## Volume front matter

## Series title page

# Complete Course of Patrology

Or a universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts. Most carefully corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily to be preferred to all others if the following matters are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. Twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; thirteen hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# Complete Works

[Column 0009]

## Continuation of the second part of the works of Rabanus Maurus

[Column 0009]

*(Written around the year 844.)* Twenty-two books of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, **On the Universe**.

# Preface to Louis, Most Invincible King of France

[Column 0009]

[Column 0009A] To the most excellent lord and most worthy of every honor, Louis, king, Rabanus, the most worthless servant of the servants of God, wishes eternal blessedness in Christ.

Having heard the good reputation of Your Majesty, which is proclaimed throughout all the provinces of Germany and Gaul and resounds with frequent praise in nearly every part of Europe, I rejoice greatly and implore the mercy of the Lord, that he may grant this reputation to reach a salutary end with good increase. For this reason I wished not to have the little works of my labor—which, with the grace of Christ himself granting it, I have expended in the service of Christ by expounding the Sacred Scriptures as best I could—without sharing them with you. Rather, I sent to Your Veneration certain treatises and commentaries written on the divine books.

[Column 0009B] Recently, too, because when I was in your presence you said that you had learned that I had newly composed a minor work on the proper meanings of words and the mystical significance of things, and because you asked that it be sent to you by my lowliness, I gladly did what you requested and sent you the work itself, completed in twenty-two books. If it pleases Your Serenity, have it reread in your presence; and if anything in it should be found worthy of correction, take care, together with your most discerning readers, to correct it as reason dictates.

For many matters are expounded in it concerning the natures of things and the proper meanings of words, as well as the mystical significance of things. I judged that it should be arranged in this way so that the prudent reader might find, set out continuously, the historical and mystical explanation of each individual thing, and might thus in some measure satisfy his desire by finding in it both the manifestation of history and that of allegory.

Therefore it seemed to me that no better beginning could be made for this work than with our very Creator, who is the head and beginning of all things: for whatever naturally exists is either the author and creator of all things or a creature established by him. For “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11); he “made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Ps. 120).

[Column 0010A] Thus I first discussed in writing something about our supreme good and true Creator—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one and only almighty God—in accordance with the smallness of my understanding, to the extent that divine grace granted me the ability. Afterwards I undertook to speak about heavenly and earthly creatures, not only about their nature but also about their power and effects, so that the diligent reader might find in this work both the properties of nature according to the historical sense and the spiritual significance according to the mystical sense, set out together.

And since it was not fitting for me to be silent about the holy men mentioned in the Old and New Testaments, about their mystical actions, or about the places in which they lived, I decided to transfer their names, and those of the places, from the Hebrew language into Latin, so that I might more easily explain their mystical significance.

[Column 0010B] I have also added to this present work no small amount concerning the Catholic faith and Christian religion; and, conversely, concerning the superstition of the pagans and the error of heretics; concerning philosophers and magicians and false gods; concerning the languages of the nations; concerning kingdoms; concerning the names and relationships of soldiers and citizens; concerning the human being and his parts, and the remaining living creatures; concerning stones, woods, and herbs that grow from the earth; concerning various arts and crafts, and many other matters. It would be lengthy to enumerate all these in the preface. For the present, therefore, let what I have said about them suffice; but in the chapters of the individual books I have taken care to enumerate them more fully.

For I decided to divide this entire work, as I said above, into twenty-two books, corresponding to the number under which Blessed Jerome, the interpreter of the divine law, declared that he had comprised the Old Testament. From his interpretation and exposition I have clarified certain obscure matters in this work.

But you, my chosen lord and dearest of kings, after receiving what I have sent you, use it as is fitting, and allow it to be useful both to you and to those placed under your rule, so that your good study may bring spiritual advancement to many and become for both you and them a spiritual exercise and an increase of heavenly joy.

[Column 0011A] Imitate the example of that wise man who uttered the following praise of wisdom, saying:

“I called upon her, and the spirit of wisdom came to me; and I preferred her to kingdoms and thrones, and I considered riches as nothing in comparison with her. I did not compare any precious stone with her, for all gold in comparison with her is a little sand, and silver in her sight will be reckoned as clay. I loved her above health and beauty, and I resolved to have her instead of light, because her radiance is unquenchable. All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands. I rejoiced in all things, because this wisdom went before me. I learned her without deceit, and I share her without envy, and I do not conceal her honor.

[Column 0011B] For she is an inexhaustible treasure for human beings; those who have used her become participants in the friendship of God, because she is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. For in her hand are both we and our words, and all wisdom, and knowledge and discipline concerning works.

For she herself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the earth, the power of the elements, the beginning and the end and the middle of times, changes of seasons, the completion of times, changes of customs, divisions of times, the courses of the year, and the arrangements of the stars; the natures of animals, the fierceness of wild beasts, the force of winds, the thoughts of human beings, the differences of trees, and the powers of [lacuna]—and I learned whatever things are hidden and unforeseen. For wisdom taught me, the craftsman of all things” (Wis. 7).

[Column 0011C] Hence also in the Book of the Nations and Kings we read that the Lord approved the request of Solomon, who asked him to give him an understanding heart so that he might judge his people and discern between good and evil. There it is written as follows:

“The request pleased the Lord, because Solomon had asked for such a thing. And the Lord said to Solomon: Because you asked for this and did not ask for many days, nor for riches or the lives of your enemies, but asked for wisdom to discern judgment, behold, I have done for you according to your words and have given you a wise and understanding heart, to such an extent that no one before you has been like you, nor will anyone like you arise after you.

[Column 0012A] “But I have also given you those things that you did not ask for, namely riches and glory, so that among all the kings of former days no one has been like you. And if you walk in my ways and keep my precepts and my commandments, as David your father walked, I will lengthen your days” (1 Kings 3).

From this it is clear that whoever is a true lover of wisdom, a diligent keeper of God’s commandments, and a faithful executor of his will to the end has him as protector, and in the future life as the most faithful rewarder of good devotion and giver of eternal joy.

[Column 0012B] Therefore, my lord king, above all else let it always be your concern to learn divine wisdom, and command those subject to you to do the same, so that you may rightly be called a king—one who strives to govern yourself and all who obey you according to the will of God and to lead them into the way of truth.

Thus it will come about that when the King of kings appears and the Lord of lords sits upon his throne of majesty, and all the nations have been gathered before him to receive, according to the quality of their merits, either reward or punishment, then you, standing with your people at his right hand, may hear that gracious sentence of the Lord which he will pronounce to all his elect, saying:

“Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

[Column 0012C] And so, incorporated into the assemblies of the saints, you will go with him into eternal life, where together with the holy angels you will rejoice happily in the sight of his glory forever.

May the majesty of almighty God preserve you here for a long time unharmed, and afterward bless you with everlasting joy in the kingdom of heaven.

# Second Preface: To Bishop Hemmo [Haymo]

[Column 0011]

[Column 0011D] To the most reverend lord, and to the Father Hemmo, bishop, rightly venerable and worthy of honor with every duty of charity, Rabanus, the unworthy servant of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in Christ.

Holy Father, mindful of your good devotion, which you possessed in childhood and youth through the exercise of letters and meditation on the Sacred Scriptures, when you read with me not only the divine books and the expositions of the holy Fathers upon them, but also the diligent investigations into the natures of things made by the wise men of this world, which they composed in their descriptions of the liberal arts and in their investigations of other matters—

after divine providence freed me from the care of external affairs and raised you to the office of pastoral care, I considered what I might produce in writing that would be pleasing and useful to Your Holiness, so that you might have briefly noted, by way of remembrance, what you had previously read at length and abundantly expressed in the great extent of many books and in the eloquent speech of orators.

For it is not unknown to me what sort of harassment you endure, not only from the pagans who are your neighbors, but also from the crowds of peoples who, through the insolence and depravity of their conduct, cause no small annoyance to Your Paternity and for this reason do not permit you to devote yourself to frequent prayer and constant reading.

[Column 0012D] While I was considering all these matters carefully, it came to mind that, following the custom of the ancients who wrote many things about the natures of things and the etymologies of names and words, I should compose for you a small work in which you would have written not only about the natures of things and the properties of words, but also about the mystical significance of those same things, so that you might find, set out continuously, the historical and mystical exposition of each individual matter.

But you, chosen lord and dearest of bishops, after receiving what I have sent you, use it as is fitting, and allow it to be useful both to you and to those placed under your rule, so that your good study may bring spiritual advancement to many and become for both you and them a spiritual exercise and an increase of heavenly joy.

[Column 0013A] Imitate the example of that wise man who uttered the following praise of wisdom, saying:

“I called upon her, and the spirit of wisdom came to me; and I preferred her to kingdoms and thrones, and I considered riches as nothing in comparison with her. I did not compare any precious stone with her, for all gold in comparison with her is a little sand, and silver in her sight will be reckoned as clay. I loved her above health and beauty, and I resolved to have her instead of light, because her radiance is unquenchable. All good things came to me together with her” (Wis. 7).

For the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy about the teaching of divine wisdom, exhorted him to this very thing, saying:

“By proposing these things to the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and of the good teaching which you have attained. Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity. Meditate on these things, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Attend to yourself and to doctrine; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. 4).

[Column 0013C] Therefore it is fitting for you to put nothing before meditation on the divine law and the teaching of the word of God. Nor should you in any way abandon these on account of worldly care and secular business, because such matters constitute the greatest impediment to the divine work among those who misuse them.

For, alas, many men of this time are found among ecclesiastical persons who, having abandoned the office of preaching and spiritual conduct, consider themselves great if they are placed over earthly affairs and frequently take part in disputes among secular people, so that they preside in their assemblies as arbiters and become judges of their conflicts.

[Column 0014A] Yet the Apostle in no way approves this, for he says:

“No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has presented himself. And whoever competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2).

Again, elsewhere he says:

“If you have those who are contemptible, appoint them to judge secular affairs” (1 Cor. 6).

It is far better for a bishop to labor in the teaching of the word of God for the salvation of the souls entrusted to him than to occupy himself with arranging and deciding civil disputes, and to devote himself to the various contentions of people who, out of earthly greed, continually provoke lawsuits and quarrels, each one striving to overcome the other in such matters.

For nowhere in the Sacred Scriptures do we read that the Savior himself or his disciples did or taught this. Nevertheless, it is found written in the Gospel that a certain man asked our Mediator to command his brother to divide his inheritance with him. He replied:

“Man, who appointed me judge or divider between you and the rest?” (Luke 12.)

[Column 0014B] In this he showed that he did not wish the teachers of the Gospel to be occupied with, or take part in, the cares and quarrels of secular people. For it is not the same office to preach the Gospel of Christ to the people from the church pulpit and, in the court of secular affairs, to decide legal disputes among quarrelling parties.

Since these things are being written, my lord, I do not want you to think that I am establishing a new rule of life for you, but rather that I am briefly recalling, for remembrance, what was proclaimed long ago by holy men.

For I believe that you would rather please your Creator beneficially in your inward sight than be vainly elevated outwardly by human favor.

[Column 0014C] Therefore, what you have begun to do well in the service of God, strive to complete by always doing it better and better to the end, so that, performing God’s service perfectly both in the earliest and in the final periods of your life, you may happily attain the fullness of the heavenly reward.

Thus, at the final judgment, the supreme master of the household himself may say to you, together with the other elect:

“Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25).

# Book One

[Column 0013]

## Chapter One: Concerning God

[Column 0013D]

The first name of God among the Hebrews is called **Heli**. Some have interpreted it as “God”; others, explaining its etymology, have interpreted it as **scyros**, that is, “strong,” because he is oppressed by no weakness but is strong and sufficient for accomplishing all things.

The second name is **Eloim**; the third, **Eloe**. Both are rendered in Latin as “God.”

This name has been transferred into Latin from a Greek designation. For in Greek, God is called *theos*—[perhaps δέος]—and *febor* [φόβος], that is, “fear.” Hence the name of God is derived from the fact that he is feared by those who worship him.

“God,” properly speaking, is the name of the Trinity, referring to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The remaining names set out below concerning God also refer to this Trinity.

The fourth name is **Sabaoth**, which is rendered in Latin as “of armies” or “of powers.” Concerning him the angels say in the Psalm:

“Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers?” (Ps. 23.)

There are many powers in this arrangement, such as angels, archangels, principalities, and powers, and all the orders of the heavenly army. Yet he is their Lord; for they are all beneath him and subject to his dominion.

The fifth name is **Elion**, which is rendered in Latin as “Most High,” the one who is above the heavens, as it is written of him:

“The Lord is Most High, and his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. 112).

He is called “Most High” as being exceedingly lofty. For *ex* is used in the sense of “very,” as in *eximius*, meaning “highly eminent.”

The sixth is **Ieie**, that is, “He who is.” God alone, because he is eternal—that is, because he has no beginning—possesses the name of essence.

This name was conveyed to holy Moses through an angel. When Moses asked what the name was of the one who was commanding him to go to the people to free them from Egypt, he replied:

“I am who I am; and you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3).

This is as though, in comparison with the one who truly is because he is unchangeable, mutable things were almost nonexistent. For what is said to have been is no longer; and what is said will be does not yet exist.

[Column 0015B] God alone knows being; he does not know having been or being destined to be. The Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, truly is. Compared with his essence, our being is nonbeing.

Hence in conversation we say, “As God lives,” because he lives by an essence that does not possess death.

The seventh is **Adonai**, which is generally interpreted as “Lord,” because he rules over every creature, or because every creature serves his dominion. Thus “Lord” and “God” may mean either that he rules over all or that he is feared by all.

The eighth is **ia**, which is used only of God; it also sounds in the final syllable of *alleluia*.

The ninth is **tetragrammaton**, that is, “of four letters,” which is used specifically among the Hebrews for God: *iod, he, vau, he*, that is, two *ia* syllables. Doubled, these form that ineffable and glorious name of God.

It is called ineffable not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot in any way be bounded by human sense and understanding. Since nothing worthy can be said about him, he is ineffable.

The tenth is **Saddai**, that is, “almighty.” He is called almighty because he can do all things—not from suffering what he does not will, but from doing what he wills. If the former were attributed to him, he would by no means be almighty. He does what he wills, and from this he is almighty.

He is also called almighty because everything that exists everywhere belongs to him. For he alone holds dominion over the whole world.

There are also certain other names predicated substantially of God, such as immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable, and eternal. Therefore he is rightly placed before every creature.

He is immortal, as it is written of him:

“He alone possesses immortality” (1 Tim. 6),

because there is no change in his nature.

For every mutability may properly be called mortality. Accordingly, the soul is also said to die—not because it is changed and transformed into a body or into some other substance, but because, in its own substance, whatever it now is or was in another condition is shown to be mortal insofar as it has ceased to be what it was.

Thus God alone is called immortal, because he alone is called unchangeable and incorruptible. He is incorruptible because he cannot be corrupted, dissolved, or divided. Whatever can be divided can also perish. He can neither be divided nor perish; therefore he is incorruptible.

He is unchangeable because he always remains and does not know how to change. He is not perfected, because he is perfect; nor does he fail, because he is eternal.

[Column 0016A] He is eternal because he is without time; for he has neither beginning nor end. Hence he is also everlasting, because he is always eternal.

Some believe that *eternal* is derived from *aether*, just as heaven is regarded as his dwelling. Hence the saying:

“Heaven, even the heaven of heavens, belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 113).

These four terms signify one and the same thing. For the same reality is designated whether God is called eternal, immortal, incorruptible, or unchangeable.

God is called invisible because the Trinity has never appeared to mortal eyes through its own substance, except through the appearance of an underlying creature, and of a corporeal one at that. For no one can see the manifestation of God’s essence itself and live, as was also said to Moses.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

“No one has ever seen God” (John 1).

[Column 0016B] He is invisible and therefore must be sought not with the eye but with the heart.

He is impassible because he is affected by none of the disturbances to which human frailty succumbs. No passions touch him, such as lust, anger, desire, fear, sorrow, envy, and the like, by which the human mind is disturbed.

When God is said to become angry, to be jealous, or to grieve, this is said according to our manner of speech. For there is no disturbance in God, with whom there is perfect tranquility.

He is called simple either because he does not lose what he possesses, or because he himself is not one thing and what is in him another. In a human being, for example, being is one thing and wisdom another; he may exist without being wise.

God possesses essence and possesses wisdom, but what he possesses is what he is; and all things are one in him. Therefore he is simple, because nothing can be added to him.

Both what he is and what is in him exist essentially, except insofar as he is related to any particular person.

He is supremely good because he is unchangeable. A creature is good, but not supremely good, because it is changeable; and although it is good, it cannot also be supreme goodness.

[Column 0016C] God is called incorporeal or bodiless so that he may be believed or understood to be spirit and not body. For when he is called spirit, his substance is signified.

He is immeasurable because he contains all things, while he himself is contained by none; rather, all things are confined within his omnipotence.

He is called perfect because nothing can be added to him. Yet perfection is also spoken of with reference to the completion of some deed. Since God was not made, how is he perfect? Human poverty has taken this term from common usage, as it has taken the other words as well, so that what is ineffable may somehow be expressed. Human speech says nothing worthy of God, and the same is true of the other terms.

He is called Creator because all the things of the world were created by him; for nothing exists that did not derive its origin from God.

He is one because he cannot be divided, or because nothing else can possess an equal measure of power.

All these things said about God pertain to the whole Trinity, because of the one and coeternal substance—whether in the Father, in his only-begotten Son, or in the form of God, in the Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of God the Father and of his only-begotten Son.

[Column 0017A] There are also certain terms applied to God from our customary language, taken from our limbs or from lower things. Although he is invisible and incorporeal in his proper nature, forms of things are nevertheless attributed to him on account of the effects of causes in him, so that he may more easily make himself known according to our manner of speaking.

Because he sees all things, he is called an eye; because he hears all things, he is called an ear; because he turns away, he walks; because he waits, he stands.

In other similar expressions, a likeness is drawn from human minds to God, as when he is said to forget and to remember.

Hence the prophet says:

“The Lord of hosts swore by his soul” (Isa. 14);

not because God possesses a soul, but because he speaks according to our human manner of feeling.

For in the Sacred Scriptures the face of God is understood not as flesh but as divine knowledge, by the same reasoning by which someone is known through seeing his face.

[Column 0017B] Thus in prayer one says to God:

“Show us your face” (Ps. 68),

as though one were saying, “Give us knowledge of yourself.”

Likewise, the footprints of God are spoken of because God is now known through a mirror. But in the future the Almighty will be found in perfection, when he is presented face to face to each of the elect, so that they may contemplate the very form whose footprints they now strive to grasp—that is, the one whom they are said to see through a mirror.

Position, appearance, place, and time are likewise spoken of God not properly but metaphorically.

He is said to sit upon the cherubim, which pertains to position; and to be clothed with the abyss as with a garment, which pertains to appearance; and:

“Your years will not fail” (Ps. 100),

which pertains to time; and:

“If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Ps. 138),

which pertains to place.

[Column 0017C] In the prophet, too, the appearance of a chariot carrying hay is applied to God. All these things are said figuratively of God, since none of them pertains to the proper nature of his substance.

And because, as we have said, human limbs, bodily appearance, and human emotions are attributed to God figuratively, we briefly note what we recall having been written about these matters.

The head of the Lord is divinity itself, because he is the beginning and creator of all things. The Lord’s hair is written of as white in the prophet Daniel, because he is “ancient of days” (Dan. VII). The eyes of God [the Lord] are divine inspection, because he sees everything, as the Apostle says: “For all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV). The eyelids of God [the Lord] are the hidden and spiritual mysteries contained in the divine commandments [Col. 0017D], as in the psalm: “His eyelids question the sons of men” (Ps. X), that is, they test the sons of men.

The Lord’s sense of smell is his delight in the conduct or works of the saints, as in Genesis: “And the Lord smelled the odor of sweetness” (Gen. VIII). The mouth of the Lord is his Son, or his word addressed to human beings, as in the psalm: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I); and elsewhere: “They provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger” (Lam. I). The tongue of the Lord is his Holy Spirit, as in the psalm: “My tongue is a pen” (Ps. XLIV). The face of the Lord is his manifestation through his Son to human beings, as in Exodus: “My face shall go before you” (Exod. XXXIII); and in the psalm: “The face of the Lord dismissed them.”

The Word of the Lord is the Son, as in the psalm: [Col. 0018A] “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV). The arm of the Lord is the Son, through whom he has done all things, as in the prophet Isaiah: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII). The right hand of God, that is, the Son, is mentioned in the psalm: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought strength” (Ps. CXVII). Again, the right hand of the Lord is glory or everlasting blessedness, as it is said of the Son in the Gospel: “He sits at the right hand of God” (Mark XVI). Again, the right hand of God is all the elect, as in Deuteronomy: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII).

The wings of the Lord are divine protection, as in the psalm: “In the shadow of your wings I shall hope” (Ps. LVI). The shoulders of the Lord are divine patience, by which he deigns to bear the weak, as in Deuteronomy: “He received them and carried them upon his shoulders” (Deut. XXXII). The hands of the Lord are divine activity, as in the prophecy: [Col. 0018B] “Have not my hands made all these things?” (Isa. LXVI). The finger of the Lord is the Holy Spirit, by whose operation the tablets of the Law are said to have been written in Exodus; and in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God.”

The fingers of the Lord are the lawgiver Moses, or the prophets, as in the psalm: “I shall behold the heavens”—that is, the books of the Law and of the prophets—“the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII). Wisdom is the Son of God, as the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I); and as Solomon says: “The wisdom of the Lord reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. VIII).

The womb of the Lord is the secret of divinity, from which he brought forth the Son, as in the psalm: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX). The feet of the Lord are the stability of eternity, as in the psalm: “And darkness was under his feet” (Ps. XVII). The throne of the Lord is the angels, or the saints, or the very power of reigning [Col. 0018C], as in the psalm: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Ps. CXVIII). The seat of the Lord—that is, the same as above, the angels or saints, because the Lord sits in them—is mentioned in the psalm: “God sits upon his holy seat” (Ps. XLVI).

The descent of the Lord is his visitation of human beings, as in Micah: “Behold, the Lord will go out from his place and will descend, trampling upon the heights of the earth” (Mic. I); and, in an adverse sense, as in Genesis: “The Lord descended to see the tower” (Gen. XI). The ascent of the Lord is the elevation of the assumed human being from earth to heaven, as in the psalm: “Who ascended above the heavens of heavens toward the east” (Ps. XXXIV). The standing of the Lord is the patience of the Godhead, by which he endures sinners for repentance, as in Habakkuk: “He stood and measured the earth” (Hab. III); and in the Gospel: “Jesus stood and commanded him to be called [Col. 0018D] to him” (Mark X), that is, to heaven.

The passage of the Lord is the assumption of flesh, by which, through being born, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, he made a certain passage, as in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song II). The steps of the Lord are his coming or visitation. The ways of the Lord are the operation of the Godhead, as in Job concerning the devil: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job XL); likewise, the ways of the Lord are the Lord’s commandments, as in Hosea: “How straight are the ways of the Lord, and the just walk in them” (Hos. XIV). The footprints of the Lord are the signs of his secret works, as in the psalm: “And your footsteps will not be known” (Ps. LXXVI).

The knowledge of the Lord means that he causes us to know; hence he says to Abraham: “Now I know that [Col. 0019A] you fear God” (Gen. XXII), that is, “I have caused you to know.” Not to know God means to reject, as in the Gospel: “I do not know you” (Matt. VII). The remembrance of the Lord is his mercy, by which he looks upon and pities whomever he wills, as in Genesis: “The Lord remembered Noah” (Gen. VIII); and elsewhere: “The Lord remembered his people” (Ps. LXXVII).

The repentance of the Lord is a change in affairs, as in the Book of Kings: “I repent that I made Saul king” (1 Kings V). Likewise, the anger of the Lord is the vengeance of the Godhead against sinners, according to the vengeance of one who suffers, not according to the equity of one who judges, as in the psalm: “In his anger and in his wrath he will trouble them” (Ps. II). The sleep of the Lord is when his faith is not at all awake in the hearts of certain people, as in the psalm: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII). The wakefulness [Col. 0019B] of the Lord means that through the foreknowledge of the Godhead he is always present in the guardianship of his elect, as in the psalm: “Behold, he shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. CXX).

For the Lord to sit means to reign, as in the psalm: “God sits upon his holy seat” (Ps. XLVI). The footstool of the Lord is thought by some to be the human being assumed by the Word, or his saints, as in the psalm: “Adore his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. XCVIII); likewise, the footstool is the submission of the humbled, as in the psalm: “Until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX). The walking of the Lord is the manifestation of the Godhead in the works of his elect, as in the prophet: “And I will walk among them, and I will be their Lord” (Lev. XXVI). The trumpet of God is an audible voice, as in the Apostle: “At the command and at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet [Col. 0019C] of God he will descend from heaven” (1 Thess. IV).

## CHAPTER II. On the Son of God

Christ is found in the divine Scriptures under many names. For he is the only-begotten Son of God the Father; although he was equal to the Father, he assumed the form of a servant for our salvation. Accordingly, certain names in him are assumed from the substance of divinity, and certain others from the dispensation of the humanity he assumed.

Christ is called by the Greek word *Christos*, from *chrisma*, that is, “anointed.” Priests and kings among the Jews were therefore anointed with sacred anointing in the Old Testament; and Christ is called “the Anointed,” because he is king and priest. He was anointed not with material oil but with the oil of gladness, that is, the Holy Spirit, above all his [Col. 0019D] participants [companions]. Christ is called *Messiah* in Hebrew.

*Jesus* is interpreted from Hebrew, through the Greek *soter*, into Latin as “salutary” or “savior,” because he came as salvation for all nations. *Emmanuel* signifies in Latin from Hebrew “God with us,” namely, that God, born through the Virgin, appeared to human beings in mortal flesh.

He is called God because of the substance united with the Father; Lord, because of the creature serving him; God and man, because he is Word and flesh. He is called only-begotten because of the excellence of his divinity, since he has no brothers; firstborn, because of his assumption of humanity, in which, through the grace of adoption, he deigned to have brothers, so that he might be their firstborn.

He is called *homoousios* with the Father because of the unity of substance. [Col. 0020A] For “substance” or “essence” is called *ousia* in Greek; *homos* means “one.” Joined together, the two terms sound as “one substance.” He is called Beginning because all things are from him and because nothing existed before him. He is called End either because he deigned humbly to be born and die in the flesh at the end of the ages, or because whatever we do we refer to him; and when we have reached him, we have nothing further to seek.

He is the mouth of God because he is his Word. For just as, in speaking of words made through the tongue, we often say “that tongue” or “this tongue,” so “mouth” is used for the word of God, because it is customary for words to be formed by the mouth. He is called Word because through him the Father created or commanded all things; Truth because he does not deceive but grants what he promised; Life because he gives life to all; Image because of his equal likeness to the Father; Figure [Col. 0020B] because, assuming the form of a servant, he represented in himself the image and immeasurable greatness of the Father through the likeness of his works and virtues; and the hand of God because all things were made through him.

Hence he is also called right hand, because of the effect of the work of the whole creation, which was formed through him; arm, because all things are held together by him; power, because he possesses in himself all the authority of the Father and can do all things; wisdom, because he reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom; splendor, because he makes manifest; light, because he illuminates; brightness, because he opens the eyes of the heart to contemplate the truth; sun, because he enlightens; rising, because he is the source of light and causes us to rise to eternal life; and fountain, because he is the origin of things, or because he makes those who are thirsty drink.

He is also called Alpha and Omega because he is the beginning [Col. 0020C] and the end. He is the Paraclete, that is, the advocate, because he intercedes for us with the Father and takes care to remove our sins; the bridegroom, because, descending from heaven, he joined himself to the Church so that the two might be one flesh.

He is called angel because he announces the Father’s will and his own; hence in the prophet he is read to be the angel of great counsel, although he is God and Lord of the angels. He is called sent because the Word became flesh. He is called man because he was incarnate; mediator because he brought us from death to life; prophet because he revealed the future; priest because he offered himself as a sacrifice for us; shepherd because he is the guardian; teacher because he is the revealer; Nazarene from the place Nazareth; and, in respect of merit, that is, “holy” or “clean,” because he committed no sin.

Christ also takes names from other, lower [Col. 0020D] things, so that he may be more easily understood. He is called bread because he is flesh; vine because we have been redeemed by his blood; flower because he is chosen; way because through him we go to God; door because through him we enter to God; mountain because he is strong; rock because he is the firmness of believers; cornerstone either because he joins two walls from opposite directions—that is, from circumcision and uncircumcision—into the one structure of the Church, or because in himself he makes peace between angels and human beings; stone of stumbling because, coming in humility, unbelieving human beings stumbled over him, and he became a rock of offense.

He is called foundation because faith is founded upon him, or because the catholic Church has been built upon him. [Col. 0021A] He is called lamb because of innocence; sheep because of gentleness; ram because of preeminence; kid because of the likeness of sinful flesh; calf because he was sacrificed for us; lion because of kingship and strength; serpent because of death and wisdom. He is likewise called worm because he rose again; eagle because after the resurrection he returned to the stars.

It is not surprising that he is represented by lowly symbols, since he is known to have descended even to the sufferings and insults of our flesh. Although he is the coeternal Son of God the Father before the ages, after the fullness of time came, he assumed the form of a servant for our salvation and became the Son of God, the son of man.

Thus certain things are said of him in Scripture according to the form of God, and certain things according to the form of a servant. By way of example, two [Col. 0021B] statements are recalled so that each may be referred to its proper category. According to the form of God he says of himself: “I and the Father are one” (John X). According to the form of man he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIII).

People who understand less what is said and to what it refers wish to transfer to the form of God what was said because of the form of a servant. Conversely, what was said according to the form of God, so that the persons might be referred to one another, they wish to make names of nature and substance; and they thus create error in the faith. For human nature was joined to the Son of God in such a way that from two substances there came to be one person.

Therefore only the man endured the cross, but because of the unity of the person, God too is said to have endured it. Hence it is written: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified [Col. 0021C] the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II). We confess that the Son of God was crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of humanity; not through the permanence of his own nature but through his assumption of ours.

Accordingly, bodily limbs are also attributed to the Son of God, as are bodily appearances, of which we have already set down some above and shall add others here.

The Apostle says that God is the head of Christ, and Christ the head of the Church, as in the passage: “For the head of a woman is man; but the head of man is Christ; and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. XI). The body of Christ is the holy Church, as the same Apostle also shows.

The white hair of Christ in the Apocalypse signifies the multitude of saints made white, where it is written: “His head and his hair were white [Col. 0021D] like white wool and like snow” (Apoc. I). The antiquity and immortality of majesty are shown in the whiteness of the head. The righteous, especially, cling to him like hairs: like wool because of the sheep who will be at the right hand, and like snow because of the innumerable multitude of those made white and of the elect granted from heaven, who shine like snow.

The eyes of Christ are the evangelical commandments. Hence it is read in Genesis: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine” (Gen. XLIX), that is, than the teachings of the old law. Likewise, the eyes of Christ are the teachers through whom the Church sees what is right, as in the Song of Songs: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water” (Song V). They are fittingly compared to doves because of simplicity, and to streams of water because of divine charisms [Col. 0022A].

The teeth of Christ are the apostles and preachers of the New Testament; hence it is written: “His teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX). They cut people away from errors and, as though by eating them, transfer them into the body of Christ. By the name “milk” the teaching of the Law is signified.

The tongue of Christ is the evangelical discourse: “My tongue has cleaved to my jaws” (Ps. XXI). The throat of Christ is the preachers of the Gospel. For of his throat it is written in the Song of Songs: “His throat is most sweet” (Song V). In the throat the inward sweetness of his words is recalled; whoever tastes it does not hunger.

The lips of Christ are the proclaimers of the Word, as in the Song of Songs: “His lips drip the first myrrh” (Song V). The beard of Christ is the man assumed by the Word, or all the perfect, as in the psalm: “Like ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII).

The hands of Christ are the workers of righteousness, prepared for every good work, as in the Song of Songs: “His hands are fashioned of gold [Col. 0022B]. My fingers are full of myrrh” (Song V). In the hands works are signified; in the fingers, discernment; and in myrrh, self-restraint and sufferings, which are most approved when self-restraint or sufferings are undertaken solely for the love of God and neighbor.

The right hand of the Lord is the New Testament; the left, the Old. Again, the right hand is everlasting blessedness; the left, the present life, as the Church says in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II). Again, the right hand is the elect; the left, all the reprobate, as in the Gospel: “He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” [Col. 0022C] (Matt. XXV).

The breasts of Christ are evangelical teaching, as in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song I). The Lord’s breasts are the two Testaments; hence it is read in the Apocalypse: “And a golden girdle around his breasts” (Apoc. I).

The belly of Christ is the bath of regeneration, from which he generates his elect as sons through the grace of adoption. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your belly is ivory” (Song V). The entrails of the Lord are the secret of divinity, or the hidden sacraments in sacred Scripture; hence it is written in Exodus: “The head with the feet and entrails shall be eaten” (Exod. XII).

His legs are the apostles or the other preachers, supporting the whole body of the Church; concerning them it is said in the Song of Songs: “His legs are like [Col. 0022D] marble columns” (Song V). The feet of the Lord are the man assumed by the Word, or the holy apostles; concerning them it is written in Deuteronomy: “Those who approach his feet shall receive his teaching” (Deut. XXXIII); and in the psalm: “We shall adore in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. CXXXI).

The bones of Christ are the strong members of the Church, which is his body; concerning them it is written in the psalm: “All my bones have been scattered” (Ps. XXI). The flesh of Christ is the weak in the Church; concerning them it is said in the psalm: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh” (Ps. XXVI).

The garments of the Lord are the flesh he assumed; hence it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “Behold, a man clothed in linen” (Ezek. IX), that is, in clean flesh. Likewise, the garments of Christ are all the elect, as in Job: “Surround yourself with your beauty, and clothe yourself in splendid garments” (Job XL).

The tunic of Christ is his Church, represented by the tunic of which it is written in the Gospel: “Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be” (John XIX). The robe of Christ is the flesh he assumed, cleansed by the wine of his passion; hence it is written in Genesis: “He shall wash his robe in wine” (Gen. XLIX). Accordingly, the cloak of Christ is the holy Church, sprinkled with his blood; hence also the preceding passage: “In the blood of the grape his cloak” (ibid.).

The loincloth [Col. 0023A] of the Lord is the Jewish people, corrupted by the vice of pride; concerning it, it is written in Jeremiah: “As a loincloth clings to the body, so I called this people to myself, says the Lord” (Jer. VII). The belt of Christ is his righteousness or faith. Hence it is read in Isaiah: [Col. 0023B] “Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his kidneys” (Isa. XI). The footwear of the Lord is the mystery of the Incarnation, about which John the Baptist says in the Gospel: “I am not worthy, kneeling down, to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Luke III).

## CHAPTER III. On the Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and possesses their substance. For nothing other than what the Father himself is could proceed from the Father.

The Holy Spirit is called by this name according to what is referred to something else. For just as Father and Son are spoken of relationally, so the Holy Spirit is likewise spoken of in a certain way relationally in relation to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. But the relation [Col. 0023C] of the Holy Spirit cannot be turned back reciprocally in the same way as that of Father and Son.

For the Father is called the Father of the Son, and the Son is called the Son of the Father. But the Holy Spirit is spoken of uniformly in relation to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. We say “the Holy Spirit,” “the Spirit of the Father,” but conversely we do not say “the Father of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his Son. Likewise, we say “the Holy Spirit,” “the Spirit of the Son,” but we do not say “the Son of the Holy Spirit,” lest the Holy Spirit be understood to be his Father.

The same Spirit is also called the gift of God, because God is the giver of his gift. In these names the rule of relation may be turned back reciprocally, so that one may say “the giver of the gift” and “the gift of the giver,” because in these terms the customary [Col. 0023D] reciprocal relation belonging to the category called “relative” can be found.

Therefore this gift of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, who proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, is a certain ineffable communion of the Father and the Son. Perhaps he is therefore so called because the same name can apply to the Father and the Son. For he is properly called by what they are called jointly: the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy. Thus, so that the communion of both might properly be signified by names that separately apply to each person, he is called the Holy Spirit. He is the third person in the Holy Trinity, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with them.

And this Trinity is one God [Col. 0024A], alone good, great, eternal, and almighty. Unity, divinity, greatness, goodness, omnipotence, and whatever is said substantially of God belong to him in himself. This is not to be understood or said in the same way with relative names, for one cannot say “the Father is Father to himself,” or “the Son is Son to himself,” or “the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit to himself”; rather, these relative names refer to another person.

Nor is the name “Spirit” always understood according to what is referred to something else; it is also understood according to what signifies a certain nature. For every incorporeal nature is called spirit in the sacred Scriptures. Hence this name applies not only to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but also to every rational creature and to the soul [Col. 0024B].

The Holy Spirit is not called begotten, lest two sons be suspected in the Trinity. He is not proclaimed unbegotten, lest two fathers be believed in the Trinity. He is called proceeding, on the testimony of the Lord, who says: “When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV); and again: “He,” he says, “will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you.”

Here he proceeds not only according to nature, but he continually proceeds in order to carry out the works of the Trinity without ceasing. The difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds is that the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore the Apostle says: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ [Col. 0024C], he is not his” (Rom. VIII).

For the Father is never read to have been sent, but the Spirit is sent, as in the Lord’s saying: “The Paraclete,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of all things” (John XIV).

*Paraclete* is interpreted in Latin from the Greek as “comforter,” from consolation; for *paraklesis* is translated as “consolation.” Christ sent him to those who were mourning after he himself had ascended into heaven from their sight. A comforter is sent to the sorrowful, according to that saying of the same Lord: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V). He also says: “Then the sons of the bridegroom will mourn when the bridegroom has been taken away from them” (Matt. IX). Likewise, he is called Paraclete because he gives consolation to souls that lose temporal joy [Col. 0024D].

Others interpret *paraclete* in Latin as “speaker” or “advocate.” For the Holy Spirit himself says, “He teaches”; through him the word of wisdom is given; by him sacred Scripture was inspired.

The Holy Spirit is therefore called sevenfold because of the gifts which, from the fullness of his divinity, individuals merit to receive in portions according to their worthiness. For he is called the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. XI).

The “principal spirit” is read of in the fiftieth psalm. Since the word “spirit” is repeated there three times, some have understood the Trinity, especially because it is written: “God is Spirit” (John IV). For what is not a body and yet exists seems to remain as spirit. Some understand the Trinity to be signified there: in the principal [Col. 0025A] Spirit, the Father; in the upright Spirit, the Son; in the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is therefore called the gift of God because he is given. The word “gift” is derived from giving. It is very well known that the Lord Jesus Christ, after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, gave the Holy Spirit; when believers were filled with him, they spoke in the languages of all nations. He is the gift of God insofar as he is given to those who through him love God. In himself he is God; among us he is a gift. Yet eternally the Holy Spirit is a gift, distributing the gifts of grace to individuals as he wills (1 Cor. XII).

He also imparts to prophets as he [Col. 0025B] wills and forgives sins to whom he wills; for our sins are not forgiven without the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is properly called love, either because by nature he joins together those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he brings it about in us that we remain in God and he in us. Hence among the gifts of God nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit.

He is also grace. Because grace is given freely, not according to our merits but by the divine will, it is therefore called grace. Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name “wisdom,” although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the term “love,” although the Father and Son are universally love.

That the Holy Spirit is the finger of God is most clearly declared in the books [Col. 0025C] of the Gospel. When one Evangelist had said: “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke XI), another expressed the same thing in this way: “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons” (Matt. XII).

The Law was therefore also written by the finger of God, given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb; and on the fiftieth day after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ the Holy Spirit came. He is called the finger of God so that his operative power together with the Father and the Son may be signified. Hence Paul also says: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. XII).

Just as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so we are marked by the Spirit, who is the finger of God and the spiritual seal.

The Holy Spirit is recorded as having come in the form of a dove so that his nature might be declared through the bird’s simplicity and innocence. Hence the Lord also says: “Be simple like doves” [Col. 0025D] (Matt. X). This bird bodily lacks bile, possessing only innocence and love.

The Holy Spirit is therefore called by the name of fire because in the Acts of the Apostles he appeared like fire through the division of tongues and sat upon each one of them (Acts II). He gave the apostles the grace of different languages so that they might be made capable of instructing the peoples of the faithful.

The fact that he is remembered as having sat above each individual has this purpose: it is to be understood that he was not divided among many, but remained whole in each, as is generally the nature of fire. For burning fire has this property: however many look toward it, however many gaze [Col. 0026A] upon the crimson crest of its splendor, to that many it grants the sight of its light and to that many it gives the mystery of its gift, while nevertheless remaining whole in itself.

The Holy Spirit is called by the name of water in the Gospel, when the Lord cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII). The Evangelist explained what he meant, for he continued: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

But the water of the sacrament is one thing, and the water that signifies the Spirit of God is another. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place in the soul; through the Holy Spirit, however, the soul itself is cleansed and nourished.

The Holy Spirit is therefore called anointing, as the Apostle John testifies [Col. 0026B] (1 John II), because just as oil, by its natural weight, rises above every liquid, so in the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne above the waters. Hence the Lord is read to have been anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle John also calls the Holy Spirit anointing, saying (ibid.): “And may the anointing [and the anointing] which you received from him remain in you. And you have no need for anyone to teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about everything.” For the Holy Spirit himself is invisible anointing.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Same Trinity

The Trinity is so called because a whole is made one from certain three things, as it were a *trinity*: for example, memory, understanding [Col. 0026C] and will, in which the mind possesses within itself a certain image of the divine Trinity. Although they are three, they are one, because each remains in itself and all are in all.

Therefore, all Scripture of the Old and New Testament, divinely inspired, if it is understood catholicly, declares this: that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, of the same substance and one essence, united by an inseparable unity of divinity [*indivinitatis* / *divinitatis*]. Thus there are not three gods but one: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the Father; [Col. 0026D] and the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, he too is coequal with the Father and the Son and belongs to the unity of the Trinity.

This Trinity is one God, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, as blessed Paul testifies when he says: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen” (Rom. XI). Therefore we most firmly believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son.

For the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. In it the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

This is shown to us especially at the very beginning [Col. 0027A] of the sacred Scriptures, where God says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). When he said “image” in the singular, he showed that there is one nature in whose image man was made; but when he says “our” in the plural, he showed that the God in whose image man was made is not one person.

If the one essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person, it would not say “in our image” but “in my image,” nor would it say “let us make” but “let me make.” If three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons, it would not say “in our image” but “in our images.” But man is said to have been made according to the one image of the one God, so that the essential divinity of the holy Trinity might be indicated.

The prophet Isaiah likewise did not conceal this Trinity of persons and unity of nature [Col. 0027B] revealed to him, when he says that he heard the seraphim crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI). In the fact that “holy” is said three times, we clearly recognize the Trinity of persons; in the fact that “Lord God of hosts” is said once, we recognize the unity of the divine nature.

It must plainly be believed without any doubt that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, the Father almighty, eternal, and unchangeable; that each of them individually is God, and all together are one God; that each individually possesses a full, perfect, and eternal substance, and all together possess one substance.

For whatever the Father is insofar as he is God, insofar as he is substance [Col. 0027C], and insofar as he is eternity, that the Son and the Holy Spirit are. Likewise, whatever the Son is insofar as he is God, insofar as he is substance, and insofar as he is eternity, that the Father and the Son are. There is one divinity in the three, one essence, and one omnipotence.

Whatever can be said substantially of God: if you are asked about the Father alone, what the Father is, answer: “God.” If you are asked about the Son, answer: “God.” If you are asked about the Holy Spirit, answer: “God.” If you are asked together about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, answer not “gods” but “one God,” almighty and unchangeable.

It must be known that certain things are said substantially of God, such as “God,” “great,” and “almighty,” and whatever is said of him in himself, signifying the substance of divinity. Certain things, however, are said relationally [Col. 0027D], such as “Father” in relation to the Son, “Son” in relation to the Father, and “Holy Spirit” in relation to the Father and the Son. In himself, whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit, he is called God.

Therefore, insofar as the Father is God, he is substance; because the Son is of the same substance, unquestionably the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. But “God,” insofar as it means “Father,” is said relationally, because it is not the name of substance but refers to the Son.

We do not say that the Son is Father in the same way that we say that the Son is God; nor do we say that the Father is Son in the same way that we say that he is God. “God” is said substantially, whereas “Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are said relationally.

## CHAPTER V. On the Angels

[Col. 0028A]

The angels are called *angeloi* in Greek, *malaoth* in Hebrew, and are translated into Latin as *messengers* (*nuntii*), because they announce the Lord’s will to peoples. The designation “angel” is a name of office, not of nature. They are always spirits, but when they are sent they are called angels. For this reason painters, by artistic license, give them wings, to signify their swift movement everywhere; likewise, according to the fables of the poets, the winds are said to have wings, evidently because of their speed. Hence Holy Scripture also says: “Who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103).

Holy Scripture attests that there are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, powers, principalities, cherubim, and seraphim. We shall explain, by interpreting them, why the designations of these offices have been given as they have.

They are called angels because they are sent from heaven to announce things to human beings. For *angelos* in Greek means “messenger” in Latin. Archangels are translated from Greek as “chief messengers.” Those who announce small or minor matters are called angels; those who announce great matters are called archangels. They are called archangels because they hold primacy among the angels; for *archos* in Greek is translated “prince” in Latin. There are also leaders and princes, under whose authority the offices of the individual angels have been assigned.

That archangels preside over angels is attested by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking in me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: Run, speak to that young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall” (Zech. 2). For if the higher powers did not in these angelic offices arrange the lower powers, the angel would in no way have learned from another angel what he was to say to the man.

Some of the archangels are called by personal names, so that their power in their work may be indicated by the names themselves. Gabriel in Hebrew is rendered in our language as “strength of God.” Wherever power or strength is manifested, Gabriel is sent. Thus, at the time when the Lord was to be born and to triumph over the world, Gabriel came to Mary to announce him who deigned to come in humility in order to defeat the powers of the air.

Michael is interpreted as “Who is like God?” Whenever something of marvelous power occurs in the world, this archangel is sent. His name derives from the work itself, because no one is able to do what God can do.

Raphael is interpreted as “healing” or “medicine of God.” Wherever the work of healing is necessary, this archangel is sent by God, and for that reason he is called the medicine of God. Thus the same archangel was sent to Tobit, applied healing to his eyes, and, removing his blindness, restored his sight. The interpretation of the name therefore also indicates the angel’s office.

Uriel is interpreted as “fire of God,” just as we read that fire appeared in the bush. We also read that fire was sent from above and accomplished what had been commanded.

### [Col. 0028B]

Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and virtues—the orders through which the Apostle encompasses the whole heavenly society—are understood as orders and dignities of angels. In accordance with this distribution of offices, some are called thrones, others dominions, others principalities, others powers, according to the particular dignities by which they are distinguished from one another.

### [Col. 0029A]

The virtues are understood to be certain angelic ministries through which signs and miracles take place in the world; for this reason they are called virtues. The powers are those to whom hostile virtues are subject, and they are called powers because the evil spirits are restrained by their authority, so that they do not harm as much as they desire.

The principalities are those who preside over the ranks of angels. Because they arrange the angels subject to them for the fulfillment of the divine mystery, they have received the designation “principalities.” For some administer, while others attend, as is also said through Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten times a hundred thousand attended him” (Dan. 7).

### [Col. 0029B]

The dominions are those who also surpass the virtues and principalities. Because they exercise dominion over the other ranks of angels, they are called dominions.

The thrones are ranks of angels who in Latin speech are called seats. They are called thrones because the Creator presides over them and arranges his judgments through them.

The cherubim are likewise said to be exalted heavenly powers and angelic ministries. From Hebrew their name is translated into our language as “multitude of knowledge.” They are exalted ranks of angels; because, being placed nearer to God, they are more fully filled with divine knowledge than the others, they are called cherubim—that is, “fullness of knowledge.”

### [Col. 0029C]

These are the two creatures made of metal above the mercy seat of the ark, signifying the presence of the angels, in whose midst God is manifested.

The seraphim likewise constitute a multitude of angels. From Hebrew their name is translated into Latin as “burning” or “kindling.” They are called burning because no other angels stand between them and God; and therefore, the nearer they stand before him, the more they are inflamed by the brightness of the divine light.

These designations of the ranks of angels are so particular to the order of each that they are nevertheless, in part, common to all. For although [*licet*] thrones, the seats of God, are specially designated in the order of certain angels, the Psalmist nevertheless says: “You who are seated upon the cherubim” (Ps. 79). These orders of angels are therefore called by private names because they have received that same office more fully in their own order; and although the offices are common to all, the names are nevertheless properly assigned to their respective orders.

### [Col. 0029D]

For, as was said above, particular offices have been entrusted to each, and it is clear that they merited them at the beginning of the world. Since angels preside over both places and human beings, the prophet bears witness through an angel, who says: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. 10). From this it is apparent that there is no place over which angels do not preside.

This is the order or distinction of the angels who, after the fall of the wicked angels, remained in the heavenly *jugore* [perhaps *vigore*, “strength”]. For after the apostate angels fell, these were strengthened by the perseverance of eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven, the words are repeated at the beginning: “Let there be a firmament” (Gen. 1), clearly showing that after the ruin of the wicked angels those who remained attained the firmness of eternal perseverance. They are no longer turned aside by any fall, nor do they fall through pride; rather, they remain steadfast in the love and contemplation of God, finding nothing sweet except him by whom they were created.

### [Col. 0030A]

The fact that two seraphim are read of in Isaiah figuratively signifies the Old and New Testaments. They cover the face and feet of God because we cannot know what occurred before the world or what will occur after the world, but through their testimony we contemplate only what lies between. Each has six wings because in the present age we know only the structure of the world, which was made in six days. Their crying three times, “Holy, holy, holy,” one to another, demonstrates the mystery of the Trinity in one divinity.

### [Col. 0030B]

But what good is it for us to touch upon these matters concerning angelic spirits if we do not strive to apply them, through suitable reflection, to our own advancement? Since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and since we believe that the human race will ascend there in numbers equal to the number of elect angels who happened to remain there, we too ought to draw something from the distinctions of those heavenly citizens for the conduct of our own lives, and inflame ourselves by good pursuits toward an increase of virtue.

Since it is believed that as great a multitude of human beings will ascend there as the multitude of angels that remained, it follows that human beings themselves who return to their heavenly homeland should, as they return, imitate something of those ranks [perhaps *imitentur*, “should imitate”].

### [Col. 0030C]

For the distinct ways of life of individual human beings correspond to the orders of the several ranks, and by the likeness of their conduct they are assigned to their lot.

There are many who grasp small matters, yet do not cease to announce these same small matters piously to their brothers. Such people therefore run among the number of the angels.

There are some who, refreshed by the gift of divine generosity, are able both to grasp and to announce the greatest heavenly secrets. How, then, are such people not counted among the number of the archangels? [*Forte quomodo hic et infra*: perhaps “how” here and below.]

There are some who perform wonders and powerfully work signs. To what lot, then, unless to that of the virtues above, do such people correspond?

There are some who even drive evil spirits from possessed bodies, casting them out by the power of prayer and the force of the authority they have received. To what, then, do such people attain their due, unless to the number of the heavenly powers [variant: *potestatum*, “of the powers”]? 

### [Col. 0030D]

There are some who, having received virtues, surpass even the merits of elect human beings; and because they are better than the good, they also preside over their elect brothers. To what lot, then, unless to the number of the principalities, have such people been assigned?

There are some who so rule over all vices and every desire within themselves that, by the very purity of their life, they are called gods among human beings. Hence it is said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7). To what number, then, unless to that of the dominions, do such people belong?

### [Col. 0031A]

There are some who, while ruling over themselves with vigilant care, while examining themselves with attentive concern, and while always clinging to the fear of God, receive this gift of virtue: that they are able to judge rightly and to judge others as well. Since divine contemplation is present to their minds, the Lord presides in them as in his throne, examines the deeds of others, and wonderfully dispenses all things from his seat.

What, then, are such people except the thrones of their Creator? To what else are they assigned except to the number of the heavenly seats? Through them, while Holy Church is governed, even the elect are often judged for certain of their weak actions.

There are some who are so filled with love of God and neighbor that they are rightly called cherubim. Since, as we said above, cherubim means “fullness of knowledge,” and we have learned from Paul that “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13), all who are more filled than others with love of God and neighbor have received, according to the lot of their merits, a place among the cherubim.

### [Col. 0031B]

There are some who, inflamed by love of heavenly contemplation, pant only for the desire of their Creator. They desire nothing now in this world; they are nourished solely by love of eternity; they cast away everything earthly and transcend all temporal things in their minds. They love and burn, and rest in that very burning. They burn with love, and by speaking kindle others as well; those whom they touch with their word they immediately cause to burn with the love of God.

What, then, should I call such people except seraphim, whose heart, transformed into fire, shines and burns? For they illuminate the eyes of their minds toward heavenly things, and by piercing the heart they cleanse away the rust of sins through tears. Since they have been so inflamed with love of their Creator, where else have such people received the lot of their calling except among the seraphim?

### [Col. 0031C]

Woe to the soul that recognizes nothing at all in itself of these good things we have enumerated; and an even worse woe threatens it if, understanding that it has been deprived of gifts, it does not lament. Whoever is such, my brothers, is greatly to be lamented, because he does not lament.

### [Col. 0032A]

Let us therefore consider the gifts received by the elect, and with whatever virtue we possess, let us pant for the love of so great a lot. Let one who recognizes no grace of gifts in himself lament; but let one who recognizes lesser gifts in himself not envy greater gifts in others.

As we have shown above, the name “angels” may designate the heavenly powers, as in the Psalm: “Who makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103).

The Lord Jesus Christ is also called an angel typologically, that is, a messenger of the Father’s will. Hence the prophet says: “The ruler whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3).

### [Col. 0032B]

John the forerunner is called an angel in Malachi, as in the passage: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3).

Likewise, in the Apocalypse, where battles are described, we read: “I saw a strong angel of God flying through the midst of heaven” (Rev. 14).

Holy preachings are called angels, concerning which the Lord, speaking to Job about the devil, says: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 41). And elsewhere: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isa. 33). And in the Apostle: “He appeared to angels” (1 Tim. 3). They received this name not by nature but by the office of their ministry.

The devil is called an angel by the Apostle, where he says: “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we preached, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1).

### [Col. 0032C]

Similarly, unclean spirits are called angels, where the same Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more matters of this life!” (1 Cor. 6). Anyone who reads the Scriptures will be able to find similar examples.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0031]
