## SINGLE CHAPTER: ON HUMAN BEINGS WHO RECEIVED THEIR NAMES THROUGH A CERTAIN PRESAGE

### [Col. 0031C]

### I. On Adam and his descendants up to the patriarchs

Adam, as blessed Jerome transmitted, is interpreted as “human being” or “earthly,” or as “red earth”; for the flesh was made from earth, and soil was the material for making human beings.

### [Col. 0031D]

Adam bore the figure of Christ. For just as he was formed on the sixth day in the image of God, so, in the sixth age of the world, the Son of God assumed the form of flesh in order to reform humanity according to the likeness of God.

Eve is interpreted as “life,” or “calamity,” or “woe.” “Life,” because she was the origin of birth; “calamity” and “woe,” because through transgression she became the cause of dying. For calamity derives its name from falling. Others say that Eve was called both life and calamity because a woman is often the cause of salvation for a man, and often the cause of calamity and death, which is woe.

She signifies the Church, made the bride of Christ through the ministry of the washing that flowed from the side of the dying Christ.

### [Col. 0032C]

Cain is interpreted as “possession.” Accordingly, his father, expressing his etymology, said: “Cain,” that is, “I have possessed a man through God” (Gen. 4). The name also means “lamentation,” because he was killed on account of the murdered Abel and paid the penalty for his crime.

### [Col. 0032D]

This brother, who, being older, killed that same Abel in the field, signifies the earlier people, who killed Christ at the place of Calvary.

Abel is interpreted as “mourning”; by this name he was prefigured as one who would be killed. It also means “vanity,” because he was quickly released and taken away.

Abel, the shepherd of sheep, bore the type of Christ, who is the true shepherd and ruler of faithful peoples; hence he laid down his life for his sheep.

Seth, who is interpreted as “resurrection” or “placing,” received his name because, after the killing of his brother, he was born as though a resurrection and replacement for him.

Seth demonstrates Jesus Christ, in whom there is true resurrection and the life of the faithful.

Enos, according to the variety of his own language, is called “human being” or “man,” and this name suited him. For concerning him it is written: “Then the invocation of the name of the Lord began” (Gen. 4), although many of the Hebrews believe that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name of the Lord and in his likeness.

### [Col. 0033A]

Enos declares the Church living in hope until it reaches the blessedness of the promised happiness.

Enoch, the son of Cain, is interpreted as “dedication.” In his name Cain later built a city. Enoch signifies the ungodly, who are founded only in this life.

Cainan is interpreted as “lamentation” or “their possession.” Just as Cain means “possession,” so the derivative name Cainan makes “their possession.” Cainan signifies those who desire carnal pleasures and devote their concern solely to the delights of the present life.

Chus is interpreted in Hebrew as “Ethiopian,” receiving the name from [the] posterity of his race. For from him came the first Ethiopians.

### [Col. 0033B]

It is said that blessed Job lived in his land, since at the beginning of his book it is written: “There was a man in the land of Chus whose name was Job” (Job 1). The holy man’s place of residence is mentioned in order to express the merit of his virtue. For who does not know that Chus is the land of the Gentiles? The Gentile world was bound by vices because it did not know its Creator. Let it therefore be said where he lived, so that this may contribute to his praise: that he was good among the wicked. For it is not greatly praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked.

Enoch, the son of Jared, is also interpreted as “dedication,” like the earlier Enoch. He begot Methuselah, walked with God, and disappeared, because God took him (Gen. 4).

### [Col. 0033C]

This Enoch, the seventh from Adam, was transferred, and he signifies the seventh rest of the future resurrection, when the saints will be transferred into the life of perpetual immortality and will be dedicated as the dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.

Methuselah is interpreted as “dead.” The etymology of the name is evident. Some thought that he was transferred with his father and survived the flood. For this reason it is significantly rendered “he is dead,” to show that he did not live after the flood but died in that same catastrophe. For only eight human beings escaped the flood in the ark.

Methuselah signifies those who are devoted only to this world and do not seek the life to come. Although they may have lived long upon the earth, they nevertheless truly die, because they do not deserve to become participants in eternal life.

### [Col. 0033D]

Lamech is interpreted as “striking.” For this striking man killed Cain. He himself later confessed to his wives that he had committed this deed.

Lamech bears the figure of this world, whose sin Christ absolved by the shedding of his blood after seventy-seven generations of the world, according to the way the evangelist Luke records them.

Noah is interpreted as “rest.” He was therefore called “rest” because under him all things that had gone before came to rest through the flood.

### [Col. 0034A]

Through all his acts Noah signifies Christ. For Noah, as we have said, is interpreted as “rest,” and the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

Noah alone was found righteous among that people, and seven human beings were granted to him on account of his righteousness. There is one who alone is righteous and perfect, to whom the seven churches, because of the sevenfold Spirit who illumines them, are granted as one Church.

Noah therefore built the ark from incorruptible wood; so Christ fashioned the Church from human beings who would live forever. The timbers of the ark were joined together with bitumen; so the members of the Church are joined by the bond of unity and the endurance of love.

Just as Noah and his household were saved through water and wood, so Christ’s household was healed through baptism and the passion of the cross. For that ark signified the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world and, with Christ as its pilot, makes its way toward the shore of eternal rest.

### [Col. 0034B]

Moreover, after the flood, Noah became drunk from the vineyard he had planted and was stripped naked in his house. Who would not recognize this as a figure of Christ, who became drunk when he suffered and was stripped naked when he was crucified? He was naked in his own house, that is, among his own people, and among the members of his own blood, namely, the Jews. For then the mortality of his flesh was laid bare.

When Ham saw that nakedness—that is, Christ’s passion—he mocked it; and the Jews, seeing Christ’s death, scoffed at it. But Shem and Japheth, like two peoples believing from circumcision and uncircumcision, recognized their father’s nakedness, which signified the Savior’s passion. Taking a garment, they placed it upon their backs, entered backward, and covered their father’s nakedness; they did not see what they covered—the father’s private parts.

### [Col. 0034C]

In a certain way we cover Christ’s passion with a veil—that is, we honor it as a sacrament—and, giving an account of the meaning of its mystery, we cover the Jews’ disparagement. The garment signifies the sacrament, and the backs signify remembrance of past things, because the Church celebrates Christ’s passion as something accomplished, not as something it still looks forward to.

Shem is called “named,” receiving this name from a presage of his posterity. For from him came the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and the people of God; from his stock also came Christ, whose name is great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting.

Ham is interpreted as “hot.” He too received his name from a presage of the future. For his posterity possessed that part of the earth which, being nearer to the sun, is hotter. Hence Egypt is called *Cham* in the language of the Egyptians even to this day.

### [Col. 0034D]

Ham presents the figure of the Jews, who mock Christ’s flesh and death.

Japheth is interpreted as “breadth.” From him the people of the Gentiles are born. Since the multitude of believers from the Gentiles is broad, Japheth was named from that same breadth; he dwells in the churches of the Israelites.

In these three sons of Noah the second origin of the world arose, so that the three parts of the world might be filled by the three lines of descent. Shem possessed Asia through his sons, Ham Libya, and Japheth Europe. In them too the Church of Christ, destined to be planted in faith in the Holy Trinity, was prefigured.

Canaan, the son of Ham, is interpreted as “their movement.” What else is this than their deed? For he was cursed on account of the movement of his father, that is, on account of his deed. Expelled from his settlements, he left the land of his possession to the sons of his brothers, indicating the posterity of the Jews, who in the Lord’s passion received the sentence of condemnation, crying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

### [Col. 0035A]

For this reason, expelled from their homeland like ungrateful people by the Romans in vengeance for Christ’s blood, they gave place to the holy Church, in which the true worship of the one God endures forever.

Nimrod is interpreted as “tyrant.” He was the first to seize upon an unaccustomed tyranny over peoples, and he himself undertook, in impiety against God, to build a tower.

### [Col. 0035B]

Thus he expressed the devil, who, driven by the desire for pride, sought the summit of divine majesty, saying: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

Heber is interpreted as “passage” or “crossing over.” His etymology is mystical: from his stock God would cross over, so that the grace transferred to the Gentiles would not remain among them. From him the Hebrews arose.

Thus Heber, in whose house the proper language remained while the other languages were scattered, signifies our Redeemer, in whose Church the unity of faith perseveres without schism.

### [Col. 0035C]

Peleg is interpreted as “division.” His father gave him this name because he was born when the earth was divided by languages. Because of the pride of Adam’s sons, which is always hostile to simplicity and unity, the division of languages took place; and because of the humility and gentleness of Christ and his apostles, the diversity of languages was brought together.

Melchizedek is interpreted as “righteous king.” He was a king because he later ruled Salem, and righteous because, discerning the mysteries of the Law and the Gospel, he offered not the victims of animals but an offering of bread and the chalice as a sacrifice.

In his offering, therefore, he prefigured the kingship or priesthood of Christ, whose sacrament of body and blood—that is, the offering of bread and wine—is offered throughout the whole world.

### [Col. 0035D]

### II. On the patriarchs and other people of the same age

Abram was first called “father seeing the people,” with reference only to Israel. Later he was called Abraham, which is translated “father of many nations,” something that was still future through faith. The word “nations” is not contained in the name itself but is understood, in accordance with the statement: “Your name shall be Abraham, because I have made you the father of many nations” (Gen. 17).

Abraham has a threefold significance in himself. First, he signifies the Savior, when he left his kindred and came into this world; second, the Father, when he sacrificed his only Son; third, he bears the figure of the saints who received Christ’s coming with joy.

### [Col. 0036A]

That tent of Abraham represented Jerusalem itself, where for a time the prophets and apostles lived, and where the Lord, coming there first, was received by believers and hung upon the wood by unbelievers.

In the three men who came to him, the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed. Two angels accompanied him; many understand these as Moses and Elijah: the one, the lawgiver of the ancient Law, who through that same Law indicated the Lord’s coming; the other, who is announced as destined to come at the end of the world and to preach to the Jews Christ’s second coming and his Gospel.

Thus, on the mountain, when the Lord had been transfigured, these two—Moses and Elijah—were seen with him by the apostles.

The fact that Abraham saw three and worshiped one, namely the Lord and Savior, shows that he awaited his coming. In accordance with this, the Lord himself now says in the Gospel: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8).

### [Col. 0036B]

We learn from the Apostle that the two wives Abraham had, namely the free woman and the slave woman, are two covenants, from which two peoples were born: the Jews and the Church.

Lot is interpreted as “turning aside.” He did not consent to the deeds of the Sodomites, but turned aside from the illicit fires of their flesh. Lot himself, Abraham’s brother, righteous and hospitable in Sodom, deserved to escape safely from that conflagration, which was a likeness of the future judgment.

He prefigured the body of Christ, which now groans among the wicked and ungodly in all the saints, does not consent to their deeds, and at the end of the world will be delivered from their association, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

### [Col. 0036C]

Lot’s wife, however, bore the figure of those who, called by the grace of God, afterward look back and strive to return to the things they had abandoned. Concerning them the Lord himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

Consequently, she herself bore the figure of the Law, from which those who also employ a carnal understanding give birth to works of unbelief.

His two daughters signify Samaria and Jerusalem, which commit fornication under the Law through the adultery of illicit teaching.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” and the whole name has this etymology. For the elder daughter conceived him from her father. Moab signifies worldly wisdom, concerning which the Lord speaks through the prophet: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. 29).

### [Col. 0036D]

It has as the author of its sense the one who is generated from God’s creation. It appears indeed to be born from the father, which is what Moab means; but because it is adulterous and hostile to the people of God, it is generated from incest, a cave, and night.

Ammon, whose name is explained as “son of my people,” is so derived that he himself is the expression “from the father.” Ammon, from whom the Ammonites are named, is called “my people.”

According to the tropological sense, we may understand the sons of Ammon, who were begotten from Lot in the cave, conceived in drunkenness and incest, as all heretics. Concerning them the Apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

### [Col. 0037A]

They arose from turning aside; for this is how Lot is translated into our language: “They have all become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).

Sarai is interpreted as “my princess,” because she was the mother and mistress of one household only. Later, because the name was changed, with the letter *i* removed, she is called Sara, that is, “princess.”

She was destined to be the princess of all nations, just as the Lord had promised Abraham: “I will give you a son from Sara, and I will bless him, and he will become a great nation; indeed, kings of peoples shall come from him” (Gen. 17).

Hagar is interpreted as “stranger” or “converted.” She was an Egyptian, a stranger joined to Abraham and given for the purpose of begetting children; after she was despised, she was converted to Sara when rebuked by the angel.

### [Col. 0037B]

According to the Apostle, Abraham’s wives, Sarai and Hagar, bear the figure of the two covenants, as we said above. One of them, namely Sarai the free woman, signifies the Church and bore the Christian people, which is not according to the flesh but was called into freedom; Christ set it free with that freedom.

The other, namely Hagar the slave woman, the mother of Ishmael—whose name is interpreted as “hearing of God”—expresses the Synagogue. She generated the Jewish people into slavery and did not deserve to receive the inheritance with the son of the free woman; cast out with her mother, Ishmael wanders in the desert of this world.

Isaac received his name from laughter. His father had laughed when Isaac was promised to him, marveling with joy. His mother too laughed, because he was promised through the three men, doubting with joy. From this circumstance he received his name.

### [Col. 0037C]

Isaac is interpreted as “laughter.” Who, then, was prefigured in Abraham, as was said above, through the sacrifice of his son, except the exalted Father? And who in Isaac except Christ?

For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so the Lord delivered his only-begotten Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood on which he was to be placed, so Christ carried upon his shoulders the wood of his cross, on which he was to be crucified.

The two servants who were left behind and were not brought to the place of sacrifice signified the Jews. Living as slaves and possessing a carnal understanding, they did not comprehend Christ’s humility or passion.

Because they did not understand Christ’s passion, they did not reach the place of sacrifice. But what was prefigured in Isaac was transferred to the ram, because Christ is a sheep. He is himself son, ram, and lamb: son because he was born, ram because he was sacrificed.

### [Col. 0037D]

But what does it mean that that ram was caught by its horns in the thorns, except that Christ was crowned with thorns by the Jews and finally fastened to the wood of the cross? Concerning him it is written: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. 3).

Rebecca was betrothed to him by Abraham’s servant. Her name is interpreted as “patience,” or “she who has received much,” because through the ancient Law, which the servant himself signifies, the Church, the bride of our Lord Jesus Christ, was prepared by the oracles of the prophets. Receiving the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, she patiently awaits the promises of the future Church.

Her sons were Esau and Jacob.

### [Col. 0038A]

Esau has three names and is called differently for distinct reasons. He is called Esau, that is, “red,” because of the cooking of the red lentil dish by which he was so named, and by eating it he lost his birthright.

He was called Edom because of the redness of his body; in Latin this means “blood-colored.” He was called Seir because he was bristly and hairy. When he was born, he was entirely hairy, like a skin; and therefore he is called by three names: Esau, that is, “red”; Edom, that is, “blood-colored”; and Seir, that is, “hairy,” because he did not possess gentleness.

He signifies the Jewish people, made bloody, red, and hairy by their impious persecution of Christ and the prophets, and made hideous by the covering of sins.

Jacob, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” either because at birth he grasped the sole [*plantam*] of his brother as he was being born [Col. 0038B], or because he later deceived his brother by cunning. Hence Esau also said: “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me twice” (Gen. XXVII). He is indeed called Israel, “the man who sees God.” For he received this name when, having wrestled throughout the whole night, he prevailed in the contest with the angel and was blessed at the rising of the morning star. Therefore, because of his vision of God, he was called Israel, just as he himself said: “I have seen the Lord, and my soul has been saved” (Gen. XXXII). Here he represents Christ, or the people of the Gentiles, who by the blessing of God the Father was placed before the former people, the Jews.

These two sons of Rebekah, as we have said, signify two peoples, the Synagogue and the Church. And just as, in time, the Jewish people serves the lesser people of the Christians, so it can also be said of each of us that there are two nations and two peoples within us, namely, those of vices and virtues. But the one is lesser, the other greater. For the wicked are always more numerous than the good, and vices outnumber virtues; nevertheless, in us too the people of grace surpasses the other people, and the greater serves the lesser. The flesh, indeed, serves the spirit, and vices yield to virtues.

Isaac, therefore, bears the image of God the Father; Rebekah, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the former people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church and of Christ. Isaac’s growing old signifies the consummation of the world; the dimming of his eyes signifies that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been neglected before him. The fact that the elder son is called “greater” signifies the Jews’ acceptance of the Law. The fact that the father loves his food and his catch signifies human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts through teaching. The fact that Isaac desired to eat from the hunt of his elder son signifies that almighty God desired to be nourished by the good works of the Jewish people.

But while that son delayed, Rebekah substituted the younger, because, while the Jewish people seeks good works outside, the mother, Grace, brought in the Gentile people, so that the almighty Father might be offered the food of good works and the younger might receive the blessing of the elder brother. He provided those same foods from domestic animals, because the Gentile people, not seeking to please God through outward sacrifices, says through the voice of the Prophet: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay with praises to you?” (Ps. LV).

The fact that Jacob covered his hands, arms, and neck with the skins of young goats [Col. 0039A] means that the Gentile people, not being ashamed to confess itself a sinner, put to death within itself the sins of the flesh. The fact that he was clothed in the garments of his elder brother means that he was clothed in good works with the precepts of Holy Scripture, which had been given to the elder people, and that the younger uses them in the household; the elder, going outside, left them within, while that Jewish people could not possess them because it attended only to the letter in them.

The fact that Isaac did not recognize the same son whom he blessed means that the Lord says concerning the Gentile people through the Psalmist: “A people whom I did not know shall serve me” (Ps. XVII). The fact that he did not see him present, yet saw what would happen to him in the future, signifies that almighty God, through his prophets, proclaimed that grace would be granted to the Gentiles—a grace which he did not show them in the present through outward appearance, because at that time he left them in error; nevertheless, because he would one day gather them, he foresaw grace for them through the blessing.

Accordingly, after his father’s blessing, Esau, stirred by the goads of envy, deceitfully devised the murder of his brother Jacob. This is precisely what the Jewish people also premeditated against Christ: it not only handed the Lord over to the cross’s gallows, but also persecuted those who believed in him even to the shedding of blood.

But Jacob, fleeing his brother’s plots, left his ancestral home and his parents and went to a distant region in order to take a wife for himself. In the same way Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people of Israel—and his homeland, namely Jerusalem and all the regions of Judea, went to the Gentiles, taking the Church from them for himself, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. II).

As Jacob was going to Mesopotamia, he came to the place now called Bethel. He placed a great stone beneath his head, and while sleeping he saw a ladder set up and leaning upon heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending. When he had seen this, he awoke and anointed the stone, saying: “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII); and after saying these things he departed.

This sleep of Jacob is the death or passion of Christ. The stone beneath his head, which is in a certain manner specifically called a stone, and which was also anointed, signifies Christ: “For the head of a man is Christ” (I Cor. XI). For who does not know that Christ was named from anointing?

The house of God, because Christ was born there, in Bethlehem. The gate of heaven, because there he descended to earth and there again ascended to heaven. The raising up of the stone is the resurrection of Christ.

Moreover, the ladder is Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John XIV). Through him the angels ascended and descended. In these angels the preachers of Christ in the Gospel are signified: they ascend when, in order to understand his surpassingly exalted divinity, they rise above the whole of creation and find him in the beginning as the Word of the Lord, through whom all things were made; they descend when they find him made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law (Gal. IV).

For in that ladder erected from earth to heaven—that is, from flesh to spirit—those who are carnal progress, as though ascending, and become spiritual. For the spiritual also descend in a certain manner to nourish them with milk, when they cannot speak to them as to spiritual people but as to carnal people.

He himself is above in his head; he himself is below in his body, that is, the Church. We therefore understand him to be the ladder, because he said: “I am the way” (John XIV). One ascends to him in order that he may be understood in the heights; one descends to him in order that the little one may be nourished by his rains. Through him they raise themselves up, so that they may await him in exaltation; through him they also humble themselves, so that they may proclaim him with sublimity and moderation.

Now it must be explained what the four wives of Jacob signify, two of whom were free women and two slave women. We have seen the Apostle understand, in the free woman and the slave woman whom Abraham had, the two Testaments; but there, what is said would appear more easily through one and one. Here, however, there are two and two. Moreover, there the son of the slave woman is disinherited; here, the sons of the slave women receive the land of promise together with the sons of the free women. Therefore something is certainly signified here.

Although Jacob’s two free wives may be thought to pertain to the New Testament, in whose freedom we have been called, nevertheless they are not two without reason: it is because two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ—one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the love of God.

Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” while Rachel is interpreted as “vision,” or “beginning,” or “word.” The activity of this life, in which we live by faith, is laborious in its works and uncertain as to the outcome by which it may reach the benefit of those whom we wish to help. She is Leah, Jacob’s first wife, and for this reason she is also said to have had weak eyes. “The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our plans are uncertain” (Wis. IX).

The hope of eternal contemplation of God, possessing certain understanding of the truth, is Rachel. Hence she is also described as “beautiful in face and lovely in appearance” (Gen. XXIX). Every devout and earnest person loves her, and on her account serves the grace of God, because our sins, even if they are like scarlet, “shall be made white as snow” (Isa. I). Laban, too, is interpreted as “whitening”; Jacob served him on account of Rachel. For no one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness except in order to live peacefully in the Word, from which the Beginning, who is God, is seen.

Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman, is interpreted as “grown old.” From an old life devoted to carnal perceptions, bodily images are conceived even when something is heard concerning the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity.

Leah also receives sons from her slave woman, inflamed by the desire to have a more numerous offspring. We find that her slave woman, Zilpah, is interpreted as “mouth.” Therefore this slave woman represents those whose mouth was present in the preaching of evangelical faith, but whose heart was not. Concerning them it is written: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). Concerning them the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. II).

Nevertheless, so that through this condition the free wife Jacob, the laboring woman, might also receive sons as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Whatever they tell you, do; but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). Hence the Apostle also says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice” (Phil. I), as though she too rejoiced when the slave woman gave birth to a more numerous offspring.

Jacob’s servitude, therefore, for seven years on behalf of his two wives signifies the time of the present life, because it unfolds through seven. In it the Lord assumed the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father’s will unto death. He served for sheep, and our Lord says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. XX). He fed the sheep, and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John X). He took for himself, as the profit of his wages, a varied flock; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations.

He stripped the bark from three rods and placed them in the watering troughs, so that his sheep might multiply while looking at them; and our Lord set before the faithful people, in the water of baptism, the three names of the persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that whoever contemplated this with a full heart might become a sheep of God.

After the long servitude which Jacob endured with his father-in-law for the sake of his wives and his wages, God commanded him to return to his homeland. Then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hurried away with his wives. But Laban pursued him furiously to Mount Gilead and searched for the idols that Rachel had stolen from him, but did not find them. What this signifies figuratively must therefore be considered. Although Laban previously represented another person, he now represents the devil.

Laban, indeed, is interpreted as “whitening.” “Whitening” is not improperly understood as the devil, because although he is dark by merit, he disguises himself as an angel of light (II Cor. XI). Jacob served him—that is, the Jewish people in its reprobate portion, from whose flesh the Lord came incarnate.

Laban can also signify this world. He follows Jacob furiously because he tries, by persecuting them, to crush the elect, who are members of our Redeemer. Jacob took away his daughter—that is, the daughter either of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church to himself. He also took her away from her father’s house, because it is said to her through the Prophet: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XLIV).

What else is signified by the idols except avarice? Hence Paul also says: “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. III). Laban therefore came to Jacob and did not find the idol, because, after displaying the world’s treasures, the devil found no trace of earthly desire in our Redeemer; but Rachel concealed what Jacob did not possess by sitting upon it.

Through Rachel, who is called the sheep of God, the Church is signified. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise up after you have sat down” (Ps. CXXVI). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting upon them, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Concerning this covering of vices the Prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI).

Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument, and so forth. Mystically, among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone in the likeness of Christ is a witness, and the heap of stones is the multitude of believers. The man who wrestled with Jacob most evidently bore the type of Christ. Yet Jacob prevailed over him because he willed it, so that he might represent the mystery of the Lord’s passion.

There Jacob appeared in the type of the Jews—that is, he prevailed over God in the offspring of his body, as though entering into combat with him in his weakness, as with a weak man, and growing strong in his passion, just as it is written when they said: “Crucify him.” Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from that same angel whom he had overcome as victor. The imposition of his name was itself a blessing.

Israel is interpreted as “seeing God,” which will be the final reward of all the saints. Moreover, that same angel touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame. Thus Jacob was both one and the same man, blessed and lame: blessed in those from the same people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers.

For in the sinew of the thigh are the health of the race and its multitude. There are indeed many in the lineage who, degenerating from the faith of their fathers and straying from the commands of their author, limp in the error of their own seed. Concerning them it was prophetically foretold: “And they have limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII). Yet after its strength had been touched, that people not only limps but also grows numb, so that it can no longer beget sons.

Finally, the fact that the same patriarch added that he had seen God face to face, while earlier he relates that a man wrestled with him, signifies that the same God was destined to become man and wrestle with the people Jacob represented.

Dinah, whose name is rendered as “cause”—for she became the cause of the quarrel at Shechem. She goes out in order to see the women of a foreign region when any mind, neglecting its own pursuits and concerning itself with the activities of others, wanders outside its proper character and proper order.

Shechem, the ruler of the land, violates her, because the devil corrupts the mind intent upon external concerns. “His soul was joined to her” (Gen. XXXIV), because he rejects the one united to him through iniquity; and because, when the mind recovers from guilt, he afflicts it; and, as it tries to weep over what it has committed, he soothes its sadness with the blandishments of false hope.

The zeal that Jacob’s sons displayed in avenging the violation of their sister morally admonishes the shepherds of the faithful to care for the souls entrusted to them, lest they be defiled violently either by bodily wrongdoing or by spiritual fornication. They should always be ready, according to the Apostle, to avenge every disobedience resisting the truth, and to strike the violator with the sword of excommunication, lest he escape unpunished for so great a crime.

Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, whose name is interpreted as “son of vision”—for when Leah gave birth to him, she called his name Reuben, saying: “Because God has seen my humiliation” (Gen. XXIX)—signifies the Jewish people, which in a certain manner saw God, that is, recognized him through the acceptance of the Law. But it violated the bed of God the Father when it fastened upon the gallows of the cross the flesh which Christ had taken to himself.

In another sense, he signifies the elect people from among the Jews, to whom divine mercy granted that, although by denying and crucifying God it had delivered itself over to eternal death, yet, pierced with remorse at the preaching of the holy apostles, it might repent of its error [Col. 0043B] and live by faith.

Simeon is interpreted as “hearing.” Thus Leah spoke when she gave birth to him: “Because God has heard me” (Gen. XXIX). He represents the scribes of the Jews, who indeed received the voice of God delivering the precepts of the Law to them, but in their fury killed the prophets, and in their anguish pierced Christ—the firmest wall in which believers are fortified with stable strength—with the punctures of nails.

Levi, who is interpreted as “added,” is the author and figure of the chief priests who crucified the Lord. In another sense Levi signifies the apostolic choir and the entire army of martyrs, as well as the head of the martyrs. These words also apply to every order of the perfect, who, dying for the Lord, fulfilled the perfection of love and, renouncing everything, attained the summit of evangelical teaching, like true Levites who have no share in the earth but say with the Prophet: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

Hence Moses says to the Lord in Levi’s blessing: “Your perfection and your doctrine are for your holy man, whom you tested in temptation and judged at the waters of contradiction” (Deut. XXXIII). For this holy man was tested, as the Apostle says, “in all things according to likeness [Latin *pro* supplied], except sin” (Heb. IV). But the devil brought upon him his greatest temptation when he stirred the minds of the Jews against his death with such obstinacy that they all cried out with one voice: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). For the waters of contradiction are the Jewish people, who rose up against Christ and his saints in the flood of persecutions.

Judah is called “confession,” because when Leah gave birth to him, she rendered praise to the Lord, saying: “Now for this I will confess to the Lord” (Gen. XXIX), that is, “I give thanks.” He signifies Christ, who rested in the chamber of the tomb like a secure lion, in a kind of sleep of the body, and after conquering the power of death rose on the third day.

Fighting against the hostile powers on the cross, he gathered to himself the holy Church from all the nations, like a true vine, washed it with the wine of his blood, and made it superior to all its enemies.

Issachar, whose name is interpreted as “reward.” This was because Leah had bought from her son Reuben the entrance of the man that was owed to Rachel by means of the mandrakes. Hence, when he was born, Leah said: “God has given me my reward” (Gen. XXX).

His father Jacob called him a strong ass in his blessing (Gen. XLIX), placing his shoulder beneath the burden, because he labored greatly in working the land and transporting to the sea what was produced within his borders. He signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which placed its shoulder beneath the burden of the cross and beneath the fulfillment of Christ’s commands, who said: “For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI).

Zebulun, whose name is interpreted as “dwelling,” because Leah, now confident of dwelling with Jacob, said: “My husband has dwelt with me” (Gen. XXX). He signifies that same Church, which dwells beside the waves of this life, endures all the temptations and storms of the world, and through its teachers summons the peoples of every nation to the mountains of virtue, where praises are to be rendered to the Lord.

Naphtali is also interpreted as “he converted me,” or “he enlarged me,” or indeed “he entangled me.” The cause or comparison gives rise to his name. Hence Rachel said, when Bilhah, her slave woman, had given birth to him: “God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed” (Gen. XXX).

His father said to him in his blessing: “Naphtali is a released hind, giving beautiful words” (Gen. XLIX). Alternatively: “Naphtali is a watered field.” The Hebrew word *aila* signifies both. It signifies either that hot springs arise in that tribe, or that it was watered by the flow of the Jordan near Lake Gennesaret.

The Hebrews, however, wish “a watered field” and “beautiful words” to be prophesied on account of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law. The released hind signifies seasonal crops and the speed of a more fertile land; but it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because the Savior taught there above all—as is also written in the Gospel.

In another sense, he represents all holy preachers who, like harts leaping, raise themselves toward heavenly things and bring the words of teaching to all believers.

Dan is interpreted as “judgment.” For when Bilhah gave birth to him, Rachel, her mistress, said: “The Lord has judged me, and, hearing me, has given me a son”; she expressed the reason for his name.

According to Jacob’s prophecy, he is said to be “a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path” (Gen. XLIX). Some say that the Antichrist is foretold by these words as destined to arise from this tribe, because in this passage Dan is asserted to be both a serpent and one who bites; moreover, among the tribes of Israel Dan was the first to camp toward the north, signifying the one who says that he will sit at the sides of the north. Concerning him the Prophet says figuratively: “From Dan the snorting of horses was heard” (Jer. VIII).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. In Greek, *cerata* means “horns.” That serpent is said to be horned; through it the Antichrist is rightly signified, for he will arm himself against the life of the faithful not only with the bite of a deadly preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? He is therefore a serpent on the road because he urges those to walk in the breadth of the present life whom he flatters as though sparing them; but he bites because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom.

Thus he is again a *cerastes* on the path, because when he finds people faithful and sees them binding themselves within the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks them not only with the crafty wickedness of persuasion but also destroys them through the terror of power in the anguish of persecution. After the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of power.

In this passage, by the name “horse” he indicates the world, which, through its pride, foams along in the course of fleeting times. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the world’s extremities, this *cerastes* is said to bite the horse’s hoof. To bite the horse’s hoof is to strike the ends of the age, so that its rider falls backward; for whoever is exalted by worldly dignity in iniquities is said to fall backward.

Moses says in the blessing: “Dan is a lion’s cub; he pours forth abundantly from Bashan” (Deut. XXXIII). The lion, through its strength, bears the figure of Christ; conversely, through its ferocity, it signifies the devil. The Antichrist, therefore, is the son of the ferocious devil.

He pours forth abundantly from Bashan because he is full of confusion. Bashan is interpreted as “confusion,” or “fatness,” or “locust.” Fatness signifies the excess of his avarice and luxury. He resembles a locust in that, just as the locust destroys vegetation, so he destroys the beauty of virtues.

Gad was named from an occurrence or from a battle array. For when Zilpah gave birth to him, his mistress Leah said: “By fortune”—the same as what is said, “in readiness” or “in an occurrence.” His father Jacob says of him in the blessing: “Gad, girded, will fight before him, and he himself will be girded behind” (Gen. XLIX).

This refers entirely to the fact that, when he returned after fourteen years to the sons whom he had divided into an inheritance beyond the Jordan, before Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, he found a great battle against the neighboring nations and fought bravely after defeating the enemies [*dimicaret* / *dimicavit*]. Read the book of Joshua and Chronicles.

Moses says of him: “Blessed in breadth is Gad; like a lion he rested and seized the arm and the crown of the head; and he saw his principality, for a teacher was placed in his portion; he was with the princes of the people and performed the justice of the Lord and his judgment for Israel” (Deut. XXXIII).

In Gad’s blessing Moses seems, according to the historical sense, to foretell the power of the brave men or judges who came from that tribe, such as Jephthah, who was very distinguished and noble in deed among the other judges.

According to the allegorical interpretations, however, Gad is interpreted as “girded” and represents the Lord Jesus Christ, who, about to fight against spiritual wickedness, appeared girded with the power of his divinity in the weakness of our flesh. He was blessed in breadth when he received from the Father a most extensive kingdom throughout the whole world, not only from the Jews but also from all nations, in fulfillment of what the Prophet had foretold: “From the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great and terrible among the nations” (Mal. I).

Because through the humility of his passion he grew to such glory of exaltation, the statement concerning his death is aptly added: “Like a lion he rested; he seized the arm and the crown of the head,” and so forth (Deut. XXXIII). In the resting of the lion the power of the Savior himself is expressed: by the arm of his strength he bent worldly powers to his religion. His power was made manifest when kingdoms and all nations were subjected to him.

For he was a helper and fellow worker to the apostles, the princes of God’s people, as they preached the Gospel throughout the world, as the Evangelist says: “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” [Col. 0046B] (Mark XVI).

Asher, whose name is interpreted as “blessed,” because when Zilpah had given birth to him, Leah said: “Blessed am I, and women shall call me blessed” (Gen. XXX). He represents the Lord Jesus Christ, whose bread is rich in the mouth of believers, because he also provides delicacies to kings—that is, he gives the sacraments of his body and blood to the saints, who are rightly called kings because they govern themselves well and govern those subject to them.

According to Moses’ prophecy, he is blessed in sons and pleasing to his brothers, when those who believe in him and are reborn through his grace have filled the whole world in their likeness. He granted his brothers—that is, the apostles and saints—so great a share of the grace of his love that they rejected the ceremonies of the Law and rejoiced and exulted in receiving evangelical truth, because they were considered worthy to suffer disgrace for his name. To all the faithful they proclaimed, saying: “Consider it all joy when you fall into various temptations” (James I).

How such abundance of Christ’s love exists in them is explained figuratively when it is added: “He dips his foot in oil” (Deut. XXXIII). As our head, the Lord Christ, ascended into heaven, he anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit in the greatest abundance the apostolic choir, which by its harmonious preaching was to traverse the whole world, like a foot still standing upon the earth. By the power conceived from this anointing it would not fail through any labor but would always flourish with the vigor of unfading joy.

He also provided it with the protection of an incorruptible shoe, concerning which it follows: “Iron and bronze are his footwear.” Its days of youth become like those of old age, because his body, which is the Church, flourished in virtues at the beginning of its faith, abounded in wisdom, and shone with miracles. Thus also at the end of the age the vigor of faith and the ardor of love persevere in the elect until the end.

He is the most upright rider of heaven, because after his resurrection he ascended above all the heavenly virtues and angelic powers and sits at the right hand of the Father (Eph. I). “His magnificence is that the clouds run” (Deut. XXXIII): namely, the teachers and preachers of the Gospel disseminate the word of God throughout the whole world.

“His arms are everlasting” (ibid.), because his victory becomes perpetual for all his enemies. He will cast the enemy, the devil, from before his face, and he says: “Crush him,” when death, the last enemy, will be destroyed, and all the elect, clothed in immortality and incorruption, will enter the eternal kingdom in triumph.

Joseph was named from the fact that his mother had desired another addition for herself; hence his name means “increase.” Pharaoh called him *Sephaneth*, which in Hebrew is said to mean “finder of hidden things,” because he revealed obscure dreams and foretold the coming sterility.

Nevertheless, because this name is given in Egyptian, it must be explained according to that language. Thus *Sephaneth*, in the Egyptian tongue, is interpreted as “Savior of the world,” because he freed the world from the impending destruction of famine.

The fact that Joseph, sold by his brothers, was exalted in Egypt signifies our Redeemer, handed over by the Jewish people into the hands of his persecutors and now exalted among the Gentiles.

His father says to him in the blessing: “A son who increases and is beautiful in appearance. The daughters ran upon the wall, but they embittered him, and they quarreled with him, and they envied him, having arrows,” and so forth (Gen. XLIX).

This prophecy, after the Lord’s passion, bore the likeness of the Father’s voice, because the Father addresses Christ, returning to heaven after his victory, saying: “Joseph, an increasing son.” An increasing son, indeed, among the Gentiles, because when he had abandoned the Synagogue’s people on account of their unbelief, he enlarged for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all the nations.

David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI). “An increasing son and beautiful in appearance.” For his beauty surpasses that of all others, according to what is sung of him in the psalms: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV).

“The daughters ran upon the wall,” that is, the churches that believed in Christ. Inflamed by love of Christ’s beauty, they ran upon the firmness of faith as upon a wall, so that they might behold the true bridegroom through contemplation and be joined and cling to him with the kiss of love.

“But they quarreled with him” when the people of the Synagogue, calumniating him with false testimonies, plotted to suppress the holy God. “They envied him, having arrows.” No one, indeed, shot arrows at Joseph or any weapon of injury; but this happened specifically to Christ.

“His bow rests in the strong one.” For Christ placed his bow and weapons in God, who is a strong defender. By his power all the wickedness of the faithless will be brought down. “And the bonds of his arms were loosed,” the bonds with which his brothers had bound him and led him to Pilate, or with which they suspended him upon the wood.

For they were torn apart by the hand of the almighty Jacob—that is, by the hand of the almighty God of Jacob—from whose thigh the Lord himself, the good shepherd, came forth, the stone and strength of believers in Israel.

“The God of your father shall be your helper.” Who helped the Son except God the Father alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; let my soul receive him”? And the Almighty will bless you with the blessings of heaven above and with the blessings of the abyss lying below. For he subjected all things to him: heavenly things through the blessing of heaven, and earthly things through the blessing of the abyss lying below, so that he might rule over all angels and human beings.

“With the blessings of the breasts,” that is, either of the two Testaments, in one of which he was announced and in the other demonstrated; or with the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed because by them the holy Virgin milked drink for the Lord from herself. Hence that woman in the Gospel said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke XI).

“With the blessings of the breasts and of the womb.” Here too the womb of that same mother is blessed, namely, the virginal womb which gave birth to Christ the Lord for us. Concerning it the Prophet Jeremiah says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. I).

“The blessings of your father have been strengthened in you by the blessings of your fathers.” He says: The blessings of your heavenly Father, which were given to you, have been strengthened from the summit of heaven and from the abyss; that is, they have prevailed over the blessings of your fathers. For the blessing of the almighty Father in the Son grew stronger beyond the merit of all the holy patriarchs, so that none of the saints could be made equal to him.

“Until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Concerning them the Lord says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see” (Luke X). These saints, therefore, are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness. They are also called eternal because they obtain eternal life and do not perish with the world, but are believed to be eternal.

“Let them come upon the head of Joseph.” All these blessings are placed upon Christ’s head, which he received when he became incarnate. And upon the crown of the Nazarite, concerning whom it is written: “For he shall be called a Nazarite” (Mal. II), that is, “holy of God.” He is among his brothers because he is the head, exalted above all, namely, above all the saints, whom he also calls brothers in the psalms.

Benjamin, whose name is interpreted as “son of the right hand,” which signifies strength. For when his mother was dying, she called his name Ben-oni, that is, “son of my sorrow”; but his father changed it, naming him “son of the right hand.” Benjamin, however, prefigured the figure of the apostle Paul, because he was both the least of the apostles and arose from his tribe. He is the ravening wolf: in the morning, a persecutor tearing apart; in the evening, a teacher feeding others.

But what Moses said in Benjamin’s blessing [Col. 0048D]—“The beloved of the Lord shall dwell securely; he shall abide in him as in a chamber all day long, and shall rest between his shoulders” (Deut. XXXIII)—seems, according to the historical sense, to touch upon the fact that Benjamin was loved by the patriarch and at the same time prophet, namely his father Jacob, who was filled with the Spirit of God; and that, by God’s dispensation, the place where worship was chiefly destined to be offered was assigned to that tribe, namely Jerusalem, where the temple and altar of God were built. Therefore it is added: “He shall abide as in a chamber all day long,” because Jerusalem was at that time the place which the Lord chose so that his name might be there.

Allegorically, however, our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the beloved of God the Father, of whom he said: “This is [Col. 0049A] my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III). He remains in the strength of the Father, because he sits at the right hand of Power, and reigns in the heights. But this may also be understood of his humility, because divinity dwells securely in that humility, which he joined to himself in the unity of person. That he will dwell in a chamber and rest between his shoulders signifies that the Church has been joined to the heavenly Bridegroom in the Virgin’s womb, and that in the strength of Christ’s power and in his works she possesses the greatest confidence and rest of mind.

Manasseh was so named because his father had forgotten his labors. Thus in Hebrew he is called “forgetfulness”; he bears the figure of the former people.

Ephraim, whose name is interpreted as “fruitful,” or “increase” [Col. 0049B], or “increase,” because God increased him. He signifies the people of the nations, who through the patriarch’s blessing were placed before the greater people of the Jews.

Thamar is interpreted as “bitterness on account of dead men.” She is also called “the one who changes,” for she changed herself into the attire of a prostitute when she slept with her father-in-law.

Phares is interpreted as “division,” because he divided the membrane of the afterbirth; from this division he received the name “Phares,” that is, “divider.” Hence the Pharisees, who separated themselves from the people as though they were righteous, were called “the divided.”

Zara, his brother, in whose hand was the scarlet thread, is interpreted as “rising,” either because he appeared first or because many righteous men were born from him, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles [Col. 0049C].

Thamar changes her attire, and she also changes her name: she becomes the Church from the Synagogue. Yet the name of bitterness remains wholly in her—not the bitterness in which she ministered to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. Judas, moreover, means “confession” in Latin. Therefore bitterness must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be prefigured; by this repentance the Church, established among all the nations, is made fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke XXIV).

The attire of a prostitute itself is also a confession of sins. Thamar bears the figure of the Church called from the nations, sitting in this attire at the gate of Enan or Enachin, which is interpreted as “fountain” [Col. 0049D]. For she ran like a deer to reach the springs of water, to come to the seed of Abraham. She is said to be borne while he did not know her [the wording is corrupt], because this was foretold of him: “A people whom I did not know shall serve me” (Ps. XLIV).

She received secretly a ring, a necklace, and a staff (Gen. XXXVIII), because she is marked by calling, adorned by justification, and exalted by glorification. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also [Col. 0050A] justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII). But these things, as I said, take place secretly, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also occurs.

A promised kid is sent to her as to a prostitute (Gen. XXXVIII). The kid is a reproach for sin, sent through the same Odollamite as though he were rebuking and saying: “Generation of vipers” (Matt. III). But the reproach for sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had changed her.

Afterward, through the public signs of the ring, necklace, and staff, she overcame the Jews who judged rashly, whose person Judas himself was already bearing; they still say today that this people does not belong to Christ and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forth, they will undoubtedly blush and be confounded, and they will confess that we have been justified [Col. 0050B] more than they.

For the Church is said to have the pledges with her. She is accused by the Jews as though she were an adulteress against the law; but she displays the staff, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the adornment of the lawful law; and the ring, the pledge of immortality.

When Scripture says that Thamar gave birth and had twin sons in her womb—of whom the first, called Zara, extended his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it; then, when he drew his hand back inside, the second, called Phares, extended his hand and came forth at birth—this corresponds figurally to the fact that Israel extended its hand into the works of the law, but withdrew it, polluted with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. Afterward the earlier people, namely the nations, comes forth first, so that those who were last might become first, and those who were first might become last.

[Col. 0050C] Job, however, as some suspect, is called Johab in the Book of Genesis, and is believed to have been born in the fourth generation from the stock of Esau. The Hebrews, on the contrary, assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor. For I found it written in the Book of Hebrew Questions that Eliphaz, who is read as one of Job’s three friends, was the son of Esau by his wife Ada. Job is also rendered in Latin as “sorrowing.” And rightly “sorrowing,” because of the striking of his flesh and the sufferings of his pains; for his calamities were represented by the etymology of his name. Thus, in his deeds and words, he expresses the person of the Redeemer, of whom it is written: “He himself bore our pains and carried our sicknesses” (Isa. LIII).

Job’s wife, who urged him [Col. 0050D] to curse, represents the perversity of carnal people.

His three friends, however, bear the figure of heretics, who under the appearance of giving counsel pursue the effort to lead people astray.

Eliud, who spoke proudly against him, represents a proud and arrogant teacher who, through his harsher rebuke, accuses and censures the crowd of the faithful within the holy Church.

[Col. 0051]

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning certain other men and women whose names are recorded in the Old Testament

[Col. 0051A]

Pharaoh is not the name of a man but of an honorific title, just as among us kings are called “Augusti” even though they are designated by their proper names. Pharaoh is rendered into Latin as “denying him,” namely God, or “dispersing,” or “uncovering,” specifically the people of God, whose oppressor he was.

He therefore bore the figure of the devil, who in the captivity of this age attempted to destroy God’s people and burden them with earthly works of vice.

His eunuch was Potiphar, whose name is interpreted as “mouth inclined to learn.” He bought Joseph, when Joseph was sold by his brothers. So also the chaste evangelical people, through the price of faith, bought Christ, when he was sold by the Jews, his near kinsmen in [Col. 0051B] blood. He is rightly called “mouth inclined to learn,” because he submits himself to teachers in order to learn divine wisdom.

Pharaoh therefore saw a dream, which Joseph interpreted, because Christ revealed to the nations the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, which the devil did not know. The seven years of abundance, displayed in the seven full ears of grain or in the seven fat cows, signified the gifts of the seven spiritual graces, through which the abundance of faith overflows in generous devotion. On the other hand, the seven barren and thin years prefigured the famine of truth and righteousness in the last times.

Joseph, who had assumed the figure of Christ, earned a chariot, and a herald went before him; Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. And our Lord, after he had been sold by Juda [Col. 0051C], as Joseph was by his brothers, and had risen from the prison of the underworld, mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom. Of this it is written: “The chariot of God is ten thousand” (Ps. XCVII). He received authority from the Father to preach and judge, as the apostle Paul says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

He also received a ring, namely the high priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked on their foreheads and hearts with the sign of salvation. Through the sign of the cross the figure of the eternal King is expressed.

He is clothed in a linen robe, that is, in holy flesh whiter than linen, and in the robe of immortality. He also received a golden chain, that is, sound understanding.

A herald goes before him, namely either John the Baptist, who, going before him, proclaimed [Col. 0051D], “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. III). He will also have another herald, the trumpet of the angel, because he himself will come with the angel’s trumpet (I Thess. IV).

The king also said to Joseph: “I am Pharaoh. Without your command no one shall move hand or foot in the whole land of Egypt.” And he changed his name and called him, in the Egyptian language, “savior of the world” (Gen. XLI). What could be clearer concerning Christ, when under the figure of Joseph the Savior is shown to be not merely the Savior of one land, Egypt, but of the whole world?

[Col. 0052A] Pharaoh’s daughter, who gathered Moses, exposed on the bank of the river (Exod. II), is the Church of the nations, which found Christ at the river of the saving washing.

Jannes is interpreted as “maritime,” or “where there is a sign.” For he yielded before Moses’ signs, and his own sign failed. Hence the magicians also said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII).

Jambres is interpreted as “leathern sea,” or “sea on the head.”

Moses is interpreted as “taken from water.” Pharaoh’s daughter found him exposed on the bank of the river. She gathered him, adopted him as her own, and called his name Moses because she had taken him from the water.

He bore the figure of Christ, who rescued God’s people from the yoke of the devil’s slavery and condemned the devil himself to eternal [Col. 0052B] punishment. Moses struck Egypt with ten plagues and instructed God’s people in the desert with ten commandments, because Christ, through the commandments of the Gospel by which he nourishes believers in the desert of this world, reproves and condemns unbelievers.

By striking the rock with his staff, he brought forth a spring of living water. So also Christ, tasting death through the Passion of the cross, brought forth blood and water from his side; with these two sacraments the holy Church is clothed.

Moses led the people through the desert, but nevertheless did not bring them across the Jordan into the promised land, because although the Old Testament promised in its writings the future homeland in heaven, no one attained access to the heavenly kingdom except under the leadership of Jesus Christ.

He likewise introduced his people through the streams of baptism [Col. 0052C] into the land of the Church, giving his elect the promise of eternal life and making earthly people citizens of heaven.

Moses therefore took one of the seven daughters of Raguel, whose name is interpreted as “feeding of God,” or “God, his friend.” Her name was Sephora, interpreted as “beauty,” or “pleasing.” She bore a son whom he called Gersan, interpreted as “sojourner.” She also bore another, who was called Eliezer, interpreted as “my God is my help.”

This occurred when the Redeemer joined to himself, in a spiritual marriage, the sevenfold Church from the Gentile people. Although she is sevenfold through the gift of the Holy Spirit, she is nevertheless one in the Catholic faith. Of her he says in the Song of Songs: “My dove, my chosen one, is one to her mother” (Song VI).

She bore one son who is called “sojourner,” and another who is called “help of [Col. 0052D] God.” These names aptly correspond to the Christian people summoned from circumcision and uncircumcision. They are sojourners because, while dwelling in this world, they now journey away from their heavenly homeland; nevertheless, they will never lack God’s help.

Aaron is interpreted as “mountain of strength.” For this reason, taking the censer, he stood in the midst of the living and the slain to meet them, and, like a strong mountain, shut out the destruction of death.

Through his priesthood he [Col. 0053A] expressed the priesthood of Christ. Just as Aaron cleansed the people with the blood of sacrifices, so Christ washed away the sins of the world through the sacrifice of his blood.

Aaron’s severed staff also blossomed again and produced fruit. So the tree of Christ’s cross, through Christ’s Passion, produced for the whole world the evergreen vitality and fruit of perpetual life. It demonstrated that Christ’s priesthood would remain forever and would be beneficial to those who believe in him.

Mary, Aaron’s sister, prefigured the Synagogue.

Moses’ Ethiopian wife represented the Church from the Gentiles, joined to Christ. For this reason the Synagogue, reproaching Christ out of jealousy, was immediately covered with the contagion of leprosy.

Eleazar is interpreted as “my God is my help,” or “help of God.” He bears the figure of the holy [Col. 0053B] teachers, who assist the holy Church by word and example. One of them says: “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (I Cor. III).

Amalek, who is interpreted as “licking people,” or “licking with his army,” signifies the devil. He always desires the destruction of humanity and seeks through crafty schemes to deceive God’s people. Resisting God’s people when he encountered them, he is overcome by the sign of the cross.

Sihon, king of the Amorites, whose name is rendered in Latin as “temptation of the eyes,” likewise signifies the devil, who, by the lie of deception, transformed himself as though into an angel.

Og, king of Bashan, whose name is interpreted as “conclusion,” strives to close off, through the difficulty of vices, the way of our [Col. 0053C] faith, so that the passage to the promised kingdom of eternal life may not lie open to us.

The seventy elders, upon whom the Spirit of God fell, displayed the languages of the seventy generations spread throughout this world; from them many believers received the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Dathan and Abiram, and the others who separated themselves from Moses and Aaron and attempted to usurp the sacrifice, designate the wickedness of heretics and the destruction of those who divide themselves from Christ’s priests and from the fellowship of the Church and receive profane sacrifices.

Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “empty people,” and who, though falling, had open eyes, represented those who through faith possess knowledge of God but fall because their works have become darkened.

[Col. 0053D] Phinehas is interpreted as “sparing the mouth.” He pierced Zimri with a dagger together with the Midianite prostitute; that is, he appeased the Lord’s anger so that he might spare. For this Phinehas, who killed Zimri and the prostitute in their adulterous union in this manner, bore the figure of the holy teachers who, with the spiritual sword of God’s word, killed the Jews and heretics in the embrace of false doctrine and in the intercourse of sin.

Zimri is interpreted as “a star provoking” or “making bitter.” The name is properly formed from bitterness, because by sinning he made the people bitter.

The man who gathered wood on the Sabbath signifies the one whom the day of judgment finds in sin, so that he does not deserve to receive the rest of the eternal Sabbath.

[Col. 0054A] The twelve spies bore the figure of the scribes and Pharisees, who turned the Israelite people away so that they would not trust that they could attain the grace of the divine promise through Christ.

The two bearers who carried a cluster of grapes from the promised land on a wooden pole upon their shoulders expressed the significance of the two peoples. The first, the Jewish people, walking against Christ, turns its back; the second, the Christian people, looks upon and follows Christ, whom it carries behind itself.

Joshua, whose name is interpreted as “savior,” himself, as a figure of Christ, saved the people from the desert and brought them into the promised land.

This Jesus sent two spies to the city of Jericho, and they were received by the prostitute Rahab. That leader Jesus of the people showed the Lord Christ in himself [Col. 0054B] both by his name and by his deed.

Jericho, however, is the world. To it the Lord Christ sent the two Testaments to examine the conduct of human beings. For, in order to test more fully the faith of believers or the stubbornness of rebels, before the coming of his judgment he sent the Law and the Gospel like two spies.

Rahab, whose name is interpreted as “breadth,” or “hunger,” or “impetus,” bears the figure of the Church gathered from foreign and alien nations. Previously, while living in the desires of the flesh, she fornicated with idols. Concerning people like these the Lord said to the Jews that they would go before them into the kingdom of heaven.

This woman therefore receives the Lord’s Testaments alone and preserves them faithfully; she does not hand them over to enemies at all, being willing to endanger herself so long as she keeps them unharmed and safe [Col. 0054C]. She firmly believed that the world would fall, just as Rahab believed that the city would fall. For her own salvation and that of all her people she made a covenant with the Lord’s Testaments. In her house she placed scarlet, that is, the sign of blood. Whoever is found outside her will in no way escape the ruin of the age and the burning of the world.

Achan, who coveted what had been devoted to destruction at Jericho, signifies the wicked Christian who, after receiving the faith, desires worldly customs or the enticements of the world.

Caleb, whose name is interpreted as “like a heart,” or “dog,” signifies the Catholic teacher who is wise in heart and strong and vigorous in the practice of the virtues.

He asks Joshua to grant him the opportunity to engage in combat with the dialecticians of the world, with those who affirm falsehoods as truths, so that he may refute and overcome them and overthrow [Col. 0054D] everything they have built upon their false assertions.

Finally, when Jesus saw his eagerness, he blessed him, that is, because he asked for and heard such things.

But you also, if you wish to devote yourself to study, meditate wisely upon the law, and become stout-hearted in the law of God, can overthrow those magnificent and fortified cities—that is, the assertions of falsehood—so that you too may deserve to be blessed by Jesus and to receive Hebron.

Hebron is interpreted as “joining,” or “marriage.” This may perhaps be shown by the fact that Abraham the patriarch purchased a double cave there, in which the remains of the patriarchs lie: Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebekah, and Jacob with Leah.

Thus the prudent and wise [Col. 0055A] Caleb receives his inheritance in the memorials of the patriarchs. Jesus assigns him Hebron, the metropolitan city of the Anakim nations, and it has remained his possession to this day.

Othniel, whose name is interpreted as “his time is God,” or “answer of God,” signifies the rulers of churches and judges, to whom, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, judgment has been given not only concerning deeds but also concerning souls.

For it is written of Othniel: “And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war, and the Lord delivered Chusar Sathon the king into his hand.” Why was this? Because the Spirit of the Lord was in him, and his hand was strengthened against Chusar Sathon. And it says: “The land rested under that judge for forty years” (Judg. V).

You see how abundant is the divine mercy. The children of [Col. 0055B] Israel served for eight years because of the sins of many; because of the righteousness of one, they continued in peace for forty years.

Adonibezek, whose name is interpreted as “lord of lightning,” signifies the devil, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI). Yet all his power and authority are vanity.

The sons of Judah—that is, the sons of confession—and the sons of Simeon—that is, the sons of hearing—fight against him when all the faithful battle him with the shield of faith and the weapons of the virtues. They seize him and cut off the extremities of his hands and feet when they strive manfully to cut away the beginnings of evil action and corrupt example, so that the effectiveness of his wicked deceit may not find an opportunity for sudden deception, once his power to cause harm has been taken away through spiritual combat.

[Col. 0055C] Eglon, king of the Moabites, whose name is interpreted as “whirled about,” or “orbit,” bears the figure of the devil, who exhausts God’s people and, because of their sins, places them under servitude.

Ehud, the judge, whose name is interpreted as “glorious,” and who was ambidextrous and had a two-edged sword, killed him. Thus the Catholic teacher confines and destroys the devil, who whirls about in the arguments of philosophers, by evangelical and prophetic speech. He extinguishes every meaning of corrupt doctrine and crude understanding that exalts and raises itself against the spiritual knowledge of Christ.

The saving angels may also be signified in the figure of Othniel or Jacob, because, as we have often shown, we are attacked not only by hostile powers, but the divine and good powers are also sent by the Lord for our help.

The Lord also sends us his [Col. 0055D] heavenly power, by which we may be freed from the yoke of demonic servitude. May that power do everything for us with right and favorable power, and recall us from what leads to destruction to that true way, of which he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV)—Jesus Christ our Lord.

Shamgar, whose name is interpreted as “name of a sojourner,” or “there a settler,” and who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with a plowshare and defended Israel, signifies teachers from the nations who cultivate the Lord’s field. They do not always use the sword of strict judgment against their adversaries, but sometimes, through rustic and simple admonition, drive vices and sins from the souls of their hearers.

The number six, which, when multiplied [Col. 0056A], reaches six hundred, bears the figure of this world, which is said to have been completed in six days. Therefore he is said to have struck six hundred with a plow who, through Christ’s cross, has crucified the world.

Deborah, whose name is interpreted as “bee,” signifies the sweetness of prophecy and the sweetness of heavenly teaching.

She lived beneath a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah is interpreted as “lofty,” and Bethel as “house of God.” Prophecy has its seat beneath a palm tree, because “the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. XCI), namely between the heights and the house of God. For prophecy contains nothing base, nor does it teach us to seek what is upon earth, but what is in heaven and in the heights.

She first called Barak to herself; his name is interpreted as “flashing.” A flash has light, but not permanent [Col. 0056B] light; for it shines only for a short time and then ceases. Therefore Barak seems to me to bear the form of the former people, who were called first of all through prophecy and flashed with the splendor of the law, but did not remain.
