When Deborah—that is, prophecy—had said to Barak, that is, the former people: “The Lord God of Israel commands you: Go up to Mount Tabor, and take ten thousand men,” and the rest that is written (Judg. IV), let us hear what Barak answered prophecy in the person of the people:

“Unless you go up with me, I will not go up, because I do not know the day on which the Lord sent his angel with me.”

As an excuse this is true, but as a promise it is false. It is certain that they went up the mountain of God; but that they promised they would go [Col. 0056C] up with prophecy is false. For they did not follow prophecy so as to believe in him concerning whom all prophecy was written beforehand, namely Christ.

Therefore Deborah says to him: “I will go with you; nevertheless, know that your primacy will not be on the way on which you are going, but the Lord will deliver Sisera into the hand of a woman.”

She clearly shows that primacy will not remain with that people, nor will the palm of victory endure with it, but Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman named Jael.

Jael is also interpreted as “ascent,” and signifies the Church, through which one ascends into heaven. To her Sisera is delivered; his name is interpreted as “vision of a horse,” that is, the proud devil and instigator of carnal vices.

That Jael pierced Sisera’s temples with wood expressed the triumph of the Church, which killed the devil’s dominion with the standard [Col. 0056D] of the cross.

Gideon is interpreted as “the testing of their iniquity.” For he was instructed by frequent proofs, as though by an omen that he would achieve victory against his enemies; from this future testing he derived the etymology of his name.

This Gideon, who went to battle with three hundred men, bore the figure of Christ, who through the sign of the cross carried away victory from the world. For the number three hundred is contained in the letter Tau, which displays the form of the cross.

Abimelech is interpreted as “my father is king.” Gideon therefore seems to have borne the image of Christ; his seventy sons signified the seventy languages or nations, who through a second regeneration deserved to become sons of God.

Abimelech, the son of a slave woman, is understood to have borne the figure of Antichrist. Having gathered lost nations [Col. 0057A], he will wickedly usurp a kingdom for himself and slaughter all the saints by force, persecution, and every form of cruelty.

Jonathan, however, the younger one, was a figure of the saints. Just as Jonathan withdrew by flight while the other brothers were killed, so no one will be able to escape the persecution of Antichrist except the one who withdraws by flight and ascends the mountain of blessing.

This is the mountain which the saints will surround, and which holy Moses, as has already been said above, placed in the blessings in Deuteronomy.

Tola, whose name is interpreted as “worm,” or “scarlet,” signifies those who, kindled by the ardor of twofold love, rightly exercise leadership over the Christian people.

[Col. 0057B] Jair, whose name is interpreted as “illuminating,” signifies our Redeemer, who is leader and king of the Christian people. The names themselves aptly demonstrate this. Jair is interpreted as “illuminating,” and Gilead as “heap of testimony.”

Our Lord is rightly called “illuminating,” of whom it is written in the Gospel: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I); and to whom the Prophet says in the Psalms: “You illuminate wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV).

He is therefore from Gilead, because his knowledge is received from the sacred Scriptures; whoever seeks him there with a believing heart undoubtedly finds him.

Jephthah is interpreted as “opening,” or “it has been opened.” After his victory he sacrificed his daughter, displaying the figure of the Redeemer, who, departing from the presence of his brothers—that is, the Jews—received [Col. 0057C] primacy among the nations. He fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation as though bound by an oath, and, like a daughter, offered his own flesh to the Lord for the salvation of Israel.

We read that the Only-Begotten swore to the Father, as the Psalm says: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI), namely, that he would fulfill the sacrament of religion in the Passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race.

Samson is interpreted as “their sun,” or “strength of the sun.” He was renowned for his strength and delivered Israel from its enemies. He prefigured the death and victory of our Savior, either because he drew the nations from the jaws of the devil like a honeycomb from the mouth of the lion under command, or because after his death he gained many and, by dying, destroyed more than he did while alive.

[Col. 0057D] Delilah, whose name is interpreted as “little poor woman,” or “pitcher,” and who shaved Samson’s head, signifies the Synagogue, which crucified Christ at the place of Calvary.

Boaz, whose name is interpreted as “in strength,” or “in whom there is power,” expressed Christ, the true Bridegroom of the Church.

Ruth is interpreted as “hastening.” She was a foreigner from the Gentile people. Having left her homeland, she hastened to cross over into the land of Israel, saying to her mother-in-law: “Wherever you go, I will go” (Ruth I). This foreign woman, who married an Israelite man, displayed the Church coming to Christ.

Hannah is interpreted as “his grace.” Although she was first barren by nature, she was ultimately made fruitful by God’s grace. She, who was barren and afterward became fruitful, bears the figure of Christ’s Church, which was formerly barren among the nations but now flourishes throughout the whole earth with the offspring of innumerable fruitfulness.

[Col. 0058A] Eli is interpreted as “my God.” This rejected priest prefigured the rejection of the priesthood of the Old Testament. Although it had been established by God through Moses for its appointed time, it did not remain, because another and better priesthood was destined to come and remain forever—namely that of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom it is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Hophni, “unshod,” was the son of Eli and had been chosen for the service of the priesthood; his loss was expressed by his name. For the Apostle says: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. I). And the [Col. 0058B] Prophet says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace!” (Isa. LII).

He is therefore interpreted as “unshod,” so that by his name it might be signified that the priesthood of the Old Testament had been taken away from the former people.

Phinehas, after Hophni, is interpreted as “mute mouth”; by this the silence of the former priesthood and teaching is signified. These priests, then, who were killed when the ark was captured by the nations, signify that the succession of the former priesthood had been extinguished and that the covenant of the law had been transferred to the worship of the nations.

Samuel is interpreted as “his name is God.” After Eli had been rejected, Samuel succeeded him in the priestly ministry. He foretold the succession of the new priesthood after the old priesthood had been cast aside.

Jesse, whose name is interpreted as “sacrifice of the island,” or “incense” [Col. 0058C], signifies the former people, who, having been led across the Red Sea by Moses, offered sacrifice to God according to the law in the desert.

From him, according to the flesh, was born our David, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is King of kings and Lord of lords.

Saul is interpreted as “request.” For it is known that the Hebrew people requested him as their king and received him, not according to God but according to their own will. This king of the Jewish people indicates the rejection of that people, or the emulation of the same people, who attempted to destroy David—that is, Christ—by an unjust judgment.

David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” because he was exceedingly strong in battles, and also “desirable” in his [Col. 0058D] lineage, namely in the line from which the Prophet had foretold: “The Desired One will come to all the nations” (Hag. II).

He expressed the image of our Savior, either because he endured unjust persecution in the persecution of the Jews, or because, strong of hand, he overcame and bound the strong devil and distributed his spoils throughout the whole world.

Goliath designates the devil, whose pride Christ’s humility cast down.

Jonathan is interpreted as “gift of a dove.” He signifies those who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, receive the gift of true faith and devotion toward our David.

Uriah is interpreted as “my light is of God.” He signifies the devil, who by pretense transformed himself into an angel of light. The Church had previously been joined to him in marriage; afterward Christ desired her as she [Col. 0059A] washed herself, that is, purified herself from the stains of the world through the water of the washing.

Absalom is interpreted by antiphrasis as “peace of the father,” because he waged war against his father, or because David is read as having remained reconciled to his son in that war, to such an extent that he mourned his death with great grief.

He bears the figure of the Jews or of the traitor Judas, who raised sedition against the true David, envying him and plotting against his rule.

Solomon is said to have had three names. His first name was Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because there was peace during his reign. His second name was Jedidiah, because he was beloved and pleasing to the Lord. His third was Coeleth [Col. 0059B], which in Greek is called *ekklesiastes*, and in Latin “preacher,” because he spoke to the people.

These things therefore announce the figure of Christ, who built a house for the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem—not from wood and stones, but from holy people.

To hear his wisdom, the queen of Ethiopia came, that is, the Church from the nations. She came from the ends of the earth to our peaceful and beloved one, pleasing to the Lord, of whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III), in order to hear his wisdom.

After hearing him and seeing his services [Col. 0059C], she burst forth in his praise, saying: “Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants, who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, who was pleased with you and set you upon the throne of Israel; because the Lord loved Israel forever and appointed you king, so that you might execute judgment and justice,” and so forth (III Kings X).

Rehoboam is interpreted as “breadth of the people,” and this too by antiphrasis, because after ten tribes had separated from him, only two remained to him.

Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, and Jeroboam, his servant, under whom Israel was divided into two parts, designate that dissension which occurred at the Lord’s coming: one part, the believers from the Jews, reigns with Christ, who arose from the family of David; the other part followed Antichrist, to whose worship they have been bound through the error of an abominable servitude.

Alternatively, Rehoboam signifies wicked rulers in the Church, who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect to care for their subjects and delight [Col. 0059D] in the multitude of those who obey them, while nevertheless they do not show proper concern for those entrusted to them.

Jeroboam means “judgment,” or “the cause of the people,” or, as some say, “division,” because in his reign the people of Israel were divided and severed from the kingdom of David’s stock; for he was the cause of the people’s division. He signifies heretics, who love dissension, split the unity of the Catholic faith by their heresies, and thus, being obedient to them, give themselves over to the worship of evil spirits. Jeroboam is also interpreted as “judging the people.” For heretics appear to judge the people when they make them followers of their error.

Abijah, whose name means “the Lord is father,” or “the father was,” [Col. 0060A] represents the scribes and Pharisees, who seemed to rule the Jewish people but lost the fatherhood and dignity of their name. By their traditions they violated the Law. Thus, as the Hebrews assert, after capturing Bethel, Abijah preserved idols as a stumbling-block for Israel; and for this reason he was struck down by the Lord and died.

Asa, whose name means “taking away” or “lifting up,” at the beginning of his reign restored divine worship and did what was good and pleasing in the sight of the Lord. He overturned the altars of the idols and smashed their images (1 Kings 15). Thus he earned the Lord’s favor, so that when he fought against the Ethiopians he won a victory and slaughtered them to the point of annihilation. Since the Lord fought for him and aided his army, [Col. 0060B] they were crushed. But afterward, falling back into worse conduct, he sought the help of the Assyrians against Baasha, king of Israel, and gravely offended the Lord by seizing and imprisoning the prophet Hanani, whom the Lord had sent to rebuke him for this. Therefore, with God justly repaying him, he fell into an exceedingly severe illness and the most violent pain in his feet, and died of it. Even in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but, trusting rather in the art of physicians, was deceived.

He thus typologically represents those who begin with a good beginning but end with an evil conclusion. After renouncing idolatry and rejecting service to demons, having received the grace of baptism and the anointing of sacred chrism, they immediately undertake works of piety at the beginning of their lives. But in more vigorous age, and near [Col. 0060C] the end of this present life, when they ought to have devoted themselves to virtue, they relapse into vices and delight in wicked deeds.

Jehoshaphat, whose name means “God is judgment,” is therefore a king who represents the people of believers from the nations. Having abandoned the error of their ancestors, they came to our Redeemer; washed in holy baptism and anointed with sacred chrism, they received from Christ the Christian name and royal dignity. To them the apostle Peter says in his Epistle: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (1 Peter 2). The interpretation of his name confirms this well. According to some, Jehoshaphat is interpreted as “the Lord’s dowry,” or “one who has been endowed.”

The Church of the nations, therefore, purchased at the price of Christ’s blood, [Col. 0060D] and endowed with the pledge of the Holy Spirit, earned a share in the heavenly Bridegroom and fellowship in the kingdom. To her were given immeasurable riches, whether in the gathering of diverse nations to the faith or in the acquisition of various virtues, together with abundant glory of spiritual wisdom.

But Ahab the impious, who reigned in Samaria, represents heresiarchs, who lead a crowd of the lost astray through error and plunge them into the precipice of eternal death. The fact that Jehoshaphat was related to Ahab and went down to him in Samaria, offering him assistance against his enemies, figuratively demonstrates those who incline from the Catholics toward friendship with heretics. Although they do not depart from the path of right faith, [Col. 0061A] they nevertheless do not completely avoid association and communion with those who are in error. This can in no way be without guilt, especially since the apostle Paul says that a heretical person must be avoided after a first and second correction (Titus 3).

Joram, whose name means “who is exalted,” was born of the religious Jehoshaphat but declined into treachery and made the sons of Judah commit fornication, imitating the fornication of Ahab’s house. He can signify those who, instructed in the Catholic faith and regenerated through Christian baptism, were being formed by the Church’s sacraments; but, abandoning the truth of the faith, they follow the errors of heretics. They not only themselves deviate from the path of sound doctrine but also strive to lead others with them through the byways of error. Hence Elijah—that is, the prophetic word—rebukes them, [Col. 0061B] because every sanction of the divine books condemns such people and, with good reason, reproaches them through the gravest testimonies for their perversity.

Ahaziah, whose name means “grasping the Lord,” signifies the scribes and Pharisees, teachers of the old Law, who held Scripture but nevertheless did not keep the Lord’s Law. Therefore Jehu, whom the Lord sent through the prophet Elisha to eradicate Ahab’s house and kill the priests of Baal, struck Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, and caused the most impious queen Jezebel to be thrown down from the palace at Jezreel.

For Jehu may typologically designate the rule of the nations, which the Lord and our Redeemer ordained to exercise judgment in the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets himself, persecuted his [Col. 0061C] apostles, and to destroy it by a just vengeance. It would also overthrow the empty priesthood that it had vainly retained after Christ’s coming, overturn the temple, cast down from the height of royal power the impious synagogue that had always thirsted for the blood of the saints, and kill its rulers.

Athaliah, then, who sought to extinguish David’s seed and destroy the royal line, aptly expresses the impiety of the Synagogue. Through the wickedness of its mind, the Synagogue lay in wait for David’s seed—that is, Christ—and always harbored hatred against him, because it seemed at one time to reign while it observed the ceremonies of the Law for a limited time. Athaliah is interpreted as “the Lord’s temporality.”

But through the courage of Jehosheba, whose name means [Col. 0061D] “the Lord’s fullness”—that is, the Church, in which true delights are found—Joash was preserved. Joash means “the Lord’s memory,” namely Christ, in whom there is remembrance of the Lord’s name, lest through the *credulitas* (“credulity”; perhaps a corrupt reading) of the raging enemy he be slain in the hearts of the elect. Rather, he is nourished in the house of Jehoiada the high priest, whose name means “beloved of the Lord.” Concerning him the Father’s voice says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3).

His house is the holy Church, where, abiding in the faith of the elect, he daily brings about the growth of his body, until at the time of judgment he raises the scepter and power of the kingdom against those who were thinking of oppressing it, and consigns the murderess of the saints to eternal punishments.

[Col. 0062A] Amaziah, whose name means “taking away the people,” signifies wicked rulers who, through harmful error or their evil examples, remove God’s people from true religion and lead them into error and depraved conduct. Like Amaziah, they pretend in some matters to be good, but are not, because they do not have a perfect heart in the worship of God. Instead, always wavering and unstable, they prove to serve the devil rather than God.

Uzziah, whose name means “the Lord’s strength,” bore two names, since the one called Uzziah in Chronicles is named Azariah in the Book of Kings. Uzziah means “the Lord’s power,” and Azariah “the Lord’s help.” He is rightly called “the Lord’s power” or “the Lord’s help,” because, as long as he acted rightly and was assisted by divine aid, he successfully [Col. 0062B] fought many wars and triumphed everywhere over his enemies. But after he presumptuously attempted what was unlawful, he was struck with leprosy and at once darkened the dignity of his name and honor.

This king, whose forehead was covered with the contagion of leprosy as punishment for his crimes, indicates the kingdom of the Jews, who bear on their forehead the disgrace and stains of their faithlessness, where they refused to carry the sign of the cross.

Jotham, whose name means “completed” or “perfect,” followed the beautiful etymology of his name. For he did what was right in the sight of the Lord and built the high gate of the temple. According to the mystical sense, whom does this king Jotham, whose life and deeds are praised, better represent than our Redeemer? Concerning him the Psalmist says: “For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised, [Col. 0062C] and terrible above all gods” (Psalm 95).

His name itself expresses his perfection. For Jotham is interpreted as “completed” or “perfect.” Concerning the Lord and Savior, Paul writes to the Hebrews: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things he suffered, and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him” (Hebrews 5).

He himself built the high gate of the house of the Lord, because through him the entrance to the heavenly kingdom stands open to the faithful: “I am the door,” he says; “if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). This gate is rightly called high, because the Psalmist says of it: “The Lord is exalted above all nations; his glory is above the heavens” (Psalm 113).

The holy teachers are also called gates, because through their [Col. 0062D] preaching we learn the entrance to life. Heretics are likewise called the gates of hell, because, according to the Lord’s own testimony, they cannot prevail against the Church built upon the rock.

Ahaz means “grasping.” Accordingly, Ahaz, who was born of a righteous father but fell into treachery and the crime of idolatry, signifies heretics. Though instructed in the sacrament of faith by Catholic fathers, they turn toward apostasy and do not fear to offer divine worship to the images of their errors. They sacrifice the fruit of their womb—that is, the result of their evil meditation—to demons in the fire of zeal. For just as Ahaz, after stripping the house of the Lord and the houses of kings and princes, gave gifts to the king of Assyria, yet [Col. 0063A] gained nothing by it, so they melt the gold of keen intellect and the silver of eloquence into the worship of idols, so that they may perish.

They call upon Egypt and go to the Assyrians when they seek protection from the powers of this world. But in their passage they are captured and killed, because “cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17).

Hezekiah means “grasping the Lord,” or “the Lord’s strength.” He did not vigorously carry out God’s work only by himself and his own people; rather, through messengers he also summoned others to similar zeal. He represents the Lord and Savior, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and who is the head of every principality and power (Colossians 2), “the strong and mighty Lord in [Col. 0063B] battle” (Psalm 24).

He washed away with his blood the transgressions of the fathers and all the violations committed under the Law, and he fully restored the worship of piety in the Church. He sent his envoys to summon the nations to the faith: first the prophets, then the apostles. Through the preaching of his Gospel he brought very many people, not only from Judea but also from other nations, to the Catholic faith and true religion.

The fifteen years added to Hezekiah’s life for his good work signify all the saints, to whom the five books of Moses’ Law together with the ten words of the Decalogue were given for the pursuit of eternal life, so that through the completion of the Law and the commandments they might attain the fullness of the heavenly kingdom.

Manasseh, whose name means “forgetful”—for through [Col. 0063C] many crimes and sacrileges he had abandoned and forgotten God—is truly an example of those who repent and confess their sins in the Lord’s mercy. He teaches us that after committing crimes no one should despair of God’s mercy, but should rather, through fitting repentance, hope for forgiveness, provided that he completes it properly.

Amon means “faithful” or “honest.” This is more properly understood as having been said of him by antiphrasis, rather than according to the truth, for since he was an idolater, how could he have been faithful? He represents heretics, who, although they pretend to be good and worshipers of God, are nevertheless proved, by wandering and leading others into error, to serve the devil rather than God.

[Col. 0063D] King Josiah, whose name means “Where is the incense of the Lord?”—for this is the proper etymology of his name—offered to God the incense of sacred prayer and the sacrifice of good works. He burned the images made by earlier kings, celebrated the lawful Passover, and expelled many idols from the temple of the Lord.

In this he signifies Christ, who undertook his passion and, casting out all the detestable things of the nations from the temples of our bodies, crushed them by burning them in the fire of his power and threw them into the torrent of this age.

Jehoahaz, whose name means “held back,” signifies wicked rulers whom the people of the land—namely, carnal people devoted to earthly desire—choose according to their own ways as persons who agree with their [Col. 0064A] vices. Pharaoh bound them at Riblah and led them into Egypt, when the devil, weakening the hearts of prelates through a multitude of flatterers, deceives them. Riblah means “multitude”; thus he plunges them, bound in spiritual Egypt with the chains of sin, into the dark abyss.

Jehoiakim is the same as Eliakim. For Jehoiakim means “Where is the preparation?” and Eliakim “the resurrection of God.” He signifies pastors of the faithful who have been equipped and adorned with knowledge and exalted with power, but who are proved by these very gifts to serve the devil rather than God and to be subjected to various vices.

It must be understood that once someone has enslaved himself to any vice, he will be subject not to one but to many [Col. 0064B] masters. Thus Jehoiakim, whom Pharaoh had previously compelled to pay tribute to him, was now forced by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to serve him for three years.

What else, then, is it to be a servant of the king of Babylon than to be subjected to the ancient enemy by the pleasure and consent of his persuasion, and, in thought, word, and deed, to be wholly devoted to vices, as though freely possessed by him?

Jehoiakim, or Jeconiah, who was led into Babylon together with his mother and the treasure of the Lord’s temple, signifies the fall and ruin of the pastors and rulers of the Church. Deceived by the craft of the true Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—they are led into the confusion of errors and vices. Those who, through the Lord’s grace and good zeal, ought to have raised others to true religion by the word of teaching and good [Col. 0064C] examples are themselves slaughtered by various vices and swallowed up by the death of sins.

For this is what the name Jehoiakim signifies: “one who raises up,” or “one who rises.” Together with him, the Lord’s most precious vessels were carried away into captivity, because those who excelled at the height of power or shone with moral uprightness, corrupted by the examples of the wicked, passed together with them as booty to the devil.

Zedekiah, whose name means “the Lord’s righteous one.” The king of Babylon put out his eyes at Riblah. Riblah is translated into Latin as *multa haec*, “many things”; therefore it signified those who become entangled in the activity of this world’s wickedness and, taken captive by the devil, lose the eyes of understanding.

[Col. 0064D] Jeroboam, whose name means “judging the people,” separated the ten tribes from the house of David and from the temple of God and led them into idolatry. He signifies heretics, who love dissension, split the unity of the Catholic faith by their heresies, and thus, being obedient to them, give themselves over to the worship of evil spirits.

Ahab, whose name means “the father’s brother,” was an unjust king and had a wicked wife. He signifies the persecutors of Christians, and especially the Jewish people dwelling with the synagogue, who persecuted the prophets and saints of God sent to them to announce God’s will and teach the precepts of his Law. From this people Christ also deigned to assume flesh.

Ahab therefore coveted the vineyard of Naboth, [Col. 0065A] whose name means “clear” or “confession.” Naboth was a Jezreelite—that is, one of “God’s honor” or “God’s seed,” namely our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, whose vineyard is the Israelite people. Isaiah says of it: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5).

Ahab wanted to make it into a garden of vegetables—that is, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to have germinated, he wanted to transplant fragile doctrines through Pharisaic superstition. When Naboth refused to give him the vineyard—that is, when Christ refused to consent to the superstitions of the Pharisees—the impious wife Jezebel, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, plotted his death.

Jezebel means “one who dwells with” or “empty flow,” which aptly suits the synagogue. It seemed to dwell in the house of the Lord, but through various desires it flowed away into vanity.

Jezebel therefore sent [Col. 0065B] letters to the elders and nobles who were in the city, so that, after false witnesses had been introduced, they might give false testimony against Naboth, claiming that he had “blessed” God and the king. Then they led him outside the city and stoned him to death. In this way the synagogue, through the high priests, scribes, and Pharisees, plotted Christ’s death.

This Ahab, therefore, despising the true prophets of God, listened to false prophets and, thus deceived by the devil, perished by the sword of the enemy. So also the Jewish people, despising the teachers of the Gospel and following the forerunners of Antichrist, as well as the very head of the wicked, will fall into eternal death.

Ahaziah, whose name means “grasping God,” was Ahab’s son. He persecuted God’s prophets, and especially Elijah. He signifies the Jewish people, and especially [Col. 0065C] the rulers of the synagogue, who, devoted to sins and vices, rejected the truth from themselves and indeed persecuted it.

Thus we read in the Gospel that the rulers and Pharisees sent officers to seize Jesus. The house of Ahaziah, therefore, is the synagogue of the Jews, surrounded on every side by the legal commandments as by the latticework of an upper chamber. But just as Ahaziah fell through the latticework by which he ought to have been protected and suffered a serious illness, so the Jewish people, exceeding the guardianship of the Law, fell into the incurable sickness of sins. Because they abandoned divine assistance there, they did not deserve to find remedies for salvation.

Nebuchadnezzar, whose name means “the prophecy of a narrow flask,” or “prophesying such a sign”—on account of the dream [Col. 0065D] of future events that he is said to have seen and that Daniel interpreted—or “a sitting in the recognition of distress,” on account of those whom he led into captivity—represents the devil. He conquered the people of the heretics through the captivity of error and led them from Jerusalem, that is, from the Church, into Babylon, that is, the confusion of ignorance.

The chief of the cooks, who overthrew the walls of Jerusalem, signifies this: all who serve the desire of the belly destroy the virtues of the soul.

Jesus the high priest represented Christ. Through him it is shown that we have returned from the exile of this world to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Among the Hebrews, Zerubbabel is said to be composed of three complete names: *Zo*, “this one”; *ro*, “teacher”; [Col. 0066A] and *babel*, which properly corresponds to Babylon. Thus the name Zerubbabel means “this teacher from Babylon.” He was born in Babylon, where he became prince of the Jewish people.

Judith means “praising” or “confessing.”

Esther means “hidden.” These women also, who bear the figure of the Church, punish the enemies of the faith and rescue the people from destruction.

Susanna means “lilies” or “her grace.” She prefigured the Church, which the Jews falsely accuse as though she were an adulteress.

Tobias bears the image of the ancient Law. The Jewish sparrows blind his eyes while they wrongly understand and obscure the sacrament of light.

Tobias his son bore the image of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0066B] who illuminates with the brightness of his power what was a hidden and blinded figure, darkened by the obscurity of the Law.

The seven Maccabees, who endured the most bitter tortures under Antiochus and were crowned most gloriously, signify the sevenfold Church. From the enemies of Christ she suffered a great slaughter of martyrs and received the crown of heavenly glory.

## CHAPTER II. On the Prophets

Those whom the pagans call *vates*, our people call prophets, as though they were *praefatores*, “foretellers,” because they speak beforehand and truly announce future events. Those whom we call prophets were called “seers” in the Old Testament, [Col. 0066C] because they saw what others did not see and perceived beforehand what was hidden in the mystery. Hence it is written concerning Samuel: “Let us go to the seer” (1 Samuel 9). Hence Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isaiah 6). The heavens were opened to Ezekiel, and he saw visions of God.

The etymologies of the names of certain prophets should be noted. Their names clearly show what they had foretold in their future deeds and words.

Elijah means “the Lord God.” He was so named as a foreshadowing of the future. For when he contended in sacrifice with the four hundred priests of Baal, he invoked the Lord’s name, and fire descended from heaven upon the burnt offering. When all the people saw this, they fell [Col. 0066D] on their faces and said: “The Lord himself is God” (1 Kings 18). For this reason he first received such a name, because through him the people later came to know the Lord God.

The same name is also interpreted as “the strong Lord,” either because he killed those same priests or because he endured Ahab’s hostility. He demonstrates Christ, because just as Elijah was carried upward into heaven by a fiery chariot, so Christ took his flesh—the flesh in which he was born, suffered, and rose again—into heaven.

The widow to whom Elijah was sent to be fed is the Church, to which Christ is read to have come through faith. Her flour—or flour and oil—was blessed and did not run out: this is the grace of Christ’s body and the anointing of chrism, [Col. 0067A] which is supplied daily throughout the whole world and is never diminished.

The seven thousand men of whom the Lord said to Elijah that they had not bent the knee before Baal signify the number of saints who, filled with the sevenfold Spirit of grace, renounced the devil.

Elisha means “the Lord’s salvation.” He too received his name as a foreshadowing of the future. Indeed, he performed many miracles and, driving away famine, saved the people from death. He figured the same Lord and Redeemer, who, descending from the height of the mountain—that is, from the sublimity of heaven—humbled himself from the form of God to the form of a human being, joined his limbs to dead members, and applied the medicine of his body to our mortality.

[Col. 0067B] The boys who mocked Elisha, crying, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead!” (2 Kings 2), and who were attacked and killed by wild beasts, indicate the Jewish people. In childish folly they mocked Christ crucified at the place of Calvary, and, seized by two bears—that is, Titus and Vespasian—they perished.

Elisha’s servant, who was sent with a staff to raise the woman’s son, displays the type of the ancient Law. Transmitted to the human race, it accomplished nothing except to show, in the rod, the austerity of servitude alone. The dead son of the Shunammite represents the human race. Over him Christ, as though yawning, spiritually breathes the Spirit of sevenfold grace, through which the sinner may revive from death.

Naaman the Syrian signifies the people gathered from the nations, [Col. 0067C] polluted by the stains of sins and purified by Christ through the sacraments of baptism.

Isaiah means “the Lord’s salvation,” and rightly so. More than the others he proclaims the Savior of all nations and his sacraments. He also expressed the form of the evangelists and apostles, who proclaimed all Christ’s sacraments not as through a figure but as though they were present.

Jeremiah means “the Lord’s exalted one,” because it was said to him: “I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms” (Jeremiah 1). In his word and sufferings he figured the death and passion of the Lord Savior.

Ezekiel means “the strength of God.” He too bore the image of Christ, who urges the people placed in this earthly [Col. 0067D] exile onward through saving commandments.

Daniel means “the judgment of God.” This is so either because, in the judgment of the elders, he delivered the sentence of divine examination when he discovered their falsehood and rescued Susanna from destruction, or because, discerning with an acute mind the visions and dreams in which future events were shown through individual riddles, he disclosed them (Daniel 9).

He was called “a man of desires” because he did not eat the bread of desire and did not drink the wine of lust. By maintaining a celibate life, he also displayed the likeness of the continence of those who live in holy leisure and do not misuse the earthly abundance of possessions.

Hosea means “savior” or “one who saves.” When he prophesied God’s anger against the people of Israel because of the crime of idolatry, [Col. 0068A] he foretold salvation for the house of Judah. For this reason King Hezekiah of Judah is shown to have removed the idols that earlier kings had consecrated and to have cleansed and purified the temple of the Lord.

He demonstrated the figure of Christ, who took the Church from the fornication of the nations into his own body.

Joel means “the Lord God,” or “beginning with God,” or “was of God.” This is what his name’s uncertain etymology seems to express. He typologically indicates those who, through the door of faith, begin to know the mystery of divine knowledge.

Amos means “a people torn away.” His prophecy was directed to the people of Israel, who had already been torn away from the Lord and served golden calves, or who had been torn away from the kingdom of David’s line.

He is therefore a shepherd and farmer [Col. 0068B] who is a type of Christ. Transferred from the pastoral care of animals—that is, from the rule of the Hebrews—he now feeds other flocks among the nations.

Obadiah means “servant of the Lord.” Just as Moses was the Lord’s servant and the Apostle the servant of Christ, so this man, sent as an envoy to the nations, sees and proclaims things worthy of prophetic ministry and service. Hence he is called “the servant of the Lord.”

In Samaria he fed one hundred prophets, and he signifies all preachers of the faith who, in this world, refresh all believers with the nourishment of the holy Scriptures.

Jonah means “dove,” or “one who grieves.” “Dove” refers to his lament, since he was in the whale’s belly for three days. “Grieving” refers either to the sorrow he felt over the salvation of the Ninevites or to the ivy that suddenly [Col. 0068C] withered, whose shade had protected him from the sun’s heat.

He is the son of Amittai, the same person as the son of the widow of Zarephath, according to the Jews. Elijah raised him, and afterward his mother said to him: “Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of truth is in your mouth” (1 Kings 17). For this reason the boy was called Amittai. *Amittai* means “truth” when translated from Hebrew into Latin, and because Elijah spoke truth, the one who was raised was called the son of truth.

Jonah, both by his speech and by his shipwreck, figures Christ’s passion, death, and resurrection: either because he was thrown from the ship into the sea as though from the cross onto the earth, or because he was received into the whale’s belly, as though into an earthly tomb, and was enclosed there for three days and three [Col. 0068D] nights. He also foretold, through the figure of Nineveh, the repentance of the world.

In what follows he represents the Jews, who not only did not wish the salvation of the nations to come, but hated it when it came. Nineveh represents the nations, while Jonah stands for the Jews. Just as the salvation of the Ninevites provoked Jonah to jealousy, so the redemption of the nations became a stumbling-block to the Jews.

He is rightly also read to have sat east of the city beneath the shade of the ivy (Jonah 4). Thus that same people, separating itself from the salvation of the Church and wasting away in grief, sitting beneath the shadow of the Law, strives to move its tongue against Christ, who is the East. That shadow was withered by a worm, because, when Christ came, the old things passed away: “and behold, [Col. 0069A] all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5).

He prophesied under Uzziah, king of Judah, when Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah also prophesied.

Micah, whose name means “Who is this?” or “Who is that?” or “humility,” signifies the one who says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11), and concerning whom the Prophet said: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

To him the word of God came, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Through his dispensation, first the prophets and afterward the apostles were sent to preach the word of God.

As far as the historical sense is concerned, according to the order of the captivity—since Samaria, the metropolis of Israel, was captured first, and afterward Jerusalem, the city of Judah—the title of the prophecy is placed first [Col. 0069B] concerning Samaria and second concerning Jerusalem.

As far as mystical meanings are concerned, since Samaria is always understood as heresies and Jerusalem as a type of the Church, we say that the word of the Lord came to the humble coheir of Christ from the Church’s various doctrines, because perhaps he had committed a sin and woven together the volume of the entire order.

Nahum means “germ” or “consoler.” He rebukes the city of bloodshed and, after its overthrow, consoles Zion, saying: “Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace” (Nahum 1).

He also bears the type of the holy preachers who rebuke and convict the city of bloodshed—that is, spiritual Babylon—demanding from it the germ of faith and good works. If they repent of [Col. 0069C] their sins, they promise them the consolation of forgiveness.

Habakkuk means “embracing.” Either because he was beloved of the Lord he is called “embrace,” or because, in contending with God, he assumed the name of one who embraces—that is, one who wrestles. No one else dared with so bold a voice to challenge God to a dispute about justice, asking why such great injustice of events occurs in human affairs and in this world.

He signifies the faithful people who, raised upon high places, contemplate the Lord on the cross, saying: “Horns are in his hands; there his glorious strength has been established” (Habakkuk 3).

Zephaniah means “the Lord’s mirror” or “the Lord’s secret,” both of which are appropriate to the prophets. They know the mysteries of God. Hence it is said to Ezekiel: [Col. 0069D] “I have appointed you as a watchman” (Ezekiel 3). And elsewhere: “The Lord does nothing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3).

He signifies those who, through the secret of contemplation, advance toward an increase of merits.

Haggai is rendered in Latin as “festive,” and its sound is joyful. He prophesies that the destroyed temple will be rebuilt and announces the joy of return after the mourning of captivity.

Zechariah means “the Lord’s memory.” When the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation had been completed, the Lord remembered his people through Zechariah’s preaching. At Cyrus’s command the people of God returned, and the city and temple were rebuilt.

These two prophets [Col. 0070A] bore the figure of the saints who, amid the life of our pilgrimage, sing beforehand the future time of liberation.

Malachi means “the angel of the Lord,” that is, “messenger.” Whatever he spoke was believed as though it had been commanded by the Lord; for this reason the Seventy translated his name in this way, saying: “The burden of the word of the Lord over Israel by the hand of his angel.”

He bore the type of our Savior, who is called “the angel of the great counsel.”

Ezra means “helper.”

Nehemiah means “consoler from the Lord.” These names were received through a certain foreshadowing of future events. For they became a help and consolation to all that people returning to their homeland. They rebuilt the Lord’s [Col. 0070B] temple and restored the work of the walls and towers.

They therefore bear the type of the apostles and preachers of Christ’s Gospel. After the faithful had departed from the Babylon of this world and returned to the promised land, these men daily rebuild God’s spiritual structure through words and examples. What had previously collapsed through the negligence or sloth of its former inhabitants, they recover through persistent effort and complete zeal, together with their devoted fellow workers.

Hananiah means “the grace of God.” He is also called Shadrach in the Chaldean language, a name interpreted as “my beauty.”

Azariah means “the Lord’s help.” He is also called Abednego, which is translated into Latin as “I serve in silence.”

Mishael means “who is the people of the Lord?” He is also called Meshach, [Col. 0070C] which means “laughter” or “joy.” These three boys bore the figure of the saints who offered their bodies in persecution.

Asaph means “synagogue,” signifying the congregation that believed, not the one that remained obstinate. For after the Lord’s resurrection we read that many thousands of Jews confessed the faith, as the Acts of the Apostles testify among other things.

Ethan means “strong.” This Ethan, like Heman, was one of King David’s singers, as the Books of Days [Chronicles] relate: namely, the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, from the congregation of Merari, son of Levi. Alternatively, he belonged to those wise men whose wisdom is ranked below Solomon’s in the Book of Kings: “He was wiser,” it says, “than Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman” (1 Kings 4).

This song, therefore, possesses such great [Col. 0070D] knowledge that it deserved to be inscribed under the name of that most wise man.

Eman was the son of Johel, son of Samuel, of the family of Caath, son of Levi, one of the singers whom David appointed over the others for singing when the Ark was brought up. Eman is interpreted as “his brother.” By this name the Lord Christ calls those who are devoted to his commands and works, as he says in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. XII). Israelites means “those who see God”; this is plainly what happens to those who, through the ministry of obedience, are radiant with the holy light of the Lord.

Idithun is interpreted as “one leaping over them,” signifying one who in mind transcends earthly things and leaps over those who, clinging to the ground and bent toward the earth, think of what is below, while he dwells in the heights of the mind and philosophizes in free song about the power of God. [Col. 0071A]

The sons of Chore, like Eman, Echan, Asaph, and Idithun, were not psalm-writers but singers, chosen by David for psalmody; yet, because of the significance of their names, they were appropriately attached to the titles of the psalms.

Chore, therefore, means “calvary” or “skull.” In the place designated by this name the Lord was crucified; and therefore the sons of Chore are rightly so called, since they devote themselves wholly to serving the sacrament of his Passion.

Zacharias is interpreted as “memory of the Lord,” because he sings of remembering the Lord’s holy covenant.

John the Baptist is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord,” because he is the boundary of prophecy, the herald of grace, or the beginning of baptism, through which grace is administered. [Col. 0071B] These are the prophets of the Old and the New Testament, whose end is Christ, to whom the Father says: “I have appointed you as a prophet among the nations” (Isa. LX).

## How many kinds of prophecy are there?

There are seven kinds of prophecy. The first kind is ecstasy, that is, an excess or rapture of the mind; for example, Peter is seen in a state of mental astonishment when the vessel was lowered to him (Acts X).

The second kind is vision; as it is read in Isaiah: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne with various living creatures” (Isa. VI).

The third kind is a dream; for example, Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder supported in heaven (Gen. XXVIII).

The fourth kind is through clouds; as God speaks to Moses and to Job after the plague. [Col. 0071C]

The fifth kind is a voice from heaven; as it sounded to Abraham, saying: “Do not lay your hand upon the boy” [Col. 0072A] (Gen. XXII), and to Saul on the road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

The sixth kind is a received parable; as in Solomon’s Proverbs, and in the case of Balaam when he was summoned to Balak (Num. XXII).

The seventh kind is the filling of the Holy Spirit; as occurs in nearly all the prophets.

Others have said that there are three kinds of visions. One is according to the eyes of the body; for example, Abraham saw three men beneath the oak of Mamre; Moses saw fire in the bush; and the disciples saw the transfigured Lord on the mountain between Moses and Elijah; and other instances of this kind. Another is according to the spirit, by which we imagine the things that we perceive through the body; for example, Peter saw that disk lowered from heaven with various living creatures, and Isaiah saw the Lord on the highest throne—not bodily, but spiritually. For no bodily form encloses or limits God; but just as many things are spoken figuratively rather than literally, so also many things are shown figuratively. The third kind of vision is neither through bodily senses nor through any part of the soul by which images of things are grasped in a bodily manner, but through the mind’s inner vision, by which understood truth is perceived; for example, Daniel, endowed with understanding, saw what Belshazzar had seen bodily. Without this kind, the other two are either fruitless or even lead into error. [Col. 0072B]

Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit governs all these kinds. Not only a good person but also an evil person can possess prophecy. For we find that King Saul prophesied. He was pursuing holy David, and, filled with the spirit, began to prophesy. [Col. 0072C]

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0071]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the persons who pertain to the New Testament

[Col. 0071C]

First of all, it must be noted that the four Evangelists figuratively express our Lord Jesus Christ under the forms of four living creatures. Matthew, announcing the same Redeemer as born and suffering, compares him to the likeness of a human being. [Col. 0071D] Mark, beginning in the wilderness, assumes the figure of a lion and proclaims Christ’s unconquered kingdom and power. Luke likewise, through the mystical face of a calf, preaches Christ as destined to be sacrificed for us. John, however, through the figure of an eagle, shows the same Christ, after the resurrection of his flesh, to have flown back into heaven.

These four Evangelists—or, rather, the four Gospels that they wrote—were expressed figuratively by the four rivers of Paradise flowing from one spring and watering the whole surface of the earth. Similarly, the four living creatures mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel in his book, when he says, “There were four faces belonging to one, and four wings belonging to one, and the hands of a human being under their wings” (Ezek. I), represented the same figures by their fourfold significance. So too the four wheels, of which the same prophet relates that they were beside the living creatures, moved in four directions, and did not turn back when they moved, bear the same significance. Likewise, the four faces, of which it is written that one was the face of a cherub, another the face of a human being, the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle, indicate the same thing.

There are also four regions of the world, and the four changes of the seasons provide human beings with the annual fruits. In the same way, the holy Church of Christ, spread throughout the four regions of the world, is nourished and strengthened by evangelical teaching throughout the whole duration of this age. Therefore the holy teachers, who illuminate the entire world through the four Gospels, especially commend to us four virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—so that, living according to them, we may offer service pleasing to God.

Likewise, the Gospel says that four thousand were fed by the Lord with seven loaves; and a paralytic is brought to Christ for healing by four men. Apart from these examples, in many other places of Holy Scripture the number four intimates this same figure to us, and it would be superfluous to recount all of them here. [Col. 0072D]

[Col. 0073A] The apostles as a whole also bear the type of the entire Church, because they received the same power of forgiving sins. They possess the form of the patriarchs, since through the word of preaching they spiritually begot the people of God throughout the whole world.

Accordingly, we must consider the mystical number of the twelve apostles, and the figures by which it is marked out in sacred Scripture. Just as God the Father, through his only-begotten Son and in the power of the Holy Spirit, completed the first creation of the world through six days of work, so also, by doubling that same number six—whence twelve results—the Lord Jesus Christ renewed the lost and almost destroyed world through his twelve apostles.

And just as, through the twelve months in the circuit of the year, the fruits of the world are renewed by the generosity of almighty God for the use of the human race through varying conditions, [Col. 0073B] so through the teaching of the twelve apostles the human race faithfully began to bring forth the fruit of good works for God. This is the true Mazaroth, that is, the “sign-bearer,” through whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, illuminates the whole world at all times.

And just as the day turns through twelve hours from sunrise to sunset, so Christ, the true day, enlightens his faithful through his twelve apostles toward the beginning of right conduct, which is understood by the rising of the sun. Whoever perseveres in it until sunset—that is, until the end of life—will be saved forever.

And just as Jacob, whose name means “supplanter,” begot twelve sons to possess the promised land, so Christ, who supplanted the devil, chose twelve apostles and entrusted to them the promised land—that is, the blessing of the heavenly kingdom—and gave them power to tread upon scorpions and serpents and upon every power of the enemy. [Col. 0073C]

Likewise, just as Moses measured out the camp on every side, that is, toward the east and west, north and south, through the twelve tribes around the tabernacle of God, so Christ, through the twelve apostles, announcing the fourfold Gospel throughout the four regions of the world, invited all who believe in him to the eternal tabernacles, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI), and I will receive you into the tabernacles of eternal life.

And just as there were twelve springs at Celim, where the people, exhausted and exceedingly thirsty, drank their fill, so through the twelve apostles the entire multitude of the faithful is given drink from the teaching of the sacred faith and is called by holy preaching to the joys of eternal life. [Col. 0073D]

Joshua, too, who expressed the figure of Christ both in name and in deed, sent twelve spies to explore the promised land, which God had promised to give to Abraham, his beloved, and to his offspring. So Christ sent twelve apostles among the multitude of all nations to evangelize the kingdom of God, as the Psalmist says of them: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Twelve men from the twelve tribes of Israel crossed the Jordan on dry feet and, lifting twelve stones, set them up there as a sign and an everlasting testimony for their descendants. These men bore the figure of the twelve apostles, who fixed the trophies of their office in holy baptism and left to believers the distinguishing marks of their preaching. [Col. 0074A]

These twelve men alone were sent to preach an everlasting testimony—that is, the Gospel of the kingdom of God—to all the nations throughout the world. They have also been sent in the holy Church as a testimony to all believers, because whoever wishes to reach the joys of eternal life must necessarily follow their preaching and teaching in all things. Their successors now in the holy Church are all preachers of the truth, announcing and preaching the word of eternal salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord.

For King Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” placed the bronze sea—that is, a basin—upon twelve bronze oxen before the Temple, [Col. 0074B] where the priests and ministers of the altar washed their hands when they entered the sanctuary of the Lord. In the same way, Christ placed the bronze sea—that is, confession of the true faith, or confession of sin, or the teaching of Holy Scripture—upon the shoulders of the twelve apostles. Through their teaching, all faithful people who have been imbued with it are cleansed from every defilement by confession of the true faith and repentance for their sins, and are made worthy to enter the eternal sanctuaries of their Lord and possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

There were also twelve holy gates in the city of Jerusalem, through which all who remained in it and all who came into it entered and departed. These expressed the figure of the twelve apostles, who are truly the gates of spiritual Jerusalem. Through their preaching and teaching, the gates of the heavenly kingdom have been opened to all who come from every direction into the holy Church. They have also been given, together with their successors in the Church, the power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, so that those whom they bind on earth through guilt may be bound in eternal torments, while those whom they loose as they confess and repent of their sins may be loosed in heaven. Having received the remission of all sins here, and aided by their prayers through the grace of God, may they deserve to reach the joys of eternal blessedness.

This much has now been said generally about the apostles of Christ; it is sufficient for the present. What their names signify specifically we shall say shortly in what follows. [Col. 0074C]

The seventy-two disciples signify the illumination of the whole world through the Gospel of the Trinity; for the entire world is completed in twenty-four hours. This number, tripled on account of the same Trinity, becomes seventy-two. They are sent in pairs because they are to preach the love of God and of neighbor, or because of the mystery of the two Testaments. [Col. 0074D]

Zacharias, as stated above, is interpreted as “memory of the Lord.”

Elisabeth is interpreted as “the fullness of my God” or “the oath of my God.” Elisabeth bears the type of the Old Law or of prophecy, just as her husband Zacharias represents the priesthood of the Old Law. Thus, just as the mute Zacharias announced the name of John by writing it; just as the ancient priesthood expressed, under a type, the priesthood of Christ and the grace of the New Testament; and just as Elisabeth, hearing Mary’s greeting, when the infant leaped in her womb, filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed the mother of the Lord blessed and fortunate: so the spirit rejoiced in the letter at the coming Christ, and the entire sequence of the Old Testament, pregnant with the Holy Spirit, heralded to the whole world the blessed and saving incarnation of the Savior. [Col. 0075A]

John bore the form of the Law, which announced Christ and proclaimed the remission of sins through the grace of the washing.

Joseph the betrothed, who was the guardian of her virginity, signifies Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, whose virginity is preserved by him in true faith from that time to the end.

Maria is interpreted as “illuminatrix,” or “star of the sea.” For she bore the light of the world. In the Syriac language Maria is called “Lady”; and fittingly so, because she bore the Lord of heaven and earth and of every creature. Mystically, however, she bears the figure and appearance of the Church, which, although betrothed to Christ, remains a virgin. [Col. 0075B]

The Magi prefigured the peoples of the nations, who would come to know the light of faith. Through the number of the gifts they indicated that Christ is God through frankincense, a suffering human being through myrrh, and the king of all ages through gold.

Herod, who inflicted death upon the infants, expressed the figure of the devil; or of the nations, which, desiring to extinguish the name of Christ from the world, raged to the death of the martyrs.

The mute who are healed in the Gospel signify those who confess the faith of Christ.

The blind signify those who did not understand the faith that they believed. [Col. 0075C]

The deaf signify those who do not obey the commands of God. The lame are those who do not walk rightly on the path of God’s commandments and neglect to fulfill the commands that bring salvation.

The prudent man who built his house upon a rock signifies the faithful teacher who places the foundation of his teaching and life in Christ. But the one who built his house upon sand represents the doctrines of heretics, who build in such a way as to produce a great ruin.

The leper whom Christ first healed when he came down from the mountain indicates the human race stained by the contagion of sins. When the Redeemer descended from the height of heaven, as from a mountain, he cleansed it from the varied worship of demons and restored it to the unity of faith. [Col. 0075D]

The centurion signifies the faith of the nations. The servant and the daughter of the Canaanite woman, whom Christ saves without coming to them, likewise reveal those nations whom the Lord did not visit in bodily presence but saved through faith in the word. The Canaanite woman herself bore the figure of the Church from the nations, which, like a dog, seeks crumbs from the table of the masters—that is, to be filled with the teachings of the apostles and prophets.

Peter’s mother-in-law, burning with fever, signifies the synagogue kindled by the heat of carnal desires. Her daughter is that part of the believers which was entrusted to Peter to govern.

The rejected scribe, who followed the Lord for the sake of profit, signifies those who desire the faith of Christ not for the Lord’s sake but for worldly gain. [Col. 0076A]

The demoniac whom the Lord healed from the legion in the region of the Gerasenes signifies the gentile people subject to the worship of many demons.

The swineherds who fled and reported in the city what had happened signify the rulers of the impious. Although they flee from the faith of Christ, they nevertheless marvel at and proclaim his powers in astonishment.

The paralytic lying on a bed is a soul whose life has become disordered in its body. When it has been healed by the grace of Christ through the remission of sins, it immediately rises after recovering its former strength and carries the bed of its flesh, on which it had lain weak, back to the house of the virtues, so that it may confine itself within the secrets of its conscience and no longer run about in exterior pleasures in a dissolute manner. [Col. 0076B]

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom the Lord was going to heal, was preceded—before he came to her—by the woman who suffered from a flow of blood and touched him from behind and was healed. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue bore the type of Judea; the woman who suffered from the flow of blood bore the figure of the Church from the nations. When this Church believed after Christ’s preaching, Passion, and Ascension, it touched the Lord, as it were, from behind, and was found worthy to receive salvation before the synagogue.

The two blind men sitting beside the road signify both peoples, Jews and nations, drawing near to Christ through faith. He said: “I am the way” (John XIV). [Col. 0076C]

The blind and mute man possessed by a demon, who is recorded as having been healed by the Savior, indicates those who are converted from the idolatry of the nations to faith in the Lord. When the worship of demons has been driven from their hearts and they have received the former light of faith, their tongue is afterward released for praising the Lord, so that they may confess him whom previously they denied.

The man with a withered hand signifies a soul unfruitful in works of mercy. When he is told, “Stretch out your hand” (Luke VI), he is admonished always to extend alms to the poor.

The man from whom the unclean spirit went out and then occupied him again signifies a repentant man, whose mind, through subsequent negligence, is more fiercely occupied by carnal pleasure, together with seven spirits of vices: anger, envy, gluttony, vainglory, and pride. [Col. 0076D]

The householder bringing forth new and old things from his treasure is Christ, bringing forth from his impenetrable knowledge the two Testaments: the Old, in which earthly happiness is promised, and the New, through which the kingdom of heaven is hoped for.

The man who sowed a mustard seed in his field is Christ, who sowed faith in the world, in which the birds of heaven—that is, spiritual souls—rest.

The woman who hid leaven in three measures signifies the knowledge of spiritual teaching fervent with love of the Trinity. [Col. 0077A]

The man who found a hidden treasure in a field is the one who, having sold everything in this world, acquires Christ and eternal life.

The five thousand men who were fed with five loaves and two fish are the ecclesiastical peoples, who are refreshed by Christ through the five bodily senses with the nourishment of spiritual law, and are filled by the two Testaments, as though by twin fish.

The four thousand men who are fed with the other seven loaves are the same Church of the nations, which is spread through the four regions of the world and restored by the abundance of the sevenfold grace.

The one who repeatedly fell now into fire and now into water signifies the world. Fire demonstrates anger that inflames, while water demonstrates carnal pleasure; seized by these, the world is continually hurled downward by daily falling. [Col. 0077B]

Moses and Elijah, who appeared with the Lord on the mountain, are understood as the Law and the Prophets, through whose voices the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and glory are declared.

The man who had a hundred sheep, and who, leaving them, seeks the lost sheep and, having found it, carries it back on his shoulders, expressed the figure of Christ. Leaving the ninety-nine ranks of angels in heaven, he found among the nations the sheep that had perished in Adam, as the good shepherd, and carried it back to Paradise on the shoulders of his cross. [Col. 0077C]

The woman who found the lost drachma is the Church. When she finds the soul dragged away by the devil’s snares through repentance, she produces joy for both angels and human beings.

The debtor of ten talents signifies people who are liable to God through transgressing the ten commandments. But just as sins are forgiven us when we ask the Lord, so each of us must forgive following the Lord’s example, lest, by refusing to forgive the small debts of those who sin against us, we be compelled to pay our greater debts with the interest of punishments.

The rich man who is compared to a camel indicates the person of the Jews, who glory in the power of the Law. Because they worship it for earthly reasons, they do not possess the kingdom of heaven. There the people of the nations, twisted by crimes and weighed down by the burdens of sins, enter more easily, as through the eye of a needle, through the narrowness of sufferings and labors. [Col. 0077D]

The householder who hired workers for his vineyard and promised them the payment of a denarius is Christ, who calls everyone to the worship of faith and promises them the reward of perfect blessedness.

The workers hired at the first hour are those who attained the worship of faith from the beginnings of childhood. Those hired at the third hour are those who came to faith in adolescence. Those hired at the sixth hour are those who believed in the age of youth. Those who came at the ninth hour are those who, declining from youth into old age, received Christ’s grace. Those who came at the last hour are those who, already decrepit and called to Christ at the final period of their life, came to him. Yet they receive the same reward of eternal blessedness as those who came earlier. In the former Christ preserves justice, since they labored from the first hour of life; in the latter he bestows mercy, since they labored for one hour of life. [Col. 0078A]

The two sons sent to work in the vineyard display the type of the two peoples. The first son sent represents the people of the nations, called through the understanding of nature to cultivate the divine work. Yet, in contempt, he proved obstinate and refused, saying that he would not go. When the Lord came, however, he corrected his former disobedience by subsequent obedience.

The second son sent represents the Jew, who, through knowledge of the Law, replied: “Whatever the Lord says to us, we will do” (Exod. XXIV). But he is condemned because he not only transgressed in confessing the Law, but also extended parricidal hands against the Lord of the vineyard. [Col. 0078B]

The man who planted a vineyard bears the figure of God, who founded Jerusalem. In it he built a tower and dug a winepress—that is, an altar and a temple—and surrounded it with a hedge, meaning that he fortified it with the protection of angels. The tenants to whom he leased the vineyard are the people of Israel, who possessed Jerusalem under divine worship.

The servants who were sent at the time of the fruits and killed by the tenants are understood as the prophets, whose blood was shed by the Jews when the prophets sought from them the fruit of justice and of the Law. [Col. 0078C]

The son sent last, whom the tenants cast out of the vineyard and killed, is Christ, whom the Jews crucified, casting him outside the gates of Jerusalem. The tenants whom the lord of the vineyard destroyed are understood as the same Jewish people, who, as we see, were once scattered and slain. The farmers to whom the vineyard was ordered to be transferred signify the apostles or the successors of the apostles.

The king who made a wedding feast for his son is understood as God the Father, who joined flesh from a virgin to Christ.

The servants who were sent to call those who had been invited are the apostles and prophets, who summoned the Jews through the Law and the Gospel. But they, pressed sometimes by the storms of earthly affairs, sometimes by the burden of the flesh and the Law, despised the solemnity of the Lord’s coming. It is clear that the nations entered into the joys of eternal life. [Col. 0078D]

The angry king who sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city is God the Father, who raised up Vespasian Caesar of the Romans. He devastated the people with the sword and utterly overthrew the city of Jerusalem together with all that belonged to it, so that it could no longer wage war.

The man without a wedding garment at the table, who fell silent when the king spoke and whom the king ordered his servants to take away and cast into the outer darkness, is the one who rests in faith with the others; but if, on the day of judgment, he is found to have a garment polluted by works of the flesh, he is immediately ordered by the angels to be taken away and plunged into the hell of eternal fire. [Col. 0079A]

The two debtors, one of whom owed the moneylender five hundred denarii and the other fifty, signified the people of the Jews and of the nations. The one who owed fifty denarii bore the type of the Jews; the one who owed five hundred expressed the figure of the nations. Existing always as a debtor from the beginning of the world, the latter had not paid off the bond of sin through repentance. When Christ came, however, he finally believed and received the more abundant fruit of mercy. Therefore, because more was forgiven him by Christ, he loves Christ more, as it is written: “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more” (Luke VII).

The seven brothers who had one wife and died without children are understood as unbelieving people who, in the present life—which runs its course through a cycle of seven days—spent their whole lives without the fruit of justice. [Col. 0079B]

The two in one bed signify those who, withdrawn from the crowds, appear to devote themselves to a certain leisure of life.

The two women grinding at the mill signify those who are carried about by the affairs of temporal things.

The two in the field signify those who work in the ministry of the Church as in the Lord’s field. When the adversity of the world comes—that is, at night—some of them remain in the faith and are taken up to life, while others depart and are left for punishment.

The five wise virgins are understood as all holy souls. Since, through the five bodily senses, they admit no corruption of the heart, they are counted by the number five. The five foolish virgins, who do not have oil in their vessels, are those souls who indeed possess bodily integrity but do not preserve within their conscience the testimony of good works. They boast before human beings in their outward appearance, but not in their hearts before God. Because they do not carry the brightness of the mind in the vessels of their breasts, at the Lord’s coming they are shut out from the joy of his kingdom. [Col. 0079C]

The man traveling to a distant country, who entrusted his goods to his servants, is Christ. After his Resurrection, returning to heaven, he entrusted evangelical grace to evangelical merchants to put out at interest. The first servant, in the five talents given to him, received the five books of the Law, which he increased through the teaching or practice of the ten commandments. The second, in the two talents, received the two Testaments and doubled them by piously dispensing them in a moral and mystical sense. The third, under the figure of one talent, obscured the gift of grace that he had received in earthly pleasures; therefore he was cast into hell, because he produced no fruit from it. Others understood in the first servant the five senses of the heart and body that were received; in the second, understanding and action; and in the one, reason.

The young son of the widow, whom the Lord raised from the dead outside the gates of the city, signifies the one who openly commits some deadly crime, but, hearing the word of the Lord, rises from the death of sin, begins to live in Christ through repentance, and is restored to his widowed mother—that is, to communion with the Church. [Col. 0080A]

The man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers represents Adam in his race. When he descended from the heavenly Paradise into the world, he fell among the angels of darkness.

The Samaritan who came down and healed his wounds is Christ, our guardian, who descended from heaven and healed the human race from the wounds of sins.

The innkeeper signifies the apostles or their successors, who restore our weakness through evangelical preaching.

Martha, who welcomed Christ into her house and served him, signifies the Church in this life, welcoming Christ into her heart and laboring in the work of justice. [Col. 0080B]

Her sister Mary, who sat beside Christ’s feet and listened to his word, represents the same Church in the future age, ceasing from every work and resting in the sole contemplation of Christ’s wisdom.

The man who asked his friend at midnight for three loaves expresses the likeness of anyone who, in the midst of tribulation, asks the Lord to give him knowledge of the Trinity.

The rich man whose field produced abundant crops signifies a person devoted to luxury and abounding in sins. The Lord rebukes him because, in the uncontrolled flow of his desires, he wishes to sin still more, saying: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII). [Col. 0080C]

The five in one house—that is, father, mother, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law—between whom two are divided against three and three against two, signify the human race separated from one another in faith and religion: partly in the division of schism, signified by the number two, and partly in the number of the Trinity, signified by three.

For the son is divided against his father—that is, the people coming from the nations against the devil, with whom it had previously been joined. The daughter is also divided against her mother—that is, the people believing from among the Jews against the impious synagogue. The daughter-in-law is likewise divided against her mother-in-law—that is, the Church from the nations against the mother of her Bridegroom, the synagogue, from which Christ had been begotten according to the flesh.

All these are separated from one another, renouncing one another, as some seek earthly glory and others heavenly glory.

The nineteen Galileans upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them signify the destruction of the Jewish people. For nineteen is expressed among the Greeks by the letters iota and theta; by these figures the name “Jesus” is written. Since they were unwilling to believe in him, they were struck down together by the Romans along with their city. [Col. 0080D]

The man who planted a fig tree in his vineyard is Christ, who founded the synagogue for the Jewish people. When the Lord ordered it to be cut down as though useless, the apostles, as tenants, dug for it a ditch of humility. Manure was also applied—that is, confession of sins—and thus, by believing at the end, it will be changed for the better and will produce abundant fruits of justice.

The woman who had been ill for eighteen years and was raised upright by the Lord is a type of the Church, which attained the salvation of faith at the end of the ages. This world is completed in six ages, but its duration has a threefold division: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace. Six times three makes eighteen. By this number the period of our salvation is indicated, when, freed from the bonds of Satan by which we were bent over, we are raised upright and receive the gift of salvation and the hope of heavenly contemplation. [Col. 0081A]
