The man suffering from dropsy, whom the Lord healed, represents those whom the overflowing flood of carnal pleasures weighs down.

The man with two sons is to be understood as God, possessing two peoples. The elder bore the figure of the Jewish people, which remained in the worship of God; the younger [Col. 0081B] represented the nations, which, abandoning the Creator, became slaves of idols. When the younger returns in the poverty of faith, God the Father mercifully receives him. For his conversion he sacrifices his only Son under the figure of the calf; he also gives him the ring of faith and clothes him in the robe of immortality. Although the Jewish brother is tortured by envious jealousy, the angelic chorus nevertheless sings for joy at his salvation.

The wasteful steward, whom the master ordered removed from his stewardship and who, by defrauding his master, remitted part of what his master’s debtors owed so that he would have something by which to live in the future, is presented as an example for us. For if he deserved to be praised by his master who, by defrauding him, provided for his own future from another’s goods, how much more can we please Christ if, from our own goods, we show mercy to those in need, so that through them we may be received into eternal tabernacles? [Col. 0081C]

The rich man who was clothed in purple signifies the former flourishing pride of the Jews, through the splendor of imperial power or the excellence of honor.

The beggar covered with sores represents the gentile people humbled by confessions of sins. The five brothers of that rich man who was tormented in hell are understood as the Jews, who are placed under the five books of the Law.

The ten lepers whom the Lord cleansed signify heretics, who possess diversity in the variety of their colors—that is, the diversity of their schisms. For this reason they are sent to the priest, so that, with every variety of error removed, they may receive the sacrament of unity. [Col. 0081D]

The unjust judge, who did not fear the Lord but nevertheless heard the widow who continually pleaded with him, is a comparison demonstrating how great the hope should be of one who continually entreats God, since the widow’s persistent pleading prevailed even in the ears of an unjust judge. The widow herself can signify the Church, perseveringly seeking vengeance from her enemies, that is, the devil and heretics.

The Pharisee praying in the Temple is the people of the Jews, who exalt their merits on the basis of the justifications of the Law. The publican, however, is the people of the nations, who, placed far from God, confesses their sins. One of them departed in pride without being justified; the other, humbled by confessing, deserved to draw near and was exalted. [Col. 0082A]

The blind man sitting beside the road represents the gentile people, who through Christ’s grace deserved the illumination of faith.

Zacchaeus, whose name is interpreted as “just,” or “justified,” or “to be justified,” is the gentile people, small in the merits of grace, who, nevertheless, raised up from earthly actions through the tree of the Lord’s cross, contemplate the mystery of Christ.

The nobleman who went away to a distant region to receive a kingdom for himself signifies our Redeemer, who reached the ends of the earth to receive a kingdom among the peoples of the nations.

The citizens who did not want him to reign are understood as the Jews, who rejected Christ as king. [Col. 0082B]

The servant who, having received one mina, acquired ten, signifies teachers who, having received the grace of the Gospel, were blessed in the ten categories of discourse and acquired many in the faith by teaching them. Therefore, when the Lord Christ comes, they are praised because they have gained profit. But the one who acquired five from one signifies those who, keeping God’s commandments, attain knowledge of the law written in the five books of Moses, and by teaching it put it out at interest for the use necessary to salvation. The one who kept the single mina itself in a cloth shows the person who treated the grace-gift entrusted to him delicately and idly. Hence rightly he will lose the grace bestowed, who through negligence disdained to preach, so that it may be increased for the one who labored from it. [Col. 0082C]

The widow who cast two small coins into the treasury demonstrates the faithful soul, which keeps in the treasury of the heart the fruit of love for God and neighbor.

The bridegroom is Christ, whose wedding is celebrated with the Church; in whose union water is changed into wine, because believers pass through the grace of the washing to the crown of the Passion.

The master of the feast is understood as Moses, who marvels that through Jesus a better and holier people has been gathered in the Gospel than that former people led out from Egypt. The wine’s being exhausted shows that the grace of the Holy Spirit has been taken away from the Jews and contributed through the apostles among the Gentiles.

The Samaritan woman is mystically understood as the Synagogue, subject to the five books of the Law as though to five husbands, according to the carnal sense. The Lord mercifully urges her to draw living water—that is, to receive the grace of the washing, or the hidden understanding of the Law. [Col. 0082D]

The adulterous woman, whom the Jews bring to the Lord to be stoned, is the Church. Having formerly abandoned God, she had committed fornication with idols; the jealous Synagogue wished to kill her. Christ saves her through the forgiveness of sin and does not allow her to perish, for he knows how to pardon sinners.

Simon the leper is the Gentile people, who was cleansed by the Redeemer.

The woman who anointed the Lord’s head with perfume is the Church, which brings the fruit of its labor and the fragrance of its faith to the praise of God and the glory of Christ. [Col. 0083A]

That angel at whose descent the water was stirred, and which was enclosed by five porticoes, is Christ. At his coming the Jewish people, enclosed within the five books of the Law, was troubled. For when the angel descended, the water was stirred and the sick person was healed; when Christ descended from heaven, that same people was stirred in his Passion, and the world was healed.

The man blind from birth, whom the Lord sent to wash at the pool of Siloam after anointing his eyes, signifies the human race, corrupted from birth—that is, from the first human being—by the darkness of error [or: errors]. The Lord smeared his eyes with spittle and mud because “the Word became flesh” (John I); and he commanded that his eyes be washed in the pool [Col. 0083B], so that, baptized in Christ, he might receive the light of faith and believe in him who appeared visibly in the world.

Lazarus, whose name means “helped,” whom the Lord raised from the tomb after he had lain there four days and stank, signifies the world, which had been corrupted by the most grievous habit of sin. Yet he is raised on the fourth day of death. The first day of death is the mortality derived from Adam, the stock of death. The second day of death is the transgression of the natural law. The third day of death is the violation of the law that was given. The fourth day of death is contempt for evangelical preaching; on that day the Lord, looking upon his work, graciously deigned to raise him.

The servant of the high priest, whose right ear was cut off, is the Israelite people, which became enslaved through unbelief. He loses his right ear when he passed over to the left-handed understanding of the letter. In those who believe, the Lord restores his hearing to faith and makes him obedient to the commandments of the Gospel. Caiphas is interpreted as “investigator,” or “shrewd,” or “vomiting with the mouth.” For with his mouth he unjustly condemned the righteous, although he had announced this through a prophetic mystery. For that same high priest, who tore his garment in the Lord’s Passion, indicates the Hebrew people stripped of the priesthood and emptied of the kingdom by its being torn apart.

Barabbas, who is released to the Jews, signifies the Antichrist, whom they, in their error, deserved to receive in place of Christ. Barabbas is interpreted as “son of the master”—without doubt the master of those Jews, who is the devil, the author of murders, who is condemned in them to this day. [Col. 0083D]

Herod and Pilate, who, although they were at odds, were joined in friendship during the Lord’s Passion, indicate that the two peoples—the people of the circumcision and the Gentiles—were at first divided from one another, but through the Lord’s Passion were united in faith.

Herod is interpreted as “leathern” [or “wearing skins”]. He signifies the Antichrist as one who changes his skin; and Pontius Pilate, “turning aside the counsel,” signifies the counsel of the Jews. For after receiving water he washed his hands, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matthew XXVII). Pilate is interpreted as “the mouth of the hammerer”; he signifies the devil, who is the hammer of the whole earth.

Simon of Cyrene, whom they compelled to carry the cross, is understood as the Gentile people, which, a stranger to the Law, becomes obedient to the Gospel of the cross. He himself became Christ’s victor and the bearer of faith. [Col. 0084A]

The two thieves represent the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. One, unbelieving, blasphemes Christ hanging on the cross; the other, faithful, rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

The four soldiers who made four portions for themselves from Jesus’ garments prefigured the four regions of the world, which divided Christ’s utterances among themselves, as it is written: “I shall rejoice over your utterances, as one who finds abundant spoils” (Psalm CXVIII).

The holy women who followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him from their possessions, and who were also present at his Passion, standing nearby, and after his burial, when the others had departed, remained sitting opposite the tomb—namely Mary Magdalene; Mary the mother of James and Joseph, who was also the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother; and the mother of the sons of Zebedee, whom Mark calls Salome (Mark XVI); together with the other women whom we read of in the remaining Gospels—these clearly bear the figure of humble souls devoted to the Lord. The more deeply they fear their own frailty in conscience, the more fervently they serve the footsteps of his Passion in this world, in which rest is being prepared for the future. And if they are perhaps able, through pious attentiveness, to imitate this, they carefully consider the order in which that same Passion was completed. [Col. 0084B]

The women who announce the resurrection to the Lord’s apostles are understood as the Law and the Prophets, who preached the glory of Christ’s resurrection as forerunners before it was revealed. [Col. 0084C]

Mary Magdalene, therefore, is the same person as the sister of Lazarus and Martha, from whom the Lord cast out seven demons. She is not another woman, but the one who, as Luke writes, while still a sinner, once came and drenched the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance, and anointed them with the ointment of a devout confession. Because she loved greatly, she obtained forgiveness for many from the merciful Judge (Luke VII). Justified shortly before his Passion and made familiar to the Lord, she poured holy oil not only on his feet, as the same John relates, but also on his head, as Matthew and Mark testify.

She is called Magdalene from the place Magdala. For Magdalene is interpreted as “tower.” Mystically, however, she signifies the faith and piety of the holy Church, which by preaching spreads the fragrance of knowledge of Christ throughout the world. [Col. 0084D]

So also Martha, whose name is interpreted as “irritating” or “provoking,” bears the type of the Church. By laboring daily in good works, she irritates the devil and his members and provokes God’s elect to faith through pious deeds and words.

The seven disciples with whom the Lord is described as having dined after the resurrection indicate the seventh-day rest of the resurrection, in which all the saints will be satisfied through Christ with the nourishment of eternal blessedness.

The chief priests, who, after learning the truth of the Lord’s resurrection from the guards of the tomb, gave them a large sum of money so that they might lie and say that the Lord’s body had been stolen by his disciples, prefigured those who, because of earthly greed, sell the truth and purchase wickedness. Moreover, all who misuse the temple’s offerings and the gifts contributed for the Church’s use for other purposes by which they satisfy their own pleasure are like the scribes and priests who redeem falsehood in exchange for the Savior’s blood. [Col. 0085A]

The fact that after his resurrection the Savior appeared to the eleven disciples in Galilee, on a mountain, is not without mystery. It signifies that the body which, by being born, he had assumed from the common earth of the human race, when rising again had already been lifted above all earthly things and clothed with heavenly power. [Col. 0085B]

He appeared on a mountain to admonish the faithful that, if they desire to see there the height of his resurrection, they should here pass from lowly desires to desires of the heights. The name Galilee is interpreted as “transmigration” or “revelation.” For then, with unveiled face, as the Apostle testifies, gazing upon the glory of the Lord, we shall be transformed into the same image—all of us who now reveal our way to him and follow his footsteps with unfeigned faith (II Corinthians III).

Now it must be said what Christ’s apostles signify through the interpretation of their names or through the manner of their deeds. In short, “apostles” is interpreted as “sent.” Their name itself indicates this. For just as in Greek angels are called messengers in Latin, so in Greek apostles are called “sent” in Latin. Christ sent them to evangelize throughout the whole world, so that some of them even penetrated among the Persians and Indians, teaching the nations and performing great and incredible miracles in Christ’s name. Thus, with signs and wonders bearing witness, people believed what they said. Most of them have the reasons for their names from these matters.

Peter received his name from “rock”—that is, from Christ, upon whom the Church is founded. Peter did not receive the name “rock” from Peter; rather, Peter received his name from the rock, just as Christ is not called from Christian, but Christian is called from Christ. Therefore the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI). Peter had said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; [Col. 0085D] then the Lord said to him: “Upon this rock, which you have confessed, I will build my Church.” For the rock was Christ, upon whose foundation Peter himself was also built.

He is called Cephas because he was established as the head of the apostles. Cephale in Greek means “head,” and that name is embodied in Peter.

Simon Barjona means “son of a dove” in our language. It is both a Syriac and a Hebrew name. Bar means “son” in Syriac; jona means “dove” in Hebrew; in both languages the expression is Barjona. Others take it simply to mean that Simon—that is, Peter—was the son of John, according to the question: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John XXI). They believe that the text was corrupted through scribal error, so that instead of bar Joanna—that is, “son of John”—bar Jona was written, with one syllable removed. Joanna is interpreted as “the Lord’s grace.” They therefore hold that Peter had three names: Peter, Cephas, and Simon Barjona.

Simon is interpreted in Hebrew as “hearing” and “obedient.” Peter, however, bears the person of the Church, which has the power to forgive sins and to lead people from the underworld to the heavenly kingdoms. [Col. 0086A]

Saul is called “temptation” in Hebrew, because he was formerly engaged in the Church’s trial. For he was a persecutor; he had this name because he persecuted Christians. Later, when his name was changed, Saul became Paul, which is interpreted as “wonderful” or “chosen.” “Wonderful,” either because he performed many signs, [Col. 0086B] or because he preached Christ’s Gospel among all the nations from East to West. “Chosen,” as the Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have chosen them” (Acts XIII).

In Latin, Paul is named from “little.” Hence he himself says: “I am the least of the apostles” (I Corinthians XV). When Saul, he was proud and exalted; when Paul, humble and little. Therefore we say: “I shall see you shortly,” that is, “after a little while.” For because he became little, he himself says: “I am the last of the apostles, and the least of all the saints” (ibid.).

Cephas and Saul were therefore called by changed names so that they might be new even in name, like Abraham and Sarah. Paul signifies the conversion of the Church from the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, whose apostle and teacher he himself was. For just as Paul first remained rebellious in unbelief and afterward, washed through the grace of baptism and imbued with the faith of Christ, remained humble and devoted, so also the Gentile people first inflicted persecution on Christians before receiving Christ’s Gospel; but afterward, devoted to God, it did not hesitate to pour out its own blood for him. [Col. 0086C]

Andrew, Peter’s brother, “fleshly and co-heir of grace,” according to the Hebrew etymology, is interpreted as “handsome” or “answering.” In Greek usage he is called “manly,” from *aner*, “man.” He represents the ecclesial people, who are handsome in the beauty of right faith [Col. 0086D] and answer with good works, because what they believe in their heart they practice in their deeds. They also act manfully in God’s commandments and perform righteousness, so that they may become acceptable and pleasing to their Creator.

John received his name through a kind of prophecy, in accordance with his merit. It is interpreted as “in whom there is grace,” or “the Lord’s grace.” Jesus loved him more than the other apostles. He bears the type of those who, exalted by the grace of contemplation, diligently cling to their Creator and consider nothing dearer than him. They can say with the Psalmist: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God, so that I may proclaim all his praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm XXVII).

It should nevertheless be noted that in the Gospel exposition, when Peter [Col. 0087A] and John ran to the tomb after Christ’s resurrection, John arrived first but did not enter; Peter, coming afterward, immediately entered and found the linen cloths lying there, and so forth (John XX), as the events are related there.

There, therefore, John bears the type of the Jewish people, which comes first to the Lord through knowledge of the Law, just as John came first to the tomb, but did not enter. For it received the commandments of the Law through the prophets; it heard about the Lord’s incarnation and Passion; and through the testimonies of sacred Scripture it had long before prophesied many things about him, far and wide. But when it saw him present, it rejected him, despised him as a human being, and refused to believe that he had become mortal. Just as it came first to the tomb, so it stood empty and idle.

But Peter followed afterward and entered; through him the Church of the Gentiles is signified. As soon as it heard about Christ, the mediator of God and human beings, it believed that he whom it knew to have died was the living God. Then that other disciple also entered, the one who had come first to the tomb (ibid.), because at the end of the world Judea too is gathered into the faith of our Lord, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI). [Col. 0087B]

James, son of Zebedee, is named from his father, whom he left with John and followed the true Father. These are the sons of thunder, who were also called Boanerges because of the firmness and greatness of their faith. This is James, the son of Zebedee and brother of John, who after the Lord’s ascension is revealed as having been killed by Herod.

James, son of Alphaeus, is given this surname to distinguish him from the former: just as the other is called the son of Zebedee, so this one is the son of Alphaeus. Both therefore took their additional name from their father. This is James the younger, who in the Gospel is called the Lord’s brother, because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary, the Lord’s mother. John the Evangelist calls her “Mary of Clopas,” naming her from her father, or from the family of her Gentile origin, or for whatever other reason he assigned her that name. [Col. 0087C]

Alphaeus in Hebrew is rendered in Latin as “thousandth” or “learned.”

Philip: “mouth of lamps” or “of hands.”

Thomas: “abyss,” or “twin”; hence he is also called Didymus in Greek. These two bear the type of preachers who, penetrating the abyss of the sacred Scriptures, bring forth from their mouths the light of preaching to illuminate the nations. [Col. 0087D]

Bartholomew: “son of the one who suspends waters,” or “son of the one who suspends me.” This is Syriac, not Hebrew. He likewise signifies holy teachers, who by their preaching suspend the waters—that is, the peoples—in aspiration toward the heavenly Father, whose sons they are.

Matthew is rendered in Hebrew as “gifted.” He is also called Levi, from the tribe from which he arose; but in Latin he received his name from the work of a publican, because he was chosen from among the publicans and transferred into the apostolate. In the writing of the Gospel he shows how great a gift of grace he merited after his conversion, giving an example to all who practice worthy repentance for their sins, so that no one may despair of forgiveness: “For the Lord is pleased with those who fear him, and with all who hope in his mercy” (Psalm CXLVI). [Col. 0088A]

Simon the Cananaean is named to distinguish him from Simon Peter, from Cana, a village of Galilee where the Lord changed water into wine. He is the one who in another Gospel is written as “the Zealot.” For Cana is interpreted as “zeal,” showing that whoever receives the office of preaching through God’s dispensation ought to possess zeal for righteousness, because “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

Judas of James, who elsewhere is called Lebbaeus, has a figurative name derived from the heart; we may render it diminutively as “little heart.” In another Gospel he is written as Thaddaeus. And rightly, since his name is figured from the heart, he turns the whole intention of his mind toward God, so that he may please him in all things, whose servant he has shown himself to be. [Col. 0088B]

Judas Iscariot took his name from the village in which he was born, or received it from the tribe of Issachar, as a portent of the future, to his own condemnation. For Issachar is interpreted as “reward,” signifying the price of the betrayer, for which he sold the Lord, as it is written: “They took my reward, thirty pieces of silver, the price at which I was valued by them” (Zechariah XI). Through the betrayal of his master, he acquired for himself a memory of eternal destruction.

Matthias, who alone among the apostles is mentioned without a surname, is interpreted as “gifted,” with “in place of Judas” understood. For the apostles elected him in Judas’s place [Col. 0088C] when the lot was cast between the two.

Alternatively, Matthias is interpreted as “little,” and Joseph, who was appointed with him by lot, is called Barsabbas—that is, “son of quietness.” Concerning these two, Arator thus played in his metrical work:

> They set up two, Joseph surnamed Just,
>
> And Matthias, whose name, they say, sounds in the Hebrew tongue as
>
> “God’s little one,” and confirms this by calling him humble. O how far human judgments differ
>
> From judgments above! The one who was just
>
> In human praise is surpassed by the little one’s merit.
>
> The twelve signs of the choir shine forth,
>
> And cast the radiance of heaven over the earth.

It should also be noted that Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, a man learned in every respect, reports that both of these men, who were appointed by lot to the apostolate, had belonged to the number of the seventy disciples.

[Col. 0088D]

Mark: “exalted by command,” certainly because of the Gospel of the Most High, which he preached.

Luke: “himself rising,” or “himself raising.” These two Evangelists—Mark and Luke—one chosen from the Jews and the other from the nations, signify the two orders of preachers: one from the Jews and the other from the Gentiles, sent to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world. They also followed the prince of the apostles and the teacher of the Gentiles: Mark followed Peter, to whom the apostolate of the circumcision was entrusted; and Luke followed Paul, who was the teacher and master of the Gentiles. Thus each rightly followed the footsteps of his master and worthily fulfilled the office of his ministry. [Col. 0089A]

Barnabas is interpreted as “son of prophecy” or “son of consolation.” Together with Paul, he was separated from the apostles by the judgment of the Holy Spirit to preach the Gospel among the Gentiles, so that he might reveal to them the gift of prophecy and, through words and deeds, provide what was suitable for eternal consolation.

Nicodemus, who came to the Lord by night and learned from him the mystery of the second birth, signifies those who come with devoted hearts to the teachers of the Church in order to learn true wisdom from them. Yet they remain placed in the darkness of ignorance and doubt until they are enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose power Jesus explained to Nicodemus himself.

For it is related in the Gospel that this same Nicodemus came during the Lord’s Passion, carrying a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, so that together with Joseph, who was from Arimathea, he might bury the Lord’s body. But this too is not without mystery, because those who truly cling to the Savior’s discipleship store the memory of his death and resurrection in the secret place of their hearts, together with the perfumes of sacred virtues. Living justly and piously, they await the day of the resurrection and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us “to cleanse for himself a people acceptable to him, zealous for good works” (Titus II). [Col. 0089B]

Nathanael is interpreted as “gift of God,” because deceit—that is, pretense—was not in him. His imitators are all the elect, who come to the Lord with simple devotion and keep his commandments.

## CHAPTER II. On Martyrs

[Col. 0089C]

“Martyrs” in Greek are called *testes*—“witnesses”—in Latin. Hence testimonies are also called *martyria* in Greek. They are called witnesses because they endured sufferings for the testimony of Christ and fought for the truth even unto death. The reason we call them not *testes*—which we could certainly say in Latin—but *martyrs* in Greek is that this Greek word sounds more familiar to the ears of the Church, just as we use many Greek names in place of Latin ones.

The first martyr in the New Testament was Stephen, whose name in Hebrew is interpreted as “standard,” because he was first in martyrdom for the imitation of the faithful. The same name, however, is rendered from Greek into Latin as “crowned,” and this prophetically, so that what would follow in reality might first resound in the name as a prophecy of the future. [Col. 0089D] For he suffered and received what he was called. Stephen means “crown”: he was humbly stoned but sublimely crowned.

There are two kinds of martyrdom: one in open suffering, the other in the hidden virtue of the soul. For many, enduring the devil’s hostile snares and resisting every carnal desire, have become martyrs even in a time of peace by sacrificing themselves in their hearts to almighty God. If a time of persecution arose, they too could become martyrs.

## CHAPTER III. On the Church and the Synagogue

“Church” is Greek and is rendered in Latin as “convocation,” because it calls everyone together. [Col. 0090A] “Catholic” means “universal,” from *apo to Catholico*, that is, “according to the whole.” For it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain parts of the regions; rather, spread throughout the whole world, it extends everywhere.

The Apostle also approves this when he says to the Romans: “I give thanks to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans I). Hence “universality” too is named from “one,” because it is gathered into unity. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI).

But since the Church is one, why is it written by John as seven churches (Revelation I), unless to signify that the one Catholic Church is filled with the sevenfold Spirit? We likewise know that Solomon said of the Lord: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars” (Proverbs IX). Nevertheless, there is no doubt that these seven are one, since the Apostle says: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Timothy III).

The Church began at the place where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the 120 who were sitting together in one place. Because of the present pilgrimage, the Church is called Sion, since, placed at a distance from this lengthy pilgrimage, it gazes upon the promise of heavenly things. For this reason it received the name Sion, that is, “watchtower” or “contemplation.” But because of the peace of the future homeland it is called Jerusalem. For Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” There, with all adversity abolished, it will possess in present sight the peace that is Christ.

“Synagogue” is Greek and is called “congregation” in Latin. This name properly belonged to the Jewish people. Their gathering is properly accustomed to be called a synagogue, although it too has been called a church. [Col. 0090C] The apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a church—either for the sake of distinction, or because there is some difference between a congregation, from which synagogue takes its name, and a convocation, from which the Church receives its name. Animals, especially sheep, are accustomed to be gathered, and we properly speak of their flocks as being gathered; but we usually say that human beings are convened.

## CHAPTER IV. On Religion and Faith

Philosophers called a doctrine *dogma* from “thinking,” that is: “I think this is good; I think this is true.”

Religion is so called because through it we bind our souls to the worship of God by the bond of service to the one God. The word is compounded from *relegendo*, “choosing again”—so that in Latin religion appears analogous to *eligio*, “choice.”

There are three things sought in human beings for the worship of God in religious observance: faith, hope, and charity. In faith: what must be believed; in hope: what must be hoped for; in charity: what must be loved.

Faith is that by which we truly believe what we are in no way able to see. For we cannot now believe what we see. The name “faith” properly derives from the fact that what has been said or promised is entirely fulfilled; hence faith is so called because what has been agreed between two parties—so to speak, between God and a human being—is brought about. From this also comes *foedus*, “covenant.”

Hope is so called because it is a “foot for proceeding,” as though from *est pes*, “there is a foot.” Hence, by contrast, despair: there the foot is lacking, and there is no ability to proceed, because while someone loves sin, he does not hope for future glory. [Col. 0091A]

Charity is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “love” or “affection,” because it binds two things within itself. For love begins from two: namely, the love of God and of neighbor. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Romans XIII).

This is greater than all things, because whoever loves also believes and hopes. But whoever does not love, even if he performs many good works, labors in vain. All love, however, is more commonly called *amor*. The name *dilectio* is usually applied only to better things.

Under the title “Church,” moreover, a certain distinction is found, so that within sacred orders and certain professions the faithful differ from one another.

## CHAPTER V. On Clerics

[Col. 0091B]

The clergy and clerics are so called because Matthias was chosen by lot, whom we read was the first to be ordained by the apostles. For *cleros* in Greek means “lot” or “inheritance.” Clerics are therefore so called either because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because they possess the Lord’s portion.

In general, all who serve in Christ’s Church are called clerics. Their ranks and names are these: doorkeeper, psalmist, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and bishop.

The order of bishops is fourfold: patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. “Patriarch” in Greek is interpreted as “highest of the fathers,” because he holds the first—that is, apostolic—place. Since he exercises the highest honor, he is designated by this name, as in the cases of the Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian patriarchs. [Col. 0091C]

“Archbishop” is a Greek term meaning “highest of bishops.” He occupies the place of the apostles and presides over both metropolitans and the other bishops. He stands above the individual provinces, and the other priests are subject to his authority and teaching; without him the remaining bishops may do nothing. For the care of the whole province is entrusted to them.

All the ranks designated above are called bishops by one and the same name; some, however, use a private title for the sake of distinguishing the powers they have received individually.

“Patriarch”: father of princes. For *archon* means “prince.”

“Archbishop”: prince of bishops, just as “metropolitan” derives from the measure of cities.

The word “episcopate” is so called because the one placed above watches over those below, undertaking care of his subjects. For *skopein* in Latin means “to look attentively” or “to supervise.” Bishops are interpreted from Greek into Latin as “watchers.” A watcher is the one placed in charge in the Church, because he watches over and looks after the conduct and life of the peoples placed beneath him.

A pontiff is the chief of priests, as though “the way of those who follow.” He is also called the high priest and the highest pontiff. He makes priests and Levites; he arranges all the ecclesiastical orders; and he shows what each person ought to do. [Col. 0092A] Formerly, pontiffs were also kings. For it was the custom of the ancestors that the king should also be a priest or pontiff. Hence Roman emperors too were called pontiffs.

Vates, “seers,” are named from the power of the mind. The meaning of the term is manifold: at one time it signifies a priest, at another a prophet, and at another a poet.

An antistes is called a priest because he “stands before.” For he is first in the order of the Church and has no one above him.

The name priest is composed from Greek and Latin, as though it meant “one who gives the sacred.” For just as a king is named from ruling, so a priest is named from sanctifying. He consecrates and sanctifies.

The priests of the pagans were called flamines. On their heads they wore [Col. 0092B] a cap in which there was a short rod, with some wool at its top. Since they could not bear this in the heat, they began to bind their heads only with a thread. For it was unlawful for them to walk with their heads completely bare. Hence they were called flamines from the thread they used, as though *filamines*. On feast days, however, after setting aside the thread, they put on the cap as a mark of the priesthood’s eminence.

“Presbyter” is interpreted from Greek into Latin as “elder,” not because of age or decrepit old age, but because of the honor and dignity they have received. Hence among the ancients the same persons were both bishops and presbyters, because one is a title of dignity and the other of age.

Presbyters are called priests because they give the sacred, as bishops do. Although bishops are priests, they nevertheless possess the summit of the pontificate, because neither do presbyters sign the forehead with chrism nor give the Spirit, the Paraclete; that the latter belongs only to bishops is demonstrated by a reading from the Acts of the Apostles. Hence among the ancients the same persons were bishops and presbyters, because, as we have just said, one is the name of dignity and the other of age. [Col. 0092C]

Levites are named from the name of their ancestor. The Levites arose from Levi, and through them the ministries of the mystical sacrament were performed in God’s temple. In Greek they are called deacons and in Latin ministers, because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of ministry belongs to the deacon.

“Hypodeacons” in Greek are what we call subdeacons. They are so called because they are subject to the commands and duties of the Levites. They themselves receive the offerings from the faithful in God’s temple and carry them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars. Among the Hebrews they are called *Nethinim*.

Readers are named from reading, and psalmists from singing psalms. The former proclaim to the peoples what they should follow; the latter sing in order to stir the hearers’ souls to compunction. Some readers also pronounce their words so mournfully that they compel certain people to grief and lamentation. They are likewise called announcers, because they announce things beforehand. Their voice is so great and clear that it fills the ears even of those who are far away. [Col. 0092D]

A cantor is so called because he modulates with his voice in song. In the art of music two types are said to exist, insofar as learned people have been able to name them in Latin: the *praecentor* and the *succentor*. The *praecentor* is the one who sends forth the voice first in song; the *succentor* is the one who responds by singing afterward. The *concentor* is the one who sings in harmony; whoever does not harmonize does not sing together and will not be a *concentor*.

Acolytes are called *ceroferarii* in Latin, “candle-bearers,” from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered. At that time they light and carry the lamps—not to drive away darkness, since the sun is shining brightly at the same time, but to demonstrate a sign of joy. Thus, under the figure of bodily light, that light is shown of which we read in the Gospel: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into the world” (John I).

[Col. 0093B]

Exorcists are called from Greek in Latin “those who adjure” or “those who rebuke.” For they invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over catechumens or over those who have an unclean spirit, adjuring it through him to depart from them.

Doorkeepers are also called gatekeepers. In the Old Testament they were chosen to guard the temple, so that nothing unclean in any respect might enter it. They are called doorkeepers because they preside over the temple doors. Holding the key, they guard everything inside on both sides; exercising judgment between the good and the wicked, they receive the faithful and reject the unfaithful.

## CHAPTER VI. On Monks
A monk is so called by a Greek etymology because he is solitary [Col. 0093C]; for *monas* in Greek means “solitude” or “singularity.” Therefore, if the word *monk* means “solitary,” what is a solitary man doing in a crowd? For there are several kinds of monks.

**Cenobites** are those whom we may call people living in community. For *cenobium* means a community of many.

**Anchorites** are those who, because of their cenobitic life, seek the deserts and live alone in the wilderness; and they are called by this name because they have withdrawn far from human beings. Anchorites imitate Elijah and John, while cenobites imitate the apostles.

**Hermits** are likewise anchorites, withdrawn from human company and seeking the desert and deserted solitudes. For *eremus* means, as it were, “a remote place.”

**Abba**, a Syrian word, means in Latin “father” [Col. 0093D]. Paul explained this when writing to the Romans: “By whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII), using two languages. For *abba* is the Syrian word for “father,” and he again names it in Latin, that is, “father.”

## CHAPTER VII. On the Other Faithful

The word **Christian**, as its interpretation shows, is derived either from “anointing” or from the name of its author and creator. Christians are named from Christ, just as Jews are named from Judah. A designation is given to followers from the name of their teacher. Formerly, however, Christians were called by the Jews, as a term of reproach, “Nazarenes,” because our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene from a village of Galilee [Col. 0094A]. Let no one glory in being a Christian who has the name but not the deeds. When the work follows the name, he is most certainly a Christian, because he shows himself to be a Christian by his deeds, walking as the one walked from whom he also received his name.

**Catholic** is interpreted as “universal” or “general.” For the Greeks call the universal *catholicon*.

**Orthodox** means one who believes rightly and lives rightly according to what he believes. For *orthos* in Greek means “right,” and *doxa* means “glory”—that is, “a man of right glory.” One who lives otherwise than he believes cannot be called by this name.

**Neophyte** in Greek may be rendered in Latin as “new” and “an inexperienced believer,” or “one recently reborn.”

A **catechumen** is so called because he is still hearing the teaching of the faith and has not yet received baptism. For *catechumen* in Greek is rendered in Latin as “hearer” or “one being instructed” [Col. 0094B].

A **competent** is so called because, after instruction in the faith, he seeks the grace of Christ. Hence they are also called *competentes*, “those who ask.”

**Laic** means “of the people.” For *laos* in Greek means “people.”

**Proselyte**, that is, “newcomer” and “circumcised person,” who was incorporated into the people of God, is a Greek word.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Heresy and Schism

**Heresy** is called in Greek from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself from heresy and schism what seems better to him—for example, the Peripatetics, Academics, Epicureans, and Stoics, or any others [Col. 0094C] who, devising a perverse doctrine, withdrew from the Church according to their own judgment. Thus *heresy* is named from the Greek word signifying “choice,” by which each person, according to his own judgment, chooses for himself whatever he wishes either to establish or to accept. We, however, are permitted to introduce nothing from our own judgment, nor to choose what anyone else has introduced according to his own judgment. We have the apostles of God as our authorities, because they too did not choose anything from their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully handed on to the nations the teaching they had received from Christ. Therefore, even if an angel from heaven should preach otherwise, he will be called accursed (Gal. I).

**Sect** is named from *sectari*, “to follow and hold.” For we call sects the dispositions of minds and the institutions faithfully maintained in matters of discipline [Col. 0094D], or the purpose which they follow by holding to it, forming opinions in the practice of religion very different from those of others.

**Schism** is so called from the rending of minds. A schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as the others; he delights only in the division of the congregation. Schism arises when people say, “We sanctify the unclean,” and other statements of the same kind.

**Superstition** is so called because it is a superfluous or superimposed observance. Others say that the term comes from old men who, having survived many years, rave and err through age in a kind of superstition, not knowing what the ancients worship or what things the ignorant adopt from the ancients. Lucretius, however, says that superstition is the “standing above of things,” that is, of heavenly and divine things, which stand above us—but he is wrong [Col. 0095A]. In order that the doctrines of heretics may easily be recognized, their causes or names must be set forth.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Heresies of the Jews

There are heresies among the Jews. Some of them, discovering doctrines contrary to the faith of Christ, became authors of perverse teachings. Their names are as follows:

1. Ephnaeans  
2. Galileans  
3. Marboneans  
4. Genistae  
5. Meristae  
6. Sadducees  
7. Pharisees  
8. Herodians  
9. Samaritans  
10. Hemerobaptists

The **Ephnaeans** say that Christ taught them complete abstinence.

The **Galileans** likewise say that Christ came and taught them not to call the Lord “Caesar” and not to obey his commands [Col. 0095B].

The **Marboneans** say that he is himself the Christ who taught them to baptize in every matter.

The **Genistae** presume upon the fact that they are descended from Abraham. For when the people of God came to Babylon, many of them, abandoning their wives, attached themselves to Babylonian women. Others, content with Israelite marriages, or born from them, separated themselves from the whole people when they returned from Babylonia and adopted for themselves a name of boasting.

The **Meristae** divide the Scriptures, refusing to believe all the prophets and saying that the prophets prophesied under different spirits.

The **Sadducees** are interpreted as “just,” for they claim for themselves what they are not. They deny the resurrection, saying: “It was said to Adam in Genesis, ‘You are from the earth, and into the earth you shall go’” (Gen. III) [Col. 0095C]. They accept only the five books of the Law and reject the prophecies of the prophets.

The **Pharisees** deny that Christ has come and agree in no respect with those mentioned above. The Pharisees and Sadducees are indeed opposed to one another. For *Pharisees* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “divided,” because they preferred to the people’s justice the justice of the traditions and observances that they call *deuterosis*; hence they are called “divided” from the people, as though by their justice.

The **Herodians** arose during the time of the Savior. They magnified Herod, saying that he himself was the Christ.

The **Samaritans** are likewise interpreted as “guardians.” They were transferred into the land of the ten tribes in place of Israel, after the people had been captured and deported to Babylon [Col. 0095D]. In part, they retain the customs of the Israelites without the Law. They do not accept the prophets and are separated from all Jews in their observances. Their superstition is unquestionably known to everyone.

The **Hemerobaptists** are so called because they wash their clothing and bodies every day. Moreover, many other kinds of heresies are found which, having arisen in Christian times, have customarily attacked the catholic faith through their inventors and followers. Father Augustine also describes them quite explicitly in his letter to the deacon Quodvultdeus. But since that learned man, enumerating ecclesiastical doctrines in his definitions, clearly set out what ought to be believed and what ought to be avoided, we have decided to omit the catalogue of heretics and insert in this work the principles of the catholic faith [Col. 0096A].

## CHAPTER X. On the Definitions of the Right Faith and of Ecclesiastical Doctrines

We believe that there is one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is called Father because he has a Son; Son because he has a Father; and Holy Spirit because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father, therefore, is the principle of the Godhead: just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds—not born, because he is not the Son; nor unbegotten, because he is not the Father; nor made, because the Holy Spirit is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son [Col. 0096B].

The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says, nor is the divinity separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes. Rather, the Father is one in person, the Son another in person, and the Holy Spirit another in person; yet in nature there is one God in the holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The Father did not assume flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but only the Son, so that the one who was the Son of God in the divinity of God the Father might himself become the son of man in humanity [Col. 0096C], lest the name “son” pass to another who was not a son by birth. Thus the Son of God became the son of man: born according to the truth of nature from God as the Son of God, and according to the truth of nature from man as the son of man. In both births he possessed the name of son by being born, not by adoption or designation; and he was true God and true man, one Son.

Therefore, there are not two Christs or two Sons, but one Son, God and man. For this reason we also call him “only-begotten,” remaining in two substances, as the truth of his nature bestowed them—not with the natures confused or mixed, as the Timotheans wish, but united in association. God therefore assumed man, and man passed into God, not through a changeability of nature, as the Apollinarists say [Col. 0096D], but through God’s condescension. Thus God was not changed into human substance by assuming man, nor man into divine substance by being glorified into God, because alteration or changeability of nature brings about both diminution and abolition of substance.

We believe that the Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation. The Son of God was therefore born from a human being, but not through human agency—that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Hebion says. Rather, he drew flesh from the body of a virgin and did not bring it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches affirm. He was not born merely in appearance, that is, without reality, as Valentinus says, nor in *dokēsis* [Greek: δοκήσει], that is, putatively or imaginatively, but with a real body—not merely flesh from flesh, as Marcianus teaches [Col. 0097A], but true God from divinity and true man from flesh: one Son in divinity, the Word of the Father, and God in humanity, consisting of soul and flesh.

His soul was not without sensation and reason, as Apollinaris says, nor was his flesh without a soul, as Anomocus teaches. Rather, he had a soul with its reason and flesh with its senses. Through these true senses he endured the pains of his flesh both during the Passion and before it. He was not born from a virgin in such a way that, by being born as a man, he received the beginning of his divinity—as though he had not been God before he was born from the virgin, as Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus taught—but the eternal God was born as man from a virgin.

Nothing created or servile is to be believed in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, holds; nothing unequal, as Eunomius teaches; nothing equal by grace, as Aetius holds; nothing earlier or later, greater or lesser, as Arius teaches [Col. 0097B]; nothing external or serving another, as Macedonius teaches; nothing inserted by persuasion or stealth, as Manichaeus teaches; nothing corporeal, as Melito and Tertullian teach; nothing corporeally formed, as the Anthropomorphites and Vadianus teach; nothing invisible to itself, as Origen teaches; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus teaches; nothing differing in character or will, as Marcion teaches; nothing in the essence of the Trinity reduced to the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian teach; nothing singular in function or incommunicable to another, as Origen teaches; nothing confused, as Sabellius teaches. Rather, it is one perfect reality, because the whole is from one and is one, yet not solitary, as that condemnable teaching of Silvanus and Praxeas of Pentapolis presumes.

The Son is therefore *homoousios*—“of the same substance”—with the Father in divinity. The Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son. One Son is *homoousios* with God and man, remaining God in his humanity, in the glory of the Father, desirable for the angels to behold, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshiped by the angels and by every creature. He is not a man apart from God, nor Christ alongside God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but man in God and God in man [Col. 0097C].

There will be a resurrection of dead human beings, but one resurrection and once only—not a first resurrection of the just and a second of sinners, as is imagined in a fable, but one resurrection of all. If that is said to rise which falls, then our flesh truly rises, just as it truly falls. There will not, according to Origen, be a transformation of bodies—that is, another new body in place of the flesh—but the same corruptible flesh, both of the just and of the unjust, will rise incorruptible [Col. 0097D], so that it may either suffer punishment for sins or remain in eternal glory according to its merits.

All human beings will rise. If all will rise, then all die, so that the death derived from Adam may rule over all his children. Yet the privilege remains in the Lord that is specially said of him: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV); his flesh did not see corruption. We have accepted this interpretation, transmitted by a very great multitude of the Fathers.

Nevertheless, there are also other equally catholic and learned men who believe that those who will be found alive at the Lord’s coming will be transformed into incorruption and immortality while their souls remain in their bodies, and that this will be reckoned for them as resurrection from the dead: they will lay aside mortality through transformation, not through death. Whichever view one accepts, one is not a heretic unless one becomes heretical through contentiousness. It is sufficient under the law of the Church to believe that there will be a resurrection of the flesh from death.

When we say in the Creed that at the Lord’s coming the living and the dead will be judged, we do not mean that the just and sinners will be judged, as Diodorus seems to think. Rather, “the living” means those who will be found in the flesh, who are believed either still to be destined to die or, as others hold, to be transformed, so that, once raised or renewed, they may be judged together with those who died previously [Col. 0098A].

After the resurrection and judgment, we must not believe that there will be a restoration of all things, as Origen deliriously teaches: that demons or impious human beings, as though cleansed by punishments after their torments, might return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or that human beings might be granted association with the just. He thinks this would accord with divine mercy, lest anything rational should perish among creatures, but that all should be saved in some manner. Rather, let us believe in the Judge of all and the just giver of rewards, who said: “The impious will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life” (Matt. XXV), so that they may receive the fruit of their works [Col. 0098B].

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I), and water, from nothing. While darkness still concealed the water itself and the water hid the earth, the angels and all the heavenly powers came into being, so that God’s goodness would not be idle but would have beings in whom, through many ages [Col. 0098C], he might display his goodness. Thus this visible world was made and adorned from the material that God had created.

Nothing incorporeal and invisible is to be believed to exist in nature except God alone—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is believed to be incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and holds all things together. For this reason he is invisible to all creatures, because he is incorporeal.

Every creature is corporeal. The angels and all the heavenly powers are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual natures to be corporeal because they are bounded in place, just as the human soul is enclosed by flesh, and as are demons, who possess the substance of an angelic nature. We believe that intellectual natures without flesh are immortal, since they have nowhere to fall and therefore do not require resurrection after a ruin [Col. 0098D].

Consequently, human souls did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, as Origen invents. Nor are they sown along with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latins affirm, as though the succession of nature required it. Rather, we say that only the body is sown through marital union.

The creation of the soul is known only to the Creator. By God’s judgment the body is joined, compacted, and formed; once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being consisting of soul and body may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance.

Nor do we say that there are two souls in one human being, as James and other Syrians write [Col. 0099A]: one animal soul, by which the body is animated and which is mixed with blood, and another spiritual soul, which supplies reason. Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in a human being, which both gives life to the body through its association with it and governs itself through its reason. It possesses freedom of choice, so that in the thought of its own substance it may choose what it wills.

We believe that only the human being possesses a substantial soul, which lives when separated from the body and retains its senses and faculties vigorously. It does not die with the body, as the Arab asserts, nor will it later perish, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially.

The souls of animals are not substances. They arise together with the flesh through the vitality of the flesh itself and end with the death of the flesh [Col. 0099B]. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are driven, so to speak, by all the impulses of nature. The human soul does not die with the flesh, because it is not sown with the flesh, as we said above. Rather, when the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, the soul is created and infused by God’s judgment, so that the human being may live within the womb and then proceed by birth into the world.

A human being consists of two substances only: soul and flesh. The soul has its reason, and the flesh has its senses; yet the flesh does not move these senses without the soul’s association, while the soul retains its rational faculty even without the flesh.

There is no third substance in a human being, namely spirit, as Didymus contends. Rather, the spirit is the soul itself, either because of its spiritual nature or because, as it breathes in the body, it is called spirit [Col. 0099C]. The soul is called *anima* because it is given for living or for giving life, animating the body.

But since a third element is introduced by the Apostle together with soul and body, let us understand “spirit” as the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle prays that this grace may remain whole in us and not, through our fault, be diminished or depart from us, because the Holy Spirit will flee what is feigned.

From the very first creation of the world, the human being was entrusted to the freedom of his will, so that, with the vigilance of the mind striving to preserve it, he might also persevere in keeping the commandment, if he wished to remain in that for which he had been created. But after he fell through the serpent’s seduction by means of Eve, he lost both the goodness of nature and the vigor [Col. 0099D] of his free will, though not his power of choice, lest what he corrected should not be his own sin, and lest what he had not regretted by his own choice should be forgiven without merit.

Freedom of choice therefore remains for seeking salvation—that is, rational will—but only after God has first admonished and invited the person to salvation, so that he may choose, follow, or act upon the opportunity for salvation, namely, through God’s inspiration. But that he should attain what he chooses, follows, or undertakes through that opportunity, we freely confess to be God’s work.

We have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy. That we assent to the saving inspiration lies within our power. That we attain what we desire in order to assent to the admonition is a divine gift. That we do not fall after obtaining the gift of salvation belongs to our vigilance [Col. 0100A] and equally to heavenly assistance. That we fall belongs to our power and our negligence.

There is one baptism, but it is found in the Church, where there is one faith, and where it is administered in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if some people have been baptized among heretics who baptize with the confession of the holy Trinity and then come to us, they are to be received as baptized, lest the invocation or confession of the holy Trinity be annulled. But they must first be taught and instructed in what sense the mystery of the holy Trinity is held in the Church.

When they understand and believe, or agree to confess, what is taught, they are to be confirmed in the integrity of the faith by the laying on of hands. If they are children or simple-minded people who cannot understand the teaching, those who present them according to the custom of baptism shall answer on their behalf. Strengthened by the laying on of hands [Col. 0100B] and by chrism, they are to be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.

But those who were baptized among heretics without the invocation of the holy Trinity and who come to us must, we decree, be baptized, not rebaptized. For we must not believe that those were baptized who were not immersed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit according to the rule established by the Lord. Such are the Paulianists, Proclianiborites, or Spurisifori; the followers of Photinus, now called Bonosians; the Montanists and Manichaeans, varied shoots of impiety; and others of their origin, order, or plague who introduce two unknown principles, as Cerdo and Marcion do; or contrary principles, as Manichaeus does; or three barbarous principles, as Secianus and Theodocus do; or many principles, as Valentinus does; or the teaching that Christ was a human being without God, as Cerinthus [Col. 0100C], Hebion, Harithemon, and Fotmus hold.

If any of these should come to us, they are not to be asked whether they have been baptized or not. They are to be asked only whether they believe the faith of the Church, and then they are to be baptized with ecclesiastical baptism.

I neither praise nor condemn receiving communion of the Eucharist every day. Nevertheless, I urge communion on every Lord’s Day, provided that the mind is not disposed toward sinning. For I say that someone who still has the will to sin is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified by it.

Therefore, even if someone is troubled by sin, but no longer has the will to sin, and, intending to communicate, makes satisfaction with tears and prayers, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, who is accustomed to forgive sins upon devout confession, let him approach the Eucharist [Col. 0100D] without fear and in confidence. I say this, however, of someone who is not weighed down by capital or mortal sins.

As for one oppressed by mortal crimes committed after baptism, I urge him first to make satisfaction through public penance and then, if he wishes, to be reconciled by the priest’s judgment and joined to communion, rather than receive the Eucharist to his own judgment and condemnation. We do not deny that mortal crimes may also be absolved through private satisfaction, but only after the person has first changed his secular way of life, confessed devotion to religion through correction of life, and shown continual—or rather perpetual—mourning, with God’s mercy. He must act contrary to the sins for which he repents and receive the Eucharist every Lord’s Day, supplicant and submissive, until death.

True penance is not committing what one must repent of and mourning what has been committed [Col. 0101A]. The satisfaction of penance is to exclude the causes of sins and not give access to their suggestions.

In the divine promises, let us expect nothing earthly or transitory, as the Melicians hope; not sexual union, as Cerinthus and Marcion deliriously teach; not anything pertaining to food or drink, as Terrenus, on the authority of Papias, together with Tertullian and Lactantius, accept; nor should we hope that Christ’s kingdom will exist on earth for a thousand years after the resurrection and that the saints will reign with him in delights, as Nepos taught. He fabricated a first resurrection of the just and a second of the impious, with ignorant nations that do not know God preserved in the flesh in the remote corners of the earth between these two resurrections of the dead [Col. 0101B].

After the thousand years of earthly rule, these nations are to be stirred by the devil to battle against the reigning just. While the Lord fights for the just, they are to be restrained by a rain of fire, and then, together with the other dead in impiety, they are to be resurrected in corruptible flesh for earthly punishments.

We believe that no one comes to salvation unless invited by God; that no one who has been invited works out his salvation unless God assists him; that no one deserves assistance unless he prays; and that no one perishes by the will of God, but by permission and according to the choice of his free will, lest the freedom of power once granted to human beings be forced into servile necessity.

Evil, or malice, was not created by God, but invented by the devil, who himself was created good by God [Col. 0101C]. Since he was entrusted with free will, as a rational creature, and had received the capacity for thought, he turned his knowledge of good toward evil. By thinking many thoughts he became the inventor of evil, and he envied in others what he had lost in himself. Not content to perish alone, he persuaded others, so that he who had been the inventor of his own malice might also become the author of that of others. Thus evil or malice spread among the other rational creatures.

From this we know that nothing is immutable by nature except God alone—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who cannot be changed from good, because he possesses goodness by nature and cannot be anything other than good.

The angels who persevere in the blessedness in which they were created do not possess goodness by nature in such a way that they could not be changed along with the others. Rather, by preserving a good will through their free choice, they preserved the goodness of their condition and their faith toward their Lord [Col. 0101D]. Hence the Lord himself rightly calls them holy angels: they maintained the holiness of their free will and did not deviate from the good by the example of their companions.

Marriage is good, but for the sake of children, not under the pretext of the lust of fornication. Continence is better, but it is not sufficient for blessedness if it is maintained solely for love of chastity. If it is chosen together with this intention in order to devote oneself to the Lord, it is good; otherwise, separation from marriage will seem rather a divorce than chastity.

Virginity is more precious than either of these goods, because it conquers both nature [Col. 0102A] and struggle: nature through bodily integrity, and struggle through the peace of chastity.

It is good to receive with thanksgiving whatever God has commanded to be eaten. To abstain from certain things, not as though they were evil but as though they were unnecessary, is not evil.

To moderate the use of meat according to necessity and season is properly Christian. To call marriage evil, or to compare it with fornication or sexual immorality, or to believe that foods are evil or created for an evil purpose for those who consume them, is not Christian. It belongs specifically to the Encratites [printed: Enerachitae] and Manichaeans.

To equate marriages with virginity consecrated to God, and to believe that those who abstain from wine or meat for love of chastising the body thereby gain no additional merit, is not Christian but Jovinianist [Col. 0102B].

With complete faith we must believe that blessed Mary, the mother of Christ God, gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin after giving birth. We must not accept the blasphemy of Helvidius, who said: “A virgin before giving birth, not a virgin after giving birth.”

We must not believe that the elements, that is, heaven and earth, will be destroyed by fire, but that they will be changed for the better. The form of the world—that is, its appearance, not its substance—will pass away.

It is good to distribute one’s resources to the poor with proper administration. It is better to give everything at once, with the intention of following the Lord, and, freed from anxiety, to lack possessions with Christ.

A man who has married two wives after baptism is not to be ordained a cleric [Col. 0102C]; nor is one who had one woman indeed, but a concubine rather than a lawful wife; nor one who took a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute in marriage; nor one who, overcome by anger or by a just or unjust fear, mutilated himself by cutting off any member of his body; nor one convicted of having taken interest or known to have performed on the stage; nor one who publicly laments mortal sins; nor one who at some time became insane in a frenzy or was afflicted by the devil’s breath; nor one who offers money through ambition, in imitation of Simon Magus.

The bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed martyrs, are to be honored with the utmost sincerity as though they were members of Christ [Col. 0102D]. Their basilicas, named after them, are to be approached with the most devout affection and the most faithful devotion, as places dedicated to divine worship. Anyone who acts against this judgment is considered not a Christian but an Eunomian and a Vigilantian.

For the baptized alone there is a path of salvation. We must not believe that any catechumen, however distinguished by good works at death, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, in which all the sacraments of baptism are completed.

The person to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest and responds when questioned. The martyr does the same before his persecutor: he confesses his faith and responds when questioned. After confession, the one is either sprinkled with water or immersed; the other is either sprinkled with blood or immersed in fire. The one receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands [Col. 0103A]; the other becomes a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in him.

The one communicates in the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the other dies together with Christ himself. The one confesses that he will renounce the works of the world; the other renounces life itself. All sins are forgiven in the one; in the other they are extinguished.

In the Eucharist, pure water alone must not be offered, as some are deceived by an appearance of sobriety. Rather, wine mixed with water must be offered, because wine too was present in the mystery of our redemption, when he says: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine” (Matt. XXVI). The water that was given after the meal was also mixed with it. Moreover, when his side was pierced by the lance, water came out with blood [Col. 0103B], showing that wine was expressed with water from the true vine of his flesh.

Our flesh is good, and very good, since it was created by the one and good God. It is not evil, as Sethianus, Opinatus, and Patricianus wish; nor the cause of evil, as Florinus taught; nor compounded from evil and good, as Manichaeus blasphemes. Since it is good by creation, it becomes good or evil for us through the soul’s free choice—not through a change of substance, but through the reward of its actions. For it is the flesh itself that is placed before the tribunal of Christ, in order that the soul may suffer in the body according to what it has done, whether good or evil.

In the resurrection from the dead, the form of the sexes will not be changed. A dead man will rise in the form of a man, and a woman in the form of a woman, not lacking sex, but retaining the natural appearance that belongs only to the condition of this life [Col. 0103C], lest the resurrection not be genuine if what rises is not what falls.

Before the Lord’s resurrection, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the debt of Adam’s transgression, until the authority of the Lord liberated them from their servile condition through his undeserved death. After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, all the souls of the saints are with Christ. When they depart from the body, they go to Christ, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with him they may be transformed into complete and perpetual blessedness.

Likewise, the souls of sinners, placed in hell under fear, await the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with them they may be turned toward eternal punishment.

We confidently believe that penance abolishes sins, even if someone repents of his offenses in the final breath of life and confesses his sins through public or suppliant lamentation [Col. 0103D]. For God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had been lost, remains immovable. Therefore, because his will does not change, whether through correction of life, if time is granted, or through humble confession, if life is immediately ended, forgiveness of sins may confidently be expected from him who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that the sinner should turn from destruction through repentance and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live.

If anyone thinks otherwise concerning God’s most just mercy, he is not a Christian but a Novatianist [Col. 0104A].

We are certain that the devil does not see the inner thoughts of the soul. We have learned, however, that he gathers them from bodily movements and indications of the emotions. The secrets of the heart are known by him alone to whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men.”

Not all our thoughts are always stirred up by the devil’s prompting. Sometimes they arise from a movement of our own free will [Col. 0104B]. Good thoughts, however, always come from God.

We do not believe that demons enter the soul substantially through an energetic force, but that they are joined to it by application and oppression. To enter the mind is possible only for the one who created it, who, subsisting incorporeally by nature, is capable of entering his own creation.

We have learned from God himself that even sinners can perform signs, wonders, and healings in the Lord’s name. When they help others through this presumption, they harm themselves through ambition for human glory, boasting in a false gift not deserved by their merits.

We rightly believe that a person can become a Christian through signs and wonders, but not yet a holy person if he acts with intemperate and harsh conduct. Through temperate and peaceful conduct, however, a person can become both holy and a perfect man of God even without the efficacy of signs [Col. 0104C].

No holy or just person is without sin; nevertheless, he does not thereby cease to be just or holy when he holds holiness with sincere devotion. We acquire holiness not through the powers of nature but through the assistance of our purpose by God’s grace. Therefore all the saints truthfully declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to mourn—if not through the accusation of conscience, then certainly through the instability of transgressive nature.

Passover, that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, cannot be celebrated before the passing of the vernal equinox and the beginning of the sixteenth day of the moon, the moon having been born in that same month.

Because of recent legislators who say that the soul alone was created in the image of God [Col. 0104D], so that, since God is rightly believed to be incorporeal, the soul too may be believed incorporeal, we freely confess that the image is found in eternity and the likeness in moral character.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0103]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Holy Scriptures, That Is, the Old and New Testament

[Col. 0103D]

The Old Testament is so called because, when the New came, it ceased. The Apostle refers to this (2 Cor. 5): “The old things have passed away; and behold, all things have become new.” The New Testament, on the other hand, is so named because it renews. For no one learns it except those who have been renewed from oldness by grace and who already belong to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven.

The Hebrews, following Ezra’s authority, count the Old Testament as twenty-two books, corresponding to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

The first order, that of the Law, consists of five books [of Moses]. The first is *Bresith*, which is Genesis; the second *Ellesmoth*, which is Exodus; the third *Vaiecra*, which is Leviticus; the fourth *Vaiedaber*, which is Numbers; the fifth *Helleaddabarim*, which is Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Thorath* and the Latins call “the Law.” Strictly speaking, however, “the Law” is the work given through Moses.

The second order is that of the Prophets, containing eight books. The first is *Josuae bennum*, called in Latin *Jesus Nave*; the second *Sobthim*, which is Judges; the third Samuel, which is First Kings; the fourth *Malachim*, which is Second Kings; the fifth Isaiah; the sixth Jeremiah; the seventh Ezekiel; the eighth *Tharistra*, that is, the book of the Twelve Prophets. Because these books are joined together on account of their brevity, they are counted as one.

The third order is that of the Hagiographa, that is, those who write holy things. It contains nine books.
