The first is Job; the second the Psalter, which is divided into five divisions; the third *Masloth*, which is Solomon’s Proverbs; the fourth *Coeleth*, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth *Sirasirim*, which is the Song of Songs; the sixth Daniel; the seventh *Dabretamin*, which is “Words of Days,” that is, Paralipomenon, also called the Chronicle; the eighth Ezra, which among the Greeks and Latins is divided into two books; the ninth Esther.

Together these five, eight, and nine books make twenty-two, as stated above. Some add Ruth and *Cinoth*, which in Latin is called the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, making twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament, corresponding to the twenty-four elders who stand in the presence of God.

Among us there is a fourth order of the Old Testament: those books that are not in the Hebrew canon. The first is the Book of Wisdom; the second Ecclesiasticus; the third Tobit; the fourth Judith; the fifth and sixth Maccabees. Although the Jews separate these among the apocrypha, the Church of Christ honors and proclaims them among the divine books.

In the New Testament there are two orders. The first is evangelical, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second is apostolic, containing fourteen Epistles: two by Peter, three by John, one each by James and Jude, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse of John.

Others divide the Old and New Testaments into seventy-two books. The first five are the books of the Law of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. These are followed by sixteen historical books: Joshua and Judges, one book each, together with Ruth; four books of Kings; two of Paralipomenon; Tobit and Esther; two books of Ezra; and two of Maccabees.

Above these are sixteen prophetic books: one each of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, together with one book for each of the Twelve Prophets. These are the prophetic books.

After these are counted eight books written in different meters among the Hebrews: Job; the book of Psalms; Proverbs; Ecclesiastes; the Song of Songs; Wisdom; Ecclesiasticus; and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Thus the books of the Old Testament total forty-five.

The New Testament begins with the four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. These are followed by the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul, after which come the seven canonical Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude. There are also the Acts of the twelve Apostles, whose seal is the Apocalypse of John, which is the revelation of Jesus Christ. [lacuna]

These are the seventy-two canonical books. For this reason Moses chose seventy elders to prophesy, and for this reason our Lord Jesus commanded seventy-two disciples to preach. Since seventy-two languages had been spread throughout the world, the Holy Spirit fittingly provided that there should be as many books as nations, so that peoples and races might be built up to receive the grace of faith.

These are the new and the old things brought forth from God’s treasury, through which all the mysteries of the sacraments are revealed. These are the two Seraphim who continually sing *hagios*—“holy”—in confession of the Holy Trinity and, uttering their hymn, break forth in song.

These sacred writings, these books, possess complete number and authority. Nothing else is to be compared with them. Whatever lies outside them is in no way to be received among holy and divine things.

These two Testaments are prefigured in many places in sacred Scripture. For they are the two millstones that the Law forbids to be separated or taken as a pledge, because neither Testament is to be removed from the other, since both are necessary for preparing heavenly bread, so that they may provide nourishment for souls.

Likewise, the two Cherubim placed beside the ark signify the two Testaments protecting the Church of God. The prophet Habakkuk likewise describes two living creatures, in whose midst God is made known.

The whole of both Testaments is divided in three ways: into history, morality, and allegory. These three are again divided in many ways: what has been done and said by God, by angels, or by human beings; what the Prophets announced concerning Christ and his body; what concerns the devil and his members; what concerns the old and the new people; and what concerns the present age, the future kingdom, and judgment.

## CHAPTER II. On the Authors of These Books

According to Hebrew tradition, the following are considered the authors of the Old Testament.

First, Moses set forth the cosmography of divine history in five volumes, which is called the Pentateuch. *Pentateuch* is derived from five volumes: for *pente* in Greek means “five,” and *teuchos* means “volume.”

The book of Genesis is so called because it contains the beginning of the world and the generation of the age. Exodus recounts the departure from Egypt and the exodus of the people of Israel, and for this reason it received its name.

Leviticus is so called because it treats the ministries of the Levites and the various sacrifices, and because the whole Levitical order is recorded in it.

The book of Numbers is so called because it enumerates the tribes that went out from Egypt and contains the description of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness.

Deuteronomy is called by a Greek word that is translated into Latin as “the second law,” that is, repetition, and as a prefiguration of the evangelical law. It contains what was written earlier in such a way that everything found in it is nevertheless new.

The book of Joshua received its name from Jesus son of Nun, whose history it contains. The Hebrews assert that Joshua himself was its author. In its text, after the crossing of the Jordan, the kingdoms of the enemies are overthrown, the land is divided among the people, and through its individual cities, villages, mountains, and boundaries, spiritual realities are prefigured, including the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem.

Judges is named from the leaders of the people who governed Israel after Moses and Joshua, before Saul, David, and the other kings existed. Samuel is believed to have published this book.

The Book of Samuel describes Samuel’s birth, priesthood, and deeds, and therefore received its name from him. Although this book contains the history of Saul and David, it is attributed to Samuel because he anointed Saul as king and David as the future king. Samuel wrote the first part of the book, while David wrote what follows, down to its end.

The book of *Malachim* is so called because it arranges in chronological order the deeds of the kings of Judah and of the Israelite nation. *Maloch* in Hebrew is translated into Latin as “of kings.” Jeremiah first brought this book together into a single volume, for previously it had been scattered among the histories of the individual kings.

*Paralipomenon* is a Greek word that we may translate as “things passed over” or “things remaining.” For matters omitted or not fully reported in Samuel or the Books of Kings are explained here in summary and briefly.

Some think that Moses wrote the Book of Job; others attribute it to one of the Prophets; still others believe Job himself wrote it after the wound of his suffering, reasoning that the one who endured the struggles of spiritual warfare should himself narrate the victories he sought.

Among the Hebrews, the beginning and end of the Book of Job are composed in prose. Its middle section, from the passage “Perish the day on which I was born” (Job 3) to “Therefore I condemn myself and repent” (Job 42), proceeds entirely in heroic meter.

The Book of Psalms is called *Psalterium* in Greek, *Nabla* in Hebrew, and *Organum* in Latin. It is called the Book of Psalms because, while one prophet sang to the psaltery, a chorus responded in song.

The Hebrew title in the psalms is written *isphr tha blm*, which is translated as “a volume of hymns.”

The authors of the psalms named in their titles are Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Jeduthun, the sons of Korah, Heman the Ezrahite, and others whom Ezra gathered into one volume.

The Hebrews hold that all the psalms are composed in metrical poetry. Following the practice of the Roman Horace and the Greek Pindar, they now proceed in iambics, now resound in Alcaics, now thunder in Sapphics, moving in trimeter or tetrameter feet.

Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, published three volumes according to the number of his names. The first is *Masloth*, which the Greeks call *Parabolas* and the Latins Proverbs, because in it he displays, through comparative likenesses, figures of speech and images of truth, while leaving the truth itself for readers to understand.

He called the second book *Coeleth*, which in Greek is called Ecclesiastes and in Latin “the Preacher,” because its discourse is not directed specifically to one person, as in Proverbs, but generally to opposing parties, teaching that everything we see in the world is fleeting and brief and therefore not to be desired.

He entitled the third book *Sirasirim*, which is translated into Latin as the Song of Songs. Through an epithalamial poem it mystically sings of the union of Christ and the Church.

It is called the Song of Songs because it is preferred above all the songs found in the sacred Scriptures, just as certain things in the Law are called holy, while the Holy of Holies is greater than they.

The poems of these three books are said to have been composed among their people in hexameter and pentameter verses, as Josephus and Jerome write.

Isaiah, more an Evangelist than a Prophet, published his book, whose entire text proceeds in eloquent prose. Its Song, however, proceeds in hexameter and pentameter verse.

Jeremiah likewise published his book together with the *Threni*, which we call the Lamentations, because they are used in sorrowful circumstances and at funerals. In them he composed a fourfold alphabet in different meters. The first two are written as if in Sapphic meter: three connected verses beginning with a single letter conclude a heroic section. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and its verses begin with three letters, that is, three verses at a time. The fourth alphabet is like the first and second.

Ezekiel and Daniel are said to have been written by certain wise men. The beginning and end of Ezekiel are enveloped in many obscurities. Daniel announces the kingdoms of the world in the Syriac language and marks the time of Christ’s coming with the clearest proclamation.

These are the four Prophets called Major because they composed lengthy volumes.

The Book of the Twelve Prophets is marked by the names of its authors. They are called Minor because their discourses are brief, and therefore they are joined together in a single volume. Their names are Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

The book of Ezra is marked by the title of its author. In its text the discourses of Ezra and Nehemiah are included together. No one should be troubled by the fact that it is called one book of Ezra: the second, third, and fourth are not found among the Hebrews but are counted among the apocrypha.

### [Col. 0109A]

Ezra is believed to have written the book of Esther. In it the same queen is described as having, under the figure of the Church, rescued the people of God from servitude and death. After Haman—whose name is interpreted as “iniquity”—was killed, a celebration of the day was established for posterity.

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews. Hence even its title bears more strongly the mark of Greek eloquence. The Jews assert that it belongs to Philo; for this reason it is called Wisdom, because in it the coming of Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father, and his passion are clearly expounded.

The Book of Ecclesiasticus was certainly composed by Jesus son of Sirach, a Jerusalemite and grandson of Jesus the high priest. Among the Latins this book is marked with Solomon’s name because of the similarity and equality of its eloquence.

It is called Ecclesiasticus because it was produced with great care and judgment concerning the teaching of the whole Church and religious conduct. It is also found among the Hebrews, but is regarded as apocryphal.

It is entirely uncertain by which authors Judith, Tobit, and the Books of Maccabees were written. They bear, however, the names of those whose deeds they recount.

The four Evangelists separately composed the four books of the Gospels.

Matthew was the first to write the Gospel in Hebrew letters and language, beginning his evangelizing in Judea with Christ’s human birth and saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). He signified that Christ descended bodily from the seed of the patriarchs, as had been promised in the Prophets through the Holy Spirit.

Mark, filled with the Holy Spirit, wrote Christ’s Gospel in Greek. He followed Peter in Italy as his disciple. He began with the prophetic Spirit, saying: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord” (Mark 1), to show that after assuming flesh Christ preached the Gospel in the world. For Christ himself was also called a prophet, as it is written: “And I have appointed you a prophet among the nations.”

Luke, the most learned in Greek speech of all the Evangelists, wrote the Gospel in Greece as a physician for Bishop Theophilus. He began with the priestly Spirit, saying: “There was in the days of Herod, priest of Judea, a certain Zacharias,” indicating that after his bodily birth and the preaching of the Gospel Christ became a sacrifice for the salvation of the world.

For he is the priest of whom it is said in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). When Christ arrived, the priesthood of the Jews fell silent; the Law and prophecy ceased.

John wrote the Gospel last, in Asia, beginning with the Word, to show that the same Savior who graciously chose to be born and suffer for us was himself the Word of God before the ages, that he came from heaven, and that after his death he returned again to heaven.

These are the four Evangelists whom the Holy Spirit signified through Ezekiel in the four living creatures. They are called four living creatures because through the four regions of the world the faith of the Christian religion was spread by their preaching.

They are called living creatures because the Gospel of Christ is preached on account of the human soul. They were also full of eyes within and without, because the Gospels foresee what was spoken by the Prophets and what had been promised earlier. Their legs were straight because there is nothing crooked in the Gospels. They had six wings covering their legs and faces, for what had been covered was revealed at Christ’s coming.

The word “Gospel” means “good announcement.” In Greek, *eu* means “good,” and *angelion* means “announcement”; hence *angelus* is interpreted as “messenger.”

The Apostle Paul wrote fourteen Epistles. Of these, he wrote nine to seven churches; the others to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon.

As for the Epistle to the Hebrews, among most Latins it is uncertain whether it is his, because of the difference in style. Some suspect that Barnabas wrote it; others that it was written by Clement.

Peter wrote two Epistles bearing his name. They are called catholic because they were written not to one people or city only, but generally to all nations.

James, John, and Jude wrote their own Epistles.

The Acts of the Apostles recounts the beginnings of the Christian faith among the nations and the history of the nascent Church. It is established that Luke the Evangelist was the author of the Acts of the Apostles. In this work the infancy of the emerging Church is woven together and the history of the Apostles is preserved; hence it is called the Acts of the Apostles.

The Evangelist John wrote the Book of the Apocalypse at the time when he was handed over to exile on Patmos for preaching the Gospel.

“Apocalypse” is translated from Greek into Latin as “revelation.” Revelation means the manifestation of things that had been hidden, as John himself says: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known openly to his servants” (Rev. 1).

These are the writers of the sacred books. Speaking through the Holy Spirit, they composed them for our instruction, for rules of living, and for the standard of faith.

Other volumes are called apocryphal. They are called apocrypha, that is, “secret,” because they are brought into doubt. Their origin is hidden; nor is it evident through which fathers the authority of true Scriptures has reached us in a succession that is wholly certain and well known.

Even if some truth is found in these apocrypha, they have no canonical authority because of the many falsehoods they contain. The prudent rightly judge that the books should not be believed to belong to those to whom they are attributed. For heretics produce many works under the names of the Prophets and more recent works under the names of the Apostles. All these, under the name of apocrypha, have been excluded from canonical authority after careful examination.

## CHAPTER III. A Brief Annotation Indicating What Is Contained in the Sacred Canonical Books

Concerning, therefore, the discussion of the Old and New Testaments, the order of the books, and their number, I shall briefly and rapidly append short introductions to their contents.

Genesis, according to the historical account, describes the making of the world, the creation of humanity, the flood, the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the deeds of the patriarchs up to Israel’s entrance into Egypt.

Exodus contains the Hebrews’ servitude, the people’s departure from Egypt, the protecting cloud, the crossing of the Red Sea, and Pharaoh’s drowning with his chariots; the singing of glory; the encounters in the wilderness; the food of manna; the streams turned into sweetness; the commandments of the Decalogue; the battle with Amalek; the ark of the covenant; and the dedication and offering of the tabernacle.

Leviticus describes the law of sacrifices, the variety of histories, the garments of the high priests, and the ministries. It also arranges the kinds of food and the various sins, together with purifications and sacrifices.

### [Col. 0111B]

In Numbers the tribes that went out from Egypt are counted, and the mysteries of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness are signified.

In Deuteronomy, which is the second law, the things that Moses spoke to the people between Pharan and Hazeroth and as far as Kadesh-barnea are recounted: namely, commandments and promises, curses for sins, promises, and blessings. There Moses sings his song and pronounces blessings upon the children of Israel. There, having looked upon the promised land, he dies and is buried.

Some Hebrews count only four books as belonging to the Law—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers—and regard Deuteronomy as a repetition of these, as a kind of meditation on the Law. Their reasoning is that the first four contain the proper accounts of the events, whereas this book contains them all as if by repetition.

In the book of Joshua, the children of Israel, led by Joshua, cross the Jordan and are circumcised in the age [saeculo; reading uncertain]. Then, after the Canaanite nations have been overthrown, they receive the land of their inheritance by lot.

The book of Judges contains Israel’s sins and servitudes, together with its cries and God’s acts of mercy.

The Book of Ruth presents the history of that Moabite woman, from whose family line David descended. The Hebrews append this little book to Judges because the events recorded in it are said to have occurred at that time. The Latins, however, because it traces the royal line of David, arising from Ruth the Moabite, more correctly argue that it belongs with the Book of Kings.

The Book of Kings, although among the Latins it has been arranged in four parts because of its length, is divided among the Hebrews into two volumes. In the first of these Samuel writes that the ark of the Lord passed from the Jews to the nations, that the priesthood of Eli was mystically transferred to Samuel, and that the rule of King Saul was transferred to David.

The book of *Malachim* arranges in chronological order the kings of Judea and of the Israelite nation and their deeds. It relates that Israel itself, because of the error of idolatry, was carried away into Assyria. Finally, it teaches that Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem, captured and led away the ruler and the people, and overthrew the city and the temple.

### [Col. 0112A]

Among the Hebrews, Paralipomenon is contained in a single volume and is called by them *Dabrejamin*, that is, “Words of Days.” Among us, because of its length, it is divided into two parts.

This history contains the order of generations and times, and in it there is no small instruction in the sacred Scriptures. For matters that in the history of the Old Testament were either wholly omitted in their proper places or perhaps not fully arranged are completed here in summary and briefly. Its sequence, drawn alongside the kings or kingdoms, reaches all the way to the time at which the text of the Books of Kings also ends.

The Book of Job contains the grievous losses and afflictions of that holy man, the insulting words of his comforters, and his lamentations in which he deplores the misery of the whole world. It also contains God’s consolations to him from the whirlwind and his double reward of goods at the end.

From his own sufferings and words, Job expressed an image of Christ. His wife represents those attached to carnal things who, placed within the Church, scandalize the life of spiritual people by their conduct. His friends represent heretics and the figure of perverse doctrines. Elihu, who presses Job with severe reproach, signifies those who preach within the Church arrogantly and who, through pride of heart and the vanity of knowledge, display whatever they say as examples of arrogance.

The Book of Psalms, although contained in a single volume, was not produced by one and the same author. For there are nearly ten prophets who wrote them at different times: Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Heman, Jeduthun, the sons of Korah, Asir, and Aahab or Ezra. Some are also thought to belong to Haggai and Zechariah.

Concerning those without titles, the tradition of the ancients is this: when the superscription naming an author has preceded them, the others that follow without a title are believed to belong to that same author.

This book is marked by allegorical and typological mysteries. In particular, it resounds with the fact that Christ was born, suffered, and rose again: truly the whole instrument of the Psalms resounds with these things.

It must nevertheless be understood that among the Hebrews all the psalms had been mixed together and disordered. Ezra was the first to gather them into one volume, arrange them in order and number, and, through the hidden mystery of the sacrament, place some before others in the sequence, although the later ones may appear later in time. Thus, according to the course of the history, Psalm 3 is later than Psalm 50, but because of the mystery it is earlier in the order. The others are arranged in the same way, because the Holy Spirit preordained them as he wished.

Solomon published three volumes. The first is the Book of Proverbs; the second is called Ecclesiastes; the third bears the title Song of Songs. In these three books he composed the disciplines of three kinds by which knowledge of things is attained.

In the first he teaches ethics, that is, morality; after this physics, which comprehends the quality of nature; and finally theory, that is, contemplation.

In Proverbs, while teaching moral matters through a common manner of speaking, he offers a higher understanding and fits the preservation of the commandments and the instruction of heavenly doctrine into brief words and concise maxims. Proverbs explain one thing under other words and are understood differently from the way they are spoken: they contain more in the force of their meanings than in the sound of their words. The Greeks call them *paraemias* [*parathimiai*].

Ecclesiastes, examining the nature of things, reproves everything in the world as fleeting and vain and, having observed the fragility of all things, warns that the world must be renounced.

In the Song of Songs, rising beyond visible things and contemplating what is heavenly or divine under the form of bridegroom and bride, he declares the unity of Christ and the Church. Stirring the soul to love heavenly things, he urges it to attain communion with God.

The following must not be omitted. Our teachers transmit that among the Hebrews there was an observance that no one was permitted to read this book unless he was already a man of perfect knowledge and strengthened faith. Otherwise, through the weakness of infancy and ignorance of faith, its teaching might not so much educate unstable minds as turn them toward bodily desires.

Their teachers customarily hand all the Scriptures over to children, including those they call *deuteres*, but reserve these four until the end: the beginning of Genesis, concerning the creation of the world; the beginning of Ezekiel, where he writes about the Cherubim; its end, which contains the description of the Temple; and the Song of Songs.

The Book of Wisdom, which is called *Panarethon*, announces openly the coming of Christ, who is the Wisdom of God the Father, and his passion.

Ecclesiasticus describes at abundant length the discipline of almost all moral matters and the conduct of holy religion. It is called Ecclesiasticus because it was delivered in the midst of the assembly of the people, that is, before the Church. Because of its great similarity of meaning and equality of eloquence, it is marked with Solomon’s name. It is established that this book was published by Jesus son of Sirach and was held in equal veneration with the other books of the sacred Scriptures.

### [Col. 0113D]

The prophet Isaiah, whose name is interpreted as “the salvation of the Lord,” after a coal sent from the altar purified his lips so that he might be made worthy of the prophecy of the Holy Spirit, beholds in a mystery two Cherubim representing the two Testaments, with twelve wings, that is, the Apostles, who rushed about with winged speed through their preaching. They cover the face and feet of the one seated on the throne of God, that is, they conceal either the things that existed before the beginning of the age or those that will exist after the form of this world has passed away.

After the vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem, however, he turns his prophetic discourse against the other nations surrounding them and, according to the character of their places and the diversity of their lives, announces the evils that are to come upon them.

After Jerusalem’s captivity, he threatens the ruin of Babylon; then the slaughter [possibly “destruction”] of the Philistines, the devastation of Moab, the extermination of Damascus, the disturbance of Egypt, and the desolation of the deserted sea; also the siege of Edom, the flight and destruction of Arabia, the ruin of the Valley of Zion, and the overthrow of Tyre or of the four-footed creatures.

Figuratively, however, in the vision the synagogue of Judea is cast down and the Church is joined to the Lord. In the ruin of Babylon, the confusion and pride of the whole world are condemned, and its end is shown. In the devastation of Moab, the error of secular knowledge is changed into silence and mourning. In the overthrow of Egypt, the idolatries of the whole world are destroyed and the building of the Lord’s temple is proclaimed. In the crushing of the Philistines, the mourning of those who reject Christ’s yoke and raise themselves against the knowledge of God is revealed.

Through Damascus the preaching to the nations and the ruin of the Jewish people are shown. Through the burden of the deserted sea, the temptation of this age is declared, and the things that are to come upon it are revealed.

Through Idumea the sun of righteousness rises for the nations, and darkness is removed from the Jewish peoples. Through Arabia the water of baptism is proclaimed, to be offered to those who flee the errors or blasphemies of the nations.

Through the Valley of Zion, the destruction of Jerusalem and of the heretics who have fallen from the height of the Church is proclaimed. Through Tyre, the nations are urged to abandon error and turn to Christ the Lord. The rest of Isaiah concerns either Christ, the Church of the nations, or the consummation of the world.

He prophesied for approximately seventy years under four kings of Judah, successive in order and lineage: Uzziah, Jotham [the transmitted text reads “Mathan”], Ahaz, and finally Hezekiah, under whom a large part of his volume is woven together down to the end of the prophecy.

Jeremiah is interpreted as “the exalted prophet of the Lord.” He speaks simply and is easy to understand, and in all his words and sufferings he presented an image of our Redeemer.

After he had destroyed the kingdoms of the devil in the type of Christ and built up the empire of righteousness and faith, he was commanded to preach among all nations: namely, Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, and Kedar; and against the kingdoms of Assyria, Elam, and Babylon.

He saw a watchful rod of divine correction and power. He also saw a seething pot, that is, he beheld the Jewish people burning with the fire of carnal desires. He saw two baskets of figs as a prefiguration of the two peoples. He descended to the potter’s house and saw the reduction of the former vessel and the restoration of the new one, signifying the decline of the former people and the succession of the future one.

He also took the cup of punishment and offered it to all the nations. He received a linen loincloth as an example of the Jewish people and, when it had rotted, cast it away in despair beyond the rivers of the nations.

He also displayed Babylon’s golden cup, by which the world was intoxicated—the deadly vessel of idolatry—and was commanded to cast into the Euphrates the book bound to a stone, to demonstrate the destruction of Babylon or, figuratively, of the whole world.

He rebuked sinners and summoned them to conversion. Finally, he lamented the ruin of Jerusalem, the destruction of the Temple, and the dispersion of the nation.

He began in the twelfth year of Josiah, king of Judah, and his prophecy extended through four kings: Josiah, Eliakim, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, under whom Jerusalem was overthrown. He prophesied for seventy-two years and four months, excluding the period during which, after Jerusalem had been overthrown, he was in Egypt with the people.

Ezekiel, whose name means “strength of God,” figuratively representing Christ, stands beside the river Chebar and, containing splendid mysteries, sees the likeness of the glory of God and the four living creatures in the likeness of the four Gospels, and wheels containing one another as a type of the two Testaments. He sees the charioteer—that is, Christ—shining below with the fire of judgment and above with electrum, that is, with the radiance of divinity. He also eats the book of divine law, in which are written the lament of penitents, the song of the righteous, and the woe of those who did not repent after sinning.

Afterward he receives a brick on which a representation of besieged Jerusalem is drawn; alternatively, mysteries are depicted under the type of Christ and of that same Jerusalem—that is, of the whole Church, which was formed from the side of Christ. This prophet is also commanded to sleep on his left side as a type of the death of sinners, who, placed on the left, will endure eternal punishments. Finally, he is commanded to sleep from the left side onto the right because of the hope of those who, through the amendment of their conduct, will obtain the glory of the resurrection.

He sees on the ground two rods joined to one another in the likeness of circumcision and the Gentiles, [Col. 0115C] or an eagle flying under Nebuchadnezzar, a figure of Christ, occupying the empire of the whole world with great wings and winged speed. Moreover, under the appearance of the prince of Tyre, he laments the blessedness of the devil, which he lost, and deplores his great ruin with lamentation. Finally, carrying a reed or cord, he measures, under the figure of the saints, the mystical Jerusalem.

Among these mystical matters, certain moral teachings also lie beneath the surface. He threatens the false prophets and commands the watchmen not to keep silent about wickedness. He also proclaims to sinners four punishments of vengeance and prophesies that souls will return to their bodies. He shows, too, that each person will render an account to the Lord for himself, and that the stain of a father’s sin will no longer harm holy offspring. In the figures of Oholah and Oholibah, he rebukes all the depravity of Samaria and Jerusalem and casts their shameful birth in their teeth. He also frequently calls the captives to repentance and, after their transgression, admonishes the people to return in conversion.

He prophesied while exiled in Chaldaea in the thirty-fifth year of his life and the fifth year of the captivity, and there completed his prophecy.

Daniel means “judgment of God.” He is also clearer than all the prophets in his testimony concerning Christ, because he not only proclaimed him, as the others did, but also defined the time of his incarnation and passion in sequence by the order of kings and the number of years, so that he seems not so much to prophesy future events as to narrate things already completed.

He frequently sees visions of four kingdoms and presents their differences under various images. He also shows that the Antichrist is the little horn, that is, one who will reign for a short time. He wrote much about the consummation of Israel or of the world, about the day of judgment, and about the kingdom of the saints. At the end of his prophetic book he includes the story of Susanna and the tale of Bel and the Dragon.

This book, among the Hebrews, is written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldaean language. He prophesied in Babylon, at the same time as Ezekiel.

Hosea the prophet, whose name means “saving,” is the first of the Twelve. He is deeper than the others in his sayings and more difficult to understand. He speaks to those tribes that were called Samaria, the house of Joseph, and Israel. Through Ephraim he rebukes the heretics who, withdrawing from the unity of the Church for whatever reason, became participants in idols. Through Samaria he indicates the error of those same heretics, who falsely claim to be guardians of God’s commandments while, under the pretext of truth, worshiping falsehood.

Historically, he declared that the Jews would believe in Christ at the end of time. He also foretold the third day of the Lord’s resurrection. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, at the same time as Isaiah.

Joel means “one who begins.” Proclaiming prophecy only concerning Judah and Jerusalem, at the beginning of his book he calls Jerusalem from luxurious banquets to mourning and also announces its destruction. He likewise proclaims the calling of the Gentiles and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the gathered believers.

He prophesied under Jotham, king of Judah, at the same time as [Col. 0116C] Micah.

Amos, whose name means “burden,” prophesied in Samaria and Jerusalem, describing three and four crimes of the nations under the figure of the whole world. The first crime is that all sinned in Adam. The second is that, while in the state of nature, they did not understand the law because they had forgotten reason. The third is that of those who did not obey the law that had been given. The fourth, unpardonable, is that of those who did not believe in Christ.

Because of these crimes the Lord thunders that he will bring fire—that is, the sentence of eternal judgment. He proclaims Christ’s coming in accordance with the truth of the Lord, saying: “I establish the thunder, and create the spirit, and announce his Christ to human beings” (Amos IV). The remaining matters that he related concerning Amaziah, Jeroboam, and Israel are to be referred figuratively to the heretics.

He prophesied under King Uzziah, at the time when Hosea and Isaiah also prophesied.

Obadiah, whose name means “servant of the Lord,” is the shortest of all the Prophets in number of words, but equal in the grace of his mysteries. Speaking against Idumaea, he mystically rebukes the pride of the former Edom—namely, his audacity in killing his brother Jacob, that is, Christ, on Mount Zion, that is, Jerusalem. He announces the future salvation and the Holy One, who is the Lord, and he thunders that the Lord’s kingdom will be established on the mountain that figuratively represents the Church of the Gentiles.

He prophesied under Josiah, king of Judah, at the time when Micah also prophesied.

[Col. 0117A] Jonah, whose name means “dove,” represents Christ’s passion, death, and resurrection both in his speech and in his shipwreck. He was either thrown from the ship into the sea, as from the cross onto the earth, or, having been received in the belly of the sea-monster, he was confined for three days and three nights as in the burial of the earth.

Because he foretold the repentance of the world through the figure of Nineveh, he subsequently bears the type of the Jews, who not only did not wish the salvation of the Gentiles to come, but, when it came, regarded it with hostility. Nineveh signifies the figure of the Gentiles, whereas Jonah in this passage represents the Jews. For just as the salvation of the Ninevites provoked Jonah to jealousy, so the redemption of the Gentiles became a stumbling block to the Jews.

It is fitting, too, that he is said to have sat opposite the city toward the east [Col. 0117B] under the shade of an ivy plant. Thus that same people, separating itself from the salvation of the Church and wasting away in grief, strives to move its tongue against Christ—that is, against the East of the Church—sitting under the shade of the Law. This shade was almost dried up because, when Christ came, the old things passed away, and behold, all things became new (2 Corinthians V).

He prophesied under Uzziah, king of Judah, at the time when Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah prophesied.

Micah means “Who is this?” or “Who is such a one?” or “humility.” The prophet Micah threatens Samaria with the anger of the Lord because of its idols and announces the coming destruction of the people of Israel. He also indicates the place in which Christ would be born.

He prophesied under Uzziah, at the time of Zephaniah.

Nahum, whose name means “consoler,” announces that the idols of the nations will be destroyed, as well as Jerusalem, the city of blood. After its destruction, the feet of the one announcing peace—that is, the coming of the Savior—proclaim it.

Habakkuk, “embracing,” or “a strong wrestler,” at the beginning of his book describes the devil with his members and his ways; at the end, he announces the coming and passion of the Savior.

Zephaniah, “watchman of the mysteries of God,” sees the future captivity of the city of Jerusalem by the Romans, through the voice of a cry from the Fish Gate and through the crushing of the hills—that is, of Mount Zion, which is the hill of Jerusalem. He also proclaims the overthrow of other nations and thunders the terror of divine judgment.

He also speaks against Moab and Ammon; through them, as neighboring peoples of the people of God, heretics close to Catholic sacraments are rebuked. He prophesies the third day of Christ’s resurrection and announces that, at Christ’s coming, the whole world will serve under one yoke of the Lord.

He prophesied under Josiah, as did Jeremiah.

Haggai, whose name means “festive,” in the text of his prophecy commanded that the temple of the Lord be restored. He proclaims the crushing of the nations, or foretells the shaking of the whole world, and under the figure of Zerubbabel prophesies Christ’s coming. He prophesied in the seventieth year of the captivity of the people, preceding Zechariah in his prophecy by only two months.

Zechariah, whose name is interpreted as “memory of the Lord,” after prophesying the Lord’s anger against the fathers, saw a man seated on a red horse, signifying through the figure of Christ’s body the rosy blood of his passion or the merits of the people of the Gentiles. He also sees four horns, or smiths, representing the nations that scattered Judah and Israel and crushed them beneath a heavy burden.

Likewise he beholds Jesus, clothed in the filth of the flesh and in mortality under the figure of a priest. When these have been removed, he sees him clothed in immortality and glory. He also sees the stone, which is Christ, having seven eyes—that is, the fullness of the sevenfold Spirit.

Among these things he beholds a tower and an extinguished firebrand, that is, the devil; a lampstand, representing Christ, with seven lamps, which are the seven gifts of the Spirit; and two olive trees placed to the right and left of the lampstand, representing the type of the two Testaments.

He also takes up two rods, “cord” and “beauty,” as a type of the Jews and the Gentiles. Then he sees two women—that is, the peoples of the Jews and the Gentiles—lifting an ephah, that is, diabolical teaching, into another place. He also sees a mass of lead, which is the exceedingly heavy weight of sin, or a flying scroll on which human sins and punishments are recorded.

He sees four chariots running under one yoke of evangelical preaching. After this he sees horses sent out for the preaching of the world: the first red, through the suffering of martyrdom; the second black, through the squalor of repentance; the third white, through the brightness of baptism; the fourth variegated, through the variety of virtues.

He also sees the trumpets of the saints, bearing the figure of those through whom the Lord sings his commandments to the world. He sees an angel in whom two opposing peoples are joined, or, figuratively, he describes a stake as Christ fixed in the hearts of the peoples. He also sees the work and intention of the shepherds of the Antichrist on the left. He sees a horse as a figure of the people of the heretics and its rider as the devil. He also proclaims a fountain opened in the house of the true David in the laver of regeneration.

Whatever else he wrote either recounts the Lord’s coming, or his passion, or the end of the age, or his judgment. He prophesied for two years under Darius, king of the Medes, at the same time as Haggai, in the seventieth year of the temple’s destruction and the captivity of the people.

Malachi, whose name means “Angel of the Lord,” at the beginning of his book demonstrates the hatred of the Jews toward Esau and the love of the younger people toward Jacob. In what follows he rejects the former sacrifices of Judaea and announces that the sacrifice will be transferred to the Gentiles. At the end he announces the Lord’s coming.

He also proclaims the day of judgment, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishments of the wicked. He declares that John was sent before the Lord’s first coming and announces that Elijah is to be sent before the second coming.

Among these matters he explains certain moral teachings appropriate to discipline. He rebukes the people—or the priests—who despise the name of God and violate his sacraments with polluted offerings and sacrifices. He also teaches that bishops ought to be learned and blameless and that they should instruct the peoples in the truth without respect of persons. He rebukes the contentious, commands that tithes and first fruits be paid to the people of the Church, and reproves those who despise their wives and seek the love of other women. Likewise, he rebukes those who, lamenting their own misery, praise the prosperity of those who enjoy the good things of this world.

He was the last to prophesy in Babylon, at the time of Haggai and Zechariah.

Esdras writes that, when the period of the captivity had been completed, under Cyrus, king of the Persians, the people of God returned to Jerusalem. Under Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak the priest, or under Nehemiah, the walls of Jerusalem, the temple, and the altar were restored, the rights of the priests reinstated, and the worship of the holy religion adorned with many works and with gifts from the nations and the princes of the Persians.

Although the books of the Maccabees are not included in the canon of the Hebrews, they are nevertheless counted by the Church among the histories of the divine books. They foreshadow the battles between the leaders of the Hebrews and the peoples of the Persians, the battle of the Sabbaths, and the noble triumphs of the Maccabees, as well as the treaty of friendship with the Roman people and the embassies.

Likewise, concerning the preface to the New Testament: although the preaching of the Gospels is fourfold, it is nevertheless one, because it proceeded from the one and same mouth of the Trinity. These are the four rivers flowing from one source of Paradise, which in a twofold manner proceed from one mouth and pour throughout the whole world the heavenly streams of grace and faith through the ministry of their words.

This is that chariot of the Lord in Zechariah, carried throughout the world, by which he subdues to himself the necks of all nations under a gentle yoke. These are also the creatures that the prophetic vision records under the appearance of four living beings: a man, a lion, a calf, and an eagle.

The first, as a man, signifies the order of human birth. The second, like a roaring lion, immediately at the beginning of its discourse makes known the strength of divine power. The third, introducing the priest’s victim, intimates death in the likeness of a calf. The fourth, following the manner of an eagle, eagerly flies across heaven and earth and penetrates the birth of the Word through the understanding of hidden mysteries.

Of these, the three creatures that walk on the earth, following the active life, treated only those matters that Christ as man performed temporally on earth. The fourth creature, with the sharpness of contemplation, gazes upon heavenly things and gradually arranged many of the mysteries of divinity in its works.

Of these, the first and the last proclaimed what they heard from Christ’s mouth, or what they saw him do and perform; the two remaining, those in the middle, proclaimed only what they learned from the Apostles. Matthew wrote his Gospel in Judaea; afterward Mark in Italy; third, Luke in Achaia; last, John in Asia. Of these, only Matthew touched upon the history of the preaching in Hebrew style; the others published theirs in the eloquence of the Greek language.

Paul set down fourteen of his epistles of preaching in writing. Of these, he wrote some to seven churches because of the type of the sevenfold Church, preserving rather than exceeding the number of the mystery, because of the sevenfold efficacy of the Holy Spirit.

He wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Thessalonians, to the Colossians, and to the Hebrews. He later published the remaining letters to individual persons, so that he might again turn that number seven toward the mystery of unity.

The subjects of these Epistles are as follows. First, he praises highly the faith of the Roman people. He rebukes the Corinthians with a twofold teaching. Among the Galatians he excludes the works of the Law through the grace of faith. He magnifies the Ephesians in the faith they received. He praises the Colossians because they stood firm in faith. He rejoices that the Philippians guarded the Gospel. In the first Epistle he boasts that the Thessalonians grew in faith and works; in the second, that they bravely endured persecutions.

Through Timothy and Titus he instructs the Churches. He asks Philemon concerning the reformed slave Onesimus. Finally, he strengthens the Hebrews who had believed in Christ but later, frightened by Jewish persecutions, had withdrawn from the faith, and he calls them back to the grace of the Gospel.

Peter wrote two Epistles, which are now called Catholic. He wrote them to those who, having believed from the circumcision, were living scattered among the nations. They seem to some to be rather plain, yet they are so full of profound meanings that those who can search out the sense of divine knowledge through them behold great mysteries revealed to them as through a small receptacle.

James, the brother of the Lord, wrote one Epistle pertaining to the edification of the Church. Its meaning seems to pour an immense clarity of knowledge into its readers.

The Apostle John wrote three Epistles. The first, commending the duty of charity, is wholly concerned with love of God and fraternal affection. The second, written to the Elect Lady, urges the practice of love; it also identifies deceivers and warns that heretics should be avoided. He wrote the third to Gaius, in which he praises him for his devotion to truth and his work of mercy. He then identifies the insolence of a certain Diotrephes and bears witness to the truth concerning Demetrius.

The Epistle of Jude rebukes those who blaspheme Christ and certain immoral persons under the example of the wicked, who, because of their pride and sensuality, have been handed over to everlasting fires. Concerning them he admonishes the Church to rebuke them and exhort them to repentance.

The history of the Acts of the Apostles describes the faith and work of the nascent Church. Its author is Luke the Evangelist. It contains what was accomplished in Judaea and among the Gentiles through the grace of the Holy Spirit, both by Peter and by the other Apostles.

In John’s Apocalypse, after he is commanded to write to the seven Churches, he beholds the Son of Man seated on a throne, the twenty-four elders, and the four living creatures falling down before the throne. In the right hand of the one seated is a book sealed with seven seals, in which war, scarcity, death, the cry of those slain, and the end of the world are recorded.

It then writes of twelve thousand servants of God who are marked on their foreheads. There seven Angels sound trumpets, followed by hail and fire mingled with blood upon the earth. There a third of the earth is burned by fire; a third of the sea becomes blood; and the shining stars themselves lose a third of their brightness. There locusts of demons are brought forth from the smoke of the well, receiving power to harm those who are not marked with the blood of the Lamb.

Moreover, the Evangelist eats the book of the covenant, sweet in the mouth through the preaching of the word but bitter because of the difficulty of the work. He measures the heavenly temple. He describes the words of the twenty-four elders, the ark of the covenant, and the woman clothed with the sun, as well as Michael’s battle with the dragon and the dragon’s downfall.

He also beholds the figure of the Antichrist, possessing seven heads of kingdom, horns of power, and the number of a man. Among these things he recounts the Song of the new covenant, observes Angels carrying scales, and likewise sees the destruction of the beast and the blessedness of those who preserved the garments of their bodies—that is, themselves—without the pleasure of the flesh.

He then relates the destruction of the Babylonian harlot, the marriage of the Lamb, the coming of judgment, the destruction of the Antichrist, the eternal punishment of the devil, and, finally, the resurrection of the dead, the renewal of heaven and earth, and the description of Jerusalem. He also describes the river of Baptism, which cleanses the world, and the tree of life, our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Library

“Library” takes its name from the Greek, because books are stored there. For *biblion* means “of books,” and *theca* means “a repository.”

Esdras the scribe restored the library of the Old Testament after the Law had been burned by the Chaldaeans, when the Jews had returned to Jerusalem. Inspired by the divine Spirit, he corrected all the books of the Law and the Prophets that had been corrupted by the nations and arranged the whole Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

Among the Greeks, the tyrant Pisistratus is believed to have first established a library. Xerxes afterward carried it away to Persia after it had been enlarged by the Athenians and after he had burned Athens. Much later, Seleucus Nicator brought it back to Greece.

From this arose among kings and other cities the zeal to collect volumes of various nations and to translate them into the Greek language through interpreters. Later Alexander the Great, or his successors, devoted themselves to furnishing libraries with every kind of book, especially Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, exceedingly skilled in all learning. He rivaled Pisistratus in his zeal for libraries and brought into his own library not only the writings of the nations but also the divine Scriptures.

For in his time seventy thousand books were found at Alexandria. He also asked Eleazar the high priest and arranged for the Scriptures of the Old Testament to be translated from Hebrew into Greek by seventy interpreters, and he kept them in the Alexandrian library.

Indeed, as some maintain, they were separated individually into separate chambers and interpreted everything through the Holy Spirit in such a way that nothing was found in one of their copies that differed from the others either in wording or in the order of the words.

There were also other interpreters who translated the sacred writings from Hebrew into Greek, such as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. There is also that common translation whose author is not apparent; for this reason, lacking the interpreter’s name, it is called the fifth edition.

Moreover, Origen discovered the sixth and seventh editions through remarkable labor and compared them with the other editions. The presbyter Jerome, equally skilled in three languages, likewise translated these Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin and rendered them with elegance. His translation is rightly preferred to the others, for it is both more faithful to the words and clearer in the transparency of its meaning.

## CHAPTER V. On the Diversity of Short Works

[Col. 0122B]

There are three kinds of short works.

The first kind consists of *Excerpta*, which are called *scholia* in Greek. In them, matters that seemed obscure or difficult are touched upon briefly and in summary.

The second kind consists of *Homilies*, which the Latins call *verbum* (“a word”); these are delivered before the people.

The third consists of *Tomi*, which we call books or volumes. Homilies speak to the common people; *Tomi*, that is, books, are concerned with more extensive discussion.

A dialogue is an exchange between two or more persons, which the Latins call *sermones* (“discourses”). For what the Greeks call *dialogoi*, we call *sermones*. A discourse is so called because it is “sown” between the two parties. Hence Virgil says: “They were sowing many things among themselves.”

A treatise is a multifaceted exposition of one subject, because it handles a meaning by touching upon many ways of understanding it in itself.

A discourse, a treatise, and a word differ. A discourse requires another person; a treatise is directed specifically toward oneself; a word is directed toward everyone. Hence one also says: “He addressed a word to the people.”

Commentaries are so called as if from *commenta* (“things devised”). They are interpretations, such as commentaries on the law and commentaries on the Gospel.

An apologetic is a defense, in which certain people customarily respond to their accusers. It consists solely in defense or denial, and its name is Greek.

A panegyric is a licentious and wanton form of speech in praise of kings; in composing it, people flatter them with many lies. This evil arose among the Greeks, whose frivolity, equipped with skill and incredible abundance of speech, raised up many clouds of falsehood.

The books of the Fasti are those in which kings and consuls are recorded. They are named from *fasces*, that is, from the powers of office. Hence Ovid’s books are also called the *Fasti*, because they were published concerning kings and consuls.

A proem is the beginning of a speech. Proems are the beginnings of books, fitted before the narration of the case to prepare the ears of the listeners. Many skilled in Latin have preserved this name without translation. Among us, however, the term is translated as *preface*, as though it meant “a preliminary speech.”

Precepts are teachings that instruct either what should be done or what should not be done. What should be done, for example: “Love the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy VI), and: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus XX). What should not be done, for example: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (ibid.).

Likewise, the precepts of the pagans either command or forbid. They command what should be done, as in: “Naked, plow; naked, sow.” They forbid, as in: “Do not plant the hazel among the vines, nor seek the upper branches.”

Among the Hebrews, Moses was the first to write precepts. Among the Latins, the seer Marcius was the first to compose precepts, among which is the following: “Speak last; act first” [the transmitted text is uncertain].

“Parable” and “problem” indicate by their names that they ought to be examined more deeply. A parable presents the likeness of some matter. Although the word is Greek, it is now used as a Latin term. It is well known that in parables, which are called likenesses of things, matters are compared with the things under discussion.

Problems, which in Latin are called propositions, are questions containing something that must be resolved through discussion. A question arises when one asks whether something exists or what sort of thing it is.

An argument is so called as though from *argutum* (“cleverly devised”), or because it is cleverly invented to establish matters.

The Greeks properly call a letter *epistola*, which is translated into Latin as “sent.” *Styla*, or *styli*, means “sent” or “sent forth.” Before the use of parchment, messages in letters were written on smoothed wooden tablets; hence their bearers were called *tabellarii*.

A codex is a collection of many books; a book is a single volume. The word *codex* is transferred from the codices of trees or vines, like *caudex* (“trunk”), because it contains within itself a multitude of books, as though of Romans [the final comparison is obscure].

A *volumen* is a book, so called from rolling, as among the Hebrews there are the volumes of the Law and the volumes of the Prophets.

A *liber* is the inner layer of bark that clings to the wood. Virgil says: “The deep bark clings to the elm.” Hence the thing in which we write is also called a *liber*, because before the use of paper or parchment, volumes were made and joined together from the bark of trees. For this reason writers were also called *librarii*, after the books of trees.

Those who sell books were formerly called *bibliopolae*. The Greeks call a book *biblos*. *Librarii*, that is, copyists, are also called *antiquarii*. But *librarii* are those who write both new and old works, whereas *antiquarii* write only old works; hence they received their name.

The scribe received his name from writing, the function being expressed by the quality of the word. The instruments of the scribe are the reed and the pen. Through these, words are impressed upon pages. The reed belongs to a tree; the pen to a bird. Its tip is divided in two while unity is preserved throughout the rest of the body—I believe because of the mystery, so that the Old and New Testaments might be signified by the two points, through which the mystery of the Word is expressed, poured out in the blood of the Passion.

The reed is called *calamus* because it deposits liquid. Hence among sailors *calare* means “to lower” or “to place.” The pen is called *penna* from *pendere*, “to hang” or “to fly,” for it belongs, as we have said, to birds.

The leaves of books are so called either from their resemblance to the leaves of trees or because they are made from *folles*, that is, skins, which are customarily stripped from slaughtered animals. Their parts are called pages because they are joined to one another.

Lines of writing are commonly called *versus* because the ancients wrote in the manner in which the earth is plowed. They first drew the stylus from left to right; then they turned from below and again moved toward the right. Such lines are still called *versus* by country people.

A *scheda* is something still being corrected and not yet reduced to book form. It is a Greek word, as is *tomus*.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Canons of the Gospels

Ammonius of Alexandria first devised the Canons of the Gospels. Eusebius of Caesarea later followed him and composed them more fully. They were made so that through them we might discover and know who among the other Evangelists said similar things and who said things proper to himself.

There are ten in number.

1. The first contains the numbers in which all four said the same things: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
2. The second contains those in which three said the same things: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.
3. The third contains those in which three said the same things: Matthew, Luke, and John.
4. The fourth contains those in which three said the same things: Matthew, Mark, and John.
5. The fifth contains those in which two said the same things: Matthew and Luke.
6. The sixth contains those in which two said the same things: Matthew and Mark.
7. The seventh contains those in which two said the same things: Matthew and John.
8. The eighth contains those in which two said the same things: Luke and Mark.
9. The ninth contains those in which two said the same things: Luke and John.
10. The tenth contains matters that each of them said individually and distinctively.

Their arrangement is as follows. Beside each Evangelist, a certain number is attached to the chapters. Beneath these numbers there is a kind of panel marked with red pigment, indicating in which canon the number beneath the panel is located.

For example, if it is the first panel, it belongs to the first canon; if the second, to the second; if the third, to the third. Proceeding in this manner, one reaches the tenth. Therefore, if, after opening any Gospel, one wishes to know which of the other Evangelists said similar things, one takes the adjacent chapter number and looks for that number in the canon it indicates. There one will find who said what. Then, in the body of the text, one will find, in each Gospel, the passages sought that are designated by those numbers and that the Evangelists are said to have spoken concerning the same matters.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Canons of the Councils

*Canon* is Greek; in Latin it is called a *rule*. A rule is so called because it leads rightly and never draws something elsewhere. Others say that it is called a rule either because it governs, because it provides a standard for right living, or because it corrects something distorted and crooked.

The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. In the preceding years, while persecution was raging, no opportunity was given for instructing the peoples. Consequently, Christianity was divided into various heresies, because the bishops were not permitted to assemble together except in the time of the aforementioned emperor.

He granted Christians the freedom to gather openly. Under him also, the holy fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea from every city of the world and, in accordance with the Evangelical and Apostolic faith, handed down the Creed after the Apostles.

Among the other councils, there are four venerable synods that principally embrace the whole faith, like the four Gospels or the four rivers of Paradise.

The first, the Council of Nicaea, consisting of 318 bishops, was held while Constantine Augustus was emperor. In it, the blasphemy of the Arian impiety concerning the inequality of the Holy Trinity was condemned. That is, Arius asserted that God the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father, and the same holy synod defined the contrary through the Creed.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] The passage is exceedingly corrupt and seems to require restoration as follows: Arius asserted that God the Son was not consubstantial with God the Father; the holy synod defined the contrary through the Creed.]

The second synod, consisting of 150 fathers, was assembled at Constantinople under the elder Theodosius. It condemned as a heretic the bishop Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God, and demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son. It supplied the form of the Creed that the whole confession of Greeks and Latins proclaims in the Churches.

The third synod, the first Council of Ephesus, consisting of 200 bishops, was held under Theodosius Augustus the Younger. It condemned Nestorius with a just anathema because he asserted two persons in Christ, showing that one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

The fourth synod, that of Chalcedon, consisting of 630 priests, was held under the emperor Marcian. In it, with one judgment of the fathers, it condemned Eutyches, the Constantinopolitan abbot, who declared one nature of the Word of God and the flesh, as well as his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and once again Nestorius together with the remaining heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ God was born from the Virgin in such a way that we confess in him the substance of both the divine and the human nature.

These are the four principal synods that proclaim the doctrine of the faith in its fullest form. But if there are other councils that the holy fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, decreed, their decisions remain established with the full force of the authority of these four; their acts are contained in this work.

We understand *synod* to be translated from the Greek as “company” or “assembly.” The name *council* (*concilium*) is derived from Roman custom. For when cases were being heard, everyone came together and deliberated with a common purpose. Hence *concilium* was named from common purpose, as though from *communicilium*. For *cilia* are the eyelashes.

Hence *considium* is also called *consilium* (“counsel”), with the letter *d* passing into *l*. An assembly (*coetus*) is a meeting or gathering, from *coire*, that is, “to come together.” Hence it is also called a *conventus*, just as an assembly or council is formed from the association of many into one.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Paschal Cycle

[Col. 0125D]

Bishop Hippolytus was the first to write about the Paschal cycle, in the time of the Emperor Alexander. After him, the highly esteemed authors Eusebius of Caesarea, Theophilus of Alexandria, Prosper, likewise an Aquitanian by birth, and Victorinus published various cycles, enlarging the calculations concerning this same feast. The blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, calculating its reckoning for ninety-five years—five times nineteen—most briefly noted on which day of the calendar, or under which moon, the Paschal solemnity ought to be celebrated. [Col. 0126A]

It is called a cycle because it is arranged in a circle and, as though set out in a ring, completes the sequence of years without variation and without any artificial contrivance. Hence poems composed in a simple form for any subject were called cyclical. From this also comes the term *laterculum*, because it contains the sequence of the courses of the years. After its completion one must return to the beginning.

In ancient times the Church celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, whichever day it happened to fall on. The holy Fathers prohibited this practice at the Council of Nicaea, determining that one should observe not only the Paschal moon—[the text then proceeds to inquire]—but also the day of the Lord’s resurrection. For this reason they extended Easter from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first, so that Sunday [Col. 0126B] would not be omitted.

The word *Pascha* is not Greek but Hebrew. Nor is it derived from *passion*—although *pascimin* [perhaps *Paschin*] is said in Greek to mean “to suffer”—but it is called *pascha* from the Hebrew word for “passing over,” because at that time the people of God passed over from Egypt. Hence also in the Gospel (John XIII): “When Jesus knew that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father.”

Its night is kept vigil throughout because of the coming of our King and God, so that the time of his resurrection may find us not sleeping but watchful. There are two explanations for this night: either because during that same night he received life again when he suffered, or because at the hour at which he rose he will later come to judge.

We celebrate Easter in such a way that we recall not only Christ’s death and resurrection, but also examine [Col. 0126C] the other matters attested concerning him, for the purpose of signifying the sacraments. Because of the beginning of new life and the new person whom we are commanded to put on and to put off the old, purging out the old leaven so that we may be a new dough—for “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V)—the first month of the new [months] among the months of the year has therefore been mystically assigned to the celebration of Easter.

That Easter is celebrated on a day of the third week—that is, on whichever day falls between the fifteenth and the twenty-first—signifies this: throughout the whole period of the world, which is conducted according to the number seven, this sacrament has now disclosed the third age. The first age was before the Law; the second was under the Law; the third is under grace, where [Col. 0126D] the sacrament previously hidden in prophetic mystery has now been revealed. For this reason also, on account of these three ages of the world, the Lord’s resurrection lasts three days.

The fact that the Paschal day is sought during the seven days from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-first is because of the number seven, by which the totality of things is often signified; this number is also attributed to the Church because it resembles totality. Hence the apostle John wrote in the Apocalypse to seven churches (Apoc. I). The Church, while still established in this mortality of the flesh, is signified in Scripture by the name of the moon, on account of its very mutability.

The varying practices of opinion concerning the Paschal feast sometimes generate error. [Col. 0127A] The Latins seek the moon of the first month from the third day before the Nones of March through the third day before the Nones of April; and if the fifteenth moon falls on a Sunday, they defer Easter to another Sunday. The Greeks observe the moon of the first month from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day of the Nones of April; and if the fifteenth moon falls on a Sunday, they celebrate holy Easter. Such disagreement between the two groups therefore disturbs the Paschal rule.

A common year is one that has only twelve moons, that is, 354 days. It is called common because two such years often proceed joined together in such a way that they follow one another in the Paschal solemnity. An embolismic year, however, is always solitary. [Col. 0127B]

An embolismic year is one that is shown to have thirteen lunar months, that is, 384 days. It is the year divinely revealed to holy Moses, in which those who lived farther away were commanded to celebrate the Passover in the second month. The name *embolismus* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “additional increase,” because it makes up the number of days lacking from common years, in which eleven lunar days are found to be missing.

Embolismic and common years are discovered as follows. If there are 383 days from the fourteenth moon of the preceding Easter to the fourteenth moon of the following Easter, the year is embolismic; if there are 354, it is common.

[Col. 0127C]

A leap day is one day added every four years. For each year, a quarter of an *as* accumulates; when it has completed an *as* in the fourth year, it makes a leap year. It is called *bissextus* because “twice six” multiplied makes an *as*, which is one day; similarly, *quadrans* derives from multiplication by four, since the sun makes the bissextile year under the course of the days.

Intercalary days are so called because they are inserted so that the reckoning of the moon and sun may agree. *Calare* means “to place”; *intercalare* means “to insert,” or, as others wish, *calare* means “to call.” For the Greek verb *kalo* means “I call.” They say that the pontiff, after the people had been called into the Capitol near the senate-house, at the *curia calabraria*, which is close to Romulus’ hut, announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones. He pronounced the days occurring on the fifth by saying the word *kalo* five times, and those occurring on the seventh by repeating it seven times. [Col. 0127D]

The Greeks call them *epacts*; the Latins call them annual lunar additions. These revolve upon themselves through the number eleven up to thirty, and the Egyptians add them so that the lunar measurement may be brought into agreement with the solar reckoning. The moon is known to shine according to its course for twenty-nine and a half days. Thus the lunar year contains 354 days, and eleven days remain in relation to the course of the solar year; the Egyptians add these, and therefore they are called additions. Without them one cannot determine what day of the moon it is in any year, month, or day.

These epacts are always found on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in whatever moon falls on that day. They are contained in a nineteen-year cycle. But when they have reached twenty-nine epacts, which is the nineteenth cycle, in the following year one must not add eleven to twenty-nine and announce thirty-eight; instead, after subtracting thirty, one returns to the beginning and announces eleven.

[Col. 0128A]

# Chapter IX. On the Canonical Offices and on What Is Read and Sung in the Church

It is clear that there are many kinds of offices, but the principal one is that which is performed in sacred and divine matters. *Officium* is derived from *efficere*, “to accomplish,” as though it were *efficium*, with one letter changed for the elegance of speech; or certainly because each person should do what harms no one but benefits everyone.

The evening office is at the beginning of night. It is named from the star Vesper, which rises as night begins. Concerning this office the Psalmist says: “The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXI). [Col. 0128B] The lifting of the hands signifies pious activity, whether exercised in almsgiving or carried out in some commendable manner of life. The evening sacrifice perhaps signifies that offering which religious devotion customarily presents to the Lord at the end of life, when we practice repentance and cleanse ourselves with humble supplication, as it is said in the fiftieth psalm: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.”

Our evening comes when, with death approaching, we leave this light. It is therefore necessary that we frequently admonish no one to despair, but rather to wipe away his final deeds with a fountain of tears.

The morning office is at the beginning of light. It is named from the star Lucifer, which rises as morning begins. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “In the mornings I will meditate [Col. 0128C] on you” (Ps. LXII). For he returns to what he said above: “To you I keep watch from the light” (ibid.). The faithful rightly keeps watch in the mornings, since even amid his prosperity he cannot forget the author of light. To such people the Apostle says: “You are sons of light and sons of the day” (I Thess. V). Through the significance of these two periods it is shown that God must always be praised by day and by night.

*Missa* occurs at the time of the sacrifice, when the catechumens are sent outside, the Levite crying: “If any catechumen remains, let him go outside.” It is called *missa* because those who are known not yet to have been regenerated may not be present at the sacraments of the altar.

A choir is a multitude gathered for sacred things. It is called a choir because at first they stood around the altars in the form of a crown. Others have said that *chorus* derives from harmony, which consists in charity, because if it does not possess charity it cannot respond suitably. When one person sings, it is called *monody* in Greek and *sicinium* in Latin; when two sing, it is called *bicinium*; when many sing, it is a choir. [Col. 0128D]

A choir is an assembled multitude of voices harmonized for sweetness. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing psalms to him with the tambourine and psaltery” (Ps. CXLIX). He now says that the Lord’s name is to be praised in the choir—in that choir which suffers no dispersion, no weariness, and no scandal, but, gathered through the excellence of its merits, abides always in the dearest unity. Another psalm explains what sort and size this choir is: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” [Col. 0129A] (Ps. CXII).

*Antiphon* is translated from Greek as “reciprocal voice,” namely, when two choirs sing psalms alternately, changing their order, or when one responds to one. The Greeks are said to have invented this kind of singing.

The Italians transmitted the responsories. Those who sing them call them responsories because, when one has ended, another responds. The difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person speaks the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses.

It is called a reading because it is not sung like a psalm or hymn, but is read only. In the former there is melody; in the latter only pronunciation is required.

[Col. 0129B]

A canticle is the voice of one singing in gladness. A psalm is so called because it is sung to the psaltery, which history reveals the prophet David used with profound mystery. These two terms are set against each other alternately in certain psalm titles according to musical art. For “the canticle of a psalm” is when the voice of the singer later expresses what the instrument plays. “The psalm of a canticle,” however, is when the art of the accompanying instrument imitates what the human voice has first uttered.

A psalm is named from the psaltery. Hence it is not customary for it to be composed from another work.

There are three stages in singing: first, that of the *succentor*; second, that of the *incentor*; third, that of the *accentor*.

[Col. 0129C]
