Some wish *diapsalma* to be a Hebrew word meaning “always the same,” because it confirms that the things between which it is placed are everlasting. Others consider it a Greek word meaning an interval in singing psalms: a *psalm* being what is sung, and a *diapsalm* the silence inserted during the singing. Just as in a psalm the joining of voices is carried along in song, so the diapsalm is their separation, displaying a certain rest within the distinct continuation. Hence it is also probable that the sentences should not be joined in singing wherever a diapsalm has been inserted, because it is inserted to indicate a change of meanings or persons.

A hymn is the song of those praising. In Greek it is interpreted in Latin as *laus*, “praise,” because it is a song of joy and praise. Properly speaking, hymns contain praise of God. If there is praise but not of God, it is not a hymn. If, however, it is said and sung in praise of God, then it is a hymn. Its opposite is the *threnus*, which is a song of lamentation and mourning.

*Alleluia* is the interpretation of two words, namely “praise God,” and it is Hebrew. *Ia* is one of the ten names [Col. 0129D] by which God is called among the Hebrews. *Amen* means “truly” or “faithfully,” and it too is Hebrew. These two words, *amen* and *alleluia*, may not be translated completely into the language of Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, or pronounced in another language. Although they can be interpreted, the Apostles nevertheless preserved the antiquity of their proper language because of their greater sacred authority.

For these names are so sacred that John also reports in his Apocalypse that, through revelation by the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly army, like the voice of many waters and mighty thunder, saying “amen” and “alleluia” (Apoc. XIX). Therefore both words ought to be spoken on earth just as they resound in heaven.

*Hosanna* cannot be wholly transferred in the interpretation of another language. *Osi* is interpreted as “saving”; *anna* is an interjection signifying the movement of the soul in a suppliant attitude. *Osi anna* is said in full, but we, corrupting the middle vowel and eliding it, say *osanna*, as happens in verses when we scan them. For the first letter of the following word, arriving, excludes the last letter of the preceding word. In Hebrew it is therefore said *osanna*, which is interpreted as “saving things,” with either “your people” or “the whole world” understood. [Col. 0130A]

*Offertory* received its name for the following reason. *Fertum* means an offering that is presented on the altar and sacrificed by priests. From this it is called *offertory*, as though derived from *fertur*, “it is offered.” It is called an *oblation* because it is offered.

[Col. 0130B]

Gifts are properly called divine presents; those of human beings are called *munera*. For they are called services when the poor render them to the rich in place of gifts. Thus a *munus* is given to a human being, but a *donum* to God. Hence in temples also we speak of *donaria*, offerings.

*Munera* are also those things received or given for souls. Two things are offered: a gift and a sacrifice. A gift is whatever is made of gold, silver, or any other material. A sacrifice, however, is a victim and whatever is burned or placed on an altar.

Everything given or dedicated to God is either dedicated or consecrated. What is dedicated is given through words, and hence receives its name. Those who think that dedication signifies consecration are therefore mistaken.

The ancients called it *immolation* because the victim was placed upon the mass of the altar and slaughtered. Hence slaughter follows immolation. Nowadays, however, [Col. 0130C] the term immolation is appropriately applied to the bread and chalice. *Libation* is the offering of the chalice alone. Hence the saying: “And he shall pour a libation of the blood of the grape” (Gen. XLIX). So too one of the secular poets says: “Now pour libations, he says, to Jupiter.” To pour a libation, therefore, properly means to pour out; the name was taken from a certain Liber, who discovered the use of the vine in Greece.

# Chapter X. On Victims, Whole Burnt Offerings, and Sacrifices, and What Their Several Kinds Signify

[Col. 0130D]

Among the ancients, *hostiae* were sacrifices made before they went to meet enemies. *Victimae* were sacrifices that they offered after victory over conquered enemies; victims were greater sacrifices than hostiae. Others thought that *victima* was so called because it fell when struck, or because it was led, bound, to the altars.

A *holocaust* is an offering in which everything offered is consumed by fire. In ancient times, when they administered great sacrifices, they used to consume entire victims in the sacred flame; these were called *holocausta*. In Greek, *holon* means “whole,” and *kausis* means “burning”; thus *holocaust* means “wholly burned.”

Among the Latins, *ceremonies* are all sacred rites, which the Greeks call *orgia*. Properly, however, the learned thought that *ceremonies* was derived from *carere*, “to lack,” as though *carimoniae*, because human beings lacked for their own use the things offered in divine rites. This name is also used in the sacred writings.

Others believe that *ceremonies* properly refers to Jewish observances, namely abstinence from certain foods according to the Old Law, because those who observe them lack the things from which they abstain.

[Col. 0131A]

*Sacrifice* is said as though it meant “a sacred act,” because it is consecrated through mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s Passion endured for us. Hence, at his command, we call this the body and blood of Christ. Although it is made from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament through the invisible working of God’s Spirit.

The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and chalice *Eucharist*, which is translated into Latin as “good grace.” And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

Five kinds of offerings were commanded by the Law to be brought for sacrifice: those of cattle, sheep, goats, birds, fine flour, and libations. Thus, in that same context, hostiae, victims, holocausts, sacrifices, and libations are mentioned as having been offered.

Cattle—cows and calves—[Col. 0131B] signify either the works of the Lord’s Incarnation, or the cultivators of the Lord’s field, that is, teachers, or the practitioners of the commandments of the Law.

Sheep and lambs signify either the Savior himself, who, according to Isaiah, was led like a sheep to the slaughter (Isa. LIII), and is shown by John to be the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John I), or they signify all simple and innocent people in the Church.

Goats or kids offered as victims signify either the flesh of the Savior, which was without sin yet was offered to God the Father for the sins of the human race, so that through his death the author of sin, the Devil, might be slain; or they signify penitents for their sins, who kill themselves for God through the affliction of the flesh.

Birds signify either Christ’s humanity—for through the turtledove [Col. 0131C] and the dove, Christ’s flesh joined to the Spirit is mystically shown, offered to God in the sacrifice of a pleasing fragrance during the Passion—or they signify contemplation in the perfection of the saints.

Flying creatures are people devoted to contemplation, who do not mix themselves at all with earthly affairs. Even if necessity should demand it, they immediately fly back to higher things, aided by the testimony of the Gospel in which the Lord says: “Consider the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matt. VI).

Therefore, a person devoted to contemplation and perfected in the consideration of higher things—for this is what the matters mentioned above have taught—if he offers his manner of life as an offering, should present his gift from turtledoves or doves, that is, in spiritual knowledge and gentleness. For this work requires that his consideration of the Law not exceed its bounds by becoming occupied with vain things.

The turtledove possesses knowledge, so that by its example [Col. 0131D] the people of the Jews were reproached, as Jeremiah proves. For he says: “The turtledove, swallow, and stork observe the time of their coming, but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord” (Jer. VIII).

The dove is clean and simple, and announces the presence of the Holy Spirit. Such ought to be those who devote themselves to contemplating the Scriptures. Hence Hezekiah says: “I will meditate like a dove” (Isa. XXXVIII).

Fine flour is the sacrifice of a libation, or the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, which is consecrated on the altar and received by the faithful for the increase [Col. 0132A] of their salvation. Alternatively, it expresses the figure of the Catholic Church, which mystically is the body of Christ and abounds in spiritual grace.

It is formed from suitable members, like fine flour collected from many grains of believers. Separated from the letter by the mill of the Law and the Gospels, joined together through the water of baptism, anointed with the oil of chrism, solidified by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and made through humility of spirit into a sacrifice pleasing to God, it is an offering.

Similarly, joined together from many persons like grapes in a cluster, crushed in the press of the Passion and temptations, it pours forth spiritual wine.

We read in the Scriptures that the Lord rejected the victims of cattle [Col. 0132B] and the legal sacrifices and desired a spiritual sacrifice. Hence the saying: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. XLIX). And again: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls,” he says, “or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (ibid.). “The sacrifice of praise will honor me; and there then is [the one] to whom I will show God’s salvation.”

Elsewhere: “I will go around and offer in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation; I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord” (Ps. CXV). Hence in the psalm the holy Church, dedicating herself entirely to God, says: “I will offer you whole burnt offerings rich in marrow, with incense” (Ps. LXV), and what follows.

The command that God’s offering be without leaven and without honey indicates that nothing voluptuous, nothing sweet according to this world, and nothing lacking some sharp element of truth pleases God. Hence the Passover is eaten with bitter herbs.

By contrast, [Col. 0132C] salt is commanded to be mixed into all sacrifices, so that everything we offer for the honor of Christ may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

The oil offered in sacrifice signifies that whatever we spend on the worship of Christ and the devotion of the saints we should do entirely with cheerfulness: “Nothing,” as the Apostle says, “from sadness or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

Thus, in a moral sense, we offer a calf to God when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational impulses; a kid when we conquer wantonness; a dove when we preserve simplicity; and a turtledove when we maintain chastity. This species of bird is said to preserve one faithful marriage.

We offer fine flour and unleavened bread [Col. 0132D] when we conduct our present life without malice and wickedness. For example, a person offers fine flour when he offers a manner of life devoted to agriculture, navigation, or some other ordinary occupation, yet sprinkled with oil, because every soul needs the oil of divine mercy, and no one can escape the present life unless the oil of heavenly compassion is present to him.

It must also be noted that, in relation to mortality, the weight of temptations is expressed by the oven; firmness of spirit and strength of mind by the frying pan; and manifold assault is fittingly signified by the griddle.

# Chapter XI. On the Divine Sacraments, Where It Is Shown What Must Be Done in Them by Human Beings

[Col. 0133A]

A sacrament occurs in a celebration when an act is performed in such a way that it is understood to signify something which must be received as holy. The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood of the Lord. They are called sacraments because, under the covering of bodily things, divine power works the salvation of these same sacraments in a more hidden manner. Hence they are called sacraments from hidden or sacred powers.

They are therefore fruitfully performed within the Church because the Holy Spirit, dwelling in it, secretly effects the same result through the sacraments. Whether they are administered by good or bad ministers within the Church of God, [Col. 0133B] nevertheless, because the Holy Spirit mystically gives them life—the Spirit who once appeared visibly in apostolic times—the gifts are neither increased by the merits of good administrators nor diminished by the works of bad ones: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III). Hence in Greek it is called *mysterion*, because it contains a hidden dispensation.

*Baptism* is translated from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” It is called immersion because there a person is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and becomes something altogether different from what he was.

Previously we were disfigured by the ugliness of sins; in the immersion itself we are made beautiful through the whitening of virtues. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up, as though made white?” (Cant. III).

Its mystery is completed in no other way than under the designation [Col. 0133C] of the Trinity, that is, through the naming of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the Lord says to the Apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

For just as every word is established by three witnesses (Deut. X), so the sacrament is confirmed by the threefold number of the divine names.

The reason baptism is given through water is this. The Lord wished that the invisible reality should be bestowed through a fitting, tangible, and visible element, over which the Holy Spirit was also borne in the beginning (Gen. I). For just as water cleanses the body externally, so through its ministry the soul too is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit.

Its sanctification takes place as follows. When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends [Col. 0133D] from heaven and sanctifies the waters through himself, having healed them; and they receive the power of purification, so that in them both flesh and soul, defiled by sins, may be cleansed.

It must also be known that although apostolic teaching (Eph. IV) proclaims one faith and one baptism, there are nevertheless many kinds of baptism that cleanse a person from sins and confer progress in holiness.

For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, as he was about to ascend into heaven, the Lord said to his disciples: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I).

Here it must be noted that the Lord’s baptism in the Holy Spirit, about which John had foretold, does not refer only to the time when the Apostles and the other faithful of that period were baptized with water for the remission of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit given them by the Lord. It also refers to the time when, sent by the Lord himself, they received more fully the same gifts of the Holy Spirit from heaven. [Col. 0134A] Even now, whoever receives baptism for the remission of sins is baptized in the Holy Spirit, through whose gift all sins are washed away and people are helped to advance in good works.

Again, the Savior is read to have said of himself in the Gospel: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and I am constrained until it is completed” (Luke XII). In this he clearly intimated the sacrament of his Passion, since through the shedding of his blood he washed his body—that is, the holy Church—from the filth of all sins. Hence it is written: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Apoc. I).

For this reason also [Col. 0134B] the martyrdom endured by the faithful for Christ’s name is believed to be the purification of all sins, as the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). Concerning this the Truth himself testifies, saying: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). And again: “Whoever wishes,” he says, “to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever loses his soul for my sake will preserve it for eternal life” (Matt. XVI).

Moreover, there are other forms of cleansing by which souls are purified from transgressions and sins. Souls are believed to be released from the bonds of sins [Col. 0134C] through confession and true repentance accompanied by contrition and tears.

Hence there is the testimony of James: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (Jas. V). The Psalmist likewise says to the Lord: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities; I said, ‘I will confess my iniquities to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Ps. XXXI). And elsewhere: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI).

By “bed” we understand bodily pleasure, which a person can wash with tears, even if they are few, if he happens through heavenly inspiration to grieve over it. The “couch” signifies the accumulation of sins, which we are commanded to water—that is, to wash more abundantly—so that from sinners we may become righteous, from mourners joyful, and from the sick completely healthy.

[Col. 0134D]

That true repentance cleanses a person and leads him to the heavenly kingdom is shown by the Lord, who says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. IV).

A person is also cleansed from the filth of the soul through good works and almsgiving. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. XXV). Whoever cleanses his own deeds through the pursuit of a good way of life washes his hands among the innocent.

The Savior also says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI). And elsewhere it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Tob. IV).

[Col. 0135A]

Pure prayer also helps a person obtain eternal salvation. Preaching of the word of God helps as well. Pure love of true charity also helps. Hence James says: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (Jas. V). And again: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (ibid.).

Finally, the Savior showed that love brings about the remission of sins when, speaking to Simon in the Gospel about the sinful woman who watered his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with perfume, he said: “Amen, I say to you, many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII). Hence it is also written elsewhere: “Charity covers a multitude of sins,” and, “Charity covers all transgressions” (Prov. X).

[Col. 0135B]

*Chrism* is called *unction* in Latin from the Greek. From its name Christ too is so called, and after the washing a person is sanctified. For just as the remission of sins is given in baptism, so through anointing the sanctification of the Spirit is applied. This derives from the ancient discipline by which people were accustomed to be anointed for the priesthood and kingship; from this also Aaron was anointed by Moses.

Although this is performed bodily, it advances spiritually, just as in the grace of baptism the visible act is that we are immersed in water, while the spiritual effect is that we are cleansed from sins. This is also signified by the ointment which the sinful woman is said to have poured over Jesus’ head.

The laying on of hands is performed so that, through the laying on of hands, the Holy Spirit, the Advocate, may be invited. Then that Paraclete willingly descends from the Father after the bodies have been cleansed and blessed; and, recognizing the baptismal water as though it were his former seat, he rests upon it. For we read that in the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters (Gen. I).

Concerning the two remaining sacraments, namely the body and blood of the Lord, one may ask why, among all the fruits of the earth, he chose wheat and wine especially for this purpose, as though these surpassed all the fruits of the earth in dignity and became more precious than all others.

We believe that this can be explained as follows. The Lord preferred that the sacraments of his body and blood be received by the mouths of the faithful and made into their nourishment, so that through a visible work an invisible effect might be shown.

For just as material food nourishes and strengthens the body externally, so the word of God nourishes and strengthens the soul inwardly: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV); and, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

[Col. 0135D]

The Truth himself says: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI). Christ’s flesh is truly food because it truly feeds a person and nourishes him for eternal life; and his blood is truly drink because it truly satisfies forever the soul that hungers and thirsts for righteousness.

People can have temporal life without this food and drink, but they absolutely cannot have eternal life, because this food and drink signifies the eternal fellowship of the Head and his members. “Whoever eats my flesh,” he says, “and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI). [Col. 0136A]

The sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is taken from the Lord’s table by some for life and by others for destruction. The reality itself, however, is life for every person and destruction for no one: whoever becomes a participant in it is joined as a member to Christ the Head in the heavenly kingdom. For the sacrament is one thing, and the power of the sacrament another. The sacrament is received by the mouth; by the power of the sacrament the inner person is nourished.

Therefore, because bread strengthens the body, it is appropriately called the body of Christ; and because wine produces blood in the flesh, it is referred to as Christ’s blood. Although these things are visible, once sanctified by the Holy Spirit they pass into the sacrament of the divine body.

# Chapter XII. On Exorcism

[Col. 0136B]

*Exorcism* is Greek; in Latin it is *conjuratio*, “conjuration,” or a speech of rebuke against the Devil, so that he may depart. Thus it is said in Zechariah: “And he showed me Jesus the great priest standing before the angel of God, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘The Lord rebuke you, Satan; the Lord rebuke you, who has chosen Jerusalem’” (Zech. III).

To rebuke and conjure against the Devil is exorcism. It must therefore be understood that it is not God’s creature in infants who is exorcized or expelled by breathing upon them, but the one under whose power are all who are born with sin. For he is the prince of sinners.

# Chapter XIII. On the Creed

[Col. 0136C]

Through the Greek language, *symbolum* is interpreted as “sign” or “knowledge.” When the Apostles were about to depart to evangelize among the nations, they established for themselves this sign or indication of their preaching.

It contains the confession of Trinity and Unity, the unity of the Church, and the entire sacramental teaching of Christianity. This creed of our faith and hope is not written on paper and with ink, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart.

# Chapter XIV. On Prayer and Fasting
Prayer is called a petition. For to pray is to ask, just as *exorare* means to obtain by entreaty. Prayer, moreover, is defined by place and time. By place, because it is not to be offered everywhere, since Christ forbids us to pray in public; rather, we should pray wherever opportunity presents itself or necessity requires it. For it is not counted as contrary to the commandment that the Apostles prayed and sang to God in prison, with the guards listening.

[Col. 0136D]

As for time, it is said: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V). But this applies to individual prayer. There is also an observance of certain common hours, which mark the intervals of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and likewise certain hours of the night. These hours of prayer have been divided for this reason: so that, if we happen to be detained by some task, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty. These times are found in Scripture. For the Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the disciples assembled together at the third hour (Acts II); and on the day when Peter experienced the vision of fellowship in the vessel, he had gone up at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer (Acts X). Likewise, at the ninth hour he went with John to the temple (Acts III), when he restored the paralytic to his former health.

[Col. 0137A]

We also read that Daniel observed these times in prayer. Certainly, we are taught by the discipline of Israel that we should worship at least three times a day. For we are debtors to the Three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. There are, of course, also other prescribed prayers, owed without any reminder at the beginning of day and night, or during the vigils; likewise, one should not first take food before prayer has been offered. For the refreshment of the Spirit must be placed before earthly things.

Whoever wishes his prayer to fly to the Lord should give it two wings: fasting and almsgiving. Then it rises swiftly and is heard.

Fasting is frugality in food and abstinence from nourishment. Its name is derived from a certain part of the viscera, which is always thin and empty and is commonly called the *jejunum*. Hence the name *jejunium* is thought to have been derived, because through hunger its viscera remain empty and drained.

[Col. 0137B]

Fasting is also called a station. The term “station” derives from a military example, because no joy that comes upon a camp breaks the soldiers’ station. For joy administers discipline more slowly, while sadness administers it more earnestly. Thus soldiers, never forgetful of their oath, are especially obedient to their stations.

Some, however, distinguish between fasting and a station. Fasting is the abstinence of anyone on any day indiscriminately, not according to a law but according to personal will. A station, on the other hand, is the observance of appointed rules, times, or days—for example, fasting on Wednesday and Friday, prescribed according to the ancient Law.

[Col. 0137C]

Concerning this station, that man said in the Gospel: “I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke XVIII), that is, on the fourth and sixth days of the week—Wednesday and Friday.

There are also appointed times established by legal and prophetic institutions at fixed periods: such as the fast of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months; or, as in the Gospel, those days “on which the bridegroom was taken away” (Matt. IX); or the observance of Lent, which throughout the world, by apostolic institution, is observed around the period bordering on the Lord’s Passion.

Some add a third kind to these, which they call *xerophagy*—that is, abstinence from moist foods. Hence this name was given because some people use dry foods.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Satisfaction of Repentance and on Exomologesis

[Col. 0137D]

Repentance (*poenitentia*) is so called as if from *punishment* (*punientia*), because a person punishes himself through repentance for what he has done wrong. For those who truly repent do nothing except ensure that what they have done wrong is not left unpunished. By not sparing themselves in this way, they obtain mercy from the One whose profound and just judgment no contemptuous person will escape.

[Col. 0138A]

Repentance is complete when one mourns past sins and does not admit future ones. The latter is like a second baptismal font: if, with the devil attacking, some sin should slip in, it is cleansed through satisfaction. Satisfaction consists in excluding the causes and suggestions of sins and in not repeating the sin thereafter.

Reconciliation is what is applied after the completion of repentance. For just as we are reconciled to God when we first turn from paganism, so we are reconciled when, after sinning, we return through repentance.

*Exomologesis* is a Greek word which is translated into Latin as *confessio*, “confession.” This word has a twofold meaning. For confession may be understood as praise, as in: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI); or it may mean that each person confesses his sins to the One from whom he seeks forgiveness, whose mercy is unfailing.

[Col. 0138B]

Thus the Greek word *exomologesis* expresses and designates the practice by which we confess our offense to the Lord—not as though he were ignorant, since nothing is hidden from his knowledge, but because confession is the declared recognition of a matter that was previously unknown to the person confessing.

Someone may have thought it useful and pleasurable to rob, commit adultery, or steal. But once he recognizes that these things expose him to eternal damnation, he confesses his error in light of that knowledge. Confession of error is confession that one must cease from it. Therefore one must cease from sins when confession is made. Confession comes first; forgiveness follows. Otherwise, the one who recognizes his sin but does not confess what he has recognized remains outside forgiveness.

[Col. 0138C]

Accordingly, *exomologesis* is a discipline of prostrating oneself or humbling oneself before others: bending the body through clothing and nourishment of sackcloth and ashes, darkening it with filth, casting down the spirit with grief, and changing those things in which one sins through a sorrowful treatment of oneself.

*Litaniae* is a Greek term; in Latin these are called *rogationes*, “supplications” or “petitions.” The difference between litanies and *exomologesis* is that *exomologesis* is performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are prescribed for entreating the Lord and obtaining some act of his mercy. But now both words are used with one meaning, and in common usage it makes no difference whether they are called litanies or *exomologesis*.

The term *supplicatio* has, in a certain sense, been retained from paganism. Among them, festivals were either regular or proclaimed. They were called proclaimed because the ancient poverty of the Romans offered sacrifices from contributions, or at least from the goods of condemned persons. Hence punishments (*supplicia*) are also called supplications (*supplicationes*), which were made from the goods of those who had suffered punishments. Sacred objects were made from the possessions of accursed persons.

## BOOK SIX

[Col. 0137]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Man and His Parts

[Col. 0137D]

Nature (*natura*) is so called from the fact that it causes something to be born. For it has the power of giving birth and of making. Some have said that Nature is God, from whom all things have been created and exist.

Kind or generation (*genus*) is so called from generating (*gignere*), and its name is derived from the earth, from which all things are generated; for in Greek they call the earth *Ge*.

Life (*vita*) is so called because of vigor, or because it contains the power of being born and growing. Hence trees are also said to have life, because they are generated and grow.

Man (*homo*) is so called because he was made from *humus*, earth, as it is also said in Genesis: “And God created man from the soil of the earth” (Gen. II). Properly speaking, man is called *homo* from *humus*. By a transferred usage, however, the whole man is understood from both substances—that is, from the union of soul and body.

The Greeks called man *anthropos*, because he looks upward, raised from the earth for the contemplation of his Maker. The poet Ovid expresses this when he says:

> While all the other animals look down toward the earth,  
> He gave man a face raised upward, and commanded him  
> To look upon the heavens (*tueri*) and lift his countenance  
> Upright toward the stars.

He therefore looks up toward heaven, so that he may seek God, [Col. 0139B] not fix his gaze upon the earth like cattle, which nature fashioned bent down and obedient to the belly. The human being, moreover, is twofold: the inner human being is the soul, and the outer human being is the body.

The soul (*anima*) received its name from the pagans because it is wind. Hence the Greeks call wind *anemos*, because we seem to live by drawing air through the mouth. But this is manifestly false, since the soul is generated long before air can be drawn into the mouth, and it already lives in the mother’s womb. The soul therefore is not air, as some thought who were unable to conceive of its incorporeal nature.

Because the human being consists of two natures, “human being” sometimes signifies the human body and sometimes the rational soul. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Even if our outer human being is being corrupted, the inner is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV); and elsewhere, that “Christ dwells in our inner human being through faith in our hearts” (Eph. III).

Likewise, in the Psalm the prophet presents different kinds of human beings, saying: “What is the human being, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. VIII). “What is the human being?” must be pronounced with contempt: that is, he is fragile and perishable, a follower of Adam, who, mingled with the ancient sin, has been enclosed in shared depravity. The Lord is mindful of him when he forgives his sins and bestows the gifts of his mercy, as he will say in another psalm: “But the sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV). This, then, is what it means to be mindful: to confer such salvation of grace upon sinners.

“Or the son of man, that you visit him.” Here we must now rise in tone, because this signifies the Lord the Savior, who, unlike other mortals, was not born from two human beings, but proceeded from the Holy Spirit and the womb of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, like a bridegroom from a glorious bridal chamber.

It follows: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII). Here the humility and glory of the Lord the Savior are related. He was made lower, not by the necessity of ministerial service, but by the spontaneous will of his loving-kindness, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II). It follows: “A little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII), because he accepted the cross for the salvation of all. For in that respect the Creator of the angels was made lower than the angels.

He rightly said “a little” [Col. 0140A], because, although he assumed a mortal body, he nevertheless had no sins. He was crowned with glory and honor when, after the exceedingly great and wondrous faith of the whole world in his resurrection, God exalted him—insofar as he had become human.

Christ is human, as in Isaiah: “Cease from the human being, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa. II). And in the Psalm: “The human being will approach the deep heart” (Ps. LXIII). Concerning this human being another prophet also says: “And he is a human being, and who will know him?” The fact that “human being” is to be understood in two ways is shown by the Lord when he says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Any human being, any human being from the house of Israel who sets his impurities in his heart” (Ezek. XIV), and so forth.

Thus, as we said above according to the Apostle, he shows us a twofold human being: the inner and the outer. For many who possess the bodily face of a human being assume the forms of various beasts, which the Prophet longs to have destroyed when he prays: “Lord, in your city you will destroy their images” (Ps. LXXII). Those of whom it is written, “When the human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII), are not human beings who are truly human, but human beings who are beasts.

Again, the one who heard in the Gospel, “Serpents, brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III), is not a human being who is truly human, but a human being who is a serpent. And those of whom it is written, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air have nests” (Matt. VIII), and concerning Herod, “Tell that fox” (Luke XIII), are not human beings who are truly human, but human beings who are foxes.

Those, however, who possess both uses of the name “human being,” if they go astray, are corrected by punishments so that they may understand that the Lord himself is God.

Rational human beings are understood in the passage of the Psalm: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV). Likewise, human beings can mean sinners, as in the Psalm: “But you will die like human beings” (Ps. LXXXI). Sometimes, however, “human being” signifies any sinner and persecutor, or even the most wicked Antichrist, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Arise, O Lord; let not the human being prevail” (Ps. IX). He is the worst human being, whom the human condition cannot withstand, and in whom there will be such cunning or power that only the Lord’s might will be able to overcome his wickedness.

We also read in the Apostle: “Our old human being”—that is, the human being of sin—“was crucified together with Christ, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. VI). Hence he commands us (Eph. IV) to put off the old human being with his deeds and to put on the new, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. He calls all sins and crimes together “the body,” which he says is destroyed through a good life and the Catholic faith. The crucifixion of the inner human being is understood as the pains of repentance and the wholesome anguish of self-restraint, by which the death of ungodliness is put to death.

The Evangelist declares that spirit and soul are the same when he says: “I have power to lay down my soul” (John X), and again: “I have power to take it up” (ibid.). Concerning this same soul of the Lord, the Evangelist mentioned above spoke at the time of his Passion, saying: “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John XX). For what is it to give up the spirit except to lay down the soul?

But “soul” is so called because it lives. “Spirit” signifies either spiritual nature or that which breathes into bodies. Likewise, “mind” (*animus*) is the same as soul, but the soul is the principle of life, while the mind is the principle of deliberation. Hence philosophers say that life can remain even without mind, and that the soul can endure without understanding. Hence also come the words “mindless” and “insane.” For “mind” (*mens*) is so called because it knows, and “mind” (*animus*) because it wills.

The mind (*mens*) is so called because it stands out in the soul, or because it remembers. Hence those who do not remember are called mindless. Therefore it is not the soul itself but what excels in the soul that is called mind, as its head or eye. Hence the human being, according to the mind, is said to be the image of God.

All these faculties are joined to the soul in such a way that they are one reality. For according to the operations of its causes the soul has received different names. Memory, too, is mind; hence those who do not remember are called mindless. Thus, when it gives life to the body, it is soul; when it wills, it is mind; when it knows, it is understanding; when it recalls, it is memory; when it indicates what is right, it is reason; when it breathes, it is spirit; when it perceives something, it is sense. For from this it is that “mind” is called “sense,” because of the things it perceives; hence the word “judgment” (*sententia*) also derives its name.

The meaning of “spirit” is manifold. Sometimes the very God is indicated by the name “Spirit,” as when it is written: “God is Spirit” (John IV). It also signifies the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the angel says to Mary in the Gospel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I). And the Apostle says: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (I Cor. II), and again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III).

Sometimes “spirit” signifies the angelic nature. Hence the Psalmist says: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. CXXX). Sometimes it signifies the human soul, as we showed above. Sometimes it signifies holy men who possess the beauty of the virtues and are spiritual. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI).

Sometimes “spirit” is called reason, which is superior in the soul, as in Daniel: “Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord” (Dan. III). Sometimes “spirit” signifies the soul of animals. Hence Solomon says: “The spirit of animals goes downward” (Eccles. III).

Sometimes it signifies the human voice. Hence the Apostle says: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV). Sometimes it signifies a heavenly rebuke. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “At your rebuke, O Lord, at the rebuke of the spirit of your wrath” (Ps. XVII). He therefore shows that preachers of the word, inflamed by the Holy Spirit, rebuked sinful peoples so that they might withdraw from their vices.

Sometimes it signifies wind, as in: “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. XLIX). In the opposite sense, the name “spirit” denotes spiritual vices. Thus one speaks of the spirit of pride, the spirit of anger, the spirit of sadness, and the spirit of fornication.

Sometimes the devil himself is indicated by the name “spirit” [Col. 0142A]. Hence it is said: “The good spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord attacked him” (I Reg. XVI). And in the Gospel the Truth himself says: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a human being, it passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and does not find it” (Matt. XII). Shortly afterward he adds: “Then it takes seven spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there” (ibid.), that is, with the fullness of every vice. Hence the last state of that human being becomes worse than the first.

“Body” (*corpus*) is so called because, once corrupted, it perishes. For it is dissoluble and mortal, and will at some time be dissolved. “Flesh” (*caro*) is named from creation. For the male’s seed is a growth, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived. Hence parents are also called creators.

Flesh is composed of the four elements. Earth is in the flesh, air in the breath, moisture in the blood, and fire in vital warmth. Each of the elements has its own part in us; the structure, once dissolved, shows what is owed to each.

Flesh and body, however, signify different things. Flesh is not always present in body, but body is always present in flesh. For flesh is what lives, and this is also body; but body that does not live is not flesh. “Body” is said either of what is dead after life or of what has been formed without life. Sometimes, even with life, something is body and not flesh, as grass and wood.

Mystically, “body” signifies bodily creation or the corrupted nature of the human being. Hence we read in the Apostle that there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. And elsewhere he says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (I Cor. XV; Wis. IX).

According to allegory, “flesh” sometimes signifies the outer human being, sometimes the letter of the law and the carnal sense, and sometimes human wisdom, which thinks contrary to God. For it is written in the Apostle: “The wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace” (Rom. VIII). What he says, “The wisdom of the flesh is death,” is one and the same as what he says elsewhere: “The letter kills” (III Cor. III).

Therefore the wisdom of the flesh is death. Whose death? Without doubt, the soul’s. For one who understands the law according to the flesh—that is, according to the letter—does not come to Christ, who is life. Therefore the wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace. The one who understands the law spiritually possesses the life and peace that is Christ.

In another sense, the wisdom of the flesh is sin, which generates death. It is called “wisdom” even though it is a foolish thing because, to worldly people, errors conceived from visible things—whether in thought or in action against the law of God—appear to be wisdom.

“For,” says the Apostle, “the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. VIII). For how could the wisdom of the flesh—that is, carnal understanding—not be hostile to God, when it opposes Christ, does not receive him whom God sent, and says: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XVII)?

It must be noted that he did not say that flesh is hostile, but the wisdom of the flesh—that is, not the substance, but the actions, thoughts, or assertions [Col. 0143A] that arise from error. The wisdom of the flesh is, first, the disputation invented by human beings concerning the order of the stars; then, the delight taken in visible things. These are hostile to God because they equate the Lord of the elements and the Maker of the world with the things he made, asserting that nothing can happen except what the order of the world contains.

For this reason they deny that God caused a virgin to give birth or that the bodies of the dead should rise, because, they say, it is foolish that God should have done anything beyond what human wisdom understands. Hence it is also written: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). And again: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV), that is, a sinful and bloodstained life does not deserve to possess eternal life.

Nor will corruption possess incorruption. Rather, holy and righteous men, changed and made immortal through the resurrection of the flesh on the day of judgment, will pass together with Christ into the everlasting kingdom.

The bodily senses are five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Of these, two are opened and closed, while two are always open. The senses are so called because through them the soul moves the whole body with the subtle power of perception. Hence they are also called “present things,” because they are before the senses, just as things are “before the eyes” that are present to the eyes.

Sight is what philosophers call vitreous humor. Some assert that vision is produced either by the outermost ethereal light or by an inner, luminous spirit coming from the brain through narrow passages, passing through the membranes, and issuing into the air; then, by the mixture of similar matter, it produces sight.

Sight is so called because it is more lively than the other senses, more excellent or swifter, and more vigorous, just as memory is among the activities of the mind. It is closer to the brain, from which everything flows. Hence we say that things belonging to the other senses are “seen,” as when we say, “See how it sounds; see how it tastes,” and so forth.

Hearing is so called because it absorbs voices, that is, because it receives sounds when the air is struck. Smell (*odoratus*) is as though it were the touching of the scent of air; for it is perceived when the air is touched. Thus it is also called *olfactus*, because it is produced by odors. Taste (*gustus*) is named from the throat (*guttur*). Touch (*tactus*) is so called because it handles and touches and spreads the power of sensation through all the limbs. For by touch we test whatever we cannot judge through the other senses.

There are two kinds of touch: either it comes from outside and strikes us, or it arises within the body itself. Each sense has been given its own nature. What is to be seen is apprehended by the eyes; what is to be heard, by the ears; soft and hard things are assessed by touch. Flavor is conveyed by taste, and odor by the nostrils.

In many places of Holy Scripture these five bodily senses mystically express the number five, as in the Savior’s parable (Matt. XXV), where it is related that a servant received five talents from his master and presented them back to that master with an increase. Likewise in the other passages where the number five is inserted, it either mystically signifies the five books of the Law or the five bodily senses.

It must be noted that these same senses, which are described in the outer human being, are likewise shown to exist in the inner human being according to their proper mode, because spiritual realities must be sought out not with bodily senses but with spiritual ones.

Hence the divine voice says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “See that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. XXXIII). And in the Psalm: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. LXXVII). And in the Gospel the Truth himself says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI). And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Apoc. II). And in the Psalter: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). And the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ both among those who are perishing and among those who are being saved” (II Cor. II). And in the Gospel the Lord shows that the hemorrhaging woman touched him by faith more than bodily, saying: “Someone touched me, for I also felt power go out from me” (Luke VIII).

Thus we must observe with every caution what pertains to the bodily senses and what pertains to the dignity of the soul, lest perhaps a confused order and irrational judgment should seem somewhere to conflict with the truth.

The first part of the body is the head. It was given this name because all the senses and nerves take their beginning from it, and from it arises the whole cause of life. For all the senses appear there. Hence it in a certain way represents the person of the soul, which governs the body.

The head, which is the first part of the body, as we said above, signifies according to allegory either Christ, who is the head of the body, the Church (Eph. V), or the divinity of the Savior. Hence we read in the Apostle: “The head of a woman is the man, the head of a man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI).

Sometimes “head” is used for the preeminence of the mind. Hence it is written: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX). This means: at all times let your works and conduct be pure, and let the oil of charity and mercy not fail from your mind.

Sometimes “head” is used for a beginning, as in: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Ps. XXXIX); and, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I); and, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John I).

Sometimes the name “head” designates the primacy of any office. Hence the apostles and teachers of the Church are called the heads of the nations, because they are leaders and teachers of faithful peoples.

Likewise, the head signifies the beginning of good works, such as the human will, as in Leviticus: “He shall place his hand upon the head of his sacrifice” (Lev. I). Similarly, in certain passages the leaders and princes of the wicked are reckoned under the name “heads.” Hence it is said: “Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head” (Ps. XXXIX). To show that the number of unbelievers is greater than that of the devoted, he says that the faithless Jews have multiplied beyond the number of the hairs, that is, of those who rightly believe.

The crown of the head (*vertex*) is the part where the hair of the head is gathered and in which the hair is turned; hence it receives its name. When understood in a good sense, the crown of the head signifies the summit of righteousness or the perfection of all virtues, as in Solomon: “For a crown of graces will receive your crown” (Prov. IV).

The crown of the head is also used in a bad sense when it signifies the height of wickedness, as in the Psalmist: “Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Ps. LXVII). The heads of the enemies are the leaders of the Jewish rebellion, and without doubt also the teachers of heretics. The former persecuted Christ in the flesh; the latter, still more cruelly, rage even against his divinity, if it is permissible to say so. Such men seek for themselves the enmity of accusations, so that they may appear able to walk over and scrutinize even the crowns of the hair.

The skull (*calvaria*) is named from the bare bones, by a process of inflection, and is pronounced as a neuter noun. At Golgotha, which is interpreted as “Skull,” because the heads of the condemned were cut off there, the Lord was crucified, so that where previously there had been a place of condemnation, there the standards of martyrdom might be raised. And just as he became a curse of the cross for us, was scourged, and was crucified, so for the salvation of all he was crucified like a guilty man among guilty men.

Hair of the head (*capilli*) is so called as though from “hairs of the head,” formed both to provide beauty and to protect the brain against the cold and defend it from the sun. In the hair, however, the adornment of righteousness and the beauty of virtues are represented in the faithful soul. For good merits and instruction in wisdom, a manifold reward is reserved for it in eternal blessedness. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “But even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. X).

Hair also signifies the virtues of the soul. Thus in the Book of Judges it is read of Samson (Judg. XVI) that, after he lost his hair, he was immediately captured by his enemies and lost the light of knowledge. Hair can also signify faithful peoples, who by their multitude provide the Church with its greatest adornment. Hence in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom says to the bride: “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have gone up from Mount Gilead” (Song VI). For Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” which aptly suits the united multitude of the saints.

Hair is also found in a contrary sense in the Psalm, where it signifies vices: “They have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me” (Ps. XXXIX). Nor is hair compared with sins without reason, since by the Lord’s command in the Old Testament priests were shaved in this same manner.

“Hairs” (*pili*) are so called from the skin (*pellis*) from which they emerge, just as *pilo* is said from *pila*, the vessel in which pigments are stored. Hairs signify the carnal thoughts that Holy Scripture admonishes us to shave from our hearts. Hence in the Book of Numbers the Levites are commanded to shave all the hairs of their flesh.

The hairs of the flesh are every superfluity of human corruption. The hairs of the flesh are the thoughts of the former life, which we cut away from the mind in such a manner that we are not wearied by any grief at their loss. For “Levite” means “one who has been taken up.” All Levites must therefore shave the hairs of the flesh, because the person taken up for divine service ought to appear pure before God’s eyes from all carnal thoughts, lest the mind produce illicit thoughts and, like hairs that bear fruit, make the beautiful appearance of the soul misshapen.

The hair or mane (*caesaries*) is named from cutting, and therefore belongs especially to men; for it is fitting for a man to be shorn, but not for a woman. Nevertheless, in Deuteronomy (Deut. XXI) we read that a captive woman was ordered, before marriage, to shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she had been captured.

This signifies the soul, which was beautifully created by God: if we find it in pagan conduct and wish to unite it to the body of Christ, it must lay aside the adornment of idolatry, put on the mournful garments of repentance, and lament its father and mother—that is, every memory of the world and its carnal allurements. Then, with the razor of God’s word and teaching, all the sin of its unbelief, which is dead and empty, must be shaved away—for this is what the hair of the head and the woman’s nails signify—and at last, cleansed and purified in the saving bath, it must be joined to the saints of God. This is when it no longer possesses on its head anything dead, nor in its hands anything of those things that through unbelief are called dead, so that it carries nothing unclean or dead either in its senses or in its actions.

Locks (*comae*) properly mean hair that has not been cut, and the word is Greek. For the Greeks call locks *caimos*, from cutting; hence they also say *keirein*, “to shear.” From this they are also called curls (*cirri*), which the Greeks likewise call *mallon*. Mystically, the locks of the head are companies of saints who cling to Christ the head in faithful service. Hence in the Song of Songs the bride says of the Bridegroom: “His locks are like lifted palm branches, black as a raven” (Song V).

These locks are called “lifted palm branches” because of the Lord’s head; lifted because of victory; black because of contempt among human beings; black because of afflictions.

Tresses (*crines*) properly belong to women. They are called tresses because they are divided by ribbons; hence they are called “partings,” from which they are divided and tied again. Mystically, tresses signify works of virtue that a human being possesses through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Hence in the Book of Judges it is read that, as long as Samson had the seven tresses of his head intact, he was unconquered; but after he was shorn through the woman’s deceit, his strength departed from him. For whoever preserves spiritual virtues through the grace of the Holy Spirit remains unharmed. If he is emptied of spiritual grace because of sin, he becomes weak and lies exposed to capture by his enemies.

Tresses can also signify generosity in almsgiving. Hence in the Gospel (Luke VII) the woman who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears wiped them with her hair and anointed them with perfume, to teach us that we ought to show compassion to Christ’s least members, distribute our superfluous possessions to the poor, and bring them aid with the fragrance of good virtues. Concerning them the Lord himself will say at the end: “Whatever you did for one of these least of my brothers, you did for me” (Matt. XXV).

Sometimes companies of the faithful are also expressed by tresses, as in the Song of Songs, where the Bridegroom says to the bride: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one tress of your neck” (Song IV). In the wounding of the heart, the greatness of Christ’s love for the Church is understood: it is formed in the holy unity of the saints, signified by the eyes, and in the pious unity of the subject people, signified by the tresses.

The temples are the parts that lie to the right and left beneath the skull. They are so called because they move, and through that movement change at certain intervals, like times. They signify the vigils of the body, which a human being ought to maintain with due measure in the condition of the present age until the sleep of death comes.

Hence the Prophet, speaking in the person of Christ, says in the Psalter: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI). All these things are known to apply rationally to Christ’s humanity. This sleep is to be understood as the rest of death. The movement of the eyelids and temples also demonstrates his vigilance before death, since in truth the temples of our head cannot have rest when the eyes are known to remain watchful, stirred by frequent movements.

First he placed “sleep,” and afterward explained how that sleep itself would be fulfilled. The Lord’s death is therefore rightly compared to sleep, because it was received only as a three-day repose, which brought no corruption to the body but rest.

The face (*facies*) is so called from image or likeness. For in it lies the whole figure of the human being and the recognition of every person. The countenance (*vultus*) is so called because through it the will of the mind is revealed; for according to the will it changes into various expressions. “Face” is therefore understood simply of each person’s natural appearance, whereas “countenance” signifies the quality of the mind.

The face is understood in two ways: bodily and spiritual. For if the inner human being did not have a face, the Apostle would not say: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III). And again: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII).

The face also signifies the highest disclosure in the mind, as in the Gospel: “Wash your face” (Matt. VI). It is clear that now we see images through faith, but then we shall see the realities themselves, that is, after the resurrection in eternal glory.

As for what the Lord said to Moses, “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII), and, according to John’s testimony, “No one has ever seen God” (John I), this is to be understood as meaning that in this corruptible life no one can possess a perfect contemplation of God.

The fathers of the Old Testament, living in this life, saw the Lord through certain images by which he wished to reveal himself; but he reserved the glory of his future vision for those who will see him perpetually in heavenly blessedness. Nor is it contrary to the force of that same statement to say, “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII), since whoever sees wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, lest he continue to be held by love of it.

No one who still lives carnally sees her, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies by that very act through which, either in the intention of the heart or in the effect of his works, he separates himself with his whole mind from the pleasures of this life. Therefore no one has seen God and lived, as though it were plainly said: no one has ever seen God spiritually and continued to live carnally in the world.

The countenance is sometimes used for understanding, sometimes for will and affection. For when the Prophet said in the Psalm, “I have been cast away from the face of your eyes” (Ps. XXX), the Son speaks to the Father in the form of a servant: “I hoped that your grace would not forsake me when the sorrow of the Passion prevailed. In the fear of death I was cast away from the face of your eyes,” that is, from the sight of your mercy.

He fittingly attributed a face to the eyes, because the eyes most especially signify the wills of the mind. The countenance is so called because it shows through its signs what the heart wills (*velle*), just as the eyes of the divinity, when they look upon someone, promise their grace.

The statement, “The face of the Lord is upon those who do evil” (Ps. XXXIII), declares that the face of the Lord—that is, his understanding—is directed toward the wicked, whom he attends to without looking favorably upon them. He does not look favorably upon them, yet he nevertheless knows their deeds.

The forehead (*frons*) is named from the openings of the eyes. Through its appearance it expresses a certain image of the soul and the movement of the mind, whether it is joyful or sad. According to allegory, the forehead signifies modesty or shamelessness of mind.

Hence a person is said to blush when he is pierced with remorse for his sins and strives to improve himself. Conversely, the shameless forehead of Jerusalem is reproached by the Prophet as he condemns its crime, when he says to it: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute” (Jer. III).

Again, the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads. Like adamant and like flint I have made your face” (Ezek. III). The house of Israel has a worn and brazen forehead, bold in insolence, hard of heart, and compared with scorpions. Therefore I gave you a very hard countenance and a forehead that no shame could overcome.

From this we learn that it is sometimes a gift of God’s grace to resist shamelessness and, when circumstances require, to crush forehead against forehead. This is granted so that our modesty and human shame may not fear the plots of adversaries.

In the same prophet we read (Ezek. IX) that the Lord commanded the man clothed in linen, who had a writer’s inkwell at his loins, to pass through the middle of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and to mark a *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groaned and grieved over all the abominations committed in its midst.

This letter bears the form of Christ’s cross; it is marked upon the foreheads of the faithful and confirmed in the hearts of the elect. Hence the Psalmist says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV). For just as the coin of the emperor bears his image, so the marks of the heavenly prince are impressed upon the faithful.

The eyes (*oculi*) are so called either because the coverings of the eyelashes conceal them, so that they may not be harmed by the injury of some object striking them, or because they have a hidden light—that is, light concealed or placed within. Among all the senses they are closest to the soul. For in the eyes lies every judgment of the mind. Hence disturbance or joy of spirit appears in the eyes.

The eyes are also called lights (*lumina*), either because light flows from them, or because from the beginning they hold enclosed light, or because they pour forth light received from outside by placing it before the faculty of sight.

The eye therefore demonstrates not only bodily sight but also the gaze of the heart. The Psalmist shows this when he says: “I lifted my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. CXX); and in Jeremiah: “Lift up your eyes and see” (Jer. III). For when he says “I lifted,” he shows that he had advanced toward some contemplation. To lift is to transfer something to higher things.

“I lifted my eyes”—that is, the sight of my heart, concerning which it is written: “Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII).

For if you understand these as bodily eyes, what could he have accomplished by gazing at mountains planted with forests or rough with rocks? But if you seek the meaning spiritually, it is altogether profitable to believe that he lifted the eyes of his heart either toward holy men, divine books, or exalted angels, who are truly mountains in greatness and firmness. Hence appropriate assistance was also expected.

And in the Gospel the Truth himself says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matt. V). Here he called the thought and sense that fly about in different directions an “eye”; by the right hand he indicates the beginnings of the will and affections.

We can also understand this saying in another way. It seems to me that in this passage the eye may appropriately be understood as a most beloved friend. For we can rightly call a member what we love intensely, and also a counselor, because an eye is as though it shows the way in divine matters, since it is the right eye. The left eye, then, may be a beloved counselor in earthly matters pertaining to the needs of the body.

Likewise, in the Gospel passage where the Lord says to his disciples, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke X), faithful understanding and a simple affection are shown, by which the Lord is to be contemplated.

And in the statement in which the Savior says, “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. VI), he designates by the eye the intention of the heart and the understanding of the mind, because when there is a good intention and desire—
When we do anything to please God, the whole body of our work is illumined. But if the intention is perverse, the work accomplished through it will also be dark. Some say that the two eyes signify the active and contemplative life [Col. 0149D]. Finally, when we read that the eyes of the Lord look upon us—as in: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him,” and “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXII)—this reveals the continual grace of the Godhead, because his mercy protects those whom he knows to fear him.

For we must understand that the eyes of the Lord contemplate the good and the wicked in every place, since nothing is hidden from him: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV). Yet he looks upon the good with mercy, while condemning the wicked through judgment.

The pupil is the central point of the eye, in which the power of sight resides. Because small images appear to us there, it is called the *pupilla*, “little one”; for little boys are called *pupilli*. Many call it a *papula*. It is called the pupil because it is pure and undefiled, like young girls. Physicians say that the pupils which we see in the eyes are absent from those who are about to die, three days before death; when they are no longer visible, certain despair follows.

The circle by which the white parts of the eye are separated from the pupil by a distinct blackness is called the corona, because by its roundness it adorns the circumference of the pupil. Mystically, the pupil of the eye signifies the intention of a pure heart, by which righteousness is discerned and truth is distinguished from falsehood. Hence the Prophet prays in the psalm, saying: “Guard me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye” (Ps. XVI).

The pupil is, as we have shown above, the transparent part of the eye situated in the middle, by which we distinguish the colors of bodies in their various qualities. It is called *pupilla* because of its smallness, as though *pusilla*, “tiny.” Christ is fittingly compared to it, for he has been appointed in his judgment to separate the righteous from sinners [Col. 0150B]. Most appropriately, therefore, he asks to be guarded as the pupil of the eye, since through it we distinguish visible things and nothing in our body is more precious.

The eyelids are the folds of the eyes, called *palpebrae* from their fluttering, because they are always moving. They meet one another so that by their constant motion they may refresh the sight. They are fortified by a rampart of hairs, so that, when the eyes are open, anything that falls into them may be repelled; and when they close in sleep, the eyes may rest hidden, as though wrapped up.

At the upper edge of the eyelids, where the two closed lids touch one another, hairs project in an orderly arrangement, demonstrating their protection of the eyes. Thus they readily ward off approaching injuries, lest harm result from them; they keep out dust and any thicker substance, and, by cutting the air, also temper it, making the vision clear and serene [Col. 0150C].

Mystically, the eyelids may be understood as the hidden dispensations of God that take place in human beings. Hence it is said in the Psalm concerning the Lord: “His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. X). Since the ministries of bodily members are often allegorically applied to the Lord, the text says that he not only looks upon the children of men with his eyes, but also then examines—that is, considers—them, when he is thought to neglect them as though sleeping.

The eyelids of God are his judgments. Through them he closes some things to us and opens others. By opening, they question us whether we are not lifted up when we understand; by closing, they question us whether we do not despise what we are unable to understand.

Likewise, in Job it is written concerning Leviathan: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn. His sneezing is the splendor of fire” (Job XLI) [Col. 0150D]. Since sneezing shakes the head most violently, the sneezing of this creature is called that final upheaval by which it enters the condemned man and exercises dominion over the proud through him. Properly, therefore, its sneezing is called the splendor of fire. Fire appears before the eyes of the reprobate when it shines through the power of signs.

“And his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.” His counselors are signified by his eyes, and they are rightly compared to the eyelids of dawn. By the eyelids of dawn we understand the final hours of the night, during which night seems to open its eyes, already displaying the beginnings of the coming light.

Some think that tears are called *lacrimae* from the laceration of the mind; others believe that they are so called because the Greeks call them *dakrya* [printed: *darsiria*] [Col. 0151A]. What tears poured from a contrite heart can accomplish, the Prophet shows when he says: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. XLI). Let those who do not desire to weep for the Lord hear this: continual tears have brought not hunger but rather satiety. Nor is this undeserved, since that weeping is food for souls, strengthening for the senses, release from sins, refreshment for minds, and baths for offenses.

Through these tears, however, he signifies that the people can be taught through afflictions. We must understand day as prosperity and night as sorrow.

The eyelashes are coverings by which the eyes are protected. They are called *cilia* because they conceal the eyes and cover them with secure protection. The eyebrows are so called because they are placed above the eyelashes. They are covered with hairs for this reason: to provide a defense for the eyes and repel the sweat flowing down from the head [Col. 0151B]. The space between the eyelashes and the eyebrows is called the *intercilium*; it is without hairs.

What the eyebrows signify has been said above, where the Lawgiver commands that, in the purification of a leper, the hair of the head, the beard, the eyebrows, and every hair on the body be shaved.

The cheeks are the lower parts beneath the eyes, from which the beard begins. For the Greeks call the beard *geneion*; hence *genae*, because beards begin to grow there. Accordingly, in allegory the cheeks sometimes signify virtues and sometimes spiritual fathers.

For the Bride says of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by the perfumers” (Song V). In the cheeks of our Savior are expressed his modesty, mercy, and also his severity. The beds of spices signify his virtues, sweetness, and reputation for glory [Col. 0151C]. The perfumers are the prophets and apostles, and those who disclosed the future mysteries of his incarnation.

Again, the Bridegroom says of the Bride: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from your eyes” (Song VI). The holy spiritual Fathers are the cheeks: wondrous in virtues, venerable in conduct, and unashamed to glory in the cross of Christ.

These things that are seen are very great, but those that are unseen and reserved for the future are much greater: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

Again, the Bridegroom says to the Bride: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like a tower” (Song I). This means: “I have adorned you with so great a virtue of salutary modesty that you do not allow the chastity of the faith promised to me to be corrupted by any seduction of depraved teachers” [Col. 0151D].

The *malae* are the projecting parts beneath the eyes, placed there for their protection. They are called *malae* either because they project beneath the eyes in a rounded form, which the Greeks call *mela*, or because they are above the jaws. The jaws are a diminutive of *malae*, just as *paxillus* is from *palus*, and *taxillus* from *talus*.

The jaw therefore signifies either teachers or bodily discipline, by which the brutish and disobedient are restrained. For what is written in the Book of Judges—that Samson destroyed and struck a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, or the jawbone of a young ass (Judg. XV)—typologically expresses the deeds of our Savior.

What is signified here by the jawbone of an ass except the persons of the Church’s preachers? Our Redeemer, holding the simplicity and patience of preachers by the power of his hand, slew carnal people in their vices; and when the jawbone had been thrown upon the ground, it afterward poured forth water, because the bodies of preachers given over to death displayed great miracles to the peoples [Col. 0152A].

But what is written in the Psalm—“Do not become like a horse and a mule, in which there is no understanding; constrain their jaws with bridle and bit” (Ps. XXXI)—is stated in these comparisons for the following reason. A horse, without the rider’s discernment, serves the rider’s will and runs wherever anyone mounts it. A mule, however, patiently receives the burdens with which it is loaded. For this reason neither has understanding: the horse does not choose whom it should obey, and the mule does not understand whose burdens weigh it down.

He therefore forbids such people to be ensnared by diabolical frauds and weighed down by the burdens of vices, lest, by obeying wrongly, they become more devoted to the party of pride [Col. 0152B].

When he says “with a bridle,” this refers to the horse; for *frenum* is said from restraining (*retinendo*) the wild animal. The ancients called a horse *ferum*. “With a bit” refers to the mule.

The jaws are the aids of animals by which food is chewed, so that bodily life may be sustained. Allegorically, therefore, he says that the jaws of the disobedient must be restrained—that is, that their provisions of food should be given more sparingly, so that, confined by the necessity of fasting, they may be subjected to the Creator’s command.
