The ancients called it a beard because it belongs to men, not women. The beard signifies the apostles or apostolic men. Hence the passage: “Like ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which ran down upon the edge of his garment” (Ps. CXXXII).

We rightly call the beard the apostles, since it is an indication of the strongest manhood and remains fixed beneath its head, that is, Christ. After overcoming many sufferings by divine favor, the apostles proved themselves steadfast men through the grace of God. By preserving the rules they had received from the Lord, they showed that they had remained beneath their head.

But lest you perhaps understand this as the beard of just anyone, he adds “Aaron,” who, presenting a figure of Christ, already bore Christ himself in a certain image in his priesthood.

“Which ran down upon the edge of his garment.” The edge of the Lord and Savior’s garment signifies the Church, because the Holy Spirit descended to its extremities when he sanctified the baptized to the end of the age through the graciousness of his mercy [Col. 0152D].

The ears received their name from drawing in voices. Hence Virgil says: “I drank in the voice with these ears.” Or, because the Greeks call the voice itself *auden*, the ears were called *aures* from hearing, through a change of letter, as though *audes*. A voice, rebounding through their winding passages, produces a sound by which they receive the sense of hearing.

Through the ears, as we have already said, the inner hearing of the soul is mystically signified, whether obedience to God’s commands, the hearing of faith, or understanding. Hence it is written: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI)—that is, let him understand with his heart.

Again, in a negative sense: “Make their ears dull, lest perhaps they hear” (Isa. VI).

We also ask God to hear our prayers. Hence the Psalmist says: “Hear, O Lord, my justice; attend to my prayer” (Ps. XVI)—that is, receive our prayers with merciful affection. To “attend” belongs to the eyes, while to “hear” belongs to the ears; but these words have been joined so that one effect of both actions may be understood.

Whatever the ear hears, the eye sees, the hand touches, the palate tastes, or the nose smells is perfectly known to God by the power of contemplation alone.

The nostrils are so called because through them odor or breath never ceases to flow, or because through smell they admonish us to recognize and know something. Hence, in opposition to the knowledgeable, the inexperienced and uneducated are called ignorant. The ancients used to say that to have smelled something was to have known it.

In the sense of smell, the discernment of good and evil is signified. In Sacred Scripture, the word “nostrils” may signify at one time foolishness, at another the instigation of the ancient enemy, and at another foreknowledge.

Foolishness regarding knowledge is signified by the nostrils, as we taught above with Solomon’s testimony: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman without sense” (Prov. XI) [Col. 0153B].

By the nostrils are understood the exhaled snares and instigation of the ancient enemy, as the Lord testifies concerning him in the Book of Job: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (Job XLI). It is as though he were saying: From his perverse investigation of human hearts arises the most wicked darkness of thought, by which the eyes of those who see are darkened.

Foreknowledge is also signified by the nostrils, as it is said through the Prophet: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” (Isa. II). The breath of our Redeemer is said to be in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be understood to consist in foreknowledge [Col. 0153C].

The nostrils sometimes signify the snares of the ancient enemy. For the Bridegroom says to the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song VII). In the nose, the dispensers of the word of God are signified on account of discernment; they are called a tower because they occupy the most eminent place in the Church.

Again, in the nostrils the breath of faith and good virtues is expressed, as in Job: “The divine spirit is in my nostrils” (Job XLI).

In a negative sense, the meaning of the nostrils is drawn from the passage in which the Lord speaks to Job concerning Leviathan: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” (Job XL), that is, from the devil; for from the snares of miracles even a dark uncertainty is generated for a moment.

Again, concerning Behemoth he says: “With stakes you will pierce his nostrils.” What are the stakes except the sharp counsels of the saints, which pierce the nostrils of this Behemoth, since by keeping watch they scrutinize his most cunning snares and, by overcoming them, pierce them? Or are the Lord’s own words the stakes by which Behemoth’s nostrils are pierced?

When he doubted that God had become incarnate, he wished to learn this by testing him through requested miracles, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. IV). But he heard these words from the Lord: [lacuna]; and by these sharp points of his sayings the investigation of the ancient enemy was struck down [Col. 0153D].

The mouth is so called because through it, as through a door, we take in food and cast out spittle; or because from the place where food enters, speech also goes forth.

The mouth sometimes signifies the Word itself, that is, Jesus Christ, who announces to us his own will and that of the Father. At other times it signifies the Holy Spirit, as in: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I). It is he himself who speaks, though he causes others to speak. For although speech is brought forth through the ministry of another, the Holy Spirit nevertheless speaks, whose commands are proclaimed, as the blessed Apostle Peter says: “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke when moved by the Holy Spirit” (II Pet. I).

At times the mouth reveals the inner thought of a person, as in: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom” (Ps. XXXVI). He does not say “meditates,” but “will meditate,” referring to the future. Here we must understand the mouth as thought, because what it will say follows concerning the tongue. He will meditate wisdom, not through reading the Scriptures, but through the purest vision of the heart. There wisdom is not gathered by letters but is freely bestowed through heavenly generosity [Col. 0154B].

Similarly, the mouth is used in the opposite sense when it is said to the sinner: “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit” (Ps. XLIX). The mouth stands for deceitful thought, and the tongue for false praise or an evil counsel.

The mouth signifies good or evil speech, as in the Gospel: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. XII; the supplied citation reads XLIX).

Sometimes the mouth stands for the words themselves, as in the Apocalypse: “In their mouth,” that is, in their words, “no lie was heard” (Apoc. XIV). And in the psalm: “My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding” (Ps. XLVIII).

Wisdom pertains to the exposition of divine matters, while understanding pertains to the ordering of probable matters [Col. 0154C]. Thus all divine speech is indicated by these two virtues.

The lips are named from licking. What is above we call the *labium*; what is below, because it is thicker, the *labrum*. Some say that men have *labra* and women *labia*.

The lips sometimes stand for a hidden word, sometimes for a manifest one. For the hidden word, as in Solomon: “The lips of the righteous consider acceptable things, but the mouth of the wicked perverse things” (Prov. X). For the manifest word, as in the Psalm: “My lips will praise you” (Ps. LXII).

Again, in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom says to the Bride: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet” (Song IV). The scarlet ribbon signifies the doctrine of truth. The Bride’s lips are likened to scarlet because the Church never ceases to proclaim the price of the Lord’s blood, by which she was redeemed; or because holy preaching burns with the ardor of charity [Col. 0154D].

Again, the Bridegroom says of the Bride: “Her lips drip lilies, distilling first myrrh” (Song V). Her lips are the words of doctrine; they are lilies because they promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom; they drip first myrrh because they proclaim that one must reach it by despising present desires.

Varro thinks that tongues received their name from binding food; others think it is because the tongue binds together the articulated sounds of words. Just as a plectrum strikes the strings, so the tongue is struck against the teeth and produces vocal sound. Thus the tongue, because it forms speech, stands for utterance. Hence we speak of kinds of tongues, because the sounds of words are different.

“For they were speaking in various tongues of the mighty works of God” (Acts II), because they had received the grace of the Holy Spirit to be able to speak God’s praise in every tongue [Col. 0155A].

The tongue also signifies right or perverse doctrine, as in Solomon: “The lips of the wise spread wisdom; the tongue of the perverse will perish” (Prov. XV).

The Greeks call teeth *odontes*, and from them the Latin seems to have derived the name. Teeth sometimes signify the teachers of the Church, as in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep” (Song IV). In the teeth the more perfect and more suitable persons for governing the Church of God are signified. They grind up the pronouncements of the Sacred Scriptures and reduce them to food for faithful souls.

Again, in the Psalm the Prophet says to the Lord: “You have crushed the teeth of sinners” (Ps. III), that is, the biting words of slanderers who oppose divine authority with wicked doctrines [Col. 0155B].

Teeth are said to derive their name from taking away (*demendo*). Thus the tongues of slanderers are very aptly called teeth, because just as teeth remove portions of food, so these people, by slander, gnaw away at the reputations of others.

Teeth signify understanding or good and evil speech, as in Exodus: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. XXI).

Our palate is positioned like the heavens; hence *palatum* is derived from *polus*, “pole.” The Greeks likewise use a similar term, because by its concavity it resembles the heavens.

Just as the palate rises above the tongue and words are formed beneath it, so our speech ought to subordinate itself to heavenly wisdom and spiritual doctrine, so that it may bring forth useful teaching that benefits its hearers.

The throat (*fauces*) is named from pouring forth voices, because through it we utter (*famur*) sounds [Col. 0155C]. The windpipe is so called either because through it air—that is, breath—is carried from the lungs, or because it holds the vital breath in narrow and constricted passages. Hence it emits the sounds of the voice. Those sounds would all be alike if the movement of the tongue did not create differences in the voice.

The throat may signify the judgment of understanding, as in: “Where are my throats? Do they not meditate wisdom?” (Job VI). The throat also signifies the keeping of God’s commandments. For just as a person ought to utter words through the sounds of the throat, so a Catholic teacher ought to demonstrate the fruit of his preaching by keeping God’s commandments.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “My tongue has cleaved to my throat” (Ps. XII) [Col. 0155D]. Since every taste is perceived on the palate, one must consider why he said “to my throat.” The throat is the passage of our gullet, where no sweetness is sensed once it has been swallowed. But since he was about to speak plainly of the Lord’s eloquence, he wonderfully placed that part of the body so that the speech might quickly reach the innermost places of our heart.

Again, it is written: “I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII). Christ labored crying out when the faithless did not listen to him; his throat became hoarse because the sacrilegious people did not hear his words at all.

The chin is so called because the jaws arise from it, or because they join there. Since the beard projects most prominently from the chin, it shows that the gentleness of true doctrine ought to be present there, and that no fraud or malice should be mixed with it.

Hence, when Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand but secretly sent a sword with his left and spilled his entrails (II Sam. XX) [Col. 0156A], holding the chin with the right hand means flattering someone as though with acts of kindness; but he sends the left hand to the sword who strikes secretly out of malice.

The neck is so called because it is rigid and clings like a column bearing and supporting the head, as though a *capitolium*. Its front part is called the throat, its rear part the nape. The nape is so called because through that part the brain is directed to the spinal cord, as though through a road of the brain.

The ancients used *cervices* only in the plural. Ostensius was the first to use *cervix* in the singular. In the singular, *cervix* signifies the bodily member itself; in the plural it often denotes obstinacy. Cicero says in the *Verrines*: “You accuse a praetor—break your neck” [Col. 0156B].

The neck signifies the beauty of understanding or the strength of preaching, and also the holy teachers, as in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like necklaces” (Song I); and again: “Your neck,” he says, “is like the tower of David” (Song IV). The tower of David is the Catholic Church; the neck is the holy preachers. Hence steadfast firmness exists in that same city, and it is unconquerable on every side [the supplied text reads *inexplanabilis*, probably for *inexpugnabilis*].

The neck or nape is also understood in a negative sense, as in this testimony concerning wisdom: “By his own power he has trampled the necks of the proud and exalted.” And in the Psalm: “The Lord,” he says, “will cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. CXXVIII).

Scripture testifies that necks stand for pride, saying: “I see that this people is stiff-necked” (Exod. XXXII). And blessed Stephen, rebuking the Jews in his passion, says: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did” (Acts VII) [Col. 0156C].

A corresponding recompense is therefore given to such people: the necks which they wickedly raised against the Lord are subjected to his yoke through salutary humility. We often remember this having happened to persecutors, who became preachers of the holiest religion, although previously they had defended idols with the most wicked persuasions.

The *gurgulio* receives its name from the throat. Its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils, possessing a channel through which the voice is transmitted to the tongue so that it may collide into words; hence we also say *garrire*, “to chatter.”

The throat sometimes signifies the sweetness of God’s law, as the Bride says of the Bridegroom: “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (Song III). In the throat the inward sweetness of his words is recalled, by which one tastes and does not hunger.

He is altogether desirable because he is wholly God and wholly man, upon whom the angels desire to gaze (I Pet. I): God in the majesty of the Father, man in the virginity of his mother; in the former, Creator, in the latter, Savior.

The throat is also understood in the opposite sense, as in: “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully” (Ps. XIII). Through the figure of a parable, the comparison is shown to be highly apt. The throat of a liar is a tomb of the dead when he rolls about in his jaws a destructive vanity that inflicts the evil of death.

It is therefore rightly called the tomb of those whose speech was deadly. For just as open tombs exhale foul odors, so the throat of these people brought forth poisonous words [Col. 0157A].

The gullet, which is named from swallowing, sometimes stands for the taking of food or drink; sometimes for gluttony—that is, feasting and drunkenness—which is called *gastrimargia* and is one of the eight principal vices.

Against it Truth himself says to the disciples: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI). And the Apostle says: “Not in feasting and drunkenness,” because drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God (Rom. XIII; I Cor. VI).

The shoulders are called *humeri*, as though arms, to distinguish human beings from mute animals, so that humans are said to have shoulders and animals arms. Properly speaking, *armi* belong to quadrupeds.

The shoulders signify work or the burden of that same work, as when Exodus prescribes the *superhumerale*, the shoulder garment, as part of the priestly vestment [Col. 0157B].

The arms are named from strength. For in Greek *barys* signifies “heavy” and “strong.” In the arms are the muscular masses of the flesh, and there is the conspicuous strength of the muscles. These are the *thori*, that is, muscles; they are called *thori* because the twisted viscera seem to appear there.

The shoulder is sometimes used for a burden, sometimes for strength. For in the blessing of Issachar it is said that he was a strong ass and placed his shoulder beneath the burden (Gen. XLIX). By this is understood the simple Gentile people, who raise themselves to the strength of good works because they are journeying toward the homeland of eternal life.

Thus he also places his shoulder beneath the burden, because, desiring to reach the promised rest, he willingly carries out all the works of the commandments.

In Isaiah we read concerning the Lord and Savior that dominion was made upon his shoulder (Isa. LIII), because he himself carried his cross; or the shoulder reveals the strength of the arm, as the same Isaiah says: “The Lord has revealed his holy arm to all the nations” (Isa. LII). And again: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII).

The elbow is so called because we recline upon it in order to take food. The elbow sometimes signifies the author and redeemer of the human race, as in the construction of Noah’s ark: “And in a cubit,” he says, “you shall complete its summit” (Gen. VI). The ark is completed in one cubit because there is one author and redeemer of the holy Church, without sin, through whom and toward whom all who know themselves to be sinners make progress.

The two cubits signify the two commandments of charity. Hence the Ark of the Covenant, which bore the type of the Church, is said to have been two cubits in length [Col. 0157D].

According to some, the *ulna* is the extension of both hands; according to others, it is the cubit, which is more correct, because in Greek *olene* means “cubit.” The *ulna* signifies good action. Hence Simeon is said to have received Christ in his arms and blessed the Lord (Luke II).

For what is it to receive Christ in one’s arms except to embrace him with pious works as with our own limbs? Through the arms the activity of virtues is expressed. When someone feeds Christ who is hungry in one person, gives him drink when he is thirsty in another, welcomes him as a stranger in another, clothes him when naked in another, and visits him when sick or imprisoned in another, by these devoted actions he undoubtedly embraces Christ himself [Col. 0158A].

The armpits are called the underarms because the movement of the arms begins there in the manner of wings. Some call them *ascellae* because from them things are *cilled*, that is, moved. Hence *ascilla* is derived from the fact that all things are moved there, for *cillere* means “to move.”

The armpit is sometimes used for desire arising from idleness. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “All the idle person’s desire is in desire” (Prov. XXVI). And again: “The lazy man hides his hand under his armpit, and he is weary if he brings it to his mouth” (ibid.).

The lazy and idle person desires carnal leisure more than the exercise of virtues. He hides his hand under his armpit and does not wish to make his actions agree with his profession, especially since it is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X) [Col. 0158B].

Hence Wisdom also says elsewhere: “Those who work in me will not sin” (Ecclus. XXIV). Truth himself likewise says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII).

The hand is so called because it is the function of the whole body. It supplies food to the mouth; it performs and administers everything; through it we receive and give. By an abusive extension, “hand” also means a craft or an artisan; hence we speak of the price of a hand.

The hand sometimes signifies power, as in the Psalmist’s words to the Lord: “In your hands are the times.” And the patriarch Jacob says to his son Judah: “Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies” (Gen. XLIX) [Col. 0158C].

At times it signifies discernment in judgment, as in: “He stretched out his hand in repaying them” (Ps. LIV). Here “hand” signifies the power of judgment, which is displayed when he makes that distinction between the good and the wicked.

The hand sometimes stands for good action, as in the Psalm: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII). And elsewhere: “I sought God with my hands” (Ps. LXXVI).

The hand also signifies the power of the soul or a good work, as in the Psalm: “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Ps. CXXVII).

In the opposite sense, hands are understood in the passage: “Repay them according to the work of their hands” (Prov. XII).

The right hand is called *dextera* from giving. It is given as a pledge of peace; it is offered as a witness of faith and salvation. Hence Tully says: “I gave the public pledge at the command of the senate”—that is, the right hand [Col. 0158D]. Therefore the Apostle says: “They gave me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship” (Gal. II).

The left hand is called *sinistra*, as though “without the right hand,” or because it allows a thing to be done. It is named from *sinere*, “to allow.”

The right hand sometimes designates Christ, the Son of God, on account of his effective power. Concerning him it is written: “The right hand of the Lord has done valiantly; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. CXVII).

Sometimes it signifies eternal blessedness; hence Christ is said to sit at the right hand of God, that is, to reign in eternal blessedness.

Sometimes it signifies the election of the saints. Hence the righteous are said to stand at the Judge’s right hand (Matt. XXV), that is, as worthy of eternal blessedness, while sinners stand at the left, that is, among the rejected, who have been handed over to punishment [Col. 0159A].

Here is fulfilled what is written elsewhere: “In the right hand of God is a fiery law” (Deut. XXXIII), while the reprobate are at his left.

The reprobate will therefore be placed at the Lord’s left. They loved the left—that is, present things—with burning desire as long as they lived, and they had no desire for eternal things, which are signified by the right hand.

Again, the right hand signifies love of eternal life, and the left the pleasure of praise in the present age. Hence it is said: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

What is “in secret” except the good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes or disclosed in words? [Col. 0159B]

Again, the right hand signifies the future life and the left the present. Hence it is written concerning the Lord: “In his right hand is length of days, and in his left hand riches and glory” (Prov. III), because here the saints gather the riches of virtues, and in the future they will receive the contemplation of the face of God.

Elsewhere, too, the right hand is found to signify prosperity or the favor of men, and the left adversity in this life or reproach, as in Isaiah: “This is the way; walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. XXX). Thus day sometimes signifies prosperity and night adversity.

At times the right hand expresses good works that please the Lord, and the left evil works that displease him.

Some wish the right hand to signify a friend, or wife, or children, or any relatives, as in the Gospel: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you” (Matt. V) [Col. 0159C].

The palm is the hand with the fingers spread, just as the fist is formed with them contracted. The fist is named from the *pugillus*, “handful,” just as the palm is named from the spread branches of the palm.

The palm sometimes signifies the breadth of eloquence, while the fist signifies the narrow treatment of arguments and the conclusion of syllogisms. Hence one of the wise, discussing Dialectic and Rhetoric, says: “Dialectic and Rhetoric are like the clenched fist and the open palm in a man’s hand.”

The former concludes arguments in brief speech; the latter ranges over the fields of eloquence in expansive discourse. The former contracts words; the latter spreads them out. Dialectic is sharper for discovering things, while Rhetoric is more eloquent in expressing what has been discovered. The former requires a few serious students; the latter frequently proceeds among crowds [Col. 0159D].

The palm also signifies the generosity of almsgiving, and the fist its restraint. Hence it is written in Solomon’s Proverbs concerning the prudent woman: “She stretches out her palms to the poor” (Prov. XXXI). And elsewhere it is written: “Let your hand be extended to give and contracted to gather” (Ecclus. VII).

The Prophet also speaks of the palm and the fist, demonstrating the Lord’s power: “He measures the heavens with his palm and encloses the earth in his fist” (Isa. XL).

In the Lord’s Passion it is written: “Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows; others slapped him in the face, saying: ‘Prophesy to us, Christ; who is it that struck you?’” (Matt. XXVI).

What is said—“They spat in his face”—signifies those who reject the grace of his presence [Col. 0160A]. They strike him with blows who prefer their own honors to his. They slap him in the face who, blinded by unbelief, assert that he did not come, driving away and rejecting his presence.

The error of heretics concerning Christ is confined to three kinds. They are mistaken either about his divinity, or about his humanity, or about both.

The fingers are so called because there are ten of them, or because they are joined together becomingly. For they contain both number and order [the supplied text ends here].
most perfect, and a most fitting order. In Scripture, however, fingers are allegorically understood as the distribution of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For it is written in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11)—that is, by the power of the Holy Spirit—“then surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (ibid.). And in Exodus it is read that the law was written by the finger of the Lord (Exod. 31), which many have wished to understand as the Holy Spirit. And in the Psalm it is read: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8).

The glorious Church rightly says this concerning the future, though before the Lord’s coming it still existed in the patriarchs and holy men. For she says: “I shall see the heavens”—that is, the books of the Gospels, which are rightly called heavens, because they contain the Lord the Savior, who said: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). Therefore I consider the work of the fingers to have been mentioned here so that he might clearly show that the divine books were perfected through the cooperation of the Holy Trinity, just as it is read elsewhere: “He hung the mass of the earth upon three fingers” (Isa. 40). This too must be received as a similar sacramental expression. For a finger is called the effect of divine operation, which most suitably applies to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, to the one God.

Again, by fingers discrimination or the exercise of good works is expressed. Hence, concerning that virtuous woman whom Solomon describes at the end of his Proverbs, it is written: “She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle” (Prov. 31). “She put her hand to strong things” means that she directed her zeal toward the perfect works of Christ’s charity; and “her fingers grasped the spindle” means that, with the equity of discernment, she fashions the weaving of the heavenly robe through works of charity. Here the highest discernment is necessary, so that we may do good for the sake of eternal reward and not temporal praise.

We call the nails *ungulae* from the Greek; for the Greeks call the nail *onyx*. By the nail, then, the extremity or end of anything is indicated. For it is written in Genesis, where Jacob blessed his son Dan, saying: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. 49). Some transfer this prophecy to the Antichrist, supposing that he will come from the tribe of Dan. In this passage they judge the horse to mean the one who, through his pride, foams in the course of passing times. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the final things of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves; for to bite the horse’s hoof is to reach the extremities of the age by striking them.

“So that its rider may fall backward.” The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted in the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not on his face, just as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall on one’s face is, in this life, for each person to recognize his own sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, is to depart suddenly from this life without knowing to what punishments one is being led.

Again, concerning the horse it is written in Job: “The earth is dug by its hoof” (Job 39). The strength of labor is commonly recognized in a horse’s hoof. What, then, is signified by the hoof except the perfection of virtues in a holy preacher? He digs the earth with his hoof when, by the example of his works, he drives earthly thoughts from the hearts of his hearers.

The trunk is the middle part of the body, from the neck to the groin. Concerning it Virgil says:

> The head is carried by the neck.  
> The trunk is supported by the hips, knees, and legs.

The trunk, which is without head and hands, signifies the weakness and inactivity of anyone. Hence it is written of Judith (Judith 13) that, when she cut off Holofernes’ head, she rolled out his headless body. Since Holofernes represents the devil, his headless body shows that, once his power has been cut off, the enemy himself is altogether weak and feeble. Thus Christ’s warriors may more confidently trust that they can conquer the most wicked judge when they thoroughly learn that he is fragile and conquerable.

The chest is so called because it is *pexum*—smooth or combed—between the projecting parts of the breasts. Hence also *pecten* (“comb”) is so called because it makes the hair smooth. The chest signifies inward reflection and the reasoning of wisdom. Thus John is read to have reclined upon the Savior’s chest (John 13), from which he drew heavenly teaching of wisdom.

But the chest bears an opposite meaning when it signifies the cunning of deceit and wickedness. Hence it is said to the serpent: “Upon your chest you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3). The serpent walks upon its chest because all the devil’s steps consist of wickedness and deceit. In the sinner, it indicates the cunning and craftiness of his thoughts, by which he creeps toward those whom he wishes to deceive. He eats earth when he feeds and delights upon the error of sinners, and, seducing them, drags them to destruction.

The breasts are so called because they are round, like apples, by way of a diminutive expression. They are called *ubera* because they are rich in milk, or because they are moist with fluid, being full of milk like clusters of grapes.

In the breasts and nursing breasts, holy teachers are mystically represented, for they nourish the faithful with the milk of sacred teaching; or the two peoples coming from circumcision and from the Gentiles. Hence in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom says to the bride: “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle” (Song 4). The two breasts, as we have said, are the teachers of both Testaments; or the two peoples coming from circumcision and from the Gentiles. Through humility they understand themselves to be small and sinners, yet, running in charity, they pass over all the obstacles of the world.

The breasts also signify the perceptions of the heart, as in Isaiah: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isa. 32)—that is, practice self-restraint against carnal perceptions.

The skin is called *cutis*, because it is the first covering on the body and, being placed over the body, is the first to suffer an incision. For in Greek “incision” is *cutis*. The same is *pellis* (“hide”), because, by covering the body, it repels external assaults and endures rains, winds, and the heat of the sun. Once removed from the body, the hide is immediately called leather.

In the skin or hide, by which an animal is externally enclosed, the human body may mystically be represented, since it covers within itself the nature of the soul that is alive; or the holy Church, whom Christ—who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14)—gives life to and governs. She is worn down externally by afflictions and strengthened inwardly by virtues.

Hence it is written in Job: “My skin has dried up and contracted” (Job 7). And again: “My wrinkles bear witness against me” (Job 16). And again: “My bone cleaves to my skin, my flesh being consumed” (Job 19). Since Christ and the Church are one person, what is signified by the bone except the Lord himself? What by the flesh except the disciples, who at the time of his Passion understood weakly? And what by the skin, which remains outside the flesh in the body, except those holy women who served the Lord by preparing material assistance?

He therefore says: “My bone cleaves to my skin, my flesh being consumed.” This means: those who ought to have clung most closely to my strength were consumed by fear at the time of my Passion; but those whom I had appointed for external ministries I found faithfully clinging to me during my Passion.

Hence it follows: “Only my lips remain around my teeth” (Job 19). What is signified by the lips except speech? What by the teeth except the apostles? Immediately after the Passion they still knew how to converse about the Lord, but they were afraid either to preach him or to bite into the vices of unbelievers.

*Arvina* is fat adhering to the skin. *Pulpa* is flesh without fat, so called because it throbs; for it often springs back. Many also call it *viscum* (“birdlime”), because it is sticky.

Sometimes *arvina* signifies the fatness of love, as in Leviticus, where fat and *arvina* are commanded to be offered to God in peace offerings. Again, *arvina* signifies an abundance of earthly goods, as in Job, where it is written of the proud man: “He ran against God with an uplifted neck and armed himself with a fat neck” (Job 15). To run against God with an uplifted neck is to commit boldly those things that displease the Creator. The wicked man arms himself against God with a fat neck because, swelling with temporal possessions, he rises against the commandments of truth as though from the magnitude of his flesh.

Of him it is added: “Fatness covered his face” (ibid.). Fatness covered his face because the abundance of desired earthly goods weighs down the eyes of the mind. “And fat hangs from his sides” (ibid.); that is, whoever clings to a powerful and wicked man also swells with his power, as though with the fatness of possessions.

Again, fatness signifies divine grace, as in the Psalm: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62). But fat is also taken in a bad sense when it signifies the thickness of wickedness, according to the Psalmist: “They have enclosed themselves in their fat” (Ps. 16).

Members are the parts of the body. Joints, by which the members are joined together, are called *artus*, from *artare* (“to constrict”); their diminutives are *articuli*. For just as we call the larger limbs *artus*, such as the arms, so we call the smaller limbs *articuli*, such as the fingers.

When members are understood in a good sense, they signify the saints and elect of God, who are members of Christ’s body, because he is the head, while the Church is his body, and members are derived from a member. The Apostle demonstrates this at length, showing that some members are glorious and stronger, while others are less honorable and weaker. This results from the diversity of virtues and from the zeal for examining or teaching.

The eyes in Christ’s body may be those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night; the ears, those who diligently hear the word of God and obey his commandments; the mouth and tongue, holy preachers; the hands, those who work well or give alms; the feet, those who walk in the way of God’s commandments; and other things of this kind, which would take too long to enumerate.

Members have another meaning when their sense is drawn toward the devil’s side. For just as all the saints belong to Christ’s body, so all the wicked belong to the body of the Antichrist. Hence it is written in Job concerning Leviathan: “The members of his flesh cling firmly to one another” (Job 41). His flesh consists of all the reprobate, who do not rise through desire toward an understanding of the spiritual homeland. The members of his flesh are those who join themselves to such people when they act perversely and go before them in iniquity.

But one member of the body is one thing, and a member of a member another. And just as it is harmful if unity is absent from good members, so it is harmful if it is not absent from evil ones, while the water of the Red Sea is divided into two parts as the chosen people travel toward the promised land.

The nerves are called by a Greek derivation; the Greeks call them *neura*. Others think they are called nerves in Latin because the joints adhere to one another by means of them. It is entirely certain that nerves constitute the body’s greatest substance of strength. For the denser they are, the more greatly they increase firmness.

In nerves, the joining together of virtues is signified. For just as joints and bones are fastened together by nerves, so virtues and good works are joined by the glue of love. Hence it is written in Job: “You have joined me together with bones and nerves. You have granted me life and mercy, and your visitation has guarded my spirit” (Job 10). The heavenly visitation guards the human mind when it does not cease either to enrich it with virtues or to strike and pierce it with a scourge.

Again, the meaning of the word is drawn in another direction when it is written in the same book concerning Behemoth: “The nerves of his testicles are intertwined. His bones are like tubes of bronze” (Job 40). This Behemoth has as many testicles as he possesses assistants of his iniquity. They are intertwined because the arguments of his preachers are bound together by deceitful assertions, so that they may pretend to be straight while persuading others of crooked things.

“His bones,” he says, “are like tubes of bronze.” What else are the bones of the Antichrist than those who are stronger in his body? Since in their hearts iniquity has become exceedingly hardened, his entire bodily structure subsists through them. His bones are rightly compared to bronze tubes because, after the manner of an insensible metal, they possess the sound of right living but do not possess the understanding of right living.

The joints are called the heads of the bones because there they adhere, joined by nerves or by a kind of glue.

Bones are the solid supports of the body. For upon them all its posture and strength depend. Allegorically, bones should also be understood as the strength of the mind. When this fails, its vigor slips away, just as the body cannot be held together when its bones are shattered.

Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled” (Ps. 6). And elsewhere: “All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34). It is evident that bones possess neither sense nor voice; but, as we have often said, the strength of the spirit and steadfastness of mind are to be understood. They are rightly compared with bones because, just as bones hold the body together, so these strengthen holy intentions.

Therefore let the bones, not the flesh, speak this mystery—that is, firmness, not relaxation—because no one but the strength of the mind can utter such a hymn.

“Who” is negative, because no one can be like him, since the Holy Trinity is one and unique. The creature is greatly unlike the Creator. The former serves; the latter rules.

Again, the penitent says: “My bones have been roasted as in a frying pan” (Ps. 41). Just as, through a favorable reputation, the bones of those who have merited well—that is, the strength of their minds—grow fat when their conscience rejoices in happy recollection, as Solomon says, “A good reputation fattens the bones” (Prov. 15), so, through an adverse recollection of sins, the sinner’s virtue contracts as though it were being fried, while he greatly fears human reproaches and the judgments of his own conscience.

Or the sinner is here being fried because he fears future fires and conflagrations. For whoever fears that he will burn is already chilled by the terror of that very fire.

Again, bones signify the virtues of the saints, as in the Psalm: “He guards all their bones; not one of them will be broken” (Ps. 33).

Marrows are so called because they moisten the bones. For they irrigate and strengthen them. Marrow signifies the inward thought of the mind. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings” (Ps. 65). Marrow-filled burnt offerings are sacrifices that we present to the divine presence from a pure and innermost heart. For when we offer the sacrifice of a contrite heart, it must have within it the purest faith; within it must be faithful works, which, in place of marrow, render the offering most pure, lest what we sacrifice before the divine presence be dry and empty.

The vertebrae are the upper parts of the bones, gathered together in larger knots; they are so called because they turn with the bending of the limbs. Cartilages are soft bones without marrow. The ears, the partition of the nostrils, and the ends of the ribs possess this kind; so do the coverings of bones that move. They are called cartilages because, when struck, they lack pain under slight friction.

Cartilage sometimes signifies the pretense of virtues. Hence it is written in Job concerning Leviathan: “His cartilage is like plates of iron” (Job 41). Cartilage has the appearance of bone but does not have the strength of bone. What, then, does it mean that his cartilage is compared to iron plates, except that those who are weaker in him are more wicked in carrying out evil?

Therefore his cartilage is said to be like iron because those in his body who are not capable of displaying virtues are inflamed more fiercely against the slaughter of the faithful.

Some think that the ribs are so called because the inner organs are guarded by them and all the softness of the belly is protected by their enclosure.

The side is so called because, when we lie down, it is hidden; it is the left part of the body. Movement is more agile on the right side, while the left is stronger and better suited to bearing a burden. Hence it is called *laeva*, because it is more suitable for lifting and carrying something. It carries the shield, sword, quiver, and other burdens, so that the right hand may be free for action.

It should be noted that the word “side” is a synonym and is suitable for signifying many things. We speak of a person’s side, an animal’s side, the side of a building, and the side or dimension of land; all these must be interpreted in their proper places according to their particular meanings.

Nevertheless, a person’s side, which protects the intestines together with the ribs, can signify the concealment of inward counsels. Hence it is written that the Creator formed a woman from one rib taken from the side of the sleeping Adam (Gen. 2), mystically prefiguring that the mysteries of salvation would come forth from Christ’s side as he slept in death upon the cross—namely, blood and water—from which the Church, his bride, would be formed.

In the tropological sense, it must be understood that we do not reach the height of contemplation unless we cease from the oppression of external cares; nor do we behold ourselves unless, returning to the secret of silence, we are lulled to rest from every disturbance outside us. Thus we may know that one thing in us is rational, which rules, and another is animal, which is ruled.

Our silence was well represented by the sleeping Adam, from whose side a woman immediately proceeded. For whoever is carried away toward understanding inward things closes the eyes of the mind to visible affairs. Then he distinguishes within himself both what ought to rule manfully and what can be subject in weakness, so that one thing in him may be able to rule like a man, and another, like a woman, may be ruled.

The back extends from the neck to the loins. It is called *dorsum* because it is the harder surface of the body, strong like a stone, both for carrying and for enduring. The word *terga* is so called because we lie supine upon it on the ground, something only a human being can do. Dumb [brute] animals lie either on their belly or on their side. Hence in animals the back is improperly called the shoulder blades.

The back and rear, because they are the posterior parts of the body, signify either flight, as in the Psalmist’s words, “You have given me the back of my enemies” (Ps. 17), or rejection, as it is written elsewhere: “They turned their backs” (Jer. 49). This can signify the turning away of the wicked from divine worship and their contempt for true religion, just as it is written in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezek. 8) that the men standing with their backs turned toward the temple looked with their faces toward the rising sun.

Again, in the back or rear bodily pains are signified, which holy men will endure when blows are inflicted. Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “You have placed tribulations upon our back” (Ps. 65)—namely, the blows that Paul endured and the rest of the faithful multitude suffered. They were humbled by these blows so that they might reject the devil’s pride together with the world’s pleasures.

Again, the rear signifies forgetfulness of past things. Hence in prayer we ask God to cast our past sins behind his back—that is, to consign them to perpetual oblivion.

That the back and rear signify contempt of God is shown by Isaiah, who says to the Israelite people: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing from behind you” (Isa. 30). A person is admonished to his face when, created for righteousness, he receives the commandments of uprightness. But when he despises those same commandments, he has, as it were, turned the back of his mind toward his Creator’s face.

Yet behold, he still follows behind and admonishes, because although he has already been despised by us, he nevertheless does not cease to call us. We have, as it were, given our backs to him face to face when we despise and trample upon his words. But he who stands behind us and sees what is despised nevertheless recalls us when we have turned away; through commandments he cries out, and through patience he waits.

The space between the shoulder blades is called *interscapulum*, because it lies between the shoulder blades.

In the allegorical sense, the shoulder blades can signify the burden of a load, as in the passage where Abraham took bread and a skin of water and placed it upon Hagar’s shoulders (Gen. 21); or they can signify various works, according to what is written of God in the Psalm: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders” (Ps. 90).

The Lord’s shoulders are the works of his wonders, through which divine power is shown as though by certain shoulders. Therefore, whenever shoulders, eyes, or an arm are attributed to God, we must take the greatest care that the mind does not imagine anything bodily in him. To confine him who fills and embraces all things without limit within bodily features is to fall into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites.

For almighty God, drawing us toward himself, humbles himself down to our level. In order to disclose lofty things, he condescends to humble ones, so that the mind of the little ones, nourished by things it knows, may rise to seek things unknown. Hearing certain things in relation to itself, it may move toward him who is far above it as though by certain steps.

Thus it happens that through Scripture he sometimes draws certain very dissimilar likenesses of himself from human bodies, sometimes from minds, sometimes from birds, and sometimes even from insensible things.

Very often he draws a likeness of himself from human bodies. Thus, through the Prophet, it is said to the person who hopes in him: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders” (ibid.), although it is certain that in his own nature God has neither eyes nor shoulders nor any other bodily features. But because we see through the eye and bear burdens upon the shoulders, God is said to have an eye because he sees all things, and to overshadow us with shoulders because he tolerates us and, by the very fact that he tolerates us, preserves us.

He says: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders,” as though he were saying to the sinful person who begs forgiveness after sin: “The Lord will protect you with the same compassion with which he has tolerated you. He overshadows you with his shoulders—that is, while carrying you, he defends you.”

The spine is the joint of the back. It is so called because it has sharp little spines. The joints of this structure are called *spondylia*, on account of the part of the brain that is said to pass through them in a long course to the other parts of the body.

The sacred spine is the lowest part of the continuous spine, which the Greeks call *hierón ostoun* (“sacred bone”), because it is the first thing formed when the infant is conceived. For that reason it was also the first thing offered by the Gentiles to their gods, and hence it is called the sacred spine.

The spine is sometimes used for the strength of the body, sometimes for the pride of the mind, and sometimes for all sins. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “I was turned in my distress when my spine was broken” (Ps. 31). The spine is what raises and supports the whole body. Here it is rightly used for pride, which, when broken, does not cast a person down to destruction but rather raises him toward salvation. For when bodily strength and prosperity are broken, the innermost thoughts of the mind must necessarily be recalled to humility of heart.

In this passage sin as a whole is clearly expressed by the spine, because, while drawing the mind toward pleasure, it tears it as though by pricking. Hence, in the voice of the righteous and penitent, it is said: “I was turned in my distress when my spine was broken.” The mind is turned toward lamentation so that the sting of sin may be broken through repentance.

Varro says that the loins are called *renes* because streams of obscene fluid arise from them. For the veins and marrows exude a thin liquid in the kidneys, and this liquid, liquefied again in the kidneys by venereal heat, flows downward.

The kidneys sometimes signify steadfastness of mind, because just as they support the body, so steadfastness guards the mind. Hence the Prophet says: “My kidneys were loosened” (Ps. 72). He said that his kidneys had been loosened because he had sought the happiness of worldly things with careless desire.

Again, the kidneys are the inward parts of the heart, as in the Prophet: “I am the Lord, searching the kidneys and hearts” (Jer. 17).

The kidneys also sometimes signify the pleasure of the flesh arising from wandering thoughts. Hence the Psalmist asks: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. 25). If he did not know that the pleasure of lust resides in the kidneys, he would not have asked that they be burned. He asks that human pleasures and thoughts be purified by the heat of the Lord’s word.

For this reason the Israelites are rightly commanded in Exodus to have their kidneys girded when eating the Passover (Exod. 12). Whoever eats the Passover ought to have his kidneys girded, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through vices, may subdue pleasures, and may restrain the flesh from lust.

The loins are so called because of the wantonness of lust, since in men the cause of bodily pleasure is located there, just as in women it is located in the navel. Hence at the beginning of his speech the Lord says to Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38), so that preparation for resistance might be present in those places where lust is accustomed to exercise dominion.

The navel is the middle place of the body. It is so called because it is the *umbus* of the hips. Hence *umbo* also denotes the central boss of a shield, from which it hangs. The infant hangs from the navel in the womb, and through it is nourished.

The loins sometimes express strength of spirit, according to the Apostle: “Gird the loins of your mind” (Eph. 6); and sometimes the lust of the flesh, as has been said above. Hence concerning Behemoth the Lord says to Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is in the navel of his belly” (Job 40). The generative seed is said to be in the loins in men and in the navel in women, as we have shown above.

For this reason Truth says to the disciples: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). For this reason Peter, restraining lust from the heart, admonished them, saying: “Gird the loins of your mind” (1 Pet. 1). For this reason Paul, saying that the priesthood of Levi was tithed through Abraham at the time of Melchizedek, when Levi was still hidden in Abraham’s body, declares: “For he was still in the loins of his father” (Heb. 7).

Since the seed of lust is contained in women in the navel, we learned this from the testimony of the Prophet, who, under the figure of a prostituted woman, rebuking the wantonness of Judea, says: “On the day of your birth your navel was not cut” (Ezek. 16).

The *ilium* is called by a Greek word because we wrap things around there. In Greek, *eiluein* means “to wrap around.”

The testicles signify the strength of virtue in the male sex. Hence it is read in Leviticus: “You shall not offer to God any animal whose testicles are crushed, bruised, cut, or removed” (Lev. 22).

A person has crushed testicles when, as wickedness gradually increases, he crushes the offspring and signs of his virtues by which a man can be recognized. He is rightly rejected because he has harmed himself in such matters.

A person has bruised testicles when he has yielded to the temptations and tribulations inflicted upon him and has betrayed the strength of his soul. He ought not to suffer this, nor to yield at all to the approaching and afflicting enemy.

A person has cut-off and removed testicles when, by one wicked action, an impious mind cuts away and removes him—as with a knife, like a savage and predatory hand—from the union that exists in virtues.

The belly, abdomen, and womb differ from one another. The belly is what digests food that has been received; it appears externally, extends from the chest to the groin, and is called *venter* because it transmits the nourishment of life throughout the body.

The abdomen is what receives food and usually cleanses it. Sallust says: “Pretending that his abdomen was being cleansed.” It is called *alvus* because it is washed or cleansed; for from it the filth of excrement flows.

Only women have a womb, in which they conceive, shaped like a little cup. Nevertheless, authors often use *uterus* for the belly of either sex, not only poets but others as well. It is called *uterus* because it is double and divides from each side into two parts, which, spreading in different directions and being filled, curve around in the shape of a ram’s horn; or because it is filled internally with a fetus. Hence also *uter*, because it has something within it, such as limbs and internal organs.

According to the allegory, the belly signifies the capacity of reason or the affection of the soul. Hence the prophet Habakkuk says: “My belly was troubled within me” (Hab. 3). And Jeremiah says: “I suffer pain in my belly, and the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jer. 4).

Again, the Psalmist says: “My eye was troubled in anger, my soul and my belly” (Ps. 30). The literal sense has referred this to the indignation of enemies; but the eye signifies understanding, which we continually trouble and confuse whenever we fear impending dangers.

Our belly is the abdomen, in which we store swallowed food. It is plainly compared with memory, because just as the belly receives food that has been transmitted into it, so the recesses of memory suitably receive knowledge of things.

He therefore says that his belly, that is, his memory, was troubled. In it he had stored what the Lord had promised him concerning his glorification. But when the flesh saw dangers threatening it, it was inevitable that it should be disturbed by fear.

The womb sometimes signifies the secret of nature and sometimes the hidden counsel. Hence the Father says to the Son in the Psalm: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109)—that is, from the secret of my substance, from the very deity itself: wholly from the whole, almighty from almighty, light from light, the highest from the highest. No investigation and no sense can reach this.

For how can he be comprehended of whom it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). This is a wondrous brevity and a sufficient measure for our weakness, because we can grasp no more, while believing this is entirely sufficient.

Again, it is written in Job: “From whose womb did the ice come forth?” (Job 38). What does it mean that the Lord first presents himself as the father of rain, but afterward says that ice comes forth from his womb and declares that he begets frost from heaven, except that, in a wondrous manner, he first waters the soil of our hearts so that it may receive the seeds of the word through the rain of hidden grace? Then, lest it flow forth too freely in the virtues it has conceived, he restrains it by the inward discipline of his dispensation.

We call not only the intestines *viscera*, but everything beneath the hide, from *viscum*, which lies between the skin and the flesh. There are also the vital *viscera*, that is, the places surrounding the heart, called *viscera* because life—that is, the soul—is contained there. There are also the *viscera*, the heads of the nerves, joined together from blood and nerves.

Mystically, the *viscera* signify affection, pity, and mercy. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “Through the tender mercies of our God, by which the dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). And the Apostle says: “If there is any affection and mercy” (Phil. 2).

The *viscera* also take on an opposite meaning, as in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Judas: “His viscera were poured out” (Acts 1)—that is, the designs of his wickedness were disclosed.

The heart derives its name from the Greek designation, which they call *kardia*, or from *cura* (“care”). For in it every anxiety and the source of knowledge resides. It is situated near the lungs so that, when anger is kindled, it may be tempered by the moisture of the lungs. It has two arteries, one of which, the left, contains more blood, while the right contains more breath. Hence we examine the pulse in the right arm.

The heart is appropriately adapted to signify many things. Sometimes it denotes the soul, sometimes understanding, sometimes counsel and a hidden word, and sometimes understanding again.

The heart denotes the soul, as in Solomon: “With all vigilance guard your heart, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4). The heart denotes understanding, as in the Psalmist: “My heart and my flesh rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83). Although both expressions appear to pertain to the flesh, there is no doubt that “heart” can refer to understanding. For when we wish to praise someone’s wisdom, we undoubtedly praise that person’s heart.

Counsel is expressed under the name of the heart, because it precedes action, as the Savior testifies in the Gospel: “From the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, murders, and the rest” (Matt. 15). Concerning this the Psalmist says: “With deceitful lips, in a heart and a heart, they have spoken wicked things” (Ps. 11). By saying “with a heart and a heart,” whenever we wish to express deceitful people, we declare their hearts to be double, as Solomon [James] says: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James 1).

When we wish to indicate the simple, we testify that they have one heart, as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). We likewise call those “double-tongued” who do not remain steadfast in one judgment.

For diligence and devotion, the word is used in the passage: “With my whole heart I have sought you” (Ps. 85). This too is the Lord’s gift, that he declares himself to have sought God with his whole heart—that is, with complete devotion. For he would not have sought him unless he had first been sought.

The designation “heart” has yet another meaning when it signifies death, hell, or the grave. Hence the Savior’s statement to the Jews: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. 12).

The fish that swallowed Jonah in the sea signifies the death that Christ suffered in the world. Jonah was therefore in the belly of the sea-monster three days and three nights. And our Savior was in death and in the tomb three days and three nights. Then what is read in Hosea was fulfilled: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O …”
in the lower regions (Hos. 13). And just as Jonah did not remain in the belly of the fish but was cast out onto dry land, so also our Savior’s soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption; rather, he rose in glory.

Likewise, concerning Leviathan the Lord says to Job: “His heart will be hardened like a stone and will be compressed like a smith’s anvil” (Job 41). The heart of the ancient enemy will be hardened like stone, because no repentance leading to conversion will ever soften him; he will be fitted only for the blows of eternal vengeance. Leviathan, therefore, is compressed like a smith’s anvil, for he will be confined by the bonds of hell, so that he may be beaten by the continual blows of eternal punishment.

The *praecordia* are the places near the heart, through which perception is received; they are called *praecordia* because the heart and thought have their origin there. Under the name *praecordia*, the rational activity of the soul may be understood, as in Isaiah’s words to the Lord: “My soul desired you in the night, and with my spirit within my *praecordia*” (Isa. 26).

The pulse is so called because it throbs; by its indication we discern either sickness or health. Its motion is of two kinds: simple, consisting of a single leap, and compound, irregular and uneven, consisting of several movements. These movements have fixed intervals. A pulse that strikes in a dactylic rhythm is healthy so long as it is without defect. If it becomes quicker, like those called *dorcadacizantes*, or slower, like those called *mirmicizontes*, these are signs of death.

Veins are so called because they are channels through which the flowing blood travels, and streams distributed throughout the body by which all the limbs are irrigated. The word *vena* is also used of water, from which a spring boils forth. This may likewise signify the progress of spiritual grace and teaching. Hence it is written in the Book of Proverbs: “Let your vein be blessed” (Prov. 5). Elsewhere: “A vein of living waters,” that is, wisdom—a sweet draught and health-giving drink.

[Col. 0171B] Blood derives its name from a Greek etymology, because it is nourished, sustained, and lives. It is called blood while it remains in the body; when poured out, it is called *cruor*. For *cruor* is so called either because, once poured out, it runs downward, or because it falls while running. Some interpret *cruor* as corrupted blood that is discharged. Others say that blood is so called because it is sweet.

Pure blood is found only in the young. Physicians say that blood diminishes with age; hence old people also have trembling. Properly speaking, blood is the possession of the soul. For this reason women customarily tear their cheeks in mourning. This is also why purple garments and purple flowers are offered to the dead.

Blood sometimes signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, as in the Savior’s words in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). Indeed, the Law commanded the Israelite people (Exod. 12) to place some of the blood of the Passover lamb on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which they ate the Passover, so that they might escape the destroyer’s slaughter. In the same way, the blood of Christ cleanses our conscience from dead works so that we may serve the living God, and it frees us from the power of the enemy and from the persecution of the ancient adversary (Heb. 9).

Blood is also given another meaning when it signifies either carnal activity or the corruption of mortal nature. Thus the Prophet prays to the Lord: “Deliver me from blood-guilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50). And again: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. 5). A man of blood is one stained with human blood, as well as one who deceives a living person. The Apostle likewise says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Cor. 15).

The lung derives its name from Greek. For the Greeks call the lung *pneumon*, because it is the heart’s fan, in which there is *pneuma*, that is, spirit, by which they are stirred and moved. Hence they are called lungs. In Greek, *pneuma* means “spirit”; by blowing and agitating the air, it expels and draws it in. From this the lungs move and palpitate: they open themselves to receive the breath and contract in order to expel it. It is an organ of the body.

[Col. 0172A] The liver has its name because fire has its seat there, and from there rises to the brain; from there it is distributed to the eyes, the other senses, and the limbs. By its heat it transforms into blood the juice drawn from food, which it supplies to each limb for nourishment and sustenance. According to those who discuss natural philosophy, pleasure and desire reside in the liver. In the liver—that is, in the *epate*—we may therefore understand pleasure or desire to be signified.

Hence the command in the Law (Lev. 3–4) that the portion of the liver, together with the belly, kidneys, and fat, be offered to God: for we ought to turn our desire toward God’s will rather than toward the world. In the Book of Tobit (Tob. 6) we read that the angel commanded Tobit to gut a fish and place its heart, gall, and liver in a small chest, and then, at the angel’s command, to place the liver upon live coals so that it might have power to drive away the demon.

[Col. 0172B] In the liver, by whose heat the food received is cooked in the stomach, we are taught to strive, through mature judgment, to cook thoroughly the fleeting thoughts of the flesh and send them away into the privy, lest we in any way consent to the devil’s having a place in the chambers of our hearts. Rather, by the strength of faith and sacred prayers, let us hasten to drive him out.

The fibers of the liver are its extremities, like the outermost parts of leaves on the stalks, or like projecting tongues. They are called *fibrae* because among the Gentiles they were brought by diviners to the altars in the sacred rites of Phoebus; once offered and burned, they received prophetic answers. This fittingly accords with what we said above: that a portion of the liver was commanded to be offered to God, so that what belongs to God might be offered to God rather than to empty and deaf idols, in which there is only fraud and deception.

The spleen is so called from *supplementum*, because it exists on the opposite side of the liver, in an empty space. Some even think that it was made for the sake of laughter, for we laugh through the spleen. This organ of the viscera also admonishes us not to rejoice and be glad in the world’s empty happiness, but in the Lord, lest we open our mouths to foolish laughter. Concerning this Wisdom says: “I counted laughter as error” (Eccl. 2). Rather, let us wipe away our sins in the present age through mourning, so that in the life to come we may enjoy eternal joy. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5).

We grow angry through the gall, we understand through the heart, and we love through the liver. When these four elements are joined together, the animal is complete.

Gall is so called because it is a little sac containing the humor called bile. Gall signifies the bitterness and deceitfulness of a perverse mind. Hence the blessed Apostle Peter said to Simon, who sought deceitfully to obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity” (Acts 8).

For this reason it is also written in Job concerning the wicked: “His bread in his belly will be turned into the gall of asps within him” (Job 20); that is, the satisfaction of transient pleasure will be turned to bitterness at the end of retribution. For then the wicked will see that they have been killed by the poison of the ancient serpent, when, delivered over to avenging flames, they are tormented together with that same persuader of theirs.

Alternatively, “His bread in his belly will be turned into the gall of asps within him”: while they glory in knowledge of the sacred Law, they turn the drink of life into a draught of poison for themselves. Again, in the Song of Deuteronomy we read concerning the Jews: “Their grape is the grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness” (Deut. 32)—the very people who gave our Savior, hanging on the cross, vinegar mixed with gall to drink.

The stomach is called *os* in Greek because it is the mouth or entrance of the belly: it receives food and passes it on to the intestines. In the stomach we may sometimes understand anger and indignation of mind to be signified. Hence we say that angry people “stomach” things, because they cannot conceal their fury within but cast it outward in a violent eruption of insults.

The intestines are so called because they are enclosed in the inner part of the body. They are arranged in long coils in the manner of circles so that they may gradually digest the food they receive and not be obstructed by food added afterward. In the intestines, therefore, the hidden things of the mind and inward thoughts may be understood. Hence it is written: “Touched with anguish of heart within” (Gen. 6). And in the Book of Job we read: “My intestines boiled with pain without respite” (Job 30).

For this reason, too, Leviticus commands that the intestines of the sacrificial victim, together with its head and feet, be washed with water and burned to the Lord as a burnt offering and a pleasing odor. The command that the intestines—or *interanea*, as another edition reads—be washed with water together with the feet announces the sacrament of baptism under figurative preaching. For the one who washes the intestines cleanses the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the completion of the sacrament. And he knows that “the one who is clean has no need except to wash his feet” (John 13).

The womb is so called because the fetus is generated in it. It receives the seed and cherishes it; once cherished, it gives it bodily form; once formed, it divides it into limbs.

The *vulva* is so called as if from *valva*, that is, “door” or “gate” of the belly: either because it receives the seed or because the fetus proceeds from it. The vulva signifies inward secrets. Hence it is written in Job: “Who enclosed the sea with doors when it burst forth as though proceeding from the womb?” (Job 38). For at that time it confronted the human race with the commandments of the Law, when the world, still near its origin, was emerging from its own beginning toward the progress of carnal life. To proceed from the womb is to appear bodily in the light of the glory of the present age.

The inner parts of the soul are also called a vulva, where good or evil is conceived. The Church also has an inward vulva, namely faith, from which corrupted heretics have brought forth a miscarriage from the mother, as the Psalm says concerning them: “Sinners have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood” (Ps. 57).

The bladder is so called because, like a vessel of water, it is filled with urine collected from the kidneys and is distended with fluid. Birds do not possess it. Urine is so called either because it burns or because it is discharged from the kidneys. By its condition the future state of health or sickness is revealed. This fluid is commonly called *lotium*, because it makes clothing washed—that is, cleansed.

Semen is what, once cast, is received either by the earth or by the womb for the generation of fruits or offspring. It is a fluid produced by the cooking of food and drink and diffused through the veins and marrow, from which it sweats forth. It collects in the kidneys like bilge water; expelled through intercourse and received in a woman’s womb, it is formed into a body by the heat of the viscera and by the irrigation of menstrual blood.

The name “seed” is appropriately applied to various kinds of things, because the seed of every animal is the source from which its origin arises. There is also seed of trees, grasses, and vegetables, from which they derive their origin, as we read that the Lord said concerning the fruits of the earth in Genesis (Gen. 1): “Let the earth bring forth green grass and produce seed, and a fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth,” and so forth.

In the Gospel parable (Luke 8), the Savior says that the seed is the word of God, because from it proceeds the fruit of good virtues.

Menstruation is the superfluous blood of women. It is called *menstrua* from the circuit of the moon’s light, during which this flow customarily occurs. In Greek, the moon is called *mene*, from which women’s menstrual discharges receive their name.

Woman is the only menstruating animal. Through contact with this blood, crops fail to sprout, wine turns sour, grasses die, trees lose their fruit, iron is corrupted by rust, and bronze blackens. If dogs eat anything contaminated by it, they become rabid. Asphalt glue, which cannot be dissolved by iron or water, is itself polluted by this blood and falls apart spontaneously.

After many days of menstruation, semen cannot generate because the menstrual blood is no longer present by which it may be moistened and irrigated. Thin semen cannot adhere to the female organs; it slips away and lacks the power of adhesion. Thick semen likewise lacks the power to generate, because it cannot mix with menstrual blood on account of its excessive thickness. Thus males or females may become sterile through excessive thickness or excessive thinness of semen or blood.

Some say that the human heart is formed first, because all life and wisdom reside in it; then, by the fortieth day, the whole body is completed—something, as they report, learned from abortions. Others say that the fetus begins from the head. Hence, in the eggs of birds, we see the eyes formed first.

The fetus is so called because it is still warmed and nourished in the womb. Its second covering is called the *folliculus*, which is born together with the child and contains it; it is so called because it accompanies and follows.

They say that children resemble their fathers if the father’s seed is stronger, and their mothers if the mother’s is stronger; in this way the features of the face are reproduced. Those who reproduce the appearance of both parents are conceived from paternal and maternal seed mixed in equal measure. They become like grandparents and great-grandparents because, just as many seeds are hidden in the earth, so seeds are hidden within us that will reproduce the features of our parents.

They say that boys are born from paternal seed and girls from maternal seed, because every birth consists of a double seed; whichever part is greater, once it gains strength, determines the likeness of the sex.

[Col. 0175A] Allegorically, the flow of blood may be understood as the obscenity of idolatry and the pollution of error. The menstrual period may likewise be understood as the time when almost the whole world was involved in error and idolatry. It is forbidden to approach or have intercourse with a menstruating woman, because a Catholic person may not share either in the idolatry of pagans or in the heresy of heretics.

The thighs are so called because it is in this part that the female sex differs from the male. They extend from the groin to the knees. The word *femina* is derived from *femur*, referring to the parts by which we cling to the backs of horses when riding. Hence in former times warriors were said to have lost their horses “under the thighs.”

The thigh signifies the lineage of descendants, as we read in Genesis concerning Jacob: “He touched the breadth of his thigh, and he limped” (Gen. 32). The thigh also signifies human flesh, as in Jeremiah: “After you showed me, I struck my thigh” (Jer. 31). At times the thigh signifies the Lord’s Incarnation, and at times carnal pleasure.

Thus in the Psalm the Prophet is read to have said to the Lord: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty” (Ps. 45). He says, “Gird your sword,” using a metaphor drawn from a warrior who girds himself with a sword before battle so that he may strike down the enemy.
