Here, however, we should understand the sword as the word of preaching. The Lord himself bears witness to this in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10). The Apostle says likewise: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

The word of God is called a sword because by the blow of its power it penetrates human hearts made corporeal by vices; and human weakness cannot resist where that glory of strength deigns to enter.

The thigh signifies the Incarnation of the Lord and Savior, as we read in Genesis: “The ruler will not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs” (Gen. 49). In the same mystery Abraham also made his servant swear (Gen. 24). When he added, after touching his thigh, “O most mighty,” he did so so that you might believe in the revered Incarnation, which divine power assumed.

Similarly, the supremely wise man says: “His sword is upon his thigh.” This may appropriately be understood to signify that carnal desire must be restrained by the word of God. For in what follows—“in your appearance and your beauty” (Ps. 45)—we clearly recognize both natures: “appearance” pertains to humanity, and “beauty” to divinity. The appearance in which salvation appeared to the world is blessed; the beauty from which all beautiful and comely things derive is most fittingly proclaimed.

We also read in the Song of Songs that the bridegroom says to the bride: “The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artist” (Song 7). Here the concord of two peoples, made fruitful by spiritual offspring, is signified in the joining of the thighs. They are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artist—that is, established by the ineffable generosity of our Creator. In the necklaces, good works are expressed.

The groins may signify the fury of lust or anger. Hence in the Book of Kings we read that Abner struck Asahel in the groin with the butt end of his spear and pierced him through (2 Sam. 2). Whom else did Asahel represent except those whom furious rage seizes and drives headlong? They must be avoided with all the greater caution in the same violent impulse, the more fiercely they are carried away by their madness.

Thus Abner—whose name in our language means “the father’s lamp”—fled. For when the tongue of teachers, which indicates the heavenly light, sees someone’s mind being carried away through the precipices of rage, and, when confronted by an angry person, refrains from returning verbal darts, it does not wish to strike the pursuer. When Abner therefore stopped in the face of the pursuer, he pierced him not with the point of the spear but with its butt end. To strike with the point is to confront someone with the force of open reproof; to strike the pursuer with the butt end is to touch the furious person calmly in certain ways and, as though sparing him, to overcome him.

Asahel immediately fell dead, because when agitated minds sense both that they are being spared and that they are nevertheless being touched inwardly and calmly by the reasoning of the responses, they immediately fall from the position to which they had raised themselves. Those who recoil from the force of their own heat under the blow of gentleness die, as it were, without a sword.

The hips are said to be like joined axles. The thighs move in them, and their concave parts are called vertebrae, because the heads of the thighs turn within them. The *suffragines* are so called because they are broken—that is, bent—below, not above, as in the arms.

The knees are the joints of the thighs and legs. They are called *genua* because in the womb they are opposite the cheeks. There they adhere to one another and are related to the eyes, which indicate tears and compassion. For the knees are named from the cheeks.

Finally, a human being is generated and formed in a folded position, with the knees raised, by which the eyes are formed so that they become hollow and recessed. Hence Ennius says: “And the cheeks press tightly against the knees.” This is why, when people prostrate themselves at someone’s knees, they immediately weep. Nature intended to remind them of their mother’s womb, where they sat as though in darkness before coming into the light.

The knees may mystically signify a confession of humility, as in the Apostle’s words: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. 3). Hence Peter also fell at Jesus’ knees, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5).

At times the knees signify the strength of faith. Concerning this, the divine voice says to the prophet Elijah in the Book of Kings: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent their knees before Baal” (1 Kings 19).

At times, again, the knees are understood as signifying the members of Christ, as in the Psalm: “My knees have grown weak from fasting” (Ps. 109). Yet the Gospel testifies (Matt. 4) that Christ the Lord fasted for forty days and forty nights; we do not read that his knees grew weak, but only that he was hungry. If this hunger is referred to the knees—that is, to the stability of the body, upon which we always stand—it can be applied with some difficulty. If this presents a problem, it is better to refer “knees” to his members, which truly grew weak when his apostles were scattered during his Passion. For what could have been weaker than that Peter denied him and the rest of the faithful company hid themselves?

The ankle is named from *talus*, for the *talus* is a prominent roundness. Hence the rounded summit of a temple is also called a *talus*. The *talus* is beneath the leg, below the heel. The ankle signifies the end of any matter, just as it lies beneath the legs and the prominence of the body.

Hence we read that Jacob made his son Joseph a long, many-colored tunic (Gen. 37), that is, one woven in variegated colors. It is called a long tunic because it descended as far as the ankles and was distinguished by the marvelous variety of the craftsman’s work. Allegorically, this tunic signified the variety of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ.

In another way, Joseph alone is described as having a long tunic, although he is said to have persevered in righteousness to the end among his eleven brothers. What, then, is the long tunic except a completed action? Just as a tunic extended downward covers the ankle of the body, so a good action covers us before God’s eyes all the way to the end of life. Hence Moses commands that the tail of the sacrificial victim be offered on the altar (Lev. 3:7), so that every good work we begin may also be completed with a persevering end.

The feet derive their name from a Greek etymology. The Greeks call them *podas*, because they move forward on the ground by alternating steps while remaining fixed upon it. The feet signify the course of the present life and the stability of mind and faith, as in the Psalm: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. 121); that is, the steps of our works remain firmly in the faith and religion that the holy Church holds in the present age.

The meaning of the feet is turned toward its contrary in the prophetic testimony: “Why do you limp on both feet?” (1 Kings 18)—that is, you are unstable and overturned in word and deed, and inclined toward evil.

Again, it is written in the Psalm concerning the Jews: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. 14). By “feet” he means the progress of their counsel, by which we advance from a beginning to the outcomes of affairs. By saying “swift,” he showed that they lacked moderation in their plans for shedding blood—understand, the blood of the Lord and Savior—so that the enormity of their wicked deed might increase.

The feet also signify the course of life or the stability of mind and faith, as in the Psalm: “Make my steps firm in your paths” (Ps. 16).

The soles are named from their flatness. They are not rounded, as in four-footed animals—for otherwise a two-footed human being could not stand—but are formed flat and elongated so that they might make the body stable. The soles are the forward parts of the feet, which also consist of many bones.

The soles signify the end of our way of life. Hence it is written in Isaiah concerning the Jewish people: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. 1)—that is, from one extreme to the other. Their entire way of life had been pierced by the thorns of vices and sins, and no soundness of right faith or good works appeared in them.

Hence it is written in the Psalm concerning the traitor Judas: “The one who ate my bread has magnified his supplanting against me” (Ps. 40). He had received the bread of teaching from the Savior’s mouth and lived with him in common fellowship with the other apostles; yet, while they were unaware, he plotted the crime of betrayal with the Jews, so that he might hand him over with a kiss. O deaf disciple, utterly hardened in an unteachable heart! Who could believe that he had received any virtue in his mind from such great goodness, when he proved to be so cruel a murderer of his own father?

The heel is a part of the sole, named from its callus, by which we tread the earth; hence the word *calcaneus*. The *solum* is the lower part of the foot, so called because by it we imprint traces upon the earth. *Solum* is also said of everything that supports something, as though it were solid. Thus the earth is a *solum* because it supports all things, and the sole of the foot is a *solum* because it bears the entire weight of the body.

The heel is the supplanting of vices, or the final course of life. Concerning the heel it is written in the Psalter of the wicked: “They themselves will watch my heel” (Ps. 56). This is the devil’s custom, or that of those known to be his servants: to watch our heel—that is, our final state—with treacherous cunning. Thus the Lord foretold to the serpent: “She will watch your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3). The devil knows that our final circumstances are judged, and he wishes to overturn them so that we may reach the peril of guilt.

Footprints, by which we leave behind an indication of our passing as we move along on our feet, sometimes mystically signify stability in the virtues, as in the Psalm: “That my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. 16). Transferred to another meaning, they show the wandering path of sinners, as in the words: “The way of the wicked passes like the track of a ship” (Wis. 5).

Nor do I think it should be left unsaid that there are things in our body made solely for usefulness, such as the viscera; things made for both usefulness and beauty, such as the senses in the face and the hands and feet on the body, whose usefulness is great and whose appearance is most comely; things made solely for beauty, such as the nipples in men and the navel in both sexes; and things made for sexual distinction, such as the genitals, a long beard, and a broad chest in men; in women, smooth cheeks and a narrow chest, with broadened loins and flanks for conceiving and carrying fetuses.

# CHAPTER II. On the Position and Condition of the Human Body

Standing signifies standing firm in faith, as in the Apostle: “Stand firm in the faith” (I Cor. 16). Walking signifies striving toward God, as in the Psalm: “And I walked in a broad place” (Ps. 118). Sitting signifies resting humbly in God, as in the Gospel: “But you, sit in the city.” And in the Book of Kings it is said of David: “And he sat before the Lord” (II Sam. 7). Lying down signifies succumbing either to vices or to temptations. Hence it is read in the Gospel: “And he found him lying in bed” (Mark 7). Running signifies prospering in good works. In the Apostle: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (I Cor. 9); and in the negative sense: “Their feet run to evil” (Prov. 1). Ascent signifies progress in the Lord. In the Psalm: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. 83). And in Exodus: “The children of Israel went up from Egypt armed” (Exod. 13). Ascent is also used negatively, signifying the presumption of pride, as in the Gospel: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10). Descent signifies falling away from God. In the Gospel: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke 10). And in Isaiah: “Woe, because you climb onto horses in order to go down to Egypt” (Isa. 30).

# CHAPTER III. How Human Members Are Ascribed to the Devil

It must be understood that when the members of a human being and human actions are ascribed to the devil, they are not to be understood historically but allegorically, because such figures are found in many places in sacred Scripture. For the devil is the head of all evils. Hence it is read in Habakkuk: “You struck the head of the house of the wicked” (Hab. 3).

The devil’s body is wicked human beings. Thus concerning Behemoth it is read in the book of blessed Job: “His body is like cast shields” (Job 41). His eyes—or his teeth—are heretics or all wicked teachers, as it is written in the aforementioned book: “His eyes are like eyelids; around his teeth is terror” (ibid.). The devil’s nostrils are his wicked inspirations, as in Job: “Smoke comes forth from his nostrils” (ibid.). The devil’s mouth is his speech, by which he addresses human hearts through hidden thoughts, as in Job: “From his mouth flames proceed” (ibid.).

The devil’s tongue is the wisdom of this world or the doctrine of heretics, as in Job: “And you will bind his tongue with a cord” (Job 40). The devil’s bones are all those who are powerful and strong in wickedness, or heretics, as in Job: “His bones are tubes of bronze” (ibid.). His cartilage signifies those less powerful than those called bones, as in Job: “His cartilage is like plates of iron” (ibid.). The devil’s breath is a hidden inspiration through which he makes the hearts of sinners burn with carnal love, as in Job: “His breath makes the coals burn” (Job 41).

The devil’s face is the coming of Antichrist or his manifest wickedness, as in Job: “Poverty goes before his face” (ibid.). The devil’s flesh is all those who are weak in his body and less capable of sinning, as in Job: “The members of his flesh cling together” (ibid.). The devil’s testicles are either heretics or wicked thoughts that subtly bind sinners with their chains, as in Job: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined” (Job 40). The devil’s tail is Antichrist or the habit of sinning, as in the statement: “He tightens his tail like a cedar” (ibid.).

For the devil to sleep means for him to rest in the heart of the reprobate, as in Job: “Under the shade he sleeps in the secrecy of the reed” (ibid.). For the devil to feed means to take delight in the sins of the wicked, as in Job: “The mountains bear grass for him” (ibid.).

What concerns the human being and the parts of the body has already been discussed in part above. Let us now add the stages of human life.

# BOOK SEVEN

## [Col. 0179] CHAPTER I. On the Stages of Human Life

There are six stages of life: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age.

The first age is infancy, the age of the child being born into the light; it extends through seven years. The second age is childhood, that is, the pure age, not yet capable of generating; it extends to fourteen years. The third is adolescence, mature for procreation; it extends to twenty-eight years. The fourth is youth, the strongest of all the ages, ending in the fiftieth year.

The fifth age is that of the older person, that is, maturity (*gravitas*). It is the decline from youth into old age—not yet old age, but no longer youth—because it is the age of the older person, whom the Greeks call *presbytēs*. For among the Greeks an old man is called not *presbyter* but *gerōn*. This age begins at fifty and ends at seventy.

The sixth age is old age, which does not end at any fixed number of years. After those five ages, however long life may continue, it is assigned to old age. Extreme old age (*senium*) is the final part of old age, so called because it is the limit of the sixth age.

In these six periods philosophers have described human life, in which a person changes and proceeds until reaching the limit of death. Let us therefore pass briefly through the aforementioned stages of life, demonstrating their etymologies in the human being.

An infant is a person of the first age. He is called *infans* because he still does not know how to speak (*fari*), that is, he cannot speak. For speech is not yet fully articulated, since the teeth have not yet been properly arranged.

Infants mystically signify little ones in wickedness, as in the Psalm: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. 8). Nursing children signify those making progress in the faith of Christ.

A weaned child signifies Christ, of whom Isaiah says: “Upon the holes of the asp and in the den of the basilisk, the weaned child shall put his hand” (Isa. 11). The weaned signify the perfected, as though withdrawn from the simple food of instruction. Here and above, *ablactatus* means “driven away from milk,” away from the breasts.

A little child (*parvulus*) mystically signifies Christ, as in Isaiah: “A little child is born for us” (Isa. 9). Little ones also signify those humble through the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Ps. 114). In the negative sense, in Hosea: “Let their little ones be dashed to pieces” (Hos. 14).

Little ones signify wicked thoughts before they are perfected in action, as in the Psalm: “Blessed is he who shall seize your little ones and dash them against the rock” (Ps. 136), that is, against Christ.

A boy (*puer*) is so called from *puritia*, “purity,” because he is pure and does not yet possess the down and blossoming of the cheeks. These are *ephebi*, that is, tender adolescent youths, so called from *hēbē* (“youth”), and not yet men.

The word *puer* is used in three ways: of birth, as in Isaiah, “A child is born for us” (Isa. 9); of age, as in “eight-year-old” or “ten-year-old.” Hence the line: “Already, as a boy, he bore the tender neck of kings.” And of service and purity of faith, concerning which the Lord says to the prophet: “You are my boy; do not fear” (Jer. 1), even though Jeremiah had long since passed beyond the years of childhood.

The boy mystically signifies Christ, as in the Gospel: “The child Jesus grew” (Luke 2). The word is also used negatively: “A boy of a hundred years shall die,” that is, a sinner of consummate folly, as in Isaiah (Isa. 65).

The saints are called boys because of their purity, as in Isaiah: “Behold, I and the boys whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. 8). In another sense: “Do not become boys in understanding, and so forth” (I Cor. 14).

A girl (*puella*) is a little one, as though *pupilla*, “pupil” or “little doll.” Hence we call people orphans (*pupilli*) not on account of their condition but on account of their childish age. They are called *pupilli*, as though “without eyes,” that is, deprived of their parents.

Strictly speaking, those are called orphans whose fathers died before they received a name from them; the others are called bereaved. *Orphans*—that is, those who are also *pupilli*—is a Greek name; *pupilli* is Latin. For in the Psalm, where it is read, “You will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 9), the Greek has *orphano*.

The meaning of this statement is as follows. By “orphan” he does not mean one whose carnal father has died, but one whose father—the world—has been buried. You will find many orphans deprived of a visible father who are blasphemers, oath-breakers, and—something especially common at that age—licentious. Such people are shown to be alien from the Lord.

But the help of God cannot be separated from those orphans whose father, the devil, is shown to have been extinguished in their sinful actions. And observe that he says, “You will be their helper,” so that when you see them suffering in the flesh, you should not doubt that they will be delivered.

It is also written in the Psalter: “He will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners” (Ps. 145). The orphan and the widow are those who look upon the Lord with a pure mind, deprived of human consolations. Christ receives them in order to vindicate them by his protection. But when he has received them in accordance with his mercy, he will destroy the devil, who is the way of sinners—that is, he will make him alien from the boundary of his kingdom.

Pregnant women mystically signify the souls of the faithful who have recently conceived the word of God but have not yet given birth to it in action. Thus in Exodus, concerning contentious teachers, it is said: “If two men are quarreling, and someone strikes a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage” (Exod. 21)—that is, if he causes the word of faith to be lost.

Concerning these souls of the faithful, Amos speaks of heretics: “They have ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead” (Amos 1). Pregnant women may also signify the souls of sinners, filled with thoughts of desires, concerning whom it is said in the Gospel: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days” (Matt. 24).

A woman giving birth signifies one who conceives words of faith in the ear of the heart and produces them in confession or action, as it is said in Jeremiah concerning the faithful: “Among them shall be the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and the woman giving birth” (Jer. 31). In the negative sense: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. 7).

The firstborn signifies Christ, concerning whom it is said in the Law: “Every firstborn that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. 13). The firstborn also signifies the Jewish people, as in the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. 4).

The firstborn daughter signifies the primitive life, for which it is written in the Law: “You shall redeem all the firstborn of your sons” (Exod. 13).

Pubescent youths (*puberes*) are so called from *pubes*, the shameful part of the body, because these places then first begin to grow down. Some think that puberty is named from the years, so that a person is considered pubescent after completing fourteen years, even if he reaches puberty very late. The most certain sign of puberty is a bodily condition that displays maturity and the ability to generate.

A *puerpera* is a woman who gives birth while still in her girlhood years. Hence Horace is praised for the verse:

> “The woman in childbed, having borne her first offspring.”

They are called *puerperae* either because they are burdened by childbirth or because they give birth to children for the first time. Hence the poet says of the mother of the Savior:

> “Hail, holy mother, having borne the King as a woman in childbed.”

An adolescent (*adolescens*) is so called because he is mature for generating, or from growing and increasing.

Adolescents signify the faithful who are making progress through their works, as in the Letter of John: “I write to you, adolescents, because you have conquered the evil one” (I John 2). In the negative sense: “For youth and pleasure are vanity” (Eccl. 11).

A young man (*juvenis*) is so called because he begins to be able to help, as with young oxen, when they have passed beyond the stage of calves. A young man is situated in the very increase of age and prepared to provide assistance. For to help is the work of a human being who contributes something.

Just as the thirtieth year is the year of full maturity among human beings, so among cattle and beasts of burden the third year is the strongest. Young men signify those who are eager for God, as in the Letter of John: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you” (I John 2). In the negative sense, as in the Psalm: “Their young men fire consumed” (Ps. 77).

Infants, adolescents, and young men mystically signify those who grow in the grace of God and resist the devil courageously. Hence the apostle John says in his Letter: “I write to you, adolescents, because you have conquered the evil one. I write to you, infants, because you have known the Father. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and you have conquered the evil one, and the word of God remains in you” (I John 2).

The terms boy, adolescent, and young man are also found used negatively when they signify folly of understanding or wantonness of behavior. Hence it is written: “Folly is bound up in the heart of a boy, but the rod of discipline will drive it away” (Prov. 22). Thus in the Book of Kings it is read concerning Rehoboam that, abandoning the counsel of the elders, he followed the counsel of the adolescents and young men (I Kings 12).

For this reason the Apostle also commands: “Do not become boys in understanding, but be little ones in wickedness” (I Cor. 14). A little one is understood to be humble and simple in mind, as in the Lord’s testimony in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

The term *parvulus* has another meaning where the Apostle says: “When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I understood as a little one, I reasoned as a little one; but when I became a man, I put away the things that belonged to a little one” (I Cor. 13).

A man (*vir*) is so called because there is greater strength in him than in women. From this, too, *virtue* takes its name; or he is so called because he acts forcefully toward a woman.

Mystically, a man sometimes signifies Christ, whose wife is the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. 5).

A man is also understood as spiritual understanding in the history of Scripture. Again, a man signifies the spirit that rules in the soul. Hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “Go, call your husband” (John 4)—that is, return to your understanding.

The word man is also used in the contrary sense, as in the Pentateuch: “A virgin of very beautiful appearance, whom no man had known” (Gen. 24)—that is, the devil, who often corrupts the mind through thought.

The word man signifies Christ in the testimony of Zechariah: “Behold, a man will come, and his name is Orient” (Zech. 6). And elsewhere: “Return, returning children, because I am your husband” (Jer. 3).

Again, man and wife signify Christ and the Church, as in the Apostle: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. But I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5).

Man and wife also signify soul and flesh, with children signifying the works generated by both, as in Exodus: “He shall serve you with your wife and children” (Exod. 21). Likewise, man and wife signify the devil and the city of Babylon, that is, the gathering of all evils.

A woman (*mulier*) is so called from softness (*mollities*), as though *mollier*, with the letter *l* removed or changed. The two sexes are separated by the strength and weakness of their bodies. But the reason the man has the greater strength and the woman the lesser is so that she might be patient with the man—namely, so that lust would not compel men, because of resisting women, to seek something else or rush toward another sex.

The word woman refers to the female sex, not to the corruption of virginity; this is clear from the language of sacred Scripture. For Eve, immediately formed from the side of her husband and not yet touched by a man, was called woman, as Scripture says: “And he formed her into a woman” (Gen. 2).

Mystically, woman signifies either the Church because of the generation of children, concerning which it is read in Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31). This sevenfold woman also contains the mystery of the Church, as in Isaiah: “Seven women will take hold of one man” (Isa. 4).

Or woman signifies the soul or human flesh, which ought to be subject to the command of the spirit and governed by its rule. Hence the Apostle says: “The head of the woman is the man, and the head of the man is Christ” (I Cor. 11). The spirit then rules the soul or flesh well if it has itself deserved to be ruled by the Spirit of Christ, because “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8).

Women also signify the souls of the faithful, though weak, as the prophet says concerning heretics: “You have driven the women of my people from the house of my delights” (Mic. 2).

Woman or wife signifies wisdom, as in the statement: “Rejoice with the wife of your youth” (Prov. 5). This woman has borne sons, not daughters—that is, virtues, not vices.

Again, woman is understood in the negative sense. The woman is the city of Babylon, which bears the figure of the whole world, as in the Apocalypse: “I saw a woman drunk with the blood of the saints” (Rev. 17). Woman also signifies heretical depravity, as in Solomon: “A foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements” (Prov. 9). Women signify the two peoples, Jewish and heretical, as in Zechariah: “Behold, two women carrying an amphora” (Zech. 5)—that is, the devil, who is the head of all iniquity.

The adulterer signifies the devil or demons, as in Isaiah: “But you, draw near, sons of the sorceress, offspring of the adulterer and the prostitute” (Isa. 57).

The prostitute signifies carnal propagation, the Jewish people, or the sinful soul. The harlot signifies the sinful soul which, having abandoned the heavenly husband—that is, Christ—conceives adulterous fruits of iniquity from the devil, as in Jeremiah: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot” (Jer. 3).

A brothel, that is, a place of prostitution, signifies the conscience of a sinful person, or the body in which he commits adulterous intercourse with demons, as in Ezekiel: “And I will destroy your brothel” (Ezek. 16).

A *virago* is so called from the greener age of youth, just as *virga* (“branch” or “rod”) and *vitula* (“heifer”) are so called. Alternatively, she is named from incorruption, as though *virago*, because she does not know the female condition.

She is called *virago* because she acts as a man, that is, performs manly deeds and possesses masculine vigor. In ancient times strong women were called *viragines*. A virgin is not properly called a *virago* unless she performs a man’s duty; a woman, however, if she performs manly deeds, is rightly called a *virago*, as in the case of an Amazon.

The woman who is now called *femina* was formerly called *vira*, just as from *servus* comes *serva*, and from *famulus*, *famula*; so from *vir* came *vira*. Some think that the name *virgin* (*virgo*) is derived from this.

Mystically, a virgin signifies either the holy Catholic Church, which is incorrupt in faith, or the faithful soul, which does not consent to be defiled by the suggestions of the devil or corrupted by the errors of heretics. To her the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you as a chaste virgin to present you to Christ” (II Cor. 11).

Virgins signify the souls of those who practice continence, abstaining from the corruption of the world through the five bodily senses, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins” (Matt. 25). Virgins also signify the souls of those who practice continence not for eternal reward but for human praise. Hence the passage continues: “And five were foolish” (ibid.). And in the prophet Amos: “On that day the beautiful virgins shall faint” (Amos 8).

Lamps signify works of righteousness, as in the Gospel: “They took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matt. 25).

The barren woman mystically signifies the holy Church before the advent of our Savior, as in Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear” (Isa. 54). And in the Psalm: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house” (Ps. 112).

A woman (*femina*) is so called from the parts of the thighs (*femora*), where the appearance of the sex is distinguished from the man. Others think, by a Greek etymology, that *femina* is derived from fiery force, because she desires intensely. They say that women are more lustful than men both among human beings and among animals. Hence excessive love was called feminine by the ancients.

When woman is understood positively, she signifies Mary, the mother of the Lord, concerning whom the prophet says: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31); or she signifies the humility of those subject to others. When understood negatively, she signifies the lust of the licentious.

An older person (*senior*) is still in the green of life. Hence Ovid says in Book Six:

> “The older man between the young man and the old man.”

The term *senior* signifies either the dignity of teaching or maturity of counsel. Hence the Apostle Peter says in his Letter: “The elders who are among you I exhort, as a fellow elder and witness of the sufferings of Christ” (I Pet. 5). And John says: “The elder to the elect lady” (II John). And: “The elder to the most dear Gaius” (III John).

Some think that old men (*senes*) are so called from a diminution of understanding, because through extreme age they become foolish. For physicians say that people of colder blood are foolish, while the prudent are warm. Hence old men, in whom warmth has already grown cold, and children, in whom it has not yet become warm, understand less. For this reason the age of infants and that of old men have something in common. Old men rave because of excessive age, children because of wantonness, and infants because they do not know what they are doing.

*Senex* is masculine, just as *anus* is feminine.

When an old man (*senex*) is understood positively, he signifies a person of complete righteousness and tested knowledge, as in Genesis: “Abraham died old and full of days” (Gen. 25). And in Solomon: “The gray hair of human beings is understanding, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4).

When used in the contrary sense, it signifies dullness of understanding and the foolishness of error. Hence it is written in Solomon: “When he had already grown old, his heart was led astray” (I Kings 11).

Old age brings with it both good and evil. Good, because it frees us from powerful masters, imposes a limit upon pleasures, breaks the impulses of lust, increases wisdom, and grants more mature counsels. Evil, because old age is most wretched through weakness and aversion. Diseases come upon us, and old age is sorrowful. For there are two things by which the powers of the body are diminished: old age and illness.

Old age sometimes signifies the troubles of the present time; sometimes, the whiteness of virtues. Thus the prophet prays to the Lord in the Psalter, saying: “Do not cast me away in the time of old age” (Ps. 70). He begs not to be cast away by the Lord in the time of his old age, when the strength of the body grows weary and needs greater assistance.

But we should understand this old age not only as the completion of bodily years. It also applies when, through frequent tribulations and martyrdoms, the strength of the soul grows old.

The whiteness of virtues is signified by the passage: “My old age is in abundant mercy” (Ps. 91). Old age has a white head. This likeness, as I think, is rightly applied here to the Church, because all the merits of the saints will shine with the purest light, like the gray hairs of the head.

Nor did he add the word “my” without reason. Human old age, wounded by grave illnesses, moves toward its end; it is burdened with complaints and disfigured in color. By contrast, the old age of the Church leads to everlasting life, marvelous blessedness, and incomparable beauty, so that its members may shine like the angels of God.

Let what has now been said about the sex of human beings and the stages of life suffice. Something must now be said about the succession of generations.

## CHAPTER II. On the Lineage of Generation

A father is the one from whom the beginning of a lineage arises. Therefore he is called the head of the household (*paterfamilias*). A father (*pater*) is so called because, after the completion of the act of fathering (*patratio*), he begets a son. For *patratio* is the completion of the sexual act. Lucretius:

> “And rightly, the fathering of fathers.”

Progenitors (*genitores*) are so called from begetting (*gignere*); parents (*parentes*) as though from *parientes*, “giving birth”; and creators (*creatores*). For *crementum* is the seed of the male, from which the bodies of animals and human beings are conceived. Hence parents are called creators.

The word father is used in Scripture in many ways. A person is called father either naturally, as God is the Father of all, from whom all things exist because all things have their origin from him; or by generation, as one is named from having begotten a son, as in the passage: “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob” (Matt. 1), and so forth; or because a nation’s descendants arose from him, as in the Gospel the Jews say to the Lord: “Abraham is our father” (John 8), and the rich man placed in hell called Abraham his father (Luke 16).

The first human father is understood to be Adam, as in Isaiah: “Your first father sinned” (Isa. 43). Father may also signify the world or the devil, as in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). And in Zechariah: “Where are your fathers?” (Zech. 1).

Again, fathers signify the apostles or prophets, as in the Psalm: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. 44). Teaching is also called fatherhood, as Paul says to certain believers: “Though you have countless teachers, you do not have many fathers. For I begot you through the Gospel in Christ” (I Cor. 4).

The term father is also used honorifically, as monastic discipline teaches monks: they should call the one appointed as their pastor “abbot” and “lord.”

But a question arises. Since the Lord commanded his disciples, saying, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, because one is your Father, who is in heaven; nor be called teachers, because one is your teacher, Christ” (Matt. 23), why did the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, say that he was a father? Or how do they call one another “fathers” in ordinary speech, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, contrary to this command?

The matter is resolved as follows: one thing is a father or teacher by nature, and another by indulgence or concession. When we call a human being “father,” we pay honor to his age; we do not show him to be the author of our life. For we do not have the beginning of life from them, but through them we have received the passage of life.

A teacher is likewise so called by association with the true teacher. And, not to repeat endlessly: just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and the one Teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an adopted or figurative sense.

A mother (*mater*) is so called because something is produced from her; *mater* is as though *materia*, “matter.” For the father is the cause.

Mother signifies the Church, as in the Psalm: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112). Mother also signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, as in the Apostle: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Gal. 4).

Again, the mother is understood as the synagogue of the Jews, as in the prophet Jeremiah: “In your crimes I dismissed your mother” (Jer. 50). Father or mother may also signify Babylon or carnal generation, as the Psalmist says: “For my father and my mother have abandoned me” (Ps. 26).

The head of a household (*paterfamilias*) is so called because he cares for all the servants placed in his household with a father’s affection, as though they were sons, and does not distinguish the condition of servants from the affection due to sons, but embraces them as one member. Hence the name *paterfamilias* arose. Those who rule their servants unjustly should by no means think that they deserve this name.

Who is to be understood mystically as the head of a household, the evangelical parable teaches, where it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20).

Who could more fittingly bear the likeness of the head of a household than our Creator, who rules those whom he created and possesses his elect in this world as a lord possesses subjects in his house? He has a vineyard—namely, the whole Church—because from righteous Abel to the last elect who will come at the end of the world, it has produced as many saints as though it had sent forth branches.

A woman who is head of a household (*materfamilias*) is so called because, through a certain legal formality, she passes into the household. The marriage tablets are the instruments of her purchase. Alternatively, just as a *matrona* is the mother of the first child, as it were the mother of one born, so a *materfamilias* is a woman who has borne several children. For a household begins from two persons.

Spiritually, the mother of all the faithful is the holy Church, which daily gives birth to children for God through the divine sacraments and the word of the Gospel. The heavenly Jerusalem is likewise called our mother, as the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4).

The word household (*familia*) is also used improperly, rather than strictly, for servants. Allegorically, the household of Christ is the Christian people who live in the holy Church, as we have shown above. Hence the priest says in prayer to the Lord: “We ask you, Lord, continually to guard your household,” because it cannot otherwise be kept unharmed unless it is fortified by his protection.

A grandfather (*avus*) is the father of one’s father, called from *aevum*, “age” or “antiquity.” A great-grandfather (*proavus*) is the father of one’s grandfather, as though “near the grandfather.” A great-great-grandfather (*abavus*) is the father of one’s great-grandfather, now far removed from the grandfather. A great-great-great-grandfather (*atavus*) is the father of one’s great-great-grandfather. A fourth-generation ancestor (*tritavus*) is the father of one’s great-great-great-grandfather, as though *tetravus*, “the fourth above the grandfather.” But *tritavus* is the final name in the sequence of kinship.

## CHAPTER III. On the Orders of Sons
The order of sons is divided into four classes: only-begotten, firstborn, middle, and last. “Firstborn” means one before whom there was no one; “only-begotten,” one after whom there is no one; “middle,” one among all the others; “last,” one after all the others, and likewise the least, counting from the unit. [Col. 0187D] “Last” is so called because he is new, since the others, by preceding him, are older.

Sons are also called by four modes: by nature, imitation, adoption, and instruction. By nature, as when the Jews are called the sons of Abraham. By imitation, as when Gentiles who imitate Abraham’s faith are called sons, the Gospel saying: “God is able from these stones to raise up sons for Abraham” (Matt. 3); or as when the Lord calls those same Jews sons of the devil (John 8), not because they were born from him, but because they imitated him. By adoption also, which no one can fail to understand according to human custom; or as when we call ourselves God’s sons not by nature but by adoption: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). By instruction, as when the Apostle calls his sons those to whom he preached the Gospel.

[Col. 0188A] Sons of the people are the faithful, reborn in the Church through the preaching of the apostles, as the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Cor. 4). To these the Lord says through the Psalmist: “Come, sons, hear me” (Ps. 33). “Sons” can mean the disciples of heretics, as in Job: “If his sons are multiplied, they shall be for the sword” (Job 27). “Sons” can mean all the reprobate, as in the Epistle of John: “By this the sons of God and the sons of the devil are manifest” (1 John 3).

“Daughter” means the faithful soul or the Church, as in the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see” (Ps. 44). In a negative sense: “Wretched daughter of Babylon” (Ps. 136). “Daughters” means the souls of the saints, as in the prophet: “I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me” (Jer. 7). “Sons” can also mean all the reprobate, as in Isaiah: “Prepare the sons of slaughter in the iniquity of their fathers” (Isa. 14).

[Col. 0188B] Sons are called *liberi* (“free persons”) in the laws so that by this term they may be distinguished from slaves: for just as a slave is under the power of his master, so a son is under the power of his father. Hence emancipation is also performed for a son, so that he may be free from his father, just as manumission is performed for a slave, so that he may become freed from his master. They are likewise called *liberi* who are born from a free marriage. For children born of a free man and a slave woman are of servile status: the one who is born always assumes the inferior status of the parent.

“Natural children” are called the sons of freeborn concubines, whom nature alone has begotten, not the respectability of marriage; they are likewise called boys, from puberty. An adopted son is one who has been transferred by mancipation from the authority of his lawful father, grandfather, or great-grandfather into another’s authority; he bears the name of both, as in Fabius Aemilius or Scipio Paulinus.

[Col. 0188C] Mystically, adopted sons are understood to be Christians, whom God the Father, sending his only-begotten Son, adopted in place of sons through immense grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle says to believers: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore he is no longer a slave but a son. And if a son, then also an heir through God” (Gal. 4).

[Col. 0188D] Twins are not only two born together, but also more than two. Of twins, one is an abortive child; the other, who has been legally born, is called *volpicus* [a term of uncertain meaning]. In Scripture, twins are understood allegorically as two peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles. Those twins born to Rebecca by the patriarch Isaac prefigured them. Thus Rebecca, when she went to worship and consult the Lord, received this answer from him: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25).

This may also be understood tropologically in another way. [Col. 0189A] Indeed, it can be said of each of us that there are two nations and two peoples within us, namely vices and virtues. One is lesser, the other greater. For the wicked are always more numerous than the good, and vices outnumber virtues; yet in us also, by God’s grace, one people overcomes the other, and the greater serves the lesser. For the flesh will serve the spirit, and vices yield to virtues.

A *posthumous child* is so called because he is born after the burial of his father, [Col. 0189A] that is, after his death. He has also received the name of the deceased. For the law decreed that one who is born after the deceased should be called by the deceased’s name.

A *bastard* (*nothus*) is one born of a noble father and an ignoble mother, as from a concubine. This is a Greek name, and has failed in Latin usage. Opposed to him is the *spurious* child, who is born of a noble mother and an ignoble father. “Spurious” also means one born of an uncertain father and a widowed mother, as though merely the son of a spurious woman; for the ancients called the female nature *spurious*. In Latin, *spurii* means, as it were, “outside purity,” that is, unclean.

For we read in the Book of Kings that a spurious man named Goliath [Col. 0189B] came forth from the camp of the Philistines, whom David defeated and struck down (1 Kings 17). This signifies our Redeemer, who, strong of hand, overthrew Goliath—whose name is interpreted “one who migrates” and signifies the devil’s pride—in single combat, and freed the people of God from his fear.

A *grandson* is one born from a son. He is called, as it were, “born afterward.” First a son is born, then a grandson. For it is a degree of succession. Hence also *posterity*, as it were, “a later generation.” A grandson may be of either sex. For the term *granddaughter* is used in law to distinguish the succession that has been lost.

A *great-grandson* is one conceived and born from a grandson. He is called *pronepos*, as it were, “born farther afterward.” From this degree the term *progeny* also begins to be used, because among them posterity does not extend far. [Col. 0189C] Just as those born much farther below are called progeny, so those above are called great-grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers, who are also called progenitors, as it were, “generating farther onward.”

A great-grandson is so called because he cannot be near. A great-great-grandson is so called because he is separated from the grandson; for between him and the grandson stands the great-grandson. An *adnepos* is the son of a great-great-grandson. A *trinepos* is the son of an *adnepos*, because he is fourth in order after the grandson, as it were a *tetranepos*. We do not say “younger descendants” except whenever the name of the degrees runs out—for example, son, grandson, great-grandson, great-great-grandson, *atnepos*, and *trinepos*. When these degrees have come to an end, we rightly say “younger descendants,” just as we use “greater ancestors” for the father’s father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, great-great-great-grandfather, and *tritavus*.

## CHAPTER IV. On Agnates and Cognates

[Col. 0189D]

*Agnates* are so called because they take the place of children when sons are lacking. They are recognized first in the family because they come through persons of the male sex: for example, a brother born from the same father, or the son of a brother, a grandson, or again an uncle on the father’s side.

*Cognates* are so called because they too are joined by the relationship of kinship. They are ranked after agnates because they come through persons of the female sex; they are not agnates, but are cognates by natural law in another way.

A *near relative* is so called because of nearness of blood. *Consanguineous relatives* are so called because they are born from one blood, that is, from the seed of one father.

[Col. 0190A] In sacred Scripture, therefore, not only are those called cognates who appear historically to be joined by a certain closeness of blood relationship, but also those whom spiritual kinship joins in faith and good works. This is shown where the faithful from the Gentiles are called the seed of Abraham. Hence the Apostle says: “Not all who are descended from Abraham are called sons of Abraham; but those who are of Abraham’s faith are considered his seed, because those who are of faith are sons of Abraham” (Rom. 9).

“Near relatives” are mystically understood as those who are near in faith, as in Solomon: “Come and eat and drink and be intoxicated, you who are near” (Wis. 2). *Neighbors* are those who are nearby, as in Exodus: “He shall take his neighbor who is joined to his house” (Exod. 12). And in Solomon: “A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away” (Prov. 27).

[Col. 0190B] *Brothers* are so called because they are from the same fruit, that is, born from the same seed. *Germani* are those who spring from the same mother, not—as many say—from the same germ; such persons are merely called brothers. Thus brothers are from the same seed, while *germani* spring from the same mother.

They are called *uterine siblings* because they are born of different fathers and from one womb; for the womb belongs only to the woman.

It is established that in the divine Scriptures the term “brothers” is used in four ways: by nature, by nation, by kinship, and by affection.

By nature, as Esau and Jacob, Andrew and Peter, James and John. By nation, as all Jews are called brothers among themselves. Hence Deuteronomy says: “If you buy your brother who is a Hebrew” (Deut. 15). And the Apostle says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9).

[Col. 0190C] By kinship, brothers are those who belong to one family, that is, one fatherland. The Latins interpret these as *paternitates*, “paternities,” when from one root a multitude of a family spreads forth. In Genesis Abraham said to Lot: “Let there be no quarrel between me and you, nor between your shepherds and my shepherds, for we are all brothers” (Gen. 13). Yet Lot was not Abraham’s brother, but the son of his brother Aaron.

In the fourth way, brothers are called such by affection. This is divided into spiritual and common affection. Spiritual affection is why all Christians are called brothers: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (Ps. 132). Common affection is when, since all human beings are born from one father, we join ourselves to one another in equal kinship, as Scripture says: “Say to those who hate you, ‘You are our brothers.’”

*Germana* is understood in such a way that a *germanus* is one who springs from the same mother.

[Col. 0190D] Mystically, Christ is a brother, of whom the Song of Songs says: “My brother is mine, and I am his” (Song 8). “Brothers” means the apostles or all the saints, as in the Psalm: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21). In a contrary sense, as in Job: “My brothers have passed me by like a torrent” (Job 6).

“Friends” means the apostles or all the saints, as in the Gospel: “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). In a contrary sense: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. 22).

*Companions* means the apostles, as in the Song of Songs: “Lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions” (Song 1).

A *sister* is understood as a brother is, for a sister is from the same seed. She is so called because she alone is held with her brothers in the lot of agnation.

[Col. 0191A] Mystically, the name “sister” may be understood of the holy Church or the faithful soul. Hence in the Song of Songs the bridegroom says to the bride: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses all spices” (Song 4). In the breasts, the holy teachers are understood, because of the consolation of the weak and the nourishment of the little ones, which is expressed by milk. In the bosom, the sweetness of grace is signified, which is more beautiful than the austerity of the law. In the fragrance of the perfumes, the sweetest reputation of the faith spread abroad is intimated, for it is scattered throughout the whole world. This faith is also preferred to the old law, which for a long time lay confined within Judea alone.

[Col. 0191B] The sons of brothers are called *patrueles* because their fathers were full brothers to one another. *Consobrini* are so called because they are born either from a sister and a brother or from two sisters, as it were “sharing the sister.” *Matrueles* are the sons of a maternal aunt. *Sobrini* are the sons of *consobrini*.

A *paternal uncle* is the father’s brother, as it were another father. Hence, when a father dies, the paternal uncle first takes charge of the orphan and protects him by law as though he were his son.

A *maternal uncle* is the mother’s brother. His name appears to have the form of a diminutive, because it is shown to derive from *avus*, “grandfather.”

An *aunt on the father’s side* is the father’s sister, as it were another mother. An *aunt on the mother’s side* is the mother’s sister, as it were a second mother.

A *father-in-law* is so called because he gives his daughter. A *son-in-law* is so called because he takes a daughter. A son-in-law is also so called because he is taken in to increase the family. A father-in-law and mother-in-law are so called because either a son-in-law or a daughter-in-law is associated with them.

A *stepfather* is one who marries a woman who has a son or daughter by another man. He is called *vitricus*, as it were *novitricus*, “a new father,” because a new man is brought in by the mother.

A *stepson* is one born from another father. He is thought to be called *privignus*, as it were *privigenus*, “previously begotten,” and is therefore commonly called “born earlier.”

[Col. 0191C] These words appear to be declined according to gender: *genitor*, “father,” and *genitrix*, “mother”; *agnati*, “male agnates,” and *agnatae*, “female agnates”; *cognati*, “male cognates,” and *cognatae*, “female cognates”; *progenitores*, “male progenitors,” and *progenitrices*, “female progenitors”; *germani*, “male full siblings,” and *germanae*, “female full siblings.”

## CHAPTER V. On Marriages

[Col. 0191C]

The word *vir* signifies the male sex, not marriage, unless one adds *vir ejus*, “her husband.” *Maritus*, however, signifies a spouse even without addition, and comes from *mas*, “male,” as it were “masculine.” It is a primary word, whose diminutive is *masculus* and whose derivative is *maritus*.

A *bridegroom* (*sponsus*) is so called from *spondere*, “to pledge.” Before the use of marriage tablets, men exchanged guarantees with one another, in which they pledged that they consented to the rights of marriage, and they supplied sureties. Hence it became customary to call the man *sponsus* from *spondere*, “to pledge,” and likewise the woman *sponsa*. Properly, however, *spondere* means “to be willing” or “to pledge.” Thus a man is called *sponsus* not because something is permitted to him, but because he pledges and provides sureties.

Christ is the bridegroom because from the beginning he was promised by the Father, as in the Psalm: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18). The bride is the Church, which was indeed promised through divine pledges, as in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come from Lebanon” (Song 4), that is, from the brightness of baptism.

“Wedding” means the joining of the Word of God and the flesh, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding for his son” (Matt. 22). “Wedding” also means the fellowship of angels and human beings made through the Lord Christ, as in the Gospel: “And you are like men waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0192A] The bridal chamber is the womb of the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalm: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18). Bridal chambers are the hearts of the saints, as in Ezekiel.

A kiss is reconciliation between a human being and God, as when it is said of the prodigal son: “And he kissed him” (Luke 15). And in the Apostle: “We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5). In a contrary sense: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22).

Laughter means everlasting joy, as it is said in Solomon concerning the Church: “And she shall laugh on the last day” (Prov. 31). In a contrary sense: “I also will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1).

[Col. 0192B] An *earnest* (*arrabo*) is so called, as it were, a “good pledge.” Whatever is given for marriage is given well, because marriage is good. But what is given on account of fornication or adultery is evil; therefore it is not an earnest. It is called an earnest from the thing for which it is handed over. An earnest is not only a marriage pledge, but also anything given for any promised matter so that it may be fulfilled.

Suitors, petitioners for marriage, are called *proci* from praying and seeking. A *brideswoman* (*pronuba*) is so called because she presides over those who marry and joins the bride to the man; she is also called a *paranymph*. For *nympha* means a bride at a wedding, and *nympha* also refers to the service of leading the bride, a term that likewise alludes to the name of the bride.

[Col. 0192C] Spouses (*conjuges*) are so called because of the yoke imposed upon those joined in marriage. For brides and bridegrooms are accustomed to be placed under a yoke for the sake of future harmony, so that they may not separate. More properly, however, they are called spouses from the initial pledge of the arrangement, even though marital intercourse is not yet known between them; thus Mary is called Joseph’s wife, although there had been and would be no intercourse of the flesh between them.

A *matron* is a woman who has already married. She is called *matrona*, as it were “mother of one born,” or because she can already become a mother. Hence the term *matrimonium*, “marriage,” is also derived.

A distinction is made between a matron and a *materfamilias*. Matrons are women who have entered into marriage; mothers are those who have given birth; *matresfamilias* are those who have passed into their husband’s family through a certain formality of law.

A *monogamist* is one who has married only once. For among the Greeks *monos* means “one,” and *gamos* is interpreted as “marriage.” A *digamist* and a *trigamist* are named from the number of wives, as it were a husband of two or three.

[Col. 0192D] A *widow* is so called because, when she and her husband had been two, she did not after the death of her first husband attach herself to the partnership of another man. For those who marry another after the death of their first husband are not called widows. Alternatively, a widow is so called because she is alone and does not preserve the rights of marriage in partnership with another man.

A brother’s wife is called a *fratrissa*; the husband’s brother is called a *levir*. The wives of two brothers are called *janitrices*, as it were “those who tread the same doorway” or travel through the same door.

A man’s sister is called a *glos*. A sister’s husband has no special name, nor does a wife’s brother.

Marriage is the lawful union and condition of those eligible for marriage. Conjugal union is the marriage of legitimate persons for coming together and being joined to one another.

[Col. 0193A] A wife is taken for three reasons. The first is for offspring, concerning which we read in Genesis: “And he blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply’” (Gen. 1). The second is for assistance, concerning which it is said there in Genesis: “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2). The third is for incontinence. Hence the Apostle says that the one who cannot contain himself should marry (1 Cor. 7).

In choosing a husband, four qualities are usually sought: excellence, lineage, beauty, and wisdom. Of these, wisdom is the more powerful.

Virgil refers these four qualities to the effect of love in Aeneas, saying that Dido was driven to love him by them:

By beauty:

> “What a face he bore! . . .”

By excellence:

> “. . . How strong in breast and arms!”

By speech:

> “. . . Alas, by what fates  
> Was he tossed! What wars, he said, had he endured!”

By lineage:

> “I believe indeed—and my belief is not vain—that he is of the race of the gods.”

Likewise, in choosing a wife, four things impel a man to love: beauty, lineage, wealth, and character. It is better, however, if character is sought in her more than beauty. But now women are sought whom either wealth or appearance, rather than moral uprightness, commends.

Women remain under the power of men because they are often deceived by levity of mind. Therefore it was fitting that they should be restrained by the authority of men. For this reason the ancients also wished unmarried women, even when they had reached full maturity, to remain under guardianship because of this very levity of mind.

[Col. 0193C] Mystically, under the name “man” either Christ is understood, who is the bridegroom of the Church, or the spirit of the human being, that is, the mind and reason, which governs the soul and rules over it. For the man and his wife are Christ and the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. 5).

Likewise, bridegroom and bride signify the same reality. The bridegroom is Christ, as we showed above, because he was promised by the Father from the beginning. Hence it is read in the Psalm: “In the sun he has set his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18). His bride is the Church, which was indeed promised through divine pledges. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come” (Song 4).

[Col. 0193D] “Lebanon” is interpreted as “brightness,” that is, a soul made white by good works. The bridegroom urges her three times to come: first, while she lives in the flesh through good works; second, after putting off the flesh, to receive blessed life; third, after receiving the body, to enjoy perfect joy after the resurrection.

In a contrary sense, “man” is used as in Genesis: “A virgin, very beautiful in appearance, whom no man had known” (Gen. 24)—that is, the devil, who often corrupts the mind through thought.

Spiritual marriage, that is, the union of Christ and the Church, contains many good things, because in Christ what we said is especially evident concerning the choice of a husband: excellence and wisdom, lineage and beauty. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). And the prophet says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). And in the Psalm it is read of him: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44).

[Col. 0194A] In his wife, likewise, the four qualities we previously numbered are found: beauty, lineage, wealth, and character. Concerning her beauty it is said in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely, like Jerusalem” (Song 1, 4). Concerning her lineage the blessed Apostle Peter says: “You are a royal and priestly race” (1 Pet. 2). Concerning her wealth it is written: “In the works of his hands are abundant riches.” Almost all sacred Scripture proclaims the uprightness of her character. Therefore it is not necessary to set down an example from it.

[Col. 0194B] This man, then, is a virgin in the flesh and a monogamist in spirit, because he knows no other bride besides the holy Catholic Church. To her the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2). He gave his wife a dowry when he poured out the price of his blood for her. He gave an earnest when, granting her the grace of the Holy Spirit, he promised her an eternal inheritance in heaven. Hence the Apostle says concerning that same Spirit: “He is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. 1).

## CHAPTER VI. On Death

Death is so called because it is bitter, or from Mars, who is the producer of deaths, or from the bite of the first human being, who incurred death by biting the fruit of the forbidden tree (Gen. 3).

There are three kinds of death: premature, untimely, and natural. The death of infants is premature; [Col. 0194C] that of young people untimely; that of the old is deserved, that is, natural.

The living sometimes signify the righteous, who remain in eternal life. Hence the saying: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Wis. 4). In a contrary sense: “I praised the dead more than the living” (Eccl. 4), that is, those brought to completion with a good end rather than those living in sins.

The dead sometimes signify sinners or unbelievers, as in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8). In a good sense: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14). Hence it is written in the Psalter: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 113). And in the Apostle: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

[Col. 0194D] Death signifies not only the death of the flesh but also the destruction of the soul and of the condemned in hell. Hence it is written: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Elsewhere the Savior says: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall never see death” (John 8). And again: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me shall not die forever” (John 11). And it is written in the Psalter: “The death of sinners is very evil” (Ps. 33).

He calls the death of sinners that which cannot be looked upon by human beings, and declares it to be not merely evil but exceedingly evil. Truly it is exceedingly evil, because eternal punishment accompanies it.

Sinners who are alive to the world and dead to God are understood in the Psalm: “They descend alive into hell” (Ps. 54).

[Col. 0195A] A *corpse* is something that lies unburied. It is called *cadaver* from falling, because it can no longer stand. While it is being carried, we call the procession a funeral; when it has been burned, the remains; when it has been placed in a tomb, it is already buried.

By common usage it is called a body, as in the verse: “When bodies are deprived of light.”

Mystically, corpses signify the bodies of unbelievers, as in the prophet: “And I will fill the valley of Jehoshaphat with the corpses of the dead” (Joel 3). In another sense they are used in the Psalter: “They have given the corpses of your servants” (Ps. 78).

A deceased person is called *defunctus* because he has completed the duty of life. For we say that those who have completed their appointed duties have “performed their office.” Hence also the expression “having discharged honors.” Thus *defunctus* means one released from the duty of life, or as it were one who has completed his day.

[Col. 0195B] A buried person is so called because he is now without pulse and palpitation, that is, without movement. To bury is to place a body in the ground. We call *humare* “to cover over,” that is, to cast earth upon it.

“Buried,” however, signifies one overwhelmed by vices or condemned in hell. Hence it is said: “The rich man also died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16).

Allegorically, a tomb signifies the body of a sinner, retaining within itself a soul dead through vices. And in the Gospel it is said: “For you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people on the outside, but within are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. 23).

Sometimes, however, a tomb signifies the memory of the Lord’s death and resurrection, as in Isaiah: “And his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. 11).

## CHAPTER VII. On Portents

[Col. 0195C]

## Portents

Varro says that portents are things that appear to be born contrary to nature; but they are not contrary to nature, because they occur by the divine will, since the will of the Creator is the nature of every created thing. Hence even the pagans call God sometimes “nature,” sometimes “god.”

A portent, therefore, occurs not contrary to nature, but contrary to nature as it is known. Portents (*portenta*), omens (*ostenta*), monsters (*monstra*), and prodigies (*prodigia*) are so called because they seem to foretell, display, show, and predict certain future events. Portents are said to derive their name from *portendere*, “to fore-show,” that is, to indicate beforehand. Omens are so called because they seem to show something future. Prodigies are so called because they “speak forth” (*porro dicant*), that is, they predict what is to come. Monsters derive their name from admonition (*monitus*), because by signifying something they demonstrate it [Col. 0195D], or because they immediately show what has appeared. This is the proper usage of the terms, though it is often corrupted through the misuse of writers.

Some creations of portents appear to have been established as signs of future events. God sometimes wishes to indicate what is to come through harmful things being born, just as through dreams and oracles he warns and signifies to certain peoples or persons an impending disaster; this has also been confirmed by many instances. A fox born from a mare, it is said, foretold the dissolution of Xerxes’ kingdom. In Alexander’s time, a monster was born from a woman whose upper bodily parts were human but dead, while its lower parts belonged to various animals and were alive; it signified the king’s sudden killing [Col. 0196A], for the worse parts had survived the better.

But these monsters, which are given as signs, do not live long: as soon as they are born, they die. There is a difference between a portent and a portentous birth. Portents are things that are transformed, as when a woman in Umbria is said to have given birth to a serpent. Hence Lucan writes:

> “And her own infant terrified the mother.”

Portentous births undergo only a slight alteration, as, for example, those born with six fingers.

Portents or portentous beings occur in various ways. Some exceed the ordinary human measure in the size of the entire body, as did Titan, who, according to Homer, lay stretched out over nine *iugera*. Others are malformed throughout the body, such as dwarfs, or those whom the Greeks call Pygmies, because they are of cubit height. Others have abnormal size in particular parts, such as an ill-formed head or superfluous limbs, like those with two heads (*bicipites*) or three hands (*trimani*), or *cynodontes*, “dog-toothed,” who have a double set of teeth. Others lack parts, where one side is greatly deficient compared with the other, such as one hand compared with the other, or one foot compared with the other. Others are dismembered, being born without a hand or head; the Greeks call such beings *steresioi*. Others occur by “numeria” [sic], when only a head or a leg is born.

Others are transformed in part: one may have the face of a lion or a dog, or the head or body of a bull, as they recount that the Minotaur was born from Pasiphaë; the Greeks call this *heteromorphia*. Others are transformed throughout into a portent of another kind of creation, as history says that a calf was born from a woman. Others, without being transformed, have their organs in altered locations, such as eyes in the chest or forehead [Col. 0196C], ears above at the temples, or, as Aristotle records, a man who had his liver on the left side and his spleen on the right.

Others differ according to conformation: on one hand several fingers may be naturally joined and fused, while on the other there are fewer, or the same may occur with the feet. Others result from premature or excessive development, such as those born with teeth, or with beards, or gray hair. Others combine many kinds of difference, as in the multifarious portent we mentioned in the case of Alexander. Others arise from the mixture of sex, as in those called *androgyni* and hermaphrodites.

Hermaphrodites are so called because both sexes appear in them. For among the Greeks *erma* means “male,” and *aphrodi* “female.” They have a male right breast and a female left breast; by intercourse with one another they both beget and give birth.

Just as certain human monsters occur among individual peoples, so among the whole human race there are certain monstrous peoples, such as giants, Cynocephali, Cyclopes, and others. The giants are named, according to the etymology of the Greek word, because the Greeks regard them as *gegenes*, that is, “earth-born,” since in fable the immense earth bore them, producing beings of vast size like herself. *Ge* means “earth,” and *genos* means “race,” although the common people also call them “sons of the earth,” whose origin is uncertain.

Some ignorant transgressors against the sacred Scriptures falsely suppose that angels had intercourse with the daughters of men before the Flood, and that giants were born from them—men of extraordinary size and strength, by whom the earth was filled.

The Cynocephali are so called because they have canine heads [Col. 0197A]; their very barking reveals them to be beasts rather than human beings. They are born in India. India likewise produces the Cyclopes, who are called Cyclopes because they are said to have one eye in the middle of the forehead. They are also called *agriophagitae*, “wild-beast eaters,” because they eat only the flesh of wild animals.

In Libya they believe that the Lemnians are born as headless trunks, having their mouths and eyes in their chests. Others are born without necks and have their eyes in their shoulders.

At the farthest point of the East, monstrous peoples are described. Some, without noses, have misshapen faces whose entire surface is flat. Others have a lower lip so prominent that, when they sleep in the heat of the sun, it covers the whole face. Others have mouths fused shut except for a small opening, through which they draw nourishment with reed stalks [Col. 0197B]. Some are said to be without tongues and to communicate by nodding or bodily movement.

The Panotii are said to live near Scythia, with ears so large and spread out that they cover the entire body. In Greek, *pan* means “all,” and *othi* means “ears.” The Artabatitae in Ethiopia are said to walk bent forward like cattle. None of them lives beyond the age of forty.

The Satyrs are little men with hooked noses, horns on their foreheads, and feet resembling those of goats. Such a being Saint Antony saw in the desert; when questioned by the servant of God, it is said to have replied:

> “I am mortal, one of the inhabitants of the desert, whom the pagan world, deceived by various errors, worships as fauns and satyrs.”

Some say that there are wild men whom certain people call fig-fauns (*Faunos ficarios*).

A people called Sciopodes is said to live in Ethiopia, each having a single leg and remarkable speed. The Greeks call them Sciopodes because, when lying on their backs in the heat, they shade themselves with the size of their feet [Col. 0197C]. The Antipodes in Libya have their feet turned backward behind their legs and eight toes on each foot. The Hippopodes in Scythia have human form but horse’s feet.

In India, they say, there is a people called the Macrobii, twelve feet tall. There is also a people there of cubit height, whom the Greeks call Pygmies from the cubit; the common people call them *septemcaulini*, because seven of them rest beneath a single stalk. We have spoken of them above. They inhabit the mountains of India, near which lies the Ocean.

They also report that in the same India there is a race of women who conceive at the age of five and do not live beyond their eighth year [Col. 0197D].

They invent other fabulous portents of human beings that do not exist, interpreting them as explanations of things, such as Geryon, king of Spain, who was said to possess a triple form. In fact, there were three brothers of such harmony that, though they had three bodies, they were as one soul.

The Gorgons, too, are said to have been prostitutes with serpent-like hair who turned those looking at them into stones, and to have possessed one eye, which they used in turn.
