In reality, they were three sisters of equal beauty, as though they had one eye; they so stupefied their spectators that people thought they turned them to stone.

They imagine that there were three Sirens, partly virgins and partly birds, with wings and claws. One sang with her voice, another with pipes, and the third with the lyre; by their song they drew sailors who had been enticed by them into shipwrecks [Col. 0198A]. In truth, they were prostitutes who, because they led passers-by into poverty, were fancied as bringing about shipwrecks. They are said to have had wings and claws because love both flies and wounds, and to have lived amid the waves because the waves created Venus.

They also say that Scylla was a woman girdled with canine heads and barking, situated beside the strait of the Sicilian sea. Sailors, terrified by the whirlpools formed where the waters meet, thought that the waves barked; the roaring vortex of the ebbing tide collides with and swallows them.

They invent certain monsters among irrational animals, such as Cerberus, the dog of the underworld with three heads. Through him they signify the three ages by which death devours human beings: infancy, youth, and old age [Col. 0198B]. They think that he was called Cerberus as if from *creovorus*, “flesh-eating.”

They also speak of the Hydra, a serpent with nine heads, called in Latin *Caedra*, because when one head was cut off, three grew in its place. But it is established that the Hydra was a place from which waters flowed, devastating a neighboring city. When one channel was blocked, many others burst forth. Hercules, seeing this, burned the place itself and thus closed the channels of the water. The Hydra received its name from water.

Ambrose mentions it by way of comparison with heresies, saying:

> “For heresy, like a certain Hydra of fables, grew through its wounds; and whenever it is repeatedly received, it sprouts forth, destined for the fire and doomed to perish in the flames.”

They also invent the Chimaera, a three-formed beast whose head is that of a lion, whose hind parts are those of a dragon, and whose middle is that of a goat [Col. 0198C]. Certain natural philosophers say that it was not an animal but a mountain in Cilicia, which in some places nourished lions and goats, in others burned, and in others was full of serpents. Bellerophon made this mountain habitable. Hence he is said to have killed the Chimaera.

The Centaurs received their name from their appearance—that is, from a human being mixed with a horse. They are said to have been Thessalian horsemen; but because, rushing through battle, they appeared to be one body composed of horses and men, they were called Centaurs.

The Minotaur took its name from bull and man: such a beast is said in fable to have been confined in the Labyrinth. Concerning it Ovid writes:

> “The half-bull man and the half-man bull.”

The Onocentaur is so called because it is said to be half human in appearance and half ass; likewise the Hippocentaur, because in them the nature of horses and human beings is thought to have been joined.

It should also be noted that prophetic actions are sometimes called portents when they foreshadow something future. Thus the Lord says to Ezekiel:

> “Son of man, I have made you a sign and a portent to the house of Israel” (Ezek. XII).

Accordingly, the same prophet is said to have been ordered to sleep for a time on his right side and then for a time on his left side, in order to prefigure what the Lord intended to bring upon the Israelite people as punishment.

It is likewise recorded of Isaiah that he walked naked and barefoot in order to prefigure the devastation of the land of the Jews and the captivity of the Israelite people. In this way the other prophets also represented future events through their actions and prophecies [Col. 0199A].

Similarly, signs, portents, and prodigies are recorded as having occurred in the New Testament. Joel also appears to predict this in his book:

> “And it shall be that after these things I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh. Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your elders shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my servants and handmaids in those days I will pour out my spirit, and I will give prodigies in heaven and on earth: blood and fire and vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel II).

Therefore it is not necessary for us to discuss at greater length the portents recounted in the books of the pagans. But we must believe that whatever truly occurs in the world and is described as a change in nature can happen only by the ordinance and will of God, who does everything justly and orders all things rightly, because “the Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works.”

## Chapter VIII. On Cattle and Beasts of Burden

Adam gave the first names to all living creatures, assigning each one a name according to its original institution and in keeping with the condition of the nature it was to serve. The nations, however, gave names to each animal in their own languages.

Adam did not impose those names according to the Latin or Greek language, or according to the language of any barbarian nation, but in the language that was one for all before the Flood and that is now called Hebrew [Col. 0199C].

In Latin, *animalia* or *animantia* means “living creatures,” because they are animated by life and moved by spirit. Allegorically, however, animals signify brutish people who think only about earthly things. Hence it is said:

> “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God; they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. II).

The Psalmist likewise says:

> “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Ps. LXVII).

The animals were the nations emptied of true religion. But when they came to the Lord, they became enriched through his help, so that they lacked nothing and were filled with rational and complete light. They will dwell in the Church when, by his mercy, they receive the worship of true religion.

The Apostle also says:

> “There is an animal body, and there is a spiritual body. The spiritual is not first, but the animal; afterward the spiritual” (1 Cor. XV).

The animal body signifies the condition of the present life, so long as a human being bears a mortal body. The spiritual body signifies the immortality of the future life, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption. The animal body exists while it is sustained by food so that it may live; the spiritual body exists when, transformed into life, it will need none of these things.

All that was said above is contained in this meaning: the animal body dies and will rise again as a spiritual body, which will neither eat nor grow weak nor be foul-smelling nor be diseased by nature. The animal body is from Adam; the spiritual body comes through Christ in the resurrection of the dead.

Animals that chew the cud, which are described as clean in the Law, are holy people who continually meditate on the divine commandments with mouth, heart, and deed, as in the Psalm:

> “The meditation of my heart is always in your sight” (Ps. XVIII).

Animals that do not chew the cud are sinners and unclean people who pay no attention to the law of God and do not devote themselves to meditation upon it.

Animals that both divide the hoof and chew the cud, which are described as clean in the Law, are believers who believe in both Testaments and, as though in two claws, establish the foot of their works in the pattern of a proper walk.

Animals that chew the cud but do not divide the hoof, which are said to be unclean, are the Jewish people, who meditate upon the Old Testament with their mouths but do not receive the New.

Horned animals, which are commanded to be offered in sacrifice to God and whose flesh is granted as food for the faithful—calves, rams, goats, deer, does, and roebucks—signify the virtues of the saints, bearing the horns of virtues against the devil and the vices of sinners.

Mystically, the horn signifies Christ’s kingdom in the Gospel:

> “And he raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant” (Luke I).

The seven horns signify powers throughout all time. Hence in the Apocalypse:

> “I saw a Lamb as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Rev. V).

The horns signify the trophy of Christ’s cross. In Habakkuk:

> “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. III).

The horns signify the devil’s pride, or his powers in the present age, or the kingdom of Antichrist in the Apocalypse. In Daniel, they signify the kingdoms of this world. In the Psalm they signify pride:

> “And my humility from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. XXI).

And elsewhere:

> “I shall break all the horns of sinners” (Ps. LXXIV).

Quadrupeds are so called because they walk on four feet. Some of them resemble domestic animals but are not under human care, such as deer, does, and wild asses; yet they are not wild beasts like lions, nor beasts of burden capable of serving human use.

We call everything that lacks human speech and form *pecus*. More particularly, the term *pecora* is usually applied to animals that are either suitable for eating, such as sheep and swine, or useful to human beings, such as horses and oxen.

There is a distinction between *pecora* and *pecudes*. In general, the ancients used *pecora* to signify all animals. *Pecudes*, however, refers only to animals that are eaten, as if from *pecu-edentes*, “those that eat.” More generally, every animal is called *pecus* from grazing (*pascere*) [Col. 0200D].

Beasts of burden (*jumenta*) derive their name from the fact that they aid our labor or our burdens by carrying, plowing, or otherwise assisting us. The ox draws a cart and turns the hardest clods of earth with the plowshare; the horse and ass carry loads and relieve human labor in walking. Hence they are called *jumenta*, because they help human beings. They are animals of great strength.

Mystically, beasts of burden are the faithful in the Church, but those lacking spiritual understanding, as in the Psalm:

> “You will save human beings and beasts of burden, Lord” (Ps. XXXV).

Again, beasts of burden signify those lacking understanding and eloquence:

> “I became like a beast of burden before you” (Ps. LXXII).

Elsewhere, beasts of burden signify lustful people, concerning whom Joel says:

> “The beasts of burden have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

Some also hold that the beast of burden is the body of Christ. Hence the Gospel passage:

> “He placed him upon his beast of burden and led him into an inn” (Luke X).

Cattle (*pecudes*) signify simple people of limited intellectual ability, whom the Lord illumines through the grace of the Holy Spirit, makes his flock, and causes to be numbered among his sheep. Hence the Psalmist says of Christ:

> “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, sheep and oxen, and moreover all the cattle of the field” (Ps. VIII).

Cattle sometimes signify sinners and those devoted to pleasures, as in Zechariah:

> “Feed the cattle destined for slaughter” (Zech. XI).

And in the Psalter:

> “Sheep and oxen, and moreover the cattle” (Ps. VIII).

Cattle also signify simple people lacking subtlety of reasoning, as in Solomon:

> “Know well the face of your cattle, and consider your flocks” (Prov. XXVII).

Sheep signify the chosen Christian people, as the Lord says to the apostle Peter in the Gospel:

> “Feed my sheep” (John XXI).

They are compared to sheep because, with the Lord’s help, they conduct themselves innocently; moreover, they cast off their fleece without feeling pain. Just as a sheep does not reproach the shearer, so the righteous person does not accuse the greed of the one who strips him.

Oxen signify preachers, who caused human hearts to bring forth a harvest of virtues by sowing heavenly commandments within them. Nor is the word “moreover” without significance, because not only are the saints subject to him, but sinners also. For Christ the Lord often triumphs with greater glory over those who have been converted.

They are cattle while they graze in the freedom of the fields—that is, in the pleasure of this world. They are sheep when they are enclosed within the Lord’s fold.

Elsewhere the divine voice says:

> “All the beasts of the forests are mine, the beasts of burden on the mountains, and the oxen” (Ps. XLIX).

The beasts of the forests signify the nations that lived amid the thickets of this world in the fiercest superstition. The beasts of burden on the mountains are simple people established in the Catholic Church, known to dwell upon the summit of faith. The oxen signify the apostles and prophets, who labored constantly in the Lord’s field.

Accordingly, through these fitting allusions he prefigures the Catholic Church, which is to be gathered from the various regions of the world.

There is a distinction between herds (*armenta*) and flocks (*greges*). Herds consist of horses and oxen; flocks consist of camels, goats, and sheep.

The sheep is a soft-fleeced animal, defenseless in body and peaceful in spirit. It is said to derive its name from the offering, because among the ancients, at the beginning, sheep rather than bulls were slaughtered in sacrifice.

Some sheep are called *bidentes*, “two-toothed,” because among their eight teeth they have two that are higher. The pagans especially offered these in sacrifice.

Sheep, as we have said, signify innocent and simple people among the Christian people. At times the sheep also typologically demonstrates the gentleness and patience of the Lord himself, as Isaiah says concerning the innocent death of the Savior:

> “Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and he will not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

In the Gospel, sheep signify the faithful people:

> “My sheep will hear my voice” (John X).

And in the Psalter:

> “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, sheep and oxen” (Ps. VIII).

The two sheep signify the peoples of the nations, whom a man—that is, Christ—will nourish, as is read in the Prophet:

> “In those days a man will nourish a young cow and two sheep; and because of the abundance of milk he will eat butter” (Isa. VII) [Col. 0202A].

The sheep of the reprobate are mentioned in the Psalter:

> “Like sheep they have been placed in hell, and death will feed upon them” (Ps. XLVIII),

that is, the devil.

The ram (*vervex*) is said to derive its name either from its strength, because it is stronger than the other sheep; or from *vir*, “male,” because it is a male; or because it has worms in its head, whose irritation causes the rams to shake themselves against one another and strike each other with great force.

The ram (*aries*) likewise is called *apo tou areos*, that is, “from Mars.” Hence among us the males in flocks are called *mares*; alternatively, it is so called because this animal was first sacrificed by pagans upon altars. Hence the saying:

> “A ram is slaughtered at the altar.”

Rams signify the apostles or leaders of the churches. Hence in Isaiah:

> “The rams of Nebaioth will minister to you” (Isa. LX).

And in the Psalter:

> “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII).

Like leaders of flocks, they led the Christian people into the causes of the Lord. He calls “sons of rams” those whom the apostles begot through preaching, not those who are shown to be outsiders through corrupt doctrine.

Rams are rightly compared with the apostles because, as we have said, these animals are especially strong in the forehead and, by repeatedly charging against whatever is set before them, knock it down. This is what the apostles did when, through preaching, they shattered various superstitions and the most firmly established idols by a kind of frontal assault with the heavenly word.

The ram is called *aries* as though from *a fronte ruens*, “charging headfirst.”

In another sense, rams signify wicked leaders, concerning whom Ezekiel says:

> “With goats and lambs and rams” (Ezek. XXVII).

The lamb (*agnus*) is said by the Greeks to be called *apo tou agnou*, as though meaning “pious.” The Latins, however, think that it received this name because, more than other animals, it recognizes its mother: even if it has strayed in a large flock, it immediately recognizes the parent’s voice by its bleating.

The lamb mystically bears either the person of our Savior, whose innocent death saved the human race, concerning whom John says:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I),

or the innocent life of any Catholic, who recognizes the voice of his mother—that is, the Church—and, by obedience, clings to her side and obeys her commandments.

The holy are represented by lambs in the Gospel:

> “Feed my lambs” (John XXI).

Lambs also signify wanton people in Isaiah:

> “My sword is drunk with the blood of lambs and goats” (Isa. XXXIV).

The ewe signifies the active life in Leviticus:

> “Let him do penance and offer a ewe from the flock or a she-goat” (Lev. V);

the latter is a figure of the contemplative life.

The seven lambs and seven ewes commanded by the Law to be offered to God in sacrifice signify the fullness of all the saints, or the mystery of innocent works. Twin offspring signify the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and love of neighbor. In the Song of Songs:

> “All are bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Song VI).

Goats (*haedi*) are named from *edendo*, “eating,” for they are small, very fat, and pleasant in taste. From the same root come *edere*, “to eat,” and *edulium*, “food.”

Allegorically, goats signify sinners, who at the end will be placed on the judge’s left, just as the righteous, signified by sheep, will be placed on the right. Hence Truth himself says in the Gospel:

> “He will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left” (Matt. XXV).

Sometimes the righteous are also designated by this name, on account of their confession of sins, as in Jeremiah:

> “Depart,” he says, “from the midst of Babylon; go out from the land of the Chaldeans, and be like goats before the flocks” (Jer. I).

The goat signifies Christ because of his likeness to sinful flesh, as in Deuteronomy:

> “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Deut. XIV).

The goat signifies Antichrist, as in the Gospel:

> “You never gave me a goat, so that I might feast with my friends” (Luke XV).

The sheepfold is the Church, as in the Gospel:

> “And there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John X).

The shepherd is Christ, as in the Gospel:

> “I am the good shepherd” (ibid.).

Shepherds are the apostles or the other leaders of the churches, as in the Prophet:

> “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and doctrine” (Jer. III).

Wicked shepherds are the corrupt priests, as in Jeremiah:

> “The flock is scattered, because there is no one to gather what has been scattered,” and so forth (Jer. X).

The guardian is the Lord, as in Job:

> “I have sinned against you, O guardian of humankind” (Job VII).

In Isaiah:

> “Guardian, what of the night? Guardian, what of the night?” (Isa. XXI).

The guardians are the apostles or the other preachers. In Isaiah:

> “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed guardians; all day and all night they will never be silent” (Isa. LXII).

Hirelings signify the Jewish people, as in the Gospel:

> “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance?” (Luke XV).

The tenant signifies a heretic; the hireling, the Jewish people. In Leviticus:

> “A tenant of a priest or a hired servant shall not eat of it” (Lev. XXII),

that is, of the sacrifice of the Lord’s body [Col. 0203C].

The goat (*hircus*) is a lustful, wanton animal, always burning with desire for intercourse. Because of lust, its eyes look sideways; hence it received its name. According to Suetonius, *hirci* are the corners of the eyes. Its nature is so exceedingly hot that its blood alone is said to dissolve a diamond, which neither fire nor iron can subdue.

The goat that was offered in the Law for sins represents the person of sinners, who, by shedding blood—that is, by tears of repentance—dissolves the hardness of sins. Hence the Church says to the Lord in the Psalter:

> “I will offer you oxen with goats” (Ps. LXV).

Goats signify sinners or the nations, as in Daniel:

> “And behold, a he-goat was coming from the north” (Dan. VIII).

The two goats in Leviticus signify the two peoples, Jews and nations, coming from the stock of sin. Others have understood the two goats as Christ and Barabbas.

Oxen, as we said above, signify preachers, who successfully plowed human hearts and planted fruitful seeds of the heavenly word in their understanding.

Goats signify those who devote themselves to devilish perversities and clothe themselves in shaggy vices. The goat is called *hircus* as though from *hirsutus*, “shaggy.” Yet the Church offers such people together with oxen when, after conversion, they confess Christ the Lord.

That thief who hung on the cross was a goat, and soon became an ox when he turned to the confession of truth. For he said:

> “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII).

Some say that male and female goats (*capri* and *caprae*) derive their names from cropping shrubs; others say that they crop rough things; still others think that the females are called so from the clatter of their legs.

Wild goats, which the Greeks call *dorkades* from *apo tou oxu derkesthai*, “to see very sharply,” dwell on high mountains. Although they are far away, they nevertheless see everyone who approaches. The same is true of she-goats.

The ibexes are likewise so called, as though *abices*, because they occupy steep and lofty places like birds and live in the mountains, so that from their heights they scarcely appear to human sight. Hence the southern region calls ibexes “birds,” since they inhabit the waters of the Nile.

These animals, as we have said, live among the highest rocks. Whenever they sense danger from wild animals or human beings, they throw themselves down from the highest rocky peaks and receive the impact safely upon their horns.

The goat signifies the flesh of the Savior—that is, the likeness of sinful flesh—as in Solomon:

> “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle” (Song II).

Goats also signify sinners or the nations, as in Daniel:

> “Behold, the he-goat of the goats” (Dan. VIII),

that is, the prince of sinners.

Thus goats sometimes signify the righteous who come from the nations, as in Solomon:

> “Your hair is like a flock of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead” (Song IV).

The bridegroom likewise says to the bride:

> “Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (ibid.).

The fact that these animals, terrified by the hostility of wild animals or human beings, cast themselves down from the highest cliffs and are received unharmed upon their horns signifies that the righteous and all who fear God—meditating upon the law of God in the two Testaments and fulfilling it through the two commandments of charity—are preserved unharmed from every adversity [Col. 0204C].

The flock signifies the congregation of the faithful, abandoning its former way of life in baptism, as in the Song of Songs:

> “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (ibid.).

A flock also signifies a collection of sinners. In Jeremiah:

> “Gather them like a flock for slaughter” (Jer. XII).

Deer are called *cervi* from the Greek *apo ton ceraton*, “from the horns,” for *cerata* means “horns” in Greek.

Deer are enemies of serpents. When they perceive themselves weighed down by illness, they draw the serpents from their caves with the breath of their nostrils; after overcoming the poison’s danger, they restore themselves by eating them. They themselves revealed the herb dittany. After feeding on it, they shake out the arrows they have received.

They marvel at the whistling of pipes: with ears raised they hear acutely, but with ears lowered they hear nothing. When they swim across immense rivers or seas, they place their heads upon the haunches of those in front, and, taking turns with one another, feel none of the burden’s exertion.

The deer signifies holy men who desire God. Hence the Prophet says:

> “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI).

The animal is first harmless, then exceedingly swift, and thirdly, when its desire burns, thirsty. It draws serpents through its nostrils; after devouring them, stirred by the heat of their poison, it hastens with all possible speed to a spring of water. It loves to be satisfied with sweet and very pure water.

This beautiful comparison ardently stimulates our own desire: when we have swallowed the poisons of the ancient serpent and burn within our deepest throat, we should hasten immediately to the spring of divine mercy, so that what is contracted through the adversity of sin may be overcome by the purity of the sweetest draught.

Nor is it without significance that he said “to springs of water,” not simply “to waters.” For Christ the Lord is the spring of waters, from whom everything that refreshes flows. Streams can often dry up, but a spring of water is always irrigated. Therefore it is rightly said that we must hasten to the flowing source of sacred origin, where our desire can never suffer hunger.

Elsewhere it is written:

> “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. CIII).

Deer also signify the patriarchs. Hence in the Song of Songs, concerning the Savior who was born from their stock according to the flesh, it says:

> “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle and a fawn of deer” (Song II) [Col. 0205B].

Deer signify the apostles. In the Psalter:

> “The voice of him who prepares the deer” (Ps. XXVIII).

The hind signifies the Lord’s flesh. In Solomon:

> “A most beloved hind and a most pleasing fawn; let her breasts intoxicate you” (Prov. V),

that is, evangelical doctrine.

Hinds signify the apostles because they give birth spiritually. In Job:

> “Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth, or have you watched the hinds giving birth?” (Job XXXIX).

The deer, as we said, devours poisonous serpents, crosses thorny places, possesses extraordinary agility, and loves to dwell in the highest mountains.

It is rightly compared with the faithful, who devour the devil when they turn his wickedness toward the praise and glory of the Lord. They leap over the vices of this world as though over thorns by their good conduct, and they dwell in the mountains—that is, in the apostles and prophets, who through their holy preaching have deserved to be firm summits in this world [Col. 0205C].

The Greeks call *tragelaphi* animals that have the same appearance as deer but shaggy shoulders like goats and chins covered with long, bristling beards. They are found nowhere except around the Phasis.

Fawns are the offspring of deer.

The doe (*damula*) is so called because it flees from the hand; it is a timid and defenseless animal. Martial writes of it:

> “The boar is feared for its tooth; horns defend the stag;  
> What are defenseless does but prey?”

These animals likewise signify either Christ or innocent human beings. Hence also the bride says of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer” (Song II). Christ, therefore, in the assumption of flesh and the humility of the gazelle, is compared to a gazelle; but in the variety of virtues and the innocence of a fawn of the deer, that is, of the patriarchs from whom he derived his origin according to the flesh.

The hare (*lepus*) is so called as though it were “light-footed” (*levipes*), because it runs swiftly. Hence in Greek it is called *lagos*, from running; for it is a swift and very timid animal. The hare signifies people who fear God, who place their trust not in themselves but in their Creator. Hence we read in Solomon: “The little hare is a feeble people that makes its burrow in the rock” (Prov. XXX). Hence it is said in the Psalm: “The rock is a refuge for hares and hedgehogs” (Ps. CIII). The rock, however, is Christ. Hence it is written of Moses (Exod. XXXIII) that “the little hare of the Lord, Moses,” stood in the cleft of the rock, because in the passion of the Redeemer he placed the hope of his salvation.

The hedgehog [Col. 0206A], which we call *ericius*, is an altogether timid animal, yet by nature always armed. Its skin is protected on every side by extremely sharp and very dense bristles; nevertheless its natural defense is not sufficient for it. So that it may not be caught by any deception, it always has refuge among rocks. To this is aptly compared the person who, bristling with his sins and fearing the future judgments, is known to have Christ the firmest rock as his refuge.

The sow (*sus*) is so called because it works over pasture—that is, it searches for food in worked earth. The boar (*verres*) is so called because it has great strength. The pig (*porcus*) is as though “filthy” (*spurcus*): for it stuffs itself with dung, plunges into mud, and smears itself with slime. Horace: “And the sow that delights in mud.” Hence we also speak of filth (*spurcitia*) and of bastard offspring (*spurii*). We call the hair of pigs bristles (*setae*); *setae* is said to derive from *sus*, and from them shoemakers (*sutores*) are so called, because they sew—*suunt*, that is, stitch together—hides with bristles.

Pigs signify sinners, the unclean, or heretics. Concerning them the Law commands that, because they split the hoof but do not chew the cud, their flesh should not be touched by the faithful. Although these people receive both Testaments, of the Law and of the Gospel, they are unclean because they do not chew spiritual food. Pigs also signify negligent penitents who return to the things over which they had wept, just as Peter says in his Epistle: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (II Pet. II).

When a dog vomits, it certainly casts out the food that weighed upon its breast; but when it returns to its vomit, it is again burdened by what had relieved it. Thus those who mourn their offenses certainly cast out through confession the wickedness of mind with which they had been badly filled and which weighed them down inwardly [Col. 0206C]; but after confession, when they return to it, they take it up again.

The washed sow, while being washed, is made dirtier; and one who mourns an offense but does not abandon it subjects himself to a heavier guilt. He despises the very pardon that he could have obtained by weeping, and, as though wallowing in muddy water, he rolls himself in it, because, while by his tears he withdraws the purity of life, he makes those very tears filthy before the eyes of God.

Pigs also signify unclean and lustful people. In the Gospel: “If you cast us out, send us into the pigs” (Matt. VIII). And there also: “Do not cast your pearls before pigs” (Matt. VII). The pig likewise signifies an unclean spirit. In the Gospel: “And he sent him into his own estate to feed pigs” (Luke XV).

The pig likewise signifies the unclean and sinners. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm [Col. 0206D]: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things; they are satisfied with pork, and they will leave what remains to their little ones” (Ps. XVI). He speaks of the Jews, of the uncleannesses that are hidden by the Lord—that is, are known to be forbidden. “Pork” refers to polluted things, which among the other precepts of the Old Testament are marked as unclean. They transmitted the remnants of their sins to their children when they cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

Likewise, in Solomon the sow signifies a sinner who understands correctly but lives lustfully: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful but foolish woman” (Prov. XI). Likewise, the sow signifies the filthy thoughts of carnal people, from which evil deeds proceed as though cooked, in Isaiah: “Those who eat swine’s flesh [Col. 0207A] and have profane broth in their vessels” (Isa. LXV).

The boar (*aper*) is named from ferocity, with the letter *f* removed and *p* substituted. Hence among the Greeks it is called *suagros*, that is, “wild.” For everything that is wild and untamed we improperly call “belonging to the countryside.” Others say that the boar is so called because it dwells in rough places.

The boar signifies the ferocity of the rulers of this age. Hence it is written in the Psalm concerning the Lord’s vineyard: “The boar from the forest has devastated it, and a solitary wild beast has consumed it” (Ps. LXXIX). He devastated it beyond its boundaries and homeland and scattered it everywhere—what happened among the Jewish people. Perhaps we should understand Vespasian as the boar, since he proved strong and savage against them. By this name, however, it signifies that he was opposed to the Jews, because this animal was regarded, among other things, as having the uncleanness of the forest—that is, of the nations—which are rightly compared to dense forests, because they had not yet been planted with fruitful growth.

By “the solitary wild beast” he recalls his son Titus, who crushed the survivors of the war with such great devastation that, like the fodder of grasses, he consumed the nation and the city in a terrifying ravaging. This had to happen to the vineyard whose wall appeared to have been thrown down. Spiritually, however, because of its excessive ferocity and strength, the boar can be understood as the devil. He said “from the forest” because his thoughts are always uncultivated and wild.

The young bull (*juvencus*) is so called because it begins to be useful to human beings in cultivating the earth, and because among the pagans a young bull was always sacrificed to Jupiter everywhere, never a mature bull; for age was also considered in sacrificial victims.

The bull (*taurus*) is a Greek name, as is *bos*. Indian bulls are tawny in color, swift as birds, and have hair turned in the opposite direction. They turn their heads around with whatever flexibility they wish; with the hardness of their backs they repel every weapon, in savage ferocity.

The bull signifies Christ. In Genesis: “In their anger they hamstrung the bull” (Gen. XLIX). Bulls also signify the powers of this age, goring humble peoples with the horn of pride. Concerning them Jeremiah says: “You bellowed like bulls” (Jer. L). And elsewhere: “And bulls with the mighty” (Isa. XXXIV).

Bulls can be understood in both a favorable and an unfavorable sense. In a favorable sense, as in the Gospel: “Behold, I have prepared my banquet, and the fattened animals have been killed, and everything is ready” (Matt. XXII). What, then, are signified by the bulls except the Fathers of the Old Testament? For since, by permission of the Law, they had received the power to strike their adversaries in requital of hatred, what else were they, so to speak, than bulls, who wounded their enemies with the horn of bodily strength?

What, on the other hand, are signified by the fattened animals except the Fathers of the New Testament? As they receive the grace of inward richness, they are lifted by the wings of their contemplation toward higher things, relying upon eternal desires.

In an unfavorable sense bulls are understood, as in the Psalm: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. LXVII). Here by bulls he signifies untamed heretics who, with necks held erect, lead innocent souls astray and draw them into their own flock, deceiving them by wretched persuasion. The cows of the peoples are women of exceedingly fickle and pliable will [Col. 0208A], who follow the teachers of unbelief as bulls and are led by them.

The Greeks call an ox *boun*. The Latins call it *trio*, because it wears down (*terat*) the earth, as though *terion*. Naevius: “Here the rustic driver of the oxen.” Its broad hanging skin, from the chin to the legs, is called the dewlap (*palearia*) from the skin itself, as though *pelearia*.

In oxen, therefore, the madness of the lustful, the laborious strength of preachers, and the humility of the Israelites are at various times expressed. That the madness of the lustful is designated by the name of an ox, Solomon indicates. After describing the wantonness of the woman who gives evil counsel, he adds: “Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to the sacrifice” (Prov. VII).

Again, that the labor of the preacher is expressed by the name of an ox, the words of the Law testify, saying: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. XXV; I Cor. IX).

Again, because the Israelite people is figured by the name of an ox, the Prophet asserts this when, announcing the Redeemer’s coming, he says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey the manger of its lord” (Isa. I). And there also: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey” (Isa. XXXII).

The ox also signifies the devil in his members, that is, in heretics. Hence in Job: “He will eat grass like an ox” (Job XL).

The cow (*vacca*) is as though *boacca*. It belongs to the class of nouns whose form changes according to gender, like *leo*, *leaena*, and *draco*, *dracaena*. At times it bears a favorable meaning, as in the Law (Num. XIX), where a red cow, of full age and one that has not drawn a yoke, is commanded to be sacrificed for the purification of the Lord’s sanctuary. Strength is usually designated by the masculine gender, and weakness by the feminine [Col. 0208C]. What, then, is signified by the cow except the weakness of the Lord’s incarnation assumed for sacrifice? Concerning this it is written: “For although he died in weakness, yet he lives by power” (II Cor. XIII).

This cow is rightly called red, because his humanity was reddened by the blood of his passion. The age of the Lord’s humanity is complete; all his work is perfect. In that humanity there was no stain, for it is truly written of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

It is rightly added: “And it shall not have borne the yoke” (Num. XIX). Since the Lord submitted to no one, he bore no yoke. It is rightly said: “He sacrificed it before the Lord” (ibid.). For our Redeemer was put to death in the sight of human beings, but he is sacrificed in the sight of the Father, because what was punishment before human eyes was sacrifice before the Father’s eyes.

The cow is understood in an unfavorable sense when it expresses the wantonness of a sinful person, as in the prophetic passage: “Ephraim is a wanton cow” (Hos. IV). And again: “Ephraim,” he says, “is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck” (Hos. X).

The cow signifies the Jewish people believing in Christ, as in Isaiah: “A man will nourish a cow and two sheep; because of the abundance of milk he will eat butter” (Isa. VII)—that is, Christ.

Cows signify the faithful in the Church, whose figure was borne by those cows that carried the Lord’s ark back from the land of the Philistines. Cows signify souls filled with carnal vices, as in the Psalter: “The assemblies of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. LXVII). Cows signify the wealthy of this age, as in Amos: “Hear the word of the Lord, fat cows” (Amos IV).

The calf and heifer (*vitulus*, *vitula*) are named from greenness, that is, from the greenness of youth, like a virgin. A heifer is therefore small and has not yet calved; once it has calved, it is a young cow, like a cow.

The calf is understood favorably when it demonstrates the innocence of the faithful or the sincere praise of pious devotion. Hence it is written: “We shall render the calf of our lips” (Hos. XIV). And in the Psalm: “They shall place calves upon your altar” (Ps. L).

He placed calves either for the innocent, whose age is still at its beginning and whose neck is shown to be free from the yoke of sin—and therefore he retained this wording, to indicate that the act of the former Law had been an image of future things—or he promises those preachers of the Gospel whose figure the Evangelist Luke assumes in the form of a calf. They would not strike the air with bellowing, but would fill the whole world with the preaching of the Lord’s faith. Or perhaps we should understand as calves more particularly those who offered their souls as an oblation of sweetness upon the sacred altars.

For Father Augustine too, when he was discussing those Gospel figures, says in one place that the Lord himself is the calf who offered himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of all. Therefore, whether the reference is understood of young men, preachers, or martyrs, the Prophet could promise to the Lord’s altars only such calves as he knew to be fitting for the Christian religion.

The calf signifies Christ in the Gospel: “Bring the fattened calf and kill it” (Luke XV). And [Col. 0209C] in another sense: “And you shall crush them like the calves of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII).

Calves signify saints growing in faith and having necks freed from the yoke of the Law. Calves signify wanton Jews. In the Psalm: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me” (Ps. XXI).

The meaning of calves is therefore taken in an unfavorable sense when it signifies the wantonness and lust of the perverse. Thus the children of Israel, with a perverse mind, practiced idolatry in the likeness of a calf in the desert; and Jeroboam, abandoning God’s temple in Jerusalem, fashioned an image of a calf and honored it with divine worship.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “They made a calf at Horeb and worshiped a sculpted image” (Ps. CV). Horeb is interpreted as “Calvary,” where afterward the Lord is known to have been killed in the flesh on the gallows of the cross. Thus, under the same name, already then in that desert at Horeb, the impious violated the worship of the Lord by their wicked presumption, and their posterity was to crucify the Lord Christ at the place of Calvary.

I also think that this should be considered: he says, “They worshiped a sculpted image,” because in Exodus we read that the cast calf was fashioned from collected ornaments, as a monstrous sort of portent. But here we must understand two things as having been stated: namely, that they worshiped the calf in the desert, and that they worshiped carved images or idols in the land of promise. He himself will say this in what follows: “And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (ibid.).

Their glory was the divinity they worshiped. Through that unhappy exchange, persisting in it, they deserved to reach the point [Col. 0210A] where, abandoning God the Creator of heaven and earth, they made for themselves the likeness of a calf eating hay.

Something must therefore be inserted here concerning the blood, fat, and richness of the cattle that were offered in the Law. Blood is, as some maintain, the power of the soul. Permission to discuss its nature is not granted, because its hidden origin is known to God alone; but according to the precept of the Law it is poured out at the base of the altar, that is, it is reserved for divine power and understanding. For what is it to eat blood except to dispute the origin of the soul?

Blood signifies the works of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV). Blood signifies sin, as in Amos: “Blood has touched blood; therefore the land will mourn” (Hos. IV). To touch blood with blood is to join sins to sins, since every sin that kills the soul is compared to blood, as the Prophet says of the sinner: “His blood is upon his own head” (Hos. XII).

Fat signifies the richness of divine grace. In the Psalm: “May he be filled with fat and richness” (Ps. LXII). Fat signifies the compunction of the hearts of the saints. In Leviticus: “And having placed the burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fats of the peace offerings” (Lev. VI). Fat signifies the understanding of spiritual grace, as in the Psalm: “And he satisfies you with the fat of grain” (Ps. CXLVII).

The fats that cover the genital organs, which are forbidden to be eaten, are thought by some to signify the origin of the soul, just as was said above concerning blood, in Leviticus. Fat signifies the thickness of wickedness, as in the Psalm: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat” (Ps. LXXII). And there also: “They have enclosed themselves in fat” (Ps. XVI).

Thickness signifies hardness of heart. In the Prophet: “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Isa. VI); and in Job: “His thickness covered his face, and fat hangs from his sides” (Job XV).

Marrow signifies holy thoughts or compunction proceeding from the innermost heart, in the Psalter: “I will offer you marrow-filled burnt offerings” (Ps. LXV). In an unfavorable sense it is spoken of the reprobate in Ezekiel: “And their iniquities are in their bones” (Ezek. XXXII).

The buffaloes (*bubali*) are so called by derivation because they resemble oxen. They are so untamed that, because of their ferocity, they do not accept a yoke upon their necks; Africa produces them. Aurochs (*uri*) are wild oxen in Germany, with horns extended so far that vessels of remarkable capacity are made from them for royal tables.

In buffaloes or aurochs may be understood proud teachers and rulers of the people, who possess the likeness of good teachers in the rank or office they hold, but, swollen with pride and trusting in the horns of worldly power rather than in divine assistance, choose to lord it over the clergy rather than to become an example to the flock. Against them the Lord threatens through the Prophet, saying: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and killed what was fat; but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up the broken, bring back the cast-off, or seek the lost; but you ruled them with harshness and power” [Col. 0211A] (Isa. XXXIV).

Camels (*cameli*) received their name either because, when they are loaded, they lie down so as to become shorter and lower—for the Greeks call *camai* “low” and “short”—or because their back is curved. For *camur*, in a Greek word, signifies “curved.” Although other regions also produce them, Arabia produces the greatest number. They differ among themselves: Arabian camels have two humps on their backs, while those of other regions have one.

In sacred language, the name camel sometimes expresses the Lord and sometimes the pride of the nations, as though something twisted were swelling above. The dromedary (*dromeda*) is a kind of camel smaller in stature but swifter, from which it also takes its name. For *dromos* in Greek means “running” or “speed.” It is accustomed to travel more than one hundred miles in a day. This animal, like the ox, sheep, and camel [Col. 0211B], chews the cud. “Chewing the cud” (*ruminatio*) is so called from *ruma*, the projecting part of the throat through which food that has been swallowed is brought back up by certain animals.

The camel either signifies Christ’s humility, because he bore the burdens of our sins, or the Gentile people converted to the Christian faith. When the Lord says in the Gospel, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX), he shows that it is easier for Christ to suffer for those who love the world than for those who love the world to be converted to Christ. He wished himself to be understood by the name camel, because he voluntarily humbled himself and took upon himself the burdens of our weakness. In whom could what is written be understood more clearly than in him: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sir. III)?

By the needle, piercings are signified; by the piercings, the pains undertaken in the passion. Thus he calls the eye of the needle the narrowness of the passion, by which, when the garments of our nature had been torn, he deigned in a certain manner to mend them—that is, to restore them—so that after our fall we might rejoice, better reformed, in fulfillment of the Apostle’s testimony: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

Others understood the camel as the Lord Jesus Christ, because by humbling himself he bore the burdens of our sins. The camel signifies the love of the world, whose figure was borne by that camel from which Rebecca, when she was about to marry Isaac, descended and left it.

Camels signify sinners distorted in character, as in Judges: “And their camels were as numerous as locusts” (Jud. VII). And in Isaiah it is written concerning Jerusalem: “A flood of camels will cover you; the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba will come, bringing gold and frankincense, and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (Isa. LX).

This sentence signifies the gathering of the nations into the Church of Christ. Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, fertile in camels. The whole province is called Sheba, from which the queen of Sheba came to Solomon. Kedar is the region of the Saracens, who are called Ishmaelites; and Nabaioth is one of Ishmael’s sons. From their names the desert is called a place lacking crops but full of animals.

Thus, through the familiar names of barbarian nations neighboring the Ishmaelites, the conversion of the whole world is proclaimed. In this passage, Mathan is interpreted as “iniquity,” Ephah as “released” or “pouring out,” and Sheba as “conversion” or “captivity.” Kedar means “darkness,” and Nabaioth “prophecies.”

Therefore herds of camels—that is, the wealthy and sinners—released from the bonds of iniquity and pouring out their souls to God, will cover Jerusalem with gifts. All will come from captivity and will bring, through their conversion, the gold of faith and the frankincense of sacrifice, progressing so far that they will also proclaim God’s salvation to others.

The ass and the little ass (*asinus*, *asellus*) are named from sitting, as though *aseddus*. This name, which was more properly applicable to horses, was assumed by this animal because, before human beings captured horses, they began to ride this one. It is a slow animal and offers no resistance; as soon as a human being wished, he placed it beneath himself.

By the name of asses, male or female, are sometimes designated the wantonness of the lustful, sometimes the gentleness of the simple, and sometimes the foolishness of the nations. The ass, mystically, because it is a brutish and lustful animal, signifies either the Gentile people—as we have said—upon which the Lord deigned to sit as he proceeded toward Jerusalem, so that he might make it subject to him and lead it to the heavenly homeland; or the foolish person who pursues nothing but the lust of this world.

Hence Jacob said to his son Issachar, whose name is interpreted as “reward”: “Issachar is a strong ass lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and the land that it was excellent, and he placed his shoulder under the burden and became a servant subject to tribute” (Gen. XLIX).

The Gentile people, whom the Lord purchased with the price of his blood, was formerly like a brutish and lustful animal, existing by no reason. [Col. 0212C] Now, however, it is strong: it subjects the hidden things of its mind to our Savior and, submitting its neck to the rule of the Redeemer, bears the yoke of evangelical discipline. Hence it has become a servant subject to tribute—that is, it offers to its king and Christ the gifts of faith and good works.

The ass also signifies a foolish person. In Deuteronomy: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass” (Deut. XXII), that is, you shall not join a foolish person to a wise person in preaching.

The ass signifies the synagogue of the Jews. In Genesis: “Binding his colt to the vine, and his ass’s foal to the vine, O my son” (Gen. XLIX). The ass signifies the body of a human being; hence it is written in the book of Judges: “You who ride upon shining asses” (Jud. V). There also, concerning the she-ass of Caleb’s daughter, which bears the image of the soul, it is said: “When she sighed, sitting upon the ass” (Jud. I).

The firstborn of an ass signifies the beginnings of a life of lust, as in Exodus: “You shall redeem the firstborn of an ass with a sheep” (Exod. XXXIV). The ass then signifies a foolish person when it shows a person bearing the burdens of sin and practicing the lusts of the flesh to the end of life.

Hence it is written that when Ana was feeding the asses of his father Sebeon, he found warm springs in the desert. Therefore the Prophet says of the lustful: “Their flesh is like the flesh of asses” (Ezek. XXIII).

*Onager* is interpreted as “wild ass.” For the Greeks call an ass *onos* and a wild animal *agrios*. Africa has these animals large and untamed, wandering in the desert. Each male rules over herds of females; when males are born, they grow jealous of them and bite off their testicles. To prevent this, the mothers hide them in secret places.

The onager signifies either the Jewish people or a hermit. It signifies the Jewish people in the Psalms, where it is written: “The wild asses await their thirst” (Ps. CIII). After saying above that the beasts of the forests are watered by flowing waters, he now places the wild asses as awaiting their thirst: namely, the Jews, who neglected to drink from the streams of divine mercy.

The onager is a woodland ass, which is said among other animals to have an especially fat heart. The more patient this species is when domesticated, the more savage it becomes when it grows wild amid the forests that retain it. The obstinate Jews are rightly compared to these animals, because they have been hardened by mental ferocity and callous foolishness and do not readily consent to be satisfied with life-giving drinks. For when he says “they will await,” he signifies what has often been said: that at the end of the age, when Elijah and Enoch come, the multitude of the Jews will believe.

Again, in the book of Job the Lord is reported to have said: “Who let the wild ass go free, and who loosed its bonds, and so forth?” (Job XXXIX). The implied answer is: “unless I.” The onager, which dwells in solitude, signifies the life of those who live apart from the crowds of the populace. He is therefore set free who, trampling upon earthly desires and seeking burdens of temporal things, is relieved of them through security of mind. And “who loosens his bonds?” The implied answer is: “unless I.” The bonds of every saint are loosened when, by divine assistance, the inward restraints of carnal desires are broken.

“To whom I gave the wilderness as his dwelling and his tents in the land of salt” (ibid.). For withdrawn men—that is, those alienated from carnal desires—inhabit this silence of mind, so that they are not pressed down by a crowd of carnal desires. The tents of this onager are in a land of salt. Saltiness ordinarily inflames thirst. Thus holy men, as long as they dwell in the tents of this life, are kindled by the daily heat of their desire for the heavenly homeland.

The onager also signifies any arrogant person, that is, a lover of empty glory, as in Jeremiah: “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of its soul, drew in the wind of its love” (Jer. II), that is, the spirit of pride. The onagers signify the rulers of the Jews, as in Jeremiah. “The wild asses also stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons” (Jer. XIV).

Horses (*equi*) are so called because, when they were joined to four-horse chariots, they were made equal and paired as equals in form and likeness in running. A *caballus* was formerly named from *cao*, because as it walks it hollows the earth by impressing its hoof—something the other animals do not do. Hence it is also called *sonipes*, because it makes a sound with its feet.

The horse sometimes bears a favorable meaning and sometimes an unfavorable one. In a favorable sense, as in the prophet Habakkuk: “You mounted upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Hab. III). And in Job the divine voice says: “Will you give strength to the horse, or clothe its neck with neighing, and so forth?” (Job XXXIX). Here the horse signifies holy preachers, whose rider is the Lord, who gives them strength—that is, steadfastness of mind—and the sound of sound preaching.

Conversely, concerning another kind of horses it is written in the song of Exodus: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” [Col. 0214A] (Exod. XV). And again: “Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea” (ibid.).

There are horses whom the Lord mounts and who go throughout the whole earth, concerning whom it is said: “And your riding is salvation.” But there are horses who have the Devil and his angels as riders. Judas was his horse; yet as long as he had the Lord as rider, he belonged with the others to the riding of salvation, and, sent with the Apostles, he brought salvation to the sick and healing to the infirm. But when he submitted himself to the Devil—for after the morsel Satan entered into him (John XIII)—led by that one’s reins, he began to ride against the Lord and our Savior.

All who persecute the saints are neighing horses; but they have riders by whom they are driven, namely evil angels, and therefore they are fierce. The Lord, therefore, cast horse and rider into the sea, and it became salvation for me.

Horses signify sinners and lustful people, as in Jeremiah: “Stallions; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V). The horse signifies carnal power. In Isaiah: “Woe to those who mount horses in order to descend into Egypt” (Isa. XXX). And in the Psalm: “Those who mounted horses fell asleep” (Ps. LXXV).

The red, variegated, black, and white horses that are read to have appeared in the prophet Zechariah either designate the correction of sinners or the consolation of converts. For it is written in Zechariah, with the Lord saying: “I am angry with the wealthy nations. For I was angry only a little, but they added to the evil” (Zech. I). And again the same prophet says: “I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse; and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the deep; and behind him were red, variegated, and white horses, and so forth” (ibid.).

The night in which the vision is seen mystically signifies the obscurity of the vision. The man who rides upon the red horse is the Lord and Savior, who assumed the dispensation of our flesh. The myrtles that were in the deep, among which he is described as standing, signify the angelic powers, which ministered to him even while he was present in the flesh.

The red, variegated, and white horses signify the Apostles and apostolic men. Some of them were crowned in martyrdom and are called red; others are called variegated because of their works, teaching, and variety of signs; others, adorned with the beauty of virginity and the integrity and purity of heart, received the privilege of seeing God as their reward.

The Apostles were sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with evangelical preaching. After completing their work, they returned to the Angel of the Great Counsel, who stood among them, and said to him: “We have traversed the earth and completed the work that was entrusted to us; and behold, the whole earth is inhabited and rests from the wars of vices, and what had previously been deserted by the Lord is now his dwelling.”

When he says, “In the seventieth year he will have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah,” the meaning is this: true peace will not come except in the seventieth year, that is, in the eternal Sabbath; nor will Jerusalem—that is, the eternal Church—rest in perpetual quiet except after the labor of the six ages, when it will rest without any disturbance in the seventh.

The consoling words are gifts of the Holy Spirit and the pledge of our inheritance, which we shall receive after the captivity of Babylon—that is, of this world.

When we read of two-horse chariots and four-horse chariots in the prophets, according to allegory this indicates either the periods of kingdoms or their authority and activity. For we read of two-horse chariots in Isaiah and of four-horse chariots in Zechariah. Thus it is written there: “I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots going out from between two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot variegated, strong horses” (Zech. VI).

The horses of the first chariot were red, bloodstained, and murderous, terrifying because of Babylon’s cruelty. In the second chariot were black horses: the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, which, with the one seated in the two-horse chariot going forth by the decree of King Ahasuerus, brought the Jews the grim message of universal death. In the third chariot were white horses: the Macedonians, under whose rule we read of the Maccabees’ victory over Antiochus. In the fourth chariot were variegated, strong horses.

For we know that among the Roman rulers some were merciful toward the Jewish nation, such as Gaius Caesar, Augustus, and Claudius; while others were persecutors and terrifying, such as Gaius, Nero, Vespasian, and Hadrian.

When the Prophet asked what the angel who spoke to him meant by what he was seeing, the angel who spoke within him answered and explained that these were the four winds of heaven—that is, the four regions of the world, which in Greek are called *climata*—which stand before and obey the Lord’s will. For none of these four kingdoms that we have mentioned did anything without the Lord’s will [Col. 0215C].

Thus, according to allegory, in the four-horse chariot the two Testaments may be understood, or the preachers of those Testaments in the commandments of love, or even the two peoples and the teachers of those peoples, namely the Jews and the nations, over whom Christ presides and to whom he grants fitting governance.

Likewise, in the four-horse chariot the four Evangelists or the four Gospels may be understood, or the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. These fittingly belong to the Lord’s chariot, because through them he guides his chosen along the way of righteousness and leads them to the everlasting kingdom.

The chariot (*currus*) is named from running (*cursus*), or because it appears to have wheels. The chariot mystically signifies either the fellowship of the holy angels or the unanimity of holy human beings [Col. 0215D], in whom the Lord exercises the governance of his will.

Hence we read that Elijah was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II), so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed assistance from another. Those things were accomplished and displayed through angels as forms of assistance, because he could not even ascend by himself into the aerial heaven, weighed down as he was by the weakness of his nature.

But our Redeemer is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was carried above all things by his own power. He was returning there where he was, and from there he was returning where he remained, because he who ascended into heaven through his humanity also contained both earth and heaven through his divinity.

It is likewise written in the Psalm: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing; the Lord is among them” (Ps. LXVII). The unanimity of the saints, therefore, is the power of the Lord, upon which he sits as a charioteer and which he directs toward the service of his will.

But to show that this chariot was devoted not to horses but assigned to human thoughts, he says: “Ten thousandfold”—which is rightly understood to refer to innumerable peoples, not to horses. He adds: “Thousands of rejoicing,” which must certainly be understood of the faithful. And to show the fullness of joy,
He says: “The Lord is among them”—a culmination of great rejoicing and a wondrous sweetness of every good thing.

Elsewhere, the chariot is understood in another sense as the company of the wicked, bound by the chain of sins; concerning this it is written in the Song of Exodus (Exod. 15), as we showed above.

Moreover, [Col. 0216B] individual riders are said to run because each person separately passes through the course of this life, one following another at a different time, yet all by the single road of mortality toward their own appointed end in death. Riders can be understood in a good or a bad sense. In the good sense, when they signify those who subdue vices; in the bad sense, when proud people who place their confidence in worldly power are prefigured.

The word *mule* (*mulus*) is derived from Greek. In Greek, it is so called because, having been subjected to the millers’ yoke, it makes the millstones travel slowly in a circle while grinding. The Jews assert that Ana, a great-great-grandson of Esau, was the first to have herds of mares mounted by donkeys in the wilderness, so that from them new animals, contrary to nature, might be born—mules. They also say that for this reason wild asses were sent to [Col. 0216C] the she-asses, and that he himself discovered this kind of mating, so that the fastest asses might be born from them.

Since the mule is a beast that carries burdens, it signifies those who follow folly. Absalom followed this folly when, seated on a mule and raising sedition against his father, he deservedly perished. Accordingly, the Psalmist restrains his hearers, saying: “Do not become like a horse and a mule, in which there is no understanding. Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle” (Ps. 31).

He therefore forbids such people to be ridden by diabolical deceits and weighed down by the burdens of vices, lest, by obeying wickedly, they become still more devoted to the cause of pride. But what, then, does he say should be done to such people—namely, to irrational animals? By these comparisons he subjects foolish people [Col. 0216D] to the truth.

For when he says “with a bridle,” he refers to the horse. *Frenum* (“bridle”) is so called from restraining (*retinendo*) the wild creature. For the ancients called a horse *ferum* (“wild”). “With a bit” refers to the mule. Thus these two animals mentioned above are restrained by these reins, so that they proceed at the command of the one giving orders and do not run wild according to their own desires.

The jawbones are bodily aids of animals, by which food is chewed so that bodily life may be sustained. He therefore says figuratively and allegorically that the jaws of the disobedient must be restrained—that is, that provisions should be supplied more sparingly—so that, confined by the necessity of fasting, they may be subjected to the command of the Creator.

Human ingenuity compelled different animals to mate, and thus discovered another kind through adulterous mixture, just as Jacob also produced likenesses of colors contrary to nature [Col. 0217A] (Gen. 30). For his sheep conceived offspring of the sort whose shadows they saw reflected in the water beneath the rams mounting above them.

Finally, it is also reported that the same practice is followed with herds of mares: noble stallions are placed before the eyes of mares during mating, so that, seized by the sight, they may conceive and produce offspring resembling them. For this reason, some people instruct pregnant women not to look upon the ugly faces of any animals, such as dog-headed creatures and apes, lest, encountering them visually, they give birth to similar offspring [Col. 0218A].

They say that this is the nature of women: whatever they have seen or conceived in their minds at the final heat of pleasure, when conception takes place, such offspring they also produce. Indeed, during sexual intercourse an animal conveys external forms inward; and, once filled with their impressions, it seizes those appearances and transforms them into its own nature.

Among living creatures, those born from different kinds are called *bigenera* (“two-kind creatures”): the mule from a mare and a donkey; the *bardo* from a horse and a she-ass; the *hybrida* from boars and sows; the *tityrus* from a sheep and a he-goat; and the *muscus* from a she-goat and a ram. The *muscus*, moreover, is the leader of the flock.

# BOOK EIGHT

## Chapter One: On Beasts

### [Col. 0217]

The designation “beasts” properly applies to lions, leopards, tigers, wolves, foxes, dogs, monkeys, and the rest that rage either with their mouths or with their claws, except for serpents. They are called *beasts* (*bestiae*) because of the force with which they rage; they are called *wild animals* (*ferae*) because they exercise their natural freedom and are carried wherever their desire leads them. Their wills are free: they wander here and there, and wherever their spirit directs them, there they go.

The name *lion* (*leo*) has been adapted from Greek into Latin. In Greek it is called *leon*, and it is a hybrid name because it is partly corrupted; *leaena* (“lioness”), however, is wholly Greek, as is *dracaena*. That *leaena* is called *lea* is an usage introduced by poets.

In Greek, *leo* is interpreted in Latin as “king,” because the lion is chief of all beasts. Its kind is said to be threefold. Of these, the short ones with curly manes are unwarlike; the long ones with smooth hair are fierce. Their courage is indicated by their forehead and tail; their strength is in their chest; their firmness in their head. When surrounded by hunters, they gaze at the ground so that, when they see the hunting spears, they will not be frightened. They fear the noise of wheels, but fire even more. When they sleep, their eyes remain watchful. When they walk, they cover their tracks with their tail so that the hunter may not find them.

When they have produced a cub, the cub is said to sleep for three days and three nights. Then, as though shaken by the father’s growl or roar, the place of its lair is said to awaken the sleeping cub.

Toward human beings the nature of lions is gentle, so that they cannot become angry unless they have been injured. Their mercy is evident in continual examples: they spare the fallen, allow captives whom they encounter to return to their homeland, and kill a human being only when driven by great hunger.

The lion, which is king of beasts, represents Christ through its strength, for Christ is King of kings and Lord of lords. Concerning him it is written in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, to open the book and to break its seven seals” (Rev. 5). Hence the patriarch Jacob said in blessing Judah his son: “Judah is a lion’s cub. You have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. 49). For Christ, in being born, became little, and, ascending the cross, redeemed captive peoples from the power of the devil.

### [Col. 0218B]

He is rightly compared with a sleeping cub for three days and three nights, because, lying in the tomb for three days, he fulfilled the sleep of death and by death itself conquered the dominion of death. Concerning him it is written in Genesis: “Like a lion’s cub, who will rouse him?” (Gen. 49).

Lions signify the leaders of the Church. Hence, in the Lord’s temple, lions together with oxen are commanded to be made of bronze on the bases of the temple.

Again, figuratively, the lion signifies the fearless company of holy teachers, whose roar—that is, the voice of their preaching—terrifies their adversaries. Hence it is written: “The lion is strongest among beasts; he fears no encounter” (Prov. 30). And in Amos: “The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3).

Again, the lion is used in an opposing sense when its savagery is being shown, as in the words of the Apostle Peter: “Be watchful and pray, because your adversary the Devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5). Again, it is written in Job: “The roar of the lion, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken” (Job 4).

The name “lioness” sometimes designates the holy Church, and sometimes Babylon. Because the Church is bold against her adversaries, she is called a lioness, as is confirmed by the words of blessed Job. Indicating Judea, abandoned by the Church, he says: “The sons of the merchants have not trodden it, nor will the lioness pass through it” (Job 28).

The Church is called a lioness in Job: “Will you catch the lioness’s prey, or fill the lives of her cubs?” (Job 39). The lioness’s cubs are the Apostles, as in the same passage.

Sometimes the name “lioness” expresses the city of this world, that is, Babylon. It is unrestrained in the savage cruelty with which it rages against the lives of the innocent. Joined to the ancient enemy as to a most savage lion, it conceives the seeds of his perverse persuasion and gives birth from itself to reprobate sons resembling him, as cruel cubs.

The cubs of lions are all the reprobate who have been generated for an iniquitous life through the error of wicked spirits. Together they constitute the whole city of the world that we have called Babylon; yet individually they are called sons of Babylon, as it were cubs not fully of a lioness. Just as all the Church is called Zion, while each of the saints is called a son of Zion, so each of the reprobate is called a son of Babylon, while all the reprobate together are called Babylon.

The lion signifies the Devil because of his strength and cruelty, as in the Psalm: “Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion” (Ps. 7); and elsewhere: “He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, like a lion in his den” (Ps. 10).

Lions are the powers of this age, as in Jeremiah: “My people were a scattered flock; lions drove them away” (Jer. 50).

The cubs of lions are demons or wicked people, as in the Psalm: “In the midst of lion cubs I lay down, troubled” (Ps. 56). And elsewhere: “The young lions roar, that they may seize and seek their food from God” (Ps. 104).

The lair of lions is the present world, or any kingdom of this world, as in Nahum: “Where is the lair of the lions and the pasture of the lion cubs?” (Nah. 2).

Again, the lair of lions is the hearts of the reprobate, as in the Psalm: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together and will lie down in their dens” (Ps. 104).

### [Col. 0219B]

The tiger is so called because of its swift flight. For this is how the Persians and Medes name an arrow. It is a beast marked with various spots, remarkable for its strength and speed. The river Tigris takes its name from it because it is the swiftest of all rivers. Hyrcania produces more of these animals.

Mystically, the tiger signifies the Devil’s cunning. Hence it is written in Job: “The tiger perished because it had no prey, and the lion cubs were scattered” (Job 4). Here he repeats under the name “tiger” the one whom he had marked by the name “lion.” Satan is called a lion because of his cruelty, and appropriately a tiger because of the variety of his many-sided cunning.

At one moment he presents himself to human senses as he is, ruined; at another he appears as an angel of light; at another he persuades the minds of fools by flattering them; at another he drives them toward guilt by terrifying them; at another he openly attempts to persuade them to vices; at another he cloaks himself in his suggestions under the appearance of virtue. Thus this beast, which is dappled with such great variety, is rightly called a tiger.

Among the Seventy translators it is called *myrmicoleon* (“ant-lion”), because this animal, concealed in dust, kills ants carrying grain, as we have said. In the same way, the apostate angel, cast down from heaven to earth, lies in wait along the path of their activity for the minds of the righteous, who are preparing for themselves the perfection of good works. When he overcomes them by ambush, he kills them unexpectedly, like ants carrying grain.

The panther is so called either because it is friendly to all animals except the dragon, or because it rejoices in the fellowship of its own kind and returns whatever it receives in the same likeness. *Pan* means “all” in Greek. It is a beast covered with small circles, so that black or white is distinguished by tawny circles resembling eyes.

It gives birth only once. The reason is evident. When the cubs have grown together in the mother’s womb and have acquired the strength needed for birth, they cannot tolerate delay. Therefore they tear with their claws the womb burdened with offspring, as though it were obstructing the birth. The mother pours out—or rather, is forced by pain to release—the offspring. Thereafter, because the birth passages have been damaged and scarred, deposited seed is not received but springs back fruitlessly. For Pliny says that animals with sharp claws often cannot give birth safely; the cubs injure them internally as they move about.

### [Col. 0220A]

The leopard is second after the panther. It is a variegated and extremely swift species, rushing headlong toward blood; for it leaps violently to death.

Mystically, the leopard signifies the Devil, filled with various vices, or any sinner sprinkled with the spots of crimes and different errors. Hence the prophet says: “The Ethiopian has not changed his skin, nor the leopard his spots” (Jer. 13).

Again, the leopard signifies the Antichrist, sprinkled with the variety of his malice, as in the Apocalypse: “The beast that rose from the sea was like a leopard” (Rev. 13). He speaks of those who persist in the blackness of sins and in the variety of their errors.

Elsewhere, however, it is written: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa. 11). This was fulfilled at Christ’s coming, when those who had formerly been fierce led their lives with the innocent, and those who had been polluted by the spots of errors, doing penance, turned to the truth of the faith.

The leopard is born from the adultery of a lioness and a panther and produces a third origin. Pliny likewise says in his *Natural History* that a lion mates with a panther, or a panther with a lioness, and that from their intercourse degenerate offspring are produced, as a mule is produced from a horse and a she-ass.

The rhinoceros—called in Greek *rhinokerōs*—is interpreted in Latin as “horn in the nose.” It is also called *monoceros*, that is, “unicorn,” because it has one horn in the middle of its forehead, four feet in length, so sharp and powerful that whatever it attacks it either tosses into the air or pierces. It is always at war with the elephant and throws it down after wounding it in the belly.

It is said to be so strong that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. But, according to those who have labored with painstaking investigation to describe the natures of animals, a virgin girl is placed before it. When it approaches, she opens her lap, and the animal, setting aside all its fierceness, lays down its head there. Thus, lulled to sleep, it is suddenly found defenseless by those seeking to capture it. It is also described as being the color of boxwood.
