When it engages elephants in combat, it is said to strike the belly of its opponent with the horn it uniquely bears on its nose. By wounding the softer parts, it easily lays low those who attack it.

This rhinoceros, or monoceros—that is, unicorn—can therefore signify the people who, having taken from the Law not works but only pride among all human beings, carried a single horn, as it were, among the other beasts. Hence, while announcing his Passion, the Lord says through the singing prophet: “Save me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 22).

There were as many unicorns, or certainly rhinoceroses, among that people as there were those who, with singular and foolish pride, trusted in the works of the Law against the declarations of the truth.

To blessed Job, who bears the type of the holy Church, it is said: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job 39). It is as though it were said more openly: Will you bend under the authority of your preaching that people whom you see proudly raging in their foolish exaltation at the death of the faithful? You are to understand: as I, who see it raised against me on its single horn, nevertheless immediately subject it to myself whenever I will.

### [Col. 0221A]

We can compare the rhinoceros to the Apostle Paul. He was formerly a persecutor and blasphemer, as it is written concerning him: “Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, to the synagogues, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9).

Endowed with knowledge of the divine Law, when he rebukes the gluttony of others, he strikes the elephant in the belly with his horn. He had struck elephants in the belly when he said: “Many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3). And again: “Such people,” he says, “do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly” (ibid.).

Thus, with his horn, this rhinoceros now strikes not human beings but beasts: when Paul, by the strength of his teaching, does not attack the humble, who should by no means be destroyed, but kills the proud worshipers of the belly.

Let us hope that what we have learned was written concerning Paul has also been accomplished in others. For many were converted from the pride of that people to the grace of humility. While the Lord subdued their savagery under the yoke of inspired fear, he clearly subjected to himself the strength of the rhinoceros.

The rhinoceros may be understood as Christ the Lord because of his unconquerable strength, as in Deuteronomy: “His strength is like that of the rhinoceros” (Deut. 33).

As we said above, the rhinoceros also signifies the strong or the powers of this age, as in Job: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job 39).

The monoceros, that is, the unicorn, is Christ, as in the Psalm: “And beloved as the son of unicorns” (Ps. 29), that is, singular in power, and the one kingdom of the saints.

The unicorns are the proud, or those who possess one testament, as in the Psalm: “And from the horns of unicorns my humility” (Ps. 22).

The Greeks are thought to have named the elephant from the magnitude of its body, because it displays the form of a mountain. For in Greek *lophos* means “mountain.” Among the Indians it is called *barrus*, from its cry. Hence its voice is called *barritus*, and its teeth are called ivory.

Its trunk is called *promuscis*, because with it the animal brings food to its mouth. It is like a snake and fortified with an ivory rampart.

The ancient Romans called these animals “Lucanian oxen”: “oxen” because they saw no animal larger, and “Lucanian” because Pyrrhus first opposed them to the Romans in battle in Lucania. This species of animal is suited to warfare. The Persians and Indians fight from them, placing wooden towers upon them as though upon a wall and hurling javelins.

They are strong in intelligence and memory. They move in herds. They greet by the movement of which they are capable. They flee from a mouse. They mate turned away from one another.

When they give birth, they release their young in water or on islands because of dragons, since elephants are their enemies and are killed when entangled by them. They carry their young for two years and give birth no more than once, producing not several but only one offspring. They live for three hundred years.

Elephants were formerly born only in Africa and India; now only India produces them.

The elephant signifies a sinner monstrous in crimes and filthy with the deformity of his offenses. Nevertheless, such people are often converted to Christ. Hence it is written in the Book of Kings that monkeys and elephants were brought to Solomon (1 Kings 10), because he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2), and by his blood cleansed our conscience from dead works.

The griffin is so called because it is a winged quadruped. This species is born in the Hyperborean mountains. In every part of its body it is lion-like, but resembles an eagle in its wings and face, and is extremely hostile to horses. It also tears living human beings apart.

These creatures can signify the ferocity of persecutors and the pride of the arrogant, who are hostile to people who follow Christian simplicity and live rationally.

### [Col. 0222B]

The chameleon does not have one color but is sprinkled with a variety of colors, like the leopard. It is called this because the little body of the chameleon changes with the greatest ease according to the colors it sees; the bodies of other animals do not change so readily.

The giraffe is so called because, although it is like a leopard and sprinkled with white spots, its neck resembles that of a horse, its feet those of an ox, and its head that of a camel. Ethiopia produces it.

It is not without reason that the color and form of these beasts are transferred to signify various errors and vices wherever mention of them is found in Scripture.

The lynx is so called because it is counted among the kind of wolves. It is a beast with a back marked by spots like a leopard, but it resembles a wolf. They say that its urine is changed into a precious stone called *ligurius*. It is proved that the lynxes themselves are aware of this, for they cover their discharged liquid with sand as far as they can, through a kind of natural envy, lest such excretion pass into human use.

Pliny says that lynxes admit no offspring beyond one. This beast likewise represents envious and deceitful people, who prefer to harm rather than benefit others. Intent on earthly desires, they uselessly preserve for themselves things that are superfluous to them but could benefit others.

Beavers are so called from *castrare* (“to castrate”), because their testicles are useful in medicines. When they sense a hunter pursuing them because of these organs, they castrate themselves and bite off their own organs, thereby depriving themselves of their strength.

Concerning them Cicero says in the *Scaurian Speech*: “They ransom themselves with that part of the body for which they are especially sought.” Juvenal says: “He makes himself a eunuch, wishing to escape the loss of his testicles.”

These are also called *fibres*, and are likewise called Pontic dogs.

The prudence of some animals is therefore astonishing; but much more astonishing is the stupidity of certain human beings, who judge that the creature God created within them is an instrument of vice.

For this reason heretics arose who cut off their own genitals, so that they might more easily preserve abstinence from marriage, misinterpreting the Lord’s statement: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). This should rather be understood as referring to the cutting off of pleasures and lust than to the mutilation of bodily members. Accordingly, canonical authority has commanded that such people be excommunicated and brought to penance.

The bear is said to have been named because it forms its offspring with its mouth, as though it had “begun” them (*orsus*). For they say that bears produce shapeless offspring and that a kind of flesh is born, which the mother forms into limbs by licking it. Hence the verse: “Thus the bear shapes the cub with her tongue when she brings it forth.”

But this is caused by the premature birth. It gives birth on the thirtieth day. Thus it happens that premature fertility produces shapeless offspring.

The bear’s head is weak, but its greatest strength is in its arms and loins. Hence bears sometimes stand upright.

Allegorically, the bear sometimes signifies the Devil lying in wait for the flock of God; at other times, savage and cruel rulers. Hence it is written in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 2) that two bears came out of the forest and devoured the boys who mocked the prophet Elisha. This signifies the two Roman princes, namely Vespasian and Titus, who came forth from the forest of the nations and devoured the Jewish boys who mocked our Savior crucified at the place of Calvary.

Again, in the same book: “A lion and a bear came and carried off a ram from the flock” (1 Kings 17).

The wolf is transferred into our language from a Greek derivation. The Greeks call wolves *lycoi*. In Greek, *lykos* is said to derive from bites: driven by the madness of rapacity, it slaughters whatever it finds.

Others say that wolves are called *leopoi*, as though “lion-footed,” because they have the strength of a lion in their feet. Thus whatever they press with their foot does not remain alive.

It is a rapacious beast, desirous of blood. Country people say that a person loses his voice if the wolf sees him first. Hence, when someone suddenly falls silent, it is said: “There is a wolf in the story.” If the wolf realizes that it has been seen beforehand, it lays aside its bold ferocity.

Wolves mate for no more than twelve days throughout the year. They endure hunger for a long time, and after long fasts devour much. Ethiopia produces wolves with maned necks, and so variegated that they say no color is absent from them.

The wolf is therefore rarely found to have a good signification, but more often an adverse one. It signifies either the Devil, as in the Gospel: “The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep” (John 10); or heretics and deceitful people, concerning whom the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7). And again: “He sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees” (John 10).

It is nevertheless read that the patriarch Jacob said this in the blessing of his son Benjamin: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. 49).

By these words the Apostle Paul is designated, descended from the tribe of Benjamin. In the morning he seized the prey—that is, at the beginning he devastated the faithful whom he could; but in the evening he divided the spoils, because, having later become faithful, he distributed the sacred words with wondrous stewardship to those who listened.

The name “dog” appears to have a Greek etymology in Latin. In Greek it is called *kynos* (*kyōn*), although some think it was named from the sound of its barking because it makes a noise; hence also *canere*, “to sing” or “sound.”

Nothing is more intelligent than dogs. They possess more sense than other animals. They alone recognize their names, love their masters, defend their masters’ homes, expose themselves to death on behalf of their masters, run willingly with their master to the hunt, and do not abandon their master’s body even after death.

Finally, their nature is such that they cannot exist apart from human beings. In dogs two things are to be looked for: either strength or speed.

The dog has various meanings. It signifies either the Devil, or the Jew, or the gentile people. Hence the prophet prays to the Lord in the Psalm: “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog” (Ps. 22).

The dog is also used in a favorable sense, as in Ecclesiastes, where it is written: “A living dog is better than a dead lion” (Eccl. 9). Here, I think, the lion is to be understood as the Devil, and the dog as a gentile or a sinful person. The latter is called better because he can come to faith and repentance.

Hence it is written concerning the Jews: “They shall return at evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go around the city” (Ps. 59).

Dogs signify mute or wicked priests, as in Isaiah: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56).

Dogs signify the Jews, as in the Psalm: “For many dogs have surrounded me” (Ps. 22).

Dogs signify the gentile people, as in the Gospel: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15).

Dogs signify heretics, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not bring the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God” (Deut. 23). And in the Apostle: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers; beware of the mutilation” (Phil. 3).

The dog is a very voracious and troublesome animal. It customarily guards with its barking those houses in which it knows that its appetite can be satisfied with bread.

The Jews are rightly compared with such dogs. Having been fattened by the gift of the Christian faith, they will hasten to defend the Church of God with clamorous preaching, as happened in the case of the Apostle Paul: the one who had formerly been a persecutor of the Christian name was afterward joined to the Apostles by divine grace.

Dogs also signify quarrelsome or slanderous people, tearing one another apart, as in the Apostle: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5).

The offspring of any beasts are improperly called “cubs”; properly, the young of dogs are called *catuli*, a diminutive form.

*Lycisci* are dogs born, as Pliny says, from wolves and dogs when they happen to mate with one another. Indian bitches, tied in forests at night, are also customarily exposed to tigers, by which they are mounted; from the same litter dogs are born so fierce and strong that they throw lions down in combat.

The cubs therefore signify the gentiles. Hence in the Gospel the Syrophoenician woman, to whom the Lord said, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15), answered him: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

The table is sacred Scripture, which supplies us with the bread of life. The children’s crumbs are the inner mysteries of Scripture, by which the hearts of humble children are accustomed to be nourished.

The little dogs therefore do not eat crusts but crumbs from the children’s bread, because those who have been converted to the faith—formerly despised among the gentiles—seek in the Scriptures not the surface of the letter but the spiritual meaning, by which they may advance in good works.

The fox is called *vulpes*, as though *volupes*. It has twisting feet and never runs along straight paths but through winding turns. It is a deceitful animal that deceives by ambush. When it has no food, it pretends to be dead; thus it seizes and devours birds that descend as though to a corpse.

Mystically, the fox signifies the deceitful Devil, the cunning heretic, or a sinful human being. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel concerning Herod: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13).

And elsewhere he says: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests” (Matt. 8), expressing heretics by the foxes and wicked spirits by the birds of heaven. These seek hiding places in human hearts where they may insert their perverse suggestions and fulfill their most evil desires.

Again, the fox signifies the Devil or demons, as in the Psalm: “They shall be handed over to the power of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes” (Ps. 63). And in Jeremiah: “Because of Mount Zion, which has been laid waste” (Lam. 5), “foxes have walked upon it.”

The foxes signify heretics in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song 2), that is, the communities of the faithful.

And in the Book of Judges it is said of Samson: “He caught three hundred foxes and tied torches to their tails” (Judg. 15).

The monkey’s name is Greek, meaning “with compressed nostrils.” Hence we call them *simiae*, because they have flattened noses and ugly faces, with wrinkles disgracefully folded; goats too are said to have a compressed nose.

Others think that monkeys were called *simiae* in Latin because a great likeness of human reason is perceived in them, but this is false.

They are skilled in recognizing the elements. They rejoice at the new moon and grow sad at the half and waning moon. They carry their young, whom they love, before them; those who are neglected cling to their mother.

There are five kinds of them. Among these, the *cercopitheci* have tails. A monkey with a tail is called by some a “thigh.”

The *sphinges* are covered with hairy manes and have prominent breasts; they are docile, having lost their wildness.

The *cynocephali* are likewise similar to monkeys but have a face shaped like that of a dog, from which they take their name.

The *satyrs* have a very pleasing face and are restless in their gesticulating movements.

The *callitrices* differ completely in appearance from the others. They have a long beard on the face and a broad tail.

Monkeys signify people crafty in mind and foul with sins. Sometimes, through conversion and repentance, they are led to our Peace and serve him, as was said above concerning the elephants and monkeys that were brought to Solomon.

The *enhydros* is a little animal so called because it lives in water, especially in the Nile. If it finds a crocodile sleeping, it first rolls in mud, then enters through its mouth into its belly and, tearing out all its internal organs, thus dies.

The ichneumon is called in Greek because by its smell both wholesome foods and poisonous ones are revealed. Concerning it Dracontius says: “The swine-like creature foretells the power of every poison.” It is called *suillus* (“swine-like”) from its bristles.

It also pursues serpents. When it fights an asp, it raises its tail, which the asp begins especially to watch as though it were threatening. When the asp transfers its force toward it, it is deceived and seized.

The *melo* is so called either because of its perfectly round body or because it seeks honeycombs and constantly captures honey.

The *musio* is so called because it is hostile to mice. The common people call it *caus* from *captura*, “capture.” Others say it is called this because it *catat*, that is, “sees.” For it sees so sharply that, by the brilliance of its vision, it surpasses the darkness of night. Hence from the Greek comes *catus*, meaning “clever” or “ingenious.”

Christ is the hunter, as in Isaiah according to the Seventy: “Behold, he will come as a lion or a lion’s cub over the prey that he has taken” (Isa. 31).

Hunters are the Apostles or other preachers, as in Jeremiah: “I will send them hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain” (Jer. 16).

The hunter is the Devil, represented by that giant hunter Nimrod, “before the Lord,” as in Genesis (Gen. 10).

Hunters are wicked people, as in the prophet: “My enemies hunted me down like a bird, without cause” (Lam. 3).

The *lamia* signifies the Devil or demons, as in Jeremiah: “Even the lamia uncovered her breast and suckled her young” (Lam. 4).

Again, the lamia signifies a heretic or any hypocrite, as Isaiah says: “The lamia lay down and found rest for itself” (Isa. 34).

## Chapter Two: On Small Animals
The mouse (*mus*) is a small animal; its name is Greek, but everything derived from it is Latin. Some say that mice (*mures*) are so called because they are born from the moisture of the earth. For *mus* means “earth,” whence also *humus*. At the full moon their liver grows, just as certain marine creatures increase, and then diminish again as the moon wanes.

The shrew (*sorex*) is a Latin word, so called because it gnaws and cuts through things like a saw. [Col. 0226C] The ancients, however, called it *saurix*, just as they called the lame man *clodus* for *claudus*. The weasel (*mustela*) is so called as though it were a “long mouse,” for *telum* (“weapon” or “shaft”) derives from length. By its cunning it is deceitful in houses where it raises its young: it moves and changes its dwelling, and also pursues snakes and mice. There are two kinds of weasels. One is wild and differs in size; the Greeks call these *ictides*. The other wanders about in houses. Those who say that the weasel conceives through its mouth and gives birth through its ear are mistaken. The weasel represents theft, as is shown in Leviticus.

The mole (*talpa*) is so called because it is condemned to perpetual blindness in darkness. It has no eyes; it is always digging the earth, casting up soil, and eating the roots beneath crops.

Mystically, mice signify people who gape after earthly possessions out of greed and steal booty from another’s property [Col. 0226D]. The weasel figuratively represents those who pollute their natural intelligence with the deceit of wickedness and spend their whole life in ambushes and frauds. The mole, therefore, which is condemned to perpetual blindness, signifies either idols—blind, deaf, and mute—or the idolaters themselves, who always wander in the darkness of ignorance and folly. Of them it is written in Isaiah: “That you may worship moles and bats” (Isa. II), that is, that the blind may worship the blind. Of them Scripture says elsewhere: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII).

Alternatively, it figuratively represents heretics or false Christians. For just as the mole, without eyes, is always digging the earth, casting up soil, and eating the roots beneath crops [Col. 0227A], so they, deprived of the light of true knowledge, devote themselves to earthly acts, to the desires of the flesh, and to the allurements of pleasures; and wherever they can, they try with the tooth of wickedness to gnaw away and overthrow the roots of good works.

Dormice (*glires*) are so called because sleep makes them fat. For we say *gliscere*, “to grow.” They sleep throughout the winter and lie motionless, as though dead; in summer they revive. They can therefore signify those who, through the torpor of laziness, become useless and refuse to work profitably. Of them it is written: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him” (Prov. XX). For whoever now grows sluggish in idleness during the time of the present life will beg in vain on the day of judgment, when it is harvest-time, because he will in no way possess the joy of heavenly life with the righteous [Col. 0227B].

The hedgehog (*hericius*) is an animal covered with spines. It is said to have received its name because it raises itself when it encloses itself with its spines, by which it is protected on every side against attacks. As soon as it senses something, it first raises itself, then curls into a ball and draws itself back within its armor. It possesses a certain prudence. For when it has detached a grape from the vine, it rolls over it on its back and thus carries it to its young.

Mystically, the hedgehog signifies sinners filled with the prickles of vices and skilled in the cunning of wickedness, as well as in frauds and robberies—people who by deceit seek food for themselves from the labors of others. Of them it is written: “There the hedgehog has its lair and nourishes its young” (Isa. XXXIV). Likewise, there is the statement written in the Psalm: “A rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. CIII) [Col. 0227C].

The *herinacius* is the same as the *hericius*: an altogether timid animal, always naturally armed by providence, whose skin is reinforced everywhere by the sharpest and densest bristles. Yet its natural protection is not sufficient for it, lest it be caught by some stratagem; it always has refuge among the rocks. This is appropriately applied to the person who, bristling with sins and fearing future judgments, is known to have Christ, the firmest rock, as his refuge.

The cricket (*grillus*) takes its name from the sound of its voice. It walks backward, bores into the earth, and chirps at night. The ant hunts it: an ant tied to a hair is thrown into its burrow, after dust has first been blown in so that it cannot hide; thus it is dragged out by the ant’s embrace.

The ant (*formica*) is so called because it carries crumbs of grain; it possesses great diligence. It provides for the future and prepares in summer what it will eat in winter [Col. 0227D]. At harvest it chooses wheat and does not touch barley; when rain falls upon its grain, it throws it all out.

They say that in Ethiopia there are ants the size of dogs, which dig up gold-bearing sand with their feet. They guard it so that no one may carry it away, and pursue those who try to take it until they kill them.

According to allegory, the ant signifies a provident person or a useful worker. Hence Solomon exhorts us in Proverbs, saying: “Go to the ant, O lazy one; consider its ways, and learn wisdom from it. Although it has no guide, overseer, or ruler, it prepares its food in summer and gathers at harvest what it may eat” (Prov. VI). By this he urges everyone to care for himself. If so tiny an animal, with no teacher but nature alone as its guide, strives to provide for the future, how much more ought a human being, with God as teacher and teachers giving admonition, to gather the fruits of works in the harvest of this life and store them in the granary of life, so that he may have something to live on in the day of cold—that is, of judgment—when he can no longer work? [Col. 0228A]

The ant-lion (*formicoleon*) is so called because it is either the lion of ants or, in fact, both ant and lion. It is a small animal greatly hostile to ants. It hides itself in the dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is called both lion and ant because it is an ant to other animals, but a lion to ants.

Frogs (*ranae*) are named from their croaking, because they make a din around their native marshes and return the sound of their voices with incessant cries. Frogs signify demons. In the Apocalypse: “I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming from the mouth of the dragon” (Apoc. XVI); these are spirits of demons [Col. 0228B]. Frogs also signify heretics, who dwell in the mire of the basest opinions and never cease barking with empty chatter, as is read in Exodus.

## CHAPTER II. On Serpents

The name *anguis* denotes a kind of serpent that can bend and twist; hence it is called *anguis*, because it is angular and never straight. Among the pagans, serpents were always regarded as spirits of places. Hence Persius: “Paint two serpents for the boys; the place is sacred.”

The *coluber* is so called either because it inhabits shadows or because it glides along slippery tracks in sinuous coils. For anything that slips while it is being held is called *lubricum*, such as a fish or a serpent [Col. 0228C].

The horned serpent (*cerastes*) is so called because it has horns on its head resembling those of rams. The Greeks call horns *cerata*. It has four little horns, by the display of which it lures animals as though with bait and kills them. It covers its entire body with sand and gives no indication of itself except on the side from which it catches the birds or animals it has enticed. It is more winding than other serpents, so that it seems not to possess a spine.

By the names *coluber* and *cerastes*, the devil or Antichrist is signified, as in the prophecy spoken by the patriarch Jacob concerning his son Dan: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road and a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. XLIX). For Antichrist is called not only a serpent but also a horned serpent [Col. 0228D]. *Cerata* in Greek means “horns,” and this serpent is said to be horned, as we have mentioned above. Through it the coming of Antichrist is appropriately indicated, because he will arm himself against the life of the faithful with the poisonous bite of his preaching and also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus he becomes a serpent on the road, because he invites those whom he spares, as though flattering them, to walk in the broad expanse of the present life; but he bites on the road, because he destroys with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom. Again, he becomes a horned serpent on the path, because when he finds people who are faithful and who constrain themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he not only obstructs them with the wickedness of cunning persuasion but also oppresses them with the terror of power [Col. 0229A], and amid the anguish of persecution he exercises the horns of power after the benefits of feigned sweetness.

In this passage the horse signifies the world, which in its pride foams along the course of passing time. Since Antichrist strives to seize the world’s final things, that horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. To bite the horse’s hoof is to reach the ends of the age by striking them: “so that its rider falls backward.” The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted in the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, not on his face, as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall on one’s face is, in this life, for each person to recognize his sins and mourn them in repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, is to depart suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led [Col. 0229B].

And because Judaea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob is fittingly changed at this same point into the voice of the elect, saying: “I shall await your salvation, Lord” (Gen. XLIX)—that is, I believe faithfully in the true Christ, who is to come for our redemption, not in Antichrist as the unbelievers do.

The serpent received its name because it creeps along by hidden approaches. It does not advance with open steps but crawls by the minute efforts of its scales. Those that move on four feet, such as lizards and geckos, are called not serpents but reptiles. Serpents are reptiles because they crawl on their chest and belly. They have as many poisons as kinds, as many dangers as species, and as many pains as colors.

The serpent signifies the devil, as in Genesis: “The serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. III). It may also signify wicked people and heretics, of whom the Psalmist says: “They have sharpened their tongues like serpents; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. XIII). Here the wickedness and deceit of heretics are beautifully described. Their tongues signify words which, polished on the whetstones of wickedness, strive to wound the hearts of the simple. They are rightly compared to serpents, because they spew forth venom in their speeches. Hence they are compared to deaf asps. They contend with such a purpose that, through the obstinacy of their minds, they never wish to be overcome by the truth.

The significance of the serpent is also taken in another direction, as in the Gospel: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III). There the serpent signifies Christ’s death, which saved the human race—the race that the ancient serpent, through its wicked persuasion, deprived of the salvation received from the Creator [Col. 0229D].

The dragon (*draco*) is the largest of all serpents, or of all the animals upon the earth. The Greeks call it *draconta*, from which the Latin word *draco* is derived. It is often said to be drawn from caves into the air, and the air is stirred because of it. It is crested, with a small mouth and narrow passages through which it draws breath, and it sticks out its tongue. Its power lies not in its teeth but in its tail; it harms more by striking than by biting. It is harmless with respect to venom, but venom is unnecessary for it to cause death, because if it coils around someone, it kills him. Even the elephant is not safe from it despite the size of its body. Lurking beside the paths along which elephants customarily walk, it ties their legs together in knots and kills them by suffocation [Col. 0230A].

It is born in Ethiopia and India, amid the very blaze of unbroken heat.

Mystically, the dragon signifies either the devil, his ministers, or the persecutors of the Church—wicked men. Its mystery is found in many passages of Scripture, in the Psalter, in the Book of Job, and also in the Apocalypse of John.

The Psalmist says of it: “You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of dragons upon the waters” (Ps. LXXIII). He established the liquid abysses of the Red Sea when the water was divided into two sides so that the navigable sea might become a land route [Col. 0230B]. “You crushed the heads of dragons upon the waters” fittingly explains the mystery of the earlier miracle, because that prefiguration of the passage through the Red Sea signified the waters of holy baptism. There the heads of dragons—that is, unclean spirits—are brought to nothing when the saving fountain cleanses the souls which they pollute with the filth of sins.

But when it is added, “You crushed the head of the great dragon, and so forth” (ibid.), although above he had spoken in the plural—“the heads of dragons”—thereby intending spiritual wickednesses, he now uses the singular and places “dragon,” as though to indicate Satan himself. The stronger he is, the more wicked he is. When he is mentioned in the singular, it is utterly denied that he dwells among the evil spirits [Col. 0230C]. His head was crushed when his pride was cast out of heaven and he did not deserve to retain his native brightness, having stained himself by voluntary darkness.

He added: “You gave him as food to the people of Ethiopia.” We rightly understand the Ethiopians to be sinners, who were formerly most foul through their dark minds, but, converted to God, took him as food when they are satisfied by speaking against him. Even today, when we wish to indicate someone utterly wicked, we call him “the devil.” For he is a scoffer at every sin that is committed, the author of every error; and just as he persecutes Christians, so he is torn apart by all through execrable denunciation. Thus it happens that he who was formerly revered by pagans is now gnawed by Christians with the bites of reproaches [Col. 0230D].

Alternatively, the faithful who have already been converted can have the devil as food when they advance through his machinations and temptations. When he persecutes them, they become martyrs; when he afflicts them, they are crowned with the reward of patience. Therefore the devil is rightly called the food of those whom he leads through repeated hardships toward harmful desires.

The asp (*aspis*) is so called because it injects and spreads poison through its bite. The Greeks call poison *ios*; hence *aspis*, because it kills with a poisonous bite. It has various kinds and species, with differing effects for causing harm.

It is said that when the asp begins to suffer under an enchanter who summons it with certain spells in order to draw it from its cave, if it does not wish to come out, it presses one ear against the ground and stops and covers the other with its tail [Col. 0231A]. Thus, not hearing those magical voices, it does not come out to the enchanter.

Of this the Psalmist says: “Their anger is like the anger of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers or the spells which the skilled enchanter utters” (Ps. LVII). By this serpent the anger of the Jews is defined with extremely apt comparison. The anger of obstinate people is irretractable: so that they may not hear the preaching of teachers, they deliberately procure voluntary deafness for themselves.

The habit of the asp is compared to this evil. To avoid hearing the enchanter’s words and leaving its hiding places, it is said to stop one ear by curling its tail around it and to press the other into the ground. The Jews are rightly compared to it, for with the ears of their hearts stopped, they refused to hear the most salutary commandment of holy Scripture [Col. 0231B].

The term “stopping” (*obturare*) is derived from the practice of priests, who filled their ears with incense so that, when foreign words intervened, the memory of the chants would not be confused and disturbed.

The *dipsas* is a kind of asp, called in Latin *situla* (“water-pot”), because whoever it bites dies of thirst.

The *hypnalis* is a kind of asp that kills by sleep. Cleopatra applied it to herself and thus was released from life by death as though by sleep.

The *haemorrhois* is an asp so called because it sweats blood in the person who is bitten by it, so that, when the veins are dissolved, it vomits out whatever life remains through the blood. In Greek, blood is called *haima*.

The *praester* is an asp that always runs with its mouth open and steaming. The poet refers to it as follows: “And, stretching wide its mouth, the greedy *praester*, steaming.” Whoever it strikes swells up and dies through enormous bodily distension. Once the body has swollen, putrefaction follows.

The *seps* is a putrefying asp which, when it bites a person, immediately consumes him, so that he melts entirely in the serpent’s mouth [Col. 0231C].

The basilisk (*basiliscus*) is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *regulus*, because it is the king of serpents, so much so that serpents flee when they see it, since it kills them by its odor. If it merely looks at a human being, it kills him. Indeed, no flying bird passes unharmed within sight of it; however far away it may be, the bird is burned by its mouth and swallowed.

Yet it is defeated by weasels, which people introduce into the caves where it hides. When it sees them, it flees; the weasel pursues and kills it. For the parent of all things has established nothing without a remedy [Col. 0231D].

It is half a foot long and marked with white spots. Basilisks, like scorpions, pursue dry places, and after they have come to water they make people hydrophobic and delirious.

The *sibilus* is the same as the *regulus*; it kills by hissing before it bites or burns.

The basilisk signifies the devil, who openly kills the unwary with the poison of his wickedness. But he is overcome when, together with the other harmful creatures, he is confronted by the soldier of Christ who places all his hope in Christ, whose power overcomes and tramples all hostile forces.

The Prophet also speaks of this in the Psalms: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC). Here the divine power is expressed, which will command such raging forces. All these names suitably apply to the devil: he is an asp when he kills secretly; a basilisk when he openly spreads poisons; a lion when he persecutes the innocent; and a dragon when he swallows the negligent with impious voracity [Col. 0232A].

But all these forces have lain prostrate beneath the feet of the Lord at his glorious coming. For only he was able to subdue such ferocity who is shown to exist as coeternal and consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity. If we diligently examine these matters through the preaching of the holy Fathers and are not disturbed by any insane heretical perversity, everything will stand before us in complete truth, just as it has been stated.

The scorpion (*scorpio*) is an earthly creature, although it is more properly assigned to the class of worms. It is an animal armed with a sting, and it received its Greek name from the fact that it pierces with its tail and spreads poison through a wound shaped like a bow. It is characteristic of the scorpion that it does not strike the palm of the hand [Col. 0232B].

The scorpion signifies the devil or his ministers. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy” (Luke X). Elsewhere the Lord says in the Gospel: “For which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent?” (Luke XI).

Three things are especially necessary for us: faith, hope, and charity. Faith enables us to believe rightly; hope enables us always to await God’s promises with good patience; charity enables us diligently to love him with all our heart, all our mind, and all our strength, and to love our neighbors as ourselves.

In faith the fish is signified [Col. 0232C], in hope the egg, and in charity the bread. Conversely, hardness is expressed by the stone, unbelief by the serpent, and despair by the scorpion. In baptism faith is received, by which one lives in the world. Hope is represented by the egg, because the chick is not yet visible in the egg, but is expected from it. Charity, because it conquers everything, is compared to bread.

The viper (*vipera*) is so called because it gives birth by force. When its belly groans in labor, the young, unwilling to await nature’s release, gnaw through its sides and burst forth, bringing about the death of their mother.

Lucan writes: “The viper’s coils mate in a body torn apart.”

It is also said that the male inserts himself into the viper’s mouth and pours out his seed, while she, driven into madness by the pleasure of lust, bites off the male’s head with her mouth. Thus both parents perish: the male while mating, the female while giving birth [Col. 0232D].

The viper signifies wicked people and also heretics, who carry within themselves the poisons of wickedness. Hence John the Baptist said to the Jews who came to him deceitfully: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III). Evil offspring imitate the actions of evil parents and are therefore called a brood of vipers. By envying the good and persecuting them, by repaying certain people with evil, and by seeking injuries against their neighbors, they follow the ways of their former carnal ancestors, like venomous children born from venomous parents.

The *enhydris* is a serpent that lives in water; for the Greeks call water *hydor*.

The *hydros* is an aquatic serpent. Those bitten by it swell up. Some call the illness it causes *boa*, because it is cured by ox dung [Col. 0233A].

The hydra (*ydra*) is a dragon with many heads, such as existed in the marsh of Lerna in the province of Arcadia. In Latin it is called *excedra*, because when one head was cut off, three heads grew in its place; but this is fabulous. For it is established that the hydra was a place that spewed forth waters devastating a neighboring city. When Hercules saw this, he burned the place itself and thus blocked the channels of the waters. The hydra was named from water.

The *celidros* is a serpent also called *cersidros*, as though “earth-serpent.” It lives both in water and on land. The Greeks call earth *cirson* and water *hydros*. Wherever it glides, it makes the earth smoke. Macer describes it thus:

“Whether foaming backs exhale poison,

[Col. 0233B] … or the earth smokes where the foul serpent glides.”

The salamander (*salamandra*) is so called because it is effective against fires. Of all poisonous creatures it possesses the greatest power. Other creatures strike individuals, but this one kills many at once. If it creeps into a tree, it infects all the fruit with poison and kills those who eat it. Even if it falls into a well, the force of its poison kills those who drink from it.

Thus, resisting fires, it alone among animals extinguishes flames. It lives in the midst of fire without pain or destruction; indeed, it not only does not die but extinguishes the fire.

To recapitulate briefly what has been said above: the serpent is the devil or impious people, as in the Gospel: “Serpents, brood of vipers” (Matt. XIII).

The serpent is Christ on account of his wisdom; its figure was borne by that bronze serpent which Moses hung upon a piece of wood, by looking upon which those struck by serpents were healed [Col. 0233C]. And in the Gospel: “Be wise as serpents” (Matt. X).

The serpent is the devil in Genesis: “The serpent was more cunning than all the animals which the Lord God had made” (Gen. III).

The head of the serpent is the first suggestion of sin, as in Genesis: “She will crush your head” (ibid.).

The breast of the serpent is a type of pride, or the wickedness of a swollen heart, as in the statement: “You will walk upon your breast” (ibid.).

The dragon is the devil, as in the Psalter: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Ps. CIII). And elsewhere: “You crushed the head of the great dragon” (Ps. LXXIII).

Dragons are demons, as in the Psalter: “You crushed the heads of dragons” (ibid.).

Dragons are the princes of the nations, as in the Prophet: “The wild beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons and the ostriches” (Isa. XLIII).

Leviathan, that is, the serpent, is the devil. In Isaiah: “The Lord will visit Leviathan, the twisting serpent, with his hard sword, and he will kill the whale that is in the sea” (Isa. XXVII).

The serpent is the devil, as in Job: “By his hand as midwife the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job XXVI)—that is, through the medicine of our Lord Jesus Christ the devil was cast out of human hearts [Col. 0233D].

The *regulus* is the devil or demons, wounding human hearts by the breath of their thoughts, as in Jeremiah: “Behold, I will send you basilisks against which there is no enchantment, and they will bite you” (Jer. VIII). And in Deuteronomy: “In which there was a burning serpent” (Deut. XVIII).

The asp is the hardness of the hearts of sinners who do not lend the ear of their hearts to the holy preaching. In the Psalm: “Like a deaf asp that stops its ears” (Ps. LVII). It is also taken in another sense, as in Job, concerning the wicked: “The head of asps will rise” (Job XX)—that is, the inspirations of the devil or demons [Col. 0234A].

The asp and the basilisk signify sin and death. In the Psalm: “You will walk upon the asp and basilisk, and trample the lion and dragon” (Ps. XC), that is, the devil and Antichrist.

The viper is the devil or his ministers, as in the Gospel: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. III). And in Job: “The tongue of the viper will kill him” (Job XX).

The scorpion is the devil. In the Gospel: “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke X).

There are also other kinds of serpents, such as *admoditae* [possibly *ammodytae*], *elefantiae*, and *camedracontes*. Finally, as great as the number of names, so great is the number of deaths.

All serpents are naturally cold, and they do not strike unless they become warm. When they are cold, they touch no one. Hence their poisons do more harm by day than by night. They are numbed by the chill of night, and rightly so, because they are cold from the nighttime dew. For these cold pests, cold by nature, draw the body’s heat into themselves. Therefore in winter they grow numb in coils, while in summer they are loosened.

This is why, whenever someone is struck by the poison of a serpent, he first becomes numb; then, when the poison has been heated within him and flares up, it immediately kills the person.

Poison (*venenum*) is so called because it travels through the veins. For once the pestilence has been infused, it runs through the veins, increased by the body’s vitality, and takes away the soul. Hence poison cannot do harm unless it has touched a person’s blood. Lucan writes: “The serpent’s destructive plague lies in mixed blood” [Col. 0234C].

All poison is cold. Therefore the soul, because it is fiery, flees cold poison. Among the natural gifts which we see to be common to us and to irrational animals, the serpent surpasses other creatures by a certain lively subtlety of sense. Hence it is also read in Genesis: “The serpent was wiser than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. III).

Pliny says—if one may believe it—that the head of a serpent remains alive even if it escapes with two fingers’ breadth attached to it. Therefore it exposes its entire body to the person striking at its head.

All serpents have dull sight and rarely look directly ahead. This is not without reason, since they do not have eyes in the forehead but at the temples, so that they hear more readily than they see. No animal moves its tongue with such speed as the serpent, so that it appears to have a threefold tongue, although it has only one [Col. 0234D].

The bodies of serpents are naked, so that wherever they go they leave tracks marked by moisture. Their tracks are such that, although they seem to lack feet, they crawl by means of their ribs and the efforts of their scales, which are arranged evenly from the top of the throat to the bottom of the belly. They lean upon their scales as though upon claws and upon their ribs as though upon legs.

Therefore, if any part of the body from the belly to the head is struck by a blow, the serpent is weakened and can no longer move forward. Wherever the blow falls, it loosens the spine by which the “feet” of the ribs and the movement of the body were driven.

Serpents are said to live for a long time, so that when they cast off their old skin they are thought to cast off old age and return to youth [Col. 0235A]. The cast-off skins of serpents are called *exuviae*, because when they grow old they strip them off; once stripped, they return to youth. They are also called *exuviae* and *induviae*, because they are removed and put on.

Pythagoras says that a serpent is created from the marrow of a dead human being, which is in the spine. Ovidius also mentions this in the books of the *Metamorphoses*, saying:

“There are those who believe that, when the spine has rotted in the closed tomb,  
human marrow is changed into a serpent.”

If this is believed, it rightly comes to pass that just as death comes to human beings through the serpent, so the serpent comes through the death of a human being.

It is said that a serpent does not dare touch a naked human being. Wise reader, once you have learned these kinds of serpents and their properties, whenever you read about them in Scripture, do not hesitate to try to draw something from them into the spiritual sense.

## CHAPTER IV. On Worms
The worm is an animal that is usually generated from flesh, wood, or any earthly substance without sexual union, although some are also born from eggs, such as the scorpion. Worms are of the earth, water, air, flesh, leaves, wood, or clothing.

The spider, a worm of the air, is so called from its nourishment from the air, because with its tiny body it draws out long threads. Always intent upon weaving its web, it never ceases to labor, continually enduring loss in its craft.

The leech, a worm of the water, is so called because it sucks blood. It lies in wait for those who drink; and when it slips into the throat, or attaches itself anywhere, it draws blood. When it has become drenched with an excess of blood, it vomits up what it has taken, so that it may suck again fresher blood.

The blister beetle (*cantarida*), an earth-worm, when applied to the human body, immediately produces, by its own burning action, blisters filled with fluid.

The many-footed creature (*multipes*), an earth-worm, is named from its multitude of feet. When contracted, it folds itself into a ball. It is born beneath stones from moisture and earth.

The slug (*limax*), a worm of mud, is so called because it is born in mud or from mud. Hence it is always regarded as filthy and unclean.

The silkworms (*bombyces*) are worms of leaves; from their weaving silk is produced. They are called by this name because, when they are emptied out, they generate threads, and only air remains within them.

The caterpillar (*eruca*), a worm of leaves, wrapped in a vegetable or vine-leaf, is named from *erodere*, “to gnaw.” Plautus mentions it:

> “He imitates the worthless and harmful creature  
> wrapped and entangled in a vine-leaf.”

But it does not fly away, like the locust, leaving what it has only half-eaten as it runs here and there. Rather, it remains amid the doomed crops and, with its slow movement and sluggish bites, consumes everything.

The Greeks call worms of wood *teredones*, because they consume it by boring through it. We call them *termites*—for that is what wood-worms are called in Latin—which trees cut down at an inauspicious time produce.

The moth (*tinea*), a worm of clothing, is so called because it clings to the fabric and remains in it until it eats it away. Hence the word *pertinax*, “persistent,” because it presses repeatedly upon the same object.

Worms of flesh include the *hemicraneus*, the intestinal worm (*lumbricus*), the *ascarides*, the *costi peduculi* (skin-lice), lice, fleas, nits, the *tarmus*, the tick, the *usia*, and the bedbug.

The *hemicraneus* is called a worm of the head.

The intestinal worm (*lumbricus*) is so called as though from *lumbicus*, because it glides, or because it is found in the loins.

The *ascarides*, or skin-worms, are so called from the feet. Hence those in whose bodies lice swarm are called *pediculosi*, “lousy.”

Fleas are so called because they are nourished more by dust.

The nit (*lendix*) is the same as the *tarmus*, and is named from *lens*, “nit.”

The *tarmus* is a worm of bacon.

The tick (*ricinus*) is called the dog-worm because it is found in dogs’ ears. *Cenos* is the Greek word for “dog.”

The *usia* is a worm of the pig. It is so called because it burns: wherever it bites, the place burns so severely that blisters form there.

The bedbug (*cimex*) is named from its resemblance to a certain herb whose stench it possesses.

Strictly speaking, a worm is born in rotting flesh. The moth is in clothing, the caterpillar in vegetables, the wood-worm in timber, and the *tarmus* in bacon.

The worm does not crawl, like the serpent, with open strides or by the exertion of scales, because it has no firmness of spine like the snake. Rather, extending the parts of its little heart straight ahead in stages, contracting those that are contracted and unfolding those that are extended, it produces movement and thus glides along when agitated.

Mystically, the worm may signify Christ because of the humility of the humanity he assumed, as in the Psalm:

> “I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm XXI).

It may also signify the memory of the sinful soul established in the punishment of hell, concerning which it is written:

> “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah LXVI).

The spider signifies human frailty. Hence the Psalm says:

> “And you have caused his soul to waste away like a spider” (Psalm XXXVIII).

The spider has a delicate body. It does not live upon the ground, but in higher places it weaves extremely fine webs through the digestion of its entrails, just as silk is said by some to be drawn out by certain worms. To this tiny body, therefore, the soul of one who has been rightly converted and afflicted is appropriately compared. Wearied by prolonged observances and vigils, it abandons earthly things and, enlivened by divine fear, produces the most refined works of virtue.

After this, he returns to the beginning of his proposition: although the soul is rebuked and wastes away, nevertheless it is confounded by human frailty amid the variety of different adversities.

The spider also signifies the devil’s deceit, as in Isaiah:

> “They have woven spiders’ webs” (Psalm LIX).

The leech, moreover, is the devil. Hence the saying in Proverbs:

> “The leech has two daughters, saying, ‘Give, give’” (Proverbs XXX).

The devil’s daughters are lust and avarice, by which the bloodthirsty enemy afflicts the human race.

The caterpillar likewise may signify the devil, who never ceases to gnaw away, through evil suggestions, the shoots of virtue growing in a person and to uproot them through vicious practices.

Therefore, wherever Scripture mentions the moth and rust, their mystical meaning must be sought. Allegorically, rust may signify arrogance and vainglory. Wherever these are found, they obscure all the beauty and strength of the virtues and squander the treasure of spiritual gifts. Hence the prophet says:

> “God scatters the bones of those who please themselves, and all arrogance is an abomination before God.”

The moth signifies an inward vice of the soul. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal” (Matthew VI).

The moth, which secretly gnaws clothing, signifies envy, which tears apart good endeavor and never ceases to destroy the harmony of unity.

The thieves are demons and heretics, concerning whom the Truth says:

> “All who came are thieves and robbers” (John X).

## CHAPTER V. On Fish

Fish (*pisces*) are so called from the same source as *pecus*, “cattle,” namely from feeding (*pascere*).

These creatures are called reptiles because they swim in such a way that they possess the appearance and nature of crawling. Although they plunge into the depths, they crawl while swimming. Hence David says:

> “This is the great and wide sea, in which are reptiles without number” (Psalm CIII).

Some kinds of fish are amphibious. They are so called because they have the use of walking on land and the function of swimming in water. *Amphi* in Greek means “both”: that is, they live both in water and on land, such as seals, crocodiles, and hippopotamuses—that is, river horses.

Human beings gave names to cattle, beasts, and birds before they gave them to fish, because those creatures were seen and known earlier. As the kinds of fish gradually became known, names were established for them: some from their resemblance to land animals, such as frogs, calves, lions, black merles, peacocks marked with various colors on their backs and necks, white and variegated thrushes, and others that claimed names for themselves according to the forms of terrestrial animals.

Others were named from the habits of land animals: sea-dogs from land dogs, because they bite; wolves because they pursue others with shameless greed; from color, such as *umbrae*, because they are the color of shadow; and *auritatae*, because they have the color of gold on their heads. *Varii* are named from their variety; these are commonly called trout.

Others are named from their shape: the *orbis*, which is round and is composed entirely in the head; the *solea*, because it is solid like footwear; and, from sex, the *musculus*, because it is the male of the whale. The whale is said to conceive through intercourse with it. Hence there are the *musculi* of shellfish, from whose milk oysters conceive.

Whales (*ballenae*) are beasts of immense size. They are named from emitting and pouring out water, for they cast up waves higher than other sea-beasts. *Ballein* in Greek means “to emit.”

They are called *cete*, that is, “monsters,” because of their enormity. They are enormous kinds of beasts, with bodies as large as mountains. Such was the whale that received Jonah, whose belly was so vast that it possessed the likeness of hell, as the prophet says:

> “He heard me from the belly of hell” (Jonah II).

Sea-horses are so called because their front part is that of a horse, while their rear part dissolves into a fish.

The *bocas* are said to be sea-oxen, as though *boacas*.

The *caerulei* are named from their color, for *caeruleum* is green mixed with black, as is the sea.

Dolphins have a well-established name because they follow human voices, or because they gather together in herds to music. Nothing in the sea is faster than they, for they often leap over ships as they spring. When they sport in the waves and strike themselves against the masses of water in a sudden leap, they seem to signify storms. These are properly called *Simones*.

There is also a kind of dolphin in the Nile with a serrated back. By cutting into the tender bellies of crocodiles, they kill them.

Sea-pigs are those commonly called swine. While seeking food in the manner of pigs, they dig up the ground beneath the water. They have the function of a mouth around the throat, and unless they plunge their snout into the sand, they cannot gather food.

The crocodile is named from its saffron-colored appearance. It is born in the Nile and is a four-footed animal, powerful both on land and in water. It is generally twenty cubits long, armed with enormous teeth and claws, and has such a hard hide that it repels from its back even blows from strong stones. At night it rests in the water and by day on land. It broods over its eggs on the ground, while the male and female take turns keeping watch.

Some fish with serrated crests kill it by cutting into the tender parts of its belly.

It is said to be the only animal that moves its upper jaw.

The hippopotamus is so called because it resembles a horse in its back, mane, and neighing. It has an upturned snout beginning at the first teeth and a twisted tail. It remains in the water by day and grazes the crops at night. The Nile also produces it.

The mullet (*mullus*) is so called because it is soft and extremely delicate. Its flesh is said to restrain lust but to dull the sharpness of the eyes; people who have often eaten it, however, smell of fish.

When a mullet is killed in wine, those who drink from it develop a distaste for wine.

The *mugil* is named because it is very agile. When it senses that the fishermen have laid their traps, it immediately turns backward and leaps over the net, so that one might see the fish flying.

The eel (*anguilla*) received its name from its resemblance to a snake. Its origin is in mud. Hence, when caught, it is so slippery that the harder one presses, the more quickly it escapes.

They say that the eastern river Ganges produces eels thirty feet long.

When eels are killed in wine, those who drink from that wine develop a distaste for wine.

The sea-dragon has spines in its gills directed toward its tail. When it strikes, it pours out poison in every direction in which it lashes; hence its name.

The Greeks call the moray eel *minana*, because it coils itself into circles. They say that it is entirely female and conceives from a serpent. For this reason fishermen call and catch it with a hiss, as though it were a snake; yet it is difficult to kill with a blow of a club.

Shellfish and snails are so called because, when the moon wanes, they become hollow—that is, empty. The bodies of all enclosed marine animals and shellfish swell as the moon increases and empty as it declines. When the moon is waxing, it increases moisture; when it enters its decline, moisture diminishes. This is what the natural philosophers say.

*Conchae* is the name in its primary form; *cochleae* is a diminutive, as though *conchulae*.

There are many kinds of shellfish, including pearl-bearing shells, which are called snails. In their flesh a precious stone is solidified. Those who have written about the natures of animals say that these creatures approach the shores at night and conceive the pearl from heavenly dew. Hence they are called *coelôe*.

The *murex* is a sea-snail. It is named from its sharpness and roughness, and is otherwise called *conchylium*. When cut with iron, it emits tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made. Hence it is called *ostrum*, because this dye is extracted from the moisture of its shell.

Those shellfish that have legs and are hostile to oysters are called *canchri*, or crabs. They live on the flesh of oysters by a remarkable art. When a crab cannot open the oyster’s strong shell, it waits until the oyster opens the shell’s closures. Then the crab secretly inserts a small stone, preventing the oyster from closing, and eats away its flesh.

Some say that if ten crabs are tied together with a bunch of basil, all the scorpions in the vicinity will gather at that place.

There are two kinds of crabs: river crabs and sea crabs.

The oyster (*ostrea*) is so called from the shell by which the softness of its inner flesh is protected. The Greeks call the shell *ostrea*. *Ostrea* is neuter, while its flesh is referred to in the feminine gender.

The “males” (*musculi*) are snails, as we have said, from whose milk oysters conceive. They are called *musculi* as though *masculi*, “males.”

The sponge (*spungia*) is named from *fingere*, “to shape,” that is, “to cleanse and wipe.” Hence Cicero says:

> “And the blood was shaped away with sponges,”

that is, “was wiped away.”

It is shown to be an animal by the blood adhering to rocks. Hence, when it is cut off, it gives off blood.

The hollow sponge mystically signifies the deceitful unbelief of the Jews, concerning whom it is written in the Gospel:

> “But placing a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, they offered it to his mouth” (Matthew XXVII).

Among these creatures, some live in the water and move about, such as fish; others stand fixed in place, such as oysters, *icini*, and sponges.

Some sponges are called male because their tubes are slender; others female because their tubes are denser, larger, and continuous. Others are harder; the Greeks call them *tragoi*, and we may call them “goats” because of their roughness. Their softest kind is called *penicilli*, because it is suitable for eye swellings and useful for wiping away eye discharge.

White sponges become so through treatment. During the summer they are spread out in the sun and, like Punic wax, absorb whiteness.

Pliny says that there are 144 names of all animals living in the water, divided among kinds of monsters, serpents common to land and water, crabs, shellfish, locusts, *polerides*, polyps, soles, and lizards, such as the squid and similar creatures.

Many of these recognize the order of their seasons through a certain natural understanding; others wander in their proper places without change.

Among fish, some females conceive through intercourse with a male and give birth to young. Others lay eggs conceived without receiving a male; these eggs are afterward fertilized by the casting of the seed of a male of the same kind. Those touched by this gift become capable of generation; those not fertilized remain sterile or decay.

In Scripture, the word “fish” sometimes designates good people and sometimes evil people. Thus in the Gospel the Savior tells the parable of the net cast into the sea:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out and, sitting beside the shore, chose the good into their vessels, but threw the bad outside” (Matthew XIII).

In this parable the holy Church is compared to a net. It has been entrusted to fishermen, and through it each person is drawn from the waves of the present age toward the eternal kingdom, lest he be plunged into the depths of eternal death.

It gathers fish of every kind because it calls the wise and foolish, free and slave, rich and poor, strong and weak to the forgiveness of sins. The shore signifies the end of the world; the net signifies the holy Church, which it was drawing.

The good fish—that is, good people—are then received into vessels, that is, they will be led into eternal dwellings. The bad, however, will be cast outside, into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Fish may also signify the wise men of this world, as in the Psalter:

> “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Psalm VIII).

The birds of heaven are proud people, who, puffed up by the wind of boasting, are carried aloft through the empty air and despise humble things when they have been raised higher. Birds are so called from their frequent flying.

The fish of the sea may perhaps signify philosophers, who investigate the nature of this world with wandering curiosity. For just as fish, with their heads foremost, open paths for themselves through the sea’s confused swellings, so these people, with their heads bent down, search out the veins of reality through continual human reasoning.

Since there are also fish of rivers, it is not without significance that he says “of the sea,” on account of those who appear wise to themselves. Yet such people, and those like them, are happily subjected beneath the feet of the Lord when they come to embrace the Christian religion.

Fishermen signify the Apostles or other preachers. Hence it is read in the Gospel:

> “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matthew IV).

In a negative sense, Isaiah says:

> “The fishermen shall mourn” (Isaiah XIX).

Fish signify the saints. In the Gospel:

> “And they drew in a net full of large fish” (John XXI).

Fish signify the reprobate. In the Gospel:

> “But they threw the bad outside” (Matthew XIII).

And in Amos:

> “The fish of the sea were also gathered together” (Hosea IV).

The fish signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, touched by the fire of tribulation. In the Gospel:

> “They set before him a portion of a roasted fish and a honeycomb” (Luke XXIV).

The two fish joined to the five loaves signify the two Testaments of the Law, or the two commandments of love, or the two persons—the royal and the priestly. In the Gospel:

> “And after taking the five loaves and the two fish” (Matthew XIV).

The hook signifies the divinity of the Son of God, which lay hidden beneath the bait clothed in flesh. Concerning this hook the Lord says to Job:

> “Can you draw out Leviathan with your hook?” (Job XL).

The ancient enemy of the human race, like a fish, bit the bait of the Lord’s body in his Passion and was killed by the endurance of the divinity.

Again, in a negative sense, the hook signifies the devil, as Habakkuk says:

> “He will draw it all up with his hook” (Habakkuk I).

## CHAPTER VI. On Birds

There is one name for birds, but their kinds are diverse. For just as they differ in appearance, so they differ in nature.

Some are simple, such as doves; others are crafty, such as the partridge. Some submit themselves to the hand, such as the hawk; others are fearful, such as the *garamentes* [uncertain reading]. Some delight in the company of human beings, such as the swallow; others love a secluded life in deserts, such as the turtledove. Some feed only on seed when they find it, such as the goose; others eat flesh and pursue plunder, such as the kite.

Some are [*incuriae*, perhaps *inviae*—uncertain], remaining always in the same places. Others are migratory and return at their proper seasons, such as storks and swallows. Others are gregarious, that is, they fly in flocks, such as starlings and quails. Others are solitary wanderers, that is, solitary because of the ambushes from which they plunder, such as eagles, hawks, and all creatures of that sort.

Some make a racket with their voices, such as swallows; others produce extremely sweet songs, such as the swan and blackbird. Others imitate human words and voices, such as the parrot and magpie.

There are also innumerable others, differing both in kind and in habits. It is difficult for anyone to discover how many kinds of birds there are. No one could penetrate all the deserts of India, Ethiopia, or Scythia and know their kinds and differences.

Birds (*aves*) are so called because they do not have fixed paths; they run about through trackless places. Alternatively, they are so called because they direct their wings upward and climb to lofty places by the rowing of their wings.

*Volucres* are named from flying (*volare*). For from the same root as “to fly” we also derive “to walk.” *Vola* is the middle part of the foot or hand; in birds, the *vola* is the middle part of the wings, by whose movement the feathers are stirred. Hence they are called *volucres*.

The offspring of all birds are called *pulli*, “young,” but the offspring of four-footed animals are also called *pulli*, as is a small human being. Newborn young are so called because they are *polluti*, “stained.” Hence a black garment is called *pullus*, “dark.”

Wings are the members in which feathers are fixed in rows and provide the means for flying. They are called wings because birds use them to embrace, nourish, and warm their young.

Feathers (*pennae*) are named from hanging (*pendere*), that is, from flying; hence also “to hang.” Birds move with the aid of their feathers when they entrust themselves to the air.

*Pluma* is as though *piluma*. For just as quadrupeds have hair, birds have feathers.

Many names of birds are evidently formed from the sound of their voices, such as crane, raven, swan, peacock, kite, owl, cuckoo, jackdaw, and others. The variety of their voices taught human beings what they should be called.

Birds signify angels, as when, in Job, the birds of heaven are said to have nests at the origin of wisdom.

Birds signify proud people. In the Psalter:

> “Sheep and oxen, all of them, and also the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea” (Psalm VIII).

Flying creatures signify the Apostles or all the saints. In the Gospel:

> “My bulls and flying creatures have been slaughtered” (Matthew XXII),

that is, the fathers of the New and Old Testaments.

Flight signifies the ascent of the saints to the Lord God, or understanding in Scripture. In the Psalter:

> “I shall fly and rest” (Psalm XVII).

Birds and flying creatures have various meanings. Sometimes they signify angels, as in the saying:

> “The birds of heaven announce his voice” (Ecclesiastes X).

Sometimes they signify holy people, as in the testimony concerning the mustard seed, which is indeed the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown is greater than all vegetables:

> “It becomes a tree, so that the birds come and dwell in its branches” (Matthew XIII).

The preaching of the Gospel is the smallest of all disciplines in the eyes of the wise men of this world, but it grows into a tree, so that we should understand the birds of heaven—whether as the souls of believers or as powers devoted to the service of God—to come and dwell in its branches.

I think that the branches of the evangelical tree, which grew from the mustard seed, are the varieties of doctrines in which each of the birds mentioned above finds rest.

Birds signify demons. Hence in the Apocalypse all the birds are addressed:

> “Birds that fly through the midst of heaven, come to the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings,” and so forth (Revelation XIX).

And in Solomon:

> “Whoever relies on a lie is fed by the wind” (Proverbs X).

He himself likewise pursues the flying birds.

The bird signifies the Savior. Hence, concerning Judaea, which was not going to believe in him, Job says:

> “The bird did not know the way” (Job XXVIII).

The bird signifies the Jewish people. The prophet says:

> “Zion has become like a flying bird” (Isaiah XVI).

Figuratively, concerning this people, Deuteronomy commands:

> “If you walk along the road and find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting over the young or eggs, you shall not take it together with its young. You shall let the mother go, but keep the young” (Deuteronomy XXII).

This is understood of the Apostles, who were taken from that same people through Christ the Lord, while the people itself was left behind.

The bird signifies the devil in Job:

> “Will you play with him as with a bird?” (Job XL).

At times, however, birds signify evil spirits, which seize the seed placed along the road, according to the Gospel parable (Luke VIII). The road, therefore, is the mind worn smooth and dried out by the constant traffic of evil thoughts, so that it is unable to receive and germinate the seed of the word. Consequently, whatever good seed falls upon the vicinity of such a road perishes, because, trampled down by the wicked passage of evil thought, it is carried away by demons.

They are rightly called the birds of heaven, either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature or because they fly through the air.

Wings in Scripture signify the two commandments of love, by which one ascends to the heavenly kingdom, or the two Testaments, as is shown in the two wings of the cherubim and in Ezekiel’s living creatures, which covered their bodies with two wings.

The six wings signify the divine preaching announced throughout this world through both Testaments, in which the world was made in six days. In Isaiah:

> “Six wings to one and six wings to the other” (Isaiah VI).

Wings signify pride, as Job says concerning the heretic:

> “When the time comes, he raises his wings on high” (Job XXXIX).

Feathers also signify the sacred Scriptures, as in the Psalm:

> “The feathers of the dove are silvered” (Psalm LXVII).

Feathers signify the souls of the saints, or their virtues. In the Psalm:

> “And he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm XVII).

And elsewhere:

> “If I take wings before the dawn” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

A nest signifies the Church or the rest of the saints on high, as in the Psalm:

> “The sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest, where it may place its young” (Psalm LXXXIII),

that is, its children.

Alternatively, a nest signifies a good conscience, in which the offspring of good thoughts are warmed and brought forth into action, so that afterward they may be called children. Thus the Psalter says:

> “Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Psalm CXXVII).

Sometimes, however, young birds are understood negatively, as in Solomon:

> “And let the young of the eagles devour him” (Proverbs XXX).

An egg, as some wish, signifies hope. Hence it is read in the Gospel:

> “Or which of you, if he asks his father for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” (Luke XI).

Eggs signify the disciples of heretics. In Job:

> “He will leave his eggs upon the ground” (Job XXXIX).

Again, eggs signify the preaching of heretics. In Isaiah:

> “Whoever eats from their eggs shall die” (Isaiah LIX).

Young birds signify the saints. In the Psalm:

> “And the turtledove a nest,” and so forth (Psalm LXXXIII).

And elsewhere:

> “And the young of the ravens that call upon him” (Psalm CXLVI),

that is, the faithful from among the unbelieving nations.

The young of eagles signify the faithful in the Church, as in Job:

> “Its young will lick up blood” (Job XXXIX),

that is, the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion.

The eagle is named from the sharpness of its eyes. It is said to possess such great power of vision that, while carried over the sea on motionless wings and hidden from human sight, it can see tiny fish swimming from such a height. Descending like a thunderbolt, it carries its captured prey to shore on its wings.

It is also said not to turn its gaze away from the sun’s ray. Hence it exposes its young, suspended by their claws, to the sun’s rays. Those whose gaze it sees to remain unmoving it preserves as worthy of their lineage; but those who turn their eyes away it casts aside as degenerate.
