In sacred Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes designates evil spirits who seize souls; sometimes the powers of the present age; sometimes the most subtle understanding of the saints; and sometimes the incarnate Lord, who swiftly traverses the lowest places and soon returns to the highest.

By the name of eagles, ambushing spirits are represented, as Jeremiah attests:

> “Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations IV).

The word “eagle” represents earthly power. Hence through the prophet Ezekiel it is said:

> “A great eagle, with great wings, long limbs, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon, seized the marrow of the cedar, and tore off the top of its branches” (Ezekiel VII).

The word “eagle” represents either the subtle understanding of the saints or the flight of the Lord’s Ascension. Thus the same prophet, describing how he saw the four Evangelists under the form of living creatures, testifies that the faces of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared to him (Ezekiel I). The fourth creature, unmistakably signifying John by the eagle, abandoned the earth in flight because, through subtle understanding, he penetrated the inner mysteries of the words by contemplation.

The sharpness of the sight of all other birds is surpassed by that of the eagle, so that when it fixes its eyes upon the rays of the sun, the flashing of the light does not cause it to close them.

At God’s command the eagle is raised up: the life of the faithful, obeying the divine orders, is suspended in the heights. It is also said to build its nest in lofty places because, despising earthly desires, it is already nourished by hope of heavenly things.

It builds its nest in lofty places because it does not construct the dwelling of its mind in a low and base manner of life.

The Lord is an eagle in Deuteronomy:

> “As an eagle protects its nest, he received them” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

The eagle signifies the divinity of the Son of God. In Solomon:

> “There are three things too difficult for me, and the fourth I do not understand at all,” and so forth (Proverbs XXX).

The eagle signifies the saints in Job:

> “Will the eagle be raised at your command, and will it build its nest in lofty places?” (Job XXXIX).

And in the Gospel it is read:

> “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew XXIV).

The eagle signifies the devil or Antichrist. In Ezekiel:

> “And behold, one great eagle” (Ezekiel XVII).

The eagle signifies an impious nation, or a city that rushes upon the plunder of others. Thus through Micah against Samaria it is said:

> “Make your baldness broad like an eagle’s” (Micah I).

The vulture (*vultur*) is thought to have been named from its slow flight. Because of its size, it does not have a swift flight.

Some say that certain vultures do not mate, but conceive and produce offspring without sexual union, and that their offspring live for nearly a hundred years.

Vultures, like eagles, sense corpses even beyond the seas. Flying at a great height, they see from above many things hidden by the obscurity of mountains.

The Mediator between God and human beings, our Redeemer, is rightly signified by the name of the vulture. Remaining in the height of his divinity, as though from a lofty flight he saw the corpse of our mortality below, and lowered himself from the heavens to the depths.

He deigned to become human for our sake; and, while seeking the dead creature, he found death among us, although with himself he was immortal.

The eye of this vulture was the very intention of our resurrection, because, by dying, he freed us from eternal death.

That faithless people of the Jews saw him as mortal, but paid no attention to the fact that by his death he would destroy our death. Therefore the bird did not know the way, nor did it behold the eyes of the vulture: for although it saw the one whom it held in death, it did not wish to see how much glory of our life would follow from his death.

Hence persecution also flared up into cruelty. The people refused to receive the words of life and drove away the preachers of the kingdom of heaven by prohibition, violence, and blows.

The vulture signifies the sinner who seizes prey from another’s death, as in Leviticus:

> “You shall not eat the vulture or anything like it” (Leviticus XI).

Cranes (*grues*) take their name from their own voice, for they murmur with such a sound. When traveling, they follow one another in a written order. Lucan says of them:

> “And the letter, scattered among the wings, perishes in confusion.”

They seek the heights so that they may more easily see the lands toward which they are heading. The bird that leads the flock disciplines it with its voice. When it becomes hoarse, another takes its place.

At night they divide the watches and take turns keeping guard, holding small stones in their raised toes so that sleep may be kept away. By their cries they indicate what must be avoided.

Their age is revealed by their color, for they grow black in old age.

Cranes may therefore signify those who live together in monasteries but do not disdain to follow one leader. They practice vigils, are solicitous for one another, and are not sluggish in producing nocturnal songs in psalmody.

Hence it is said:

> “The cranes follow one another and fly in written order.”

Storks (*ciconiae*) are named from the sound they make as they rattle, as though *cicaniae*. This sound comes from their mouths rather than their voices, because they produce it by striking their bills.

They are messengers of spring and companions in community. Enemies of serpents, they fly across the sea and travel in a gathered flock to Asia. Ravens go before them as leaders, and the whole group follows like an army.

They show exceptional devotion toward their young. They tend them so assiduously that, through constant brooding, they lose their feathers. For as much time as they spend raising their offspring, so much time are they in turn nourished by their own young.

The stork therefore signifies prudent people and cautious servants of God in their way of life. They pursue serpents and regard their poisons as nothing, because they attack evil spirits with their poisonous suggestions and reduce them to nothing.

Concerning them Jeremiah says:

> “The turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have known the time of their coming” (Jeremiah VIII),

that is, the time when the holy Church will be gathered into one at the coming of the Savior.

The *olor* is a bird that the Greeks call the swan. The *olor* is so called because it is entirely white with feathers. No one remembers a black swan. *Olor* in Greek means “whole.”

The swan (*cygnus*) is named from singing, because it pours forth the sweetness of song in measured tones. It sings sweetly because it has a long, curved neck, and its voice must struggle through a long and winding passage to produce various melodies.

It is said that in the northern regions many swans fly toward harpers who play before them and sing together in harmony with the music.

*Olor* is the Latin name; in Greek they are called *cygni*.

Sailors say that the swan gives them a favorable omen, as Aemilius Macer says:

> “The swan is always the happiest bird among omens.”

> “Sailors desire it, because it does not plunge into the waves.”

The swan, with its lofty neck, signifies pride. It is called *struthio* (“ostrich”) in Greek. Although this creature appears to have feathers like a bird, it does not rise any higher from the ground. It neglects to brood its eggs; once they have been laid, they are brought to life merely by the warmth of the dust. Mystically, hypocrites are signified by the ostrich. Hence the Prophet says: “The beast of the field has glorified me, the dragons and the ostriches” (Isa. XLIII). For what is expressed by the name “dragons” except malicious minds in the open, which continually crawl along the earth through the lowest thoughts? And what is signified by the name “ostrich” except those who pretend to be good, who retain the life of holiness in appearance, as though it were the feather of flight, but do not practice it in their deeds [Col. 0245D]? The Lord therefore declares that he is glorified by the dragon or the ostrich, because he often converts both those who are openly evil and those who are hypocritically good to his service through their innermost thoughts.

Or certainly the beast of the field glorifies the Lord—that is, the dragons and ostriches glorify him—when the Gentiles exalt the faith that is in him, although they had formerly been members of the devil in this world. Therefore he reproaches malice under the name of dragons, and marks hypocrisy under the name of ostriches. The Gentiles, as it were, received feathers but could not fly: they possessed the nature of reason but did not know the practice of reason.

The ostrich may also signify heretics or philosophers, who wish to exalt themselves with the feathers of wisdom, but nevertheless do not fly away [Col. 0246A]. Hence it is read in Isaiah: “And it shall be the lair of dragons and the pasture of ostriches” (Isa. XXXIV).

The heron (*ardea*) is so called as if from *ardua*, “lofty,” on account of its high flights. Lucan says: “And the heron, which dares to fly.” It fears rain and flies above the clouds so that it cannot feel the storms of the clouds; but when it has flown higher, it signifies a storm. Many call it Tantalus. This bird can signify the souls of the elect, who fear the disturbance of this age lest they be caught in the storms of persecution at the devil’s instigation, and therefore raise their minds above all temporal things toward the serenity of the heavenly homeland, where God’s countenance is continually seen.

The phoenix is a bird of Arabia, so called either because it has a Phoenician color or because it is singular and unique throughout the whole world. For the Arabs call it the solitary phoenix. Living for more than five hundred years, when it sees that it has grown old, it gathers branches of aromatic plants and builds itself a funeral pyre. Turning toward the sun’s ray, it feeds the fire destined for itself by the beating of its wings, and thus rises again from its ashes [Col. 0246B]. It can also signify the resurrection of the righteous, who, having gathered the spices of the virtues, prepare for themselves after death the restoration of their former vigor.

The cinnamolegus is likewise a bird of Arabia. It is so called because it builds its nests in lofty groves from cinnamon branches. Since human beings cannot climb there on account of the height and fragility of the branches, they attack the nests with lead-weighted arrows and thereby bring down the cinnamon, selling it at a very high price because merchants value cinnamon more than other commodities [Col. 0246C].

The parrot is born on the shores of India. It is green, with a crimson collar, a large tongue broader than those of other birds, and consequently it articulates words, so that if one does not see it, one might think that a human being was speaking. By nature it greets people, saying “Ave” or “Chaire”; it learns other names through instruction. Hence the verse:

> “Parrot, from you I shall learn the names of others:  
> These words I have learned to say: ‘Caesar, hail.’”

The kingfisher (*alcyon*), a bird of the sea, is so called as if “ocean bird,” because in winter it builds its nests on the waters of the ocean and raises its young there. While it keeps watch, the sea is said to grow calm across the extended waters, with silent winds, for seven days, and nature itself to provide assistance for raising its offspring.

The onocrotalus is a bird with a long bill, which the Greeks call *onocrocolon* [Col. 0246D].

The crocodile is a kind of flying creature, so called as if “eating the heart.”

The bat (*vespertilio*) receives its name from the time of day, because, fleeing the light, it flies about in the evening twilight. Driven by rapid movement and suspended from the extremely thin membranes of its arms, it resembles a mouse. It makes a sound less like a voice than a shriek. In appearance it is at once winged and four-footed, something not ordinarily found among other birds. Bats are the monstrous forms of idols, devoted to darkness, as it is read in Isaiah: “That you may worship moles and bats” (Isa. II).

The owl (*noctua*) is so called because it flies at night and cannot be seen by day; when the sun’s brightness has arisen, its sight is dulled. The island of Crete does not have this bird, and if one comes there from elsewhere, it immediately dies [Col. 0247A]. Some call the owl the *corvus marmus*. The owl, however, is not the *bubo*, for the *bubo* is larger. The owl signifies people who flee the light of truth and are bound to darkness. Hence in Leviticus the eating of this bird is forbidden.

The *bubo* receives its compounded name from the sound of its voice. It is a wild bird, heavily burdened with feathers, always held back by sluggish heaviness; it haunts tombs by day and night and continually remains in caves. Of it Ovid says:

> “And the hideous bird becomes the messenger of coming grief,  
> The sluggish owl, a dread omen to mortals.”

Finally, among augurs it is said to portend evil. The *bubo* signifies those devoted to the darkness of sins and fleeing the light of righteousness. Hence it is counted among the unclean animals in Leviticus.

The *lucina* bird received its name [Col. 0247B] because by its song it commonly signals the rising of the approaching day, as though *lucinia*; it is also called *acedula*. Of it Cicero says in the *Prognostics*:

> “And the *acedula* exercises its morning songs.”

Perhaps typologically this can signify holy preachers, who announce the rising of the future light and exhort the faithful, with watchful minds, to attend to its coming.

The *ulula* is named from wailing and mourning. When it cries, it either imitates weeping or moaning. Hence among augurs, if it laments, it is said to indicate sadness; if silent, prosperity. This bird can signify the wailing of sinners in hell. Thus, when the Prophet speaks of Babylon’s devastation, he says that “owls” are reported to dwell in its houses, “as also the onocrotalus and the hedgehog” (Isa. XIII) [Col. 0247C].

The jackdaw (*graculus*) is named from its chatter, not—as some wish—from flying in flocks, since it is clear that its name comes from its voice. It is an exceedingly talkative species and troublesome in its sounds. It can signify either the empty loquacity of philosophers or the harmful verbosity of heretics.

The magpie (*pica*) is so called as though “poetical,” because it expresses words with distinctions of sound like a human being. Hanging from the branches of trees, it makes a troublesome noise through its incessant chattering. Although it cannot articulate its tongue in speech, it nevertheless imitates the sound of the human voice. Concerning it someone aptly says [Martial]:

> “Talkative magpie, with a distinct voice I greet you, my master;  
> If you do not see me, you would deny that I am a bird.”

The woodpecker (*picus*) took its name from Picus, son of Saturn, because he used it in augury [Col. 0247D]. This bird is said to possess something divine, as shown by the fact that on whatever tree it nests, a nail or anything else driven into it cannot remain fixed for long: as soon as the bird settles there, the object immediately falls out. But let each person judge this as he wishes. Its voice, however, can signify the loquacity of heretics or philosophers, as we said above concerning the jackdaw.

The peacock (*pavo*) takes its name from the sound of its voice. Its flesh is so hard that it scarcely feels decay and is not easily cooked. Concerning it someone says:

> “You marvel whenever it unfolds its jeweled wings,  
> Yet you can hand this hard creature over to the cruel cook.”

The peacock that was brought to Solomon from distant regions and has various colors in its feathers signifies the Gentile people coming to Christ from the distant parts of the earth [Col. 0248A]. By his grace, they also shine with the adornment of many virtues.

The cock (*gallus*) is so called from castration. Among all birds, it alone has its testicles removed; for the ancients called castrated men *galli*. Just as the female of a lion is called a *leaena*, and the female of a dragon a *dracaena*, so the female of a cock is called a hen.

The cock signifies a holy man or an evangelical teacher who, placed beneath the darkness of this world, announces the future light of eternal life. Concerning him Solomon says: “A cock girded about, and there is no king who can resist him” (Prov. XXX). And in Job: “Who,” he says, “gave the cock understanding?” (Job XXXVIII.) The cock is also used in another sense, as in Isaiah: “I will carry you away as a cock is carried away” (Isa. XXII).

The hen signifies wisdom, or the holy Church, or a righteous creature, as in the Lord’s testimony concerning Jerusalem: “How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII) [Col. 0248B].

The goose (*anser*) received a fitting name from its continual swimming. From this species some are called *germanae*, because they nourish their young more than the others do. The name *anes* was derived from the name *anser*, either through derivation, through resemblance, or because it too frequently swims. This bird bears witness to the watches of the night through its continual cackling. No animal senses the smell of a human being as keenly as a goose. Hence by its cackling the approach of the Gauls to the Capitol was detected. It can signify prudent people who are carefully watchful over their own custody.

The diver (*mergus*) receives its name from its continual diving. It often submerges its head and gathers signs of storms beneath the waves; foreseeing a tempest at sea, it heads toward the shore with a cry [Col. 0248C]. The diver signifies the lustful person, always intent upon the desire of the flesh, as is shown in Leviticus.

The coot (*fulica*) is a tame and black bird, smaller than a duck but similar in bodily form. It delights to remain in ponds. It is a bird of the waters, making its nest in the middle of the water or on rocks surrounded by water, and always delighting in the deep sea. When it senses a storm, it flees and plays in shallow water. It aptly refers to those being baptized, who persevere in the grace of the most sacred font. Hence it is written: “The house of the coot is leader”—that is, the sacred font is the leader of all Christians, while it brings them to the kingdoms of heaven [Col. 0248D].

The turtledove (*turtur*) is named from its voice. It is a chaste bird, always dwelling on mountain ridges and in desert solitudes. It flees human dwellings and human society and remains in the woods. The dove, by contrast, loves human hospitality and is always a gentle inhabitant of houses.

The turtledove signifies the body of Christ, which is the Church, on account of the diversity of the nations. Concerning it Scripture says: “How beautiful are your cheeks, like those of a turtledove!” (Song I.) And in the Psalm: “The turtledove has found a nest where she may place her young” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Doves (*columbae*) are so called because their necks change colors with each turn. They are tame birds, living among crowds of people [Col. 0249A] and without gall. The ancients called them *veneriae*, because they frequent nests and conceive love through kissing.

The dove signifies God. In Jeremiah: “At the face of the sword of the dove each one shall turn to his people, and each shall flee to his own land” (Jer. XLVI).

The dove signifies the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel: “And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove upon him” (Matt. X).

The dove signifies the Church on account of simplicity of heart. In the Song of Songs: “A beautiful dove, girded with gold and jewels” (Song II).

The doves signify the apostles. In Isaiah: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX.)

The dove signifies the Jews. In Zephaniah: “Woe to the provoking dove; she has not listened to the voice” (Zeph. III).

The dove signifies simplicity of mind. The two dove’s chicks express the twofold lament of repentance. Hence it is read in Leviticus: “But if his hand is not able to offer a sheep, let him offer either two turtledoves or two young doves” (Lev. V) [Col. 0249B].

The wood pigeon (*palumbes*) is called a chaste bird because of its conduct, since it is the companion of chastity. It is said that, once it has lost its bodily mate, it goes about alone and does not seek sexual union again. The turtledove, as we said above, represents the type of the holy Church, because apart from Christ the Lord it knows no other consort. Likewise, the dove signifies the Holy Spirit or the Church, concerning which it is written: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song VI). And again: “The feathers of the dove are silvered” (Ps. LXVII), because the dove possesses innocence and shines with the silvery brightness of divine utterances [Col. 0249C].

The dove is also used in another sense, as in Hosea: “Ephraim is a dove without understanding, without a heart” (Hos. VII).

Again, the turtledove signifies the Holy Spirit, or a holy man, or spiritual understanding, as in the Song of Songs: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song II). The dove is called the Holy Spirit when there is a clear exposition of sacred Scripture; the turtledove, however, is understood as the Holy Spirit when minds are raised by the lofty and obscure mysteries of Scripture.

The partridge (*perdix*) receives its name from its voice. It is a deceitful and unclean bird. The male rises against the male, and reckless lust forgets its sex. It is so fraudulent that it steals another bird’s eggs and broods them; but fraud bears no fruit. For when the chicks hear the voice of their true mother, by a kind of natural instinct they abandon the one that brooded them and return to the one who gave them birth. The partridge therefore signifies the devil, concerning whom it is written in Jeremiah: “The partridge broods what it did not hatch; he makes his riches without judgment. In the middle of his days he will abandon them” (Jer. XVII). Thus the devil, through the leaders of the heretics, gathered peoples whom he had not begotten and joined to himself a multitude of the deceived; afterward he abandoned them and was shown by the judgment of all to be utterly foolish [Col. 0249D].

It is established that quails (*coturnices*) are named from the sound of their voice. The Greeks call them *ortyges*, because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They have fixed seasons for arriving: when summer has passed, they cross the seas. The *ortygometra* is the one that leads the flock [Col. 0250A]. When a hawk sees her approaching the land, it seizes her. Therefore the entire flock is concerned to entice the leader of the foreign race, through whom they may avoid the first dangers. Their favorite food is the seed of poisonous plants, for which reason the ancients forbade people to eat them. This is the only animal, apart from the human being, that suffers from falling sickness.

The quails given as food to the children of Israel are held by some to represent the figure of the historical law; concerning this it is read in Exodus.

Sparrows (*passeres*) are flying creatures named from their smallness; hence they are called little and small. Concerning one it is written in the Psalm: “The sparrow has found a house for herself” (Ps. LXXXIII). And elsewhere: “Like a solitary sparrow on a roof” (Ps. CI). Again, in another sense, in the Psalm: “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow” (Ps. X).

Sparrows also signify the saints. In the Psalter: “There the sparrows will build their nests [Col. 0250B]” (Ps. CIII).

The sparrow is extremely swift because of its great speed. It does not tolerate living in the woods but eagerly seeks out a house in the holes of walls. When it has found one, it rejoices with immense joy, believing that it will no longer be exposed to the snares of various adversities. Thus the soul rejoices when it senses that its dwelling in the kingdom of heaven has been prepared.

The sparrows that were commanded to be offered in the cleansing of a leper in Leviticus signify the mystery of Christ’s passion, through which we are cleansed from the filth of sins. Paul demonstrates this when he says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI). In this rite the living sparrow, cedar wood, twisted scarlet, and hyssop are dipped. All these things are included in the power of baptism, which, as we have said, is a figure and signification of the Lord’s passion [Col. 0250C].

The living sparrow, whom we necessarily understand as the divinity of the Only-Begotten, is also dipped in the blood of the sparrow that was killed and in water—that is, in the grace of baptism—for they are baptized not in the passion of a human being but of God and human being. After this, the living sparrow is released into the field so that it may fly. Thus the impassible divinity was inseparable from the flesh that suffered. It is therefore baptized inseparably in blood, so that, alive and impassible, it may fly away into the field—that is, it is sent forth into the breadth of contemplation, while our understanding releases it and yet holds it beneath this contemplation.

There is another meaning of the sparrow, as we said above. Hence it is read: “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow” (Ps. X).

There are also many kinds of sparrows [Col. 0250D]. Some delight in holes in walls; others seek dewy valleys; some desire barren mountains. But the Prophet now speaks of those who are carried by a very light impulse toward the highest places of the earth, so that they may rightly be judged similar to those who, through the fickleness of an inconstant mind, are transferred to the most wicked teachings. For in the Psalm the Prophet says:

> “I have become like a pelican in solitude;  
> I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.  
> I have watched and have become like a solitary sparrow on a roof” (Ps. CI).

Through these names of birds, as I think, various kinds of penitents are declared to us.

The pelican is an Egyptian bird, similar to the stork in the size of its body. It is always affected by natural leanness [Col. 0251A], because, as the physiologists hold, its intestine is stretched through its internal organs and transmits whatever food it takes without any digestion. Consequently it is not filled with its own fat, since it is restored by only a very small amount of nourishment. It does not fly in flocks like other birds but comforts itself in solitary delight. One kind is said to inhabit ponds; another, as has been said, lives in deserted and secluded places. Through this kind of bird hermits are beautifully signified: having abandoned human society, they torment themselves in the fear of the Lord through secluded affliction.

The text continues: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” Another kind of penitent is introduced. In Greek the *nycticorax* means “night-raven.” Some have said that it is an owl, others a *noctua* [Col. 0251B]; still others testify that it resembles a raven in size and color and is found especially in the regions of Asia. Just as the brightness of day conceals it, so the coming of night reveals it. Contrary to the habits of birds, it begins to keep watch and seek food precisely when all living creatures prepare themselves for sleep.

So this penitent seeks the food of the soul during the night with attentive diligence: sometimes devoting himself to psalmody, sometimes giving alms, sometimes secretly visiting prisons. He wishes to have God alone as his witness, for the darkness of night does not remove anything from God’s sight. Notice that, just as the pelican signifies the hermit and solitary, so the night-raven declares the one who keeps himself within a dwelling and withdraws from public view. The night-raven may also signify Christ or a holy man despised among the faithful [Col. 0251C].

The sparrow is a small bird, as we said above, but it is exceedingly alert and cautious. It is not easily caught in snares, nor is it deceived by greed for food through the gluttony of its belly. Because of its weakness, and lest it itself be seized by a predator or its young be devoured by serpentine attacks, it alone among birds, protected by its vigilance, hastens to the high roofs of houses. Thus it is kept apart from suspected dangers, although it is exposed to many perils.

It is rightly compared with the person who fears the devil’s snares and, withdrawing especially to the enclosure of the Church, perseveres most safely in watchfulness upon its height. He says “solitary” because charity makes one out of many; “on a roof” because of the height of faith and the strength of mind.

It should also be considered how this petitioner began with the larger birds, the pelican and the night-raven, and reached the very smallest size of the sparrow. For as he descends gradually through repentance, he is great at the first stage, moderate at the second, and at the third entirely tolerable through the very habit of repentance [Col. 0251D]. These birds, figuratively, are a parable of people differing in kind but alike in the quality of their habits.

The swallow (*hirundo*) is so called because it does not take food while sitting, but catches and eats it in the air. It is a chattering bird, flying through winding circles and twisting circuits, and very skillful in building nests and raising its young. It also possesses a certain foresight: it abandons and avoids what is about to fall and does not seek high places. Other birds do not attack it, nor is it ever prey [Col. 0252A]. It flies across the sea and remains there during winter.

The swallow represents penitents on account of their sins. Its shrill voice sounds more like weeping than melody, and instead of singing it commonly produces groans, like the dove. Hence Hezekiah says in his prayer: “Like a swallow’s chick, so I will cry out; I will meditate like a dove” (Isa. XXXVIII).

The penitent is therefore nourished by his tears and, raising his heart to things above, seeks for himself the food of heavenly nourishment. Hence the Prophet says: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI). And again: “I ate my bread like ashes, and mingled my drink with weeping, because of the face of your anger and indignation; for, lifting me up, you have cast me down” (Ps. CI).

The Greeks call it the *upupa*, because it looks upon human excrement and feeds upon foul smoke. It is an exceedingly filthy bird, helmeted by projecting crests and always dwelling among tombs and human dung [Col. 0252B]. This bird signifies wicked and sinful people who continually delight in lingering amid the filth of sins.

The raven (*corvus*, or *corax*) receives its name from the sound of its throat, because it croaks. It is said that this bird does not fully provide food for its young after they are hatched until it recognizes in them, from the blackness of their feathers, a likeness to its own color. Once it sees them entirely dark with feathers and recognizes them, it feeds them more abundantly.

The raven first attacks the eyes of corpses. It signifies the blackness of sins or demons, as in Solomon: “May the ravens dig it out from the valleys” (Prov. XXX).

The raven [Col. 0252C] also signifies the Gentile people, as in Job: “Who prepares food for the raven, when its young cry out to the Lord, wandering because they have no food?” (Job XXXIX). Food is given to the raven’s young—that is, to the children of the Gentiles—when their desire is refreshed by our conversion.

Again, the raven is used in a good sense, as in the Song of Songs concerning the bridegroom: “His locks are like fir trees, black as ravens” (Song V).

The raven is Christ in his members, that is, in the saints, as in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like raised palm branches, black like a raven” (ibid.).

The raven signifies the blackness of sin or unbelief, as in the Psalm: “And the young of the ravens that call upon him” (Ps. CXLVI).

The raven signifies the sinner’s tardiness in repenting and his postponement from day to day through vain hope, as in Zephaniah: “The voice of one singing [Col. 0252D] at the window, a raven on its thresholds” (Zeph. II).

The crow (*cornix*) is a long-lived bird, called by the Latins by a Greek name. Augurs claim that it manages human concerns through signs, points out the paths of ambushes, and predicts the future. It is therefore a great sacrilege to believe that God entrusts his counsels to crows. Among its many supposed omens, they also attribute to it the prediction of rain through its cries. Hence the verse:

> “Then the wicked crow calls for rain with a full voice.”

But let us set aside these uncertainties and attempt to write about more certain matters.

The kite (*milvus*) is soft both in strength and in flight, as though a soft bird. Yet it is exceedingly rapacious and always lies in wait for domestic birds [Col. 0253A]. The kite signifies a rapacious or proud person, as in the Psalm according to the Hebrews: “The fir tree is the kite’s home.”

The hawk (*accipiter*) is more heavily armed in spirit than in talons, carrying greater strength in a smaller body. It takes its name from *accipere*, “to seize,” that is, from catching. It is eager to seize other birds and is therefore called *accipiter*, “the taker” or “raptor.” Hence Paul says: “For you endure it if someone takes” (II Cor. XI). He did not say, “if someone robs,” but “if someone takes.”

Hawks are said to be harsh toward their young. When they see that the young are able to attempt flight, they provide them with no food; instead they beat them with their wings and cast them from the nest, forcing the tender young to hunt, lest, once grown, they become sluggish.

The hawk sometimes signifies a holy man, as one who seizes the kingdom of God [Col. 0253B]. Concerning it it is written in Job: “Does the hawk grow feathered in your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south?” (Job XXXIX.) That is: Have you granted understanding to any of the elect, so that, when the Holy Spirit blows, he may spread the wings of his thoughts, cast off the burdens of his former way of life, and take up the feathers of the virtues for a new flight?

Through this hawk renewed Gentile society may also be signified.

The *capus* is called *capus* in the Italian language, from *capere*, “to seize.” Our people call it a falcon; it is also known by another name, *herodius*. This bird too can signify rapacious people.

That certain birds are counted among the unclean in Leviticus and Deuteronomy is shown by Scripture, which says:

> “Eat all clean birds; you shall not eat the unclean: namely, the eagle, the griffin [Col. 0253C], the sea-eagle, the *ixion*, the vulture, and the kite according to their kinds; and every species of raven; the ostrich, the owl, the gull, and the hawk according to their kinds; the heron, the swan, the ibis, the diver, the purple bird, the night-raven, the onocrotalus, and the plover, each according to its kind; the hoopoe also and the bat; and everything that creeps and has feathers shall be unclean and shall not be eaten” (Lev. XI; Deut. XIV).

Among unlawful and exceedingly avoidable things, one should count anyone devoted to contemplation who bears the sort of stains that the lawgiver signifies through the birds just enumerated. He says: “The eagle, the griffin, the sea-eagle, the kite, and the vulture according to their kinds.” Through these he signifies rapacious people who wickedly pursue what belongs to others and rejoice in unjust profits.

For since some are found in churches [Col. 0253D] among those thought to devote themselves to contemplation—people who do not attend to it as they ought but are vainly puffed up—let them hear Paul saying:

> “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with piety, he is arrogant and knows nothing, but is sick with disputes and controversies over words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that piety is a means of gain” (I Tim. VI).

These animals therefore signify those who seek their food through plunder. Some of them attack other birds and are nourished by their hunting. Others enter houses [Col. 0254A] and carry off whatever they find, sparing not even the food of those who possess it. Some people resemble these: they penetrate houses and take captive little women burdened with sins; Paul rebukes them (II Tim. III).

The vulture delights in quarrels and wars on account of the corpses left by battles, to such an extent that it even follows an army. One who devotes himself to contemplation must not therefore feed and nourish himself on the misfortunes of others.

The creatures of the raven kind are without affection. This is made clear by the fact that the raven sent out by Noah transgressed from him on its first flight (Gen. VIII). Judas was like it toward his master and Lord.

The ostrich is indeed a bird, but it cannot fly and occupies its entire life around the earth. Such are some who serve God while entangling themselves in the affairs of the world [Col. 0254B].

The owl—called *glaucus* by the Seventy—is said to have keen sight at night but to enjoy less use of its eyes when the sun appears. Such are those who glory in contemplation and knowledge of the law but are unable to grasp the light of evangelical conduct.

The gull is an animal that lives in both elements, water and land. As a bird it flies, but as an aquatic creature it swims. Those who simultaneously honor circumcision and baptism are not improperly compared with it. Paul says to them: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V).

The hawk is among the rapacious birds. It has another characteristic for which the lawgiver included it: it becomes tame and cooperates in rapacity. Those who appear tame and peaceful in disposition but associate with the powerful, the greedy, and the rapacious imitate it [Col. 0254C].

The night-raven is a creature that seizes and works only at night. Such are the Gentiles occupied in the intelligible works of night: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, the worship of idols, and similar things.

The ibis and the purple bird, and the creatures whom the Seventy call the pelican, the swan, the heron, and the plover, are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the heights of the earth and the waters. We must not imitate these animals or pull food from what is below, but from heavenly things. The person who devotes himself to contemplation strives toward higher things in mind and awaits from God not only intelligible food but also bodily food. Hence the Lord says:

> “Do not be anxious for your soul [Col. 0254D], what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matt. VI).

The hoopoe is a mournful animal and loves grief. “The sorrow of the world produces death” (II Cor. VII). Therefore the one who loves God ought always to rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things, because joy is the fruit of the spirit.

Bats fly close to the earth, using their wings as feet when they walk. This is unworthy of those who devote themselves to contemplation. For those whose flight is around the earth undoubtedly have their contemplation occupied with earthly things.

Therefore do not be unbelieving or doubtful that the lawgiver also placed the animals now enumerated as figures and signs of those from whom people devoted to contemplation ought to abstain [Col. 0255A].

But you will say: How is it that the food of these animals, rather than their imitation, is prohibited, when the Prophet David compared himself with the pelican and the night-raven, saying: “I have become like a pelican in solitude; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling” (Ps. CI)? Through the eagle Moses himself signifies God speaking to Israel: “How I carried you on the wings of eagles” (Deut. XXXII). The Prophets also call Christ a lion. Yet Peter, conversely, says that the lion is the devil (I Pet. V). Christ is not therefore a lion in the same respect in which the devil is called a lion; far be this from us, far be such impiety.

Rather, because the animal is at once royal, rapacious [Col. 0255B], and fierce, and because it produces both a praiseworthy dignity and a blameworthy activity, what it has that is praiseworthy is understood in Christ’s kingdom, while what is blameworthy in the devil—that is, rapacity and savageness—is understood there. Considering the eagle in the same way, we find this without any doubt. Because of its lofty flight, Moses took it as a figure of God. But because it is rapacious, he said that its meat should be abstained from.

The Prophet David, mourning a person established in sin, compared him to the night-raven as one living in the night. Through the pelican, as an animal that loves solitude, he represented one who has perhaps been abandoned by friends or deprived of the company of relatives and others of the same kind.

Augurs say that signs are established [Col. 0255C] in the posture, movement, flight, and voice of birds. They call those birds *oscines* that give omens through their mouths and songs, such as the raven, crow, and woodpecker. They call *alites* those that appear to show the future by their flight. If their signs are unfavorable, they are called *inhibae*, because they inhibit—that is, forbid; if favorable, they are called *praepetes*. They are called *praepetes* because all birds, when flying, seek what is ahead.

They make a third kind of augury in birds, which they call common, mixed from both kinds: namely, birds that give omens both from their mouths and from their flight. But the faith of Christ does not admit these things.

All kinds of birds are born twice. First eggs are produced; then, through the warmth of the mother’s body, they are formed and brought to life. Eggs are called *ova* because they are moist (*uvida*). Hence *uva*, “grape,” also receives its name because it is full of moisture within. That which has moisture on the outside is called *humidum*; that which has it within is called *uvidum* [Col. 0255D].

Some, however, think that *ovum* has a Greek origin. They say that it comes from *oa* with the letter *v* removed. Some eggs are conceived by an empty wind, but only those conceived through male intercourse and penetrated by seminal breath are capable of generation. They say that eggs possess such power that wood drenched with them will not burn; nor will a garment touched by them be scorched. Mixed with lime, they are also said to glue together fragments of glass.

## CHAPTER VII. On Bees

[Manuscript: On Small Birds]

Bees are so called either because they bind themselves to one another with their feet, or because they are born without feet. For afterward they acquire both feet and wings. These industrious creatures occupy assigned dwellings for the task of producing honey; they construct their homes with indescribable skill, make honeycombs from various flowers, and fill their woven waxen structures with countless offspring. They have an army and kings; they wage battles; they flee smoke; and they are provoked by tumult. For many have discovered that they are born from the corpses of oxen. To produce them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, so that worms may be generated from the putrefied blood, and these later become bees. Properly, however, bees are called those born from oxen, just as hornets are born from horses, drones from mules, and wasps from asses.

The Greeks call *castros* [reading uncertain] the larger creatures produced at the outermost parts of the honeycombs; some think that they are called kings because they lead the armies. A drone is larger than a bee but smaller than a hornet. It is called a drone because it consumes the labor of others, as though from *fagus* (“one who eats”). For it devours what it has not labored to produce. Of it Virgil says:

> They drive the idle swarm of drones from the feeding troughs.

Bees represent virginity or wisdom, as in Solomon’s saying:

> Go to the bee, and learn what kind of worker it is.

They have another signification where it is read in the Prophet:

> The Lord whistled for the fly that is at the end of the rivers of Egypt in the desert, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria (Isaiah 7).

There he figuratively indicates Pharaoh by the fly and Nebuchadnezzar by the bee: they chastised the sinful people of the Jews with deserved scourges. It is also read in the Psalm:

> They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns (Psalm 117).

Bees surround the honeycomb when, through waxen houses, they store away their sweetest liquids; and when they think they are laying up provisions for themselves, they make something from which human beings can satisfy their desires. It is evident that the Jews fulfilled this, when they subjected something most sweet to the whole world to bitter efforts.

Thorns signify the sins of the world. The Jewish people, violently driven on by them in their transgressions, seethed like crackling fire. Yet even in them the Lord’s grace was vindicated, when, converted to the Lord, they were most sweetly filled with that honey which they had stored up unknowingly.

Drones, which consume the labor of others, signify idle people languishing in sloth, who prefer to have nourishment supplied to them from the works of others rather than from their own sweat. Concerning them Paul writes to the Thessalonians:

> We hear that some among you are walking disorderly, doing no work, but meddling. To such people we announce and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they should eat their own bread (2 Thessalonians 3).

Hornets (*scabrones*) are called from *caballus*, that is, “horse,” because, as some think, they are created from horses. Just as hornets are born from the rotten flesh of horses, so beetles often arise from them again; hence they have received their name. Bulls are terrestrial or woodland beetles resembling the tick.

Wasps or hornets signify pursuing enemies or fear of enemies, as in the Lord’s promise in the Law, which he gave to Israel through Moses:

> The Lord will send hornets ahead of your entry, which will destroy the Canaanite, Hivite, and Perizzite (Wisdom 12).

It is not found anywhere in the history of the Old Testament that the Lord sent hornets or wasps ahead of the children of Israel against their enemies. Rather, by these animals, which fight with stings, he signifies the fears of compunction among their enemies, by which they were pierced and driven away.

Concerning the beetle it is written in the Prophet:

> And the beetle cried out from the wood.

Some think that this was said of the Lord, who, suspended on the cross, prayed for his persecutors, saying:

> Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing (Luke 23);

or of the thief who cried out to Christ on the cross, saying:

> Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom (ibid.).

The locust is so called because it has long legs, like a spear. Hence the Greeks call both the marine and terrestrial locust *astakos* [ἀστακός]. Sometimes the locust signifies unstable and wandering peoples, as in the Gospel concerning John:

> His food was locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3);

for the conversion of the peoples to the faith of Christ became his delightful and sweet nourishment.

Likewise, in Exodus it is read that the locust was sent into Egypt as the eighth plague (Exodus 10). By this kind of plague, some think that the fickleness of the human race—divided and discordant within itself—is rebuked.

The locust signifies the people of the nations, as in Solomon:

> The locust has no king, yet it goes forth in companies (Proverbs 30).

Likewise, locusts signify demons, as in the Apocalypse:

> Locusts came out of the smoke (Apocalypse 9).

And in the Book of Judges:

> Their camels were like locusts (Judges 7).

The locust signifies pride or the wandering of the mind, as in Joel:

> What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten (Joel 1).

In another sense, locusts are to be understood as representing the fickleness of frivolity, like wandering souls leaping into the pleasures of the world.

Likewise, by the signification of the locust—which harms human crops more than all other small creatures—the tongues of flatterers are expressed. When they observe the minds of earthly people producing some good, they corrupt them by praising them immoderately. The fruit of the Egyptians is the work of those who seek empty glory; locusts destroy it when flattering tongues incline the worker’s heart to desire passing praise. Locusts eat the grasses when flatterers exalt the words of speakers with popular approval. They also devour the fruits of trees when, through vain praises, they weaken the works of certain people who are already, as it were, strong.

The fly comes from the Greek, as does *mus* (“mouse”). These creatures, like bees, sometimes revive after being killed in water and left for the space of an hour.

In Greek it is called *cynomya*, that is, “dog-fly.” For *kyno* [κύων] in Greek means “dog.” Flies signify unclean spirits or sinners who pursue the squalor of vices and corrupt the oil of mercy and charity with the filth of their crimes. Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes:

> Dead flies ruin the sweetness of the perfume (Ecclesiastes 10);

for an evil person mixed with the good contaminates many. Just as flies, if they die in perfume, destroy its odor and flavor, so cunning soils wisdom and malice prudence.

In the fourth place Egypt is struck by flies (Exodus 8). The fly is an insolent and restless creature. What else is signified by it but the insolent anxieties of carnal desires? Egypt, therefore, is struck by flies because the hearts of those who love this world are battered by the restlessness of their desires.

The translators of the Septuagint, however, rendered it *cynomya*, that is, “dog-fly,” by which doglike behavior is signified: in such people the will of the human mind and the lust of the flesh are reproved. At this point the dog-fly may also signify the forensic eloquence of human beings, by which, like dogs, they tear one another apart.

The gnat is so called from its sting, by which it sucks blood. For it has in its mouth a tube shaped like a thorn, with which it pierces the flesh in order to drink blood.

*Scinifes* are extremely small flies, very troublesome because of their stings. By them the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague. This creature is suspended by its wings and flits through the air, but it is so subtle and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eye unless the observer looks sharply. When it settles on the body, however, it pierces it with an exceedingly painful sting, so that although no one can see it flying, he immediately feels its arrival.

This kind of creature is therefore compared with heretical subtlety. Heresy pierces souls with the subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such cunning that the deceived person neither sees nor understands from where the deception comes. Yet, by blaspheming against the Trinity, heretics scatter the faith of the whole world.

The *bruchus* signifies gluttony of the belly. Hence also the earlier statement:

> What the caterpillar left, the bruchus has eaten (Joel 1).

Rust signifies anger of the heart, as in Joel:

> What the bruchus left, the rust has eaten (ibid.).

The caterpillar signifies the itching of lust, concerning which it was also said above:

> What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten (ibid.).

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0257]

## PROLOGUE. On the World and Its Four Regions

[Col. 0257D]

In sacred discourse there is therefore a great discernment of interpretation. Often, in certain passages, both the historical sense and the allegory must be preserved; often, in others, only the allegory is to be sought; and sometimes it is necessary to retain only the historical sense. In certain passages, as we have said, history and allegory must be held together, so that the slower minds may be nourished by the history and those quicker in understanding by the allegory.

Thus, when the people saw the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain while God was speaking, they were terrified and asked that the Lord speak to them through Moses. Hence it is written:

> The people stood far away, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was (Exodus 20).

The crowd of the people is unable to penetrate the darkness of allegories, because it belongs to very few to investigate spiritual understanding. Since the minds of the carnal are often nourished by history alone, the people stood far away while God was speaking. But since spiritual people penetrate the cloud of allegories in order to understand God’s words spiritually, Moses approached the darkness in which God was.

Therefore, in this work, where we have decided to write about the variety of things and their various significations, we first identify the things themselves and then briefly discuss their meanings. Beginning with the world, we shall subsequently set forth its parts in our exposition.

The world is heaven and earth, the sea, and the works of God that are in them. Concerning it is said:

> And the world was made through him (John 1).

The world is called *mundus* in Latin by philosophers because it is in perpetual motion, like heaven, the sun, the moon, the air, and the seas. No rest has been granted to its elements; therefore it is always in motion.

The Greeks applied to the world the name of an ornament because of the diversity of the elements and the beauty of the stars. Among them it is called *cosmos* [κόσμος], which signifies “ornament.” For we see nothing more beautiful in the world with the eyes of the flesh.

The world is understood historically as the joining together of all the elements. At other times, according to allegory, it is used in a good sense, and at other times in the contrary sense.

The world is understood historically where the Evangelist says:

> He was in the world, and the world was made through him (ibid.).

And where the Lord says:

> I came as light into this world (John 12).

He was in the world, and the world was made through him, because he was God, wholly present everywhere: without labor he governs, and without burden he sustains what he made. In this world, which he had first created through his divinity, he later appeared as a human being born.

But what follows—

> And the world did not know him (John 1)—

signifies human beings deceived by love of the world and, by clinging to the creature, turned away from recognizing the majesty of their Creator.

As we have said, the world is understood in two ways: one way in sinners and another in saints. When the Lord says to the Father:

> So that the world may believe that you sent me (John 17),

and elsewhere:

> So that the world may know that I love the Father (John 14),

he calls “the world” those who were going to believe, or those who at that time believed that Christ, the Son of God, had been sent by the Father into the world for the salvation of the human race.

But when he says:

> Righteous Father, the world did not know you, but I knew you (John 17),

it did not know him because it was condemned by justice. But the world that was to be saved knew you through mercy. Christ himself reconciled it—not by merit, but by grace.

Hence Jesus is called the Savior of the world, that is, of the Catholic Church, because he is the Savior of all, and especially of the faithful.

When the Lord is read to have said:

> For the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me (John 12),

he shows here that the devil is prince of sinful human beings, not of God’s creatures. Whenever the figure of the world is used in an evil sense, it indicates nothing except lovers of that world and not of God.

Far be it from us to believe that he is prince of heaven and earth and of all creatures, which are generally called by the name “world.” Everything serves its Creator, not its deceiver; its Redeemer, not its destroyer. Everything is governed by divine dispensation and is not overturned by the enemy’s cunning, except for those human beings who, of their own will and not from any necessity, subject themselves to the devil.

Sometimes even the ambition for earthly things is signified by the name “world.” Hence the apostle John says:

> Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2).

By “everything that is in the world,” he means all who dwell in the world in their minds and inhabit the world through love, just as those whose hearts are above inhabit heaven, although in the flesh they walk upon the earth. Everything that is in the world—that is, the lovers of the world—has nothing but the desire of the flesh and of the eyes, and the pride of life. By these names of vices he embraces every kind of vice.

The desire of the flesh is everything that pertains to bodily pleasure and luxury, among which the chief things are food, drink, and intercourse. Solomon compares these three to leeches.

The desire of the eyes is manifested in learning wicked arts, watching shameful or unnecessary spectacles, acquiring temporal possessions, and discerning and criticizing the faults of one’s neighbors.

The pride of life occurs when someone boasts of his honors. By these three things human desire is tested; by these Adam and the Lord himself were tested.

They say that there are four climates of the world, that is, regions: east and west, north and south.

The East is named from the rising of the sun. The West is so called because it makes the day set and perish: for it conceals the world’s light and brings darkness upon it.

The North is named from the seven stars of the axis, which revolve in that region. It is properly called the *vertex*, because it turns, as the poet says:

> Meanwhile the heavens turn . . . .

The South is so called either because the sun makes midday there, as though *medidies*, or because the ether then shines more purely. For *merum* means “pure.”

Mystically, the East signifies the Lord the Savior, concerning whom it is written in Luke:

> The Dawn from on high has visited us (Luke 1).

And in the prophet Zechariah:

> Behold, the man whose name is Dawn (Zechariah 6).

The East signifies the Jewish people, or the illumination of faith, as the Church is described in Isaiah:

> From the East I will bring your offspring (Isaiah 43).

The West signifies the people of the nations. Hence also above:

> And from the West I will gather you (ibid.).

The West also signifies the decline of a better life, or the setting of death. Hence it is written to sinners in the Prophet:

> The sun will set for you at noon (Amos 8).

And the Psalmist says:

> Then, he says, make way for him who rises above the setting; the Lord is his name (Psalm 67).

Likewise, setting signifies the cooling of the incitements of lust after the heat of temptation. Thus in Deuteronomy, concerning one who is polluted by nocturnal sleep—that is, by a hidden thought—it is commanded that he not return to the camp before washing his garments and waiting until the sun has set.

Again, the East designates the beginning of our good life, and the West the inclination toward an evil way of life, as in the Psalm:

> As far as the East is from the West, so far has he removed our iniquities from us (Psalm 103).

We were in the West when we were held bound by the chain of sin. But we are in the East when the true Sun visits us through the water of regeneration and causes the darkness of our sins to depart.

Thus our iniquities are as far removed from us when our sins are marked out as the clear day can be from the dark night.

Alternatively, the East signifies the kingdom of God, while the West signifies Gehenna, which is separated from the dwelling of the blessed as greatly as Abraham says when speaking to the rich man:

> Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed (Luke 16).

The northern region of the world, from which frost and dryness proceed, figuratively displays the devil or the coldness of unbelief. Concerning it it is written:

> You created the north and the sea. Tabor and Hermon rejoice in your name; your arm is with power (Psalm 88).

By the north he designates the devil, who said:

> I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High (Isaiah 14).

Hence it is read elsewhere:

> The north is a harsh wind, which is called “right” by another name, either because the devil arrogates to himself the name of the right, as though he were good, or because for those who look toward the West—that is, toward sin—it becomes the right side.

The north signifies the people of the nations, as in Isaiah:

> I will say to the north, “Give” (Isaiah 43).

And in the Psalter:

> The sides of the north are the city of the great king (Psalm 47).

And in Job:

> From the north comes gold (Job 37).

The southern and austral region of the world is called from the south wind. By its heat it disperses cold and melts ice, signifying the grace of the Holy Spirit, who by the heat of charity drives away the coldness of unbelief and dissolves the hardness of sins.

Hence it is written:

> Turn, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south wind (Psalm 125).

This wind also signifies the Jewish people, who possess the light of knowledge in the Scriptures and in the Law and Prophets, just as the north signifies the gentile people dwelling in the darkness of unbelief and the foolishness of error. Through the Gospel, the grace of Christ summoned both peoples to himself.

Likewise, in the north the adversities of the world are designated, and in the south its consolations. Through this twofold struggle the Church is tested, and through steadfastness of faith it spreads the wonderful fragrance of virtues.

Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs:

> Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow (Song of Songs 4).

“Arise” is the word of one permitting, not commanding.

The south is also understood in the contrary sense, as in the Psalm:

> From the ruin and the noonday demon (Psalm 90).

The noonday demon is an immense danger kindled by the heat of persecution, where ruin is often feared.

The south wind signifies the Church, which first brought forth Christ from the Jews, as in the Prophet:

> You who dwell in the southern land, bring water to the thirsty (Isaiah 21),

that is, baptism to believers.

And in Job:

> From the north comes gold, and from the south [and toward God] fearful praise (Job 37).

The south wind is the holy Church, kindled by the warmth of faith.

## CHAPTER ONE. On Atoms

[Col. 0262A]

Philosophers call certain parts of bodies in the world *atoms*, so exceedingly small that they are neither visible to the sight nor subject to *tomē*, that is, division. Hence they are called *atoms*. In the morning they flit about through the whole world in restless movements and are said to be carried here and there, like the finest dust seen scattered through windows in the rays of the sun.

Some gentile philosophers have thought that trees, grasses, and all crops arise from these, and that fire, water, and everything else are generated from them and consist of them. Atoms are found either in body, in time, or in number.

In body, for example, there is a stone. You divide it into parts, and divide those parts into grains, such as grains of sand. Then divide the grains of sand again into the finest dust, until, if possible, you reach some tiny portion that can no longer be divided or cut. This is the atom in bodies.

In time, the atom is understood as follows. You divide a year, for example, into months; months into days; and days into hours. These parts still admit division, until you arrive at such a point of time, such a small particle of a moment, that it cannot be prolonged by any delay and therefore can no longer be divided. This is the atom of time.

In numbers, for example, eight is divided into four, four again into two, and two into one. Hence one is an atom, because it is indivisible; so too is clay [the text appears corrupt here]. For you divide speech into words, words into syllables, and a syllable into letters. The letter is the smallest part, an atom, and cannot be divided.

An atom, therefore, is that which cannot be divided, as a point is in geometry. For *tomos* [τόμος] means “division” in Greek, while *atomos* [ἄτομος] means “indivision.”

The value of indivisible unity in things, for demonstrating mystical meaning, is clearly indicated by Scripture, since it shows that unity itself is the beginning of all things. The Apostle says:

> One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in us all, who is blessed forever (Ephesians 4).

Hence the same Apostle commands us to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, so that there may be one body and one Spirit, just as we were called in one hope of our calling.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Elements

[Col. 0262D]

The Greeks call *hylē* [ὕλη] a certain first matter of things, formed in no way at all but capable of receiving all bodily forms. From it these visible elements were formed, and therefore they received their name from it.

The Latins call this *hylē* “matter,” because everything unformed from which something is to be made is always called matter. They also appropriately called it “woodland” or “forest,” since forests consist of matter.

The Greeks call the elements *stoicheia* [στοιχεῖα], because they agree with one another through a harmony of association and a certain communion. For they are said to be joined together among themselves by a natural principle: beginning with fire and proceeding down to earth, and again from earth up to fire. Fire ends in air, air is condensed into water, and water thickens into earth; then earth is dissolved into water, water becomes rarified into air, and air is thinned into fire.

Therefore all the elements are present in all the others, but each receives its name from that which it possesses in greater measure. They have been distributed by divine Providence according to their proper portions. The Creator himself filled heaven with angels, the air with birds, the sea with fish, the earth with human beings, and the churches with living creatures.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Heaven

Heaven is so called because, like an engraved vessel, it bears the impressed lights of the stars, as though they were signs. In the holy Scriptures heaven is called the firmament because the course of the stars has been established and strengthened by fixed laws.

Sometimes “heaven” is also understood as the air, where winds, clouds, storms, and whirlwinds arise.

In sacred Scripture, even those things that can be understood historically are often to be understood spiritually, so that faith may be maintained in the truth of the history and spiritual understanding may be grasped in the mysteries of allegory.

Thus we know that the Psalmist says:

> For I will see the heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you established (Psalm 8).

Here, according to the truth of the history, the statement is entirely reasonable: the heavens are indeed God’s works, and the moon and stars were created and established by him.

But if the Psalmist asserts only the historical meaning and not also the mystical one, having professed that the heavens are God’s work, why, when he is about to speak of the moon and stars, did he not also enumerate the sun, which we know to be his work? If he were speaking according to history alone, when he intended to name the lesser light he should first have named the greater light, so that he might mention the sun before the moon and stars as having been established.

But because he was speaking according to mystical understanding, so that we should understand the moon as the holy Church and the stars as holy people, he did not wish to name the sun, since he was speaking to that eternal Sun concerning whom it is written:

> But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise (Malachi 4).

According to allegory, heaven sometimes signifies the Lord himself, the Savior, as in:

> Heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord (Psalm 113),

because he is the Holy of Holies and God of gods. Thus he is rightly called the heaven of heavens, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells.

At other times it signifies the angelic powers, as in Genesis:

> In the beginning God made heaven and earth (Genesis 1).

He first called heaven the firmament because these were the heavens that had initially been created well, but afterward were called the firmament because they received the power of immutability so that they could no longer fall.

To them the Prophet says elsewhere:

> Hear, O heavens, because the Lord has spoken (Isaiah 1).

Likewise, by the name “heavens,” prophets, apostles, and holy people are signified, as in:

> The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 18);

for by discussing Christ’s coming they filled the whole world with holy exhortations.

Concerning these heavens it is said elsewhere:

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power (Psalm 32);

because, after the ascension, Christ sent the Holy Spirit from above, and the apostles were strengthened in faith and knowledge.

Thus, in the beginning God made heaven (Genesis 1), that is, spiritual people who meditate upon and seek heavenly things in it. He also made carnal people, who have not yet set aside the earthly human being.

Sometimes heaven signifies contemplation of heavenly things, as in:

> They ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses (Psalm 106).

We ascend to the heavens when we penetrate the highest things; but we descend to the abysses when, from the summit of contemplation, we are suddenly cast down by shameful temptations.

Very often in the holy Gospel the present Church is called the kingdom of heaven. The congregation of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven.

Since the Lord says through the Prophet:

> Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet (Isaiah 66),

and Solomon says:

> The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom (Proverbs 15),

while Paul says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1), it is clearly proved that God [the source text is defective here], that is, reigns and decrees his judgments.

This heaven and air, as we said above, is also recognized as that heaven in which Elijah is described as having been carried away, and concerning which the Apostle speaks of unclean spirits:

> Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6).

Another Apostle says:

> The heavens that now exist, and the earth, have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire until the day of judgment (2 Peter 3).

Sometimes sacred Scripture is designated by the name “heaven,” concerning which it is said:

> Stretching out heaven like a skin (Psalm 103).

From it the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and, from the ancient fathers, the stars of examples and virtues shine upon us.

It is stretched out like a skin because, having been set forth through its writers in the language of the flesh, it is unfolded before our eyes through the words of teachers.

The Lord covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters because the heights of sacred discourse—that is, those things it tells us about the nature of divinity or eternal joys—are still unknown to us and known secretly only to the angels.

For elsewhere in the Psalter it is read:

> Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord (Psalm 148).

Although we read in Genesis that one heaven was made, the Apostle Paul also called them by the plural number (2 Corinthians 12), reporting that he was caught up into the third heaven and there learned things which it is not lawful for a human being to speak. Here, too, they are named in the plural.

Perhaps the matter is consistent for this reason. We say that there is one palace surrounded by many chambers and many spaces; so perhaps we call the parts of heaven “heavens,” while its whole structure and interior show it to be one.

Genesis reports that there are waters above the heavens. For it says:

> And he divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament (Genesis 1).

The firmament is understood as the divine Scriptures in the Church, because heaven will be folded up like a book. Above this firmament he separated the waters, that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who have no need to receive this firmament in order to hear the word of God by reading the Law. They always see him and love him.

But he placed the firmament of his Law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, by receiving it, they might learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the Parts of Heaven

That same place is called *aether*, where the stars are, and the term signifies the fire that has been separated from the whole world and raised on high. Strictly speaking, *aether* is the element itself, while *aethera* is the splendor of the ether.

The luminaries stand in the firmament of heaven—that is, fixed in the firmament of God’s Law. These are the evangelists and teachers of sacred Scripture, who remain joined to it through their exposition and display the light of wisdom to all below.

At the same time there appeared, etc., the multitude of shining stars—that is, the multitude of diverse virtues in the Church—which, shining in the obscurity of this life as in night, divide within the firmament of Scripture sensible and intelligible things, as between the light of the perfect and the darkness of the peoples. They are signs of virtues and miracles.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Gates of Heaven

There are two gates of heaven: the East and the West. Through one gate the sun emerges; through the other it withdraws.

The gates of heaven signify the divine Testaments. Hence the Psalmist says:

> He commanded the clouds above and opened the gates of heaven (Psalm 77).

For the clouds—that is, the preachers—were commanded, through the gates of heaven, that is, the holy Scriptures, to announce through glorious preaching the coming of the Lord Savior, who is truly received as manna when he is tasted in the worshipful communion.

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Hinges

There are two hinges of the world: the North and the South. Heaven revolves upon them.

These hinges signify the conduct of the present Church, which extends throughout the whole world and, living according to the two Testaments or the two commandments of charity, directs the course of the present life while tending toward the homeland to come.

Hence it is written:

> The hinges of the earth belong to the Lord, and he has set the world upon them (1 Samuel 2).

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On Light
Light was first formed by the Creator after the creation of heaven and earth, in order to manifest and make known the works of God. Light itself is a substance; radiance proceeds from light—that is, the brightness of light—but authors confuse these terms. Accordingly, the word “light” expresses various meanings. Sometimes it reveals God himself, that is, the whole holy Trinity together; sometimes the Son of God; sometimes holy men; sometimes Holy Scripture; sometimes [Col. 0266A] the preaching of the Gospel; and sometimes the holy Church.

We must understand that the name “light” is common to the entire Trinity. For it is written: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1). Therefore, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, we rightly recognize that this has been said of the whole Trinity: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.” Hence the Psalmist rightly says of the Savior: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35).

That Christ is the true light he himself demonstrates in the Gospel, saying: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8). Concerning him the evangelist John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens everyone coming into the world” (John 1)—that is, everyone who is enlightened [Col. 0266B] either by natural intelligence or by divine wisdom. For just as no one can exist from himself, so no one can be wise from himself; rather, this is possible through the illumination of him concerning whom it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Sirach 1).

Holy men are rightly called light, since the Lord says to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5). The apostle Paul likewise says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5). Yet there is a great difference between the light that is illuminated [printed: “who is illuminated”] and the light that illuminates: between those who receive a share in the true light so that they may shine, and that perpetual light which is sufficient not only to shine in itself but also, by its presence, to illuminate whomever it touches.

Sometimes we understand Holy Scripture as light, as in the verse: [Col. 0266C] “Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Psalm 118). Knowing, therefore, that the night of this age is entangled in various stumbling-blocks—containing snares in one place, crags in another, and elsewhere the deepest wastelands—he testifies that the word of the Lord shines for his feet, lest, in the absence of the true light, he fall into a ruin that he could not avoid by his own foresight. This word must be understood as that which was sown through the Scriptures by the mouth of the prophets. He aptly called this word a lamp, which has been given for human use to dispel the deepest blindness of night, just as the apostle Peter says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter 1).

Likewise, light is the illumination [Col. 0266D] of faith, or the gift of the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4).

Likewise, light and darkness signify the elect and the reprobate, as in Job: “Do you know where light dwells and where darkness dwells, so that you may lead each to its boundaries?” (Job 38).

Likewise, light and darkness signify righteousness and iniquity, as the Apostle says: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, but whoever hates him walks in darkness” (1 John 2).

The lamp also signifies the preaching of the Gospel.
