Hence the Savior says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Luke 11). To put a lamp under a bushel, therefore, is to place bodily advantages above the preaching of truth, so that someone does not preach the truth because he fears suffering some hardship in bodily and temporal matters.

[Col. 0267A] This lamp may also be interpreted as referring to the humanity of the Savior. For he lights the lamp who fills the vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity. He certainly did not wish to hide this lamp from believers or place it under a bushel—that is, enclose it within the measure of the Law—or confine it within the boundaries of the one Jewish nation. He calls the Church the lampstand, upon which he placed the lamp, because they fixed the faith of his incarnation upon our foreheads, so that those who wished faithfully to enter the Church might be able openly to behold the light of truth.

The holy Church is also designated by the name “light,” as in the verse: “Clothed in light as with a garment” (Psalm 103). [Col. 0267B] “Light” signifies the Church, concerning which it is written: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song of Songs 3). “Made white” is understood as “illuminated.” It is rightly perceived as a garment of the Lord Savior, possessing neither spot nor wrinkle. For it is itself bright—that is, made white—and adorned with every beauty of virtue. To it the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3). This was also signified by that tunic which could not be divided at the time of the Passion. This is the one of which it is said: “Clothed in light as with a garment” (Psalm 103).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Luminaries

The luminaries placed in heaven illuminate day [Col. 0267C] and night according to the disposition of their Creator and fulfill the course of their appointed service. The sun, moon, and stars, according to their nature, possess allegorical meanings. After the Psalmist had incited the angelic powers to praise God, he then urged these luminaries to praise the Lord, saying: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light” (Psalm 148).

## CHAPTER IX. On the Sun

The sun, moon, and stars, as some say, are governed by a power proper to themselves; nevertheless, since they are visible to bodily eyes, it is not unreasonable to conclude that they are inferior to the powers that are not seen, although they appear to adorn the appearance of heaven with beautiful light. [Col. 0267D] For those things reached by our sight, although bright and subtle, are plainly bodies; and they must yield to those things that subsist by invisible power.

Therefore the Prophet commanded the sun, moon, and stars to praise the Lord, whether by their own nature or through other sensible and discernible substances, because they merited existence through the Creator’s gift. The consideration of so many lights can arouse immense wonder, since they both enable mortal eyes to see and themselves establish life through splendid radiance.

Thus, in Holy Scripture the sun sometimes signifies the Lord Savior, sometimes the glory of his saints, sometimes the splendor of wisdom, sometimes the beauty of virtues, and sometimes, conversely, the heat of persecution and the tribulation of the present life.

[Col. 0268A] The sun expresses the Savior insofar as, just as it itself gives radiance to the other heavenly bodies—the moon and stars, as some maintain—without assistance from them, so Christ, shining by his own power and needing no one’s help, grants the holy Church and all the saints the splendor of wisdom and virtues. Hence it is written in the Prophet: “For you who fear the Lord, the Sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing is in his wings” (Malachi 4). Elsewhere, in the person of sinners, it is said: “The Sun of righteousness has not risen for us” (Wisdom 1).

That the sun signifies the resurrection of the saints through the splendor of glory is shown by Truth itself, which says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13).

[Col. 0268B] The Psalmist testifies that the sun signifies wisdom, saying: “He made the sun rule the day, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 135). This may be understood spiritually as meaning that, in his mercy, the Lord pours the sun of wisdom into his saints, so that they may see those things that certainly belong to his command.

The sun’s signification of the beauty of virtues and good works is demonstrated by that saying of the Lord addressed to the Apostles: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

The sun signifies the sharpness of wisdom, as is said in Job of certain wise but reprobate beings, with reference to the devil: “The rays of the sun will be under him” (Job 41)—the faith of the Church being understood. Concerning him the Prophet Joel says: “[Col. 0268C] The sun will be turned into darkness” (Joel 2), because the faith of the Church will be darkened by unbelief in the hearts of the reprobate during the final persecution.

The sun is manifest action, as is said in the Psalter concerning the body assumed by the Lord: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18).

Finally, that the sun’s signification can be expressed in an opposite sense is shown by that Gospel parable which the Lord spoke concerning the different kinds of seed, saying: “Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of soil. When the sun rose, it was scorched; and because it had no root, it withered” (Luke 8).

[Col. 0268D] The rocky places, covered with a thin layer of soil, which can quickly cause the seed they receive to germinate but do not possess the strength to establish a root, are plainly those hearts which, instructed by no devotion to discipline and softened by no trials of temptation, delight for a time merely in the sweetness of the word they have heard and in heavenly promises, but withdraw at the time of temptation.

The sun is prosperity, and the moon is the adversity of the world, as in the Psalter: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120).

## CHAPTER X. On the Moon

The moon, which waxes and wanes at monthly intervals and does not shine with its own light but is illuminated by the borrowed splendor of the sun, sometimes signifies in Scripture this mortal and wretched life, and sometimes the present Church.

Thus it is read in the Gospel [Col. 0269A] parable (Luke 10) that a man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers. They also stripped him, inflicted wounds, and departed, leaving him half dead. This man is understood as Adam together with the whole human race. Jerusalem is understood as that heavenly city, from whose blessedness Adam fell through deprivation and was cast out into this mortal and wretched life. This is aptly signified by Jericho, which is interpreted as “moon,” since it is always unstable and perishable amid the various struggles of its deficiencies.

The robbers may be understood as demons, who, by deceiving Adam, stripped him of the glory of blessed immortality and deprived him of the garment of innocence.

That the moon represents the Church is shown by the verse: “He made the moon for the seasons; the sun knows its setting” (Psalm 103). [Col. 0269B] The moon is the Church, which, having been made in the course of time, sometimes happens to diminish and sometimes to grow; yet it diminishes in such a way that it is always restored when its fullness returns. We rightly understand the sun in this passage as the Lord Savior. He therefore “knew his setting,” that is, he recognized the glory of his Passion, when he said to his disciples: “The hour has come, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Matthew 26).

Likewise, the moon signifies the passion of the martyrs, as it is said through the prophet Joel: “The moon will be turned into blood” (Joel 2), that is, drenched with the blood of his martyrs.

Likewise, the moon signifies the present age, because it is always changing. Concerning this, the Apocalypse says of the Church: “And the moon under her feet” (Revelation 12).

[Col. 0269C] Sometimes Scripture censures the unstable quality of the human mind under the figure of the moon, as in Wisdom: “A fool changes like the moon,” because “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Sirach 27).

It should also be noted that the moon largely determines the time of the Paschal festival. This solemnity is celebrated especially when the sun’s light, benefiting human souls, first gains victory over the shadow of night by increasing. We then observe the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, in which we celebrate Easter.

This is the month in which the world was formed and the first man was placed in the seat of paradise. Through the mysteries of this solemnity we hope to receive again our first robe and the first kingdom of heavenly blessedness, from which we departed into a distant land. Concerning the glory of that kingdom, the blessed Apostle Peter says: [Col. 0269D] “We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3). John likewise says in his Apocalypse: “And the one seated on the throne said: Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21).

We also observe the third week of that same month at Easter, which most fittingly corresponds to the joys of the Lord’s resurrection. For his most holy resurrection took place on the third day, and in the third age of the world—that is, with the coming of heavenly grace—the whole dispensation of his life in the flesh, consummated in the glory of the resurrection, appeared to the world.

He graciously came to illuminate the first ages of the world through the natural law given through the patriarchs, the middle ages through the written Law given through the prophets, and the final ages through spiritual grace, coming in person.

[Col. 0270A] The moon’s own change at that time also offers us a most beautiful spectacle of the heavenly mystery. The moon, made in the form of a rounded figure, receives light from the sun, as we said above, and is therefore always bright on the half of its orb that faces the sun, while the other half is always dark. From the first day to the fifteenth, it has an increase of light toward the earth but a decrease toward the heavens. From the fifteenth day to the last, the increase of that same light, turned away from earthly things, gradually returns toward heavenly things.

This change of the moon rightly signifies the mysteries of Paschal joy, by which we are taught, through contemplation, to turn all the glory of our mind away from visible pleasures and perishable favors and to raise it toward the light of heavenly grace alone.

[Col. 0270B] Or, if we take pleasure in interpreting both of its changes positively, we may understand that the moon’s increasing light toward human eyes signifies the grace of virtues through which the Lord, appearing in the flesh, illumined the world. Concerning these things it is said: “Jesus increased in wisdom and age and grace with God and men” (Luke 2). Its increasing return toward the heavens signifies the glory of his resurrection and ascension. This glory came forth perfect at once in itself, but in the minds of the faithful it does not cease to increase through certain advances of its light until the end of the age.

For when the Lord rose from the dead, he appeared first to individuals and pairs, then to larger groups—sometimes seven, sometimes eleven—and finally to more than five hundred brothers at once (1 Corinthians 15). At last he appeared to all the disciples; [Col. 0270C] as they watched, when he was about to ascend into heaven (Acts 1), he commanded them to be witnesses of his dispensation in Jerusalem, throughout all Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

The moon aptly grows toward our eyes while gradually moving away from the sun; but when it grows toward the heavens, it returns to the sun at equal intervals. This is what he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I am leaving the world and going to the Father” (John 16). The Psalm also says of him: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its summit” (Psalm 18).

Since, then, the moon signifies, by that increase of light which it unfolds from the sun toward our eyes, the teaching and virtues of the Lord Savior in the flesh up to the time of his Passion; and since, by its return toward the sun, through which it gradually withdraws toward the invisible face of heaven, it demonstrates the wonders of his resurrection and later glory, it is rightly proclaimed fitting for the joys of Easter from the fifteenth day onward [Col. 0270D; the printed text is uncertain: “a quinta decima paschalis non gaudiis apta”].

Taking these indications of Paschal time from the observance of the Law, we heirs of the New Testament also append the Lord’s Day, which Scripture calls “one” or “the first day of the Sabbath.” Not without reason, for it is distinguished by the condition of the first light, marked by the triumph of the Lord’s resurrection, and always remains desirable to us because of our own resurrection as well.

[Col. 0271A] The seven days of the moon—that is, from the fifteenth day to the twenty-first—through which it naturally proceeds toward the Lord’s Day, announce in part the universality of the Church, which throughout the world has been redeemed by the Paschal mysteries. Scripture often uses the number seven to signify universality. Thus, when the Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118), this is best understood in the same sense as his other statement: “His praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

John testifies that the perfection of the whole Catholic Church is specially represented by this figure. Writing to the seven churches of Asia, he reveals the mysteries of the universal Church throughout the world. Hence, in all the admonitions he writes to each of the seven, he took care to insert this verse: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2). What he said to each one, he proves that he said to all the churches.

[Col. 0271B] The Paschal season also commends to us a moral sense: in the name of Easter [Pascha], so that every day we may make a spiritual passage from vices to virtues; and in the month of new things, in which the ripened fruits, by their arrival, proclaim the cessation of the old, so that, stripping off the old man with his deeds, we may be renewed in the spirit of our mind and put on the new man, who was created according to the Lord in righteousness, holiness, and truth (Ephesians 4).

Thus, nourished by the varied abundance of virtues and sheltered as though beneath the leaves of a pleasant tree, we may sprout like joyful and fruitful crops at the full moon, bearing the perfect radiance of faith and understanding and being separated from the darkness of sin.

In the same lunar light, when it turns back toward heaven—a movement that begins with the fifteenth moon—we are taught that the greater we become, the more we should humble ourselves in all things, each of us saying with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15).

[Col. 0271C] Since this grace, the gift from above, was poured out more manifestly in the third age of the world, the beautiful sequence of the figures fittingly signifies that in the third week of the moon its light, which had until then increased toward the earth, begins already to increase toward heavenly things. We are beautifully commanded to observe this in the Paschal season, so that, never forgetting the grace we have received, we may remember to repay its giver by obedience at each stage of our spiritual passage.

Alternatively, in the moon’s increase toward human beings we may see a type of the active life, and in its return toward heaven a type of the contemplative life. Or in one movement the love of neighbor is signified, and in the other the love of our Creator. Its progress as it turns this way admonishes us to perform good works outwardly; its movement in the other direction, [Col. 0271D] to perform those same good works with regard only to the reward above. Here it teaches that our light should shine before men, so that they may see our good works; there, that they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Stars and Constellations

There is this distinction between stars, constellations, and heavenly signs. Stars and constellations and signs differ among themselves in the following way. A star is any individual star; constellations are formed from many stars, such as the Hyades and Pleiades; heavenly signs are large stars or stellar figures, such as Orion and Boötes. Writers, however, confuse these names, using “signs” for stars and “stars” for constellations.

Stars are also said not to possess their own light but to be illuminated by the sun, like the moon.

[Col. 0272A] Constellations are understood sometimes in a positive sense and sometimes in an opposite sense. They are taken positively when they signify the saints and elect of God who are in the Church. Thus the Lord says to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (Genesis 22). The Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15).

Christ is the star, as in the Apocalypse: “I am the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22). Elsewhere: “A star shall rise out of Jacob” (Numbers 24). And in the Apocalypse: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches” (Revelation 1). The apostle Paul also writes to seven churches, though not the same ones as John; and the seven places are figures of the whole Church, which possesses the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

[Col. 0272B] Hence the Psalmist says of the Creator’s work: “The moon and stars to rule the night, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 135). We should understand the moon, as we have already said, as the Church; and the stars as its various orders, distinguished by holiness, such as bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the others who, like stars, are known to radiate through a heavenly manner of life. All these have been given authority over the night—that is, over the darkness of this age—so that through them the darkened hearts of mortals may shine.

Likewise, the stars are the saints or the learned, because they shine in this world through works of virtue, as in the Psalter: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Psalm 146).

The heavenly signs are the holy angels, as in Job: “When the morning stars praised me” (Job 38).

[Col. 0272C] Constellations are taken in an opposite sense when they signify either wicked angels, heretics, or hypocrites. The Apocalypse testifies that wicked angels fell from heaven when it says that the dragon dragged a third of the stars down with him to the earth.

The apostle Jude designates heretics under the name of constellations in his Epistle, saying: “Wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.” Hypocrites, who appear to imitate the saints through outwardly feigned forms of virtue, nevertheless fall like stars from heaven to earth, when they are separated from the company of the saints and numbered among sinners.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Pleiades

[Col. 0272D] What the Pleiades and Arcturus signify may be observed in the passage in which the Lord spoke to the blessed Job. For he says: “Can you bind together the shining stars of the Pleiades, or can you disperse the circle of Arcturus?” (Job 38).

The Pleiades are called stars *apo tou pleiotēta*, that is, “from plurality.” They were created so near to one another and yet so separate that they are together and nevertheless cannot be joined, so that they are united in their constellation but separated in contact.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Arcturus

Arcturus illumines the hours of night in such a way that, placed upon the axis of heaven, it turns through its various positions and nevertheless does not set. It does not revolve outside its course, but, situated in its place, it inclines toward all the regions of the world without ever falling.

[Col. 0273A] For what do the shining Pleiades, which are also seven, signify other than all the saints, who amid the darkness of the present life illuminate us with the light of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit? From the very origin of the world to its end they were sent at different times to prophesy; in one respect they are joined to one another, and in another they are not joined.

The stars of the Pleiades, as was said above, are joined in their constellation but separated in contact; they are situated together and nevertheless pour forth rays in the vicinity of their light, each in turn. So all the saints, appearing at different times for preaching, are separated by the vision of their hand [Col. 0273A–B; printed: *visione suae magnus*; supplied reading *manus*, “hand”], but joined in the intention of their minds.

[Col. 0273B] They shine together because they preach one thing; but they do not touch one another because they suffer at different times. How far apart in time were Abel, Isaiah, and John! They were separated in time, but not in preaching.

In Arcturus, however, which by its revolution illumines the spaces of night without setting, not the life of the saints produced individually but the whole Church together is designated. It suffers hardships but does not incline toward the collapse of its proper state. It endures the cycle of labors but does not hasten toward setting with the passing ages.

For Arcturus is not led down to the lower pole together with the night; rather, while it itself revolves, the night comes to an end. Thus, while the holy Church is shaken by innumerable tribulations, the shadow of the present life is brought to an end. Night passes while the Church stands, because, while it endures in its safety, the mortality of this life runs its course.

[Col. 0273C] Arcturus, therefore, which arises from the regions of cold, may signify the Law; and the Pleiades, which rise from the East, may signify the grace of the New Testament. The Law came, as it were, from the North, terrifying its subjects with such harsh rigidity that, for their offenses, it commanded some to be overwhelmed with stones and others to be punished by death with the sword.

The Pleiades, which, as we said above, are also seven, indicate the grace of the New Testament all the more clearly, since we all plainly see that through it the sevenfold Holy Spirit illumines the faithful with the light of his gifts.

[Col. 0273D] Wherever Arcturus turns, it displays the Pleiades, because throughout everything that the Old Testament says, the works of the New Testament are announced. Beneath the text of the letter, the mystery of prophecy is concealed.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Orion and the Hyades

The blessed Job similarly expressed the mystical meaning of Orion and the Hyades, saying: “He who made Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades, and the inner regions of the South” (Job 9).

The Orions rise at the very height of the winter season, and by their rising they stir up storms and disturb seas and lands. What, then, are designated by the Orions after Arcturus except the martyrs? When the holy Church is raised to the condition of preaching, they came forth, as it were, into the face of heaven in winter, destined to suffer the weight of persecutors and their afflictions.

[Col. 0274A] He aptly added the Hyades immediately afterward. They come forth into the face of heaven when spring is becoming young, and they spread out when the sun is already exerting the strength of its heat. They cling to the tracks [printed: *vitiis*, “faults”; corrected reading: *vestigiis*, “tracks”] of that sign which the wise men of the world call the Bull, from which the sun begins to increase and rises with greater heat to extend the spaces of day.

Who, therefore, are designated by the name of the Hyades after Orion except the teachers of the holy Church? After the martyrs had been withdrawn, they came to the knowledge of the world at a time when the faith shone more clearly. When the winter of unbelief had been suppressed, the sun of truth warmed the hearts of the faithful more deeply [printed: *calet*, “is warm”; corrected reading: *calefacit*, “warms”]; when the storm of persecution had been removed and the long nights of unbelief had been completed, they arose in the holy Church when a brighter year was already opening for it through the springtime of faith.

Nor are the holy teachers inappropriately designated by the name of the Hyades. In Greek speech, *Hyades* means “rain,” and the Hyades received their name from rains because, when they rise, they undoubtedly bring showers. They were therefore aptly expressed by the name of the Hyades, because, brought forth as it were into the face of heaven for the establishment of the universal Church, they poured the rains of holy preaching over the arid ground of the human heart.

[Col. 0274B] When he had said, “He who made Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades,” he immediately added: “and the inner regions of the South.” What, in this passage, is signified by the name “South” except the fervor of the Holy Spirit? When someone has been filled with this, he burns with love for his spiritual homeland.

[Col. 0274C] The inner regions of the South are therefore those hidden orders of angels and the most sacred recesses of the heavenly homeland, which the warmth of the Holy Spirit fills. There the souls of the saints arrive, both now when they have been separated from their bodies and later when they have been restored to their bodies, and they are hidden, as it were, in the secret places of the South.

## CHAPTER XV. On Lucifer

Lucifer is sometimes taken in a positive sense and sometimes in an opposite sense. It is taken positively when it signifies either the Lord Savior or the light of wisdom.

The Lord Savior is signified by that statement in the Book of Job: “Do you bring forth Lucifer in his time?” (Job 38). Christ therefore made himself known as Lucifer, because he rose from the dead at dawn and by the splendor of his light pressed down the darkness of our mortality. John aptly says to him: “The bright and morning star” (Revelation 22).

By appearing alive after death, he became for us the morning star, because, by providing in himself an example of resurrection, he showed us what light would follow.

[Col. 0274D] The light of wisdom and sound understanding is shown by that statement of the blessed Peter, who says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend until the day dawns and Lucifer rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1). Lucifer himself is our enlightened understanding, which will be illuminated by the light of true wisdom and perfect charity.

Lucifer is placed in the opposite sense where, through the prophet Isaiah, in the burden of Babylon and under the figure of the king of Babylon, the apostate angel is addressed: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn,” and so forth (Isaiah 14). There his fall from eternal brightness into infernal darkness is shown.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Evening

[Col. 0275A] Evening signifies either the end of the world and the coming of Antichrist, or the setting of the death of our Redeemer.

Evening signifies the coming of Antichrist in that passage from Job mentioned above, where, after the bringing forth of Lucifer, it is subsequently read: “And you cause evening to rise over the sons of the earth” (Job 38).

The Lord causes evening to rise over the sons of the earth because, in accordance with their deserts, he permits Antichrist to rule over the unbelieving hearts of the Jews. They are justly subjected by the Lord to this evening because they themselves willingly wished to be sons of the earth. Seeking earthly rather than heavenly things, they were blinded from contemplating the glory of our Lucifer. While they desire evening to rule over them, they are overwhelmed by the punishment of the damnation that follows.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Air

[Col. 0275B] Air is emptiness containing a great deal of light and possessing more rarefaction than the other elements. Concerning it Virgil says: “Following through the long void.”

Air is called *aer* either because it carries the earth or because it is carried by the earth. It belongs partly to earthly matter and partly to heavenly matter. The subtle air, in which windy and stormy movements cannot exist, belongs to the heavenly region. The more turbulent air, which becomes bodily through the exhalations of moisture [printed: *exaltationibus humilis*], is assigned to the earth, and from itself produces many forms.

[Col. 0275C] When it is disturbed, it makes winds; when stirred more violently, fires and thunder; when contracted, clouds; when thickened, rain; and when its mists freeze, snow. When turbulent, with denser freezing clouds, it produces hail; when stretched out [corrected reading: *distentus*], it produces clear weather.

It is established that dense air is a cloud, and that a cloud is rarefied and loosened air. Air signifies the emptiness of anything whatsoever. Hence the Apostle says: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (1 Corinthians 9), that is, not pursuing empty things.

Air also signifies the insubstantiality of worldly minds, as in Job: “Suddenly the air will be compressed into clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away” (Job 37). What, then, are signified by the air except the minds of worldly people, which, devoted to the innumerable desires of this life, are scattered fluidly here and there in the manner of air?

[Col. 0275D] The air is compressed into clouds when unstable minds are strengthened with the solidity of virtue through the grace of the heavenly Spirit [printed: *spectus*; corrected reading: *spiritus*, “Spirit”]. The passing wind therefore drives away the clouds because mortal life, running its course, hides the holy preachers bodily from our eyes.

Sometimes air signifies the preachers of the divine word, as in the Psalmist: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Psalm 17). The same applies to the prophets, the preachers of the word. For although someone may think that he understands their sayings, he can scarcely reach the full power of what they have said as it truly is, just as the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13)—when he sees the very thing in which he believed and is understood to behold the very thing he hoped for.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Clouds

[Col. 0276A]

Clouds (*nubes*) are so called from *nubendo*, “covering,” that is, covering the sky; hence also *nuptae*, “married women,” because they veil their faces; and hence Neptune (*Neptunus*), because he “marries,” that is, covers sea and land. The density of air produces clouds. For winds gather the air together and form clouds; hence the saying: “And the air is gathered into a cloud.”

Mystically, clouds sometimes signify the incarnation of Christ, unburdened by any weight of sin, or the virgin Mary; sometimes the protection of the Holy Spirit; and sometimes the prophets and holy preachers. The incarnation of Christ is signified by Isaiah’s words: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will descend into Egypt” (Isa. XIX). Likewise in Exodus: “The Lord,” he says, “went before them to show them the way, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire” (Exod. XIII). For this cloud going before them is Christ, and likewise a pillar, because he is upright, firm, and supports our weakness: shining by night but not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.

It may also, not improperly, be understood in this way: the mystery of Christ is manifest in the flesh, as in daylight, or as in a cloud; but in the judgment it will be like the terror of night, because then there will be great tribulation in the world, like fire, and it will shine upon the righteous but burn the unrighteous.

That passage in the Gospel where the Lord was transfigured on the mountain before three disciples also has this meaning: “And behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them” (Matt. XVII). Because Peter sought a material dwelling, he receives the shelter of the cloud, so that he may learn that at the resurrection the saints will be protected not by the covering of houses but by the glory of the Holy Spirit.

It should also be noted that, just as at the Lord’s baptism in the Jordan, so also at his glorification on the mountain, the mystery of the entire Holy Trinity is revealed. There, the Father was shown in the voice, the Son in the baptism, and the Holy Spirit in the dove; here, the Father is shown in the voice, the Son in the glorification, and the Holy Spirit in the cloud. For plainly we shall praise his glory—which in baptism we confess by believing—when we see him in the resurrection.

That clouds signify the prophets or preachers of the divine word is shown by the Psalm: “The multitude of the sound of waters; the clouds gave forth their voice, [like] a stormy sea” (Ps. LXXVI). Thus, in the holy churches, the various prayers of the peoples resound. But why was the sound of a multitude of waters produced? He fittingly adds: “because the clouds gave forth their voice.” We have often said that clouds signify preachers, of whom it is written: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V). They gave forth their great voice when they proclaimed the Lord’s commandments throughout the whole world, just as another psalm had already proclaimed: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

A cloud is divine protection, as we read in Exodus that the cloud overshadowed the tabernacle of the covenant. A cloud is the obscurity of the Scriptures, as in the Psalter: “He who covers the sky with clouds” (Ps. CXLVI).

## CHAPTER XIX. On thunder, lightning, and flashes of lightning

Thunder (*tonitruum*) is so called because its sound terrifies. For *tonus* means “sound”; it sometimes shakes everything so heavily that the sky seems to have split open. When the most violent winds of a storm suddenly force their way into the clouds, the whirlwind grows stronger and seeks an exit from the cloud it has hollowed out; with great force it tears it apart and is thus borne to our ears with a dreadful crash [*fragore*].

Thunder sometimes signifies the divine voice in Scripture, as in the passage: “The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice” (Ps. XVII), since he was about to speak great mysteries. For in the Gospel the almighty voice of the Father says: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John XII); and therefore many, as is recorded there, believed that it had been thunder.

The Most High gave his voice when it was said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, XVII).

At other times thunder signifies the preaching of the Gospel, as in the passage: “The voice of the thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI). Thus, in the wheel—that is, in the world—the voice of his thunder went forth when the preachers of Christ filled the circuit of the whole world with thunderous words.

With thunder, lightning is also expressed, but lightning appears more quickly because it is bright; thunder, on the other hand, reaches the ears more slowly. Lightning (*fulgur*) and the thunderbolt (*fulmen*) are named from the striking of a heavenly dart: for *fulgere* means “to strike” and “to smite.” Thunderbolts are produced by clouds colliding. The collision of all things creates fire, as we see in stones and likewise through the friction of wheels. In the same way fire is produced in clouds: first there are clouds, then fires. It is certain that thunderbolts are formed in the clouds from wind and fire and are discharged by the force of the winds. The fire of the thunderbolt has greater power because it is made from subtler elements than our fire, that is, the fire used by us.

It has three names: *fulgur*, “flash,” because it touches; *fulgor*, “brightness,” because it sets fire to and burns; and *fulmen*, “thunderbolt,” because it splits. For this reason it is also depicted with three rays.

Flashes of lightning, or coruscations, mystically express the divine terrors in Scripture, which appear in flashing miracles; or they express the communications [*comminationes*, “threats”] written in the divine law, as in the passage: “Your flashes of lightning illuminated the world; the earth saw and was shaken” (Ps. LXXVI). By “flashes” he means the divine commandments, radiant with the light of truth, which drove away the darkness of humanity throughout the whole world by their illuminating revelation.

The text reads *alibuta* [*alibi ita*, “elsewhere, thus”]: “He multiplied flashes of lightning and troubled them” (Ps. XVII), that is, he performed many miracles, which moved the hearts of those who witnessed them just as frequent flashes of lightning customarily terrify those who see them. “He troubled them”: he speaks of those who were troubled when they recognized through manifest proofs that he had risen.

## CHAPTER XX. On the celestial rainbow

The celestial rainbow is so called from its resemblance to a curved golden bow [*arcus*]. *Iris* is its proper name, and it is called *iris*, as though from *aeris*, “of the air,” because it descends through the air to the earth. It shines from the sun when hollow clouds receive the sun’s ray from the opposite side and form the appearance of a bow. It has various colors because thin water, bright air, and dark clouds, when illuminated, create various colors in it.

The celestial rainbow is a sign of the covenant that God established between himself and human beings and every living creature, so that he would not destroy it by a flood. Its appearance in the clouds, and the fact that it shines only from the sun, signifies that those do not perish in the flood who recognize the power of Christ in the prophets and in all the divine Scriptures, as though in the clouds of God.

Because in the same rainbow the color of water and of fire is displayed together—being blue on one side and reddish on the other—it is evident that it bears witness to both judgments: one yet to come and the other already past. That is, the world will be consumed by the fire of judgment; it will not again be destroyed by the water of a flood.

The rainbow, that is, the bow, is said to bear the figure of God’s two judgments: the first, through the flood; the second, through fire, as in the Apocalypse: “And a rainbow around him” (Rev. IV).

Clear weather signifies the remission of sins granted through the blood of Jesus Christ after the darkness of sins, as in the Gospel: “In the evening you say: ‘It will be fair, for the sky is red’” (Matt. XVI).

## CHAPTER XXI. On fire

Fire, which is the fourth element of the world, sometimes expresses the zeal of God; sometimes the Holy Spirit; sometimes charity; sometimes desire; sometimes malice; sometimes understanding; sometimes tribulation; sometimes anger; and sometimes pleasure.

It denotes the zeal of God in the sentence: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV). It demonstrates the Holy Spirit, who appeared at Pentecost over the apostles in tongues of fire, illuminating them with the light of wisdom and kindling their hearts with zeal for righteousness.

It signifies charity when it expresses the fervor of love, as in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

It signifies desire when it denotes excessive ambition for earthly things. Hence, in Exodus, the Lord commands concerning observance of the Sabbath: “You shall not kindle fire,” he says, “in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day” (Exod. XXXV). He forbids the fire of desire to be kindled both in human bodies and in all gatherings.

Fire signifies malice when it reveals an evil heart always bent toward lower things. Concerning this fire it is said: “This fire will consume the adversary,” because an evil heart wastes away through its own malice. Just as the fire of love lifts the mind upward, so the fire of malice entangles it.

Fire signifies tribulation, as in the Psalm: “You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire” (Ps. LXV).

It signifies anger when it displays heavenly vengeance, as in the passage: “I will consume them with the fire of my anger,” says the Lord (Ps. LVII); and elsewhere: “For,” he says, “a fire has been kindled by my anger, and it will burn down to the depths of hell” (Ps. XVII).

Fire signifies pleasure when it displays the burning of lust, as in the passage: “All are adulterers; their hearts are like a burning coal of fire” (Hos. VII). Unless the remedy of repentance comes to their aid, the wood of eternal punishment will follow them, where there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth and everlasting torment.

Concerning this it is written in Isaiah: “Behold, all of you who are kindled by fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire.” Sinners have within themselves hay, wood, straw, thorns, thistles, and leaves, all of which are handed over to eternal burning. Yet they are summoned to salvation, and it is said to them: “Walk in the light of your fire and in your flames,” and so forth, so that in punishments and sufferings they may stand apart from [*distant*; *effugiant*, “may escape”] the power of God and return to salvation.

Likewise, fire is understood in the sacred writings as understanding, whether good or evil. Thus, in Leviticus, it is said of the sons of Aaron, who offered strange fire before the Lord and were there consumed.

Smoke is sometimes used in a favorable sense and sometimes in the opposite sense. For when the Psalmist says: “Smoke rose up in his anger, and fire burned from his face” (Ps. XVII), smoke is used here in a good sense. Just as earthly smoke stirs up useless tears, so smoke kindled by the heat of repentance pours forth a fruitful stream of tears in his anger—that is, at the time when he troubles sinners with fear of the future judgment, so as to bring them to the remedy of conversion.

Fire is the charity of God, increasing through the progress of the virtues; the more it is desired, the more effectively it grows. He rightly says, “from his face,” because through his illumination charity is granted to those who abandon their sins.

But when it is said elsewhere concerning sinners: “As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish” (Ps. LXVII), the punishment of sinners is foretold. Smoke is a dark mass rising from this corruptible flame; the higher it rises, the more it is diluted into emptiness. Sinners are rightly compared to it, because from the flame of their wickedness they produce smoky deeds. Although these rise to greater heights through pride, they must necessarily waste away through their own elevation, like smoke.

## CHAPTER XXII. On burning coals

Burning coals signify the soul’s illicit desires, which pollute the course of human actions. Hence the passage: “When he walks upon coals, his feet will not be burned” (Prov. VI).

For this reason it is written in Job concerning Leviathan: “His breath makes coals burn” (Job XLI). What does he call coals except the minds of the reprobate, set alight by inward desires? Leviathan’s breath kindles coals as often as secret suggestion draws human minds toward illicit pleasures. A flame comes forth from his mouth because whatever he himself says, and whatever he says through his preachers, is fire by which not gold or silver but wood, hay, and straw are burned.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On charcoal

Charcoal signifies the blackness of sins. Hence the passage: “Coals were kindled by him” (II Sam. XXII). By kindled coals he means sinners, who, like dead coals, are darkened in the blindness of this world; but then, when repentance kindles them, they revive, and from dead embers begin to become living coals.

Likewise there is the passage read in the Psalm: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, together with coals” (Ps. CXIX). Some have wished to understand “desolating coals” as the most loathsome sinners, extinguished by evil deeds; their dread and remembrance are known to lay waste our vices, when we fear to commit such acts as we know they endured.

It may also be understood that we should take “desolating coals” as prayers kindled by the fire of charity. These cleanse and purify us from vices in such a way that what the devil had bound within us is perceived, through divine favor, to have been laid waste and overthrown.

Or perhaps it refers more properly to what Isaiah says: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand he held a burning coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs. He touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, this has touched your lips; behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and I have cleansed your sins completely’” (Isa. VI). This is now accomplished through the grace of the holy cross, when we mark our lips with remembrance of the Lord.

Perhaps it is not without reason that we call the sign of the cross a desolating coal, since it drives away the sins of believers, although to the faithless it appears extinguished.

Likewise there is the passage where it is written: “As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who sent him” (Prov. X). Here smoke expresses the vanity of those who pursue the desire of this world more than devotion to the word of God.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On ashes

Ashes signify the emptiness of human frailty. Hence it is written in Solomon: “Why is earth and ash proud?” (Ecclus. X).

Cinders (*favilla*) signify the same thing. Thus Job says: “I repent in cinders and ashes” (Job XLII). To repent in cinders and ashes is, after contemplating the highest essence, to recognize oneself as nothing other than cinders and ashes.

Hence also, in the Gospel, the Lord says to the reprobate city: “If the mighty works that have been done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. XI). In sackcloth are shown the harshness and contrition of sinners; in ashes is shown the dust of the dead. For this reason both are customarily used in repentance, so that through the prickling of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and through the ash-dust of ashes may consider what we have become through judgment.

A log and a brand signify the human race, which through the Lord Jesus Christ has been drawn from perpetual burning, as righteous [the printed text reads *se in justum*; *semiustum*, “half-burned,” is supplied], as in Zechariah: “Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?” (Zech. III).

Two brands signify the two powers of this world and the heretics who, by common agreement, persecute the Church, as in Isaiah: “Do not fear the two tails of these smoking brands” (Isa. VII).

## CHAPTER XXV. On winds

Wind is air set in motion and stirred up, receiving different names according to the various regions of the sky. It is called *ventus* because it is vehement and violent. Its force is so great that it not only uproots rocks and trees but also disturbs heaven and earth and stirs up the seas.

There are four principal winds, or spirits. The first blows from the east and is called the Subsolanus; from the south comes the Auster; from the west the Favonius; and from the north the wind of that same name. Each has two companion winds on either side.

The Subsolanus has the Vulturnus on its right and the Eurus on its left. The Auster has the Euroauster on its right and the Austro-Africus on its left. The Favonius has the Africus on its right and the Corus on its left. The north wind has the Circius on its right and the Aquilo on its left.

These twelve winds turn the globe of the world with their blasts. Their names have been assigned for particular reasons, as those who have written about the etymologies of their names show. We intend, however, to speak only of those that we find more frequently mentioned in Scripture.

Wind is sometimes used in a good sense and sometimes in the opposite sense. It is used in a good sense in the passage: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. CXXXIV). Here we may reasonably understand the apostles to be represented, whose preaching traversed the whole world like a swift wind.

Likewise there is the passage written elsewhere: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII). This expresses the Lord’s ascent above the heavens and the powers of heaven, where he is now seated at the right hand of the Father and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The statement that he “flew upon the wings of the winds” fittingly displays his immense speed, when the report of his birth, passion, and resurrection spread throughout the whole world. For what could be said to be swifter, when, while he lay in the cradle, the splendor of the star announced him, and as soon as he was born he was seen in another part of the world?

Winds also signify souls. Hence it is written: “He made weight for the winds” (Job XXVIII). Souls are commonly signified by the speed and loftiness of winds. Thus souls receive weight, so that they no longer leap away from the purpose of God in light motion but remain fixed in him with the grave steadfastness of constancy.

Or certainly, to make weight for the winds means to temper the glory of virtues granted here to the elect by mingling it with weakness.

In the opposite sense wind is used in the Gospel: “The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck against that house” (Matt. VII). Here by rain they wish manifold temptations of the devil to be understood, by rivers open and manifest persecutions, and by winds malignant spirits.

Likewise the passage in Job is to be understood in the opposite sense: “A scorching wind carried him away” (Job XXVII). The scorching wind is called the malignant spirit, which kindles the flames of desires in the heart so that it may drag a person toward eternal punishments.

Winds also signify spirits of pride, as it is said in Hosea concerning heretics: “A spirit has bound him in its wings” (Hos. IV).

Likewise: “The wind shall feed all your shepherds” (Jer. XXII); and elsewhere: “He who relies on lies feeds on wind” (Prov. X).

The eastern wind is called the Subsolanus because it rises beneath the rising sun. It signifies the preaching of the Gospel, which proceeded from the true Sun and illuminated the whole world with the light of faith and wisdom. Hence it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of justice shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. IV).

The Auster is named from drawing up water. It also makes the air heavy and nourishes clouds. In Greek it is called *Nothus*, because it sometimes corrupts the air. For the pestilence that arises from corrupted air is carried by the blowing Auster into other regions. But just as the Auster produces pestilence, so the Aquilo drives it away.

The Auster sometimes signifies the warmth of faith, as in the Psalm: “Like a stream in the south wind” (Ps. CXXV). Sometimes it signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden” (Song IV). Sometimes it signifies the fervor of love, as it is said in the Psalter: “He stirred up the south wind from heaven and brought in the southwest wind by his strength” (Ps. LXXVII).

It is used in the opposite sense when it signifies the heat of desire, which seizes human minds with the pestilence of vices and introduces the sickness of sins into the human race.

The western wind is called *Zephyrus* in Greek because flowers and shoots are brought to life by its breath. In Latin it is called *Favonius*, because it fosters what is coming to birth.

This wind is found in a good sense when it signifies the setting of Christ, the true Sun; from this setting all the shoots of virtues and good works arise in the world. It is used in the opposite sense when it signifies the decline of the better life. Hence the prophet says to sinners: “Your sun shall set at midday” (Amos VIII).

The Aquilo is so called because it compresses the waters and scatters the clouds. For it is a cold and dry wind. It signifies either the devil or unbelieving people, and thus the abundance of iniquity and the lack of charity. Hence it is written in the prophet: “From the north evils shall blaze forth upon the earth” (Isa. XIV).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the breeze and the sea wind

The breeze (*aura*) is named from the air, as though *aeria*, “airy,” because it is the light movement of air. Stirred air produces a breeze. Hence Lucretius also speaks of “airy breezes.”

The sea wind (*altanus*) is so called by derivation from *altum*, “the deep,” that is, the sea. For there is another blast along the shores, which we have called the breeze; the breeze is on land.

The breeze signifies the tranquility of a good mind contemplating God. Thus Elijah, standing on the mountain before the Lord, when he saw a great wind overturning the mountains, said: “The Lord was not in the wind” (III Kings XIX). After the commotion, there was fire, and he said: “The Lord was not in the fire”; and after the fire came “the sound of a gentle breeze.” When Elijah saw this, he covered his face with his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave.

The Lord is said not to be in the wind of upheaval or in the fire, but he is not denied to be in the sound of the gentle breeze. For when the mind is lifted up into the height of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to perceive is not God; but when it perceives something subtle, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. We perceive, as it were, the sound of a gentle breeze when, through sudden contemplation, we taste something of uncircumscribed truth.

The tranquility of the sea, which they call the *altanus*, signifies the peace of the Church in the world. As the breeze of the Holy Spirit blows, the Church strives, after the storm that has arisen in the world, to reach securely the desired harbor of eternal rest on a prosperous course. This is like the voyage of the Lord with his disciples in the boat: when the little boat was covered by the waves, the Lord arose, commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (Matt. VIII).

In a tropological sense, each of us, instructed in the catholic faith and marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross, when we intend to leave the world, surely boards the ship with Jesus and attempts to cross the sea. Yet he who neither slumbers nor sleeps, the guardian of Israel, often seems to sleep while we are sailing. This happens when, amid the repeated struggles of the virtues, the force of unclean spirits, wicked people, or our own thoughts grows tumultuous, and the brightness of faith is darkened, the height of hope withers, and the flame of love grows cold.

But amid such storms we must hasten to that helmsman and diligently awaken him who does not serve the winds but commands them. At once he will restrain the storms, restore tranquility, and grant the harbor of salvation.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the whirlwind

A whirlwind is a swirling movement of winds. It is called *turbo* from the earth whenever the wind rises and sends the earth whirling around.

A whirlwind signifies the force of persecutions or tribulations, as in Isaiah: “He became the strength of the poor, the hope from the whirlwind” (Isa. XXV).

A storm (*tempestas*) is named either from time, as historians commonly speak when they say “at that time,” or from the state of the sky, because by its magnitude it arises over many days.

A whirlwind either signifies the Lord’s scourge sent upon a person or the persecutions of wicked people. For we read in Job: “The Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said” (Job XXXVIII).

I observe something that deserves attention: if he had spoken to Job while Job was sound and unharmed, the Lord’s speech would have been said to come from tranquility. But because he speaks after the breath has been broken, he is described as having spoken from the whirlwind.

The Lord speaks differently to his servants when he advances them inwardly through compunction, and differently when he restrains them through severity so that they do not become proud. Through the Lord’s gentle speech the sweetness of his love is shown; through the terrifying speech his power, which must be feared, is revealed. By the former the soul is persuaded to advance; by the latter, the soul that advances is restrained. Through the former it learns what to desire; through the latter, what to fear.

By the former he says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in your midst” (Nah. I). By the latter it is said: “The Lord is in the storm and in the whirlwind of his ways.”

He is gentle when he comes to dwell in our midst. But when he reveals himself through storm and whirlwind, he disturbs the hearts he touches and rises up to subdue their pride, making himself known as powerful and terrible.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “You will pursue them in your storm, and in your anger you will trouble them” (Ps. LXXXII). “In the storm” means at the time of judgment.

Likewise, a storm signifies the examination of judgment, as in the Psalm: “Around him is a mighty storm” (Ps. XLIX). It is rightly compared to a storm, first because it is unexpected, and then because it suddenly causes confusion with its crash; the sudden magnitude of the danger removes the possibility of deliberation.

A storm is a kind of violent uprising of the air caused by rain, in which the matter is brought to a violent conclusion while we are harassed by an excess of waters.

The passage continues: “And in your anger you will trouble them.” I have often said that anger cannot properly be attributed to the Divinity; rather, the expression is taken from human beings, who, when they judge criminals, are moved by the heat of their spirit and cannot proceed to condemn a person unless they are stirred up by the crimes he has committed.

The persecution of the wicked is signified by that verse spoken in the person of the Lord: “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm submerged me” (Ps. LXVIII). How does he who walked upon the seas with fixed steps, and extended his right hand to Peter so that he would not sink, say that he was submerged by a storm?

Here the depth of the sea signifies the vast madness of the people. A storm is also the stirred-up sedition of deranged people. It submerged the Lord and Savior when it brought him to the cross.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the tempest

Tempests arise either from rivers or from winds. Nothing, however, is swifter than winds. Hence poets represent both winds and rivers as winged because of their speed, as in “the winged force of the south wind.”

A tempest signifies the stormy fury of persecutors, who afflict the Church of Christ partly with threats and partly with blows and torments. But sometimes the Lord converts the minds of the persecutors to a better state, so that, cleansing themselves from their former crimes through repentance, they turn to good works.

For it is written in the Psalm: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of tempests, which fulfill his word” (Ps. CXLVIII). Allegorically, fire, hail, snow, and ice, as has been said, signify people who in this world have passed from turbulent and very evil ways to the most peaceful pursuits of devotion. “Who fulfill his word”: who else but those who have deserved to come from stormy and wicked ways to the grace of confessing him?

At other times, while they persist in evil actions, eternal punishment will torment them. Hence it is written: “He will rain snares upon sinners, fire, sulfur, and the spirit of tempests; this is the portion of their cup” (Ps. X). It is fire when fiery care consumes them; sulfur, because their thoughts are defiled by a detestable stench; the spirit of tempests, when they confuse themselves with a tumultuous mind; “the portion of their cup,” that is, the measure by which they become drunk with polluted deeds.

# BOOK TEN

## CHAPTER I. On times

Times (*tempora*) receive their name from *temperamentum*, “regulation” or “measured arrangement,” either because the span of each is separately ordered, or because all the courses of mortal life are regulated by moments, hours, days, months, years, lustrums, ages, and periods of life.

The reckoning of time is therefore distinguished according to a threefold method. It proceeds either by nature, by custom, or by authority.

Authority itself is divided in two ways: human authority, as when Olympiads of four years, market weeks of eight days, and indictions celebrated in cycles of fourteen years are observed. The Greeks, Egyptians, and Romans, each according to his own understanding, also ordered that the day formed from the quarter-days should be intercalated in February or August.

Divine authority ordained that the Sabbath be observed on the seventh day, that in the seventh year people abstain from agricultural labor, and that the fiftieth year be called the Jubilee.

By the guidance of nature it was discovered that the solar year consists of 365 days and a quarter, while the lunar year lasts 354 days when ordinary and 384 days when embolismic; the entire course of the moon is contained within a nineteen-year cycle.

It was also discovered that the wandering stars move around the zodiac in their appointed courses. Nature was not, according to the madness of the pagans, a creative goddess, one among many, but was created by the one true God, who, when he set the stars in the heavens, commanded them to serve as signs and for seasons, days, and years.

Time, called *chronos* (Greek: χρόνος), runs from the beginning of the world to the end of the age, divided, as we said above, into moments, hours, days, months, years, lustrums, ages, and periods of life.

It signifies the fitting distribution of the divine will. Hence the passage: “The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them food in due season” (Ps. CXLIV); and likewise: “It is time to act, Lord; they have dissolved your law” (Ps. CXVIII).

Thus the devout people, in the time of Antiochus, rejected the attempt of the Jewish populace to pollute the law of the Lord through the worship of demons. It is as though a sick person cries out to a physician that it is time to come to his aid, lest, as the diseases grow worse, the people’s health be destroyed: “It is time to act,” not to delay what is necessary.

Through the law and the prophets he had commanded that, since he was the true Lord, humanity should worship him with the deepest devotion. But because the stubbornness of the Jews despised this to their own destruction, the faithful people cries out: “It is time to act,” that is, for you to appear as salvation for the world, dissolve sins, conquer death, and overthrow the devil himself together with his host. This is the Lord’s action: to come at the time foretold.

Hence it was also said through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. XLIX; the printed reference reads “Isa. XCIV”). And the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. 6).

Everything the Lord does is completed according to the most fitting arrangement, so that it ought not to happen beforehand except when he, in his mercy, grants it. Hence it is always beneficial for us to have patience, to await what has been commanded, and to ask for what is beneficial. The time to act is known by him who is the ruler.

## CHAPTER II. On moments

A moment (*momentum*) is the smallest and narrowest measure of time, named from the motion of the stars. It is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when one thing yields to another and succeeds it.

A moment therefore signifies the briefest passage of time, as in the Apostle: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (I Cor. XV). By “the twinkling of an eye” he wishes to signify the extreme brevity of the moment, so that from the speed of the resurrection you may recognize how great God’s power is.

Another edition has: “in an atom and in the twinkling of an eye.” The smallest of all things, and that which cannot be divided by any method, is called in Greek *atomon* (ἄτομον), that is, “indivisible” or “uncuttable.” Because of its smallness it is more visible to grammarians than to calculators. Since grammarians divide a verse into words, a word into feet, feet into syllables, and syllables into temporal units, assigning two temporal units to a long syllable and one to a short syllable, and have nothing further into which they can divide it, they have chosen to call this an atom.

## CHAPTER III. On hours

[Col. 0286C]

Hora is a Greek word, though it sounds Latin. For hora means a boundary or limit of time, just as the boundaries of the sea, rivers, and garments are called horae. An hour is the twelfth part of the day, namely, the “artificial” [or “articulated”: *articularis* / *artificialis*] day—that is, from sunrise to sunset—not the natural day, which extends from one sunrise to the next and is completed in twenty-four hours. Indeed, twelve hours complete the day, as the Lord attests when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks by day, he does not stumble” (John 11). Although here he has allegorically called himself the day and his disciples, who were to be illumined by him, the hours, he nevertheless defined the number of hours according to the customary human reckoning.

It should be known, then, that hora is sometimes used for a period of time, [Col. 0286D] and sometimes for an age of the world. It is used for a period of time in Paul’s statement: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans 13). This relates to what was said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 13). By this is signified the time of the Gospel, in which we ought to advance toward merit—that is, rise from sleep, do good, as though in the daytime, that is, openly, and take care that, by living purely, we may come to the promised reward, [Col. 0287A] having shaken off the sleep of ignorance or negligence.

Hora is used for an age of the world in the Epistle of John, where he says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2). By “the last hour” he means the final period of the world, which is now taking place, in accordance with that parable of the Lord in which he tells of laborers hired for the vineyard. The first hour extends to the times of Noah; from the times of Noah, the third hour; from the times of Abraham, the sixth hour; from the giving of the Law, the ninth hour; from Christ to the end of the age, the eleventh hour, in which the coming of Antichrist has been prophesied.

Likewise, the first hour is infancy or childhood; the third hour, adolescence; the sixth hour, youth; the ninth hour, old age; the eleventh hour, extreme decrepitude. Hence the example given above.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Days

[Col. 0287B]

Day is air illumined by the sun, taking its name from the fact that it separates and divides the darkness. For when, at the beginning of creation, darkness was over the face of the abyss, “God said: Let there be light; and there was light. And God called the light Day” (Genesis 1). This definition is divided in two ways, namely, popularly and properly.

Popularly, the whole period during which the sun is present above the earth is called a day. Properly, however, a day is completed in twenty-four hours, that is, by the sun’s circuit as it traverses the whole sphere. Since it always carries the daylight with it everywhere, it is believed to be raised through no smaller expanse of air beneath the earth at night than above the earth by day.

Before the creation of the sun, however, what is now accomplished by the sun was accomplished by the circuit of the primordial light. [Col. 0287C] On the first and second days it traversed the waters of the abyss, which had covered the whole earth; on the third, it traversed the empty air by its circuit.

Thus, as far as we who follow the traces of our fathers are permitted to conjecture, when God said, “Let there be light,” immediately the darkness that had covered the abyss departed. Light emerging from the East between the waters covered the entire surface of the earth with the breadth of its radiance, reaching at once the northern, southern, and western regions. Then, gradually withdrawing as the full span of one day was completed, it descended by circling beneath the lower regions of the earth. With dawn preceding it, it completed the second and third days in a similar order. It differed from solar light only in lacking the nourishment of heat; and, since the stars did not yet exist, it left those ancient nights dark with their primeval darkness.

Day, however, has several meanings according to allegory. Sometimes it signifies the Lord the Savior; sometimes his saints; sometimes knowledge of the Holy Scriptures; sometimes charity; sometimes the radiance of virtues; sometimes temporal prosperity; sometimes the day of judgment; and sometimes eternal blessedness.

Day signifies the Lord in the Gospel statement: “Whoever walks in the day does not stumble” (John 11), because whoever follows the Savior’s teaching will not fear the stumbling-blocks of sins.

Likewise, day signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, as in the Psalm: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Psalm 117 [118]).

It is understood that day signifies the Apostles and the saints of God in the Psalmist’s verse: “Day pours forth speech” [Col. 0288A] (Psalm 18 [19]); that is, the Lord, shining upon the Apostles with divine radiance, made known to them words of heavenly light. Conversely, in what follows—“Night declares knowledge to night” (ibid.)—Judas is understood to have betrayed Christ to the Jews.

We can also understand day as knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, because in it the light of righteousness and true wisdom shines for those who understand rightly. Hence the Apostle admonishes us to be intent upon meditating on God’s law “until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts” (2 Peter 1).

That daylight signifies charity is shown by John in his Epistle, when he says: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light” (1 John 2).

Day also signifies the Gospel, as in the Song of Songs: “Until the day breathes and the shadows are removed” [Col. 0288B] (Song of Songs 2).

Day signifies the present life, as in the Gospel: “I must do the works of him who sent me, while it is day” (John 9).

Again, day signifies the future life of the righteous, as in Isaiah: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day” (Isaiah 60).

Day and night signify the righteous and sinners, righteousness and iniquity, in the Apostle: “We are not of the night or of darkness. For you are all sons of light and sons of God” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Day and night signify prosperity and adversity, as in the Psalm: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Psalm 41 [42]). Likewise: “By day I will cry out, my God, and you will not answer; and by night, and it shall not be reckoned folly for me” (Psalm 21 [22]).

Day signifies the radiance of virtues and the beauty of upright conduct in Paul’s statement: “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day” (Romans 13). For if the order of knowledge drives away our ignorance, and, turning away from unworthy actions, we pursue all that is pious and honorable, we are placed in the light and walk honorably as though in the day.

Therefore, in what is written, “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Psalm 41 [42]), we ought to understand day as leisure, in which the Lord’s commandments are learned. His law is absorbed in a time of tranquility. For then there is leisure to learn, when there is nothing that ought to impede us.

It follows: “And by night he declared it.” What is said in the night is declared in tribulation. First the words of the law are learned in a time of leisure; but their fruit is shown in affliction.

That the name “day” signifies the time of judgment is shown by the Gospel statement: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5), and by the Apostle’s words: “The day will disclose it” (1 Corinthians 3).

The Prophet shows that day is used for eternity when he says to the Lord: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 83 [84]). Such are the courts of the Lord in which, as he has testified above, he desired and languished. In them one day is rightly desired, because it is eternally unending: it does not arise with the coming of the sun, nor end with its setting; it is not followed by tomorrow, nor preceded by yesterday. Remaining unchanging, it consists in perpetual unity.

“Above thousands” signifies this world, in which thousands of days come to an end. One day signifies a thousand years, as in the Psalm: “For a thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Psalm 89 [90]).

Some understand the two days to figure the Old and New Testaments, as in the Psalm: “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Psalm 95 [96]).

Day signifies knowledge of the Trinity, as in Exodus: “We shall go a journey of three days and sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exodus 35).

Likewise, the three days contain a figure of the Savior’s passion, burial, and resurrection, as in Hosea: “The Lord will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live” (Hosea 6).

The sixth day signifies the present world, which is said to have been made in these six days. Hence the six days are said to bear the figure of six thousand years, as in the Apostle: “One day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day” [Col. 0289B] (2 Peter 3).

The seventh day, which is written to have been sanctified for God’s rest, signifies the rest of all the saints after the course of the present life.

The seven days contain all the time and work of the present life, which revolves through these seven days. They also contain the mystery in which we are commanded to celebrate Passover: that is, to pass from worse things to better through amendment of life, and not to eat leaven, which is the corruption of sin, but to walk in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5).

The eighth day bears the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection. Likewise, the eighth day signifies the future resurrection of all and the day of judgment, whose mystery is prefigured by the title of the sixth Psalm, namely, “For the eighth.”

“Today” signifies the eternity of the Godhead, begun by no beginning and to be closed by no end. Hence in the Psalm the Father speaks to the Son, saying: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2). For with the Lord there is neither yesterday nor tomorrow, but always today.

Today signifies all present time, as in the Psalm: “Today, if you hear his voice” (Psalm 94 [95]), as though it said: at whatever time.

Tomorrow signifies future time, as in the Gospel: “Do not worry about tomorrow, what you will eat or what you will drink” (Matthew 6). Likewise there: “For if God so clothes the grass—that is, sinners—which is in the field today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace, that is, into everlasting burning,” and elsewhere: “Lest your children say tomorrow to our children: You have no share in Israel” (Joshua 22).

## CHAPTER V. On the Parts of the Day

[Col. 0289D]

There are three parts of the day: morning, midday, and the final period.

Morning is mature and full light, no longer twilight. It is called *mane* from *manus*, “hand.” For the ancients called a good thing *manus*. What is better than light?

Morning signifies the time of regeneration in baptism, when a person begins to be a child of light; or the light of good works; or the time of resurrection. Hence: “To you I shall pray, Lord, in the morning, and you will hear my voice” (Psalm 5).

The Church, which knows that it had the darkness of sins and was gathered from the night of this world, then rightly believes that it is heard when it bursts forth into the light of the true resurrection.

Morning signifies the time of resurrection in what follows: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see that you are not a God who wills iniquity” (Psalm 5) [Col. 0290A]. On the day of judgment, when all people rise from the sleep of death, the equity of God’s judgment will appear, when he gives to each according to his works.

Midday is called *meridies*, as though *medidies*, “middle-day,” either because it is then that the day is clearer. For *merum* means “pure.” It signifies plain teaching together with the clarity of good works, as in the Song of Songs, where the bride says to the bridegroom: “Tell me where you feed your flock, where you make it rest at midday” (Song of Songs 1).

Elsewhere midday is used in an opposite sense, as in the Psalm: “From ruin and the noonday demon” (Psalm 90 [91]). The noonday demon is a terrible danger kindled by the heat of persecution, where ruin is often feared when human weakness is overcome.

Likewise, “from the noonday demon” is understood as “from what is manifest, not hidden.”

The final period is the last part of the day, when the sun turns its course toward setting. It is so called because it is what remains for the final part of the day and declines toward evening.

Evening therefore signifies either the end of human life, or the end of the world, or future repentance. That evening signifies the death of Christ is declared by the Psalmist: “In the evening weeping will lodge, and in the morning joy” (Psalm 29 [30]).

Weeping lodged in the evening when Christ our Lord was slain. Then truly weeping lodged, while for three days the crowd of the faithful groaned together and the nature of the world was shaken by his setting.

In the morning joy also arose, when, at morning-time, the Lord’s resurrection was proclaimed, as the Gospel bears witness, and the disciples were granted to behold the immortality of their Lord’s presence.

Evening signifies the end of the world, when the time for working has already ended. Hence it is said: “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9).

It signifies future repentance, where sinners are described as being cast into the outer darkness.

The Psalmist embraces these three times in one verse, saying: “In the evening, morning, and midday I shall tell and proclaim, and he will hear my voice” (Psalm 54 [55]). These words announce great mysteries to us.

Evening signifies the time of the betrayal, when Judas is known to have betrayed him to the cohorts that were seeking him.

Morning signifies the time when he was brought before Pontius Pilate to be heard.

Midday signifies the sixth hour, when, as the Evangelist says, he was hung upon the cross [Col. 0290D].
