“I shall tell” refers to the evening, because it is evident that he then spoke all the things that the wicked Judas had planned to do.

“I shall proclaim” answers to the morning, when, after Pilate said, “Are you the king of the Jews?” he proclaimed: “For this I was born,” and the other things that the Lord said there.

He also joined to these words, “and he will hear my voice.” This refers to midday, when on the cross he said: “It is finished,” and gave up his spirit.

Likewise, evening signifies the Passion, morning the resurrection, and midday his ascension into heaven.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Night

Night is so called because it harms sight or human activities, or because in it thieves and robbers find an opportunity to harm others.

Night is the absence of the sun, when the earth is covered by shadow, until the sun returns from setting to rising. The poet, describing its nature, indicates this when he says:

> From Ocean comes night,  
> enveloping earth and heaven with a great shadow.

Solomon likewise expressed it in the sacred writings: “He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song of Songs 6). With elegant meaning he calls the retreat of night the inclination of the shadows.

For according to the conditions of the regions through which the sun’s course extends, and because the obstruction of the earthly mass excludes its radiance from us, that shadowing—which is the nature of night—is raised so high that it appears to extend even to the stars. It was therefore rightly indicated, by the contrary change—that is, by the rising of the light—that the shadows incline, and that night is depressed and driven away.

Philosophers say that this shadow of night is raised as far as the boundary between air and ether. They say that, with darkness sharpened like pyramids, it sometimes reaches and obscures the moon, which travels in the lowest orbit of the planets. No other heavenly body suffers such an eclipse—that is, a failure of its light—because, around the boundaries of the earth, the radiance of the sun freely sees those things that are far from the earth; and therefore it always makes the regions of the ether beyond the moon full of daylight, whether illumined by its own radiance or by that of the stars.

The shadow of night was given to mortals for bodily rest, so that humanity, eager for work, would not grow weak and perish through unbroken labor. It was also given so that certain living creatures that cannot bear the sun’s light—and even beasts that fear human presence—might have the opportunity to roam about and seek food, as the Psalmist sings in God’s praises: “The sun knows its setting; you established darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest pass through,” and so forth (Psalm 103 [104]).

Just as day mystically signifies in Scripture the light of faith and the equity of righteousness, as well as prosperity and happiness, so night signifies injustice, unbelief, and every adversity.

Night signifies unbelief in the Apostle’s testimony: “We are not children of night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Iniquity is expressed through the meaning of night in blessed Job’s statement: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said: A man has been conceived” (Job 3). Hence the Psalmist testifies that he was conceived in iniquities and born in sins (Psalm 50 [51]).

Blessed Job therefore wishes to perish the hope brought by the apostate angel, who, pretending to be day, shone forth with a promise of divinity, but, showing himself to be night, darkened for us the light of our immortality.

May the ancient enemy perish, who displayed the light of promise but brought the darkness of sin; who, flattering us, made himself known as though day, but through blindness produced by worldly advantages led us even to dark night.

Adversity is therefore expressed under the name of night, when the Psalmist testifies that he cries out in the night—that is, in tribulation—and yet has not been heard.

Likewise, the Psalmist says: “In the day of my tribulation I sought the Lord with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 58 [59]).

Under the name of night he signifies the life of this world, which, although it appears to possess light, is darkened by the obscurity of sins.

Night also signifies the prison of hell, when he says: “Perhaps darkness will trample me, and night will be my illumination in my delights” (Psalm 138 [139]). How, then, could he be trampled by darkness when night was illumination for him in his delights? He shows that the prison of hell was truly illumined when Christ shattered the devil’s power and, in his mercy, freed humanity.

Night signifies the present life, as in the Psalm: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place” (Psalm 133 [134]). Likewise: “By night before him, and I was not deceived” (Psalm 58 [59]).

Night signifies the future age for sinners, as in the Gospel: “The night will come, when no one can work” (John 9).

Night is the life of sinners, as in the Apostle: “Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Night is blindness of heart or vain security, as in Job, where it is said of the impious: “At night a storm will carry him away” (Job 27). And in the Gospel: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12).

Night signifies future tribulation, as in the Gospel: “On that night two will be in one field; one will be taken and one will be left” (Luke 17).

Night signifies the tribulation of the present life in its appointed time, as in the Gospel: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him: Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11)—that is, knowledge of the Trinity.

Midnight signifies the hidden judgment of the Lord, as in the Gospel: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming” (Matthew 25).

Midnight signifies death arriving unexpectedly, as in Job concerning the reprobate: “And at midnight they will be taken away” (Job 34).

The first watch signifies the first age of human beings, namely infancy or childhood; the second watch, adolescence and youth; the third watch, old age, as in the Gospel: “And if he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants” (Luke 12).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Seven Parts of the Night

The parts of the night are seven: twilight, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn [the enumeration appears to name six terms, although the heading says seven].

Twilight is uncertain light. For we call *creperum* “uncertain,” that is, something between light and darkness.

Evening is named from the western star, which follows the setting sun and precedes the darkness that follows. Virgil speaks of it:

> Before day, evening will set the sun  
> Beneath the closed Olympus.

The time of silence is when everyone is silent. For *conticescere* means “to be silent.”

The dead of night is the middle and inactive period of the night, when nothing can be done and everything is quiet in sleep. Time is not understood in itself except through human actions. The middle of the night lacks activity; therefore it is an inactive period, as though without time—that is, without the activity by which it is distinguished. Hence the expression: “You came at an inopportune time.” It is therefore called *intempesta*, because it lacks time, that is, activity.

Cockcrow is so called because roosters announce the light.

Morning is the interval between the departure of darkness and the coming of dawn. It is called *matutinum* because at this time morning begins.

Dawn is, as it were, the small light of day already beginning. It is also called *aurora*, which precedes the sun.

Aurora is the beginning of the brightening day and the first radiance of the air. In Greek it is called *eos* (“dawn”), which we call *aurora* by derivation, as though *eurora*. Hence the lines:

> … Joyful with Eastern  
> Eurus’ horses …

And:

> And the Eastern battle-lines …

Evening therefore signifies the beginning of night, or the beginning of tribulation that follows worldly prosperity; or the beginning of the turning away of the wicked, who, turned away from the true light of God’s commandments, fall into the darkness [Col. 0293B] of sins.

For when someone departs from truth and righteousness and falls into the darkness of errors and sins, he is rightly called by the name of evening, because he becomes a companion of Antichrist, who is called “Evening” in the Scriptures.

The dead of night—that is, the middle of the night—signifies either the depth of sins or the withdrawal from worldly affairs and the diligence of good people in praising the Lord. Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness” (Psalm 118 [119]).

It is not without significance that he says, “At midnight I rose.” For he knows that at this time the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck down. He also knows that at that time the chains of Peter, Paul, and Silas, placed in prison, were loosed. He knows also that the bridegroom will come at midnight; therefore at that same time he rises for praise, lest he remain outside the closed door among the foolish virgins.

Nor is it without significance that he says, “I rose,” because one always rises when one hastens to the Lord’s praises.

“To give thanks” here means “to praise,” because what follows is: “for the judgments of your righteousness.” For if he had wished confession of repentance to be understood, he would have said, “for your mercy,” not “for the judgments of your righteousness.”

Cockcrow signifies the conversion of sinners. At that same time Peter, who had wandered in the darkness of forgetfulness by denying the Lord, corrected himself through the remembrance of the light he had already hoped for; and, having attained the presence of that true light, he fully restored everything that he had changed.

I think that this cock should be understood as one of the teachers, who, awakening you as you lie prostrate and rebuking those who are drowsy, says:

> Awake, you righteous, and do not sin.

Morning, or dawn, signifies the time of the Lord’s resurrection, or the person’s complete conversion from sins to righteousness. Hence the Psalmist says to the Lord: “To you I keep watch from the light; and in the mornings I shall meditate upon you, because you have become my helper” (Psalm 62 [63]).

We keep watch for him whenever we sleep amid the ambition of the world. For we attain those things if we hasten to abandon these.

He rightly added: “In the mornings I shall meditate upon you” (Psalm 107 [108]); and elsewhere: “I shall rise at dawn.” This was when the time of the Lord’s resurrection shone forth, and he would then behold his praises, when he had animated the human race by the example of his resurrection.

Morning signifies the day of judgment or the resurrection of the dead, as in the Psalm: “In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth” (Psalm 100 [101]).

Aurora signifies the Church, because after the darkness of sins she has been illumined by the light of faith, as in Job: “And you showed the dawn its place” (Job 38).

## CHAPTER VIII. On Darkness

Darkness is so called because it holds shadows.

Darkness sometimes signifies the depth of the divine Scriptures; sometimes ignorance; sometimes the unbelief of sinners; and sometimes the punishment of Gehenna.

The depth of the Scriptures is signified by the prophetic testimony: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17 [18]); and elsewhere: “Darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illumined like day; its darkness is like its light” (Psalm 138 [139]).

By darkness he means the mystical and profound matters of the divine Scriptures, in accordance with what we read in Proverbs: “He understands the parable and the dark saying” (Proverbs 6).

Likewise, in another Psalm we read: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Psalm 17 [18]). These darknesses, then, are not darkened but rather illumined by the Lord, because the preaching of the prophets was fulfilled when he came.

Darkness signifies ignorance in the Apostle’s statement concerning sinners: “Their heart is darkened by darkness” (Ephesians 4).

The unbelief of the wicked is indicated by the Gospel statement: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1).

For Christ is the light of human beings, and by the presence of his knowledge he illumines all human hearts that are worthy of being illumined. But the darknesses are the foolish and the wicked, whose blinded hearts the light and [eternal—an uncertain or corrupt reading] wisdom clearly reveals for what they are, although they themselves are entirely unable to grasp the rays of that same light through understanding. It is as though a blind person were flooded with the sun’s radiance and yet could not see the sun, by whose light he is suffused.

Darkness signifies the devil or demons, as in the Prophet: “Darkness pursues his enemies,” that is, the Lord’s enemies (Nahum 1).

The punishment of Gehenna is signified by darkness in the Gospel statement concerning the sinner: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22).

Whoever, therefore, is darkened in the present life by the inner darkness of unbelief and sins must, unless suitable repentance comes to his aid, be cast after the end of this present life into the outer darkness, where there is the punishment of death and everlasting horror dwells.

Shadow is therefore sometimes used in a good sense and sometimes in a bad sense.

It is used in a good sense when it signifies God’s protection and the guardianship of the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “Under the shadow of your wings I hope, until iniquity passes away” (Psalm 56 [57]). And elsewhere: “Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye; under the shadow of your wings protect me” (Psalm 16 [17]).

He most appropriately asks to be guarded as the apple of the eye, since through it we distinguish visible things and nothing more precious is found in our body.

It follows: “Under the shadow of your wings protect me.” Here another figure [*schema*] is introduced, called in Greek *parabolē* and in Latin *comparatio*, “comparison,” when something unlike is joined to something else for the sake of some instruction.

Wings are compared with a father’s protections. For mercy and charity are like the Father’s wings, under which he appropriately begs to be protected.

And in the Gospel: “Behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them” (Matthew 17). And elsewhere: “Under his shadow we shall live among the nations” (Lamentations 4).

Shadow signifies the Old Testament, as in Solomon: “Until the day should appear and the shadows be removed” (Song of Songs 4).

Shadow signifies human life, as in Job: “He flees like a shadow” (Job 14).

Shadow signifies the death of the flesh, as in the Psalm: “The shadow of death has covered us” (Psalm 43 [44]).

Shadow is used in a bad sense when it signifies either bodily death or the punishment of Gehenna, as in: “Although I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me” (Psalm 22 [23]).

And elsewhere: “They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Psalm 87 [88]). This indicates the place of sinners, because the dead of transgressors endure shadowy and dark realms, since no joy shines for them, immersed as they are in the perpetual darkness of their sadness. Therefore, according to the character of the places, this word varies in its manifold meaning.

*Caligo* is a shadow produced by the density of the air. It is called *caligo* because it is especially generated by the heat of the air.

According to allegory, however, *caligo* signifies the covering of divine secrets. Hence we read in Exodus: “The people stood far off, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was” (Exodus 20).

The crowd of the people is unable to penetrate the darkness of allegories, because it belongs to very few to investigate spiritual understanding. Since the minds of the carnal are often nourished only by the historical account, “the people stood far off” while God spoke. But because spiritual people penetrate the cloud of allegories and understand God’s words spiritually, “Moses approached the darkness in which God was.”

Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “Darkness is beneath his feet” (Psalm 17 [18]), because God is not seen by those below with the same clarity with which he rules above.

This statement can also be understood in another way: here the darkness is the Devil, who clouds human minds, preventing them from seeing the splendor of truth, while he possesses them.

“Beneath his feet”: for undoubtedly, by the majesty of the Lord the Savior, the accursed wickedness of demons is trampled down, as it is said in the ninetieth Psalm: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90 [91]).

Likewise, *caligo* signifies the blindness of heart of persecutors. Hence the Lord says to Job: “Who shut up the sea with doors when it burst forth, proceeding as though from the womb, when I made the cloud its garment and wrapped it in darkness as in the swaddling clothes of infancy?” (Job 30).

The raging sea is clothed with a cloud, because the cruelty of persecutors is clothed in the covering of its folly. It is unable to see the clear light of truth, and through blindness it does not recognize what it accomplishes through cruelty.

Because the persecutors of the Church, unsettled by instability of heart and devoted to this world, have childish rather than great thoughts, they are restrained by heavenly judgment, lest they be able to persecute as much as they wish.

Likewise, shadow and darkness sometimes signify sins, as in: “Those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1); and sometimes the delight of sins, as in what is said of the devil in Job: “Under the shadow, in the secret places of reeds and rushes and in green places” (Job 40).

And because shadow is not far from the air, of which it is the shadow, so death is not far from punishment. Hence it is also said in Job: “Where there is the shadow of death, and there is no order, and everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10).

## CHAPTER IX. On the Weeks
Hebdomad takes its name in Greek from the number seven. In ordinary human usage it consists only of seven days; but by the authority of Sacred Scripture it is distinguished in many forms, all of which, unless I am mistaken, look toward one end: namely, to remind us that after the perfection of good works we should hope for perpetual rest in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The first and singular hebdomad, from which the others derive their form, is sublime through divine activity. For the Lord completed the adornment of the world in six days and rested from his works on the seventh. Here we should note that the number six is not perfect because the Lord completed the works of the world in it; rather—as Augustine says—the Lord, who was able to create everything simultaneously, graciously chose to work in that number because it is perfect. It is filled by its own parts, namely the sixth, the third, and the half, which are one, two, and three, and together make six.

Following the example of this divine hebdomad, a second is commanded for human observance, as the Lord says: “For six days you shall labor and do all your work; but on the seventh day, the Sabbath of the Lord your God, you shall do no work. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and he rested on the seventh” (Exod. XX). In ancient times this hebdomad was reckoned by the people of God as follows: the first day of the week, or “one of the week,” or “of the Sabbaths”; the second day of the week; the third; the fourth; the fifth; the sixth; and the seventh day, or the Sabbath. This does not mean that all the days of the Sabbaths—that is, the days of rest—were individually designated as first, second, third, and the others in their order, as though that day which excelled by its distinctive name and observance were simply one among them.

The third kind of hebdomad is observed in the celebration of Pentecost: seven weeks of days, completed by one day—that is, fifty days. On that day Moses also ascended the burning mountain and received the law from heaven, while Christ sent down from heaven the grace of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire.

The fourth was the hebdomad of the seventh month, which was almost entirely devoted to distinguished solemnities. Among these the Day of Atonement was especially prominent. On that day alone during the year the high priest, leaving the people outside, entered the Holy of Holies, after the annual fruits—that is, grain, wine, and oil—had first been gathered in their proper order. This signified that Jesus, the great high priest, after completing the dispensation of the flesh, would enter the gates of the heavenly kingdom through his own blood, so that he might now appear before the face of God for us, while we, still placed outside, await and love his coming. Here we should note that just as certain unclean persons were seen by the law to be purified on the first, third, and seventh days, so the first, third, and seventh months were each made solemn by their own ceremonies.

The fifth was the hebdomad of the seventh year, throughout which the entire people, by command of the law, rested from agricultural labor, as the Lord says: “For six years you shall sow your field, but in the seventh you shall cease” (Lev. XXV).

The sixth is the hebdomad of the jubilee, that is, of remission. It is formed by seven hebdomads of years, namely forty-nine years. When this period was completed, that is, when the fiftieth year began, the trumpets sounded more loudly, and according to the law the ancient possession returned to everyone.

The seventh kind of hebdomad is the one used by the prophet Daniel. Following the custom of the law, he comprises each hebdomad in seven years, but by a new method abbreviates those years, defining each by twelve lunar months. He adds the intercalary months—which customarily arise from the eleven epact days of the year—one at a time in the native reckoning in the third or second year; but when they reached the number twelve, he inserted them together as a complete year. He did this not out of envy toward those seeking knowledge of the truth, but, in the manner of prophecy, to exercise the understanding of those seeking it. He preferred his pearls to be sought by the children through fruitful toil rather than to be scattered for swine to trample in contemptuous disdain.

But so that these matters may become clearer, let us now examine the angel’s own proclamation to the prophet:

“Seventy hebdomads,” he says, “have been abbreviated concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX).

There is no doubt that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the law and the prophets, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. The seventy hebdomads, divided into periods of seven years, indicate four hundred and ninety years.

We should note, however, that he does not say that these hebdomads were simply marked out or counted, but that they were abbreviated, secretly warning the reader that years shorter than usual are being indicated.

“Know therefore,” he says, “and understand: from the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the ruler, there shall be seven hebdomads and sixty-two hebdomads; and the street and the walls shall again be built in the distress of time” (ibid.).

From Ezra’s account we learned that Nehemiah, when he was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, in the twentieth year of that king’s reign, in the month of Nisan, obtained permission from him to restore the walls of Jerusalem. The Temple had been built long before, Cyrus having permitted its construction. Nehemiah completed this work—as has been said—in a time of distress, being so fiercely attacked by neighboring peoples that, as we are told, the builders individually fought with swords girded at their waists, using one hand for battle and the other for restoring the wall.

From that time, therefore, until Christ the ruler, count seventy hebdomads: that is, four hundred and ninety years of twelve lunar months, which are four hundred and seventy-five solar years. For the Persians ruled from the aforementioned twentieth year of King Artaxerxes until the death of Darius for one hundred and sixteen years. From then the Macedonians held power until Cleopatra’s death for three hundred years. Thereafter the Romans held the monarchy until the seventeenth year of Tiberius Caesar for fifty-nine years. These together, as we said, make four hundred and seventy-five years, and are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles. For nineteen times twenty-five makes four hundred and seventy-five.

Since seven intercalary months accrue in each cycle, multiply twenty-five by seven: the result is 175, which are the intercalary months of 475 years. If you wish to know how many lunar years these can make, divide 175 by twelve. Twelve times fourteen makes 168, and fourteen years result, with seven months remaining. Add these to the 475 years written above: together they make [the number is corrupt in the source]. Add also the seven surplus months and the portion of the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign in which the Lord suffered, and you will find that from the appointed time until his Passion the seventy abbreviated hebdomads—that is, 490 lunar years—were completed.

At his baptism, however, when the Holy of Holies was anointed and the Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove, not only had seven and sixty-two hebdomads been completed, but a portion of the seventieth hebdomad had already begun:

“And after the sixty-two hebdomads,” he says, “Christ shall be slain, and there shall not be his people who will deny him.”

Christ was not slain immediately after the sixty-two hebdomads, but at the end of the seventieth hebdomad. He separated this hebdomad from the others—as far as we can conjecture—because he was going to report more about it. For Christ was crucified in it, and by the faithless people he was denied not only in his Passion but continuously from the time when he began to be proclaimed by John.

What follows—“And the people with the ruler who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed” (ibid.)—does not belong to the seventy hebdomads. It had been foretold that these hebdomads would extend up to Christ’s rule; but Scripture, after foretelling his coming and Passion, also shows what would happen afterward to the people who refused to receive him.

By the coming ruler it means Titus, who in the fortieth year of the Lord’s Passion so destroyed the city and sanctuary together with the Roman people that not one stone remained upon another. But after briefly anticipating these events, it immediately returns to explain the outcome of the hebdomad that it had passed over:

“He will confirm the covenant with many for one hebdomad” (Dan. IX)—that is, the very last one, during which either John the Baptist, or the Lord, or the apostles converted many to the faith through preaching.

“And in half of the hebdomad sacrifice and offering shall cease” (ibid.). The middle of this hebdomad was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, with Christ’s baptism having begun, the purification effected by sacrifices gradually began to be held in little esteem by the faithful.

Likewise, what follows—“And in the Temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and desolation shall endure until the consummation and the end” (ibid.)—refers to later times. The truth of this prophecy is attested both by the history of the ancients and by the events of our own times.

The eighth kind of hebdomad is uniform and stands alone without the cycle of revolution. It is completed as a figure corresponding in every respect to the first hebdomad, as the ages of this world pass away.

On the first day light was made, and in the first age humanity was placed in the delight of Paradise. When light had been divided from darkness, evening came; and when the sons of God had been separated from the wicked offspring, giants were born not long afterward, and the whole earth was corrupted, until the Creator, repenting that he had made humanity, determined to destroy the world by a flood.

On the second day the firmament was balanced in the midst of the waters. In the second age the ark was borne in the midst of the waters, supported on one side by the spring of the abyss and drenched on the other by the cataracts of heaven. Its evening came when the sons of Adam, moving eastward from the place where they had gathered to build the tower of pride, were punished by the division of languages and scattered from one another.

On the third day, when the waters had been gathered into one place, dry land appeared, adorned with woods and grasses. In the third age, when the nations had been established in the worship of demons, Abraham the patriarch abandoned his kindred and homeland and was made fruitful through the offspring of the saints.

Evening also came, when the Hebrew people, compelled by the pressure of evils, asked for a king against the will of God. Once appointed, he first slaughtered the Lord’s priests and prophets; afterward he himself, together with the whole people, perished by the sword of the Philistines.

On the fourth day heaven was adorned with luminaries. In the fourth age that people, distinguished by heavenly faith and glorious through the kingdom of David and Solomon, was also ennobled throughout the world by the height of the most holy Temple. But it too received an evening, when, as sins multiplied, that kingdom was destroyed by the Chaldeans, the Temple was demolished, and the whole people was transported to Babylon.

On the fifth day fish and birds were brought forth from the waters: the former remain in their native streams, while the latter fly through air and over land. In the fifth age, when the peoples of Israel had multiplied in Chaldea, one part, supported by the wings of heavenly desires, sought Jerusalem; another, deprived of the flight of virtues, remained among the waters of Babylon.

Evening followed, when, as the Savior’s coming was already near, the Jewish people, because of the magnitude of their crimes, became tributary to the Romans and was moreover subjected to foreign kings.

On the sixth day the earth was filled with its living creatures, and the first human was created in the image of God. Soon afterward, a woman was fashioned from the rib taken from the side of the sleeping man. In the sixth age, while the prophets proclaimed him, the Son of God appeared in the flesh—the one who had created humanity in the image of God. Sleeping on the cross, he poured blood and water from his side, from which he consecrated the Church for himself. The evening of this age, darker than the others, will come in the persecution of Antichrist.

On the seventh day, having completed his works, God rested. Sanctifying it, he commanded that it be called the Sabbath; it is not said to have had an evening. For in the seventh age the souls of the just, after the excellent labors of this life, rest perpetually in the next life. It will never be stained by any sorrow, but will instead be increased by the greater glory of the resurrection.

This age began for humanity when the first martyr, Abel, entered—bodily indeed into the tomb, but in spirit into the Sabbath of perpetual rest. It will be completed when, having received their holy bodies, they possess a double inheritance in their own land; everlasting joy will be theirs.

This is also the eighth age, on account of which the sixth psalm is inscribed. I believe that during the six ages of this world we must pray for the seventh or eighth age of the world to come. Because the righteous will receive joys in it, while the reprobate will receive punishments, the Psalm begins, proceeds, and ends in great terror:

“Lord, rebuke me not in your anger,” etc. (Ps. VI).

## CHAPTER X. On the Months

The months are so called from the measure by which each is measured; but more correctly from the moon, which in Greek is called *mēnē*. Among the Hebrews as well, as Jerome testifies, the moon—which they call *yare*—gave its name to the months. Hence Jesus son of Sirach, who certainly wrote in Hebrew, says when speaking of the moon: “The month is according to its name” (Sir. XLIII).

The ancients were accustomed to reckon their months not by the course of the sun but by that of the moon. Therefore, whenever Sacred Scripture—whether in the law or before the law—indicates on what day of the month something happened or was said, it signifies nothing other than the moon’s age. The Hebrews, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted (Rom. III), have always continued, according to the ancient custom of their ancestors, to observe the months by the moon.

They call the first month, consecrated to the rites of Passover, Nisan. Because of the moon’s wandering course, it now falls in March, now in April, and sometimes occupies several days of May. It is more properly assigned to April, because it always either begins in that month, ends in it, or is wholly contained within it, provided that the rule mentioned above is observed: the moon that is fifteenth after the equinox makes the first month of the following year, while the one that occurs before it makes the last month of the preceding year, and so in order.

Their second month, Iar, corresponds to May; the third, Sivan, to June; the fourth, Thammuz, to July; the fifth, Ab, to August; the sixth, Elul, to September; the seventh, Tisri, to October. Because of the gathering of crops and the very important festivals celebrated in it, Tisri is called the new year. The eighth, Marcheshvan, corresponds to November; the ninth, Chislev, to December; the tenth, Tebeth, to January; the eleventh, Shebat, to February; and the twelfth, Adar, to March in the same manner.

Because the lunar cycle consists of twenty-nine and a half days, these months alternate between thirty and twenty-nine days. After the second or third year has been completed, they intercalate an additional month, which is formed from the eleven epact days that accrue annually.

I am therefore moved by no small difficulty concerning how our predecessors count the day on which the law was given—which is the third day of the third month—as the fiftieth day from the slaughter of the lamb. They assign seventeen remaining days to the first month, since thirteen earlier days had passed before Passover, then thirty days to the second month and three to the third, making fifty days altogether. Yet it is clear that two lunar months do not end in sixty days but in fifty-nine. Thus, if the paschal month is reckoned as thirty days and retains seventeen days of its course after Passover, the second month ought to end not in thirty but in twenty-nine days. Consequently, the total of the period mentioned would contain no more than forty-nine days—unless perhaps we should think that, by synecdoche, a very common rule of Sacred Scripture, the whole is being reckoned from a part.

However these matters may have been handled or calculated, it is nevertheless clear that the Hebrews were accustomed to observe their months according to the course of the moon.

The same understanding should be applied to Genesis, where Noah is said to have entered the ark with his companions on the seventeenth day of the second month and to have left it on the twenty-seventh day of that same month after the flood. The year there is described as a complete solar year, that is, 365 days, because the moon that is, for example, seventeenth on the Nones of May in the present year will appear on the twenty-seventh on the day before the Nones of May in the following year.

It should certainly be noted that those are greatly mistaken who believe that a month is, or was defined by the ancients as, the time during which the moon traverses the zodiacal circle. For, as more careful investigation of nature has taught, the moon completes the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, but completes the course of its own movement in twenty-nine days and twelve hours, allowing for its leap.

Thus it is more correctly defined as follows: a lunar month is the circuit and renewal of the moon’s light from new moon to new moon. A solar month is the sun’s passage through one-twelfth of the zodiac—that is, the circle bearing the signs—which is completed in thirty days and ten and a half hours. It is longer than a lunar month by twenty-two and a half hours, from which eleven and a quarter epact days ordinarily accrue each year.

Twelve times twenty-two makes 264, which are the hours of eleven days; this is readily apparent because eleven times twenty-four produces the same total. Moreover, twelve times six and a half makes seventy-eight, which are the hours of a quarter of a day each year. Since the moon’s twelve months are, as has been said, eleven days and a quarter shorter than the same number of solar months, in completing them it traverses the zodiac thirteen times.

Allegorically, however, the month, which receives its name and order from the moon, signifies the gathering together or progress of the holy Church. Hence Job says: “Who will grant me that I might be as in the months of former times?” (Job XXIV). What does he signify by the name “months” except gatherings of souls, or, at times, perfection, represented by the month?

Let the Church, therefore, through Job’s words remember the perfection of former times, and recall how much perfection of preaching brought her in profit through the souls she gathered.

The twelve months, corresponding in number, are the Apostles, as in the Apocalypse: “Yielding its fruit each month” (Rev. XXII).

The month, like the Sabbath, is also found to stand for eternal rest, as in Isaiah: “From month to month and from Sabbath to Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI), so that from carnal Sabbaths and months there may arise spiritual and delightful Sabbaths. This Sabbath-rest is reserved for the people of God, as is the spiritual month, when the moon is completed from point to point and runs through its ordered course so as to make a complete calendar month.

That the moon, which is illuminated by the sun, signifies the Church illuminated by Christ requires no explanation; nor does the fact that the Sabbath signifies rest.

“They shall come from new moon to new moon and from Sabbath to Sabbath.” Having passed through the six days in which the world was made, they hasten toward the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, in which true rest exists.

“All flesh shall come to worship before my face,” says the Lord (Isa. LXVI)—not only the Jewish people, nor in Jerusalem alone, but the whole human race everywhere throughout the world shall worship the Father in Spirit and truth (John IV).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Four Changes of the Seasons

There are four changes of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They are called *tempora* because of the tempering of their qualities: they moderate one another through moisture, dryness, heat, and cold. They are also called courses, because they do not stand still but run their course.

It is established that after the world was made, the seasons were divided according to the character of the sun’s course into three months each. The ancients distinguish the months of each season as follows: the first month of spring is called new, the second mature, and the third declining. Summer is similarly divided into new, mature, and declining; likewise autumn; and likewise winter, whose months are called new, mature, and declining or final.

Hence the expression: “At the fall of extreme winter.”

Spring is so called because it becomes green. For then, after winter, the earth is clothed with grasses, and everything bursts into flower.

Summer is called as though from “burned,” that is, scorched and dry, for heat is dry.

Autumn is named from the stormy season, when the leaves of the trees fall and everything ripens.

Winter received its name from the reasoning of the hemisphere, because the sun then revolves through a shorter circle. Hence this season is also called *bruma*, as if from Greek *brachys*, “short,” or from food, because the appetite for eating is then greater. Gluttony is called *broma* in Greek. Hence those who have an aversion to food are also called *imbrumati*.

*Hibernus* lies between winter and spring, as though from *hievernus*, and often signifies the whole of winter by a part.

These seasons are also assigned to the several regions of heaven. Spring is given to the East, because at that time everything rises from the earth. Summer belongs to the South, because that region burns with greater heat. Winter belongs to the North, because it is sluggish with cold and perpetual frost. Autumn belongs to the West because of the serious diseases it brings; hence at that time the leaves of all the trees fall.

Autumn’s abundance of disease is caused by the boundary between cold and heat and by the conflict within it of contrary elements.

Mystically, spring signifies the newness of Baptism, or the renewal of life after the cold of unbelief and the torpor of sluggishness; alternatively, it signifies the resurrection of bodies after death. Hence the Lord commanded in the law that the month of new things and the beginning of spring should be observed, when the Lord led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt through the Red Sea, in which he also commanded them to celebrate Passover (Exod. XIV). At the same season the Savior rose from death after his Passion and granted us the hope of resurrection.

Summer is a foreshadowing of the joy to come and expresses the fervor of charity. Hence the Psalm says: “You made summer and spring” (Ps. LXXIII). Solomon likewise says: “For now the winter is past and gone; the flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song II).

Summer signifies future blessedness, as Solomon says: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him” (Prov. XX).

Through these two seasons he signifies the faithful distinguished by differing qualities of character. Some are like summer, fervent with the heat of faith and brought even to martyrdom; others, tempered by gentleness, are like spring, serving the Lord with steady devotion. For he himself made all these things and all others, and by his grace what is displayed in human good will is granted.

Autumn, in which crops are gathered, is also the season of harvest and vintage. It signifies the time of universal judgment, when each person will receive the reward of his work and reap the fruit of his labor, according to the Apostle:

“We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil; for whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (II Cor. V; Gal. VI).

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “The harvest is the consummation of the age, and the reapers are the angels of God” (Matt. XIII).

And elsewhere: “The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and sleep and rise, night and day, while the seed germinates and grows, though he does not know how” (Mark IV). For the earth bears fruit of its own accord: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit has appeared, he immediately sends the sickle, because the time of harvest has come.

Then the Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and bind the weeds into bundles to burn them; but they will gather the wheat into his barns (Matt. XIII).

Autumn sometimes also signifies past times of salvation, as in Micah: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers grapes in autumn” (Mic. VII).

Winter signifies tribulation or the end of mortal life. Hence the Lord instructed his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV).

If we understand this saying as referring to the captivity of Jerusalem, when it was captured by Titus and Vespasian, they should pray that their flight not occur in winter or on the Sabbath. In the one case the severity of the cold prevents them from going into solitude and hiding in the mountains and deserts; in the other, it would be a transgression of the law if they wished to flee, or imminent death if they remained.

But if it is understood of the consummation of the world, he commanded that our faith and love for Christ not grow cold, nor that we become sluggish as idle people in the work of God on the Sabbath of virtues.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Year

The year received its name either from renewing all things that have passed away according to the natural order, or from the circuit of time, because the ancients used to denote a year by the word *circum*, as Cato says in the *Origins* of the Orators: “A year, that is, a circuit, a boundary.” From this comes *ambire*, used for “to go around.”

There is a lunar year, a solar year, a year determined by the wandering stars, and a single year belonging to all the planets, which is specially called the great year.

The lunar year is understood in four ways. The first is when the moon, traversing the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, returns to the sign from which it departed. The second is longer by two days and four hours; this is customarily called a month, when, after twenty-nine days and twelve hours have passed, the moon, now diminished, returns to the sun from which it had newly departed.

The third is completed in twelve such months, that is, in 354 days, and is called common because two such years most often run together.

The fourth is called in Greek *embolismos*, that is, an increase or addition, and has thirteen months, that is, 384 days [the numerical reading is uncertain in the source].

Among the Hebrews both kinds begin with the beginning of the paschal month and end there. Among the Romans, however, the year begins with the new moon of January and ends there.

There is also a solar year, when the sun returns to the same positions among the stars after 365 days and six hours—that is, a quarter of a complete day. This fraction, taken four times, requires one day to be inserted; the Romans call it the leap day, so that the sun may return to the same circuit.

Every fourth solar-cycle year is bissextile, one day longer than the other three. When it has been completed, the sun returns to all the positions of the signs at the same hours of days and nights at which it was four years earlier.

The year of the wandering stars is the period in which each of them traverses the circuit of the zodiac, as we said above.

The great year is when all the wandering stars together return each to its own position. The great paschal cycle also displays this.

The great paschal cycle is completed in 532 years by multiplying the solar and lunar cycles together. Whether nineteen times twenty-eight or twenty-eight times nineteen is multiplied, the number 532 results. Thus the same great cycle contains twenty-eight lunar nineteen-year cycles and nineteen solar cycles, each normally completed in twenty-eight years.

It has nineteen sets of seven leap years, that is, 133; and twenty-eight times 228 solar months, that is, 6,384. The lunar months amount to twenty-eight times 235, that is, 6,580. The days, excluding leap days, are twenty-eight times 6,935, that is, 194,180. With the leap days added, they are 194,313; when it has completed the aforementioned total in the proper order of months and days, it immediately turns back upon itself and continually restores everything pertaining to the course of the sun or moon in the same manner in which it had passed before.

Only the years of the Lord’s Incarnation advance along their fixed path toward increase. The indictions, however they proceed in their order, move nothing in the course of the stars and therefore nothing in the order of the paschal calculation.

Allegorically, years sometimes signify eternity and sometimes the brevity of human life. In the prophetic passage where it is said to God, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI), his nature is declared through brevity, because he alone knows how to exist without needing another helper in order to be.

Elsewhere, where it is written, “Our years shall meditate like a spider” (Ps. LXXXIX), the comparison expresses the wickedness of our life. A spider is a weak and extremely delicate creature that weaves certain deceitful webs in order to obtain food for itself from passing flies. Thus the years of those devoted to criminal works are occupied in devices and crafty schemes.

What follows—“The days of our years in them are seventy years; and if in strength, eighty years,” and so forth—would seem, if we wished to understand these years literally, to be contradicted by the fact that many people live good lives into their nineties, while others are worn out by weakness before reaching seventy. Thus what is said here would appear unable to stand.

But we more appropriately adapt the number seventy to the law, which commanded the observance of the Sabbath day; and we most suitably assign eighty to the Christian people, who venerate the eighth day of the Lord’s resurrection with holy celebration.

He added eighty “in strength,” because we truly began to possess strength when the Lord our Savior appeared to us. These, then, are the days of years that grant us the brightness of a credible life.

Some consider the year to be the Lord Jesus Christ, as in the Psalm: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance” (Ps. LXIV).

The year is also the present time from the Lord’s advent until the end of the world, in which repentance and the remission of sins are proclaimed, as in Isaiah: “To proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord and a day of retribution” (Isa. LXI).

Hence in the Gospel the gardener says to his master concerning the barren tree: “Let it remain this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of manure on it” (Luke XIII).

The six years about which the law gives instruction—namely, that if a Hebrew servant has been bought for a price, he should serve his master, and in the seventh go out to freedom (Exod. XXI)—signify the present time, because the world was made in six days.

Jubilee is interpreted as “the year of remission.” It is a Hebrew term and a number formed by seven hebdomads of years, that is, forty-nine years. In it the trumpets were sounded, the ancient possession returned to everyone, debts were remitted, and freedoms were confirmed.

We also celebrate this number in the days of Pentecost after the Lord’s resurrection: guilt having been remitted, the written record of the entire debt having been canceled, we receive freedom from every bond and welcome the grace of the Holy Spirit as it comes upon us.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Age

Ages consist of generations, and they are called ages because they follow one another. As some depart, others succeed them.

For this reason some call the fiftieth year an age, which the Hebrews call a Jubilee. For the same reason the Hebrew servant who, because of his wife and children, loves his master and is subjected to servitude with his ear pierced is commanded to serve “forever,” that is, until the fiftieth year (Exod. XXI).

Sometimes “age” refers to the present life, as in: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CXXXV). The age signifies the course of this life, in which all who sin are wretched, and in which it is permitted for our hearts to be converted and mercy to be sought. For confession of sin brings condemnation there where judgment is known to exist.

Sometimes it refers to eternity, as in: “He remembered his covenant forever” (Ps. CIV), because whatever the Lord has promised will remain through him with everlasting firmness.

Sometimes it signifies past time, as in: “The mercy of the Lord is from the age” (Ps. XL), that is, it was revealed from the beginning of the world among his faithful. And “unto the age of the age” means in the present age and in the future age.

Thus, when “age” is used three times here, it absolutely designates the eternity of the Lord, since he is shown to be merciful before the age, in the age, and after this age.

*Age* is often used for one year, as in annals; for seven years, as in the case of a human being; for a hundred years; or for any period of time. Hence an age is a period constructed from many ages, and the word *aetas* is formed as though from *aevitas*, that is, a likeness of an age.

For *aeon* is perpetual age, whose beginning and end are unknown. The Greeks call these *aeons*; among them the word is sometimes used for an age and sometimes for eternity. From them it has also passed into Latin.

The word *age* is used in nearly two ways. It may refer to a human being, as in infancy, youth, and old age; or to the world. The first age of the world extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the migration of Judah into Babylon; the fifth from then until the Savior’s coming in the flesh; and the sixth, which is now in progress, until this world comes to an end.

Thus the age of the world can be compared to the ages of a human being.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Six Ages of the World
## Of the Six Ages of This World

We have touched briefly above upon the six ages of this world, and upon the seventh or eighth age of rest and heavenly life, in comparison with the first week, in which the world was adorned. Now, in comparison with the lifespan of a single human being—who in Greek is commonly called by philosophers *microcosmos*, that is, “the smaller world”—we shall explain the same matters somewhat more fully.

The first age of this world, therefore, extends from Adam to Noah. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 1,657 years; according to the translators of the Septuagint, 2,242 years [Col. 0307A]; and, according to both editions, ten generations. This age was entirely destroyed by the Flood, just as the forgetfulness that commonly overwhelms every person’s infancy destroys the first age of each human life. For how many people are there who remember their infancy?

The second age extends from Noah to Abraham. According to the Hebrew authority, it comprises ten generations and 222 years; according to the translators, however, it comprises 1,072 years and eleven generations. This was, as it were, the childhood of the people belonging to God, and therefore language was discovered in it—that is, Hebrew. For it is in childhood that a person begins to learn to speak, after infancy, which is so called because one cannot yet *fari*, “speak.”

The third age extends from Abraham to David. According to both authorities, it comprises fourteen generations and 942 years. This was, as it were, a kind of adolescence [Col. 0307B] of the people of God. Since at this age a person begins to be capable of generating offspring, the evangelist Matthew consequently took the beginning of his genealogy from Abraham, who was also appointed father of the nations when he received a changed name (Gen. XVII).

The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian captivity. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 473 years; according to the Septuagint translation, twelve more. According to both books, it contains eighteen generations, although the evangelist Matthew, for the sake of a definite mystery, sets them at fourteen. From this age, as from the period of youth, the times of kings began among the people of God. For among human beings this is ordinarily the age suited to governing a kingdom.

The fifth age, as it were an old age, extends from the Babylonian captivity to the coming of the Lord and Savior in the flesh. [Col. 0307C] It too contains twenty-four generations and extends over 589 years. During this period the Hebrew people, wearied as though by oppressive old age, are shaken by increasingly frequent evils.

The sixth age, which is now in progress, has no fixed sequence of generations or periods of time; rather, like an age of decrepitude, it is destined to be consumed by the death of the entire world. Those who have overcome these sorrowful and labor-filled ages of the world by a blessed death now await, having entered the seventh age of the perpetual Sabbath, the eighth age of blessed resurrection, in which they will reign forever with the Lord.

## CHAPTER XV. On Festivals

“Festival” (*festivitas*) is derived from “festal days,” as though from *festiditas*, because on those days only divine matters are performed. Opposed to them are the *fasti*, on which justice is proclaimed—that is, spoken. “Solemnity” (*solemnitas*) is said from sacred things, having been adopted in such a way that, on account of the religion [Col. 0307D] of Christ, it ought not to be changed; it is named from *solum*, that is, from what is firm and solid. “Celebration” (*celebritas*) is so called because on those occasions not earthly things but heavenly things alone are performed.

Easter is the first of all festivals; its name has already been discussed above.

Pentecost, like Passover, was a celebrated day among the Hebrews. It is observed after five decades from Passover, and from this it received its name. For *pente* in Greek means “five.” On that day, according to the Law, the loaves of the Presence were offered from the new crops. The jubilee year in the Old Testament represented its figure, and now, again through the figure of its promise, foreshadows eternal rest.

“Epiphany” is called in Greek *epiphaneia*, and in Latin “appearance” or “manifestation.” On that day Christ appeared to the Magi, to be worshiped, through the indication of a star [Col. 0308A]; this was a figure of the firstfruits of the believing nations. On that day also the sacrament of the Lord’s Baptism took place, as well as the beginning of the signs performed by the Lord, including the changing of water into wine.

There are two Epiphanies. The first is that on which Christ, having been born, appeared to the shepherds of the Hebrews when an angel announced him. The second is that on which, from the people of the nations, the Magi were led by a star to the cradle of the manger to worship him.

The Hebrew solemnity of *Scenopegia* is translated from Greek into Latin as “the dedication of tabernacles.” It was celebrated by the Jews in memory of the expedition during which, after setting out from Egypt, they lived in tabernacles; hence the name *Scenopegia*. For *skēnē* in Greek means “tabernacle.” This solemnity is celebrated among the Hebrews in the month of September.

[Col. 0308B] Among us *Neomenia* is called the Calends. Among the Hebrews, however, since the months are reckoned according to the course of the moon, and the moon is called *mēnē* in Greek, the term *neomenia* arose, meaning “new moon.” Among the Hebrews these days of the Calends were solemn days by legal institution, concerning which it is said in the Psalter: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of your notable solemnity” (Ps. LXXX).

*Encaenia* means a new dedication of the temple. For in Greek *kainon* means “new.” Whenever something new is dedicated, it is called *encaenia*. The Jews celebrated this solemnity of the temple’s dedication in the month of October.

It is called Palm Sunday because on that day the Lord and our Savior, as the prophet sang (Zech. IX), is said to have sat upon a donkey as he was making his way toward Jerusalem. Then, as he proceeded, crowds of people went out to meet him with palm branches [Col. 0308C], crying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Matt. XXI).

The common people call this day *capitilavium* because it is then customary to wash the heads of the infants who are to be anointed, so that they may not approach the anointing soiled by their observance of Lent.

On this day the Creed is delivered to the candidates for baptism, because of the proximity of the solemnity of the Lord’s Passover, so that those who are already hastening to receive the grace of God may recognize the faith that they are to confess.

It is called the Lord’s Supper because on that day the Savior celebrated the Passover with his disciples. This is still celebrated today, as it was handed down; on that day the holy chrism is also prepared, and the beginning of the New Testament and the cessation of the Old Testament are declared.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Sabbath

[Col. 0308D]

The Sabbath is named by the Hebrews, according to the interpretation of its name, “rest,” because on it God rested when the world had been perfected. Indeed, on that day the Lord rested in the tomb, in order to confirm the mystery of that rest, which was commanded to the Jews to be observed as a shadow of things to come. But after Christ fulfilled its figure in his own tomb, its observance came to rest.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Lord’s Day

The day is therefore called the Lord’s Day because on it the resurrection of our Lord was revealed. This day was not declared for the Jews but for Christians in the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0309A], and from that event it began to have its own festival.

For the Jews alone were given the Sabbath to celebrate, because previously it signified the rest of the dead. But there was no resurrection of anyone who, having risen from the dead, would [Col. 0310A] not die again. After such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body—so that he might go before, as the head, that which the body of the Church would hope for at the end—the Lord’s Day, that is, the eighth day, which is also the first, began to be celebrated.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0309]

## CHAPTER I. On the Diversity of Waters

[Col. 0309A]

There is great diversity in the nature of waters. Some are saline, some nitrous, some alum-bearing, some sulphurous, some bituminous, and some provide remedies for diseases [Col. 0309B]. Historians are found to have reported many things about these waters.

For it is said that near Rome the waters of the Albula heal wounds. In Italy, the spring of Cicero cures injuries of the eyes. In Ethiopia there is a place where bodies, when washed with its water, shine as though with oil. The spring of Zama in Africa makes voices melodious. Those who drink from Clitorius, a lake of Italy, develop a distaste for wine. On the island of Chios, they say, there is a spring that makes people dull-witted. In Boeotia there are two springs: one brings memory, the other forgetfulness. The spring of Cyzicus removes the love of Venus. The lake of Boeotia is frenzied; whoever drinks from it is inflamed with the ardor of lust.

In Campania there are waters said to remove infertility in women and madness in men. Whoever drinks from the red spring of Ethiopia [Col. 0309C] becomes delirious. The spring of Lechnus in Arcadia prevents miscarriages. In Sicily there are two springs, one of which makes a barren woman fertile, while the other makes a fertile woman barren.

In Thessaly there are two rivers. They say that sheep drinking from one become black, those drinking from the other become white, and those drinking from both become variegated. Lake Clitumnus in Umbria produces very large cattle. They say that the hooves of pack animals are hardened in the marshes of Reate.

In the Asphaltite Lake of Judea nothing that possesses life can sink. In India there is a pond called Siden in which nothing floats, but everything sinks. By contrast, in Africa’s Lake Apuscidamus everything floats and nothing sinks.

The spring of Marsyas in Phrygia ejects stones; in Achaia water flows out of stones. The Styx is so called because whatever is drunk from it kills immediately. The lake of Gelonium in Sicily drives away those who approach it by its foul odor.

There is a spring in Africa near the temple [Col. 0309D] of Ammon that binds the earth with the bonds of moisture; it even hardens ashes into a clod. The spring of Job in Idumaea is said to change color four times a year—that is, dusty, bloody, green, and clear—retaining one of these colors for three months at a time.

Among the Troglodytes there is a lake that becomes bitter three times a day and then just as often becomes sweet. The spring of Siloam at the foot of Mount Zion does not bubble continuously, but at fixed hours and on fixed days. In Judea, once, a stream dried up every Sabbath.

In Sardinia, hot springs heal the eyes and expose thieves, for their crime is revealed by blindness. In Epirus, they say, there is a spring in which burning torches are extinguished and extinguished torches are lit. Among the Garamantes, they say, there is a spring so cold by day that it cannot be drunk, and so hot by night that it cannot be touched.

[Col. 0310A] In many places, moreover, waters flow perpetually, hot enough only to heat baths. Some lands contain much sulphur and alum. Thus, when cold water comes through heated veins, it becomes intensely hot when touched by the nearby heat of sulphur. [Col. 0310B] Such water does not flow out hot from its source, but is changed as it comes. Waters carry sulphur and alum with them, both substances full of fire and growing hot through the slightest movements.

Since different kinds of water have different effects, they can express appropriate meanings in Scripture wherever necessary. For it is fitting that the meanings of those things found in Scripture should be carefully sought; things that occur elsewhere, however, need not be explained.

In Holy Scripture, waters sometimes signify the Holy Spirit, sometimes sacred knowledge, sometimes corrupt knowledge, sometimes tribulation, sometimes peoples flowing away, and sometimes the minds of those who follow the faith.

[Col. 0310C] The infusion of the Holy Spirit is signified by water, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says” (John VII), “rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist adds immediately afterward: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

Holy knowledge is again signified by water, as it is said: “He gave them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Sir. XV).

Corrupt knowledge is also commonly called water. Thus in Solomon, the woman who represents heresy entices with crafty persuasions, saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX).

The name of waters sometimes signifies tribulations, as the Psalmist says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. LXVIII).

[Col. 0310D] Peoples are signified by water, as John says: “The waters are peoples” (Apoc. XVII).

Water also signifies not only the flow of peoples running onward, but also the minds of the good who follow the teachings of faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. XXXII). The Psalmist likewise says: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Ps. XXVIII).

Some hold that waters are angels, as in the Psalm: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII).

Waters are nations, as in the Apocalypse: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations” (Apoc. XVII).

Water signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, because he washes away filth and refreshes the thirsty, as in Jeremiah: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II). And in the Psalm: “Like water I have been poured out” (Ps. XXI).

[Col. 0311A] Water signifies the streams of divine preaching, as in Isaiah: “He gave waters in the desert” (Isa. XLIII), that is, among the people.

Water signifies the obscure preaching of the saints, as in the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII). And elsewhere: “Because of the multitude of the sound of the waters, the clouds gave forth a voice” (Ps. LXXVI).

Water signifies baptism, as in Isaiah: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV). And in Ezekiel: “I will pour clean water over you” (Ezek. XXXVI). Likewise there: “And behold, water was coming out from the right side” (Ezek. XLVII), that is, from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Some hold that water signifies the pouring out of tears: “If I am washed as with waters of snow” (Job IX).

Water signifies the doctrine of the righteous, as in Solomon: “The words from the mouth of a man are deep water” (Prov. XVIII). Likewise there: “Drink water from your own cistern” (Prov. V).

[Col. 0311B] Some think that water signifies charity, as in the Psalm: “He who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. CIII)—the heaven of divine Scripture—because, according to the Gospel, the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon the two commandments of charity.

Waters signify the persecutions of this world, as in Job: “Will you raise your voice in the cloud, and will the force of the waters cover you?” (Job XXXVIII).

Waters signify the temptations of the devil, as in the Psalm: “I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Ps. LXXX).

Waters signify the baptism of heretics, as in the Psalter: “Deliver me from many waters” (Ps. CXLIII).

Waters signify the multiplication of sins, as in the Psalter: “He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters” (Ps. XVII).

Water signifies the doctrine of heretics, as in Solomon: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX). And in Isaiah: “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine” (Isa. I).

[Col. 0311C] Water signifies excessive speech, as in Solomon: “Whoever releases water,” that is, the tongue, “is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. XVII).

Water signifies the lust of the flesh, as in Solomon: “The earth is not satisfied with water” (Prov. XXX), that is, the human flesh is not filled with lust. And in the Gospel it is said of a certain lunatic: “He often falls into the fire, and frequently into the water” (Matt. XVII).

## CHAPTER II. On the Sea

The sea is the general gathering of waters. For every collection of waters, whether salt or fresh, is loosely called a sea, according to the passage: “And he called the gatherings of waters seas” (Gen. I).

[Col. 0311D] Properly, however, it is called the sea because its waters are bitter. The reason why the sea does not increase, although it receives all rivers and all springs, is first that its own vastness does not perceive the inflowing waters; then that its bitter water consumes the fresh stream; or that the clouds themselves draw much water upward; or that the winds carry some of it away and the sun dries up some; finally, that it is filtered through certain hidden openings in the earth and, returning to the source and headwaters of all things, flows back again.

Hence it is also written in Ecclesiastes: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. I). Here, metaphorically, human beings are understood by the name of waters and rivers: they return to the earth from which they were taken [Col. 0312A], but the earth is not filled by their multitude.

## CHAPTER III. On the Ocean

The Greeks and Latins call it the Ocean because it surrounds the world in the manner of a circle. Likewise, because it shines like the sky with a purple color, it is called Ocean, as though *cyaneos*, “blue.”

This is the body of water that embraces the shores of the lands and advances and recedes with alternating tides. For when winds breathe into the depths, it either drives the seas away or sucks them back.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Mediterranean

The Great Sea is that which flows from the Ocean in the west, turns toward the south, and then extends toward the north [Col. 0312B]. It is called Great because the other seas are smaller in comparison with it.

It is also called the Mediterranean because it reaches through the middle of the land as far as the East, separating Europe, Africa, and Asia.

## CHAPTER V. On the Red Sea

The Red Sea was so called because it is stained with rose-colored waves. It does not, however, possess the nature that it appears to display. Rather, the gulf is corrupted and stained by the neighboring shores, because all the land surrounding the sea is red and close to the color of blood. For this reason the brightest red pigment is seen there, along with other colors by which painting is varied.

Since the earth possesses this nature [Col. 0312C], it is repeatedly washed by the waves, and whatever adheres to it is carried off into the color. For this reason red gems are also found on these shores. A stone of this kind, wrapped in such soil, when rubbed among the sands, takes both the color of the earth and that of the sea.

This sea is divided into two gulfs. The one to the east is called the Persian Gulf, because the Persians inhabit its shore; the other is called the Arabian Gulf because it lies around Arabia.

Allegorically, the sea signifies either baptism, or worldly wisdom, or the present age seething with the waves of persecutions, or sinners tossing amid the waves of vices.

The sea signifies baptism in the passage of the Apostle: “All were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. X). There the true Pharaoh with his army is submerged, and the true Israelite is delivered from the pursuing enemy.

[Col. 0312D] Again, the sea signifies baptism in the Apocalypse: “And before the throne there was, as it were, a sea of glass” (Apoc. IV). That bronze sea which Solomon made in the temple of the Lord prefigured this sea of baptism.

The sea also signifies divine Scripture because of its immeasurable knowledge, as in Ezekiel: “And their appearance,” that is, the appearance of the wheels, “was like the appearance of the sea” (Ezek. I).

The eastern sea signifies the Jewish people; the westernmost sea signifies the people of the nations. Hence we read in Zechariah, in reference to the water of baptism: “Half of them toward the westernmost sea” (Zech. XIV).

The sea signifies worldly wisdom, as in the Psalm: “The birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, which travel the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII). The fish of the sea [Col. 0313A] perhaps signify philosophers, who investigate the nature of this world with wandering curiosity. Just as those fish, moving headfirst, open paths for themselves through the confused flood of the sea, so philosophers, casting out a net, search out the principles of things through continual human labor and reasoning.

Although there are also fish of rivers, it is not without significance that the Psalm has said “of the sea,” because of those who seem wise in their own eyes.

The sea also signifies the present age, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea” (Matt. XIII). In Habakkuk: “You sent your horses into the sea,” that is, the apostles, “stirring up many waters” (Hab. III), that is, the nations.

The desert sea is likewise the present world, as in Isaiah: “The burden of the desert sea” (Isa. XXI).

[Col. 0313B] Again, the sea signifies the people of the nations, as in the Psalter: “Therefore we will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV), that is, the apostles.

And in the Gospel: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,’ and it would obey you” (Luke XVII).

In this sea the innumerable snares of the devil and the wickedness of demons are also shown to crawl about, as though by certain waves the unstable will of souls were shaken. Thus the Psalmist says: “This sea, great and spacious; there are creeping things without number, small animals and great; there the ships will pass. This dragon, whom you formed to sport in it” (Ps. CIII).

They themselves make the sea spacious by compelling people to suffer shipwreck, for there is no doubt that the person who is submerged in the abyss of sins endures enormous waves.

[Col. 0313C] The sea is called *mare* from *meando*, “going,” because it always goes and returns. These innumerable spirits, however, have been comprehended by God, who counts the sand of the sea and the drops of rain. And lest they be left wholly incomprehensible, he defined them by quantity, not by quality.

Thus it is said of them: “Small animals and great,” because among them there are found beings of every kind of wickedness, both greater and lesser. “There,” namely, in that impure sea which he earlier mentioned.

The ships rightly signify the Churches, which escape the dangerous waves of the world by the wood of the glorious cross. They carry the peoples who have believed through the sign of faith.

There also dwells the wicked and pestilential dragon, who is mocked by the angels of God through their most just rebukes, and also by faithful men when they flee from his incitements to vice with detestation of his error.

[Col. 0313D] That the sea signifies sinners is shown by the Psalmist, who says: “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Ps. CXIII). We have often said that the sea should be understood as the sinners of this age, who, like waves, toss about in swollen thoughts.

Jordan, however, should be understood as any river, since rivers carry people away with various desires and lead them into that great sea through wicked precipitousness. These two forces, which were carrying the human race away through different pleasures, were driven backward and returned from their accustomed courses when the Lord came.

The heart of the sea signifies the hearts of human beings, as in the Psalter: “The mountains will be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV).

[Col. 0314A] The heart of the sea also signifies Judea, because it is said to lie in the middle of the world. Hence in the book of Ezra the following is said of the Savior: “I saw a man ascending from the heart of the sea” (4 Esdras XIII). And in Ezekiel: “O Tyre, which is situated in the heart of the sea” (Ezek. XXVII).

The depth of the sea signifies eternal condemnation, as in the Gospel: “It is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be cast into the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVIII).

The tongue of the sea of Egypt signifies the philosophy of this world, as in Isaiah: “And the Lord dried up the tongue of the sea of Egypt” (Isa. XI).

The shore of the sea signifies the end of the world, as in the Gospel: “And sitting beside the shore, they gathered the good into vessels but threw the bad outside” (Matt. XIII).

The Ocean that surrounds the world is indicated by the saying of blessed Job, in which he says: “Am I the sea, or a sea monster [Col. 0314B], that you have enclosed me in a prison?” (Job VII).
