Cosmographers say that the sea monster dwells especially in the depths of the Ocean. The sense of this passage may therefore be that he called the world the sea allegorically, and the sea monster the devil, who is held within the confines of this world and is to be condemned at its conclusion.

We often read that “prison” is used for punishments, because all penalties pertain to a prison. Thus, for all the evils that blessed Job suffered, he called it a house of torments, as though he had been confined within that same house.

The Red Sea therefore signifies either the sacrament of baptism or the flowing and turbid condition of this age, through which the saints pass unharmed while sinners are overwhelmed by the judgment of God.

[Col. 0314C] Concerning it we read in the Psalm: “He divided the Red Sea into divisions, and led Israel through the midst of it; he shook off Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea” (Ps. CXXXV).

Men of ancient authority said that the Red Sea was divided into twelve sections, corresponding to the number of tribes of the Jews. For this reason the expression is given in the plural, “into divisions,” lest we should think that the Red Sea was crossed by a single route.

This can also be understood suitably in a spiritual sense. The Red Sea is the mingled depth of this world, which we cross by many divisions when, converted toward the land of the living, we hasten there by the Lord’s gift.

We cross the sea of this world in one way through almsgiving, in another through continual prayer, in another through virginity, and in another through outstanding charity. Thus, by many divisions, we cross the sea of this world [Col. 0314D] to the Lord, who shakes off the devil and his ministers in the fountain of salvation, when by the power of his might he removes him from us.

He said that he “shakes him off,” as one throws away a woman, in order by this swiftness both to show the power of the divinity and to reveal that they are earthly filth.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Abyss

The abyss is an impenetrable depth of waters, or caverns of hidden waters through which springs and rivers issue forth, or which themselves flow secretly underground. Hence it is called the abyss. For all rushing waters return through hidden channels to the womb of the abyss.

[Col. 0315A] The abyss signifies the depth of Scripture, as in the Psalm: “Abyss calls to abyss” (Ps. XLI), that is, the Old Testament announces the New, and the New calls the Old to bear witness: “At the voice of your cataracts” (ibid.), that is, in the preaching of the saints.

The abyss is also the immensity of waters, as it is written in Genesis: “And the fountains of the great abyss were broken open” (Gen. VII).

The abyss signifies the ineffable judgments of God, as in the passage: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV).

The abyss signifies hell, as the Apostle says: “Or who will descend into the abyss?”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead (Rom. X).

The abyss signifies human hearts darkened by crimes, as in the saying of blessed Job: “The abyss will say, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea will say, ‘It is not with me’” (Job XXVIII).

[Col. 0315B] The abyss is also compared with superstitious people and persecutors of the Church. Just as a cloak covers what lies beneath it, so they covered the world with the most foul superstition, so that they seemed to overwhelm with bodily torments not only ordinary people but even holy and eminent men themselves, to their own destruction. Thus it is said in the Psalm: “The abyss was clothed as with a garment; and the waters will stand like mountains” (Ps. CIII).

The abyss again signifies human hearts darkened by crimes, as in Amos: “The Lord called for judgment, and it devoured the great abyss” (Amos VII).

The abyss signifies the eternal condemnation of sinners, as in Job: “He considered the abyss as growing old” (Job XLI), that is, the devil, through his ministers, will suppose that the punishment of the wicked will one day come to an end.

[Col. 0315C] The abyss signifies hell, as in the Gospel: “The spirits,” that is, the demons, “begged him not to send them into the abyss” (Matt. VIII).

## CHAPTER VII. On Tides and Straits

The tide pertains to the Ocean, while a strait pertains to either sea. For a tide is the advance or retreat of the sea, that is, its unrest. Hence tidal inlets are so called, through which the sea alternately advances and recedes.

A strait is so called because there the sea is always boiling. A strait is a narrow and, as it were, boiling sea, named from the boiling of its waves.

Allegorically, the world seethes with the waves of persecutions. Through various regions it either advances or recedes; it also boils with hatred and raises disturbances, and it can never maintain a condition of perfect tranquillity in the deep [Col. 0315D].

Hence it is also written in the Gospel (Mark VI) that the Lord sent his disciples to board a little boat and go ahead of him across the strait until he dismissed the crowds, while they labored at rowing because of the contrary wind.

This mystically signifies the varied labors of the holy Church, which, amid the hostile waves of the world and the blasts of unclean spirits, strives to reach the rest of its heavenly homeland, as though a secure station on the shore.

But the wind does not cease before the Savior goes up into the boat, because in whatever heart God is present through the grace of his love, the immense battles of vices and of the hostile world or evil spirits immediately subside into rest.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Lakes and Ponds

[Col. 0316A]

There are also certain seas that do not mingle with the waves of the Ocean or with the Great Sea; these are called lakes and ponds.

A lake is a receptacle in which water is retained and does not mingle with the waves, such as Lake Asphaltites, Lake Benacus, and the others that the Greeks call *limenas*, that is, “ponds.”

Springs flow into rivers, and rivers run into straits. A lake remains in one place and does not flow out; it is called a lake as though it were a “place of water.” A lake is also called a pond when a great quantity of water gathers in one place. For a pond is so called because water stands there and does not run onward.

Lake Asphaltites, also called the Dead Sea, is so named because it produces nothing living [Col. 0316B] and receives nothing belonging to the kind of living things. It has neither fish nor birds accustomed to the water and delighted by diving; rather, whatever living creature one attempts to submerge in it, by whatever method it is sunk, immediately springs back up. Even when thrown into it with great force, it is promptly cast out again.

Nor is it moved by the winds, because bitumen resists the whirlwinds and holds all the water stagnant. It is not suitable for navigation, because everything without life sinks into its depths. It supports no material except what is coated with bitumen. They say that a lighted lamp floats upon it, but when its flame is extinguished, the light sinks.

This is also called the Salt Sea, or Lake Asphaltites—that is, the Bitumen Lake. It lies in Judea between Jericho and Zoara. Its length extends toward Zoara of Arabia for 580 stadia, and its width reaches 150 stadia toward the vicinity of Sodom [Col. 0316C].

Ponds signify the philosophy of this world, as in Isaiah: “I will make rivers into islands, and dry up ponds” (Isa. XLII).

Mystically, however, the Dead Sea—which produces nothing living, receives nothing from the class of living things, and sinks everything lacking life into its depths—lies beside the land of Sodom and Gomorrah, cities that the Lord overthrew by raining fire and sulphur from heaven. It signifies the perversity of the present age, where the devil reigns among the lost and is joined by no fellowship with those who live in God’s life. Rather, he plunges those who lack true life into the depth of hell.

The stench of the flesh is expressed by sulphur, and the burning of carnal desire by fire. Sulphur has a stench, and fire has heat. Therefore, [Col. 0316D] those who had burned with perverse desires from the stench of the flesh deserved to perish together by sulphur and fire, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

The Lake of Tiberias was named from the town of Tiberias, which Herod once founded in honor of Tiberius Caesar. It is in Judea and is healthier than all the other lakes, being in some way more effective for the health of bodies.

Lake Genesar is the largest lake in Judea. It extends for 140 stadia in length and spreads for forty in width. Its waters are stirred by breezes that it generates not from winds but from itself. Hence it is called *Genesar* in Greek, as though meaning “producing a breeze for itself.”

Indeed, throughout the lake’s broader spaces it is stirred by frequent breezes, and therefore its water is purer, sweet to drink, and suitable for drinking [Col. 0317A].

If we knew what *Genesar* signifies in Latin, we would understand how Jesus, through the figure of the apostles and the ship—that is, the Church—leads it, rescued from the shipwreck of persecution, to the shore and makes it rest in the most tranquil harbor.

*Genesar* is interpreted as “the beginning of rising,” as we find in the book of Hebrew names. Complete tranquillity will then be granted to us when, through Christ, the inheritance of Paradise is restored to us and the joy of the first robe is returned.

The word “lake” in general is used either for hell, or for a hollow burial place, or for the deepest calamity of this world. It is called a lake because it lies hidden beneath the earth itself.

A lake signifies hell, as in the Psalmist: “They placed me in the lowest lake [Col. 0317B], in darkness and the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII). Likewise in that testimony of the prophet Zechariah, where he says to the Lord himself: “By the blood of your covenant you brought out your prisoners from the lake in which there is no water” (Zech. IX).

This is understood as follows: “By the blood of your passion, O Savior, you set free by your mercy those who were held captive in the prison of hell, where there is no mercy.”

A lake also signifies a burial place, as in the Psalmist: “I have been counted among those who descend into the lake” (Ps. LXXXVII). He condemns those who thought that the Lord and Savior had died in the ordinary manner, and who compared that singular and marvelous passion with the deaths of other human beings.

Again, by the name of a lake [Col. 0317C] the deepest calamity of this world is expressed, as in the passage: “To you, O Lord, I cried; my God, do not be silent toward me, and I shall be like those who descend into the lake” (Ps. CXLII).

This age is a lake, which is believed to be pleasant and tranquil, but whose depths and dimensions are unknown.

A lake signifies grief or a fall into death, as in the Psalter: “He opened a pit and dug it” (Ps. VII). And elsewhere: “They prepared snares for my feet” (Ps. LVI).

A pool (*lacuna*) signifies heretics, as in the prophet: “Those who made pools for catching fish” (Isa. XIX).

## CHAPTER IX. On Springs
Vascho is the name of a spring in the tribe of Benjamin, and it is interpreted as “turning of a generation.” Rogel is the name of a spring in the tribe of Benjamin [Col. 0317D]; it is interpreted as “bringing downward.” Sames is a spring in the tribe of Benjamin, and it is interpreted as “sun.” Areth is the spring beside which Gideon encamped (Judg. VII); it is interpreted as “craftsman,” and rightly so, because there the people who were to fight with Gideon were tested by the Lord’s command beside the waters.

A spring can also mystically signify either the Lord Christ, or the grace of the Holy Spirit, or the laver of Baptism, or the origin of virtues. It signifies Christ in the passage in Genesis (Gen. II) where the spring is said to be in the middle of Paradise, from which four rivers proceeded—that is, the four Gospels proceeding from the spring of salvation for the watering of the human race.

Likewise, a spring signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit in the Lord’s words in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will have in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV).

The sacrament of Baptism is shown by the words of the prophet Zechariah: “On that day there shall be a spring opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman” (Zech. XIII). This spring, issuing from the house of God, is said to flow toward the Church and toward knowledge of the Scriptures, so that we may all be reborn in Christ and, in the water of Baptism, our sins may be forgiven us. Nothing is more unclean than a menstruous woman, who makes whatever she touches unclean; and the filth of the unrighteous is washed away by Christ’s Baptism.

The spring signifies the Savior, as in Jeremiah: “They have forsaken me, the spring of living water” (Jer. II).

The spring signifies Baptism in Joel: “And a spring shall come forth from the house of the Lord and irrigate the whole land” (Joel III).

In another sense, as in the prophet: “The river shall be dried up at its source” (Isa. XIX).

Springs signify holy preachers, as in Isaiah: “You shall draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior” (Isa. XII).

In another sense, through Joel: “The beasts also looked to you; the springs of water dried up.”

Springs signify heretics in Peter’s Epistle: “These are springs without water” (II Pet. II).

The spring signifies the origin of the human race in Solomon: “Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is shattered over the spring” (Eccl. XII)—that is, the human body through death.

Thus the spring signifies the origin of virtues in the Psalmist’s words: “For with you is the spring of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). He says to Christ the Lord: “For with you is the spring of life”—that is, the beginning of all good things and the origin of virtues—from which we are perfectly filled whenever we receive some gift from his mercy.

The same interpretation applies to this passage: “He sends forth springs in the valleys; the waters shall pass through the midst of the hills” (Ps. CIII). The omnipotent God grants the gifts of spiritual grace to the humble; hence the valleys are mentioned here, and the divine waters there always surge forth. They will pass through the midst of the hills—that is, of proud heretics—without producing any fruit.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Rivers

A *fluvius* is a perpetual flow of waters, named from flowing continually. Properly speaking, however, a *flumen* is the water itself, while a *fluvius* is the course of the water [Col. 0318D]. The *flumen* therefore comes before the *fluvius*: the water precedes the flow.

There are two kinds of rivers: one is a torrent, the other a living river. Concerning the latter Virgil says:

> Until I have washed myself in living water.

A torrent is water coming with force. It is called a torrent because it increases through rain and becomes parched through drought—that is, it dries up.

The allegory of a river or stream is sometimes turned toward the good and sometimes toward the contrary. Rivers are understood in a good sense where the Savior says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII)—that is, spiritual graces flow forth from the secrecy of the heart.

So also in the Psalter: “The rush of the river”—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—“makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV), that is, the Church of God.

And elsewhere: “The river of God is filled with water” (Ps. LXIV).

The same applies to the Psalmist’s words: “Your heights and your waves have passed over me” (Ps. XLI). We suitably apply the heights and waves to the sacred Scriptures. They are the things he earlier called “abysses”; there the waves of parables also play upon the surface, while the depth of their meanings grows through devout investigation. The righteous man therefore says that these have passed over him, because in his eagerness for their knowledge he had immersed himself in their examination.

Sometimes rivers signify the teaching of the apostles and evangelists together with good works, as in the passage: “The rivers have raised their voices” (Ps. XCII); and: “The rivers shall clap their hands together” (Ps. XCVII).

Isaiah likewise says: “I shall place rivers in the islands” (Isa. XLII).

In the contrary sense, rivers are mentioned when they signify the turbid course of this world and the inundation of sins, as in the passage: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI).

It should be observed that he does not say “in the rivers,” but “upon the rivers.” Those who are still in these rivers are carried away by the inundation of sins; but those who sit safely above the banks have already been delivered from those waves by divine favor.

Hence elsewhere he says of the saints: “They shall pass through the rivers on foot” (Ps. LXV)—that is, through the turbid streams of this world they shall proceed by the secure step of virtues, through the grace of Christ, toward the future homeland, where the source of our joy and eternal salvation has been prepared.

Rivers signify the force of persecution in the Song of Songs: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor could rivers overwhelm it” (Song VIII).

The river signifies the philosophy of this world or the doctrine of heretics in the Psalter: “You dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. LXXIII). Ethan is interpreted as “strong,” that is, the devil, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “When the strong man, armed, guards his courtyard,” and so forth (Luke XI).

In another way, in Job: “He will swallow up the river and will not marvel, and he will trust that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job XL).

By the name of the river is signified the course of the human race, which, as though arising from the origin of its own spring, rises by birth and, flowing downward to the lowest places, passes through death. By the name of the Jordan, however, the baptized are signified. It is as though he were saying: Before the world’s Redeemer, Behemoth swallowed up the world without wonder; but—what is more grievous—even after the Redeemer’s coming he trusts that he can swallow some who have been baptized.

Some rivers received their names for particular reasons. Among these, several that are celebrated in histories should be noted.

The river Gihon issues from Paradise and surrounds the whole of Ethiopia. It is called by this name because, through the increase of its overflowing, it irrigates the land of Egypt. *Ge* means “land” in Greek. Among the Egyptians it is called the Nile because of the mud that it carries, which produces fertility. Hence the Nile was also called as though it were “drawing along the fertile mud” [the printed form is uncertain: *nean y len*]. Formerly the Nile was called *Melo* in Latin.

It appears in Lake Nilides, from which it is received southward by Egypt; there, driven back by the northern winds, it swells as its waters struggle backward and produces the inundation of Egypt [Col. 0320A].

The river Ganges, which Holy Scripture calls the Pishon, issues from Paradise and proceeds toward the regions of India. It is called Pishon, that is, “crowd,” because it is filled by fifteen great rivers joining it and becomes one river.

It is called Ganges after Ganges, king of India. It is said to rise, like the Nile, and to burst forth over the lands of the East.

The Tigris is a river of Mesopotamia, rising from Paradise, proceeding toward the Assyrians, and, after many windings, flowing into the Dead Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, running with extraordinary swiftness like a tiger.

The Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia, rising from Paradise and exceedingly rich in gems; it flows through the middle of Babylon. It received its name from crops or abundance. For in Hebrew *Euphrata* is interpreted as “fertility” [Col. 0320B].

Mystically, these four rivers, as was said above, signify the four Gospels written by the four Evangelists.

The river Gihon, which is interpreted as “breast” or “precipitous,” signifies the Gospel of Matthew. It was the first to be written, by the author himself in the Hebrew language. Beginning with the genealogies of the Savior, it briefly records the Lord’s birth, the arrival of the Magi to the Savior, and the slaughter of the infants by Herod. It then recalls his Baptism, his fasting in the desert, and the temptations by which he was tested by the devil; next it proceeds to the preaching of the Gospel and the performance of miracles. Thus, reaching his Passion, it shows that he rose from the dead, appeared to his disciples in Galilee, and sent them to preach the Gospel [Col. 0320C]. In this way it waters the land of Ethiopia and the spiritual Egypt with the four streams of its teachings, so that they may produce the fruit of faith and good works. Accordingly, the evangelist himself is described in ecclesiastical history as having preached the Gospel in the regions of Ethiopia and having completed his course by martyrdom.

The Ganges, that is, the Pishon, interpreted as “crowd” or “change of mouth,” signifies the Gospel of Mark. It says little about the Savior’s genealogy according to the flesh; but it gathers into one book, in a crowd, the account of his preaching and miracles, which the other Evangelists narrate more fully. Thus, reaching the Passion of Christ and his resurrection from the dead, it shows that he ascended into heaven and that, after his Ascension, the apostles preached him throughout the world [Col. 0320D].

The Tigris can also appropriately correspond to the Gospel of Luke. Beginning with the priesthood of Zechariah and the birth of John, it next announces the angel’s message to the Virgin Mary and the Savior’s birth. Then, recalling his genealogy in connection with the account of his Baptism, it proceeds to explain his preaching and the performance of his miracles. Moving swiftly through everything, and describing the Lord’s Passion and resurrection, it briefly and concisely includes his Ascension into heaven and the disciples’ praise of the Lord in the Temple.

The river Euphrates, interpreted as “fruit-bearing” or “growing,” corresponds most fittingly to the Gospel of John. Beginning with the Savior’s divine generation, he described especially those matters that pertained to explaining his divine nature [Col. 0321A]. Thus he irrigated the land of the Church so that it might produce spiritual growth and the fruit of virtues, and he bestowed upon it the riches of spiritual knowledge.

The river Jordan is named from two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan. When these, although far apart, were joined together into one channel, the river thereafter came to be called Jordan. It rises beneath Mount Lebanon and divides Judea and Arabia; after many windings, it flows near Jericho into the Dead Sea.

Mystically, the Jordan, which is interpreted as “their descent,” and in which the Savior was baptized, signifies the grace of Baptism. There we must put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth (Eph. IV). There too we must descend from the pride of the devil and become participants in the humility and gentleness of Christ.

For three reasons, therefore, the Savior received Baptism from John (Matt. III). First, because he had been born a human being, he might fulfill all the righteousness and humility of the Law. Second, that by his own Baptism he might confirm John’s Baptism. Third, that by sanctifying the waters of the Jordan through the descent of the dove, he might reveal the coming of the Holy Spirit in the washing of believers.

What is written in Joshua son of Nun (Josh. III), where the passage of the children of Israel through the channel of the Jordan is recounted, has this meaning: when the priests carrying the ark of the Lord’s covenant placed the soles of their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the waters below flowed away and failed, while those that came from above stood in a great mass [Col. 0321C].

The part of humanity that, after receiving holy Baptism, again gives itself over to worldly affairs and the enticements of lust, and drinks the salty cup with greed, is represented by that part of the waters which flows into the sea and perishes in its salty waves. But the part that remains stable and preserves its sweetness represents those who hold unfalteringly to the gift they have received from God.

The Jabbok is a river, and its name is interpreted as “sand” or “struggle.” After crossing it, Jacob wrestled against the one who had appeared to him, and he was called Israel. It was between Amman—that is, Philadelphia—and Garasan, at the fourth milestone from it [Col. 0321D]; proceeding farther, it mingles with the river Jordan.

The struggle of the man who wrestled with Jacob signifies, according to allegory, the Passion of Christ. Jacob is seen there in the type of the Jews—that is, in the offspring of his body—to have prevailed against God, and, as with a weak man, to have entered into struggle with his flesh and grown strong in his Passion, as is written when they said: “Crucify him.”

According to tropology, however, Jacob, who contends with the angel, expresses the soul of each perfect man devoted to contemplation. For when the soul strives to contemplate the Lord, it is placed, so to speak, in a contest. At one moment it seems to prevail, because through understanding and feeling it tastes something of the unbounded light.

Ella, Aber, and Gozan [Col. 0322A] are the names of rivers in the land of the Medes, to whose mountains Israel was led captive. Ella is interpreted as “weakness”; Aber as “bruise” or “face”; and Gozan as “their shearing.” This may signify the injury of those who, having been led out of the land of the Church, live in the pleasures of the world, where they suffer various wounds from vices.

Abana is a river of Damascus, and its name is interpreted as “its stones,” signifying the hard sterility of the wicked, who do not know how to produce the fruit of virtues.

The Chobar is the river beside which the prophet Ezekiel was placed and saw a vision. Its name is interpreted as “heaviness,” while Ezekiel means “strength of God.” Ezekiel therefore came beside the river Chobar because the strength of God, through the mystery of his Incarnation, deigned to draw near to the human race, which bears the burdens of its sins and flows daily from its birth toward death [Col. 0322B].

The spring, or pool, of Siloam, at the foot of Mount Sion, as was said above, boils up with continuous waters, though at uncertain hours and days. It signifies the sacrament of Baptism. Accordingly, when the Lord had spread saliva mixed with mud over the eyes of the man born blind, he said to him: “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam,” which is interpreted as “sent.”

What the Lord did is clear. Illumination took place in the blind man, but a great mystery concerning the human race is commended here. He spat upon the ground and made mud from the saliva, because “the Word became flesh” (John I); and he anointed the blind man’s eyes. He had been anointed and yet did not see. The Lord sent him to the pool called Siloam.

It belonged to the Evangelist to commend to us the name of this pool, and he said that it is interpreted as “sent” [Col. 0322C]. Now you recognize who was sent. For unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. He therefore washed his eyes in the pool that is interpreted as “sent”; he was baptized in Christ. Thus, when the Lord in a certain way baptized him in himself, then he illuminated him; when he anointed him, perhaps he made him a catechumen.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Torrents

A torrent is, as we said above, water coming with force. There are certain proper names of torrents which, according to their interpretation, possess a mystical significance.

Such is the torrent Kishon, which is interpreted as “their hardness.” It is beside Mount Tabor, where the battle against Sisera was fought, and it signifies the obstinacy of the proud, which is crushed by the Lord’s power.

The torrent Cademi is beside which Deborah waged war. Its name is interpreted as “useless resurrection,” signifying the resurrection of sinners, who will rise not to life but to everlasting punishment.

The torrent of the Chorathites lies beyond the Jordan, in which Elijah was hidden opposite that same river. Its name is interpreted as “division” or “knowledge.”

Chimarus—that is, the torrent Kidron—lies between the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem, where the evangelist John relates that the Lord Savior was betrayed. Kidron is interpreted as “darkness” or “sorrow,” and it signifies the blindness of the Jews, who came with tumult to seize Jesus [Col. 0323A].

A torrent is suddenly stirred by winter rains. It is both rapid and muddy, because it does not pour forth from a pure spring but is befouled by earthly contaminations. To it the turbid course of this world is rightly compared: it flows from no spring of truth but is compounded from every storm of evil.

Hence it is said: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Ps. CXXIII).

And again: “He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head” (Ps. CIX). Israel therefore rightly declares that it too has passed through it; hence it is proclaimed that its head drank.

In all these passages there is one true confession: we are delivered from such great dangers solely by the Lord’s mercy.

The torrent also signifies the teaching of the wicked in the Psalter: “You broke open springs and torrents” (Ps. LXXIII).

Again, the torrent signifies the force of temptation in the Psalter: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me” (Ps. XVII).

A torrent is also found in a good sense, as in the passage: “You shall give them to drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV).

We said that a torrent is a swift river which descends through the sudden flooding of rains. The wisdom of Christ is well compared to it, because it is sudden and so rapid that it reaches the end it intends without any delay.

Rivulets are so called because they are led off for irrigation—that is, to bring water into the fields. For *rigare* means “to bring in water.” The word signifies the flow and irrigation of heavenly grace, because human hearts are watered so that they may produce the fruit of teaching and good works.

Hence the passage: “The rock poured out for me streams of oil” (Job XXIX)—that is, Christ poured out the gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0323C].

In the Psalm: “Water its streams; multiply its generations; it shall rejoice in its showers when it springs forth” (Ps. LXIV).

Here he also calls the apostles, or other faithful people, “streams,” because they have always drunk from that river filled by God. But lest you should think the drink itself exceedingly slight, he says that the streams themselves are to be made drunk, so that they may reach such fullness as is sufficient abundantly for themselves and allows them to provide for others in the future.

He therefore returns to the singular number, which we said corresponds to ecclesiastical unity. For he says, “Multiply its generations”—namely, those of the stream that flowed forth from the holy river—so that through successive generations blessed preaching may not fail but may multiply. Thus the Catholic Church may always grow, and those who are now being instructed in the sacred doctrine may afterward be seen teaching others [Col. 0323D].

Showers are drops that fall from roofs. They penetrate not by weight but by persistence; and how far they differ from streams is also made clear to us by ordinary observation. Therefore every faithful person will rejoice in his beginnings when he springs forth. We are truly reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, and by the Lord’s own condescension we are prepared for glory. Great joy is ours then, when, laying aside the oldness of the ancient man, we are admitted to the joys of new regeneration.

Rivulets signify the preaching of the saints in Isaiah: “Upon every high mountain and upon every elevated hill shall be streams of flowing waters” (Isa. XXX).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Wells

A well is a hollowed-out pool from which water is drawn; it is named from drinking. It can be understood in a good sense or in the contrary sense.

The well of the oath, which Abraham dug (Gen. XXI), is Beersheba in the region of Gerar.

The well of vision is in the desert, where Isaac dwelt.

The well of judgment is in the region of Gerar to the present day.

Again, the well of the oath, where Isaac and Abimelech swore an oath, is called the town of Isaac.

There are also many other wells in the Holy Scriptures, which are shown to be in the region of Gerar and near Ashkelon.

The following can therefore be understood in a good sense. In Genesis we read that Isaac dug wells (Gen. XXVI), wells which his father Abraham’s servants had dug; but the Philistines, envying him, stopped them up by filling them with earth, and so forth.

Who is this Isaac except our Savior? When he descended into this torrent of Gerar, he first of all wished to dig those wells which his father’s servants had dug. Moses had dug the well of the Law; David, Solomon, and the prophets had written the books of the Old Testament. Yet the Jews’ earthly and sordid interpretation had filled them.

When Isaac wished to cleanse their mouth, to show that whatever the Law and the prophets had said, they had said about him, the Philistines quarreled with him—that is, the Jews alienated from the kingdom of God. But he descended and departed from them, and cannot remain with those who do not want water in the wells but earth. He says to them: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII) [Col. 0324C].

Isaac therefore dug a new well—or rather, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; Peter and James; Jude and the apostle Paul. All of them dug the well of the New Testament and found living water, which becomes “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV).

Those who think only of earthly things still quarrel over this. They neither allow new things to be established nor old things to be cleansed. They oppose the evangelical wells and resist the apostles. And because in everything they contradict and dispute, it is said to them: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, behold, we now turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

After this Isaac dug a third well and called the name of that place “Broadness,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us, and he has caused us to increase upon the earth” (Gen. XXVI) [Col. 0324D].

Truly Isaac was enlarged. He filled the whole earth with knowledge of the Trinity and established the breadth of the Church throughout the world. Formerly God was known only in Judea; he was named in Israel (Ps. LXXV). But now “their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

In the contrary sense is that well beside which the Savior is read to have sat, wearied from his journey, while the Samaritan woman wished to draw water with a jar (John IV).

The jar perhaps signifies love of this world—that is, desire—which people draw there from the dark depth whose image the well bears, namely, from earthly conduct. Once they have tasted the pleasure, they burn again with desire for it, just as whoever drinks of that water will thirst again.

But one who believes in Christ ought to renounce the world. By leaving the jar behind, he should show that he has abandoned worldly desire—not merely believing with the heart unto righteousness (Rom. X), but also confessing with the mouth unto salvation and proclaiming what he has believed [Col. 0325A].

The well also signifies either the devil or hell, as in the passage: “Nor let the well press its mouth against me” (Ps. LXVIII). Sinners likewise press their mouth shut when they persist in the worst will until the time of their death.

The cistern signifies right understanding, as in Solomon: “Drink water from your own cistern and flowing water from your own well” (Prov. V).

The cistern signifies a heretic or perverse understanding, as in Jeremiah: “They dug for themselves broken cisterns” (Jer. II).

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Whirlpools

A whirlpool is properly a deep pool in a river. Allegorically it signifies the storms of persecutions that oppose the elect in this world.

Hence it is written in Jonah: “All your whirlpools and your waves have passed over me” (Jon. II). No one doubts that the swelling waves of the sea passed over Jonah and that the savage storm roared around him as a mystery of Christ. For no human being can endure all temptations without Christ.

And because all persecutions and everything that happens are not inflicted apart from God’s will, they are called God’s whirlpools and waves. They did not overwhelm Jesus but passed over him, threatening shipwreck without bringing it about [Col. 0325C].

“All the persecutions and storms,” he says, “by which the human race is troubled, and all their little boats that were being broken, roared over my head.” I therefore endured the storms and broke the raging whirlwinds, so that they might sail more safely.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Rains

Rains are so called because they flow like rivers. They arise from the breath of the earth and sea. When they have been lifted higher, either dissolved by the heat of the sun or compressed by the force of the winds, they are distilled upon the earth.

Showers (*imbres*) pertain both to clouds and to rains. They are called by a Greek word because they make the earth drunk so that it may germinate. From them all things are created.

Rains or showers signify heavenly gifts and God’s precepts or commands, which water the earth—that is, human beings—and stir them to produce the growth of good works [Col. 0325D].

Hence the passage in the Psalm: “God will set apart a voluntary rain for your inheritance” (Ps. VII). This explains what he said above: “The heavens dripped” (ibid.). That voluntary rain was the manna, which the Jewish people, eager to eat, obtained at that time. For, to satisfy its desire, the world received an unheard-of miracle. That rain was voluntary, unlike the rain that is generally spread everywhere.

And elsewhere he says: “I shall command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V)—not these visible clouds, which either pour down waters or are condensed into a bodily mass [Col. 0326A], but certain powers of the Lord who serve according to an intellectual order. This statement is filled with many meanings; it also refers to the apostles and prophets.

The early and latter rain is understood as the Old and New Testament, as in the prophet Joel: “He will cause the early rain and the latter rain to descend for you at the beginning” (Joel II)—that is, in Christ.

Sometimes rain is found in a bad sense, as in the passage where the Savior says that rain descended upon a house founded on sand and overthrew it (Matt. VII). This rain is the devil; the rivers are all the antichrists who think against Christ; the spiritual winds of wickedness daily plot the destruction of human beings.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning a Drop

A *gutta* is a drop that remains; a *stilla* is one that falls. Hence *stillicidium*, as though “a falling drop.” *Stiria* is Greek for “drop”; from it a diminutive is formed, so that we say *stilla*.

A drop signifies spiritual teaching. Hence the words of the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs, addressed to the bride: “Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one; for my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the night” (Song V).

The head is Christ God; the locks are the gatherings of the faithful. In the dew and drops of the night is shown the cold love that many have toward God and their neighbors. Therefore the Lord necessarily arouses each of the faithful to zeal for preaching.

Showers of drops signify light instructions, of which it is said: “She shall rejoice in her showers when she springs forth” (Ps. LXIV) [Col. 0326C]. These pertain to Christians who are beginners, when narrow beginnings cannot yet receive the widest-ranging doctrine.

Of them the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). At first, the dryness of faith is enlivened by certain drops; afterward it is irrigated by abundant streams. Then, as the preceding verse says, with the Lord’s help we arrive at the fullness of that river. Thus through these three stages the order of the divine gift is revealed.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Snow

Snow is named from the cloud from which it comes. It sometimes signifies the whiteness of righteousness, as in the Psalm: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L).

And again: “When he separates the heavenly kings over the earth, they shall be whitened in Salmon” (Ps. LXVII) [Col. 0326D].

The kings are the apostles, holy bishops, and the other faithful, who by divine favor have worthily learned to rule their bodies. They shall be whitened above the snow in Salmon—that is, they shine above the whiteness of snow—because they are known to govern the Church faithfully and in due order in Salmon, which is interpreted as “shadow,” that is, under divine protection.

“Whitened” is sometimes used in a bad sense, as also in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Lord will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII).

The Gospel also bears witness to this: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII) [Col. 0327A].

Snows signify the outpouring of Baptism, as in Job: “He who fears the frost, snow will fall upon him” (Job VI). They understood the frost here as present tribulation.

Likewise it is written in Job: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or have you seen the treasuries of hail?” (Job XXXVIII).

What else is understood in the cold of snow or the hardness of hail than the life of the wicked, which grows cold through torpor and strikes through the hardness of malice?

“These things,” he says, “I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war” (ibid.), so that when our adversary the devil strives to tempt us, he may use their behavior against us as though they were his weapons.

Or treasures are held in snow and hail because many who are cold with the torpor of iniquity are taken up into heavenly grace and shine with light in the holy Church, while with the blows of their teaching they hammer upon perverse knowledge [Col. 0327B].

Hence the text clearly continues: “These things I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war.”

Saul became snow and hail against the hearts of his adversaries, either through the whiteness of righteousness or through the correction of stern eloquence.

It should also be noted that snow sometimes expresses the charm of whiteness, just as brilliance expresses terror. Hence the angel who announced the glory of the Lord’s resurrection was both terrifying in condemning the wicked and kind and gentle in comforting the elect.

For the same angel who appeared to terrify the impious guards of the tomb with fear and cast them to the ground like the dead refreshed the holy women who visited that same tomb with kindly consolation [Col. 0327C].

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Ice

Ice is formed from frost and water, as though *gelacies*, that is, “frozen water.” Frost is so called because the earth is constricted by it. For *ge* means “earth.”

The earth is gripped by a more severe frost when the night has been clear. Ice signifies the hardness of sins, as in Solomon: “As ice in clear weather, so your sins shall be dissolved” (Sir. XXXIII).

And in the Psalm: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy wind, which do his word” (Ps. XLVIII). Allegorically these signify people who in this world have come from turbulent and exceedingly evil conditions to the most tranquil practices of devotion.

Who are those who “do his word” except those who have deserved to come from stormy and wicked conditions to the grace of confessing him [Col. 0327D]?

For the Lord speaks to Job as follows: “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who gave birth to the frost from heaven?” (Job XXXVIII).

By frost or ice we understand the hearts of the Jews, cold and constricted by the torpor of unbelief. Through the mysteries of the Law and the prophecy they were held within the bosom of grace, as though within the Creator’s womb. But because, when the Lord came, constricted by the cold of unbelief, they lost the warmth of love, they came forth like ice from the Creator’s womb.

“And who,” he says, “gave birth to the frost from heaven?” It is as though the frost came forth from heaven, because a cold people of unbelievers proceeded from the sublime offspring of the saints. The Lord is said to have given birth to them because he permitted them to emerge cold.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Frost and Hail

Frost is the cold of the morning. It received the name *pruina* because it burns like fire. *Pyr* is the Greek word for “fire.” In truth, the word pertains both to cold and to heat, because one expression signifies two different things on account of their having one effect.

The force of heat and cold is similar, and both split rocks. Heat burns, as in the passage:

> Unhappy Dido is burning.

Cold also burns, as in the passage:

> Or let the penetrating cold of the north wind burn.

According to allegory, frost signifies abstinence, because through it the body’s heat grows cold. Concerning this the Psalm says: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Ps. CXVIII) [Col. 0328B].

Frost signifies the malice of the perverse. Hence it is read in the Psalm: “He killed their vineyards with hail, and their walls with frost” (Ps. LXXVII).

Frost is also the malice that precedes and anticipates others, preventing alien labors from reaching their fruits.

Hail signifies God’s threat, by which he scourges the obstinate, as in the Psalm: “Hail and coals of fire” (Ps. XVII).

In another sense: “He killed their vineyards with hail” (Ps. LXXVII).

Hail is the blow that is to come, as in Isaiah: “He will strike it down with a whirlwind and with a stone of hail” (Isa. XXX).

And elsewhere: “I shall cast down great stones from above” (Ezek. XIII).

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Dew

[Col. 0328C]

Ros is a Greek word, which they call *drosos*; others think that it is called *ros* because it is sparse and not thick, like rain. Ros signifies the word of the Lord, because it moistens the hearts of earthly human beings so that they may bring forth fruit, as it says in the Psalm: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. CXXXII).

Ros is a thin and light rain that does not come in drops, but penetrates the hardness of earthly dryness through exceedingly minute particles. Through it all growing things cohere and are brought to various fruits by the gift of its tempering. Hermon is the Hebrew name of a mountain situated beyond the River Jordan; interpreted, as it has been handed down by the fathers, it signifies “anathema.” The dew, therefore, of this mountain, nourishing sinners who have lain hidden under the curse of anathema, descends upon Mount Zion when, by the Lord’s generosity, they have attained the remedy of a godly way of life. For Zion signifies the Catholic Church, which receives the nations that had been placed under the danger of anathema.

Likewise, dew signifies the teaching of preachers, as it says in the Book of Job: “Who is the father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?” (Job XXXVIII), as though he were saying: “Who but I, who freely sprinkle the dry earth of the human heart with drops of knowledge, like dew?” The drops of dew are the holy preachers of Christ, who, amid the evils of the present life, like parched fields amid the darkness of a dry night, pour over the fields of our hearts the grace of heavenly generosity.

## CHAPTER XX. On Mist

[Col. 0329A]

*Mist* (*nebula*) is so called from the same source as *cloud* (*nubila*), namely, from *obnubere*, “to cover over,” that is, to cover the earth; or because it causes clouds to fly. Moist valleys exhale mists, which become clouds; from these comes cloudiness, and from cloudiness, snow. Mists seek the lower regions when the sky is clear, and the upper regions when it is cloudy.

Mystically, mist signifies either the obscurity of the Scriptures or the darkness of error. Hence, at the dedication of the Temple, when the mist filled the house of the Lord, the priests could not stand and minister because of the mist (III Kings VIII). This statement indicates the proud chief priests and teachers of the Jews who, while disdaining to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, lost their due ministry of faith [Col. 0329B] through the mist of error. Thus the mist filled the synagogue, that is, the house of the Lord, and because of the mist the priests could not minister: for, while they disdained to investigate the mystical meanings covered by the veil of the letter in the Old Testament amid the dark obscurities of allegories, they lost the due ministry of faith because of the mist.

Thus the Lord says to Job: “Will you raise your voice in the mist?” (Job XXXVIII). In the mist, therefore, the Lord uttered the voice of his teaching to the Jews when he also related openly what concerned himself. For what is clearer than: “I and the Father are one” (John X)? What is clearer than: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII)? But because the minds of the hearers had been filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening mist concealed it, like a ray of sunlight that had been sent forth.

Mist is also the veil of God’s mysteries, which holy teachers investigate through meditation. Hence it is written in the Prophet: “Mist is the dust of his feet” (Nahum I). Likewise, mists signify heretics, of whom the Apostle Peter says: “These are fountains without water and mists driven by storms” (II Peter II).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Flood

The flood (*diluvium*) is so called because, through the destruction caused by waters, it wipes out everything that it inundates. The first flood occurred under Noah, [when], angered by the crimes of human beings, the Almighty covered the whole world, destroyed everything, and [made] one expanse of sky and sea. We still see evidence of it in stones that we often find in remote mountains, concreted with shells and oysters and even hollowed out by water.

The second flood occurred in Achaea, in the times of the patriarch Jacob and of Ogyges, who was the founder and king of Eleusis and gave his name to the place and the period. The third flood occurred in Thessaly, in the times of Moses or Amphictyon, who reigned third after Cecrops. In his time an inundation of waters destroyed most of the peoples of Thessaly, while a few were saved by taking refuge in the mountains, especially on Mount Parnassus. Around this mountain Deucalion then held royal power; he received those who fled to him on rafts and sheltered and fed them between the twin peaks of Parnassus. For this reason, Greek stories say that the race of human beings was restored from stones, because of the innate hardness of the human heart.

Rivers too, when swollen beyond their customary level by unusually heavy rains, whether through prolonged duration or through magnitude, overflow and destroy many things; they too are called floods. It must be understood, however, that when rivers rise beyond measure, they not only inflict present damage but also signify certain things to come.

Mystically, when the flood is understood in a good sense, it signifies Baptism; when in the opposite sense, the error of heretics. For in that statement of the Psalmist in which he says, “The Lord inhabits the flood, and the Lord will sit as king forever” (Ps. XXVIII), the sevenfold Spirit comes first with the virtues and, in the third order, reaches by wondrous arrangement the fullness of the Trinity. By saying “Lord” three times in these two verses, he shows that the holy Trinity inhabits the flood, that is, the waters of Baptism, as it is said in the Gospel: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

But let us ask why the flood is used here for the sacred fonts. Rightly so, because what happened under Noah bore the likeness of holy Baptism. For just as this purifies souls from the filth of sins, so that flood wiped away the shameful crimes of the world. The flood is therefore rightly used for Baptism, since it is clearly understood to have been accomplished in its likeness.

Since the word “Lord” is repeated three times without distinguishing the persons, the first occurrence may be understood as having been spoken of the Holy Spirit: “The Lord inhabits the flood.” It follows: “And the Lord will sit as king forever” (Ps. XXVIII). We properly understand this of the Son. “The Lord will give strength to his people”: we appropriately recognize this as concerning the Father. “His people” signifies the Christian people, whom he acquired through the gift of holy Baptism. He also adds: “And he will bless his people with peace.” He did not say “they will bless,” but “he will bless,” because the Lord our God is one; “with peace,” because of that Gospel saying: “My peace I give you, my peace I leave you” (John XIV). For the peace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one.

The flood is likewise used in the opposite sense in the verse in which the Prophet says: “In the flood of many waters they shall not approach him” (Ps. XXXI). For the flood of many waters is the error of very wicked human beings who, wavering amid various depraved ways, establish for themselves manifold doctrines that they have in no way received from the true teacher. This statement especially indicts heretics, who in the flood of their perversity raise stormy and shipwreck-producing questions.

# BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0331]

## CHAPTER I. On Earth

[Col. 0331A]

Earth is situated in the central region of the world, remaining at an equal distance from all parts of the heavens, like a center. In the singular number it signifies the whole globe; in the plural, its individual parts. Its names arise from different explanations. For it is called *terra* from its upper part, where it is worn away; *humus* from its lower part; or from *humida terra*, “moist earth,” as beneath the sea. It is called *tellus* because we gather its fruits. It is likewise called *arva* from plowing and cultivating.

Properly speaking, earth is called dry in distinction from water. As Scripture says (Gen. I), God called the dry part “earth.” For dryness is the natural property of earth. If it is moist, it obtains this through affinity with water.

Some say that its movement is caused by wind in its hollows, whose motion moves it. Sallust writes: “Winds driven headlong through the hollows of the earth, and bursting forth, caused certain mountains to collapse, and the mounds sank.” Others say that generative water moves within the earth and shakes it at the same time, like a vessel, as Lucretius says. Others call the same earth a “sponge,” whose often-hidden collapses shake everything placed above it. Chasms in the earth are caused either by the movement of subterranean water, by frequent thunder, or by winds bursting forth from the hollows of the earth.

Earth has many mystical meanings. Sometimes it signifies the heavenly homeland, as in: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXV). And in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek,” he says, “for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V).

Sometimes it signifies the flesh of the Lord and Savior, as in: “You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXIV). For the patriarch Jacob signifies the faithful people, who were freed from the captivity of the devil through the incarnation of the Savior.

Likewise, earth signifies the holy Virgin Mary, from whom the Lord graciously chose to be born. Hence the saying: “Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV). This passage may also be understood in another way. Truth springs from the earth when confession of sins is offered; righteousness looks down from heaven when forgiveness of sins takes place. This occurred in the prayer of that tax collector (Luke XVIII). Truth sprang from the earth when, looking down to the depths and confessing his sins, he entreated the Lord; righteousness looked down from heaven when the tax collector went down justified rather than that Pharisee.

Earth also signifies the Church, as in: “The earth is the Lord’s” (Ps. XXIII). Although we know that earth is often used in both a good and an evil sense, here we must understand it as the Church, which serves the Lord especially with a pure mind. For although all things were created by him, we properly call that his which venerates him as its creator. Therefore the Church is rightly understood as the fruitful earth of good things, because it nourishes and contains the people.

It follows: “And its fullness” (ibid.), that is, the holy multitude by which the Church is filled. But lest you should perhaps think that the earth mentioned above meant some restricted region, he now says: “the world” (ibid.), that is, the universal Church, which is contained within the circuit of the whole world. Observe also that he says: “Those who dwell in it,” that is, not those who come and go, but those who endure with a fixed stability of mind. For to dwell means to remain; this does not belong to those who wander and is incompatible with change. Only that person dwells in the Church who perseveres in the truest faith until his death, as another psalm also says: “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXII).

Earth signifies the human being himself, as in the Gospel: “Other seed fell upon good earth” (Luke VIII). Likewise, in Genesis the dry land is called earth, as in: “And he called the dry land Earth” (Gen. I), signifying the people thirsting for the fountain of faith and bringing forth the germ of good works.

Earth is used in an evil sense when it signifies the corruption of human nature, sinners, or lost people. The corruption of nature is demonstrated by that sentence of the Lord addressed to the sinful human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). Sinners are also marked by the name earth where the Lord says to the serpent: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (ibid.), that is, “You will draw sinners into your portion and destruction, and feed upon their iniquities.”

Likewise, it is written elsewhere: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. XVII), that is, those who turn away from you through apostasy shall be numbered among sinners.

Earth signifies carnal power, as in Ecclesiasticus: “Why does earth and ash boast?” (Sir. X).

Deserted earth signifies the Jewish people or all sinners, as in Jeremiah: “A deserted and uninhabited land, in which no one dwells, nor does any son of man pass through it” (Jer. VI), that is, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Sinners are dust, as it is said in Isaiah concerning the devil: “And dust shall be the serpent’s bread” (Isa. LXV). And elsewhere: “Not so the wicked, not so; but they are like dust” (Ps. I).

Mud signifies the bond of heavenly medicine, as in the Gospel: “He made mud and anointed my eyes” (John IX). In another sense it signifies the bond of sinners, as in the Psalm: “Deliver me from the mud, so that I may not cling to it” (Ps. LXVIII).

Mud signifies the deception of the flatterer, or the false soothing of heretics, as in Ezekiel: “They were building a wall, while others were plastering it with mud without tempering it” (Ezek. XIII).

## CHAPTER II. On the World

The world (*orbis*) is so called from the roundness of a circle, because it is like a wheel. Hence a small wheel is also called an *orbiculus*. The Ocean, flowing around it on every side, surrounds its boundaries in a circuit.

Accordingly, according to the historical sense, it signifies the whole world; according to the allegorical sense, the universal Church; or, in the opposite sense, the wicked, who are frequently designated by the name earth. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “He will judge the world in righteousness” (Ps. IX). They are to be judged by the Lord, because through their stubbornness they are freed by no remission.

“People” signifies those who among the Hebrews were proved faithful and those who came devotedly from the nations.

It should rightly be investigated that here too he speaks of “the world,” while in the Psalm he says, “His lightning flashes have illumined the world” (Ps. LXXVI), and in many other places, using the same figure, declares that the earth is enclosed. Again, the hundred-sixth Psalm encompasses the spaces of the earth by its four cardinal points, saying: “From the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. CVI). There is also a very clear example of this in the Gospel, where it says: “He will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and he will gather them from the four corners of the earth” (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore I rightly judge that it must be investigated how both a square and a circle can apply to the earth, since the figures themselves, as geometers say, are judged to be different.

Scripture calls the form of the earth a circle because, for those who look toward its extremity, a circle always appears; the Greeks call this circle the *horizon*. It says that the earth is formed by four cardinal points because the four cardinal points signify the four corners of a square, which are contained within the aforesaid circle of the earth.

For if you draw individual straight lines from the cardinal point of the East toward the South and toward the North, and likewise, if you extend individual straight lines from the cardinal point of the West toward the aforesaid cardinal points, namely the South and the North, you form a square of the earth within the aforesaid circle.

But how this demonstrative square ought to be inscribed within a circle, Euclid clearly explains in the fourth book of the *Elements*. Therefore Holy Scripture rightly calls the surface of the earth both a circle and a world, and says that it is contained by four cardinal points.

The world is divided into three parts: one is called Asia, another Europe, and the third Africa. The ancients did not divide these three parts of the world equally. For Asia extends from the South through the East as far as the North; Europe from the North as far as the West; and Africa from the West as far as the South.

Thus Europe and Africa clearly occupy one half of the world, while Asia alone occupies the other half. These two parts were formed because between them the Great Sea enters from the Ocean and divides them. Therefore, if you divide the world into the two parts of East and West, Asia will be in one, and Europe and Africa in the other.

These three parts, together with the islands adjacent to them, contain the entire human race. The world was fittingly divided into three parts because it was destined to be imbued with faith in the holy Trinity and instructed by the teaching of the Gospel.

Hence it is written in the Savior’s parable (Matt. XIII) that a woman took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened. That is, the holy Church hid the leaven of evangelical teaching in the hearts of the faithful, among the human race that was sown in the world from the three sons of Noah, until it should transform its entire natural flavor into the worship and service of God through true faith and spiritual knowledge.

## CHAPTER III. On Paradise

Paradise is a place situated in the eastern regions. Its name is translated from Greek into Latin as *hortus*, “garden.” In Hebrew, moreover, it is called *Eden*, which in our language is interpreted as “delights.” Joined together, the two terms produce “garden of delights.”

It is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree, and also contains the tree of life. There is neither cold nor heat, but a perpetual temperateness of spring. From its midst a spring bursts forth, waters the entire grove, and divides into four rivers that arise from it. After the sin of the human being, access to it was closed. For it is enclosed on every side by a flaming sword, that is, it is girded by a wall of fire, whose blaze almost joins it to heaven.

The cherubim also—that is, a guard of angels—were stationed above the blazing sword to drive back evil spirits, so that humans might be kept away by the flame and evil angels by the angels, lest access to paradise be opened to any flesh or spirit of transgression.

Paradise, that is, the garden of delights, mystically signifies either the present Church or the land of the living, where those who are worthy will live forever through right faith and good works. Concerning it, the Lord said to the thief confessing on the cross: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

In another sense, however, paradise, as we have said, signifies the holy Church, of which it is written in Genesis: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of pleasure from the beginning” (Gen. II). Paradise is the Church; thus we read of it in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride” (Song IV).

Paradise is planted from the beginning because the Catholic Church is understood to have been founded by Christ, who is the beginning of all things. The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ, the river from the Father’s fountain; it waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of Baptism. Concerning this the Prophet aptly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river leaping forth upon thirsty land.”

The earth is watered by the four rivers flowing out from paradise; the solid structure of our mind is held together by prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, because the whole structure of good works rises through these four virtues. Thus the four rivers of paradise water the earth, because when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is tempered against the entire heat of carnal desires.

Likewise, allegorically, the four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels sent forth for preaching among all nations. The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints, and their fruits are their works. The tree of life is, of course, Christ, the Holy of Holies; whoever stretches out his hand toward him will live forever.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is free choice of the will, which has been placed within us for discerning good and evil. Whoever, having abandoned the grace of God, tastes from it will die the death.

## CHAPTER IV. On Regions
India, so called from the river Indus, by which it is bounded on its western side. It stretches from the southern sea as far as the rising of the sun, and from the north as far as Mount Caucasus. It contains many peoples and towns, as well as the island of Taprobane, filled with gems and elephants; Chryse and Argyre, rich in gold and silver; and Tyle, whose trees never lose their leaves. It also has the rivers Ganges, Indus, and Hypasis, which make the Indians renowned. The land of India is made exceptionally healthy by the breath of the Favonius; it harvests crops twice a year and enjoys the Etesian winds in place of winter. It produces dark-colored people, huge elephants, the beast called the monoceros, the bird parrot, ebony wood, cinnamon, pepper, and aromatic reed. It also exports ivory and precious stones—beryls, chrysoprases, diamonds, carbuncles, lychnites, pearls, and unions—things in which the ambition of noble women burns. There are also golden mountains there, which it is impossible to approach because of dragons, griffins, and monsters of immeasurably huge people.

Parthia is generally called the region extending from the borders of India as far as Mesopotamia. Because of the unconquerable valor of the Parthians, Assyria and the other neighboring regions likewise took their name from it. For within it are Aracusia, Parthia, Assyria, Media, and Persida. These regions, joined to one another, begin at the river Indus and are bounded by the Tigris; they lie in mountainous and rougher places and contain the rivers Hydaspes and Arbis. They are separated from one another by their own boundaries and take their names from their respective founders.

India, which lies in the eastern part and is the first to receive the rising sun, can signify the primitive Church established among the Jewish people. It first beheld the coming of the sun of righteousness and, through its teachers, preached throughout the whole world the true light that had dawned upon this world. It also possessed in abundance the gold of wisdom, the silver of eloquence, and gems of every virtue; it had no shortage of ever-green trees, that is, many people flourishing in the greenness of right faith. Yet it was not entirely without a multitude of beasts, since it encountered many persecutors of the Christian name and foresaw the rise of the poisonous teachings of heretics. Nevertheless, by the power of Christ it overcame all the devil’s fabrications.

Assur is interpreted as “depressing,” that is, the devil depressing the human race, as in the psalm: “For, he says, Assur also came with them” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Assur likewise signifies the devil or the powers of this age, as in Isaiah: “Woe to Assur, the rod of my fury” (Isa. X). Likewise there: “Do not fear, my people, inhabitant of Zion, because of Assur” (ibid.). “For with the rod he will strike you, and he will raise his staff over you on the way to Egypt.”

Again, Assur signifies the Antichrist, as in the prophet Micah: “Then there will be peace for our land when seven shepherds and eight leaders of men arise in it” (Mic. V), that is, preachers of the Law and of the Gospel; “and they will track down Assur,” that is, the Antichrist, “in the pit of Vembroth,” that is, in the condemnation of the devil.

Assyria was named from Assur, son of Shem, who first inhabited that region after the Flood. On the east it touches India, on the south Media, on the west the Tigris, and on the north Mount Caucasus, where the Caspian Gates are. In this region the first use of purple was discovered. From there came the first perfumes for hair and body, and the fragrances through which the luxury of Romans and Greeks poured forth.

Assyria, named from Assur—who, as some wish, is interpreted as “directing” or “walking”—and which also first seized worldly supremacy through insolence, signifies the arrogance of worldly empire. Concerning it, it is also written in Genesis: “From that land Assur went out and built Nineveh and the city of Rehoboth” (Gen. X). From this land of the Assyrians imperial power sprang up. They founded the great city from the name of Ninivel, son of Ninus; the Hebrews call it Nineveh, and all the prophecy of Jonah concerns either its destruction or its repentance.

Assyrians are interpreted as “those who depress,” that is, the impious or demons, as in Jeremiah: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?” (Jer. II.) They are also understood in a favorable sense, as Isaiah says: “Israel will be a third with the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth” (Isa. XIX).

Kedar is a Hebrew name which in our language is interpreted as “darkness.” It pertains to the lovers of this age, who, wrapped in dark deeds, love those things through which they are known to perish. But, to understand briefly the origin of this word, Kedar was the son of Ishmael, who gave his name to his people; their borders extended as far as the Medes and Persians. They are now called Saracens. By this name sinners are appropriately signified, among whom the Church still sighs to dwell.

Media and Persida were named from the kings Medus and Perses, who attacked those provinces in war. Media, extending across the Parthian kingdoms from the west, is enclosed by Armenia on the north; on the east it looks toward the Caspian regions, and on the south toward Persida. This land produces the medicinal tree, which no other region brings forth. There are two Medias, greater and lesser.

Persida extends from the east toward the Indians; on the west it has the Red Sea, on the north it touches Media, and on the south Carmania, which is attached to Persida. In these regions lies the celebrated town of Susa. In Persida the magical art first arose. After the confusion of languages, the giant Nimrod went there and taught the Persians to worship fire. For all the peoples in those parts worship the sun, which in their language is called “El” [reading uncertain].

The Persians and Medes, who held the kingdom after the Assyrians, signify the rule of the nations that at times foster the people of God with their assistance. Hence we read in the histories of the ancients that Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, who had been foretold in the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa. XLIV, XLV), released the Jewish captivity and ordered the Temple of God to be built. For this reason he was also called the servant of God, and for this reason the Lord’s aid was promised to him, so that he might subject nations before him and turn the backs of kings: and rightly so. For “Medes” and “Persians” are interpreted as “measuring” or “measured.” The measure by which they measured was measured back to them.

Mesopotamia possesses a Greek etymology, because it is enclosed by two rivers. For on the east it has the Tigris, and on the west the Euphrates. It begins in the north between Mount Taurus and Caucasus; to the south of it lies Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and finally Arabia Eudaemon.

Mesopotamia, which is interpreted as “raised up,” and from which Jacob took a wife, signifies the Gentile world, from which Christ chose for himself the Church as a bride without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V). For just as Jacob, leaving his home, country, and parents, went to a distant region to take a wife for himself, so Christ left his parents according to the flesh—that is, the Israelite people—and his country—that is, Jerusalem and all the regions of Judaea—and went to the Gentiles, taking the Church from them, so that what was said might be fulfilled: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved” (Hos. II).

The chief city of the region of Babylonia is Babylon, from which the region also received its name. It was so renowned that Chaldaea, Assyria, and Mesopotamia sometimes passed into its name. The giant Nimrod first founded this city. Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, enlarged it and built the city wall with bitumen and baked brick. It took its name from confusion, because there the languages of those building the tower were confused and mixed together (Gen. XI).

Babylonia, which is interpreted as “confusion,” in which the rule belonged to the Chaldeans—who are interpreted as “like demons” or “like fierce men”—signifies the city of the devil, in which there is everlasting confusion and where the fierceness of demons appears in the overthrow of human beings.

In it Nabuchodonosor reigned. His name is interpreted as “prophecy of a narrow flask,” and he signifies the devil. For he laid waste to the city of God and burned the Temple, because he persecutes the holy Church with hatred and desires to overthrow by the fire of worldly desire those who were the temple of God. For thus we read concerning him:

“Nabuzardan, commander of the army, servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord, the house of the king, and the houses of Jerusalem; and he burned every house with fire, and all the army of the Chaldeans that was with the commander of the soldiers destroyed all the walls of Jerusalem around it. And the rest of the people who remained in the city, and the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the common people, Nabuzardan, commander of the army, transferred, and so forth” (IV Kings XXV).

Nabuzardan, whose name is interpreted as “winnowing fan” or “prophecy of another’s judgment,” signifies the Antichrist, who comes by God’s just judgment upon sinners. He is, of course, the commander of the army of the king of Babylon. When the ancient enemy—who is both the king of confusion and the prince of all the wicked, both evil spirits and impious human beings—invades the faithful people, he burns the intelligible Jerusalem, the house of the Lord, and the house of the king and the houses of Jerusalem, that is, the rulers and those who seemed to dwell in the vision of peace, overthrowing them when inflamed by desire. He burns every house with fire when he disturbs each person’s conscience through the flame of unlawful love. He destroys all the walls of Jerusalem around it when, among those who despair, he dissolves the purpose of prayer and the pursuit of virtues, which he knows can prevail against him, lest they return through hope of forgiveness to divine aid and grasp the defenses of a more corrected life.

And when he leads the people into captivity, he leaves winegrowers and farmers from the poor of the land, because, by taking captive through vices those who could have been useful in word and example, he entrusts cultivation to foolish and dull people, so that not the wine of spiritual grace and the grain of sound doctrine may bear fruit in the vineyards and fields of the peoples, but rather the thorns and thistles of vices may grow.

Babylon may also be the world or Rome, as we read in the Apocalypse: “And Babylon the great came into remembrance before the Lord, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath” (Apoc. XVI). And in Isaiah: “And that glorious Babylon among the kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; it will not be inhabited to the end” (Isa. XIII). And in Jeremiah: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk; suddenly Babylon fell, and she was shattered” (Jer. LI).

Arabia was so called, that is, “sacred.” For this is what its interpretation signifies, because it is a region producing incense-bearing fragrances. Hence the Greeks called it Eudaemon, and our people call it “blessed”; in its forests myrrh and cinnamon grow. There the phoenix bird is born, the sardonyx gem and the iris are found, as well as malachite and paederos. It is called Saba from the son of Cush, who was named Saba. This region extends eastward in a narrow strip of land toward the Persian Gulf; Chaldaea closes it on the north, and the Arabian Gulf on the west.

Arabia, which is interpreted as “humble” or “level,” signifies earthly pleasure. Hence it is written in the psalm: “The kings of Arabia and Saba will bring gifts” (Ps. LXXI). “Arabians” stands for people who deal in sweet things and delight themselves with earthly pleasure. For just as that country soothes the senses with various spices, so these people are invited to the softest pleasures by worldly allurements.
