The kings of Arabia, therefore, are those who subject the blandishments of the body to strict discipline. Likewise Saba, from which the Sabaeans are named, although it excels in bodily pleasure and is filled with pleasant fragrances, nevertheless offers more agreeable gifts of virtue through its converted people.

Syria is said to have been named by a certain Syrian native after his own name. On the east it is bounded by the Euphrates, on the west by Our Sea and Egypt; on the north it has Armenia and Cappadocia, and on the south the Arabian Gulf. Its position extends to an immense length but is narrower in breadth.

Syria signifies the pride of the nations, which often afflicted the people of God. Hence it is written (III Kings XX) that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his whole army, along with thirty-two kings, horses, and chariots, and, advancing, fought against Samaria, besieged it, and so forth.

Mystically, Ben-hadad, the enemy of Israel, signifies the devil, the enemy of all good, who gathers various armies of evil spirits to overthrow the people of God. But he is conquered through the young men of the princes of Israel, when the wicked enemy is put to flight through good hearers of the holy teachers—those who strive to fulfill in their deeds what they hear with their ears. His entire army is thrown into confusion by the soldiers of Christ.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, also fled on horseback with his cavalry. Then the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck Syria with a great blow. What does it mean that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, is described as fleeing on horseback with his cavalry, except that the prince of all the wicked—the devil, whose eyes are raised high, for Syria is interpreted as “the lofty”—trusting in the horse of his pride, flees with his horsemen, namely, all the proud? Since he is the head over all the sons of pride, he is overcome and put to flight by the army of Christ, that is, by the humble and those who fear God.

Syria contains the following provinces: Commagene, Phoenicia, and Palestine, of which Judaea is a part, excluding the Saracens and Nabataeans.

Commagene, the first province of Syria, was named from the city of Commagene, which was once regarded as its capital. It has Armenia to the north, Mesopotamia to the east, Syria to the south, and the Great Sea to the west.

Phoenix, the brother of Cadmus, went from Thebes of the Egyptians into Syria and reigned at Sidon; he called that province Phoenicia after his own name. It is the [city] where Tyre is located, to which Isaiah speaks. It has Arabia to the east and the Red Sea to the south.

The province of Palestine had the city of Philistim as its capital, now called Ascalon. From this city the entire surrounding region was called Palestine. On the east it meets the Red Sea; on the southern side it is bordered by Judaea; on the north it is divided from the territory of the Tyrians; and on the west it is bounded by the Egyptian frontier.

The region of Judaea was named from Judah, from whose tribe it had kings. It was formerly called Chanaan, either from the son of Ham or from the ten nations of the Canaanites; after these had been expelled, the Jews possessed the same land. Its length begins at the village of Arfa and extends as far as the village of Juliadis, where Jews and Tyrians share a common settlement. Its breadth extends from Mount Lebanon to the Lake of Tiberias.

In the middle of Judaea lies the city of Jerusalem, like the navel of the region and of the whole earth, rich in various resources, fertile in crops, distinguished by its waters, and abundant in balsams. Therefore, according to the favor of the elements, the Jews believed it to be the land promised to the fathers, flowing with milk and honey, although by this means God was promising them the privilege of resurrection.

“Jews” is interpreted as “confessors,” and Judaea is interpreted as “confession.” Mystically, it signifies the holy Church, in which the Lord is always praised through right faith, devout confession, and good works. Jerusalem, interpreted as “vision of peace,” also holds its type, because there he is seen who is our peace and who made both one (Eph. II).

It must also be noted that, according to history, Jerusalem is the city in which the Lord was crucified, buried, and rose from the dead. To it the Savior says in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you,” and so forth (Matt. XXIII), expressing the very people who dwell in Jerusalem and its surrounding territories.

Allegorically, it signifies the present Church, concerning which it is written: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI). Tropologically, it signifies the faithful soul, which contemplates the Lord with a pure mind. According to anagogy, therefore, it signifies the heavenly homeland and the dwelling of the holy angels and human beings in heaven, concerning which the Apostle says: “The Jerusalem that is above is our mother” (Gal. IV). The Apostle John sufficiently describes it in his Apocalypse and mystically depicts its structure as being made from precious stones, that is, holy human beings.

Samaria, a region of Palestine, took its name from a certain town called Samaria, once a royal city in Israel, now called Sebastia after the name of Augustus. This region lies between Judaea and Galilee, beginning at a village called Eleas and ending in the land of Ararat. Its terrain is similar in nature and differs in no way from Judaea.

Samaria is interpreted as “watch,” and it was so named because, when the ten tribes had been transferred by the Chaldeans, other nations were substituted for them to guard the land. Samaritans are customarily understood as representing idolatry. For, separated from the Jewish people, they had devoted the honor of their souls to images of many animals, namely, golden calves.

Heretics may also be understood in the Samaritans. They appear to possess knowledge of God’s Law, but they do not cease to color the images of their errors; therefore, separated from the people of God, they can have no communion.

Ituraea and Trachonitis are regions whose tetrarch was Philip, as we read in the Gospel. Trachonitis is called the land beside the desert of Arabia, which is joined to Bostra. Ituraea is a Syrian word and is interpreted as “mountainous.”

Galilee is a region of Palestine, so called because it produces people of a lighter complexion than Palestine. It is twofold, upper and lower, though they are connected with one another and adjoin Syria and Phoenicia. Their land is rich, productive, and very fertile in crops.

Galilee is interpreted as “wheel,” or “transmigration,” or “revelation.” It sometimes signifies the course of the present life, as in the Gospel where it is said of the Savior: “He left Judaea and came again into Galilee” (John IV). What does “he left Judaea” mean except that he left the unbelief of those who refused to receive him and rejected the stone they ought to have built? He went through the apostles into Galilee, that is, into the revolving course of this world, commanding the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

That Galilee signifies transmigration is shown by the words that the angel spoke to the women at the Lord’s tomb after his resurrection: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, I have told you” (ibid.). For our Redeemer had already transmigrated from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from punishment to glory, and from corruption to incorruption. He is first seen by the disciples in Galilee after the resurrection, because we shall see the glory of his resurrection afterward, if now we transmigrate from vices to the height of virtues.

He who is announced in the tomb is shown in transmigration, because the one recognized in the mortification of the flesh is seen in the transmigration of the mind.

According to the interpretation of Galilee as “revelation,” he is no longer to be understood in the form of a servant, but in that form in which he is equal to the Father, which he promised to those who love him in John, saying: “And I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John XIV). This is not according to what they were already seeing, and what, after rising with his scars, he later showed not only to be seen but also to be touched. Rather, it is according to that ineffable light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John I), according to which he shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

He went before us there, and when he came to us he did not depart from there; and when he went before us there, he did not abandon us. That will be the revelation, truly in Galilee, when we shall be like him. There we shall see him as he is (I John III). It will also be the more blessed transmigration from this age into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we may deserve to be separated to his right hand.

The region of Pentapolis lies on the border of Arabia and Palestine. It was named from the five cities of the wicked, which were consumed by heavenly fire. Once the land was exceedingly fertile around Jerusalem; now it is deserted and burned. Because of the crime of its inhabitants, fire descended from heaven and dissolved that region into eternal ashes. There a kind of shadow and appearance is still seen in the ashes and in the trees themselves.

Green fruit grows there beneath so convincing an appearance of ripeness that it awakens the desire to eat it. If you pluck it, it splits open and dissolves into ash, exhaling smoke as though it were still burning. The name Pentapolis is derived from a number, as though it meant “the region of five cities.”

These five cities were established there: Sodom, which is interpreted as “silent cattle”; Gomorrah, interpreted as “fear of the people” or “rebellion”; Admah, interpreted as “soil,” “earth,” or “earthly”; Seboim, interpreted as “of the roes” or “of the does,” or “its station is the sea” or “the station of the sea”; and Segor, interpreted as “small.”

Since this region was burned by divine judgment on account of its crimes, it signifies those who abuse the five senses of their bodies in luxury and pleasure concerning earthly things. They are liable to eternal fire unless repentance and correction of their perverse ways come to their aid beforehand.

Egypt, formerly called Aeria, later received its name from Egyptus, the brother of Danaus, who reigned there. On the east it is joined to Syria and the Red Sea; on the west it has Libya; on the north, the Great Sea; while to the south it recedes inland and extends as far as the Ethiopians. It is a region unaccustomed to the rains of heaven and ignorant of rainfall. Only the Nile, flowing around it, irrigates and fertilizes it by its inundation. Hence it is fertile in crops and supplies a large part of the lands with grain. It is also so rich in other goods that it fills the whole world with necessary merchandise.

Egypt is interpreted as “tribulation that hems in,” and it signifies the vain labor that the wicked exercise in this world, burning with greed, pursuing the profits of the age, and conducting worldly business. There they will never find rest for their souls; rather, from the tribulation of this life they will arrive at everlasting confinement.

Egypt can also signify the world converted to God, as in the psalm: “Ambassadors will come from Egypt” (Ps. LXVII). And in Isaiah: “On that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt. For they will cry to the Lord because of the face of the one who oppresses them, and he will send them a Savior and defender who will deliver them” (Isa. XIX).

It is also understood in a negative sense, as in Ezekiel: “When I make the land of Egypt desolate. The land will be deserted of its fullness when I strike all its inhabitants” (Ezek. XXIX). Amos likewise says: “Egypt will be in desolation and Idumaea in the desert of destruction” (Joel III).

Scythia, like Gothia, is said to have been named from Magog, son of Japheth. Its land was once immense. For in the east it extended to India; in the north, through the Maeotian marshes [Metocides], between the Danube and the Ocean, as far as the borders of Germany. Later it became smaller, extending on the right-hand side of the east, where the Syrian Ocean stretches as far as the Caspian Sea, which lies to the west. From there it was drawn southward as far as the ridge of Caucasus. Hyrcania lies beneath it; on the west it has many peoples wandering widely because of the infertility of the lands. Some of these inhabit fields, while others, monstrous and savage, live on human flesh and blood.

Many lands of Scythia are rich, though more of them are uninhabitable. For although in many places they abound in gold and gems, access by human beings is rare because of the ferocity of the griffins. This homeland possesses the finest emeralds. The blue stone and the purest crystal are also found in Scythia. It has the great rivers Oschus, Phasis, and Araxes.

Scythia, which lacks warmth and is always hardened by cold, can signify those who are strangers to the warmth of the Holy Spirit and remain under the rule of the one who said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Concerning them Christ says: “Iniquity will abound; the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). Their savagery feeds on human flesh and lives on human blood, since they do not cease to harm the innocent and, through greed, turn the necessary expenses of others into their own profit.

Those who dwell in the rich and habitable land among these people signify those who, converted from the error of the Gentiles and from idolatry, come to the land of the Church. There, bright with sincere faith and ever-green with the gems of precious virtues, they live by a heavenly way of life in expectation of the future homeland. Their citizenship, according to the Apostle, is always in heaven (Phil. III). Though walking in the flesh, they do not wage war according to the flesh; rather, they seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, and they set their minds on the things above, not on those upon the earth.

Armenia was named from Armenus, a Thessalian companion of Jason. After losing King Jason and gathering his multitude, which had been wandering in different places, Armenus founded Armenia and named it after himself. It lies between Taurus and Caucasus and extends from Cappadocia to the Caspian Sea. To the north it has the Ceraunian Mountains, from which the river Tigris rises, and in whose mountains the ark is said to have come to rest after the Flood.

Ararath is interpreted as Armenia, or “mountain made warlike.” Ararath itself is Armenia. For the ark is said to have come to rest in the mountains of Ararath after the Flood, and it is said that traces of it remain there to this day.

Jeremiah also mentions these mountains in his vision against Babylon. Josephus likewise, in the first book of his *Jewish Antiquities*, presenting the history of secular literature, says:

“Observing that the earth had been freed from the Flood, Noah allowed seven more days to pass. Then, releasing all the animals and beasts through the open enclosures, he himself went out with his offspring, sacrificing offerings to God and rejoicing with his children. The Armenians call this place the place of departure or going forth. For the inhabitants of those regions testify that the ark first came to rest there, and all who wrote barbarian histories record that certain traces of the timbers of this ark survive, as well as the Flood. Among them is Berosus the Chaldean, who, reporting on the Flood, said this: ‘It is said that some part of this ship remains in Armenia near the mountain of the Carduchi, and that certain people tear away bitumen from it and carry it around; they use it especially for those who are purified and cleanse themselves.’”

Jerome the Egyptian, who wrote the antiquities of the Phoenicians in fine language, also reports this, as do Naseas and many others, and likewise Nicolaus of Damascus in the twenty-seventh book. There is a mountain in Armenia above Immades called Beris, to which many are believed to have fled during the Flood and to have been saved there. Others, floating in the hull of the ark, are said to have reached its summit, and the wood of the ark was customarily displayed for many generations. I believe that these were none other than those whom Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, set forth in his books.

Mystically, Ararath, or Armenia, can signify the rule of this world or the people of the nations. It is rightly called a “mountain made warlike,” because, torn away from the height of pride and the error of idolatry, it submits itself to the holy Church, which is the ark of the living God. She contains within herself every kind of living creature, that is, every kind of human being, and, standing upon the height of virtues, awaits future devotion in the heavenly kingdom.

A city gave Cappadocia its proper name. It lies at the head of Syria; on the east it touches Armenia, on the west Asia Minor, on the north the Cimmerian Sea and the Themiscirian plains, which belonged to the Amazons, and on the south Mount Taurus, beneath which lie Cilicia and Isauria as far as the Gulf of Cilicia, which faces the island of Cyprus. Its land is, above all others, a nurse of horses. The river Halys flows through it; it once separated the kingdoms of Lydia from the Persians.

Cappadocia is interpreted as “redeemed by the hand.” Typologically, it can also signify the holy Church, which through the work of Christ our Lord has been redeemed from the power of the devil.

Asia Minor is enclosed by Cappadocia on the east and surrounded on every other side by the sea. To the north it has the Euxine Sea, to the west the Propontis, and to the south the Egyptian Sea. It contains the provinces of Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia, Isauria, and Lycia.

It contains these seven cities: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Asia is interpreted as “raised up” or “walking upward,” signifying the Church advancing toward heavenly things by the steps of virtues. Hence John writes in the Apocalypse to the aforementioned seven Churches that are in Asia.

Ephesus is interpreted as “my will” or “my counsel,” signifying the Church chosen by the will and counsel of God. Smyrna is interpreted as “their song,” that is, the confession of the faithful. Pergamum is interpreted as “dividing their horns,” that is, the Church cutting apart the fears of heretics or the temptations of aerial powers. Thyatira is interpreted as “illuminated,” namely, the Church illuminated by the sun of righteousness. Sardis is interpreted as “the beginning of beauty,” that is, the Church of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the beginning of beauty. Philadelphia is interpreted as “saving,” that is, the Church saving her own peoples. Laodicea, interpreted as “an agreeable tribe,” signifies the Church, which is pleasing to God.

Galatia was named from the ancient peoples of the Gauls, by whom it was occupied. For the Gauls, summoned to aid by the king of Bithynia, divided the kingdom with him after achieving victory. Thereafter, mingled with the Greeks, they were first called Gallograeci and are now called Galatians from the ancient name of the Gauls; their region is called Galatia. Galatia is interpreted as “magnificent” or “transferred,” and rightly so, because, transferred from error, it became magnificent through the power of faith.

Phrygia was named from Phrygia, the daughter of Aesop. It was also called Dardania from Dardanus, son of Jupiter, concerning whom Homer says:

> Whom Jupiter first begot in the heavenly citadel.

For he indeed, having set out from the city of Corycus, first came into Phrygia. It is a region lying above the Troad: on its northern side it borders Galatia; to the south it is adjacent to Lycaonia; on the east it adjoins Lydia; and on the west it is bounded by the sea of the Hellespont. Its region is Troy, which Tros, king of the Trojans and father of Ganymede, named after himself. There are two Phrygias, Greater and Lesser. Greater Phrygia contains Smyrna; Lesser Phrygia, Ilium. Lycaonia [lacuna]. Phrygia, moreover, is interpreted as “a cutting apart of breasts”; Lycaonia, however, is interpreted as “for raising up.”

Lydia was named after Lydus, the brother of the king, who had remained in the province. On the west it is joined to Lesser Phrygia; on the east it contains the city of Smyrna, which the river Meles surrounds. The Pactolus and Hermus flow around its fields, exceedingly rich in golden sands. Lydia is interpreted as “cleansed” or “purified.”

Isauria is said to have received its name from the situation of the place, because it lies open on every side to the blowing of the winds. It contains the metropolitan city of Seleucia.

Cilicia derived its name from a certain Cilix, whom they say was born in Phoenicia and assert to have been older than Jupiter. It extends chiefly across plains, receiving Lycia on the west, the Issic Sea on the south, and the ridges of Mount Taurus behind it. The Cydnus cuts across it; its mother-city is Tarsus. In it also lies the town of Corycus, from which a great quantity of excellent saffron comes, more fragrant in its scent and more golden in color. Cilicia is interpreted as “assembly,” or “mourning,” or “assumption,” or “its sound.” Figuratively, it represents the person of penitents, who daily lament their sins in fasting and prayer and implore pardon from the Lord.

Lycia was so named because it is joined to Cilicia on the east. For it has Cilicia to the east, the sea to the west and south, and Caria to the north. There is Mount Chimaera, which exhales fire in its nightly eruptions, just as Mount Etna does in Sicily and Vesuvius in Campania. Lycia is interpreted as “weeping.”

Albus is a region of the Idumaeans, now called Gabalene, near the city of Petra.

The Amalekite region lies in the desert south of Judaea, extending to the city of Petra for those traveling toward Aila. Scripture also recalls it, saying: “Amalek dwells in the land of the south” (Num. 13). Near it another Canaanite also lived, who fought against the children of Israel in the desert; concerning them it is written: “The Amalekite and the Canaanite dwell in the valley” (Num. 14).

Argob is the region of the king of Bashan, above the Jordan, in the allotment of half the tribe of Manasseh. To this day there is a village near the Arabian city of Gerasa, fifteen miles from it toward the west, called Arga, which Symmachus interprets as “measure.” Argob, however, is interpreted as “cursed height.” And what is “cursed height” if not the arrogance of pride, which is interpreted as “a curse of sorrow”?

Hermon is a region of the Hebrews, which Jesus possessed. The Hebrew from whom I learned the Scriptures by his instruction asserts that Mount Hermon rises above Paneas. The Hivites and Amorites once possessed it; from there summer snows are now carried to Tyre for the sake of luxury.

Cene, a region of the princes of Edom, is interpreted as “possession.”

Evila is the place where the purest gold—called *zaab* in Hebrew—and the most precious gems, the carbuncle and emerald, are produced. It is a region extending toward the east, around which the Pishon, flowing out of Paradise, makes its circuit; our people, changing its name, call it the Ganges. One of the younger sons of Noah was also called Evila. Josephus reports that he, together with his brothers, possessed the territory from the river Cophene and the region of India as far as the place called Hicira. Ishmael is also said to have lived in the wilderness of Evila, which Holy Scripture says is in the desert of Sur, opposite Egypt, and extends as far as the land of the Assyrians. Evila is interpreted as “grieving” or “in labor.”

Ephratha is the region of Bethlehem, the city of David, in which Christ was born. It is in the tribe of Judah, although many mistakenly think it lies in the tribe of Benjamin, beside the road where Rachel was buried, five miles from Jerusalem, in the place called Hippodrome by the Seventy, as we read in the Book of Chronicles. Ephratha is interpreted as “fertility” or “dusty.”

Elath is the region of the princes of Edom and the city of Esau, ten miles east of Petra. Elath is interpreted as “on the ground,” or “solitary,” or “one.”

Philistim, now called Ascalon, and the region around it are in Palestine. Philistim is interpreted as “a double ruin.”

Gerara, from whose name the region is called Geraritis, lies beyond the Doric region, twenty-five miles south of Eleutheropolis. It was formerly the boundary of the Canaanites on the southern side and the metropolitan city of Palestine. Scripture records that it lay between Kadesh and Sur—that is, between two deserts, one of which adjoins Egypt, to which the people reached after crossing the Red Sea. The other extends from Kadesh as far as the wilderness of the Saracens. Gerara is interpreted as “he saw rumination,” or “walls.”

Gesse is a region of Egypt in which Jacob lived with his children. Gesse is interpreted as “approaching their touching,” or “nearness.”

Idumaea is the region of Esau, which received its name from the fact that he was called Edom. It lies around the city of Petra, now called Gabalene.

Jotheth is a region of the princes of Edom in the same Gabalene about which we spoke above.

Messe is a region of India in which the sons of Joktan, son of Eber, lived. Messe is interpreted as “rare water” or “elevation.”

Theman is a region of the princes of Edom in the land of Gebal, taking its name from Theman, son of Eliphaz, son of Esau. To this day there is a village called Theman, five miles from the city of Petra, where there is also a garrison of Roman soldiers. But the place from which Eliphaz, king of the Themanites, came was also called Theman, as was each of the sons of Ishmael. It should be known, moreover, that the whole southern region is called *Theman* in Hebrew. Theman is interpreted as “the south wind” or “the southwest wind.”

Kedar is the region of which we read in Ezekiel, “the princes of Kedar”; Jeremiah and Isaiah also recall this name in their vision of Arabia. It is a region in the wilderness of the Saracens, named after Kedar, son of Ishmael. Kedar is interpreted as “darkness” or “mourning.”

Gotha is a region of the Assyrians. Gotha is interpreted as “beginning.”

Decapolis, as we read in the Gospel, is a region of ten cities beyond the Jordan, around Hippo, Pella, and Gadara.

Fathures is a region of Egypt, according to Ezekiel and Jeremiah, in which the fugitive Jews lived. Fathures is interpreted as “exploration of the mouth,” or “a morsel of light,” or “the mouth of a turtledove.”

Gellam Sur is a region of the foreign peoples. Gella is interpreted as “migrate” or “for one migrating.”

Gessur is a region of foreigners in Syria. Gessur is interpreted as “beside my light,” or “drawing near to my light.”

Galilee is the name of a region. There are two Galilees, one of which is called Galilee of the Gentiles, near the borders of Tyre. There Solomon gave King Hiram of Tyre twenty-five cities in the allotment of the tribe of Naphtali. The other Galilee is around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun. Galilee is interpreted as “rolling,” or “completed transmigration,” or “wheel.”

Gamela is a region of the Idumaeans, for which Aquila and Symmachus give the interpretation “valley of salt.”

Macha is a region of the king of Gessur. Macha is interpreted as “softened” or “broken.”

Masagam is a region of the Moabites, as Jeremiah writes. Masaga is interpreted as “seeking” or “retaining.”

Misor is a region of Moab, according to Jeremiah. It is interpreted as “straight,” or “level,” or “tribulation.”

Masfath is a region of the Moabites, as we read in Jeremiah. It is also mentioned above in Isaiah. Masfath is interpreted as “having the seasons of a rush of waters.”

Maon is a region of the Moabites, according to Jeremiah. Maon is interpreted as “dwelling place.”

Magedan is the place whose borders the evangelist Matthew records that the Lord reached; Mark also recalls the same name. It is now called the region of Magedana, around Gerasa. Magedon is interpreted as “of its fruits,” or “its upper rooms.”

Nebeoth is the region of which Isaiah writes. Nebeoth is interpreted as “prophesying.”

Ophir is the place from which, as we read in the Books of Kings, gold was brought to Solomon. One of the descendants of Eber was also named Ophir. Josephus reports that those descended from him lived from the river Cophene as far as the region of India called Hieria; I think that the region received its name from him. Ophir is interpreted as “disgrace.”

Reblatha is a region of the Babylonians, or a city now called Antioch. Reblatha is interpreted as “this much,” or “multitude.”

Saron, which Isaiah also mentions, saying, “Saron has been turned into marshes” (Isa. 33), is to this day the name of the region between Mount Tabor and the lake of Tiberias. The whole land visible from Caesarea of Palestine as far as the town of Joppa is also called Saronas. Saron is interpreted as “prince of sorrow.”

Sefela, as Isaiah writes, is interpreted by Aquila as “level country” and by Symmachus as “valley.” To this day the entire region near Eleutheropolis, level and flat and extending toward the north and west, is called Sefela.

Thalassar is a region of Syria. Thalassar is interpreted as “the suspended prince.”

The region of the Ethiopians rises from the river Indus beside Egypt, reaches the Nile and the Ocean to the south, and lies close to the sun itself.

Canaan, son of Ham, possessed the land from Sidon to Gaza, which the Jews afterward possessed after expelling the Canaanites. Canaan is interpreted as “their movement,” or “merchant,” or “humble.” Canaan figuratively signifies the greedy and avaricious, those devoted to frail possessions and worldly business, whom it is clear must be removed from their dwelling places, because “the world is passing away, and its desire” (1 John 2).

Pontus is a region of many peoples beside the Pontic Sea, which separates Asia and Europe. Pontus is interpreted as “inclining.”

Saronas, interpreted as “level country,” is a region of Palestine extending as far as the town of Joppa. Sarona is also interpreted as “singing sorrow.”

After Asia we turn our pen to Europe. Europe, according to the accounts of the pagans, was the daughter of Agenor, king of Libya. Jupiter carried her off from Africa and brought her to Crete, and named the third part of the world after her. This Agenor was the son of Libya, from whom Libya—that is, Africa—is said to have received its name. Thus it appears that Libya received its name first, and Europe afterward.

Europe, divided into the third part of the world, begins at the river Tanais and descends westward along the northern Ocean as far as the borders of Spain. Its eastern and southern part, rising from the Pontus, is joined entirely to the Great Sea and ends at the islands of Gades.

The first region of Europe is Lower Scythia. Beginning at the Maeotian marshes, it extends between the Danube and the northern Ocean as far as Germany. In general, because of the barbarian peoples who inhabit it, this land is called Barbaria. One part of it is Alania, which reaches the Maeotian marshes; after this comes Dacia, where Gothia is also situated; then Germany, where the Suebi inhabited a very large area.

Germany, after Lower Scythia, is enclosed between the Danube, the Rhine, and the Ocean. It is bounded on the north and west by the Ocean, on the east by the Danube, and on the south by the river Rhine. It is a land rich in strength, with numerous and formidable peoples. Hence it was called Germany because of the fertility by which it produces peoples. It produces Hercynian birds [the Hercynian Forest], whose feathers shine through at night. It also breeds wild bison, aurochs, and elk. It supplies gems, crystal, and amber, as well as green Gallic stone and white thunderstone.

There are two Germanies: Upper Germany beside the northern Ocean, and Lower Germany around the Rhine.

Among the provinces that the Danube separates from the barbarian lands to the Mediterranean Sea, the first is Moesia, so called from the yield of crops. Hence the ancients called it the granary of Ceres. On the east it is joined to the mouths of the Danube; on the southeast to Thrace; on the south to Macedonia; and on the west to Istria.

After Moesia comes Pannonia; after it, Noricum, a cold and less fertile land; after Noricum, Rhaetia, rich in crops, which borders Belgic Gaul.

Thrace is said to have received its name from Thiras, son of Japheth, who came there. Others say that Thrace was named from the savagery of its inhabitants. To the east lie the Propontis and the city of Constantinople; to the north extends the Ister; to the south it adjoins the Aegean Sea; and to the west Macedonia lies beneath it. Various peoples once inhabited this region: the Bessi, Massagetae, Sarmatians, Scythians, and many other nations. It is extensive and therefore contained very many peoples. The river Hebrus flows through Thrace and also touches many barbarian nations.

Greece was named after a Greek king who inhabited the whole region. Andromache bore Molossus to Pyrrhus, and from him one part of Epirus was called Molossia.

There are seven provinces of Greece. The first, from the west, is Dalmatia; then Epirus; then Hellas; then Thessaly; then Macedonia; then Achaia; and two in the sea, Crete and the Cyclades. Illyricum, in general, is the whole of Greece.

Dalmatia is said to have derived its name from Delmi, the largest city of that province. To the east it adjoins Macedonia; to the north, Moesia; to the west it is bounded by Istria; and to the south it is enclosed by the Adriatic Gulf.

Epirus was named after Pyrrhus, son of Achilles. One part of it is Chaonia, previously called Molossia after Molossus, son of Pyrrhus, whom he had by Andromache. After Pyrrhus was killed through the plotting of Orestes, Helenus took Andromache and held the kingdom of his stepson, who had succeeded his father. From him that part of Epirus was called Molossia. Helenus later called it Chaonia after his brother Chaon, whom he is said to have killed unknowingly while hunting, as a kind of consolation for his dead brother.

Hellas was named after King Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha. From him the Greeks were earlier called Hellenes. This is the land of Attica, formerly called Acte. A certain Cranous, a native of Greece, had a daughter named Attis, after whom the land of Attica was called. It lies between Macedonia and Achaia and is joined to Arcadia on its northern side.

This is true Greece, where the city of Athens stood, mother of the liberal arts and nurse of philosophers. Greece possessed nothing brighter or nobler than Athens. In it also lies the plain of Marathon, once famous for the bloodiest battle, according to tradition.

There are two provinces of Hellas: Boeotia and the Peloponnese.

Boeotia was named for the following reason. When Cadmus, son of Agenor, was seeking his sister Europa, carried off by Jupiter, at his father’s command, and could not find her, he feared his father’s anger and, taking courage, chose exile. By chance he followed the tracks of an ox he had seen and embraced the place where it had lain down. Thus he named the place Boeotia after the ox, and there he built the city of Thebes, where civil wars once thundered and where Apollo and Hercules—the elder, the Theban—were born.

The same region was called Aonia after a certain spring consecrated to Apollo and the Muses, which is in Boeotia.

The Peloponnese is the second part of Hellas, ruled by and named after Pelops.

Thessaly was named after King Thessalus. It is joined to Macedonia on the southern side, with Pieria behind it. Thessaly has many rivers and towns, especially Thessalonica; Mount Parnassus, once consecrated to Apollo, is also there.

Thessaly was the homeland of Achilles and the origin of the Lapiths. They are said to have been the first to tame horses with bridles. Hence they were called centaurs. Solid gold coins were first made in Thessaly, and the practice of taming horses was also discovered there.

At first Macedonia had the name Emathia, from King Emathius. But Macedo, the maternal grandson of Deucalion, after gaining power there, changed the name and called it Macedonia after himself. On the east it borders the Aegean Sea; on the south, Achaia; on the west, Dalmatia; and on the north, Moesia.

It was the homeland of Alexander the Great and is a region rich in veins of gold and silver. It produces the stone called *paeanitis*. Mount Olympus is there, rising so high with its lofty peak that neither clouds nor winds are felt at its summit.

Achaia was named after King Achaeus; both the city and the province bear the name. It is almost an island, for except on its northern side, where it joins Macedonia, it is surrounded on every side by the sea. On the east it has the Myrtoan Sea; on the southeast, the Cretan Sea; on the south, the Ionian Sea; and on the southwest and west, the islands of Cassiope. Only on the northern side is it joined to Macedonia or the land of Attica.

Its chief city is Corinth, the glory of Greece. The Inachus is a river of Achaia.

Arcadia is a gulf of Achaia, spread out like a plane-tree leaf between the Ionian and Aegean Seas. Arcas, son of Jupiter and Callisto, after bringing the Pelasgians under his rule, named it Arcadia after himself.

It is also Sicyonia, after King Sicyon, from whom the kingdom of the Sicyonians was named. Arcadia has the great river Erymanthus and also the asbestos stone, which, once kindled, is never extinguished. The whitest blackbirds are also born there.

Pannonia was named from the Apennine Alps, by which it is separated from Italy. It is a strong region, rich in soil, enclosed by two sufficiently swift rivers, the Drabus and the Savus. It is joined to Noricum and Rhaetia, which have Moesia to the east, Istria to the southeast, and the Apennine Alps to the southwest. To the west it has Belgic Gaul; to the north, the source or boundary of the Danube, which separates Germany and Gaul.

Italy was first occupied by Greek peoples and called Greater Greece; afterward, from the name of the king, it was called Saturnia, and then Latium, because Saturn, driven from his dwelling places by Jupiter, hid there. Later it was named after King Italus, who ruled there.

Its length is greater than its width, extending from the northwest toward the southeast. It is bounded on the south by the Tyrrhenian Sea, on the north by the Adriatic, and on the west by the ridges of the Alps. It is a land most beautiful in every respect, delightful for the fertility of its soil and the abundance of its pastures. It has the lakes Benacus and Lucrinus; the rivers Eridanus and Tiber; and the warm springs of Baiae. It produces gems, *syrtitis*, *lyncurium*, and coral, as well as boa serpents, wild lynxes, and the birds of Diomedes.

Italy and Spain are both called Hesperia because the Greeks sail by the star Hesperus both to Italy and to Spain. They are distinguished in this way: if one says simply “Hesperia,” Italy is meant; if one adds “the farther” or “last,” Spain is meant, because it lies at the end of the west.

Tuscia is a part of Italy. Umbria, as histories relate, was so named because it survived the watery disaster of rains; for this reason it was called Umbria in Greek. It lies on the ridges of the Apennine mountain, in the southern part of Italy.

Etruria is a part of Italy, so called because its boundaries stretched as far as the bank of the Tiber, as though to “other boundaries.”

For *eteros* means “other,” and *oros* means “boundary.” Previously Rome’s boundary held only one bank of the Tiber. Others think Etruria was named after an Etruscan prince.

It is also called Tyrrhenia, after Tyrrhenus, the brother of the Lydian king, who came from the east [by lot] with part of the people of Maeonia to Italy.

This is also Tuscia, but we should not say *Tusciam*, because we nowhere read that form. Tuscia was named from the frequency of sacrifice and incense.

Gaul was named from the whiteness of its people. *Gala* in Greek means “milk.” Mountains and the severity of the climate exclude the sun’s heat from that region, with the result that the whiteness of the bodies is not colored.

To the east the ridges of the Alps protect it; to the west the Ocean encloses it; to the south the steep Pyrenees; and to the north the waters of the Rhine and Germany, whose beginning is Belgica.

Aquitania is a region with rich, pasture-bearing soil, suitable for the use of animals, and watered by rivers and springs. It is irrigated by two great rivers, the Rhine and the Rhône.

Belgis is a city of Gaul, from which the province was called Belgica. It is called Cisalpine because it lies on this side of the Alps, or Transalpine—that is, beyond the Alps, toward the north.

Rhaetia is a land that remains springlike in winter and summer. The sun there is mild, the climate pleasant, and the air pure and gentle. It was therefore named from being beside the Rhine.

Aquitania was named from the oblique waters of the river Loire, because for the greater part the river forms its boundary and almost surrounds it in a circle.

Spain was first called Iberia from the river Iberus. Later it was called Hispania after Hispalo. It is the true Hesperia, named after Hesperus, the western star. It lies between Africa and Gaul, closed on the north by the Pyrenees and on every other side surrounded by the sea. Its climate is temperate; it is fertile in every kind of fruit and exceedingly rich in gems and metals.

Great rivers flow through it: the Baetis, the Minius, the Iberus, and the Tagus, which carries gold like the Pactolus.

It has six provinces: Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Baetica, and, across the straits in the region of Africa, Tingitania.

There are two Spains: Citerior, which extends in the northern region from the Pyrenees to Carthage; and Ulterior, which extends southward from Celtiberia to the Strait of Gades. They are called Citerior and Ulterior, as though “on this side” and “beyond”; or *circa*, as though “on this side of the lands,” and “beyond”; or because one is the last, or because there is no other land after it.

Let this suffice concerning the regions of Europe. Now let us speak briefly about the parts of Africa.

Libya was so called because *Libs*—that is, the southwest wind—blows from there. Others say that Epaphus, son of Jupiter, who founded Memphis in Egypt, fathered by his wife Cassiope a daughter named Libya; she later possessed a kingdom in Africa, and from her name that land was called Libya.

Some think Africa was named as though *aprica*, because it is open to the sky and sun and free from the terror of cold. Others say that Africa was named after one of the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, who was called Afer, of whom we spoke above.

It begins at the borders of Egypt and extends southward through Ethiopia as far as Mount Atlas. On the north it is joined to and enclosed by the Mediterranean Sea and ends at the Strait of Gades. Its provinces are Libya Cyrenaica, Pentapolis, Tripolis, Byzacium, Carthage, Numidia, Mauretania Sitifensis, Mauretania Tingitana, and, around the sun’s heat, Ethiopia.

Libya Cyrenaica is the first part of Africa. It was named after the metropolitan city of Cyrene, which lies within its borders. Egypt is to its east; the Greater Syrtes and the Trogodytes to its west; the Libyan Sea to the north; and Ethiopia, various barbarian nations, and inaccessible deserts to the south. These deserts also produce basilisk serpents.

Pentapolis was named in Greek from its five cities: Cyrene, Berenice of Ceutria, Apollonia, and Ptolemais. Ptolemais and Berenice were named after kings. Pentapolis is joined to Libya Cyrenaica and assigned to its borders.

The province of Tripolis is likewise designated by the Greeks according to the number of its three great cities: Oea, Sabrata, and Leptis Magna. To the east it has the Greater Syrtes and the Trogodytes; to the north, the Adriatic Sea; to the west, Byzacium; and to the south it extends to the Getuli and Garamantes as far as the Ethiopian Ocean.

The region of Byzacium received its name from two most distinguished towns, one of which is called Hadrumetum. It lies below Tripolis, extending for two hundred thousand paces or more. It is fertile in olives, and its soil is so exceedingly rich that seeds cast there grow again with almost a hundredfold increase of grain.

Zeugis, where great Carthage is located, is itself true Africa. It lies between Byzacium and Numidia, joined on the north to the Sicilian Sea and extending southward as far as the region of the Getuli. Its nearer parts are fertile in every respect, while the farther parts are full of wild beasts and serpents, as well as great wild asses wandering in the desert.

Getulia is the Mediterranean part of Africa.

Numidia was so called by its inhabitants, who wandered here and there because they had no fixed dwelling. For in their language “uncertain and wandering dwellings” are called *Numidia*. It begins at the river Ampsaga and ends at the boundary of Zeugis. To the east it has the Lesser Syrtes; to the north, the sea extending toward Sardinia; to the west, Mauretania Sitifensis; and to the south, the peoples of Ethiopia.

It is a region extremely rich in plains; where it is wooded, it raises wild beasts; where it is steep with mountain ridges, it produces horses and wild asses. It also possesses an excellent marble called Numidian marble. Its chief cities are Hippo Regius and Rusicada.

Mauretania was named from the color of its peoples. The Greeks call black *mauron*. Just as Gaul received its name from the whiteness of its people, so Mauretania received its name from blackness.

Its first province is Mauretania Sitifensis, which contains the town of Sitifis, from which the region is said to have derived its name. Mauretania Caesariensis was a colony; Caesarea was a city, and the province received its name from it.

Both provinces, therefore, joined together, have Numidia to the east, the Great Sea to the north, the river Muluccha to the west, and Mount Astrix to the south. The mountain separates the fertile land from the sands extending as far as the Ocean.

Mauretania Tingitana was named after Tingis, the metropolitan city of the province. This is the farthest part of Africa. It rises from seven mountains and has the river Muluccha to the east, the Strait of Gades to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west, and to the south the Gaetulian peoples, who wander as far as the Hesperian Ocean.

It is a region that produces the fiercest dragons and ostriches. Formerly it was also full of elephants, which now only India produces.

The chief town of the Garamantian region was Garama. It lies between Cyrenaica and Ethiopia. There is a spring there which grows cold in the heat of day and becomes warm in the cold of night.

Ethiopia was named from the color of its peoples, whom the nearness of the sun scorches. Indeed, the power of the stars is revealed by the color of human beings. There is perpetual heat there. For all of it lies beneath the meridian axis. Toward the west it is mountainous; in the middle, sandy; and toward the east, desert. Its territory extends from the western side of Mount Atlas eastward as far as the borders of Egypt.

It is bounded on the south by the Ocean and on the north by the river Nile. It has very many peoples, terrifying in their varied faces and monstrous appearance, and is also filled with a multitude of wild beasts and serpents. There are the rhinoceros and camelopard, the basilisk, and enormous dragons, from whose brains gems are extracted. Hyacinth and chrysoprase are also found there, and cinnamon is gathered there.

There are two Ethiopias: one around the rising of the sun, the other around its setting, in Mauretania.

Beyond the three parts of the world there is a fourth part, interior and across the Ocean, in the south. It is unknown to us because of the sun’s heat; at its borders, the Antipodes are fabulously said to live.

Nearest to Spain is Mauretania, then Numidia, then Carthaginensis; after this we come to Getulia, afterward Ethiopia, and then the regions scorched by the sun’s heat.

It should certainly be known that some provinces were first named after their founder, and afterward the name of the province was given to the people. Thus from Italus came Italia, and again from Italia came Italus; and so we use the name of the people in the same form as the name of the founder from whom the name of the province was derived.

Hence it happens that from one man a city, a region, and a people are named.

The provinces received their names from their circumstances. For when the territories of peoples had belonged to various kings, and the Romans, by conquering, reduced them under their own authority, they called the distant regions provinces.

A homeland (*patria*) is so called because it is common to all who are born in it.

“Land” (*terra*), as we said above, signifies the element; “lands” signify individual parts, such as Africa and Italy, and likewise particular places. For places and stretches of land throughout the world contain many provinces within themselves. Just as in a body one place is a single part containing many limbs, and just as a house contains many rooms, so lands and places are called stretches whose parts are provinces.

Thus in Asia there is Phrygia; in Europe, Gaul and Rhaetia; in Spain, Baetica. Asia is a place; Phrygia is a province of Asia; Troy is a region of Phrygia; Ilium is a city of Troy.

Likewise, regions are parts of provinces, which the common people call districts, as in Phrygia, Troy; and in Gallaecia, Cantabria and Asturias.

A region (*regio*) was named after its rulers. Its parts are territories. A territory (*territorium*) was so called as though *tauritorium*, “land trampled by oxen and the plow.” For the ancients marked the boundaries of possessions and territories by drawing a furrow.

## Chapter V. On the Islands
Islands are so called because they are in the open sea, that is, situated in the sea. In many passages of Holy Scripture they signify either the Churches of Christ or, more particularly, certain holy men who are battered by the waves of persecution but are not destroyed, because they are protected by God. For it is written in the Psalter: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad” (Ps. 96). Since, therefore, the Lord reigns throughout the whole world, the Churches established everywhere rejoice. They are rightly compared with islands, because, surrounded by the waves of the world, they are battered by the multitude of persecutions barking around them. Yet, just as these islands are not harmed by raging waves, so the holy Churches are proved not to be exempt from the disturbances of their adversaries; rather, they shatter upon their own rocks those who rush against them with billowing crests.

Observe also that he says “many,” not “all,” because of heretical perversities, which impose the name of Churches upon their errors.

Likewise, an island signifies the Jewish people, as in Ezekiel: “Son of man, speak to the inhabitants of the island” (Ezek. 39).

There are very many islands called by their proper names, but their names are found recorded in only a few passages of Holy Scripture. [Col. 0354A] Therefore, we do not believe that it is necessary in this work to seek out all their names. Nevertheless, we do not hesitate here to set down the etymologies of some of them according to the tradition of our predecessors, since perhaps it will please the reader to find something of this sort stated in our little work, and thus to have material from which, wherever it seems appropriate, he may transfer their meanings to spiritual understanding.

Chios is an island before Bithynia, which some now call Chia.

Gindus is an island opposite Asia; its name is interpreted as “ecstasy of the mind.”

Miciliae is an island opposite Asia, seven miles away. Its name is interpreted as “from infirmity,” or “a command of humility.”

Samothrace is an island in the gulf of Pathmos.

Britain is an island of the Ocean, separated from the whole world by the intervening sea and named from the designation of its people. [Col. 0354B] It lies opposite Gaul, toward the view of Spain. Its circuit is forty-eight times seventy-five thousand paces. It has many large rivers, hot springs, and a rich and varied abundance of metals; jet is found there in great quantities, as are also pearls.

Thanatos is an island of the Ocean, separated from Britain by the strait of Gaul. It has grain-producing fields and exceedingly fertile soil. It is called Thanatos from the death of serpents: although it itself has none, earth carried from it and brought to other lands immediately kills snakes.

Thule is the last island of the Ocean, between the northern and western regions, beyond Britain. It takes its name from the sun, because, as some say, the sun produces the summer solstice there, and beyond it there is no daylight. Hence its sea is sluggish and congealed.

The Orcades are islands of the Ocean beyond Britain, numbering thirty-three. Twenty of them are deserted, while thirteen are inhabited.

Scotland, also called Hibernia, is an island near Britain. It is narrower in extent of land but more fertile in situation. It stretches from the southwest toward the north. Its front parts face Iberia and the Cantabrian Ocean; hence it is called Hibernia. It is called Scotland because it is inhabited by the peoples of the Scots. There are no snakes there, few birds, and no bees, to such an extent that if anyone scatters imported dust or pebbles from that island elsewhere among beehives, the swarms abandon their honeycombs.

Gades is an island situated at the end of the province of Baetica. It separates Europe from Africa; the Pillars of Hercules are seen there, and from there the tide of the Ocean enters through the mouths of the Tyrrhenian Sea. It is separated from the mainland by one hundred and twenty paces. The Tyrians, coming from the Red Sea, occupied it and called it Gadir in their language, that is, “enclosure,” because it is enclosed by the sea. A tree grows there resembling a palm, whose gum, when used to stain glass, produces the gemstone called “thunderstone.”

The Fortunate Islands, by their name, signify that they bear every good thing, as though happy and blessed in the abundance of their fruits. By their own nature they produce the apples of precious forests; their hilltops are clothed with vines that grow spontaneously; and, in place of herbs, the common vegetation consists of grain and vegetables. Hence the error of the pagans and the poems of secular poets, because of the fertility of their soil, have imagined that these islands are paradise. They lie in the Ocean opposite the left side of Mauritania, near the far west, separated from one another by intervening sea.

The Gorgades are islands of the Ocean opposite the promontory called Hesperuceras. They were inhabited by Gorgons, women swift as birds, with hairy and rough bodies; the islands were named from them. They are two days’ sailing from the mainland.

The Hesperides Islands were named from the city Hesperis, which was at the end of Mauritania. They lie beyond the Gorgades beneath the Atlantic shore, in the innermost recesses of the sea. In their gardens, fables imagine a sleepless dragon guarding golden apples. It is said, however, that there is a tidal sea there, so twisted by its billowing sides that, to those viewing it from a distance, its movement resembles the winding of a snake.

Chryse and Argyre are islands situated in the Indian Ocean. They are so fertile in their abundance of metals that many have reported that they possess a golden surface and a silver one; hence they received their names.

Taprobane is an island beneath India toward the east wind, from which the Indian Ocean begins. It extends 875,000 paces in length and 625,000 stadia in breadth. A river flowing through it divides it, and the whole island is filled with pearls and gems. One part is filled with wild animals and elephants, while human beings inhabit the other. They say that on this island there are two summers and two winters in a single year, and that spring flowers twice.

Tylos is an island of India that bears leaves throughout the entire year.

Thus far, the islands of the Ocean.

There are also the islands situated in the Great Sea from the Hellespont to Gades.

Cyprus received its name from the city of Cyprus, which is on the island. On it is Paphos, consecrated to Venus, in the Carpathian Sea, near the south wind. It was once famous for its wealth, especially for its copper, since the first discovery and use of this metal took place there. Its name is interpreted as “sad” or “grief.”

Crete is an island of Greece, with one part extending toward the Peloponnese. It was first called Macaronesus because of the temperateness of its climate; afterward it was called Crete, after a certain native named Crete, who is said to have been one of the Curetes, among whom Jupiter was hidden and brought up. It is an island of Greece, stretching in a very long tract between east and west. To the north it is washed by the waters of Greece, and to the south by Egyptian waters. It was once famous for its hundred cities, whence it was also called Hecatompolis. It was the first to become renowned for oars and arrows; the first to establish laws in writing; and the first to teach cavalry formations. The practice of music began there with the Idaean Dactyls. It is rich in goats but poor in deer; it produces no wolves, foxes, or other harmful wild beasts anywhere; there are no snakes or owls there, and if they are brought in, they die immediately. It is rich in vines and trees. The herb dittany grows in Crete, as does alimos, which, when chewed, prevents hunger for a day. It also produces venomous phalangia and the stone called the Idaean dactyl. The term for this island, however, is intermediate between Syrian and Hebrew.

Abydos is an island in Europe, situated above the Hellespont and separated from it by a narrow and dangerous sea. It is called Abydos in Greek because it is the entrance to the Hellespont, where Xerxes built a bridge of ships and crossed into Greece.

Cos is an island adjoining the province of Attica, where the physician Hippocrates was born. As Varro testifies, it first became famous in the art of weaving for women’s adornment. Its name is interpreted as “shaking off” or “awaiting.”

The Cyclades were formerly islands of Greece. They are thought to have been called Cyclades because, although they extend in a wide circuit from Delos, they are situated around Delos; for the Greeks call a circle kyklos. Others think that they were called Cyclades not because they were arranged in a circle, but because of the reefs situated around the same island. They lie toward the Hellespont, between the Aegean and Malean Seas, and are also surrounded by the Myrtoan Sea. Their total number is fifty-three. They extend 500,000 paces from north to south and 200,000 from east to west. Their chief city is Rhodes.

Delos lies in the middle of the Cyclades. It is said to have been called Delos because, after the flood remembered as having occurred in the time of Ogyges, when continuous night had overshadowed the world for many months, it was illuminated by the sun’s rays before all other lands. It received its name from this circumstance, because it had first been made visible to human eyes; for delon in Greek means “manifest.” It is also called Ortygia because quails were first seen there; the Greeks call quails ortygas. On this island Latona gave birth to Apollo and Diana. Delos is the name both of a city and of an island.

Rhodes is the first island of the Cyclades from the east. It is said that a rose was discovered there while a city was being founded; from this the city and island were called Rhodes. In this city stood the bronze Colossus of the Sun, seventy cubits high. There were also one hundred other smaller colossi on the same island.

Tenedos is one of the Cyclades, situated to the north. A city was once founded there by a certain Tene, from whom the city—and more properly the island—received its name. [Col. 0356C] This Tenes was disgraced because he had intercourse with his stepmother. Fleeing to the island, he took possession of it, since it had no inhabitants; hence it was called Tenedos. Thus Cicero says: “They hold him himself, from whose name Tenedos is named.”

Carpathos is one of the Cyclades, situated to the south toward Egypt. The Carpathian Sea was named from it. It received its name because its fruits ripen quickly. It lies between Egypt and Rhodes. Large and spacious ships are also called Carpathian ships from this island.

Cythera is one of the Cyclades, situated on the western side. Its earlier name was Porphyris. It was called Cythera because Venus was born there.

Icaria is one of the Cyclades and gave its name to the Icarius Sea. It is inhospitable, with projecting rocks between Samos and Myconos, and has no bays suitable for harbors. It is said that the Cretan Icarus perished there in a shipwreck, and that the place received its name from the man’s fate.

Naxos, formerly called Dionysias, as though Dionaxos, surpasses the other islands in the fertility of its vines. It is eighteen miles from Delos. From it Jupiter is once said to have set out against the Titans.

Melos is one of the Cyclades and the roundest of all the islands; hence it received its name. History says that Philomelus was born of Jason, and that Plutus—“Pareantum” is uncertain in the transmitted text—was begotten of Philomelus; he called the island and town Paron after his own name. It was first called Minoia, then Paron; concerning it Virgil writes, “and snowy Paros,” for it produces the whitest marble, which is called Parian. It also produces sardonyx, a stone superior to marbles but the least valuable among gems.

Chios is called in the Syrian language by a name meaning “mastix,” because it produces mastic. For the Syrians call mastic chios.

Samos is an island in the Aegean Sea, where Juno was born. From it came the Samian Sibyl and Pythagoras of Samos, from whom the name of philosophy is said to have been derived. It is said that earthen vessels were first discovered on this island; hence such vessels were called Samian.

Sicily was named Sicania after King Sicanus; afterward it was called Sicily after Siculus, the brother of Italus. It was formerly called Trinacria because of its three promontories: Pelorus, Pachynus, and Lilybaeum. Trinacria is a Greek word, corresponding in Latin to “three-cornered,” as though divided into three sections. It is separated from Italy by a narrow strait and looks toward the African Sea. Its soil is fertile in crops and rich in gold, yet it is penetrable by caves and channels and full of winds and sulphur. Hence Mount Etna burns there; and in its strait are Scylla and Charybdis, by which ships are either swallowed up or dashed to pieces. It was once the homeland of the Cyclopes and afterward the nurse of tyrants. It is fertile in grain and was the first land in the world to be broken by the plow after seed had been entrusted to the soil.

Its chief city is Syracuse. It has the spring Arethusa and the river Alpheus, producer of great horses. Comedy was first invented on this island. It first produced the agate stone from the river Achates. Its sea also produces coral; it produces Agrigentine salts, which dissolve in fire and crackle in water. Its entire circumference measures 3,000 stadia.

Sallust says that Sicily was once joined to Italy, but that the intervening space was divided by the force of the sea and split through a narrow passage.

Tapsus is an island ten stadia from Sicily, lying low and level. Hence it received its name; Virgil writes, “and lying Tapsus.”

The Aeolian Islands, islands of Sicily, were named after Aeolus, son of Hippotas, whom poets imagined to have been king of the winds. But, as Varro says, he was the ruler of these islands; and because he predicted future winds from their mists and smoke, he seemed to the ignorant to hold the winds under his power. They are also called Aeolian or Vulcanian Islands, because, like Etna, they burn. There are nine, each with its own name. The first was called Lipara by a certain Liparus, who ruled it before Aeolus. The second is called Hiera because it has very high hills. The others are Strongyle, Didyme, Ericusa, Hephaestias, Phaenicusa, Evonimos, Ericodes, and Phaenicodes. Because some of them burn at night, they are called Aeolian or Vulcanian. Some of these did not exist at the beginning but later rose from the sea and have remained there to the present.

The Stoechades are islands belonging to the people of Massilia, sixty miles from the mainland, opposite the province of Narbonensis, where the Rhône River flows into the sea. They are called Stoechades in Greek, as though “standing in a row,” because they are arranged in order.

Sardus, the son of Hercules, came from Libya with a great multitude, occupied Sardinia, and gave the island its name. In the African Sea it projects eastward, broader toward the east than the west, resembling a human footprint, with nearly equal sides turned toward the south and north. Hence, before commerce, Greek sailors called it Ichnos, that is, “footprint.” The land extends 140 miles in length and forty in breadth. Neither snakes nor wolves are produced there; only the solifuga, a small creature harmful to human beings. No poison grows there except a plant mentioned by many writers and poets, resembling wild marjoram, which contracts the mouths of human beings and kills them as though laughing. Sardinia has hot springs that bring healing to the sick; they also bring blindness to thieves if, after taking an oath, they touch their eyes with the waters.

The inhabitants of Corsica gave the island its beginning, naming it after their leader. A Ligurian woman named Corsa once saw a bull from the herd she tended near the shore regularly swim across and return after intervals, its body having grown larger. Wishing to learn what unfamiliar pasture it was seeking, she followed the bull in a boat as it departed from the others and continued to the island. When the Ligurians learned from her return about the fertility of the island, they sailed there on rafts and named it after the woman who had been its discoverer and leader. In Greek the island is called Cyrne, after Cyrnus, the son of Hercules, who inhabited it. Virgil refers to it as “Cyrnean yews.” It is separated from Sardinia by a strait of twenty miles and surrounded by the gulf of the Ligurian Sea, facing Italy. It is angular, with many promontories, and produces very rich pasture and a stone that the Greeks call cathochites.

Ebusus is an island of Spain. It is called this because it lies not far from Zanio, as though “Ebozos.” It is seventy stadia from that place, and snakes flee from its soil. Opposite it lies Colubraria, which is full of snakes.

The Balearic Islands are two islands of Spain: Aphrosiades and Gymnasiae, the larger and the smaller. Hence the common people called them Majorca and Minorca. Slings, by which stones are hurled, were first invented on these islands. Hence they were called Balearic; for ballein in Greek means “to hurl.” Thus come ballista, as though “something hurled,” and fundibulum. Virgil writes: “with the lash of a Balearic sling.”

## CHAPTER VI. On Promontories

It is common to islands that they project outward, and their projecting places are called promontories. Thus Sallust writes of Sardinia: “It projects more broadly toward the east than toward the west.”

The promontory of Sigeum is in Asia, where the Hellespont widens more openly. It was called Sigeum because of the silence of Hercules: when he was denied hospitality by Laomedon, king of the Trojans, he pretended to withdraw and then came silently against Troy. This is expressed by the word sige, “silence.”

Malea is a promontory of Greece that enters the sea and extends for fifty miles. The waves there are so violent that they seem to pursue sailors. The promontory received its name from Maleus, king of the Argives.

Pelorus is a promontory of Sicily facing north. According to Sallust, it was named after the helmsman of Hannibal, who was buried there.

Pachynus is a promontory of Sicily facing south. It was named from the thickness of the air, for pachus means “fat” or “thick.” It is swept by the south wind.

Lilybaeum is a promontory of Sicily facing the setting sun. It was named after the city of the same name situated there.

Borion is a promontory of Numidia. It received this name because it faces the north wind.

Hippo Rhegium was later so called because it is interrupted by the level sea.

Calpe is a promontory of Spain.

Promontories, which stand upon the summits of islands and provide them with protection against the waves of the sea, can, according to allegory, represent holy teachers who preside over the Churches of God and strengthen and encourage them amid the waves of persecutions, so that they may not be overwhelmed by the storm of tempests and the flooding of waves.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0359]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Mountains

[Col. 0359A]

Mountains are swellings of the earth. They are called “very high” because they rise above the surrounding land. Some, however, have been named from particular causes; among these we should note those most celebrated in common opinion.

Mount Caucasus extends from India to Taurus. According to the variety of peoples and languages, it is called by different names wherever it runs. Where it rises in the east to a loftier height, it is called Caucasus because of the whiteness of its snows. For in the eastern language caucasus means “white,” that is, shining white with very dense snow. Hence the Scythians who adjoin the same mountain called it Croacasis. Among them casim means “whiteness” or “snow.”

Mount Taurus is also called Caucasus by many.

Mount Ararat is in Armenia. Historians testify that the ark came to rest there after the flood. Hence traces of its timbers are still seen there to this day. Ararat is interpreted as “descending from a watchtower.”

The mountain of the Moabites is the mountain to which Balak, son of Sephor, brings Balaam the diviner to curse Israel (Num. 22). Its summit, because of its steep precipice, is called “the Cut,” and it overlooks the Dead Sea not far from the Arnon.

Fogor, or Bethfogor, is a mountain of the Moabites to which King Balak brings Balaam the soothsayer, on the ridge of Libiad. Another village, Sodor, can also be seen not far from Bethlehem; it is now called Faor.

Abarim is the mountain on which Moses died. It is said to be Mount Nebo in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, above the Jordan, on the ridge of Pisgah. It is shown to those ascending from Libiad toward Herbum, still retaining its ancient name beside Mount Fogor; the surrounding region is still called Pisgah from it.

Abarim is interpreted as “in the crossing,” which can signify the end of the law, since Moses, the giver of the law, was placed upon that mountain of virtues and passed from this life. The Israelite people could not cross the Jordan and enter the promised land through Moses; this was accomplished through the leadership of Jesus—that is, our Savior—who brings his faithful from the desert of this world through the sacrament of Baptism into the land of the living and the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Hermon is a mountain of the Amorites. It is said of it that the Phoenicians call it Sanior, while the Amorite called it Sanir. A notable temple is said to stand on its summit, held in pagan worship, in the region of Paneas and Lebanon. The land of the children of Israel beyond the Jordan, from the rising of the sun, extends from the steep slopes of the Arnon to Mount Hermon.

Hermon is interpreted as “anathema” or “sadness.” It signifies the worship of idols and the pride of arrogance, which is rightly called anathema, because every fellowship and association with it is forbidden to holy and faithful men, since, according to the Apostle, “there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Belial” (2 Cor. 6).

Catachryseia, that is, “toward the breeze.” These are mountains rich in gold in the desert, far from the stations of Coreb. Moses is said to have written Deuteronomy near them. Because a bronze temple, which in our time has collapsed, stood there, they judge that the neighboring mountains are full of veins of gold.

Mount Choreb is the mountain of God in the region of Midian, near Mount Sinai, above Arabia, in the desert. Joined to it are the mountain and desert of the Saracens, which they call Faran. It seems to me that the same mountain is called by two names, now Sinai and now Choreb.

Choreb is interpreted as “bald,” “dryness,” or “solitude”; Sinai as “temptation,” “red,” or “my amphora.” There Moses received the law and wrote, at the Lord’s command, a rule of life for the inexperienced people. Yet the temptation of the faithless was not absent there, nor did the shedding of blood entirely cease.

Mount Galaad is the mountain to which Jacob, a fugitive, came on the seventh day of his journey. It is joined at the rear to Phoenicia and Arabia by the hills of Lebanon and extends through the desert. As far as that place beyond the Jordan, a certain Seon, king of the Amorites, dwelt. The aforementioned mountain fell by lot to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh.

Jeremiah also says: “Galaad, you are to me the beginning of Lebanon” (Jer. 22). From this mountain the city founded upon it also received its name; Galaad, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, captured it from the hand of the Amorites.

Galaad, interpreted as “heap of testimony” and “migration of testimony,” signifies Holy Scripture, in which the covenant and agreement between God and human beings are read as established. In it, too, the reconciliation of the human race with the Lord through Christ is proclaimed.

There is also a Mount Galaad in the desert, where the children of Israel pitched their camp.

Mount Gebal is in the promised land, where an altar was constructed at Moses’ command. Near Jericho there are two neighboring mountains facing one another; one is called Garizim and the other Gebal. The Samaritans, however, think that these two mountains are near Neapolis, but they are seriously mistaken. They are very far from one another, and the voices of those blessing or cursing could not possibly be heard by each other, as Scripture records.

Gebal is interpreted as “ancient abyss.” Mount Garizim is the mountain upon which the wicked stood; curses resounded beside the aforementioned Mount Gebal. Garizim is interpreted as “division” or “cutting off.”

Who, then, are those who walk beside Mount Garizim, and who are those who walk beside Mount Gebal? Those who walk in this place beside Mount Garizim, chosen to bless, figuratively indicate those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise. Those half who walk beside Mount Gebal, where the curses were pronounced, indicate those who fulfill what is written in the law not from love of blessings or promises but from fear of future punishments, so that they may attain salvation.

All of them walk around the ark, for they do not withdraw from the bosom of the Church. Yet we know that those are nobler who do what is good out of desire for goodness itself and love of eternal blessing than those who pursue good because they fear evil.

Mount Olivet lies east of Jerusalem, and Jesus taught his disciples there. This mountain signifies the height of virtues and spiritual graces distributed to the faithful as gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Naban, called Nabo in Hebrew, is a mountain above the Jordan opposite Jericho, in the land of Moab, where Moses died. To this day it is shown six miles from the city of Esbus, toward the east. Naban is therefore interpreted as “at the conclusion,” and signifies the end of the law, just as does the death of Moses, because, according to the Apostle, “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

Or is the mountain on which Aaron died, near the city of Petra, where to the present day the rock is shown that Moses struck and from which he gave water to the people. Or is interpreted as “anger,” and rightly so, because there, on account of the doubt of Moses and Aaron in bringing forth water from the rock, they were forbidden to bring the children of Israel into the promised land.

Mount Gaas is in the tribe of Ephraim. On its northern side Jesus, son of Nun, was buried, and to this day his notable tomb is shown near the village of Thamnas.

Mount Seir is in the land of Edom, where Esau lived in the region of Gebalene. Because Esau was hairy and shaggy, that region received the name Seir, that is, “hairy.” The Horites had previously lived in those places; Chodor-laomor killed them. Isaiah also mentions Mount Seir in his vision of Idumea.

What Seir, interpreted as “hairy” or “shaggy,” signifies can easily be recognized by anyone who reads and correctly understands the history of Jacob and Esau. Jacob, the simple man, signifies the simplicity of the Church; Esau, hairy and shaggy, represents the Jews and heretics, filthy and foul with the bristles of their vices.

Baal Hermon is a mountain near Lebanon, on the borders of the Philistines.

The mountains of Gilboa belong to foreigners and lie at the sixth milestone from Scythopolis. There is also a large village there called Gelbus. Saul and Jonathan fell on these mountains, and for this David cursed them, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you,” and so forth (2 Sam. 1).

What, then, had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong when Saul died, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them, and the word of the sentence should dry them of every green growth? [Col. 0362A] Since, however, Gilboa is interpreted as “a flowing down,” and through Saul, the anointed one, his death expresses the death of our Mediator, the mountains of Gilboa rightly signify the proud hearts of the Jews. While these flow downward into the desires of this world, they became involved in the death of Christ, that is, of the Anointed One. Because the anointed King died bodily among them, they themselves are dried of every kind of dew.

Thabor and Hermon are mountains of the province of Syria, whose names bring forth great mysteries.

Thabor means “coming light,” and specially signifies the coming of the Lord Savior, concerning whom it is said: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1).

Hermon signifies “his anathema,” that is, the anathema of the devil, which the devil received from Christians when the Lord came. For it was fitting that the dark devil should be overcome by the present light.
