Therefore these will rejoice in the name of the Lord, as the faithful say elsewhere: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113).

Lebanon is the highest mountain of the Phoenicians, remembered by the prophets. It is called from incense, because incense is gathered there. The part of it lying above it and facing east is called Antilebanon, that is, “opposite Lebanon.”

Lebanon can signify the holy Church, cleansed from sins by sacred Baptism and whitened by the brightness of virtues. Hence it is said in the psalm: “All the trees of the forest and the cedars of Lebanon, which you planted, will be satisfied” (Ps. 103). The trees of the forest signify the peoples of great nations who have come to the Catholic Church from thorny and uncultivated peoples. These trees indicate people of ordinary station; the cedars of Lebanon, however, signify the noble and powerful, who are known to rise above the human race like cedars.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.” The power of this world seems to be a kind of celebration, where rich and powerful people, lofty and tall, are born as though on Mount Lebanon. Yet they have reached true religion through the gift of the Lord.

Mount Sophim is in Ephraim, in the region of Ramathaim. Sophim is interpreted as “watchtower” or “crag,” and signifies the summit of perfection. Hence it is read in the Book of Kings that there was a certain man from Ramathaim Sophim, from Mount Ephraim—that is, in the lofty contemplation of virtues—so that the height of his mind might not be cast down or its unity divided by any thoughts lying beneath or barking around it.

Mount Sion is situated in the southern part of the city of Jerusalem and rises above the city. Hence Sion is interpreted as “mirror” or “contemplation.” It signifies the holy Church, which with a pure heart and simple intention contemplates the vision of heavenly peace and beholds God himself, who rules and reigns above all things.

Mount Sinai is in the region of Midian, above Arabia, in the desert. Concerning it the Apostle writes: “Mount Sinai is in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now is, and is in bondage with her children” (Gal. 4). It signifies the carnal synagogue of the Jews, holding to observance of the law, which the Apostle compared with Hagar, Sarah’s slave woman.

There are also other notable mountains mentioned only in the histories of the pagans. It will be sufficient to recall their names here together with their etymologies.

The Acroceraunian Mountains were named for their height and the strikes of lightning. For in Greek ceraunos means “thunderbolt.” They lie between Armenia and Iberia, beginning at the Caspian Gates and extending to the source of the Tigris River.

The Hyperborean Mountains of Scythia were so called because Boreas blows above them, that is, beyond them.

The Riphaean Mountains are in the upper part of Germany and were named from the perpetual blowing of winds. For in Greek riphe means “rush” or “impulse.”

Mount Olympus in Macedonia is exceedingly lofty, so that clouds are said to be beneath it. Concerning it Virgil writes:

> “Olympus surpassed the clouds.”

It was called Olympus, as though *ololampus*, that is, “as if heaven.” This mountain divides Macedonia from Thrace.

Mount Athos is in Macedonia. It too is higher than the clouds and so lofty that its shadow reaches Lemnos, which is seventy-six thousand paces away.

Mount Parnassus is in Thessaly near Boeotia. It rises toward heaven with a double summit and divides into two ridges, Cyrrha and Nissa. It received its name because Apollo and Liber were worshiped on its separate ridges. These ridges are called after two brothers, Cithaeron and Helicon; Helicon was named after Helicon, the brother of Cithaeron.

The Apennine Mountains were called, as it were, the Poenine Alps, because Hannibal, when coming to Italy, opened those same Alps. Hence Virgil writes:

> “He will let the Alps be entered, opened.”

For after the wars in Spain Hannibal broke through them with vinegar. Juvenal writes:

> “And he broke the mountain with vinegar.”

From this the places he broke through are called the Apennine Alps.

Mount Etna was named from fire and sulphur, and hence also gave rise to the name Gehenna. On the side from which the east and southwest winds blow, it has caves full of sulphur, extending as far as the sea. These caves receive the waves into themselves and create wind; when the wind is agitated, it creates fire from the sulphur. Hence the appearance of a blaze.

The Pyrenees were likewise named from their frequent fires of lightning; for in Greek pyr means “fire.” This is the range that lies between Gaul and Spain like a deliberately placed barrier.

Solorius is so called from its singularity, because it alone among the mountains of Spain appears higher than all the others.

Mount Calpe is at the farthest limits of the Ocean. It separates Europe from Africa and is said to be the end of Atlas. Concerning it Lucan writes:

> “Calpe of Hesperia, and it filled the highest Atlas.”

Atlas was the brother of Prometheus and king of Africa. They say that he first devised the art of astrology, and for that reason he was said to support the heavens. Thus, because of his learning in that discipline and his knowledge of the heavens, his name was transferred to a mountain in Africa, which is now called Atlas and which, because of its height, seems to support the heavens and the stars like a mechanism [Col. 0364A]. Sometimes he signifies the Lord Savior; sometimes the holy Church; sometimes the apostles and prophets, or holy men, on account of the loftiness of their virtues. Conversely, he sometimes represents proud and inflated people in the power of worldly rule; sometimes heretics; and sometimes the devil himself.

For a mountain signifies the Lord Savior in prophecy, where it says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it will be lifted above the hills, and all nations will go to it,” and so forth (Isa. 2). A mountain signifies the Church where the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they will not be shaken forever” (Ps. 124). And again: “Like the dew,” he says, “of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132). Zion, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” signifies the Church, as we have said, upon which the abundance of divine grace descends, and which God daily beholds: “For there God, the God of gods, will be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83).

Hermon is the Hebrew name of a mountain situated beyond the Jordan River; its interpretation, as stated above, signifies “anathema” or “that which is devoted to destruction.” Therefore, the dew of this mountain, nourishing sinners who have lain under the arousal of the anathema, descends upon Mount Zion when, by the Lord’s gift, they attain the remedy of conversion. For Zion signifies the catholic Church, which receives the nations that had been placed under the danger of anathema.

The mountains signify the apostles and prophets, where it is said: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103). The deer are the faithful, who leap over the vices of this age like thorns through good conduct and dwell in the mountains—that is, in the apostles and prophets—who by their holy preaching have deserved to be solid peaks in the world.

Likewise, mountains signify holy men or the divine books in that passage of the Psalmist where he says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Ps. 120). If you seek this spiritually, it is entirely profitable to believe that he lifted the eyes of his heart either toward holy men, or toward the divine books, or toward the exalted angels, who in their greatness and firmness are truly mountains. Hence also the appropriate help was understood to be given.

The mountain is the Jewish people, concerning which Daniel says: “A stone was cut out without hands” (Dan. 2)—that is, Christ, conceived without male seed—and by his faith he filled the whole world [Col. 0364D].

They draw the meaning of mountains in the opposite direction as well. Hence it is written: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 96). Here the mountains signify people who both pursue the heights of this world and grow hard through senseless superstition. They are wonderfully compared with melting wax, because they flow into repentance all the more readily the more firmly they had believed themselves immovable in their hardness.

Mountains signify the rich and the powers of this world, as in Job it is said concerning the devil: “The mountains bear herbs for him” (Job 40), which means the vices of the flesh.

The mountain signifies the devil because of his swelling pride, as in Isaiah: “Raise up a sign over the dark mountain” (Isa. 13). And in Jeremiah: “Behold, I am against you, pestilential mountain” (Jer. 51).

The mountain signifies the doctrine of heretics, as in the Prophet, in the person of the Church: “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee like a sparrow to the mountain’?” (Ps. 10).

Mountains signify demons, or heretics, or the scribes of the Jews. In Jeremiah: “Give glory to the Lord your God, before your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jer. 13). And in the Psalm: “As far as from the deserted mountains” [the text supplies: *Neque a*, “nor from,” in place of *Usque ad*] (Ps. 74).

The two mountains described in Zechariah as bronze (Zech. 6) signify the two Testaments of the Law, from between which the Lord’s chariot—that is, the preaching of the four Gospels—proceeds.

Thus mountains signify heretics where it is said: “Lest your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jer. 13). For the Prophet warns us to beware lest the steps of our works, stumbling against the proud teaching of heretics, fall into the darkness of error [Col. 0365B].

The mountain signifies the devil where it is written in the Apocalypse (Rev. 8) that a great mountain was thrown into a lake of burning fire and sulfur, because the devil’s defiance is condemned to eternal Gehenna.

The foundations of the mountains are the hopes of the proud. In the Psalm: “The foundations of the mountains were shaken” (Ps. 17).

## CHAPTER II. On Hills

Hills are the more prominent ridges of mountains, like necks. Mountain ridges are called *juga* because they are joined together by proximity. A mound is, as it were, swelling earth. A mound is also a heap of earth where there is no memorial.

Hills signify good people of lesser merit than mountains. They are people of moderate attainment, who nevertheless praise the Lord by good works, as the Prophet testifies, saying: “The mountains and hills sang praise before God” (Ps. 148).

A hill is also used in another sense, as in the Gospel: “Every mountain and hill will be humbled” (Luke 3).

The ridges of mountains are appropriately compared with the saints, who are joined and united to one another by brotherly love and, living in fellowship, reject every separation caused by schism.

## CHAPTER III. On Valleys

Valleys are low places, as though cut away from the earth, and *convalles* are depressed areas of land between mountains.

There are proper names for valleys, such as Aialon, a valley and precipitous place, above which, when Jesus once prayed, the moon stood beside a village that is still called Aialon, east of Bethel, three miles distant from it, near the cities of Agaba and Saul’s Rama. The Hebrews, however, assert that Aialon is a village near Nicopolis, at the second milestone for those traveling to Aelia.

Coelastitanorum—that is, “the valley of the giants”—was the place against whom David fought.

Codas, that is, the Valley of Jehoshaphat, lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; read the prophet Joel.

The Valley of Rephaim was the valley of the Philistines, on the northern side of Jerusalem.

A valley signifies contrition of heart and humility, as in the Psalm: “The valleys will abound with grain” (Ps. 64). The valleys signify humble peoples, because nothing is humbler than those who descend into a kind of hollow. Therefore these humble people abound in grain—that is, in spiritual teaching and the help of virtues—like that publican who did not dare to raise his eyes toward heaven and did not trust in any presumption of merits (Luke 18); he abounded in grain. Because he was a humble valley, he was raised up: for, by the Lord’s favor, he had cast himself down [Col. 0366A].

A valley is also used in another sense, as in the Prophet: “The valley of the sons of Hinnom” (Jer. 19), in which the punishment of Gehenna is expressed.

Valleys signify heretics, Jews, or sinners falling from the height of the Church, as in Isaiah: “The valley of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 10). And elsewhere: “The valley of the sons of Hinnom” (Jer. 19).

A valley signifies those humble in heart, concerning which the voice of Christ speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field” (Song 2), that is, the glory of the world; “and the lily of the valleys,” namely, the glory of the humble.

## CHAPTER IV. On Fields

[Col. 0366B]

A field is a level expanse of land. It is called a field because it is low underfoot, neither raised up like the mountains, but open and extended and lying out in its own breadth. Hence in Greek it is called *pedion*. It took its name from Greek etymology: for the Greeks call something short *chamai*.

The ground is everything that supports, and is so called from its solidity.

Under the name of fields, the divine Scriptures are sometimes signified, because they provide faithful souls with a suitable *pactum* [probably *pastum*, “nourishment”], as in the Psalm: “And your fields will be filled with abundance” (Ps. 64).

At other times a field signifies evenness and gentleness of character, as in the Psalmist: “The fields will rejoice, and everything in them” (Ps. 95). Here we should likewise understand fields in a good sense, because we call those things full which are stretched out in most beautiful evenness. Thus he calls fields men who excel in the praise of righteousness, not swollen with pride, not rough with anger, but perfectly level in gentle meekness.

The field is understood as the world because it is open. The Prophet Habakkuk says of it: “The word”—that is, the Son of God—“went forth and cast himself into the field.” And in the Psalm it is written: “As he set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Tanis.”

Tanis is a city of Egypt, where the wonders that are read about took place. The signs were certainly traces impressed upon the hard hearts of the Egyptians, as though by a seal. The wonders were, as it were, things speaking beforehand—that is, things prefiguring what was to come. For all those plagues occurred in ancient times with some symbolic significance. They were therefore rightly called signs and wonders, because what was done in Egypt was shown forth as such.

We said that Tanis is interpreted as “a humble command,” which is recognized as necessary and salutary for us in this age, where we ought to be humble and prostrate, always seeking the assistance of pardon.

The field is understood in the opposite sense when it signifies luxury in pleasures and the loosening of discipline, because the way that leads to life is narrow, while the way that leads to death is broad and spacious (Matt. 7).

## CHAPTER V. On Forests

[Col. 0367A]

Forests are vast and wooded places where trees spring upward to a great height.

A forest, or woodland, mystically signifies the barrenness of the nations. Hence the Psalmist says: “Then all the trees of the forest will exult before the face of the Lord, as he comes” (Ps. 95 [96]). Trees of the forest by themselves produce bitter and barren fruits; but once grafted, they grow fat with the sweetest abundance. Thus the nations, which previously had been like trees of the forest, when brought to fruitful cultivation, will rejoice with great gladness before the face of the Lord.

But when he says “all the trees,” he wishes that part to be understood which could be grafted into good works and changed.

The forest signifies the people of the Church, as in the Prophet: “Those who dwell in the wilderness will sleep securely in the forests” (Ezek. 34) [Col. 0367B].

The forest of the southern field signifies the Jewish people, as it is said in the Prophet Ezekiel concerning the forest of the southern field: “Behold, I will kindle in you a fire of life, and it will devour every green tree and every dry tree” (Ezek. 20).

## CHAPTER VI. On Places

Names of places are found in the divine books that are not without mystical significance. But we think it would be too long to explain what all of them signify typologically. Therefore we give only their names with a historical explanation, leaving the mystery of each for the discerning reader to investigate.

Aenam, on the road to Thamnam [Col. 0367C], is now a deserted place, near the large village of Thamna, situated between Aelia and Ospolis. There is also a spring in the place mentioned above, Ena. Hence Ena, that is, “spring,” received its name; an idol standing there is worshiped with the greatest veneration in that region.

The Hebrews, however, assert that Ena does not signify a place but a fork in the road, where one must carefully choose one of two roads. Ena is also interpreted as “their heart.”

Areatat is a place beyond the Jordan, where Jacob was once mourned, three milestones from Jericho and two thousand paces from the Jordan. It is now called Bethagla, which is interpreted as “place of a circle,” because there, according to the custom of mourners, they went around Jacob’s funeral procession.

Aelim was the camp of the children of Israel and a place in the wilderness where Moses, after departing from the Red Sea, found eleven springs and seventy palm trees [Col. 0367D]. For Elim is interpreted as “strong rams,” as is read in Exodus: “The children of Israel came to where there were twelve springs” (Exod. 15)—that is, the teaching of the apostles.

Aelus is in the wilderness, where the children of Israel camped. Aelus is also interpreted as “ferments,” or “mix.”

Aseroth is a part of the wilderness where Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses (Num. 12). The Hevites once lived at Aseroth as far as the city of Gaza. The Hebrews, however, think that these places were called not Aseroth but Aserim. Aseroth is interpreted as “courtyards” or “vestibules.”

Asemona was a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness. Asemona is interpreted as “his mouth,” from *os*, “bone,” and not from *os*, “mouth.”

Atheraim, for which Aquila and Symmachus translated “the way of the spies,” was where, in the wilderness, battle was fought against the Canaanite who had broken out from the south against Israel.

Areopolis was filled with garrisons of soldiers distributed on every side; they testify to an entrance full of blood and terror. It once belonged to the Moabites, and later Sihon, king of the Amorites, acquired it by right of war. The land of the children of Israel beyond the Jordan also begins at the Arnon and extends as far as Mount Hermon and Lebanon.

Ar is a place or town on the Arnon, called Er by the Seventy Translators with a lengthened vowel. Ar is interpreted as “he raised up,” or “watchfulness.”

Aesinion is a place in the wilderness; indeed, the word itself signifies uncultivated and deserted land.

Araboth of Moab is where the people were carefully numbered [possibly *sedulo*, “diligently,” rather than *saeculo*, “in the age”]. Aquila interprets it as “the lowlands” or “the level places of Moab.”

Abelsathim is a place in the wilderness south of the Moabites. It is interpreted as “mourning of the shores” or “of the banks.”

Beniacan is a camp of the children of Israel in the wilderness. Benacham is interpreted as “son of necessity.”

Beroth of the sons of Jachim is a place in the wilderness where Aaron died. It is still shown at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra, on Mount Urtica. Beroch is interpreted as “wells.”

Bonos, that is, “the hill of foreskins,” is a place at Gilgal where Jesus circumcised the people of Israel, at the second milestone from Jericho. The stones that were brought there from the Jordan, as Scripture records, are still shown today.

Bethdago is a place where the two tribes of Zebulun and Issachar share a boundary. Bethago is also interpreted as “their house of festivity.”

Chaspi is where Tamar gave birth to the twin sons of Judah. It is now shown as a deserted place near Adullam, in the territory of Eleutheropolis [Col. 0368C]. Chaspi is interpreted as “the immense *calio*” [reading uncertain], or “sacrifice to me.” This has been discussed more fully in the books of Hebrew Questions.

Emechachor is interpreted as “the Valley of Achor,” that is, “a mound and disturbance,” where Achan was crushed by stones because he had taken something from the anathema. It is a place near Jericho, not far from Gilgal.

Some therefore wrongly think that the Valley of Achor was named after the man who was stoned, whereas he was called Achan, not Achior or Achar.

Fanuel is the place where Jacob wrestled throughout the night and earned the name Israel, near the torrent of Jabbok. Fanuel is interpreted as “the face of God,” because there he saw the Lord.

Golgol and Galgal are near the place where Mounts Gerizim and Ebal are said to be. Galgal is a place near Jericho. Therefore the Samaritans are mistaken when they wish to show Mounts Gerizim and Ebal near Neapolis, since Scripture testifies that they are near Galgal. Galgal is interpreted as “revelation.”

Golathmaim is a place interpreted as “possession of water.”

Goliath is a place near the Jordan in the tribe of Benjamin, where the sons of Reuben established an altar to the Lord (Josh. 22). Goliath is interpreted as “revelation” or “migration.”

Iroth is a place in the wilderness to which the children of Israel came after crossing the Red Sea. Iroth is therefore interpreted as “length.”

Letabutha is a place in the wilderness where torrents of water are displayed.

Lobon is a place of solitude beyond the Jordan, where Moses is read to have written Deuteronomy [Col. 0369A]. Lobon is interpreted as “entrance” or “one who finds.”

Mirra or Mara, which is interpreted as “bitterness,” that is, the letter of the Law, is the place where Moses, after applying a piece of wood, turned the waters to a sweet taste. Hence it is read in Exodus: “The children of Israel came to Myrrha or Mara, and they could not drink the water of Myrrha or Mara because it was bitter” (Exod. 15).

Raphidim is a place in the wilderness near Mount Horeb, where water flowed from the rock, and it was called “temptation.” There also Jesus fought against Amalek near Paran. Raphidim is interpreted as “relaxed hands,” or “health of judgment,” or “a vision of a sufficient ear for them.”

Scene, that is, “tabernacles,” is the place where Jacob lived after returning from Mesopotamia. In the Hebrew language it is called Sochoch [Col. 0369B].

Sior is a place opposite Egypt. Even today a village named Sior is shown between Aelia and Eleutheropolis, in the tribe of Judah. This is discussed more fully above in the books of Hebrew Questions. Sior is interpreted as “little” or “turbulent.”

Selo is in the tribe of Ephraim. The ark of the covenant remained there, and the tabernacle of the Lord, until the time of Samuel. It is eleven miles from Neapolis, in the region of Atrapitena. We also read that a patriarch’s son was called Selon. Selo is interpreted either as “his dismissal” or “petition.”

Abennezer is interpreted as “stone of help,” or “stone of helpers.” It is the place from which the Philistines took the ark of the covenant, between Aelia and Ashkelon, near the village of Bethsamis [Col. 0369C].

Asiongaber: at this place Jehoshaphat’s fleet was battered by the force of a storm. It is said to be Issia itself, not far from Ailo, on the Red Sea.

Ahia is a place in the region of the asses. Ahia is interpreted as “vulture,” or “incense.”

Elim is the well of Dimon. Isaiah also recalls this place in the same vision.

Acheldemach, that is, “the field of blood,” is still shown at Aelia, south of Mount Zion.

Ennon is near Salim, where John baptized (John 3), as it is written in the Gospel according to John. The place is still shown at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis, to the south, near Salem and the Jordan. Ennon is interpreted as “he gave me.”

Baalthamar is near Gaba, where the children of Israel engaged in battle against the tribe of Benjamin. To this day a village called Bethamari is found in the places mentioned above. Baalthamar is interpreted as “having a palm tree.”

Bechacar: the people of Israel pursued the foreigners as far as this place and called it “the stone of help.” For Betachar is interpreted as “house of business,” or “of a lamb.”

Berasan is the place to which David sent part of the spoils.

Baurim is the place as far as which her husband pursued Michal, Saul’s daughter, in tears. Baurim is interpreted as “the chosen” or “young men.”

Ergab is the place to which Jonathan, Saul’s son, directed the boy while practicing with military spears. Aquila and Symmachus translated it as “stone.”

Esthama is the place to which David sent someone. Esthama is interpreted as “the mercy of God.”

Fel monialmoni, which Aquila translates as “that one” or “this one,” and Symmachus as “I do not know,” is the place to which they transferred the ark of the covenant from Azotus. It is now called a large village.

Getham is interpreted as “Antipatris” and “Jamnia”; another village is also called Gethim. Getha is interpreted as “his winepress,” or “humble excavation.”

Gallim was the place from which came Phalti, who, after David’s flight, had taken his wife Michal. Isaiah also mentions this place. There is also said to be a village of Ekron called Gallim. Gallim is interpreted as “marshy places” or “heaps.”

Gel is the place where Jehu, king of Israel, struck Ahaziah, king of Judah, near Jibleam. Gel is interpreted as “division” or “cutting off.”

Gethsemane is the place where the Savior prayed before his Passion. It is at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and a church is now built above it [Col. 0370B]. Gethsemane is interpreted as “valley of olive presses.”

Golgotha, “the place of the skull,” is where the Savior was crucified for the salvation of all. It is still shown at Aelia, north of Mount Zion.

Navoth is a place in Ramah where David sat; we have discussed it in the books of Hebrew Questions. Navoth is interpreted as “conspicuous,” or “exclusion from sitting.”

Ramah, for which Aquila translates “exaltation” or “he will be exalted,” is the place written about in Jeremiah (Jer. 31). There is also another place in the tribe of Benjamin near Bethlehem, concerning which it is said: “A voice was heard in Ramah” (Matt. 3). Ramah is interpreted as “lofty.”

Sofamoth is the place to which David sent someone. Sofamoth is interpreted as “the lip of death.”

Thelamage is the place to which Abner sent to David. It should be known, however, that Aquila translates this word as *Extemble*, while Symmachus translates it as “for himself.”

Saforvaim is the place from which the Assyrians migrated and settled in Samaria, and from them the Samaritan nation took its beginning. Isaiah also mentions them.

Thafeth: we read in Jeremiah, “Aram Thafeth” [the printed reading is uncertain]. To this day there is a place in the suburbs of Aelia called by this name, near the pool of the fuller and a field.

Acheldemach is therefore interpreted as “the little one has come.”

Thabat is where battle was fought against Midian. Thabath is interpreted as “mud.”

Topheth is in the Valley of the Sons of Hinnom, where the people worshiped images. It is a place in the suburbs. Topheth is therefore interpreted as “protection of the mouth,” or “of Gehenna.”

## CHAPTER VII. On Rugged Places

Rugged places are places into which winds run from every direction and break themselves, as Naevius says: “Into the mountains, where the winds broke the place.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Dens of Wild Beasts

Dens are dark hiding places of wild beasts and lairs of wolves. Hence brothels are also called *lustra*, by way of contrast, because they are scarcely illuminated.

Cliffs signify pride, as in Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the cliffs” (Jer. 14).

A cave signifies a sinful person, as is said in Job concerning the devil: “The beast will dwell in his cave” (Job 37) [Col. 0371A].

## CHAPTER IX. On Sacred Groves

A sacred grove is a place enclosed by dense trees, drawing light away from the ground. It may also be called such from the fact that it shines with many lights. [Things] were also done there on account of pagan religion and worship.

When groves are mentioned in the divine books, they signify the error of the pagans, because they frequently sacrificed to idols there. Thus in the Prophet: “the grove of Dazin,” that is, of Adonis, who was Venus’s lover, where he was mourned by the deluded as though he were dead.

## CHAPTER X. On Desert Places

Deserts are so called because they are not sown and therefore are, as it were, abandoned. Such are the places of forests and mountains, contrary to the most fertile lands, where the soil is exceedingly rich.

A desert is sometimes used for Paradise, which man abandoned when he sinned, as in the Gospel (Luke 15), where the man who had a hundred sheep left the ninety-nine in the desert and went to seek the one sheep that had perished.

At other times the desert signifies the neediness of the present life, as in the Psalmist: “In a desert and trackless and waterless land, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary” (Ps. 62). “In a desert,” he says—that is, in the needy and barren destitution of this world. He continues, “and in a trackless place,” because the world has no way within itself except the Lord Savior, who is the path of the blind and the saving straightness of those who wander.

He adds: “And waterless,” that is, barren and fruitless. We call a place watery when it is watered by abundant waters; waterless means dry and infertile, so that rightly the soul grows hard through excessive dryness. By these three names, therefore, the neediness of this world is indicated.

Sometimes we call Judea a desert because it was rejected and abandoned by the Lord on account of its unbelief.

Sometimes the Gentiles are signified, concerning whom it is written: “It will rejoice and exult in the way” (Isa. 35). There is also this: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54).

## CHAPTER XI. On Trackless Places

Trackless places are secluded and hidden places, as though outside the road. They are also called pathless places. Hence *aviaria* are secluded places, remote from the road or accessible only to birds. Thus the poet says: “The uncultivated bird-haunts redden with berries.”

Trackless places mystically signify the errors of heretics, who neglect to keep the way of truth and do not wish to follow the footsteps of him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). For everyone who does not keep the path of righteousness is rightly said to pass through trackless places.

## CHAPTER XII. On Pleasant Places

Verrius Flaccus says that pleasant places are so called because they provide only love and attract people to be loved. Varro says they are so called because they are without service and no business is conducted in them, as though *amunia*, that is, “without fruit,” from which no fruit is paid out [Col. 0372A]. Hence those who provide nothing are also called *immunes*, “exempt” or “without obligation.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On Sunny Places

Sunny places are those that enjoy the sun, as though *aneu phrices*, that is, “without cold,” or because they are under an open sky. Shady places, by contrast, are as though covered by the sky and are opposite to sunny places.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Slippery Places

A place is clearly called slippery because someone slips there. The word *lubricum* is used not of something that slips, but of that in which someone slips.

## CHAPTER XV. On Summer Places

Summer places are shady places where animals avoid the heat of the sun during summer. Statius: “And the summer retreats of shady Lycaeus opened.”

Pleasant and sunny places can signify forms of virtue, where the sun of righteousness shines and the moderation of a good life is established.

Conversely, slippery places can signify vices, where the steps of upright conduct cannot stand firm. The person who follows the luxury of the age and greedily desires to possess the delights and riches of this world proceeds on slippery ground. In all these things the fall of human life is near, and the deception of souls is certain.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Shipyards and Harbors

Shipyards are places where ships are built; they are also called *textrina*. A station is where ships remain for a time; a harbor is where they winter. An unsafe harbor (*importunum*) is one in which there is no refuge, as though there were no harbor.

A harbor is a place removed from the access of winds, where people customarily prepare winter quarters. It is called *portus* from the carrying away of merchandise. The ancients called it *bajas*, from the carrying of goods, with the same declension as *baja, bajas* and *familia, familias*.

If ships can spiritually signify churches, which move upon the open sea of this world and are shaken by the waves of temptations and the storms of persecution, then the station or harbor of ships can appropriately be understood as the firmness of faith, where the souls of the saints desire to find the tranquility of rest.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “And he led them into the harbor of their desire, and delivered them from their necessities” (Ps. 106). It shows that the Lord provides consolation to those who labor. After dangers, the weary commonly emerge from their toil, rejoicing that they have been delivered from great disaster, when they have begun to reach the safest harbor.

A harbor is called *portus* from carrying ships. What follows is a repeated but exceedingly pleasing conclusion: that the mind in distress might be delivered from all its necessities [Col. 0372D].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Shore

The shore is land near water and the sea. It is called *littus* because it is struck by the wave, or because it is washed by water. Cicero, in the *Topics*: “The shore is where the wave is struck.”

The shore signifies the end of the world, as in the Gospel, where it says that the Lord’s net draws fish to the shore (Matt. 13). There the good fish are gathered into vessels, while the bad are cast out.

By the shore the state of immortality is signified. Hence we read in the Gospel that the Lord sat on the shore, while the disciples are described as laboring in a boat. After the Resurrection the Lord stood on the shore, whereas before his Resurrection he had walked before his disciples upon the waves of the sea.

The reason for this is readily understood if the circumstance then present is considered. For what does the sea signify except the present age, which is battered by the tumult of events and the waves of corruptible life? And what is signified by the solidity of the shore except the permanence of eternal rest?

Since the disciples were still involved in the waves of mortal life, they labored in the sea. But because our Redeemer had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh, after his Resurrection he stood on the shore [Col. 0373B], as though he were speaking to his disciples of the mystery of the Resurrection, saying: “I no longer appear to you in the sea, because I am not with you in the waves of disturbance.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Caves

A cave is a hollow beneath the earth that can be seen through. In Greek it is *spelaion*; in Latin, *spelunca*.

Caves designate the dark hearts of sinners, as in the Prophet: “And darkness over the caves forever” (Isa. 32).

*Spiracula* are the name given to all places of pestilential spirit, which the Greeks call *charoneia* or *Acherontea*. Varro also calls such a place a *spiraculum*. They are called *spiracula* because they are places where the earth emits breath.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Chasms

A chasm is a deep rupture in the earth, as though from *itus*, “going.”

Strictly speaking, a chasm is the opening of a human mouth, transferred from wild beasts, whose greed is displayed by the opening of their mouths.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Deep

Strictly speaking, *profundum* means, as it were, “that whose bottom extends far forward.” By an abuse of language, however, *profundum* can refer either upward or downward, as in: “The seas and lands, and the deep heaven.”

The deep sometimes signifies the secret of wisdom; sometimes the innermost compunction of the heart; sometimes the voracity of sinners; and sometimes the prison of hell.

The depth therefore signifies divine wisdom, whose bottom—that is, whose end—no one can reach [Col. 0373D].

It signifies the compunction of the heart in the Psalm where it says: “From the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. 129). From this depth Peter poured forth glorious tears. From this depth the publican beat his blameworthy breast; he had descended so deeply into sin that he did not even raise his eyes toward heaven. From this place Jonah silently cried out to the Lord, having entered hell alive when he was placed in the belly of the sea-monster. The sea-monster was the prophet’s oratory.

The deep signifies the voracity of sinners or persecutions where it says: “Deliver me from those who hate me and from the deep waters” (Ps. 68).

It signifies the prison of hell where it says: “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let its open mouth press upon me” (ibid.) [Col. 0374A].

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Abyss

Abyss is the name of excessive depth. It is called *barathrum*, as though “black chasm,” from its depth.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Erebus

Erebus is the depth and recess of the underworld.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Place of Cocytus

Cocytus is a place of the underworld, concerning which Job speaks as follows: “He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus, and it will draw every human being after it, and innumerable ones before it” (Job 21).

The wise men of this world thought that the river Cocytus was in the underworld. But let us understand the voice of the blessed man: in Greek, *Cocytos* means “the lamentation of the infirm.” These are the infirm who refuse to act manfully.

We customarily call the small stones of rivers *glareae*, which flowing water carries along. These pebbles designate those who are always devoted to their pleasures and are dragged downward by the river, as it were, and who daily move toward lamentation through their own falls, so that afterward they may mourn eternally.

“He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus,” because the ancient enemy offers people as many kinds of vices as he draws them into, giving them, as it were, so many drinks of his sweetness. It is therefore rightly said: “He was sweet to the pebbles of Cocytus,” because he is bitter to the elect but pleasant to the reprobate.

“And it will draw every human being after it, and innumerable ones before it.” Since drawing every human being is more than drawing innumerable ones, why is it first said, “It will draw every human being,” and then, as an increase, “innumerable ones” is added? Reason requires that what is less should be stated first, and afterward what is greater as an increase.

But it must be understood that saying “innumerable” was more than saying “all.” It draws every human being after it because within three and a half years it binds under the yoke of its condemnation all those whom it finds occupied in the pursuits of carnal life. But it drew innumerable ones before it because, although it could not draw all carnal people throughout the course of more than six thousand years, there are nevertheless many more whom it found to seize over so long a period.

Tartarus is so called either because everything there is disturbed—*apo tes taraches*, “from disturbance”—or, more truly, *apo ton tartarizein*, that is, “from the trembling of cold,” which means being chilled and frozen, because it lacks the light of the sun. For there are neither vapors there, which are produced by the sun’s light, nor winds, which are stirred by its movements, but perpetual torpor. In Greek, *tartarizein* is read as “to shudder and tremble.”

For there is weeping and gnashing of teeth there (Matt. 22).

Gehenna is a place of fire and sulfur. They think it is called after a valley consecrated to idols, beside the wall of Jerusalem, formerly filled with the corpses of the dead. There the Hebrews sacrificed their children to demons, and the place itself was called *Gehennon*. Therefore the place of future punishment, where sinners are to be tortured, is designated by the name of this place.

It is read that Gehenna is twofold, consisting of fire and cold [Col. 0375A].

The underworld is called *inferus* because it is below. Just as, according to the body, everything lower is heavier if it maintains the order of its weight, so according to the spirit everything lower is sadder. Hence in the Greek language the origin of the name by which the underworld is called is said to resound with the meaning that it contains nothing pleasant [Col. 0376A].

Just as the heart of an animal is in the middle, so the underworld is said to be in the middle of the earth. Hence we read in the Gospel: “In the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12).

The philosophers, however, say that the underworld is called *inferi* because souls are carried down from here to there.

# BOOK FOURTEEN

## CHAPTER ONE. On Public Buildings

[Col. 0375A]

The city is a multitude of people united by the bond of fellowship [Col. 0375B], named from *citizens*, that is, from the inhabitants themselves. For the city itself consists of walls, whereas the *civic community* is called not stones but inhabitants. There are three kinds of association: of families, peoples, and cities.

A city (*urbs*) is so called from *orb* (“circle”), because ancient cities were made in a circular form; or from the *urbus*, the part of the plow with which walls are marked. Hence the following verse:

> And he chose a place for his kingdom and enclosed it with a furrow.

For the site of the future city was marked out by a furrow, that is, by a plow. Cato says: “Whoever,” he says, “founds a new city shall plow with a bull and a cow, and where he has plowed he shall make the wall; where he wishes the gate to be, let him lift up the plow and carry it across, and let him call it a gate.” A city was therefore surrounded by a plow with a differing kind of animals because of the mingling of families and as an image of one who sows and produces fruit. [Col. 0375C] A city is founded by the plow and overturned by the plow. Hence Horace:

> And the hostile plow would imprint itself upon the walls.

Some have said that *oppidum* (“town”) derives from the opposition of its walls; others from the storage of resources, because it is fortified, because it is a gathering of inhabitants, and because it offers mutual aid against the enemy. For at first human beings, as naked and unarmed, had neither defenses against wild beasts nor shelters from cold and heat, nor were people themselves sufficiently safe from one another. At length, by natural ingenuity, they wove huts and cottages for themselves from woodland shelters, branches, reeds, and brushwood, so that life might be safer and access denied to those who might do harm. This is the origin of towns, which, because they offered aid, were therefore said to have been called *oppida* [Col. 0375D]. A town differs in size and walls from a village, a fort, and a rural settlement.

Cities are called either colonies, municipalities, villages, forts, or rural settlements. Properly, a *civitas* is one founded not by newcomers but by those born in the same soil; therefore cities founded by their own citizens are called *civitates*, not colonies. A colony, however, is one filled with new settlers because of a shortage of native inhabitants. Hence *colonia* is named from the cultivation of the land.

There are therefore proper names of cities and towns, as well as of villages; but among them we have judged that certain more notable ones should be set down here in this little work.

**Achath** is the city of Nimrod’s kingdom in Babylonia. The Hebrews, moreover, say that this is a city of Mesopotamia, [Col. 0376A] now called Nisibis, besieged and captured by a certain consul Lucullus, and a few years ago handed over to the Persians by the emperor Jovian. *Achath* is interpreted as “a shelter.”

**Aggai** lies toward the western side of Bethel, not far from it. Bethel is situated, for those traveling from Neapolis to Aelia, on the left side of the road, about twelve miles from Aelia, and to this day a village, though small, is visible. A church has also been built there, where Jacob slept while going to Mesopotamia. Therefore he gave that place the name Bethel, that is, “house of God.” *Aggai* is interpreted as “inquiry” or “festivity.”

**Arbohc** is written corruptly in our manuscripts as *arboc*, whereas in Hebrew it is read as *arbe*, that is, “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were buried there, together with the great Adam, as is written in the Book of Jesus, although some suppose that Adam was buried at the place of Calvary. This is the same place as ancient **Celibron** [Col. 0376C], formerly the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling-place of giants; later it was the kingdom of David, a priestly and refuge city in the tribe of Judah. It lies about twenty-two miles south of Aelia. The oak of Abraham, which is also a holm oak, was said to remain until the reign of King Constantius; its trunk, however, is visible at the present time. Although a church has now been built there by our people, the place around the terebinth is superstitiously honored by all the nations, because Abraham once received angels as guests beneath it.

This place was first called Arbe; afterward it received its name from Cebro, one of the sons of Caleb. Read the Book of Chronicles. *Cebron* is interpreted as “marriage” or “eternal vision.”

[Col. 0376D] **Adama** is one of the five cities of the Sodomites, overturned together with the others. *Adama* is interpreted as “soil,” “earth,” or “earthly.”

**Astaroth** was the ancient city of Og, king of Bashan, where giants lived. Later it fell by lot to the tribe of Manasseh, in the region of Patana, and it is separated by six miles from Abra, a city of Arabia. *Astaroth* is interpreted as “folds for sheep,” or, according to another interpretation, “they make an explorer.”

**Arabbi** is the boundary of the province of Judea, facing east toward the tribe of Judah. There is also now a large village called Arabbi, nine miles from Neapolis for those descending eastward toward the Jordan and Jericho; it is called by the name of Crapitene, and the boundary of the Amorites is also called “from Akrabbim.” From this place the tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the foreigners, as is written in the Book of Judges. [Col. 0377A] *Arabbi* is interpreted as “scorpions.”

**Achar** is called in Hebrew *emechachur*, which is interpreted as “valley of tumult” or “of disturbance,” because Israel was thrown into tumult and confusion there, and Achan was once stoned there on account of the theft of the anathema. It lies north of Jericho and is still called by this name by the inhabitants of that region. *Achar* is interpreted as “disturbance” or “tumult.”

**Accaron**, in the tribe of Dan—or, as I think, in the tribe of Judah on the left—is an ancient city of the Canaanites, once a satrapy of Palestine. It was indeed assigned to the tribe of Judah, but was not held by it, because the tribe could not expel the former inhabitants. To this day there is a large village of Jewish inhabitants called Accaron between Azotus and Jamnia. Accaron is the Tower of Strato, later called Caesarea. *Accaron* is interpreted as “instruction,” “sorrow,” or “barrenness.”

**Azotus** is still an important municipality of Palestine and is one of the five cities of the Allophyles. It was assigned to the tribe of Judah but was not retained by it, because it could not at all expel the ancient settlers. *Azotus* is interpreted as “the burning of my uncle’s fire.”

**Ascalon** is a famous city of Palestine, formerly one of the five satrapies of the Allophyles. It was assigned by lot to the tribe of Judah but was not retained by it, because it could not overcome its inhabitants. *Ascalon* is interpreted as “hung,” “fire,” or “infamous.”

[Col. 0377C] **Emach** is a city that fell by lot to Reuben. Even now a village called Amathus lies across the Jordan, almost twenty-one miles to the south. On investigation, however, I found that the city of Coelesyria is called Emath; in Greek it is now called Epiphania. *Emach* is interpreted as “a people still remaining.”

**Bethlehem**, the city of David, fell within the lot of the tribe of Judah. Our Lord and Savior was born there, six miles from Aelia toward the south, beside the road that leads to Hebron. The tomb of Jesse, the father of David, is also shown there; and about a thousand paces away stands the Tower of the Flock, by a certain prophecy signifying beforehand the shepherds who were witnesses of the Lord’s Nativity. On account of the same place, the tomb of Archelaus, once king of the Jews, is also shown; it marks the beginning of the path that turns from the public road toward our cells. Bethlehem was also the name of the son of Ephrathah, that is, of Mary, as is read in Chronicles. According to some, this city was founded by the Jebusites and was first called Ephrata. When Jacob pastured his flocks there, he gave the place the name Bethlehem by a prophecy concerning the future. It is interpreted as “house of bread,” on account of that bread which descended from heaven there.

**Bala**, which is Segor, is now called Gozara. Of the cities of the Sodomites, it alone was preserved at Lot’s request. It overlooks the Dead Sea, and a garrison of Roman soldiers has been stationed there. It is also frequented by its own inhabitants, and balsam and dates are produced there, signs of its ancient fertility. No one should be troubled that Segor is also called Zoara, although the same name means “little” or “smaller”; rather, Segor is Hebrew, while Zoara is Syriac. *Bala* is interpreted as “swallowed up.”

**Damascus** is a famous city of Phoenicia. By the same name Abraham’s servant-woman’s son, Masech, was also called. It is agreed that Damascus in Syria was founded and named after Damascus, the son of Abraham’s steward. *Damascus* is also interpreted as “drink of blood” or “kiss of blood.”

**Dan** is a village four miles from Paneas for those traveling toward Tyre. It is still called by this name and is the northern boundary of the province of Judea. The river Jordan, bursting forth from that place, received its name from it. The Hebrews call *Jor*—[the text reads] *richron*—a river or stream. *Dan* is interpreted as “judgment” or “judging.”

**Dothain** is where Joseph found his brothers pasturing their flocks. It is still shown ten miles north of Sebaste. *Dothaim* is therefore interpreted as “pasture,” “their green place,” or “a sufficient withdrawal.”

**Dehon** also, and **Dibon**, were camps of the children of Israel in the wilderness. There is another very large village called Dibon near Paran. Although it had formerly belonged to the children of Moab, and afterward Sihon, king of the Amorites, had held it by right of war, it was captured and possessed by the children of Israel and fell to the tribe of Gad. *Dibon* is interpreted as “abundantly” or “understanding sufficiently.”

[Col. 0378C] **Esebon** was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, in the land of Gilead. Although it had belonged to the Moabites, it was possessed by the Amorites by right of war. *Esebon* is interpreted as “thought” or “a belt of mourning.”

**Engaddi** lies in the tribe of Judah, where David hid in the wilderness, in the plain of Jericho—that is, in that level region. To this day there is a very large Jewish village called Engadda beside the Dead Sea; balsam comes from there; [lacuna], which vineyards Solomon calls “the vineyards of Engaddi.” *Engaddi* is interpreted as “spring of the kid.”

**Endor** is in the tribe of Manasseh, where the woman skilled in divination was consulted by Saul, king of Judea. *Endor* is interpreted as “spring of generation.”

**Gaza** is the city of the Enehorites (*Enehorum*, as printed), in which the Cappadocians lived after the former inhabitants had been killed. Among the ancients it was directly beside the Canaanites near Egypt; it fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, but that tribe could not retain it, because the Enacim—that is, the giants of the Allophyles—resisted with great strength. It remains to this day a distinguished city of Palestine. It was called Gaza because King Cambyses of the Persians placed his treasures there when he made war on the Egyptians. In the Persian language, *gaza* means “treasure.” *Gaza* is interpreted as “his strength.”

**Gabaath**, in the tribe of Benjamin, is the city of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, where Eleazar was buried. There is now a village called Gabatha twelve milestones from Eleutheropolis. *Gabaath* is interpreted as “the hill of a cousin.”

**Jericho** is traditionally said to have been founded by the Jebusites, from whom it is believed to have taken its name. After Joshua crossed the Jordan, he overthrew it and killed its king. In its place Ozam, from Bethel in the tribe of Ephraim, built another city, which our Lord and Savior graciously honored by his presence. This city too, at the time when Jerusalem was being attacked by the Romans, was captured and destroyed because of the faithlessness of its inhabitants. In its place a third city was built, which still exists today; the remains of both earlier cities are visible to the present day. *Jericho* is also interpreted as “its fragrance” or “moon,” and signifies the passing away of mortal life.

**Jerusalem**, in which Adonibezek reigned and which afterward the Jebusites held, received its name from them. David later exterminated them and made the city the metropolis of the whole province of Judea, because he bought there the site of the Temple and left the expenses of its construction to his son Solomon. Josephus reports that this is the Salem mentioned in Genesis under King Melchizedek (Gen. XIV). It was in the tribe of Benjamin.

The name *Jebus* is found in Scripture to have four kinds of significance. It is the same city as Jerusalem. Jerusalem, according to history, denotes the earthly city, in which the holy Church itself is signified; according to allegory, it expresses the holy Church; according to tropology, it designates the faithful soul; and according to anagogy, it prefigures the heavenly homeland, as we have shown above.

**Sion**, the same city, is named from the mountain situated in its southern part, and possesses a mystical meaning. *Sion* is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” and signifies the Church, the faithful soul, or the heavenly homeland.

According to history, Sion is the people of the Jews, or the city itself on Mount Sion, which is also called Jerusalem. Thus we read in the prophet Amos:

> The Lord will roar from Sion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice. (Amos I)

For from that same people the Lord was born according to the flesh. Isaiah says of this:

> From Sion the law will go forth, and the word from Jerusalem. (Isa. II)

And Micah writes:

> Sion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall be like a heap of stones. (Mic. III)

According to allegory, Sion designates the holy Church, as in the Psalm:

> Praise your Lord, Sion. (Ps. CXLVII)

Hence Isaiah says:

> Arise, arise; clothe yourself with your strength, Sion. (Isa. LII)

Micah writes of the same subject:

> Rise and thresh, daughter of Sion, for I shall make your horn iron and your hoofs iron. (Mic. IV)

According to anagogy, Sion designates the heavenly homeland. Hence the Apostle says:

> You have approached Mount Sion and the city of the living God, Jerusalem. (Heb. XII)

The daughter of Sion is the Church or the holy soul. Thus we read in Zephaniah:

> Sing praise, daughter of Sion; rejoice, Israel. (Zeph. III)

The sons of Sion are the sons of the Church. Hence we read in the Psalm:

> Let the sons of Sion rejoice over their king. (Ps. CXLIX)

And Joel says:

> You sons and daughters of Sion, rejoice in the Lord your God, who has given you a teacher of righteousness. (Joel II)

**Moab**, named from one of the sons of Lot who was called Moab, is a city of Arabia now called Areopolis. The city and the region are called Moab from its name; for this reason the city itself possesses, as it were, a proper designation: Rabbatha Moab, that is, “Great Moab.” *Moab* is interpreted as “from part,” that is, “from the devil.”

**Ammon** means “son of my people” or “a turbulent people,” namely the Jews, according to some, or heretics. Thus we read in Deuteronomy:

> The Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth generation, shall not enter the Church of the Lord forever. (Deut. XXIII)

And Zephaniah says of this:

> As I live, says the Lord, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah. (Zeph. II)

They are also understood in a favorable sense, as in Isaiah:

> The sons of Moab shall be obedient. (Isa. XI)

**Roboch** is a city of the Assyrians, which Assur built after returning from the land of Shinar. *Roboth* is interpreted as “inclination” or “streets.”

**Sidon** is a distinguished city of Phoenicia, formerly the northern boundary of the Canaanites and afterward of the region of Judea. It fell by lot to the tribe of Asher, but the tribe did not possess it, because it was unable to drive out its enemies. The Phoenicians, coming from the Red Sea, founded this city and called it Sidon because of the abundance of fish. For the Phoenicians call a fish *sidon*. They also founded Tyre in Syria, Utica in Africa, Hippo, Jebtin, and other cities on the maritime coasts. *Sidon* is also interpreted as “hunt of death.”

**Shinar** is the plain of Babylon, where the tower stands. From there Assur departed and built Nineveh. *Shinar* is therefore interpreted as “shaking of teeth” or “their stench.”

[Col. 0380C] **Sodom** is the city of the impious, consumed by divine fire beside the Dead Sea. *Sodom* is also interpreted as “silent animal,” “blindness,” or “their likeness.”

**Seboim** was likewise a city of the impious, dissolved into eternal ashes.

**Sora** is a city near Sodom, also called Segor and Zora, of which we have spoken above.

**Salem** is a city, and **Sichem** [is] of the Shechemites. **Sea** too is another village, shown to the present day near Aelia toward the east by this name. At the eighth milestone from Scythopolis, a village called Salumias is likewise found. *Salem* is interpreted as “peace” or “one who gives back.”

**Thamna**, where Judah sheared his sheep, is still shown as a very large village in the territory of Diospolis, for those traveling toward Aelia, in the tribe of Dan or Judah. There is another city of the princes of Edom called Thamna. The concubine of Eliphaz, the son of Esau, was also called Thamna; she bore him Amalek, from whom came the Amalekites. *Thamna* is interpreted as “a completed portion” or “a given consummation.”

**Arimathem** is the city of Elkanah and Samuel, called Ophini, in the Thamnitic region of Diospolis. Joseph, who is mentioned in the Gospel as being from Arimathea (Matt. XXVII), was from there. *Arimathem* is interpreted as “their height.”

**Bethsamis** is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin. It is still shown, for those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Nicopolis, at the tenth mile toward the east. *Bethsamis* is interpreted as “house of the sun.”

**Bethsaida** is a city in Galilee, belonging to Andrew, Peter, and Philip, near the lake of Gennesareth. *Bethsaida* is interpreted as “house of fruits” or “house of hunters.”

**Bethphage** is a little village on the Mount of Olives, to which the Lord Jesus came. *Bethphage* is interpreted as “house of the mouth of the valleys” or “berries.”

**Bethany** is a village two miles from Aelia, on the side of the Mount of Olives, where the Savior raised Lazarus. His tomb is still shown there, with a church now built over it. *Bethany* is interpreted as “house of affliction” or “house of obedience.”

**Bethsaida** is the pool in Jerusalem called the Sheep Pool, which may be interpreted by us as “belonging to animals.” It once had porticoes. Two pools are also shown there: one is usually filled by winter rains, while the other, reddening wondrously as though with bloody water, bears within it the signs of an ancient work. For it is said that the priests used to wash sacrifices in it, from which it received its name.

**Capernaum** is a town in Galilee of the nations, situated beside the lake of Gennesar, within the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali. *Capernaum* is interpreted as “field” or “village of consolation.”

**Emmaus**, from which Cleopas came, whom the evangelist Luke mentions, is now the distinguished city of Nicopolis in Palestine. *Emmaus* is interpreted as “a rejected people.”

[Col. 0381C] **Ephraim** lies near the wilderness, to which the Lord Jesus came with his disciples. *Ephraim* is therefore interpreted as “a fruitful people” or “sharp”; we may derive it from increase, “those who increase.”

**Phanuel** is the city built by Jeroboam. *Phanuel* is interpreted as “face of God.”

**Modin** is a village near Diospolis, from which the Maccabees came. Their tombs are still shown there.

**Mello** is a city built by Solomon.

**Nazareth** is the place from which our Lord and Savior was called a Nazarene. To this day there is a village in Galilee, facing the legion, fifteen miles toward the east, near Mount Tabor, called Nazara. *Nazareth* is interpreted as “his flower,” “his little branch,” “purity,” “separation,” or “custody.”

**Saba** is the royal city of Ethiopia, which Josephus reports was called Meroe by King Cambyses, after the name of his sister. *Saba* is also interpreted as “captive.”

**Sareptha** is a town of the Sidonians situated on the public road, where Elijah once lived. *Sareptha* is interpreted as “burning” or “the affliction of bread.”

**Tharsis** is the place from which gold was brought to Solomon. Josephus thinks that it is the city of Tarsus in Cilicia. *Tharsis* is interpreted as “investigation of joy.”

**Thersa** is where Asa was king of Israel. *Thersa* is interpreted as “contemplation.”

**Acheldemach** is the Field of Blood, still shown in Aelia on the southern side of Mount Sion. To this day, following the custom of the Jews, the earth covers some of the lowly dead, while others are left to decay in the open air.

**Antioch** is a city of Coelesyria, where the apostles Barnabas and Paul were ordained. There is another Antioch in the province of Pisidia in Asia, where these same men, preaching to the Jews, said:

> It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you rejected it, and so forth. (Acts XIII)

**Alexandria** is a city of Egypt, where the tomb of the blessed evangelist Mark is venerated. *Alexandria* is interpreted as “removing the narrowness of darkness.”

**Attalia** is a maritime city of Pamphylia. *Attalia* is interpreted as “its time,” or, better, “the Lord’s decline.”

**Amphipolis** is a city of Macedonia. There is another of the same name in Syria. *Amphipolis* is interpreted as “a people falling by the mouth.”

**Apollonia** is also a city of Macedonia. There is another in Africa, called Pentapolis. *Apollonia* is interpreted as “discipline” or “their synagogue.”

**Athens** is a city in Achaea. *Athenians* are interpreted as “investigators,” “respondents,” “humble,” or “scattered in time.”

**Areopagus** is the court of Athens, interpreted as “village of Mars,” because Mars was once judged there by twelve gods. *Areopagus* is also interpreted as “first” or “solemnity”; but this is forced, since it is the name of the Athenian court, which received its name from Mars.

**Antipatris** is a city of Palestine, now ruined, which Herod, king of Judea, named after his father. *Antipatris* is interpreted as “giving praise.”

There are two cities called **Caesarea** in Judea, in the land of promise: Caesarea of Palestine, situated on the seacoast, and another Caesarea Philippi, which Scripture mentions in the Gospel. *Caesarea* is interpreted as “the possession of a prince.”

**Corinth** is a maritime city of Achaea. *Corinth* is interpreted as “their way of life.”

**Lydda** is a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea. *Lydda* is interpreted as “usefulness.”

**Seleucia** is a new city of Syria, founded by Seleucus, who also founded Antioch. *Seleucia* is interpreted as “lifting itself up,” or “an experiment of the journey,” or “one going forth to the calling.”

**Salamis** is a city on the island of Cyprus. *Salamis* is interpreted as “sent.”

**Tyre** is the metropolis of Phoenicia in the tribe of Naphtali. *Tyre* is also interpreted as “affliction,” as we have said above.

**Troas** is a maritime city of Asia. *Troas* is interpreted as “rest.”

**Thessalonica** is a city of Macedonia. *Thessalonica* is interpreted as “hastening to strengthen or fashion a shadow.”

When *city* or *urban community* is understood in a favorable sense, it signifies either the holy Church or the faithful soul. Thus it is written in the Psalm:

> Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain. (Ps. CXLIV)

And again:

> The force of the river makes glad the city of God. (Ps. XLV)

That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes glad the holy Church of God, or the faithful soul of any holy man. Much is written on this subject in the Apocalypse. Hence:

> I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, adorned like a bride for her husband. (Rev. XXI)

The cities of Judea likewise signify the Churches of Christ or the souls of the faithful. Hence it is written in the Psalm:

> The cities of Judah shall be built, and so forth. (Ps. LXVIII)

Citizens are mystically called the faithful. Thus the Apostle says:

> But you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household. (Eph. II)

A city can also signify the hearts or bodies of the impious, as in the Psalm:

> You have destroyed their cities. (Ps. IX)

And in the Gospel:

> And you have burned their cities with fire. (Matt. XXII)

When *city* is used in the contrary sense, it signifies spiritual Babylon, namely the city of the devil, which will be plunged into the depth of the abyss, where the dwelling-place of demons and every unclean spirit is. Over it the kings of the earth will weep, those who committed fornication with it; and the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over it (Rev. XVIII).

For the Apostle says:

> We have no abiding city here, but we seek the one that is to come. (Heb. XIII)

That is, the heavenly homeland and the fellowship of the holy angels.

A **municipality** is a place that, while retaining the status of a city, obtains from a prince some right of lesser or greater office. It is called *municipium* from *munera*, that is, offices, because it renders only its *munia*, that is, its due taxes or obligations [Col. 0383C]. For liberal and famous cases, and those that proceed from the prince, are not conducted there; these belong to the dignity of the city.

The municipality likewise signifies the future homeland in heaven and the everlasting glory of the saints. Hence the Apostle says:

> But our citizenship is in heaven. From there we await the Lord Savior, who will refashion the body of our lowliness so that it conforms to the body of his glory. (Phil. III)

A **village** is so called from neighboring dwellings, or because it has only roads and no walls. It is without the protection of walls, although the dwellings themselves within a city are also called villages. It is called *vicus* because it takes the place of a city, or because it has only roads without walls.

Villages, or the country estates of the nations, can mystically express their roads, locations, or earthly activities, because they are situated outside the city, that is, outside the fellowship of the people of God. Hence the Lord’s command in the Gospel parable: when those who had been invited to the wedding refused to come, he ordered his servants to go out into the streets and villages of the city and invite to the wedding whomever they found (Luke XIV). That is, because the Jewish people delayed coming to the Lord’s wedding, he commands the multitude of the nations to enter in its place, so that the wedding feast of those reclining at table might be filled.

The ancients called a **fort** (*castrum*) a town situated in a very high place, as though it were a “high house.” Its plural is *castra*, and its diminutive is *castellum*. Forts or castles can signify the dwelling together of good people or of the holy angels.

Thus we read in Exodus of the camps of the children of Israel, where they encamped, and in Genesis of the place where the patriarch Jacob met the angels of God (Gen. XXVIII). He called the name of that place *Manaim*, that is, “camps.” There is no doubt that the camps of God which Jacob saw on his journey were a multitude of angels, since Scripture calls them the army of heaven.

**Rural settlements** (*pagi*) are places suitable for buildings, inhabited by people among the fields. These are also called **meeting places** (*conciliabula*), from the gathering and fellowship of many people into one place.

**Crossroads** (*compita*) are places where country people customarily gather. They are called *compita* because many places in the fields meet or converge there, and country people come together in them.

**Suburban areas** are buildings situated around or beside a city, as though beneath the city. Suburban buildings and sites can signify the locations of various nations that may be brought into the service of the city of God, that is, the holy Church, when through the zeal of preachers they are summoned to receive the word of God and become catechumens. If they persevere in the faith, they will thus be joined to the unity of the holy Church.

**Walls** (*moenia*) are the walls of a city, named because they fortify the city, as though they were the city’s defenses, that is, its protections. *Munium* is said to derive from “made by hand”; similarly, walls are named from fortification, as though fortified, because they fortify and protect the interior of the city.

Walls have two meanings. Sometimes, improperly, *walls* refers to all the public buildings of a city, as in:

> We divide the walls and open wide the buildings of the city.

Properly, however, walls are only the walls themselves. A wall is adorned with towers and battlements. A **forward wall** (*promurale*) is a structure serving as a defense for a wall; it is situated immediately before the wall.

The walls of the holy city, according to mystical interpretation, are either assemblies of the righteous or the heights of sacred virtues. The wall of that city signifies the unconquerable firmness of faith, charity, and hope. The Lord himself may also be understood as the great wall protecting the Church on every side, of whom Isaiah says:

> The city of our strength is saved; he will place a wall in it. (Isa. XXVI)

The forward wall signifies the Lord’s protection and the intercession of the holy patriarchs, prophets, and other holy preachers, who accomplish the same thing by teaching the hearts of believers. Alternatively, the wall signifies faith, and the forward wall good works. It is not enough to possess the wall of faith unless faith itself is strengthened by good works.

This wall, and this forward wall or surrounding wall, is represented by living stones that, according to the prophet, roll upon the earth. Likewise, walls and fortifications are the divine Scriptures, or the prophets, as is read in the Psalm:

> Let the walls of Jerusalem be built. (Ps. L)

**Towers** are so called because they are rounded and tall. Something is *teres* when it is round together with height, like a column. Although towers may be built square or broad, they nevertheless appear round to those viewing them from a distance, because every appearance of their angles disappears and is worn away over the long span of air, and they look round. [Col. 0385A]

In the meaning of a tower, the Savior himself is understood, as in:

> The name of the Lord is a very strong tower. (Prov. XVIII)

A tower also signifies divine Scripture, as it says in the Song of Songs:

> Your neck is like the tower of David. (Song IV)

It may also signify the excellence of virtues or the eminence of teachers, who hold the first place in the Church. Hence it says in the Song of Songs:

> Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon. (Song VII)

By the nose, the ministers of the word of God are designated on account of discernment; they are compared to a tower because they hold the most eminent place in the Church.

A tower is sometimes placed in the contrary sense: it signifies the height of pride. Thus the sons of Adam are read in Genesis to have built a lofty tower, where their language was confused (Gen. XI). A tower can also signify the Church, as in Micah:

> And you, tower of the flock, misty daughter of Sion. (Mic. IV)

That is, overshadowed by the divine mysteries. Some understand this tower as the Virgin Mary.

Towers can also signify the hearts of the reprobate, constructed by the malice of duplicity, as in Zephaniah:

> Against every fortified wall and against every lofty tower. (Zeph. I)

## CHAPTER II. On Gates

A **gate** is so called because something may be brought in or carried out through it. Properly, the gate of a city or of a camp is meant, as was said above.

A gate is sometimes understood in a favorable sense and sometimes in an unfavorable one. It is understood favorably when it signifies the Lord himself, through whom the entrance to eternal life lies open to us. Hence he says:

> I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will go in and go out and find pasture. (John X)

A gate also signifies the faith of Christ. Hence it is written:

> They enter the city through the gate,

because one must enter the Church of God through right faith. The gate of Christ, or faith, is meant in the Psalm:

> This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. (Ps. CXVII)

The gate can signify the womb of the Virgin Mary or the canon of the Old Testament, as in Ezekiel:

> I saw a gate in the house of the Lord, and it was closed. (Ezek. XLIV)

Gates can signify the holy Scriptures, the apostles, or good works, as in the Psalm:

> Lift up your gates, you everlasting doors, and the king of glory shall enter. (Ps. XXIII)

Gates can also signify human hearts, or the entrances of the mind, formerly occupied by the devil and afterward possessed by Christ, as in Genesis:

> Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies. (Gen. XXIV)

That is, Christ shall possess them.

The gates are also understood as the holy teachers who open for us, through their doctrines, the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. In the contrary sense, however, heretics and false teachers are expressed under the name of gates, through which the lost enter Gehenna. Concerning them the Lord says to Peter:

> You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. (Matt. XVI)

And the Psalmist says:

> You lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Sion. (Ps. IX)

The gate of death is the devil or every worldly enticement, because through it one unhappily enters into eternal destruction. Having therefore been delivered from those mortal gates, he promises that in these gates of the Church, which grant everlasting blessedness, he will proclaim the praises of the Lord; through them his exalted name is celebrated throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER III. On Ways

**Ways** are the narrow spaces themselves that lie between villages. The word *way* is found used in either a favorable or an unfavorable sense.

It is favorable where the Lord says:

> I am the way, the truth, and the life. (John XIV)

And the Psalmist says:

> I have chosen the way of truth. (Ps. CXVIII)

That is, the doctrine of truth.

In the contrary sense there is another way, concerning which the same prophet, entreating the Lord, says:

> Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law. (Ps. CXVIII)

And in Solomon it is written concerning the prostitute:

> Her house is the way to hell. (Prov. VII)

The name *ways* also expresses those of which the Lord says through the prophet:

> I shall judge each one according to his ways, says the Lord God. (Ezek. XXXIII)

A way is called narrow and constricted when it leads to life, and broad and spacious when it leads to death (Matt. VII).

The way signifies the present life, as in the Gospel:

> Agree quickly with your adversary, while you are with him on the way. (Matt. V)

The way signifies the books of the Law and the Prophets, as in Jeremiah:

> Stand upon the ways, and see and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way. (Jer. VI)

A **path** signifies the divine commandments, as in the Psalm:

> Lead me in the path of your commandments. (Ps. CXVIII)

## CHAPTER IV. On Streets
Broad streets are the permanent and wider roads of cities, named from their breadth, according to the proper usage of the Greek language. Broad streets, moreover, are found used sometimes in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one. In a good sense, when they signify the breadth of believers among the nations. Hence it is written: “Wisdom cries aloud outside, and in the streets she raises her voice” (Prov. I). Sometimes they signify the eternal blessedness extended among the saints, as in the Apocalypse: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold, and throughout all your alleys they shall sing alleluia” (Apoc. XXI). In a bad sense, however, a broad street is used when it signifies the breadth of worldly pleasures, because—as we said above—the road that leads to death is broad and spacious [Col. 0386D] (Matt. VII).

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Sewers

Sewers (*cloacae*) are so called because waters are filtered through them. They say that Tarquinius Priscus first constructed them at Rome, so that whenever a flood of rain occurred, the waters might be discharged through them beyond the city, lest, during the greatest and continuous storms, the force of the waters should overthrow the level ground or the foundations of the cities.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Forum

The forum is a place for conducting lawsuits, named from *fari*, “to speak.” These places are also called *prostra*; hence the name, because, after the capture of the Carthaginians’ ships in the Punic War, their beaks (*rostra*) were removed and fixed in the Roman forum, so that it might bear the mark of victory. [Col. 0387A]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the Senate House

The senate house (*curia*) is so called because there the senate administers concern for all matters.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Praetorium
