The praetorium is so called because the praetor presides there to examine cases.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Gymnasium

A gymnasium is generally a place of exercises. At Athens, however, it was a place where philosophy was learned and the study of wisdom was practiced. For *gymnasium* is called in Greek what in Latin is called *exercitium*, “exercise”—that is, meditation. Baths and places for the races of athletes are also gymnasia, because there people train themselves in the pursuit of their particular art. [Col. 0387B]

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the Capitol

The Capitol at Rome was so called because it was the highest head of the Roman city and religion. Others say that, when Tarquinius Priscus was opening the foundations of the Capitol at Rome, he found in the place of the foundation a human head marked with Etruscan letters; and therefore he called it the Capitol.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Citadels

Citadels are the elevated and fortified parts of a city. [Col. 0387C] For whatever places in cities are safest are called citadels (*arces*) from *arcere*, “to repel” the enemy; hence also *arcus* and *arca*. A citadel sometimes signifies worldly power or secular wisdom; at other times, the summit of true wisdom and the height of the virtues.

Thus we read that David conquered the citadel of Zion, driving out the Jebusites from it and expelling from it the blind and the lame who hated David’s life; and that thereafter he called it the city of David. For our Savior, casting out evil spirits from the multitude of the nations—or from any particular soul—and illuminating it for himself through the light of wisdom, rightly causes it then to be called the citadel of Zion, that is, “the contemplation and vision of peace.” Of it the Psalmist then rightly says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. His place has become established in peace, and his dwelling place in Zion” (Ps. LXXV).

They think that the Circus at Rome was so called from the circuit of horses, because horses run there around the turning-posts. The theater, on the other hand, was named from the spectacle, because there the people stood above and watched, contemplating theatrical performances. [Col. 0387D]

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the Amphitheater

The amphitheater was so called because it is composed of two theaters. For the amphitheater is circular, whereas the theater is formed from the middle of the amphitheater and has the shape of a semicircle.

A labyrinth is a building entangled with walls, such as the one made by Daedalus in Crete, where the Minotaur was confined. Whoever entered it could not find the way out without a ball of thread. [Col. 0388A] The arrangement of this building was such that, when its doors were opened, a terrifying thunderous sound was heard within; one descended by more than a hundred steps. Inside were images and monstrous figures; innumerable passages, divided into sections, led through the darkness, along with other features designed to confuse those entering, so that it seemed impossible to come from its darkness into the light.

There are four labyrinths: the first Egyptian; the second Cretan; the third on Lemnos; the fourth in Italy. All were constructed in such a way that not even the ages could destroy them.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the Lighthouse

A lighthouse is a very large tower, which Greeks and Latins alike, from the use of the thing itself, called a *pharus*. It is so called because by the sign of its flames it can be seen from far away by sailors. [Col. 0388B] Ptolemy is said to have built such a lighthouse near Alexandria at a cost of eight hundred talents.

Its purpose is to display fires during the nighttime course of ships, to give warning of—and enable sailors to avoid—shoals [or: to avoid shoals] and of the entrances to harbors, so that sailors deceived by the darkness might not strike the rocks. For Alexandria has treacherous approaches, full of deceptive shoals. Hence in harbors they call the structures built to provide illumination *phari*. For *phos* in Greek means “light,” while *orasis* means “vision.” Hence also the morning star is called in Greek *phosphoros*, “light-bearer.”

Spiral towers are tall and round, and are called *cochleae*, as though “circular” or “ring-shaped,” because in them one climbs as if around a circle and a revolving circuit. Such is the tower at Rome, one hundred seventy-five feet high.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Baths

[Col. 0388C]

Baths (*thermae*) are so called because they are hot. For the Greeks call heat *thermon*.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Bathhouses

The name *balnea* was given to bathhouses from the washing away of sorrow. For the Greeks call them *balaneion*, because they remove anxiety of mind.

These places are also called gymnasia, because there athletes exercise with their bodies oiled and their limbs rubbed by the hands. For *gymnasium* in Greek is called *exercitium* in Latin, “exercise,” as we showed above.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the Changing Room

The *apodyterium* is the place where the clothing of those bathing is deposited; it is so called from removing one’s clothes, for *apoduein* in Greek means “to undress.” [Col. 0388D]

*Popina* is a Greek word which among us is corruptly called *propina*. It is a place beside public baths where, after bathing, people recover from hunger and thirst. Hence the terms *propina* and *propinare* are also used. For *peina* in Greek means “hunger,” since this place removes hunger.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Shops

In former times *tabernae* were the small and simple cottages of common people in the streets, closed with beams, bars, or boards. Hence also the term *tabernariae*, because people were accustomed to sit there.

They were called *tabernae* because they were constructed from boards and pieces of wood. Although they no longer preserve the former appearance, they still retain the ancient name.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Market

[Col. 0389A]

The *macellum* was so called because animals are slaughtered there and sold to buyers. The market (*mercatus*) was named from commerce. It is customary there to sell or buy goods. Likewise, a *teloneum* is the place where the goods of ships and the earnings of sailors are paid out. There the collector of the customs duty sits, intending to set a price upon the goods and demanding it aloud from the merchants.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the Prison

A prison is a place from which we are forbidden to depart; it is called *carcer* from *coercere*, “to restrain.”

Allegorically, a prison sometimes signifies the tribulation of the present life, in which the elect are afflicted for a time. Concerning this the Prophet says: [Col. 0389B] “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. CXLI). At other times it signifies the custody of hell, as in the Gospel: “The judge will hand you over to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison,” and what follows (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Dwellings

*Habitatio*, “dwelling,” is named from *habere* or *habitare*, “to have” or “to dwell,” as in “to dwell in houses.”

A house (*domus*) is named from a Greek designation. For the Greeks call roofs *domata*. A house is the dwelling of one family, just as a city is the dwelling of one people, and the world is the dwelling of the entire human race.

The ancients called every building an *aedes*. Others think that *aedes* took its name from *edere*, “to eat,” giving as an example the line of Plautus:

> If I had invited you to the house for lunch.

[Col. 0389C]

Hence also *aedificium*, “building,” because it was originally made for eating.

The house signifies the flesh assumed by the Savior in the holy Church, as in Solomon: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX). And in the Psalm: “We shall go into the house of the Lord with agreement” (Ps. CXXI).

The house signifies the hearts or bodies of the faithful, as in Exodus: “You shall place some of the blood of the lamb on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which you will eat it” (Exod. XII).

The house signifies the hearts of the reprobate, as in Isaiah: “Thorns shall spring up in their houses” (Isa. XXXIV)—that is, the anxiety of the world.

The house of the devil signifies the assembly of all evil people, as in Solomon: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your labors be in another’s house” (Prov. V).

An *aula* is a royal house, or a spacious dwelling enclosed by four porticoes. An *atrium* is a large hall, or a broader and more spacious house; it is called an *atrium* because three porticoes are added to it on the outside. Others say that *atrium* means, as it were, “blackened by fire and wood.” It becomes black from smoke. [Col. 0389D]

The hall signifies the holy Church or the conscience of a perfectly pure soul; for it is the royal hall and dwelling of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Cor. III).

A house therefore sometimes signifies the holy Church, as in: “Holiness befits your house, Lord, throughout the length of days” (Ps. XCII); sometimes the heavenly Jerusalem, concerning which it is written: “I rejoiced in those things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI); and sometimes the holy soul in which God dwells. [Col. 0390A]

Atria signify either the holy Church or the entrance of faith. Hence it is written: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (ibid.). This signifies those who are already within the innermost chambers of the Church, or those who have been deemed worthy to enter and depart.

They say that the bedchamber (*thalamus*) received its name for the following reason. When the Sabine women had been carried off by the Romans, and one of them, distinguished above the others for her beauty, was being carried away amid everyone’s great admiration, an oracle answered that she should be given to Thalassius, the commander. Since this marriage turned out successfully, it was established that the name *thalamus* should be repeated at all weddings. [Col. 0390B]

The Egyptians also, in their own language, call the places where newlyweds enter and lie down *thalami*, “bedchambers.”

Mystically, the bedchamber signifies the womb of the holy virgin Mary, in which our nature was joined to the Word of God; that is, the holy Church was joined to Christ, the Son of God. Or it signifies the hearts of the saints, in which the soul is joined through love to the invisible Bridegroom, so that it burns with desire for him and no longer covets anything that is in the world. It counts the length of the present life as punishment, hastens to depart, and desires to rest in the embrace of love in the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom.

The dining room (*coenaculum*) was named from the communal sharing of food. Hence also *coenobium*, “community.” For the ancients used to eat publicly and together; no one had a private banquet, lest pleasures kept secret should give rise to luxury. [Col. 0390C]

The dining room therefore signifies the holy Church, in which Christ consecrated the mystery of his passion and the sacrament of his body and blood. It is also the place where the Holy Spirit came in the form of fire upon the one hundred twenty believers, and where speech in various languages was given to them through that same Spirit.

A *triclinium* is a dining room so called from the three couches of those reclining at table. Among the ancients, the furnishings were laid out in the place of the banquet. For *cline* in Greek means “bed” or “reclining,” from which the word *triclinium* was formed.

The *triclinium* expresses faith in the Trinity, where holy souls, resting in faith, hope, and charity, await entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

A chamber (*cella*) was so called because it conceals and hides us. A bedroom (*cubiculum*) is so called because we sleep there and, sleeping, rest. A sleeping place (*cubile*) is a place for lying down; a retreat (*secessus*) is so called because it is a place “without access.”

Spiritually, the bedroom signifies the secret place of the heart. Hence the Gospel man is commanded to pray to the heavenly Father. Thus he is told: “But when you pray, enter your bedroom, and, with the door closed, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI). [Col. 0390D]

A lodging house (*diversorium*) was so called because people come together there from different roads.

*Hospitium* is a Greek word for a place where someone dwells temporarily under the law of hospitality and then, passing onward again, departs from it. Hence also *metatum*, “a changed place,” because it is changed. Thus we read: “And they encamped,” meaning “they moved their camp.” For an army does not remain there but passes through.

A lodging house may signify the present Church, to which nations come together from every direction seeking a dwelling, and, remaining in that lodging, awaiting access to the heavenly homeland.

An underground chamber (*hypogaeum*) is a building constructed beneath the earth, which we call a cave or cavern.

A sun terrace (*solarium*) is so called because it is open to the sun and the breeze. Such was the place where David saw Bathsheba bathing and fell in love with her. [Col. 0391A] Its mystery is clear: Christ, seeing the Church from the nations cleansing herself from sins through the tears of repentance and the sacrament of baptism, desired her beauty and wished to take her as his bride.

A *xenodochium* is a dwelling made for receiving travelers. Thus, when Antiochus was besieging Jerusalem, Hyrcanus, the leader of the Jews, opened David’s tomb and removed from it three thousand talents of gold. From these he gave three hundred to Antiochus so that he would abandon the siege. To remove the odium of this deed, he is said to have been the first to establish guesthouses from the remaining money, in which he would receive the poor and travelers. Hence the institution took its name. For *xenodocheion* in Greek is rendered in Latin as “the reception of travelers.” [Col. 0391B]

Where the sick are gathered from the streets, the place is called in Greek a *nosocomeion*; there the bodies of the wretched, exhausted by illnesses and hunger, are cared for.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Buildings

A *sacrarium* is properly the place in a temple where sacred objects are kept, just as a *donarium* is the place where offerings are deposited, and *lectisternia* are called the places where people customarily sit. Thus a *sacrarium* is named from the carrying in and carrying away of sacred things; a *donarium*, because gifts which people customarily offer in temples are placed there.

An oratory is consecrated solely to prayer; no one ought to do anything in it except that for which it was made, and from this it receives its name. The *penetralia* are the secret places of oracles, and are called *penetralia* from *penitus*, “within.” [Col. 0391C]

A monastery is the dwelling of one monk. A *sterium* is a station—that is, the dwelling of a solitary person. A *coenobium* appears to be compounded from Greek and Latin: it is the dwelling of many persons living together in common. For *koinon* means “common” in Greek.

Temples (*fana*) were so called from the ropes by which the error of the Gentiles constructed temples, in order that the consuls might hear the responses of demons. The ancients called temples having fountains *delubra*, in which people were washed before entering; they are called *delubra* from washing (*diluere*). These are now churches with sacred fonts, in which the faithful who are reborn are cleansed; and by a fitting presage they are called *delubra*, for they are for the washing away of sins.

The font in churches is the place of the regenerate, in which seven steps are arranged in the mystery of the Holy Spirit: three in descent and three in ascent; but the seventh is also the fourth, namely, one like a son of man, extinguishing the furnace of fire, the support of the feet, the foundation of the water, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. [Col. 0391D]

Basilicas were formerly called the dwellings of kings, whence they have their name. For *basileus* means “king,” and basilicas are royal dwellings. But now divine temples are called basilicas because in them worship and sacrifices are offered to God, the King of all.

A *martyrium* is a place of martyrdom, by Greek derivation, because it has been built in memory of a martyr, or because the tombs of holy martyrs are there.

Some say that an altar (*ara*) is so called because victims burned there blaze; others derive *arae* from prayers, which the Greeks call *aras*. [Col. 0392A]

A pulpit is so called because the reader or psalmist, placed there in public, may be seen by the people and heard more freely. A lectern (*analogium*) is so called because discourse is preached from it—for *logos* means “discourse” in Greek—and because it is set higher up.

A tribunal is so called because from it the priest imparts the precepts for living. It is a place situated on high, from which all may hear him. Alternatively, a tribunal is named from a tribe, because a tribe is summoned to it.

In Holy Scripture a tribunal sometimes signifies the power of divine majesty, because it will judge the world, as in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes upon the seat of his majesty, then all nations shall be gathered together” (Matt. XXV); and in the Apostle: “We shall all,” he says, “stand before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the things proper to his body, according as he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V). [Col. 0392B]

Sacred places are those established for divine worship—for example, those in which altars are customarily consecrated by pontiffs performing sacrifice. According to the ancients, the holy places (*sancta*) are the outer parts of the temple; but the holy of holies is the more secret place of the temple, to which no one had access except priests alone. It is called the holy of holies because it is holier than the outer sanctuary, or because it is holier by comparison with holy things, just as the Song of Songs surpasses all songs.

The word *sanctum* is named from the blood of victims. For among the ancients nothing was called holy unless it had been consecrated or sprinkled with the blood of a victim. Again, *sanctum* is that which has been sanctioned. To sanction is to confirm and to defend against injury by the infliction of a penalty. Thus laws and customs too are said to be holy. [Col. 0392C]

A propitiatory is, as it were, an oratory of propitiation; for propitiation is appeasement. Oracles are so called because answers are given from them, and *oracula* derives from *os*, “mouth.”

What materials the Lord required for the construction of the tabernacle, he himself makes known in Exodus, saying to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take first-fruits for me: from every man who offers willingly, you shall receive first-fruits for me” (Exod. XXV). We too offer the first-fruits of our goods to the Lord when, if we do anything good, we attribute it all to divine grace.

“These,” however, “are the things which you must receive: gold, silver, and bronze; hyacinth, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine linen; goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, violet skins, and sethim wood; oil to prepare the lamps; spices for ointment and sweet-smelling incense; onyx stones and gems to adorn the ephod and the breastpiece. And they shall make me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell in their midst” (ibid.). [Col. 0392D]

All these things which the Lord commanded the former people to offer materially for making the sanctuary ought also to be offered with spiritual understanding by us, who are spiritual children of Israel—that is, who desire to be a people imitating the Lord and seeing [God]. We offer him gold when we shine with the brightness of true wisdom that is in right faith; silver, when confession is made with our mouth unto salvation; bronze, when we rejoice to spread abroad that same faith by public preaching; hyacinth, when we lift our hearts upward; purple, when we subject the body to suffering; scarlet twice dyed, when we burn with the twofold love, that is, of God and neighbor; fine linen, when we possess chastity of the flesh; goats’ hair, when we put on the garb of repentance and mourning; rams’ skins dyed red, when we see the leaders themselves of the Lord’s flock baptized in their own blood; violet skins, when we hope that after death we shall have spiritual bodies in heaven; sethim wood, when, after the thorns of sins have been purged away, we shall serve the Lord alone with clean flesh and soul; oil to prepare the lamps, when we shine with the fruits of charity and mercy; spices for ointment and sweet-smelling incense, when we spread the renown of our good action far and wide, as an example of good living for many; onyx stones and gems to adorn the ephod and breastpiece, when we proclaim with worthy praise the miracles of the saints, by which they adorned thoughts devoted to God and works of virtue, and use these, where need requires, in aid of our faith. [Col. 0393A]

Since we are accustomed to bear burdens on our shoulders, the ephod—that is, the shoulder-garment—rightly signifies the works of the righteous and pious labors for the Lord. Since the breast is the seat of thoughts, the rational and pure thoughts of the elect are rightly expressed in the breastpiece, which is a garment of the breast; onyx stones and gems adorn the ephod and breastpiece when the emblems of miracles are joined to the outstanding deeds and thoughts of the greatest Fathers. [Col. 0393B]

We read in the Old Testament concerning the construction of the tabernacle, which Moses made in the desert, and concerning the building of the temple, which Solomon built in the land of promise. In each building holy places and the holy of holies are mentioned, and their mysteries are readily evident to those who understand rightly, because both houses signify the holy Church.

Yet because the former house was on the journey by which the land of promise was reached, whereas this one was built in the land of promise itself, in the city of Jerusalem; because the former was frequently carried from place to place by the ministry of the Levites, to be brought at last into the land of the promised inheritance, whereas the latter was constructed at once in the homeland itself and the royal city, to stand always upon an inviolable foundation until it fulfilled the office of heavenly figures committed to it: in the former the labor and exile of the present Church, and in the latter future rest and blessedness, may be figured. [Col. 0393C]

Or certainly, because the former was made for the children of Israel alone, while this one was made also by proselytes among the nations, the Fathers of the Old Testament and that ancient people of God may principally be represented in the former, and the Church gathered from the nations figurally expressed in the latter. Nevertheless, when the structure of either house is more fully examined in its spiritual sense, it is shown to suggest in manifold figures both the daily labors of the present Church and everlasting rewards in the future, the joys of the heavenly kingdom, the election of the first Church in Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ. [Col. 0393D]

The holy place, separated from the sanctuary by a hanging veil, signifies the present Church, which moves in the pilgrimage of this world; the holy of holies signifies that Church which is in heaven. For the holy Church itself, consisting of holy angels and human beings, partly still journeys below and partly reigns above in the heavenly homeland, still has its citizens separated from one another by the dividing veil of heaven.

Paul the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, gives full testimony of this when he declares that Christ, the true high priest, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption, not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood.

Finally, in Holy Scripture the tabernacle sometimes signifies the body of the Lord and Savior, as in the Psalm: “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII). Again, God’s tabernacle is the holy Church, or the faithful soul dwelling in the pilgrimage of the world. Hence we read in the Psalm: “For I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. XLI); and in the Apostle: “The tabernacle which God pitched, and not man” (Heb. VIII). In Exodus the Lord is reported to have spoken thus to Moses concerning this tabernacle: “You shall make me a sanctuary, and from there I shall be seen by you” (Exod. XXV). [Col. 0394A]

The columns of the tabernacle are the teachers of the Church, as we read in the Apostle: “James and John and Cephas, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. II). The bars or poles that held together the boards or columns signify Holy Scripture or the harmony of holy preachers; thereby their strength and firmness are displayed. The bases of the columns are the books of the Law and Prophets; the head of the column is Christ. In the Apostle: “Christ is the head of man” (I Cor. XI). [Col. 0394B]

The curtains of the tabernacle are the multitude of the faithful, suspended by the cords of faith and the precepts of Scripture; the violet loops of the curtains are heavenly precepts; the eleven goat-hair coverings are expressed under the figure of sinners; the fifty rings signify the hope of future rest; the holy of holies is that heavenly homeland and the eternal joys of the kingdom of heaven; the two cherubim are the two Testaments of the Law; the ark of the Testament is the Church. Hence we read in the Psalm: “Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. CXXXI).

The propitiatory above the ark is Christ, at the head of the Church. In the Epistle of John: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II). The four golden rings by which the ark was carried are the four books of the Gospels, by which the Church is proclaimed, girded about through the four parts of the world. The poles of incorruptible wood, inserted into the rings, are strong preachers, ever intent upon evangelical preaching with an incorrupt mind. [Col. 0394C]

The golden urn is the Savior’s flesh, pure and filled with the sweetness of everlasting divinity. The table is the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the refreshment of the elect, or the unity of faith; of him the Psalmist says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. XXII). The table made of sethim wood may also signify Holy Scripture, put together from the strong words and deeds of the holy Fathers. Since it shows us what the joys of eternal blessedness are and how they may be attained, it surely supplies us with the food of salvation and life. [Col. 0395A]

The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of divine speech according to the differing capacity of hearers. The loaves of presentation always set upon the table are spiritual teachers, who meditate day and night on the law of the Lord and offer the refreshment of the heavenly word to all who enter the Church.

Twelve loaves, therefore, on the table of the tabernacle signify the twelve Apostles and all their followers in doctrine within the Church. The candlestick signifies the body of the Lord, or the holy Church, or divine Scripture. In Zechariah: “I saw two silver candlesticks on the right side of the altar” (Zech. IV). The seven lamps placed upon the candlestick signify the sevenfold sacrament of the Church, or faith. In Exodus. [Col. 0395B] The lamp signifies the faith of the Church, or works of righteousness. In Solomon: “Therefore the lamp will not be extinguished throughout the whole night.”

The bronze pegs in the tabernacle signify the patriarchs and prophets. The peg signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, fixed in the hearts of the faithful, as Isaiah speaks of him: “I will fix him in a faithful house” (Isa. XXII). The peg signifies the stimulus of compunction, as it is written in Deuteronomy: “You shall have a place outside the camp, to which you shall go for the necessities of nature, carrying a peg on your belt” (Deut. XXIII).

The circle signifies the spiritual circuit in the Scriptures. In Exodus. The little chains signify the testimonies of the Scriptures, holding one another together. The vessels in the tabernacle signify the faithful in the Church. Hence the Apostle says: “But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware” [Col. 0395C] (II Tim. II).

The door of the tabernacle signifies the present life, or entrance into faith, or the beginning of good works. Hence in Leviticus: “And he shall bring him to the door of the tabernacle, and shall place his hand upon the head of his victim” (Lev. IV).

The golden altar signifies divinity itself, or the height of faith. In Exodus: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exod. XX). For in the Old Testament two altars are recorded as having been made: one was the altar of burnt offering, on which victims were sacrificed; the other was the altar of incense, on which incense was offered to the Lord.

The altar of burnt offering, in general, signifies the life of the righteous, who customarily crucify their flesh daily, with its vices and desires, and offer it to God as a living sacrifice. The altar of incense, however, which was made for burning incense, signifies the particular life of certain perfect people. It was not without reason that the flesh of animals was burned on one altar and incense was burned on the other: for the first prefigured those who do not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but, as though sacrificing these desires to the Lord, dedicate all the senses of their bodies to his will through the fire of his Holy Spirit. The second expresses the type of those who, with greater perfection of mind, after all the enticements of the flesh have been utterly extinguished and lulled to rest, offer to the Lord only the vows of their prayers. They have nothing in the flesh that attacks them, nor anything in their conscience concerning sin by which they may be troubled and afraid; rather, through the outpouring of tears, they more sweetly desire to come and stand before the face of God.

Hence this altar was appropriately placed inside, near the veil and [Col. 0396A] the ark, while the other was placed outside, before the tabernacle. For the former plainly represents those who shine before the sight of the holy Church as examples of every virtue; the latter represents those who, through the ardor of desire and contemplation of future blessedness, draw very near even while detained in the body.

Appropriately, the former is commanded to be covered with bronze and the latter with gold. Bronze is more sonorous than the other metals and endures for a long time; gold, however, to the extent that it is inferior in sound, surpasses bronze in brilliance. The former signifies externally the preaching of teachers; the latter inwardly indicates the splendor of divine love, where one is abundantly illumined by the light of contemplation of God.

The altar may also mystically signify the hearts of the elect, in which a sacrifice of praise and good devotion is offered to the Lord; or the height of faith, as in the Psalm: “Then you shall place calves upon your altar” [Col. 0396B] (Ps. L). Some say here that the calf itself is the Lord, who offered himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of all. Therefore, whether this is understood of young men, or of preachers, or of martyrs, the prophet could nevertheless promise such calves for the Lord’s altars, since he knew them to be suited to the Christian religion.

The altar signifies the assumed body of the Savior. In Exodus: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. XX). The altar signifies the holy Church. In Deuteronomy: “When you have crossed the Jordan, build an altar of stones that iron has not touched” (Deut. XXVII), that is, of holy faithful people whom no schism of heresies or stain of sin has defiled.

Again, the altar signifies the pastures of the Scriptures, as in the Psalm: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXV). Again, the altar signifies the hearts of the saints. In Leviticus: “But the fire on the altar shall always burn” (Lev. VI), that is, the ardor of charity.

The horns of the altar signify the height of the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalm: “Appoint the solemn day amid the throngs, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII).

The bronze altar signifies the hearts of carnal people. On this altar flesh was burned as a burnt offering, signifying those who lament carnal works.

Incense signifies the prayers of the saints. In the Psalm: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, O Lord” (Ps. CXL). Sacrifice signifies an offering of righteousness. In the Psalm: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV). A holocaust, that is, “wholly burned,” signifies total zeal of faith or mortification of the flesh. For there is a certain fire of charity that takes all a person’s members into its own service, so that it does not permit them to serve sin. And in the Psalm: “I will offer you holocausts full of marrow” (Ps. LXV). A peace-offering signifies a work of mercy; it is called a peace-offering because the offering resists the devil and reconciles a person to God. In the Psalm: “Take offerings, and enter into his courts” (Ps. XCV). The fat of the peace-offerings signifies compunction of heart and an outpouring of tears. In Leviticus: “And he shall burn the burnt offering laid upon it” (Lev. V).

In the bull is pride, which is slaughtered by the knife of self-restraint in the ark of the heart. In the ram is anger. In the goat is lust. In the calf is carnal pleasure. In the lamb is wantonness. In the kids are various sins. Through the turtledove and the pigeon, purity of chastity and simplicity of heart are offered as a sacrifice to God. In fine flour is purity of mind, or works of mercy. In firstfruits are the beginnings of good works, or good will. In tithes is the perfection of good works.

The priest is the Lord Jesus Christ, as in the Psalm: “You are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Priests signify the saints, as in Isaiah: “You shall be called the priests of the Lord and ministers of our God” (Isa. LXI); and in a bad sense, in Malachi: “You priests, why have you polluted my name?” (Mal. II.)

The garments of the priests signify works of righteousness, as in the Psalm: “Let your priests, O Lord, be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI). Again, the priest’s garments signify the people of the faithful. In Leviticus: “He shall not uncover his head, nor tear his garments” (Lev. XXI).

The hyacinth-colored tunic signifies the Church of Christ, adorned with his blood. In Exodus: “And they made a hyacinth-colored tunic, and so forth” (Exod. XXXIX).

The shoulder-piece signifies the strength of action, indicated by the shoulders. In Exodus: “And they made the shoulder-piece of gold and hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen” (ibid.).

The breastplate signifies doctrine, or truth, or the declaration of reason from the breast. In Exodus: “And they made the breastplate by woven workmanship” (ibid.).

The twelve stones in the breastplate, three placed in each of four rows, show that faith in the Trinity, the evangelical message, and the doctrine of the twelve Apostles must always be present upon the priest’s breast.

The *poderis*, that is, the inner tunic. In Exodus: “And they made the priestly garment, the *poderis*, beneath the shoulder-piece, woven work, entirely hyacinth-colored” (ibid.).

The golden bells inserted into the garments signify the word of preaching joined to works [Col. 0397C]. The pomegranates intermingled with the bells signify unity of faith and harmony of charity.

The golden plate on the forehead signifies a prefiguration of the cross or manifest judgments. In Exodus: “And they made the golden plate, and they formed upon it letters engraved with the sign of the Lord’s holiness” (ibid.).

The Holy of Holies signifies the mysteries of God, or the kingdoms of heaven. In the Apostle: “For Jesus did not enter into a sanctuary made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God” (Heb. IX).

“Temples” is a general term. For the ancients called any large places temples; and they were called temples as though they were broad roofs. But a designated place facing east was also called a temple, from contemplation. Its four parts were: the front toward the sunrise, the rear toward sunset, the left looking toward the north, [Col. 0397D] and the right looking toward the south [variant: facing]. Hence, when they built a temple, they looked toward the equinoctial east, so that a line drawn from east to west would make the right and left parts of the sky equal, in order that one who consulted or prayed might look directly toward the east.

Mystically, the temple signifies either the body of the Lord, concerning which he himself says in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, says the Lord, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II); or the assembly of the saints, to whom the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III).

If, therefore, he was made the temple of God through the humanity he assumed, and we become the temple of God through his Spirit dwelling within us, it is evident that that material temple represented all of us, namely, the Lord himself and his members, which we are: it represented him as a uniquely chosen and precious stone founded upon the foundation; but us as living stones built above the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, that is, above the Lord himself (Eph. II).

The house that King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width. The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the Church, by which, in the exile of this pilgrimage, she patiently endures every adversity until she reaches the homeland for which she waits.

The width signifies charity, which, with the bosom of the mind enlarged, knows how to love not only friends in God but also enemies for the Lord’s sake, until the time comes when, whether her enemies have been converted to her peace or utterly destroyed, she may rejoice with her friends alone in God.

The height proclaims hope of future reward. In view of this hope, one willingly despises all lowly things, whether those that delight or those that oppose, until, having passed beyond both, one may deserve to see only the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

The works that Hiram the craftsman from Tyre made for Solomon have a spiritual significance. The cast sea, ten cubits in diameter, round from rim to rim all around, bears the figure of sacred Baptism, by which we are cleansed for the remission of sins.

The twelve oxen that carried it signify the twelve Apostles [Col. 0398C] and all those who, in their place, have undertaken to govern the holy Church in Christ.

Likewise, the twelve basins in which the victims were washed signify sacred Baptism and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. The remaining vessels, which the aforementioned craftsman fashioned from bronze in clayey earth, signify the various kinds of holy people who are formed in clayey earth—that is, in sacred Scripture—for the service of God.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Entrances

“Entrance” (*aditus*) is so called from *adire*, “to approach,” because through it we enter and are admitted.

A vestibule is either the entrance of a private house or the space adjoining public buildings. It is called a vestibule because through it the doors are clothed, or because it clothes the entrance with a roof, or from *stare*, “to stand.”

The vestibule sometimes signifies faith, through which one enters the Church; sometimes humility, because no one can ascend to the steps of spiritual gifts except through the virtue of humility. Hence it is written: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI.)

The vestibule may also signify faith. It is itself before the steps and the door, because we first come to faith and afterward enter the entrance of heavenly life through the steps of spiritual gifts. One does not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith one proceeds to virtues. Through faith, therefore, one comes to works, but through works one is established in faith.

Thus the vestibule is before the steps, because the person who first believes is the one who afterward ascends by the steps of virtues to the entrance of the door.

The spiritual steps signify ascent, as in the title of the Psalter: “A Song of Ascents.”

The ivory steps signify the chaste examples of the ancient fathers: “From the ivory steps, by which they delighted you.” By these steps of virtues the true believer rightly ascends to the entrance of the door.

A portico is more a passageway than a place for standing, like a gate; and it is called a portico because it is open. A portico sometimes signifies the entrance of a house. Hence it is written in the Book of Kings: “There was a portico before the temple, twenty cubits, corresponding to the width of the temple,” and so forth (III Kings VI).

The portico that stood before the temple, being nearer, customarily received the light of the sun. What could more openly signify, in a figurative sense, that part of the age which preceded the times of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0399B]? In it are the patriarchs and prophets, who first received the Sun of righteousness rising upon this world and bore witness to the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, whether by living, preaching, being born, or even dying.

The door (*janua*) is named from a certain Janus, to whom the pagans consecrated every entrance and exit. Hence Lucan:

> “May the iron threshold of warlike Janus restrain.”

It is the first entrance of a house; the other openings within the door are generally called doors (*ostia*).

An *ostium* is an opening by which we are prevented from entering somewhere, and is so called from *obstare*, “to stand in the way.” Others say that it is called *ostium* because it detains an enemy; for there we expose ourselves to adversaries. Hence the mouths of the Tiber are called *ostia Tiberina*, because they are set against enemies.

Doors (*fores*) and folding doors (*valvae*) are fastenings. But *fores* are so called because they open outward (*foras*), whereas *valvae* turn inward and are double and foldable; general usage, however, has confused these terms. *Claustra* are so called because they are closed.

The door signifies the thought of the mind, or the entrance of the heart, as in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter your room and, having shut the door upon yourself, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI).

Entrance signifies entry into the Church through faith, and exit through the dissolution of the flesh into divine contemplation, as in the Gospel: “He shall enter and go out, and shall find pasture” (John X). And in the Psalm: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit, from this time forth and forever” (Ps. CXX).

Again, the door sometimes signifies the opening of faith, as in the Apostle: “For a great and evident door has been opened to me” (I Cor. XVI).

The door or gate of the Lord’s temple therefore signifies the Lord the Savior, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John XIV). Thus he himself says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

The door of the portico signifies prophetic speech, which, as though by a straight road, led those entering to the door of the temple, because it openly proclaimed the grace of the Lord the Savior, by which he was to redeem the world.

The entire structure of the portico, therefore, signifies all the faithful of that time; the door in the portico represents the teachers, who opened to the others the light of life and the gate of entrance to the Lord. And appropriately there is one door, on account of the harmonious faith and love of truth in all the saints.

This portico was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the temple [Col. 0400A], because the ancient righteous, through the long-suffering of devoted minds, desired to come to the enlargement of the Church in the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

It is also read in the Book of Kings (III Kings VI) that Solomon made two small doors at the entrance of the sanctuary. This signifies that good angels and holy human beings perfectly love the Lord and their neighbor; no one will be able to enter the door of life except through this twofold love. Or it signifies that the same door of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely, Jews and Gentiles.

The doorposts have five angles, because the hall of heaven receives not only the souls of the elect but also, at the judgment, opens its doors to bodies endowed with immortal glory.

The hinge is the place on which a door turns and continually moves. It is called *cardo*, from the Greek *apo tes cardias* (“from the heart”), because, just as the heart governs the whole human being, so that wedge governs and moves the door. Hence the proverbial expression, “the matter is on the hinge.”

The thresholds of doors are so called because they are transverse, like a boundary (*limes*), and through them one enters or goes out, as in a field.

Doorposts and jambs (*antes*) are named as though from “behind” and “before.” The jambs are so called because they stand before the door, or because we approach them first before entering the house; the doorposts are so called because they stand behind the door.

The hinge can signify steadfastness in right faith. The doors turn upon this, because outside the rule of faith the order of love cannot in any way separate itself.

It is also read in the Book of Kings: “The hinges of the doors of the temple were of gold” (III Kings VII). If the doors of the inner house, the Holy of Holies, signify angelic ministries that open for us, after we have departed from the body, the entrance to heavenly life; and if the doors of the temple signify holy teachers and priests, who by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood first open to us the thresholds of the present Church—what are the hinges of both sets of doors except the senses and hearts of those same angels or holy people, by which they cling immovably to the contemplation and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the ministry divinely entrusted to them?

Again, the hinge is used in a bad sense, as in Solomon, where he says: “As a door turns on its hinge, so the lazy person on his bed” (Prov. XXVI). The lazy person, therefore, on the bed of his body turns like a door on its hinge, because he proposes now to go out to work and now to return for rest; yet he never ceases to lie in his wickedness.

The thresholds [Col. 0400D] of doors signify the humility and gentleness of good morals, because in them the steps of the virtues are perfected, and through them the entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies open, as the Lord himself says: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. XXIII). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V); and the Psalmist says: “The meek shall possess the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. XXXVI).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Walls of Buildings

A foundation is so called because it is the base of a house; likewise *caementum* is derived from *caedere*, “to cut,” because it rises from large stones.

Allegorically, the foundation signifies Christ, or his catholic faith, upon which the Church has been founded. Hence it is written in the Apostle: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). And again: “You are built upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets” (Eph. II), that is, upon their teaching.

It is also read in the Psalm concerning the city of God, that is, the Church: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI), that is, Christ the Lord, who so sustains his Church that no shaking can make her totter. Rightly, therefore, she took her beginning from him, whom it is certain to be the beginning of all things.

A wall (*paries*) is so called because there are always two equal sides, either at the flank or at the front. For whether it is four-sided or six-sided, the sides that face one another will be equal. Otherwise the structure is misshapen.

We call ruins of walls *parietinae*, as though “wall ruins”: they are standing walls without a roof and without inhabitants or dwellers.

A corner is so called because it joins two walls into one.

The wall signifies the body of the Savior, as in the Psalm: “Like a leaning wall and a tottering fence” (Ps. LXI); and elsewhere: “Behold, he stands behind our wall” (Song II).

The wall signifies the pretense of hypocrites, and in Ezekiel: “They were building a wall, but they were plastering it with mud without straw” (Ezek. XIII).

The windows signify the hearing of faith or the understanding of the heart, as in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the lattice.”

Windows signify sight, hearing, smell, and the other senses of the flesh, as in Jeremiah: “Death entered through our windows” (Jer. IX).

The window signifies the thought of the heart, or the very intention of the mind, as in Zephaniah: “The voice of one singing in the window, a raven on its thresholds” (Zeph. II).

A painting on a wall signifies wicked thoughts in the human heart, as in Ezekiel: “And behold, all the idols of the house of Israel were painted on the wall” (Ezek. VIII).

The walls of God’s temple are the faithful from both peoples, that is, from the Jewish and Gentile peoples, from whom Christ built his Church. Hence it is read in the Book of Kings concerning Solomon: “He built the walls of the house within with cedar boards, from the floor of the house to the top of the walls, and he covered it with cedar wood up to the rafters” (III Kings VI).

Within, indeed, the house was clothed with cedar; on the outside, the stone itself of which it had been made shone with such brilliance that it seemed to have been woven of white marble.

According to the mystical meanings, the walls of the temple are the peoples of the faithful, from whom the holy universal Church consists. Their expansion throughout the world is signified by the width of the walls; their hope and every intention raised toward heavenly things by the length; or, certainly, the height of the wall, which consists of rows of stones placed one upon another, signifies the present state of the Church, in which the elect, all built upon the foundation of Christ, succeed one another in their order through the courses of time, each bearing the others and fulfilling the law of Christ, which is charity.

A corner is that which joins two walls into one. In Scripture, a corner, or something angular, is understood as Christ, because he joins two walls into one, namely, believers from Jews and Gentiles. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII).

Under the allusion to builders, the futile work of the Jews is explained. For they alone among human beings still appeared to be building while worshiping one God in the world, whereas the other nations were destroying themselves through the worship of idols. Builders always direct their work toward the corner, so that the solidity of the joined walls may be completed.

The Jews, however, did not complete the structure of their faith, because, like madmen, they thought that the very one who was the strongest cornerstone should be despised.

The Lord Christ is called the cornerstone in a tropological sense, as has been expounded in countless places, because he joined to himself two peoples coming from different directions, Gentiles and Jews, like twin walls, into one grace of solidity.

The prophets said various things about this stone, the Apostles about it, and many others about it.

The word “corner” (*angulus*) is derived from the Greek, namely from *gony*, which in Latin is *genu*, “knee,” because, by its bending, it forms the appearance of a corner with corresponding shape. Among the Greeks, the origin of the word is entirely preserved in its derivatives, such as *tetragonus*, *pentagonus*, and similar terms.

Summits (*culmina*) are so called because in ancient times roofs were covered with thatch, as rustic roofs are now. Hence the top of a roof is called its summit.

Vaults (*camerae*) are curved structures looking inward, and are named from their curvature. For in Greek *campulon* means “curved.”

Coffers (*laquearia*) are what cover and adorn a vault; they are also called *lacunaria*. Properly, *lacus* means “a hollow,” as Lucilius says: “The houses and lakes resound.” Its diminutive is *lacunar*, as in Horace: “Nor does a golden coffer shine in my house.” From this comes another diminutive, *lacunarium*, which by transposition of letters gives *laquearium*.

Roofs or coffers can be understood as the holy teachers. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The beams of our houses are cedar, our coffers cypress” (Song I).

By her houses she names the various gatherings of the faithful throughout the world, from all of which the universal Church consists. The beams and coffers signify the various orders of the faithful of the Church in those same houses.

Both are customarily placed high, but beams are made for support, whereas coffers contribute more to the beauty of houses than to their support. The beams therefore signify holy preachers, by whose word and example the structure of the same Church is held together so that it can stand. Through the strength of their teaching they ward off the storms of heretical assault, lest they overthrow it.

The coffers are likened to the simpler servants of Christ, who know how to adorn the Church by their own virtues rather than spread it through words of doctrine, and how to fortify it against the assaults of false teachings.

The coffers hang down, fastened to the beams, because it is necessary that all who despair of shining in the holy Church through lofty virtues should cling with their whole mind to the sayings and examples of the highest fathers, by which they may be suspended from the pursuit of earthly things.

These beams are rightly called cedar and the coffers cypress, because both trees are known to be entirely incorruptible in nature, remarkably tall, [Col. 0403A] and of exceptional fragrance. This aptly suits those who can say with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II); and: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

The roof signifies the intention of heavenly action, that is, the contemplative life, as in the Gospel: “Let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house” (Matt. XXIV).

Again, the roof signifies the human body, as in the Gospel: “What you hear in the ear, preach upon the roof” (Matt. X).

The roof is also understood as the veil of the Law and the obscurity of the holy Scriptures.

An apse (*absida*) is translated from Greek into Latin as “bright,” because, having received light, it shines through an arch. But some learned authorities consider it uncertain whether one should say *absidam* or *absidem*, since the gender of the word is ambiguous.

A shell vault (*testudo*) is the sloping vault of a temple. In the form of a tortoise shell, the ancients made the roofs of temples; this was done so that the roof might reproduce the image of heaven, which is understood to be convex. Others hold that a *testudo* is a place in the opposite part of the atrium for those approaching.

Arches are so called because they are curved by a narrow enclosure; they are also called vaults (*fornices*).

Pavements originated among the Greeks as works of art made from pictures; *lithostrota* were made from small fragments and tesserae stained in various colors. They are called pavements because they are paved (*paveantur*), that is, beaten or struck. Hence also comes *pavor*, “fear,” because fear strikes the heart.

*Ostracus* is a pavement made of fired brick, so called because broken pottery is struck into it with lime mixed in. The Greeks call a potsherd *ostracon*.

The pavement signifies the humiliation and affliction of the soul, or its inclination toward earthly things, as in the Psalm: “My soul has clung to the pavement” (Ps. CXVIII). [Col. 0403C]

A pavement is the solid surface of some ground constructed to be extremely smooth, and is rightly compared with our body, since it too is smoothed with a similar polish. He therefore says that he has clung to his flesh; there is no doubt that this is a fault. If the soul clings to the body, it favors sins; if it is separated from it in will, it favors virtues.

The pavement signifies the humility of the faithful who patiently receive the teaching of the saints, as in Ezekiel: “And before the treasury was a pavement laid with stone” (Ezek. XL).

It is also read in the Book of Kings (III Kings VI) that Solomon covered the pavement with gold inside and outside, that is, in the sanctuary and in the temple itself. Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold inside and outside, because our peaceful King completely and fully separated the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven from the baseness of mortals through the gift of eternal love.

The *compluvium* is so called because the portions of water around it converge there.

Tesserae are the pieces with which dwellings are paved; they are named from *tesserae*, that is, square stones, by diminutive formation.

Bases are the supports of columns, rising from the foundation and bearing the weight of the structure placed upon them. *Bases* is also the name, in the Syriac language, for a very strong rock.

Columns are named from their length and roundness; the weight of the entire structure is raised upon them. The ancient proportion for columns was that their height should be three times their width.

There are four kinds of round columns: Doric, Ionic, Tuscan, and Corinthian, differing from one another in the measure of their thickness and height. A fifth kind consists of those called Attic, having four or more angles with equal intervals between their sides.

Capitals are so called because they are the heads of columns, just as the head is above the neck.

Epistyles are placed above the capitals of columns; the word is Greek and means “laid upon.”

Mystically, the bases can be understood as the books of the divine Testaments, upon which all the teaching of the holy preachers rests.

The columns are the Apostles and teachers of the Gospel. They were prefigured by the two columns that Hiram is said to have made in the construction of the Lord’s temple, as it is written in the Book of Kings and Chronicles: “Hiram completed all the work of the king in the house of God,” that is, the two columns and the epistyles and capitals, and certain net-like structures that covered the capitals above the epistyles (II Chron. [Col. 0404B] IV).

These are the columns of which Paul says: “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be columns, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Gal. II).

By these words he seems, as it were, to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they signified and why two were made. For they signify all the holy Apostles and teachers, spiritual people who are strong in faith and action and raised toward heavenly things in contemplation.

There are two of them so that by preaching they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church. They stood in the portico before the doors of the temple and wonderfully adorned its entrance on both sides with their dignity and beauty.

The door of the temple is the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John XIV); and as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

The columns placed on either side stand before that door when the ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.

The capitals of the columns, that is, their uppermost part, are the inmost thoughts of faithful teachers. Just as the head directs the limbs, so all their works and words are directed by their thoughts devoted to God.

The two capitals placed above these heads signify the two Testaments. Through meditation upon and observance of them, the holy teachers submit themselves with all their mind and body.

Hence each capital appropriately had a height of five cubits, because the writing of the Mosaic Law is contained in five books. The entire series of the Old Testament also encompasses five ages of the world.

The New Testament proclaims nothing other than what Moses and the prophets had foretold would be proclaimed through it.

The appearance of chains and the likeness of a net in the capitals signify the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints, concerning which the Lord is praised in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed around with a variety of diverse spiritual gifts” (Ps. XLIV).

Or certainly, the many interlacings of chains and the spreading of the net indicate the manifold persons of the elect. By listening faithfully to and obeying the words of the holy preachers, they cling to them; like nets and little chains placed above the capitals of the columns, they present to all who look upon them the wonder of their interconnectedness [Col. 0405A].

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Storerooms

A treasury (*aerarium*) is so called because formerly stamped bronze (*aes signatum*) was stored there. This was once the customary practice, before gold and silver had been stamped. Although money was later made from these metals, the name *aerarium* nevertheless remained from the metal from which money had its beginning.

An armory (*armarium*) is a place where instruments of any arts are kept; an arsenal (*armamentarium*) is a place where only weapons are kept. Hence Juvenal says: “Whatever weapons the arsenals of heaven possess.” Both words are derived from *arma*, that is, arms, the limbs by which people exercise themselves.

A library is a place where books are stored. For in Greek *biblos* means “book,” and *theca* means “repository.”

A storeroom (*cellarium*) is so called because table supplies are collected there, or because whatever necessities remain for food are stored there. The difference between a *promptuarium* and a *cellarium* is that a *cellarium* is for a few days, whereas a *promptuarium* is for a long period.

A *promptuarium* is so called because necessities for food are brought forth from it, that is, produced or taken out.

*Promptuaria* are sometimes understood in a bad sense, as in the Psalm: “Their storehouses are full, bursting forth from this one thing to that” (Ps. CXLIII).

The storehouses that the common people call storerooms signify the hearts of heretics, where various kinds of things and foods have been deposited. The more abundantly these are stuffed, the more they emit diverse eruptions of foul exhalation.

If you overcome them by authority, they turn to the wickedness of interpretations; when, with the Lord’s help, they have also been defeated there, they turn to the tricks and slanders of sophists—wandering and unstable, because they cannot possess the root of truth.

Hence they are compared with harsh odors, which deceive the hearts of the simple with foul speech.

A warehouse (*apotheca*), or granary, may be called in Greek by a term meaning “repository” or “place of concealment,” because people store in these places the crops they have cultivated. Hence by the Greek name *entecham* we call a stored and abundant substance of a thing.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Workshops and Workrooms
The *ergasterium* is a place where some work is done: for in Greek, *ergon* means “work,” and *sterion* means “station,” that is, “of workers.” *Ergastula* too are named from the same Greek word; they are places where criminals are assigned to perform some work, as gladiators and exiles commonly are—those who cut marble and yet are bound under the custody of chains.

The *genetheum* [*gynaeceum*] is so called in Greek because women gather there to practice wool-working; for “woman” is called *gyne* in Greek. A *pistrinum* is so called as though it were *pilistrinum*, because grain was formerly pounded with a pestle. Hence among the ancients millers were called not *molitores* but *pistores*, as though *pinsors*, from pounding (*pinsere*) grain. For the use of the mill did not yet exist; they pounded grain with a pestle. Hence Virgil also says:

> Now roast the grain in fire; now break it with stone.

A *clibanus*, that is, an oven, is said to be named by derivation from *far* (“grain”), because bread made from it is baked there. The *clibanus* (as we have said) signifies everlasting burning, as in the Gospel: “For if the grass, which is today in the field and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” (Matt. VI). Hence the *clibanus* signifies the tribulation of the present life, as in Jeremiah: “Our skin, that is, our flesh, has been burned like an oven by the face of the storms of famine” (Lam. V).

A *clibanus* is a rounded form made from a bronze vessel for baking bread, burning within beneath consuming flames. In this likeness sinners are rightly placed: at the future judgment they will be tormented both by anguish of spirit and by penal suffering, because they lived with an obstinate mind against the Lord’s commandments. Of them it is said in the Psalm: “You will place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence” (Ps. XX). The Lord’s presence is the day of judgment, when the Son of Man will be seen by human beings; but only the righteous will also behold him in contemplation of his divinity.

A *torcular* is so called because grapes are trodden there and the juice produced from them is pressed out. A *forum* is a place where grapes are trodden; it is so called either because grapes are carried there (*feratur*), or because they are struck there by the feet (*feriatur*). Hence it is also called a *calcatorium*, though this word has many meanings.

A *torcular* signifies an altar, because offerings and fruits are brought there, as in Isaiah’s song: “And I dug a winepress in it” (Isa. V). Likewise, the *torcular* signifies future tribulation, as in the Apocalypse: “He himself trod the winepress of the wine of the wrath of the fury of God” (Rev. XIX). Thus the *torcular*, which according to the usage of Holy Scripture is sometimes used for the vengeance and punishments of sinners and sometimes for the gathering of new fruits, is used for penalties and torments when Jeremiah, lamenting in the Lamentations the overthrow of Jerusalem, says: “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep” (Lam. I).

In a favorable sense, psalms are inscribed “for the winepresses”: the eighth and the eighty-third. For the title of the eightieth Psalm reads: “For the end; for the winepresses; of Asaph.” The “fifth Sabbath” is the fifth day from the Sabbath, called by the Gentiles Thursday and by us the fifth feria. On it God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things having living souls, and winged creatures beneath the firmament of heaven,” mystically signifying that men of diverse virtue would be born from the waters of baptism.

The intention of this title, therefore, is as follows: “for the end” designates the Lord Christ; “for the winepresses,” the Church tested by persecutions; “Asaph,” the congregation; “the fifth Sabbath,” baptism. From this it is gathered that the Psalm will speak in the Lord’s Church of the congregation brought to new birth. Historically, Asaph speaks of this matter; but it is better understood spiritually by the Christian people.

A *lake* signifies hell, as in the Psalter: “They placed me in the lowest lake,” and elsewhere: “They led my life down into the lake of death” (Ps. LXXXVII).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Fortifications

A fortified place, or fortification, is so called because it is made by hand. A *cohors* [Al., *cors*] is so called either because it confines everything within, that is, encloses it, or because by its obstruction it restrains outsiders and prevents them from approaching.

A *vallum* is what is raised by a mass of earth, so that a protective barrier may be extended. It is named from *vallis* (“valley”). For *valli* are so called because they are fixed in the ground and pulled up. *Intervalla* are the spaces between the heads of the ramparts, that is, between the stakes by which the rampart is made; hence other spaces too are named from the stakes.

An *agger* is a heap or accumulation of any material, by which ditches or valleys can be filled. Properly, an *agger* is earth heaped up and placed close to a constructed rampart; but improperly we call walls and all fortifications *aggeres*.

In Scripture, a rampart or embankment signifies the constriction of enemies by which they hem in those whom they wish to harm. Hence the Lord says to Jerusalem in the Gospel: “The days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and hem you in on every side, and cast you and your children who are within you down to the ground” (Luke XIX). This signifies the human soul—which ought to have been a vision of peace—being brought into distress because of its sins.

For who are greater enemies of the human soul than evil spirits? They besiege it as it departs from the body; while they cherish it, placed in the love of the flesh, with deceptive pleasures, they hem it in, dragging it into fellowship with their own damnation. Thus, when it is caught at the very extremity of life, it sees by what enemies it is surrounded and yet cannot find a way of escape, because it is no longer permitted to do the good works which, when permitted, it scorned to perform.

*Maceriae* are long walls by which vineyards and other places are enclosed. For the Greeks call “long” *macron*. Hedges are the fortifications of planted fields, and from this they receive their name.

Mystically, a wall or hedge signifies the protection of angels by which God’s people—called through the prophet the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth—were surrounded and defended. Hence it is written in Isaiah: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill” (Isa. V). And shortly afterward: “I will remove its hedge, and it will be for plundering. I will tear down its wall, and it will be for trampling” (ibid.). In the Gospel the Lord himself presents the parable, saying: “There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge” (Matt. XXI).

Likewise, in the Psalter we read of the same vineyard: “You have destroyed all its walls; you have made its fortifications a terror” (Ps. LXXIX). Thus a wall is something that fortifies places prepared for some useful purpose, as a defense. It is not built by mixing it with any other material, but is constructed, like a wall, solely by joining stones together. In its likeness Scripture sets forth that simple and unconquerable divine defense which had to be removed so that the Jewish people could be devastated by the assault of enemies.

It is beautifully said: “You have made its fortifications a terror,” so that, because of their sins, they would fear the Lord himself, by whose protection they had been accustomed to be fenced in.

A wall therefore signifies the cross of Christ, as some wish to understand it, as in the Psalm: “Like a wall leaning over and a wall struck down” (Ps. LXI).

*Caulae* are protections for sheep, or enclosures for sheepfolds. The word is Greek, with the *c* removed; for the Greeks call the shelters of animals *aulae*. Allegorically, just as sheep signify religious people who are gentle and live innocently, so sheepfolds signify the holy Church, where Christ’s sheep are placed, preserved, and defended from beasts.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Tents

*Tabernacula* are the tents of soldiers, in which, while on campaign, they avoid the heat of the sun, storms of rain, and the hardships of cold. They are called *tabernacula* because curtains stretched by ropes, with boards standing between them, were hung up to support the tents.

A *tentorium* is so called because it is stretched by ropes and stakes; hence even today *praetendere* (“to stretch out before”) is used.

Mystically, a tent or tabernacle signifies either the present Church, just as that Mosaic tabernacle was constructed in the desert as a prefiguration of it; or the congregation of the faithful from the nations, as in the Psalmist: “How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII); or the condition of the human body, of which the Apostle says: “As long as we are in this tabernacle, we groan, being burdened, unwilling to be unclothed but to be clothed upon” (II Cor. V).

A tabernacle also signifies the mind’s thought, as in blessed Job: “Fire devours the tabernacles of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job XV). For just as the body dwells in a tabernacle, so the mind dwells in thought; but fire devours the tabernacles when the heat of avarice ravages the thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Tombs

[Col. 0408C]

A *sepulcrum* is named from one who has been buried. Formerly, each person was buried in his own house; afterward this was forbidden by law, lest the bodies of the living should be infected by contact with the stench itself.

A *monumentum* is so called because it reminds the mind of the deceased. When you do not see a monument, what is written is fulfilled: “He was forgotten as one dead from the heart.” But when you see one, it admonishes the mind and brings you back to remembrance, so that you remember the dead. Thus monuments are called *memoriae* (“memorials”) because they admonish the mind.

A *tumulus* is so called as though it were *tumens tellus*, “swelling earth.” *Sarcophagus* is Greek, because bodies are consumed there: for *sarx* means “flesh” in Greek, and *phagein* means “to eat.”

*Mausolea* are the tombs or monuments of kings, named from Mausolus, king of the Egyptians. After his death, his wife constructed a tomb of extraordinary size and beauty, to such an extent that even today all costly monuments are called *mausolea* from his name.

A *pyramid* is a type of tomb, square and rising to a summit beyond every height that can be made by hand. Hence they are said to surpass the measure of shadows and to have no shadow. Such a building rises so that it begins broadly and ends narrowly, like fire—for *pyr* means “fire.”

Egypt possesses these monuments. Among the ancients, powerful people were buried either beneath mountains or in houses. From this arose the practice of constructing pyramids over corpses or placing enormous columns there.

Mystically, a tomb sometimes signifies hidden wickedness or the preaching of heretics. Hence the Psalmist says: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. XIII). The tomb is the throat of one who lies, rolling in his jaws a destructive vanity that inflicts the evil of death. He rightly added “open”: if it were closed, it would give off less stench.

Sometimes it signifies the foul conduct of a sinner and a greedy man. Hence the same Psalmist says: “Their tombs are their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII), because they choose to persevere in the avarice and luxury they have begun.

A tomb also signifies hypocrites, who outwardly display simulated righteousness but inwardly are full of wickedness and sorrow. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel that they are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead (Matt. XXIII).

Sometimes, however, a tomb is understood in a favorable sense, as in Eliphaz’s statement to blessed Job: “You will enter the tomb in abundance” (Job V). What is signified by the name “tomb” except the contemplative life? It buries us, as though dead to this world, when it hides us away within from earthly desires.

He therefore says: “You will enter the tomb in abundance.” The perfect man enters the tomb in abundance because he first gathers the works of the active life and afterward, through contemplation, completely hides from this world the sense of the flesh, dead to it.

A tomb is also understood as the memory of the Lord’s death and resurrection, as in Isaiah: “And his tomb will be glorious” (Isa. XI).

A tomb signifies the body subjected to sins, or all who simulate righteousness, as in the Gospel: “Woe to you, Pharisees and scribes, who are like whitewashed tombs” (Matt. XXIII).

A pit signifies the damnation of sinners, as in the Psalm: “That you may restrain him from evil days, until a pit is dug” (Ps. XCIII).

A pit signifies the damnation of the devil or Antichrist, as in the prophet: “They will track down Assur,” that is, Antichrist, “in the pit of Nebroth” (Zech. X).

A *fovea* signifies deceit or a snare leading to death, as in the Psalm: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit that he made” (Ps. VII).

A pit signifies heretical deception, as in Solomon: “A prostitute is a deep pit, and another man’s wife is a narrow well” (Prov. XXIII).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Rustic Buildings

A *casa* is a rural dwelling woven from stakes, branches, and reeds, by which people can protect themselves from the force of cold or the harshness of heat.

A *tugurium* is a little hut made by vineyard keepers as a covering for themselves, as though it were a *tegurium* (“covering”): either to turn aside the heat and rays of the sun, or so that from it they might drive away people or little creatures that commonly lie in wait for ripening crops. Country people call it a *capanna*, because it accommodates only one person.

A *casa* or *tugurium* can signify the poverty of the present life. Hence we read that our fathers dwelt in little huts in the land of their pilgrimage (Heb. XI). Through the *tugurium*, Isaiah expresses a worthless dwelling and one soon to fall in this world, as in the words: “Zion will be like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field” (Isa. I).

## CHAPTER XXX. On Fields

A field is called *ager* in Latin because something is done (*agitur*) in it. Others more clearly believe that *ager* derives from Greek; hence a farm is called *choragros* in Greek.

A *villa* is named from a rampart, that is, an embankment of earth, which is customarily established as a boundary.

*Possessiones* are widely extending fields, public and private, which at the beginning people did not acquire by formal conveyance but each occupied and possessed as he was able; hence they received this name.

A *fundus* is so called because a patrimony is founded or established upon it. A *fundus* is to be understood as either an urban or a rural building.

A *praedium* is so called because it is especially foreseen by the head of a household, that is, because it appears beforehand, as though *praevidium*; or because the ancients held fields they had taken in war as booty.
