Every field, as Varro teaches, is divided in four ways: it is either *arvus*, that is, arable; or *consitus*, that is, planted and suitable for trees; or *pascualis*, which is given over only to grasses and animals; or *floreus*, containing gardens suitable for bees and flowers. Virgil followed this classification in the fourth book of the *Georgics*.

By the name “field” the human race, dwelling in this world, is expressed. Hence we read in the Gospel parable: “The field is the world” (Matt. XIII), in which the holy word of God is sown. But it produced fruit according to the difference of the soil: good soil produces a hundredfold fruit of good works; bad soil produces thorns and thistles of vices, and is also near to a curse.

A field also signifies the Church, as in Genesis: “Behold,” Isaac said, “the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which God has blessed” (Gen. XXVII). And in the Gospel: “They bought from them the potter’s field for the burial of strangers” (Matt. XXVII).

A field also signifies the Jewish people. Concerning this field Solomon says to the priest Abiathar: “Go to your field at Anathoth” (II Kings II).

A field also signifies the discipline of the Christian religion, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field; when a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells everything he has and buys that field,” and so forth (Matt. XIII).

This treasure signifies heavenly desire. The field in which the treasure is hidden signifies the discipline of the pursuit of heaven. The man who finds this treasure signifies the humble and religious, because they rejoice greatly when they receive a good desire. Then, having sold—that is, despised—the pleasures of the flesh and all earthly delights, they trample underfoot everything in the world through the discipline of heavenly vigilance. Nothing that flatters the flesh now pleases them; nothing that destroys the life of the flesh is feared by the spirit.

Alternatively, this treasure is understood as Christ; and the field is Holy Scripture, in which knowledge of our Savior is stored. Whoever, by his grace revealing him, comes to know him must despise all the delights of the world and hasten toward knowledge of him through continual practice of good works.

When the treasure has been found, it is hidden so that it may be preserved, because no one can preserve the pursuit of good will in the work of God if he does not hide it from human praise.

The ancients called uncultivated fields *rura*, that is, woods and pastures; but they called a cultivated field *ager*. For the *rus* is where honey, milk, and livestock can be found. Hence one is called *rusticus*. These were the first and leisurely blessings of country people.

A *seges* is a field in which seed is sown. Hence Virgil says:

> That crop at last answers the hopes  
> of the greedy farmer.

A *compascuus ager* is a field left by those who divided the lands for common pasture among the neighbors.

An *alluvius ager* is so called because a river gradually flows into the field.

An *arcifinius ager* is so called because it is not contained by fixed measurements of lines; rather, its boundaries are kept in place by the obstruction of rivers, mountains, and trees. Hence in such fields no *subsitum* [Al., *subsecivorum*] intervenes.

A *novalis ager* is land newly plowed for the first time, or land that lies fallow in alternate years in order to renew its strength. For *novalia* are once productive and once empty. *Novalia* can signify fruitful labors newly begun. Hence the prophetic saying: “Renew your fallow ground” (Hos. X), as though he were saying: “Exercise yourselves in useful pursuits, lest idleness make you barren.”

Thus it is also written elsewhere: “There is much food in the fallow fields of the fathers” (Prov. XIII), that is, abundant delights of virtues are found in the teachings and examples of holy teachers.

An *area* is a level surface of boards. It is called *area* from its flatness and evenness; hence also *ara*. Others say that it is called *area* because bronze pieces are given for threshing grain, as though *aerea*; or because only dry things are threshed upon it.

Mystically, the threshing floor signifies the Church. Hence John the Baptist is read to have said of Christ in the Gospel: “His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III). By the winnowing fan, that is, the shovel, the discernment of just judgment is signified; by the threshing floor, the present Church is designated. In it, unquestionably—and this is very grievous—“many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII): few grains are destined for the dwellings above, in comparison with the many that are to be consigned to everlasting flames.

The cleansing of this threshing floor is now carried out individually, when each perverse person is either expelled from the Church for manifest sins or condemned after death by divine severity for hidden sins. It will be completed universally at the end, when the Son of Man sends his angels and they gather from his kingdom all scandals (Matt. XIII).

The Lord therefore has the winnowing fan in his hand—that is, he holds the discernment of judgment in his power—because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Measures of Fields

[Col. 0412A]

We call measures of roads *milliaria*; the Greeks call them *stadia*, the Gauls *leugae*, the Egyptians *schaeni*, and the Persians *parasangae*. Each has its own proper extent.

A *milliarium* is bounded by one thousand paces. It is called *milliarium*, as though *milliadium*, having five thousand feet.

A *leuca* ends at one thousand five hundred paces.

A *stadium* is one-eighth of a *milliarium*, consisting of one hundred twenty-five paces. They say that Hercules first established it and measured it by the distance he could cover in a single breath; for that reason he called it a *stadium*, because at its end he drew breath and at the same time stopped.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Roads

[Col. 0412B]

A road is a route along which a vehicle can travel, and it is called *via* from the movement of vehicles. For it allows two tracks because of the movement of vehicles going and coming.

Every road is either public or private. A public road is one situated on public land, along which passage and the movement of the people are open. Such a road leads either to the sea or to towns. A private road is one assigned to a neighboring municipality.

The word *via* has several meanings. Sometimes it is understood in a favorable sense, and sometimes in the contrary sense.

The road signifies the Lord Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Through him we proceed to eternal life, and by his gift we receive true blessedness.

Sometimes the word “road” designates the divine commandments and the rules of the holy Scriptures. Hence the Psalmist says: “I ran the way of your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. XXIV).

Sometimes it signifies a person’s life. Hence the Prophet says: “I declared my ways, and you heard me” (Ps. CXVIII).

The meaning of “road” is drawn in the contrary direction when, because of the path of an evil mind, it indicates the practice of evil works, as in the prophetic saying: “Remove from me the way of iniquity” (ibid.). And in the Book of Wisdom we read: “There are ways that seem right to people, but their ends lead to hell” (Prov. XVI).

Hence it is called a broad road, that is, one widened by the allurements of vices, as in the Gospel: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII).

The narrow road is one made strict or pressed by tribulations, concerning which it is written: “How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life!” (ibid.).

A straight road is one adorned with God’s commandments, as in Isaiah: “Make straight,” he says, “the paths of God” (Isa. XL).

A crooked road is one that deviates from God’s commandments, as in the same prophet: “The crooked ways will become straight, and the rough places into level roads” (ibid.). For that road is level which has been made even by obedience to God’s commandments.

Elsewhere we read: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right; those on the left are perverse” (Prov. IV).

A *strata* is so called as though it were a road worn by the feet of the common people. Lucretius says:

> And the roads already worn down by the feet of the common people.

It is also called *dilapidata*, that is, paved with stones. The Carthaginians are said to have first paved roads with stones; afterward the Romans laid them throughout nearly the whole world, to keep the people from idleness because of the straightness of the routes.

An *agger* is the raised middle of a paved road, laid with piled-up stones. It is named from *agger*, that is, from accumulation. Historians call it a military road, as in the verse:

> Like a snake often caught upon the raised road.

An *iter* or *itus* is a route along which a person can go in any direction. *Iter* and *itiner* have different meanings. An *iter* is a place easy to pass through, and from this we also use the word *itus*. An *itiner* is a journey along a long road, and also the labor of walking by which one reaches the destination one desires.

A *semita* is half an *iter*, from *semi-itus*. A *semita* belongs to human beings; a *callis* belongs to wild animals and cattle.

A *callis* is a narrow and well-trodden route for livestock between mountains, named from the callus of the feet, or from the hardened hoofs of animals.

*Tramites* are transverse paths through fields or straight roads; they are so called because they cross over.

*Divortia* are bends or branchings of roads, that is, roads extending in different directions. Now *diverticula* are divergent and divided roads, or transverse paths situated at the side of a road.

A *bivium* is so called because it is a double road. *Compita* are so called because several roads meet in them, as in *trivia* and *quadrivia*.

This too must be observed in each passage where these names of roads are marked: their meaning is to be understood from the preceding or following passages of the same writing. For in this way their fitting sense can readily be discerned, whether they belong to a favorable or an unfavorable meaning.

# BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0413]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Philosophers

[Col. 0413B]

Philosophers are so called from the Greek designation, which in Latin is interpreted as “lovers of wisdom.” For a philosopher is one who possesses knowledge of divine and human matters and follows the entire path of right living. The name “philosophers” is said first to have arisen from Pythagoras. [Col. 0413C] For when the ancient Greeks had previously arrogantly called themselves Sophists—that is, wise men, or teachers of wisdom—he was asked what profession he followed and modestly replied that he was a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom, since claiming to be wise seemed exceedingly arrogant. Thereafter it pleased later generations that, however much anyone seemed to excel either himself or others in knowledge concerning matters belonging to wisdom, he should be called nothing other than a philosopher.

Philosophers themselves are divided into three classes: they are either physicists, ethicists, or logicians. They are called physicists because they treat of natures, for nature is called *physis* in Greek. They are called ethicists because they treat of morals; for custom is called *ethos* among the Greeks. They are called logicians because they add reasoning to the study of natures and morals; for reason is called *logos* in Greek.

[Col. 0413D] Physics, however, is divided into seven parts: Arithmetic, Astronomy, Astrology, Mechanics, Medicine, Geometry, and Music. Arithmetic is the science of numbers. Astronomy is concerned with the rising and setting of the stars. Astrology is the study of the stars—their nature and power—and of the motion of the heavens. Mechanics is expertise in the craft of working metals, wood, and stones. Medicine is the science of remedies, devised for the balance and health of the body. Geometry is the discipline of measuring the dimensions of places and the sizes of bodies. Music is the division of sounds, the variety of voices, and the modulation of singing.

Ethics, however, is divided into four parts: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Prudence leads a person to recognition of the truth. Justice preserves love of God and neighbor. Fortitude overcomes adversity and scorns death. Temperance restrains vicious pleasures and governs everything.

Logic is divided into two kinds: Dialectic and Rhetoric. Dialectic is a sharp disputation that distinguishes the true from the false. Rhetoric is the discipline competent for persuasion in every matter.

Philosophers themselves were divided according to their sects. Some received their names from their founders, such as the Platonists, Epicureans, and Pythagoreans; others from the places where they held their meetings and established their schools, such as the Peripatetics, Stoics, and Academics.

The Platonists were named after Plato. They assert that God is the creator of souls and that angels are the creators of bodies; they say that souls return through many cycles of years into different bodies.

The Stoics were named from a place. For there was a portico at Athens which the Greeks called *Stoa*, in which the deeds of wise men and the histories of brave men were painted. The wise gathered in this portico and philosophized, and from it they were called Stoics; for a portico is called *stoa* in Greek. Zeno first established this sect.

They deny that anyone can become blessed without virtue. They assert that every sin is equal, saying: the one who steals straw is as guilty as the one who steals gold; the one who kills a small bird is as guilty as the one who kills a horse. For it is not the animal but the intention that makes the crime. They also say that the soul perishes together with the body, and they deny that the soul, which contains virtue, is either immortal or eternal. Yet they seek eternal glory while admitting that they are not eternal.

The Academics were named after Plato’s villa, the Academy of Athens, where Plato himself taught. They believe that everything is uncertain. But just as it must be admitted that many things are uncertain and hidden—things which God willed to exceed human understanding—so nevertheless many things exist which the senses can grasp through penetrating reason. Arcesilaus, a Cyrenaic philosopher, discovered this sect. Democritus was his follower, and he said that truth lay hidden in obscurity like something in a deep well whose bottom cannot be found.

The Peripatetics were named from walking about, because Aristotle, their founder, used to dispute while walking. They say that a certain part of the soul is eternal, while the greater part of it is mortal.

The Cynics were named from the impurity of their shamelessness. For, contrary to human modesty, it was their custom to have intercourse openly with their spouses. They judged it lawful and honorable to lie openly with one’s wife, because marriage is legitimate, and they publicly preached that this should be done—as dogs do in streets and alleys. Hence they also took their title and name from dogs, whose life they imitated.

The Epicureans were named after a certain philosopher, Epicurus, a lover of vanity rather than wisdom, whom philosophers also called a pig because, wallowing in filth, he asserted that bodily pleasure was the highest good. [Col. 0415B] He also said that the world was neither equipped nor governed by any divine providence, but assigned the origin of things to atoms—that is, indivisible and solid bodies—from whose chance collisions all things arise and have arisen. They assert that God does nothing, that everything consists of bodies, and that the soul is nothing other than a body. Hence he also said: “I shall not exist after I have died.”

The Gymnosophists are said to philosophize naked in the shadowy solitudes of India, wearing coverings only over their genitals. For *gymnasium* is so called because young men exercise naked in the field, where they cover only their private parts. They also abstain from procreation.

The Theologians are the same as the physicists. They are called Theologians because in their writings they spoke about God.

[Col. 0415C] Their opinions differed as they sought to determine what God was. Some, understanding him in bodily terms, said that this visible world, composed of the four elements, was God, as did Dionysius the Stoic. Others understood him spiritually as mind, as did Thales of Miletus. Some said that God was the soul moving through all things and giving them life, as did Pythagoras. Some said that God was timeless and unchanging, as did Plato. Some said that he was a mind set free, as did Cicero. Some said that he was both spirit and mind, as did Maro [Virgil].

They discovered God only in name, but did not explain him as they had found him: “They became futile in their thoughts; claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1).

The Platonists assert that God is caretaker, arbiter, and judge; the Epicureans say that he is idle and inactive. The Platonists affirm that the world is incorporeal; [Col. 0415D] the Stoics, that it is corporeal. Epicurus said it arose from atoms, Pythagoras from numbers, and Heraclitus from fire. Hence Varro also calls fire the soul of the world, because it governs everything in the world just as the soul governs us. He says this most foolishly, for, when the soul is in us, “we ourselves are”; when it departs, “we die.” Therefore, when fire departs from the world through lightning, the world also dies.

These errors of the philosophers also introduced heresies into the Church. From them came the aeons and certain forms—I know not what; from them, among Arius’s followers, the Trinity of the Godhead, and among Valentinus’s followers, Platonic madness; from them, Marcion’s better God of tranquility, for it had come from the Stoics. Epicurus supplies the basis for saying that the soul perishes, and the denial of the restoration of the flesh is taken from the empty school of all the philosophers. Wherever matter is made equal to God, there is the teaching of Zeno. Wherever something is read about a fiery God, Heraclitus intervenes.

The same material is tossed about among heretics and philosophers, and the same arguments are entangled. But, rejecting the errors of the gentiles and heretics—[spretis: “despised”]—we must state what true philosophy is according to the understanding of the Catholic Fathers.

Philosophy, therefore, is inquiry into nature and knowledge of human and divine matters, insofar as it is possible for a human being to investigate them. Philosophy is also uprightness of life, the pursuit of right living, meditation on death, and contempt for the world—something especially fitting for Christians, who, having trampled underfoot the world’s ambition, live in disciplined imitation of the future homeland.

The subject matter of philosophy, therefore, consists of knowledge and opinion. [Col. 0416B] Knowledge exists when something is perceived through certain reasoning—for example, that a solar eclipse is caused by the interposition of the moon, or the historical text in the Scriptures, which expresses the truth of things accomplished, or the faithful instruction of moral life. Opinion exists when an uncertain matter remains hidden and cannot be defined by any firm reasoning—for example, the magnitude of the heavens, the depth of the earth, or discussion of invisible and incomprehensible things.

Philosophy is therefore divided into three parts: Physics, Ethics, and Logic, as we showed above. In Physics, then, the cause of inquiry is considered; in Ethics, the order of living; in Logic, the method of understanding. The divine words of Scripture consist in these three kinds of philosophy. For they customarily discuss nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes; morals, as in Proverbs and throughout the books generally; or logic—which our theologians claim for themselves—as in the Song of Songs and the holy Gospel.

Theological philosophy is also that which is called contemplative: by it, having surpassed visible things, we contemplate divine and heavenly matters with the mind alone. True philosophy is likewise divided into two parts, contemplative and practical.

Practical philosophy consists in the operations necessary for this mortal life. Through it, the manner of living, honorable desire, and practices directed toward the virtues are exercised; through the other, God is loved and worshiped in hope and faith.

Therefore, whoever desires to be wise and wishes to arrive at recognition of true wisdom and contemplation of truth itself must read the Holy Scriptures attentively according to the rule of the Catholic faith. He must also strive to exercise himself in the sacred virtues by living well according to their teachings, and endeavor to keep a pure heart free from every evil desire and worldly craving. In this way, with God’s help, he will be able to reach the desired good.

The Psalmist shows this to us when he says: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of God. Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. 118). Here Truth itself also says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0417A] We must therefore first understand that certain things are so clear and noble that they should not be sought for any other advantage, but should be loved and pursued solely for their own dignity—namely virtue, knowledge of the truth, and good love. The true philosophers understood these things in human nature and honored them with the greatest zeal.

Virtue, therefore, is a disposition of the soul, the adornment of nature, the rule of life, and nobility of character. It has four parts: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Prudence is knowledge of things and natures. It has three parts: memory, understanding, and foresight. Memory is that by which the mind recalls what has been. Understanding is that by which it perceives what is. Foresight is that by which something future is anticipated before it occurs.

The definition of justice is as follows: justice is a disposition of the soul that assigns to each thing its proper dignity. In it the worship of divinity, the rights of humanity, and the equity of the whole of life are preserved.

Justice is constituted partly by natural law and partly by customary practice, because its parts incorporate a certain natural right: religion, piety, gratitude, vindication, observance, and truth. Their definitions may be given as follows.

Religion is the care and ritual observance owed to a certain superior being whom they call divine. Piety is the dutiful and diligent service rendered to those joined to us by blood and to benevolent fellow citizens. Gratitude contains remembrance of friendships and services, together with the willingness to repay them. Vindication is the defense or avenging by which right, injury, and altogether anything harmful are repelled. Observance is the respect and honor shown to people who precede us in some dignity. Truth is the declaration of what is, what was, or what will be.

Justice is therefore observed through customary practice, so that it is considered according to agreement, an equitable judgment, and law. An agreement is something jointly settled among certain persons, though not among everyone. An equitable judgment is something established by the opinions of one or more eminent men. Law is written right for an entire people, prescribing what it must avoid or observe.

The third kind of virtue is fortitude, which is defined as follows: fortitude is the endurance of dangers and labors with a great spirit. Its parts are magnificence, confidence, patience, and perseverance.

Magnificence is the understanding and administration of great and lofty matters, accompanied by a certain broad and splendid purpose of mind. Confidence is that by which the mind places great trust in itself, together with firm hope, in great and honorable matters. Patience is the voluntary and enduring bearing of difficult or arduous things for the sake of honor or usefulness. Perseverance is a stable and lasting continuation in a course of action carefully considered as good.

The final kind of virtue is temperance, whose definition is as follows: temperance is the rational, firm, and moderate rule of desire and of the other improper impulses of the mind. Its parts are self-restraint, clemency, and modesty.

Self-restraint is that by which every evil desire is governed and controlled through the great guidance of deliberation. Clemency is that by which injury and hatred are restrained with a mild spirit. Modesty is that by which concern for propriety is preserved everywhere throughout life, whether in the conduct of the mind or in the movements of the body.

[Col. 0418A] Hence the person who observes these things possesses exceptional honor before human beings and praise before God. But it is lamentable that, while those philosophers preserved these virtues solely because of the dignity of the virtues themselves, we Christians depart from them in many ways through deviant error—although the Truth himself, Christ Jesus, promises eternal-glory rewards to those who now observe them in faith and charity.

These, then, are the eminent virtues to be understood and observed in our religion, that is, the Christian religion. Wisdom is the virtue by which God is understood and feared according to the measure of the human mind, and his future judgment is believed. Justice is the firm maintenance of love of God and observance of his commandments. Fortitude is the virtue by which the ancient enemy is conquered and the adversities of the world endured. Temperance restrains lust, represses greed, and quiets and governs every impulse of the mind.

The end to be kept in view in all these virtues is that God and neighbor be loved. For what is easier: to love beautiful sights, sweet flavors, pleasant sounds, fragrant odors, delightful touches, the honors and felicities of the world—which recede like a fleeting shadow—or to love God, who is eternal beauty, eternal sweetness, eternal pleasantness, eternal fragrance, eternal delight, perpetual honor, and unfailing happiness? This is especially so since the divine [Scriptures] deal with us in no other way than by commanding us to love God and our Lord with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves.

For we have a promise from him who does not know how to deceive: “My yoke is sweet,” he says, “and my burden is light” (Matt. 11). The love of this world is more laborious than the love of Christ. For what the soul seeks in the world it does not find—namely, happiness and eternity—because this lowest beauty passes away and recedes; either it abandons the lover or is abandoned by the lover.

Let the soul therefore keep its proper order: let it love what is above, namely God; let it rule what is below, namely the body; and let it nourish and cherish associated souls through love. Thus, purified and freed from its burdens by sacrifices, the soul may fly back from this laborious and wretched life to rest and enter into the joy of its Lord.

In the sacred Scriptures, Christ is sometimes signified by the name “Wisdom,” as in the Apostle: “I speak of Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). Sometimes it signifies heavenly doctrine, as in the Apostle: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the rulers of this age has known” (1 Cor. 2). Wisdom is also sometimes called the philosophy of this world. Hence Solomon says: “The wisdom of men is not with me” (Prov. 30). And the Apostle says: “God made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1).

God is called wise in Job, as in the passage: “God is wise in heart and mighty in strength” (Job 9). The saints are also called wise in Hosea, where it is written: “Who is wise, and shall understand and know these things? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just walk in them” (Hos. 14).

Again, philosophers, Jews, or heretics are called wise, concerning whom the Apostle says: “For claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1). According to the world, therefore, the saints are fools. Hence the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world and the weak things, to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). But the wise of this world are fools before God. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “The foolish and the fool shall perish together” (Ps. 48).

## CHAPTER II. On Poets

As to where poets received their name, Tranquillus says:

When, near the beginning of Christianity, human beings had cast off their savagery and begun to live by reason, and had come to know themselves and their gods, they devised both a built environment and speech, each necessary to the other. For the worship and magnificence of the gods, they therefore devised temples more beautiful than houses and images larger than human bodies. In the same way, they thought the gods should be honored in speech of a more august kind. They exalted their praises in more splendid words and more pleasing rhythms. Since this was accomplished through a certain form called poetry, the result was called a poem, and its makers poets.

Varro says that *vates*—“seers” or “poets”—were so called from the force of the mind, or from shaping poems, that is, bending or modulating them. Accordingly, poets were once called *vates* in Latin, and their writings were called prophecies.

Lyric poets are called so from the Greek *apo tou lyrein*, that is, “from the variety of songs”; hence the lyre also received its name.

Tragic poets were so called because at the beginning the prize for those who sang was a goat, which the Greeks call *tragos*. Hence Horace wrote:

> He who competed in tragic song for a worthless goat.

Later tragic poets gained great honor, excelling in the subjects of their stories, which they fashioned in the likeness of truth.

Comedians were so called either from a place, because they performed throughout villages, which the Greeks call *komai*, or from feasting. For people customarily came to hear them after eating. Comedies proclaim the deeds of private persons; tragedies, however, recount the affairs of states and the histories of kings.

Some poets were called theologians because they composed songs about the gods. The poet’s task is to take things that truly happened and transfer them into other forms through indirect figures, with some embellishment. Hence Lucan is not counted among the poets, because he seems to have composed histories rather than a poem.

There are three kinds of poems. One is concerned with actions or imitations, which the Greeks call *dramatikon* or *mimetikon* [the source prints *micticon*, with *mimiticon* as a correction]. Another is narrative, which the Greeks call *exegetikon* or *panegyrikon*. The third is common or mixed, which the Greeks call *koinon* or *mikton*.

*Dramatikon* is active: speaking characters are introduced without the poet’s intervention, as in tragedies and plays. For *drama* is called a play in Latin. A work of this kind is written as follows:

> Where are your feet taking you, Moeris, or by what road does the way lead into the city?

In our tradition, the Song of Songs was written in this form, where the alternating voice of Christ and the Church is clearly found, although the writer does not intervene in the dialogue.

*Exegetikon*, or narrative poetry, is that in which the poet himself speaks without the intervention of any character. Such are all three books of the *Georgics* and the first part of the fourth, as well as the poems of Lucretius and similar works. Among us, the parables and Ecclesiastes were written in this form; in their own language, like the Psalter, they are composed in meter.

*Koinon* or *mikton* is that in which the poet himself speaks and speaking characters are introduced. Such are Homer’s *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, Virgil’s *Aeneid*, and among us the history of blessed Job, although in its own language it is not entirely poetic but is written partly in metrical and partly in rhythmic speech.

## CHAPTER III. On the Sibyls

[Col. 0420B]

All female prophets are generally called Sibyls, a Greek term. For *sios* means “god” in the Aeolic dialect, and *boulē* means “mind” in Greek—thus, “the mind of God.” Since they customarily interpreted the divine will for human beings, they were therefore called Sibyls.

Just as every prophesying man is called either a seer or a prophet, so every prophesying woman is called a Sibyl. The name derives from the office, not from the proper meaning of the word.

The most learned authorities report that there were ten Sibyls. The first was Persian; the second Libyan; the third Delphic, born in the temple of Delphic Apollo, who prophesied before the Trojan War, and whose many verses Homer inserted into his work. The fourth was the Cimmerian, in Italy.

The fifth was the Erythraean, named Erophyla, born in Babylon. She prophesied to the Greeks who were setting out for Ilium that Troy would perish and that Homer would write lies. She was called Erythraean because her songs were discovered on that same island.

The sixth was the Samian, who was called Phemonoe and received her surname from the island of Samos, where she was from.

The seventh was the Cumaean, named Amalthaea. She brought nine books to Tarquinius Priscus, in which the Roman decrees were written down. She is the Cumaean Sibyl. Of her Virgil wrote:

> Now the final age of the Cumaean song has come.

She was called Cumaean from the city of Cumae in Campania; her tomb still remains in Sicily.

The eighth was the Hellespontine, born in the Trojan territory. She is said to have lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus.

The ninth was Phrygian, and she prophesied at Ancyra.

The tenth was the Tiburtine, named Albunea.

The songs of all these women are circulated, and it is very clearly established that they wrote much about God, Christ, and the nations. The most celebrated and distinguished among them is said to be the Erythraean, who wrote certain things about Christ. At the beginnings of her verses the following Greek words are contained:

> *Iēsous Christos Theou huios sōtēr*  
> “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.”

These verses, whose initial letters yield the meaning we have stated, contain the following, as someone translated them into existing Latin verses:

[Col. 0421A]

> The sign of judgment: the earth is wet with sweat.  
>   
> From heaven the King will come, destined to be for all ages,  
>   
> Present in the flesh, surely, to judge the world.  
>   
> Hence the unbelieving and the faithful shall see God,  
>   
> The Most High, with the saints, at the very end of the age.  
>   
> Thus the souls will be present with the flesh, whom he himself judges,  
>   
> When the world lies uncultivated amid dense thorns.  
>   
> They will cast away the images of men and all their wealth as well.  
>   
> Fire will burn the lands, the sea, and the heavens,  
>   
> Searching out the dark gates; it will shatter the doors of Hell.  
>   
> For the free light of the saints will be given to all flesh,  
>   
> While the guilty will be consumed by eternal flame.  
>   
> Then each person will speak, revealing hidden deeds and secrets,  
>   
> And God will open hearts to the light.  
>   
> Then there will also be mourning, and all will gnash their teeth.  
>   
> The sun’s radiance will be taken away, and the chorus among the stars will perish.  
>   
> The heavens will be rolled up, and the moon’s splendor will pass away.  
>   
> He will cast down the hills and raise the valleys from below.  
>   
> Nothing among human things will remain lofty or high.  
>   
> Now the mountains and the blue depths of the sea are made level with the plains.  
>   
> All things will cease; the shattered earth will perish.  
>   
> Thus alike the springs and rivers will be scorched by fire.

[Col. 0421B]

> But then the trumpet will send forth a mournful sound from the lofty  
>   
> World, lamenting crime and its manifold woes.  
>   
> And the earth, gaping open, will display Tartarean chaos.  
>   
> And kings will be made to stand before this Lord, every one of them.  
>   
> From heaven will fall a stream of fire and sulfur.

In these Latin verses, translated somehow from the Greek, the meaning produced when the letters at their beginnings are joined could not appear, because the letter Υ occurs in Greek and no Latin words could be found beginning with that same letter while also fitting the sense. These are the fifth, eighteenth, and nineteenth verses.

Finally, if we join the letters at the beginnings of all the verses, we do not read the three verses that have been written. Instead, we remember the letter Υ as though it itself had been placed in those verses. [Col. 0421C] The result, in five words, is “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” But this is expressed in Greek, not Latin. There are twenty-seven verses, a number that produces a solid square of three. For three multiplied by three makes nine, and when those nine are multiplied in such a way that a figure rises in breadth and height, they reach twenty-seven.

Of these five Greek words—*Iēsous Christos Theou huios sōtēr*, which in Latin means “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior”—if you join the initial letters, they form ἰχθὺς, that is, “fish.” In this name Christ is mystically understood, because in the abyss of this mortal life, as in the depth of the waters, he was able to remain alive—that is, without sin.

This Sibyl, whether Erythraean or—as some more firmly believe—Cumaean, contains nothing in her entire poem, of which this is a small excerpt, that pertains to the worship of false or fictitious gods. Indeed, she speaks against them and against their worshipers in such a way that she seems to belong among those who pertain to the City of God.

Lactantius also inserts into his work certain prophecies of the Sibyl concerning Christ, although he does not specify which Sibyl. But what he set down separately, piece by piece, I have judged should be presented together, as though it were a single extended passage, since he mentioned it in several short sections:

> “Afterward he will come into the hands of unbelievers. They will strike God with impious hands and spit poisonous spittle with unclean mouths. Yet he will simply offer his holy back to the blows; receiving the blows, he will remain silent, lest anyone recognize that he is the Word, or from where he came to speak to the dead, and he will be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar. They served this inhospitable table to the Lord. Foolish one, you did not understand your God playing with mortals, but you crowned him with thorns and mixed the dreadful gall. The veil of the temple will indeed be torn, and at midday there will be an exceedingly dark night for three hours. He will die by death, having received sleep for three days; then, returning from the underworld, he will come first into the light, displaying the beginning of the resurrection by restoring the dead.”

Lactantius brought forward these Sibylline testimonies piecemeal and at intervals in the arrangement of his work, as the passages he intended to prove seemed to require. We, however, have taken care to distinguish them only by headings, so that later writers may not neglect to preserve them, placing them in a single connected sequence without inserting anything.

## CHAPTER IV. On Magicians

The first of the magicians was Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus [printed *nimis*], king of the Assyrians, killed in battle. Aristotle writes of him that the indications in his volumes show that he composed two million verses. Many centuries later Democritus expanded this art, at the time when the discipline of medicine also flourished through Hippocrates.

Among the Assyrians, however, magical arts are abundant, as Lucan testifies:

> … Who could know the fates from the entrails?  
>   
> Who could reveal the birds or observe the lightning of heaven,  
>   
> Observe them, and search out the stars with Assyrian care?

[Col. 0422C]

Thus the vanity of magical arts, transmitted by evil angels, prevailed for many centuries throughout the entire world through a certain knowledge of future things and the summoning of the dead. Their inventions include haruspices, auguries, and those things called oracles, as well as necromancy.

There is nothing surprising in the sorceries of magicians, whose arts of wrongdoing and enchantment developed so far that they even resisted Moses with signs very like his, turning rods into dragons and water into blood.

What more need be said? If it is permissible to believe the story of the pythoness—that she summoned the soul of the prophet Samuel from the hidden places of the underworld and displayed it to the eyes of the living—provided, that is, that we believe it was the prophet’s soul and not some phantasmal illusion produced by Satan’s deception.

Prudentius says this about Mercury:

[Col. 0422D]

> He is said, taking up the power of his wand,  
>   
> To have recalled extinguished souls into the light …  
>   
> … and to have condemned others to death.

A little later he added:

> For by magical muttering this wicked art knows  
>   
> How to summon subtle shapes  
>   
> And skillfully enchant sepulchral ashes.  
>   
> It likewise knows how to strip others of life.

Magicians are those whom the common people call sorcerers because of the magnitude of their crimes. They also shake the elements, disturb human minds, and kill by the violence of a spell alone, without anyone having swallowed poison.

Hence Lucan also wrote:

> The mind, polluted by no taint of swallowed poison,  
>   
> Perishes when bewitched …

They dare to summon demons and stir them up, so that each may destroy his enemies [Col. 0423A] by evil arts. They also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead. Necromancers are those whose incantations make the dead appear to have been revived, to prophesy and answer questions. *Necros* in Greek means “dead,” while *manteia* means “divination”; to revive them, blood is added to the corpse. For they say that demons love blood; therefore, whenever necromancy is practiced, blood is mixed with water, so that they may be more easily attracted by the color of blood.

Hydromancers are so called from water. For hydromancy consists in summoning the shadows of demons by gazing into water, and seeing their images or deceptions, and hearing some things from them there; when blood has also been added, they are said to seek answers even from the underworld. This form of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians.

[Col. 0423B] Varro says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. Hence the terms geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy. Diviners are so called as though they were “full of God,” for they pretend to be filled with divinity and, by cunning fraud, conjecture the future for human beings.

There are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Enchanters are so called because they complete their art by means of words. *Arioli* are so called because around the altars of idols they utter abominable prayers and offer deadly sacrifices, and through these ceremonies receive responses from demons.

Haruspices are so called as though they were “inspectors of hours”: for they observe days and hours in conducting business and performing works, and consider what a person ought to observe at each particular time. They also inspect the entrails of animals and foretell the future [Col. 0423C] from them.

Augurs are those who attend to the flight and voices of birds, as well as to other signs or observations that unexpectedly occur to human beings; they are also called auspices. For auspices are the things observed by travelers on a journey. They are called *auspicia*, as though *avium aspicia*, “observations of birds,” and *auguria*, as though *avium garria*, that is, the voices and speech of birds. *Augurium* is also as though *avigerium*, because birds carry it. There are two kinds of auspices: one pertaining to the eyes, the other to the ears. To the eyes belongs flight; to the ears, the voice of birds.

Pythonesses are named after Apollo Pythius, because he was the originator of divination. Astrologers are so called because they augur from the stars. *Genethliaci* are named from their consideration of birth-days. They describe the origin of human beings through the twelve signs of heaven and attempt, from the course of the stars, to foretell the character, actions, and circumstances of those being born—that is, under what sign each person was born, or what effect the life of the one born will have.

These are the people commonly called mathematicians. The Latins call this kind of superstition *constellationes*, that is, “markings of the stars,” describing how the stars are positioned when each person is born. At first these interpreters of the stars were called magi, as in the case of those who announced in the Gospel that Christ had been born; afterward this name was reserved for mathematicians alone. Knowledge of this art was permitted up to the Gospel, so that after Christ had been born no one thereafter might interpret another person’s nativity.

Horoscopes are so called because they observe human births by hours, assigning them a different and varied [Col. 0424A] fate. Sortilegers are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the knowledge of divination through certain things they call “the lots of the saints,” or who promise the future by examining any kind of Scripture.

Those whose limbs twitch are called salisators, because whenever any part of their limbs leaps, they declare that this signifies something favorable or sad for them.

To all these practices also belong the amulets of accursed remedies, which must be despised, whether in incantations, in characters, or in any objects that are hung up or tied. In all these things there is a work of demons, arising from a certain deadly association between human beings and evil angels. Therefore all these practices must be avoided by a Christian and utterly rejected and condemned with abhorrence.

The Phrygians were the first to devise augury from birds; Mercury is said to have been the first to devise magic illusion. It is called *praestigium* because it dazzles and obstructs the sharpness of the eyes.

As for magical arts, incantations, and various superstitions, which pagans and false Christians appear to follow in their divinations and perverse observances, it is easy to discover what the divine law decrees in the authorities of the Old and New Testaments.

The divine law detests such people, for in the book of Exodus it says:

“You shall not allow sorcerers to live in your land” (Exod. XXII).

And again:

“He who sacrifices,” it says, “to gods other than to the Lord alone shall be put to death” (ibid.).

And in Leviticus:

“You shall not eat with blood; you shall not practice augury, nor observe dreams; and you shall not cut your flesh for the dead, nor make figures or marks upon yourselves. I am the Lord” (ibid.).

And again:

“Do not turn to magicians,” it says, “nor inquire of diviners, lest you be defiled through them” (ibid.).

And again:

“A man or a woman in whom there is a pythonic or divining spirit shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones. Their blood shall be upon them” (Lev. XX).

In Deuteronomy it likewise says:

“When you enter the land that the Lord your God is about to give you, take care that you do not imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you one who makes his son or daughter pass through fire, or one who consults diviners, observes dreams, or practices augury; nor a sorcerer, nor an enchanter, nor one who consults pythonic spirits or diviners, or seeks truth from the dead. For the Lord abhors all these things. [Col. 0424D] And because of such crimes he will destroy them at your entrance. You shall be perfect and without blemish with the Lord your God. Those nations whose land you will possess listen to augurs and diviners; but you have been instructed otherwise by the Lord your God” (Deut. XVIII).

And immediately afterward it follows what must be followed and obeyed:

“The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your people and from your brothers, like me; him you shall hear, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, when you assembled and said: ‘I will no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor will I see this great fire any more, lest I die.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘They have spoken well in all things. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth; he will speak to them everything that I command him. But whoever refuses to hear his words, which he will speak in my name, I myself will be his avenger’” (Deut. XVIII).

This prophet, therefore, and Lord of all the prophets, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), the author of both Testaments, rejects and despises all errors, divinations, and harmful arts, not only in the Old but also in the New Testament. He does not wish truth or healing to be sought from anyone other than himself, because he, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true and almighty God, who alone works great wonders.

Therefore in the Gospel he invites everyone to himself, saying:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden light” (Matt. XI).

And again:

“I am,” he says, “the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

This one, therefore, according to Paul’s testimony, is “the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers” (I Tim. IV). Peter also says of him:

“There is no other name given to human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

In this name also, great signs and healings are performed daily in the Church through the prayers of the faithful. For he himself says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. Go and preach the Gospel” (Luke X; Mark XVI). “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”

Why, then, is it necessary to seek salvation from anyone other than the almighty physician? Or what reason is there for wishing to learn knowledge and wisdom from anyone other than the source of all wisdom and knowledge? Of him it is written:

“All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him and is before him. Who can count the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who can investigate the wisdom of God, which precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all others, and the understanding of prudence is from eternity. The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the heights, and its ways are eternal commandments” (Sir. I).

For whoever wishes to have salvation without the Savior, and thinks that he can become prudent without true wisdom, will not be saved but sick; he will not be prudent but foolish. He will labor in continual sickness and, foolish and senseless, remain in harmful blindness. Accordingly, every inquiry and every remedy sought from diviners and magi, or from the demons themselves in the worship of idols, ought rather to be called death than life. Those who pursue such things, unless they correct themselves, are heading toward eternal destruction.

For, as the Psalmist says, “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. LXXV): through deceived human beings they daily strive to deceive others, so as to make them participants in their own destruction.

## CHAPTER V. On Pagans

Pagans are named from the *pagi* of the Athenians, where they originated. For there, in rural places and villages, the pagans established groves and idols, and from such a beginning they acquired the name *pagans*.

Those who are without the law and who, because they did not believe, are called *gentiles* are so called because they are as they were born—that is, as they descended in the flesh—under sin, serving idols and not yet regenerated. Accordingly, those who were called *gentiles* in Latin are called *ethnici* in Greek. For *ethnos* in Greek means “nation,” and *ethnici* in Greek means *gentiles* in Latin.

After faith, those who believe from among the nations ought no longer to be called nations or gentiles, just as after faith one can no longer be called a Jew, as the apostle Paul testifies when he says to Christians: “For when you were gentiles,” that is, unbelievers, and so forth.

They are also called apostates who, after receiving Christ’s baptism, return to the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices. This is a Greek name.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Gods of the Nations

Those whom pagans assert to be gods are reported to have once been human beings, and after their deaths began to be worshiped among their own people according to the merits of each person’s life: Isis in Egypt, Jupiter in Crete, Juba among the Moors, Faunus among the Latins, and Quirinus among the Romans. Likewise, Minerva at Athens, Juno at Samos, Venus at Paphos, Vulcan at Lemnos, Liber at Naxos, and Apollo at Delphi.

Poets also added their praises, and by composing songs raised them to heaven. [Col. 0426C] For they are said to have discovered various inventions of the arts: medicine from Aesculapius [the text reads “Scolapius,” corrected contextually], metalworking from Vulcan. They are also named from their activities, as Mercury, who presides over merchandise, and Liber, from liberality.

There were certain brave men or founders of cities, and when they died, the people who had loved them fashioned images of them, so that they might have some consolation from contemplating their likenesses. But, as demons persuaded succeeding generations, this error gradually crept in among them, so that those whom their predecessors had honored merely in memory of their names, later generations considered and worshiped as gods.

The use of images arose when, from longing for the dead, people established likenesses or effigies of them, as though they had been received into heaven. In their place, demons presented themselves on earth to be worshiped, [Col. 0426D] and persuaded the deceived and ruined to sacrifice to them.

Images are called *simulacra* from likeness, because the hand of the artist imitates their faces in stone or another material, in whose honor the images are fashioned. Thus *simulacra* means either that they are similar or that they are simulated and fabricated. Hence they are also false.

It should be noted that the Latin term is found among the Hebrews. Among them, an idol or image is called *selem*. The Jews say that Ishmael was the first to make an image from clay; the pagans, however, maintain that Prometheus was the first to fashion images of human beings from clay, and that from him arose the art of making images and statues. Hence poets also falsely represent human beings as first made by him, figuratively, because of their effigies.

Among the Greeks, Cecrops was the one under whom the olive first arose on the citadel and the city of Athens received its name from Minerva. He was the first of all to name Jupiter, to discover images, to establish altars, and to sacrifice victims—things never before seen in Greece.

*Idololatria* is interpreted as “the service or worship of idols.” For *latreia* in Greek means “service” in Latin, and, insofar as true religion is concerned, this service is owed to one God alone. Just as impious pride, whether of human beings or demons, either commands or desires that it be offered to them, so pious humility, whether of human beings or holy angels, refuses the worship offered to them and points out to whom it is owed.

An idol is an image made and consecrated in human form, according to the interpretation of the word. For *eidos* in Greek means “form,” and from it, by diminution, *idolum* is derived; among us it likewise gives *formula*, “a little form.” Therefore every form or little form demands to be called an idol. Hence *idolatry* is every service and servitude performed around any idol.

Some Latins, however, ignorant of Greek, incompetently say that *idolum* derives its name from *dolus*, “deceit,” because the devil introduced the worship of the creature under the divine name.

They say that demons are named by the Greeks as though from *daimonias* [Greek *daimonias*], that is, “skilled” and “knowledgeable” in matters; for they foresee many future events and therefore commonly give many responses. They possess knowledge of things beyond human weakness, partly through the keenness of a subtler sense, partly through the experience of a very long life, and partly through angelic revelation by God’s command.

They are vigorous by the nature of aerial bodies. [Col. 0427C] Before their transgression they bore heavenly bodies; after their fall, however, they were changed into an ethereal quality. They were permitted to occupy not the purer regions of the air but these gloomy ones, which are for them like a prison until the time of judgment. These are the transgressing angels, whose prince is the devil.

In Hebrew, *diabolus* means “flowing downward,” because he disdained to stand peacefully at the summit of heaven but, falling downward under the weight of pride, collapsed. In Greek, *diabolus* means “accuser,” either because he reports to God the crimes into which he himself entices people, or because he accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated charges. Hence in the Apocalypse an angelic voice says:

“The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, he who accused them before our God day and night” (Rev. XII).

*Satan* in Latin means “adversary” or “transgressor.” He is the adversary because he is the enemy of truth and always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints. He is also the transgressor because he became a violator of the law. “He did not stand in the truth in which he was created” (John VIII).

He is likewise the tempter, because he asks that the innocence of the righteous be tested, as is written in Job.

He is called Antichrist because he will come against Christ—not in the way that certain simple people understand the name Antichrist, as though he were called that because he would come before Christ, that is, because Christ would come after him. Rather, *Antichrist* in Greek means in Latin “opposed to Christ”; for *anti* in Greek signifies “against” in Latin.

When he comes, he will falsely claim to be Christ, fight against him, and oppose Christ’s sacraments and his truth. He will also attempt to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem and restore all the ceremonies of the old law.

But the one who denies that Christ is God is also an Antichrist, for he is opposed to Christ. All who go out from the Church, are cut off from the unity of faith, and are themselves antichrists.

Bel is a Babylonian idol, whose name is interpreted as “old.” This Belus was the father of Ninus and the first king of the Assyrians; some call him Saturn. This name was later worshiped among both the Assyrians and the Africans. Hence in the Punic language *Bal* means “god.” Among the Assyrians, Bel is called, according to a certain arrangement of their sacred rites, both Saturn and the sun.

Beel-phegor is interpreted as “the idol of disgrace.” It was an idol of Moab, called Baal, on Mount Phegor, which the Latins call Priapus, the god of gardens. He came from Lampsacus, a city of the Hellespont, from which he was expelled; because of the size of his male member, the Greeks transferred him into the number of their gods and consecrated him as the divinity of gardens. Hence he is said to preside over gardens because of their fertility.

Beelzebub was an idol of Accaron, whose name is interpreted as “man of flies,” for *zebub* means “fly.” This most filthy idol was called “man of flies” because of the filth of idolatry.

*Behemoth* in Latin means “animal,” because he fell from the heights to earthly things and, according to his deserts, became like a brute animal. He is also Leviathan, that is, “the serpent from the waters,” because he moves with cunning in the shifting sea of this world.

Leviathan is interpreted as “their addition”—whose, that is, if not of human beings, to whom he once brought the guilt of transgression in paradise and to whom, by daily persuasion, he adds or extends it all the way to eternal death.

The pagans attempt, through vain stories, to turn certain names of their gods into natural explanations, interpreting them as composed in terms of the causes of the elements. But all this was fabricated by poets, so that they might adorn their gods with various figures, even though histories confess that these beings were ruined and full of disgraceful infamy. For wherever truth ceases, there is entirely room for fabrication.

Saturn is designated by the pagans as the source of the gods and of all posterity. The Latins are said to have named him from *satus*, “sowing,” because the sowing of all things belongs to him; or from the length of time, because he is filled with years. Hence the Greeks say that he bears the name *Chronos* (Χρόνος), that is, “time.”

The story that he devoured his children means that time rolls back into itself the years that it has produced; or it refers to seeds returning to the place from which they arise. They say that he cut off the genitals of his father Caelus, because nothing is born in heaven from seeds. “He holds a sickle,” they say, to signify agriculture; or years and seasons, because they return into themselves; or wisdom, because it is sharp within.

In certain cities, pagans sacrificed their children to Saturn, because poets handed down that Saturn was accustomed to devour his children.

Jupiter is said to have been named from *iuvare*, “to help,” and *Jupiter* is as though *iuvans pater*, “helping father,” that is, one who provides for all. They even called him, as a special title, “Jupiter the Best,” although he was incestuous among his own and impure among strangers.

Sometimes they represent him as a bull because of the abduction of Europa. In fact, he was in a ship whose emblem was a bull. At other times they say that he sought intercourse with Danaë in the form of a shower of gold, signifying that the woman’s chastity was corrupted by gold; at other times he appears in the likeness of an eagle, because he carried off a boy for sexual violation; at other times as a serpent, because he crawled; and as a swan, because he sang.

These are therefore not merely figures, but plainly crimes grounded in reality. It was consequently shameful to believe in gods of the sort that human beings ought not to be.

They say that Janus is as though the gate of the world, heaven, or the months. They give Janus two faces because of east and west. When, however, they make him four-faced and call him double Janus, they refer this to the four regions of the world, or to the four elements or seasons. But in inventing this, they make not a god but a monster.

They declare Neptune to be the waters of the world, and say that he is called Neptune as though “thundering through the cloud.” They wish Vulcan to be fire, and say that Vulcan is named as though “flying brightness,” or as though *Volicanus*, because it flies through the air. For fire arises from the clouds.

Hence Homer also says that he was hurled from the air to the earth, because every bolt of lightning falls from the air. Vulcan is therefore imagined as born from Jupiter’s thigh because lightning bolts arise from the lower air.

Vulcan is called lame because by nature fire is never straight but has, as it were, the appearance and movement of a lame thing. They say that this same Vulcan is the patron of the smiths’ furnace because no kind of metal can be melted and worked without fire.

Pluto in Greek is *Diespiter* or *Ditis pater* in Latin; others call him Orcus, as though “receiver of the dead.” Hence a vessel that receives water is also called an *orca*. He is also Charon in Greek.

They wish Liber to have been named from *liberamentum*, “release,” because, as males engage in intercourse, they are freed through his benefit when their seed is discharged. This same Liber is painted with a womanly and delicate body; they say that women were assigned to him, and wine, to arouse lust.

Hence his forehead is encircled with a vine shoot. But he has a wreath of vine leaves and a horn because, when wine is drunk pleasantly and moderately, it produces joy; when drunk beyond measure, it provokes quarrels—that is, it gives, as it were, horns.

He is also called Lyaeus, from the Greek *apo tou luein*, “from loosening,” because the limbs are relaxed by abundant wine. In Greek he is also Dionysus, from Mount Nysa in India, where he is said to have been raised. There is also a city called Nysa, in which this same Liber is worshiped; hence he is called Nisaeus.

Mercury is interpreted as speech. For he is called Mercury as though *medius currens*, “running in the middle,” because speech runs among human beings as an intermediary. Hence he is also called Hermes in Greek, because speech or interpretation—something pertaining to speech—is called *hermeneia*.

He is also said to preside over merchandise because speech serves as an intermediary between sellers and buyers. He is therefore imagined with wings because words travel more swiftly; hence he is represented as swift and wandering. His wings on his head and feet signify that speech becomes winged as it passes through the air.

He is called a messenger because through speech all thoughts are announced. They call him the master of theft because speech deceives the minds of those who hear it.

He holds a staff with which he separates serpents, that is, poisons; for those who are fighting and disagreeing are calmed by the speech of an interpreter. Hence, according to Livy, ambassadors of peace are called *caduceatores*. Just as wars were declared through the *fetiales*, so peace was made through the *caduceatores*.

Hermes is called in Greek *apo tes hermeneias*, “from interpretation,” and in Latin *interpres*, “interpreter.” Because of his virtue and knowledge of many arts, he was called *Trismegistus*, that is, “thrice-greatest.”

Why they represent him with a dog’s head is explained in this way: among all animals, the dog is considered the most keen-scented and perceptive kind.

They say that Mars is the god of war, and that he is called Mars because fighting is done by men, as though *Mars* were *maris ars*, “the art of males.” There are, however, three customary forms of warfare: among the Scythians, where both women and men go into battle; among the Amazons, where women alone fight; and among the Romans and other nations, where only males fight.

They also interpret Mars as though “the producer of deaths,” for death is named from Mars. They call him an adulterer because the outcome is uncertain for those who wage war. He stands bare-chested so that each person may expose himself to war without fear in his heart.

Mars is called Gradivus among the Greeks [variant: Thracians], either because those who fight advance their step in battle, or because they march energetically.

[Col. 0430C] They believed Hercules to be the god of courage. In Greek he is called *Heracles*, as though *heris cleos*, “glorious in strife,” from *heris*, “strife,” and *cleos*, “glory”; or as though *hero-cleos*, which in Latin we call “the fame of brave men.” But, as Sextus Pompeius writes, he was a farmer. Hence he is said to have cleansed the stable of King Ancheus of dung, because fertilizing fields with manure is properly the work of farmers.

Although they call Apollo a diviner and physician, they also called him the sun, as though *solum*, “the sole one”; Titan, as though one of the Titans who did not act against Jupiter; and Phoebus, as though *ephebus*, “a young man.” Hence the sun is also painted as a boy, because it rises daily and is born with a new light.

They say that this same Apollo is also called Pythius, from Python, a serpent of immense size, whose poison was no more frightening than its magnitude. Apollo struck him down with arrows and carried away the spoils of his name, so that he would be called Pythius. Therefore, as a mark of victory, he established that the Pythian rites should be celebrated.

They likewise say that Diana, his sister, is the moon and the guardian of roads. Hence they wish her to be a virgin, because a road [the source apparently reads *via*; the intended word may be *virgo*, “virgin”] produces nothing. For the same reason both are imagined with arrows, because those two heavenly bodies send rays from heaven down to earth.

Diana is called as though *duana*, because the moon appears by day and by night. They also affirm that she is called Lucina because she shines; and Trivia because she is imagined in three forms. Virgil writes of her:

> The three faces of the virgin Diana,

because she is called the same Luna, the same Diana, and the same Proserpina. But when the moon is represented,

> [lacuna] in a somewhat shining garment she gleams;

when she shines with her quiver fastened beneath her, she is the virgin Latonian;

when she sits reclining upon a throne, she is the Plutonian consort.

Diana is called Latonian because she was the daughter of Latona.

They say that Ceres, that is, the earth, was named from producing crops, and they call her by many names. They also call her Ops, because the earth is made better by work; Proserpina, because crops sprout forth from her; Vesta, because she is clothed with grasses and various things, or from her power of standing.

They likewise imagine her as Tellus and as the Great Mother, tower-crowned, with a tympanum, a cock, and the clatter of cymbals. She is called Mother because she produces very many things; Great because she produces food; Nourishing because she feeds all living creatures with her fruits. For the earth is the nurse of food.

Her image is represented with a key because the earth is closed in winter and opened in spring, so that crops may be born. They wish her tympanum to signify the orb of the earth. She is said to ride in a chariot because she herself is the earth, suspended in the air. She is supported by wheels because the world revolves and is ever-turning.

They place tame lions beneath her to show that there is no race on earth so savage that it cannot be subjected to or conquered by her. The towered crown that she wears on her head shows that the cities placed upon the earth stand as though marked by towers.

Seats are imagined around her because, although everything moves, she does not move. Her attendants, the Corybantes, are imagined with drawn swords, signifying that everyone ought to fight for his native land.

They made eunuchs (*galli*) serve this goddess, signifying, they say, that those lacking seed ought to follow the earth, since everything is found in it. The command is given, they say, that those who cultivate the earth should not sit idle, for there is always something for them to do.

The sound of the cymbals is the clatter of tools used in cultivating the fields. For this reason they are made of bronze, because the ancients cultivated the earth with bronze before iron was discovered.

They also maintain that this same Vesta is fire, since there is no doubt that the earth contains fire, as is shown by Etna and Vulcan. For this reason they call her a virgin, because fire is an inviolable element and nothing can be born from it, since whatever it seizes it consumes [the text reads *assumat*; context suggests *absumat*, “consumes”].

Ovid, in the *Fasti*, writes:

> Nor should you understand Vesta as anything other than living flame.
>
> You see that no bodies are born from flame.

[Col. 0431D] Therefore they also say that virgins serve her, because just as nothing is born from a virgin, so nothing is born from fire.

They say that Juno is as though *Janona*, that is, a gate, for the purification of women, because she opens, as it were, the gates of mothers to their children and the natures of brides to their husbands. Such is the philosophers’ interpretation.

The poets, however, assert that Juno is the sister and wife of Jupiter. They interpret Jupiter as fire and air, and Juno as water and earth, from the mingling of which all things are generated. They call her his sister because she is a part of the world, and his wife because, mingled with him, she unites with him.

Hence Virgil writes:

> Then the almighty Father, the aether, descended in fruitful rains
>
> joyfully into the lap of his glad consort. [lacuna]

Minerva is called Athene among the Greeks, that is, “woman.” [Col. 0432A] Among the Latins, however, she was called Minerva, as though “goddess” and “gift” of various arts. They say that she was the discoverer of many skills; hence they interpret her as art and reason, because nothing can be contained without reason. Since reason arises from the mind alone, and they believe that the mind resides in the head and brain, they therefore say that she was born from Jupiter’s head, because the understanding of the wise person, who discovers everything, is in the head. For this reason the head of the Gorgon is represented on her breast: there is all prudence, which confounds others and proves the ignorant to be stone-like. We also see this on ancient statues of emperors, in the middle of the breastplate, to suggest wisdom and courage.

This Minerva is also called Tritonia. For Triton is a marsh in Africa, around which she is said to have appeared at a virginal [Col. 0432B] age. On this account she was called Tritonia. Hence she was believed to be a goddess all the more readily because her origin was less known.

She was called Pallas either from the island of Pallene in Thrace, where she was raised; or from *apo tou pallein to doru*—that is, “from shaking the spear”; or because she killed the giant Pallas.

They say that Venus was so called because a woman does not cease to be a virgin without force. The Greeks call her *Aphrodite* because she generates from foam of blood. For *aphros* in Greek means “foam.” As for the story that Saturn cut off the genitals of his father Caelus and poured the blood into the sea, and that Venus was born when the sea-foam congealed from it, they explain it as follows: sexual intercourse consists in the substance of salty moisture. Thus Venus is called *Aphrodite*, because intercourse is foam of blood, which consists of the fluid and salty juice of the inward parts. Venus is called the wife of Vulcan because the function of sexual love does not exist without heat. Hence the saying: “The old man is cold toward Venus.”

As for the claim that Saturn cut off the genitals of his father Caelus, and that they created Venus when they fell into the sea, this is imagined because nothing is created unless moisture descends from heaven to earth.

They say that Cupid was so called on account of love. He is the demon of fornication, and he is represented with wings because nothing is found lighter or more changeable than those in love. He is depicted as a child because love is foolish and irrational. He is imagined holding an arrow and a torch: the arrow because love wounds the heart; the torch because it inflames it.

The Greeks call him Pan; the Latins call him Silvanus, the god of rural people, whom they fashioned in the likeness of nature. Hence he is also called *Pan*, that is, “all.” [Col. 0432D] For they imagine him with the universal appearance of the elements. He has horns in the likeness of the rays of the sun and moon; his hide is marked with spots because of the stars of heaven. His face is red in the likeness of the ether. He carries a pipe of seven reeds because of the harmony of heaven, in which there are seven sounds and seven distinctions of voices. He is hairy because the earth is clothed with vegetation. From the knees downward his body is ugly, on account of trees, wild animals, and cattle. He has the hooves of a goat to show the solidity of the earth. They call him the god of things and of all nature. Hence they say that *Pan* means “all things.”

Isis is called “earth” in the language of the Egyptians, and they wish her to be the earth. Isis was, however, queen [Col. 0433A] of the Egyptians, the daughter of King Inachus. Coming from Greece, she taught the Egyptians letters and instructed them in cultivating the land; for this reason they also called the earth by her name.

Serapis, the greatest of all the Egyptian gods, is the same as Apis, king of the Argives. He was carried by ships to Egypt, and when he had died there, he was called Serapis. The reason is that the chest in which a dead person is placed—what they call a sarcophagus—is called *soros* in Greek; thus, as it were, “the tomb of Apis.” They began to worship him there as one buried, before his temple had been constructed. First he was called Sorapis; then, with one letter changed, Serapis.

Apis was a bull among the Egyptians, consecrated to Serapis and named from him. Egypt worshiped him as a divine being because he gave certain clear signs concerning the future. He appeared [Col. 0433B] in Memphis, accompanied by a hundred priests, who suddenly sang before him as though possessed.

The Jews made an image of his head for themselves in the wilderness.

Fauns are said to have been named from *fari* (“to speak”), or as though from *apo tēs phōnēs* (*apo tes phones*), because they seemed to disclose future things by their voice, not by signs. For pagans consulted them in sacred groves, and they gave them responses not by signs but by voices.

They say that a genius is so called because it possesses, as it were, the power of generating all things, or from the generation of children. Hence among the nations beds were called “genial” when they were spread for a newly married husband.

These and other things are the fabulous inventions of the pagans. They are interpreted in such a way that, although they are not understood, they are nevertheless worshiped to the condemnation of those who worship them.

They say that Fate is whatever the gods speak, whatever Jupiter speaks. Thus they call it *fatum* from *fari*, that is, from speaking. If this word were not already accustomed to being understood in another sense, toward which we do not wish to incline human hearts, we could reasonably call fate *fatum* from *fari*. For we cannot deny that it is written in the sacred writings: “God has spoken once; I have heard two things,” and so forth (Ps. LXI).

What is meant by “he has spoken once” is that he has spoken immutably, that is, unchangeably, just as he knows unchangeably everything that will happen and everything that he himself will do.
