They imagine three Fates at the distaff and spindle, twisting threads from wool with their fingers, on account of the three times: the past, which has already been spun and wound onto the spindle; the present, which is drawn between the fingers of the spinner; and the future, in the wool wrapped around the distaff, which still must be transferred by the spinner’s fingers to the spindle, as the present is transferred into the past. [Col. 0433D]

They say that the Parcae were called by an antiphrastic expression, because they spare least of all. They wished there to be three of them: one who begins a person’s life, another who weaves it together, and a third who breaks it. We begin when we are born; we exist when we live; we cease to exist when we die.

They say that Fortune derives her name from things that happen by chance, as though she were a goddess who mocks human affairs with various accidents and chance events. Hence they call her blind, because, rushing indiscriminately upon anyone, without examining merit, she comes alike to the good and the wicked.

They distinguish Fate from Fortune. Fortune, they say, belongs to things that come by chance, with no evident cause; Fate, however, is assigned and fixed for each individual.

They also say that there are three female Furies, with hair consisting of serpents, on account of the three passions that produce many disturbances in human souls and sometimes compel people to transgress, so that they do not permit them to have regard for reputation or danger: anger, which desires vengeance; greed, which desires wealth; and lust, which seeks pleasures. They are called Furies because they strike the mind with their goads and do not allow it to be at rest.

They suppose that the Nymphs, goddesses of waters, were so called from clouds. For waters come from clouds, and their name is derived from this; they are goddesses of waters, as it were, the divine powers of streams.

They also call these same beings Muses, and likewise Nymphs—not without reason, since the movement of water produces music.

Among the pagans the Nymphs have various names. The Nymphs of mountains are called Oreads, those of forests Dryads, those of fields Hamadryads, those of springs Naiads, and those of the sea Nereids.

They say that the Heroes derived their name from Juno. For Juno is called *Hera* in Greek, and therefore, according to the Greek story, some son of hers was called Eros. The story signifies something mystical by this: air is assigned to Juno, and they wish the Heroes to dwell there. By this name they call the souls of the dead who have acquired some merit, as though they were *aeroae*, that is, “airy men” worthy of heaven because of their wisdom and courage. [Col. 0434B]

The pagans called all the gods whom they worshiped at home Penates. They were called Penates because they were in the *penetralia*, that is, in secret places. How these gods were called, or what names they had, is unknown.

They call the gods of the dead Manes, whose power they assert to lie between the moon and the earth. They also think that *mane* (“morning”) derives from them, and that they were called Manes from the air, which is *manus*, that is, thin or rare; or because they spread widely through the breezes; or because, in contrast with the savage, they are gentle, and so they are called by an opposite name. [Col. 0434C]

Apuleius, however, says that they are called Manes by antiphrasis, that is, “gentle and restrained,” although they are terrifying and savage, like the Parcae and the Eumenides.

They say that Larvae are demons made from human beings who had been guilty of evil deeds. Their nature, they say, is to frighten children and chatter in dark corners.

Lamiae, whom the stories say were accustomed to seize and tear infants, are specifically named from tearing.

The hairy spirits, who are called Panites in Greek and Incubi in Latin, are also called *Invi* from *inire*, “to enter,” because they have intercourse everywhere with animals. They are also called Incubi from *incumbere*, that is, from violating or having sexual intercourse. For they are often wicked even toward women and carry out intercourse with them. The Gauls call these demons Dusii because they practice this impurity continually. [Col. 0434D]

The being whom the common people call an Incubus, the Romans call Faunus ficarius, the “fig-tree Faun.”

Horace says to him:

> Faunus, lover of fleeing Nymphs,  
> May you pass gently through my lands  
> And my sunny fields.

But after rejecting false gods and the inventions of human beings, concerning which the Psalmist says, “All the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. XCV), let us explain the distinction conveyed by the name itself.

Thus the gods of the nations are demons, who benefit no one but always deceive and mock those who believe in them. For although demons are called *daemones* in Latin as though they were “knowing beings” (*daimonias*), in human speech the word is an insult. [Col. 0435A] Thus we use it for those whom we judge worthy of execration—and rightly so, since there is no true knowledge in them: they do not follow the will of their Creator. In the same way we call philosophers “wise.”

But the Apostle attacks these people with a definitive judgment, saying: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. III). Therefore, knowing this, we must regard them as lacking understanding.

A demon is therefore a certain substance created by God, altogether excellent, just as are the good angels. Through the pride proper to it, however, it reached the point where, having abandoned its natural dignity, it always persists in evil works.

Yet elsewhere it is written: “God stood in the assembly of gods, but in the midst he distinguishes gods” (Ps. LXXXI).

In one remarkable brief statement Jesus Christ is declared to us. For it is he who is God who stood in the assembly, he who sat at the [Col. 0435B] right hand of the Father. These positions are bodily expressions. For if you consider his majesty, he is wholly everywhere and full everywhere. Nor can one say that the nature of the Godhead stands or sits, because it is confined by no determination of place.

Thus John the Baptist also says of him: “But there stands among you one whom you do not know” [Col. 0436A] (John I).

He adds “of gods” so that you may understand more clearly that this was said of human beings, among whom Christ is known to have lived bodily, just as the prophet Jeremiah foretold: “After these things he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Bar. III).

For we often find this statement made about human beings. Thus he also says to Moses: “I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII). And later the Psalm itself will say: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). In this way we also call human beings sons of God.

But if you refer the expression to the nature of the Godhead, there is one Word who should truly and properly be called by this name.

Sometimes we call angels and higher powers “gods” in an improper sense, as the Apostle says: “Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth. For us there is one God, the Father” (1 Cor. [Col. 0436B] VIII).

It follows: “But God distinguishes in the midst” (Ps. LXXXI), that is, the apostles and the righteous, who have followed the admonitions and faith of his majesty. To distinguish belongs to foreknowledge and to the divine understanding, which snatches us from the mass of sin and leads us to the kingdoms of heaven.

Hence the Apostle also says: “For who distinguishes you?” (1 Cor. IV).

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 0435]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Languages of the Nations

[Col. 0435B]

The diversity of languages arose in the building of the tower after the Flood. For before the pride of that tower divided human society into different sounds of signs, there was one language of all nations, which is called Hebrew. The patriarchs and prophets used it not only in their speech but also in the sacred writings.

At the beginning, however, there were as many languages as nations. Later there were more nations than languages, because many nations arose from one language.

Here “languages” means words produced by the tongue, according to that mode of expression in which the agent is named by the thing effected, just as “mouth” is often used for words and “hand” for writing.

There are three sacred languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which excel throughout the whole world. For in these three languages Pilate wrote the charge against the Lord above the cross. Hence, because of the obscurity of the holy Scriptures, knowledge of these three languages is necessary, so that one may turn to another if the speech of one language introduces any uncertainty concerning a word or its interpretation.

The Greek language is considered more distinguished than the other languages of the nations. It is more sonorous than Latin and all other languages. Its variety is divided into five forms. The first is called *koinē*, that is, “mixed” or “common,” which everyone uses. The second is Attic, namely, Athenian, which all the writers of Greece used. The third is Doric, which the Egyptians and Sicilians have. The fourth is Ionic. The fifth is Aeolic, in which the Aeolians spoke. Such are the established distinctions observed in the Greek language. [Col. 0436C] Their speech is divided in this way.

Some have said that there are four Latin languages: ancient, Latin, Roman, and mixed.

The ancient language is the one used by the earliest inhabitants of Italy under Janus and Saturn, an uncultivated language, as is evident in the songs of the Salii.

Latin is the language spoken under Janus and the kings of Tuscia by the other inhabitants of Latium; in it the Twelve Tables were written.

Roman is the language that arose among the Roman people after the expulsion of the kings. The poets Naevius, Plautus, and Virgil, and among the orators Gracchus, Cato, Cicero, and the others, poured it forth.

The mixed language arose after the empire had expanded more widely, when peoples and customs entered the Roman state together with it. It corrupts the integrity of speech through solecisms and barbarisms.

All the peoples of the East strike their language and words in the throat, as do the Hebrews and Syrians. All the peoples of the Mediterranean strike their speech against the palate, as do the Greeks and Asians. All the peoples of the West break their words against the teeth, as do the Italians and Spaniards.

Syriac and Chaldaean are close to Hebrew in speech and agree in many respects, including the sound of the letters. Some think that Hebrew itself is Chaldaean because Abraham came from the Chaldaeans. But if this is accepted, how is it that in Daniel the Hebrew boys are commanded to be taught the language they already knew?

Every human being can acquire any language—whether Greek, Latin, or one of the languages of other nations—either by hearing it or by learning it from a teacher through reading.

Although knowledge of all languages is difficult for anyone, no one is so lazy that, living among his own people, he does not know the language of his own people. For what else should he be considered but worse than dumb animals? They utter the cry of their own kind; he is worse because he lacks knowledge of his own language.

It is difficult to discover what language God spoke at the beginning of the world when he said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I), for at that time languages did not yet exist.

Likewise, it is asked in what language he later sounded in the external ears of human beings, especially when speaking to the first man, or to the prophets, or when the voice of God speaking sounded bodily: “You are my beloved Son.” Some believe that this was the one and only language that existed before the diversity of languages.

Among the various nations it is believed that God speaks to them in the same language that the human beings themselves use, so that they may understand him. [Col. 0437B] God speaks to human beings not through his invisible substance but through a bodily creature, through which he also wished to appear to human beings when he spoke.

The Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels” (1 Cor. XIII). Here it is asked in what language angels speak. This does not mean that angels have some languages of their own; it is said by way of exaggeration.

It is likewise asked in what language human beings will speak in the future, but this is nowhere found. For the Apostle says: “Whether tongues will cease” (ibid.).

We placed the discussion of languages before that of nations because nations arose from languages, not languages from nations.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Names of the Nations

[Col. 0437C]

A nation is a multitude arising from one origin, or distinguished from another nation by its own particular grouping, such as Greece and Asia. From this comes the term “gentility.” A nation is so called because of the generations of families, that is, from *gignere*, “to beget,” just as *natio* comes from *nasci*, “to be born.”

The nations by which the earth was divided are seventy-three: fifteen from Japheth, thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem. These total seventy-three—or rather, as calculation demonstrates, seventy-two—and an equal number of languages began to exist throughout the earth; as they increased, they filled provinces and islands.

The five sons of Shem each separately begot one nation. The first was Elam, from whom came the Elamites, rulers of Persia. The second was Asshur, from whom the empire of the Assyrians sprang. The third was Arphaxad, from whom the nation of the Chaldaeans arose. The fourth was Lud, from whom came the Lydians. The fifth was Aram, from whom came the Syrians, whose capital was Damascus.

The sons of Aram, grandchildren of Shem, were four: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.

Uz founded Trachonitis, which held supremacy between Palestine and Coelesyria. Job came from there, according to what is written: “There was a man in the land of Uz” (Job I).

The second was Hul, from whom came the Armenians. The third was Gether, from whom came the Arcanians or Curians. The fourth was Mash, from whom came those who are called Maeonians.

The descendants of Arphaxad, son of Shem: Eber was the grandson of Arphaxad, from whom came the Hebrews. Joktan, the son of Eber, was the ancestor of the Indians. Sale, the son of Joktan, was the ancestor of the Bactrians, although others suspect that they were exiles from the Scythians.

Ishmael, the son of Abraham, was the ancestor of the Ishmaelites, who are now called Saracens under a corrupted name, as though from Sarah, and Hagarenes from Hagar. Nabaioth, the son of Ishmael, was the ancestor of the Nabataeans, who inhabit the region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea.

Moab and Ammon, the sons of Lot, were the ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites. Edom, the son of Esau, was the ancestor of the Idumaeans.

These are the nations that came from the stock of Shem.

The Hagarenes derive their name from Hagar. As we have said, they are called Saracens by a perverse name because they boast that they were born from Sarah. The Ishmaelites are interpreted as “obedient to themselves,” that is, sinners who do what they desire. Hence it is read in the Psalm: “The tents of the Idumaeans and the Ishmaelites” (Ps. LXXXII).

The Hagarenes are interpreted as “proselytes,” that is, sinners alienated from the assembly of the Church. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon, Amalek and the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre” (ibid.).

Edom, from whom came the Idumaeans, is interpreted as “red” or “blood-colored.” It signifies the Jewish people, bloodstained because of the killing of Christ and the prophets. Hence it is written in Obadiah: “Thus says the Lord to Edom: Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly despised. The pride of your heart has lifted you up” (Obad. v. 2).

The Idumaeans are interpreted as “bloodstained” or “earth,” that is, demons or sinners, as it is read in the Psalm: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations’” (Ps. CXXXVI).

The Idumaean people also represent the nations. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: “You shall not abhor the Idumaean, because he is your brother; nor the Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land. Those born from them in the third generation shall enter the assembly of the Lord” (Deut. XXIII), that is, through faith in the Trinity and the washing of regeneration.

Seir, interpreted as “rough” or “hairy,” signifies the Jewish people. Hence it is read in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The Lord will come from Sinai, and he has dawned for us from Seir” (Deut. XXXIII).

Amalek is interpreted as “licking,” that is, the devil. Hence it is read in Exodus: “With a hidden or mighty hand the Lord wages war against Amalek from generation to generation” (Exod. XVII).

The Amalekites are interpreted as “the licking people,” that is, sinners who seek earthly things. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Gebal and Ammon and Amalek and the foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre” (Ps. LXXXII).

The Philistines are the same as the Palestinians, because the Hebrew language does not have the letter *p*; instead it uses *ph* in Greek. Thus the Philistines are called Palestinians, plainly from their city. They are also called Allophyli, and likewise foreigners, because they were always enemies of Israel and were separated far from their race and fellowship.

The Philistines are interpreted as “those who fall by the cup,” that is, enemies of the Church who exalt themselves through their own knowledge. Hence it is read in the Prophet: “What have I to do with you, Tyre and Sidon, and all the territory of the Philistines? Quickly and swiftly I will repay your recompense upon your own head” (Joel III).

They are also understood in a favorable sense. Hence it is read in the Psalm: “These Allophyli have been subjected” (Ps. LIX).

The Canaanites were named from Canaan, the son of Ham, whose land the Jews possessed. From his lineage came Emor, the brother of Shechem, from whom the Amorites were named. The Canaanites are interpreted as “unstable” or “immovable,” and they signify sinners who do not possess the foundation of faith. Hence it is read in the Song of Exodus: “All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away” (Exod. XV).

The Egyptians were named from a certain king called Egypt; previously they were called Aerei. In the Hebrew language, however, Egyptians is interpreted as “those who afflict,” because they afflicted the people of God before they were delivered by divine aid.

The Egyptians are interpreted as “those who afflict,” that is, the impious or demons who oppress the faithful of the Church. Hence it is read in Exodus: “The Egyptians afflicted them with harsh labor” (Exod. I).

Armenius, one of the number of Jason’s leaders who went to Colchis, gathered the multitude that had wandered about after the loss of King Jason and founded Armenia, giving the nation its name from his own. It is a Persian frontier, which separates the Scythians from them.

A man was surnamed Scytha; from his frontier, some say, the Scythians derived their name. They have always been regarded as a most ancient nation. They founded the kingdoms of the Parthians and Bactrians, and their women also founded the kingdoms of the Amazons.

The Massagetae are descended from the Scythians. They were called Massagetae, as though “heavy Getae,” that is, strong Getae. For Livy uses “heavy silver” to mean masses. These are the people who live in the northern regions between the Scythians and the Albanians.

The Amazons were so called either because they lived together without men, as though *amazosai*; or because their right breasts had been burned away so that the shooting of arrows would not be obstructed, as though *aneu mazou*, “without a breast.” For they exposed the breast that they had burned. Titianus calls them “one-breasted women.” For *amazon* means, as it were, *aneu mazou*, “without a breast.”

It is now established that they no longer exist, since some were destroyed to the last person by Hercules, some by Achilles, and some by Alexander.

The Albanians are a region and people of Asia. They believe themselves descended from Jason. They are born with white hair because of the continual snows, and the color of their hair gave the people their name; hence they are called Albanians. Their pupils are gray, that is, variegated, so that they see better at night than by day. The Albanians were neighbors of the Amazons.

They say that the Ugnos, formerly called Huns, were later called Avars after their king. They first lived in the farthest Maeotis, between the icy Tanais and the savage peoples of the Massagetae. Then, on swift horses, they burst through the rocks of the Caucasus, where the barriers of Alexander restrain savage peoples. They held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians.

The nation of the Trojans was formerly called Dardanian, after Dardanus. Dardanus and Jasius were brothers who set out from Greece. Jasius reached Thrace, Dardanus Phrygia, and there Dardanus first ruled. After him came his son Erichthonius, and then his grandson [Col. 0440A] Tros, from whom the Trojans were named.

The Galatians are known to be Gauls. Summoned by the king of Bithynia to assist him, they divided the kingdom with him after winning the victory. Thus, mixed with the Greeks, they were first called Gallo-Greeks; now, from the ancient name of the Gauls, they are called Galatians.

The Greeks were first called Thessalians, after Thessalus; later they were called Greeks, after King Graecus. For properly speaking, the Thessalians are Greeks.

They say that the Lapiths were a people of Thessaly who formerly lived around the river Peneus and were named from Lapitha, the daughter of Apollo.

The Sicyonians are Greeks, named after King Sicyon. They were first called Aegialeans, after King Aegialeus, who first ruled the Sicyonians; from him the city Aegialea was also named. It is now called the Peloponnese, after its king Pelops. The same people are also called Arcadians, after King Arcas, the son of Jupiter and Callisto.

The Danaans were named after King Danaus. They are also called Argives, after their founder Argus. After Apis, king of the Greeks, died, his son Argus succeeded him in the kingdom, and from him the Argives were named. After his death they also began to regard him as a god, honoring him with a temple and sacrifice.

The Achaeans, also called Achivi, were named after Achaeus, the son of Jupiter. They were called Pelasgi because they seemed to have arrived in Italy in spring with their sails spread, like birds. Varro records that they first landed in Italy; the Greeks, however, say that the Pelasgi were named after Pelasgus, the son of Jupiter and Larissa.

The Myrmidons were the companions of Achilles; the Dolopes were those of Pyrrhus. The Myrmidons were so called on account of their cleverness, as though *myrmeces*, that is, ants. Eratosthenes, however, says that the Myrmidons were named after the leader Myrmidon, the son of Jupiter and Eurymedusa.

Cranaus succeeded Cecrops as king of the Athenians. His daughter Attis gave her name to the region and people, and from her they were called Attici, that is, Athenians.

Ion, a brave man, called these same Athenians Ionians after his own name.

The Macedonians were formerly called Emathians, after King Emathion; later they were called Macedonians.

The Epirotes were first called Pyrrhidae, after Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles. Later, under King Pyrrhus as leader, they ventured to cross into Italy.

Dorus was the son of Neptune and Ellepis, and from him the Dorians derive their origin and name. They are a part of the Greek people, and from them the third language of the Greeks, called Doric, also received its name.

The Lacedaemonians were named after Lacedaemon, the son of Semele. Having long persisted in war against the Messenians, they feared that through the length of the conflict they would lose the hope of offspring. They therefore commanded that their virgins should have intercourse with the young men left at home. Thus, from the promiscuous intercourse of virgins and husbands, young men were born of uncertain fathers and were called Parthenii from the known chastity of their mothers. For they are the same as the Spartans, who are also called Lacedaemonians.

The Thracians are said to have arisen from and been named after a son of Japheth called Tiras, as stated above. The pagans, however, think that they were named from their character, because they are savage; for they were the fiercest of all peoples.

Hence many fabulous stories are told about them: that they sacrificed captives to their gods and were accustomed to carry human blood in the bones of skulls. Virgil says of them:

> Alas! Flee the cruel lands, flee the greedy shore!

That is, the lands of the cruel and greedy.

The people of the Istrians derive their origin from the Colchians. They were sent to pursue the Argonauts, and when they entered the river Ister from the Black Sea, they were named from the river, by which they withdrew from the sea.

The Romans were named after Romulus, who founded the city of Rome and gave his name to the nation and the state. [Col. 0441B] Previously they had been called Saturnians after Saturn and Latins after Latinus. Latinus was the king of Italy, who called the people Latins after his own name; later they were called Romans.

They were also called Quirites because Romulus was called Quirinus, since he always used a spear, which in the Sabine language is called *quiris*.

Italus, Sabinus, and Sicanus were also brothers. From them names were given to peoples and regions. From Italus came Italy, from Sabinus Sabinia, and from Sicanus the Sicanians; they are also called Sicilians.

The Etruscans are a people of Italy. Their name is said to derive from the abundance of sacrifices and incense, that is, from *apo tou thuein* (“from sacrificing”).

The Umbrians are a people of Italy but descendants of the ancient Gauls, who inhabit the Apennine mountain. Histories report that they survived the time of the watery disaster of the rains; for this reason they were called *Ombrious* in Greek.

The Marsi, a people of Italy, were named after Marsyas, the companion of Liber, who taught them the use of vines. For this reason they made a statue of him, which the Romans later carried away after conquering the Marsi.

The Greeks call the Marsi *Uscos*, as though *ophiouchous*, because they possess many serpents, and *ophis* means “serpent.” They are said to remain unharmed by the magical power of their incantations. They inhabit a region of the Apennine mountain together with the Umbrians.

The Goths are thought to have been named after Magog, the son of Japheth, from the similarity of the final syllable. The ancients called them Getae more often than Goths. They are a brave and exceedingly powerful people, tall in bodily stature and terrifying in their manner of warfare. Lucan writes of them:

> On this side let the Dacian press, on that the Getan meet the Iberians.

The Dacians were offspring of the Getae. They are thought to have been called Daci as though *Dagi*, because they were created from the stock of the Goths. Of them the poet says:

> You will go far, all the way to the northern Dacians.

The Bessi were barbarians, believed to have been named from the multitude of their oxen. Concerning them someone writes:

> He who inhabits the middle of the land, or that man  
> Who, rich in many cattle, wears a cap,  
> The dweller on the bank.

The Gipedes used foot combat more than cavalry combat, and were named for this reason.

The Sarmatians rode armed across open plains before Lentulus kept them back at the Danube. From their devotion to arms they are therefore thought to have been called Sarmatians.

A river called the Lanus is said to lie beyond the Danube, from which the Alans were named. Likewise, the peoples living near the river Lemannus are called Alemanni. Lucan writes of them:

> They abandoned the tents fixed beside the hollow Lemannus.

The Lombards are commonly said to have been named from their long beards, which were never cut.

The river Vindelicus bursts forth from the edge of Gaul. The Vandals are said to have lived beside this river and to have derived their name from it.

The peoples of Germany were so called because they have immense bodies and are savage nations, hardened by the most severe cold. They drew their character from the very harshness of the climate: they are fierce in spirit and always untamed, living by raiding and hunting. Their peoples are numerous, varied in weapons, different in dress, discordant in language, and uncertain in the origin of their names: the Tolleraces, Amsivarii, Quadi, Tungri, Marcomanni, Bructeri, Camasi, Blangiones, and Ubantes. Their barbarous savagery, even in their names, expresses a certain horror.

The Suebi were a part of the Germans at the northern extremity. Lucan writes of them:

> From the farthest North he pours forth the blond-haired Suebi.

Many have reported that they consisted of a hundred districts and peoples. They are thought to have been called Suebi after Mount Suevo, which begins Germany from the rising of the sun, and whose regions they inhabited.

The Burgundians, after the interior of Germany had once been conquered by the Romans, were placed by the emperor Tiberius along the boundaries of the military camps. They grew into a great nation and took their name from those places, because the frequent settlements established along the boundaries are commonly called *burgi*, “forts” or “settlements.”

Later, rebelling against the Romans, more than eighty thousand armed men settled along the bank of the Rhine and acquired the name of a nation.

The Saxon people live on the shores of the Ocean and in impassable marshes. They are capable through courage and agility. Hence they are called Saxons because they are a hard and extremely strong race of men, surpassing the other peoples devoted to piracy.

The Franks are thought to have been named after a certain leader of their own. Others believe that they were named from the savagery of their character. For their customs are uncultivated and their spirits naturally fierce.

Some suspect that the Britons were called by a Latin name because they are brutish. They are a people placed within the Ocean, with the sea spread around them, as though outside the inhabited world. Virgil writes of them:

> The Britons divided from the whole world.

The Scots have their name in their own language from their painted bodies, because they mark themselves with tattoos of various designs using iron needles and ink.

The Gauls were named from the whiteness of their bodies. For *gala* means “milk” in Greek. Hence the Sibyl also calls them this when she says of them:

> Then their milk-white necks  
> Are entwined with gold.

According to differences in climate, human faces, colors, bodily sizes, and differences of character also arise. Thus we observe that the Romans are serious, the Greeks lighthearted, the Africans changeable, and the Gauls naturally fierce and keener in intellect. Climate produces this by nature.

The Gauls called the Senones were formerly called Xenones, because they had received Liberus as a guest. Later the *x* was changed into an *s*.

Vacca was a town near the Pyrenees, from which the Vaccaei were named. The poet is believed to have spoken of them:

> The Vaccaei wandering widely.

They inhabit a very extensive wilderness of the Pyrenean heights. They are also called Vascones, as though Vaccones, with the *c* changed into an *s*.

Gnaeus Pompey, after subduing Spain and hastening to return for his triumph, brought them down from the Pyrenean heights and gathered them into one town. Hence the town received the name “city of the gathered.”

The Spaniards were first called Iberians from the river Iberus; later they were called Spaniards from Hispalo.

Galicians (*Galleci*) are so called from the whiteness of their complexion, and hence they are also called Gauls (*Galli*); for they are fairer than the other peoples of Spain. They claim Greek ancestry for themselves and therefore possess natural cleverness. For they say that, after the end of the Trojan War, Teucer—hated by his father Telamon because of the death of his brother Ajax, and not being received into the kingdom—went to Cyprus and [Col. 0443C] there founded a city named Salamis after his ancient homeland. From there he proceeded to Galatia and, having established settlements, gave the people their name from that place.

Asturians (*Astures*) are a people of Spain, so called because they live around the river Astur, enclosed by mountains and dense forests.

Cantabrians (*Cantabri*) are a people of Spain, named from the name of the city and of the river Ebro, upon which they are situated. Their spirit is stubborn, more inclined to banditry and warfare, and they are always ready to endure blows.

The Celtiberians (*Celtiberi*) came from the Celtic Gauls, from whose name the region Celtiberia was called. For they settled beside the river Ebro in Spain and came to be called Celtiberians from the combination of the two names: the Ebro and the Gauls who were called Celts.

[Col. 0443D] The Africans (*Afri*) were named after one of Abraham’s descendants, who was called Afer. He is said to have led an army against Libya, settled there after defeating its enemies, and caused his descendants, from the name of their ancestor, to be called Afri and Africa.

The Carthaginians (*Poeni*) were named from the Phoenicians, who departed with Dido. The Tyrians, however, were named from Tyre, a Phoenician city from which they set out and came to the coast of Africa.

The Gaetuli (*Getuli*) are said to have been Getae who, embarking on ships in a huge migration from their own lands, occupied the regions of the Syrtes in Libya. Because they had come from the Getae, they were called Gaetuli, the name being derived from that origin. Hence there is also a belief that, among the Goths, on account of their ancient kinship, the Moors are called their close relatives by blood.

At the beginning Africa was called Libya; afterward Africa; then Gaetulia; and finally Mauretania and Numidia. The Moors and Numidians, as the Africans believe, received their origin and name as follows. After Hercules died in Spain, his army, composed of various peoples, wandered about seeking settlements for itself after losing its leader. From among them the Medes, Persians, and Armenians were carried by ship to Africa and occupied the regions nearest the sea. But when the Persians could not find materials in the fields with which to build dwellings, and an unfamiliar language prevented commerce, they wandered through open fields and various wildernesses. Because of their wandering journeys, they called themselves Numidians in their own language—that is, “wandering and roaming without a city.”

[Col. 0444B] The Medes mingled with the Libyans who inhabited the region nearest Spain. The Libyans gradually corrupted their name, calling the Medes *Mauri* in their barbarian language, although the Greeks call them *Mauri* because of their color: for the Greeks call black *mauron*. Blown upon by the heat of the torrid climate, they acquire a dark complexion.

Massilia is a city of Africa not far from Atlas and the gardens of the Hesperides. From this city the Massylians (*Massylii*) were named, whom we corruptly call Massulae. Virgil writes of them:

> Here a priestess of the Massylian people  
> was shown to me.

The Gaulalians (*Gaulalii*) are peoples who wander from the south as far as the Ocean of the Hesperides. The island of Gauloe gave them their name; it lies near Ethiopia, where no serpent is born or lives.

The Garamantes are a people of Africa living near Cyrene. They were named after King Garamantes, the son of Apollo, who founded there a city called Garama after his own name. They are close neighbors of the Ethiopian peoples. Virgil writes of them:

> The farthest Garamantes.

They are called “farthest” because they are savage and removed from human society.

The Hesperians (*Hesperii*) are those who dwell around Spain, for Spain is called Hesperia.

The Ethiopians (*Aethiopes*) were named after the son of Ham, who was called Cush, from whom they derive their origin. For *Cush* in Hebrew means “Ethiopian.” Once, rising from the river Indus, they settled near Egypt, between the Nile and the Ocean, in the south, beneath the immediate neighborhood of the sun. They consist of three peoples: the Hesperians, the Garamantes, and the Indians. The Hesperians belong to the West, the Garamantes to Tripoli, and the Indians to the East.

The Ethiopians are interpreted as “darkness” or “gloom,” that is, the impious, among whom the devil moves as though surrounded by darkness.

The Troglodytes, a people of Ethiopia, were so named because they possess such speed that they can catch wild animals by running.

The Panphagi and the Hini [variant: *hi*] are in Ethiopia. Their food is whatever can be eaten, including everything that grows by chance; hence their name. The Ichthyophagi are so called because they are successful at hunting in the sea and live only on fish. They occupy the mountainous regions beyond India; after subduing them, Alexander the Great forbade them to eat fish.

The Anthropophagi are an exceedingly savage people settled beneath the region of the Syrians [variant: *Seres*]. Because they eat human flesh, they are called Anthropophagi, “man-eaters.” Thus, as happened with these peoples, the names of the other nations too have been altered over the centuries—whether from kings, places, customs, or any other causes—so that their original source is no longer revealed by the passage of time.

As for those called Antipodes, on the supposition that they stand opposite our footsteps, or that they are placed beneath the earth and tread with their feet against the footprints of our feet, this is not to be believed in any way, since neither the solidity of the earth permits it nor does its center. Nor is it established by any knowledge of history; rather, poets conjecture it as though reasoning it out.

[Col. 0445B] The Titans are said to have been certain peoples in Greece, powerful and outstanding in strength. The myths say that the earth, angered against the gods, created them to avenge her. Hence they are called Titans, from *apo tēs tiseōs*—that is, “from vengeance”—because they were supposedly armed against the gods to avenge their mother, the earth. The myths invent that Jupiter overcame and destroyed them in war, and that they perished when thunderbolts were hurled from heaven.

## CHAPTER III. On the Vocabulary of Kingdoms and Military Affairs

A kingdom (*regnum*) is named from kings (*reges*), for just as kings are called from ruling (*regnare*), so a kingdom is named from kings. All nations have possessed kingdoms in their respective periods—the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Egyptians, and Greeks—whose turns the lot of time has rolled onward in such a way that one was succeeded by another. Among all the kingdoms of the earth, however, two are handed down as more glorious than the rest: first that of the Assyrians, and afterward that of the Romans, ordered and distinguished from one another by their times and locations. For just as the former came first and the latter afterward, so the former arose in the East and the latter in the West. Indeed, at the end of the former, the beginning of the latter immediately followed. The remaining kingdoms and kings are regarded as appendages of these.

But among all kingdoms, the kingdom most to be desired is that which remains stable and fixed, rests in eternal peace, and will have no end. The king of this kingdom is Christ, of whom the prophet says:

> His dominion shall be multiplied,  
> and there shall be no end of peace  
> upon the throne of David  
> and over his kingdom,  
> to establish and strengthen it  
> in judgment and justice,  
> from now and forever.

(Isa. IX.)

Of this kingdom the angel also says to Mary:

> The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

(Luke I.)

To possess this kingdom, he himself calls us daily through the sacred Scriptures and the preachers of the Gospel, so that we may hope for and desire heavenly things and strive to reach them through right faith and good works. On the day of judgment, when the King of kings himself sits upon the throne of his majesty and all nations are gathered before him, he invites his elect, who will be at his right hand, saying:

> Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.

(Matt. XXV.)

In this world, moreover, those kingdoms are praiseworthy which are subject to the true King, namely the Lord Christ, who extends and governs the Church throughout the whole world, among various peoples and in different places, according to his will.

To these kingdoms the Prophet speaks in the psalm, saying:

> Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God;  
> sing praises to the Lord;  
> sing praises to God,  
> who has ascended above the heaven of heavens toward the East.

(Ps. LXVII.)

By saying “kingdoms of the earth,” he wished to signify the whole human race. For although there are peoples who have no kings, this expression nevertheless includes whatever peoples are understood to exist. The word “sing” refers to purity of soul; “sing praises” refers to the holiest works, which are approved and accepted by the Lord.

“He who has ascended above the heaven of heavens”: this is certainly the Lord, who descended from heaven to liberate the nature of our weakness and likewise ascended above the heavens of heavens, because he sits at the right hand of the Father. By “toward the East,” or by what he said, he clearly indicated Jerusalem, which is situated in the eastern regions. Hence, while the apostles looked on, the Lord ascended into heaven.

Kings (*reges*) are called from ruling (*regere*); for just as a priest is named from sanctifying, so a king is named from ruling. But one does not rule who does not correct. Therefore the name is rightly retained by doing right and lost through sinning. Hence among the ancients there was this proverb:

> You will be king if you act rightly;  
> if you do not act rightly, you will not be king.

The chief virtues of kings are justice and piety. Piety, however, is praised more highly in kings, for justice by itself is severe.

Among the Greeks kings are called *basileis*, because, like bases, they support the people; hence bases also bear crowns. For the more highly anyone is placed, the more heavily he is burdened with the weight of duties.

Tyrants are called in Greek what in Latin are likewise called kings; for among the ancients there was no distinction between a king and a tyrant, as in the verse:

> It will be part of my peace to have touched the tyrant’s right hand.

They were also called *tyrones*. For a *tiro* is a strong man, of the sort about whom the Lord speaks:

> Through me kings reign,  
> and tyrants possess the earth.

(Prov. VIII.)

Later, however, it became customary to call the worst and most wicked kings tyrants—those who exercise among the peoples a desire for luxurious domination and the most cruel rule.

Mystically, a king is understood as God, as in the psalm:

> But God is our king before the ages.

(Ps. LXXIII.)

The queen is the holy Church, as in the psalm:

> The queen stood at your right hand.

Likewise, kings are the apostles or the other saints, as it is read in the psalm:

> God who gives vengeance,  
> and is powerful in his kingdom,  
> gives strength to our kings.

(Ps. XVII.)

Queens are likewise the souls of the perfect, who are not servants of sin, as it is said in the Song of Songs:

> There are sixty queens.

(Song VI.)

Saintly men are rightly called kings because, by the authority of the Spirit, they govern their souls according to the will of God and subject them in obedience to the King of kings, namely the Lord Christ. In the words of the Psalmist:

> He shall rule from sea to sea,  
> and from the river to the ends of the earth.  
> The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts;  
> the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents,  
> and all the kings of the earth shall adore him;  
> all nations shall serve him.

(Ps. LXXI.)

When it says, “He shall rule,” it means that the Lord Christ, of whom the preceding verses sing and the following verses will speak, will become widely known through religious worship.

This cannot in any way refer to Solomon, the son of David, who is known to have been king only among the Jewish people. For if you understand these seas as our seas and the verse as signifying the circuit of the whole world, you will not be able to perceive its meaning.

The kings of Arabia, therefore, are those who subject the allurements of the body to rigorous discipline. Likewise, “Sheba,” from which the Sabaeans are named, although it excels in bodily pleasure and is filled with delightful fragrances, offers through its converted people more pleasing gifts—the gifts of virtues.

When it says, “All the kings of the earth shall adore him,” he wished us to understand all nations by “all the kings,” because there is no nation that does not worship its own creator in some part of its people.

In another sense, kings are understood as wicked teachers, as the prophet says:

> They have become kings, but not from me.

(Hos. VIII.)

A tyrant can typologically signify either the devil or the Antichrist, who always strive to act in opposition to the rule of Christ. They are followed by wicked people who, pursuing earthly desire, choose rather to oppress the Christian people cruelly than to govern them with moderate administration and preside over them properly and prudently.

Consuls (*consules*) are called from consulting (*consulere*), just as kings are called from ruling (*regere*), or from reading (*legere*). For when the Romans could not endure the proud rule of kings, they established annual offices and appointed two consuls for themselves. Royal arrogance consisted not in the benevolence of one who gave counsel but in the pride of one who dominated.

These men were called consuls either because they consulted for the citizens or because they governed all things by counsel. They were nevertheless chosen to be changed every year, so that no arrogant man might remain long and a more moderate one might quickly take his place. Hence there were two equals: one administered civil affairs and the other military affairs. They ruled for 464 years.

Consuls can rightly be called masters of the Church—that is, bishops, presbyters, and others who, according to the tradition of the holy Scriptures, assist and govern the people subject to them through counsel. He introduced this name of authority from the tradition of the pagans because it suits ecclesiastical dignity for all matters, internal and external, to be conducted prudently with counsel, according to what is written:

> Do everything with counsel,  
> and afterward you will not regret it.

(Sir. XXXII.)

As for the title of Caesar or Augustus, I think it applies to our Lord only in the sense of monarchy, because he alone reigns in heaven and on earth, and because all things stand under his rule.

Monarchs are those who possess sole authority, such as Alexander among the Greeks and Julius among the Romans. Hence the word “monarchy”: *monos* in Greek means “single,” and *archē* means “rule.”

Tetrarchs are those who hold a fourth part of a kingdom. For *tetra* means “four,” as was the case with Philip in Judaea.

“Prince” signifies both rank and dignity, as in Virgil’s verse:

> Turnus, the first, hurled the blazing torch,

where “prince” means “first.”

A prince is named from the sense of taking, because he is the first to take, just as a *municipes* is named from receiving civic duties (*munia*).

It is therefore read in the prophet concerning Christ (Isa. IX) that he is the prince of peace, whose principate is upon his shoulder, because on the cross he draws all things to himself (John XII). Therefore every knee bends to him and every tongue confesses, because he lives and reigns in the glory of God the Father forever (Phil. II).

Of this prince it is likewise read in Ezekiel:

> The prince shall sit in it—that is, in the closed gate—and shall eat his bread.

(Ezek. XLIV.)

The apostles and teachers of the Church of God are also called princes, concerning whom it is written in the psalm:

> The princes of the people have gathered with the God of Abraham.

(Ps. XLVI.)

And again:

> You shall appoint them princes over all the earth;  
> their principate has been greatly strengthened.

(Ps. XLIV.)

For by their admonitions they govern the Church until the end of the world, and on the day of judgment they will be judges with Christ. To them he himself says:

> When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

(Matt. XIX.)

Again, saints are princes, as in Solomon:

> I saw servants on horses—that is, sinners in carnal power—and princes walking like servants upon the earth.

(Ecclus. X.)

In the opposite sense, princes are understood as those of whom the prophet says:

> Princes have arisen, and I did not know them.

(Isa. XIX.)

The prince may also signify the devil or the Antichrist, as the Lord speaks of him in Ezekiel:

> Son of man, raise a lamentation over the prince of Tyre,

that is, over the prince of tribulation.

(Ezek. XXVIII.)

A leader (*dux*) is so called because he is the leader of an army. But not everyone who is a prince or leader can immediately be called a king. In war it is better to call someone a leader than a king, for this name expresses one who leads in battle.

Hence Virgil speaks of “Evander the leader.” Sallust writes:

> The more eagerly each man wished to appear good in the presence of the leader;

he did not say “in the presence of the consul.”

A leader can truly be called one who walks in the path of justice and leads those who follow him through right faith and good works into eternal life. Hence the Prophet beseeches the Lord, saying:

> Lead me in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.

(Ps. LXXXV.)

And elsewhere:

> Your good Spirit, he says, will lead me into the right way.

(Ps. CXLII.)

The Savior himself is therefore read as leader in the Gospel through the prophet, where it is written:

> And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall go forth a leader who will govern my people Israel.

(Matt. II.)

The Lord Jesus Christ is likewise understood as leader in that passage of Isaiah:

> Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher of the nations.

(Isa. LV.)

And elsewhere:

> My servant David shall be prince in their midst.

(Ezek. XXXIV.)

The holy preachers are leaders because they draw the flocks of the faithful after them.

In the opposite sense, leaders are heretics, Jews, or wicked teachers, as in the Gospel:

> Leave them; they are blind leaders of the blind. If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.

(Matt. XV.)

The Lord is strong, as it is read in the psalm:

> The Lord is strong and powerful.

And in Job:

> Wise in heart and strong in power.

(Job IX.)

The strong are the saints, as in the Song of Songs:

> Behold, sixty strong men surround Solomon’s bed, from among the strongest of Israel.

(Song III.)

The strong one is the devil, as in the Gospel:

> When the strong man, armed, guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace.

(Luke XI.)

The patricians (*patricii*) were so called because, as fathers provide for their children, so they provide for the commonwealth.

Prefects (*praefecti*) are so called because they preside with praetorian authority.

Praetors are the same as prefects, being, as it were, those set over others.

Presidents (*praesides*) are so called because they protectively hold the guardianship of some place.

Praetors are also, as it were, teachers and leaders of the state. They are likewise quaestors, as though they were investigators, because they preside over inquiries. Counsel and legal cases are in their hands.

The *proceres* are the princes of the state, as though they were those who go before, because they surpass everyone in honor.

Tribunes are so called because they assign rights to soldiers or to the plebs.

Chiliarchs are those who command a thousand; we call them “commanders of a thousand.” The name is Greek.

Centurions are so called because they command one hundred soldiers, just as *quinquagenarii* are so called because they command fifty soldiers, and *decani* because they are placed over ten soldiers.

These ranks of superiors are properly maintained in the Church. Each superior, according to his proper rite and order, cares for his subjects so that they do not proceed along the byways of error or persist in unjust deeds. They must also take care that no one harms another or oppresses anyone by violence, but that they lead a moderate life in mutual concord and peace.

Hence in the Old Law (Exod. XVIII), Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, gave him the advice that he should appoint over the people tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and commanders of ten, so that they themselves might decide and judge lesser matters, while he might administer to his subjects the things that pertain to the Lord.

For this reason the Apostle also commanded the Hebrews, saying:

> Obey your superiors in the Lord and submit to them; for they keep watch as though they would give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would not be profitable for you.

(Heb. XIII.)

And again:

> Remember, he says, your superiors, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.

(Ibid.)

A soldier (*miles*) is so called either because there were formerly a thousand in a single unit, or because he was chosen as one out of a thousand. Romulus was the first to take soldiers from the people and give them this name. Liber first taught the order of military service.

A soldier is called ordinary or extraordinary. An ordinary soldier serves according to rank and has not yet attained any grade of honor; he is a common soldier, that is, a humble member of the military. An extraordinary soldier is one who is promoted out of the ranks because of valor.

The discharged are called veterans: they are released from military service and are no longer engaged in active warfare. For to serve as a soldier is called *mereri*, from the pay that soldiers earn. They are likewise called veterans because they are no longer in active warfare but, after the labors of military service, receive the benefit of rest.

Cavalry soldiers are so called because they sit on horses and serve in the cavalry order.

Recruits (*tirones*) are called strong young men who are selected for military service and are capable of bearing arms. They are judged not merely by their profession of birth but by their appearance and bodily health. Hence they are called recruits, and until they have been tested by the military oath, they are not soldiers.

It was the custom of Roman military service that young men first be trained in arms after reaching puberty. Recruits served at sixteen years of age, and until then they lived under guardianship alone.

Those enrolled in military service are so called because they are entered on tablets by the one who is to lead them. Those transferred are so called when they pass from one legion to another; they are called transferred because their names are entered for transfer.

*Optiones* are so called because they are chosen, for *optare* means “to choose,” as in the verse:

> And he chose a place for his kingdom,

that is, “he selected it.”

Guards (*excubitores*) are so called because they are always keeping watch. They are soldiers who keep watch in porticoes for the protection of the king. Daytime guards are called *excubiae*; nighttime guards are called *vigiliae*, hence “watchmen.”

The *velites* were a type of Roman military force, named from *volitare*, “to fly about.” Young men selected for their agility, with their arms, sat behind the cavalry. When they approached the enemy, they leapt down from the horses and immediately, fighting on foot on another side while the cavalry who had carried them engaged the enemy, threw the foe into confusion.

Once, Hannibal’s elephants were driven back by these *velites*. When they could no longer be restrained by their own people, they were killed by driving a craftsman’s chisel between their ears.

Military service (*militia*) is called from soldiers (*milites*), or from “many,” as though *multitia*, the business of many; or from the burden of affairs, as though *moletia*.

A legion consists of six thousand armed men and is named from the chosen (*electi*), as though it meant “chosen for arms.” Strictly speaking, the Macedonian formation is called a phalanx, the Gallic formation a *caterva*, and ours a legion.

A legion has sixty centuries, thirty maniples, twelve cohorts, and two hundred troops of cavalry.

A century is a division of the army into groups of one hundred soldiers. Hence those who command them are called centurions.

The *subcenturiati* are not those who belong to the first century but those who belong to the second, as though they were beneath the first century. Nevertheless, they too are closely arrayed and stationed in the fighting lines, so that if the first line fails, these men—whom we have called those under the second century—may come to the aid of the first when it is hard-pressed. Hence *subcenturiatus* is used to suggest a force equipped with concealed arms.

A maniple consists of two hundred soldiers.

Maniples are so called either because the soldiers were the first to begin battle by hand, or because, before standards existed, they made for themselves bundles—*manipuli*—of straw or some kind of grass to serve as standards. From this standard the soldiers were called *manipulares*. Lucan writes of them:

> At once he calls the armed maniples to the standards.

A troop (*turma*) consists of thirty cavalrymen. For the Roman cavalrymen in one tribe numbered three hundred; ten were supplied from each century, and a troop was formed.

A cohort has five hundred soldiers.

There are three types of military service: the oath of service, the summons, and the levy.

The oath of service is that in which, after his selection, each soldier swore that he would not withdraw from military service until he had completed his terms of service—that is, the periods of military duty. These are those who complete full military service, for they are bound to it for twenty-five years.

A summons occurs when, in the event of a sudden war, not only soldiers but also others are called out. Hence a consul was accustomed to say:

> Let whoever wishes the commonwealth to be safe follow me.

A levy is made amid an uprising, when the danger threatening the city does not permit individuals to swear an oath; instead, a multitude is suddenly gathered and, in the tumult of anger, brought together. This is also called an uprising.

In battle formation there are generally these arrangements: the battle line, the fleet, the knot, the wedge, the wings, the horns, and the column. These forms and names borrow their designations from the things from which they are transferred.

The battle line (*acies*) is so called because it is armed with iron and with the sharp points of swords.

An army (*exercitus*) is a multitude of one kind, named from exercise.

A wedge (*cuneus*) is a multitude of soldiers gathered together. Because it comes together into one, this gathering itself was called a *cuneus*, as though *couneus*, since all are forced into one.

The *classes* were so called because of the division of the army that Romulus instituted. For the Greeks call division *claein*. Later these divisions were called maniples. Hence Virgil writes:

> Here they used to fight with fleets; here, in battle line.

Later, the word *classis* was also applied to a fleet of ships.

A knot (*nodus*) is properly a dense multitude of infantry, just as a troop is a multitude of cavalry. It is called a knot because of its difficulty, since it can scarcely be untied.

The wings (*alae*) in an army are said to consist of thirty cavalrymen. Cavalry are called wings because they protect the infantry in the manner of wings.

The horns (*cornua*) are the extremities of the army, because they are bent inward.

A column (*agmen*) is so called because it is extended lengthwise, as usually happens when an army travels; it derives from *agere*, “to go.” Plautus writes: “Where are you going, and where is he himself?” It is an army on the march.

A column is so called because it is extended lengthwise, as usually happens when an army proceeds through the gates. Anything else is called a column only improperly.

The soldiers of Christ are those who fight against the devil and battle courageously against vices. When they have completed and fulfilled their contest, they are promised not an earthly reward but eternal life.

The Apostle wrote to the Corinthians concerning such men:

> Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but powerful through God for the destruction of enemies’ plans, destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God and taking every understanding captive into obedience to Christ, and being ready to punish every disobedience.

(II Cor. X.)

## CHAPTER IV. On Citizens

[Col. 0451D]

It has been said in part about the names of commands and military service. Next we briefly treat the names of citizens.

Citizens are so called because, coming together into one community, they live together, so that communal life may become both more refined and safer. Citizens are understood mystically in a favorable sense, as in the Apostle: “But you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. II). They are also understood in an unfavorable sense, when they are assigned to spiritual Babylon—that is, to the faction of the devil.

A house is the dwelling of one family, just as a city is that of one people, and the world is the dwelling of the whole human race; “house” also denotes a lineage. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIV). After mocking the idols of the Gentiles, in the third section he says that the praises of the Lord’s saints are to be celebrated with the mouth; but, proceeding through these two verses by different offices, he admonishes us that the praise of the faithful ought to resound to the true Lord.

In Israel every righteous person is included, one who rejoices in divine contemplation; afterward he counts them individually. In Aaron are the priests; in Levi, the remaining ministers; finally, those who serve the Lord in any honorable manner. Thus the whole people, divided into its various parts, are commanded to praise the Lord with devotion.

“Race” (*genus*) is derived from “begetting” and “generating,” or from the definition of those begotten from particular ancestors. Nations bounded by their particular kinships are called peoples (*gentes*).

A people (*populus*) is an assembly of human beings joined together by agreement in law and harmonious fellowship. A people differs from the commoners (*plebs*) in this respect: the people consists of all the citizens, including the elders, whereas the commoners are the remaining populace of the city without the elders. Thus the people is the entire citizen body, while the populace is the commoners; *plebs* is so called from plurality. For the number of younger people is greater than that of the elders. It is said to derive from the Greek *polis*, that is, “city” or “plurality.” Hence the people is also so called; in Greek, however, the people is *laos*, from “stones.”

The populace (*vulgus*) is a multitude dwelling here and there, as though each person lived wherever he wished.

In the Holy Scriptures, the name “people” signifies either the Jewish nation devoted to the worship of the one God and instructed by the precepts of the Lord’s law, or the Christian people, which is recognized as being more devoted to God. [Col. 0452C] Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Know that the Lord is God: he himself made us, and not we ourselves; but we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIX). For although the activity of the flesh supplies the ministry of our birth, nevertheless he is shown to bring us into this world who caused all things to come into existence.

It follows: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” He comes to the faithful people through most beautiful comparisons, showing what they are: sheep, because they are simple, and he himself is their true shepherd; “of his pasture,” that is, the abundant and sweet feast of the divine Scriptures. These are the pastures by which the faithful soul is nourished and led to the pleasant places of future blessedness.

Tribes are called distinct councils and assemblies of peoples. They are called tribes because, at the beginning, the Romans were divided by Romulus into three groups: senators, soldiers, and commoners. Although these tribes have now multiplied, they retain their former name.

Mystically, tribes likewise signify either the twelve tribes of the Israelite race or the assemblies of the saints in the Church. When the prophet speaks of mystical Jerusalem, he adds: “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to your name, O Lord” (Ps. CXXI).

By saying “there,” he signifies the city of Jerusalem, of which he earlier said: “whose participation is in unity” (ibid.). And so that you might understand it to be heavenly, he added: “they went up.” The blessed continually ascend to it, because they advance through unceasing exercise. He then added “tribes,” in which the people of Israel had been distributed. For just as that nation had twelve tribes according to the number of Jacob’s sons, so the Roman people had thirty-five councils.

In these tribes he signifies the saints who confessed that the Lord Savior is God. But, in order to separate these tribes of the faithful from the unbelieving, he added “the tribes of the Lord.” They could not truly be his unless they had believed in him with a pure mind. For it is clear that there were other tribes belonging to the devil, which preferred to separate themselves from Christ through impious will; to them he said in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII).

He briefly indicated what these tribes of the Lord were like by adding “a testimony for Israel,” that is, those who bear witness to holiness.

Among the ancient Romans there were censors; for “censor” is the name of a judicial dignity. To censor is to judge. Censors are also judges of estates, called from the assessment of property; they are called judges as though they were “speaking the law” to the people, or because they deliberate according to law. To deliberate according to law is to judge justly; and one is not a judge if justice is not in him.

In the Holy Scriptures, unjust men are also found set in place of censors of equity. Likewise there are unjust judges who followed in their judgments injustice rather than equity; many examples of this are found.

The Senate received its name from age, because its members were elders. Others understand senators to have been so called from *sinere*, “to permit,” because they gave the power to act. The *senatus consultum* was named from deliberating and discussing, because it is carried out in such a way that it gives counsel and cannot cause harm.

The senators were called “fathers,” as Sallust says, from their resemblance to caretaking. For just as fathers nourished their sons, so they nourished the republic. They were called “enrolled fathers” (*patres conscripti*) because, when Romulus had chosen ten senatorial councils, he entered their names on golden tablets before the assembled people; hence they were called enrolled fathers.

Municipal citizens (*municipes*) are those born in the same municipality. They are named from the performance of duties, because they undertake public offices. *Munia* means offices; hence those who hold no office are called exempt (*immunes*). Municipal citizens are original inhabitants who perform their duties in the place.

It is also read in the Scriptures that the citizenship of the saints is in heaven (Phil. III), because there they receive everlasting offices.

Private persons (*privati*) are outsiders excluded from public offices; the term is the opposite of one who holds a magistracy. They are called private because they have been released from the offices of the council.

Mercenaries are those who serve for wages. They are also called *barones*, a Greek name, because they are strong in their labors.

Mystically, mercenaries signify those who serve the Lord not solely out of divine love but for temporal reward. Of them it is written in the Gospel that the prodigal son, repenting, said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance, while I perish here from hunger?” (Luke XV).

Elsewhere the Truth himself says: “The hired servant, who is not the shepherd and whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees” (John X).

Publicans are called the contractors of the taxes of the treasury or of public revenues, because they collect public taxes, or because they pursue profits through the business of the world; hence they received that name. In the Gospel they are also read of as having come to the Savior together with sinners, because those who conduct public business in earthly affairs are rarely free from the burden of sins. But when they truly turn to the Lord through repentance, they become righteous from sinners.

A steward (*villicus*) is properly the governor of a country estate, and therefore receives his name from *villa*. Sometimes, however, according to Cicero’s interpretation, *villicus* signifies not the governance of an estate but the administration of the whole household: that is, an administrator of all possessions and estates.

In the Gospel parable, the steward is compared with one who makes himself guilty in earthly affairs but strives to acquit himself through almsgiving. Hence it is written that the steward, accused before his master of having squandered his goods, provided for his future by remitting debts to his fellow servants (Luke XVI). Therefore, after explaining the parable, the Lord himself said to his disciples: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (ibid.).

Agents, likewise called administrators, are so named from acting and caring. Procurators are so called because they perform the function of an administrator, as a proconsul does that of a consul.

Mystically, procurators, or guardians and agents, may be understood as the prophets, by whose words we were daily instructed concerning the coming of the Savior. Hence the Apostle says by way of example: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, though he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and agents until the time appointed by the father” (Gal. IV).

Rightly are those said to be under guardians who, possessing the spirit of fear, have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption. The age of infancy fears both sins and the pedagogue; it does not dare to believe itself free, although by nature it is master. According to both interpretations—whether we understand guardians and agents as prophets or as angels—this child remains under agents and guardians until he has reached the proper time of the mature man.

Just as the legal age among the Romans is fixed at twenty-five years, so, for the perfection of the human race, the coming of Christ is reckoned as the appointed time. As soon as he comes and we all grow into a mature man, the pedagogue and guardian depart from us. Then we enjoy the authority of the master and possession of the inheritance in which, though born to it beforehand, we were in a certain sense considered strangers.

Colonists (*coloni*) are resident cultivators from elsewhere, named from the cultivation of the land. They come from another place, cultivate leased land belonging to someone else, and owe a condition to the soil of their birth on account of agriculture, because the estate has been leased.

Colonists are spoken of in four ways: Roman colonists, Latin colonists, auxiliary colonists, and colonists of private land.

Tenants (*inquilini*) are so called as though they were “inhabiting another’s property.” They do not possess a dwelling of their own but live on another’s land.

There is a difference between a tenant and a newcomer. Tenants are those who move away and do not remain permanently. Newcomers or resident settlers are called adventitious, but they remain; hence they are called inhabitants, from inhabiting.

Newcomers mystically signify the saints who migrate from worldly error to the holy Church. Of them the Prophet says: “The Lord guards the newcomer and the orphan” (Ps. CXLV)—that is, the one who has come from the city of Babylon, the city of the devil, to Jerusalem, the city of the Lord Savior. He guards this person provided that he remains among the dwelling-place of the elect.

Natives (*indigenae*) are those born there, in the same place where they live. “Inhabitant,” however, indicates not a native but a newcomer.

Pilgrims are so called because their parents, from whom they originated, are unknown; they come from a distant region. Thus we read in the Psalmist: “Do not be silent toward me, for I am an inhabitant with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII).

An inhabitant is one who, arriving as a stranger, cultivates the land for a time, not one who remains in the region of his native country. This happens to every saint who is received into the divine city. Sin made us all strangers and held us captive in a wicked region; but when his mercy receives us, we are inhabitants, because we have arrived there—that is, we are transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem by his drawing us.

Therefore he says “with you,” so that you might understand that he had been an inhabitant not in the city of the devil but in the city of the Lord. He added “and a pilgrim,” because he begins to be where he was not. A pilgrim is so called as though he were “going farther.”

And, so that you might understand this to have been a general judgment, he says: “As all my fathers were.”

Urban inhabitants are called Romans, because they live in Rome; those who live elsewhere are called townspeople. Rome alone is called a city; the other places are towns.

Household servants (*famuli*) are those born from a household of slaves.

Slaves (*servi*) derived their name from this: those who could lawfully have been killed by the victors in war were preserved; they became slaves, being so called from being preserved.

Mystically, the slave is Christ in the abasement of the flesh, as is said of him in Isaiah: “Behold my servant; I will receive him” (Isa. XLII).

A slave is also the faithful teacher in the Church, as we read in the Gospel: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent servant?” (Matt. XXIV). The term also has an opposite meaning, referring to a wicked teacher, where it continues: “But if that evil servant says in his heart…” (ibid.).

A slave is the sinful human being, as in Solomon: “A servant is not corrected by words, because he understands what you say but disdains to answer” (Prov. XXIX).

Again, “servants” are the saints, as in Joel: “Even upon my male and female servants I will pour out my spirit” (Joel II).

As we have said, household servants or slaves may be understood in both a favorable and an unfavorable sense, because Scripture speaks of servants of righteousness and servants of sin. It says: “Whomever a person serves, to him he is also made a servant” (Rom. VI). And the Apostle says: “Having been freed from the service of sin, you became servants of righteousness” (ibid.); the same applies to female servants.

Female servants (*ancillae*) are named from a support, for *ancon* in Greek means “elbow,” whence we also use the word *ancon*. Allegorically, the female servants of God are holy souls who serve his will with ready devotion.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a female servant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

Again, female servants are the Apostles, because of the weakness of the flesh, just as it is said concerning the devil: “And you shall bind him with your female servants” (Job XL).

Again, female servants are the souls of sinners, as in Nahum: “The captive soldier was led away, and his female servants groaned as they threatened” (Nah. II).

Christ is poor, or the faithful people, as the Apostle says: “For your sake he became poor, though he was rich” (II Cor. VIII). And in the Psalm: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. XXXIII).

The poor are the saints who are humble in spirit, as in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V). And in the Psalter: “He has not despised or scorned the prayers of the poor” (Ps. XXI).

In another sense, the poor are the rich of this world, empty of virtues, as in the Apocalypse: “You say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy,’ and you do not know that you are poor and a beggar” (Apoc. I).

The needy (*inops*) is the humble people of the Gentiles, as in the Psalter: “Raising the needy from the earth” (Ps. CXII). And elsewhere: “Rescuing the needy from the hand of the stronger” (Ps. XXXIV)—that is, from the power of the devil.

A possession (*mancipium*) is whatever can be seized or subjected by the hand, such as a human being, a horse, or a sheep. These beings are considered possessions as soon as they are born. Even those included among wild beasts are considered possessions once they have begun to be captured or tamed.

Freeborn persons (*ingenui*) are so called because they possess freedom by birth, not through an act, as freedmen do. Hence the Greeks call them *eugenoi*, “of good birth.”

A freedman (*libertus*) is so called as though “released,” for previously he had been bound under the yoke of slavery.

Among the ancients, the sons of freedmen were called *libertini*, as though born from freedmen. Now, however, *libertinus* refers either to one made or possessed by a freedman.
