Spiritually, freedmen are those who make good use of Christian freedom. Hence the Apostle says: “For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, he who was called while free is Christ’s slave” (I Cor. VII).

The latter is truly a slave who acts without understanding. The ancient authorities likewise held that all wise people were free, while all foolish people were slaves. Hence Solomon says: “Slaves will serve the wise as free men” (Eccli. X).

Thus the one who believes, although temporarily a slave because he acts wisely by believing in Christ, becomes the Lord’s freedman. If sins make people slaves—as Ham, the son of Noah, became a slave because of sin and folly—then, when a person receives remission of sins, he becomes a freedman.

Likewise, the Apostle says: “He who was called while free is Christ’s slave” (I Cor. VII). It is progress to pass from being free to becoming Christ’s slave. For he who was free from God—which is the greatest crime—therefore, having lost a bitter and harmful freedom, receives a condition of servitude that is beneficial, as the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you, for it is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matt. XI).

A manumitted person (*manumissus*) is so called as though “sent forth by the hand.” Among the ancients, whenever they freed someone, they led the person around after striking him with a slap; hence they were called manumitted, because they were released by the hand.

Later, Roman citizens came to be made under the consuls through wills in the city of Rome. They were called Roman citizens because, having been made free by testament, they were enrolled among the number of Roman citizens.

At first, they were permitted to live in the city of Rome. Other freedmen, however, were forbidden to remain either in the city of Rome or within seven miles of the city. Nevertheless, we read that the Apostle Paul, compelled by necessity because of the uprising that had arisen, called himself a Roman citizen.

Far more glorious is the fact that, together with the other faithful, he called himself a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. Hence, writing to the Ephesians, he says: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and newcomers, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II). That is, they have been established upon the New and Old Testaments: for what the apostles preached, the prophets foretold as future. This means that not only we, but also the heavenly powers, are together made a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit.

The name “heir” was imposed by the assessment of property, for he paid the tax of the agent. In this term there is the first succession of inheritance and lineage, as in sons or grandsons.

A substitute heir (*prohaeres*) is one who performs the role of an heir, as though “in place of an heir.” He is either appointed or substituted.

Mystically, heirs may be understood as the saints of God and those who will become possessors of the heavenly homeland. Hence the Apostle, writing to the Romans, says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. And if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII).

Thus, in order to make us ready to obey God the Father, he exhorts us with this hope, saying that we shall become heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. Since the hope of the reward is great, we should be all the more devoted to the things of God, setting aside concern for worldly matters.

What it means to be a fellow heir of the Son of God is taught to us by the Apostle John. Among other things he says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (I John III).

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

[Col. 0457]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Dust and Clods of Earth

[Col. 0457B]

Dust (*pulvis*) is so called because it is driven by the force of the wind. It is lifted by its breath, neither resisting nor knowing how to remain still, as the Prophet says: “Like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I).

Mire (*limus*) is so called because it is smooth. Mud (*coenum*) is a chasm of mire. Ash (*cinis*) is named from burning, for it is produced by it. Ash-dust (*favilla*) is so called because it is produced by fire; for *phos* in Greek means “fire.”

A clod (*gleba*) is so called because it is a globe. It is compacted by the gathering of dust and united into a single mass. Earth bound together is a clod; loose earth is dust.

Some think that mud (*lutum*) is named by antiphrasis because it is not washed, that is, not clean. For all mud is unclean.

A wallow (*volutabra*) is so called because pigs roll about there. Marshiness (*uligo*) consists of the filth of mire or muddy water.

Dust signifies the corruption of human nature or the fickleness of the human mind, as in the Psalms, where it is written of the sinner: “And he shall be like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. I). Dust, as we said above, is the disintegration of earth. When an earthly human being is inflated by the deceptive wind of pride, he is cast away from the solidity of the land of the living like dust, because in his fickleness he cannot hold fast to the foundation of the commandments.

Mire signifies the earthly material of the human body, as in the passage: “Then the Lord formed the human being from the mire of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. II). This means that he created in him the substance of soul and spirit in which he was to live.

In another sense, mire expresses the mud and filth of vices in which a human being is polluted. Mud likewise has a double meaning: human flesh and the pollution of vices.

Hence we read in the Gospel that the Lord made mud from spittle and opened the eyes of the man born blind: “For he spat on the ground and made mud from the saliva” (John IX). The Word, having become flesh, imbued the human race with faith in his incarnation. The race was blind from birth—that is, from the origin of the first human being—and so he sent it to the pool of Siloam, that is, to the sacrament of baptism.

Conversely, mud is used when it signifies the filth of vices. Thus Peter says of sinners: “For what is stated in the true proverb happened to them: ‘The dog has returned to its vomit,’ and ‘The washed sow to its wallowing in mud’” (II Pet. II).

Clay (*argilla*) is named from Argos, where vessels were first made from it. It signifies Holy Scripture. Hence we read in the Book of Kings (III Kings VII) that all the vessels which Hiram made for Solomon in the house of the Lord were of bronze; the king cast them in clayey soil in the region of the Jordan.

Clearly, the vessels of the house of the Lord were cast in the region of the Jordan, in the river in which our Lord chose to be baptized. Having been immersed in its waters, he turned the element of water into a washing away of sins for us.

The clayey earth from which molds were made for casting the vessels of the Lord—what can it better be understood as than Holy Scripture, from which we receive the rule of right living? Just as clay hardened by fire displays the form of the Lord’s vessel, showing how great and what kind the vessels ought to be, so Scripture shows us the rule of righteousness that we are to follow. It also sets before us the examples of the saints who persevered undefeated in the fire of tribulations and are to be followed in all things.

Chalk (*creta*) takes its name from the island of Crete, where it is of better quality. Cimolian chalk is white; it is named from Cima, an island of Italy. One of these softens the precious colors of garments and brightens those darkened by sulfur with a certain luster; the other gives brilliance to gems.

Silver chalk (*creta argentaria*) is likewise called white because it restores brightness to silver.

Samian earth is named from the island of Samos. It is adhesive and white, smooth to the tongue, and useful for medicines and vessels.

Sulfur (*sulphur*) is so called because it is kindled by fire. [Possibly *ur*] means “fire”; for its power is perceived in boiling waters. Nothing else is more easily ignited. It arises in the Aeolian Islands, between Sicily and Italy, which are said to burn. It is also found dug out in other places.

There are four kinds of it. One is dug out, translucent, and greenish; physicians alone use this kind among all the varieties. Another, called a clod, is used only by fullers. The third is liquid, used for fumigating wool, because it gives whiteness and softness. The fourth is especially suitable for making lamp-wicks.

The power of sulfur is so great that, placed on fires, it detects epileptic illnesses by its odor. Anaxilaus, carrying around a wine-cup with a coal placed beneath it, caused the reflection of the flame to cast a dreadful pallor, like that of the dead, upon the guests.

What is expressed by sulfur if not the stench of flesh? And what by fire if not the burning of carnal desire? When, therefore, the Lord determined to punish the carnal crimes of the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, he made the stain of their crime known through the very character of the punishment. Sulfur has a stench; fire has heat. Those who had burned with perverse desires from the stench of the flesh therefore deserved to perish together by sulfur and fire, so that through a punishment corresponding to their crime they might learn what they had done through unrighteous desire.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Clods Formed from Waters

Bitumen emerges in the Judean Lake Asphaltites. Sailors approach its floating clods in small boats and collect them. In Syria, however, mud continually boils up from the earth. Both substances become thick and unite through density; the Greeks call both *pissasphaltos* [Greek: “bitumen”]. Its nature is burning and akin to fire, and it cannot be broken apart by either water or iron, except by the impurities of women. It is useful for joining the timbers of ships.

Mystically, bitumen, which is an extremely hot and powerful adhesive, signifies the ardor of love, which, with great strength, endures everything in order to preserve spiritual fellowship. Hence, concerning the construction of the ark which Noah built at the Lord’s command, we read in Genesis: “Make yourself an ark from smoothed wood; make small rooms in the ark, and coat it with bitumen inside and outside, and so make it” (Gen. VI).

Noah constructed the ark from timbers that would not decay; Christ builds the Church from human beings who will live forever. The ark demonstrated the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world.

That the same ark was commanded to be made of squared timbers on every side signifies the stable life of the saints, prepared for every good work. For whichever way you turn a square, it will stand firmly.

The fact that the timbers of the ark are joined with bitumen inside and outside signifies, within the joining of unity, the endurance of charity: lest, when scandals assail the Church, whether from those who are inside or those who are outside, the brotherly bond yield and the bond of peace be broken.

Alum (*alumen*) is named from “light,” because it gives light to colors being dyed. It is a saltiness of the earth, produced in winter from water and mud and matured by the summer sun. There are two kinds: liquid and thick.

Some think that salt (*sal*) is so called because it leaps in fire. It flees fire, although it is fiery; but it follows nature, since fire and water are always hostile to one another.

Others believe that salt is named from the sea and the sun. It is naturally produced from seawater, from foam left at the edges of shores or cliffs and dried by the sun. There are also lakes, rivers, and wells from which it is drawn; afterward it is carried into saltworks and dried by the sun. Rivers too become thickened into salt, while the remaining stream flows beneath the ice.

Elsewhere it is gathered after the sand has been removed, increasing during the nights of the moon. In Cyrenaica, ammoniac salt is found beneath the sands. There are also natural mountains of salt, in which it is cut with iron like stone. In some places it grows to such hardness that they make walls and houses from masses of salt, as in Arabia.

There are also differences in the nature of salt. In one place it is mild, in another extremely salty. Ordinary salt crackles in fire. Tragasaean salt neither crackles in fire nor leaps. Agrigentine salt, which withstands the flames of Sicily, leaps in water and flows in fire.

Mystically, salt signifies the seasoning of wisdom. Hence the Lord says to the Apostles in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted? It is good for nothing thereafter except to be thrown outside and trampled by people” (Matt. V).

They are called this because through them the entire human race is seasoned; for “earth” signifies human nature. In the salt, however, is the wisdom of the word. By calling his Apostles, filled with heavenly and divine wisdom, the salt of the earth, the Savior shows that those are to be judged foolish who savor only earthly things. Pursuing an apparent abundance of temporal goods, or fearing their lack, they lose eternal things, which can neither be given nor taken away by human beings.

It must also be noted that the nature of salt makes the earth barren. Hence the Psalm says: “He made a fruitful land into saltiness” (Ps. CVI). We also read that certain cities were sown with salt by the wrath of their conquerors, so that no plant might grow in them.

Allegorically, this also suits apostolic teaching: when the strongholds of adversaries have been destroyed and the reign of sin overthrown, the salt of wisdom restrains the luxury and foulness of the fleshly earth of the world from producing the growth of vices.

Again, because salt is suitable for seasoning foods and drying meat, it properly demonstrates that through the preaching of the Gospel the flow of pleasures is restrained. Human nature, once the worms and decay of sins have been excluded, is preserved unharmed for its Creator through obedience to his commandments.

It is good to hear the word of God frequently, to season the hidden places of the spiritual heart with the salt of wisdom, and indeed to become, together with the Apostles, the salt of the earth—that is, to suffice for instructing the minds even of those who still savor earthly things.

But if someone, once enlightened by the seasoning of truth, returns to apostasy, by what other teacher can he be corrected, since he has rejected the sweetness of wisdom that he himself tasted, either terrified by the adversities of the world or enticed by its allurements?

Just as salt, once it has lost its savor, is no longer useful for seasoning foods or drying meat and is fit for no purpose, so it is not useful for the earth—as another Evangelist testifies—because when thrown upon it, it prevents growth. Nor is it useful for the manure heap of agriculture; mixed with fertile clods, it naturally extinguishes rather than nourishes the seeds of crops.

Thus a person who turns back after recognizing the truth can neither bear the fruit of good works himself nor cultivate others. He must be thrown outside—that is, separated from the unity of the Church—so that, according to another parable, his enemies may mock him and say: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV).

Nitrum takes its name from the place where it is found. It arises in the town or region of Egypt called Nitria, from which medicines are made and the filth of bodies and garments is washed away.

Its nature is not very different from salt. It possesses the power of salt and arises similarly, whitening through the drying of shores. For just as the heat of the sun produces salt on the seashore by hardening into stone the seawater that a stronger force of winds or the heat of the sea itself has cast onto the farther shores, so in Nitria, where longer summer rains soak the earth, the heat of the heavenly bodies is so great that it cooks the rainwater across the breadth of the sands into a stone resembling salt or ice in appearance. Yet it possesses neither the cold rigidity of ice nor the taste of salt. In accordance with the nature of salt, however, it hardens in heat and flows and liquefies in cloudy weather.

The natives collect and preserve it, and when the need arises they use it as a cleansing agent.

Hence the Prophet says to sinful Judea: “If you wash yourself with nitrum and multiply for yourself the herb *borith*, you are stained in your iniquity, says the Lord God” (Jer. II).

It crackles in water like quicklime. It itself disappears, but makes the water suitable for washing. Observing what figure this nature represents, Solomon says: “Vinegar in nitrum, and one who sings songs to a very bad heart” (Prov. XXV).

For if vinegar is poured into nitrum, the nitrum immediately becomes hot and boils over. Likewise, when a perverse mind is reproved through correction, it becomes worse because of the correction and is inflamed into the iniquity of murmuring, from the very thing by which it ought to have been restrained from iniquity.

Above I mentioned the prophetic statement: “If you wash yourself with nitrum and multiply for yourself the herb *borith*, etc.” (Jer. II). For “the herb *borith*,” the Septuagint translated *poian*, signifying the herb of fullers. According to the custom of the province of Palestine, it grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as nitrum.

Our nitrum and the fuller’s herb *poian* signify repentance. Ecclesiastical preaching, which rebukes, reproves, and corrects the sinner, resembles milder nitrum. One who is stained by a light blemish of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions.

But grave sins, which lead to death, can be washed away neither by nitrum nor by the herb *borith*; they require more severe torments. “For each one’s work, whatever it may be, the fire will test, and by fire it will be revealed” (I Cor. III).

Beautifully he adds: “You are stained in your iniquity before me” (Jer. II). Even if you appear clean to human beings, you are not clean to me, who know the consciences of all.

*Aphronitrum* in Greek, in Latin “foam of nitrum,” is the foam of nitrum. Concerning it, someone [Martial] says:

> You are rustic; you do not know what I am called by my Greek name.  
> I am called the foam of nitrum: if you are Greek, [you know me as] aphronitrum.

It is collected in Asia, dripping from caves, and then dried by the sun. It is considered best if it is as light as possible and especially crumbly, almost purple in color.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Common Stones
Stones, as denser than earth, are also commonly distinguished. A *lapis* (“stone”) is so called because it injures the foot: a *lapis* is movable and scattered, whereas rocks (*saxa*) adhere and break away from mountains. *Petra* is Greek. *Silex* is a hard stone, so called because fire leaps forth from it. *Scopulus* (“crag”) is named from a projecting rock, as though from *speculari* (“to observe”), or from the covering of ships, from the Greek *apo tou skepein* (“from covering”).

The stone or rock has many meanings. Sometimes it signifies Christ because of the firmness of faith and the solidity of truth, as in the Psalm: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 117 [118]). And the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Sometimes, however, the apostles or holy men, or the works of the virtues themselves, are signified by the name “stone.” Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: “The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone” (Rev. 21). And in the Psalm it is written concerning the saints: “Your servants have taken pleasure in its stones, and they will pity its earth” (Ps. 101 [102]). And elsewhere: “The holy stones,” he says, “are rolled upon the earth.”

Again, stones sometimes signify the order of those set over the Church, concerning whom Jeremiah says: “The stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4)—that is, at the head of broad and spacious roads that lead to destruction.

Sometimes they signify the Jewish people, concerning whom it is said in the prophet: “Take the stones out of the way and pile them up” (Jer. 50). Likewise, stones signify the hardness of the hearts of the Gentiles, concerning whom the Lord says: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3). Rocky ground also signifies the barrenness of the hearts of the reprobate. Thus it is written in the Gospel (Luke 8) that the seed which fell on rocky ground had no root: the hearts of the reprobate cannot produce an appropriate fruit, because they believe for a time and, at the time of temptation, withdraw from the state of righteousness.

Again, concerning the devil’s hardness, it is written in the Book of Job: “His heart will be hardened like a stone” (Job 41), because it is never softened by any repentance leading to conversion.

Gypsum is related to lime, and its name is Greek. There are many kinds of it, but the best of all comes from *lapis specularis* (“transparent stone,” or selenite). Quicklime is so called because, although cold to the touch, it contains hidden fire within. Its nature produces something marvelous: after it has been burned, it is set on fire by water, which normally extinguishes fire; and it is extinguished by oil, which normally kindles fire. Its use is necessary in building construction. For stone cannot adhere more firmly to stone unless it is joined with lime. Lime made from white, hard stone is better. This may signify the bond of charity by which the elect who belong to God’s spiritual building are joined to one another, because they shine with the whiteness of virtues and display in themselves the beauty of good works.

Sand is named from its dryness, not—as some wish—from its adhering in buildings. It is tested if, when pressed by the hand, it makes a grating sound, or if, sprinkled on a white garment, it leaves no stain.

Mystically, sand signifies the instability of earthly people, or the unfruitfulness of the Jewish people, who, gaping after earthly desires, neglected to produce spiritual fruits. Concerning them it is written: “I will number them, and they will multiply upon the sand” (Ps. 138 [139]). And in the Gospel (Matt. 7) we read that the wise man builds his house upon a rock, while the foolish man places his upon sand.

The foundation which the Apostle Paul, the architect, laid is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon this stable and firm foundation, itself founded upon a solid mass, Christ’s Church is built. But upon sand, which is fluid and cannot be joined together or reduced to a single bond, rests all the speech of the heretics, which is built for the purpose of collapsing.

## CHAPTER IV. On the More Notable Stones

The magnet is an Indian stone named after its discoverer. It was first found in India in this manner: while the same Magnes was tending cattle, it adhered to the nails of his sandals and to the tip of his staff; afterward it was found in various places. It is rusty in color, but it is tested when placed beside iron and made to draw it toward itself. For it grips iron so firmly that it makes a chain of rings; hence the common people call it “living iron.”

The *gagates* stone was first found in Sicily, thrown up by the flow of the river Gagates, from which it is also named, although it is abundant in Britain. It is black, smooth, and glossy, and burns when brought near fire. Writing made upon objects of earthenware with it is not erased. When burned, it drives away snakes, exposes demoniacs, and detects virginity. Remarkably, it is kindled by water and extinguished by oil.

Asbestos is a stone of Arcadia, the color of iron, which received its name from fire because, once kindled, it is never extinguished. Human art contrived something mechanical from this stone, which the Gentiles, captivated by the sacrilege, would marvel at. In the end, they say that there was a shrine of Venus in a certain temple, and in it a lamp burning under the open sky so persistently that no storm and no rain could extinguish it.

*Selenites*, interpreted in Latin as “lunar,” is so called because they say that its inner whiteness waxes and wanes with the moon. It is found in Persia.

## CHAPTER V. On Marbles

*Marble* is named in Greek from its greenness; and although other colors are later found, it nevertheless retains its original name from greenness. The colors and varieties of marble are innumerable. Not all of them, however, are cut from cliffs; many are scattered beneath the earth and are of the most precious kinds.

Thus Lacedaemonian marble is green and more cheerful than all others; it was first found among the Lacedaemonians, from whom it also took its name. Parian marble is of extraordinary whiteness and is called *lychnites*. It is found on the island of Paros, and from this it is called Parian. *Lygdinus* is of a size no larger than plates and mixing bowls and is itself suitable for perfumes.

Parian marble is white in color and signifies the purity of the elect. Hence we read that, in Solomon’s temple, the walls of the temple were built from this stone. This signifies that the holy Church has been built from the pure life and thoroughly approved conduct of the saints.

Alabaster is a white stone marked with various colors, from which that little vessel of the Gospel ointment was made (Matt. 26). They hollow it out for perfume vessels because it is said to preserve them unspoiled exceptionally well. It is found around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, and is whiter than other varieties; the most highly esteemed is found in India.

Mystically, alabaster can signify Holy Scripture, which contains precious ointment—that is, spiritual knowledge—which fills the whole world with its fragrance. Hence we read in the Gospel of a woman who had an alabaster vessel of precious ointment and poured the ointment over the head of Jesus as he reclined. This signifies the Church proclaiming Christ’s divinity throughout the whole world.

The same woman also anointed the Lord’s feet with the same ointment, because she commends with devout preaching and venerates with dutiful service that aspect of his nature by which he deigned to touch the earth—that is, to live among human beings.

## CHAPTER VI. On Ivory

[Col. 0464C]

Ivory (*ebur*) is named from *barro*, that is, “elephant.” Horace says: “What do you want, woman, most worthy of black elephants?” Ivory signifies continence in chastity. Hence it is written in the Psalm concerning the Church: “Myrrh and drop and cassia from your garments, from ivory houses, etc.” (Ps. 44 [45]).

The prophet said where the most glorious beauty of the bride comes from, she who stands placed at the Lord’s right hand: namely, “from ivory houses.” This signifies the ornaments of palaces clothed in abundant ivory.

Let us not, however, understand ivory as suited only to wealth. The elephant, whose bones these are, is said to possess extraordinary chastity: among four-footed animals it is outstanding in intelligence, mates temperately with its female, and does not take a second wife. This is appropriately applied to chaste women, because those are recognized as having dwelt in ivory houses who, through chastity, followed the commandments of Christ the Lord. The most learned Fathers, Augustine and Jerome, approved this interpretation.

## CHAPTER VII. On Gems

After the varieties of marble come gems, which contribute much beauty to gold through the loveliness of their colors. The kinds of gems are said to be innumerable; we shall note only those that are principal or best known.

Gems are so called because they shine through like gum. They are called precious stones because they are highly valued, or so that they may be distinguished from common stones, or because they are rare. Everything rare is called great and precious, as we read in the Book of Samuel: “The word of the Lord was precious in Israel” (1 Sam. 3), that is, rare.

Precious stones are understood to be the holy apostles and all the saints, from whom the city of the great King is constituted in the Apocalypse. Likewise, nine names of precious stones are read in Ezekiel, in which the nine orders of angels are expressed. Hence the prophet says against the devil: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28). And shortly afterward: “Among the stones of fire you walked, perfect in beauty, from the day of your creation” (ibid.).

The most precious stones are also enumerated in Exodus, that is, those placed in the high priest’s breastpiece, and in the Apocalypse, in the construction of the spiritual city. For it is written in Exodus:

“In the first row there shall be a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald; in the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper; in the third, a *lygurius*, an agate, and an amethyst; in the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl” (Exod. 28).

In the Apocalypse likewise we read:

“The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth onyx, the sixth sardonyx, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh hyacinth, the twelfth amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate being made from one pearl” (Rev. 21).

The various names of the stones indicate either varieties of virtues, fragrance, or diversity, by which the whole heavenly Jerusalem is constructed. For it is difficult for each person to flourish in every virtue.

Finally, when Isaiah was describing the adornment of the same city, saying, “Behold, I will set your stones in order, and I will lay your foundations in sapphires, etc.” (Isa. 54), he immediately added: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord” (ibid.).

### The First Foundation: Jasper

There are many kinds of jasper. One is green and appears tinged as though with flowers. Another resembles an emerald but is of a denser color; they believe that it drives away all phantoms. Another is snowy and resembles the foam of marble waves, glowing red as though mixed with blood.

Jasper therefore indicates the unfading green of faith, which is steeped in the sacrament of the Lord’s passion through the waters of baptism and, as its merits advance, is furnished with every flower of spiritual grace. Whoever possesses this faith drives away empty fears, as the blessed Apostle Peter warns: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5).

Such a person can say with the bride: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5). Hence, appropriately, in the Apocalypse the wall’s structure is made secure and in Isaiah the battlements of the same city are both fortified and adorned with this stone.

Two stones—jasper and sardius—are said to bear the figure of God’s two judgments: the first by the water of the flood, the second by fire. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: “The one seated upon the throne was like a jasper stone and a sardius” (Rev. 4).

Jasper also signifies the testimonies of Scripture, as in Isaiah: “Your battlements shall be of jasper” (Isa. 54).

### The Second Foundation: Sapphire

Moses explained both the color and the sacramental meaning of this stone when, describing God’s appearance, he said: “Under his feet was something like a pavement of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24).

Ezekiel likewise says that the place in which God’s throne is situated has the likeness of sapphire, and that the glory of the Lord consists in its color. Whoever bears the heavenly image, being such a person, can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

When struck by the sun’s rays, sapphire emits from itself a blazing brilliance. Thus the person always intent upon heavenly things, renewed daily by the rays of divine light in the souls of the saints, seeks eternal things in a manner made more contrite and more ardent, and urges himself more deeply in their pursuit.

Since it is said to be found in the Red Sea, it signifies that through the Lord’s passion and the washing of sacred baptism the minds of mortals are raised sublimely to embrace heavenly things.

### The Third Foundation: Chalcedony

“Chalcedony” (Rev. 21). Chalcedony shines like a pale lamp-flame and has brilliance in the open air, not in a house. This represents those who, supported by heavenly desire, nevertheless remain hidden from human beings and, as though in secret, perform their fasts, almsgiving, and prayers. But when they are ordered to come into public service in teaching or in other uses of the saints, they immediately show what brilliance they possessed within.

For it is said to resist engraving, but when rubbed by the rays of the sun or by the fingers, if it becomes incandescent, it draws straw toward itself. This appropriately corresponds to those who permit their strength to be overcome by nothing, but instead unite even the more fragile to the authority of their own light and ardor.

Of one such person it is said: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5): burning with the love of faith, shining through speech. They continually renew the light of their virtues with the oil of inward charity, lest it fail.

The fact that it is born among the Nasamones, a province of Ethiopia, indicates those who, under the burning heat of love, nevertheless remain obscure in reputation, as though sullied by dark skin.

### The Fourth Foundation: Emerald

“Emerald” (Rev. 21). Emerald is of such intense greenness that it surpasses all green herbs and twin leaves, dyeing the air around it with reflected greenness. It is enhanced by unmixed wine and green oil, although it is endowed by nature.

There are many varieties; the more distinguished are Scythian, followed in second place by Bactrian and in third by Egyptian emeralds.

It signifies souls ever green with faith. The more they are tested by the adversity of the world, represented by the figure of Scythia, the more they strive both to conceive in hope the unfading inheritance preserved in heaven and to spread it among their neighbors through preaching. Through the cup of the Lord’s passion and the inward richness of charity given through the Holy Spirit, they advance toward contempt for the world.

The land that is the homeland of this stone also corresponds to them most beautifully. It is a rich but uninhabitable land, for although it abounds in gold and gems, griffins possess everything—most savage winged creatures, or rather flying beasts. They are four-footed and, in body, resemble lions, but in head and wings are very like eagles.

The Arimaspians fight with them. These men are distinguished by having one eye in the middle of their forehead, so that they may obtain these stones, with the savage creatures seizing them and the Arimaspians guarding them.

The Psalmist had heard of this land, abundant in treasures of virtues, when he said: “Behold, I have fled far away, and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54 [55])—that is, by withdrawing his mind far from the world’s allurements.

In this land he had encountered hostile beasts when, rebuking them, he said: “Let deceitful lips become mute, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and contempt” (Ps. 30 [31]).

He also revealed with delighted wonder that he had found desirable treasures there, when he continued: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (ibid.), and so forth to the end of the Psalm.

Against such winged creatures, eager to snatch away from us the seed of the divine word, the vigilant among the saints strive with a simple concentration born of heavenly desire, as though with one admirable eye, so that they may seek out and dig up the gem of faith and of the other virtues.

For the higher any virtue is, the fewer devotees it has and the more severe a persecution it endures from unclean spirits. Like dreadful griffins, earthly through the abasement of their merits but winged through the proud elevation of their minds, these spirits strive with unwearied labor not to possess spiritual riches for their own use, but to take them away from human beings.

And because such sublimity of faith became known to the world through the Gospel, emerald is appropriately placed fourth, on account of the four books of the Gospel.

### The Fifth Foundation: Sardonyx

Sardonyx derives its whiteness from onyx and its redness from sardius, and from both it received the name *sardonyx*. There are many varieties.

One resembles red earth. Another appears two-colored, as though blood shone through a human fingernail. Another consists of three colors: black beneath, white in the middle, and snowy above.

To it are compared people who are reddened by bodily suffering, white through purity of spirit, but despised in their own minds through humility, professing with the Apostle: “Though our outward person is being destroyed, yet our inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). And again: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but by this I am not justified” (1 Cor. 4).

Likewise the Psalmist says: “Although a human being walks in the image of God” (Ps. 38 [39]), that is, in the virtue of the mind, “yet he will be troubled in vain,” that is, through the weakness of the flesh.

Since this suffering is found in bodily weakness—for “those who kill the body cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10)—and humility descends from the frailty of the same body, when it is said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7), sardonyx is rightly inserted as the fifth foundation.

For it is certain that our body subsists through the five senses.

### The Sixth Foundation: Sardius

Sardius, which is wholly blood-red in color, signifies the glory of the martyrs, concerning which it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115 [116]). It is fittingly placed sixth, since our Lord was both incarnate in the sixth age of the world and crucified on the sixth day for the salvation of the whole world.

### The Seventh Foundation: Chrysolite

Chrysolite shines like gold and has blazing sparks. By its appearance are represented those who shine with the understanding of true heavenly wisdom and pour forth words of exhortation to their neighbors, or signs of virtues, like sparks of fire.

Of such people Arator also says:

> Love presses upon their minds;  
> ardor seethes in their speech.

Because this is accomplished only by the gift of spiritual grace, chrysolite is most appropriately the seventh foundation. The grace of the Holy Spirit is customarily represented by the number seven. Concerning it the Apocalypse says above: “And from the seven spirits who are before his throne” (Rev. 1).

This meaning is also consistent with the fact that a certain variety of the same stone is found in a bluish and verdant color. Hence among the Hebrews it is called *tharsis*, from its resemblance to the color of the sea.

Green signifies the integrity of faith, which is called the beginning of wisdom; water, in a figurative sense, pertains to the Holy Spirit, as the Lord testifies: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive (John 7).

### The Eighth Foundation: Beryl

Beryl is such that, if you consider water struck by the sun’s brilliance, it returns a reddish and beautiful color. But it shines only if it is polished and shaped into a hexagonal form. Its brilliance is sharpened by the reflection from its angles.

It signifies people who are indeed shrewd in understanding but shine still more brightly through the light of heavenly grace. That water signifies depth of meaning is attested by Solomon, who says: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man” (Prov. 18).

But neither human nor divine wisdom possesses perfect brilliance unless it is also brought to completion through works. For perfection of action is often signified by the number six, especially since the work of this world was completed in that number.

Beryl is said to burn the hand of whoever holds it. This plainly indicates that whoever is joined to a holy man is refreshed by the fire of his good conduct.

### The Ninth Foundation: Topaz

Topaz is as rare in discovery as it is precious in price. It is said to have two colors: one of the purest gold and another shining with an ethereal brightness. It has a rosy richness and a modest purity. It resembles chrysoprase in size or color, because it shines most intensely when struck by the sun’s brightness, surpassing the most precious brilliance of all gems and uniquely summoning the eager delight of the eyes to its appearance.

If you wish to polish it, you darken it; if you leave it to its own nature, it radiates.

It is said to be marvelous even to kings, so that they recognize that they possess nothing comparable among their riches. The beautiful quality of its nature is most suitably compared with the beauty of the contemplative life.

Holy kings, whose heart is in God’s hand, rightly prefer this life to all the riches of good works and every jewel of the virtues. They direct toward it the gaze and focus of their pure minds, embracing the sweetness of heavenly life in their hearts all the more ardently the more frequently they have been struck by the brilliance of heavenly grace.

Holy men therefore possess a golden color from the flame of inward charity, and an ethereal color from contemplating heavenly sweetness. Yet they often become cheapened, as though worn down, by the turmoil of the present age. For the mind cannot easily, at one and the same moment, be driven by earthly labors, afflictions, cares, and pains, and also gaze with the tranquillity of a peaceful mind upon the joys of heavenly life.

Rather, it cries out with a groan: “My eye is troubled because of anger; I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6).

The fact that topaz is said to be found on the island in the Thebaid called Topazion, from which it received its name, is to be understood in two ways: both because those principal regions of Egypt abound in communities of monks, and because whoever dwells near the sun of justice is crowned with the radiance of ethereal light.

Just as the perfection of the active life is beautifully placed in the eighth order, so the gem of contemplative sweetness is placed in the ninth—either because the nine orders of angels, whose life it imitates, are found in Holy Scripture, or because it is only one—so to speak—degree of death away from the ten of perfect blessedness.

The prophet sighed for that summit with the greatest longing, saying: “Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz” (Ps. 118 [119]); that is, above every brightness of approved action and every height of contemplative joy possible in this world, I delighted in the sweetest love of your commandments. Their first and greatest is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6).

It is absolutely certain that this cannot be perfectly accomplished except at the summit of the heavenly kingdom.

### The Tenth Foundation: Chrysoprase

Chrysoprase is green mixed with gold; some varieties also draw forth a purple radiance, with golden drops interspersed. It is found in India.

It signifies those who, having earned the greenness of their eternal homeland through the radiance of perfect charity, also reveal it to others through the purple light of their martyrdom.

Because, in despising the present life, they prefer eternal glory and follow the examples of the Lord appearing in the flesh, they now display the brightness of their merits like India—that is, near the rising of the sun. Desiring and awaiting that they may shine like the sun in the kingdom of the Father and reign with their King, with whom they now suffer, they are rightly placed in the tenth position.

For through the ten, by which the workers of the Lord’s vineyard are rewarded, the image of the eternal King to be received is signified. There, what could not be achieved at an earlier stage will be fulfilled: the Decalogue will be completed in all things through perfect love of God and neighbor.

### The Eleventh Foundation: Hyacinth

Hyacinth is found in Ethiopia and has a blue color. The best is neither rare nor dulled by density, but shines through a balance of both qualities and draws forth a gently purified bloom.

It does not glow uniformly. It changes with the appearance of the sky: in clear weather it is transparent and pleasing, but under cloud it vanishes and withers before the eyes.

It indicates souls always devoted to heavenly contemplation and, as far as is permitted to mortals, approaching an angelic manner of life. They are commanded to preserve the virtue of discernment with every vigilance, lest, being skilled in every subtlety of understanding, they dare to seek things higher than themselves and investigate things too difficult for them (“It is the glory of God to conceal a word,” Prov. 25—that is, to philosophize cautiously about God or about the human Christ), or, again, falling sluggishly into indolence, relapse into the weak beginnings of faith and the elementary first principles of God’s words.

Rather, walking along the royal road, equipped with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, they should proceed. By suitable observance of time, changing their appearance with the sky, they should say to those who watch them: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5).

Like a hyacinth surrounded by cloud, it says: “You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own hearts” (2 Cor. 6).

And again: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). Then, as though seen in clear light, it says: “But we speak wisdom among the mature” (ibid.).

### The Twelfth Foundation: Amethyst

Amethyst is purple, mixed with a violet color, and shines like a rose, giving off certain small flames. Some varieties do not appear wholly fiery purple but rather red like wine.

Its purple beauty signifies the appearance of the heavenly kingdom; its rosy and violet colors signify the humble modesty and precious death of the saints. Their minds are chiefly raised to the heights of faith even when they are seen cast down by suffering at the lowest levels, always remembering amid adversities the Lord’s promise: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

They spread the flame of charity not only among one another but also toward their persecutors, and, kneeling, they implore: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7). While drinking the cup of suffering, they are instead continually inebriated by the remembrance of that wine which gladdens the human heart and which the Lord promised he would drink anew with his disciples in the kingdom of the Father.

Thus, in jasper the greenness of faith is represented; in sapphire, the height of heavenly hope; in chalcedony, the flame of inward charity; in emerald, the steadfast conduct of that same faith amid adversity; in sardonyx, the humility of the saints amid their virtues; in sardius, the reverend blood of the martyrs; in chrysolite, spiritual preaching amid miracles; in beryl, the perfect action of preachers; in topaz, their ardent contemplation.

In chrysoprase are represented both the work and reward of the blessed martyrs; in hyacinth, the raising of teachers toward heavenly heights and, for the sake of the weak, their humble descent to human concerns; in amethyst, the continual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom in the minds of the humble.

Onyx is so called because it contains whiteness mixed within it in the likeness of a human fingernail; for in Greek they call a fingernail *onycha*. India or Arabia produces it. The varieties differ from one another: Indian onyx has fiery specks surrounded by white bands, while Arabian onyx is black with white bands. There are five varieties.

We read in Exodus that, at the Lord’s command (Exod. 28), Moses made for his brother Aaron a shoulder-piece of gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, and, engraving the names of the sons of Israel on two onyx stones, set them, enclosed and encircled with gold, into the shoulder-piece.

Its mystical meaning is evident. Precious stones are precious works of spiritual virtues. The priest bears precious stones on his shoulders, with the names of the Fathers inscribed upon them, when he himself is admirable to all through the brightness of good works and teaches that this same brightness was not newly invented by him but handed down to him through the ancient authority of the Fathers.

He bears these on his shoulders for a twofold reason: so that he himself may proceed humbly subject to the Lord’s commandments, and so that he may always set before his hearers heavenly examples—whether his own or those of the Fathers—for them to follow.

Carbuncle is so called because it is fiery like a coal, whose brilliance is not overcome even by night. It shines in darkness so strongly that it seems to send [or: dart] flames toward the eyes. There are twelve varieties, but the superior ones are those that appear to glow and pour out something like fire.

This stone can signify the word of God, which shines upon us through the apostolic order and the preachers of the Gospel in the obscurity of this world and drives away the darkness and gloom of sins. Hence it is written: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1).

*Lyncurius* is so called because it is formed from the urine of the lynx, hardened over time. Like amber, it is tawny and attracts nearby leaves by its breath.

Since this gem is among the red gems, it can signify the passion of the martyrs. Stirred by the divine Spirit, they attract the leaves of words; through prayer or preaching they reconcile their persecutors to themselves and lead them to the unity of faith.

Agate is one of the black gems. It was first found in Sicily beside the river of the same name, and afterward in many lands. It is black, with black circles in the middle, joined and variegated with white, resembling hematite. If it is believed, it averts storms and stops rivers.

It too can signify those who, because of their desire for heavenly life, hold the world in contempt and await the crown of eternal life.

Coral is produced in the sea. It is branching in form, green in color, and especially red; its veins are white and soft under water. Once removed, it immediately hardens and reddens; when touched, it quickly becomes stone. It is therefore usually seized and pulled out with nets, or cut with a sharp instrument; for this reason it is called coral.

Among us Indian pearl is as precious as coral is among the Indians. Magicians claim—if one believes them—that coral resists lightning.

This stone therefore rightly represents those who are drawn out of the waves of the sea—that is, from the softness of worldly conduct—and grow hard through the strength of continence. They display in themselves the solidity of right faith and the beauty of good works, so that they can rightly be pleasing to the holiest men.

Alabandine is named from the region of Alabanda in Asia and resembles purple in appearance. In the East it is melted by fire and cast for use as glass. Its color imitates chalcedony but is redder, and figuratively it displays the blood of the martyrs.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Pearls

The pearl is the first among white gems. The Indians say it is called *margarita* because this kind of stone is found in the shells of the sea. A pebble is born within the flesh of the shellfish, just as a little stone is found in the brain of a fish. It is produced from heavenly dew, which shellfish draw in at a certain season of the year.

Some of these pearls are called *uniones* (“single pearls”), an appropriate name because only one, never two or more together, is found.

White pearls are better than those that turn yellow. Youth or the gathering of morning dew makes the former white; old age or evening air produces the latter darkened.

Mystically, the pearl signifies evangelical teaching, or the hope of the kingdom of heaven, or the charity and sweetness of heavenly life. Hence we read in the Gospel parable (Matt. 13) of a man seeking good pearls. When he found one precious pearl, he went away and sold everything he possessed and bought that field.

For whoever has perfectly come to know the sweetness of heavenly life, insofar as human possibility allows, willingly abandons everything he had loved on earth. In comparison with it, everything becomes worthless. He leaves what he possesses, scatters what he has gathered, and his mind burns with desire for heavenly things. Nothing earthly pleases him; whatever had pleased him by its earthly appearance is despised as deformed, because only precious charity shines in the mind.

## CHAPTER IX. On Crystals
Crystallus is described as a shining, watery substance in color, being snow hardened into ice over many years; hence the Greeks also gave it its name. It is produced in Asia and Cyprus, and especially in the Alps of the north, where even in summer the sun is not found to be exceedingly hot. Thus its own prolonged, age-old hardness produces the material called crystal. When placed opposite the rays of the sun, it catches the flame so powerfully that it can provide fire to dry sponges or leaves. It is also used for drinking vessels, though it can endure nothing except cold.

Crystal sometimes signifies the sacrament of baptism, sometimes the steadfastness of the holy angels, and sometimes also [Col. 0472D] the Lord’s incarnation. It signifies baptism in the passage written in the Apocalypse: “Before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal” (Rev. IV). Because of the faith of truth, baptism is compared to glass, in which nothing other than what it contains within is seen outwardly. Baptismal grace is likewise represented by crystal, which is formed from water into ice and a precious stone.

That crystal signifies the solidity of the angels, or the Lord’s incarnation, is proved by the testimony of the prophet Ezekiel, who says: “And above the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of a firmament, like the appearance of a terrifying crystal, spread out above their heads” (Ezek. I). The heavenly powers can indeed be understood by the name “firmament.” This firmament is rightly described as resembling the appearance of crystal, because crystal is exceedingly strong, yet solidified from water. Likewise, when the angelic nature was created, it received free will: whether it wished to persist in humility and remain in the sight of almighty God, or fall into pride and fall away from blessedness, it was like water. But since, when the others fell, the holy angels remained in their blessedness and received this as a gift—that they could no longer fall at all—their nature, since it can no longer be moved into change, was hardened as though into the likeness of crystal.

Likewise, before human nature was assumed by the Creator of all things, it was earth. For there was no firmament: to the sinful man it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). But after it was assumed by the author of all things, raised up into heaven, and set above the angels, what had been earth became firmament. The firmament that is seen, whose likeness it possessed, is then added when it says: “Like the appearance of a terrifying crystal” (Ezek. I).

Crystal, as has been said, freezes from water and becomes strong. We know, therefore, how great is the mobility of water. But the body of our Redeemer, because it was subject to suffering even unto death, was in a certain respect like water: for by being born, growing, becoming weary, hungering, thirsting, and dying, it passed through the successive moments of time in a state of change, even unto the Passion. Water, therefore, was changed into crystal when the weakness of its corruption was transformed through the resurrection into the firmness of incorruption. [Col. 0473C]

The Indian diamond is a rough stone, rusty in color, with the brilliance of crystal. It is never found larger than a hazelnut’s kernel. It yields to no material—not even iron or fire—and it never becomes hot. Hence, according to the Greek interpretation, it received the name “indomitable” [perhaps: “invincible strength”; the text reads *indomita jus*]. Yet although it is unconquered and scorns iron and fire, it is split by fresh goat’s blood and softened by being warmed in it; thus it is shattered by many blows of iron. Sculptors use its fragments like gemstones for ornamenting and perforating other stones.

It also conflicts so strongly with the magnet stone that, when placed nearby, it does not allow iron to be drawn by the magnet; or, if the magnet brought near has seized the iron, the diamond snatches it away. It is also said, in the manner of electrum, to detect poisons, [Col. 0473D] to drive away vain fears, and to resist magical arts. There are six varieties of it.

This stone signifies the hardness of the hearts of the Jews, who were always unyielding and unmanageable with regard to repentance. Thus we read in the prophet Jeremiah: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond claw upon the breadth of their heart” (Jer. XVII). Their sin, therefore, indelible and, so to speak, impossible to erase by any means, is written with an iron stylus and a diamond claw. By the iron stylus, therefore, a powerful sentence is signified; by the diamond claw, the eternal end. Their sin is said to be written with an iron stylus upon a diamond claw because the guilt of the Jews is preserved for endless punishment by the powerful judgment of God. [Col. 0474A] At the Passion of the Savior they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

Alternatively, this may be understood as having been said about Judas the betrayer and his companions. Concerning him the Truth says: “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom he will be betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI).

## CHAPTER X. On glass.

Glass is so called because it shines through to the sight with transparency. In other metals, whatever is contained within is hidden; but in glass, any liquid or substance is revealed outwardly as it is inwardly, and in a certain manner, though enclosed, it remains open to view. Its origin was as follows. [Col. 0474B]

In a part of Syria called Phoenicia, bordering on Judaea, near the foot of Mount Carmel, there is a marsh from which the river Belus arises. It flows for five thousand paces into the sea near Ptolemais. As its sands are washed clean of impurities by the flowing water, the following story is told. When the ship of merchants carrying natron was driven ashore and they were preparing a meal at scattered places along the coast, and there were no stones on which to raise their vessels, they placed lumps of natron from the ship beneath the vessels. When these were kindled, the sand of the shore mixed with them, and streams of a new, transparent substance flowed forth. This was the origin of glass.

Soon, as ingenuity is resourceful, the art was not content with natron alone but experimented with other mixtures. It is cooked over light, dry wood, with cyprus and natron added, in continuous furnaces, until the mass melts like bronze and forms lumps. [Col. 0474C] Afterwards it is melted again from these lumps in workshops. Some of it is shaped by blowing, some is worn down on a lathe, and some is engraved in the manner of silver. It is also dyed in many ways, so that it imitates hyacinths, sapphires, emeralds, onyxes, and the colors of other gemstones. No other material is better suited to mirrors. The highest esteem, however, belongs to white glass, and next to that, glass resembling crystal. Thus glass has displaced vessels of silver and gold for drinking.

Formerly it was also made in Italy, throughout Gaul, and in Spain: white sand was ground and pounded with a very soft pestle and millstone. It has already been stated above that glass signifies the sacrament of baptism, in which we are cleansed from every stain of sins and restored to purity. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse concerning the structure of the heavenly city: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. XXI). [Col. 0474D] The Church is represented by gold; it is often described as adorned in golden lampstands and bowls because of its devotion to wisdom. Glass, however, refers to true faith, because what is seen outwardly is also present inwardly, and among the saints of the Church nothing is feigned or hidden from view. It may also refer to that time when thoughts are seen and revealed to one another.

## CHAPTER XI. On metals.

“Metal” is said in Greek to derive from *apo tou metallan*, because its nature is such that wherever one vein appears, there is hope of searching for another. There are seven kinds of metals: gold, silver, bronze, electrum, tin, lead, and iron, which subdues all things. [Col. 0475A]

## CHAPTER XII. On gold.

Gold is named from *aura*, that is, from brilliance, because when the air is reflected it shines more brightly. Hence Virgil also says:

> From there the varied brilliance of gold flashed back through the branches.

That is, the splendor of gold. For it is natural that the brilliance of metals shines more brightly when reflected by another light. Hence goldsmiths are also so called, because their luster makes things brilliant.

Gold can signify the splendor of wisdom, or the spiritual understanding of the sacred Scriptures, or the excellence of charity, as in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. XLIV). Therefore the grace of charity appeared above the other virtues, because its radiance surpasses them all; and the light of wisdom is most brilliant, being perceived especially through meditation on the Scriptures. [Col. 0475B]

Refined gold is called *obrizum* because it shines with radiance. It is of the finest color; the Hebrews call it *ophaz*, and the Greeks *cirron*. Concerning refined gold, in Job, where Scripture speaks of divine wisdom, we read: “Refined gold shall not be given in exchange for it” (Job XXVIII). For what is signified by refined gold if not the holy angels? They are rightly called refined gold: gold because they shine with the brightness of righteousness; refined because they have never had any taint of guilt.

Righteous human beings, however, so long as they live mortally in this corruptible flesh, may indeed be gold, but they cannot at all be refined gold, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX). For although in this life they may shine with the great brightness of righteousness, they are nevertheless by no means free from the stains of sins.

Again, in the same book we read: “If I thought gold was my strength, and said to refined gold, ‘My confidence’” (Job XXXI). What do we understand as gold in this passage except the capacity for excellent understanding? And what as refined gold except the mind which, while being purified in the fire of love, always preserves within itself the brightness of beauty through the daily renewal of fervor? A mind that strives always to begin anew through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness.

Holy men, however, do not count gold as their strength, because, however greatly they may shine in intelligence, they consider themselves nothing through their own powers. Even when they are able to understand everything vigorously, they first desire to understand themselves, so that the light of their intelligence, like the sun, may first illuminate the place in which it rises and afterwards everything else toward which it expands as it advances. Otherwise, if they devote themselves to knowing others while failing to know themselves, the sun’s ray will grow dark precisely where it rises. [Col. 0475D]

Again, God is understood by gold, as Christ is described in the Song of Songs: “His head is the finest gold” (Song V). In the Apostle: “The head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI).

Gold is the spiritual meaning in divine Scripture, as in the Psalm: “The back parts of his body are in the green of gold” (Ps. LXI). Gold also signifies the saints, concerning whom it is written in Job: “Gold shall come from the north” (Job XXXI), that is, those believing in Christ, with the Apostle of the Gentiles preaching [perhaps omit *praedicante*, “preaching”]. And in the Psalm: “He shall live, and gold from Arabia shall be given to him” (Ps. LXXI).

Gold signifies wisdom, as in Exodus, where it is first prescribed that this very material be used in the priestly adornment. Gold also signifies all the reprobate who have been rejected by the Lord but chosen by human beings. Concerning the devil, it is said in Job: “He spreads gold beneath himself like clay” (Job XLI); and in Habakkuk: “His food is choice” (Hab. I).

## CHAPTER XIII. On silver.

Silver is not far removed from the Greek name, for the Greeks call it *argyros*. [Col. 0476B] It possesses the remarkable property that, although white, when pressed against the body it leaves black lines.

Quicksilver is so called because it stirs up the substances into which it is poured. It is also called liquid because it runs. It is found especially in mines or in silver-smelting furnaces, adhering to their surfaces in drops that have solidified; it is also often found in very old sewage and in the mud of wells.

Mystically, silver expresses the divine utterances, or the literal or historical understanding, as in the prophet’s statement against heretics: “You took my silver and my gold and placed them in your shrines” (Joel III). And in the Psalm: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI). By the likeness of a bright metal, he defined the pure utterances as silver tested by the fire of the earth, which is usually most pure when it has been cleansed through frequent smelting. “Tested” or “purified” is set against what he says of sinners: “They have spoken deceitful lips, with a heart and a heart” (ibid.). And so that the distance might be understood as very great, he added, “purified sevenfold.” This number appears to refer to the sevenfold Spirit: the fear of God, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. Through these, the divine word remains in the blazing furnaces with the radiant flash of truth. [Col. 0476C]

Silver also signifies the confession of the mouth or the purity of chastity. In Exodus: “Everyone who is generous of heart shall offer the firstfruits to the Lord: gold, silver, and bronze” (Exod. XXV).

Again, silver signifies the Jewish people in Jeremiah: “Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them” (Jer. VI). [Col. 0476D]

Silver also signifies the speech of preaching. Hence in Exodus the pillars of the tabernacle are said to be silver-plated.

## CHAPTER XIV. On bronze.

Bronze is named from the brilliance of bronze, just as gold and silver are. Among the ancients, however, the use of bronze was known before that of iron. With bronze they first plowed the earth; with bronze they conducted the contests of war; and bronze was held in greater esteem. Gold and silver, on account of their uselessness, were rejected. Now the reverse has occurred: bronze lies neglected, while gold has risen to the highest honor. Thus revolving time changes the conditions of things, and what was once held in esteem finally becomes honored by no one. [Col. 0477A]

Later the use of bronze passed to statues, vessels, and especially the structures of buildings, as well as to the preservation of monuments. Public decrees were also written on bronze.

Bronze expresses vanity or the emptiness of faith, as in the Apostle: “I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII).

It has another meaning in the Psalmist’s words: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow” (Ps. XVII). Here the prophet shows how one ought to fight against the devil. The arms are the prophets and Apostles of Christ, through whom he has carried out the desire of his will. He compares them to a bronze bow because God’s servants do not know how to grow soft in preaching; rather, remaining in heavenly strength, they pierce the hearts of devoted people by sending forth salutary words like arrows shot from afar. [Col. 0477B]

Bronze also signifies the divine Scriptures. Hence in Isaiah: “Instead of bronze I will bring gold, and instead of iron I will bring silver, and instead of wood, bronze” (Isa. LX). And concerning the promised land, which is the Church, he says in Deuteronomy: “Its stones are iron, and from its mountains—that is, from its teachers—the ores of bronze are dug” (Deut. VIII).

Bronze signifies the strength of repentance or the sound of preaching, as in Exodus: “Everyone who is generous of heart shall offer to the Lord gold, silver, and bronze” (Exod. XXV).

Bronze also signifies the Church’s strength in the long endurance of patience. Hence the passage in Job: “A stone dissolved by heat is changed into bronze” (Job XXVIII).

Again, concerning the Antichrist, we read in the same book: “He regards iron as straw, and bronze as rotten wood” (Job XLI). [Col. 0477C] This marks the rigidity of his obstinacy.

Again, bronze signifies murmurers under the scourges of God, as in the prophet: “All these have turned into the dross of silver: bronze, tin, and lead in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek. XXII).

*Aurichalcum* is so called because it possesses both the brilliance of gold and the hardness of bronze. The name is compounded from the Latin and Greek languages: bronze is called *chalkos* in Greek. It is made from bronze and much fire, and by chemical treatments it is brought to a golden color.

Corinthian bronze is a mixture of all metals, which chance first mingled when Corinth was captured and burned. For when Hannibal had captured this city, he gathered all the bronze statues onto one pyre and burned them. From this mixture, craftsmen took the material [Col. 0477D] and made bowls. Thus Corinthian objects arose from all the metals combined into one, neither this nor that. Hence to the present day, whether made from the original material or in imitation of it, bronze or vessels are called Corinthian bronze or Corinthian vessels.

In the Apocalypse (Rev. I) we read of the likeness of the Son of Man that “his head and his hair were white, like white wool and like snow; his eyes were like a flame of fire; and his feet were like aurichalcum, burning as in a furnace.” By the fiery feet he means the Church of the last time, which must be tested and proved by severe pressures. For aurichalcum is bronze brought to a golden color by much fire and chemical treatment.

Another translation, which says “like the aurichalcum of Lebanon,” [Col. 0478A] signifies that the Church in Judea, whose mountain is Lebanon, will be persecuted especially in the last days. By dross may be understood the Jewish people, or all the reprobate, rejected and cast away from the natural metal because of the defect of sin. In the prophet: “All these have turned into the dross of silver,” and so forth (Ezek. XXII).

## CHAPTER XV. On electrum.

Electrum is so called because in the sun’s rays it shines more brightly than gold and silver. For the sun is called *elector* by the poets. This metal is purer than all other metals.

There are three kinds of it. One flows from pine trees and is called amber; another is a metal found naturally and held in esteem; the third is made from three parts gold and one part silver. Even if you dissolve the naturally occurring material, you will find no difference between what is born and what is made: both are of the same nature. [Col. 0478B]

Natural electrum has such a nature that at a banquet and by lamplight it shines more brightly than all metals and reveals poison. [Col. 0478B] For if poison is poured into it, it gives off a hissing sound and emits various colors in the manner of the heavenly rainbow.

Concerning electrum, it is written in the vision of the prophet Ezekiel: “And I saw something resembling electrum, like the appearance of fire within it all around, from his loins upward; and from his loins downward I saw something like the appearance of shining fire around him, like the appearance of a bow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day” (Ezek. I). [Col. 0478C] What does it mean that the appearance of a man is seen upon the throne as a form of electrum, except that in electrum gold and silver are mixed, so that one substance is made from two metals? In it, the brilliance of gold is tempered by the silver, and through the brilliance of gold the appearance of silver becomes bright.

In our Redeemer, however, both natures—that is, divinity and humanity—are united with each other without confusion and inseparably, so that through his humanity the brilliance of his divinity could be tempered to our eyes, and through his divinity the human nature in him could shine and, having been exalted, possess a radiance beyond what it had when created.

## CHAPTER XVI. On tin.

[Col. 0478D] The etymology of tin is *apochorizon*, that is, “separating” and “distinguishing.” For by means of fire it separates metals mixed and adulterated with one another, and divides bronze and lead from gold and silver. It also protects other metals from fire. Bronze, although its nature is extremely hard, like that of iron, is burned and consumed if it is without tin.

Tin spread over bronze vessels makes their flavor more agreeable and restrains the poisonous force of verdigris. Mirrors are also tempered with it. White lead is made from it, just as from lead.

Allegorically, tin can signify sophistical speech and the pretense of heretics. Hence in Ezekiel, where the commerce of Tyre is mentioned, it is written: “The merchants of Carthage filled your markets with silver, iron, tin, and lead, from the abundance of all kinds of wealth” (Ezek. XXVII). Thus they multiply the markets of Tyre not with gold or precious stones, but with silver, iron, tin, and lead: possessing the elegance of eloquence and weapons for assault; in tin, the likeness of eloquence, which falsely imitates silver; and in lead, the gravest impiety, in accordance with Zechariah, in whom a woman sat upon a talent of lead, and the Egyptians were sunk into the depths like lead. [Col. 0479A]

A lengthy discussion of each of the metals would follow, but we must strive for brevity. Tin also signifies a pretense of holiness, as in the prophet: “All these have become for me the dross of silver, bronze, tin, and lead” (Ezek. XXII).

## CHAPTER XVII. On lead.

[Col. 0479B] Lead is so called because the depth of the sea was first sounded with it, after a line had been made from it. There are two kinds of it, black and white; but the white is better, and it was first discovered in the islands of the Atlantic Sea. It is also produced in Lusitania and Galicia, at the surface of the earth, in sandy soil, black in color and heavy in weight.

Small stones are mixed with it, especially from dried-up torrents. They wash these sands, and they cook what settles at the bottom in furnaces. Black and heavy stones are also found in gold mines when water is added; while the gold is gathered, they remain with it. Later, when separated, they are melted and resolved into white lead. Hence lead has the same heaviness as gold.

So too the desire for the world and greed for money are burdensome and oppress their lover with the heaviest iniquity.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On iron.

[Col. 0479C]

Iron is so called because it encloses *farra*, that is, the seeds of the earth’s crops. [Col. 0480A] It is also called steel, *chalybs*, from the river Chalybs, where iron is tempered with the greatest skill. Hence the material itself is used metaphorically for steel, as in: “the wound-dealing steel.”

The use of iron was discovered after the other metals; later its character was turned into a reproach. For the material with which the earth was first cultivated is now used to pour out blood.

Mystically, iron signifies tribulation and distress, as in the Psalm concerning Joseph: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. CIV). Here iron indicates the tribulation of harsh necessity, which ranges through the soul when it is pressed by anxiety, as it already suffers the evils of future things that it does not cease to fear.

A similar expression occurs in the Gospel, where Simeon says to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul” (Luke II), signifying that the glorious mother would possess the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion. We believe that this type of expression should be noted among the distinctive features of divine Scripture.

Iron also signifies the strong members of the Church, as in the book of Job: “Iron is taken from the earth” (Job XXVIII); and in Deuteronomy: “Its stones are iron” (Deut. VIII). In the same place it is said of the Church: “Iron and bronze are its sandals” (Deut. XXXIII).

Again, iron signifies keenness of mind, whence Solomon says: “Iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend” (Prov. XXVII).

Again, iron is the word of reproof, as in Deuteronomy: “If someone goes with his friend innocently into the forest to cut wood, and the iron comes out of his handle and kills his friend” (Deut. XIX).

Again, iron signifies the enemy’s ambushes, as Solomon says: “As iron rusts, so does his wickedness” (Ecclus. XII).

# BOOK EIGHTEEN.

[Col. 0479]

## CHAPTER ONE. On weights.

[Col. 0479C]

The nature of weights and measures is useful to know, for everything bodily, as it is written, “from the highest to the lowest,” has been arranged and formed according to measure, number, and weight (Wis. 11). Nature has assigned a weight to all corporeal things, and its own weight governs everything.

Moses, the first to precede all the pagan philosophers in time, related numbers, measures, and weights to us in various places of his Scripture. Afterward Phidon of Argos established the system of weights in Greece; although others were more ancient, he was more experienced in this art. A *pondus* (“weight”) is so called because, balanced on a steelyard, it hangs (*pendet*); hence also *pensum*. By an extended usage, a *pondus* is one pound. Hence *dipondium* was also coined, as though “two weights”; this name remains in use even now.

A *trutina* is a balance with two pans for weights, hanging with equal equilibrium, made for weighing talents and hundredweights, just as a small balance is used for small and modest sums of money.
