It was also called *moneta*, and likewise *statera*, taking its name from number, because, balanced by two pans and one central rod, it stands equally. The *examen* is the central cord by which the balance’s steelyard is controlled and the pans are made equal; hence on the pans it is also called the *amentum*.

[Col. 0480C]

In the steelyard, the power of equity or of divine governance is signified, as in Isaiah: “And he weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills in a steelyard” (Isa. 40); that is, he judges the greater and the lesser, the powerful and the weak, the noble and the ignoble, with justice, “because he will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth” [Col. 0480D] (Ps. 9). Hence Job also says: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance” (Job 6).

Who else is expressed under the name of the steelyard except the mediator of God and human beings? He came to weigh the merit of our life and brought justice and mercy with him together; but, making the pan of mercy outweigh our sins, he lightened them by sparing us.

The pound of weight mystically signifies observance of justice, because in it what is equitable and what is contrary to equity are tested. Very many proofs of this are found in Scripture, and some of them must necessarily be listed here.

The prophet therefore testifies: “The Lord is just and loves justice; his countenance has seen equity” (Ps. 10). He says that God loves the just because he knows how to regard none but those who know how to preserve justice. He adds, “His countenance has seen equity”—that equity, namely, which he himself nevertheless graciously grants. For humanity possesses nothing good of itself except what it has received from the Lord, the giver of all good things.

Hence it is also written in Proverbs: “Whoever follows justice is loved by the Lord” (Prov. 21); and elsewhere it is said of wisdom: “Whoever is steadfast in justice,” he says, “will apprehend it” (Sir. 15).

Each weight, moreover, has a definite measure designated by its proper names. The *chalcus* is the smallest part of a weight, a quarter of an obol, consisting of lentil-seed grains. It is called *chalcus* because it is small, just as a *calculus* is a stone so tiny that it can be trodden upon without inconvenience.

The *siliqua* is one twenty-fourth of a solidus, taking its name from the tree whose seed it is.

The *ceratum* is half an obol, containing one and a half siliquae; Latin calls it a *semiobolus*. Greek *ceratum* is interpreted in Latin as *siliqua cornu* (“horn-pod”).

An obol is weighed as three siliquae; it contains two ceratia and four chalci. Formerly it was made of bronze in the shape of an arrow, and therefore received its name from the Greeks, namely “arrow.”

A *scrupulus* consists of the weight of six siliquae. Among the Greeks it is called a *gramma*. *Scrupulus* is formed by diminutive usage from a small stone, called a *scrupus*.

A drachma is one-eighth of an ounce and the weight of a silver denarius. It consists of three scruples, that is, eighteen siliquae. The drachma’s likeness is applied to the human being in the Gospel parable, where the Lord says: “Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it, and so forth” (Luke 15).

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself is signified both by the shepherd and by the woman. Since the image of a human being is expressed on the drachma, the woman lost the drachma when the human being, created in the image of God, departed through sin from the likeness of his Creator.

But the woman lights a lamp, because the Wisdom of God—the Son of God himself—when he assumed human nature from Mary’s womb and appeared in humanity, was shaken by awareness of our mortality and saw that he could return by the cross to immortality, from which humanity had fallen through sin.

The denarius is so called because it was reckoned at ten coins. Allegorically, the denarius signifies the future reward of the saints, which is promised to them here for their good labor and given in the future. Hence in the Gospel the master of the household is read to have given a denarius to the workers in his vineyard at the end of their labor (Matt. 20).

Two denarii signify the two precepts of charity, or both Testaments, that is, the New and the Old; hence it is said in the Gospel: “And on the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper” (Luke 10).

The *solidus* is so called because nothing seems to be lacking from it; for the ancients called what was whole and complete *solidum*. It is also called *nomisma*, because it is marked with the names and image of rulers. At the beginning there was one coin, one silver piece; this originated among the Assyrians. The Jews say that Abraham was the first to bring this form into the land of Canaan.

Among the Latins the solidus is also called a *sextula*, because six of them make an ounce. This, as we have said, the common people call a gold solidus. One-third of it they called a *tremissis*, because, when sent three times, it makes a solidus.

The impression of a coin in the census signifies the image of the Creator in the human soul, which is sought from each of us when the faith of right belief, together with good works, is required of us. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to those who were testing him: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22).

The coin that was displayed bore Caesar’s image; therefore he commanded that the coin, tribute, money, and earthly honors be rendered to Caesar. God, however, himself formed us—that is, the image of God—in ourselves; this image is not painted in gold but formed in human beings.

A sextula taken twice makes a *duella*; taken three times, it produces a *stater*. A stater is half an ounce, weighing three gold pieces; hence it is called *stater*, because it stands at three solidi. It is also a *semi-ounce*, because it contains half an ounce; and a *semissis*, because it is half a weight, as if half an *as*.

The Hebrews likewise call the *quadrans* a *codrans*. It is called a quadrans because it weighs a quarter of an ounce.

The Gospel speaks of the quadrans when it recalls the delivery of a guilty person into prison: “Amen, I say to you, you will not go out from there until you repay the last quadrans” (Matt. 5).

A quadrans is a kind of coin, as though two small coins. Hence in another Gospel (Mark 12) that poor widow is said to have put a quadrans into the treasury, while in another Gospel she is said to have put in two small coins (Luke 21)—not because the Gospels disagree, but because one quadrans contains two small coins.

This is therefore what he says: “You will not leave the prison” (Matt. 5) “until you repay even your small sins.” The repayment of the last quadrans may reasonably be understood either as referring to the fact that nothing is left unpunished—as when we also say “down to the dregs” when we wish to express that something has been carried out so exactly that nothing remains—or as signifying, under the name of the quadrans, the final earthly sins.

For the earth is found to be the fourth and final part of the divided members of this world: beginning with heaven, you count the air second, water third, and earth fourth.

The *sikel*, which in Latin is improperly called a *siclus*, is a Hebrew name. Among the Hebrews it has the weight of an ounce. Among the Latins and Greeks, however, it is a quarter of an ounce and half a stater, weighing two drachmas. Therefore, when *sikel* is read in the divine writings, it means an ounce; when it occurs in pagan writings, it means a quarter of an ounce.

An ounce is so called because, by its unity, it binds together—that is, encompasses—the whole of the lesser weights. It consists of eight drachmas, that is, twenty-four scruples, and is therefore regarded as the standard weight, because the number of its scruples measures the hours of day and night; or because, counted twelve times, it makes a pound.

A pound is completed by twelve ounces and is therefore a type of perfect weight, because it consists of as many ounces as the year has months. It is called *libra* because it is *libera* (“free”), and contains within itself all the weights mentioned above.

A *mina* in weights is measured at one hundred drachmas, and the name is Greek. The mina signifies the ten words of the Law divinely given to human beings, so that they might work with them and produce spiritual profit. Hence it is read in the Gospel (Matt. 25) that the nobleman who went away to a distant region entrusted his money to his servants; when he returned, each one reported what he had made profitable.

This nobleman is our Redeemer, who went away to a distant region because, after completing his Passion and resurrection, he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God. On the day of judgment he will come to demand from each debtor the money he had entrusted to them: “And he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. 16; Rom. 2).

The talent is said to be the greatest weight among the Greeks, for nothing is smaller than the chalcus and nothing greater than the talent; its weight varies among different peoples.

Among the Romans, a talent is seventy-two pounds, as Plautus shows when he says that two talents are one hundred forty-four pounds. There are three kinds: the lesser, the middle, and the greatest. The lesser consists of fifty pounds; the middle of seventy-two pounds; the greatest of one hundred twenty.

The *centenarius* takes its name from the number one hundred because it is a weight of one hundred pounds. The Romans established this weight because of the perfection of the number one hundred.

Under the name of talent, the fullness and perfection of gifts are signified. Hence in the Gospel parable the Lord says (Matt. 25) that a man setting out on a journey called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them: to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Thus by the five talents the gift of the five senses—that is, knowledge of external things—is expressed. By two, understanding and action are signified; by the name of one talent, understanding alone is signified.

Ten thousand talents signify the working out of the ten commandments of the Law in the Gospel, where it is written: “And one was brought who owed ten thousand talents” (Matt. 18).

The talent is also used in a bad sense in Zechariah: “I saw,” he says, “iniquity upon a talent of lead” (Zech. 5).

In the most ancient times, before gold and silver had been discovered, people used bronze. Bronze money was first in use, silver followed, and gold came afterward; nevertheless, it retained the name from what had come first.

Hence *aerarium* (“treasury”) was also so called, because originally only bronze was in use and only bronze was stored away, before gold and silver had been coined. Although money was later made from those metals, the name *aerarium* remained from the metal from which it had begun.

A treasure is named, according to the Greek expression *apo tes theseos*, “from placing,” that is, from something stored away. For *thesis* means “placing,” and the word is compounded from Greek and Latin. The Greeks call something stored away *thesis*; the Latins call gold *aurum*, so that, when joined together, it sounds like “stored gold.” *Auraria* takes its name from gold.

The Gospel parable gives a clear indication of the meaning of treasure, where the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds hides; and for joy over it he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matt. 13).

The treasure is the heavenly desire. The field in which the treasure is hidden is the discipline of devotion to heavenly things. The person who sells everything and buys that field renounces the pleasures of the flesh and tramples all his earthly desires under the guardianship of heavenly discipline, so that nothing pleasing to the flesh may be permitted and the spirit [or Spirit] may shrink from nothing that destroys the carnal mind.

This treasure, in which “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2), is either the word of God, which appears hidden in the flesh of Christ, or the Holy Scriptures, in which knowledge of the Savior has been stored. When someone finds him in them, he must despise all the profits of this age so that he may possess the one whom he has found.

Tributes (*tributa*) are so called because formerly they were exacted individually through the tribes, just as now they are exacted through individual territories. It is therefore established that the Roman people were divided into three parts, so that those in the individual parts were called *tribuni*. Hence the expenses that peoples paid were also called *tributa*.

*Vectigalia* are tributes named from carrying (*vehere*). *Stipendium* is named from money being weighed out (*stips pendenda*). For the ancients were accustomed to weigh money rather than count it.

[Col. 0484C]

Let us briefly explain what the rich, who possess treasures, and riches signify mystically. God is called rich, as in the Apostle: “God, who is rich in mercy” (Eph. 2). The rich are the saints, as in the Apostle: “Because you have become rich in him in all wisdom and understanding” (1 Cor. 1).

The Jewish people are rich, of whom it is said in the Gospel (Matt. 19): “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven.” Others understand this rich person as any proud individual.

The rich are the Jewish philosophers, or the proud of this world, as in the Psalter: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. 33); and elsewhere: “He sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1).

Riches are the virtues of the soul, or the word of wisdom, as in the Apostle: “Because you have become rich in him in all wisdom and understanding” (1 Cor. 1); and in Solomon: “The riches of a man are the possession of his own soul” (Prov. 13). The word is also used in another sense for a heretic, as it is read in Job: “His riches, which he devoured, God will draw out from his belly” (Job 20).

Money, therefore, is the divine word, as in the Gospel: “You ought to have entrusted my money to the money-changers” (Matt. 25).

A purse is the storing up of treasure in God, as in the Gospel: “Make purses for yourselves that do not grow old” (Luke 12). A purse is also the gathering of avarice, as in the prophet Haggai: “He who gathered wages put them into a pierced purse” (Hag. 1).

The merchants are the Apostles. But in Job, with reference to the body of the devil—that is, all the wicked—it is said concerning those same merchants: “His friends will cut him up; merchants will divide him” (Job 40). The word is likewise used in a bad sense in Ezekiel: “Merchants with lambs and goats come to you” (Ezek. 27).

*Moneta* is so called because it warns (*monet*) that no fraud should be committed in metal or weight.

A *nomisma* is a solidus, whether gold, silver, or bronze. It is called *nomisma* because it is marked with the names and images of rulers.

Formerly a silver coin was called *argyrus*, because it was struck principally from silver. Coins (*nummi*) were named from Numa, king of the Romans, who first marked them among the Latins with images and inscribed upon them the title of his name.

Three things are sought in a coin: metal, figure, and weight. If any one of these is lacking, it will not be a coin.

The mystical meaning of coins has been explained above.

There are three kinds of silver, gold, and bronze: coined, fashioned, and unworked. Coined is what is found in coins; fashioned is what is found in vessels; unworked is what is found in ingots, which is also called *grave*, that is, a mass.

Metals came to the knowledge of human beings in the following way. When burning forests, for whatever reason, melted the earth, the heated veins poured out streams of whatever kind of material they contained, whether bronze or gold. As the flow ran into lower places in the earth, it took the shape that either the flowing stream or the hollow receiving it had formed. Captivated by the brilliance of these things, people lifted the masses that had been cast up and saw in them the marks of the earth represented. From this they devised the idea that melted metal could be brought into every shape.

## Chapter II. On Measures

[Col. 0485C]

A measure is any thing bounded according to its proper extent or time. It is either of the body or of time. Of the body, as the length and shortness of human beings, pieces of wood, and columns. The sun itself, too, has its own measure within its orbit, which geometers dare to investigate.

Of time, as the measure of hours, days, and years; hence we also speak of measuring the feet of hours—that is, of measuring time. For it is read in the Book of Wisdom that God disposes all things according to measure, number, and weight (Wis. 11).

In these three definitions, as I think, the following can be understood: that in measure quality is established, in number quantity, and in weight proportion. These are balanced in the judgment and mercy of God, because everything is enclosed within these two limits. Within them God established this world, governs it, and will judge it; within them God the just judge can be comprehended.

Everything, therefore, that we have said above or shall say is now hidden from us in the conclusion of these three things; it will then be unlocked by the keys of God’s judgment and mercy, so that it may be known when, at the Lord’s coming, “the hidden things of darkness will be brought to light and the counsels of hearts will be revealed” (1 Cor. 4), so that each person may receive praise from God or punishment.

More properly, a measure is so called because by it crops and grain are measured, both liquids and dry goods, as by modii, urns, and amphorae.

The smallest part of measures is the *cochlear*, which is half a drachma and weighs nine siliquae. Tripled, it makes a *choncula*. A choncula is filled by one and a half drachmas.

A *cyathus* is weighed at ten drachmas. Some also call it a *causatus* or *lassatus*. An *oxyba­phus* is made when five drachmas are added to ten.

An *acetabulum* is one quarter of a hemina and weighs twelve drachmas.

A *cotula* is a hemina containing six cyathi. It is called *cotula* because in Greek *cote* means “a cutting”: a hemina is cut into two equal parts from a sextarius, making a cotula.

A hemina weighs one pound; doubled, it makes a sextarius. A sextarius is two pounds. Taken twice, it is called a *bilibris*; taken four times, it becomes, in Greek, a *choenix*; folded five times, it makes a *quinaris* or *gomor*. Add a sixth, and it produces a *congius*, for a congius measures six sextarii, from which it also gave the sextarius its name.

The stater and the bilibris are mentioned in the Apocalypse in the description of the third seal:

“When he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying, ‘Come and see.’ And behold, a black horse, and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand. And I heard as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: ‘A bilibris of wheat for a denarius, and three bilibres of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil.’ And behold, a black horse, and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand. And I heard as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, and so forth” (Rev. 6).

The black horse is the crowd of false brothers who have the balance of right profession but harm their companions through works of darkness. For when it is said in the midst of the living creatures, “Do not harm,” it is shown that there is someone there who does harm.

Concerning this horse and the one preceding it the Apostle says: “Outside, battles; inside, fears” (2 Cor. 7).

“A bilibris of wheat for a denarius, and do not harm the wine and the oil.” Beware, he says, lest by a very bad example you scandalize your brother, for whom Christ died, and who bears the marks of the sacred blood and chrism. For whether perfect in merit or among the very least in the Church, provided that they are imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity, all have been redeemed by the same perfect price of the Lord’s blood.

Nor is it without reason that perfection of faith or work is expressed by a bilibris rather than by a simple pound: both kinds of perfection rest upon the twofold root of charity.

A *metreta* is a measure of liquids. It takes its name from measure: for the Greeks call a measure *metron*, and from this it is called *metreta*. Although an urn, amphora, and other such names are also names of measures, this one received the name particularly from the perfection of the number ten.

A *metron* pertains to every measure. For *metreta* in Greek means “measure” in Latin. A cyathus is a measure, an amphora is a measure, and whatever contains more or less is a measure. But this name specifically claimed for itself the designation because it is the measure of the perfect number, namely ten.

Hence it is written in the Gospel, concerning the wedding feast where the Lord changed water into wine: “There were six stone water-jars set there according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three metretae” (John 2).

Water-jars are vessels prepared for receiving water; for in Greek water is called *hydor*. Water signifies the knowledge of Holy Scripture, which is accustomed both to wash its hearers from the filth of sins and to give them drink from the fountain of divine knowledge.

The six vessels containing it are the devoted hearts of the saints, whose perfection of life and faith has been set before the human race as an example of right belief and living, through the six ages of the passing world—that is, up to the time of the Lord’s preaching.

The vessels are appropriately made of stone, because the inner hearts of the righteous are strong, as those solidified by the faith and love of that person. “Each holding two or three metretae”: the authors and ministers of Holy Scripture sometimes speak only of the Father and the Son, as in the verse, “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103)—for Christ is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1)—and sometimes they also mention the Holy Spirit, according to the statement of the same psalmist: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32).

The *modius* is so called because it is perfect according to its own measure. It is a measure of forty-four pounds, that is, twenty-two sextarii. The reason for this number is drawn from the fact that at the beginning God made twenty-two works.

On the first day he made seven works: the formless matter, the angels, light, the higher heavens, the earth, and the air. On the second day, the firmament alone. On the third day, four: the seas, seeds, crops, and plantations. On the fourth day, three: the sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth day, three: fish, aquatic reptiles, and birds. On the sixth day, four: wild beasts, cattle, terrestrial reptiles, and human beings.

Thus twenty-two kinds of things were made in six days. There are also twenty-two generations from Adam to Jacob, from whose seed the whole nation of Israel was born; twenty-two books of the Old Testament up to Esther; and twenty-two letters of the alphabet by which the teaching of the divine Law is constituted.

According to these examples, the modius of twenty-two sextarii was established by Moses according to the measure of the sacred Law. Although different nations ignorantly add to or subtract from the weight of this measure, among the Hebrews it is preserved by divine ordinance according to this reasoning.

The modius is named from *modus*, “measure.” Hence also *modica*, “moderate,” since the modius gave its name to *modica*. We improperly, rather than properly, use *modica* for small things.

In Holy Scripture, the modius signifies the equity of justice. Hence the Lord commanded in the Law: “You shall not have a greater and a lesser modius, but a just modius and an equal sextarius” (Deut. 25).

The modius also signifies the human body or the literal sense of the Law. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a modius” (Luke 8; 11).

To put a lamp under a modius is therefore to place bodily advantages above the preaching of truth, so that someone does not preach the truth because he fears suffering some inconvenience in bodily and temporal matters. Whoever obscures and covers the light of good teaching with temporal advantages puts a lamp under a modius.

But the person who places it upon a lampstand subjects his body to the service of God, so that the preaching of truth is above and bodily service below. Nevertheless, through that bodily service the teaching shines forth more brilliantly, since it is displayed through temporal functions—that is, through voice, tongue, and the other movements of the body.

A *satum* is a kind of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, holding one and a half modii. Its name is drawn from the Hebrew language. Among them *satum* means “taking” or “lifting,” because the person who measures takes up and lifts the same measure.

Elsewhere *satum* is also a measure holding twenty-two sextarii, approximately a modius.

Hence it is written in the Gospel (Matt. 13) concerning the woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened. This woman signifies the holy Church, which places the teaching of the Gospel and the understanding of the Holy Scriptures in human hearts until it unites the three parts of the world—the world that arose from the three sons of Noah—turning the threefold square toward the faith of holy charity, so that spirit, soul, and body, brought together into one, do not disagree among themselves.

Apart from this, the three measures of flour can also be understood as those fruits of the Lord’s seed: the thirtieth, the sixtieth, and the hundredfold, that is, of the married, the continent, and virgins.

He appropriately says that the leaven was hidden in the flour until the whole was leavened, because charity, stored in our mind, ought to grow until it transforms the whole mind into its own perfection.

A *bath* is called by the Hebrew language from the mill for olives, which among them is called *bath* or *batha*. It holds fifty sextarii, the amount that is crushed in one turn of the mill.

An *ephi* is therefore a measure of three modii, as is shown in the Book of Ruth. A *gomor* is a measure of three Attic *chenices*. Hence whenever the tenth part of an ephi is commanded to be offered in sacrifice in Leviticus and Numbers, the measure of a gomor is understood to have been expended.

The ephi has the same measure for dry goods as the bath has for liquids.

An amphora is so called because it is lifted from both sides. In Greek it is said to have been named from its shape, because its doubled handles appear to imitate ears. It holds a square foot of wine or water, but three Italian modii of grain.

A *cadus* in Greek is an amphora containing three urns.

An urn is a measure called a *quartarius*. Properly, however, an urn is a vessel customarily used for storing the ashes of the dead; concerning it the poet says: “He is covered by the sky who has no urn.”

A *medimnus* is a measure of five modii. In Latin it is called *medimnus*, that is, “half,” because it measures five modii, which is half of the perfect number ten.

An *artaba* is a measure among the Egyptians of seventy-two sextarii. It is formed from the number because of the seventy-two nations or languages that filled the world.

A gomor weighs a load of fifteen modii. A *corus* is completed as a measure of thirty modii. It derives from the Hebrew language and is called *cora*, from its likeness to a hill. For in Hebrew *coria* means “hills.” Thirty modii heaped together appear like a hill and make a camel’s load.

Concerning the amphora it is written in the prophet Zechariah:

“And behold, a woman sitting in the middle of the amphora, and he said: ‘This is wickedness.’ And he threw her into the middle of the amphora and placed a mass of lead in its mouth,” and so forth (Zech. 5).

Here the amphora signifies the great measure of the iniquity of the Jews, concerning which the Savior says to them: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. 23).

Over this measure of all sins sat wickedness in the middle, which we may call by another name idolatry and denial of God. A mass of lead was therefore placed in the mouth of the synagogue of the Jews, so that its arrogance might be silenced.

This wickedness of the synagogue, which sat upon the sins of Israel and gloried in its crime, was afterward cast into the midst of Babylon and oppressed by the evil of captivity—or certainly by the angel—so that what had previously lain hidden in crime might fall silent in eternal silence.

We read in the Gospel (Luke 16) that the steward of iniquity reduced the debts of his master’s debtors, who owed their master a great debt: one owed one hundred cadi of oil, another one hundred cori of wheat. He ordered the first to write fifty instead of one hundred cadi of oil, and the second to write eighty instead of one hundred cori of wheat.

By these matters we are instructed that, by showing mercy through the remission of debt, we ourselves may obtain remission of our debts from the merciful Lord.

## Chapter III. On Number
[Col. 0489C] For the numerical system, in many instances, reveals to us a venerable mystery through typological significance according to allegory. Thus the first number, that is, one, refers to the unity of the Godhead. Concerning this it is written in Exodus: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI). Likewise, one pertains to the unity of the Church or of faith. Hence it is written concerning the believers in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). Again, one looks to the unity of faith or to the perfection of works. Hence in Genesis it is written concerning the ark: “And you shall finish its top at one cubit” (Gen. VI). Once more, one expresses the unity of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “And he saw there a man not dressed in a wedding garment” (Matt. XXII).

The number two refers to the two Testaments; hence it is written in the Book of Kings: “And he made two cherubim, ten cubits in size” (III Kings VI). Likewise, two pertains to the two commandments of charity, whence he says in the Gospel: “On these two commandments depend the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII). Again, two expresses two dignities, namely, the royal and the priestly; their figure was borne by those two fish joined to the five loaves in the Gospel. Once more, two signifies the mystery of the two peoples, that is, the Jews and the Gentiles. Hence it is written in Zechariah: “And there shall be peace between those two” (Zech. VI). Two also signifies the agreement of soul and body; hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If two of you agree on earth,” etc. (Matt. XVIII). Concerning this Amos also says: “Will two walk together unless they have agreed?” (Amos III). Likewise, two bear the prefiguration of the elect and the rejected. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then two will be in the field: one will be taken and the other will be left” (Matt. XXIV).

The number three, therefore, pertains to the mystery of the Trinity, as in the Epistle of John: “There are three,” he says, “who bear witness” (I John V). Likewise, three refers to the mystery of the Lord’s passion, burial, and resurrection; hence it is written in Hosea: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live” (Hos. VI). Again, three serves to express faith, hope, and charity; the three cities in Deuteronomy, to which the homicide who has unwillingly killed his neighbor is commanded to flee, are said to bear the figure of these virtues [Col. 0490B]. Likewise, three signifies three periods: the first before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace. Hence we read in the Gospel parable: “Behold, these three years I have come seeking fruit on the fig tree, and I find none” (Luke XIII). Again, three prefigures the threefold activity of human beings, whether in good or evil, namely, in thought, word, and deed, as the Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw” (I Cor. III). Once more, three indicates the threefold profession of the faithful, namely, of clerics, monks, and married persons. Concerning this threefold profession in the Church the Lord speaks through Ezekiel, saying: “If these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in their midst, they would save neither son nor daughter; they alone would be saved” (Ezek. I).

The number four, therefore, pertains to the four Gospels, as in Ezekiel: “And in the midst of them was the likeness of four living creatures” (Ezek. I). Likewise, four leads to the mystical significance of the four holy virtues, namely, prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, by which the souls of the saints are refreshed through the Lord’s generosity. Hence it is written: “Those who had eaten were about four thousand men, and he dismissed them” (Mark VIII). Again, four pertains to the four regions of the world, from which the holy Church is gathered. Hence it is said through the prophet: “From the east I will bring your offspring, and from the west I will gather you; I will say to the north, ‘Give,’ and to the south, ‘Do not withhold’” (Isa. [Col. 0490D] XLIII). Similarly, four may be referred to the four elements of the world, from which the human body is composed, since the constitution of the body is chiefly strengthened and sustained by them. For it is written in the Gospel that a paralytic was carried on a bed by four men.

The number five, therefore, sometimes derives its significance from the five books of Moses’ law, concerning which the Apostle says: “I would rather speak five words with my understanding in the Church” (I Cor. XIV); or from the five bodily senses, namely, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins” (Matt. XXV), for five of them were foolish and five wise. Likewise there: “And to one he gave five talents” (ibid.). Hence also the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “For you have had five husbands” (John IV).

The number six refers in its significance to the six days in which God created the whole creation, as in Exodus: “For in six days God made heaven and earth” (Exod. XX); or to the entire period of the present age, which proceeds through six ages. Hence the Lord, the perfecter of all his work, coming into the world in the sixth age, suffered on the sixth day, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from the dead on the Lord’s Day.

The number seven, therefore, has a manifold significance, because sometimes it refers to the seventh day, on which, when all things had been completed, the Lord rested. Thus the souls of the saints, after the labor of good works, rest from all their work in eternal blessedness [Col. 0491B]. At other times it pertains to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is written in the Apocalypse: “Seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent throughout the whole earth” (Apoc. V). Likewise, seven churches are read of in the Apocalypse, represented by seven lampstands and seven stars (Apoc. I). In them the fullness of the saints is present, as the same book testifies: the seven lampstands are the seven churches, and likewise the seven stars.

Again, by seven the whole present time of this age is designated, since it revolves through the cycle of seven days. Conversely, by the number seven the fullness of sin—that is, the totality of the seven chief vices—is represented. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the unclean spirit: “Then he goes and takes with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in they dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Luke XI). Hence also it is read in Solomon: “Do not believe him, for there are seven wickednesses in his soul” (Prov. XXVI), that is, in the devil’s.

Again, seven demonstrates the perfection of God’s scourges, as in Leviticus: “The Lord will chastise you sevenfold for your sins” (Lev. XXVI). Moreover, seven and eight bear the figure of the Law and the Gospel; hence it is written in Ecclesiastes: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Eccles. XI). Similarly, seven and eight possess the mystery of rest and resurrection. Eight pertains to the day of the Lord’s Resurrection and to the future resurrection of all the saints. Concerning this it is written in the title of the sixth psalm: “For the end, for the eighth.”

[Col. 0491D] Nine is especially suitable for demonstrating the mystery of the Lord’s passion, because the Lord himself, crying out with a loud voice at the ninth hour, gave up his spirit. Likewise, there are said to be nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim. This is signified by the ninety-nine sheep in the Gospel parable, left in the desert or on the mountains. Likewise, nine signifies the imperfection of God’s commandments or the incompleteness of all good things, as it is written in Deuteronomy concerning the bed of Og, king of Bashan, who is a type of the devil, that its length was nine cubits.

The number ten, therefore, sometimes refers to the Decalogue of the Law. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will sing to you on a ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. XXXII). Likewise, by the same number the perfection of works or the fullness of the saints is signified; their figure was represented by the ten curtains that were made in the tabernacle of the testimony at the Lord’s command.

The number eleven bears the figure of transgression of the Law or of sins. The eleventh psalm, which was prefigured in the mystery of this number, also shows this, saying: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. XI). Hence in the tabernacle of the covenant, goats’ hair coverings of the same number are commanded to be made in the likeness of sinners.

Twelve pertains to the apostles, as is demonstrated in the Gospel, where we read: “These are the names of the twelve apostles” (Matt. X). Hence the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Did I not choose you twelve?” (John VI). Likewise, twelve pertains to the mystery of all the saints, who, chosen from the four regions of the world through faith in the Trinity, make of themselves one Church. The twelve precious stones from which the city of the great King is built in the Apocalypse bear the figure of these chosen ones. These are the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, seeing the Lord with understanding.

Thirteen pertains to the fullness of the Law and to faith in the Trinity, as in Ezekiel: “And he measured the height of the gate at thirteen cubits” (Ezek. XL). Fourteen refers to the mystery of the Lord’s birth, as is clearly demonstrated at the beginning of Matthew’s Gospel: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations” (Matt. I). The same fourteen also pertains to the present and future age, as is shown in Leviticus, where it is written concerning a woman who has given birth to a female that she is unclean for two weeks, that is, for the present and future ages.

The number fifteen bears the mystery of the Law and the Gospel, of rest and resurrection. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Paul is said to have stayed with the Apostle Peter for fifteen days.

Sixteen pertains to the number of the sixteen prophets. Seventeen pertains to the mystery of all the prophets, because the ten commandments of the Law operate through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

Twenty pertains to the perfection of works that operate through charity. For the Decalogue of the Law, doubled by the two commandments of love, produces twenty. Hence the two cherubim—which signify the fullness of knowledge—are said to have had twenty cubits in the temple [Col. 0492D].

Twenty-two pertain to the mystery of the divine books according to the letters of the Hebrews. Some say that the number twenty-four pertains typologically to the twenty-four books of the Old Testament, according to the Hebrew tradition. Other Fathers understood the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments under the same number. In the Apocalypse: “And upon thrones were twenty-four elders seated” (Apoc. IV).

Twenty-five, through the five senses of the body multiplied within themselves, attain to the mystery, as is made clear in Ezekiel.

The number twenty-eight pertains to the mystery of the Law and the Gospel. Under the mystery of this number, the curtains of the tabernacle are said in Exodus to have had twenty-eight cubits in length [Col. 0493A].

Thirty pertains to the fruit of the faithful married, as in the Gospel: “And it will yield fruit, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold” (Matt. XIII).

Thirty-two pertains to the mystery of the age in which our Lord dwelt in the flesh. Hence, as some think, the Apostle says: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

The number forty bears the mystery of the Law and the Gospel. Likewise, forty pertains to the mystery of Lent. Hence it is written in the Gospel concerning the Lord: “He was led by the Spirit into the desert for forty days” (Matt. IV). Again, forty contains the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0493B], for it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And he spent time with them for forty days” (Acts I).

Moreover, the number forty is said to figure the whole present time of this age: for there are four regions of the world, and every visible creature consists of four elements. The number ten, perfected for good or evil, when multiplied by four completes forty. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “For forty years I was near this generation” (Ps. XCIV). In the Flood, the Lord rained upon the earth for as many days and nights according to this number; and in the prophet Jonah it is written: “After forty days Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III). Historically, this did not happen in that city [Col. 0493C]; but in the world, of which that city was a figure, it will be fulfilled.

Forty also pertains to the number of encampments in the wilderness, or to the number of generations from Abraham to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Fifty pertains to Pentecost or to the coming of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled” (Acts II). Likewise, fifty pertains to the forgiveness of sins; in the mystery of this number the fiftieth psalm was placed.

The number sixty pertains to the mystery of all the perfect. Hence he says in the Song of Songs: “Behold, Solomon’s bed”—that is, Christ’s Church—“sixty mighty men surround it, from the mightiest of Israel” (Song III). Likewise, sixty is assigned to the fruit of widows or of those who practice continence [Col. 0493D]. Hence we read in the Gospel: “And it will yield fruit, another sixtyfold” (Matt. XIII).

Seventy is said to pertain to the mystery of the ancient fathers. As their figure, Solomon is said to have chosen seventy thousand laborers for the construction of the temple, who carried materials on their shoulders. Seventy and eighty together pertain to the figure of the Law and the Gospel, as it is written in the psalm: “The days of our years are seventy years; and if by reason of strength, eighty years” (Ps. LXXXIX).

Seventy-two pertains to the number of the elders of Moses and of the disciples whom the Lord chose for the preaching of the Gospel.

Seventy-five pertains to the number of the souls who are said in the Acts of the Apostles to have gone down with Jacob into Egypt [Col. 0494A].

Eighty pertains to the souls of certain Christians who cling to the Lord by faith alone and not by works. Concerning them it is written in the Song of Songs: “There are seventy queens”—that is, the souls of the perfect—“and eighty concubines” (Song VI).

One hundred pertains to the fruit of martyrs or virgins, as in the Gospel: “And it will yield fruit, another a hundredfold,” etc. (Matt. XIII).

The number one hundred twenty shows the perfection of the Law and the Gospel through a figure. Hence Moses the lawgiver is described as being one hundred twenty years old; and on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit descended upon one hundred twenty believing souls who had gathered in the upper room of Zion. We also read that before the Flood one hundred twenty years were allotted to human beings for repentance. The height of Solomon’s temple was one hundred twenty cubits. This fact—that the entire height of the temple was one hundred twenty cubits—refers to the same mystery: the primitive Church in Jerusalem, on account of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men.

Thus, as the natural progression of number advances from one through twelve, and the sums of all the terms are collected together, they amount to one hundred twenty. For fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, is sometimes customarily referred to as signifying the future life, which is now enacted in the Sabbath-rest of the faithful souls; but it will be perfected at the end of the age through the resurrection of immortal bodies.

The number one hundred fifty-four pertains to the mystery of the elect. In their figure, the fish of this number are reported in the Gospel to have been caught by the Apostles after the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 0494C].

Three hundred pertains to the number of the perfect, who, triumphing over the world through the cross of Jesus, carry away the victory. In their likeness Gideon is written to have chosen fighters of the same number in the Book of Judges (Judg. VII).

Five hundred, as some think, pertains in its mystery to the five ages of the world. When these had passed, the Savior deigned to visit the world. As his type, Noah, when he was five hundred years old, divinely inspired, prepared the ark for the salvation of his household.

The number one thousand signifies the perfection of blessedness. Hence it is read in the Song of Songs: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one, and in it he has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit” (Song VIII). The vineyard, that is, the Church, abundant in the fruit of faith, belonged to the peaceful one, that is, to the Lord Christ, who entrusted it to keepers, namely, the prophets, apostles, and angelic dignities. For its fruit the man himself brings a thousand silver pieces, that is, the perfection of recompense.

One thousand two hundred bear the figure of apostolic teachers, who, abandoning everything in the world, do not cease to labor in the word of preaching. They are given a twofold reward, which is signified by the two hundred. Concerning them it is written: “A thousand are yours, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who guard its fruits” (Song VIII).

The number seven thousand pertains to the mystery of all the elect, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, are gathered through the week of this world into the kingdoms of heaven [Col. 0495A]. Concerning this it is said in the Book of Kings: “I have left seven thousand men for myself” (III Kings XIX).

Six hundred fifty thousand pertains to the mystery of the children of Israel who went out from Egypt, as in Exodus.

The number ten thousand pertains to the Decalogue of the Law, as in the Gospel: “And one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents” (Matt. XVIII).

One hundred forty-four thousand pertains to the mystery of the elect who, as some hold, will believe in Christ from among the Jews at the end of the world (see above).

Again, one hundred forty-four thousand pertains to the mystery of all virgins, concerning whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “And no one could sing that song except those one hundred forty-four thousand” (Apoc. XIV); and shortly afterward: “For they are virgins, and no falsehood was found in their mouth” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV. On Music and Its Parts

Music is the skill of modulation, consisting in sound and song; and it is called *musica* by derivation from the Muses. The Muses, moreover, were called *apo tou mosthai*—that is, “from seeking”—because, as the ancients wished, through them the power of song and the modulation of the voice were sought. Their sound proceeds from a perceptible thing, passes away into past time, and is impressed upon the memory. Hence poets invented the story that the Muses were daughters of Jupiter and Memory; for unless sounds are retained in human memory, they perish, since they cannot be written down.

Moses said that Jubal, who belonged to the line of Cain before the Flood, was the discoverer of the art of music. The Greeks, however, say that Pythagoras discovered the beginnings of this art from the sound of hammers and the extension of struck strings [Col. 0495C]. Others relate that Linus of Thebes, Zethus, and Amphion were the first to become distinguished in the art of music. After them this discipline was gradually developed, especially, and increased in many ways; and it was considered just as disgraceful to be ignorant of it as to be ignorant of letters.

It was introduced not only into sacred rites but also into all solemn occasions and every joyful or sorrowful circumstance. For just as hymns were sung in divine worship, so at weddings hymenaeal songs, and at funerals dirges and laments, were sung to the accompaniment of flutes. At banquets, lyre or cithara was passed around, and a convivial kind of songs was arranged for each of those reclining at table.

Thus no discipline can be perfect without music, for nothing exists without it. Indeed, the world itself is said to have been composed according to a certain harmony of sounds [Col. 0495D], and heaven itself revolves under the modulation of harmony. Music moves the emotions and provokes the senses into different dispositions. In battles too, the concert of trumpets inflames the fighters; and the more vehement the blast, the stronger the spirit becomes for combat. Indeed, song also encourages the rowers. Music soothes the mind for enduring every kind of labor, and the modulation of the voice consoles the fatigue of individual tasks. Music also calms agitated spirits, as we read concerning David (I Kings XVI), who by the art of modulation rescued Saul from an unclean spirit. Music even summons beasts, as well as serpents, birds, and dolphins, to listen to its modulation.

But whatever we say, or whatever moves us inwardly through the pulsations of our veins, is shown to be joined to the powers of harmony through musical rhythms [Col. 0496A].

The parts of music are three: harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. Harmonic music is that which distinguishes [discerns] the high and the low in sounds. Rhythmic music is that which examines the movement of words, whether the sound coheres well or badly. Metric music is that which recognizes the measure of different meters by a dependable method—for example, the heroic, iambic, elegiac, and so forth.

Every sound, however, which is the material of songs, is by nature threefold. The first is harmonic, which consists of the singing of voices; the second is organic, which consists of breath; the third is rhythmic, which receives numerical patterns through the striking of the fingers. For sound is produced either by the voice, as through the throat; or by breath, as through a trumpet or flute; or by striking, as through a cithara or anything else that becomes melodious when struck.

The first division of music, which is called harmonic—that is, modulation—pertains to comic actors, tragic actors, choruses, or all who sing with their own voice. It produces movement from soul and body, and from movement it produces sound; from this is gathered the music that in a human being is called the voice.

The voice is air struck by the breath, from which words are named; properly speaking, it is the voice of human beings or of irrational creatures and animals. In other cases, sound is abusively, not properly, called “voice,” as in the verse:

> The voice of the trumpet roared, and the voices were broken against the shores.

A voice is perfect when it is high, sweet, and clear: high, so that it may rise aloft; clear, so that it may fill the ears [Col. 0496C]; sweet, so that it may charm the minds of the hearers. If any of these qualities is lacking, the voice will not be perfect.

The second division is organic, consisting of those things which, when filled by breath blown through them, are animated into vocal sound: such as trumpets, reeds, pipes, organs, pandora, and similar instruments.

The third division is rhythmic, pertaining to strings and striking, to which are assigned the various kinds of citharas. The tympanum also, the cymbal, the sistrum, bronze and silver castanets, and other objects which, struck with metallic rigidity, return a ringing sound with sweetness, belong here, along with things of this kind.

“Song” signifies spiritual knowledge, as in the psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. XXXII). To psalm is to practice a good work. “Song” refers to the contemplative life; “to psalm” refers to the active life, as above.

Jubilation is a cry expressed with greater spiritual fervor, or an ineffable joy that the human tongue cannot fully express, as in the psalm: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

First of all, I shall come to the sounds of the organ—for it is reckoned greater than all these kinds in sound and extraordinary power. It is hollow and joined together from two elephant hides, and, driven by the bellows of twelve smiths, it produces an immense sound like thunder through twelve bronze pipes, so that it is unquestionably heard distinctly for a thousand paces, or even farther. This is confirmed by the accounts of the Hebrews concerning the organs whose sound is heard from Jerusalem as far as the Mount of Olives, and beyond [Col. 0497A].

Many say that there are two kinds of organ. The first is the one we have described; the other is the one which the prophet placed before the Israelite exile in Babylon and which is suddenly written about in these words: “By the rivers of Babylon,” etc. (Ps. CXXXVI). This whole passage signifies the Gospel of Christ figuratively and spiritually. For that organ too is joined together from two skins—that is, from the harshness of the two laws—and through the twelve bellows of the smiths, that is, through the patriarchs and prophets, it emits an immense sound through twelve bronze pipes, that is, through the Apostles, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII), that is, the voice of the Gospel throughout the whole world, as it is written: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI).

For through a thousand paces—that is, through the perfect number ten, the number of the words of the Law—its sound is fulfilled [Col. 0497B]. In the willows, that is, through the labor of each teacher and through the movement of his lips, the Gospel is preached.

Likewise, the organ signifies a human being or the Lord’s body, as in the psalm: “Praise him with strings and organ” (Ps. CL). In another sense it signifies the empty joy of the wicked, as in Job: “They hold the tympanum and cithara, and rejoice at the sound of the organ” (Job XXI).

The trumpet, therefore, concerning which it is written in Daniel: “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, flute, cithara,” etc. (Dan. III), is made in various figures and forms. For one kind is the trumpet of gathering the people, another of recruitment, another of victory, another of pursuing enemies, another of closing off cities, and so forth.

The trumpet of gathering, according to those most knowledgeable about such matters, is understood in this way: through three bronze pipes rolled together at the head, by means of four bronze sound-conduits, which produce fourfold sounds through a bronze foundation, it emits an exceedingly loud and powerful bellowing [Col. 0497C]. Thus the Gospel, in the threefold confession of the three persons of the Holy Trinity, is divinely inspired in the narrow head—that is, in Christ’s birth—and through the four bronze sound-conduits, that is, through the four Evangelists, and through the bronze foundation, namely, the stability of faith and works, it sends forth throughout the whole world a voice with an immense cry, as though in the manner of a trumpet of gathering.

Concerning the flute it is related that it is a square, hollow, and very broad bronze vessel, in the shape of a crown, with a bronze and iron pipe joined to it, which is fastened at its upper end to a tall and beautifully formed wooden structure. On each side, twelve bronze vessels hang on chains, with twelve pipes placed in the middle [Col. 0497D]. Thus three vessels are fashioned on each side around the circumference. When the first vessel is set in motion, and the pipes of the twelve vessels placed in the middle are set in motion, they produce together a great cry and an exceedingly loud crash.

The *bumbulum*, then, together with its pipes—that is, the teacher in the midst of the Church—is accompanied by the Holy Spirit, who speaks within it. It is fastened to a tall tree, that is, to Christ, whom the wise compare to the tree of life; it hangs upon a chain, that is, upon faith, and does not join itself to the earth, that is, to carnal works. The twelve Apostles are the pipes, that is, the divine utterances.

The cithara, concerning which it is written in the Forty-Second Psalm, “I will confess to you upon the cithara, O God, my God,” is an instrument especially customary among the Hebrews. It is constructed with twenty-four strings in the shape of the letter delta—as the most expert authorities transmit—and by the fingers of Pindar it is set in motion with varied sounds and ringing performances in different modes. The cithara of which we are speaking spiritually represents the Church. With the teachings of the twenty-four elders, and having a threefold form in the shape of the letter delta, it signifies faith in the Holy Trinity; and by the hands of the apostolic order, which is its preacher, it is set in motion in diverse melodies of the Old and New Testament—differently in the letter and differently in the figurative meaning.

The psalterium, called in Hebrew *nablum*, in Greek *psalterion*, and in Latin “the instrument of praise,” is mentioned in the Fifty-Fourth Psalm: “Awake, psalterium and cithara.” It is not shaped like a cithara, but like a square shield, with ten strings, as it is written: “Upon a psalterium of ten strings I will sing to you” (Ps. CXLIII). Its strings are stretched from one side to the other, so that, by the gesture of the hand that sets it in motion from below upward, they signify the psalterium rising from the underworld to the kingdom of heaven. The instrument is commonly called a song and is named from *psallere*, “to pluck”; the chorus responds to its sound in harmony.

It resembles the barbarian cithara, as some maintain, in the shape of the letter delta. The difference between the psalterium and the cithara is that the psalterium has above it the hollow wood from which the sound is returned, while the strings extend downward and are sounded from above. The cithara, however, has the hollow part of the wood below. The Hebrews used a ten-stringed psalterium because of the number of the Ten Commandments of the Law.

The cithara signifies a devout breast, in which virtues—spiritual goods—are present like strings, as in the Psalm: “Awake, psalterium and cithara” (Ps. CVII), that is, works together with faith. It is also understood negatively, as in Isaiah: “Cithara and lyre and tambourine and wine are in your feasts” (Isa. V); this designates the luxury of those devoted to pleasure. The psalterium signifies good works, as in the Psalm: “A pleasant psalterium with the cithara” (Ps. XVIII). Likewise, the ten-stringed psalterium signifies the performance of the ten commandments of the Law, as in the Psalm: “Sing to him upon the psalterium of ten strings” (Ps. CXLIII). Again, in the same place: “Upon the ten-stringed psalterium,” he says, “with song and cithara” (Ps. CXCI), that is, with understanding and faith.

Concerning the trumpet, the psalterium, and the cithara it is written in the Psalm: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psalterium and cithara” (Ps. CL). These musical instruments are arranged in a meaningful order: let the trumpet resound to the King, let the psalterium sing to God, and let the cithara, together with the others, sing to the Bridegroom. It is evident that these instruments are not literally present there; rather, all these things are clearly to be referred through mystical allusions to Christ the Lord, who is King and God and the Bridegroom of the holy Church.

Among the most learned Hebrews, the sambuca is an unknown instrument. In ancient times, however, it is reported to have existed among the Chaldaeans, as it is written: “When you hear the sound of the trumpet, the pipe, the cithara, the sambuca, and so forth” (Dan. III). Among the Hebrews, the trumpet is called *bucin*; then, by diminution, *bucina*. Among the Hebrews, *sambuca* is interpreted as “sun,” as it is written: “Samson—their sun.” It is therefore called *sambuca* among them because many think it is the bark of some tree, made sonorous by an application of wax and honey, and capable of being moved like a trumpet from a tree branch. It is accordingly called *sambuca* because it can be made only during the summer and can last until the time of cold weather. For, in accordance with ordinary usage, it dries out. It represents those who praise the Lord in their prosperity but cannot praise him in the cold season—that is, in a time of tribulation or persecution—because of the infidelity of their lives and the abundance of their riches.

The lyre is called *lyra* from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ λύρειν, “from producing a variety of sounds,” because it produces different tones. They say that the lyre was first invented by Mercury in the following manner. When the Nile, receding into its channels, had left various animals scattered across the fields, a tortoise was also left behind. After it had decayed and its sinews remained stretched within the shell, Mercury struck it, and it produced a sound. In imitation of it Mercury made a lyre and handed it over to Orpheus, who was especially devoted to this art. Hence it is believed that by the same art he applied not only wild beasts but also rocks and forests to the modulation of song. Because of their love of study and praise of song, musicians invented the fiction that this instrument had even been placed among the stars in the fabrications of their myths.

Mystically, the lyre signifies the exultation of the saints. Thus it is read in Chronicles: “With lyres and nabla” (1 Chron. XV); and it is understood negatively, as in Amos: “I will not hear the songs of your lyre” (Amos V).

The tambourine is a hide or skin stretched over wood on one side. It is the middle part of a *symphonia*, resembling a sieve; it is called a tambourine because it is in the middle. Hence the central pearl is also called a tambourine. Like a *symphonia*, it too is struck with a rod.

The tambourine should be explained in a few words, since it is a small object and can be carried in a woman’s hand, as it is written in Exodus: “Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand” (Exod. XV). It is also a trumpet with a single pipe at its narrow head through which one blows. Thus, too, the small amount of knowledge of the Old Law was formerly in the hand of the Jewish synagogue.

The tambourine also signifies a body made lean by fasting, as in the Psalm: “Praise him with tambourine and chorus” (Ps. CL). The chorus likewise is a simple skin with two bronze pipes: one blows through the first, and through the second the voice is emitted. It represents the former people, who had received a narrow understanding of the Law and, through the narrowness of their will to preach, proclaimed all things weakly.

If, however, we carefully and wisely contemplate earthly things, they are to be understood spiritually and mystically. In another sense, the chorus is the harmony of charity, as in the same passage: “Praise him with tambourine and chorus” (ibid.); and it is understood in another sense in Jeremiah: “Our chorus has been turned into mourning” (Lam. V); and elsewhere: “My organ into the voice of those who weep” (Job XXX).

Cymbals are certain basins which, when struck against one another, touch each other and produce a sound. They are called cymbals because they are struck together with dancing movements. For when the Greeks say *cymbala ballematica*, they mean dancing cymbals. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals” (Ps. CL).

We ought to understand the well-sounding cymbals as our lips; they are rightly placed among the musical instruments because they bear a certain resemblance to cymbals, and through them the human voice is demonstrably able to produce the sweetest harmony. Harmony is the joining together of diverse things brought into a single concord; this also occurs in the human voice when the individual durations and syllables are brought into one concord of sound.

The sistrum is named after its female inventor. Isis, queen of the Egyptians, is said to have invented this kind of instrument. Juvenal writes:

> “May Isis strike my eyes with her angry sistrum.”

Women therefore also strike it, because a woman was the inventor of this kind. Hence among the Amazons the sistrum was the instrument by which the army of women was summoned to war.

The little bell takes its name from the sound of the voice, just as do the clapping of hands and the creaking of doors.

The *symphonia* is commonly called a hollow piece of wood with a skin stretched over both sides; musicians strike it here and there with rods, and from the concord of high and low it produces the sweetest song.

# CHAPTER V. On Medicine

Medicine is that which either preserves or restores the health of the body; its subject matter concerns diseases and wounds. To it belong not only those things supplied by the art practiced by those properly called physicians, but also food and drink, clothing and covering—in short, every defense and protection by which a healthy body is preserved against external blows and accidents.

The name *medicine* is thought to have been derived from *modus*, that is, “moderation.” For through it nature is greatly distressed, but rejoices in moderation. Hence those who drink potions and antidotes either too abundantly or too frequently are afflicted. Every excess brings not health but danger.

Among the Greeks, Apollo is said to have been the founder and discoverer of the medical art; his son Aesculapius enlarged it through reputation and practice. But after Aesculapius perished by a stroke of lightning, the practice of healing is said to have been forbidden, and the art failed together with its author. It remained hidden for nearly five hundred years, until the time of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. Then Hippocrates, born on the island of Cos to Asclepius as father, brought it back into the light.

Health is the integrity of the body and the balance of the hot and moist element, which is blood. Hence health is called *sanitas*, as though it were the condition of the blood.

By the general term “diseases” all bodily afflictions are included. The ancients called them *morbi* in order that, through the very name, they might demonstrate the force of death that arises from them. Between health and disease lies treatment; unless treatment corresponds to the disease, it does not lead to health.

All diseases arise from four humors: blood, yellow bile, melancholia, and phlegm. By these the healthy are governed, and by these the sick are harmed. When they grow excessively beyond the course of nature, they produce illnesses. Just as there are four elements, so there are four humors, and each humor imitates its element: blood imitates air, yellow bile fire, melancholia earth, and phlegm water. These four humors, like the elements, preserve our bodies.

Blood takes its name through a Greek etymology because it invigorates, sustains, and gives life. The Greeks called yellow bile *cholera* because it comes to an end within the span of a single day. Hence *cholera*, that is, “little gall,” is so named; it is the discharge of bile, for the Greeks call bile *chole*.

Melancholia is so called because it consists of the dregs of black blood mixed with an abundance of bile. The Greeks call black *melan*, while they call bile *chole*.

In Latin, blood is called *sanguis* because it is sweet; hence people dominated by blood are gentle and agreeable. They called phlegm *phlegma* because it is cold; for the Greeks call coldness *phlegmōn*. From these four humors, as we have said, the healthy are governed and the sick are harmed. When they grow excessively beyond the course of nature, they produce illnesses.

From blood and bile arise acute disorders, which the Greeks call *oxea*. From phlegm and melancholia proceed lingering diseases, which the Greeks call *chronia*. *Oxea* is an acute disease that either passes quickly or kills more rapidly, such as pleurisy or frenzy. For among the Greeks *oxy* means “sharp” and “swift.” *Chronia* is a prolonged disease of the body that persists for a long time, such as gout or consumption (*phthisis*). Among the Greeks, *chronos* means “time.”

Some ailments received their names from their particular causes. Fever is named from heat, for it is an excess of warmth. *Phrenesis* is so called either from the impairment of the mind—for the Greeks call the mind *phrenes*—or because the sick person gnashes his teeth.

The practice of medicine must not be despised, since we read that holy men also used it, and since it is written concerning it in Ecclesiasticus:

> “Honor the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him. For all healing is from God, since the Most High created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not reject it” (Ecclus. XXXVIII).

But, leaving aside what writers of secular literature have composed concerning diseases and the medical art, it is sufficient here to recall what we read in the divine books. For the Law also speaks of various kinds of diseases, and the prophet Isaiah assisted Hezekiah, king of Judah, through medical treatment (Isa. XXXVIII). The Apostle Paul also said that a little wine was beneficial to Timothy (1 Tim. V).

Languor is the disease of vices, as it is read in Exodus: “If you observe my commandments, I will not bring upon you any of the languor that I brought upon Egypt” (Exod. XV).

Infirmity signifies the inability of the mind, as in the Apostle: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV).

Fever is carnal desire, burning insatiably, as the Gospel figuratively describes Peter’s mother-in-law as feverish (Matt. VIII).

The paralytic signifies a soul dissolved by vices and weighed down by sins in the languor of its flesh, as it is said in the Gospel: “Behold, a paralytic was being carried on a bed by four men” (Mark II).

The dropsical person signifies a greedy man. For just as the dropsical person becomes thirstier the more he drinks, so the greedy man, the more money he gathers, breathes more intensely in the heat of avarice.

Leprosy is the false and varied teaching of heretics, or the unbelief of the Jews, or the contamination of sins, as in Leviticus:

> “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: If a man’s flesh and skin has a different color, or a pustule, or something like a shining mark—that is, the sore of leprosy—he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons. When he sees the leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color, it is leprosy, and he shall be separated according to his judgment” (Lev. XIII).

Lepers are heretics who blaspheme the Lord Jesus Christ. Lepers in the beard are heretics who hold perverse opinions concerning the incarnation of the Savior or concerning the holy Apostles. Lepers over the entire body are those who mix their blasphemy, described above, throughout the whole sequence of the Scriptures.

A swollen leprosy signifies inflated pride. A low or subdued leprosy signifies pretense of heart or hidden blasphemy. A red leprosy signifies anger of heart. A white leprosy is hypocrisy.

Leprosy in a house is total unbelief among the people. Leprosy in clothing signifies vices of the flesh. Leprosy in living flesh signifies sins in the soul. Flying leprosy signifies any vice. A flow of seed arising of itself signifies immoderate speech. Nocturnal pollution signifies the hidden thought of sins.

A menstruating woman is the soul polluted by unclean thoughts, as it is said in Jeremiah: “All who seek her will not fail; in her menstruation they will find her” (Jer. II).

A flow of blood is the outpouring of sins.

The weakening of the limbs is the weakening of minds, as it is read in Leviticus:

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons: A man of your seed throughout your families who has a blemish shall not approach the altar or offer bread to his God—if he is blind, lame, has a twisted nose, a broken hand, is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a skin disease, a continuing scab, or is heavy-bodied, and so forth” (Lev. XXI).

A person is called blind when, deprived of the light from above, he has no idea at all where to direct the step of his conduct. Concerning this blindness Malachi says to the priests: “If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is that not evil?” (Mal. I). It is also understood positively in the Gospel: “If you were blind, you would not have sin” (John IX).

A mute is one who does not preach the word of God or sing praise to God. A deaf person is one who refuses to hear the word of God. A person has a severed ear when he does not display obedience to God’s commandments.

A person is bleary-eyed when he possesses intellectual capacity for understanding, but worldly anxiety does not allow him to contemplate things above. A person has a twisted nose when he is not capable of distinguishing good from evil. A person has a severed tongue when he makes no confession of the true faith. A person has a broken hand when he remains idle, deprived of right action.

A person is lame when he sees where the steps of his conduct should lead, but weakness of mind does not allow him to act rightly. It is also understood positively in the Gospel: “Bring in here the poor and the weak” (Luke XIV).

A person is bleary-eyed when earthly desire, weighing him down, does not allow him to lift the eyes of his mind to contemplate heavenly things.

A person has crushed testicles when he does not possess vigorous thoughts against vices. A person is heavy-bodied when a wicked thought continually weighs upon his mind. A person has a scab on his body when the lust of the flesh ravages his mind. A person has a skin disease when avarice rules in his heart. Others have understood this skin disease as the assemblies of heretics.

A person is cut off when, because his own sins demand it, he has been separated from the body of Christ, which is the Church.

Christ is the physician, as in the Gospel: “Those who are healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX).

Resin is heavenly medicine, as Jeremiah says: “Is there no resin in Gilead, that is, in the Church? Or is there no physician there?” (Jer. VIII). Again, in the same book, concerning the soul weakened by the sickness of sins: “Apply resin to its pain, if perhaps it may be healed” (Jer. LI).

Odor is so called from the air. *Thymiama*, a Greek word, means “fragrant”; for *thyme* is a flower that gives off a scent, concerning which Virgil writes: “And they smell of thyme.”

*Incense* is so called because it is consumed by fire while it is offered. It signifies the purity of prayer; hence it is said in the Psalm: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

And in Exodus the Lord says to Moses:

> “Take for yourself aromatics: stacte, onycha, galbanum of good fragrance, and the clearest frankincense. They shall all be of equal weight. You shall make a compound incense, the work of a perfumer, carefully mixed and pure” (Exod. XXX).

We make compound incense from aromatics when we give off fragrance upon the altar of good works through the multiplicity of virtues. It becomes mixed and pure because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good works is offered.

To reduce the aromatics to powder is to wear down the virtues through reflection and examine them carefully. Fragrant incense made from perfumes is a sweet burning that, consumed by coals, sends a most precious smoke upward and delights those who smell it with pleasurable joy. So too the prayer of the blessed, kindled by the fire of charity, is offered before the divine presence; it is raised all the more by the weight of humility and compunction.

The Lord rejoices in virtues as in good fragrances. For that the Lord receives holy prayer as a most fragrant odor is also read in the Apocalypse, where it is said:

> “An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, holding a golden censer, and the smoke of the prayers ascended from the angel’s hand into the presence of the Lord, so that he might give from the prayers of the saints what is before the Lord” (Rev. VIII).

# BOOK NINETEEN

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Cultivation of Fields

Cultivation is the means by which grain or wine is obtained through great labor; it is named from cultivating. For the wealth of the ancients consisted in these two things: feeding well and plowing well.

The cultivation of a field includes burning, plowing, fallowing, burning the stubble, manuring, harrowing, and weeding.

Burning is the fire by which the field expels its useless moisture. Plowing is so called because people first cultivated the earth with bronze before the use of iron had been discovered.

There are therefore two kinds of plowing: spring plowing and autumn plowing. Fallowing is the practice by which, in alternate years, an empty field recovers its strength. Manuring is the sprinkling of fertilizer. Manure is so called either because it is spread over the fields or because what overflows in the city must be wiped away, since it is filthy.

*Fimus* is also the material thrown over fields. It is called *fimus* because it becomes *mus*, that is, manure, commonly called fertilizer, because through its nourishment it makes plants joyful and renders the fields rich and fertile.

Harrowing occurs when, after sowing, farmers release the oxen and break up the large clods with hoes. It is called *occatio*, as though it were “blinding,” because it covers the seeds. Thus to harrow is to cover seeds, vines, or trees with earth.
