Weeding is pulling plants from the earth. For *rus* means “earth.” A furrow is named from the sun because, once cut open, it receives the sun. *Veruactum* is so called as though it were *vere actum*, “done in spring,” that is, plowed in spring.

The first plowing is the opening of the soil, when the field is still hard. Sowing is so called as though it were “the action of the seed,” or “the action of the sower.” To sow is so called because this should be done under a clear sky, not during rains. Hence there is also Virgil’s saying: “Plow naked; sow naked.”

The harvest is named from *metere*, “to reap,” that is, “to cut back.” A crop is named from the seed that we cast, or from cutting.

Spiritually, in the sacred Scriptures, fields signify the hearts of believers, in which the fruits of virtues germinate. Hence the Apostle says to believers: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. III).

God is the farmer, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer” (John XV). The Apostles, or the other preachers, are also farmers. The tenants signify the saints. Hence he says in the Gospel: “He will destroy the wicked miserably, and will lease his vineyard to other tenants” (Matt. XXI).

The laborers are the Apostles or the other preachers. It is read in the Gospel: “Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. IX). In another sense, laborers are heretics, as the Apostle says: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil laborers, beware of mutilation” (Phil. III).

Fields are therefore burned with fire so that all useless moisture may be expelled, when through zeal for God every excess of vices is burned away from the hearts of the elect, lest anything harmful germinate there.

Fields are plowed when, through the preaching of teachers, crowds of believers are cultivated and prepared to receive the seed, for the seed is the word of God, as the Lord himself demonstrates in the Gospel (Luke VIII).

Manure is therefore cast upon the field so that it may bear better fruit, because through remembrance of sins the faithful are summoned to repentance, so that the shoot of right faith and the fruit of good works may grow more vigorously in the furrows of righteousness.

The furrows are the hearts of the faithful, as in the Psalm: “Water its furrows” (Ps. LXIV); and in Job: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it” (Job XXXI).

The seed is divine preaching, as in the Gospel: “The one who sows went out to sow his seed” (Matt. XIII). The seed is also the preaching of heretics, watered with the water of foolishness, as in the Pentateuch: “Every seed upon which water has fallen shall be unclean” (Lev. XI).

The plowman is the cross, or the ministry of preaching, or the beginning of good works, as in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX).

To plow is to exercise the ministry of preaching. Hence it is read in the Book of Kings: “And he himself was one of the twelve plowmen” (3 Kings XIX).

To sow is to scatter the word of preaching in the hearts of the faithful, as in the prophet: “And they will sow fields” (Ps. CVI).

The crops are the peoples of the faithful, whom spiritual farmers—that is, holy teachers—cleanse and purge, lest anything useless or poisonous grow there.

The harvest is the abundance or multitude of the faithful, as the Lord says to the Apostles in the Gospel: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for harvest” (John IV; Matt. XIII).

In another sense, the harvest is the consummation of the age; the harvesters are the angels of God; the wheat is the elect, and the weeds are the reprobate.

The crops are therefore gathered and bound into sheaves so that they may be placed in the Lord’s granary, when holy men, bearing sheaves of virtues, are received into the heavenly dwelling. Thus it is said in the Psalm: “Those who come shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV), that is, reaping the reward of good works.

The weeds signify scandals or those who live wickedly, as it is written in the Gospel: “The enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat” (Matt. XIII); and shortly afterward: “Bind the weeds into bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my granary” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER II. On Grains

Properly speaking, grains are those that have ears; the remaining produce is called crops.

Spiritually, grain signifies either our Redeemer himself, who says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the ground dies, it remains alone” (John XII), or holy men, who are members of his body.

Grain also signifies the word of preaching, as Solomon says: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI).

Wheat likewise signifies the elect, who belong to the Lord’s granary, as we have shown above.

Rye is a kind of wheat, named from sowing; for its form is especially prominent in bread.

Barley is so called either because it becomes dry before the other kinds of grain or because its ear has rows. It signifies the letter of the Old Law, which was given as food to the carnal Jews. Hence it is read in the Gospel that the Lord satisfied five thousand people with five barley loaves (John VI).

Again, it is written in Genesis concerning Isaac: “Isaac sowed and found a hundredfold of barley in that year” (Gen. XXVI).

The ear is so called because it dries first. The stalk is the very stem of the ear, which grows from the roots; it is called *culmus* as though it were *calamus*, “a reed.”

The husk is the case of the grain, in which the kernel is kept inside. Furnished with a protective barrier over the ear, it prevents the fruit of the ear from being stripped by the bites of small birds or crushed underfoot. It also signifies the carnal observance of the Old Law, in which the marrow of spiritual meaning lies hidden.

The beginnings of ears signify the beginning of faith or the beginning of good works, as it is said in Job concerning heretics: “They took away the ears from the hungry” (Job XXIV).

Stubble signifies those who are dry with respect to faith, or empty people, as in the Apostle: “Wood, hay, stubble” (1 Cor. III); and in the prophet: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest” (Mic. VII), that is, I have found no fruit of good works.

Stubble and chaff signify sinners who are fit for eternal fire. Hence it is written: “But he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III). It is also written in Jeremiah: “What has chaff to do with wheat? says the Lord” (Jer. XXIII).

Heaps signify the gathering of the faithful into the threshing floor of the Church, or the perfected preaching of the saints, as it is said in Job concerning heretics: “They sat in the shade among their heaps” (Job XXIV).

## CHAPTER III. On Legumes

Legumes are named from *legere*, “to gather,” as though they were “selected”; for the ancients gathered whatever was best. Alternatively, they are so called because they are gathered by hand and do not require cutting.

There are many kinds of legumes, among which beans, lentils, peas, faselus beans, chickpeas, and lupins appear more agreeable for human use.

Mystically, legumes can signify restraint of lust and the mortification of the body. Hence in the prophet Daniel (Dan. I), Daniel himself and the three youths with him, despising royal delicacies, desire to eat legumes. By crushing carnal desires, they rightly may be called men devoted to spiritual desires.

## CHAPTER IV. On Vines
Noah first established the planting of the vine, while the age was still primitive. Among the Greeks, however, Liber is known as the discoverer of the vine; hence the pagans also wished to regard him as a god after his death. *Vitis* (“vine”) is so called because it has the power of taking root quickly. Others think that vines are so called because they entwine with one another by means of tendrils and, creeping over neighboring trees, bind themselves to them; for their nature is flexible, so that, like arms, they clasp whatever they have seized. *Labrusca* is a wild vine that grows along the edges of the earth; hence it is called *labrusca*, from the lips and extremities of the earth. The tips of vines and shrubs are called *flagella* (“lashes”), because they are agitated by the wind. A *palmes* is the soft substance of the vine, which, sent out through young branches, bears fruit. *Corymbi* are rings that bind and clasp whatever is nearest, lest the vine shoots, loosened too far, be scattered by blasts of wind. *Uvae* (“grapes”) are so called because inwardly they are full of moisture, juice, and richness. For that is *humidum* which has moisture externally, and *uvidum* which has it internally, as in a grape berry or cluster. A *racemus* is part of a cluster, and *botryo* is Greek. [Col. 0506D–0507A]

Mystically, the vineyard may be understood as the Church or the people of Israel. Concerning the latter it is written in Isaiah:

> A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill; he fenced it, cleared it of stones, planted it with a choice vine, built a tower in its midst, constructed a winepress in it, and expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes, and so forth (Isa. V).

That the people of Israel are called God’s vineyard is also shown at the end of this song, where we read:

> The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved plant.

And in Psalm 79:

> You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.

In the Gospel also, the Lord constructed a parable in almost the same words with which the prophet now speaks (Matt. XXI):

> There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a fence, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, and leased it to cultivators, and so forth.

And in Jeremiah we read:

> I planted you as a wholly true, fruitful vine. How have you turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine? (Jer. II.)

Thus Jerusalem, as we have said, is mourned, and its ruin is sung in prophetic language.

For the Church and for the people formerly belonging to the nations, another song was composed, concerning which we read in the Psalms:

> Sing to the Lord, all the earth; proclaim his salvation from day to day; proclaim his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples (Ps. XCV).

By a metaphor, as we have said, he describes the Jewish people as a vineyard, which he fenced with the aid of angels and from which he removed stones—whether idols or everything else that could impede the worship of God. He planted it as a *sorech* vine, which Symmachus alone interpreted as “chosen.” He also built a tower in its midst, namely, the temple in the middle of the city, and constructed a winepress in it, which some think signifies the altar. Thus it is said in Isaiah’s song:

> And I dug a winepress in it (Isa. V).

The winepress is the tribulation that is to come, as in the Apocalypse:

> He himself trod the winepress of the wine of the wrath of the fury of the Lord (Apoc. XIX).

For just as all grapes are brought together and trodden in the winepress so that wine may be pressed from them, so the altar receives the fruits of the whole people and consumes the sacrificed victims, according to what is read concerning Benjamin:

> Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats, and in the evening he gives food (Gen. XLIX).

Everything that is said about the vineyard can also be applied to the state of the human soul, which, planted by God for good, has produced not grapes but wild grapes, and afterward has been handed over to beasts to be trampled, since it has not received the rain of divine teaching because it despised what had gone before.

The following practices especially apply to vines: digging around them, pruning, propagation, and digging. To *oblaqueare* is to open the earth around the root and make it like a basin. To *putare* is to cut away the unnecessary rod from the vine, whose shoots grow luxuriantly; for *putare* means “to cleanse,” that is, “to cut off.” *Traducere* means “to lead across” or “to transfer.” To propagate is to lay down a vine shoot buried in the earth and, as it were, plant it farther along. Hence *propagines* (“propagated shoots”) are named from *propagare* and *protendere* (“to extend”). To dig is, as it were, to make a pit and to foster it.

If anyone considers all these things carefully, he will be able to find them spiritually applied to the instruction of the Church. Thus the bride says in the Song of Songs:

> The flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come (Song II),

that is, so that, once the useless shoots of empty religion have been cut away, the future fruit of faith may be prepared.

Allegorically, the vine signifies Christ, who says in the Gospel:

> I am the true vine (John XV).

The meaning of vineyard or vine is also transferred to another sense, as in the song of Deuteronomy:

> Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot is from Gomorrah (Deut. XXXII).

The vine shoots are allegorically understood as the Apostles or the saints. Hence the Lord says to the Apostles:

> I am the true vine, and you are the vine shoots, and so forth (John XV).

Likewise, the grape signifies the fruit of righteousness; conversely, it is read in another sense:

> Their grape is a grape of gall; their cluster is bitterness in them (Deut. XXXII).

Elsewhere the cluster signifies the Church or the body of the Lord. Hence it is written in the Book of Numbers (Num. XIII) that two men carried a cluster on a pole from the promised land, because the two orders of preachers bring the incarnation of Christ to believers by voice and word: what the prophets announced as future, the Apostles testify has already come.

The vintage is mystically understood as the consummation of the age, or as vengeance upon the people. Hence it is read in the Psalm:

> All who pass along the way gather it as a vintage (Ps. LXXIX);

and Joel says:

> Send out the sickles and harvest the vineyard of the earth, for its grapes are ripe (Joel III). [Col. 0508B–C]

The vineyard is the Church, as it is said in the Song of Songs:

> There was a vineyard belonging to the Peaceful One, and he entrusted it to guardians (Song VIII),

that is, to the Apostles.

The vineyard also signifies the Jewish people, as in the Psalter:

> You brought a vineyard out of Egypt (Ps. LXXIX).

The vineyard signifies the people of the faithful, as in Solomon:

> Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards (Song II).

Vineyards signify actions of good works, as in the prophet:

> They shall plant vineyards (Isa. LXV).

In another sense, as it is read in Solomon:

> I passed by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, nettles had filled everything (Prov. XXIV).

The winepress, as we said above, signifies the altar, because offerings are brought there as fruits. In another sense, the winepress signifies the pressure of tribulations, in which the faithful are tested. Hence it is written in the title of certain psalms:

> For the end, concerning the winepresses.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Trees

The name of trees, as also of grasses, is believed to have been derived from *arva* (“fields”), because they cling to the earth with roots fixed in it. The two are nearly alike for this reason: one arises from the other. For when you cast seed into the earth, grass first springs up; then, nourished, it rises into a tree, and within a short time you receive a young tree from what you had seen as grass.

An *arbustum* is a young and tender tree into which grafting can be made; it is called *arbustum*, as if from *arboris hasta* (“the spear of a tree”). Others take *arbustum* to mean a place where trees are found, like *salictum* (“a willow grove”); likewise, *virectum* is a place where young green shrubs grow. [Col. 0508D–0509A]

A tree signifies the human race, as in the saying:

> A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard (Luke XIII; Matt. VII, XII).

A good tree is also called a good man, and a bad tree a bad man. Some think that in this passage the tree should be understood more as the will of a person than as the person himself, and the good fruit as good works, but the bad fruit as evil works.

The root mystically signifies origin. Hence it is written in the Apostle:

> If the root is holy, so are the branches (Rom. XI).

Again, concerning the sinner it is said:

> God will destroy you forever; he will tear you up and carry you away from your tent, and your root from the land of the living (Ps. LI).

Branches express the offshoot of anything, transferred either to a good or to an evil sense. In a good sense, there is the Gospel passage concerning the mustard seed, of which the Lord says:

> It becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches (Matt. XIII).

In another sense it is written in Daniel:

> Cut down the tree and its branches (Dan. IV).

And in Solomon:

> Let the imperfect branches be cut off (Wis. IV).

A leaf signifies the word of teaching. Hence it is written in the Psalm concerning that wondrous tree planted beside streams of water, which gives its fruit in its season and whose leaf does not fall (Ps. I). This tree signifies our Lord Jesus Christ because of the suffering of the cross. The fruit of his virtues is food for believers, and his leaves do not fall because under no circumstance do his words depart from the truth.

These are the spiritual waters; these are the healing leaves, concerning which blessed John says in the Apocalypse:

> He showed me a river of the water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, through the middle of its street. On either side of the river was the tree of life, producing fruit twelve times, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of that tree were appointed for the healing of the nations (Apoc. XXII).

A flower mystically signifies Christ, who says in the Song of Songs:

> I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys (Song II).

Flowers signify the growth of good conduct, as in the Song of Songs:

> The flowers have appeared on the earth (ibid.),

that is, the beginnings of faith and righteousness have blossomed in the world as the Church of Christ has grown.

A flower also signifies the glory of this present age. In Isaiah:

> All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass (Isa. XL).

Apples signify the fruits of the saints in their virtues, as in the Song of Songs:

> Let him eat the fruit of his apples (Song IV).

Again, the bride says to the Bridegroom:

> All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you (Song VII).

The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises of the New and Old Testaments. It is clear that the Church refers all of these to the grace of Christ.

Again, apples signify the sweetness of sin. Hence it is read in Amos:

> What do you see, Amos? And I said: A hook for apples (Amos VIII),

that is, the punishments of sinners.

Things are called ripe because they are suitable for eating; likewise, things are called unripe because, before they become ripe, they are hard to eat. Allegorically, ripe things are those that are perfect, while unripe things are those recognized to be imperfect.

Forests or wooded places mystically signify the nations, or even sacred Scripture shaded by allegorical testimonies, as in the saying:

> God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shady and dense mountain (Ps. CXXXI).

Concerning this it is written in the Psalm:

> We found it in the fields of the forest.

The fields of the forest indicate the hearts of the Gentiles, which, having been cleansed by the Lord, were opened into the purity of a plain from sins like wild and thorny places.

From these forests two bears emerged—namely, the two kings of the Romans—at the command of the typological Elisha, and, forty-two years after his ascension into heaven, they devoured the Jewish boys. Forests signify the Gentiles, as in the Psalm:

> The boar from the forest destroyed it (Ps. LXXIX).

Dense places—that is, shadowy woodland—signify the hidden places of divine Scripture, as in the Psalm:

> The Lord has revealed the dense places, and in his temple all will speak of his glory (Ps. XXVIII).

The fear of the Lord revealed the dense places when, ignorance having been laid aside, devoted peoples gathered for understanding of the divine law. For this reason they all give glory in his Church, according as each receives the gifts of that sevenfold spirit. For glory, as we have often recalled it being said, is praise produced by the celebration of many.

Again, a wooded place signifies the people of the Church, concerning whom it is written in the prophet:

> Those who dwell in the wilderness shall sleep securely in the wooded places (Ezek. XXXIV).

Again, the southern forest represents the Jewish people. Hence Ezekiel says:

> Thus says the Lord concerning the forest of the southern field: Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree and every dry tree (Ezek. XX).

Trees are called *ligna* because, when burned, they are converted into light; hence *lychnum* (“lamp”), because it gives light.

A little rod is called *hastula* from *tollere* (“to lift” or “take away”). *Fomes* is a little rod struck from trees by cutting; alternatively, it is a charred twig or hollowed wood, taking its name from fungi, because it readily catches fire. Virgil refers to this:

> And he snatched a flame from the tinder.

Trees are found placed both in a good and in an evil sense. In a good sense:

> The fields will rejoice, and all the trees of the forests before the face of the Lord, because he comes (Ps. XCV).

In an evil sense:

> Whoever cuts wood will be endangered by it (Eccl. X),

because whoever is an executor of sins will be assigned to eternal fire.

Some also think that trees signify angels. Thus in the prophet Ezekiel it is said concerning the devil:

> No tree of paradise was made like him (Ezek. XXXI).

And shortly afterward:

> The cedars were not taller than he (ibid.).

The tree signifies Christ or the saints in the Psalm:

> He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water (Ps. I).

And in the Gospel:

> If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry? (Luke XXIII.)

A tree signifies a human being in Ecclesiastes:

> If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north (Eccl. XI),

that is, toward good or toward evil, wherever it falls, there it will remain.

Trees signify the testimonies of the Scriptures in Leviticus:

> The fire on the altar shall always burn, and the priest shall nourish it by placing wood on it every morning, each day (Lev. VI).

Solomon’s saying agrees with this testimony:

> Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow (Eccl. I).

The tree signifies the cross of Christ in the Book of Wisdom:

> Blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes (Wis. XIV).

And in the Psalm:

> The Lord has reigned from the wood (Ps. XCV).

Trees signify sins in Deuteronomy:

> If someone goes with his neighbor innocently into the forest to cut wood (Deut. XIX).

A *torris* is a burned piece of wood, which common people call a *titio*, drawn from the hearth, half-burned and extinguished.

*Quisquiliae* are bits of straw mixed with twigs and dry leaves; they are the refuse of the earth.

Mystically, a *torris* or *titio* signifies vain wisdom, which is opposed to true wisdom. Hence we read in the prophet Isaiah that the Lord said to the prophet himself:

> Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Jasub, who has been left, at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field, and say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and let your heart not be afraid because of the two tails of these smoking firebrands, in the anger of the fury of Rezin the king of Syria and the son of Romelia. For Syria has taken counsel against you for evil, as have Ephraim and the son of Romelia, saying: Let us go up against Judah, stir it up, tear it away to ourselves (Isa. VII).

The two tails of the smoking firebrands, as we said earlier, are secular wisdom and heretical speech, whose end is burning. They took counsel in vain in order to rise up against Judah and, as though against one negligent and asleep, seize him and join him to their errors.

*Caries* (“decay”) is the rotting of wood. This name is so called because it occurs in wood lacking strength. Decay can signify the rottenness of sins. Hence carnal people, consumed by the worms of desire, become unfit for the spiritual building belonging to the city of God. [Col. 0511A–C]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Proper Names of Trees

The palm is so called because it is an ornament of the victorious hand, or because its branches are spread out in the manner of the human palm. It is a tree distinguished by victory, with a tall and beautiful shoot, clothed in enduring foliage and preserving its leaves without any replacement. The Greeks call it *phoenix*, because it lasts a long time, taking its name from that Arabian bird which is said to live for many years. Although it grows in many places, it does not bring its fruit to maturity everywhere; it does so most often in Egypt and Syria. Its fruits are called *dactyli* (“dates”) because of their resemblance to fingers. [Col. 0511C–D]

The palm is also called as though it were *pacis alma* (“nourisher of peace”), since it is the prize for those who win in the contest, as the Apostle says:

> Now I press on toward the palm of the heavenly calling (Phil. III).

Above the earth it is rough and uneven, marked by certain swellings; but when it has risen toward the heights, it is filled with the sweetness of its most delightful fruits and stretches out adorned, as it were, with rays. So the conduct of the righteous in this world is full of harsh labors, but in the heights it is proved most beautiful.

The palm can signify people who are always green with the beauty of virtues and gain victory over all spiritual vices. Hence they receive from the Lord the prize of the eternal crown, concerning which it is written in the Psalm:

> The righteous will flourish like the palm; he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon (Ps. XCI).

And in the Song of Songs the bride says concerning the bridegroom:

> His locks are like raised palms, black as a raven (Song V).

The locks are the companies of saints who cling to God in faithful service; the raised palms are on account of the Lord’s head; the blackness is on account of their contempt among human beings—or the raised palms signify victory, and the blackness, afflictions.

The laurel is named from the word of praise, for with it the heads of victors were crowned amid praises. Among the ancients it was called *laudea*; afterward, with the letter *d* removed and *r* substituted, it was called *laurus*, just as *auriculae* (“little ears”) were initially called *audiculae*, and *medidies* became *meridies* (“midday”). The Greeks call this tree *daphne*, because it never lays aside its greenness; for this reason, in particular, victors were crowned with it. It is also the only tree that is believed not to be struck by the flash of lightning. This tree can fittingly signify the victories and unfading crowns of the martyrs.

The apple is called *malum* by the Greeks because its fruit is the roundest of all fruits; hence these are true *mala*, because they are exceedingly round. *Mala Matiana* (“Matian apples”) are named from the place from which they were first brought. For many trees received their names from the provinces or cities from which they were imported. Virgil shows what is customarily sought from an apple by lovers.

*Cydonian apples* took their name from a town on the island of Crete, concerning which the Greeks commonly say that Cydonia is the mother of the Cretan cities. From its fruit *cydonitum* is made. Wine is also made from it, by which the desires of the sick are deceived; for in appearance, taste, and smell it reproduces the likeness of any old wine.

*Melimelum* (“honey-apple”) is named from its sweetness, either because its fruit has the taste of honey or because it is preserved in honey.

Allegorically, the apple signifies the Lord Christ. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs:

> As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the daughters; beneath his shadow I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my palate (Song II).

That is: just as an apple surpasses the trees of the forest in sight, smell, and taste, so Christ surpasses all those who are called sons of God—though they are sons by grace, while he alone is so by nature. When he who, coming forth, was always sought as present, I rest and remain secure, because he refreshes me with the heavenly sweetness of his grace.

The pomegranate is called *malum Punicum* (“Punic apple”) because its species was brought from the Punic region. It is also called *malumgranatum* (“seeded apple”), because within the roundness of its rind it contains a multitude of seeds.

The Punic apple signifies the Church, or the unity of faith and harmony of peace. As a figure of this, the Israelite scouts in the Book of Numbers (Num. XIII) carried a pomegranate together with a cluster and figs from the promised land. In Exodus, pomegranates are commanded to be joined with golden bells in the priestly vestment.

The pomegranate signifies the assembly of holy and elect men. Hence the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs:

> Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you (Song VI).

The cheeks are the spiritual fathers of the holy Church, remarkable in virtues, venerable in conduct, and unashamed to glory in the cross of Christ. What is seen in her is already very great, but what is not seen is much greater and is reserved for the future.

The pomegranate can also signify the Church gathered from many nations, or possessing diverse graces within herself. Hence concerning her it is written in the Song of Songs:

> Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruit of apples (Song IV).

The fig is called *ficus* in Latin from *fecunditas* (“fertility”), for it is more fruitful than other trees: it produces fruit three or four times each year, and as one fruit ripens another arises. Hence *caricae* (“figs of Caria”) are also named from abundance.

Mystically, the fig signifies the synagogue of the Jews, as in the Gospel:

> The fig tree withered immediately (Matt. XXI).

And in Habakkuk:

> The fig will not bear fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines, and so forth.

The fig of the vineyard, together with the olive, was the synagogue of the Jews when it offered to God the sweetness of good works, the ardor of fervent love, and the richness of a merciful spirit. But this fig tree, when the Lord came to it for the third time—that is, in the giving of the law through Moses, in continual rebuke and exhortation through the Prophets, and in the offering of grace through himself—neglected to bear the fruit of virtue. Therefore, condemned to eternal barrenness, it was delivered over to a curse.

The fig also signifies the ancient law. Hence it is said in the Gospel:

> A certain man planted a vineyard—that is, the Jewish people—and in the vineyard he planted a fig tree (Matt. XXI; Luke XIII).

The leaves of the fig tree are the harshness of the law, or the itching of vices. Hence the passage in Genesis:

> They took fig leaves and made themselves coverings (Gen. III),

that is, girdles for the genitals.

The *caprificus* (“wild fig”) is so called because it tears apart the walls on which it grows; for it breaks through and emerges from the hiding places in which it was conceived. Others think that it is called *caprificus* because the fig tree is made fertile by its agency.

The *morus* (“mulberry”) is so called by the Greeks; the Latins call it *rubus* (“red tree”), because its fruit is red like a shrub. It is a wild tree bearing fruit by which, in the wilderness, the hunger and want of shepherds are relieved. Its leaves, when thrown upon a snake, are said to kill it.

Thus the *rubus*, as some think, is a prefiguration of the Virgin Mary, because from the thorny growth of the human body she brought forth the Savior like a rose—or because it endured the force of the divine brightness without being consumed. Hence it is read in Exodus:

> The Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush; and he saw that the bush was burning but was not consumed (Exod. III).

The *sycomorus*, like the mulberry, has a Greek name. It is called *sycomorus* because its leaves resemble those of the mulberry. The Latins call it *celsa* (“lofty”) because of its height, since it is not short like the mulberry. Others say that it is a wild fig.

Hence the prophet Amos says to Amaziah:

> I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet; but when I was a herdsman and was gathering mulberries, the Lord took me as I followed the flocks (Amos VII).

This means that the Lord took up a humble and rustic shepherd, sent him to his people Israel, and commanded him to leave his land and go to Samaria.

The sycamore also signifies vain knowledge. In Jeremiah:

> Dragons—that is, demons—will dwell with foolish fig trees (Jer. L).

In a good sense, however:

> Zacchaeus climbed into a sycamore tree (Luke XIX).

The walnut is so called because the shade or dripping of its leaves harms other trees. The Latins call it by another name, *juglans*, as if *Jovis glans* (“Jupiter’s acorn”), for this tree was consecrated to Jupiter. Its fruit has such power that, when thrown among suspicious herbs or mushrooms prepared as food, it strikes down, removes, and extinguishes whatever poisonous substance is in them.

In general, *nuces* (“nuts”) are all fruits covered with a harder shell, such as pine nuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, chestnuts, and almonds. Hence they are also called *nuclei* (“kernels”), because they are covered by a hard shell.

By contrast, all soft fruits are called *mala* (“apples”), with an indication of the lands in which they first grew, such as Persian, Punic, Matian, and Cydonian apples, and so forth.

Mystically, the walnut tree signifies the Church or a holy man who bears the sweetness of the fruits of virtues hidden in the heart. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs:

> I went down to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valley (Song VI).

For the garden of nuts is the present Church, where we do not clearly see one another’s consciences; but when the shell of the body has been broken through temptation, the taste of inward sweetness will appear.

The fruits of the valley are the fruit of humility. The holy Church descends through holy teachers in order to see who are advancing toward good fruits and who still need the watering of instruction.

Nuts also signify the incarnation of the Lord the Savior, or, as some think, the mystery of the Holy Trinity. Hence in the Book of Numbers it is written concerning Aaron’s rod:

> And it blossomed with nuts (Num. XVII).

The almond is a Greek name; in Latin it is called *nux longa* (“long nut”). Others call it *nucicla*, as though “little nut.” Concerning it Virgil says:

> When the many nuts clothe themselves in blossom in the forests …

For it is the first of all trees to clothe itself in blossom and anticipates the other young trees in bringing forth fruit.

Hence it signifies the primitive Church, which believed from the Jews. Concerning it Solomon says:

> The almond tree will blossom.

This statement can also be understood otherwise according to allegory. Ecclesiastes says:

> The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper will be scattered, because the human being will go to the house of his eternity (Eccl. XII).

They teach that these expressions signify human limbs: in the blossoming of the almond, gray hair; in the swelling of the locust, the moisture of the feet; and in the scattering of the caper, the cooling of desire. When these things occur to an old man at the final period of life, then he must return to the earth, as it were to the house of his eternity.

We may also rightly understand this house of eternity as that future land concerning which it is written:

> I shall please the Lord in the land of the living (Ps. CXIV).

It is read in Genesis (Gen. XXX) that the patriarch Jacob took green rods of poplar and almond and of plane trees, partly stripped them of their bark, and placed them in the channels where water was poured out before the sheep, so that when the flocks came to drink, they might have the rods before them and conceive at the sight of them.

What does it mean to place green almond and plane-tree rods before the eyes of the flocks, except to offer the lives or teachings of the ancient fathers as examples to the peoples through the sequence of Scripture? Since these are straight according to the test of reason, they are called rods. From some he removes part of the bark, so that in what is stripped the inner whiteness may appear; on others he preserves part of the bark, so that they remain outwardly as they had been. Thus the color of the rods becomes varied, with the bark partly removed and partly retained.

Before the eyes of our consideration, therefore, the teachings of the fathers who preceded us are placed like variegated rods. When we often flee the literal meaning, we remove the bark, as it were; and when we often follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inner whiteness of allegory is revealed; and when the bark of outward understanding is retained, green examples are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed these rods in channels of water, because our Redeemer fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge through which we are inwardly watered. Rams mate with the sheep while gazing upon these rods, because our rational spirits, when fixed upon their meaning, are mingled with each of our actions, so that they produce such offspring of works as the examples of those who preceded us appear in the words of instruction.

The chestnut is called by the Latins by a Greek word; the Greeks call it *castanon*. Its fruit is enclosed in pairs, like testicles, within a husk; when they are expelled, they are as though castrated. As soon as this tree has been cut down, it is accustomed to sprout again like a forest.

This tree can signify the assembly of the continent, which through chastity of body produces many fruits of virtue.

The holm oak is called *ilex* from *electus* (“chosen”), for human beings first chose the fruit of this tree for food. Hence the poet says:

> Mortals first chewed the acorn in their throats.

Before the use of grain, ancient people lived on acorns. The holm oak, however, contains the mystery of the cross of Christ. Hence it is read that Abraham dwelt beside the holm oak of Mamre, because in mystery it prefigured the passion of Christ.

The beech and the *aesculus* are believed to have been called fruit-bearing trees because formerly human beings lived on their fruits, took their food from them, and had nourishment from them. *Aesculus* is named from *esca* (“food”), while *fagus* derives its name from Greek. For *phagein* [φαγεῖν] in Greek means “to eat.” By this fact we are admonished to practice abstinence, so that we may strive rather to be content with a frugal diet than eagerly devote ourselves to fleshly banquets.

*Xyliglycon*, which the Latins corruptly call *siliqua* (“carob pod”), received this name from the Greeks because the fruit of its wood is sweet. They call wood *xylon* [ξύλον] and sweet *glyky* [γλυκύ]. The juice pressed from the fruit of this tree is called *acacia* by the Greeks.

Mystically, the carob pod signifies either the pleasure of the world or secular wisdom. Hence in the Gospel (Luke XV) the prodigal son, while feeding pigs and suffering hunger, is said to have desired the carob pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him any.

For the food of demons is drunkenness, luxury, fornication, and every vice. These things are pleasing and wanton, and they caress the senses with pleasure; as soon as they appear, they invite people to use them. For this reason the luxurious young man could not be satisfied with them, because pleasure always produces hunger for itself, and what has passed does not satisfy. When Satan has seized someone by his art and placed his own yoke upon him, he no longer takes pains to entice him toward an abundance of vices, knowing that he is already dead. We see many idolaters in this condition, worn out by the misery and want of bread.

The food of demons is also the poetry of poets, secular wisdom, and the pomp of rhetorical language. All these delight people by their own sweetness; and while they captivate the ears with verses flowing in sweet rhythm, they also penetrate the soul and conquer the inner chambers of the heart. But when they have been read through with the greatest zeal and labor, they offer their readers nothing except empty sound and the clamor of words. No fullness of truth and no nourishment of righteousness is found there; those devoted to them remain hungry for truth and in want of virtues.

The pistachio is so called because the shell of its fruit resembles the scent of *nardus pistica*, concerning which we shall speak later.

The pine, a pitch-producing tree, is named from the sharpness of its leaves; for the ancients called something sharp *pinum*. One kind of pine the Greeks call *pitin*, another *peuken*, which we call the pitch pine, because it exudes pitch; for they also differ in appearance.

On the islands of Germany, the tear of this tree produces amber. For the falling drop, hardened by cold or warmth, becomes solid and forms a gem, receiving a name from its nature, namely *succinum*, because it is the tree’s sap.

The pine is believed to benefit everything planted beneath it, just as the fig is harmful to everything. The fear of Gehenna can be signified by the pine and pitch pine: just as the pine is believed to benefit everything that stands beneath it, so the fear of Gehenna will benefit those who repent of their sins because of fear of punishment.

Conversely, the fig—that is, carnal luxury—harms all who follow it and abuse permitted things through the enticements of pleasure.

The pine also signifies those who are light or agile in the Church and ready for every good work. Hence it is read in Isaiah:

> The fir, the box tree, and the pine together (Isa. LX).

Again, the pine signifies the rich of this world, as above.

Pitch signifies the pollution and blackness of sins. In Solomon:

> Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it (Ecclus. XIII).

The fir is so called because, more than other trees, it extends far and rises to a great height. Its nature is free from earthly moisture and therefore makes it supple and light. Concerning it Virgil says:

> And the fir, destined to see the sea’s disasters,

because ships are made from it.

Some call it the Gallic tree because of its whiteness; it is without knots. The fir, because of its height and its long-lasting strength, fittingly represents the mind of the elect, which scorns all lowly desires, is always intent upon contemplation of heavenly things, and is singularly excellent in the virtue of patience.

Hence in the Book of Kings it is written concerning Solomon and the building of the temple:

> And he covered the floor with fir boards and overlaid them with gold (III Kings VI).

The sheets of gold placed upon the marble and the fir boards are the breadth of charity arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Just as gold is more precious than the other metals, so charity, with a singular brightness, shines more splendidly than the other virtues in the temple of God.

In another sense, the fir has a meaning in Zechariah, where it is said:

> Howl, fir, because the cedar has fallen (Zech. XI).

The cedar, which the Greeks call *kedros*, is understood as *kaiomenēs dryos hygros*, that is, “the sap of a burning tree.” Its leaves resemble those of the cypress; its wood has a pleasant fragrance and lasts a long time, nor is it ever destroyed by moths. Concerning it Persius says:

> And words worthy of cedar. [Col. 0516D–0517A]
namely, because of its enduring permanence. Hence in temples ceilings are made from this wood because of its longevity. The resin of this wood is called cedar resin; it is so useful for preserving books that those coated with it neither suffer from moths nor grow old with time. It grows in Crete, Africa, and Syria.

For, as we have said, the cedar is by nature an altogether imperishable tree, of pleasant fragrance and shining appearance, which drives away and kills snakes when its scent is kindled. All these qualities suit the perfect, whose patience is unconquerable, whose reputation for virtue is outstanding, whose presence is most pleasing to all good people, and whose authority in defeating and refuting those who resist the truth is utterly steadfast. They shine, both in this life and in the future, with an eminence surpassing that of the other saints.

Indeed, the cedar mystically signifies Christ or the holy Church. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Like a cedar I have been exalted in Lebanon” (Ecclus. XXIV). Likewise, the cedar typologically represents the prophets and apostles. Thus it is said in the Psalm: “All the trees of the forest will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon, which you planted; there the sparrows will build their nests” (Ps. CIII)—that is, spiritual men dwell in the teaching of the prophets and apostles.

Again, cedars represent proud heretics, or philosophers, or even demons. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and crush them” (Ps. XXVIII). And in Isaiah: “Upon all,” he says, “the cedars of Lebanon and the lofty trees” (Isa. I).

Cypress is called *cyparissus* in Greek because its crown rises from a rounded base into a point. Hence it is also called *conoeides*—that is, “a lofty roundness.” Its fruit too is called a cone, because its roundness resembles a cone. Hence cypresses are called cone-bearing. The wood of this tree has almost the same strength as cedar; it is suitable also for the beams of temples, and with its impenetrable solidity it never yields to weight, but endures with the firmness it possessed at the beginning.

The ancients used to place branches of cypress near the funeral pyre, so that, while corpses were being burned, the pleasantness of its fragrance might overpower their odor. Cypress also expresses constancy in that it is suitable for healing bodily ailments and does not lose the beauty of its foliage under any assault of the winds. It therefore represents the activity of those who adorn the holy Church with the higher ornaments of virtue.

For the cypress signifies Christ or the Church. Hence the passage: “Like a cedar I have been exalted in Lebanon, and like a cypress on the mountains of Hermon” (Ecclus. XXIV). Likewise, cypress represents the prophets, patriarchs, or holy teachers. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypress” (Song I). The beams and ceilings are the teachers in the holy Church, both for protection and for adornment; cedar and cypress signify their outstanding virtues and the fragrance of their good life.

Juniper is called by the Greeks either because it narrows from a broad form into a slender one, like fire, or because it retains an enclosed fire for a long time—so much so that, if live coals are covered with its ashes, they remain until the following year. For *pyr* means “fire” in Greek. Concerning this tree it is written in the Book of Job: “Their food was the root of junipers” (Job XXX).

The juniper tree has prickles instead of leaves. What it produces is so bristling that it can prick anyone who handles it, like thorns. A thorn is every sin, because while it draws the mind toward pleasure, it tears it as though by pricking. What, then, is signified by the root of juniper except avarice, from which the thorns of all sins arise? Concerning this Paul also says: “The root of all evils is desire” (I Tim. VI). It arises secretly in the mind, but openly produces the prickles of every sin in action.

Ebony grows in India and Ethiopia. Once cut, it hardens into stone. Its wood is black and its bark smooth, like that of the laurel. Indian ebony is mottled with small white and reddish-brown markings; Ethiopian ebony, which is considered superior, is marked by no spots at all, but is black, smooth, and hornlike.

The plane tree is so called from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and broad; for the Greeks call broad things *platos*. Scripture expresses both the name and the form of this tree when it says: “Like a plane tree I have spread out in the streets” (Ecclus. XXIV). It has very delicate and soft leaves and resembles the vine.

Mystically, this tree signifies the Lord Christ, who is spread throughout the whole world in his members and everywhere displays to the faithful saving examples of gentleness and innocence. Concerning him it is written in the Psalm: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. I). The Lord Christ is rightly compared, as I think, to a fruit-bearing tree because of the cross, which he accepted for the salvation of humanity.

Likewise, the plane tree signifies the saints, as though spread out with the leaves of preaching. Hence it is read in Ezekiel: “The plane trees were equal to its foliage” (Ezek. XXXI).

The oak is called *quercus* or *quernus* because the gods of the gentiles used to utter responses to those seeking oracles beneath it. It is a very long-lived tree, as we read of the oak of Mamre, beneath which Abraham dwelt; it is said to have endured for many centuries, even into the reign of the emperor Constantine. Its fruit is called a gall, of which one kind is wild.

*Robur* generally means whatever is strongest in any material. This tree can typologically signify the patience and long-suffering of the saints, by which they firmly endure every adversity, persevere in steadfastness of spirit, and bear everything with equanimity. As I have said, the saints, strong in faith and virtues, are mystically represented by the oak in Isaiah, where we read: “And it will be displayed like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads out its branches” (Isa. VI). Elsewhere, in another sense: “And above all the oaks,” he says, “of Bashan” (Isa. II).

The ash is said to be so called because it grows especially in rough and mountainous places. Hence, by derivation, *fraxinus*, just as *montanus* comes from *mons*. Concerning it Ovid wrote:

> [. . .] and the ash useful for spears.

It can signify the weapons of virtue that the saints use against their enemies.

The yew is a poisonous tree, from which poisonous substances are also called *toxica*. The Parthians and other peoples make bows from it. Hence the poet says:

> [. . .] the yew of the Ityreans is bent into bows.

This tree can represent the deceit and poisonous doctrines of heretics, which produce death and bring destruction upon those who are wounded by them.

The alder is so called because it is nourished by a stream; for it grows close to water and does not easily live away from the waves. Hence it is tender and soft, because it is nourished in a moist place. The elm received its name because it thrives better in boggy and damp places. In mountainous and rugged places it is less vigorous.

These two trees can signify those who progress more through the irrigation of the sacred Scriptures and humility of conduct than those who trust in their own power.

The poplar is so called because a multitude grows from its cutting. There are two kinds: one white and the other black. The white poplar is so called because its leaves are white on one side and green on the other. Thus it is two-colored, bearing something like the signs of night and day, whose seasons are marked by the rising and setting of the sun. Poplars also produce resin around the river Eridanus—or, as others report, in the territory of Syria.

The poplar signifies the shoots of chastity, as some maintain, in Leviticus. In a negative sense it is understood in Hosea, where it is said: “Under the poplar and terebinth, because its shade is good” (Hos. IV).

The linden is said to have been so called because it is useful for making weapons, owing to the brilliance and lightness of what is thrown. It is a kind of very light wood, and is also highly useful to bees in making honey. So too gentleness is praiseworthy in teachers, and the preaching of the word is exceedingly sweet.

The willow is so called because it sprouts quickly—that is, grows rapidly. It is a pliant tree, suitable for binding vines. Its seed is said to have this property: if someone drinks it in a cup, he becomes childless; it also makes women infertile.

In the mystical sense, willows are the faithful in the Church, rooted near the streams of divine preaching, as in Isaiah: “And like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLIV). Again, willows are unfruitful people. Hence the passage in Job: “Willows of the torrent will surround him”—that is, the devil (Job XL); and elsewhere: “They will lead them down to the willow by the torrent” (Isa. XV).

The poplar, willow, and linden are soft woods suitable for carving. The significance of the poplar and the others has already been explained above.

Tamarisk, which the Latins call *tamarix*, is named from its bitterness; for its taste is exceedingly bitter. This tree grows in the wilderness and in rocky soil. From it, too, they say that *misethra*—that is, hatred—is aroused by magical arts.

A likeness concerning this tree is given by the prophet Jeremiah, who says:

> Thus says the Lord: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He will be like a tamarisk in the desert and will not see prosperity when it comes, but will dwell in dryness in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabited” (Jer. XVII).

This is said of the Jewish people, who dwell in the desert, bear no fruit, and are in a land of salt that produces no fruit, and in an uninhabited land that has neither God as a guest nor the protection of angels nor the grace of the Holy Spirit nor the knowledge of teachers.

The myrtle is named from the sea because it is chiefly a coastal tree. Hence Virgil wrote:

> Shores most joyful with myrtles;

and:

> Lovers of the myrtle shores.

For this reason it is called *myrine* by the Greeks. The books of physicians state that this tree is suitable for many female needs. The myrtle signifies the people of the gentiles. Hence mention is made of this tree in the prophet Zechariah, where we read:

> And behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the depths, etc. (Zech. I).

The Hebrews think that this man is the archangel Michael, who is the avenger of iniquities and sins in Israel. They understand his standing among the myrtles that were in the depths to mean the prophets and saints who lived amid the captive people and were themselves in the depths.

The lentisk is so called because its point is pliant and soft; for we call anything flexible *lentum*. Hence we speak of a pliant twig and pliant vines. Virgil wrote: “and pliant vines,” meaning flexible vines. Its fruit exudes oil, while its bark produces resin called mastic, of which the greatest quantity and the best quality is produced on the island of Chios.

The lentisk is mentioned in the Book of Daniel, where the story of Susanna is written and where the responses of the elders concerning the *schinus* and *prinus* are displayed. The Latins interpret *schinus* and *prinus* as holm oak and lentisk; their meaning is made clear there.

The terebinth is a Greek name. It produces the finest of all resins. We also read in Genesis that the patriarch Jacob, having summoned his entire household in accordance with the Lord’s command, said to them:

> “Throw away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments. Arise, and let us go up to Bethel, that we may make there an altar to the Lord, who heard me in the day of my tribulation and was my companion on the journey.”

So they gave him all the foreign gods they possessed, and the earrings that were in their ears. He buried them beneath the terebinth that is behind the city of Shechem (Gen. XXXV).

This signifies that the Church rejects all the idols of the gentiles and consigns them to perpetual oblivion, so that the worship of the one true God alone may everywhere be celebrated.

The terebinth signifies the saints, as in Isaiah: “And it will be displayed like a terebinth” (Isa. VI). In another sense, as in Hosea: “Under the poplar and terebinth, because its shade was good” (Hos. IV).

Boxwood is a Greek name, partly corrupted by the Latins. Among the Greeks it is called *pyxos*, an evergreen tree whose smooth wood is suitable for the tips of writing instruments. Hence Scripture says: “Write it on boxwood, and carefully engrave it in a book” (Isa. XXX).

Boxwood signifies the gentle in the Church, who, although they possess no spiritual fruits, nevertheless remain green through their perpetual confession of faith. Hence the passage in Isaiah: “The fir, the boxwood, and the pine” (Isa. LX).

The reed is so called because it dries quickly. The ancients called it *canna*; Varro later called it *arundo*. It should certainly be known that the Latin word *canna* was borrowed from the Hebrew language, for among the Hebrews a reed (*calamus*) is called *canna*.

The reed signifies the changeability of the human mind. Hence the Lord says to the Jews concerning John:

> “What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matt. XI.)

But John was not a reed shaken by the wind. He could never be bent to one side or the other; he neither favored empty praises nor yielded to adversities.

The golden reed signifies the incarnation of the Savior, or the divine Scripture, as in the Apocalypse: “And in his hand a golden reed” (Apoc. XXI).

Likewise, the *calamus* signifies the preaching of the saints, as in Isaiah: “The green growth of reed and rush will arise” (Isa. XXXV). The rush is the faithful person who always remains in the Church beside the streams of divine law, as in Job: “Can the papyrus live without moisture, or does the reed grow without water?” (Job VIII.)

The paliurus is an exceedingly rough and thorny plant. Paliurus is the defense of sin or impurity of mind. Hence in Isaiah: “And paliurus in its fortifications”—he who is upright among them is like paliurus, and like thorns from a hedge (Isa. XXXIV; Mic. VII).

The rhamnus is a kind of bramble, which the common people call the bear’s thorn. It is exceedingly rough and thorny. *Sentix* is so called from *situs*, meaning uncultivated ground, where thorns and brambles grow. Our ancestors called every thorny tree a *vepres*, because it seizes by force.

Concerning the rhamnus, therefore, we read in the Psalm:

> Before your thorns produce rhamnus, like living things, so he will swallow them up in wrath (Ps. LVII).

The rhamnus, as we have said, is a particularly troublesome kind of thorn. At first it grows as a very soft herb; but once it has thickened with maturity, it produces pointed twigs, and afterward its stakes harden into the firmness of trees.

This passage therefore threatens the Jews that they will be swallowed up before their wickedness grows strong through long age. Likewise, it is said elsewhere of such people: “Men of blood and deceit will not divide their days” (Ps. LIV). The rapidity of their destruction follows: “Like living things, so he will swallow them up in wrath” (LVII). He rightly said “like living things,” because they seem to live but are dead. Every sinner who lives in wickedness is dead to the truth.

The Lord himself interprets thorns as riches and worldly anxieties when he explains the parable of the sower in the Gospel, saying:

> “What fell among the thorns are those who have heard the word, but as they go on their way they are choked by anxieties, riches, and pleasures of life, and bear no fruit” (Luke VIII).

Similarly, in allegorical interpretation thorns can express the filth of vices, which prick the human mind with illicit desires and provoke it to sin.

Thistles signify the stings of vices or temptations, as in Genesis: “It will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). And in the prophet: “Sin,” he says, “is a burdock and a thistle of Israel” (Hos. X).

The removal of sins is represented by brambles in Isaiah: “All the mountains that are hoed with the hoe will not be approached by the terror of brambles and thorns” (Isa. VII).

The itching of lust is represented by nettles in Isaiah: “Thorns and nettles will arise in their houses”—that is, in the hearts of the reprobate (Isa. XXXIV).

The wild olive is so called because its leaves resemble those of the olive, though they are broader. It is a wild, bitter, and fruitless tree. When a branch of the olive is grafted into it, it changes the power of the root and transforms it into its own quality.

The tears of the wild olive are of two kinds. One resembles gum without any sharpness of quality; the other resembles a drop of ammoniacum, collected by distillation and biting to the taste.

The olive is called *elaios* in Greek, from which the Latin word *oliva* is derived. The tree itself is the *olea*, its fruit the olive, and its juice oil. It is the distinguished tree of peace, and its fruit is called by various names.

The wild olive signifies the fruitless gentiles, who, while they were without Christ, could not produce the fruit of right faith and good works. But after they were cut away from their ancient error and converted to the faith of Christ, they were immediately grafted into the root of the patriarchs and prophets and became sharers in the root and richness of the olive. The Apostle discusses this elegantly in his letter to the Romans (Rom. XI). The Prophet, singing in the Psalter about the body of Christ, which is the Church, says:

> “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God forever and ever” (Ps. LI).

Oil sometimes signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, sometimes charity, and sometimes mercy. Conversely, it has another meaning where the Psalmist says: “But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. CXL).

Oil, in the good sense, is the cause of splendor, nourishment for light, and a source of both brightness and health. In the bad sense—as it is understood here—the sinner’s oil is feigned affection. Entering our minds gently through flattering and soothing words, like the richness of oil, it softens the rigor of truth and leads them toward harmful thoughts through the ostentation of counterfeit love.

The olive signifies Christ in the Church. Hence it is read in Ecclesiasticus: “Like a beautiful, fruit-bearing olive tree, the Lord has called your name” (Ecclus. XXIV). And shortly afterward: “Fire blazed in it.”

Oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit in Deuteronomy: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest rock” (Deut. XXXII); and in Job: “The rock poured out streams of oil for me” (Job XXIX); and elsewhere: “The yoke will rot before the face of oil” (Isa. X).

Oil signifies works of mercy, as in the Psalm: “And my flesh was changed because of oil” (Ps. CVIII).

Oil signifies gladness of mind, as in the Gospel: “When you fast, anoint your head” (Matt. VI). And in the Psalter: “That he may gladden his face with oil” (Ps. CIII).

Oil signifies the testimony of a good conscience, as in the Gospel: “But the prudent took oil in their vessels” (Matt. XXV).

Oil signifies the deceiver’s speech, in the Psalm: “But let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. CXL).

Oil signifies the subtle and flattering deception of heretics. Thus Solomon speaks of the same corrupt teaching: “His throat is smooth with oil” (Prov. V). And in Hosea: “They carried oil into Egypt” (Hos. XII)—that is, to deceive the minds of worldly people.

Ointment signifies the name of the Savior. In Solomon: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song I).

Ointment signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit in Solomon: “Dead flies”—that is, demons—“destroy the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. X).

The ointment of chrism signifies anointing. According to some, this is meant in the Psalter: “They have been multiplied by the fruit of grain and oil” (Ps. IV); and much is related about it in Exodus.

Oil signifies the soothing remedy of gentle persuasion in divine preaching, as in the Gospel: “And drawing near, he bound up his wounds, pouring in wine and oil” (Luke X).

*Amurca* is the watery part of oil. It is named from its rising away from the oil—that is, because it separates from the oil—and is its dregs. The Greeks call it *amorgen*, borrowing the word from Latin.

*Gumen* is a Greek name; for the Greeks call it *kommi*. Resin the Greeks call *retinen*, for in Greek *reon* means anything that flows.

It is the tear exhaled as sweat from woods, such as cherry, lentisk, balsam, or other trees and shrubs that are said to sweat. The same is true of the fragrant woods of the East, such as balsam, ferula, or amber, whose tear hardens into a gem.

The first and finest resin is terebinthine resin. It is brought from Arabia Petraea, Judea, and Syria, from Cyprus and Africa, and also from the Cycladic islands. The second is lentisk resin, called mastic; it is transported from the island of Chios. The third is pine resin.

## CHAPTER VII. On aromatic trees

Aromatics are all substances of fragrant odor sent from India or Arabia, or from other regions. They seem to have acquired the name *aromata* either because, placed upon altars, they appear suited to divine invocations, or because they are thought to enter and mingle with the air. For what is scent except air that has been touched?

Aromatics signify various ornaments of virtue. Thus, in the Book of Kings, we read of the queen of Sheba: “Such aromatics as these were never brought, as the queen of Sheba gave to Solomon” (III Kings X).

Spices signify various fragrances of virtue; likewise, in the passage above: “with all the powders of the perfumer.”

Frankincense is an immense and branching Arabian tree with very light bark. Its branches resemble those of the maple, and it exudes an aromatic white sap like an almond; when chewed, this sap dissolves as though into powder. When broken, it is fatty within and easily catches fire when placed upon it. Among us it is called “male” because by nature it is round, shaped like testicles; the rest is flat and almost rough and is less good.

It is adulterated by mixing in resin or gum, but it can be recognized by its distinctive properties. Frankincense placed upon fire burns; resin smokes; gum melts when heated.

Frankincense is so called from pounding. It is also called Lebanon, after the mountain of Arabia where the Sabaeans live. Their mountain is called Lebanon, and frankincense is gathered there.

Myrrh is an Arabian tree five cubits high, resembling the thorn called *achanton*. Its drop is green and bitter; hence it received the name *myrrh*. Its naturally flowing drop is more valuable, while that extracted by cutting the bark is judged inferior.

The Arabs keep its branches burning in fires. From their highly harmful smoke, unless the fragrance of storax counteracts it, people often contract incurable diseases.

Troglodytic myrrh is named from an Arabian island where the better and purer kind is collected.

Different aromatics signify different kinds of virtue, with which the holy Church is adorned. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs:

> “Who is this who comes up through the desert like a column of smoke, from the aromatics of myrrh and frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song III.)

The Synagogue marvels at how the people of the gentiles, cleansed by no mystery of circumcision and instructed by no admonition of the prophets, suddenly ascended from the lowest pleasures, through the desert of paganism and idolatry, to the heights of virtue and the embrace of the bridegroom. Kindled by the fire of love, it strives toward heavenly things with every effort of virtue, through the mortification of bodily pleasures, the purity of prayers, and the fragrance of every virtue.

Hence it is also written: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense” (Song IV), because myrrh expresses mortification of the flesh, while frankincense expresses devotion in prayer.

Again the bridegroom says: “I gathered my myrrh with my aromatics” (Song V). Myrrh expresses passion or mortification; aromatics express all virtues. He gathers myrrh with aromatics when he brings martyrs, together with the other elect, to the maturity of their rewards.

Again, through the Prophet this is said of the Lord the Savior: “Myrrh and drop and cassia from your garments?” (Ps. XLIV.)

The holy body of the Lord is understood to have been a kind of garment of the divinity. For just as the limbs of mortals are covered by clothing, so the majesty of the Word appeared hidden from the eyes of the faithful beneath the veil of flesh. From this garment, therefore—that is, from the mystery of the incarnation—myrrh, drop, and cassia are appropriately said to have come.

Myrrh signifies the death that he accepted for the salvation of all. The drop, called ammoniacum, cures hardenings contracted by some necessity; it is aptly compared with the Lord’s incarnation because by holy preaching it dissolves the hardness of the human heart.

Cassia, which our people call *fistula*, signifies the redemption of the human race through the water of baptism, since this kind of herb is said to be found in watery places. These substances also possess a sweet fragrance, so that both the power of the herbs and the sweetness of their scent may rightly be compared with the holy incarnation.

The drop signifies the force of the love of God, and the tree of charity is understood, as in the passage above: “A bundle of drops is my beloved to me” (Song I).

Storax is an Arabian tree resembling the Cydonian apple. Around the rising of the Dog Star, its twigs pour out tears through openings. Its distillation, when it falls upon the ground, is not clean; but when it is preserved in a hollow of its own bark, it is clean. That which adheres to the twigs and reeds is clean and whitish; afterward it becomes yellow because of the sun. Storax of the reeds itself is fatty, resinous, fragrant, moist, and emits something like a honeyed liquid.

Storax is so called because it is the flowing and congealed drop of a tree. For the Greeks call a drop *stiria*. In Greek it is *styrax*, and in Latin *storax*.

The sons of Israel brought this spice, together with the other aromatics, into Egypt and offered it to Joseph as a gift. This signifies the good gifts of goodwill and sacred virtues that holy men offer to our Savior during their pilgrimage in this world—gifts in which he delights, so that he may be favorable and grant their petitions.

Bdellium is a tree of India and Arabia. Its tear is better in Arabia: it is bright, somewhat whitish, smooth, fatty, evenly waxlike, easily softened, not mixed with wood or earth, bitter, and of good fragrance. That from India is dirty, black, and in larger lumps. It is adulterated by mixing in gum, which does not make the taste equally bitter.

Mastic is the drop of the lentisk tree. It is called *granomastix* because it is shaped like grains.

The pepper tree grows in India on the side of Mount Caucasus that faces the sun. Its leaves resemble those of the juniper, and its forests are guarded by snakes. But when the pepper is ripe, the inhabitants of that region set the forests on fire. Thus the snakes are driven away by the fire, and black pepper is produced from the flame.

The natural color of pepper is white, though its fruit has different forms. What is unripe is called long pepper; what remains untouched by fire is white pepper; but what has a wrinkled and rough skin takes both its color and its name from the heat of the fire.

If pepper is light, it is old; if heavy, it is fresh. The fraud of merchants must be avoided. They often sprinkle very old pepper with moistened silver foam or lead so that it will become heavy.

Aloe grows in India and Arabia. It is a tree of exceedingly fine and powerful fragrance. Indeed, its wood is burned on altars in place of incense, and it is thought to have acquired its name from this.

Concerning aloe, the Gospel says this about the burial of the Lord:

> Then Joseph came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came—the one who had first come to Jesus by night—bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds (John XIX).

Hence in the Song of Songs the following is written in praise of the bride:

> “Myrrh and aloe with all the finest ointments” (Song IV).

Myrrh and aloe are aromatic trees that express continence of the flesh; “with all the finest ointments” means with all the gifts of virtue.

Cassia grows in Arabia. It is a branch with a strong bark and purple leaves like those of pepper. In its power it resembles cinnamon, but it is inferior in strength. Therefore twice its weight is mixed into medicines in place of cinnamon.

Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender like a reed. It grows in the regions of India and Ethiopia, as a short shrub only two cubits high, of a somewhat blackish or ash-colored hue, with extremely slender branches. What grows thick is despised; what develops more slenderly is excellent. When broken, it emits a visible breath resembling a cloud or powder.

Concerning these trees it is written in the Song of Songs:

> “Fistulae (cassia-pods) and cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon” (Song IV).

Fistula, which is also cassia, is an aromatic but modest tree; therefore it signifies those who are humble in spirit. Mystically, cassia is right doctrine or the reputation of good works, as in the Psalter: “And cassia from your garments” (Ps. XLIV).

Likewise, cinnamon signifies those who despise themselves, because it too is a short but fragrant and sweet tree. So humility has great praise and sweetness before God. Just as fistula and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon signify their exalted actions.

Aromatic reed is named from its resemblance to the common reed. It grows in India, jointed with many knots, yellowish, and fragrant with a pleasant scent. When broken, it splits into many parts, and in taste resembles cassia with a slight, biting sharpness.

The reed is therefore commanded to be mixed with the other aromatics—that is, with myrrh, cinnamon, and cassia—in the oil for sacred anointing, so that God’s tabernacle and all its vessels may be sanctified. The ointment with which the tabernacle is anointed is the chrism with which the faithful people are anointed; in them the divinity dwells as in a tabernacle.

This ointment can also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or the fragrance of righteousness spread far and wide. Concerning it the Apostle says:

> “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge” (II Cor. II).

The balsam tree was originally found in Judea within an area of only twenty *jugera*. Later, after the Romans had taken possession of that region, it was propagated over very broad hills. Its trunk resembles that of a vine, and its leaves resemble those of rue, though they are whiter and evergreen.

The tree is called balsam; its wood is called *xylobalsamum*, its fruit or seed *carpobalsamum*, and its juice *opobalsamum*. It receives these additional names because, when struck with iron claws, the bark distills drops of extraordinary fragrance through openings. An opening is called *ope* in Greek.

Its drop is adulterated by mixing in cyprine oil or honey. Genuine balsam is distinguished from honey if it coagulates with milk, and from oil if, when dropped into or mixed with water, it is easily dissolved. Moreover, if woolen garments are soiled with it, they are not stained. Adulterated balsam does not coagulate with milk; like oil, it floats upon water and stains clothing.

Pure balsam has such power that when the sun grows hot it cannot be held in the hand.

Mystical mention of this liquid, that is, balsam, is made in the Book of Jesus son of Sirach, where it is written:

> “And unmingled balsam is my fragrance” (Ecclus. XXIV).

And in the Song of Songs, the bride speaks of the bridegroom as follows:

> “While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will remain between my breasts. My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of En-Gedi” (Song I).

The Lord therefore became a cluster of Cyprus in the resurrection, whereas in the Passion he had been a bundle of myrrh. He is also rightly remembered as being in the vineyards of En-Gedi. For, as we said earlier, balsam grows in the vineyards of En-Gedi; it is customarily mixed into the olive oil used in the preparation of chrism and consecrated by episcopal blessing, so that all the faithful may be marked with this anointing through the laying on of the priest’s hand, by which the Holy Spirit is received.

## CHAPTER VIII. On aromatic or common herbs
There are also the names of certain herbs whose names echo some characteristic of them and thus have an explanation. Yet you will not find the etymology of every herb, since their names also vary according to place.

Folium (“leaf”) is so called because it is gathered floating without any root along the shores of India. The Indians pierce it with linen, dry it, and store it. It is said to be a herb of paradise, resembling nard in taste.

Nard is a spiky herb; hence it is also called by the Greeks *nardostachys* (“spike of nard”). One kind is called Indian, another Syrian—not because it grows in Syria, but because the mountain where it is found faces India on one side and Syria on the other. The Indian nard is multiform, but the Syrian is better: light, tawny, hairy, with a small and highly fragrant spike, resembling cyperus. If it remains in the mouth for a long time, it dries the tongue.

Celtic nard takes its name from a region of Gaul. It grows more often in the Alps of Liguria and in Syria, as a small shrub whose roots are gathered into a bundle and fastened with cords. Only its flower is valued for its good fragrance; its clusters and little roots are judged useful for our purposes.

Nard signifies the fragrance of the virtues of the saints in the Church. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I). That is, while Christ the King rests in the blessedness of heavenly seclusion, the virtue of the saints in the Church supplies us with great sweetness of grace. [Col. 0527C]

Likewise, in the same book the bridegroom speaks of the bride’s glory: “Your emissions are a paradise of pomegranate trees, with the fruits of orchards, cyprus with nard” (Song IV).
