Nard and saffron signify the holy Church through the irrigation of sacred Baptism; the paradise of pomegranate-tree emissions signifies the holy martyrs; “with the fruits of orchards” means with the fruit of the virtues of the saints.

Cyprus is an aromatic tree signifying the blessing of heavenly grace. Nard expresses the type of the Lord’s Passion, while saffron expresses the fervor of charity. Cyprus is joined to nard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer for Christ. Likewise, nard is joined to saffron when, through Christ’s charity, we willingly accept death.

Saffron is named from a town in Cilicia called Corycus, although it also grows elsewhere; but it is neither so abundant nor of such quality elsewhere as in Cilicia, and therefore it took its name from the place where it is superior. For many things have taken their names from places where more of something “comes” (*pervenit*; perhaps *provenit*, “is produced”) and where it is better.

The finest saffron is fresh, of good fragrance, slightly pale, elongated, whole rather than broken into fragments, of a good scent, staining the hand when picked, and slightly sharp. If it is not of this kind, it is recognized as either old or adulterated by soaking.

Cyprus also signifies incorruption; nard, strength; and saffron, the martyrs.

Hyssop is a low-growing herb whose roots penetrate rock. It signifies the humility of repentance, or Baptism, as in the Psalter: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50).

Costus is the root of a herb that grows in India, Arabia, and Syria, though the Arabian variety is better. It is white and light, pleasant, and of agreeable fragrance. The Indian is dark in color and light, like fennel stalk; the Syrian is heavy in weight, boxwood-colored, and pungent in smell. The best, however, is white, light, dry, fiery to the taste.

The flower signifies either Christ, who blossomed from the rod of the root of Jesse, or the pattern of righteousness, as in the psalm: “The righteous man,” he says, “shall flourish like the palm tree” (Ps. 91).

The rose is named from the appearance of its flower because it is red with a shining color. The rose signifies the martyrs, as in the saying: “They shall spring up like a rose beside flowing waters” (Ecclus. 39). [Col. 0528B]

Lilies are a herb with a milky flower; hence the name, as though *laclia* (“milk-like”), since although the leaves are white, a golden appearance shines within. The lily signifies Christ, who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). And again: “That he may feed in the gardens and gather lilies” (Song VI), as though he were saying: “I am the beauty of the world and the glory of the humble.”

Speaking of his bride, he says: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song II), because the whiteness of her chastity is proved by tribulations, and the fruit of preaching is greater than that of repose.

Virginity may also be expressed by the lily, because virginal chastity is more excellent than the other virtues, as is shown in the Apocalypse.

The violet received its name from the power of its fragrance. There are three kinds: purple, white, and yellow.

The violet also signifies confessors, because of the likeness of their bruised bodies. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “Flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song II); to them also the kingdom of heaven has been promised. [Col. 0528C]

Ivy is so called because it clings to trees by creeping over them. Of it Virgil wrote:

> Among the victorious laurels, let ivy creep for you.

Some say that *hedera* (“ivy”) was so called because in ancient times it was given to goats as food beyond their abundance of milk.

According to the natural philosophers, ivy indicates cold earth, for it is an antidote to drunkenness: if someone drinks while crowned with ivy, it counteracts intoxication.

Ivy bears the type of the Jewish people, who at one time flourished but did not long remain in their former verdure. Thus, in the book of the prophet Jonah, the ivy under whose shade Jonah sat dried up at the rising of the worm at dawn on the following day. This signifies the resurrection of that worm who said: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21). The Jewish people, once flourishing in the patriarchs and prophets, dried up through unbelief.

Galbanum is the sap of a fennel-like plant.

Dicte is a mountain of Crete, from which the herb dittany received its name. Because of it, as Virgil says, a wounded doe traverses the Dictean glades. For the herb has such power that it expels iron from the body and shakes out arrows. Thus wounded animals, by feeding on it, eject arrows embedded in their bodies. Some Latins call it *poleium Martis* (“Mars’s pennyroyal”) because it shakes out weapons of war.

Mandrake is so called because it has sweet-smelling fruits as large as the apple called the Matian apple. Hence the Latins call it *malum terrae* (“earth-apple”). Poets call it *anthropomorphon* (“human-shaped”), because its root resembles the form of a human being. Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink by those whose bodies must be cut open for medical treatment, so that, being rendered sleepy, they may not feel the pain.

There are two kinds. The female produces fruits resembling plums, with leaves like lettuce; the male has leaves like beet.

Of the mandrake the bride says in the Song of Songs: “The mandrakes have given forth fragrance at our gates” (Song VII). Because of its many kinds of medicinal power, the mandrake is compared with the virtues of the saints. The doctors of the Church are its gates. At such gates the mandrakes give forth fragrance when spiritual people spread the palm of virtue from themselves far and wide.

It is read in Genesis (Gen. 30) that Reuben, the son of Leah, went out into the field, found mandrakes, and gave them to his mother Leah. This signifies the good reputation that every diligent person gains from worldly people and ought to bring back to Mother Church.

Thus the Apostle says concerning one to be ordained bishop: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3). Although such people may have little understanding, they nevertheless often repay the labor of those who care for them with the splendor of praise and the honor of a good reputation. [Col. 0529B]

Herbs signify the eternal verdure of paradise and the pasture of holy souls, as in the Gospel: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will enter and go out, and will find pasture” (John 10). And through Ezekiel: “On the high mountains of Israel, there I shall feed them in green pastures” (Ezek. 34).

Conversely, concerning the aridity of their mind, the Jews are addressed through Jeremiah: “Their eyes have failed, because there was no grass” (Jer. 14).

Grass signifies the life of the flesh, as in Job concerning the devil: “To him the mountains”—that is, luxurious rich men—“bring forth grass” (Job 40).

Grass signifies the life of mortals, as in the psalm: “In the morning let him pass away like grass” (Ps. 89).

A meadow is a place whose abundance of hay protects cattle. The ancient Romans gave it this name because it is immediately ready and requires no great labor of cultivation; meadows are places that can be mown.

Mystically, a meadow may signify the holy Church or sacred Scripture, in which flowers of various virtues are found and spiritual nourishment is prepared for pious creatures—that is, faithful people. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song II), that is, in the leisure of faith and righteousness they flourished in the world as the Church grew.

For this reason she also says to the teachers: “Sustain me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I languish with love” (ibid.), as though she were saying: “Console me with the examples both of those beginning and of those completing the way of salvation, while I still languish in the weariness of this pilgrimage from love of the vision above.”

The meadow is also disclosed as divine Scripture, as in Solomon: “The meadows are opened, and green herbs appear” (Prov. 27).

It is also understood in a negative sense, as in Solomon: “Let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through” (Wis. 2).

Oats . . . darnel . . . tares—which poets always call “unfortunate darnel,” because it is useless and unproductive—mystically signify sinners and vices. Hence it is said in the Gospel (Matt. 13) that the enemy sowed tares over the Lord’s crop.

Hay is so called because flame is fed by it; for *phos* in Greek means “flame.” For *enim* (“for”; alternatively *autem*, “however/indeed”), hay allegorically signifies the fragility of human nature. Hence it is read in the psalm concerning sinners: “For like hay they shall quickly wither, and like the green herb they shall soon fall” (Ps. 36).

Hay is beautiful while it is green and flowering, but when it has dried, it immediately withers as its color changes. So are the ungodly: shining with a kind of flourishing joy, they dry up through a premature end.

At first they are compared with hay, so that they might wither; now with field vegetables, so that they might fall. For he did not say “garden vegetables,” but “herbs,” to indicate rather those most worthless plants that grow spontaneously through the fields.

Hay signifies the history of the Law or temporal things, as in the psalm: “Who produces hay on the mountains” (Ps. 146).

Hay signifies sinners, as in the Gospel: “For if the grass, which today is in the field and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” (Matt. 6).

Vegetables are called *olera* from *olla* (“pot”), where, once gathered, they are boiled. Therefore let us compare the hay of the world with the nobles, who readily prosper and are clothed, as it were, with the great grace of verdure. Let the vegetables of the field represent the ordinary and humble, which rise abundantly in uncultivated places and retain the wild and rough quality of their nature. But the former quickly withers, and the latter soon fall.

## CHAPTER IX. On Vegetables

A garden is so called because something is always growing there. While other land produces something once a year, a garden is never without fruit.

*Olus* (“vegetable”) is derived from *alere* (“to nourish”), because at first human beings were nourished by vegetables, before they ate crops and meat. They were nourished only by the fruits of trees and by vegetables, just as animals are by herbs.

The garden signifies the holy Church, in which various kinds of virtues are produced. Hence the Bridegroom says of the bride: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV).

The enclosed garden is the Church, because it produces the manifold shoots of spiritual works. It is a fountain because it overflows with saving doctrine. It is enclosed because it remains established, anointed under the Lord’s protection; it is sealed by the word of faith.

The garden has another meaning in the following passage from the Book of Kings, where it relates that King Ahab said to Naboth the Jezreelite: “Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it a garden of vegetables, because it is nearby and close to my house,” and so forth (1 Kings 21).

Naboth, whose name is interpreted as “conspicuous,” signifies the Lord Savior, who is the seed called Jezreel, because he is the true Son of God. He possessed a vineyard, of which it is written in Isaiah: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5).

Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “father’s brother,” coveted this vineyard: that is, the Jewish people, from whom Christ was pleased to assume flesh, coveted it in order to make it a garden of vegetables—that is, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to have germinated, to transplant every fragile doctrine through Pharisaic superstition.

But when Naboth refused to give him the vineyard—that is, when Christ did not consent to the superstitions of the Pharisees—his wicked wife Jezebel, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, plotted his death.

The garden signifies the inward delights of paradise. Hence it is said: “Enter into my garden, my sister, my bride” (Song V).

The garden also signifies the Jewish people, of whom it is said: “My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices” (Song VI).

Again, the garden signifies a certain pretense of hypocrites, as in Isaiah: “Those who consider themselves pure in the gardens” (Isa. 66).

The little bed signifies the Virgin Mary in the Song of Songs: “My beloved has gone up to his garden, to the bed of spices” (Song VI).

The little beds signify the hearts of the saints, fragrant with the scent of virtues. It is said above: “The beds of spices planted by the perfumers” (Song V).

The vegetable signifies simple and open preaching, as in the Apostle: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. 14). [Col. 0531B]

The smallest vegetable signifies a good work by which certain hypocrites strive to please human beings, as in the Gospel: “Woe to you, hypocritical Pharisees, who tithe mint and dill and cumin and every vegetable” (Matt. 23).

Onions and garlic signify corruption of mind and the bitterness of sin, which, the more they are eaten, the more they torment with pain. Hence in the Book of Numbers the children of Israel are read to have murmured and said: “The cucumbers and melons, the leeks and onions and garlic come to mind. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna” (Num. 11).

Mustard is so called because its leaves resemble those of the turnip. Mystically, this herb signifies the Gospel of Christ, as the Lord himself shows when he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed,” and so forth (Matt. 13). Sown in the hearts of believers, it germinates and produces the fruit of right faith and good works.

The Greeks call the radish *raphanos*; we call it *radix* (“root”), because it strives wholly downward, whereas the other vegetables shoot upward. Whoever has soaked its seed and stained his hands with it will handle snakes with impunity. Its root also whitens ivory, and as food it resists poisons.

For poisons, its roots are beneficial, as are walnuts, lupins, citron, and celery—but against poison yet to come, not against poison already received. Hence among the ancients these were customarily served at table before other dishes.

Figurally, this vegetable can express self-restraint and caution, which are highly effective against the poisonous suggestions of the devil and against the vices of the flesh.

Lettuce is so called because it overflows with an abundance of milk, or because it fills nursing women with milk. In men also it restrains sexual activity.

There is a wild lettuce which we call *sarralia*, because its back is shaped like a saw. The children of Israel were therefore commanded to eat wild lettuces at Passover with the roasted flesh of the lamb.

Wild lettuces are extremely bitter. The lamb’s flesh must be eaten with wild lettuces so that, when we receive the body of the Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves in tears for our sins, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind its perverse love of life.

Cucumbers are sometimes bitter, although they are said to grow sweet if their seed is soaked in honeyed milk. Concerning cucumbers and melons it is read in the Pentateuch that the children of Israel desired them, scorning manna—just as carnal desire rejects spiritual food and despises it.

The gourd is a herb requiring support from another. It signifies the weak and uneducated, who need the assistance of others to sustain them lest they fall. Gourds are mentioned in the prophet Jonah (Jon. 4).

Celery is so called because the crown—*apex*, that is, the head—of ancient victors was crowned with it. Hercules was the first to carry this herb around his head. For at one time he wore before the people a crown of poplar, at another of wild olive, and at another of celery. Its roots effectively combat the dangers of poisons.

Species of this kind are *petroselinum*, *hipposelinum*, and *olioselinum*.

*Petroselinum* is so called because it resembles celery and grows among rocks and steep mountains; we may call it “rock celery.” *Selinon* in Greek means “celery.” The finest and most esteemed variety is Macedonian, sweet in taste and aromatic in smell.

The Latins call fennel *feniculum*, because the sap of its clusters or root sharpens the sight. Its power is said to be such that snakes shed their annual old age by tasting it. The Greeks call this vegetable *marathron*.

What vegetables that are effective against poison signify mystically has already been explained above.

Lovage takes its name from a region, for it grows especially in Liguria. It is aromatic in smell and sharp in taste.

Coriander takes its name from the Greek word *corion*. Its seed, given in sweet wine, makes people more inclined toward sexual intercourse; if given in excessive quantity, it fosters madness. It is also said that gray hair can be dyed with coriander.

It is read in Exodus that manna was like coriander seed, white and somewhat translucent. Thus the word of God has the whiteness of chastity and the light of spiritual knowledge; by it faithful souls are nourished daily.

Rue is so called because it is extremely hot. One kind is wild and more powerful, but both are proved to be intensely hot. We learn from weasels that it resists poisons: when they have fought with a snake, they arm themselves by eating rue.

Rue signifies the faith of Christ, which is exceedingly powerful against the poisons of the ancient serpent.

# BOOK TWENTY

[Col. 0531]

## CHAPTER I. On Wars

[Col. 0531D]

King Ninus of the Assyrians was the first to institute wars. Not content with his own boundaries, he violated the bond of human society and began to lead armies, ravage the possessions of others, slaughter free peoples, or subject them. He subdued the whole of Asia with a new form of servitude, extending to the borders of Libya. From that time the world began to rage in mutual bloodshed through alternating slaughter.

There are four kinds of war: just, unjust, civil, and more-than-civil.

A just war is one undertaken, as prescribed, to recover property or to repel enemies. An unjust war is begun out of fury rather than legitimate reason. Concerning this Cicero says in *The Republic*: “Those wars are unjust which are undertaken without cause.” For no war can be just except one waged either for vengeance or for repelling enemies.

Tullius likewise added, with a brief interruption: “No war is considered just unless it has been announced, formally declared, and waged after restitution has been demanded.”

Civil war is a revolt and outbreak of tumult arising among citizens, such as that between Sulla and Marius, who waged civil war against each other within one people.

More-than-civil war is where not only citizens but also relatives fight, such as the war between Caesar and Pompey, when son-in-law and father-in-law fought against each other. In that struggle, indeed, brother fought brother and father bore arms against son.

Lucan:

> . . . The brother’s rewards fell upon the brother.

Again:

> . . . For whom the severed neck of his father  
> would yield . . . .

Wars are therefore called internal, external, servile, allied, and piratical.

Piratical wars consist of scattered bands of brigands across the seas, sailing in light and swift *myoparones*, who ravage not only ships carrying supplies but also islands and provinces. Gnaeus Pompey first suppressed and defeated them with remarkable speed, after the prolonged devastation they had inflicted on land and sea.

Just as the war waged against enemies is called war, so the disturbance aroused by civil sedition is called tumult. Sedition is disagreement among citizens, so called because some go apart from others.

Some think that disagreement of minds is called sedition, which the Greeks call *diastasis* (“separation”). Cicero explains how the two differ: “There can be war without tumult; but there cannot be tumult without war.” For what else is tumult but such disturbance that a greater fear arises? Hence *tumultus* is also understood as though from *timor multus*, “great fear.”

Tumult is more serious than war. For in war there are periods of leave; in tumult there are none.

War, battle, and engagement differ. War is the whole conflict, as in the Punic War; its parts are battles, such as those of Cannae and Trebia. Again, within a single battle there are many engagements: one is fought on the wings, another in the final line.

War, therefore, is the whole; battle is the action of one day; an engagement is a part of the battle.

War was formerly called *duellum*, because there are two sides of combatants, or because one side makes the other victorious and the other vanquished. Later, after a letter was changed and removed, it was called *bellum*.

Others think it was named by antiphrasis, because it is dreadful, as in “dreadful wars,” although war is in fact the worst thing.

Engagements are called *praelia* from pressing the enemy; hence also *prela*, the beams with which grapes are pressed.

A battle is called *pugna* because at the beginning people used to fight in war with their fists, or because they initially began wars with fists. Hence *pugna* may sometimes refer to a fight between two people without weapons.

These are the wars of worldly people, who struggle over worldly power. Among Christians, however, and faithful servants of God, there is another manner of fighting, about which the Apostle writes: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6).

And again: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified” (1 Cor. 9).

Wars or battles also signify the struggle against spiritual wickedness or against conflicts with vices, as in the Apostle: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (ibid.).

Again, war or struggle signifies the devil’s battle against the saints, as in Jeremiah: “They shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail” (Jer. 1).

Holy men always fight against vices and the temptations of the devil, and against the allurements of the flesh and the enticements of pleasures, so that they may be holy and undefiled in God’s sight, perfecting sanctification in his fear. Christ is their peace; he says to his disciples: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2).

Four things occur in war: battle, flight, victory, and peace.

The word *pax* (“peace”) seems to have been taken from *pactum* (“agreement”). Later peace is received; first, a treaty is made.

A treaty is peace made between combatants. It is called *foedus* either from *fides* (“faith”) or from *fictialibus* [*faecialibus*], that is, priests, because treaties were made through them, just as wars were conducted by secular men.

Others think that *foedera* (“treaties”) was derived from a sow being killed foully and cruelly, since her death was wished upon anyone who broke away from the peace.

Virgil:

> And they joined treaties with the slaughtered sow.

The parts of a treaty are truces. *Induciae* (“truces”) are so called as though from *in dies otii*, “days of rest.”

## CHAPTER II. On Triumphs

Every kingdom of this world is sought through wars and extended through victories.

Victory is so called because it is attained by force—that is, by strength. For this is the law of nations: to repel force with force. A victory gained by deceit is shameful.

A complete victory consists either in the killing of the enemy, in stripping him of his possessions, or in both. Yet a victory achieved through immense losses is not pleasing. This is what Sallust praises: commanders who brought home victory with an unbloodied army.

A procession is called *pompa*, in the Greek sense, from *apo tou pompeuein*, that is, “to be displayed publicly.” Victory precedes the procession because those going into this contest first make a vow for victory.

A trophy is called *trophaeum* from *apo tes tropes*, that is, from the turning and flight of the enemy. For one who put the enemy to flight deserved a trophy; one who killed him deserved a triumph. The latter is called *triumphus* from *apo tes triambes*, that is, from exultation.

A triumph is owed for a complete victory, a trophy for a partial one, because the victor has not yet achieved a full victory: he has not conquered the army but only put it to flight. Writers nevertheless confuse these names.

It was the Roman custom for those celebrating a triumph to be carried in four-horse chariots, deriving from the fact that earlier commanders were accustomed to enter wars in this manner.

Those who won in a conflict were crowned with a golden palm, because the palm has spines; but one who struck down a fleeing enemy without a conflict was crowned with laurel, because that tree has no thorns.

An army is destroyed in two ways: either by extermination or by dispersal.

Sallust says: “The enemies had either been crushed or scattered.” Virgil expresses both in turn. For extermination:

> . . . Bury the submerged ships.

For dispersal:

> Either drive them apart, or scatter their bodies upon the sea.

[Col. 0535B]

The spoils of enemies are called *praeda*, *manubiae*, *exuviae*, and *partes*.

*Praeda* is named from *praedari* (“to plunder”); *manubiae* because they are taken away by hand; they are also called *exuviae* from *exuere* (“to strip”), because they are stripped away; and *partes* from equal division, according to the rank of the persons and the just distribution of labor.

*Spolia* (“spoils”) is derived from *pallia* (“cloaks”), as though from *ex pallia*, because cloaks are stripped from the defeated.

Our victory is Christ, whose triumphal sign is the cross, by which he conquered the devil and overcame death. His spoils, which he took from the enemy, are human beings who believe in God. Rescued from the devil’s power, they are joined to their legitimate king.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “When a strong man armed keeps watch over his courtyard, everything he possesses is at peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

Victory signifies the triumph over the devil or the adversary, as in the Apostle: “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory” (1 Cor. 15).

The *bravium* is the appointed reward of good merits, as in the Apostle: “I pursue the appointed prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3).

The crown of eternal glory is the reward for righteousness, as in the Apostle: “From now on a crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4).

Peace is Christ, because he is the one who made both one (Eph. 2).

Peace of the flesh signifies concord against the spirit, concord directed toward good, as in the psalm: “Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem” (Ps. 121).

It is also understood in a negative sense of Jews or heretics, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not speak peaceful words to him at any time” (Deut. 2).

## CHAPTER III. On Instruments of War

[Col. 0535D]

War-signals are so called because the army receives from them the signal for fighting, victory, and retreat. For the army is either warned by the voice of a trumpet or by a signal.

## CHAPTER IV. On Trumpets and Horns

The *buccina*, by which a signal is given in the presence of the enemy, is named from its sound, as though *vocina* (“little voice”). For pagans and country people were summoned to crossroads by the *buccina* for every purpose.

Properly, therefore, this was a signal for country people, concerning which Propertius wrote:

> The horn was already summoning the ancient Quirites to arms.

Its blast is called *buccinium*.

The Tyrrhenians were the first to invent the trumpet. It is called *tuba*, as though *tofa*, that is, “hollow.” Likewise, *tuba* is like *tibia* (“flute” or “pipe”).

The ancients distinguished between the trumpet and the horn. The sounding horn announced the urgency of war. Virgil:

> . . . The horn gave  
> the dreadful signal . . . .

The trumpet, however, announced battles:

> But the trumpet gave a terrifying sound . . . .

Its sound varies. Sometimes it is played so that battle may begin; sometimes so that the fleeing may be pursued; sometimes it is played for retreat.

A retreat is so called because the army withdraws to safety. Hence the signals for retreat are said to be sounded.

The trumpet or horn signifies the voice of holy preachers, which resounds throughout the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel and summons the spiritual soldiers of Christ to battle. By teaching, warning, and exhorting, they instruct God’s people and show what must be done and what must be avoided.

Whoever keeps watch over himself according to its indications and lives according to its teaching will receive eternal life.

## CHAPTER V. On Weapons

Weapons, in general, are instruments for all things; hence the places where they are stored are called armories.

Weapons are also called missiles of every kind. But *arma* are the things by which we defend ourselves, whereas *tela* are the things we throw.

Weapons are of two kinds: those with which we strike and those with which we protect ourselves.

*Arma* is properly so called because it covers the *armi* (“shoulders” or “upper arms”). The word may be derived from *armus*, “shoulder,” as in:

> . . . The spear, driven through his broad shoulders,  
> trembles . . . .

Or it may come from the Greek *apo tou Areos*, that is, “from Ares.”

Mystically, weapons signify the sayings of sacred Scripture or *exercitus* (“army”) [perhaps *exercitiis*, “exercises”] of the virtues. Hence the Apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal but spiritual, powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds” (2 Cor. 10)—that is, of vices and errors by which hostile people, urged on by the devil, fight against the soldiers of Christ.

The armory is sacred Scripture or right faith. From it spiritual weapons are brought forth against the enemies of the Christian faith and the attackers of true religion.

Weapons also signify divine protection and his assistance to the saints, as in the Psalter: “Take hold of weapon and shield” (Ps. 34).

Weapons signify works of righteousness against the vices of the devil, as in the Apostle: “Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist” (Eph. 6).

Weapons signify works of sin or the devil’s snares, as in the psalm: “He will burn the weapons and shields with fire” (Ps. 45).

## CHAPTER VI. On Swords
The sword (*gladius*) is generally called an *ensis* in battle, but *ensis* denotes only the iron. The *gladius*, however, denotes the whole weapon. Properly speaking, it is called *gladius* because it divides the throat (*gulam*), that is, cuts the neck. For this purpose it was first made; for limbs are more often cut with axes, whereas the neck is cut only with a sword. The sword’s edge (*acies*) is so called from its sharpness.

The hilt (*capulus*) is so called either because it is the head of the sword or because it is grasped there, so that the weapon may be held. Otherwise, the edge of the iron does not permit this. The point (*mucro*) belongs not only to a sword but to the sharp end of any weapon. It is named from its length: for the Greeks call something long *makron*; hence also *machaera*. A *machaera* is a long sword sharpened on one side.

A *framea* is a sword sharpened on both sides, which the common people call a *spatha*; it is the same as a *romphaea*. *Framea* is so called because it is made of iron: just as one says “iron implement,” so one says *framea*; therefore every sword is a *framea*.

The sword is understood both in a good and in a bad sense. In the good sense, as in the Apostle: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). In the bad sense, as in the Psalmist: “Sinners have drawn the sword” (Ps. XXXVI).

The sword of the sinner is any deceit that seeks to harm another. For the man who strives to despoil the poor draws out the sword of his perverse plan; and the man who desires by evil persuasion to deceive innocent souls displays the sword of his most wicked thought. “They have drawn out” signifies “they have unsheathed”: what previously lay hidden in thought, as though concealed in a scabbard, appears after being drawn out, when the thoughts have been revealed.

The *framea* signifies divine vengeance against the wicked, as in the Psalm: “Pour out the sword, and shut it against those who persecute me” (Ps. XXXIV). Elsewhere: “Deliver my soul from the sword” (Ps. XXI); for he asked to be freed from the death that he was about to undergo, through the gift of resurrection. *Framea* is a synonymous term, signifying either a spear, or a sword, or any weapons by which the future outcome of the cross was appropriately foreshadowed, since it is often brought about through such weapons. At first he said, “Deliver my soul”; now he asks that the Church, which is his one Church—that is, the catholic Church—be delivered, so that it may be understood that he rejected new doctrines and the assemblies of the lost under the name of unity.

The *framea* also signifies vengeance inflicted upon the innocent, as in the Psalmist’s words concerning sinners: “The swords of the enemies have failed completely” (Ps. IX). “Of the enemies” is a genitive expression, that is, of the devil, whose sword is testified to have failed. *Framea* is a Hebrew word signifying the sword with which that enemy raged. By the words “completely” the consummation of the age is understood, when the devil’s power is proved to be destroyed by that almighty sword. Concerning it he said in the seventh Psalm: “Unless you repent, he will brandish his sword,” and so forth (Ps. VII).

The *spatha* is named from suffering, according to a Greek word: for the Greeks say *pathein*, “to suffer,” whence we say *patior* and *patitur*. A *semispathium* is a sword named from half the length of a *spatha*, not—as the foolish common people say—“without space,” because it is swifter than an arrow.

The *pugio* is named from stabbing and piercing through. It is a small, double-edged sword, worn at the side. It is also called a *clunabulum*, because it is fastened at the hips.

The *sica* is named from cutting. It is a short sword, used especially by those who practice brigandage among the Italians; from it they are also called *sicarii* [Col. 0538A].

The sword has many meanings, and is understood both in a good and in a bad sense, as we have shown above. For the sword signifies the word of God and the severity of the Law and the Prophets, as in the Apocalypse: “And a sword was proceeding from his mouth” (Apoc. I), that is, the word of the Lord.

The sword is the power of the love of God, as in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X).

The swords in the hands of the saints are the testimonies of divine Scripture from both Testaments of the Law, brought to a sharp point, as in the Psalm: “And swords sharp on both sides in their hands” (Ps. CXLIX). And in the Apostle: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

The swords are the two Testaments of the Law, as in the Gospel according to Luke: “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke XXII).

The sword is the preaching of heretics, as in Solomon: “Which has swords for teeth” (Prov. XXX). And in the Gospel: “Everyone who strikes with the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI).

The sword is the devil’s seduction, as in the Psalter: “You who delivered your servant from the evil sword” (Ps. CXLIII).

The sword is everlasting condemnation, as in Job: “If his sons are multiplied”—that is, the disciples of heretics—“they shall be for the sword” (Job XXVII).

The sword is God’s judgment, as in Jeremiah: “Before the sword of the dove each one shall turn to his own people” (Jer. XLVI).

The sword is vengeance or the word of the Lord, as in the Apostle: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. IV).

The *romphaea* is the same as the term explained above.

The *machaera* is a deceitful discourse, full of ambushes, as in the Psalm: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI).

Axes (*secures*) are the insignia carried before the consuls. The Spaniards, borrowing the term through the usage of the Franks, call them *franciscas*. Such insignia used to be carried before the consul, so that the practice of war would not be lost through disuse, nor the sight of swords be forgotten through idleness.

An axe is an iron implement with which wood is cut for human use. Mystically, it signifies either evangelical preaching or the sentence of judgment, as in the Gospel: “For now the axe has been laid at the root of the trees” (Matt. III).

The tree of this world is the whole human race. The axe is our Redeemer, who consists, as it were, of a handle and iron: he is held by reason of his humanity, but cuts by reason of his divinity. This axe has already been laid at the root of that tree, because although he waits in patience, what he is about to do is already apparent.

The name “axe” may also signify the preaching of the evangelical word, because, according to the Apostle, “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts” (Heb. IV). The prophet Jeremiah likewise compares the word of the Lord to an axe cutting rock.

Or the axe signifies the sentence of the Most High’s judgment, which has been laid at the roots of the tree—that is, at the end of the kingdom of the Jewish people—in order to cut off from the land of the living those who refused to believe in Christ.

## CHAPTER VII. On Spears

A *hasta* is a shaft with iron attached; its diminutive is *hastile*. The word *hasta* derives from *astus*, whence also *astutia*, “craft.”

A *contus* has no iron; it consists only of a sharp point. Virgil:

> “And iron-shod poles, and shafts with sharpened point.”

A *contus* is as though from *conitus*, for a *conus* is a sharp rounded form.

In its symbolic meaning, a spear or spear-shaft may signify the devil’s temptation, through which the ancient enemy envies the salvation of the human race and prepares its destruction. Thus Scripture reports concerning the giant Goliath: “The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam,” and so forth (1 Sam. XVII).

The battle of the Philistines against Israel may appropriately be understood as the battle of evil spirits against the Church of God. From the camp—namely, the Philistine camp—there comes forth a bastard man named Goliath, of extraordinary size. He may rightly signify the devil’s pride, which our David, engaging it in single combat, struck down and thus delivered God’s people from its fear. David killed the lion and the bear: the bear signifies the devil, who now secretly lies in wait for human beings; the lion signifies Antichrist, who will rage openly in the future.

A *lancea* is a spear having a thong in the middle. It is called *lancea* because it is balanced and hurled with an equal thong. The *amentum* is the strap of javelins and spear-shafts, fitted around the middle of the spears; hence it is called *amentum*, because the middle of the spear is bound and the weapon is thrown.

A club (*clava*) is such as Hercules had. It is so called because it consists of iron nails fastened together, and is a cubit and a half in length. It is also called a *cateja*, which Lucilius calls a *caia*. It is a kind of Gallic weapon made from especially tough wood. When thrown, it does not fly far because of its weight, but wherever it reaches, it shatters with tremendous force; if thrown by a skilled craftsman, it returns to him.

The lance may signify the pain of the Passion or the opening of the sacraments. Thus it is written in the Prophet: “They wounded me with their lances.” And during the Lord’s Passion one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out (John XIX).

The Evangelist therefore used an elegant word when he did not say, “He struck” or “wounded” his side, or anything similar, but “opened,” so that there might in some manner be opened there the door of life, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed—without them one does not enter into life, which is true life. That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water makes the saving cup temperate; it supplies both washing and drink.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Arrows

An arrow (*sagitta*) is named from a swift shot, that is, a rapid blow. It is carried by feathers like a bird, so that death may swiftly travel to a human being. The Cretans were the first to use such arrows. As we have said, feathers are fastened to them so that they may be light and fly swiftly [lacuna].

Small darts (*spicula*) are short arrows or spears, named from their resemblance to ears of grain.

A *scorpio* is a poisoned arrow shot from a bow or from machines of war. When it reaches a person, it injects the venom with which it pierces; hence it received the name *scorpio*.

Concerning arrows it is written in Job: “The arrows of the Lord are in me, and their indignation drinks up my spirit” (Job VI). Here, under the name of arrows, the sentence of divine punishment is signified. The holy man, therefore, considering the misery of his exile and lamenting that he groans beneath the persecutions of the Lord’s judgment, says: “Therefore my words are full of pain, because the arrows of the Lord are in me.” It is as though he said: “I do not rejoice in the condemnation of exile; rather, placed under judgment, I grieve, because I recognize the force of persecution.”

The arrow is the Lord Jesus Christ, wounding the hearts of his elect for their salvation, as in Isaiah: “He hid me like an arrow in his quiver” (Isa. XLIX).

The arrow is the divine commandment, as in the Psalter: “The arrows of the little ones became their wounds” (Ps. LXIII), that is, of the apostles. Elsewhere: “He sent forth his arrows and scattered them” (Ps. XVII).

Arrows are the enemy’s ambushes or the discourse of heretics, as in Jeremiah: “A wounding arrow is the tongue of the enemy” (Jer. IX).

At times, as we have said, the name “arrows” expresses the sentences of divine Law. Hence the Psalm says: “Your arrows are sharp, O Most Powerful” (Ps. XLIV). Elsewhere, the sharp arrows are the words of the Lord, the Savior of humanity: “The sharp arrows of the Mighty One” (Ps. CXIX), piercing hearts for their salvation. They wound in order to heal; they strike in order to free; they overthrow in order to raise up.

Arrows have another meaning in the Psalm’s statement: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X). The comparison with the archer remains: just as the archer has arrows in his quiver, so the enemy carries poisonous words in his heart.

“ In darkness” means either when the Church is troubled by persecutions, when carnal people are thought to be more easily changed by fear of danger, or in a hidden plan, when they think it more advantageous to deceive Christians because they believe that their schemes are unseen. But when he says “the upright in heart,” he shows that their ambushes are empty and ineffectual.

## CHAPTER IX. On Quivers

A quiver (*pharetra*) is a case for arrows, named from carrying missiles, just as a *feretrum* is the bier on which a corpse is carried. These words share an etymology because the quiver carries death, while the bier carries the dead.

*Coriti* properly are cases for bows, just as quivers are cases for arrows.

The quiver is either sacred Scripture, from which the arrows of divine judgments are brought forth and the prophets and apostles send the missiles of preaching; or it is the humanity of our Savior, who speaks in Isaiah: “He made me like a chosen arrow, and hid me in his quiver” (Isa. XLIX).

When he says “chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not all are chosen. These arrows are the prophets and apostles, who run throughout the whole world. Concerning them it is also sung elsewhere: “Your arrows are sharp, O Most Powerful; peoples shall fall beneath you” (Ps. XLIV). Again: “The sharp arrows of the Mighty One, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX).

Christ, however, among the many arrows and numerous sons, is the one chosen arrow and the only-begotten Son, whom he hid in his quiver—that is, in a human body—“so that the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily in him” (Col. II), and so that he might be the faith of things hoped for. Of him it is also said above: “You are a hidden God” (Isa. XLV), and “we did not know.”

The bride, wounded by this arrow, speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song II).

A scabbard (*vagina*) is so called because the point or sword is carried in it.

A case (*theca*) is so called because it covers whatever has been received, with the letter *c* put in place of *g*. Others maintain that it is called *theca* from the Greek word because something is stored there; hence *bibliotheca* means a repository of books.

The scabbard signifies the concealment of a plan or the postponement of judgment. Thus it is written in the Psalm: “Unless you repent, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. VII).

This threatens the obstinate Jews, who, having despised the Lord’s Law, served idols with most abominable rites. Unless they repent, he will brandish his sword against them—that is, he will send his only Son in radiant glory.

We call that “brandished” which is seen at one moment to display light and at another trembling shadows. This was fulfilled in the incarnation of Christ the Lord, when he showed the darkness of his divinity to the faithless but its light to the faithful.

A bow (*arcus*) is so called because it wards off the adversary; hence fortresses are called *arces*, because enemies are driven away from them. The bow is also named from its form, because its ends are curved like arches [Al., “more tightly”].

In the mystical sense, the bow is the evangelical word, as in Genesis: “His bow remains firm” (Gen. XLIX), that is, the Lord’s; and in the Apocalypse: “A bow was given to him” (Apoc. VI).

The bow is the doctrine of heretics, as in the Psalter: “For behold, sinners have bent their bow” (Ps. X). Again, concerning the bow, it is written in the Psalm: “He bent his bow and prepared it” (Ps. VII).

We therefore appropriately understand the bow as the Scripture of the New and Old Testaments, because, through two curved arcs, as it were, it embraces the necks of the devoted. To the faithful it shows a gentle yoke; to the obstinate it reveals terrifying weapons. The words “he bent it” were added so that his patience would not be thought to be lax.

What follows—“And in it he prepared the vessels of death; he made his arrows for the burning ones” (ibid.)—shows the distribution of divine majesty. Through the bow, that is, through the Old and New Testament, as has already been said, the effect of death comes, and through its arrows life is bestowed.

From this bow went forth arrows, that is, the apostles, who sent salutary commandments in the manner of arrows, with burning—that is, desirous—hearts. Thus the wicked would be wounded, while effective healing would come to the faithful.

## CHAPTER X. On Slings

A sling (*funda*) is so called because stones are poured from it, that is, discharged.

A *ballista* is a kind of engine of war, named from hurling missiles. For *ballein* in Greek means “to throw.” It is twisted by the striking force of sinews and hurls either spears or stones with great power; hence it is also called a *fundibalus*, as though “pouring out and discharging.”

A tortoise formation (*testudo*) is effective against a ballista: it is a formation made of shields joined together by their bosses.

The sling is the Church, as it is said concerning Antichrist in Job: “All the stones of the sling have become stubble to him” (Job XLI). And in Zechariah: “They shall cast them into the stones of the sling” (Zech. IX).

Concerning the sling, we read in the Book of Kings: “David chose for himself five very smooth stones from the brook, put them in the shepherd’s bag that he carried with him, took the sling in his hand, and went out against the Philistine” (1 Sam. XVII). This signifies that Christ, through the five books of the Law in the unity of love, overcame the devil by the sling of preaching and condemned and destroyed him with his own sword—that is, with his own wickedness [Col. 0542B].

## CHAPTER XI. On the Battering Ram

The battering ram (*aries*) received its name from its form, because it strikes the wall with force in the manner of fighting rams. The head of a strong, knotty tree is covered with iron; suspended by ropes and operated by many hands, it is driven against the wall. Then it is pulled backward and hurled forward with greater force. Thus, by repeated blows, the side of the wall is shaken, gives way, is hollowed out, and makes a breach and an opening for those about to enter.

A sack filled with straw, lowered into the place struck by the ram, is a remedy against its impact. For when the sack’s loose interior receives the blow, the impact of the ram is softened and dissipated; harder things more readily yield to softer ones.

*Plutei* are wicker screens covered with rawhide, held before the enemy during military work.

Rams are the goads of temptation or the assaults of persecution, as in the words: “And you shall place rams around it” (Ezek. IV).

## CHAPTER XII. On Shields

A *clypeus* is a large shield, so called because it conceals the body and withdraws it from danger, from the Greek *apo tou kleptein*, “to hide.” Placed before the body, it protects it by its defense from spears and javelins.

The *clypeus* belongs to infantry, while the *scutum* belongs to cavalry. The *scutum* is so called because it shakes off the blow of weapons; to resist missiles, the shield is held before the body.

Concerning the shield it is written in Proverbs: “Every word of God is a burning shield to those who hope in him” (Prov. XXX). The whole Church of Christ knows this, and especially those experience it who, with God dwelling with them, despise the pride of earthly wisdom.

For every word of divine authority both kindles the hearts of the elect with the fire of love and illumines them with knowledge of the truth. It consumes the filth of vices, if it finds any in them, and protects those who hope in him from the ambushes of enemies and from every adversity.

Again, it is written in the Song of Songs: “A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song IV). This signifies the testimonies of the holy Scriptures.

The *umbo* is the central part of a shield, like a navel.

An *ancile* is a short, round shield, of which Virgil speaks:

> “And on his left arm he carried a sacred shield.”

The *ancile* is so called from *ancisio*, “cutting,” because it is, as it were, cut away on every side, that is, round. Ovidius:

> “And they call it an *ancile*, because it is cut away on every side;  
> Every angle is absent wherever the eye observes it.”

A *pelta* is a very small shield shaped like a half-moon. The Book of Kings mentions it: “King Solomon made two hundred shields of pure gold and three hundred *peltae* of tested gold” (1 Kings X).

A *cetra* is a leather shield without wood, used by Africans and Moors. Concerning it the poet says:

> “The left side is covered by the *cetra*.”

A *parma* is a light weapon, as though *parva*, “small”; it is not a *clypeus*. A *testudo* is also called a shield, for a *clypeus* is made in the form of a tortoise. A *testudo* is likewise a curved joining of shields in the shape of a tortoise.

In the various kinds of weapons, soldiers also take their names from animals, as with the ram. Sallustius says: “In the manner of a military hedgehog.”

The shield signifies either faith, as in the Apostle: “Taking the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Eph. VI); or divine assistance, as in the Psalmist: “Take up arms and shield, and rise to my aid” (Ps. XXXIV).

The shield also signifies hardness of heart or the defense of sin, as in Jeremiah: “You will give them, Lord, the shield of heart—your labor” (Lam. III).

*Arma* is derived from *arcere*, “to ward off,” because by means of them we ward off the most violent enemies. Therefore, in ordinary human usage, this is said of the weapon that arms the hand so that it may crush the enemy.

In truth, however, the arms and shield are the Lord’s will alone: he protects the endangered and conquers the adversary. The shield is also called as though it were “engraved” (*sculptum*), because the ancients marked their deeds upon it.

When Scripture says “take up,” does this mean that a foreign defense is taken from him for a time? He is always prepared for the outcomes of events, since he is proved omnipotent. He is not thought to rise from rest, as though he had ever lain down; rather, he is shown never to have lain down.

Arms therefore pertain to iron garments by which human safety is defended; the shield is for repelling the enemy’s blows, so that the missiles intended for human destruction fall frustrated.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Breastplates

A *lorica* is so called because it lacks thongs (*loris*); it is woven solely from iron rings.

A coat of mail made of scales (*squama*) is an iron breastplate formed from iron or bronze plates linked together in the manner of a fish’s scales. It is named from the brilliance and likeness of those scales.

Breastplates are also polished and covered with haircloth.

The breastplate signifies the observance of righteousness, which protects a person and preserves him unharmed from the enemy. Just as a person is difficult to wound in those places especially that preserve life when he wears a breastplate of virtue, described as *conservatam* [variant: *consertam*, “fastened together”], with hooks and iron rings holding one another together, so a person surrounded by a many-layered garment of righteousness will neither receive an arrow in the liver like a deer, nor fall into desires, and will calm passions with a pure heart.

God is the craftsman of this breastplate. He fashions every kind of armor for each of the saints; he does not allow them to perish from the dart of pleasure or to be struck and tormented by the burning arrows.

The breastplate is also understood in a bad sense, as in Ezekiel: “Against Gog, all shielded and wearing breastplates” (Ezek. XXXVIII).

## CHAPTER XIV. On Helmets

A *cassis* is made of a sheet of metal; a *galea* is made of leather. For *galeros* means “leather.” They say that the *cassis* was named by the Etruscans. They call a helmet *cassus*, I believe, from the head.

The crest-support (*apex*) is what projects from the top of the helmet and to which the crest is fastened. The Greeks call it *konos*. A *conus* is the curve that projects from the helmet, above which the crests are placed.

The helmet or *cassis*, which defends our head—that is, our mind—against the enemy’s weapons, is hope in the Lord our Savior. Therefore the Apostle urges us to put on the helmet of salvation, since we wage war against exceedingly savage enemies, skilled in every kind of deception.

For this reason we must remain vigilant with every care and concern, so that, however they may attempt to attack us, they may find us fortified and prepared. God must help those whom he sees keeping watch in prayer and awaiting victory from his weapons.

In such warfare a sober mind and a pure conscience are necessary, because the battle is not against fleshly things but against spiritual wickedness. Against earthly enemies the body is strengthened by nourishment and the mind is inflamed by food, so that it may gain courage to resist. Against spiritual wickedness, however, one must fight spiritually and take up the weapons of sobriety and abstinence, so that, filled with the Holy Spirit, we may overcome unclean and wandering spirits.

Thus we shall gird our loins in truth if we are prepared to resist error. For everyone who wishes to work girds himself, so that, once the impediment has been removed, he may work more diligently.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Forum

The *forum*, a place for conducting lawsuits, is named from *fari*, “to speak.” This place is also called the *rostra*, because, after the ships of the Carthaginians had been captured in the Punic War, their beaks (*rostra*) were removed and fixed in the Roman forum, so that they might serve as a sign of that victory.

There are four meanings of *forum*. First, it is a place left in a city for holding markets. Second, it is the place where magistrates customarily judge. Third, it is the place mentioned above, which we have called a *calcatorium*. Fourth, it means the flat spaces on ships. Concerning these Virgil says:

> “And he opens the decks.”

The forum consists of a case, a law, and a judge.

A case (*causa*) is so called from the event (*casus*) through which it arises. It is the matter and origin of a dispute, before examination has yet taken place. While it is being presented, it is a case; while it is being examined, it is a judgment; when it is concluded, it is justice.

A judgment (*judicium*) is so called as though *juris dictio*, “the pronouncement of law”; justice (*justitia*) as though *juris status*, “the state of the law.”

A judgment was formerly called an inquiry. Hence we call those placed in charge of judgments *quaestores* or *quaesitores*, “inquirers.”

Concerning a case it is written in the Psalter: “Arise, Lord, and judge your cause” (Ps. LXXIII). After everything he has said, he now turns the matter into a judge’s case, so that he may move more effectively the one to whom the nature of his affair is being disclosed. He now turns his words to the Lord himself, asking him to judge his case against those who do not cease to assail him with the most wicked murmuring.

He judges his cause when he makes the erring recognize what is manifest, so that, once converted, they may proclaim what they had rejected in their foolish thoughts.

Concerning judgment it is written: “Give your judgment to the king, O God” (Ps. LXXI). *Judicium* is so called as though *juris dictum*, that is, because the law is pronounced in it. To prove most clearly that this is truly a petition, he repeats the same request in the following clause: “And your justice to the king’s son.” This repeats what was said above: “Give your judgment to the king.” You frequently find such repetition in the divine Scriptures for expressing the same matter.

*Negotium* has several meanings. Sometimes it means the conduct of some affair, to which leisure (*otium*) is opposed; sometimes the prosecution of a case, which is litigation. It is called *negotium* as though *nec otium*, “not leisure,” that is, activity without leisure.

In legal cases one speaks of *negotium*; in commerce, of *negotiatio*, where something is given so that greater profit may be gained.

*Jurgium* is so called as though *juris garrium*, “the quarrel of law,” because those who plead a case dispute according to law.

*Lis* first took its name from the contest over boundaries, concerning which Virgil says:

> “A boundary had been set to divide the dispute among the fields.”

A case rests either upon argument or upon proof. Argument never provides evidence through witnesses or documents; it discovers the truth solely through investigation. Hence *argumentum* means an ingenious discovery. Proof, however, rests upon witnesses and the reliability of documents.

A matter may be praiseworthy, namely, when one labors in spiritual pursuits, as in the Gospel: “Conduct your business until I come” (Luke XIX). Hence spiritual merchants are said to be those who seek good pearls.

Conversely, another matter is blameworthy, namely, what is pursued in worldly desire. Concerning this the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. II).

Cases likewise are sometimes praiseworthy and sometimes blameworthy. They are praiseworthy when they concern the virtues; they are blameworthy when they pertain to worldly contentions.

The Psalmist says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. XLII). He does not ask that his sins be examined, but that he be freed from the company of the wicked. It would be dangerous to say merely “Judge me” unless he had added “and distinguish my cause,” that is, “separate me from the mixture in which I endure in this world, and at some time, once separated from the impious, establish me among the chosen people.”

He adds, “from an unholy nation,” that is, from the perverse and wickedly living.

In another prophet we read that the Lord rebuked sinners, saying: “Behold, you keep watch for lawsuits and contentions, and you strike with the fist wickedly” (Isa. LVIII). How blameworthy this is, is clear.

In every judgment six persons are sought: a judge, an accuser, a defendant, and three witnesses.

A judge (*judex*) is so called as though “one who speaks the law to the people,” or because he argues according to law.

In the sacred Scriptures the judge is sometimes our God himself, who judges all things according to equity. Hence the Prophet says: “God is a just judge, strong and patient” (Ps. VII).

Human beings are also called judges. Thus it is written in the Law: “Appoint judges in your gates, who shall judge the people with equity” (Deut. XVI).

An accuser (*accusator*) is so called as though *adcausator*, “one who calls to a case,” because he summons to trial the one whom he accuses.

The accuser signifies the devil, concerning whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “Rejoice, heavens, and all who dwell in them, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down” (Apoc. XII).

A defendant (*reus*) is named from the matter (*res*) for which he is sued. For although he may not be conscious of any crime, he is nevertheless called a defendant as long as he is sued in court concerning some matter.

In the Scriptures, *reus* is used for a guilty person and sinner. Hence: “Whoever kills a human being is guilty of death” (Exod. XXI).

Witnesses were formerly called *superstites*, “survivors,” because they were brought forward concerning the standing of the case. Now, with part of the name removed, they are called *testes*.

A witness is considered according to status, nature, and life: according to status, if free and not enslaved—for often a slave suppresses the testimony of truth through fear of his master; according to nature, if male and not female, for:

> “Woman is ever a changeable and mutable thing …”

Life, if innocent and upright in conduct; for if a good life is lacking, it will lack faith. Justice cannot have fellowship with a criminal.

There are two kinds of witnesses: either by stating what they have seen, or by reporting what they have heard. Witnesses offend in two ways: when they either utter falsehoods or cover true things with silence.

In Holy Scripture, those are called witnesses who truthfully report what they have seen and heard. Thus God himself says to his apostles: “And you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I). Hence, when Peter and John had been detained by the Jews and forbidden to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus to anyone, they answered them: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves; for we cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts IV).

Therefore those who persevere in right faith and in confessing Christ’s name even unto death are called martyrs—that is, witnesses of Christ. By speaking rightly and acting well in their lives, and likewise in their deaths, they offered the Lord a faithful testimony. Thus the Apostle, enumerating the virtues of the saints, added at the end, saying: “All these were found approved by the testimony of faith” (Hebrews XI).

And, to recapitulate everything briefly: God is the judge, as we showed above, as in the Psalter: “God is a just judge, strong and patient” (Psalm VII). The apostles are judges, as in the Gospel: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX). The apostles and the other faithful are witnesses, as in the Apostle: “We testify concerning God that he raised Jesus Christ from the dead” (Acts IV, V). Christ is a witness, as in the Apocalypse: “Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness” (Apocalypse I); and in Isaiah: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples” (Isaiah LV).

False witnesses are the Jews or heretics, as in the Psalm: “For unjust witnesses have risen against me” (Psalm XXVI). And in Deuteronomy: “If an unjust witness stands up and brings false testimony against his neighbor” (Deuteronomy XIX).

Judgment is the discernment of good and evil, as in the Psalter: “If you truly speak justice, judge rightly, children of men” (Psalm LVII). Judgment is the separation of the good from the company of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “And he will separate them from one another” (Matthew XXV); and in the Psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Psalm XLII).

Judgment is future condemnation, as Truth speaks in the Gospel concerning the faithful: “Whoever believes in me will not be judged” (John III). Conversely, concerning the reprobate: “But whoever does not believe has already been judged” (ibid.), that is, condemned.

Judgment consists in reproving or condemning the unjust, as in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matthew VII); and in the Apostle: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Romans XIV).

Judgment is the confession of the penitent; for when he accuses himself and praises God’s judgment, that is true judgment. Concerning this judgment the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying: “Bring me to remembrance, and let us be judged together” (Isaiah XLIII); and in Job: “And do you consider it worthy to open your eyes upon such a one and bring him with you into judgment?” (Job XIV); and in the Apostle: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians XI).

Judgment is the presumption of certain people who exalt themselves on account of their own righteousness; to them the Lord answered through Jeremiah, saying: “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me” (Jeremiah II).

The enemy is understood allegorically as the devil, as in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew XIII). Enemies are the Jews or heretics, as in Micah: “A man’s enemies are his household” (Micah VII)—that is, Christ’s household.

The adversary is the divine word, because it commands things contrary to human will, as in the Gospel: “Agree with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matthew V). The adversary is the devil, as in Zechariah: “And Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zechariah III).

The cruel one is the devil, as in Solomon: “Do not give your honor to strangers”—that is, to demons—“or your years to the cruel one” (Proverbs V). Strangers are demons, Jews, or heretics, as in the Psalm: “For strangers have risen against me” (Psalm LIII). Outsiders are demons, as in Solomon: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in a foreign house” (Proverbs V).

The thief is the devil, as in Hosea: “And the thief strips, while the robber is outside” (Hosea VII). Robbers are demons, in Job: “His robbers came together” [the text also reads, “came all together”] “and made their way through me” (Job XIX). Thieves and robbers are heretics or the teachers of the Jews, in the Gospel: “All who came are thieves and robbers” (John X).

The thief is death arriving unexpectedly, as in the Gospel: “Know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Matthew XXIV). The thief is the day of judgment, in the Apostle: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians V).

## CHAPTER XVI. On Spectacles

Spectacles, as I believe, are generally called pleasures that do not defile by themselves, but through what takes place there. They are called *spectacula* because a public viewing (*inspectio*) is provided there for people. They are also called *ludicra*, because they take place in games or on stages.

Concerning the spectacle we read in the Apostle: “We have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels and to human beings” (1 Corinthians IV). Enoch and Elijah will be a spectacle to such an extent that their bodies will be thrown into the street in the sight of the entire unbelieving people. So too the apostles became a spectacle, because they were publicly mocked and exposed to the insult and death that they suffered.

He called angels and human beings “the world,” because there are also evil angels, as David says in Psalm LXXIV: “He afflicted them through evil angels.” There are also evil and unbelieving human beings; the insults suffered by the apostles are their amusement. The world is called unbelief because it follows visible things.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Gymnastic Game

The gymnastic game is the glory of speed and strength. Its place is called a gymnasium, where athletes exercise and the speed of runners is tested. Hence it happened that the exercises of almost all arts came to be called gymnasia.

Formerly, those competing in the games were girded so that they would not be naked. Later, when a certain runner suddenly fell prostrate and lifeless after his girdle had been loosened, the archon Hippomenes, by decree of the council, permitted them thereafter to exercise naked. From that time the place was called a gymnasium, because young men exercise naked in the field, covering only their private parts.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Kinds of Gymnastic Contest

There are five kinds of gymnastic contest: jumping, running, throwing, strength, and wrestling. Hence they say that a certain king, having that many adolescent sons, ordered them to compete for the kingdom in the same number of events.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Jumping

Jumping is so called as if from “springing upward” (*exsilire in altum*); for a jump is either to spring higher or farther. Mystically, jumping signifies progress in the virtues, as in Isaiah: “Then the lame man will leap like a stag” (Isaiah XXXV).

“To leap” means to rejoice with all one’s strength in the Lord, as it is said of David in the Book of Kings: “And he leaped before the ark of the Lord with all his strength” (2 Kings VI). In another sense, in the Gospel: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance” (Luke VII).

## CHAPTER XX. On Running

Running is named from the speed of the legs; for running is the swiftness of the feet. Mystically, running refers to the passing of the present life, or to the contest in which Christ’s soldiers labor in this world. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that those who run in the race all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it” (1 Corinthians IX)—that is, so that you may receive the palm of victory and the full reward of your labor.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Throwing

Throwing (*jactus*) is named from throwing (*jacere*). Hence the fishing net is also called a “throwing implement” (*jaculum*). This art consists in striking stones taken up for the purpose from a distance, throwing spears with measured force, and shooting arrows from a bow.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Strength

Strength is the magnitude of bodily power in labor and weight. Strength pertains to spiritual exercise, so that by virtues we may conquer and overcome vices.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Wrestling

Wrestling is named from the clasping of the sides, upon which those who compete at close quarters lean. In Greek terminology they are called athletes. Our wrestling, however, is spiritual, not carnal; for, as the Apostle testifies (Ephesians VI), “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Wrestling Ground

The place of wrestling is called a *palaestra*. They say that *palaestra* was named either from *apo tēs palēs*, that is, “from wrestling,” or from *apo tou pallein*, that is, “from the motion of a powerful fall”—namely, because in wrestling they seize their opponents around the middle, almost shaking them; among the Greeks this is called *pallein*.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Contest

What the Latins call contests, the Greeks call *agōnes*, from the crowds by which they are celebrated, since every gathering and assembly is called an *agōn*. Others think that they were called *agōnes* because they were held in circles, in places as it were “without an angle” (*sine angulo*).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Kinds of Contest

The kinds of contest are these: magnitude of strength; speed in running; skill in shooting arrows; endurance in standing; bodily movements performed to the cithara and the flutes; contests concerning character, appearance, and the modulation of singing; contests of land warfare and naval battle; and contests in enduring punishments.

From the worldly contest the Apostle took an example for the spiritual contest, saying: “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things. They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one,” and so forth (1 Corinthians IX).

Let us inquire what he means by “all things,” so that through comparison with the bodily contest we may acquire instruction for the spiritual contest. Those who strive in this visible contest to compete lawfully are not permitted to use whatever foods the appetite of desire may suggest, but only those which the discipline of the contests themselves prescribes.

They must abstain not only from forbidden foods, drunkenness, and every kind of gluttony, but also from all idleness, leisure, and sloth, so that through daily exercises and continual training their strength may increase. Thus they are removed from every anxiety and sorrow, from secular occupations, and even from marital affection and activity, so that they know nothing besides the practice of their discipline and are not at all entangled in any worldly concern. They hope only to obtain from the one who presides over the contest the means of daily sustenance, the glory of the crown, and worthy rewards commensurate with the praise of victory.

Therefore, if we understand the discipline of the worldly contest, by whose example the blessed Apostle wished to instruct us, it teaches us with what vigilance we ought to act and with what purity we ought to guard the chastity of our body and soul—those who must daily feed on the sacred flesh of the Lamb.

For what they desire to attain in bodily purity, we must also possess in the conscience of our heart. In that contest the Lord sits as judge and *agonthea* [*agonotheta*]—the president of the contest—and continually awaits the struggle of our race and competition. Thus he requires that we not even permit those things which we shudder to admit openly to become inflamed within us through guarded thought, and that we not be polluted by hidden desire in those matters over which we are ashamed even in human thought.

Although such things may escape human notice, no secret can elude the knowledge of the holy angels or of almighty God himself, nor can they remain hidden. In this respect the gift is greatly different; and therefore we must be more diligent, since a spiritual crown is reserved for us, not woven from earthly and fading flowers but set with eternal gems, in the form of a royal diadem.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Circensian Games

The circensian games were instituted for the sake of sacred rites and celebrations of the gentile gods. Hence those who attend them appear to serve the worship of demons.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Circuses

At the circus, where the horses are released, the starting gates are called *carceres*, from the same thing as the prison (*carcer*) located in a city. Just as condemned and confined people are held there, so horses are restrained here so that they do not leave before the signal is given.

Spiritually, prison signifies present or future punishment, as in the Psalmist: “Lead my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Psalm CXLI). The elders wished this prison to be understood in two ways: either as the painful narrownesses of this world, which we suffer while established in this body; or, more especially, as the custody of hell, from which it is not permitted to escape under the frail law of human nature.

The prison (*carcer*) is so called as if from *arcer*, because it bars those enclosed within from going out. But the reason why he desired to be freed from this prison follows: “That I may confess your name.” For then praise is offered in confession by all the faithful to the Father, when it is clear that he was led out of the prison of hell by the miracle of the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Charioteers

The art of the circus includes the charioteer and chariot, horsemen, and footmen. A charioteer is properly so called because he drives and guides the chariot, or because he strikes the yoked horses. For *haurit* means “he strikes,” as in: “He strikes the open flank.” He is also called an *agitator*, that is, a driver or beater, from *agere*, “to drive.”

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Chariot

The chariot (*currus*) is named from running (*cursus*), or because it appears to have wheels; hence *carrus*, as if from *cursus*.

Allegorically, the chariot is understood in two ways. Either the angelic army is represented in it, as we read in the Book of Kings that Elijah was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot (2 Kings II). This was accomplished and the assistance displayed through angels, since he could not ascend even to the aerial heaven by himself, burdened as he was by the weakness of his nature.

Or it signifies the fellowship of all the saints, as in the Psalmist: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing; the Lord is among them” (Psalm LXVII). The unanimity of the saints is therefore the Lord’s chariot, which he rides like a charioteer and governs according to his will by a saving law.

To show that this chariot is not devoted to horses but assigned to human thoughts, he says: “Ten thousandfold,” which is rightly understood of innumerable peoples, not horses. He adds: “Thousands of rejoicing,” which certainly must be understood of the faithful. And to show the fullness of joy, he says: “The Lord is among them”—the culmination of great exultation and the wondrous sweetness of every good.

At times, however, the chariot is understood as the fellowship of the wicked, bound by the chain of sins. Hence it is written in Exodus: “He threw Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea” (Exodus XV).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Horses Used for Racing
