Quadrigas, bigas, trigas, and sejugas are named from the number of horses and from the yoke. The gentiles consecrated quadrigas to the sun, bigas to the moon, trigas to the gods below, sejugas to Jupiter, and the desultores—those who leap from one horse to another—to Lucifer and Hesperus.

They yoke a quadriga to the sun because the year turns through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They yoke a biga to the moon because it competes with the sun in a double course, or because it is seen by day and by night; they yoke one black horse and one white horse.

They dedicate trigas to the gods below because they carry human beings away through three ages: infancy, youth, and old age. A sejuga, the largest chariot, runs for Jupiter because they believe him to be the greatest of their gods.

In Holy Scripture, quadrigas signify either the four Evangelists or the four Gospels, or the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. In these the sum of all virtues consists; they also raise a human being to the height of perfection and lead him to the heavenly kingdom.

In these, moreover, the two Testaments or the two peoples of the faithful are understood—namely, those from the Jews and from the nations—whom the heavenly charioteer leads according to his will. Hence the Psalmist says: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Psalm LXXXV).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Seven Laps

A quadriga runs seven laps, corresponding either to the course of the seven stars, by which they say the world is governed, or to the course of the seven days of the present life. When these have been completed, life’s end is brought to completion; their finish is the chalk-line—that is, judgment.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Horsemen

Individual horsemen are said to race because each person individually completes and passes through the course of this life. One follows another at a different time, yet all travel by one road of mortality to their own goal, death.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Footmen

They say that footmen run on foot because human beings run toward mortality on their feet. For this reason they run from the upper part toward the lower, that is, from east to west, because mortals are born and die.

They run naked because a human being has no lasting remains in this world. They run along a straight course because there is no distance between life and death. But they invent these things in order to try to excuse their vanities and sacrileges.

Horsemen signify those who accomplish a task with the aid of others. Footmen signify those who complete the course of the contest by their own labor. Thus the Prophet says to the Lord concerning the horsemen: “You ascend upon your horses, and your riding is salvation”—that is, you ascend into the hearts of your elect through the illumination of grace, by which, with you guiding them, they proceed along the path of the virtues and, carrying you throughout the world by proclaiming the Gospel, announce the life of perpetual salvation to the world.

Concerning the footmen, Scripture likewise says: “He will guard the feet of his saints, and the wicked will be silent in darkness” (1 Samuel II). The Lord will guard the feet of his saints—that is, he will direct the works of his elect into the way of justice. “And the wicked will be silent in darkness,” because they will be sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew VIII, XXII); there they will be crushed—that is, they will cease from the arrogance of their pride.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Colors of the Horses

The same gentiles also associated the colors of horses with the causes of the elements. They likened rose-colored horses to the sun, that is, to fire; white horses to air; green horses to earth; and blue horses to the sea.

They also wished rose-colored horses to run for summer, because they are fiery in color and at that time everything turns yellow. They assigned white horses to winter, because it is icy and everything grows pale in the cold. They assigned green horses to spring because then the vine-leaf becomes dense with green color. They assigned blue or red horses to autumn, and also consecrated them to Mars, from whom the Romans are said to arise. Hence Roman standards are adorned with scarlet, because Mars rejoices in blood.

But these things are vain and contrary to the Christian faith. Therefore you must observe, Christian, how many unclean names the circus possesses. Consequently, the place occupied by so many spirits of Satan will be foreign to you; for the devil and his angels have filled the whole of it.

Nevertheless, in the Apocalypse we read that John saw a white, red, black, and pale horse; their diversity seeks a spiritual interpretation.

The white horse signifies the Church, whitened like snow by grace. Upon it sat the one who had a bow, and to him a crown was given; “and he went out conquering, so that he might conquer” (Apocalypse VI). This signifies the Lord, seated above the Church, bearing the weapons of spiritual doctrine against the ungodly and obtaining victory for his own.

The red horse, upon which sat the one who had taken peace from the earth, signifies the people of the left hand, made bloodstained by their rider, the devil, who always delights in discord.

The black horse, upon which sat the one who held a balance in his hand, is the multitude of false brothers. They possess the balance of right profession, yet they injure their companions through works of darkness.

The pale horse, however, on which sat the one whose name was Death and whom Hell followed, signifies heretics. They deceive themselves into thinking they are Catholics, although they are worthy of death as their inhabitant, and they drag an army of the lost behind them.

For the devil and his ministers are called, by metonymy, Death and Hell, because they are the cause of death and hell for many.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Theater

The theater is the structure enclosing the stage, having the shape of a semicircle, in which everyone standing looks on. Its form was originally round, like an amphitheater; afterward, the theater was made from the middle of the amphitheater.

The theater was named from spectacle, from the Greek *apo tēs theōrias*—“from viewing”—because the people stood above and watched the games being performed there.

The theater is also a brothel, because after the games were finished, prostitutes stood on display there. It was likewise called a *lupanar*, from the same prostitutes, who are called she-wolves (*lupae*) because of the vileness of their publicly exposed bodies. Prostitutes are called *lupae* from their rapacity, because they seize and prey upon wretched people.

Brothels were established by pagans so that the modesty of unfortunate women might be publicly exposed and so that both those who committed such acts and those who suffered them might be objects of mockery.

Mystically, the theater can signify the present world, in which those who follow the luxury of this age hold God’s servants up to ridicule and rejoice as they watch their sufferings. Hence the Apostle says: “We have been made a spectacle in this world to angels and human beings for God’s sake” (1 Corinthians IV).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Combat with Wild Beasts

The combat with wild beasts consisted in young men receiving beasts that had been released and voluntarily fighting them at the cost of their lives—not as a crime, but in madness.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Abomination of These Games

These spectacles of cruelty and exhibitions of vanities were instituted not only through human vices but also at the command of demons. Therefore a Christian should have nothing to do with circus madness, the indecency of the theater, the cruelty of the amphitheater, the savagery of the arena, or the luxury of the games.

For whoever presumes to do such things denies God and becomes a transgressor of the Christian faith. He desires again what he renounced long ago in baptism: the devil, together with his pomp and works.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Ships

I have decided henceforth to note in part the names of certain arts by which something is manufactured.

*Artifex* is a general name, so called because he makes an art, just as a goldsmith (*aurifex*) is one who works gold. For the ancients said *faxo* for *facio*, “I make.”

A *nauclerus* is called the master of a ship, because the ship is his allotted property. *Cleros* in Greek means “lot.” The others on the ship are under his command.

A *gubernio*, also called a *gubernator*, is so called as if from *cohibernator*, because by his prudence he restrains the winter storms at sea. A sailor (*nauta*) is named by derivation from *navis*, “ship.” *Navita* is a poetic form for *nauta*, just as *Mavors* is used for *Mars*; the correct form is *nauta*.

A rower (*remex*) is so called because he carries an oar. The nominative form is pronounced *remex* in the same way as *tubex*.

An *epibata*, a Greek term, is called in Latin one who “comes aboard” or “arrives.” He has no business on the ship but, after paying his fare, intends to travel to other lands.

Some say that *navis*, “ship,” is so called because it seeks a skilled (*gnavus*) helmsman—that is, an experienced, wise, and energetic one who knows how to contain and steer it amid maritime dangers and accidents. Hence Solomon says: “The intelligent person will possess the rudders” (Proverbs I).

Mystically, a ship signifies either the Church, as in the Gospel: “The ship was tossed in the midst of the waves” (Matthew XIV); and in the Psalm: “This sea is great and spacious,” and so forth, “there the ships will pass” (Psalm CIII).

Ships rightly signify the Churches, which escape the dangerous waves of the world by means of the wood of the glorious cross, carrying peoples who have believed through the sign of faith. Christ dwells in these ships. If he is awakened by believers, he tells the most violent storm to be still, and it becomes still.

Elsewhere the same Prophet says: “By a mighty wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm XLVII), because through the grace of the Holy Spirit the doctrine of the philosophers, who crossed the sea of this world by disputing, has been emptied out by preachers.

The Lord of the ship, therefore, is the Savior himself, who is also its helmsman, because by his Spirit he rules and steers it until he brings it to the harbor of eternal salvation.

In another sense, a ship is understood as in Isaiah: “Howl, ships of the sea” (Isaiah XXIII). By this name philosophers or heretics wandering through empty questions are signified.

Rafts (*rates*) were the first and most ancient kind of vessel, joined together from rough beams and planks. Ships made in their likeness were called *ratariae*. Now *rates* is used improperly for ships; properly, rafts are beams joined together.

A *trieris* is a large ship, which the Greeks call a *dourkōn*. Concerning it Isaiah says: “The great trieris will not pass through it” (Isaiah XXXIII).

Liburnian ships (*liburnae*) are named from the Libyans. They are merchant ships, concerning which Horace says:

> Twice by Liburnian ships amid the lofty vessels.

Ram-bearing ships (*rostratae naves*) are so called because they have bronze rams at the prow, to prevent them from striking and colliding with rocks.

Long ships are those we call *dromones*. They are so called because they are longer than the others. Their opposite is the *musculus*, a short vessel. *Dromo* is named from running (*decurrere*); for the Greeks call a course *dromon*.

A fleet (*classis*) is named by a Greek term, *apo tōn kalōn*, that is, “from the timbers.” Hence *calones* are also small boats that carry wood for soldiers.

A *barca* is a vessel that carries all the ship’s cargo to the shore. On the open sea, because of the excessive waves, the ship receives it into its own embrace; when it approaches the harbor, the ship returns to the barca the service that the barca rendered to it at sea.

A *paro* is a pirate vessel, and is called this from those who use it. A *myoparo*, as if “a very small paro,” is a skiff made of wicker which, covered with rawhide, provides a type of vessel. Germanic pirates use such craft along ocean shores or in marshes because of their agility. Concerning them a history says:

> “The race of the Saxons,” it says, “relies on myoparones, not on strength; they are prepared for flight rather than for war.”

*Celoces*, which the Greeks call *celetes*, are swift biremes or agile triremes, suitable for the service of a fleet. Ennius writes:

> The oiled keel of a swift vessel glides over the gray waters.

A *lembus* is a short boat, also called by another name a *cymba* and a *caupolus*, as is a *linter*, that is, a *carabus*, which they use on the Po and in marshes.

A *carabus* is a small skiff made of wicker which, covered with rawhide, provides a type of vessel.

The various kinds of ships can represent different gatherings of the good and the wicked. In them the good devise good things, while the wicked devise evil. Likewise, the various equipment of ships signifies different arts, in which the good strive to be useful, while the wicked strive to cause harm.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Parts and Equipment of Ships

The stern (*puppis*) is the rear part of a ship, as if from “behind” (*post*); the prow (*prora*) is the front, as if from “before” (*priora*).

The *cumba* is the lowest part of a ship, because it rests upon the waters. The keel (*carina*) is named from running (*currere*), as if *currina*.

The *fori* of ships are their concave sides, named from carrying a load, or the ship’s decks, which are laid down. They are called *fori* because they bear the movement of those walking upon them or project outward.

*Transtra* are the planks on which the rowers sit. They are so called because they lie across the ship; Virgil calls them *juga*, “yokes.”

Oars (*tons ae*) are named from removing and striking away the waves, just as barbers (*tonsores*) are named from cutting and striking away the hair.

The *palmula* is the extreme width of an oar, named from the palm of the hand, by which the sea is driven.

Yards (*antennae*) are so called because they are placed before the stream (*ante amnem*); for the stream flows past them. The horns are the end-parts of the yards, named by a figure of speech.

The mast (*malus*) is the ship’s tree by which the sails are supported. It is called *malus* because it has the appearance of an apple at the top, or because it is surrounded by certain wooden mallets (*malleoli*), through whose rotation the sails are more easily raised.

The rudder (*clavus*) is the device by which the steering oar is controlled. Ennius writes:

> So that I may hold the straight rudder and steer the ship.

A *porticulus* is a small mallet carried in the hand, by which the rowers are given rhythm and signals. Plautus writes:

> Keep the *porticulus* in your hand for speaking and for silence.

A *tonsilla* is an iron or wooden hook to which the ship’s ropes are fastened when it is fixed on the shore. Ennius writes:

> They seize the hooks and drive the curved ones into the shore.

An anchor (*anchora*) is an iron tooth. Its name derives from the Greek etymology that it grasps either rocks or sand like a human hand; for “hand” in Greek is *cheir*. Among the Greeks it has no aspiration, for it is pronounced *ancyra*. Hence the ancients pronounced it without aspiration.

The anchor signifies sound intention and a good disposition of mind, by which a person reaches toward God and eternal life. Hence the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “We have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us, which we have as a safe and firm anchor of the soul, entering even into the interior of the veil, where Jesus, our forerunner, entered for us,” and so forth (Hebrews VI).

## CHAPTER XLI. On Sails

The Greeks call sails *armena*, because they are moved by the air. Among the Latins, however, sails are named from flying (*volatus*). Hence the expression:

> We spread the wings of the sails.

Sails of ships can therefore typologically express human wills, which are driven by the wind—that is, by spiritual impulse—toward the course of a good life or toward destruction in an evil one. For the good Spirit of God leads a person into the right way, while an evil spirit leads him into a crooked way.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Ropes

Ropes are so called because they were formerly wrapped in wax for use as lights; hence also *funalia*, “torches.”

Cables (*restes*) are so called either because they hold rafts together or because nets are stretched with them. *Rudentes* are the ropes of ships, named from their excessive creaking.

Ropes or cables can express the restraints of pleasures, which hold human souls back from falling headlong. A rope signifies the faith of the Trinity, as in Solomon: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Ecclesiastes IV).

Ropes signify faithful peoples woven together in faith in the Trinity, as in the Psalm: “The ropes have fallen to me in pleasant places” (Psalm XV). Ropes signify the prolongation of sins, as in Isaiah: “Woe to those who draw iniquities with cords of vanity” (Isaiah V).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Nets
A net is called *rete* either from holding fish, or from the ropes (*restes*) by which it is stretched. A small net is called *simplagium*, from *plagae*; for properly speaking, *plagae* are the ropes by which nets are stretched around their lower and upper edges. A *funda* is a kind of fishing net, so called because it is cast to the bottom; it is also called *jaculum*, from throwing (*jactare*). Plautus: “Indeed, you were formerly a good javelin-thrower.” A *tragum* is a kind of net, named from being dragged. It is also called a *verriculum*; for *verrere* means “to drag.”

Nets, or seine-nets, mystically signify the preaching of the Gospel. Hence the Apostles, typological fishermen, are sent by the Lord into the sea of this age, so that by their doctrines they may rescue people from worldly errors and lead them to the true faith of God. Concerning the seine-net the Gospel reads as follows:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a seine-net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it out and, sitting beside the shore, gathered the good into vessels, but threw the bad outside” (Matt. XIII).

Under this parable, therefore, the holy Church is compared to a seine-net—for it has been entrusted to fishermen, and through it people are drawn from the waves of the present age toward the eternal kingdom, lest they be submerged in the depths of everlasting death. It gathers fish of every kind, because it calls the wise and foolish, the free and the enslaved, the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak to the forgiveness of sins. Hence the Psalmist says of it: “To you all flesh shall come” (Ps. LXIV).

This seine-net is then filled universally, when the whole of the human race is brought to its conclusion at the end. They draw it out and sit beside the shore, because just as the sea signifies the world, so the shore of the sea signifies the end of the world. At that end, the good fish are gathered into vessels and the bad are thrown outside: each of the elect is received into the eternal dwellings, while the reprobate, deprived of the light of the eternal kingdom, are dragged away into the outer darkness.

For nets sometimes signify the devil’s deception, as in the Psalm: “Sinners shall fall into his net” (Ps. CXL).

A *conopeum* is a net in the form of a tent, by which gnats are kept out; the Alexandrians use it especially, because abundant gnats are born there from the Nile. Hence it is also called *conopeum*, for *Canopea* is Egypt. It is likewise read in the Book of Judith concerning Holofernes (Judith X) that he had a *conopeum* and used it.

The column that stood at the head of Holofernes’ bed signifies the hardness of an evil heart, which produced the error of false security. The sword hanging bound to it signifies the malice of an evil intention. The hair of his head signifies the exaltation of a proud mind; his neck, the obstinacy of wicked action; and the *conopeum*, that is, the net against flies, signifies the snares of deceitful thought.

Therefore our Judith commends to her maidservant the guarding of the doors, because the holy Church commands each of the faithful to maintain vigilance for the catholic faith. She herself prays with tears, because she seeks heavenly assistance with the innermost devotion of her heart. She approaches the column and loosens the dagger, by which she may cut off the head of the most wicked enemy, when, having exposed the malice of the hardened heart, she cuts away from the enemy the opportunity for insolent temptation. She also removes the *conopeum*, because she exposes his frauds, by which he strives to entangle the simple and unwary. Thus she exposes the enemy’s headless body, when she shows that the enemy himself is weak and feeble in every respect, so that the soldiers of Christ may more confidently believe that they can conquer the most wicked enemy once they fully learn that he is fragile and conquerable.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the smiths’ furnace

[Col. 0558A]

The smith (*faber*) derives his name from making (*facere*) iron. From this the term was extended to craftsmen or workshops dealing with other materials, with an added specification, such as “woodworker” (*faber lignarius*) and the like, evidently because of the strength of the work.

In the smiths’ furnace, the pagans say that Vulcan is the originator. Figuratively, through Vulcan they signify fire, without which no kind of metal can be melted and extended. For there is scarcely anything that cannot be produced by fire. In one place it makes glass, in another silver, in another lead, in another vermilion, in another pigments, and in another medicines. By fire stones are reduced to bronze. By fire iron is produced and tempered. By fire gold is perfected. By fire, when stone has been burned, cement and walls are joined together. By cooking, fire whitens black stones; by burning, it darkens white wood. From glowing embers it makes black coals; from hard wood it makes fragile material, and from rotten material it makes something imperishable. It loosens what is tight and tightens what is loose; it softens what is hard and hardens what is soft. It also has medicinal uses, for it often benefits the countryside. It is also known to aid against the pestilence contracted through the obscuration of the sun.

In its work, fire produces one thing with the first flames, another with the second, and another with the third. Fire also has another kind of diversity within itself: one kind serves human use; another appears in divine judgment—whether the fire that draws lightning from heaven, or that which belches forth from the earth through the peaks of mountains. Fire is so called because nothing can be produced from it; for it is an inviolable element, consuming everything it seizes.

The mystical significance of fire has already been discussed above, where the four elements were treated. If anyone wishes to compare what is written here with those discussions, he may perhaps be able to explain still more mysteries from their operations.

God is understood as the smith, because he fashioned the whole structure of heaven and earth, as in the Gospel: “Is this not the son of the smith?” (Matt. XIII).

Smiths signify holy preachers, as the Book of Kings says: “Moreover, no blacksmith was to be found throughout Israel” (1 Kings XIII).

Smiths also signify the kingdoms of the nations, which from the four parts of the world oppress the people of Israel and other humble persons under the burden of servitude, as in Zechariah: “And behold, four smiths” (Zech. I).

A workshop consists of two things, winds and flame. Flame is properly so called because it is stirred up by the blowing of bellows. A furnace is named from fire; for *phos* [Greek: “fire”] means fire. A kiln (*caminus*) is a furnace, a Greek derivative from *kauma* [Greek: “burning heat”]. A furnace or kiln can typologically express either the excessive tribulation of the present time, as in the prophetic testimony: “The Lord delivered you from the iron furnace” (Jer. XI)—that is, from Egypt, where the people of God were afflicted by great tribulation—or it can signify the torment of Gehenna, as in the Gospel: “Throw them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII).

An anvil is the object on which iron is hammered, and is named from *cudere*, because there we hammer something—that is, produce it by striking. For *cudere* means to cut and to strike. The ancients did not call it *incus* but *intudem*, because metal is hammered on it, that is, extended. Hence a *tudes*, a hammer, is named from hammering—that is, extending.

Concerning the anvil, it is written in the Book of Job, when Leviathan is described: “His heart is hardened like a stone, and it is compressed like a smith’s anvil” (Job XLI). A smith fixes the anvil so that it may receive blows alone. For this purpose the anvil is set up, to be struck by repeated blows. Thus Leviathan will be compressed like a smith’s anvil, because he will be confined by the bonds of hell, so that he may be hammered by the continual blows of eternal punishment. Even now he is struck, when the righteous are saved while he lies in wait, wasting away in pains.

Other vessels are formed upon the anvil; the anvil itself, however, is not transformed by all those blows into another vessel. Therefore Leviathan is rightly compared to an anvil: while he persecutes us, we are fashioned; but he himself is continually struck and is never changed into a useful vessel.

A hammer is so called because, when something is hot and soft, it strikes and shapes it. In sacred Scripture, the devil is sometimes signified by the name “hammer,” through whom the sins of transgressors are now struck. At other times heavenly chastisement is understood, because either the elect feel blows from above so that they may be corrected from wicked paths, or righteous anger strikes the reprobate, showing them, by anticipating eternal punishments, what they will deserve in the future.

Since the ancient enemy is expressed by the designation “hammer,” the Prophet bears witness when he contemplates the force of the final judgment against him, saying:

> “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered!” (Jer. L.)

It is as though he were saying: Who could comprehend with what whirlwind, when the final judgment comes, the one through whom the Lord strikes and fashions his vessels for use in ministry will be broken in eternal condemnation?

Again, heavenly chastisement is expressed by the hammer. This is signified when Solomon was building the Temple, where it is said:

> “When the house was being built, it was built from dressed and finished stones; neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built” (1 Kings VI).

For what did that house signify except the holy Church, which the Lord inhabits in the heavens? For its building, the souls of the elect are brought forward like polished stones. When they are built in heaven, no hammer of discipline resounds there any longer, because we are brought there as dressed and finished stones, to be arranged in places appropriate to our merit.

Likewise, hammers are God’s threats against sinners, as in Jeremiah: “Are not my words like fire, and like a hammer crushing rocks?” (Jer. XXIII).

Likewise, hammers are the scourges of sinners, as Solomon says: “Hammers striking the bodies of fools” (Prov. XIX).

Tongs (*forcipes*) are virtually *ferricipes*, because they seize and hold glowing iron; or they are so called because with them we seize and hold something hot, as though *forvicapes*, since *forvum* means “hot.” Hence we also call people *formosi*—handsome—when the heat of their blood creates beauty through redness.

Concerning the tongs, it is written in Isaiah: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken from the altar with the tongs” (Isa. VI). Accordingly, in the tongs by which the coal is grasped, the two Testaments are signified; they are joined to one another by the unity of the Holy Spirit, and through angelic ministry the word of God is brought to cleanse the prophet’s lips, so that he may be able worthily to announce God’s will to the people.

A file (*lima*) is so called because it makes something smooth; for *limum* means “smooth.” In it can be expressed the duty of a good teacher, who makes people’s minds gentle with pleasing words, makes them receptive to hearing the word of God, and disposes them to fulfill his will through good works.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

[Col. 0559]

## CHAPTER I. On the construction of walls

[Col. 0559C]

[Col. 0559D] In the construction of walls and ceilings, the Greeks assert that Daedalus was the inventor. For he is said to have been the first to learn the craft from Minerva. The Greeks call smiths or craftsmen *tectones*, that is, builders. Architects, however, are masons who lay out the foundations; hence the Apostle says of himself: “As a wise architect, I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. III).

*Machiones* are so called from the machines on which they stand because of the height of the walls.

## CHAPTER II. On layout

A building has three parts: layout, construction, and beauty. Layout is the description of the site or ground and of the foundations.

## CHAPTER III. On construction

[Col. 0560C]

[Col. 0560D] Construction is the building of bricks and height. It is called construction or fitting together because it binds and makes stones, clay, and wood adhere to one another. For dipping iron into water is *strictura*. Unless heated iron is plunged into water, it cannot be tightened and made to cohere.

Construction is also named from the multitude of stones and timbers, hence *strues*, a heap or structure. Building and restoration are different. Building is a new construction; restoration is what is repaired in the likeness of the earlier structure. For the ancients used *instar* to mean likeness; hence they also said *instaurare*, “to restore.”

Construction consists of a foundation, stones, lime, sand, and wood. A foundation is so called because it is the bottom of a building. It is also called *caementum*, from cutting, because it rises from cut stone. Its mystical significance has already been discussed above.

Stones of different kinds are suitable for structures. Their significance, as has already been said above, can be understood in both a favorable and an adverse sense. They are called living stones—that is, saints—who are suited to the heavenly construction; and there are senseless, hard stones, which cannot be cut at all by spiritual tools, because they are never softened by repentance that brings conversion, nor do they consent to be joined to one another by the cement of lime—that is, by the bond of charity.

Sand, which in itself is weak, fluid, and unstable, acquires firmness when mixed with the addition of lime and is considered useful for building. So too the barrenness of sinners, which in itself is not useful, nevertheless, through conversion to the fellowship of the saints, acquires the stability of good works and, through the commandment of love, becomes useful for the building up of the holy Church.

In works of clay, baked bricks are suited to walls and foundations, and curved tiles and roof tiles to roofs. Tiles (*tegulae*) are so called because they cover buildings, and curved tiles (*imbrices*) because they receive rain. *Tegula* is the name of the primary form, whose diminutive is *tigillum*.

Bricks (*laterculi*) are so called because they are formed broad by being enclosed on every side by four boards. Unbaked bricks (*lateres crudi*) are likewise named from being made broad in wooden molds. The frameworks of these molds are called *crates*, in which they customarily carry the mud for the same unbaked bricks. They are woven structures of reeds, called *crates* from the Greek *apo tou cratein*, that is, because they hold one another.

Some think that mud (*lutum*) is so called by antiphrasis—that is, by a contrary expression—because it is not clean. For everything that has been washed is clean.

The nature of clay constructions can, according to mystical interpretation, be referred to the creation of the human condition, because it is written:

> “God formed man from the mud of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul” (Gen. II).

Our God is the potter, as the prophet Jeremiah and the Apostle Paul demonstrate. For in the prophet Jeremiah we read something of this kind: God commanded him to enter the potter’s house and see him fashioning a vessel that had collapsed from his hands; gathering it again, he fashioned it according to his will. “And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: Can I not do with the house of Israel as this potter does?” (Jer. XVIII).

Wisdom also says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

God therefore has power over us, just as a potter has power over clay, to make from the same mass vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor.

Concerning bricks, it is written in Genesis, where it mentions the construction of the tower:

> “When they had departed from the East, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And one said to his neighbor: Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire. And they had bricks for stone and bitumen for mortar. And they said: Come, let us make for ourselves a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven, and let us make our name famous before we are scattered throughout all the lands” (Gen. XI), and so forth.

This tower signifies the pride of this world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they had moved away from the East—that is, departed from the true light—and came to the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking of the teeth,” they immediately build a tower of their impiety against the Lord and fashion, with wicked audacity, the pride of their doctrines. They wish, through illicit curiosity, to penetrate the heights of heaven itself. But just as those people were divided from one language into many through pride, so heretics, separated from the unity of the confession of faith, are divided among themselves by the diversity of their error, as though by the discord of language.

A channel (*canalis*) is so called because it is hollow in the manner of a reed. It is more properly pronounced in the feminine gender than in the masculine.

Concerning channels, it is written in Genesis:

> “Jacob therefore took green poplar rods, almond rods, and rods from plane trees, and partly stripped them of their bark. He placed them in the channels where water was poured out, and the flocks came to the well opposite the animals, so that they might conceive when they came to drink,” and so forth (Gen. XXX).

Its mystery is as follows: What does it mean to place green almond rods and rods from plane trees before the eyes of the flocks except to offer, through the sequence of Scripture, the lives and teachings of the ancient Fathers as an example to the peoples?

Because these rods are straight according to the test of reason, they are called rods. Jacob removes part of the bark from them so that, in what is stripped, the inner whiteness may appear; and he preserves part of the bark so that the exterior may remain in truth as it had been. The color of the rods becomes greener when the bark is partly removed and partly retained.

Before the eyes of our contemplation, therefore, the teachings of the preaching Fathers are placed like varied rods. In them, when we often flee from the literal meaning, we remove the bark, as it were; and when we often follow the literal meaning, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inner whiteness of allegory is revealed; and when the bark is retained, the green examples of the outward understanding are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed these in channels of water, because our Redeemer fixed them in the books of sacred knowledge, through which we are inwardly nourished. The rams mate with the ewes while looking at them, because our rational spiritual understandings, when fixed upon their meaning, are mingled with individual actions, so that they produce such offspring of works as the examples of their predecessors, seen in the utterances of the precepts, display.

Water pipes (*fistulae*) are so called because they pour out and discharge water. For in Greek *stellein* means “to send forth”; their forms are made according to the quantity of water and the measure of their capacity. Mystically, pipes can signify the mouths of preachers, from which the waters of doctrine are poured into the hearts of their hearers: from good teachers, healthy and sweet waters; from bad teachers, bitter and harmful waters.

## CHAPTER IV. On beauty

Thus far, the parts of construction. What follows concerns the beauty of buildings. Beauty is whatever is added to buildings for the sake of ornament and elegance, such as coffered ceilings decorated with gold, panels of precious marble, and paintings in various colors.

## CHAPTER V. On coffered ceilings

Coffered ceilings have already been discussed, because they represent the splendor of Christ’s simpler servants who are nevertheless exalted in virtue, and they provide beauty to the Church.

## CHAPTER VI. On marble panels

Panels are slabs of marble; hence marble-covered walls are called paneled.

## CHAPTER VII. On mosaic pavements

[Col. 0563B] Mosaic pavements are produced by the skilled art of painting with small panels and tesserae colored in various hues. Tesserae are named from *tesserae*, that is, square little stones, by diminution.

The Gospel mentions a mosaic pavement where, during the Lord’s Passion, Pilate is said to have sat in the tribunal at a place called *Lithostrotos* (John XIX), which in Hebrew is *Gabbatha*. This reveals that the varied fabrication of false accusers could not overcome the simple assertion of truth. Rather, the one who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again gave himself for us, so that by the shedding of his blood he might wash away the varied stains of our sins.

## CHAPTER VIII. On plasterwork

[Col. 0563C]

*Plastice* is the art of forming and representing figures and images on walls with gypsum, and of painting them with colors. *Plattein* is a Greek word meaning in Latin “to fashion likenesses from earth or gypsum.” To make some form by impressing clay is also *plastice*; hence the human being is called *protoplastus*, because he was first formed from mud.

## CHAPTER IX. On painting

Painting is an image that expresses the appearance of some thing and, when seen, brings the mind back to remembrance.

## CHAPTER X. On colors

Colors are so called because they are perfected by the heat of fire or the sun, or because at first they were strained so that they might be of the greatest fineness.

Some colors arise naturally or are produced: naturally, such as *sinopis* [red ochre], *rubrica* [red pigment], *paritonium*, *melinum*, *eretria*, and *auripigmentum* [orpiment]. The others are fashioned either by art or by mixture.

Different colors signify different kinds of virtues, by which God’s creature is adorned in the image of its Creator: the redness of *sinopis* or vermilion signifies the ardor of charity; purple signifies martyrdom and sufferings endured for Christ’s name; orpiment signifies the splendor of wisdom; blue and hyacinth signify heavenly conduct; ceruse signifies the whiteness of chastity; and the other kinds signify the virtues as the occasion of the time and the order of reason require.

## CHAPTER XI. On the instruments of buildings

[Col. 0564A]

The structure of walls ought to be made according to the square and to correspond to the plumb line. The square (*norma*) is named from a Greek word, outside which nothing can be made straight. It is composed of three rulers, two of them two feet long and the third two feet and ten inches long, polished to equal thickness and joined together at their outer points so that they form the shape (*schema*) of a triangle. That is the square.

A ruler (*regula*) is so called because it is straight, virtually *rectula*, and has no obstruction. A plumb line (*perpendiculum*) is what is always hung down.

In construction, unless everything is made according to the plumb line and a fixed rule, all structures must be defective: some parts will be small, some reclining, some sloping downward, and others lying backward. For this reason everything badly constructed collapses.

In the square, the rule, and the plumb line, therefore, the principle of equity is to be understood, so that we may make all our works according to the tradition of the holy Scriptures, the rule of right faith, and the plumb line of sound doctrine. In accordance with what the divine commands teach, our works will then lead us to salvation. Otherwise the person who works outside these principles loses his labor, because “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

A trowel (*trulla*) is so called because it pushes and presses down—that is, it encloses stones with lime or mud. The mason’s trowel signifies God’s spiritual building, which the supreme Craftsman himself carries out in the construction of his Church.

Hence it is written in the prophet Amos:

> “And behold, the Lord was standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand was a mason’s trowel. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A mason’s trowel. And the Lord said: Behold, I will place the trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I will no longer continue to build it up or show it mercy, and the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste” (Amos VII).

The Lord, who is the builder of the wall and the cornerstone, threatens to withdraw his trowel—the aid of his protection—from the people of Israel. When the Lord withdraws his protection and, so to speak, the garment of the wall through the cessation of the trowel, then the high places of the idols will be demolished, and the sanctuaries of the ten tribes will be laid waste or destroyed.

According to the anagogical interpretation, the Lord Christ speaks and stands upon the strongest wall, upon his apostles and saints, whom he granted to be called a very strong wall. Hence he also said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

That wall, unless it is defended by the Lord’s aid, loses all its strength. But under his protection it is so strong that it is said to it: “If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you” (Isa. XLIII). The more it is struck by temptations, the stronger it becomes, and it rejoices amid blows for the name of the Savior.

Stairs (*scalae*) are named from *scandere*, that is, “to ascend.” They adhere to walls. The word *scalae*—“stairs”—is either singular in sense or plural, since the noun exists only in the plural, like *litterae*, which signifies a letter.

Mystically, stairs signify the progress of the saints through their preaching. Hence it is read in Genesis (Gen. XXVIII) that Jacob saw in a dream a stairway standing upon the earth with its top touching heaven.

This dream of Jacob is the death or Passion of Christ. The stone at his head, which is in a certain way also specifically called “anointed,” signifies Christ. For “the head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. XI); and who does not know that Christ is named from anointing?

The house of God is called Bethlehem, because Christ was born there. The gate of heaven is so called because there he descended to earth, where he later ascended again to heaven. The raising up of the stone is Christ’s resurrection.

The stairway, moreover, is Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John XIV). Upon it angels ascended and descended (Gen. XXVIII); in these are signified the Evangelists, the preachers of Christ. They ascend when, in order to understand his most exalted divinity, they rise beyond the whole of creation and find him “in the beginning,” the Word with God, through whom all things were made (John I). They descend when they find him made from a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. IV).

## CHAPTER XII. On woodworkers
A *lignarius* is generally called a worker in wood. *Carpentarius* is a specific designation: he makes a *carpentum*, [Col. 0565C] just as a *navicularius* is so called because he is a maker and craftsman only of ships. A *sarcitectus* is so called because, from boards joined together here and there, he repairs a single body of roofing; he is likewise a *lignarius*, because he applies roofing to wood.

Carpenters, then, and builders in wood, and roof-builders may be understood typologically as the holy teachers and preachers of the Gospel. Through their words and good examples they prepare a spiritual building for God. Either they build a dwelling for God from those who have newly come to faith, or, from those whom heretics and schismatics had corrupted through error, they restore them to God’s spiritual building by reproving and correcting them. Hence in Exodus we read of carpenters, and in the Book of Kings of woodworkers and masons who will restore the dilapidated parts of God’s house.

[Col. 0565D] *Materia* is therefore the name given to every piece of wood from which something is made: whether you apply the term to a door or to a statue, it will be *materia*. *Materia* must always be understood in relation to something, just as we call the elements the *materia* of things, because we see that the things that exist are made from them; and *materia* is so called, as it were, from *mater*, “mother.” Mystically, human creation may be understood by *materia*. Thus the supreme Craftsman, through his artisans—that is, through holy teachers—prepares manifold adornment for the Church and builds vessels suitable for his service.

*Trabes* (“beams”) are so called because, placed crosswise, they hold the two walls together. *Tigna* (“timbers”) and *trabes* are different: joined timbers make a beam, whereas beams are timbers that have been hewn. Concerning [Col. 0566A] beams, it is written in the Book of Kings: “Solomon placed beams in the house all around on the outside, so that they would not be attached to the walls of the temple,” and so forth (III Kings VI).

Who, then, are typologically signified by the beams of the house that carried the paneling, if not the holy preachers? While they themselves hold a lofty and honorable place in the Church of God, by their preaching they raise the weak and fragile above the desires of the weak, and suspend them in the desire and hope of heavenly things. They are also aided by their intercessions, so that they may persevere in what they have begun.

Again, *trabs* has another meaning in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matt. VII). Here the beam may be understood as a greater sin, and especially [Col. 0566B] envy; the splinter as a lesser sin, or sudden anger.

*Asseres* (“boards”) are named from *asse*, because they are laid singly and are not joined together. *Scindulae* (“shingles”) are so called because they are split, that is, divided. Since boards fit together to form the roof of a house, they may rightly be understood as repentance, or as charity, which “covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV). The Prophet likewise says in the Psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI).

*Epigri* and nails are what make wood adhere to wood. Nails are called *clavi*, as though *chalabi*, because they are made of *chalybs*, that is, iron; for *chalybs* means iron. Mystically, nails may be understood as the preaching of the saints, piercing human hearts. Hence it is written in Solomon: “The words of the wise are goads, and like nails driven firmly [Col. 0566C] in” (Eccles. XII).

Boards were called *tegulae* by the ancients, from *tegere*, “to cover”; hence also *tagulae*. The joining of boards is called a *commissura*. Boards may signify faithful hearers, who are supported by beams or timbers—that is, by holy teachers. Their joining may likewise be understood as unity and charity.

*Sectio* (“cutting”) is so called from following what has been begun; for *secare* means to pursue and follow. The word *serra* (“saw”) comes from its sound, that is, from its screeching. It can signify the persecution inflicted on Christians by unbelievers. Hence we read in the Apostle: “They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they died by the killing of the sword” (Heb. XI). Scripture also tells that the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two with a wooden saw.

A *circinus* (“compass”) is so called because, by bending, it produces a circle. Its measure is formed by a doubled line that had previously been extended as a single line across [Col. 0566D] its width. The point in the middle of the compass is called by the Greeks the *centrum* (“center”), toward whose middle everything converges.

Concerning the compass and the other instruments of the craftsman, Isaiah writes, where he speaks of the maker of an idol:

> The ironsmith worked it with a file over coals, and formed it with hammers, and worked it with the strength of his arm. The woodworker stretched out the rule, formed it with an adze, made it with a square, turned it with the compass, and made the image of a man, like a handsome human being dwelling in a house (Isa. XLIV).

Whatever is said concerning idols may also be referred to the leaders of heresies. With a crafty heart they construct images of their doctrines and falsehoods, [Col. 0567A] and they worship what they know to have been fabricated by themselves. Their own error is not enough for them unless they deceive the simple by their flattery—those who think that gain is godliness and devour widows’ houses (I Tim. VI). Abusing the ignorance of the common people, they fashion their doctrine by dialectical skill, as though with an axe, drill, file, and marking tool; they forge it with a hammer and gild it with the beauty of rhetorical speech. Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame (Phil. III).

An *securis* (“axe”) is so called because trees are cut down with it, as though *succuris*. It is also called *securis*, as though *semicuris*: for it is sharp on one side and digging on the other. Among the ancients it was called a *penna*; when it has an edge on both sides, it is a *bipennis*. A *bipennis* is so called because it has a sharp edge on either side, as though it had two wings; for the ancients called something sharp *pennum*. [Col. 0567B]

Concerning the axe John the Baptist said to the Jews: “Even now the axe has been laid at the root of the trees” (Matt. III). The tree of this world is the entire human race. The axe is our Redeemer, who consists, as it were, of a handle and iron: he is held by his humanity, but cuts by his divinity. This axe has already been laid at the root of this tree, because, although he waits patiently, what he is going to do is nevertheless apparent.

The axe may also signify the preaching of the Gospel, because, according to the Apostle, “the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul, flesh, and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts” (Heb. IV). The prophet Jeremiah [Col. 0567C] likewise compares the word of the Lord to an axe cutting down rock. Or the axe signifies the judgment of the Most High, which has been laid at the roots of the trees—that is, at the end of the kingdom of the Jewish people—in order to cut from the land of the living those who refused to believe in Christ.

An *ascia* (“axe” or “adze”) is named from *hastulae*, the small pieces that it removes from wood; its diminutive is *asciola*. It has a short handle, and at the opposite end resembles either an ordinary hammer or a hollow or two-pronged rake.

Concerning the axe, adze, and double axe, it is written in the Psalter, where the destruction of the Lord’s temple is recalled: “They cut down its doors with axes together; with the double axe and the adze they threw it down” (Ps. LXXIII). By the axe he indicates the tribulation of this age; by the adze, the persecution of the wicked, by which they pursue the saints even to [Col. 0567D] destruction; and by the double axe, the twofold affliction with which wicked people torment God’s elect in word and deed.

A *scalprus* (“chisel”) is so called because it is suited to carving and making holes, as though *scalforus*; its diminutive is *scalpellus*. A *terebra* (“drill”) is named from the woodworm called a *terebra*, which the Greeks call *teredon*. Hence the drill received its name: because, like the worm, it makes a hole by wearing away, as though *terefora*, or “piercing through.”

To build is to do good works or to teach rightly, as in the Apostle: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones” (I Cor. III). In the opposite sense, concerning the Jewish people, Malachi says: “They will build, and I will destroy” (Mal. I).

To destroy [Col. 0568A] is to practice evil works or to teach wrongly, as in Solomon: “One builds, and another destroys” (Ecclus. XXXIV). In a good sense, Jeremiah says: “To destroy and to build” (Jer. I).

To cleanse is to purge from vices, as in the Gospel: “He touched him, saying, ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matt. VIII).

# Chapter XIII. On the Invention of Woolworking

The Gentiles celebrate a certain Minerva for many accomplishments. They say that she first revealed the use of woolworking, that she first set up the loom and dyed wool. They also call her the inventor of the olive tree, of building, and the discoverer of many arts. For that reason craftsmen commonly pray to her; but this is a poetic [Col. 0568B] fiction.

Minerva is not actually the mistress of these arts. Rather, because wisdom is said to be in a man’s head, and Minerva is imagined to have been born from Jupiter’s head—that is, to represent intelligence—therefore the understanding of the wise person, who discovers everything, is in the head. For this reason Minerva is also called the goddess of the arts, because nothing is more excellent than intelligence, by which all things are governed.

# Chapter XIV. On the Vestments of Priests

There are eight kinds of priestly garments in the Law.

The *poderis* is a priestly linen garment fitted closely to the body and descending to the feet; hence its name. The common people call it a shirt.

The *abaneth* is the priestly belt, round and woven in a multicolored pattern from scarlet, purple, and hyacinth, so that flowers and [Col. 0568C] gems appeared to be distinguished within it.

The *pileum* is a round cap of fine linen, like half a sphere, covering the priest’s head and fastened at the back of the head with a band. The Greeks and our people call it a *tiara* or helmet.

The *machin* is an ankle-length tunic, entirely hyacinth-colored, having at its feet seventy-two bells and an equal number of intermingled and hanging pomegranates.

The *ephod*, which is interpreted in Latin as “overgarment,” was a shoulder-garment worn over the other clothing. It was woven from four colors and gold, and on each shoulder it had two emerald stones enclosed in gold, on which the names of the patriarchs were engraved.

The *logion*, which in Latin is called the *rationale* (“breastpiece”), was a double cloth woven with gold and four colors. It was a span square and contained twelve most precious [Col. 0568D] stones woven into it. This cloth was attached to the shoulder-garment opposite the high priest’s chest.

The *petalum* was a golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, bearing the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, written in Hebrew letters.

The *badim*, or *feminalia*, were linen breeches reaching to the knees, by which the priest’s private parts were covered.

Mystically, the *poderis* signifies chastity of body and soul maintained to the end. The belt signifies restraint, abstinence, and the mortification of carnal desires.

The four principal colors—hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen—from which the high priest’s vestment was woven together with gold have a mystical meaning. Gold represents spiritual [Col. 0569A] wisdom; hyacinth, a heavenly manner of life; purple, martyrdom; twice-dyed scarlet, the perfection of charity, which rests on two commandments, namely love of God and of one’s neighbor; and fine linen, chastity and purity.

The linen cap, or *tiara*, which covered and adorned the priest’s head, also admonishes him to consecrate all the senses of his head to God, so that his eyes may not see vanity, his ears may not willingly hear reproach against his neighbor, his mouth may not abound in wickedness, and his tongue may not contain deceit. Nor should his heart be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness, nor his sense of smell embrace the bed of a prostitute perfumed with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon.

The hyacinth-colored tunic shows what the priestly life ought to be: continually intent only on heavenly [Col. 0569B] desires, having, according to the Apostle, its way of life in heaven (Phil. III), and constantly awaiting the coming of its Savior.

This tunic, like the linen one, reached down to the feet. For this reason both are called *poderis* in Greek, to show that nothing weak or filthy should remain in the priestly life. Rather, everything he does should be covered with the beauty of virtues in every limb, from head to foot, and should be as splendid as an ethereal color.

The *ephod*, woven with gold and four colors and containing precious stones inscribed with the names of the sons of Israel, signifies good works according to the examples of the holy fathers and the practice of the virtues.

The *logion*, or rationale, which was placed on the priest’s [Col. 0569C] chest, shows that a priest and ruler of God’s people must do everything rationally and always distinguish good from evil by careful examination.

The fact that the rationale had four rows, each of which contained three stones, what does it typologically disclose to us except that, in the virtues distinguished principally into four categories, we should hold an unfeigned faith in the Holy Trinity?

In the varied beauty of the stones we may rightly understand not only the manifold splendor of priestly conduct and thought, but also the spiritual gifts of the virtues and the miracles of healings, concerning which the Lord himself said to the apostles: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matt. X).

The golden *petalum*—that is, the golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, on which “Holy of the Lord,” namely [Col. 0569D] the Lord’s name, was engraved—was a more sacred part of his clothing than the rest, and rightly so. Just as divine power surpasses all the things it created, so his name ought to stand above and beyond the rest of the high priest’s clothing and adornment, occupying the highest place on his forehead as though sanctifying everything.

It signifies the confidence of our profession, which we carry on our forehead, each of us saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

But because the other matters have been treated above, the *feminalia*, which are commanded to be made for covering the flesh of shame, specifically signify that part of chastity which restrains the desire for marital intercourse. [Col. 0570A] Without it, no one can receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he either remains a virgin or dissolves his marriage in violation of the bonds of marital union.

# Chapter XV. On the Various Names of Garments

There are various names for garments: *tegmen*, *tegumen*, *indumentum*, *vestimentum*, and others.

* Tegmen* is so called because it covers the limbs, just as *tegumen* refers to coverings that cover bodies.

*Vestimentum* is that which extends to the footprint, as though *vestigimentum*, “something reaching to the foot,” as with an ankle-length tunic. But the customary usage of writers confuses this distinction.

*Indumentum* is what is put on beneath or next to the body, as though *intumentum*.

*Vestitus* (“dress”) is distinguished [Col. 0570B] from *cultus* (“attire”), since *cultus* is understood more broadly. *Cultus* is likewise distinguished from *habitus*. For *habitus* belongs to nature, whereas *cultus* belongs to human arrangement.

Most garments are named either from the time when they are especially in use, or from the places where they were first made or are chiefly sold, or from the kind of color, or from the names of their discoverers.

When *vestitus* is understood in a good sense, it mystically signifies either faith, with which those reborn in Christ’s baptism are clothed, or charity. Thus the Prophet says in the Psalter concerning the adornment of the Church: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV).

When he says “in a garment of gold,” we must relate the gold to the splendor of charity, because the holy Church shines, surrounded by virtue. And so that you would not understand [Col. 0570C] charity alone to be present there, he said “in a garment gilded with gold,” not “golden.” For we call something “gilded” when the appearance of gold is spread over and attached to another material. Charity appeared above the other virtues because it surpasses them all by its radiance.

He adds: “Surrounded with variety.” Let us examine why the Church of God is praised for the variety of its garment, when simplicity and unity are entirely appropriate to it. By this variety he either signifies the many languages, because every nation, according to its own homeland, sings to the Creator in the Church, or the most beautiful diversity of virtues.

The Church is adorned with the gold of the apostles, the silver of the prophets, the gems of virgins, the scarlet of martyrs, and the purple of penitents. This, then, is the variety of unity, woven together from all nations by a godly way of life to please the eyes of the Lord.

[Col. 0570D] The most ancient garment of human beings was the *perizoma*, that is, a loincloth, by which only the genitals are covered. At first the earliest mortals made it for themselves from leaves of trees, when, after the transgression, they were ashamed and covered their private parts. Certain barbarian peoples, although naked, still retain its use to this day.

These garments are also called *campestria*, because young men who exercise naked in the field cover their private parts with them.

The *perizoma* that our first parents sewed from fig leaves and used to cover themselves signifies those who embrace the harshness of the world while clinging to the itching of carnal pleasure. Deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace, they gather coverings of falsehood like fig leaves [Col. 0571A] and make loincloths of perversity for themselves when they lie about the Lord or about the Church.

The *tunica* is called an ancient garment because it makes a sound when the wearer moves; for *tonus* means “sound.” At first there were leather tunics, with which Adam and Eve were clothed after their offense and expulsion from paradise.

A *talaris tunica* is so called because it descends to the ankles and flows down to the feet, just as a *pectoralis* was so called because among the ancients it was short and covered only the chest, although now it is more ample.

A *manicleata* or *manicata* tunic is so called because it has sleeves; the Greeks call it *cheiridoton*.

The tunic as a garment signifies the integrity of faith, which the Apostle Peter is recognized as having. In the Gospel we read of him: “When Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around him and threw [Col. 0571B] himself into the sea” (John XXI). By the firmness of faith he escaped the dangers of this world and overcame its temptations.

It is likewise read in Genesis (Gen. XXXVII) that the patriarch Jacob made for his son Joseph a *tunica polymita* or *talaris*, that is, an *astralogon* [*astragalon*], or a sleeved garment. The ancients, however, made greater use of *colobia*.

The many-colored tunic that his father made for Joseph signified allegorically the diversity of peoples gathered from all nations into the body of Christ.

In another interpretation, Joseph—who is described as having persevered in righteousness to the end among his eleven brothers—is said alone to have had an ankle-length tunic. What, then, is the ankle-length tunic except a perfected action? Just as a long tunic covers the body’s ankle, so a good action covers us before the eyes [Col. 0571C] of God to the end of life.

A *dalmatica* is a garment first woven in the province of Dalmatia in Greece: a white priestly tunic with purple stripes.

*Serica* is so called from *sericum*, “silk,” or because the Seres first sent it.

*Holoserica* is entirely silk; for *holon* means “whole” or “entire.”

*Tramoserica* has linen warp and silk weft.

*Holoporphyra* is entirely purple; for *holon* means “whole.”

*Byssina* is a white garment made from a certain kind of coarser flax. Some also consider *byssus* to be a particular kind of flax.

The garment is the faith of the Church, or the diversity of virtue, or the diversity of nations, as in the Psalter: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV). And in Isaiah: “Rise, rise, put on your strength, Zion; [Col. 0571D] put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, holy city” (Isa. LI).

The name “garment” signifies Christ’s assumed body, as the Prophet says: “And behold, a man clothed in linen” (Ezek. IX).

Christ’s garment also signifies faithful peoples. The garment of the saints signifies works of righteousness, or the faithful of Christ, as the Apostle says: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

The garment of the wicked is their works of iniquity, as in the Psalmist: “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double cloak” (Ps. CVIII).

The garment signifies human flesh, as we read in Solomon: “At all times let your garments be white” (Eccles. IX), that is, not soiled by any pollution of lust.

The garment signifies the hypocrisy of hypocrites, as in the Gospel: “They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

The wedding garment signifies faith, or [Col. 0572A] (as some wish) charity, as in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matt. XXII).

The linen garment signifies the virtue of the soul, or the purity of chastity, as in Leviticus: “The priest shall be clothed in linen garments and linen undergarments” (Lev. VI).

*Linea* is so called because it is made solely from flax.

*Linostema* is a garment woven from wool and linen. It is called *linostema* because it has linen in the warp and wool in the weft.

The linen garment signifies the mortification of carnal life. The *linostema*, woven from wool and linen, signifies the person of hypocrites, who display kindness toward their neighbors while presenting deceitful wickedness. What, then, is signified by wool except simplicity? And what by linen except subtlety? Often a subtle and clever person outwardly displays the simplicity of gentleness while inwardly concealing the subtlety [Col. 0572B] of malice.

Such a person puts on the garment of his conduct as though it were made from wool and linen when he displays simplicity on the surface while preserving the subtlety of malice in his mind.

A *lumbare* (“loincloth”) is so called because it is tied around the loins or clings to the loins. In Egypt and Syria it is worn not only by women but also by men.

Accordingly, Jeremiah took his loincloth across the Euphrates and hid it there in a cleft of the rock; afterward he found it torn. Some call this garment a *renale*, because it is tied around the kidneys.

Concerning the loincloth the Lord said to Jeremiah:

> For just as the loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, says the Lord, so that they might be my people, my name, my praise, [Col. 0572C] and my glory; but they did not listen (Jer. XIII).

The belt or loincloth that is joined around the kidneys is the people of Israel. Taken from the earth, like linen, and unwashed, it possessed neither softness nor whiteness, yet through God’s mercy it clung to him.

When this linen and loincloth sinned, it was carried across the Euphrates—that is, to the Assyrians—and was hidden there. In other words, it was in some way swallowed up by the multitude of great and innumerable nations and counted as nothing.

After a long time, the same prophet, acting as a type of the Lord, freed the people from captivity. Yet even after their return they did not obey the Lord’s commands. Instead, they followed foreign gods, and at last even laid hands on the Son of God, wasting away in eternal destruction.

Every [Col. 0572D] holy man is also God’s loincloth. Taken from the earth and from the clay of the earth, he is joined in a certain way to fellowship with God. Whatever appears shameful in God’s Church, he covers and surrounds with greater diligence, lest it be exposed to the bites of pagans and heretics.

If this loincloth touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, so that it is soaked with the moisture of the Assyrian region, it loses its former strength, rots, and falls apart. Even if it returns to God’s use, it cannot recover its former beauty—not because of any hardness in God, but through its own fault: because people refuse to hear his words and walk in the perversity of their hearts, doing whatever seems right to themselves.

The belt is mystically understood as the girding of spiritual work, as in the Psalter: [Col. 0573A] “You girded me with gladness” (Ps. XXIX).

The *balteus* signifies the girding of virtues, or watchfulness of mind. Hence we read in Deuteronomy: “You shall have a peg in your belt” (Deut. XXIII), that is, the goad of compunction.

In another sense, Job says: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” (Job XII).

The garment commonly called an *armelausa* is divided and open in front and behind, but closed only around the shoulders; the word is formed as though from *armiclausa*, with a letter removed.

We call them *camisae* because we sleep in them, in *camae*, that is, in our beds.

*Feminalia* are so called because they cover the thighs. They are also called *bracae*, because they are short and cover the private parts of the body.

# Chapter XVI. On the Characteristic Dress of Certain Peoples

[Col. 0573B] *Sarabara* are loose and flowing garments, concerning which it is written in Daniel: “And their *sarabara* were not changed.” Publius also says: “Why, then, did the Parthians hang *sarabara* in your belly?”

Among some peoples, *sarabara* are called certain coverings for the head, such as those that we see painted on the heads of magi.

The *mastruca* is a Sardinian garment made from the skins of wild animals. Cicero says concerning it in his speech for Scaurus: “The man whom royal purple did not move was changed by the *mastruca* of the Sardinians.”

The *mastruca* is understood as though “monstrous,” because those who put it on are transformed, as it were, into the appearance of wild beasts.

The Apostle speaks of certain holy people who lived under the Old Testament: “They wandered,” he says, “in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted; the world was not worthy of them” (Heb. [Col. 0573C] XI).

This shows that holy men who are driven by the desire to advance toward eternal life do not wish to enjoy the pleasures of the present life through indulgence. Rather, through self-restraint they strive to possess an abundance of virtues, adorned with which they may deserve to enter the banquet of the eternal King.

# Chapter XVII. On Men’s Cloaks

A *pallium* is a garment by which the shoulders of those who minister are covered, so that while they minister they may move about unencumbered.

Plautus says:

> If you are going to do anything, hang your cloak on your shoulders,  
> and let the agility of your feet proceed as far as it is able.

The *pallium* is said to derive its name from skins, because in former times the ancients wore leather overgarments, as though *pellea*. Or it may derive from *palla* by a process of derivation.

A *chlamys* is [Col. 0573D] worn on one side. It is not sewn together but fastened with a clasp; hence it received its name from the Greek.

The *chlamys* signifies the adornment of praise, as in Solomon: “He made a cloak for her husband,” that is, a garment fashioned, as it were, from the two Testaments.

A *toga* is so called because it covers and conceals the body with its covering. It is a clean cloak, round in shape, spreading widely and falling in a swelling fold. Coming from beneath the right side, it is placed over the left shoulder. We see a similar form in the coverings of statues or paintings, and call such statues *togatae*.

The Romans used the toga in peacetime, but in wartime they used military cloaks. The proper measure of a toga is six cubits.

The *toga palmata* was so called because it was [Col. 0574A] awarded to those who returned from the enemy bearing palms. It was also called the *toga picta*, because it had victories woven into it together with palms.

The *pallium* is understood in a good mystical sense, as in the saying: “A cloak of praise instead of a belt of mourning” (Isa. LXI).

In an opposite sense, the *pallium* is placed in the Psalm, where it is said concerning the Church: “He founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever. The abyss, like a cloak, is his covering” (Ps. CIII).

The abyss signifies a very great multitude of waters, which is generally placed both in a good and in an evil sense. Here it is rightly compared with the superstitious and persecutors, because just as a cloak covers what lies beneath it, so they covered the world with the most shameful superstition. They seemed to overwhelm not only ordinary people but also holy and outstanding men themselves with bodily tortures, to their own destruction.

*Diplois* is a Greek name, derived from the fact that it is a double covering.

Horace [Col. 0574B] writes:

> Against whom patience covers herself with a double cloth.

It is a military garment, the use of which first began during campaigns in Gaul, from booty taken from the enemy. Hence came the senatorial saying: “Having laid aside your togas, Quirites, go to your military cloaks.”

*Sagum* is a Gallic name. It is called *sagum* because among them it was originally square or fourfold.

The Prophet says: “Let them be covered, like a double cloak, with their shame” (Ps. CVIII).

He therefore asked that those who have now been stripped by unbelief be clothed in the understanding of both laws. The shame of the Jews is their failure to understand the Law, which so often foretold that the Lord the [Col. 0574C] Savior would come.

Or the passage may express the kind of saying commonly found in proverbs: “Let them be clothed in a double cloak of shame,” while they are ashamed before God and human beings.

The mystical meaning of the *sagum* has been sufficiently explained in the construction of Moses’ tabernacle; we refer the reader to that discussion.

A *paenula* is a cloak with long fringes, mentioned in Paul’s Epistle to Timothy (II Tim. IV).

A *casula* is a hooded garment. It is a diminutive of *casa*, because it covers the whole person, like a small house; hence also *cuculla*, as though “a small cell.”

In Greek it is likewise called *planeta*, because it wanders about with its edges moving freely. Hence the stars are called *planetae*, that is, “wandering,” because they move about in their wandering course and motion.

Allegorically, the *casula* may [Col. 0574D] express the garment of right faith, in which the fullness of good works consists. Hence it is written: “In his garment good things rest through him” (Ecclus. XIV).

The *melotes*, also called a *pera* (“wallet”), is a goatskin hanging from the neck and fastened around the waist. It is properly a garment necessary for the exercise of work. Some believe that it was formerly made from the skins of badgers; hence it was called *melotes*.

Fringes are called . . . [lacuna] The edges of garments, that is, their ends, derive their name from a Greek word. For the Greeks call a boundary *oron*. [Col. 0575A]

Spiritually, fringes signify the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, which the woman suffering from hemorrhage touched and was immediately healed.

Fringes also signify the extremity of human life. Hence it is said concerning the Church in the Psalm: “She is surrounded with variety in golden fringes” (Ps. XLIV), because all perfection is at the end, where charity is not merely seen as gilded, but already appears in its fullness, like gold.

# Chapter XVIII. On Women’s Cloaks
Regillum is a richly adorned cloak of queens, from which it also takes its name. Peplum is a matron’s purple mantle, marked with a design, whose fringes gleam at their upper edge with golden thread. Palla is a square mantle of women’s dress, reaching down to the feet and fastened in an ordered arrangement with jewels. It is called *palla* from Greek *pallein*, that is, “from movement,” because such a garment moves about at its edge, or because it is gathered into rippling folds and curls.

*Theristrum* is a little mantle with which, even today, the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia veil themselves; by it they are protected from the heat under a most secure shade. *Anaboladium* is a linen covering for women, by which the shoulders are covered; the Greeks and Latins call it a *sindon*. Concerning the *theristrum*, it is also written in Isaiah; and in Genesis the following is written about Rebecca:

> Rebecca also, when she saw Isaac, descended from the camel and said to the servant, “Who is that man who is coming across the field to meet us?” He said to her, “He is my master.” Then she quickly took up her mantle and covered herself. (Gen. XXIV)

When Rebecca sees Isaac, she asks the servant who that man is and learns the answer: so too holy Church daily understands, through the words of the prophets and apostles, what she ought to believe concerning her Redeemer. She immediately covered herself with a mantle, because she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior the more subtly the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life, and because she is ashamed that she has acted perversely. She took care to cover herself with a mantle because, when she saw the Lord, she blushed at the weakness of her conduct; and she who had previously been carried freely upon the camel, after descending is covered by shame.

Mystically, therefore, the *sindon* expresses the purity of chastity.
