Hence we read that Joseph wrapped the Lord’s body in it, because he demonstrated that it would be utterly pure through ineffable chastity and ought to be received sacramentally by pure people. Likewise, concerning the strong woman, it is written in Proverbs:

> She made a *sindon* and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite. (Prov. XXXI)

In the linen of the *sindon*, its fine weaving signifies holy preaching, in which the mind rests gently, because in it the mind of the faithful is refreshed by heavenly hope. Hence animals are shown to Peter in a linen cloth (Acts X), because the souls of sinners, gathered together mercifully, are held within the gentle repose of faith.

Thus she made and sold this *sindon*: she gave by speaking the faith that she had woven by believing, and received from unbelievers a life of upright conduct. She also delivered a girdle to the Canaanite, because through the vigor of demonstrated righteousness she restrained the disordered works of paganism, so that she might hold by living what is commanded, as it is written in the Gospel:

> Let your loins be girded. (Luke XII)

*Stola* is a matron’s covering, which, with the head and shoulder covered, is thrown from the right side over the left shoulder. It is called *stola* in Greek because it is placed over the body. In Latin it is also called *ricinium*, because one half of it is thrown back; in common usage it is called a *mavort*. It is called *mavort* as though from *Mars*, for it bears the sign of marital dignity and authority. “The man is the head of the woman” (I Cor. XI); therefore it is also placed over the woman’s head.

The *stola* signifies the garment of baptism or faith, as in the Gospel:

> Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him. (Luke XV)

The *stola* also signifies future reward and immortality; at times it signifies the honor of dignity or of sacred rank. Hence it is written:

> He will clothe him with a robe of glory. (Eccli. VI)

Future reward is signified by the *stola* where the Apocalypse records that the souls of the saints, who cried out to the Lord after the shedding of their blood and sought vengeance, received this answer:

> They should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers who are to be killed, just as they were, should be complete. (Apoc. VI)

For now the souls of the saints have individual robes, rejoicing in their immortality; but when their bodies rise again, according to Isaiah, they will possess double garments in their own land (Isa. LXI). The desire for the resurrection is not rejected; rather, it is delayed because of the increase in the number of brothers who are to be gathered.

Indeed, the joy of the souls themselves can be represented by white robes, when, through the Lord’s revelation, they learn both that the wicked will finally be condemned and that, until the end of the age, many will be joined to their number through martyrdom. Filled with inward charity, they prefer to be content with this consolation and to have their joys deferred until then, for the completion of the number of their brothers [*differri*, “to be deferred”].

## CHAPTER XIX. On Bedding and the Other Garments in Use

A *stragulum* is a variegated garment, distinguished by the craftsman’s hand in diverse patterns. It is so called because it is suitable for spreading over a bed and for covering the body. Concerning it Solomon says:

> She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing.

The variegated garment, which through its varied weaving is customarily made especially strong, signifies the Church’s vigorous works and the diverse ornaments of her virtues. Concerning these the Prophet sang in praise of the supreme King, that is, of that man:

> The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety. (Ps. XLIV)

As has been shown above.

Pillows are so called because they are placed beneath the neck or elbow. *Pulvillus* is named from *pulvinare*, which is the bed of the wealthy. *Culcitrae* are so called because they are stuffed—that is, filled—with feathers or padding, so that they may be softer and warmer.

Pillows, cushions, and mattresses can allegorically signify the flatteries of false teachers and flatterers, who deceive those to whom they promise impunity for evil deeds and pledge the rewards of life to the unworthy. Through the prophet it is said to them:

> Woe to you who sew cushions beneath every elbow and pillows to deceive souls, and so forth. (Ezek. XIII)

*Tapeta* are so called because at first they were spread beneath the feet, like *tapedia*. Carpets can signify the ornament of eloquence. Hence the prostitute says in Proverbs:

> I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread over it embroidered carpets from Egypt. (Prov. VII)

In the bed woven with cords, the prostitute signifies the softness of repose. In the embroidered carpets from Egypt she also signifies the enticements of the eyes, by which, when they are ensnared through a shameful gaze, she more easily penetrates the hidden places of the mind in order to seduce them.

Since cords sometimes signify divine commandments, by which they restrain us from our pleasures and bind us back, heretics promise through a web of heavenly words to prepare a wholesome bed for their hearers, on which they may rest with an unconstrained heart amid the tumult of vices. But in reality they build for them with those cords of sins a place of destruction, where their feet and hands, bound forever, will be condemned. Concerning this the Lord says in the Apocalypse:

> I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation. (Apoc. II)

In the embroidered carpets from Egypt, therefore, the ornament of eloquence and the subtlety of dialectical art are understood—an art that originated among the pagans—through which the heretical mind boasts that it has woven for itself the sense of a pernicious doctrine, like a prostitute weaving the couch of her crime.

*Mantelia* now denotes cloths for covering tables; as the name itself indicates, they were formerly provided for wiping the hands. *Mappae* are cloths for banquets and prepared meals, serving as if they were hand-towels; hence they are so named. Their diminutive is *mappella*, or *mandeba*, from *mandere*, “to chew.” *Sabanum* is a Greek word. *Facitergium* and *manutergium* are named from wiping the face or the hands.

These linens belong to the service of the table and to human service; yet they are also known to belong to the use of sacred service and to the ministry of the altar, when clean linens are placed upon the table—that is, the sacred altar—and little cloths are held in the hands of priests and ministers, so that the people may always see them prepared for the service of God.

*Vela* are so called because by being placed before something they veil the interior parts of houses. *Aulaea* are painted, large curtains. They are called *aula* because they were first invented in the hall of King Attalus of Asia, whose kingdom was inherited by the Roman people.

*Curtains* are *aulaea*, that is, coverings made of hides, such as are mentioned in Exodus, by which the tabernacle was covered externally. They are called *cortinae* from *corium*, “hide,” because they were first made from skins. Hence in the same tabernacle the Law commands that curtains be made from the skins of red rams and from violet-colored skins.

The Arabs call *cilicia* coverings woven from goat hair, from which they make tents. Anyone who reads Exodus can recognize that veils, curtains, and goat-hair coverings were made in the Lord’s tabernacle at the divine command; from this, with sound understanding, one can investigate the fitting mystery, especially since ten curtains of various colors are commanded to be made, variegated in appearance [*variegatae*, “variegated”]. For holy universal Church is built from many persons of the elect, from many churches throughout the world, and from the diverse flowers of virtues; its entire perfection is contained in the number ten.

The *saga*, therefore, by which the tabernacle is covered, are the rulers of holy Church. Through their diligence and labor, the flock of that Church is protected and fortified with unceasing care: lest the life and faith of the elect be corrupted by heretical seduction; lest they be defiled by the wickedness of false Catholics; lest they be touched by the filth of temptations to vice; and lest poverty of temporal resources drive them into sadness.

## CHAPTER XX. On Wool and Linen

*Wool* is named from *laniare*, “to tear away,” that is, “to pluck”; hence *vellus*, “fleece,” is also so called, because formerly wool was plucked rather than sheared. *Linen* grows from the earth, and its name is derived from Greek: for the Greeks call linen *linarion*, or it is so called because it is soft and gentle.

Mystically, wool, since it is the garment of sheep, can signify all works of piety and simplicity that we perform for our neighbors. Linen, which grows green from the earth but through long and varied labor loses its natural moisture and reaches the grace of a new whiteness, can signify the chastisement of our flesh. While through abstinence we burn out the innate filth of vices, we make the flesh worthy to put on Christ, according to the Apostle:

> For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. (Gal. III)

Thus concerning wool and linen, Proverbs says of the strong woman:

> She sought wool and linen, and worked with the counsel of her hands. (Prov. XXXI)

The strong woman seeks wool and linen and works with the counsel of her hands when holy Church diligently searches for the fruits of piety by which she may exercise herself and considers how she may cleanse herself from carnal allurements. She does both with the most prudent counsel—that is, solely with regard to heavenly reward.

*Stuppa* is hemp or flax. According to ancient orthography it was called *stippa*, because the cracks of ships were caulked with it; hence those who arrange it in bundles are called *stippatores*. It can signify the despised teaching of the word among the proud, which nevertheless frequently helps the needs of peoples laboring amid the waves of this age.

*Byssus* is a kind of very white and extremely soft linen, which the Greeks call *papates*. Concerning *byssus* it is also written in Proverbs:

> Fine linen and purple are her clothing. (Prov. XXXI)

Byssus signifies the purity of upright conduct; purple signifies the shedding of the precious blood of the martyrs. Byssus is white in color; purple, however, is dyed from the blood of marine shellfish, which is also called *ostrum*, because it is dyed from the moisture of the shell. Hence the Fathers beautifully said that holy Church, blooming with the flowers of the elect, possesses lilies in peace and roses in war.

Likewise, because byssus grows green from the earth but through long and manifold exercises, after losing its natural moisture and greenness, is brought to the beauty of a white garment, so the Church is clothed in byssus when the elect chastise their bodies and subject them to servitude. She is clothed in purple when they practice that same continence not for popular approval but to obtain the blessedness of the eternal kingdom.

In the present, this garment of virtues appears contemptible to those who do not understand it; but in the future its true nature will be clearly revealed. Hence John beautifully reports in the Apocalypse that he heard the voice of the saints saying:

> Let us rejoice and exult, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it has been granted to her to clothe herself in shining, pure linen. (Apoc. XIX)

The linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Conversely, the meaning of linen and purple is taken in the Gospel in the opposite direction, where it is written:

> There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen. (Luke XVI)

Here the ambition of worldly wealth is expressed: for a time it smiles upon the greedy, but soon, fading away, it leads them to eternal mourning.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Colors of Garments

Among the Latins, *purple* is named from the purity of light; among the Greeks it is called *porphyra*, with aspiration, whereas among us it is *purpura*, without aspiration.

*Ferrugo* is a nearly black-purple color, produced in Spain, as in the verse:

> Bright with Iberian rust.

It is called *ferrugo* because all purple in its first dyeing has this kind of color.

The Greeks call *coccum* what we call red or vermilion; for it is a little worm from woodland foliage. Since *coccus* has the appearance of fire, it is rightly compared with the most ardent love of the saints. Hence some of them who had conceived this love while the Lord was present and accompanying them said:

> Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us? (Luke XXIV)

In contrast, it is said of the reprobate:

> Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold. (Matt. XXIV)

This is, as it were, dyed twice when we burn with love of God and neighbor, loving him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, just as we love ourselves.

*Hyacinth*, because it imitates the appearance of bronze and of the sky, signifies the minds of the elect who seek heavenly things with every hope and desire. Commending to us the mystery of this color, the Apostle says:

> If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. (Col. III)

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Implements of Garments

*Tela* is named from the length of its warp threads; its derivative is *telaria*. *Tela* also denotes length. The warp signifies either the prolongation or the ordering of judgment. Hence it is written in the Prophet:

> And the web that he has woven over all the nations of the earth. (Isa. XXV)

For the Lord prepares rewards everywhere according to their proper merits, in order to judge.

The *distaff* (*colus*) is so called because of its length and roundness, resembling a column. The *spindle* (*fusus*) is so called because through it what has been spun is poured out. In the distaff the knowledge of Scripture is expressed; in the spindle, the application of discernment. Hence it is written in Proverbs concerning the strong woman:

> She put her hand to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle. (Prov. XXXI)

Women commonly hold the spindle in the right hand and the distaff in the left. Wrapped around the distaff is wool, which is drawn out as thread and passes onto the spindle to be spun.

Often in Scripture the right hand signifies eternal life, while the left signifies God’s present gifts: namely, abundance of possessions, peace in the times, health of bodies, knowledge of Scripture, and perception of heavenly mysteries. When, by the Lord’s generosity, we receive these and similar goods, we transfer the wool of the immaculate Lamb, spun from the distaff, from the left hand to the right. For from the goods of our Redeemer and from the examples of his works we make for ourselves a robe of heavenly glory and a garment of nuptial charity.

Spun thread, from which threads are made, expresses earthly labor, by which people prepare clothing for themselves for future reward. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel, wishing to withdraw us from worldly desire and prepare us for future glory:

> Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they do not labor or spin, and so forth. (Matt. VI)

The *warp* is so called because it stands upright. The *weft* is so called because it is sent through the cloth along a straight path. It is the thread running among the warp threads. These two can signify right faith together with good works.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Adornment

*Ornaments* are so called because through their adornment the mouth and face are beautified. In ornaments, however, the varieties of virtues and the diverse graces of spiritual gifts, which adorn human souls, can be understood. Hence in Ezekiel the Lord says to Judea:

> I clothed you with fine garments and adorned you. (Ezek. XVI)

And elsewhere it is written:

> I adorned you with necklaces. (Isa. LXI)

Conversely, in Solomon it is written:

> Behold, a woman in the adornment of a prostitute. (Prov. VII)

That is, in the sophistical speech of heretical depravity and the false color of virtues.

The first ornament is the crown, an emblem of victory or a sign of royal honor. It is placed on the heads of kings to signify the peoples spread throughout the world, by whom the king, as though by his head, is encircled and crowned.

The name *crown* is said to have arisen because at the beginning people ran around altars; it was formed and named after the image of a circuit or chorus. Roman emperors and certain kings of the nations use golden crowns. The Persians wear tiaras: kings wear them straight, satraps curved. The tiara was discovered by Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians; from that time to the present that nation has retained this kind of ornament.

The Athenians wore golden cicadas, some on the crown of the head and others on the forehead. For the insignia of all kingdoms are not the same. The seers of the pagans used a fillet, a pointed cap, or a cap with a brim.

Mystically, the crown signifies the reward of eternal glory for righteousness. Hence the Apostle says:

> I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me. (II Tim. IV)

Just as the completion of spiritual progress leads to the crown, so their reward is rightly called by the name “crown.”

The crown also signifies the circle of the Lord’s disciples, or the gathering of the whole Church around Christ. Concerning this the Psalmist says:

> You placed a crown of precious stone upon his head. (Ps. XX)

And again:

> You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness. (Ps. LXIV)

The crown can appropriately be understood as signifying the gathering of the disciples who surround him, because a circle of apostles desiring to hear him surrounded him as he taught. This was the crown of his head, this the royal diadem—not an ornament that adorned Christ when placed upon him, but one that was itself adorned by Christ the Lord.

In this crown we may rightly also perceive the circle of the whole world, in which the universal Church is signified.

Conversely, a crown is used when it signifies an encirclement of tribulation. Hence it is written:

> Crowning, I crowned you with tribulation. (Isa. XXII)

Some say that a *diadem* is a head ornament of married women, woven from gold and gems, which is fastened at the back by bringing its ends around itself; hence it is called in Greek from the fact that it is bound in front.

An *infula* is a white priestly headband, shaped like a diadem, from which ribbons hang on either side and bind the *infula*. The *infula* was sometimes broad and sometimes twisted, made of white and scarlet material.

An *apex* is a sewn cap worn by pagan priests. It is named from *apiendo*, that is, “binding,” for the rod that was on the cap was fastened with a thread made from the wool of a sacrificial victim.

A *galerum* is a cap made from the skin of a slaughtered sacrificial victim. The *pileus* is named from the victim’s skin from which it was made.

The *cydaris* also belonged to priests; many call it a *mitre*. A *mitre* is a Phrygian cap covering the head, such as is the head ornament of dedicated women. The *pileus* belongs to men, whereas the *mitre* belongs to women.

*Redimicula* are the bands by which a mitre is tied. The *pileus*, as we said above, was made from skin; the mitre, however, is made from wool.

A *ricula* is a mitre for a virgin’s head. *Vittae* are bands woven into the hair, by which flowing hair is tied back; they are called *vittae* because they bind.

A *taenia* is the hanging end of the bands, of various colors. A *vitta* is also the band by which a crown is bound; the *taenia* is the final part of the band that hangs from the crown.

*Discriminalia* are women’s head-ornaments. They are so called because they distinguish their head from a man’s; for *discriminare* also means “to divide.”

Hairpins are used among women to hold the structure of their hair in place, so that it does not flow too loosely and scattered hairs are not dispersed [*dissipentur*, “be dispersed”].

Earrings are named from the openings of the ears, from which precious grains of stones hang. In Greece, girls wore them in both ears; boys wore them only in the right ear.

*Torques* are golden rings hanging from the neck down to the breast. Men wear *torques* and *bullae*, whereas women wear necklaces and chains. *Torques* are so called because they are twisted; *bullae* because they resemble in roundness the bubbles that swell in water when stirred by the wind.

A *monile* is an ornament made from gems, customarily hanging from a woman’s neck; it is named from *munus*, “gift.” This is also called a *serpent*, because it consists of certain golden vessels and various gems arranged in the form of a serpent. Some call it a *segmentum*, as Juvenal says:

> Segments and long garments;

although we also speak of *segmentatae vestes*, as he himself says:

> And the little girl had slept in segmented cradles.

The word *monile* often signifies all the ornaments of married women—that is, whatever is given to them as a gift.

A *muraena* is the common name for a chain woven from the gold metal, which is made pliable in rods and joined in a winding arrangement resembling the serpent called the *muraena*, and which is fitted for adorning the neck. It is sometimes woven from rods of gold and silver. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs:

> We will make golden *muraenulae* for you, studded with silver. (Song I)

In the *muraenulae*, holy Scripture is displayed: inwardly it shines with the gold of spiritual meanings, and outwardly it gleams with the silver of heavenly speech.

Right-hand ornaments are common to men and women, since the right hands of both sexes are meant.

*Armillae* properly belong to men. They were awarded to soldiers as a reward for victory, on account of their valor in arms; hence they were formerly commonly called *viriolae*. In meaning, an *armilla* does not differ from a circle, since it too surrounds and constricts the place where it is worn. An *armilla*, however, extends more broadly, while a circle is round.

*Fibulae* are ornaments with which women adorn the breast, or by which men fasten a mantle on the shoulders or a belt around the loins.

*Lunulae* are women’s ornaments: little golden bosses hanging in the form of the moon.

*Specula* are mirrors in which women look at their faces. A mirror is so called either because the image is returned from its brightness, or because women looking into it examine the appearance of their faces and add whatever ornament they see to be lacking.

*Periscelides* are ornaments for women’s legs, by which their steps are adorned.

*Olfactoriola* are women’s little vessels in which perfumes are carried.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Rings

*Annuli* are so called as diminutives from *anuli* and *circuli*, which are rings worn around the arms and legs. Hence their signs are also called *sigilla*, diminutively: for *signa* are larger, while *sigilla* are, as it were, smaller signs.

People first began to wear rings on the finger next to the thumb because a certain vein extends from that finger all the way to the heart; the ancients thought that vein ought to be marked and adorned with some distinction.

Among the Romans, rings were issued publicly and not without distinction. Jewelled rings were given to men of exceptional rank, plain rings to the rest. Neither a slave nor a freedman wore a gold ring in public. Freeborn men used gold rings, freedmen silver, and slaves iron.

A ring demonstrates the seal of faith, as in the saying:

> Put a ring on his hand. (Luke XV)

That is, place upon him the sign of faith in good works.

In Isaiah, where many ornaments are enumerated and mention is made of mitres and other things, it is written:

> On that day the Lord will take away the ornaments of the shoes, the little crescents, the torques, the necklaces, the armlets, the mitres, the headbands, the leg ornaments, the little necklaces, the perfume vessels, the earrings, the rings, the gems hanging from the forehead, the changes of clothing, the mantles, the linens, the hairpins, the mirrors, the sindons, the ribbons, and the theristra. (Isa. III)

Their mystical meaning has been clearly explained by the holy teachers.

Isaiah describes women’s necklaces, and through these the insignia of cities; or, according to the anagogical sense, the various ornaments of virtues. Women have little bosses hanging like the moon; we transfer these to the ornaments of the Church, which are illumined by the Sun of righteousness.

The *torques*, which hang down as far as the breast, signify the understanding and authority of the mind in the heart. The *monilia*, which in one expression signify all ornaments, and the armlets signify good works, such as Rebecca received at her betrothal. The mitres signify the ornaments of the head, and the *discriminalia*, so that one may possess judgment concerning individuals. The *periscelides* signify the adornment of our walk, as we hear:

> Your foot will not stumble. (Prov. III)

And:

> He will rescue my feet from falling. (Ps. XXIV)

The *muraenulae*, woven from rods of gold and silver, signify the meaning of Scripture. The *olfactoriola* signify the saying:

> We are the good fragrance of Christ. (II Cor. II)

The earrings signify that we should not hear the judgment of bloodshed, but the Lord’s words:

> Let the one who has ears to hear hear. (Matt. XI, XIII)

The rings signify that we are marked for the Lord’s service, him “whom God the Father has sealed” (John VI). Hence it is said to the prince of Tyre:

> You are the seal of likeness. (Ezek. XXVI)

The prodigal son (Luke XV), when he was received with the robe, also received a ring, shoes, and gems hanging from the forehead, by which our faces are adorned. Concerning the adornment of his head we also read in the Psalm:

> Like oil upon the head, which runs down upon the beard of Aaron. (Ps. CXXXII)

According to the anagogical sense, the *mutatoria* are those things of which it is said:

> They will go from strength to strength. (Ps. LXXXIII)

The linens signify that, washed in the Lord, we may enjoy his delights, according to what is written in the Psalms:

> You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. (Ps. XXXV)

The daughters of Zion lost all these things because they walked with an outstretched neck and displayed pride through the gestures of their eyes, believing that what they possessed belonged to their own power and not to the Lord’s grace.

Women have hairpins by which the structure of their hair is held in place, so that it does not flow too loosely and the scattered hairs are not dispersed. They also have mirrors in which they examine their faces and, if they see anything lacking, add it to their adornment. They also have *theristra*, which we may call mantles; Rebecca was wrapped in one, and even today the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia are covered with them.

Thus, because of their pride, the daughters of Zion lost the hairpins by which the rule of all the commandments was fastened. They lost the mirrors that, in Exodus, the women who remained at the doors of the tabernacle offered for the construction of the Lord’s basin. Concerning these the Apostle Paul also spoke:

> Now we see through a mirror in an enigma. (I Cor. XIII)

They lost the *sindones* and ribbons by which they covered their shoulders and restrained the mind as it flowed here and there; and they lost the *theristrum*, by which they were protected under a most secure shade in the heat.

The earrings signify obedience or a sound understanding of Scripture. Hence in Exodus men together with women offered armlets, earrings, rings, and right-hand ornaments.

Sometimes these things take on a negative meaning, as in the passage in Exodus concerning the fornication with the cast idol, where Aaron said:

> Take the golden earrings from the ears of your wives and daughters and bring them to me. (Exod. XXXII)

And in the Book of Judges Gideon said to the people:

> Give me the earrings from your spoils. (Judg. VIII)

The Ishmaelites were accustomed to have golden earrings—that is, to have those who obeyed them. Shortly afterward it says:

> Israel prostituted itself with it. (Ibid.)

The *torques* signify the glory of preaching, as in Ezekiel:

> I put armlets on your hands and a torque around your neck. (Ezek. XVI)

In the negative sense, in the Book of Judges:

> Apart from the golden torques of the camels. (Judg. VIII)

That is, the ornamented eloquence of sinners.

The *armlets* signify the beauty of work or virtue, as in Exodus:

> Men together with women offered armlets. (Exod. XXXV)

The *dextralia* signify upright action, as above. They also signify discernment between good and evil, as above.

The ring, as we said earlier, signifies the seal of faith:

> Put a ring on his hand. (Luke XV)

The ring also signifies the sealing of sacred law. For the mystical and hidden understanding of holy Scripture is not open to everyone. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse:

> I saw a book in the right hand of the one seated, sealed with seven seals. (Apoc. V)

And elsewhere:

> The words are closed and sealed. (Dan. XII)

Mirrors also signify divine commandments or the examples of the fathers who preceded us. Hence it is written in Exodus:

> He also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. (Exod. XXXVIII)

That is, from holy souls who daily keep watch in observance of God’s commandments.

In *polymitus*, the varied spiritual gifts of virtues are understood, as in Ezekiel:

> I anointed you with oil and clothed you in varied garments. (Ezek. XVI)

In the opposite sense:

> Your merchants, that is, those of Tyre, traded in violet cloth and chests of precious embroidered goods. (Ezek. XXVII)

## CHAPTER XXV. On Belts

A *cinctus* is a broad girdle; a *semicinctium* is narrower; and the diminutive of both is *cingulum*. Thus *cingulum* is named as a diminutive from *cinctus*.

Young men used a *cinctus* in athletic exercise to cover their modesty; hence it was also called a *campestris*.

The *cingulum* signifies spiritual action, as in the Psalm:

> You girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced. (Ps. XXIX)

A *balteus* is a military belt. It is so called because standards hang from it to display the total strength of a military legion, namely six thousand six hundred, which is the number from which they themselves are constituted. Thus a *balteus* is named not only from the fact that it is girded on, but also because weapons hang from it.

The *balteus* signifies being girded with virtues or watchfulness of mind, as in Deuteronomy:

> You will have a peg in your belt. (Deut. XXIII)

That is, a goad of compunction amid the multiplication of virtues.

The meaning of *balteus* is taken in the opposite sense in Job, where it is written:

> He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord. (Job XII)

*Zona* is a Greek word; the Greeks call it *zonarion*, while we call it a *cingulum*.

A *strophium* is a golden belt with gems, concerning which Cinna says:

> With a *strophium* she girded her tender breasts;

but Prudentius says:

> This name is fastened to the gem, the *strophium*.

A *zona* signifies mortification of the body. Hence the Gospel says concerning John the Baptist:

> John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his loins; his food was locusts and wild honey. (Matt. III)

Behold, the poverty of his food and clothing is praised; the same discipline is condemned in the rich man. It says that he had hair, not wool, because austere clothing gives one impression, while softer luxury gives another.

The leather belt with which Elijah too was girded is a symbol of mortification. Further, what follows—“his food was locusts and wild honey”—was fitting for an inhabitant of the wilderness, so that he might satisfy not the delicacies of food but the necessity of human flesh.

A *redimiculum* is what we call a *succinctory* or *bracile*. Descending over the neck and divided at the sides of the neck, it surrounds the hollows of both armpits and girds them on either side. Thus, by constricting the breadth of the garments, it draws them toward the body and joins and arranges them. In common usage it is called a *bracile*, as though *brachiale* (“arm-band”), although it is now a girdle not for the arms but for the loins.

Monks living in Egypt adopted the customary use of this garment, so that their arms might be unimpeded for every work and they might be made ready for action, striving with all their strength to fulfill the Apostle’s command:

> These hands have ministered not only to me but also to those who were with me; nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment, but working in labor and weariness night and day, so that we might not burden any of you. (II Thess. III)

And:

> If anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat. (Ibid.)

It is called a *succinctory* because, as has been said, it is drawn beneath the arms, surrounds the hollows of the armpits, and girds them on either side.

The *succinctory* signifies the firm foundation of righteousness and truth. Hence Isaiah says concerning the Lord:

> Righteousness will be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his kidneys. (Isa. XI)

For he has become for us from God wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption (I Cor. I). In the Gospel he said:

> I am the light and the way, the life and the truth. (John XIV)

Concerning him it is said in the Psalms:

> Truth has risen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven. (Ps. LXXXIV)

Hence the Apostle exhorts the Ephesians:

> Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness. (Eph. VI)

A *fascia* is a band by which the breast is covered and the breasts are compressed; as the belt is tightened, the breast is made narrower and more closely constricted. It is called *fascia* because it binds the body in the manner of a bundle. Hence also come the *fasciolae* by which wounds are bound.

In a *fascia*, the vigilant custody of the mind regarding perverse thoughts and harmful desires can be understood. A woman—that is, a faithful soul—applies this to herself for her preservation. Hence the prophet says:

> Can a woman forget her ornament, or the breast-band of her chest? And so forth. (Jer. II)

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Shoes
Stitchers are so called because, inserting the bristles of pigs as thread, they sew—that is, stitch—hence they are almost *setores*. Shoemakers, however, are not called *caligarii* from the callus of the feet, but from *calo*, that is, “wood,” without which footwear cannot be sewn; the Greeks call these wooden forms *calopodes*. At first they were made only from willow; hence footwear is called *calceamenta*, either because it is made on a *calus*, that is, a piece of wood, or because it is trodden underfoot.

Footwear therefore mystically signifies the preaching of peace, concerning which the prophet says: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who preach good things!” (Isa. LII). And the Apostle says: “Having your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). Hence it is also written in Ezekiel: “I shod you with hyacinth,” that is, with heavenly hope, “and with footwear,” evidently after the example of the fathers who preceded us. Concerning this we read in Exodus: “And you shall have footwear on your feet” (Exod. XII).

Footwear also signifies the works of mortality, or the examples of wicked people, from which the Lord forbade the Apostles in the Gospel, saying: “Neither shall you carry footwear on the way” (Matt. X). *Ocreae*, or leg-coverings, are footwear because they cover the legs. *Cothurni* are the shoes worn by tragedians who were about to speak in the theater and sing verses in a high, resounding voice. It is a kind of footwear shaped like sandals, worn by heroes; but it is made in such a way that it fits either the right or the left foot.

*Soleae* are footwear in which only the soles of the feet are covered, and they are named from the sole of the foot. There are also material *soleae*, made from woven leather or other material. Mystically, *soleae*, or sandals, signify discrimination in teaching. Hence the Lord in the Gospel according to Mark (Mark VI) commanded the disciples to put sandals or *soleae* on their feet, so that the foot might be neither covered nor completely bare against the ground. Mystically, this signifies that the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rely upon earthly advantages.

*Socci*, whose diminutive is *socelli*, are so called because they have a pouch into which part of the sole is inserted. *Caliculae* … *Caligae* are named either from the callus of the feet or because they are tied; for *socci* are not tied but merely slipped on. *Caliculi*, or *caligae*, are described in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XII), where the Apostle Peter is said to have been instructed by an angel to put on his *caligae* and follow him. This signifies that, released from earthly bonds, he might go more freely to preach the Gospel.

*Corrigiae* are so called from leather, or from being tied together, almost as if they were *colligiae*. Thus *corrigiae* mystically signify the binding of the mystery. Hence John the Baptist says concerning the Lord: “Whose shoe-strap I am not worthy to loosen” (Mark I), that is, to reveal the mysteries of his incarnation; or, alternatively: “I am not worthy to carry his footwear,” that is, to claim for myself the bridegroom’s name.

# BOOK TWENTY-TWO

[Col. 0587]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Tables and Foods

[Col. 0587A]

Daedalus was the first to make a table and a chair. A certain Apicius was the first to arrange the equipment of the kitchen; having spent his wealth on it, he died by his own hand—and rightly so, because one who serves gluttony and greed for food destroys both soul and body.

The word *mensa* is derived from eating and eating together, for it has no other use. To cook therefore signifies that one ought to meditate carefully on the Lord’s word in the heart, that is, to “boil it down” in the mind, as it were. Frequent mention of this word is found in the Book of Leviticus.

To eat mystically signifies to receive divine words spiritually and to enjoy eagerly that bread which descended from heaven (John VI). Hence it is written in Joel: “And you shall eat, eating, and shall be satisfied, and you shall praise the Lord your God” (Joel II).

A *torus* is so called from twisted grasses, which are placed beneath the shoulders of those reclining. *Stibadium* is named from *stipites*, “stumps,” as though *stipadium*; for it was formerly written in this way.

Among the Greeks, *convivium* is derived from *compotatio*, *symposion*; among us it is more correctly called from *convictus*, “living together,” or because it includes conversation about life. It is also called *convivium* from the multitude of those eating together; for a private meal is *victus*, but it is not a *convivium*.

There are three aspects of a banquet: reclining, eating, and drinking. Reclining, as in: “I was ordered to recline on painted couches.” Eating and drinking, as in:

> After the first rest following the feast, and the tables removed,  
> They set out great mixing bowls and crown the wines.

A banquet mystically signifies either meditation on Sacred Scripture, in which spiritual refreshment is received, or the future recompense, where the fullness of all good things is believed to have been prepared for holy and worthy people. Hence it is written in the Prophet: “By the Lord a banquet of rich foods shall be prepared on this mountain, a banquet of marrow-filled foods and purified wine” (Isa. XXV).

*Cibus*, “food,” is so called because it is taken by the mouth, just as *esca*, “fare,” is so called because the mouth takes it. *Victus* is properly so called because it preserves life; hence to call someone to food is called *invitare*, “to invite.” *Alimonia*, “nourishment,” is so called because by its expenditure the body is nourished. The young receive it for growth, the old for perseverance; for flesh cannot endure unless it is strengthened by nourishment.

Food signifies either the preaching of the Lord’s word or the will of God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). And in the Prophet: “He fed them,” he says, “with the fat of wheat” (Ps. LXXX); this signifies either manna or the body of the Lord Christ. We call the corporeal fatness of animals *adeps*, “fat”; this word has been transferred improperly to wheat in order to indicate that some inner goodness is present in it.

*Victus* signifies necessary food, not luxurious food. Hence the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing,” or, as we read in other copies, “Having nourishment and coverings, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI). As though he were saying: It is enough to have those things that are necessary for our use. For these alone shall we enjoy; but if other things are accumulated, let us leave them to others in due measure.

“Having nourishment and coverings, let us be content with these”: he says “coverings,” not “clothing,” since in some Latin copies the expression is not properly rendered—that is, things that cover the body, not things that flatter the glory of dress.

*Opulentia*, “wealth,” is derived from *opes*, “resources.” If you examine it, you will find that it keeps to moderation; for how can something that is excessive provide assistance, when it is more troublesome than too little? The term *opulentia* applies not only to bodily things but also to spiritual things, because, as the text has it, *opes fuerunt* [sic], that is, earthly riches.

Likewise, the Scriptures speak of the riches of virtues, which make a person richer than earthly riches do. For the human spirit is tormented by earthly desires and worldly greed, but it is consoled and nourished by love of heavenly things. Hence the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded or to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us with all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life” (I Tim. VI).

*Epulae*, “feasts,” are named from the abundance of provisions. Simple feasts are divided into two necessities—bread and wine—and two superfluities, which are sought from land and sea for the sake of eating. *Dapes*, “banquets,” belong to kings; *epulae*, “feasts,” to private persons.

*Deliciae*, “delicacies,” are so called because people take pleasure in them and desire them pleasantly. When *epulae* carry a good meaning, they express the spiritual joy of the saints in the good things of virtues and wisdom. Hence the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not on the old leaven, nor on the leaven of malice and wickedness,” and so forth (I Cor. V). That is: possessing the joy of renewal, let us flee former deeds, casting every impurity away from us, for it is corruption. Just as leaven corrupts the whole mass (Ibid. and Gal. V), so an evil life corrupts the whole person.

Likewise, *dapes* and spiritual *deliciae* signify the delights of good actions and sacred knowledge, which nourish the soul. Conversely, when a person abuses earthly pleasures and bodily food, he causes harm not only to the soul but also to the body.

*Pulmentum*, “stew,” is named from *puls*, “porridge”; whether only porridge or something mixed with it is consumed, it is properly called *pulmentum*. We read that the patriarch Isaac desired a stew from his son Esau (Gen. XXVII), which Jacob nevertheless supplied successfully. Isaac, being well refreshed by it, returned to him a full blessing in exchange. This signifies that, while the former people remained occupied in external observance, the people of the Gentiles, offering to God the Father a stew of good will and innocence, deserved to receive the grace of eternal blessing.

*Satiēs* and *saturitas* differ from one another. *Satiēs* can be said even of a single food, from the fact that it is sufficient; *saturitas*, however, takes its name from *satura*, which is composed of a varied arrangement of foods.

*Satiēs* is sometimes used in a good sense and sometimes in the opposite sense. In the good sense, when it signifies an abundance of virtues in the present or the fullness of recompense in the future. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The Lord satisfied five thousand men” (Matt. XIV). And the Prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI).

It is used in the opposite sense when Scripture says concerning the impious: “They shall be satisfied with their punishments,” that is, they shall abound in future torments.

Likewise, *saturitas* is found used in both a good and an adverse sense. In the good sense, where the Prophet says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. XXI). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V).

In the evil sense, where the Psalmist says concerning the Jews: “They were satisfied with swine’s flesh and left what remained for the little ones” (Ps. XVI). For they were filled with the filth of their sins, having opposed the Son of God, and they transmitted the remnants of their sins to their children when they cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

*Crapula* is immoderate voracity, as it were “raw food”; by its rawness the heart is burdened and the stomach becomes indigested. Immoderate voracity is a vice; only so much is healthy as is sufficient for support and for nature.

By allegory or tropology, *crapula* is understood more in the adverse than in the good sense, because it refers more to vices than to virtues. Hence the Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come suddenly upon you,” and so forth (Luke XXI).

*Prandium*, “midday meal,” is named from the preparation of eating. Properly, however, the ancients called the food of all soldiers before battle *prandium*. Hence comes the commander’s address: “Let us dine, as though we were going to sup in the underworld.”

They say that *coena*, “supper,” is called from the fellowship of those eating. For the Greeks call what is common *koinon*; hence *communicantes*, “sharing together,” because they come together communally, that is, in common. Among the ancients it was customary to eat and feast publicly and communally, lest isolation produce luxury.

Supper is an evening meal, which the ancients called *vesperna*; for midday meals were not customary.

Mystically, *prandium* signifies the nourishment of the present age, in which the faithful are fed by the words and examples of the holy prophets and Apostles. Hence it is written in the Gospel parable: “The king said to his servants: Tell those who have been invited, ‘Behold, I have prepared my meal; bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered, and everything is ready’” (Matt. XXII).

*Supper* may be understood as the end of the world, when the Lord will repay each person according to his works. Hence, in the Gospel parable, when the worthy reclined at the banquet, the one who did not have a wedding garment was cast out from the company of the others into the punishment due to him. For while the elect recline in heavenly rest, only the rejected will be cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Bread is called *panis* either because it is set beside every food or because every animal desires it. For in Greek *pan* means “all.”

*Cibarius* is bread given to servants for food, not for delicacy. *Fermentatius* is bread made with leaven; *azymus* is unleavened. For *azymos* means “without leaven,” “pure.” *Acrozymus* is lightly leavened, as though *acroazymus*.

Bread is understood both in a good and in an evil sense. In the good sense, when it signifies Christ or his word. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread who descended from heaven” (John VI). And again: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (Ibid.).

Bread signifies faith, as in the Gospel: “Who among you,” he says, “will have a friend and go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves’?” (Luke XI).

Bread is also understood as charity. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Which of you, if his father asks for bread, will give him a stone?” (Ibid.).

Again, ten loaves are understood as the fullness of all the saints who keep the Decalogue; and the twelve loaves that were changed each Sabbath upon the table of the Presence (Exod. XXV) possess the sacramental significance of the twelve Apostles.

Bread is placed in the opposite sense when it signifies the teaching of heretics. Hence it is written in Solomon: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasing” (Prov. IX). Again, there: “Do not desire,” he says, “his foods, in which there is the bread of deceit” (Prov. XXIII).

Unleavened bread signifies purity of mind without the leaven of malice, as the Apostle says: “In the unleavened bread of sincerity” (I Cor. V).

*Similago*, “fine flour,” signifies the multitude of the faithful, purity of mind, the practice of mercy, and the strength of charity. Hence it is written in Leviticus: “But if he offers a gift, let his offering to God be fine flour” (Lev. II).

*Subcineritius panis*, “under-the-ashes bread,” is bread baked beneath ashes and turned over; it is the same as *focacius*, “hearth-cake.” Under-the-ashes bread signifies an offering of humility, as in Genesis: “Quickly knead three measures of fine flour and make under-the-ashes bread” (Gen. XVIII). In another sense: “Ephraim has become like under-the-ashes bread that is turned over” (Hos. VII).

*Clibanicius* is bread baked in a baking vessel. Concerning clibanicius bread it is written in Leviticus: “When you offer a sacrifice baked in an oven, it shall be of fine flour, loaves without leaven, kneaded with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil” (Lev. II).

Rightly, therefore, the sacrifice is said in this passage to have been baked in an oven, to announce the birth of Christ—namely, in the womb of the Mother of God. That oven is necessarily called *clibanus*; for just as the oven received the bread and the fire from above, so the Mother of God received from above the bread of life, namely God the Word, and the fire of the Spirit’s presence in her womb.

Therefore, receive the words of the Apostles as loaves, and those of the prophets as wafers. For as loaves are more suitable than wafers for nourishment, so the words of the Apostles are more suitable than the words of the prophets. Both, however, are unleavened, because they contain no leaven from another teaching—for example, from secular wisdom, which one should accept.

*Placentae* are made from spelt or other grain; some call them *liba*, because they please and are pleasing. *Dulcia*, “sweet cakes,” are kinds of baked goods, named from their taste; they are eaten sprinkled with honey.

*Crusta* is the surface of bread; it is also called *fragmenta*, “fragments,” because it is divided as something broken.

Jeremiah mentions *placentae*, where the people are rebuked because they baked cakes or hearth-cakes for the queen of heaven. This signifies heretics or schismatics: whatever they bake and prepare in heresy from secular wisdom, they offer not to God but to evil spirits.

And it is written in the Psalm: “He sends his crystal like pieces of bread” (Ps. CXLVII). The substance of crystal is rightly compared with hardened sinners, who, constricted by the cold of unbelief, freeze more each day. The Lord sends them forth like pieces of bread when he causes converts to proclaim his mighty works, so that the hungry people may eat heavenly bread.

We call pieces *fragmenta* because they are parts of some body. They signify the diverse gifts of teaching that the Lord has often deigned to display through his saints to those who observe them [perhaps “to sinners”].

*Fermentum*, “leaven,” is named from *fervere*, “to boil,” because it cannot be contained for more than one hour; as it grows, it rises beyond its limits.

*Farina*, “flour,” and *furfures*, “bran,” are named from *far*, “spelt,” whose refuse they are. *Amolum* is the flower of the flour, extremely fine because of its lightness and expelled from the millstone; hence it is called *amolum*, as though “from the millstone.”

Leaven is understood as faith in the Gospel, where it is written: “A woman took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour” (Matt. XIII). Leaven also signifies corruption of the mind through sin, as in Exodus: “Everyone who eats what is leavened,” he says, “his soul shall perish” (Exod. XII).

Flour signifies the multitude of the faithful, as in the Gospel: “A woman took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour” (Matt. XIII), which is the mystery of the Trinity.

Flour signifies a good or evil work, as in the Prophet: “There is no handful among them making flour; and even if there were, strangers would consume it” (Hos. VIII).

*Carnes*, “flesh,” are so called because they are *carae*, “dear,” or from *creare*, “to create”; hence the Greeks call flesh *kreas*.

Flesh signifies the sacrament of the Lord’s body in the Gospel: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood” (John VI).

Flesh signifies the historical sense of the Law, as some wish to understand it, in Exodus: “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be satisfied with bread” (Exod. XVI)—that is, after the illumination of faith and the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, you shall feed on spiritual food.

Flesh signifies the outer person, as it is written in the Apostle: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V); and blood signifies carnal action. Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. L).

Flesh and blood also signify the greed of the belly and lust, as the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV).

That is called *crudum*, “raw,” which is bloody; it is something cooked with blood. Yet something cooked for a long time is also called “cooked.” *Assum* is what burns, as though *arsum*, “burned.” *Elixum* is what is cooked in water alone. For *lixa* means water because it is dissolved; hence the dissolution of lust is called *luxus*, and limbs displaced from their proper place are called *luxa*.

The command in the Law concerning eating the flesh of the lamb at Passover is: “You shall not eat anything raw from it, nor cooked in water, but only roasted by fire” (Exod. XII).

What do the raw flesh of the lamb signify except his humanity, rejected without consideration and without reverent reflection? For whatever we contemplate carefully, we, as it were, cook in the mind. But the lamb’s flesh must be eaten neither raw nor cooked in water, because our Redeemer must be regarded neither as merely a human being nor considered, through human wisdom, in terms of how God could have become incarnate.

Whoever believes our Redeemer to be merely human—what else does he eat than raw lamb’s flesh? He has refused to cook it through understanding the Redeemer’s divinity. Whoever attempts to examine the mysteries of his incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to cook the lamb’s flesh in water; that is, he wishes to penetrate the mystery of his dispensation through lax or dissolved knowledge.

*Frixum*, “fried,” is named from the sound made when something burns in oil. *Frixura*, “frying,” signifies fear of punishment. Hence the Psalmist says: “My bones have been fried as in a frying-pan” (Ps. XXX).

Just as, through a favorable opinion concerning good merits, the bones—that is, the strength of the spirit—grow fat when the conscience rejoices in a happy recollection, as Solomon says, “*Farina* [*fama*, ‘reputation’] good makes the bones fat” (Prov. XV), so, through an adverse recollection of sins, virtue contracts as though fried, while a person greatly fears the reproaches of others and the judgments of his own conscience. Or the sinner is fried when he fears future fires and conflagrations; for one who fears that he will burn already grows cold from the terror of that burning.

*Salsum*, “salted,” is as though sprinkled with salt, with three syllables removed as though from the middle.

Salt signifies the seasoning of wisdom, as Truth himself says in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). And again: “Have salt in yourselves” (Mark IX).

Again, salt signifies the discredited knowledge of the Jews in Leviticus: “I shall rain,” he says, “dust and salt upon that land.”

* Salsugo*, “saltiness,” signifies contrition of heart, as it is said in Job concerning the wild asses—that is, monks: “His tents are in a land of saltiness” (Job XXXIX).

Again, *salsugo* signifies the unbelief of the Jews, or the barrenness of the mind, in the Psalter: “A fruitful land into saltiness” (Ps. CVI).

*Jus*, “broth” or “sauce,” is named by the masters of the kitchen from *jus*, “law,” because it is the law of its seasoning. The Greeks call it *zomos*.

To cook therefore signifies careful meditation. To meditate carefully on the Lord’s word in the heart is to boil it down in the mind, as it were; this is demonstrated in Leviticus.

To eat is to receive divine words spiritually and to enjoy eagerly that bread which descended from heaven. Hence in Joel: “And you shall eat, eating, and shall be satisfied, and you shall praise the Lord your God” (Joel II).

Hunger signifies the poverty of faith and the reception of the divine word in the Gospel: “There arose a severe famine in that region, and he himself began to be in need” (Luke XV). And in Isaiah: “Therefore my people were led away captive because they had no knowledge, and its nobles perished from hunger” (Isa. V). And in Amos: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I shall send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII). And in the Psalm: “To rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine” (Ps. XXXII).

Concerning this hunger for the word of God, it is said of the righteous man in the Psalm: “I was young and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI). And in Solomon: “The Lord will not kill the soul of the righteous with hunger” (Prov. X).

Thirst is the same as what was mentioned above: the dryness of the heart where the word of the Lord is absent. In Isaiah: “Their multitude ‘has lacked thirst’ [*siti caruit*; or *exaruit*, ‘has dried up’]” (Isa. V). And in Jeremiah: “Keep your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst” (Jer. II).

In a good sense: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V).

*Lac*, “milk,” is derived from a Greek word because of its whiteness. The Greeks call white *leukon*. Milk and blood are what nourish and what is nourished: we are nourished by milk, and we live by blood.

The breasts from which milk proceeds signify the teaching of the four Gospels. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song IV).

Milk is also understood as the ancient Law delivered through Moses. Hence in Genesis it is said concerning the preachers of the New Testament: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Gen. XLIX).

Milk also signifies simple teaching in the Apostle, where it is said: “As to little ones in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able” (I Cor. III). Here *milk* is understood as a small measure of understanding.

Hence it is also written in Isaiah concerning the Church of the Gentiles: “You shall be suckled at the breast of kings” (Isa. LX), that is, you shall be nourished by the preaching of holy teachers.

Milk also signifies sincerity of mind in the Epistle of Peter, where he says: “Desire rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation” (I Pet. II). For elsewhere it is written: “Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the milk of the flock?” (I Cor. IX).

*Quactum*, as though *coactum*, “pressed together,” that is, as though coagulated. When another substance is received into it, it coagulates.

“Coagulated” is used both in a good and in an evil sense. In the good sense, as in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “A coagulated mountain, a rich mountain” (Ps. LXVII). *Coagulatum* signifies concretely formed charity. The rich mountain is Christ or the Church.

In the evil sense, where it is written: “Their heart has coagulated like milk” (Ps. CXVIII), signifying that it has been congealed by vices.

Cheese signifies spiritual understanding, as some wish to interpret it, in the Books of Kings, where it is written concerning David: His father said to him, “Take an ephah of porridge,” that is, a measure of three *modii*, “and ten cheeses, and carry them to the commander” (I Sam. XVII). This bears the figure of the ten commandments of the Law together with faith in the Holy Trinity.

Butter signifies the evangelical word derived from the milk of the Law, as is narrated in Genesis concerning Abraham (Gen. XVIII), who offered the Lord butter with the other foods—that is, with a calf and milk—at the meal.

Butter also signifies the fruit of the Church, which believed from among the Jews. Hence it is written in Isaiah concerning the Lord: “He shall eat butter and honey” (Isa. VII). Our Savior is nourished by butter, that is, by the faith of believing Jews, and by honey, that is, by the sweetness of the love of the faithful from the Gentiles.

*Mel*, “honey,” is a Greek-derived name, which is believed to have received its name from bees. For a bee is called *melissa* in Greek.

Formerly honey was made from dew and was found on the leaves of reeds. Hence Virgil too says:

> At once the heavenly gifts of aerial honey.

Indeed, even to this day in India and Arabia it is found clinging to branches in the likeness of salt.

Honey also mystically signifies the sweetness of God’s commandments. Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII).

Honey also expresses, by figurative meaning, the sweetness of the Savior himself, concerning whom it is said in the Song of Deuteronomy: “They sucked honey from the rock” (Deut. XXXII); and the Psalmist says: “He satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX).

Honey is placed in the opposite sense when it signifies the sweetness of sin and a voluptuous life. For this reason the Law also prohibited it from being offered in God’s sacrifice.

A *favus*, “honeycomb,” is so called because it is eaten rather than drunk. For the Greeks call eating *phagein*.

By allegory, the honeycomb is the flesh of the Savior, full of the sweetness of divinity, as in the Gospel: “And they placed before him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb” (Luke XXIV).

The honeycomb is also divine Scripture, filled with the honey of spiritual wisdom, as in the Song of Songs: “I ate my honeycomb with my honey” (Song V).

In the opposite sense, the honeycomb is used where it signifies the seductive deception of heretics. Hence it is read in Proverbs: “The lips of a prostitute drip with honeycomb” (Prov. V).

Physicians, and those who have written about the nature of human bodies—especially Galen in the books whose title is *Peri ugias* (“On Health”)—say that the bodies of children, young people, and men and women in the prime of life burn with an innate heat. Foods that increase heat are harmful to these ages, while cold foods are beneficial when consumed. Conversely, for the elderly, who suffer from phlegm and cold, hot foods and old wines are beneficial.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Drink
## Chapter II. On Drink

“Drink” (*potio*) is so called from the Greek derivation; for the Greeks call it *poton*. Water is so called generally because its surface is level. Hence also “waters” (*aequora*), and therefore we call it “fresh” (*recentem*), because aged water is not useful, as wine is: it must be taken immediately from a river, spring, or well. For aged water becomes foul. Water is the natural drink and is generally common to everyone; hence it is healthier than the others.

“Drink” sometimes signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Psalm 35). In another sense: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” [Col. 0595A] (Romans 14).

Wine (*vinum*) is so called because its drinking fills the veins with blood. Others call it *lyaeum*, because it releases us from care. The ancients called wine *venenum*; but after the poisonous juice that brings death was discovered, this was called *vinum*, and that other substance *venenum*. Hence Jerome, in the book he wrote on preserving virginity, says that young women ought to shun wine as they would poison, lest they drink it while inflamed by the heat of youth and perish. For this reason, among the ancient Romans women did not use wine except on certain days for the sake of religious rites.

We call it “pure wine” (*merum*) when we mean unmixed wine. For we call anything pure and unadulterated *merum*, just as we call water pure when it has been mixed with nothing. Hence also *merenda*, because in ancient times, at that hour, pure bread was given to children and laborers; or because they ate at midday—that is, alone and separately—not, as at breakfast or dinner, at a common table. We believe that the time after midday is likewise called *meridies* because it is “pure.”

Wine has many meanings. Sometimes it signifies the blood of Christ, as in the Gospel: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6). Sometimes it signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as in: “New wine must be put into new wineskins” (Mark 2). Sometimes it signifies divine speech or compunction of heart, as in the Psalm: “You gave us wine of compunction” (Psalm 59). Sometimes it signifies divine judgment, as in the Apocalypse: “He himself has trodden the winepress of the wine of the wrath of the fury of the Lord” (Apocalypse 19). [Col. 0595C] Sometimes it signifies Holy Scripture and sound doctrine; hence Isaiah says to the Jews: “Your tavern-keepers mix water with wine” (Isaiah 1). Sometimes it signifies works of lust, as the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5). And elsewhere: “Wine is a wanton thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous” (Proverbs 20).

“Pure wine” (*merum*) signifies either sincerity of judgment or truth, or even the warmth of faith, as in the Psalm: “Full of pure wine, mixed” (Psalm 74). Therefore blessed Ambrose, in his hymn for the holy Epiphany, proclaimed this splendidly, with an extraordinary radiance of words. What he called “pure” (*meri*) indicates sincerity—what is always pure and always clear. For it brings restored human beings to the glory of virtue, not to the vice of drunkenness. What he called “mixed” signifies the New and Old Testaments, which, mingled together, produce a most healthful drink for souls. [Col. 0595D]

Spiced wine signifies fervent love, adorned with the various spices of the virtues. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine and the must of my pomegranates” (Song of Songs 8).

Must is wine taken immediately from the vat. It is believed to be called *mustum* because it contains mud and earth mixed into it. For *mus* means “earth,” whence also *humus*; and such is the force of its fermentation that vessels, however large, if left full of it without a vent, immediately burst.

Must signifies the newly given grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles we read that the Jews said of the Apostles: “These men are full of new wine” [Col. 0596A] (Acts 2). Although they interpreted this maliciously, in truth the Apostles were filled with divine grace, from which they gave many people drink in a health-giving drunkenness.

Vinegar (*acetum*) is so called either because it is sharp (*acutum*) or because it is watered (*aquatum*); for wine mixed with water quickly turns to this taste. Hence also *acidum*, as though *aqu idum*, “watery.” Mystically, vinegar signifies corrupted purity of mind. Thus it is written in the Psalm: “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68). Matthew reports that, when the Lord said, “I thirst” (Matthew 27), they offered him gall mixed with vinegar, so that the bitterness and harshness of the drink might truly indicate the faithlessness of the Jews. He said, “I thirst,” because he could not find in them the faith he desired; they offered their own exceedingly bitter ways, in which they were converted by no compunction. The harshness of vinegar is likewise understood as the corruption of the mind. Hence in the Book of Numbers (Numbers 6), the Nazirites who consecrated themselves to the Lord were forbidden to consume both wine and vinegar.

*Sycer* is every drink, apart from wine, that can intoxicate. Although its name is Hebrew, it has a Latin sound, since it is made from the juice of grain or fruit, or from the fruit of palms pressed into liquid; alternatively, cooked grains are strained with water made richer, as it were, by their juice, and the resulting drink is called *sycer*. *Sycer* signifies drunkenness, from which all Holy Scripture forbids us. Hence in the Law the Lord said to Aaron: “You and your sons shall not drink wine, nor anything that can intoxicate, when you enter the tent of testimony” (Leviticus 10)—that is, when you enter upon divine service and spiritual teaching. For the tent of testimony is the touching or apprehension of heavenly things. Therefore the Apostle not only forbids us to become drunk, but the prophet Isaiah likewise condemns drunkenness, saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening,” and so forth (Isaiah 5). *Sycer* also signifies the sweetness of sin and the enticement of pleasure. Hence the angel testified concerning the Lord’s forerunner: “He shall drink neither wine nor sycer” (Luke 1), because he was fasting and devoted to abstinence.

Drunkenness is sometimes understood as sobriety of mind, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “These men are drunk” (Acts 2). In another sense, drunkenness and gluttony signify the fullness of vices, as in the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21). And in Solomon: “As a thorn comes into the hand of a drunkard” (Proverbs 26). [Col. 0596D]

Lees (*fex*) is so called because, rising up in the vessel, it clings to it. Lees signifies the final judgment. Hence it is written concerning the lees in the Psalm: “Yet its lees have not been emptied” (Psalm 74). Here we must understand “lees” not as filth, but as the lowest and final sediment of wine. For how could that which he previously declared to be pure and unmixed have lees? But so that you might understand that this lees had not yet been reached, he returns to the full cup, saying: “All the sinners of the earth shall drink” (ibid.). Here he signifies what we have often said: that at the end of the age the Jews will drink from this cup together with the other sinners, when they are judged worthy to believe and are joined to the Catholic Church in united faith.

## Chapter III. On Eating Vessels

A vessel (*vas*) is so called from eating (*vesci*), because food is placed in it. Its diminutive is *vasculum*, as though *vesculum*.

Earthenware vessels (*fictilia*) are so called because they are made and shaped from earth. To shape (*fingere*) means to make, form, and mold; hence potters are also so called. An earthen vessel (*vas fictile*) is not something “fictitious,” that is, false, but something formed so that it exists and has a certain shape. Hence the Apostle says: “Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Romans 9).

It is said that earthen vessels were first invented on the island of Samos, made from chalky earth and hardened by fire; hence they were called Samian vessels. Later people discovered how to add red pigment and shape vessels from red earth. It is clear that the use of earthen vessels is older than the casting of bronze or silver. Among the ancients there were neither golden nor silver vessels, but earthen ones: casks were devised for wine, jars and pitchers for water, vessels for baths, and the rest of the objects used by human beings were either made on a wheel or fashioned by hand.

The form of earthen vessels therefore pertains to the lot of human nature. Hence it is written: “God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Genesis 2). Yet when these vessels have been thoroughly fired by the fire of the Holy Spirit, they become precious vessels fit for the service of God. Precious vessels, golden and silver, are the saints who shine with the splendor of wisdom and the radiance of eloquence. Conversely, wooden or earthen vessels are those who still fall somewhat short of perfection. Hence the Apostle says: “In a great house there are not only golden and silver vessels, but also wooden and earthen ones; some are for honor, but others for dishonor” (2 Timothy 2). The great house, he says, is the Church, consisting of many human beings. Therefore not all within it can be equal. For even in a very large house all vessels cannot be found to be alike; among golden and silver vessels, wooden and earthen ones are also seen. Some are worthy of honor, while others are contemptible and assigned to a particular use.

Then, because the division of vessels was natural, lest anyone suppose that the same was true among us, he added: “If anyone purifies himself from these things, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, and prepared for every good work” (ibid.). What natural material accomplishes there, free choice accomplishes here. Whoever separates himself from what is worse is a useful vessel for the honor of God; others are for dishonor. This lies within our choice and power: whether we choose what is better or what is worse.

Chased silver or gold vessels are vessels marked inside or outside with prominent figures. Their name derives from *caelum*, a kind of tool that people commonly call a *cilio*.

*Chrysendeta* are gilded vessels; the word is Greek. *Anaglypha* are vessels sculpted in relief. For in Greek *ano* means “above,” and *glyphen* means “to carve”; hence *anaglypha*, that is, “carved above.”

Chased or relief-work vessels signify the saints, distinguished and adorned with the insignia of various virtues. The vessels called gilded signify those whom the gift of perfect love adorns. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44). We must apply gold to the splendor of love, by which the holy Church, surrounded, shines. And lest you understand love alone to be present there, he said “in a gilded garment,” not “in a golden one.” We call something gilded when the appearance of gold is laid over and attached to some material. Love’s grace appeared above the other virtues because its radiance surpasses them all.

He adds, “clothed all around with variety.” Let us inquire why the Church of God is praised for the variety of her garment, when everything fitting for her is simple and one. By this variety he either signifies the many languages, because every nation in the Church sings to its Creator according to its own homeland, or the most beautiful diversity of virtues. She is adorned with the gold of the Apostles, the silver of the prophets, the gems of virgins, the scarlet of martyrs, and the purple of penitents. This, then, is the variety of unity, woven from all nations so as to please the eyes of the Lord through holy conduct.

The dish (*discus*) was formerly called *iscus*, from the likeness of a shield; hence also *scutella*. Later it was called *discus* because it gives or places food, and from it come the terms for those reclining at table. Alternatively, it comes from the Greek *apo tou dicein*, “because they throw.”

A *paropsis* is a square, four-sided vessel, that is, one with sides of equal projections. A *patena* is so called because it is a broad and open dish with an extended rim.

The Gospel speaks of a dish and a *paropsis* (Matthew 14): at the beheading of John, mention is made of a dish; and in the account of the Savior’s Passion, a *paropsis* is mentioned (Matthew 26). Through these examples all of us who detest Herod’s lust and Judas’s avarice are warned to flee lust and cruelty and to avoid every kind of fraud or betrayal.

A table (*mensa*) is so called from *mensis*, “month,” because on that day banquets were celebrated according to the custom of the nations. Concerning the table the prophet says: “You have prepared a table before me” (Psalm 22). The Church’s table is a blessed banquet, a joyful feast, the satisfaction of faith, and heavenly food. Yet it is clear that this table has been prepared against those who, sunk in some perversion, grievously distress the Church of God by their error. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11)—the body given, of course, for the remission of sins and the possession of everlasting life.

Remember also that “table” is used both in a good and in a bad sense, as the Apostle says: “You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10). The table is likewise the altar of Christ, from which the faithful receive the mystery of his body and blood.

Again, the Lord’s table is the intellectual feast of both Testaments, at which those who hunger for the Lord’s delights with eager minds are nourished as at a banquet and desire to be filled with the health-giving drunkenness of the Holy Spirit. This became a stumbling block to the Jews, as the Psalmist testifies: “Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling block” (Psalm 68), when those Jews rejected the spiritual banquet of Christ.

In Exodus (Exodus 25) the Lord commanded Moses to make a table of setim wood and to prepare for its service various vessels—that is, dishes, bowls, censers, and cups—in which libations were to be offered, and so forth. The Lord’s table made of setim wood is Holy Scripture, produced by holy men.
