The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of divine speech, adapted to the differing capacities of its hearers. For the wise are to be taught in one way, the foolish in another; the rich in one way, the poor in another; the healthy in one way, the sick in another; the old in one way, the young in another; men in one way, women in another; celibates in one way, married people in another; rulers in one way, subjects in another. Yet all these vessels pertain to the offering of libations, because when a prudent teacher speaks variously according to the diversity of his hearers, everything is found within the rule of Holy Scripture, and these teachings rouse the hearts of the listeners to offer vows of good works to the Lord.

Hence it is also written in the Book of Numbers that the leaders would offer at the dedication of the altar various vessels—that is, dishes, bowls, and mortars. These naturally have a mystical meaning. The dishes, which have a narrow mouth, mysteriously express the narrowness of the letter of the Law and the obscurity of prophetic speech. Bowls, however, which are said originally to have been made of glass—for the Greeks call glass *hyalon*—and which have a broad opening at the top, suggest the brightness and clarity of the evangelical meaning, in which all the mysteries of the Law and the prophets have been explained, as well as the plain expression of apostolic teaching, in which those things that were previously hidden in riddles have been brought into the light and expounded. And what else is signified by a golden mortar than the heart of the elect, full of divine wisdom and containing within itself the spices of the virtues?

## Chapter IV. On Drinking Vessels

A cup (*poculum*) is named from drinking (*potare*); it is every vessel in which the practice of drinking takes place. Mystically, a cup signifies the chalice of the Lord’s blood, which so intoxicates that it heals the mind, restraining it from sins rather than leading it to sin. This drunkenness makes the sober; this fullness empties away evils. Whoever is not filled with that cup is left eternally hungry in poverty.

It is also found in a negative sense, as Isaiah says: “I received from your hand the cup of ruin, the cup of my wrath and indignation” (Isaiah 61). He also added what is especially glorious, since such gifts lead to the kingdom of heaven. Concerning this cup the Gospel says: “Whoever drinks from the water that I shall give will never thirst, but the water that I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4).

Bowls (*paterae*, *phialae*) are so called either because we usually drink from them or because they are open and have widely spread rims. Bowls signify the holy teachers in the Church, filled with extensive knowledge. Concerning this there is also material in Exodus.

In sinners, however, bowls signify the portion of divine wrath, as in the Apocalypse: “Seven final bowls full of God’s wrath” (Apocalypse 16).

A *crater* is a cup with two handles, and the name is Greek. Among the Greeks it is declined as masculine, *hic crater*; in Latin it is feminine, *haec cratera*. Hence Persius writes:

> If for you, silver mixing bowls.

Virgil writes:

> They set out great mixing bowls and crown the wines.

At first they were made from interwoven branches. Hence they were called *craterae*, from the Greek *apo tou cratein*, “because they hold one another together.”

There are also *cyathi* and *scyphi*. *Cymbia* are likewise kinds of cups; the name *cymbium* is derived from the likeness of a ship’s *cymba*.

An *amystis* is a kind of cup from which one drinks in a single draught—that is, in one breath.

*Bachea* were first named from Bacchus, which means wine; later the term passed into use for water vessels.

*Calices*, *calathi*, and *schalae* are kinds of cups formerly made of wood, and from this they received their names. For the Greeks called every kind of wood *calon*.

The cup signifies Holy Scripture, that is, the two Testaments, as some hold. Thus in the Gospel according to Luke it is recorded that at Passover the Lord gave the Apostles two cups, one before the supper and another after the supper (Luke 22).

Figuratively, the cup also expresses the punishments of sinners in the Psalter: “Fire and sulfur and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Psalm 10). Again, the cup is the tribulation of the present life, and punishment upon all nations, in Jeremiah: “Take this cup and give all the nations to drink from it” (Jeremiah 25).

An *ampulla* is, as it were, a broad bubble; it resembles in its roundness the bubbles that form from the foam of water and swell in the wind. We have already spoken above about the mystical meaning of vessels, and it is not necessary to repeat what has already been fully explained.

## Chapter V. On Wine and Water Vessels

An *oenophorus* is a vessel carrying wine. For *oinos* means “wine.” Concerning it there is the line:

> The bottom turns in the wine vessels; our judgment is overturned.

*Phlascas* is derived from a Greek word. These vessels were originally made for carrying and storing bowls, and from this they received their name. Later they came into use for wine, while retaining the Greek name from which they had originated.

*Lagena* and *situla* are Greek names, modified in part so that they would become Latin. The Greeks say *lagenos*; we say *lagena*. They say *sicile*; we say *situla*.

Lagenas signify human hearts, which retain the wine of wisdom, as in the prophet: “Every little flask shall be filled with wine” (Jeremiah 13).

A *hydria* is so called by derivation as a kind of water vessel; for the Greeks call water *hydor*. The *hydria* signifies human flesh, as in the Book of Judges: “And he gave them into their hands, empty water jars” (Judges 7). And in Solomon: “Let the water jar be shattered over the spring” (Ecclesiastes 12)—that is, carnal desire, concerning which it is read in the Gospel: “She left her water jar and went into the city” (John 4).

The six water jars in the Gospel (John 2) signify the six ages of the world, in which the water of legal wisdom was changed by Christ into the wine of spiritual grace.

A *situla* is so called because it is suitable for the thirsty to drink from; the Greeks call this vessel a *cadus*. Mystically, the *situla* signifies the flesh of Christ. Hence it is written in the Book of Numbers: “Water flows from his water jar” (Numbers 24).

A *catinum* is an earthen vessel; it is better spoken of in the neuter gender than the masculine, just as *salinum* is a vessel suitable for salt.

A *catinum* has the same meaning that we attributed to the *paropsis*, in which the Savior’s betrayer was revealed.

A *scyphus* is a vessel in which we wash the hands.

An *orca* is a large jar; *seriola* is a straight row or a wine vessel, first devised in Syria. *Cilicises* were so called from Cilicia, from which they were first brought.

The *scyphus* signifies knowledge of the Law. Hence Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack (Genesis 44), because heavenly doctrine shone forth in Paul’s body through his eloquence.

An *orca* is a kind of amphora; its smaller form is *urceus*, and its diminutive is *urceolus*.

A *dolium*: [lacuna] *Cupos* and *cupas* are thought to be so called from *capere*, “to take,” that is, to receive water or wine; hence also *caupones*, tavern-keepers.

A *uter* is named from *uterus*, “womb.” Concerning the wineskin the Psalm says: “I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your righteous judgments” (Psalm 118). A wineskin emptied of its natural heat by frost is drawn tight through the benefit of conversion. When it has thus been happily seasoned, what follows takes place: it can in no way forget the Lord’s righteous judgments.

The wineskin signifies mortal flesh; the frost indicates the benefit of conversion. Through this, our flesh, which is inclined to vice, is contracted by the discipline of repentance. The heat of faith increases in proportion to the bodily flame that has been withdrawn.

The Gospel also mentions wineskins, when the Lord, speaking of the preaching of faith, says: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins, otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine is spilled; but they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9). By the old wineskins he signifies carnal people, and by the new wineskins spiritual people, who are suited to receive the wine of heavenly grace.

A *mulgarium* is a vessel in which animals are milked; it is also called a *mulctrum*, from the milk that is milked there. A *mulgarium* is likewise a pastoral vessel into which milk is poured, and it signifies the Old Law, in which was contained the milk of simple teaching suited to the inexperienced.

A basin (*labrum*) is so called because infants were customarily washed in it; its diminutive is *labellum*. It is also called an *alveus*, because washing was customarily done in it.

A basin is read of in Exodus, placed before the entrance of the Lord’s temple. There the priests washed their hands and [Col. 0601D] feet when they were about to enter the tent of testimony and when they were about to approach the altar. This signifies cleansing through the tears of compunction.

The condition of tears and compunction is distinguished in two ways. First, whoever turns to the Lord must pray for forgiveness for the sins he has committed, pouring out tears. If he perseveres in this for a long time, accompanied by worthy fruits of repentance, then it remains for him, made more secure by the forgiveness he has received, to long with eager desires for the time when he may be found worthy to see the face of the Creator among the most blessed choirs of angels.

A basin (*pelvis*) is so called because the feet are washed in it. The basin in which the Lord poured water and washed the feet of his disciples (John 13) signifies holy prayer. Through prayer, divine grace, after the washing of baptism, cleanses our works from earthly stains. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever has been bathed has no need except to wash his feet; he is entirely clean” (ibid.).

How can both be true—that he is entirely clean and yet his feet must be washed? Only because he is entirely clean in the bath of holy baptism, but is again soiled by the dust of earthly habitation. Therefore he must again be washed through the grace of divine compassion, although previously that same grace had cleansed him entirely, as the Apostle John testifies: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Every day, therefore, he washes our feet, the one who intercedes for us; and every day we confess in the Lord’s Prayer that we need to have our feet washed when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

## Chapter VI. On Oil Vessels

A *lenticula* is a small oil vessel made of bronze or silver, named from *linire*, “to anoint.” With these, kings and priests were anointed. It signifies Holy Scripture, in which the promise of the Holy Spirit is contained, through whose grace we are anointed and sanctified for God (Apocalypse 1), and made spiritual kings and priests.

## Chapter VII. On Cooking and Baking Vessels

All vessels prepared for cooking are called *cocula*. Plautus writes:

> All mercy has been cooked out for me in bronze pots, and so forth.

An *olla* is so called because water boils in it when a fire is placed beneath it, so that the vapor may be sent upward more forcefully. Hence also *bulla*, “bubble,” which is sustained in water by the breath of the wind.

A *patella* is so called as though *patula*, “open”; it is a pot with a more open mouth.

Mystically, the *olla* is understood by some as a family lineage. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Moab is the pot of my hope” (Psalm 59), on account of Ruth. The *olla* also signifies eternal condemnation, as in Joel: “Their faces shall be turned into a pot” (Joel 2).

Again, the *olla* is the Jewish people, inflamed by carnal desire, concerning which Jeremiah says: “I see a boiling pot” (Jeremiah 1). Under the name of the *olla*, the present world, or the human race, or any sinful soul subjected to the fire of tribulation is likewise indicated. Concerning this the Lord said to Ezekiel: “Set the pot upon the coals, empty, until its bronze becomes hot” (Ezekiel 24).

A *cacabus* and a *cucuma* are named from the sound of boiling. These names are common to Greek and Latin; but whether the Latins borrowed the words from the Greeks or the Greeks from the Latins is uncertain.

*Lebetes* are bronze vessels, so called in Greek; they are smaller pots prepared for cooking. Concerning the *lebes* it is written in Ezekiel: “Thus says the Lord God: Set the pot and pour water into it, and put into it pieces of bones and flesh,” and so forth (Ezekiel 24). There, under the likeness of the pot, he describes the city of Jerusalem; under the cooking of the bones and flesh, he expresses the torments of the strong and the weak within it; and through the boiling of the red fire itself, he signifies the city’s destruction on account of its iniquities.

According to the tropological meaning, this city and pot signify the present world, which lies in the power of the Evil One (1 John 5). On the day of judgment it will be kindled by divine fire, and the city of bloodshed will be placed upon burning coals, so that what is written in Isaiah may be fulfilled: “Having coals of fire, he sat upon them” (Isaiah 50). What is also written will be fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10). The Lord says that he will not have mercy, nor pass over the sins of the world, nor spare the impious, nor be appeased, so that the paths of the wicked may perish, according to what is placed at the end of the first Psalm: “The way of the wicked shall perish.”

A *sartago* is named from the sound it makes when oil burns in it. The *sartago* also signifies the tribulation of the present life, as in the Psalm: “And my bones”—that is, the strong members of the Church—“have been fried as in a frying pan” (Psalm 30). Again, the *sartago* signifies zeal for righteousness against sins and compunction for a brother’s weakness. In Ezekiel: “And you, son of man, place a frying pan between yourself and the city” (Ezekiel 4). The Apostle speaks of this frying pan: “Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (2 Corinthians 11).

A millstone (*mola*) is so called from its roundness, like an apple (*mala*)—as is also the case among the Greeks. The millstone expresses the circuit of the present life and earthly labor. In the Gospel: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone drawn by an ass be hung around his neck and he be sunk into the depths of the sea” (Matthew 18).

Hence Isaiah says against Babylon: “Take the millstone and grind flour” (Isaiah 47). And elsewhere: “Those who grind shall be killed” [the supplied text reads “their idle ones”] “in a small number” (Ecclesiastes 12).

The two millstones signify the two Testaments of the Law, as some hold. Hence it is read in the Gospel: “Then two will be grinding at the mill; one will be taken and one will be left” (Matthew 24). The two millstones also signify hope and fear, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not take the lower or the upper millstone as a pledge” (Deuteronomy 24).

A sieve (*cribrum*) is so called because grain runs through it, as though *currifrugum*. Allegorically, the sieve is the separation of the faithful from association with unbelievers. It is mentioned in Amos (Amos 9), and in the Gospel the Lord says to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat,” and so forth (Luke 22).

## Chapter VIII. On Storage Vessels

A treasury (*gazophylacium*) is a chest in which are collected, in the temple, those things sent for the needs of the poor. The word is composed from the Persian and Greek languages. In Persian, *gaza* means “riches”; in Greek, *phylaxion* [*phylace*] means “custody.”

Mystically, the treasury is the hearts of the saints, full of the riches of wisdom. This is sufficiently demonstrated in the prophet Ezekiel and in the Gospel.

A chest (*arca*) is so called because it bars and prevents sight. Hence also *archivum* and *arcanum*, that is, “secret,” from which others are kept away.

The mystical significance of the chest is fully demonstrated in Exodus, where the construction of the ark of the Lord’s covenant is narrated. It signifies either the incarnation of the Lord or the holy Church, in which the divine Testaments are stored. The ark of Noah likewise plainly holds the type of the holy Church.

A *loculus* is a place made for putting something inside, or for guarding clothes or money. Hence it is called by a diminutive form. A *loculus* is mentioned in Genesis, where Joseph’s tomb is described, and in the Gospel there is mention of the purse of Judas the betrayer.

*Scrinia* are vessels in which books or treasures are kept. Hence among the Romans those who preserve books and ecclesiastical treasures are called *scriniarii*.

A sack (*saccus*) is named from *sagum*, because it is made by sewing that material together, as though *sagus*. It is the garment of penitents and the container of humble or worthless things.

A purse (*marsupium*) is a small bag for coins, which the Greeks call *marsupon*. Some Greek names are slightly modified into Latin for the sake of Roman speech.

*Sitarciae* are sailors’ bags, so called because they are sewn together.

An *involucrum* is so called because it holds something wrapped inside itself.

A *fiscus* is a public purse; hence *fiscellae* and *fiscinae* are also derived from it. Tax collectors have this purse, and they put into it the public revenue that is paid to kings. *Fiscus* is the original form, *fiscina* the derivative, and *fiscella* the diminutive.

Mystically, a small purse (*sacculus*) is the storing up of good works. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old” (Luke 12). In another sense, this is understood from what is read in Solomon: “Let us possess together a purse, or money bag” (Proverbs 1)—that is, avarice. [Col. 0604C]

Allegorically, a *pera* signifies concern for food and livelihood. Hence the Lord commanded: “Carry neither purse nor bag on the road” (Luke 10).

## Chapter IX. On the Basket

A basket (*canistrum*) is woven from split reeds, and from this it is named. Others assert that the word is Greek.

The basket signifies the tongue of the teacher, in which the unleavened loaves are offered by the prescription of the Law—that is, the word of the Gospel as a sacrifice to the Lord—just as it is read that this was done at the anointing of Aaron and his sons.

A *cophinus* is a vessel woven from branches, suitable for removing dung and carrying earth. Concerning it the Psalmist speaks for Israel: “His hands served in the basket” (Psalm 80). It is called *cophinus* as though *covus* or *cavus*, “hollow.”

Although this may seem to be said historically, when the Jewish people in Egypt served under various necessities—sometimes making bricks, sometimes carrying earth in baskets—we apply it more carefully to the fathers of Christians. From their backs God turns away the burdens of sins when they prostrate themselves in blessed humility, as he himself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

We call those baskets *cophini* through which we throw away the refuse of filth so that the purity of the place may shine forth. Therefore those who are occupied with the uncleanness of sins hold their hands in them; but we are freed from this servitude by the Lord when we are cleansed from the filth of our crimes.

The twelve baskets also signify the Apostles, in which the leftover fragments from the five loaves and two fish were collected (Matthew 14).

A *sporta* is either made from broom (*spartum*) or so called because it carries something away. It is also read in the Gospel that the Apostles took seven full baskets from the fragments of the seven loaves. This signifies that the apostolic teachers gather into themselves those things from the mystical teachings of the Holy Spirit that the people are unable to consume.

## Chapter X. On Lighting Vessels

The ancients called fire *focus*; for *fos* is “fire” in Greek and *ignis* in Latin. Hence, according to certain philosophers, all things are generated from it, and truly nothing is born without heat. Thus the poet says of the north:

> Nothing is brought forth by barren cold.

Varro says that *foci* are so called because they nourish fires. For the fire itself is the flame. Whatever nourishes the fire is called a *focus*, whether it is an altar or something else in which the fire is maintained.

A lamp (*lucerna*) is named from *lychnos*. Hence *lu* is short, as Persius writes:

> The arranged lamps vomited forth a thick cloud.

[Cols. 0605C–0614B]

If it were said “from light,” the verse would not scan. *Lychnus*, however, is as though from *lucinius*, for it is the wick of a lamp. The lamp of the Church is faith or works of righteousness. Hence it is written in Solomon: “Therefore her lamp will not be extinguished throughout the night” (Prov. XXXI). Likewise, “lamp” signifies prophetic speech or preachers of divine law. Thus the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet” (Ps. CXVIII). And in the Gospel it is written of John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V).

*Candelabrum* is named from *candela*, as though *candelaferum*, “that which carries a candle.” Mystically, the candlestick signifies the Lord’s body, or the holy Church, or divine Scripture. Hence it is read in Zechariah: “I saw two silver candlesticks on the right side of the altar” (Zech. IV). For the seven lamps placed upon the candlestick—as is read in Exodus—signify the mystery of the sevenfold Church and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

*Cereus* derives its name from *cera*, “wax,” from which it is formed. Concerning it one says:

> Here I, a wax-candle, shall provide you nocturnal fires:
>
> When daylight has been withdrawn, I am another light for you.

The wax candle, which is lit to illuminate the darkness of night, signifies the teaching of a faithful preacher, which enlightens souls that believe and obey the word of God. Likewise, it is written of wax in the Psalm: “As wax melts before the fire, so sinners will perish before the face of God, and the righteous will feast” (Ps. LXVII). For in God’s judgment sinners perish before his face just as wax is consumed by the fire close at hand.

*Lacunaria* are suspended lights, as though *lucanaria*, that is, “shining in the air.” *Funalia* are so called because they are contained within wax; they are named from *funis*, “cord,” since before the use of papyrus our ancestors used to surround cords with wax. Hence funerals (*funera*) are also so called.

A *lampas* is a flame shining at the top, called so because it seems to display the movement of something gliding. Concerning the lamps, it is read in the Gospel (Matt. XXV) that the five wise virgins had their lamps with oil, because the elect keep in their hearts the oil of mercy and charity, which the foolish virgins do not have. Therefore, when the wise enter the wedding feast, the foolish are rejected; and their works, which appeared bright outwardly before human beings, are darkened inwardly at the Judge’s coming, and they receive no reward from God, because for them they received from human beings the praises that they loved.

Likewise, lamps signify the shining hearts of the saints, always radiant with the light of knowledge, as in the Song of Songs: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” (Song VIII). Elsewhere too it is written: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich” (Job XII); this signifies that teachers are despised in the hearts of the proud.

*Fax* is so called because it makes a fire (*focus*); its diminutive is *facula*. A *laterna* is so named because it contains light enclosed within. It is made of glass, with the light shut inside so that no gust of wind can reach it, and it can easily be carried everywhere to provide illumination.

A *pyra* is a structure that is customarily built from wood in the shape of an altar so that it may burn. For *pur* means “fire.” But a *pyra* is a heap of wood when it has not yet begun to burn; it is a *rogus* when it has begun to burn; and once it has been burned out it is called a *bustum*.

A *pharus* is a very large tower, which Greeks and Latins alike called a *pharus* from the common use of the thing itself, because it could be seen from far away by sailors as a signal of flame. As we said above, Ptolemy is said to have built one of this kind near Alexandria at a cost of eight hundred talents. Its purpose is to display fires for ships traveling at night, announcing shoals and the entrances to harbors, lest sailors deceived by the darkness run upon rocks. For Alexandria has approaches made treacherous by deceptive shoals. Hence, in harbors, structures built to shine ahead as a service are called *phari*. For *phos* means “light,” and *oros* means “sight”; hence the bringer of light is called in Greek *phosphoros*.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Beds and Seats

*Lecticae* are so called from beds of herbs (*lecti herbarum*). *Stratus* is named from *sternere*, “to spread,” as though *storiatus*. In these alone the ancients reclined for sleeping, before woolen bedding had been devised. *Storia* means something spread upon the ground.

A *cama* is short and close to the ground; for the Greeks call something short *kamai*.

Concerning beds and bedding, the Prophet says in the Psalter:

> Every night I shall wash my bed;  
> I shall water my couch with my tears (Ps. VI).

If you wish to understand this literally, he was indeed washing with tears the bed that he had polluted during the nights. Yet it is possible that there had been such an abundance of tears that he could be said to have washed not only his face but also his bed. It is therefore better to understand “bed” as bodily pleasure, against which, as though in our decaying chamber, we struggle when we resist pleasure—a pleasure that a person can wash away with even a few tears if, moved by heavenly inspiration, he happens to weep over it.

A *cubile* is a place for lying down. *Grabatum* is Greek. A *bajunola* is a bed carried on a journey, from *bajulare*, that is, “to carry away.”

Concerning the bedchamber it is written in the Psalter:

> Be pierced with remorse upon your beds (Ps. IV).

The dwelling of wild animals is properly called a *cubile*, from *cubare*, “to lie down.” He therefore aptly called fierce thoughts “bedchambers,” although the word is sometimes used figuratively in a good sense, as in the passage concerning the saints:

> They shall rejoice upon their beds (Ps. CXLIX).

For when he says, “Be pierced with remorse upon your beds,” he means, “Do penance.” For through a certain remorse of soul the desired conversion takes place, as if he were saying: “Abandon your wicked thoughts before you commit crimes.”

A *grabatum* signifies endurance of brotherly charity. Hence it is written in the Gospel that the Lord said to the paralytic whom he had healed:

> Rise, take up your bed, and walk (Matt. IX),

that is: “Leave your former sins; come to the aid of your brothers’ needs. In everything you do, see that you do not fix your mind upon this world, but hasten to behold the face of your Redeemer. Rise by doing good; carry your bed by loving your neighbor; and walk by awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God.”

Allegorically, a bed signifies either rest in Christ, or the contemplative life, or bodily sickness, or an opulent life, or the deception of heretics, or the tribulation of the future life.

The bed of the Church is rest in Christ, as in the Song of Songs:

> Behold, Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men surround it (Song III).

Likewise, the bed signifies spiritual rest, that is, the contemplative life, in Solomon:

> Upon my little bed by night I sought him whom my soul desires (ibid.).

And in the Gospel:

> Then there will be two in one bed: one will be taken, and one will be left (Luke XVII).

Again, the bed signifies the human body or the infirmity of the flesh in the Psalm:

> May the Lord sustain him upon his bed of pain (Ps. XL).

And elsewhere:

> Every night I shall wash my bed (Ps. VI).

The bed signifies an opulent life, as is said in Amos concerning the rich of this world:

> You who sleep upon ivory beds (Amos VI).

In the Church, the bed signifies the deception of heretics, concerning which it is written in Solomon:

> I have woven my bed with cords (Prov. VII),

that is, with the bonds of sins.

The bed signifies the tribulation of the future life. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse:

> Behold, I cast her upon a bed; and those who commit adultery with her will be in great tribulation (Apoc. II).

A *pulvinar* is the bed of the rich; hence also *pulvillus*, “little cushion.” A *pulvillus* signifies the deception of flatterers. Hence it is written in the Prophet:

> Woe to you who sew cushions beneath every elbow and pillows for heads, to ensnare souls (Ezek. XIII).

The *sponda* is the outer part of a bed, while the *pluteus* is the inner part.

*Geniales lecti* are properly beds spread for girls who are marrying; they are so called from the begetting of children.

*Cunabula* are little beds in which infants customarily lie. They are so called because they are used for childbirth, as though *cynabula*. For *kuein* in Greek means “to give birth.” The word is often used figuratively for the nourishment of infants.

A *feretrum* is so called because the dead are carried upon it. Mystically, it also signifies the favors of flatterers or the evil habits of people in which those dead in sins desire to lie. Hence, when the Lord wished to raise a dead man, he ordered the bier to stand, because he forbade him to remain longer in sins through the snares of flattery.

*Scamna* are platforms placed beside higher beds; they are so called from *scandere*, “to climb.” Hence *scabella* are also placed beside low beds or seats for climbing up. A *scabellum* is also called a *suppedaneum*. For the Greeks call it *hypopodion*, the Latins *scabellum*, and others *suppedaneum*, because it is beneath the feet.

The footstool signifies the subjection of the humbled, as in the Psalm:

> Until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet (Ps. CIX).

A *sedes* is so called because among the ancient Romans there was no custom of reclining at table; hence people were said to sit together. Therefore—as Varro says in *On the Life of the Roman People*—men began to recline and women to sit, because reclining was an unbecoming sight in a woman.

Mystically, a seat signifies the bearing of one who reigns or judges. Hence it is said in the Psalm:

> Your seat is forever and ever (Ps. XLIV);

and again:

> You sit upon the throne, judging equity (Ps. IX).

And in the Gospel the Lord says to the apostles:

> You will sit upon seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. XIX).

Cathedras are seats of teachers, and mystically signify the power of teaching, or the teaching of the law of Moses, or even the teaching of heretics.

The *cathedra* signifies teaching or power in the Psalter:

> Let the seat of the elders praise him (Ps. CVI).

It signifies the teaching of the law of Moses in the Gospel:

> The scribes and priests and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat (Matt. XXIII).

It signifies the teaching of heretics in the Psalm:

> He did not sit in the seat of pestilence (Ps. I).

For to sit is to teach.

A *solium* is the seat upon which kings sit for the protection of their bodies. According to some, it is derived from *soliditas*, as though *sodium*. According to others, through the figure of antistichon, it is as though *sodium*, from *sedere*, “to sit.” Hence *sella* is also said as though *seda*, and *subsellia* as though *subsedia*.

In the sacred Scriptures, the *solium* signifies the bearing of one who reigns and the excellence of divine majesty. Hence the Lord is read in Isaiah and Micah as sitting upon a lofty and exalted throne (Isa. VI). For the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is shown by this expression in the bearing of one who reigns: he reigns forever and sits upon his holy seat.

*Tripodes* are little platforms having three feet; candlesticks are also *tripodes*, because they likewise have three feet.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Vehicles

A *carrum* is named from the axle (*cardo*) of wheels; hence *currus* are also so called, because they appear to have wheels. A *rota* is named from *ruere*, “to rush,” and *rotundum*, “round,” is derived from *rota*.

A *rheda* is a type of vehicle with four wheels. The ancients called such vehicles *retae*, because they had wheels.

A *carpentum* is a ceremonial type of vehicle, as though a ceremonial carriage.

A *plaustrum* is a vehicle with two wheels, by which loads are carried. It is called *plaustrum* because it rolls, as though one were to say *pilastrum*.

Mystically, a wheel signifies either the world, or human life, or the soul’s changeability, or the instability of the human mind.

For it is written in the Psalm:

> The sound of your thunder is in the wheel (Ps. LXXVI).

“In the wheel,” therefore—that is, in the world—his thunderous voice went forth when Christ’s preachers filled the circle of the whole world with words like thunder.

In Ezekiel, wheels are discussed in many ways. It is read there (Ezek. I, X) that one wheel appeared beside the living creatures upon the earth, and afterward there is an account of four wheels, whose appearance and workmanship were as though one wheel were within another wheel. Whoever considers the wheel and its course through time will see that the world has been completed by apostolic speech.

A wheel within a wheel is also the joining of the two Testaments, which are indicated by Jacob’s ladder (Gen. XXVIII), Isaiah’s tongs (Isa. VI), and the two-edged sword, or by the mutually connected books of the Gospel, whose course and stature extend toward heaven (Apoc. I).

Concerning wagons it is written in Genesis (Gen. XLV) that Pharaoh sent a wagon through Joseph to carry the aged Jacob and his children. This signifies that teachers provided timely comfort to weak hearers, so that they might more easily cross the journey of the present life.

Likewise, in the prophet Amos the Lord is read as saying:

> Behold, I shall creak over you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay, and flight will perish from the swift, etc. (Amos II).

Here it is shown that the Lord complains of being burdened by the crimes of the Jews, for which he brought swift vengeance upon them.

Likewise, the circuit of the wheel signifies the labor of the present life in Solomon:

> And the wheel shall be broken above the cistern, and again you will set them like a wheel (Eccles. XII).

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the Remaining Things Used in Daily Life

A *baculus* is said to have been invented by Bacchus, the discoverer of the vine, as a support for people overcome by wine. Just as *baculus* comes from Bacchus, so *bacillum*, “little staff,” comes from *baculus* by diminutive formation.

The staff signifies support for human weakness. Hence the Prophet says to the Lord:

> Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps. XXII).

The rod pertains to the justice and strength of the Lord the Savior, as it is said in the Psalm:

> The rod of equity, the rod of your kingdom (Ps. XLIV).

The staff pertains to human assistance: by it the foot is carefully planted, and the whole body is supported as it leans upon the stick. The patriarchs used such staffs, as Jacob says:

> With my staff I crossed this Jordan (Gen. XXXII).

Likewise, in Exodus the Lord says to the children of Israel:

> You shall gird your loins, and, holding staffs in your hands, you shall eat in haste (Exod. XII).

*Vectes* are so called because they are carried (*vehi*) by the hands; with them doors and rocks are levered out.

*Vectes* sometimes signify holy teachers, by whom, according to divine ordinance, the ark of the Church or the Lord’s table was carried, as is written in Exodus. At other times *vectes* signify the strong bars of hell, or sinners whom the Lord is read to have broken, according to the passage:

> He shattered bronze doors and broke iron bars (Ps. CVI).

The bronze doors are the vicious habits of human beings, which shut us up in the courts of sins so that they cannot grant us permission to go out. The iron bars may appropriately be understood as unclean spirits, who are known to guard those doors of sins so that we may not leave by passing around them.

*Scalae* are the progress of the saints, as is read in Genesis:

> Jacob saw in dreams a ladder standing upon the earth, whose top touched heaven (Gen. XXVIII).

*Scopae* are superstitious cares pursued through vainglory, as in the Gospel:

> He came and found the house empty, swept with brooms and adorned (Luke XI).

In another sense, as in Isaiah:

> I shall sweep him with a sweeping broom (Isa. XIV),

that is, with the satisfaction of repentance.

According to etymology, if *forfices*—the scissors of tailors—are said to derive from *filum*, they are written with *f*: *forfices*. If they derive from *pilus*, “hair,” they are written with *p*: *forpices*, the shears of barbers. If they derive from *accipere*, “to take,” they are written with *c*: *forcipes*, because they grasp (*capiunt*) something hot (*formum*), which are the tools of smiths. The ancients called something hot *formum*; hence *formosus*, “beautiful.”

A *novacula* is a broad piece of iron drawn out to a certain fineness and made extremely sharp for shaving hairs. Although, when pressed against it, it cuts the harvest of the beard, it leaves the substance of the body unharmed.

In the razor, too, the fraud and deceit of Antichrist are expressed. Hence it is written in the Psalm:

> Your tongue devises injustice like a sharpened razor; you have practiced deceit (Ps. LI).

He appropriately compared the deceit of the most savage man to a sharp razor, because just as the razor does not injure the man, so the Antichrist does not strike the soul of the righteous under any affliction. He can shave away everything outwardly attached, like hairs; but he makes the inner parts of the soul more beautiful when he strives to remove worldly things from it.

A *clavis* is so called because it closes and opens. *Catenatum* is so called because it holds by seizing.

Mystically, a key signifies the opening of spiritual understanding. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to the lawyers:

> You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves have not entered, and you have hindered those who were entering (Luke XI).

Thus the key also signifies the virtues of justice, mercy, and piety in the Gospel, where the Lord says to Peter:

> I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI).

Likewise, keys signify the sharp preaching of the saints, piercing human hearts, as in Solomon:

> The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep (Eccles. XII).

As we have said, a key signifies the opening of the holy Scriptures, or the power of binding and loosing, or the right of introducing someone to life or casting someone down to death, as is said through Isaiah concerning the Savior:

> I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; he will open, and no one will close (Isa. XXII).

And in the Apocalypse:

> I hold the keys of death and hell (Apoc. I).

*Horologia* are so called because in them we read—or rather gather—the hours. For such an instrument is placed in a sunny place, where a shadow runs from a peg along lines, so that it indicates whichever hour of the day it may be.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Agricultural Implements

An *aratrum* is named from *arare*, “to plow” the earth, as though *araterrium*.

A *vomer* is so called because it tears up the soil by force, or from *evomere*, “to vomit forth” the earth. Concerning it Lucretius writes:

> The hooked iron share of the plow  
> Secretly wears away in the fields  
> And acquires brightness through its wearing away.

*Ligones* are so called because they lift the earth, as though *levones*.

Mystically, the plow signifies the work of evangelical preaching, by which the cultivation of the Lord’s field is carried out. With the share of the divine word, vices are uprooted and harmful desires eradicated, and thus the soil of human hearts is prepared to receive the seeds of virtue.

But everyone who earnestly takes hold of the spiritual plow must look ahead, so that he may make a straight furrow and not turn away from the path of truth. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX).

The shares and mattocks are exercises of preaching. Hence the Prophet says concerning teachers:

> They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks (Isa. II).

The *sarculus* likewise signifies the same thing, as above in Isaiah:

> All the mountains, he says, that shall be hoed with the hoe (Isa. VII).

For, as we have said, to plow or dig is to carry out the work of preaching.

Hence the gardener says in the Gospel:

> Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and apply manure (Luke XIII).

And it is written in Deuteronomy:

> You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together (Deut. XXII).

The saying from the Book of Job agrees with this passage:

> The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys were feeding (Job I).

The word *stercus*, “manure,” therefore has several meanings. The sacrifices of the Jews are manure. Hence it is written in Isaiah:

> Their corpses became like manure in the midst of the streets (Isa. V).

Manure also signifies the recollection of sins, placed at the root of the heart of those who commit them. Hence it is said in the Gospel:

> Until I dig around it and apply manure (Luke XIII).

Manure signifies the lust of sin, concerning which it is read:

> The animals rotted in their own manure (Joel I).

Human manure signifies the most foul odor of sins, since every sin stinks. Hence the passage in Ezekiel:

> You shall cover the manure that comes out of a human being before their eyes (Ezek. IV).

*Cultelli* are named from *cultus*, “cultivation,” because in former times people used them to prune trees and vines before sickles had been invented.

A *falx* is used to prune trees and vines. *Falces* are so called because soldiers first used them to cut fern (*filix*), whence comes the following:

> The assured peace of a leader has bent me to peaceful uses:
>
> I am now a farmer; formerly I was a soldier.

A *falcastrum* is named from its resemblance to a sickle. It is a curved iron tool with a long handle for cutting through dense thickets. These are also called *runcones*, with which thorn bushes are cut; the word derives from *runcare*, “to clear.”

Sickles signify the preaching of the saints, which removes what is superfluous and leaves what is necessary. Likewise, a sickle signifies the cutting off of the flesh through death, or divinity itself, which encompasses and judges all things. Hence it is written in Joel:

> Send forth sickles and harvest the vine of the earth (Joel III).

And in the Apocalypse:

> He had in his hand a sharp sickle (Apoc. XIV).

A *ventilabrum*, winnowing fan, signifies the scrutiny of justice. Hence it is read concerning it in the Gospel:

> His winnowing fan is in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his granary, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. III).

The threshing floor signifies the Church in the Gospel:

> He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor (ibid.).

The threshing floor also signifies the present world, concerning which it is read in the Prophet:

> Daughter of Babylon, threshing floor of mine (Jer. LI).

The heaps signify the gathering of the faithful to the threshing floor of the Church, or the perfected preaching of the saints, as is said in Job concerning heretics:

> Among their heaps they spend the noonday (Job XXIV).

Wheat signifies the saints or the elect in the Gospel:

> He will gather the wheat into his granary (Matt. III).

Grain signifies Christ’s body or the evangelical word in the Psalm:

> He fed them with the fat of grain (Ps. LXXX).

A grain of wheat signifies Christ in the Gospel:

> Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone (John XII).

Grain signifies the word of preaching in Solomon:

> Those who hide grain will be cursed among the peoples (Prov. XI).

The granary signifies the kingdom of heaven in the Gospel:

> He will gather the wheat into his granary (Matt. III).

A *prelum* is the beam by which crushed grapes are pressed; it is named from *premere*, “to press,” as though *pressorium*. A *prelum* is also the device by which oil is pressed. A *lacus* is the vat into which the liquid flows and from which, by pressing grapes or olives, wine and oil are extracted.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Garden Implements

A *rota* is so called as though from *ruere*, “to rush.” It is a machine by which water is drawn from a river. Lucretius writes:

> We see wheels turned in the rivers, and water-lifting devices.

*Haustra*, that is, “wheel,” are named from *haurire*, “to draw up water.”

A *girgillus* is so called because it turns in a circle. It is a piece of wood movable upon a transverse pole, from which a rope with a bucket or leather vessel is lowered into a well to draw water.

The wheel signifies the course of life. Hence the passage in Ecclesiastes:

> Before the silver cord is broken, and the golden band returns, and the pitcher is shattered above the spring, and the wheel is broken above the cistern, and the dust returns to its earth (Eccles. XII).

For when the pitcher is shattered, it ceases to draw water; and if the wheel by which water is lifted from the cistern and well is broken, the use of the water is interrupted. So also, when the silver cord is severed and the stream of the soul returns to its sources, the human being will perish.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Horse Equipment

*Phalerae* are ornaments for horses, and the word is Greek.

*Frena* are so called because they compel horses to snort, or because horses bite them—that is, press and gnaw them with their teeth. Hence nursing piglets are called *nefrendes*, because they have not yet gnawed anything, that is, crushed it with their teeth. Hence also *faba fresa*, “ground bean.”

*Lupata* are extremely harsh bits. They are called *lupata* from wolves’ teeth, which are uneven; hence their bite is especially harmful to a dog.

*Capistra* are named from the head of beasts of burden.

A *sella* is named from *sedere*, “to sit,” as though *sedda*.

An *antella* is as though “before the saddle,” just as a *postella* is “behind the saddle.”

*Cingulum*, “belt,” is neuter in gender when applied to human beings; for animals it is feminine, since we say *has cingulas*.

A *sagma*, commonly corrupted in popular usage into *sauma* or *salma*, is named from the spreading of saddlecloths. Hence one says *caballus sagmarius*, “pack horse,” and *mula sagmaria*, “pack mule.”

A *capulum* is a rope, from *capere*, “to seize,” because untamed beasts of burden are caught with it.

*Calcaria* are so called because they are tied to the heel of a person, that is, to the rear part of the feet, to spur horses when they must fight or run, on account of the animals’ sluggishness or fear. Spurs (*stimuli*) are also named from fear or from *stigo*.

*Strigiles* are named from *tergere*, “to wipe,” because horses are rubbed down with them.

A *character* is a glowing, fiery piece of iron with which marks are branded onto livestock. *Character* in Greek means *forma* in Latin, “form” or “mark.”

A *cauterium* is as though *cauturium*, because it burns, and because a watchful and severe precaution is taken in its use: when it is seen whose mark it is, greed is restrained. It is sometimes used as a sign and sometimes as a treatment, so that the force of disease may be dried up by the heat of fire.

*Habenae* are named from *habere*, “to hold,” because with them we hold horses; hence horses are also called *habiles*, “manageable.” They are likewise called *retinacula*, from *retinere*, “to restrain.”

*Lora* [lacuna].

In these things, therefore, discipline is signified for insolent and brutish people. Hence the Psalmist says:

> Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding; bind with bridle and bit the jaws of those who do not draw near to you (Ps. XXXI).

Here he now admonishes the human race in general not to submit itself to wandering errors. Let us examine why these comparisons have been made.

A horse, without the judgment of its rider, is carried wherever its impulse leads, and whoever mounts it, it rushes forth. A mule, however, patiently accepts whatever burdens are placed upon it. Neither has understanding in this respect: the one does not choose whom it should obey, and the other does not understand under what burdens it is weighed down.

He therefore forbids such people to be ensnared by diabolical deceits and burdened with the weights of vices, lest by obeying wrongly they become even more committed to the side of pride.

But what is said to be done to people of this kind—that is, to imprudent animals? By these comparisons he subjects foolish people to the truth against their will.

When he says “with a bit,” this pertains to the horse. For *frenum* is named from restraining the wild (*ferum*); the ancients called a horse *ferum*. “With a bridle” pertains to the mule. These restraints therefore restrain the aforementioned animals so that they proceed at the command of the one giving orders and are not carried away by their own wills.

The jaws are aids of animals by which food is chewed so that the life of the body may be sustained. Allegorically, therefore, he says that the jaws of the disobedient must be restrained—that is, that supplies of food should be given more sparingly, so that, confined by the necessity of fasting, they may submit to the Creator’s command.

For allegory is, as has often been said, when one thing is said and another is signified. And since we have said that in this passage the Lord Christ is speaking, “restrain” is understood as addressed to the Father. Nevertheless, the holy Trinity has one will, one power, and one cooperation.

[Cols. 0613–0616C]

# THE THIRD PART OF ALL THE WORKS OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, OR WRITINGS COMPOSED WHILE HE WAS ARCHBISHOP AND OTHER WORKS PUBLISHED BY HIM WITHOUT A DATE

## EXCERPT FROM PRISCIAN’S ART OF GRAMMAR

### Concerning the Voice

The authority of the philosophers shows that the property of the voice consists in the striking of the air, regardless of the manner in which the blow is made. They also divided it into four kinds: articulate, inarticulate, literate, and illiterate.

Of these, there is no doubt that two joined together—namely, articulate and literate—produce the principal and useful, indeed necessary, voice, because it alone is recognized as capable both of letters and of understanding. The others are not equally useful, because they cannot be grasped simultaneously by nature and by understanding. Yet if someone wishes to investigate them as they come together individually, one will undoubtedly find that they produce a voice without understanding; and if they are used in that way, they lack letters. This does not happen with the kinds mentioned above.

### Concerning the Letter

A letter is the smallest part of articulate speech, that is, speech that consists in the composition of letters. It is “smallest” with respect to the entire comprehension of literate speech. For speech is whatever we say—for example, if you say, “The orator came and taught.” This can be divided into individual words: “The orator came,” and “he taught”; the words themselves into syllables, *o* and *ra* and *tor*; and the syllables into letters. A letter itself cannot be divided into smaller parts; hence philosophers call it an *atomos*, that is, indivisible.

Scaurus defined it as follows: “A letter is the form of a voice that can be written.” For an element is the smallest force, the indivisible matter of articulate speech, and the beginning of each thing, from which it takes its growth and into which it is resolved; its figure is called a letter.

The ancients also called letters “elements,” by analogy with the elements of the world, because just as those elements, by coming together, complete every body, so these letters, joined together, preserve speech, and, separated, dissolve it.

The difference between elements and letters is therefore that the elements properly refer to the pronunciations themselves, that is, the force of the sound that is heard and understood. Their figures, however, are letters. “A,” “b,” and “c,” and every other such sign, are the name both of the pronunciation and of the figure. What is read is an element; what is understood is a letter; what is written and named is both.

A letter is called *littera*, as though *legitera*, because it is read, because it shows a path to those who read, because of the erasure (*litura*) it undergoes, and because it is repeated through reading.

All the letters used by the Latins are twenty-three, and they have three kinds of differences. The first difference has two qualities: they are either Latin or Greek. There are twenty-one Latin letters and two Greek letters: the vowel *y* and the semivowel *z*, which entered their usage because of Greek names.

There are also five others which, after the reception of the Christian faith, even if they are not received in the order of the alphabet, are nevertheless contained in the pages of the divine writings: *h*, because of the name of Jesus; *Α* and *Ω* because of the authority of divine speech, “I am Alpha and Omega”; and, because of the name of Christ, *ΧΡΙ*.

The second difference among letters likewise has two qualities: some are vowels and some consonants.

The third difference is among consonants: some are semivowels, some mutes, some liquids, and some double letters.

There are five vowels: *a, e, i, o, u*.

There are seven semivowels: *l, m, n, r, s, x, z*.

There are nine mutes: *b, c, d, f, g, k, p, q,* and *t*.

Vowels are so called as though “sounding,” because they produce a voice by themselves and lend a voice to other letters. Consonants are so called because they sound together with vowels; and they are aptly called consonants because two sounds sound together.

Semivowels are so called because they do not have a full voice, just as people are called semimen and semigods, not because they are half-men or half-gods, but because they are not complete gods or complete men. If you remove the vowel from them, they nevertheless retain a thin sound and a kind of hiss. Thus, if you say—[Note: Something is missing.]—and remove the vowel *e*, a certain hissing and thin sound nevertheless remains.

Mutes are so called not because they are entirely without a voice, but because, in comparison with letters that sound well, they possess only a small portion of voice. Thus a woman is called *informis*, “without form,” not because she lacks all form, but because she is badly formed. We call someone cold not because he is entirely without heat, but because he possesses only a very small amount of it.

All Latin vowels are *dichrona*, that is, they can be shortened and lengthened, whereas the Greeks have three such vowels: *α, ι,* and *υ*. The Greek *ε* and *ο* are always short, while *η* and *ω* are always long.

The vowels are short in words such as *amor, erit, iter, operis,* and *utique*; they are long in *aera, erecta, ivit, omen,* and *utile*.

Among these vowels, *i* and *u* pass into the power of consonants when they are paired with one another, as in *Juno* and *vita*, or when they are joined to vowels, as in *vates, velox,* and *vox*, and *i* in *iecur* and *iocus*. These letters are also called medial, because in certain words they have a middle sound, neither their natural nor their proper sound, but blend alternating sounds between themselves, as in *vir optimus*.

When *i* is placed after *n*, with the consonantal function of the Aeolic digamma, it is short. When followed by *d, m, r, t,* or *v*, it appears to have the Greek *y* sound, as in *video, vim, virtus, vita,* and *vix*.

Although contracted, *u* nevertheless has the same sound, namely *y*, when placed between *q* and *e, i,* or *ae* in a diphthong, as in *atque, quis,* and *quae*. The same is true when it occurs between *g* and those same vowels within a single syllable, as in *pingues, anguis,* and *linguae*.

*I* appears as a double consonant when it is placed between two vowels, and therefore it always makes the preceding syllable long, as in *maius, peius,* and *eius*. For these words cannot be pronounced otherwise than if one *i* is pronounced with the preceding syllable and the other with the following one. Therefore the ancients always wrote two *i*s in these words.

When *v* is placed in the position of a consonant, it has among the Latins precisely the same force in every respect as the Aeolic digamma. The voice of that digamma arose from *vau*, in place of which Caesar wished this figure, namely *F*, to be written.

Among the Aeolians the digamma is sometimes written as a single consonant and sometimes as a double consonant. Thus our *v* appears to have the place of a single consonant, as in:

> Yet Venus, the mother, not terrified in spirit without reason;

It also has the force of a double consonant in the perfect and pluperfect tenses of the third and fourth conjugations, in which *i* placed before the consonant *v* is lengthened, while, when the *v* is removed, it is shortened, as in *cupivi, cupii, cupiveram, cupieram*; *audivi, audii, audiveram, audieram*.

At times, however, metricians use this digamma, with *v* and *i* placed in the position of a consonant, in place of a shortened vowel, as Horace did when he made *silvae* a three-syllable word in this verse of the *Epode*:

> And the snows draw Jupiter down,
>
> Now the sea, now the woods.

For it is an iambic dimeter joined to a heroic penthemimeral line.

And Aurelius Prudentius, in the *Psychomachia*:

> The noble [woman], accompanied by her husband—for Job was nearest.

It should be understood that the Aeolian digamma was adopted for the sake of aspiration, so that they might avoid the harshness of the breath, and also to avoid hiatus. We follow them in many cases, though not in all, as when, avoiding aspiration, we say *vespera* (“evening”), *vis* (“force”), and *vestis* (“garment”); and avoiding hiatus, as in *clauus*, *argiuus*, *pauo*, *ovum*, *ovis*, *bouis*.

Among the consonants, then, *l* and *r* are liquids; some add *m* and *n*. When these follow *f*, a semivowel, and the six mute letters—namely *b, c, d, g, p, t*—they generally lose the force of a consonant in verse, at the poet’s discretion, and render a syllable short. For this reason Priscian taught that *f* is more nearly a mute. [Note: [Col. 0616D] The passage is corrupt.] If any mute is placed before a liquid, *f* occupies among us the place of the Greek mute letter φ, except that it is not pronounced with the lips fixed in the manner of φ.

The letters *k* and *q*, although in shape and name they seem to differ in some way from *c*, nevertheless possess the same power both in the sound of words and in metre. *K* is entirely superfluous, for there seems to be no reason why it should be written when followed by *a*: whether *Carthago* and *caput* are written with *k* or with *c*, they produce no difference either in the sound or in the force of that consonant. [Col. 0617A] *Q*, on the other hand, seems to be written for no other reason than to show that the following *v*, placed before another vowel in the same syllable, loses the force of a letter in metre.

*H* is a sign of aspiration and has nothing else belonging to a letter except its shape, as Priscian says. Some grammarians nevertheless say that it is a letter, because, after the manner of a consonant, it often makes a short syllable long in metre. When *c* is joined to it, it represents the Greek χ; when *p* precedes it, it signifies φ. Likewise, when *t* precedes aspiration, it stands for θ. If *p* and *s* are placed together, they assert that the Greek letter ψ is represented. These letters occur in foreign words such as *Chimaera*, *philosophus*, *thelesfor*, and *psalmigraphus*.

Moreover, *h* is never placed after vowels except in interjections such as *ah* and *oh*, which signify the feeling of one who is troubled or grieves. [Col. 0617B]

*S* also has a peculiar power and frequently loses its force in metre. Sometimes, when placed at the beginning of a word before another consonant, it lengthens the final syllable of the preceding word when that syllable ends in a short vowel; sometimes it leaves it short. Some also say that, when placed in the middle of a word before another consonant, it disappears after the manner of the liquids, as in Virgil’s line:

> *Hortatur Mnesteus, Nunc, nunc insurgite remis.*  
> “Mnestheus urges them: now, now rise to the oars.”

*X* is understood sometimes as *cs*, sometimes as *gs*, as in *apex, apicis* (“summit”), and *grex, gregis* (“flock”). It sometimes changes into the consonant *v*, as in *nix, nivis* (“snow”), and also into *c*, as in *nox, noctis* (“night”). It also takes the place of aspiration, as in *veho, vexi* (“I carry, I carried”), and *traho, traxi* (“I draw, I drew”); but these forms seem to be declined contrary to the rule.

*Z* is used only in Greek words. [Col. 0617C] In place of it, some of the ancients used the vowel *i*, while others habitually wrote two *s*’s. Thus *jugum* was said as though from Greek *zugon*, and *Jupiter* as though from *zeuspater*. Likewise *Messentius*, *petissare*, *tablissare*, and other such forms show the ancient usage.

Furthermore, we must make clear that all consonant letters have this characteristic: all semivowels begin with *e* and end in themselves, except *x*, which begins with *i*; and all mutes begin with themselves and end in *e*, except *k*, *g*, and *h*. Finally, it should be noted that three things belong to every letter: its name, by which it is called and pronounced; its shape, by which it is seen and marked when written; and its force, by which it is distinguished and understood, according to its own character, from the other letters in metrical usage—whether it is a vowel, a consonant, a double consonant, a semivowel, a mute, or a liquid. [Col. 0617D]

According to some authorities, order also belongs to letters: one precedes and another follows, so that *a* is first, *b* follows, *c* is third, and the remaining letters proceed in order. *A* is therefore first among the letters in all nations because it is the first to open the voice of those who are born.

## On the syllable

A syllable properly is a gathering or joining of letters, pronounced under one accent and with one breath. By an abuse of terminology, however, we also call the sounds of individual vowels syllables. In Greek, *syllable*—συλλαβή—is called in Latin *conceptio* or *complexio*, “conception” or “joining.” The word *syllable* is derived from *ἀπὸ τοῦ συλλαμβάνειν τὰ γράμματα*, that is, “from the conception [Col. 0618A] of letters”; for *συλλαμβάνειν* means “to conceive.” Hence that is truly a syllable which arises from several letters. Beginning with a single letter, a syllable in Latin speech can extend to no more than six letters, as in *a, ab, est, mars, stans, stirps*.

It should be understood that no syllable contains three vowels. Hence *u* and *i* are not otherwise joined in diphthongs than when they are placed in the position of consonants, as in *siluae* and *Troiae*. *U* alone can be joined to a diphthong when it loses the force of a letter, as in *quae* and *linquae*. Often a single long vowel is found in place of a diphthong, as in *inquiro* for *quaero*, *includo* for *claudo*, *occido* for *caedo*, *illido* for *laedo*, *Nilus* for *Neilus*, and *musa* for *moysa*. Conversely, a diphthong may be used in place of a long vowel, as in *lavor, lautus*; *faveo, fautus*; and *avis, auceps*. [Col. 0618B]

It should also be noted that when three consonants precede a vowel, only two can follow it, as in *monstrans* and *scrobs*. Again, when three consonants follow, only two can precede them, as in *stirps*. Three consonants cannot otherwise be joined at the beginning of a syllable unless the first is *s*, the second after *s* is *c*, *p*, or *t*, and the third is *l* or *r*, as in *sculptile*, *splendens*, *scriba*, *stratum*, and *sprevit*.

At the end of a word, however, we find the reverse: the first consonant is a liquid, followed by a mute, and the last is *s*, as in *urbs* and *stirps*. Such is the rule concerning two consonants placed together in a syllable. Semivowels precede other semivowels in the same syllable, as in *Mnesteus*, *amnis*, *Smyrna*, and *smaragdus*. Those who write *zm* are in error, for a double consonant can never stand at the beginning of a syllable together with another consonant. [Col. 0618C]

Lucan demonstrates this in the tenth book:

> *Terga sedente crebro maculae distincta smaragdo*  
> “The backs, with the emerald set, are marked by frequent spots.”

For unless *s* stood before *m*, it could not have been removed in metre. *S* often loses the force of a consonant in metre when placed before another consonant in the same syllable; *z*, however, does so only when a short vowel follows it and another letter immediately follows *z*.

At the end of a syllable, all liquids generally stand before *s*, as in *puls*, *ars*, *hyems*, and *pons*. Likewise they stand before *x*, except *m*, as in *falx*, *lanx*, and *arx*. In many cases *b* and *g* precede a following *d*, as in *bdelyros*, *bdellium*—a kind of stone—and *mygdonides*. *C* and *p* precede a following *t*, as in *lectus* and *aptus*.

No semivowel precedes a mute at the beginning of a word, except *s* followed by *b*, *c*, *q*, *p*, or *t*, as in *asbestus*, *scutum*, *squalens*, *sperat*, and *stans*. [Col. 0618D] Nearly all mutes also precede liquids, as in *blandus*, *claret*, *abodlas*—a barbarian name—*glacies*, *tlemus*, *planus*, *flavus*, *abnuo*, *Cnidum*, *Ariadne*, *Gneus*, *Aetnam*, *contempnit*, *Brennus*, *creber*, *Drances*, *gratus*, *frater*, and *pratum*, *tractus*. Before *m*, however, only *c*, *d*, *g*, and *t* are found, as in *Alcmenae*, *Admetus*, *dragma*, and *rhythmos*.

But if a syllable ends in two consonants, the first must be a liquid and the second one of *s* and *χ*, as we showed above; or *c* and *t* with *n* preceding them, as in *hinc*, *dicunt*, *amant*, and *hunc*. *S* also precedes *t*, as in the preposition *post*, the conjunction *ast*, and the anomalous verb [Some copies: “anomalous verbs”] *sum, es, est*.

[Col. 0619A] For *b* and *s*, or *p* and *s*, are written in place of the Greek ψ, according to the form of the genitive, as in *Arabs, Arabis*; *Pelops, Pelopis*; *caelebs, caelibis*; and *princeps, principis*. Some, however, as we explained above, think that the Greek ψ should be written only as *ps*. Although the rule of the genitive requires the spelling just mentioned, they say that the relationship of the sound makes *ps* more appropriate. This, however, should be understood: at the beginning of a syllable, *ps* must in every case stand for ψ, as in *psittacus*, *pseudulus*, and *ipse*. *Nubo* likewise makes *nupsi*, and *scribo* makes *scripsi*, although analogy compels us to write them with *b*; euphony prevails, and it likewise requires us to pronounce and write *nuptam*, not *nubtam*, and *scriptum*, not *scribtum*, with *p* rather than *b*.

[Col. 0619B] Finally, all syllables are either long, short, or common. Long are those that are always long; short are those that are always short; common are those that are sometimes short and sometimes long, according to the poet’s choice.

Long syllables arise in two ways: by nature and by position. Those long by nature are of two kinds: either through the lengthening of individual vowels, as in *navis*, *sedes*, *finis*, *omen*, and *unus*; or through the joining of two vowels, which they call a diphthong. Diphthongs are so called because they contain two sounds—*phthongi*, that is, “voices”—for individual vowels have their own sounds, as in *aevum*, *poena*, *augustus*, *eurus*, and *ei*, which is an interjection expressing grief or fear, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* 2:

> *Ei mihi, qualis erat, quantum mutatus ab illo!*  
> “Alas for me! What he was, and how changed from that man!”

When *ae* is pronounced by poets as a diaeresis in the genitive case, it is written according to the Greeks with *a* and *i*, whether in proper names, as *Aeneai* and *Anchisai*, or in common nouns, as *pictai* and *aulai*. Both vowels are long. Virgil writes in Book 3:

> *Aulai medio libabant pocula Bacchi,*  
> “In the middle of the hall they poured cups of Bacchus,”

for *aulae*. Cicero likewise writes:

> *Atque oculos urget pedibus pectusque nopai,*  
> “And it presses the eyes with its feet and the breast of the scorpion,”

for *nopae*, that is, “of the scorpion.” [Col. 0619C]

Syllables become long by position in three ways: when a short vowel ends before two consonants, as in *ast*; before one double consonant, as in *dux*; when a vowel ends in one consonant and is followed by another, as in *arca*; when it is followed by the double consonant *x*, as in *axis*; or when it is followed by *i* placed in the position of a consonant, as in *Troja*. This positional length is sometimes divided in metre among three syllables, as in:

> *Arma virum tabulaeque et Troia gaza per undas*  
> “Arms, the man, and tablets, and Trojan treasure through the waves.”

A syllable may also end in a consonant or be followed by *u* and *i* placed in the position of consonants, as in *aduena* and *adiutor*. [Col. 0619D]

Short syllables are those that have none of these features.

Each syllable has the following attributes: pitch, aspiration, quantity, and number of letters. Pitch may be acute, grave, or circumflex, and must be fixed in every word. Likewise, aspiration may be rough or smooth. Quantity is one or two—or, as some prefer, one and a half and two and a half, as well as three and four.

A syllable has one time when a vowel is short by itself and is followed by a single consonant, as in *caput*. It has one and a half times in common syllables, about which we shall speak later, as in *lacrymae*. Long syllables, whether long by nature or by position, have two times, as in *da* and *ast*. They have two and a half times when a single consonant follows a naturally long vowel, as in *sol*. They have three times when two consonants or one double consonant follow a naturally long vowel, as in *mons* and *rex*. [Col. 0620A] There are four times when, for example, one places together in a verse *lex prima*, *lux clara*, *pax plena*, and similar expressions. The vowel is naturally long in *le*, *lu*, and *pa*, and has two times; it is followed by the double consonant *x*, which has one time, and then by a mute and a liquid, which likewise have one time each and complete the measure. All these joined together make four times. Nevertheless, in metre each syllable must be taken as occupying either one or two times. Metricians regard the remaining quantities as superfluous.

The number of letters also belongs to the syllable, because, as we said above, among Latins a syllable may contain no fewer than one and no more than six letters. It should also be made clear that every syllable begins its calculation with the vowel, whether it is long or short. The consonants that follow are then considered, not those that precede. Preceding consonants do not benefit the vowel that follows but the preceding vowel. For example, if one says *gens* and *stirps* together, the *n*, the two *s*’s, and the *t* give their quantity to the preceding vowel, namely *e*; likewise *r*, *p*, and *s* are joined to the preceding *i*. [Col. 0620B]

Common syllables arise in nine ways. By these, syllables that are naturally long are transferred to short, by poetic license, or those naturally short are transferred to long.

The first kind occurs when a short vowel in the same word is followed by two consonants, the latter of which is a liquid. It is naturally short in:

> *mens tenebris obscura suis*  
> “a mind darkened by its own shadows,”

[Col. 0620C] but long by position in:

> *mortisque tenebris*  
> “and in the shadows of death.”

It should be understood that not only mute consonants placed before *l* or *r*, but also those placed before *m* or *n*, make common syllables among the ancient poets, as in Ovid:

> *Pisconsamque Cnidon gravidamque Amathunta metallis.*  
> “And Pisconian Cnidos and Amathus, rich in metals.”

The second kind occurs when a short vowel ends in a consonant and is followed by the letter *h*. It is naturally short in:

> *Porcinum tenuere gregem, niger, hispidus, horrens*  
> “They kept a swinish herd, black, bristling, and shaggy,”

but long in:

> *Vir humilis moesto dejectus lumine terram*  
> “A humble man, cast down, his gaze sorrowfully fixed upon the ground.”

The third kind is a common syllable when a word ending in a short vowel is followed by two consonants, the first of which is *s*. It is [Col. 0620D] naturally short in Fortunatus:

> *Ordinibus variis alba smaragdus inest.*  
> “White emerald is present in varied arrangements.”

It is long by position in Sedulius:

> *Adveniat regnum jam jamque scilicet illud.*  
> “May that kingdom come, surely, now and now.”

The letter *s*, when placed before two other consonants—namely a mute and a liquid—at the beginning of the following syllable, is likewise found to make a common syllable, as in Horace, *Satires* 1:

> *Linquimus insani ridentes praemia scribae.*  
> “We leave laughing at the mad scribe’s rewards.”

The fourth kind of common syllable occurs when, after any foot, one short syllable remains from a word and is either ending in a vowel followed by a consonant belonging to the next word, or ending in a consonant [Col. 0621A] followed by another vowel. It is naturally short in:

> *Cujus onus leve est, cujus juga ferre suave est.*  
> “Whose burden is light, whose yoke is pleasant to bear.”

It is long in:

> *Frondea ficus erat, cujus in robore nullum.*  
> “There was a leafy fig tree, in whose trunk no …”

The fifth kind occurs when a part of speech ends in a diphthong and is immediately followed by another vowel. It is long in *musae Aonides* (“Aonian Muses”), but short in:

> *Insulae Ionio in magno.*  
> “Islands in the vast Ionian Sea.”

Virgil writes in Book 7:

> *Stipitibus duris agitur sudibusve praeustis.*  
> “It is driven on by hard stakes or fire-hardened poles.”

In this way, as in the preceding one, later poets very rarely use the common quantity; instead, they generally make synaloepha, as Prosper does:

> *Non nostrae hoc opis est, sed ab illo sumitur hic ros,*  
> *Qui siccam rupem fundere jussit aquas.*  
> “This is not within our power, but this dew is received from him, who commanded waters to pour from the dry rock.”

[Col. 0621B] The sixth kind occurs when a long vowel is followed by another vowel. It is long in:

> *O utinam in thalamos invisi Caesaris issem*  
> “Would that I had gone into the halls of the hated Caesar!”

It is short in:

> *Te Corydon, o Alexi, trahit sua quemque voluptas*  
> “You, Corydon, O Alexis, your own pleasure draws each of you.”

Virgil likewise writes in Book 5:

> *Infindunt pariter sulcos, totumque dehiscit*  
> *Convulsum.*  
> “Together they cleave the furrows, and the whole, torn apart, gapes open.”

Modern versifiers are accustomed to make this kind of shortening within the same part of speech, as in:

> *Eoi venere magi . . . .*  
> “The eastern Magi came …”

and:

> *Splendidus auctoris de vertice fulget Eous.*  
> “The radiant East shines from the author’s crown.”

The seventh kind occurs when a pronoun ending in the letter *c* is immediately followed by a vowel. It is long in Sedulius:

> *Non quia qui summus Pater est, et Filius hic est*  
> “Not because he who is the highest Father is also here the Son,”
> *Sed quia quod summus Pater est et Filius hoc est.*  
> “But because what the highest Father is, the Son is also.”

[Col. 0621C] It is short in:

> *Hic vir, hic est, tibi quem promitti saepius audis.*  
> “This is the man, this is he whom you often hear promised to you.”

One adverb ending in *c* also makes a common syllable. It is long in Paulinus:

> *Donec aspirante Deo conatibus aegris*  
> “Until God lends breath to our feeble efforts,”

but short in Prosper:

> *Morbo obsessis praestanda est cura medendi,*  
> *Donec in aegroto corpore vita manet.*  
> “For those afflicted by disease, care for healing must be provided, as long as life remains in the sick body.”

The eighth kind occurs when a short vowel in the same part of speech is followed by the Greek double consonant *z*. It is long in Juvencus:

> *Difficile est terris affixos divite gaza*  
> “It is difficult for those fixed to the earth amid rich treasure,”

but short in the same author:

> [Col. 0621D] *Et gaza distabat rerum possessio fulgens.*  
> “And the splendid possession of riches stood apart.”

The ninth kind is that every final syllable of a verse, in whatever metre, is *adiaphoros*, that is, indifferent. At the poet’s discretion, a short syllable is lengthened and a long one shortened. There are countless examples of this in every metre.

It should be understood that those who say that the letter *x* can make a common syllable in metre are mistaken. When it follows a vowel in the same part of speech, whether that vowel is naturally long or naturally short, *x* always makes it long, as in *pax*, *lux*, *vox*, *rex*, *lex*, and likewise *fax*, *nex*, *nix*, *nox*, and *nux*. But when *x* occurs at the beginning of a word, it cannot lengthen the final vowel of the preceding word, as in:

> *Pontibus in stratis conduxit littora Xerxes.*  
> “Xerxes joined the shores with bridges laid across.”

[Col. 0622A] As Varro says, all consonants of syllables are either rough, as in *trux* and *crux*; smooth [Perhaps *lenes*, “gentle”], as in *luna* and *lana*; tall, having a long final or penultimate vowel, as in *mansuetudo* and *facilitas*; harsh, having a mute at the end, as in *hic* and *hoc*; barbarian, as in *gaza* and *mammon*; Greek-like, as in *hymnos* and *zenon*; hard, as in *ignotus* and *cognitus*; or soft, as in *aedes* and *ludus*. Those who wish to make smooth and flowing verses must observe these distinctions completely, striving to avoid whatever weighs upon the ear in sound or causes it to stumble, and assigning the highest importance to euphony in poetry.

## On initial syllables

[Col. 0622B] The investigation of initial syllables in all parts of speech is difficult. The person best able to distinguish them is the one who diligently studies the principles of feet and the scansion of verses in metre. For although many words, according to the character of their analogy, end with the same termination, few agree in their beginnings.
