Since these matters require an elaborate exposition, it is enough for us to mention briefly only what we have found extracted from the most reliable writers on the arts.

A syllable is recognized as long either by a diphthong—written in five ways, namely *ae, oe, au, eu,* and *ei*; wherever these are found, they always show that the syllable is naturally long—or by example. In the scanning of metre and the identification of feet, one asks whether a syllable is long or short. For example, if you do not know whether the first syllable of the common noun *Musa* [Col. 0622C] is long or short, Virgil’s line may occur to you:

> *Musa, mihi causas memora, quo numine laeso*  
> “Muse, tell me the causes: by what violated divinity …”

You will find that *mu* is long, because every heroic verse must have a long first syllable, since at the beginning of a verse in this metre there is always either a spondee or a dactyl.

In elegiac poetry there are likewise ready examples for investigating syllables. The first verse, the hexameter, almost always contains a dactyl in the fifth foot, whose first syllable is long and whose following two are short. Similarly, the succeeding pentameter always closes the verse, after its first two feet and the colon, with two dactyls and one extra syllable. Virgil is said to have composed the following epitaph for himself [Col. 0622D] before his death:

> *Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc*  
> *Parthenope: cecini pascua, rura, duces.*  
> “Mantua gave me birth; the Calabrians took me; now Naples holds me. I sang of pastures, country lands, and leaders.”

It is scanned as follows: *Mantua*, a dactyl; *me genu*, a dactyl; *it Cala*, a dactyl; *bri rapu*, a dactyl; *ere te*, a dactyl; *net nunc*, a spondee. In the second verse: *Partheno*, a dactyl; *pe*; *ceci*, a dactyl; *ni*, the colon; *pascua*, a dactyl; *rura du*, a dactyl; *ces*, the colon.

As we said, in the first verse the fifth foot shows *e* to be long and *re* and *te* short. In the following verse, *pa* is long and *scu* and *a* short; likewise *ru* is long and *ra* and *du* short, and the same foot is displayed. Although in other positions of a verse the spondee and dactyl may alternate, in these examples the feet do not mislead us.

Fortunatus, in a little book that he composed in praise of blessed Mary, writes:

> [Col. 0623A] *Rorarunt coeli nubes, justumque pluerunt:*  
> *Quem Salvatorem germine Virgo dedit.*  
> “The clouds of heaven poured down dew and rained upon the just one: the Virgin, from her offspring, gave him as Savior.”

This is scanned as follows: *Rora*, a spondee; *runt cae*, a spondee; *li nu*, a spondee; *bes ju*, a spondee; *stumque plu*, a dactyl; *erunt*, a spondee. In the second verse: *Quem Sal*, a spondee; *vato*, a spondee; *rem*, the colon; *germine*, a dactyl; *Virgo de*, a dactyl; *dit*, the colon.

Thus, just as in the preceding example both verses had dactyls in every position except one spondee, so now both verses have spondees in every position except the three places mentioned above.

Sometimes the character of the first syllable can be discovered from the form of a compound. If you do not know what kind of syllable occurs in *pius* or *probus*, you can learn it from the compounds *impius* and *reprobus*, although this method sometimes fails in certain syllables. Thus, when we say *nubere*, the *nu* is long. Calpurnius writes in Book 10:

> [Col. 0623B] *Nubere vis Prisco, non miror, Paula, sapisti.*  
> “You wish to marry Priscus; I am not surprised, Paula—you have shown good sense.”

But in *pronuba*, *innuba*, and *connubium*, the *nu* is short in the compound. Virgil writes in *Aeneid* 6:

> *Et Bellona manet te pronuba nec face tantum.*  
> “Bellona, as matron, awaits you, and not with the torch alone.”

The same poet writes in Book 4:

> *Connubio jungam stabili, propriamque dicabo.*  
> “I shall join her to you in a firm marriage and dedicate her as your own.”

Likewise, in *lux, lucis*, *lu* is long, but in the derivative *lucerna* it is short. *Homo* is short everywhere; *humanus* is always long. In:

> *Itur in antiquam silvam*  
> “One goes into the ancient forest,”

the *i* is long; in:

> *Superumque ad lumen ituras*  
> “Those who will go toward the light of the gods,”

the *i* is short. Such examples, however, are rarely found.

If any part of speech is compounded with prepositions, we recognize its initial syllables from them. Nearly every syllable in the compound retains the character of the preposition itself, as in *deceptus*, *eductus*, and *abundans*, *reluctans*: *de* and *e* are long, while *ab* and *re* are short. [Col. 0623C]

The prepositions *ad*, *ob*, *in*, and *sub* are used with different quantities in verbs. They are shortened when they produce a disyllabic word, as in *adit*, *obit*, *init*, and *subit*. They are indifferent when they make a trisyllable, as in *adicit*, *obicit*, *inicit*, and *subicit*. They are lengthened when they produce a tetrasyllabic word, as in *adicio*, *obicio*, *inicio*, and *subicio*.

The syllables written with *prae* and *quae* at the beginning are likewise long, as in *praemium*, *praescivit*, *quaerens*, and *quaesivit*. But they are shortened in *pretium*, *precor*, *premo*, *prehendo*, and *queror*—that is, “I set forth a complaint”—and in words derived or compounded from these, such as *adprecor*, *preces*, *comprimo*, *apprehensus*, *conqueror*, *querela*, and the conjunction *que*.

The same prepositions are also shortened in compounds, as in *dehinc*, *profectus*, *profusus*, *professus*, *profatus*, *proavus*, *pronepos*, and so forth.

[Col. 0623D] There are also some verbs whose initial syllables change according to tense. In every perfect and pluperfect tense, or only in one future subjunctive tense, the initial syllables listed below are long. In the other moods and tenses they are short.

Those of the first conjugation are:

- *lavo, lavi, laveram, lavissem, laverim, cum lavero* — “I wash, I washed, I had washed, I had washed [in the subjunctive], I may have washed, when I shall have washed.”
- *juvo, juvi, juveram, juvissem, juverim, cum juvero* — “I help, I helped, I had helped, I had helped [in the subjunctive], I may have helped, when I shall have helped.”

Those of the second conjugation are:

- *sedeo, sedi, sederam, sedissem, sederim, cum sedero* — “I sit, I sat, I had sat, I had sat [in the subjunctive], I may have sat, when I shall have sat.”
- *faveo, favi, faveram, favissem, cum faverim, favero* — “I favor, I favored, I had favored, I had favored [in the subjunctive], I may have favored, when I shall have favored.”
- *moveo, movi, moveram, movissem, moverim, cum movero* — “I move, I moved, I had moved, I had moved [in the subjunctive], I may have moved, when I shall have moved.”
- *foveo, fovi, foveram, fovissem, foverim, [Col. 0624A] cum forero* — “I cherish, I cherished, I had cherished, I had cherished [in the subjunctive], I may have cherished, when I shall have cherished.” [The printed *forero* may be corrupt.]
- *voveo, vovi, voveram, vovissem, cum voverim, vovero* — “I vow, I vowed, I had vowed, I had vowed [in the subjunctive], I may have vowed, when I shall have vowed.”
- *paveo, pavi, paveram, pavissem, cum pavero* — “I fear, I feared, I had feared, I had feared [in the subjunctive], when I shall have feared.”
- *caveo, cavi, caveram, cavissem, cum caverim, cavero* — “I beware, I took care, I had taken care, I had taken care [in the subjunctive], I may have taken care, when I shall have taken care.”
- *video, vidi, videram, vidissem, cum viderim, videro* — “I see, I saw, I had seen, I had seen [in the subjunctive], I may have seen, when I shall have seen.”
- *neo, nevi, neveram, nevissem, cum neverim, nevero* — “I spin, I spun, I had spun, I had spun [in the subjunctive], I may have spun, when I shall have spun.”
- *fleo, flevi, fleveram, flevissem, cum fleverim, flevero* — “I weep, I wept, I had wept, I had wept [in the subjunctive], I may have wept, when I shall have wept.”
- *cieo, civi, vel cii, civeram, civissem, cum civerim, civero* — “I set in motion, I set in motion, or *cii*, I had set in motion, I had set in motion [in the subjunctive], I may have set in motion, when I shall have set in motion.”

The verbs of the third conjugation that follow the same rule are:

- *fugio, fugi, fugeram, fugissem, cum fugerim, fugero* — “I flee, I fled, I had fled, I had fled [in the subjunctive], I may have fled, when I shall have fled.”
- *cudo, cudi, cuderam, cudissem, cum cuderim, cudero* — “I forge, I forged, I had forged, I had forged [in the subjunctive], I may have forged, when I shall have forged.”
- *capio, cepi, ceperam, cepissem, cum ceperim, cepero* — “I take, I took, I had taken, I had taken [in the subjunctive], I may have taken, when I shall have taken.”
- *lego, legi, legeram, legissem, cum legerim, legero* — “I read or gather, I read or gathered, I had read or gathered, I had read or gathered [in the subjunctive], I may have read or gathered, when I shall have read or gathered.”
- *facio, feci, feceram, fecissem, cum fecerim, fecero* — “I make, I made, I had made, I had made [in the subjunctive], I may have made, when I shall have made.”
- *jacio, jeci, jeceram, jecissem, cum jecerim, jecero* — “I throw, I threw, I had thrown, I had thrown [in the subjunctive], I may have thrown, when I shall have thrown.”
[Col. 0624B]

- *lino, levi, leveram, levissem, cum leverim, levero* — “I smear, I smeared, I had smeared, I had smeared [in the subjunctive], I may have smeared, when I shall have smeared.”
- *emo, emi, emeram, emissem, cum emerim, emero* — “I buy, I bought, I had bought, I had bought [in the subjunctive], I may have bought, when I shall have bought.”
- *sero, sevi, severam, sevissem, cum severim, severo* — “I sow, I sowed, I had sowed, I had sowed [in the subjunctive], I may have sowed, when I shall have sowed.”

Some of these, in the present tense and certain other tenses, show by their position that they have a long initial syllable; but those whose vowel is naturally short are subject to this rule:

- *rumpo, rupi, ruperam, rupissem, cum ruperim, rupero* — “I break, I broke, I had broken, I had broken [in the subjunctive], I may have broken, when I shall have broken.”
- *cerno, crevi, creveram, crevissem, cum creverim, crevero* — “I discern, I discerned, I had discerned, I had discerned [in the subjunctive], I may have discerned, when I shall have discerned.”
- *sperno, sprevi, spreveram, sprevissem, cum spreverim, sprevero* — “I despise, I despised, I had despised, I had despised [in the subjunctive], I may have despised, when I shall have despised.”
- *fundo, fudi, fuderam, fudissem, cum fuderim, fudero* — “I pour, I poured, I had poured, I had poured [in the subjunctive], I may have poured, when I shall have poured.”
- *vinco, vici, viceram, vicissem, cum vicerim, vicero* — “I conquer, I conquered, I had conquered, I had conquered [in the subjunctive], I may have conquered, when I shall have conquered.”
- *tero, trivi, triveram, trivissem, cum triverim, trivero* — “I rub, I rubbed, I had rubbed, I had rubbed [in the subjunctive], I may have rubbed, when I shall have rubbed.”
- *frango, fregi, fregeram, fregissem, cum fregerim, fregero* — “I break, I broke, I had broken, I had broken [in the subjunctive], I may have broken, when I shall have broken.”
[Col. 0624C]

- *fodio, fodi, foderam, fodissem, cum foderim, fodero* — “I dig, I dug, I had dug, I had dug [in the subjunctive], I may have dug, when I shall have dug.”
- *odio, odi, oderam, odissem, cum oderim, odero* — “I hate, I hated, I had hated, I had hated [in the subjunctive], I may have hated, when I shall have hated.”

Of the fourth conjugation:

- *venio, veni, veneram, venissem, cum venerim, venero* — “I come, I came, I had come, I had come [in the subjunctive], I may have come, when I shall have come.”
- *eo, ivi, vel ii, ieram, iissem, cum ierim, iero* — “I go, I went, or *ii*, I had gone, I had gone [in the subjunctive], I may have gone, when I shall have gone.”
- *queo, quivi, quiveram, quivissem, cum quiverim, quivero* — “I can, I could, I had been able, I had been able [in the subjunctive], I may have been able, when I shall have been able.”

Conversely, some forms are long in the present tense but become short in the perfect, such as:

- *pono, posui* — “I place, I placed”;
- *cogo, coegi* — “I compel, I compelled”;
- *do, dedi* — “I give, I gave”;
- *sto, steti* — “I stand, I stood.”

The compounds of *sto* behave likewise: *praesto*, *asto*, *persto*, *resto*.

All verbs whose perfect forms are reduplicated are shortened in their initial syllables, such as the following second-conjugation verbs:

- *pendeo, pependi* — “I hang, I hung”;
- *mordeo, momordi* — “I bite, I bit”;
- *spondeo, spopondi* — “I promise, I promised”;
- *tondeo, totondi* — “I shear, I sheared.”

The following belong to the third conjugation:

- *posco, poposci* — “I demand, I demanded”;
- *curro, cucurri* — “I run, I ran”;
- *disco, [Col. 0624D] didici* — “I learn, I learned”;
- *cano, cecini* — “I sing, I sang”;
- *tango, tetigi* — “I touch, I touched”;
- *tendo, tetendi* — “I stretch, I stretched”;
- *pendo, pependi* — “I weigh, I weighed”;
- *pello, pepuli* — “I drive out, I drove out”;
- *tundo, tutudi* — “I beat, I beat”;
- *pungo, pupugi* or *punxi* — “I prick, I pricked”;
- *parco, peperci* — “I spare, I spared”;
- *pedo, pepedi* — “I fart, I farted”;
- *fallo, fefelli* — “I deceive, I deceived”;
- *cado, cecidi* — “I fall, I fell”;
- *tollo, tetuli* — “I raise or remove, I raised or removed”;
- *pario, peperi* — “I give birth, I gave birth”;
- *pango, pepigi* — “I fasten or compose, I fastened or composed,”

and so forth.

In words written with the same letters, it should also be noted that *liber*, if it means “book” or “bark,” has a short *li*; if it means “free,” it has a long one. *Pila*, if it means a vessel, has a long *pi*; if it means a ball, it has a short one. *Securus* (“safe”) has a long *se*, while *securis* (“axe”) has a short one. *Domus* has a short *do*; *doma*, meaning “roof,” has a long one.

*Plaga*, when it means “climate,” has a short *pla*; when it means “punishment,” it has a long one. *Palus, paludis* (“marsh”) has a short *pa*; *palus, pali* (“stake”) has a long one. *Populus*, when it means “the people,” has a short *po*; when it means “tree,” it has a long one. [Col. 0625A] *Nitens*, from *nitor* (“shine”), has a short *ni*; from *nisus* (“effort”), it has a long one.

Likewise, *educo, educis* (“I lead out”) has a long *du*; *educo, educas*, meaning “I nourish,” has a short one. *Concido*, *decido*, *incido*, and *occido*, when they refer to falling, have a shortened *ci*; when they refer to cutting, it is lengthened.

*Colo, colis* (“I cultivate”) has a short *co*; *colo, colas* (“I strain or filter”) has a long one. *Placeo, places* (“I please”) has a shortened *pla*; *placo, placas* (“I appease”) has a long one. *Pareo, pares*, meaning “I appear” or “I obey,” has a long *pa*; *paro, paras*, meaning “I prepare,” and *pario, paris* (“I give birth, you give birth”), have a short one.

*Parentēs*, when it means “those who appear,” has a long *pa*; when it means “parents,” it has a short one, as does *parientēs* (“those giving birth”).

*Incipio, incipi, inciperam, incipissem, cum inciperim, incipero* — “I begin, I began, I had begun, I had begun [in the subjunctive], I may have begun, when I shall have begun.”

*Satago, sategi, sategeram, sategissem, cum sategerim, sategero* — “I am busy, I was busy, I had been busy, I had been busy [in the subjunctive], I may have been busy, when I shall have been busy.” Its simple verb behaves likewise: *ago, egi, egeram, egissem, cum egerim, egero* — “I do or drive, I did or drove, I had done or driven, I had done or driven [in the subjunctive], I may have done or driven, when I shall have done or driven.”

[Col. 0625B] *Dico, dicis* (“I say, you say”) has a long *di*. Its compounds are likewise lengthened, as in *condico*, *praedico*, *contradico*, and *interdico*. *Dicas*, from *dico*, has a short *di*; its compounds are likewise shortened, as in *praedico*, whence *praedicator* (“preacher”); *dedico* (“I dedicate”); and *abdico* (“I renounce”).

*Idem*, if it is neuter, is shortened; if masculine, it is lengthened in both numbers.

*Levitas*, if it denotes instability of mind or lightness of weight, has a short *le*; if it denotes softness of touch—whence wood smoothed for construction is called *levigata*—it has a long one.

*Lego, legis* (“I read or gather, you read or gather”) has a short *le*; *lego, legas* has a long one.

*Citum*, from *cio, cis* of the fourth conjugation, has a long penultimate; from *cieo, civi* of the second conjugation, it has a short penultimate.

*Ico* has a short penultimate in the present, but lengthens it in the perfect, *ici*, whence *ictus* (“struck”).

[Col. 0625C] The adverb *ne*, when used to prohibit or deny, is long; when used in a question or rebuke, it is shortened.

*Labor*, when it is a noun, is shortened; when it is the deponent verb “I slip,” it is lengthened, as in:

> *Labitur invalidae deformis gloria formae.*  
> “The disfigured glory of an infirm form slips away.”

*Liquor*, if it is a noun, is shortened; if it is a verb, it is lengthened, as Virgil writes in the *Georgics*:

> *Liquitur, et Zephyro putris se gleba resolvit.*  
> “It melts, and the crumbling clod dissolves beneath the West Wind.”

## On medial syllables

We recognize medial syllables in three ways: by position, by diphthongs, and by accent. We have, as I think, discussed position and diphthongs sufficiently above; now let us discuss accents.

Accent is, as some have correctly judged, the vigor and soul of the voice. For just as no voice exists without a vowel, so no voice exists without accent. [Col. 0625D] *Accent* is so called as though from *adcantus*, “singing beside,” because it is next to song, just as an adverb is so called because it stands beside a verb. In Greek it is called *prosodia*, whence the Latins gave it that name: Greek *pros* means Latin *ad*, “to” or “toward,” and Greek *ōdē* means Latin *cantus*, “song.”

Of the accents, two are necessary for the matters we are treating: the shortened and the lengthened, because they show metricians the quantity of time that each syllable ought to possess. The other accents serve more particularly pronunciation, writing, or orthography.

The shortened accent occurs in syllables that we utter without any pause in the voice, as in *macula* and *tabula*. The lengthened accent occurs in those that we express with some delay in the voice, as in *majestas* and *libertas*, because every long syllable occupies twice as much time as a short syllable occupies once.

Accents of pronunciation indicate medial syllables in the following way. In three-syllable words, if the penultimate syllable is short and is long neither by nature nor by position, the accent is transferred to the antepenultimate, and the penultimate is pronounced more quickly, as in *maenia* and *vincula*. But if the penultimate is long either by nature or by position, it retains the accent, whether circumflex or acute, as in *natura* and *potestas*. [Col. 0626A]

It should nevertheless be understood that forms of verbs pronounced with a short *i*, when they occur in the middle and change that *i* into *e*, are everywhere shortened, as in *legis, lege, legere*, except when they are followed by three consonants, *b*, *m*, and *t*, as in *legebam*, *legemus*, and *legetur*.

[Col. 0626B] As for words that are polysyllabic, we must investigate them by examples, position, and forms, as well as by accents. If we ask of which syllables *truculentissimorum* consists, we learn from an example that its first and second syllables are short, as in:

> *Domini truculentos persequor hostes.*  
> “I pursue the lord’s savage enemies.”

We learn that the third and fourth are long by position, and the fifth short by accent, because when we say *truculentissimus*, we prove that the penultimate is short. We pronounce the sixth with a circumflex accent and thereby show that it is long.

Likewise, if we ask of which syllables *cornigerorum* consists, we find that the first is long by position and the second short by accent, since in *corniger* the penultimate is short. We discover from the form of the compound that the third is short, because *corniger* is a common noun formed from *cornu*, “horn,” and *gero*, “I bear.” In *gero, geris*, *ge* is also short, and it is likewise shortened in compounds. [Col. 0626C]

We show that the fourth is long by accent. The character of the final syllable we shall demonstrate through the individual parts of speech in the discussion that follows.

We recognize medial syllables in six ways: by diphthongs, by the position of consonants, by the composition of parts, by rule, by examples from authors, and by accent. We have already discussed diphthongs and the position of letters above, when treating the syllable; now we shall speak of the remaining matters.

Medial syllables are therefore distinguished by the composition of parts, because almost all component parts of compounds retain in composition syllables of the same quantity that they had as simple words, except when they had been shortened from their earlier state, or when, after vowels have been removed, a joining of consonants has taken place, as in *parricida* (“parricide”), from the noun *parens* (“parent”) and the verb *caedere* (“to kill”); and *quadrigae* (“four-horse chariots”), for *quadrijugae*; *bini* (“two each”), for *bis uni* (“twice one”); and *deni* (“ten each”), for *decies uni* (“ten times one”). [Col. 0626D]

The same happens when two consonants meet in composition—that is, the final consonant of the preceding word and the initial consonant of the following word—and by this position they lengthen a syllable that was short in the preceding member, as in *paterfamilias* (“father of a household”), *ejusmodi* (“of this kind”), *satisfactio* (“satisfaction”), and *uterque* (“each of the two”). This occurs especially with prepositions that end in a consonant and are naturally short, such as *inter* (“between”), *subter* (“under”), and *super* (“above”); they are lengthened by position in *interfector* (“killer”), *superstes* (“survivor”), and *subterfugit* (“he escaped beneath” or “he evaded”). Otherwise they almost always preserve the rule mentioned above, as in *benevolus* (“benevolent”) and *malevolus* (“ill-disposed”): since they were simple words with all their syllables short, they remain likewise in composition.

For whatever compounds are formed from the verbs *gero* (“carry”), *fero* (“bear”), *teneo* (“hold”), *possum* (“be able”), *facio* (“make”), or *gigno* (“beget”), all shorten their medial syllables, because those verbs themselves, in their simple form, shorten their first part, as in *corniger*, *cornigeri* (“horn-bearing, of the horn-bearer”); *aliger*, *aligeri* (“winged”); *armiger*, *armigeri* (“weapon-bearing”); *lauriger*, *laurigeri* (“laurel-bearing”); *congero*, *degero*, *congerans*, *degerans* [perhaps *congerens*, *degerens*] (“I heap together,” “I carry away,” “heaping together,” “carrying away”). [Col. 0627A]

Likewise: *astrifer*, *astriferi* (“star-bearing”); *stellifer*, *stelliferi* (“star-bearing”); *somnifer*, *somniferi* (“sleep-bringing”); *vocifero*, *vociferans* (“I raise my voice,” “raising one’s voice”); *auferens* (“carrying away”), from *aufero*; *confero*, *conferens* (“I bring together,” “bringing together”).

Likewise: *omnipotens* (“all-powerful”); *armipotens* (“mighty in arms”); *almipotens* (“nourishingly powerful”); *omnitenens* (“holding all things”); *arcitenens* (“bow-bearing”); and *contineo*, *continens* (“I hold together,” “holding together”); *detineo*, *detinens* (“I hold back,” “holding back”).

Likewise: *pacificus*, *pacifico*, *pacificans* (“peaceful,” “I make peaceful,” “making peaceful”); *magnificus*, *magnifico*, *magnificans* (“magnificent,” “I magnify,” “magnifying”); *mirifico*, *mirifice*, *mirificans* (“I make wonderful,” “wonderfully,” “making wonderful”); *glorifico*, *glorifice*, *glorificans* (“I glorify,” “gloriously,” “glorifying”), and similar forms.

Likewise: *verbigena* (“word-born”); *terrigena* (“earth-born”); *nubigena* (“cloud-born”); *trojugena* (“Troy-born”); *unigenitus* (“only-begotten”); *primogenitus* (“first-begotten”). It must be understood that all these words, when their first member ends in *i*, shorten that *i*. [Col. 0627B]

The rule supplied by the authors is so abundant in material, so distinguished by manifold varieties, and so supported by suitable testimony that scarcely anyone could commit all of it to memory or explain it in a concise account. Yet it ought not to be entirely passed over by us. Although we cannot expound it all in this brief work, we shall nevertheless make an effort to touch upon it in its more notable places.

Thus, when Priscian wrote about the derivation of nouns, he investigated with great acumen the penultimate or antepenultimate syllables of each ending. We too have followed his authority here, but, for the sake of brevity and according to the affinity of the endings, we have combined the material that he arranged separately under other classes. [Col. 0627C]

Among derivative nouns ending in *-a*, if they have *i* before the *a*, they always shorten it, as in *sapientia* (“wisdom”) and *acrimonia* (“sharpness”). Nouns of the second declension ending in *-cus* likewise shorten the antepenultimate *i*, as well as the penultimate, unless they are names of regions derived from such forms: *amicus*, *amici*, *amicitia* (“friend, of a friend, friendship”); *inimicus*, *inimicitia* (“enemy, enmity”); *pudicus*, *pudicitia* (“modest, modesty”).

The same applies to certain other disyllabic nouns of the same declension: *laetus*, *laeti*, *laetitia* (“joyful, of a joyful person, joy”); *durus*, *duri*, *duritia* (“hard, of a hard thing, hardness”); *moestus*, *moesti*, *moestitia* (“sad, of a sad person, sadness”); *stultus*, *stulti*, *stultitia* (“foolish, of a fool, folly”).

The same is true of those whose nominative and genitive are alike in the third declension. Their derivatives arise from the dative, just as the former arise from the genitive: *segnis*, *segni*, *segnitia* (“sluggish, of sluggishness, sluggishness”); *tristis*, *tristi*, *tristitia* (“sad, of sadness, sadness”).

When a consonant precedes the final *a*, derivative or verbal nouns have three forms: *-la*, *-na*, and *-ra*. [Col. 0627D]

The ending *-la* is long when preceded by *e*: *cautus*, *cauti*, *cautela* (“cautious, of the cautious person, caution”); *tutus*, *tuti*, *tutela* (“safe, of safety, protection”); *custos*, *custodi*, *custodela* (“guardian, of a guardian, guardianship”); *mandatum*, *mandati*, *mandatela* (“command, of a command, commission”); *cliens*, *clienti*, *clientela* (“client, of a client, clientele”).

Note that all these forms take the final vowel of the genitive—if they are nouns of the second declension—or of the dative—if they are nouns of the third declension—changing it into long *e* before adding *-la*. Those formed from second-conjugation verbs, however, remove the *s* from the second-person form and add *-la*: *candeo*, *candes*, *candela* (“I shine,” “you shine,” “candle”); *suadeo*, *suades*, *suadela* (“I persuade,” “you persuade,” “persuasion”).

Those ending in *-na* have a penultimate syllable that is always long, either by nature or by position: *officium*, *officina* (“office, workshop”); *medicus*, *medicina* (“physician, medicine”); *rex*, *regis*, *regina* (“king, of a king, queen”); *leo*, *leaena* (“lion, lioness”); *doctrix*, *doctrina* (“female teacher, teaching”); *piscis*, *piscina* (“fish, fishpond”); *cocus*, *cocina* and *culina* (“cook, kitchen”); *cantus*, *cantilena* (“song, song or chant”); *far*, *farina* (“grain, flour”); *lux*, *lucis*, *lucina* (“light, of light, Lucina”); *luceo*, *lucerna* (“I shine, lamp”); *lateo*, *laterna* (“I lie hidden, lantern”). [Col. 0628A]

*Fiscina* (“basket”) shortens its penultimate syllable, as do *fuscina* (“trident”), *mutina* (“Mutina”), and *pagina* (“page”). This is because they are not derivatives but primitives. The same applies to *sagana* (“witch”); for *sagana* and *saga* have the same meaning.

All words ending in *-ra* have a form like the feminine participles of the future tense; hence their penultimate *u* is unquestionably long: *scriptura* (“writing”); *censura* (“censure”); *pictura* (“painting”); *tonsura* (“shearing”); *usura* (“use”); *litura* (“erasure”); *natura* (“nature”); *armatura* (“armor”).

It must be noted that all the forms mentioned above, namely those ending in *-a*, properly belong to the feminine gender. A few verbal nouns of masculine or common gender are nevertheless found: *hic scriba* (“this male scribe”), from *scribo*, with long *i*; from *lego*, *le*—*collega* (“colleague”); from *fugio*, *hic et haec perfuga* (“male or female deserter”); from *assequor*, *assecula* (“female follower”); from *advenio*, *advena* (“newcomer”); from *convenio*, *convena* (“guest”), with the penultimate syllable shortened in these forms; in *conviva* (“guest, table-companion”), it is long. [Col. 0628B]

*Propheta* (“prophet”), *poeta* (“poet”), and *proreta* (“pilot”) are primitives and lengthen their penultimate *e*.

Among feminine patronymics ending in *-ne*, which are forms in *-iadis*—the text reads *iadis linquae*, apparently corrupt—the penultimate *i* is long if the primary name did not have the same vowel: *Adrestos*, *adrestine*; *Nereus*, *nerine*. But if the primary name did have *i*, a lengthened *o* is found before *-ne*, as in *acrisios*, *acrisione*.

Derivative neuters ending in *-e* include *sedile* (“seat”), *civile* (“civil thing”), *monile* (“necklace”), and *cubile* (“bed”); they have a long penultimate syllable. Since most arise from common-gender forms whose masculine and feminine end in *-ilis*, the penultimate syllables of these neuters are recognized from the rules governing those forms.

A few masculine or common nouns ending in *-o* are found: *Cicero*, from *cicer* (“chickpea”); *Capito*, from *caput* (“head”); *labeo*, from *labe* (“a stain”); *latro*, from *lateo* (“to lie hidden”); *leno* (“pimp”), naturally long, from *lenio* (“to soften”); *Cato*, from *catus* (“shrewd”); *comedo* (“glutton”), from *comedo* (“I eat”); *epulo* (“banqueter”), from *epulor* (“I feast”), with the penultimate syllable naturally short; *palpo* (“flatterer”), from *palpo* (“I flatter”), has it long by position. [Col. 0628C]

Most feminine derivatives end in *-io*, *-go*, or *-do*, sometimes in one and sometimes in another.

Words ending in *-io* are generally formed from perfect participles. Their genitive, after *o* has been added and *i* shortened, produces nouns of this kind: *oratus*, *orati*, *oratio* (“spoken, of the spoken thing, speech”); *accusatus*, *accusati*, *accusatio* (“accused, of the accused person, accusation”); *status*, *stati*, *statio* (“stationed, of the stationed thing, station”); *datus*, *dati*, *datio* (“given, of the given thing, giving”); *nexus*, *nexi*, *nexio* (“bound, of the bound thing, binding”); *abolitus*, *aboliti*, *abolitio* (“abolished, of the abolished thing, abolition”); *lectus*, *lecti*, *lectio* (“read or chosen, of the read or chosen thing, reading or choice”); *munitus*, *muniti*, *munitio* (“fortified, of the fortified thing, fortification”).

*Internectus*, *internecti*, *internecio* (“slain, of the slain, slaughter”) was formed for euphony by removing the *t*.

All diminutives that have *i* before *o* shorten it, as I have said: *homuncio* (“little man”).

Words ending in *-go*, whether derivative, primitive, or compound, have a penultimate syllable long either by nature or by position: *virago* (“heroine”); *compago* (“joint, framework”); *Carthago* (“Carthage”); *sartago* (“frying pan”); *caligo* (“mist”); *uligo* (“moisture”); *rubigo* (“rust”); *ferrugo* (“iron-rust”); *aerugo* (“verdigris”); *virgo* (“virgin”); *margo* (“edge”). The sole exception is *ligo* (“spade”), whose penultimate syllable is short; and this is unsurprising, since it is masculine and the only disyllabic word having a vowel before *-go*. [Col. 0628D]

Derivative nouns ending in *-do* arise from nouns, verbs, or participles. Before *-do* they have either long *e*, or *i*, or *u*: *acris*, *acredo* (“sharp, sharpness”); *dulcis*, *dulcedo* (“sweet, sweetness”); *intercapio*, *intercapedo* (“I intercept, interruption”); *torpeo*, *torpedo* (“I am numb, numbness”); *libet*, *libido* (“it pleases, desire”); *cupio*, *cupido* (“I desire, desire”); *formido*, *formidas*, *formidinis* (“fear, you fear, of fear”). The latter formed a verbal noun resembling the primitive verb because the verb itself had that form by position.

In *-tudo* we find *fortitudo* (“strength”); *magnitudo* (“greatness”); *habitudo* (“condition”); *amplitudo* (“extent”); *firmitudo* (“firmness”); *celsitudo* (“height”); *suavitudo* (“sweetness”); in all of which the antepenultimate *i* is shortened. *Testudo* (“tortoise”), from *testa* or *testu*, is a bodily term. [Col. 0629A]

Moreover, all words ending in *-do*, even when they are not derivatives, lengthen a penultimate *u*, whether by nature or by position: *hirundo* (“swallow”); *arundo* (“reed”); *hirudo* (“leech”).

Among derivative nouns ending in *-al*, if their primitives have a penultimate syllable long by nature or position, they too have a long penultimate syllable: *cervix*, *cervicis*, *cervical* (“neck, of the neck, cervical”); *tribunus*, *tribunal* (“tribune, tribunal”); *vectus*, *vectigal* (“carried, tax”); *lupercus*, *lupercal* (“Lupercus, Lupercal”). But if the primitive has a short syllable, the derivative also has it short: *torus*, *toral* (“couch, relating to a couch”); *animus* and *anima*, *animal* (“spirit or soul, animal”). [Col. 0629B]

Derivative or compound forms ending in *-um* have various patterns. Some have long *e* or shortened *i* before *-um*: *olivetum* (“olive grove”); *coriletum* (“hazel grove”); *rosetum* (“rose garden”); *dumetum* (“thicket”); *quercetum* (“oak grove”); *scutetum* (“shield-shaped ornament”); *myrtetum* (“myrtle grove”).

Others have *iu*: *augurium* (“augury”); *solarium* (“sundial”); *ponarium* (“fruit basket”); *solatium* (“consolation”); *suavium* (“kiss”); *basium* (“kiss”); *odium* (“hatred”); *remedium* (“remedy”); *concubium* (“marriage or cohabitation”); *palladium* (“Palladium”); *officium* (“duty”); *connubium* (“marriage”); *convivium* (“banquet”); *exsilium* (“exile”); *consilium* (“counsel”); *judicium* (“judgment”); *meritorium* (“earned reward”); *municipium* (“municipality”); *praesidium* (“protection”); *domicilium* (“dwelling”).

Derivative nouns having consonants before *-um* also have various forms. Some end in *-bulum*, a form resembling diminutives, and arise from nouns or verbs: *cuna*, *cunabulum* (“cradle”); *vesta* or *vestis*, *vestibulum* (“vestment or clothing, vestibule”); *thus*, *thuris*, *thuribulum* (“incense, of incense, censer”); *voco*, *vocas*, *vocabulum* (“I call, you call, word or name”); *concilias*, *conciliabulum* (“you reconcile, meeting-place”); *stas*, *stabulum* (“you stand, stable”); *pasco*, *pabulum* (“I feed, fodder”); *prosto*, *prostibulum* (“I stand publicly, brothel”); *patior* or *patio*, *patibulum* (“I suffer or endure, gallows”).

[And it should be observed that in all these words the penultimate syllable is shortened; but the antepenultimate, if it contains *i*, is also shortened, as in *vestibulum*, *patibulum*.] [Col. 0629C]

If, however, the antepenultimate contains *a*, it is lengthened, as in *cunabulum*, *pabulum*. *Stabulum* is excepted, since it shortens its *a*; and this is unsurprising, since the verb *stabulo*, *stabulas* also shortens the same syllable. So too do *stabilis* (“stable”), *status* (“standing”), and all forms derived from the verb *sto*, *stas* (“I stand, you stand”), except the one supine *statum*, and the noun *stamen* (“thread”), and *statura* (“stature”), which is both a noun and a participle. *Staturus* and *staturum* likewise lengthen the syllable, although *status*, *stata*, *statum* shorten it.

Some words ending in *-culum* are derived from the second-person form of a verb: *devertis*, *deverticulum* (“you turn aside, small side-road”); *verris*, *verriculum* (“you sweep, broom”); *vehis*, *vehiculum* (“you carry, vehicle”); *perior*, *periris*, whence *peritus* (“experienced”) and the compound *imperitus* (“inexperienced”), and *periculum* (“danger”); *oras*, *oraculum* (“you speak, oracle”); *propugnas*, *propugnaculum* (“you defend, defense”); *obstas*, *obstaculum* (“you obstruct, obstacle”); *miraris*, *miraculum* (“you wonder, miracle”); *perpendis*, *perpendiculum* (“you weigh, plumb line”); *specio*, *specis*, *speculum*, by syncope for *speciculum* (“I look, you look, mirror”); *fero*, *fers*, *ferculum* (“I bear, you bear, tray”). [Col. 0629D]

It must be understood that all these forms shorten the penultimate *u*. The same applies to diminutives ending in *-culus*, *-cula*, *-culum*, and *-ulus*, *-ula*, *-ulum*: *igniculus* (“little fire”); *tantulus* (“so little”); *regulus* (“little king”); *navicula* (“little ship”); *tantula* (“so little”); *corpusculum* (“little body”); *capitulum* (“little head” or “chapter”). All those that have *i* in the antepenultimate likewise shorten it: *dulciculus*, *dulcicula*, *dulciculum* (“little sweet thing”); *monticula* (“little mountain”); *fidicula* (“little lyre”); *corniculum* (“little horn”); *versiculus* (“little verse”); *anicula* (“little old woman”); *geniculum* (“little knee”).

*Cuticula* (“skin”) is excepted, for it lengthens the *i* in the antepenultimate syllable. Juvenal writes:

> The contracted skin drinks in the summer sun,

and likewise *apicula* (“little bee”). Words that have *e* before *-cula* lengthen it: *vulpecula* (“little fox”); *nubecula* (“little cloud”); *diecula* (“little day”). [Col. 0630A]

Other verbal nouns end in *-mentum*: *vestio*, *vestis*, *vestimentum* (“I clothe, clothing”); *hortor*, *hortaris*, *hortamentum* (“I encourage, you encourage, encouragement”); *orno*, *ornas*, *ornamentum* (“I adorn, you adorn, ornament”); *sacro*, *sacras*, *sacramentum* (“I consecrate, you consecrate, sacred rite”); *fundo*, *fundas*, *fundamentum* (“I found or pour, you found or pour, foundation”); *moneo*, *monitus*, *monimentum* (“I advise, advised, monument”); *alui*, *alitus*, *alimentum* (“I nourished, nourished, nourishment”); *munivi*, *munitus*, *munimentum* (“I fortified, fortified, fortification”).

It must be understood that these have a lengthened or shortened antepenultimate syllable according as the penultimate syllables of the perfect-tense forms of the verbs from which they derive are long or short.

There are also derivatives in *-monium*, with *i* shortened before *mo* or after it: *patrimonium* (“patrimony”); *matrimonium* (“marriage”); *testimonium* (“testimony”).

Among derivative words ending in *-en*, with *m* preceding, almost all are verbal and neuter. If they arise from the first conjugation, they have a long penultimate syllable: *solor*, *solaris*, *solamen* (“I console, you console, consolation”); *foro*, *foras*, *foramen* (“I bore through, you bore through, opening”); *curvas*, *curvamen* (“you bend, curvature”); *oblectas*, *oblectamen* (“you delight, delight”); *purgo*, *purgas*, *purgamen* (“I cleanse, you cleanse, cleansing”); *irrito*, *irritas*, *irritamen* (“I provoke, you provoke, provocation”); *ligas*, *ligamen* (“you bind, bond”). [Col. 0630B]

If they arise from the second or third conjugation, they have shortened *i*: *moneo*, *mones*, *monimen* (“I advise, you advise, memorial”); *rego*, *regis*, *regimen* (“I rule, you rule, governance”); *tego*, *teg is*, *tegimen*, and by contraction *tegmen* (“I cover, you cover, covering”); *specis* or *specie*, *specimen* (“you look” or “appearance, example”). Or they have lengthened *a* when the verb ends in *-uo*: *acuo*, *acumen* (“I sharpen, sharpness”); *fluo*, *flumen* (“I flow, river”); *nuo*, *numen* (“I nod, divine will”). *Numen* means the nod or will of God. Hence Virgil writes:

> The winds without my divine will.

That is, “without my nod.” From *luo* comes *lumen* (“light”), by which all things are washed clean—that is, purified from darkness.

Forms arising from fourth-conjugation verbs have lengthened *i*: *munio*, *munimen* (“I fortify, fortification”); *lenio*, *lenimen* (“I soften, soothing”); *molior*, *molimen* (“I undertake or strive, effort”).

A few masculine derivatives ending in *-en* are found: *pecten* (“comb”), from *pectendo* (“combing”); *filamen* (“thread”), from *filo* (“I spin”), which after syncope of *i* we call *flamen*; and masculine compounds from *cano* (“sing”) have a shortened penultimate *i*: *tubicen* (“trumpeter”); *cornicen* (“horn-player”); *fidicen* (“lyre-player”). The sole exception is *tibicen* (“flute-player”), which alone lengthens the penultimate *i* because two short *i* sounds have been contracted by synaeresis into one long syllable. [Col. 0630C]

Among derivative words ending in *-ar*, if a consonant precedes *-ar*, the penultimate syllable is lengthened: *caesus*, *caesar* (“cut, Caesar”); *lacus*, *lacunar* (“lake, ceiling-panel or hollow”); *lupa*, *lupanar* (“she-wolf, brothel”). If a vowel precedes it, the syllable is shortened: *laqueus*, *laquear* (“coffered ceiling”).

Among derivatives ending in *-er*, most have *s* or *t* before *r*: *equester* (“equestrian”); *pedester* (“on foot”), and diminutives likewise: *antester* (“little priestess”); *parasitaster* (“little parasite”); *antoniaster* (“little Antony”); *catulaster* (“little puppy”). Most verbal forms retain the shortened consonant: *rubeo*, *ruber* (“I am red, red”); *pigro*, *piger* (“I am sluggish, sluggish”); *macero*, *macer* (“I make thin, thin”).

Words ending in *-or* and *-ur* are formed from verbs by removing *o*: *coloro*, *color* (“I color, color”); *laboro*, *labor* (“I work, labor”); *honoro*, *honor* (“I honor, honor”); *decoro*, *decor* (“I adorn, beauty”); *adoro*, *ador* (“I adore, adoration”); *murmuro*, *murmur* (“I murmur, murmur”); *auguro*, *augur* (“I augur, augur”); *saturo*, *satur* (“I satisfy, full”). The feminine of *satur* is *satura*, and the neuter is *saturum*.

Others add *r* to the verb: *amo*, *amor* (“I love, love”); *furo*, *furor* (“I rage, rage”).

Others change the ending *-us* of participles into *-or* while preserving their accent: *senatus*, *senator* (“senate, senator”); *monitus*, *monitor* (“advised, adviser”).

It must be understood that all comparatives ending in *-or* always have a shortened penultimate *i*: *senior* (“older”); *doctior* (“more learned”); *fidelior* (“more faithful”), masculine and feminine alike; and likewise their neuters, *doctius* (“more learned”) and *fidelius* (“more faithful”).

Among derivative words ending in *-as*, if they have *i* or *e* in the penultimate syllable, they shorten it: *probus*, *probi*, *probitas* (“upright, of an upright person, uprightness”); *bonus*, *boni*, *bonitas* (“good, of a good person, goodness”); *timidus*, *timidi*, *timiditas* (“fearful, of a fearful person, timidity”); *pius*, *pii*, *pietas* (“dutiful, of a dutiful person, piety”); *socius*, *socii*, *societas* (“ally, of an ally, society”); *capax*, *capaci*, *capacitas* (“capable, of a capable person, capacity”); *felix*, *felici*, *felicitas* (“fortunate, of a fortunate person, happiness”); *celer*, *celeri*, *celeritas* (“swift, of a swift person, swiftness”); *auctor*, *auctoritas* (“author or originator, authority”). [Col. 0631A]

Some lengthen *e*: *pauper*, *paupertas* (“poor, poverty”); *uber*, *ubertas* (“fertile, fertility”); *major*, *majestas* (“greater, majesty”). Some of these are common-gender forms, such as *primas* (“chief”); *optimas* (“best”); and *ultima*, with circumflex accent.

Derivative and verbal forms ending in *-es* shorten it: *eques*, *equitis* (“horseman, of a horseman”); *struo*, *strues* (“I build, structure”); *sepio*, *sepes* (“I enclose, hedge”).

Verbal forms ending in *-es* with a long vowel include *luxurio*, *luxuries* (“I live luxuriously, luxury”); *illuvio*, *illuvies* (“I wash over, alluvial matter”).

Patronymics of this form also occur, such as *Anchisiades* (“son or descendant of Anchises”).

This form, used by our writers, must be discussed more carefully. If the Greek nominative ends in *ας* (*-as*) and the genitive in the diphthong *ου* (*-ou*), a short *a* is found before *-des* in the patronymic: *Pelias*, *Peliades* (“Pelias, descendant of Pelias”); *Aeneas*, *Aeneades* (“Aeneas, descendant of Aeneas”); *Menoetius*, *Menoetiades* (“Menoetius, descendant of Menoetius”); *Lerchios*, *Lerchiades* (“Lerchios, descendant of Lerchios”).

Virgil, in Book IX, used *Aeneides* more against the rule, by poetic authority, changing the shortened *e* and *a* into lengthened *i*:

> Let it suffice, Aeneid, that Numanus has fallen  
> By your weapons without penalty to you . . . .

*Hippotes*, *hippotades*; *Butes*, *Butades*; *Corinetes*, *Corinetides*: in these the penultimate *i* is short.

The following are exceptions, however, since against the rule they lengthen the penultimate vowels: *aeolides*, *demades*, *codrides*, *licoorgides*, *lagides*, *belides*, *everides*, *licomedides*. Among the Greeks these have a diphthong in the penultimate syllable; in its place we use long *i*. [Col. 0631B]

Derivative and verbal words ending in *-is* have many different forms. Some end in *-alis*, some in *-elis*, some in *-ilis*, and some in *-ulis*: *curialis* (“curial”); *fidelis* (“faithful”); *docilis* (“teachable”); *virilis* (“manly”); *curulis* (“curule”). Others end in *-aris*, with long *a* preceding: *Apollinaris* (“of Apollo”); *scholaris* (“scholastic”). Others end in *-ensis*: *Atheniensis* (“Athenian”). Others have two consonants before *-is*: *agrestis* (“rural”); *muliebris* (“womanly”); *Samnis* (“Samnite”); *insignis* (“remarkable”).

Words ending in *-alis* or *-ale*, if formed from nouns of the first declension, take *-lis* or *-le* after the nominative of the primitive and lengthen the penultimate *a*: *curia*, *curialis* (“senate-house, curial”); *memoria*, *memorialis* (“memory, memorial”); *mensa*, *mensale* (“table, table-related”); *via*, *vialis* (“way, relating to a way”).

If they are formed from nouns of the second declension, they take the final *i* of the genitive. If from nouns of the third declension, they change *-is* into long *a* and add *-lis*: *Martius*, *Martii*, *martialis* (“of Mars, of Mars, martial”); *fluvius*, *fluvii*, *fluvialis* (“river, of a river, riverine”); *liber*, *liberi*, *liberalis* (“free, of a free person, liberal”); *theatrum*, *theatri*, *theatralis* (“theater, of a theater, theatrical”); *caput*, *capitis*, *capitalis* (“head, of the head, capital”); *virgo*, *virginis*, *virginalis* (“virgin, of a virgin, virginal”); *cardinis*, *cardinalis* (“of a hinge, cardinal”); *hospitis*, *hospitalis* (“of a guest, hospitable or hospital”); *navis*, *navalis* (“ship, naval”); *dotis*, *dotalis* (“dowry, dotal”); *floris*, *floralis* (“flower, floral”); *corporis*, *corporalis* (“body, corporeal”); *caelibis*, *caelibalis* (“unmarried, celibate”); *juvenis*, *juvenalis* or *juvenilis* (“young, youthful”); *princeps*, *principis*, *principalis* (“chief, of a chief, principal”); *vox*, *vocis*, *vocalis* (“voice, of the voice, vocal”). [Col. 0631C]

If they derive from nouns of the fourth declension, the final *s* is removed; if from the fifth, *es* is removed from the nominative and *-alis* is added: *manus*, *manualis* (“hand, manual”); *census*, *censualis* (“assessment, financial”); *species*, *specialis* (“appearance or species, special”).

Verbal forms of the first conjugation ending in *-alis* are also found: *penetro*, *penetralis* (“I penetrate, inner or sanctuary-related”). [Col. 0631D]

Few derivative nouns ending in *-elis* are found: *fidus*, *fidi*, *fidelis* (“faithful, of a faithful person, faithful”); *crudus*, *crudi*, *crudelis* (“raw or cruel, of a cruel person, cruel”); *patruus*, *patrui*, *patruelis* (“paternal uncle, of a paternal uncle, cousin”); *frater*, *fratris*, *fratruelis* (“brother, of a brother, cousin”).

Note that all forms changing the final syllable of the genitive into long *e* have taken *-lis*. *Frater*, however, from *fratris*, changed the *is* into *u* and took *-elis*.

All forms in *-ilis* derived from nouns, as well as neuters in *-ile*, have a long *i*: *aedis*, *aedilis* (“temple, aedile”); *senex*, *senilis* (“old man, senile”); *anus*, *anilis* (“old woman, old-womanish”); *puer*, *puerilis* (“boy, boyish”); *vir*, *virilis* (“man, manly”); *scurra*, *scurrilis* (“buffoon, buffoonish”); *civis*, *civilis* (“citizen, civil”); *servus*, *servilis* (“slave, slavish”); *quintus*, *quintilis* (“fifth, of the fifth month”); *sextus*, *sextilis* (“sixth, of the sixth month”); *gens*, *gentilis* (“people or clan, gentile”); *hostis*, *hostilis* (“enemy, hostile”); *subtel*, *subtilis* (“fine or delicate, subtle”). *Par*, *parilis* (“equal, equal or corresponding”) is excepted.

*Exilis* (“thin, slight”) will likewise preserve the rule of denominatives, having been made from *agrem* [lacuna] *factum*. [Note: [Col. 0631D] The passage is corrupt and simultaneously incomplete.]

Verbal or participial words ending in *-ilis* shorten the same penultimate *i*: *fero*, *fertilis* (“I bear, fertile”); *utor*, *utilis* (“I use, useful”); *futtuo*, *futtilis* (“I copulate, worthless or trivial”); *volo*, *volatilis* (“I fly or wish, flying”); *textus*, *textilis* (“woven, textile”); *altus* or *alitus*, *altilis* (“raised or nourished, nourishing”); *fictus*, *fictilis* (“fashioned, made of clay”).

Likewise, all forms ending in *-bilis* shorten the penultimate *i*. If they arise from first-conjugation verbs, they have a long *a* in the antepenultimate: *amo*, *amas*, *amabilis* (“I love, you love, lovable”); *penetro*, *penetras*, *penetrabilis* (“I penetrate, you penetrate, penetrable”); *paro*, *paras*, *parabilis* (“I prepare, you prepare, preparable”); *miror*, *miraris*, *mirabilis* (“I wonder, you wonder, wonderful”), except *stabilis* (“stable”).

Lucan writes in Book V:

> How he would not look down upon all things  
> From a summit not firm but trembling.

Those arising from second-, third-, or fourth-conjugation verbs, if they have *i* in the antepenultimate, shorten that as well: *doceo*, *docibilis* (“I teach, teachable”); *credo*, *credibilis* (“I believe, credible”); *utor*, *utilis*, *utibilis* (“I use, useful, usable”); *sensio*, *sensi*, *sensibilis* (“I perceive, I perceived, perceptible”); *audio*, *audibilis* (“I hear, audible”). [Col. 0632B]

It must nevertheless be understood that some are derived from the present, some from the perfect, and some from the future: from the present, *doceo*, *docibilis*; from the perfect, *plausi*, *plausibilis* (“I applauded, worthy of applause”); from the future, *flebo*, *flebilis* (“I shall weep, tearful”), whence it has a long *e* before *b*.

Words ending in *-aris* are derived from nouns by changing the final part of the genitive into long *a* and adding *-ris*: *populus*, *populi*, *popularis* (“people, of the people, popular”); *singulus*, *singuli*, *singularis* (“single, of a single thing, singular”); *Apollo*, *Apollinis*, *Apollinaris* (“Apollo, of Apollo, Apollonian”); *schola*, *scholae*, *scholaris* (“school, of a school, scholastic”); *peculium*, *peculii*, *peculiaris* (“property, of property, peculiar or private”); *mola*, *molae*, *molaris* (“millstone, of a millstone, molar”); *velum*, *veli*, *velare* (“veil, of a veil, veiling”), neuter. [Col. 0632C]

In forms ending in *-ensis*, if they are derived from first- or second-declension nouns, they change the final part of the singular or plural nominative into *-en* and add *-sis*: *circa* [perhaps *circus*], *circensis* (“circus, pertaining to the circus”); *Sardinia*, *Sardiniensis* (“Sardinia, Sardinian”); *castrum*, *castrensis* (“camp, camp-related”); *Athenae*, *Atheniensis* (“Athens, Athenian”), which has *i* for the sake of euphony.

If they are nouns of the third declension, they remove the final *s* of the genitive and add *-ensis*: *pistoris*, *pistoriensis* (“of a baker, baker-related”); *Carthaginis*, *Carthaginensis* (“of Carthage, Carthaginian”).

Words having two consonants before *-is* are formed either from the nominative of their primitives by removing its final letter and adding *-bris*: *salus*, *salubris* (“health, healthy”); *mulier*, *muliebris* (“woman, womanly”); or from the genitive by changing its final part into *e* and adding *-stis* or *-stris*: *ager*, *agri*, *agrestis* (“field, of a field, rural”); *terra*, *terrae*, *terrestris* (“earth, of the earth, terrestrial”). [Col. 0632D]

Words ending in *-tis* have their penultimate syllable long either by nature or by position: *Samnitis*, for *Samnis* (“Samnite”); *Tiburtis*, for *Tiburs* (“Tiburtine”); and *ceretis* or *ceritis*, for *Ceres*, whose penultimate syllable is sometimes shortened and sometimes lengthened.

Words ending in *-us* have different forms and meanings, because this ending includes possessives, superlatives, diminutives, derivatives, denominatives, and verbals. Their types must be explained one by one.

We call possessives not only those that signify possession but also those that have the form of possessives. Some gentile nouns have a form resembling possessives, as in *Romanus civis* or *Romanus ager* (“a Roman citizen” or “Roman land”). Others are proper names, gentile names, and possessives at once: *Latirus*, the son of Faunus; and *Latinus*, a Latin citizen or Latin land.

Some are proper names alone, such as *Quintilianus* and *Julianus*. Others stand in place of patronymics, such as *Octavianus Caesar* and *Aemilianus Scipio*. Others are surnames, such as *Africanus* and *Persicus*. Others are derived from materials: *ferreus* (“iron,” made of iron), *aureus* (“golden”), *argenteus* (“silver”), *marmoreus* (“marble”). Others derive from diseases, such as *cardiacus* (“cardiac”). Others derive from professions, such as *mechanicus* (“mechanical”) and *grammaticus* (“grammatical”). Others derive from disciplines, such as *Aristotelicus* (“Aristotelian”) and *rhetoricus* (“rhetorical”). Others resemble their primitives, such as *Thracius* for *Thrax* (“Thracian”).

The forms of possessives that we have received from the Greeks are these. There is the ending *-cos*, which we have changed to *-cus*, preceded by short *a*, *i*, or *y*: *Hebraicus* (“Hebrew”); *Cypriacus* (“Cyprian”); *Italicus* (“Italian”); *grammaticus* (“grammatical”); *rhetoricus* (“rhetorical”); *Libycus* (“Libyan”), the only one with *y* before *-cus*. [Col. 0633A]

Possessives, both Greek and Latin, also end in *-us*, preceded by shortened or lengthened *e*, shortened *i*, lengthened *o*, or the diphthong *ae*. With short *e* before *-us* are *Hectoreus* (“of Hector”); *Agenoreus* (“of Agenor”); *Caesareus* (“of Caesar”); *Romuleus* (“of Romulus”); *aureus* (“golden”); *argenteus* (“silver”); *ferreus* (“iron”); *ligneus* (“wooden”); *marmoreus* (“marble”), and almost all words relating to material.

A few occur without *e*: *quernus* (“oak”); *colurnus* (“hazel”); *abiegnus* (“fir”). Some have long *e*: *spondeus* (“spondaic”); *phebeus* (“of Phoebus”). The same occurs when *e* stands for a diphthong: *Achilleus* for *Achilleios* (“of Achilles”); *Alpheus* for *Alpheios* (“of the Alpheus”); *Pythagoreus* for *Pythagoreios* (“Pythagorean”). Virgil, however, shortens it in *Tiphoeus*:

> Son of the highest father, who scorns the weapons of Typhoeus;

but it is also said *tiphoeus*, *tiphos*, or *tiphon*.

Foreign words especially have lengthened *e* before *-us*: *Pharisaeus* (“Pharisaic”); *Matthaeus* (“Matthew”); *Judaeus* (“Jewish”). They have shortened *i*: *martius* (“of March”); *hereditarius* (“hereditary”). The Romans lengthen *i* according to the Greeks in only a few names: *Phtius Dius*, *Phtia Dia*, *Conius Cius*, *Argius*, *Langius*, *Lycius*, *Sperchius* [the transmitted forms are uncertain]. [Col. 0633B]

Sometimes *u* functions in place of digamma and lengthens the penultimate *i*: *argivus* (“Argive”); *nominativus* (“nominative”); *genitivus* (“genitive”); *imperativus* (“imperative”); *optativus* (“optative”), and similar forms. There is lengthened *o*: *herous* (“heroic”); *eous* (“eastern”). There is the diphthong *ae*: *Sabaeus* (“Sabaean”); *Cretaeus* (“Cretan”); *Ptolomaeus* (“Ptolemaic”); *Timaeus* (“Timaean”); and *cubaea* (“of Cuba”).

In words ending in *-nus*, if the penultimate syllable has *a* or *e*, it is lengthened: *Romanus* (“Roman”); *Hispanus* (“Spanish”); *fontanus* (“of a spring”); *montanus* (“mountain”). *Dardanus* is a proper and primitive name, and therefore has shortened *a*; likewise *terrenus* (“earthly”); *egenus* (“needy”); *alienus* (“foreign”); *amenus* (“pleasant”).

The *i* before *-nus* is sometimes lengthened: *camerinus* (“of Camerium”); *reginus* (“royal”); *masculinus* (“masculine”); *vicinus* (“neighboring”); *femininus* (“feminine”); *follinus* (“of a bellows”); *marinus* (“marine”); *taurinus* (“of a bull”); *porcinus* (“swine-related”). It is sometimes shortened, namely in words derived from trees: *oleaginus* (“olive-tree”); *faginus* (“beech-tree”); and in those derived from temporal adverbs: *cras*, *crastinus* (“tomorrow, tomorrow’s”); *horno*, *hornoctinus* (“this year, of this year”); *diu*, *diutinus* (“for a long time, prolonged”). [Col. 0633C]

There is also long *u* before *-nus*: *tribunus* (“tribune”). Other forms have length by position and are derivative: from *heri* (“yesterday”), *hesternus* (“yesterday’s”); from *aetas* (“age”), *aeternus* (“eternal”); from *dies* (“day”), *diurnus* (“daily”); from *semper* (“always”), *sempiternus* (“everlasting”). [Col. 0633D]

Superlatives end in *-mus*, and all have a short penultimate *i*: *infimus* (“lowest”); *optimus* (“best”); *doctissimus* (“most learned”); *humillimus* (“humblest”); *minimus* (“smallest”); *celeberrimus* (“most celebrated”); *maximus* (“greatest”). A few are excepted, having a long vowel before *-mus* and deriving from an adverb or preposition: from *extra* (“outside”), *extremus* (“outermost”); from *supra* (“above”), *supremus* (“highest”); from *post* (“after”), *posterior* (“later”) and *postremus* (“last”).

Diminutives also have many forms and occur in all three genders: *-culus, -cula, -culum*; *-ulus, -ula, -ulum*; *-olus, -ola, -olum*. Their penultimate syllable is always short: *igniculus* (“little fire”); *anicula* (“little old woman”); *corpusculum* (“little body”); *tantulus* (“so little”); *silvula* (“little wood”); *capitulum* (“little head” or “chapter”); *sergiolus* (“little Sergius”); *unciola* (“little ounce”); *lauriolum* (“little laurel”); and also *homuncio* (“little man”) and *aculeus* (“little thorn”), whose penultimate syllables are short.

Other diminutives are lengthened only by position: *agellus* (“little field”); *capella* (“little goat”); *novellum* (“little new thing”); *pugillus* (“little fist”); *anguilla* (“little eel”). Others are lengthened both by nature and by position: *pauxillus*, *pauxilla*, *pauxillum* (“very little”); *ullus*, *ulla*, *ullum* (“any”).

As for the antepenultimate syllables of these forms, what we said above should suffice for this brief treatment.

In the endings of denominative and verbal forms, various patterns are found, divided among *-ius*, *-uus*, *-bus*, *-cus*, *-quus*, *-dus*, *-lus*, *-rus*, *-sus*, *-tus*, and *-stus*. [Col. 0634A]

Words ending in *-ius*, such as *nuntius* (“messenger”); *Virgilius* (“Virgil”); *Silvius* (“Silvius”); *saucius* (“wounded”); *scius* (“knowing”); *nescius* (“ignorant”); *Fabricius* (“Fabricius”), all shorten the penultimate *i*. If they have *i* in the antepenultimate, they shorten that as well: *tribunitius* (“tribunitial”); *advectitius* (“conveyed”); *patricius* (“patrician”). If they have *a*, they lengthen it: *gallinacius* (“of a hen”); *membranacius* (“membranous”).

Words ending in the divided sequence *-uus* shorten the penultimate *u*: *annuus* (“annual”); *patruus* (“paternal uncle”); *ambiguus* (“ambiguous”); *vacuus* (“empty”); *menstruus* (“monthly”). [Col. 0634B]

In *-quus*: *obliquus* (“oblique”), with the penultimate syllable long by nature; and *longinquus* (“distant”), long by position.

In *-cus* or *-bus*: *parcus* (“sparing”); *superbus* (“proud”).

Words ending in *-dus* either shorten the penultimate syllable: *herbidus* (“grassy”); *turbidus* (“turbid”); *uvidus* (“wet”); *rabidus* (“mad”); *timidus* (“fearful”); *aridus* (“dry”); *squalidus* (“filthy”); *frigidus* (“cold”); or lengthen it by position: *errabundus* (“wandering”); *moribundus* (“dying”); *amandus* (“to be loved”).

Words ending in *-lus* likewise shorten the penultimate syllable: *credulus* (“credulous”); *pendulus* (“hanging”); *bibulus* (“drinking”).

Few denominative or verbal words ending in *-rus* lengthen the penultimate syllable: *honor*, *honorus* (“honor, honorable”); *odor*, *odorus* (“smell, fragrant”); *decor*, *decorus* (“beauty, beautiful”); *canor*, *canorus* (“song, melodious”). [Col. 0634C]

Words ending in *-sus*, if they have *o* in the penultimate syllable, lengthen it: *curiosus* (“curious”); *herbosus* (“grassy”); *spumosus* (“foamy”); *saxosus* (“rocky”); *scelerosus* (“wicked”); *odiosus* (“hateful”).

Verbal words ending in *-tus*, if they have *i* before *-tus*, shorten it: *sonitus* (“sound”); *habitus* (“condition or habit”). In denominatives, if they derive from first-declension nouns, they have a long penultimate *a*: *barbatus* (“bearded”); *stellatus* (“starred”); *trabeatus* (“wearing the *trabea*”); *purpuratus* (“clad in purple”).

If they derive from second- or third-declension nouns, some have long *a*, others long *i*: *pallium*, *palliatus* (“cloak, cloaked”); *annulum*, *annulatus* (“ring, ringed”); *gratus*, *avitus*, *maritus*, *cerritus*, from *grates* (“thanks”), *avo* (“from grandfather”), *mare* (“sea”), and *cerere* (“from Ceres”).

Forms derived from fourth-declension nouns have long *u* before *-tus*: *cornutus* (“horned”); *verutus* (“armed with a spit”); *astutus* (“cunning”); *versutus* (“crafty”). *Manuleatus* (“handed” or “with a hand-shaped form”), from *manus* (“hand”), is excepted and has a long penultimate *a*. [Col. 0634D]

All words ending in *-stus*, *-xus*, *-ptus*, or *-ctus* lengthen their penultimate syllable by position: *honestus* (“honest”); *moestus* (“sad”); *robustus* (“strong”); *laxus* (“loose”); *flexus* (“bent”); *fluxus* (“flowing”); *acceptus* (“accepted”); *aptus* (“fitted”); *sanctus* (“holy”); *amictus* (“clothed”).

## On the singular nominative

The nature of the singular nominative is recognized most clearly by the following rule for each ending.

Nouns ending in *-a* with a short vowel are Greek or Latin, masculine, feminine, or neuter: *hic poeta* (“this poet”); *scriba* (“scribe”); *haec musa* (“this Muse”); *Roma* (“Rome”); *hoc toreuma* (“this embossed work”); *emblema* (“emblem”); *hic et haec auriga* (“male or female charioteer”). [Col. 0635A]

Latin neuters ending in short *-e* include *hoc monile* (“this necklace”) and *mare* (“sea”).

Greek feminine nouns ending in long *-e* include *haec Euterpe* (“Euterpe”); *Libye* (“Libya”); *schole* (“school”); *Andromache* (“Andromache”).

Latin or Greek neuters, or indeclinables of every gender, ending in long *-i* include *hoc gummi* (“gum”); *sinapi* (“mustard”); *hic et haec et hoc frugi* (“thrifty,” of any gender); *nihili* (“worthless”); *mancipi* (“of a slave or chattel”); *hujusmodi*, *illiusmodi*, *ejusmodi*, *istiusmodi* (“of this kind,” “of that kind,” “of that sort,” “of this sort”); and *cordi* (“dear”), *nauci* (“worthless”). *Nauci* also means “the shell of a nut” and is used for “nothing.”

Latin or hybrid masculine, feminine, or common nouns ending in short *-o*—although poets frequently lengthen it—include *hic Cicero* (“Cicero”); *leo* (“lion”); *haec virgo* (“virgin”); *Carthago* (“Carthage”); *hic et haec homo* (“man or human being”); *nemo*, *neminis* (“no one”), compounded from *non* (“not”) and *homo* (“person”). [Col. 0635B]

Those retaining *o* in their oblique cases retain it lengthened: *Cicero*, *Ciceronis* (“Cicero, of Cicero”). Those changing it into *i* pronounce the penultimate syllable short: *virgo*, *virginis* (“virgin, of a virgin”).

Greek feminine nouns ending in long *-o* include *Manto*, *Dido*, *Sapho*, and *Erato*. They are either declined in Greek fashion, as *Manto*, *Mantus*, where *Mantus* is the genitive, or they form the genitive according to Latin usage by adding *-nis*, while retaining the long *o*, as *Dido*, *Didonis* (“Dido, of Dido”).

Virgil writes in Book X:

> The son of prophetic Manto and of the Tuscan river.

Latin neuters ending in *-u* include *cornu* (“horn”); *gelu* (“frost”); *genu* (“knee”). Although some writers on the grammatical arts think there is a difference in quantity in these forms—for they say that the nominative, accusative, and vocative are short, while the remaining cases are long—these nouns are nevertheless found in actual usage with the same length in all their cases, and not without reason. For every ending in *-u*, wherever it occurs, is lengthened: *fluctu* (“wave”); *Panthu* (“Panthus”); *tu* (“you”); *diu* (“for a long time”). [Col. 0635C]

Ovid writes in Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*:

> And her left knee pressed against her right ham,  
> With fingers joined together in the fashion of a comb.

Here the accusative is unquestionably present, and it is lengthened. Virgil likewise writes in Book I:

> Bare at the knee, and her flowing folds gathered into a knot.

For just as he joined *sinus collecta* (“her gathered folds”)—an accusative—to the nominative, so also he joined *nuda genu* (“bare at the knee”).

There are two neuters ending in *-c*: *halec* (“salt fish”), which is long, as Martial writes:

> Capers and rotting turnips swimming in *halec*;

*halec* is a kind of fish. The other is *lac*, *lactis* (“milk”), whose declension is disputed.

There are two neuters ending in *-d* with a short vowel: *aliud* (“another thing”) and *quid* (“what”), as well as their compounds *aliquid* (“something”); *siquid* (“if anything”); *nequid* (“lest anything”).

Latin and barbarian masculine or neuter nouns ending in short *-al* include *hic Hannibal* (“Hannibal”); *hoc tribunal* (“tribunal”); *cervical* (“neck-pillow”). Neuters lengthen the *a* in their oblique cases. [Col. 0635D]

One masculine monosyllable ends in long *-al*: *hic sal*, *salis* (“salt”), which nevertheless shortens the vowel in the oblique cases.

Latin neuters ending in short *-el* include *hoc mel* (“honey”) and *fel* (“gall”).

Barbarian names ending in long *-el* include *hic Daniel*, *Michael*, and *Gabriel*.

Latin masculine or common nouns ending in short *-il* include *hic pugil* (“boxer”); *hic et haec vigil* (“watchman or watchwoman”); and *nihil* (“nothing”), an indeclinable compound of *non* (“not”) and *hilum* (“a trifle”), which is unquestionably a noun meaning “anything at all.” [Col. 0636A]

One Etruscan feminine name ends in long *-il*: *haec Tanaquil*, that is, “the wife of Tarquinius Priscus.”

The masculine Latin noun ending in *-ol* is *hic sol*, *solis* (“sun”), which is long.

Masculine or common Latin nouns ending in short *-ul* include *hic consul* (“consul”) and *hic et haec exsul* (“male or female exile”).

One indeclinable word of every gender ends in short *-am*: *hic et haec et hoc nequam* (“worthless,” “scoundrel,” or “good-for-nothing”).

Latin or Greek neuters ending in short *-um*—Greek forms ending in *-on*—include *hoc templum* (“temple”); *regnum* (“kingdom”); *lignum* (“wood”); *pelium* (“basin or vessel”); *hostorium* (“measuring rod”), the piece of wood by which a *modius* (“measure”) is leveled.

Comic poets use many women’s names having the form of neuters. For the sake of their meaning they regularly placed feminine articles before them: *haec Dorcium* (“this Dorcium”); *haec Glycerium* (“this Glycerium”); *haec Sophronium* (“this Sophronium”). The neuter article, however, is customarily used either as a term of flattery or to indicate youthfulness.

Greek masculine or feminine nouns ending in *-on*, *-an*, or *-in* are all lengthened: *hic Titan* (“Titan”); *Pean* (“Paian”); *Pan* (“Pan”); *hic delphin* (“dolphin”); *haec trachin* (“Trachin”); *hic Memnon* (“Memnon”); *haec Sidon* (“Sidon”).

It must be understood that all words ending in *-in* also end in *-is* with a long vowel: *delphis* (“dolphin”); *trachis* (“Trachin”); *Eleusis* (“Eleusis”). [Col. 0636B]

Nouns ending in *-on* preserve the rule mentioned above in their Greek genitives: the penultimate syllable remains long or short according to Greek usage: *Memnon*, *Memnonos*; *Simon*, *Simonos*; *Lacoon*, *Lacoontos*; that is, *Memnon*, *Memnonis*; *Simon*, *Simonis*, with the penultimate syllable shortened; *Lacoon*, *Lacoontis*, with the penultimate syllable lengthened; and *canon*, *canonis* (“rule, of a rule”).

Latin masculine or neuter nouns ending in short *-en* include *hic flamen* (“priest”); *cornicen* (“horn-player”); *fidicen* (“lyre-player”); *tubicen* (“trumpeter”); *tibicen* (“flute-player”); *hoc numen* (“divine power”); *carmen* (“song”).

Latin masculine nouns ending in long *-en* include *hic lien* (“spleen”); *rien* or *ren*, *renis* (“kidney”); *splen* (“spleen”). Greek forms include *hic Damen*, the proper name of a historian; *Seben*, the name of the hero who was a companion of Ulysses and lived at Temesa; and the feminine forms *haec siren* (“siren”) and *Trizen* (“Troezen”). [Col. 0636C]

Latin, Greek, and barbarian masculine or neuter nouns ending in short *-ar* include *hic Caesar* (“Caesar”); *Bostar*; *hoc nectar* (“nectar”); *calcar* (“spur”). But neuters, if derivative, lengthen their *a* in the oblique cases: from *lupa* (“she-wolf”), *lupanar*, *lupanaris* (“brothel, of a brothel”); from *lacus* (“lake”), *lacunar*, *lacunaris* (“ceiling-panel or hollow, of a ceiling-panel”); from *laqueus* (“coffered ceiling”), *laquear*, *laquearis* (“ceiling-panel, of a ceiling-panel”); from *calx* (“heel”), *calcar*, *calcaris* (“spur, of a spur”).

Latin masculine, neuter, or common nouns ending in long *-ar* are either monosyllables or compounds of monosyllables: *hic Nar*, *Naris* (“Nar,” the name of a river), which retains the long *a* in its oblique cases; *hoc torcular* (“press”); *pulvinar* (“cushion”); *hic far*, *farris* (“grain”), lengthened by position in the oblique cases; *hic et haec et hoc par* (“equal”), *dispar* (“unequal”), and *impar* (“uneven”), which shorten their *a* in the oblique cases. [Col. 0636D]

Virgil writes in the *Bucolics*:

> The god delights in an uneven number.

Lucan writes in Book VIII:

> Therefore, with equal purpose and upon equal altars, he rose.

Likewise, *lar*, *laris* (“household spirit, of a household spirit”).

Plautus writes:

> I am the household Lar.

Virgil writes:

> And the Trojan household Lar, and the inner shrine of gray Vesta.

It must be noted that if we wish *nar* to signify “nose,” it is better to pronounce the nominative like the genitive: *haec naris*, *hujus naris* (“this nose, of this nose”), as Ovid writes in Book VI of the *Metamorphoses*:

> Their hair flowed down, together with their noses and ears.

Lucan, in Book XI, uses the genitive:

> One cuts off the ears of one man, another the breathing passages  
> Of a hooked nose.

Among feminine, masculine, neuter, and common Greek or Latin nouns ending in short *-er* are *hic puer* (“boy”); *pater* (“father”); *Alexander*; *Menander*; *haec mater* (“mother”); *hoc tuber* (“swelling”); *hic et haec pauper* (“poor man or woman”). [Col. 0637A]

Greek masculine nouns ending in long *-er*, and one Latin—or rather non-Latin—neuter noun, include *hic Hiber*, *Hiberi*, meaning “Spanish,” and its compound *Celtiber*. When speaking of the people who live near the Armenians, however, we say *Hiber*, *Hiberis*. Also: *hic aer*, *aeris* (“air”); *hoc ver*, *veris* (“spring”).

Virgil shortens *aether* (“ether, sky”) in Book VIII:

> For suddenly a flash, hurled from the ether,  
> Came with a crash, and all the vessels suddenly fell.
although some other grammarians say that this is long. Masculine nouns ending in short **-ir** include *vir*, *levir*, and compounds of *vir*, such as *duumvir*, *triumvir*, and so forth; also one masculine ethnic name, *Trevir*; and one feminine noun, *Gaddir, Gaddiris*, that is, Tarcessus, a city of Spain, which the Tyrians now call *Gaddir*, having changed its name. There is also one indeclinable neuter noun, *ir*, which the Greeks call θήναρ (*thēnar*). Some add *abaddir*, ὁ βετηλός (*ho betēlos*), genitive *abaddiris*: this is the name of the stone which Saturn swallowed instead of Jupiter, and which they imagined to be a god.

Masculine, feminine, neuter, and common nouns, both Greek and Latin, are found ending in short **-or**, for example *Nestor*, *orator*, *uxor*, *aequor*, and *auctor* in all three genders. It must also be noted that in this ending, when Latin masculine, feminine, or common nouns are involved, the *o* is long in the oblique cases: *doctor*, *salinator*; *uxor*, *soror*; *auctor* in both genders; *pallor*, *pudor*, *macor* or *marcor*, meaning emaciation—genitives *doctoris, uxoris, auctoris, marcoris*.

Those, however, that change *o* into *i* in the penultimate syllable have a short vowel: *ordo, ordinis*, except for *memor* and *immemor* in all three genders, genitives *memoris, immemoris*. These derive from the verb *memoro* and retain the penultimate syllable of that verb. So too *indecor, indecoris*, in both genders.

Virgil, Book XI:

> Yet your queen does not leave you dishonored.

Its simple form, *decor, decoris*, is also short among the ancients when it is used for *decorus, decora, decorum*. Since these forms are derived or compounded from *decus, decoris*, they retain the declension of that word. Likewise, compounds from *corpus* retain its declension, such as *bicorpor, tricorpor, bicorporis, tricorporis*.

Virgil, Book VI:

> Dolphins and the harsh ones (or Harpies), and the shadowy forms of three-bodied beings—

The feminine noun *arbor, arboris* likewise has a short penultimate syllable in the genitive, since it is derived from *robur* and preserves that word’s declension. Compounds of *puer* also have a short vowel: *Puplipor, Marcipor, Pupliporis, Marciporis*. According to Probus, the ancients said these for *Puplii puer* and *Marci puer*—“Publius’s boy” and “Marcus’s boy.”

Neuter nouns and all Greek nouns likewise have a short *o* in the oblique cases: *marmor, marmoris*; *aequor, aequoris*; *Hector, Hectoris*; and *actor, actoris*, when *Actor* is a Greek proper name.

Virgil:

> He shakes the spoil of the Auruncan Actor, trembling.

To summarize briefly the rule stated above: among neuter and Greek nouns ending in **-or**, as well as those derived or compounded from primitive forms with a short penultimate syllable, the penultimate syllable remains short in the oblique cases. The others lengthen it, except *cor*, which assumes a *d* and lengthens itself by position in the genitive, and *aaor* [reading uncertain], whose derivative Virgil lengthens in Book VII:

> And they place honey-cakes and sacrificial offerings  
> upon the grass for the feast.

Latin masculine, common, and neuter nouns end in short **-ur**, such as *satur*, *turtur*, *augur* in both genders, and *tibur*. Also included are those that have short *u* instead of *o* throughout the oblique cases: *robur, roboris*; *ebur, eboris*; *femur, femoris*; and *jecur, jecoris*, or *jecinoris*. The genitive appears to derive from the nominative *jecinus*, which is no longer in use.

Only one common noun of both genders is found with long **-ur**: *fur*, genitive *furis*.

Greek masculine, feminine, neuter, and common nouns occur with short **-as**: *Arcas*, a proper name, genitive *Arcadis*; *Pallas, Palladis*; *Ceras*, a place-name, genitive *Ceradis*; and *arcas*, an ethnic name, in both genders, genitive *arcadis*.

Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, neuter, and common nouns occur with long **-as**: *Aeneas*, *Maecenas*, *civitas*, *vas, vasis*; *vas, vadis*, which is short in the oblique cases; *mas, maris*; *fas* and *nefas*; and *nugas* in all three genders, an indeclinable form. Also: *Capenas, Capenatis*; *primas, primatis*; *optimas, optimatis*; *Arpinas*; *Crotonas*; *Pontias*; and *Larinas*. These have a circumflex accent on the final syllable because their full ancient forms were *Arpinatis* and *primatis* in both genders.

Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns of two or three genders ending in short **-es** are understood to be short in two ways. First, when the short *e* changes into *i* in the genitive, as in *miles, militis*; *trames, tramitis*; *sospes, sospitis* in both genders; *pedes, peditis*; *eques, equitis*; and *superstes, superstitis* in both genders. Second, when the penultimate *e* remains short in the genitive, as in *seges, segetis*; *teges, tegetis*; and *praepes, praepetis* in all three genders.

The same applies to forms derived from verbs: from *tero, teris*, *teres, teretis* in all three genders; from *habeo, habes*, *hebes, hebetis*; from *indigeo*, *indiges, indigetis*; from *impeto*, *impes, impetis*; and from *interpretor*, *interpres, interpretis*.

Greek as well as Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with long **-es**: *Anchises*, *Ermogenes*, *Chremes*, and *Verres*. Latin forms with a long vowel occur in five ways:

1. when they belong to the fifth declension, such as *dies* in both genders, genitive *diei*;
2. when the genitive has the same number of syllables as the nominative, such as *proles, prolis*; *caedes, caedis*; and *strages*;
3. when a genitive that increases in syllable-count has a long *e* in the middle, such as *merces, mercedis* and *haeres, haeredis*;
4. when the nouns are monosyllabic or derived from monosyllables, such as *pes*, *semipes*, *bipes*, *quadrupes*, and *cornipes*;
5. when they have *i* before final *-es*, such as *aries*, *paries*, *abies*, and *quies*.

All these, however, except *quies, quietis*, and its compound *inquies, inquietis* in all three genders, are short in the oblique cases, just as *pes, pedis* and its compounds are.

Virgil:

> The hoofed horse stands and fiercely bites the foaming reins.

Juvenal, Book IV:

> The filthy digger, in his great chain, expresses disdain.

Virgil, Eclogue III:

> The ram himself is believed, and now dries his fleece.

The same poet, *Aeneid* II:

> The guards can bear it; [it] totters under the repeated battering-ram.

Virgil, Eclogue VII:

> The poplar belongs beside the rivers, the fir upon the high mountains.

The same poet, *Aeneid* II:

> They build and weave the cut firwood into the sides.

Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with short **-is**: *Paris, Paridis* or *Paris*; *collis, collis*; *Thetis, Thetidis*; *cuspis, cuspidis*; and *utilis* in both genders, genitive *utilis*.
