Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with long **-is**: *delphis, delphinis*; *Aris*, a proper name, genitive *Arinis*; *soteris, soterinis*; *Dis*, the proper name of Pluto, genitive *Ditis*; *dis* as a common noun in both genders, genitive *ditis*; *vis, vis*; *glis, gliris*; *Samnis, Samnitis*; and *lis, litis*.

Greek and Latin masculine, neuter, and common nouns occur with short **-os**: *Delos, Delei*. All Greek nouns ending in **-os** that have a diphthong in the genitive are short: *os, ossis*. The ancients also pronounced this as *ossum*. Likewise, *compos, compotis* in all three genders.

Seneca, *Phaedra*:

> with a fulfilled vow;

this is an Adonic verse.

Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, common, and neuter nouns occur with long **-os**: *heros, herois*; *nepos, nepotis*; *dos, dotis*; *cos, cotis*; *lepos, leporis*; *mos, moris*; *flos, floris*; *ros, roris*; *bos, bovis* in both genders, though the penultimate syllable is short in the genitive; *os, oris*; *custos, custodis* in both genders; *sacerdos, sacerdotis* in both genders; and *impos, impotis*.

Latin masculine, feminine, neuter, and common nouns of two or three genders occur with short **-us**: *lepus*; *pius*, *sanctus*, *justus*, *dignus*; *Venus*; *manus*; *tempus*, *nemus*, *munus*; *Ligur, Liguris* in both genders; and *vetus, veteris* in all three genders.

Greek masculine nouns occur with long **-us** when their Greek genitives end in **-dos** and the Latins change *dos* into *dis*: Οἰδίπους, τοῦ Οἰδίποδος—Latin *Oedipus, Oedipodis*; *Melampus, Melampodis*.

Latin nouns ending in the aforementioned long **-us** are without doubt feminine and belong to the third declension. They also retain a long *u* in the oblique cases: *servitus, servitutis*; *senectus, senectutis*; *juventus, juventutis*; *tellus, telluris*. No Latin masculine, neuter, or common noun ends in long **-us**, except one epicene noun borrowed from Greek, which changed Greek *y* into long Latin *u*: *mus, muris*—the Greeks write μῦς (*mys*). The following neuter nouns are exceptions: *rus, ruris*; *crus, cruris*; *jus, juris*; *plus, pluris*; and *thus, thuris*. The following are common: *grus* in both genders and *sus* in both genders. These two, however, are short in the oblique cases: *gruis* and *suis*.

Virgil, *Aeneid* X:

> The Thracian cranes give the signal …

Horace, *Satires* II:

> carrying torn-apart  
> limbs of a crane, scattered with much salt and not without grain.

*Palus, paludis* is also short, as in Virgil:

> and the barren marsh, long unproductive and suited to oars.

Greek masculine and feminine nouns occur in **-ys**: *amphibrachys, amphibrachys*; *Capys, Capyis*; *Erinys, Erinnyis*.

One masculine Latin noun ends in the diphthong **-aes**: *praes, praedis*. There is also *aes, aeris*; its plural oblique forms are rarely used, as in *aera, aerarum, aeribus*.

Two feminine Latin nouns end in the diphthong **-aus**: *laus, laudis* and *fraus, fraudis*.

Greek nouns ending in the diphthong **-eus** either change *us* into *i* in the genitive, as *Titheus, Tithei*, or change the diphthong *eus* into long *es* in Latin: Ἀχιλλεύς, *Achilles*; Περσεύς, *Perses*; Οὐλιξεύς, *Ulixes*. Ovidius gives the genitive in *-ei* in Book XIV of the *Metamorphoses*:

> Neritus, Macareus, companion of experienced Ulysses;

From this it is clear that the Latins also habitually pronounced these names both with **-eus** and with **-es**.

Nouns ending in **-ans**, **-ens**, **-ons**, or **-uns** are always long by position in the nominative because of their consonant clusters. Consequently, in the other cases they always have the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable long by position. All are Latin and masculine, feminine, or common: *dodrans*, *quadrans*; *glans, glandis*; *infans* in all three genders; *Ufens*; *mens*; *parens* in both genders; *prudens* and *sapiens* in all three genders; *mons*; *frons*; *insons* in all three genders; *sons, sontis*; and *Arruns*.

Similarly, nouns ending in **-ars**, **-ers**, **-ors**, **-urs**, or **-uls** are long by position. They are Latin masculine, feminine, or common nouns: *Mars*; *ars*; *iners, inertis* in all three genders; *Mavors*; *cohors*; *sors*; *concors* in all three genders; *Tiburs, Tiburtis* in all three genders, although it is also an ethnic name; and *puls, pultis*.

One feminine noun has short **-ems**: *hiems*.

Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> Pray for moist solstices and calm winters.

Greek and Latin masculine and feminine nouns occur with short **-abs**: *Arabs, Arabis* and *trabs, trabis*.

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> the eastern homes of the Arabs and the painted Gelonians.

Latin nouns of every gender occur with short **-ebs**: *caelebs, caelibis* in all three genders. One Latin feminine noun has long **-ebs**: *plebs*.

Latin feminine nouns occur with short **-obs**: *scobs, scobis* and *scrobs, scrobis*.

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> and surpassed the earth with filled-in trenches.

One masculine noun has short **-ybs**: *Chalybs, Chalybis*.

Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> But the naked Chalybes, and the Pontus rich in iron …

One feminine noun ends in **-urbs**, preserving its quantity by position in the oblique cases: *urbs, urbis*.

One feminine noun has short **-aps**: *daps, dapis*.

Masculine nouns and nouns of all genders occur with short **-eps**: *manceps, mancipis*; *particeps, participis* in all three genders; and *adeps* or *adipes, adipis*, which occurs in both genders. Varro, *On Agriculture* II, uses *adipes* in the feminine.

One Latin feminine noun has long **-ops**: *Ops, Opis*, that is, the Mother of the Gods.

Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

> and Ephyrē, and Ops, and Asia Deiopeia.

There is also one common noun with short **-ops**, *ops, opis* in all three genders, meaning “abundance.” From it is formed *inops, inopis*, in all three genders.

Greek masculine nouns are also found with this ending: *Pelops*, *Aethiops*, *hydrops*, *merops*, genitives *Pelopis, Aethiopis, hydropis, meropis*.

Lucan, Book VI:

> or tear away Ephyrē from the broad realms of Pelops.

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> What groves of the Ethiopians, white with soft wool …

The same poet, Book III:

> and the meropes and other birds from their rich stalls.

Greek nouns occur with long **-yps**, such as *Cinyps, Cinyphis*.

Virgil, *Georgics* III:

> Meanwhile the shaggy goats of Cinyphus shear  
> their white beards and hoary chins, and their flowing bristles.

One Latin noun, always long by position, ends in **-irps**: *stirps, stirpis* in both genders.

One neuter noun has short **-t**: *caput, capitis*.

Latin and Greek masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with short **-ax**: *Pheax, Pheacis*; *Ajax, Ajacis*; *pax, pacis*; and *audax, audacis*, *capax*, *pervicax*, *rapax*, *fallax*, *pellax*, *vorax*, *tenax*, *emax*, and *sagax* in all three genders.

Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with short **-ex**: *Lelex, Lelegis*; *grex, gregis*; *apex, apicis*; *ilex, ilicis*; and *artifex, artificis* in all three genders.

Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with long **-ex**: *rex, regis*; *lex, legis*; and *exlex, exlegis* in all three genders.

Latin masculine and feminine nouns occur with short **-ix**: *calix, calicis*; *fornix, fornicis*; *varix, varicis*; *pix, picis*; *nix, nivis*; and *salix, salicis*.

Greek and Latin masculine, feminine, and common nouns occur with long **-ix**: *phoenix, phoenicis*; *cornix, cornicis*; *nutrix, nutricis*; and *pernix, pernicis*, *felix, felicis* in all three genders.

It must be understood that the Greeks consider *i* and *y* before *x* short even when they are lengthened in the oblique cases, as in *phoenix, phoenicos* and *bombyx, bombycos*. They say, however, that *a*, according to the genitive, may be either long or short even in the nominative, as in κόλαξ, κόλακος (*kolax, kolakos*). The Latins, however, say that all vowels of two quantities—that is, δίχρονοι (*dichronoi*)—placed before *x* in the nominative are lengthened or shortened according to the genitive.

One feminine noun has short **-ox**: *nox, noctis*, and its common compound *pernox* in all three genders. Although these always have length by position, they are understood to have a naturally short vowel because *nox* is said to derive from the verb *noceo*.

Feminine nouns and nouns of all genders occur with long **-ox**: *vox, vocis*; *velox, velocis*; *ferox, ferocis*; and *atrox, atrocis* in all three genders.

Barbarian or Latin masculine and feminine nouns occur with short **-ux**: *volux, volucis*; *nux, nucis*; *crux, crucis*; *dux, ducis* in both genders; and *trux, trucis* in both genders.

The masculine noun *Pollux, Pollucis* and the feminine noun *lux, lucis* have long **-ux**.

Greek masculine and feminine nouns occur with short **-yx**: *sandyx, sandycis* and *Styx, stycis*.

Latin feminine nouns ending in **-aex**, **-aux**, **-alx**, or **-anx** are always long either by diphthong or by position: *faex, faecis*; *faux, faucis*; *falx, falcis*; and *lanx, lancis*.

One common noun ends in **-unx**: *conjunx* in both genders. It is nevertheless short in the oblique cases: *conjugis, conjugi*, and so forth.

One feminine noun ends in **-arx**, always long by position: *arx, arcis*.

I have said that some of these nominative endings are partly short and partly long, although they are always long by position, so that the nature of their quantity might become clear and could be seen in the oblique cases, where the quantity is not due to position.

## On the oblique cases

The singular genitive of the first, second, fourth, and fifth declensions is long in its final syllable: *hujus poetae, docti, fructus, speciei*. The genitive of the third declension is short: *hujus fortis*, except for one monosyllable, *vis, vis*.

The singular dative likewise always has a long final syllable: *huic poetae, docto, forti, fructui, speciei*. It must be noted that fifth-declension nouns whose penultimate syllable in the nominative contains *i*, such as *facies* and *dies*, retain a long *e* in the genitive and dative: *hujus* or *huic diei*, *hujus* or *huic faciei*. But if they have a consonant before *-es*, although they divide the *e* in the same way, they nevertheless shorten the penultimate syllable in both the genitive and dative: *fides, fidei*; *spes, spei*; *plebes, plebei*; *res, rei*.

The accusative is therefore always short: *hunc poetam, doctum, fortem, fructum, speciem*.

The singular vocative is everywhere like its nominative, except when, in the second declension, *-us* changes into short *-e*: *doctus, docte*. The same occurs with proper names of that declension that have *i* before *-us*: when *-us* is removed from the nominative, the vocative has a long final syllable—*Virgilius, o Virgili*; *Sallustius, o Sallusti*. There is also one common noun that makes its vocative both with short *e* and with long *i*: *filius, o filie* or *o fili*.

It must also be noted that these proper names whose vocative ends in *i*, although they have a short penultimate syllable, retain the accent on that syllable. The reason is that their original, fully formed vocatives ended in *e*, such as *Virgilie* and *Mercurie*. The acute accent, which the ancients placed on the antepenultimate syllable, was transferred by later speakers—who favored the short form—to the penultimate syllable through the loss of the final letter.

Horace, Book I of the *Odes*:

> Mercury, eloquent grandson of Atlas.

The same poet, in the same book:

> That man, mourned by many good people, died;  
> by none more mourned than by you, Virgil.

The singular ablative is always long: *ab hoc poeta, docto, fructu, specie*, except in the third declension, specifically in nouns whose ablative ends in *e*. All these are short: *ab hoc patre*, *ab hoc matre*, except one, which is long: *ab hac fame*.

Virgil, Book VI:

> He throws before him a morsel; that one, opening his three throats  
> in ravenous hunger …

Lucan, Book X:

> At the command of hunger, many birds and wild beasts  
> made the gods of Egypt …

This lengthening occurs because the ancients declined this noun more according to the fifth than the third declension: *hujus* and *huic famei*, not *hujus famis* or *huic fami*.

Furthermore, whenever the third declension sends its ablative in *i*, that ablative is always long.

Juvenal, Book V:

> Besides, the pain of the side, together with watchful fever.

Virgil:

> Standing high upon the stern …

Statius, *Thebaid* I:

> And ancient Lerna pours forth and foams with poison.

The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative in the masculine, feminine, and common genders are always long: *hi* and *o poetae*, *hos poetas*; *hi* and *o magistri*, *hos magistros*; *hi*, *hos*, and *o sapientes*; *hi*, *hos*, and *o magistratus*; *hae*, *has*, and *o res*. In the neuter they are short: *haec* and *o mandata*; *haec* and *o capita*; *haec* and *o dogmata*; *haec* and *o cornua*.

Moreover, the two dual-number nouns *ambo* and *duo*, when masculine, are long, as Virgil says in Eclogue VII:

> Both flourishing in age, both Arcadians;

when neuter, they are short.

The plural genitive always ends in short *-um*. To determine its penultimate syllable, the following principle is clear: one should identify the singular case from which it derives. Since the plural genitive of the first, second, and fifth declensions arises from the long singular ablative of those declensions, it preserves the same length in its penultimate syllable: *ab hoc poeta, horum poetarum*; *magistro, magistrorum*; *die, dierum*. When the plural genitive descends from the short ablative of the third declension, if it has *i* as its penultimate syllable, that *i* is always short.

In the fourth declension, however, this same case is formed not from the long ablative, as some believe, but from the singular nominative: *s* is removed and *-um* added. Both *u*s are therefore short.

Virgil:

> Receive these as well, that they may be memorials of my hands  
> for you, boy …

Juvenal, Book I:

> the inward parts of great houses and of the future master.

The plural dative and ablative are long when they end in *-is*: *his* and *ab his poetis, magistris*. When they end in *-bus*, they are shortened: *his* and *ab his patribus, fluctibus, rebus*. It must also be noted that when *i* or *u* precedes *-bus* in these cases, the penultimate syllable is short.

Virgil, Eclogue:

> The daughters of Proetus filled the fields with false lowing.

And again:

> O unhappy maiden, now you wander in the mountains.

Ovid, *Fasti* III:

> Fresh must is the nearest reward from your pools.

But when *a* or *o* precedes *-bus*, the syllable is long: *his* and *ab his natabus, filiabus, deabus, equabus, mulabus, libertabus, asinabus*; and *his* or *ab his ambobus, duobus*.

The fifth declension always has a long penultimate *e* in these cases: *his* and *ab his diebus, faciebus*.

Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> For even on festival days the laws and religious ordinances  
> permit certain tasks to be performed.

In Greek nouns declined according to Greek forms, the singular genitive is short when it ends in *-dos* or *-ros*: *archados, poematos*. The dative is short when it ends in *-i*, as *Palladi*. The accusative is short when it ends in *-a* or *-on*, as *Thesea, Delon*.

Virgil, *Georgics* III:

> Pelion, fleeing, filled the air with a sharp neighing.

The vocative is otherwise long when it ends in *-a*: in masculine nouns it is long, as *Aenea*; in feminine nouns it is short, as *cathedra*. A vocative ending in *-e* is long: *schole, synagoge, pentecoste, parasceve, Tydide*, except those whose nominative ends in *-os*, such as *petros, petre* and *Phoebos, Phoebe*. A vocative ending in *-i* is short: *Nai, Alexi*.

Virgil, Eclogue IX:

> Where are you going, Moeris? Do your feet lead you into the city,  
> or does the road?

A vocative ending in *-o* is long: *Dido, Sappho*.

The plural nominative and vocative are short when they end in *-a* or *-s*: *poemata, rhetores*.

Rufinus, *On Metrical Feet*:

> The rhetors usually tell you about deeds in a spondee.

They are otherwise long, as *ecclesiaste*. The genitive is long: *philenon, laon, cedron*. A dative ending in *-i* is short, as *arcasin*; otherwise it is long, as *lays*. An accusative ending in *-as*, when it derives from a singular genitive ending in *-os*, is short: *arcados, arcadas*.

Lucretius:

> Holding flaming torches in their right hands;

Otherwise it is lengthened, as *ecclesias*.

## On the pronoun

A pronoun ending in *o*, *e*, *is*, *er*, or *us* in the singular nominative is short: *ego, ille, ipse, iste, is, meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester*. A pronoun ending in *u* is long, namely *tu*, and is pronounced with a circumflex accent.

A pronoun ending in the letter *e* is regarded by poets as common in quantity: it is shortened or lengthened in verse. The reason is that most authors added the syllable *-ce* to it in all its cases: *hicce, huncce, hocce, hisce, hosce, hasce*. When the vowel following it was removed by apocope, the two remaining letters *-ce* were accustomed to make the preceding syllable long.

Virgil, *Aeneid* XI:

> This was what you were doing, gracious mother, when through weapons and fires  
> you rescue me …

The carelessness of scribes omitted one *c*, although the oldest Roman books still testify that they consistently wrote two *c*s in this pronoun.

There are also two common-gender pronouns, *nostras* and *vestras*, with long final syllables. Their complete forms were *nostratis* and *vestratis*. Since the syllable *-ti-* was syncopated, the accent of the complete form remained on *a*, and the final syllable became circumflexed. Thus their neuter ends in *e*: *nostrate, vestrate*. This shows that their nominatives were also pronounced by the most ancient speakers as forms in *-tis*, according to analogy.

There are nine mobile nouns which, because they follow the declension of pronouns, some have placed among the pronouns. All are short in the singular nominative in every gender, except one, which has a diphthong in the feminine: *quae* and *qui*, when used for the indefinite or interrogative *quis*. *Quis* and *quid* are short.

The nine are:

* *unus, una, unum*;
* *solus, sola, solum*;
* *totus, tota, totum*;
* *alius, alia, aliud*;
* *ullus, ulla, ullum*;
* *nullus, nulla, nullum*;
* *alter, altera, alterum*;
* *uter, utra, utrum*;
* and its compound, *neuter, neutra, neutrum*.

Likewise, the feminine forms of all pronouns ending in *-a* in the nominative, and the neuter forms ending in *-um* or *-ud*, are short: *illa, ipsa, ista*; *illud, istud, ipsum*.

The singular genitive of pronouns ending in *-i* or *-ae* is long: *mei, tui, sui*; *meae, tuae, suae*. Otherwise it is short: *illius, nostratis*. It must be noted that a genitive ending in *-ius*, whether in pronouns or nouns, always has a naturally long penultimate *i*, although poets frequently shorten it by the license granted to them. The sole exception is *alterius*, which, because it exceeds its nominative by only two syllables, always shortens the penultimate *i*. *Alius*, on the other hand, always lengthens its penultimate *i* in every case.

The singular dative is always long: *nostro, illi, illae*, except *mihi, tibi, sibi*, which may be used with either quantity.

Priscian testifies, and many poets confirm by their meters, that *cui*, *huic*, and *ei* are monosyllables.

Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

> To each place we assigned its laws; she rejected  
> our marriage …

The same poet, *Georgics* I:

> From its root the pole extends to eight feet;

This is maintained everywhere. Nevertheless, these forms are occasionally made disyllabic by diaeresis, especially *ei*, to prevent it from being taken as an interjection. When they are divided, they shorten the penultimate syllable.

Juvenal shows that *ei* and *eis* are divided by diaeresis in Book V:

> He fills even the adulterers and gives them to those same catamites.

Statius divides *huic* into two syllables:

> A false one to assume wings and horns for this grim creature.

In the same work:

> You may see the descendants gladly granting laws to this gift.

Terentianus shortens both syllables of *cui* in *On Letters*:

> Yet the proximity of places causes each thing to arise;

The same poet, in the same work:

> In order, shining, to whom Synope gives its name,

This is a sotadean verse composed of two major ionics and three trochees. It scans as follows: *verum ut cui*, an ionic; *quae est proximi*, an ionic; *tas lo*, a trochee; *cis o*, a trochee; *riri*, a trochee; [spondee]. Likewise: *ex ordine*, ionic; *fulgens cui*, ionic; *dat no*, trochee; *men Sy*, trochee; *nopes*, trochee.

The singular accusative is always short: *illum, illa, illud*, except when it ends in *e* and is lengthened by position, as *hunc* and *hanc*, or when it ends in long *e*, as *me, te, se*.

The vocative follows the rule of its nominative: *tu, o tu*. Although the vocative of pronouns or nouns ending in *-us* ends in *-e*, it retains the same short quantity.

It must be noted that *meus*, which according to the rule ought to form the vocative *o mee*, changes its two short *e*s into one long *i* for the sake of euphony.

Terence, *Adelphoe*:

> O my Aeschinus, O my brother;

Nor should one therefore think that *o* is a pronoun merely because in the vocative it serves in place of an article before a noun or pronoun. It is without doubt an adverb of calling and wishing. It is also an interjection expressing grief. There is no difference between this vocative *o* and *heus*: just as we say *heus juvenes*, “hey, young men,” so we say *o juvenes*, “O young men.”

The singular ablative is always long: *a me, ab illo*, except for the two forms that follow the third declension: *ab hoc*, *ab hac*, or *ab hoc nostrate, vestrate*.

The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative are short only when they end in *-a*: *illa, nostra*. The plural genitive is always short: *nostrorum, vestrorum, illorum, nostrorum*, unless it ends in *-i*, as *nostri*. The dative and ablative are long when they end in *-is*: *meis, tuis, illis, vobis*; when they end in *-bus*, they are short: *quibus, nostratibus, vestratibus*. These forms also shorten the penultimate syllable.

Virgil, Eclogue VI:

> by what course he sought the deserted places, and to whom before.

## On verbs

Since the accidents of verbs are numerous and the rules concerning verbs are varied, I now intend to write for you in this place, Lucius, sweetest of boys, those matters that pertain to the usefulness of the art of meter, as they have been handed down to us by our teachers, or as far as I myself have been able to investigate them according to the limited measure of my small ability. I shall carefully set them down in flowing prose—not only the rules concerning final syllables, but also those concerning penultimate and antepenultimate syllables, knowledge of which is no less necessary for poets than knowledge of nouns, insofar as the brevity of this little work permits.

Therefore, if you are indeed quick-witted, you will be able to infer everything else more easily, provided that you now strive to grasp these matters attentively.

In all verbs, the following endings are shortened:

* *o*, as in *amo, doceo, pono, nutrio, amabo, docebo*—although authority varies;
* *m*, as in *amabam, docueram, ponam*;
* *r*, as in *amor, docebar, ponerer, nutriar*;
* *t*, as in *amat, docebat, posuerat, nutriret*;
* *us*, as in *amamus, docemus*;
* *re*, as in *amare*;
* *te*, as in *docete*;
* *tis*, as in *ponitis*;
* *stis*, as in *amavistis*;
* *ris*, as in *doceris, ponebaris*;
* *se*, as in *nutrivisse*.

The following are long:

* *a*, as in *ama*;
* *e*, when it occurs in the imperative of the second conjugation, as *doce*;
* *i*, as in *nutri, amavi, amavisti, doceri*;
* *u*, as in *amatu*;
* *c*, as in *fac, dic*;
* *as*, as in *umas, docebas, posueras*;
* *es*, as in *doces, amares, posuisses*.

But *t*, when in the third-person plural it is preceded by *l*, *n*, *s*, or *r*, makes the syllable long by position: *amant, docebant, ponerent, nutrierint*. The same applies to *vult, fert, est*.

Finally, knowledge of penultimate and antepenultimate syllables is chiefly acquired from the four conjugations, because all verbs that are declined according to analogy belong to four conjugations.

The first conjugation is that which, in the indicative mood, singular number, present tense, second person, active and neuter voice, ends in long *-as*: *amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant*.

According to the form it has in the present tense, the imperfect and pluperfect indicative of all conjugations are declined, as are the future optative and present subjunctive of the second, third, and fourth conjugations:

* *amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant*;
* *amabam, amabas, amabat, amabamus, amabatis, amabant*;
* *docebam, docebas, docebat, docebamus, docebatis, docebant*;
* *ponebam, ponebas, ponebat, ponebamus, ponebatis, ponebant*;
* *nutriebam, nutriebas, nutriebat, nutriebamus, nutriebatis, nutriebant*;
* *amaveram, amaveras, amaverat, amaveramus, amaveratis, amaverant*;
* *docueram, docueras, docuerat, docueramus, docueratis, docuerant*;
* *posueram, posueras, posuerat, posueramus, posueratis, posuerant*;
* *nutriveram, nutriveras, nutriverat, nutriveramus, nutriveratis, nutriverant*;
* *doceam, doceas, doceat, doceamus, doceatis, doceant*;
* *ponam, ponas, ponat, ponamus, ponatis, ponant*;
* *nutriam, nutrias, nutriat, nutriamus, nutriatis, nutriant*.

For this reason, all these forms lengthen the penultimate *a* in the first- and second-person plural.

In the passive voice, these same tenses likewise follow the declension of the present tense, except for the pluperfect:

* *amaris, amatur, amamur, amamini, amantur*;
* *amabar, ambaris, amabatur, amabamur, amabamini, amabantur*;
* *nutriebar, nutriebaris, nutriebatur, nutriebamur, nutriebamini, nutriebantur*;
* *docebar, docebaris, docebatur, docebamur, docebamini, docebantur*;
* *ponebar, ponebaris, ponebatur, ponebamur, ponebamini, ponebantur*;
* *docear, docearis, doceatur, doceamur, doceamini, doceantur*;
* *ponar, ponaris, ponatur, ponamur, ponamini, ponantur*;
* *nutriar, nutriaris, nutriatur, nutriamur, nutriamini, nutriantur*.

For this reason, these forms too have a long penultimate syllable in the second and third persons singular and in the first and third persons plural, while they lengthen the antepenultimate syllable in the second person plural.

The second conjugation is that which, in the indicative mood, singular number, present tense, second person, active and neuter voice, has a final long *-es*: *doces, docet, docemus, docetis, docent*.

This conjugation is followed in every conjugation by the present, imperfect, perfect, and pluperfect of the optative, by the imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive, and, in the first conjugation, by the future optative and present subjunctive:

* *doces, docet, docemus, docetis, docent*;
* *amarem, amares, amaret, amaremus, amaretis, amarent*;
* *docerem, doceres, doceret, doceremus, doceretis, docerent*;
* *nutrirem, nutrires, nutriret, nutriremus, nutriretis, nutrirent*;
* *amavissem, amavisses, amavisset, amavissemus, amavissetis, amavissent*;
* *docuissem, docuisses, docuisset, docuissemus, docuissetis, docuissent*;
* *posuissem, posuisses, posuisset, posuissemus, posuissetis, posuissent*;
* *nutrivissem, nutrivisses, nutrivisset, nutrivissemus, nutrivissetis, nutrivissent*;
* *amem, ames, amet, amemus, ametis, ament*.

These too, like the preceding forms, lengthen the penultimate *e* in the first- and second-person plural according to the pattern of the present tense.

In the passive voice, these same tenses imitate the present tense, except for the perfect and pluperfect:

* *doceris, docetur, docemur, docemini, docentur*;
* *amarer, amareris, amaretur, amaremur, amaremini, amarentur*;
* *docerer, docereris, doceretur, doceremur, doceremini, docerentur*;
* *ponerer, ponereris, poneretur, poneremur, poneremini, ponerentur*;
* *nutrirer, nutrireris, nutriretur, nutriremur, nutriremini, nutrirentur*;
* *amer, ameris, ametur, amemur, amemini, amentur*.

These forms have a long penultimate syllable in the second and third persons singular and in the first and third persons plural, and a long antepenultimate syllable in the second person plural.

The third conjugation is that which, in the second-person singular of the present indicative, in the active and neuter senses, shortens the final *is*. According to its likeness, the future indicative of the first and second conjugations is inflected, as is also that of the fourth conjugation in those verbs whose first-person present ends in *-eo*. Likewise the perfect subjunctive and the future perfect, as in:

*pono, ponis, ponit, ponimus, ponitis, ponunt*;  
*amabo, bis, bit, bimus, bitis, bunt*;  
*docebo, bis, bit, bimus, bitis, bunt*;  
*ibo, ibis, ibit, ibimus, ibitis, ibunt*;  
*quibo, bis, bit, bimus, bitis, bunt*;  
*amaverim, ris, rit, rimus, ritis, rint*;  
*docuerim, ris, rit, rimus, ritis, rint*;  
*posuerim, ris, rit, rimus, ritis, rint*;  
*nutriverim, ris, rit, rimus, ritis, rint*;  
*amavero, ris, rit, et rel.*;  
*docuero, ris, rit, et rel.*;  
*posuero, ris, rit, et rel.*;  
*nutriero, ris, rit, et rel.*

Therefore [the source reads *Id [Et] ideo*, “and therefore”] these forms are shortened in those places where, as we said above, the corresponding forms are lengthened. Likewise, in the passive, the future indicative of the first or second conjugation is inflected on the model of the present, as in:

*ponor, poneris, ponitur, ponimur, ponimini, ponuntur*;  
*amabor, amaberis, amabitur, amabimur, amabimini, amabuntur*;  
*docebor, doceberis, docebitur, docebimur, docebimini, docebuntur*.

All these are shortened in the same way, whether the short *i* remains unchanged or changes into a shortened *e*.

The fourth conjugation, however, in the second-person singular of the present indicative, active and neuter, has a lengthened *i* before *s*, and in the passive, common, and deponent forms before the final syllable, as in:

*nutrio, nutris, nutrit, nutrior, nutriris*.

It also differs from the third conjugation in this respect: it preserves everywhere as long the long *i* which it received from the second person in the present tense, as in the imperative:

*nutri, nutrīto, nutrīre, nutrītor*;

and in the infinitive:

*audire* or *audiri*,

and in all other similar forms. You must therefore remember that, just as the neuter verb follows the rule of the active verb in every conjugation, so the passive, common, and deponent forms do likewise; and by means of their syllables you can investigate their formation.

It should be noted, moreover, that first-conjugation verbs not only lengthen the *a* which they produce in the form of the present tense, according to the rule stated above, in the other tenses; they also always have long the *a* which they had received from the second-person singular of the present indicative, whether it falls in the penultimate, antepenultimate, or fourth syllable from the end:

[Col. 0649A]

in the following tenses and moods, whose forms are given below:

from the present: *donas, donamus, donatis*;  
imperfect: *donabam*;  
perfect: *donavi*;  
pluperfect: *donaveram*;  
future: *donabo*.

Present imperative: *dona, donate*;  
future imperative: *donato, donatote, donanto*;  
imperfect optative and subjunctive: *donarem*;  
pluperfect: *donassem*;  
perfect subjunctive: *donaverim*;  
future: *donavero*;  
present infinitive: *donare*;  
perfect infinitive: *donavisse*.

And in the passive present indicative:

*donaris, donatur, donamur, donamini, donantur*;

imperfect:

*donabar, donabaris*;

future:

*donabor, donaberis*;

present imperative:

*donare*;

future imperative:

*donator*;

imperfect optative:

*donarer, donareris, donaretur, donaremur, donaremini, donarentur*;

present infinitive:

[Col. 0649B]

*donari*.

So too with all the verbs of this conjugation, except the one monosyllabic verb *do, das*, which contrary to the rule shortens the penultimate syllable in most forms, as in the imperfect, future, infinitive, participle, and supine, unless it is lengthened by position and in the verbal noun:

*damus, datis, daris, datur, dabam, dabo, darem, dare, datus, daturus, datum, datu, dator*,

and the forms regularly made from these, such as *dabamini*. In all these forms *da* is short. Virgil says in Book I of the *Aeneid*:

> Scarcely out of sight of Sicilian land, into the deep,  
> joyfully they were giving their sails.

In the same work:

> May Bacchus, giver of joy, and kindly Juno be present.

In the same work:

> O you who have suffered heavier things, God will also bring an end to these.

The same author, in the same work:

> If Italy is granted to the allies, and the king received—

The same author, in Book VI:

> To whom I had been given as guardian, I clung, and guided his course.

The same author, in Book III:

> And father Anchises was ordering me to give my sails to the fates.

Persius:

> Why do we not give to the gods what, from a great dish,  
> the bleary-eyed offspring of great Messalla cannot give?

Virgil, in Book IV:

> Bring the flames quickly, give the weapons, drive the oars.

Lucan, in Book IV:

> But he will give the commanders the greatest moments of fate.

Second-conjugation verbs likewise always lengthen the *e* which they originally carried long from the second-person singular of the present indicative, wherever they have it in their moods or tenses:

from *docēs*: *docemus, docetis*;  
imperfect: *docebam, docebas, et rel.*;  
future: *docebo, docebis, et rel.*;  
present imperative: *doce, docete*;  
future imperative: *doceto, docetote, docento*;  
imperfect optative: *docerem, doceres, et rel.*;  
present infinitive: *docere*.

Likewise, in the passive present indicative:

*doceris, docetur, docemur, docemini, docentur*;

imperfect:

*docebar, docebaris, et rel.*;

future:

*docebor, doceberis, et rel.*;

present imperative:

*docere, docemini*;

future imperative:

*docetor, docentor, doceminor*;

imperfect optative or subjunctive:

*docerer, docereris, et rel.*;

present infinitive:

*doceri*.

Those forms which arise from a shortened *e* in the first-person indicative preserve it everywhere, as in *doceo*; present imperative, *doceat, doceant*; future optative or present subjunctive, *doceam, doceas, et rel.*; and in the passive, the same moods and tenses:

*doceatur, doceamur, doceantur*,

and:

*docear, docearis, et rel.*

It must also be understood that this conjugation does not alone shorten *e* before *o* in the first person of the indicative; in the other conjugations as well, other vowels are similarly shortened before *o*. In the first conjugation, *e* or *o*, as in *inchoo, meo, creo*; in the third, *i* or *u*, as in *facio, ruo, induo*. In the fourth conjugation likewise *i*, or *e*, is shortened, as in *eo* and *audio*. This does not occur only in these forms, for one will rarely find in Latin words a penultimate vowel before another vowel that is lengthened.

We said “rarely” because in the verb *fio* authors lengthen the penultimate syllable, as Virgil says in the *Bucolics*:

> Let everything—even the middle of the sea—become sea; live, forests.

The penultimate syllable of a genitive ending in *-ius* is also indeterminate [the preceding source reading, *Initio [Forte et in ius]*, is uncertain], as we mentioned earlier. In Greek words this is often found, as in *Menelaus, spondaeus, diacamilla*.

The third conjugation likewise ends the singular present indicative in a short *is*. It should be noted that all verbs of this conjugation, if they change a short *i* at the end or in the middle of the verb into *e*, shorten it everywhere, as in:

*legis, lege, legere, legerer*,

except when, in the middle of the verb, it is followed by one of three consonants—*b*, *m*, or *t*—as in:

*legebam, legebar, legemus, legemur, legetur*.

Otherwise they shorten *i* wherever it stands in the middle of the verb, as in:

*legimus, legitis, legite, legito, legitur, legimur, legimini, et rel.*

Those forms of the fourth conjugation which arise from the second person of the present indicative, as we said above, always have a long *i*, as in the indicative from *audis*:

*audimus, auditis*.

Imperative: *audi, audite, audito, auditote*;  
optative: *audirem, audires, et rel.*;  
infinitive: *audire*;  
passive present indicative: *audiris, auditur, audimur, audimini*;  
imperative: *audire, auditor*;  
optative or subjunctive: *audirer, audireris, et rel.*;  
infinitive: *audiri*.

Those forms which arise from the first person always have a short *i*, as in the third-person plural of the present indicative:

*audio, audiunt*;

and in the future of the same mood:

*audiam, audies, et rel.*;

present imperative:

*audiat, audiamus, audiatis, audiant*;

future:

*audiunto* or *audiuntote*;

imperfect optative or subjunctive:

*audiam, audias, et rel.*

And in the passive, in the same moods and tenses:

*audiuntur, audiar, audieris, et rel.; audiatur, audiamini, audiantur, audiuntur, audiar, audiaris, et rel.*

This is especially evident in those fourth-conjugation verbs whose first-person indicative ends in *-eo*: the forms that arise from the second person have a long *i*, as in:

*is, imus, itis, ibam, ibas, ivi, iveram, ibo, ite, et rel.*

Those arising from the first person are pronounced with a shortened *e*:

*eo, eunt, eam, eas, et rel.*

It should therefore be noted that the imperfect indicative of the third or fourth conjugation does not come from the second person, as in the first and second conjugations—*amabam, docebam*—but from the first person, with final *o* changed into long *e* and *-bam* added:

*faciebam, induebam, legebam*,

and:

[Col. 0651A]

*audiebam, serviebam, muniebam*.

The vowel, wherever it occurs before *e*, is nevertheless shortened. If in the fourth conjugation the *e* has been removed by syncope, the *i* is lengthened, as in:

*audibam, venibam, ibam*.

The perfect, therefore, in the inflection of the active verb, ends in long *i* in the first-person indicative; and at the same time it naturally has this lengthened vowel in the penultimate syllable of the second-person singular and plural, as in:

*amavisti, amavistis*.

In the third-person singular, as also in the first-person plural, it shortens it:

*amavit, amavimus*.

In the third-person plural it changes the same lengthened *i* in the penultimate syllable into long *e*:

*amaverunt* or *amavere*;  
*docuerunt* or *docuere*.

It should also be understood that the pluperfect indicative, the perfect subjunctive, and the future arise from the aforesaid tense by changing long *i* into short *e*, throughout all conjugations, in all persons and both numbers:

*amavi, amaveram, amaverim, amavero*.

Likewise, the pluperfect optative or subjunctive and the infinitive perfect derived from them arise from the same tense:

*utinam* or *cum amavissem, amavisse*;  
*docuissem, docuisse*.

These forms have a long *i* both by nature and by position.

It is therefore very useful to know what the penultimate syllables of the tense mentioned above—that is, of the first-person singular of the perfect indicative—are like before the final *i*, especially since all perfect and pluperfect forms of the other moods look to it as their source and preserve in these syllables the quality which they received from it unchanged.

In verbs ending in the syllable *-vi*, every penultimate syllable is long, either by nature or by position:

*amavi, lavi, vovi, movi, cupivi, munivi, audivi*.

But verbs of the third and fourth conjugations ending in *-ivi*, if the consonant *v* is dropped, shorten the penultimate *i*:

*cupivi, cupii; arcessivi; sivi, sii; munivi, munii; audivi, audii*.

Verbs of all conjugations are found ending in divided *-ui*: first conjugation, *tonui, secui*; second, *tenui, habui*; third, *annui, posui*; fourth, *aperui, prosilui*. Every penultimate syllable of this form—that is, of forms ending in divided *-ui*—is shortened.

In perfect forms ending in *-si*, the penultimate syllable is lengthened either by nature or by position. By nature:

*rideo, risi; suadeo, suasi; evado, evasi; haurio, hausi*.

By position:

*maneo, mansi; repo, repsi*.

Perfect forms ending in *-xi* always lengthen the penultimate syllable:

*frigeo, frixi; pelliceo, pellexi; pergo, perrexi; diligo, dilexi; sancio, sanxi; vincio, vinxi*.

The third-conjugation verb *bibo*, *bibi*, and its compounds, such as *ebibo*, shorten the penultimate syllable both in the present and in the perfect.

*Scindo* and *findo*, although long by position in the present, nevertheless shorten the penultimate *i* in the perfect:

*scidi, fidi*.

Likewise:

*contingo, contigi; attingo, attigi*.

Two first-conjugation monosyllables, *sto* and *do*, shorten their penultimate syllables in the perfect:

*steti, dedi*.

The same is true of their compounds:

*resto, restiti; reddo, reddidi*.

Some third-conjugation verbs repeat syllables at the beginning, others at the end. Those that repeat at the beginning, if they have a short penultimate syllable in the present, also shorten it in the perfect:

*cado, cecidi; cano, cecini; pario, peperi*.

But if the penultimate syllable is naturally long in the present, it is also lengthened in the perfect:

*caedo, cecidi; pedo, pepedi*.

If the penultimate syllable is long by position in the present, sometimes it is preserved in the perfect; when a consonant is removed, it is shortened. It is preserved in:

*posco, poposci; parco, peperci; fallo, fefelli; tendo, tetendi; pendo, pependi; curro, cucurri*.

When a consonant is removed, it is shortened in:

*disco, didici; pello, pepuli; tango, tetigi; pango, pepigi; pungo, pupugi; tundo, tutudi*.

Those verbs that repeat at the end always shorten the penultimate syllable:

*credo, credidi; vendo, vendidi; perdo, perdidi; prodo, prodidi; condo, condidi; addo, addidi; abdo, abdidi; abscondo, abscondidi*.

Three fourth-order verbs compounded from *pario*—*reperio, comperio, deperio*—shorten the penultimate syllable in the perfect:

*reperi, comperi, deperi*.

These and all forms that appear to be compounded from the same verb always have a short *pe* syllable, wherever it occurs:

*aperio, aperui; cooperio, cooperui; experior, operior*.

Lucan, in Book IV:

> We hand over the western peoples and open the eastern lands.

## On irregular verbs

Among irregular verbs we shall now briefly explain, as far as we can, the principles governing lengthening and shortening.

*Fero*, an irregular active verb, always has its first syllable short in every mood and tense, except when it is lengthened by position. In the second-person singular of the present indicative it undergoes syncope—that is, contraction:

*fero, fers*.

For this reason all forms arising from the second person preserve its contraction:

*fers, fert, fertis; fer, ferte, ferto, fertote, ferre*.

All these forms, except the one *fer* of the singular present imperative, are long by position.

In all other moods, tenses, and persons it follows the rule of the third conjugation, namely that forms taking their rule from the first person follow the regular inflection:

*fero, ferebam, feram*.

Its perfect, however, is irregularly formed—that is, *tuli*, which is properly the perfect of another verb, *tollo, tollis, tuli*. This perfect, and all forms arising from it, shorten the first syllable:

*tuli, tulisti; tuleram, tuleras; tulissem, tulisses; tulerim, tuleris; tulero, tuleris; tulisse*.

In the passive it is likewise shortened, except when lengthened by position; then it returns to the analogy and is inflected according to the rule of the conjugation mentioned above, except that in the perfect and forms arising from it it changes its letters. Thus the present indicative is:

*feror, fereris, fertur, ferimur, ferimini, feruntur*;

the imperfect:

*ferebar, ferebaris, et rel.*;

the perfect:

*latus sum, es, est, et rel.*

Everything else is inflected according to analogy. That this perfect must have its first syllables lengthened is shown by the past participle from which it is formed. Lucan, in Book IV:

> They pray, bearing the branch of Cecropian Minerva.

And in the same work:

> And after the citadels of burned Phocis had been transferred.

It should be noted, however, that *aufero, affero, infero, suffero, confero, profero, praefero, transfero, circumfero, antefero*, and all verbs that appear to be compounded from this verb, preserve its inflection in both voices.

The neuter verb *volo*, whether it changes its first syllables into *e* or preserves them with *o*, nevertheless always shortens them by nature:

*volo, volumus, volui, volueram, voluerim, voluero, et cetera*;

*velim, velis, velit, et rel.*

In these forms, however, *e* is lengthened by position:

*vellem, velles, et rel.*

The second-person singular of the present indicative is naturally lengthened:

*vis*.

In the future optative, or present subjunctive, the final syllable of the second-person singular and the penultimate syllable of the first- and second-person plural are likewise naturally lengthened:

*velis, velimus, velitis*.

In the other plural forms, whether the penultimate syllable is *u*, as in *volumus*, or *i*, as in *voluerimus*, they are always short. But where the form belongs to the first conjugation, as *volebam, volueram*, or to the second, as *vellem, velles, voluissem, voluisses*, they follow the rule of the conjugation whose form they possess.

Two other verbs are compounded from this verb: *nolo* and *malo*. *Nolo* is formed from *non* and *volo*, and therefore, like its simple verb, always lengthens the first part.

Martial, in the *Epigrams*:

> I do not wish to recite my epigrams to you,  
> you are quick not to listen, but you wish to recite.

And Albanus, in the *Monastica*:

> Do not believe everything that people say.

*Malo* is likewise compounded from *magis* and *volo*, but its *ma* is lengthened. Virgil, in Book III of the *Georgics*:

> And those whom they would rather keep for breeding-stock.

The irregular active verb *edo* alters its second person:

*es*,

with the *e* before *s* long. In all persons and tenses that ordinarily arise from this second person, one finds the conjugational rule altered, although the *e* received, lengthened, from the second person remains everywhere:

*es, est, este, esto, estote, essent, esse*.

In the plural of the present indicative, however, it follows the rule of the third conjugation, with *e* everywhere shortened:

*edimus, editis, edunt*.

Likewise in the imperfect and future:

*edebam, edam*.

And in all forms that ordinarily arise from the first person, namely in the third-person imperative:

*edat*,

and in the future optative, which is also the present subjunctive:

*edam, edas, edat, et rel.*

The first syllable is shortened, as Martial says of the dove:

> Doves delay and dull the loins of one whose groin is tormented;  
> let him who wishes to be lustful not eat this bird.

From this verb are derived *comedo, ambedo, abedo, circumedo*, which preserve its inflection in both voices.

It should nevertheless be understood that the ancients inflected this verb not in its shortened form but fully according to the third conjugation:

*edo, edis, edit*,

with the first syllable shortened, and so forth. Cato, in *To His Son on the Orator*:

> The hare brings much sleep, for the man who eats it.

And Virgil, in Book IV of the *Georgics*:

> Who would doubt it? For often the unknown *stillio*—a lizard—eats away the honeycombs.

And Martial:

> The barbarian himself never eats his own birds.

Here *e* is long everywhere.

The substantive verb *sum* is irregular throughout all moods, numbers, and persons; its first syllables are naturally short:

*sum, es, et sumus*;

imperfect:

*eram, eras, et rel.*;

perfect:

*fui, fuisti, fuit, fuimus, et rel.*;

pluperfect:

*fueram, fueras, et rel.*;

future:

*ero, eris, erit, et rel.*;

optative:

*fuissem, fuisses, et rel.*;

perfect subjunctive:

*fuerim*;

pluperfect:

*fuissem*;

future:

*fuero*.

There is only one exception: the future optative, or present subjunctive:

*sim, sis, sit, simus, sitis, sint*.

Here the second-person singular monosyllable is lengthened, as is the penultimate syllable in the first- and second-person plural.

Yet in this verb also certain persons are lengthened by position: the third-person plural of the present indicative, *sunt*; the second-person plural, *estis*; the second-person future imperative, *esto, estote*; the present optative, *essem, esses, esset, et rel.*; and the present infinitive, *esse*.

Likewise, compounds recognizable by their inflection as derived from it may be either lengthened or shortened:

*possum, assum, praesum, desum, absum, intersum, prosum, supersum*.

This can be demonstrated by many examples. Martial, in the *Epigrams*:

> You sing beautifully, and dance beautifully, Atticus, beautifully;  
> you are handsome through the art of the lyre, handsome through the art of the lyre.

The same author, in the same work:

> Surely you cannot stiffen while you are safe?

Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> Come here, Galatea; for what pleasure is there in the waves?

And the same author:

> Come here; let the mad waves strike the shores.

The same author, in the same work:

> Not everyone can do everything.

And the same author:

> These things will always be yours, even when the solemn gifts—

Likewise:

> Here, nevertheless, you will be able to rest with me tonight.

Likewise:

> Fortunate boy, you will now be another like him.

*Memini* and *odi* also have the force of both present and past in the indicative, with the final syllable lengthened. In the other tenses and moods they follow the third conjugation. For *novi*, the present is formed from *nosco*.

## On gerunds

Gerunds, participles, or supines are five in forms of this kind:

*amandi, amando, amandum, amatum, amatu*.

We have already discussed their final syllables; now we must discuss the penultimate syllables, since it is especially useful to know them, because the past and future participles arise from them:

*amatu, amatus* or *amaturus*,

as do verbal nouns:

*auditor, auditio*.

A certain rule of the other parts of speech seems to arise from this, a rule particularly useful for recognizing medial syllables and a very clear guide to the whole system. We shall explain it more fully below.

The first three supines always lengthen their penultimate syllables by position, although the vowel is naturally short or long, throughout all conjugations:

*amandi, amando, amandum*;  
*monendi, monendo, monendum*;  
*gemendi, gemendo, gemendum*;  
*nutriendi, nutriendo, nutriendum*.

The two that follow will now be explained.

All first-conjugation verbs whose perfect ends in *-vi*, changing *-vi* into *-tum*, form a supine with a lengthened penultimate syllable:

*amavi, amatum; donavi, donatum; oravi, oratum; flavi, flatum; juvi, jutum*,

and from the last:

*adjuvi, adjutum*.

Likewise, in the other conjugations, whatever verbs end in the aforesaid syllable in the perfect—that is, in *-vi* or *-ii*—lengthen the penultimate syllable in the supine:

*movi, motum; nevi, netum; favi, fautum; cupivi, cupitum; solvi, solutum; volui, volutum; calui, calutum; audivi* or *audii, auditum; munivi, munitum*.

The exceptions are:

*livi, litum; sivi, situm; ivi, itum; quivi, quitum; civi, citum; sevi, satum; cognovi, cognitum; agnovi, agnitum*,

and their compounds:

*obitum, aditum, praeteritum, nequitum*.

From *ambio* the supine or participle also lengthens the penultimate *i*. Ovid, in Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> He ordered the shores to be placed around the encircled land.

When it is a noun, however, the same syllable is shortened.

Perfect forms ending in divided *-ui* either lengthen the penultimate syllable by position in the supine:

*secui, sectum; mico, micui, mictum; docui, doctum; tenui, tentum; rapui, raptum; aperui, apertum*;

or have *u* as their penultimate syllable:

*acui, acutum; indui, indutum*.

All the rest are shortened:

*vetui, vetitum; crepui, crepitum; candui, canditum; studui, studitum; habui, habitum; monui, monitum; vomui, vomitum; gemui, gemitum; fremui, fremitum; tremui, tremitum*.

There is one with *u* as its penultimate syllable that is nevertheless short:

*rui, rutum*,

and its compounds:

*obrui, obrutum; dirui, dirutum; erui, erutum*.

Perfects ending in *-si* or *-xi* always lengthen the penultimate syllable of the supine, either by nature or by position:

*risi, risum; indulsi, indultum* or *indulsum*; *lusi, lusum; laesi, laesum; ussi, ustum; luxi, luctum; auxi, auctum; duxi, ductum; dixi, dictum; vinxi, vinctum; sanxi, sanctum; flexi, flexum; fluxi, fluxum*.

The supine of *steti* ought to be *statum*, with the penultimate syllable lengthened; hence Lucan, in Book XI:

> [lacuna] the faith of the gods will stand—

whereas *datum* and *datus*, as we showed above, shorten the penultimate *a*.

It should nevertheless be noted that nouns derived from this verb shorten the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable:

*status, stata, statum, stabilis*.

Lucan, in Book X:

> Whose fixed times the blasts—

The same author, in Book V:

> How, from no stable but trembling summit, she might look down upon everything.

The very ancient writers produced various compounds from it:

*asto, astitum* and *astatum*;  
*praesto, praestitum* and *praestatum*,

with *i* shortened and *a* lengthened.

It should be understood that in no other supine, participle, or participial noun is the penultimate syllable shortened, except in the two forms mentioned above, *datus* and *status*, and in one deponent verb of the second conjugation, *reor, ratus*, and one active verb of the third conjugation, *sero, sevi, satum, satus*.

It is difficult to find an *e* of the verb changed into *a* in a participle or supine except in the forms mentioned above. In compounds of the supines or participles mentioned above, it changes into shortened *i*:

*satus, insitus, obsitus*.

Virgil, in Book II of the *Georgics*:

> To transform it into another’s kind, and for grafted apple trees to bear altered pears.

Perfects ending in *-di* form the supine either in *-sum*, lengthening the penultimate syllable by position:

*fodi, fossum; prandi, pransum; pandi, pansum; defendi, defensum; momordi, morsum; sedi, sessum; scidi, scissum; fidi, fissum*,

or in *-itum*, with a short penultimate syllable—especially those verbs that repeat the final syllable in the perfect:

*reddidi, redditum; credidi, creditum; perdidi, perditum; condidi, conditum; vendidi, venditum*.

*Vidi* and its compounds *providi* and *invidi* naturally lengthen the penultimate syllable in the supine:

*visum, provisum, invisum*.

In *fudi, fusum*, the *u* is long.

Verbs ending in *-gi* in the perfect shorten the penultimate *i* in the supine:

*fugi*,

and its compounds:

*confugi, perfugi, refugi*,

which form:

*fugitum, confugitum, perfugitum, refugitum*.

Likewise *legi* forms *lectum*; *egi*, *actum*; *fregi*, *fractum*; and their compounds, such as *collegi, collectum*.

A perfect ending in *-bi* shortens the penultimate syllable in the supine:

*bibi, bibitum; ebibi, ebibitum*.

*Compesco*, *deposco*, *posco*, and *disco* form their supines from the present by changing *o* into shortened *i* and adding *-tum*:

*posco, poscitum; compesco, compescitum; deposco, deposcitum; disco, discitum*.

*Peperci*, or *parsi*, forms *parsum*.

*Feci* and *jeci* form *factum* and *jactum*; *ici* forms *ictum*. *Reperi*, *comperi*, and the other forms of the same origin lengthen the penultimate syllable by position in the supine:

*compertum, repertum, expertum, opertum*.

Some deponent and common verbs naturally lengthen the penultimate syllable in the supine; some naturally shorten it; some lengthen it by position alone; and some have it long both by nature and by position, although the position is straightforward. We shall explain those in which the syllable is lengthened or shortened by nature.

All deponent and common verbs that have *a* as the penultimate syllable in the supine lengthen it:

*irascor, iratum; criminor, criminatum*,

except the one mentioned above:

*reor, ratum*.

Those that have shortened *i* in the penultimate syllable belong to the second or third conjugation:

*vereor, veritum; intueor, intuitum; polliceor, pollicitum; adipiscor, adipiscitum*.

*Obliviscor* ought also to form *obliviscitum*, but through synaeresis it forms *oblitum*, with lengthened *i*.

Those that lengthen *i* belong to the fourth conjugation:

*mentior, mentitum; metior, metitum; largior, largitum*.

Verbs that are uncertain between the third and fourth conjugations sometimes have their penultimate syllable lengthened by authors and sometimes shortened, as *potior, orior, morior*.

Virgil, in Book III of the *Aeneid*:

> He breaks every law, cuts down Polydorus, and with gold  
> gains possession by force.

The same author, in Book II:

> [lacuna] We are overwhelmed by the weapons  
> of our people, and the most miserable slaughter arises.

Lucan, in Book IV:

> He does not die without cost, the man who challenges an enemy at the throat.

Naevius, in Book II of the *Iliad*:

> He penetrates deeply and gains possession of the chamber.

Lucilius, in Book III:

> Anyone who attacks can disturb the soul.

Ennius, in Book XIV of the *Annals*:

> Now is that day when the greatest glory  
> displays itself to us, whether we live or die.

Their supines are:

*ortum, potitum, moritum*,

with the penultimate *i* shortened according to the third conjugation or lengthened according to the fourth.

Therefore those that have *u* as their penultimate syllable in the supine lengthen it:

*loquor, locutum; sequor, secutum; utor, usum*,

and their compounds:

*alloquor, allocutum; consequor, consecutum; abutor, abusum*.

Those that form supines from irregular verbs either lengthen them by position, as:

*tero, tersum; volo, vultum*,

or by nature, as:

*edo, esus*,

and its compounds:

*comedo, comesus; ambedo, ambesus; adedo, adesus*.

Virgil, in Book XI:

> And clung to the doorposts that had been eaten away.

The same author, in Book III:

> May he compel them to consume the tables gnawed by their jaws.

Another supine of this verb is also found:

*esitus*,

with shortened *i*, derived from *edo, edis, edit*, in its complete conjugation.

It should be understood that a supine ending in *-um*, when combined with the infinitive *ire*, forms the future infinitive:

*oratum ire, doctum ire, lectum ire, auditum ire*.

Very often, however, the most ancient writers added *esse* to the neuter future participle and expressed the future infinitive in this way, saying:

*oraturum esse* instead of *oratum ire*, and *facturum esse* instead of *factum ire*.

## On adverbs

With regard to adverbs, it is necessary to examine their forms according to each ending, so that we may carefully explain which are primitive and which derivative; from this the rule of lengthening or shortening may become clearer.

Those ending in *-a* are either primitive, such as *ita*, which alone has a shortened *a*, although some also regard *puta* as an adverb and therefore say that Persius shortened it:

> “This, suppose, is not right; that is bad; that is more correct.”

Or they are compounds, such as:

*praeterea, interea, postea, antea*,

all of which lengthen the final *a*.

Or they are ablatives of nouns used as adverbs:

*una, qua, nequa, Roma*,

of which no one doubts that the *a* is long.

Those ending in shortened *e* are either primitive:

*pone, pene, prope, nempe, quippe, saepe, inde*,

or compounds derived from *inde*:

*deinde, subinde, exinde, proinde*.

All these have an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable, either because they contain the prefixed element *de*, as some think—hence we often find *exin* and *dein*—or because separated prepositions receive the grave accent; when they are joined, however, they take an acute accent to show that they are compounded. The same occurs with the conjunction *si* and the adverb *ne* when they precede *quando*:

*siquando, nequando*.

For the sake of distinction from *aliquanto*, which seems to have a similar sound, *aliquando* has an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable.

Or they are derivatives from verbs:

*peragro, peregre; punio, impune; abundo, abunde; rito*, from which come *irrito* and *rite*.

We also find nouns ending in shortened *e* used as adverbs:

*facile, forte, sublime*,

although *facile* and *sublime* are accusatives, while *forte* is an ablative.

Likewise, *sponte sua* and *mane primo* are shown to be nouns by their combination with other case forms, as in *domi suae*.

*Pote* arises from *potis*, namely *hic potis*, *haec potis*, and *hoc pote*. Hence Persius:

> “How can I? Do you want me to say it? You are trifling with yourself, baldhead.”

That is: “How is it possible?”

From *hic potis, haec potis, hoc pote* comes the comparative:

*hic potior, haec potior, hoc potius*,

and the superlative:

*potissimus*.

From these also come the adverbs *potius* and *potissime*, and from *pote* the compound adverb *utpote*.

No primitive forms ending in lengthened *e* are found. There are, however, derivatives from second-declension nouns whose dative ends in *-o* and is changed into long *e* to form an adverb:

*huic claro, clare; pigro, pigre; pulchro, pulchre; valido, valde*,

with syncope; *fabro, affabre; sano, sane; fero, fere*.

The exceptions are *bene* and *male*, from *bono* and *malo*, ending in shortened *e*. They have irregular comparatives:

*bene, melius, optime*.

Some lack forms in comparison:

*pie, piissime; ulterius, ultime, novissime*.

Many of the nouns mentioned above are used as adverbs in the very form of their dative:

*falso, consulto, postremo, sedulo, auspicato, augurato, manifesto, privato, precario, merito*.

They often shorten the final *o* when they pass into an adverbial meaning:

*cito, sero, modo*.

Juvenal, in Book III:

> And soon, having snatched away what remains  
> from the consumed nobility—

Virgil, in Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> Only ask the gods for pardon, when the sacrifices have been completed.

Statius, in Book I of the *Thebaid*:

> Late mindful of the marriage chamber, Phoebus,  
> you prepare mournful consolations for death.

Necessity is expressed by *necessario*, and *necesse* requires a substantive verb. Adverbs are also formed from nouns of the fifth declension, lengthening *e*: *pridie*, *hodie*, *postridie*; *meridie* too is used as an adverb, although it is a noun.

Adverbs ending in long *i* are also found, but few are primary, such as *heri*. Other nouns are generally used adverbially in the genitive, such as *domi*, *Taurominii*, *Lampsaci*, *Tyri*, *Ephesi*, *belli*; in the dative, such as *vesperi*, *sorti*; and also in the ablative, such as *qui*, used for *quomodo* (“how”) or *inde* (“from there”). Two are found with short *i*: *ubi* and *ibi*, and compounds formed from them, such as *sicubi* and *inibi*.

Among primary forms ending in *o* are *quando*, temporal in meaning, and its compounds *siquando*, *nequando*, and *aliquando*, which have an acute accent on the antepenultimate syllable, lest they be thought to consist of two divided parts, as stated above, or for the sake of distinction. Derived forms are *a facto*, *fatuito*; *ab omni*, *omnino*; *a fortuitus*, *fortuito*; *a cis*, *citro* and *citra*; *ab in*, *intro*, *intra*, and *infra*. There are also compounds, *praesto* and *perfecto*.

Other nouns, or pronouns, are used adverbially, as shown above: *falso*, *merito*, *solito*, *sedulo*, *cito*, *sero*, *vero*, *utro*, *utroque*, *aliquo*, *eo*, *illo*. When they are used as adverbs, however, they are sometimes found with a shortened *o*, because *o* is indifferent in verbs and adverbs.

Only a few denominatives ending in *u* are found, such as *diu*, and its compound *interdiu*; from *nox* comes *noctu*. *Astu*, however, is an indeclinable noun, like *cornu*. Nouns in the diphthong *ae*, genitive in form and used in place of adverbs, are *Romae*, *Cosae*, and *Capuae*.

Among primary forms ending in *c* are *sic* and *donec*, which the ancients also called *donicion*. Derived from pronouns are *illic*, *istic*, *huc*, *illuc*, *istuc*, *hinc*, *illinc*, *istinc*, *hac*, *istac*, and *illac*. All of these, whether by nature or by position, lengthen their final syllable, [Col. 0659B] except *donec*, and are circumflexed at the end if they have a naturally long vowel. Compounds are also found: *adhuc*, *abhinc*, and *dehinc*.

Few forms ending in short *l* are found, such as *semel*, *pol*, and *aedepol*, as well as the conjunction *vel* when it is understood as “very.” For all adverbs ending in *m* are short, whatever vowel precedes them: *utinam*; primary forms include *clam* and *coram*; derived or compound forms include *nequicquam* and *nequaquam*, with the penultimate syllable lengthened. Moreover, *quam*, when it expresses likeness, comparison, or choice, is used adverbially. Virgil, in Book XII:

> How easily the sacred bird is taken from the high rock.

Sallustius: “The Pontic Sea is sweeter than the other seas.”

Likewise *bifariam*, *trifariam*, and *omnifariam* are compounds formed from *fero* and prefixed words.

Primary forms ending in *em* are *item* and *tandem*; compounds include *idem*, *ibidem*, *indidem*, and *identidem*. Forms ending in *im* are denominatives and verbal or participial forms: from *pars*, *partim*; from *vir*, *viritim*; from *vicis*, *vicissim*; from *ostium*, *ostiatim*; from *status*, *statim*; from *raptus*, *raptim*; from *saltus*, *saltuatim*; from *cursus*, *cursim*; from *strictus*, *strictim*; from *sensus*, *sensim*; from *singuli*, *singillatim*; from *fatus*, *affatim*, or rather from the Greek ἄφενος, that is, “abundantly,” whence *fa* is also shortened; from *privatus*, *privatim*; from *paulus*, *paulatim*; from *singultus*, *singultim*; from *tractus*, *tractim*; from *carptus*, *carptim*; from *ductus*, *ductim*; and especially *praesertim* and *confestim*.

There are few primary forms ending in *um*: *iterum*, *sursum*, *rursum* and *rursus*, *prorsus* and *prorsum*. Derived or compound forms are *dextrorsum*, *sinistrorsum*, *deorsum*, *orsum*, “toward the east,” and “toward the west,” as well as *deorsum*. These seem to be compounds because they are pronounced under a single accent; it is better, however, to say that the nouns placed above incline toward them. Similarly, *actutum* is derived from *actus*, that is, “speed.”

Virgil, in Book III:

> The dutiful Aeneas will promptly restore the rest,  
> and Aeneas [is] sound—  
> “Carius” (“more dear”) [source context uncertain].

Neuter nouns are also found in the same ending in place of adverbs, such as *multum*, *primum*, *nimium*, and *parum* for *parvum*.

Two forms ending in long *n* are found: *non* and *en*; the rest have short *n*, such as *forsan* and *forsitan*. All primary forms ending in *r* are shortened: *cur*, and *per* when it means “very.” Derived from nouns or participles of the third declension are forms ending in *-ter*. But if the nominative ends in *-ens*, they change the *is* of the genitive into *r*: *sapiens, sapientis, sapienter*; *prudens, prudentis, prudenter*. Others take *-ter* from the dative, with the penultimate syllable shortened: *fortis, forti, fortiter*; *utilis, utili, utiliter*; *audax, audaci, audaciter*, or, by syncope, *audacter*.

*Facilis* is excepted: instead of *faciliter*, it has *facile* in adverbial use, with short *e*. *Difficilis*, however, makes *difficulter*. At times the ancients used neuter nouns as adverbs, as *sublime volans* (“flying loftily”) for *sublimiter*, and *utile*, *acuile* (“usefully,” “sharply”) for *utiliter*, *acuiliter*.

It should be noted that in this ending those adverbs that come from the second declension, contrary to this rule, end both in long *e* and in short *r*: from *durus*, *dure*, *duriter*; from *largus*, *large*, *largiter*; from *humanus*, *humane* and *humaniter*; from *inhumanus*, *inhumane* and *inhumaniter*; from *firmus*, *firme*, *firmiter*. Other examples are *insane*, *insaniter*; *severe*, *severiter*; *benigne*, *benegniter*; *aspere*, *asperiter*; *proterve*, *proterviter*. Usage, however, now rejects these forms.

From *tres* and *quattuor* arise the adverbs *ter* and *quater*. There are also compounds, *obiter*, *paulisper*, *tantisper*, and *parumper*.

Among primary forms ending in long *as* is *cras*. I find denominatives in this ending with the final syllable circumflexed, such as *alias*. Forms ending in long *es* are *sodes* and *Hercules*, as well as numerical adverbs—that is, those formed from numbers, from five through one thousand: *quinquies*, *sexies*, *decies*, *vicies*, *centies*, *quingenties*, *millies*.

With short *is* are *bis* and *nimis*, which we also say as *nimium*. *Satis*, which is also used in place of a positive noun and accepts a comparative, as *satius* for “better,” is likewise short.

Juvenalis, in Book III:

> This is preferable to saying, “I saw it before the judge.”

There is one form with long *us*, the primary form *plus*. Primary forms with short *us* include *penitus*, *rursus*, *prorsus*, and *secus*; derived forms include *a caelum*, *caelitus*; *a stirps*, *stirpitus*; *a fundus*, *funditus*; *a radix*, *radicitus*; *ab humanus*, *humanitus*; *divinus*, *divinitus*. Yet one also says *divine*, *humane*, and *humaniter*.

*Eminus* and *cominus* are also local adverbs. *Adversus*, which is also a nominative, is used like *nullus* for “least of all.” All comparatives resembling the neuter gender of comparative nouns are also adverbs: *doctius*, *clarius*, *prudentius*, *ocius*, *satius*, *felicius*, *sapientius*. There are also forms which, although not derived from nouns, have comparatives or diminutives: *saepe, saepius, saepissime*; *ultra, ulterius, ultime, ulterior, ultimus*.

For adverbs of this kind are not derived from nouns; rather, nouns arise from adverbs: *supra, superius, supreme, superior, supremus*; *citra, citerius, citime, citerior, citimus*; *extra, exterius, extreme, exterior, extremus*; *infra, inferius, infime, inferior, infimus*; *diu, diutius, diutissime, diutior, diutissimus*; *nuper, nuperius, nuperrime*.

Adverbs with long quantity by position are found ending in *-rs*, such as *fors*. Virgil, in Book II:

> Perhaps he makes vows and heaps the altars with gifts,

which, like *forsan*, *forsitan*, *forte*, *fortasse*, and *fortassis*, is derived from the noun *fors*. *Fors*, *forsan*, and *forsitan* express doubt; *forte* denotes an occurrence, in the sense “by chance”; *fortasse* and *fortassis* are used for “rashly.”

Forms ending in *-ns* include *totiens*, *quotiens*, *multotiens*, and *aliquotiens*. Forms ending in *-x* include *vix*, *mox*, and *pax*, a Greek word when it means “only.” Forms ending in *-nc* are *nunc*, *hinc*, *illinc*, and *istinc*. Ending in *-ps* is *deinceps*.

## On the Participle

The final syllables of all participles follow the rule of nouns through all their cases: participles of the past and future tenses follow movable nouns, such as *justus, justa, justum*; *amatus, amata, amatum*; *amaturus, amatura, amaturum*; *amandus, amanda, amandum*. Present participles, however, are declined according to fixed nouns: *infans, infantis*; *emens, ementis*; *amans, amantis*; *docens, docentis*; *legens, legentis*; *audiens, audientis*. From these principles participles derive their rules for lengthening and shortening syllables according to case and gender.

The knowledge of the penultimate and other syllables is acquired from the verbs from which participles are derived. The present participle is formed from the imperfect indicative by changing the final syllable—that is, changing *-bam* into *-ns*: *amabam, amans*; *docebam, docens*; *legebam, legens*; *faciebam, faciens*; *muniebam, muniens*. Exceptions are verbs of the fourth conjugation ending in *-eo*, which, contrary to the rule for the others, have a long *i* before *-bam*: *ibam*, *quibam*. The same can also occur in other verbs: *polibam* for *poliebam*, *insignibam* for *insigniebam*. Nevertheless, this did not prevent the participles from being formed according to the rule of perfect forms: we say *iens*, *audiens*, *quiens*, *poliens*, and *insigniens*.

These same participles, however, when formed from fourth-conjugation verbs ending in *-eo*, anomalously have *eu* in place of *ie* in their oblique cases: *iens, euntis*; *quiens, queuntis*. Their compounds behave likewise: *prodiens, prodeuntis*; *nequiens, nequeuntis*.

Future participles, if formed from active, neuter, or deponent verbs, are made from the final form of the supine by adding *-rus*: *amatu, amaturus*; *doctu, docturus*; *lectu, lecturus*; *auditu, auditurus*; *statu, staturus*; *cursu, cursurus*; *molitu, moliturus*; *vertitu, vertiturus* [perhaps *verritu, verriturus*].

A common verb, which has two participles in the future tense—one active, ending in *-rus*, and the other passive, ending in *-dus*—forms the one ending in *-rus* according to the rule just stated: *criminatu, criminaturus*; the one ending in *-dus* follows the future passive.

Future passive participles are formed from the past participle of the present tense by changing the final *-tis* into *-dus*: *amans, amantis, amandus*; *docens, docentis, docendus*; *legens, legentis, legendus*; *audiens, audientis, audiendus*; *transiens, transeuntis, transeundus*; *praeteriens, praetereuntis, praetereundus*.

Past participles ending in *-tus*, *-sus*, or *-xus* are likewise formed from the final form of the supine by adding *s* and shortening *u*. They arise from passive, common, deponent, neuter-passive, and some neuter verbs. From passives: *amatu, amatus*; *domitu, domitus*; *doctu, doctus*; *deletu, deletus*; *mersu, mersus*; *pexu, pexus*; *auditu, auditus*. From common verbs: *criminatu, criminatus*; *osculatu, osculatus*. From deponents: *for, fatu, fatus*; *loquor, locutu, locutus*. From neuter-passives: *gavisu, gavisus*; *factu, factus*. From neuter verbs, only a few past forms arise: *coenatu, coenatus*; *pransu, pransus*; *placitu, placitus*; *nuptu, nuptus*.

*Mortuus* is an exception. From *morior*, by analogy, it ought to have formed *moritu, moritus*, and from this *moriturus*; but the past form is *mortuus*, not *moritus*. Likewise *potum* is used by syncope for *potatum*, and from it comes the participle *potus*.

Virgil, in the *Bucolics*:

> And drive the fed sheep to drink, Tityrus, and while they drink—

And the same poet, in the *Georgics*:

> And in whatever way they might drink, they would rejoice in the endive’s fibres.

Lucan, in Book V:

> Thus the cranes, when winter drives them away, leave the icy Strymon  
> To drink from you, Nile.

*Lautus*, *lauturus*, is used for *lavatus*, *lavaturus*. *Ortu*, *ortus*, and *oriturus* are likewise formed.

The rules stated above are also observed in irregular forms: *latu, latus, laturus*; *ferens, ferentis, ferendus*; *esu, esus, esurus*; *edens, edendus*; and likewise in their compounds.

The ancients also produced from *sum* the participle *ens*, from which *potens* is formed. The future form seems rather to arise from the verb *fio*, whose past is *factus* and present *fiens*; nevertheless, it may also be thought to come from *fui*. *Facio* has *factu*, the past *factus*, the future *facturus*, and the present *faciens*. *Findo* produces *findens*, *fissus*, and *fissurus*.

It should also be understood that when supines are lacking, participles are likewise lacking—both future participles ending in *-rus* and past participles formed from them. This is found in all meditative and inchoative verbs, in which the two final forms of the supine are lacking. When these are lacking, the participles of the aforementioned tenses are also lacking: for example, *parturio*, *esurio*, *horresco*, and *calesco*. The same is often true of neuter verbs of the second conjugation, or of the third conjugation ending in *-uo*: *tepeo*, *egeo*, *caleo*, *ferveo*, *stupeo*, *lateo*, *candeo*, *niteo*, *aestuo*, and *luo*.

Nevertheless, supines or future participles are very rarely found in some such verbs: *doleo, doliturus*; *careo, cariturus*; and many other defective forms occur. The same applies in other meanings or classes of verbs, both to supines and to the forms derived from them: *urgeo*, *spuo*, *metuo*, *timeo*, *medior*, *ambigo*, *scindo*, *vergo*, *arceo*, *mando*, *mandis*. In whatever tense verbs are defective, their participles are defective as well.

*Ferior* and *vescor* also lack a past tense and participles of that tense. *Coepi* has neither present nor future, nor a participle, but only the past participle *coeptus*. Similarly, *odi* has *osus*, from which come *perosus* and *exosus*; *novi* has *notus*; and *memini* has *meminens*, because *memini*, like *odi*, has the force both of the present and of the past, as we have already said. *Nosco* produces *noscens*.

Impersonal verbs likewise lack supines and the participles formed from supines: *piget*, *pudet*, *taedet*, *poenitet*, *liquet*, *licet*, *libet*, and *oportet*. Yet the compound *pertaesum* is found, as are *poenitens*, from which comes *poenitentia*, and *libens* and *licens*, from which come *licentia* and *licitus*.

It should also be understood that when verbs are compounds, their participles are derived from those compounds: *efficio, efficiens*. For if they are compounded in themselves, they do not pass into the force and meaning of nouns until the verbs have first been compounded; the same is true when they are compared, as in *nocens, innocens* and *sapiens, insipiens*.

Although I may seem to be composing these matters out of sequence, since I have undertaken to write about the quantity of syllables, I have nevertheless inserted them without uselessness, because the character of words will be clearer if their origin is first investigated carefully.

It should also be noted that all past and future participles follow, in their penultimate or antepenultimate syllables, the rule of the supines from which they are derived, with a few exceptions. Thus *statum, statu* produces a long penultimate syllable from the supine. In the participle or verbal noun, however, it is shortened: *status, stata, stabilis*, except only in the future participle *staturus, statura, staturum*, which is also a noun. As we showed above when writing about gerunds or medial syllables, there is no need to repeat this, especially since we are hastening to other matters.

## On the Conjunction

We can also explain the final syllables of conjunctions briefly; nevertheless, so that their quantity may be more clearly understood, we think it necessary to indicate their lengthening or shortening together with their classes. There are fourteen classes of conjunctions: copulative, continuative, subcontinuative, adjunctive, causal, effective, approbative, disjunctive, subdisjunctive, assertive—or elective or presumptive—adversative, negative, collective or rational, and completive.

The copulative class joins both words and meaning: *et*, *-que*, *ac*, *atque*, *quidem*, *quoque*; *quando* when it is used for *quod*; *at*, *ast*, *sed*, *autem*, and *vero* when it is used for *autem*.
