These join the meaning with affirmation, and all are shortened except *ast*, whose quantity is produced by position.

Continuative conjunctions signify the order of a preceding matter in relation to what follows, as in “If he snores, he sleeps.” Likewise *sive*, *sin*, and *seu*. Three of these are lengthened: *si*, *sin*, and *seu*; one is shortened, *sive*.

Subcontinuative conjunctions show the cause of a continuation that follows together with the being of things, such as *quo*, *quia*, and *-que*, and they are short.

Adjunctive conjunctions are joined to subjunctive verbs, such as *cum*, *ut*, *dum*, and *quatenus*; all are short. The difference between adjunctive and properly causal conjunctions is that the latter are uttered with affirmation, the former with doubt.

Causal conjunctions signify the cause of what precedes: *si*, *etsi*, *etiamsi*, *siquidem*, *quando*, *quandoquidem*, *quin*, *quin etiam*, *nam*, *namque*, *ni*, *nisi*, *nisisi*, *si enim*, *etenim*, *sed*, *interea*, *quamobrem*, *praesertim*, *item*, *itemque*, *caeterum*, *alioquin*, and *praeterea*. All are shortened except *interea* and *praeterea*, and those which have *i* before *n* in their final syllable, such as *quin* and *alioquin*.

Effective conjunctions are almost the same as causal conjunctions, but effective conjunctions nevertheless express some effect more fully in themselves, as when I say: “He is moved, for he walks; he rests, for he sits.”

It should also be noted that the causal conjunctions which some have placed in a single class are divided by Apollonius, the father of Herodian, into five classes, which we have listed above: continuative, subcontinuative, adjunctive, causal, and effective, on account of a certain distinction that they appear to possess among themselves.

Nouns, pronouns, adverbs, and prepositions are also found used in the place of causal conjunctions. Nouns include *qua causa*, *qua gratia*, *qua propter*, *quam ob rem*, and *quas ob res*. Pronouns include *ideo* and *eo*. Adverbs include *quando* and *etiam*. Prepositions with pronouns include *praeterea* and *interea*, which follow the force of their origin in respect of quantity.

Approbative conjunctions approve a matter. Virgil, in Book XII:

> “And indeed I have deserved it, nor do I plead against it,” he said.

Terence, in the *Phormio*:

> “So indeed a relative, but we—”

Causal conjunctions are also used as approbative conjunctions. Virgil, in Book II of the *Aeneid*:

> Gods, if there is any divine compassion in heaven that cares for such things—

The same poet, in Book I:

> If there is any justice anywhere—

It should be understood that when approbative conjunctions are used, they are joined to the indicative mood.

Disjunctive conjunctions join words but separate meaning, signifying that one matter exists and the other does not: *-ve*, *vel*, *aut*. Within this class are certain doubtful or interrogative conjunctions, such as *aut*, *an*, *ne*, and *necne*, which is shortened. Sometimes they are used indicatively, sometimes doubtfully. Indicatively: “Is it light or night?” Doubtfully: “Is it useful, or is it not useful, to seek wealth?”

Subjunctive conjunctions have the form of disjunctives but signify that both things exist, either together, as copulatives do—for example, “Alexander or Paris,” meaning “Alexander, who is also called Paris”—or separately but together in the statement, as: “All day this man either reads or thinks.” This means that he both reads and thinks, but does not do both at the same time: he reads at some hours and thinks at others.

All disjunctive conjunctions are shortened except those consisting of diphthongs, such as *aut* and *seu*.

Assertive, elective, or dissertive conjunctions are used when, from several propositions, we show that we choose one: “I wish to be rich rather than poor.” *Quam* here is both an accusative used with an infinitive noun and an adverb of comparison, as in Terence’s *Phormio*:

> How unfairly it has been arranged!

It is also a duplicative conjunction used as an adversative, as in *quamquam*.

Adversative conjunctions signify opposition to what agrees: *tamen*, *quamquam*, *quamvis*, *etsi*, *etiamsi*, and *saltem*. They are short except those ending in vowels.

Negative conjunctions are *ne* and *neque*; they are short.

Collective or rational conjunctions are *ergo*, *igitur*, *itaque*, *quando*, with the penultimate syllable accented; *quapropter*, *quin*, *alioquin*, *imo*, *utique*, *ita*, *quippe*, *atquin*, and *scilicet*. By inference these gather together what was said above—that is, they confirm it by reasoning. They are conjunctions, although some appear to be adverbs. Their final syllables are shortened except those that have *i* before *n*, as stated above.

Completive conjunctions are *vero*, *autem*, *quidem*, *equidem*, *quoque*, *enim*, *nam*, *namque*, *porro*, and *porro autem*, as well as nearly all conjunctions inserted for ornament or meter, without any necessity of meaning. They are called completive conjunctions. Nevertheless, such forms occur among the other classes as well. If I say, “Aeneas, indeed, was both pious and brave,” *vero* is completive, because if it is removed, the meaning remains complete.

## On Prepositions

The following prepositions govern the accusative: *ad*, *apud*, *ante*, *adversus*, *cis*, *citra*, *erga*, *contra*, *extra*, *inter*, *intra*, *infra*, *juxta*, *per*, *prope*, *propter*, *ob*, *pone*, *secundum*, *post*, *trans*, *ultra*, *praeter*, *supra*, *usque*, and *penes*: twenty-eight in number.

The following govern the ablative: *a*, *ab*, *abs*, *e*, *ex*, *de*, *pro*, *prae*, *cum*, *clam*, *coram*, *palam*, *sine*, *absque*, and *tenus*: fifteen in number.

The quantities of accusative-governing prepositions are distinguished as follows. *Ad* is short. *Adversus* has its first two syllables long by position and its final syllable short. In *apud* both syllables are short. *Ante* lengthens its first syllable by position; the next is short. *Cis* is long. In *citra*, *ci* is short and *tra* long. In *supra*, *su* is short and *pra* long. In *circum*, the first syllable is long by position and the second short. *Circa*, *erga*, *contra*, *extra*, *intra*, *infra*, *juxta*, and *pone* have all their syllables long. In *inter*, the first syllable is lengthened by position and the second is short. *Per* is short. Both syllables of *prope* are short. In *propter*, the first is long and the second short. *Ob* is short. In *praeter*, the first syllable is long and the next short. In *usque*, the first is long and the second short. Both syllables of *penes* are short.

The following prepositions govern the ablative: *a*, *ab*, *abs*, *cum*, *coram*, *clam*, *de*, *e*, *ex*, *pro*, *prae*, *palam*, *sine*, *absque*, and *tenus*. *A*, *abs*, *de*, *e*, *ex*, and *prae* are always long, whether used independently or in composition, except that *de* is shortened in the compound *dehinc*. *Ab*, *cum*, and *clam* are always short unless the position of the following part lengthens them.

*Pro* is sometimes shortened and sometimes lengthened in composition. It is shortened in *proavus* and *pronepos*; some confirm that in these cases it is compounded from the adverb *procul*, and therefore shortened, as are all forms that similarly have shortened *pro*, such as *profatur* and *protervus*. Others say that, following the example of the Greeks, among whom *pro* is a shortened preposition, our ancestors likewise shortened it in certain compounds.

*Coram*, *palam*, and *absque* have their first syllables long and their subsequent syllables short. Both syllables of *sine* and *tenus* are short.

Although we think enough has been said about the quantities of prepositions, we nevertheless wish to speak about them more clearly, because their usage is rarely described fully by authors.

## On the Lengthening and Shortening of Cases

In the first declension, the singular nominative, accusative, and vocative are short. The genitive, dative, and ablative are long, and all cases in the plural are long, except that the genitive, dative, and ablative, when they end in *-bus*, are short for the sake of distinction.

In the second declension, the singular nominative, vocative, and accusative are short. The genitive, dative, and ablative are long, and all plural cases in the masculine and feminine genders are long, except the genitive. In the neuter gender, the singular nominative, accusative, and vocative are short; the other three are long; and all the remaining plural cases are short except the dative and ablative.

In the third declension, the nominative and vocative are sometimes short and sometimes long; the genitive is always short, as is the ablative unless it ends in *i*; the singular accusative and dative are long. In the plural, the nominative, accusative, and vocative are long in the masculine and feminine genders, while the dative and ablative are short. The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative in the neuter gender are short.

In the fourth declension, the singular nominative and vocative, and the accusative in the masculine and feminine genders, are short. The genitive, dative, and ablative are long. In the plural, the nominative, accusative, and vocative are long; the genitive, dative, and ablative are short. In neuter nouns, the nominative, accusative, and vocative are short, while the other three are long. In the plural, all are short.

In the fifth declension, all singular cases are long except the accusative. In the plural, the nominative, accusative, and vocative are long; the other three are short.

## On the Force and Various Power of Meters

Since, in the preceding book, I believe that I explained sufficiently to you, most dear one, according to the capacity of my ability, the force of letters and syllables, the various sounds of all the parts of speech, and the rules of metrical feet, insofar as seemed sufficient for a first introduction to the art of meter, I think that I have done enough. It remains for me to explain, as far as I can in this following book, the force of meter itself and its most subtle structure, the reason why and by which authors it was invented or established, and by whom it is found to have been changed or varied.

First, it must be noted that, as has been investigated by the most eloquent and trustworthy students of history, concern for poetry existed earlier among the Hebrews than among the gentiles. For Moses, who composed the songs of Exodus and Deuteronomy in hexameter verse—as Josephus and Origen write—is found to be older than all those whom the Greeks consider most ancient: Homer and Hesiod, the Trojan War, and, much earlier still, Hercules, Musaeus, Linus, Chiron, Zethus, Amphion, Perseus, Orpheus, Castor, Pollux, Aesculapius, Liber, Mercury, Apollo, and the other gods of the gentiles, their sacred figures and prophets, and even the deeds of Jupiter himself, whom Greece placed at the summit of divinity.

Job also, whom many place in the same period as Moses, according to the testimony of the writers mentioned above, proceeds throughout in hexameter verse, in dactyls and spondees. But we shall speak of these matters more fully below, when we write about the kinds of meter.

Thus the historian Tranquillus, an ancient writer, reports the following about the poets of the gentiles and their poems:

[Note: [Col. 0665D] The passage is corrupt.]

> “When human beings had first laid aside their wildness and begun to have an ordered way of life, to know themselves and their gods, and to possess moderate worship and necessary speech, they devised, in accordance with the grandeur and religion of both, what was appropriate to themselves and to their gods. Accordingly, they made temples more beautiful than their houses and statues larger than their bodies. Thus they also thought that those whom they honored should be honored with speech that was, as it were, more august; and they exalted their praises both with more illustrious words and with more pleasing rhythms. Because this kind of composition is produced through a certain form called *poesis*, it was called a *poema*, and its makers were called poets.”

Poetics, therefore, is a metrical structure of a fictitious or true narrative, composed with an appropriate rhythm and foot and adapted to usefulness and pleasure. It is called *metrum* because it is bounded by definite measures and intervals of feet. For “measure” is called μέτρον in Greek. Therefore one foot is not a meter, nor one and a half feet, because meter is made up of feet; and feet cannot properly be called such when there are nowhere two of them. Thus meter is more than one foot.

Poetics differs from a poem and from poetry in this respect: poetics means the art itself, whereas a poem is a part of a work, such as a tragedy; poetry is the woven structure and body of the entire completed work, such as the *Iliad*, the *Odyssey*, and the *Aeneid*.

There are three kinds of poem. It is either active or imitative, which the Greeks call *dramaticon* or *mimeticon*; narrative or declarative, which the Greeks call *exegeticon* or *apangelticon*; or common or mixed, which the Greeks call *koenon* or *micton*.

*Dramaticon*, or the active kind, is that in which the characters alone act, without any intervention by the poet, as in tragic and comic plays. The first *Bucolic* was written in this form, as was the work that begins, “Where are you going, Moeris?”

*Exegeticon*, or the narrative kind, is that in which the poet himself speaks without the intervention of any character, as in the three books of the *Georgics* and the first part of the fourth. The poems of Lucretius and other similar works belong here.

*Koenon*, or the common kind, is that in which the poet himself speaks and introduces speaking characters, as in the whole of Homer’s *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, Virgil’s *Aeneid*, and other similar works.

Among the Greeks, the active or dramatic poem has four kinds: tragic, comic, satiric, and mimetic. Among the Romans these are called *praetextata*, *tabernaria*, *atellana*, and *planipes*.

In Greek tragedy there is a presentation of heroic fortune in adversity. According to some, *tragoedia* is derived from *tragos* and *ode*, because in ancient times a goat—*tragos*—was offered as a prize to tragic poets for their song; it was sacrificed more generously on a festival day for this very purpose because, as Varro says, goats graze upon the vine.

Horace, in the *Art of Poetry*:

> He who contended in tragic song for a cheap goat  
> Soon also stripped the rustic satyrs naked. . . .

Virgil, in *Georgics* II:

> Not for any other fault is the goat slain  
> At every altar for Bacchus.

Others think that tragedy was named from the lees, which certain Greeks call *tryga*, through a change of letters, with *y* changed into *a*. For in former times, before Thespis discovered masks, such plays were performed with faces smeared with lees, as Horace again testifies:

> Thespis is said to have discovered an unknown kind of tragic Muse  
> And to have carried his poems in wagons—  
> Poems that men with faces stained with lees  
> Would sing and act.

Others thought that it was derived from wine, because *tryx* was once the name used for it; from this comes *trygetos*, which even today means the vintage, because wine was given more generously to the singers among the Athenians on the festival of Liber Pater. Lucilius is a witness to this practice.

Comedy is a presentation of private and civic fortune without danger to life. *Comoedia* is said to be derived ἀπὸ τῶν κωμῶν. For *comae* are villages, that is, gatherings of country people. Thus, as Varro says, the young men of Attica were accustomed to go around the villages and, for the sake of their earnings, recite this kind of poem; or else the name came from local festivals. After people had moved from the countryside to Athens and the Hiladian games [the reading is uncertain: *hi ludi*] had been established, as the Compitalian games were at Rome, they went out to sing and were called from the urban comic song.

Comedy was also said to have received its name either because it presents the fortunes of villages—that is, of humble households—not those of public and royal figures, as tragedy does; or ἀπὸ τοῦ κώμου, that is, from reveling, because in ancient times the revelries of young lovers were sung in such plays.

Comedy therefore differs from tragedy in that heroes, commanders, and kings are introduced in tragedy, while humble and private persons appear in comedy. In tragedy there are mourning, exile, and slaughter; in comedy, love affairs and the abduction of maidens. Furthermore, in tragedy the endings are frequently, indeed almost always, sad despite earlier happy circumstances, with a change for the worse in the [hiberorum, sic] and former fortunes.

For this reason the Greeks distinguished them by different definitions: one was called ἀκίνδυνος [the source has the corrupt form ἀκινδίνοσπε], the other τύχης περίστασις [the source has the corrupt form τίχυς περίστασις]. Sorrow is proper to tragedy. Therefore, when King Archelaus asked Euripides to write a tragedy about him, Euripides refused and prayed that nothing tragic might happen to Archelaus, showing that tragedy is nothing other than a presentation of miseries.

The first comic poets were Sussurim, Bullus, and Magnes. These men recited certain humorous pieces of the old school, less skillfully and in an old-fashioned manner. In the second age were Aristophanes, Eupolis, and Horace, who attacked the vices of leading men and composed extremely biting comedies. The third age belonged to Menander, Phile, and Philemon, who softened all the harshness of comedy and followed varied plots involving Greek errors. The Romans translated their plays, and it is agreed that among the Romans Livius Andronicus was the first to write comedy in the Latin language.

Some maintain that Epicharmus, while living in exile on the island of Cos, was the first to practice this kind of poetry regularly, and that comedy was therefore named from Cos.

In earlier times they used headdresses rather than masks, so that the nature of the color might indicate the age of the characters, since they were white, black, or red. The first to use masks was the outstanding actor Roscius Gallus, because his eyes were distorted and he did not pronounce the role of the parasite attractively enough when wearing masks.

Satire is called a poem—and not necessarily a slanderous one among the Romans—composed in the sharp style of comedy for attacking the vices of human beings. Such works were written by Lucilius, Horace, Persius, and formerly by Carmem [reading uncertain]. Because it consisted of various poems, it was called *satyra*; works of this kind were written by Pacuvius and Ennius.

According to others, *satyra* was so called either from the satyrs, because ridiculous and shameful matters are similarly expressed in this poem, as though they were spoken and performed by satyrs; or from a platter filled with various and numerous first fruits that was carried in ancient religious rites. Because of the abundance and fullness of its contents, it was called a *satyra*. Virgil also mentions this type of platter in the *Georgics*, saying:

> On platters and dishes we return the steaming entrails.

And again:

> We shall bring platters and sacrificial cakes.
whether from a certain kind of sausage stuffed with polenta and pine nuts and sprinkled with mulsum. Others add pomegranate seeds. Others think it was named from the *lex Satyra*, which embraced many matters in a single proposal, since satiric poetry likewise embraces many poems at once. Lucilius mentions this law of the *satyra* in his first book: “made aedile by the *satyra*, who frees him from the laws.” The fourth species of drama among the Greeks is the mime, so called because it imitates human affairs. It is therefore an imitation—without reverence—of any kind of speech, or of shameful actions with wantonness, since certain plays by Greek poets were composed so as to be especially suited to bodily movement. For a play is called by the Greeks *παρὰ τὸ δρᾷν*, that is, “from acting,” because it was displayed more by actions and movements. Indeed, they say that a play is “acted,” not “recited,” by its actors; nevertheless, in Latin plays there are many songs that are sung. Horace therefore interprets both meanings when he says of a play:

> Either the action is performed on the stage, or what has been performed is recounted.

Thus the Latins called the four species mentioned above by their own proper names, as we have already stated: they called the tragic *praetextata*, the comic *tabernaria*, the satiric *atellana*, and the mimetic *planipes*. But just as we have taken care to explain what the Greek names meant according to the understanding of the ancients, so let us not omit to explain the Latin names, which are more native to us.

Tragedies and comedies, in their beginnings among the Latins, were called *togatae*, because everything seen in public honor was included without distinction. The *togatae* were later divided into *praetextatae* and *tabernariae*. Plays are called *togatae* when they are written according to the customs and dress of men wearing the toga, that is, Romans—for the toga is Roman. Varro likewise says that Greek plays are named *palliatae* from their dress. It should also be noted that although *toga* is a general term, common usage applies it specifically to *tabernariae*, since Faunus calls them *togatae*, and poets do so as well, as Horace says:

> Whether those who taught *praetextatae*, or those who taught *togatae*.

There are nearly as many species of *togatae* as of *palliatae*. The first species of *togatae* are those called *praetextatae*. In them the affairs of commanders are treated, and Roman kings or generals are introduced publicly; in the dignity and exalted status of their characters they resemble tragedies. They are called *praetextatae* because the deeds of kings or magistrates, who wear the *praetexta*, are generally included in such plays.

The second species of *togatae* are called *tabernariae*. They correspond to comedies both in the lowly status of their characters and in the similarity of their plots. Magistrates and kings are not introduced in them, but humble persons and private households. Since such houses were once covered with boards, these plays were called *tabernariae*.

The third species of Latin plays are those called *atellanae*, after Atella, a city of the Oscans, where they first began. In plots and comic sayings they resemble the Greek satiric plays.

The fourth species is the *planipes*, which in Greek is called *μίμος*. It was called *planipes* in Latin because the actors entered the stage on flat feet, that is, barefoot—not like tragic actors in buskins, nor like comic actors in slippers—or because in former times they performed not on the raised stage but on the level ground of the orchestra, with the mimetic instruments set there. The writer of *togatae* mentions the performance of the *planipes* in an aedilician play: “[The text is corrupt: *Datur in est Scaurus exsultat planipes*.]” If, however, they had made any plays in slippers, the *palliati* performed them.

A *togata* differs from a *praetextata* tragedy in this respect: in tragedy heroes are introduced. Thus Pacuvius wrote tragedies with heroic names, such as *Orestes*, *Chryseus*, and similar titles. In a *praetextata*, however, the titles bear Latin names, such as *Brutus* or *Decius*, likewise *Marcellus* or *Africanus*, and similar names.

A *tabernaria* differs from a comedy because Greek customs and Greek characters are introduced in comedy, such as Laches, Sostrata, Geta, and Demipho; in the *tabernaria*, however, the characters are Latin.

Two men chiefly brought *tabernariae togatae* onto the stage: Afranius and Gaius Quintius. Terence and Caelius wrote comedies.

A Latin *atellana* differs from a Greek satiric play because in the satiric play characters who are satyrs are generally introduced, or characters resembling satyrs in their comic nature, such as Olicus and Bosiridis. In the *atellana*, however, the characters are Oscan, such as Maccus.

There are three species of *exegematic*, that is, narrative, poetry: *angelitic*, historical, and didactic.

*Angelitic* poetry is that in which maxims are written, as in the book of Theognis and the *Monastica* of Albinus. This species is found scattered through many poems. *Chriae* are also assigned to it.

Historical poetry is that in which genealogical narratives are composed, such as the poem on the generation of the world, and on the situation and character of the various nations, and the book of Alcimus, and similar works.

Didactic poetry is that which contains the philosophy of Empedocles and Lucretius. It also includes astrology, Aratus’ and Cicero’s *Phaenomena*, Virgil’s *Georgics*, and similar works.

There are two species of common or miscellaneous poetry. The first is heroic, as in the *Iliad* and the *Aeneid*; the second is elegiac, which is also called lyric, as in Archilochus and Horace.

# The Glosses on Donatus the Greater Begin

How many definitions are there among grammarians? Six.

The first is substantial: “A noun is a part of speech with case.”

The second concerns sound: the word *nomen* (“name”) is said as though it were *notamen* (“a mark”).

The third is numerical: there are eight parts of speech.

The fourth is accidental: six things happen to a noun.

The fifth is specific: a body or thing in its proper sense.

The sixth is etymological: *homo* (“human being”) is said to derive from *humus* (“earth”), and *humus* from *humor* (“moisture”).

But *verum* means “but”; [the gloss adds: “*verum id per se designat*,” “the true denotes a body or thing in itself”]. A proper thing is, as Priscian says, an art belonging specifically to any author, such as the *Arithmetica* of Nicomachus or the *Grammatica* of Aristarchus. A common thing is, for example, a discipline or an art.

Others say that a proper thing consists of names such as the names of angels—Michael, Gabriel, and so forth—whereas common things are the names of virtues, such as piety, prudence, and the like. Some do not hesitate to affirm the matter in this way: God is a proper thing, whereas an angel is a common thing.

There are four species: Publius is a praenomen, Cornelius a proper name, Scipio a cognomen, and Africanus an agnomen. These four species of names belong to one man.

Other names are first [the text is abbreviated and uncertain]. They do not derive their origin from elsewhere; the number of their syllables often increases, though not always, as in *paulum*, *paululum*, *pauxillum*, and *pauxillulum*.

There are names wholly [abbreviation, perhaps “of Greek declension”]. These are proper names among the Greeks, but among us they are placed among the species of common nouns, because their interpretations are common nouns: *Themisto*, “perceptive”; *Calypso*, “rational”; *Pan*, “all” or “the whole.”

They are wholly of Greek declension, that is, they should not be declined in Latin by one who knows both languages. They are called *notha*, that is, partly noble. For the Greeks say *Achilleios*, while Latins say *Achilles*; Greeks say *Agamemnon*, while Latins say *Agamemno*.

Likewise, there are *sermo* and the remaining homonyms, that is, words with one name or one voice (*uninomia vel univoca*).

A *nepos* is the son of a son; a person is called *luxuriosus* or *prodigus* (“extravagant,” “wasteful”).

There are synonyms and polyonyms, that is, words with many names or many voices (*plurinomia vel multivoca*).

An *aries* is an animal; *aries* is a sign in the heavens; *aries* is a machine for destroying the fortifications of walls. *Acies* may mean the sharpness of the eyes, the edge of a sword, or the battle line of an army.

In words that are Greek, [the abbreviation apparently means “we shall preserve the Greek rule more closely”] than the Latin one, because the ending they have in Greek is likewise preserved in Latin.

*Agamemnonicae*, *Mycenae*: that is, because Agamemnon ruled there.

Other words have intermediate meaning, because when I say “great,” the meaning still hangs in suspense; or they have intermediate meaning because they may refer either to good or to evil, as in “a great teacher” and “a great robber.”

Another category concerns homeland. A homeland is the city in which someone is born, or the land adjoining the city.

“First” applies to many, because it has the form of a superlative.

“Former” applies to two, and has the form of a comparative because it makes a comparison between two.

*Comedo* means “a glutton” or “a moth.”

*Palpo* means “a little bird,” “a butterfly,” “a blind man,” or “a robber.”

There are three kinds of comparison. Comparison is the bringing together of similar things, by which one is preferred to another through comparison with it. Sometimes the comparative, and the further, higher, and lower forms derived from the adverbs *ultra*, *supra*, and *infra*, are used.

The positive degree is complete in meaning and free from case: “the Pontic Sea is sweeter than the other seas.” The comparison would be greater if he said simply “sweet”; it signifies less because what is bitter is compared with bitterness.

Now, “older”: [note: “Now old, but with a youth still harsh and green.” Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.303]. Here a comparative is used for a positive, for Charon is not being compared with anyone else.

## On Gender

“This muse.” *Musa* is interpreted as “seeking”; it is derived from sound and is the goddess of poetry. The nine names of the Muses are: Melpomene, Euterpe, Polyhymnia, Terpsichore, Urania, Clio, Calliope, Erato, and Thalia.

It is *epicoenon*, that is, “of common gender,” because we include animals of both genders under one grammatical gender. Others call it “super-mixed,” not because the nature of the sexes itself is mixed, but because of our understanding: when we see certain animals, we do not know whether the individual is male or female.

*Eunuchus* is a comedy, that is, a work of Terence, and that noun is of feminine gender. The same applies to *Orestes* and *Centaurus*.

A *poema* is a poet’s work; an *emblema* is abundance; a *porrum* is a vegetable. *Cepe* is neuter in the singular and is the name of a vegetable.

A *forum* is a marketplace or the decking of ships.

A *stirps* means shoots that grow beside a tree, or offspring.

A *pampinus* is a vine leaf. These words have uncertain gender, that is, they may be masculine or neuter; for a double nominative is found, as in *frenus* and *frenum*, *clypeus* and *clypeum*.

*Vulgus* and *specus* have the same ending in both masculine and neuter gender.

In the feminine [the abbreviations probably mean “we often use the feminine forms for the trees themselves”], because it is sometimes found in the masculine gender, as in *oleaster*.

*Scutum* (“shield”) is so called from its roundness.

A woman who makes bread is called a *pistrilla*; the word may also mean the vessel in which water and flour are mixed, or a diminutive name for the house itself.

*Toreuma* means a turning or engraving, a bubble that forms in water, or, as some say, the sound of the chest.

*Euterpe* is the name of a Muse.

*Gummi* is a kind of resin suitable for medicine.

*Frugi* means thrifty or modest.

*Nihili* means the same as *nihil* (“nothing”).

A *pumilio* is a small little man.

## On Number

*Numerus* (“number”) is said to derive from counting coins, or from a certain goddess Numeria.

The singular means certainty of quantity.

The plural is uncertain, that is, a multiplication of units.

There is also a dual number. It is called dual because it is neither singular nor fully plural. It is incorrect to say *omnis duo* (“every two”). Likewise, it is inappropriate to say *omnes duo* (“all two”) or *ambo* (“both”), as is customary with the other names of numbers. We say *omnes tres*, *omnes quatuor*, and so forth.

Pompeius explains it this way: “The dual is that which signifies two only. When I say *duo* (‘two’), I can signify neither one nor many.” Priscian, however, completely undermines this reasoning.

There are also nouns common in number, because in both numbers they have certain cases with one and the same ending.

Some are always plural. The *manes* are spirits, so called either because they always remain, or because they flow through the air—that is, pass into new bodies.

*Quirites* is the name of the common people on the island of Crete, just as the Roman *Quirites* are said to have received their name from a certain Sabine city, that is, from chariots.

*Cancelli* (“latticework”) is plural because this object cannot be made from one thing but only from many. The same applies to *scopae* (“broom”), *scalae* (“ladder”), *quadrigae* (“four-horse chariot”), and so forth.

*Kalendae* (“Kalends”): at the lighting of the new moon, the priest of the idols customarily said repeatedly, *calo, calo*, that is, “I call.” Hence the Kalends are called “the callings.”

*Nundinae* means purchases. At sacrificial festivals, commercial transactions are usually conducted. Alternatively, *nundinae* means nine days counted backward from the Ides to the Nones.

*Feriae* means days of rest. They are said to derive from *fari* (“to speak”), because different things are pronounced at assemblies.

*Quadrigae* means, as it were, “four-yoked,” from the four horses that draw them.

*Nuptiae* means marriage; it is accomplished only through two persons.

*Pus* may mean the corruption of blood, a pool of water, a swelling in the body, or a guard. Hence, some say, the body is called *corpus* as though it meant “the guard of the heart”; but it is better to say that *corpus* is so called because it can decay.

“By measure” applies to liquids; “by weight” applies to dry things.

*Moenia* means buildings made for the defense of a city.

*Floralia* are the festivals of the goddess Flora, held in spring when sacrifices were offered to Earth.

*Saturnalia* are the festivals of Saturn.

*Compitalia* are festivals of Ceres, called from *compita*, that is, from many roads.

*Populus* means something that cannot consist of one individual.

*Concio* means an assembly, or the speech itself.

Athens and the other such names are cities of Greece.

## On Figure

Figure is the third category of quantity.

*Potens* (“powerful”) derives from the verb *possum* (“I can”), or rather, as Priscian says, from the noun *potis* (“powerful”).

*Suburbanus*: whatever belongs specifically to the jurisdiction of the city is suburban. Many say that a suburban person is one who lives beneath the city, that is, near the wall outside it; others say it is one who lives underneath the city, in buildings constructed below ground.

*Efficax* means sharp, as though capable of producing effects.

*Municeps* means one who receives public offices or obligations.

*Ineptus* means one who is not suitable.

*Insulsus* means one who is not salty, that is, foolish.

*Pinnipotens* means powerful with wings, as an eagle.

*Nugigerulus* means a worthless bearer.

*Inexpugnabilis*: a place is *pugnabilis* if it can be attacked; *expugnabilis* means very attackable; *inexpugnabilis* means one that cannot be conquered in any way. Others say that *pugnabilis* and *expugnabilis* are the same, as Pompeius proves.

*Praetor* means judge.

In *senatusconsultum*, *senatus* is the genitive of the fourth declension, whereas *consultum* is a nominative, meaning “counsel.”

## On Cases

There are six cases: the nominative, from *nominare* (“to name”); the genitive, from *generare* (“to generate”); the dative, from *dare* (“to give”); the accusative, from *accusare* (“to accuse”); the vocative, from *vocare* (“to call”); and the ablative, from *auferre* (“to take away”). Of these, two are called straight cases. This is not, however, true of all nouns of the second declension that signify quality or quantity.

The remaining cases are oblique, that is, bent back. In addition, some call one case Latin, because it was discovered by the Latins, and call it the seventh because it occupies the seventh place.

*Monoptota* are words that use one ending through all their cases, such as the names of numbers and letters.

*Aptota* are words that have only one case, such as *sponte* (“of one’s own accord”).

*Diptota* have two case forms, such as *pascha* (“Passover”).

*Triptota* have three case forms, such as *musa* (“muse”).

*Tetraptota* have four case forms, such as *magister* (“teacher”).

*Pentaptota* have five case forms, such as *doctus* (“learned”).

*Hexaptota* have six case changes, such as *unus* (“one”).

*Frugi* means abstinent or thrifty, because it spares the crops.

*Nihili* means useless, one who is worth nothing.

*Nequam* means unjust or wicked.

*Fas* means what is right to say.

*Nefas* means what it is impious to say.

“Numbers are declined,” that is, the names of numbers are declined.

“This brick” [*hunc laterem*]: all the cases of that noun are found except the nominative and vocative.

*Ditione* means “by authority.”

*Sponte* means “by will.”

*Tabo* means “by plague” or “by putrefaction.”

*Natu* means “by birth.”

“Ignorant of war” means one who has never experienced war.

“Untroubled by loves” means one who loves no one.

“An enemy to evils”: it is more correct to say, “he is an enemy to me,” than, “he is my enemy.”

“Suitable to equals” means fitting to similar things.

“Loathing wars, foreseeing the future.” This is figurative, that is, not proper usage. For when I say “loathing wars” and “foreseeing the future,” they naturally take a genitive: *praescius futurorum*, “foreseeing future things.” Alternatively, it is figurative because they are placed almost in the position of participles, as “hating” or “having hatred for wars.”

But these [the text implies: these forms] are only those that are not *aptota*. If the *e* is lengthened, the letter *e* is lengthened when the word becomes a noun of the fifth declension. But this rule [the abbreviations probably mean “is understood of feminine gender”], because all nouns of the fifth declension are feminine, except *dies*, which is found in both genders, and *meridies*, which is always masculine.

“By way of distinction”: this is so that there may be a distinction between the plural accusative and the plural nominative and vocative. If they were alike, an error arising from ambiguity would result. Or it is so that there may be a distinction between the ablative of these nouns and those ending their ablative in *-e*, as in *ab hoc patre* (“from this father”).

Singular nominatives ending in the syllable *-is*, which form their singular ablative in *-i*, more correctly pronounce the plural accusative with *-is* than with *-es*. Alternatively, this may be so that such an accusative distinguishes those nouns that form the plural genitive of nouns in *-um*. Therefore nouns that form their plural genitive in *-ium* more properly form their plural accusative in *-is*.

“From this house.”

Nevertheless, in accordance with the second declension, we commonly use three cases: the singular ablative, and the plural genitive and accusative.

“From this *jugerum*.” A *jugerum* measures 240 feet in length and 120 in width.

Let us remember that *verum* is used for *sed* (“but”).

*Euphonia* means good sonority.

“What analogy”: that is, the comparison of similar things, as in *doctus*, *aptus*, *humus*, *domus*. It is formed in eight ways, through the six accidents of the noun, its ending, and the principle of its tenses.

If any one of these elements is lacking in the noun to which the comparison is made, the rule of analogy will no longer stand, as with *lupus* (“wolf”) and *lepus* (“hare”): *lupus* forms *lupa* (“she-wolf”), whereas *lepus* remains fixed.

*Nequam*, *nihili*: according to Priscian, these nouns are *monoptota*.

*Emblema* means abundance or a natural figure in marble.

*Stemma* means ornament.

*Poema* means a poet’s work.

“In these rules,” that is, in the ablatives.

*Analogia* means proportion.

*Trieterida* means sacrifices performed every three years.

## On Anomalous Verbs

A question arises concerning the difference among anomalous, unequal, and defective verbs.

Those are called anomalous that begin with the same letters but do not have the same form, as *volo*, *vis* (“I wish,” “you wish”).

Those are called unequal that do not begin with the same letters, as *sum*, *es* (“I am,” “you are”), and the rest.

Defective verbs are defective sometimes in their moods, sometimes in their tenses, and sometimes in their persons, as *cedo*, *cedite* (“give way,” “give way, plural”), and the rest.

## On Feet

Syzygies are five-syllable feet. They are called *syzygiae* among the Greeks, as though they were certain declensions. But they are not feet; they are called pentasyllables or hexasyllables because they do not proceed beyond five or six syllables. Therefore a name in verse should not exceed these syllables, as in *Carthaginensium*, *Hierosolymitanorum*, and *Constantinopolitanorum*.

Each foot has an *arsis* and a *thesis*, that is, the raising and placing of the voice. For the feet of the voice could not be properly arranged unless they were raised in alternating sequence, as in *arma*: *ar* is the elevation, *ma* the placement.

By dividing these two elements, the legitimate feet are determined. Division is equal whenever the *arsis* and *thesis* are allotted equal measures of time. It is double whenever one of them exceeds the other twofold. It is sixfold whenever one exceeds the other sixfold.

In the single division, one is found in excess; in the double division, one is lacking. For “sixfold” means half. It is triple when the greater part contains the whole of the lesser three times—that is, three and one. It is *epitritus* when the lesser is contained by the greater together with its third part.

The parts of feet are divided either equally, or twofold, or sixfold, or threefold, or by an *epitritus*. We therefore divide the following by equal measure: the spondee, as *aestas* (“summer”); the pyrrhic, as *fuga* (“flight”); the iamb, as *parens* (“parent”), by double division; and the trochee, as *meta* (“turning point”), by double division.

We therefore divide the following equally:

- Spondee, as *aestas*.
- Pyrrhic, as *fuga*.
- Dactyl, as *carmina* (“songs”).
- Anapest, as *Erato*.
- Dispondee, as *oratores* (“speakers”).
- Proceleusmatic, as *avicula* (“little bird”).
- Diamb, as *propinquitas* (“kinship”).
- Ditrochee, as *cantilena* (“song”).
- Antispast, as *Solonius*.
- Choriamb, as *armipotens* (“mighty in arms”).

By double division we divide the following feet:

- Trochee, as *meta*.
- Iamb, as *parens*.
- Molossus, as *Aeneas*.
- Tribrach, as *macula* (“spot”).
- Lesser ionic, as *Diomedes*.
- Greater ionic, as *Junonius*.

By triple division we divide only the amphibrach:

- Amphibrach, as *carina* (“keel”).

The following belong to sixfold division:

- Amphimacer, as *insulae* (“islands”).
- Bacchius, as *Achates*.
- Antibacchius, as *natura* (“nature”).
- First paeon, as *legitimus* (“lawful”).
- Second paeon, as *colonia* (“colony”).
- Third paeon, as *Menedemus*.
- Fourth paeon, as *celeritas* (“swiftness”).

The following remain, divided by the *epitritus*:

- First epitrite, as *sacerdotes* (“priests”).
- Second epitrite, as *conditores* (“founders”).
- Third epitrite, as *Demosthenes*.
- Fourth epitrite, as *Fescennius*.

When these four feet are doubled, they produce sixteen.

A pyrrhic joined to a pyrrhic is a proceleusmatic, as *avicula*.

A pyrrhic joined to a spondee is a lesser ionic, as *Diomedes*.

A pyrrhic joined to an iamb is the fourth paeon, as *celeritas*.

A pyrrhic joined to a trochee is the third paeon, as *Menedemus*.

A spondee joined to a pyrrhic is the greater ionic, as *Junonius*.

A spondee joined to a spondee is a dispondee, as *oratores*.

A spondee joined to an iamb is the third epitrite, as *Demosthenes*.

A spondee joined to a trochee is the fourth epitrite, as *Fescennius*.

An iamb joined to a pyrrhic is the second paeon, as *colonia*.

An iamb joined to a spondee is the first epitrite, as *sacerdotes*.

An iamb joined to an iamb is a diamb, as *propinquitas*.

An iamb joined to a trochee is an antispast, as *saloninus*.

A trochee joined to a pyrrhic is the first paeon, as *legitimus*.

A trochee joined to a spondee is the second epitrite, as *conditores*.

A trochee joined to an iamb is a choriamb, as *armipotens*.

A trochee joined to a trochee is a ditrochee, as *cantilena*.

# The Exposition of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, on the Proverbs of Solomon (C, G)*

## Book One

## Chapter One

> The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel.

In Greek, *parabolae* are called “comparisons” in Latin. Solomon gave this book that title so that we might know that what it says is to be understood at a deeper level and not according to the letter. In this he signifies that the Lord would speak to the crowds through parables. Likewise, by the proper name and peaceful condition of his kingdom, he announces the everlasting kingdom of Christ and the Church. Of that kingdom it is written: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace upon the throne of David and over his kingdom” (Isaiah 9). Just as the construction and dedication of the temple signify the building of the Church, which will be dedicated forever at the time of the resurrection, so he intimates here the same reality. For he is himself declared to be the son of David and the king of spiritual Israel by the testimony even of the crowds, who met him as he entered Jerusalem with palm branches and praises.

It should be noted, however, that the Vulgate edition says *paroemiae*, that is, “Proverbs,” where the Hebrew has *Masloth*. Yet even this name does not depart from the truth. What are rightly called parables because they are so hidden may also, not inappropriately, be called proverbs, since they are matters that deserve to be frequently on the lips of speakers and retained in memory. Proverbs too are often expressed so obscurely that they may rightly be marked by the name “parables,” as the Lord testifies when he says: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but shall announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John 16).

The usefulness of Solomon’s proverbs is shown in Proverbs 1 by the continuation of the title, where it adds:

> To know wisdom and discipline.

To know wisdom and discipline means to have truly learned how one ought to believe rightly and how one ought to live: to know where to direct the heart’s intention and what one ought to undertake in action.

What it adds—

> To understand the words of wisdom and to receive instruction in doctrine—

admonishes those whom it teaches not only to embrace the wisdom they have themselves received and to know how to serve the discipline of the virtues they have learned, but also willingly to listen to the words of the prudent, by which they may advance toward greater perfection, and to take care diligently to understand them.

> Justice, judgment, and equity.

Justice consists in those things that we do well according to the rule of truth. Judgment consists in what we do rightly with our neighbors through sound discernment. Equity consists in striving, with sincere intention, to please God alone in the things we rightly do and judge.

> That astuteness may be given to the simple, knowledge and understanding to the young.

He calls “simple” those who have only recently begun to lend an ear to wisdom, and “young” the person who has already made some progress in listening to it. Perhaps for this reason he calls the simple by the plural and the young person by the singular. For the teaching of wisdom receives people devoted to different movements of the soul and different ways of life, and advances them through instruction toward one perfection of virtue. Of them it is rightly said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul.”

“Let astuteness,” he says, “be given to the simple.” This is necessary for the inexperienced and foolish, so that they may recognize and avoid the cunning of sophistries, lest they be led away by the deceptions of false arguments from the simplicity of true wisdom, which leads to life.

> To the young, knowledge and understanding.

For whoever prudently avoids falsehood will consequently receive knowledge of the truth.

This has been the prefatory title. From here the actual text of the proverbs begins.

> A wise person who hears will become wiser.

Because Solomon was a lover of wisdom, and because, when given the choice, he asked for and received wisdom, he fittingly begins his proverbs with wisdom. By saying that a wise person becomes wiser when he hears a word, he shows that no one can become so wise in this life that his wisdom cannot increase. It is always characteristic of the wise to listen to the sayings of their elders, and sometimes even of their juniors, and to apply to themselves whatever usefulness they hear in them and store it away in their hearts.

Thus the lesser wise person heard the greater: the queen of Sheba heard Solomon and returned wiser. Moses heard his father-in-law, much inferior though he was, and returned wiser. The disciples heard Christ and were found worthy to receive the Spirit of Wisdom. Nicodemus heard; Gamaliel heard; his disciple—then Saul, now the apostle Paul—heard the wise word of the Gospel, and they became wiser. Even Paul, when he had been caught up to the third heaven and heard words that it is not lawful for human beings to speak, nevertheless, after returning to earth, said: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be brought to an end” (1 Corinthians 13).

> And the understanding person will possess the means of governing.

Let no one boast of his own knowledge. Whoever neglects to hear and understand the words of the wise frequently does not know how to govern his own life properly. How much less can one who has scorned submitting himself to the discipline of the fathers be perfected under the governance of another?

When it says, “The one who hears will become wiser,” it refers to knowledge of the things that are known through wisdom. When it adds, “And the understanding person will possess the means of governing,” it refers to the uprightness of life that is learned and taught through that same wisdom.

The beginning of the Proverbs fittingly agrees with the beginning of the title, which reads: “The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, for knowing wisdom and discipline.”

> Understand the parable and its interpretation, the words of the wise and their riddles.

This gift the Wisdom that taught the disciples, appearing in the flesh, gave to those who humbly listened to her: they were to understand both his parables, which the crowd could not understand, and the riddles of the prophets and the Law—that is, their obscure sayings—in a spiritual manner, and to be able to clarify them for their own hearers. He also reserved the same mysteries of spiritual understanding for the succeeding teachers of the Church who piously sought and knocked.

> The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

There are two fears of the Lord. The first is servile fear, which is called the beginning of knowledge and wisdom; the second is friendly fear, which accompanies the perfection of wisdom.

Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom because whoever begins to become wise after the error of sins is first seized by divine fear, lest he be led to punishments. Perfect love, however, drives out this fear. In its place comes the holy fear of the Lord that endures forever and ever. Charity does not exclude it but increases it. This is the fear with which a good son fears offending, even in a small matter, the eyes of his most loving father.

In the beginning, through servile fear, the soul still fears that it may be subjected to punishments by an angry Lord. Both fears, however, will cease in the life to come, whereas charity will never fail but will remain eternally in the fullness of wisdom. This is to know the true and one God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent.

Wisdom and discipline fools despise. He had said of the wise man that, when he hears the word, he becomes wiser and learns rightly to govern his actions. Conversely, he says of fools that they not only fail to attain the wisdom of sound doctrine and the discipline of a pure way of life, but even disdain to know them. Accordingly, when Wisdom itself preached in the flesh, all who were wise hastened joyfully to it; but the Pharisees and the chief priests spurned both its saving words and its deeds. It should also be noted that he describes the wise man in the singular, but fools in the plural, because fools are more numerous than the wise, and the whole company of the wise follows one uniform path of devotion. The erroneous have a different doctrine and a different manner of life.

Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not abandon the law of your mother. Until this point he has discussed both sides in proverbial fashion; from here he begins earnestly to admonish every faithful person not to prefer the flatteries of the reprobate to the discipline of divine law. For the keeping of the former is followed by a crown, while their crimes are followed by eternal death. Hence he rightly calls him “son,” whom he takes care to instruct with a father’s concern. This may also be understood as spoken in the person of God the Father; by “mother,” however, the Church is to be understood, which at that time was called the Synagogue. It should be noted that he commands us to love the discipline of the father in such a way that we abandon the law of the mother for no reason. For it is not enough for someone to say that he loves God and obeys his commands if brotherly charity does not follow in the unity of the Church. Nor does he forbid us to understand the mother herself as the grace of God by which we are saved. For among the Hebrews also the spirit that bestows grace is designated by a feminine noun.

So that grace may be added to your head, and a necklace to your neck.

It was the custom among the ancients for those who competed lawfully to receive a crown on their head and a necklace around their neck. Therefore, if we keep the discipline of our Creator and the decrees of the mother of grace, the splendor of spiritual virtues increases from day to day. Grace is added to the head when charity, the principal ornament of the mind, is kindled more ardently. A necklace is also added to the neck when the preaching of the word—which proceeds through the neck—is strengthened by the radiance of perfect action. And, lest it be despised by its hearers, it is taught through the unbroken joining of the virtues. Moreover, for those who observed the decrees of the Mosaic law when the Lord came, the grace of the New Testament was added, together with the hope of the heavenly kingdom, whose extraordinary splendor, after the pattern of a crown and a necklace, will never be brought to an end. For us too, when eternal light is bestowed for the good works that divine grace has enabled us to perform, grace is surely added to the head and a necklace to the neck, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Because from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John 1)—that is, the grace of blessed recompense in return for the grace of right action.

My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. Sinners entice those whom they deceive in two ways: either they lure them by flatteries into committing crimes, or they exalt deeds already committed by their favors, as though they had been performed laudably. In both respects Wisdom urges its hearers not to consent to such people.

“If they say: Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood.” This passage may be understood generally of robbers who set ambushes for the innocent and inflict death and loss; it may also be understood particularly of those who handed over the very Author of life to death.

“Let us conceal snares against the innocent without cause.” They did this when they said: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Mark 12), and many things of this kind. For he was truly innocent, who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2). Truly they were laying their snares without cause against the one by whom they had been harmed in nothing, but rather had experienced his numerous benefits.

“Let us swallow him alive, like the underworld, and whole, like one descending into the pit.” The impious desired to destroy the Lord in such a way that every memory of his virtues and teaching would be removed, and even the fact that such a person had ever lived among them would be consigned to oblivion.

“We shall find every precious possession; we shall fill our houses with spoils.” They were speaking about the people whom they saw clinging to Christ. For they thought that, if they killed him, they could separate from his love and following all who had believed, and fill their assemblies with such spoils of souls in their houses. A similar saying appears in the Lord’s parable: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matthew 21).

“Cast in your lot with us; let there be one purse for us all.” A purse is a bag of coins. The passage clearly concerns robbers, since, in order to acquire more companions in crime, they promise them a share in the booty they have seized. The persecutors of our Redeemer likewise joined to themselves as many as they could; but those whom they saw following him they drove away from the Synagogue and deprived of their fellowship.

My son, do not walk with them; keep your foot from their paths. He forbids those among the Jews who believe in Christ to share in fellowship with the Jews who persecute Christ. Accordingly, all who believed were together, and Peter speaks to these same people: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.”

For their feet run to evil and hasten to shed blood. The impious hasten not only toward the evil that they commit temporarily, but also toward the evil that they will suffer perpetually, whenever they hurry to commit murder or perpetrate any other crime. For to the extent that they are visibly led toward completing their crime, they approach invisibly toward enduring punishment for it. These words may be understood particularly of the ambushes laid for our Savior; the following verse, however, is inserted generally concerning his faithful, who likewise endure the malice of the wicked.

But in vain is a net spread before the eyes of winged creatures. In vain is the snare of persecution or death laid for the elect, who possess the wings of hope and charity and of the other virtues, by which, while they live, they desire heavenly things and, after death, are worthy to attain them. They also have the eyes of the mind, by which they see both that the evils they endure from the impious will quickly pass and that the good things they have earned through endurance will remain forever. With these same eyes they foresee both the swift completion of the pride of the reprobate and the everlasting duration of the punishments that follow. The “net” may also be understood as the destructive teaching of the wicked, which he has woven from the passage where he says: “If sinners entice you, do not consent.” Such a net is spread in vain before those who contemplate heavenly things with pure eyes of heart, who know how to say with the Prophet: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Psalm 124). For one whose way of life is in heaven easily avoids the snares laid upon the earth. Thus the wicked prepare both nets in vain for the good: if they persuade them to wickedness, they are overcome by the wisdom of the righteous; if they inflict adversity, it is despised through patience. Moreover, the tempters themselves are destroyed by their own ambushes, and therefore he rightly adds:

And they themselves lie in wait for their own blood and devise treachery against their own souls. “Against their blood,” so that they may be punished by temporal death; “against their souls,” so that they may also be condemned to eternal destruction of soul. Although this applies to all who lie in wait for blood and think that they must live by deceit, it is especially fitting for the Jews, who concealed snares for the innocent Lord and endeavored by deceit to ensnare his Apostles, strengthened by the wings of virtue. They were acting against their own blood and their own souls: fearing that they would lose an earthly kingdom, they killed the King of heaven and earth; they persecuted the citizens of heaven on earth. Thus they lost both the kingdom they possessed on earth and the kingdom they could have acquired in heaven. In general, however, it must be said that whoever has the eyes of faith opened and has received from the Lord wings like a dove, with which to fly to eternal rest, is ensnared in vain by the traps of the wicked; by attempting this, the wicked destroy themselves instead.

Thus the paths of every greedy person seize the souls of those who possess wealth. By “the paths of the greedy person” he means his subtle thoughts, by which he diligently seeks how to increase his money. Such paths seize for destruction the souls of those who possess wealth—that is, of those who devote themselves beyond reason to their financial possessions. Therefore, he says, not only do those who, out of love of money, devote themselves to the robbery and slaughter of the innocent destroy themselves by doing this; in the same way, though with lesser guilt, all the thoughts of the greedy that prefer gold to God drag them to destruction. Alternatively: “Thus the paths of every greedy person seize the souls of those who possess wealth,” with the result I have mentioned: every greedy person kills and strips those who abound in possessions, so that he himself perishes by doing this. For why would he kill the poor, whom he sees to possess nothing and from whom he finds no spoils? Up to this point the persecutions that the Jews inflicted upon Christ are described; to this point belong the things that he himself, after his Passion, speaks to those same persecutors through the Apostles.

Wisdom preaches outside; in the streets it raises its voice; at the head of the crowds it cries aloud. The Wisdom of God is Christ, who, while dwelling in the world, disclosed the mysteries of his divinity to a few and commanded them not to preach before his Passion and Resurrection that he was Jesus Christ, nor to tell anyone of the glory they had seen on the mountain. At that time he displayed the power of his majesty more by deeds than by words, fulfilling the prophecy that said: “No one will hear his voice in the streets” (Matthew 12). After the Resurrection, however, Wisdom preached outside, because, when the Spirit had been sent from above, it openly declared itself to the world through the Apostles. In the streets it raised its voice because, in the broad public spaces, it openly repeated what it had previously taught to a few, fulfilling the word that it spoke to those same heralds: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10). At the head of the crowds it cried aloud because it also openly brought to remembrance, even before the rulers who seemed to have prevailed against it so that it would be crucified, the guilt of the murder they had committed, and called them to the remedy of patience.

“In the doorways,” it says, “at the gates of the city it utters its words.” The city of the Lord is the Church, united from both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. The doorways of its gates are the teachers, who bring believers into it by preaching the word. Wisdom uttered its words in the doorways of its gates when it spoke in its Apostles, one of whom said: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13). The doorways of the city’s gates may also be understood as the principal synagogues, in which Wisdom disputed when, speaking through the Apostles, it recalled to grace even the Pharisees who were learned in the law and the priests, so that, as Luke says, “a great many of the priests also became obedient to the faith.”

What, then, this same Wisdom cried aloud, he adds:

“How long, little ones, will you love infancy? How long, little ones in understanding, will you love the ceremonies of the Old Testament while the New Testament is shining forth? How long will you prefer Moses to Christ and the law to the Gospel? How long will you place above the decrees that the Son himself, coming in perfect understanding, bestowed those decrees that were given through a servant to peoples who were still immature? How long,” he says, “will you do these things? You have already seen Christ in the flesh; you have already seen him performing miracles and teaching. You not only despised him, but also killed him. At least now love him, raised from the dead and presiding in heaven, and he will forgive you the crime you committed.”

And fools will desire the things that are harmful to them, and the imprudent will hate knowledge. The words following the preceding “how long” must be supplied: “How long will they desire? How long will they hate?” They desired what was harmful and hated knowledge because they followed the surface of the letter of the law and refused to receive the mysteries of the Gospel, which that very letter signified.

Turn to my correction. Through the mouths of the Apostles he reproved the Jews because they had been unwilling to believe, and even then, after he had risen and ascended, he urged them to turn back.

Behold, I will pour out my spirit to you, and I will make my words known to you. “If you still neglect to turn back,” he says, “I will pour out upon you the vengeance you have deserved, and I will show that the words I foretold concerning your destruction are true.” He calls his spirit the power of vengeance. Of it Moses says: “You sent your spirit, and the sea covered them”; and in the book of blessed Job it is said that the wicked perished when God breathed, and were consumed by the spirit of his anger.

Because I called, and you refused. He says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. First by doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the Devil, and afterward by suffering on the cross.

You despised all my counsel. He says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3).

And you neglected my reproofs. He says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11). And, in general: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3).

I too will laugh at your destruction and mock you. The Psalm says of these same people: “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Psalm 2). This does not mean that the Lord laughs with his lips or mocks with his nose; rather, that power is signified by this language which he gave to the Apostles, so that they might foresee that the impious would be able to plot nothing against him beyond what he himself permitted. Rather, they were to foresee that all their undertakings would be brought to nothing, while his glory after the Passion would be spread throughout the world. Therefore, even when they saw the pride of the impious at its greatest strength, they were to despise it as nothing.

When what you feared has come upon you. They said to one another: “If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11).

When sudden calamity rushes upon you and destruction comes like a storm. He refers to the siege of Jerusalem and the conquest of the whole province by the Romans. The Lord himself foretold this when he saw the city in the Gospel and wept over it.

When tribulation and distress come upon you, then they will call upon me, and I will not answer. The Jews are not recorded as having called upon the Lord during any siege, but only as having trusted in arms, although they witnessed the desolation of their homeland and the ruin of the Temple with the deepest anguish. If some did call upon him then, since they did not wish to understand the guilt for which they were punished and thus truly repent, they cried out in vain to the one they had despised. Hence they are rightly said to have suffered tribulation together with distress. Tribulation was present in the things by which they were oppressed outwardly; distress was present in the fact that inwardly they found no consolation from God. The saints, on the other hand, when they are outwardly oppressed by adversities, are enlarged in heart by the sure hope of salvation, knowing that they are heard by the one whose words commanding them to listen they remember. Hence the Prophet says: “When I called upon you, you answered me, O God of my righteousness; in tribulations you enlarged me” (Psalm 4).

This entire correction of Wisdom may also be understood generally of all the reprobate, because on the day of judgment they will cry out to the strict Judge, asking that the gate of the kingdom be opened to them, but will not deserve to be heard. For the following words also:

“They will rise early and will not find me,” plainly designate the time of the final judgment, when some rise to eternal life and others to everlasting disgrace.

Because they hated discipline and did not accept the fear of the Lord. They are rightly deprived of salvation who not only lack the fear of the Lord and discipline—the beginning of wisdom—but also pursue them with hatred. In contrast, the son of salvation says: “I hated the wicked, but I loved your law” (Psalm 118).

Therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way. He means the way about which he had said above: “Their feet run to evil.” “Because,” he says, “they were unwilling to walk in my ways in order to live, they will receive the reward of their ways, so that they may perish forever.” In contrast, it will be said of those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways: “I shall eat the labors of your fruits; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm 127).

And they shall be filled with their own counsels. Because they refused to consent to my counsel, by which I had determined to save them, they shall be filled with their own counsel, by which they said: “Let us conceal snares against the innocent without cause” (Proverbs 1). In place of the Savior they chose a robber for themselves, so that they might be ravaged by robbers and condemned among robbers. The same may also be understood of all who despise the word of God.

The turning away of the little ones will kill them. By “little ones” he means not those who are young in age, but those who are immature in understanding. Of them it was said above: “How long, little ones, will you love infancy?” They could have been not little ones but perfect in understanding if they had not turned their hearing away from the counsel of Wisdom. But to the extent that they turned away, they devoted themselves to eternal death.

And the prosperity of fools will destroy them. When, with no adversities delaying them, they have carried out what they had planned while saying, “We shall find every precious possession.” Again: “The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.” For often the mind, having turned away from fear of the Creator, suffers the just Creator’s anger in this way: in the things in which it sins, it seems to endure no adversity. But, as blessed Job says: “Let him spend his days in prosperity, and in a moment let him descend to the underworld” (Job 21).

But whoever listens to me will rest without terror. This may be understood both in the present life and in the future, because one who serves the Lord perfectly is frightened by no adversities. Rather, he rejoices in adversities and, even in death itself, delights as though at an entrance into life. With the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit, he always bears a breast that is quiet, free from useless thoughts and the disturbances of temptations. The rest of the seventh day mystically signified this in the law. But when he has departed from the world, he will rest not only without fear of evils, but also in great joy at the resurrection he hopes for, like Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham.

And he will enjoy abundance, with the fear of evils removed. Now, abundance consists in good works, when even the fear of those who kill the body has been taken away; then, abundance consists in joys in the bosom of blessedness. For one may contemplate how great is the abundance of every good thing there, where there is glory from the one from whom all good things come, with every fear of anything that could thereafter bring adversity completely removed.

## CHAPTER II

My son, if you receive my words and hide my commands within yourself. He hides God’s commands within himself who, hearing them, carefully stores them in his heart, in accordance with the one who says: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you.” For we must take the greatest care lest, according to the parable of the Gospel, demons carry them away like seed cast beside the road.

“So that,” he says, “your ear may hear wisdom.” The person whose ear does not hear wisdom is shown to be the one who receives God’s words only through the hearing of the body, but neglects to retain them in memory and put them into practice. If, therefore, you receive God’s commands with fixed love, for learning and keeping them, first hold to the way of humility; for this is what he adds next:

Incline your heart to know prudence. To incline the heart to know prudence is to humble it for the knowledge of prudence and to cleanse the heart, so that it may become worthy to receive the mysteries of truth. Hence the same Wisdom, speaking to the Father, says: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10)—that is, you have hidden them from the proud and revealed them to the humble.

For if you call upon wisdom and incline your heart to prudence. We ought to call upon no one—that is, invite no one into us by prayer—except God. Therefore, when he teaches that Wisdom must be called upon, he plainly shows that he is not proposing for us to pursue just any wisdom, that is, knowledge of heavenly or earthly things, but the very knowledge of the Godhead. In receiving this wisdom lies the highest perception of blessedness, as Wisdom itself attests when it pleads for us to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). It should also be noted that he urges us both to call upon wisdom and to incline our own heart toward knowing prudence, because it is plainly necessary both to seek divine help in everything and, with the Lord assisting us, to do whatever good we are able to do. We must believe that we can do nothing without him; nor, without our own effort, may we believe that we are to be saved by him.

If you seek it like money and dig it out like treasures. If you seek wisdom with as much care as the greedy seek money—or certainly if you seek wisdom as diligently as though you were going to acquire through it boundless and unspeakable riches—you will receive the rewards that are explained below. Whoever digs out treasures removes the earth and makes a deep pit; he persists diligently in his labor until he reaches the treasures he seeks. Likewise, whoever desires to find the treasures of wisdom must purge whatever earthly thing he discovers to be within himself, cut away carnal enticements, make within himself a pit of humility, and not cease from acting until he recognizes that he has found the vein of truth.

Then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God. If you seek with an attentive heart, you will arrive at the experience of the Lord’s beloved fear. In this life alone, it is not the beginning but the perfection of heavenly wisdom; therefore perfect love does not cast it out, but makes it remain forever. You will also find the knowledge of his divinity, which makes one blessed forever.

Because the Lord gives wisdom. This verse looks back to what he said above—“if you call upon wisdom,” and so forth—up to where he says, “and you will find the knowledge of God.” Wisdom, that is, the Lord, must be called upon in order to receive wisdom because wisdom cannot be possessed from ourselves, but is given by the Lord. Let Pelagius be silent: the Apostle also refutes him when he says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4). And the Apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask it of the Lord” (James 1).

And from his mouth come knowledge and prudence. In this verse the ineffable and coeternal birth of Wisdom from God the Father may be understood; elsewhere Wisdom itself says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn” (Ecclesiasticus 4). The mouth of the Lord may also be understood as his saints. Hence it is often said in the prophets that “the mouth of the Lord has spoken,” and from his mouth knowledge and prudence are born, because unless he sanctifies the human mouth, unless he graciously makes it his own, it is entirely unable to speak perfect wisdom.

He will preserve the salvation of the upright and protect those who walk in simplicity. Uprightness and simplicity are virtues akin to one another, and they cannot be separated from each other. Therefore Wisdom does not seek one without the other; rather, wherever both are found together, it preserves and protects those people. Thus it is said of blessed Job: “That man was simple and upright” (Job 1)—simple, namely, through the innocence of gentleness; upright, through the caution of discernment. Simple because he desired to harm no one, but rather to benefit everyone; upright because he allowed himself to be corrupted by no one.

Preserving the paths of justice and guarding the ways of the saints. They call the general commandments of God the ways of the saints, and the more demanding disciplines of heavenly life the paths of justice, which are accessible only to the perfect. Wisdom preserves both, so that at whatever level of virtue they may stand, it may assist the upright and the simple.

Counsel will guard you, and prudence will preserve you, so that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the man who speaks perverse things. By “the evil way” he means wicked works; by “the man who speaks perverse things,” he means teachers of wicked action. They call the evil way wicked when they say, “Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood”; they call him one who speaks perversely who is the author of this persuasion.

Those who abandon the straight path and walk along dark ways. Beautifully he opposed dark ways to the straight path, because the path of right action is traveled in the light and leads to the joys of the heavenly light.
