But, as the Lord says, “everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed” (John 3); and such a person will receive an end in outer darkness.

Those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. Those who do evil rejoice for this reason: they walk along dark ways and do not know where they are going. If they saw that they were heading toward punishment, they would certainly restrain their step and correct their harmful joy with salutary weeping.

So that you may be delivered from the strange woman and from the foreign woman who makes her words smooth. This verse depends upon the preceding words, where it was said: “Prudence will preserve you.” The meaning is: Prudence will preserve you so that you may be delivered from the strange woman. Earlier Solomon warned his hearer, whom he was striving to teach wisdom, not to join himself to robbers—not to run together with a thief if he saw one—but to walk rightly and simply. Now he warns him not to place his portion among adulterers. The preceding words, “so that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the man who speaks perversely,” can also be understood particularly of them. For what speech is more perverse than persuasion to sexual immorality? This chapter begins at the passage where he says: “My son, if you receive my words and hide my commands within yourself.”

The foreign woman may also be understood as the depravity of heretics, alien from the members of Christ and the Church, which is accustomed to deceive the hearts of the innocent by the smoothness of eloquence and the flatteries of the tongue. Hence the Psalmist says: “They have softened their words more than oil, yet they are arrows” (Psalm 54).

And she has abandoned the guide of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God. This is clear concerning the adulterous woman, because she has abandoned her first husband and forgotten God’s covenant—namely, the covenant that, with God as witness, she made with her husband at the time of marriage, that they would preserve mutual fidelity and chastity. It is also clear concerning the heretical mind, because it has abandoned the teacher from whom it learned the faith of the Church and has forgotten the covenant of its God—that is, the faith of the Lord contained in the Creed, which it promised on the day of baptism to preserve.

For her house has inclined toward death, and her paths toward the impious. The whole way of life of the adulterous woman leads to destruction. Although she may appear gentle and mild, she will experience no less punishment at the end than those who serve open wickedness by robbery. The house of the adulterous woman may also be understood as her flesh, in which she submits herself to disgrace and lust; at the time of the final judgment, this flesh will rise not to life but to everlasting death. The house of heretics, too, because it is built upon sand, even when it appears to stand, inclines toward collapse; by its own growths, as by certain paths, it tends toward association with the impious—that is, toward the punishments of evil spirits.

All who enter into her will not return, nor will they grasp the paths of life. He says “to her,” meaning to death, not to the woman. For one who has been joined to an adulterous woman may, with the Lord’s help, return and merit life through repentance; one who has been defiled by heresy may return to salvation by recovering his senses. But whoever has once been seized by eternal death will never return to the way that seeks the life of the blessed. This is said particularly against the Origenists, who promise heretical prostitutes and every crowd of the immoral—and, moreover, the Devil himself and his angels—forgiveness of sins, life, and a kingdom in heaven after the innumerable ages of the universal judgment have supposedly been completed.

They misunderstand Isaiah’s words: “The wicked will be shut up in prison, and after many days they will be visited” (Isaiah 24), as though he had said that the wicked would be saved after the long period of judgment had ended. On the contrary, he grants them no salvation, but signifies that those who, in this present time of death, deserve to be shut up in the prison of punishments because of the enormity of their crimes will be visited at the time of the resurrection only briefly, so that, once they have received their bodies, they may be condemned more severely at the judgment and immediately afterward be confined forever in harsher punishments.

Nevertheless, the words “all who enter into her will not return” may also rightly be understood in this way: “into her,” that is, into the prostitute or into her house. They will not return because, as far as nature is concerned, once corrupted by its own wicked will, it has no ability to return by itself; it returns only through the grace of God, by which it is helped and restored so that it may grasp the paths of life. The weight of iniquity is designated by this saying, so that when someone returns, he may not attribute it to himself but to the grace of God—not to works, lest he should perhaps boast.

So that you may walk in the good way and keep the paths of the righteous. By “the good way” he means the unity of right faith, concerning which the Lord says: “I am the way” (John 6), and elsewhere: “No one can come to the Father except through me” (ibid.). By “the paths of the righteous” he names the many examples of the saints. This verse depends upon what was said above, “Prudence will preserve you,” as does the statement, “so that you may be delivered from the strange woman.”

For the upright will dwell in the land, and the simple will remain in it. Here too the simple are joined to the upright, as above when he said: “He will preserve the salvation of the upright and protect those who walk in simplicity.” For simplicity without uprightness is disordered and foolish, whereas uprightness without simplicity is excessively severe and harsh. When joined together, however, both virtues make a perfect person. The difference between the two verses is this: in the first, the Lord is said to assist the righteous while they struggle in the present; in the second, to crown them as victors in the future.

By the name “land” the Church is designated, since it habitually brings forth spiritual fruit for God. The righteous dwell and remain in it because not even death separates them from its fellowship. When this life has ended, they reach that part of it which reigns with Christ in heaven.

But the impious will be destroyed from the land, and those who act wickedly will be removed from it. These words may be understood not as spoken generally of all the reprobate, but particularly of those who seemed to belong to the land of the Lord—that is, to the Church—and yet, because their merits demanded it, are removed from it. Some are removed by the Church’s open judgment, such as Simon, Arius, and Porphyry; others by the secret judgment of the invisible Judge, such as countless people who appear good to human beings. He calls open apostates impious, but calls all who, after receiving the mysteries of faith, in some way degenerate from its chastity those who act wickedly.

Both groups, however, will be destroyed in the future recompense from the land of the living, because “the wicked will not dwell near the Lord, nor will the unjust remain before his eyes” (Psalm 5). And rightly so: since he has said much about the ways of the wicked and the good, he adds, in the conclusion [perhaps: “in the enclosing summary”], what the end of each will be. He had done the same in the preceding parable, which forbade fellowship with robbers, saying of the end of the wicked, “the prosperity of fools will destroy them,” and saying of the good, “whoever listens to me will dwell without terror.”

The verses about which we have most recently spoken may also be understood of the ancient people of God: when they lived rightly, they remained happily in their own land; but when they sinned, they were expelled by their enemies.

## CHAPTER III

My son, do not forget my law, and let your heart keep my commands. Here he teaches that one must devote oneself to works of mercy, not trust in one’s own strength, but seek help from God. In a fitting order, after restraining the person he instructs from cruelty and chastising him for lust, he adorns him with good actions.

For length of days, years of life, and peace will be added to you. So that the hearer would not be disturbed by the burden of keeping the commands, he first set forth assured rewards, and then enumerated the commands. By “length of days” he signifies everlasting light; by “years of life,” passage beyond this mortality; by the increase of peace, the state of blessedness itself once attained. Concerning this Isaiah says: “He multiplied his dominion, and there will be no end of peace” (Isaiah 9). The earlier people of God were also given this in the present life, so that, when they obeyed God’s law, they might live for a long time in peaceful rest.

Let mercy and truth not abandon you. Because truth must be spoken by your mouth, mercy, which must be shown to your neighbor, should not therefore depart from your deeds. For in this way it comes about that God’s mercy and truth always accompany you: mercy, namely, which blots out your sins; truth, which fulfills his promises.

Surround them around your throat, and write them on the tablets of your heart. By “the throat,” where the instrument of the voice is located, he signifies speech; by “the tablets of the heart,” the breadth of thought. Thus let the virtue of mercy and truth, fixed in the root of the mind, come forth through the voice of the speaker, so that the hidden purposes of the heart may be pleasing in secret and the duties of speech may help our neighbors. He rightly teaches that the virtues are to be surrounded around the throat, since the voice of the speaker is formed inwardly in the throat but surrounds what is outside. For insofar as it arouses others to live well, it binds the preacher himself to act well. Let action not pass beyond the word, lest one’s life contradict one’s voice.

And you will find grace and good instruction in the sight of God and human beings. Before God, a person finds grace and good instruction when, through constant practice of the virtues, he continually merits the Lord’s favor, so that day by day he becomes more perfect and better than himself. But he also finds grace and good instruction before human beings when his works are such that he is rightly praised and offers his neighbors an example of how to live.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not rely on your own prudence; acknowledge him in all your ways, and he himself will direct your steps. Do not fear that, because of your own weakness, you cannot keep God’s commandments; nor, conversely, suppose that you can fulfill them by your own strength and know them by your natural understanding, unless you are instructed by his law. Rather, in learning and in acting, seek his frequent help, and he, in his mercy, will grant that you may fulfill what he has commanded.

Do not be wise in your own eyes. Someone may perhaps think that this is the same command as the preceding one, “Do not rely on your own prudence.” But there is a great difference. A person relies on his own prudence when he prefers what seems to him necessary to do or say over the decrees of the Fathers. But a person is wise in his own eyes when, even in matters that he has been able to understand correctly through the teaching of the Fathers, he exalts himself above others as though he were more learned. What true human wisdom is, he subsequently shows.

Fear the Lord and depart from evil. It is as in Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil—that is understanding” (Job 28). For all who are perfect ought to restrain themselves from every evil in such a way that they always recall, with fear, the presence of the divine majesty. It should also be noted that above he urged us to have confidence in the Lord, whereas now he urges us to fear God. There he strengthens the hearts of the weak, lest they despair, by promising God’s help; here he restrains the strong, lest they presume upon themselves, by recalling divine fear.

For it will be health to your navel and irrigation to your bones. In the bones, solid works of virtue are signified; in the navel, which is central in the lower part of the body, the still weak and imperfect action of good is signified. Therefore, if you fear God and, trusting not in your own strength but in heavenly protection, strive to abstain from evil, it will be health to your navel and irrigation to your bones: through these, the weakness of your works will recover strength toward perfection, and your stronger deeds will receive from them the means to become still more firm.

Honor the Lord from your substance and from the firstfruits of all your crops. Many give much to the poor, but from the substance and crops of others, which they have seized by force and fraud. Many give from what is their own, but in giving do not honor the Lord, because they act for human favor and not out of love for the heavenly observer. Whoever therefore desires the fruit of almsgiving to profit him should give both from his own possessions and in honor of the Creator, so that human beings—who are his creation and were made in his image—may be refreshed. We are commanded to honor the Lord not only from the substance of money that we extend to the poor, but also from the substance and firstfruits of every good work that we perform and of all the heavenly grace that we receive. This means seeking his praise in everything and not our own. The person also honors the Lord from his substance and from the firstfruits of his crops who attributes everything good that he does not to his own strength and merits but to heavenly grace, remembering that saying: “Without me you can do nothing.”

And your granaries will be filled with abundance, and your winepresses will overflow with wine. The Lord says in the Gospel: “But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6). If the righteous can have treasures in heaven, because there they find true riches, then they can certainly have granaries and winepresses as well, because they will hunger and thirst no more: “And your granaries will be filled with abundance,” because, he says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16). “Your winepresses will overflow with wine,” because the inner sweetness of eternal things kindles the hearts of all the faithful in praise of their Creator. Hence he says: “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). But even in the present life the Lord sometimes grants the teacher who supplies the needy with the bread of the word and the cup of spiritual grace greater gifts for supplying them, as his reward. Whoever generously provides earthly support to the needy is made richer by being repaid with a heavenly recompense.

My son, do not reject the Lord’s discipline, and do not fail when you are corrected by him. Some serve the Lord in prosperity but go astray in adversity. Therefore Wisdom, having taught a person to live well in prosperity, also urges him not to fail under correction, lest, when weakness, poverty, and human persecution arrive, he lose the devotion that he seemed to preserve in tranquility.

For the Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and, as a father with his son, he takes pleasure in him. Therefore, the less we ought to murmur at the scourge by which we are chastised, the more certainly we recognize in it the pledge of a father’s love. Hence he himself also says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3). It should be noted, however, that in place of this wording the Seventy Translators said: “But he scourges every son whom he receives.” It is astonishing why the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews in Hebrew, chose to follow this version more closely.

Blessed is the person who finds wisdom, and who abounds in prudence. Because he had been consoling those placed under discipline and correction, he adds to what he had begun, making clear that true human blessedness does not consist in being free from adversity in the present, but in rejoicing in the apprehension of eternal wisdom. This means knowing the Lord’s will in this life and enjoying his vision in the future. And appropriately, when he had said, “Blessed is the person who finds wisdom,” he immediately added, “and who abounds in prudence.” For there are people who find wisdom by receiving the teaching of truth with the ear, but neglect to abound in prudence because they do not wish to open wide the breast of their heart to receive its fullness.

Her acquisition is better than the business of silver and gold. Whoever has acquired the riches of wisdom need not fear the correction of poverty, because the heavenly gift surpasses earthly treasures incomparably.

Her first and purest fruits. If, according to Ecclesiasticus, the root of wisdom is fearing God, what are the fruits of wisdom except seeing God? And these fruits are first and purest—either because God, who is seen, is from the beginning, and nothing defiled enters into his vision; or because human beings were created first for contemplating him. Hence the younger son, when he returned penitently to the Father, is remembered as having received his first robe. Or it may be because newly worked and unalloyed gold is usually the purest; and our first robe is truly to be understood as blessedness, which the Lord promises will be restored to us more perfectly in the resurrection.

She is more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired can be compared with her. The brightness of this wisdom is preferred not only to earthly riches but also to heavenly riches—even to the very sight of the angels. Hence the prophet says: “What do I have in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72), and so on to the end of the psalm.

Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory. By the vision of his divinity he grants the elect perpetual light, while in the present life he enlightens and strengthens them through the mysteries and gifts of his incarnation. To those who sell all that they possess in order to acquire him, he gives a hundredfold in this time and, in the age to come, eternal life. At this point, according to the ancient translation, the following is included, which our books do not have:

> From her mouth proceeds righteousness; she carries law and mercy upon her tongue.

I thought this ought to be noted because those verses are often found inserted in the works of the Fathers.

Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful. Her actions and teachings, which are contained in the Gospels, are beautiful because they far surpass the measure of the divine and pure human being; and all her commandments lead to eternal peace. Everything that he accomplished in it pertains to reconciling mortals to God, making the human race peaceful with the angels, and displaying to his own examples of preserving peace and love toward one another.

She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her. Just as Moses testifies that the tree of life was placed in the middle of paradise, so the Church is made alive through the Wisdom of God, namely Christ. Through the sacraments of his flesh and blood she now receives the pledge of life, and in the future she is blessed by his present sight.

The Lord founded the earth by wisdom; he established the heavens by prudence. God the Father created all things through the Son. In a typological sense, he founded the earth by wisdom when through him he placed the holy Church upon the solidity of faith. He established the heavens by prudence when through that same one he enlightened the lofty hearts of preachers.

By his wisdom the abysses burst forth. This occurs when, in the days of Noah, all the fountains of the great abyss were torn open, and when, through their daily course, springs and rivers flow from the abyss through the veins of the earth. In another sense, the abysses burst forth by wisdom when, through the grace of Christ being generously bestowed, the depths of the heavenly mysteries become known to the faithful.

And the clouds grow by his dew. This is clear according to the literal sense. Allegorically, however, the clouds are the teachers of the Churches, lofty through contemplation and life and watering the hearts of their hearers, as though they were the earth subject to them, through their teaching. They grow by dew because, with the finest discernment, they examine their virtues: those by which they may make progress, by which they may seek high things, and by which they may be displayed as an example to their inferiors.

My son, do not let these things slip from your eyes. Take care lest, wearied by temporal discipline, you lose the grace of wisdom, which is so great.

Keep the law and the counsel. The law is wisdom, which says: “If you wish to enter into life, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness,” and so on (Exod. 20). The counsel of wisdom is what he immediately adds: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell everything that you have,” and so on (Matt. 19).

And it will be life to your soul. Your soul has life with God if you keep his decrees, however much the flesh may be oppressed by the discipline of correction or even by death.

And grace to your throat. The mind’s understanding therefore has its own throat, since it says: “Your utterances are sweet to my throat” (Ps. 118). Through these it judges the words it hears; through them it examines, by discerning judgment, the things and deeds of individuals that it sees; and by embracing some it receives them, while by rejecting others it despises them. In this throat, when we keep the Lord’s law and counsel, grace is multiplied. For the more diligently someone obeys the divine commands, the more sweetly he conceives love for him. The Psalmist desired that grace should be present in our throats when he said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

Then you will walk confidently in your way. We walk confidently in our way when, trusting in God’s grace, we make progress in our good conduct. If, therefore, we humbly submit to his commands, we shall both experience the taste of heavenly love more sweetly in the throat of our mind and continually obtain an increase in good works. We shall also, with his help, be defended in temptations so that we do not fail. This is what follows:

And your foot will not stumble. For “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8).

If you sleep, you will not fear; you will rest, and your sleep will be sweet. Do not fear sudden terror or the powers of the wicked rushing upon you.

For the Lord will be at your side, and he will guard your foot lest you be captured. The literal sense is clear: the person who remembers that he lives innocently and justly before God sleeps and wakes securely, rests and walks securely. But when the righteous person sleeps in death, he not only fears none of the powers of evil spirits but also rests in peace and securely awaits the day of resurrection, because he has God everywhere as his protector and guardian. Thus it is in the psalm: “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me” (Ps. 22).

Do not withhold good from the one who is able to do it; if you are able, do good yourself. We marvel that those whom we remember as once small and unlearned have now become so illustrious.

[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0695D] The end of the third chapter and the beginning of the fourth are missing.]

## CHAPTER IV

[lacuna] And he taught me and said: Let your heart receive my words. Whoever rereads the Book of Chronicles will find that David the father gave such admonitions to Solomon. But why does Solomon call himself an only child before his mother, when Scripture testifies that a uterine brother preceded him, unless it is because that child, having been born soon before and dying without a name, was as though he had never existed?

And acquire prudence in all your possessions. Remember to act wisely in everything good that you possess. Or: “In all your possessions acquire prudence”—despise everything earthly that you possess, provided that you gain wisdom. Solomon himself asks for this when, given a choice, he preferred love of wisdom to all things; and in the Gospel, the person who sought the precious pearl, after finding it, sold everything he had and bought it.

He will give increase of graces to your head; an illustrious crown will protect you. This is clear concerning Solomon: when he despised everything for the sake of wisdom, having received wisdom he shone with the elevation of greater glory. But if [perhaps “if” is missing] we embrace wisdom in our head—that is, in the governing faculty of the mind—the greater grace of the Spirit is increased, and in the future the crown of life will also be given. Having explained what he had received as words from the Father, he returns to teaching his hearer the wisdom with which he began.

Listen, my son, and receive my words, so that the years of your life may be multiplied. That is, so that you may receive the gifts of eternal life.

I will lead you along the paths of righteousness; when you enter them, your steps will not be cramped. The paths—that is, the actions—of righteousness seem narrow and confined when they are first begun. But when they make progress, they already seem spacious and broad through habit, as the Psalmist testifies. After he had said to the Lord in his foolishness, “Because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16), he later sang, already making progress: “I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118). Therefore, even if the paths of righteousness seem narrow to you when you begin to enter them, once you have entered them your mental steps will not be confined; rather, as the Lord says, you will find that his yoke is easy and his burden light. The reprobate enter the broad way in this life, but on the last day, with hands and feet bound, they will be cast into darkness. The feet of the elect, however, are directed into the way of peace.

And when you run, you will have no stumbling block. The more eagerly you run to fulfill God’s commandments, the less you will fear adversities that might hinder you. For all who toil in wicked action find a stumbling block in the middle of their course, because, suddenly and without foreseeing it, they are snatched away to punishment.

They eat the bread of impiety and drink the wine of iniquity. Through their criminal actions the wicked delight as though in dishes set before them. Indeed, they drink the wine of the condemned and rejoice in removing ears of grain from the hungry, as Holy Scripture testifies to be the custom of the impious.

But the path of the righteous is like shining light, proceeding and growing until the perfect day. The works of the righteous are carried out in the light of knowledge, and they lead to eternal life, which is the perfect day.

The way of the wicked is dark; they do not know where they will fall. The apostle John says of them: “The one who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him; but the one who hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2). In contrast, it is said above to the wise person, “When you run, you will have no stumbling block” (Prov. 4), that is, no scandal.

With all vigilance guard your heart, because from it life proceeds. There are people who seem to live rightly to human beings, but because they do not act with a right intention, their perverse intention is rejected by God, who looks upon the heart, as is the life that was believed to be good. Therefore, guard the purity of your heart with every diligence, because the manner of your life will be assessed according to its examination.

Remove from yourself a wicked mouth, and let lips that slander be far from you. This should be understood in two ways: guard your own mouth so that it does not speak anything wicked, and guard your lips so that they do not become accustomed to slander; also flee from others whom you know to be subject to this vice, lest they corrupt you.

Let your eyes look straight ahead, and let your eyelids go before your steps. Learn carefully the way of justice in which you ought to walk, and in everything you plan to do, diligently foresee what end it will reach. This is what it means for the eyelids of eyes that see straight to go before your steps: to anticipate through attentive thought the good work you are about to do and, by meditation, to foresee whether it is according to God.

Direct the path for your feet. That is, do not go astray in your actions or in your faith.

And all your ways will be established. Do not be moved from your good purpose by fickleness of mind. Hence the Apostle also says: “Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1 Cor. 15).

Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. The right way is understood as the good way, and the left as the reprobate way. We are therefore forbidden not to walk on the right way, but to turn aside toward the right. A person turns aside toward the right when he is unjust; toward the left when he wishes to claim for himself that he is righteous. He turns aside toward the right when he presumes upon his own strength; toward the left when, because of his weakness, he despairs of being able to be saved. He turns aside toward the right when he serves folly; toward the left when he wishes to be wiser than one ought to be. The same understanding applies to the other virtues and vices.

Turn your foot away from evil. That is, do not deviate from the truth either in this direction or in that, because the virtues require discernment, and every excess is a vice.

For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right. That is, he chooses them; they please him. Therefore he will say to those who displease him and are rejected: “I do not know you” (Matt. 7), which means: “I have not chosen you; you do not please me.”

But he himself will make your course straight, and he will lead your journeys onward in peace. If you turn your foot away from evil, and, with the Lord’s help, strive to do the good things I have taught, he will graciously assist your efforts, so that you may walk rightly now and then be able to reach everlasting peace.

## CHAPTER V

My son, attend to my wisdom and incline your ear to my prudence. Up to this point he had generally admonished his hearer. From here, under the figure of a prostitute, he prohibits him from the wickedness of heretics.

So that you may guard your thoughts, and your lips may preserve instruction. The thoughts by which you believe correctly; the lips by which you profess that same faith in simple, customary, and ecclesiastical words. But according to the literal sense as well, the person who clings to a prostitute defiles even his lips, whether by kissing or by speaking shameful things.

For the lips of a prostitute are a dripping honeycomb. When the sweetness of wisdom resounds in the mouth of a heretic not merely to the point of sufficiency but to excess, falsehood is regarded as truth by fools because it is seen to be expressed skillfully.

And her throat is smoother than oil. Catholic faith is consecrated by the oil of the Holy Spirit. Those who prefer their own opinions to the faith of the Fathers display their throat as smoother than oil. The point is also clear concerning the prostitute, since she seeks both sweetness of speech and beauty of body in order to capture the wretched.

But her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword. A drink of wormwood grows bitter inside, in the entrails; a sword strikes the limbs outside. Therefore, to show that at the final punishment the wicked will burn inwardly and be surrounded outwardly by punishments for their sins, he asserts that they will be tormented by the bitterness of wormwood and cut down by the sword. Why the sword is called two-edged, the Lord explains when he says: “But fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10).

Her steps are wandering and untraceable. The notions of heretical deception are wandering, because some deny that Christ is God, others that he is human; some deny that he assumed flesh, others that he had a soul; some confess that he was born from a virgin, others deny it; some deny the Holy Spirit, others that God is the Father; others prohibit confessing that forgiveness should be granted to sinners. This pestilence spreads into so many paths that its number cannot be fully investigated. Catholic truth, however, is neither wandering nor untraceable, because it is known as one and the same truth by the faithful throughout the whole world.

Keep your way far from her, and do not approach the doors of her house. The Apostle also says, “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6), because the first remedy of this life is to remain far from those whose presence either inclines toward vice or contributes to it. But it benefits weak hearers to be completely separated from listening to heretics.

Do not give your honor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel. Do not subject the honor with which you were created in the image of God to the will of unclean spirits, nor spend at the pleasure of the pitiless adversary the span of life that you have received. For whoever is subjected to any crime is thereby enslaved to the dominion of evil spirits.

Lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your labors be in another’s house. Do not assist the works of demons by applying either the ingenuity of your mind or the strength of your body to committing crimes. Do not increase another’s house—that is, the number of the lost—by adding yourself to it. He aptly said, “Let your labors be in another’s house,” because there are people who, according to the Prophet, labor in order to act wickedly; and if only it were hidden how much labor heretics undertake against the Church!

And you will groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body. This should be placed before the preceding words; the sense is: “Lest perhaps . . .” Therefore, preserve yourself chaste, lest you be forced to groan in punishments when not only carnal pleasures have passed away, but also, once the body itself has been abandoned, the soul is compelled to give an account of everything it did through the body. Yet this also often happens in the present life: those who in youth dispersed their possessions by living luxuriously may fail through poverty in old age; and, as the heat of the flesh cools and the flower of youth withers, they see others using the possessions that they had sold for lust, and in late repentance they say what follows:

Why did I hate discipline, and why did my heart not accept correction? By discipline he means the faith of the Church; by corrections, the rebukes by which heretics are reproved for having departed from the Church. The literal sense concerning fornicators is also clear.

I was almost involved in every evil in the midst of the Church and the synagogue. “Church” and “synagogue” are Greek names and signify the same thing in Latin: an assembly of many people gathered together. If they are distinguished more precisely, *ecclesia* means “convocation,” while *synagoga* means “gathering.” The former people of God were called by both names. Now, however, for the sake of distinction, that people is called the synagogue, while ours is called the Church—rightly, because of the greater faith and knowledge, since an irrational creature too can be gathered. Thus God said: “Let the water be gathered into one gathering” (Gen. 1). But only a rational and sentient creature can be summoned.

Sometimes, however, these names also signify assemblies of evil people. Hence the saying: “Fire blazed in their synagogue, and I hated the assembly of the wicked” (Ps. 105). Therefore, when the contemptor of wisdom says in late repentance, “I was almost involved in every evil in the midst of the Church and the synagogue,” he seems, as he considers the magnitude of his condemnation, to recognize that there was scarcely any crime in which he himself was not entangled, since he deserved to undergo such torments. And this added to the accumulation of his misery: he was not the least among sinners but rather stood in the middle, almost as their leader. Certainly, although bodily present in the midst of the gatherings of the saints, he did not fear living a life alien to them. This should also be understood specifically of heretics, since neither the sayings nor the examples of the ancient or the recent Fathers were able to recall them from error.

Drink water from your own cistern and flowing water from your own well. Enjoy the affection and devoted services of your own wife.

Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets. Give your son and daughter in marriage to others, and do this openly, with many people aware of it.

Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share in you. Retain alone in your power the marriages by which you join your children to others; do not allow prostitutes and harlots to share in your offspring.

Let your vein be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth. Preserve such temperance with the woman whom you received as a young man, and preserve it when she has grown old, so that you may rightly obtain the blessing of faithful chastity in your children.

A most dear doe and a most pleasing fawn. Let that wife always be most dear to you who, like a doe pursuing serpents, pursues prostitutes and drives them from her home. Let a son be born from her, himself a most pleasing lover of chastity.

Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times. Take continual delight in her love. He does not teach that one should always persist in marital intercourse, but he urges that, while the first wife is alive, one should neither take another nor ever join oneself to a prostitute.

In another sense, the earlier statement, “Drink water from your own cistern and flowing water from your own well,” teaches that one must beware of heretics and attend to the guardianship and reading of the Scriptures. Preserve, he says, the knowledge that you preach to others yourself, and pour it out through the irrigation of your speech.

Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets. Once you have preserved them yourself, then preach to others as well, and distribute the divine utterances among a great multitude of hearers according to each person’s capacity.

Keep them for yourself alone. We divide the waters in the streets and yet possess them alone when we pour preaching broadly into the world but have no desire whatsoever to gain human praise through it.

Let strangers not share in you. Unclean spirits share in the teacher when, while he preaches, they corrupt his mind through the arrogance of pride, through heresy, or through any other vice. He alone possesses the waters when, faithfully joined to the members of the Church, he keeps himself free from the company of strangers.

Let your vein be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth. Let your teaching, and all who are born from it, be in the blessing of the Church; and rejoice with her to whom you have been joined from youth—that is, from the beginning of your time of believing. A most dear doe and a most pleasing fawn: let her breasts intoxicate you at all times; take continual delight in her love. The most dear doe—or “most pleasing,” as some books have it—is the holy Church, which is accustomed to hate and crush the serpent’s teaching. The most pleasing fawn is her people, delightful through the variety of their virtues and always inflamed by emulation toward that same chaste faith. We are intoxicated by her breasts when we are instructed against the deceits of heretics through the pages of both Testaments. To take continual delight in her peace and love is a great occasion for practicing the virtues.

Why are you seduced, my son, by a stranger, and embraced in the bosom of another? This should be understood both of the prostitute and of heresy.

The Lord observes the ways of a person and considers all his steps. Let adulterers not think that they can be concealed by the darkness of night or by walls; nor let heretics think that their volumes can be hidden, because darkness will not be darkened before the Lord, and night will be illuminated like day.

His iniquities capture the impious person, and he is bound by the cords of his sins. There is a distinction between a sinner and an impious person. Everyone who falls into either small or great crimes is called a sinner. An impious person, however, is one who either never received the faith or, through the enormity of his crimes, has been anathematized from the faith he received. This includes heretics and Catholics entangled in public crimes. They are bound by the cords of their sins and perish through the unceasing increase of their wickedness. For just as a person making a rope continually increases it by twisting and winding strands together, so the twisted structure of evil works grows.

Such are the books of heretics: by joining perverse things to perverse things, they do nothing by writing except bind themselves more tightly.

He himself will die because he did not have discipline, and he will be deceived by the multitude of his folly. Because he had discussed much concerning adultery and heretics, he shows in his customary concluding manner what the end of such people is: they advance toward eternal death because they hated the discipline of life. He calls their folly a “multitude” because heretics claim to be wiser than the holy Fathers, or because the wicked, while doing works of darkness, think either that the Lord does not see them or that they can easily endure his wrath.

## CHAPTER VI

My son, if you have pledged yourself for your friend, you have given your hand as surety to a stranger. The literal sense is plain: he advises the person who has stood surety for a friend to urge that friend anxiously to repay the money he owes, so that both he and the friend may be freed from the creditor. Allegorically, in this section he instructs the teacher how he ought to conduct himself, and in the following section he instructs any unoccupied person. For the teacher is told: “If you have pledged yourself for your friend, you have given your hand as surety to a stranger.” This means plainly: if you have accepted responsibility for a brother’s soul, placing it at risk through your conduct, you have already bound your mind to the care of an anxiety that previously was absent.

You are ensnared by the words of your mouth and captured by your own speech. Since, when you are compelled to say good things in preaching to those entrusted to you, you must first keep yourself what you have said.

Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor. Run about, hasten, rouse your friend. Remember not only to remain vigilant by living well yourself, but also to separate through preaching the one over whom you preside from the torpor of sin.

Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber. A person gives sleep to his eyes when he entirely neglects the care of his subjects. He lets them slumber when he recognizes their blameworthy deeds but, because of weariness of mind, does not correct them with the rebuke they deserve.

Rescue yourself like a doe from the hand, and like a bird from the snares of the fowler. As a bird seeks to escape from a snare, or a doe from the hand of one who captures it, so strive to free yourself from the pledge of your hearer’s life by instructing him for his salvation. Indeed, because the doe is an animal naturally clean, swift in running, and keen in sight, it is called in Greek *dorkas* (δόρκας), from *derkein* (δέρκειν), “to see.” A bird is accustomed to seek high places by flying. Therefore, when you are occupied in teaching those under you, strive to be clean from every sin, energetic in good works, perceptive in detecting the snares of evil people, and supported by the wings of the virtues, so that, when the task of preaching has been completed, you may deserve to fly upward and enter the pastures of heavenly life.

Go to the ant, you lazy person, and consider its ways and learn wisdom. Here he urges every unoccupied person that, if he is not sufficient to teach others, he should at least not neglect to care for himself; and if he cannot be taught wisdom by a human being, he should learn from the ant the wisdom of working.

Although it has no guide, teacher, or ruler, it prepares food for itself in summer and gathers in the harvest what it will eat. If such a tiny animal, lacking a ruler and devoid of reason, foresees the future for itself under the guidance of nature, how much more ought you, created in the image of God and called to see his glory, assisted by the teaching of teachers and having the Creator himself as your guide, to gather in the present the fruits of good works by which you may live eternally in the future. This life is compared to harvest and summer because, amid the heat of temptations, it is the time for gathering the future rewards of merits. The day of judgment, however, is compared to the rigors of winter because then no opportunity remains for laboring for life; each person is compelled only to bring forth from the storehouse of his former conduct what he stored there. Hence the Lord also commands, saying: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath.” In winter, opportunity is lacking; on the sabbath, permission according to the law is lacking for gathering the fruits of life and escaping everlasting want.

How long will you sleep, you lazy person? When will you rise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep. How long, he says, will you sleep in vices? When can you rise to good works, while weighed down by harmful torpor and always saying, “Let me lie here a little longer, and afterward I will rise through repentance”? It happens that, while you continually postpone the good work, the Judge who will punish your evil deeds suddenly appears. This is what follows:

And poverty will come upon you like a traveler, and want like an armed man. Poverty and want are the final punishment, in which the condemned deserve none of the riches. It will come like a traveler because it is unforeseen and sudden; like an armed man because it cannot be resisted perpetually. The literal sense is clear: laziness is the nurse of poverty and want. But if you are diligent, your harvest will come like a fountain. The earthly fruits that we reap are not compared to a fountain but to a cistern, because they nourish the one who gathers them for a time and fail in due season. But for the person who is diligent in laboring for heavenly riches, his harvest comes like a fountain, because he receives an unfailing reward for his labors.

And want will flee far from you. For, he says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16).

A man who has apostatized, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he signals with his eyes, rubs his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil in his crooked heart, and at all times sows quarrels. He had spoken about heresies and other kinds of vices, had instructed the teacher, and had roused the sluggard; but now he rebukes the schismatic. Here it should be noted that, when he wished to describe the sower of quarrels, he first called him an apostate [Col. 0704A], because unless, in the manner of the proud angel, he had first fallen away inwardly from the presence of his Creator through the aversion of his mind, he would not afterward have come forth to sow quarrels. For it is rightly said that “he signals with his eyes, rubs his foot, and speaks with his finger.” The inner faculty is the guard that keeps the external members in due order; therefore, whoever has lost the stability of his mind flows outward into instability of movement and, by his external restlessness, shows that he has no inward root.

There are six things that the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests. He indicates, by sowing discord, the same person whom he described more fully above as hateful to the Lord. But when he speaks of the Lord’s soul, he speaks in human fashion, so as to signify that he hates such people with full intention and not lightly. So it is said in Isaiah: “Your new moons and your festivals my soul has hated” (Isa. I).

[Col. 0704B] Haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising the worst thoughts, feet swift to run to evil, one who utters lies, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers. He enumerates six capital crimes, yet, by comparison with the sower of discord, he sets them down as though they were lesser. For that deed is plainly more serious by which the unity and brotherhood joined together through the grace of the Holy Spirit are torn apart. Anyone may raise his eyes arrogantly, lie with his tongue, pollute himself with homicide, devise evil against his neighbor, subject his members to other crimes, or give false testimony [Col. 0704C] against someone; but this should not be considered identical with what he named above as “a lying tongue.” A lie can be told without being directed against one’s neighbor. Indeed, blessed Augustine teaches in the book he composed On Lying that there are eight kinds of lies. I say, then, that anyone who has been ruined may inflict evils of this kind either upon himself or upon others while the peace of the Church remains intact; but what Donatus and Arius and their followers did was more serious, for by sowing discord they tore apart the harmony of fraternal unity.

Keep, my son, the commandments of your father, and do not abandon the law of your mother. Now, under the guise of the adulterous woman, he forbids listening to heresy.

[Col. 0704D] Bind them continually upon your heart, and surround your throat with them. Hold God’s commandments fixed in your thoughts and in your speech. Fortify yourself on every side with the sweetness of these things, lest you slip with your tongue.

When you walk, let them go with you; when you sleep, let them guard you; and when you awake, speak with them. Let your meditation on the divine law be so constant that, whenever you are awake and occupied with something, you recall it with diligent attention; when you sleep, rest in its remembrance; and when you awake, call it first to mind. Thus it will happen that, while awake, you will neither offend, nor be harmed by nocturnal fear. Alternatively: when you walk in progress toward righteousness, let God’s commandments go with you, so that they may instruct you; when you sleep in death, let them guard your soul lest the enemy seize it; and when you awake in the resurrection, [Col. 0705A] speak with them, seeking the rewards that they promised you if you kept them.

Do not be captured by her signals. This is clear concerning the adulterous woman; but even if heretics appear to live well and conduct themselves appropriately, beware lest you be seduced by their doctrines.

For the price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread. Remember that the pleasure of fornication is brief, but the fornicator’s punishment is eternal. Just as a single loaf drives away hunger only for the day, and afterward the one who departed satiated after eating the bread becomes hungry again, so the one who enters a prostitute’s house dispels his lust for an hour, but after a little while it returns more fiercely.

Can a man hide fire in his bosom without his garments being burned? Permission to read the books of heretics is granted only to one who is so firmly established in [Col. 0705B] the Catholic faith that neither by sweetness of words nor by cunning can he be separated from it.

It is not a great fault when someone has stolen, and so forth. Theft is said not to be a great fault in itself, but by comparison with a greater one, namely adultery. Just as Jerusalem, which sinned more grievously, is told: “Sodom has been justified in comparison with you”—not because Sodom’s sins were nonexistent or few, but because Jerusalem sinned more abundantly.

For the jealousy and fury of a husband will not spare on the day of vengeance, nor will he yield to anyone’s prayers, nor accept many gifts as a ransom. This is to be understood of the Lord: he who now spares the reprobate will not spare them on the day of death; he will not yield to the prayers of those who cry out to him too late; nor will he accept gifts, since there will then be neither time nor opportunity for them. For he is jealous when anyone presumes to corrupt his bride, that is, the Church [Col. 0705C], or any faithful soul.

## CHAPTER VII

My son, keep my words, and so forth. This passage, like the preceding one, explains the matter more fully under the person of the harlot.

And my law as the apple of your eye. Guard carefully what I teach, as though you could see nothing rightly without it.

Bind it upon your fingers. Write it upon the tablets of your heart. By “fingers” he means actions; by “the tablets of the heart,” the breadth of thought. Finally, another translation reads: “Describe it upon the breadth of your heart.”

Say to Wisdom, “You are my sister,” and call Prudence your friend [Col. 0705D], so that she may guard you from the strange woman and from the foreign woman who makes her words sweet. Join Wisdom, that is, the teaching of the Church, to yourself with sisterly affection, so that it may preserve you from the pollution of heresy, which is proved foreign to the chastity of the Church.

For from the window of my house, through the lattice, I looked out, and I saw the little ones. Literally, it is clear that the gaze of wise teachers diligently observes the actions of the weak and of the strong. But the eternal Wisdom of God looks forth from heaven and sees all the sons of men. Solomon appropriately says that he looked out from the window of his house through the lattice in order to judge the deeds of the little ones. Whoever looks out through a latticed window is indeed able to consider fully the things taking place outside [Col. 0706A], yet those who dwell outside and below cannot see him. For this is what the Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

I consider a foolish young man who passes through the street near the corner. He calls the adulterer “young” not because of his age, but because of his instability. He passes through the street because he has abandoned the narrow way that leads to life; he is near the corner because he turns aside from uprightness.

And he walks near the way of her house. Because he has turned aside from the way of truth, he rightly approaches the way and house of the harlot—or of the heretic—which, as we have explained, is situated both in the street and near the corner.

In the darkness, as the day grows toward evening, in the night’s gloom and darkness. For such a man, through the blindness of his heart, [Col. 0706B] is already hastening toward the darkness both of sin and of condemnation.

And behold, a woman meets him, dressed like a prostitute and prepared to capture souls. All this is evident literally concerning the works of a prostitute. But heretical teaching attempts to deceive anyone whom it finds unwary and foolish. It appears in the dress of a prostitute because it shines with filthy eloquence. It is prepared to capture souls because, whoever it can associate with itself, it destroys by spiritual death.

Talkative and restless, unable to remain at peace. Desiring to disturb the peace of the Church.

Unable to remain in her house on her feet. For no heresy is content with its first disciples. They are its household, but it always seeks new people whom it may deceive [Col. 0706C].

Now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners. Outside, when it seizes pagans; in the streets, when it seizes the pleasure-seekers; near the corners, when it seizes other heretics.

She seizes the young man and kisses him. She tests the unstable man with the blandishments of deceitful words.

And she flatters him with an impudent face, saying: “I owed sacrifices for salvation; today I have paid my vows.” Literally, the meaning is clear: the prostitute confesses that she has always prepared a magnificent banquet [“very magnificent” in the text]. But heretics, in everything they do, either claim or desire to be considered to offer themselves as a sacrifice to God for their own salvation. For the Lord also said to his disciples: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John XVI).

[Col. 0706D] I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread over it embroidered coverings from Egypt. Beds woven from cords—or, according to another translation, from threads—are usually made better than those constructed from wood, leather, or any other material. By the bed woven from cords, therefore, the prostitute signifies the softness of repose. By the embroidered coverings from Egypt she also attempts the enticements of the eyes, by which, once they have been ensnared through a sinful gaze, she may more easily penetrate the secret places of the mind in order to seduce them. But because divine commandments are sometimes represented by the name “cords”—for by restraining us they bind us back from our pleasures—heretics promise, by weaving together heavenly words, to prepare for their hearers a salutary bed on which they may rest with a free heart from the tumult of vices. [Col. 0707A] In truth, however, they construct for them with those cords a place of perdition, where their feet and hands will be bound forever and they will be condemned. Concerning this the Lord says in Revelation: “I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornication. Behold, I cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation” (Rev. II).

By the embroidered coverings from Egypt, the ornament of eloquence and the cunning of dialectical art—which originated among the pagans—is understood. Through it the heretical mind boasts that it has woven for itself the bed of its crime out of the meaning of its deadly teaching, as a prostitute does.

I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon. Such people promise that they possess the fragrance of heavenly virtues, with which they will furnish their own hearts and those of their followers as though they were handsome beds [Col. 0707B], and so claim that they can say with the apostles: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II).

Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts (*uberibus*) until daybreak. Heretics boast that they will satisfy one another with the cups of holy teaching and be joined together by the grace of the virtues until eternal light follows their deeds.

For the man is not in his house; he has gone on a very long journey. “Christ,” they say, “is not bodily in the Church. Having risen from the dead, he ascended into heaven and left us the ministry of governing his Church, that is, his household.”

He took a purse of money with him. He carried with him the glory of resurrection and the splendor of immortality, by which he would gladden and enrich the citizens of that homeland.

He will return to his house on the day of the full moon. [Col. 0707C] At the time when the Church of his elect has completed its number, he will return for judgment.

Immediately he follows her, like an ox led to sacrifice. That is, like a fool who is himself led, unknowingly, to destruction.

And all the strongest have been slain by her. Such as Solomon, the wisest of men; Samson, the strongest; and David, the gentlest—all by a woman’s snare. Such also was Origen, by a heretical woman (*haeretica*). Whoever denies that, after the apostles, he was a teacher of the Church for as long as he held right understanding is in error.

Her house is the way to hell, penetrating the depths of death. But concerning the Church the Lord says: “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). By “the depths of death” he means the most severe torments of Gehenna, as though they were [Col. 0707D] narrower and darker places, into which heretics and fornicators are known to be plunged. So it is said concerning the saints who suffer for the Lord in this life: “The jailer put them into the inner prison” (Acts XVI)—that is, a harsher, fouler, and darker place.

## CHAPTER VIII

Does not Wisdom cry out, and does not Prudence give her voice? Has not the Lord spoken openly to the world and said nothing in secret? (John XVIII.) Why, then, neglecting his Gospel, do wretched people gather instead to listen to heresy or to the persuasion of lust, which whisper in a corner?

At the highest and lofty summits, standing beside the way, in the midst of the paths, near the gates of the city. On the mountain [Col. 0708A] he taught both his disciples and the crowds; he often preached along the roads to those who gathered and healed those who needed care. At the very gate of the city of Nain, while raising a dead man, he commended by the example of the miracle the words he had taught. Why, then, do you follow those who in hidden places raise their tongues against him?

At the very doors she speaks, saying: “O men, I call to you, and my voice is addressed to the sons of men.” She cries to men—that is, to vigorous hearers of the word, of either sex. For those who are feminine, that is, weak-minded, cannot receive the words of Wisdom.

Understand cunning, little ones, and pay attention, you who are foolish. This is manifestly about the Lord, since while he himself was in the world he spoke his word to every age, sex, and condition. Indeed, he even cried out while standing in the temple: “If [Col. 0708B] anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII). And now, through the teachers of the Church—for they are his city’s gates—he preaches to wise men and women, to the foolish, to the old, and to the little ones. False teaching, by contrast, secretly and privately seeks those whom it can seduce.

Listen, for I am about to speak of great things. Great indeed, because he both promised and guaranteed the kingdom of heaven, taught the faith of the Holy Trinity, and proclaimed countless other things that the prophets left for him to speak.

And my lips will be opened so that they may proclaim what is right. His lips are the two Testaments, joined to one another by their harmonious testimony to the truth. When he himself appeared in the flesh, they were opened throughout the whole world for the proclamation of [Col. 0708C] salvation through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Receive my discipline, and not money; choose teaching rather than gold. “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matt. VI).

I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and I am present with learned thoughts. “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII).

Arrogance, pride, a crooked way, and a double tongue I detest. Arrogance and pride are found in those who consider themselves better than others; a crooked way in those who openly do evil; and a double tongue in those who possess nothing firm in the good things they say, but change their words according to the pleasure of their hearers.

[Col. 0708D] Counsel is mine, and equity; prudence is mine, and strength. Let no human presumption exalt itself: only God’s Wisdom possesses the fullness of the virtues, and from her human weakness has received whatever virtue it possesses.

Through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just; through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice. By “kings” he means the apostles or other saints, who know how first to govern themselves well and then the Church subject to them. He calls “lawgivers” the hearers of both Testaments and the later writers of the Church; “princes” and “the powerful,” the other teachers and rulers of the faithful. All of them possess whatever they are by means of Wisdom alone [Col. 0709A]. For he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me. The Gospel says similarly: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV). Those who watch early for Wisdom are those who, with the mind’s continually renewed zeal, strive to attain the vision of Christ.

With me are riches and glory, noble wealth and justice. By “noble wealth” he means lofty wealth, signifying heavenly gifts. For in Greek “noble” is *Yperephanos*, that is, “appearing above”; therefore Wisdom rightly says that *Yperephana* riches are with her, because whatever gifts are given from heaven to the faithful are proved superior to all the riches of the world. This is made still clearer by the addition of [Col. 709B] justice. For the unjust often possess earthly wealth and glory, but we await at the resurrection, as Peter says, “new heavens and a new earth according to his promises” (II Pet. III), in which justice dwells.

The Lord possessed me as the beginning of his ways. The ways of the Lord are his works, through consideration of which people arrive at faith or knowledge. “His invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made from the creation of the world” (Rom. I). His ways are also the illuminations by which he reveals himself both to angelic spirits and to human minds. At the beginning of these ways Wisdom was possessed, because at the beginning of the newborn creation he had the Son, who ordered all things together with him. But lest anyone think that the Son began to exist at the beginning of these ways [Col. 0709C] or at some time before them, he carefully added:

Before he made anything from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity; and from ancient times, before the earth existed, and so forth, until he says: “When he established the foundations of the earth, I was with him arranging all things.” A similar passage occurs in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. All things were made through him” (John I). Therefore let those perish who deny that the power of God and the Wisdom of God, namely Christ, was from the beginning—or rather, that before anything that can be spoken or conceived, he was begotten from the Father himself.

Another translation begins this passage as follows: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works.” The Fathers [Col. 0709D] understand this to have been said of the Lord’s incarnation, saying that, for the sake of a certain mystery, he said, “The Lord created me,” and not, “The Father created me.” “The flesh,” they say, “acknowledges the Lord; glory signifies the Father; creation confesses the Lord; love knows the Father.” “The beginning,” or “in the beginning of his ways.” And he himself says: “I am the way,” because, rising from the dead, he made a path for his Church to the kingdom of God and to eternal life. “For his works,” because he came to redeem the works of the Father and free them from slavery to corruption: Christ’s flesh was for the works, while his divinity was before the works.

And I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times. Playing in the inhabited world, and my delight was to be with the sons of men. By “playing” he means rejoicing. He was therefore playing before the Father day by [Col. 0710A] day, because, as the prophet says, from the beginning, from the days of eternity, he rejoiced to be one with the Father (Mic. V). He was playing at all times in the inhabited world because, when the times of the world and of creation began to exist, the Son himself remained what he was with the Father. This is said so that no one might claim that he began together with creatures and times. And his delight is to be with the sons of men because he desires to rest in their love and to lead us, through the grace of our good works, to see him.

Blessed is the man who hears me, who watches daily at my doors and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway. He calls the Holy Scriptures and their teachers his doors and the posts of his doorway, without which we cannot enter the life he promises.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0710B] Wisdom built herself a house. Since he had spoken sufficiently about the eternity of Christ’s divinity, he adds a discussion of the humanity he assumed. Wisdom therefore built herself a house because the Son of God himself created the man whom he would receive into the unity of his person.

She hewed out seven pillars. He raised up churches throughout the world through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. They uphold her house—that is, the mystery of her incarnation—by believing, worshiping, and preaching, lest its memory be removed through the wickedness of the faithless [the reading *in probitate* is uncertain]. Or, certainly, the house of Wisdom is the Church of Christ, while the pillars are the teachers of the holy Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, such as Jacob, Cephas, and John. Wisdom hewed out these pillars because she raised up the minds of preachers, separated from [Col. 0710C] love of the present age, to bear the structure of that same Church.

She sacrificed her victims. She preserved the Church through her own sufferings; or she permitted the lives of preachers to be slaughtered in persecution. These victims are opposed to the victims of the harlot, to which she invites fools, as we read above when she says: “I owed sacrifices for salvation; today I have paid my vows.”

She mixed her wine and set her table. To those unable to grasp the secrets of his divinity, he disclosed the mysteries of the humanity he assumed, and, opening to us the nourishment of Holy Scripture, prepared it for us.

She sent her maidservants to call people to the fortress and to the walls of the city. He chose weak and despised [Col. 0710D] preachers, who would gather faithful peoples for the buildings of the heavenly homeland above.

“If anyone is little, let him come to me.” And she spoke to the foolish. By “little ones” he means the humble; by “foolish,” those who possess nothing from the arrogance of worldly wisdom. He calls such people so that his teaching may make them wise and exalted.

Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. In the bread, the divine utterances are expressed; in the mixed wine, the joined natures of his divinity and humanity in the one person of Christ are represented, as stated above. Or, certainly, in the bread of his body and the mixed wine of his most holy blood, the mystery by which we are nourished at the altar, that is, at his table, is shown.

[Col. 0711A] Abandon childishness and live, and walk in the ways of prudence. After offering the meal, he adds counsels for life, so that those whom he has refreshed with the mysteries of his incarnation may also be instructed by the words of his teaching.

Whoever instructs a scoffer does himself an injury, and whoever rebukes the impious brings a blemish upon himself. It is as though you asked: Why did Wisdom invite little ones and the foolish above all others to her banquet? “For this reason,” she says, “because the one who tries to impress the word of wisdom upon someone who refuses to hear labors in vain, since that person believes himself wiser than his teacher and greater than he.”

Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you. It is not to be feared that, when rebuked, the scoffer may heap insults upon you; rather, one must take care that he does not become worse by being driven into hatred. Therefore, at times you should refrain from correcting him [Col. 0711B]—not out of fear for yourself, but for the sake of his love.

Rebuke the wise man, and he will love you. By “wise man” he means one who is making progress, that is, a lover of wisdom, whom above he called little because of his humility. The perfectly wise person has no need to be rebuked.

A foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing nothing at all, sat at the doorway of her house, upon a seat. This woman is heresy, plainly opposed to Wisdom, which sang of her mysteries above. She too sat at the doorway of her house—that is, in teachers of falsehood—because through deception they introduce wretched people into the inner chambers of faithlessness. She sits upon a seat because she usurps for herself the chair of preaching. This is the chair of pestilence on which the blessed man [Col. 0711C] refuses to sit. In a high place of the city. He speaks also of Wisdom, because she gives her voice at the highest and loftiest summits; but the former is raised up in the sublimity of virtues, while this one is lifted up by the arrogance of self-exaltation.

To call passersby who walk along the way and proceed on their journey. Heresy often calls Catholics to faithlessness when it sees them walking the straight path, wishing to cross the way of this world quickly and hasten toward the eternal homeland.

Whoever is little, let him turn aside to me, and she spoke to the foolish. Wisdom also appears to invite the little and the foolish to her [Col. 0712A] banquet in almost the same words. But there is a difference: Wisdom simply invites them to come to her, whereas the other urges those whom she calls to turn aside toward her. Wisdom summons to the right path of action those whom she sees wandering; the other teaches those walking rightly to depart from their journey and turn aside toward her.

Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasing. Wisdom openly set out her table and mixed her wine; but the foolish woman, possessing nothing pure, gathers all whom she can to stolen waters and hidden bread. The Catholic Church openly spreads before the world the banquets of the daily utterances, commands that the mysteries of Christ’s divinity and humanity be celebrated, and, in the mixed wine, offers her hearers both historical and allegorical knowledge, so that each may be refreshed according to his capacity with the drinks of life. [Col. 0712B] The teaching of heretics secretly sets its decrees above the public faith and confession. Possessing nothing spiritual, it boasts that it teaches a more pleasing knowledge than Catholic teachers, so that people may more readily hear and practice what the Church forbids to be said and believed openly. Thus the foolishness thought to be knowledge may be drunk more sweetly because its forbidden hearing is stolen. “Stolen waters” may signify the baptism of heretics, and “hidden bread” their sacrifice. Literally, however, the adulterous woman asserts that a forbidden and illicit union is sweeter in stolen waters and hidden bread.

And she did not know that giants are there, and that her ways are in the depths of hell. The adulterous woman does not know, and the heretic does not know [Col. 0712C] that unclean spirits inhabit their houses. Those who suffer eternal punishments in the depths of hell delight, as though at sumptuous banquets, in the deeds of the lustful and in the doctrines of heretics. But when the sacraments are rightly celebrated in the Church of Christ, when the word of Christ, who is the Wisdom of God, is heard and preserved, it is clear that angelic powers are present there and that they are the faithful’s fellow banqueters in the heights of heaven. “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (John VI).

## BOOK TWO: THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON

[Col. 0711]

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0711D] The Proverbs of Solomon. He introduces a new title because a new kind of discourse begins. He no longer discusses at length, as before, the individual aspects of good and evil, but describes the actions of both in alternating verses.

A wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother. Whoever faithfully preserves the mysteries received through faith gladdens God the Father; but whoever stains them by evil conduct or heresy grieves the mother, the Church.

[Col. 0712D] Treasures of wickedness will not profit, but justice will deliver from death. It often delivers from temporal death, as in the case of Daniel and the three young men, and it always delivers from eternal death. But treasures gathered through wickedness, even if they sometimes appear to rescue a person from bodily death, nevertheless bring greater harm through the wickedness by which they were acquired than benefit through what was given for the sake of life.

The Lord will not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger, and he will overthrow the plots of the wicked. Even if the wicked sometimes afflict the righteous with hunger or even kill them, [Col. 0713A] their soul will not be harmed, for the Lord consoles it in the life to come, or in the glory of his vision. He also turns those same plots of the wicked back upon them by judging them justly.

A slack hand produces poverty, but the hand of the strong prepares riches. Whoever lives negligently in this world will lack good things in the future; but whoever serves the Lord valiantly will be rewarded with the riches of eternal blessedness.

Whoever gathers in the harvest is a wise son, but whoever snores in summer is a son of shame. Whoever gathers the souls of the faithful for Christ is a wise son; indeed, the harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Whoever, in this acceptable time, grows torpid even about caring for his own salvation will be put to shame on the day of reckoning.

[Col. 0713B] Blessing is upon the head of the righteous, but iniquity covers the mouth of the wicked. To the righteous it will be said in judgment: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV). But the mouth of the wicked, which served feasting, drunkenness, and evil conversations, will be condemned by the iniquity it practiced. Finally, iniquity covered the mouth of the rich man who, placed in torments, sought relief for the tongue by which he was punished more severely for his many crimes.

The memory of the righteous is with praises, but the name of the wicked will rot. In this life they exalt the good, whether living or dead, with praises; but they detest both the deeds and the name of the wicked. In the life to come, the righteous live in the praises of God, while the honor, name, and praises of the reprobate are exchanged for the rotting punishments of Gehenna: “where their worm [Col. 0713C] does not die and their fire is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI).

Whoever walks simply walks securely, but whoever perverts his ways will be exposed. Whoever knows how to live simply despises all deceptive adversities, because he trusts that by this way he will come to joys, saying with the prophet: “The Lord is the defender of my life; whom shall I fear?” and so forth (Ps. XXVI). But whoever walks in crooked ways, whether he wishes it or not, is exposed and receives what his deeds deserve; for nothing is hidden that will not be revealed.

Whoever signals with his eye causes pain. Whoever mocks someone with the signals of his eyes does not escape without the pain of punishment or remorse.
