Of such people the Psalmist says: “Those who hate me without cause and were winking with their eyes” (Ps. XXXIV). Or certainly, “whoever signals with his eye causes pain,” [Col. 0713D] because a foolish son is grief to his mother.

A fool will be beaten by his lips. By his own lips, by which he deserved to be condemned; for “death and life are in the hand of the tongue.” Or he will be beaten by the lips of those from whom he received a sentence of condemnation because he could not be corrected. Thus the Psalmist, when he says, “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. CXIX), asks the Lord for both: that he himself may not have lying lips or a deceitful tongue, and that he may not be deceived by the wickedness and deceit of others.

The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life. And the Lord says concerning teachers: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

And iniquity covers the mouth of the wicked. The wicked are those who, [Col. 0714A] by defending and concealing either their own errors or those of their neighbors, prevent them from reaching healing. The prophet condemns this and prays that the Lord not incline his heart toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins.

Wisdom will be found on the lips of the wise, and a rod on the back of one who lacks understanding. The rod on the back is vengeance in what follows, that is, in the life to come; the famous blow by which the Philistines were struck on their buttocks expresses this well. Whoever does not wish to carry the rod on his back should carry wisdom on his lips, speak the praises of Christ, and proclaim his commandments. But because one ought always to praise the Lord, though not always to teach, and because it is not fitting for the wise to teach everyone everything he knows, the text rightly adds:

[Col. 0714B] The wise conceal knowledge. They know, namely, that there is a time to be silent and a time to speak. Hence the prophet says: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled myself, and I was silent concerning good things” (Ps. XXXVIII); and the Apostle: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

But the mouth of the fool is near to confusion. For he either speaks good things disorderly or openly speaks evil.

The substance of the rich man is his city of strength; the poverty of the poor is their fear. The rich trust in riches as in a fortified city; the poor therefore fear lest their resources fail, because they know themselves to be needy. Spiritually, whoever is rich in God through good works trusts in him as in an impregnable city, because no enemy can overcome him. [Col. 0714C] But those who are constricted by a lack of virtues lack heavenly riches because, through harmful fear, they dread enduring hard labors for the Lord.

Lying lips conceal hatred, and whoever utters an insult is a fool. If, then, you desire to be truthful and wise, conceal neither hatred in the secrecy of your heart nor hatred through an insult of the mouth; rather, let your heart be filled with love and your mouth with truth.

As if in jest, a fool commits crime; but prudence is wisdom for a man. Prudence takes its name from foreseeing. Therefore, the fool is one who rejoices in crime. It belongs to the wise—and to one worthy of the name “man”—to foresee that laughter will be mingled with sorrow and that the joys of sin will be followed by the punishment of retribution.

[Col. 0714D] What the wicked fears will come upon him; the desire of the righteous will be granted. He speaks of the wicked person who sins knowingly. The wicked therefore fears seeing the strict Judge; the righteous desire to depart and be with Christ. The former fears being deprived of earthly joys and being punished with eternal vengeance; the latter fear that their sojourn may be prolonged and desire to receive the rewards for which they have struggled. For both, what they hold in their hearts will come to pass.

Like a passing storm, the wicked will not remain; but the righteous is like an everlasting foundation. He speaks of the persecutions of the Church by those who seek to overthrow the house of faith. But because that house is established on the true foundation, which is Christ, they themselves immediately perish.

As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who sent him. As the faithlessness of heretics causes annoyance and tears to good teachers, so the Catholic who lives badly is burdensome through his inertia to those who commanded him to show his faith by his works. The eyes and teeth are the preachers of the holy Church: they are accustomed both to foresee the right paths and to supply spiritual nourishment. Vinegar, which degenerates from wine, and smoke, which rises from fire and vanishes, figuratively indicate those who withdraw from the sweetness and charity of the Church through pride and sluggishness and then attack it even with their words. John speaks of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us,” and so forth.

The fear of the Lord will add days, but the years of the wicked will be shortened. Those who faithfully serve God will be given eternal light; but those who are enslaved to wickedness lose, together with this [Col. 0715B] life, the goods they loved.

The expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked will perish. It is clear that the righteous rejoice in expectation of the life to come, although they are troubled by the affliction of present distress; hence the saying: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounds me, my exultation” (Ecclus. 51). But the wicked, who think that they will find rest in the future—or, certainly, that there will be no existence after death—are deceived. Nor does this contradict the statement made above, that “what the wicked fears will come upon him.” For there are some who, knowing that a judgment of good and evil is to come, nevertheless sin through negligence, despair, or even deliberately. For such people, the destruction they fear will indeed come. There are others who believe that the evils they commit will either never be punished [Col. 0715C] or, because they judge their deeds to have been good, will be rewarded with a proper recompense. Of them it is rightly said: “The hope of the wicked will perish.” For he subsequently adds concerning those who sin knowingly:

“The strength of the simple is the way of the Lord, and terror to those who do evil.” If, he says, you cannot grasp the hidden meanings of Scripture, nevertheless do not despair of salvation; instead, walk in the way of the Lord, do the good things you know, and you will be numbered among the strong. But rightly let those tremble who disdain to do the right things they know, because certain evils remain for them to suffer.

## CHAPTER XI

“A deceitful balance is an abomination to the Lord, but an accurate weight is his will.” He speaks not only of a deceitful balance in the measurement of money, but also in judicial discernment. For whoever hears the case of a poor man one way, that of a powerful man another way, that of a companion one way, and that of a stranger another, plainly weighs with an unjust balance. So too does the person who judges his own good deeds better than those of his neighbors, and his own faults lighter, weigh with a deceitful scale. Likewise, the one who lays unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders but himself is unwilling to touch them with even one finger; and the one who does good publicly but evil in secret—is detested by the Lord for the injustice of a deceitful balance. But the person who acts sincerely in all things, who distinguishes one case from another with an even scale, clearly conforms to the will and action of the righteous Judge.

“Where there is pride, there too will be insult.” For the proud either behave insultingly, through contempt or ignorance of discipline, and inflict insults on their neighbors, or certainly because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23).

“But where there is humility, there is wisdom.” “You have hidden these things,” he says, “from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to infants” (Matt. 11)—that is, to the humble.

“When the wicked man dies, there will be no further hope.” Alas, Origen passes over this statement disastrously, since he believed that life would be given to all the wicked and sinners after the universal and final judgment. It should be noted, however, that although there is no hope of pardon for the wicked after death, there are nevertheless people who can be freed after death from lesser sins by which they died bound—either by being chastised with punishments or by being absolved through the prayers, almsgiving, and celebration of Masses offered by their relatives. But such things are done before the judgment and concern lesser offenses. Those who think that they will be freed only after a long period following the judgment are deceived, and perhaps the following statement applies to them:

“And the expectation of the anxious will perish.” There is one kind of anxiety by which the good are always girded for fulfilling God’s commandments; there is another by which the wicked, sinning knowingly, anxiously fear when they will be carried away to eternal punishment. Therefore the expectation of those who serve God with an anxious mind will rightly be crowned; but the expectation of those who despise God and, even before his judgment, condemn themselves while their own conscience accuses them will perish. This verse is rendered very differently in the ancient translation, which says: “The hope of a righteous dead man will not perish, but the glory of the wicked will perish.”

“The righteous man is delivered from distress, and the wicked is handed over in his place.” Every martyr is delivered from the distress of suffering after death, and the persecutor who afflicted him is handed over to punishment on his account. Jacob was crowned by martyrdom; Peter was delivered from prison; and Herod, who persecuted them, was visibly consumed by worms and invisibly carried away to the place “where their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66).

“The pretender deceives his friend with his mouth, but the righteous will be delivered by knowledge.” The heretic, pretending to teach Catholic doctrine, deceives his hearer. But those who rightly follow the truth of the Gospel will be delivered by Catholic knowledge, so that they may not be carried away by heretical deceit.

[Col. 0716D] “Whoever despises his friend is deficient in heart, but the prudent man will keep silent.” We should not despise or mock someone who is shown to love us sincerely, even if through lack of understanding he does something ineptly. Whoever does this is unworthy of wisdom. But every prudent person keeps silent publicly about such people’s faults and corrects them privately. This same point is pressed more firmly in the following verses:

“Whoever walks deceitfully reveals secrets, but whoever is faithful conceals his friend’s confidence.” Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother,” and so forth (Matt. 18). Hence the following is rightly added:

[Col. 0717A] “Where there is no governor, the people will fall; but where there are many counselors, there is safety.” Lest you think that, if you cannot correct your friend’s faults, you ought therefore to conceal them still further, he rightly says that a people without a governor will fall, but will be saved where there are many counselors. Thus he shows that what you cannot correct alone should be disclosed to several people, so that all may correct it through united effort.

“He will be afflicted by evil who guarantees a stranger.” The literal meaning is clear, but a person is a stranger to the company of the saints if he neglects to correct his sins through repentance. Whoever grants such people the grace of communion or promises them eternal life, because he has guaranteed a stranger, has plainly made himself worthy of punishment before the eyes of the strict Judge.

“But whoever guards against snares will be secure.” Secure in the future will be the person who is now rightly fearful, diligently cures his own faults through repentance, and keeps himself free from the society of the impenitent.

“An evil man who joins hand to hand will not be innocent.” Whoever joins hand to hand does not, in fact, accomplish anything. But an evil man who joins hand to hand will not be innocent, because even if he withdraws his hands from an evil action for a time, he cannot possess innocence of heart. Hence it is preceded by:

“An evil heart is an abomination to the Lord. But the seed of the righteous will be saved.” This is what was said above: “A faithful reward awaits the one who sows righteousness.” Or certainly, “the seed of the righteous will be saved,” because those who follow the examples of the righteous who came before them also follow their footsteps in order to see the joys of salvation. Concerning them Isaiah says: “All who see them will recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61).

“A beautiful but foolish woman is like a golden ring in a pig’s snout.” If you fix a golden ring in a pig’s snout, nevertheless the animal hastens to turn over the earth with its nose and plunge into a wallow of mud. Likewise, if a foolish woman has received beauty of face or dress, she nevertheless loves to turn her face toward low things, to carry her comeliness everywhere for the overthrowing of the little flowers of chastity, and to soil herself with the filth of pleasure.

Alternatively: Whoever acquires the ornament of divine utterances through meditation but pursues these things by living badly has a golden ring in a pig’s snout, yet does not cease, after the manner of swine, to dig up the earth, because he has stained with unclean action what he received through the fragrance of knowledge. Therefore such a soul is considered a beautiful but foolish woman: devoted to carnal allurements, she is beautiful through knowledge but foolish through conduct.

Alternatively, this may be understood because he saw heretical doctrine shining with the splendor of eloquence, yet not corresponding to a fitting understanding of wisdom. “A golden ring,” he says, “in a pig’s snout”—that is, beautiful and elaborate speech in the perceptions of a foolish mind. Gold hangs from its speech, yet, because of the weight of its earthly intention, it does not look upward in the manner of swine. He explained this by adding: “A beautiful but foolish woman” in understanding.

“The desire of the righteous is wholly good, but the expectation of the wicked is fury.” The righteous always desire righteousness to reign everywhere. But even when the wicked appear to cease from carrying out their wickedness, they nevertheless, according to the purpose of their savage mind, direct themselves toward inflicting the violence of fury on anyone at all. This is what was said above: “An evil man, hand in hand, will not be innocent”; likewise, “the expectation of the wicked is fury,” because anger often burns more fiercely when enclosed in silence within the mind.

“Some distribute their own possessions and become richer.” For they receive a hundredfold in the present age, and in the age to come eternal life.

“Others seize what is not theirs and are always in want.” “Always in want,” he says—not only in torments, where they do not receive even a drop of water with which they might be refreshed for a moment, but also in the present life, where, although they seize countless things, the miser is always needy.

“The soul that blesses will be made rich, and whoever gives others drink will himself also be given drink.” Whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives inwardly an increase of spiritual richness. And while he does not cease to intoxicate the minds of his hearers with sacred oil, he himself grows intoxicated with an abundant draught of grace.

“Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell it.” Whoever keeps within himself the words of holy preaching will be cursed among the peoples, because he is condemned for the punishment of many whom he could have corrected, solely through the guilt of his silence. He is the lazy and wicked servant who, for retaining the talent he had received, was sent into outer darkness. Those who sell grain are the people who impart the word of life to their hearers, from whom they receive the price of faith and confession. The Lord says: “Trade until I come” (Luke 19). Blessing comes upon their head when the Lord says to each person returning from such trade: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (ibid.).

“Whoever seeks good rises early in the right way, but whoever investigates evil will be overcome by it.” To seek the good things that you ought to do, by which you may reach heavenly goods, is to rise early in the right way—that is, as the light of knowledge increases, to gird oneself for good work. Or certainly, he rises early in the right way, that is, toward life, at the time of the resurrection, whoever now seeks good at the time of action. But whoever diligently investigates the evils he may say or do will then be held back by their weight from reaching the higher things of the kingdom.

“Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will sprout like a green leaf.” Whoever longs for present goods and gives no thought to the future will at the end lack both. But those who do good in the present in hope of future rewards rightly receive what they hope for. A green leaf on a tree signifies future fruits that it has not yet displayed; so the righteous sprout like a green leaf because, having been saved in hope, they do not cease to advance in the grace of faith and virtues until they reach the fruit of the recompense they desire.

“Whoever troubles his own house will possess winds, and whoever is foolish will serve the wise.” Whoever does not fear to disturb his mind with the tumult of harmful thoughts opens it to the blasts of evil spirits, by which he will be overwhelmed. And the fool who persecutes the wise serves him even by ruling over him, because by oppressing him he makes his patience more proven, so that, when the fool is condemned, the wise man may receive the prize for which he contended.

“The fruit of the righteous is the tree of life.” The reward of the righteous is the vision of Christ. He himself is Wisdom, of whom it was said: “She is the tree of life to those who embrace her”; and in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will grant to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2). The righteous now await this fruit, as long as they sprout like a green leaf, as was said above.

“And whoever receives souls is wise.” Whoever undertakes the care of souls for the Lord—to teach them when they go astray, to console them when they are sorrowful, to support the needy with temporal goods, to draw the resistant toward the remedies of salvation, or to govern those deprived of a shepherd, so that he may lead many to the Lord together with himself—such a person, I say, is wise. For through these things he provides for his own soul, so that he may reign more sublimely with the Lord.

“If the righteous man receives on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner?” If the holy martyrs suffered so much, what torments do you think await those unrighteous people who afflicted them? If Job, Tobias, and the other elect of God received so much adversity in this life, why are you troubled if affliction touches you briefly, when you lie so far beneath their footsteps? Indeed, although you ought neither to call yourself nor believe yourself wicked, you should not deny that you are a sinner—that is, that you have some sins, whether small or great, open or hidden. Rather, you ought to confess this, lest you deceive yourself and truth be unable to exist in you.

Therefore, if the righteous received on earth—Abel, martyrdom, and Job, an example of patience—how much more did the wicked, such as Antiochus and Herod, and the sinners in the Gospel, such as the paralytics, receive punishment, since they could be healed by the Lord only after their sins had first been forgiven? It should be noted that Peter placed this statement in his Epistle according to the ancient translation, saying: “And if the righteous man will scarcely be saved, where will the wicked and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4).

## CHAPTER XII

“Whoever is good will draw grace from the Lord, but whoever trusts in his own thoughts acts wickedly.” The connection between these verses is as follows: the one who is good does not trust in his own thoughts, but seeks the grace of the Lord and, through it, receives the ability to live devoutly. Whoever trusts in his own thoughts cannot be good. For whoever does not take care to ask for the grace of heavenly assistance rightly persists in wicked action.

“A diligent wife is a crown to her husband, but she who does things worthy of disgrace is rottenness in his bones.” The literal meaning is plain: a good and chaste wife gives honor to her husband. In all things, and through her virtues, she governs the household well and, as it were, adds grace to his crown. But the adulterous woman, even if she appears beautiful outwardly, inwardly pollutes her members with the stench of lust. Spiritually, however, the Church offers herself as no other crown than the crown of Christ. “All those who surround him will offer gifts,” and the son of Sirach speaks of the high priest himself standing beside the altar, “with a crown of brothers” around him. Or “bones”—that is, virtues—which the decay of an evil doctrine corrupts in the faction of heretics.

“The thoughts of the righteous are judgments, but the counsels of the wicked are deceitful.” The righteous carefully examine their actions to see whether they please the Lord, lest, because of insufficient vigilance, the heavenly Judge should secretly arrange adversity against them, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11). But the reprobate, forgetting the fear of God, force their plans toward the fraud they intend to commit.

“Turn the wicked, and they will be no more; but the house of the righteous will remain.” When the wicked are turned from this life, they will no longer be what they were, because after death they do not find what they believed they would find. Deceived in their hope, they receive torments instead of rewards. But the house of the righteous—that is, the Church, which partly journeys inwardly and partly reigns in heaven—never fails. Whatever members of it arrive there from here, they find there the joys they had hoped for.

Alternatively: “Turn the wicked, and they will be no more.” There was much wickedness among the gods of the nations, much among the sects of heretics, much in the tricks of magicians, and much in the persecutions of pagans. But when these things were overthrown by the Lord’s gift, their memory of wickedness was also removed. Their foolish writings and doctrines themselves were carried off by fire, as we read that happened at Ephesus in the time of the apostles.

“But the house of the righteous will remain,” because no length of time has been able either to hide or remove the holy Church, corrupt anything from its Scriptures, or violate its faith in any respect. It may also be understood in this way: “Turn the wicked, and they will be no more”—turn them from wickedness, and they will no longer be wicked but righteous. For this reason another translation says: “Wherever the wicked turns, he will be destroyed.” In contrast, it is said of the saints: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Rom. 8).

“A man will be known by his doctrine.” Scripture commonly calls those who are endowed with divine virtues “men.” Hence the Apostle says: “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully” (1 Cor. 16). Therefore each person will be known to be a man by his doctrine, because if he teaches what is right and fulfills it in his actions, he is shown to be holy.

“But whoever is empty and senseless will be exposed to contempt.” [Col. 0720D] For he has despised the strength of a manly spirit.

“Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself than the renowned man who lacks bread.” Better is the unlearned and simple brother who, by doing the good things he knows, earns life in heaven than the person renowned for learning, who has even held the office of teacher of Scripture but lacks the bread of love. Concerning that part of love which pertains to one’s neighbor, he adds next:

“The righteous man knows the souls of his animals”—that is, he pities and sympathizes with the dullness and weakness of those entrusted to him.

“But the inward parts of the wicked are cruel.” They not only fail to sympathize with their subjects but also act according to what the Lord says: “They beat the boys and the maidservants, saying, ‘My master delays in coming’” (Matt. 24).

“Whoever works his land will be satisfied with bread, but whoever pursues idleness is utterly foolish.” Whoever exercises his soul in spiritual pursuits will now be filled with virtues and then with the banquets of rewards. But whoever refuses to labor for the salvation of his soul will then be counted among fools, even if now he appears glorious through either divine or worldly wisdom.

“The desire of the wicked is the stronghold of the worst.” The wicked desire to imitate those who went before them in evil and to speak about their life and deeds. Or certainly, the desire of the wicked is the stronghold of the worst because all his desire tends toward this—even though he does not know it—that he may be shut up with the former unrighteous in the prison of eternal death. But because such people encounter an end they least foresee, he says in contrast concerning the good:

“But the root of the righteous will prosper.” For the faith and love of the elect, by which they are rooted in Christ, do not deceive them. Rather, continually increasing toward greater perfection, they will receive in the future more than they know how to hope for.

“Everyone will be filled with good things from the fruit of his mouth.” The fruit of the mouth is good speech, for whoever speaks evil does not produce fruit with his mouth but harm. Therefore everyone who speaks good things will be endowed with eternal goods—provided that in his conduct he does not contradict what he says. This is precisely what he adds with vigilance:

“And according to the works of his hands it will be repaid to him.” For a teacher’s speech does not become fruitful in any other way unless he himself first does the good things he teaches.

“A fool immediately displays his anger, but whoever conceals an injury is shrewd.” Whoever desires to avenge himself in the present is a fool; whoever, for the Lord’s sake, disregards an injury is wise. Another translation renders this verse as follows: “The fool declares his anger at the same hour, but the shrewd man conceals his disgrace.”

It does not, however, determine that the disgraceful passion of anger should be concealed from the wise, as though it were to be hidden in such a way that, while condemning its haste, it did not forbid its delay. Rather, if anger should burst forth through the necessity of human weakness, it judged that it should be concealed so that, while wisely covered for the moment, it may be removed more wisely and destroyed forever. For this is the nature of anger: when delayed, it weakens and dies; when expressed, it blazes ever more fiercely.

“There is one who makes a promise and is pierced as if by the sword of conscience.” Some promise that they will obey the truth, but when a frightening or flattering temptation presents an obstacle, they abandon what they began, yet their conscience is pierced as if by the sword of their promise.

“But the tongue of the wise is health.” For both they themselves advance toward life by fulfilling the good things they promise, and by preaching they show others what they should follow.

“The lip of truth will be firm forever, but whoever is a sudden witness fashions a lying tongue.” The faith of the Church will always remain. But whoever suddenly introduces new doctrines is a minister of heretical falsehood.

“A crafty man conceals knowledge.” Here “crafty” is understood positively—that is, as wise and prudent. Such a person sometimes deliberately conceals his knowledge, for two reasons: either because he is unable to speak to weak hearers as to spiritual people, but must speak to them as to carnal people; or because he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine.

“And the heart of fools provokes folly.” This happens when the wicked, desiring to know more than they ought, leap so far forward in meditation that they seize folly in place of wisdom. Or, attempting to teach others what they are not yet able to grasp, they provoke them to even greater folly. Like people bringing sunlight to wounded eyes, they take away the little light that their hearers seemed to see.

“The hand of the strong will rule, but the slack hand will serve tribute.” The perfect not only overcome the battles of vices but also rule over the elect brothers through a greater grace of virtues. Those who are lax in spirit and do not fear becoming entangled in sins pay daily the tribute of vices to the devil, the worst tax collector. If they do not escape his dominion during life through repentance, then, after death, delivered to him, they are sent by him into the prison of eternal punishments, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel parable. Yet we should not despair of the correction of such people, since he immediately adds:

“Sorrow in a man’s heart will humble him, and he will be made joyful by a good word.” It is necessary that the sorrow of repentance first humiliate the sinner beneficially, and that afterward, through the judgment of the priest, the word of reconciliation granted to him may make him joyful.

“Whoever overlooks an injury for the sake of a friend is righteous.” If this is rightly said of a general generosity in money and of a sincere friend, how much more worthy of the crown of righteousness is the person who, for the sake of the one who said, “I say to you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body” (Matt. 10), either sells what he possesses and gives it to the poor, gladly accepts the seizure of his goods, or hands over his own flesh to be mortified or killed in suffering.

“But the way of the wicked will deceive them.” This happens when they rejoice either in retaining what is their own or in seizing what belongs to others. Hence it is rightly added:

“The fraudulent man will not find profit, and a man’s substance will be the price of gold.” Money acquired through fraud brings more loss to the soul than profit to the treasury. Whoever knows how to distribute his own substance for the Lord will receive heavenly gifts in place of earthly things, with the Lord himself granting the reward.

Alternatively: “The fraudulent man will not find profit, and a man’s substance will be the price of gold.” The person who, with a fraudulent mind, pretends to be good while living wickedly in secret will not find the goods of the life to come. But whoever truly acquires the substance of spiritual virtues will purchase from it the glory of the everlasting kingdom. This he states more plainly in the following words:

“In the path of righteousness there is life, but the crooked way leads to death.” The path of righteousness acquires the substance of virtues, by which the eternal glory of life—more precious than gold—is purchased. But the crooked way on which the fraudulent man walks, having lost the temporal profit he desired, leads toward the everlasting death he refused to foresee.

## CHAPTER XIII

“A wise son accepts his father’s instruction, but a scoffer does not listen when he is rebuked.” The difference between the wise and the fool is so great that the wise person may at some time, through progress in instruction, become capable of teaching the one who taught him; but the scoffer does not know how to listen even when he is rebuked.

“The lazy man both wishes and does not wish, but the soul of those who work will be made rich.” The person who wishes to reign with God but does not wish to labor for God is rightly marked by the name “lazy.” Rewards delight him when they are promised, but struggles frighten him when they are commanded. Concerning him James says: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James 1); and the son of Sirach: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclus. 2).

But those who carry out the Lord’s commands do so because their souls are refreshed by the perfect sweetness of heavenly things, according to the one who entreats the Lord, saying: “Let my soul be filled as with the richness of fat” (Ps. 62). Or certainly, “the soul of those who work will be made rich,” because those who toil for the Lord in devout labors will receive a heavenly and unfading reward after their labors.

“There is one who is as if rich, though he has nothing, and there is one who is as if poor, though he possesses many riches.” The man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day seemed rich to himself. But because he did not possess God, he discovered at the end that what he had possessed was nothing. Hence it is said of such people: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75).

Lazarus, by contrast, seemed poor, lying at the rich man’s gate and covered with sores. Yet he possessed many riches: he had the virtue of humility, and he carried in his heart the Creator of all riches, namely God. What true riches are worth, and what true poverty accomplishes, he reveals by adding:

“The riches of a man are the redemption of his soul, but whoever is poor does not endure rebuke.” Whoever wishes his soul to be redeemed from future wrath should gather the riches of good works. For whoever lacks such riches cannot endure the rebuke of the strict Judge. Concerning this the Psalmist asks: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger” (Ps. 30). The poor in spirit, however, are not rebuked by the Lord there; rather, they receive the blessing of eternal inheritance.

“The light of the righteous brings joy, but the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished.” The light of the righteous, which gives joy forever, is the hope of future things. The lamp of the wicked, which is suddenly extinguished, is the happiness of the passing world.

“Among the proud there are always quarrels, but those who do everything with counsel are guided by wisdom.” Heretics are always quarreling among themselves, and the other reprobate also quarrel, since they do not know the unity of faith and truth. But the faithful, who do not cease to enjoy the counsel of the divine utterances, are guided by the moderation of wisdom, which does not allow them to quarrel.

“Substance acquired hastily will diminish, but whoever gathers little by little with his hand will multiply.” Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation (1 Tim. 6), nor do they possess forever the riches they acquire or desire. But whoever persists in righteous labors in order to receive the substance of heavenly rewards will receive manifold gifts of heavenly blessedness. Concerning this he appropriately adds:

“Hope that is deferred afflicts the soul, but desire that comes is a tree of life.” As long as the hope of eternal things is deferred, it afflicts the souls of the faithful, either because the goods they love are delayed or because the evils they endure are imposed. But when what they desire has come, they easily forget what they had endured, because they begin to live forever with their Redeemer, whom they sought with their whole intention. He himself is the tree of life to those who embrace him.

“Whoever reproves a matter binds himself for the future.” Whoever reproves a good matter binds himself for the future, because by doing what he ought not to have done he prepares for himself the punishment by which he will be bound. But the person who reproves an evil matter also binds himself for the future—not so that he may suffer punishment for the reproof, but so that after reproving it he may conduct himself more cautiously. For what he rightly criticizes in others he must not himself commit with impunity, as the Apostle cries out: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. 2).

[Col. 0724C] “But whoever fears the commandment will dwell in peace.” It is therefore better for each person to fear his own weakness, lest he violate the divine commands, than to tear apart the faults of others with a foolish mouth. The Apostle says again: “If a person is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6).

“The astute man does everything with counsel, but whoever is foolish will reveal folly.” When he teaches that everything should be done with counsel, “counsel” should be understood as divine counsel, implanted in the sacred utterances, rather than human counsel. The person who lives outside this counsel is foolish, even if he naturally appears astute and prudent. Concerning him it is rightly added:

“The messenger of the wicked falls into evil.” But he calls Arius, Sabellius, and the others angels—that is, messengers of Satan—who, because they neglected the counsel of the divine Scriptures, fell into the evil of the torments of Gehenna.

“But a faithful ambassador is health.” That is, every Catholic preacher acquires eternal health for himself and for his hearers.

“If desire is fulfilled, it delights the mind; fools detest those who flee evils.” Every desire, whether good or evil, delights the soul when it reaches fulfillment. But fools who rejoice in carnal desires detest those who, out of love for heavenly things, despise pleasures of the lowest sort.

[Col. 0725A] “Whoever walks with the wise will be wise, but the companion of fools becomes like them.” To walk with the wise is to imitate the actions of the wise. Therefore, however simple and uneducated a person may be, and even if he cannot grasp the secrets of wisdom, if he nevertheless follows the examples of the wise in his manner of life, he will rightly be numbered among the wise.

But whoever loves fools—not because they are human by nature, but because of their folly, since they are mimics, actors, or people of that sort—not in order to instruct and correct them, but in order to make them worse by encouraging them, such a person, even if he appears wise through intelligence or learning, will be marked as a companion of fools and held under condemnation.

“A good man leaves heirs, sons and grandsons, and the sinner’s substance is stored up for the righteous.” We often see good people die without children. Indeed, the Lord promises greater rewards to those who have preferred the chastity of virginity to the begetting of children. Yet the substance of the righteous is also taken away by sinners. The Apostle glorifies those who gladly accepted the seizure of their possessions.

Therefore this should be understood spiritually: the good and righteous Lord, ascending into heaven through his Passion, left as heirs of his teaching the apostles and their successors. The multitude of the nations, which had been the substance of the devil, was converted to his faith. For Christ entered the house of that wicked and strong adversary, crushed him with greater power, seized the weapons in which he trusted, and distributed the spoils, as he himself testifies in the Gospel.

Or certainly, the sinner’s wisdom was stored up for the righteous when the kingdom of God was taken away from the Jews and given to a nation producing its fruits.

“There is much food in the new fields of the fathers, gathered by others without judgment.” Whoever diligently devotes himself to gathering riches and, after accumulating them, does not distribute them to the poor for the redemption of his soul, but reserves them for others to distribute after him, acts without right judgment. This is said literally in the preceding verse: “The sinner’s substance is stored up for the righteous.” It applies especially when a person has enough to live on by right of his paternal inheritance and no necessity compels him to gather money. This is what he means by “much food in the new fields of the fathers.”

According to the spiritual meaning, there is much food of heavenly nourishment in the sayings and examples of the venerable fathers. The person who busies himself with reading, meditating on, and explaining these things, yet serves not his own salvation through them but rather that of others, acts without reason if he himself differs from what he reads either through reprehensible actions or through the impiety of heretical understanding.

Such a person acquires support not for himself but for others in the new fields—that is, in the works or sayings of the fathers cultivated by excellent instruction. Those who read his treatises discover through them the secrets of spiritual meaning by which inward realities are perceived. What follows appropriately suits both interpretations:

“Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but whoever loves him diligently instructs him.” A good father diligently instructs his son, and a Catholic teacher his disciple, so that he may not turn toward iniquity.

The ancient translators rendered the preceding verse as follows: “Righteous men will enjoy riches for many years, but the wicked will perish swiftly.”

“The righteous eats and fills his soul, but the belly of the wicked is insatiable.” The righteous receives the foods of wisdom that are shown to have arisen in the new fields of the fathers—that is, in the works and words of the righteous who came before—and he brings them to the nourishment of his soul by living well.

But “the belly of the wicked,” that is, the capacity of the heretics’ understanding, is insatiable, because, as the Apostle says: “Always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3). Why do they not deserve to be filled with knowledge? Because they are never refreshed by the foods of their fathers’ instruction, but gather these foods for others without judgment.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0726B]

A wise woman builds her house; but the foolish one tears down even what has been built, with her hands. Every faithful soul, and the catholic Church throughout the world, builds for itself a dwelling in the heavenly homeland through good works. But the reprobate, by living badly and sometimes openly resisting, scatter what has been rightly ordered by the good. Why fools tear apart the deeds of the wise is shown in the words that follow:

“Whoever walks on the right path and fears God is despised by one who walks on an infamous road.” Religion is an abomination to the sinner, and it seems foolish to unbelievers when the faithful, for fear of God, not only cast away fear but even laugh at the tortures of those who kill the body. Appropriately, the text continues:

[Col. 0726C] “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride, but the lips of the wise guard them.” Fools, through empty talk, afflict the humble whom they despise; but those same humble persons, through the teaching of wisdom, fortify themselves lest they be deceived.

“Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty; but where there are abundant crops, there the strength of the ox is manifest.” These words belong with what precedes. By oxen he means catholic teachers, by the manger the assembly of hearers, and by the crops the fruits of good works. The proud person therefore fears in vain and, with unlearned eloquence, beats the ears and hearts of his subjects. For where there are no learned preachers, the crowd of common people gathers in vain to hear; but where abundant works of virtue appear, it is most clearly evident that it was not a heretic who chattered uselessly, but one who labored for the fruit of the word—one who knows both how to name the word itself with a pure mouth and how to walk along the way of truth with a straight step of discernment.

Nor is it strange that we have said hearers are signified by the manger, since the ox is fed from the manger, while the teacher customarily nourishes those who hear with the word. Yet we must observe that the manger is also filled by the ox’s labor, and that the ox itself is refreshed by its own fruit from the manger; for the faithful preacher both refreshes his hearers with the word and himself advances before the Lord through that same refreshment. This is represented in the deed of Elijah: while he feeds the widow of Zarephath, he himself is fed.

“The scoffer seeks wisdom and does not find it; the teaching of the prudent is easy.” Caiaphas, who said to the Lord, “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ” (Matthew XXVI), sought badly to find what he asked, and therefore did not deserve it. But the disciples, who had humbly submitted themselves to hearing the truth, after receiving the grace of the Spirit, were counted worthy not only to recognize Christ as the Son of God but also to understand the hidden things of Scripture.

The teaching of the prudent was also easy when Cornelius, together with his household, and others like them, humbly heard the word, immediately believed, and, having received the Holy Spirit, spoke in all languages. Even now, whoever is prudent easily grasps the teaching of the catholic faith while being catechized; heretics, however, because they seek perversely, never find it at all.

“Go against a foolish man, and he does not know the wisdom of prudent lips.” The scoffer does not find the wisdom he seeks because, even if you proceed openly against his folly in debate, he does not know how to understand what you say. So it was with Arius, who maintained that the word “consubstantial” could nowhere be found in Scripture, although these statements were plainly set before him: “I and the Father are one” (John X), and “The Word was God” (John I), together with other such passages.

The teaching of the prudent is easy because the lips of prudence have wisdom—that is, because all lips governed by the restraint of prudence find it sweet to speak and hear only of wisdom and strive to devote themselves to its meditation.

“The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not admit a stranger into its joy.” The souls of the elect have bitterness so long as they are kept from eternal joys; the reprobate also have bitterness when they are afflicted by perverse desires. But because the elect walk in the light, they foresee with what joy their bitterness will be changed.

The reprobate, blinded by their own will, do not see what they suffer in the present, nor foresee what they will suffer in the future. Therefore they will remain strangers to the future joys of the good, since they have not learned to share in their present bitterness. Hence the text appropriately adds:

“The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tents of the just will flourish.” One ordinarily uses a house for a dwelling and tents on a journey. Therefore the house of the wicked will be destroyed, because in death the reprobate will lose the habitation of the present life in which they always desired to remain; and, since they had not foreseen it, they will undergo the exile of perpetual damnation.

But the tents of the just will flourish, because their present manner of life—in which they are inhabitants with the Lord yet pilgrims—will, as their merits increase without ceasing, reach the sweetest fruit of the heavenly homeland.

“The innocent believes every word, but the astute considers his steps.” John forbade this kind of innocence and taught that this kind of astuteness should be possessed when he said: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from the Lord” (1 John IV).

“The wise person fears and turns away from evil; the fool leaps across it and is confident.” Just as it belongs to a fool to trust in his own boldness and wish to leap across a swift torrent or a broad chasm, while it belongs to the wise to turn aside toward level ground or a bridge, so the person who avoids sins as far as he can, fearing that he may be entangled in evils, is wise.

But the fool sins contemptuously, flattering himself either that he will later repent of what he has done or that, if he should suddenly die, he will bravely endure the punishments of the underworld.

“The impatient person will commit folly, and the deceitful man is hateful.” The impatient person is indeed blameworthy, but the deceitful person is much worse and more hateful to God, even though he may be considered better by human beings. The former displays his folly openly to all; the latter, although perverse in heart, often pretends to simplicity and justice and delights in being called holy according to human judgment, although by divine examination he is reckoned among the reprobate.

“The wicked will lie before the good, and the impious before the gates of the just.” At the final judgment the reprobate, who oppressed the just in the present life, will be condemned while the just are crowned. What is said by “before”—that is, before the good and before the gates of the just—does not refer to proximity of place but to the vision of the good, since they will always behold the torments of the wicked, so that they may endlessly give thanks to their deliverer.

Therefore Isaiah says of them: “They shall go out and see,” he says, “the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be until the satisfaction of vision to all flesh” (Isaiah LXVI). When it says “they shall go out,” this does not signify the movement of feet but the gaze of the eyes: those placed within the kingdom send their sight outward, whenever they wish, to behold the punishments of the wicked.

“The crown of the wise is their wealth; the folly of fools is imprudence.” The wise do not regard anything earthly as their wealth, but only the crown which they will receive in the future for their virtues. The greatest folly of fools is that, improvident concerning eternal things, they rejoice only in present advantages; for “imprudence” is so called as though it meant lack of foresight.

“A faithful witness delivers souls, but the deceitful man brings forth lies.” Christ, who is the faithful witness, delivers souls, as we read in the Apocalypse; and, as the Apostle says, “He gave the good confession before Pontius Pilate” (1 Timothy VI).

The devil brings forth lies, and is rightly called deceitful, because he declares that the evils he suggests should be done are good, and promises eternal joys to those whom he is preparing for the torments of hell.

Likewise, the catholic teacher delivers souls when he faithfully—that is, rightly—preaches the testimonies of Scripture; and the heretic brings forth lies. Or, as another edition more plainly translates it, “the deceitful man kindles by a lie,” the souls, that is, of those whom he deceives by his error.

“In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength, and for his children there will be hope.” The fear of the Lord grants confidence of strength, because our mind looks upon the terrors of temporal things with greater courage the more truthfully it submits itself in fear to their Creator.

Those governed by divine fear are called the children of the fear of the Lord, just as those who pursue virtues are called children of virtue, and those who belong to the joys of the resurrection are called children of resurrection. For them there will be hope, according to the Psalmist: “Those who fear the Lord, hope in the Lord” (Psalm CXIII). Concerning this hope he adds:

“The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, that it may turn one away from the ruin of death.” This, then, is the hope of those who fear the Lord: that, turning away from the ruin of death, they may deserve to reach him who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Earlier it was said, “The law of the wise is a fountain of life, that it may turn one away from the ruin of death”; and now it is said, “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, that it may turn one away from the ruin of death.” From this it is clear that there is no prior law by which the wise person should avoid death and acquire eternal life than possessing the fear of the Lord. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Sirach I).

“In the multitude of the people is the dignity of the king, and in the scarcity of the populace is the disgrace of the ruler.” Wherever there is a multitude serving God, there especially is the glory of Christ. But where there are only catechumens, or candidates for baptism, or newly born infants still held under the kingdom of the devil—and who, hastening at the proper time to be reborn in Christ, are there—there the manifest disgrace of the prince of this world is seen.

Or certainly, in the assemblies of heretics, which are always fewer than the churches of Catholics, the disgrace of those who separate these people from ecclesiastical unity is evident.

“The health of the heart is the life of the flesh; envy is the rottenness of the bones.” By flesh are signified certain weak and tender things, and by bones strong deeds. Therefore he rightly says, “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh,” because, if innocence of mind is guarded, even whatever is weak outwardly is eventually strengthened.

And rightly he adds, “Envy is the rottenness of the bones,” because through the vice of jealousy even what appears strong to human eyes perishes before the eyes of God. For bones to rot through envy is for even strong things to decay.

“An intelligent servant is pleasing to the king.” He is the one to whom it is said: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew XXV).

“An unprofitable servant will endure his anger.” He is the one of whom the same Lord says, “Cast the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV

“A gentle answer breaks anger, but a harsh word arouses fury.” Whoever humbly receives the words of the one rebuking him already draws near to pardon for the guilt he has incurred. But whoever, in pride, resists the one correcting him provokes against himself the greater anger of the strict Judge.

“The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge, but the mouth of fools bubbles over with folly.” The tongue of the catholic Fathers adorns knowledge of divine utterances by explaining more fully what canonical Scripture previously set forth obscurely.

The mouths of heretics bubble over with folly because they understand the statements of sacred Scripture perversely and place their own opinions above its authority. The words “the mouth of fools bubbles over with folly” may also be understood of pagan philosophers, such as Porphyry and Julian, who poured forth the streams of their folly against the teachers of the Church.

[Col. 0730A] “A soothing tongue is a tree of life, but the undisciplined one crushes the spirit.” The tongue of a catholic teacher leads to the fruit of everlasting life. But whoever does not know the measure prescribed by ecclesiastical discipline will crush both his own spirit and the spirit of those who hear him by speaking badly.

“The house of the just has abundant strength, but in the fruits of the wicked there is turmoil.” The house of Christ, that is, the Church, possesses abundant strength, so that it cannot be destroyed by rain, winds, or the rivers of frequent temptations. But in the works of the devil continual turmoil rages, by which he attempts to overthrow that same house of Christ either through false interpretations or through open adversaries.

“The lips of the wise will scatter knowledge; the heart of fools will be unlike itself.” The lips of Catholics will scatter knowledge of the true faith by preaching. The heart of heretics will be unlike itself, because it conceives faithlessness in place of knowledge in order to teach it.

This can also be understood in another way: the heart of fools will be unlike even itself, since through the mutability of diverse thoughts it displays itself as changeable and never remains what it was. In contrast, concerning Hannah, when she prayed to the Lord with attentive mind, it is said: “Her countenance was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel I).

“The sacrifices of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord; the vows of the just are pleasing.” The Lord abhors the prayers, works, and sacrifices of heretics, but he accepts the vows of those who affirm the catholic faith through just works.

“The teaching of those who abandon the way is evil; whoever hates rebukes will die.” The teaching of those who abandon the way of truth is evil. Concerning them the Lord says: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

Yet, if such persons repent after being rebuked, the way back to pardon remains open. But if they do not heed ecclesiastical correction, certain destruction already awaits them.

“All the days of the poor are evil; a secure mind is like a continual sacrifice.” As long as the people of God are poor in the present life, their whole time is filled with afflictions and hardships, because they have not yet reached the riches of heavenly goodness and everlasting dwelling. Hence the Apostle warns: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians V).

The reprobate, however, who lack fear of God and use the world securely, are continually refreshed, as it were, by the banquets of fools. Hence it is rightly added:

[Col. 0730D] “Better is a little with the fear of the Lord than great and insatiable treasures.” This is like the statement in the Psalm: “Better is the little of the just man than the many riches of sinners” (Psalm XXXVIII). It is better, therefore, while preserving the fear of God, to lack wealth or even daily food than to abandon the fear of God through the desire to acquire more.

“Better is an invitation to vegetables with love than to a fatted calf with hatred.” Whoever displays to his neighbors examples of good works for them to imitate invites them, as it were, to a banquet by which they may be refreshed.

It is better, however, to invite them to vegetables with love than to a fatted calf with hatred. It is much more useful to preserve the innocence of a simple life with love than to shine outwardly with greater miracles of virtue while failing to cleanse the interior of the mind from the filth of hatred.

Therefore, when some say at the end, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matthew VII), the Lord himself will say: “I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (ibid.).

“The way of the lazy is like a hedge of thorns.” He calls lazy those who are reluctant to practice righteousness. When they desire the way of God, suspicions arising from their fears prick them like thorns in obstructing hedges. But because this does not usually hinder the elect, he adds:

“The way of the just is without stumbling.” In their manner of life, whatever adversity may meet them, the just do not stumble, because by a leap of eternal hope and inward contemplation they overcome the obstacles of temporal adversity.

“A person rejoices in the judgment of his mouth, and an opportune word is best.” It is indeed human to rejoice in one’s opinion as though it had been wisely expressed. But the truly wise person carefully considers not only the matters he is to speak about, but also the suitability of the place, the time, and the person to whom he is speaking.

“The path of life is above the instructed, so that he may turn away from the lowest hell.” By “instructed” he means one who is perfect not only in knowledge but also in conduct. For such a person the path of life is rightly opened from above, and for him the gate of heaven stands open.

The lowest hell, from which he is delivered, is the final punishment of damnation. The first hell is the blindness of the sinful soul, which lacks knowledge of the true light. Concerning it the Psalms say: “They descend alive into hell” (Psalm CXIII)—that is, those who know descend into sin.

“The Lord demolishes the house of the proud and makes firm the boundaries of the widow.” The Lord demolishes the gatherings of heretics and the other persecutors of the Church, and makes firm throughout the world that same Church, his bride, for whose life he deigned to die.

“The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the Lord, but the pure speech that is most beautiful will be established by him.” The Lord abhors the thoughts of heretics, indeed all thoughts contrary to piety. The pure speech of the true faith will be established by him when, at the judgment, he will repay fitting rewards not only for all deeds but also for all words.

He abhorred the evil thoughts of those who said, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (Luke VII), and he established as most beautiful the pure speech of the one who said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI), when he replied: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.).

“The light of the eyes gladdens the soul; a good reputation makes the bones fat.” The human mind is rightly delighted when it recognizes that, with the Lord revealing them, it has received the light of heavenly mysteries.

Another edition expresses this more plainly: “Seeing good things, the eye delights the heart.” These are certainly the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Whoever contemplates them with the eye of the mind is rightly delighted in heart, even if outwardly he appears to walk in sadness because he is afflicted by the enemy.

That most blessed reputation by which we know that not only our deeds and words but also our thoughts lie open in heaven to the descending angels provides the richness of love and faith to our virtues, so that they may not wither through failure. For the more certainly we hold that the secrets of our heart, together with the outward acts of our work, lie open to the divine gaze, the more eagerly we strive to enrich the strength of our good action with the oil of his love, lest it grow weary.

“An ear that hears the rebukes of life dwells among the wise.” The disciple who obediently accepts the rebukes of his teachers often advances so far that he rises to the teacher’s chair. Thus Paul, who humbly submitted himself to the rebuke of his Creator, later reached the seat of apostolic dignity in exaltation.

## CHAPTER XVI

“It belongs to a person to prepare the soul, and to the Lord to govern the tongue.” It is certain that we cannot prepare the mind, govern the tongue, or do anything good without grace, for he says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). How, then, does it belong to a person to prepare the soul and to God to govern the tongue?

Unless this specifically signifies the time of persecution, about which the Lord says: “When they hand you over, do not think about how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should say” (Matthew X).

[Col. 0732C] “All the ways of human beings are open to his eyes; the Lord is the weigher of spirits.” The Lord sees the ways—that is, the actions—of all people, both good and evil, and he distinguishes, as on a precise balance, what each person’s spirit thinks in secret. Hence it is rightly added:

“Reveal your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be directed.” We reveal our works to the Lord when, knowing that nothing is hidden from him, we recall him in everything we do and ask his help in all things. When we do this devoutly, the result is that not only the works themselves but also our inward thoughts proceed under his direction.

“The Lord has made everything for himself, even the wicked for the evil day.” The Lord had no cause for making any visible or invisible creature except his own will: namely, that he might display his goodness to rational creation, which he intended to make eternally blessed. He also, with just severity, condemned the one who of his own will abandoned the goodness of his Creator—that is, the devil together with his followers.

“Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord; even if hand is joined to hand, he will not be innocent.” Whoever attributes to himself the good he does, even if he seems to perform no evil with his hands, has already lost innocence of heart, because he has placed himself before the giver of good things. Therefore his Creator abhors him as guilty, since he sees him to be ungrateful for his benefits.

[Col. 0733A] “When a person’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace.” Such is the holiness of divine religion that often even those who are outside hold it in reverence; and although they differ in religion, they begin to live at peace with those whom they see serving God perfectly.

Thus, because the ways of Daniel and of the three young men pleased the Lord, he turned to peace even their enemies, who had cast them into the fire or among beasts. Because the ways of the holy preachers pleased the Lord, he converted many of their persecutors not only to peace but also to the same faith and unity of religion.

“Better is a little with justice than abundant fruits with iniquity.” The Lord also says: “Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke VI). And again: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (ibid.).

This may also be understood in this way: it is better to serve God devoutly in a simple manner of life than, while abounding in many virtues—for example, almsgiving, prayers, fasting, teaching, and chastity—to despise the deeds of one’s neighbors and glory in one’s supposedly unique exaltation.

“Divination is on the lips of the king; his mouth will not err in judgment.” He signifies the king of whom it is said: “Give the king your judgments” (Psalm LXI).

For which temporal king is there who never errs in judgment and in whose lips there is divination? This king directs not only the words and deeds of his own people, but also the pagan seers—commonly called diviners—who answer those who consult them; whatever they arrange is determined by him judging inwardly.

The prophet Micaiah testifies that, for the deception of Ahab, the most wicked king, a spirit was sent from the throne of the heavenly Judge to fill the mouths of his prophets and arm them to persuade him to do what would destroy him.

The mouth of the eternal King did not err in this judgment. Rather, he permitted the wandering prophets to speak to the wicked king what, because of his preceding sins, he had deserved to hear.

Ezekiel likewise says to the sinful and doomed people of the Ammonites: “When you saw vain things and divined lies” (Ezekiel XXI). This is not the divination of demons, but the judgment of God, who gave an end to those whose wickedness was complete.

Another translation renders this verse more clearly concerning the Lord: “Nothing false will be said to the king, and nothing false will come out of his mouth,” because he can neither be deceived by any liar nor ever lie himself.

“A weight and a balance are the judgments of the Lord, and all the stones of the world are his works.” He calls the just and strong in faith “the stones of the world,” such as the Apostle Peter desired those to be whom he admonished: “You also, like living stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (1 Peter II).

No one, therefore, from the beginning of the world has been chosen by his own virtue and made suitable for the heavenly building; rather, this is the work of the one who established all things by weight, measure, and number, distributing to each the measure of faith and gifts as he willed.

“Just lips are the delight of kings.” He means holy kings, who are accustomed principally to rule over vices and to be surrounded by the virtues of the soul like ranks of obedient companions. Concerning such kings the Lord says: “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X).

Otherwise, earthly kings often greatly hate just lips, as Herod hated those of John, for which reason he also punished him by beheading him.

“Whoever speaks rightly will be directed.” He will reach eternal life with the straight steps of his deeds.

On the other hand, “a man of many words will not be directed upon the earth.” This does not conflict with what is said about Antiochus: “Deceit will be directed in his hand.” Scripture does not say that this man would be directed, since it foresaw that he would become perverse and most wicked. Rather, it says that deceit would be directed in his hand because the frauds and crimes he planned were brought without hindrance to the result he intended. Yet, after accomplishing them, he himself perished eternally, as he deserved.

“The indignation of a king is messengers of death.” The messengers of death are the angels of Satan—that is, heretics and vain philosophers, indeed all who announce to their neighbors words by which they may be snatched away from eternal death. The more they serve the author of death, the more gravely they offend the giver of life.

Yet the way of repentance is not closed to such people, for it follows:

“And a wise man will appease him.” By recovering his senses he can appease the Lord whom he happened to offend by speaking foolishly.

“In the cheerfulness of the king’s face there is life.” Whoever deserves to see the cheerful face of Christ will be granted eternal life with him.

Otherwise, on the day of judgment, as it is written, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III). But then the reprobate will see him angry, while the just will see him serene.

“And his clemency is like the late rain.” In Judea the late rain customarily comes even now when the harvests are already ripe. The Lord also promises the early rain, saying through the prophet: “I will give you the early rain and the late rain upon the earth” (Joel II).

The early rain, or seasonal rain as it is called elsewhere, is when we first received the seeds of belief in Christ. The late rain is when, having been taken from this life with the fruits of virtue ripe, we are stored in the Lord’s granary.

The king’s clemency is rightly compared with the late rain, because the fruit of life that we receive by acting well is produced not by the freedom of our will but by the watering of heavenly grace.

“The one instructed in the word will find good things; and blessed is the one who hopes in the Lord.” Not only will the person instructed to preach the word of God find good things with him, but even the one who has learned to place his hope in the Lord, although he is not capable of preaching to others, shares in the same blessedness.

“Whoever is wise in heart will be called prudent, and whoever is sweet in speech will receive greater things.” Whoever preserves unimpaired in his heart the wisdom of the catholic faith he has learned rightly receives the name of prudent.

But whoever also knows how to preach that same wisdom skillfully and defend it against heretics will receive greater rewards for his greater labor.

[Col. 0735A] “The fountain of life is the instruction of its possessor; the teaching of fools is folly.” When he said “of its possessor,” he did not add what the possessor possessed. What, then, should we think he intended, unless perhaps instruction itself? The full sense would be: “The fountain of life is the instruction of one who possesses his instruction.”

This is plainly to say that the preacher truly opens the ways of life to his hearers who himself practices what he preaches, who possesses firmly in his heart the love of the word in which he instructs others. He does not merely cast into the earth seed retained in memory, as though gathered in the fold of his garment.

For this reason the teaching of fools is folly: even if they have learned through habitual instruction what good things to say, they nevertheless despise in their foolish hearts the good things they themselves say.

“Well-arranged words are a honeycomb; sweetness of soul is health to the bones.” Many people, through eloquence, can pleasantly pronounce good things to those who love and favor them, although they themselves do not love those things.

Only those words contribute to the health of your bones—that is, to the spiritual growth of your virtues—which proceed from the inward sweetness of your soul.

“The soul of the laborer labors for itself, because its mouth compelled it.” Literally, it is clear that, expelled from paradise, human beings perform daily labor lest they perish. His mouth compelled him when, after speaking with the serpent, he touched what was forbidden, so that he might endure prolonged exile with labor and eat bread in the sweat of his face.

But the mouth also compels the teacher to labor, because he must do good. For it says:

“An impious man digs evil, and fire burns on his lips.” The prophet also says: “They labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah IX).

This may be understood especially of the heretic, who breaks up the most beautiful and flourishing fields of divine utterances with the harmful plowshare of his tongue, so as to extract from their inner boundaries impious meanings that are not actually there. Fire burns on his lips, by which he destroys himself and his hearers forever.

Hence James also says: “The tongue is placed among our members; it defiles the whole body and inflames the wheel of our birth, being inflamed by Gehenna.”

“An unjust man flatters his friend and leads him along a way that is not good.” This may be understood both of the heretic and of every supporter of evil, when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the one who acts wickedly is blessed.

[Col. 0735D] “The one who thinks perversely with staring eyes, biting his lips, accomplishes evil.” To accomplish evil is worse than merely to do it. But it is not only the person who performs something perverse and harmful through the members of his body who accomplishes evil; the one who deliberately plans to commit evil does so as well.

The proud commonly bite their lips in indignation, and they commonly keep their eyes staring, seeing nothing present, while for a time they silently ponder things with an attentive mind. Hence it may be inferred that the text speaks of one who thinks perversely with staring eyes—that is, one who investigates in this way the evils he intends to do, without seeing what retribution will follow upon his evil deeds in the future.

“Better is the patient man than the strong man; and whoever rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities.” It is a lesser victory to capture cities, since they are outside oneself and are conquered. Greater is what is conquered through patience, because the spirit itself is overcome and subjects itself to itself when patience lays it low in humble endurance.

“Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord.” Just as lots are openly cast into the lap but are held concealed in the lap, so it belongs to divine judgment to determine whose lot will hold the prize. In the same way, human deeds are presently open to one another, but whose merit they are will become clear in the future, when the judgment of each person is brought forth and made manifest, as though from the lap of divine examination.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of sacrifices with strife.” It is better to perform small good deeds with love, without the skill of preaching—in this sense the morsel is dry—than to shine more brilliantly with virtues mixed with discord.

“The crown of the elders is the children of their children, and the glory of children is their fathers.” By elders he means the patriarchs and prophets, who are celebrated with fitting praise by the children of their children—that is, by the successors of the apostles. And it is the glory of the preachers of the New Testament that they were found worthy to be children of the ancient fathers.

“A most precious jewel is the expectation of one who asks; wherever it turns, it understands wisely.” Whoever faithfully awaits future rewards rejoices as though possessing the most splendid jewel. In the Gospel, too, the wise merchant sold everything he had to acquire the precious pearl—that is, heavenly desire.

Such a person, whether adversity or prosperity befalls him, is not turned from his purpose, wisely understanding that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans VIII).

“The wicked always seeks quarrels; but a cruel angel will be sent against him.” The cruel angel is an unclean spirit sent by the Lord against sinners, either to afflict them in the present—as he did the Egyptians, against whom he sent “the anger of his indignation, indignation and anger and tribulation, sent through evil angels”—or even to snatch them through death into eternal destruction.

In contrast, “the angel of the Lord is sent around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

[Col. 0736D] “It is easier to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool confident in his folly.” It was easier for the holy teachers to confront the fury of paganism after some peoples had been snatched away to them and, through preaching, converted from its beastly savagery to the piety of faith than to confront any heretic confident in the faithlessness of his doctrine.

The reason is that the former struggle was against outsiders, while the latter was against their own entrails.

The malice of the ancient enemy may also be understood under the name of the bear. We snatch away her cubs when, by catechizing and baptizing those who were sons of the devil, we join them to the company of the children of God. This is often accomplished with much less effort than trying either to bring a heretic back to the right faith or to restore a badly behaving Catholic to a state of good conduct.

[Col. 0737A] “Whoever lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels.” To let water loose is to release the tongue into a flood of speech. In the opposite, favorable sense it is said: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Proverbs XVIII).

Whoever, therefore, lets water loose is the beginning of quarrels, because the person who does not restrain the tongue destroys concord. Hence, conversely, it is written: “Whoever imposes silence on a fool appeases anger” (Proverbs XXVI).
