“What does it profit a fool to possess riches when he cannot buy wisdom?” What did it profit the unbelieving Jewish people to possess the riches of Scripture when they could not understand Christ in them? What does it profit the heretic to abound in the same riches when he cannot learn from them the unity of the faith? What benefit is it to a bad Catholic to possess the riches of the true faith when he has neglected to possess the wisdom of pious action?

“At all times the one who is a friend loves, and a brother is proved in distress.” Whoever truly loves the Lord preserves his love for him at all times and does not abandon the one whom he confessed in the tranquility of peace when he enters the distress of suffering.

A foolish man claps his hands when he has given surety for his friend. Foolish is the man who, having undertaken the direction of his brother’s soul, boasts of his own achievements instead of providing him, with humble compassion, whatever salutary assistance he can.

A joyful mind makes a flourishing age; a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones. Whoever rejoices in the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit is also adorned with the blossom of good action and awaits the fruits of heavenly rewards. But whoever is distressed by the sorrow of the world, which produces death, cannot at all possess the richness of divine love in the strength of the virtues he appears to exercise; rather, like one whose bones have been dried up, he withers, because in the good actions he performs he has lost the grace of love.

[Col. 0737C] Wisdom shines in the face of the prudent; the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth. Indeed, in the face of the Lord and Savior the wisdom of his divinity shone forth, which, appearing in the flesh, he demonstrated by the testimony of his miracles and teaching. But the eyes of the unbelieving Jews were directed rather toward fulfilling earthly desires than toward his salutary admonitions. More generally, prudent people often display the gravity of their understanding even in their very countenance, yet fools do not raise the eyes of their mind to admire and follow it; [Col. 0737D] instead, they seek with all their attention how they may reach the end of carnal pleasures.

It is not good to inflict harm on the righteous, nor to strike a ruler who judges rightly. This may be understood of the very Prince and Judge of the ages, who willed to suffer for our salvation, and also generally of all the rulers of the Church, who have either been stripped of their possessions by the impious or even consumed by death.

## CHAPTER 28

When the impious comes into the depth of sins, he despises them, but disgrace and reproach follow him. Whoever has once been wrapped in the long darkness of sins and despairs of the light now, through despair, releases the restraints of sinning everywhere. Yet such a person cannot in any way escape the reproach of future condemnation, since no remembrance of divine fear restrained him from the practice of his wickedness.

Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and a flooding, overflowing spring of wisdom. The words of the wise are compared with water because they wash and irrigate the minds of their hearers, lest they remain disfigured by the filth of sins or waste away from lack of heavenly teaching and, as though from a harmful drought, perish. And because certain mystical and hidden meanings lie concealed in the same words of teachers, to be grasped through more diligent effort, while other meanings flow openly and are easy for all hearers to understand, he rightly says that these words are both deep water and an overflowing torrent. It may also be divided in this way: since the Scripture of the Old Testament was expressed typically, the words from a man’s mouth are called deep water, because the Lord and the apostles openly disclosed to the world the mysteries of both Testaments. To these may be joined the phrase, “an overflowing torrent, a spring of wisdom.”

Whoever is soft and negligent in his work is a brother to one who destroys his own work. Whoever does not strictly carry through the good things he has begun imitates, through negligent slackness, the hand of one who destroys.

The substance of the rich is a fortified city, and like a strong wall surrounding it. Earthly substance cannot always defend a person; indeed, many have been captured or killed because of their riches. Thus Ecclesiastes also says: “Riches preserved to the harm of their lord perish in the worst affliction” (Eccles. V). It is therefore better understood as praising the substance of virtues: whoever abounds in these wards off all the enemy’s ambushes as though by an impregnable wall.

Whoever answers before he hears demonstrates that he is foolish and worthy of confusion. Whoever desires to be a teacher before learning does not avoid the harmfulness of folly. Whoever hastily seeks to judge the deeds of his neighbors before fully discerning the case of both parties likewise demonstrates that he is worthy of confusion.

A man’s spirit sustains his weakness. The same man says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” This may be understood of any holy man who supports the weakness of the flesh with strength of mind, lest he yield in temptations.

But who can sustain a spirit quick to anger? Whoever is easily provoked to anger cannot sustain himself, so that, once angry, he often says things which, later, when calm, he regrets having said, and frequently does not even know what he has said. Nevertheless, his madness is sometimes endured very easily through the moderation of the wise and is quickly quieted.

A man’s gift enlarges his way and makes room for him before rulers. The gift of charity, or of the other virtues that the faithful receive from the Lord, enlarges the path of their activity, because the more they are filled inwardly with the grace of the Spirit, the more widely they multiply their steps in good works outwardly; and among the great rulers of the Church they will in the future receive the height of honor. Alternatively, the Savior’s spiritual gift, which he brought to the world, enlarged his way, so that he might come to the nations of the whole world through the presence of his faith and love; and he caused not only peoples but even the rulers of earthly affairs to renounce their desires and willingly obey him.

A righteous man is the first accuser of himself. His friend comes and will examine him. Whoever is truly righteous, when he sees the errors of sinners, first turns the eye of consideration upon himself. After carefully accusing himself of his own frailty, he then kindly extends his speech to correct others. But he who deigned to say to his faithful ones, “I have called you friends, because whatever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV), comes into his heart through the presence of divine contemplation. He recognizes how pure it is from the stain of wickedness and rewards its humility with a fitting recompense.

[Col. 0739B] A brother helped by his brother is like a fortified city, and their judgments are like the bars of cities. When both peoples—the Jews, that is, and the nations—agree with one another in fraternal love in Christ, they build one city of the Catholic Church. And just as bars fortify the gates of cities, so the teachings of both Testaments defend the Churches throughout the world, which together constitute one Catholic Church, from the assaults of unbelievers.

The poor man will speak with entreaties, and the rich man will answer harshly. The humble in spirit humbly adore the Lord, like that publican of the Gospel; the proud boast of their merits, like the Pharisee.

A kindly man will be more a friend for companionship than a brother. The people who believed from the nations are more loved by the Lord than the Jewish people who persisted without faith, among whom he was born according to the flesh. This may also be understood of the apostles born from the Jews, because they loved those who believed from the nations more than the unbelievers of their own people.

## CHAPTER 19

Better is a poor man who walks in his simplicity than a rich man who twists his lips and is foolish. A simple hearer of the word of God is better, if he completes in action whatever he has been able to understand in the Scriptures, than any learned man who twists his lips, in the things he has keenly understood, to preach heresy.

Where there is no knowledge in the soul, there is no good; and whoever is hasty with his feet stumbles. Knowledge of heavenly life is necessary for the human soul, since without it no one can be blessed forever. Yet whoever, with unbridled faculties of mind, desires to know more than is fitting often incurs the offense of heretical folly through rash speculation. This was mystically signified in the first parents of the human race: while they hastened, out of a desire for greater knowledge, to touch what was forbidden, they departed from the state of blessedness in which they had been created and fell into the punishment of misery and mortality.

A man’s folly undermines his steps, and in his mind he rages against God. It is characteristic of fools that, when they abandon the way of truth by sinning, they do not admit that they have gone astray but refer the origin of their guilt back to their Creator, as though he himself had given them an occasion for sinning—either by making man frail or by admitting a crafty enemy to tempt him. Thus, after the transgression, when rebuked by the Lord, the first parent of our race immediately fled to a defensive excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me of the tree, and I ate” (Gen. III); and the woman herself said: “The serpent deceived me.” For both of them were casting back upon the Creator what they had done: the man, that he had received from the Lord as a companion the woman through whom he perished; the woman, that the Lord had placed in paradise the serpent that would deceive her. In contrast, the wise man prays the Lord not to incline his heart toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins.

But the man who undermines his own steps also rages in his mind against God when, despising the divine commands through his own laziness, he further reproaches the Lord himself with an insane mind, as though he had imposed unbearable burdens upon human beings.

Riches add many friends, but from the poor even those whom he had depart. The riches of the heavenly kingdom, which the holy teachers preach as to be granted to the faithful, win many friends both for those same preachers and for the Lord who bestows them. But from philosophers and the other teachers of the nations, since they certainly do not know how to promise future blessedness, even those whom they had depart—namely, those converted to faith and to the most certain hope of the Lord’s promise.

Whoever merely follows words will possess nothing, but whoever is master of his mind loves his own soul. The Apostle also says: “It is not the hearers of the law who will be justified before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II).

A false witness will not go unpunished, and whoever speaks lies will perish. He had reproved the person who merely pursues words of knowledge without the effectiveness of action; now he reproves the person who corrupts the very words of divine authority by interpreting them wrongly. The fact that the same matters are often repeated is an indication of certainty, as Joseph said when interpreting the king’s dream, because it is the word of God and will truly be fulfilled.

Pleasures do not suit a fool, nor does it suit a servant to rule over princes. The pleasures of the Scriptures do not suit a heretic, because he does not know how to use them well; nor should one who is still proved to be a servant of sin be preferred to the righteous in the government of the Church.

A man’s teaching is recognized through patience. The perfection of ecclesiastical teaching is shown through the patience of its teachers. For when they preferred to subject their bodies to afflictions and death rather than cease from the duty of teaching, they clearly demonstrated how salutary was the teaching they took such pains to defend. Alternatively, “A man’s teaching is recognized through patience,” because the less patient a person is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be. For he cannot truthfully impart good things by teaching if, in his life, he does not know how to tolerate the evils of others with equanimity. It is rightly added:

And his glory is to pass beyond wickedness. For the perfection of a teacher is to endure the wickedness of others patiently while also carefully observing his own frailty, so that he does not engage in wicked action. Neither the purity of one’s own conduct without tolerance of external disturbance nor the strength to endure adversity outwardly is sufficient if, inwardly, one still weakly favors wicked impulses.

As the roaring of a lion, so is the king’s anger; and as dew upon the grass, so is his cheerfulness. He speaks of the Lord the King, who at the judgment will appear cheerful and gracious to the righteous but terrifying to the unjust.

A foolish son is the sorrow of his father. God, who in his nature is always impassible and peaceful, is nevertheless said to grieve in our manner when he considers that human beings, whom he created to believe in and praise him, serve the wicked enemy rather than himself. Hence Moses says of him: “It repented him that he had made man on the earth, and he was touched with inward grief of heart: I will destroy,” he says, “the man whom I created from the face of the earth” (Gen. VI).

And a contentious woman is like a roof continually dripping. Just as roofs continually dripping receive rain from heaven but do not distribute it for any useful purpose, instead channeling it to the annoyance of the inhabitants, so the church of heretics turns the heavenly gifts of words, not toward the salvation of souls but toward the use of its own wickedness, by misinterpreting them and quarreling against Catholics. Dripping roofs receive clean drops of rain, but make them dirty beneath the house; likewise, the heretic takes in with the bodily ear the clearest words of the heavenly oracle, but when he touches them with a polluted heart, he serves them to his hearers mixed with filth.

[Col. 0741C] Sloth induces sleep. A person is called idle who, although he seems to be awake through right understanding, grows sluggish because he does nothing. But idleness adds savor because, when one ceases from the pursuit of good action, even the vigilance of right understanding is gradually lost. It is rightly added:

And the slack soul will hunger. Because it does not direct itself upward by drawing itself taut, it spreads itself below through desires. And while it is not tightened by the vigor of refined pursuits, it is wounded by the hunger of weak desire; to the degree that it neglects being bound by discipline, it scatters itself hungrily through the desire of its wills.

He lends to the Lord who has mercy on the poor, and he will repay him his due. The Lord himself proves the truth of this statement when he promises that he will give himself to those who practice almsgiving.

Discipline your son; do not despair; but do not set your soul on his destruction. If you see someone entrusted to you erring, take care to correct him diligently. But if he refuses to be healed, act toward him carefully and temperately, so that he finds nothing at all in your words or deeds by which he might sin further. The following statement supports this meaning:

Whoever is impatient will suffer loss; and when he has seized something, he will add another. If, provoked by the hardness of the brother whom you began to instruct, you yourself fall into the vice of impatience, you certainly incur the loss of your virtue. And if, by rebuking him too harshly, you take away the hope of salvation and repentance that he had, you will render a strict account to the Judge for having scandalized your brother.

The literal sense is clear: whoever through impatience serves poverty by theft or robbery harms his own soul; and when he takes away his neighbor’s property, he will have to render an account—not necessarily to a human being because of this, but certainly to the eternal Judge. Hence another edition translates this verse as follows: “A man thinking evil will be afflicted with great loss; and if he has been destructive, he will add his own soul.” For when, in his violence, he has taken away money, he will unwillingly give his soul in exchange for it.

A needy man is merciful. By “needy” he means the humble man who continually remembers that he is in need of everlasting goods. Such a person, in order to obtain mercy from the Lord, never refuses to show mercy to his neighbor. Of him he subsequently adds:

And a poor man is better than a lying man. Better, indeed, is the humble in heart, who trusts nothing to his own works, than the man who, thinking himself worthy of the name “man” because of the excellence of his virtues, is deceived unknowingly, having lost the good things he accomplished through pride.

The lazy man hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it to his mouth. No one is so lazy that he thinks bringing his hand to his mouth, even to eat, is labor; but for the lazy man it is labor to extend his hand to his mouth, because every sluggish preacher refuses to do what he says. To bring the hand to the mouth is to make one’s deeds agree with one’s speech.

An unjust witness mocks judgment—namely, the judgment expressed in the command, “You shall not bear false witness,” and certainly the future judgment, of which it was said above: “A false witness will not go unpunished, and whoever speaks lies will perish.”

And the mouth of the impious devours iniquity. Just as a hungry man eagerly desires to be refreshed by food, so the impious ardently seeks to be satisfied by carrying out iniquity.

Judgments are prepared for mockers, and hammers for striking the bodies of fools. Even if the reprobate, as was said earlier, mock the judgment of divine command and threat, judgments of condemnation nevertheless await them, which will strike them without end in the furnace of Gehenna like hammers striking red-hot iron.

## CHAPTER 20

Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him. Whoever now, through laziness, has neglected to labor in the service of God will beg when the day of the kingdom comes, and nothing will be given him, because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. The kingdom of God is rightly compared with summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow pass away and the days of eternal life shine with the brightness of the everlasting sun.

The righteous man who walks in his simplicity will leave blessed children after him. This cannot always stand according to the literal sense. Blessed Samuel, a righteous and simple man, left sons unlike himself; and Ahaz, an unjust and reprobate man, left behind him a blessed son, Hezekiah. But he calls the children of the righteous those who follow the example of the righteous. Hence now all the elect are called children of Abraham because of faith, as the Apostle testifies: “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. III). [Col. 0743A] Blessedness is promised to them not in this age but in the age to come. Hence it is rightly added:

A king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his gaze. Although in this life the elect suffer the evils inflicted by the reprobate, when the day of universal judgment appears all evils will be scattered; and once the righteous have been crowned with the Lord, only the unjust will undergo punishment. This also happens now in part, when one of the saints emerges victorious from the world and the persecutor who afflicted him receives what his deeds deserve.

This verse may also be understood of the elect, because they sometimes have evils hidden in the mind that cannot be seen by other human beings, yet the Lord observes them and destroys them through the hidden visitation of grace. Thus it is written: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter; and Peter remembered the word of the Lord,” and so forth (Luke XXII).

Who can say, “My heart is clean; I am pure from sin”? Notice that he does not say, “Who can have a clean heart and be pure from sin?” but, “Who can say,” he says, “My heart is clean; I am pure from sin?” For there are people who, through the gift of divine grace, can, according to human measure, possess purity both of heart and of conduct. Hence the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). And in the Psalm: “Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. XXIII).

For if no one has a clean heart and no one is pure from sin, it necessarily follows that no one ascends the mountain of the Lord and no human being stands in his holy place. But since it is certain that many will ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in his holy place, it remains that there are many who are pure in heart and, according to the measure of human possibility, pure from sin. Nevertheless, no one declares himself pure in heart and free from sin without presumption. For it is foolish boasting to praise oneself, and rash for anyone to glory in his own innocence or righteousness.

And because there are people who habitually praise their own deeds as though they were strong while condemning the deeds of their neighbors as worthless, it is rightly added:

A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure—both are abominable to the Lord. A person who has one weight in his own house and another measure judges himself one way and his neighbor another. He always searches his own actions for what may be praised, but those of others for what may be blamed. The Lord therefore rightly abominates such a person, because the more he pleases himself without merits, the more deservedly he displeases the heavenly Examiner.

But because it is dangerous for anyone to judge another’s conscience, whose intention he cannot know, he gives advice concerning the judgments by which we ought to direct the judgment of our heart toward our neighbor. For it follows:

A boy is known by his pursuits, whether his works are clean and upright. Whoever you see devoted to virtues—for example, to moderation, chastity, listening to the wise, and observance of God’s commandments, especially humility and simplicity—understand that his works are clean and upright. But whoever you discover following the opposite path, either correct and discipline him as a person of unclean and crooked heart, or, if you cannot do this, take care to avoid and shun him, lest you yourself be harmed by him.

It should not seem contradictory that this passage testifies that the works of a diligent boy are clean and true, while above it said: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin?’” In this verse it commends the effort to live rightly; in that one it discourages presumption concerning one’s own purity. Here it teaches the purity and uprightness that the righteous can possess in this life; there it warns that the subtlety of the divine examination, by which God judges human deeds and intentions, must always be kept before one’s eyes.

Hence the ancient interpreters translated that passage in this way: “When the king sits upon the throne of judgment, who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is pure from sin?” They also rendered the verse we are expounding more explicitly, saying: “The young man who is with the righteous will have a straight path.” For whoever walks with the wise will be wise, just as, by contrast, one who is the friend of fools will become like them.

The Lord made both the hearing ear and the seeing eye. By the hearing ear he means the obedient hearer of the word; by the seeing eye, the learned teacher. Therefore, when someone sees himself instructed in the knowledge of the Scriptures and fit to proclaim the word of God, let him not despise the simplicity of his brother, who, although less learned for preaching, is no less ready to learn or to fulfill the good things he has learned. Rather, let him remember that the one who gave him the greater grace of knowledge also granted the brother the spiritual gifts he possesses. He gave these gifts not only for the recipient’s own sake but also for the benefit of his brother, giving each person grace according to the measure of his gift.

Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you; open your eyes and be filled with bread. Do not love the sleep of sin and inactivity, concerning which the Apostle says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII). If you do not wish to keep watch properly now, do not let that most grievous poverty seize you in the future, where, although thirsty, you may be unable to find even a single drop of water. Open the eyes of your heart to sacred vigils, and by living rightly seek for yourself an abundance of heavenly joys.

“Bad, bad,” says every buyer, but when he has departed, then he will boast. Thus the person who desires to purchase eternal rewards in heaven must say that what he has to endure in the present is bad, so that, when he has departed, he may then rejoice, clearly perceiving that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

Gold and a multitude of precious stones, and a precious vessel, are lips of knowledge. This is the boast of the wise buyer, who, as long as he is making his purchase, calls what is happening to him bad, but when he has departed rejoices that he has bought wisely. So too the buyer of the heavenly kingdom will rejoice when he has departed from here, discovering that the lips of knowledge—that is, the spiritual teaching he employed—are to be compared with gold, gems, and precious vessels.

The bread of deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel. In whatever member a person has sinned more greatly, in that member he will suffer greater torments in punishment. Hence it is rightly said that whoever sins more with his tongue will burn more in it, since his mouth is said to be filled with gravel, which is a burning stone. This is known to have happened to the rich man who feasted splendidly every day: when burning in hell, he asked Lazarus to cool his tongue. For he who had indulged continually in empty words while feasting burned especially in his tongue.

Whoever reveals secrets, walks deceitfully, and enlarges his lips—do not associate with him. If someone wishes to enter your friendships and you see him revealing the secrets of his former friend, beware of him as a treacherous man.

An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end. Those who desire through the wickedness of greed to multiply their possessions in this life will in the future become disinherited from the eternal patrimony.

Alternatively: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end.” Whoever rashly takes the rank of government before learning to be subject will at the end lack the reward of blessing owed to good rulers. Whoever approaches the ministry of the altar ignorant and presumptuous will likewise lose on the last day the grace of the recompense promised to those who minister well. It may also be understood in this way: whoever wishes to avenge his injuries in the present will lack the crown of patience in the future. This meaning seems especially suited to what follows:

Do not say, “I will repay evil”; wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you. The following verse also establishes this when it says:

A weight and a weight, a deceitful balance—both are an abomination to the Lord; it is not good. The person who, when he sins, asks the Lord for pardon, yet refuses to forgive the person who sins against him and repents, has a double weight and a deceitful balance in his heart. He strives by prayers to move God, who is divine, to show mercy, while he himself, being human, cannot be moved to mercy by any human prayers.

He is rightly abominated by the Lord as an unjust weigher, because he measures his own injuries as heavier than those of the Lord. For example, he is unwilling to forgive one who has violated his wife, while asking that he himself be forgiven if perhaps he has defiled a virgin betrothed to Christ, or has stained with some filth of vice his own soul, consecrated to God in baptism.

The steps of a man are directed by the Lord. Whenever human beings walk along a right path, this does not happen through the freedom of human choice but through the governance of the one to whom Isaiah says: “You have accomplished all our works for us” (Isa. XXVI).

But who among human beings can understand his own way? In this, he says, it is clearly shown that whatever good a person possesses he does not possess from himself but through the grace of God; nor can he, through the freedom of his own choice, understand what he will be or how and for how long he will live.

It is the ruin of a man to devour the holy and afterward retract his vows. Since it is a sin to harm any human being, how much more is it so when someone has offended or injured the saints of God and has not feared to treat them, like a worthless slave, according to the pleasure of his own desire. Thus the forty men in the Acts of the Apostles vowed that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul; and, as we often read, pagans vowed to their gods that they would devour the blood of Christians.

An ancient edition placed this verse according to another meaning, saying: “It is a snare for a man hastily to preserve something of his own. But after he has made a vow, he repents.” Since eternal condemnation awaits both groups—those who despise their vows and those who persecute the saints in order to fulfill their vows—it is rightly added:

A wise king scatters the impious and bends an arch over them. It was customary among the ancients, when they had won a victory over an enemy, to erect arches for themselves on which they recorded the praises of their valor, as we read in the account of Saul. Therefore our Lord and King not only destroys the wickedness of the impious at the end, but also celebrates forever, together with his elect, the great glory of that triumph.

An ancient translation has this verse as follows: “A wise king is the winnower of the impious, and he sends a wheel of evils upon them”—that is, a punishment that will never be brought to an end. Opposed to this wheel is the crown of eternal life that God sends to those who love him.

The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man, searching all the hidden places of the belly. When the illumination of divine inspiration enters the mind of a human being, it enlightens and reveals that mind to itself. Before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the mind could carry perverse thoughts but did not know how to weigh them.

The exultation of young men is their strength, and the dignity of the old is their gray hair. By gray hair he means wisdom. The affairs of any well-ordered city, and the matters of the holy Church, are rightly conducted when the stronger members devote their necessary strength to their tasks, while the elders, endowed with greater prudence, give sound counsel concerning what must be done.

The bruise of a wound will wipe away evils, and blows in the innermost parts of the belly. When we are struck outwardly, we are recalled silently and sorrowfully to the memory of our sins; and through what we suffer outwardly we grieve more deeply over what we have done inwardly. Thus, amid the body’s open wounds, the hidden wound of the belly washes us more thoroughly, because the secret wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of evil action.

The mind is often signified by the word “belly,” because just as the belly consumes food, so the mind, by pondering, digests cares.

As the divisions of waters, so is the heart of the king in the hand of God. Why does he say that the heart of the king, rather than that of all human beings, is in God’s hand, when it is written, “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Ps. XCIV), unless perhaps he calls every saint a king, since each one knows how to conquer the battles of vices in himself and to be surrounded by the army of virtues?

For just as the Lord fills widely the boundaries of the earth and the air with the manifold divisions of waters, and also covers the heights of the heavens with waters, so he inclines the king’s heart wherever he wishes. Just as he grants the divisions of grace, according to his will, to angels and human beings, so also he makes the hearts of the saints worthy through whatever gifts he wishes to bestow. There is no place here for a Pelagianist claim by which anyone could be saved without the grace of God.

## CHAPTER 21

A man’s perverse way is alien; but whoever is pure has a straight work. To live rightly before the Lord is proper to the human condition. Hence he says elsewhere: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is every human being” (Ecclus. XII). But whoever lives perversely is plainly walking a way alien to human nature. A perverse action is therefore alien and contrary to nature. Whoever is pure in his work rightly carries out what he originally received by nature.

It is better to sit in a corner of the roof than with a contentious woman in a shared house. So true is it that it is better to sit in a corner of the roof—that is, in the secluded height of a more continent life—than with an evil woman in a house that you share with her, that even if the best possible woman were offered to you as a wife, it would be better, for the companionship of the Lamb, to spurn marriage and lead a celibate life.

Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard. This statement must be understood generally, and not only of one who is needy or physically infirm. For even a person who, in the case of another’s sins, is found to exercise judgmental severity rather than hold it with compassionate grief shows that he has not yet been purified of the filth of vices and is not worthy to receive the hearing of divine mercy.

A hidden gift will extinguish anger, and a gift in the bosom the greatest indignation. Whoever desires to appease the anger of the strict Judge, which he has deserved by sinning, should give alms to the poor—not with any pleasure in human approval, but solely out of love for the Creator, who sees what is hidden in hearts. Thus the gift becomes hidden; thus it becomes useful for calming the Creator’s anger, if it is offered with no regard for external reward. In this way what he himself commanded will be fulfilled: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI).

It is joy to the righteous to do judgment, and terror to those who practice iniquity. The righteous man rejoices when he labors at good works, because he hopes that for these he will be rewarded with everlasting goods. But while the reprobate do the evil things they know God has forbidden, although they may take carnal pleasure in the accomplishment of their lust, they cannot be without inward terror of mind, because they do not doubt that they will suffer everlasting punishment for the evils they have wickedly done in time.

[Col. 0748A] A man who has strayed from the way of teaching will dwell in the assembly of giants. By “giants” he means unclean spirits, concerning whom blessed Job also says: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters, and those who dwell with them” (Job XXVI)—that is, proud and wickedly powerful demonic spirits, who are subjected to punishment and tormented together with the human beings they deceived. All who have strayed from the way of truth will be joined to their assembly, as the Judge himself testifies, who foretold that he would say to them: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

For the just, the ungodly is given, and for the upright, the wicked. The just and the upright seem to be the same, but there is a difference between the ungodly and the wicked: all the wicked are reprobates, whereas the ungodly are those who, entangled in greater crimes, either never received the mysteries of the holy faith, or, after receiving them, returned to apostasy. Hence, in this passage, “ungodly” may be understood to mean every persecutor of the faithful, while “wicked” generally designates all evil people. “For the just, the ungodly is given,” when a persecutor who handed a martyr over to death is punished. “For the upright, the wicked,” those who, seeing their righteousness, refused to imitate them. Herod is condemned not only for the innocent whom he impiously delivered to death, but also receives an increased condemnation because, although he was a Jew and knew the words of the prophets, he refused to follow the faith of the Magi in seeking the Lord. Hence the Lord says: “The queen of the South will rise in judgment with this generation and will condemn it,” and so forth (Luke 11). Not because she will condemn it by her own power and authority, but because, by comparison with her, those who knew of her devotion will be condemned, since they pretended not to care about wisdom even though they could have done so much more easily.

A desirable treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the righteous; a foolish man will dissipate them. The brightness of good works, always pleasing to the Lord, and the richness of love shine forth in the Church of the saints. Blessed Pope Gregory, in his homilies on the Gospel, gave this verse according to the ancient translation: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” But the reprobate hasten not only to fail to attain virtues, but also to persecute them, and, insofar as they can, to overwhelm the good. This verse may also properly be understood of any martyr, in whose dwelling—that is, in whose body—the holy soul, namely God’s treasure, is preserved, and in whom the anointing of spiritual grace abounds; but the foolish persecutor can tear apart such a dwelling. Yet he cannot touch the treasure held within the dwelling, nor the oil. Hence the Lord teaches that we should not fear those who kill the body and, after that, have nothing more they can do.

The wise man ascends the city of the mighty and destroys the strength of its confidence. By “the city of the mighty” he means the world, which was once foolishly subjected to the tyranny of evil spirits and served them, placing its confidence for life in the worship of those who are not gods but the works of human hands. He entered this city when he was born in the flesh—the one who is the power and wisdom of God—and through his preachers destroyed the worship of the gods in whom those ignorant of the truth had trusted. He taught that confidence must be placed in the faith of heaven, which could never be destroyed. Every day, too, the wise man ascends the city of the mighty and destroys the strength of its confidence when a faithful teacher refutes, by the affirmation of faith and the discipline of ecclesiastical correction, the arguments of philosophers, heretics, or even the obstinate contradictions of carnal brethren, by which they strive to defend and lessen the guilt of their crimes, and when, laying them bare, he abolishes them.

A false witness will perish; an obedient man speaks of victory. Whoever testifies that he serves God but does not carry out his words in his deeds will perish. But whoever faithfully submits to the divine commands, as he promises, has speech that reaches victory, because while he strives through disobedience to overcome his desires, he afterward receives the palm of victory through the justice of the Judge.

An ungodly man obstinately hardens his face, but the upright man corrects his way. Judas, because he was ungodly in heart, although the Lord himself reproved him, refused to restrain the evil he had begun. Peter, however, because he was upright in heart—that is, a lover of uprightness—when the Lord looked upon him, immediately corrected through repentance what he had done wrong by denying him. There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord. Whatever the heretics devise and seize upon is empty, vain, and useless.

The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation. It is the task of a person devoted to God, in a time of persecution, to prepare his spirit and offer his body to danger. But it belongs to divine assistance that victory and salvation should follow the labor of the contest once begun.

A good name is better than great riches. He means a good name not one praised by crowds of ignorant common people, but one commended by the testimony of the faithful, even if they are few. For he did not refuse to have a good name; rather, he sought to be praised only by the good, saying: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” A good name, therefore, is the name of religion, rightly preferred to worldly riches. Even if someone were to gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it merely so that his name might be written in heaven, and his memory established eternally among both angels and holy human beings.

Good favor is above silver and gold. He signifies that favor by which someone is praised by the good for a good work. Indeed, on account of the gifts of merit bestowed upon him, the Father who is in heaven is glorified.

The rich and the poor meet one another; the Lord is the maker of both. Do not honor the rich because of their riches, nor despise the poor because of their poverty; instead, venerate this in both of them: that they are a work of God, since they were made in the image and likeness of God.

The shrewd man sees evil and hides himself; the innocent passes by and suffers harm. Many of the rulers believed in the Lord, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. Because they were shrewd, they saw the evil of the persecution that threatened them and hid the faith of their devotion, which they had conceived only briefly. But the innocent apostles passed along the straight road of the confession they had begun; they were afflicted with blows, chains, imprisonment, and even punished with death. Many people to this day follow one or the other of these examples, both in the struggle of faith and in ordinary conduct.

The ancient interpreters translated this verse more clearly, but with a different meaning: “The crafty man, seeing the wicked being punished, himself receives severe discipline. But the foolish, passing by, were afflicted with harm.”

The end of moderation is the fear of the Lord; riches, glory, and life. By “moderation” he means constancy in good works, and by “the fear of the Lord” that fear which endures forever and ever. For the perfection of virtues is plainly to ascend to this state of mind, in which we are afraid to offend the Creator even slightly, placing nothing at all before the remembrance of him—what elsewhere is called perfect love, which casts out servile and foolish fear, by which each person fears that, if he sins, he may perhaps deserve to be subjected to punishments. When he adds “riches, glory, and life,” he signifies things in the future. Thus: “The end of moderation is the fear of the Lord; riches, glory, and life.” For the perfection of virtues in this life is to fear the Lord with holy fear—that is, to worship him with sincere love. The end of virtues in the future is to receive from the Lord the riches of the promised inheritance, the glory of the heavenly kingdom, and life without end. Hence Peter says: “When you see him, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.”

Weapons and swords are in the way of the perverse; the guardian of his soul withdraws far from them. This should be understood in two ways. The perverse are always armed to harm their neighbors by wicked word or deed, and the vengeance of divine judgment always awaits them, already prepared. But whoever seeks to save his soul eternally flees far from such weapons and swords: he restrains both his mind and his hand from injuring his neighbors, and takes careful precaution lest he himself be struck by the severity of the just Judge.

There is a proverb: “A young man according to his way; even when he grows old, he does not depart from it.” It is clear that many, by the gift of the Lord, are changed in old age from the vices they possessed as young people. Conversely, when the Lord abandons some, they abandon near old age the virtues by which they seemed to shine in youth. Yet because people much more often continue throughout the rest of their lives the habits with which they were imbued from youth, he calls it a proverb: whatever each person has begun as a young man, he does not change in old age. He does not, however, assert that this always happens. He sets forth this proverb so that he may persuade his hearers to pursue virtues from their earliest years, lest in old age they be unable to learn the pursuits to which they had disdained to devote themselves in tender youth. For also:

> A jar will long retain the scent with which it was once imbued when new.

And Greek history relates that Alexander, the most powerful king and conqueror of the world, could not rid himself, either in character or in gait, of the faults of his tutor Leonidas, with which he had been infected while still a little boy.

The rich rule over the poor, and whoever borrows is the servant of the lender. This is clear according to the literal sense. But the rich in virtues also rule over them in the judgment of the hidden Examiner—or rather, they will in the future become judges of those who lack the riches of virtues. And whoever receives the word of saving doctrine from a teacher is the servant of that same teacher—that is, he is bound to fulfill everything which the teacher, by the authority of his heavenly instruction, commands.

Whoever sows wickedness will reap evils. It is certain that whoever teaches wickedness either by word or by example will receive punishment. But since it follows:

> And the rod of his anger will be brought to completion,

he seems chiefly to mean the wickedness carried out with a harsh and impious mind: practicing robbery, oppressing people with servitude, tearing them apart with tortures, killing them, taking away a widow’s ox as a pledge, or refusing to avenge oneself upon an adversary when one has the power to do so. Such a person will deservedly be consumed by the rod of his anger, because, as the Lord says, “All who take the sword will perish by the sword”—that is, those who unjustly rage against others bring destruction upon themselves by that very rage. But since he had spoken of the ungodly, he then adds, by contrast, concerning the godly:

Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed; he gave his bread to the poor. This resembles the saying of that same Judge, who, distinguishing the merciful from the wicked, says: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth. The breads given to the poor may be understood not only as bodily nourishment, but also as spiritual instruction by which the soul is refreshed.

## CHAPTER XXII

Cast out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him; causes and insults will cease. Cast the heretic whom you cannot correct out of the Church; when you take away his freedom to preach, you provide assistance to Catholic peace.

Whoever loves purity of heart, because of the grace of his lips, will have the king as a friend. Whoever preaches what is right with a pure heart will be numbered among those of whom the Prophet said to that same King and Creator of the ages: “But to me, your friends, have been greatly honored.” But if someone displays the grace of his lips by preaching what is right while neglecting to preserve purity of heart, he should by no means be thought capable of enjoying the friendship of the eternal King.

The eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge, and the words of the wicked are overthrown. Heavenly inspection always preserves in the Church the knowledge of the truth that he taught. But the words of heretics—or rather, every speech contrary to devotion and justice—are not preserved because the Lord governs; they are overturned together with their author.

The lazy man says: “There is a lion outside; I will be killed in the middle of the streets.” Often the person who is lazy in performing good works and timid about confessing the faith he holds in his heart says to himself: “I dare not publicly profess the faith I have learned, lest the ungodly persecutor, because he hates the faithful, kill me. I am afraid to go out publicly to practice the actions of virtue, lest perhaps the more grievous adversity of the ancient enemy hold me [perhaps: assail me]—or, possibly, some perverse person with his crowd ridicule me, overwhelm me with insults, afflict me with injuries, or, as happened to many righteous people, destroy me with tortures and death because my life is at odds with his.” “There is a lion outside; I will be killed in the middle of the streets,” he says. This is plainly to say that as soon as the words and works of virtue begin to be displayed publicly, persecution by human beings or unclean spirits will immediately arise; and I am unable to resist temptations, but will be defeated at the very beginnings of my good purpose.

The mouth of the foreign woman is a deep pit; the one with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it. Whoever willingly embraces the words or kisses of a prostitute is, as it were, already knocking at the gate of the infernal abyss, and will quickly be swallowed up unless he cautiously withdraws his foot, and unless he restrains his other limbs from the pit’s vicinity. No one falls into this punitive pit except a son of wrath.

Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will cleanse it. We know many children endowed with wisdom: Jeremiah, while still a boy, received the mystery of prophecy; and Daniel writes that God gave the boys who practiced abstinence knowledge and discipline in every word and in wisdom. We must therefore understand that in this passage “children” signifies not those young in age but those small in understanding, such as the Apostle forbade his hearers to be when he said: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness” (1 Corinthians 14). Such children—that is, minds devoted to folly, wantonness, or laziness—must be chastised by youthful discipline and led to the right path of life by the rigor of the wise.

Whoever slanders the poor in order to increase his riches will himself give to one richer and will be in need. It is clear that rapacious people lose everything alike: both what they take from the poor and what they seemed to possess justly, when, at the examination of the severe Judge, they receive punishments for what they have done. But the person who slanders a brother poor in spirit, disparaging his virtues so that through this kind of denigration he may eagerly increase the riches he desires—that is, a greater glory of human praise, as though he were thereby considered more holy—such a slanderer deservedly loses whatever good action he seemed to possess and remains at the end empty of the fruit of virtues.

Thus far extends the heading of Solomon’s Proverbs that was set above. From this point he is shown to have adopted a new kind of expression, so that what follows seems to be spoken not as though to someone else whom he was teaching, but as though he were reasoning alone with himself. The first verse of the Proverbs is therefore: “A wise son gladdens his father, but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother.” The last is the one to which we have now reached in our exposition. From here he returns to his earlier manner of speaking, addressing specifically the person whom he will instruct. It begins as follows:

Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise; apply your heart to my doctrine. He makes a beautiful beginning to the new mode of expression, commanding the person he is teaching to apply his ear to hearing and his heart to understanding what the wise speak: “For it will be beautiful for you when you preserve it in your belly, and it will overflow upon your lips” [Note: We were unable to supply this lacuna from a written exemplar, because what was written on one side obscured the writing on the other.].

[lacuna]

It may be understood of any poor or needy person, concerning whom it was said: “For to you the poor man has been left; you will be the helper of the orphan.” But since it follows:

> And he will pierce those who pierced his soul,

it is better understood of the one who, although he was rich, became poor for us, and who not only became poor in order to enrich us, but also deigned to be crucified in order to redeem us. Wisdom therefore forbids its hearers to inflict violence and death upon the Lord preaching in the flesh, because certain destruction awaits those who have not feared to lay hands upon the author of life.

Do not be a friend to an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his paths and take a stumbling-block for your soul. Although this may generally be understood of every angry or furious person, nothing prevents it from being understood specifically of those who raged with insane minds against the Savior and his disciples. All who believed in him and cared for their salvation are forbidden their friendship and companionship, lest through proximity to the wicked they too perish. The case of Judas Iscariot proves that this can happen.

In general, however, it must be said that just as perfect men ought not to flee from perverse neighbors, because they often draw them toward uprightness and are themselves never drawn toward perversity, so all the weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils they frequently see but cannot correct.

Do not be among those who drive in their hands and offer themselves as sureties for debts; for if he has nothing with which to repay, why should he take away the covering from your bed? Do not be among those who, although free and at leisure for themselves, fix themselves in the care of the salvation of wicked people, promising that they will give an account to the Lord for their souls. For if the one for whom you gave surety has no good works by which to make you free and secure, what benefit is it to you that you yourself should be judged on the day of judgment for his soul? You will lose the garment of righteousness with which you seemed to be clothed and will be shown to stand naked of the adornment of virtues, because you were unable to fulfill what, as the Lord witnessed, you had promised.

This is not said to mean that you should refuse the care of governing souls when it has been regularly imposed upon you, but so that you may not rashly usurp for yourself, without anyone commanding it, the office of teacher and bishop.

Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established. Do not move the boundaries of the faith that the Catholic teachers established from the beginning.

Have you seen a man swift in his work? He will stand before kings and will not be before the ignoble. Whoever you see swift in his work—that is, diligent and attentive in the good work he ought to perform—know that he will stand on the day of the final examination before the apostles, who will sit with Christ to judge the world, because he will have kept their commands. He will not be placed among the ignoble teachers whose error he avoided; that is, he will not be placed on the Judge’s left.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When you sit to eat with a ruler, pay careful attention to what is set before you, and place a knife at your throat, if indeed you have your soul under your control. Everything is said allegorically. When you sit down to read with a teacher, so that you may be refreshed by the bread of the word, understand carefully what is written and preserve discernment of sacred reading in your speech—if indeed you are such a person, and sufficiently educated, as to have your soul under your control, rather than being carried about in your mind like an unlearned person by every wind of doctrine. He used “throat” for speech because the voice is in the throat, and “knife” for discernment because, when we are refreshed by food, we prepare it by cutting it with a knife. A person sits down to eat and places a knife at his throat when one who diligently meditates on divine things brings forth carefully chosen words from his mouth and does not continually turn upon his tongue words other than those of the heavenly oracle. This is done by one who has his soul under his control—that is, who has learned to preserve an immovable state of a wise mind amid the errors of deceptive sages. Hence he rightly adds:

Do not desire his foods, in whom there is the bread of deceit. This plainly means: Do not desire to listen to the speeches of one who is accustomed to deceive his hearers with the sweetness of false doctrines.

Do not labor to become rich. He signifies the riches of knowledge, which we are forbidden to seek beyond the measure of our capacity.

But set a limit to your prudence. He means the limit of which it was said above: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established”—that is, the boundaries of the truth and faith handed down by the fathers.

Do not raise your eyes toward riches that you cannot possess, for they will make themselves wings like eagles and fly into heaven. Do not raise your mind to investigate the secrets of divinity that you cannot penetrate; these are open only to the citizens of heaven.

Do not eat with an envious man, and do not desire his foods, for he estimates what he does not know like a diviner and interpreter. Do not speak about the Scriptures with a heretic who envies human salvation, preferring to deceive rather than to be corrected. For just as a diviner and interpreter of dreams estimates what he does not know, so the heretic, who does not understand, presumes to interpret the Scriptures as he pleases.

“Eat and drink,” he says to you, but his heart is not with you. “Learn and do securely what I teach,” he says, although he himself has no firm faith in what he teaches, knowing that he has fabricated from his own heart what he teaches.

You will vomit out the foods you have eaten and lose your fine words. You must either abandon through repentance the perverse opinions you learned from heretics and be corrected, or be compelled after death to suffer punishment for them. You will also lose the words of confession by which you had thought that, while they were preaching, you ought humbly to favor them.

Do not speak in the ears of fools, for they will despise the doctrine of your speech. The saying in the Gospel is similar: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine,” and so forth (Matthew 7). If he above warned you not to listen to the doctrines of heretics, so now he urges you not to be led by love of empty glory into thrusting the secrets of truth indiscriminately upon unclean people.

Do not touch the boundaries of the little ones, nor enter the field of orphans, for their kinsman is strong. He himself will judge their case against you. He calls the Lord the kinsman of the little ones and orphans, because when he was in the flesh he deigned to become more the companion of the poor than of the rich. Otherwise, the same Lord is the Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. The little ones and orphans may also appropriately designate those of whom the Lord says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me. For I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Whoever touches their fields and boundaries—that is, whoever harms their good way of life by disturbing it—does not escape the judgment of the Lord.

Let your heart not envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord all day, because you will have hope at the end, and your expectation will not be taken away. If throughout the day—that is, throughout the whole period during which you remain in the light of this world—you strive both to avoid the examples of sinners and to fear the Lord, you have hope of blessed reward at the end, when you reach the end of this life. This is confirmed by the one who says: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.”

Do not be among the banquets of sinners, nor at the feasts of those who bring together meats for eating. To bring meats together for eating means, in a conversation of detraction, to exchange accusations about the lives [perhaps: vices] of one’s neighbors. Their punishment is then immediately added:

Because those who devote themselves to drinking and contribute their shares will be consumed, and drowsiness will be clothed in rags. *Symbolum* is a Greek word and is interpreted as “contribution” or “sharing.” There is a contribution of words, as occurs in councils, and also of money or other things, as the present passage teaches. Those devote themselves to drinking who become intoxicated with the disgrace of another’s life. To give a contribution means that, just as each person ordinarily contributes his share of food for eating, so in a conversation of detraction each contributes words. But those who devote themselves to drinking and give their contributions will be consumed, because, as it is written: “Every slanderer will be uprooted.” Drowsiness is clothed in rags because death will find despised and destitute of every good work the person whom, here, the languor of his detraction occupied in seeking accusations against the life of another.

Let your father rejoice, and let your mother who gave birth to you exult. Let God the Father rejoice in your righteousness; let the Church your mother rejoice; and let the priest who regenerated you through the grace of baptism and instructed you from childhood also rejoice in your good works.

For whom is there woe? For whose father is there woe? The question is asked, by way of discussion, for which crimes of human beings the greatest punishment is reserved by the Lord. He answers through his reasoning: without any doubt, for those who through drunkenness descend into lust. “For whom,” he says, “is there woe? For whose father is there woe?” He calls woe eternal destruction, concerning which the Lord says: “Woe to that man through whom the stumbling-block comes” (Matthew 18). He calls the father of the one upon whom woe is impending either the person from whom someone outwardly received examples of wicked action in order to sin, or certainly the devil, who inwardly poured the poison of his deadly suggestion into the heart. It was of him that it was said to the Jews: “You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father.”

For whom are quarrels? For whom are pits? Quarrels, because the person whom drunkenness has rendered incapable of controlling his senses does not know how to preserve peaceful concord. Pits, because the person who is as though deprived of his mind and does not know how to distinguish good from evil does not hesitate to fall everywhere into the mire of every vice. The drunkard very often falls into that pit of which it was said above: “For the prostitute is a deep pit, and the foreign woman a narrow well” (Proverbs 23).

For whom are wounds without cause? For whom is redness of the eyes? Wounds without cause, because many people, filled beyond measure with wine, have received wounds through swelling in their limbs, suffering them with scarcely any cause. Redness of the eyes, because immoderate drinking of wine has produced bodily dimness of vision in many and blindness of the inner senses.

Are they not those who linger over wine and devote themselves to drinking cups? He does not forbid drinking wine as necessity requires, but he forbids lingering over wine beyond the proper time and usefulness, and competing with one another in emptying cups, according to the saying of Isaiah: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah 5).

Your eyes will see foreign women, and your heart will speak perverse things. It is a familiar and almost natural vice, after the poisons of drunkenness have spread through the heart, to pursue desire for women, accompanied also by the depravity and shamefulness of speech.

And you will be like one sleeping in the middle of the sea, and like a drowsy pilot who has lost the rudder. He sleeps in the middle of the sea who, placed amid the temptations of this world, neglects to anticipate the movements of invading vices, as though they were towering heaps of waves. He is like a drowsy pilot who loses the rudder when the mind loses the diligence required to steer the ship of the body.

And you will say: “They struck me, but I did not feel pain; they dragged me, and I did not notice. When will I awake and again find wine?” The voice of one struck and sleeping is expressed. The mind, sleeping through its neglect of vigilance, is struck and does not feel pain, because just as it does not foresee the evils threatening it, so it does not recognize what it has perpetrated. It is dragged and feels nothing, because it is led by the allurements of vices, yet is not awakened to guard itself. It desires to awake so that it may again find wine, because, although it is oppressed by the sleep of torpor and neglects its own protection, it nevertheless strives to awaken to the concerns of the world so that it may always be intoxicated by pleasures. While it sleeps concerning what it ought diligently to watch over, it desires to watch over what it could have laudably slept through.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Do not envy evil men, nor desire to be with them, and so forth. Do not desire to imitate those whom you see entangled in the vices mentioned, but take care rather to devote yourself to wisdom.

By instruction the storerooms will be filled with every precious and beautiful substance. The storerooms are the hearts of the righteous, which are filled with the gifts of virtues only through the instruction of wisdom.

A wise man is strong, and a learned man is robust and powerful. Not everyone who is strong is wise, but every wise person should be called strong, because even if he is weak in body, provided he has wisdom, he conquers all the battles of the strong adversary—that is, of the devil.

Wisdom is too high for a fool; he will not open his mouth in the gate. A fool cannot attain wisdom, for it is high above one who lies in the depths of vices. Even if he presently thinks himself wise in some respect, at the gate of the city—that is, at the departure from this life—he will discover that what he considered wisdom amounted to nothing.

Whoever thinks about doing evil will be called a fool. Lest you think that only someone whom you see as dull and slow-witted should be considered a fool, he openly shows that the one who consents even in thought to the suggestions of sin is to be called a fool, even if he appears sharp-minded. The person who, though dull in understanding, has nevertheless resolved to obey the commands of God that he was able to learn is not a fool.

If you have lost hope when exhausted on the day of distress, your strength will be diminished. Nothing is more detestable than despair. Whoever possesses it loses the steadfastness of courage both in the ordinary labors of this life and—what is most harmful—in the struggle of faith.

Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction. This may be understood mystically: rescue those who are deceived by heretics by preaching the right faith; free, by displaying examples of good works, those who are being dragged to destruction by Catholics who live wickedly. If you see people who have fallen or are about to fall in the struggle of persecution, strive to restore them to life by earnest exhortation. If you see some about to perish from hunger or cold, refresh them by giving food and clothing.

Eat honey, my son, because it is good, and the honeycomb is very sweet to your throat; so too is the doctrine of wisdom to your soul. It is very easy to see why he compares the doctrine of wisdom to honey and the honeycomb: just as honey surpasses other foods in sweetness, so wisdom surpasses other teachings. But there is a difference between the meanings signified by the two. Honey, which is readily available to eat, suggests the moral surface of the literal text. The honeycomb, from which honey is pressed out of wax, figuratively announces allegorical speech, in which, once the veil of the letter has been withdrawn, the sweetness of the spiritual meaning is perceived with somewhat more labor or delay.

Do not lie in wait and seek wickedness in the house of the righteous, nor destroy his rest. Do not seek some opportunity by which you may disparage a righteous man. If he falls, he quickly removes his foot and is free of the fault, which is not repeated in his action. But the ungodly fall in such a way that they do not return afterward. As he adds next:

For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the ungodly will collapse into evil. How is the person called righteous who is said to fall—that is, to sin—unless he is speaking of light and daily sins, without which no righteous person could exist in this life? For through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, surprise, necessity, and the weakness of the flesh, every day, whether unwillingly or willingly, we often incur guilt. Yet the righteous rises again, precisely because he is righteous, and his fall through human frailty does not prejudice his righteousness. Hence, when he spoke of the righteous person’s fall, he did not add “into evil.” For although it is evil that they fall, they take care by rising quickly that they may not remain stuck in the evil into which they had fallen.

Or this may be understood in contrast concerning the reprobate. “But the ungodly,” he says, “will collapse into evil,” because when the ungodly have fallen—or, more seriously, collapsed, as Scripture says—when they have committed capital crimes, they consent so pleasurably to their fall that they disdain to be lifted from it through repentance.

When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he is ruined, let your heart not exult, lest perhaps the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn his anger away from him. Above he forbade setting traps for the righteous; now, in order to make you perfect in all things, he also forbids you to insult enemies when they have sinned or suffered some adversity. Otherwise, if by the Lord’s mercy they return to repentance and the salvation of their soul, and begin to have faithful friendship with you, you may then be ashamed because you once despised those whom divine grace had preserved for life. As much as you can, therefore, grieve with those who lie fallen and help them so that they may rise. If your desire and effort are followed by success, you will rejoice over the one who has been healed, whom you had grieved to see suffering. If not, you will nevertheless not lack the fruit of your goodwill before the Lord. Certainly the saying should be understood thus: do not rejoice at the fall of your enemy, lest perhaps the Lord, by casting down your pride—which undoubtedly displeases him—in this way humble you, so that while you fall into sin, he may recover and be healed.

Fear the Lord, my son, and the king. In accordance with what he himself says: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Mark 12). Nor does anything prevent us from understanding “Father and Son” as designated in the Lord and the king, since they are to be worshiped with one and the same honor of divinity. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.

And do not associate with slanderers. Namely, with those who, while claiming to know God the Father, refused to receive the Son of God appearing in the flesh.

For suddenly their destruction will arise, and who knows the ruin of both? He means both the slanderer and the one who, by favoring him, associates himself with him: the rulers who disparage Christ and the people deceived by them; the heresiarchs who tear faith apart and the hearers who listen to them.

These things too are unknown to the wise. The implied sense is: when each of the reprobate is suddenly snatched from the world by a sudden death [Perhaps the *qui* is redundant]; or else, “these things too are to be observed by the wise,” namely, what I have taught, so that they may not associate with slanderers. For nearly the whole human race is endangered by this particular vice. Therefore, wishing to remedy this same fault, blessed Father Augustine had these verses written on his table:

> Whoever loves to assail the life of the absent with words  
> shall know that this table is forbidden to him. [Col. 0759B]

An ancient edition states the verse more clearly: “I say these things to you who recognize wisdom.” This can fittingly serve as the beginning of the following sentences.

To recognize a person in judgment is not good. Above he taught that the king is to be feared, and now he forbids recognizing persons in judgment. From this it follows that subjects ought to offer temporal obedience to rulers in such a way that they never stray from the path of truth out of regard for their rulers’ reverence or fear.

He will kiss the lips of the one who gives a right answer. A kiss is a sign of peace and love. Therefore, the one who gives a right answer will kiss the lips, because whoever, disregarding partiality, follows only the words of justice—even if he perhaps seems burdensome and severe to the foolish—will nevertheless find many prudent people with whom he may live in peace, and many who will embrace his words with love. Often, too, he will receive as friends and companions those whom he had endured as opponents of his sound assertions, once they have been converted to better things.

Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house. What is it to cultivate the field diligently after preparing one’s work, except to cultivate our conduct for the harvest of recompense after pulling out the thorns of iniquity? And what is it to return, after cultivating the field, to the building of the house, except that from good works we generally learn what purity of life we should also construct in our thoughts? For he builds the house of his mind well who first cleanses the field of his body of the thorns of vices, lest, if the thorns of desires grow in the field of the flesh, the entire structure of the virtues within be destroyed as the famine of goodness increases.

Do not be a false witness against your neighbor; do not flatter anyone with your lips; do not say, “As he has done to me, so will I do to him,” and so forth. These things pertain to the cultivation of our field—that is, to the practice of good conduct: not to harm an innocent neighbor by false testimony, not to grant any sinner greater confidence to sin by flattery, and not to repay evil with evil. In this way, when you have first properly ordered your outward actions, you subsequently reach the task of cultivating the purity of the inner person as well, and, as it were, after cultivating the field, you begin to adorn and build more deeply the dwelling of the mind with pious thoughts. Since the reprobate neglect to do this, it is rightly added:

I passed by the field of a lazy man and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, nettles had completely filled them, and thorns had covered its surface. To pass by the field and vineyard of the lazy and foolish man is to examine the life of anyone who is negligent. Nettles or thorns fill it, because in the hearts of the negligent there sprout the itching earthly desires and the stings of vices, in accordance with what is written: “Every idle person is ruled by desires.”

And its stone wall had been destroyed. The stone wall lies destroyed in the vineyard or field of the foolish man when anyone who is negligent loses the defenses of the virtues he had begun, either deceived by the wickedness of evil people or by the cunning persuasion of unclean spirits.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0759]

### CHAPTER XXV

These too are the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, collected. Here he begins to speak in a new order, so that, rather than addressing an audience as before, he may himself discuss and examine what the reasoning of truth contains. In these sayings, nevertheless, every reader or hearer may recognize with complete clarity what ought to be desired and what ought to be avoided. These proverbs are said to have been collected by the men of Hezekiah because perhaps, until his time, they had been dispersed among many people, just as they had received them once spoken from the mouth of the wisest king. Through his diligence, however, they were gathered into one collection and inserted into the body of this little book. It should certainly be noted that these proverbs contain far more allegorical language than the others, namely, through the comparison of things that appear suited to serve as figures.

It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to investigate a matter. The glory of the Lord who appeared in the flesh is to display to mortal eyes more of the nature of his humanity than of his divinity, and to confess himself as the Word—that is, the Son of God—more through the miracles of his works and mystical utterances than through open declarations. Hence in the Gospel he much more often used to call himself the Son of Man than the Son of God. The glory of his faithful disciples, moreover, is diligently to investigate his word, by which he mystically signifies that he is also God, even where he does not say so openly. Such is the saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X), and other passages of this kind. Finally, concealing the eternity of the Word and displaying the weakness of the flesh, he said: “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” (John VI.) The foremost of kings, having investigated his saying, which he had often heard before, answered him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid.), [Col. 0761A] and by this investigation he earned no small glory. For immediately he heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” and so forth (Matthew XVI).

Heaven above, earth below, and the heart of kings unsearchable. Just as human beings cannot fathom the height of heaven or the depth of the earth, so the knowledge of the prophets and apostles, who learned the secrets of divinity through the revelation of the Spirit, surpasses the capacity of our weakness.
