Remove the dross from silver, and a most pure vessel will emerge. Remove the surface of the letter from sacred Scripture, and you will find the purest meaning hidden beneath the lowliness of the letter, and spiritual mysteries concealed beneath the carnal figures of the ceremonies.

Remove impiety from the royal face, and his throne will be established in justice. Remove the impiety of persecuting Christians from the mind of Saul—or of any other zealot for the Law—and when they begin to preach Christ, the justice and teaching-seat of their doctrine will be established, which their impiety had previously been driving away, so long as they resisted the justice of God and strove to put their own justice first [Perhaps “his” for “their”]; [perhaps “his own” for “their own”]. Likewise, “Remove impiety from the face of the king, and his throne will be established in justice.” For those who preside over peoples, if they wish their throne to be firm, should always display faces full of cheerfulness and favor, lest, becoming too harsh through arrogance, they fall into the murmuring of the people.

Do not appear glorious before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men, and so forth. Above he warned the ruler; now he warns the subject. For just as he told the ruler to display cheerful faces to his subjects, so he admonishes the subject not to appear arrogant in the sight of his superiors, but rather, placed in an ordinary position, to deserve to be summoned to a higher one. This resembles the saying of the Lord: “When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place,” and so forth (Luke XIV). We may also understand the king and ruler as signifying the Lord, before whom we must always humble ourselves, as the apostle Peter admonishes when he says: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Peter V).

What your eyes have seen, do not bring forth hastily in a quarrel, lest afterward you be unable to correct it when you have disgraced your friend. And in the Gospel the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone,” and so forth (Matthew XVIII).

Golden apples in settings of silver is one who speaks a word in its time. Sacred writings are most aptly compared to settings of silver—settings, namely, because they provide rest for the souls of those who hear them; silver, because they shine brilliantly with the virtues of the Fathers. Hence it is written: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested in fire.” Whoever, by expounding and displaying the same divine sayings as full also of spiritual meanings and mysteries, adds golden apples to the ornament of these settings, does so beautifully. These meanings are aptly called apples because they have grown from the tree of life, that is, from the wisdom of God; they are aptly called golden apples because they pour the knowledge and love of perpetual brightness into minds. Thus, “Golden apples in settings of silver is one who speaks a word in its time,” because the person who knows how to preach the word of God suitably, according to the capacity of his hearers, sometimes repeats literally the examples and sayings of the Fathers, through whose keeping one reaches eternal rest; at other times, removing the veil of the letter, he discloses in them the sweeter fruits of spiritual meanings with which to nourish the pious desires of his hearers.

A golden earring and a shining pearl is one who reproves a wise person and an obedient ear. The humble hearer is rightly compared to a golden earring, because, while willingly lending his ear to one who rebukes and teaches, he is already preparing himself to receive the splendor of heavenly wisdom and is already drawing near to the vision of the light above. The learned teacher is rightly likened to a shining pearl, because, while he displays the correction of conduct and the knowledge of heavenly things to minds that desire and piously seek them, he adds to the golden ornament the greater and more gracious brilliance of a burning gem.

As the cold of snow on the day of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to the one who sent him: he makes his soul rest. It seems entirely inappropriate for it to snow during harvest. For below we also read: “As snow in summer and rain in harvest, so glory is unfitting for a fool.” Yet in the exceedingly hot regions of Palestine it is very pleasing to those harvesting if a sudden cold, such as usually comes with snow, arrives; it cools somewhat the sun’s burning, wipes away the laborers’ sweat, and moderates their burning breaths. The faithful messenger is rightly compared to such cold, because by acting prudently he gives rest to the mind of the one who sent him.

Mystically, however, the faithful messenger is the catholic teacher; the one who sends him is the Lord. The day of harvest in the heat is the time of preaching amid the fury of persecutors, of which it is said: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few” (Matthew IX). The cold of snow during harvest is the slight respite of preachers from the persecution of their opponents. Thus it is rightly said: “As the cold of snow on the day of harvest, so a faithful messenger to the one who sent him makes his soul rest.” For just as it is desirable for preachers of the word, when they receive some cooling relief from the rage of unbelievers and are not deprived of the opportunity to teach, so it is evidently pleasing to the Lord who sent them to preach when they faithfully fulfill the commission they received from him even amid the opposition of adversaries. Finally, as Luke reports, when the disciples returned from their preaching ministry, he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and gave thanks to the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,” and so forth (Luke X).

Cloud and wind, but no rain that follows, is a glorious man who does not fulfill his promises. This seems similar to what he said above: “Do not flatter anyone with your lips.” But that verse specifically contains the warning not to receive a person by making promises and then deceive him by failing to fulfill them. This verse, however, can contain both that meaning and what the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy III).

By patience a ruler will be softened, and a gentle tongue will break hardness. When you have offended the Lord by sinning, you can nevertheless merit his clemency if you patiently endure the adversities inflicted upon you for your sins and subdue the hardness of your former obstinacy through humble satisfaction.

You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, having been filled, you vomit it up. You have found the heavenly sweetness of understanding, supplied to you through the labor of spiritual fathers, as through the work of the wisest bees. Take care, therefore, not to desire to know more than you ought to know, lest, while you seek to understand the highest things beyond your strength, you lose even what you had understood well. This verse can also be understood figuratively as referring to what follows:

Withdraw your foot from your neighbor’s house, lest, when you have been filled, he hate you. Even if you find the conversation or visit of some neighbor sweeter than honey, it is nevertheless better to make him always love your arrival by coming more rarely than to remain with him for so long on even one occasion, or to come to him so often, that he grows weary of seeing you and seeks to prevent you from returning.

A rotten tooth and a weary foot is one who hopes in the faithless on the day of distress and loses his cloak on the day of cold. Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being and makes flesh his arm.” He is rightly compared to a rotten tooth and a weary foot, because whoever does not know how to place his one true good—that is, adherence to God—and his hope in the Lord God can neither receive the food of life nor reach the dwelling of the salvation he desires. Such a person loses his cloak on the day of cold, because although in the calm of the present life he appears clothed in the habit of religion, when the severity of just judgment arrives he will appear completely naked of the adornment of justice, and unworthy of the company of those of whom it is written: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Revelation XVI).

Vinegar on soda is one who sings songs to a most wicked heart. Soda takes its name from the province of Nitria, where it commonly grows, and it differs little in appearance from ammoniac salt. For just as the heat of the sun produces salt on the seashore by hardening into stone the seawater that a great force of winds, or the heat of the sea itself, has cast onto the farther shores, so in Nitria, where in summer prolonged rains soak the earth, the heat of the stars is so intense that it cooks the rainwater itself throughout the breadth of the sands into a stone, quite similar in appearance to salt or ice, but possessing neither the cold rigidity of ice nor its false taste. Yet, in accordance with the nature of salt, it remains solid in hot weather but flows and melts in cloudy air. The local inhabitants collect and preserve it, and when necessary use it for their animals.

Therefore the prophet says to sinful Judea: “If you wash yourself with soda and multiply for yourself the herb called *borith*, you are stained in your iniquity, says the Lord God.” It crackles in water like quicklime and itself indeed disappears, but makes the water suitable for washing. Observing how its nature suited the figure, Solomon says: “Vinegar on soda, and one who sings songs to a most wicked heart.” For if vinegar is poured onto soda, the soda immediately grows hot and boils over. Likewise, when a perverse mind is rebuked through correction or urged toward good through the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse through the correction and is inflamed into the iniquity of murmuring by the very means through which it ought to have been restrained from iniquity.

If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. This can be understood both of bodily nourishment and of spiritual nourishment.

For you will heap burning coals upon his head, and the Lord will repay you. He is not speaking of the fires of punishment; wisdom would not teach you to provide good things to your enemy for the sake of his destruction. Rather, the burning coals upon his head signify the warmth of charity in his heart. It sometimes happens that an enemy, overcome by repeated acts of kindness and having the hardness of hatred softened, receives the heat of charity in his mind, becomes a friend from an enemy, and begins rightly to love in return the one whom he had unjustly hated.

The north wind disperses rain, and a sad face the slanderous tongue. If you listen to a slanderer with a cheerful face, you provide him fuel for slander. But if you listen with a sad face, then, as a certain man of God said, he learns not willingly to say what he has learned is not willingly heard.

It is better to sit in the corner of a roof than in a shared house with a quarrelsome woman. A rooftop is both elevated and secluded. For *doma* in Greek means “roof” in Latin. Accordingly, in the Acts of the Apostles, where Peter ascended to the upper part of the house to pray, the Greek text uses *doma* for “upper part.” It is better, therefore, for a person to remain in the height of the virtues, free from the bonds of marriage and secluded from the desires of this world, than to be subjected, amid the carnal use of pleasure, to the daily insults of a wicked woman.

Cold water for a thirsty soul, and good news from a distant land. The Psalmist says: “As a deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Cold water, which restrains the thirsting person’s heat, and a messenger who comes from afar bearing unexpected news and joys, are therefore compared. For the sweetness of the divine vision consoles the soul that has long desired it and frees it from the heat of present tribulations. Likewise, angels descend daily from a distant land—that is, from the heavenly homeland—into the world, strengthening the righteous amid temptations through hope of heavenly things, or, once the battles of temptation are finished, leading them to the palm of everlasting reward.

A spring muddied by the foot and a corrupted fountain is a righteous person falling before the wicked. The mouth and tongue of the righteous person, who meditates on wisdom and speaks judgment, are a spring and fountain of life. If it happens that the devil overcomes this person and brings him down into a fall, the spring is rightly called muddied when the adversary tramples it, and the fountain corrupted. It often happens that those who shone with greater knowledge eventually fall into the pit of foolishness because they desire to know more than is granted to human frailty. Hence what follows:

As it is not good for one who eats much honey, so the one who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. If the sweetness of honey is taken in excess, the food that delights the mouth destroys the life of the eater. The investigation of majesty is sweet, but whoever desires to search it out more deeply than the knowledge of humanity permits is crushed by its very glory, because, like honey taken in excess, it breaks apart the mind of the investigator while the night overtakes it. The wise person must attend not only to avoiding the search for things higher than himself and the scrutiny of things stronger than himself, but also to ensuring that what he could rightly and usefully know is not made less useful to him by excessive speech. Hence it is suitably added:

As an open city without the encircling protection of walls, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking. For just as it has no wall of silence, so the city of the mind lies open to the arrows of the enemy. When a person casts himself outside himself through words, he displays himself as open to the adversary, who overcomes him with as little effort as the defeated person himself fights against himself through excessive speech.

### CHAPTER XXVI

As snow in summer and rain in harvest, so glory is unfitting for a fool. This verse too warns that the office of teaching should not be entrusted to the unlearned. Snow in summer and rain during harvest are the persecutions of unbelievers during the time of preaching the Gospel. When they perhaps press too heavily, they impede the warmth of love in many and spoil the fruits of good works. Glory granted to a fool is rightly asserted to be like these things, because if the teaching chair is given to an unlearned person, the Church is harmed by this just as it is by the persecution of unbelievers. The disaster of the Arian storm proved this to be entirely true.

As a bird flying elsewhere and a sparrow going wherever it will, so an undeserved curse will come upon someone. Words are rightly compared to birds, because they fly through the air from the mouth of the speaker all the way to the ears of the hearer, as though carried across. But they differ in this respect: a bird can fly wherever it pleases and settle in a place where it has no definite necessity or benefit, whereas the words we speak do not simply scatter into the wind and disappear. Everything returns to its author: words spoken well help the speaker, while words uttered badly burden him, so that we are compelled to give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word.

How much more, then, do curses oppress not someone else but the person who curses—both those hurled against an innocent person from a malicious mind and those uttered indiscriminately against anyone by the foolish habit of the negligent? For “those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God.” He does not say “an undeserved curse” without reason, because there is also a curse uttered not undeservedly, but sent forth in the anger of divine justice’s severity against the impious, as in the saying of blessed Peter to Simon Magus: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts VIII). The same applies to the anathemas pronounced against apostate heretics by ecclesiastical judgment. Concerning these the Lord says to that same Church: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven.”

Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself. These statements should not seem mutually contradictory: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” and “Answer a fool according to his folly.” Both agree according to the differences of times and persons, since the fool is both disregarded because he does not receive wisdom and his foolish pride is struck down by another kind of folly, in accordance with what the Apostle also says: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians XII).

Lame in the feet and drinking iniquity is one who sends messages through a foolish messenger. It may happen that some wise person sends a fool as his messenger, not knowing that he is a fool; nevertheless, he himself does not lose the glory of his wisdom because he believed, concerning someone unknown to him, the good report he had heard. He is lame in his feet and drinking iniquity because he has lost the outward gait of good works, while inwardly he intoxicates the depths of his understanding by drinking in folly.

As one who casts a stone onto a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool. Whoever grants a fool—that is, a heretic—the honor of teaching commits no less a sin than one who worships the gods and shrines of the gentiles with empty devotion.

As when a thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard, so is a proverb in the mouth of fools. A thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard when, in the works of one who serves carnal enticements, the stings of crimes arise. A proverb proposed by a fool is rightly compared to this. For although a fool may know how to utter words of wisdom, he does not know how to avoid in them the stings of vices with which he wounds either himself or his neighbor. Often an imprudent teacher, even when saying good things, secretly seeks either his own praise from others or the condemnation of others.

As a dog returns to its vomit, so an imprudent person repeats his folly. When a dog vomits, it has surely cast out the food that was weighing down its chest. But when it returns to its vomit, from which it had been relieved, it is burdened again. Likewise, those who confess their sins cast out the wickedness by which they had been badly filled and which weighed upon the innermost parts of their minds; but after confession, when they desire to resume it, they become burdened again.

Have you seen a man who seems wise to himself? The fool has more hope than he. In explaining this, the Lord says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX).

The lazy man says, “There is a lioness on the road, a lion in the paths.” As a door turns on its hinge, so the lazy man turns on his bed. When many hear a word of exhortation, they make excuses about the devil, saying that they indeed wish to begin the way of justice but are hindered by Satan from completing it. Thus, through such excuses, they always turn on the hinge of their torpor like a door, proposing now to go out to work and now to return to rest, yet never ceasing to lie in their perverse ways.

The lazy man seems wiser to himself than seven men who speak judgments. By the seven men who speak judgments he means those who, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, have supplied us with the knowledge of sacred Scripture. The fool considers himself wiser than they, because some people so turn their minds away, through foolishness, from doing what the Lord commands that they claim that none of these things can or ought to be fulfilled by a human being. As though wiser than those who wrote the divine utterances, they assert that a person cannot do what those writers, under the direction of the Holy Spirit, commanded human beings to do—or rather, what they showed that many people had accomplished with the help of the grace of that same Spirit.

As one who seizes a dog by the ears, so is one who passes by and impatiently involves himself in another’s quarrel. The Apostle says: “Do not quarrel over words; it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (2 Timothy II). Therefore, whenever a person is simple in understanding and his ear is caught by the biting speech of two people quarreling with each other, he quickly begins himself, like a dog, to bark and generate disputes. But the wise person avoids this entirely.

The words of a whisperer seem simple, yet they reach the innermost parts of the belly. He calls the whisperer an instigator of strife and a double-tongued person, one who simulates praise in his words while seeking to hear something from which he may sow quarrels.

### CHAPTER XXVII

Do not boast about tomorrow, since you do not know what the coming day will bring forth. Never be secure about the future, because even if today you see yourself serving the Lord, you cannot foresee at all what you may be in the future or how you will end your life. For blessed is the person who is always fearful.

A stone is heavy and sand is burdensome, but the anger of a fool is heavier than either. It is indeed burdensome enough for someone to be weighed down as though by a stone’s weight by even one capital crime, or to be burdened like grains of sand by countless lesser sins. But the anger of a fool is heavier than both, because the more clearly these are shown to be evil, the more sharply they pierce the mind so that it may be corrected. Anger, however, because it is not a bodily but a spiritual vice, burdens a person all the more as it is less detected. Thus he does not simply say “anger,” but “the anger of a fool,” heavier than stone and sand. For wise people strive to examine and correct not only their actions and speech but also the movements of their minds.

Anger has no mercy, nor can anyone bear the force of an enraged fury once it breaks forth. He is not speaking of every kind of anger. For it is written of a very gentle and moderate man that he went out from Pharaoh “exceedingly angry” (Exodus XI). But he is speaking of the anger of the fool, whom he had mentioned in the preceding verse: once it has flared up, it immediately loses the inner organs of compassion and knows only how to loosen the reins to its own fury. Otherwise, useful and necessary anger is spoken of in the saying: “Anger is better than laughter,” because through the sadness of the face the mind of the offender is corrected.

Open rebuke is better than hidden love. Here “hidden love” means illicit love, such as adulterous love, which wise people rightly conceal because of its disgrace, lest it be rebuked. Open rebuke is rightly preferred to it, because it is unquestionably better to love someone secretly out of a desire to correct him.

The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates. It is better to endure the wounds of affliction inflicted by the Lord, who, as a father, is accustomed to educate us as sons, than to be deceived by the flatteries of the devil. To deprive us of our heavenly inheritance, the devil customarily favors our errors, as though the evil we do were insignificant, while the tribulation that rages beyond measure against our sins is endured under the Lord’s ordering.

A satisfied soul will trample the honeycomb, but to a hungry soul even bitter things will seem sweet. The soul of the rich, who have their consolation and to whom the Lord says, “Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger” (Luke VI), despises the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom when it hears it. But the soul of those who hunger and thirst for justice regards even the world’s adversities endured for the Lord—and indeed death itself—as sweet, knowing that through the cup of bitterness it will come to the joys of eternal salvation.

As a bird migrating from its nest, so is a man who leaves his place. Just as a bird that neglects its nest abandons the eggs or young it had brooded to the plunder of other birds or animals, so the person who abandons the keeping of the virtues in which he was progressing becomes himself a betrayer of those same virtues he had seemed to possess, handing them over to unclean spirits. Hence he says elsewhere: “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place.” This means plainly: if the temptation of the ruler of the world—that is, the devil—should press upon you, take care not to abandon the good work to which you were devoted.

A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away. A neighbor who binds your spirit to him in brotherly fellowship is better for you than a blood brother who has neglected to share with you the common rights of faith and devotion. The Lord clearly proved this in the parable of the man wounded by robbers who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and of the Samaritan who cared for him.

Whoever blesses his neighbor, rising early with a loud voice, is like one who curses him. He blesses his neighbor with a loud voice who exalts him with the favor of excessive praise, either by favoring his evil deeds against justice or by praising his good deeds beyond what is proper. But such a person is likened to one who curses because he greatly harms the person whom, by praising him, he either gives confidence in evil action or diminishes the simplicity of a pure heart in a right action, so that he completes the good work he had begun with a view to heavenly reward out of love for passing praise.

Iron sharpens iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend. The consolation and counsel of wise people who instruct one another everywhere by mutual advice are very good: “Iron sharpens iron.”

Sheol and destruction will never be filled; likewise, the eyes of human beings are insatiable. The torments of hell will not be filled by reaching an end; likewise, the desires that seize human beings are insatiable in their longing to sin. They therefore suffer punishments without end because they had a will to sin without end, if only they had possessed a nature capable of living without end.

Know well the face of your sheep and consider your flocks.

For you will not always have authority, but a crown will be given through generation after generation. This is said to the shepherd of the Church. Take diligent care of those over whom you happen to preside; recognize the minds and actions of each one. If you find in them anything that soils them with vice, remember to correct it quickly. For you will not always have authority to feed the Lord’s sheep, but the crown you will receive is eternal if, in your time, you have rightly administered the office entrusted to you.

The meadows are open, green plants have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains. The pastures of heavenly sacraments, which had long been closed by legal figures, are now open. The new greenness of evangelical truth and grace has appeared, and the writings of the ancient Fathers have been gathered as fodder for the Lord’s flock. These things were taken away from the proud Jews by the sickle of divine judgment and given to the humble peoples of the Church for spiritual support, in accordance with the Lord’s saying to them: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew XXI).

Lambs for your clothing and goats for the price of a field. He calls the innocent “lambs” and the penitent “goats.” You will be clothed with the wool of lambs when, as a shepherd, you yourself advance through the good conduct of obedient disciples; seeing their praiseworthy deeds, you will become more glorious yourself both in the adornment of virtues and in the warmth of love. You will purchase a field with goats when, by calling sinners to repentance, you acquire for yourself a higher place in the land of the living.

Let the milk of goats be sufficient for your food, for the needs of your household, and for the sustenance of your maidservants. Feed the flock entrusted to you with such diligence that you will not lack fresh milk in summer or in the cold, but that it will always be sufficient for you and yours. That is, devote yourself so assiduously to teaching that you may even advance former penitents to the office of teaching, so that through those who formerly, because of the foulness of their vices, seemed destined to be placed on the judge’s left, rational and undeceiving milk of the word may now be supplied to the little ones in understanding.

Milk becomes food for maidservants when those who do not yet serve the Lord with perfect love but still serve him with servile fear are refreshed by the life-giving banquets of the word through the example or words of those who have been saved through repentance, and are helped to advance toward greater growth in the virtues.

Someone explained the words, “The meadows are open, green plants have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains; lambs for your clothing and goats for the price of a field,” in this way: “The tombs are laid open, resurrected bodies have appeared, sinners have been separated from the saints. Hay for burning from the high places. The lambs have been separated to the right and the goats to the left; the lambs for the king’s clothing, because he himself said, ‘I will dwell in them’ (2 Corinthians VI); the goats are sold for the price of the saints, whom they know, into the fires.” [Col. 0770A]

### CHAPTER XXVIII

The wicked flee when no one pursues. Whoever is not strong in faith, even when no persecutor is pressing upon him, nevertheless sometimes abandons the faith of his own accord [“Never” is redundant, or should perhaps be read as “sometimes”], whenever, through robberies, perjuries, fornications, sorceries, or other crimes of this kind, he makes himself like an unbeliever.

The righteous man will be confident like a lion, without fear. A lion does not tremble when beasts confront it, because it knows that it prevails over them all. Thus the security of the righteous man is rightly compared with that of a lion: when he sees anyone rising up against him, he returns to confidence of mind and knows that he overcomes all his adversaries, because he loves only the one whom he never loses from sight.

Wicked men do not consider judgment, but those who seek the Lord take note of everything. The elect take note of everything: that the universal judgment will come, and by which works rest, and by which works eternal punishment, will be repaid.

Whoever deceives the righteous on an evil road will fall into his own destruction, and the upright will possess his goods. Whoever deceives lovers of righteousness through heretical teaching so that they deviate from the truth incurs the punishment he deserves for his evils. But whatever good he possessed—whether through useful writing or through a continent way of life—passes to others for their benefit, namely to those who, reading or hearing these examples, take from him—even though they know he has perished—examples for their own salvation.

In the rejoicing of the righteous there is much glory. For they rejoice not in present riches but in future eternal goods; they are glad not over the things of the world, which they see, but over the Creator of the world, whose vision they hope for, as the Psalmist says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Psalm 31). Or certainly, in the rejoicing of the righteous much glory is produced, because whenever the elect happen in this life to rejoice over the Church’s prosperous circumstances, much glory is given to the Lord through the faith and good works of many.

[Col. 0770D] When the wicked reign, there is the ruin of men. Just as many begin to give glory to God when they see the righteous rejoicing in their progress in virtue, so whenever the reprobate hold power, they show many to be accomplices in their faithlessness. This can rightly be understood both of pagans, heretics, and wicked Catholics.

Blessed is the man who is always fearful, but he who is hard of heart will fall into evil. The anger of the coming judgment will then be borne with all the greater severity insofar as it is now scarcely feared amid one’s sins. Hence it is written elsewhere: “On the day of good things do not forget evils, and on the day of evils do not forget good things.” Thus the two must be joined together, so that one is always supported by the other.

[Col. 0771A] A roaring lion and a hungry bear: a wicked ruler over a poor people. This may be understood both of pagan rulers and of heretics, who with bestial savagery test either the patience or the wisdom of the poor people—that is, of the holy Church.

A man who persecutes a life unto blood, even if he has fled as far as the pit, no one will support him. [Note: [Col. 0771D] There was some blank space at this point in the manuscript.] Whoever works his land will be satisfied with bread, but whoever pursues idleness will be filled with poverty. Whether it is the soil of a field or the soil of the body, whoever cultivates it will be satisfied: the former with grain, the latter with virtues. Whoever scorns both will be filled with poverty.

A man who hastens to become rich and envies others does not know that poverty will overtake him. Certainly, whoever strives to increase his wealth neglects sin. Like birds caught when they greedily look at food from the earth, he does not recognize the snare of sin by which he will be strangled. Whoever desires the goods of the present world does not understand what losses he will suffer in the future.

When the wicked rise up, men hide themselves; but when they have perished, the righteous will multiply. He calls them “men”—those whom he calls righteous—because they preserve the just and established order of human nature given by God. Hence, in the book of blessed Job, a certain penitent sinner is told: “He will look upon men and say: I have sinned” (Job 33). This plainly means: he will look upon those who rightly preserve the nature of human creation, and they will recognize that by sinning they have made themselves like animals.

The meaning is therefore clear: when the persecution of the wicked is raging, the faithful are often hidden, often unable or not permitted to appear publicly, as the Lord says: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matthew 10). But when, with the persecutors destroyed, the persecution has ceased, the glory of the faithful shines more brightly after their afflictions. Moreover, many unbelievers, having seen the condemnation of unbelief, receive the grace of faith, in accordance with what is written: “When the pestilent man is scourged, the simple will become wiser” (Proverbs 21).

## CHAPTER XXIX

A man who speaks flattering and deceitful words to his friend spreads a net for his steps. Whoever praises his neighbor with deceitful words prepares snares for him, so that, made more secure by his careless action or speech, he may fall into danger. But let us see whether the nets of the deceitful ensnare the man around whose steps they are spread, or rather the man by whom they are spread. The text continues:

The snare will entangle the sinful man who acts wickedly, and the righteous man will praise and rejoice. The snare of sinners therefore does not harm the righteous, even if it kills him bodily. The ambushes that the wicked prepare for their neighbors condemn the wicked themselves forever, while the righteous rejoice and praise the Creator’s just judgment, either for their own deliverance or for the destruction of the wicked.

Finally, the ancient edition plainly placed at the end of the preceding verse: “He surrounds his feet with nets.” For, because of the ambiguous Greek word αὐτοῦ, either interpretation is possible. For, as it is said elsewhere: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it himself.”

[Col. 0772A] A wise man who contends with a fool will find no rest, whether he becomes angry or laughs. If a wise teacher contends with an unbelieving and stubborn man, whether he recounts the torments of the reprobate or the joys of the good, he labors in vain with the senseless man. Whether he urges him to the lamentation of repentance or explains the rewards of good works, he is not heard by the fool. Hence the Apostles also said to the Jews: “We lamented for you, and you did not mourn; we sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matthew 11).

A fool pours out his entire spirit. When impatience drives him, he is moved to pour out his whole spirit. Turmoil therefore expels it more quickly, because no discipline of wisdom restrains it within.

[Col. 0772B] But the wise man delays and reserves it for the future. When injured, he does not desire to avenge himself immediately, because, even while enduring, he wishes to spare. Nevertheless, he does not fail to recognize that everything will be avenged at the final judgment. The ancient translation has this passage as follows: “The wicked man pours out all his anger, but the wise man distributes it gradually, piece by piece.” For the fool is inflamed to vengeance by the disturbance of anger, whereas the wise man gradually weakens and drives it out through mature deliberation and moderation.

The poor man and the creditor met one another; the Lord is the enlightener of both. The poor man is the humble hearer of the word of God; the creditor is the man who entrusts to him the money of that same word by preaching. They meet when they come together in one and the same grace of devotion. The Lord is the enlightener of both, because neither could preach without the gift of divine grace, nor could the other believe. For the truthful judgment of truth remains: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

A king who judges the poor in truth will have his throne established forever. So too the Psalmist says of Christ the King: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom” (Psalm 44).

The rod and reproof will give wisdom, but a child who is left to his own will brings shame upon his mother. Concerning this rod the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4). The child whom he very frequently urges to be corrected and instructed is the people of God. If they are not disciplined by the priests’ continual admonitions and rebukes, they bring shame upon the Church, since those outside disparage the religion of the Christian faith. Thus what follows is rightly added:

When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered; but blessed is he who keeps the law. For when priestly instruction ceases, the discipline of divine law is immediately loosened, by which the people ought to reach the rewards of blessedness.

Have you seen a man swift to speak? There is more hope of folly than of his correction. Folly is indeed a grave vice, but loquacity is no lighter. For it often happens that some dull man, ignorant even of letters themselves, receives the words of saving correction more quickly, whereas one endowed with an abundance of speech strives more to display boastfully what he knows—or thinks he knows—than to listen to the words of the wise.

[Col. 0773A] Whoever delicately nourishes his servant from childhood will later find him rebellious. Whoever delicately nourishes his body from childhood, though he ought to subject it to the spirit, will find it wanton and uncontrollable when it reaches the years of adolescence. Another translation expresses this verse beautifully: “He who is delicate from childhood will be a servant, but at last he will be grieved in himself.” For he will be late in repenting of his evils, grieving within himself because he remembers that, while still young, he refused to restrain himself from his pleasures according to the rule of the prudent.

An angry man provokes quarrels, and whoever is quick to indignation will be more prone to sins. Anger is the door of all vices; when it is closed, rest will be granted to the virtues within.

Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul; he hears an adjuration and does not disclose the matter. Wisdom teaches its hearer not only to abstain from sins but also to restrain himself from the company of sinners, lest he deserve to hear from the strict judge: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers.” For not only the thief is held guilty, but also the man who, knowing of the theft, refuses to disclose it when the owner seeks the money he has lost, although he is able to do so.

[Col. 0773C] But lest anyone claim that, out of fear of a more powerful person, he can neither separate himself from the company of thieves nor disclose what he knows, the text appropriately adds:

Whoever fears man will quickly fall, but whoever hopes in the Lord will be lifted up. To this the Gospel saying applies: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

## CHAPTER XXX

The words of the Gatherer, son of the Vomiter. Up to this point are the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, translated. From here there are again words of Solomon, spoken by him on another occasion; perhaps he is now called by the name which in Greek is Ecclesiastes, translated into Latin here as “Gatherer.” For a church is called a gathering.

The vision spoken by the man with whom God is, and who, strengthened because God dwelt with him, said. “The vision,” he says, “which he spoke,” because, by contemplating more secret things in God’s presence, he disclosed outwardly through speech to human beings what he had seen. For whoever is strengthened by the Spirit of God speaks the following words with a humble heart:

I am the most foolish of men, and the wisdom of men is not with me. “The sons of this age are wiser in their generation than the sons of light” (Luke 16). And the Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3). He himself also says concerning himself and those like him, in whom God dwells: “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block indeed to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1).

I have not learned wisdom, yet I know the knowledge of the holy ones. Solomon did not learn wisdom from a human being, but received it freely when God offered it, so that he might know the knowledge of the holy. The Apostle too, who says, “We are fools for Christ’s sake” (2 Corinthians 4), again says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2)—a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed.

Who has ascended into heaven and descended? This knowledge of the holy, which is considered foolishness by the wise of this age, is so because the Son of God, after his death and resurrection, ascended into heaven in the flesh he had assumed, and at the time of our resurrection will descend from heaven to judge the living and the dead.

Who has held the spirit in his hands? Every spirit—human, angelic, that of animals, and that of storms—is held by God’s power so that it may not fail.

Who has gathered the waters as though in a garment? Of him the Psalmist also says: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Psalm 33).

Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth? Even now the Lord raises up and sustains everything that lives and grows throughout the world—human beings, animals, and plants—so that each may continue in its own life. On the day of judgment he will raise the whole human race from death, from the four winds of heaven.

What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know? He speaks of the name of God the Father and of the Son, whose mystery worldly wisdom cannot know by nature. Nevertheless, through the things it sees to have been wondrously made, it can understand that there is one God who made all things. “If you know,” he says—that is, you who, boasting of your wisdom, presume to call the mysteries of our faith foolishness.

Every word of God is fiery, a shield for those who hope in him. The whole Church of Christ knows this, and those know it especially who, with God dwelling with them, despise the arrogance of earthly wisdom. For every word of divine authority both kindles the hearts of the elect with the fire of charity, illuminates them with the knowledge of truth, consumes whatever filth of vices it finds in them, and defends all who hope in it from the ambushes of enemies and from every adversity.

But we must examine more carefully the property of the Greek expression πεπυρωμένον, which the Latin translation does not explain in a single word. Hence it is translated sometimes as “ignited” and sometimes as “tested by fire,” as in: “Your word is greatly ignited,” and “silver tested by fire” (Psalms 118 and 11). In Greek both are expressed by the one word τὸ πεπυρωμένον. Likewise, the passage that sounds very similar to this saying of Solomon—“The words of the Lord are tested by fire, that is, πεπυρωμένα; he is the protector of all who hope in him” (Psalm 17)—uses the same term.

Πεπυρωμένον therefore signifies something that has been purified by being melted in fire. For just as metals melted by fire contain no foreign or useless impurity within them, but everything remaining in them is genuine, perfect, and cleansed of every taint of vice, so the word of the Lord, bearing witness within itself to faith in eternal goods, has this saying of the Lord: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished” (Matthew 5). All things are true and, having been tested by fire, are free from every ambiguity of empty superfluity.

Do not add anything to those words, lest you be reproved and be found a liar. Do not corrupt the words of the holy Scriptures, as certain heretics are known to have done so that they would not be convicted by them.

Two things I have asked of you; do not deny them to me before I die. Keep vanity and lying words far from me. Do not give me mendacity or riches; grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance, and so forth. Thus the man with whom God is, his speech irradiated by the fire of the divine word, addresses his voice to the Lord, beseeching him never to prefer the vanity of the world or lying words to the truth of the heavenly Scriptures, and not to fall again into forgetfulness of eternal things through either abundance or want of transitory goods.

A generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother. When above he asked the Lord to grant him purity of life, he suddenly turns his gaze to contemplate the wickedness of the perverse and indicates by how many miseries it is entangled and how far it stands from the truth. “There is,” he says, “a generation of the impious which, even if it does any good, destroys it”—namely, by failing to honor its parents.

A generation that seems pure in its own eyes, yet is not washed from its filth. The Psalmist speaks of this generation: “For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves” (Psalm 52).

A generation whose eyes are exalted and whose eyelids are raised on high. The Psalmist avoided the company of this generation when he said: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes raised high” (Psalm 130).

A generation that has swords for teeth and devours with its molars. Of this the Psalmist says: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongues are a sharp sword.”

So that they may devour the needy from the earth and the poor from among men. The persecutors of the Church arm their tongues for this purpose: to slaughter Christ’s innocent and humble people.

If you wish to consider this carefully, you will find that these generations are the most wicked assemblies of Jews and heretics. The generation of the Jews cursed its father—namely, the one who said, “Israel is my firstborn son”—when it denied his Son as he came in the flesh. It did not bless its mother, the Synagogue, because it stripped her of the knowledge of her former faith concerning Christ, which she had possessed in the patriarchs and prophets.

The generation of the Novatians seems pure in its own eyes, saying that it has no need of repentance, yet it cannot be clean from the filth of sins, since by denying forgiveness to sinners it closes off the fountain of repentance.

Likewise, the generation of the Arians has exalted eyes and raised eyelids directed above God, asking what existed previously, whether there was a time when the Son did not exist, and what the power of the Holy Spirit is—whether equal or unequal.

Likewise, the generation that has swords for teeth is that assembly which strives to disclose its faithlessness to others. Just as bodies are commonly laid low by swords, so it seeks to subject the souls of its hearers to eternal death through the poison of wicked speech.

A leech has two daughters who say, “Give, give.” The leech is the devil, who is incessantly inflamed by a thirst for committing sins and persuading others to sin. He has two daughters, because there are two particular enticements of the human race that imitate this disposition [animum] of the ancient enemy. The more freely the reins of lust are loosened, the more harmfully it delights; and, as one of the poets said:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.

There are three things that are never satisfied, and a fourth that does not say, “Enough”: the underworld, the mouth of the womb, and the earth, which is not satisfied with water; but fire does not say, “Enough.” The underworld is never filled. Likewise, the prostitute, its neighbor, is not satisfied with the pleasures of the body; and the greedy man never says, “Enough.”

Some interpret the underworld as the devil, who is insatiable in human seduction; the mouth of the womb and the earth that is not satisfied with water as above; and the fire that does not say, “Enough” as the burning of Gehenna, which never ceases but burns with infinite heat those who refused to put an end to their sins.

The eye that mocks its father and despises the birth of its mother—may the ravens of the torrents pluck it out, and the young of the eagle devour it. When the perverse criticize divine judgments, they mock the father. Likewise, when heretics deride and scorn the preaching of the holy Church, they despise the birth of their mother, because they came forth from her, though they speak against him. “They went out from us,” it says, “but they were not of us.”

When Catholic preachers, proceeding from the streams of the divine Scriptures, refute their purpose by reproving them, they are, as it were, plucking out the wicked eye with ravens from the torrents. And the young of the eagle devour it. Holy teachers are called ravens because, through the grace of humility, they confess the blackness of sin within themselves. They are called the young of the eagle because they have been reborn through the grace of the one who, in the form of the humanity he assumed, flew up to heavenly things. Hence elsewhere they are also called “the sons of the bridegroom.”

There are three things too difficult for me, and a fourth that I utterly do not know: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon the earth, the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, and the way of a man in his youth. As far as the historical sense is concerned, it is as it is written. But because he speaks in parables, the way of an eagle in the sky is difficult to find—that is, the subtlety of the enemy, by which he flies around the hearts of heavenly men and is detected only with great difficulty.

Likewise, the way of the serpent upon the earth signifies the devices of the poisonous enemy, who never ceases to lie in wait for those whom he sees established upon the rock of faith. The way of the ship in the midst of the sea signifies the way of iniquity, which moves with such subtlety through the bitter waves of this world, stirred by the blasts of unclean spirits, that its course can scarcely or not at all be detected.

That the eagle signifies the evil enemy is attested by the prophet, who says: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations 4)—that is, the men who persecuted us were so savage that they seemed more cruel than the demons themselves.

That the serpent often signifies the devil was demonstrated both in the transgression of the first man and when the wise man said: “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

That the ship signifies the instability of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine is shown by the prophet, who says: “And the Chaldeans glorying in their ships” (Isaiah 43). This signifies unclean spirits exalting themselves over the weakness and instability of the human mind and rejoicing as victors over its ruin.

Just as those things are so crafty that they cannot be discovered, so it is difficult to conceive of the young man who has abandoned the way of truth: with what wandering thoughts his foolish and errant mind turns aside at every hour and into how many reflections it strays.

Such also is the way of the adulterous woman, who eats, wipes her mouth, and says: “I have done no evil.” The mind of the adulteress, like the things mentioned above, is always unstable and wandering. When she has been able to conceal the shame of her act, she denies that she has committed any crime.

There are four things that are least among those on earth, yet they are wiser than the wise. The righteous often seem lesser on earth than the reprobate—that is, humbler and more despised by this world. Yet they are wiser than the world’s wise because they savor eternal and heavenly goods and, in order to seek what those others do not know, desire to endure every adversity of the world with courage.

The ants are a weak people who prepare their food in the harvest. The people of the Church, in order to preserve strength of mind, show themselves weak for a time when adversaries rage, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). In this life they prepare for themselves the fruits of good works, by which they may merit everlasting life.

The little rabbits are a feeble people who place their dwelling in a rock. Here too he signifies the people of the Church, who are called feeble either because, as we said above, they do not seek to avenge their own injuries, or because they have learned to place no confidence in their own strength but to hope for salvation in the help of their Redeemer. This is to place their dwelling in a rock, under whose protection they avoid hostile attacks, as the Lord says with the Psalmist: “Be for me a very strong rock and a fortified house, to save me, because you are my rock and my fortress.”

In place of “little rabbit,” the ancient translation has “hyrax” (*chyrogrillus*). It is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear. It is abundant in the regions of Palestine, and it is accustomed always to live in caves of rocks and holes in the earth.

It should be noted that in the psalm where we sing “Rock, a refuge for hedgehogs,” some manuscripts have “for rabbits,” and others “for hyraxes.” Likewise, in this saying of Solomon, certain copies have “hedgehog” in place of “little rabbit.” Moreover, in the book of Hebrew Names we find that the same Hebrew word, *saphan*, in Jeremiah, has been interpreted by Saint Jerome as “hyrax,” “rabbit,” and “hedgehog.”

A locust has no king, yet it goes forth in companies. Some interpret the locust as the people of the nations, who once existed without a king—that is, without Christ, without a prophet, and without a teacher—and, not gathered into the unity of faith, hasten to spiritual battle against the devil.

The locust may also be understood as the harmonious unity of anchorites. Though they are ruled in their hiding places by no human instructor, they nevertheless serve Christ with tireless perseverance, each in his own place, and are accustomed to consume the shoots of carnal pleasures as they grow wrongly.

The lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in the palaces of kings. The lizard supports itself with its hands because it has no wings by which it might be carried. Dwelling in the palaces of kings, it signifies the humility of those who, although naturally slow in understanding, nevertheless by the skillful diligence of their efforts attain either knowledge of the divine Scriptures or the grace of the virtues by which they may merit entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

Often birds, which feathers lift for flight, perch in thorn bushes; but the lizard, which has no feathers for flying, supports itself with its hands and occupies the king’s building. For often the clever, while they grow sluggish through negligence, remain in wicked actions, whereas the simple, whom the feather of intellect does not assist, are lifted by the virtue of their works to obtain the walls of the eternal kingdom.

There are three things that walk well, and a fourth that walks successfully: the lion, strongest among beasts, which fears no encounter; a cock with girded loins; and a ram—and there is no king who can resist it. Here the lion is the one of whom it is written: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered.” He is called strongest among beasts because in him “what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.” He fears no encounter, for he says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

The cock with girded loins signifies the holy preachers who announce the true morning amid the darkness of this night. Their loins are girded because they restrain the flowing excesses of lust in their own members.

And the ram—and there is no king who can resist it. Whom else should we understand here as the ram except the first order within the Church, the priests? Of them it is written: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28). By their examples they draw the people who walk after them like a following flock of sheep. No king at all can resist those who live spiritually and rightly, because whatever persecutor confronts them cannot impede their purpose.

And because after these things the Antichrist will appear, the text adds this fourth figure, saying:

There is one who appeared foolish after he was raised on high; for if he had understood, he would have placed his hand over his mouth. He will indeed be raised on high when he falsely claims to be God. Yet once raised on high he will appear foolish, because in that very exaltation he will fail at the coming of the true one.

If he had understood, he would have placed his hand over his mouth—that is, if he had foreseen his punishment when he began to grow proud, he would not, once well created, have been raised up in such a display of arrogance.

This should not disturb anyone because it was said above: “A fourth that walks successfully.” He said that three walk well and the fourth successfully. For not everything that is successful is good, nor in this life is everything that is good successful. The lion, the cock, and the ram walk well, but not successfully here, because they suffer the battles of persecution. The fourth walks successfully but not well, because the Antichrist proceeds in deceit; yet for the brief duration of the present life that deceit prospers for him.

Whoever presses the breasts firmly to draw out milk expresses butter; and whoever milks with excessive force draws out blood. We press the breasts firmly when we weigh the words of sacred speech with subtle understanding. By this pressure, while seeking milk, we find butter, because while we seek nourishment even through a slight understanding, we are anointed with the abundance of inward richness.

But this must not be done excessively or continually, lest, while milk is sought, blood issue from the breasts. For when the words of sacred speech are examined more than they should be, they fall into a carnal understanding. The one who milks with excessive force draws out blood, because what is perceived through an excessive wandering of the spirit becomes carnal.

And whoever provokes anger produces discord. The preceding parable explains what this signifies according to the literal sense. Whoever addresses his neighbor with measured speech receives a pleasing reply, as though he were expressing butter from breasts in which he sought milk. But whoever provokes anger and discord in a brother’s heart through an unsuitable word, like one milking the breasts beyond measure, finds blood instead of milk.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### THE WORDS OF KING LAMUEL. THE VISION WITH WHICH HIS MOTHER INSTRUCTED HIM

Lamuel is interpreted as “in whom is God.” He is the one referred to above as “the vision,” with the same name translated into Latin, because he spoke as “the man with whom God is.”

The mother who taught him this vision is best understood as divine grace, which invisibly instructed him in his heart with the understanding of wisdom that he himself would outwardly minister to human beings. Nevertheless, it can also rightly be understood as Solomon’s fleshly mother, who taught him these things when he was a child. Since he recognized that they had been wisely spoken, he wished to insert them into his Book of Proverbs. Therefore, after the title says “the words of King Lamuel,” it rightly immediately adds: “the vision with which his mother instructed him.” For when he was anointed king and received the spirit of wisdom, he saw in that same Spirit how wisely his good mother had instructed him.

What, my chosen one? What, chosen son of my womb? You should understand: What shall I say to you, my son, who, born from my womb, have been chosen for kingship?

What, chosen one of my vows? That is, you who have been chosen for that which I desired with complete devotion.

Do not give your substance to women. The literal sense is clear, but we are also forbidden to stain the substance of our virtues with the corruptions of vices.

And your riches to the destruction of kings. He gives his riches to destroy kings who corrupt human hearts with earthly pleasures, so that they will not seek the heavenly goods in which they could reign forever with the Lord. Kings are destroyed through riches when those who have been united by faith to the body of the supreme King nevertheless, through the allurements of the world, deserve to be uprooted from the land of the living.

Do not give wine to kings, O Lamuel; do not give wine to kings. These words and those that follow are clear according to the literal sense. Allegorically, however, he commands that wine, in which there is lust, must not intoxicate the minds of the faithful, who are members of the eternal King.

For there is no secret where drunkenness reigns. No heavenly secrets are contemplated where carnal pleasure reigns; such people pursue only those visible things that belong to the flesh.

Lest he drink and forget judgments and alter the cause of the poor man’s children. Lest, intoxicated by earthly allurements, he forget Christ’s poor people, for he himself was made poor for our sake.

Give strong drink to those who are grieving, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit. Let them drink and no longer remember their poverty or their sorrow. Here he calls “strong drink” and “wine” the everlasting consolation of divine wisdom. It is to be offered to those hearts that refuse to be consoled by lowly things and receive whatever happens in the present with a bitter spirit, clinging with their whole mind only to the heavenly joys they do not yet see, in accordance with him who said: “My soul refused consolation; I remembered God, and I was delighted.”

Likewise: “Give strong drink to those who are grieving, and let those who are bitter in spirit drink wine,” and so forth. Pour abundantly into those who are weighed down by grief and sadness on account of repentance for their former actions the sweetness of spiritual knowledge, like wine that gladdens the human heart. Refresh them with the abundant draught of saving speech, lest those of this kind, submerged by continual grief and deadly despair, be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

Open your mouth for the mute and for the causes of all the children who pass away. Speak on behalf of the poor, who cannot speak for themselves in judgment, and take care to defend those who, with the heavenly homeland in view, hasten to pass more quickly through the road of this life.

Alternatively, he commands that one open one’s mouth for the mute by preaching the word of faith to the people of the nations, who previously did not know how to utter the divine words, and by extending concern for salvation not only to the Jews but also to all the nations throughout the world.

Open your mouth, decide what is just, and judge the needy and the poor. Just as in the preceding verse he commanded that one open one’s mouth for the cause and deliverance of the poor, so here he admonishes one to chastise and judge the poor person himself when he goes astray, with justice. In accordance with this Moses also says: “You shall not pity the poor in judgment” (Exodus 33). The prophet indicates that the Lord does both when he says: “He will judge the poor in righteousness and reprove in equity for the meek of the earth” (Isaiah 11).

Thus far the words of Lamuel.

From this point the most wise of kings, Solomon, sings the praises of the holy Church in a few verses, but with the fullest truth. For this poem consists of twenty-two verses, corresponding to the order and number of the letters of the Hebrews, so that each verse begins with one of the individual letters. Through the most perfect order of the alphabet, it symbolically indicates how fully the virtues and rewards are here described either of every faithful soul or of the whole holy Church, which is made one from all the elect souls.

Who can find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the remotest bounds.

The Catholic Church is called the strong woman: namely, the woman accustomed to beget spiritual children for God from water and the Holy Spirit; strong because, for faith in her Creator, she scorns all the adversities and prosperities of this age alike. He himself, appearing in the flesh, found her indeed weak, but by his discovery of her—that is, by his gracious visitation—made her strong. [Col. 0781B] Hence, after her redemption, as he was returning to heaven, he joyfully said to the heavenly citizens: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the sheep that had been lost” (Luke XV).

Therefore, seeing the human race entangled in innumerable errors, and seeing that no patriarch, no prophet, and no one at all among the elect could suffice for its salvation except the sole mediator between God and human beings, Solomon says: “Who can find a strong woman? Her price is far from, and from the remotest ends of the earth”; as though he openly proclaimed his amazement at the future grace of the Lord: Who is of such virtue, who possesses such merit, that from so many unbelieving and wicked nations of the world he will gather for himself one Church of the elect, which by his grace he will make strong and inseparable, despite all opposition? [Col. 0781C]

Certainly, one like us is not meant here, nor is he to come in our time; rather, at the end of the ages God-Man will descend from heaven, to redeem us by his passion and death. This is what is meant by “far from, and from the remotest ends of the earth is her price”: “far from,” namely, in the period of time that intervened between Solomon’s days and the Virgin’s giving birth; “from the remotest ends,” because his going forth was from the highest heaven, and because he offered himself as the only price for our redemption. Hence the Apostle says: “He loved us and handed himself over for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians V).

[Col. 0781D] The price of the holy Church may also rightly be understood as having been set far away, because the incarnation of the Word of God, his life among human beings, his passion, and his resurrection were far removed from the condition of our nature. For he was born both when he wished and from the mother whom he wished; he lived in the world without sin; he departed from the world by the death he wished and in the manner he wished; and he likewise held the time of his resurrection and ascension in his own power. Such things were as far removed from us as heaven is from earth. But because the Lord, who redeemed the Church, granted her not only to receive the word of salvation, but also steadfastly to fight for it and to preach it throughout the world, it is rightly added:

Her husband’s heart trusts in her, and he will have no need of spoils.

He calls the Lord and Redeemer of the holy Church her husband—the one who also deigned to become her price. [Col. 0782A] Hence the Apostle says to believers: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Corinthians I).

The statement “Her husband’s heart trusts in her” is plainly drawn from human custom. For just as a man who has a strong, faithful, and chaste wife trusts her completely, because she can do nothing against his will, cannot be touched even by an adulterous thought, willingly endures every adversity for love of him, and desires to convert to his friendship as many as she can, so indeed—so indeed—our Lord and Redeemer trusts in the Church. For he knows the spirit of grace that he has given her; he knows the power of love that he has poured into her heart. Therefore he does not doubt that she can in no way be corrupted from the integrity of her faith, but also [Col. 0782B] that she will persist in gathering more people into the unity of that same faith.

This is what follows: “And he will have no need of spoils.” The Church despoils the devil when, through her preachers, she recalls to the path of truth those whom he had deceived. It is rightly said that “he will have no need of spoils,” because the Church will never cease restoring to the faith of Christ souls liberated from diabolical fraud, until, when the course of the world has been completed, the predetermined number of her members has also been fulfilled.

But because whatever good the holy Church, or any faithful soul, does is received from above, it is rightly added:

She will repay him with good and not with evil all the days of her life.

The soul repays Christ with good when, living rightly in response to the gifts of life received from him, it strives also to make known to others [Col. 0782C] what, with his help, it has been able to learn or do. After saying “She will repay him with good,” he rightly adds at once, “and not with evil,” because there are certainly people who repay the good they have received from the Lord with evil: either by defiling the mysteries of faith they received with heretical filth; or by blaspheming the faith they preserve in their profession through wicked deeds; or by corrupting through evil conversation the good morals by which they serve together with right faith.

Nor do those repay the Lord with the good they have received who do not take care to persevere until the end of their present life in what they have begun well. Therefore, after saying “She will repay him with good and not with evil,” to show the necessity of perseverance in goodness he added, “all the days of her life.” A similar saying occurs in the Gospel: [Col. 0782D] “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days” (Luke I).

The works, and the fruits of righteousness or holiness, to which the person who strives gratefully to repay the good received from the Lord should devote himself are subsequently indicated:

She sought wool and flax, and worked by the counsel of her hands.

The strong woman—that is, the holy Church—has also been accustomed to receive and observe the beginning of this verse according to its literal meaning, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah LVIII).

She does not work through useless and blind labor, but with this purpose: that at the judgment [Col. 0783A] she may deserve to hear from her husband, the Lord Christ: “I was naked and you clothed me; and whatever you did for one of these least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew XXV).

She works “by the counsel of her hands,” that is, through those persons by whom she gives alms to the poor. In their devout work she uses that health-giving counsel: when she distributes and gives to the poor, she is not praised by people for a time, but her righteousness remains for ever and ever, and her horn is exalted in glory.

Mystically, wool may be understood as all the works of piety and simplicity that we bestow upon our neighbors, since wool is the clothing of sheep. In flax, which grows green from the earth but through long and manifold exercise loses its natural moisture and reaches the grace of a new whiteness, the chastisement of our flesh may be signified. While through continence we burn away the inborn [Col. 0783B] filth of vices, we make it worthy to clothe us with Christ, according to the Apostle’s saying: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III).

The strong woman therefore seeks wool and flax and works by the counsel of her hands when the holy Church diligently seeks by what fruits of piety she may exercise herself and how she may cleanse herself from carnal enticements; and she does both with the wisest counsel, that is, solely with regard to the reward from above. The following verse also speaks more clearly of this reward:

She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.

He calls a merchant an *institor*, because in ancient usage he is so called from his diligent pursuit of acquiring and multiplying [Col. 0783C] merchandise.

The strong woman therefore became like a merchant’s ship, because just as a merchant’s ship, loaded with goods that are more plentiful in its homeland, seeks foreign lands across the sea so that, after selling what it brought there, it may carry home things more valuable, so the holy Church, and every perfect soul, rejoices to be laden with the riches of virtues by which it may purchase greater gifts of divine grace.

For the exchange is excellent when, by doing the good we are able to do, we first receive this reward from the Lord: that we may always advance toward doing greater things; and thereafter we receive eternal life.

The holy soul therefore became like a merchant’s ship. It crosses, in desire, the waves of the present age; it meditates on the eternal joys that it hopes to receive in heaven alone; [Col. 0783D] and, to obtain them more abundantly, it strives eagerly to do whatever it can and bravely to overcome whatever adversity arises.

Of this it is rightly said that “she brings her bread from afar,” because in all the temporal good things she does, she awaits only an eternal reward. She desires only the satiety of the living bread, namely, that bread of the one who mercifully and powerfully promises his hearers: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI).

By contrast, the person who receives his bread close at hand, and does not bring it from afar across the seas, is the one who, in what appears to be righteous living, seeks only the rewards of human approval and does not strive, with any thought of enduring life, to rise above and trample upon the things that slip away below. Of such people he himself thunders terribly: [Col. 0784A] “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew VI).

She rose in the night, gave food to her household, and provisions to her maidservants.

Just as the whole course of the passing age is varied by the perpetual alternation of day and night, with day naturally established for work and night for rest, so the whole period of the present Church is ordered by a kind of twofold state of rest and work.

She rests, as it were, at night when some of her faithful, interrupting for a time their external concerns, begin to devote themselves to themselves and to care spiritually for themselves—by exercising themselves more privately in sacred readings, prayers, tears, or other such pursuits.

She rises at night when, in these same faithful, she earnestly girds herself to undertake the care [Col. 0784B] of her neighbors as well. She is accustomed to perform this work of fraternal service in two ways: she both calls those who were wandering outside to the grace of faith, and never ceases to rouse those who have already been imbued with the sacraments of faith to devote themselves more fully to good works.

Hence it is rightly said: “She gave food to her household, and provisions to her maidservants.” She gives food to her household when she reconciles to the fellowship of those who preceded them in faith the people whom, by teaching, she has been able to rescue from the ancient enemy. She gives provisions to her maidservants when, so that the humble who obey her commands with due fear may not grow weary under their pious labor, she refreshes them with the remembrance of the heavenly reward.

She considered a field and bought it; from the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard.

He calls the field the possession [Col. 0784C] of the heavenly inheritance, of which the patriarch speaks while blessing his son: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis XXVII).

The fragrance of the saints is like the fragrance of a full field that the Lord has blessed, because with the whole intention of their minds they contemplate what the fullness of blessing will be in the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

The Church therefore considered a field and bought it because she diligently learned what the joys of everlasting life are, and for the sake of obtaining them she strove to labor as much as she could. She also planted a vineyard from the fruit of her hands, because from the fruitful deeds or words of her faithful she established Holy Scripture, through which she might intoxicate the minds of her hearers with faith and love of their Redeemer.

Nor is it inappropriate if we understand the Church herself—who is represented by the strong woman [Col. 0784D]—to be figured under the name of the vineyard, and those who are the woman’s children to be the vineyard’s branches. The woman planted the vineyard when the primitive Church, sending preachers throughout the world, scattered the seeds of faith.

She considered the field when she perceived that the whole world, bristling with the thorns of vices, needed a spiritual cultivator. She bought it when, sending teachers everywhere, she entrusted the talent of the word to those who would hear, so that, once they believed, she might subject them to the most blessed service of Christ.

She planted a vineyard in that same field when, through a full instruction in evangelical truth, she established the Church among newly believing peoples.
