She planted this vineyard from the fruit of her hands because the apostles and their successors [Col. 0785A] instructed the peoples they taught not only by word, but also joined signs of miracles to the words of their teaching as a testimony to good works.

Even to this day—or rather, until the end of the age—the strong woman considers the field and buys it, and from the fruit of her hands plants a vineyard, because the holy Church is always diligently seeking those whom she can convert to the faith. Whoever she finds teachable, she buys for the service of Christ by giving the payment of the word, and strives to plant Christ’s vineyard in them, or rather to make them Christ’s vineyard.

And because anyone who desires to teach another must first abstain from evil himself and exercise himself in good works, it is rightly added:

She girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm. [Col. 0785B]

The Church girded her loins with strength when, intent upon the desires of heavenly things, she disdained to succumb to carnal enticements. She strengthened her arm when she prepared herself to perform works of virtue.

It is rightly said first that she girds her loins with strength and afterward strengthens them, because the action of a good work cannot be acceptable to God if a person does not first restrain the looseness of lust from both flesh and mind. Hence the prophet says: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah I). And the Lord himself says: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.” Let your loins be girded, lest you be subjected to lust; let your lamps be burning, so that you may shine with good works.

She tasted and saw that her commerce was good; her lamp will not [Col. 0785C] be extinguished at night.

When he says “her commerce,” he is clearly referring to the field of which he said above: “She considered a field and bought it.”

The holy Church tasted; every perfect soul tasted—that is, it recognized with the innermost desire of the mind—that the commerce of imperishable life is good, life which we purchase in heaven as an eternal reward after abandoning temporal enticements. She also tasted—that is, she learned openly—that it is good, through the urgency of preaching, to lead to the life of truth all whom she is able to lead. Therefore she cannot afterward be delayed by any darkness of tribulations, not even by death. [The reading *post est* is uncertain; the sense appears to be “cannot be delayed.”]

A lamp is extinguished at night, although it appears to burn during the day, because, as the Lord says, “they believe for a while, and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke VIII). The lamp of those people is also extinguished in the middle of the night [Col. 0785D] who are proved, when the Judge comes, not to have had the oil of love in the vessels of their hearts, while, after the rumor of false virtues has been lost, they pay the true penalties of their dark deeds.

If we wish to understand “night” here as rest, in accordance with what was said above, “She rose in the night”—that is, she prepared herself for work after rest—it is aptly said that the lamp of the holy Church is not extinguished at night. For when she rests from the business of action, she is more freely available to the light of heavenly contemplation; and when she ceases from public works, she takes greater care to devote herself either to hearing sacred reading or to divine praises, following the example of the industrious woman, who is accustomed not only to devote herself during the day to necessary labors, but also, at night, often having lit her lamp, to take an equal care of her household [the reading *parilemm* is uncertain]. [Col. 0786A]

She put out her hands to strong things, and her fingers grasped the spindle.

By “strong things” he means perfect works in the love of Christ, to which the Church joyfully submitted herself in the sure expectation of a heavenly reward. For example: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy’; but I say to you, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,” and so forth (Matthew V). Concerning the preservation of virginity: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew XIX). Concerning the contempt of riches: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor,” and so forth (ibid.).

The people of the Synagogue, to whom it was said, “If you are willing and obey, you shall eat the good things of the land,” were so much weaker in the work [Col. 0786B] of righteousness as they were less uplifted by the hope of eternal reward.

But the Church, which hears from the Lord, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew IV), rightly endures even hard things with patience because of this command. Hence again he says of her strength: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew X).

“And her fingers,” he says, “grasped the spindle.” Women commonly hold the spindle in the right hand and the distaff in the left. For wool is wound around the distaff, to be drawn out as thread and pass, through spinning, onto the spindle.

In Scripture the right hand often signifies everlasting life, while the left signifies God’s present gifts: the abundance of possessions, the peace of the times, bodily health, knowledge of the Scriptures, and the understanding of heavenly mysteries.

When, by the Lord’s generosity, we receive these and similar [Col. 0786C] goods, we carry them as wool wound around a distaff in the left hand. But when we begin beneficially to exercise them for love of heavenly things, we transfer the wool of the immaculate Lamb from the distaff to the spindle, from the left hand to the right. For from the goods of our Redeemer and from the examples of his works we make for ourselves a robe of heavenly glory and a garment of nuptial love.

The fingers by which we are said to grasp the spindle signify the very intention of discernment by which each person acts. No members of the body are divided into more joints or adapted to more flexing than the fingers.

Whoever, therefore, can truthfully say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0786D] (Philippians III), has truly grasped the spindle with the fingers of his right hand, because he has learned to labor for eternal goods with attentive discernment.

It is rightly said that they “grasped,” so that the earnestness and haste with which we ought to act in the uncertainty of this life for rewards that are certain with God may be commended more vividly.

What the strong woman—that is, the holy Church, or every perfect soul—has worked through the intellectual spindle is explained next:

She opened her hand to the needy and extended her palms to the poor.

This may also be understood of works of almsgiving generally performed for the poor; but it is better understood of the word of God, which bestows the garment of salvation upon souls. The blessed Job boasts of this, saying: [Col. 0787A] “I put on righteousness, and clothed myself with it as with a garment, and with my judgment as with a diadem” (Job XXIX).

The Church opened her hand to the needy when she revealed the mysteries of faith to those ignorant of them through the workers of truth. She extended her palms to the poor when she scattered preachers far and wide to instruct nations lacking eternal salvation.

She will not fear the cold of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in double garments.

The cold of snow is the hearts of the reprobate, stiffened by the chill of their faithlessness. Of them the Lord says: “Because lawlessness will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew XXIV).

The worst one is signified by snow [the manuscript adds *designatur*], who, falling from heaven into the depths of darkness because of the merit of his original pride, nevertheless presumes to display himself as an angel [Col. 0787B] of light to the foolish and to present the appearance of his merits as resembling snowy whiteness to those unaware of his deceptions. It is characteristic of the Lord and his angels, indeed, to signify the brightness of their virtue by a snowy appearance.

The Church will not fear the cold of the snow mentioned above for her household, because, by the Lord’s promise, she believes that the gates of hell will not prevail against her.

“All her household are clothed in double garments”: with wisdom, namely, to repel the heretical teachings of false brothers, and with patience, to endure the battles of open enemies. Or they are clothed in double garments because they possess the promise of the life that now is and of the life that is to come: now, during their temporal pilgrimage, they are aided by divine assistance so that they may not fail; then, in the perpetual habitation of their homeland, [Col. 0787C] they will be sustained by the grace of the divine vision so that they may live happily forever.

Again, her household is clothed in a double garment, one of works and the other of the mind. They possess the coverings of faith and deeds, being imbued with the sacraments of their Redeemer and formed by his examples. Thus is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III).

The cold of snow may also be understood as eternal torments, which we read are mingled with fire and cold, when it is said: “Where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew VIII). Fire and smoke ordinarily produce weeping in the eyes, while cold produces gnashing in the teeth. Hence blessed Job, speaking of the eternal punishments of the reprobate, says: “They pass to excessive heat, from the waters of snow” (Job XXIV).

But the Church will not fear these things for her household, because whoever perishes did not belong to her [Col. 0787D] household, nor will they be clothed in her spiritual garment, even though for a time they appeared to be instructed in her mysteries.

Finally, we read in the Gospels that a man who had presumed to enter the house of that banquet in filthy garments of works was expelled from it and cast into the outer darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth. He was rightly bound over to the cold of punishment, because he had neglected to possess the garment of piety.

She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing.

The variegated garment, which is usually made extremely strong through varied weaving, signifies the strong works of the Church and her diverse ornaments of virtue. Concerning these the Prophet sang in praise of the supreme King, that is, of that husband: “The queen stood at your right hand in [Col. 0788A] a garment of gold, clothed all around with variety” (Psalm XLIV).

“Fine linen and purple are her clothing.” Fine linen signifies the purity of a chaste manner of life; purple, the outpouring of precious blood. Fine linen is white in color, while purple is produced from the blood of the living creature called the purple-fish, and itself bears the appearance of blood.

Hence the Fathers beautifully said that the holy Church, blooming with the flowers of the elect, has lilies in peace and roses in war.

Again, because fine linen arises green from the earth but, through long and manifold exercises, loses its natural moisture and greenness and is brought to the beauty of a white garment, while purple is royal attire, the Church is clothed in fine linen when the elect chastise their bodies and subject them to service; she is clothed in purple when they exercise that same [Col. 0788B] continence not for popular approval, but to obtain the blessedness of the everlasting kingdom.

In the present, this garment of virtues appears contemptible to those who do not understand it; but in the future its true character will plainly be revealed. Hence John beautifully reports in the Apocalypse that he heard the voice of the saints saying: “Let us rejoice and exult, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself, and it has been granted to her to clothe herself in shining, white fine linen. For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints” (Revelation XIX).

Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land.

The husband of the holy Church and of every faithful soul is the Lord. He appeared ignoble when he stood before the governor’s tribunal to be judged, when he received insults, scourging, spitting, and death itself on the cross. [Col. 0788C] But he will appear noble when he comes to judge the world in righteousness, with all the angels accompanying him. Then, he says, “he will sit on the seat of his majesty, and the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another,” and so forth.

“Her husband is noble at the gate,” because the ancients customarily sat at the gates to judge, so that those coming to the city from elsewhere might immediately receive the judge’s answer already prepared; neither would peasants or shepherds be astonished by the unfamiliar buildings of the city, nor would the city’s inner peace be marred by the frequent disputes of litigants.

The Lord will therefore be noble at the gates of his city, because he who is now thought by many to be contemptible will, when the end of the age has arrived and he has opened the entrance to the heavenly homeland for the elect, already be revealed as sublime to all.

“He will sit with the elders [Col. 0788D] of the land,” namely, with those to whom he himself promises: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIV).

She made a linen garment, sold it, and gave a girdle to the Canaanite.

In the fine woven linen of the *sindon* the subtle fabric of holy preaching is signified. The mind rests gently in it, because the minds of the faithful are refreshed by eternal hope. Hence animals are shown to Peter in a linen cloth, because the souls of sinners, gathered mercifully together, are held in the gentle rest of faith.

She therefore made a linen garment and sold it because she gave by speaking the faith that she had woven through believing, and received life from unbelievers [Col. 0789A] in right conduct. She also gave a girdle to the Canaanite because, through the vigor of demonstrated righteousness, she destroyed the slack works of paganism, so that what is commanded might be held in life: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII).

The name Canaan is fittingly used: Canaan both produced the people of the Gentiles and is interpreted as “changed.” Thus the Gentiles converted to the faith are signified—those who, through a most blessed change, migrated from vices to virtues and from the devil to Christ.

Hence Psalm XLIV is written in his praise, with the title: “For the end; for those who will be changed; for the sons of Korah; a song for the Beloved.” The sons of Korah are interpreted as “sons of Calvary.” They are the children of the Lord’s cross, saying: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 0789B] (Galatians VI).

How they are changed is taught by the continuation of that same psalm, where the Beloved himself—that is, the Lord—says to the Church: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.” He desires her to be changed, commanding her to forget the house of her former father, that is, of the ancient enemy, so that he may have her as a daughter.

Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day.

Strength is for enduring the wickedness of the perverse; beauty is for exercising the grace of virtues. Beauty is hers because she practices righteousness; strength is hers because she suffers persecution for righteousness. Therefore she will laugh on the last day—that is, she will rejoice in the reward of the heavenly kingdom, whereas she suffered grief in the struggle of the present life.

It is customary in Scripture to use laughter for joy, [Col. 0789C] just as the Lord says: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you will laugh” (Luke VI); and blessed Job: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter.”

The Prophet placed a similar sentence concerning the Lord and Savior of this strongest woman, saying: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength” (Psalm XCII).

When he preached the Gospel of the kingdom, he pleased some and displeased others; some spoke well, while others slandered, tore at, mocked, and reviled him. To those whom he pleased, therefore, he put on beauty; toward those whom he displeased, strength.

Imitate your Lord, then, so that you may be his garment. Be adorned with beauty toward those who delight in your good works; be strong against detractors.

[Col. 0789D] She opened her mouth to wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue.

She opened her mouth only for the purpose of teaching wisdom, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians IV). Or certainly, she opened the mouth of her heart to learn inwardly from Wisdom itself the truth that she would teach others outwardly.

Since the Church does both, what follows appropriately agrees with both meanings: “And the law of kindness is on her tongue”—that is, the law by which she did not immediately punish sinners after the manner of the Mosaic law. She plainly received an example of this mercy from the divine Wisdom itself, our Lord and Savior, when a sinful woman was brought before him: “Let the one among you who is without sin first cast a stone at her” [Col. 0790A] (John VIII). Thus, on the condition that she sin no more, he had mercy on her and released her from the crime she had committed.

She considered the paths of her household, and did not eat her bread idly.

She considers the paths of her household because she examines carefully all the thoughts of her conscience. She does not eat bread idly because, having understood and received this from sacred Scripture, she presents it before the eyes of the eternal Judge, [Note: Something appears to be missing.] of the heavenly homeland.

The paths of her household are the commandments of righteousness by which one reaches the dwelling of eternal life. The soul rightly considers these paths when it carefully observes by what actions one must reach heavenly things and does not cease diligently to practice what it has learned must be done.

Nor does she eat bread idly when, receiving the sacrifice of the Lord’s [Col. 0790B] body, she strives to imitate in action what she celebrates in the mystery, taking great care lest, by eating the Lord’s bread and drinking the cup unworthily, she eat and drink judgment upon herself; rather, by suffering for Christ, shedding tears, and devoting herself to good works, she follows, as far as she can, his passion and examples.

The statement that the strong woman does not eat bread idly may also be taken simply, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (II Thessalonians III). He also says of himself: “These hands have ministered to my needs and to those who were with me.” Hence, rightly rebuking luxurious widows, he adds: “At the same time they learn to go around from house to house,” not merely being idle, but also being talkative and curious (I Timothy V).

[Col. 0790C] Her sons rose up and called her most blessed, and her husband praised her.

What he certainly knew would happen he reports prophetically as though it had already occurred. The sons of the Church—all the elect—will rise in the last age, restored from the mortality of the flesh. Then they will proclaim their mother, who begot them from water and the Holy Spirit, most blessed. Now she is despised by unbelievers as though she were wretched; and truly, as the Apostle says, “If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we are of all people most pitiable” (I Corinthians XV). But because in the present we strive for another life, when what we shall be has appeared, we shall rightly proclaim our mother most blessed—she who, gathered from all the righteous, is called the one dove, bride, and beloved friend of Christ.

Her husband also will rise and praise her, saying at the judgment: [Col. 0790D] “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matthew XXV).

He himself, indeed, rose from the dead as the firstfruits of those who sleep; but on the day of judgment he will demonstrate more manifestly to all whom he judges worthy of his praise how great is the glory of that resurrection of his.

What is said—“Her sons rose up and called her most blessed”—may also appropriately be understood as occurring in the present age, whenever any of the faithful, having passed beyond the hardships of the world, is led to the heavenly kingdoms.

To sit pertains to humiliation, and to rise to glory. Hence it is said that formerly they should repent in sackcloth—that is, being humbled. And the Prophet says: “I sat alone because of the presence of your hand, for you filled me with threats” (Jeremiah XV). The Psalmist likewise says: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; [Col. 0791A] rise after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm CXXVI).

This is plainly to say: Why do you seek to rejoice in the present, when joy is reserved for the elect in the future? In this life—that is, before the light of heavenly reward—you cannot possess the glory of true happiness. Rather, after you have been humbled here for a time, hope to be truly exalted there forever, you for whom everything that appears joyful and sweet to lovers of the world is bitter.

The sons of the Church therefore rise and proclaim her most blessed when, exalted by heavenly goods, they behold how great is the blessedness of that homeland [Col. 0791B] of which they have deserved to become participants, and celebrate it with due praise in the divine vision.

Her husband also praises her when he rewards the good things that he himself bestowed.

The words with which he praises her are subsequently shown:

Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all.

By “many daughters” he means the churches of heretics and the crowds of wicked Catholics. They are called daughters either of Christ or of the Church because they too were reborn through the Lord’s sacraments and began to preserve the adoption of children [F. omits *rennerunt*]. Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”

They gathered riches—namely, good works: prayers, fasts, almsgiving, affliction, chastity of the flesh, restraint of the tongue, [Col. 0791C] meditation on the Scriptures, and other such things. These are true riches of the spirit when they are performed with pure simplicity of mind; but when they are done without the faith that works through love, they benefit those who perform them nothing.

Those daughters also gathered riches in vain of whom the Lord says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will confess to them, ‘I never knew you’” (Matthew VII).

But the Catholic Church surpasses all daughters of this kind. With chaste faith and perfected works, she follows the footsteps of her Redeemer.

[Col. 0792A] “Deceitful is grace, and beauty is vain; the woman who fears the Lord—she shall be praised.”

The praise that a person receives from human beings is deceitful grace; the beauty of chastity or good works that a soul lacking divine fear displays before people is vain. But that conscience is truly worthy of praise which preserves the fear of God in all things. For this fear is the beginning and guardian of every virtue, as Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. I); and again: “He who fears God neglects nothing.” Hence blessed Job flourished incomparably in virtue during prosperity and remained unconquerable to his enemy in adversity, because he could truly say: “For I always feared God as though waves were swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight.”

[Col. 0792B] The grace of pretenders, therefore, is deceitful, and the adornment of fools’ works is vain. But the Church, which is preserved in fear throughout the time of her sojourn, will rightly be praised by her Bridegroom and enter with him through the gate of the heavenly kingdom, because she will offer him the lamps of her virtues, burning for his coming to judgment. How he praises her is taught in the concluding verse:

“Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.”

These are the words of that man of whom it was said, “Her husband also, and he shall praise her”—that is, of God and our Savior. At the end he will command the angels to bring the Church, after the contest of this life and after the crushing weight of earthly afflictions, into the joys of the heavenly kingdom and to join her to himself as the companion of immortal life, according to the Gospel saying:

[Col. 0792C] “But gather the wheat into my barn” (Matt. I).

“Give,” he says, “to her from the fruit of her hands,” because she took care to bear the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, modesty, self-control, faith, and patience. In return, render to her the reward owed her. “And let her works praise her in the gates”—that is, in the judgment, or at the entrance into the heavenly homeland. Let it not be the empty favor of human beings, but the works themselves, which I performed while he examined, approved, and rewarded them—he by whose grace, granted to me, I accomplished these things. May he himself mercifully grant that we may deserve to be praised by him in the future, while in the present life we praise him with worthy service. Amen.

[Col. 0793]

# The Twenty Books of the Exposition of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, on the Prophet Jeremiah

## Preface to the Emperor Lothar

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A] After the little commentaries which my small ability published on the Heptateuch, the Books of Kings, and Chronicles; after my brief explanations of the histories of Esther, Judith, and the Maccabees, as well as of the Book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, and after the labors of my other small works, I finally laid my hand to Jeremiah, so that, having gathered the opinions of the holy Fathers from every side, I might also open up, at least somewhat, the meaning of this prophet to the eager reader.

A necessity imposed this task upon me: I was nowhere able to find the explanations of blessed Jerome on this prophet complete, but only the first six books, which extend almost to the middle of the prophetic volume. Nor could the most diligent man, Cassiodorus the Senator, claim to have found them; yet he testifies that he wrote twenty books on the subject. Therefore, at the urging of our brothers, who study the divine books together with us, I devoted myself to the task of writing. Thus, what I could not produce from a single expositor and interpreter of the divine books, I might at least provide from several teachers and their different volumes, thereby satisfying their request.

For it is said that Origen explained this prophet in forty-five homilies in the Attic language. Of these I found only fourteen translated, and they helped me considerably in this work. The explanations of the other prophets which that aforementioned interpreter of divine law produced also lucidly expounded Jeremiah’s meaning in many places. Likewise, blessed Pope Gregory greatly assisted me in composing this work. In his various little works, as is his custom, he explains the meaning of the divine books and has unraveled many testimonies from this prophet as well.

[Col. 0793B] Having considered all these things, I resolved to compose a single work, but decided to divide it into twenty books, lest the length of the books weary the reader; rather, their brevity might make him more attentive to examining each point. No one ought to call me presumptuous or superfluous in composing this work, as though, after the finest and most eloquent expositors, I, a man without eloquence and of slender understanding, wished by a rash undertaking to obscure the studies of great men. He will see that I have gathered their opinions and preserved their meanings everywhere. Although in some places, for the sake of brevity, I have used my own words, I have indicated externally the names of those whose words or meanings appear on the page.

This work also offers a sufficiently useful abridgment: a reader who finds gathered together in one place what he would otherwise have had to seek through many books of the Fathers no longer needs to labor in searching, since another’s work has provided for his repose.

[Col. 0793C] Recently, therefore, a letter from Your Excellency, O Emperor, reached us. It urged my small ability to explain the book of this prophet to you and to carry the final part of the prophet Ezekiel—from the place where blessed Pope Gregory concluded its exposition in the tenth homily, in a moral and allegorical sense—through to the end in a moral and mystical sense.

This seemed to me arduous and exceedingly difficult: what the most learned and eloquent teachers of the Church judged beyond their strength and, with astonishment, avoided, I, weak and feeble—sick not only in body but also diminished in understanding—was stubbornly attempting to undertake as though I were fit for it. Although I have never been anything great, I now feel myself to be very different from what I once was. Weighed down by serious illness, I now lie in my little bed more often than I sit in my study for writing or reading.

[Col. 0794A] Therefore, since “my harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep” (Job XXX), I would rather weep over my sins than sound music in song, saying to the Lord with the Prophet:

“I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart. And all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you. My heart is troubled within me, and my strength has deserted me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII).

“Have mercy on me according to your great mercy, blotting out my iniquity” (Ps. I), “for my soul trusts in you” (Ps. LVI).

“Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me” (Ps. LXX).

[Col. 0795A] For this reason, then, setting aside the other matters—or rather reserving them for a suitable time, if perhaps the Lord, through the boundless grace of his mercy, should wish to grant me health and provide me with the ability to read and write—I now entrust to your devotion and authority the present work of exposition, namely, on the prophet Jeremiah. I began it while your father of blessed memory, the Emperor Louis, was still alive, and completed it after his death. May you possess it and read it, and may you use it together with our brothers for the cultivation of good study.

Since the opinions of many people differ, their abilities are unlike, and their judgments waver, I have chosen to seek you alone as judge—both favorable and most wise—most holy and august Emperor Lothar. Divine wisdom illumines your mind and does not permit it to be corrupted by the deceit of the envious or led astray by the cunning of the perverse; preserving it in the rule of equity and justice, it diligently guides you along the way of truth.

[Col. 0795B] To you, therefore, as an impartial judge, I offer this work, so that it may be tested and approved by your examination and protected by your authority against the bites of envious rivals. Since I have you as a favorable and kindly judge, I consider the false opinions of others worthless. As one who loves what belongs to your jurisdiction and as a devoted executor of your holy will, I shall remain faithful to you, by Christ’s grant, for as long as I live.

May the eternal goodness of God and his majesty, which excels above all things, protect the most serene and pious Augustus unharmed from his enemies on earth for a long time, and afterward make him reign blessed forever in heaven.

[Col. 0795C] [Note: [Col. 0795D] What follows has been drawn from the homilies of Origen. EDIT.]

God is ready to do good, but toward those who deserve punishment he is a dissimulator—although he can, while remaining silent and without announcing what is to come, punish those whom he has once judged worthy of punishment. He never does so immediately. Even if he has condemned them, he declares what he has always purposed to declare: that those who were condemned because of their offense may be freed from condemnation through repentance.

Although we can take many examples of this from Scripture, the examples that arise at present are sufficient for us to proceed to contemplation of what has been read. The Ninevites had been condemned by God as sinners, for it is said: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III). God did not wish to punish those who had been condemned without warning. Rather, giving them an opportunity for repentance and conversion, he sent to that foreign people a prophet of the Hebrews, so that, when he said, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,” those who had been condemned might not perish but, by doing penance, might obtain God’s mercy.

[Col. 0795D] Those who lived in Sodom and Gomorrah had already been destined for a dreadful destruction, as is evident from the words God spoke to Abraham. Nevertheless, the angels did what was theirs to do, wishing to save those whom they had judged unworthy of salvation. They said to Lot: “Is there anyone here who belongs to you—a son-in-law, or sons, or daughters?” (Gen. XIX). They did not fail to know that those people would not follow Lot, but they displayed both their own kindness toward human beings and that of the one who had sent them.

[Col. 0796A] We find something similar written in Jeremiah. The time of his prophecy is recorded: when he began to prophesy and when he finished. Therefore, whoever reads the Scriptures, if he attends carefully to the reading and seeks the intention of what is written, may say: “The historical heading has been prefixed, stating when Jeremiah began and when he completed his prophecy. What relevance, then, does the historical chronology have for me?”

By reading I have learned that he began to prophesy in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah, until the thirteenth year of his reign. Then he prophesied in the days of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the completion of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, king of Judah. By reading I have learned that his prophecy extended through three kings, until the captivity of Jerusalem, in the fifth month.

[Col. 0796B] What, then, are we taught by these things, if we attend to the reading? God had condemned Jerusalem because of the sins they had committed, and this was the final sentence: that they should be handed over to captivity. Nevertheless, since God loves human beings and does not wish anyone to perish, before the time of devastation drew near he sent this prophet also, so that through his words the people might be converted to repentance.

He sent him under the second king after the first; he also sent him under the third. What more need be said? Captivity was already imminent, and God still urged them toward salvation, granting, so to speak, even one day’s opportunity for repentance. Hence it is written that Jeremiah prophesied until the captivity of Jerusalem and until the fifth month.

[Col. 0796C] The hands of the enemy had already bound them in chains, yet God was, in a manner of speaking, still saying this: “Behold, you have become captives; even though late, do penance. Ask me, and I will spare you. I can rescue from captivity those whom I handed over.”

We therefore possess something necessary in this heading, which records the times of the prophecy: according to his clemency, God always exhorts human beings toward salvation, so that when sin ceases, captivity also may come to an end.

We can understand these things also as applying to us. If we sin, we too shall become captives. For handing a sinner over to Satan differs in no way from the fact that the Jews were handed over to Nebuchadnezzar. God delivered them to the adversary because of their repeated impieties; in the same way, because of the sins we have committed, we shall be handed over to a spiritual Nebuchadnezzar.

[Col. 0796D] “And those whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme,” says the Apostle concerning other sinners (I Cor. V).

Consider how great an evil it is to sin, so that I may be handed over to Satan, who takes captive the souls of those whom God abandons. God does not abandon those whom he leaves without cause or judgment. For when he has sent rain upon a vineyard, and the vineyard has produced thorns instead of grapes, what should he do except command the clouds not to rain upon the vineyard?

Therefore, because of the offenses of which we are conscious, our captivity is near at hand. It will happen that we shall be handed over—if we do not repent—to Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians, who will torment us visibly.

[Col. 0797A] With these things already approaching, the words of the prophets, the words of the Law, the words of the Apostles, and also the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ exhort us to repentance and call us to salvation. If we listen, we believe him who said: “And I also will repent of all the evils that I have said I would do to them.”

These matters belong to the preface.

# Book One

[Col. 0797]

## Chapter One: On Jeremiah’s Sanctification and Mission; on the Watchful Rod and the Boiling Pot

[Col. 0797A]

“The words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were at Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The word of the Lord came to him in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the completion of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the captivity of Jerusalem, in the fifth month.” (Jerome.)

The other prophets—Isaiah, Hosea, and Joel—lived before the captivity of the ten tribes of Israel, or of the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Others came after the captivity, such as Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah. Jeremiah and Ezekiel, however, composed their prophecies when the captivity was imminent: one of them in the land of Judah, the other in Babylon.

While he was still a boy, Jeremiah began to prophesy in the thirteenth year of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah. He prophesied during Josiah’s reign for nineteen years, afterward under his son Jehoiakim for eleven years, and under Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, for eleven years, until the fifth month, when Jerusalem was captured by the Babylonians.

Joahaz and Jeconiah each reigned for three months—one of them having been led into Egypt, the other with his mother into Babylon—and these months are included in the years mentioned above. Thus, from the beginning of his prophecy until the captivity of Jerusalem, in which he himself was captured, he prophesied for forty-one years, apart from the period when he was taken into Egypt. There he prophesied at Tahpanhes, as this very volume relates.

[Col. 0797C] In place of “The words of Jeremiah,” the Septuagint has, “The word that came to Jeremiah,” with this meaning: that the words of Jeremiah are the word of the Lord.

He was of the lineage of the priests who lived opposite the north side of Jerusalem, three miles away, in the village of Anathoth. At the same time, the Lord’s remarkable clemency is evident: although the captivity was already near and the Babylonian army was surrounding Jerusalem, he nevertheless summoned the people to repentance, preferring to save those who were converted rather than destroy those who were sinning.

In place of “deportation,” which all the others translated with one accord, the Septuagint has “captivity.”

Thirty-five years after the beginning of Jeremiah’s prophecy, Ezekiel began to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been captured with him.

[Col. 0797D]

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; I gave you as a prophet to the nations.”

This does not mean that Jeremiah existed before conception, as the heresy supposes, but that the Lord foreknew that he would exist. To him, things not yet done are already done, according to what the Apostle says: “Who calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV).

What is said of being sanctified in the womb we should understand according to the Apostle’s statement: “But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the nations” (Gal. I).

John the Baptist also was sanctified in the womb, received the Holy Spirit, moved in the womb, and spoke through his mother’s mouth (Luke I).

When he said, “I gave you as a prophet to the nations,” this means what we shall later read concerning him: that he prophesied not only to Jerusalem but also to many surrounding nations.

Some understand this passage as referring to the Savior, who was properly the prophet of the nations and called all peoples through the Apostles. He truly was sanctified in the womb before he was formed in the virginal womb and was known to the Father before he came forth from his mother’s womb, since he is always in the Father, and the Father is always in him.

[Col. 0798C]

“And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child.”

The Septuagint has: “And I said: O Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am young.”

He rejects the office because, on account of his age, he cannot sustain it, with the same modesty with which Moses also says that he has a thin and weak voice (Exod. IV). Moses, however, is rebuked as though he were of mature and vigorous age; Jeremiah is excused on account of his childhood, which is adorned with modesty and shamefastness.

[Col. 0798D]

“And the Lord said to me: Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for you shall go to all those to whom I send you, and you shall speak all that I command you. Do not fear their presence, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.”

“Do not consider your age,” he says. “For from another prophet you have learned: ‘A person’s gray hair is his wisdom’ (Wis. IV). Let it be enough that you are willing to go; you will have me as your companion, and with my help you will accomplish everything.”

“Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX).

Nor should you consider the multitude of those to whom and against whom you will speak. Consider me, who am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. The Lord delivers him—not by keeping the prophet free from persecutions and troubles, since we read that he suffered many things, but by enabling him to overcome everything through endurance and not yield to distress.

[Col. 0799A]

“And the Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.”

It should be noted that here the hand of God is sent to touch the prophet’s mouth, and he is told: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.” But in Isaiah it is written:

“Then one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he held a live coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar. And he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins” (Isa. VI).

There, because Isaiah was of mature and perfect age, and because he himself simply confessed that he had unclean lips and dwelt among a people of unclean lips, one of the seraphim was sent to touch his mouth—not with his hand, but with tongs and a coal—and to take away his iniquities and cleanse his sins.

Here, however, the hand of God himself is sent—the hand through which he accomplished all things and which elsewhere is called his arm—not to take away sins, for Jeremiah had committed few sins on account of his childhood, but to grant him the grace of speech.

Ezekiel, moreover, devours a book written inside and outside, containing both the divine mysteries and the plain historical account (Ezek. II). Jeremiah’s mouth is touched and the Lord’s words are given to him, so that he may receive confidence for preaching.

Beautifully, in accordance with the literal sense, a hand is sent, so that, seeing the likeness of human limbs, he may not shrink from the touch of a hand.

(Gregory.) It should be understood, however, that some people laudably desire the office of preaching, while others are also laudably compelled and drawn into it. We recognize this clearly if we consider the actions of the two prophets just mentioned. One of them willingly offered himself to be sent to preach; the other refused to go, trembling.

When the Lord asked Isaiah whom he should send, Isaiah immediately offered himself, saying: “Here am I; send me” (Isa. VI). Jeremiah, however, is sent, yet humbly resists being sent, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child.”

[Col. 0799C] Thus, an outwardly different voice proceeded from each, but it did not arise from a different source of love. There are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor.

Through the active life, Isaiah, desiring to benefit his neighbors, seeks the office of preaching. Through the contemplative life, Jeremiah, desiring diligently to cling to the love of his Creator, objects to being sent to preach. What Isaiah laudably desired, Jeremiah laudably feared: Jeremiah, lest he lose the gains of silent contemplation by speaking; Isaiah, lest, by remaining silent, he suffer the losses of diligent work.

But this must be carefully observed in both: the one who refused did not resist completely, and the one who wished to be sent first saw himself purified by the altar’s coal. Thus no one should dare approach the sacred ministries without having been purified, nor should one whom heavenly grace has chosen contradict it proudly under the appearance of humility.

Since it is very difficult for anyone to know that he has been purified, the office of preaching is more safely declined. Yet, as we have said, it must not be stubbornly declined when heavenly will is recognized as calling one to undertake it.

[Col. 0799D] Moses wonderfully fulfilled both requirements: he neither wished to preside over so great a multitude nor refused obedience. He would perhaps have been proud if he had accepted the leadership of an innumerable people without trembling; and again he would have been proud if he had refused to obey the command of the Creator. In both respects, therefore, he was subject: fearing to preside over the people, he did not wish to do so; yet he consented, relying on the strength of the one who commanded.

“Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, to tear down, to destroy, to overthrow, to build, and to plant.” (Jerome) What we have added from the Hebrew—“to overthrow,” or “to depose”—is not found in the Septuagint. It should also be considered that four sorrowful things are followed by two joyful ones. For good things cannot be built unless evil things have been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst have been uprooted: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15). And the building that has no foundation upon rock, but has been constructed on sand, is undermined and destroyed by the word of God (Matthew 7). But that which Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth and destroy at the arrival of his coming—that is, every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine—he will destroy forever. Moreover, whatever is raised up against the knowledge of God, and trusts in its own wisdom, which is folly with God, he will overthrow and depose, so that lowly things may be built in their place, and in place of the higher things that have been destroyed and uprooted, those things may be constructed and planted which accord with ecclesiastical truth; and what the Apostle says may be fulfilled: “You are God’s building, God’s cultivation” (1 Corinthians 3).

Many understand this passage as referring to the person of Christ. For Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord”: he destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him on the height of the mountain; he overthrew the hostile powers, erasing the bond of errors on the cross. Concerning these things he also speaks figuratively—τροπικῶς, that is, allegorically—in the psalm, after the truth of the historical account: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together as one” (Psalm 2). In place of these things—uprooted, destroyed, ruined, and dragged down to lower regions—the Church of God is built and planted.

There is, however, no doubt that the person of Jeremiah is intended. For we read in what follows that he receives in his hand a cup full of unmixed wine and is commanded to offer it to all the nations round about.

(Origen) Mystically, whoever receives words from God, taking up the grace of heavenly speech, receives them for this reason: that he may uproot and overthrow kingdoms and nations. But since kingdoms and nations are named, I do not want anyone who has received divine words to understand kingdoms and nations bodily. Rather, considering that human souls are governed by sin, in accordance with what is written in the Apostle, “Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body,” and seeing also the many forms of transgression, let him interpret “kingdoms” and “nations” as the various sins that have possessed human souls. These, then, are the things that will be uprooted and undermined by the words of God, which were given either to Jeremiah or to the other saints.

Nor are we unaware that there are some who refer these things—regarding them as greater than Jeremiah—to our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ. It must be understood that many of these statements can apply to the Savior, and we too shall insert them. A few, however, of the things spoken to Jeremiah narrow the interpretation, since, as many judge, they cannot be referred to God.

What, then, are the statements that can apply to the Lord?

“To all those to whom I send you, you shall go, and everything that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their presence, for I am with you, to rescue you, says the Lord.”

These words do not yet seem to be ineptly referred to the Savior. But the words that follow make the interpretation difficult with respect to Jeremiah:

“And the Lord extended his hand to me and touched my mouth, and said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy and to build.”

Unless perhaps we understand it in the way stated above: that he received in his hand a cup full of unmixed wine and was commanded to offer it to all the nations round about. What nations did Jeremiah uproot? What kingdoms did he overthrow, so that it could rightly be said to him, “Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and undermine”? What power did he have to destroy, so that he should hear “and to destroy”? Whom did he build up, so that “and to build” might appropriately be added? Jeremiah said, “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me.” And how was building and planting given to him?

These statements, as we said, do not restrict the interpreter when they are referred to the Savior. Jeremiah is a figure of the Savior in these matters. But the words that follow also bring difficulty in exposition to the most learned person: how can they be made to agree [the Latin addition in some copies reads: “with the Lord”]?

“And I said: Who are you, Lord and ruler? Behold, I do not know how to speak.”

How can “I do not know how to speak” be fitted to him who is the power of God, who is wisdom, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily? And there is also the statement that “I am a young man,” as though he had not answered well. For if the Lord says to him, “Do not say, ‘I am a young man,’” it is clear that he is being rebuked as one who has spoken incorrectly.

These are the statements that do not seem to apply to the Savior. The preceding ones, however, are easily referred to him. Here the interpreter’s discourse is constricted.

We know Jesus Christ to be God. We seek to explain the words that were spoken in accordance with the dignity of his person. Therefore it is necessary for us to call the holy Scriptures as witnesses. Our understandings and explanations have no credibility without these witnesses. And what is said, “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (2 Corinthians 13), applies more to the proof of the interpreter than to the number of any people. To establish the Word of my understanding, I shall take two witnesses from the New and Old Testaments, and three witnesses from the Gospel, the prophet, and the apostles; thus “every word shall stand.”

How, then, shall we be able to join these statements to the Savior? Let the Old Testament bear witness to me: “For before the child knows good or evil,” and so forth. Let Isaiah also bear witness: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7). There too it is added, “before the child knows.”

If testimony must also be taken from the Gospel, Jesus, not yet a man but still an infant, was making progress because he had emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2). No one makes progress who is already perfect; rather, the one who needs progress makes progress. Therefore he was making progress in age, making progress in wisdom, and making progress in grace with God and human beings. For if he had emptied himself when he descended to us, then, in emptying himself, he again took up those things of which he had previously emptied himself.

What is improper about his having progressed in wisdom, progressed in age, and progressed in grace with God and human beings—and about these statements being true of him: “before the child knows good or evil,” and the other things we have inserted concerning him?

But someone may say to me: Even if you can understand the statement about the Savior as meaning that he does not know, and the other things of this kind, which are less significant—even if you accept that he was a child—do you not offend the Only-begotten and Firstborn of all creation by thinking this way, him who was announced before he was conceived, when the angel Gabriel said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1), and do you dare to say that he does not know how to speak?

Therefore I shall see whether I can bring forward in this passage something worthy of the Savior: how, if he did not know certain things, his not knowing them might be greater than his knowing them. Let us use his own voice to show how there are certain things he does not know. He replied to those who said to him: “Did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform miracles?”—“Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matthew 7).

Do you think that when he says, “I do not know you,” this demonstrates a lesser power in him, or a greater and astonishing one, because he does not know the wicked and those destined to perish? For he knows the distinctions among them; he knows what is better. “The Lord knows those who are his,” and if anyone does not know, he is not known.

Therefore, as is established, the sinner is not known by God. Someone among the hearers may say to me: You have shown that God does not know sinners; you have shown that he does not know those who practice iniquity, since they are not worthy of his recognition. How, then, will you prove that it is something great and glorious that he said, “I do not know how to speak”? Speaking is human, and he always uses speech—whether, for example, in the language of the Hebrews or of the Greeks or in the speech of other peoples.

Therefore, if you ascend to the Savior and know that in the beginning he was the Word with God, observe that he does not know how to speak, since what is called “speaking” is human. But he does not know it because he knows greater things.

If you also compare the languages of angels with human languages, and know that he is greater even than the angels, as the Apostle testifies concerning him in the Epistle he writes to the Hebrews (Hebrews 1), you will understand that he was greater than the angels even in languages, when he was only the Word of God with the Father.

Thus he speaks, and in a certain sense receives instruction in things not great but lower and lesser. Just as I learn to stammer, forcing myself to do so when I speak with little children—for, so to speak, I do not know how to speak like a child, nor, being so old, how to converse with children in broken words—in the same way the Savior, while dwelling in the magnificence of God’s glory and remaining in the Father, does not speak human things. He does not know how to address the Pharisees [or: “to address those who are below”]. But when he comes in a human body, he says at the beginning: “I do not know how to speak, because I am a young man”: young in respect of the dispensation, old in accordance with the fact that he is the Firstborn of all creation; young because he came at the completion of the ages and at the final period of this life.

He therefore says: “I do not know how to speak.” For I know how to speak certain greater things; I know how to speak certain better things than this mortal speech. Do you want me to speak in earthly terms? I have not yet assumed human frailty. I possess your speech; I am your Word. I know how to speak to you; I do not know how to speak to human beings, because I am young.

“Do not say, ‘I am a young man,’ for to all those to whom I send you, you shall go.”

Then he moved his hand to touch his mouth, so as to give him words with which he might uproot kingdoms. Yet the Savior did not need words in order to receive them, since he was in the Father, where there was nothing in heaven deserving to be overthrown. But now he receives lesser things, temporarily setting aside [in another copy: “postponing”] the greater.

And thus this is confirmed, just as elsewhere he had gloriously said: “I do not know you, because you are workers of iniquity” (Luke 13). Now too, although he is God, he gloriously received words and said in accordance with the magnificence of his glory, “I do not know how to speak”—that is, “I do not know human speech.”

“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.”

If God knows everyone, why does he say to Jeremiah, as though he were distinguished from the others, “I knew you”? Does the Lord know only those who are worthy of his knowledge, and recognize those who are his? Does neither the Father nor the Son know those who are unworthy, saying, “I do not know you”?

We human beings, when endowed with some distinction, have judged some people worthy of our acquaintance and others unworthy; and those whom we do not wish to know or hear, we do not know. What, then, do you suppose concerning the God of the universe? He wishes to know Pharaoh; he wishes to know the Egyptians, but they are unworthy of his knowledge. They themselves make it so that they are not known. He knows Moses; he knows the prophets, and anyone who resembles them. You must labor greatly before you begin to be known by God.

He knew Jeremiah before he formed him in the womb; another of the prophets he began to know at the age of thirty, another at forty. These are ineffable statements concerning the Savior and are not to be investigated too carefully. But concerning Jeremiah, they require the ears of those who possess knowledge of the Scriptures, so that they may understand how he says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from your mother’s womb, I sanctified you.” God sanctifies certain people for himself.

He does not wait for this man to be born before sanctifying him; rather, he sanctifies him before he comes forth from the womb. If, as I said, you refer this to the Savior, it is not wrong to say that he was sanctified before he was born. If you understand it of the Lord, he was not merely sanctified before he came forth from the womb, but had been holy always, from an infinite time before. Here, however, he was sanctified before he came forth from the womb.

“I have appointed you a prophet among the nations.”

If you ask how Jeremiah was appointed a prophet among the nations, observe what follows, when he is commanded to prophesy to all the nations. For this is the kind of superscription found in the prophecies that Jeremiah uttered concerning all the nations—Elam, Damascus, Moab—and you will understand that he prophesied to all the nations, in accordance with what was said: “I have appointed you a prophet among the nations,” provided that you wish to regard these words as spoken about Jeremiah.

But if you transfer the interpretation to the Lord, he truly preached among all the nations. He is, like the other comparable titles, a prophet, just as he is high priest, Savior, and physician; similarly, he is also a prophet. Moses, announcing him, called him not merely a prophet but an extraordinary prophet among all others, saying: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him. And whoever will not listen to that prophet shall perish from his people” (Deuteronomy 18).

This is the prophet appointed among the nations. He received from God grace poured upon his lips, so that not only when he was bodily present, but also now, when he is present in power and in spirit, he may prophesy to all the nations and by his prophecy draw people from the whole world to salvation.

As for what he says—“The Lord extended his hand to me and touched my mouth, and said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot”—he is blessed in such a way that, by the words given to him by God, he uproots many kingdoms that the devil showed to Christ: kingdoms of demons and kingdoms of sin.

For it is written: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.”

But just as there are very many kingdoms, so likewise there are many nations; and no kingdom can be called a kingdom unless it contains nations under itself. For example, let it be said: Fornication reigns in the sinful person. It is necessary that the kingdom of fornication have its nations. That general sin itself—avarice and deceit—from which scarcely anyone is free has its own kingdom, and under one kingdom it possesses many nations, namely, through the very many forms of avarice.

For this reason the words of the Lord are necessary, so that kingdoms of this kind, together with their nations, may be uprooted. The Savior shows this in the Gospel, saying: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15).

There are certain things planted within our souls that the heavenly Father did not plant: all the worst thoughts—murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies—are plantings that the heavenly Father did not plant. But if you wish to know whose planting such a thought is, listen: “An enemy did this, who sowed weeds among the wheat.”

Behold, God is at work; the devil is at work; both have seeds. If we give the devil room, the enemy will sow a planting, which the heavenly Father did not plant and which therefore must be uprooted. But if, having driven the devil away, we give room to God, God rejoices over the ruling faculty of our heart and scatters his seed.

Let no one suppose that God gave Jeremiah some grievous command when he appointed him for the uprooting of kingdoms and nations. This is an indication of God’s goodness: to uproot vices through words, to destroy kingdoms hostile to the heavenly kingdoms, and to overthrow nations that wage war with their own people—to uproot and overthrow them.

There is a building of the devil, and there is a building of God. Whatever is built upon sand belongs to the devil, for it is not established upon anything stable or firm. But what is built upon rock belongs to God. Hence it is said to those who belong to him: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3).

“To uproot and overthrow and destroy nations and kingdoms.”

If something is uprooted and the uprooting itself has not been destroyed, what was uprooted still remains. If a house is demolished and its stones remain intact in the ruin, the house has been dispersed but not destroyed. Therefore God’s kindness is necessary, so that both the uprooting itself and the entire overthrow may perish.

Read more carefully how uprooted things are destroyed: “But he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire”; and: “Bind the bundles of weeds and hand them over to the fire” (Matthew 3). In this way the things that have been uprooted perish.

If you wish to know how the overthrow too is reduced to nothing, and how the material of the worst building is crushed into dust, consider the house that, because of leprosy, is commanded to be dismantled and cast out (Leviticus 14). Once it has been reduced to dust, it is thrown outside the city, so that not even a stone of it remains, in accordance with what is written: “I will erase them like the mud of the streets” (Psalm 17).

For wickedness must utterly perish. Something has been overthrown; let those stones also that have been destroyed be crushed, lest they be usable for another building that the devil might construct.

What benefit is it to me if, in place of the things that have been uprooted and undermined, better things are not planted and built in me? Therefore the words of God first do what is necessary: they uproot, destroy, and ruin; after this they build and plant.

We have always observed in the sacred Scriptures that those things which seem sorrowful are named first, and then those which are more joyful are mentioned second: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deuteronomy 32). He did not say first, “I make alive,” and afterward, “I kill.” For what God once makes alive cannot be killed, either by him or by another; rather: “I will put to death, and I will make alive.”

Whom will I put to death? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. And I will make him alive, so that Paul may become an apostle of Christ Jesus.

The first thing is that evils be taken away from us. The Lord cannot build in the place of an evil building. “For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? What fellowship does light have with darkness?”

Wickedness must be uprooted from its deepest foundations; the worst building must be entirely removed from our souls, so that afterward the words of God may build and plant.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see a watching rod. And the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word to accomplish it.”

(Jerome) In place of “watching rod,” the Septuagint translated “almond staff.” We must therefore work so that the Hebrew etymology may be briefly understood by a Latin reader. The term for “almond” is given; that for “watch,” “watchful,” or “to watch” is [uncertain: the Hebrew terms are absent from the supplied text]. Hence also, later on, a watchful leopard is designated by this name. From the word for “almond,” therefore, because of the similarity of the terms, the name alludes to the meaning of “watchful.” The same is written in Daniel, according to Theodotion, where a cutting and sawing—σχίνου καὶ πρίνου, that is, of holm oak and mastic—are decreed for the adulterous elders.

Likewise, at the beginning of Genesis, the woman is called from the man, as though she were a kind of *virago*, because she was taken from the man. In place of “almond staff,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “watching rod”; Theodotion translated “almond rod.”

The rod watches, considering everything concerning the people, so that it may strike and correct those who sin. Hence the Apostle also writes to sinners: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4).

This is the rod or staff of which David also speaks: “Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me” (Psalm 22). He beautifully added, “They have comforted me.” For the Lord corrects in order to amend.

And just as an almond has a very bitter outer covering and is enclosed by an extremely hard shell, so that, once the harsher and harder parts have been removed, the sweetest fruit is found, so every correction and the labor of self-restraint appears bitter for the present, but produces the sweetest fruits. Hence there is also that ancient saying: “The roots of learning are bitter, but its fruits are sweet.”

Some understand the watching and almond rod as the Lord, of whom Isaiah says: “A rod will come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isaiah 11). Hence Aaron’s rod, which was thought to have died, is said to have blossomed in the Lord’s resurrection.

“And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see? And I said: I see a boiling cauldron, and its face is from the face of the north. And the Lord said to me: From the north evils will be opened [or: will blaze] upon all the inhabitants of the land.”

(Jerome) Punishments are assigned to sinners in successive stages, so that they may gradually come to salvation. Those who refuse to be corrected by the striking rod are sent into a bronze and burning cauldron. Ezekiel writes more fully about this cauldron, which is kindled from the face of the north and signifies the king of Babylon and the city of Jerusalem.

And beautifully it is added: “From the north evils will blaze upon all the inhabitants of the land”—either the land of Judah or, certainly, the whole earth. Concerning them it is also written in the Apocalypse: “Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth.”

For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth, but newcomers and pilgrims. One of them says: “I am a sojourner upon the earth and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Psalm 38). Another says: “Few and evil are the days of my life, during which I sojourn upon the earth” (Genesis 47). Hence Peter writes the Catholic Epistle to the newcomers and pilgrims of Pontus, Galatia, and Cappadocia.

And in accordance with the mystical interpretations, Solomon says: “The north wind is a harsh wind.”

(Maurus) It is called “right” by name because, although it is harsh in itself, it is left-handed and has an extremely stubborn neck, refusing to accept God’s yoke; this applies to those who have stiffened under its cold and lost the warmth of faith, who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet, who call light darkness and darkness light. No one escapes the sharpness of this smoke. For no one is without sin, not even if his life is only one day long.

Concerning this cauldron, therefore, in the Book of Job (Job 4), where the Lord speaks to Job about the creation of Leviathan, we read: “Smoke comes forth from his nostrils, like a cauldron burning and boiling. His breath makes coals burn, and flame goes forth from his mouth.”

(Gregory) The cauldron is kindled when the human mind is stirred by the persuasions of the evil enemy. The cauldron boils when it is already inflamed, even through consent, by the desires of wicked persuasion. It casts out so many waves, as it were by boiling, by which it extends itself in its wicked acts into outward actions [variant: “through as many wicked acts as it extends itself”].

The present prophet had seen this boiling of the carnal conscience—that is, of the cauldron—coming from the smoke of Leviathan, when he said: “I see a burning cauldron, and its face is from the face of the north.”

For the cauldron of the human heart is kindled from the face of the north when, through the instigation of the adversary, it is inflamed with unlawful desires. For the one who says, “I will place my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Psalm 14), kindles the mind he has once seized with the blasts of his wicked persuasion, as though with fires placed beneath it. Thus the mind, not content with present things, continually burns with desire: it seeks things that should be despised and despises things it has acquired; now it longs for its own advantages, now it opposes another’s interests even to its own harm; now it satisfies the allurements of the flesh; now, as though carried to some summit by the pride of thought, setting aside bodily concerns, it raises itself wholly in a form (*typo*) [variant: *typho*, “pride”] of exaltation.

Since, therefore, the heart is led through various desires and is inflamed by the instigation of this Leviathan, its smoke is rightly said to resemble a burning and boiling cauldron. For the conscience, blown upon by his temptations, rises up through as many boiling surges as the thoughts with which it swells within itself.

Truth explains this still more clearly in other words when it adds: “His breath,” it says, “makes coals burn.” What does he call coals except the minds of reprobate people, kindled in earthly desires? They burn whenever they desire something temporal, because desires burn and do not allow the soul to be quiet or whole.

Therefore Leviathan’s breath kindles coals as often as his hidden suggestion draws human minds toward unlawful pleasures. He inflames some with the torches of pride, others with those of envy, others with those of lust, and others with those of avarice.

He placed the torch of pride beneath Eve’s mind when he stirred her to despise the words of the Lord’s commandment (Genesis 3). He also kindled the flame of envy in Cain’s heart when he grieved over his brother’s accepted sacrifice and thereby proceeded all the way to the crime of fratricide (Genesis 4). He burned Solomon’s heart with the torches of lust, subjecting him to such love for women that, led as far as the worship of idols, he forgot reverence for the Creator while pursuing the pleasure of the flesh (1 Kings 21). He also consumed Ahab’s mind with the fire of avarice when he drove him with impatient desires to seek another man’s vineyard and thereby dragged him into the guilt of murder (1 Kings 21).

This Leviathan therefore breathes upon the coals with as much force as the effort of his hidden suggestion uses to inflame human minds toward unlawful things. Hence it is rightly added at once: “And flame goes forth from his mouth.”

The flame of his mouth is the instigation of hidden speech itself. He directs words of wicked persuasion toward each person’s mind; but what goes forth from his mouth is flame because the mind burns with desires when it is stirred by his suggestions. He suggests these things daily and does not cease suggesting them until the end of the present life.

But he spreads himself more wickedly when, coming through that condemned man, he displays himself more openly in the glory of this world. Then greater smoke comes forth from his nostrils, because the instigation strikes human hearts more powerfully when they have been terrified by admiration for his signs. Then his breath makes the coals burn more fiercely, because the minds of the reprobate, which he finds already hot with love of temporal glory, he sets ablaze through the blasts of his suggestion until they practice cruelty. Then flame goes forth from his mouth, because whatever he speaks through himself and whatever he speaks through his preachers is fire by which fruitless wood is burned.

The mind of those who have no desire to become precious metals is touched by the fire of earthly desire. Therefore whoever does not want to be affected by the flame of his mouth should, in accordance with the judgment of the true teacher, take care to be found not as wood, hay, and straw, but as gold, silver, and precious stone. For the fire of his persuasion burns all the more strongly as each person makes himself more yielding to consent.

But since it is impossible for a mind placed in this corruptible flesh never to be touched by the heat of his persuasion, it remains that, scorched by his wicked blasts, it should turn without ceasing to the help of prayer. The wave of tears quickly extinguishes the flame of his suggestions.

“For behold, I shall summon all the families of the kingdoms of the north, says the Lord; and they shall come and set each one his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its surrounding walls, and upon all the cities of Judah. And I shall speak my judgments with them concerning all their wickedness, because they abandoned me, poured libations to foreign gods, and worshiped the work of their hands.”

(Jerome) There is no doubt that many nations and the kings of individual nations were subject to the king of Babylon. When he besieged Jerusalem, they set their throne and especially their tents all around it and at the exits of the gates, so that none of those who were shut in could escape. Not only Jerusalem but also all the cities of Judea were surrounded by a similar siege.

“And,” he says, “when the city has been captured, then I shall speak to them, showing that my judgments were right and that each received what he deserved—not on account of the other vices to which human condition is subject, but especially on account of idolatry, through which they abandoned me and worshiped the works of their hands.”

Some take this passage in a favorable sense: namely, that those who have been boiled in the bronze cauldron, having first been purified through torments, afterward become rulers of Jerusalem; and that, after the Lord has pitied them, he then reproaches them because, after abandoning him, they worshiped images. But this is a forced and perverse interpretation, lest an unlearned commentator bring false accusation.

“Therefore you, gird your loins, arise, and speak to them everything that I command you.”

Job too is commanded to gird his loins (Job 4), and the apostles (Luke 12) are told to hold in their hands the lamps, namely, of evangelical preaching, with their loins girded—loins which Elijah (2 Kings 1) and John the Baptist (Matthew 3) mortified with leather belts.

Therefore whoever is going to speak the words of God must gird his loins, knowing that all the strength of the devil is in his loins (Job 40), and that the righteous man says in the Psalms: “My loins are filled with illusions” (Psalm 37).
