When he has girded his loins, let him hear what is written: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5), so that, always watchful and rising from sleep, he may speak what the Lord has commanded him.

“Do not be afraid of their presence, for I shall not make you fear their faces.”

Or, as the Septuagint and the other interpreters have it: “Lest perhaps I make you fear.” According to our translation, the sense is: Do not be afraid of their presence, for with me as your helper you will not be able to fear them. According to the Septuagint: “Do not be afraid of their presence”; hold fast to the confidence of my command.

For if you do not offer what you possess so as to cease fearing, I shall abandon you and hand you over to fear; and in a certain sense I shall seem to make you afraid, when I abandon you to dread.

This signifies that the truth must always be loved and that one must not fear the multitude of people who do not endure rebuke but set ambushes for the person by whom they are corrected.

The words that follow according to the Septuagint—“For I am with you, to deliver you, says the Lord”—are not found in the Hebrew. The sense is: “I shall rescue you,” not so that no one may lie in wait for you, but so that, while enduring ambushes, you may not sin.

“For behold, I have given you this day [or: behold, I have appointed you on this day] as a fortified city, and as an iron pillar, and as a bronze wall over all the land: against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests, and the people of the land. And they shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail, because I am with you, says the Lord, to rescue you.”

The divine discourse describes why the prophet ought not to fear.

“I,” he says, “have set you, or given you, this day”—that is, in the present life, while it is called “today”—as a most strongly fortified city. Not as one house, nor a tower, nor some walls, but as the entire city that, set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden (Matthew 5). Concerning it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86); and: “I am a fortified city, a city under siege” (Isaiah 27).

“And as an iron pillar,” he says, concerning which the Apostle writes: “The pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Timothy 3). Hence Peter and John, who were thought to be pillars of the Church, gave the right hand of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas.

Nor is this enough, but he says: “And as a bronze wall,” which is not marred by rust, nor destroyed when beaten by rains, but grows stronger with age.

You will be such a person against kings and princes and the people—not of just any place, but of the land: those who think earthly things and do not know heavenly things, who possess the image of the earthly one (χοϊκός, “earthly”) and not of the heavenly one.

“These,” he says, “shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail.” Why, I ask, is there such great strength that neither kings, nor princes, nor priests, nor peoples can prevail against one man?

The answer follows: “Because I am with you, says the Lord, to rescue you.”

If at some time the kings of Judah—whose name is interpreted as “confession”—and their princes and priests, namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons, together with the vile and ignoble common people, should rise up against a holy man, let him possess the firmness of faith and cease to fear, because with the Lord’s help he will overcome.

## CHAPTER II

He rebukes them on account of the priests and shepherds; concerning the fountain of living water and the muddy cistern; and that Jerusalem is an adulteress, degenerating and forgetting her God.

“And the word came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying.”

(Jerome) This is not found in the Septuagint, but has been added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion. He interpreted the Hebrew word *carath*, for which we said “cry out” or “preach,” as “read.” For because of its ambiguity, the word can signify reading, crying out, or preaching. We should understand “the ears of Jerusalem” as meaning the ears of its inhabitants.

“Thus says the Lord: I remember you, showing compassion for your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown.” The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: I remembered the mercy of your youth and the love of your perfection.” This is stated more fully in Ezekiel, when the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and, under the person of a wife, unites her to his embraces; or, to show a more ardent affection, he calls her a girl, a young woman, and a betrothed bride. For what we have not yet possessed, we desire more eagerly to possess. “When,” he says, “you followed me in the wilderness, I distributed to you, as though they were the ornaments and dowry of a betrothal, the adornments of the Law and the necklaces of words.” He refers all this not to her merit but to his own mercy, through which she also obtained love. This too, which we have set down—“in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown”—is not found in the Septuagint.

“Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his produce. All who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord.” When Israel is called the firstfruits of the Lord’s produce, this shows that the people gathered from the nations came after the firstfruits, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “Remember your congregation, which you established [or possessed] from the beginning” (Psalm LXXIII). Firstfruits, moreover, always belong to priests, not to enemies. What follows—“all who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord”—has this meaning: just as those who devour the firstfruits, since they are by no means of the priestly race, are guilty of crime, so those who defile Israel will be subjected to evils, in accordance with what the holy man says in the twenty-sixth psalm: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh, those who afflict me, my enemies, they themselves grew weak and fell.” For those who carry out God’s sentence will not on that account be free from punishment, and evils will come upon them: “For scandals must come, but woe to the one through whom scandals come” (Matthew XVIII).

[Col. 0811B] “Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What injustice did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me, walked after vanity, and became vain?” Another prophet also bears witness to this meaning: “My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Answer me: for I brought you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery” (Micah VI). Both names, Jacob and Israel, are used not with reference to the two and the ten tribes, but of the whole people, since Jacob himself was later called Israel (Genesis XXXII). He traces the offense back to the fathers, not because the sins of the fathers are imputed to their children, but because the children, possessing the likeness of their fathers, are punished also for their parents’ crime. We often read that God shows mercy to children because of holy fathers. The fathers of the sinful people, however, abandoned God—not briefly, but over a long period—and instead of God they followed vanity, namely idols, which profit their worshipers nothing; and they became like them, according to what is written: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Psalm CXIII).

“And they did not say: Where is the Lord, who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through an uninhabited and impassable land, through a land of thirst and the image of death, through a land in which no man walked and no human being dwelt?” In place of “man,” the Septuagint translated “son of man,” and in place of “the image of death,” “the shadow of death” has been added from Theodotion. Although this is clear according to the historical sense, we must consider according to the spiritual interpretation (*anagoge*, ἀναγωγή) that, as long as we are in this world and are being led out of Egypt, we gradually ascend. First we pass through “the wilderness” and “an uninhabited land,” which a holy person ought not to inhabit, and “an impassable land,” to indicate the difficulty of the journey. Then we pass “through a land of thirst,” where we always desire greater things and are not content with what is present; and through “the image,” or “shadow,” “of death,” for we always stand in danger, and everywhere the devil stretches out his snares. We pass “through a land in which no man walked,” namely, one who has attained perfect maturity in Christ. For we shall all rise “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians IV). Nor does the person who is a man of God, or a son of man, ever dwell in that land; he is always hastening toward greater things. From this it is evident that perfection is not on the way, but at the end of the way and in the dwelling prepared for the saints in the heavenly places, to whom it is said: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm CXXXIII). In vain, therefore, does the new heresy [Note: [Col. 0811D] namely, that of the Pelagians] infer from the Old Testament that perfect victory is found here, where there is struggle and conflict and the outcome of future things is uncertain.

“And I brought you into the land of Carmel, so that you might eat its fruit and its good things. And you entered and defiled my land, and you made my inheritance an abomination.” In place of the labor of the exceedingly difficult journey, I gave you abundance of all things. This is what Carmel signifies; in Hebrew it is called *chermel*, and in our language its name means “knowledge of circumcision.” Just as that people polluted and violated the holy land, fertile in all things, through idolatry, so we, having received the knowledge of true circumcision, eat its fruit; and if negligence creeps in, we defile God’s land and make his inheritance abominable.

“The priests did not say: Where is the Lord? Those who hold my law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal, and followed idols.” After such great benefits, they turned the privileges of their dignity into contempt, so that the priests did not seek the Lord; the teachers of the Law did not know the one whom they ought to have taught others; and the preachers, through negligence, became transgressors. The prophets, who dispute before the peoples, do not speak for God but for an idol, and they worship their own fabrications. These words may be used against the teachers of our own order, who devour God’s people like bread and, through evil works, do not call upon the Lord.

(Gregory.) Truth therefore asks to be unknown by them, and declares that it does not know the leaders of the ignorant, as in the Gospel: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Matthew VII). For surely the wicked, while they do not know what belongs to the Lord, are not known by the Lord, as Paul testifies when he says: “But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored” (1 Corinthians XIV). This ignorance of shepherds often corresponds to the merits of their subjects. Although, because their own guilt demands it, they do not possess the light of knowledge, strict judgment nevertheless governs matters so that, through their ignorance, even those who follow them may stumble. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew XV).

“Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and I will dispute with your children.” (Jerome.) So that he may not seem to strike through power, he contends with them by reason as with equals, in accordance with what David sings and the Apostle employs: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm L; Romans I). By adding “still,” he testifies that he has often done this. And by adding “with your children,” he shows that the children also possess a similar stubbornness to that of their evil parents. He secretly signifies that their children too, at the Lord’s coming, followed their fathers’ ancient denial of God.

“Cross over to the islands of Cethim and see; send to Cedar and consider carefully, and see whether anything like this has happened: whether a nation has changed its gods—and surely they are not gods. But my people have changed their glory for an idol [or for that from which it will gain no benefit].” He compares something incomparable and sets the true Lord against false gods. “Go,” he says, “to the islands of Cethim,” which we ought to understand either as Italy or as the western regions, since the island of Cyprus, in which a city bears this name, is near the land of Judea; from that island also came Zeno, the leader of the Stoics. Cedar is a region of the wilderness and of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens. Against this very region, the prophecy of this prophet is woven at its conclusion; David also mentions it when he says: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul was long a sojourner” (Psalm CXIX).

The meaning is: Go either toward the west or into the wilderness, and see whether any nation has done what you have done. None of them has despised its gods or exchanged wooden and stone gods for golden ones; instead, following its ancient error, each has held to what it received from its ancestors. And this, although none of their gods exists, but all are images fashioned by human hands. But my people have exchanged truth for falsehood and preferred an idol to me, an idol that will not be able to help them in a time of need.

We can also say this against those who pursue vices with greater zeal than virtues, whom the Apostle admonishes, saying: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification” (Romans VI).

We must also recognize that no one who is engaged in prayer is permitted to conceive of or imagine anything bodily concerning the divine majesty, in accordance with the heresy of the Anthropomorphites. It is reported in the books of the *Collations* that Serapion, a very ancient monk, was deceived by this error. Since God is Spirit, those who worship God must worship him in spirit. Yet it is not surprising that a very simple man, never thoroughly instructed concerning the substance and nature of the Divinity, could, through the fault of rusticity and the habit of an ancient error, remain until now in deception and, to speak more accurately, persist in his former error. This error is not introduced by a recent illusion of demons, but by the ignorance inherited from earlier paganism.

For just as, according to that error’s custom, demons were worshiped when represented in human form, so now they think that the incomprehensible majesty of the true God’s name must be worshiped within the limits of some image. They believe that they possess or grasp nothing unless they have an image set before them, one which they continually invoke in prayer and carry in their minds, keeping it always fixed before their eyes. Against this error the following judgment is appropriately directed: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man.” Jeremiah also says: “My people have changed their glory for an idol.”

Although this error, by the origin we have described, has become deeply rooted in the minds of certain people, it has nevertheless also been contracted by those who have never been defiled by pagan superstition, through ignorance or rusticity under the pretext of the testimony that says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Thus the heresy of the Anthropomorphites emerged under the occasion of this detestable interpretation; with obstinate perversity it maintains that the immeasurable and simple substance of the Divinity is composed according to our features and human form. Yet anyone instructed in Catholic doctrines will detest this pagan blasphemy and will attain such purity in prayer that he will mingle with his supplication not only no image of the Divinity, nor bodily features—which it is even unlawful to utter—but will admit into himself no memory of any saying, no appearance of any deed, and no form of any figure.

“Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and be utterly desolate, O its gates, says the Lord. For my people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.” The Septuagint: “The heaven was astonished at this, and shuddered exceedingly and vehemently”; the rest is similar. Heaven, to which it was said, “Attend, O heaven, and I will speak,” and, “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth,” sees God’s commands trampled underfoot, shudders, and cannot conceal its astonishment. For every creature groans and grieves together over human sins.

The people of God commit two contrary acts. First, they abandon God, who is the fountain of life and who gave the commandment: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Second, as it is written in the same place: “You shall have no gods before me”; instead, they follow demons, whom he calls cracked cisterns because they cannot keep God’s commandments.

We must also observe that a fountain is perpetual and possesses life-giving waters. Cisterns and pools, however, are filled either from torrents or with muddy waters, earth, and rain.

(Maurus.) Of those waters that flow from the fountain of living water Isaiah says: “And there shall be streams of flowing waters upon every high mountain and every elevated hill” (Isaiah X). And again: “I will open rivers on the bare hills and fountains in the midst of the fields.” Let us understand the mountains and hills as those who have been raised up to the heights by virtues, who hunger and thirst for righteousness and whom the Lord invites to drink. Whoever drinks of his waters will never thirst. Hence we read in the psalm: “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel” (Psalm LXVII). And in the Gospel it is said (John VII) that whoever drinks of the waters of Jesus will have rivers of living water flow from his belly.

The holy man says to God: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Psalm XXXV), from which a most pure river proceeds. Concerning it Scripture again says: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God” (Psalm XLV). And elsewhere: “The river of God is filled with waters.” Isaiah says: “He will drink water from the fountains of the Savior” (Isaiah XII). Concerning these things the Psalms also sing: “Bless the Lord God from the fountains of Israel” (Psalm LXVII). And he says: “He made the wilderness into pools of water and the impassable land into streams of water.”

Of these waters the Savior also spoke mystically in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John VII). And again: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” “Now,” the evangelist says, “he spoke this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

(Jerome.) He calls the gates the gates of heaven, concerning which it is also written in the twenty-third psalm: “Lift up your heads, O gates, and the king of glory shall enter.” In place of this the Septuagint translated: “Lift up your gates, O princes.” More will be said about them in its proper place. Nor should anyone be troubled because Aquila and Symmachus translated “heavens,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated “heaven.” The Hebrew word has a common number: both “heavens” and “heaven” are called by the same name, just as Thebes, Athens, and Salonae are plural in form.

“Is Israel a servant or a household slave?” I think that from this passage the Jews, lifted up in pride, said to the Savior: “We are Abraham’s seed and have never been slaves to anyone; how then do you say: You will be free?” (John VIII), not knowing that everyone who commits sin is sin’s servant and that each person serves the one by whom he is overcome. Though therefore born from Abraham, the friend of God, they became through their own fault like the sons of Ham, to whom it was said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.”

“Why then has he become prey? Lions roared over him and gave forth their voice; they made his land a wilderness, his cities were burned, and there is no one who dwells in them.” The divine word asks the question so that it may answer itself. By lions it means the rulers of Babylon, who made his land a wilderness and destroyed his cities by fire. Or certainly, according to the spiritual interpretation (*anagoge*, ἀναγωγή), let us understand the lions as hostile powers or the leaders of heretics, who, desolating the land of the Church, laid waste all its cities with heretical fire, with that fire of which it is written: “All adulterers, like an oven, their hearts” (Hosea VII). They truly give forth their voice. In this same prophet, under the figure of the partridge, they cry: “They gather what they have not brought forth and make riches without judgment” (Jeremiah XVII). His cities were therefore devastated and destroyed because they do not have God as their inhabitant, as Scripture says: “There is no one who dwells in them.”

“The sons also of Memphis and of Tahpanhes violated you to the crown of your head. Has not this happened to you because you abandoned the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you along the way?” What we have rendered “at the time when he was leading you along the way” is not found in the Septuagint. He names two great cities of Egypt, Memphis and Tahpanhes, and says that their sons violated Israel to the crown of its head, in the sense in which Isaiah says: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isaiah I). Such was the lust of the Egyptians, who are large in body, that they spared no member but violated everything.

According to the literal sense, this refers to the idols of Egypt; according to the spiritual understanding, to teachers of perverse doctrine, who pollute the purity of the Church with their own shamefulness. These things will happen to Israel because it abandoned the Lord its God, especially at the time when it ought to have followed him as its leader.

According to the tropological sense, to be violated to the crown of the head means that, after practicing evil works, one is finally corrupted even in the very height of faith. When the most wicked spirits entangle a person’s soul in evil works but cannot corrupt the integrity of faith, they pollute, as it were, the lower members but do not reach the crown. Whoever is corrupted in faith, however, is violated even to the crown. For the evil spirit reaches from the lower members to the highest when, by polluting the active life, it corrupts the chaste loftiness of faith with the disease of unbelief.

“And now what have you to do with the way to Egypt, to drink the water of the Seor? And what have you to do with the way to Assyria, to drink the water of the river?” (Jerome.) We translated *Seor* as “muddy,” which is what the Hebrew word signifies; the common edition has “Geon.” Since above he had mentioned the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who violated Israel to the crown of its head, he now names Egypt itself more clearly. There is no doubt that the Nile has muddy waters and that “the river of Assyria” signifies the Euphrates, since Scripture says that the land of promise extends from the torrent of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.

Those who have abandoned Christ, the fountain of life, and dug for themselves pools belonging to heretics, which cannot hold the waters of doctrines, must necessarily fall under the lions that reduce their land to a wilderness, destroy all their churches, pollute them to the crown of the head, and make them drink muddy waters and the streams of the Assyrian and northern river, from which evils blaze forth over the earth.

“Your wickedness will rebuke you [or your transgression will instruct you], and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to have abandoned the Lord your God, and that the fear of me is not in you, says the Lord God of hosts.” It must be observed that wickedness, or transgression, after it has filled the transgressor and, like quail, has produced nausea, may instruct the one who repents. He is commanded to see what he has abandoned, what he has followed, and how, despising good and sweet things, he chose evil and bitter ones. All this happened because he abandoned the Lord his God and does not possess his fear. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs IX); because he did not possess it, he is handed over to evil and bitterness.

“From ancient times you broke my yoke [or your yoke], you tore my bonds [or your bonds], and you said: I will not serve. For on every high hill and under every leafy tree you were lying prostrate as a prostitute [or there you spread yourself in fornication].” He speaks to Israel as to a prostitute, because it broke the bonds of marriage and said, “I will not serve”—understood, the lord or husband—but lay prostrate in idolatry on every high hill and under every leafy tree. Pleasant and elevated places are always dedicated to idols.

This may also be said of one who was a Christian from the beginning and was partly instructed in sacred writings, but later, through desire for secular literature—signified by the hills—and attractive eloquence—represented by leafy trees—prostrates himself before demons. Under the pretext of learning and elevated knowledge, they pollute the souls of believers and cause them to spread their legs before every passerby.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0817]

[Col. 0817B] After the rebuke in which the Lord reproached the Jews for exchanging their glory for an idol and abandoning the fountain of living water, digging for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water, he again calls them to remember him under another comparison, so that they may recall how, in their fathers, they were chosen and planted by him like a vineyard in the land of promise, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, you drove out the nations and planted it; you made a way before it, you planted its roots, and it filled the land,” and so forth (Psalm LXXIX). Concerning this, too, it is now said through Jeremiah:

“But I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed. How have you been changed for me into a degenerate vine?” The Septuagint: “But I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jerome.) In place of “choice vine,” or “fruitful vine,” the Hebrew has the word used in Isaiah’s song (Isaiah V). It is a kind of excellent vine, by whose shoot the Lord says that he planted Israel, and he wonders how the true seed and chosen vine have been changed into bitterness and have therefore become a foreign vine. Let no one be secure if the Lord’s planting, the true seed, and the vine of *Sorech* can be so changed by its own fault that, through bitterness, it withdraws from the Lord and becomes a foreign vine.

(Maurus.) Concerning this vine mentioned above, it is written in Isaiah: “I will sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a fertile place” (Isaiah V). The prophet sings a lamentable song for the people of Israel, composed by the one of whom it is written in the Gospel (Luke XIX): “When he saw it”—without doubt Jerusalem—“he wept over it and said: If only you too had known the things that are for your peace; but now they will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with fortifications, hem you in, overthrow you, and your children with you.” And again (Matthew XXIII): “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.”

Thus Jerusalem, as we have said, is mourned, and its ruin is sung in prophetic speech. But for the Church and for the people once belonging to the nations, another song has been composed, concerning which we read in the Psalms: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth; announce his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples.” And again: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.”

(Jerome.) Here too we must consider the Creator’s mercy: the one who said in the Gospel, “I am the true vine,” also granted to his disciplines [variant: disciples] and to the people believing in him that they might be a choice or true vine, if they wished to remain in that in which they were planted.

“If you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the herb *borith*, you are stained by your iniquity before me, says the Lord God.” In place of the herb which we translated as it is found in the Hebrew, the Septuagint translated *poa* (πόα), meaning the herb of fullers. According to the custom of the province of Palestine, it grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as natron. Natron and the fuller’s herb signify repentance. Ecclesiastical speech, which argues, rebukes, and corrects the sinner, resembles more biting natron. Whoever is stained only with the lighter dirt of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions. But grave sins, which lead to death, can be washed away neither with natron nor with the herb *borith*; they require more severe torments. For the fire will test what sort of work each person’s work is, and it will be revealed in the fire.

He fittingly added: “You are stained by your iniquity in my sight,” meaning that even if you seem clean to human beings, you are not clean to me, who know the consciences of individuals. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII).

“How can you say: I am not defiled; I did not go after the Baals? Look at your ways in the valley.” Or “the ravine,” which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is not preserved here] and which the Septuagint translates as *polyandrion* (πολυάνδριον), a word that in our language can be rendered “a tomb of a multitude.” “In vain,” he says, “do you refuse to confess your crimes and boast of your purity, although you have been polluted by the filth of idolatry, and shamelessly deny that you worshiped the idol Baal. Look at the valley of the sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Siloam, and there you will see the shrine of Baal, whom, after abandoning the Lord, you worshiped.”

The addition “know what you have done” opens the closed eyes of the denier, so that he may see what he is ashamed to look upon. According to the tropological sense, we should convict by their deeds the brazen shamelessness of those who refuse to confess their vices. Such people do not walk on the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, but on the broad and spacious way by which many enter, which leads to death (Matthew VII). Hence it is significantly called *polyandrion*, whether according to the historical sense because a multitude was there killed and destroyed by the evil of idolatry.

[Col. 0819B] “A swift runner spreading out his ways, a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul drew in the wind of her love. No one will turn her aside; all who seek her will not fail; they will find her in her menstruation.”

The Septuagint: “Toward evening her voice howled; she spread out her ways over the waters of the wilderness; in the desire of her soul she was carried by the spirit. She was handed over; who will turn her? All who seek her will not labor, and in her humiliation they will find her.”

In this passage the Septuagint edition differs greatly from the Hebrew truth, yet each has its own meaning. Since above she said, “I am not defiled,” and he was speaking as though to a woman who had behaved shamefully, he describes her fornication. “As,” he says, “a light-footed doe”—which we rendered by the general term “runner,” while Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion more pointedly translated *dromas kouphē* (δρομὰς κούφη), “a swift runner”—she spreads out her ways and rushes swiftly toward the preliminary stages; and, like a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, she draws in the desire of her soul the wind, or spirit, of her love. For among the Hebrews one name denotes both “wind” and “spirit.” Thus Israel, or Jerusalem, was carried with every impulse toward the desire of lust and burned with every love of idols. No one could turn her from this impulse by force of admonition—not because the prophets were unable to do so, but because of the perverse will of the one desiring it.

“Whoever,” he says, “seeks her will not have to labor greatly; they will find her in her menstruation and uncleanness.” In place of this, Aquila translated *neomenia* (νεομηνία), that is, “new moon” or “Kalends”; Symmachus translated “month”; the Septuagint and Theodotion translated “humiliation.”

According to the Septuagint, the meaning is this: the prostitute Jerusalem, like the woman described in Proverbs (Proverbs V and VI), howled toward evening with her voice and invited lovers to lust. She opened the paths of her shame and spread her legs before every passerby. There was a pleasant place with flowing waters, made more delightful when wilderness surrounded it, so that no one might see the fornicator.

“In the desire,” he says, “of her soul, she was carried by the spirit”—*pneumatophoreito* (πνευματοφορεῖτο)—either she was led by a perverse spirit, or she drew in the refreshment of love, or certainly she sang the songs of her shame. “She was handed over,” he says, “to her vices and lust; no one will be able to convert her. All who wish to find her will find her in the humiliation of her shame, so that she can never be satisfied by love of pleasure.”

(Gregory.) A wild ass is an untamed ass, and rightly in this book heretics are compared with wild asses, because, abandoned to their pleasures, they are released from the bonds of faith and are alien to reason. The wild ass is accustomed to the wilderness because, since it does not cultivate the soil of its heart through the discipline of virtue, it dwells where there is no fruit. It draws in the wind of its love in the desire of its soul because what it conceives in its mind from the desire for knowledge is directed toward inflation, not edification. Against such people it is said: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians VIII).

“Keep your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst. And you said: I have despaired; I will not do it. For I have loved strangers, and I will walk after them.”

The Septuagint: “Turn your foot from the rough way and your throat from thirst. She said: I will act manfully, because I have loved strangers and have walked after them.”

(Jerome.) Those who are about to celebrate Passover are commanded to have shoes on their feet (Exodus XII). The Apostle also praises the feet of those who are prepared for the Gospel, so that, while they walk through the wilderness of this world, they may not be exposed to poisonous creatures, which must be trampled down and crushed by the evangelical foot. We keep the throat from thirst when we receive the Savior’s command, which says (John VII): “Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink.” She denied in desperation concerning evil that she would do what the Lord commanded, and she explained the reason, saying: “I have loved strangers, and I will follow them,” thinking, in her shameless confession, that she could avoid the charges against her.

According to the Septuagint, the way of sinners is rough, and it is turned by the Lord into a level way. Anyone who follows heretics should be marked by the condemnation of these verses. She said, “I have despaired,” or, “I will act manfully in my evil purpose and will be strengthened in my error.” It is necessary that whoever follows foreign ecclesiastical teaching should love strangers and follow in their footsteps—whether demons or the leaders of heretics, who are alien to God.

“As a thief is put to shame when he is caught, so the house of Israel has been put to shame, they and their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, saying to a piece of wood: You are my father; and to a stone: You gave me birth.” Although the face of thieves is shameless and brazen, they nevertheless blush when they are caught in theft. Thus Israel too, saying to a piece of wood, “You are my father,” and to a stone, “You gave me birth,” calling its own manufactured objects its parents, is put to shame when caught in its idolatry. And lest we think that this is said only of the common people, he names their kings, princes, priests, and prophets. Let us use this testimony whenever our own princes and those who are regarded as leaders in the Church are caught in shameful sins.

“They turned their back to me and not their face.” When a teacher gives an order, the sign of obedience is to listen with the head bowed; but to turn the back is a sign of contempt, as it is written elsewhere: “They turned their shoulder away from me” (Zechariah VII). Those who cast God’s words behind them turn their back toward him and not their face. “They despised my commands,” God says, “to such an extent that they were unwilling even to hear them, but they indicated the swelling of their spirit by the gesture of their body.”

“And in the time of their affliction they will say: Arise and deliver us.” Those who did not perceive God through benefits will perceive him through torments.

“Where are your gods whom you made for yourself? Let them arise and deliver you in the time of your affliction.” It is a shameless request, in a time of need and distress, to seek help from one whom they despised in peace. It should be read with the feeling of one rebuking: “Let your gods whom you made for yourself deliver you,” so that, while God is the creator of human beings and human beings have made a god, necessity may prove what power those gods possess whom you previously worshiped in security. Concerning this it is written in Isaiah: “Where are your gods whom you made for yourself? Let them arise and save you in the time of your troubles.” Thus he speaks specifically to the Jews, because the multitude of their synagogues would not be able to deliver them during the siege.

“According to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah.” (Jerome.) Either the same gods or separate and different ones were worshiped by the individual cities, so that they might not even seem to have agreement in impiety; rather, superstition warring against itself followed different errors. What follows—“and according to the number of the ways of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal”—was added by the Septuagint.

[Col. 0821C] “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all abandoned me, says the Lord.” Human perversity is inclined to excuse itself, so that whatever it suffers deservedly may appear to be suffered unjustly, and it may refer its own guilt to God’s judgment. “In vain,” he says, “do you present complaints and accuse the judge of injustice, when what you suffer is the result of your own impiety.” What follows—“and you all acted wickedly against me”—was likewise added by the Septuagint.

“I struck your children without cause: they did not accept discipline.” In place of this, the Septuagint rendered, “You did not accept,” and the sense in the Hebrew is: The very ones who were struck refused to accept discipline. In the Septuagint, however, the meaning is: I struck your children so that you might be instructed by their death. And lest you should perhaps say, “You were unwilling to correct the sinners,” learn from the wounds of your children that I wished to heal you with a harsher medicine. Concerning this it is written in Isaiah: “I struck your children without cause; you did not accept discipline.” Hence he speaks in anger through Hosea: “I will not visit upon your daughters when they have fornicated, nor upon your brides when they have committed adultery” (Hos. IV). And through Ezekiel: “Let my jealousy depart from you, and I will not be angry with you any longer” (Ezek. XVI). Concerning these things we also read in the Psalms: “There is no firmness in their wound; they are not in the troubles of men, nor will they be scourged with men” (Ps. XXXV).

“Your sword devoured your prophets.” Not my prophets, but your prophets. By no means my sword, but your sword devoured them—the sword which you endured on account of your sins. The Septuagint, moreover, does not have “your”; they simply translated, “The sword devoured your prophets,” so that the meaning may be either the hostile sword or my sword, by which your sins were pierced.

“Your generation is like a ravaging lion.” The Septuagint: “Like a ravaging lion, and you were not afraid.” The sword, he says, which devoured your prophets—undoubtedly referring to the diviners of Baal and the idols—will ravage everything like a lion; and yet your generation, which ought to have been corrected by the killing of a few, persisted entirely in its crime. According to the Septuagint, however, the sense here is this: Thus the Lord’s sword, which indicated the sword of the adversaries, devoured and tore apart your false prophets like a lion that, in its great hunger, tears apart the prey it has found; and yet, even by the punishment of your prophets, you were unable to turn to better things.

“See the word of the Lord. Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a late land? Why then did my people say, ‘We have withdrawn; we will not come to you again’?” The Septuagint: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Have I become a wilderness to Israel, or a land full of thorns, because my people said, ‘We will not serve, nor will we come to you’?” Moses also saw the voice of God (Exod. XXXIII), and the apostle John says that he saw and touched the word of God (I John I). He wonders how the people of Israel could have regarded God as a wilderness, while they pursued idols as though they were the crowded centers of cities. A late land is one that does not receive the rains of instruction, and it is full of thorns because it had not been cultivated. The people, therefore, once God’s people, are all the more criminal because they withdrew from the Lord and do not wish to return any longer to their God. Great is the offense of refusing to appease the one whom you have offended.

“Will a virgin forget her adornment, or a bride the band around her breast? Yet my people have forgotten me for innumerable days.” Through these words we learn that Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. But if he is the bridegroom, the words are his concerning whom John the Baptist also speaks: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). Therefore, whoever withdraws from the Lord loses her adornment and forfeits the understanding of the teachings, which is signified by the breast. Hence the evangelist John also reclines upon the Lord’s breast (John XIII). And among other things the breast of the victims is set apart for the priests (Num. XVIII). The greater the number of days during which we forget God, the greater is the punishment of the sin—a sin which even the length of ages has been unable to tame.

“Why do you strive to display your good way in seeking love? You have even taught others your evil ways, and upon your wings—or hands—was found the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent. I did not find them in pits, but in all these places, or beneath every oak.” In vain, he says, you seek to defend yourself by skillful words and, as though to earn love, wish to display your good works. You even taught others your ways and became an example to all of evil deeds. And indeed upon your wings—or hands—was found the blood of the innocent, whom you sacrificed to idols, or whose souls you destroyed by the likeness of sacrifices. We have supplied “the poor” from the Hebrew; it is absent from the Septuagint. These poor and innocent ones, he says, I did not find murdered in pits, as commonly happens through the ambushes of robbers, but in all the places I have mentioned above—or beneath the oak, which in Hebrew is called *ella*. This too has its meaning, so that the sense is: in all these places, or beneath the oak and terebinth, beneath whose shade and foliage, as in pleasant places, you enjoyed the crimes of idolatry.

“And you said, ‘I am without sin and innocent; therefore let your anger turn away from me.’ Behold, I will contend with you in judgment, because you said, ‘I have not sinned.’ How utterly vile you have become—or how utterly you have despised—repeating your ways!” These words should be used against those who refuse to acknowledge their sins but, in a time of affliction and distress, say that they are suffering unjustly what they suffer; they provoke God’s anger all the more because it is a greater sin not to mourn what they have done but to put forward empty excuses for their sins. “I will contend with you in judgment,” he says, “because you have said, ‘I have not sinned,’” as though this were a greater sin: to have one thing in one’s conscience and to proclaim another in speech. Let the new heresy learn from the old that the greatest possible expression of God’s anger is the refusal humbly to confess one’s sin, while shamelessly boasting of one’s righteousness.

“And you will be put to shame by Egypt, as you were put to shame by Assyria. For you will also go out from there, and your hands will be upon your head, because the Lord has shattered your confidence—or hope—and you will have nothing prosperous in it.” To avoid the attack of the Egyptians, they fled for refuge to the Assyrians, whose protection proved useless. We read that they were defeated by the Egyptians; then, again, to escape the anger of the Assyrians, they relied on the help of the Egyptians, whom history records as having been overcome by the Assyrians. They are therefore rebuked because, abandoning hope in God, they rely upon human assistance, which has all been shattered and overturned, so that no benefit can be found in it. Hence he says, “You will also go out from there,” that is, from Egypt, just as you went out from the Assyrians; “and your hands will be upon your head,” and you will mourn that you waited in vain for aid from the Egyptians. Let us recall the historical event when Tamar, corrupted and violated by her most wicked brother Amnon, placed her hands upon her head, which had been sprinkled with ashes, and thus returned to her house (II Kings XIII).

## CHAPTER III. That she fornicated with many lovers, and concerning the two sisters. Here follows the word of the Lord against the Assyrians, etc.

“It is commonly said” (for which the Septuagint translated, “It is said only”): “If a man divorces his wife, and she leaves him and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will that woman—or that land—not then be polluted and defiled? Yet you have fornicated with many lovers—or shepherds.” The Hebrew word *re‘im*, written with four letters—resh, ayin, yod, mem—signifies both “lovers” and “shepherds.” If we read it *re‘im*, it means “lovers”; if *ro‘im*, “shepherds.”

“Nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (or, “You were returning to me, says the Lord”). In the Hebrew, even after fornication he receives the penitent and urges her to return to him. In the Septuagint, however, he does not call her to repentance but censures the shamelessness of the prostitute, because after adultery she dares to return to her husband. By saying, “Will that woman be defiled,” whereas in the Hebrew we read “land,” he leaves an example and speaks more plainly about the land of Israel, which is compared to an adulterous woman. Let us use this testimony against those who abandon faith in the Lord and, entangled in the errors of heretics, pretend after many fornications and the deception of souls to return to the former truth—not to lay aside the poisons in their hearts, but to insinuate themselves among others.

(Gregory.) Behold, an argument from justice is proposed concerning a woman who has fornicated and been abandoned, and yet when we return after a fall, not justice but mercy is shown to us. From this we should certainly conclude: if such mercy is shown to us when we sin, with what wickedness do we sin when we do not return after our offense—and what pardon will there be for the wicked from him who does not cease to call them after their guilt? This mercy in calling after an offense is aptly expressed elsewhere by another prophet, when it is said to the turned-away person: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing you behind your back” (Isa. XXX). The Lord admonished the human race face to face when, in paradise, as its creator, he instructed the human being standing in freedom of choice what he ought and ought not to do. But the human being turned his back upon God’s face when, in pride, he despised his commands. Yet God did not abandon him in his pride: to recall the human being, he gave the Law, sent angels to exhort him, and appeared in the flesh of our mortality. Therefore he admonished us while standing behind us: even after being despised, he called us back to the restoration of grace. What could be said generally of all must therefore be understood particularly of each individual. Each person, as though placed before God, hears the words of his admonition when, before committing sins, he knows the commands of God’s will. To stand still before his face means not yet to despise him by sinning. But when, abandoning the good of innocence and choosing iniquity, a person pursues it, he turns his back upon God’s face. Yet behold, God still follows behind and admonishes him. Even after the offense, he persuades him to return to himself; he calls back the offender, and, without considering the deeds committed, opens the bosom of his mercy to the one who returns. We hear the voice of one admonishing us behind our backs if, after our sins at least, we return to the Lord who invites us. We must therefore be ashamed of the mercy of the one who calls us if we do not wish to fear his justice, because his mercy is despised with a more serious wickedness precisely because, even after being despised, he does not disdain to call us.

“Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not been cast down. You sat by the roads, waiting for them, like a robber in the wilderness, or like an abandoned raven.” (Jerome.) In place of “robber” and “raven,” the Hebrew has a word that can also signify the Arabs, a people devoted to brigandage who, even to this day, raid the borders of Palestine and ambush travelers going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The Lord also recalls this event in the Gospel (Luke X). Therefore lift up your eyes, Jerusalem, and look around here and there, and see where you have not been cast down by fornication. Just as robbers customarily set ambushes for travelers at evening and in deserted places, so you, like the prostitute in Proverbs (Prov. VII), sat by the roads at evening, in order to kill by your intercourse the souls of those who fornicated with you; for this reason the whole earth has been polluted by your fornications (Ecclus. IX). Significantly, according to the *anagoge*, those who promise to abandon heretical errors are commanded to lift their eyes straight ahead. Unless they begin to see what is straight, they cannot condemn their former perversity.

“And you polluted—or killed—the land by your fornications and by your wickedness. Therefore the drops of rain were withheld, and there was no late rain—or, you had many shepherds to your offense.” The land was killed, or polluted, because of the killing of those who perished through the fornication of idolatry. Therefore the blessing of all things was removed, so that they suffered a drought of the word of God. Or else it had shepherds through whom it offended God: those who ought to have been teachers, restraining others from error, became authors of impiety.

(Gregory.) At times in sacred discourse the brightness of preachers is signified by the name of the sun, as it is said through John: “The sun became like sackcloth” (Rev. VI). At the end of time the sun is shown as like sackcloth because the shining life of preachers appears harsh and despised before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also represented by the brightness of the stars, because while they preach what is right to sinners, they illuminate the darkness of our night. Hence, when preachers are taken away, it is said through the prophet: “The drops of rain were withheld.” Since the sun shines by day and the stars illuminate the darkness of night, and since in sacred discourse the designation “day” often signifies the eternal homeland while “night” signifies the present life, the holy preachers become like the sun to our eyes when they open for us the contemplation of the true light. They shine like stars in the darkness when, through the active life, they arrange earthly matters for our future needs.

“You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed.” The Septuagint: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute; you have become shameless toward everyone.” (Jerome.) Because above she had said, “I have not sinned,” and had sinned all the more by denying her crimes, she is now accused as a brazen woman of excessive shamelessness—not merely brazenly presenting herself to one or another, but showing shame before no one. Let us use this saying against the assembly of heretics who glory in their errors.

“At least from now on call me, ‘My Father’; you are the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry forever, or will you persist to the end?” Let heretics be ashamed, those who refuse to turn to better things and to return to the Father, their creator, and let them hear: “At least from now on call me, ‘My Father’; you are the guide of my virginity.” He betrothed our soul to his embraces, and teaches it how it ought to pray and perform repentance. But the more merciful he is, who shows a way of salvation after fornication, the more wretched is the prostitute who does not wish to receive healing after her wounds.

“Behold, you have spoken and have done evil, and you have been able.” Instead of words of repentance, you blasphemed with words of pride; you fulfilled your evil thought and displayed your strength against your husband, so that you were able to do what you had discussed in speech.

“And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what faithless Israel has done? She went away for herself upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and fornicated there. And I said, after she had done all these things, ‘Return to me’; but she did not return. And her treacherous sister Judah saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her, given her a bill of divorce, and yet treacherous Judah, her sister, was not afraid. She went away and herself also fornicated, and by the ease of her fornication she polluted the land; she committed adultery with stone and wood. And in all these things her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood, says the Lord.”

The torments of some are remedies for others. When a murderer is punished, he indeed receives what he has done, but others are deterred from crime. Therefore, when the ten tribes called Israel had been captured by the Assyrians and transferred to Media (IV Kings XVII), the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, which ought to have feared a similar fate and turned to God with their whole mind, surpassed the crimes of the ten tribes. They pursued idols to such an extent that they placed a statue of Baal in the temple of God—a statue that is called in Ezekiel an idol set up to provoke the Lord’s jealousy and rivalry (Ezek. XVIII).

He speaks figuratively of two sisters because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were born from one stock. He calls the former “faithless” and the latter “treacherous.” The former utterly turned away from God, immediately worshiping golden calves at Dan and Bethel; the latter, although she possessed the temple and the worship of the true God, gradually withdrew from the Lord through imitation of her sister (III Kings XII). She is therefore called “treacherous.”

According to the *anagoge*, however, this prophecy concerns heretics. While they imagine that they pursue knowledge of a false name through heretical subtlety, they climb the mountain of pride; and, captivated by the pleasures of this flesh, beneath every leafy and pleasant tree they expose their fornication. When they are handed over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh, it frequently happens that the house of Judah—that is, of confession and true faith—is not at all frightened by the example, but commits much greater crimes, polluting the land of the Church by the ease of its fornication and committing adultery with stone and wood by following doctrines hostile to God.

But if an ecclesiastical man wishes to correct one who has gone astray, cut away the rotten flesh, and bring back to repentance those who have followed falsehood, while they nevertheless continue, under the appearance of ecclesiastical truth, to pursue their ancient error, it may be said of them: “In all these things treacherous Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood.”

This prophecy took place in the days of the just King Josiah, under whom Jeremiah also began to prophesy.

(Origen.) If you have understood the two peoples—Israel and the nations—understand the transmigration of Israel in the people of the Jews, and that it is written of it: “I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce.” For God truly dismissed the people of Israel and gave them a bill of divorce, so that, by leaving them, he might establish an example. The law of Moses commands that a woman displeasing her husband be given a bill of divorce and dismissed; then it permits the husband to take another wife (Deut. XXIV). In accordance with this sense, understand that the Jews received a bill of divorce and were utterly abandoned by the Lord. Where now among them are the prophets? Where are the signs of mighty works? Where is the manifestation of God? There is no temple, no sacrifices, no other worship expressed in the volumes of the Law. They have been expelled from their regions, and thus the Lord gave Israel a bill of divorce.

After them came we, who in the Scriptures are called Jews. We are Jews because of the tribe of Judah, from whose stock the Savior descended; we have turned to the Lord, and our final state—would that it were not fulfilled, at least in this present time—will be similar to, or rather worse than, the sins of Judah. You should believe that worse things will happen to us at the consummation of the age, since they happened to the Jews. Hear the Savior preaching in the Gospel: “When iniquities have multiplied, the love of many will grow cold; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV). And elsewhere: “He will perform signs and wonders in heaven and on earth to deceive, if possible, even the elect” (Luke XXI). Such unbelief will arise throughout the whole human race that our Savior, because he knew what would happen, said: “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith upon the earth?”

Indeed, if we judge our faith and not our numbers, and consider the will of human beings rather than their assemblies, we shall find it difficult to discover one who is faithful amid so great a number of Churches. They were truly faithful when the sacrifices of martyrs were being offered, when we returned sadly to the Church after accompanying their bloody funerals; and the whole multitude was immense when catechumens, immediately upon receiving their first faith, were taught concerning the postponement of martyrdom. When women and the weaker sex remained fearless even unto death, then truly there were signs from heaven; then wonders were performed on earth; then there were few, indeed, but truly faithful people, entering the narrow and constricted way that leads to life.

But now, when we have become more numerous: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII). Of so many who profess one faith in Christ, very few are found to possess a faith worthy of true blessedness. If, therefore, it first says, “I dismissed Israel because of its sins and left it under threat,” while Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not wish to turn to me, it speaks of our sins. We read what the Jewish people suffered, yet we are not afraid and do not say, “If God did not spare the natural branches, how much less will God spare us?” If Christ, who is the gracious and most merciful God, uprooted those who boasted that they were a good olive tree and sprang from the root of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, according to their deserts, how much less would he spare us if we did similar things?

See the kindness and severity of God. He is neither merely kind and not severe, nor merely severe and not also kind. If he were only kind, we would despise his goodness; if he were severe, despair of salvation because of the sins we have committed would plunge us into vice. But now, [the text is corrupt: “quasi Deus(?) necessariam … homines”], we human beings have need both of his goodness for repentance and of his severity for offenses; thus he is both severe and kind.

We who are Judah, reading in the sacred books, find that God dismissed Israel from all the places in which its dwelling was contained and in which it committed adultery, and gave it a bill of divorce. Although we ought, from what they suffered, to turn to better things and observe that they were handed over to captivity and killed by their enemies because of their sins, and that their cities were burned with fire, nevertheless—although, as we have said, we ought to reckon these things with ourselves, “because if God did not spare the natural branches, how much less will he spare us” (Rom. XI)—if he dismissed those who descended from the race of the patriarchs because of their sins, what it is necessary for us, called from the nations, to suffer—we pay no attention to any of this.

We were called so that they might be moved to jealousy when they saw those who were once servants, now free, and formerly without honor, now made children of God. But if they suffered so much, how much worse will we suffer if we sin? If someone newly purchased has entered the house of his buyer and master, he asks one of his fellow servants which of the former servants offended the master and what punishment he received. If he wishes to remain in the master’s house, he takes care not to do what he hears those men did who proved worthy of blows, tortures, and exile. Then, investigating most carefully what those did who earned freedom from their master, he strives with every effort to do what he knows they did.

So, too, let us who were not servants of God but of idols and demons, and who afterward were gathered from the nations and believed in Christ, read Scripture. Let us see who was justified and who offended the Lord, and with complete vigilance let us strive to do what we read the righteous did. Let us beware of falling into what befell those who were handed over to captivity and expelled from God’s inheritance.

“And treacherous Judah was not afraid,” he says, “but went away and herself also fornicated.” After the fornication in which Israel first fell, Judah also fornicated, and her fornication came to nothing; she committed adultery with wood and stone. When we sin against God with a hardened heart, we do nothing other than fornicate with stone; when we sin in our will, we commit adultery beneath every wooded tree.

“And in all these things treacherous Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood.” We too have turned to the Lord, but because we have not turned with our whole heart, it is said: “Treacherous Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood.” Nor does he say merely, “Treacherous Judah did not turn to me,” and stop there. Rather, he says, “Treacherous Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood,” to show that those who turn, if they do not turn from the heart, turn in falsehood and not in truth.

Therefore let us read the histories and prophets of the Old Testament, and if we find any who were justified, let us imitate the things by which they were justified. Let us read the Gospels and the whole New Testament; let us read the Epistles of the apostle Paul; and let us write all of them upon our hearts, living according to the heavenly commands, so that a bill of divorce may not be given to us also, but that we may become heirs with Christ Jesus.

“And the Lord said to me: Faithless Israel has justified her soul in comparison with treacherous Judah.” (Jerome.) “Israel is more righteous,” he says, “in comparison with Judah, because she perished at the beginning, whereas Judah could have been corrected by Israel’s tortures.” Let the new heresy learn from the old that Israel is said to have been justified in comparison with one who was worse. Nor is this surprising concerning sisters of one nation, since Sodom also receives the name of righteousness in comparison with Jerusalem, when the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Sodom was justified by you” (Ezek. XVI); and the tax collector becomes righteous in comparison with the Pharisee.

“Go and cry out—or read—these words toward the north, and say: ‘Return, faithless Israel,’ says the Lord, ‘and I will not turn away—or establish—my face from you—or against you—for I am holy—or merciful,’ says the Lord, ‘and I will not be angry forever. Nevertheless, know your iniquity, for you have acted treacherously—or impiously—against the Lord your God; you have scattered—or poured out—your ways among strangers beneath every leafy tree, and you have not heard my voice,’ says the Lord.”

The Hebrew word may be understood as both “call” or “cry out” and “read.” Hence Aquila and Symmachus translated it “cry aloud,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it “read.” The word is directed toward the north, against Babylon and the Assyrians, toward the ten and the two tribes, and their return is foretold. “I will not turn away my face from you,” he says, or, “I will not establish my face against you,” so that I may receive you not with the severity of judgment but with a merciful countenance. For I am holy and merciful, so that I will no longer remember your iniquity or recall that you withdrew from the Lord, that idols pleased you in his place, and that you fornicated beneath every shady and leafy tree.

This also appropriately applies to heretics and to the negligent within the Church, who are daily summoned to repentance through ecclesiastical men and to whom the words “you did not hear my voice” can properly be applied. Every heretic dwells in the north, has lost the warmth of faith, and cannot hear the Apostle’s command, “Fervent in spirit.” Because he has surrendered himself to pleasures, he has withdrawn from the Lord, scattered his ways among foreign doctrines, and followed pleasure. No heresy is constructed except for the sake of the throat and the belly, so that it may deceive little women weighed down with sins, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (II Tim. III). Concerning them it is truly said: “Those who devour my people as though they were bread” (Ps. XIII). Christ’s apostle also marks them as “those who devour widows’ houses” (Matt. XII).

“When I have had mercy on you,” he says, “do not think yourself righteous, but always remember your iniquity and know that you have fornicated against the Lord. Lower the neck of your pride, so that you who offended God through arrogance may please him through humility.” To the words mentioned above, “I will not establish my face against you,” the prophetic saying applies: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. L).

“Turn, returning children—or wandering and withdrawing children,” says the Lord, “for I am your husband—or your ruler. I will take one from a city and two from a clan, and I will bring you into Zion. I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and instruction. When you have multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, says the Lord, they will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant—or testament—of the Lord’; it will not rise upon the heart, nor will they remember it, nor will it be visited, nor will it be made again.”

The Jews think that this was fulfilled after the return from Babylon under Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel—even though not everyone returned—and that this is what is signified: “I will take one from a city and two from a clan.” But it is better understood as referring to Christ’s coming, when the remnant was saved, as the Apostle says and explains: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Rom. IX). Then they were brought into Zion, concerning which it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). Shepherds according to his heart were given to them—the apostles and apostolic men—and they fed the multitude of believers not with Jewish ceremonies but with the knowledge and teaching of Christ, after the preaching of the Gospel had been sown throughout the whole world.

They will no longer place their confidence in the Lord’s ark, which was the custodian of the Mosaic Law; they themselves will be the temple of God. Nor, like the wandering Nazarenes, will they devote themselves to hidden sacrifices, but they will pursue spiritual worship. Others understand this as referring to the end of time, when, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI).

“At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will be gathered to it in the name of the Lord, to Jerusalem, and they will no longer walk after the perversity of their evil heart.” The Lord will not sit upon the ark of the covenant and the cherubim, to whom that people formerly said, “You who sit upon the cherubim, reveal yourself” (Ps. LXXIX); rather, all who believe with a perfect mind will be the throne of God. Or, better, the whole passage should be understood of the Church, when all the nations are gathered in the name of the Lord into Jerusalem, in which there is the vision of peace. They will no longer walk after the perversity of their evil heart, doing what they desire or following their own errors, but will say with the Prophet: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has received me” (Ps. LXII).

“In those days the house of Judah will go to the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north to the land that I gave to your fathers.” This is fulfilled specifically at Christ’s coming, when people from all twelve tribes believed the Gospel together. Leaving the land of the north, of the harshest cold, and withdrawing from the dominion of the devil, they then received the promised land that had been pledged to their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I recently published a small book on the promised land [Note: See Jerome’s Letter 129, to Dardanus.].

“But I said: How shall I place you among children and give you a desirable land, a glorious inheritance of the armies of the nations? And I said: You will call me ‘Father,’ and you will not cease to walk after me.” In place of “a glorious inheritance of the armies of the nations,” which the Septuagint translated “a named inheritance of God Almighty of the nations,” Theodotion translated more significantly, “a renowned inheritance of the strength of the mightiest of the nations,” signifying Christ, who is the leader and Lord of all the nations that believe in his name and passion.

He himself said to Israel, “You will call me ‘Father’”; and, “Whoever believes in me believes in the Father.” He himself promised, “I will place you among children,” namely, among the number of my children who believed in me from the people of the nations, and to whom I gave the desirable land. “For as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John I).

“But just as a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me,” says the Lord. This is Christ’s voice concerning the Jewish people, to whom he had said: “I will place you among children, give you the desirable land, and you will call me ‘Father’ and will not cease to walk after me.” How, he says, does a woman despise not her husband but her lover, once she has been joined to him, when she sees him serving her lust and realizes that the law of nature has been changed in her, through which she had once been subject to her husband, as the Lord says: “Your turning shall be toward him” (Gen. III)? In the same way the house of Israel—that is, the Jewish people—despised the Lord and Savior to its own destruction.

“A voice was heard on the roads—or on the lips—the weeping of the children of Israel, because they made their way wicked; they forgot the Lord their God. Turn, returning children, and I will heal your apostasies—or your contritions.” Symmachus translated this as “your conversions.” God gladly receives the penitent and runs to meet the son exhausted by poverty and squalor; immediately he clothes him in his former garments and restores glory to the one who returns—provided only that he returns with weeping and lamentation. Through his own fault he made his way wicked and forgot the Lord his God and Father.

The prophetic word now speaks to them: “Turn, returning children.” I call you children for this reason: because, having understood your sins, you return to your parent with weeping and lamentation. When you have returned to the Lord, he says, he will heal all your contritions—or apostasies—from which you had withdrawn from the Lord, or certainly your conversions. Although we return to the Lord by our own will, unless he draws us and strengthens our desire by his help, we cannot be saved. Let us understand this both of the Jewish people returning to the Lord and of heretics who abandoned the Lord.

“Behold, we have come to you, for you are the Lord our God. Truly the hills were liars, and the multitude—or strength—of the mountains. Truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.” Let the penitent say this, abandoning all pride and the multitude—or height—of mountains and hills by which he exalted himself against God; let him speak after being cast down in humility: “Truly in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.”

“Confusion consumed the labor of our fathers from our youth; their flocks and herds, their sons and daughters.” All the labors of heretics, concerning which it is written, “Those who search searched in vain,” from the youth of those whom they had deceived—their sons and daughters, who had advanced in heresy—were held oppressed by confusion, like herds by lust. Hence they add:

“We shall sleep in our confusion, and our disgrace will cover us, because we have sinned against our God, we and our fathers, from our youth to this day, and we have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God.” Let Israel speak this, Israel that did not listen to its Lord; let every heretic who does penance speak it also. Yet part of salvation is to confess and recognize one’s sins. “Say first your iniquities,” he says, “that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43). For Israel truly abandoned Christ the Lord, its God, and sinned against him—not only at the time when he was seen in the flesh, but also before his coming. Hence they say: “We and our fathers, from our youth to this day, have not listened to the voice of our God,” who was speaking to our fathers: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also; for he wrote about me” (John 5).

## CHAPTER IV. Forgiveness is promised if they wash themselves; the prophet grieves over the destruction of his nation.

“If you return, Israel, says the Lord, return to me.” (Jerome.) For this the Septuagint translated: “If Israel turns, says the Lord, it will turn to me.” The sense is: If it returns to me, it will return from captivity; or, alternatively, when it offers what it has. “For to the one who has, it will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.”

According to the Hebrew, however, the sense here is: If you return to me, Israel, and, desiring salvation once and for all, say that you have sinned and have not listened to the voice of the Lord your God, turn back completely. Believe in the one whom you denied, and then your return will be complete.

“If you remove your stumbling-blocks from before me, you will not be shaken.” Therefore, when we are shaken and say, “But my feet almost slipped” (Psalm 72), we suffer this not from weakness of nature, but because we set our stumbling-blocks and idols before the Lord.

“And you will swear: ‘The Lord lives,’ in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness; and the nations will bless him and praise him.” How, then, does the Gospel prohibit us from swearing (Matthew 5)? Here, however, “you will swear” means “you will confess,” and it is said in condemnation of the idols by which Israel used to swear. Accordingly, the stumbling-blocks are removed, and he swears by the Lord.

When it says, “The Lord lives,” in the Old Testament this is an oath for the condemnation of the dead gods by whom every idolater swears. At the same time, we must observe that this oath has truth, judgment, and righteousness as its companions: if these are absent, it will not be an oath but perjury. And when he says that Israel will do this, and through the apostles will become a teacher of the nations, then all the nations will bless—or be blessed—in him and will praise him, because salvation will have come forth from Israel.

“For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and Jerusalem: Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns. Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest perhaps my indignation go forth like fire and burn, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness—or inventions—of your thoughts.”

For what we rendered, “Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskin of your hearts,” Symmachus wrote, “Purify yourselves for the Lord, and remove the wickednesses of your hearts,” understanding circumcision as cleansing and foreskins as vice.

This is commanded to the men of Judah and Jerusalem who pursue the true faith and dwell in the Church: they must not sow upon thorns, which the Gospel discourse signifies (Matthew 13), since these choke the seed of God. Rather, they must first break up new ground and dig out all the brambles and remove the thorns, so that clean fields may receive clean seeds.
