This is what is said elsewhere: “Do not cast your pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to dogs” (Matthew 7). For how can one whose mind is filled with the troubles of the world hear the word of God, conceive the seed, and bear fruit?

What follows—“Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts”—is commanded to no one other than the man of Judah and the inhabitant of Jerusalem, so that they may abandon the killing letter and follow the life-giving Spirit. For if you do not do this, he says, my indignation will go forth like fire, and it will burn, and there will be no one to extinguish it. He therefore foretells the threat in advance so that he may not be compelled to carry it out. We find the same in the case of the Ninevites, to whom the sentence of judgment was announced so that by repentance they might avert the impending wrath.

All these evils will come because of the wickedness—or inventions—of our thoughts. Where are those who say that there is no sin in thoughts, when, according to the Gospel truth, all vices proceed from the heart?

(Maurus.) But the Lord, who does not desire the death of a sinner but his conversion and life, first commands us not to commit sins, to walk in the way of righteousness, and to obey his commandments. Then, if we sin and transgress his commandments, he urges us to turn from our sins in repentance, and thus promises forgiveness of the offense. Thereafter he also commands us to keep the way of discipline and to exercise ourselves vigorously in good works.

Thus, after the prophet admonished the Israelites to turn from error to the Lord and to walk in truth, judgment, and righteousness, and to cleanse the field of the heart from the filth of crimes, he urges them, as those preparing to fight against the fiercest lion, to arm themselves with spiritual weapons, to enter the fortified cities of the sacred Scriptures, and to raise the banner of the cross, fighting manfully against the most wicked enemy. This is made clear at the beginning of the following book.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0833]

“Announce it in Judah, and make it heard in Jerusalem. Speak and sound the trumpet in the land; cry out loudly and say: ‘Gather together, and let us enter the fortified cities. Raise the signal in Zion. Take courage, and do not stand still, because I am bringing evil from the north, and great destruction.’”

(Jerome.) Let Judah hear this, and Jerusalem, in which there is confession of faith and in which the peace of Christ dwells, and to which it was said through Isaiah: “Climb up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40). Let it cry out loudly and thus command: “Let us enter the fortified cities.” The wars of heretics are rising up; let the fortifications of Christ hold us secure. Raise the sign of the cross upon the watchtower, that is, upon the height of the Church. Take courage, you who are afraid; do not stand still, but run to the help of Christ. “For I am bringing,” he says, “evil from the north, and great destruction”—truly, Nebuchadnezzar, who is permitted by me to exist in this world for this reason: so that your strength and victory may be demonstrated.

“A lion has come up from his lair, and the destroyer of nations has risen; he has gone forth from his place to reduce your land to a wilderness. Your cities will be laid waste, remaining without an inhabitant.”

This is, as we said, the true Nebuchadnezzar, concerning whom Peter also speaks: “Our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5). He has come up, either from the abyss into which he is to be bound and to which he begs not to be sent, or as the destroyer, or devastator, of nations who has risen—the one of whom it is said: “He will rule over all his enemies” (Psalm 9), and who boasts in the presence of the Lord: “I have traversed the whole earth and trampled it” (Job 2).

Who is there whom the devil’s poisons do not touch, except the one who can say: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14)? This one often reduces the whole land of the Church to a wilderness, so that those who have gone out from the Church fight against the Church. Of these the evangelist says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

The cities of the land of Judah are devastated, while the assemblies of heretics flourish. If someone is a supporter of the authors of perverse doctrines, this may be said of him: “A lion has come up from his lair, and the destroyer of nations has risen,” and so forth.

“Because of this, gird yourselves with sackcloth; mourn and howl, because the anger of the Lord’s fury has not turned away from us.” Or, as the Septuagint translated, “from you.” We cannot otherwise avoid the lion and the most savage beast unless we do penance and turn to the Lord not only in mind but also in deed. As long as he devastates the Church and lays waste the land of Judah, and also ravages Jerusalem, the wrath of God is evident.

“And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: The heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests shall be stupefied, and the prophets shall be dismayed.”

When the destroyer is devastating the Lord’s Church and the Lord’s anger remains against us, every aid will be useless. The heart of the king will perish, though his heart ought to be in the hand of God, and the heart of the princes, who were thought to be wise. For God made the wisdom of the world foolish, because through it they did not know God (1 Corinthians 1).

The priests themselves, who ought to teach the law of the Lord and defend the peoples subject to them from the lion’s fury, will, stupefied by a kind of torpor, be turned into madness. For this is how the Septuagint translated it, expressing bewilderment and loss of mind. And the prophets will be dismayed, or, as Aquila translated the Hebrew word, they will be insane. For who would not go mad and lose heart when he saw his former princes, kings, priests, and prophets under the lion?

“And I said: ‘Alas, alas, alas, Lord God!’” For this the Septuagint translated, “O Lord God.” “Have you then deceived this people and Jerusalem by saying, ‘There will be peace for you’? And behold, the sword has reached to the soul.”

Because he had said above, “At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will gather to it on the mountain of the Lord, in Jerusalem,” and now says, “The heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests shall be stupefied, and the prophets shall be dismayed,” the prophet too is disturbed and thinks that God has deceived him. He does not understand that the former promise was made for a time far in the future, whereas this will happen in the near future, in accordance with what the Apostle also says: “Has God rejected his people? By no means” (Romans 11).

The sword reaches to the soul when nothing vital remains in the soul. At the same time, this also shows that unless the sword comes first—the sword that cuts away and purifies the soul’s vices—peace and the promise do not follow.

“At that time it will be said to this people and to Jerusalem: ‘A scorching wind—or a wind of dew—on the roads that are in the wilderness, the roadways of the daughter of my people: not for winnowing and cleansing. A spirit full of these things will come to me.’”

When the sword has reached the soul and the threshing floor has been completed, then a wind will come from the wilderness—not to cleanse and winnow it, so that the chaff may be scattered here and there and the grain stored in the granaries, but a spirit full of these things will come, not to the people but to me, so that my wheat may be scattered.

Among the Hebrews, “wind” and “spirit” are called by the same name; according to the character of the context, we must understand either wind or spirit. Others explain this passage in such a way that, after the threshing floor has been cleansed, the remnant may be saved. Hence it is also written: “The spirit of fullness will come to me,” as the evangelist says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1), and we will receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Historically, understand the scorching wind as Nebuchadnezzar, who consumes everything. Tropologically, understand it as the hostile power that, coming from the wilderness and solitude—where there is no dwelling-place of God—attempts to overthrow his Church.

“And now I will speak my judgments with them.”

Aposiopesis, in accordance with Virgil’s line:

> Whom I … but it is better to calm the troubled waves.

Thus, intending to speak of prosperity, he restrains himself and joins sad things to sad things. For these are the judgments that God speaks with his former people, so that they may know that they are justly enduring what they endure.

“Behold, he will rise like a cloud, and his chariots like a storm. His horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, for we have been devastated.”

He sees the future as present and describes the Babylonian army, whose chariots and the clatter of their wheels are compared to a most savage storm, while the speed of the horses is compared with eagles. When the prophet had said this and pointed out the approaching enemies with his finger, the people groan and feel not what is future but what has already happened, saying: “Woe to us, for we have been devastated.”

The same may be referred to the Church: every day the army of the true Nebuchadnezzar attacks us, and the chariots of Pharaoh and all his cavalry surpass the assault of eagles. If the ecclesiastical man understands this, believing the saying, “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved,” he will say: “Woe to us, for we have been devastated.”

[Col. 0837A] “Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved. How long will harmful thoughts remain within you?”

When the people say, “Woe to us, for we have been devastated,” the prophet—or rather, God through the prophet—responds: “Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem,” with the water of which Isaiah also speaks: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1), the water of saving baptism, the water of repentance.

He speaks to the metropolis of the Jews, so that through the city the peoples may be understood: How long will you remain subject to wicked thoughts, which proceed from your heart? In the Holy Scriptures, however, we must understand “heart” as soul and understanding.

“For there is the voice of one announcing from Dan and making known an idol—or grief—from Mount Ephraim.”

In accordance with the position of the land of Judea, the divine discourse now speaks. The tribe of Dan, situated near Mount Lebanon and the city now called Paneas, faces north, from where Nebuchadnezzar will come. He describes the idol Bel—or grief, or iniquity—as coming from Mount Ephraim. For after the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one travels to Jerusalem.

Dan ([term omitted in the supplied text]) is interpreted as “judgment,” and Ephraim ([term omitted in the supplied text]) as “fruitfulness.” Therefore the Lord’s judgment will come upon the land that has offended the Lord, together with the full abundance of punishment.

“Tell the nations: ‘Behold, it has been heard in Jerusalem that watchmen are coming from a distant land, and they have raised their voice against the cities of Judah. Like watchmen of fields, they have encircled her, because she provoked me to anger,’ says the Lord.”

He wants all the surrounding nations to know God’s sentence, and, when Jerusalem has been scourged, to accept discipline. A report, he says, is commonly told in Jerusalem that adversaries are coming from a distant land, and that the roar of a howling army is rising against her. They besiege the city and shut it in with fortifications so carefully that you would think them not adversaries but guardians of fields and vineyards.

All this happened not through the strength of the enemies but through the fault of Jerusalem, because she provoked God to anger. For if hostile powers have no authority over swine (Matthew 8), how much less over human beings—and over human beings who were once citizens of God’s city?

“Your ways and your thoughts have done this to you—this is your wickedness, because it has touched your heart with bitterness.”

He turns in apostrophe to the city of Jerusalem, saying that its ways and thoughts, by which it sinned both in deed and in speech, caused everything that came upon it; and that its wickedness, which is bitter in itself, touched its heart and penetrated the inward parts of its soul. Whatever therefore happens to us happens through our own fault: we turn the sweet God into bitterness and compel him to rage, though he is unwilling to do so.

“My belly, my belly, I grieve; the senses of my heart are troubled. I will not be silent, because my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle. Destruction has been called upon destruction, and the whole land has been devastated. Suddenly my tents were devastated, in an instant my tent-curtains.”

Where we rendered “are troubled” according to Symmachus, and where the Hebrew reads [term omitted in the supplied text], the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered it μαιμάσσει, a word whose meaning remains unknown to the present day. Aquila used ὀχλίζει, which itself also signifies “to cause tumult.” Let this be said about the word, concerning which I know that there is great dispute among many.

The voice of the prophet—and, through the prophet, of God speaking—is introduced as grieving over the destruction of his people, with his inward parts torn asunder like those of a human being. So too the Savior grieved over the death of Lazarus (John 11) and wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19), nor did he wish to conceal his grief in silence.

(Gregory.) The mind is therefore rightly understood by the name “belly,” because just as offspring is conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind; and just as food is contained in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind.

(Jerome.) Every blast of the trumpet and roar of battle therefore disturbs his affection, while evils are heaped upon evils and the entire land of the two tribes is devastated. “While I did not expect it,” he says, “my former tents and tent-curtains were ravaged when Babylon raged, and my former dwellings fell as plunder to the enemies.”

God says the same when he sees the tumults and dissensions of sedition in the Church, and sees people shouting throughout the day in their assemblies and turning God’s rest into war. Hence it follows: “How long will I see those fleeing and hear the sound of the trumpet?” Either those fleeing from the Babylonian king, or those fleeing from me and withdrawing from my service?

“For my foolish people has not known me. They are foolish and senseless children. They are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good.”

The cause of the destruction, devastation, flight, and trumpet is that the people have become foolish—not by nature, but through the determination of their will. Their foolishness is proved by this: they did not know God. Thus, instead of wise children, they became foolish and senseless children.

For what greater foolishness can there be than for Israel not to know the Lord, when the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master’s manger (Isaiah 1), and to despise him who was present, whom it had always desired to see?

What follows—“They are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good”—must be understood with “wisdom” meaning wickedness. So too the children of this age are said to be wiser than the children of light, and the unjust steward is reported to have acted wisely in certain matters (Luke 16); and the serpent in paradise is read to have been more prudent than all the beasts (Genesis 3).

True wisdom, therefore, is that which is joined to the fear of God. Otherwise, where there are ambushes and evasions, it must be called not wisdom but cunning and craftiness.

For what we rendered, “My foolish people has not known me,” the Septuagint translated, “The rulers of my people have not known me,” making the fault lie more with the teachers than with the people who lack knowledge of God.

“I looked at the earth, and behold, it was empty and void; and at the heavens, and there was no light in them. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were moving, and all the hills were shaken. I looked, and there was no human being, and every bird of the heavens had departed. I looked, and behold, Carmel was a wilderness, and all its cities had been destroyed before the Lord and before the face of his burning wrath.”

The prophet sees in the spirit what is going to happen, so that the people, hearing it, may be terrified and, after doing penance, may not suffer what they fear. The earth is empty because its inhabitants have been destroyed; the heavens have no light, because the people cannot see in the magnitude of their terror. The mountains and hills have no safe hiding-places, and, by hyperbole, they appear to move and be shaken. He looked around in every direction, and not even a bird could be found.

For the mute elements also feel God’s anger, and irrational animals are afraid. The whole world now shows this to be true: when a multitude of human beings has been slain, even the birds, which usually follow inhabitants, have departed and perished.

Carmel itself, which rises above the Great Sea, planted with olive trees, filled with shrubs, and dense with vines, will come to such desolation that it will possess the devastation of a wilderness. All the cities too will become deserted. The cause of all these evils is that the Lord’s anger has been provoked by the fault of the sinful people.

Whatever we have said historically about Jerusalem and Judea, let us refer to the Church of God when it has offended God and has been devastated either by vices or by persecution, so that where once there was a chorus and joy of virtues, there may be found a multitude of sins and sorrows.

“For thus says the Lord: ‘The whole land shall be a wilderness, yet I will not make a complete end. The land shall mourn, and the heavens above shall grieve, because I have spoken. I have purposed, and I have not repented, nor have I turned away from it.’”

God’s mercy is mingled with his anger: the whole land is deserted, but it is not brought to a complete end, so that there may be people who understand his clemency. The heaven above will also appear sad, and the land itself will mourn because the Lord’s sentence has reached its conclusion; nor has he repented of what he purposed and spoke.

God’s repentance is spoken of when the sentence previously announced is withdrawn and the raging anger does not reach its full end. He threatened through Jonah (Jonah 3), but the multitude of tears and groans overcame the impending sword.

“At the voice of the horseman and of the one shooting arrows—or drawing the bow—every city—or region—fled. They entered the rugged places and climbed the rocks.”

What follows, “and they entered the thickets—or caves,” was added by the Septuagint.

“All the cities have been abandoned, and no one dwells in them.”

The divine discourse describes the army of the raging Babylonian: because of its terror, the whole people abandoned the city, climbed every height, and nevertheless could not avert the Lord’s anger. Whatever, as we said above, is understood historically against Jerusalem can be referred to the Church when it has offended God and been handed over to its adversaries, whether in a time of persecution or, certainly, through vices and sins.

“But you, devastated woman, what will you do?” For “devastated woman,” which in Hebrew Aquila alone translated in this way, the others rendered “wretched” and “pitiful,” because of her own guilt: she offended the merciful God and was handed over to her adversaries.

Accordingly, it follows:

“When you dress yourself in scarlet, adorn yourself with a golden necklace, and paint your eyes with antimony, you will adorn yourself in vain. Your lovers have despised you; they seek your life.”

He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman. Once you have offended God and, as though abandoning your husband, have forsaken the Creator, you seek adornments in vain. Your lovers, the demons, have despised you, and they will seek not the impurity of sexual intercourse but the destruction of your soul.

The same is to be understood spiritually against those who have lost conjugal affection and the chastity of true faith. “If,” he says, “you dress yourself in scarlet”—that is, if you take up faith in the blood of Christ; if you adorn yourself with a golden necklace”—that is, if you devote yourself to meditation on spiritual meaning and understanding; and if you paint your eyes with antimony”—that is, if you pursue the mysteries and seek to know the secrets of God—you will adorn yourself in vain.

For you had prepared these things also for your lovers; therefore the narrow bed cannot contain both, and God does not receive the ornaments by which you formerly pleased your lovers.

“For I heard a voice like that of a woman in labor, anguish—or groaning—like that of a woman giving birth: the voice of the daughter of Zion, fainting and spreading out her hands. ‘Woe is me, for my soul has failed because of the slain.’”

He describes the city of Jerusalem lamenting and crying out in the likeness of a woman giving birth, that is, one delivering her first offspring. For just as a woman in labor, who has not yet experienced the pain of childbirth, almost dies and, suffering anguish, can scarcely breathe, collapsing with her hands spread out, so the daughter of Zion, when she sees her children slain, bursts into these words and says: “Woe is me, for my soul has failed because of the slain.”

Two examples are compared in one chapter: a woman giving birth to children and a woman mourning them, so that whatever a woman suffers in bearing children or through the deaths of her children, Jerusalem may suffer in the case of its peoples.

## CHAPTER V. The Lord seeks faith among the people; the prophet goes to the obstinate and announces devastation because of the sins of the princes and priests; their catalogue is reviewed.

“Go around the streets of Jerusalem, look, consider, and search in its squares to see whether you can find a man who practices justice and seeks faith, and I will be merciful to it. Even if they say, ‘The Lord lives,’ they will swear falsely.”

(Jerome.) Great is the love of justice: unlike the exchange between Abraham’s question and God’s answer, God will not spare the city for ten righteous men (Genesis 18); but if he finds even one in Jerusalem, which is already on the verge of perishing, who practices justice and seeks faith—or, as Symmachus translated, “truth”—God will nevertheless have mercy on Jerusalem.

And because it could happen that some among the people would be found who pretended to worship God and swore by the Lord, he forestalls this objection. God is not pleased with empty words but with the truth of faith, and he says: “I do not love those who swear by me and swear falsely, but those whose hearts and lips agree.”

“Lord, your eyes look upon faith. You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline. They hardened their faces more than rock and refused to return.”

After the words of the Lord, by which he had commanded, “Go around the streets of Jerusalem,” and so forth, the prophet speaks to the Lord: “Lord, your eyes look upon faith,” which in Hebrew is [the Hebrew term is omitted in the supplied text]. It is not the works of the Jews, in which they exulted according to the ceremonies of the law, but the faith of Christians, through which we have been saved by grace.

From this chapter we learn that punishments are inflicted so that vices may be corrected. Accordingly, he says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline.” Through all tortures and scourging Jerusalem is not corrected; beyond all this, it does not even have the shame of its vices, but, hardening its forehead like rock in shamelessness, it refuses to turn toward better things.

(Gregory.) Every divine stroke is therefore either a purification of our present life or the beginning of the punishment to come. It is concerning those who profit from scourging that it is said: “You fashion pain according to the commandment” (Psalm 93). When the wicked person is scourged and corrected, because he refused to hear the commandment, he hears pain. Pain is therefore fashioned as a commandment for the one who is restrained from evil works by pain, as though pain were taking the place of a commandment.

But concerning those whom scourging condemns and does not free, it is said: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline.” These scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment. Hence through Moses the Lord says: “A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it will burn to the depths of the underworld.”

With respect to the stroke inflicted in the present, it is rightly said: “A fire has been kindled by my anger”; but with respect to eternal condemnation, what follows is aptly added: “and it will burn to the depths of the underworld.”

Although some customarily say that what is written is true: “God will not judge twice for the same thing,” they nevertheless fail to consider what the prophet says concerning the wicked: “Crush them with double confusion,” and what is written elsewhere: Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.

“If we nevertheless agree with them that no fault can be struck twice, this must be understood of those who are struck because of sin and die in their sin: their punishment begins here and is completed there. Thus, for those who refuse every correction, there is one scourge, which begins temporally but is completed in eternal punishments, so that for those who utterly refuse to be corrected, the stroke of present scourges is already the beginning of the torments to come.”

“But I said: ‘Perhaps they are poor and foolish, ignorant of the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God.’”

Often those who are poor among the common people are designated by the name “foolish.” Hence now also through Jeremiah it is said: “I said, ‘Perhaps they are poor and foolish, ignorant of the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God.’”

[Col. 0842A] “I will therefore go to the nobles and speak to them, for they know the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God.”

(Jerome.) Here “poor” and “nobles” do not refer to poverty and wealth; rather, he compares the people with their rulers. The sense is: Seeing the stubbornness of the unbelieving people, and that they refused to accept discipline with hardened faces, I reasoned this out with myself: Perhaps the common, undistinguished people cannot know the teaching of God, and therefore are excusable, because through ignorance they are unable to know God’s commandments.

I will therefore go to the priests and to those who rule the people, and I will speak to them, for they know the will of the Lord and understand the judgment of their God. He says this in the language of one who doubts, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “I will send my son; perhaps they will respect him” (Matthew 21), so that through the ambiguity of the sentence and the suspension of the words the freedom of the human will might be shown.

“And behold, these men broke the yoke completely; they burst the bonds. Therefore the lion from the forest struck them, the wolf devastated them at evening, and the leopard kept watch over their cities. Everyone who goes out from them will be captured, because their transgressions have multiplied and their apostasies have grown strong.”

Those whom I thought to be teachers proved to be worse than their disciples; and the greater the authority of the wealthy, the greater the insolence of their sins. They broke the yoke of the law, as the Apostle says: “Why then are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we are saved, just as they were” (Acts 15).

They also burst the bonds of God’s commandments—not those of the Pharisees—concerning which it is said in the second Psalm: “Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us.”

Because they did all these things, “the lion from the forest struck them,” namely, the Babylonian kingdom; “the wolf devastated them at evening,” signifying the Medes and Persians. For this, in Daniel’s vision (Daniel 7), a bear is set down, with three rows of teeth in its mouth; “the leopard kept watch over their cities,” prefiguring Alexander’s assault and his swift attack from the West all the way to India.

He calls it a leopard because of its variegated nature and because it fought against the Medes and Persians with the many nations subjected to it. “And it had,” he says, “four heads in the beast, and authority was given to it.”

Because he is not prophesying about the future but speaking about the past, he has woven the history as though these events were already immediately about to occur. He is silent, however, about the Roman Empire, concerning which perhaps it is said: “Everyone who goes out from them will be captured.”

He gives the reasons why they suffered these things: their transgressions had multiplied, and they persisted in their violations. Hence it is said: “Their apostasies have grown strong.”

The fact that the Hebrew word placed at the beginning signifies “watchfulness” is demonstrated in the present passage. Where we said “the leopard keeping watch,” the Hebrew reads [the Hebrew wording is omitted in the supplied text].

According to the tropological interpretation, those who are thought great in the Church, because they break the yoke and burst the bonds, are therefore handed over to shameful passions, so that they do what is unfitting.

“Because of this, how can I be merciful to you? Your children have forsaken me and swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery; they indulged themselves in the house of a prostitute. They became lustful horses toward women and were made stallions for me. Each one neighed for his neighbor’s wife. Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord, and shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation?”

A catalogue of Jerusalem’s sins: God says that he does not know on what grounds he might show it mercy. “Your children,” he says, “have forsaken me.” They are no longer mine but yours, because they swear by those who are not gods. “I filled them, and they committed adultery.”

Let those who, after receiving riches from the Lord, lie immersed in them and serve lust hear this. “They became lustful horses toward women.” For “stallions,” the Hebrew has [the Hebrew wording is omitted in the supplied text], which all the translators rendered with one voice as ἕλκοντες, that is, “drawing” or “pulling,” so that the size of their genitals might be indicated, in accordance with the saying of Ezekiel: “Their flesh was like the flesh of donkeys” (Ezekiel 23).

This is what is written elsewhere: “They have become like foolish beasts and have been made like them” (Psalm 48). At the same time, he displays such madness of lust that he calls not merely the appetite for pleasure but also χρεμετισμός—that is, “neighing”—and preserves the metaphor of horses raging with desire.

“When you have done these things,” he says, “are you not worthy of a visitation?” Observe that here “visitation” is used for punishment and chastisements, in accordance with what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Psalm 88).

“And shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation?” Once it has been bound by sins, it is no longer called the people of God but a nation from which God’s soul has withdrawn, in accordance with what is written: “Your new moons and Sabbaths and feast days my soul hates” (Isaiah 1).

What is expressed in the Old Testament as affection is written in the New Testament as a reality, when the Savior says: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10).

“Go up upon its walls (or fortifications) and destroy them; but do not make a complete end. Remove its branches (or supports), for they are not gods. For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord.” [Col. 0843D] He commands the nations of whom he had said above: “The lion from the forest struck them, the wolf laid them waste, and a leopard in their cities,” to go up upon the walls of Jerusalem, or its fortifications, and destroy it; but they are not to make a complete end, so that a remnant may be saved and there may be someone to proclaim the glory of God among the nations. Thus he mingles clemency with severity. When he adds, “Remove its branches, or supports,” he commands that all the means of assistance be taken away—means they lost through their own fault, because the house of Israel and the house of Judah transgressed against the Lord, signifying the ten tribes and the two. Let the Church hear this: the walls and fortifications of those who have no hope in the Lord and transgress against him will quickly be destroyed; nevertheless, a complete end will not be made [Col. 0844A] because of the judge’s clemency, and not because of the merits of the offenders.

“They denied the Lord and said: He is not the one (or: These things do not exist), and evil will not come upon us; we shall not see the sword, and we shall not suffer hunger. The prophets spoke into the wind, and there was no answer (or: speech) in them; therefore these things shall happen to them.” Because they denied God, or lied against the Lord, they said: “He is not the one by whose judgment all things will happen; rather, all these things occurred by chance. Nor will what the prophets’ voices threaten come upon us; we shall neither see the sword nor endure the famine of a siege. Whatever the prophets said, they said into the wind; all of it passed away ineffectually, and they had no answer—that is, no oracle—or the word of God was not in them. [Col. 0844B] Therefore they will suffer what the following speech describes.” Let the negligent Church, which rejects God’s providence, hear this: it too will endure sword and famine unless it believes that what is announced will come.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth into fire, and this people into wood, and it will devour them.” You said: “The prophets spoke into the wind, and what they threaten will not come.” Therefore, O prophet, I place my words in your mouth, words possessing the power of fire; and I will turn this people into wood, so that through your speech and prophecy the unbelieving may be consumed. Thus God is called a consuming fire, so that, if we build upon Christ as our foundation, he may consume in us the hay, wood, and stubble (Deut. IV).

[Col. 0844C] “Behold, I will bring upon you, house of Israel, a nation from far away, says the Lord: a strong nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, nor understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open grave; all are mighty. It will eat your crops and your bread; it will devour your sons and your daughters; it will eat your flocks and your herds; it will eat your vine and your fig tree; and it will crush your fortified cities, in which you place your confidence, by the sword. Nevertheless, in those days, says the Lord, I will not make a complete end of you.”

The prophets will not speak to you into the wind after a long time, nor as you falsely suppose. Even now I will bring upon you the nation of the Babylonians, which will come from far away—a strong nation. In Hebrew it is written [Col. 0844D] “an ancient nation,” whose dominion once belonged to the giant Nimrod (Gen. X), a nation whose language you will not know, or, as it is written in Hebrew, “nor will you understand what it says.” For it is some consolation amid evils to have enemies whom you can address and who understand your pleas. As for what follows, “Its quiver is like an open grave”—which is not stated in the Septuagint edition—it signifies Babylonian weaponry. There is no doubt that the kingdom of the Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians is supremely skilled in archery. At the same time he describes the devastation of the land of Judea, the slaughter of many, the driving away of livestock, and the overthrow of cities and walls, since everything will be seized by the enemy’s sword. Yet amid such great evils he will not destroy them utterly, but will preserve a remnant—either those who were led away to Babylon and then released to cultivate the fields of the land of Judea, or those who, after the heat of persecution, preserved the Lord’s faith by flight or confession.

“And if you say: Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us? You shall say to them: Just as you abandoned me and served a foreign god, or foreign gods, in your own land, so you shall serve foreigners in a land that is not your own.” It is great foolishness not to know why they suffered these things, since they committed such great sins. The brief answer to those who ask is: “Just as you served a foreign god”—that is, Baal—or the foreign gods of all the nations in the land of Judea, so you shall serve foreign gods in a land that is not your own: [Col. 0845B] clearly, Babylon and Chaldea. For if a foreign religion delights you, why is it necessary to adopt a distant error? Live with such people—indeed, serve those whose gods you worship.

This may also be understood of heretics, concerning whom it is written: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” (1 John II). The Lord casts heretics out of the Church, those who for a long time, under his name, venerated the images of their own falsehoods, so that outside they may worship what previously they worshiped within, and the chaff may be separated from the wheat.

“Announce this to the house of Jacob, and make it heard in Judah, saying: Hear, foolish people, who have no heart: you have eyes, yet do not see; you have ears, [Col. 0845C] yet do not hear.” He draws sinners back to salvation in many ways. He calls the people foolish because, as though abandoning wisdom, they have abandoned its author; and he compares them to images, concerning which it is written: “They have eyes, and do not see; they have ears, and do not hear. Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them” (Ps. CXIII). Properly, however, he speaks to Judah and to the house of Jacob. Israel had already been exiled in Assyria for a long time. At the same time he gives us to understand that, even without a commandment, we ought by natural understanding to recognize what is right.

“Will you not therefore fear me, says the Lord, and will you not grieve before my face (or: will you not fear)? I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance that will not pass away. They will be shaken and will not be able (or: it will be troubled and will not be able); its waves will swell (or: roar), but they will not pass beyond it. But this people has acquired an unbelieving and rebellious heart; they have turned away and gone off, and have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives us the early and latter rain in its season, preserving for us the fullness of the annual harvest.”

He recounts his benefits in order to convict the ungrateful. “Will you not fear me,” he says, “who have granted you such things? I do not seek the love of the perfect, but the fear of beginners”—I who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, who by my command restrained so powerful an element and the immense masses of its depths at the shores, according to what is written: “He issued a command, and it will not pass away” (Ps. CXLVIII). Things that lack the capacity for hearing hear and perceive me; but my former people, made foolish through their own fault, not only despise the Lord but even provoke the gracious Lord. “They have turned away,” he says, from me, turned their backs on me, and gone away with hurried steps. Nor did a silent conscience draw them back, so that they might say in their hearts: “Let us fear him who gives us the early and latter rain.”

Through all this he indicates the abundance of the annual harvest; for this reason Aquila’s first edition and Symmachus translated the term as “weeks.” In Hebrew, the word written here, because of its ambiguity, signifies both “weeks” and “fullness.”

“Your iniquities have turned these things aside, and your sins have withheld good from you.” [Col. 0846B] Therefore, whenever the sea also crosses its boundaries or the rain is withdrawn, the Lord’s hand has by no means been shortened so that he cannot do these things. Rather, our sins have turned aside the things coming to us, so that they might go to others who have not sinned. “And they have withheld,” he says, “the good already coming to us,” according to what is written literally: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V).

We may understand the early and latter rain as the Law and the Gospel, and as the various callings from the first hour until the eleventh, in which the workers of the vineyard are promised one reward, eternal life (Matt. XX).

“For impious men have been found among my people, lying in wait like birdcatchers, setting snares and traps for catching men. As a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.” Since the early and latter rain, and all good things, were turned away from them, the reasons are now given: impious men were found among his people. He did not say “unjust men and sinners,” as the new heresy wishes, but “impious.” Impiety openly denies God; iniquity and sin, if they confess their error, easily bend God toward mercy. What we rendered “lying in wait like birdcatchers,” which is not found in the Septuagint, Aquila and Symmachus translated as “like a birdcatcher’s net.” Even one who appears good and upright among them sets ambushes like a birdcatcher, while they hunt one another to death and fill their houses with the losses and damages of others, so that the philosophers’ saying may be fulfilled: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.” [Col. 0846D] Would that such people existed only among those who appear to be outside, whom the Lord judges, and that those whom he possesses did not fill our own assemblies. Avarice is the root of all evils, so that when people come to us we look not at their faces but at their hands.

“Therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed beyond my words most wickedly. They have not judged the cause; they have not directed the cause (or: judgment) of the orphan. And they have not judged the judgment of the poor (or: widow). Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on a people such as this?”

If I wished to note individually everything omitted in the Septuagint edition, it would take too long. “Those who set ambushes,” he says, “and rejoice in the nakedness of others have therefore become great and rich,” because they have done the things mentioned above. “They have grown fat and sleek,” according to what is written: “The beloved grew fat and sleek and kicked” (Deut. XXXII). They passed beyond my words for their own harm, because the consciousness of their wealth led them to say what appears in the Gospel: “Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke XII).

They passed beyond them to their own evil, despising everyone and not setting God’s judgment before their eyes. They disregarded the orphan and the poor; for this the Septuagint said “widows,” although the Hebrew does not contain this, since it properly means “the poor,” not “widows.” As for what follows—“Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on a people such as this?”—it has already been explained above.

“Astonishing and wondrous things have occurred in the land: the prophets prophesied falsehood (or: injustice), the priests applauded with their hands, and my people loved such things. What, then, will you do at the end (or: after these things)?”

Above he had said: “I will go to the great men and speak to them; perhaps they have known the way of the Lord.” And behold, these men had all the more broken the yoke and torn the bonds. Now he describes who the great men are: namely, the prophets and priests, of whom some proclaim future events, while others determine from the Law what must be done. “And behold,” he says, “while they prophesied falsehood, the priests applauded with their hands.” To show that the people too were not without guilt, since they were led astray by such men, it is written: “And my people loved such things.” Once my people, after loving such things they ceased to be mine. What, then, will they do when the final time of judgment arrives, or when the necessity of captivity comes? Hence it is astonishing and wondrous that no one was found, either among the leaders or among the people, who thought rightly.

## CHAPTER VI

The coming of Nebuchadnezzar and the deportation of the people because of the priests’ avarice; and because the people does not hear the sound of the trumpet.

“Strengthen yourselves, children of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem; blow the trumpet in Tekoa; and raise a sign (or: banner) over Beth-haccerem, because evil has been seen (or: appeared) from the north, and great destruction.” (Jerome.) No one is unaware that Jerusalem is situated in the tribe of Benjamin. We also see daily with our own eyes that Tekoa is a village situated in the hill country and twelve miles from Jerusalem. There is another village among us, likewise situated in the hill country, which in the Syriac and Hebrew language bears this name. What he says, therefore, means this: because Nebuchadnezzar is now about to come from the north and captivity is near, “O inhabitants of Jerusalem, take up arms; blow the trumpet loudly in Tekoa; and raise a banner in Beth-haccerem,” he says, so that you may be able to resist the enemies.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand”; Tekoa as “trumpet”; Beth-haccerem as “village of the vineyard.” Let us refer all these things to the Church, so that, if it sins and the attack of persecution comes, it may prepare itself to resist.

[Col. 0848A] “I have compared the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman; shepherds and their flocks will come to her. They have fixed (or: will fix) their tents around her; each one will pasture those who are under his hand. Consecrate (or: prepare) war against her; rise, and let us go up at noon.”

The beauty of Jerusalem, which is Zion itself, is described—one name referring to the whole city, the other to the city’s citadel. For Zion is interpreted as “citadel,” that is, “watchtower,” and she is compared to a beautiful woman. Just as lovers are said to come to a woman, so shepherds are said to come to this city. The Hebrew word is especially elegant: written with four letters, it signifies “lovers” if read one way and “shepherds” if read another, so that, according to the metaphor of a beautiful woman, lovers are understood, or, according to the city’s overthrow, shepherds. [Col. 0848B] Some of them hasten to violate the prostitute; others to besiege and overthrow the city.

By the shepherds and their flocks let us understand the leaders and the army of the Chaldeans. They will fix their tents all around in the siege of the city, “and each one will pasture those who are under his hand”—namely, his own troops and companies. These leaders, or shepherds, will say to their flocks: “Consecrate war against Jerusalem, for it is the Lord’s command; rise, and let us go up at noon.” Let us attack in broad daylight, not by night and ambush, for no one can resist us.

“Woe to us, because the day has declined, because the evening shadows have grown longer (or: failed). Rise, and let us go up by night, and let us destroy its houses.” They say, “Rise, and let us go up at noon,” and let us fight in the clear light. These reply: “Woe to us, because the evening shadows have grown longer,” in accordance with Virgil’s lines:

> And now from afar the highest rooftops of the farmsteads smoke,  
> and the shadows fall longer from the lofty mountains.

The sense is: If we suffer these things by day, what will we suffer at night? Again, those who had said above, “Consecrate war against her and rise,” now urge one another to battle, saying: “Rise, and let us go up by night,” so that the adversaries may know that victory depends not on the time but on strength. “And let us destroy her houses,” which are uselessly protected by the strength of their walls.

[Col. 0848D] “For thus says the Lord of hosts: Cut down its wood (or: woods); pour out (or: bring) a rampart around Jerusalem.” “For this reason,” they say, “we are confident of victory, because it is the Lord’s command, ordering the Chaldeans: Cut down wood and bring earth for the rampart of the future fortifications.” This shows that, before the crown of victory comes, the city is not to be captured immediately, but after a long siege, as we read later.

“This is a city of visitation (or: deceit); every calumny (or: oppression) is in its midst. Just as a cistern (or: pool) makes its water cold, so she has made her wickedness cold.”

The Lord commanded that the trees be cut down and that ramparts be poured out [Col. 0849A] all around, because the time of her visitation has arrived, so that she may receive what is due for her sins, the greatest of which is συκοφαντία—that is, “false accusation”—by which she oppresses the innocent through calumny. Just as a cistern or pool makes its water cold, so the wickedness present in the midst of Jerusalem has lost all the warmth of life.

It should also be noted that those inflamed by the Holy Spirit are called fervent, whereas evil things are cold. Hence it is also written: “When in the last days iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). I think this also is expressed by: “I have become like those who go down into the pit” (Ps. XXVII). Let the Latin reader understand this, so that it will be enough to say it once: among the Greeks, “pit” does not mean a pond, but a cistern, which is called in Syriac and Hebrew. In the present passage, instead of “pit,” which all have translated in the same way, the Hebrew says:

(Maurus.) Concerning this pit, in the burden of Babylon through Isaiah, it is said to Nebuchadnezzar: “Yet you shall be brought down to the underworld, to the depth of the pit” (Isa. XIV). The saints have the wings of an eagle and the wings of a dove, and they can say: “I will fly away and rest.” But the impious, resembling the Egyptians, have been submerged like lead in mighty waters and sunk into the depths like a stone. Sometimes “the pit” signifies the depths of hell. These are the testimonies: “I have become like those who go down into the pit, and they placed me in the lowest pit” (Ps. XXVII). For just as a pit receives waters descending into it, so hell receives souls. [Col. 0849C] Banaias descended into such a pit (1 Chron. XI) in a time of snow and cold, and killed a lion there. Hence the heretics abandon the Lord, the fountain of living water, and dig for themselves cracked cisterns incapable of holding water.

Among these pits are those who do not possess the fervor of the Holy Spirit and are not like the prophet Jeremiah, who, according to the Septuagint interpreters, said: “I found hot water in the desert.” When their love grew cold, they lost the color of the Holy Spirit. Hence he says: “As a pool cools water, so wickedness cools those who possess it.” Would that, according to the Apocalypse of John (Rev. III), they were “either hot or cold”—that is, either that they believed or that they did not believe at all—so that through lukewarmness and a pretended faith they would not be rejected by the Lord.

[Col. 0849D] “Let iniquity and devastation be heard in her; before me there is always weakness and a wound. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest perhaps I make you a deserted, uninhabitable land.”

The Septuagint has: “Impiety and misery will be heard in her, before her face; through every grief and scourging you will be instructed, Jerusalem, lest perhaps my soul depart from you, lest I make you an impassable land that is not inhabited.”

(Hier.) Through these words we learn that the Lord chastises every son whom he receives. Jerusalem is therefore instructed through blows and torments so that she may be corrected, God’s soul may not depart from her, and she may not be reduced to desolation. Whenever, then, we are subjected to repeated afflictions, let us recall this verse for our consolation: [Col. 0850A] “Through every grief and scourging you will be instructed, Jerusalem.”

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: They will gather Israel’s remnant as grapes in a vineyard, even to the last cluster. Turn your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket.”

The Septuagint has: “For thus says the Lord of powers: Gather grapes, gather grapes like the remnant of Israel; return like a grape-gatherer to his basket.” Some receive these words in a favorable sense, others in an unfavorable one. In the favorable sense, when Jerusalem has been devastated, the remnant is saved. In the unfavorable sense: not even one cluster or small bunch should remain in the vineyard; everything will be gathered. Whatever you find, cast it into the basket like a grape-gatherer, so that, just as he drags the clusters to the winepress, you may drag the captives [Col. 0850B] to Babylon.

“To whom shall I speak, and whom shall I warn, so that he may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised (or: your ears), and they cannot hear. Behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach to them, and they will not receive it.”

They cannot hear because they were unwilling to circumcise their ears. Yet their inability is not free from punishment, since it arises from contempt and unbelief. Therefore, if anyone does not receive God’s words and does not possess understanding of his commandments, he has uncircumcised ears. At the same time, it should be noted that circumcision in Scripture is spoken of in three forms: of the foreskin, of the heart, and of the ears. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI). By our own will, therefore, we do not receive the word of God, and for that reason it becomes a reproach to us, so that what was given for salvation is turned by our fault into punishment.

[Col. 0850C] “Therefore I am full of the Lord’s fury; I have labored, enduring it.”

The Septuagint has: “I have filled my fury and endured, and I have not consumed it.”

According to the Hebrew, this is spoken in the person of the prophet, who foresees the coming wrath of God and is full of the Lord’s fury and anger, and can endure no longer, nor dare to implore the Lord on behalf of sinners. According to the Septuagint, however, a new sense is introduced: the Lord himself speaks and says, “I have filled my fury by striking the sinful people, yet I have restrained it and have not poured it out entirely, so that a remnant may be saved.” This seems to me to be contradictory to itself: for if he has filled his fury, how did he restrain it so that he would not complete it?

“Pour out (or: he poured out) fury upon the child [outside], and upon the assembly of young men together. For a man will be captured with a woman, an old man with one full of days. Their houses will pass to others, together with their fields and wives.”

Either the prophet, in the spirit, commands the coming Chaldean to pour out the Lord’s fury upon the children and not to spare even an innocent age; or he certainly reports what happened to the assembly of young men together, who had taken up arms to resist. A man will be captured with his wife; those sweetest names between them will together experience captivity—an old man with one full of days. Thus old age is not the final stage of life, but refers to those who are full of days, whom in our language we call spent or decrepit.

It follows: “Their houses will pass to others,” through the evil of captivity, “together with their fields and wives,” so that both the wife and the property may pass to the enemies. Whatever we understand literally concerning Jerusalem, let us refer spiritually to the Church, if it has offended God.

“For I will stretch out my hand over the inhabitants of the land, says the Lord. For from the least to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice; and from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. And they treated the brokenness of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: Peace, peace, when there was no peace.”

What is said in Hebrew, “I will stretch out my hand over the sinners (or: inhabitants) of the land,” is always rendered by the Septuagint as “I will continually raise it up.” Both expressions refer to the posture of one who strikes, according to what is written: “And still the hand of the Lord is extended (or: exalted)” (Isa. V). The inhabitants of the land, however, are always at fault. Hence in the Apocalypse it is frequently said: “Woe to the inhabitants of the earth” (Rev. VIII).

From the least to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, in accordance with the apostolic saying: “Avarice is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). And from prophet to priest, all practice deceit: some by prophesying falsehood, others by perversely interpreting the law of God. For the prophet also says elsewhere: “Seek the law [Col. 0851C] from the priests” (Jer. XVIII).

“And when,” he says, [Col. 0852A] “they were doing such things, they announced every prosperity to my people; and as though they wished to heal the wound and disgrace of my daughter, they said: Peace, peace, when there was no peace at all.” This is to be understood especially of priests and teachers who promise prosperity to the rich and to those whom they see established in the highest honor, and proclaim God as merciful, thereby preparing them all the more for punishment and wrath.

“They were confounded because they committed abomination. Indeed, they were not confounded with confusion, and they did not know how to blush.”

This should be read more precisely according to the Hebrew: “And when,” he says, “they had done such things, were they ashamed? Did they blush at their crimes? Rather, they increased their sin through contempt and did not know how to blush.” Here he used “did not know” for “were unwilling,” or because, through excessive contempt and the fault of an ingrained evil, they could not even understand.

“Therefore they will fall among those who are falling; at the time of their visitation they will collapse, says the Lord.”

“Because,” he says, “they did not know how to blush, and not only did they possess no action but not even knowledge or awareness of repentance, therefore those who previously stood among them will fall among those who collapse through their own vices. When the time of their visitation and punishment arrives, they will be joined to all who are falling.” It is great impiety not only not to guard against sins, but also to refuse to understand them, and to have no distinction between good and evil works.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0851]

Knowing that the Lord is just and merciful, the prophet, as is his custom, terrifies sinners by proclaiming the punishments that are to come upon them; yet he does not cease to call them to repentance and improvement of life. Therefore, after testifying that, because of the uncircumcised ears of the Jews and the hardness of their hearts, he was full of the Lord’s fury and wearied, since in the spirit he saw a great punishment threatening sinners, he now again urges them to meditate on God’s law and to observe his commandments, so that, walking in the good way, they may find refreshment [Col. 0851D] for their souls.

“Thus,” he says, “says the Lord: Stand on the roads and see, and ask about the ancient paths, what the good way is; walk in it, and you will find refreshment (or: purification) for your souls. And they said: We will not walk (or: go). And I appointed watchmen over you; listen to the sound of the trumpet. And they said: We will not listen. Therefore hear (or: they heard), nations, and know, assembly (or: you who pasture flocks), how much I will do to them. (Or, according to Symmachus: ‘And know the testimony that is in them.’) Hear, O earth.” (Hier.)

The Gospel parable (Matt. XIII), if understood, will provide the interpretation of this passage. In it the good merchant is said to sell all his pearls in order to buy one exceedingly precious pearl with their price. In this way, through the patriarchs and prophets, we come to the one who says: “I am the way” (John XIV).

We must therefore stand among the prophets, contemplate them with the greatest care, and ask about the ancient or everlasting paths, which have been worn by the footsteps of many saints. In Greek they are more significantly called τρίβοι, “well-trodden paths.” We must ask what the good way is in the Gospel (Matt. VII), and walk in it. When this way has been found, it provides refreshment or purification for the souls of believers.

[Col. 0852D] But they answered in the opposite manner: “We will not walk in the way of the Gospel”—the prophet speaking here specifically of the Jews’ unbelief. Immediately he adds: “And I appointed watchmen over you.” There is no doubt that the chorus of the apostles is indicated, according to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III). And I commanded you to hear the sound of the trumpet—either the commandments of the Gospel or the teaching of the apostles—according to Isaiah: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who announce Jerusalem” (Isa. XL).

They said: “We will not listen,” and, invited to the dinner, they refused to come. Therefore it is said: “Hear, nations.” The apostles followed this principle when they spoke in Lycaonia: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts XIII).

“And know, assembly”—not a Jewish assembly, but one of all nations—or “you who pasture flocks,” bishops, presbyters, and the entire ecclesiastical order—or “know the testimony that is in them”: “The testimony of God is trustworthy, imparting wisdom to the little ones” (Ps. XVIII). To them the Lord also says: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke XII); and, “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isa. VIII).

Know, therefore, how much I will do to the unbelieving people. When it adds, “Hear, O earth,” the whole world is summoned to hear, just as we read at the beginning of Isaiah: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (Isa. I), namely, to what the Lord will do to the Jewish people.

(Maurus.) Therefore that man is an ecclesiastical teacher who moves tears, not laughter; who rebukes sinners; who declares no one blessed or happy, and does not anticipate the judgment of his judge, since holy Scripture says: “Do not call anyone among human beings blessed before death” (Prov. XVII). But elsewhere also we read: “He who blesses his friend in the morning with a loud voice is no different from one who curses him.” Therefore, scorning human judgments, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their criticisms, but let us enter the straight way and the paths worn by the holy prophets, and let us hear Jeremiah saying: “Stand on the ways and see, and ask about the everlasting paths of the Lord, what the good way is, and walk in it.”

And if at any time we have gone astray and, like human beings, have traveled along a crooked road, let us await the Lord’s promises through Ezekiel, where he says: “I will give them another way and another heart.” Therefore, according to the true tradition of the Lord, the straight way is gentle and easy, although it may be felt as hard and rough. For those who serve faithfully and devoutly, when they have taken the Lord’s yoke upon themselves and learned from him because he is gentle and humble in heart, now laying down, in a certain manner, the burden of earthly passions, do not labor but, with the Lord’s provision, find rest for their souls, just as he himself testified through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “Stand on the ways and see, and ask about the ancient paths, what the good way is, and walk in it, and you will find refreshment for your souls.”

For their crooked ways will immediately become straight, and [Col. 0853D] their rough places into level roads. Tasting, they will see that the Lord is sweet; and hearing Christ proclaim in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI), they will understand what follows once the burdens of vices have been laid down: “For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light.”

The Lord’s way therefore has refreshment if it is kept according to his law. But we are the ones who procure pains and torments for ourselves through turbulent exertions, while we prefer to pursue the crooked and perverse ways of this world, even with the greatest danger and difficulty. When, however, by this conduct we have made the Lord’s yoke heavy and hard for ourselves, through blasphemy against the Spirit, we complain about the yoke itself—or about Christ who imposes it—as though it were harsh and rough, according to the saying: “The folly of a man corrupts his way, but he blames God in his heart.” And according to the prophet Haggai, when we say that the way of the Lord does not direct, the Lord rightly answers us: “Is my way not directing? Are your ways not rather crooked?”

And truly, if we wish to compare the shining flower of virginity and the sweet-smelling purity of chastity with the foul and fetid wallows of lust; the quiet and security of monks with the dangers and hardships in which the people of this world are entangled; the rest of our poverty with the devouring sorrows and sleepless cares of the rich, in which they are consumed day and night not without the greatest danger to their life—we shall very easily prove that the yoke of Christ is most sweet and his burden exceedingly light.

“Behold, I will bring evils upon this people, the fruit of their thoughts (or: aversion), because they did not hear my words and cast away my law.” (Hier.) He calls “evils” the punishments and penalties suffered by those who are being chastised—not upon the nations called to the truth of the Gospel, but upon the people who answered: “We will not listen.” They will receive the fruit of their thoughts, or of their aversion, as David says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Ps. CXXVII). The reason is evident: they did not hear the Lord’s words and cast away his law.

“Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and fragrant cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me.”

No one doubts that frankincense comes from Sheba. Hence there is also Virgil’s line:

> And a hundred altars grow warm with Sabaean frankincense.

The prophetic word shows that the cane—which is called in Hebrew, but which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as “cinnamon”—comes from a distant land, so that we may understand India, from which many spices come by way of the Red Sea. Physicians call this kind of aromatic substance κασία σύριγγος, “cassia of the reed.”

The sense is: “In vain do you bring me the most fragrant spices for making the perfumes prescribed by the Law, and burn your burnt offerings, while you do not carry out my will in the Law,” according to what was written above: “They did not hear my words, and they cast away my law.” This properly applies to those who offer sacrifice from plunder and the stripping of the poor, and think they redeem their sins through almsgiving from iniquity, although Scripture says: “The wealth of a man is the ransom of his soul”—wealth gathered not from iniquity, but from labor and righteousness.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give this people over to ruin, and they shall fall among them (or: into weakness, and they shall become weak in it), fathers and sons together, neighbor and kinsman, and they shall perish.”

We see fulfilled everything that the Lord threatened against that people. For daily they fall in their blasphemies, possessing no strength within themselves, but being wholly weakness. The sons follow the blasphemies of their fathers, and daily receive that imprecation: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). And not they alone, but also their neighbors and kinsmen—all who follow the Law and the prophets according to the letter that kills, and not according to the life-giving Spirit—shall likewise perish, because they have sinned alike.

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people is coming from the land of the north, and a great nation shall arise from the ends of the earth. It shall seize bow and shield (or: a *zebynna*); it is cruel (or: shameless), and it will not show mercy. Its voice shall roar like the sea, and it shall mount horses, prepared like a man for battle against you, daughter of Zion.”

This is properly prophesied concerning the Babylonians, who are to come against the people of Jerusalem. The entire array of weapons and the assault of the combatants are described, so that, shaken by the terror of their voice, they may repent and appease the most merciful God. Finally, he gives an occasion for supplication when he says, “against you, daughter of Zion.” We may apply this testimony figuratively to a time of persecution, when all the devil’s fury is aroused against us and there is no mercy; and, like the waves of a most violent sea, they overwhelm those who resist.

“We have heard his report; our hands have become weak. Distress has seized us, pains like those of a woman in labor.”

The people replied—the people whom the prophet, or rather the Lord through the prophet, had threatened with the Babylonians—that even before they came, they had been overcome by fear and could not raise their hands, and that anguish had seized them like the pain of a woman in labor, than which they declare that they have felt nothing more severe.

“Do not go out to the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy is terror all around.”

The Gospel teaches (Matt. 24) that one must not go out into the field or descend from the height of the rooftops, but must heed the words, “On the mountain save yourself” (Gen. 19), toward which we are commanded to go and ascend in Isaiah and Micah (Isa. 2; Mic. 4). Literally, however, they are ordered not to go outside or abandon the walls, but to protect themselves with strong fortifications.

“Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes; make mourning for an only child (or: a beloved child). Make for yourself bitter (or: pitiful) lamentation, for suddenly the devastator (or: misery) will come upon us (or: upon you).”

After saying above, “Do not go out to the fields, and do not walk on the road, for the sword of the enemy is terror all around,” and after also prohibiting flight, he teaches what they must do: namely, turn to repentance and possess in it the firmest and safest armor. Where we have translated, “Make mourning for an only child,” the Hebrew has a word that sounds more like “solitary” than “only child.” For if it meant “beloved” or “lovable,” as the Septuagint translated it, it would have used that term—the same name God gave Solomon. Nothing is more painful than losing one’s only or solitary son.

And where we translated, “for suddenly the devastator or misery will come upon us,” the Septuagint has “upon you,” although God has spoken much more mercifully, testifying that whatever is to come upon his people will also come upon himself. The devastator properly signifies either Nebuchadnezzar or the devil.

“I have appointed you as a strong tester in my people, and you shall know and test their ways. All these princes are turning aside (or: disobedient), walking deceitfully (or: perversely); they are bronze and iron; all of them are corrupt. The bellows have failed” (which the Greeks more precisely call *physētēr* [φυσητήρ, “bellows”]). “The lead has been consumed in the fire; the smelter has smelted in vain (or: the silversmith). For their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away.”

A strong tester is given to the unbelieving people, which in Hebrew is [the Hebrew term is omitted in the supplied text] and means either “fortified,” according to Aquila, or “closed and surrounded,” according to Symmachus and the Septuagint—like a very strong city, so that he may fear none of the people’s plots. “When you have tested,” he says, “and have learned the way of the sinful people, then understand that silver mixed with bronze cannot in any way be purified.”

For just as lead is mixed with adulterated and corrupted metals so that the foreign material may be separated, and, if it should perhaps not be purified, all the lead is consumed and reduced to nothing, so every utterance of teaching and prophetic speech perishes in those who disdain to listen. Let us also say of such people: “Like deaf adders they stop their ears, so that they may not hear the voices of those who charm” (Ps. 57). In vain has the silversmith or smelter smelted, for their wickednesses have not been consumed. Therefore they are called not silver but rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away. The princes are those who depart from the Lord, or are disobedient, who walk perversely and deceitfully.

**(Gregory.)** Concerning this smelting, it is written in Job: “Silver has its sources of veins, and gold has a place where it is smelted” (Job 28). Silver ordinarily signifies eloquence, and gold the splendor of life or wisdom. And because heretics take such pride in the brilliance of their eloquence that they are supported by no authority of the sacred books—and those books are, as it were, veins of silver for our speech, because from them we derive the origin of our discourse—he recalls them to the pages of sacred authority, so that, if they desire to speak truth, they may take from there what they are to say.

“And gold,” he says, “has a place where it is smelted.” As though he were plainly saying: The true wisdom of the faithful, whose place is the universal Church, suffers tribulation from you persecutors, but it will be purified from every stain of sin by the fire of your persecution. Hence it is written: “Gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Ecclus. 2).

This passage may also fittingly be understood as a rebuke of the heretics’ foolish suffering. For they often suffer much for the name of Jesus Christ our Lord and Redeemer, and hope to become martyrs of his passion. To them the voice of holy men now says: “Gold has a place where it is smelted.” For, in accordance with what has already been said by us and by others before us: Whoever suffers outside the unity of the Church may suffer punishment, but cannot become a martyr, because gold has a place where it is smelted.

What then do you say to this, heretics? You wish to be smelted through affliction of the flesh, even through martyrdom, but you do not know the place where you ought to be smelted. Hear what the voice of the holy preacher says: “Gold has a place where it is smelted.” Seek, therefore, the place of smelting; find the furnace in which gold can properly be purified. There is one Church, and whoever wishes to be smelted in it can also be purified from every stain of sin. If, while situated outside it, you endure anything bitter for God, anything involving tribulation, you may be burned, but you cannot be purified.

Let Jeremiah speak; let him show how wholly devoid of power is the fire of your smelting: “In vain has the smelter smelted, for their wickednesses have not been consumed.” Behold, an external fire smelts and applies the punishment of harsh suffering, yet does not burn away the guilt of error; it inflicts the torments of cruel punishments, yet does not increase the merits of good deeds.

The Apostle Paul also indicates how powerless is this fire of smelting, which is endured outside the Catholic Church, saying: “If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Some hold perverse opinions about God; others hold correct opinions about the Creator, but do not preserve unity with their brethren. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by the commission of schism.

Thus, in the first part of the Decalogue itself, the guilt of both parties is restrained, when the divine voice says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and immediately it adds: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12). Whoever thinks perversely about God plainly does not love God; whoever thinks correctly about God but is divided from the unity of the holy Church plainly does not love his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as a companion.

Whoever is divided from this unity of Mother Church—whether by heresy, through holding perverse opinions about God, or by the error of schism, through failing to love his neighbor—is deprived of that charity of which Paul says: “If I hand over my body,” and so forth (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER VII. One must not place confidence in the temple but in good works; one must not pray for that people; concerning the rejection of sacrifices

“‘The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord, and proclaim (or: read) this word there, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, you who enter through these gates to worship the Lord.’”

**(Jerome.)** This is not found in the edition of the Septuagint, but was added from Theodotion’s version of the Hebrew. The prophet is commanded to stand at the Lord’s gate, through which the multitude of the people enters to worship the Lord, so that on this occasion they may hear what the Lord commands. From this we understand the hardness of the Jewish people: they regarded the prophets as liars and madmen, since they were compelled by the opportunity and public prominence of the place to hear the words of the Lord, and not because the words were the Lord’s.

“‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Make good (or: direct) your ways and your practices (or: your inventions), and I will dwell with you in this place (or: I will make you dwell in this place).’”

The most merciful physician desires to heal all the wounded with medicine. When he says, “Make good (or: correct) your ways,” he shows that they are perverse and contain nothing good.
