And because it is natural for each person to love his birthplace alone and to hold nothing dearer than his homeland, he promises rewards to those who obey. “I will dwell with you,” he says, so that I may make you secure in your dwelling; or, according to Symmachus, “I will establish you in a firm dwelling,” as he translated it: “And I will establish you in this place.”

“‘Do not trust in lying words, saying: The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this. For if you make your ways good (or: direct them) and your practices; if you execute judgment between a man and his neighbor; if you do not oppress the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow (or: if you do not mistreat them); if you do not shed innocent blood in this place; and if you do not walk after foreign gods to your own harm, I will dwell with you (or: I will make you dwell) in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers from age to age.’”

What the Septuagint added at the beginning of this chapter—“in lying words that will in no way profit you”—is not found in the Hebrew. He commands both the Jewish people then and us today, who appear to be established in the Church, not to place our confidence in the splendor of buildings, gilded ceilings, or walls clad in marble slabs, saying: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.” That is the temple of the Lord in which true faith, holy conduct, and the chorus of all virtues dwell.

Finally, he adds: If you make your ways straight, if your thought does not go after error, if you pursue justice, if you do not do evil or shed innocent blood, if you do not cause the simple to stumble, and if you do not walk after foreign gods, worshiping the perverse doctrines that you have fabricated from your own heart to your own harm, then either I will dwell with you in this place that you call the temple of God, and in the land that I gave to your fathers—namely, to the apostles and apostolic men—or certainly I will make you dwell there in a firm station from beginning to end.

This can also apply to those virgins who boast of their chastity and display their purity with an impudent face, while their conscience contains something else. They do not know the Apostle’s definition of virginity: “that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 1). For what does bodily chastity profit a mind that has been defiled, if it does not possess the other virtues described by the prophetic word?

“‘Behold, you trust in lying words (or: liars), which will not profit you: stealing, killing, committing adultery, swearing falsely, offering libations to the Baals, and going after foreign gods whom you do not know. And you have come and stood before me in this house in which my name has been invoked, and you have said: We have been delivered (or: We have ceased), because we have committed all these abominations.’”

That they place their confidence in the temple in vain is demonstrated by the sins that follow. For what does it profit them to enter boldly across the threshold of God’s house, stand there with head held high, and have not only their hearts but also their hands polluted by theft, murder, adultery, perjury, sacrilege, and the worship of gods whom they do not know?

No one doubts that these things happen spiritually in the Church, when people consider the prosperity of the present age, do not reckon with their sins, and suppose that God is unaware of them because punishment does not immediately follow. Rather, they burst into such madness that they think themselves delivered because, after their evil deeds, they have also withdrawn from the worship of the Lord.

“‘Has this house (or: my house), in which my name has been invoked in your eyes, become a cave of robbers? I—I am he; I have seen it, says the Lord.’”

I think that the passage in the Gospel was taken from this place, where it is written: “My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a cave of robbers” (Matt. 21); or, as it is written in another Gospel, “a house of commerce” (John 2).

The Church of God is turned into a cave of robbers when thefts, murders, adulteries, perjuries, sacrilege, the invention of heresy, and every crime are practiced in it; when its leaders burn with the torches of greed; and when a shabby—or certainly not shabby—little cloak possesses the wealth of former kings.

Hence he adds: “I—I am he; I have seen it, says the Lord.” My eyes have observed what you think is hidden; the darkness of your treasures does not escape my consciousness. “Though he was rich, he became poor for us” (2 Cor. 8), but now he is ashamed of our riches and says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6).

“‘Go now to my place at Shiloh, where my name dwelt at the beginning, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of my people Israel.’”

From past events he teaches about the present. To those who say, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord,” and rejoice in the splendor of their costly house, he recalls Shiloh, where God’s tabernacle was first located. Concerning it, the psalm says: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh” (Ps. 77; 1 Sam. 4), so that just as that place collapsed into ruins and ashes, so the temple too may fall when it has become the dwelling of similar sinners.

Therefore, just as Shiloh is an example of the temple, so the temple is an example for us when the time comes for that testimony: “Do you suppose that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18.)

“‘And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord, and I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking, and you have not listened; and I called you, and you did not answer: I will do to this house in which my name has been invoked, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave you and your fathers, as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you away from my presence, as I cast away all your brothers, the whole seed of Israel [or: Ephraim].’”

What we have rendered, “rising early and speaking,” is not found in the Septuagint. God rises early—not because there is any time when he is without dawn, but because, after the rest of night, when bodily strength has been restored, the human soul is more vigorous and, being in no way occupied with pleasures or the desire for food, is able to hear and do what is said.

Hence we read in the psalm: “In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and see” (Ps. 5). And in Isaiah: “From the night (or: at dawn) my spirit rises early to you, O God, for your commands are light upon the earth” (Isa. 26). Therefore the Apostle Paul calls them children of light (Eph. 5), not of night or darkness, nor sleeping as the others sleep—those who do not perceive God’s commands.

Because God called them, rising in the night, in order also to free them from darkness, he threatens to do to the temple in Jerusalem what he did to the place of Shiloh (1 Sam. 4–5), where the tabernacle was first located, so that similar sins might be struck by an equal judgment.

And just as the Lord rejected the seed of Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes called Israel, which had rulers because of Jeroboam son of Nebat, from the tribe of Ephraim, which was also called the tribe of Joseph—so he testifies that he will likewise reject Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah together with Benjamin. He rejected Shiloh, and he will reject the temple; he rejected the ten tribes, and he will reject the two. Whatever is said to that people, let us understand as also applying to us if we do similar things.

“‘Therefore, do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf (or: nor ask that they obtain mercy); and do not oppose me, for I will not hear you.’”

So that the prophet might not appear to ask and fail to obtain what he requested, God commands him not to intercede for the sinful people who practice no repentance. When he says, “Do not oppose me,” he shows that the prayers of the saints can oppose God’s anger. Hence the Lord also says to Moses: “Let me alone, so that I may strike this people and make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32). And in the Psalms it is written: “Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Ps. 105). Aaron also took a censer, stood between the fire and the people who were burning, and the wrath of God ceased (Num. 16).

For this reason we read in Isaiah: “You shall raise up the foundations of generation after generation, and you shall be called the builder of walls, turning the paths into rest” (Isa. 58).

**(Jerome.)** Instead of “builder of walls,” Aquila translated, “one who opposes the raging anger of God.” Finally, Symmachus translated it, “one who sets up a wall against the one striking.” Such were Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, who resisted the Lord’s anger and, as though they had built a wall, set a boundary to his indignation.

The same is said to Jeremiah: “Do not stand before the Lord,” lest he wish to resist his anger and, by his prayers as by a wall, shut in his indignation. To Moses, as though the Lord were held back by him, he says: “Let me alone, and I will strike this people” (Deut. 9).

Such a builder of ramparts, walls, and hedges turns the paths into rest, so that God’s anger may no longer rage, but the Lord may be appeased toward them, and all the paths of his indignation may come to rest.

It must be understood, however, that there are two things that prevent our prayers from being heard by the Lord: an uncorrected and persistent error, and an unrepentant heart. Error itself never merits pardon; but whoever has truly been rid of it and withdraws from sharing in it will receive pardon. As long, therefore, as this error remains in people, they retain their condemnation, and it will never be undone, because error always merits punishment.

The Lord said that for those who sin against the Holy Spirit there would be no forgiveness either in this age or in the age to come. Yet how many do we know who, having sinned against the Holy Spirit—various heretics, such as Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians—have returned to the Catholic faith, received forgiveness for their blasphemy here, and taken hope of obtaining pardon in the future. The Lord’s judgment is not thereby untrue, nor can it be thought to have been in any way annulled, since, concerning such people, if they remain what they are, it persists forever as something that can never be forgiven. But when they are no longer such, the punishment imposed is consequently removed.

The statement of the blessed Apostle John also applies: “There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that one should pray for it. And there is a sin not leading to death; I do say that one should pray for it” (1 John 5). The sin leading to death is found in those who remain in the same sin.

There is no sin, indeed, for which the Church either does not pray that it be forgiven or, by the power divinely granted to it, cannot absolve those who desist from it or release those who repent. To it is said: “Whatever you forgive on earth will be forgiven also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

All things are included in these words—however many, whatever magnitude, and whatever kind they may be—while the true force of the Lord’s sentence nevertheless remains: the sentence that declares that such sin will never be forgiven remains in force for those who persist in it, but does not remain against those who afterward withdraw from it.

**(Augustine.)** In the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s people are gathered into one, the unclean spirit is cast out—the spirit that is divided against itself. The unrepentant heart speaks against this gratuitous gift and against this grace of God. Impenitence itself is the spirit of blasphemy, which will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come. For it speaks against the Holy Spirit by whom those whose sins are all forgiven are baptized, and whom the Church receives so that those whose sins it forgives may be forgiven.

Whether in thought or with the tongue, such a person speaks a very evil and exceedingly impious word: Although God’s patience leads him to repentance, by the hardness of his heart and his unrepentant heart he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.

This impenitence—for so, by some single name, we can to some extent call the blasphemy and the word against the Holy Spirit that has no forgiveness forever—this impenitence, I say, against which both the herald and the judge cried out, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. 3); against which the Lord opened the mouth of evangelical preaching; and against which he foretold that the Gospel itself would be preached throughout the whole world.

After he rose from the dead, he said to his disciples: “It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24). This impenitence has absolutely no forgiveness either in this age or in the age to come, because repentance obtains forgiveness in this age, and that forgiveness avails in the future.

But this impenitence, or unrepentant heart, cannot be judged as long as a person lives in this flesh. No one is to be despaired of, as long as God’s patience leads that person to repentance. Nor does the one who does not want the death of the wicked—rather, that the wicked should turn and live—snatch the wicked away from this life.

A person is a pagan today; you do not know whether tomorrow he may become a Christian. A Jew is an unbeliever today; what if tomorrow he believes in Christ? He is a heretic today; what if tomorrow he follows the Catholic truth? He is a schismatic today; what if tomorrow he embraces Catholic peace? What if those whom you mark as belonging to any kind of error, and whom you now condemn as utterly beyond hope, repent before they finish this life and find true life?

For the Lord is merciful, compassionate, patient, and greatly merciful; we must never despair of his mercy. Therefore the prophet Jeremiah, lest we think God cruel because he does not even permit himself to be entreated, gives the reasons why he does not hear, saying:

“‘Do you not see what these people are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The sons gather wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women mix fat to make cakes (or: *chavonas*) for the queen (or: army) of heaven, and they pour libations to foreign gods, provoking me to anger. Do they provoke me to anger, says the Lord? Is it not rather themselves, to the shame of their own faces?’”

**(Jerome.)** “Do you wish,” he says, “to hear, prophet, why I told you, ‘Do not pray for this people’? They do the following things: inside and outside, in the streets and at the exits of Jerusalem, the sons carry wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women mix fat with flour in order to make *chavōnas* [χαυῶνας], which we have translated as ‘cakes,’ or ‘preparations,’ so that every kind of sacrifice may be indicated, for the queen of heaven, whom we must understand as the moon; or certainly for the army of heaven, so that we may understand all the stars.

“After this they pour libations to foreign gods—not because such gods exist, but because under their names they burn incense to demons—and by doing these things they provoke me to anger. The wretched do not understand that this conflict does not injure me, whom anger never changes, but injures themselves, bringing shame upon their own faces and everlasting disgrace.”

**(Maurus.)** Moses, in prophetic spirit and in the person of the Lord, had foretold these things concerning them in the song of Deuteronomy: “They provoked me with foreign gods, and with their abominations they angered me. They sacrificed to demons and not to God” (Deut. 31–32). They did this of their own will, because it lies within our free choice to choose good or evil.

**(Jerome.)** Whatever we do, therefore, we do not injure God, who can never be injured; rather, we prepare destruction for ourselves, storing up wrath for the day of wrath. He assigned different tasks to sons, fathers, and mothers or wives so that no age might be found that had disagreed with their impiety.

“‘Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my fury and my indignation have been smelted (or: have dripped) upon this place, upon human beings and animals, upon the tree of the countryside, and upon the produce of the land; and it shall burn, and it shall not be extinguished.’”

Because he had said above, “Do they provoke me to anger?” how does he now say, “Behold, my fury and my indignation have dripped upon this place”? The meaning is: I do not naturally become angry, but they act in such a way as to provoke me to anger and make it seem that I change my nature. Let them therefore experience me as angry, since, insofar as it lies within them, they try to make me so.

And beautifully he does not say, “My fury has been poured out upon this place,” but “has dripped,” to signify a measured punishment. Yet if there is such harshness in a drop of fury, what will happen if the whole rain is poured out? The phrase “has been smelted” (or: “the indignation has been smelted”) may also be understood to mean that what he long refused to do, he is compelled to do by the multitude of their sins.

When God becomes angry, human beings and the things belonging to human beings will likewise experience destruction. “And it shall burn,” he says—there is no doubt that he means the Lord’s fury—“and it shall not be extinguished,” because the people do not do the things by which it could be extinguished.

“‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat meat. For I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I led them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this word I commanded them, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way that I have commanded you, so that it may be well with you.’”

Having rejected their temple, he consequently rejects their sacrifices as well, indirectly accusing them of sacrificing victims not out of reverence for him but from a desire for feasting. When he says, “I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I led them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices,” it is clearly understood that he first gave the Decalogue, written on stone tablets by the finger of God.

After the offense of idolatry and the making of the calf (Exod. 31), he later commanded that sacrifices be made to him rather than to demons, removing the pure religion of the commandments of God and permitting the shedding of sacrificial blood and the desire for meat.

“‘And they did not listen, nor did they incline their ear, but they went according to their wills (or: desires) and according to the perversity of their evil heart; and they became backward and not forward, from the day when their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day.’”

When I said, “Hear my voice, and I will be your God,” and so forth, they did not listen or incline their ear, but made the desires of their own hearts their rule. Contrary to the Apostle’s teaching—who forgot what lay behind and stretched forward to what lay ahead—they did the opposite: they desired the past and despised the future.

When he says, “From the day when their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day,” he says that they spent the whole intervening time in offense against the Lord. Hence the grace of the Gospel was necessary, preserving them not through their own merit but through the Lord’s mercy.

“‘And I sent to you all my servants the prophets, day after day, rising early and sending them. But they did not listen to me, nor did they incline their ear; they hardened their neck, and they acted worse than their fathers.’”

The Lord’s anger, therefore, was justly smelted and dripped upon a contemptuous people, hard of neck and unwilling to hear the words of God. We have explained above how God sends prophets either in the night, at dawn, or during the day.

“‘And you shall speak all these words to them, and they will not listen to you; and you shall call them, and they will not answer you. And you shall say to them: This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God and did not receive discipline. Faith has perished and has been taken from their mouth.’”

“Do not doubt,” he says, “that they have hardened their neck and acted worse than their fathers. Behold, I give them an opportunity for repentance. I do not speak in order that these things may happen, but because they are going to happen, I therefore foretell them. At least now speak to them my words; then they will not listen to you, and you will call them, and they will not answer you. For they will be so proud that, when you call them to listen, no one will deign to answer.

“And you shall say to them: ‘This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God and did not receive discipline.’” As I said before, he fittingly calls them not his people but a nation. Although this was partly fulfilled in the time of the prophets, and preceded in shadow and image, it is more fully completed in Christ, when they refused to receive discipline and despised the voice of their Lord.

Hence he elegantly adds: “Faith has perished”—which properly belongs to Christians—“and has been taken from their mouth,” namely, every confession of being a child of God and of faith.

“‘Cut off your hair and throw it away, and take up (or: upon your lips) lamentation, because the Lord has rejected and abandoned the generation of his wrath.’”

When Job heard of the death of his sons and daughters, we read that he cut off his hair (Job 1). Among the ancients, cutting one’s hair was the common practice of all who mourned; now, by contrast, letting the hair grow long is a sign of grief.

All lamentation and prophetic mourning is taken up for this reason: “because the Lord has rejected and abandoned the generation of his wrath.” There is no doubt that this signifies the Jewish people, and that it properly refers to the time of Christ, when faith perished and was taken from the mouth of the people who blasphemed the Lord.

“‘For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight, says the Lord. They have set up their abominations in the house in which my name has been invoked, to defile it; and they have built the high places (or: an altar) of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and daughters in the fire—something I did not command and did not conceive in my heart.’”

That the sons of Judah placed a statue of Baal in the temple of God, we learn at the beginning of Ezekiel. The high places, which in Hebrew were called [the supplied text is missing the Hebrew term], or the altar of Topheth, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, signify the place irrigated by the springs of Siloam. It is pleasant and wooded, and even today offers the delights of gardens.

This error of paganism occupied all the provinces, so that they sacrificed victims at the sources of springs and in the most pleasant groves, preserving every form of perverse superstition as a religious practice.

In the Hebrew language, *Topheth* is interpreted as “breadth.” It is reported in the book of Joshua son of Nun that this place, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom and is called in Hebrew [the supplied text is incomplete], is also described by the Greek word *pharanga* (φάραγγα), that is, “valley”; the name may signify either a person’s name or “grace.”

The Hebrews relate that Gehenna received its name from this place, because the entire Jewish people perished there by offending God. In that same place they also consecrated their sons to idols in the fire, or offered them as burnt offerings—something he had not commanded them and no provision of the Law had ordered (2 Kings 17).

If Jephthah offered his virgin daughter to God (Judg. 11), it is not the sacrifice that is pleasing, but the intention of the one making the offering. For if a dog, an ass, or any unclean animal had first met the father returning from the slaughter of his enemies, he ought not therefore to have offered it to God.

«Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when it shall no longer be said, “Topheth,” nor “the valley of the son of Ennon,” but “the valley of slaughter”; and they shall bury in Topheth, because there will be no place. And the corpses of this people shall become food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth, and there will be no one to drive them away.»

This signifies the time of the siege which they endured from the ninth year of King Zedekiah to the eleventh year (IV Kings 25). And the valley itself will no longer be called Gehennon—that is, the valley of Ennon, or of the sons of Ennom—but, because of the slaughter of so many, the valley of slaughter. So great, moreover, will the carnage be [Col. 0865D] that in the place formerly devoted to religious worship there will be innumerable graves; and those whom they cannot bury will be torn apart by birds and devoured by beasts. There will be no one to drive away such creatures, fearing similar things and being prevented from carrying out the duties of burial. We pass rapidly over what is clear, so that wherever there is an obscure passage we may linger. For the length of the book itself may weary its readers—how much more if we were to discuss it at greater length?

«And I will silence from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy, the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a desolation.»

When the place of idolatry has been turned into graves, so that where they had offended God, there their unburied corpses may lie, all joy will be removed from the former city of Jerusalem [Col. 0866A] and from the other cities that had been under its rule; everything will be filled with mourning, lamentation, and desolation.

## CHAPTER VIII

Threat against those who remained from the captivity; rebuke of the unrepentant people; the voice of the penitent; the arrival of the enemies; the city’s wailing.

«At that time, says the Lord, they shall bring out of their tombs the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its princes, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of those who dwelt in Jerusalem. And they shall spread them out before the sun and the moon and all the host of heaven, which they loved, served, followed, sought, and worshiped. They shall not be gathered up and shall not be buried; they shall lie as dung upon the face of the earth. And all those who remain of this evil family, in every place where I have cast them and which has been left desolate, shall choose death rather than life, says the Lord of hosts.»

(Jerome.) Everything that the prophetic utterance describes we see happening in our own time—not only to Jerusalem, which suffered these things at the hands of the Chaldeans and the Romans, but throughout the whole world, so that tears have dried up and everything has been filled with the bones of the dead. And because, according to ancient custom, people used to place gold and certain ornaments belonging either to women or to men in tombs, greed broke and dug up these objects as well, so that they might be exposed to the sky and the light. Therefore the bones of the kings of Judah and of its princes, and also of the priests and prophets and of the entire people who had been [Col. 0866C] in Jerusalem, were brought out from the burial mounds and exposed to the sight of the sun, the moon, and all the stars, so that those whom they had served after abandoning God might look upon them, and so that, consumed, they might be dissolved into dung and ashes. But if anyone from the multitude was able to escape, wherever he came he would prefer death to life and regard destruction as a remedy for his unhappy soul.

«And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Does one who falls not rise again, and does one who has turned away not return [or: not turn back]?»

After such great evils he calls those who have been able to remain to repentance; or, before the one whom he has threatened comes, he urges them to conversion and grants a place for repentance. What is written according to the Hebrew—«And one who has turned away shall not turn back»—signifies that if one who has turned away from God wishes to turn toward better things, he can also turn God’s anger toward better things, withstand the one who is coming, and avoid the blows through prayers.

«Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning-away? They have grasped falsehood and have refused to return.»

The more, he says, I called them to repentance, the more they withdrew from me—not so much from a desire to sin as from a desire to overcome me. For they firmly grasped falsehood, whether idols or whatever wicked things are contrary to truth and justice, and they refused to return. He did not say, “They were unable,” but rather that they pursued wickedness with every effort. Our task, however, is that each day, as God’s grace draws us, we should humbly follow; or else, resisting him with a stiff neck and uncircumcised ears, as it is written, we deserve to hear concerning Jerusalem:

«Does one who falls not rise again, or does one who has turned away not return? Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning-away? They have hardened their necks; they have refused to return?»

«I paid attention and listened: no one speaks what is good. There is no one who repents of his sin and says, “What have I done?” All have turned to their own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle.»

(Jerome.) Although called back to repentance, they disdain listening; nor is it enough for them to have sinned against the Lord and spoken blasphemy. Rather, like horses rushing with fiery speed into battle, [Col. 0867B] they do not reflect on their sin and do not say, “What have I done?” (Genesis 8). By this we may understand either that these words are spoken of the whole human race, which is inclined toward vices, or of the time of the Savior, when «all turned aside; together they became worthless; there was no one who did good, not even one» (Psalm 13). Hence he himself cried out mystically: «Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed» (Psalm 11). But if this is so, where are those who say that it lies within our will to be entirely without sin? «No one speaks what is good,» he says (Matthew 11), because we shall also give an account for an idle word on the day of judgment.

«The kite knows its appointed time in the sky; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming; but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord.»

For the kite, which Symmachus translated, the Septuagint and Theodotion have placed the Hebrew word itself; and again, for the swallow Symmachus translated “cicada,” which in Hebrew is called [Hebrew term absent in the supplied text]. But for what we rendered “stork,” Aquila and Symmachus translated exactly as it is written in Hebrew, whereas the Septuagint rendered it “sparrows of the field.” The sense, however, is one and the same as that found at the beginning of Isaiah: «The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood» (Isaiah 1). Even small birds know their seasons and understand when, hastening toward warmer regions, they ought to escape the severity of winter, and again, at the beginning of spring, return to their customary regions. Here, however, “sky” should be understood as the air above us.

«How can you say, “We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us”? Truly, the lying stylus of the scribes has wrought falsehood.»

He speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, who boast of their knowledge of the law while writing iniquity. And when he says:

«The wise have been put to shame; they have been terrified and captured.»

This does not mean that those who do such things are truly wise. Rather, he calls them “wise” so that they may be condemned by their own judgment, and so that their wisdom may, conversely, be proved folly, as Paul says: «You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?» (Romans 2). «For they have rejected the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them.» [Col. 0868A] In vain, therefore, do they boast of knowledge of the law when they destroy its teaching by their actions.

«Therefore I will give their wives [or: women] to foreigners, their fields to heirs, because from the least to the greatest all pursue greed, from prophet to priest; all practice falsehood [or: iniquity]. And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people to her shame, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there was no peace.»

They received the reward of their deeds: those who rejected the word of the Lord were themselves rejected by him. “Their wives,” he says, “and their possessions I will hand over to enemies.” And lest my sentence be thought cruel, let the listener recognize the reasons: «From the least to the greatest, all are devoted to greed.»—«For greed is the root of all evils» (1 Timothy 6). «From prophet to priest»: those who ought to restrain others from sin are the first to be subject to crimes. They all practice either iniquity, while plundering what belongs to others, or else falsehood, so that there is no truth in their mouths. And after these things, like good physicians, they wished to heal the wounds of others with words, though they themselves were pierced with wounds from every disgraceful act. We see these things daily among our own people as well, as the Apostle says: «You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?» etc. (Romans 2). When they see sinners and the rich, they wish to heal the brokenness of the daughter of God’s people—that is, the Church—to the shame either of those who are deceived or of those who deceive others, saying to people covered with every crime, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace and the war of sins threatens them.

[Col. 0868C] «They were ashamed who committed abomination. Indeed, they were not ashamed with shame, and they did not know how to blush.»

This should be read ἐρωτηματικῶς—that is, interrogatively—so that the sense is: “Were they ashamed of their crimes? Did they understand the abominations they had committed?” Not at all. Rather, they rushed into such madness that they neither wished to correct their vices through shame nor, in hope of forgiveness, confess their crimes.

«Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time of their visitation they shall fall, says the Lord.»

These are the rewards of those who did not know how to be ashamed: those whose dignity was higher than that of the people shall be mixed with the people’s ruin. «For from the least to the greatest all pursue greed, and from prophet to priest all practice falsehood.» The time of visitation, however, is the captivity that is near.

«Gathering, I will gather them, says the Lord. There is no grape on the vines, and there are no figs on the fig tree. The leaf has fallen, and I have given them what has passed away.»

What the time of visitation is, at which sinners will fall, he teaches more clearly when he says: «Gathering, I will gather them.» Without doubt this means in Jerusalem, so that they may be besieged by the Chaldeans for a long time and endure the evils of hunger. “When,” he says, “the seasons pass, when autumn follows summer and the leaves of the trees fall in winter, you will see everything from a distance but will obtain no food from it. For there is no grape on the vines for you, since you do not partake of the fruit of the vines; and there are no figs on the fig tree for the besieged people, who see the fruit of their trees being plundered by enemies.” “The leaves,” he says, “will fall after summer and autumn have passed.” For I gave them what they could see passing away and would lose with greater grief: the abundance of all things, which they were not permitted to touch.

«Why are we sitting? Come together and let us enter the fortified city [or: fortified cities], and let us be silent there [or: let us be cast there], because the Lord our God has silenced us and has given us water to drink—water of gall. For we have sinned against the Lord. We hoped for peace, but there was no good; for a time of healing, and behold, terror.»

The voice of the people is introduced, responding, confessing their vices, and encouraging one another to enter the walled cities—or one city, Jerusalem, since the other cities had already been captured. «And let us be silent there,» it says, «because our Lord has silenced us.» For we have no confidence to make supplication; or, “Let us be cast there,” like dung. He himself gave us water of gall, because we turned God, who is sweet, into bitterness. And the reason why we drank such waters is clear: «For we sinned against the Lord and hoped for peace,» although we had done no good work; and we thought that a time of healing had come for us, while everything was being filled with fear and terror. The change of speakers, especially in the prophets, makes the meaning difficult. But if each statement is assigned to its proper place, cause, and time, what seemed obscure will become clear.

«From Dan the snorting of his horses is heard; the whole land is shaken by the sound of the neighing of his warhorses [or: cavalry]. And they came and devoured [or: they will come and devour] the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants.»

Therefore, contrary to what the Septuagint translated above, the people did not say, “Let us enter fortified cities,” but “the fortified city,” signifying Jerusalem. Hence he now adds, «the city and its inhabitants.» He describes Nabuchodonosor coming from Dan through Phoenicia with his army. The Jordan River rises in that region. And what the Septuagint expresses as future, the Hebrew, in accordance with the truth of the event, records as already accomplished.

«For behold, I will send among you serpents, basilisks [or: evil, or, as the Septuagint translated, deadly], for which there is no spell; and they shall bite you, says the Lord.»

Who those are who come from Dan, whose snorting is heard, and who reduced the whole land to desolation, the same prophetic speech demonstrates under another figure, calling them evil or deadly serpents, or, as Aquila translated, basilisks—called in Hebrew [Hebrew term absent in the supplied text]. I do not understand what his second edition intended when it said “watchers,” unless perhaps because of the similarity of the word. «For which,» he says, «there is no spell.» In vain do they pour out prayers to the Lord against the ancient serpent, the twisting serpent, when they have despised God’s commandments. Let us use this passage against those who, despising the Savior’s words, are handed over to hostile powers.

«My pain is beyond pain; my heart within me mourns.»

For this, the Septuagint joined the words to the preceding sentence [Col. 0870A] and rendered them: «And they shall bite you, says the Lord, incurably; with the pain of your hearts you shall faint.» In Hebrew, however, the word does not signify so much pain—the Greek ὀδύνη—as μειδίαμα, which we may interpret as “the grimace of a mouth contracted by pain and bearing a likeness to laughter.” These words should be read ἐμφατικῶς—that is, emphatically—as spoken in the person of God lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem and unable to endure its miseries.

«Behold, the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people from a distant land.»

He describes the weeping and wailing of the city of Jerusalem when the enemies have entered it.

«Is the Lord not in Zion, or is its king not in her?»

Or, “The Lord himself is king”; or else “Lord” refers to the Father and “king” to the Son, according to what is written under the name of Solomon: «O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son» (Psalm 71). But the reason why the voice of the cry is in Jerusalem and the cry itself comes from a distant land is clear: the Lord is not in her, and her king has departed from her.

«Why, then, did they provoke me to anger with their carved images and with foreign vanities?»

“The Lord,” he says, “departed from them because they provoked me, who was their Lord and king, to anger through the worship of idols.”

«The harvest has passed; summer has ended, and we have not been saved.»

Again the people speak, shut up in Jerusalem by a prolonged siege: the seasons have changed, the cycle of the years has run its course, and all their hope has proved futile and passed away.

«Over the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am broken; I mourn, and astonishment has seized me.»

God replies that in Jerusalem’s affliction he himself appears afflicted and, in human likeness, is crushed by astonishment.

«Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why, then, has the scar of the daughter of my people not formed over?»

Not only in the present passage but also in many other testimonies of Scripture we find balm in Gilead used as a figure for repentance and medicine. God now wonders why Jerusalem’s wounds have not been healed and why the skin has not yet been covered with scars, because there are no prophets or priests whose medicinal treatment might heal them.

## CHAPTER IX

The prophet’s lament and tears for his people; glorying only in the Lord; lament because of the abandonment of the people by their shepherds, iniquity, and vengeance.

[Col. 0870D]

«Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?»

(Jerome.) “Even if,” he says, “I were wholly changed into weeping, and there were no drops of tears but an abundance like a river, I still could not worthily mourn the slain of the daughter of my people.” For the evils are so great that by their magnitude they surpass all the pain one could bear. This may be understood as spoken both in the person of the prophet and in that of the Lord.

[Col. 0871A] «Who will give me an inn for travelers in the wilderness, so that I may abandon my people and depart from them?»

The Septuagint: «Who will give me a final lodging in the wilderness, so that I may abandon my people and depart from them?»

“It is better,” he says, “to dwell in the remotest wilderness than to remain amid such human crimes.” Hence the Savior also said in the Gospel: «How long shall I endure you?» (Matthew 17). And elsewhere it is written: «At that time the one who understands will sit and be silent, for it is an evil time» (Lamentations 3; Micah 2).

«For they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors. They have stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth. They have strengthened themselves in the land, because they have gone from evil to evil, and they have not known me, says the Lord.»

Sinners pass from evil to evil when they exchange one idol for another and advance from sins to sins; or certainly when they pass from the evil of the siege to captivity. Of the saints it is said: «They go from strength to strength» (Psalm 83). Of sinners, however: «They have gone from evil to evil.» The cause of all their miseries is that they did not know the Lord; they are an assembly of transgressors who arm their tongues like a drawn bow for blasphemy. They have strengthened themselves in the land so that they deserve to hear: «You are earth, and to earth you shall go» (Genesis 3).

«Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him place no trust in any of his brothers, because every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will proceed deceitfully. A man will mock his brother, and they will not speak truth. For their tongue has learned to speak falsehood [or: they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood]. They have labored to act wickedly [or: they have acted wickedly], and they did not stop in order to turn back. Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit, in deceit [or: usury upon usury, and deceit upon deceit]. They refused [or: were unwilling] to know me, says the Lord.»

This passage should be used in a time of persecution and distress, when faith is rare or nonexistent; when one must trust neither brother nor neighbor, and «a man’s enemies are those of his own household» (Micah 7); when, according to the Gospel, «the father will hand over the son, and the son the father, and two will be divided against three and three against two» (Matthew 10). (Gregory.) For when the cunning adversary sees that he is being driven back from the hearts of the good, he seeks out those who are especially loved by them. Through their words he speaks with flattering sweetness—through those who are loved more than the others—so that, while the power of love pierces the heart, the sword of his persuasion may easily break into the innermost defenses of righteousness.

(Jerome.) What follows, «They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood,» or «Their tongue has learned to speak falsehood,» shows that the habit of lying has in a certain way been turned into nature, and that they deliberately act so as to do wicked things. And what follows, «Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit,» or «in deceit,» is addressed specifically to the prophet: he dwells among a lying people. Or, as the Septuagint translated it, «usury upon usury, and deceit upon deceit,» they daily increase their crimes and have no remorse for what they did before, but heap new offenses upon earlier ones. By doing these things they strive with all their might not to know the Lord, who commanded that such things not be done.

«Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will melt them [or: test them with fire] and examine them. What else shall I do because of the daughter of my people?»

Whenever we are subjected to distress, receive evils from God, and are tested by persecutions, whatever adulterated material there is in us is refined by the fires of tribulations and miseries. «The silver of the Lord, tested by fire, approved by the earth, purified sevenfold» (Psalm 11).

«Their tongue is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit. With his mouth each speaks peace with his friend, but secretly he sets an ambush for him. Shall I not visit them for these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?»

Every heretic who wounds the hearts of hearers who do not know the Scripture—«Guard your heart with all vigilance» (Proverbs 4)—possesses a wounding arrow and speaks deceitfully. Although with his mouth he promises peace to his neighbor, secretly he lays an ambush. In the verses that follow, where he says, «Shall I not visit them for these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?» this prophet frequently uses the same formula: after listing each of their evil deeds, he declares that he is right to do what he does.

«Over the mountains I will take up [or: take up, you] weeping and lamentation, and over the beautiful places [or: paths] of the wilderness, mourning, because they have been burned [or: have failed]; because there is no man [or: human being] passing through. They did not hear the voice of the possessor [or: substance]; from the bird of the sky to the cattle they have migrated and departed.»

When the Babylonian army came upon the land and laid everything waste, the desolation of the province is prophesied: there will be mourning on the mountains and weeping in the desert, or on the paths of the wilderness; everything will have failed and been burned, and no one will remain to walk upon the land, since all have been slain and nothing remains that can breathe and live. Hence the Septuagint translated “possessor” as “substance”—a word that in Hebrew is [Hebrew term absent in the supplied text]. Here “substance” does not mean οὐσία, that is, essence, but possessions and riches. What follows, «From the bird of the sky to the cattle they have departed and gone away,» shows what we have often said: God’s anger is felt by all things, and not only the birds of the air but also the fish of the water fail.

According to the allegorical sense, weeping is taken up over the mountains and lamentation over the beautiful places of the wilderness when the leaders of the Church sin, when no substance of God is found in her, and the voice of the Lord who possesses the Church is not heard through holy and apostolic men. «From the bird of the sky to the cattle»: from those who can rise to lofty things down to the irrational and more simple, they have departed from the assembly of God.

«And I will make Jerusalem into heaps of sand [or: into a place of migration], and into dens of dragons; and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, because there is no inhabitant.»

When ecclesiastical men and all the teachers have failed, then Jerusalem is given over to migration, or to heaps of sand, so that heretical speech may prevail in her and she may become a den of dragons. [Col. 0874A] Her cities will be reduced to solitude, and there will be no habitation of the divine word in her—that word of the one who says: «I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God» (Leviticus 26).

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0873]

[Col. 0873A] The prophet, describing in many ways the calamity that befell the Jews through the Chaldean captivity—even to the point of weeping—was himself shaken by it. Hence above he says: «Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes? And I will weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people.» Adding also the causes of the various transgressions for which they endured this evil, he now asks questions of his people in search of an understanding hearer to whom he may speak, instructing them what they must avoid so as not to arouse the Lord’s anger against themselves. For this reason Holy Scripture reveals to human beings the kinds of transgression and lays open the sequence of virtues, so that they may know how to avoid evil and do good, and thus deserve to escape the Lord’s anger and find his grace. For it follows:

«Who is the wise man who understands this, and to whom the word of the Lord’s mouth may come, so that he may proclaim it: Why has the land perished and been burned like a desert, because there is no one passing through it? And the Lord said: Because they abandoned my law, which I gave them, and they did not listen to my voice, and they did not walk in it, but went after the perversity of their heart and after the Baals, which they learned from their fathers.»

(Jerome.) The prophet asks whether he can find in Jerusalem any wise person to whom the word of the Lord may come, who might proclaim the Lord’s will and give the reasons why Judea has been reduced to a wilderness, and, when all have been killed, no one has remained to pass through it. He introduces the Lord as giving the answer and explaining the reasons: they abandoned his law, which he had given them; they did not listen to his voice; they did not do what had been commanded; but they went after the perversity of their own heart. Therefore we must place our trust not in our own will but in the Lord. «The heart is perverse in all things» (Jeremiah 17). And: «From our heart proceed evil thoughts» (Matthew 15). «They went after the Baals,» he says, «which they learned from their fathers.» Baal is the idol of the Sidonians and is singular in number; Baalim, however, is plural. Therefore we must follow neither the error of parents nor that of ancestors, but the authority of Scripture and the command of God who teaches.

«Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood [or: distress], and I will give them water of gall to drink; and I will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers have known; and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed.»

This may be prophesied both of the time near at hand, when they were captured by the Chaldeans, and specifically of the present time, when they were scattered among nations that neither they nor their fathers had known. Throughout the world they were divided and fed with wormwood, or with necessities and distress. They received water of gall to drink, which either signifies the greatness of their evils and the everlasting yoke of captivity, or else that through ignorance of God’s law they will accept the Antichrist in place of Christ. The sword is sent after them so that they may be consumed even unto destruction. Or certainly it is the sword that divides them and does not permit them to consent to evil, so that they may perish in that which is evil.

«Thus says the Lord of hosts: Consider [or: understand], and call for the mourning women to come; and send to those who are wise, that they may come quickly [or: speak], hasten, and take up a lamentation for us. Let our eyes [or: your eyes] pour out tears, and let our eyelids [or: your eyelids] flow with water, because the voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion [or: in Zion].»

Because of the future captivity [Col. 0874C] and overthrow of Jerusalem, he commands that mourning women be summoned. In mourning they customarily provoke the people to tears with a plaintive voice and by striking their arms with their hands. This custom continues to the present day in Judea: women with their hair unbound and their breasts exposed stir everyone to weeping with a measured voice. God joins himself to them in compassionate feeling—or the prophet does—so that he says that he himself suffers and feels whatever the people endure. As for what follows, «because the voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion,» the nature of this voice immediately follows.

«How devastated we are, and how greatly confounded! Because we have abandoned the land, because our tents have been cast down [or: we have cast down our tents].»

This is the voice of those lamenting in Zion: «How devastated we are, and how greatly confounded!» Immediately they answer themselves and explain the causes of their devastation, saying: «Because we have abandoned the land» through our own fault and sin, and our tents have been cast down—tents that we once possessed like temporary travelers. Let the crowds of believers in the former persecution say this as well: they were devastated and confounded because they abandoned the Lord’s land and deserted their tents.

«Therefore hear, women, the word of the Lord, and let your ears receive the word of his mouth. Teach your daughters lamentation, and each her neighbor mourning, because death has climbed through our windows and entered our houses, to destroy the children outside and the young men from the streets.»

In the preceding chapter he had said: «Call for the mourning women, and let them come; and send to those who are wise, that they may come quickly.» Now, as if speaking to women present, he speaks in condemnation of the priests, teachers, and all the men, so that when these cease to teach, the women may hear the word of the Lord, receive the words of his mouth, and teach their daughters and neighbors mourning and the causes of tears: «Because death,» he says, «has climbed through our windows and entered our houses.» Although this may also be understood spiritually—because death enters for the destruction of the soul through all the senses of the sinner—it may also be understood of the assault of the Babylonians. Their strength and speed in battle were so great that they did not wait to have the doors opened, but climbed through windows and over roofs in order to lay waste to the houses of Jerusalem. The children who are outside, and the young men who go out from Jerusalem, perish—those to whom John also writes (1 John 2). They do not enter by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life but walk through the streets, concerning which it is written: «How broad and spacious is the way that leads to death!» (Matthew 7).

(Gregory.) Since the soul is invisible, it is not touched by the delight of bodily things except insofar as, being joined to the body, it has in the body’s senses certain openings through which it may go out: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch are, as it were, paths of the mind by which it comes forth and desires what lies outside its own substance. Through these bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks upon external things and, looking, desires them. Hence Jeremiah also says: «Death has climbed through our windows and entered our houses.» Death climbs through windows and enters houses when desire, coming through the bodily senses, enters the dwelling of the mind. In contrast, Isaiah says of the righteous, as we have often mentioned: «Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?» (Isaiah 60). The righteous are said to fly like clouds because through the bodily senses they do not look upon external things with predatory intention, and carnal desire does not carry them outward. Whoever, however, carelessly looks outward through these bodily windows often falls into the pleasure of sin even against his will; bound by desires, he begins to want what he did not want. For the soul, rushing headlong because it did not foresee beforehand how to avoid seeing carelessly what it might desire, begins blindly to desire what it has seen. Thus the prophet’s mind, which had often been lifted up and occupied with inner mysteries, carelessly saw another man’s wife and afterward, darkened, joined himself to her unlawfully. But the holy man who, having received the bodily senses as subordinate servants, presides over them like a most just judge, sees faults before they arise and, as if death were lying in ambush, closes the windows of the body.

«Speak: Thus says the Lord: The corpse of a man [or: the corpses of men] shall fall like dung upon the face of the land [or: field], and like grass behind the one who reaps, and there will be no one to gather it.»

(Jerome.) The Hebrew word written with three letters, [Hebrew term absent in the supplied text], has no vowels in the middle. According to context and the reader’s choice, if it is read DABAR, it signifies “word”; if DEBER, “death”; if DABBER, “speak.” Hence the Septuagint and Theodotion joined it to the preceding chapter, saying: «Destroy the children outside, the young men in the streets, with death.» Aquila and Symmachus, however, translated λὰλησον—“speak”—so that God commands the prophet to speak what follows: «Thus says the Lord,» and so forth. The sense is this: when death has climbed through our windows and entered the houses of Jerusalem, and the children and young men outside have perished in the streets, then their corpses, or the bodies of the dead, will lie like dung upon the face of the earth and like straw left behind the reapers, which is not gathered because it is useless. By this he wishes to show that such slaughter will take place in Jerusalem and around the city that no one will remain to bury those who have fallen.

«Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches. Rather, let the one who glories glory in this: that he knows [or: understands] and knows me, that I am the Lord who practices mercy, justice, and judgment upon the earth. For these things please me [or: for in these is my will], says the Lord.»

All human pride is removed, since their wisdom, strength, and wealth are reckoned as nothing. The only glory is to know and understand that he is the Lord who practices mercy, judgment, and justice upon the earth: that everything is governed by God’s providence [Col. 0876C] and justice, and that the things which seem to us to have no rational explanation are nevertheless full of justice and reason. For these things alone please God, and in them is his will. Where, then, are those who say that human beings are ruled by their own choice, and that free will has been granted in such a way that God’s mercy and justice are removed? Hence the Apostle, taking up this testimony, gives the example: «Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord» (1 Corinthians 10).

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will visit judgment upon everyone who has the foreskin circumcised: upon Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who are tonsured at the hairline, who dwell in the desert, because all the nations have a foreskin, but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.” To some extent many peoples, and especially those who to this day border Judaea and Palestine, are circumcised—particularly the Egyptians, Idumaeans, Ammonites, and Moabites, and the entire region of the Saracens, who dwell in the desert, concerning whom it is said: “upon all who are tonsured at the hairline, who dwell in the desert.” Therefore Judah, who is mixed with the nations mentioned above, ought not to boast that he does not have their foreskin but is circumcised according to the law of God, since others also do these things while not observing the commandments of the law and remaining ignorant of the God of Israel. Circumcision, which was given as a sign, is of no benefit unless the Lord’s commands are fulfilled; just as the hair, which signifies a people, does not signify bodily strength [Col. 0877A] or the power of warriors. What follows—“all the nations have a foreskin, but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart”—has this meaning: apart from the Egyptians, Idumaeans, Ammonites, and Moabites, and the Ishmaelites dwelling in the desert, among whom for the most part some are circumcised, all the other nations throughout the whole world are uncircumcised in the flesh, whereas the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart, not in flesh. The former uncircumcision leads to death, for it is of the flesh; the latter is of the spirit.

## CHAPTER X. The people are warned not to fear the constellation of the heavens; an indictment of idolatry; and Jerusalem’s lament over her affliction

“Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: Do not learn the ways of the nations, and do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear, because the laws of the peoples are futile.” (Jerome) He speaks particularly against those who venerate the heavenly bodies, which were appointed as signs of years, seasons, months, and days. From these they suppose that the human race is governed and that earthly affairs are regulated by the causes belonging to the heavens. When he says, “the laws—or statutes—of the peoples are futile,” he demonstrates that all human wisdom is ineffectual and possesses no usefulness.

“For a tree is cut from the forest, the work of the craftsman’s hands, with an axe. He adorns it with silver and gold, and fastens it with nails and hammers so that it will not come apart—or be moved. They are fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree [Col. 0877C] and will not speak; when carried, they must be lifted, because they cannot walk. Therefore do not fear them, for they can do neither harm nor good.”

This is a description of the idols worshiped by the nations. “He cuts a tree,” he says, “from the forest”: therefore the material of idols is perishable and corruptible. “The work of the craftsman’s hands.” Since the craftsman is mortal, whatever he fashions is mortal as well. “He adorned it with silver and gold”: so that by the brilliance of both materials he may deceive the simple. This error has passed even to us, so that we suppose religion to consist in riches. “He fastened it with nails and hammers, so that it will not come apart—or so that it will not be moved.” What power do idols possess, when they cannot stand by themselves unless they are fastened with nails and hammers? “They were fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree”: they possess the beauty of metals and are adorned by the art of painting, but they have no usefulness by which they might provide any fruits to their craftsman. “And they will not speak,” for they contain nothing living within themselves. Concerning them it is written: “They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have ears, but they will not hear” (Psalm 113). “When carried, they must be lifted”: the one who carries them is stronger than what is carried. Indeed, in the one there is understanding, while in the other there is a figure without understanding. “Therefore do not fear them, for they can do neither good nor harm.” Many gentiles customarily worship demons so that they may not harm them, and entreat others to grant them benefits. Hence there is also that line of Virgil:

> A black sheep for winter, a white one for favorable west winds.

Whatever we have said about idols can be applied to all doctrines opposed to the truth. They too make immense promises and devise in their own hearts an image of empty worship. They boast of great things and, as though by golden ideas and eloquence gleaming with the splendor of silver, bind the perception of the ignorant in order to deceive the simple. Their inventors exalt them, although they possess no usefulness; their worship properly belongs to the nations and to those who are ignorant of God.

“There is none like you, Lord; you are great, and your name is great in might. Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For honor is yours. Among all the wise men of the nations and in all their kingdoms, there is none like you. Together they will be proved foolish and senseless. Their doctrine of vanity is wood, silver wrapped around it—or beaten out—and brought from Tharsis, and gold from Ophir, the work of a craftsman and the hands of a metalworker. Hyacinth and purple are their clothing; all these are the work of craftsmen—or wise men. But the Lord God is true; he is the living God and the eternal King. At his indignation the earth will be shaken, and the nations will not endure his threat.”

These words are not found in the Septuagint, but in most copies they have been added from the edition of Theodotion. Although they appear clear according to the literal sense, they contain great difficulty according to the allegorical sense.

There is none like the true God among those gods who are fashioned by heretical art. All will fear him who is King of the nations. “For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Proverbs 9), and from it we advance toward true love. “Honor is yours,” he says: in truth there is beauty, but in falsehood disgrace. Although heretics may appear wise to themselves according to the wisdom of the world, which is being destroyed, yet in all the kingdoms by which they tear the Church apart, the divine word says, “there is none like you.” “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1).

Their doctrine is at once wise and foolish: according to the quality of their intellect, it is either worthless and compared with wood, or like silver because of the elegance of their eloquence. “It is brought from Tharsis.” According to Josephus, Tharsis is either a region of India, or indeed every sea is called Tharsis. It has a likeness to heaven, yet is wrapped in an artifice of words. If it wishes to deceive, it will not be able to do so. “And gold from Ophir”: among the Hebrews gold is called by seven names, one of which is what we may call *obrizum*, so that it may shine on the surface of the idols, which inwardly are wood and worthless material. They are covered with hyacinth and purple so that by their outward surface they may deceive the eyes, while promising themselves the color of heaven and the heavenly kingdoms. Yet all these are the works of the wise who are considered wise by the world but are fools before God.

“But the Lord our God is the true God”: therefore all those things are lies, “and he himself is the living God.” Thus those things that are fashioned are dead. “And the eternal King”: the shadows of the heretics prevail for a time, but over a long period they decay. “At his indignation the earth will be shaken”: those who have earthly works and fashion earthly images; “and the nations will not endure his threat”: not the people of the Lord, but the multitude of the nations, which cannot withstand God’s threat.

“Thus you shall say to them: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from beneath these heavens.” These words should be spoken to false gods, which have been skillfully constructed. They made neither the heavens nor the earth. Those who are fellow workers with Christ are called gods, and through ecclesiastical teaching they build a great part of the Lord’s house.

“The Lord who makes—or made—the earth by his strength, prepares the inhabited world in his wisdom, and by his prudence stretches out the heavens. At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heavens, and he raises—or brings forth—the clouds from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning into rain, and brings forth the wind—or winds—from his treasuries. Every human being has become foolish through his knowledge; every craftsman is confounded by the carved image, because what he cast is false and there is no spirit in them. They are vanity and works worthy of laughter. At the time of their visitation they will perish. The portion of Jacob is not like these. For he is the one who formed all things, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name.”

He who makes the earth by his strength is God the Father, but he makes it by his strength, the Lord and Savior. For Christ is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1). He himself is also prudence, in whom he stretches out heaven. “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 32), speaking to the Son: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1).

(Origen) The Prophet takes up, in a certain way, three virtues of God—strength, wisdom, and prudence—and assigns particular works to each: the earth to strength, the inhabited world to wisdom, and heaven to prudence. Hear, then, the order of Scripture: “The Lord who made the earth by his strength, established the inhabited world by his wisdom, and by his prudence stretched out heaven.”

We too, therefore, in our earth—for it was said to Adam, “You are earth”—need the strength of God, because without it we cannot accomplish what resists the flesh. But when our members upon the earth have been put to death, then they obey the will of the spirit. For, according to the Apostle, “by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh are put to death” (Romans 8).

“The Lord, therefore, who made the earth by his strength.” But if you also come to this earth and consider what is written in Job 26—at least according to the most accurate copies—how he established it upon nothing, you will find the strength of God sustaining the balance of the earth in the middle of the world.

I shall now come to the inhabited world, which in Greek is called *oikoumenē*, that is, “inhabited.” I know my soul inhabited; I know a deserted soul. For if it does not have God the Father; if it does not have the Son saying, “I and my Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 4); if it does not have the Holy Spirit, the soul is deserted. It is inhabited, however, when it is full of God, when it has Christ and the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, Scripture speaks in different and various ways of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwelling in the human soul. David too, in the psalm of confession, asks for three spirits, saying: “Establish me with a princely spirit; renew a right spirit within me; and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50). What are these three spirits? The princely spirit is the Father; the right spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Spirit who is holy.

We have said this in confirmation of the fact that the inhabited world was fashioned in the wisdom of God. “Wisdom will assist the righteous more than ten men who have power in a city. But he who rejects wisdom and discipline is wretched; his hope is empty, his labors senseless, and his works useless,” says the Wisdom that bears the title of Solomon.

Therefore, insofar as we can, let us strive through labor so that our habitation may be raised up by the wisdom of God. It fell and collapsed from its height when we came into this place of miseries. Our habitation fell after we sinned, acted wickedly, behaved unjustly, and conducted ourselves impiously; and after its fall it needs to be raised up.

But if you do not wish this interpretation to be applied, let us seek the common fall of the whole world, so that afterward God may accordingly be proclaimed as the one who raises it up after its fall. Whoever exists in this world fell before being raised; and if he fell, he consequently had to be raised. No one is lifted up without a fall; but if he has been raised, let us see what fall preceded it.

Through sin we all fell into the inhabited world, and the Lord, “who raises up the fallen” (Psalm 144), lifted us who were lying prostrate. In Adam we all die, and thus the inhabited world fell and needs to be raised up, so that in Christ we may all be made alive.

We have therefore handed down a twofold interpretation of the inhabited world: one, concerning how individual souls are either inhabited or deserted; the other, concerning how the entire world fell together.

“And by his prudence he stretches out heaven.” Wisdom was not adopted fortuitously in the stretching out of heaven. You will also find it said in Proverbs: “God founded the earth by wisdom, but prepared the heavens by prudence” (Proverbs 3).

There is therefore a prudence of God, which I do not want you to seek outside Christ. For everything that belongs to God is Christ: he is his wisdom, his strength, his justice, his holiness, and his redemption; and, to come to the present point, he is also prudence. But although he is one in substance, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings.

Wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. When he is called wisdom, he instructs you in the disciplines of divine and human matters; when justice, he is understood as the distributor and judge of merits; when holiness, that virtue is described which makes those who believe in God holy.

Understand his prudence here, then, as doctrine and demonstration of good, evil, or neutral things. In this way heaven is now said to have been stretched out in his prudence.

But hear how heaven is stretched out by him whose prudence stretches it: “Because I stretched out my words, and you did not pay attention.” He asserts that there is a certain extension of words, just as heaven is now said to be extended, in accordance also with what is written elsewhere: “He stretches out heaven like a skin” (Psalm 103).

Our soul too, which had previously been contracted, is stretched out so that it may be capable of the wisdom of God.

But, to return to the subject, we have said that heaven was made by his prudence, and now we affirm that those who bear the heavenly man are heavens. For if it is said to sinners, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3), why should it not be said to the righteous, whose is the kingdom of heaven: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”? Or, if because of the earthly man it is said to one who bears the image of the earthly, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” why should it not fittingly be said, because of the heavenly man, to one who bears the image of the heavenly: “You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go”?

Each of us, then, either has heavenly works or earthly ones. If earthly things have been made, they lead him who stores them up on earth rather than in heaven to the earth related to them. Conversely, those things that have been performed according to virtue carry their treasurer upward to the heavenly regions related to them.

(Jerome) “At his voice he gives a multitude of waters in the heavens.” For all the Lord’s teaching flows from heavenly things, as David says: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and when it was weakened, you restored it” (Psalm 67). “And he raises—or brings forth—the clouds from the ends of the earth” (Psalm 67). The clouds to which the Lord commanded that they should not rain upon Israel are brought forth from the ends of the earth. One such cloud said: “For I think God has displayed us apostles as the last, as though condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to this world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Corinthians 4).

(Origen) For what is written—“your truth reaches to the clouds”—cannot refer to lifeless clouds. The truth of God reaches those clouds that hear the Lord’s command and know where to bring the rains and from whom to withhold them. Concerning these clouds it is said: “And I will command my clouds not to rain upon it rain” (Isaiah 5).

As for those said to consist of condensed air: if there is no rain, God did not command them not to rain upon a vineyard or any region; rather, they do not appear at all, as we read in the Third Book of Kings. At the time of the drought no cloud appeared, and afterward, according to Elijah’s prophecy, a sign of future rain was shown in the shape of a man’s footprint; then, after the cloud had gathered, rain descended upon the earth.

But to these clouds, as it were, having a real subsistence, it is commanded to withhold rain when the soul is unworthy of heavenly rain, and it is said: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it rain.”

Thus each of the saints is a cloud. Moses was a cloud and spoke as a cloud: “Give ear, O heaven, and I shall speak; let the earth hear the words from my mouth; let it await my words like rain” (Deuteronomy 32). If he had not been a cloud, he would never have said, “Let it await my words like rain, and let my utterances descend like dew.” As a cloud he said: “Like rain upon the grass, like frost upon the hay, because I have invoked the name of the Lord.”

Isaiah likewise spoke as a cloud: “Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 1). Since he himself was a cloud and knew other clouds prophesying with him, he therefore said prophetically: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon the earth rain.”

But if we now say who the clouds are, let us see how God brings forth clouds from the end of the earth. The Savior says: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be last of all” (Mark 9). Paul kept this commandment and was last in this world, saying: “For I think God has displayed us apostles as the last, as though condemned to death, because we are a spectacle in the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Corinthians 4).

If, therefore, some saint, keeping the Savior’s commandment, becomes last in this life, let him be a cloud. God brings forth clouds not from the first people of the earth, not from consuls, not from commanders, not from the wealthy: “For blessed are the poor, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).
