You see how God brings them forth from the ends and gives bodily form to the clouds. Therefore, if we wish to become clouds to which the truth of God may reach, let us become last of all, and both in feeling and with our mouth say: “For I think God has displayed us apostles as the last.” Even if I am not an apostle, I may nevertheless become last, so that God, bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth, may bring me forth.

“And he made lightning into rain.” For when the rain of teachings has come from heaven and has satisfied the parched hearts of human beings, then you will find flashes and bright lightning bolts of wisdom.

Those who investigate natural causes say that lightning is generated by the collision of clouds, like harder flints which, when struck together, release fire between them. Thus thunder roars together with the lightning: thunder indicating the sound of the collision, and lightning the brightness of the light struck forth.

If you have understood the example, now consider rational clouds. Moses was a cloud; Jesus Nave was a cloud. If these speak with one another, lightning flashes from their words. Jeremiah and Baruch were clouds; let them speak to one another, and you will see lightning gleaming. You too can find such collisions of clouds in the holy Scriptures, from which fires may be emitted.

To come also to the New Testament: Paul and Silvanus came together as two clouds. Behold, the brilliance of their letters illuminates the whole world.

“He made lightning into rain and brought forth winds from his treasuries” (Psalm 134). The winds that blow over the earth are not therefore in God’s treasuries, with their nature plainly understood, including how and for what reason they exist. Rather, there are certain treasuries of winds, treasuries of spirits: the spirit of wisdom and understanding; the spirit of counsel and strength; the spirit of wisdom and piety; the spirit of the fear of God; and spirits of fortitude, affection, and love.

You too can gather these winds from the Scriptures and discover the treasuries of these spirits. Where are these treasuries? Certainly they have their dwelling in him in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden—in Christ. From there these spirits arise, so that one may be wise, another faithful, another learned, and another may possess whatever gift of God he has received. “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12).

“He therefore brought forth clouds from the end of the earth, made lightning into rain, and brought forth winds from his treasuries,” and we suppose, according to God’s mercy, that we shall hasten toward these treasuries.

And because there are many treasuries, perhaps, according to the order of those who rise again, there will also be rest in the treasuries of God. What I mean is this: the resurrection of the dead will occur in certain orders. The Apostle says: “Each person will rise in his own order” (1 Corinthians 15); the orders of those who rise again are not mixed together arbitrarily.

There will be one order in this or that treasury of God, and another order in another treasury of God. Yet all these treasuries have one treasury, “in which are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

Just as I possess one most precious pearl through many other pearls, so I come to the treasury of treasuries, the Lord of lords, and the King of kings, when I have become worthy to dwell with the spirits abiding in God’s treasuries.

(Jerome) “Every human being has become foolish through knowledge.” Although Paul, Peter, Moses, and Abraham are wise, in comparison with God all their wisdom will be reckoned as nothing. Hence “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.”

Every human being has been made foolish through knowledge.

(Origen) If every human being has been made foolish through knowledge, then: “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13). “He has been made foolish through knowledge”: seeing through a mirror, seeing in an enigma, seeing only a small portion; and, if it is permissible to say so, recognizing only the smallest part of that small portion.

Conversely, you will understand what it means that “every human being has been made foolish through knowledge.” In comparison with the sins of Jerusalem, the sin of Sodom is righteousness. “Sodom was justified in comparison with you,” it says (Matthew 10).

Just as the sins of Sodom do not possess righteousness in themselves but are justified in comparison with greater crimes, so, conversely, Paul’s knowledge is reckoned folly in relation to that heavenly knowledge and that complete understanding of reason. Therefore “every human being has been made foolish through knowledge.”

Ecclesiastes, I think, detected something of this kind and said: “I said, ‘I shall become wise,’ and it withdrew farther from me than it had been; profound and deep—who can find it?”

We wish to say something boldly, if permitted: this thing that descended into the world emptied itself, so that the world might be filled by its emptying. If that which descended into the world emptied itself, then the emptying itself is wisdom, since “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.”

If I had said “the foolishness of God,” how the hunters of words—always devoted to accusation—would brandish their poisonous tongues against me! But Paul, as one who was wise and possessed apostolic authority, dared to say that all earthly wisdom—the wisdom that was in himself, in Peter, and in the other apostles, and that had descended into this world—is the foolishness of God. For in comparison with that wisdom which the earthly realm cannot contain, that wisdom which is heavenly and exceeds the limits of the world, what descended to human beings is the foolishness of God. Yet that same foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.

Which human beings? Not fools, certainly, but the wise—whether you call them the wise men or rulers or seers of this age. For these wise men of the age, what we have explained is true: “The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.”

We wish to insert something marvelous: “The wisdom of the world is foolishness with God,” and God has made the wisdom of the world foolish. In his wisdom he made the wisdom of the world foolish, and the wisdom of the world cannot grasp the wisdom of God; thus the former is proved to be foolishness.

For the wisdom of God did not deem it worthwhile to descend entirely in order to refute the wisdom of the world. Rather, it descended only a little, as much as was necessary—what constituted the foolishness of God—so that by this small thing, this foolishness of God, the wisdom of the age might be made foolish. The wisdom of the age was not capable of sustaining the greatness of the wisdom that came into it.

But let us introduce an example so that it may clearly be understood how the foolishness of God made the wisdom of the world foolish. Let me pretend for a moment that I, who am thought to know something, am conversing with some foolish and uneducated person who understands nothing and asks nothing requiring subtle argument. To expose his foolishness, do I need to employ the skill of dialectical art and the acumen of profound thoughts? Would I not, with the utterance of a single brief and modest statement that nevertheless seemed extremely sharp to his understanding, prove him foolish and senseless?

So, in order to make the wisdom of the world foolish, it is not necessary for the wisdom of God to descend and wrestle with that wisdom which is below. The foolishness of God is sufficient, because “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.” My Savior and Lord assumed all these opposites in order to dissolve opposites by opposites, so that we might be strengthened by his weakness, made wise by his foolishness, and, having been initiated into these things, might ascend to the wisdom and power of God, Christ Jesus.

(Jerome) “Every craftsman is confounded by the carved image,” who fashioned images from his own heart, and what he cast is false. But if every human being has been made foolish through knowledge, then everything false and foolish that he has made is foolish, and there is no spirit in them.

It should be noted that in this chapter too, among the Hebrews, wind and spirit are called by one name. He calls it the spirit of sanctification, which cannot be found in the minds of heretics. [Col. 0884D]

“They are vanity and a work worthy of laughter.” For who would not laugh when he has seen the images of the heretics? Either what they say is rustic, and it is wood; or it is composed in beautiful speech, and silver is discovered; or it is fabricated from their own understanding, and they vainly promise the image of gold.

“At the time of their visitation they will perish.” Heresy has strength for a time, so that the elect may be revealed and proved (1 Corinthians 11). But when God’s visitation comes and his eye looks upon foolish things, everything falls silent.

“The portion of Jacob is not like these”—the portion of those who have supplanted the Jews and daily destroy the heretics. The portion of the saints, however, is God, concerning whom the Prophet says: “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 72). “For he who formed all things is himself,” who made and fashioned all things, both in soul and in body.

“And Israel is the rod of his inheritance.” Everyone who is upright in God, or who sees God with understanding, is the scepter of his inheritance, whose name is the Lord Almighty, or “of hosts.” For this is what “Lord of hosts” signifies: what is written in Hebrew as “Lord Sabaoth.”

“Gather from the earth your confusion, you who dwell under siege, because thus says the Lord: Behold, this time I will cast far away the inhabitants of this land, and I will afflict them so that they will not be found.”

The Septuagint reads: “He gathered from outside his substance, which dwells in a fortified place, because thus says the Lord: Behold, I will supplant the inhabitants of this land, and I will afflict them so that they will not be found.”

(Jerome) Jerusalem is commanded to gather into the most strongly fortified city whatever substance it has outside, and to prepare provisions for a prolonged siege. For he is no longer threatening the future and distant time as before, but the captivity that is near and about to come immediately.

“Gather,” he says, “from outside and from the earth”—that is, from the fields—“your substance into confusion.” Whatever you have is worthy of confusion. Although you prepare these things, understand that the Lord’s words concerning them are as follows: “Behold, this time”—at this moment—“I will cast away,” or hurl like a sling, “far away the inhabitants of this land.” In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “I will supplant them and make them fall.” In place of the Hebrew word, Aquila and Symmachus translated *sphendonēsō* (σφενδονήσω), “I will hurl like a sling.” The meaning is: “I will cast them away with every force, as with a sling; I will besiege them in such a way, and afflict and confine them so greatly, that all will be found in the city and will be unable to escape the evil.”

“Woe is me because of my crushing, my grievous wound.” The Septuagint reads: “Woe because of your crushing, your grievous wound.” According to the Hebrew, Jerusalem herself is speaking, declaring that she has been severely afflicted and is suffering an incurable wound. According to the Septuagint, however, the prophet speaks to Jerusalem and laments her over her crushing and her wound.

“But I said: Surely this is my weakness—or my wound—and I will bear it—or it has seized me.” Jerusalem herself is speaking: “Whatever I suffer, I suffer through my own fault. I understand my wound, which has seized me; or I will endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him.”

“My tent has been devastated; all my cords have been broken—or all my skins have been torn; my children have gone out from me—or my sheep—and they do not remain. There is no one who will further stretch out my tent—or there is no longer room for my tent—and raise up my skins.”

Jerusalem laments the overthrow of her city as though it had been so easy that one would think not that her walls and all her fortifications had been uprooted from their foundations, but that a tabernacle or tent had simply been taken away. “My tent,” she says—that is, my dwelling—“has suddenly been removed.”

“All my cords have been broken”: he preserves the metaphor of the tent. Or, “all my skins have been torn. My children have gone out from me,” or “my cattle.” What was added by the Septuagint does not fit the historical sense. During a lengthy siege, how could sheep and cattle have been taken away from Jerusalem? Even if they had been there, famine would have consumed them. “And they do not remain,” he says, or “they are not present.” For they were not transferred to Chaldaea; a large part of them was killed. “There is no one who will further stretch out my tent”: there is no one who will restore me and lay the foundations of my walls, which have been thrown down to the ground.

“For the shepherds acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord; therefore they did not understand, and their whole flock was scattered.” Through the metaphor of shepherds and sheep, the guilt of the rulers and the scattering of the people are described. Since the rulers acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, whom they ought to have sought with their whole heart, they therefore neither foresaw nor understood the evils that were coming—or they did not understand the Lord—and the entire multitude of Jerusalem was scattered here and there.

“The sound of a report—behold, it comes—and a great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling place of dragons—or a den of ostriches.”

As Symmachus translated it, “of sirens,” in place of which the Hebrew has [the source is materially incomplete here].

The prophet’s words are: “Behold,” he says, “the sound and roar” of the coming Babylonian is heard, and a great commotion—or earthquake—from the land of the north, so that it may reduce all the cities of Judaea to desolation after killing their inhabitants, and make dragons dwell there in place of human beings, together with every venomous creature; or ostriches, an animal likewise familiar to the desert, which is born and nourished in wastelands. Alternatively, we may understand sirens as certain monsters and phantoms of demons.

Let us refer all these things, which both the preceding and the present discourse have described, to the times of the Church’s persecution, when the Lord’s tents are overthrown and every habitation of the Church is reduced to desolation. And that all these things come about is the fault of the shepherds, who acted foolishly, did not seek the Lord, and did not understand him; therefore the whole flock was scattered.

“I know, Lord, that a person’s way does not belong to him, nor is it the man’s to walk and direct his steps.”

Let the new preachers blush—those who say that each person is governed by his own choice—since this prophet too says, “A person’s way does not belong to him,” and David sings in his lyric song: “The steps of a person will be directed by the Lord, and he will greatly desire his way” (Psalm 36).

Or the meaning here is: “What we suffer at the hands of the Babylonians is not the result of their strength, but of our merit and your indignation.”

“Correct me, Lord, yet with judgment, and not in your fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing. Pour out your indignation upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the provinces—or generations—that have not called upon your name; for they have consumed Jacob, devoured him, and exhausted his place, and have scattered—or reduced to desolation—his honor (or pasture).”

We read this passage in the Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor [Col. 0887A] correct me in your anger” (Psalm VI). The meaning is: We certainly deserve everything we suffer, and we deserve things far greater than what we endure. Nevertheless, I ask this: correct me as a father, not as an adversary; amend me as a son, and do not punish me as an enemy. “For you chastise every son whom you receive” (Hebrews XII), and through every pain and scourging you correct Jerusalem. But the enemies who did not know you, and the provinces or regions that did not call upon your name, ought not to experience your judgment, but your indignation. You handed us over so that we might be corrected, but they made their yoke heavier. They spared neither the old nor afflicted the little ones; they consumed and utterly devoured us, and reduced Jerusalem to such desolation that they destroyed everything belonging to both public [Col. 0887B] and private buildings and killed your people. It should also be noted that the Lord is said to rage, not because he is subject to human disturbances, but because we who sin, unless we hear that the Lord is angry, will not fear him. Hence the Apostle also writes (Romans II): “The goodness and patience of God urge us to repentance; but according to our hardness and impenitent heart, we are storing up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment.”

## CHAPTER XI. On the curse of the one who does not hear the word of the Lord; on the punishment for sin committed: the impious is not sanctified by his sacrifices. On the olive tree and the prophecy of Christ’s cross.

[Col. 0887C] “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this covenant—or testament—and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel.”

It is not stated in the heading at what time, under which king, or in which year of his reign this prophecy was made. But we understand either that it should be joined to the preceding prophecy and its period, or certainly that, after some interval of time following the earlier prophecy, this word of the Lord was addressed to the prophet. It should also be noted that Aquila and Symmachus consistently translated the term as “covenant,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as “testament.” Properly speaking, the discourse is now directed to Jerusalem and to the men of the tribe of Judah.

[Col. 0887D] “Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying: Hear my voice and do everything that I command you, and you shall be my people, and I shall be your God.”

It is not because of privileges of lineage, nor because of the offense of circumcision and the leisure of the Sabbath, but because of obedience that God becomes the God of the people of Israel, and Israel becomes his people. Here he speaks as though to servants, so that they may please God. In the Gospel, however, the Lord says to the disciples: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I heard [Col. 0888A] from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). Once they have become friends, they pass from being friends into being sons: “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John I). Therefore he commands friends and sons: “Be perfect, just as your Father is perfect” (Matthew V), commanding likeness, not equality. In the former passage there is obedience to commandments; here, likeness to God.

And when he says, “on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace,” he gives us to understand that the kiln and blazing iron furnace signify the magnitude of tribulation and punishment, not some place of punishment prepared out of iron.

(Origen.) What is this word that came from the Lord, whether to Jeremiah, Isaiah, or any of the prophets? Is it the word that was in the beginning [Col. 0888B] with God? I know no other word of the Lord besides the one about which the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). We must understand that this is the benefit of believers: that the Word comes to each individual. For what does it profit me if he descends into the world and I do not possess him? Conversely, even if he does not come to the whole world, but I become like the prophets, I possess him. I shall say that the same Word came also to Moses, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and each of the saints. And what the Lord said to the disciples—“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII)—was fulfilled in deed even before his coming, which he made manifest to all. For [Col. 0888C] he was with Moses, Isaiah, and all the saints. How could they have spoken the word of God without the coming of the Word himself?

We who are ecclesiastical people ought to pay particular attention to this: we wish the God of the Law and the Gospel to be one and the same—the same God in ancient times, now, and throughout all ages, forever and ever. Let us therefore hear what he says: “Hear the words of this Testament and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

We are the men of Judah because of Christ; there is no doubt that our Lord arose from Judah. The name Judah itself can also be shown, according to the Scriptures, to refer to Christ. The men of Judah are not the unbelieving Jews, but we who believe in Christ. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the back [Col. 0888D] of your enemies” (Genesis XLVIII). “Your brothers shall praise you”: it was not Judah, Jacob’s son, whom his brothers praised; rather, it is this Judah whom his brothers praise. For this Judah says: “I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I shall sing hymns to you” (Psalm XXI).

It is said to that Judah: “Your hands shall be upon the back of your enemies.” Where is it found that that Judah placed his hands upon the back of his enemies? History records nothing of the kind concerning him. But if you consider the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who destroyed the devil, stripped the principalities and powers, exposed them publicly, and triumphed over them on the cross, you will see how the prophecy was fulfilled concerning this Judah: “Your hands shall be upon the back of your enemies.”

[Col. 0889A] And now the word is spoken to the men of Judah. No one doubts that it is spoken to us Christians, because of Christ, who was born from the tribe of Judah. The word is also spoken to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, namely, to those who dwell in the Church. This is the city of the great King; this is the vision of peace. Peace is multiplied and perceived in us, provided that we are sons of peace.

“Hear, therefore, the words of this Testament, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and say to them: Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this Testament, which God commanded your fathers.”

Who hears the words of the Testament that God commanded the fathers more fully: we who believe in Christ, or those who, by not believing in Christ, did not even believe Moses? To them the Savior says: “If you believed [Col. 0889B] Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me; but if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John V.) Thus they did not believe Moses; but we, believing in Christ, believe the Testament handed down through Moses. And it is said to us, so that we may not become accursed: “Cursed is the man who will not hear the words of this Testament, which he commanded your fathers.”

Are those people therefore accursed? For they did not hear the Testament that God commanded their fathers. “On the day,” he says, “when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace.”

God also brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace—especially according to the spiritual understanding of what is written in John’s Apocalypse: the place where the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt. For if someone is called Egypt spiritually [Col. 0889C], and is not Egypt according to the bodily understanding, there is no doubt that, if you understand spiritual Egypt and have gone out from it, you are one who is coming out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace; and to you it is said: “Hear my voice and act according to all these things.”

Then God’s promise is made to those who hear, if they do everything that the Lord commanded, saying: “You shall be my people, and I shall be your God.” Not everyone who says that he is the people of God is the people of God. The people of the Jews, claiming themselves to be God’s people, deserved to hear: “You are not my people”; and it was said to them, “Not my people,” and again this people was called “not a people.” “For they,” he says, “were zealous against me over what is not God.” Concerning them he says: “They provoked me with their idols, [Col. 0889D] and I shall make them jealous over what is not a nation; I shall provoke them with a foolish nation” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

We, therefore, have been made the people of God, and righteousness is announced to the people who will be born from the nations. This people is born suddenly. It is written in the prophet [Col. 0890D]: “Has a nation been born all at once?”—when the Savior ascended to heaven, and five thousand believed in one day, with another three thousand added on the following day (Acts V). Truly then it was possible to see a people born all at once by the word of God, and suddenly the barren woman giving birth, to whom it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Galatians IV).

The Church, deserted by the Law, was also deserted [Col. 0890A] by God; but the Synagogue, having the Law as its husband, also had God. What, then, does God promise? “You shall be my people, and I shall be your God.”

He is not the God of everyone, but only of those to whom he has given himself. Thus he was the God of the patriarch to whom he said, “I am your God,” and again to another, “I shall be your God,” and concerning others: “I shall be their God.” Do we perhaps at some point attain what I am describing individually, so that God may be the God of all and our God?

But if you wish to learn more fully whose God he is, and to whom he grants the designation of his name, he says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus III). Explaining this very statement, the Savior says: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Luke XX). Who is dead? Certainly the sinner, who does not possess the one who says: “I am life.” Who possesses [Col. 0890B] dead works—the one who has not yet repented of dead works, concerning which the Apostle says: “Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works” (Hebrews VI).

If, then, God is not the God of the dead but of the living, and we know him to be living, whoever lives according to Christ becomes his participant. And if we wish him also to be our God, let us renounce dead works, so that he may fulfill his promise in us, saying: “And I shall be your God.”

“Thus I may establish the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day.”

(Jerome.) The fathers appear to receive the promise when the sons receive it, and Abraham’s promise is fulfilled in his descendants. We should understand the land flowing with milk and honey hyperbolically as signifying an abundance of all things, as in the following passage (Virgil, Eclogue III):

“May honey flow [Col. 0890C] for them, and may the rough bramble bear amomum.”

And again:

“And everywhere he held back wines running in streams.”

Or, certainly, in a tropological sense, let us understand the land flowing with milk and honey as the Church of Christ, in which, through faith, we are raised as little ones and infants, so that we may be able to receive solid food.

“And I answered and said, Amen, Lord.” In place of this, the Septuagint translated, “Let it be, Lord” (for this is what amen means). The Lord had said: “I swore to your fathers that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus III), as is confirmed by the facts themselves to this day. The prophet, zealous for his people, takes up the Lord’s voice and desires that what has been given may be true and endure forever. Hence he says: “Truly, Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised”; or, “Let it be, Lord”—that is, “May what you have given always remain.”

“And the Lord said to me: Proclaim—or read—all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this covenant, and do them.”

The most merciful God frequently foretells what is to come, so that at last a mind slow to believe may be softened. He foretells it both in the city of Jerusalem and outside it, in the countryside, so that those whose danger is shared may also share the same repentance.

[Col. 0891A] “For I solemnly warned your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, even to this day. Rising early each morning, I warned them and said: Hear my voice. But they did not hear, nor incline their ear; instead, each went after the perversity of his evil heart. And I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do.”

Up to this point this is not found in the Septuagint. What follows—“and they did not do them”—was included by them and joined to the end of the preceding chapter, where it is written: “Hear the words of this covenant and do them, and they did not do them.”

What it means for God to rise early, repeatedly to press his words upon them through the prophets, to lead them out of Egypt, and to admonish them again and again, saying, “Hear my voice,” while they went after the perversity of their heart, and afterward to repay them with what they deserved to receive, we have already explained.

[Col. 0891B] “And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers, who refused to hear my words. Thus they too have gone after foreign gods, to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant, which I made with their fathers.”

For “conspiracy,” which we have translated according to Symmachus, Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated σύνδεσμον (*syndesmon*), which we may render “a binding together.” Hence Athaliah, when she discovered that a plot was being prepared against her in the temple (2 Kings XI), used the same word: “Conspiracy, conspiracy!”

Scripture properly employs this word when the movement toward sin is not a sudden and accidental transgression, but is directed toward wrongdoing through prepared ambushes and conspiracy, and when they act with one mind and a single [Col. 0891C] purpose to despise God’s commandments. It says that fathers and sons, with one mind and one judgment, disregarding God, worshiped idols—both Israel, that is, the house of the ten tribes, and the house of Judah, that is, the two tribes whose rule was in Jerusalem—so that, since they shared one purpose in contempt of God, their punishment in enduring captivity might also be equal.

(Origen.) If we sin—although we are called men of Judah because of Christ—and sinners are found among our number, it is said concerning us: “A binding together—or conspiracy—has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” When there are such people in the Church of God, in whom the snare of iniquity and the bonds of sin are found, so that what is said about the sinner applies [Col. 0891D] to them—“Each person is bound by the bonds of his sins”—then God says: “A binding together has been found among the men of Judah.”

Yet a binding together will not be found among us. But how will it not be found among us if, even to this hour, such a binding remains in some? Rather: “Release every bond of iniquity; undo the oppressive obligations; scatter every unjust contract; break your bread for the hungry.”

Thus a binding together has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. “They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers.” To whose iniquities have they returned? He does not simply say “fathers,” but adds “their former fathers.”

We have said that these things are spoken concerning us and the sinners among us. How, then, have the sinners [Col. 0892A] among us returned, not merely to the iniquities of their fathers, but to those of their former fathers?

We have two kinds of fathers, and one kind consists of the worst fathers. Before we believed, the devil was our father, as the Gospel saying shows: “You were born from the devil as father” (John VIII). But when we believed, we became children of God. If, therefore, we sin afterward, we return not simply to the iniquities of our fathers, but to those of our former fathers.

To establish this point—that we have two kinds of fathers—we shall also use David’s testimony in the forty-fourth Psalm, which says: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm XLIV). The father says: “You shall forget your father’s house,” as though he began by saying, “Hear, daughter.”

[Col. 0892B] Thus our fathers are of two kinds. But he says: “Forget the house of your former father.” If, therefore, after forgetting the house of your former father, you turn back again to sins, you have fallen into what is now called sin: “They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers.”

A little earlier I said that the devil was our father before God became our Father. But even now, if we do not have the devil as father—as we also establish from John’s Epistle, where it is written, “Everyone who commits sin is born from the devil” (1 John III)—then, if everyone who commits sin is born from the devil, we are born from the devil as often as we sin. Unhappy is the person who is always begotten by the devil; exceedingly blessed, in turn, is the person who is always born from God.

I shall not say that the righteous person [Col. 0892C] was born from God only once; rather, through each individual work of virtue, the righteous person is always born from God. To prove this more fully, let us also speak of the daily birth of our Savior, clearly establishing in the righteous what preceded in the Lord. Our Savior is the splendor of glory; but splendor is not born once and then ceases to be born. Rather, whenever the light from which the splendor arises comes forth, the splendor of glory also arises.

Thus the Savior is always being born, and for this reason he says, “Before all the hills he begets me,” not, as some have incorrectly read it, “he begot me.” If the Lord is always born from the Father, then you too, in his [Col. 0892D] likeness, provided that you possess the spirit of adoption, are always begotten by God through each act of understanding and each deed, and you become a son of God in Christ Jesus, to whom belong glory and dominion forever and ever.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bring upon them evils from which they will not be able to escape. They will cry out to me, and I shall not hear them. The cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry out to the gods to whom they offer libations, but they will not save them in the time of their affliction.”

(Jerome.) God does not hear in a time of need and distress because they themselves refused to hear the word of the Lord [Col. 0893A]. Saul also suffered this (1 Samuel XXVIII). When, terrified by the armies of the Philistines, he had not deserved to receive the word of the Lord, he turned to the pythoness to learn from idols what he ought to have obtained from the Lord through persistent prayer and tears.

From this we learn that, even if the Lord does not hear us, we must not cease, nor flee to demons, who cannot help their worshipers, but to the Lord’s assistance. He is quickly moved when angry and changes his sentence if those with whom he is angry also change.

Everything now being said concerns the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, upon which captivity is impending.

“For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah; and according to the number of your streets, O Jerusalem, you set up altars of shame on which to offer to the Baals.”

Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles (2 Kings XXI; 2 Chronicles XXXIII), and we shall find that Judah and Jerusalem did things far worse than Israel [Col. 0893B]: they had as many forms of idols as they had cities, and as many altars for their own shame as there were streets and street-corners in Jerusalem, on which they sacrificed victims to the idols called Baals.

“You, therefore, do not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf, because I shall not hear them when they cry out to me in the time of their affliction.”

Jeremiah is commanded not to wish to intercede with the Lord for those upon whom the sentence has already been completed. His prayer must not appear ineffective, nor be unheard because of their own crimes. “Do not pray,” he says, “for them, nor take up praise,” as though, by recalling the mercy of the earlier history through which I have always pitied them, and by praising me, you might strive to change my sentence.

Even if [Col. 0893C] you do this, I shall not hear those who are forced to petition me in a time of necessity. From this we learn that it is useless for someone to pray for another when the person for whom God is entreated does not deserve to receive.

“What is my beloved doing in my house, having committed many crimes? Will holy flesh remove your wickedness from you, in which you exulted? O abundant, beautiful, fruitful, splendid olive tree—the Lord called your name. At the sound of its speech, a great fire was kindled in it, and its thickets were burned.”

He calls the people of Judah beloved and most dearly loved because they placed idols in his temple and worshiped [Col. 0894A] them there. They think that they appease God’s anger if they sacrifice many victims and glory in the multitude of sacrifices, which cannot remove the wickedness of sins.

He compares Jerusalem, or the whole Jewish people, to a beautiful and fruitful olive tree. Raised up through pride, it did not act humbly and did not recognize its Creator and Lord. Lifted up in pride and speaking arrogantly, it was set ablaze by the Lord’s fire, so that its branches or thickets were burned and reduced to nothing—that is, the whole people was destroyed by the sword of its enemies.

This same sense is written elsewhere, where it is said to Jerusalem: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed; how have you been changed into bitterness, a strange vine?” When its walls are destroyed, the boar from the forest lays it waste, and all the beasts devour its fruits, let us [Col. 0894B] apply this chapter to the leaders of the churches: “What is my beloved doing in my house, having committed many crimes?”

Or certainly let us apply it to the rich who, while plundering what belongs to others and not removing the wickedness from their hearts, think that they deserve God’s mercy: “Will holy flesh remove your wickedness from you, in which you exulted?” But now the names of those who make offerings are publicly recited, and the redemption of sins is turned into praise. They do not remember the widow in the Gospel (Mark XII), who, by putting two small coins into the treasury, surpassed the gifts of all the rich.

“And the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has spoken evil against you because of the evils committed by the house of Israel and the house of Judah, which they perpetrated against themselves to provoke me, offering libations to the Baals.”

The Lord your God called you and planted you as an abundant, beautiful, fruitful [Col. 0894C] olive tree. But because a flame descended upon you at the sound of the great God’s speech and consumed all your branches, therefore the one who had planted you has now spoken evil against you—not through an unjust sentence or a sudden perversity of speech, but because of the evils committed by the house of Israel and the house of Judah, which they deliberately practiced by offering libations to the Baals in order to provoke me to anger.

Although God can do whatever he wills, he gives reasons so that he may not appear to act unjustly, according to what is written: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm L).

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0893]

[Col. 0893D] Since many passages in the Book of Jeremiah unfold pure history, and many others seek mystical interpretation, there are also among them some passages that can be understood in two ways—that is, according to history and according to allegory. The prudent reader must carefully consider what properly fits each statement, and should allegorize in such a way that he does not lose the truth of the historical account; likewise, he should rely on the historical account in such a way that he does not neglect to receive the benefit of allegory wherever appropriate.

It should also be noted that the prophets and Psalms are obscure and difficult to understand because the speaker’s identity often changes within [Col. 0894D] a different narrative. While the reader is attending to one matter, he is suddenly carried over to another. This is demonstrated in many places in Sacred Scripture and also in the present passage. For while the prophet, speaking from the Lord’s word, rebuked Judah for its crimes and idolatry, and testified to the Lord’s voice addressed to him, forbidding him to pray for the people because they were unworthy of pardon, he suddenly turned, in his own person, to recounting Christ’s Passion, saying:

“But you, Lord, showed me, and I understood; you revealed to me their designs. And I [Col. 0895A] was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter, and I did not know that they had devised plots against me, saying: ‘Let us put wood into his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, so that his name may no longer be remembered.’ But you, Lord Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the kidneys and the heart, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you I have revealed my cause, Lord my God.”

(Jerome.) It is the consensus of all the churches that these words are understood to have been spoken by Christ under the person of Jeremiah: the Father showed him how he ought to speak and revealed to him the designs of the Jews; and he himself, like a lamb led to the slaughter, did not open his mouth. The words “and I did not know” are to be understood with “sin” supplied, according to the Apostle’s statement: “He who [Col. 0895B] knew no sin was made sin for us” (2 Corinthians V).

And they said: “Let us put wood into his bread,” namely, the cross into the Savior’s body. For he himself says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). And: “Let us root him out—or crush him—from the land of the living.” For they conceived this crime in their minds, intending to erase his name forever.

(Origen.) If God’s utterances are found in the Law and the Prophets, in the Gospels and the Apostles, the disciple of God, who learns the divine words, must acknowledge God as his teacher. According to the Psalmist, “He who teaches human beings knowledge” (Psalm XCIII) is God.

The Savior also testifies that no one ought to be called teacher upon earth, saying: “Do not call anyone your teacher upon earth, for one is your [Col. 0895C] teacher, the Father who is in heaven” (Matthew XXIII). The Father who is in heaven instructs human beings either by himself, or through the Son, or through the Holy Spirit. To come down to lesser examples, he instructs through Paul, through Peter, and through any other of the saints—provided only that God the Spirit and God the Word descend and teach.

Why have we said this? Because the prophet says: “Make it known to me, Lord, and I shall understand.” For I cannot know unless you reveal it to me. But if, with you showing me, I am able to know what I do not know, then I shall see the thoughts of each person, understand what each one is doing, and whose will is at work.

The statement that follows—“Come,” they say, “let us put wood into his bread”—is exceedingly difficult. The bread of Jesus by which we are nourished is interpreted as his word. Therefore, because [Col. 0895D] he was teaching, some people wished to place stumbling blocks in his teaching; and, crucifying him, they said: “Come, let us put wood into his bread.” When the master’s crucifixion is joined to Jesus’ word and teaching, wood is put into the bread.

Those plotting against him said: “Come, let us put wood into his bread.” But I shall add something remarkable: the wood placed in his bread made the bread better. Take an example from the Law of Moses. Just as the wood cast into bitter water made it sweet, so the wood of Jesus Christ’s Passion, cast into his teaching, made his bread sweeter.

Before the wood was put into his bread, when it was merely bread and there was no wood, its sound had not gone out into the whole [Col. 0896A] earth. But afterward, when it received strength through the wood, the word of his Passion was spread throughout the entire world. As a figure of this, water in the Old Testament was also made sweet by the touch of wood.

I declare that the uncomprehended Law is bitter water. But when the wood of Jesus Christ comes and my Savior’s word descends into it, then it is sweetened and becomes of the most pleasing flavor—the Law of Moses being understood as well as read.

Thus, when they said, “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” they also added: “And let us crush him from the land of the living, and his name shall no longer be remembered.” They killed him as though they would utterly erase his name. But Jesus knows why and how he dies. Therefore he says: “Unless a grain [Col. 0896B] of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much fruit” (John XII).

Thus Jesus’ death became an ear of wheat, returning sevenfold and much more than had been sown. If his death produced such abundant crops, of what fruitfulness will his resurrection be? Our Savior, therefore, was not crushed or erased from the land of the living, nor was his memory removed from the memory of the faithful.

(Jerome.) On the contrary, the Son speaks to the Father according to the mystery of the assumed body, and calls down his judgment while praising his justice. He invokes God as the examiner of the kidneys and heart, asking him to repay the people what they deserve, and says: “Let me see your vengeance upon them”—namely, upon those who persist in crime, not upon those who turn to repentance.

[Col. 0896C] Concerning the latter he said on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXV [as printed]). He reveals and lays open his cause to the Father, because he was crucified through no merit of his own, but because of the people’s crime, saying: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John XIV).

The Jews and those among us who Judaize understand these words as spoken by Jeremiah, asserting that, because of his prophecy of future events and the evils of the impending captivity, he suffered these things from the people. But I do not know how they can prove that Jeremiah was crucified, since Scripture does not mention this—unless perhaps they suppose that they planned it but did not carry it out.

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life and say: ‘You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and you shall not die at our hands.’ Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘Behold, I shall visit punishment upon them: their young men shall die by the sword, their sons and daughters shall die of famine, and no remnant of them shall remain. For I shall bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation.’”

This appears to contradict the preceding interpretation, by which we wish to establish that the words were spoken in the person of Christ and not of Jeremiah, who actually lived in the little town of Anathoth, three miles from Jerusalem. But if we understand the etymology of the town Anathoth, which is interpreted as “obedience,” it will plainly be shown that the “men of Anathoth,” who once obeyed the Lord’s commands, are a designation for all the Jews, and especially the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, upon whom the final sentence came, so that they would perish amid the evils of the siege, by sword, famine, and pestilence.

(Origen.) Figuratively, the name Anathoth is now being taken up. The entire mystery concerning the Jewish people is contained in it. For Anathoth, as we have said, is interpreted as “obedience.” Since, therefore, there was obedience to God among that people, just as there was his kingdom—and what we know was foretold happened to that kingdom: “The kingdom shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits”—so now the men who are in Anathoth, that is, in “obedience,” seek the life not of Jeremiah; for no history records this, since history does not say that the men of Anathoth sought his life.

We have the Books of Kings; Scripture mentions Jeremiah there, but nothing of this sort is recorded. We have Chronicles, and the very volume of the prophet that we are now interpreting: the men of Anathoth said nothing. But they seek the life of my Lord Christ, “who say: ‘He prophesied not in the name of the Lord.’” We also read that the Jews forbade Christ to teach this, saying: “Otherwise you will die at our hands.” “Behold, I shall visit punishment upon them: their young men shall fall by the sword, and their sons and daughters shall die of famine.” They did not perish by the sword in Jeremiah’s time, but after the Lord’s advent. Then famine also came upon them—not famine of bread or thirst for water, but famine of hearing the words of the Lord. For it is no longer said among them: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.” This is the famine of the prophetic voice that has ceased among them.

But why should I speak of prophets? No teachers or instructors remain anywhere in Judaea. And although there are countless people who claim wisdom for themselves, the word of the Lord is no longer in them. That prophecy has been fulfilled:

“The Lord shall remove from Judaea and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water, the giant and the mighty man, the warrior and the judge, the prophet and the arbiter, the elder and the captain of fifty, the marvelous counselor, the wise architect, and the intelligent hearer.”

There is no longer anyone among them who can say: “As a wise architect, I laid a foundation” (1 Cor. III). The architects have departed from them and come to the Church; they have laid Christ Jesus as the foundation. All who believed after them build upon him.

(Hieronymus.) To free ourselves from every difficulty of interpretation, let us follow the rule that the prophets performed many things as types of the Lord and Savior, and that whatever has been fulfilled in Jeremiah with reference to the present time should be understood as being prophesied concerning the Lord in the future.

## CHAPTER XII

*The dispute with the Lord concerning the murmurers; the binding of Jerusalem’s captivity; the rejection of the Synagogue; the condemnation of the shepherds; concerning those who have turned to the Lord.*

“Indeed, you are righteous, Lord, if I dispute with you (or: because I satisfy you); nevertheless, I shall speak judgments to you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why is it well with all who transgress and act unjustly? You planted them, and they have taken root; they advance (or: they have begotten sons and produce fruit). You are near to their mouths and far from their kidneys”—that is, from their inward conscience.

(Hieronymus.) This dispute is directed against all who act unjustly, and the substance of the seventy-second psalm is briefly contained in it, where he prophesied:

“How good God is to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the prosperity of sinners,” and so forth (Ps. LXXII).

More particularly, however, it is spoken against heretics, whose way prospers although they are wicked. They beget sons—those whom they have deceived into heresy—and they transgress and act unjustly, so that they plunder the Church. While they persist in the perversity of their doctrine, they boast that they have been planted by God, have taken root, have begotten sons, and have produced fruit. Although they frequently repeat the name of Christ, they do not have God dwelling within them, in accordance with Isaiah’s words: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX).

“And you, Lord, know me; you have seen me and tested my heart in relation to you. Gather them like a flock for slaughter, and sanctify them for the day of killing.”

There is no scandal, he says, in the fact that the wicked—or all heretics—flourish for a time: “For you, Lord, know me, and you have seen me, and you have tested my heart in relation to you.” whom God the Father knows as he knows his own Son: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X).

Let heretics advance, he says; let them beget sons and produce fruit; let you be near their mouths and far from their inward conscience. Nevertheless, it is no small consolation that they are fattened like livestock for slaughter. Gather them into the city of Jerusalem, or into their own assemblies, so that they may be slaughtered like sacrificial victims and sanctified when they have been slain by the ecclesiastical sword. For the killing of heretics is the salvation of those who had been deceived.

“How long shall the land mourn, and every plant of the region wither, because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it? Animal and bird have perished, because they said: ‘He will not see our end’ (or: ‘God will not see our ways’).”

(Hieronymus.) Whatever good or evil happens in the world does not occur without providence or by chance, but by God’s judgment. The land is now barren; the grass withers. Do you wish to know the reason? The wickedness of its inhabitants causes this, so that both the animals upon the earth and the birds of heaven perish, because all these things were created for human use. They have risen to such blasphemy that they say God does not know their ways and does not know what each person will suffer.

When he says “How long,” he signifies that God’s anger continues, because the mind of sinners is not changed.

“If you have grown weary running with foot soldiers, how will you be able to compete with horses? If you are confused in a land of peace, what will you do amid the pride (or: roar) of the Jordan?”

If, he says, the frequent captivity imposed by neighboring nations has wearied you—the Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines, and Idumeans—what will you do in the long captivity that will lead you as far as Chaldaea? He compares foot soldiers with horsemen because, both according to history and in reality, all Persia, all Chaldaea, and the armies of those regions take pride in their cavalry.

The nations I mentioned above, however, because of the difficulty of their terrain, are suited less to battle than to brigandage. He preserves the metaphor and says: If you have failed from weariness while running with foot soldiers, what will you do if you wish to match your course with horses? Even if you had some confidence in your own land, what will you do when you cross the Jordan and endure its torrents?

“For even your brothers and the house of your father, although they fought against you and shouted after you with a full voice, do not trust them when they speak good things to you.”

You will be covered by such grievous floods of the Jordan, he says, and the multitude of horsemen coming from far away will devastate you, so that even your brothers—the Idumeans—and the house of your father, who were born from the stock of Lot (Gen. XIX), Moab and Ammon, will themselves, in the time of need and distress, fight against you and mock you.

Therefore beware of wishing to trust them or to place hope in kinship, through which they rage against you with greater hatred than your enemies. This may also be understood of the Savior: his brothers and the house of his father fought against him and shouted with full voice, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him! We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

“I have abandoned my house; I have forsaken my inheritance. I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies. My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest. It raised its voice against me; therefore I hated it.”

He who spoke in the Gospel, “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV), and again, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII), now threatens the same things through the prophet and says that he has done what he is going to do.

The Lord’s inheritance is Israel, and it is the portion of his inheritance. When he says, “I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies,” this means: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X).

The Jewish people, once the Lord’s inheritance, became like a lion in the forest against him when it cried out against him with a united voice during his Passion. And because it raised its voice against him, he therefore hated and rejected it; what was once beloved and most dear is now called hateful.

(Origen.) Nor is it surprising that it was then compared with a savage beast. To this present day there are lions in the forest anathematizing the Lord Jesus, blaspheming him, and lying in wait for those who believe in his name.

“Is my inheritance for me a speckled bird? Is it a bird dyed all over? Come, gather together, all you beasts of the earth; hasten to devour it.”

(Hieronymus.) The Septuagint reads: “Is my inheritance for me a hyena’s cave, or a cave surrounding it over it? Go, gather together all the beasts of the field, and let them come to eat it.”

The speckled and entirely dyed bird, according to the literal sense, he calls a peacock. Israel, he says, possessed such beauty, and Jerusalem was adorned with such virtues, that there was nothing good that could not be seen in it. Since, therefore, what had once been my inheritance—that is, the people of Israel—became like a lion in the forest and raised its voice against me, I detested it with utter hatred. Therefore come and gather together against it, all you beasts of the earth—that is, the multitude of various nations—and devour it, since it did not know its Lord.

But if, as the Septuagint and the other interpreters have translated it, we read: “Is my inheritance for me a hyena’s cave?” let us refer this to the uncleanness of the nocturnal beast that lives on the corpses of the dead and is accustomed to dig bodies out of tombs, and that feeds on every kind of uncleanness. Such is Israel, offending its Lord and delivered over to the bites of every beast.

(Origen.) The beasts of the field came and devoured the Jewish people. Consider how the hearts of all have been consumed by hostile powers. If God did not spare them but said, “Go and gather the beasts,” how much more will he not spare us? If we do not keep his law, if we neglect the word of the Gospel, he will again say: “Go and gather the beasts and hand it over to them.” But let us trust in the Lord and say in prayer: “Do not hand over to the beasts the soul that confesses you” (Ps. LXXIII).

Let us repent of our sins; let us confess the offenses we have committed, and we shall not be handed over to the beasts. Rather, angels will come, carry us in their bosom from earthly places to heavenly ones, and transfer us from the present age into everlasting eternity.

“Many shepherds have destroyed (or: corrupted) my vineyard; they have trampled (or: polluted) my portion. They have made my desirable portion into a desolate wilderness (or: an impassable place). They have laid it waste (or: it has been laid waste).”

(Hieronymus.) Let those who desire to be rulers of peoples hear these words. On the day of judgment they will have to render an account not only for themselves but also for the flocks entrusted to them. Because of them, the Lord’s portion is trampled and polluted, so that where God once had his lodging, there the dwelling place of beasts may be.

Others understand not the leaders of the people and priests, but the leaders of the enemies, who laid Jerusalem—that is, the Lord’s vineyard—waste.

“And it mourned over me: the whole land has been utterly desolated, because there is no one who considers in his heart. Over all the paths of the wilderness devastators have come, because the sword of the Lord will devour from one end of the land to the other; there is no peace for all flesh.”

The Septuagint reads: “Therefore the whole land has been utterly devastated,” and so forth.

What we have rendered, “And it mourned over me,” is joined according to the Hebrew with the preceding verse, so that the sense is: “They have laid it waste”—that is, my inheritance—“and it mourned over me,” deprived of my help.

According to the Septuagint, however, God says that the land has been laid waste and reduced to desolation because of him, since there is no one who considers in his heart and there is no peace for all flesh. For flesh cannot receive the peace of God: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII).

According to the Hebrew, moreover, all Judaea is desolate because there is no one who considers God in his heart, nor any survivor who can escape. For devastators—the hostile army—came along every path of the wilderness, and the sword of the Lord devoured from boundary to boundary; nor was there any respite for those fleeing from the city. Hence it is said: “There is no peace for all flesh.”

(Origen.) If you wish to understand this more subtly—“Because of me the whole land has been destroyed”—consider how the land within you has been destroyed, and then you will see that after the coming of Jesus Christ the things spoken have been fulfilled.

Our members upon the earth have been put to death, so that the earth no longer performs its works. Among the righteous there are no longer the things with which the flesh was formerly indulged: no fornication, no uncleanness, no further licentiousness, no service of idols, no sorceries, and so forth.

The Lord says: “What do you suppose, that I have come to bring peace upon the earth? I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). Truly, before he descended, there was no sword upon the earth; the flesh did not lust against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh. But when he came, we were taught which things belong to the flesh and which to the spirit.

His teaching, like a sword thrust in, divides the flesh—that is, the earth—from the spirit and destroys it, because we carry the death of Jesus in our body and no longer live according to the flesh. The spirit, however, lives, and we sow not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that we may reap not corruption from the flesh but eternal life from the spirit.

“They sowed wheat and reaped thorns; they received an inheritance, and it will not benefit them.”

The Septuagint reads: “You sowed wheat and reaped thorns; their clerics will not benefit them.”

(Hieronymus.) They expected better things, he says, and the worst came upon them; they hoped for prosperity and suffered adversity. They received from the Lord an abundance of all things, but it will not benefit them.

According to the Septuagint, however, all heretics sow as though they were sowing wheat, but reap thorns. The Lord expected them to produce fruit, but they produced no judgment, only an outcry.

This is also said of ecclesiastical people who squander the words of God and his teaching through evil conduct. Concerning them it is added: “Their clerics will not benefit them.” What benefit will the title of bishop or presbyter, or the remaining ecclesiastical order, be able to give them, when they are rather weighed down by their dignities, and “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI), and the more that has been entrusted to them, the more will be required of them?

(Origen.) You must understand that we are not immediately saved merely because we are clergy. For many presbyters perish, while laypeople are found to be most blessed. We must both deserve and possess the clerical order in accordance with its requirements.

Since there are certain clerics who do not live in such a way that they themselves receive the fruit of their order and are an adornment to their dignity, therefore, those who have expounded this prophet say that he said: “Clerics will not benefit them.”

The usefulness of the clerical office does not consist in someone sitting among the ranks of presbyters, but in his walking worthily according to his position and according to the Lord’s commands.

But, beloved, do not suppose that this has been said only about us. Divine majesty admonishes both us and you to live according to the commands of the Scriptures—or, if it is better expressed: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments.”

More is required of me than of a deacon, and more of a deacon than of a layperson. Whoever holds the citadel of the entire Church will render an account for the whole Church. For this reason the apostle Paul, since much had been entrusted to him, said: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that each be found faithful” (1 Cor. IV).

“You shall be put to shame because of your fruits (or: because of your boasting), because of the anger of the Lord’s fury (or: because of reproach in the Lord’s presence). Thus says the Lord against all my worst neighbors who touch the inheritance that I assigned to my people Israel: ‘Behold, I shall uproot them from their land, and I shall uproot (or: cast out) the house of Judah from their midst. And when I have uprooted them, I shall turn (or: return), and I shall have mercy on them, and I shall bring them back (or: make them dwell), each man in his inheritance and each man in his land.’”

(Hieronymus.) This is said to those for whom their clerical and ecclesiastical order will be of no benefit, so that they may be put to shame because of their boasting and because of reproach before the Lord.

When he adds, “against all my worst neighbors,” according to the literal sense the neighbors of the Holy Land are the Idumeans, Philistines, Moabites, and Ammonites. According to the tropological sense, however, they are all heretics, who are reckoned under the name of Christ. They are neighbors rather than inhabitants of the Holy Land, and they touch and devastate God’s inheritance.

It is said concerning them that they will be removed from the midst of the land, and that the house of Judah will be taken away from their midst. Once they have been uprooted and freed from the jaws of heretics, they will obtain God’s mercy and be brought back into their inheritance and their land.

(Origen.) There are many things in which, by boasting, we display our foolishness. For example, if some people boast of numerous possessions, it is said to them: “Be put to shame because of your boasting.” If someone walks about rejoicing in the most expensive garments or in a house adorned with many riches—for such boasting is foreign to the boasting of the saints—it is said to him: “Be put to shame because of your boasting.”

But this is too little. Hear what the divine word says in Jeremiah, commanding us not to boast even in our wisdom:

“Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but let the one who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jer. IX).

Do you wish to boast and, boasting, not hear, “Be put to shame because of your boasting”? Boast like the apostle and say: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

Do you wish to boast and not hear, “Be put to shame because of your boasting”? Hear the apostle Paul boasting, and learn how he speaks: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. XII).

“And it shall be: if they diligently learn the ways of my people, so that they swear by my name, ‘As the Lord lives,’ just as they taught my people to swear by Baal, they shall be built up in the midst of my people. But if they do not listen, I shall uproot that nation with utter uprooting and destruction, says the Lord.”

If those who have been transferred from heresy into the Church learn the ways of God’s people, swear by the Lord’s name and not by the names of idols that they have fashioned from their own hearts, they will be built up by the Lord and will become part of his people.

But if, after being transferred into the Church, they retain the remnants of perverse doctrines and do not listen to God’s words, that nation will be uprooted from the midst of God’s people with perpetual uprooting and destruction, and no place for repentance will be left to them.

We see this daily and prove it by experience: heretics pretend that their faith is true in order to deceive the simple. They do not themselves turn to the faith; rather, they draw the faithful into unbelief.

## CHAPTER XIII

*Concerning the rotten loincloth and the wineskin; concerning the drunkenness of the wicked, the dark mountains, and the transfer of Judah because of its iniquities and impenitence.*

“Thus says the Lord to me: ‘Go and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth (or: girdle), and place it upon your loins; you shall not put it into water (or: it shall not pass through water).’ And I acquired the loincloth according to the word of the Lord, and placed it around my loins.

Then the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: ‘Take the loincloth (or: girdle) that you acquired, which is around your loins, and arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole in the rock.’

And I went and hid it in the Euphrates, as the Lord had commanded me. And after many days the Lord said to me: ‘Arise, go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth (or: girdle) that I commanded you to hide there.’

And I went to the Euphrates, dug, and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth (or: girdle) had rotted, so that it was fit for no use.

Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: So will I cause the pride (or: injury) of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem to rot, along with this most wicked people, who refuse to hear my words and walk in the perversity (or: direction) of their wicked heart. They have gone after foreign gods, to serve them and worship them. And they shall be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use.

For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, says the Lord, so that they might be my people, my name, my praise, and my glory; but they did not listen.’”

(Hieronymus.) The girdle or loincloth that is joined to God’s loins is the people of Israel. Taken from the earth in the likeness of linen, unwashed, it possessed neither softness nor whiteness, yet through his mercy it clung to God.

When it sinned—for this linen and loincloth is endowed with reason—it was led across the Euphrates, that is, among the Assyrians, and was hidden there: in other words, it was somehow swallowed up by a multitude of great and innumerable nations, and was considered worthless.

After a long period, the same prophet, acting as a type of God, delivered the people from captivity. Yet even after its return it did not obey God’s commands. Instead, it followed foreign gods, and at last it even laid hands upon the Son of God and decayed through eternal betrayal.

Every holy man is also God’s loincloth. Taken from the earth and from earthly clay, he is joined to God’s fellowship and, in a certain sense, covers and encloses with greater care those things that appear shameful in God’s Church, lest they be exposed to the bites of pagans and heretics.

If that loincloth touches water and crosses the streams of the Euphrates, so that it is saturated with the moisture of the Assyrian regions, it loses its former strength, rots, and dissolves. Even if it returns to God’s service, it cannot possess its former beauty—not because of any harshness on God’s part, but through its own fault, because it refuses to hear his words and walks in the perversity of its heart, or does whatever seems right to itself.

The divine word itself also explains why it used this comparison, saying: “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I joined and made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me”—namely, the ten tribes and the two tribes—“so that they might be my named people, my praise, and my glory.” Yet in spite of all this they did not listen to me, but followed their own vices.

(Origen.) After this we ask why it is called a linen girdle. Linen grows from the earth. When the seed has been cast into the soil, it first sprouts as grass; then, to pass over countless stages, it is brought from the harvest into the house, combed, washed, beaten, pounded, and, with immense labor, so to speak, threshed, until it becomes something from which a girdle or some other necessary article can be made.

So too all of us who derive our origin from the earth, who are woven into God’s girdle, require much care: we must be combed, washed, and rid of the color of earth. For linen has one color at its origin and another after it has been cleansed through labor. Its natural color is darker—we call it black—but after its preparation it is brighter.

Something similar, I say, happens to us at the beginning. We are black when we are regenerated, when we believe, when we say in the Song of Songs: “I am black and beautiful” (Song I). We have a soul like that of the Ethiopians.

Then why are we washed? So that we may become white, so that through diligence we may attain the brightness that was not implanted in us by nature, in accordance with what is written in the same passage: “Who is this that comes up made white?”

We become pure, white linen, and thus, when we have become worthy of God’s fellowship, we are woven into his girdle and are never removed from him—provided that we always retain the whiteness he has granted us.

Since, therefore, the Jews and the whole house of Israel proved unworthy of God and were cast away by him, he has girded himself with us in their place. We must not suppose that, after casting away the girdle, he remained ungirded and immediately wove another for himself.

This girdle is the Church gathered from the nations. It must understand that if God did not spare those who came first, neither will he spare it if it abandons him, if it does not prove worthy of his loins, if it does not cling to the Lord and become one spirit in Christ Jesus.

Therefore let the one who can say, “But for me, clinging to God is good” (Ps. LXXII), beware lest through negligence he be separated from the Lord’s loins, cross the Euphrates, and be handed over to the power of the king of Assyria. Let him beware lest he be occupied not in the most solid rock but in a hole of a rock that has become rotten and corrupted—that is, in the filth and vices of heretics—and come to such a degree of decay that he can no longer return to the Lord’s service or become his girdle.

“Therefore you shall say to them—or to the people—this word [Col. 0905B]:

‘Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Every flask (or wineskin) shall be filled with wine.’

And they will say to you: ‘Do we not know that every flask (or wineskin) shall be filled with wine?’

And you shall say to them:

‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings who sit from the stock (or sons) of David upon his throne, and the priests and prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. And I shall scatter them, each man from his brother, and fathers and sons alike, says the Lord. I shall not spare (or desire them), and I shall not grant pardon, nor show mercy, so as not to destroy them.’”

(Jerome.) The Hebrew word [the Hebrew term is absent from the supplied text] was translated by Aquila in his first edition as “flask,” in his second as [the term is absent], by Symmachus as “bowl,” by the Septuagint as “wineskin,” and by Theodotion as “vessel.” Every such vessel is filled not with oil, nor water, nor honey, nor milk, nor any other liquid material, but with wine and drunkenness. This shows that we are a fragile vessel, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4), and that it cannot fail to be fulfilled in you which is written: “For good does not dwell in my flesh”; and again: “For I do not do the good that I desire, but I practice the evil that I do not desire” (Romans 7). And afterward: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (ibid.)

By this drunkenness, through which we forget God’s commandments and every human condition is filled with vices and sins, the Prophet says: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142)—not in comparison with God, as the ancient and modern heretics and the patrons of heretics wish, but with respect to his knowledge. “For man sees what is in the face, but God sees what is in the heart” (1 Samuel 16); and what appears clean to us in our heart is discovered to be filthy in his eyes.

(Origen.) The Lord says that every wineskin must be filled with wine, and the people reply: “Do we not know, knowing this, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?” This can indeed be interpreted, according to the poverty of my understanding, if we first examine the differences among wines, so that afterward we may discuss the wineskins and establish the truth of what has been said: that every wineskin will be filled with wine. If someone is good, so to speak, among the wineskins, the wineskin will be filled with the wine of his goodness; if he is evil, then, in proportion to his evil, he will be filled with evil wine.

How, then, can we derive the distinctions among wines from the Scriptures? The following has been written about evil wine: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah; their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them; their wine is the poison of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deuteronomy 32). But of the good wine it says: “How excellent is your inebriating cup!” (Psalm 22.)
