Wisdom summons people to her bowl, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9).

There is therefore wine from Sodom, and there is wine that Wisdom has mixed. Again: “A vineyard came to be for the beloved on a hill, in a fertile place” (Isaiah 5)—a vineyard planted by God, called the vineyard of Sorech, a certain chosen vineyard, marvelous among all vineyards. [Col. 0906B] There is also another vineyard, that of the Egyptians, which the Lord strikes, according to what is written: “He struck their vineyard with hail, and their sycamores with frost” (Psalm 77).

Let us therefore consider all human beings, figuratively speaking, to be capable of wine. We can give no other name to those capable of wine than “wineskins,” and say that the wicked person is full of wine from the vineyards of Sodom and Egypt, full of the wine of Israel’s enemies; but that the holy person, and the one who progresses in the virtues, is full of wine from the vineyard of Sorech—the wine of which it is written, “How excellent is your inebriating cup!”—the wine that Wisdom has mixed.

These things have been understood by me with respect to wickedness and virtue, so that we may recognize how every wineskin is filled with wine. But if wineskins are filled with wickedness or virtues, it follows that they are filled with punishments because of wickedness and with blessings because of virtue.

Let the sacred writings provide testimony as to how torments or promises are called “wine.” “Take this cup of pure wine, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you.” Jeremiah speaks these words concerning what follows: “They shall drink, vomit, rave, and fall.” Thus, in this passage he called punishments “pure wine”: they drink pure wine, that is, they are worthy of pure torments. There are others who drink punishments, but not wholly pure ones; they are tempered to some degree.

“For there is a cup in the hand of the Lord, of pure wine, full of mixture; and he has poured from this into that; yet its dregs have not been emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink from it” (Psalm 74). If you wish to perceive the cup of blessing, which the righteous drink, it is enough to cite Wisdom’s testimony, where she says: “Drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9). Nevertheless, observe the Savior ascending on the day of Passover to a large upper room furnished and cleansed, celebrating the feast with his disciples and offering them the cup, concerning which it is written in the Gospel: “Take and drink; this is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins. Do this whenever you drink, in remembrance of me. Amen, I say to you, I shall not drink it from now on until I drink it with you in the kingdom of God” (Matthew 26).

You see the cup of the New Testament; you see the cup of punishments, which we explained above, full of pure wine. There is also another cup, which is mixed and handed to you in return for your good or evil deeds. For he understands those who completely depart from piety and altogether reject religion, to such an extent that they live by chance and like beasts, drinking the cup of pure wine that we brought forth from the book of Jeremiah. But those who have not completely departed, who are sinners and are judged unworthy of the cup of the New Testament, yet often do good works and often do the opposite, drink a cup mixed with pure wine.

“For God has poured from this into that.” What does he mean by “from this into that”? I see two cups. He has poured from this into that, yet its dregs have not been emptied. Consider the cup of your good works in one hand of the Lord. But if I may say something somewhat boldly: let the cup of virtues be in his right hand, and the cup of vices in his left.

When, therefore, you begin to be tormented because of your sins—since you have also done good works—the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of wine mixed with wine. He has poured from this into that: that is, from the cup which was in the right hand into the one held in the left. For you cannot drink only the cup of good deeds, as though you had done nothing but good, nor again only the cup of sins, since you have also performed some good deeds. Therefore he has poured from this into that, so that, according to the balance of your works, your punishment may be mixed for you, either more diluted or purer, and according to your merits the sting of divine anger may either be blunted or sharpened.

But if you are good and have kept God’s commandments, consider what you say: “I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115).

Every wineskin, therefore—whether good or evil—will be filled with the wine appropriate to its quality. No oil will be poured into it, nor any liquid from elsewhere, except the wine of Sodom or of Sorech. He will spare no one who is about to punish sinners. No one will be freed from punishments because he has been called a prophet, or because he is a priest: not only the obscure common people and the worthless crowd, but also the kings of the churches from the stock—or sons—of David, who sit leaning back with their necks held high, with their bellies thrust forward over his throne; the priests themselves, who hold the second rank in ecclesiastical honor; and the prophets, who appear to possess knowledge of the Scriptures; and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem will be filled according to the variety of their sins—or of Judah, as the Septuagint added.

When they have become drunk, they will be scattered from one another’s company: fathers will be separated from sons and sons from fathers, so that they may be polluted by different heresies and, under the name of Christ, fight among themselves and wage war against their mother, the Church, which gave them birth. Hence he says: “I shall not desire them, but shall hate them with everlasting hatred.”

God gathers the righteous; he separates sinners. Accordingly, as long as human beings had not moved from the east, they were not scattered. But when they moved from the east, and one man said to his neighbor, “Come, let us build a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven” (Genesis 11), God spoke, saying: “Come, let us go down and confuse their language” (ibid.). A little later it says: “Behold, the Lord scattered them from that place over the face of the whole earth.” The people of Israel, too, before they sinned, were in Judea; after their sins, they were scattered throughout the whole world.

Understand something similar concerning all of us. There is a church of the firstborn—that is, of those who are enrolled in the heavens—where there are Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Blessed are those who will be gathered there. But sinners will be divided from one another, even so that they may be tormented together by their punishment.

I know that certain kings, when people have plotted against their rule, are accustomed to deporting them to deserted islands and to ordering this as a great punishment, so that they will not endure the deprivation of exile in one place. A wife is banished to one part of the world, children to another, so that even in their calamities they may not enjoy the comfort either of mother and son or of brother and brother.

In the same way, the sinner, through a certain providence of God, endures the bitterer torments of solitude if he is sent alone into exile, so that, once corrected, he may return to his former condition. Just as you restrain your relatives or children—not through accidental or irrational anger, but because you wish through blows to recall them from the error into which they have fallen—so God draws back through pains and torments those who could not be converted by speech to the state in which they formerly were, in accordance with the Scripture that says: “Through every pain and scourge you shall correct Jerusalem.”

Thus, to increase the pain of punishment, he separates those who are being corrected from one another. For punishment is in a certain way made lighter if many people situated in the same place console one another through mutual conversation.

If it is necessary to introduce yet another explanation of the division of the wicked, we shall offer this one as well. When the wicked are together, they think about wicked things and, persevering in their former depravity, add sins to sins. Conversely, when the good are together, they speak about honorable matters. Thus wicked thought is dissolved and reduced to nothing when it has no conversation with another who is more wicked. Therefore, by God’s providence, the worst are separated from the worst for their own benefit also, so that through solitude and deprivation of companionship they may eventually desist from their former crimes.

“‘I shall not spare,’ he says, ‘and I shall not grant pardon, nor show mercy.’”

Heretics rise up against these and similar statements, saying: “Do you see what kind of creator the God of the prophets and of the law is, and what he says: ‘I shall not spare and I shall not show mercy in their destruction’? How can he be good?”

I shall take the example of a good judge who, for the common benefit, does not show mercy to certain people, so that we may perceive how God, sparing many, does not spare one. I shall also take the example of a physician, showing that he does not spare one bodily member so that he may spare all the members.

Let us suppose that a judge has undertaken to provide quiet to the city and peace to the people over whom he presides. If a murderer is brought before him, handsome in appearance and still in the vigor of life, while on one side his mother pleads with disheveled hair that he have mercy on her old age, and on the other his wife laments in a tearful voice that he not kill her husband, with little children standing around who will soon be bereaved, what will the judge do? Will he have mercy on the criminal or not?

He will carry out what benefits the city as a whole. If he has mercy, the murderer will return to his former crime; but if he persists in judicial severity, one man will perish and the entire people will be protected.

So, if God spares the sinner and, showing him mercy, refuses to punish him for his crime, who would not take license for evil? Those who are now at least terrified because of punishments—will not the time come when they invade everything and rush headlong into whatever vices they wish to fulfill?

We can often observe the same thing happening in churches. Someone has sinned and, after his sin, requests communion. If what he asks is granted, forgiveness becomes harmful to everyone, and, once the restraints have been loosened, a path is opened to crimes. But if, after reasonable deliberation—not as a merciless or cruel judge, but as one providing for a single person while considering the salvation of all—he has considered the harm to the people caused by forgiving one person, there is no doubt that he will cast one person out of the Church in order to preserve many unharmed.

Now consider a physician as well. If he stops cutting a wound that must be cut, if he does not burn what requires cauterization because of the pain—since recovery comes from such remedies—how the illness grows and the chronic disease worsens! But if, so to speak, a rash surgeon approaches the wound and burns the lesion, he cures the one who is cut and burned, because he has assumed a little severity, even though he may appear not to show mercy to the sick person for the moment.

So too God cares not for one human being alone but for the whole world; he orders heavenly and earthly things and all things everywhere. In providing what is beneficial to one person, he provides much more what he judges beneficial for the entire world and for all human beings. He does indeed provide what benefits the individual, but in such a way that that person’s advantage does not become everyone else’s harm.

Therefore eternal fire has been prepared, as have Gehenna and the outer darkness. All these things have been established not so much for the one who is to be punished as for the sake of all human beings.

But if you wish to accept Scripture as a witness to this matter—that sinners, even though they are already hopeless and entirely beyond cure, are tormented for the instruction of others—listen to Solomon speaking in Proverbs: “When the pestilent person is scourged, the foolish person will become more prudent” (Proverbs 19). He did not say that the one who is scourged would become more clever and wiser because of his own correction, but that the foolish person is turned from folly to prudence because of the punishment of the pestilent person. This is signified by the very term “cleverness”: he is turned toward cleverness when he sees others suffering punishment for the sins to which he himself is liable.

It therefore benefits us, if we are so worthy of salvation, that others are tormented for our benefit. And just as Israel’s sin was useful for the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some is useful for the salvation of others. For this reason God is good and merciful.

“‘I shall not spare,’ he says, ‘and I shall not show mercy in their destruction’”—not because of the cruelty of the sentence, but because of the truth of the judgment.

(Jerome.) For those who slaughtered those peoples will themselves perish forever. This may also be understood simply according to the historical sense: the kings, priests, prophets, and entire people of Jerusalem will be made drunk with the Babylonian cup and overwhelmed by the evils of captivity.

“‘Hear and perceive with your ears; do not be lifted up, because the Lord has spoken.’”

(Origen.) Let us therefore consider from these very words what it means to hear and to perceive with the ears. “To perceive with the ears” means, as it seems to me, to hear with the ears what is being said. But if the preceding command, “Hear,” is stated in distinction from the command that follows, “Perceive with the ears,” then the latter commands us to receive what is said into the mind and understanding.

There are certain things not only in this passage but throughout Scripture that are easy and readily understood and that, as soon as they are read, provide benefit to the readers. There are other things that are more sacred and ineffable and, so to speak, wrapped in certain obscurities. Concerning those things, then, that lie hidden and require exposition, I think it is now said, “Hear”; but concerning those that, without the interpreter’s scruple, are beneficial to the hearer, “Perceive with the ears.”

(Jerome.) Since he had said above, “Every wineskin shall be filled with wine,” so that the kings, priests, prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem would also be filled with drunkenness, he therefore joins this statement and says: “Hear and perceive with your ears,” both outwardly and inwardly, both in mind and body. “And do not be lifted up” through pride, considering your frailty and that no one, according to the quality of his sin, is free from this drunkenness.

Thus a person is destroyed and corrupted and is unworthy of God’s mercy when he exalts himself against him through pride. For although the human race is afflicted by many vices, it is oppressed above all by this sin. Nor is pride of only one kind. One person is exalted irrationally and like a fool in matters more deserving of shame, or at least exceeds the proper measure of exaltation. Another, as though deceived by a plausible line of reasoning, is lifted up over matters he considers worthy of glory, although it is dangerous to glory even in such things.

I shall give examples to make this clearer. Some boast that they are sons of leaders and were born into noble families. Such people cannot display even the shadow or image of their exaltation. Others are elated because they have the power to kill a person and, as they themselves think, possess the dignity to cut off the heads of whomever they wish; their glory lies in their shame.

Others applaud themselves for their wealth—not true wealth, but the wealth that belongs below. Others grow proud over splendid houses and extensive possessions, although there is no basis for glorying in any of these things.

What appears plausible and, as some think, worthy of glory is when someone is exalted by his wisdom, or is conscious that he has not touched women for ten years, or has remained chaste and undefiled from childhood. Again, another is lifted up because he has carried chains for Christ.

All these things appear right and seem to provide some persuasion in favor of glorying. But even in these matters, if we follow the truth, no one is reasonably exalted, because glorying even in good things is not without danger.

Paul had material for boasting: visions, revelations, signs, and powers within himself; the labors he endured for Christ’s sake; and his struggle to lay a foundation among the churches he established where Christ had not yet been named (2 Corinthians 12). All these were grounds for boasting and, if it is appropriate to say so, plausible reasons that could support honorable self-display.

But because even in such matters it is dangerous to be lifted up, the gracious and provident Father, just as he bestowed upon him visions and various gifts, so, for the protection of his gifts, handed him over to an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he be exalted. For this reason he begged the Lord that the angel of Satan, who had been assigned to him according to God’s providence, might depart from him.

But the Lord answered him—for Paul was worthy of the Lord’s answer—and said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

Nothing, therefore, should be a cause of boasting, since Scripture says: “Before destruction a man’s heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.”

“‘Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark and before your feet stumble against the dark mountains. You will wait for light, and there will be the shadow of death, and they will be placed in darkness’ (or, according to the Hebrew: ‘and he will place it in the shadow of death and in darkness). But if you do not listen, your soul will weep in secret, from the face of pride (or insult).’”

(Jerome.) Those to whom the divine word had said, “Hear, perceive with your ears, and do not be lifted up,” he now summons to repentance, so that before they are led to Babylon and their feet stumble against dark or shadowy mountains, they may give glory to God.

Hence sinners are often told: “Give glory to God” (Psalm 67). That Babylon and the entire region of the Chaldeans are called dark or shadowy mountains, we read at the beginning of Isaiah, in the prophecy against Babylon, where it is written: “Raise a banner upon the dark mountain” (Isaiah 13). The Hebrew expression is absent from the supplied text.

He therefore commands them to repent before they are led into captivity and experience the evils of servitude. And while they expect light, they will sit in darkness. “But if,” he says, “you do not wish to listen to me, your soul will weep in secret”—according to Aquila, “in darkness”; or, according to the Septuagint, “from the face of pride”—so that even their groaning and weeping may not be free, lest the eyes of their conquerors be offended.

We can also interpret the passage in this way. The Savior says: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work any longer” (John 6).

(Origen.) He called this age “day,” but the consummation of the world “darkness” and “night,” because of the punishments that are to come.

(Jerome.) Isaiah also prophesied concerning that time: “For the stars and Orion and all the adornment of heaven will not give their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light” (Isaiah 13). Zephaniah likewise agrees in the same words, saying: “A day of tribulation and distress, a day of misery and destruction, a day of darkness and storm, a day of cloud and gloom” (Zephaniah 1).

(Origen.) If you consider that grievous event after the consummation of the world, which nearly the entire human race will suffer because of the things it has sinned, you will see how darkness will occupy everything and no one will be able at that time to glorify God—for he is not glorified only by words and voices.

Glorify him in chastity, justice, and beneficence; glorify him in courage, patience, piety, wisdom, and the remaining virtues. God is to be glorified in this way. If I introduce the opposite, do not think that I am glorifying him, but blaspheming him.

I shall present Scripture as a witness to my understanding, showing how the chaste glorifies God and the licentious dishonors him. For the latter destroys and corrupts his temple like Nebuchadnezzar and, according to the Apostle, dishonors God through transgressing the law. Thus the righteous glorifies God, while every sinner heaps insults upon him.

(Jerome.) Before the time of judgment arrives and our feet stumble against the dark mountains—that is, the hostile powers appointed over torments and sufferings—let us repent, lest, while waiting for light, we become enveloped in the darkness of night.

Let us know that, unless we do this, the soul either of God or of the prophet will weep because of the pride of those who refuse to hear God’s words. Hence the prophet himself says:

“‘Jerusalem shall weep (or, “weeping, she shall weep”), and my eye shall shed a tear’”—I cannot conceal my grief with silent groans. The entire cause of the torments is that the Lord’s flock has been taken captive.

Let us say to the Jews and to our own Judaizers, who follow only the simple and death-dealing historical sense: Unless you listen secretly—that is, in the mystery, or in the darkness that God has made his hiding place (Psalm 17)—and, according to Solomon, understand the parable and the obscure word, the prophet’s soul will weep, or their own soul will weep, because of the face of pride, while through stubbornness they resist God.

(Origen.) Hence there will be continual weeping and perpetual tears, because the Lord’s flock has been taken captive and corrupted by the word of Nebuchadnezzar. Observe how remarkable this is: he does not say, “You will weep if you do not listen secretly,” but, “Your soul will weep.”

There is a weeping belonging to the soul alone, and perhaps this is the weeping of which the Savior says: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 24). That threat by which he announces mourning and tears to those who laugh also concerns this weeping, which the prophet now recalls, saying: “Unless you listen secretly, your soul will weep because of insult.”

When you have suffered insult, then you will weep, and your eyes will shed tears, because the Lord’s flock has been crushed. If we consider the condition in which the Jews now are and compare it with their former happiness, we shall see how the Lord’s flock has been crushed; and because they judged themselves unworthy of salvation, the word has turned to the nations.

If, then, that flock has been crushed, and we are the wild olive tree grafted contrary to nature into the good olive tree of the patriarchs, should we not fear even more that this flock of the Lord may also be crushed? For it will happen that this flock too will one day be crushed, in accordance with what the Savior said: “When iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24).

Of whom is this said—“the love of many will grow cold”? Is it not of those who are called Christians? Of those concerning whom this word is spoken: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18.) Is it not of us?

Therefore let us take the greatest care that, day by day, this flock of the Lord may improve, grow strong, and remain whole, and that, with all crushing removed from our souls, we may become perfect in Christ Jesus.

“‘Say to the king and to the mistress (or, “Say to the king and to the powerful”): “Humble yourselves; sit down, because the crown of your glory has descended (or, “has been removed”) from your head. The cities of the south are closed, and there is no one to open them. All Judea has been transferred (or, “all Judah has been transferred”), with the transference (or captivity) completed.”’”

(Jerome.) The prophet is commanded to speak to King Jeconiah and his mother, whom he calls “mistress,” “ruler,” or “queen,” so that they may humble themselves and sit in the dust. For they had lost their royal dignity and were to be handed over to the king of Babylon.

“The cities of the south are closed”—that is, the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem, which faces south near the wilderness—and there is no one to open them, since they are surrounded by siege.

“All Judea has been transferred (or, all Judah has been transferred), with the transference completed,” or, “it has received what it deserved,” and “it has been fulfilled in it”; for this is how the Septuagint translated the passage.

The person who understands “the king” as Christ, “the powerful” as angels or apostles, and interprets them as taking on a body of humility, sitting in the dust, and losing from their heads either royal power or the crown and glory of strength, is raving in this passage.

He also interprets “the cities of the south are closed” as the underworld, which is opened to no one, and understands all Judah’s glory to have been transferred when, during the Passion, the following was fulfilled: “All have turned aside together; they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one.”

The Hebrew word [the Hebrew term is absent from the supplied text] was translated by Aquila and Symmachus as “ruler” and “mistress.” The Septuagint understood it as “the powerful.”

“‘Lift up your eyes and see those who are coming from the north. Where is the flock that was given to you, your glorious sheep? What will you say when he visits you? For you yourself teach them against yourself and instruct them for your own destruction.’”

The inhabitants of Jerusalem are commanded to lift up their eyes and see the Chaldeans coming from the northern region. The city itself is questioned, and it is said to her:

“Where is the flock that was given to you, your glorious sheep?” Where is your people, whom you had received from God? Where is that great and glorious multitude, so large that you believed the population of the entire province had been gathered into one place?

“What will you say when the Lord visits you with his rod and hands you over to the Babylonian enemies, whom you yourself taught against yourself—or for your own destruction—from the beginning, so that you might flee to their aid and follow their idols? Under the pretext of your friendship, they learned by what route they ought to come against you.”

Let the negligent Church hear this: she herself teaches her adversaries how they can seize her through spiritual captivity and tear apart her flock with the cruelty of beasts.

“‘Will pains not seize you, like a woman in labor? But if you say in your heart, “Why have these things come upon me?” Because of the multitude of your iniquity your most shameful parts have been exposed, and your feet have been defiled (or dishonored).’”

While you are unaware, let sudden captivity seize you just as childbirth suddenly seizes a woman. But if you wish to complain and ask why you have been handed over to your enemies, hear plainly that the multitude of your iniquity has brought these things upon you, so that, like the clothing of a prostitute being lifted, your disgrace may be exposed and your public fornications revealed.

From this we learn that, while sins are still minor, God acts patiently and awaits our repentance. But if we wish to join offenses to offenses and heap up sins, our shameful parts will be exposed and our feet displayed to everyone, either in the present age or in the future.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 11), when Daniel’s statement is fulfilled: “These will rise to everlasting life, and those to everlasting reproach and everlasting confusion” (Daniel 12).

“‘Can an Ethiopian change his skin, or a leopard its spots? And can you do good when you have learned evil?’”

Those who wish to assert different natures use this testimony against the Church. They say that the blackness or diversity of sins is so great that it cannot pass into whiteness and the beauty of a single color. They do not attend to what follows: “And you can do good when you have learned evil.”

Whatever is learned belongs not to nature but to effort and to the will of the individual, which, through excessive habit and love of sinning, is transformed into nature. But what is impossible for human beings is possible for God, so that the Ethiopian and the leopard may indeed appear unable to change their nature. Yet it is he who works in the Ethiopian and the leopard, as the Apostle says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ” (Philippians 4).

Hence he says elsewhere: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that is in me” (1 Corinthians 15). And: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2). Again we read: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4.)

For these reasons “let the wise man not boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches” (Jeremiah 4), nor the chaste person in his chastity, knowing that in all these things it is Christ’s power, not the power of those who boast in their own virtues.

“‘And I shall scatter them like straw carried away by the wind in the wilderness. This is your lot and the portion of your measure from me, says the Lord’ (or, “and the portion of your disobedience against me”).”

Because through their excessive habit of evil they could not change their nature—not through any fault of the Creator, but through the practice of an ingrained crime—I shall scatter them into the wilderness like straw carried away by the wind, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “Like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1).

He turns his speech toward Jerusalem herself, saying that this is her lot and this is her portion, because she herself chose for herself a measure that was heaped up, complete, and overflowing—or the portion of her disobedience by which she refused to obey the Lord. “By the measure with which he has measured, it will be measured back to him” (Luke 6).

“‘Because you have forgotten me and trusted (or hoped) in falsehood, therefore I have stripped you (or shall strip you), and I shall expose your thighs and your hind parts before your face. And your disgrace, your adulteries and your neighing, the crime (or alienation) of your fornication, shall appear.’”

The cause of Jerusalem’s dispersion is that she forgot God and trusted—or hoped—in falsehoods. Whoever trusts in the things of this world apart from God forgets God. Therefore her thighs or hind parts are exposed, so that she may see her own disgrace; and what ought to have been behind becomes what is in front, so that she herself may see what she has done and her disgrace may appear not only to her but to everyone.

“Your adulteries,” he says, “and your neighing” reveal not only lust but the madness of lust, in the manner of mares that desire intercourse, as in that Virgilian passage:

> “[…]
> Hippomanes indeed, which the shepherds call by that name,
> drips as a sluggish poison from the groin.”

Let us ask Jesus that neither in the present age nor in the age to come he may expose our thighs and hind parts, but that he may erase our iniquities and prevent all our crimes from being revealed.

“‘Upon the hills in the field I saw your abominations. Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be cleansed (or, “because you have not been cleansed”) after me—how long still?’”

I hear of your idols not only in the midst of the city of Jerusalem but on every hill and throughout all the regions. Therefore it is said to her:

“Woe to you, Jerusalem, because you have not been cleansed after me,” so that although you boasted that you followed my footsteps and proclaimed the confession of my name, you were nevertheless never purified, because you forgot me and trusted in falsehoods.

Therefore he rebukes her and says: “How long still?” The meaning is: How long shall I wait for you? How long shall I endure you? How long will you forget me completely and despise my commandments?

The person who fornicates on the hills and in the fields and is never cleansed is the one who, with his neck held stiff through pride, is not humbled beneath the mighty hand of God but trusts in his crimes and vices.

BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0915]

[Col. 0915C] No one who rightly understands can doubt that Sacred Scripture is harmonious with itself, because whatever is asserted in one book is by no means denied in another, where rewards are promised to the righteous and punishments to sinners, and the scourges of the wicked and consolations of the good are described—especially since it is there recorded that, through the very elements of the world, a fitting recompense has been allotted to each of the two orders according to the Creator’s will. Thus these same things are found written not only in the history of ancient times but also in the prophetic books. For in the Book of Wisdom we read:

> “He armed creation for the vengeance of its enemies, and the world fought with him against the senseless” (Wis. 5).

Hence also it is said through the Psalmist:

> “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm wind fulfill his word” (Ps. 148).

And again:

> “He does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.”

Accordingly, the people of the Jews, lacking the verdure of right faith and barren in the fruits of good works, are read here also, in the present prophet, to have been struck not only by the hostile sword but also by a change in the air. It is of this that the text now speaks.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the lack of rain; the voice of the penitent; fasts and prayers do not benefit the obstinate; mourning over the people’s contrition, etc.

> “The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words about the drought.”

(Hieron.) All things concur with God’s anger; hence even the sun sets at midday over sinners, and the moon, stars, and other things do not give their light. It should be thought that there was no rain during the time of the siege, so that the besieged might endure a scarcity of water. The city uses one spring, that of Siloam, and not even that continuously; to the present day, moreover, the lack of rain causes a shortage not only of crops but also of drinking water.

> “Judah mourned (or: Judea), and its gates collapsed (or: were emptied), and they were darkened (or: enveloped in darkness) over the land, and the cry of Jerusalem rose up. Their elders sent their youngest (or: their younger men) to the water; they came to draw (or: to the wells), but found no water. They brought back their vessels empty. They were confounded and afflicted (or: put to shame), and covered their heads because of the devastation of the land (or: and because the works of the land had failed), because rain did not come (or: there was no rain) upon the land. The farmers were confounded and covered their heads.”

In a time of drought, when the multitude suffers hunger for hearing and learning the word of God, Judea mourns—she who previously boasted of possessing the worship of God and the confession of true faith. Her gates are either emptied or collapse. We must refer these gates to the senses, through which instruction is conceived in the soul. Then everything is darkened and enveloped in shadows, and reason and the word of teaching no longer reign in Jerusalem; instead there are shouting and confusion.

The elders too, who ought themselves to go to draw water, send the younger men—some of whom are gray-haired in wisdom, while others are not gray-haired in wisdom. They therefore come to the wells and do not find the waters that history tells us the patriarchs found. They bring back their vessels empty—not because there had been no water, but because they were unable to find it.

“They were confounded and afflicted, or: put to shame, and covered their heads,” because they could not say with the Apostle:

> “But we all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3).

Because of the devastation of the land—or: because the works of the land had failed—through which we advance toward knowledge of God; and the cause is clear, because rain did not come upon the land.

> “For the clouds were commanded not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5).

The farmers also, one of whom says:

> “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3),

and in another place:

> “We are God’s fellow workers,”

cover their heads and are confounded, understanding that without God’s grace and assistance they strive in vain.

> “For even the hind (or: hinds) gave birth in the field (or: gave birth), and abandoned (or: abandoned them), because there was no grass.”

(Greg.) This statement is spoken about teachers who carelessly abandon the children begotten by them; hinds, therefore, are rightly compared with teachers. For holy teachers, after killing vices as though they were serpents extinguished, live like hinds, and from the very extinction of vices burn more ardently for the fountain of life. Hence the Psalmist says:

> “As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 42).

They too, while they pass through the fleeting moments of this temporal existence like certain rivers, out of compassion bear one another’s burdens, because with vigilant care they observe what is written:

> “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6).

Hence it is said through Job:

> “Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth, or have you watched the hinds giving birth?” (Job 39).

The southern region calls ibices birds that inhabit the waters of the Nile; the eastern and western regions, however, call small four-footed animals ibices, whose habit it also is to give birth among the rocks, because they know how to live only among rocks. If at times they fall from the high peaks of cliffs, they catch themselves unharmed upon their own horns. For when they fall headfirst, they strike their heads; and when they first set their horns against the impact, the whole body is kept from the injury of the fall.

It is also the habit of hinds to kill serpents they find and tear their bodies apart with their bites. It is said, moreover, that whenever they cross rivers, they place the burdens of their heads upon the backs of those in front, and, taking turns with one another, feel none of the burden’s toil.

To watch hinds giving birth, then, is to weigh with careful consideration the labors of fathers who beget spiritual children. One must look attentively at the fact that this statement is impressed with such vigilance that it says, “Have you watched?” For it is the task of very few to weigh what labor there is in the preaching of fathers, with what pains and efforts they give birth, as it were, to souls in faith and conduct; how carefully they scrutinize themselves so that they may be strong in their commands, compassionate in weaknesses, terrifying in threats, gentle in exhortations, humble in displaying authority, condemning in their contempt for temporal affairs, and unyielding in enduring adversities.

And yet, while they firmly do not attribute their strength to themselves, how great is their pain over those who fall, their fear concerning those who stand, the ardor with which they seek to attain some things, and the anxiety with which they preserve others once they have been acquired. Since it is the task of very few to weigh these matters, the words are rightly addressed to him: “Have you watched the hinds giving birth?”

Nothing prevents the fact that, when God speaks of teachers, he designates them under the form not of male deer but of hinds. For those are truly teachers who, while they are fathers through the vigor of discipline, know how to be mothers through the compassion of their hearts. They endure the labors of holy conception and carry within the womb of charity the children they are to bring forth for God. In giving birth, mothers labor more greatly: they sustain the conception growing within the womb through many months, and they do not deliver what has emerged from the womb without great pains.

> “And the wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the wind like dragons, their eyes failed because there was no grass (or: hay).”

(Hieron.) Great is the sterility when even hinds give birth in the field and abandon their offspring because there is no grass or hay—so that those who draw serpents from their caves by the scent of their nostrils and kill poisonous creatures do not partake of the food of grace.

The wild asses too, of whom it is written:

> “Who sent the wild ass free into the wilderness?” (Job 39),

leaving the level plains and open country, stand upon the rocks and cannot run. They draw in the wind like dragons, and their eyes fail, so that they cannot see the clear light.

When rational nourishment is withdrawn, this drought often occurs in the churches: deer and wild asses are found among the peoples, and they waste away through lack of teachers. There are those who can learn, but there are none who can teach.

> “If our iniquities have answered (or: resisted) us, O Lord, act for the sake of your name, for our apostasies (or: sins) are many. We have sinned against you, O hope of Israel, its savior in the time of tribulation.”

If we wonder why the rains do not descend upon the land, why everything withers in dryness, let us hear the answer: Our iniquities have resisted us. Therefore, Lord, not according to our deeds but according to your holy name, overcome our many apostasies. For we have sinned against you, whom the secrets of the heart do not deceive; and we await you, who are the true hope and expectation of Israel and who save them in the time of tribulation, according to what is written:

> “To the Lord I cried when I was in distress, and he heard me” (Ps. 120).

Let us also say in a time of drought and scarcity of water:

> “We have sinned against you and done evil before you” (Ps. 51);

we await your coming, for you save Israel not through its merit but through your mercy.

[Col. 0919A]

> “Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay? Why will you be like a wandering man, or like a strong man who cannot be saved?”

The Septuagint: “Why have you become like a stranger in the land, and like a native turning aside to stay? Will you be like a sleeping man, and like a man who cannot be saved?”

The Jews understand this passage as follows: Why do you separate yourself from your people and, like a traveler seeking refreshment for only a single hour, do not care what lodging you use, but, since you are about to pass on elsewhere, do not save your people and abandon the once-famous temple?

Our interpreters, however, think that this is spoken of Christ’s future dispensation: that he will be a foreigner in the land, making use of the earth’s hospitality for a short time, and, like a man passing through yet strong, will leave Israel and proceed toward the multitude of the nations, passing from place to place, from people to people, and from the temple to the Church.

But where the Septuagint has:

> “Will you be like a sleeping man, and like a man who cannot be saved?”

the comparison expresses not the reality of the matter, according to what is written:

> “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord?”

This does not mean that the Lord sleeps, of whom it is said:

> “He will not slumber or sleep, who keeps Israel” (Ps. 121),

but that he appears to sleep to those whom he abandons. Finally, in what follows it does not say, “a sleeping man who cannot be saved,” but “like a man”; in both instances ἀνθρωποπαθῶς—anthropopathically, that is, in human terms—is written.

[Col. 0919C]

> “But you are among us, O Lord, and your name has been invoked over us; do not abandon us (or: do not forget us).”

You who, among the Jews, were to be like a stranger, a traveler, and a wandering man, abandoning your ancient dwelling, dwell among us. Your name has been invoked over us, so that we are called Christians. Therefore do not abandon us or forget us, for all the prophets’ mouths have sung of your future coming.

> “Thus says the Lord concerning this people: Because it loved (or: they loved) to move its feet, and did not rest (or: they did not spare), and the Lord was not pleased (or: God did not take pleasure in them), now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins.”

When the people say, “Why have you become like a stranger, a traveler, and a wanderer, abandoning your dwelling?” the Lord replies to his former people: Do you wish to know the reason? Listen to what is said. The people loved to move their feet and did not remove them from the fetters of sins—or: did not rest and could not stand. Therefore I too abandoned it, and I take no pleasure in it.

He who delayed for a long time and, through patience, refused to punish sinners, because they persisted in crime, will now remember their iniquities and, as though they were sick and unable to perceive God, will visit their sins, so that they may cease sinning.

It should be noted in the Holy Scriptures that the feet of sinners are always moving, while the saints are told with Moses:

> “But you, stand here with me” (Deut. 5).

And elsewhere it is written:

> “Praise the Lord, servants, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 135).

[Col. 0920A]

> “And the Lord said to me: Do not pray for the good of this people. When they fast, I will not hear their prayers; and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, for with sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them.”

It is foolish to pray for one who has sinned unto death, as John says:

> “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5).

Every iniquity is sin, and there is sin not unto death. Fasts, prayers, sacrifices, and burnt offerings are beneficial when we turn away from vices and mourn our former sins. But if, while remaining in our crimes, we think that we can redeem ourselves from the ears of God by vows and sacrifices, we are gravely mistaken, treating God as unjust.

For whoever has once been handed over to the sword, famine, and pestilence can be rescued by no prayers. Hence the prophet too is told not to ask in vain for what he cannot obtain.

[Col. 0920B]

> “And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God (or: who are, Lord God). The prophets say to them: You shall not see the sword, and famine shall not be among you, but he will give you true peace in this place. And the Lord said to me: The prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them, nor did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, a fraudulent divination, and the deceit of their own heart.”

Let teachers who promise prosperity to sinners who remain in their vices hear this—those who say to the rich: You shall not see the sword of God’s torments, and famine shall not be among you. You will be filled, they say, with the words of God, and the Lord will give you the truest peace in this place, whether the Church or Jerusalem.

Where, according to the Hebrew, he says “ah, ah, ah” three times, he responds to what came before, where the Lord had threatened:

> “With sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them.”

Since the prophets—or rather, the false prophets—made false promises, the Lord therefore spoke through Jeremiah: Do not listen to the words of the false prophets, who were not sent by me but came of their own will. Hence they should not be called prophets but diviners, since they speak deceit to the people.

It is far better to correct sins through fear of punishments than, through hope of prosperity, to become subject to divine judgment.

[Col. 0920D]

> “Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, whom I did not send, saying: There shall be neither sword nor famine in this land: By sword and famine let those prophets be consumed. And the peoples to whom they prophesied shall be cast out upon the roads of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there shall be no one to bury them—them, their wives, their sons and daughters—and I will pour out their evil upon them (or: their evils).”

Let the false prophets beware, those who overthrow the people of God by promising prosperity, lest they themselves perish and the deceived people likewise be destroyed. Let them lie upon the roads of Jerusalem, trampling the Lord’s commands, and perish from famine and sword, with no one to bury them or cover their disgrace with the dust of repentance.

For the prophets themselves, the people, their wives, sons, and daughters—in short, the entire generation—will be cast upon the refuse heap without anyone to perform their funeral rites. How many lie upon the roads of Jerusalem! How many do we see unburied, receiving the evils they suffer when the Lord pours them out!

[Col. 0921A]

> “And you shall say this word to them: Let my eyes shed tears (or: let your eyes shed tears) day and night, and let them not be silent (or: cease), for the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a most grievous wound.”

This passage is understood in two ways: either God himself mourns his people and his eyes do not cease to weep, or else he commands the eyes of the peoples to flow with tears, and says that what must be mourned is no light matter, since the virgin daughter of his people has been struck by the greatest crushing and an intolerable wound. Others think that these words are spoken in the person of the prophet.

[Col. 0921B]

> “If I go out into the fields, behold, those slain by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, those weakened by famine (or: by the pain of hunger). The prophets and priests too have gone away into a land they did not know.”

There is just cause for mourning: the virgin has been crushed, the daughter struck, and the people destroyed. For, he says, if I wish to go outside, I shall see the slain; if I enter the city, I shall see those weakened by hunger, scarcely clinging to their bones through the necessity of famine.

And what wonder is it to say this about the common people and the lowly masses, when even the prophets and priests—who prophesied prosperity to others and who ought to have explained the commands of the law—have themselves gone into a land they did not know and endured the evil of captivity?

Let our prophets hear this, and understand that through their negligence there is no security either within or without; that they scandalize those who are outside and allow those who are within to perish from hunger; and that those who were the authors of sinning become partners in its torments.

[Col. 0921C]

> “Have you utterly rejected Judah, or has your soul abhorred Zion? Why then have you struck us, so that there is no healing? We hoped for peace, and there is no good; and for a time of healing, and behold, confusion.”

The prophet wonders that the Lord has so suddenly rejected Judah and Jerusalem—that is, the kingdom of the two tribes, in which both the worship of God and the ceremonies of the temple existed—and has struck it with so great a wound that no remedy can be applied.

“We hoped,” he says, “for peace and a time of healing,” but there is no good; instead, there is confusion, so that where the worship of God and tranquility had formerly been, everything is filled with seditions and the hostile roar of war.

Whenever, therefore, our Zion and our Judah are rejected, and God’s soul abhors them, let us by no means be surprised, but rather say what follows:

[Col. 0921D]

> “We acknowledge, O Lord, our impieties and the iniquities of our fathers, because we have sinned against you.”

We, he says, and our fathers alike neglected what we had received in our madness, and the measure of our ancestors has been filled in us, so that whatever had been lacking in them might be completed by our accumulation.

Hence it is said of Judah:

> “Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be erased; let them always be against the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth” (Ps. 109).

[Col. 0922A]

> “Do not give us over to reproach for your name’s sake, and do not bring dishonor upon us. Remember the throne of your glory; do not annul your covenant with us.”

Let us not think that the throne of God’s glory is only the temple of Judea, which has often been destroyed, but every holy person, in accordance with what is written:

> “You have struck his throne down to the ground.”

It is struck down and destroyed when, through a multitude of sins, it has offended God. Yet the one who perishes through his own fault is sustained by the Lord’s mercy, which is changed into severity of judgment if the Lord annuls his covenant by which he promised that we would be saved.

[Col. 0922B]

> “Are there among the idols of the nations any that can cause rain, or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O Lord God, whom we have awaited? For you made all these things.”

After many and varied statements, he returns to the title of the prophecy, in which it is written:

> “The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words about the drought.”

What he says, therefore, means this: Since the images of demons cannot make it rain, and the heavens cannot of themselves give their rain, you, Lord our God, whom we have always awaited, in whom we place our hopes and direct our vows, you must give your rain; for all things are yours. Whatever good exists cannot be given without you, to whom it belongs.

Let us also say this against heretics, who cannot bestow the rain of teachings. Although they promise that they are heavens and boast that this has been written about them:

> “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 19),

yet they cannot give the showers of doctrine. For God alone instructs his people and grants the varieties of grace to those who await him.

## CHAPTER XV. The Lord does not hear the prayers of Moses and Samuel; the Lord’s Passion and vengeance against the Jews are proclaimed; the voice is transferred to the preacher.

[Col. 0922C]

> “And the Lord said to me: If Moses and Samuel should stand before me (or: against me), my soul is not toward this people.”

We read that these men stood against the Lord’s anger on behalf of the people and turned aside the sentence that was already impending. “Even if,” he says, “they should stand either in my presence or against me”—to one of whom God said:

> “Let me alone, and I will strike this people”—

I will nevertheless not hear, because the crimes of the offending people have reached their completion.

Why, with so many other fathers passed over and left aside, are Moses and Samuel alone brought forward? Their remarkable power of obtaining what they sought is shown by the statement that even they are said to be unable to intercede—as though the Lord were openly saying: I do not even hear those whom, because of the great merit of their petition, I by no means despise.

Why, then, are Moses and Samuel preferred to the other fathers in their supplication? Only because these two alone, throughout the entire sequence of the Old Testament, are read to have pleaded even for their enemies.

One was attacked by the people with stones, yet he entreated the Lord for those who stoned him. The other was cast down from leadership, yet when asked to pray, he confessed, saying:

> “Far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you.”

[Col. 0923A]

“If Moses,” he says, “and Samuel should stand before me, my soul is not toward this people,” as though he were openly saying: I do not even now hear those whom I know to pray for their enemies because of the great merit of their virtue.

The virtue of true prayer, therefore, is the height of charity; and each person obtains what he rightly asks when his spirit, in making the petition, is not darkened by hatred of an enemy.

Something similar is found in Ezekiel (Ezek. 14):

> “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, when a land sins against me by committing a transgression, and I stretch out my hand over it, and break its staff of bread, and send famine into it, and cut off man and beast from it—if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, should be in its midst, they shall deliver their own souls by their righteousness, says the Lord of hosts. But if I also bring the most grievous beasts upon the land to lay it waste, and it becomes impassable because no one can pass through it on account of the beasts, if these three men are in it, as I live, says the Lord, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters; they alone shall be delivered, but the land shall be desolated. Or if I bring a sword upon that land and say to the sword, ‘Pass through the land,’ and cut off man and beast from it, and these three men are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone shall be delivered,” and so forth.

It may be asked: Since Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as well as Moses and the other patriarchs and righteous prophets, were also righteous, why are only these men mentioned? The answer is readily given.

Noah could not delay the approaching flood of the whole world, because the entire earth had corrupted its ways; but he preserved his sons, who perhaps possessed the same virtue and had been kept for the propagation of the human race.

Daniel did not soften the captivity of the Jewish people that was drawing near, despite all his tears. Job, however, did not deliver either his house or his children—not because of sins, but for the sake of testing.

Others say that these three men alone saw prosperity, adversity, and prosperity again; therefore they are named together, and this is secretly signified: just as they saw good and evil and then joy again, so the people of Israel, who had first enjoyed good things and afterward endured the yoke of captivity, may, if they repent, return to their former happiness.

But if Noah, Daniel, and Job, gathered together and placed in one location, cannot rescue the sinful land—that is, those who dwell on the land—from the anger of God, what must be said of those who think that sinful children can be delivered from the fires of Gehenna through the merits and virtues of their parents?

Thus neither can a father deliver a transgressing son, nor will a mother of holy conduct give an immodest daughter the rewards of chastity. Conversely, the vices of parents will not harm their children, but the soul that has sinned will itself die.

Lot, dwelling in Sodom (Gen. 19), but a stranger in spirit and flesh, did not deliver his wife, who had looked back, but only his daughters, who perhaps had not sinned. And Josiah, a holy man, not only did not save the sinful people through his virtues, but also died in their sins (2 Kings 22 and 23).

If at times the Lord promises to show mercy to the descendants of Abraham and David on account of their forefathers, it must be noted that he does not spare those who persist in crimes, but those who repent, so that the conversion of the children may be aided by the merits of their fathers.

Since these things are so, and the prayer of such great men cannot save the sinful land from the individual punishments, the Lord God says: Because Jerusalem has sinned wickedly, I will bring four punishments upon her at once—the sword by which she is slaughtered by enemies; the famine which she suffers during the siege; the beasts by which fugitives are devoured in deserts and wild places; and pestilence, which always follows famine and scarcity, and for which the Vulgate edition has translated “death.” “I will bring these,” he says, “upon her, so that neither human beings nor animals remain in her.”

[Col. 0924B]

> “Drive them out (or: send them forth) from my presence, and let them go forth.”

Sinners do not depart from God by place but by will, although we also read that Adam and Cain were driven from the presence of God (Gen. 3 and 4).

> “And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go forth?’ you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity. And I will visit four kinds upon them, says the Lord: the sword for slaughter, dogs for tearing apart, and the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth for devouring and scattering.”

The prophecy of Ezekiel also demonstrates the four punishments to which the Jewish people were handed over (Ezek. 14): the sword, pestilence, famine, and beasts, together with captivity. Among the beasts, understand also the dogs and birds, to which the bodies were handed over to be torn apart, devoured, and scattered. For it could not happen that, when the Creator was neglected, all creation would not rise up against sinners.

[Col. 0924C]

> “And I will give them over to trembling (or: agitation) and distress for all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for all that he did in Jerusalem.”

We read in the Book of Chronicles that Manasseh returned to Jerusalem after his captivity and repentance and reigned there. But just as the merits of the saints descend to their descendants, as in the case of David and others, so the crimes of sinners reach their descendants if their children and grandchildren commit similar acts.

When he says, “I will give them over to trembling or agitation and distress for all the earth,” this was partly fulfilled under the Babylonians and is now fulfilled completely, when the impious people imitated the most wicked king who filled Jerusalem from gate to gate with the blood of the righteous. From this we learn that peoples are often destroyed through the crime of kings, rulers, and governors.

[Col. 0925A]

> “For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve for you? Or who will go to ask for your peace?”

(Orig.) I shall give an example. Suppose that some rebellious and treacherous enemy has been condemned against the emperor of this land. All mercy is withdrawn from him, lest, while someone pities the condemned man, he begin to offend the one who condemned him.

There are also some who add severity, so that they do not even grieve over him, carefully avoiding the appearance, through the sadness of their face, of being displeased with the king’s judgment.

If you understand the example, then consider the sinner condemned by God because of many sins, and see how, although innumerable angels preside over the human race, he is judged worthy of mercy by not even one of them.

Each of the angels perceives that it is God who has condemned him, that it is the Creator who rejects him, and that the sin is of such a kind that the merciful and compassionate God has in some sense been compelled to pronounce a sentence against him. They do not spare him, they do not grieve, they do not pity, and they do not return to ask peace for him.

(Hieron.) No one can plead with God, once offended, on behalf of sinners’ crimes, because a creature cannot be as merciful as the Creator, nor can one who is so unrelated to others spare them as the Lord spares his own.

(Orig.) Jerusalem, therefore, which added this also to its former crimes—that it crucified my Lord Jesus—and whose crime rose to such a height that the Savior himself said of it:

> “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

Therefore it was abandoned and remains desolate to the present time. The angels who had always assisted it, through whom even the law of Moses was given—“through angels in the hand of a mediator”—destroyed it and said: It has been overwhelmed by many crimes; it killed Jesus and laid hands upon the Lord our God.

As long as it committed lesser sins, we could plead for it, entreat the Lord, and spare it. But in this matter, who can spare it? If a man sins against another man, they will intercede for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will intercede for him?

> “Jerusalem has committed a great sacrilege; it has perpetrated a great crime.”

It has been made an object of God’s threat, and it is said to it:

> “Who will spare you, Jerusalem, or who will grieve over you?”

We will not grieve over Jerusalem, or over its calamities, or over all that people. Through their offense, salvation has come to us, to provoke them to jealousy. And because it sinned in such a way that, by the Lord’s voice, it was said, “Who will spare you, Jerusalem?” I too say to the murderess of my Lord: Who will spare you, Jerusalem, and who will grieve over you?

I shall now pass from the humility of the literal sense to the spiritual understanding, with reason opening the way before me, so that I may see how every soul worthy of God’s peace is now called Jerusalem.

After divine instruction, the one who had previously been Jebus became Jerusalem. History reports that the name of this place had been Jebus and that later, after its name was changed, it was called Jerusalem. The descendants of the Hebrews, however, say that Jebus is interpreted as “Trampled.”

Thus Jebus, “trampled,” our soul, trampled by opposing powers, was transformed and became Jerusalem, “Vision of Peace.” If, after being changed from Jebus into Jerusalem, you sin, and regard the blood of the covenant as common—as some have done—it will be said of you also:

> “Who will spare you, Jerusalem, and who will grieve over you?”

For who will grieve if you are such as to betray Jesus? Whenever any one of us sins—especially whoever commits great sins—he sins against Jesus. But if he also departs from the faith, he does spiritually to Christ what Jerusalem did bodily.

Therefore:

> “How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as common the blood of the New Testament by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

If you have trampled upon Jesus, the Son of God; if you have insulted the Spirit of grace, who will spare you? Who will grieve over you? Who will return to ask for the things that belong to your peace?

The sinful soul betrayed Jesus himself, who both prayed for and granted the things that belonged to peace. Who can thereafter pray for you, turning toward the things that are for your peace?

Knowing, therefore, that it is impossible for those who

> “have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift, have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away”

to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and expose him to contempt, let us strive with every effort lest it also be said of us:

> “Who will spare you, Jerusalem, or who will grieve over you, or who will return to ask for your peace?”

[Col. 0926C]

> “You have forsaken me, says the Lord; you have gone backward.”

(Hieron.) The reason is given why no one pities Jerusalem, grieves for it, or pleads for its peace. Although, according to the Apostle, it ought to forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead, it has instead turned backward and desired the meat of Egypt.

But consider what it means to walk backward, or to stretch forward toward what lies ahead.

(Orig.) The righteous, forgetting what lies behind, stretches forward to what lies ahead. The sinner remembers what lies behind and does not desire what lies ahead. Whoever remembers what lies behind transgresses the law of Jesus, who said:

> “Let him not turn back to take up his cloak.”

He is disobedient to his command. Remember Lot’s wife: she despises the Savior’s command:

> “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

[Col. 0926D]

> “And I will stretch out my hand over you and kill you. I have grown weary of pleading (or: of being entreated).”

For this the Septuagint translated: “I will by no means spare them any longer.”

(Hieron.) A hand stretched out is an indication of one who strikes; the killing signifies that the anger against sinners has reached completion. What he adds—“I have grown weary of pleading (or: of being entreated)”—has a twofold meaning: either that God has now become exhausted by repeatedly forgiving them, or that he is weary from continually calling them to salvation.

“‘And I will scatter them with a winnowing shovel at the gates of the land [Col. 0927A] (or: of my people). I have killed and destroyed my people, yet they have not turned back from their ways.’ What profit is there in my being entreated so often, when they do not turn back from their exceedingly evil ways, nor repent? For I scattered them like a winnowing shovel, so that I might cleanse my threshing floor; and I scattered them at the gates of the land, so that they might, as it were, tread the thresholds of hell. And I killed and destroyed my people, so that, compelled by the necessity of their evils, they might avoid the evils hanging over them.

“‘Her widows have been multiplied for me beyond the sand of the sea. I brought upon them, against the mother of a young man, a destroyer at midday; I sent suddenly upon the cities terror.’ By various remedies God desires to save sinners, so that those who had despised him when he was gentle might fear him when he threatened. Her widows were multiplied beyond the sand of the sea: when their husbands had been killed and their children lost, the mothers experienced the destroyer—not at night and by ambush, but in broad daylight—in order to show the open force of a stronger adversary. ‘I sent,’ he says, ‘upon the cities.’ There is no doubt that he means Judah and the sinful people: terror came suddenly upon them, so that, the more sudden the evil had been, the more difficult escape would be.

“‘She who bore seven (or: very many) has grown weak (or: has cast away), or has become empty; her soul has failed; her sun has set while it was still day (or: midday); she has been confounded and put to shame. And I will give her survivors to the sword, in the sight of their enemies, says the Lord.’ We have often said that the Hebrew word may mean either ‘seven,’ or an oath, or ‘very many.’ Hence the interpretation also differs: Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion render it ‘seven,’ while Symmachus has ‘very many.’ She who had been rich in children was suddenly made childless, perished in broad daylight, and was confounded in the desolation of her solitude. ‘But her remnant,’ he says, ‘I will hand over to the sword,’ so that no one might escape death and the wrath of God.

“Others refer this to the synagogue, which grew weak so that the multitude of the Church might increase, according to what is written: ‘The barren woman has borne seven (or: very many), and she who had many children has grown weak’ (1 Samuel 2). Thus also ‘her sun has set’—the sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing (Malachi 4)—and therefore she has been covered with eternal shame, losing her people by the spiritual sword.”

(Gregory.) Hence it is written in Job: “By day they encounter darkness, and as in night, so they will grope at midday” [Col. 0927D] (Job 5). By day they encountered darkness: those who, in the very presence of truth, were blinded by the error of unbelief. For by day one clearly sees, whereas by night our sight is obscured. Therefore the persecutors of our Redeemer, while they saw the miracles of divine power and nevertheless doubted his divinity, suffered darkness in the daytime, because they lost their sight in the light. Hence the Light himself admonishes them, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12). Hence also the prophet again took upon himself the voice of penitents, saying: “We stumbled at midday as though in darkness, and among the darkened as though dead” (Isaiah 21). Again he said: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said: Morning comes, and also night” [Col. 0928A].

For the watchman comes from the night, because the protector of the human race appeared manifest in the flesh; yet Judah, pressed down by the darkness of its unbelief, did not recognize him at all. Appropriately, from the watchman’s voice it is added: “Morning comes, and also night.” For through his foreknowledge a new light shone upon the world, and yet ancient blindness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. Well is it said: “As in night, so they will grope at midday.” By groping we seek what we do not see with our eyes. But the Jews had seen his manifest miracles and still sought him as though groping, when they said: “How long will you take away our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.”

“‘Woe is me, my mother, why did you give birth to me, a man of strife (or: of judgment), a man of discord (or: one who is judged), throughout the whole earth.’” (Jerome.) This may be understood by synecdoche of Jeremiah, since he was judged not throughout the whole world, but in the land of Judah. Yet it truly applies to the Lord and Savior, who speaks in the Gospel (John 9): “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” Of him it is written: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2).

For which philosopher, which Gentile, which heretic does not judge Christ, imposing laws upon his birth, passion, resurrection, and substance? Nor is it surprising that, according to the reality of the body he assumed, Christ should say: “Woe is me, my mother,” since elsewhere, plainly appropriate to his person, it is said: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest, and like a cluster of grapes at the vintage, with no ear of grain to eat as firstfruits.” And lest we suppose that the usefulness of the groans is being referred to the Word of God—who it is that mourns—the passage immediately continues: “Woe is me, my soul, for the one who turns back from the earth has perished.” This does not mean that we divide the persons, as the impious do, but that the one and same Son of God speaks now according to the flesh and now according to the Word of God.

(Origen.) For the Word of God does not suffer death, but the human being who experiences these emotions, as we have often explained. If you consider the martyrs condemned everywhere and brought from the individual churches before the tribunal, you will see how Jesus Christ is condemned through each martyr. For he himself is the one who is judged in those who bear witness to the truth. Receive this faithfully, knowing that he did not say that you were in prison when you were in prison, nor that you were hungry when you were hungry, nor that you were thirsty when you were thirsty, but that he spoke of himself: “I was in prison, and you came to me; I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25).

Thus, even if a Christian is condemned, he is not condemned for any other reason, nor for his crimes, but solely because he is a Christian: it is Christ who is condemned. Consequently, Jesus is condemned throughout the whole earth whenever the one who is condemned for his sake is condemned. Christ is heard not only before the judges of this age and the powers of tribunals; even when a Christian suffers slander from someone and is summoned to litigation, Christ is also judged unjustly then [Col. 0929A]. Everywhere Christ is condemned and distinguished: some condemn him, while others do not condemn him. If he is not condemned, he is received. You open the door to him, and he comes to you; you believe in him, and he eats with you. But if, upon hearing about the Christian religion, you do not receive it, you do nothing other than condemn Jesus as a liar, as a deceiver of human beings, as one who leads the world into error: “as one whom you bore—a man who is judged and distinguished throughout the whole earth.”

All who utterly refuse to believe in him condemn him; those who believe yet still doubt distinguish him. Christ therefore undergoes two things among human beings: he is condemned by unbelievers and distinguished by those who doubt. If you bear the image of the heavenly, having laid aside the image of the earthly, you are not the earth condemning him, nor the earth in which he is judged and distinguished [Col. 0929B].

“‘I have not lent at interest, nor has anyone lent at interest to me; all curse me.’” In place of this, the Septuagint has: “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me.” Theodotion has: “I was not indebted, nor was anyone indebted to me.”

Jeremiah proclaimed the divine commandments. No one paid attention to what he proclaimed. Therefore, like a physician who willingly and readily offers medicines to the sick, yet finds that they do not regard him as a sober practitioner of healing but act according to their own will, he says: “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me.” In a certain way, the one who treats obtains a benefit if he sees the fruit of his labor in the sick person; and through the joy of his mind he himself also gains an advantage, according to what is said elsewhere: “Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who listen.” Thus the teacher joyfully obtains this benefit from his hearers if they make progress by listening, reaping, as it were, the fruit of their salvation.

Jeremiah says that he has no place among the Jews; therefore, he says, no one has benefited me. For if what I say ought to benefit my hearers, but the hearers reject what is said, I say: “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me,” because I have not obtained the benefit obtained by the one who is made blessed while speaking into the ears of those who listen.

(Jerome.) But because the various editions have different words here, the sense of all of them, in the person of Christ, is this: No one offered himself to receive the coins worthy of me; nor did anyone lend to me by caring for the holy and the poor, making me his debtor; or: I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me. For no one wished to receive as much as I desired to give. “Nor has anyone benefited me”: the salvation of the creature is the Creator’s profit.

Or certainly: “I was not indebted, nor was anyone indebted to me.” No one gave me as much as I desired to receive, nor made me his debtor in anything. And what follows—“nor was anyone indebted to me”—has this meaning: how could anyone owe me interest when he did not deign to accept a loan? “All,” he says, “curse me.” For which heretic or person in error does not curse Christ, believing perverse things and blaspheming still more perversely?
