[Col. 0930A] “The Lord says: ‘Surely your remnant will be for good; surely I came to your aid in the time of affliction, in the time of tribulation and distress, against the enemy.’”

(Jerome.) These words may also be understood as spoken by Jeremiah, who was compelled to prophesy at a most evil time, when captivity was already imminent, and to endure harsh treatment from an unbelieving people. In response to what he had said above—“Woe is me, mother, why did you give birth to me, a man who is judged and distinguished throughout every age,” and the rest—the Lord replied: Do not consider the present, but the future. Your survivors and your last days will be for good. Indeed, even now, when your enemies desired to overwhelm you, I was present with you, and you were protected by my help.

This may be referred both to Jeremiah and, according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, to the Savior. In place of what we have translated according to the Hebrew—“All curse me”—up to the point where it says “in the time of tribulation against the enemy,” I find the following in the common edition: “My strength has failed among those who curse me; let it be, Lord, with those who direct them, if I have not stood by you in the time of their affliction and in the time of their tribulation, for good against the enemy.”

The sense is: “My strength has failed in the things that curse me,” for they do not understand my power, which is perfected in weakness; and the more they curse me, the more my strength has failed in them.

(Origen.) Let us see whether, with the sense and language he himself grants us, we can say something more manifest than what has been said: “He was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1). The “true light” is the Son of God, “which enlightened every human being coming into this world.” Whoever is rational becomes a participant in the true light. Every human being is rational. Since all human beings are rational, the light is diminished in some of them.

If you see a soul enslaved to vices and passions, you will see how the power of the Word fails in it. If you see one who is holy and just, you will see that each day the power of God advances and grows; and you will apply to such a person what is written about Jesus. For Jesus did not progress only in himself in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings; rather, in each of those who receive an increase of wisdom, age, and grace, Jesus also progresses in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings [Col. 0930D].

(Jerome.) The prophet or the Lord joins these words and says: “Let it be, Lord, with those who direct them”—that is, let the curses spoken by the enemies come upon me, and let them be directed toward good, if I did not stand before you in the time of their tribulation and distress, when the enemy was laying them waste and hastening to capture them; if I did not stand in your sight, plead with you for them, and say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

(Origen.) He stood before the Father as the propitiation for our sins and entreated him in the time of our evils. For he did not stand after the time of our affliction; rather, while we were still sinners, Jesus Christ died for us. And who is the enemy except the devil, who afflicted us and oppressed us under the yoke of slavery? Against him the Savior stood, and, liberating us from captivity, restored us to freedom. These things the Lord spoke prophetically.

(Jerome.) We also often discover Jeremiah in this book praying for the people.

“‘Will iron be allied with iron from the north, and bronze?’” Symmachus: “Will iron injure iron from the north, and bronze?” The Septuagint and Theodotion: “If iron will know, and the bronze covering?” The reason for the variation is clear. For the word written in the present passage, because of the ambiguity of its pronunciation, signifies both friendship and hostility. But if it is read with the letter that resembles another letter, it signifies knowledge and recognition.

The meaning is this: Do not grieve that the people are your enemy. Since you announce hard things, the one who is hard cannot love you. Or the reference is to the Babylonians, who come from the north: they are the hardest iron against this people, which is harder still and untamed like bronze; they cannot be joined in friendship. Or the very hard iron means that the people of Israel are unworthy of the knowledge of God, having reached such wickedness that they are enclosed by a harder metal, bronze [Col. 0931B].

“‘I will give your riches and your treasures for plunder, without payment (or: without a price), because of all your sins and throughout all your boundaries. And I will bring your enemies (or: I will make you serve your enemies) from a land that you do not know, because a fire has been kindled in my anger; it will burn against you.’”

“I will hand over,” he says, “all your substance to your enemies without any price, because of the sins you have committed throughout all your boundaries. Therefore I will bring your enemies—or make you serve them—in the land of the Chaldeans, because my fire, once kindled in my anger, will burn against you and cannot be extinguished. You supplied the material for your own burning, so that my fire might consume as wood, hay, and straw the things that are in you. Thus the cause of the burning is not in the Lord, but in those who supplied fuel for the blaze.”

(Origen.) But who are these treasures of sinners that God grants for plunder and gives up in exchange for all their sins? Are they perhaps the treasures that they stored up for themselves on earth? Each human being stores up treasure for himself—if he is a sinner, on earth; if he is righteous, in heaven—as the Gospel teaches us. Or does the passage mean something of this kind? Behold, Jeremiah is one treasure; Isaiah is another treasure; Moses was a treasure, and so were the others. God took these treasures away from the people, and through Christ, who said, “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21), he gave them to us.

“Therefore I will give your treasures for plunder because of your sins”—your treasures were given to us, because the words of God were first entrusted to them and afterward assigned to us. We assert that what is written—“The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits”—has already been fulfilled, not in the sense that Scripture has been taken away from them. For they have the Law and the Prophets; they have the books of the divine writings, but without understanding. Thus the kingdom of God has been taken away from them, since the meaning of Scripture has been removed from them and the interpretation of the Law and the Prophets has ceased among them.

They read everything and do not understand, that prophecy having already been fulfilled after the Lord’s coming: “Say to this people: ‘You will hear by hearing and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not know; for the heart of this people has grown dull’” (Isaiah 6). Likewise, what is said by Isaiah: “The Lord will take away from Judah and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, the giant and the warrior, the judge, and the prophet, and the arbitrator, and the prudent architect, and the wise hearer” (Isaiah 3).

The Lord took all these away from them and handed them over to us, who are from the Gentiles, if only we are willing to receive them: “I will give your treasures for plunder, in exchange for all your sins and throughout all your boundaries.” What he says is this: all these things have been repaid to you because of your sins, which have spread throughout all your boundaries. For there is no boundary of that people that has not been filled with its sins, nor could every boundary fail to be filled with their sins.

As far as they were able, they killed righteousness; they killed wisdom, if Christ is wisdom; they killed truth, if Christ is truth. Therefore, because of their cruel outcries against the Son of God, they lost all these things. And when Jesus Christ my Lord rose again, he did not appear further to his murderers, but was shown victorious from the dead to those who believed in him [Col. 0932C].

After the words of threat that we have explained to the people, the one who had prayed above completes his prayer and joins what follows to the preceding words:

“‘You know, Lord; remember me, visit me, and protect me from those who persecute me. Do not receive me in your patience. Know that I have suffered reproach for you. Your words were found, and I ate them (or: consume those who reject your words). And your word became for me the joy and gladness of my heart, because your name was invoked over me, Lord God of hosts.’”

(Jerome.) The words “You know” are not found in the Septuagint. Blessed is that conscience which suffers reproach for God. Hence he says: “Your words were found,” the words that you spoke through my mouth, “and I ate them”—that is, they were turned into food for me. Or, according to Symmachus: “I received them,” so that they might be turned for me into joy, though earlier they had been a reproach. Hence the Babylonians also confess that what Jeremiah had foretold as future has been fulfilled.

Or the sense is this: I experienced distress and endured the miseries of the persecuting people; nevertheless, I rejoiced.

(Origen.) The Savior can also say these things: he suffered persecution from the people up to the cross, but not in patience. What does “not in patience” mean? You had always been long-suffering toward this sinful people. But because it also raised its insolence against me, do not be long-suffering. And in fact God was not patient. If you consider the times of the Lord’s passion and of Jerusalem’s downfall, when it was overthrown, you will see how God did not use patience toward them. For from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar until the overthrow of the Temple there are counted forty-two years, because a short period ought to have been left for repentance, on account of those who were going to believe through the signs and wonders of the apostles.

“Know how I received reproach for you from those who despise your words.” It may be that the prophet says this, despised by the sinful people against whom he was preaching. For he says elsewhere: “I have completed my days in derision.” He therefore suffers reproach from those who disdain to hear the words of God and asks that he may have God’s help, saying: “Know how I have received reproach for you from those who despise your words; consume them.”

The prophet may also say this, but it suits the Savior more, after whose passion came the consummation of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Jewish people. And “your word will be for me a joy”—he does not say “is,” but “will be.” For in the present time it brings me prisons, exiles, insults, and labors. But the end of all these things will be joy, and your word will be for me the joy and gladness of my heart, because your name has been invoked over me, Lord Almighty. Even if Christ says this, it does not conflict with the meaning, for the Father’s name has been invoked over him.

“‘I did not sit in the council of those who play, and I rejoiced (or: feared) before the face of your hand; I sat alone, because you filled me with bitterness. Why has my pain become perpetual (or: why are those who trouble me strengthened), and my wound incurable has refused to be healed (or: my wound is strong—how shall I be healed)? I have become like deceitful waters without faith (or: like treacherous water that cannot be trusted).’”

The Hebrews believe that these words are spoken in the person of Jerusalem: that she sat alone, was filled with bitterness, and her pain became perpetual. And just as waters pass away, so the words of the prophets, by which they had falsely promised her prosperity, passed away deceitfully.

It is better, however, to understand these words as spoken in the person of the prophet, or as the words of a holy man who did not sit in the council, or secret gathering, of those who play—either because he feared the hand of God hanging over him, or rather because he gloried in having no share with evildoers. “I sat alone,” he says, according to what is written: “I did not sit with the council of vanity, and I will not enter with those who act unjustly. I hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the unjust” (Psalm 25). And elsewhere: “I am solitary until I pass over. From the face,” he says, “of your hand I sat alone” (Psalm 140), while I fear you and continually await your hand hanging over me.

I did not wish to sit in the council of those who play, but I consumed my bitterness so that I might prepare joy for myself in the future. Nor did I have intervals of relief from my pain; I was oppressed by unbroken misery, so that I expected no remedies [Col. 0934A]. For those who troubled me prevailed, and my wound became strong. Yet I had this consolation: that it was like deceitful and passing water. For just as passing waters, while they flow, appear and then slip away, so, with your help, the whole onslaught of my enemies passed away.

(Origen.) “‘I did not sit,’ he says, ‘in the council of those who play, but I feared before the face of your hand.’” Our Savior also did not sit in the council of those who play. Teaching that he had risen, he says: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13). For the divine Word left the council of the Jews and gathered for himself another council from the Gentiles.

As for what he says, “I sat alone,” the statement itself, without exposition, edifies the hearers: when there is a multitude of sinners and it cannot tolerate anyone living righteously with it, it is not unfitting to flee their gatherings and imitate the prophet who says: “I sat alone.” Imitate Elijah also, who lamented pitifully (1 Kings 19): “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug up your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek to take my life.”

“‘I sat alone,’ he says, ‘because I have been filled with bitterness.’” If the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted, it is advantageous for you, withdrawing from every sweetness, to be filled with bitterness in the present age. And it should be noted that he does not say, “I ate bitterness,” but “I have been filled with bitterness”—that is: the weight of the persecutions of the world has pressed upon me so greatly that I became full of bitterness.

“Why are those who trouble me strengthened against me?” Jeremiah suffered much from those who did not wish to hear the truth. And in this world they were stronger than he, because the kingdom of God is not from this world, but from another region of the living, as the Savior says (John 18): “If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would labor so that I would not be handed over to the Jews.”

Thus they are strengthened against him in this world. And because the righteous person is weaker than those who persecute him, consider the sufferings of the martyrs. The judge sits on lofty tribunals, belching and amid luxuries as he pronounces sentences; the Christian, in whom Christ dwells, is judged, filled with bitterness, and subjected even unto death, while his enemies are strengthened against him.

As for what he says, “My wound is firm”—whether you understand it of the Lord’s cross, of the righteous, or specifically of Jeremiah, it will not conflict with the meaning—“My wound is firm; how shall I be healed?” The Savior too can say, “How shall I be healed?” announcing his resurrection after the wounds of the nails.

(Origen.) And so can the righteous person, who receives healing after his wounds. Again, what he says—“I sat alone from the face of your hand, because you filled me with threat”—may be understood in this way: the face of God’s hand is that stroke of righteous judgment which drove the proud human being from paradise (Genesis 3) and excluded him into the blindness of the present exile. His threat is the terror of the punishment still present. After the face of the hand, threats still terrify us, because the punishment of the present exile has struck us through the experience of judgment; and if we do not cease from sinning, it still consigns us to eternal punishments [Col. 0935A].

(Jerome.) Would that the Lord grant us also not to sit in the council of those who play and of those who think nothing of the future, nor to be crushed by adversity, but always to fear through the judgment of God and to say with the prophet: “I sat alone, because I have been filled with bitterness.” Therefore let him rejoice in the present age; the text concerning “the counsel of the wise and the hidden, secret gathering of those who play” is syntactically uncertain. May it be good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God, to be filled with reproaches, and to await the judgment of my judge. When its end arrives, experience will show that all sadness and bitterness have receded like flowing waters.

“‘Therefore, thus says the Lord: If you turn back, I will restore you, and you will stand before my face. And if you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be like my mouth. They will turn to you, and you will not turn to them. And I will make you for this people a strong bronze wall; they will fight against you, but they will not prevail, because I am with you to save you and rescue you, says the Lord. And I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the hand of the strong (or: pestilential).’”

It is evident that the preceding words were spoken not by Jerusalem but by the prophet. The Lord answered him: If you turn the people away from their sins, I too will turn you from tribulation to joy, and you will stand before my face, as angels stand in the presence of God, daily seeing his face.

“And if you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be like my mouth.” Do not think, he says, that there is no reward for a good work if, through your words, you separate my saints from the number of sinners. You will be like my mouth and will be joined to my commandments. For they ought to imitate you, not you them.

Nor should you be afraid and say: “Why has my pain become perpetual, and my wound strong”—or incurable—“so that I despair of being healed?” For I will make you like a bronze wall, exceedingly strong, so that you may resist the adversaries with all your strength; you will have me as your helper, and I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked—or pestilential—and redeem you either by my blood or, for the present, by my help.

Let us consider how great a reward belongs to the teacher’s speech if he is able to free someone from error and lead him out from the number of sinners.

(Origen.) But what is said in another translation—“If you turn back, I will restore you”—seems to me to signify a certain mystery in the word “I will restore you.” For no one can be restored except to the place from which he had previously departed. For example, if a member of my body has been separated from its framework, the physician attempts to restore it to its former place. If someone has been separated from his homeland and sent into exile, and afterward, through the clemency of those able to release exiles, is restored to freedom, he returns from where he had been expelled. A soldier who has been cast out of his rank is likewise restored to his rank if he receives pardon.

So now it is said to the mortal race—that is, to us human beings, who had turned away from God: “If you turn back, I will restore you.” For the end of the promise is restoration, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 3), “until the times of the restoration of all things,” which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets in Christ Jesus.

CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the future calamity of the Jews; concerning the Christian people that will come from the Gentiles.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘You shall not take a wife, and you shall not have sons or daughters in this place. For thus says the Lord concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them, and concerning their fathers from whose stock they were born: They will die in this land by deaths from disease; they will not be mourned, and they will not be buried. They will be like dung upon the face of the earth, and by sword and famine they will be consumed; and their corpses will be food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth.’”

(Jerome.) If, at the time of the imminent captivity, the prophet is forbidden to take a wife, lest he should have the tribulation of the flesh and, in addition to his own grief, be tormented by the miseries of his wife and children, how much more does the Apostle command (1 Corinthians 7), since the time has been shortened and the consummation is near, that even those who have wives should live as though they had none.

Hence the criticism of the new heretics is superfluous, for we have shown that second and third marriages do not proceed from the Law, but from concession. For it is one thing to do what is good in itself; it is another for something to be permitted so that you may not do worse things. He himself also gives the reasons why he wishes young widows to marry, adding: “For some have already turned back after Satan” (1 Timothy 5). At the same time, he is a teacher of continence and perpetual chastity, and, blasphemously making himself equal to God, praises marriages of three or four unions. I would call these not so much marriages as consolations of misery and the last plank of shipwrecks—unless perhaps he grants indulgence to his Amazons so that, even into decrepit old age, they may experience the wars of lust.

The reason why the prophet is forbidden to take a wife is evident: with the siege near, everyone would perish by pestilence, sword, and famine, and the number of the dying would be so great that the duty of burial would be overwhelmed; instead, the corpses would lie in a dung heap, to be torn apart by birds and beasts. It should also be noted that wasting away through diseases and prolonged illness is an expression of God’s anger. Thus Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, was consumed by illness (2 Chronicles 21); and the Apostle teaches that those who have violated holy things become sick, waste away, and die (1 Corinthians 11).

“‘For thus says the Lord: You shall not enter a house of feasting, nor go to mourn, nor console them, because I have taken away my peace from this people, says the Lord, mercy and compassions; and great and small will die in this land. They will not be buried, nor will they be mourned; they will not cut themselves, nor will baldness be made for them. They will not break bread among them in mourning, to console them over the dead; nor will they give them the cup to drink, to console them over their father and mother. And you shall not enter a house of feasting, to sit with them and eat and drink.’”

The Apostle commanded that one should not even eat with those who turn away from God (1 Corinthians 5); and, even more strongly: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to such a person” (2 John 10). The Savior also forbids the apostles to greet anyone on the road (Luke 10). Hence Elisha forbids Gehazi to offer a greeting while he is going to heal the boy (2 Kings 4).

It is customary to bring food to mourners and prepare a feast, which the Greeks call περίδειπνα (“funeral feasts”), and which our people commonly call parentalia, because funeral rites are celebrated for parents. Divine Scripture also says elsewhere: “Give wine to those who are in mourning” (Proverbs 31), so that they may forget their grief.

The prophet is therefore commanded not to console anyone from the people, not to join the banquets of God’s enemies, and not to celebrate funeral rites over the deaths of the dead. For it is one thing to die according to the common law of nature; it is another for God’s judgment to have killed someone.

“I have taken away,” he says, “my peace from this people”; they are unworthy of mercy, and I will spare no age, but great and small alike will perish, so that they will also lack burial: “They will not cut themselves,” he says, “nor will baldness be made for them.”

This was a custom among the ancients, and it persists to the present day among some Jews: in mourning they cut their arms and make baldness. We read that Job also did this (Job 1 and 2). Hence the prophet is told not to break bread among them, nor enter to console them over the dead; not to give them drink, nor enter the house of feasting, nor associate with those who have been prepared for God’s judgment [Col. 0937C].

But if this is said about mourners, what will happen to heretics, whose word spreads like cancer and who daily lay out funerals in the Church for those whom they have deceived?”

“‘For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will remove from this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. And when you announce to this people all these words, and they say to you: “Why has the Lord spoken against us all this great evil? What is our iniquity, and what is our sin that we have committed against the Lord our God?” you shall say to them: “Because your fathers abandoned me,” says the Lord, “and went after foreign gods, served them, and worshiped them; but me they abandoned, and they did not keep my law. Yet you have acted worse than your fathers.”’

When the Church sins, every joy and all gladness are taken away from her—of which the Apostle says: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV)—as well as the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, concerning which it is written: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III). But if, he says, the people ask you why they are suffering these things and seek the causes of their misery, you shall answer them: “Because your fathers abandoned me,” says the Lord—those who preside over you in the churches and went after foreign gods, whose god is their belly, and greed, and luxury, and glory in their shame; and they served them. For by whatever someone is overcome, of that he is also the slave. “And they worshiped them”: for each person worships what he loves.

“And me they abandoned, and they did not keep my law.” It is the particular duty of priests not only to teach the law but also to practice it, so that they may instruct the peoples subject to them and the flock entrusted to them not merely by words but by examples. And lest they perhaps say, “The sentence is unjust: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge,” he adds: “Yet you have acted worse than your fathers,” so that just punishments may be inflicted upon those who have sinned worse than their fathers.

“‘For behold, each one walks after the perversity of his evil heart, so as not to listen to me. And I will cast you out of this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers know, and there you will serve foreign gods day and night, who will not give you rest.’”

Once abandoned by the Lord, they do what is unfitting: they go after the desires of their evil heart, from which the worst thoughts proceed. Therefore they are separated from the Church, so that they may go into a distant land which neither they nor their fathers knew before they sinned, and there serve foreign gods. These are not gods, but are considered gods through the error of those who worship them. By adding “day and night,” he shows the continual persistence of sinners in their wickedness, since by day they serve their crimes and by night their lust. “Who will not give you rest.” There is no doubt that he signifies the false gods, of whom he said: “And there you will serve foreign gods.” Whatever, therefore, we sin, whatever we do day and night, and whatever evil deeds we commit, is the rule of demons, who never give us rest but always drive us to increase our sins and heap sin upon sin.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 0937]

The Lord is pious and merciful, just and true, patient and greatly merciful. Knowing the frailty of the human race and the changeability of the earthly heart, he mingles times with times, blandishments with terrors, hard things with gentle things, and joyful things with sorrowful ones. Hence at one time he threatens sinners with punishments, while at another he promises consolation to the afflicted. This is why, after the Lord had earlier commanded sinful Judea through the prophet, saying: “Behold, I will remove from this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride,” and so forth, he subsequently added words of consolation. For if he had always commanded harsh things and never interspersed gentle ones, he might drive them into despair and take away from them every hope of salvation. Therefore it now follows:

“‘Therefore behold, days are coming,’ says the Lord, ‘when it will no longer be said: “As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of Egypt,” but: “As the Lord lives, who brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands to which I had cast them”; and I will bring them back into their land, which I gave to their fathers.’”

(Jerome.) The future restoration of the people of Israel is clearly foretold, followed by the mercy which, according to the literal sense, was partly fulfilled under Zerubbabel, Jesus the high priest, and Ezra; according to the spiritual understanding, it is described as being fulfilled more truly and perfectly in Christ. A time will come, he says, when it will no longer be said that the people were brought back from Egypt by Moses and Aaron, but that they were brought back from the land of the north, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, released the captives. “And from all the lands,” he says: this will not be fulfilled in the time of Cyrus but at the end of the age, as the Apostle says: “After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). We can also understand this of the persecutions that have befallen our people from the days of Nero—of whom the Apostle writes, “And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (II Tim. IV)—to the time of Maximinus. In what way the Lord had mercy on his people and brought them back into their land is beyond doubt: namely, into the Church, which he gave to their fathers, the apostles and apostolic men.

“‘Behold, I will send many fishermen,’ says the Lord, ‘and they will fish for them. And after this I will send them many hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain and from every hill and from the clefts of the rocks, because my eyes are upon all their ways. They have not been hidden from my face, and their iniquity has not been concealed from my eyes. And I will repay first double their iniquities and their sins, with which they polluted my land through the carcasses of their idols and filled my inheritance with their abominations.’”

There are different interpretations of this chapter. The Jews believe that the Chaldeans are signified, described under the name of fishermen, and afterward the Romans, who are compared with hunters and hunted the unhappy people from the mountains, hills, and clefts of the rocks. The Lord says that he did this because he looked upon their ways and repaid the iniquities with which they had polluted the land by venerating images and defiling his inheritance with the abominations of idols.

Our people, however, more correctly and properly think that the prophet foretold these things concerning the future. Since he had said above, “I will bring them back into their land, which I gave to their fathers,” he now shows how they are to be brought back: first, he sends apostles, to whom the Savior said, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV); afterward, hunters, whom we can understand either as ecclesiastical men or as angels. When the time of consummation arrives, they will hunt the saints from the mountains of lofty doctrines, from the hills of good works, and from the clefts of the rocks—that is, from the apostles and apostolic men.

For not only is Christ the rock, but he also granted to the apostle Peter that he should be called a rock (I Cor. X; Matt. XVI). Those resting in his understanding are rightly said to have been transferred from the rock. He shows that either the apostles or those who are afterward to be hunted had sins and received double their iniquities. “For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten much” (Luke XII). It should be known that the Hebrew has “first,” while the Septuagint edition omits it. When he says, “I will repay first double their iniquities and their sins,” he suggests that after they have received evil things, they will also receive good things.

Those who are afterward to be transferred polluted the Lord’s land with the carcasses of their idols and filled his inheritance with their abominations, so that the whole world might become subject to God and be preserved not by its own merit but by his mercy. The words we have given here from the Hebrew, “They have not been hidden from my face,” are not found in the Septuagint.

(Origen.) Therefore, when you have been drawn out through the disciples of the Lord from the waves of this age, change the vices of the body and change the perceptions of your soul. You are not that fish which moves about in false waters; rather, drawn out from the deep whirlpool, turn toward better things, according to the apostolic saying (II Cor. III): “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as though from the Spirit of the Lord.”

And when you have been freed by the apostles and disciples of Jesus from the waves of the sea, do not seek the deep, but come to the mountains, the prophets; come to the hills, the righteous. Let your dwelling be there, so that when the day of death arrives, hunters may be sent. Let some of the fishermen who have been appointed over the taking up of souls receive you, together with the other saints, from the hill, the mountain, and the higher place.

Nor can these hunters be permitted to take people from anywhere else than from the mountains and hills. What follows is, “from the clefts of the rocks.” From this, how can we understand rocks and the clefts of rocks? I come to Exodus and seek an occasion for interpretation; there I find that Moses wished to see God, and that God promised him, saying: “Behold, I place you in the cleft of the rock, and you shall see my back, but you shall not see my face” (Exod. XXXIII).

If you consider what is called the rock there, and what is the opening of the rock in which Moses stands upon the rock, and from the cleft of the rock beholds God through the opening of the rock, you will understand the other rocks and the openings of the rocks as well. What, then, is the rock? The Lord Jesus Christ: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (I Cor. X); and in the thirty-ninth psalm it is said, “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX).

What is the opening of the rock? Behold God: in God the Father, the Word who is God—you will see the whole rock. Behold the dispensation of the assumed body: you will see the opening of the rock, through which the human gaze, according to the capacity of its weakness, looks upon the back of God.

For this is what he says: “And you shall see my back.” I have found one cleft of one rock; I seek other rocks and other clefts. I come to the choir of the prophets and apostles and say: all imitators of Christ are rocks, just as he who taught is the rock. And just as he has an opening through which God’s back is seen, so each of the righteous who, through his words, opens a way to understanding God has made himself an opening of the rock.

Since you do not know when the hunters will be sent, beware lest you ever descend from the mountain, leave the hills, or come out from the clefts of the rocks. For if you are found outside, you will hear what those outside deserve to hear: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII.)

You observe the one descending from the mountains and hills; you observe the one standing outside the opening of the rock: see how he wanders and considers good those things which are nothing, saying, “I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up” (ibid.). He judged grain and the usefulness of earthly fruits to be good, not knowing that true goods are not born in the cursed earth but in the heavenly regions.

He will treasure for himself on earth because he believes that treasures are on earth. But if someone, taking up his cross, follows the Lord Jesus and treasures for himself in heaven, it is not said to him, “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you.” Rather, the hunters, coming and seeking living creatures from the mountains and hills and from the clefts of the rocks, will receive him also together with them and carry him from the hunt to the higher realms of blessedness.

“‘Because my eyes are upon all their ways.’” God has his eyes upon all the ways of such people—those who dwell in the mountains, walk upon the hills, and live in the clefts of the rocks. “They have not hidden themselves from my face.” Those who are holy do not hide themselves from the face of the Lord; the unjust, however, hide themselves from his face. After Adam transgressed the heavenly commandment, “he heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the afternoon, and he hid himself” (Gen. III). The holy person does not do this, but through the conscience of his actions has confidence before God: “If our conscience does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him.”

Yet although Adam had sinned, his mind had not fallen entirely into perfect wickedness; therefore he hid himself from the face of God. But when the most wicked fratricide perceived what he had done (Gen. IV), “he went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod.” If you compare the two kinds of evil, it is better to hide from the face of God than to flee from him. In one person a wound of conscience has been inflicted: seeking darkness and secrecy, he is unable to raise his eyes to heaven. In the other, however, insolence born of despair neglects God.

“‘They have not hidden themselves, therefore, from my face, nor have they hidden their iniquities from my eyes.’” Those whom we mentioned above as righteous—those who did not hide themselves from the face of God—were at one time in sins, when they were in the sea from which the fishermen drew them out. Therefore, lest they suppose that they came from the deep to the mountains not through God’s mercy but through their own merit, the divine word admonishes them—and in them us—of their former sin. For this reason, after prosperous and happy things, it introduces sorrowful ones: “Nor have their iniquities been hidden from my eyes; and I will repay them first double their injustices.”

Some have removed the word “first,” either because they did not understand what was written, or because the Septuagint translators, as with other passages, wished to remove it according to their own arrangement. God knows. Comparing this passage with the other editions, we find it written: “And I will repay them first double their injustices.” This shows that, even if they have been made worthy of God’s blessedness by their later deeds, nevertheless, because they once sinned and were not free from human vices, they must first receive what is due for their offenses. And see whether the reasoning is not true.

Who does not receive punishment for sins? Surely the one who, after belief and baptism, hears the Lord saying, “Your sins are forgiven you; sin no more” (Matt. IX; John VIII). But if, after the washing and forgiveness of sins, we return again to our former filth, and, still imperfect in understanding, depart from the footsteps of the apostles, or commit some injustices, or even have certain sins mixed into our very righteousness, let us consider what will happen to us. When we depart from the present age, if we possess either vices or virtues, will we receive rewards for the virtues and have the sins we knowingly committed forgiven? Or will we be punished for our offenses and receive no rewards for our virtues?

Neither of these alternatives is true. We will be tormented for our sins and receive rewards for the righteousness we deserve. For if, after the foundation of Jesus Christ, you have built upon it in your heart not only gold, silver, and precious stone—if indeed you possess any gold or silver—but also wood, hay, and stubble, what do you wish to happen to you when your soul has been taken from the body? Are you to enter the holy places with your wood, hay, and stubble and pollute the kingdom of God? Or are you, because of the wood, hay, and stubble, to remain outside and receive no reward for the gold, silver, and precious stone? But neither is this just.

What, then, follows except that first, because of the wood, fire should be given to you, so that it may consume the hay, wood, and stubble? For our God is said to be a consuming fire among those who are able to understand divine things. And when the prophet says, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV), he does not specify what it consumes, leaving you to infer it from clearer passages. This fire does not consume what remains according to God’s image and likeness, nor does it consume his own creatures, but the wood, hay, and stubble that have been built upon them.

“First” has necessarily been added. First, because of injustices, we endure torments; afterward, because of righteousness, we are crowned. For the just things should not be given first and the sins repaid afterward, so that when the good things have ceased, the vices might remain eternally. Rather, we will first receive evil things and afterward good things, so that, once the vices have been removed, the virtues may remain forever.

All, therefore, whoever among us have within ourselves material for that fire, will first receive what is due for our offenses. But one of the hearers will say to me: “Explain also what follows: ‘double.’” Let it be granted that I receive punishment for sins, so that what the Apostle said may be fulfilled (I Cor. III): “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.” Why, then, do I receive double punishment for sins?

The answer is this: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten much” (Luke XII). It is fitting that those who are from the Gentiles receive single punishment for sins, but that we receive double punishment, according to the Apostle, who says (Heb. X): “For if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” Rather, there is a fearful expectation of judgment and fire; the zeal of God will consume all adversaries.

“‘Lord, my strength, and my stronghold, and my refuge in the day of tribulation’ (or: of evils).”

(Jerome.) All human strength, without the power of God—which is Christ—is considered weakness and nothing. Therefore we must flee to God and say: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation” (Ps. LXXXIX). And elsewhere: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. XC).

The day of tribulation, or of evils, is to be understood as the day of which the Apostle also says: “That he might deliver us from the present evil age” (Gal. I); and, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. V).

[Col. 0943C] “‘To you the nations will come from the ends of the earth, and they will say: “Truly our fathers possessed a lie, vanity that did not profit them.”’”

The Septuagint: “To you the nations will come from the ends of the earth, and they will say: ‘How falsely our fathers possessed idols, and there is no profit in them.’”

After Israel has been cast out and transferred through fishermen and hunters, the multitude of the Gentiles is consequently called to faith and confesses that it—or its fathers—had previously lived in error.

(Origen.) Who are these who come from the ends? Some are the first of the earth, and others are the last. Who are the first? The wise of this age, the noble, the rich, and the eminent. Who are the last? “God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the strong, and the things that were not, to destroy the things that are” (I Cor. III). “The nations will come from the ends of the earth,” as if he had said: From those people who are last upon the earth—from the foolish, the ignoble, and the despised—and they will say: “How falsely our fathers possessed images, and there is no profit in them.” This is not because idols are also true, in contrast to which they are now called false; rather, the idols, which are false by nature, have no profit in them.

“‘Can a man make gods for himself, and they are not gods?’”

(Jerome.) This too is spoken by the nations who came to the Savior from the ends of the earth, reproving both their own ignorance and that of their ancestors, through which they thought that gods could be made by human beings, although it belongs to God to make human beings.

(Origen.) People make gods for themselves not only from bodily images but also from the heart. Those who imagine another creator besides the God of the universe, another Holy Spirit, another Christ, and other ages besides those we see—these people have made gods for themselves and worshiped the works of their hands. All philosophers who have promulgated various doctrines, and all heretics who have become authors of alternative beliefs about God for wretched mortals, have made idols for themselves. They have considered the will of the soul to be God and, turning aside, have worshiped the works of their hands, thinking that what they had imagined was true.

All, therefore, who make gods for themselves either from visible matter or from false doctrines are now rebuked by the divine word, which says: “Can a man make gods for himself, and these are not gods?”

“‘Therefore behold, I will show them this time; I will show them my hand and my power, and they shall know that my name is the Lord.’”

(Jerome.) The hand of God, through which he accomplished all things, and the power of which the Apostle said, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I), are shown to the Gentiles through the completed passion of the Son. Beautifully he says, “I will show them this time.” I will show them openly, not as formerly in shadow, image, and prophecy of future things, so that after they have come to know me, they may know my name and hear from the Son: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people” (John XVII).

# CHAPTER XVII  
## On the obstinacy of the Jews; the one who trusts in man is cursed, while the one who trusts in God is blessed; on diabolical destruction; on Jeremiah’s imprecation against the sinful people; on observance of the Sabbath

[Col. 0944C]

“‘The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point, engraved upon the breadth of their heart (or: upon the breast of their heart), and upon the horns of their altars (or: shrines).’”

It was said above concerning the nations that had been converted to the Lord: “Behold, I will show them this time; I will show them my hand and my power.” Now he speaks concerning Israel, which has been cast aside: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point,” and so forth. Why this was omitted by the Septuagint, I do not know, unless perhaps they spared their own people, just as it is evident that they did the same in Isaiah: “Cease, then, from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is esteemed as exalted” (Isa. II). There are many such passages; if I wished to set them all out, I would need not merely one book but books.

The sins of the nations have been erased because, having turned to the Lord, they heard from the ends of the earth: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples; for his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever” (Ps. CXVI). And concerning those of whom he had said to Moses: “Leave me, that I may destroy this people and make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII).

But the sin of Judah, indelible and, so to speak, incapable of being erased by any means, is written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point. In Hebrew this is called *shamir*—not a fingernail called by that name, but an adamantine stone which, because it is unconquered and unbreakable, received this name. It possesses such brilliance and smoothness that one can write upon it with an iron stylus without any impediment: the hard material of iron writes upon the harder adamantine tablet, and what has been written remains forever.

For they themselves said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Thus the iron stylus signifies a firm sentence, while the diamond point signifies an eternal end. The sin of Judah is said to be written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point because the guilt of the Jews is preserved by the firm judgment of God for an infinite end. Hence it is engraved, or inscribed, upon the horns of their altars or shrines, so that the works of sacrilege may endure in everlasting memory.

But if this is so, where is that delirious old woman’s fabrication that a person can be without sin if he wishes, and that God’s commandments are easy?

(Origen.) Since it is difficult for anyone to confess himself evil, the Jews, who falsified certain copies, substituted “their sin” in this passage for “the sin of Judah.” But if you consider it figuratively, as we have often shown, that Judas is called Christ, perhaps “the sin of Judah” is our sin, since we believe in Christ who is from the tribe of Judah and born from his stock according to the flesh.

But if you wish to understand it in a more sacred sense as spoken about the betrayer Judas—“The sin of Judas is written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point, engraved upon the breast of their heart”—what follows, “their,” will oppose you. Therefore, as we said above, these things apply to us who sin: our sins are not written somewhere externally, but are engraved upon the consciousness of the heart with an iron stylus and carved with a diamond point.

That our sins are written upon the breast, understand from what follows. Before I commit sin, no image of sin exists in my heart. But once my conscience has taken on the image of sin, I possess its form, and the pageant of my offense is continually painted before the eyes of my heart. If my sin were written in ink, perhaps I could erase it. But now it is written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point; it is written upon the breast of my heart, so that I may come before the tribunal and that what Christ prophesied may be fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing is concealed that will not be made known” (Matt. X).

The consciousness of my breast will be laid bare, and when the heart is opened, the letters of my sins will be seen—letters written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point. Thus the whole multitude of sinners will read upon my breast the images of my sins, marked there. “For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed,” and “the thoughts of the accusing or defending will mutually accuse one another.” And: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts.”

To whom will this be revealed? Certainly not to him, who knows all things before they happen, but to those who will come with him. On account of the purity of their mind and body, they follow the Lamb, and he will show them the offenses expressed in the sinner’s heart, so that the righteous may rise in glory, but sinners in disgrace and eternal confusion.

“‘When their children remember their altars and their groves, their leafy trees upon the high mountains, sacrificing in the field, I will give your strength and all your treasures for plunder; your high places, because of your sins throughout all your borders. And you will be left alone, apart from your inheritance which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, because you kindled a fire in my anger; it will burn forever.’”

(Jerome.) These words also are not found in the Septuagint, for the same reason, I think, that we mentioned above: namely, lest an eternal sentence remain against them. “You will be left,” he says, “apart from your inheritance which I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know”—either under the Babylonians or, as is more true, under the Romans. For they themselves kindled the fire and provoked the most merciful Lord to anger; the fire of his fury will burn forever.

I am ashamed of the dispute among our people, who criticize the Hebrew truth. The Jews read these things against themselves, while the Church does not know what is in its own favor. Therefore let us, who are sons of the apostles, remember the iniquities of the former people and testify that they have suffered these things justly.

The high places, called *bamoth* in Hebrew, can also be understood against heretics, who have set their mouths in heaven [on high], and whose tongue has passed over the earth. They have burst into such madness that they alone have remained without the grace of the Holy Spirit and have lost the Lord’s inheritance—namely, the former truth of faith. Hence an eternal fire and slavery to demons, who are enemies and avengers, are prepared for them.

“‘Thus says the Lord: Cursed is the man who trusts (or: places his hope) in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He will be like a tamarisk in the desert and will not see good when it comes, but will dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a salt land and an uninhabited place.’”

(Jerome.) If every person who trusts in man is cursed, while Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior as holy and exalted above all virtues, nevertheless confess him to be a man, then they will be cursed, since they place their hope in man.

But if it is objected to us that we too believe in the one who says, “Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God; Abraham did not do this. You do the works of your father” (John VIII), we will answer with the apostolic statement: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way” (II Cor. V).

Finally, the same Apostle writes at the beginning of his Letter to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me” (Gal. I). For if death has been swallowed up in victory (Hos. XIII; I Cor. XV), why should not the humility of the flesh, assumed for human salvation, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that he made both one? Let us not worship a creature, but the Creator, who is blessed forever.

Cursed, therefore, is not only the one who places his hope in man, but also the one who makes flesh his arm—that is, his strength—and whatever he does, considers to be the work not of the Lord’s mercy but of his own power. For the heart of the one who does these things departs from the Lord, asserting that he can do what he cannot.

“And he will be like a tamarisk,” which in Hebrew is called *aroer*, or, as Symmachus interpreted it, “an unfruitful tree in the wilderness.” “And he will not see when good things come,” which the multitude of the nations will see, but will dwell in dryness, in the desert. This is said of the Jewish people, who dwell in the desert and produce no fruit. They are in a salt land that produces no fruit and in an uninhabited place that has no divine guest, no angelic protection, and no grace of the Holy Spirit or knowledge of teachers.

“‘Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence (or: hope). He will be like a tree transplanted (or: fruitful) beside waters, which sends its roots toward moisture and will not fear when the heat comes. Its leaf will be green (or: its branches will be leafy). In the time (or: year) of drought it will not be anxious (or: afraid), nor will it ever cease to bear fruit.’”

Let this be understood as spoken of the Jews and heretics who place their hope in man—in their Christ, that is, whom they think will come not as the Son of God but as a mere man. Conversely, the ecclesiastical man who trusts in the Lord hears: “And know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. XCIX).

He trusts in the Lord and will be compared to the tree of which the first psalm also sings: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall.” By “beside waters,” understand the grace of the Holy Spirit and his various gifts. “Which sends its roots toward moisture,” so that it may receive abundance from the Lord.

But we can also say that we have been transferred from Jewish dryness into the everlasting grace of baptism. “And he will not fear,” he says, “when the heat comes”—whether the time of healing [or: persecution], or the day of judgment. “And its leaf will be green,” or “its leafy branches will be in it,” so that it never fears dryness but continually produces the grace of every virtue.

And when the time, or year, of drought arrives, he will not fear when the Lord, in anger, commands the clouds not to rain upon Israel (Isa. V). What follows—“Nor will he cease to bear fruit”—can explain the passage written in Mark (Mark XI), where the Lord came to the fig tree and found no fruit on it, because it was not yet the season, and cursed it so that it would never again bear fruit.

The one who trusts in the Lord, and whose confidence is the Lord, will not fear even in the time of Jewish drought, but will always bring forth fruit, believing in him who once died for us and dies no more (Rom. VI), and who says, “I am life” (John XIV).

[Col. 0948A] The heart of human beings is crooked and inscrutable; who “will know it? I, the Lord, search the heart and test the kidneys, who give to each according to his way and according to the fruit of his inventions.”

The Septuagint has: “The heart is deep above all things, and the human being is—who will know him?”—and so forth similarly. The Hebrew word *enosch* is written with four letters. If it is read *enosch*, it means “human being”; but if *anusch*, it means “inscrutable,” or “desperate,” because no one is able to discover the human heart. Symmachus, however, translated this passage as follows: “The heart of human beings is inscrutable; but what man is there who can find it?”

Some of our people, indeed with a good intention but not according to knowledge, are accustomed to use this passage against the Jews, arguing that the Lord and Savior is “human being,” according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, and that no one can know the mystery of his birth, in accordance with what is written: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII)—except God alone, who examines hidden things and repays each according to his works. It is better, however, to understand it simply: that no one knows the secrets of thoughts except God alone.

For above he had said: “Cursed is the man who has his hope in man”; and, conversely: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.” Therefore, so that we would not suppose human judgment to be reliable, he added that almost all hearts are perverse. The Psalmist says: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. XVIII)—without doubt, from thoughts. And in Genesis: “But when God saw that human wickedness was great on the earth, and that every inclination of the thought of the heart was directed toward evil at all times” (Gen. VI). And again: “For the sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from its youth” (Gen. VIII). Through these passages we learn that God alone knows their thoughts.

But if it is said of the Savior, “Jesus, seeing their thoughts” (Luke IX), and no one can see their thoughts except God alone, then Christ is God, who searches hearts and tests the kidneys and will repay each according to his works.

“‘The partridge brooded’ (or, ‘gathered’) what it did not hatch.” As the Septuagint translated it: “The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch. It made its riches without judgment. In the middle of its days it will leave them” (or, “in the middle of his days they will leave him”), “and at his end he will be foolish.”

The writers of natural history say—of beasts and birds, as well as of trees and plants—whose leading authorities among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny the Second, that this is the nature of the partridge: to steal the eggs of another partridge, that is, eggs belonging to another, and to sit and brood over them; and when the young have grown, they fly away from it and abandon the parent that is not their own.

Such are the rich who seize what belongs to others and, without considering God’s judgment, make riches without judgment. They abandon these riches in the midst of their time, carried away by sudden death, when it is said to them: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII.) Nothing is more foolish than failing to consider the end and thinking what is brief to be everlasting.

Others, both on account of the foregoing history and on account of another account in which they say that the partridge is exceedingly combative and unclean, so that it defiles its food, interpret the devil under this name: he has gathered riches belonging to others for himself, saying to the Lord: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV). His riches, which had been wrongly gathered by him, will abandon him and, through the apostles, return to the Lord; and he who seemed to himself to be the wisest will, in the judgment of all, be foolish.

What the Septuagint says—“the partridge cried out”—is to be referred to the person of heretics: this partridge, the devil, cried out through the leaders of the heretics, gathered what it had not hatched, and assembled for itself a multitude of the deceived; afterward they will abandon him, and he will be proved the most foolish in everyone’s judgment.

(Origen.) For the partridge cried out through Valentinus, cried out through Basilides, through Marcion, and through all who were carried away by desire for glory belonging to another and alien from God. None of them could make heard the voice of the Lord Jesus: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X). Rather, the voice of Christ was in Paul; it was in Peter. For this reason Paul said: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (II Cor. XIII.)

The voice of the partridge gathering what it did not hatch is found in those who entangle the simple among the faithful in the snare of a heretical faction.

“Thus the partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch, making its riches without judgment. The partridge became rich.” Behold how many thousands belong to it, an immense crowd, many peoples of captives. It makes its riches without considering judgment and without having justice in its heart, doing everything without law; rightly it is accused of having made riches without judgment.

But my Jesus makes his riches with judgment. His wealth has been examined and chosen.

“In the middle of his days they will abandon him”: we are all those who once were under the power of the crying partridge. For it cried out not only through those whom we mentioned above, but generally through all who, as though calling people to piety and religion, cried out under a doctrine opposed to the truth. We, I say, abandon him in the middle of all his days. All his days, indeed, are the days of this age. But because the Lord Jesus does not rescue us at all from the present age, for this reason we abandon him in the middle of his days, and his end will be foolish.

For when was he wise, so that his end should rightly become foolish? But let us say that he was wise. “For the serpent was wiser than all the beasts upon the earth that the Lord God had made” (Gen. III). He was wise according to what is written: “I will bring the great prince of the Assyrians upon [his] understanding [wording uncertain]. And he said: By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations; I will consume their strength, and I will shake uninhabited cities.”

If anyone can understand it, let him understand how “his end will be foolish.” He who was formerly wrongly wise—for he was wiser than all the beasts upon the earth—will become the opposite of what he was: from one who was wrongly wise, he will become foolish.

You will understand what “his end will be foolish” means if you know how the Apostle also commands you to receive foolishness for your salvation. “If anyone,” he says, “seems to himself to be wise among you, let him become foolish in this age.” Notice that he did not merely say, “Be foolish and stupid,” but said it so that you may become wise.

If, then, there is a certain blameworthy wisdom, according to which the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their generation, God is good, for by opposites he overturns contrary things, so that what was said may be fulfilled: “His end will be foolish.”

When his end becomes foolish, Christ must reign until God places all his enemies beneath his feet. But when he has subjected all things to him, the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. When death has been destroyed, then the partridge’s end will come, and its end will become foolish.

“The throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, the place of our sanctification. The hope of Israel, O Lord: all who abandon you will be put to shame; those who depart from you will be written upon the earth, because they have abandoned the Lord, the vein” (or, “the fountain”) “of living waters.”

(Jerome.) Once the partridge has been abandoned because of its foolishness, the hope of Israel—that is, of God’s people and of those who believe in the Lord—is he who made all things. His throne is glorious and exalted from the beginning, and he is the place of sanctification for all believers, so that the Lord is not in a place, but wherever he is, that place is sanctified.

(Origen.) If you wish to understand these words of Christ, you will not sin; if of the Father, you will not think impiously. For there is a throne of brightness, exalted, and from the beginning the Savior; a throne of glory, because his kingdom is exalted. “Christ is our sanctification,” because both he who sanctifies and we who are sanctified are all from one.

“The support of Israel.” Just as Jesus himself is justice, himself truth, himself sanctification, so likewise he himself is support. There is nothing just without Christ, nothing holy without him, nor anything enduring that does not possess Christ within itself; for he is the support of Israel.

But if you refer this also to the Father, you will not understand it impiously: “O Lord, all who have abandoned you will be put to shame as they depart.”

(Jerome.) Those who abandon the Lord will be put to shame with everlasting shame; and those who depart or turn away from him will be written upon the earth, erased from the book of the living. For just as the one who can say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III), is written among heavenly things, so the one who abandons or turns away from the Lord will be written upon the earth with those who set their minds on earthly things.

(Origen.) Whenever each one of us sins, through the things by which he sins he abandons Christ. In abandoning the Son, he also abandons the Father. The unjust is far from justice; the defiled is far from holiness; the warrior is far from peace; and the one who begins to be under the power of the enemy becomes alienated from redemption. Whoever is outside the wisdom of God abandons wisdom.

Thus, teaching us what will happen to all who desert God, the prophet says: “All who abandon you will be put to shame, those who depart”—that is, to the extent that they abandon you, to that extent let them be put to shame—“departing from you.”

“They will be written upon the earth.” All holy people are recorded in heaven; sinners upon the earth. Jesus says to the disciples: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). “For by whatever measure they measured, it will be measured back to them” (Luke VI).

Each person is himself the cause of being written upon the earth: if he does not seek heavenly things while on earth, if his soul is always agitated by the affairs of this world, which appear good to the age. But if, hearing Jesus say, “Do not store up treasures for yourselves upon earth, where moth and worm destroy, and where thieves break through and steal; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Luke XII), he stores up treasure for himself in heaven, he himself is the cause of being written in heaven.

(Jerome.) The reason why they are written upon the earth is manifest: they have abandoned the Lord, the fountain of life, or the Lord, the fountain of living waters, who says in the Gospel: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This he said concerning the Spirit whom believers were to receive (John VII).

“Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise.”

Many physicians in the Gospel (Matt. IX) had treated the woman with the flow of blood, who had spent all her substance on them; yet she could be healed by no one except him who is the true physician and whose healing is in his wings. Therefore now also the prophet, having suffered reproaches from the people and having frequently been surrounded by ambushes, desires to be healed and saved by him, whose praise and medicine are true.

(Origen.) Therefore let the one who wishes his sick soul to be saved say confidently: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.” For healing follows the medicine when Christ deigns to cure. “Save me, and I shall be saved.” I shall also rejoice to say this if, renouncing all worldly glory, I can say the rest as well: “For you are my praise”; or when I have fulfilled the command in which it is prescribed: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, but let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord” (Jer. IX).

Blessed, therefore, is the man who renounces all glory that is below: glory in noble birth, beauty, bodily advantages, riches, and boasting. Blessed is the one who, content with one glory, says to the Lord: “For you are my praise.”

“Behold, they themselves say to me: ‘Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.’ But I have not been troubled following you as shepherd” (or, “I have not labored following you”), “and I have not desired the day of man. You know that what came forth from my lips was upright in your sight” (or, “is before your face”). “Do not become a terror to me; you are my hope in the day of affliction” (or, “do not become alien to me”), “while sparing me in the evil day.”

(Jerome.) Those who do not believe that what has been spoken will come to pass say to the prophet: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come,” considering the delay of the sentence to be a pretense. But while they say these things, he says, I have not been troubled, nor have I labored in following you, or entering after your footsteps. Nor was I content with this alone, but I did not desire the day of man—that is, either a longer life or whatever prosperity belongs to this age. And he calls him as both witness and judge: “You know.”

“Behold, they themselves say to me: ‘Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.’ But I have not labored in following after you.”

(Origen.) Jesus says to you: “Take up your cross and come, follow me”; and: “Whoever does not leave father or mother and follow me is not worthy to be my disciple” (Luke XIV). If, then, you are such a person that you always follow Christ, the more closely you follow, the less you will labor. For there is no weariness in Jacob, nor will pain appear in Israel.

Therefore he said that we should labor no longer, since we labored before we began to follow him: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). If we come to Jesus while laboring and follow him, then we shall be able to say: “But I have not labored in following after you.” And he says: “I have not desired the day of man.”

There is a day of man, and there is a day of God—that is, the day of resurrection. Every holy person desires the latter, not the former, concerning which it is written: “Woe to those who desire the day of man, for that day is darkness and not light.”

Who can say: “I have not desired the day of man”? The explanation of the word convicts us, because we do desire the day of man. Frequently, when we are sick and begin to be in the fever’s delirium and are pressed by the threshold of death, we raise our weakened hands to the brothers who visit us, asking them to pray to the Lord on our behalf and saying: “Ask for some extension of life for me; I beg you, let me remain for a little while in this light.” In remembering such things, we desire not the holy day of the Lord but the day of man.

Therefore, laying aside love of long life and desire for the human day, let us seek to see that day on which we may become participants in the blessedness that is in Christ.

It follows: “What came forth from my lips was upright in your sight.”

(Jerome.) He never lied and said nothing contrary to the Lord’s will: “Do not,” he says, “become a terror to me; you are my hope in the day of affliction.” This is clear according to the Hebrew. But according to what the Septuagint translated—“Do not become alien to me, while sparing me in the evil day”—the meaning is: Do not spare me in the present age, which is evil; but repay me according to my sins, so that I may have eternal rest. For I know that it is written: “The Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). The evil day is either the entire age or the day of judgment, for those who are tormented on account of their sins.

“Let those who persecute me be put to shame, but let me not be put to shame; let them be afraid, but let me not be afraid. Bring upon them a day of affliction, and crush them with a double crushing.”

The prophet invokes this against those who reproach him for the word of the Lord and say: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.” Let those who persecute him be put to shame, blush, and return to salvation; let those who lie be afraid, and not he who foretells the truth. When the day of vengeance arrives, may he crush them with a double crushing—with famine and the sword.

In another sense, when spiritual wickednesses are overcome by us through God’s help, they are put to shame and afflicted with great anxiety, so that they are rightly said to have been crushed with a double crushing: first, because they possessed holiness but lost it when human beings sought it, and became causes of human destruction; and second, because spiritual substances were conquered by carnal and earthly beings.

“Thus says the Lord to me: Go and stand in the gate” (or, “in the gates”) “of the sons of the people, through which the kings of Judah enter and leave” (or, “through which they enter and leave”), “and in all the gates of Jerusalem; and you shall say to them: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah, and all Judah” (or, “Judea”), “and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem who enter through these gates.”

Because, he says, they disdain to hear your words and do not come to you to inquire what the wisdom of God is, go to the most frequented place, either of the temple gates or of the city gates, through which the kings and the whole populace enter and leave, so that they may be compelled to hear and, “in season and out of season,” proclaim the word of God (II Tim. IV). Thus no excuse may remain for them—that they failed to act because they had not heard.

“Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the sabbath day, nor bring them in through the gates of Jerusalem. Do not cast burdens out of your houses on the sabbath day; do no work at all, and sanctify the sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. But they did not hear, nor incline their ear, and they stiffened their neck” (and in the Hebrew there is no “against their fathers”), “so as not to hear me and not to accept discipline.

“And it shall be, he says, if you hear me, says the Lord, so that you do not bring your burdens through the gates of this city on the sabbath day; and if you sanctify the sabbath day, doing no work on it, kings and princes sitting upon the throne of David will enter through the gates of this city. They will ride in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever.

“They will come from the cities of Judah and from the surrounding region of Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the plains, from the hill country, and from the south, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices” (or, “incense”), “and an offering” (or, “manna”), “and frankincense; and they will bring an offering” (or, “praise”) “into the house of the Lord.

“But if you do not hear me, so as to sanctify the sabbath day, and do not carry a burden, and do not bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the sabbath day, I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem, and it will not be extinguished.”

So that I would not tear apart in fragments the commandment concerning the sabbath, restored through Jeremiah, I have thought it appropriate to set it down in full, so that we may understand everything together.

He guards his soul who does not carry the burdens of sins on the day of rest and the sabbath, nor bring them through the gates of Jerusalem—which gates we must understand as virtues. “Do not,” he says, “cast burdens out of your houses.” For they are not merely to be carried but utterly cast away.

“And do no work at all”—whether servile work or any other work concerning which it is written: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI). Instead, we must do that work of which the Savior says: “Work for the food that does not perish” (John VI).

“Sanctify,” he says, “the sabbath day,” so that we may spend the whole time of our life in sanctification, as did our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
