Although God had commanded these things, they did not incline their ear—the ear of the mind, certainly, not of the flesh—but stiffened their neck, rejecting the yoke of the law and, metaphorically, resembling untamed animals.

Let us see what reward belongs to those who do not carry burdens on the sabbath day and sanctify it.

“They will enter,” he says, “through the gates of this city, kings”—those whose heart is in God’s hand and who rule their own bodies (Prov. XXI)—“and princes sitting upon the throne of David,” so that they may imitate Christ’s example; “and they will ride in chariots and on horses,” concerning which it is written: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, at Sinai, in the holy place” (Ps. LXVII). And elsewhere: “Your riding is salvation” (Hab. III).

Every man who confesses God and who dwells in Jerusalem, concerning which it was said, “His place came to be in Salem” (that is, in peace), “and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV), will dwell forever in the Church of God.

“They will come from the cities of Judah and from the surrounding region of Jerusalem,” concerning which we have already spoken; “and from the land of Benjamin,” who is the son of strength and of the right hand; “and from the plains”—which in Hebrew is called *schephela* and signifies the plain understanding of the historical sense; “and from the hill country,” namely, from lofty doctrines; “and from the south,” concerning which it is written: “God will come from the south” (Hab. III). Hence come warmth and full light, and there all cold is driven away.

“They will bring,” he says, “burnt offerings,” consecrating themselves to God; “and a sacrifice” (or, “incense”), so that they may say: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. L); and: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (I Cor. II); and elsewhere: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

“And an offering,” for which the Septuagint set down the Hebrew word *manaa* itself. Through a very bad custom—or rather, through the negligence of scribes—it is read as *manna* in our books.

“And frankincense,” concerning which it was said: “Why do you offer me frankincense from Sheba?” (above, VI).

“And they will bring an offering,” which in Hebrew is called *thoda* and can be rendered “thanksgiving,” while the Septuagint translated it as “praise.”

“Into the house of David,” without doubt meaning into the Church.

These are the rewards of those who sanctify the sabbath and are weighed down by no burden.

“But if,” he says, “you do not hear my commands and do not do what I have commanded to be done, I will kindle a fire in its gates”—that is, in the gates of Jerusalem—the fire of which it is said: “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hos. VII). This fire devours the houses, or streets, of Jerusalem, which the Septuagint translated as ἄμφοδα (*amphoda*); Aquila and Symmachus as βάρεις (*bareis*), that is, tower-like houses. In Hebrew they are called *aremenoth*.

This fire will never be extinguished, as the Apostle says (I Cor. III): “Each one’s work will be revealed as to what it is; fire will test it.” And again: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.”

But if our Judaizers reject the figurative explanation, they will either be compelled to become Jews and circumcise their foreskins while observing the sabbath, or else they will have to condemn the Savior, who commanded a paralytic on the sabbath to carry his bed. The Evangelist says: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, not only because he was breaking the sabbath, but also because he was calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John V).

## CHAPTER XVIII

The potter’s vessels are shown to the prophet; concerning Christ’s passion and vengeance upon the Jews.

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you shall hear my words. And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel” (or, “stones”), “and the vessel that he was making from clay with his hands was spoiled. And turning” (or, “again”), “he made it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his eyes to make it.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not do with you, house of Israel, as this potter does? Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so you are in my hand, house of Israel.

“Suddenly” (or, “at once”) “I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot it” (or, “remove it”), “and to destroy and ruin it. If that nation repents of its evil, concerning which I spoke against it, then I too will repent of the evil that I had planned to do to it.

“And suddenly” (or, “at once”) “I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it and to plant it. If it does evil in my eyes, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent of the good that I spoke of doing to it.”

Through all the senses one reaches the judgment and understanding of the mind—hearing, smell, taste, and touch—but what is seen by the eyes is retained more deeply in the mind. Therefore the prophet is commanded to go to the potter’s house and there hear the Lord’s commands.

When he says, “I went and descended into the potter’s house,” the potter was making a work upon the wheel, which the Septuagint, misled by the ambiguity of the word, translated as “stones.” For according to the nature of the place and the difference of pronunciation, the instrument—that is, the potter’s wheel—is called both “wheel” and “stones.”

“When,” he says, “I saw a vessel being made from clay, suddenly it was spoiled.” This happened through God’s providence, so that the craftsman’s hands, unknowingly, might shape a parable through their own error.

Again that potter, who had lost the clay vessel while the wheel was turning, made another for himself, as seemed good to him. Immediately the Lord said to the prophet: If the potter has this power, to make again from the same clay what had been spoiled, shall I not be able to do this with you, who, insofar as it depends on you, seem to have perished?

To signify free choice, he says that he announces both evils to a nation and to a kingdom—this one or that one—and again good things; yet what he has foretold does not necessarily occur. On the contrary, good things come to the wicked if they repent, and evil things to the good if, after the promises, they turn back to sins.

We say this not because God is ignorant of what a nation or kingdom will do, whether this or that, but because he leaves the human being to his own will, so that by his own will and merit he may receive either rewards or punishments. Yet whatever happens will not immediately be wholly attributable to the human being, but also to the grace of him who has bestowed all things.

Free choice must indeed be preserved in such a way that the grace of the giver excels in everything, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). “So then, it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

Furthermore, that this potter—that is, our creator and maker—is called God is testified not only by Jeremiah but also by Isaiah and the Apostle Paul. For in Isaiah it is written: “Woe to the one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the vessels of earth. Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and, ‘Your work is without hands’?” (Isa. XLV.) And the Apostle speaks in his Epistle to the Romans, saying: “Does the work say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

“Now therefore say to the man of Judah and to the inhabitant of Jerusalem, saying: Thus” (or, “so”) “says the Lord: Behold, I am shaping evil against you and devising a plan against you. Let each one turn back from his evil way; and straighten your ways and your inclinations.

“They said: ‘We have despaired’” (or, “we will grow strong”), “for we shall go according to our plans, and each one of us shall do the perversity” (or, “what pleases”) “of his evil heart.

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask the nations: Who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done so exceedingly?”

(Jerome.) The Lord fulfills the parable that he had taught both by sight and by words, and says: “Behold, I am shaping evil against you,” like a potter shaping clay. “Evil,” according to Isaiah, who says, “making peace and creating evil” (Isa. XLV), does not mean that it is evil in itself, but that it appears evil to those who suffer it.

“And I am devising a plan against you,” that is, I am imposing a sentence according to merit. Change your works, “and straighten your ways,” so that punishment may also be changed into prosperity.

But they, he says, answered in opposition: “We will grow strong,” namely, in evil works; or, according to Aquila, “we have despaired”; and according to Symmachus, “we have failed.” Both responses offend God, whether one thinks oneself unable to be saved or has failed in spirit to appease God.

“And we shall go,” he says, “according to our plans.” Where, then, is the power of free choice without God’s grace, and the judgment of one’s own will, when it is a great offense against God to follow one’s own plans and do the will of an evil heart?

Therefore he adds: “Ask the nations, and all the nations around them, who has done or heard such things, while serving idols, as the virgin Israel has done so exceedingly?” He calls her a virgin because she served one God, as the Prophet says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV).

“Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Or can the waters that burst forth, cold and flowing, be torn away?”

The Septuagint has: “Will breasts fail from the rock, or snow from Lebanon? Or will water violently carried away by the wind turn aside?”

Something similar is expressed in that passage of Virgil (Eclogue I):

> Before the light-footed deer will feed in the air,  
> and the seas will leave their fish upon the shore,  
> before his image slips from my breast.

And in another passage (Aeneid I):

> While rivers run into the sea, while shadows from the mountains  
> traverse the land, while the sky feeds the circling stars,  
> your honor, name, and praises will always remain.

How, he says, snow cannot fail from the summits of Lebanon, nor be overcome by the sun’s heat so that it all melts, and how streams flowing from the mountains do not dry up at their sources—so my name, which is stable in itself and cannot be changed forever, should not be altered. Yet, while all other things preserve nature’s order, my people have forgotten me.

For it follows:

“Because my people have forgotten me, offering libations in vain and stumbling in their ways and on the paths of the age” (or, “everlasting paths”), “so that they might walk along an untrodden road.”

Whoever forgets God and abandons him who says, “I am the way” (John XIV), pours libations to alien gods and stumbles in his own ways—not in God’s ways—and abandons the ancient and everlasting paths, which have been worn smooth by the footsteps of all the saints who worship God.

But these people walked on an untrodden road, and after abandoning the worship of God they venerated idols. For this reason the punishment that follows is imposed:

“So that their land might become a desolation and an everlasting hissing. Everyone who passes through it will be astonished and will shake his head.”

Because, he says, they abandoned the worship of God and followed the crooked paths of idolatry, their land was therefore reduced to a wilderness and became a wonder and a hissing to all, so that those who saw a land and city once flourishing collapsed into desert and ashes would marvel and be stupefied, expressing the confusion of their souls by a gesture of the body.

For this is what it means to shake the head and to display the mind’s astonishment by hissing.

We understand this to have been fulfilled more fully and more correctly after the coming of the Lord, when no Jew is permitted by law to enter the land and city that was once theirs; but when they come for lamentation, they marvel and mourn over the prophecies of the prophets fulfilled in deeds.

[Col. 0958A] “As a scorching wind I will scatter them before the enemy” (or, “enemies”); “I will show them my back and not my face on the day of their destruction.”

To this day God’s sentence remains upon the Jews: they have been scattered throughout the whole world before the enemy—the devil—or before enemy demons. Although day and night they invoke God’s name in the synagogues of Satan, God shows them his back and not his face, so that they may understand that he is always withdrawing and never coming toward them.

The day of the Jews’ destruction is the whole period after the Savior’s passion, until the consummation of the age, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved (Rom. XI).

“And they said: ‘Come, let us devise plans against Jeremiah; for the law will not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise man, nor speech from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us pay no attention to any of his words.’”

This was the thought of the Jews against Jeremiah—or against the Lord and Savior—then, and it is the thought of heretics against his servants today: to construct accusations and forestall holy men with charges, without considering what truth they speak, but only what falsehood they themselves may devise.

For they boast that among their priests, wise men, and false prophets the law of God, counsel, and eloquence remain, although Scripture says: “Wisdom will not enter a perverse soul” (Wis. I).

“Attend to me, Lord, and hear the voice of my adversaries. Is evil repaid for good, because they dug a pit for my life? Remember that I stood in your presence, to speak good on their behalf and to turn away your indignation from them. Therefore hand their children over to famine, and deliver them into the power of the sword. Let their wives be childless and widowed, and let their husbands be put to death. Let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle; let a cry be heard from their houses.”

In the type of the Savior, Jeremiah suffers all these things from the Jewish people, who are afterward devastated when the Babylonian comes. But they are fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ: when the city was overthrown, they were slaughtered by the Roman sword—not on account of idolatry, which did not exist at that time, but on account of the killing of the Son of God, when the whole people cried out together: “Take away, take away such a man; [Col. 0958D] we have no king except Caesar” (John XIX). Their curse was fulfilled in eternal condemnation: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). For they had dug a pit for Christ and had said: “Let us remove him from the land of the living” (Isa. LIII). Yet he showed such great mercy toward them and stood in the presence of the Father to speak good on their behalf and to turn away his indignation from them, that even on the cross he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

We pass quickly over what is evident, so that we may dwell on what is more obscure—not interpreting the ravings of certain people as the captivity of the heavenly Jerusalem, but pursuing a clear history and an exceedingly manifest prophecy with complete confidence regarding both words and meanings.

[Col. 0959A] “For you will suddenly bring a robber upon them, because they dug a pit to seize me and concealed snares for my feet. But you, Lord, know all their counsel against me for death. Do not be propitious toward their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from your presence. Let them become stumbling or falling before you; in the time of your fury, deal with them—or, do this to them.”

If we understand this of Jeremiah, let us refer the sudden robber to Nebuchadnezzar; if of the Savior, which is truer and better, to the Roman army. And, so that God’s judgment may appear just, he explains what they did against Christ, the Son of God, and what they suffered. As for what follows—“Do not be propitious toward their iniquity, and let their sin not be blotted out from your presence”—this is by no means contrary to the earlier statement in which he entreats the Father on behalf of the people. But after the time granted for repentance had passed, and they persisted in their crime, the people and their elders were punished not so much for themselves as for the sake of others, lest their great sin harm the rest by its example.

And what follows—“Let them become stumbling” (or “falling”) “before you”—resembles the statement of Isaiah and the apostle Peter: “And you shall not stumble as upon a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (Isa. VIII; 1 Pet. II). The Prophet also recalls this in the Psalms: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the Lord” (Ps. CXVII).

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The breaking of the little flask signifies the breaking of Jerusalem because of the idolatry of Ennon

[Col. 0959C]

“This says the Lord: Go and take an earthen potter’s flask from the elders of the people and from the elders of the priests. And go out to the valley of the son of Ennom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate (or Charsith), and you shall proclaim—or cry out, or read—there the words that I shall speak to you. And you shall say: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

In place of “the potter’s flask,” which is called *backebeck* in Hebrew, the Septuagint translated “a little jar.” For “the Potsherd Gate,” Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, *harsith*. In its place the Septuagint, following its usual practice, added the Greek letter χ for the aspiration, saying *Charsith* instead of *harsith*, just as they say *Hebron* for *Chebron*, and [Col. 0959D] *Hiericho* for *Hieriho*.

Divine Scripture wishes the people to be taught not only through their ears but also through their eyes. For, as we have already said, what reaches the mind through sight is retained more firmly than what reaches it through hearing.

“Take,” he says, “an earthen flask (or little jar) from the elders of the people and of the priests, and go out to the valley of the son of Ennom,” about which we spoke above: there was the shrine of Baal, together with a grove and sacred thicket, watered by the springs of Siloam. “The valley itself,” he says, “is beside the gate which in the Hebrew language is called *harsith*, that is, ‘earthen.’ And you shall proclaim—or read—there the words that I shall speak with you,” so that what I am about to say may be heard there.

The reason that “you shall proclaim,” “you shall cry out,” and “you shall read” are all given is that the Hebrew word [Col. 0960A] *karath* signifies all three. He wants what he is about to say to be heard both by the kings of Judah and by the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, by the royal line and by the whole people—so that those who refuse to hear may be without excuse.

“This says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing affliction (or evils) upon this place, so that everyone who hears it—or them—will have his ears ringing, because they abandoned me, made this place foreign, and poured libations there to foreign gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah knew. They filled this place with the blood of the innocent, and they built the high places of the Baals in order to burn their sons as a burnt offering to the Baals—things that I did not command (or devise), nor speak, nor did they enter my heart.”

Some foolishly refer this passage also to the heavenly Jerusalem. Rather than continually admonishing against this, it is enough to have said this much: such an explanation—or rather, such a heresy—must be avoided, for it overturns what is manifest and attempts to introduce certain illusions into the churches of Christ.

No one doubts that they placed the idol of Baal in the temple of God—or in the shrine that was in the valley of the son of Ennom—where the grove of Baal and his altar stood, upon which they sacrificed and burned their sons: things that the Lord neither devised nor spoke, nor entered his heart. This does not mean that God was ignorant of what was to come, but that he says that he does not know things unworthy of his knowledge, in accordance with the Gospel statement: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke XIII). For the Lord knows those who are his (2 Tim. II). And: “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” [Col. 0960C] (1 Cor. XIV)—or, certainly, these statements concerning God are to be understood *anthropopathically* (ἀνθρωποπάθως), as are other such expressions.

Every heretic abandons God and makes foreign the place of God’s dwelling by polluting it with his deceit. He pours libations to foreign gods whom neither he nor his fathers knew—namely, the apostles and apostolic men. The kings of Judah, that is, the patriarchs of the heretics, fill the former place of God with the blood of the deceived and the innocent. For unless a person is foolish and simple, he is not quickly overthrown. They build the high places of the Baals when they claim to be discussing lofty matters. They burn their children to an idol when they give birth to them in heresy. The Lord says that he does not know any of these things, and that they never entered his thoughts.

“Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called Topheth, nor the valley of the son of Ennom, but the Valley of Slaughter.”

The Septuagint has: “Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called ruin and *polyandrion* (πολυάνδριον) of the son of Ennom, but *polyandrion* of slaughter.” We explained above what the valley of the son of Ennom is; it is called in Hebrew [term absent in the supplied text], and from it they think that Gehenna received its name. I wonder what the Septuagint intended by placing *diaptōsis* (διάπτωσις), that is, “ruin,” in place of Topheth, and *polyandrion*, meaning “a multitude of men,” in place of “valley,” unless perhaps because the people would fall there and a multitude of men would be slaughtered—either spiritually, through the error of idolatry, or literally, by the Babylonian army, as is made clearer in what follows.

[Col. 0961A] “And I shall dissipate the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and overthrow them by the sword before their enemies and by the hand of those who seek their lives. And I shall give their corpses as food to the birds of the sky and to the beasts of the earth. And I shall make this city an object of astonishment and hissing. Everyone who passes by it will be appalled and will hiss at all its wounds. And I shall feed them the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and each one shall eat the flesh of his neighbor during the siege and in the distress with which their enemies and those who seek their lives will confine them.”

Although we know that these things also occurred to the people during the Babylonian captivity, they refer more fully to the time of the Savior, when they were besieged by Vespasian and Titus, and their city collapsed in the time of Hadrian into eternal ashes. Those who had offered their sons to idols afterward, compelled by the necessity of famine, turned them into food, and the flesh of all was given to the birds of the sky and to the beasts of the earth. Those who had abused God’s gifts for impiety and sacrificed their own entrails to idols made their own bellies the tombs of their children.

“And you shall break the flask before the eyes of the men who will go—or come out—with you, and you shall say to them: This says the Lord of hosts: So shall I break this people and this city, just as a potter’s vessel is broken, which cannot be restored again.”

It is plainly said not of the Babylonian captivity but of the Roman captivity. After the Babylonians, the city was rebuilt, the people were brought back to Judea, and [Col. 0961C] restored to their former abundance. But after the captivity that occurred under Vespasian and Titus, and afterward under Hadrian, Jerusalem’s ruins will remain until the consummation of the age. Although the Jews think that a golden, silver, and gem-studded Jerusalem will be restored to them, together with sacrifices and offerings, the marriages of the saints, and the earthly kingdom of the Lord Savior, we do not follow these beliefs, yet we cannot condemn them, because many churchmen and martyrs have said these things. Let each person abound in his own understanding, and let everything be reserved for the judgment of the Lord.

Just as an earthen and clay vessel, once broken, cannot be restored to its former appearance, so the Jewish people and Jerusalem, once overthrown, will not possess their former condition. Indeed, the name of the city itself has now been abolished, and it is called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian. Along with its former dwelling, it also lost its former name, to humble the pride of its inhabitants. The names of the holy cross and of the resurrection do not signify the city but the place; nor do they signify the former wealth by which the Jewish people perished, but the glory of holiness possessed by our humble Bethlehem, which has neither gold nor gems, but the bread that was born in it.

“And in Topheth they shall be buried (or, they shall bury), because there is no other place for burial. Thus I shall deal with this place,” says the Lord, “and with its inhabitants; and I shall make this city like Topheth (or, like ruin). And the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah shall be like the place of Topheth (or, of ruin).”

The addition found in the Septuagint—“every house of the kings of Judah shall be like the place of Topheth”—is not found in the Hebrew. And it continues:

“All the houses on whose roofs—or housetops—they sacrificed to all the host of heaven and poured out libations to foreign gods shall be unclean.”

What he had said above—“This place shall no longer be called Topheth, and the valley of the sons of Ennom, but the Valley of Slaughter”—he now states more explicitly: so great a slaughter will take place in that very spot that the people will be buried there in heaps, and the former sacred grove will become a burial mound for the dead. The city itself, which overlooks this place, will become like Topheth, for which the Septuagint translated “ruin.” The houses [Col. 0962B] of Jerusalem and the palaces of its kings will likewise be turned into similar ruins.

The reason is given: they were unclean and polluted by the crime of idolatry, because on their housetops and roofs they sacrificed to the sun, moon, and stars of heaven and burned incense. Nor were they satisfied with this error, but they sacrificed to demons and poured libations to foreign gods.

“Jeremiah then came from Topheth, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, and stood in the court of the house of the Lord and said to all the people: This says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the evils that I have spoken against it, because they hardened their necks so as not to hear my words.”

After Jeremiah had broken the flask or jar in Topheth in the presence of the elders of the people whom he had brought with him, and had prophesied in the Lord’s words concerning the breaking of the people and the city of Jerusalem, he returns and stands in the court of the house of the Lord, addressing the whole multitude that had refused to go to Topheth. The Lord, he says, will bring upon the city of Jerusalem and upon all its towns all the evils that he had spoken against it.

And, lest we think the sentence cruel, he gives the reasons why he will bring the evils: “Because,” he says, “they hardened their necks so as not to hear my words,” refusing to repent even after so many acts of impiety.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Jeremiah is struck and placed in custody; he mourns over his people and curses the day of his birth

[Col. 0962D]

“Phassur son of Emmer, the priest who had been appointed chief in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words. And Phassur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks, which were at the upper Benjamin Gate in the house of the Lord.”

In place of Phassur, the Septuagint translated Phascor, which is interpreted as “blackness of mouth.” In place of the stocks, which we have mentioned, the Septuagint and Theodotion translated “cataract”; Symmachus used *basanistērion* (βασανιστήριον) or *streblōtērion* (στρεβλωτήριον), both of which signify instruments of torture. We, following common usage, have said “stocks.” We read of this type of torture also in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XVI), when the apostles Paul and Silas were placed in the custody of the prison.

This man was the high priest of the temple, and he abuses the dignity of the priesthood that had been given to him for an evil purpose—not to teach and correct with speech, but to terrify through tortures. Hence both the Savior and the apostle Paul are beaten at the command of the high priest (John XIX; Acts XVI). Nor is it surprising if, today, the servants of God are beaten by Phascor, sent into prison, and kept in terrible custody. This power is given by God so that the faith of the prophets may be revealed. Yet the one who strikes is not greater; rather, the one who is struck is stronger.

The prophet patiently accepts God’s judgment and does not protest against the blows, but considers who is commanding them. *Emmer* means “word,” from which blackness is often generated—not through the fault of a parent but through the crime of one who degenerates. The instrument of torture by which the prophet is tormented seems to be in the region of the right side, which is interpreted as Benjamin, and at the lofty gate, which indicates not truth but the unjust power of the high priest.

“When morning came, Phassur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him: The Lord has not called your name Phassur, but Terror on Every Side.”

Here also everyone has interpreted both the priest’s name and the type of torture in the same way as above. The priest’s name is changed so that the punishment to come might be demonstrated through the name of the future. “You shall by no means,” he says, “retain the blackness of mouth and the rule of unjust power; rather, you shall be led captive to Babylon.” For “Terror on Every Side,” or “around the circuit,” means that, trembling and uncertain of your own safety, you will look around here and there and dread the adversaries coming against you.

[Col. 0963C] In place of “terror,” which is written in Hebrew, the Septuagint and Theodotion translated *metoikon* (μέτοικον), that is, “one who migrates”; the second edition of Aquila, “stranger”; the first, “one who looks around”; Symmachus, “removed,” or “gathered” and “constrained.”

“For this says the Lord: Behold, I shall give you and all your friends over to terror, and they shall fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes shall see it. And I shall give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall lead them into Babylon and strike them with the sword. And I shall give all the wealth (or strength) of this city, and all its labor, and all its price (or glory), and all the treasures of the kings of Judah into the hand of their enemies; and they shall plunder them, take them away, and lead them to Babylon. But you, Phassur, and all the inhabitants of your house, shall go into captivity. You shall come to Babylon, and there you shall die, and there you and all your friends in whose presence you prophesied falsely shall be buried.”

According to the interpretation given above, by which Phassur’s name had been changed, all the translators likewise rendered it so as to signify either terror, pilgrimage, removal, transfer, or migration. He threatens that Phassur and his friends are now about to be captured and handed over to the enemies, and that the whole people of the tribe of Judah will fall into the hands of the king of Babylon. Some will be killed by the sword, others led into captivity, and all the wealth both of the city and of the royal treasures will be seized by the enemies. Phassur himself, with all his relatives and household, will be led into captivity and will die in Babylon because he deceived the people by his lie—not by telling them true and grievous things, but by promising prosperity through falsehood.

At the same time, we should observe the prophet’s patience and prudence: although he has been sent into prison, he remains silent and conquers the injury through silence. Yet he does not conceal what he knows will come, so that perhaps the high priest who is a false prophet may cease from sinning and implore God’s mercy. We shall discuss him more fully in the following book.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0963]

[Col. 0963C] We read in the Gospel that the Lord foretold the coming of the Paraclete to his disciples in these words: “When he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment” [Col. 0963D] (John XVI). What else is indicated here than that those who were to be enlightened and strengthened by the gift of that same Spirit would, by convicting the world, correct its lovers and the despisers of God, so that they might understand by what great crime they were held captive and how great a punishment was deserved by those who preferred treachery to sound faith, injustice to righteousness, and iniquity to judgment?

But since the holy prophets, according to the measure given to them in their own time, performed the same office, reproving the impious for their unbelief and sinners for their evil deeds, what else is suggested than that the very same Spirit had enlightened the prophets of God before the Lord’s incarnation by his gift, so that they could carry out their ministry worthily—the Spirit who filled the apostles after his incarnation, so that they might convict the errors of the whole world and expose and proclaim the wickedness of the devil before human eyes?

Behold, the prophet Jeremiah reproves kings and priests for their impieties and rebukes the whole people for their crimes. Although he suffered punishments and pains from them on this account, he did not cease from the duty of preaching. He testified to the power of the Holy Spirit working within him and strengthened himself with the hope of divine consolation, saying:

“He became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones; I grew weary and could not endure it. I heard the insults of many and terrors all around, but the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior. Therefore those who persecute me shall fall and shall be weak.”

Accordingly, in accordance with the beginning of the ninth book, the following discourse will make clear how these things took place.

“You have deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived (or, ‘You have misled me, Lord, and I was misled’). You were stronger than I and prevailed (or, ‘obtained the victory,’ and ‘were able’). [Col. 0965A] I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me, because for a long time I have been speaking, crying out against iniquity and proclaiming devastation (or, ‘because with my bitter word I shall laugh at transgression and invoke misery’).” (Jerome)

The prophet says that he was deceived by the Lord because at the beginning, hearing, “I have appointed you prophet to the nations” (above, I), and again, “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and overthrow, and to build and plant” (ibid.), he thought that he would say nothing against the Jewish people but against the various nations around them. For this reason he willingly accepted the prophetic office. The opposite happened: while he proclaimed the captivity of Jerusalem, he endured persecutions and afflictions.

When he adds, “I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me,” it is because they think he has lied about everything and that all the things he foretold would come to pass were false. The prophet, too, had thought that what the Lord threatened would happen immediately, while the people believed that what had not come immediately would never come at all. I cry out concerning the devastation of Babylon and the iniquity of the enemies by which my people will be oppressed.

But if we follow the Septuagint in what it says—“because with my bitter word I shall laugh at transgression and invoke misery”—the meaning is this: I know that present sadness will be changed into future joy, in accordance with what is written: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Luke VI). Therefore I willingly endure misery, iniquity, and affliction, so that I even desire and invoke them, and may compensate for the brevity of injury with the eternity of happiness.

“For the word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and a mockery all day long. And I said: I shall not remember him (or, ‘I shall not name the Lord’), and I shall no longer speak in his name. And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones; and I grew weary (or, ‘was dissolved’) and could not endure it. For I heard the insults (or, ‘reproach’) of many and terror all around (or, ‘of those gathered from every side’): ‘Pursue him, and let us pursue him.’”

As I cried out and said that the Babylonian army was already coming and that the enemy sword was plundering everything, the word of the Lord became for me a reproach and a mockery, while they considered the delay of the prophecy a lie. Therefore I resolved in my mind not to speak any longer to the people of God in words or to name his name. Although I had made this decision overcome by shame, timidly and foolishly, nevertheless, he says, “It became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones”; or, “I was dissolved on every side,” so that I could not endure it.

The divine word conceived in the mind but not uttered by the mouth burns in the breast. Hence Paul also says (1 Cor. IX): “If I preach the Gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” And when he saw in Athens a city devoted to idolatry, he was stirred in spirit and burned with his whole mind (Acts XVII). Later, in the same volume, we read (Acts XVIII): “When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ.”

Many teachers in the Church also endure similar things to this day, hearing the reproach of many gathered around them and saying: “Pursue them, and let us pursue them.”

“All the men who were at peace with me and guarded my side, watching to see whether he might somehow be deceived so that we might prevail against him and take vengeance on him. But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior.”

When adversaries rise up, and former friends and peaceful companions turn to hostility and wish to set ambushes for us, let us not be greatly concerned. Rather, let us desire to say what the prophet also says: “But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior.”

“Therefore those who persecute me shall fall and shall be weak (or, ‘therefore they pursued me and could not understand’). They shall be greatly confounded, because they did not understand the everlasting reproach (or, ‘disgrace’) that shall never be blotted out.”

Because they persecuted him, they were unable to understand the prophetic word, and profound confusion followed their ignorance. They did not understand the everlasting disgrace that would possess them and never be erased by any forgetfulness.

Let the men who were once at peace with me and guarded my side, desiring to deceive me, say whatever they wish, provided that after persecution the just man and teacher of the Church receive such vengeance and such rewards.

“And you, Lord of hosts, tester of the righteous (or, ‘who test what is righteous’), who see the kidneys and the heart, let me see, I pray, your vengeance upon them; for to you I have revealed my cause.”

The Lord alone knows how to test righteousness, just as he alone sees the inner things of the heart. Hence Jesus, who knows the thoughts of human beings (Luke VI), is God not by progress, as certain people think, but by nature.

Something similar is expressed in the Psalms: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII). If one who is alive in virtues is not justified, how much less one who is dead through sins?

Although the righteous man knows that God is his defender, nevertheless, because of the impatience of human weakness, he desires even now to see what he knows will come. To him he will reveal his cause, as he says elsewhere: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. XXXII). Blessed is the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord (Heb. X), as the Apostle says: “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Eph. V).

“Sing to the Lord; praise the Lord, because he has delivered the life of the poor from the hand of the wicked.”

The one who is poor in spirit and does not possess the riches that have received their consolation in this age—riches of which Paul says, “provided that we remember the poor” (1 Cor. XIII)—when he has obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises the Lord in spirit and glories that he has been rescued from the hand of the wicked.

All this happens not through our merit but through the grace of the one who has delivered the poor, who does not possess the riches of a falling pride but the humility of the one who has been delivered in poverty.

“Cursed be the day on which I was born; let the day on which my mother bore me not be blessed. Cursed be the man (or, ‘person’) who announced to my father, saying: ‘A male child has been born to you,’ and made him rejoice as though with happiness. Let that man be like the cities that the Lord overthrew and did not repent. Let him hear a cry in the morning and a wail at noon, because he did not kill me from the womb, so that my mother might have been my grave and her womb an eternal conception. Why did I come out from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in confusion?”

Those who think that souls once existed in heavenly places and were cast down from a better state into a worse use this and similar testimonies, arguing that it was better to dwell in the heavens than on earth and to assume a body of humiliation. In seeking arguments for their heresy—new arguments, or rather already ancient ones—we, however, read the words of blessed Job: “Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the night on which they said, ‘A male child has been conceived’;” and, “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘A child has been born to you’” (Job III). We apply them to this testimony, understanding that it is better not to exist than to live in torments, in accordance with what is written: “Death is rest for the man whose way God has closed” [Col. 0967C] (Ecclus. XXII). And again: “Why was light given to the miserable, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul?” (Job III).

In the Gospel also we read the simple statement: “It would have been better for him if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI). This does not mean that there is someone who was not born, but that it is better not to exist than to exist in evil. For it is one thing altogether not to exist, and another thing, while existing, to be tortured without interruption.

How do we prefer a peaceful death to a miserable life? Hence Amos calls it a day of darkness and a day of affliction (Amos V), and Jacob, because he lived in labor and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil (Gen. XLVII). The apostle Paul says that Christ came “to deliver us from the present evil age” (Gal. I). And again: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. V).

The Hebrews calculate the fifth month—the month in which Jerusalem was captured and the temple overthrown—as the month of Jeremiah’s birth, using certain highly intricate and incredible arguments. If they are able to prove this, I do not know how they can interpret the testimony of Job, unless perhaps they claim that this day also prefigured, through a kind of foreshadowing and prophecy, the future destruction of the temple.

As for the curse comparing the man to overthrown cities, I think it refers to Sodom and Gomorrah, and that the whole time is to be understood as mourning, so that there may be a cry in the morning and a wail at noon. As for what follows—“who did not kill me in the womb”—they think that God is signified: “so that,” he says, “conception might have been eternal for me.” All these things are spoken hyperbolically.

Finally, he explains the reasons why he prefers death to life, and nonexistence to an evil existence, adding: “Why did I come out from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in confusion?”

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The capture of Zedekiah and the burning of Jerusalem

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord when King Zedekiah sent to him Phassur son of Melchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying: Inquire of the Lord for us, because Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us, to see whether perhaps the Lord will deal with us according to all his wonders and withdraw from us.”

Above, the high priest Phassur, or Phascor, who struck Jeremiah, [Col. 0968B] had Emmer as his father. This Phassur, however, is the son of Melchiah. This is stated so that no one may think they are the same person.

King Zedekiah sends to the prophet, wishing either to learn the people’s situation or to discover the opinion of the leaders, so that through messengers he may secretly ascertain what judgment the Lord holds concerning the city of Jerusalem and the Jewish people.

When it adds, “because Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is fighting against us,” it shows that Jerusalem was already under siege and that Zedekiah was asking the prophet about this. It should also be noted that in the prophets, especially Ezekiel and Jeremiah, the order of kings and events is not consistently observed. Rather, what according to the historical sequence happened later is sometimes reported first, and what happened first is reported afterward.

For it is one thing to write history and another to write prophecy, as in the present passage. Zedekiah, who was captured together with the city of Jerusalem, is described as sending to Jeremiah while Jerusalem was under siege. Later the history of his brother Jehoiakim, who had been king before him, and of Jehoiachin—that is, Jeconiah—the son of Jehoiakim, is narrated. We shall speak about them in what follows.

“And Jeremiah said to them: Thus you shall say to Zedekiah: This says the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold, I shall turn the weapons of war (or, the military arms) that are in your hands and with which you fight against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who are besieging you around the walls, and I shall gather them—or, *eos*, ‘them,’ the besiegers—into the midst of this city. And I shall wage war against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm (or, a lofty arm), in fury, indignation, and great anger. And I shall strike the inhabitants of this city; people and animals shall die of a great pestilence.”

“You are trying in vain,” he says, “to resist the Chaldeans who are besieging you and to prepare weapons of war. You will use them only in the middle of the city, so that you may appear to be armed. But while they besiege you, I shall wage war against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm, and I shall strike you with my fury and indignation, so that you and every breathing creature will die of famine and pestilence in the midst of the city.”

We read that this indeed happened. For without any battle array or clash of combatants, so great a siege captured the city that those who defeated it had no one left to defeat, but only people to capture. “Better,” he says, “were those wounded by the sword than those killed by famine.”

[Col. 0969A] “And after this the Lord says: I shall give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his servants, and his people, and those who remain in this city after the pestilence, the sword, and the famine into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies and of those who seek their lives. And he shall strike them with the edge of the sword, and he shall not turn aside, spare, or show mercy.”

What we have translated as “into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies” is not found in the Septuagint. In place of what we said—“he shall not turn aside, spare, or show mercy”—the Septuagint translated, “I will not spare, nor will I show mercy.”

The Hebrew is better, so that the cruel and inflexible sentence may appear to belong more to the king of Babylon than to the Lord. At first the prophecy was spoken concerning the whole city; now it is specifically foretold concerning Zedekiah and his people—those who remain after the pestilence, sword, and famine—that he will be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and killed with the sword together with his friends. Let him expect no mercy from the one whose treaty and relationship he abandoned through perjury.

“ And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. Whoever remains in this city shall die by the sword, famine, and pestilence; but whoever goes out and defects to the Chaldeans, who are besieging you, shall live, and his life shall be as spoil to him. For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good,” says the Lord; “it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire.”

To those who had been sent by the king and had come to the prophet to entreat him to inquire of the Lord on their behalf, he had given the preceding answer, including what they were to report to King Zedekiah. Now he urges them to answer the people, and gives counsel that they should defect to the Chaldeans, contrary to the king’s command—something no one is unaware was dangerous for the prophet. Hence he also invokes death upon himself and says: “Cursed be the day on which I was born; why did I come forth from the womb, that I might see trouble and sorrow?” [Jer. 20:14, 18] This is not because it is a light matter, before the city has even been captured, to advise people to surrender themselves voluntarily to captivity—as though, when shipwreck is imminent, one should order those who are about to suffer it to seize the oars and planks before the wreck and the ship’s destruction, and deliver themselves to the waves—but because it is more tolerable, however they may be captured, to remain alive than to be consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence.

There are some who explain this passage according to the allegorical sense as follows: that it is better to surrender oneself to secular disciplines, and especially to philosophy, than to remain in that Church in which there is a famine of the word of God, and in which the whole people is dying by the sword of heretics, through the scarcity of doctrine, and by heretical pestilence.

“And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, house of David. Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the slanderer, lest perhaps my indignation go forth (or: so that my indignation may not go forth) like fire, and be kindled, and there be no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your undertakings.”

What follows—“because of the wickedness of your undertakings”—is not found in the Septuagint. Since he had said above, “And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord,” he now appropriately adds, “and to the house of the king of Judah,” so that “you shall say: Thus says the Lord” is understood. For ἀπὸ κοινοῦ—“by a common construction”—joins what comes before and what follows, so that the sense is: “And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord.”

The speech is directed specifically to the royal house, because it is chiefly on account of its guilt that the city is besieged, so that it may correct its error through repentance and obtain the Lord’s mercy. “Judge,” he says, “judgment in the morning”—not in the darkness of wickedness, but in the light of justice. “And rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the slanderer”: do not show partiality in judgment, but, when the rich oppress the poor, let God’s command have greater weight with you than the power of the persecutor.

“And if,” he says, “you do this, the fire of my wrath will by no means be kindled among you, nor will it find material to consume.” In this passage the incredible mercy of God is displayed: although he had previously said, “For I have set my face against this city for harm and not for good; it shall be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire,” now, when the Lord’s sentence is already pressing upon them, he summons them to salvation. This is not because he does not know that Jerusalem is to be captured, but because human free will is preserved, so that they may appear to perish not through ignorance of what is to come, but by their own choice. So too the Savior knew that the apostle would deny him and that he himself would be crucified—indeed, he had often foretold this to the apostles—yet he nonetheless admonished them, wishing to correct them toward repentance, so that whatever they later suffered might be attributed to their own fault, [Col. 0970C] not to the hardness of the one threatening them.

“Behold, I am against you, inhabitant of the valley, the solid and level place,” says the Lord, “you who say: Who will strike (or: frighten) us, and who will enter our houses? And I will visit you.” What follows—“according to the fruit of your undertakings, says the Lord”—is not found in the Septuagint: “And I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it shall devour everything around her.”

Instead of “inhabitant of the valley, the solid and level place,” the Septuagint translated: “Behold, I am against you, who dwell in the valley of SOR [the Greek form is not reproduced in the supplied text], the level place.” Symmachus interpreted this as “rock,” Theodotion as “besieged”; Aquila’s first edition has “solid,” and the second “Tyre.” For Sor, or Sur, in the Hebrew language signifies “Tyre,” “flint,” and “constricted” [the supplied text reads *cohortatam*, apparently an OCR error for *coarctatam*].

He is speaking against Jerusalem, which has been surrounded by the siege, or which is enclosed by the Babylonian army like Tyre by the great sea, so that it cannot escape. Or else she considers herself, like an exceedingly hard rock, impregnable and strong because of the solidity of her walls and their great size, and says: “Who will be able to frighten us, and who will enter our houses?” But God speaks in opposition: “I will visit you”; you will not be able to escape my eye. I will visit you for destruction and repay you the fruit of your wickedness. And I will kindle the fire in your forest—not the Babylonian, as you suppose, nor the king of the Chaldeans, but my wrath will accomplish all these things.

He calls Jerusalem and the entire surrounding region a forest, because it has no fruit-bearing trees of good works and is prepared for burning. Beautifully he calls it a level valley, because it is accessible to enemies, rather than a lofty mountain that is difficult to climb, in accordance with what is said in Isaiah: “The vision of the valley of Zion” [Isa. 22:1].

Whatever is prophesied concerning the royal house and the metropolitan city, let us refer to the ecclesiastical order and the rulers of the Churches—those, at any rate, who have surrendered themselves to pride, wealth, and wantonness. Let them not immediately imagine that, because they are the royal house, they will be delivered from destruction. Likewise, although there were descendants of David, very few were found who pleased the Lord, such as David himself, Hezekiah, and Josiah; while a very large part of the rulers and of the royal line provoked the Lord’s anger against the whole people.

## CHAPTER XXII

The prophet is sent to preach justice to the king; Jehoiakim, king of Judah, is cast unburied outside Jerusalem.

[Col. 0971B]

“Thus says the Lord: Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and speak there this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, king of Judah, who sit upon the throne of David—you and your servants and your people, who enter through these gates. Thus says the Lord: Practice judgment and righteousness, and rescue the one oppressed by violence from the hand of the slanderer; do not wrongfully distress the resident alien, the orphan, or the widow, nor oppress them unjustly or impiously, and do not shed innocent blood in this place. For if you truly do this word, kings sitting from the line of David upon his throne shall enter through the gates of this house, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you do not hear these words, I swear by myself, says the Lord, that this house shall become a desolation.” (Jerome.)

This vision—or rather, this word of the Lord—is either given to the Prophet before Zedekiah sent messengers to him, or certainly, after he instructed the messengers what they should report to the king, Jeremiah is commanded not to speak to the king through messengers, but to go himself to the palace and speak to him there.

At the same time, let us observe the divine wisdom: through the messengers he orders grievous things to be announced, mingled with promises of prosperity if the king should be willing to practice repentance. Here, however, because Jeremiah himself is commanded to go, he does not announce calamities and the captivity that is already at hand, but warns him what he must do in order to avoid the Lord’s impending sentence.

It is proper to kings to practice judgment and righteousness, to rescue those oppressed by violence from the hand of slanderers, and to offer assistance to the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. And to impress upon them a greater concern for God’s commandments, he adds: “Do not distress them”—so that they may not only rescue them, but also not permit them, through their connivance, to be distressed by others.

“And do not shed innocent blood in this place.” To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the administration of the laws.

“If,” he says, “you do these things, O kings of Judah, you shall retain your former authority and enter the gates of Jerusalem with honor. But if you are unwilling to do so, O royal house, it will be not so much the Lord’s cruelty as your own will that reduces the whole city to desolation.”

Whatever was said to the royal house, let bishops, and their associates the presbyters and deacons, and the entire ecclesiastical order, understand as addressed to them. If they do what has been commanded, and, among other things, do not shed innocent blood by scandalizing the least and wounding the consciences of individuals, let them retain the dignity entrusted to them by the Lord. But if they are unwilling to do these things and despise them, let them themselves reduce the Church of God to desolation.

Those who are of the line of David enter through the gates of Jerusalem and sit upon his throne—he is interpreted as “strong of hand”—and they ascend chariots and horses when they restrain both their own disturbances and those of the people, enter the Church with disciplined conduct, and are accompanied by a chorus of many virtues harmonizing with them on every side. And that we may believe this to be true, he swears by himself, because, according to the Apostle, he has no one greater by whom he can swear [Heb. 6:13].

“For thus says the Lord concerning (or: to) the house of the king of Judah: Gilead, you are to me the head (or: beginning) of Lebanon. If I do not make you a desolation, uninhabitable cities! And I will consecrate against you a slayer and his weapons; and they shall cut down your choice cedars, and cast (or: throw) them into the fire. And many nations shall pass through this city, and each one shall say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord done this to this great city? And they shall answer: Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord their God, worshiped foreign gods, and served them.”

Scripture records Gilead, which half the tribe of Manasseh possessed beyond the Jordan [Gen. 31], as the mountain where Laban overtook the fleeing Jacob. According to Genesis, the mountain received the name Σορός, that is, “heap of testimony,” because there Jacob and Laban swore an oath over a heap of stones gathered together.

It is the head, or beginning, of the lofty mountain of Lebanon, which is entirely planted with cedars, in accordance with David’s song: “The Lord will shake the cedars of Lebanon” [Ps. 28:5]. And elsewhere: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” [Ps. 36:35]. And in Zechariah we read: “Open your gates, Lebanon, and fire shall devour your cedars” [Zech. 11:1].

Therefore, in the present passage, because he was speaking to the royal house, he speaks metaphorically to the temple, or to the house of the tribe of Judah: either because it itself is elevated, or because remedies for all sins were sought from the temple and sanctuary. Hence the same prophet recalls: “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has healing not risen for the daughter of my people?” [Jer. 8:22].

He therefore threatens the royal house, the city of Jerusalem, and the temple, which he calls the head of Lebanon: they shall be reduced to desolation with all their cities—not by the power of the king of Babylon, but by the command of the Lord, who says: “I will consecrate against you one who kills.”

Nebuchadnezzar and his entire army are called holy because they execute God’s sentence. “And they shall cut down,” he says, “your choice cedars”—all the powerful and rulers of the city—“and cast them into the fire,” so that the all-devouring flame may consume everything.

When all things have been destroyed, many nations shall pass through the city and temple, which they had previously been forbidden to enter, and each shall say to his neighbor why the Lord had brought upon the renowned and great city so sudden and so enormous an overthrow. “And they shall answer,” he says, those who are questioned, explaining the causes of the ruins: “Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord their God,” and worshiped idols in place of God.

Let the royal house of our own city hear this also, and its rulers, and the cedars that raise their summit to the clouds and say in their pride, “Who will see?”—let them know that they will quickly be consumed by the Lord’s flame if they refuse to obey his commands. The sacrifice of the executioner and his weapons, however, is one thing; that of priests and those who minister to the Lord is another.

“Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn over him. Weep bitterly for the one who goes away, because he shall not return again, nor see the land of his birth. For thus says the Lord concerning Sellum son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, who went out from this place: He shall not return here again, but in the place to which I have carried him, there he shall die, and he shall no longer see this land.”

Josiah, the righteous king, had three sons: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. The first of these, Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, led captive into Egypt, where he died; and in his place he appointed his brother Jehoiakim king [2 Kings 23–25]. After Jehoiakim’s death, his son Jeconiah reigned. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, led him into captivity with his mother, his officials, and his craftsmen; in his place his uncle Zedekiah reigned, who, after the capture of Jerusalem, was taken to Babylon.

The question therefore arises: who is this person who must not be mourned, who is to be led into captivity and will not return, when three were captured and carried away? The Hebrews think that this applies to all of them—that is, to Jehoahaz, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah—and that all the sons of Josiah are called Sellem, or Sellum, which means “consummation” or “completion,” because the kingdom of Judah ended in them.

I, however, think that this is spoken specifically of Zedekiah, concerning whom the prophecy of both the present and the preceding chapter is given. In him the kingdom of Judah truly ended: under him the city was captured, he was led to Babylon, and there he is recorded to have died. He is Sellum—that is, “consummation” and “completion”—the son of Josiah and king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father.

Jeconiah, however, was not Josiah’s son but his grandson, the son of Jehoiakim. Thus, from the beginning of the vision, when King Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, until this chapter, we should understand everything as being said to and about King Zedekiah.

“Woe to him who builds his house with injustice and his upper rooms without judgment; who oppresses his neighbor without cause and does not give him his wages; who says: I will build myself a spacious house and broad upper rooms; who opens windows for himself, makes cedar ceilings, and paints them with vermilion. Will you reign because you vie with the cedar? Did not your father eat and drink, and practice judgment and righteousness, when it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy for his own good. Was this not because he knew me? says the Lord. But your eyes and heart are directed toward greed, toward shedding innocent blood, toward slander, and toward the pursuit of evil works.”

The Septuagint has: “O you who build your house without righteousness and your upper rooms without judgment! Your neighbor works for him without payment, and he does not give him his wages. You built yourself a small house, airy upper rooms decorated with windows and paneled with cedar, and smeared with vermilion. Will you reign because you contend with Ahaz your father? They shall not eat and they shall not drink. It will be better for you to practice good judgment and righteousness. Now they have known; they did not judge the judgment of the humble, nor the judgment of the poor. Is this not your failure to know me? says the Lord. Behold, your eyes are not right, nor is your heart good, but they are directed toward your greed, toward shedding innocent blood, and toward iniquity and murder, so that you may do these things.”

I have set out both editions in full, so that both the Hebrew truth and the difficulty of the common edition may more easily be recognized. The speech is against Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, about whom we spoke above: Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, appointed him in place of his brother Jehoahaz, whom he had led away bound into Egypt.

We read, as the history of both Kings and Chronicles relates [2 Kings 23–24; 2 Chron. 36], that Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, ruled cruelly, proved impious, and later died; yet his burial is not recorded, although Holy Scripture ordinarily reports both the deaths and burials of all the kings. In his case it specifically reports that he died but does not say that he was buried. We shall speak of this in what follows.

The passage therefore mourns the aforementioned king because he trusts in his injustice, thinks his royal dignity will be perpetual, builds upper rooms for himself, oppresses his friends, refuses to pay those who open them for him, and imagines that the construction of his palace will be eternal.

“Will you,” says the divine word, “be able to reign forever because you wish to compare yourself with the lofty cedar,” namely with your father Josiah, the righteous king? “Your father,” it says, “ate and drank,” enjoyed royal wealth, and nevertheless did not offend God by possessing riches. Rather, he pleased him because he practiced judgment and righteousness; therefore it was and will be well with him both in the present age and in the future.

“He judged,” it says, “the cause of the poor and needy,” and did so for the refreshment of those whom he heard, specifically “for his own good.” All these things happened prosperously for him “because he knew me,” says the Lord.

But your eyes, O Jehoiakim, incline toward greed, toward shedding innocent blood, toward slander, and toward the pursuit of evil works.

According to the Septuagint, however, I cannot understand what sense the passage has. Although the other parts agree with one another to some extent, the statement, “Will you reign because you contend with Ahaz your father?”—for which the Hebrew has [the Hebrew term is not reproduced in the supplied text], and this word signifies “cedar”—clearly has no intelligible sense. Likewise, what follows—“They shall not eat, and they shall not drink”—and the rest are so scattered and confused among themselves that, without the truth of the Hebrew reading, they have no intelligible meaning.

We can take this passage, according to the anagogical sense, as directed against heretics. They build themselves not a large house, broad with the abundance of the Church, but a small one. They build it neither with righteousness nor with judgment, because they desire to seize what belongs to others.

Hence it says: “You built yourself a small house, airy upper rooms,” which are carried about by every wind of doctrine, “and decorated with windows.” They have neither a permanent building nor solid stability. “And paneled with cedar,” it says. They seem indeed to have a most beautiful paneling, but against the rains and storms of persecutions they quickly rot and collapse. “And smeared with vermilion.” They too promise the Lord’s passion and blood, but they do not reign forever, because they contend with and provoke to anger Arez—that is, “cedar”—their father.

Every heretic is born in the Church but is cast out of the Church; he contends and fights against his parent. And when it says, “They shall not eat and they shall not drink,” the body and blood of the Savior are understood, along with the rest of the same kind. It says that all error descends from the fact that they did not know God and do not have upright eyes, but that their heart is inclined toward greed, so that they seize what belongs to others and shed the blood of the deceived—for this is to commit murder. Matters that are obscure must be discussed at greater length.

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: They shall not mourn for him, saying, ‘Alas, brother!’ and ‘Alas, sister!’ They shall not lament for him, saying, ‘Alas, lord!’ and ‘Alas, illustrious one!’ He shall be buried with the burial of a donkey, rotting and cast outside the gates of Jerusalem.”

What we have supplied from the Hebrew—“They shall not mourn for him, saying, ‘Alas, brother!’ and ‘Alas, sister!’”—is not found in the Septuagint. It is specifically spoken against King Jehoiakim, and the riddle that previously seemed concealed and ambiguous among the three brothers is disclosed: the passage is not about Jehoahaz or Zedekiah, but specifically about Jehoiakim, whom Hebrew history says was killed by bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Ammonites, and Moabites. Hence in the book of Kings he is recorded as dead, while his burial is passed over in silence [2 Kings 24]. In the Book of Chronicles we read that he was bound in chains and taken to Babylon [2 Chron. 36]; nothing further is reported about him.

Appropriately, it says that he will be buried with the burial of a donkey, signifying in other words that he will be unburied—that is, torn apart by beasts and birds.

For this is the burial of a donkey:

“Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan, and cry out to those passing by, because all your lovers have been crushed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, and you said, ‘I will not listen.’ This has been your way from your youth, because you did not listen to my voice. The wind shall pasture all your shepherds (or: lovers), and your lovers (or: friends) shall go into captivity; and you shall be confounded and ashamed because of all your wickedness. You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars, how you have groaned when pains came upon you, pains like those of a woman in labor!”

By the metaphor of Lebanon and Bashan, regions and mountains beyond the Jordan, the speech is directed to Jerusalem: it has trusted in Egypt in vain—or to Jehoiakim himself, who was reigning in Jerusalem at that time and had been appointed king by the Egyptians—because he hopes in vain for help from the Egyptians, although they too will be overcome by the king of Babylon and led into captivity [2 Kings 23].

What he says, “I spoke to you,” means that God himself spoke through the prophets; or, “They spoke to you,” with my prophets understood. “And in your prosperity you said, ‘I will not listen.’” He accuses her of arrogance, because she abused the abundance of her riches in contempt of God. He relates that not only at this time, but from the beginning, when she was brought out of Egypt, she did not listen to God’s voice.

Hence all her shepherds and rulers have been scattered here and there and have submitted their necks to Babylonian captivity. The statement, “You who sit in Lebanon and nest in the cedars,” reproves the arrogance that had grown from the abundance of all things, and indicates that sudden pain and captivity would come upon her like the pain of a woman in childbirth.

What we translated as “Cry out to those passing by,” and what is written in the Hebrew as [the Hebrew term is not reproduced in the supplied text], the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as “across the sea,” while Symmachus has “from the opposite side,” indicating that the prophet’s voice must reach from Jerusalem as far as Mount Lebanon and Bashan.

“As I live, says the Lord, even if Jeconiah [Choniah], son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring upon my right hand, from there I would tear him away (or: you), and I would give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whose face you fear; and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon” (which is not found in the Septuagint), “and into the hand of the Chaldeans. And I will send you (or: cast you out), and your mother who bore you, into a foreign land in which you were not born; and there you shall die, and in the land to which they lift up their desire to return, there they shall not return.”

Above he had said, “You shall speak these things to the house of the king of Judah,” and then, “Go down to the house of the king of Judah,” and again, “Thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah.” After speaking about Zedekiah, who was the last of the kings in Jerusalem, he now returns, in reverse order, to his brother Jehoiakim, who reigned before him. With that prophecy fulfilled, he now speaks to Jehoiakim’s son, the grandson of Josiah, Jeconiah, king of Jerusalem, who is also called by another name, Joachim. He was captured by Nebuchadnezzar with his mother, his officials, his craftsmen, and many nobles, and was led into Chaldea, where he died.

The sense is therefore this: just as a signet ring does not leave the hand of its bearer and is not easily removed from the finger, so Jeconiah is in my hand; nevertheless, I will tear him away and hand him over to the king of Babylon. There he will die with his mother and all his companions, and he will no longer see the land of Judah, which he desires.

The wretched Grunnius, who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue falsehood, translated into Latin one book of the very pagan Pythagorean Sextus. He divided it into two volumes and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Sixtus, bishop of the city of Rome. In it there is no mention of Christ, the Holy Spirit, God the Father, or the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles. With his customary recklessness and madness he called this book the *Ring* [*Annulus*]. It is read throughout many provinces, especially by those who preach ἀπάθεια (*apatheia*, freedom from passions) and sinlessness.

Just as the Lord threatens to cast Jeconiah from his hand and finger like a ring, so I beseech the reader to reject that impious book and, if he wishes to read it, to read it like the other books of the philosophers, not as an ecclesiastical volume.

In commentaries and explanations, whose custom is to set forth various interpreters’ opinions, I commonly insert such expressions as: “Some say this; others maintain that; some think thus.” The wretched Grunnius, and many years later the disciples of Jovinianus, have accused and continue to accuse me of placing my own opinions under other people’s names. I do this out of kindness, so that I may not seem to attack anyone by name.

Since kindness has been turned into slander, I now say both to the one who has died and to the one who is alive and attempts to restore his heresy: their teacher Origen refers this passage to Christ, claiming that he was torn from the hand of God the Father like a ring, sent into a land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and delivered to the cross; and that his mother—undoubtedly the Synagogue—was also captured and cast out.

Yet, in mentioning these things, he is not afraid to understand the following passage concerning the Lord of majesty:

“Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as abominable (or: sterile),” and the rest.

He writes this so that his disciples may not dare to deny it, in the fifth book of the *Stromata*.

“Is this man Jeconiah a clay vessel, crushed? Is he a vessel without any pleasure (or: usefulness)? Why have he and his offspring been cast away and thrown into a land they did not know?”

Instead of what we said, “Is this a clay vessel, crushed?” Symmachus translated, “Is this refuse?” or “Is this worthless and discarded rubbish?” The Septuagint has nothing corresponding to this, but interpreted only: “Jeconiah has been dishonored like a vessel in which there is no usefulness.”

Although this is said about Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, someone dares to refer it typologically to Christ. Since the Apostle says that the Lord and Savior is the image of the invisible God [Col. 1:15], the firstborn of every creature—that is, wisdom, the Word, truth, life, and righteousness—he calls him a ring that is cast away or torn from the Lord’s hand and handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar.

“They have been cast away,” he says, “he and his offspring, and thrown into a land they did not know”—something no one doubts happened to Jeconiah.
