Jeconiah is interpreted as “the Lord’s preparation”; in the present passage its first syllable, that is, the Lord’s name, is removed, and he is called Choniah, so that he may be understood as prepared for destruction and ruin.

“Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man down as sterile, a man who shall not prosper in his days; for none of his offspring shall be a man who sits upon the throne of David and has authority any longer in Judah.”

If I wished to mark individually all the places where the Septuagint either omitted or altered things, the discussion would become lengthy, especially since a diligent reader can determine from both editions what has been changed, added, or removed.

Instead of “sterile,” the Hebrew has [the Hebrew term is not reproduced in the supplied text]. Aquila’s first edition has “sterile”; the second, ἀναύξητον, that is, “not growing”; Symmachus has “empty”; the Septuagint and Theodotion interpreted it as “abominable” and “rejected.”

A question arises: how can the prophecy stand that none of his descendants would be born who sat upon the throne of David, nor any ruler who would thereafter be in Judah, when the Lord and Savior was born from his line? Gabriel speaks of his birth to Mary:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” [Luke 1:31–33].

We can therefore say that the words omitted by the Septuagint—namely, “he shall not prosper in his days,” or “he shall not grow”—created the difficulty for those who did not know them. The Septuagint translated: “Write this man down as a rejected man, because no man shall grow from his offspring who sits upon the throne of David, a ruler thereafter in Judah.” The same statement is placed twice in the Hebrew. Thinking that it had been added to the Greek books, those who first wrote them removed it.

Let us answer, then, that in Jeconiah’s days no man succeeded him who sat upon his throne, but that much later one was born from his offspring who obtained his throne.

The passage can also be resolved in this way: a man and human being will not sit upon the throne of David, but God will sit upon it. His kingdom will not be earthly and short-lived, as David’s was, but perpetual and heavenly, as Scripture says: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

Thus Jeconiah was born from Jehoiakim, Shealtiel from Jeconiah, Zerubbabel from Shealtiel, and in due succession one arrives at Christ. But in the days of Jehoiakim no king-son succeeded him as he himself had succeeded his father. Rather, he was in captivity, and from Shealtiel and Zerubbabel until Christ no one from the royal line exercised royal power.

This is because the Hebrew reads: “In his days and at that very time”—the time in which he lived—“there shall be no man who sits upon the throne of David.” For all were captives, and thereafter no one from David’s line held authority in the land of Judah.

Hence Josephus relates that rulers came from the priestly order and the tribe of Levi; these were succeeded by Herod, son of Antipater the proselyte. Later, under Vespasian, the kingdom of this line—or rather the appearance of imperial rule—was completely destroyed.

## CHAPTER XXIII

The Lord threatens the shepherds who tear the flock; concerning the birth and passion of Christ, and concerning false prophets.

“Woe to the shepherds who scatter and tear apart the flock of my pasture (or: O shepherds who disperse and scatter the sheep of my pasture), says the Lord. Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel to the shepherds who pasture my people: You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your undertakings, says the Lord. And I will gather the remnant of my flock from all the lands to which I had driven them, and I will bring them back to their fields (or: restore them to their pastures), and they shall grow and multiply. And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they shall pasture them. They shall no longer fear, nor be terrified, and none shall be missing from their number, says the Lord.”

(Jerome.) The prophetic speech is directed to the shepherds, or spoken concerning the shepherds. Since we read that Jeconiah, the penultimate king of Judah, was of the line of David: “Earth, earth, earth, hear the words of the Lord. Write this man down as rejected (or: sterile), and none of his offspring shall sit upon the throne of David,” and since every hope of the Judaic kingdom had been cut off, the speech passes to the rulers of the Churches.

With the Synagogue and its shepherds abandoned and condemned, the speech is directed to the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they shall pasture them. They shall no longer fear, nor be terrified, and none shall be missing from their number, says the Lord” [cf. Ezek. 34:23].

The apostles will pasture the ecclesiastical flock confidently and without any fear, and the remnant of the people of Israel will be saved from all lands. They will return to their fields, or pastures, and grow and multiply.

But upon the wicked shepherds—the scribes and Pharisees—the Lord will visit the wickedness of their undertakings. We may also understand this allegorically of the rulers of the Church who do not govern the Lord’s sheep worthily: once they have been cast away and condemned, the people are saved and entrusted to others who have proved worthy, so that the remnant may be saved.

Shepherds destroy the sheep when they teach heresy; they tear and scatter them when they create schisms; they drive them out when they separate them from the Church contrary to justice; and they do not visit them when they withhold their hand from penitents. The Lord will have mercy on all of them, restoring their former pastures to them and removing the wicked shepherds.

“Behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will raise up for David a righteous branch (or: a righteous rising one), and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise (or: understand), and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely. And this is the name by which they shall call him (or: by which he shall call him): ‘The Lord our righteous one’ (or: ‘our righteousness).’” In Hebrew this is expressed by [the Hebrew term is not preserved in the supplied text]. What has been wrongly added in the Septuagint, “among the prophets,” must be removed entirely. For another chapter follows, which they have omitted. When that chapter has ended, the title is “To the Prophets,” or “Against the Prophets”; we shall discuss it in its proper place.

Accordingly, after the shepherds of the Synagogue—namely, the scribes and Pharisees—have been rejected, and the remnant of Israel saved, and the apostles of the Gospel appointed in place of the former leaders, the shepherd of shepherds, the prince of princes, the King of kings, and the Lord of lords is introduced: namely, Christ our Savior. He is properly the righteous branch, or the righteous rising one, of whom we read: “In his days righteousness shall rise” (Ps. 71). And elsewhere: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising, and he shall rise beneath him, and he shall build a temple for the Lord” (Zech. 6). Thus, just as in Isaiah he is called “Emmanuel” (Isa. 7)—that is, “God with us”—so in Jeremiah he receives the name “Our righteousness.” Hence the Apostle also says: “He was made wisdom for us by God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1).

His opponent, Antichrist, together with the devil who dwells in him, is called in Zechariah the “foolish shepherd.” Of Christ, however, it is said: “And he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.” For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5). In those days both the two and the ten tribes—Judah and Israel—shall be saved together, and from the two staffs, according to Ezekiel, one staff shall be made (Ezek. 37). His name, if according to the Septuagint he is called “the Lord,” shall be called Josedech, that is, “the righteous Lord”; but if according to the Hebrew, which reads “his name shall be called,” it shall be rendered “the Lord our righteousness.” For this is what [the Hebrew term is not preserved in the supplied text] signifies, which Symmachus translated, “Lord, justify us.”

“Therefore, behold, the days are coming,” says the Lord. “And they shall no longer say: ‘As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,’ but: ‘As the Lord lives, who brought out and led back the offspring of the house of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands to which I had driven them there’; and they shall dwell in their own land.”

This entire chapter is absent from the Septuagint. Its meaning is that God’s people will no longer be liberated from Egypt through Moses, but through Jesus Christ from the whole world, into which they had been scattered. This is partly being fulfilled even now throughout the world, and will be fulfilled completely when they come from east and west, north and south, and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—so that, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel may be saved.

“Against the Prophets” (or: “among the prophets,” or “to the prophets”). As we said above, this title is placed in the Septuagint edition at the end of the preceding chapter, where we read: “And this is the name by which the Lord shall call him, Josedech, among the prophets.” Many people, being ignorant of this, invent various delirious explanations. It would have been far better simply to confess ignorance than to make others heirs of their incompetence.

The passage, however, is directed against the prophets—indeed, against the false prophets—of Jerusalem and Samaria, whom it now calls “prophets” by the common and customary name. Concerning them it is written immediately afterward: “And among the prophets of Samaria I saw iniquity”; and at once: “And among the prophets of Jerusalem [I saw] horrible things.” Whenever he uses the conjunction “and,” he shows that what precedes was also said about the Lord’s prophets, who themselves proved similar to the false prophets.

“My heart is broken within me; all my bones trembled (or: were shaken). I became like a drunken man, and like a man intoxicated (or: stupefied with wine), because of the presence of the Lord and because of the presence of his holy words (or: also because of the presence of the beauty of his glory).”

Having contemplated the face of almighty God—that is, the Father—and having contemplated the face of the Son, “who, according to the Apostle, is called the radiance of his glory and the likeness of God’s substance” (Heb. 1), the prophet shudders in soul and body and understands that he is nothing, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. 72). Or he offers to God a sacrifice of his conscience and humility, according to what is written in the Psalms: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God will not despise a broken and humbled heart” (Ps. 50).

As for the bones that trembled or were shaken, let us understand them as those of which the same David sings: “All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34). He became like a drunk man, and like one intoxicated or stupefied by wine, possessing no understanding and no wisdom: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. 93). If this is so, where are those who proclaim perfect righteousness in human beings? If they answer that they say this concerning the saints, and not from themselves, I certainly think that no one is holier than Jeremiah, who was a virgin, a prophet, and sanctified in the womb, and who by his very name prefigures the Lord Savior. For Jeremiah is interpreted as “the Exalted One of the Lord.”

“Because the land is filled with adulteries, because the land mourned at the presence of the curse (or: oath). The fields have dried up (or: the pastures of the wilderness), and their course has become evil, and their strength is improper.”

What we have set down from the Hebrew—“because the land is filled with adulteries”—is absent from the Septuagint, which has “oath” in place of “curse.” He gives the reasons: because of adulteries and curses, or excessive oath-taking—in fact, perjuries—barrenness of crops followed. Whatever you understand literally concerning the land of Judea, apply it to the congregation of believers, because through adulteries and lies, or perjuries, barrenness of virtues and of God’s gifts arises in the churches.

“For prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I found their evil,” says the Lord. “Therefore their way shall be like a slippery path in darkness; for they shall be driven and fall upon it, because I shall bring (or: inflict) evils upon them, the year of their visitation,” says the Lord.

When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially among its leaders, let us know that this has been fulfilled: “Prophet and priest have been polluted; in my house I found their evils,” says the Lord. The house of Christ is the Church, concerning which Paul also writes to Timothy: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth” (1 Tim. 3).

Understand “prophet” as teacher, and “priest” as the dignity of ministry. If they agree with a perverse mind, their way will be slippery and in darkness, and they will not have the Lord speaking to them: “I came as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12). Hence the holy man speaks, fleeing all darkness: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4).

When they are in darkness and on a slippery path—that is, in heretical error—they will be driven and fall at every movement. The Lord will bring evils upon them—not because the evils are evil in themselves, so that the Lord inflicts evil, but because they are evils for those who endure punishments. Otherwise, the same things are both evil and good: evil in relation to those whom they torment, good in relation to those whom they correct. It should also be noted that “the year of the Lord’s visitation” means the correction and punishment of sinners, according to what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from him” (Ps. 88).

“And among the prophets of Samaria I saw folly (or: iniquity): they prophesied by Baal and deceived my people Israel.”

I think that, according to the mystical interpretation, the prophets of Samaria properly signify heretics, and all who boast of knowledge falsely so called. Just as the prophets of Samaria prophesied whatever they said by Baal—that is, by an idol consecrated to demons—so heretics, whatever they say in the Church or outside the Church in order to overthrow the people of Israel who once saw God, speak through demons. Hence he says significantly: “And among the prophets of Samaria I saw folly.” For they do not possess him of whom it is said: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1).

“And among the prophets of Jerusalem I saw the likeness (or: horrible things) of adulterers and the way of falsehood. And they strengthened the hands of the worst people, so that no one would turn back from his wickedness (or: from his most wicked way). They have all become for me like Sodom, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah.”

He says: These things were found not only in the assemblies of heretics, but also among the prophets of Jerusalem—that is, among the teachers of the Church. I saw similar things, or horrible things: they adulterated the word of God and entered by the way of falsehood, so that they might yield to the deceits of heretics and strengthen the hands of the worst people, adding their evils to their own crimes and leading those whom they ought to have corrected into destruction.

Those who do this should not think themselves unpunished. They themselves, and those whom they favor, will be like Sodom; and all who dwell with them and do not withdraw from such people will be like Gomorrah. Let the worst doctrine therefore exult as much as it wishes, and let the prophets of Jerusalem glory in what they have obtained through falsehood and in having strengthened the hands of the worst people: their end will be like that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

“Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts concerning the prophets: Behold, I will feed them wormwood (or: sufferings,” and according to Symmachus, “bitterness”), “and I will give them gall to drink (or: bitter water), because pollution has gone forth from the prophets of Jerusalem into the whole land.”

Let us use this testimony against those who send letters filled with lies, deceit, and perjury throughout the world, polluting the ears of their hearers and damaging the reputation of the simple. In them is fulfilled what is written: “From the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth into the whole land.” For it is not enough for them to swallow their own iniquity and injure their neighbors; those whom they have once hated they strive to defame throughout the world and to sow blasphemies everywhere.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you. They speak the vision of their heart, and not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who blaspheme me (or: reject my word), ‘The Lord has spoken: Peace shall be yours’; and to everyone who walks in the perversity of his heart they say, ‘No evils shall come upon you.’”

So that the people might not think themselves free from guilt if they listened to perverse teachers, he says: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy falsehood to you and deceive you.” The punishment will be equal for teacher and disciple. They do not speak from the mouth of the Lord, but those things which they have fabricated in their own hearts.

“They say to those who blaspheme me”—that is, to heretics and the perverse, or to those who reject my word. What do they say? “The Lord has spoken: Peace shall be yours.” Do not fear harsh punishments, nor be terrified by empty threats. Peace and tranquility shall be yours, and whatever we say and announce to you, the Lord has spoken. The evil that you fear because of your evil conscience shall not come upon you; rather, the good that the Lord has spoken to you shall come.

“For who was present in the council of the Lord, and saw and heard his word? Who considered his word and heard it?”

Where we have translated “in the council of the Lord,” the Hebrew has [the Hebrew term is not preserved in the supplied text]. Aquila translates it as *secretum*, “secret”; Symmachus, “word”; the Septuagint and Theodotion translate it as “substance” or “subsistence.” The sense is this: Do not believe, O uneducated multitude, the prophets who announce falsehoods to you and say, “The Lord has spoken: Peace shall be yours; no evil shall come upon you.” How could they know the secrets of God, or through whom did they learn the council of the Lord? How did the word of the divine disposition reach them? Some of our people think that in this passage they have discovered a description of God’s substance.

“Behold, the whirlwind (or: tempest) and the Lord’s indignation will go forth, and the bursting tempest will come upon the head of the impious. The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he acts and until he fulfills the thought of his heart. In the last days you shall understand his council.”

Those who had said above, “The Lord has spoken to us: Peace shall be yours,” and whom he had rebuked because they could not know what was to come or understand God’s decision—he now shows by opposites that they know nothing at all. Instead of peace and security, the Babylonian tempest will come, and it will come not upon just anyone, but upon the heads of the impious—whether the whole people or those who announced falsehoods to the people.

God’s anger and fury are not now to be appeased as in former times; rather, what he foretold and so often threatened is to be completed in deed, and his thought and decision are to be confirmed by the punishments of the impious. When the final period of captivity arrives, he says, and the triumphant conqueror has prevailed over you and bound your hands with the clanking of chains, then you will understand his council, which you now falsely boast that you know.

“I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. If they had stood in my council and had made my words known to my people, I would certainly have turned them away from their evil way and from their most wicked thoughts.”

The Apostle also explains this meaning in Romans: “And since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting, filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, depravity, greed” (Rom. 1), and the rest.

Once false teachers have surrendered themselves to lies, perjuries, and the deaths of those whom they have deceived, they do not run gradually or with considered steps, but rush headlong into destruction—both their own and that of those whom they have deceived. The Lord does not speak to them; they themselves speak as if from the mouth of the Lord. Concerning them it is also said: “If they had stood in my council”—that is, if they had wished to submit to my will and had made my words known to my people, instead of flattering them and destroying them through adulation by saying, “You have no sins; you possess perfect righteousness; holiness, chastity, and justice are found in you alone.”

Then I would not have handed them over to uncleanness and disgrace, to do what is not fitting and to follow their most wicked thoughts. Let us contemplate heretics and see how, once they despair of salvation, they surrender themselves to gluttony and luxury: they eat meat, frequently visit the baths, give off the scent of musk, and, smeared with various perfumes, seek bodily beauty. For once they cease to hope for the future and do not believe in the resurrection, they show this by their actions, although they do not reveal it in words. If they believed, they would not do these things.

In this passage, where it is written, “If they had stood in my council,” Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint have translated it in the same way as above.

“Am I a God nearby,” says the Lord, “and not a God far away? If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him?” says the Lord. “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” says the Lord.

The Septuagint has: “I am a God who draws near,” says the Lord, “and not a God far away. If a man hides himself in secret places, shall I not see him?” says the Lord. “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” says the Lord.

Aquila and Symmachus likewise interpreted it as: “Am I a God of what is near, or nearby, and not a God of what is far away?” The Septuagint and Theodotion, however, translated it with the opposite meaning: “I am a God who draws near,” says the Lord, “and not a God far away.”

The former maintain that God knows not only what is near but also what is far away, and sees not only present things but future things as well. The latter think that God is present everywhere and that there is no place where God is absent. For God draws near to everyone, and especially to the saints, as though a garment were attached to the skin; sinners, however, withdrawing far from him, will perish.

We read this meaning also in the Psalms: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138).

Amos likewise agrees with this, saying: “If they descend as far as the underworld, from there your hand will lead them out; and if they ascend into heaven, from there I will bring them down; and if they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel, searching them out I will take them away from there; and if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it will bite them” (Amos 9).

Again, in the preceding psalm: “For darkness,” he says, “will not be darkened by you, and night shall be illumined like day; its darkness is like its light” (Ps. 138). Whenever the phrase “thus says the Lord” is frequently used in the prophets, it is always added so that their words may not be despised as merely the words of prophets, but so that people may continually be reminded that the words they speak are God’s words.

[Col. 0985C] “I have heard what the prophets said, prophesying falsehood in my name and saying, ‘I dreamed’ (or: ‘I saw a dream’). How long will this remain in the heart of the prophets who prophesy falsehood and prophesy the deceits (or: desires) of their own heart? They wish (or: think) to make my people forget my name because of their dreams, which each one recounts to his neighbor, just as their fathers forgot my name because of Baal (or: in Baal).”

Since the preceding title is “Against the Prophets,” or “To the Prophets,” and we clearly understand these to be false prophets, there are many kinds of prophesying. One of them is through dreams, as occurred in Daniel. Therefore the prophetic word is also directed against those who believe in dreams and think that everything they see is a divine revelation—something that is properly disclosed to saints and servants of God.

If we read that Pharaoh (Gen. 41) and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2), wicked kings, saw dreams that proved true, this was not due to the merit of those who saw them. Rather, it was so that through the occasion of their dreams the holy men Joseph and Daniel might shine forth, and so that the tyrants’ harsh and untamed hearts might perceive the majesty of the Lord through their own conscience.

There are dreamers even today in the Church, and especially in our own flock, who proclaim their errors as the prophecy of the Lord and repeatedly thrust upon us the words, “I dreamed, I dreamed.” The Lord rebukes them, saying: “How long will this remain in the heart of the prophets who prophesy falsehood and prophesy the deceits of their own heart?”

They do this so that, just as the ancient people who came out of Egypt forgot my name, so their descendants may also forget me. Such prophecy, however, is not in the name of the Lord but in the name of Baal, which is properly the idol of the Sidonians—or Babylonian—and is called by the related name Bel.

“The prophet who has a dream, let him recount the dream; and the one who has my word, let him speak my word truthfully. What has straw to do with wheat?” says the Lord. “Are not my words like fire?” says the Lord, “and like a hammer (or: axe) breaking the rock?”

Those who deserve to possess the word of God should interpret dreams and say, “Thus says the Lord”—those to whom the Lord has spoken, in whom there is truth and not deceitful falsehood. What do the straw of heretics have to do with the wheat of the Church?

John the Baptist speaks more fully about this (Matt. 3): the Lord cleanses his threshing floor and leaves the straw to be scattered by the blasts of the winds and burned by fire, while he gathers the wheat into barns so that it may become heavenly bread. Let each believer say: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33).

The perverse doctrine is beautifully compared with straw, which has no marrow and cannot nourish believing peoples, but is crushed from empty stalks. And because heretics are accustomed to promise prosperity and open the kingdoms of heaven to sinners, saying, “The kingdoms of heaven are prepared for you; you can imitate the majesty of God so that you may be without sin. For you have received the power of free choice and knowledge of the law, by which you may attain whatever you wish,” they deceive wretched people with flatteries—especially little women burdened with sins, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth—and they deceive all their hearers through flattery (Eph. 4).

Therefore, comparing his words with the straw of heretics, the Lord says: “Are not my words like fire?” says the Lord, “and like a hammer breaking the rock?” My word, he says, announces future punishments in order to deter people from sinning; it threatens the straw of sinners with burning, so that the hard hearts of heretics, untamed like flint, may be crushed by the hammer of his word. He removes the heart of stone in order to put in its place a heart of flesh—soft, that is, and capable of receiving and perceiving God’s commandments.

The Lord says something similar through Ezekiel (Ezek. 13): the false prophets plaster their wall with their flatteries, without tempering material, and afterward it is overthrown by a violent rain and the truth of judgment. The false prophets sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, so that they may give sinners rest and prevent them from calming God’s anger with tears.

In place of “hammer,” the Septuagint translated “axe”—namely, the axe of which John the Baptist speaks (Matt. 3): “Now the axe has been laid at the roots of the trees.” This axe cuts down unfruitful trees, and this hammer crushes the hardest stones. Hence the prophet Nahum also says: “His fury”—clearly, God’s—“will consume the rulers, and the rocks will be crushed by him” (Nah. 1).

This is directed against heretics. But concerning ecclesiastical men it is written that neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house of God (1 Kings 6).

“Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets,” says the Lord, “who steal my words, each one from his neighbor. Behold, I am against the prophets,” says the Lord, “who take up their tongues and say, ‘The Lord says’” (or: “who dream a dream”). “Behold, I am against the prophets who dream falsehood,” says the Lord, “who recount them and deceive my people with their lies and with their wonders (or: astonishments) and terrors, although I did not send them and did not command them. They have benefited this people nothing,” says the Lord.

Falsehood always imitates truth, and unless it possesses some likeness of what is right, it cannot deceive the innocent. Just as prophets in the former people lied and said, “Thus says the Lord,” and “I saw the Lord,” and “The word of the Lord that came to him,” so heretics take testimonies from the Scriptures of the Old and New Instrument and steal the words of the Savior, each one from his neighbor—from the prophets, apostles, and evangelists.

They take up their tongues in order to utter the poisons of their hearts with their mouths, and they dream a dream. Of them it is truly said: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Ps. 75). Or, according to the Hebrew, “And they say, ‘He says,’” with “the Lord” understood; or certainly, “the divine word.”

The Lord now threatens that he himself will come against teachers of this kind, who deceive his people with their lies, astonishments, and miracles. They promise great, incredible, and immense things in order to deceive the wretched, and they “benefited the people of God nothing.” They fulfill the apostolic saying: “Teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain.” They are accustomed to announce prosperity to the wicked and adversity to the good.

“If this people, or a prophet, or a priest asks you, saying, ‘What is the burden of the Lord?’ (or: ‘What is the assumption of the Lord?’), you shall say to them: ‘You are the burden’ (or: ‘the assumption’). For I shall cast you away (or: dash you down), says the Lord. And the prophet and the priest and the people who say, ‘The burden’ (or: ‘the assumption’) ‘of the Lord,’ I shall visit (or: punish) that man and his house.

“Thus each of you shall say to his neighbor and to his brother: ‘What did the Lord answer, and what did the Lord say?’ And the burden (or: assumption) of the Lord shall no longer be remembered, because his word shall be a burden (or: assumption) to each person.”

Aquila translates the Hebrew word as ἅρμα (*harma*), that is, “burden” and “weight”; Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translate it as “assumption.” Wherever what the Lord threatens is grave, full of weight and labor, and impossible to bear, the title also uses ἅρμα, that is, “weight.” Wherever, however, the Lord promises prosperity, or promises better things after a threat, it is called a vision. Alternatively, the title itself clearly indicated what sort of prophecy was to follow: a burden, a vision, or the word of God.

Because prophets were accustomed to announce sad things and threaten punishments to a sinful people in order to draw them back to repentance, while the merciful and compassionate Lord delayed his sentence for a long time, the deceived people, led astray by the fraud of the false prophets, thought that what the Lord threatened would not come to pass. They turned a serious matter into a game and a joke.

When the prophets prophesied, they mocked them, saying: “Again this man sees the burden and weight of the Lord.” Thus it came about that it was no longer called a vision, but, in mockery and derision, a burden and weight.

Therefore the Lord commands that if the people, prophet, or priest asks Jeremiah what the burden or assumption of the Lord is, he should answer them and say: “You are the burden and you are the assumption.” For I shall assume you, cast you away, dash you down, and destroy you.

If anyone thereafter—whether prophet, priest, or member of the people—dares to call it “the burden” or “the weight of the Lord,” he says: “I shall visit that man and his house,” and I shall erase him forever.

Let each person therefore say to his neighbor and friend: “Do not ask, ‘What is the burden of the Lord?’ but, ‘What did the Lord answer, and what did the Lord say?’” Forget the former expression. Let neither “burden,” “weight,” nor “assumption” sound again in your mouths, because each person’s word and deed will be reckoned as a burden and weight for him, according to what is written: “You shall be justified by your mouth, and by your mouth you shall be condemned” (Matt. 15).

[Col. 0988C] “And you pervert the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God. Thus you shall say (or: they shall say) to the prophet: ‘What did the Lord answer you, and what did the Lord say?’ But if you say, ‘The burden of the Lord’”—up to this point the passage is absent from the Septuagint, and it continues:

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Because you have said this word, ‘The burden’ (or: ‘the assumption’) ‘of the Lord,’ when I sent to you saying, ‘You shall not say, “The burden” (or: “the assumption”) “of the Lord,”’ therefore, behold, I will take you up (or: assume you), carrying you, and I will cast you away, and the city that I gave to you and to your fathers, away from my presence. And I will give you to everlasting reproach and eternal disgrace, which shall never be erased by oblivion.”

The Lord commanded that the language of burden, weight, and assumption should not be used among the people, but rather the language of response and the word of God. Because the people had refused to fulfill this command, he interprets the very word against them and says: Since you have said what I did not want, even though I repeatedly sent prophets and commanded you not to say it, I will therefore fulfill in you the word of assumption, burden, and weight.

I shall assume you, take you up, carry you, dash you down, and make you fall from the heights to the ground—not only you, but also your city, which I gave to your fathers. “And I will give you,” he says, “to everlasting reproach and eternal disgrace, which shall never be erased by oblivion.”

We know that this happened at the time of the Babylonian captivity, but it is fulfilled more fully and perfectly after the Savior’s passion and resurrection, when he said: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13); and his sentence will remain until the end.

Let us also explain it in another way, at least according to the Septuagint: λῆμμα (*lēmma*) signifies not only “assumption” but also “gift” or “offering.” Since the people were always promising themselves prosperity, he says that they must no longer speak in this way, for they are unworthy of God’s gifts and offerings; rather, they are to be rejected and entirely abandoned by God’s help.

Things are often revealed through words and the interpretation of names, as the changed names of Abraham, Sarah, Peter, and the sons of Zebedee signify a change in circumstances. In this same prophet, Phassur is said to mean “terror” or “transference,” and also “settler” or “stranger.”

It should be noted that the words “of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God” are absent from the Latin and Greek codices, while the Hebrews read them differently in their books—something that properly signifies the mystery of the Trinity.

## BOOK TEN

[Col. 0989]

The tenth book of the Commentaries on Jeremiah begins with the two baskets, one of which rightly represents the sweetness of true faith, the other the bitterness of the faithlessness of heretics. Although Hananiah son of Azur opposes Jeremiah, and Shemaiah the Nehelamite wishes that the prophet be sent to prison, and the priest Zephaniah conspires in the words of the false prophets, truth can be shut up and bound, but it cannot be overcome. It is content with the small number of its own people and is not frightened by the multitude of its enemies.

## CHAPTER 24  
### The figure of the two baskets of figs; concerning the affliction of Zedekiah and the people
“Then the Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets [or, according to Symmachus, two hampers] full of figs, set before the temple of the Lord, after Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with his princes, the craftsman, and the engraver from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon. One basket had very good figs, like the figs of the first season usually are; and one basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten because they were bad. And the Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ And I said: ‘Figs—good figs, very good; and bad figs, very bad, which cannot be eaten because they are bad.’ And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: As these figs are good, so I will regard the deportation of Judah, whom I sent away from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good. And I will set my eyes upon them with favor [or, for good], and I will bring them back to this land; and I will build them up, and not overthrow them; and I will plant them, and not uproot them. And I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord. And they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, because they will return to me with their whole heart. And as for the very bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are bad, thus says the Lord: so I will give [or hand over] Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remained in this city, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt. And I will give them over to vexation and affliction [or dispersion] in all the kingdoms of the earth, for reproach, an example, a proverb, and a curse in every place to which I have driven them; and I will send against them the sword, famine, and pestilence, until they are consumed from the land that I gave to them and to their fathers.’” [Col. 0989C–0990B]

(Jerome.) Some interpret the two hampers or baskets of good and bad figs as the Law and the Gospel, the Synagogue and the Church, the people of the Jews and Christians, hell and the kingdom of heaven—one pertaining to the punishment of sinners, the other to the dwelling place of the saints. But since we know, according to the Apostle Paul (Romans 7), that the Law is good and holy, that the commandment is good and holy, and that the God of both Testaments is one, let us rather refer them to those who believed and did not believe at the coming of the Lord and Savior. Those who, stirred up by the scribes and priests, cried out, saying, “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (Luke 23), are the basket of bad figs; those from the people who believed after his ascension are to be referred to the good figs and the excellent basket or hamper.

Let us follow the simple and true historical account: that he called Jeconiah the basket of good figs, because he had surrendered himself to the king of Babylon at Jeremiah’s counsel and by God’s command, and to him the Lord promises prosperity. The basket of bad figs signifies Zedekiah, who contradicted God’s sentence, was captured, blinded, and led to Babylon, where he died (2 Kings 25). [Col. 0990C]

God so set his eyes upon those who obeyed his command for their good that he brought them back to their land, built them up and did not overthrow them, planted them and did not uproot them. He gave them a heart to know him, that he himself was the Lord, so that they might become his people and he might be their God. Thus, even in captivity, he set his eyes upon them for good and permitted them to cultivate the land, build houses, and plant orchards in the Babylonian region. Daniel, through the miracles of his signs, suddenly became a prince from a captive (Daniel 5); and the three young men were gloriously delivered from the fire of the furnace (Daniel 3). After the seventy years had been completed, under Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, Ezra, and Nehemiah, a very large part of the people returned to Jerusalem; their number is contained in the same book of Ezra (Ezra 2). [Col. 0990D–0991A]

It should be noted that this vision was given to the prophet in the time of Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been led into deportation. For he did not say “captivity,” since Jeconiah had surrendered himself voluntarily. By the craftsmen and engravers, we should understand either interpreters and teachers of the Law, or artisans and engravers of gold and precious stones, an art that is held in the highest esteem among barbarian nations. In place of “engravers,” the Septuagint translated “prisoners,” thereby signifying the misfortune of captivity; they also added “the wealthy,” which is not found in the Hebrew.

He compares the basket that had good, indeed very good, figs with the early figs, which in Greek are called *proïma* (πρωΐμα): namely, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Job, and the other holy men, concerning whom one of the Twelve Prophets says: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, and like an early fig on a fig tree I found their fathers” (Hosea 9). Hence we too are called children of Abraham. Conversely, it is said to the Jews: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8). [Col. 0991B]

These baskets, which contained good and bad figs, were not outside and beyond the Church, but before the temple of the Lord, since everything lies open to God's knowledge. The figs that are outside do not have as much bitterness as those that, after confessing the faith, have been changed by apostasy. Nor do the good figs that are not before the temple of God—such as were the philosophers of the world, who, through natural goodness and an understanding of the Creator, appeared not so much to follow virtues as to praise them—possess as much sweetness as the figs in the temple of God. [Col. 0991C]

How great is the sweetness of the figs that are in the temple of God, represented by the prophets and apostles! One of these figs said: “I gave you milk, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3); and: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4). Hence it is said that before the temple of God there were good figs, very good, and bad figs, very bad. And lest we be thought to be imposing our own interpretation, Scripture itself explains the matter: “As these figs are good,” it says, “so I will regard the deportation of Judah, whom I sent away from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good”—signifying Jeconiah and the princes who were taken captive with him.

Conversely, concerning the basket that had bad figs: “And as for the very bad figs,” it says, “which cannot be eaten because they are bad, so I will give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his princes, and those who fled to Egypt and those who remained in this city, to vexation and affliction among all the kingdoms of the earth” (below, chapter 42). When they too were captured in Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar set up his throne at Tahpanhes, and the Lord sent against them the sword, famine, and pestilence, until they were consumed from the land that he had given to their fathers. [Col. 0991D]

What he said concerning the good figs—“I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord”—is like the apostolic statement: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2). This shows that not only our works but also our will depend upon God’s help. [Col. 0992A]

In this passage the allegorical interpreter always goes astray, seeking to do violence to the force of the historical truth. He says that those taken captive and transferred to the land of the Chaldeans were captured from the heavenly Jerusalem, and that they would return again to their former place, like Jeremiah and the other holy prophets. But he says that others, who were sinners, would die in this land and in the valley of tears. I have set out the entire *pericope* (περικοπή) of this vision at once, so that I would not divide its meaning in the exposition.

## CHAPTER XXV

### On Judah’s seventy-year captivity; on the cup from which all nations drink; the shepherds and nobles are summoned to mourning

“The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah [or, over all the people of Judah], in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah.” [Col. 0992B]

(Jerome.) These events precede the preceding vision. That vision took place under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been transferred to Babylon; this one, however, took place under Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah. As I said earlier, it was not his concern to preserve the chronological sequence of the prophecies, which the laws of history require; rather, he knew that it was useful to write them in whatever order would benefit his hearers and readers. Hence some people wrongly seek in the Psalter an order corresponding to the historical sequence of the psalms, although such an order is not observed in lyric poetry.

“This is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon” (this is not found in the Septuagint; the text continues): “What Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying.”

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar assumed power in Babylon. Thus it happened that the year that was Nebuchadnezzar’s first year in Babylon was the fourth year of King Jehoiakim in Jerusalem. Finally, in the eighth year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar led Jeconiah, together with his mother and the princes, into captivity; Jeconiah reigned for only three months after the killing of his father, Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim himself was killed in Jerusalem in the eleventh year of his reign. [Col. 0992C]

“From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Ammon, king of Judah, to this day—this is the twenty-third year—the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising by night, speaking, and you have not listened.”

Jeremiah began to prophesy in the thirteenth year of the reign of Josiah, who reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years, and he prophesied under him for nineteen years. His son Jehoahaz succeeded him; when Jehoahaz was immediately led into captivity by Necho, king of Egypt, his brother Jehoiakim obtained the kingdom (2 Kings 23). In the fourth year of Jehoiakim’s reign, this word of the Lord came to Jeremiah. Accordingly, it was the twenty-third year of the prophet Jeremiah from the time he began to speak to the people, and he had never ceased preaching. Each day, at dawn and by night, he rose and spoke to the people: “And you did not listen,” he says. [Col. 0992D–0993A]

But if, as the new heretics derive from the old ones, the Law was given once for all as an aid, and commandments were established which we either perform or do not perform by the choice of our own will, how is it that the prophet continually intervenes and repeats God’s commandments every day—commandments which, if once received, should surely have been sufficient for those to whom they were given? It is to show that we always need God’s help and that what was given once can never be sufficient unless it is renewed daily by the Lord’s admonition.

“And the Lord sent to you all his servants, the prophets, rising early and sending them, and you did not listen.”

God continually admonished his people, not through one prophet but through all of them; and, as though he himself were stationed on watch and guard duty, he rose early to warn his people. “And you did not,” he says, “listen,” so that the more frequent the admonition, the greater were the sins of those who despised it. [Col. 0993B]

“Nor did you incline your ears to listen when I said: Return, each of you, from his evil way and from your very wicked thoughts, and you shall dwell in the land that the Lord gave to you and to your fathers, from age to age and forever.”

So great was the people’s hardness that it did not even assume the posture of one listening, or incline its ear when the Lord especially admonished each person to return from his evil way and his very wicked thoughts. And, O infinite mercy: he did not impose punishment for their crime, but summoned them to repentance—both from evil deeds, signified by the evil way, and from very wicked thoughts, which are counted as sin even without an accompanying deed. He promises a reward if they do what was commanded, so that they may dwell in the land that had been given to their fathers and taken away because of their children’s vices. His words “from age to age and forever,” or “from eternity to eternity,” show that God’s gifts are perpetual, if those to whom they were given prove worthy. [Col. 0993C]

“And do not go after foreign gods, to serve and worship them; nor provoke me to anger by the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you. But you did not listen to me.”

“These things,” he says, “I warned you about along with the preceding matters: that you should not serve foreign gods or worship them, and that by doing these things you should not provoke me to anger because of the works of your hands, so that I would do what I did not wish and afflict you. But you did not listen to me.” The following words—“says the Lord, so that you might provoke me to anger by the works of your hands, to your own harm”—are not found in the Septuagint. [Col. 0993D]

“Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you did not listen to my words, behold, I will send for and take all the families of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant.”

(Jerome.) Because you provoked me to anger, did evil to your own destruction, and trampled under your proud foot the one who summoned you to repentance, “I will send,” he says, “for all the families—or nations—of the north, and I will bring their ruler, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant.” The Lord sends either angels to stir up the nations or, certainly, admonishes such families to do the Lord’s will. [Col. 0994A]

When he calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant, he does not call him a servant in the sense in which the prophets and all the saints are servants, those who truly serve the Lord; rather, he calls him so because, in the overthrow of Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar serves the Lord’s will. Thus the Apostle also says: “Whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1). No one doubts that the Chaldeans lie in the northern direction from Jerusalem.

“And I will bring them against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all the nations surrounding it. I will destroy them, and make them an object of astonishment, a hissing, and everlasting desolations.”

These are the rewards of those who despise and refuse to hear God’s words. Whatever evil, therefore, is brought against us is caused by our sins. Just as all the nations were then brought against Jerusalem, so today they are brought against a negligent Church, to destroy it and make it an object of astonishment, a hissing, and everlasting desolations, so that it may serve as an example and wonder to all. Hissing is an indication of wonder and astonishment; everlasting desolation is found in those who do not have God as their ruler. [Col. 0994B]

“And I will take away from them the voice of joy, the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom, and the voice of bride, the sound of the millstone, and the light of the lamp. And all its land shall become a desolation and an astonishment.”

This is also demonstrated today in the assembly of the wicked: their teachers do not teach the word of God, but hiss like a serpent. The voice of joy and the voice of gladness perish in them, so that they never hear the Apostle’s words: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4). So too the voice of the bride—the ecclesiastical faith—and not the voice of the bridegroom, the Lord and Savior: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). The sound of the millstone disappears, so that grain is no longer ground in it and given to the people as food; so too the light of the lamp, namely, the teaching and knowledge of the prophets. Finally, John the Baptist is also called a lamp: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John 5); and another prophet says: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Psalm 118). “All the land of the heretics,” he says, “will become a desolation and an astonishment when its final folly has been revealed.” [Col. 0994C]

“And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. And when the seventy years have been completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their iniquity, says the Lord, and punish the land of the Chaldeans; and I will make it everlasting desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words that I have spoken against it, everything written in this book, all that Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.”

Just as Jerusalem receives back its former inhabitants after seventy years and, once its punishments have been completed because it obeyed God’s sentence, enjoys its former prosperity, so the king of Babylon, who was lifted up in pride and considered it the result of his own strength that he ruled over the nations rather than of the Lord’s will, will be destroyed when the Medes and Persians come. Indeed, to this day only the ruins of the city of Babylon remain. The Lord made it an everlasting desolation and fulfilled all the words contained in this very prophet’s book. For in what follows, Jeremiah’s speech describes the evils Babylon is to suffer: [Col. 0994D–0995A]

“Because they served them when they were many nations and great kings; and I will repay them according to their works and according to the deeds of their hands.”

This is not found in the Septuagint. It signifies that Jeremiah prophesied not only against Babylon but also against the other nations that were part of the Babylonian army and fought against the Lord’s people. In what follows he speaks against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, the kingdoms of Hazor and Elam, and finally against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. [Col. 0995B]

“For thus says the Lord God of Israel to me: Take from my hand this cup of the wine of fury [or unmixed wine], and you shall make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it. They shall drink and become drunk [or vomit], and they shall go mad because of the sword that I will send among them. And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord, and I made all the nations to whom the Lord sent me drink.”

The offering of the cup, and of unmixed wine—called *akratos* (ἀκράτου) in Greek—is an indication of the Lord’s fury. Concerning it, it is written in the Psalm: “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine mixed with spices,” so that all the nations that fought against God’s people may drink from the cup of the Lord’s fury. Isaiah also writes concerning Jerusalem: “You have drunk the bowl of fury, the cup of ruin; you have drained it. Therefore arise” (Isaiah 51).

This cup is drunk by all the nations so that they may vomit and go mad. A perverse interpreter takes this in a favorable sense, as though it were a purgative drink that compels everything bilious, phlegmatic, and harmful in the chest to come out and restores the body to its former health. In place of Jeremiah he takes the Savior, saying that the Savior himself offered the cup to all the nations to which he was sent, so that, abandoning idolatry, they might devote themselves to the worship of God. What follows in Scripture will show this to be contrary to the sacred text. They are not offered the unmixed cup as a remedy, as he wishes, but as punishment. [Col. 0995C]

“Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and its kings and its princes, so that I might make them a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing, and a curse, as they are this day.”

“I thought,” he says, “that I would offer the cup only to the nations, and therefore I gladly presented myself for this ministry. But among the other nations—or rather, before the other nations—I offered it to Jerusalem, to the cities of Judah, to its kings and princes, so that I might make them an astonishment, a desolation, a hissing, and a curse, as the present example also demonstrates.” Hence he says above: “You have seduced me, and I was seduced; you prevailed and you were stronger” (Jeremiah 20:7). [Col. 0995D]

“To Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and his servants, his princes, and all his people, and everyone without exception.”

After Jerusalem, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and his companions drank; the princes and the entire people drank, as did everyone who was not Egyptian but lived in his regions. The Septuagint translated these people as *symmiktous* (συμμίκτους), that is, “mixed people”: not the common people of the Egyptian region, but foreigners and immigrants. [Col. 0996A]

“And all the nations of the land of Ausitis.”

In Hebrew it is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text]. History also says that Job came from there: “There was a certain man in the land of Ausitis whose name was Job.” It must nevertheless be understood that this verse is not found in the Septuagint, and that Theodotion translated it as “island.”

“And all the kings of the land of the Philistines, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod.”

He names the Philistines generally—that is, the land of the Palestinians—and then specifies their cities: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod. He mentions only Gath indirectly, since it is included among the “remnants.” This is the meaning of the phrase “and the remnant of Ashdod”: the region of the city of Gath, which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], is neighboring and adjoining Ashdod. Isaiah also writes that the Palestinians were captured and devastated by the Babylonians. [Col. 0996B]

“Edom, Moab, the sons of Ammon, and all the kings of Tyre, and all the kings of Sidon.”

Edom contains Mount Seir and in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text]. Moab and Ammon are the sons of Lot, near the Dead Sea. Tyre and Sidon are leading cities on the Phoenician coast; they too were conquered when the Babylonian army came. Carthage was their colony. Hence the Carthaginians are called *Poeni*, as though *Phoeni*, through corruption of the language; their language is largely related to Hebrew. [Col. 0996C]

“And the kings of the lands of the islands that are beyond the sea.”

Beyond Cyprus and Rhodes, and the islands called the Cyclades (Κυκλάδες); these too were occupied by the Babylonians.

“And Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who shave their hair in a circle.”

These peoples live in the desert. They are near and intermixed with the regions of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens. Concerning them it is said: “those who shave their hair in a circle.”

“And all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the west who dwell in the desert.”

This is not found in the Septuagint. Because Dedan, Tema, and Buz, as well as the Ishmaelites, have been mentioned, he follows the geographical sequence. [Col. 0996D]

“And all the kings of Zimri.”

This too is not found in the Septuagint.

“And all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes.”

Since Elam and the kings of the Medes follow Zimri, we think that Zimri too is a region of Persia, unless perhaps, because Arabia preceded it, these kings are to be understood as desert peoples. Elam is a region of Persia beyond Babylon, whence come the Elamites. The Medes and Persians were the peoples by whom Babylon was captured and destroyed. They too drank the unmixed cup when Alexander, king of the Macedonians, offered it to them. [Col. 0997A]

“And all the kings of Babylon [or, of the north], near and far.”

Since he had listed the regions of Persia and Babylon—Elam and the Medes—he now generally includes all the kings of the north, both those who are near and those who are far away. In place of “north,” which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], the Septuagint translated *aphēliōtēn* (ἀφηλίωτην), which we may render “the east wind” or “the wind beneath the sun.”

“Each against his brother, and all the kingdoms of the earth that are upon its surface. And the king of Sheshach shall drink after them.”

To avoid the tediousness of enumerating separately all the regions of the eastern provinces, he generally includes all the kingdoms of the earth that dwell upon the land. When he says “against his brother,” the unstated meaning is: I gave them unmixed wine, so that all might rage, vomit, go mad, and fight one another in mutual battles.

The statement “the king of Sheshach shall drink after them,” which is also absent from the Septuagint, has this meaning: “All the nations round about,” he says, “will be subject to the Babylonian empire, and he will subject everything to his power, so that all the nations recounted in the preceding passage will serve him and drink from his cup.” Hence, in the vision against Babylon, it is written: “Babylon is a golden cup, intoxicating the whole earth.” [Col. 0997B]

The last king of Babylon, however, will drink this potion when Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians, offers it to him as the rider of the chariot, camel, and donkey. Anyone who has even a small knowledge of the Hebrew language will have little difficulty understanding how Babylon, which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], is understood as Sheshach.

Just as among us the Greek alphabet is read in sequence through its final letter—α, β, and so forth through ω—and then, for the memory of children, we customarily reverse the order of reading and mix the first and last letters, saying α, ω, β, ψ, so too among the Hebrews the first letter is [Hebrew letter absent], the second [Hebrew letter absent], the third [Hebrew letter absent], and so on up to the twenty-second and final letter [Hebrew letter absent], whose penultimate letter is [Hebrew letter absent]. We therefore read [Hebrew sequence absent]. When we reach the middle, the letter [Hebrew letter absent] is encountered; and just as, when read correctly, we read “Babel,” so, with the order changed, we read “Sheshach.” [Col. 0997C]

The vowels between [Hebrew letters absent] and [Hebrew letters absent], according to the custom of the Hebrew language, are not written in this name. [Note: Col. 0997D: Read thus: Between [Hebrew letters absent] and [Hebrew letters absent]; between [Hebrew letters absent] and [Hebrew letters absent].]

I think that the holy prophet prudently concealed them, lest he openly provoke the madness of those who were besieging Jerusalem and were on the point of taking possession of it. We likewise read that the Apostle did this with respect to the Roman Empire (2 Thessalonians 2), when writing about the Antichrist: “Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time”—“him” meaning the Antichrist. “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains it continue to restrain it, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2). By “the one who restrains,” I mean that he indicates the Roman Empire.

For unless this is destroyed and removed from the midst, according to the prophecy of Daniel, the Antichrist will not come beforehand. If he had wished to say this openly, he would foolishly have aroused persecution against Christians and stirred up rage against the Church, which was then being born. [Col. 0997D–0998A]

We have spoken at greater length about this chapter than the brevity of a commentary permits. Greek and Latin readers may perhaps find it tedious, since it is not found in their books. But what benefit will that be, when this same prophet later says: “How Sheshach has been captured, and the glory of the whole earth seized! How Babylon has become an astonishment among the nations?” Allegorical interpreters refer this entire passage to all the nations whom the devil has intoxicated with the unmixed cup of sins; for at the end he himself too will drink punishments and torments. Concerning him the Apostle writes: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2). Hence elsewhere he says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15). What great ability it shows to be able to translate the names of different nations according to their etymologies and fit each one to its corresponding name! [Col. 0998B]

“And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and become drunk, vomit and fall, and do not rise from before the sword that I will send among you.”

“After you have offered the cup to all the nations and fulfilled the Lord’s command, you shall again command them in the Lord’s words and say: ‘Drink and become drunk, vomit and fall, and do not rise.’ If drinking, becoming drunk, vomiting, and falling are signs of salvation, so that harmful things are expelled like a purgative drink, how does the statement that follows—‘and do not rise’—make sense? He makes clear what kind of drink causes them to fall forever: namely, ‘before the sword that I will send among you.’” [Col. 0998C]

(Maurus.) A question arises here: how can Jeremiah say that after drinking, drunkenness, vomiting, and falling, Jerusalem cannot rise, while Isaiah says to her: “Rise up, rise up; stand, Jerusalem, you who drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath to the bottom, who drank the cup of stupor and drained it to the dregs. There is no one to support her among all the sons she bore, and there is no one to take her hand among all the sons she raised. Two things have come upon you; who will grieve for you? Desolation and destruction, famine and sword—who will comfort you?” (Isaiah 51).

The matter is resolved as follows. As long as a person is drinking the cup, becoming drunk, raging, vomiting, and collapsing, he cannot rise. For he has not yet drained the Lord’s cup, nor reached the dregs so as to drink it to the bottom. But here Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem in the past tense: “You who drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury,” not “you who are drinking.” [Col. 0998D]

At the same time, it must be considered that thereafter there was neither prophet nor apostle in Judea to console her, take her hand, and raise her when she lay fallen. It is therefore clear that these words refer to the final captivity. Otherwise, history tells us that in Babylon and after Babylon she had Ezekiel and the other prophets. When he says, “Two things have come upon you,” or “two things have come against you,” and asks, “Who will grieve for you?” and then, instead of two, mentions four—desolation and destruction, famine and sword—this resembles what is sung in the Psalm: “Once God has spoken; twice I have heard this: power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy; for you will repay each one according to his works” (Psalm 62). [Col. 0999A]

There too God speaks once, declaring that he is almighty, while the prophet hears two things: that his omnipotence prevails in both directions, so that he grants mercy to those who repent and repays those who persist in sin with the punishments they deserve. Likewise here, two things come upon Jerusalem, each of which contains a pair of disasters: desolation is followed by destruction, and famine by the sword of death.

“And when they refuse to receive the cup from your hand and drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: You shall certainly drink. For behold, in the city over which my name has been invoked, I am beginning to afflict; and will you be like innocent men, free from guilt [or: will you be completely clean]? You shall not be free from guilt [or: you shall not be clean].”

(Jerome.) He subtly shows that those who refuse to carry out God’s command willingly will receive it under compulsion, and will hear: “You shall certainly drink.” Whether you wish it or not, God’s sentence must be fulfilled. If Jerusalem, the city in which God’s name was known, drank the unmixed cup of fury—for the Prophet says, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75)—how much less will you be clean, who worship idols in place of God? [Col. 0999B]

“For I am summoning the sword against all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord of hosts.”

This is the unmixed drink; this is the cup of the Lord’s fury, which is summoned not against Jerusalem alone but against the whole earth and all the surrounding nations. Concerning it he had said above: “I will send for Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring him against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all the nations surrounding it.” [Col. 0999C]

“And you shall prophesy all these words to them and say to them: The Lord will roar from on high [or: will give an answer], and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice. Roaring, he will roar over his beauty [or: he will answer over his place]. A cry like that of those who tread the winepresses will be sung against all the inhabitants of the earth. The sound [or: destruction] will reach to the ends [or: over the part] of the earth, because the Lord has a judgment with the nations; he himself is judged with all flesh. I have handed over the wicked to the sword, says the Lord.”

Let us first give the meaning according to the truth of the translation. “You shall prophesy to all the nations,” he says, “and say that the Lord roars from on high”—that is, gives an indication of his fury—according to what is written: “The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3). “And from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice,” so that he may terrify all who hear him. He will roar over his beauty, that is, over the temple.

When he has roared, a battle cry like that of those treading winepresses will be sung; and amid the shedding of mutual blood, a mournful song will be raised, which Symmachus calls *katálēgma* (κατάληγμα), and Aquila calls *iasmos* (ἰασμόν). The sound of this battle cry and song will reach to the ends of the earth, because the Lord has judgment with the nations. [Col. 0999D–1000A]

If the Lord has judgment with the nations, then the nations also possess differing merits (Hosea 4). This is relevant to the interpretation some give to the passage: “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). He has indeed been judged in that he did not believe; but those who do not believe are themselves subjected to different punishments from one another. He is judged with all flesh, so that no one may remain unjudged. But he hands the wicked—that is, those who do not believe in God—over to the everlasting sword.

Allegorical interpreters, following the Septuagint, explain this passage in such a way as to take the Lord’s explicit threat in a favorable sense. “The Lord,” they say, “will give an answer from on high” to those whom he is going to save; “and from his holy place he will utter his voice,” and will answer with a word in his own place. Those people, like harvesters filled with his fruits, will answer that sentence: “Destruction will come upon all the inhabitants of the earth.” Not upon the whole earth, but upon a part of the earth—namely, those who do not believe. For there will be judgment among the nations, and he himself will be judged with all flesh; but the wicked will be handed over to the sword. [Col. 1000B]

«Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, distress (or evil) shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind (or storm) shall go forth from the farthest heights (or extremities) of the earth. And the slain of the Lord (or, wounded by the Lord) shall be on that day from one end of the earth to its other. They shall not be mourned, nor gathered up, nor buried; they shall lie as dung upon the face of the earth.»

Let those who try to do violence to Holy Scripture be ashamed, interpreting in a favorable sense passages full of threats. I think the Lord also spoke of this passage when he said: «Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom» (Luke XXI), along with the rest contained in that Gospel saying. Let us understand these things historically, when all the surrounding nations were subdued by the king of Babylon and experienced his savage rule; or prophetically, as events that will occur after a long time, at the consummation of the world. They are called slain by the Lord—not because the Lord himself strikes them, but because, in the destruction of the wicked, the will and command of the Lord are fulfilled.

[Col. 1000D]

«Howl (or, rejoice), shepherds, and cry out; sprinkle yourselves with ashes, leaders of the flock (or, mourn, rams of the sheep), because your days have been completed, for you to be killed, and your dispersions; and you shall fall like precious vessels (or, like chosen rams). And flight shall perish from the shepherds, and deliverance from the leaders (or, rams) of the flock.»

It should be noted that only in this passage have the Septuagint translators placed rejoicing in a negative sense; in its place the other translators rendered “howling,” as it is written in the Hebrew. There is this distinction between shepherds and rams, or leaders of the flock: shepherds are the leaders of rational beings, whereas rams and leaders refer to the rich, who themselves are also called part of the flock. What follows—«Your days have been completed, for you to be killed»—means that their days will be completed when their sins have been completed; they will be scattered and fall like precious vessels, so that, once broken, they cannot be restored. And the more precious they were before, the greater will be their loss in being shattered; or else they will fall like chosen rams, so that they may be a fat victim for those eager to devour them.

«Flight,» he says, «shall perish from the shepherds,» when they have not done penance. Thus it is said to the Pharisees: «Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?» (Luke III). And we read in the Psalms: «Flight has perished from me» (Psalm CXLI). «And deliverance,» he says, «from the leaders of the flock (or, rams).» Ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, “by common construction,” the verb *shall perish* is understood.

«The voice of the shepherds’ cry and the howling of the leaders of the flock (or, the rejoicing of the rams), because the Lord has devastated their pastures. And the fields (or, beautiful places) of peace have fallen silent before the face of the Lord’s wrathful anger.»

Here too it should be noted that the Septuagint has used “rejoicing” in place of “howling.” There is this distinction between shepherds and rams: shepherds are understood to be those in the Church who rule the flock with wisdom, learning, and teaching. Rams, however, are those who appear to be leaders among the people but possess no learning or wisdom in themselves and, through excessive simplicity, are almost akin to foolishness.

When we have peace but fail to understand either the good or the beauty of peace, and instead give ourselves over to luxury, idleness, and pleasures, then the good things of peace will rest, or fall silent, and will be taken away from us because of the Lord’s wrathful anger. Then what is written will be fulfilled: «When they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will overtake them» (1 Thessalonians V). When it comes, everything will fall silent.

«He has abandoned his shelter (or, lair) like a lion (and, more accurately, “tabernacle,” for this is what the Hebrew signifies), because their land has become desolate (or, impassable) before the face of the wrath of the dove (or, before the face of the great sword), and before the face of the wrathful anger of the Lord.»

The Lord, of whom he had earlier said, «From on high he will roar, and from his holy dwelling he will give his voice; roaring, he will roar over his beauty»—he himself will abandon his tabernacle, of which it is written: «His place was made in peace, or in Salem, and his dwelling in Zion» (Psalm LXXV). He himself will desert his seat and fulfill what he spoke through this same prophet: «I have abandoned my house; I have forsaken my inheritance» (Jeremiah XII).

He abandoned his lair like a lion so that all the beasts might have power to devastate his land. For while a lion guards and presides over it, no one dares approach it. «Their land,» he says—there is no doubt that this means either the people of the Jews or certainly all the nations—«has become desolate and impassable before the face of the wrath of the dove.»

No one will be surprised that Nebuchadnezzar is understood as the Lord’s dove, if he has read above that he is called the Lord’s servant. (Maurus.) We also read in Isaiah that the Lord said: «I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have summoned my mighty ones in my wrath, rejoicing in my glory.» There he signifies the Medes and Persians, who were chosen by the Lord for the overthrow of Babylon; so now Nebuchadnezzar, who served the Lord’s command by destroying Jerusalem’s transgression, is called the Lord’s servant and dove. (Jerome.)
