In place of “dove,” the Septuagint translated “great sword.” Yet we may also understand the dove as referring to Jerusalem, because it is angry and grieved that it has lost the protection of its lion and that its land has come to desolation. «The land has been made desolate before the face of the dove’s wrath, before the face of the Lord’s fury.» (Gregory.)

What he had foretold as the dove’s wrath, he then added as the Lord’s fury, calling it the dove. For the dove is a very simple animal, and because no inequality of fury creeps into God, he called the Lord’s fury the dove’s wrath. In order to demonstrate the unshaken force of divine severity, he said “the dove’s wrath.” It is as though he were saying openly: He who, while remaining gentle, punishes, brings forth an unyielding judgment.

Therefore, even at the final judgment, while remaining unchangeable in himself, he is altered by no fluctuation or change. Yet he will not appear to the elect and the reprobate under the same appearance of unchangeability, because he will appear tranquil to the righteous and angry to the unjust. Their conscience testifies, for within themselves they bring forth the reason why they regard the one same being, though they are not affected in the same way: justice already performed makes him kindly to some, while guilt makes him terrible to others.

Who could explain their terror when it happens to the wretched both to see their sins within themselves and to see the just judge before them? This is indeed enacted daily in the practice of the present life, so that mortal hearts may be taught about the character of the judgment to come. For when two people go to judgment, one conscious of his innocence and the other of his guilt, while the judge is still silent before the verdict has been given, both see him; yet the one indebted through guilt suspects a grave anger against himself even in the judge’s silence. This anger is not announced to him by any disturbance in the judge, but by the recollection of his wickedness, because, although the verdict does not yet proclaim him guilty outwardly, conscience already accuses him gravely within.

By contrast, the friend of justice beholds the face of the judge who is about to decide, but inwardly rejoices in the testimony of a good memory. Since he has nothing within himself that he fears, he sees everything that concerns him as gentle.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the reign of Jehoiakim: how the priests wanted to kill Jeremiah, who was freed by the officials

[Col. 1002D]

«At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord and speak to all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them. Do not withhold a word, in case they listen and each one turns from his evil way, and I repent of the evil (or, cease from the evil) that I am considering doing to them, because of the wickedness of their practices.»

(Jerome.) This prophecy is earlier than the preceding one, although it was made under the same king. The earlier one was made in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah; this one, however, was made at the beginning of that same king’s reign, as Scripture says: «At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying.» Therefore, as we have often said, the historical sequence should not be woven together in the prophets, since here, under the same king, earlier events are mentioned afterward and later events beforehand.

The one who is going to speak the word of the Lord ought to stand with Moses (Deuteronomy V) and hear with the Psalmist: «You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God» (Psalm CXXXIV). He is commanded to speak to all the cities of Judah, although the Septuagint did not translate “cities,” lest it perhaps seem improper to speak in the court of the Lord’s house to cities that were not physically present. But when he speaks to the people and the citizens, he speaks to the cities themselves.

He stands beautifully in the court and vestibule of the Lord’s temple, so that, on the occasion of prayer to the Lord and worshiping him, they may be compelled to hear the prophet’s words. «Do not withhold,» he says, «the word»: although it is grievous, although the fury of those listening may be aroused against you, nevertheless say what has been commanded you. Do not fear the persecutions of those who will be stirred up against you, but obey the authority of the Lord who commands: «Perhaps,» he says, «they will listen and turn back.»

The ambiguous word “perhaps” cannot properly be applied to the majesty of the Lord, but he speaks according to our human feeling, so that free choice may be preserved for human beings, lest, because of God’s foreknowledge, they be compelled by necessity either to do something or not to do it. For something is not going to happen simply because God knows that it will happen; rather, God knows it because it is going to happen, as one who knows the future beforehand.

Yet we must understand, in accordance with this same Jeremiah, that even if the Lord has foretold evils and the people have done penance, he too will repent of what he threatened to do. And if he has promised prosperity and the people have acted negligently, God will change his decision and bring evils instead of good things. This is said in the person of Almighty God.

Indeed, here too he says: «Perhaps they will listen and each one will turn from his evil way,» so that, when they have turned, I may repent of my decision and not do what I am considering doing to them. I am considering doing it because of the wickedness of their practices; if those practices are changed, my decision too will be changed. Let us read the history of Jonah and Nineveh.

[Col. 1003D]

«And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If you do not listen to me, so as to walk in my law, which I gave you, and listen to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent to you, rising early and sending them, and you did not listen, I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.»

It therefore lies within our power either to do something or not to do it, but only in such a way that whatever good work we desire and seek to accomplish, we attribute to God’s grace, who, according to the Apostle, gave us both the will and the ability to act (Philippians II). Otherwise, it would be enough merely once to walk in the law given to us through Moses, as the foolish heresy supposes.

How, then, did he add: «So that you may listen to the words of my servants the prophets»? They were certainly sent after the law, and not once but frequently—not casually and from a position of ease, but continually and from a position of vigilance. «I sent,» he says, «my servants to you every day, rising early and sending them» (Jeremiah XXVI). If you refuse to listen to them, I will make this house—that is, the temple of God—like Shiloh, where the tabernacle was.

When the temple has been destroyed, consequently the city too will become a curse to all the nations of the earth. But just as, after the temple was built on Ornan’s threshing floor and on Mount Moriah—that is, the mount of vision, where Abraham is said to have offered his son Isaac—the worship at Shiloh ceased, and sacrifices were no longer celebrated there, so, after the Church was built and spiritual victims were offered in it, the ceremonies of the law ceased (2 Chronicles III). And the city of the Jews was made a curse to all the nations of the earth—a curse from which the Lord delivered us, as the Apostle says: «Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us» (Galatians III).

«And the priests and the prophets (or, false prophets), and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets (or, false prophets), and all the people seized him, saying: He must die, because he prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying: This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolated, because there is no inhabitant.»

The priests and prophets—whom the Septuagint rendered more explicitly as “false prophets”—are angry with Jeremiah because he proclaims the truth: when the temple and city have been overthrown, the worship will be deserted and perish, along with the profits gained from religion. Therefore they seize him and, with the people agreeing with them, condemn him to death because he said in the name of the Lord: «This house shall be like Shiloh, and the city shall be desolated, because it has no inhabitant.»

Therefore, whenever priests, false prophets, or a deceived people become angry with us because of the commandments of the Lord and the truth of faith, let us not be greatly concerned, but let us carry out the Lord’s decision, thinking not about present evils but about future goods.

«And all the people gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. And the officials of Judah heard these words and came up from the king’s house to the house of the Lord; and they sat at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord.»

Jeremiah was prophesying the words of the Lord in the temple and had said: «I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.» Immediately, when an uprising had been stirred up by the priests, the prophets, and the people, the entire crowd gathered against the prophet in the temple where the prophet was, and he was held in the hands of the priests, prophets, and crowd.

When the city officials, who were staying in the royal palace, heard this, they crossed over, or «came up from the king’s house to the house of the Lord.» It should be noted that going to the house of the Lord is an ascent. «And they sat at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord.» It was the officials’ duty to sit at the gate of the Lord’s house and there investigate the truth of the matter and the uprising.

It is called the new gate because those who sat there and presided over judgment resisted the accusations of the priests and false prophets.

«And the priests and the prophets spoke to the officials and to all the people, saying: This man deserves the sentence of death, because he prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears.»

While the officials of the city were sitting at the gate of the temple, at the new gate, having come from the king’s palace to the temple in order to calm the people’s uprising, and while the assembly of the people had gathered, the priests and false prophets accused Jeremiah. The prophet would have perished, so far as the priests and prophets were concerned, if the accusers themselves had possessed judicial authority.

From this we understand that those who appeared devoted to religion were more cruel toward the prophet, through envy of his holiness, than those who were in charge of public affairs.

[Col. 1005B]

«And Jeremiah said to all the officials and to all the people, saying: The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house (or, concerning this house) and against this city (or, concerning this city), all the words that you have heard. Now therefore make your ways and your practices good; listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you (or, the Lord will cease from the evils that he has spoken against you). But as for me, behold, I am in your hands; do with me what is good and right in your eyes (or, what is expedient for you). Nevertheless, know and understand that, if you kill me, you are delivering innocent blood against yourselves, against this city, and against its inhabitants. For in truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears.»

While the people were present, the city officials sat at the gate, and the priests and prophets accused Jeremiah the prophet and brought a charge deserving death against him. Jeremiah spoke to the officials and to all the people whom the faction of the priests and false prophets had aroused—wisely, humbly, and steadfastly all at once.

He spoke wisely in saying that he had been sent by the Lord to speak against the temple and the city, and in giving this counsel: if they were willing to hear his advice and do penance, the Lord too would change his decision. He spoke humbly when he said: «Behold, I am in your hands; do with me what is good and right in your eyes.» And he spoke steadfastly when he said: «In truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears.»

He speaks in other words as well: If you are angry because I have spoken against the Lord’s temple and city, and if the safety of the city and temple matters to you, why do you add sins to sins and make both the city and its inhabitants guilty of my blood? Therefore, whenever we too need humility because of the straits of necessity, let us assume it in such a way that we do not abandon truth and steadfastness. It is one thing arrogantly to insult the judge, which is a sign of foolishness; it is another to avoid an impending danger in such a way that you subtract nothing from the truth.

«And the officials and all the people said to the priests and prophets: This man does not deserve the sentence of death, because he has spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God.»

The people, who had earlier been led astray by the priests and false prophets, join the city officials and speak on Jeremiah’s behalf, saying that he is by no means guilty of death but prophesied in the name of the Lord and from his mouth.

The uneducated crowd quickly changes its opinion when it receives a reasonable explanation; but the anger of the accusers, especially of the priests and false prophets, cannot be changed. Therefore, while they continue to accuse and persist in their accusation, the people change—having been given hope of pardon by the Lord if they made their ways good and listened to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord too might bend his decision.

«And men from the elders of the land arose and spoke to the whole assembly of the people, saying: Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he said to all the people of Judah: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion shall be plowed like a field; Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house shall become a wooded height. Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord, and entreat the face of the Lord, and did not the Lord repent of the evil that he had spoken against them? But we are doing great evil against our own lives.»

The city officials and the people understand the truth of the judgment. The elders, whose special duty it was to know ancient events, repeat the history and compare the prophecy of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied under King Hezekiah, with Jeremiah’s prophecy, for which the danger of death threatened him. They show that Micah spoke more severe words and yet suffered nothing at the hands of the righteous King Hezekiah; rather, when they turned to repentance, the Lord changed his decision for the better.

Micah said: «Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house a wooded height» (Micah III). Jeremiah, however, said: «I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth» (above, XXIV).

They give this advice because they suppose that what Micah foretold did not actually occur, since it did not happen for a long time because of the people’s repentance. Likewise, what Jeremiah has spoken will not occur if, following his advice, they make their ways and practices good and listen to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord will not bring upon them the evil that had been threatened.

At the same time they break the fury of the accusers and join themselves to them, saying: «Therefore we are doing great evil against our own lives.» They do not mean that they ought to do it, but that, if they do it, they will harm not the accused but their own lives, which they could save by a change of decision.

«There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim, and he prophesied against this city and against this land, in accordance with all the words of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and all his officials heard these words, and the king sought to kill him. And Uriah heard this, was afraid, and fled and entered Egypt.»

The following words—«And King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt, Elnathan son of Achbor and men with him, to Egypt»—are not found in the Septuagint. Then it continues: «And they brought Uriah out of Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim, and he struck him with the sword and threw his corpse into the graves of the common people. Nevertheless, the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, so that he was not handed over into the hands of the people and they did not kill him.»

The question arises why, when Uriah son of Shemaiah from the town of Kiriath-jearim prophesied the same things as Jeremiah, he was terrified and fled to Egypt, was brought back from there, and was killed, whereas Jeremiah was able to escape. Jeremiah certainly had not fled, but, boldly persevering in his earlier declaration, was freed both by the judgment of the people and the officials and by the counsel of the elders against the accusing priests and false prophets.

The brief answer is that God’s judgment cannot be known: when the cause and the sentence are the same, one person is punished and another freed. Unless perhaps we can answer that Uriah was slain as a condemnation both of the accusers and of the people, whereas Jeremiah was preserved for God’s judgment, so that he might preach to the remnants of the unhappy people and lead them back to repentance.

We read the same thing in the Acts of the Apostles: the apostle James immediately suffered Herod’s sentence and was crowned with martyrdom, while Peter and the other apostles were preserved for the Lord’s teaching. We must also observe the steadfastness of the prophet: even when Uriah was brought back from Egypt, he did not change his declaration, but, seeing that death was being prepared for him, nevertheless spoke what the Lord had commanded.

That he was afraid, fled, and entered Egypt is not a sign of faithlessness but of prudence, lest we needlessly expose ourselves to dangers. Otherwise, we also read that the Lord and Savior slipped from the hands of those pursuing him (Luke IV; John VIII), and that he commanded the apostles: «When they persecute you in this city, flee to another» (Matthew X).

It is also asked how Jehoiakim, king of Judah, whose kingdom was small, weakened, and already on the point of perishing, could have had the authority to send men to Egypt and bring Uriah out from there. This is easily resolved if we consider that he had been appointed ruler by Necho, king of Egypt, and that this prophecy was made at the beginning of his reign.

Although Jeremiah was freed through the Lord’s assistance, the one through whom the Lord freed his prophet is nevertheless credited with this as a reward—namely, Ahikam son of Shaphan. We shall read about him later, when Jeremiah is freed from the danger of death from the muddy cistern through the counsel and protection of Ebed-melech the eunuch.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the wooden yokes and bonds to be sent to five kings, and on the warning that they should submit to Nebuchadnezzar lest they die

[Col. 1008A]

«At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying.»

(Jerome.) This is not found in the Septuagint edition, and many think it is the beginning of the following chapter. That is not at all the case; rather, it must be joined to what precedes, so that we may believe that whatever is reported as having been said and done occurred at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim. Hence he also had the authority to send men to Egypt, as though to a friendly king.

It seems to me that the Septuagint omitted this title for the following reason: they did not wish to appear to say twice what they had already placed at the beginning: «At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying.»

«Thus says the Lord to me: Make for yourself bonds and chains» (or, κλοιοί, “collars” or “yokes,” called [in Hebrew; the term is absent from the supplied text] and *boias* in common speech), «and place them on your neck, and send them to the king of Edom, to the king of Moab, to the king of the children of Ammon, to the king of Tyre, and to the king of Sidon, by the hand of the messengers who came to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah. And command them to speak to their masters: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; thus you shall say to your masters.»

The preceding vision occurred at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. This one, however, occurred under Zedekiah, who was the last to reign in Jerusalem, and under whom the city was captured and destroyed.

Jeremiah is commanded to place on his neck the chains, or wooden forks, which, as we have said, are called *boias* in common speech, and to send them to the kings of Edom, Moab, the children of Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon, through the envoys who had come to Zedekiah. He is to command them to announce to their masters that they must serve King Nebuchadnezzar and heed what follows in the prophet’s speech.

And lest the envoys and kings of these nations should perhaps reply, “Why do you not command this of your own people?” he speaks similarly to King Zedekiah and to the priests and prophets.

The allegorical interpreter (that is, Origen), always fleeing the truth of history, interprets this passage concerning the heavenly Jerusalem: its inhabitants ought voluntarily to assume bodies and descend into Babylon—that is, into the confusion of this world, which lies in wickedness—and serve the king of Babylon, clearly meaning the devil. If they refuse to do this, they will not bear heavy bodies but will perish by sword, famine, and pestilence; and they will not become human beings at all but demons.

Let him have said this, lest his defenders bring an accusation against us. For the rest, let us follow the simple and true history, lest we be wrapped in certain clouds and illusions.

«I made the earth, and humanity, and the animals that are upon the face of the earth, by my great strength and my outstretched arm; and I gave it to the one who was pleasing in my eyes.»

Although Scripture speaks here ἀνθρωποπάθως—“in human fashion,” as we human beings can speak and understand—yet God’s strength and his arm are the one of whom the Apostle also speaks: «Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God» (1 Corinthians I); and Isaiah: «Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?» (Isaiah LIII).

The evangelist John also writes: «All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made» (John I). David likewise says in his song: «By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host» (Psalm XXXII).

What he says—«I gave it to the one who was pleasing in my eyes»—signifies that all things have been granted to the human race through God’s grace. «I made,» he says, «the earth, and humanity, and the animals.» The order is reversed: in Genesis (Genesis I), living creatures are made first and humanity last; here he names humanity first and afterward what has been subjected to humanity.

«Now therefore I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant; moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field, so that they may serve him. And all the nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son’s son.»

What misery for Israel, when Nebuchadnezzar is called God’s servant in comparison with it! It is written in the Gospel: «The world was made through him, and the world did not know him; he came to his own, and his own did not receive him» (John I). Rightly, therefore, the Creator hands over his creature to whomever he wishes.

Indeed, the devil himself, whose type Nebuchadnezzar prefigured, confesses: «All these things have been handed over to me.» What he adds—«Moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field, so that they may serve him»—we should understand either simply as every kind of living creature: along with humanity, the things subject to humanity are also handed over; or else we should understand beasts, wild animals, as nations, including those that previously did not know how to serve.

By “his son” and “his son’s son,” according to the Hebrew, he means Belshazzar and Evil-merodach, about whom Daniel writes.

«Until the time of his land and of him comes.»

It is fitting that Nebuchadnezzar’s rule should not be thought eternal; he says that he too will be captured by the Medes and Persians. This is what is signified by: «Until the time of his land and of him comes.» But this too is not found in the Septuagint.

«And many nations and great kings shall serve him.»

He did not say “all,” for this belongs properly to Christ’s rule, although according to Symmachus the reading is not «Many nations and great kings shall serve him,» but «Many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude,» so that he too may serve the Medes and Persians, to whom all the nations had previously been subject.

This is what we have placed from the Hebrew: «I gave him, so that they may serve him; and all the nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his land and of him comes, and many nations and great kings shall subject him to servitude.» In the Septuagint edition, as we have already said, this is not found.

«But the nation and kingdom that will not serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and whoever will not bend his neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with sword, famine, and pestilence, says the Lord, until I consume them by his hand.»

The Lord will not merely subject sinful nations to Nebuchadnezzar; the Apostle also speaks of sinners: «Those whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme» (1 Timothy I); and elsewhere: «I handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved» (1 Corinthians V).

He also urges obedience to authorities, not only because of wrath but because of conscience, lest we be condemned by them.

«Therefore, do not listen to your prophets, diviners, dreamers, augurs, and sorcerers, who say to you: You shall not serve the king of Babylon, because they prophesy falsehood to you, in order to remove you far from your land, expel you, and destroy you. But the nation that submits its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, I will let remain in its land, says the Lord; it shall cultivate it and dwell in it.»

Here too the allegorical interpreter raves and urges those placed in the heavenly Jerusalem not to listen to their prophets, diviners, dreamers, augurs, and sorcerers, but rather to serve Nebuchadnezzar and assume bodies of humiliation, the cries of infants, and the cradles of little children.

For if they do this, once the servitude and condition of human mortality have been completed, they will return to their own land, dwell in it, and perform the works they performed before. He says that he suspects that those who have despised God’s commandments will be weighed down with human bodies, become demons and unclean spirits, and never regain their former dwelling.

But let us explain the passage simply. Among the nations too there are prophets who pretend to foretell future things by divine inspiration; there are diviners, about whom there is even a common proverb: “The wise claim to divine”; dreamers, who imitate Joseph and Daniel; augurs, who announce by the flight of birds and the cries of birds what should or should not be done; and sorcerers, whom we may call poisoners or those who serve the apparitions of demons, who are called in Hebrew [the term is absent or illegible in the supplied text].

All these, he says, deceive and mislead you, so that you will not serve the king of Babylon. For it is much better voluntarily to accept servitude, to have a friend whom you serve, and to cultivate your native land, than to serve as captives by force and necessity.

«And I spoke to Zedekiah, king of Judah, according to all these words, saying: Submit your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why should you and your people die by sword, famine, and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that refuses to serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you: Do not serve the king of Babylon, because they speak falsehood to you. For I did not send them, says the Lord; yet they prophesy falsely in my name, in order to expel you, and you will perish—you and the prophets who prophesy to you.»

After addressing all the nations, he turns to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and speaks in the same words with which he threatened the nations. The Israelite nation deserves no privilege, since it has sinned either as much as or more than the other nations. Indeed, because the rebellious people refused to listen, it was consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence.

It should be observed in Holy Scripture that those who prophesy falsely in the name of the Lord are called “prophets” in place of “false prophets.” «They do this,» he says, «in order to expel you, and you will perish—you and the prophets who prophesy to you.» Therefore the destruction of both those who are deceived and those who deceive is alike.

This is what we have placed from the Hebrew: «Under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why should you and your people die by sword, famine, and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that refuses to serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you…» This is not found in the Septuagint. For this reason I give the warning, so that the prudent reader may understand how much is lacking, passage by passage, in the Greek and Latin manuscripts.

“And I spoke to the priests and to all this people, saying: Thus says the Lord: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Behold, the vessels of the Lord will now soon return from Babylon’; for they prophesy falsehood to you.” (The phrase “now soon,” which we have inserted, is not found in the Septuagint; nor is what follows:) “Do not listen to them, but serve the king of Babylon, so that you may live. Why should this city be given over to desolation?” [Col. 1011C]

After speaking to the nations and the king, he speaks to the priests and the people, since above he had announced destruction to the prophets, saying: “That I may cast you out and you may perish,” both you and the prophets who prophesy to you. He repeats what he had said to the king and the nations: that they should not listen to the words of their prophets and say that the vessels of the Lord’s temple were already to be brought back—those vessels that had been carried away with Jeconiah, his nobles, and his mother. He urges them to submit to the king of Babylon and live, and that the city, voluntarily subjected, should by no means be delivered to the flames. In this too the Lord’s clemency is evident: he wishes to hand them over to a lighter punishment, lest they suffer a heavier one.

“And if they are prophets, and the word of the Lord is in them, let them intervene.” What follows, which we shall append to the end of this chapter, is not found in the Septuagint.

[Col. 1012A] “—of the Lord of hosts, so that the vessels that had been left in the house of the Lord, and in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem, should not come to Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, and the bases”—in place of which the Hebrew has: “and concerning the remaining vessels belonging to them that remained in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon did not carry away when he deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem to Babylon, together with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that were left in the house of the Lord, and in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon, and there they shall remain until the day of their visitation, says the Lord; then I shall bring them up and restore them to this place.” These words, as we have said, are not found in the Septuagint but have been translated from the Hebrew truth. Instead, they inserted something else that was not written, saying: “It is mine, because thus says the Lord: ‘And the remaining vessels that the king of Babylon did not carry away when he deported Jeconiah from Jerusalem to Babylon shall enter,’ says the Lord”—giving the sense rather than the words. Perhaps they thought it irrational that God should speak to pillars, the sea, the bases, and the other vessels that had remained in Jerusalem—as though we did not read that the Lord rebuked the morning worm and spoke to the sea: “Be silent and be still” (Jonah 4).

When he says, “Let them intervene before me,” or “before the Lord of hosts,” he shows that a true prophet can resist the Lord by prayers, just as Moses also stood against the Lord in the midst of the plague, to turn away the fury of his anger. Samuel did the same (1 Samuel 8), and the Lord said to Moses: “Let me alone, and I will strike this people” (Exodus 32). When he says, “Let me alone,” he shows that he can be restrained by the prayers of the saints.

“Let the prophets,” he says, “intervene, and let them demonstrate that whatever they predict has been accomplished in fact; then the prophecy will be confirmed as true.” The pillars, the sea, the bases, and the remainder of the vessels are mentioned in *Malachim* and at the end of this prophet’s book (2 Kings 24). The vessels carried away to Babylon are enumerated there, when Zedekiah was captured, the city burned, and the temple overthrown.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 1011]

[Col. 1011D] What astonishing blindness and pitiable misery among the Jews! They could never be moved either by benefits or corrected by scourges so as to submit to the command of their Creator. Rather, rebellious with stiff necks and an untamed mind, they were always contentious toward the Lord. For although his true prophets foretold future punishments when earlier kings were transgressing God’s law—and events themselves proved that what they had announced was true—the people, remaining unbelieving, chose instead to place their faith in the false prophets who promised prosperity, even while they were surrounded by enemies, daily endangered, and approaching death. Hence we now read in the later passages that Hananiah son of Azur, relying on false prophecies, utterly rejected the words of Jeremiah—or rather, the words of God through him—which also foretold their certain destruction.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT

Jeremiah answers Hananiah, who says that the people and all the vessels will return to Jerusalem after two years—“Amen”; and God punishes Hananiah for his falsehood.

[Col. 1013A]

“And it came to pass in that year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, that Hananiah son of Azur, the prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the Lord, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years of days I shall bring back to this place all the vessels of the house of the Lord.” (Jerome.)

What the Hebrew calls *prophets*—the source term is not preserved in the supplied text—the Septuagint translated as “false prophets,” so as to make the meaning clearer. Accordingly, in the present passage too he is called “a prophet”—the corresponding source term is not preserved—and not “a false prophet.”

The word of the Lord comes under King Zedekiah, in the fourth year of his reign and in the fifth month. The prophet Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been deported with Jeconiah. Hananiah nevertheless has the confidence to speak against the prophet in the Lord’s temple, because he promises prosperity to the people and falsehoods are willingly heard, especially when they promise happiness. Jeremiah had said that the remaining vessels—whether of the temple or the royal palace—and all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had left behind would be carried to Babylon. Hananiah, by contrast, promises that even those already deported will be brought back.

“—which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took from this place and carried away to Babylon. And Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles of Judah who entered Babylon, I shall bring back to this place, says the Lord; for I shall break the yoke of the king of Babylon.”

In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “Jeconiah and the exile of Judah. For I shall break the yoke of the king of Babylon,” briefly presenting the sense rather than the words of the Hebrew truth.

Hananiah the prophet promises—as it then appeared to the people—not only that the vessels but also King Jeconiah would be brought back to Jerusalem, and that the yoke of the king of Babylon, that is, his empire, would be destroyed. Since this had not yet happened, he promises that it will occur within two years, so that the nearness of the promised time may magnify the joy.

“And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet in the sight of the priests and in the sight of all the people who were standing in the house of the Lord; and Jeremiah the prophet said: Amen; so may the Lord do. May the Lord raise up your words which you have prophesied, so that the vessels may be brought back to the house of the Lord and all the exiles from Babylon to this place.” [Col. 1013D]

He wishes what the false prophet is lying about to come to pass; this is what “Amen” signifies, a word the Lord our Savior often uses in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you” (John 5). He desires, for the sake of prosperity, that the other man rather than himself should speak the truth. Hence another prophet also testifies, saying: “Would that I were not a man possessing the Spirit, and that I spoke falsehood instead” (Micah 2). Jonah, by contrast, is grieved that he has spoken falsely, and the Lord rebukes him because he would rather that his prophecy prove false than that so great a multitude should perish (Jonah 3). And so that he might not seem to confirm the false prophet’s prediction, he asserts the truth by the example of others, without injuring the man who is lying.

“But nevertheless, hear this word which I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people: The prophets who were before me and before you from the beginning, and who prophesied over many lands and great kingdoms, concerning war, affliction, and famine—the prophet who prophesies peace will be recognized as the prophet whom the Lord has truly sent when his word comes to pass.”

Jeremiah could have said to Hananiah: “You are speaking falsely; you are deceiving the people; you are not a prophet but a false prophet.” If he had said this, the false prophet could have thrown the same charge back at Jeremiah. Therefore he does not insult him but speaks to him as to a prophet.

“Not only am I a prophet, and you,” he says, “but before me and before you there were many others,” among them Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, Amos, and the rest. “They prophesied,” he says, “against many lands and not insignificant but great kingdoms,” announcing war, adversity, and scarcity of every kind. Conversely, there were others who promised peace and prosperity. The judgment of both groups was confirmed not by the flattery of falsehood but by the outcome of events.

Thus he speaks about himself by the example of others, and tells Hananiah that the truth of prophets is revealed when the end of events arrives. The Lord said the same through Moses (Deuteronomy 23): that a prophet is proved by the outcome of his prophecy. It should also be noted that he rebukes the liar not threateningly or harshly but with confidence in the truth, postponing the matter to the future so that those who hear may await the outcome of events.

“And Hananiah the prophet took the chain—or fork, which in Hebrew is called [the Hebrew term is not preserved in the supplied text]—from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it. And Hananiah said in the presence of all the people: Thus says the Lord: In this way I shall break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon within two years of days from the neck of all the nations. And Jeremiah went his way.”

The Septuagint did not translate “two years,” nor did it call Hananiah “a prophet,” lest it seem to call a prophet one who was not a prophet. Yet many things in the holy Scriptures are stated according to the opinion of the time when events are reported, and not according to the truth of what actually happened. Thus Joseph is called the Lord’s father in the Gospel, and Mary herself—who knew that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit and had answered the angel, “How will this be, since I have not known a man?” (Luke 1)—speaks to her son: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in anguish” (Luke 2).

At the same time, Jeremiah’s prudence, humility, and patience must be considered. The false prophet insults him and breaks the fork seized from his neck—something he certainly could not have done if it had been made of iron. Jeremiah remains silent and conceals his pain. For the Lord had not yet revealed to him what he should say, so that holy Scripture might quietly demonstrate that prophets do not speak solely on their own authority but by God’s will, especially concerning future events, which God alone knows.

“He went,” it says, “and departed on his way,” as though defeated, fulfilling the prophetic saying: “I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth” (Psalm 27).

“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah after Hananiah the prophet had broken the chain—or fork—from the neck of Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Go and say to Hananiah: Thus says the Lord: You have broken a wooden chain, but you shall make—or, ‘I shall make’—iron forks in its place. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have placed an iron yoke upon the neck of all these nations, so that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.”

The following words—“and they shall serve him; moreover, I have given him the beasts of the earth”—are not found in the Septuagint. In the present passage, moreover, the Septuagint does not call Hananiah “a prophet,” nor does it do so in what follows, lest, as I said earlier, it seem to call a false prophet a prophet.

But what does this imply according to the Hebrew truth? After Jeremiah the prophet went away and silently swallowed the insult, the word of the Lord came to him, so that the prophet might not speak to the false prophet boasting in his lie from his own words, but might say: “Thus says the Lord.” Yet Hananiah too, when breaking the wooden fork, spoke in the Lord’s presence with the same authority: “Thus says the Lord.” For falsehood always imitates truth.

When he added, “You have broken wooden forks, and you shall make—or, ‘you have made’—iron chains for them,” he showed that by refusing the lesser punishment Hananiah had caused a greater penalty to fall upon the people.

Here the allegorical interpreter raves, calling the wooden forks and chains “ethereal” and “brazen bodies,” namely those of demons and hostile powers. The iron forks or chains, he calls our coarser bodies, woven from nerves, bones, flesh, and veins. Those who were unwilling to undergo lesser torments in the heavenly Jerusalem according to the measure of their sin are condemned to the chains of our bodies; they endure the bonds and filth of swaddling clothes in the cries of infancy and serve the devil, the king of Babylon—that is, of this world—since Scripture says: “The world is placed in the evil one” (1 John 5), together with the beasts of the earth, which are confined within the bodies of brute animals.

An unlearned expositor and follower of Grunnius’s slander compelled me to set out openly the faults of another, which previously I mentioned discreetly, leaving them to the reader’s judgment.

“And Jeremiah the prophet said to Hananiah the prophet: Hear, Hananiah: The Lord did not send you, and you have caused this people to trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall send—or, ‘cast’—you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die.”

The following words—“because you have spoken against the Lord. And Hananiah the prophet died in that year, in the seventh month”—are not found in the Septuagint. Instead, they have only: “And he died in the seventh month.” Here too the Septuagint does not call Hananiah “a prophet,” although according to the Hebrew the holy Scripture calls him a prophet, even though Jeremiah, when reproving him, says: “Hear, Hananiah, the Lord did not send you,” and omits the word “prophet.” For how could he call him a prophet whom he denied to have been sent by the Lord?

But the truth and sequence of the narrative are preserved according to what was thought at that time, not according to what the man actually was, as we said above. “You deceived the people,” he says, “with a lie, so that they would not submit to God’s sentence; therefore know that you will die this year.”

If, whenever we die, we are freed from the prisons of our bodies, according to the testimony that heretics wrongly interpret—“Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141)—how is death now inflicted on the false prophet as a punishment? Here too it must be noted that Jeremiah, after suffering insult from the false prophet, remains silent while the word of the Lord had not yet come to him. Later, however, when sent by the Lord, he boldly rebukes the liar and announces his imminent death.

As for the fact that he died in the seventh month: those who habitually interpret this number as signifying rest may perhaps say that he died in the seventh month so that he might be freed from the evils of the body, according to the saying that is cited: “Death is rest for a man” (Sirach 21). We, however, know that the bodies of believers are temples of God, provided that the Holy Spirit dwells in them.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE

Jeremiah sends a book to the exiles; after seventy years they will be visited; and he warns them to beware of false prophets.

“And these are the words of the book which Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the remainder of the elders of the exile, to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, after King Jeconiah had gone out, together with the mistress—or queen—the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem—or nobles—and the craftsmen from Jerusalem, by the hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in Babylon, saying:

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom he carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens—or orchards—and eat their fruit. Take wives and beget sons and daughters; give wives to your sons and give your daughters to husbands, so that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there and do not be few in number. Seek the peace of the city—or land—to which I have carried you, and pray to the Lord for it, because in its peace you will have peace.”

This letter—or rather, this little book—of Jeremiah the prophet was sent to Babylon by Zedekiah’s messengers, Elasah and Gemariah, to those who had been carried away by Nebuchadnezzar with Jeconiah and his mother. Through the occasion of the royal embassy, the prophet also completed his own task, admonishing the deported people concerning what the Lord had commanded them.

He aptly said: “King Jeconiah went out, together with the mistress, the eunuchs, and the princes of Judah,” and the rest. And: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom he carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon,” so that they might appear to have been deported not by the power of the king of Babylon but by the Lord’s will.

First the word is addressed to the elders, then to the priests, third to the prophets, and fourth to all the people of God, so that, in accordance with the order of age, the prophet’s letter might reach those who were being admonished.

He warns them, not in his own words but in the Lord’s, to build houses and dwell in them, plant gardens or orchards and eat their fruit, take wives and beget sons and daughters, multiply in the place of their exile, and not be few in number. They are to seek the peace of the city or land to which he has carried them and pray to the Lord for it, giving this reason: “For in the peace of that land you will have peace.”

Because captivity was soon to follow Jerusalem on account of its short remaining time, Jeremiah was commanded neither to take a wife nor to beget children. Hence the Apostle says to us: “The time is shortened; from now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7). If, because of the narrowness of time, the use of wives is removed from those who have them, how much more is it commanded that those who do not have them should not take them!

The whole of this prophetic command was given so that they would not listen to the false prophets who, because the time was short, promised them a return to Jerusalem. They were to know that they would remain in Babylon for a long time—long enough to take wives, plant orchards and gardens, build houses, and beget children.

When he added, “Seek the peace of the city—or land,” and again, “For in its peace you will have peace,” he confirms the apostolic command: “Therefore I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and purity” (1 Timothy 2).

According to the mystical interpretation, after we have been cast out of Jerusalem—that is, the Church—because of our sins and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, of whom the Apostle says, “I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5), and again, “Those whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1), we must not become secure, grow sluggish through idleness, or utterly despair of salvation.

Rather, we must first build houses—not on sand but on rock—and such houses as the midwives built in Exodus (Exodus 1), because they feared the Lord. Next we must plant gardens or orchards, like the paradise that the Lord planted in Eden and in which he placed the tree of life, of which it is written: “She is a tree of life to those who seize her, and whoever holds her fast is blessed” (Proverbs 3).

Third, we must take wives, one of whom is Wisdom, concerning whom Solomon writes: “Love her, and she will guard you; embrace her, and she will exalt you” (Proverbs 4); and elsewhere: “I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wisdom 8). One wife, Wisdom, is not enough for us unless we also possess the other virtues—fortitude, temperance, and justice—so that we may beget from them many sons.

We shall also give our daughters to husbands, so that the truth of faith, which is represented by sons, may be joined to good works, which are represented by daughters, and good works may be joined to the soundness of faith. Begetting such sons and daughters, let us multiply in number, so that, destroying what belongs to childhood and growing into a mature man, we may deserve to hear: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2), and may say with the Apostle to our children: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4).

Let us also seek the peace of the Church, our city and our land, so that we may deserve to return to it, from which by the Lord’s judgment we were deported to dwell in the confusion of error. For if it receives us, we shall have peace.

At the same time, the Lord’s clemency must be considered. He commands us to pray for our enemies and do good to those who persecute us, so that we may not be content with our own salvation alone but may also seek the salvation of our enemies (Luke 6).

“For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets who are in your midst and your diviners deceive you, and do not pay attention to your dreams which you cause yourselves to dream. For they prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord.”

That there were prophets—or rather false prophets—diviners, and dreamers in Babylon among those whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away with Jeconiah and his mother is attested by the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote against them and whom Jeremiah likewise commanded the people not to believe (Ezekiel 13). At the time when this letter was sent, however, Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon. This message was sent at the beginning of King Zedekiah’s reign; Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of Jeconiah’s exile, which was also a year of Zedekiah’s reign.

According to the tropological interpretation, we should understand the false prophets as those who interpret the words of Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit expresses them. The diviners are those who pronounce the conjectures of their own minds and uncertain predictions of the future without the authority of divine words. The dreamers are those who do not heed what is written: “Do not give sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids” (Proverbs 6). Concerning them the Apostle Jude also says: “Likewise, these dreamers defile the flesh and reject authority” (Jude 8). Their mind is never vigilant but, crushed by the sleep of arrogance and error, is surrounded by the horror of night. To them the Apostle Paul also says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Ephesians 5).

“For thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I shall visit you and raise up over you my good word, to bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think concerning you, says the Lord—thoughts of peace and not of affliction—to give you a good end and patience—or hope. Then you will call upon me and go—or, according to Symmachus, ‘you will find’—and pray to me, and I shall hear you. You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart, and I shall be found by you—or, ‘I shall appear to you,’ says the Lord.”

“Do not believe,” he says, “your false prophets, diviners, and dreamers, who promise you an imminent return to Jerusalem. Unless the seventy years have been completed, and the king of the Persians, Cyrus, has first released the captives, you will by no means return to your homeland. Then I shall fulfill my promises in it and bring you back to this place.”

“I know the thoughts that I think concerning you,” says the Lord. He says that he knows what he is thinking, while they, along with their prophets, diviners, and dreamers, do not know. Knowledge of future events belongs to God alone.

“To give you,” he says, “an end and patience”—the end of captivity and patience amid present hardships, or hope concerning the future. “Then you will call upon me and go to Jerusalem, and you will pray, and I shall hear you.” Certainly the Lord could fulfill what he had promised without the captives’ calling upon him and praying. Yet he urges them to pray so that they may deserve to receive what has been promised.

“You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart,” in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7).

According to the anagogical interpretation, we remain amid the confusion of this world until we deserve to receive the rest of the number seven. Once repentance has been received, God will fulfill what he promised, and we shall be brought back to our proper place, the Church. For this reason the Lord seems to strike in order to heal. He will give us the end of our labor and patience; we shall call upon him and return to the Church; we shall pray and be heard; we shall seek and find him when we seek him with all our heart, and then he will appear to us.

Some interpret the seventy years according to what is written: “The days of our years are seventy years” (Psalm 89). When these have been completed, we shall return to the Lord with all our heart, be heard, and reach the end of our labor and patience. For now we possess everything in shadow and in an image.

“And I shall bring back your captivity and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I have driven you, says the Lord, and I shall bring you back from the place to which I caused you to be deported. For you said: ‘The Lord will raise up prophets for us in Babylon.’

For thus says the Lord to the king who sits upon the throne of David, and to all the people who dwell in this city, and to your brothers who did not enter into exile with you: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I shall send against them sword, famine, and pestilence, and I shall make them like worthless figs that cannot be eaten, because they are so bad. I shall pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence, and I shall make them a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth, a curse, an astonishment, a hissing, and a reproach among all the nations to which I have driven them, because they did not listen to my words, says the Lord, which I sent to them through my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them—and you did not listen, says the Lord.

Therefore hear the word of the Lord, all you exiles whom I sent out from Jerusalem to Babylon.”

Up to this point, the passages I have marked with asterisks are not found in the Septuagint. As for the other places in which one verse or a few words have been omitted, I did not record them, overcome by weariness, lest I cause boredom for the reader.

The Lord promises those who were in exile that after seventy years of captivity he will bring them back from all the nations and from every place to which he has driven them, releasing them from captivity and restoring their former condition and homeland.

“And since I myself,” he says, “will do this of my own accord, and you will return at the appointed time, you are deceiving yourselves in vain by thinking that you have prophets in Babylon who promise you false things. You should know that you must not now hope for a return, but build houses, plant orchards, take wives, beget children, multiply in number, and await the promised time.”

Hear what the Lord says to Zedekiah, who now reigns in Jerusalem, and to all the inhabitants of this city—that is, to your brothers who refused to obey my judgment and migrate with you to Babylon. They will by no means escape captivity but will die by sword, famine, and pestilence.

“And I shall make them like worthless figs,” which Theodotion translated as *sudrina*; the Second Version as “worst”; and Symmachus as “last.” In Hebrew they are called *Sed*—but through scribal error the Greek delta became established in place of the middle syllable or letter alpha, so that *suarim* is read as *sudrim*. Just as the basket—or hamper—that contained good figs is said to have contained first fruits, so the other basket, which contained bad figs, is written to have contained last figs.

“And I shall pursue,” he says, “those who now remain in Jerusalem with sword, famine, and pestilence, so that first, through the siege, and immediately afterward, those who have been able to remain and escape may be scattered throughout all lands. They will become an example to all of curse, terror, hissing, and reproach, among those to whom I shall drive you, because they did not listen to my words,” says the Lord, “which I spoke to them through my servants, rising early, sending them, and never ceasing to warn them, so that they might imitate you who enjoy secure leisure in exile until the Lord’s promise is fulfilled.

But you who obeyed my judgment and surrendered yourselves to the Babylonian king, hear what I am about to say.”

Here the delirious interpreter dreams of the ruin of the heavenly Jerusalem and supposes that the prophecy is directed against those who dwell in the Babylon of this world. He says that they did well to descend voluntarily into these bodies, build houses in the land of the Chaldeans, plant orchards, take wives, beget children, and, after seventy years, be restored through good works to their former place and to the heavenly Jerusalem. Those, however, who were unwilling of their own will to descend to earthly things are supposedly to suffer what the Lord threatens against Zedekiah and his people: because they refused to imitate their brothers and come to Babylon, he will send against them sword, famine, and pestilence—that is, the deprivation of all things—and make them like the worst figs, which cannot be eaten at all.

He will pursue them with an everlasting sword and make them a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth, so that they will become not human beings but demons and aerial powers, and among all the angels who preside over the various provinces they will be a curse, a terror, a hissing, and a reproach among all nations.

He says that they will suffer these things because they refused to hear the words of the prophets in the heavenly Jerusalem, who urged them to descend to earthly things, assume a body of humiliation, and, after repentance, possess their former place following the true Sabbath rest.

Such are the things he says; and when his disciples hear them, they think they are hearing divine mysteries, though they are merely the filth of the Grunnian fable. We, who despise these notions, are regarded by them as though we were brute animals, and they call us *pelousiōtai* (πηλουσιῶται), because, being situated in the mud of this body, we cannot perceive heavenly things.

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and concerning Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy falsely to you in my name: Behold, I shall deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he shall strike them before your eyes. From them a curse shall be taken for all the exiles of Judah who are in Babylon, saying: ‘May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire.’

Because they committed folly—or iniquity—in Israel, committed adultery with the wives of their neighbors—or fellow citizens—and spoke a word falsely in my name, which I had not commanded them. I am judge and witness, says the Lord.”

The Hebrews say that these were elders who committed folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens. To one of them Daniel said: “You who have grown old in evil days”; and to the other: “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you and desire has perverted your heart. This is how you acted toward the daughters of Israel, and they, out of fear, spoke with you; but the daughter of Judah did not endure your iniquity” (Daniel 13).

When the prophet now says, “They spoke a word falsely in my name, which I had not commanded them,” they think this signifies that these men so deceived the wretched little women who were carried about by every wind of doctrine that they told those who belonged to the tribe of Judah that Christ was to be generated from their seed. Ensnared by desire, these women offered their bodies as though they were to become the mothers of Christ.

But the statement made here—“whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”—seems to contradict the account in Daniel. Daniel asserts that, on Daniel’s sentence, they were stoned by the people; here, however, it is written that the king of Babylon roasted them in the fire. Therefore many, indeed almost all, of the Hebrews reject this story as fictitious and do not read it in the synagogues of the Jews.

“For how,” they ask, “could it have happened that captive princes and prophets had the power to have their own people stone them?” They maintain instead that Jeremiah’s account is more credible: the elders were indeed convicted by Daniel, but the sentence against them was imposed by the king of Babylon, who, as victor and master, exercised authority over the captives.

How many among our own flock resemble Ahab and Zedekiah, prophesying falsehood in the Lord’s name, committing folly in Israel, and committing adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens—those who were born in the same city of the Church! The true Nebuchadnezzar roasts them in the fire of sin, as the prophet Hosea says: “All of them commit adultery; they are like an oven heated by the baker” (Hosea 7).

Blessed is the one who removes the yoke from his youth and sits alone, filled with bitterness, and can say with David: “I have not sat in the council of the wicked, nor will I enter with those who practice iniquity” (Psalm 25).

When the prophet now adds, “I am judge and witness, says the Lord,” the meaning is this: What I say concerning these two false prophets, who speak falsely in my name a word that I did not command them to speak, I have not learned merely by report; I myself know it to be true. No one can conceal it from me or escape the truth of my judgment.

“And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say. And what follows—‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you sent letters in your own name to all the people who are in Jerusalem’—is not found in the Septuagint. They have again added from their own text: ‘I did not send you in my name.’ And then, in due order: ‘And to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest.’ And again, from the Hebrew: ‘And to all the priests.’ Then the narrative is woven together:

‘The Lord appointed you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, so that you might be leader (or instructor) and overseer in the house of the Lord over every man possessed and prophesying, so that you might put him in the stocks, and in prison (or in custody), and in the bar’ (which Symmachus renders μόχλον, “bar,” while Aquila gives the Hebrew word itself, SINAC). ‘And now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite, who prophesies to you? For on this account he sent to us in Babylon, saying: It is a long time; build houses and dwell in them, plant gardens and eat their fruit. So the priest Zephaniah read this letter in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet.’

Shemaiah, from the place Nehelam—which is interpreted as “torrent”—had been taken into Babylon with King Jeconiah, and he falsely prophesied to the people that they would soon return to Jerusalem. That he was a false prophet, however, is demonstrated by Jeremiah’s following words:

“Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah prophesied to you, though I did not send him.”

Because Jeremiah had sent letters to those who were in Babylon, saying: “Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruit; take wives and beget sons,” and had added afterward: “Let not your prophets who are among you, and your diviners, deceive you”; and then: “For these men prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them, says the Lord”—Shemaiah, recognizing that this had been written against him under the general designation of “false prophets,” sent letters to Jerusalem, to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and to the remaining priests, against Jeremiah, asking why Jeremiah was not rebuked by the priest Zephaniah, whose office it was to distinguish between prophets who spoke by the Holy Spirit and those who spoke by the contrary spirit, and to order that he be confined [Col. 1023A] in prison, so that he might suffer the penalties for his falsehood and cease any longer to lead the people astray.

Jehoiada was the priest who, after the killing of Gothalia [Athaliah], transferred the kingdom to Joash and killed the priests of Baal (2 Kings 11; 2 Chronicles 23). This, then, is what he writes: “Why do you not imitate Jehoiada the priest and kill Jeremiah the false prophet? For the Lord appointed you in place of Jehoiada, so that you might have charge of the Temple and, above all, distinguish who speak by the Holy Spirit and who by a demonic spirit.” That the discernment of spirits belongs to the Lord’s grace is also recalled by the Apostle (1 John 4).

“Why,” he says, “have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite?” What Shemaiah himself deserved as a false prophet, he transfers to the prophet, and by his lie anticipates the truth. Hence, too, the children of darkness are considered wiser than the children of light in this generation. While we act patiently and await the salvation of the wretched, these heretics forestall us and call us by their own name, leading the blind into a pit along with the blind.

“He sent to us in Babylon, saying: ‘It is a long time.’” This is the whole source of his grief: that Jeremiah, contrary to his lie, had written the truth—that the return was far off, and that they would return to Jerusalem after seventy years. Therefore they ought to build houses, plant orchards, eat their fruit, take wives, and beget children, as the preceding passage recounted. When the priest Zephaniah received this letter, which had been written specifically to him, he read it to Jeremiah, in a way reproaching him and censuring him by the very act of reading: why had he dared to write such things to Babylon?

[Col. 1023C] And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying:

“Send to all the exiles, saying: Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah prophesied to you, though I did not send him, and he made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit punishment upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite and upon his offspring. He shall have no man sitting in the midst of this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do to my people, says the Lord, because he has spoken apostasy against the Lord.”

The false prophet Shemaiah the Nehelamite, who had drawn foreign and turbid waters from a torrent, became angry that Jeremiah had written the truth against his lie, and sent letters to the priest Zephaniah, asking why the prophet had dared to write [Col. 1023D] the truth and seeking to have him confined in prison so that he would not speak. Zephaniah, too, secretly accuses the prophet when he reads the letter of the liar and boasts that he possesses his accusation. How much more guilty, then, are those who defend false prophets, cherish liars, and make the evil discoveries of others their own sins?

Let the false prophet hear, and let the priest understand what he himself deserves to hear through the prophet. Thus says the Lord:

“Behold, I will visit punishment upon Shemaiah.”

The Lord speaks this, not the prophet: he will visit Shemaiah the Nehelamite, not for his restoration but for the punishment of the liar, in accordance with what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges” (Psalm 88). Nor does he visit punishment only upon the false prophet, but also upon his offspring—all the disciples whom he deceived by his error:

“He shall have no man,” he says, “sitting in the midst of this people.”

Let the worst stock be erased from the assembly of the saints; let him not sit among those who are at rest, since he could not stand with those who were standing and did not heed the words: “If he had stood in my substance” (Jeremiah 23). And although the Lord promises the perfection of all virtues when the period of sevenfold time has been completed, he will not see the good that he was claiming for himself in the present age. All this will happen because he spoke apostasy against the Lord, saying that, once the captivity of sins had already been loosed, those people would return to Jerusalem—those to whom the Apostle issues this warning:

“Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you have reigned without us—and would that you had reigned, so that we also might reign with you!” (1 Corinthians 4).

## CHAPTER XXX

*He promises sorrow because of the captivity, and joy and vengeance against the enemies.*

“This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Write for yourself in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel and Judah, says the Lord God; and I will restore them (or make them dwell) in the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it” (MAUR.).

This passage of the prophet Jeremiah contains mystical promises, which the Jews—and our Judaizers—think are to be fulfilled at the end of the world. For they cannot yet prove that they were fulfilled under Zerubbabel. We, however, following the authority of the apostles and evangelists, and especially that of the Apostle Paul, show that whatever is promised carnally to the people of Israel has been fulfilled spiritually in us and is being fulfilled even today. There is no other dispute between Jews and Christians than this: that both believe Christ, the Son of God, was promised, but that the things said to be future under Christ are said by us to have been fulfilled, while the Jews say that they are still to be fulfilled by them.

Since, therefore, we already believe that Christ has come, we must necessarily demonstrate that the things said to be future under Christ have been fulfilled, and that we are the children of Abraham, concerning whom it is written: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” To him the promise was made: “And in your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 26). Teaching that this blessing was fulfilled in Christ, the vessel of election “did not say, ‘In seeds,’ but ‘in seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3).

“This is the word,” he says, “that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Write for yourself in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel and Judah, says the Lord God; and I will restore them (or make them dwell) in the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.”

(Hieron.) While the false prophets in Babylon were promising that the people who had been taken captive with Jeconiah would soon return, and while Hananiah son of Azzur was preaching the same thing in Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah affirmed that this would indeed happen—but not within two years, as they falsely claimed; rather, after the completion of seventy years. At that time he is commanded to write in a book and commit to memory what the Lord foretold would come. From this it is clear that the prophecy does not concern a near time, but that these things are to be fulfilled after many ages, when Israel and Judah are to return to their own land. Then what Ezekiel prophesied must also be fulfilled: that the two staffs would be joined together and that David the king would rule, concerning whom he writes: “And my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them” (Ezekiel 37). Whatever, therefore, we have said about that prophecy must also be understood in the present passage, especially since Ezekiel in Babylon and Jeremiah in Jerusalem prophesied at the same time and about the same events.

[Col. 1025B] “And these are the words that the Lord spoke concerning Israel and Judah. For thus says the Lord: We have heard a voice of terror (or fear), dread, and there is no peace. Ask and see whether a male gives birth. Why, then, have I seen every man’s hand upon his loins, like a woman in labor? And why have all faces turned into yellowness?”

First, grievous things are announced, so that joyful things may follow after the evils: health is more welcome when sickness has been driven away, and the magnitude of pain is transformed into the magnitude of joys. What he says means this: There will be such fear and such dread that, once peace has been driven away, everything will be filled with wars and bloodshed. Even men, whose proper role is to fight against adversaries, will be seized by womanly terror, and their hands will be applied not to weapons but to holding their loins, as though a woman giving birth were clasping her hips and loins. Hence the faces of all will be turned yellow, their pallor bearing witness to the fear in their hearts.

Some interpret this passage tropologically, thinking that it may be compared with the testimony: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived, and we were in labor, and we gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isaiah 26), and with the apostolic statement in which he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4). It is clear, however, that this comparison pertains not to terror but to joy, whereas the present Scripture signifies the time of Israel’s devastation and ruin.

“Woe! For great is that day, and there is none like it; it is a time of tribulation for Jacob, and he shall be saved from it.” [Col. 1025D]

He foretells a time of misery in order to introduce a time of joy. When, he says, such evils have come first that the pain of all men is compared with the pain of a woman in labor, nevertheless the time of Jacob’s tribulation—that is, of God’s people—will be changed into prosperity. “And he shall be saved from it” means, implicitly, from the time about which the discourse had proceeded. By Jacob understand the twelve tribes, which were saved not under Zerubbabel, as some falsely suppose, but through the evangelical calling.

“And it shall come to pass on that day, says the Lord of hosts: I will break his yoke from your neck, and I will burst his bonds, and strangers shall no longer rule over them; and they shall serve (or work for) the Lord their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.”

This is the David of whom the Gospel also speaks: that he will give us the ability, “having been delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, to serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.” Just as the first Adam and the second Adam are written of according to the truth of the body, so too are David, the Lord and Savior, because according to the flesh he is from David, with holy Mary contributing everything in him that was from the stock of David and possessing his origin and conception from the Holy Spirit.
