When he says, “I will break his yoke from your neck, and I will burst his bonds,” there is no doubt that, under the type of Nebuchadnezzar, this must be understood of the devil.

“Therefore do not fear, my servant Jacob, says the Lord, nor be afraid, Israel; for behold, I will save you from a distant land, and your seed from the land of their captivity. And Jacob shall return and be at rest, and shall abound in all good things, and there shall be no one whom he fears, for I am with you, says the Lord, to save you. For I will bring complete destruction upon all the nations among which I scattered you; but I will not bring complete destruction upon you. I will chastise (or instruct) you with judgment, so that you may not appear innocent to yourself (or, ‘and cleansing, I will not cleanse you’).”

This περικοπή (“section”) is not found in the Septuagint, and in most codices of the Vulgate edition it has been added from Theodotion under asterisks. The divine word promises and familiarly calls Jacob and Israel his servant, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called servants of God. Moses and the other prophets are likewise called by this title, and the Apostle Paul boasts of it at the beginning of his Epistles. Thus the two and ten tribes—that is, the twelve—may know that they are to be saved from a distant land, that their captivity is to be loosed and peace restored, and that they are to be filled with every abundance, in accordance with what is said in the Psalm: “Let there be peace within your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Psalm 121).

This will happen because they will enjoy the Lord’s presence, when the hostile nations that had captured them perish and they themselves are liberated from the nations. He teaches that they were handed over not to punishment but to instruction, so that they might be judged as his own and not destroyed as strangers: “For he who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3)—that is, he has already been sentenced to destruction.

When he adds, “So that you may not appear innocent to yourself,” or, according to Symmachus, “and cleansing, I will not cleanse you,” or according to Aquila, “When I instruct you through judgment, I will by no means make you innocent,” this signifies that the whole world needs God’s mercy and that no one, however holy he may be, proceeds securely to the Judge. This is directed against the new heresy arising from the old one, which thinks that in this world and in this mortal flesh—before this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality—perfection can exist in anyone and that anyone can fulfill all virtues at once.

“For thus says the Lord: Your fracture is incurable, your wound is grievous. There is no one to judge your case so as to bind it; there is no usefulness of remedies for you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they will not seek you. For I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel (or severe) chastisement. Because of the multitude of your iniquity, your sins have become harsh (or multiplied). Why do you cry out to me over your crushing? Your pain is incurable. Because of the multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins, I have done these things to you.”

He speaks as though to a beautiful woman, to whom he had earlier said: “I will chastise you with judgment, so that you may not appear innocent” (or innocent, in the feminine). And by a metaphor he speaks to Jerusalem, saying that she has been grievously wounded by God’s judgment and that she cannot be healed by anyone other than the one who struck her. “There is no one,” says the Lord, “to judge your case,” and no one able to lay the skin of a scar over so deep a wound. Wherever you turn, there is no remedy for you, because you have offended him who is the true and the only physician.

“All your lovers have forgotten you,” whether priests, rulers, or certainly the angelic protectors by whom you were previously surrounded before you offended the Lord. “They will not seek you,” imitating the Apostle Paul, who sought believers and not what belonged to believers (2 Corinthians 12).

“For I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel (or severe) chastisement.” A friend strikes in one way, an enemy in another; a father strikes in one way, an adversary in another. The former beats in order to correct; the latter strikes in order to kill. Hence the prophet also says tearfully: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Psalm 6).

This happened because, on account of the multitude of your iniquity, your sins became grievous. What follows—“Why do you cry out over your crushing? Your pain is incurable because of the multitude of your iniquity”—is not found in the Septuagint, evidently because “because of the multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins” is said a second time, and those who copied the text from the beginning thought it had been added.

The sense is this: The multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins caused me to strike you with the wound of an enemy and beat you with cruel chastisement. They could not be healed except by the most biting medicine [powder, burning cautery, and the sharpest iron], by which I would amputate the putrid and incurable flesh. Nevertheless, “because of the multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins I have done this to you”—not by my will, but compelled by the logic of medicine.

(Greg.) Hence it is also written in Job: “He will send it upon him, and he will not spare” (Job 20). Whenever God corrects a sinner by striking him, he sends the scourge for the purpose of sparing him. But when, by striking, he brings to an end a life that persists in sin, he sends the scourge and by no means spares. He who sent the scourge in order to spare sometimes sends it so that he may not spare.

In this life the Lord strives all the more to spare in proportion as he scourges by waiting. As he himself says through the voice of the angel to John: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Revelation 3). And elsewhere it is said: “For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

Conversely, concerning the scourge of condemnation it is written: “The sinner is caught in the works of his hands” (Psalm 9). Concerning this the Lord says through Jeremiah, when he sees peoples sinning incorrigibly—whom he now regards not as sons under discipline but as enemies under strict punishment:

“I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel (or severe) chastisement.”

And what is said here—“he will not spare”—is also declared there in other words: “Why do you cry out to me over your crushing? Your pain is incurable.” Hence the elect always take care to return to righteousness before the Judge’s anger kindles itself unquenchably against them, lest, seized by the final scourge, their life be ended together with their guilt. For the scourge then wipes away guilt when it changes the life; it does not expiate actions when it changes a person’s habits.

Every divine stroke is therefore either a purification of the present life in us or the beginning of the punishment to come. It was said concerning those who profit from the scourge: “You who devise pain by decree” (Psalm 93). While the wicked person is scourged and corrected, he who refused to hear the commandment hears pain. Pain is therefore fashioned for him through instruction when, in place of a commandment, pain restrains him from evil deeds.

But concerning those whom scourges condemn and do not free, it is said: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jeremiah 5). These scourges begin in this life and persist in eternal punishment. Hence the Lord says through Moses: “Fire has blazed up in my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths of the underworld” (Deuteronomy 32). Insofar as this concerns the present stroke, it is rightly said: “Fire has blazed up in my anger”; but insofar as it concerns eternal condemnation, what follows is suitably added at once: “and it shall burn down to the depths of the underworld.”

Although some are accustomed to say that what is written—“God does not judge twice for the same thing”—means this, they nevertheless fail to consider what is said through the prophet concerning the wicked: “Crush them with double confusion,” and what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed a second time those who did not believe.”

If, however, we grant them this—that no fault can be struck twice—this must be understood of those who are struck in sin and die in their sin. Their striking begins here and is completed there, so that for the uncorrected there is one scourge, which begins temporally but is consummated in eternal punishments. Thus, for those who altogether refuse correction, the striking of present scourges is already the beginning of the torments to come.

“Therefore all who eat you shall be devoured, [Col. 1028D] and all your enemies shall be led into captivity; those who ravage you shall be ravaged, and I will give all your plunderers as plunder. For I will bind up your scar and heal you from your wounds, says the Lord, because they called you the outcast (or dispersed one): ‘This is Zion, which had no one seeking her.’”

We recognize that these things took place under Zerubbabel, when the Babylonians and Chaldeans ravaged the Assyrians—that is, Nineveh—and in turn the Medes and Persians captured the Babylonians and Chaldeans, and Babylon was destroyed. Then Zion began to have the Lord seeking her; the scar was laid over her wound, and she was healed from her blows. This is fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ.

[Col. 1029A] Thus says the Lord:

“Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob, and I will have mercy on his dwellings (or captivity); the city shall be built upon its height, and the Temple shall be founded according to its order. And praise shall go forth from them, and the voice of those who make merry; and I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished.”

What follows—“And I will glorify them, and they shall not grow weak”—is not found in the Septuagint.

“And his sons,” he says, “shall be as from the beginning, and his assembly shall remain before me. And I will visit all who afflict him; and his leader shall be from him, and his ruler shall be brought forth from his midst; I will bring him near, and he shall approach me. For who is this who applies his heart so that he may draw near to me? says the Lord” (Hieron.).

Their type had already appeared in Zerubbabel [Col. 1029B] and Ezra, when the people returned, the city began to be built upon its height, the law of the Temple and its worship began to be observed, and the other things contained in Ezra’s volume took place. More fully and perfectly, however, this was fulfilled in the Lord and Savior and in the apostles, when the city was built upon its height, concerning which it is written: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5).

And the Temple was founded according to its order and ceremonies, so that whatever had been done carnally among the former people might be fulfilled spiritually in the Church. Then praise went forth, or thanksgiving—for this is what it signifies—so that all the apostles might say: “Grace to you and peace” (1 Corinthians 1).

And the voice of those who make merry—not with the kind of play in which the people ate, drank, and rose up to play (Exodus 32), [Col. 1029C] but with the kind in which David danced before the ark of the Lord (2 Samuel 6). “And they were multiplied and not diminished,” so that the whole world might believe in God the Savior. They were glorified, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86).

And her sons—that is, the apostles—were as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been at the beginning, princes of the Israelite race. Then the Lord visited all who had afflicted the people of God, namely, the hostile powers. And her leader was from her own midst, unquestionably the Lord and Savior according to the flesh, brought forth from the race of Israel; and her ruler was brought forth from her midst. The Father brought him near to himself, and he approached him, so that his Son might say: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14), because no one can so apply his heart to the Lord or be so joined to him as the Son is joined to the Father.

What is said according to the Septuagint—“And you shall be my people, and I shall be your God”—we see fulfilled in part in Israel and completely in the multitude of the nations.

“Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord; fury goes forth; a sweeping storm shall come to rest upon the head of the wicked. The Lord shall not turn away the anger of his indignation until he has acted and fulfilled the thought of his heart. In the last days you shall understand these things.”

The whirlwind of the Lord’s fury, and the sweeping storm and tempest, shall come to rest upon the head of either the demons or those who blasphemed the Son of God. He shall not turn away the anger of his indignation until he acts and fulfills the thought of his heart, [Col. 1030A] and Jerusalem is surrounded by an army and utterly destroyed.

Just as an artisan cannot be understood until his work has been completed, nor the skill of a physician until health has been restored, so, when Jerusalem has been overthrown and the former people rejected, believers will understand that the rejection of the Jews was the occasion of our salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXI

*After the fullness of the nations has entered, Israel comes to faith; concerning the birth of Christ and the sacrament of his body and blood; that each person will die in his own sin.*

“At that time, says the Lord: I will be God to all the clans of Israel (or to the race of Israel), and they shall be my people” (Hieron.).

Unless the Lord’s thought has been fulfilled and his fury has come to rest upon the head of the wicked, the Lord of the universe cannot be God to the clans of Israel. He says this concerning the remnant that has been saved. If what is said—“I will be God to the race of Israel,” or “to all the clans of Israel”—is brought against us, let us take as an example: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of your father” (John 8), and the Apostle writes: “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 10). From this he teaches that there is another Israel according to the spirit.

That, therefore, is Israel who sees God with the mind, or who is the Lord’s most upright one; and such an Israel shall be the people of God.

“Thus says the Lord: The people that remained from the sword found grace in the wilderness; Israel shall go to his rest.”

The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the Lord: I found θερμὸν (‘the hot one’) in the wilderness with those who had perished by the sword. Go, and do not kill Israel.”

In this passage the Latin codices, through the ambiguity of the Greek word, have absurdly translated it as *lupinos* (“lupines”) instead of “hot.” For the Greek θερμόν means both things; and this word itself is not found in the Hebrew. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as χάριν, that is, “grace.” Only the Septuagint supplied “hot,” thinking that it was the final letter. If we read the word according to its letters, it means “grace”; if it is interpreted according to its sense, it means “heat.”

The sense according to the Hebrew is this: When the Jewish people, who had remained after the Roman sword—or who at least had been able to escape the anger of the Lord’s fury—found grace in the wilderness of the nations, they would be saved among the multitude of peoples in the Church. Hence Israel will go and find his rest, which he had always hoped for and which the prophecies of the prophets had promised him.

According to the Septuagint, however, the understanding is this: The Lord found the apostles and their companions, hot and alive, in the wilderness of the nations, among those who had been killed by their unbelief and no longer possessed the heat of life. Hence the angels and those who serve in God’s ministry are commanded not to kill everyone, so that Israel may not be utterly destroyed; and it is said to them: “Go, and do not kill Israel.” Let there be some who live, some who are warm with the ardor of faith, and some who escape the cold of unbelief and death—those whom the Lord finds in the wilderness.

“The Lord appeared to me (or to him) from afar, and I have loved you with everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you in mercy. [Col. 1031A] Again I will build you, and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Again you shall be adorned with your tambourines (or, you shall take up your tambourines), and you shall go out in the dance of those who make merry. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria. Plant plantations and gather the vintage; for there shall be a day when watchmen will cry on Mount Ephraim: ‘Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the Lord our God.’”

Because Israel had offended the Lord and said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), and, “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12), and had withdrawn far from God, the Lord therefore appeared to him after a long time—not in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, after which they were again taken captive—but loved him with an everlasting love that will be destroyed by no end, and drew him in mercy. For he was saved not by merit but by clemency.

Again he says: “I will build you, and you shall be built, virgin Israel.” Let us understand this properly of the Church. Those who look to receive a golden and jewel-studded Jerusalem are mad, consecrating their own greed in the mystery of the Lord’s city. Again you shall be adorned with your tambourines, so that, with all flesh of evil works consumed in you, you may sing to the Lord in the churches. And you shall go out in the dance of those who make merry with the throngs of the nations. You shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria, not in valleys and low places, but on the mountains of Samaria, which after the captivity of the people of Israel were occupied by foreigners; to them it is said: “Plant plantations and gather the vintage.”

Then was the day of the Lord, on which the watchmen—namely, the apostles and apostolic men—cried on Mount Samaria and on Mount Ephraim, the one name signifying “watch,” the other “fruitfulness.” But what do the watchmen of Samaria say—or rather, what do they cry on Mount Ephraim? “Arise, you who lie down; leave low things behind; despise the sacrifices of victims: ‘A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God’ (Psalm 50). Let us go up to Zion,” that is, to the Church, where there is watchfulness and the vision of God. And when we have been in Zion—or rather, have gone up to it together—we shall go up to the Lord our God.

“For thus says the Lord: Rejoice with gladness, Jacob, and neigh against the head of the nations. Make a sound, blow the trumpet, and say: ‘Save your people, Lord—the remnant of Israel.’”

Significantly, not all Israel is saved, but the remnant of Israel, the Lord commanding and saying: “Rejoice with gladness, you who are of Jacob, and neigh,” referring all things to the head of the nations, because the tail has at one time been turned into the head. “Make a sound, blow the trumpet, and say.” What is it that they are commanded to say? “Save, Lord, your people.” What people? Certainly, “the remnant of Israel,” which has been saved according to election. Of this Paul too, taking up Isaiah’s testimony, says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we should have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1; Romans 9).

“Behold, therefore, I will bring them from the land of the north and gather them from the ends of the earth.” What follows—“at the feast of Passover, and she shall bear many children”—is not found in the Hebrew, but is read only in the Septuagint. In its place, among the Hebrews it is written:

“Among them shall be the blind and the lame, the pregnant and she who gives birth together: a great assembly of those returning here.”

The remnant of the people of Israel is gathered through the apostles and apostolic men, of whom we read above: “The watchmen will cry on the mountain,” and to whom it is commanded: “Make a sound, blow the trumpet, and say,” so that the remnant of Israel may be saved. The Lord himself promises that he will bring them back from the land of the north—which is the harshest wind, though by name it is called “right-hand”—from unbelief and from the coldness of the Lord’s love, and gather them from the ends of the earth, not at another time but at the feast of Passover, that is, in the days of the Lord’s passion, when the Lord was crucified. Thus was fulfilled what he himself promised in the Gospel: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12).

Then he begot a great multitude, so that Isaiah’s saying was fulfilled: “For a nation has been born at once” (Isaiah 66, according to the Septuagint). For in one day three thousand and five thousand people believed (Acts 2 and 4). But what is written in the Hebrew—“Among them shall be the blind and the lame, the pregnant and she who gives birth together: a great assembly of those returning here”—although it was fulfilled also according to the letter, in that the blind saw and the lame walked, can nevertheless better be understood according to anagogy: those who had first been blind through unbelief afterward believed the Savior; and those who were lame, to whom Elijah once said, “How long do you limp on both feet?” (3 Kings 18), afterward walked. And “the people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light” (Isaiah 9); the lame ran; and the pregnant woman bore children—a great church of those returning to the faith. The Jews think this was fulfilled when, under Ezra, after the day of Passover, they departed from Babylon to return to Jerusalem; in this there was a type, not the reality. For they could not prove that at that time all the things which we have read, and shall read, had been fulfilled.

“In weeping they will come (or, ‘go out’), and in mercy I will bring them back, and I will lead them by streams of water on a straight road, and they will not stumble (or, ‘will not go astray’) on it, because I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.”

If we read according to the Hebrew, “they will come in weeping,” we shall say that this sometimes indicates even tears of excessive joy, in accordance with the expression, “I weep for joy.” But if we follow the Septuagint, who said, “They will go out in weeping, and in mercy”—or, “in consolation I will bring them back”—we shall adopt the sense also expressed in the Psalms: “Going they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125). They wept when they were led away captive, but received the greatest consolation when they were brought back by the Lord’s mercy.

And the Lord led them through the apostles and apostolic men, full of waters and of a most abundant river, along the road—that is, of the right faith—not in the unbelief of the Jews. “And they will not,” he says, “stumble on it,” because they have ceased to be blind, of whom it was once said: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now, because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (John 9). We may understand Christ as the straight road, on which whoever walks will not stumble.

“I have become,” he says, “a father to Israel, which has been brought back, and Ephraim is my firstborn.” “For where sin once abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5). Scripture testifies that Ephraim is a type of the people gathered from the Gentiles.

He was indeed Joseph’s younger son, and he took away the primacy from Manasseh, who by nature was the firstborn (Genesis 48). But in the mystery of the cross, when the hands were crossed, he who stood on Jacob’s left received the blessing of the right hand, while he who had stood on the right was blessed with the left and reduced to second rank. And just as Jacob took the birthright from Esau, so Ephraim took it from Manasseh. The whole people of the ten tribes was called Ephraim, because Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was the first to obtain the kingdom in Samaria, belonged to this tribe (Genesis 27).

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 1033]

[Col. 1033B] In part, Jeremiah’s prophecy, when he predicts the return of the Jews, demonstrates their historical return to the land of Judah after the captivity; in part, it signifies their spiritual conversion to the faith after Christ’s coming, when the remnant was saved; and in part, it foretells the gathering of the Gentiles from the error of idolatry to faith in Christ and true religion. Therefore, after showing the belief of the former people, he now turns his discourse toward the Gentiles and proclaims that their salvation truly takes place in Christ, saying:

“‘Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and proclaim it in the distant islands, and say: He who scattered Israel will gather him, and will guard him as a shepherd guards his flock. For the Lord has redeemed Jacob and delivered him from the hand of one more powerful (or, ‘stronger’), [Col. 1033C] and they will come and praise him on Mount Zion, and they will flow together to the good things of the Lord, over grain, wine, and oil, and over the offspring of sheep and cattle. And their soul will be like a watered garden (or, ‘like a fruitful tree’), and they will hunger no more. Then the virgin will rejoice in the chorus (or, ‘the virgins’), the young men and the old men together; and I will turn their mourning into joy, and I will comfort them, and I will gladden them after their sorrow, and I will intoxicate the soul of the priests (or, ‘the sons of Levi’) with fatness, and my people will be filled with my good things, says the Lord.’” (Jerome.)

The calling of the Gentiles is clearly demonstrated, when Scripture says: “Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and proclaim it in the distant islands, and say.” What are they to proclaim to the distant islands? That the Lord who scattered Israel will himself gather him. It was therefore not the power of his adversaries that caused them to be scattered, but the Lord’s will: “And he will guard him as a shepherd guards his flock.” For the good shepherd laid down his life for his sheep (John 10).

“For the Lord has redeemed Jacob” by the price of his blood, “and delivered him from the hand of one more powerful (or, ‘stronger’).” By these words the opposing powers are shown to be stronger by nature than human weakness, insofar as strength exists in either side; but we are stronger through faith, if indeed we deserve to be delivered by him who can bind the strong man and plunder his house.

“And they will come,” he says—there is no doubt that they have been delivered from the hand of the powerful—“and they will praise” their deliverer “on Mount Zion,” that is, in the Church. “And they will flow together to the good things of the Lord”: to an abundance of all things, which is perceived not in the crops and foods of this flesh but in the variety of virtues.

“Over grain,” he says, “and wine and oil,” from which the Lord’s bread is made and the type of his blood is fulfilled; and the blessing of sanctification is shown in the words of Scripture: “Your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

“And over the offspring of sheep,” which in the Church are the simple; “and of cattle,” which have horns and drive away adversaries. But so that we may know that these blessings pertain not to the body but to the soul, it follows: “And their soul will be like a watered garden, or like a fruitful tree,” planted beside streams of water, and like the Lord’s beloved paradise [in delights]. “And they will hunger no more,” he says—not with the hunger of which it is written, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5), but with the hunger that is changed by fullness and excludes the want of all things.

“Then the virgin will rejoice in the chorus,” of whom the Apostle writes: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11). And the young men, to whom John says: “I write to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one” (1 John 2); and the old men, to whom he likewise testifies in mystical speech: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (ibid.).

“And I will turn,” he says, “their mourning into joy,” so that those whom the cross had scorched may be gladdened by the resurrection. “And I will comfort them, and I will gladden them after their sorrow,” in accordance with what the Lord says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5).

“And I will intoxicate the soul of the priests,” who possess the knowledge of God, from whose mouth those who believe in him inquire about the law of the Lord; to him the Prophet sings: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). But the words that follow according to the Septuagint, “the sons of Levi,” are not found in the Hebrew. It is therefore clear that this does not refer to priests who are sons of Levi, but to those in whose likeness Melchizedek went before.

The intoxication of the priests is also confirmed in the apostles, when they were burning with faith and were said to be full of new wine (Acts 2). Hence the place where the Lord was seized is called Gethsemane, which in our language means “valley of fatness.” And when the priests have been made fat with the Lord’s teaching, and, intoxicated at Joseph’s banquet, have said, “How excellent is your intoxicating cup!” (Psalm 22), then this too will come to pass, which the Lord now promises: “And my people will be filled with my good things.”

All these things are now granted in part; then they will be given in full, when we see face to face and the body of our humiliation has been changed into the glory of the resurrection.

“Thus says the Lord: A voice has been heard on high, of lamentation, mourning, and weeping: Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted over her children, because they are not.”

The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the Lord: A voice was heard in Rama, lamentation and weeping and mourning: Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to cease, because they are not.”

Matthew took his testimony neither according to the Hebrew nor according to the Septuagint. For after describing the slaughter of the infants, we read in his Gospel: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: A voice was heard in Rama, weeping and much wailing, Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted because they are not” (Matthew 2). From this it is clear that the evangelists and apostles did not follow an interpretation of anything from the Hebrew, but, as Hebrews from Hebrews, expressed in their own language what they read in Hebrew.

Rachel, the mother of Joseph, when she was coming to Bethlehem, was suddenly seized by the pains of childbirth and bore a son. Because she was dying in childbirth, the midwife called him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow”; but his father Jacob changed the name and called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand” (Genesis 35).

It is therefore asked how the Evangelist Matthew transferred the Prophet’s testimony to the killing of the little children, when it is plainly written about the ten tribes, whose chief was Ephrata, whereas Ephrata is not in the tribe of Ephraim but in the tribe of Judah. For this is also Bethlehem, bearing two names (δυωνύμως); hence the names of both agree. Bethlehem is called “house of bread”; Ephrata, Καρποφορία, which we may render “fruitfulness.”

Since Rachel was buried in Ephrata—that is, in Bethlehem—as Holy Scripture and the inscription on her tomb still testify, she is said to mourn the children who were killed near her and in the surrounding region.

Some Jews interpret this passage as referring to the time when Jerusalem was captured under Vespasian, and through this route the captives were sent to Rome by way of Gaza and Alexandria. Others refer it to the final captivity under Hadrian, when Jerusalem was also destroyed and an innumerable population of every age and both sexes was sold in the terebinth marketplace; for this reason, it is said to be abhorrent to the Jews to look upon that famous marketplace.

Let them say what they wish; we shall say that the Evangelist Matthew rightly took the testimony with reference to the place where Rachel was buried, so that she might have mourned as her own the children of the neighboring villages all around.

“Thus says the Lord: Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, because there is a reward for your work, says the Lord; and they will return from the land of the enemy (or, ‘enemies’). And there is hope for your future, says the Lord; and the children will return to their borders.”

This has not yet happened according to the letter. For we do not read that the ten tribes, which are exiled in the cities of the Medes and Persians, have returned to the land of Judea. But according to the spirit it was fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion, and is fulfilled down to the present, when Israel is saved from the whole world.

And Rachel is told: “Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears.” The sense is: “Stop weeping, for the Lord has regarded your former works; and your children will return from the land of the enemy,” so that you may not be held by present sorrow. “For there is hope for your future, says the Lord; and your children will return to their borders,” which their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob possessed.

But we understand it better of the little children: they receive a reward for the blood poured out for Christ, and, in place of the land of the hostile Herod, they possess the kingdoms of heaven. They will return to their former dwelling when, in place of the body of humiliation, they recover a glorious body. This is the final hope, when the righteous will shine like the sun (Wisdom 3). And the infants who were once little children and sucklings will rise, without increase of age or bodily injury and labor, as a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4).

“I have surely heard Ephraim migrating (or, ‘lamenting’): ‘You chastised me, and I was instructed, like an untamed young bull (or, ‘like a calf’), and I did not learn. Convert me, and I will be converted, because you are the Lord my God. For after you converted me (or, ‘after I was taken captive’), I did penance; and after I came to know (or, ‘after you showed me’), I struck my thigh (or, ‘I groaned’). I was ashamed and embarrassed (or, ‘from the day of shame’), and I showed you that I bore reproach from my youth.’”

God says that he heard Ephraim speaking and lamenting. There is no doubt that this signifies the ten tribes, whose first ruler was Jeroboam son of Nebat, who also made golden calves in Dan and Bethel, so that the people, deceived by this error, might cease to worship and adore the God of Israel.

“You chastised me,” he says, “and I was instructed.” All correction advances salvation: at the time it appears to be sorrowful, but afterward it produces the most peaceful fruit. And when he says “like an untamed young bull,” or “calf,” “and I did not learn,” he signifies that Ephraim was instructed through much labor and blows, so that he might be turned to repentance, yet did not improve.

“Convert me,” he says, “and I will be converted.” Therefore even the repentance we practice we cannot complete unless we rely on God’s help. For after you have converted me, and I have turned toward you, then I will know that you, Lord, are my God, and that my errors and sins will by no means destroy me: “and after you converted me, I did penance.”

Consider how great God’s help is, and how fragile the human condition, since we cannot accomplish even the repentance we practice unless the Lord first converts us. “And after,” he says, “you showed me”—whether repentance itself or knowledge of you, or, “I came to know you”—“I struck my thigh,” which is a sign of one grieving and lamenting, weeping over his former error: he strikes his thigh with his hand and confesses how greatly he had previously gone astray.

(Gregory.) What is understood by the thigh, if not the pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean by, “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that after he saw heavenly things spiritually, he extinguished everything that he had lived carnally in himself below? The more clearly the highest things were revealed, the less the lower things that had held him gave him pleasure. For the more someone begins to live above, the more he begins to die below.

According to the inclination toward carnal action, all Paul’s flesh had died when he said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

(Jerome.) “I was ashamed,” he says, “and embarrassed (or, ‘from the day of shame’).” What time is not a time of our shame? If we remember our ancient sins and all the things we have done wrongly, shall we take them into memory? And what the Septuagint said, “And I showed you,” signifies that after he groaned and recognized his sins, he then advanced to such great progress [lacuna]. [Note: What is missing here, reader, you will find in Eusebius Hieronymus, Commentary on Jeremiah, book VI, chapter 31, in our Patrologia, volume XXIV, from column 879, line 4, through column 884, note 11. EDIT.]—which they made void, and therefore the Lord disregarded them.

But now, in the Gospel, after the resurrection and ascension, he promises that he will give a covenant not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshy hearts. And when the Lord’s testament has been written in the minds of believers, he will be their God and they will be his people, so that they will no longer seek Jewish teachers, traditions, and commandments of men, but will be taught by the Holy Spirit—if only they deserve to hear: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3). “The Spirit, however, breathes where he wills,” and has various gifts; and knowledge of the one God is possession of all virtues.

“And this,” he says, “will happen because I will be merciful toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”

From the understanding of this passage (περικοπή), it is therefore clear that the preceding words are to be understood first of the Savior’s coming, when the two peoples, Israel and Judah, were joined to one another.

But if anyone is troubled by the reason he said, “I will establish with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a covenant, or new testament, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers,” let him understand that the first Church of Christ consisted of Jews, and that the Lord the Savior came to them and said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15). The apostles likewise confirmed this: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 14).

For it was not right to give the children’s bread to dogs (Matthew 15). But because the children did not wish to receive the Father when he came among them, he gave to all the power to become children of God, to those who received him.

“‘Is Ephraim a son honorable (or, ‘beloved’) to me? Is he a delicate child? For ever since I spoke concerning him (or, ‘my words are in him’), remembering him, I will still remember him. Therefore my inward parts are disturbed over him; pitying, I will pity him, says the Lord.’”

The former people were an honorable son to the Lord. He exalted them above all the other nations by many benefits and wondrous gifts, and brought them out of Egypt amid many miracles. Of them it is said through Hosea: “Because Israel was a child, I loved him, and from Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11). He instructed them sufficiently through his law and the oracles of the prophets. But because they always walked in a perverse way against his will, and, though often admonished, refused to obey him, at last he sent his only-begotten Son to summon them to repentance and correct them from error.

He felt such compassion for their misery that he is even read in the Gospel to have wept over their hardness, saying to them: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you” (Matthew 23).

Yet he did not wholly reject them. He preserved an elect remnant from them, from which came the apostles and evangelists and the primitive Church in Jerusalem: “Finally, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

“‘Set up for yourself a watchtower; place bitterness for yourself; direct your heart onto the straight road on which you have walked.’”

He summons them to make satisfaction, so that they may consider how greatly they have sinned and, practicing repentance, return to their former grace, in accordance with what is written in Revelation: “Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do your first works” (Revelation 2).

(Gregory.) In the tropological sense, the Prophet admonishes the soul of each of the elect to look carefully around in prudent discernment. As though placed on the citadel of contemplation, it should detect the approach of sin before it comes, and the more watchfully it foresees it, the more firmly it should avoid it.

To set up a watchtower for oneself is, through profound consideration, to foresee the coming struggles of vices. The mind of the elect places bitterness before itself when, even while established in the peace of virtues, it sees the evils lying in wait and refuses to rest securely.

First, it considers that it must not do any evil; second, it considers that it must not do good things carelessly. After it has subdued what is crooked, it strives also to subject what is right to itself, lest, if these things pass beyond the mind’s control, they be turned into the fault of pride.

For, as was said above, evils often arise from good things through negligence. Therefore it watches attentively to see how arrogance may arise from teaching, cruelty from justice, laxity from piety, anger from zeal, and sluggishness from gentleness.

When it does these good things, it sees how many enemies may rise against it through them. When it labors to acquire the studies of teaching, it carefully prepares its mind against the battle with arrogance. When it desires justly to punish the faults of offenders, it most shrewdly avoids allowing the cruelty of vengeance to exceed the measure of justice. When it strives to restrain itself through piety, it cautiously takes care lest it be conquered by some relaxation of discipline. When it rouses itself through the goads of righteous zeal, it takes the greatest care lest the flame of anger kindle it more than necessary. When it regulates itself with the great tranquility of gentleness, it watches vigilantly lest it grow cold through sluggishness.

“Direct,” he says, “your heart onto the straight road on which you have walked.”

(Maurus.) The straight road is the path of God’s commandments, on which one must proceed without turning aside to the left. He directs his heart onto the straight road on which he has walked when he resolves to advance his mind along the way of righteousness, which he promised at the reception of baptism that he would follow according to the teaching of the Holy Scriptures, and does not consent to turn aside either along the byways of error or into the pleasures of the world.

“‘Return, virgin of Israel, return to these your cities. How long will you dissolve yourself in pleasures, wandering daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman will surround a man.’”

(Maurus.) Although some try to refer this, according to the historical sense, to the Jews’ return from Babylon to their own land, so that they might rebuild the ruined cities and restore the ancient settlements, in accordance with what the Prophet says below—“Depart from the midst of Babylon, and go out from the land of the Chaldeans”—and again, “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own life”—nevertheless, it seems to me more appropriate to refer everything to the time of the New Testament, in which the Virgin’s birth brought forth the Savior for the whole world.

Thus the virgin of Israel, whom the Lord betrothed to himself according to Hosea (Hosea 3), in righteousness, judgment, mercy, and compassion, may return after her former pollutions, by which she was defiled through various transgressions, to the cities of the Church, and cease wandering after the luxuries of the world.

“For the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman will surround a man.” And according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “A virgin conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7).

He is rightly called “man,” in accordance with Zechariah’s words: “Behold, a man whose name is Orient; he will build the temple of the Lord, and he himself will bear glory, and he will sit and rule upon his throne” (Zechariah 6); and, “He has set his tent in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom, came forth from his chamber; he rejoiced like a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its summit” (Psalm 18).

He fought with the ruler of the world, and the strong Lord conquered the strong devil in battle; binding him, he plundered all his spoils and vessels.

[Col. 1039D] “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: They will still say this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their captivity: ‘May the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain’; and Judah and all its cities will dwell in it together, farmers and those who lead flocks. For I have intoxicated the weary soul, and I have filled every hungry soul.”

The Prophet foretells the future times of the Christian religion, in which the Lord restores the captivity of his people and calls the scattered back to their own land. Then the faithful will say to the mountain of God—to the fertile mountain, the mountain made firm, the fat mountain, the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell—that the Lord will indeed dwell there forever.

“May the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain.” Concerning this Isaiah also says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; he will teach us his ways, and we have walked in his paths, because the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2).

And because he himself is the beauty and the sun of righteousness: “For righteousness is the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins” (Isaiah 11).

“Judah will dwell in it”—that is, the one who rightly confesses God—“and all its cities together.” These are all the Churches of the Gentiles, held together by the one Catholic and Apostolic Church, which is the city of the great King, built upon this mountain and therefore unable to be hidden. There the living fountain and the rush of the river gladden this city and intoxicate [Col. 1040B] the weary soul—that is, it refreshes the faithful with the nourishment of his body and blood—and satisfies every hungry soul: “For blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

There are farmers and those who lead flocks, because the cultivators of the Lord’s field and the shepherds of his sheep, who feed them with the divine word and, following the example of the chief Shepherd, are ready to lay down their lives for their sheep (John 10), continually dwell there.

Foreseeing these things in the spirit, the Prophet immediately adds:

“Therefore I awoke as if from sleep, and I saw; and my sleep became sweet to me.”

What does he mean by saying that he was awakened from sleep, that he saw, and that his sleep became sweet to him? Surely that, through the grace of Christ, who rose from the sleep of death in glory, the Prophet himself was awakened from the sleep of weariness and sorrow by divine revelations and found the sleep of rest and peace made sweet to him by God’s gracious promises.

Hence it is also written in Proverbs: “If you sleep, you will not be afraid; you will rest, and your sleep will be sweet,” and what follows (Proverbs 3).

According to the letter, it is clear that the person who remembers living innocently and justly before God sleeps, keeps watch, rests, and walks in security. But when the righteous sleeps in death, he not only does not fear the powers of evil spirits, but also rests in peace and confidently awaits the day of resurrection, because he has God everywhere as his protector and guardian, as it is said in the Psalm: “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me” (Psalm 22).

[Col. 1040D] “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of beasts. And just as I watched over them to uproot, demolish, destroy, ruin, and afflict, so I will watch over them to build and plant, says the Lord.”

These are the days of the New Testament, in which the Lord sows the house of Israel and the house of Judah—that is, he fills the Catholic Church with the seed of man and the seed of beasts: with crowds of Jews instructed by the divine law and of Gentiles living like brute animals; or, more generally, with a multitude of intelligent people and also of the simple. For God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

“For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free” (Romans 2), but Christ is all and in all.

And just as the Lord once watched over all the nations to uproot, destroy, ruin, and afflict them because of the transgression of the first man and the many crimes they themselves added, so now, appeased by Christ’s death and the shedding of his blood, he watches over them to build, plant, and prepare for himself a people acceptable to him, devoted to good works.

“In those days they will no longer say: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’; but each person will die in his own iniquity.”

This sentence agrees with what is read in Ezekiel, where it is written:

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘What do you mean by turning this proverb into a saying among you in the land of Israel, saying: “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge”? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb will no longer be a saying for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins will itself die’” (Ezekiel 18).

The divine Scripture teaches that what was said in Exodus—“I am your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation, for those who hate me; and I show mercy to thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exodus 20)—must be understood, as must the following passage, as a parable and proverb, so that the words may sound one way while the meaning is held in another:

“The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses; and Moses called upon the name of the Lord. And the Lord passed before his face, and he called upon him, saying: ‘The Lord God is compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy, and true, preserving justice and showing mercy to thousands, taking away iniquities, injustices, and sins; yet he will not acquit the guilty, repaying the iniquities of the fathers upon the children and upon the children’s children, to the third and fourth generation’” (Exodus 34).

Until the present, we had thought that the two testimonies from Exodus quoted above were not parables but simply expressed a straightforward meaning. Although we did not dare say anything—or have the “clay vessel speak against the potter, ‘Why have you made me this way or that?’” (Romans 9)—we nevertheless suffered a hidden scandal, because it seemed unjust of God for one person to sin and another to pay the penalty for the sins.

For if he repays the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished. But the phrase that follows, “for those who hate me,” removes the scandal from the threat or command. They are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned—for the fathers, who were sinners, ought rather to have been punished—but because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God through hereditary evil and impiety, with the evil growing into the branches from the root.

Heretics who do not accept the Old Testament commonly say at this point against the Creator: “How good and just is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, though at rest, repays the sins of the fathers upon those who have not sinned?” Indeed, how great is his cruelty, to extend his anger to the third and fourth generation?”

We shall answer them that here too the clemency of the Creator God is demonstrated. To hold anger until the third and fourth generation is not cruelty or severity, but a sign of mercy: the postponement of the punishment of sin. When he says, “The Lord God is compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy,” and adds, “repaying the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children’s children,” he indicates that he is so merciful that he does not punish immediately but postpones the sentence of punishment.

But if the vengeance against sinners is postponed until the third and fourth generation, what more does he do for the righteous and holy? The text continues: “And he preserves justice and mercy for many thousands, for those who keep his commandments and carry out his precepts.”

It is written in Proverbs: “As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth, and smoke to the eyes, so iniquity is to those who use it” (Proverbs 10). From this it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that suffer and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who ate the sour grape.

The sense of this passage is that if someone wished to say, “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge,” it would be ridiculous and without coherence. In the same way, it is unjust and perverse for fathers to sin while their children and grandchildren are tormented.

“All souls are mine,” he says, according to creation, not according to merit. Thus Moses is called a man of God, concerning whom it is written, “The prayer of Moses, the man of God”; and Elijah spoke to the commander of fifty men: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down upon you and upon your fifty men” (2 Kings 1).

But a man of sin and a son of iniquity is not called a man of God, just as those who are called servants and household members of God cannot be described by the statement, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin”; and again, “By whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved.”

Just as the sins of children do not harm their fathers, so the sins of fathers do not pass over to their children. “The soul that sins will itself die”—not through abolition of its substance, but through exclusion from the fellowship of him who says, “I am life.” Yet elsewhere he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

“Every person who eats a sour grape—his teeth will be set on edge.” (Gregory.) What is the sour grape if not sin? A sour grape is fruit eaten before its time. Whoever desires to be satisfied by the pleasures of the present life hastens, as it were, to eat fruit before its time.

Therefore, whoever eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge, because whoever feeds on the pleasure of the present world has his inner senses bound, so that he can no longer chew—that is, understand—spiritual things. For by what they were delighted in outwardly, by that they become numb inwardly.

And while the soul feeds on sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, because teeth bound by the habit of sin cannot at all eat what has a just taste within.

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—the covenant which they made void, though I was their master, says the Lord.”

The Lord promises that he will give his people a new covenant—that is, the covenant of the Gospel—which is written through the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers. It is not the covenant of the ancient Law, which was written on tablets of stone and given to a hard and unbelieving nation; they themselves made it void, and for this they received the punishment they deserved.

Hence he says, “And I was their master, says the Lord”—that is, I carried out upon them a just vengeance, in accordance with what they deserved.

“‘And this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel. After those days,’ says the Lord, ‘I will give my law within them, and I will write it upon their heart; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’”

(MAURUS.) Concerning this law it is also written in Isaiah: “‘From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’ (Isa. II).” And again: “‘Hear me, you who know what is just, my people: my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not dread their blasphemies’ (Isa. LXI).”

(Hieron.) This indicates that the new people shall no longer live according to the letter, but according to the spirit, restoring the natural law in their hearts. Concerning this the Apostle also writes: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what belongs to the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. II). This law is signified in the Psalm: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted” (Ps. LXIII).

This agrees with what is read in Ezekiel: “‘I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you; and I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will place my spirit within you,’” and so forth (Ezek. XXXVI). It must be considered that the new heart and the new spirit are given through the outpouring and sprinkling of water. When the new heart and the new spirit have been given, then all hardness—which is compared to stone—will be taken away from the Jewish heart, and in place of the stony heart there will be a fleshly heart, soft and tender, able to receive the Spirit of God within itself and to have the saving letters inscribed upon it.

The apostle John calls this grace of the Holy Spirit, which God pours into the hearts of believers, an anointing, saying: “And the anointing which you received from him remains in you; and you do not need anyone to teach you, but just as his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John II). Rightly he adds “about everything,” just as in the Gospel the Lord, speaking to the disciples about the same Spirit, says: “He himself will teach you everything” (John XIV), because unless that same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless.

(Greg.) Therefore, no one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth: for unless there is one who teaches within, the teacher’s tongue also labors outwardly in vain. Nevertheless, the teacher must not cease doing what he can, in accordance with what Paul says: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. III).

(Bernard.) This passage may also be transferred to the contemplation of the future life, where the pure hearts of the elect will contemplate God in his glory: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). For then the law of God is truly written in the hearts of the faithful, when perfect knowledge of God is granted to them. Then he will be their God, and they will be his people, when nothing will separate them from their God. Rather, they will be filled with joy in his presence and will delight in his right hand forever. Concerning this it is further added:

“‘And a man shall no longer teach his neighbor, nor a man his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest,’ says the Lord, ‘because I will forgive their iniquities, and I will remember their sin no more.’”

(MAURUS.) At that time no one will need to be instructed by another, when all the elect will be in the contemplation of truth and will see God face to face. Hence Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I am known” (1 Cor. XIII).

From this John also says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III). Paul also explains this to others in different words: “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. We shall be like him” (1 Cor. III). For when we enjoy the contemplation of the immutable and eternal divinity, we too shall be immortal, and indeed we shall be like him, because we shall be blessed; yet we shall not be like the Creator, because we are creatures. For who among the sons of God will be like God? Nevertheless, this may also be understood as referring to the immortality of the body.

In this respect also we shall be like God—but only like the Son, who alone in the Trinity assumed a body, in which he rose from the dead and carried it to the heights above. For to be is proper to God: to remain eternal and unchangeable. Hence he says to Moses: “I am who I am,” and: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” We shall therefore see him as he is when we contemplate him in the very substance of his divinity.

In this life this is granted absolutely to none of the elect. Even the lawgiver himself, who was accustomed to contemplate the Lord in angelic form, entreated him, saying: “Lord, show yourself to me, so that I may see you” (Exod. III), and heard from that same Lord: “No one shall see my face and live” (ibid.). Yet, in consideration of his great holiness, he was told: “I will show you every good thing.” Hence Paul also says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII).

Thus what was answered to Moses is true: no one can see the face of God and live—that is, no one living in this life can see him as he is. For many saw him, but they saw what God’s will chose, not what nature formed. And when John says, “We shall see him as he is,” he does not mean as human beings saw him, since he appeared in the form he wished, not in the nature which, even when he was seen, remained hidden in him. Rather, he means as he is—the very thing Moses requested when he was told: “Show yourself to me.” Moses spoke with him face to face, yet no one has ever comprehended the fullness of God, not only with the eyes of the body, but not even with the mind itself.

For it is one thing to see, and another to comprehend the whole by seeing. Whatever is perceived is seen as present; but the whole is comprehended by seeing when it is seen in such a way that nothing of it remains hidden from the one who sees, or when its boundaries can be surveyed. For example, nothing is hidden from you concerning your present will, while you can survey the boundaries of your ring. I have offered these two examples: one pertaining to the mind’s vision, the other to the bodily eyes. Vision must be referred to both—that is, to the eyes and to the mind.

When he says, “Because I will forgive their iniquities, and I will remember their sin no more,” he indicates the perfect healing of the saints, when, cleansed from every stain of sins, and with death itself—which came about as the result of sins, “for the wages of sin is death” (Rom. VI)—entirely taken away, they are clothed with immortality and enjoy eternal joy.

“‘Thus says the Lord, who gives the sun for light by day, the order of the moon and stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea and its waves roar—the Lord of hosts is his name. If these laws’ (or: these ordinances) ‘should cease before me,’ says the Lord, ‘then the seed of Israel also shall cease, so that it will no longer be a nation before me all its days.’”

(Hieron.) At the beginning of Genesis we also read that the sun was placed in heaven for the light of day, and the moon and stars for the light of night. And in the Psalm: “Day announces the word to day, and night reveals knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII), indicating that day and night succeed one another.

How, he asks, can the order of things—and especially of the heavenly stars—not be changed, while the waves of the roaring sea roll toward the shores, and the crash of the waters and the dreadful sound of the swelling waves are heard? Nor can the sea advance farther than God’s command has prescribed, in accordance with: “You set a boundary which they shall not pass, nor shall they return to cover the earth” (Ps. CIII). So, he says, the seed and race of Israel shall remain perpetual by the Lord’s will and shall never cease.

The “laws” here are not to be understood as the Mosaic laws, but as the constitution and order of nature. Let us question the Jews: If the heavens will perish, and all things will grow old like a garment, and it is said to God, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI), how can the seed of Israel be perpetual? Either the seed of Israel will perish when the heavens perish, or, if it is to be perpetual, the heavens will not perish either.

But if Scripture cannot lie, and the heavens are going to perish, then the seed of Israel will perish as well—especially since Jacob says to his sons: “Come, and I will announce to you what shall happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIX). When it says “in the last days,” therefore the world will cease to exist and another administration of things will come about. This is directed against them.

As for our own people, the Gospel also demonstrates that this present world is not perpetual, saying: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. XXIV), and: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Let us state it another way: As long as this world exists, the seed of Israel and the Jewish nation will remain—not in those who are now unbelieving, but in those who believed with the Apostles and through the Apostles, so that the remnant might be saved.

“‘Thus says the Lord: If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be searched out, then I also will reject all the seed of Israel because of all that they have done,’ says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: If the heaven is raised higher above, and if the pavement of the earth is lowered below, then I will not reject the race of Israel, says the Lord, because of all that they have done.”

There is a great difference in this passage between the Hebrew and the commonly received edition. Let us first discuss it according to the Hebrew: “If the heavens above can be measured”—and their height be known—“or the foundations of the earth be searched out,” and their extremities be comprehended by reason, “then,” he says, “I will reject all the seed of Israel because of all that they have done,” says the Lord.

Just as it is impossible for us to know the summit of the heavens and the foundations of the earth, so it will be impossible for me to reject all the seed of Israel. But if I reject all the seed of Israel, then the summit of the heavens and the extremities of the earth will be measurable. This syllogism is also constructed in the Gospel, when one impossibility is compared with another: “It is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdoms of heaven” (Matt. XIX). For just as the impossible cannot occur, so neither can this occur. But if this happens, then what was thought impossible will happen.

They are therefore mistaken who interpret this passage differently, adducing also that testimony according to which the Son could have asked the Father and brought twelve legions of angels to his aid (Matt. XXV). The Septuagint translated the passage in a sense contrary to this, saying: “If the heaven is exalted higher, and the pavement of the earth is lowered below, then,” he says, “I will not reject the seed of Israel, says the Lord, because of all that they have done.”

But if this is so, the nation of Israel will be rejected. For just as the heaven cannot be higher than what it is, nor the earth lower than what it is, so the race of Israel will in no way be approved. If we see the Jews glorying in this testimony according to the Hebrew, let us agree with them that not all the seed of Israel has been rejected. For not all have been rejected, but only those who were unbelieving.

“‘Behold, the days are coming,’ says the Lord, ‘and a city shall be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line shall go out farther’ (or, according to Symmachus, ‘the cord’) ‘of its measurement, opposite it, over the hill of Gareb, and it shall go around Goath’ (or, according to the Septuagint, ‘the chosen stones’). ‘And the whole valley of ruins’ (for which Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself), ‘and the ashes, and all Aseremoth’ (which we more correctly read; Aquila translated it as ‘suburbs’), ‘as far as the torrent of Cedron, and as far as the corner of the eastern Horse Gate. It shall be holy to the Lord; it shall not be uprooted or destroyed forever.’”

Those who accept Christ’s thousand-year reign on earth in the land of Judea—namely, Jews and our Judaizing Christians—try to identify the tower of Hananel, the Corner Gate, the hill of Gareb and Goath, the valley of Phagarim, all of Asedemoth, the torrent of Cedron, and the site of the corner of the eastern Horse Gate. They say that there the sanctuary of the Lord—that is, the temple—will be established and will remain forever.

Since they cannot show that this was fulfilled after the captivity in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, they pass to the time of Christ, whom they say will come at the consummation of the world, so that Jerusalem will descend, golden and set with jewels, according to John’s Apocalypse. They say that it will be built around this extent of land, that is, from one place to the other (Rev. XXI).

They seize upon this small basis for their suspicion: that from the tower of Anathoth, which today is called Jeremiah’s and is three miles from Jerusalem, as far as the torrent of Cedron, which is mentioned in the Gospel (John XVIII)—that is, in the valley of Jehoshaphat, where there was a garden in which Judas the traitor handed over the Savior—the foundations of the city will be laid.

“We shall read,” they say, “in what follows that Anamehel, son of Shallum, was Jeremiah’s paternal cousin, whose field he bought. This is the tower of Hananel,” not knowing the Hebrew truth. Here, according to the Hebrew, it is written “from the tower of Hananel” with the middle letter; there, however: “Behold, Anamehel, son of Shallum, your paternal cousin, will come to you,” also with the middle letter.

Therefore, invoking the Lord Savior, who holds the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, and who shuts and no one opens (Rev. III), who also opened the sealed book of Isaiah and of all the prophets—and the twenty-four elders worshiped him, holding lyres, because he alone was able to disclose the divine mysteries—let us approach the building of the city to which the prophetic word is directed: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI), and: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV).

The Church is therefore built from the tower of obedience, or of grace and gifts—for this is the meaning of Hananel—as far as the Corner Gate. Although it may appear to have a lofty beginning, as long as we remain in this flesh we cannot possess the straight line of truth; rather, we stand at a corner. With the lines broken, the measuring cord extends farther opposite it—that is, the Corner Gate—over the hill of Gareb, a name which in our language means either “sojourning” or “scab,” teaching us that we are strangers and pilgrims, and that we must not have itching ears or readily consent to the novelty of evil doctrines.

(Greg.) At a corner two walls are joined. Therefore the city of the Lord is said to be built from the tower of Hananel as far as the Corner Gate, because the holy Church, beginning from the height of heavenly grace, is built as far as the entrance and reception of both peoples—namely, the Jewish and the Gentile peoples. But because, as its multitude increases, the reprobate are also gathered within it, it is appropriately added: “And it extended beyond the measuring line,” because it reaches even to those who, passing beyond the rule of justice, do not belong within the number of heavenly measure.

(Hieron.) “And it shall go around,” he says, “Goath,” for which the Septuagint translated “around,” referring to the chosen stones that roll upon the surface of the earth and are bound together by the cornerstone, as the Apostle Peter says: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. II).

“And the whole valley,” he says, “of Phagarim,” which means “ruins”; and “the ashes”—understood, “it shall go around.” Thus, although we may seem to be on the hills, we should nevertheless always fear ruin, consider the ashes, and repentantly say with David: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI). Hence it is also said to those who lie fallen: “Will he who falls not rise again?” says the Lord (Jer. VIII).

“And all,” he says, “of Sademoth,” which we translate as “the region of death,” dividing the one name into two words: one meaning “region,” and the other “death.” Aquila translated it “suburbs,” or “fields and countryside.” The region of death is the region of sinners; the suburbs are the region of pleasures. It extends as far as the torrent of Cedron, where the Lord was handed over, and which is interpreted as “darkness.”

See how many places the Church contains, and how that apostolic description—“that it might be without spot or wrinkle”—is reserved for the future and for the heavenly realm. You hear of corners, you hear of a scab, you hear of ruins and ashes, the region of death and darkness, and yet you glory in your own virtue and sinlessness?

Finally it follows: “And as far as the corner of the gate.” This corner also indicates that no true justice and no certain victory is displayed in this age. Although this corner of the gate is eastern, from where the light emerges, it is nevertheless called the Horse Gate, teaching us that we need running and struggle, so that at last we may deserve to hear from the Lord: “You mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation.”

At the eastern gate, the gate of chariots, there is the sanctification of the Lord, so that we may then consider ourselves perfect when we say to the Lord: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice; the Lord is among them” (Ps. LXVII).

Such a building, founded upon Christ, of which the Apostle also speaks—“As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (2 Cor. III)—will never be destroyed, but will remain forever. Obscure and difficult matters must be discussed at greater length, so that we may pass more briefly over what is clear.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Jeremiah prophesies in prison that Zedekiah will be led captive to Babylon, and he buys a field in Anathoth; he prays for the people; the word of the Lord concerning the burning of Jerusalem and the liberation of the captives.

“‘The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah—which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was confined in the court of the prison, which was in the house of the king of Judah. For Zedekiah king of Judah had confined him, saying: “Why do you prophesy, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord’?”’”

(Hieron.) Not only the words but also the deeds of the prophets are examples to us of virtue. Jeremiah could have announced favorable things and enjoyed the friendship of King Zedekiah, but he preferred to obey God rather than human beings, and the one who can kill both soul and body in Gehenna rather than the one who could exercise power over the body alone.

It must also be considered that this was the tenth year of Zedekiah’s reign. Jerusalem was already besieged, consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence, and close to captivity; yet Zedekiah persisted in his decision. Still, some degree of his clemency is shown by the fact that he ordered Jeremiah to be confined not in the prison itself but in its vestibule—clearly a less restrictive custody—so that he could not escape. Indeed, the whole of Jerusalem, shut in by its fortifications, was like a common prison for its inhabitants.

This was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, who began his rule in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. All the reasons for the king’s anger were the things Jeremiah spoke in God’s name and had been commanded to speak.

“‘Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall capture it. And Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape from the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon; his mouth shall speak with his mouth, and his eyes shall see his eyes. And he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain until I visit him,’ says the Lord. ‘And if you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall have no success.’”

This was the cause of the royal anger: Jeremiah preferred truth to falsehood and declared that both the city of Jerusalem and King Zedekiah would be captured. More grievously still, he said that Zedekiah would see the face of the king of Babylon and speak humbly as a captive before the madness of a most powerless king. For it is a greater terror to see the one whom you fear, and to suffer the torment of rebuking words before that of punishments.
