“And he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he shall remain.” For this the Septuagint translated: “And he shall enter into Babylon,” one expression signifying that he is dragged there unwillingly, the other that he goes abroad by his own will. “And there,” he says, “he shall remain.” He uses an ambiguous expression, lest he seem to prophesy torture and misery.

What follows—“Until I visit him, says the Lord. And if you fight against the Chaldeans, you shall have no success”—is not found in the Septuagint. He wisely tempered the sentence, which can be referred either to a good or to an evil meaning. For visitation, as I have often already said, signifies both consolation and punishment.

“And Jeremiah said: ‘The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Behold, Anamehel, son of Shallum’ (or: Sallon), ‘your paternal cousin’—which in Hebrew is expressed as “will come to you,” saying: ‘Buy for yourself my field, which is in Anathoth; for the right of purchase belongs to you by reason of kinship.’”

No one could know that the word of God had secretly come to Jeremiah unless Jeremiah himself revealed to whom it had come. He is also told beforehand that his paternal cousin Anamehel will come to him and offer him the possession of the field that had belonged to him.

The place itself, Anathoth, was among the suburban lands that, according to the law, were given to the priests throughout the individual tribes and cities (Num. XXVII). It was not lawful for property to pass from one tribe to another, or from one family to another. Hence the daughters of Zelophehad receive a portion among their brothers (Lev. XXV). In particular, the priests’ suburban lands could not be sold to anyone else until the year of remission, except to the person whom blood relationship required.

Thus his paternal cousin came to him and offered him the purchase that was owed to him by kinship. Hilkiah and Shallum were full brothers: Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, and Anamehel the son of Shallum. Hilkiah means “the portion of the Lord”; Jeremiah means “the exaltation of the Lord.” Rightly, therefore, the exaltation of the Lord is born from the portion of the Lord.

Shallum, however, is translated in our language as “peace” or “peaceful”; Anamehel means “the gift” or “grace of God.” We should not be surprised that peace is joined to grace, since this is also the opening of the apostolic letters: “Grace to you and peace” (Rom. I). First, therefore, we merit the peace of God, and after peace grace is born for us—a grace that depends not on the will of the one who possesses it, but on that of the one who gives it.

He brings the purchase of the field as a gift of God to the one who has been placed in lofty things, so that, although he may appear exalted, he nevertheless needs the grace of God.

The expression frequently sung by the bride in the Song of Songs, “My cousin” (Song V)—that is, “ὁ ἁδελφιδέος μοῦ” (*ho adelphideos mou*) is said in Hebrew. Therefore it should not be called *fratruelis*, but *πατράδελφος* (*patradelphos*), that is, *patruelis* (“paternal cousin”). That Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, is also attested by the beginning of this book.

“And Anamehel, the son of my paternal uncle, came to me, according to the word of the Lord, at the vestibule” (or: court) “of the prison, and said to me: ‘Possess’ (or: buy) ‘my field, which is in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin; for the inheritance belongs to you, and you are the relative entitled to possess’ (or: buy) ‘it.’”

What the word of the Lord had announced to the prophet as future was immediately fulfilled in deed. “Anamehel,” he says, “the grace of God, the son of my paternal uncle”—that is, the son of peace—“came to me in the vestibule of the prison and said to me” the things that the Lord had foretold he would say.

This priestly field, whose purchase and possession were being offered to Jeremiah, is in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The former name signifies “obedience,” while the latter sounds like “son of the right hand.” Appropriately, therefore, he seeks to buy it from the one in whom obedience and the virtue of the Lord were found. For this reason the Septuagint translated the word as πρεσβύτερον, that is, “elder,” which does not suit this passage.

“But I understood that it was the word of the Lord, and I bought the field from Anamehel, the son of my paternal uncle, which is in Anathoth. And I weighed out to him the silver: seventeen silver shekels. And I wrote it in a book, sealed it, and called witnesses. And I weighed out the silver on the scales, and I took the sealed book of possession, containing the stipulations, the valid terms, and the external marks.”

It was difficult, and almost incongruous—indeed, laughable—for a man who had just prophesied that Jerusalem would be captured and that all would be led away as captives or perish by sword, famine, and pestilence to buy a field in Anathoth that he would not possess.

“But I understood,” he says, “that it was the word of the Lord, and that my purchase was to be adapted as evidence and prophecy to the Lord’s purpose. Therefore, at his command, I acquired it by buying it; nor had the word concerning such a matter come to me from God without reason.”

He weighed out seventeen shekels of silver, which we render as “staters.” A shekel contains twenty obols, as is written at the end of the book of Ezekiel (Ezek. XLV). The prophet therefore bought the field for seventeen shekels. In this number David, the servant of the Lord, sang on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, saying: “I will love you, Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmness and my refuge and my deliverer. My God is my helper; I will hope in him. He is my protector, the horn of my salvation, and my support” (Ps. XVII).

That ten is a mystical number is shown by the Decalogue, which was written on stone tablets by the finger of God, and by “the day of fasting and expiation of the seventh month” (Exod. XIII). We also establish through many testimonies of Scripture that the number seven contains the true Sabbath-rest and holy rest. I could mention at least a few of these, if it were not pointless to teach what is already known.

In this number, therefore, the prophet and priest purchases the possession; it is written in a book and sealed; witnesses are called; and the silver is carefully weighed, so that all the legal requirements of sale and purchase may be observed and the possession be securely confirmed by stipulations and promises.

Let those who try to claim false wills—and sometimes not even wills—by bringing in witnesses listen to this.

“And I gave the book of possession to Baruch son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Anamehel my paternal cousin, and in the sight of the witnesses whose names were written in the book of purchase, and in the sight of all the Jews who were sitting in the court of the prison.”

Although the possession was immediately to be abandoned—or rather, purchased for posterity—and was bought by one who had no children, since he had not taken a wife, he nevertheless obediently carried out everything properly according to the Lord’s command. He gave the sealed book of possession to Baruch son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah.

Baruch means “blessed” in our language. He was the son of Neriah, whose name means “my lamp,” as the prophet says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet and a burning light for my paths” (Ps. CXVIII). Neriah likewise was the son of Maaseiah, that is, of the work and deed of the Lord.

Let us therefore observe with how many privileges of virtue Baruch, Jeremiah’s disciple, served him, in accordance with David’s saying: “He who walks in the blameless way served me” (Ps. C). Hence Elisha, Elijah’s servant, so pleased God that after his master’s translation he deserved to receive a double portion of the spirit (2 Kings II).

I say this as a warning to those who abuse the services of evil men and do not dare to cast them off, although they know that such men are joined to them by the glue of an evil conscience.

The book is entrusted to Baruch in the presence of such a man as Anamehel, who had sold the field, and of the witnesses who had signed it, whose names were kept in the book of purchase. “And in the sight,” he says, “of all the Jews who were sitting in the court of the prison”—those, namely, who had either come to console the prophet or desired, out of fear of God, to hear the Lord’s words.

“And I commanded Baruch in their presence, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these books—the sealed book of purchase and this book that is open—and place them in an earthen vessel, so that they may remain for many days. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses, fields, and vineyards shall still be possessed in this land.’”

With all those whom the preceding account mentioned present and observing, Baruch, the servant and disciple, is commanded—not by the teacher’s words but by the command of God—to take the books: one sealed, the other open.

This is the practice of purchases that remains to the present day: what the seals contain closed within is presented as an open volume to those who wish to read it. Both books are placed in an earthen vessel so that they may remain for many days.

The possession, therefore, was secure and destined to continue long afterward. It was guarded with such care lest the books of purchase, if left outside, fall prey to theft, or, if buried in the ground, be destroyed by the moisture of the earth.

All this is done so that those who witnessed it might understand that Jerusalem would again be inhabited and the fields possessed. Although they ought to have understood this by themselves without Jeremiah’s speech, they are nevertheless reminded by the words of the Lord, which say to them: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses, fields, and vineyards shall still be possessed in this land.”

This is what Jeremiah had said earlier: “I understood that it was the word of the Lord,” and for that reason he bought the field which he himself was not going to possess.

“After I had handed over the deed of purchase to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to the Lord, saying: ‘Alas, alas, alas, Lord God’ (or, ‘You who are, Lord God’). Behold, you made heaven and earth by your great strength and by your outstretched (or exalted) arm; no word (or, according to the Septuagint, nothing) will be difficult (or impossible) for you. Nothing is hidden from you, who show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the bosom of their children [Col. 1053A] after them. Most mighty, great, powerful—your name is the Lord of hosts (or, of powers). Great in counsel and incomprehensible in thought, whose eyes are open over all the ways of the sons of Adam (or, of human beings), to repay each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.’”

After the purchase of the field had been lawfully completed, and after the Lord’s declaration in which he promised that houses, fields, and vineyards would thereafter be possessed, the prophet prays to the Lord and expresses his grief with groans, saying: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God.” For this the Septuagint translated ὁ ὤν, that is, “You who are, Lord God,” in accordance with what is said to Moses: “Go, say to the people of Israel: ‘The One who is has sent me’” (Exod. III). This does not mean that there are no others; rather, it is one thing to exist by the Creator’s gracious gift, by which one continues to subsist, and another to exist by the eternity of one’s nature.

He praises God and proclaims the Creator from the created things. First, therefore, he extols in lofty words his power, mercy, and justice toward the whole human race. Then he turns to Israel and describes in celebrated language how many benefits he had bestowed upon it. After such great benefits he says that they had forgotten his goodness and provoked his clemency into bitterness, so that the city was under siege and, even before the enemy’s assault, had been consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence. He prefaced all this so that he might then introduce what appeared to be a reproach of the divine sentence: “And you say to me, Lord God, ‘Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses,’ when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans.” This, for the moment, constitutes the whole section of this passage (περικοπή). Now let us return to the individual details.

“You made heaven and earth by your great strength.” John likewise says of the Son: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John I). This is the strength of the Lord, as the Apostle confirms: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I).

“And by your outstretched (or exalted) arm.” Both expressions indicate the arm of one who strikes. This is the arm of which Isaiah also speaks: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII).

“No word will be difficult for you.” For what is impossible with human beings is possible with God (Matt. XIX); or, “Nothing is hidden from you,” according to the Psalmist’s statement: “For darkness will not be darkened from you, and night will shine like the day” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

“You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of their fathers into the bosom of their children after them.” Great is the Creator’s clemency: to extend his mercy through a thousand generations, but to display his justice immediately in the second generation—which itself, nevertheless, is mingled with mercy. For he does not immediately punish the offender, but awaits the full measure, so that if the children imitate their parents’ vice, the punishment, long deferred, may be repaid.

“Most mighty and great, powerful; the Lord of hosts (or powers) is your name.” These names indicate the Creator’s power. Properly speaking, however, the name of God is “Father,” which is revealed in the Gospel by the Lord when he says: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John XVII).

“Great in counsel.” Does anyone dare to insert himself into the Lord’s secret and pass judgment on his judgments?

“And incomprehensible in thought.” If thought cannot comprehend him, how can speech comprehend him?

“Whose eyes are open over all the ways of the sons of Adam.” Therefore, human beings vainly suppose that they can hide themselves from God’s knowledge. And what follows—“to repay each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds”—indicates that sometimes, because of his exceedingly great wisdom, his judgments may appear unjust. The Apostle explains this passage more fully in Romans: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. II). Thus, the later the vengeance upon sinners, the more just it is—after the likeness of Pharaoh, who, warned by ten plagues but not punished by them, persisted in hardness and was finally overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea (Exod. XIV).

“You established signs and wonders in the land of Egypt to this day, and in Israel and among human beings (or, earth-dwellers), and you made a name for yourself, as it is this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror. You gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers that you would give them, a land flowing with milk and honey. They entered and possessed it, but they did not obey your voice and did not walk in your law. They did not do anything that you commanded them to do, and all these evils came upon them.”

He passes from the general to the particular and briefly reviews what he had specifically done for Israel.

“You established,” he says, “signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,” by which Egypt was afflicted, “to this day, and in Israel and among human beings, or earth-dwellers.” The words “to this day” should be joined with what follows, so that we read: “And in Israel and among all mortals your signs are fulfilled daily.” Or alternatively: “You performed signs and wonders not only in Egypt, but to this day the same strength of your mercy has saved your people, and by the Creator’s power you assist the entire human race.” It should also be noted that he separates Israel from human beings, or earth-dwellers, in accordance with the statement: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV).

“And you made a name for yourself, as it is this day.” “Your praises,” he says, “are celebrated in the speech of the whole world.”

“And you brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt.” He appropriately says “your people,” for at the time when they were brought out, they were serving the Lord’s commands. You brought them out “with signs and wonders,” by which Egypt was struck, “with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror”—when you provided a way through the Red Sea for the people of Israel as they crossed and overwhelmed the Egyptian army.

“And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers that you would give them”—namely, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Therefore they received the promised land, a land flowing with milk and honey, not on account of their own merit but through the virtues of their fathers. For they were not yet able to take solid food; they were nourished by the honey and milk of infancy—or, certainly, by honey and milk as symbols of the fruitfulness and abundance of all things.

“They entered and possessed it.” Immediately there was nothing between possession and disobedience. Abundance produces security, security negligence, and negligence contempt.

“They did not obey,” he says, “your voice and did not walk in your law.” Therefore they had promised in vain in the wilderness, saying: “Everything that the Lord has commanded we will do” (Exod. XIX). The reward lies not in the promise but in the deed. This rebukes the shamelessness of those who think that human beings can fulfill everything they have promised to do.

“They did not do anything that you commanded them to do”—although they had promised that they would do so.

“And all these evils came upon them.” They were evils to those who suffered them, but according to the Lord’s judgment they were good, since he repays each according to his ways.

“Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city so that it may be captured, and the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans, who are fighting against it, because of the sword, famine, and pestilence; and whatever you have spoken has happened, as you yourself see. Yet you say to me, Lord God: ‘Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses,’ when the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans?”

It was the tenth year of King Zedekiah, for it is written: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah.” At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem. Jeremiah the prophet was confined in the court of the prison. And it is rightly said now: “Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city so that it may be captured, and the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans.” They have no one to defeat, but only people to capture. They had already been consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence, and we see that everything you said has been fulfilled. How, then, do you say to me, Lord, “Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses, when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans”?

He therefore does not reproach but asks a question; and he wishes to learn not so much for himself as for the others who were sitting in the court of the prison and perhaps were silently objecting: how could the same prophet, whom they believed to be proclaiming the truth, say both that the city was to be captured [Col. 1055D] and that he should buy a field as though he were going to possess it?

“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: ‘Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh. Will anything be difficult (or, impossible) for me, or will any word be hidden from me? Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and they will capture it. The Chaldeans will come (or, enter), fighting against this city (or, the Chaldeans will come), and they will set it on fire, burn it, and burn the houses on whose roofs they sacrificed to Baal and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods, provoking me.’”

He joins joyful things to sorrowful ones and, after Jerusalem’s destruction, promises the captive people a return. First he sets out the causes of the offense and of God’s just anger, so that the greater the guilt of the sinners, the greater the Creator’s clemency toward sinners.

“I am,” he says, “the Lord, the God of all flesh.” He does not say “the God of all nations,” or “the God of the people of Israel,” or—as he frequently says of the saints—“the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” but “the God of all flesh,” so that he may be believed to have made both rational and irrational creatures. There are some who acknowledge the Creator’s providence only as far as rational beings, but assert that irrational creatures either perish or live by chance. The prophetic word, however, declares that nothing escapes God’s providence and knowledge, because some things were created for their own sake and others for human use.

“Will anything be difficult or impossible for me, or indeed will any word be hidden from me?” We have already said that what is impossible with human beings is possible with God. Here, as in many other places, we must understand “word” as referring to things.

“What does this mean,” he says, “that ‘the word came’?” “Therefore thus says the Lord.” What had preceded, for him to use the causal conjunction and say, “Therefore thus says the Lord”? “Because,” he says, “it is my concern to govern all things, arrange everything, and repay each according to his ways, therefore I will give this city into the hands of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and they will capture it.”

First it is surrounded by an army; then, while Nebuchadnezzar is absent, it is captured, and Zedekiah is led to Riblah and handed over there to the king.

“And the Chaldeans will come,” he says, “fighting against this city.” Aquila is better, for instead of what is written, “They will come,” he translated εἰσελεύσονται, that is, “They will enter the city.” They were not absent so that they might come, since they had surrounded Jerusalem, as Scripture testifies: “The army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem”; and then: “Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city so that it may be captured, and the city has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans.” How, then, will those who were present come? Rather, he says, those who were besieging the city will enter it, capture it, set it on fire, and burn it to the ground. The Hebrew word, because of its ambiguity, means both “they will come” and “they will enter.”

They will burn the houses on whose roofs they sacrificed to Baal, the idol of the Sidonians, and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods, provoking me—so that they might be seen to act not from religious error, but from a certain defiance and insult directed against the Creator.

Just as the world is written to perish according to the statement, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV), because it lies in the power of the evil one, so the house itself and the places in which crimes were committed are subject to God’s anger. Some, contentiously, refer to the places themselves the statement that “the place where the Lord and Savior was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt”; others think that the whole world is signified under the names Egypt and Gomorrah. For just as Gomorrah was destroyed by divine fire, so the world too is to be consumed by God’s judgment.

“For the children of Israel and the children of Judah were continually (or, alone) doing evil in my sight from their youth” (Jerome).

Aquila translated the Hebrew word as πλὴν, which signifies the conjunction “nevertheless.” The first edition of Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated it as “alone”; the second edition of Symmachus rendered it διόλου, which we too have followed here in saying “continually.”

Let us first state the sense according to the Hebrew: “The children of Israel and the children of Judah were continually doing evil.” The ten tribes and the two tribes, he says, committed evil without cessation, and perseverance in the worst deeds was continually theirs. But if they were continually and always evil throughout the whole people, where is the everlasting righteousness?

According to the Septuagint, which reads, “Alone doing evil,” a question arises: Did other nations not do evil at the time when Israel and Judah were sinning? This is resolved as follows: Whoever possesses knowledge of God and turns away from him sins alone in God’s sight. Those who remain unbelieving transgress as though God neither saw nor cared. Hence David, the holy man, because he had fallen into sin with Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba, and afterward repented (II Sam. XII), says: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you”—that is, “in your sight” (Ps. L). Finally, the text adds: “Alone doing evil in my sight and before me from their youth.”

What follows—“The children of Israel, who to this day have provoked me by the work of their hands, says the Lord”—is not found in the Septuagint and has been added from the Hebrew. Since they continually sinned from their youth to the present day, God’s sentence is therefore just, and Scripture rightly continues:

“This city has been a cause of my fury and indignation, from the day on which they built it to this day, when it will be removed from my sight.”

If, from the time when the foundations of the city were laid until this day, when it was captured, burned, and removed from the Lord’s sight, it continually provoked God against itself by its vice and his indignation, where is the rest from sinners, as we have often already said?

“Because of the wickedness,” he says, “of the children of Israel and the children of Judah, which they committed, provoking me to anger—they themselves, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

Since he had said above, “This city has been a cause of my fury and indignation, from the day on which they built it to this day, when it will be removed from my sight,” and had shown that no one in general was without sin, he now lists them individually: their kings, princes, priests, and prophets; and, encompassing everything in a single expression, he says, “the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

He says this appropriately because he does not say “my kings, my princes, my priests, and my prophets,” but “their kings, their priests, and their prophets,” because they sinned.

“They turned their backs to me and not their faces.” This accords with what is written elsewhere: “They turned their shoulder away from me” (Zech. VII). Whoever prays bends his neck and prostrates himself on the ground; whoever turns his back indicates by the very gesture of his body that he disregards the one who threatens him. This, he says, they were doing.

“When I was teaching them at dawn and instructing them, they were unwilling to listen, so as to receive discipline.” Once the darkness of error and every form of idolatrous worship had been driven away, I wished daily to illuminate their hearts, having refuted their opinion, and to teach them what is right. And, so that he might preserve free choice, he adds: “They were unwilling to listen, so as to receive discipline.” It continues:

“They placed their idols in the house over which my name has been invoked, to defile it.”

It was not only at that time that Judah placed in God’s temple the statue of the idol that we read about at the beginning of Ezekiel (Ezek. VIII). Even to this day an idol is placed in the house of the Lord—which is interpreted as the Church—or in the heart and soul of believers, whenever a new doctrine is established and, according to Deuteronomy, worshiped in secret (Deut. IV): “Do you not know,” he says, “that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Cor. III).

“They built the high places (or, altars) of Baal, which are in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, to initiate their sons and daughters to the idol Molech.”

For “initiate,” the Hebrew has a word that Aquila and Symmachus translated as “to lead across,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as “to bring forward.” We have discussed more fully above the valley of the sons of Hinnom, which is called by a Hebrew name: it lies beneath the springs of Siloam, and because of its pleasantness—for it is a well-watered place—it provoked the people of Israel to luxury, which is followed by the worship of idols.

It should also be noted that in Hebrew the altars are called “high places,” for the sake of those who, in the books of Samuel and Kings, are uncertain what this word signifies. Molech is the idol of the Ammonites; its name means “king.” Divine Scripture indicates that in that very place the people served not only the idol Baal but also Molech and all the demons.

“Which I did not command them, nor did it enter my heart that they should do this abomination and lead Judah into sin.”

The tribes of Judah and Benjamin plainly worshiped images of demons in the sanctuary of Baal and Molech. The ten tribes—called Samaria, Joseph, and Ephraim—clearly wished to worship the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. So great was the evil committed by the people that God testifies that he had never conceived, nor had it entered his heart, that they would do such things. All these statements are made ἀνθρωποπάθως, that is, in language attributing human emotions or experiences to God.

“And now, because of these things, thus says the Lord God of Israel concerning this city, of which you say that it is being handed over to the hand of the king of Babylon, through sword, famine, and pestilence.”

Just as Jerusalem is prophesied against those who hope for assistance and trust in the strength of its walls—that it is to be overthrown, that the people are about to be captured, and that before the captivity they will perish by sword, famine, and pestilence—so he promises his aid to those who despair and, because of the city’s destruction, expect no salvation. Thus confidence and pride may merit a just sentence from God, while despair and humility may merit his aid.

“Behold, I will gather them from all the lands to which I drove them in my fury, anger, and great indignation; I will bring them back to this place and make them dwell securely. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God. I will give them one heart and one way, so that they may fear me all their days, and that it may be well with them and with their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant (or, establish an eternal testament), and I will not cease doing them good. I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they may not depart from me. I will rejoice over them when I have done them good, and I will plant them in this land in truth (or, in faith), with all my heart and all my soul.”

Many think that this was fulfilled in the time of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak the high priest, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied under Ezra the priest; when the temple was built, and under Nehemiah the surrounding walls were constructed. They say that those whom God had previously expelled from Jerusalem in fury, anger, and great indignation and scattered throughout the whole world were afterward brought back, made to dwell securely, and became God’s people, with the Lord as their God, together with the other things that Scripture relates.

But how this can be fitted to that period—“I will make them dwell securely, and I will make with them an everlasting covenant (or, establish for them an eternal testament)”—cannot be approved at all, since we read, and sacred history records, that they were often captured not only by neighboring nations but also by the Persians, Macedonians, Egyptians, and Romans, and that they have continued in servitude to this day.

Everything, therefore, must be referred to the coming of the Savior, which we see fulfilled spiritually in our time and in the time of faith. The remnant, according to the Apostle, has been saved, and they dwell securely in Christ. They have been given one heart, according to what is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). And “one way,” he says—the one who declares: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV).

“So that they may fear me all their days.” “For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Prov. IX). He says “all their days.” Since this does not apply to the Jews, it must be understood of our people, for whom it was, is, and will be well—not only for them but also for their children after them. With us he has made an everlasting covenant, and he will not cease doing us good.

What follows—“I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they may not depart from me”—grants free choice while nevertheless allowing the fear bestowed to remain the grace of the giver.

[Note: The material enclosed in brackets is added by Rabanus in his own words under Jerome’s name. EDIT.]

Ezekiel likewise says: “I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and observe my judgments and do them; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Ezek. XXXVI).

By these words we are most clearly taught that the beginning of good will is granted to us when the Lord inspires us—whether he draws us toward the way of salvation by himself, through someone’s exhortation, or through necessity—and that the perfection of the virtues is likewise bestowed by him. Our part is to respond, more weakly or more earnestly, to God’s exhortation and assistance; and for this we rightly merit either rewards or punishments.

(Jerome.)

“And when I have done them good,” he says, “I will rejoice.” He rejoices because he sees his creature saved. Hence there is also joy among the angels over one sinner who repents (Luke XV).

“And I will plant them,” he says, “in this land in truth,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “in faith,” so that it may properly signify the Christian people, whose religion is faith.

“With all my heart and all my soul.” If these are the words of the Lord and Savior, his heart and soul are rightly understood as those of the one who says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John X). But if we understand them as spoken in the person of God the Father, they should be interpreted according to the statement: “Your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates” (Isa. I).

“For thus says the Lord: Just as I brought upon my people Israel all this great evil, so I will bring upon them all the good that I am promising them. Fields will be purchased in this land of which you say that it is desolate, because no human being or animal remains and it has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans. Fields will be bought with money, recorded in a book, the seal will be impressed, and witnesses will be called in the land of Benjamin, in the environs of Jerusalem, in the cities of Judah, in the mountain cities, in the lowland cities (or, the Shephelah), and in the cities of the Negeb—that is, those in the south—for I will restore their fortunes, says the Lord.”

Although, according to the literal sense, these things occurred in a type after the return from the Chaldeans, when the people returned to Judea at the command of King Cyrus, they are nevertheless fulfilled more truly and fully in Christ and in the Apostles.

Then human beings and animals too were brought back into the Church, according to what is written: “You save human beings and animals, Lord” (Ps. XXXV)—the rational and the simple alike.

Then fields were bought with money, so that we might make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, who may receive us into eternal dwellings. They were recorded in a book—undoubtedly the book of the living—and the sign of the banner of the Lord’s cross and victory was impressed. Witnesses were called: the martyrs and the entire chorus of the saints.

“In the land of Benjamin,” where the Lord’s strength is; “in the environs of Jerusalem,” where there is the vision of peace and eternal security; “in the cities of Judah,” in which there is the true confession of Christ; “in the mountain cities,” one of which is the city of which it is said: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V); and “in the lowland cities,” which in Hebrew are called [Hebrew term], so that from the depths and low-lying places, through the levelness of the plains, we may climb to the heights; and “in the cities that are toward the south,” which the Septuagint translated as “the Negeb,” where there is midday and the full light of truth.

When all these things have happened, what is written will be fulfilled: “I will restore their fortunes, says the Lord.” Of this it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII)—“he received,” or, as the Apostle says, “he gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. IV).

# BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 1061]

[Col. 1061A] In the preceding twelve books I arranged, passage by passage, the material published by blessed Jerome in his exposition of Jeremiah up to this point, inserting also the opinions of other teachers that they expressed concerning the same prophet. I indicated the names of each one externally, beside their writings, so that the reader might know from the name what each had thought or said in his exposition.

Since thereafter I nowhere found the exposition of the aforementioned commentator Jerome on the present prophet, I considered it necessary to extract from expositions of other prophets what he himself appears to have recalled concerning this prophet. For there are many passages in Jeremiah that correspond to other prophets. Consequently, the meaning of this book is explained to a considerable extent through their expositions as well.

This circumstance also gave me the opportunity, wherever I did not find the writings of the earlier teachers, to dare to explain the prophetic statements in my own words by imitating their meanings—not relying on my own abilities or knowledge, but entrusting myself entirely to the grace of the one who says through the Prophet: “Call upon me in the day of your trouble; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX). And again: “Open your mouth,” he says, “and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX).

He also gives wisdom abundantly to his faithful speakers and does not reproach them, so that whatever is properly spoken may redound entirely to his honor and praise. But if anything has sounded less cautiously or inappropriately, may it be purified by the judgment of the one who once purified the prophet’s lips with a coal taken from the fire by a Cherub.

From this point, let us consider what follows in the Prophet.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE

On the conduct of Judah and Jerusalem; on the flock passing over to the hand of the one who numbers it; and on Christ’s everlasting kingdom and priesthood.

“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah a second time, while he was still confined in the court of the prison, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord, who will make and form it and prepare it—the Lord is his name: Call to me and I will answer you, and I will announce to you great and firm things that you do not know’” (Maurus).

Above it was written that King Zedekiah had confined Jeremiah in the court of the prison, which was in the house of the king of Judah, saying to him: “Why do you prophesy, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon’?” and the rest (see above, XXXII). While he was there, he bought a field from the son of his paternal uncle for seven shekels and ten pieces of silver.

There too, now for the second time, he receives a word of consolation concerning the people’s return to the land of Israel, the restoration of the city of Jerusalem, and the rebuilding of the temple.

When he says, “Call to me and I will answer you, and I will announce to you great and firm things that you do not know,” he shows that through the prayers of the prophets and of the saints who belonged to the people, the Lord was appeased for the people’s sins and revealed to them their return to their land. Yet the grace of that return still lay hidden, because it had not yet been proclaimed.

If someone thinks it should be asked how the Lord here says to the prophet, “Call to me and I will answer you,” when above he had said to him, “You must not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer for them, because I will not answer you, says the Lord,” let him understand that the Lord did not wish to avert the captivity of the Jews that was imminent. Rather, he wished to bring it about in accordance with his word. But once they had first paid the penalty due for their sin, he afterward did not deny them their return, which he now promises to accomplish.

“For thus says the Lord God of Israel concerning the houses of this city, concerning the houses of the king of Judah that have been destroyed, concerning the fortifications, and concerning the sword of those who are coming to fight against the Chaldeans and to fill them with the corpses of human beings whom I struck in my fury and indignation—for I have hidden my face from this city because of all their wickedness:

‘Behold, I will bring it a bandage and healing; I will cure them and reveal to them a prayer for peace and truth. I will restore the fortunes of Judah and the fortunes of Jerusalem. I will rebuild them as at the beginning and cleanse them from all their iniquity by which they sinned against me. I will be gracious toward all their iniquities by which they sinned against me and despised me.

‘It shall become for me a name, a joy, a praise, and an exultation among all the nations of the earth that hear of all the good things I am going to do for them. They will fear and tremble because of all the good things and all the peace that I will make for them.’”

He foretells that just as vengeance is prepared for sinners, so medicine is prepared for penitents. In the places where, through the Lord’s indignation, the corpses of the slain had lain prostrate, the dwellings of the converted will be rebuilt, and there will be an abundance of every good thing, so that from there the glory of the Lord’s name may be proclaimed everywhere and praise and joy may arise among all nations over all the good things that the Lord will do for his people.

Although some refer these things to the time when the Chaldean captivity was ended, it nevertheless seems better to me to refer them to Christian times, when the Lord spiritually and truly grants every good thing to his faithful through his Spirit—true wisdom and sacred virtues—so that they may live in complete peace and harmony.

Hence Truth itself says to his disciples: “I leave you my peace; I give you my peace. I do not give to you as the world gives peace; I give to you” (John XIV). And again: “Behold,” he says, “I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

In the return of the Jews from Babylon, however, the neighboring nations greatly harassed them and prevented them from rebuilding the temple and restoring the city walls. Later, too, in the time of the Maccabees, many wars and hardships befell them, and they could never have perfect peace and complete security, until they were expelled from their land by Roman rulers and scattered throughout the whole world.

[Col. 1063B] “Thus says the Lord: Even yet there shall be heard in this place, which you say is desolate because there is neither human being nor animal in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, which are desolate, without human being, inhabitant, or livestock—the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those saying: ‘Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for his mercy endures forever,’ and of those bringing vows into the house of the Lord. For I shall restore the fortunes of the land as at the beginning, says the Lord.”

So that the Jews might not fall into despair because of the threats of captivity, he promises them the future blessings of restoration: the place that had been made desolate because of the crimes of its inhabitants would again be inhabited by those corrected and reformed, and filled with flocks and animals. [Col. 1063C] Mystically, however, the Church of the Gentiles, which had been deserted by the Lord because of idolatry and the enormity of its crimes, is once again inhabited through faith in Christ and filled with a multitude of believers from diverse nations. To her Isaiah says: “The deserted and impassable place shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult, and shall blossom like a lily; blossoming, it shall blossom, and shall exult with joy and praise” (Isa. 35). And again: “Sing praise, he says, you barren woman who do not bear; break forth into praise and sing, you who did not give birth, for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband. For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I shall gather you” (Isa. 54).

To her, therefore, every flock of Kedar shall be gathered; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to her. There the voice of joy and the voice of gladness shall be heard, [Col. 1063D] when the Gospel is read there and the joyful alleluia is frequently sung in the churches. There the voice of Christ the bridegroom and the voice of the Church the bride are heard; Solomon composed the Song of Songs for their wedding. There the voice of those who confess the Lord daily is heard, as is the voice of those bringing vows into the house of the Lord, because the Lord will restore the fortunes of the land of the Gentiles as at the beginning, so that there may be one faith among all in belief and one language in confession. Concerning this it is further said:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet again there shall be in this desolate place, without human being and without animal, and in all its cities, a habitation of shepherds and of those who make their flocks lie down—in the mountain cities, in the lowland cities, and in the cities of the south; and in the land of Benjamin, in the surroundings of Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, flocks shall again pass under the hand of the one who counts them, says the Lord.”

These shepherds, whose habitation is in the place that had previously been desolate, are the apostles, evangelists, and teachers of the New Testament. The flocks lying down in the mountain cities, in the lowland cities, and in the cities of the south are the Churches gathered from the Gentiles. They stand upon the summit of virtues, yet do not abandon the depths of humility; rather, through the fervor of the Holy Spirit, signified by the south wind, they devote themselves to good works and maintain the obligations of love. Associated with them are the flocks that dwell in the land of Benjamin, [Col. 1064B] in the surroundings of Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, because many from that former people belong to the faith of Christ and to the number of his sheep. Of them he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10).

All these flocks, therefore, shall pass under the hand of the one who counts them, because, according to the ordering of the true shepherd, they live while observing the divine commandments. He himself records them in the heavenly kingdom, as he promised them, saying: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). That sheep from both Jews and Gentiles are the flocks of Christ, he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my own, and my own know me. Just as the Father knows me, and I know the Father; [Col. 1064C] and I lay down my life for my sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice. And there shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up the good word that I spoke to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah.”

The good word that the Lord said he would raise up is the coming of the Son of God: he who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word (John 1), would himself in the last times become flesh and dwell among us. When this Word was promised to the patriarchs, the Law foretold it; the prophets proclaimed it; and finally an angelic oracle bore witness to it before the virgin Mary, who was descended from David [Col. 1064D] (Luke 1). She herself conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin, because she brought forth God and man for the salvation of the human race—namely, the one God and our Lord Jesus Christ. Concerning him it is next said:

“In those days and at that time I shall cause a righteous Branch to sprout for David, and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteous one.’”

Isaiah foretold these days, saying: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow toward it, and many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths, for the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Isa. 2).

The Lord therefore causes the righteous Branch of David to sprout—that is, he causes Christ to descend from his lineage. He will execute judgment and righteousness in the land, because, according to Isaiah, “righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his kidneys” (Isa. 1). “And in those days Judah shall be saved”—that is, the apostles and the primitive Church in Judea. “Israel”—that is, the people summoned from the elect of the Gentiles—“shall dwell” securely “in the faith of Christ and in true religion.” Concerning this, Moses prophesied under the figure of Benjamin, saying: “The beloved of the Lord shall dwell securely in him; he shall remain as in a bridal chamber all day, and he shall rest between his shoulders” (Deut. 33), because the Church, the bride belonging to the fellowship of Christ the Bridegroom, now rejoices in hope under his protection, but in the future shall rest in blessedness.

“And this,” he says, “is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteous one.’” Concerning him another prophet says: “And they shall call his name Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Isa. 7), because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He is the Lord our righteous one, “because the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness; his face has seen equity. He has brought down the mighty from their throne and exalted the humble; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty” (Ps. 10). For he is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works.

“For thus says the Lord: There shall not cease from David a man sitting upon the throne of the house of Israel; and from the priests and Levites there shall not cease before me a man who offers burnt offerings, kindles sacrifice, and slaughters victims all the days.”

Because no one can properly apply this testimony to the kingdom of the Jewish people, to the priesthood of the Old Testament, and to the ceremonies of the ancient Law, it is necessary to transfer the whole of it to the kingdom of Christ, his priesthood, and the worship of the New Testament. Concerning the power of this kingdom, the divine voice says in the Psalms: “I shall establish his throne forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven” (Ps. 88). Concerning his priesthood it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 109).

Concerning this priest, the divine voice also says to the priest Eli (1 Sam. 2): “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall act according to my heart and according to my soul; and I shall build him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Christ all his days.” The members of this priest are the children of the holy Catholic Church, as Peter testifies, saying: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2). To this priest burnt offerings and sacrifices are offered in thanksgiving to God, and sacrifices acceptable to him shall be made all the days.

[Col. 1066A] “And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Thus says the Lord: If my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night can be annulled, so that day and night do not occur at their appointed time, then my covenant with David my servant can also be annulled, so that he has no son reigning upon his throne, and so that the Levites and priests, my ministers, do not remain.”

Above he had spoken of the creation of the sun, moon, and stars, and of their courses, so that those laws or ordinances could not be overturned. Now, in a similar way, he testifies that the covenant of day and night cannot be annulled, nor can the Lord’s covenant with his servant David be annulled, so that he should have no son reigning upon his throne, nor the Levites and priests as the Lord’s ministers. This is clearer than daylight, since, when the legal priesthood has ended, the kingdom and priesthood of Christ will remain forever. Concerning this it is further said:

“Just as the stars of heaven cannot be counted and the sand of the sea cannot be measured, so I shall multiply the offspring of David my servant, and the Levites who minister to me.”

It is read in Genesis (Gen. 16) that the Lord promised Abraham that his offspring would be multiplied like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore. There can be no doubt that this means that his spiritual offspring would be multiplied without number in the Church, and that its total is known to God alone, who numbers the multitude of the stars and calls all of them by name. His kingdom shall have no end, and his ministers shall remain forever.

“And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: Have you not seen what this people has said: ‘The two families whom the Lord had chosen have been rejected, and they have despised my people, so that it is no longer a nation before them’? Thus says the Lord: If I had not established my covenant with day and night and the laws of heaven and earth, then I too would cast away the offspring of Jacob and David my servant, so that I would not take from his offspring rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For I shall restore their fortunes and have mercy on them.”

With truthful reasoning and fitting comparison, he refutes the speech of the enemies who insulted the people of God. Just as the laws of heaven and earth, of day and night, persist in the order assigned to them and now continue without interruption, so the promise of God made to the fathers concerning their offspring is altogether stable and remains fixed by an enduring law.

By the two families whom the Lord had chosen we may understand either the royal and priestly lineage, or the two tribes that were in Jerusalem and the ten tribes that were in Samaria. The Lord chose them when he made the promise to their fathers that he would give their offspring a land flowing with milk and honey. Yet although many of them strayed from the way of truth, many others were found approved in the state of right faith and good works, because from them came the apostles and the primitive Church in Jerusalem, which was found most distinguished in evangelical teaching and most steadfast in faith.

Paul also seems to indicate this when he says: “What then? Israel did not obtain what it was seeking, but the elect obtained it; the rest were hardened” (Rom. 11). And again: “Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I myself am an Israelite, from the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

Thus it is clear that the Lord did not reject the people whom he had chosen, contrary to the claims of those who insulted them, if he took from the offspring of David rulers from the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob forever. Concerning them it is written in the Psalms: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth. They shall remember your name, O Lord, throughout every generation and lineage” (Ps. 44).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The punishment of those who do not release their male and female slaves, after promising solemnly to do so in the temple.

[Col. 1067B] “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and all his army, and all the kingdoms of the earth that were under the power of his hand, and all the peoples, were warring against Jerusalem and against all its cities, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah, and say to him: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn it with fire, and you shall not escape from his hand, but you shall surely be captured and delivered into his hand; and your eyes shall see the eyes of the king of Babylon, and his mouth shall speak with your mouth, and you shall enter Babylon. Nevertheless, hear the word of the Lord, Zedekiah king of Judah: Thus says the Lord to you: [Col. 1067C] You shall not die by the sword, but you shall die in peace; and just as they burned incense for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so they shall burn it for you; and ‘Alas, lord!’ they shall lament over you, because I have spoken this word, says the Lord. And Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that remained, against Lachish and against Azekah; for these were the fortified cities that remained among the cities of Judah.”

(MAURUS.) Although the most wicked king Zedekiah, of whom Scripture reports that he did evil before the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done, was unworthy of the Lord’s mercy, nevertheless, because the Lord’s mercies are great and exceedingly many, he admonished him repeatedly through his prophets— [Col. 1067D] that is, through Jeremiah in Judea and through Ezekiel, prophesying in Babylonia—proclaiming the captivity that was to come, in the hope that he might somehow provoke him to repentance. But his hardened mind turned the words spoken into an occasion of disgust, and he chose to persist in the wickedness he had begun rather than correct himself through reform of life. Therefore he received the punishment he deserved and suffered the vengeance of captivity together with the people subject to him.

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people who were in Jerusalem, proclaiming that each person should release his male slave and each his female slave, Hebrew man and Hebrew woman, [Col. 1068A] free, and that they should by no means dominate them—that is, over a Jew, their brother. And all the princes and all the people who had entered into the covenant heard that each person should release his male slave and each his female slave, free, and should no longer dominate them. They heard, therefore, and released them; but afterward they turned back and took again their male slaves and female slaves whom they had released as free, and subjected them as male and female servants. And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: I made a covenant with your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, saying: When seven years have been completed, each person shall release his Hebrew brother who was sold to him, [Col. 1068B] who shall serve you for six years, and then you shall release him from you as a free man. But your fathers did not listen to me, nor did they incline their ear. And you have now turned and done what is right in my eyes, proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbor; and you made a covenant in my presence in the house in which my name was invoked. But you have turned back and profaned my name, and each of you has brought back his male slave and each his female slave whom you had released to be free and their own masters; and you have subjected them, so that they are your male and female slaves,” and so forth.

It is clear here that it profits no one to begin a good work if he does not strive to bring it to a good end, since “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” [Col. 1068C] (Matt. 24). The commandment of the Law had therefore been given that the children of Israel should not hold their brothers in the condition of slaves or oppress them by force, but that at the appointed time they should return to the family and inheritance of their fathers; and that they should have male and female slaves from the nations who surrounded them. Wishing to observe this, Zedekiah and the people who were with him promised that they would do so. But they turned back, took again their male and female slaves whom they had released as free, and subjected them as servants. Therefore the Lord, angered, delivered them into the tumult of all the kingdoms of the earth and sent upon them the sword, pestilence, and famine. And because they profaned the victim of the covenant that they had cut in accordance with the terms of the established pact, they were given into the hands of their enemies [Col. 1068D] and into the hands of those seeking their lives; and their corpses became food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth. Not only was the people, because of its crimes, killed and scattered by its enemies, but their cities also were burned and demolished.

According to the tropological sense, this passage teaches us that, when we have taken our brothers under our care and they have been subjected to us for God’s sake, we must not oppress them by force or unjustly impose the violence of servitude upon them. Rather, we should treat and assist them with brotherly affection, by word and example, so that they may offer worthy service to the Lord who redeemed them with his blood, until the true Jubilee comes and each person is restored to his own dignity [Col. 1069A] and possession. Concerning this the first shepherd of the Church instructs us, saying: “Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and as one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, watching over it not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming an example of the flock from the heart. And when the chief shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Pet. 5).

## CHAPTER XXXV. By the example of the Rechabites the people are taught obedience, and a blessing is promised to the sons of Sechab.

“The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord [Col. 1069B] in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, saying:”

(MAURUS.) Since in the preceding chapter the prophet had spoken about King Zedekiah and the things done by those under him, but now once again turns the narrative to the time of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, it is plainly evident that he did not observe chronological order in his narration, as has already been said above. Rather, according to the dispensation of the Holy Spirit who spoke in him, he wished his prophecy to be written according to the suitability of the causes and the correspondence of circumstances, just as we find was done in the other sacred Scriptures, and especially in the Gospel, so that the reader may know that the sacred Scriptures were composed not by human arrangement but by divine inspiration and ordering.

[Col. 1069C] “Go to the house of the Rechabites and speak to them; and you shall bring them into the house of the Lord, into one of the chambers of the treasury, and you shall give them wine to drink. And I took Jaazaniah son of Jeremiah son of Habazziniah, and his brothers, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites, and I brought them into the house of the Lord, to the treasury of the sons of Hanan son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which was beside the treasury of the princes, above the treasury of Maaseiah son of Shallum, keeper of the vestibule. And I set before the sons of the house of the Rechabites bowls full of wine and cups, and I said to them: ‘Drink wine.’ But they answered: ‘We do not drink wine, because Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, commanded us, saying: You shall not drink wine, neither you nor your sons, forever; and you shall not build a house, and you shall not sow seed, and you shall not plant vineyards, nor shall you possess them; but you shall dwell in tents all your days, so that you may live many days upon the face of the land in which you are sojourners,’” and so forth.

To confound the pride and obstinacy of the Jews, who had always resisted the commandments of God, the prophet, at the Lord’s command, brought forward the obedient and gentle Rechabites as witnesses. They obeyed in everything the commands of Jonadab son of Rechab, their father, so that they neither drank wine nor built houses, neither sowed seed nor planted vineyards, but dwelt in tents all their days, until the necessity of the Chaldean captivity, according to everything that had been commanded them. For this reason also the Lord promises them that no man from the line of Jonadab son of Rechab will fail to stand in his presence all their days.

Mystically, however, these Rechabites signify those who, through a desire for perfection, transcend the commandments of the Law by a stricter way of life, in accordance with what the teachings of the Gospel and the examples of the Apostles convey to them. The righteous, for whom the Law was not imposed, are shown not to be under the Law in this respect: they strive not only to fulfill the righteousnesses of the Law but even to surpass them. Their devotion is greater than the legal command, and, increasing the observance of the commandments, it voluntarily adds what is beyond obligation.

Thus we read that Abraham also surpassed the commandments of the future Law. After overcoming the four kings, he refused entirely to touch the spoils of Sodom, which as victor were not unjustly owed to him, even though the king himself, whose spoils he had recovered, humbly offered them to him. He proclaimed under the testimony of the divine name: “I lift up my hand to the Lord Most High, who made heaven and earth: if from a thread to a sandal strap I take anything of all that is yours” (Gen. 14).

So too we know that David surpassed the commandments of the Law. Although Moses commanded that retaliation be rendered to enemies, David not only failed to do this but also embraced his persecutors in love, devoutly praying to the Lord on their behalf and even lamenting and bitterly mourning those who had been killed.

In the same way we prove that Elijah and Jeremiah were not under the Law. Although they could licitly have used marriage without reproach, they preferred to remain virgins. Likewise, we read that Elisha and the other men of this purpose surpassed the Mosaic commandments. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, and oppressed; the world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and in caves and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 11).

So now these sons of Jonadab are praised by the divine word because of the obedience they showed to their father, and future blessings are promised to them. They were not content merely to offer the tithes of their possessions; they rejected the estates themselves and offered themselves, rather, and their souls to God. No exchange can be made for these by any human being, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matt. 16).

Therefore we must understand that we are no longer required to observe the legal commandment, but that the evangelical word resounds daily for us: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). When we offer tithes from our possessions to God, we are still, in a certain sense, held under the burden of the Law and have not yet reached that evangelical height which rewards those who obey it with not only the benefits of the present life but also future rewards.

For the Law promised those who did its works not the rewards of heavenly kingdoms but the comforts of this life, saying: “The one who does this shall live by them.” But the Lord promises the kingdoms of heaven to his disciples and friends: “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1071A] (Matt. 5). And: “Everyone who has left house or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

Nor is it without reason. It is not as praiseworthy to refrain from what is unlawful as it is also to refrain from what is lawful, and for reverence toward him not to use things that he permitted us to use because of our weakness. It was not to be commanded universally, nor, so to speak, canonically required of everyone, since what is sought because of its wondrous sublimity cannot be grasped indiscriminately by all. Rather, all are invited by counsel and grace, so that those who are great may rightly be crowned with the perfection of virtues.

Those who are small, however, and cannot attain the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, may appear joyful, covered by the brilliance of their greater brethren like stars; nevertheless, they are separated from the darkness of the curses that are in the Law. They are neither handed over to the disasters of present evils nor punished with eternal punishment. Christ therefore does not compel anyone by necessity to those lofty summits of virtue, but calls them by the power of free choice and kindles them through the healthfulness of counsel and the desire for perfection.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Baruch is sent from Jeremiah’s prison with the book, which Jehoiakim burns; another is written against him.

“And it came to pass in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, [Col. 1071C] king of Judah, that this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Take a scroll of a book and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah, and against all the nations, from the day when I first spoke to you, from the days of Josiah even to this day. Perhaps, when the house of Judah hears all the evils that I am thinking of doing to them, each person may turn from his evil way, and I shall be merciful toward their iniquity and sin.”

(MAURUS.) O immense clemency and immeasurable goodness of our Creator, who, when despised by the proud, does not inflict the punishment of vengeance upon sinners, but promises pardon to those converted through repentance. He directs the word of preaching through the prophet not only to the single nation of the Jews but to all the nations of the Gentiles, in the hope that each person may somehow turn from his evil way and obtain, through the Lord’s mercy, forgiveness of his sins.

“Jeremiah therefore called Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord that he had spoken to him in the scroll of the book. And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying: I am confined and cannot enter the house of God. Go, therefore, and read from the scroll in which you have written from my mouth the words of the Lord, in the hearing of the people in the house of the Lord, on the day of fasting. Moreover, in the hearing of all Judah who come from their cities, you shall read to them, if perhaps their prayer may fall before the Lord and each person may turn from his evil way, [Col. 1072A] because great is the fury and indignation that the Lord has spoken against this people. And Baruch son of Neriah did according to everything that Jeremiah the prophet had commanded him, reading the words of the Lord from the scroll in the house of the Lord.”

The prophet’s prompt obedience accords with the divine clemency. For just as the Lord, through the admonition of conversion, takes account of human weakness, so the prophet, by obeying, performs the ministry of preaching for the salvation of his neighbors. Although he was confined in prison and could not accomplish this himself, he nevertheless took care to fulfill everything through an interpreter, exactly as he had been commanded.

What, then, shall we inert people say at God’s future judgment, who, though released and possessing liberty, neglect to offer the word of the Lord to our neighbors? When he who was shut behind prison bars did not use the excuse of impossibility to obstruct the Lord’s command, but hastened most diligently to accomplish through another person what he could not complete by himself, [Col. 1072B] what excuse will we have?

“Now it came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, that they proclaimed a fast in the presence of the Lord for all the people in Jerusalem and for all the multitude that had gathered from the cities of Judah in Jerusalem. And Baruch read from the scroll the words of Jeremiah in the house of the Lord, in the treasury of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, in the upper vestibule, at the entrance of the new gate of the house of the Lord, in the hearing of all the people,” and so forth.

The order is appropriate: when repentance is proclaimed, a fast of frugality is proclaimed, so that those who, by failing to guard against vices through luxury, had fallen into sin may strive through abstinence and bodily affliction to wash away those same sins. (Greg.) For we must consider most carefully that the person who remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things. In this way he may satisfy his Creator: the person who has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, and the one who remembers having sinned in great matters should reproach himself in small ones.

“Then all the princes sent to Baruch son of Neriah, son of Nethaniah, son of Cushi, saying: ‘The scroll from which you read in the hearing of the people—take it in your hand and come.’ So Baruch son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them. And they said to him: Sit down and read this in our hearing. And Baruch read in their hearing. When they had heard all the words, each was astonished, one looking at another. And they said to Baruch: Must we report all these words to the king? And they questioned him, saying: Tell us how you wrote all these words from his mouth. But Baruch said to them: He spoke from his mouth to me, as though reading all these words to me, and I was writing in the scroll with ink,” and so forth.

When Baruch was questioned by the princes of the people about how he had written Jeremiah’s words from his mouth, he replied that Jeremiah had spoken to him from his own mouth, as though reading the words. This indicates that the holy prophets and apostles, speaking by the Holy Spirit, suffered neither from a need for elaborate composition nor from a scarcity of words. Rather, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, they could produce before their hearers everything that was required, promptly and easily.

Hence Truth himself says to the disciples in the Gospel: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider beforehand how or what you shall speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Luke 1; Matt. 10). And again: “The Paraclete Spirit,” he says, “whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have said to you” (John 16).

And we should know that the grace of the Holy Spirit is necessary not only for teachers but also for hearers. For, as we have already said above, unless the same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is idle. Therefore no one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth. Unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

Behold, in the Church we all hear one voice speaking, yet we do not all equally perceive the meaning of the voice we have heard. Since the voice of the speaker is not different, why is the understanding of the voice different in our hearts? It is because, through what the speaker’s voice commonly admonishes, there is an inner teacher who teaches certain people particularly concerning the meaning of the voice.

Concerning this grace of the Holy Spirit John also says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2). A person is therefore not instructed through the voice when the mind is not anointed by the Spirit. But why are we speaking of this concerning the teaching of human beings, when even the Creator himself does not speak for a person’s instruction unless he also speaks to that person through the anointing of the Spirit?

(MAURUS.) Certainly, before Cain carried out the deed of fratricide, he heard: “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 3). But because, as his sins deserved, he could not hear the admonishing voice in the anointing, he despised it rather than obeying. So also, what follows in this chapter demonstrates that King Jehoiakim and his servants, because they were not inwardly illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit through which the prophet spoke, could indeed hear the words of God with the ears of the body, but could not hear them with the ears of the heart—those ears that the Lord requires in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11; Luke 8). And in the Apocalypse he says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2). For the account continues:

“Now the king was sitting in the winter house, in the ninth month, and a brazier filled with burning coals was placed before him.
