And when he had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the scribe’s knife and threw it into the fire that was on the brazier, until the whole scroll was consumed by the fire that was on the brazier. Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words were afraid, nor did they tear their garments,” and so forth.

O astonishing blindness of the human mind and astounding wickedness of a hardened heart! They ought to have been pierced by salutary admonitions toward repentance for their sins, yet they strove to consume the words of the Lord written in the book in the flame of fire. Moreover, they attempted to insult the prophet, whom they ought rightly to have honored because of the grace of his teaching and reproof. And why was this? Because the evil spirit, which always opposes the Spirit of grace, devised in their hearts the harshness of stubbornness rather than the gentleness of obedience, lest they should believe, repent, and be saved.

“Then the king ordered Jeremiel son of Amalech, Saraiah son of Ezriel, and Shelemiah son of Abdeel to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet; but the Lord hid them.” Thus human presumption attempts something in vain when divine authority wills to resist it. The earthly king ordered that the prophet [Col. 1074B] and his secretary be seized and sent to prison, but the heavenly King hid them—that is, protected them—so that human wickedness might not injure the innocence of the saints. “For the Lord guards all who love him, but he destroys all sinners (Ps. 144)”; and: “People shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord (Zeph. 1).”

“The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah after the king had burned the scroll and the words that Baruch had written from Jeremiah’s mouth, saying: Take another scroll again and write on it all the earlier words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim king of Judah burned, and say to Jehoiakim king of Judah: Thus says the Lord: You burned that scroll, saying, ‘Why did you write in it, announcing: The king of Babylon will surely come swiftly and devastate this land, and will cause human being and beast to cease from it?’ Therefore thus says the Lord against Jehoiakim king of Judah: There shall be none of his line who sits upon the throne of David, and his corpse shall be cast out into the heat by day and into the frost by night. I shall punish him, his offspring, and his servants for their iniquities, and I shall bring upon them, upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have spoken against them, and they did not listen.” Retribution deservedly followed the treacherous king, so that the one who burned the words of the Lord written by the prophet would have his own corpse cast into the heat by day and into the frost by night: thus his iniquities, together with those of his offspring and servants, would be punished, and all the evil that the Lord had spoken against the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem would quickly arrive. This was to show that whoever rebels against the Lord’s commands and has a hard and impenitent heart will suffer the certain vengeance of retribution, because, according to Paul’s statement, “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap; and whoever sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

It should be noted, however, that the Book of Chronicles records that Nebuchadnezzar king of the Chaldeans led this Jehoiakim to Babylon bound in chains. The Book of Kings, on the other hand, relates that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers and that his son Jehoiakim reigned in his place. But Josephus, the Jewish historian, appears to agree more closely with Jeremiah’s words. He asserts that Jehoiakim, the father of Jeconiah, was killed by the king of Babylon in Jerusalem rather than led captive to Babylon. In the tenth book of his *Antiquities* he reports as follows:

“When the king of Babylonia had entered the city, he did not at all keep faith, but killed the strongest and most handsome young men of Jerusalem together with King Jehoiakim. He also ordered Jehoiakim to be thrown outside the walls unburied. He appointed his son Jehoiakim king of the entire province. He led into Babylon as captives three thousand of those who held positions of rank; among them was the prophet Ezekiel, who was still a boy. Thus Jehoiakim came to his end. He lived thirty-six years and reigned nine years. Jehoiakim, his successor in the kingdom, a man named Onos, reigned three months and ten days.”

But whether the Jehoiakim mentioned perished in Jerusalem or in Chaldea does not seem to me worth investigating, since it is certain that, in accordance with what the prophet had foretold, his corpse was cast out into the heat by day and the frost by night. This was fittingly done so that the corpse of the one who had tried to burn the prophetic Scripture, cut from the scroll, would be afflicted by the sun’s heat and the night’s frost.

“Jeremiah then took another scroll and gave it to Baruch son of Neriah the scribe, who wrote in it from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the book that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned with fire; and many more words were added than had been there before.” What, then, is meant by the fact that the prophet, instructed by the Lord’s command after the burning of the earlier scroll, took another scroll and gave it to Baruch the scribe, who wrote in it from Jeremiah’s own mouth all the words of the book that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned with fire? It means that, although Judah was rejected because of its faithlessness, the books of the Law and the Prophets were preserved for the salvation of the nations, to whom, after Christ’s coming, all the glory of the Old Testament was transferred, because “all these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10).”

Hence it is rightly added: “and many more words were added than had been there before,” because they possess history alone, whereas we possess, together with the history, its mystical meaning. They had a veil over their hearts when Moses was read. “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Now the Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Cor. 3).”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Zedekiah commands that the Lord be entreated for himself and the people; Jeremiah is seized and sent to prison, where a portion of bread is given him daily.

“And King Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned in place of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had appointed king in the land of Judah. But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land obeyed the words of the Lord, which he had spoken through the hand of Jeremiah the prophet.” (MAURUS.) That Zedekiah reigned after Jehoiakim, who was also called Jeconiah, for nine years is reported not only by Jeremiah but also by the Book of Kings and the *Books of Days* [Chronicles]. For after his father Josiah, Jehoahaz reigned three months; after him, Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim, his brother, reigned nine years. After him, Jehoiakim son of Jehoiakim reigned three months and ten days; after him, his uncle Zedekiah, as we have said, reigned nine years. All these were wicked and exceedingly evil kings, who opposed the Law of the Lord and were devoted more to idolatry than to divine worship. Therefore they deserved the Lord’s just vengeance.

[Col. 1076B] “King Zedekiah sent Juchal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest to Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Pray for us to the Lord our God.” Jeremiah, however, walked freely among the people, for they had not put him in the custody of the prison. Zedekiah certainly did not ask the prophet to pray for himself and his people, since he refused to obey the divine commands, because it is written: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed (Ps. 28).” Hence the same prophet Jeremiah was forbidden to pray for them, when the Lord said to him: “But you must not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf, because I will not hear you, says the Lord God.”

[Col. 1076C] “Then Pharaoh’s army came out of Egypt. When the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard this report, they withdrew from Jerusalem. And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: This is what you shall say to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of me: Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which has come out to your aid, will return to its own land, to Egypt; and the Chaldeans will return, wage war against this city, capture it, and burn it with fire,” and so forth.

Josephus explains how the Chaldeans temporarily lifted the siege of Jerusalem because of the approaching Egyptians. Relating that Vaphres, king of Egypt, came to aid the Jews, he reports as follows:

“Meanwhile, when the king of Babylonia learned of this, he moved his camp against him. After devastating the province and plundering its fortifications one by one, he came with a great army to besiege Jerusalem itself. When the king of Egypt heard that Zedekiah was his friend, he gathered a very large force of soldiers and came to Judea, as though he intended to lift the siege. But the Babylonian withdrew from Jerusalem and met the Egyptians. When they engaged in battle, he defeated them and forced them to flee from Syria.

“When the king of Babylon had departed from Jerusalem, the false prophets deceived Zedekiah, saying that the Babylonians would no longer fight against him, but that their fellow countrymen who had migrated from the province to Babylon, together with all the sacred vessels that the king had removed from this temple, would return. But Jeremiah, passing through the midst of them, prophesied the opposite—and the truth—saying that those who told such things to the king were acting wickedly: the Egyptians could provide them no help, for the king of Babylonia would defeat them, return to Jerusalem, besiege it vigorously, destroy the people by famine, lead away the remaining captives, plunder their possessions, empty out the treasures of the temple, and then burn it and overwhelm the city. They would be enslaved to the king of Babylon and his descendants for seventy years. When they returned to this city, they would rebuild the temple and restore Jerusalem.

“When Jeremiah said this, many believed him, but the rulers [Col. 1077B] and the wicked said that he had lost his mind, and under this pretext they mocked him. When he decided to hasten to his homeland, called Anathoth, situated one hundred seventy stadia from Jerusalem, one of the rulers met him on the road, seized and detained him, accusing him of intending to go over to the Babylonians. But Jeremiah said that the man was lying and falsely bringing a charge of slander against him, and that he himself was hurrying to his homeland. The other, unmoved by these words, led him in chains to the master of the judges. There he endured every kind of beating and torture and was held for execution; for some time he unjustly suffered the things we have described.

“Now, in the ninth year of King Zedekiah, on the tenth day of the tenth month, the king of Babylonia encamped against Jerusalem and, remaining around it for eighteen months, besieged it with great determination and force. The Jerusalemites under siege were oppressed by two other and very great evils: the weakness of disease and the famine that pressed upon them with great severity.

“But Jeremiah the prophet, although he was in custody, did not cease; he cried out and preached openly, warning the people to open the gates and receive the king of Babylon. By doing this, he asserted, they could be saved with their entire households; otherwise they would be uprooted completely. He likewise preached that whoever remained in the city would certainly perish, either consumed by famine or by the swords of the enemy; but if they fled to the enemy, they would in some manner escape both their enemies and death.”

[Col. 1077D] “Therefore the rulers became angry with Jeremiah, beat him, and sent him to the prison that was in the house of Jonathan the scribe; for he was in charge of the prison. So Jeremiah entered the house of the cistern [or: the pit-house] in the dungeon, and Jeremiah remained there many days.

“Then King Zedekiah sent for him, brought him out, and questioned him secretly in his house, saying: ‘Is there a word from the Lord?’ And Jeremiah said: ‘There is.’ He said: ‘You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.’

“And Jeremiah said to King Zedekiah: ‘What have I done wrong against you, your servants, or your people, that you have sent me into the prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied to you and said: The king of Babylon will not come against you or against this land? Now therefore, my lord the king, hear, I beg you; may my petition prevail before you, and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there.’

“So King Zedekiah commanded that Jeremiah be placed in the court of the prison and that he be given a round loaf of bread each day, apart from the stew, until all the bread in the city was consumed. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison, and so forth.”

That Zedekiah sent Jeremiah into the depths of the prison not willingly but compelled by the force of the people and at the request of the rulers is no reason for some to excuse him. To support their opinion, they introduce the fact that, as though moved by pious feeling during the extreme famine, he ordered food to be given Jeremiah until all the bread in the city had been consumed. But one who was faithless and hostile to God could not perfectly keep faith with a human being, because, according to the judgment of truth, “whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much,” and “whoever is unrighteous in very little is unrighteous also in much (Luke 16).”

It is clear from his deeds that he did nothing pleasing to God, neither in the fear of God nor in love of his neighbor; and for this he received from God the deserved vengeance for his sins.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Jeremiah is sought for death and sent into a muddy cistern, from which he is brought out by Ebed-melech; he preaches to the king as before.

“And the rulers said to the king: ‘We ask that this man be put to death. For he deliberately weakens the hands of the fighting men who remain in this city [Col. 1078C] and the hands of all the people, speaking to them according to these words: This man does not seek the peace of this people, but its harm.’

“And Zedekiah said: ‘Behold, he is in your hands, for the king is not able to deny you anything.’

“So they took Jeremiah and threw him into the cistern of Malchiah son of Amalech, which was in the court of the prison; they lowered Jeremiah down with ropes. The cistern contained no water, but mud. Thus Jeremiah sank into the mire.”

(MAURUS.) Here it is clear that Zedekiah did not show Jeremiah mercy with sincere affection. If he truly loved him, would he have handed him over to the rulers to be thrust into prison as a punishment, merely for their favor or out of fear? Therefore his feigned compassion was fruitless, just as Pilate’s was when, during the Lord’s Passion, he took water and washed his hands before all the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it (Matt. 27).” Yet afterward he had him scourged and handed him over to the Jews to be crucified.

“Now Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king’s house, heard that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern. The king was then sitting at the Gate of Benjamin. Ebed-melech went out from the king’s house and spoke to the king, saying: ‘My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done against Jeremiah the prophet, throwing him into the cistern so that he may die there of hunger. For there is no longer any bread in the city.’

“Then the king commanded Ebed-melech, saying: ‘Take with you thirty men from here and lift Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.’

“So Ebed-melech took the men with him and entered the king’s house, which was beneath the storeroom. From there he took old rags and ancient garments that had rotted, and lowered them to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian said to Jeremiah: ‘Put these old rags and these torn and rotten garments beneath the armpits of your hands, under the ropes.’ Jeremiah did so, and they drew Jeremiah up with the ropes and brought him out of the cistern. Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.”

Just as the rulers of Zedekiah who had thrown the prophet into the cistern represented those rulers of whom Paul says, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the cosmic powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6),” who always desire to plunge Christ’s faithful into the mire of vices and the filth of sins, so this Ethiopian eunuch, moved by fear and love of God and striving to rescue the prophet, signifies the holy preachers from the nations. The Gospel says that they made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 10); moved by true charity, they strive by word and example to rescue the unjustly oppressed from the pit of destruction. His very name confirms this. For Ebed-melech means “servant of the king”—that is, of the king concerning whom it is written: “For the Lord is most high and terrible, a great king over all gods (Ps. 46).” The order of holy preachers serves him worthily when, through the word of the Gospel, it joins the nations to the Christian faith.

(GREGORY.) Since that same charity remains perpetual and unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is appropriately said in Leviticus: “This is the perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar (Lev. 6).” This fire certainly never fails from the altar, because even after this life the fervor of charity increases in their minds. For through eternal contemplation it comes about that the more the omnipotent God is seen, the more abundantly he is loved.

That we are freed from the depths of this life, aided by divine admonitions and by the examples of those who came before us, is also fittingly signified by the prophet Jeremiah being lowered into a well, since, in order to raise him from the well, ropes and old rags are lowered to him. What else are signified by the ropes but the Lord’s commands? Because, when we are placed in evil action, they both convict us and rescue us: they bind and draw us, constrain and lift us. But lest, while being pulled by these ropes, a person bound by them should be injured, old rags are lowered at the same time. For lest the divine commands terrify us, the examples of the ancient fathers strengthen us, so that, by comparing ourselves with them, we may presume that we can do what we fear because of our own weakness.

If, then, we hasten to be lifted from this depth, let us be bound with ropes—that is, let us be fastened to the Lord’s commands—and let old rags also be present, so that the ropes may hold us more securely. Let us be strengthened by the examples of those who came before us, so that subtle commands may not wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while we are being lifted.

The Apostle Paul supplied certain old rags when, in order to support those being lifted by the commands of discipline, he added the examples of the ancients to his spiritual instructions, saying: “The righteous experienced mockery and blows, and moreover chains and imprisonment; they were stoned, they were sawn apart, they were tempted, they died by the sword”; and shortly afterward: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every burden and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the contest set before us.” Again: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith (Heb. 11).”

Earlier, when he spoke of spiritual commands, he had, as it were, lowered the ropes; afterward, when he recalled the examples of the elders, he supplied, as it were, the old rags. Therefore, stirred by so many commands and aided by so many examples, let us return to our hearts, examine everything we do, and accuse whatever in us offends the rule of divine righteousness, so that our very accusation may excuse us before the strict Judge. For by this judgment of our mind we are acquitted more quickly the more strictly we hold ourselves guilty.

Nor should we waste the times in which we are free for these practices, because after the time of this life there will be no opportunity for them. It is not said without reason that there will be no leisure then; for it will no longer be in human power to come before God for judgment. We are reminded that we will not be able to do this then, so that we may not neglect what we can do now.

[Col. 1080C] But behold, worldly affairs occupy us. They are thrust upon us and draw us away from considering ourselves; they turn aside the eye of our mind. In these visible things, which our heart observes, it is scattered outside itself, and, while occupied externally, it forgets what is happening within it. The divine voice, through its terrifying judgments, places this before us like nails, so that we may awaken and that a person may tremble, at least when struck by fear, before the hidden judgments hanging over him—judgments that, pressed by the demands of time, he disguises. Sacred Scripture pierces drowsy hearts with a certain terror, lest they cling to those external things through which they have lost eternal realities. It indicates what hidden judgment decrees, so that we may not think excessively about these public matters.

“And King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah the prophet and brought him to the third entrance, which was in the house of the Lord. The king said to Jeremiah: ‘I ask you about one matter; hide nothing from me.’ Jeremiah said to Zedekiah: ‘If I tell you, will you not kill me? And if I give you counsel, you will not listen to me.’

“Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, saying: ‘As the Lord lives, who made this life for us, I will not kill you, nor will I hand you over to the men who seek your life,’” and so forth.

The prophet, foreseeing in the spirit the Lord’s future judgment upon the king and the people, namely, that the city would be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans, gave the king counsel to surrender himself voluntarily into the hand of the king of Babylon. In this way he might somehow soften his fury and receive from him a less severe sentence of captivity. But the hardened mind could not be corrected by the foresight of good counsel, just as Pharaoh’s hardened mind was softened toward repentance neither by divine reproof nor by Moses’ warning. Of him Scripture says: “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to the voice of the Lord (Exod. 7),” until, while pursuing the Israelites with his army into the waves of the Red Sea, he was drowned.

“Jeremiah replied: ‘They will not hand you over. Hear, I beg you, the voice of the Lord that I speak to you, and it will go well with you, and your life will be preserved. But if you refuse to go out, this is the word that the Lord has shown me: Behold, all the women who remain in the house of the king of Judah will be brought out to the rulers of the king of Babylon, and they themselves will say: “Your peaceful friends deceived you and prevailed against you; they have sunk your feet into the mud and the mire, and have withdrawn from you.” All your wives and your sons will be brought out to the Chaldeans, and you will not escape their hands. Rather, you will be captured into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn this city with fire,’” and so forth.

Why does Jeremiah, rebuking Zedekiah with the Lord’s word, say: “Behold, all the women who remain in the house of the king of Judah will be brought out to the rulers of the king of Babylon, and they themselves will say: ‘Your peaceful friends deceived you and prevailed against you; they have sunk your feet into the mud and the mire, and have withdrawn from you’”? He says this to show us that fickle thought and pleasure-loving counselors sink the steps of our actions into the mire of carnal desires and the mud of vices, and, when they see us submerged, withdraw from us. For once people are ruined, those who devoted themselves solely to hurling their consenters into the abyss of sin can no longer give them any useful counsel.

Thus, if we do not wish to correct ourselves from our sins through the counsel of the divine Scriptures and to free our souls from future destruction through repentance, we shall be led out with our wives—that is, carnal desires—and our children—that is, wicked deeds—to the Chaldeans, whose name is interpreted as “demons.” We shall be bound and delivered into the hand of the king of eternal confusion, who will burn our city—that is, both body and soul—with an unquenchable fire.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Zedekiah flees when the city is taken, is captured, and blinded. Jeremiah is entrusted to Gedaliah with the city; Ebed-melech is delivered.

[Col. 1081D] “And it came to pass, when Jerusalem was taken in the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came to Jerusalem and besieged it. But in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the city was opened; and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebo, Sarsechim, Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer, Rab-mag, and all the remaining princes of the king of Babylon. When Zedekiah [Col. 1082A] king of Judah and all the men of war saw them, they fled and went out of the city by night, by the way of the king’s garden and through the gate between the two walls; and they went out by the way of the wilderness. But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and captured Zedekiah in the plain of the wilderness of Jericho. Having captured him, they brought him to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon at Riblah, which is in the land of Hamath, and he pronounced judgments upon him. The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons at Riblah before his eyes, and the king of Babylon killed all the nobles of Judah. He also put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him with fetters to be taken to Babylon. The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the houses of the common people with fire, and overthrew the wall of Jerusalem,” and so forth.

(MAURUS.) The same prophet gives a fuller account below of this devastation of the city and captivity of the people; we have therefore deferred its allegorical exposition to that place, where, if the Lord grants it, we shall discuss it in writing. Yet it should be noted that the prophet Isaiah in his book set forth a corresponding account of this devastation, saying: “Depart from me; I will weep bitterly. Do not press upon me to comfort me concerning the devastation of the daughter of my people. For it is a day of slaughter, trampling, and weeping to the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, searching the wall, and the magnificent one upon the mountain. And Elam took up the quiver, the course of a man riding a horse, and the shield uncovered the wall. Your chosen valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen set their stations at the gate; and the covering of Judah shall be revealed. On that day you shall see the armory of the house of the forest, and you shall see that the breaches of the city of David have multiplied. You gathered the waters of the lower pool, counted the houses of Jerusalem, and demolished houses to fortify the wall; you made a reservoir between the two walls and the water of the old pool, and you did not look to him who made it, nor did you see its maker from afar. On that day the Lord of hosts called for weeping and mourning, baldness and girding with sackcloth. But behold, joy and gladness: killing calves and rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’ And the voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears: ‘This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die,’ says the Lord of hosts (Isa. 22).”

(JEROME.) He plainly describes the captivity that occurred in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, of which Jeremiah also speaks elsewhere: “Behold, I shall summon all the kindreds of the kingdoms of the North, says the Lord; they shall come, and each shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, against all its surrounding walls.” Lest we think this was foretold in speech and not fulfilled in deed, Jeremiah himself says: “In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the city was opened, and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the middle gate.” Then an innumerable army was spread around the city of Jerusalem; the Holy of Holies and the armory, which was planted with a grove, were laid open by hostile devastation, and the enemy entered through every part of the city where the walls had been divided.

But as for the words, “You gathered the waters of the lower pool, counted the houses of Jerusalem, and demolished houses to fortify the wall; you made a reservoir between the two walls and the water of the old pool, and you did not look to him who made it, nor did you see its maker from afar”: he relates how they prepared for the siege around the city, transferred the waters of the lower pool, which could be taken for the upper water-fortification, built walls out of demolished houses, took from each family’s houses as much as they possessed, and restored anew a cistern between the two walls and the old pool for preserving water. Yet they did not rather invoke the aid of God, the Lord who created the city and the pool—as though he had said in other words: You put your trust in man, not in God, who is man’s maker.

“And the Lord God of hosts,” he says, “called on that day for weeping and mourning, baldness and girding with sackcloth; but behold joy and gladness: killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’ And the voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears: ‘This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die,’ says the Lord God of hosts.” With captivity at hand and Jerusalem besieged, when sword, famine, and thirst pressed upon the city, Jeremiah summoned it to repentance; whereas kings, princes, and the wretched populace, in the despair of those perishing, gave themselves over to feasts. Nothing so offends God as a stiff neck after sins, and contempt arising from despair. Hence he speaks also through Amos: “For three and four impieties I will not turn him back: because he has both conceived and done it, has not repented, and moreover has taught evil (Amos 2).” Hence it is said now: “This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die.”

“Now Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had given orders concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, saying: ‘Take him, keep your eyes upon him, do him no harm, but do with him whatever he wishes.’ So Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, and Nebushazban, Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer, Rab-mag, and all the nobles of the king of Babylon sent and took Jeremiah from the court of the prison [Col. 1083D] and handed him over to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, [Col. 1084A] that he might go home and live among the people.”

The Lord is just, and his judgment is right: he renders to each according to his works. Accordingly, as through the ministers of the scourge he inflicts deserved punishments upon the proud and contemptuous, so through those same ministers he bestows upon the gentle and obedient the care due to mercy and consolation. This has now been made clear in King Zedekiah and the prophet Jeremiah through the decree of King Nebuchadnezzar. Nor is it surprising that he appoints different rewards to different persons through the same human beings, since from the same elements he bestows different recompenses upon elect and reprobate according to the quality of their merits. For the water of the Red Sea, which preserved the Israelites, worshippers of God, unharmed, killed the idolatrous Egyptians (Exod. 14). Likewise, the flame of the furnace, which cruelly killed the ministers of the king of Babylon beside the furnace, preserved unharmed in the midst of the fire the boys who praised and blessed the Lord (Dan. 3). Hence the wise man says in praise of God: “For creation, serving you its maker, is inflamed for the punishment of the unjust, and becomes gentler for the benefit of those who trust in you (Wis. 16).” This same point is shown below, when it is said:

“The word of the Lord had come to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the prison, saying: ‘Go and speak to Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, saying: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I shall bring my words upon this city for evil and not for good, and they shall be before your eyes on that day. But I shall deliver you on that day, says the Lord, and you shall not be handed over into the hands of the men whom you fear. Rather, rescuing, I shall rescue you; you shall not fall by the sword, but your life shall be yours as a salvation, because you have trusted in me, says the Lord.’”

(MAURUS.) All who hope in the Lord shall not be confounded, but “let the wicked who do vain things be confounded (Ps. 42).” Behold, the rulers who sought Jeremiah for the punishment of prison suffered the vengeance of Chaldean captivity. But this eunuch, who freed the prophet from prison, obtained perfect freedom as the Lord’s reward. If, however, you consider the allegory that we set forth above concerning this Ethiopian eunuch, you find the same meaning: when holy preachers have been delivered from future destruction, their persecutors shall perish in everlasting vengeance.

# BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 1083]

Having described the devastation of the city, the destruction and captivity of the Jewish people together with their faithless king, let us now begin to recount what happened to Jeremiah and to the remnant of the people, and how the same prophet, by the word of the Lord, admonished the very small portion of the surviving people to remain securely in their own land and serve the king of Babylon. But they, despising God’s command, chose rather to migrate to Egypt, where Nebuchadnezzar afterward found and slaughtered them, and at the same time devastated the land of Egypt. The present prophet did not pass this over in silence either, but foretold it to them beforehand as a future of clear salvation.

## CHAPTER XL. Jeremiah is set free; he foretells to Johanan Gedaliah’s death at Ishmael’s hands, which befell him.

“Here is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, had released him from Ramah, when he had taken him bound in chains among all those who were departing from Jerusalem and Judah and being led away to Babylon. The commander of the army therefore took Jeremiah and said to him: ‘The Lord your God spoke this evil concerning this place, and he brought it about; the Lord did as he had spoken, because you sinned against the Lord and did not obey his voice, and this word has come upon you. Now, behold, today I release you from the chains that are on your hands. If it pleases you to come with me to Babylon, come, and I will keep my eyes upon you. But if it displeases you to come with me to Babylon, remain here. Behold, the whole land is before you; wherever you choose and wherever it pleases you to go, go there, and do not come with me. But live with Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon has appointed over the cities of Judah. Live with him among the people, or wherever it pleases you to go, go there.’ The commander of the army also gave him provisions and gifts, and dismissed him.” (MAURUS.) It is asked how this word of the Lord is here described as having come to Jeremiah, when it is not shown what that word was or what it disclosed. Hence, unless I am mistaken, it is implied that the prophet wished secretly to indicate, through this word spoken to him, that his own release by the commander of the army had taken place through divine providence, just as that same Nebuzaradan said to Jeremiah: “The Lord your God spoke this evil, because you sinned against the Lord and did not obey his voice.” Thus, if those who sinned against the Lord and did not obey his voice were handed over into captivity according to the word of the Lord, this man, who reproved sinners and obeyed the Lord’s command, was, according to his promise, delivered from the hands of his enemies [Col. 1085C] and from the prison-house.

“Then Jeremiah came to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah, and lived with him among the people who had been left in the land. When all the commanders of the army who had been scattered through the regions, they and their companions, heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over the land, and that he had entrusted to him men, women, and children, and some of the poor of the land who had not been deported to Babylon, they came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Jonathan, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ophai who were from Netophah, and Jezaniah son of the Maacathite, they and their men. Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan swore to them and to their companions, saying: ‘Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you. Behold, I am dwelling at Mizpah, so that I may answer the command of the Chaldeans who are sent to us. But you, gather grapes, harvest, and oil, and store them in your vessels, and remain in your cities that you occupy.’

“Moreover, all the Jews who were in Moab, among the Ammonites, in Edom, and in all the regions, when they heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed over them Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, all the Jews, I say, returned from all the places to which they had fled, and came to Gedaliah in the land of Judah, at Mizpah, [Col. 1086A] and gathered wine and an exceedingly abundant harvest.”

The Lord’s mercies are exceedingly numerous, and his judgments are a deep abyss. Just as he rightly chastised sinners and transgressors of his law, so he mercifully brought the help of his consolation to the humble and obedient. Through the very enemies by whom he punished the faithful king and his rebellious ministers, he also appointed Gedaliah as protector of the remnant of his people, so that by his prudence the cultivation of the land might be carried on profitably, and those who had been scattered might be gathered again and dwell—if they were willing to obey the Lord’s commands—in their own land without fear of enemies or accusation.

Mystically, however, this same Gedaliah, whose name means “magnified by the Lord,” represents the holy preachers, who are appointed in the world by divine providence so that all the faithful and God-fearing may have a refuge and consolation by which they can endure and remain devoted to God’s service. They lay down their lives for their neighbors, and, setting up the shield of protection against the faithless, persist faithfully in their undertaken ministry even unto death. Therefore, just as the innocent Gedaliah was killed by the faithless and deceitful Ishmael, so these men, living innocently for Christ’s name, do not hesitate to undergo temporal death at the hands of persecutors of the Gospel and pursuers of the Christian religion. Concerning him it is also written:

“Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the army who were scattered through the regions came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and said to him: ‘Know that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life.’ But Gedaliah son of Ahikam did not believe them. Johanan son of Kareah said privately to Gedaliah at Mizpah: ‘I will go and strike Ishmael son of Nethaniah without anyone knowing, lest he take your life, and all the Jews who have gathered to you be scattered, and the remnant of Judah perish.’ Gedaliah son of Ahikam said to Johanan son of Kareah: ‘Do not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely about Ishmael.’”

## CHAPTER XLI. Ishmael kills Gedaliah and eighty men traveling to Jerusalem, sparing ten; Johanan flees with eight men to Egypt.

“And it came to pass in the seventh month that Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elishama, of royal descent, and the king’s nobles, and ten men with him came to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah, and they ate bread there together at Mizpah. Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the ten men who were with him arose and struck Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan with the sword, and killed the man whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land. Ishmael also struck all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldeans found there, and the men of war.

“On the second day after he had killed Gedaliah, while no one yet knew of it, eighty men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, with shaven beards, torn garments, and covered with filth; [Col. 1087A] they had gifts and incense in their hands, to offer them in the house of the Lord. Ishmael son of Nethaniah therefore went out from Mizpah to meet them, walking and weeping. When he met them, he said to them: ‘Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.’ When they had come to the middle of the city, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, together with the men who were with him, killed them beside the middle of the cistern. Ten men, however, were found among them who said to Ishmael: ‘Do not kill us, because we have a treasure in the field—of wheat, barley, oil, and honey.’ So he stopped and did not kill them with their brothers.”

(Greg.) This fraud was indeed carried out historically by Ishmael, but now it is enacted spiritually every day in the world by the ancient enemy. We must understand that the ancient enemy attacks our good deeds in three ways, so that what is done rightly before human beings may be corrupted in the sight of the interior Judge.

Sometimes he pollutes the intention in a good work, so that everything that follows in the action is not pure and clean, because he disturbs it from the beginning. Sometimes he cannot corrupt the intention of the good work, but places an obstacle in the action itself, as on a journey, so that when someone more confidently proceeds from the purpose of his mind, he is secretly overtaken by a vice and is destroyed as though by ambush. Sometimes, however, he corrupts neither the intention nor the course of the journey, but ensnares the good work at the end of the action. Since the Psalmist had perceived that snares lie in the path for those who begin well, he rightly said, filled with the prophetic spirit: “On this path on which I was walking, they hid a snare for me” [Col. 1087C].

Jeremiah indicates this well and subtly. While he took care to report events outside us, he showed what takes place within us, saying:

“Eighty men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, with shaven beards, torn garments, and covered with filth; they had gifts and incense in their hands, to offer them in the house of the Lord. Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, walking and weeping. When he met them, he said to them: ‘Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.’ When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them.”

Those shave their beards who remove confidence in their own strength. They tear their garments who do not spare themselves the rending of their inner beauty. They come intending to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord who promise to present themselves in God’s sacrifice with prayer and good works. Yet if they do not carefully watch themselves on the very path of holy devotion, Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes out to meet them. For every evil spirit, begotten in the error of pride after the example of its first father, Satan, sets himself down to lay a snare.

Of him it is also said: “He went walking and weeping.” For in order to prevail in striking down devout minds, he hides himself as though under a veil of virtue; and while he pretends to grieve together with those who truly mourn, he is admitted more securely into the depths of the heart and kills whatever virtue lies hidden within, since he often promises to raise a person to higher things. Hence he is reported to have said: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” While he promises greater things, he also takes away lesser ones. Thus it is rightly said: “When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them.” He kills the men who come to offer gifts to God in the middle of the city because minds devoted to divine things, unless they guard themselves with great vigilance, lose their life in the very course of their journey while the enemy steals upon them as they carry the offering of their devotion. No one escapes the hand of this enemy unless he hastens to repentance.

Therefore it is added there: “Ten men were found among them who said to Ishmael: ‘Do not kill us, because we have treasures in the field—of wheat, barley, oil, and honey’; and he did not kill them.” A treasure in the field is hope in repentance. Since it is not seen, it is held as though buried in the soil of the heart. Those who had treasures in the field were therefore saved, because after the fault of their carelessness they return to lamentation and do not die captive.

But when the ancient enemy strikes neither at the beginning of the intention nor in the course of the action, he displays harsher snares at the end. He besieges a person all the more wickedly the more he seems to himself to have been left alone to deceive. The prophet had perceived these snares placed at the end when he said: “They will watch my heel” (Ps. LV). Since the heel is the end of the body, what is signified by it except the end of an action? Whether evil spirits or wicked people who follow their pride watch the heel, they do so when they desire to corrupt the end of a good action.

“The cistern into which Ishmael threw all the corpses of the men whom he had struck because of Gedaliah is the one that King Asa made because of Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael filled it with the slain.”

(MAURUS.) The Book of Kings (III Kings XV) relates that Baasha, king of Israel, went up into Judah and built Ramah so that no one could go out or enter from the territory of Asa king of Judah. When Asa king of Judah heard this, he sent to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, offering him many gifts of gold and silver, so that he would break the treaty he had with Baasha king of Israel and bring him aid against him. Ben-hadad sent the commanders of his army into the cities of Israel, and they struck Aijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth—that is, the whole land of Naphtali.

When Baasha heard this, he stopped building Ramah and returned to his own land. King Asa then sent a message throughout Judah, so that no one would be excused. They took away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had built it, and King Asa built from them Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. This is what the text now says: that Asa made a cistern because of Baasha king of Israel, and that Ishmael filled it with the slain. It could have happened that, among the other buildings that King Asa constructed at Mizpah, he made this cistern mentioned by Scripture for some necessary purpose.

Mystically, however, whoever the spiritual Ishmael—the savage and cruel one whose hand is raised against everyone and always ready to do harm—kills by deceit or fraud, he will hurl into the lake of eternal sulfur and fire.

[Col. 1089A] “Ishmael took captive all the remnant of the people who were at Mizpah, the king’s daughters and all the people who remained at Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Ishmael son of Nethaniah took them captive and departed to cross over to the Ammonites. Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the warriors who were with him heard of all the evil that Ishmael son of Nethaniah had done, and taking all the men, they set out to fight against Ishmael son of Nethaniah,” and what follows.

Ishmael takes captive the remnant of the people who were at Mizpah, just as the evil spirit, by seducing them with vices, corrupts and binds with sins the faithful who are engaged in contemplation and meditation on God’s law, or in the mirror of the virtues. He also takes the king’s daughters—that is, noble souls, concerning whom Peter says: “You are a royal and priestly race” (I Peter II). He does this in order to transfer them to the Ammonites, whose name is interpreted as “people of sorrow,” and to make them participants and companions in the destruction of the condemned, who remain in everlasting sorrow.

Against him Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the warriors who are with him contend. Holy teachers and men of virtue, strengthened by God’s grace and mercy—for this is what “Johanan” signifies—fight against spiritual wickedness, bring back the captivity, and through repentance and correction of error restore it to the holy Church, so that the one who had plundered may depart in confusion and, once defeated, lose the captivity he had held unjustly. For, as the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and flee from us” (Ephesians VI).

“Then Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the warriors who were with him took all the remnant of the common people whom he had brought back from Ishmael son of Nethaniah from Mizpah, after he had struck Gedaliah son of Ahikam: warriors for battle, women, children, and eunuchs whom he had brought back from Gibeon. They departed and settled as sojourners at Geruth Chimham, which is near Bethlehem, in order to go on and enter Egypt because of the Chaldeans. For they were afraid of them, because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had struck Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land of Judah,” and so forth, up to the place written in Chapter XLIII.

## CHAPTERS XLII AND XLIII. Jeremiah is asked to consult the Lord on behalf of the remnant and receives the answer: “Do not enter Egypt.” Concerning Jeremiah’s words to the people whom Johanan leads into Egypt: Jeremiah sets up stones at Taphnis, concerning which he says that the king of Babylon will come.

“Behold, I will send for and bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne upon these stones that I have hidden; and he will set his royal seat upon them. He will come and strike the land of Egypt: those destined for death, to death; those destined for captivity, to captivity; and those destined for the sword, to the sword. He will kindle a fire in the shrines of the gods of Egypt and burn them, and he will lead them captive. He will wrap himself in the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, and he will depart from there in peace. He will shatter the statues of the House of the Sun that are in the land of Egypt, and he will burn the shrines of the gods of Egypt with fire.”

(Maurus.) This flight of the remnant of the Israelite people, and their journey into Egypt contrary to the word of the Lord, which the prophet Jeremiah unfolded at length in three chapters—that is, chapters 154, 155, and 156—Isaiah foretold long ago, one hundred and fifty years earlier, namely, the number of years between Isaiah and Jeremiah. For it is written in the book of the prophet Isaiah:

“Woe to the rebellious sons, says the Lord, who make a plan, but not from me, and weave a web, but not by my spirit, adding sin upon sin; who go down to descend into Egypt and have not asked my mouth, hoping for help in Pharaoh’s strength and trusting in the shadow of Egypt. Pharaoh’s strength will be for you a shame, and trust in the shadow of Egypt a disgrace. For your princes went to Taphnis, and your messengers reached as far as Taphnes. All were ashamed because of the people who could not benefit them; they were not for help or any advantage, but for shame and reproach” (Isaiah XXX).

(Hieron.) He foretells this history, which we read in the volume of Jeremiah: after Jerusalem had been overthrown and all its wealth and its princes had been carried away to Babylon, Gedaliah son of Ahikam, a man of royal descent, was appointed over those who remained in Judah. After he was treacherously killed with his Chaldean companions, all the commanders of the warriors, Johanan son of Kareah, Jeconiah son of Hoshea, and the rest of the common people, from the least to the greatest, came to Jeremiah the prophet and said to him:

“Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God for all this remnant, because we have been left few from many, as your eyes behold us. May the Lord your God announce to us the way by which we should go and the word that we should do.”

When Jeremiah had answered them after ten days, in accordance with the word of the Lord:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: If you remain quietly in this land, I will build you up and not destroy you; I will plant you and not uproot you, for I have relented concerning the evil that I have done to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you fear in terror.”

And shortly afterward:

“But if you say, ‘We will not remain in this land,’ and set your faces to enter Egypt, and enter there to dwell, the sword that you fear will overtake you there, and the famine about which you are anxious will cling to you in Egypt, and there you will die.”

The proud men answered Jeremiah, saying:

“You are speaking falsehood. The Lord our God did not send you, saying, ‘Do not enter Egypt to dwell there’; rather, Baruch son of Neriah has incited you against us, in order to hand us over to the Chaldeans, so that they may kill us and lead us away to Babylon.”

Finally, all the commanders of the people, gathering the remnant together with the women, the children, and the king’s daughters, did not obey the voice of the Lord. They entered Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and came to Taphnis. There Jeremiah, as a sign of the future captivity, prophesied against the disobedient people the things contained in his book.

What was therefore to happen afterward is foretold many years in advance. They are called “rebellious sons” because, having abandoned the counsel of God that they had received through Jeremiah, they followed their own will and wove their web not by the Spirit of God, which spoke through Jeremiah’s mouth. “Weaving your web” is used metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*) to signify a wicked plan. They did this in order to increase their former sins by the sin of proud contempt.

“You who went down,” he says, “into Egypt, and you did not ask my mouth”—not because they had asked, but because they did not wish to hear the prophet’s counsel. They hoped for help in Pharaoh’s strength and trusted in the protection, or shadow, of Egypt. Among the Egyptians, Pharaoh is the name of royal power; each individual king is called by a distinctive name, such as Pharaoh Neco and Pharaoh Hophra, just as if we were to place “Caesars” and “Augusti” before the proper royal names of kings.

“And Pharaoh’s strength,” he says, “will be for you a shame, and trust in the shadow of Egypt a disgrace.” Jeremiah writes that he buried stones in the city of Tanis, at the gate of Pharaoh’s house, and said to the Jewish men:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send for and bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne upon these stones that I have hidden, and he will set his royal seat upon them. He will come and strike the land of Egypt: those destined for death, to death; those destined for captivity, to captivity; and those destined for the sword, to the sword. He will kindle a fire in the shrines of the gods of Egypt and burn them, and he will lead them captive. He will wrap himself in the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, and he will depart from there in peace. He will shatter the statues of the House of the Sun that are in the land of Egypt, and he will burn the shrines of the gods of Egypt with fire.”

(MAURUS.) After the Egyptians had been overcome, the Jews who had fled to the Egyptians were also taken captive. As for what follows—“Your princes were in Taphnis, and your messengers reached as far as Tanis”—it should be read with mockery and emphasis (*ἐμφατικῶς*): they disregarded God’s counsel and sent their princes to Tanis, a city of Egypt in which Pharaoh’s royal palace stood, and where, under Moses, many signs and wonders were performed, as the Psalm says: “He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis” (Psalm LXXVII).

Isaiah likewise speaks against Egypt:

“Where are your wise men now? Let them announce to you and say what the Lord Sabaoth has planned against Egypt. The princes of Tanis have failed” (Isaiah XIX).

He says that they failed at the time when the Lord entered Egypt upon a swift cloud. We do not read elsewhere of a city of Egypt called Tanis; but from the statement, “Your messengers reached as far as Tanis,” we understand it to be the last city of Egypt, near the Ethiopians and the Blemmyes. For this reason the Septuagint translated:

“The evil messengers will labor in vain, those who trusted in the people of Egypt, who could not benefit them, and they were for everlasting reproach.”

Some think that this passage was written against the ten tribes in Samaria, because, while seeking aid from the Egyptians, they were captured by the Assyrians.

According to the tropological interpretation, all who, having despised the worship of God, return to their vomit (Proverbs XXVI), and, having lost the name of sons, are called shameless dogs, form a plan not through the Lord and make a covenant not through the Spirit of the Lord. They add sins to sins, so that, overcome by flattering vices, they also accept the perversity of false doctrines. They descend into the darkness of Egypt, seeking the help of Pharaoh, who reigns in Egypt, whose protection leads to disgrace and everlasting reproach.

For in Tanis—that is, in the command, humble and cast down—are its worst princes, evil messengers who labor in vain over a people who cannot benefit them. Just as the salvation of disciples brings joy to holy teachers, so the destruction of the deceivers destroys the patriarchs of those who had fled for help to Egypt.

## CHAPTER XLIV. The prophet rebukes the people for disobedience and idolatry; he threatens them with sword, death, and famine; they do not listen, and therefore the Lord destroys them, giving a sign.

“The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews who dwell in the land of Egypt, who live at Migdol, Taphnis, and in the land of Pathros, saying:

‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: You have seen this evil that I brought upon Jerusalem and upon all the cities of Judah. Behold, they are desolate today, and there is no inhabitant in them, because of the evil that they committed, provoking me to anger, going away and sacrificing to and worshiping foreign gods whom neither they nor you nor your fathers knew. I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them, saying: “Do not do this abominable thing”; but they did not listen or incline their ear, so that they might turn from their evil ways and not sacrifice to foreign gods,’” and so forth.

[Col. 1092D] (MAURUS.) Just as in the land of Judah the prophet opposed the remnant of the Israelites, contradicting them with the word of the Lord so that they would not enter Egypt, so also, when they had settled in the land of Egypt, he announced the word of the Lord to them: because he was angered by their disobedience, he had prepared vengeance for them, and would punish and destroy them as he had punished their fathers, by sword, famine, and pestilence.

Migdol is therefore a city of Egypt, to which the children of Israel came after they had gone out of Egypt, before they crossed the Red Sea. We also read in Ezekiel: “From Migdol to Syene.” Likewise, Taphnis is a city of Egypt, as was shown above; and Pathros is a region of Egypt, as was also shown above, according to Ezekiel (Ezekiel XXXVI) and Jeremiah, in which the Jewish fugitives lived.

When he says, “I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending them, saying: ‘Do not do this abominable thing,’” he displays the Lord’s immense clemency, and the vigilance and diligence of his prophets, who proclaimed the word of God earnestly, not lazily, to those to whom they had been sent. He rebukes lukewarm teachers who now sleep in the Church, devote themselves to leisure and worldly pleasures, and do not care to announce God’s will to his people or turn them from sins to the practice of good works.

Nor do I think it should be passed over that Isaiah called these same Jews “beasts of the south,” because of the stupidity of their understanding, by which, abandoning God’s counsel, they fled to the images of Egypt and placed their hope in Pharaoh—one who trusts in him is like someone leaning on a reed that breaks and wounds the hand of the one who leans upon it. For it is written there:

“Burden of the beasts of the south. In a land of tribulation and distress, the lioness and the lion, and from them the viper and the flying basilisk, carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts and their treasures upon the humps of camels, to a people who cannot benefit them. The Egyptians will help in vain and to no purpose” (Ezekiel XXX).

(Hieron.) The land of tribulation and distress signifies the immense desolation of the desert, through which the remnant of Jerusalem, together with Johanan son of Kareah and the daughters of King Zedekiah, fled to Egypt after taking away everything they were able to possess.

Understand the lioness and the lion’s cub metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*) as Jerusalem and its people, as Balaam says in Numbers:

“Behold, the people will rise like a lioness and lift itself like a lion. It will not lie down until it devours the prey and drinks the blood of the slain” (Numbers XXIII).

The viper and the flying basilisk—or flying offspring of asps—signify the same thing: children born worse from evil parents. Concerning them the Gospel also said: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew III).

And it is said to the land of Israel: “You are a land on which no rain fell and no shower came in the day of wrath” (Amos IV), whose princes are in its midst like roaring lions, seizing prey and devouring souls by force.

These offspring of vipers, or flying asps—that is, the princes of the people and the whole crowd of the ungodly—fled to a people who could not benefit them. Jeremiah says that the Lord would deliver Pharaoh Hophra, king of Egypt, into the hands of his enemies and into the hands of those who sought his life, so that all the men of Judah who were in the land of Egypt would be consumed by sword and famine, to utter destruction. The Hebrews therefore assert that, before Nebuchadnezzar captured Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch escaped the impending captivity by death.

“All the men who knew that their wives sacrificed to foreign gods, and all the women who stood there in a great assembly, and all the people who lived in the land of Egypt, in Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying:

‘As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you. Rather, we will certainly carry out every word that proceeds from our mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her, just as we and our fathers, our kings, and our princes did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. Then we were filled with bread, it went well with us, and we saw no evil. But from the time when we stopped sacrificing to the queen of heaven and pouring out libations to her, we have lacked everything, and we have been consumed by sword and famine. And if we sacrifice to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her, do we perhaps do this without our husbands? We make cakes for her worship and pour out libations to her.’

Jeremiah said to all the people, to the men and to the women, and to all the populace who had answered him in this way:

‘Did not the sacrifices that you offered in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem—you and your fathers, your kings and your princes, and the people of the land—come to the Lord’s remembrance and rise upon his heart? The Lord could no longer bear it because of the evil of your practices and because of the abominations that you committed. Therefore your land became a desolation, a horror, and a curse, without an inhabitant, as it is today,’” and so forth.

(MAURUS.) O crooked and perverse generation, children in whom not faith but wickedness holds sway, a foolish and senseless people, always repaying the Lord’s benefits with the opposite and provoking him by their evil deeds! See how foolishly they speak in answer to the Lord’s prophet:

“As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you; rather, we will certainly carry out every word that proceeds from our mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her, just as we and our fathers, our kings, and our princes did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. Then we were filled with bread, it went well with us, and we saw no evil.”

They forgot his benefits and his wonders, which he displayed before their fathers, and which sacred Scripture sufficiently recounts: how he rained manna upon them from heaven, and “man ate the bread of angels; he sent them food in abundance; he drove the nations out from before them and allotted their land to them by lot, by the measuring line of their inheritance, and he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents. Yet they tested and provoked God Most High and did not keep his testimonies. They turned away and did not observe the covenant, as their fathers had turned aside like a crooked bow. They provoked him to anger on their hills and aroused him to jealousy with their carved images. God heard and rejected them, and utterly reduced Israel to nothing. He gave their strength into captivity and their beauty into the hand of the enemy; he shut his people up in the sword and rejected his inheritance. Their haters ruled over them, and their enemies afflicted them” (Psalm LXXVII)—and deservedly so.

For all the mountains, valleys, and torrents were full of the worship of demons. Concerning these Jeremiah now speaks, saying that fathers and sons carried wood and kindled fire in order to make *χαυῶνας* for the army of heaven—that is, cakes or wafers for all the stars—with women grinding and mixing flour and fat, in order to provoke God to anger. There is no doubt what he means by “cakes,” whether cakes or small pastries prepared by a craftsman’s hand; for in our language this is what *χαυῶνας* signifies.

Concerning these, Moses had sung prophetically in the song of Deuteronomy, speaking in the person of the Lord:

“They provoked me with foreign gods and angered me with their abominations; they sacrificed to demons and not to God” (Deuteronomy XXXI).

“And they did this by their own will,” because it lies within our power to choose good or evil. As was said above, some call the queen of heaven the moon; others call her Juno, sister of Jupiter, or Berecynthia, wife of Saturn and mother of the gods. They falsely attributed the name of majesty to these, since “all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm XCV).

Mystically, however, all heretics, situated in the Egypt of this world—that is, in the darkness of error—offer sacrifices and libations not to the true God but to false divinities, when they compose perverse fictions and corrupt doctrines in order to deceive human beings and overturn the true faith. Therefore evils will come upon them, and they will be a desolation, a horror, and a curse, because they sinned against the Lord and did not obey his voice, and because they did not walk by the straight path of catholic confession, either in his law, or in his commandments and testimonies.

“Jeremiah said to all the people and to all the women: ‘Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah who are in the land of Egypt. Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: You and your wives have spoken with your mouths and fulfilled with your hands, saying: “Let us perform our vows that we vowed, so that we may sacrifice to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her.” You have fulfilled your vows and carried them out in deed. Therefore hear the word of the Lord, all Judah who dwell in the land of Egypt. Behold, I have sworn by my great name, says the Lord, that my name shall no longer be called upon by the mouth of any Judean man who says: “As the Lord God lives in all the land of Egypt.” Behold, I shall watch over them for evil and not for good, and all the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by sword and famine until they are completely destroyed. Those who escape the sword shall return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah—few men—and all the remnant of Judah who entered the land of Egypt to dwell there shall know whose word shall stand, mine or theirs.’”

The prophet, speaking the word of the Lord, declares that the name of the Lord shall no longer be called upon by the mouth of any Judean man who says: “As the Lord God lives in all the land of Egypt.” For those who had gone there contrary to the divine command did not deserve to have the Lord’s protection there. After their adversaries had been consumed by sword and famine, the few who could escape the sword returned from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, so that the posterity of the ancient stock might be preserved.

Spiritually, however, the name of the Lord is not called upon by the mouth of any heretic in the land of Egypt, because, as long as they remain in error, their speech is proved to be not a prayer pleasing to God but the most wicked blasphemy. Hence it is written: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner”; “Let deceitful lips be struck dumb, which speak wickedness against this one in pride and contempt.” Therefore whoever persists in the error he has conceived will perish by the sword of God’s just judgment. But those who, abandoning their error, return from the land of Egypt to the land of Judah, and thereafter rightly follow the Catholic faith in all things while doing penance, will be saved.

[Col. 1096B] “‘And this shall be a sign for you,’ says the Lord, ‘that I shall visit you in this place, so that you may know that my words against you shall truly be fulfilled for evil. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall deliver Pharaoh Ephree, king of Egypt, into the hand of his enemies and into the hand of those who seek his life, just as I delivered Zedekiah, king of Judah, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, his enemy and the one who sought his life.’”

It was entirely fitting that the Lord gave Ephree, or Vaphre, king of Egypt, as a sign of the devastation of Judah, so that when the Jews saw captured and killed the one in whom they had placed their hope of deliverance, they might return to the aid of their true liberator. Histories report that Vaphre ruled Egypt for thirty years. [Col. 1096C] In his sixth year, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, after capturing Jerusalem, burned the Temple, which had stood from the beginning of its construction for 442 years.

Clement agrees with this account in the first book of the *Stromata*, testifying that the captivity of the Jews occurred in the forty-eighth Olympiad, when Vaphres was reigning among the Egyptians and Phoenippus at Athens. He also reckons the seventy years of the Temple’s desolation up to the second year of Darius.

Josephus, in the tenth book of his *Antiquities*, relates the following about this Egyptian, saying:

“Now Nebuchadnezzar, after he had lived forty years, died, an energetic man and much more fortunate than the preceding kings. Berossus also mentions this event in the third book of his *History of the Chaldeans*, saying:

‘When the father of Nebuchadnezzar heard that the satrap appointed by him over Egypt, the regions of Lower Syria, and Phoenicia had revolted from him, and since he himself was no longer able to undertake the campaign, he entrusted a part of the army to his young son Nebuchadnezzar and sent him against the rebel. Nebuchadnezzar engaged the man who had revolted from his father, fought him, defeated him, and from this beginning brought the province under his rule.

At that time it happened that his father Nebuchadnezzar fell ill in the city of Babylon and departed this life. He had reigned twenty-one years. Nebuchadnezzar, shortly afterward learning of his father’s death, arranged the affairs of Egypt and the remaining province, as well as the captives from Egypt, Phoenicia, Syria, and the other peoples. He ordered certain friends to transport everything to Babylon with great strength and all due care. He himself came to Babylon with a few men through the desert and, having taken possession of the affairs then administered by the Chaldeans, became master of the entire paternal kingdom, after a certain very distinguished man had preserved the kingdom for him.’”

## CHAPTER XLV  
Baruch is rebuked by Jeremiah for faintheartedness; nevertheless, salvation is promised to him.

The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to “Baruch son of Neriah, when he had written these words in a book from the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,” saying:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel to you, Baruch: You said, ‘Woe is me, poor man that I am, for the Lord has added sorrow to my sorrow. I have labored with my groaning, and I have found no rest.’ Thus says the Lord: ‘This is what you shall say to him: Behold, I destroy those whom I built, and I uproot those whom I planted—and this entire land—and you seek great things for yourself? Do not seek them, because behold, I shall bring evil upon all flesh,’ says the Lord, ‘but I shall give you your life for your salvation in all the places to which you go.”’”

Still inexperienced and imperfect in enduring the sufferings that he would later undergo, Baruch was terrified by the calamity of the captivity that was already threatening the city in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. Therefore he complains that sorrow has been added to his sorrow, but he receives a divine response: he is seeking in vain to have peace granted to him when the entire people are struggling beneath the burden of various tribulations.

It seems to me, therefore, that he represents those who, amid the pressures of the persecutions with which the Church is afflicted in the present age, waver through faintheartedness, wishing to possess in the present the consolation that is promised in the future life to those who fight the good fight. “For all,” as the Apostle says, “who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Hence the Savior says to his disciples: “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 15). And again: “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be changed into joy.” And again: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Mark 8). And again: “You will be hated by all because of my name; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Luke 21). And again: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER XLVI  
The word of the Lord against Egypt and its cities; mercy is promised to Israel.

“The word that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations, concerning Egypt and the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was beside the river Euphrates at Carchemish, whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, struck down in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah.”

(MAURUS.) Until now the prophet has spoken intermittently about Judah and Israel, and about the Chaldeans and Egyptians, as the opportunity for his narrative presented itself. From this point, however, he brings forth the word of the Lord addressed individually to various nations and provinces: to Egypt, the Philistines, the Moabites, the Ammonites, Edom, Kedar, Elam, and finally Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. Isaiah called such a word by the name of a “burden.” Thus each nation may know what it has done against the Lord’s will and what punishment it will consequently suffer.

He therefore first turns his speech to Egypt, which was especially a stumbling block to the Jewish people, recalling when this embassy or oracle was delivered: in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, when Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, fought against Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, at Carchemish and was crushed and defeated by him.

But since the divine history does not openly show how this occurred, I thought it necessary to place Josephus’s account here. In the tenth book of his *Antiquities* he narrates as follows:

“Now the king of the Egyptians, after returning from the battle, summoned Jehoiakim to himself from the Syrian city called Hamath. When he came, he immediately bound him and gave the kingdom to his elder brother, born of the same father, whose name was Eliakim. He imposed upon the province a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. Jehoiakim paid this money.

But he led Jehoahaz away to Egypt; he also died there after reigning for three months and ten days. Jehoiakim’s mother was called Zebudah, from the city of Abuma. This man was by nature unjust and exceedingly wicked, neither holy toward God nor gentle toward human beings.

When he was in the fourth year of his reign, a certain man named Nebuchadnezzar assumed the rule of Babylonia. At that time he came with a great force to the city of Carchemish, which is beside the Euphrates, intending to fight against Neco, king of Egypt—for all Syria was under his authority. When Neco learned the intention of the king of Babylon, he was not at all afraid, but came to the Euphrates with great force against Nebuchadnezzar. After the battle was joined, he was defeated and lost many thousands through the fortunes of war.

The king of Babylon crossed the Euphrates and seized all Syria as far as Pelusium, except Judea. Therefore, in the fourth year of Nebuchadnezzar—which was the eighth year of Jehoiakim, king of the Hebrews—he encamped against the Jews with a large army, intending either to exact tribute from Jehoiakim or to fight him. Jehoiakim, fearing his threats and desiring peace, paid him the tribute he had ordered for three years.

But in the third year, when he heard that the Egyptians were again going to fight against Babylon, he did not pay the tribute. He himself, however, was deceived by the report [rumore] of the Egyptian war, for the Egyptians did not dare to fight against him.””
