(MAURUS.) As Scripture testifies, the Jews were always turned in their hearts toward Egypt. They trusted not in God’s strength but in a human arm and in a broken reed for support; therefore they rightly fell before their enemies. So also anyone who, abandoning the one true God, places hope in the aid of this fragile world will be unable to withstand the most wicked enemies—namely, evil spirits—but will be ensnared, captured, and crushed by their wicked devices.

Thus we can call the place in which we dwell, and the world that lies in the power of the evil one, “Egypt,” especially because, as is said, *Egypt* is interpreted as “troubling” and “returning to distress.” And truly, the broad and spacious way of this world leads to perpetual tribulation and distress. Let us therefore see what the prophet says next to Egypt.

“Prepare shield and buckler, and go forth to battle. Harness the horses and mount the riders. Stand in your helmets; polish the spears; put on your breastplates. What then? I saw them terrified and turning their backs; their warriors were struck down. They fled headlong and did not look back; terror on every side,” says the Lord. “Let not the swift flee, nor let the strong think that he can be saved. Beside the river Euphrates, toward the north, they were defeated and fell.”

By irony he urges the unwarlike and frightened Egyptians to take up arms and prepare the engines of war, though they do this in vain. For, terrified and turning their backs, they flee headlong; neither swift flight nor the strength of their arms can defend or save them against their enemies. Instead, they were suddenly defeated and fell by the sword of the Chaldeans toward the north, beside the river Euphrates.

“Who is this that rises like a river, whose channels swell like the streams? Egypt will rise like a river, and its waves will move like rivers, and it will say: ‘I shall cover the earth; I shall destroy the city and its inhabitants.’”

Because of the multitude of its peoples, he compares Egypt to a river and to streams. Through its arrogance, it rejoiced [the text reads *latitabant*, “they hid”; perhaps *laetabatur*, “it rejoiced”] that it would cover and destroy the land of Israel and the city of Jerusalem, or even the land of the Chaldeans and the city of Babylon with its inhabitants. For, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, Egypt shall be delivered into the hands of cruel rulers; a powerful king shall rule over them; the water of the sea shall dry up; the river shall be desolated and dried; the streams shall fail; and the canals shall become shallow and dry, while the reed and rush shall wither.

(HIERON.) It is natural that, when captivity comes through God’s anger, pestilence should follow his indignation, and that all the elements should rage against those who have offended God. Hence it is written by another prophet that birds in the air and fish in the waters shall fail, so that everything is withdrawn from human use.

Here we may understand the passage simply as referring to the drying up of the Nile and its channels. But if, metaphorically, we understand the kingdom by the river, its rulers by the channels, and all Egypt’s abundance by the greenery, rush, and papyrus, then Egypt’s works are described through these things, since Egypt is exceedingly fertile.

Mystically, however, when a powerful and harsh king has ruled over Egypt, all secular learning and the beauty of eloquence will dry up. The devil himself, the source of all rivers, from whom all lies arise, will be laid waste, so that the remaining rivers and channels, which were filled from the muddy waters of the Nile, will fail.

“Mount the horses and exult in the chariots. Let the warriors of Ethiopia and Libya come forth, holding shields, and the Lydians seize and shoot arrows. But that day belongs to the Lord God of hosts, a day of vengeance, to take vengeance on his enemies. The sword shall devour and be satisfied; it shall drink its fill of their blood. For there is a sacrifice of the Lord God of hosts in the land of the north, beside the river Euphrates.”

(MAURUS.) He commands them to mount horses and exult in chariots, and the warriors to come forth—that is, those who, through the pride of their minds, trust in their own power—from the regions bordering Egypt, namely Ethiopia, Libya, and Lydia, which were once regarded among the strongest nations and whose king was Croesus. Let them begin to fight so that the day of the Lord’s vengeance may take vengeance on his enemies, since they strive in vain when divine assistance is withdrawn.

Mystically, all heretics and schismatics who arise from different provinces devise things against the city of the Lord in vain, for they will not be able to overthrow it. “The gates of hell,” according to the Savior’s promise, “shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). Rather, on the day of the Lord’s vengeance, that sword will devour his enemies, of which it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32).

“And there shall be a sacrifice of the Lord in the land of the north, beside the river Euphrates”—that is, beside the flow of worldly pleasure, when they are delivered into the hands of him who set his throne toward the north and boasted that he would be like the Most High, so that he will cast them into the lake of fire and sulfur, where they will be tormented forever in both body and soul.

“Go up to Gilead and take balm, virgin daughter of Egypt. You will multiply medicines in vain; there will be no healing for you.”

(HIERON.) Gilead is a mountain joined to Mount Lebanon by the seven hills of Phoenicia and Arabia, and extending through the desert to the place beyond the Jordan where Sihon, king of the Amorites, once dwelt. The aforesaid mountain fell by lot to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh.

The Greeks call resin *rhētinē* (ῥητίνη), for in Greek *rhein* (ῥεῖν) means whatever flows. It is a tear exhaled through the sweating of trees—such as cherry, mastic, balsam, or other trees and shrubs said to sweat—as well as the fragrant trees of the East, such as drops of balsam, ferula, or amber, whose tear hardens into a gemstone.

The first is terebinth resin, the finest of all. It is brought from Arabia Petraea, Judea, Syria, Cyprus, and Africa, and also from the Cyclades islands. The second is mastic resin, called *myrtix*. This is brought from the island of Cissa. The third is pine resin, of which one kind is called *pitinēs*, another *petitinē*, one liquid and another dry; these are brought from the land of Colophon. Hence resin also took the name “Colophonian resin.”

For resin is smooth, suitable for the body, and used as medicine. Therefore Jeremiah also says: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why has healing not risen for the daughter of my people?” (Jer. 8).

Jacob also had this resin, which he sent to his son Joseph together with honey, terebinth, nuts, incense, and stacte (Gen. 43). The Ishmaelites who bought Joseph likewise carried incense, resin from Gilead, and stacte from the land of Israel into Egypt.

(MAURUS.) As we have already said above, the resin of Gilead is understood in many passages of Scripture as repentance and as the medicine of true conversion to God. Therefore the prophet exhorts Egypt and the provinces bordering it to repent of their error and evil deeds. If they do not do this, they will seek medicines from false gods in vain, since they will receive no healing from them but will find everlasting confusion. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1101B] “The nations have heard of your disgrace, and your wailing has filled the earth, because warrior has stumbled against warrior, and both have fallen together.”

Egypt’s disgrace became evident when, deprived of the aid it expected from false divinities, it fell before its enemies and collapsed through mutual slaughter with the mighty. So also heretics, who are always in disagreement and turn amid varied error, disagree with one another in many matters. Fighting at close quarters and tearing one another apart, they do not gain the victory of truth; rather, captives of error, they fall together into the pit of perdition.

“The word that the Lord spoke to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his striking the land of Egypt: ‘Announce it in Egypt and make it heard in Migdol; let it resound in Memphis; say to Tahpanhes: “Stand and prepare yourself, for the sword shall devour the things around you.”’”

The prophet speaks the word of the Lord to Egypt and to its principal places, telling them to prepare for war but also to know that the sword of the Chaldeans will devastate its entire land.

(HIERON.) Migdol is a place, as I mentioned above, to which the children of Israel came after leaving Egypt, before they crossed the Red Sea. We also read in Ezekiel: “from Migdol to Syene.” Moreover, Jeremiah reports that the Jews who had accompanied him, seeking to avoid the Babylonian attack, lived in this city of Egypt.

Tahpanhes was the metropolis of Egypt. The Psalmist declares that Moses performed many signs there (Ps. 77), which are described in Exodus: “He set his signs and wonders in Egypt, in the field of Zoan.” Memphis, too, devoted to magical arts, displays traces of its former error down to the present time.

Isaiah speaks to these cities in his oracle concerning Egypt: “The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis have withered; they have led Egypt astray, the corner-stone of its peoples” (Isa. 19). This briefly indicates that, through the Babylonian devastation, all the counsels of the magicians and the folly of those who promised knowledge of future things are exposed, and that at Christ’s coming everything is reduced to nothing. Egypt’s diviners will find no counsel by which they can suppress Christian doctrine.

It is an idiom of Scripture to use “corner” for a kingdom, because it contains peoples and, as it were, is the strongest part of an entire house. Hence Christ, who holds together the walls of two peoples, is called the cornerstone.

“Why has your mighty one rotted away? He did not stand, because the Lord overthrew him.”

(MAURUS.) By “the mighty one” he means either some idol or false god in whom the Egyptians trusted, or Pharaoh, on account of his royal power. He rightly rotted before his enemies, because he did not endure in victory but, putrefying with the decay of corruption, became foul; for the Lord’s just judgment overthrew him.

“He multiplied those who fell, and man fell beside his neighbor, and they said: ‘Rise, let us return to our people and to the land of our birth, away from the sword of the dove.’”

[Col. 1102B] Egypt multiplied those who fell, because, after its peoples had been delivered into the hands of their enemies, their pursuers struck them down. And just as the bold should have encouraged one another to fight, so the fearful incited one another to flee.

He calls Nebuchadnezzar a “dove,” not as praise but as reproach—not because of simplicity but because of stupidity. Although he had become victorious over various nations by the Lord’s gift, he gave the credit not to the one who had granted him victory but to false divinities.

It is not surprising that Nebuchadnezzar, who served by the Lord’s command in destroying treacherous Jerusalem, is called his servant and his dove, since the Medes whom he sent to overthrow Babylon are called “sanctified,” as he says through Isaiah: “I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have summoned my mighty men in my anger, exulting in my glory” (Isa. 13).

(HIERON.) The dove is therefore found used in praise, as in the command in the Gospel: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). That is, we are to be simple like doves and shrewd like serpents, imitating the simplicity of doves and the shrewdness of the serpent, so that we may neither harm others nor suffer ambushes from others. Through simplicity and prudence we are to display a balanced human character, because prudence without goodness is wickedness, and simplicity without reason is called stupidity.

The dove is also used as a reproach in Hosea, where we read: “Ephraim has become like a foolish dove without understanding. They called upon Egypt; they went to the Assyrians” (Hos. 7).

It may be asked why Ephraim is compared not to other birds but to a dove. Other birds hasten to protect their young even at the risk of their own lives. When they see a hawk, snake, raven, or crow approach their nest, they fly here and there, throw themselves upon the intruder, tear it with beak and claws, and express the parent’s grief with plaintive cries. The dove alone does not grieve for or seek its stolen young. Ephraim is rightly compared to it because, although its people were devastated in various places, it did not perceive this but was negligent regarding its own salvation.

“Call the name of Pharaoh, king of Egypt: ‘The time of tumult has arrived.’ ‘As I live,’ says the King—the Lord of hosts is his name—‘he shall come like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea.’”

(MAURUS.) The prophet commands those who have heard his prophecy concerning the slaughter of the Egyptians to announce to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, that the time of the tumult of war is near, which his enemies will wage against him.

When he confirms under the oath of the Lord of hosts that this tumult will come “like Tabor among the mountains and like Carmel by the sea,” he shows by comparing fertile places that a great overthrow threatens the Egyptians, as though fertile mountains were submerged in the sea.

(HIERON.) Tabor is the boundary of Zebulun, a mountain of remarkable rounded height in the middle of the Galilean plain, ten miles east of Diocaesarea. It was also a boundary between the tribes of Issachar and Naphtali.

Carmel, where Nabal once lived, is now a village called Chermela, ten miles from the town of Hebron, facing east; there is also a Roman garrison there.

(MAURUS.) Mystically, because Tabor is interpreted as “coming light,” or “let light come,” and Carmel as “tender,” “soft,” or “knowledge of circumcision,” they signify heretics who pride themselves on the light of secular wisdom, or Jews who are soft and pleasure-loving and glory in circumcision of the flesh. Those who remain under Pharaoh and refuse to serve Christ will be submerged in the turbulent sea of this age and will therefore come to everlasting condemnation.

“Make for yourself baggage for migration, inhabitant, daughter of Egypt, for Memphis shall become a desolation and shall be abandoned, uninhabitable.”

He commands Egypt to make baggage for migration—that is, to prepare bundles for flight—because its most famous city, where the practice of the magicians’ enchantments was especially renowned, will be turned into a desolation, and the land will be abandoned and uninhabitable.

The Lord speaks similarly to Ezekiel concerning baggage for migration, saying (Ezek. 12):

“You, therefore, son of man, make for yourself baggage for migration, and you shall migrate before them by day. You shall migrate from your place to another place in their sight, if perhaps they will look, for it is a provoking house. You shall bring out your baggage by day in their sight, like the baggage of one migrating. But you shall go out in the evening before them, as one migrating goes out before their eyes. Dig through a wall for yourself, and you shall go out through it in their sight. You shall carry it on your shoulders; you shall flee in darkness; you shall cover your face and shall not see the land, because I have made you a portent for the house of Israel.”

(HIERON.) There is no doubt that the whole content of this passage indicates the future captivity of King Zedekiah and the tribe of Judah, who was captured along with Jerusalem. Jeremiah the prophet and the history of the Kings relate that Zedekiah was captured by the Babylonians and Chaldeans and led from one place to another—from Jerusalem to Babylon.

The other actions that Ezekiel subsequently commands the prophet to perform are symbolic of what Zedekiah would actually do. “Gather your bundles,” he says, for these are the baggage of one migrating, in their sight. After they have seen what you are going to do, you shall go out in the evening in the likeness of one migrating.

We read that Zedekiah fled by night through a breach made in the wall toward the deserts of the Jordan, where he was captured by the Babylonians; this is what the pierced wall signifies. When he says, “You shall carry it on your shoulders,” the baggage is understood—whatever fugitives customarily carry for support on a journey.

“You shall bring it out in darkness,” so that no one may see you. “You shall cover your face,” either because blindness came upon him when Nebuchadnezzar removed his eyes, or so that he would not be recognized as the king himself and the concern of those guarding him would thereby increase.

“Egypt is a beautiful and graceful heifer; a goad from the north shall come against her.”

(MAURUS.) He calls Egypt a graceful heifer because its people, raised amid luxury and possessing untamed and wanton manners, refused to bear the yoke of discipline. A goad—that is, Nebuchadnezzar—shall come against her from the north and turn her to flight by the force of arms.

The following passage in Hosea is similar: “Israel is like a wanton cow that has turned aside; now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place” (Hos. 4). In the Septuagint this is rendered: “As a cow struck by the gadfly, Israel became mad; now the Lord pastures them in an open place.”

(HIERON.) Just as a wanton cow casts off the yoke, so Israel—that is, the ten tribes—turned away from the Lord’s service. For “wanton cow,” as we have said, the Septuagint translators rendered *paroistrōsa* (παροιστρῶσα), meaning one struck by a gadfly or horsefly, commonly called a *tabanus*. Virgil also refers to it in the third book of the *Georgics*:

“… whose name in Latin is *asilus*;  
the Greeks translated it as *oistros*,  
harsh, fiercely sounding; terrified by it,  
the herds scatter throughout the forests; the air  
roars, shaken by their bellowing, and the woods,  
and the dry bank of the Tanagrian river.”

Because Israel became mad and, struck by the spirit of fornication, raged with incredible fury, the Lord therefore pastures them not long afterward—but while the prophetic spirit still directs these events—like a lamb in an open place.

Since he had begun with a metaphor drawn from a wanton cow or a gadfly, he preserves it in what follows: he calls the captivity among the Assyrians and the people’s dispersion through the broadest land of the Medes the pasture of lambs, as though in a very wide field and spacious land.

The straightforward interpretation concerning heretics is evident. Just as a cow is struck by a gadfly, so heretics are struck by the devil’s burning arrows and abandon knowledge of the law. Therefore they will pasture on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and the patience of the Lord, the good shepherd, will nourish them toward destruction.

“Her hired men also, who were in her midst, have turned like fattened calves and have fled together; they could not stand, because the day of their slaughter shall come upon them, the time of their visitation.”

(MAURUS.) He calls the rulers of Egypt not shepherds but hired men, because they had not cared for the flock but devoted themselves to greed and luxury. Therefore, unable to stand before their enemies, they turned to flight. The day of vengeance and slaughter came upon them.

According to the allegory, we can understand Egypt’s hired men as false shepherds of the present Church, which is a pilgrim in this world. Seeking earthly profit, they do not dare to defend the sheep entrusted to them against destroyers.

Truth itself identifies them in the Gospel, saying (John 10): “But the hired man, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.”

(GREG.) The wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust and rapacious person oppresses the faithful and humble. But the one who seemed to be a shepherd and was not leaves the sheep and flees, because, fearing danger from the oppressor, he does not dare to resist his injustice.

He flees not by changing his position but by withdrawing his assistance. He flees because he saw injustice and remained silent. He flees because he hid himself under silence. The prophet rightly says of such men: “You did not go up to the breach, nor did you build a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13).

To go up to the breach means to oppose, with the free voice of reason, any authorities who act wickedly. We stand in battle and set up a wall for the house of Israel on the day of the Lord if, by the authority of justice, we defend faithful and innocent people against the injustice of the wicked.

Because the hired man does not do this, when he sees the wolf coming, he flees. But there is another wolf who daily, without ceasing, tears apart not bodies but minds: the evil spirit, who prowls around the folds of the faithful in ambush and seeks the deaths of souls.

Concerning this wolf it is immediately added: “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” The wolf comes and the hired man flees, because when the evil spirit tears the minds of the faithful apart in temptation, and the one who occupies the shepherd’s place does not exercise vigilant care, souls perish while he himself rejoices in earthly advantages.

[Col. 1105C] “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” when he draws one toward lust, kindles another with greed, raises another up in pride, divides another through anger; envy spurs this one, and deceit trips up that one. Thus the devil scatters the flock when, through temptations, he destroys the people of the faithful.

Against these things the hired man is kindled by no zeal and stirred by no fervor of love. Since he seeks only outward advantages, he negligently tolerates the inward losses of the flock. Hence it is immediately added: “The hired man flees because he is a hired man and has no concern for the sheep.”

The sole reason for the hired man’s flight is that he is a hired man. It is as though it were said plainly: He cannot stand in danger for the sheep because, while he presides over the sheep, he does not love the sheep but seeks earthly profit. While he embraces honor and rejoices in temporal advantages, he hesitates to oppose danger, lest he lose what he loves.

(MAURUS.) Such shepherds are like fattened calves, devoted to carnal pleasures and giving no attention to self-restraint. When the day of their slaughter and the time of their visitation comes upon them, they are consumed, because the future arrival of the heavenly Judge delivers them to the fires of Gehenna for punishment of their sins.

“His voice shall sound like bronze, because they will hasten with an army, and will come against him with axes; and, like men cutting wood, they have felled his forest,” says the Lord, “which cannot be counted: they have multiplied beyond the locusts, and there is no number to them.”

[Col. 1106A] For vengeance overtook not only historical Egypt by the just judgment of God, but will also overtake spiritual Egypt on the day of judgment—a future event that Holy Scripture now foretells throughout the whole world. Hence his voice is rightly compared with sounding bronze, because bronze rings more sonorously than other metals; and the day of the future judgment will resound more powerfully than all the admonitions that preceded it. For then “our God will come manifestly, and will not keep silence; fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest will surround him. He has summoned heaven above and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. XLIX). Then the heavenly armies will hasten to gather all scandals out of his kingdom, and with the axes of a mighty examination they will cut down the fruitless trees. Then the useless forest, which cannot be counted, will be cut down, because every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matt. VII); and the multitude of the lost, exceeding the number of locusts that toss themselves about in their brief flight, will be condemned, while the little flock to which it pleased the Father to give the inheritance will be saved. Then every thought of the carnal will be exposed to shame—thought that rested upon the pleasures of this age—when it will be handed over to the power of the evil spirits. There will no longer be permission to indulge in luxury, when punishment for sins is required. Hence it follows:

“Egypt’s daughter is put to shame and handed over to the people of the North. Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will visit the tumult of Alexandria, Pharaoh, Egypt, her gods, her kings, Pharaoh, [Col. 1106C] and all those who trust in him; and I will give them into the hands of those who seek their life, and into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hands of his servants.”

“The Lord will visit the tumult of Alexandria, Pharaoh, Egypt, her gods, her kings, and so forth,” when, because of the sins of its people and rulers, Egypt, with all its pomp and worship, was handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and to the Chaldaeans, who plundered everything and scattered the order of the kingdom. Something similar is read in Isaiah: “And I will give Egypt into the hands of cruel rulers, and a strong king will rule over them, says the Lord of hosts” (Isa. XIX). This, however, can be understood in two ways: as referring either to the time of the Chaldaeans, when Egypt was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar, or to the time of the Roman Empire, when Augustus Caesar subjugated Egypt after defeating Antony and Cleopatra. All Scripture testifies that the Babylonians were cruel: they spared neither little children, whom they wounded with their arrows, nor pregnant women. Daniel’s Scripture also testifies that the Roman kingdom was exceedingly strong (Dan. VII), explaining that the fourth beast had iron teeth and claws.

“And after this it shall be inhabited as in ancient days, says the Lord.”

Although this may seem to indicate that the kingdom of the Egyptians was not so destroyed by King Nebuchadnezzar that it could never be recovered, since kings continued there afterward until Augustus Cae[Col. 1107A]sar, nevertheless, in a higher sense it can designate the Christian times, when the worship of God was restored in the Egypt of this world, for the practice of which humanity was originally created. Of this Isaiah also says: “The Lord will strike Egypt with a plague, and he will heal it; and they will return to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them, and he will heal them” (Isa. XIX). “For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). This persecution, however, does not concern the denial of believers but their testing and crown, so that what was rejected may be destroyed and what is approved may be restored.

[Col. 1107B] “And you, my servant Jacob, do not be afraid, and do not fear, Israel, because behold, I will save you from afar, and your offspring from the land of your captivity; and Jacob shall return, and shall rest, and shall prosper, and there shall be none to terrify him. And you, my servant Jacob, do not be afraid, says the Lord, because I am with you; for I will consume all the nations to which I have driven you. But you I will not consume; rather, I will chastise you in judgment, nor will I spare you as though you were innocent.”

This promise does not properly suit the carnal Jewish people, but the spiritual people of those who believe in Christ. For it was not said to them by the divine voice that they would not be consumed, since they are now scattered throughout the whole world and possess neither kingdom nor priesthood; [Col. 1107C] rather, it concerns the Christian people, gathered from all nations. They will return from the captivity of error and their former way of life to the land of the Church, where they will rest in hope and prosper through the growth of virtues. Their adversary will not terrify them, because they have confidence in their God. They are not consumed by the persecution of enemies, but will be preserved and, like gold passing through fire, will be completely purified and tested. Unless perhaps we say that that ancient generation will not be entirely consumed before the day of judgment, because “a partial blindness has happened in Israel; but when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

It must nevertheless be understood that all human beings are tested in three ways: usually for testing, sometimes for correction, and at times in proportion to the merits of their sins. We read that Abraham, blessed Job, and many saints endured innumerable tribulations for the sake of testing. For correction, God hands over his just people to various trials because of certain small and light sins of theirs, or because of pride or impurity, in order to humble them. Thus, to use the prophet’s words (Isa. I), he smelts away the dross that he has seen to be congealed within them, sending them into the future judgment as pure gold, having purified them in the present and permitting nothing to remain in them that the fire of judgment might afterward discover and cleanse by penal torment.

In proportion to the merits of sins, however, the blow of temptation is inflicted, as the Lord threatens to send blows upon the Israelite people, saying: “I will send the teeth of beasts against them, with the fury of creatures dragging themselves over the earth”; and, “I struck your children in vain; you did not accept correction” (Deut. XXXII). Likewise in the Psalms: “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Ps. XXXI). And in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

[Col. 1108C] We also find a fourth reason, by which we know from the authority of Scripture that certain sufferings are inflicted upon some people solely to reveal the glory and works of the Lord, according to the Gospel saying: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John IX).

# BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 1107]

[Col. 1107C] In the preceding book, while passing over the prophecy of Jeremiah concerning the destruction of the remnants of the Israelite people, we suitably added the devastation of Egypt, so that when the destruction of those who trusted more in a reed-like staff and a fleshly arm than in divine help and protection had been recalled, the desolation of those in whom they trusted might consequently also be described. Now let us turn to consider what the prophet brought forth against the Philistines, Moabites, and other nations.

# CHAPTER XLVII  
## The Word of the Lord against the Philistines, and concerning their destruction

“The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah the prophet against the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza.”

The prophet Jeremiah, like Isaiah and Ezekiel, foretells for each of the nations bordering the land of the Jews the blows that were destined to come upon them, because they had been enemies of God’s people and rejoiced in their adversity. Therefore he now announces to the Philistines, as he previously did to the Egyptians, an approaching calamity, and specifies its time in a certain way: namely, before Pharaoh struck Gaza. This plague, therefore, which came upon the Philistines from the Assyrians, occurred before Gaza’s devastation.

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, waters will descend from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent; they will cover the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants.”

It should be noted that Isaiah, in the oracle against Philistia, spoke as follows: “Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of your striker has been shattered; for from the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth, and its offspring will devour the bird. The firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest securely. I will destroy your root by famine, and I will kill your remnant. Howl, gate; cry out, city; all Philistia has been overthrown. For smoke will come from the north, and there is no one who will escape its host” (Isa. XIV).

As we said above, “Philistines” signifies the Palaestinians, whom the common edition renders “foreigners,” although this is not the name of one nation but a designation of all external nations. “Do not rejoice,” he says, “O Philistia; do not insult my people because the rod of your striker, Ahaz, has been broken; because the staff accustomed to strike you appears to have been crushed by death; because the serpent has been killed. For in its place a more harmful one is born: Hezekiah, the little king, whom the Greeks call βασίλισκος (*basiliskos*, “basilisk”), who will kill you by his appearance and destroy you by the breath of his mouth.”

He calls the gate those who are in the gate, and the city its inhabitants, and directs his speech to the cities of the Palaestinians, telling them that they must wail and mourn the coming of Sennacherib, who devastates everything like a torrent. Under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came among the other nations and devastated the Philistines, to whom Jeremiah now speaks: “Behold, waters will rise from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent; they will cover the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants.” For the Assyrian came from the north, and from his heat Niniveh and the other nations that he subjected will emerge. At the time when these words were being sung, smoke was rising into the heights—that is, a report was spreading among the peoples through the successive order of all the cities—that the Phoenicians and the Palaestinians also were to be devastated. Or else the waters rose like an overflowing torrent and covered the land when the peoples of the Assyrians and those who were with them violently shook the land of the Palaestinians. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1109C] “The people will cry out, and every inhabitant of the land will howl at the sound of the pomp of his weapons and warriors, at the rattling of his chariots and the multitude of his wheels. The fathers did not look back toward their children, their hands hanging slack, because of the coming day on which all Philistia will be devastated and Tyre and Sidon will be scattered, together with all their remaining auxiliaries.”

(MAURUS.) Great indeed was the howling of the land of Philistia when death threatened each person, and no one was permitted to care for another, since the enemy raged in the slaughter of individuals; and the clatter of his weapons and warriors and the noise of his chariots surpassed the voices of those lamenting on the day when all Philistia was being devastated. By saying that Tyre and Sidon were scattered in the same disaster, he shows that those cities belonged to the association of the Palaestinians, although Tyre fell by lot to the tribe of Naphtali, and Sidon, the boundary of the Canaanites, belonged by lot to the tribe of Asher; yet the latter did not possess it, because it was entirely unable to drive out its enemies.

“For the Lord has devastated the Palaestinians, the remnant of the island of Cappadocia.”

The prophet Amos testifies that the Palaestinians came from Cappadocia, saying: “Are you not like the children of the Ethiopians to me, children of Israel, says the Lord? Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Palaestinians from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene?” (Amos IX).

The sense of this passage is as follows: I, the Lord God almighty, from whom nothing can be hidden, who touch the earth and it is shaken, who build my ascent into heaven, who call the waters of the sea and pour them over the face of the earth—my name is the Lord, and I am the creator of all things. I formed all nations from the same clay and gave them birth under an equal lot. In the end, I joined Ethiopians, Palaestinians, Syrians, and Jews—different in place and body—under the law of mortality. At my will I transfer my servants here and there, and I move entire provinces. Do not rise up in pride because I brought you out of Egypt and did not allow you, as my special people, to serve Pharaoh. I did the same for the Palaestinians, whom the Septuagint translated as “foreigners,” and who are called in Hebrew [the term is absent from the supplied source], whom I transferred from Cappadocia and settled in the regions of Palaestine. I also transferred the Syrians from Cyrene. Since all were made under equal conditions, they will be punished by my judgment under an equal sentence, and without respect of persons I will overthrow all ungodly kingdoms.

“Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon has fallen silent, together with the rest of their valleys.”

Gaza and Ashkelon were once cities of Palaestine, among the five principal cities of the Philistines. Gaza was a city of the Hivites, in which Cappadocians lived after killing its former inhabitants. Among the ancients it was the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt. It fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, but Judah could not retain it, because the Anakim—that is, the giants of the foreigners—resisted with the greatest strength. It remains to this day a distinguished city of Palaestine.

It is asked how one prophet can say that Gaza will become an everlasting mound. The answer is this: scarcely any trace of foundations remains at the site of the ancient city; the city now visible was built elsewhere in place of the one that collapsed. Ashkelon also is a famous city of Palaestine, which in ancient times was one of the five satrapies of the foreigners. Although it was assigned by lot to the tribe of Judah, it was not retained by it, because Judah could not overcome its inhabitants.

Baldness and profound silence came upon these cities because they were stripped of their works and deprived of masculine strength. Therefore the voice of joy and the voice of gladness ceased among them, and continual sorrow remained with them. In the vengeance that the prophet foretold against the Palaestinians and their cities, he signifies the future blow that will come upon heretics and schismatics, and upon all the enemies of God’s holy Church. Because they prepared ambushes for Christ’s faithful confessors, waged wars against them, and, with the devil as instigator, inflicted many kinds of persecution, they themselves will finally be handed over to the most savage enemies and subjected to everlasting ones.

“Philistines” is interpreted as “falling ones,” Tyre as “distress,” Sidon as “hunt,” Ashkelon as “fire,” and Gaza as “his strength.” All these meanings aptly suit the Antichrist and his members: falling through pride into apostasy, burning with anguish of mind, he conducts a hunt in the world so that he may seize and kill as many as he can from Christ’s Church. His strength is the notorious fire—that is, carnal desire. Hence it is read in the Book of Job: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel” (Job XL). Through lust he burns the minds of carnal people, and through fornication he kills them. But at the final judgment of the Lord, he and his followers will be scattered, together with all his auxiliaries, and he will be cast into the infernal abyss to be tortured eternally.

“How long will you cut down? O sword of the Lord, how long will you not rest? Enter into your sheath; cool yourself and be silent.”

In the historical sense we can understand this sword as Nebuchadnezzar, who, having been permitted to do so, exercised the vengeance of the Lord’s anger against various nations. To him it is also said through Ezekiel: “Sword, sword, draw yourself from your sheath to kill; sharpen yourself to slaughter, and shine, when what seemed to you were vain things and lies were divined, so that you might be given over the necks of the wounded and the ungodly, whose appointed day has come at the time fixed for iniquity. Return to your sheath, to the place in which you were created; in the land of your birth I will judge you, and I will pour out my indignation upon you” (Ezek. XXI).

The sense of this sentence is as follows: O king of Babylon, who, like a sword or blade, are prepared for slaughter; who have been sharpened to shine and kill—although your idols may have answered you, and everything answered by demons is vain, so that you might threaten the necks of the wounded and through you what the Lord had long threatened might be fulfilled—after you have completed the work that you carried out against the children of Ammon, return to your sheath, that is, to Babylon, to the place in which you were made and created. In the land of your birth I will judge you, pour out my indignation upon you, and you will be captured by the power of the Medes and Persians.

According to the ἀναγωγή (*anagogē*), or spiritual sense, we can understand the sharp sword prepared for slaughter as the devil. Of him Paul says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor. V). And elsewhere: “Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. I). It is also written in the Psalms: “He sent fury and anger and distress, a sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII).

The prophet, therefore, astonished at the magnitude of the vengeance that will come upon sinners, speaks as one who suffers and grieves to the sword of the Lord’s vengeance and asks how far it will advance and why it does not at some point cease from inflicting punishment. To this the prophet himself replies:

“How shall it rest when the Lord has commanded it against Ashkelon and against its maritime regions, and has assigned it there against Moab?”

He also shows the reason why they suffer vengeance: by provoking the Lord to anger through their sins, they deserved to receive such a sentence. Nor is it possible for anyone to turn aside an inflicted blow unless the appeased Lord commands it, by his authority, to cease from killing the guilty. Now, after the Philistines, the word of the Lord through the prophet is directed against Moab.

# CHAPTER XLVIII  
## The Word of the Lord against Moab and its cities

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Woe to Nabo, because it has been devastated and put to shame; Cariathiarim has been captured; the strong one has been put to shame and has trembled. There is no longer exultation in Moab. They have devised evil against Heshbon: ‘Come, and let us destroy it from the nation.’ Therefore you shall be silent; you shall fall silent; the sword will follow you. A voice of shouting from Horonaim: devastation and great destruction. Moab has been crushed; announce the cry to its little ones. For by the ascent of Luith, weeping, he will ascend in lamentation, because on the descent of Horonaim the enemies have heard the howl of destruction.”

(MAURUS.) He therefore foretells, in the historical sense, the devastation that the Babylonians will bring upon Moab and its renowned cities, so that because they had been enemies of God’s people and had always held them up to ridicule, those cities themselves, devastated with the other nations, might also become objects of derision. Hence it is said below: “Israel was a derision to you, as though you had found him among thieves; because of your words that you spoke against him, you will be led away captive.”

Isaiah also speaks against the Moabites in his book, saying: “The wall of Moab has fallen silent; the houses and Dibon have ascended to the high places in mourning; Moab has howled over Nabo and over Medeba” (Isa. XVI), and so forth.

Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which was Bale son of Beor, who summoned the diviner Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel (Num. XXV); there the people were initiated into the worship of Beelphegor. Nabo was a renowned city in which the idol Chamos was consecrated, also called by another name, Beelphegor. Heshbon was once the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, concerning which the same Jeremiah says: “Fire has gone out from Heshbon, and flames from the midst of Sihon” (Sup. XLIV).

Luith, of which the prophet now says, “By the ascent of Luith, weeping, he will ascend in lamentation,” we understand to be the slope of the road that leads toward the Assyrians. By this captivity is signified, because on the descent of Horonaim the enemies heard the howl of destruction. It would take too long to speak of each place individually, since it is clear that these are names either of cities in Moab or of places that have perished with those who migrated.

As circumcision is carnal, so it is spiritual; and of spiritual circumcision the Apostle says: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit and glory in the Lord and do not trust in the flesh” (Phil. III). Again, to distinguish it from the spiritual, Israel is described as carnal: “See Israel according to the flesh, and you nations in the flesh.”

Thus Moab is to be understood spiritually. Its name is interpreted as “from the father” or “paternal water”; it was conceived through incest and drunkenness, and in a certain sense seemed to have been generated by a father who was absent—or rather, unaware. In many places of Scripture we read about Moab, especially in the Book of Numbers (Num. XXII), when Balak, king of the Moabites, invited the diviner Balaam to curse Israel. Among other things, he prophesied this mystical saying against Moab: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel, and he shall strike the rulers of Moab.”

Moab signifies secular wisdom, concerning which the Lord speaks through the prophet: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX; 1 Cor. I). Since it has a mind as its author, which is generated by God’s creation, it appears indeed to be born from a father—what Moab means—but because it is adulterous and hostile to God’s people, it is generated from incest, a cave, and night. Therefore it perishes in night, that is, in everlasting error.

The Egyptians were overwhelmed in the Red Sea at the morning watch, which reveals the nocturnal period; and Lot, when the Sodomites were perishing by night, came to Zoar, and the sun rose for him (Gen. XIX). Understanding this, the blessed Apostle writes concerning the holy and perfect (1 Thess. V): “We are not of the night or of darkness, but we are children of God. For those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night.” But we who are of the day must keep watch, clothed with the breastplate of faith and charity.

Because he had abandoned the night and had already begun to be a son of God, he says to believers: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and lust” (Rom. XIII).

According to Isaiah, the Moabites perish by night: “By night Ar was devastated; Moab fell silent” (Isa. XIII). Because the wall was devastated by night, Moab fell silent. That wall, constructed by the art of dialectic, was devastated and destroyed in the same night, and fell silent for eternal duration.

It should be noted that Nabo is interpreted as “sitting” or “prophecy”; Cariathiarim as “city” or “village of forests”; Heshbon as “thoughts”; Luith as “cheeks”; and Horonaim as “a hole of sorrow.”

Since, therefore, every doctrine contrary to the truth, which arises from human thought without God’s inspiration in the darkness of error, was devastated by night, and its arguments—which are understood as its walls—were destroyed by ecclesiastical speech, they fell silent in eternal silence. Their entire faction was turned toward penitence and tears: over Nabo—that is, prophecy and sitting, meaning their teachers; and over Cariathiarim, where there are no fruitful trees but an infertile forest in which the beast dwelt, concerning which it is written in the twenty-eighth Psalm: “And he revealed the dense forests.”

There will be howling and mourning, and all the ornaments of eloquence from their headings will be removed, so that they will remain naked and deformed. If they appeared to possess any greenness in their beard, it will be shown to have been shaved by an ecclesiastical man, made effeminate and weak. They will gird themselves with the sackcloth of penitence, and on the roofs and housetops—where they formerly believed themselves exalted—and in the streets, because they do not enter by the narrow way but by the broad way that leads to death, there will be howling. They will by no means rise into pride—which is what Heshbon means—but will make void the ascent of pride. Their voice will be heard as far as the evil deeds they committed, and they will condemn themselves by their own confession of the commandment they thought was from God.

When they have done penance through Luith—that is, through the tears of their cheeks—they will climb to the altar; and as from a hole and entrance of sorrow they will raise a cry of contrition to the Lord, so that they may say: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L).

“Flee; save your lives; and you shall be like a tamarisk in the desert,” and so forth.

The prophet foretells that, when Moab perishes through Chaldaean devastation, whoever wishes to be saved should flee from there and hide in the desert, like a tamarisk, which is a low-growing tree. Spiritually, whoever wishes to save his soul should flee the crafty and deceptive teaching of philosophers and heretics, where destruction is certain, and through humble confession should repent of his error, remaining in the desert of strict abstinence and in the simplicity and truth of Catholic doctrine.

“Because you trusted in your fortifications and in your treasures, you too will be captured; and Chamos will go into captivity, together with his priest and his princes. The plunderer will come to every city, and no city will be saved; the valleys will perish, and the plains will be scattered. For the Lord has said: ‘Give a flower to Moab, because it will go forth flowering’; and its cities will be desolate and uninhabited.”

Therefore the philosophers of this world and the heretics, who trust in dialectical disputations in which they hope the treasure of wisdom lies, will be captured by the Church’s warriors, who with the shield of right faith and the word of truth attack every error of the faithless and lead its worshipers and ministers into captivity. Thus they may learn that no city—that is, no stronghold of their doctrine—can give true salvation. But the valleys will perish: their false humiliations and pretended virtues. For what appeared to flourish in human invention and secular wisdom will be reduced to desert and solitude. And because all hypocrisy and false pretense greatly displease God, the following sentence shows this:

“Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord deceitfully.”

Whoever deviates through error from the way of uprightness stands far removed from the light of truth. Therefore it is necessary that we consider not only what we do but also with what discernment we do it: first, lest we do evil in some way; and afterward, lest we do good carelessly.

The prophet urges us to perform good deeds diligently, saying: “Cursed is the man who performs God’s work negligently.” In the older translation, however, the sentence is read as follows: “Cursed is everyone who performs God’s work deceitfully and sluggishly.”

It must be understood most carefully that sluggishness arises from torpor, while deceit arises from private affection. Lesser love of God intensifies the former; the latter is created by self-love when it wrongly possesses the mind. Whoever loves himself inordinately and hastens toward the rewards of transitory goods because of what he has done rightly commits deceit against the love of God.

It must also be understood that this deceit is committed in three ways: by it, a person undoubtedly desires either the silent favor of the human heart, or the breeze of approval, or some external possession. In opposition to this, the prophet rightly says of the just man: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isa. XXXIII).

Since deceit is not found only in the acceptance of money, a gift is certainly not of one kind. There are three kinds of gifts toward which one hastens through deceit. A gift from the heart is favor sought from one’s thoughts. A gift from the mouth is glory through approval. A gift from the hand is a reward through giving.

But every just person shakes his hands free from every gift, because in what he does rightly he seeks to receive neither empty glory from the human heart, nor praise from the mouth, nor payment from the hand. The only one who does not practice deceit in God’s work is the person who, while devoting himself to good action, does not pant after rewards of bodily things, words of praise, or the favor of human judgment.

Since our good deeds cannot escape the sword of insinuating guilt unless they are guarded daily by watchful fear, it is rightly said through holy Job: “I feared all my works” (Job IX). As though he were saying in humble confession: I see what I have done openly, but I do not know what I have secretly endured in these deeds.

Often our good deeds perish through deceit acting as a thief, because earthly desires attach themselves to our righteous actions. Often they fail when sluggishness intervenes, because love grows cold and withers from the fervor with which they began. Since the stealthy intrusion of guilt is scarcely overcome even in the very act of virtue, what remains for our security except always to fear diligently even while practicing virtue?

“And cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood.”

To withhold one’s sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from the slaughter of carnal life. Concerning this sword it is again said: “And my sword has devoured flesh” (Gregory).

When such people conceal the word of preaching within themselves, let them hear the divine sentences against them with terror, so that fear may drive fear from their hearts. Let them hear how the one who refused to distribute his talent lost it along with the sentence of condemnation. Let them hear how Paul believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors precisely because inwardly he did not spare their desires when they needed to be struck, saying: “I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts XX).

[MAURUS.] This prophetic sentence of cursing can also apply to anyone who follows the luxury of the world and neglects to chastise his body and subject it to servitude, although the Apostle plainly says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V). He says of himself: “I chastise my body and subject it to servitude, lest after preaching to others I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX).

Hence he himself also says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI). And again: “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it; and whoever loses his life in this world preserves it for eternal life.”

Whoever wishes to ascend to this state should therefore purify himself through abstinence and the mortification of heart and body, because, as it is written, “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Heb. IX). Nor is this without reason: “For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. V).

Therefore whoever wishes to restrain the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God—from the shedding of this blood will undoubtedly be punished by the curse of the prophet Jeremiah: “Cursed,” he says, “is the one who withholds his sword from blood.”

This is the sword that, healthfully pouring out that guilty blood by which the material of sins is animated, cuts away and severs whatever carnal or earthly matter it finds congealed in our members. It makes those who have been put to death to vices live for God and flourish in spiritual virtues. Thus they will begin to weep no longer in remembrance of an old offense but in hope of future joys; thinking not so much about past evils as about coming goods, they will pour forth tears not from sorrow over sins but from the gladness of that eternal joy. Forgetting what lies behind—that is, carnal vices—they will stretch forward to what lies ahead: spiritual gifts and virtues.

“Moab was fertile from its youth, and it rested upon its lees; it was not poured from vessel to vessel, and it did not go into exile. Therefore its flavor remained in it, and its odor was not changed. Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall send against him arrangers and jar-overturners; they shall lay him low, empty his vessels, and shatter their jars. Moab shall be confounded by Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was confounded by Bethel, in which it had placed its trust.”

Abundance of possessions frequently leads to severe want, and excessive security is followed by a storm of calamity. For when a sluggish person uses permitted things without restraint, the vigor of the soul is dissolved in luxury, and the heart is immediately lifted up into pride. Thus he makes the God whom he could have had as his ally through humility become his adversary through pride. Hence Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV).

The downfall of the Moabites proves this most clearly. Because of the fertility of their land, their abundance of possessions, and their excessive leisure, they fell into arrogance; and they despised and mocked the people of God, who were sweating beneath the burden of tribulations, because Moab itself, free from calamity, remained unharmed. But because by the swelling of its mind and its perverse conduct it provoked God to anger, it was handed over to enemies for plunder. They searched through all its possessions and left nothing uninjured. Nor could the false divinity and idol Chemosh, their god, whom they worshiped as a true deity, in any way come to their aid, so that they would not be devastated and led into captivity—just as Israel also suffered because of the golden calves it worshiped at Bethel, placing in them its hope of deliverance.

According to the mystical meanings, however, all who trust in human philosophy and hope that through it they can possess security and everlasting life, while despising the religious faith and simple teaching of the Church, will have the arrangers and overthrowers of their doctrines come upon them, along with plunderers of the treasures they possessed in the vessels of their books—namely, wicked spirits. Then they will be confounded when, at the end of life, they see that their study and the worship of the false gods whom they proclaimed with manifold praise have profited them nothing: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm XCV). And when the future judgment has been completed, all the impious will go with the devil and his angels into eternal fire, but the righteous will ascend with their king Christ to the heavenly kingdom (Matthew XXV).

“How do you say, ‘We are strong, and powerful men for battle’? Moab has been devastated, and its cities have been cut down, and its chosen young men have descended to the slaughter, says the king—the Lord of hosts is his name. The destruction of Moab is near, that it may come, and its calamity will meet it very swiftly.”

These words are spoken so that, under the name of Moab, the world’s folly and the pride that exalts itself to heaven may be crushed. In vain does one hope to be strong who does not trust in the almighty Lord. Certain condemnation will quickly come upon him whom the protection of the supreme King does not defend; and all the strength of one who boasts while trusting in his own power or knowledge will be scattered. “The destruction of Moab is near,” he says, “that it may come, and its calamity meets it very swiftly.” For what will one day perish is not enduring, nor is what is subject to a certain end far away. Calamity therefore swiftly meets the one who does not take care to escape it through repentance and correction of life. The only refuge for those in danger is to seek from the true Savior the remedy of their salvation. Of him it is written: “Everyone who trusts will not be confounded.”

“Comfort him, all who are around him; and all of you who know his name, say: ‘How has the strong rod been broken, and the glorious staff? Descend from glory and sit in thirst, O habitation of the daughter of Dibon, for the devastator of Moab will ascend against you and destroy your fortifications.’”

The consolation by which he commands those around Moab to console it seems to me, in accordance with irony, to be understood either as a challenge or as an invitation to repentance, so that through suitable satisfaction and turning away from sins it may deserve to find relief from its oppression. For how could he have been consoled by his helpers when the divine sentence threatens that devastation will come upon him? This is made clear by the present sentence and by what follows. For it continues:

“Stand on the road and look toward the habitation of Aroer. Ask the one fleeing and the one who escaped: ‘Say, What has happened?’ Moab is confounded, because it has been defeated. Howl and cry out; announce it in Arnon, for Moab has been devastated, and judgment has come upon the plain, upon Elon, upon Jasa, upon Mephath, upon Dibon, upon Nebo, upon the house of Diblathaim, upon Kiriathaim, upon Beth-gamul, upon Beth-maon, upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, whether far away or near.”

In commanding the habitation of Aroer—which is the metropolis of the Moabites—to stand and to ask the fugitive and the one who escaped from battle what had happened, he indicates its astonishment at the sudden disaster that unexpectedly befell them. The fleeing man answered: “Moab is confounded, because it has been defeated. Howl and cry out,” and so forth—as though he were saying: What the prophetic utterance foretold to us in the person of Moab has suddenly come upon us, and Moab has been confounded, although previously it boasted that it could become victorious. Therefore he commands that this be announced everywhere with howling and crying, because ruin and devastation have come upon all its cities alike.

Mystically, however, the wise men of this world and the heretics, whom we said earlier were represented by the person of Moab, if they do not correct their folly and turn to the truth of the catholic faith, will suffer a great ruin, and all their cities—that is, the various philosophical sects that stood either far from or near to the truth—will be overthrown as the Gospel of Christ dawns. For it continues:

“The horn of Moab has been cut off, and his arm has been broken, says the Lord. Make him drunk, for he has risen up against the Lord; and Moab shall strike his hand against his vomit, and he himself shall become a laughingstock. For Israel was a laughingstock to you, as though you had found him among thieves. Because of those words of yours that you spoke against him, you shall be led captive” (Jerome).

Just as the prophet foretold against Babylon and the Philistines that they had oppressed the Jewish people, so now the devastation of the Moabites—that is, of Arabia—is foretold at the hands of the Assyrians and Babylonians, for they were devastated by both peoples: both when Sennacherib led Israel captive and when Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Jerusalem. Moab had indeed mocked both enemies, Ephraim and Judah. Thus Moab, made drunk by the cup of the Lord’s wrath, struck its hand against its own vomit—that is, in its punishment it ceased persecuting others—and it that had mocked others itself became exposed to the mockery of all.

So also the foolish wisdom of this world, which is accustomed to mock Christian simplicity, will recognize the folly of its error when it comes to its end. Truly, whatever perverse doctrines exist in the world, whatever belongs to earthly knowledge and is thought to be strong, will be overthrown and dissolved like a fire into ashes and embers, so that what was thought most powerful may be shown to be nothing.

“Abandon the cities and dwell in the rock, inhabitants of Moab; and be like a dove nesting at the mouth of a cavern.”

(Maurus.) The prophet gives the wise men of this world the counsel that they should abandon the dwellings of their errors and flee to the rock, Christ. They should take upon themselves the simplicity of that dove of which it is written in the Song of Songs: “Rise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the recesses of the wall” (Song of Songs II). Let them nest at the mouth of the cavern—that is, in the perfect confession of Christ’s passion and resurrection—and, together with good works, prepare for themselves an everlasting dwelling, where they will receive the perpetual reward of their labors.

“We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud. I know his exaltation, his arrogance, his pride, and the loftiness of his heart, says the Lord; his boasting, and that his strength is not equal to it, nor has he attempted to do what he was capable of doing. Therefore I shall lament over Moab [I shall mourn over Moab], and I shall cry out over Moab as a whole, for the men of the wall of baked clay are lamenting. With the mourning of Jazer I shall weep for you, O vine of Sibmah. Your branches have crossed the sea; they have reached as far as the sea of Jazer. The plunderer has rushed upon your harvest and your vintage. Joy and gladness have been taken away from Carmel and from the land of Moab, and I have removed the wine from the winepresses. The treaders of grapes shall no longer sing the customary work-song.”

Something similar is read in Isaiah: “We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud. His pride, his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength” (Isaiah XVI). Therefore Moab will howl over Moab; all of it will howl for itself, those who rejoice over walls of baked brick. Speak of its wounds.

Again he returns to the present situation and reproves Moab for having been lifted up far more than its strength warranted. Because of this pride, Moab howled over Moab—that is, the people over the city, or the metropolis over the province—and the whole land resounded with howls over walls of baked brick. Concerning these Jeremiah now also says: “Therefore I shall lament over Moab and cry out over Moab as a whole, for the men of the wall of baked clay are lamenting.”

Through these words he displays both the power of its former prosperity and the wounds of its sudden overthrow. It is customary in Scripture that, after raising the despairing human mind with a joyful message, it again terrifies the negligent and those unwilling to repent with a threat. For God’s goodness does not harden our heart. Let us give only one example of this. In Psalm 144 we read: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Psalm CXLV). And shortly afterward: “The Lord supports all who fall and raises up all who are bowed down. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food in due season” (Psalm CXLIV). And although he had previously said, “The Lord guards all who love him,” so that he would not make the hearer negligent, he added: “but he will destroy all sinners.”

Since, therefore, in the earlier passage he was calling those who had gone astray to repentance and urging them to turn to Christ so that they might remain forever in his faith, now, because he recognizes that many of them are incorrigible and persist in their folly, he speaks through the person of the saints who were saved from Moab and who learned its pride by their own experience. Therefore he says:

“We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud—his exaltation, his arrogance, his pride, and the loftiness of his heart,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) For what heretic is not proud? He despises the simplicity of the Church and regards the people of the Church as though they were brute animals. He rises to such a swelling of pride and insult that he arms his mouth against the Creator himself, disparaging his prophets as though on the authority of the Gospel testimony in which the Savior says: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John IX). He even calls Moses, God’s servant, a murderer, and disparages Joshua son of Nun as a bloodthirsty man, although he was of such holiness that at his command the sun and moon stood still (Joshua X). He calls David, from whose seed Christ was born, a murderer and adulterer, without considering his repentance and gentleness, by which he is compared with God’s clemency.

But although he is proud and arrogant and exults in fury, he dares more than his strength permits. Therefore Moab will howl over Moab—that is, one over another. All the various kinds of heretics and of secular wisdom will roar against one another when they are in torment. Accordingly, you who possess walls not built of squared stones, of which the temple was built, stones so well polished that neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house of God—you teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab—announce the wounds of those who have been wounded by the arrows of the heretics.

For all their thoughts, which is what Heshbon signifies, do not belong to the habitation of the city of the Lord, of which it is written: “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God” (Psalm XLV). They are suburbs, although they are believed to belong to the city of the Lord because they are beneath the city; nevertheless, they will be deserted by its protection or consumed by divine fire. Especially so is the vine of Sibmah, whose name is interpreted as “raising up height,” because it lifts itself up on high and attempts to build the tower of its pride as far as heaven.

Of this vine Isaiah also says: “The lords of the nations have cut off its branches; they reached as far as Jazer. Its branches wandered in the wilderness; they were left behind and crossed the sea. Therefore I shall weep in the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I shall drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Eleale, because upon your vintage and your harvest the sound of the treaders has rushed, and joy and gladness will be taken away from Carmel. In the vineyards there will be no rejoicing or shouting. He will not tread wine in the winepress, as he was accustomed to tread it; I have taken away the sound of the treaders” (Isaiah XVI).

The suburbs of Heshbon, of which it was written above, are deserted; and the vine of Sibmah can be interpreted not only as “raising up height,” but also as “a kind of conversion,” because it appears, in the region of Moab, to wish in some measure to turn toward the service of the Lord.

The apostles of the Lord of the nations and apostolic men completely cut off the branches and shoots of this vine of Sibmah, so that other heresies might not be born from other heresies and an endless multitude of the erring might arise. They not only cut off the branches of Sibmah, but reached as far as Jazer, which is interpreted as “their strength”—that is, to the strongest doctrines of the heretics, constructed by dialectical art, in which they seemed to possess their power. Their sword raged against them to such an extent that finally they wandered in the wilderness and had no one left for them to kill.

Although they cut off its branches, some shoots nevertheless remained because of the fault of the evil root. But the lords of the nations crossed the sea—that is, the temptations of this world, concerning which we read in the psalm: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm overwhelmed me” (Psalm LXVIII). And elsewhere: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work on great waters, they saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.”

They crossed the sea in order to behold the works of the Lord in the depths of temptations while being delivered from them. Thus the prophetic utterance mourns the strength of the heretics, namely Jazer, and the vine of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God: “and I shall drench Heshbon with my tears”—that is, their thoughts—and Eleale, by which they climbed to lofty things. But why does Jazer mourn the vine of Sibmah and drench Heshbon and Eleale with its tears? So that, while it itself weeps, it may teach them to weep also. “For,” he says, “upon your vintage and your harvest the sound of the treaders has rushed.”

The vine of the Moabites, because of the proximity of the region, is like the vine of the Sodomites, concerning which it is said: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah.” And in Psalm 77 we read of a vine transplanted from Egypt, which God strikes with hail. The harvests of Moab also grow in the valleys called Rephaim, and its vintage is false—the vine of which it was said above: “The lords of the nations have cut off its branches.” For they crush the bitter grapes and tread them beneath their feet, lest they squeeze from them the dragon’s poisons and all who drink them be destroyed.

The joy and exultation of the heretics, which they were previously accustomed to hear, will also be taken away, so that after they have repented they may deserve to hear: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V). What he added about Carmel signifies not that the heretics truly possess Carmel—that is, knowledge of spiritual circumcision—but that they falsely boast of possessing it.

When the vines have been cut down and joy and exultation have been removed from their falsely named knowledge, then none of the former treaders will remain to tread the grapes that he previously trod. Their voice will be silenced in eternal silence, and the customary work-song will not be sung—that is, the song of joy—for their mouths will be oppressed by everlasting sorrow. Celeuma, as some maintain, is a song in the winepress of the treaders, or, better, a song of sailors in a ship.

Therefore in this passage we have set down Isaiah’s statement together with its exposition, since it is almost identical with this account of Jeremiah:

“From the cry of Heshbon as far as Eleale and Jazer they have uttered their voice.”

Heshbon and Eleale are the names of cities in the province of Moab. Heshbon was once the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, concerning which the same Jeremiah says shortly afterward: “A fire has gone out from Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon.” As we have said, Heshbon is interpreted as “thought.” Therefore, alluding to the name, Jeremiah says against Heshbon: “They have thought up evils; as far as Jazer their voice has been heard.”

The city of Jazer overlooks the Dead Sea, where the boundary of the province of the Moabites lies. This indicates that the howling of the province resounded as far as its outermost limits. Hence Jeremiah now says: “From the cry of Heshbon as far as Eleale and Jasan they have uttered their voice.” Isaiah also speaks of this: “For this reason,” he says, “the armed men of Moab will howl; its soul will howl for itself” (Isaiah XV).

The Hebrew word which Aquila rendered ἐξώμους—that is, “unencumbered/ready,” with shoulders bared—Symmachus rendered as “girded.” Some think that not men but the name of a city is intended, a city now called Elusa, situated in the parts of Moab. We may also say that the entire strength of the warriors had fallen and that the whole land resounded with mutual weeping. But if the people of Elusa are understood, as Aquila wished, as having their shoulders bared, the following meaning is suggested to us: everyone bared his breast for mourning.

“Their bars extend from Zoar as far as Horonaim, the heifer of three years old.”

Concerning this Isaiah says: “Its bars reach as far as Zoar, the heifer of three years old” (Isaiah XV). We discussed this in the books of Hebrew Questions, and we now briefly note that this is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim. It was preserved at Lot’s plea and is called Bela, that is, “swallowed up.” According to the Hebrews, it was overthrown by a third earthquake. It is the place now called Zoora in the Syriac language, and Segor in Hebrew; both names mean “little.”

We may understand “the heifer of three years old” as referring to complete maturity. For just as the thirtieth year is the strongest age among human beings, so among cattle and beasts of burden the third year is the strongest. Understand the bars also as boundaries and strength, because Zoar is situated on the borders of the Moabites, separating their land from the land of the Philistines.

“The waters of Nimrim also shall become utterly bad.”

Isaiah likewise says: “The waters of Nimrim shall also be desolate, for the grass has dried up, the plant has failed, all verdure has perished. According to the greatness of the work and their visitation, they shall lead them to the torrent of the willows,” and the rest (Isaiah XV).

This settlement lies above the Dead Sea, whose waters are salty and therefore sterile. Whether Isaiah alluded to the name, or whether this happened only after the devastation although it had not happened before, the result was that even the waters were turned to bitterness. It is not, as some think, that all the grass dried up because of the genuinely sterile waters of Nimrim; rather, Scripture speaks metaphorically. The meaning is: throughout Moab the waters of Nimrim were salty and bitter, and just as no grass grows there, so drought overtakes the entire province—from Zoar to Horonaim, from one boundary to the other.

Jeremiah now says the same: “The waters of Nimrim shall become utterly bad. According to the greatness of the work and their visitation, they shall lead them to the torrent of the willows.” In place of “willows,” the Hebrew reads a word that can also be understood as “Arabs” and read as Orbim, that is, a village situated on their borders, whose inhabitants are said by many to have supplied food to Elijah on Mount Horeb. Because of the ambiguity, the name is translated also as “ravens,” “the west,” and “open places.”

The meaning is: the visitation will correspond to the greatness of the disease. Here understand “visitation” not as a remedy but as a wound. Hence in the psalm: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod” (Psalm LXXXVIII). Understand the torrent of the willows as the rivers of Babylon, concerning which David also says: “On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Psalm CXXXVI). Or understand it as the valley of Arabia, through which one travels to the Assyrians.

Spiritual Moab is girded with the sackcloth of repentance. On the roofs and housetops, where they formerly believed themselves to be exalted, and in the streets—because they do not enter by the narrow way but by the broad way that leads to death—there will be howling. They will no longer climb into pride but descend into weeping.
