Then they will understand that all their thoughts were vain, which is what Heshbon signifies, and that the fall was the ascent of pride, which is what Eleale denotes, so that their voice may be heard as far as the evil works they committed and the commandment which they thought belonged to God, condemning themselves by their own confession.

Therefore the bars—that is, those who were strong in Moab and who understood their error—will howl and begin to have hope of progress, when their soul has howled for itself. Hence the prophet, with the affection of one who suffers, speaks to those whose soul will howl for itself and says: “My heart shall cry out for Moab,” in order to call them to repentance.

Their bars and all the strongholds that they seemed to possess in their heresies will reach from Zoar—that is, as far as the little one. It is shown that they are not strong but fragile. If this Zoar—that is, small repentance—perseveres, it will lead them to perfect salvation, which is signified by the three-year-old heifer, in accordance with what we read in Genesis XV, where God commands Abraham to offer a three-year-old calf, ram, and goat: a perfect sacrifice, clearly, so that he might deserve to be God’s heir.

When they have done penance through Luith—that is, through the tears of their cheeks—they will ascend to the altar and, as though from the cavern and entrance of sorrow, raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, so that they may say: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm L).

This will happen because the waters of Nimrim—that is, the teaching of the heretics, which is compared with leopards and transgressors—will be desolate and brought to nothing. They are leopards whose variegated markings and spots are not changed, as in Jeremiah (Jeremiah XIII), and apostates, concerning whom we read in the psalm: “I have regarded all sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Psalm CXVIII).

All the grass and plants, and whatever appeared green in their speech, will also dry up. According to the greatness of their sins they were visited by God, so that they might recognize through scourges the one whom they had not perceived through benefits. Finally they will be led to the valley, or torrent, of the willows, so that no fruit may remain in them. For they say that the nature of the seed of these trees is such that whoever drinks it in a cup becomes childless. Hence the saints, who because of their sins have begun to exist in the confusion of this world, hang their instruments upon the willows of the rivers of Babylon.

A cry surrounds all the boundaries of the Moabites, either from those calling others to repentance or from those groaning over their error, so that through their howling they may offer the calves of their lips and reach the fountain of the Lord’s rams, or of the strong, since Elim signifies both.

“And I shall remove from Moab,” says the Lord, “the one who offers in the high places and sacrifices to its gods.”

(Maurus.) It is rightly said that the Lord will remove from Moab the one who offers in the high places and sacrifices to its gods, because when the kingdom failed, the practice of sacrifices ceased. Mystically, however, when the sect of human wisdom perishes, the shouting and pomp of words likewise cease, so that neither the philosophers of this world nor the heretics who have gone out from the unity of the Church find anything in their teaching that contributes any benefit to human life.

“Therefore my heart shall resound over Moab like a pipe, and my heart shall make the sound of pipes over the men of the wall of baked clay. For he has done more than he could; therefore they have perished.”

The prophet speaks with the feeling of one who grieves, either because Moab is about to fall into the power of the enemy, upon whom so many evils come, or because it is to be oppressed by such great calamities that it will become pitiable even to its enemies. Hence he says that his heart will sound like a pipe, because he is ready to utter from his heart a mournful song over its pride and yet its fragility, and an unbroken groaning because it has perished at the hands of its enemies.

“For every head shall be bald, and every beard shall be shaved. On all hands there shall be mourning, and over every back sackcloth, and on all the roofs of Moab and in its streets there shall be universal lamentation, because I have crushed Moab like a useless vessel, says the Lord.”

Isaiah speaks similarly: “On all its heads there shall be baldness; every beard shall be shaved. In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; on its roofs and in its streets there is universal howling” (Isaiah XV).

Among the ancients, shaving the beard and the head was therefore a sign of mourning. Through these things the magnitude of sorrow is displayed. The tears will not be private; public mourning and public lamentation will resound. Neither matrons nor virgins, neither the young age of children nor the broken steps of the old will be kept within their homes. Extreme captivity will know neither modesty nor weakness, “because I have crushed Moab like a useless vessel,” says the Lord.

Moab was therefore a useless vessel, less suited to good work, and for this reason it was crushed by the Lord. So too every doctrine of the philosophers, being fragile and founded upon falsehood, will be crushed and scattered when truth prevails, and will be exposed to contempt and eternal groaning.

“How has it been defeated, and how have they howled? How has Moab bowed its neck and been confounded? Moab shall become a laughingstock and an example to all who are around you.”

The region of Moab has been defeated; hence its inhabitants have howled. It has bowed the neck of its pride and been confounded. Moab will become a laughingstock and an example to all around it, because its exceedingly great pride has been cast down. So too, to the extent that human wisdom raises itself against the Lord in the arrogance of its pride, to that extent, when truth prevails, it will bear the shame of confusion before all.

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, he flew like an eagle and spread his wings toward Moab. Kerioth has been captured, and its fortifications have been seized by him.”

He calls Nebuchadnezzar an eagle because of his rapacity, since he exercised it in the devastation of various nations. When he directed his wings—that is, his advance—toward Moab, Kerioth, a most famous city, was captured, and its fortifications were seized by him. Hence it continues:

“And the heart of Moab’s strong men shall be on that day like the heart of a woman in labor, and Moab shall cease to be a people, because he gloried against the Lord. Terror, pit, and snare are upon you, inhabitant of Moab, says the Lord. Whoever flees from the face of terror shall fall into the pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For I shall bring upon Moab the year of their visitation, says the Lord.”

He rightly compares Moab’s heart with the heart of a woman in labor, because from great luxury it has come to great sorrow. It also ceased to be a people because it gloried proudly against the Lord in its own power. Thus terror of mind, the pit of deception, and the snare of captivity seized it. It happened that, when it prepared to flee from the narrowness of terror, it fell into the pit of siege; and when it attempted to escape from there, it was caught by the enemy in the snare of captivity.

Scripture shows why this happened to it by adding that the Lord brought upon Moab the year of their visitation—that is, of just retribution—so that at last, through calamity, they might experience what they had refused to understand while living in prosperity.

“In the shadow of Heshbon those fleeing from the snare stood, because a fire went out from Heshbon and a flame from the midst of Sihon, and it devoured a portion of Moab and the crown of the sons of tumult.”

He says that those fleeing from the snare stood in the shadow of Heshbon because they hoped to find some comfort in its fortification, but in vain. For the fire of vengeance, which proceeded from the merits of their deeds, overwhelmed the crown of the tumultuous sons of Moab, as the just Judge rendered retribution. Hence it continues:

“Woe to you, Moab! You have perished, people of Chemosh, because your sons have been seized and your daughters have gone into captivity.”

No fortification of their cities, nor any power of the false gods denoted by the name Chemosh, was able to rescue or defend them from the enemy. All their sons and daughters went into captivity.

So there will be perpetual woe for those who trust in human wisdom, serve various errors, refuse to hear God’s wisdom, and will not submit to the divine laws. Their sons and daughters will go into captivity together with their parents—that is, disciples together with their teachers—from which they cannot escape.

But what follows—“And I shall restore the captivity of Moab in the last days, says the Lord”—seems to me to signify the times of grace. In them, whoever among all the nations wishes to believe and to turn away from the worship of idols is granted the hope of eternal salvation, because God is not a respecter of persons; rather, in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. “And it shall be, according to the prophecy of Joel, that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel II).

## CHAPTER XLIX  
The Word of the Lord against Ammon and against Edom; against Kedar, Hazor, and Elam.

“Thus says the Lord to the sons of Ammon: Are there no sons in Israel, or has he no heir? Why, then, has Milcom taken Gad as an inheritance, and why has his people dwelt in its cities? Therefore, behold, days are coming upon you, says the Lord, and I shall cause the battle cry to be heard over Rabbah of the sons of Ammon. It shall be scattered into tumult, and its daughters shall be burned with fire. And Israel shall possess those who possessed him, says the Lord.”

(Maurus.) After Moab, therefore, the divine word turns to the sons of Ammon and reproves them because they dared to attack the land of the Israelites and invade the Lord’s inheritance. It foretells that deserved vengeance is about to come upon them and that Israel will possess those who possessed it.

“Howl, Heshbon, for Ai has been devastated. Cry out, daughters of Rabbah; gird yourselves with sackcloth. Mourn and go around among the hedges, for Milcom shall go into captivity, together with his priests and his princes.”

It has already been said above that Heshbon was a great city of the Amorites. Ar also was the metropolitan city of the Moabites; today, its name compounded from Hebrew and Greek, it is called Ariopolis. Many think that it means Ares, that is, “the city of Mars.”

Rabbah was the metropolis of the Ammonites. Today it is called Philadelphia, after the Egyptian king Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, who ruled Arabia together with Judea. Milcom, however, was the idol of the Ammonites, and its name means “my king.”

The vengeance for their crime is rightly foretold for these cities, because they had not only despised God by plundering and devastating his people, but had also worshiped an idol in God’s place as a deity, calling it “my king.” “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm LIX). And accursed is the one who serves foreign gods and refuses to render service to the one and only God, the true Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Why do you boast in the valleys? Your valley has flowed away, O delicate daughter who trusted in your treasures and said, ‘Who is coming against me?’ Behold, I shall bring terror upon you, says the Lord God of hosts, [Col. 1126D] from those who are all around you; and each of you shall be scattered from before the others, nor will there be anyone to gather the fugitives.””

By the name “valleys” he signifies an abundance of produce, in which the Ammonites trusted, supposing that they could never come to want. But by the Lord’s word their future devastation and dispersal are foretold to them. Ezekiel likewise prophesied against the sons of Ammon, saying:

“‘Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: “Aha, aha!” against my sanctuary—or, “because you rejoiced over my sanctuary, because it was polluted”—and against the land of Israel, because it was desolate, and against the house of Judah, because they have been led into captivity. Therefore I shall give you to the sons of the East, or to Eden, as an inheritance. They shall establish their sheepfolds in you and [Col. 1127A] pitch their tents in you. They themselves shall eat your crops, and they themselves shall drink your milk, or your abundance. I shall make Rabbath a dwelling-place for camels, or the city of Ammon a pasture for camels, and the sons of Ammon a resting-place for flocks; and you shall know that I am the Lord.”’”

(Hieronymus.) According to the tropological interpretation, we can understand the sons of Ammon, who were generated from Lot’s seed in a cave, and generated in drunkenness and incest, as all heretics. Concerning them the apostle John also says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2). These arose from inclination—for this is how Lot is rendered in our language:

“For all have turned aside together; they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. [Col. 1127B] 13).

Against these the prophetic face is set, or made firm, so that it may crush them by its severity; and he says to them: Because you insulted my Church at the time of persecution, since my sanctuary had been polluted by various vices—whether through the fault of those who served me, or through the cruelty of the enemies who persecuted my people—and because you considered the land of Israel, that is, those who see God in their understanding, to be desolate of the choir of virtues. And just as the sons of the house of Judah, which confesses God and possesses true faith and right confession, have been led into captivity and have ceased to serve the Lord, so, O you who insult, you shall be handed over to the sons of the East, who have proceeded from the true light, and you shall be handed over as an inheritance, so that you too may learn to confess the Lord.

By way of metaphor it is said that the sons of the East will place their sheepfolds over them, fasten their tents, drink their milk, and eat their crops; and that the city formerly characterized by pride will become a dwelling-place for camels, which, having laid aside the burden of sins, can enter through the eye of a needle; and a resting-place for flocks governed by the good shepherd. When they have done this, mingled with and handed over to the shepherds of the East, they will understand that he is the Lord. Hence it is said:

“And after this I shall restore the captives of the sons of Ammon, says the Lord.” (Maurus.) For after the heretics’ return from error to right faith, their captivity to sins will be dissolved, and they will be received into the communion of the holy Church, from which they had gone out.

“Concerning Idumaea: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Counsel has perished from the sons; their wisdom has become useless. Flee and turn your backs; descend into the abyss, inhabitants of Dedan, for I have brought the destruction of Esau upon him, the time of his visitation. If grape-gatherers had come upon you, they would not have left a cluster; if thieves had robbed you at night, they would have taken only what was sufficient for them. But I have uncovered Esau; I have revealed his hidden things, and he will not be able to conceal himself. His offspring has been devastated, as have his brothers and his neighbors, and he will not exist.” (Hieronymus.)

No one acquainted with the Scriptures will doubt that Esau, Seir, Edom, Idumaea, and Duma are called one and the same nation. And, to say nothing of the other prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, [Col. 1128A] and Amos prophesied against Idumaea and Edom. The prophet Obadiah directs his entire prophecy against this nation, because it lost the birthright and received its name from the dish of food. Esau is also interpreted as “deed.” It should be known, moreover, that in Hebrew Idumaea is never written, but always Edom; the Greek translation rendered this as Idumaea.

It is foretold to Idumaea that there will no longer be wisdom in Teman, which is interpreted as “failing,” and that their wisdom will become useless. The inhabitants of Dedan, likewise a city of Idumaea, will turn their backs; Dedan is interpreted as “kinship.” For grape-gatherers, that is, devastators, have come upon Idumaea and have not left a cluster; and they have not devastated it secretly or in part, but openly and completely—its offspring, its brothers, and its neighbors.

“‘If grape-gatherers,’ he says, ‘had come upon you, they would not have left a cluster; if thieves had robbed you at night, they would have taken what was sufficient for them. But I have uncovered Esau; I have revealed his hidden things, and he will not be able to conceal himself. His offspring has been devastated, as have his brothers and his neighbors, and he will not exist.’”

What he says is this: If thieves and robbers, who customarily break into houses at night and carry off what is in them, had entered you and, hidden by the darkness, gone around the corners of your houses, they would certainly have taken only what they thought sufficient for themselves; they would have left something in the buildings, either because they were satisfied or because they did not know it was there. If grape-gatherers had entered your vineyard, whether wishing to ravage it as enemies or to harvest it as hired workers, however carefully they gathered the grapes, they would still have left clusters hidden among the vines [Col. 1128C] and foliage, between the branches.

But the enemies who came against you at the Lord’s command—he means the Babylonians and the army of Nebuchadnezzar—searched everything. They examined all your secrets, and the caves and holes in which you live. And, to say something also about the nature of the place: the entire southern region of the Idumaeans, from Eleutheropolis as far as Petra and Aila—for this is the possession of Esau—has little dwellings in caves. Because of the excessive heat of the sun, since it is a southern province, it makes use of underground huts.

“‘I have uncovered,’ he says,” that is, I have brought into the middle what was pressed down into the earth; everything that you had shut away has been opened. When I searched your substance together with the enemies, no hidden places could conceal anything.

Alternatively: I think that the thieves and robbers who enter at night, because they are sons of night and darkness, signify heretics who do not preach the doctrines of truth. They steal what is sufficient for themselves and hasten daily to snatch things from the flocks of the Church.

These enter the vineyard of our Lord, which he transferred from the Egypt of this world, and from whose produce he promises that he will drink wine in the kingdom of his Father. They desire to ravage everything so completely that they scarcely leave a cluster in it. But the Lord acts in the opposite way: through his saints, ecclesiastical men, and teachers, he brings into the open all their secrets, hidden mysteries, and the patriarchs of Esau—for by these I understand those who first devised heresies. His first victory is that what had been concealed becomes manifest.

Hence it is said with astonishment: “How Esau was searched out! His hidden things have been discovered.” Consider Marcion and Valentinus and all the heretics: with a conscience branded by the doctrines of demons, they applaud themselves and deceive simple souls, as though initiating them into certain divine mysteries, by carefully composed speech. But when the discourse has brought into the open their thirty aeons, decades, ogdoads, dodecads, their two gods, and the monstrous Abraxas, then the wisdom of Esau is shown to be folly.

According to the tropological interpretation, this seems to me to be the meaning: Idumaea is called earthly and carnal. It rises up against the spirit, so that we may not do the things that belong to the spirit, and it hastens to draw the soul, placed in the middle, toward itself. It wishes to exact vengeance from those to whom it had previously been subject, the sons of Judah; and it remembers the ancient pain, that it had not properly possessed power. Therefore it seeks revenge upon those who, withdrawing from the flesh, followed the spirit.

For this reason the Lord himself, as avenger of the sons of Judah, stretches out his hand over Idumaea. According to Ezekiel’s prophecy, he removes from it man and beast—whatever seems to possess either reason or simple faith—in order to reduce it to a wilderness; and he does the same with Teman, which is interpreted as “failing,” and Dedan, which likewise signifies kinship. He killed them all with the sword that he placed in the hand of his people Israel, so that Edom might be overthrown and feel the Lord’s anger and fury, and understand that his vengeance had achieved this end: that it should serve the house of Judah.

This is what the Apostle also discusses when he writes: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9). He loves Jacob because Jacob supplants and overcomes what is carnal and earthly, and deserves to receive his blessings. For we live first according to the flesh and afterward according to the spirit: first there are vices, then virtues, by which the vices are overthrown, since the human heart is inclined toward evil from childhood, while mature age despises the errors of youth.

Hence David also says: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 18). Yet it must be understood that Jacob received the first blessing, and Esau the second. Finally it is said of Esau: “You shall be the servant of your brother” (Gen. 27). When the flesh has become subject to the spirit and, joined to it, ceases to be flesh, Idumaea will pass over into Judaea.

“Leave your orphans; I shall make them live, and your widows shall hope in me.” (Maurus.)

The Father of widows and orphans promises to give life to those who hope in him, to show that he himself is the one to whom the prophet says: “To you, Lord, the poor man has been abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 9). And elsewhere: “Blessing I shall bless his widow; I shall satisfy his poor with bread” (Ps. 131).

When the adversaries of God have been killed, their orphans and widows are therefore saved, because if the soul, separated from worldly luxury and secular conduct, turns itself wholly toward God and hopes in his goodness, it will have eternal life.

[Col. 1130A] “For thus says the Lord: Behold, those for whom there was no judgment that they should drink the cup shall surely drink, and will you be left as innocent? You shall not be innocent, but you shall surely drink. For I have sworn by myself, says the Lord, that Bozrah shall become desolation, reproach, wilderness, and a curse; and all its cities shall become everlasting desolations.”

“If the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4.) And if a father scourges his son, what does a wicked servant deserve? Idumaea therefore hoped in vain that it could sin with impunity, since it saw that the Lord had handed Judah over to the hands of enemies for correction because of its sins.

Bozrah, then, is not a city in Edom but in Moab, and its name is interpreted as “firm” and “fortified.” Nevertheless, because it was destined to be devastated by the Lord’s judgment, it was captured and abandoned as though it were weak. (Hieronymus.)

We must understand, according to the laws of tropology, either that this speech was made against the Jews, who are rivals of Christians and persecute their brother Jacob, the supplanting people who took the birthright from them, or certainly against all heresies and opposing doctrines. These appear to be close to us, but are more truly hostile, and they strive to drive the simple inhabitant of the house of Jacob from his paternal inheritance.

For this reason Idumaea is interpreted as “earthly,” and, because of its red color, it can also be understood as “bloody.” Therefore the Savior, carrying victory over the world to the Father, when the angels cried out, “Open your gates, O rulers, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23), [Col. 1130C] and when, in Isaiah, they asked in astonishment, “Who is this who comes from Edom, with a shining garment from Bosor, so beautiful in his white robe?” (Isa. 63), spoke to him face to face:

“Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread in the winepress?”

He speaks in triumph, displaying the palms of his cross: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no man from the nations was with me.”

There are those who refer Idumaea to the flesh and believe that the soul is summoned to battle against it, so that, by putting to death our members that are upon the earth—sexual immorality, impurity, and passion—we may obtain eternal victory in Christ.

“I have heard a report from the Lord, and an envoy has been sent to the nations. Gather together and come against her, and let us rise up for battle.” (Maurus.)

It should be known that this sentence of Jeremiah is contained in the prophet Obadiah in almost the same words, just as very many words of this chapter of Jeremiah agree with the language of Obadiah.

We have already said above that Edom and Idumaea are the same, because in Hebrew the name refers to the one who founded it, whereas in Greek it refers to the city founded by him. Jeremiah heard, or Obadiah heard, or all the prophets heard together. For all of them write against Edom, saying that an envoy has been sent to the nations—the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2). Concerning him the Father also speaks through Haggai: “I shall shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all the nations shall come” (Hag. 2). In Isaiah he is described as “the Angel of great counsel and the Father of the age to come” (Isa. 9).

We can say that he himself is the envoy and the very fortress, saying what the prophetic discourse has joined together: “Rise, and let us rise up against him,” or against her, for battle.

The envoy who has been sent to the nations speaks these words: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. 5). And lest this battle perhaps seem difficult and unfamiliar to us, he says: “You have me first in the battle line; I shall be the ἀρχιστρατηγός, the commander-in-chief of the battles.” I am the one who appeared holding a sword to Joshua son of Nun, and who defeated Amalek while Moses fought beneath the standard of my cross. Here Jeremiah, in his vision against Idumaea, does not differ greatly from these things.

“For behold, I have made you small among the nations, contemptible among human beings. Your arrogance has deceived you, and the pride of your heart, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock and strive to seize the height of the hill. Though you exalt your nest like an eagle, I shall bring you down from there, says the Lord.”

In prophetic interpretation we ought to follow our customary method: first laying the foundations of the historical account, and then, if we can, raising up lofty towers and the heights of spiritual understanding for readers.

“O Edom,” he says, “although you are the least among all the surrounding nations, and small in number in comparison with the other peoples, you raise yourself beyond your strength through pride. Although you live in caves—indeed, in rocky caverns—humble and rather poor, possessing no lofty roofs of buildings, you lift yourself up like an eagle into the heights. You swell so greatly in thought that you believe yourself to dwell among the stars. Even if you could penetrate beyond nature into the heights of heaven, I would bring you down from there and lead you back to earth, says the Lord God.”

But what has been added in Jeremiah—“and strive to seize the height of the hill”—has disclosed the riddle, signifying by the hill Mount Zion. Accordingly, he wishes it to be understood either as the city of Jerusalem itself or as the temple established in it.

Even those who discuss the nature of birds have recorded that the eagle flies higher than all other birds. It is said to possess such powerful vision that, when it is carried motionless above the sea on unmoving wings, though it is invisible to human eyes, it can see small fish swimming from such a height; and when it is near the shore, it descends like a missile and drags its seized prey to the shore with its wings.

If we have learned the history, let us follow the spiritual understanding. Although you may seem great to yourself, O heretic, and despise the smallness of the Church, you are nevertheless small among the nations and contemptible—and not merely contemptible, but, with ἐπίτασις, exceedingly contemptible.

“The pride of your heart has lifted you up.” For which heretic is not lifted up in pride, despising the simplicity of the Church and considering faith ignorance? He dwells in the clefts of the rock, raising up his throne.

Although “rock” is often used either of the Lord’s person or of firmness—hence the prophet says, “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 19), and it is said to Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16)—it is also frequently understood in the contrary sense: “I shall take away,” he says, “the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 36). And: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3).

This is especially so here, where he did not say that he dwells upon the rock on which the wise builder constructs his house, but in the clefts or caverns of the rock, signifying the divisions of heresies from the rock of Christ and from the Church.

Moreover, what is read in Obadiah—“exalting his throne, and saying in his heart, ‘Who will bring me down to the ground?’” (Obad. 3)—shows the swelling of the heretical mind, insofar as those who trust in their own mysteries and secrets are concerned. We should understand this hyperbolically as referring to those who promise themselves the kingdoms of heaven.

Hence the Apostle writes to such people: “Already you are reigning without us; and I wish that you were reigning, so that we also might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4). David likewise says: “They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has gone through the earth” (Ps. 72).

If, therefore, they have been exalted like an eagle—for they too promise themselves the likeness of eagles, which are accustomed to gather around the Lord’s corpse—and have set their nest among the stars, I shall bring them down from there, says the Lord.

For just as, while the master of the house sleeps, an enemy sows weeds among the good seed (Matt. 13), so the great eagle, with enormous wings, extended length of limb, abundant feathers, and variegated coloring, which has the habit of entering Lebanon, taking a branch from the top of a cedar, and planting it over many waters so that shoots may grow in the vineyard, is accustomed to set its nest among the stars of the Church. Concerning these it is said elsewhere: “The righteous will shine like the stars” (Matt. 13).

I said above that this can also be understood against the flesh: its strength has been diminished at Christ’s coming, it is contemptible and subject to the soul’s authority, and it is raised up in vain while dwelling in the clefts of the rock—that is, in perceptions or thoughts—and wishing to rule the soul by exalting its throne, while it believes that its works cannot be overcome. To it it is said that, although it raises itself up and imitates the heights of the eagle, and has deceived many of the saints, it has nevertheless been separated from the Lord and cast down. What we have understood concerning heretics and the flesh can also be understood against the Jews.

[Col. 1132D] “And Idumaea shall become desolate; everyone who passes through it shall be astonished and hiss at all its wounds, as Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors were overthrown, says the Lord. No man shall dwell there, nor shall a son of man sojourn in it.”

Therefore, on the day of the Lord’s wrath, the assembly of heretics—or of blaspheming Jews—will be made desolate, because afterward they will never have the power to assemble a council of the wicked. Everyone who passes through it will be astonished and hiss at all its wounds, because the punishments they will suffer for their impieties will be greatly worthy of fear and dread.

For just as sulfur and fire burned Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19) and reduced them to everlasting desolation, so fire and sulfur will rain upon sinners, and the spirit of storms will be the portion of their cup.

“Behold, like a lion he shall ascend from the pride of the Jordan to the strong beauty, for suddenly I shall make him run against it; and who is the chosen one whom I shall appoint against it? For who is like me? And who will withstand me? And who is this shepherd who will resist my face?”

Therefore, just as the Lord chastised the pride of the Jews, whom he marks by the name Jordan, so also, through the ministers of his wrath, he will punish with complete vengeance the faithlessness and envy of the Idumaeans, which they had exercised against their brothers. No one can resist his counsel and will.

Likewise, heretics and the enemies of God’s Church will not escape torments corresponding to their wicked works and doctrines. But the most savage and rapacious lion, the devil, has shut them away in Tartarus, where they will be tortured by perpetual tearing.

“Therefore hear the counsel of the Lord that he has formed concerning Edom, and the thoughts that he has thought concerning the inhabitants of Teman: Surely the little ones of the flock shall cast them down; surely they shall scatter their dwelling with them. At the sound of their ruin the earth has been shaken; the sound of their voice has been heard at the Red Sea. Behold, like an eagle he shall ascend and fly, and spread his wings over Bozrah. And the heart of the strong men of Idumaea shall be on that day like the heart of a woman in labor.”

When the devastator comes upon Idumaea and Bozrah—he compares him to an eagle spreading its wings, that is, ready to seize prey—the sound of their ruin will resound far and wide and strike terror into the neighboring provinces, because, according to the Lord’s counsel, the proud nation is paying the penalties it deserves.

Mystically, according to the Lord’s counsel, the little ones of the flocks—that is, the humble among the Church’s people, with right faith and truthful doctrine—cast down and scatter the proud doctrines of heretics.

“And the heart of the strong men of Idumaea shall be on that day like the heart of a woman in labor,” because, at the Lord’s command, all the arrogance of the heretics’ defiance will be crushed and reduced to nothing, when, according to the Psalmist:

“God will arise, and his enemies will be scattered; those who hate him will flee before him. As smoke vanishes, so they will vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so sinners will perish before the face of God. But the righteous shall feast; they shall exult in the presence of God and delight in joy and an abundance of peace” (Ps. 67).

[Col. 1133D] “Concerning Damascus: Hamath and Arpad have been confounded, for they have heard an exceedingly evil report. They are troubled in the sea; in anxiety it could not rest. Damascus has been dissolved; it has turned to flight. Fear has seized it; distress and pains have taken hold of it like a woman in labor. How have they abandoned the praised city, the city of joy? Therefore its young men shall fall in its streets, and all its men of war shall be silent on that day, says the Lord of hosts. And I shall kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the walls of Ben-hadad. Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck.”

After the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, and Idumaeans, the discourse turns to Damascus, that is, Arabia, [Col. 1134A] which was once itself a royal city and held supremacy throughout Syria. Antioch, Laodicea, and Apamea had not yet flourished; we know that these cities were enlarged under Alexander and the power of the Macedonians.

Because Damascus had always provided assistance to the ten tribes against Judah, as the history in Kings and Chronicles relates, he also signifies that devastation was approaching it from the Assyrians, when the king of the Assyrians said: “I captured Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria. Just as I captured these, so I shall capture all the kingdoms.”

Likewise, we read in the Book of Kings: “The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, captured it, and transferred it to Cyrene. He also killed Rezin, who was king of Damascus.” All these things they suffered while Hezekiah was reigning in Jerusalem.

Hamath and Arpad, therefore, which are mentioned in Isaiah [Col. 1134B] and Jeremiah, are cities of Damascus and Arabia, which the king of Assyria devastated. It should be understood, however, that Isaiah describes the nearby Assyrian captivity, whereas Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of the city of Damascus—that is, the captivity of the few whom the king of the Assyrians had left there.

Others believe that the prophecy refers to the Roman captivity, when the people of the Jews were also captured and Damascus, over which Aretas ruled, endured a similar servitude, so that everything written concerning them may be transferred to the time of Christ and the mysteries of the apostles.

For Damascus is threatened with the harsh word of captivity, which the prophet calls an exceedingly evil report; fear will seize it, with its strength dissolved, and distress and pains will agitate it like a woman in labor; fire will devour the walls of Damascus and the fortifications of Ben-hadad.

We first read the name of Damascus in Genesis (Gen. 15), where one from Damascus, before Isaac, was Abraham’s household servant and was thought to be his heir, unless Sarah’s son had been begotten according to the promise. Damascus is interpreted either as “cup of blood,” “one drinking blood,” or “blood of sackcloth.” All these meanings suit the pagan people, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty and performed deeds worthy of mourning and sackcloth.

The historical account in the Book of Chronicles relates (2 Chron. 22) that, when a year had been completed, the army of Syria went up against Joash, king of the Jews, came to Jerusalem, and killed all the leaders of the people. They sent all the booty to the king of Damascus, who had come with only a few men; and God delivered an exceedingly great multitude into their hand because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.

This must be considered according to the allegorical sense and as a type of future events: whether we can refer it to the time of the Lord’s coming. After the end of the acceptable year in which the Savior preached the Gospel, an army of the nations came up from Damascus, with a few men, against Judah and Jerusalem, which had abandoned the Lord. They carried off all the riches of their Law and Prophets and sent them to the king of Damascus—to ecclesiastical men and the teachers of the Gospel. Compared with the whole world and with the Jews scattered throughout the world, these were then few in number; yet the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands because they had abandoned the Son of God, who had previously been proclaimed through the prophets.

For this reason, I think, Saul too—who afterward received the name Paul through his excellence, and who was a zealot for the law—came from Damascus. He wished to fight against believers from the nations who were in Damascus, so that from there he might again go up to Jerusalem to attack the Jews (Acts 9).

Through Damascus the calling of the nations is signified, because they loved or drank blood. After they believe in Christ, they will cease to be the city of their former conduct, “and, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, they will be like a heap of stones in a ruin” (Isa. 17). For just as heaps of stones scattered through the fields are gathered into one mound, so from all the nations a heap of believers is assembled for the ruin of the Jewish people: when they fall and we rise. (Maurus.)

[Col. 1135B] Damascus, then, was spiritually seized by fear, distress, and pains like those of a woman in labor—that is, those who repented before God for their sins, so that they might give birth to the spirit of salvation and bring forth the fruit of good works. They therefore turned to a salutary flight, so that, abandoning idolatry, they might be converted to the true God; and those who had previously been warriors of the devil through their savagery might now become devoted soldiers of Christ through their gentleness.

“Thus says the Lord: Rise up, go up against Kedar, and devastate the sons of the East. They shall seize their tents and their flocks, their skins and all their vessels; they shall take their camels for themselves, and they shall summon terror against them all around. Flee; depart with great haste; sit in the abysses, you who inhabit Hazor, says the Lord. For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has formed a plan against you and devised thoughts against you.

“Rise up and go up against a tranquil nation that dwells confidently, says the Lord. They have neither doors nor bars; they dwell alone. Their camels shall become booty, the multitude of their cattle prey; and I shall scatter them in every wind—those who are shorn in their hair—and from every boundary of theirs I shall bring destruction upon them, says the Lord. And Hazor shall become a dwelling-place of dragons, desolate forever. No man shall remain there, nor shall a son of man sojourn in it.” (Hieronymus.)

The Book of Genesis teaches that Kedar and the Hagarenes—who are improperly called Saracens—were descended from Ishmael. They dwell throughout the entire wilderness. I think the poet also refers to them when he says, “The Barceans wandering far and wide.” And according to the book mentioned above, “he shall dwell in the presence of all his brothers,” because the very broad desert extends from India as far as Mauretania and the Atlantic Ocean.

I think this is what the title of Jeremiah means: “Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck.” Immediately it follows:

“Thus says the Lord: Rise up and go up against Kedar, and devastate the sons of the East. They shall seize their tents and their flocks, their skins and all their vessels, and they shall take their camels for themselves,” and so on to the end of the chapter.

Consider how he described the very nation of the Ishmaelites, that is, the Saracens: they live in tents; wherever night compels them, there they establish their dwellings; their wealth consists in herds, cattle, camels, and flocks; they have neither doors nor bars. They do not live in cities but in the wilderness.

These people, too, were destroyed by the Babylonians, who overturned to the ground Hazor, the city that had been the nation’s metropolis in the wilderness. Yet when the herds of camels and sheep were captured and their skins and tents divided by lot, the destruction of that nation’s name was signified, since more than a hundred thousand dromedary camels are accustomed to flee through the vast wilderness in a single day.

“He takes away,” he says, “all Kedar in the small number of archers,” an art in which they are especially skilled.

Spiritually, however, Kedar, which is interpreted as “darkness,” and Hazor, which is interpreted as “arrow of light,” signify heretics darkened in mind, who nevertheless pretend, in the pronouncements of their doctrines, to shoot arrows of light. They pretend to be sons of the East, although in truth they are sons of darkness.

Their tents and flocks, skins and vessels, camels and cattle are seized by the spiritual Chaldaeans, who, together with the mystical Nebuchadnezzar, lay them waste. For they seize teachers with their disciples, vessels of wickedness with the dead bodies of crimes, and brutish people deformed by the crookedness of sins, who hide in the abysses of their crimes, and lead them away to eternal destruction.

Although they are shorn in their hair and think themselves stripped of the hair of their vices, nevertheless, because of their sins and their most wicked hypocrisy, they are subject to everlasting death. Their city, which had always been opposed to the city of God, will become a dwelling-place of spiritual dragons. No ecclesiastical and catholic man will remain there, nor will a son of man dwell there, one who truly makes use of the reason created in him by God. Only the lost and those deceived by errors will remain there forever.

Concerning this spiritual Kedar the Psalmist says: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. 119).

He comes to the second part, where, having condemned vices, he regrets that he has a long life in the world.

“Woe is me” is the speech of one grieving, because he is wearied by the length of this world. There is no doubt that various saints have had this complaint, as Ecclesiastes says: “And I praised all the dead who have already died above all the living who are still alive” (Eccli. 4). The apostle Paul also cries out: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

The prophet therefore rightly groaned in this part, since he burned with a love very like that of the Lord. “Sojourning” signifies pilgrimage. We call those inhabitants who dwell for a time in foreign lands but are separated far from their homeland. This is rightly said of those whose way of life is always in heaven, but who are still held here in the body.

When he said, “has been prolonged,” he expressed the intense feeling of one who longs. To someone desiring to see a blessed homeland, even if the time here is proved to be brief, it nevertheless seems long.

It follows: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.” Kedar is a Hebrew name which in our language is interpreted as “darkness.” This applies to the lovers of this world, who, wrapped in dark deeds, love those things through which they are known to perish. By this name he appropriately signifies sinners, among whom the good soul sighs that it still dwells. For a good spirit must be afflicted whenever it is enclosed by association with the wicked.

“Thus was the word of the Lord made to Jeremiah the prophet against Elam, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, saying:

‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I shall break the bow of Elam and the chief of their strength, and I shall bring upon Elam four winds from the four quarters of heaven; I shall scatter them into all these winds, and there shall be no nation to which the fugitives of Elam will not come. I shall make Elam tremble before their enemies and in the sight of those who seek their life. And I shall bring evil upon them, the anger of my wrath, says the Lord, [Col. 1137B] and I shall send the sword after them until I consume them. I shall establish my throne in Elam and destroy from there kings and princes, says the Lord. But in the latter days I shall restore the captives of Elam, says the Lord.’”

We should understand Elam to be the region of Persia, from which the Elamites also derive their name. The prophet foretells that, although the Medes and Persians devastated Babylon and destroyed the kingdom of the Chaldeans, they themselves would in turn be destroyed by the Macedonians and through the power of Alexander the [Col. 1138A] Great. For he who chastised the other kingdoms on account of their iniquities did not leave this kingdom unpunished for its crimes and impieties.

The Elamites are therefore interpreted as “despisers” or “those who tempt,” and they signify the persecutors of the Church of Christ. The Lord has given them power so that, for a time, despising the Church of God and testing it through various persecutions, they may weary it. But the hour will come when vengeance will overtake them from the four quarters of heaven, and they will tremble before their enemies, because evil will threaten them from every side and a mighty storm will be at hand. “For the Son of Man will send his angels from the four winds of heaven, to gather all scandals out of his kingdom,” and they will “send those who work iniquity into the furnace of burning fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth [Col. 1138B] (Mark XIII).” There the sword of the Lord’s vengeance will consume them forever.

Nevertheless, because many among those persecutors will first be converted to the faith of Christ and received into the number of the brethren, the divine word does not remain silent when it says: “But in the latter days I shall restore the captives of Elam, says the Lord.” Those who had previously been captives of sins will later, through the grace of Christ, be free; and those who had formerly been enemies will now become friends and neighbors.

# BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 1137]

[Col. 1137C] Having completed the prophecy that the prophet uttered against various nations—that is, against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, the children of Ammon, Damascus, and Kedar, and finally against Babylon and the Chaldeans, who by the Lord’s command rebuked the other nations—he now directs his discourse against them. Those whom he previously reproved covertly in many passages he now openly exposes, expressing their devastation and complete desolation as the punishment for their crimes and sins.

## CHAPTER L. The Lord’s discourse against Babylon foretells the return of the people to Judah and Jerusalem.

“The word that the Lord spoke concerning Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans by the hand of Jeremiah the prophet: [Col. 1137D] Announce among the nations and make it heard; raise a signal, proclaim it and do not conceal it; say: Babylon has been captured, Bel has been put to shame, Merodach has been defeated; all her carved images have been put to shame, her idols have been overcome, because a nation from the north has come up against her. It will make her land a desolation, and no one will dwell in it, from man to cattle; they have been shaken and have gone away.”

(MAURUS.) Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel delivered the word of the Lord against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. In it they rehearsed its many transgressions and iniquities and foretold the deserved vengeance that would come upon it. How Babylon was overthrown by the Medes and Persians, history [Col. 1138C] reveals, and the books of the prophets do not keep silent about it.

Hence the present prophet commands that it be announced among the nations and proclaimed that Babylon has been captured, Bel put to shame, and Merodach defeated—namely, the idols that the Chaldeans worshiped as gods. All her carved images have been put to shame and their idols overcome, because a nation—certainly of the Persians and Medes—from the north has come up against her and will make her land a desolation, so that no one will dwell in it, from man to cattle.

Isaiah wrote something similar in his book, saying:

“Behold, I shall stir up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver nor desire gold, but will kill the little ones with arrows and will not pity nursing mothers; their eye will not spare the children. And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah by God. It will not be inhabited forever, nor will it be founded from generation to generation; the Arab will not pitch his tents there, nor will shepherds rest there. But beasts will be there, and their houses will be filled with dragons; ostriches will dwell there, and shaggy creatures will leap there; owls will answer in their houses, and sirens in the temples of pleasure (Isaiah XIII).”

What was hidden has been revealed. The strong and giants are by no means to be understood as angels and demons, but as the nation of the Medes, whose leader Darius was the first to destroy the Babylonian empire, after Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar and son of Evil-merodach, had been killed.

He describes the cruelty of the Medes and Persians as so great that, burning with the desire to shed blood, they despise gold and silver [Col. 1139A] and regard offered riches as filth; yet they kill the little ones with arrows, do not spare infants at the breast, and their eye does not pity the children. Let the little ones be killed, whose wounds will be no smaller than their bodies; let pregnant wombs be cut open, infants torn forth, and the cruel victor kill the children pressed to their mothers’ breasts.

Thus, to the present day, the prophecy concerning Babylon is fulfilled. Just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, so this city, once overthrown, will not be inhabited forever. In its place the Persians made Seleucia and Ctesiphon famous cities. “The Arab will not pitch his tents there, nor will shepherds rest there; but beasts will be there, and their houses will be filled with dragons; ostriches will dwell there, shaggy creatures will leap there, owls will answer in their houses, and sirens in the temples of pleasure.”

Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not even be useful as pasture for herds and cattle. The Arab and the Saracen will not pitch tents there, nor will shepherds, exhausted by the labor of following their flocks, rest there. But among the ruins and narrow spaces of the ancient wreckage there will dwell those creatures which only the Seventy translated as θηρία, that is, “beasts.” Others, wishing demons or phantoms to be understood, use the very name written in Hebrew for them.

As for what follows—“Shaggy creatures will leap there”—some understand either incubi or certain wild bulls, men whom some call Fauns or Satyrs; others understand kinds of demons. In place of “owls,” the Seventy alone translated the Hebrew word as “onocentaurs.” As for the sirens, which we have interpreted as demons, or certain monsters, or even great dragons—because they are crested and flying—all these expressions signify devastation and desolation. The destruction of the once most powerful city is so great that, because of the multitude of demons and beasts, no shepherd—that is, no seeker of the wilderness—dares enter it.

We learned from a certain Elamite brother who came from those regions and now lives the monastic life at Jerusalem that royal hunts take place in Babylon, and that beasts of every kind are confined merely by the circuit of its walls.

“In those days and at that time, says the Lord, the children of Israel will come, they and the children of Judah together. Walking and weeping, they will hasten and seek the Lord their God. They will ask the way to Zion; their faces will come here, and they will be joined to the Lord by an everlasting covenant that will never be erased by any forgetfulness.”

This promise concerns the return of the people of God from the captivity which they endured under the Assyrians or Chaldeans into the land of Judah; or, rather, it signifies the Christian age, when the children of God gather from different nations into the catholic Church and the true religion. There they will seek their Lord, asking and learning the way of truth, and turning the face of their heart toward doing God’s will. They will be joined to him by an everlasting covenant, which no forgetfulness will ever erase.

For this also, under another figure, the prophet Ezekiel describes in his book, saying:

“You, son of man, take one piece of wood and write upon it, ‘Judah and the children of Israel, his companions.’ Then take another piece of wood and write upon it, ‘Joseph, the wood of Ephraim and the whole house of Israel, his companions.’ Join them one to the other into one piece of wood, and they will become one in your hand.

“When the children of your people speak to you, saying, ‘Will you not tell us what you mean by these things?’ you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall take the wood of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel that are joined to him, and I shall place them together with the wood of Judah. I shall make them one piece of wood, and they will be one in his hand.

“The pieces of wood upon which you have written will be in your hand before their eyes. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they have gone; I shall gather them from every side and bring them to their own soil. I shall make them one nation in the land, upon the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over them all. They will no longer be two nations, nor will they be divided any longer into two kingdoms.

“They will no longer defile themselves with their idols, abominations, or any of their iniquities. I shall save them from all their settlements in which they sinned; I shall cleanse them, and they will be my people, and I shall be their God. My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd over them all.

“They will walk in my judgments, keep my commandments, and do them. They will dwell upon the land that I gave to my servant Jacob, in which your fathers dwelt; they and their children and their children’s children will dwell upon it forever. David my servant will be their prince forever.

“I shall make with them a covenant of peace; it will be an everlasting covenant with them. I shall establish them, multiply them, and set my sanctuary in their midst forever. My tabernacle will be among them; I shall be their God, and they will be my people. The nations will know that I am the Lord who sanctifies Israel, when my sanctification is in their midst forever (Ezekiel XXXVII).”

The history of the Kings relates (III Kings XXXVII) that under Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, the twelve tribes were divided. Two—that is, Judah and Benjamin, together with the Levites and priests—followed Rehoboam, who reigned in Jerusalem, and his kingdom was called Judah. The other ten tribes said, “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse [Isaiah],” and submitted their necks to Jeroboam son of Nebat, of the tribe of Ephraim, who was descended from Joseph; they served him and were called, for the most part, by the ancient name of Israel.

For a long time the kingdoms of Judah and Israel fought against one another and obeyed their own kings. First the ten tribes were captured by the Assyrians; after some time, those called Judah were led captive by the Chaldeans to Babylon. After seventy years the tribe of Judah was restored to its ancient land. The ten tribes called Israel, however, remain captive in the mountains and cities of the Medes to this day [Col. 1141A] (IV Kings XII; IV Kings XXV).

The present prophecy therefore promises from the mouth of the Lord that the two kingdoms will be joined to one another—namely, the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel. The rod of Ephraim, who was descended from Joseph, together with the remaining tribes associated with him, will be taken and joined to the rod of Judah, so that they will no longer be called Judah and Israel but will be called by one name, Judah. Under the prophet’s figure, who precedes as a type of the Lord Savior, they will be held not in two hands but in the one hand of Christ.

For he says that he will take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they were led captive, and bring them back to the land and the mountains of Israel, of which we read above. They will be called one nation and ruled under the authority of one king, so that they will no longer defile themselves with idols [Col. 1141B] and abominations. Once they have been freed from the settlements of captivity in which they sinned through every vice, they will be cleansed and become God’s people, so that the Lord will be their God.

“And my servant David,” he says, “will be king over them.” Concerning him the angel also speaks in the Gospel (Luke I), saying that he will reign over the house of Jacob and that his kingdom will have no end. His mercy will be so great that he will be called not only king but also shepherd, a title that softens the proud name of imperial rule.

After they have become one nation and dwelt in the land and mountains of Israel, they will walk in all the Lord’s judgments and keep his commandments. They will dwell not in another land but in that which he gave to his servant Jacob, where their fathers—Abraham, Isaac, [Col. 1141C] and Jacob—and the other saints dwelt. They themselves will dwell there, and so will their daughters and grandchildren, in accordance with Virgil’s line:

> And the children of children, and those who will be born from them.

They will dwell not for a short time but forever.

Would you like to know who this king and shepherd is? He is the one of whom I spoke above: “My servant David”—“who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians II).”

When they are under such a king, he will make with them a covenant of peace—not as in the Old Testament, a covenant of conflicts and wars, but a covenant of peace that surpasses all understanding. Of this the Savior says to the apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you (John XIV),” and the Prophet says: “His place has been made in peace (Psalm LXXV).”

When he has founded and established them in the Church, so that they can say, “He set my feet upon a rock (Psalm XXXIX),” then they will multiply, either in the number of believers or in the increase of virtues.

“And I shall give,” he says, “my sanctification, or my sanctuary, in their midst forever.” The Jews interpret this as the temple built under Zerubbabel. But how can what is said to endure forever be understood of that temple, when the temple built by Zerubbabel and later restored by many was burned by Roman fire?

All these things must be referred to the Church and to the times of the Savior, when his tabernacle was established in the Church, where our God was made manifest and we became his people. The result of everything is that they should know that he is the Lord and that he himself sanctifies Israel—not according to the flesh but according to the spirit—when his sanctification has been established forever in the midst of believers.

That the Lord rejected the tribe of Ephraim and chose the tribe of Judah we also read in the Psalms, where it is written: “He rejected the tabernacle of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but chose the tribe of Judah (Psalm LXXVII).” Of Judah it is written: “The prince will not fail from Judah, nor the ruler from his elders, until he comes who is to be sent, for whom it has been reserved; he himself will be the expectation of the nations (Genesis XLIX).”

Truly, at the coming of the Lord Savior, the two rods—or, as it is written in Hebrew, the two pieces of wood—were joined into one scepter. In Christ’s baptism what had long been separated is united, so that they may become one new man and one nation. They are no longer defiled by idols and abominations, but through the washing they are cleansed as God’s people; Christ rules them, and they dwell upon the land—the land of the living—which he had given to his servant Jacob, who supplanted the people of Israel in his mother’s womb.

But if we wish to understand this according to the prophecy of Hosea, which is directed almost entirely toward the ten tribes—that is, toward Joseph, Ephraim, Samaria, and Israel—we shall understand it as knowledge bearing a false name and as divided mobs of heretics. We shall say that in the final time, “when the fullness of the nations has entered and all Israel has been saved (Romans XI),” then the adversaries of the people who fought against the house of Judah and the confession of the Church will surrender themselves to the ecclesiastical faith.

Having abandoned every error, the rulers of this world who are being destroyed, and their patriarchs who led them into the abyss of blasphemies, they will rise and leave their idols and abominations, which they had fashioned from their own hearts. From all the settlements in which they had sinned they will pass to the ecclesiastical faith, be cleansed, and become Christ’s people; and he himself will be their God.

“A lost flock has become my people; their shepherds led them astray and made them wander upon the mountains. They passed from mountain to hill; they forgot their resting place. All who found them devoured them.”

(MAURUS.) This statement denotes the kings of the Israelites [Col. 1142D] who caused the people to go astray from the worship of God and turn to idolatry. The first of these was Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made the ten tribes worship golden calves, placing one in Dan and the other in Bethel. There was also Ahab, of whom Scripture says that he sold himself to do evil in the sight of the Lord, as well as the other kings of the same people, whom Scripture reproves as transgressors of God’s law.

Mystically, however, it signifies the scribes and Pharisees, or even heretics, who in the arrogance of their pride introduced destructive sects among God’s people and made them liable to various transgressions. Because they abandoned the tradition of the divine law and withdrew from the resting place of the holy Church, where the bridegroom speaks with the bride, they set Christ, who is the door, against God’s sheep—sheep which those men tear with the darts of sin and consider, and have always considered, of no importance. Hence it follows:

“Their enemies said: ‘We have not sinned, because they sinned against the Lord, the beauty of justice and the hope of their fathers in the Lord.’”

According to the tropological sense, evil priests can also be understood in these shepherds. Devoted to worldly cares and the allurements of pleasures, they become the cause of the destruction of the people entrusted to them. Concerning them the prophet says: “Evil priests are the cause of the people’s ruin.”

Although through their negligence they have committed a great sin—because, contrary to the commandment of justice and the hope of future reward, they have handed Christ’s sheep over to the bites of wolves—they are nevertheless moved by no repentance or fear of future vengeance to correct themselves from their sins. Blinded by the dust of earthly cares, they go blindly toward everlasting fire.

With what state of mind does the overseer of souls exercise pastoral honor among others while moving amid the earthly affairs that he ought to have rebuked in others? In just retribution the Lord threatens this through the prophet, saying: “It will be as with the people, so with the priest (Malachi I).” A priest is like the people when the one who performs the spiritual office does what those do who are still judged according to carnal pursuits.

“Depart from the midst of Babylon, and go out from the land of the Chaldeans; be like young goats before the flock. For behold, I shall stir up and bring against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the land of the north. They will prepare themselves against her, and from there she will be captured. Their arrow is like that of a mighty man, a killer; it will not return empty.”

According to the historical sense, the prophet warns the Israelites who were to go into captivity at Babylon not to imagine that they would possess a permanent dwelling there, but to have hope of returning to their own land. When the time of release from captivity came, they should hasten to depart, because Babylon was destined to be devastated by the Medes and Persians and the exceedingly wealthy kingdom of the Chaldeans to be turned over as spoil to its enemies.

(ORIGEN.) Mystically, just as our body exists in some place on earth, so the soul, according to its condition, exists in some place of the figurative earth. What I am saying will become clearer in this way: our body is either in Egypt, or in Babylon, or in Palestine, or in Syria, or wherever else. Similarly, the soul is in a place bearing one of these names: one is in Babylon, another in Egypt, another in the region of the Ammonites. Thus, according to the understanding of Scripture, it is distinguished by the diversity of these places in accordance with the quality of its life.

The soul is in Babylon when it is confused and troubled, when, having abandoned peace, it endures the wars of the passions, and when the tumult of wickedness roars around it. Then, as we have said, it is in Babylon, and the prophetic word is directed to this soul, saying: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul.” For as long as one is in Babylon, one cannot be saved.

When the soul also remembers where Jerusalem is, it groans and says: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land? (Psalm CXXXVI)” Because it is impossible for someone situated in Babylon to sing to God with instruments—there the instruments of God’s hymns are useless—the Prophet therefore says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion; on the willows in its midst we hung our instruments (ibid.).”

Our instruments are hanging as long as we are in Babylon, on the willows of Babylon’s rivers. But if we find Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace, then the instruments that previously hung idle are taken up in our hands. Then we continually sing psalms, constantly play the lyre, and there is no time when we do not praise God with the instruments that we hold.

Therefore, as we had begun to say, the soul is always in some figurative place of the earth. Just as the sinner is in Babylon, so, conversely, the righteous person is in Judea. Yet according to the quality of life and faith, even within Judea the soul is separated into different places. It may be in Dan, which is at the farthest boundaries of Judea; or in regions somewhat higher and better than Dan; or in the central parts of Judea; or near Jerusalem—the most blessed of all, which is situated in the middle of the city of Jerusalem.

The sinner, however, who is overwhelmed by excessive crimes, is in Babylon. One who is slightly less wicked and has not yet risen to the summit of sin dwells in Egypt and the regions of Egypt. Just as those who are in Judea do not all possess equal places—one is in Jerusalem, another in Dan, another in Naphtali, another in the territory of Gad—so, although all are in Egypt, they do not inhabit equal parts of Egypt. One dwells in Taphnis, another in Memphis, another in Syene, another in Bubastis.

The prophet Ezekiel bears witness in a voice full of mysteries to these places, explaining also the names of the regions of Egypt. If a reader is spiritual, discerning all things and judged by no one, he will allegorize not only the greater regions—Judea, Egypt, and Babylon—but also the smaller divisions of the land. Just as in Judea he reads of Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and its other cities, so in Egypt, by his understanding of the realities, he will give figurative meaning to Diospolis, Bubastis, Taphnis, Memphis, and Syene.

The divine voice therefore urges those who have been held captive by sins in the confusion of this age to depart, through conversion and correction of life, from the kingdom of the devil and the power of darkness, and through repentance to return to the land of the Church. For goats signify penitents; hence they were also offered in the law for sins.

When the Israelites hear of Babylon’s devastation and the destruction of the Chaldean kingdom, they go out. So the elect, instructed by the voices of holy teachers, are driven before the flock of preachers, so that they may go to the promised land of the future—the land of the living, which the meek and gentle will possess forever.

For when they hear the apostle John saying to them, “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. The world is passing away, and its desire (1 John II),” they depart from the confusion of vices, each striving to arrive more quickly at the dwelling of the heavenly homeland by walking in the path of virtues and advancing through good works.

“And Chaldea will become plunder; all who despoil her will be filled, says the Lord, because you rejoice and speak great things while plundering my inheritance; because you have poured yourselves out like calves upon the grass and bellowed like bulls.”

(MAURUS.) After recalling Babylon’s fall and recounting the plundering of Chaldea, he explains the reason why they suffered these things: they rejoiced at the destruction of the Jews and spoke arrogantly. They plundered the Lord’s inheritance, reveling in its devouring like a calf upon the grass, and with proud shouting, like the bellowing of bulls, they mocked the Israelites after their capture and defeat. But they did not enjoy their happiness for long; rather, they were cast down into perpetual shame. Hence it follows:

“Your mother has been greatly put to shame, and she who bore you has been made equal to dust. Behold, she will be the last among the nations, a desert, impassable and dry, because of the Lord’s anger. She will not be inhabited, but will be wholly reduced to desolation. Everyone who passes through Babylon will be astonished and hiss at all her wounds.”

Isaiah speaks similarly about Babylon in his book, saying: “That Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah by God. It will not be inhabited forever, nor will it be founded from generation to generation (Isaiah XIII).”

Thus, to the present day, as we said above, the prophecy concerning Babylon is fulfilled. It has been put to shame, made equal to dust, and reduced to desolation. Just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, so this city, once overthrown, will not be inhabited forever. In its place the Persians made Seleucia and Ctesiphon famous cities. It has become an astonishment to all nations, because the great power of its kingdom has come to such profound contempt.

According to the tropological sense, he says that at the end of the world, or at the death of each individual, all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans and the confusion of the world will depart, and everything will be overthrown just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. The order of worldly pleasures and of this world will not continue, but will perish.

“Prepare yourselves against Babylon all around, all who bend the bow; fight against her, do not spare the arrows, because she has sinned against the Lord. Cry out against her on every side; she has given her hand; her foundations have fallen. Her walls have been destroyed, for it is the Lord’s vengeance. Take vengeance upon her; as she did, do to her. Destroy the sower [or: planter] from Babylon, and the one who holds the sickle at harvest-time, from before the sword of the dove.”

The prophetic word commands the Medes and Persians and all the nations that came to their aid against Babylon to prepare weapons of war against her, renew the battle, and raise a cry against her. Just as she had been intent on devastating all the surrounding nations, including King Nebuchadnezzar, whom the prophet here calls “the dove”—not because of simplicity of mind, but because of the folly of his pride—so they should repay her with vengeance and do to her as she had done to others.

Let them cast down her walls and destroy her foundations; let them destroy from her the sower and reaper, and leave none who cultivates her land.

Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that Babylon was exceedingly powerful and situated on a square plain. From corner to corner its walls extended sixteen thousand paces—that is, sixty-four thousand paces around the circuit. Its citadel, that is, the Capitol of the city, and its tower are said to have risen after the Flood to a height of four thousand paces. It narrowed gradually from a broad base to a narrower summit, so that the overhanging weight might more easily be supported by the wider lower portions.

He describes marble temples, golden statues, streets shining with stones and gold, and many other things that seem almost unbelievable. We have related all this to show that, when God is angry, every power is polluted and compared with ashes and dust. If it were permitted, because of the barbarian nations, to enter and see the last traces of so great a city, we would see that their possession is one of ruin and [perhaps: “has gone out into”] pools of water, and would see truly fulfilled what is sung in Isaiah’s words: “I shall sweep it with the broom of destruction.” Except for the baked-brick walls, which are restored after many years in order to enclose the beasts, the entire space within is desolate.

“Each one will turn back to his own people, and each will flee to his own land.”

(HIERONYMUS.) Isaiah also places this same testimony in his book, showing [Col. 1146C] that after Babylon had been captured and the hostile army had entered through its gates, all the auxiliary forces and the troops of the various nations by which the city had previously been defended would return to their own provinces.

“Israel was a scattered flock; lions drove him away. The king of Assyria first devoured him; this last one, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, stripped his bones.”

(MAURUS.) The kings of the Assyrians—namely, Tiglath-pileser, who transferred a large part of the Jewish people into Assyria, and Sennacherib, who, after conquering the ten tribes of the Jewish nation called Israel, transferred them to the mountains of the Medes—are here called lions, because they devoured Israel.

So too Nebuchadnezzar, who finally devastated all Judea, destroyed its cities, and burned the temple of God in Jerusalem, according to what is written in the Book of Kings: “The Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of plunderers, until he had cast them from his presence.” This began from the time when Israel was torn away from the house of David and they appointed Jeroboam son of Nebat as king (III Kings XII).

For Jeroboam separated Israel from the Lord and caused them to commit a great sin. The children of Israel walked in all the sins of Jeroboam that he had committed, and they did not depart from them until the Lord removed Israel from his presence, as he had spoken through all his servants the prophets. Israel was transferred from its land into Assyria to this day.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I shall visit the king of Babylon [Col. 1147A] and his land, as I visited the king of Assyria, and I shall restore Israel to its habitation. He will feed in Carmel and Bashan, and his soul will be satisfied on Mount Ephraim and in Gilead. In those days and at that time, says the Lord, the iniquity of Israel will be sought, and it will not be found; and the sin of Judah, and it will not be discovered, because I shall be merciful to those whom I leave.”
