The Lord therefore visited the king of Babylon—that is, Belshazzar, who was the last to reign in Babylon—and his land when, through Cyrus and Darius, the Medes and Persians, he destroyed the kingdom of the Chaldeans.

So he visited Assyria through Sennacherib and his people, who blasphemed the God of Israel through their messengers. Hence the angel of the Lord went forth and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians (II Chronicles XXXII). Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, returned and lived in Nineveh. When he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword, and they fled to the land of Ararat, as the book of Isaiah bears witness.

The captivity of the Hebrews was released through Cyrus, who caused nearly fifty thousand people to return to Judea. Later, after the temple had been built and the city restored, the Israelites began to cultivate their own land.

Mystically, however, the Lord visits the king of Babylon—that is, of confusion—as he visited the king of Assyria, whose name is interpreted as “walking” or “directing.” This occurs when he destroys the devil, the king of confusion and ruler of these darknesses, just as he destroyed Antichrist and all the persecutors of the Church [Col. 1147C], who directed the weapons of their wickedness against God’s saints and shed innocent blood. It also applies to heretics, who direct the arrows of evil doctrine against the souls of the simple in order to kill them.

At the end of the world, the devil who deceived the nations will be sent into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast, Antichrist with his wicked members and persecutors, and the false prophet—without doubt the heretics—are. They will be tormented day and night forever and ever. The saints will reign with their king forever, and their souls will be satisfied with every good thing.

Then what is said will truly be fulfilled: “At that time the iniquity of Israel will be sought, and it will not be found; and the sin of Judah, and it will not be discovered.” For then the Lord will bind up the wound of his people and heal their injuries; he will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his saints, and death will be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain will be any longer, for the former things have passed away. Instead, a new people entering a new city will rejoice there forever with manifold exultation.

“Ascend against the land of rulers, and visit its inhabitants; destroy and kill what remains after them,” says the Lord, “and do according to everything that I have commanded you.” The divine speech is directed to the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, so that, ascending against the land of rulers—that is, against Babylon—and against its Chaldean inhabitants, it may visit, destroy, and kill what remains after them, so that Babylon’s posterity may utterly perish and it may no longer be inhabited. This is to occur after its desolation, according to everything that the Lord commanded. Mystically, however, this is commanded to the teachers and preachers of Christ: they are to strive to overthrow the devil’s kingdom in the world, destroy his evil works, and demolish his wickedest counsels, so that they may kill all the sinners of the earth and remove from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity. [Col. 1148A; cols. 1148B–1157C passim.]

“‘The sound of war in the land, and great destruction! How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed? How has Babylon been turned into a desert among the nations? I have ensnared you, and you have been captured, Babylon, and you did not know it; you have been found and seized, because you provoked the Lord.’” Historically, by the figure of synecdoche, he designates Babylon with its kings as the hammer of the whole earth, since it shattered and devastated very many regions of the earth. And deservedly, at its destruction, the sound of war and great devastation resounded, because its ruin brought joy to many nations.

(ORIGEN.) We must therefore ask who, spiritually, is the hammer of the whole earth, and what destruction of it has been prophesied, since it was broken before it was crushed. Who is this hammer that wishes, insofar as it can, to hinder the stones of the temple’s construction, so that, once crushed, they may not fit its foundations? Consider now whether the devil is not himself the hammer of the whole earth. I will declare confidently that there is someone who does not greatly concern himself with the hammer of the whole earth. Since the example is taken from a physical hammer, I seek a material stronger than the hammer, one that suffers nothing when struck by it. Seeking this, I find it in what is written: “Behold, a man standing upon adamantine walls, and in his hand an adamant.” History relates of adamant that it is stronger than every hammer striking it, remaining uncrushed and unconquerable.

Although the devil—the hammer—stands above it, and the dragon, like an unyielding anvil, is placed beneath it, the adamant standing in the Lord’s hand and in his presence suffers nothing. Thus the hammer and the unyielding anvil are two things opposed to the righteous adamant [another reading: “to this one”]. It is already a familiar proverb, common among the nations, that people say of those oppressed by anxieties and evils: “They are between the hammer and the anvil.” You, however, apply this to the devil and the dragon, who are always designated in Scripture by such names according to the variety of circumstances; and you say that the saint, who is like an adamantine wall or is an adamant in the Lord’s hand, cares neither for the hammer nor for the anvil. Rather, the more he is struck, the more his strength shines forth.

After this I ask who it was that broke and crushed the hammer of the whole earth. I will say that Moses could not break and crush the hammer of the whole earth, nor Abraham before him, nor Joshua son of Nun after him, nor any other of the prophets. Who, then, could break and crush so great a hammer of the whole earth? Who is he? Jesus Christ broke and crushed the hammer of the whole earth.

The prophet, now marveling at this in the Holy Spirit, says: “How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and crushed?” First it was broken, and afterward crushed. Since I have found that the Savior was the one who broke and crushed the hammer of the whole earth, I shall turn to the Gospel to see the first temptation, when the devil said to him: “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me,” and so forth (Matthew 4). I will say that at that time Jesus did not crush the hammer of the whole earth, but merely broke it. When he withdrew from him until the appointed time, and later came when that time had arrived, then the hammer of the whole earth was crushed—not merely broken as at first.

And because the hammer of the whole earth, which had previously been broken, was crushed, it is likewise broken in each one of us when we are brought into the Church and advance in faith. But it is crushed and reduced to fragments when we have reached perfection.

“‘How,’ he says, ‘has Babylon among the nations been turned into a desert? I ensnared you, and you have been captured, Babylon; you did not know it, and you have been found and seized, because you provoked God.’” From what precedes, the captivity of Babylon can be understood as occurring when, after being captured, it is undermined, overthrown, and desolated, so that nothing of confusion remains in us.

“‘You will be captured, Babylon, and you will not understand; you have been found and seized, because you resisted the Lord.’” Did Babylon alone resist the Lord, and not rather all the nations, which, having abandoned the Creator, worshiped idols and resisted the Lord? Or does he figuratively say that every soul opposed to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace—is Babylon? Hence the saints were in Jerusalem, while sinners were in Babylon. And if the inhabitants of Jerusalem sinned, they were sent into Babylon, and while remaining in Babylon they were converted to repentance. The saints, however, returned to Jerusalem.

Babylon, then, is captured and does not understand. For Babylon is not subject to the law of God. Indeed, Babylon could not be found and yet not be seized; rather, it was seized when it was found, because it resisted the Lord.

“The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath, because the work belongs to the Lord, the God of hosts, in the land of the Chaldeans.” Another edition has: “Open its storehouses, search it as a cave, and destroy it; let no remnant remain for them. Dry up all its fruits, and let them descend to slaughter. Woe to them, for their day will come, the time of their vengeance.”

Wishing to understand what is meant by “The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath,” I seek elsewhere in Scripture for the vessels of the Lord’s wrath. For a fuller comparison with this kind of scriptural passage, I find an apostolic passage, and there I find the Apostle explaining to me what the vessels of God’s wrath are. For he says: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, whom he also called—not only from the Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9; 2 Timothy 2).

In general, the Apostle divides all human beings into two classes, saying that some are vessels of mercy and others vessels of wrath. For example, Pharaoh and the Egyptians are vessels of wrath. Again, he calls himself—the first to obtain mercy—and those who, he says, in due time would believe, from both Jews and nations, vessels of mercy.

There are therefore vessels of wrath in God’s treasury. For it is written: “The Lord has opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath.” What is this treasury of the Lord in which vessels of wrath are found? Someone may perhaps ask whether only vessels of wrath are in the Lord’s treasury, and whether God’s treasury, which is the treasury of all things, does not contain vessels of mercy; or whether something else should be understood concerning God’s treasury from which his vessels of wrath are brought forth.

I will say confidently, then, that the Lord’s treasury is his Church, and that in this treasury—that is, in the Church—there are often people concealed who are vessels of wrath. A time will therefore come when the Lord opens the treasury of the Church. For now the Church is closed, and vessels of wrath dwell together with vessels of mercy; the chaff is with the grain, and the fish destined to perish and be thrown away are contained together with the good fish that had entered the net.

When he opens it at the time of judgment and brings forth from it his vessels of wrath, the one who is a vessel of mercy will perhaps say concerning the vessels of wrath going out: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. Or they went out from us so that it might be shown that not all were of us” (1 John 2).

And the discourse desires to break out into another subject. What we dare to say is this: there are vessels of wrath in God’s treasury. Outside the treasury, sinful persons are not vessels of wrath, but they are lesser than vessels of wrath. For they are servants who do not know their master’s will and do not do it. But whoever enters the Church is either a vessel of wrath or a vessel of mercy. Whoever is outside the Church is neither a vessel of mercy nor a vessel of wrath. I seek another designation for one who remains outside the Church [Note: [Col. 1149D] The sense is interrupted.]. [Note: [Col. 1151D] He attacks natal astrologers.]

[ lacuna ]

“‘The work belongs to the Lord of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans.’” According to the various interpretations, an earthly place is called by many names. Just as, with one underlying reality, the Savior has many names according to differing meanings—while he is one in underlying subject but various in his powers—so, because of the wickedness of the human race, earthly affairs, though one in underlying subject, are many according to the diversity of their meanings.

What I am saying will become clearer when, explaining the example I took from the Savior, I proceed to elucidate the matters that follow. The underlying reality of my Lord Jesus the Savior is one. With this one reality underlying all, he is called a physician in one sense, according to what is written: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke 5). In another sense he is a shepherd, insofar as he rules irrational creatures; in another sense a king, insofar as he governs rational creatures. In another sense he is the true vine, insofar as human beings grafted into him bear abundant fruit and, cultivated by the Father, the husbandman, receive the richness of the true vine through sharing in one root (John 15). According to another meaning he is wisdom; according to another, truth; according to another, righteousness. Nevertheless, the underlying reality is one.

Therefore, just as in the Savior there are many meanings corresponding to his different names, while the underlying reality is one, so earthly affairs are one in their underlying reality but many according to their meanings. We have often said allegorically that Babylon signifies earthly affairs, which are always confused by vices. Egypt likewise signifies affliction. We have said that the land of the Chaldeans is so called because many people consecrate to the stars the things that occur on earth and assert that whatever happens to us, whether it concerns our sins or the stars’ powers, comes about through their influence. The Chaldeans, therefore, are those who have devoted themselves to such beliefs.

Everyone who believes these things is in the land of the Chaldeans. If any of you follows the ravings of the astrologers, he is in the land of the Chaldeans. If anyone calculates the day of birth and, trusting various reckonings of hours and moments, accepts the doctrine that stars configured in this or that way make people lustful, adulterous, chaste, or whatever else they may be, that person is in the land of the Chaldeans.

Some now even suppose that Christians are made what they are by the courses of the stars. All of you who understand these things in this way, all of you who believe such statements, are in the land of the Chaldeans. Therefore, when God threatens those who are in the land of the Chaldeans, he threatens spiritually those who have consecrated themselves to genealogies and fate, asserting that everything that occurs among mortals depends either on the movements of the stars or on the necessity of fate.

But God, leading Abraham toward better things, said to him: “I am the one who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans” (Genesis 15). For God is powerful enough to grant us also that we may go out from the land of the Chaldeans. Let us believe that there is no other besides him who, ordering all things and governing our life according to the quality of our acquired merits, regulates its varied circumstances. For neither some flashing star, nor the star of Phaethon, as they call it, nor that of corrupted Ganymede contains the causes of our affairs.

According to one interpretation, then, the person who believes the arguments mentioned above is in the land of the Chaldeans. According to another, someone ascends upon the roofs and worships the army of heaven. Thus the work belongs to the Lord of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans, because its appointed times have come.

“‘Open its storehouses’”—it is clear who those in the land of the Chaldeans are. The storehouses of the Chaldeans are the doctrines of nativity-astrology. “Search it as a cave and destroy it.” Whoever rejects calculations based on birth, whoever uses the word of truth against them, whoever demonstrates that none of the things asserted by the astrologers is true, whoever teaches that God’s judgments are inscrutable and cannot be grasped by human beings, whoever asserts that the stars are not the causes of what happens on earth, and still less of what happens to us Christians—this person carries out the Lord’s command [the source has “magis,” “rather”; “minus,” “less,” is evidently intended].

“‘Come against her from the ends of the earth; open her, so that those who trample her may come out. Remove the stones from the road and heap them up, and kill her; let nothing remain. Scatter all her mighty men; let them descend to slaughter. Woe to them, because their day has come, the time of their visitation.’”

Just as at that time people came from every direction to devastate Babylon, to trample it, heap its stones into piles, and kill it so that nothing remained, and they scattered all its mighty men, who descended to slaughter, so now too there are many devastators and destroyers of spiritual Babylon, killers of its mighty men. The holy preachers, among those from the nations who believe in Christ, destroy the devil’s kingdom and kill the hordes of vices, so that nothing remains. For the holy teachers praise no vice and do not cease to persecute any sin; rather, according to the strength given them by God, they strive to uproot and overthrow the entire faction of the ancient enemy.

“Do not leave,” he says, “even a little of it, and dry up all its fruits.” (ORIGEN.) Who is so blessed that he can dry up all the fruits of the land of the Chaldeans and make them descend to slaughter?

“‘Woe to them, because their day has come, and it is the time of their vengeance.’” After this comes the contents of another chapter.

“‘The voice of those fleeing and of those who escaped from the land of Babylon, to announce in Zion the vengeance of the Lord our God, the vengeance of his temple. Announce in Babylon to many, to all who draw the bow: take your stand against her all around, and let no one escape. Repay her according to her work; do to her according to everything she has done, because she has risen up against the Lord, against the Holy One of Israel.’”

He now prophesies concerning those who, abandoning their ancestral customs, the nations, the laws of the nations, and the unbelief of former times, come to the word of God. For something of this kind is signified by the statement: “The voice of those fleeing who escaped from the land of Babylon,” or “of those rescued from the land of Babylon.”

Would that your voice too, O catechumens, were the voice of those fleeing Babylon: fleeing vices, fleeing sins. For the voice of those fleeing and rescued is not sufficient merely to flee from the land of Babylon; they must also be rescued from the land of Babylon, in order to announce in Zion the vengeance of the Lord our God. Thus, fleeing from the land of Babylon, you should come to Zion, the place of watchmen—to the Church of God—to announce in Zion, that is, in the Church, the vengeance received from the Lord our God, the vengeance of his people.

“Announce in Babylon to many, to everyone who draws the bow.” “To many” is significantly included. There are many who are in Babylon, but few in Jerusalem. For he does not say for this reason, “The Lord your God loved you because you were many”; rather, “You are few among all the nations.” And rightly it was said to those who were only a part: “You are few among all the nations.”

Understand this also: “Few are those who are saved,” and likewise: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate; but many walk through the broad and spacious way.” “Announce in Babylon to many, to everyone who draws the bow; let there be no one from it who is saved. Destroy and kill everything belonging to Babylon.”

Recently we spoke of Babylonian children, Babylonian men, and Babylonian offspring. Let no one from Babylon’s offspring be rescued either. Repay her according to her works; do to her according to everything she has done, because she resisted the Lord and rose up against the Holy God of Israel.

As long as you harbor within yourself thoughts of wickedness resisting piety and true faith, you have Babylonians within you. But take vengeance and kill all the sinners of the land that is within you—that is, all the Babylonians—so that, once cleansed, you may pass over to Jerusalem, the city of God in Christ Jesus.

“‘Therefore young men will fall in her streets, and all her warriors will be silenced on that day,’ says the Lord.” He uses “young men” for the strong and “warriors” for the robust. The young men of Babylon, therefore, who walk in its streets that lead to death and do not take up the narrow way that leads to life, will unquestionably fall on the day of the Lord’s visitation. Likewise, all the warriors who fought with their king, the devil, against the Church of Christ will be silenced. After the day of judgment they will no longer be granted any power to fight or harm Christ’s soldiers; rather, they will be suffocated in eternal silence.

“‘Behold, I am against you, O arrogant one,’ says the Lord God of hosts, ‘for your day has come, the time of your visitation; and the arrogant man will fall and collapse, and there will be no one to raise him up. I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it will devour everything around him.’”

(MAURUS.) The prophet speaks to the king of Babylon, announcing to him the future disaster that will also threaten his nation: moreover, that a fire will devastate his cities and the towns that were around them.

Mystically, however, he foretells the future condemnation of the most arrogant king, the Antichrist, who exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, and of his members—that is, of all the wicked. He foretells the fire that will consume all his fortifications, built through secular wisdom, and the evil councils in which he delighted to deceive human beings. Thus all his schemes and the weapons with which he attacked the worldwide holy Church of God will be devoured in eternal destruction, because they did not fear to inflict oppression and prepare captivity for God’s people. Hence it follows:

“‘Thus says the Lord of hosts: The sons of Israel and the sons of Judah suffer oppression together; all who captured them hold them fast and refuse to release them. Their Redeemer is strong; the Lord of hosts is his name. He will defend their cause in judgment, so as to terrify the earth and shake the inhabitants of Babylon.

“‘A sword against the Chaldeans,’ says the Lord, ‘and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her princes, and against her wise men; a sword against her diviners, who will become fools; a sword against her mighty men, who will be afraid; a sword against her horses, and against her chariots, and against all the common people who are in her midst, and they will become like women; a sword against her treasures, and they will be plundered. Drought will be upon her waters, and they will dry up, because it is a land of carved images, and it glories in monstrous things.’”

The sword of the Lord devours all the sinners of the earth. Historically, it destroyed not only the Chaldeans and the inhabitants of Babylon—that is, its princes, wise men, and diviners, together with all the common people, weak as women—through the Medes and Persians; it also condemned at the future judgment all who live amid the confusion of the world and, relying upon secular wisdom, worship images of error instead of truth, together with the treasures of their doctrines and works.

The doctrine of the heretics will wither and dry up, because their synagogue is a land of carved images and glories in monstrous things—that is, in false inventions. Concerning this sword the Lord himself says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand seizes judgment, I will repay vengeance to my enemies, and I will requite those who hate me. I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword will devour flesh, from the blood of the slain and from the captivity of the uncovered heads of the enemy” (Deuteronomy 32).

“‘Therefore dragons will dwell with the foolish siccarii [“assassins”; reading uncertain], and ostriches will dwell in it, and it will no longer be inhabited forever. It will not be rebuilt for generation after generation, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors,’ says the Lord. ‘No man will dwell there, nor will a son of man sojourn in it.’”

(JEROME.) When the Medes were raised up against the cities of confusion—people who count neither gold nor silver among good things, who kill infants with arrows, who show no pity to nursing children, and whose eye spares not even sons—the once-renowned city that stood in the pride of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as resembling demons, is overthrown just as Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown, so that no trace of its former habitation remains. After there has been a new heaven and a new earth, and the form of this world has passed away (1 Corinthians 7), the city of confusion will not be inhabited forever.

(MAURUS.) Since, at the beginning of this Babylonian captivity, we have already spoken historically, according to the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah, about the monsters mentioned here, let us now speak according to tropology. At the end of the world, or at the death of each individual, all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans and the confusion of the world will depart from us, and everything will be overthrown just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. The state of this world will no longer continue but will perish, and no Arab will pitch his tents there.

Concerning this it is written in the sixtieth Psalm: “Make a way for him who ascends over the setting-place; the Lord is his name.” Nor will shepherds rest there—the angels who preside over the human race and daily see the face of the Father. Rather, beasts, dragons, ostriches, satyrs, owls, and sirens will rest there. We understand all these beasts figuratively as angels or demons, and as those to whom we are handed over for punishment. In houses once devoted to pleasure, where there had been delight and joy, there will be the lament of owls or the mournful voice of sirens, which leads their hearers to death.

No one will wonder that the time of judgment is near and that the day of Babylon’s consummation is not far off if he sees Babylon overturned daily by holy men among those who believe in the Lord, and understands that eternity is near to every length of time.

We have spoken briefly about the kinds of beasts—or rather, monsters—because in the preceding discussion they were touched upon in part according to the historical sense. This too must be considered: after ecclesiastical speech and the teaching of the Savior have overthrown the city of confusion, so that it is compared with Sodom and Gomorrah, it will not be inhabited by holy men, nor will shepherds rest there, those who were accustomed to feed Christ’s flock. Rather, beasts, dragons, and satyrs will rest and dance there.

Whatever the heretics say in the synagogues of Satan is not the Lord’s teaching but the howling of demons and satyrs, whom Esau imitated. Sirens will rest in the shrines of pleasure, drawing souls into the abyss by their sweet and deadly song, so that, when the shipwreck rages, they may be devoured by wolves and dogs.

“‘Behold, a people is coming from the north, and a great nation, and many kings are rising from the ends of the earth. They will take up bow and shield. They are cruel and merciless; their voice will roar like the sea, and they will mount horses, like a man prepared for battle against you, daughter of Babylon. The king of Babylon heard news of them, and his hands grew slack; anguish seized him, pain like that of a woman in labor.’”

The historical meaning is clear: a great nation of Medes or Persians, and many kings with Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius, king of the Medes, assembled to devastate Babylon, where King Belshazzar was then reigning. While he was preparing a great banquet for his attendants and princes, he decided to use the vessels of God’s temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem, for drinking by himself and his concubines, and in this way to blaspheme God (Daniel 5).

Then he saw a hand coming from the wall and writing certain syllables on the plaster. Disturbed by this vision, he summoned the magicians, the Chaldeans, and every similar class of people who among the barbarians claimed expertise in interpreting dreams and signs of this kind, so that they might explain what had been written to him. When the magicians said that they could find and understand absolutely nothing, Daniel interpreted the writing for him and foretold the disaster that was soon to overtake him.

Therefore, exhausted by grief and sorrow, he made no preparation to resist his enemies, since on that same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom. Concerning him it is now said: “The king of Babylon heard news of them, and his hands grew slack; anguish seized him, pain like that of a woman in labor.”

“‘Behold, like a lion he will ascend from the pride of the Jordan, against the strong beauty; for suddenly I will make him run against her. And who will be the chosen one whom I shall appoint over her?’”

This passage seems to indicate that King Nebuchadnezzar, together with the Chaldeans, after overthrowing the kingdom of the Jews cruelly like a lion, devastating the land, destroying and burning the city of Jerusalem and the temple, returned to his seat in Babylon like a victor secure against his enemies, leaving the kingdom unharmed to his descendants.

But when the Lord scattered it in the vengeance carried out against it, the entire kingdom was reduced to the dominion of King Cyrus. Concerning this he now says: “And who will be the chosen one whom I shall appoint over her?” To demonstrate that this happened not through Cyrus’s own power but through the Lord’s judgment, whose will no king or human being can resist, he immediately added:

“‘For who is like me, and who will withstand me? And who is this shepherd who can resist my face? Therefore hear the counsel of the Lord that he has conceived against Babylon, and his thoughts that he has thought concerning the land of the Chaldeans: surely the little ones of the flock will drag them away; surely their dwelling will be destroyed together with them. At the sound of Babylon’s captivity the earth was shaken, and a cry was heard among the nations.’”

Isaiah also declares this most clearly, saying: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subject nations before his face and turn the backs of kings, and open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth. I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars; and I will give you hidden treasures and secret riches, so that you may know that I am the Lord who calls you by your name, the God of Israel, for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel. I have called you by your name. I have likened you [to him], and you did not know me.

“I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God. I girded you, and you did not know me, so that those from the rising of the sun and those from the west may know that there is no God besides me. I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil; I am the Lord, doing all these things” (Isaiah 45).

Knowing that in this chapter very many, not only Latins but also Greeks, fall into serious error, supposing that it is written, “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, my Lord,” so that it may be understood according to what we read elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Genesis 19), and “The Lord said to my Lord” (Psalm 109), he explains that the text does not say κυρίῳ (“to the Lord”) but “to Cyrus,” the Hebrew name of the king of the Persians who conquered Babylon and the Chaldeans. And above, with the Medes joined to him, he is called the driver of a two-horse chariot, that is, of a camel and a donkey.

He is called “anointed,” that is, “the Lord’s anointed,” which among the Hebrews was a mark of royal power. Just as among us a diadem and purple are given only to emperors, so among the Hebrews those destined to reign were anointed with oil. Hence Saul too is called “the Lord’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24). And in the Psalms we read: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not harm my prophets” (Psalm 104).

God grasped and held Cyrus’s right hand so that no one could resist his strength. We read the history of the elder Cyrus in Xenophon’s eight books, and we see Isaiah’s prophecy fulfilled. What city did not open to him? What king did not submit his back? What walls, previously impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege?

Therefore God addresses Cyrus himself: “I have given you hidden treasures and the wealth of all the cities,” so that you, who previously worshiped idols, might recognize one God through his benefits—especially since you know that your name was foretold long before you were born. Josephus too, in the eleventh book of *The Antiquities of the Jews*, reports that Cyrus had read that Isaiah had prophesied about him by name, and that for this reason he greatly loved the Jews as though they were his intimates.

“These things,” he says, “I have granted you for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel, and I have called you by your name,” just as he called Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and foretold long beforehand both Isaac and Josiah. This was so that you would not be thought to be the Christ to whom you were likened, and in whose type and image you went before: “But you did not know me,” that is, you worshiped images, not God.

“I girded you” with strength; I made you victorious over many nations; “and you did not know” your helper. At this point I cannot sufficiently marvel at the folly of readers who refer these words to Christ, through whom the world was reconciled to God.

“I,” says the Lord, “and there is no other besides me”: for apart from my Word, reason, power, and wisdom, which are in me, there is no other God. I did these things so that the whole world, from east to west, might recognize that there is no other God besides me.

“I am the Lord, and there is no other.” The Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, who speaks in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.” In the book of Ezra it is written that Cyrus wrote to all the nations that there was no god except the one God of Israel. Alternatively, it should be understood that the release of the captives and God’s mercy toward his people made God better known to all the nations.

I, therefore, who gave you strength, am the one and only God. I myself make things contrary to one another within creation: light and darkness—that is, day and night—peace and evil, that is, tranquility and war. Through these he signifies that he had been angry with his people when they suffered the darkness of captivity and the evils of servitude, and that he again showed mercy when, having been released and returned to their homeland, they received peace and joy.

## CHAPTER LI

Concerning the pestilential wind and the golden cup; concerning the destruction of Babylon, its king, and the Chaldeans; he writes in a book all the evils that will come upon Babylon.

«Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall raise up against Babylon and against its inhabitants, who lifted up their heart against me, as a pestilent wind; and I shall send winnowers against Babylon, and they shall winnow it, and they shall demolish its land, because they have come upon it from every side on the day of its affliction. He who bends his bow shall not dwell there, nor shall the armored man ascend. Do not spare its young men; destroy all its army. And the slain shall fall in the land of the Chaldeans, and the wounded in its regions, because Israel was not widowed, nor was Judah from its God, the Lord of hosts; but their land was filled with guilt against the Holy One of Israel.» (MAURUS.) These winnowers who winnowed Babylon and Chaldea are often said to have been the Medes and Persians, against whom the bow and breastplate of Babylonia could not resist. But since their enemies were everywhere victorious, they spared neither the old nor the young, nor any age or sex; rather, they killed its entire army. For they had been sent for the vengeance of the Lord’s anger, so that they might exact deserved punishment from the guilty, since they had not chastised the people of God by correcting them, but had devastated them by plunder and delivered them to destruction. Isaiah makes this clear when he says: «Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger, and the staff itself is in their hand, my indignation. I shall send him against a deceitful nation, and I shall command him against the people of my wrath to take spoils and seize booty, and to put it underfoot [Col. 1158B] like the mud of the streets. But he did not judge it so, and his heart did not reckon it thus; rather, his heart was for crushing and destroying very many nations,» and so forth (Isaiah 10). And elsewhere: «Will the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or will the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn? As though a rod should lift itself against him who raises it, and a staff should exalt itself, though it is merely wood» (ibid.). [HIERON.] Against Sennacherib—or, as many think, Nebuchadnezzar—boasting and saying, «By the strength of my hand I have acted, and by my wisdom I have understood,» and so forth, the holy prophet replied: O most foolish of mortals, do you suppose that God’s anger is your wisdom, and do you attribute his command to your own strength? It is as though the axe should boast against him who holds the axe, and the saw against him by whom it is drawn, and they should say that all the works done through the axe and saw were accomplished by their own skill; or as though someone should raise a rod and exalt a staff to strike whomever he wished, and the rod and staff themselves should boast and say that the one who was struck had been struck by them. So you too, when you are an instrument of God’s will, are lifted up in pride and boast that everything which happens has been accomplished by your own power.

Whatever is said to the Assyrian can also be referred to the pride of heretics and to the devil, who in Scripture is called an axe, a saw, and a rod: through him unfruitful trees are cut down; the hardness of unbelievers is divided and sawn apart; and those who do not receive discipline are struck with the rod. Heretics also, whose mouth is placed in heaven and whose tongue traverses the earth, misuse for what is contrary and perverse the understanding they have received from him in a good sense, so that they speak against him by whom they were created, and turn the ministry of the tongue, by which the Lord should be praised, into blasphemy. And because their land—that is, the temporal life by which they live in this world—has been filled with the guilt of error, they shall be subjected in the future judgment of the Lord to eternal torment.

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

[Col. 1157]

[Col. 1157D] I should like, if I could, to encompass Jeremiah’s prophecy against Babylon in a single book; but because the length of the discourse does not permit this, I have decided to divide it into two books. I shall also arrange matters so that, after the punishments of Babylon mentioned above, which the earlier book recounts in part, I shall make the prophet’s exhortation to the Jews according to the historical sense—or also to the faithful according to the mystical senses, that they should flee from the midst of Babylon and save their souls from the confusion of this world—the beginning of the following book.

«Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul.» Let us therefore hear what the word of God commands those who are in Babylon. «Flee,» it says, «from the midst of Babylon»: not gradually, not step by step, but flee with speed, flee with haste—for this is what it means to flee. Flee from the midst of Babylon, all you who have a soul made confused by the passion of various vices. The word is addressed to you, and the same command is given to me also. For I am still in confusion of mind, and therefore I am in Babylon.

What, then, has God commanded? He does not say, «Come out from the midst of Babylon,» for this can also be done gradually, but, «Flee from the midst of Babylon.» Therefore I also seek the reason for the wording «from the midst.» It can happen that someone is in Babylon but, while lingering at its outermost boundaries, seems in a certain way to be outside Babylon. It is another matter to stand in the middle of Babylon, so that the distance is equal on every side, and to live at its center, as though in the middle of an animal’s heart. For just as the heart is the middle of an animal, and in the Gospel according to Luke «the heart of the earth» (Luke 17) is called the middle of the earth, so it seems to me that Tyre is said to be «placed in the heart of the sea» (Ezekiel 26), and that sinners must now flee from the midst of Babylon—that is, from its heart.

Flee, therefore, from the midst of Babylon, so that, abandoning the middle of Babylon, you may begin to be at its boundaries, not in its center. If this seems obscure to anyone, it will become clearer in the following way. Whoever is deeply immersed in vices is an inhabitant of the middle of Babylon. But whoever gradually abandons evil and turns his nature toward better things, and has begun not so much to possess virtues as to desire them—that person, although he has fled from the middle of Babylon, has nevertheless not yet departed from Babylon.

According to such interpretations, Holy Scripture teaches us to believe that not even one letter has been placed there without the wisdom of God. For he who commands a person, saying, «You shall not appear before my presence empty» (Exodus 23), himself does this much more, so that he says nothing empty. The prophets, receiving from his fullness, sang those things that were taken from that fullness; and therefore the sacred books always breathe the spirit of fullness. There is nothing—whether in prophecy, the Law, the Gospel, or the Apostle—that does not descend from the fullness of the divine majesty.

For this reason, the words found in the Holy Scriptures breathe fullness even today. They breathe it for those who have eyes to see heavenly things, ears to hear divine things, and noses to perceive the things that belong to fullness. I have said this because the wording is not simply «Flee from Babylon,» but, with the necessary addition, «Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his own soul.» First one must flee from the midst of Babylon; then, after fleeing, each must save his own soul.

Nor did he merely say «save,» but, according to another edition, «restore-save» (*resalvate*). The addition of the syllable signifies a mystery: for once we tasted salvation, and afterward, falling from it because of sins, we came into Babylon. For this reason each person must save his own soul, so that he may begin to recover what he lost, according to the apostle Peter, who says: «We shall receive as the end of faith the salvation of souls» (1 Peter 1). The prophets sought and diligently investigated this salvation; they prophesied on account of our benefit. Nevertheless, it lies with us to flee from Babylon, and it is placed in our power, if we wish to raise up again what has fallen.

«Do not be silent over her iniquity, because it is the time of vengeance for the Lord; he himself will repay her in kind.» In another edition it is read thus: «Do not be cast away in her iniquity.» (MAURUS.) Whoever, by silence, consents through a perverse will or wicked action to the iniquity of Babylon, and does not rather rebuke it, is a participant in its offense and a partner in its punishment. But when someone is in the righteousness of Babylon and does not repent, it follows that he will be cast away.

Observe how Scripture, although translated from the Hebrew language into Greek, nevertheless expressed its wording meaningfully, insofar as it could accommodate distinctions among words. In another passage it says: «I have chosen to be rejected in the house of the Lord» (Psalm 83), and it does not say «cast out.» In the present passage it did not say «lest you be rejected in her injustice,» but «lest you be cast out in her injustice.» For to be cast out is one thing, and to be rejected another. What is despised and neglected is not cast out but rejected; what is entirely outside and alien to salvation and blessedness is cast out. Divine Scripture also makes this clear elsewhere, saying: «The leaders of my people shall be cast out from their house of delights because of their exceedingly wicked desires, for their clergy shall not profit them» (Micah 2).

«Do not be cast out,» he says, «in the iniquity of Babylon, because the time of her vengeance for the Lord has come.» In a marvelous sense he says that punishments are inflicted on account of the vengeance of the one who suffers them: for when someone is not avenged, he is left unpunished. I remember having said in my exposition of the Twelve Prophets what is written there: «I shall not visit your daughters when they fornicate, nor your daughters-in-law [Col. 1160D] when they commit adultery.» Therefore God does not, as some suppose, punish sinners in anger; but, if it is appropriate to speak in this way, it is a great anger not to undergo torments from God. Whoever is punished—even if he is corrected by what is called God’s anger—is punished so that he may be amended.

«Lord,» David says, «do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury» (Psalm 6). But even if you rebuke, rebuke us in judgment and not in fury. Jeremiah said: You will also find a promise of God, in which corruption is given to some, when punishment is promised to the children of Christ who sin, so that mercy may not be denied. It is written: «If his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my righteous acts, I shall visit their crimes with a rod and their iniquities with lashes; but I shall not remove my mercy from them» (Psalm 88).

Considering these things, see how the person who commits crimes up to the present time and is not punished is not yet worthy of punishment. For God’s visitation is shown by the torments inflicted upon the one visited. But as for the sinner who is corrected, I do not know what may proceed from his punishment.

This has been said because of the words, «because the time of her vengeance is from the Lord.» It follows: «He himself will repay her in kind.» God will not repay Babylon through ministers; he himself will repay her what she deserves. I wish to say something about the addition of the pronoun in the words written, «he himself»: «For he himself,» it says, «will repay her in kind.» God does not repay everyone what they deserve himself; there are some to whom he repays through others, whether punishing them or healing them through pain, as is contained in the Psalms: «He sent upon them the fury of his anger, fury and anger and distress, a mission through evil angels» (Psalm 77).

To these he did not repay himself, but used evil angels as ministers for their recompense. Perhaps to others he repays not through evil angels but through good ones, as happens to those who are punished for their crimes. You will find many such examples if you search the Scriptures.

Sometimes, however, after rejecting the service of ministers, God himself repays, as now in the case of Babylon. I fear introducing something obscure into a clear passage, something which seems to me to lie hidden if I remain silent. Nevertheless, one should dare at least to touch upon a few points when the wounds are easy and the treatment readily available.

A physician sends his servant; he sends a disciple, and through him treats the sick person—for the wounds are not serious. Sometimes, too, the person being healed needs cutting and iron; yet the physician himself does not go to him, but chooses one of his disciples who is able to treat him and uses him as a minister. But when the wounds are incurable, when deep corruption has consumed the dead flesh, and the sickness is so severe that it requires not servants or disciples, who have already approached him by their knowledge of the art, but the hands of the master himself, then the physician himself, girding his loins, hastens to cut the most terrible wound.

In the same way, when sins are lesser, God himself does not repay sinners but uses other ministers. But when, because of his deserts, a great sickness has seized a person—as now Babylon, which has been pierced by the grave wounds of its own wickedness—then God himself hastens to repay.

If you seek something similar to this, you will also find it concerning Jerusalem, and what happened to it after the prophets, because it plotted against Christ.

«Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk. All the nations drank of her wine, and therefore they were shaken; suddenly Babylon fell and was crushed.» (ORIG.) Nebuchadnezzar, wishing to deceive people through Babylon’s treacherous cup, did not mix the drink he was preparing in an earthen vessel, nor in a slightly better one—an iron, bronze, or tin vessel—or even in one superior to these, a silver vessel. Rather, choosing a golden vessel, he prepared the drink in it, so that someone who saw the beauty of the gold, delighted in the splendor of the shining metal, and fixed his eyes entirely upon its appearance would not consider what was hidden within. Taking the cup, he would drink without knowing that it was Nebuchadnezzar’s cup.

You will understand the golden cup named here in the present passage if you observe the deadly words of the worst doctrines: what arrangement of language they possess, what rhetorical beauty, and what organization of their subject matter. You will recognize how each of the poets who are thought most eloquent among their own people has prepared a golden cup and poured into it the poison of idolatry, the poison of shameful speech, the poison of doctrines that kill the human soul, and the poison of falsely named knowledge.

But my Jesus did the opposite. Knowing the devil’s golden cup, and taking precautions lest anyone coming to his faith should suppose that Christ’s cup was like the one the devil had left behind, and lest he should fear error because of the similarity of the material, he arranged that we should have this treasure in earthen vessels. I have often seen a golden cup in beautiful rhetorical adornment, and, considering the poisons of its doctrines, I have detected the cup of Babylon.

«Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord.» Babylon’s cup is not always golden. When the Lord comes for vengeance, and Babylon has been placed in the Lord’s hand, then it becomes like the earth that was once touched in Job. Nor is it continually held in the Lord’s hand, but only at the time of vengeance, when the Lord begins to repay it what it deserves. Then it will be in his hand, making the whole earth drunk.

This golden cup of Babylon made the whole earth drunk. How it made the whole earth drunk you will easily understand if you consider that all human beings are drunk. We are drunk with anger; we are drunk with grief; we are drunk in mind; we lose our senses through love, desires, and vainglory. How many cups it has prepared and how many goblets of drunkenness it has offered—what need is there to say?

«Babylon is a golden cup, making the whole earth drunk.» Observe that the whole earth is full of sins, and do not ask how Babylon made the whole earth drunk. But if perhaps you see that a righteous person is not drunk from the cup of sinners, do not suppose that Scripture lied when it said, «making the whole earth drunk,» because this person is not made drunk by Babylon and yet remains on earth.

Hear that the righteous person is not on the earth. This golden cup makes the whole earth drunk. But although the righteous person is above the earth, his manner of life is in heaven, and for this reason it is no longer fitting to say to the righteous person, «You are earth, and to earth you shall go» (Genesis 3). But, if it is necessary to speak boldly, God says to the righteous person who still remains above the earth: You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go, for he bears the image of the heavenly one.

To conclude, the golden cup makes the whole earth drunk—that is, we are all made drunk by it as long as we are earth. «The nations drank of her wine; therefore they were shaken.» Just as we see in those who drink the liquid commonly used as wine: if they drink beyond thirst and beyond measure, we see the movement of an intoxicated body, unsteady feet, the head and temples weighed down, a slack mouth, and a tongue indicating the speech of the drunk, with words cut short by lips that cling together.

In the same way, one can observe those who have drunk from Babylon’s golden cup: how they are moved, how unstable their steps are, how, with their minds weakened and their efforts wavering, they hold nothing firm but are always driven about in confusion and uncertainty.

«The nations drank; therefore they were shaken, and suddenly Babylon fell and was crushed.» When did Babylon suddenly fall? It seems to me that he is prophesying the sudden future consummation of the world. For just as in the days of the flood they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building (Luke 17), until the flood came and took them all away, and the inundation came suddenly; and likewise in the days of Lot—so also the consummation of the world will not take place in stages, but suddenly.

I think this should be compared with what is written in Joshua [Col. 1163B] (Joshua 7), when, at the mere sound of the trumpet, the city of Jericho collapsed and suddenly perished. In accordance with this comparison, Babylon too will fall at the consummation of the age, be suddenly crushed—and these things have indeed been said about the consummation.

But if you turn to the advent of my Lord Jesus Christ and see his great work, how he overturned all the doctrines of the nations concerning idols in order to free believers from the yoke of error, you will understand that, at the time of his passion, Babylon immediately fell and was crushed.

Let each one of us examine himself and observe whether Babylon has fallen in his own breast. If the city of confusion has not fallen in someone’s heart, Christ has not yet come to him. For when he comes, Babylon customarily collapses. Therefore, taking refuge in the protection of prayers, ask that Jesus come into your hearts, crush Babylon, and make all its wickedness collapse, so that he may rebuild, in place of the things that were overthrown and in place of Babylon, which had previously been built, the holy city of God, Jerusalem, in the governing center of our heart.

«Wail over her; take resin for her pain, if perhaps she may be healed.» «Wail over her,» that is, mourn for her. Then, because every soul can receive salvation and not one is incurable before God, he gives counsel to those who are able to make the journey to Jerusalem and possess the resin needed to prepare poultices, so that they may take medicines and, with all the zeal they possess, restore Babylon to health.

Let us also try to do this, beseeching God to give us rational resin, and from rational resin to teach us how to apply a poultice, oil, and a bandage. By applying these, let us bind up Babylon’s wounds, imitating the Samaritan, so that the wretched city may be healed and, once cured, cease to be what it was.

This is what he says: «Take the resin of her correction, if somehow she may be healed.» Where are the heretics? Where are those who, introducing certain natures, assert that there is a material of despair which cannot receive salvation at all? If there is a nature that perishes, what other nature could be such as Babylon? Yet God does not despise even this one. For he commanded the physicians to take resin for Babylon, if somehow it might be healed.

Some of those who had received the command took the resin for Babylon’s correction, to see whether it might be healed. They did what had been commanded: they took resin for its correction, hearing that Babylon could possibly recover its health. But because they did not find what they had hoped—for Babylon, persisting in its predetermined wickedness, refused to be healed—the good physicians give their account and say:

«We have healed Babylon, but she was not healed. Let us abandon her, and let us go each to his own land, because her judgment has reached the heavens, and it has been raised up to the clouds.» (ORIG.) See, human being, lest God at some time command the angels to prepare medicinal poultices for the sickness of your soul, to see whether you can be healed of your disease. And lest the angels reply, «We have healed this Babylon»—showing that its soul has been confused by passions—«and it has not been healed.» They do not blame their knowledge of the art or the power of the resin, but you, who did not wish to obey their commands, saying: «We have healed Babylon, and it has not been healed; let us leave her.»

The physicians, the angels of God, stood under the great physician, wishing to heal our weaknesses and divinely free the soul. But we ourselves drive them away when we do not heed their counsels.

«To their own land» means: the medical care entrusted to us by the Lord was to heal the human soul. We supplied assistance and applied medicines. It is exceedingly obstinate; it does not wish to observe what we say, and the result does not follow our efforts.

«Let us leave her, and let us go each to his own land»—to his own domestic and proper task. Beware, human being, lest the physician abandon you: whether the physician is an angel of God or any human being entrusted with the care of conveying words as medicines for salvation.

For if they abandon you and say, «Let us go each to his own land, because her judgment will approach heaven,» it is clear that their departure is your condemnation, since you are beyond remedy and unwilling to be healed. When they have abandoned you, what else will happen to you except what usually happens to those whom physicians despair of: they follow the inclination of their disease and sink into worse conditions?

Similar things also happen in the ordinary practice of this life among wise physicians. One of them approaches a sick person; as far as the art permits, the physician’s skill does not cease. But if either the illness is so great that it resists treatment, or the patient himself, through impatience of pain, does the opposite of what he is ordered, the physician abandons such a person in despair and withdraws, lest, if he expires in the physician’s hands, the cause of his death be attributed to the physician.

So we too, lest we die in the hands of the holy angels who have been sent by the Lord to heal us, are abandoned by them in despair over our soul, and they say: «There is no use applying a poultice, or oil, or a bandage, because her judgment has approached heaven and has been raised up to the stars.»

Whoever has a small sin does not raise his judgment up to heaven and the stars, for it is small and lowly. But whoever grows in crime also grows in judgment; as vices increase, punishment increases together with them. And because he sins to such an extent that his judgment is lifted up to the heavenly places, resisting God through his impiety and climbing to the heights, God brings forth his judgment in the humiliation of that judgment which the sinner had exalted. In bringing forth his judgment, he humbles the sinner, but he repays the righteous person with what is worthy of his life in Christ Jesus.

«The Lord has brought forth our righteous acts; come, and let us proclaim in Zion the work of the Lord our God.» (ORIG.) This is the voice of the angels of the Lord, or of the holy preachers, who, seeing that Babylon’s wound is incurable, urge one another to announce the work of the Lord our God and his mighty deeds in the catholic Church, which is rightly called Zion, that is, «mirror,» because it alone pertains to the contemplation of the face of God, together with the holy angels who are in heaven.

As for that earthly Jerusalem and Zion, because of the scandal of its error it can now be called Babylon more than Zion or Jerusalem. Concerning it Isaiah says: «Woe to the sinful nation, a people full of iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children. They have abandoned the Lord; they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned away backward. Where shall I strike you, as you continue to add transgression? Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it. Wound and bruise and swelling sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil. Your land is desolate; your cities have been burned with fire. Foreigners devour your region before your eyes, and it shall be laid waste as in hostile devastation. And the daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, like a city that is being devastated» (Isaiah 1).

The description, therefore, of wounds that cannot be healed expresses the Jews’ prolonged captivity.

«Sharpen the arrows; fill the quivers. The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, and his mind is against Babylon, to destroy it, because the vengeance of the Lord is the vengeance of his temple. Raise a banner over the walls of Babylon; strengthen the guard. Set up watchmen and prepare ambushes, because the Lord has planned and done whatever he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon. You who dwell upon many waters, rich in treasures, your end has come, the measure of your cutting off. The Lord of hosts has sworn by his own life: Surely I shall fill you with men as with locusts, and a battle cry shall be sung over you.» (MAURUS.) He speaks to the Medes and Persians, the devastators of Babylon, so that they may prepare their weapons to kill and destroy it in vengeance for the people of God.

Whatever the Lord planned against Babylon and threatened through his prophets to do to it, he completely accomplished, bringing it from great power and the vastness of a kingdom to a narrow end—or rather, to nothing. God is said to swear by his own life, not because he makes a decision with an oath in the human manner, but to show us that his plan and word are stable and firm, because «heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away» (Luke 21).

He therefore filled Babylon with lowly men as with locusts, because he gathered innumerable armies for its devastation. After overcoming it, they joyfully sang a triumphal song for the victory granted to them.

When he says that Babylon dwelt upon many waters, he indicates that it became rich in treasures—or, historically, that there was an abundance of water there, since the Euphrates flowed through its middle. Figuratively, he signifies that a multitude of peoples was in it.

(OROS.) For many have related that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod and restored by Ninus or Semiramis. Visible from every side across a level plain, its site was naturally very broad. Its walls, arranged in a square like a military camp, possessed a strength and magnitude scarcely credible to describe: they were fifty cubits thick and four times that height. Its circuit extended for four hundred and eighty stades. The wall was made of baked brick joined with bitumen; outside it, a broad ditch flowed around it like a river. In the front of the walls were one hundred bronze gates.

The very breadth at the top of the battlements, with dwellings for defenders arranged equally on both sides, accommodated twenty chariots in its central open space. Within stood houses, remarkable for the threatening height of their fourfold dwellings. Yet that great Babylon, that first city founded after the restoration of the human race, was soon afterward conquered, captured, and overthrown—almost without delay.

Cyrus, after subduing all those against whom he had marched, attacked the Assyrians and Babylon, a people and city then richer than all others. But the river Gindes, second in size only to the Euphrates, intercepted his advance. One of the royal horses, outstanding in whiteness and beauty, had been induced to attempt the crossing. It was swept away, hurled down, and drowned by the violent channel, whose whirlpools rose up when disturbed at the ford.

The angry king resolved to take revenge on the river, declaring that the river which had now swallowed such a splendid horse should be left fordable by women scarcely wetting their knees. Nor was he slow to carry out his threat. With his entire army, he spent a full year cutting and channeling the river Gindes through great trenches and dividing it into four hundred and sixty channels.

Having trained his excavators through this work, he also diverted the far more powerful Euphrates, which flowed through the middle of Babylon. In this way he made a dry path through fordable shallows and exposed sections of the riverbed, and captured the city which it was almost incredible among mortals either that human labor could have built or human strength could destroy.

At that time Croesus, the famous king of the Lydians, celebrated for his wealth, had come to assist the Babylonians. After being defeated, he withdrew anxiously to his kingdom. But after Cyrus invaded Babylonia as an enemy, overthrew it as a victor, and organized it as a king, he transferred the war to Lydia. There he easily defeated the army already broken in the earlier battle; he also captured Croesus and, after capturing him, granted him both his life and his patrimony.

Nor do I think the following should be passed over in silence: when King Arbatus went down into Media, the Chaldeans retained part of the kingdom and claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes. Thus power over Babylonia belonged to the Medes, while ownership belonged to the Chaldeans. But because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, the Chaldeans preferred not to call it theirs, but to call themselves hers.

Hence it happened that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, although powerful through Chaldean strength and recorded under the Babylonian name of Darius, are not counted among the illustrious kings in the number and order of kings.

Babylon, then, was dishonored in the year when Rome was, properly speaking, planted under King Proca. Babylon was finally overthrown by King Cyrus at the time when Rome was first liberated from the domination of the Tarquin kings.

«He made the earth by his strength, prepared the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding. When he gives his voice, the waters in heaven multiply. He lifts up clouds from the end of the earth; he makes lightning into rain and brings forth the winds from his treasuries.» (MAURUS.) Properly demonstrating Babylon’s overthrow, the prophetic word returns to the author of so great a disaster, because there is no power except from God, since the Most High rules in the kingdom of human beings and gives it to whomever he wishes:

«He made the earth by his strength, prepared the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens.» Through his Word—that is, his only-begotten Son, who is called his arm, power, and wisdom—he created everything that is in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, because «he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.»

He himself is the creator, arranger, and governor of all things, and he disposes everything according to his will, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: «The Lord did whatever he wished in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses; he brings clouds from the end of the earth, makes lightning into rain, and brings forth the winds from his treasuries» (Psalm 134).

(CASSIOD.) For although the works of the Lord are beyond description and the whole world cannot adequately recount what he does, all his works in the world have nevertheless been summed up here with brevity: God made everything he wished in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses. Thus you may recognize that the created things you see were made by his will, and may understand that those things which cannot appear to human eyes can be held within his power.

Heaven is used for all heavenly things; earth for everything produced from the soil; the sea, we may say, for those regions which the journeys of travelers frequent; and the abyss designates the ocean, which is unknown to us and, as some report, deep to a great extent. In all these things the Lord’s will is fulfilled without any doubt.

When he says, «bringing clouds from the end of the earth, making lightning into rain, and bringing forth the winds from his treasuries,» if you attend to the literal sense, he testifies that the secrets of nature are completed through the Lord’s administration. But because he speaks below about the Hebrew people, this can also be applied to human beings:

«He brought clouds from the end of the earth.» When he caused the prophets to rise from a lowly purpose to the heights of preaching—they are rightly compared with clouds, because by the rain of their eloquence they protect us from the heat of the coming judgment while proclaiming future things to our souls. Scripture testifies, as has often been said, that clouds should be understood as prophets, saying: «I shall command my clouds not to rain rain upon her.»

It follows: «He made lightning into rain.» The preachings of the prophets are therefore lightning when they strike enemies; they are rains when they wash the devoted clean of sins and pour upon them the rain of salvation. From this spiritual fruits spring and, by the Lord’s favor, grow together into a ripened harvest.

He added: «He brings forth the winds from his treasuries.» We appropriately understand the apostles as winds: their preaching traversed the whole world like a swift wind. Concerning them it is written elsewhere: «He makes his arrows burning» (Psalm 7). Wings are also attributed to these winds because of the speed of their movement; for he says: «He mounted above the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.»

He adds: «from his treasuries.» From them, in truth, spiritual riches could come forth.

“Every human being has become foolish through knowledge; every metalworker is confounded by the carved image, because his casting is false, and there is no spirit in them. Their works are worthless and deserving of ridicule; at the time of their visitation they will perish. Jacob’s portion is not like these, for he himself is the maker of all things, and Israel is the scepter of his inheritance: the Lord of hosts is his name.”

(MAURUS.) Therefore, rightly, after the overthrow of Babylon he rebukes the makers of idols, because the works produced by human foolishness are worthless and deserving of ridicule: for there is neither spirit, nor voice, nor understanding, nor any efficacy of works in them. Hence they will be unable to save either themselves or their worshipers on the day of visitation. Israel, however, did not act in this way, since it was a worshiper of the one God. Although many of them went astray, many nevertheless remained in the faith and were often delivered and protected by his help.

Mystically, all heretics and schismatics have become foolish, fashioning images of their errors, because their doctrines are worthless and deserving of ridicule. Therefore, at the time of visitation—that is, on the day of universal judgment—they will perish together with their authors. For such is not the apostolic and prophetic teaching that is preached in the Catholic Church. It daily proclaims to the faithful the praise of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, of the one God—because he truly is: that is, God, the creator and fashioner of all things, alone remains eternally immutable in himself; and the holy Church is the scepter of his inheritance. His name is “the Lord of Sabaoth” forever.

“You have shattered for me the instruments of war, and I will shatter nations in you and destroy kingdoms in you. I will shatter horse and rider in you; I will shatter chariot and rider in you; I will shatter man and woman in you; I will shatter old man and boy in you; I will shatter young man and virgin in you; I will shatter shepherd and his flock in you; I will shatter farmer and his team in you; I will shatter commanders and magistrates in you. And I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea for all the evil they have done in Zion before your eyes, says the Lord.”

The divine word foretells to Babylon that, just as it shattered weapons of war—that is, weapons of battle—or fighting men in the land of the Jews and in various provinces, so the Lord will shatter all nations in it, destroy kingdoms, crush horses and riders, and shatter people of every sex and age, farmers, commanders, and magistrates, so that, when the just Judge repays them, each may receive the evil he did to his neighbors. So also it will be in God’s future judgment: each of the persecutors of Christ’s Church will receive the punishment he deserves and earned by his unjust life.

[Col. 1169B] “Behold, I am against you, pestilential mountain, says the Lord, which corrupts the whole earth. I will stretch out my hand against you, roll you down from the rocks, and make you a mountain of burning. They will not take from you a stone for a corner, nor a stone for a foundation; rather, you will be destroyed forever, says the Lord.”

By the pestilential mountain he means either, historically, Nebuchadnezzar with the Chaldeans, because of the cruelty of his tyranny, which he exercised against various nations; or, spiritually, the devil, on account of his pride. Elsewhere Scripture calls him “the mountain of darkness” (Isa. XIII), because of the darkness of error. He corrupts the whole earth—that is, he pollutes earthly and carnal people with various vices. Against him the Lord stretches out the hand of vengeance, rolls him down from the rocks—that is, separates him from those who are firm in faith—and gives him over to the mountain of eternal burning, so that he may continually pay the penalties of his pride. Nor is a cornerstone taken from him for the foundation of the heavenly building; rather, he will be destroyed forever.

To this mountain belong unbelieving Jews, blasphemers, heretics, and all the impious who persist in their wickedness and refuse to turn to the Lord, so that they may become living stones suitable for God’s building. Conversely, there is another stone, mentioned in Daniel’s prophecy (Dan. II), which was cut from the mountain without hands. It struck that enormous statue on its iron feet and shattered the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold; and it became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole earth. This, then, is the stone that the builders rejected, yet it became the cornerstone (Luke XX). The Lord has done this, and it is marvelous in our eyes. Its kingdom will never be destroyed or handed over to another people; rather, its kingdom will be the kingdom of all ages, and its dominion will extend through every generation and lineage. Blessed are all who trust in it.

“Raise a banner in the land; sound the trumpet among the mountains. Consecrate nations against her; proclaim against her to the kings of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. Muster against her Tapsar; bring up the horse like a bristling locust. Consecrate against her the nation, the kings of Media, their commanders, all their magistrates, and the whole land under their authority. The earth will tremble and be shaken, because the Lord’s purpose has awakened against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon desolate and uninhabitable.”

The prophet speaks to the nations and their kings who dwelt around Chaldea and Babylon, telling them to raise their standards and weapons of war, sound their trumpets among the mountains, and summon all nations for Babylon’s overthrow. For Ararat is Armenia, and Ashkenaz was the son of Gomer, the son of Japheth, the son of Noah; from them kings arose. Indeed, Asia was possessed by the seven sons of Japheth, from Amanus and Taurus—the mountains of Coele-Syria and Cilicia—as far as the river Tanais; in Europe, as far as Gadeira, leaving their names to places and peoples. He commands the nations to be consecrated against Babylon, which was to fulfill God’s holy will by repaying it with a just recompense for its sins and making its land desolate and uninhabitable. Hence it follows:

“The mighty men of Babylon have ceased from battle; they have remained in the strongholds. Their strength has been devoured, and they have become like women. Her tents have been burned. The bars have been broken; runner will meet runner, and messenger will meet messenger, to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end. The fords have been seized, the marshes have been burned with fire, and the warriors have been thrown into confusion.”

The strength and power of Babylon failed when Cyrus and Darius came against it with their armies, and its people became unwarlike, like women. Therefore its tents were burned and all its fortifications destroyed. This also did not escape King Belshazzar, although he was at a banquet: messengers running back and forth announced to the king that his city had been captured from one end to the other, that the fords of the Euphrates had been seized, the marshes burned with fire, and all the warriors thrown into confusion. No one remained who could successfully resist the enemy.

“Because thus says the Lord God of Israel: The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time of its threshing; in a little while the time of its harvest will come.”

The people of Babylon were like a threshing floor when, through the power of their kingdom and the greatness of their wealth, they threshed and crushed the nations to which they had been sent. But the time of harvest came, when they were forced to receive what they had wickedly done. Concerning this, in the person of the Jewish people, it is subsequently said:

“Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, has devoured me and swallowed me up; he has made me like an empty vessel. He has swallowed me like a dragon; he has filled his belly with my tenderness and cast me out. May the violence done to me and my flesh be upon Babylon, says the inhabitant of Zion, and my blood is upon the inhabitants of Chaldea, says Jerusalem. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will judge your case and avenge your vengeance. I will make its sea desolate and dry up its spring, and Babylon will become heaps, a dwelling place of dragons, an object of astonishment and a hissing, because there is no inhabitant, even when lions roar. They will shake their manes like lion cubs. In their heat I will set out their drink; I will make them drunk so that they may grow drowsy and sleep an everlasting sleep and never rise again, says the Lord.
