I will lead them like lambs to the slaughter, and like rams with young goats.”

Isaiah also speaks of this sea in his book: “The burden of the desert of the sea. Like whirlwinds coming from the south, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land; a harsh vision has been announced to me.” It is therefore clear that Babylon is called the desert sea. Jeremiah confirms this here in the person of the Lord, saying: “I will make its sea desolate and dry up its land, and Babylon will become heaps of sand.” It is called a sea because of the multitude of its inhabitants. Hence above also the multitude of Egypt was compared with the sea.

The Lord destroyed Babylon through the armies of the Medes and Persians, whom he here compares with lions and lion cubs, and reduced it to heaps of sand, so that afterward it became a dwelling place of dragons, an object of astonishment, and a hissing for those who saw and marveled at its destruction, because no inhabitant remained in it. In the heat of their tribulations, therefore, they drank the cup of the Lord’s wrath and became drunk, so that they grew drowsy and slept an everlasting sleep and rose no more.

Mystically, the sea signifies the turbulence of this age. The Lord makes it desolate when he causes its luxury to cease, and the wicked who served confusion through the errors and vices of their lives will be scattered. Malignant spirits will come upon them, fierce like lion cubs, together with the lion-devil, who prowls around roaring and seeking someone to devour. They will intoxicate them with the drink of future vengeance and retribution, so that they may sleep in the drowsiness of eternal death and never rise again to life, but become victims slain by the Lord’s sword and dwell forever with spiritual dragons in the lake of hell. Concerning this and what follows, it also says:

“How Sheshach has been captured, and the renowned one of the whole earth has been seized! How Babylon has become an object of astonishment among the nations! The sea has risen over Babylon; she has been covered by the multitude of its waves. Her cities have become an object of astonishment, a land uninhabitable and desolate, in which no one dwells, nor does any human being pass through it. I will punish Bel in Babylon and cast out of his mouth what he had swallowed, and the nations will no longer stream to him. Indeed, the wall of Babylon will also fall.”

That Sheshach itself is Babylon has already been demonstrated above. How Babylon’s overthrow occurred—how the sea, that is, the multitude of peoples, together with its god, overthrew and destroyed it—has also been stated repeatedly. Let us now add a little concerning the allegory.

Sheshach is interpreted as “the linen of a sack” or “the hand of a sack,” just as Babylon means “confusion.” Sheshach was therefore captured, and Babylon became an object of astonishment, when those who practiced idolatry and were enslaved to various vices were overthrown by the waves of the coming judgment. With Bel, whose name is interpreted as “antiquity”—that is, with the ancient enemy—they will have everlasting confusion in hell, having at last repented too late. Therefore the prophetic word warns the faithful to go out and separate themselves from their fellowship, lest they perish together with them.

“Go out from her midst, my people, so that each may save his soul from the anger of the Lord’s fury, and lest your heart perhaps grow soft, and you fear the report that will be heard in the land: in one year a report will come, and after that year a report and iniquity in the land, and ruler against ruler.”

It is necessary, therefore, for everyone who wishes to save his soul to withdraw from the company of the lost and to revere the word of the Lord, who threatens the future vengeance for sins. This word is preached daily in the Church and heard by all, while the holy Scriptures testify year after year to the same thing: that the heavenly Judge will say at the final examination to those who will be at his left hand, “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Our heart must not grow soft through the desires of the flesh and make us sluggish in good works. Rather, hearing this, it should make us attentive to meditation on God’s law and vigorous in the practice of the virtues, because the iniquity of the earth will be repaid with the punishment of Gehenna, and ruler will come against ruler, so that those who were more powerful in sins may suffer more powerful torments (Wis. VI).

“Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will punish the images of Babylon. Her whole land will be confounded, and all her slain will fall in her midst. Heaven and earth, and all that is in them, will praise over Babylon, because plunderers will come against her from the north, says the Lord. And just as Babylon caused the slain to fall in Israel, so from Babylon the slain will fall throughout the whole earth.”

These are days of retribution, when the heavenly Judge will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples with equity. Then Babylon’s images—that is, the idols of error that heretics have fashioned in their doctrines—will be punished, and all their earthly way of life will be confounded. All who have gone astray and led others into error will fall beneath the sword of the Lord’s vengeance. And just as spiritual Babylon caused the slain to fall among God’s people, so its inhabitants will fall slain throughout the whole earth. Therefore heaven and earth, and all that is in them, will praise over Babylon, because the plunderer of all nations has been devastated.

“You who have fled from the sword, come; do not stand still. Remember the Lord from afar, and let Jerusalem rise above your heart.”

The prophet urges the Israelites who were in Babylon that, if they wished to be saved, they should depart from there, remember from afar the land of the Lord’s temple and Jerusalem, his desolated city, and hurry to cross over there rather than share in Babylon’s devastation. To this they respond:

“We are confounded because we have heard reproach; disgrace has covered our faces, because foreigners have come upon the sanctuary of the Lord’s house.”

They say that they are ashamed because of the reproach of neighboring nations, which mocked them as captives, as is read in the Book of Ezra, since they had been torn from their land, their dwelling places were desolate, and the sanctuary of the Lord’s temple had been destroyed. To them the prophet again responds:

“Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will punish the images of Babylon, and throughout all her land the wounded will roar. If Babylon ascends to heaven and strengthens her power on high, her destroyers will come to me, says the Lord. A voice of outcry from Babylon and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans, because the Lord has devastated Babylon and destroyed from her the great voice. Their waves will roar like many waters; their voice has made a sound, because the plunderer has come upon her—that is, upon Babylon—and her mighty men have been seized, and her bows have languished, because the Lord is a mighty avenger who repays with retribution. I will make drunk her princes and her wise men, her commanders and magistrates, and her mighty men; they will sleep an everlasting sleep and will not awaken, says the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts. Thus says the Lord of hosts: That very high wall of Babylon will be dug down by undermining, and her lofty gates will be burned with fire. The labor of the peoples will come to nothing, and the work of the nations will be consumed in fire and perish.”

He enumerates all the plagues that were to come upon Babylon, upon all its nobles, commanders, and magistrates, and upon the entire people: they would be killed by various punishments, sleep the sleep of everlasting death, and never awaken from it again.

Mystically, all these things proclaim the ruin of the faithless city that the devil constructed from the beginning, through which he continually fought against the city of God. Once God’s holy and chosen people have been rescued from death, the impious city will be plunged into eternal punishment. Concerning this city John also spoke sufficiently in the Apocalypse, saying:

“I saw an angel descending from heaven, possessing great authority, and the earth was illumined by his glory. He cried out in a mighty voice, saying: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and it has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, a prison of every unclean and hateful bird, because all the nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have fornicated with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich through the power of her luxuries.’ And I heard another voice from heaven saying: ‘Come out of her, my people, so that you may not share in her sins and receive none of her plagues, because her sins have reached to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. Repay her as she herself repaid you, and give her double for her deeds. In the cup in which she mixed the drink, mix her a double portion. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning. For in her heart she says: “I sit as queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall never see mourning.” Therefore in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be consumed by fire, because mighty is God who has judged her. And the kings of the earth who fornicated with her and lived in luxury will weep and mourn over her’” (Rev. XVIII).

And after a little he adds, saying: “‘Rejoice over her, heaven,’ and holy apostles and prophets, ‘because God has pronounced your judgment against her.’” For there is no other city than the city of the devil that receives every unclean soul, in which every impurity dwells throughout the world.

“And the merchants of the earth have become rich through the power of her luxuries.” He calls those who, for the sake of temporal abundance, entrust their souls to an unhappy commerce “rich in sins.” For excessive luxury makes people poor rather than rich.

“Come out of her,” he says, “my people, and do not share in her sins.” Isaiah says the same: “Come out from their midst, and do not touch what is unclean; purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.” Having foretold Babylon’s ruin, he introduces the departure of the elect. What is Babylon’s ruin? When Lot departs from Sodom, they will be utterly destroyed (Gen. XIX).

“Repay her,” he says, “as she repaid you.” For visible and invisible plagues go out from the Church into the world. “Give her double for her deeds.” Thus she who enjoyed temporal pleasures will be tormented by eternal punishments.

“The word that Jeremiah commanded Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah, when he went with King Zedekiah to Babylon, in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah, moreover, was chief of the prophecy. Jeremiah wrote in one book all the evil that was to come upon Babylon, all these words that were written against Babylon. And Jeremiah said to Seraiah: ‘When you come to Babylon, see and read all these words, and say: “Lord, you have spoken against this place, to destroy it, so that no one may dwell in it, from human being to cattle, and so that it may be an everlasting desolation.” When you have finished reading this book, tie a stone to it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates, and say: “Thus Babylon will be submerged, and will not rise again from the face of the affliction that I am bringing upon her, and she will be dissolved.”’”

(MAURUS.) Babylon was not submerged in the Euphrates according to the historical sense, although after its submersion it was reduced to desolation. Rather, the spiritual prophet foretells the future eternal destruction of spiritual Babylon, which on the day of judgment will be plunged into the depths of hell together with its prince, the devil. The prophets in the Old Testament also proclaimed this, and the preachers of the New Testament declare it in a firm and truthful account. Hence John narrates in his Apocalypse, saying:

“Then one mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: ‘With such force Babylon, that great city, will be thrown down, and it will never be found again. The voice of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never be heard in you again, and the light of a lamp will never shine in you again. The voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again, because your merchants were the rulers of the earth, because by your sorcery all the nations were led astray, and in her was found the blood of prophets and saints and of all who were slain on the earth’” (Rev. XVIII).

The city of this age is compared, because of the weight of its sins and its unstable error, with an unwieldy millstone: “For the wicked walk about on every side” (Ps. XI). It is rightly swallowed up by the waves of vengeance, because it oppressed the citizens of Jerusalem with waves of unbelief, when, sitting beside the rivers of Babylon (Ps. CXXXVI), they wept over the absence of heavenly Zion.

The Lord says that the authors of scandal are to be punished. The Church, indeed, is compared to a stone, but to one that is stable and firm and despises the assaults of storms. The millstone may also be understood as the crushing of punishments. For blessed Ignatius is said to have declared, when he was about to suffer: “I am God’s grain; I am ground by the teeth of beasts, so that I may become pure bread.”

“‘The voice,’ he says, ‘of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will never be heard in her again.’” He had deferred the sound belonging to the five senses, which he now says is removed from the world along with other things—as if he were saying that whatever is beautiful to the sight, harmonious to the hearing, smooth to the touch, pleasant to the smell, and delightful to the taste has been taken away from the age. Everything that pertains to the use or enjoyment of human life is also removed from the impious.

He adds the reason, saying: “Because your merchants were the rulers of the earth”—that is, because in your life you received good things, and in you the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who were slain on the earth, was shed.

Did the same city kill the apostles as well as the prophets and all the saints? This is the city that Cain founded with the blood of his brother and called by the name of his son Enoch—that is, by the name of his entire posterity (Gen. V). For seven generations of Cain are recorded. Into the building of this city all righteous blood has been poured, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah—that is, of both people and priest.

## CHAPTER LII

Jerusalem is captured by the Chaldeans; Zedekiah is blinded; the city is burned; the temple is plundered. King Jehoiachin is brought out of prison, and food is assigned to him.

“Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah. He did evil in the eyes of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done, because the Lord’s wrath was against Jerusalem and Judah, until he cast them from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.”

(MAURUS.) It should therefore be noted that this history, which recounts Zedekiah’s capture and the devastation of the city of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, is contained in nearly similar form in the Book of Kings. Hence we think that certain things already stated in the exposition of that book, which we published several years ago, should be set down here:

“It came to pass in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem. They besieged it and built fortifications against it all around. The city remained under siege until the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign. In the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month, famine prevailed in the city, and there was no food for the people of the land. The city was breached, and all its fighting men fled. They went out from the city by night, by the way of the gate that lies between the two walls and leads to the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans surrounded the city; and they went by the road that leads to the wilderness.”

The number nine, which falls short of ten, signifies the imperfection of the Law, just as eleven signifies transgression. It is therefore rightly said that Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city in Zedekiah’s ninth year, in the tenth month and on the tenth day of the month. When evil shepherds neglect to fulfill in their deeds and teaching the commandments of the Decalogue, which contain knowledge, it is necessary that the ancient enemy, with his army, surround the people entrusted to them with a siege. Having constructed fortifications of vice and error, he closes the city in by a rampart, and thus famine prevails in the city—famine, namely, of the word of God, when the bread of doctrine is not freely distributed to the people of the land.

The city was breached, and all the fighting men fled by night. The people’s guardianship was breached through the various temptations of malignant spirits. Those who ought to have defended the city with weapons flee, surrounded by the night of ignorance and the darkness of sins, because, according to the word of Truth, “the hired servant, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” (John X). The Apostle also says: “Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night” (1 Tim. V).

As for what follows—that they fled by the road of the gate lying between the two walls and leading to the king’s garden—it secretly exposes the negligence of teachers who, stationed between the double wall of the two Testaments, seek not to wage war but to escape, and to drift more in pleasures, which the garden signifies, rather than resist the enemies with the shield of faith.

“But the Chaldean army pursued the king, and they seized Zedekiah in the wilderness near Jericho, and all his companions scattered from him,” and what follows. In the Book of Kings it is written as follows (2 Kings XXV):

“Zedekiah fled by the road leading to the plains of the wilderness, and the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and seized him on the plain of Jericho. All the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him,” and what follows.

When malignant spirits surround the people, the ruler does not flee to the mountains, of which it is written, “The mountains surround him, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. CXXIV), but to the plains of the wilderness—that is, to the expansiveness of luxury. Hence it is written: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life; broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matt. VII).

“They seized him on the plain of Jericho, and all the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him.” Rightly, therefore, when the virtues of people—the virtues that ought to have defended him—desert him, he is captured in the wilderness, or on the plain of Jericho: that is, in wantonness or in the decline of carnal conduct. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon” and signifies the decline of the flesh. Hence that man who was descending from Jerusalem to Jericho is described as having fallen among robbers (Luke X).

Having seized the king, they brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, who pronounced judgment upon him—that is, exercised a just judgment against him.

“He killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, then put out his eyes, bound him with chains, and brought him to Babylon.”

(GREGORY.) When Sacred Scripture narrates Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity. The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of intimate confusion. He first slaughtered the sons before the eyes of the one watching, because he often kills good works in such a way that the soul itself, which has been captured, sorrowfully sees that it has lost them. For when the soul often groans, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, having loved the good works it produced, loses them, it considers the losses it suffers but nevertheless does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. While it is struck by the visible perpetration of wickedness, it is eventually led through the habit of sin to be deprived even of the light of reason.

Therefore the king of Babylon first put out the eyes of all Zedekiah’s sons, because the malignant spirit first removes good works and then takes away the light of understanding. Rightly does Zedekiah suffer this at Riblah. Riblah is interpreted as “many things,” for at times the light of reason is closed to one who is weighed down by the multitude of his iniquity through evil habit.

“The king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and placed him in the prison house until the day of his death.” After the soul has been bound in the confusion of sins and brought by malignant spirits into the prison house in fetters of vices, it is placed there until the day of death, because it is shut up in distress of mind and not in breadth of heart, awaiting the sentence amid the wrath of future death.

“In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—that is, the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan, the commander of the army who stood before the king of Babylon in Jerusalem, came and burned the house of the Lord, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned every great house with fire, and the whole army of the Chaldeans that was with the commander of the army destroyed the entire wall of Jerusalem all around. As for the poor of the people, the rest of the common people who remained in the city, and the fugitives who had defected to the king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the commander of the army, carried away, along with the rest of the multitude. But of the poor of the land Nebuzaradan, the commander of the army, left some as vinedressers and farmers.”

The sequence of time therefore accords with the logic of vengeance. The city is said to have been devastated in the fifth month because it despised the Pentateuch of the Law, and on the tenth day of the month because, by violating the Decalogue of the Law, it did everything contrary to the divine commandments, vainly flattering itself about its security because it inhabited holy places.

Hence, earlier, through this same Jeremiah, the Lord says:

“Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord.’ For if you thoroughly amend your ways and your practices; if you administer justice between a man and his neighbor; if you do not oppress the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow; if you do not shed innocent blood in this place; and if you do not go after foreign gods to your own harm, then I will dwell with you in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers forever and ever.

“Behold, you trust in lying words that will not benefit you: stealing, killing, committing adultery, swearing falsely, offering to the Baals, and going after foreign gods whom you do not know. Then you come and stand before me in this house in which my name has been invoked, and you say, ‘We have been delivered, because we have committed all these abominations.’

“And now, because you have done all these things, says the Lord, and I have spoken to you, rising early and speaking, but you have not listened: I will do to this house in which my name has been invoked, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and your fathers, as I did to Shiloh. I will cast you from my presence, as I cast away all your brothers, the whole offspring of Ephraim” (Jer. VII).

Nebuzaradan came; his name is interpreted as “winnowing fan,” or “prophecy of another’s judgment,” signifying the just judgment upon sinners. He was the commander of the army of the king of Babylon against intelligible Jerusalem, and he burned the house of the Lord. This occurs when the ancient enemy, who is both the king of confusion and the prince of all the wicked—of malignant spirits as well as of impious human beings—invades the faithful people. He overturns the king’s house and the houses of Jerusalem, that is, the rulers and those who seemed to remain in the vision of peace, inflaming them with desire.

He burned every house with fire when he disturbs each person’s conscience with the flame of illicit love. He destroys the walls of Jerusalem all around when he dissolves, in those who despair, the intention of prayer and the pursuit of virtues, which he knows can prevail against him, so that they may not seek divine aid through hope of forgiveness or grasp the defenses of a reformed life, while he leads the people into captivity.

“Of the poor of the land he left vinedressers and farmers,” because, by taking captive through vices those who could have been useful in word and example, he entrusts the cultivation to foolish and dull people, so that spiritual wine of grace and the grain of sound doctrine may not bear fruit in the vineyards and fields of the peoples, but rather the thorns and thistles of vices may grow up.

[Col. 1178D] “The Chaldeans also broke up the bronze columns that were in the house of the Lord, the bases, and the bronze Sea that was in the house of the Lord, and carried all their bronze away to Babylon; and they took the pots, the fire-pans, the psalteries, the bowls, the mortars, and all the bronze vessels that had been used in the service; also the pitchers, censers, jars, basins, lampstands, mortars, and cups. As many things as were of gold, gold, and as many as were of silver, silver, the commander of the army took away, together with the two columns, the one Sea, and the twelve bronze calves that were beneath the bases which King Solomon had made in the house of the Lord. There was no weight recorded for the bronze of all these vessels.”

We may understand the bronze columns and bases as teachers, who ought to have supported others by the resonance of their preaching and the firmness of their faith [Col. 1179A]. The bronze Sea, however, signifies the baptismal washing or the contrition of tears. The spiritual Chaldeans strive to remove and break all these things from the house of the Lord through the negligence of teachers, so that not even a potsherd remains from which a little ember might be carried away from the fire. For the various vessels that he enumerates also indicate the various offices in ecclesiastical orders. The evil spirits, removing these from the service of God, likewise strive to turn them to their own wicked use. Hence he says, “As many things as were of gold, gold, and as many as were of silver, silver, the commander of the army took away,” because the wicked enemy attempts to remove both precious understanding and the beauty of eloquence from the house of the Lord and carry them with him into confusion.

“Now the height of one column was eighteen cubits [Col. 1179B], and a cord twelve cubits in circumference surrounded it. Its thickness was four fingers, and it was hollow within; and there were bronze capitals upon both. The height of one capital was five cubits, with bronze latticework and pomegranates upon the crown all around; likewise on the other column. There were ninety-six pendant pomegranates, and all the pomegranates were surrounded by latticework.”

By describing the construction of the columns with their capitals, latticework, and pomegranates, he shows that the work has a mystical meaning. For just as the columns signify teachers, so also the capitals—that is, their uppermost parts—signify the hearts of faithful teachers; and the latticework expresses the various anointings of the Holy Spirit, just as the pomegranates express [Col. 1179C] the sweetness of good virtues. The spiritual Nebuchadnezzar, that is, the ancient enemy, tries through his ministers to remove all these things from the temple of God. If anyone wishes to know these matters more fully, let him read our work that we recently published as an exposition of the Book of Kings; there he will find, as I think, a sufficiently clear account of what the holy Fathers understood concerning them.

“And the commander of the army took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three guardians of the vestibule; and from the city he took one eunuch who was set over the fighting men, and seven men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city, and the chief scribe of the soldiers, who tested recruits; and sixty men from the people of the land who were found in the midst of the city. Nabuzardan the commander of the army took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. And the king of Babylon struck them and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath; and Judah was carried away from his land.”

For the devil strives to deceive and take captive by sins not only ordinary people but also the strong and the leaders in the Church. Concerning him it is written in Job: “Their food is choice” (Job 20).

He also took Seraiah, whose name means “bound,” the chief priest, when he binds the first order of the Church, which is found in bishops, with the love of earthly pleasure and the chain of vices. Likewise he took Zephaniah, whose name means “hidden,” the second priest, when he subjects to his dominion men of the second order—that is, presbyters—who, digging in the earth, had hidden the talent of God’s word [Col. 1180A]. And he took the three doorkeepers, or guardians of the vestibule: namely, those doorkeepers who ought to have opened the door of faith but, holding the key of knowledge, neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter.

“And from the city he took one eunuch who was prefect over the fighting men.” This eunuch signifies those whom sacred Scripture elsewhere calls foolish virgins (Matt. 25). They hold vessels empty of oil in their hands: they keep themselves, to be sure, from bodily intercourse, yet they were unwilling to have the oil of grace and mercy in their hearts. They are placed over fighting men to no purpose, since they make no effort to guard against arrogance.

“He took also seven men of those who saw the king’s face”: plainly, those who had been washed with Christ’s baptism and sanctified by the sevenfold Spirit, yet lost the grace they had received. Hence, handed over to seven more wicked spirits, they no longer look upon the will and commands of the heavenly King and Lord of hosts, but strive to fulfill the will of the king of vices.

“And the chief scribe of the soldiers, whom the Book of Kings calls Sophar, who tested recruits.” Sophar means “dispersing” or “dividing.” He signifies those who, instead of nurturing in the Church the inexperienced whom they ought to have trained for the service of Christ, scatter them by evil examples and separate them through error from the assembly of the faithful.

“And sixty men from the people of the land,” or from the common people, “who had been found in the city”—that is, foolish workers, who are rightly called by the name of the common people because they had neglected to learn the usefulness of divine counsels [Col. 1180C] and to fulfill them in their deeds.

Nabuzardan, the commander of the army, took all these men and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. The king of Babylon struck them and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath, because when the ancient enemy tears such prey from the Church through his wickedness and carries it away, this is what he desires, this is what he pursues with all his effort: to bring them to the destruction of eternal death. The king of confusion strikes them at Riblah—that is, amid a multitude of crimes and the love of pleasures. Hence Scripture says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and there are many who enter by it.”

“And Judah was carried away from his land”: this occurs when those who seemed in the Church to possess confession of the name of God are, through numerous crimes and sins, transferred from the land [Col. 1180D] of virtues and led away into the kingdom of confusion and error. Whoever continues to serve wickedly under that dominion and does not deserve, under the leadership of Jesus, to return to the land of Judah and rebuild the temple of the Lord there will, after the distress of the present life, be handed over to the prison of perpetual death, where their worm will never die and their fire will not be extinguished. In them will be fulfilled the saying of blessed Peter: “For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them” (2 Pet. 2), since, as the Truth testifies: “The servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12).

[Col. 1181A] “This is the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away in the seventh year: three thousand and twenty-three Judeans. In the eighteenth year Nebuchadnezzar carried away from Jerusalem eight hundred and thirty-two persons. In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nabuzardan the commander of the army carried away seven hundred and forty-five persons of the Judeans. Thus all the persons numbered four thousand six hundred.”

Three times, as the Books of Kings and Chronicles testify, Nebuchadnezzar devastated the land of Judah. The first was when he defeated and bound in chains Jehoiakim, also called Eliakim, son of Josiah king of Judah, and carried him to Babylon with the vessels of the house of the Lord, which he placed in his own temple.

The second was when he carried Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah, his son, together with his mother, the eunuchs, the nobles, and his servants, to Babylon, taking with them the most precious vessels of the house of the Lord.

The third was when he captured Zedekiah and put out his eyes, killed his sons, and put the best of them to death. He spared neither young man nor virgin, neither old man nor aged person; he burned the house of the Lord, destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, and demolished whatever was precious. If anyone escaped the sword, he was carried away to Babylon and served the king and his sons.

Therefore Jeremiah, according to the threefold number, enumerates the deportation of the Judeans from their land: first, three thousand and twenty-three; second, eight hundred and thirty-two; third, seven hundred and forty-five. Calculating their total, he says that there were four thousand six hundred persons [Col. 1181C].

Although this happened historically on account of the people’s sins, it nevertheless indicates spiritually that all who pollute the faith of the Holy Trinity through error, refuse to preserve the teaching of the four Gospels, and disdain to possess the perfection of good works are subject to the servitude of the king of Babylon [Col. 1182A]. If they do not correct themselves beforehand and free themselves through repentance, he will deprive them of the light of knowledge, lead them into captivity to perpetual confusion, and confine them in the prison of hell, where, condemned to eternal chains, they will groan forever.

“And it came to pass in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiakim king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-fifth day of the month, that Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year of his reign, raised up the head of Jehoiakim king of Judah and brought him out of the prison house. He spoke kindly to him, set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon, changed his prison garments, and he ate bread continually before him all the days of his life. His provisions were given to him as perpetual provisions by the king of Babylon, an allowance for each day until the day of his death, all the days of his life.”

I do not discover what it signifies spiritually that Evil-merodach, Nebuchadnezzar’s grandson and king of Babylon, raised up the head of Jehoiakim king of Judah, brought him out of the prison house, and exalted him with honors and riches—unless it shows us by clear indications that the divinity is powerful to exercise its judgments through the good as well as through the wicked.

For just as God condemned Zedekiah, who was incorrigible and disobedient to prophetic warnings, to blindness and perpetual captivity through Nebuchadnezzar, so through Evil-merodach he looked with mercy, after his correction, upon King Jehoiakim, though he had been a sinner, who, as if taking thought for the safety of his people and the salvation of the city, had handed himself and his mother over to the king of Babylon to be led away [Col. 1182C]; freeing him from punishments, he restored him to repose and honor. For the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. Thus, when he scourges us, he is shown to be just; and when he consoles us, he is shown to be merciful.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

[Col. 1181]

[Col. 1181C] We intend to expound the final part of the prophet Jeremiah, which is called the Lamentations, according to history and according to its mystical meaning, insofar as the Lord may wish to enlighten us by the grace of his Spirit, through whom the prophet himself spoke. First, we wish to make known that, according to some, this part is joined into one book with the rest of Jeremiah’s prophecy, while according to others it is placed separately and considered to have the name of a book in its own right. The same is true of the Book of Ruth: according to some it is joined to the Book of Judges, while according to others it is placed separately, so that the books of the ancient Law among the Hebrews are shown to number twenty-four. It is under this number that the Apocalypse of John introduces the twenty-four elders, worshiping the Lamb and offering their crowns before the four living creatures full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking toward the past and the future—and crying out with unwearied voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is, and who was, and who is to come.”

Nor do I think that this should be left unsaid: the Lamentations themselves, as blessed Jerome testifies, are alphabetic among the Hebrews and composed according to the law of meter. That renowned teacher and interpreter of divine law reports the following in his letter to Marcella:

“You should know that, according to the order of the Hebrew letters, four psalms begin with the elements of the alphabet: the thirty-sixth, the one hundred eleventh, the one hundred eighteenth, and the one hundred forty-fourth. You should also know that in the first psalms each letter has a single verse attached to it, and these verses consist of iambic trimeter; the later ones consist of iambic tetrameter, just as the Song of Deuteronomy is written. In Psalm 118, eight verses follow each individual letter, and in Psalm 144, two verses are assigned to each letter. Some think that other psalms also begin in this order, but that opinion is false.

“You also have four alphabets in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Of these, the first two are written in a manner resembling Sapphic meter, because a heroic comma concludes three connected verses that begin with one and the same letter. The third alphabet is written in trimeter, and its verses begin with letters in groups of three, three verses beginning with the same letter. The fourth alphabet resembles the first and second. The Book of Solomon’s Proverbs also ends with an alphabet, counted in iambic tetrameter from the passage where it says: ‘Who can find a strong woman?’ (Prov. 31).

“Just as in our ordinary writing one cannot proceed to read and join words unless one has first begun with the letters, so in the divine Scriptures we cannot know what is greater unless we have first made an ethical beginning, according to what the prophet says: ‘From your commandments I have gained understanding’ (Ps. 118)—namely, that after works one begins to possess knowledge of mysteries.

“But now what you requested must be completed: that the interpretation attached to each element should indicate its meaning. Aleph means doctrine; beth, house; gimel, fullness; daleth, tablets; he, this; vau and zain, this; heth, life; teth, good; iod, beginning; caph, hand; lamed, discipline or heart; mem, from them; nun, everlasting; samech, help; ain, fountain or eye; phe, mouth—from *ore*, not from *osse*; sade, righteousness; koph, calling; resh, head; sin, teeth; tau, signs. See that you understand this, lest you be deceived by the ambiguity of the letters.

“After the interpretation of the elements, the order of their meaning must be stated. Aleph, beth, gimel, daleth form the first connection: doctrine, house, fullness, tablets—that is, the doctrine of the Church, which is the house of God, is found in the fullness of the divine books.

“The second connection is he, vau, zain, heth: this, and, this, life. For what other life can there be without knowledge of the Scriptures, through which Christ himself is also recognized, he who is the life of believers?

“The third connection contains teth and iod: good, beginning. For although we now know everything that has been written, we know only in part and prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. 13). But when we have deserved to be with Christ and have become like the angels, then the teaching of books will cease.

“The fourth connection is caph and lamed: hand, heart, or discipline. Hands are understood in relation to works; heart and discipline are interpreted in relation to understanding, because we can do nothing unless we have first learned what must be done.

“The fifth connection is mem, nun, samech: from them, everlasting, help. This needs no explanation; it is clearer than daylight that the Scriptures provide eternal assistance.

“The sixth connection contains ain, phe, sade: fountain or eye, mouth, righteousness, according to what we explained under the third number.

“The seventh connection is also the final one; and in this seventh number too there is a mystical meaning: koph, resh, sin, tau—calling, head, teeth, signs. Articulate speech is produced through the teeth, and by these signs we proceed to the head of all, who is Christ, through whom we come to the everlasting kingdom.”

We have inserted these matters for this reason: to instruct the reader, so that he may know that the prophet did not publish these things according to the sequence of the letters without purpose, but that everything written concerns the mysteries of Christ and the Church.

That the aforementioned Lamentations were written not only over the devastation of the city of Jerusalem and the captivity of the Jewish people but also over the death of King Josiah is shown by the Book of the Words of the Days, where we read:

“King Josiah died and was buried in the mausoleum of his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him. Jeremiah especially mourned him; and all the male and female singers repeat lamentations over Josiah to the present day, and it became like a law in Israel.”

Therefore, in our exposition we shall first weave together the historical account; then, at suitable points, we shall insert the allegory relating either to Josiah, whose name means “the salvation of the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord,” or to the Jews, “confident of this” (sic) [Col. 1184B].

It is therefore much more appropriate for us now to lament than it was then for the prophet of God, although it is not many cities or an entire nation that is lamented, but the soul of a Christian human being, nobler than many nations and more precious than many powers. For if one who does the will of God is better than a multitude of the wicked, then the soul that was once faithful and in which God dwells was better than the multitudes of the Jews, who, ungrateful for God’s benefits, always acted in opposition to him.

Therefore their lawgiver, reproaching their faithlessness, speaks to them in these words: “For I know your contentiousness and your exceedingly stiff neck; you have always acted contentiously against the Lord” (Deut. 31). And Stephen says: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts 7).

If anyone has contemplated the temple of a human being who belongs to God, when it shone with the splendor of chastity, he will surely consider that earlier lamentation a small and very inferior one, in which the pollution of the holy of holies by barbarian hands and the destruction of the sacred buildings by hostile fire are bewailed. There the defiled cherubim, the ark, the mercy seat, the two stone tablets, and the golden urn are mourned.

The lamentation that we mourn is proved to be so much harsher and more bitter than that one as all these things were more truly and evidently present in the faithful soul than they were within the walls of that temple. This was much holier, because the temple was in it. It did not shine with the metal of gold and silver but with the virtues of the soul and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. For it contained within itself the ark and the two cherubim—that is, the faith of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit established within it.

But now none of these things appears. All have been taken away; the house of God has been stripped of all its ornaments and deprived of all the gifts that the Divinity had bestowed, and it remains deformed and ugly. Every defense and every guard has perished from it. Its door is no longer closed, nor is its entrance kept secure; rather, it lies open to all evil spirits hastening to corrupt the soul. No shameful thought, no foul desire is driven away from it. If the spirit of fornication comes, it enters; if the spirit of vainglory, if avarice, or if spirits more wicked and impure than these come, no one forbids or drives them away. No guard remains, no doorkeeper.

For formerly, just as access to the secrets of heaven was denied to such evils, so no such thought could penetrate a most pure mind. But now let us see how the text itself begins.

# CHAPTER ONE

Aleph. “How does the city sit solitary, that was full of people? She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations. The princess of provinces has become subject to tribute.”

The prophet laments the ruin of the perverse people and the overthrow of the faithless city, which always thought contrary to its Lord and opposed his commandments. Ungrateful for God’s benefits, it persecuted his prophets and finally slaughtered the heir himself. Therefore, handed over to the hands of enemies, it was devastated, so that the city that had previously ruled over various peoples and provinces was afterward oppressed by harsh servitude.

This was partially fulfilled before the Lord’s coming under the Chaldean captivity. But after the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven it was fulfilled more completely, when, under the Roman rulers Vespasian and Titus, the city was burned in vengeance for the Lord’s blood, and the entire nation was at once partly killed and partly led into captivity, according to what is written in Daniel’s vision, where the angel speaks to the prophet as follows:

“After sixty-two weeks [four weeks], Christ will be killed, and there will be no people belonging to him who will deny him; and the people with the coming leader will destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed (Dan. 9).”

And shortly afterward: “Until the consummation,” he says, “and the end, desolation will endure.”

Mystically, however, the faithful soul of a human being is mourned: once it was full of the multitude of virtues and ruled over diverse emotions, dominating the desires of the flesh; afterward, kindled by the flame of lust from evil spirits, deprived of the angels’ assistance and lacking divine fellowship, it serves as many scepters as it has vices.

Beth. “Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears were on her cheeks; there was no one among all her lovers to comfort her. All her enemies despised her and became her enemies.”

When the tribulation of captivity came on account of idolatry and the enormity of their crimes, the Jewish people grieved too late. They had often been warned by the testimony of the prophets that it would have been better for them to avoid the guilt of transgression than to mourn punitively after committing it.

The false divinities that various peoples worshiped in images had therefore been the cause of their scandal and deception. Having abandoned the true God, they had served false gods through the worship of idols, and these gods profited them nothing at the time of vengeance; rather, they harmed them greatly, so that they were made objects of mockery and confusion among their enemies.

For this reason it is also said through Ezekiel to sinful Judea: “Behold, I will stir up all your lovers against you, of whom your soul has been satisfied, and I will gather them against you from every side. They will deal with you in hatred, take away all your labors, and leave you naked and full of disgrace” (Ezek. 23).

According to the allegory, the soul deceived by the devil’s suggestion will come into the night of future destruction, where it will utter perpetual groaning without any consolation. The evil spirits that previously dragged it in various directions through the enticements of pleasures will not cease to punish it with everlasting torments once it has been placed in the outer darkness.

Therefore, to avoid this greatest grief, it is necessary to grieve profitably in the present, so that God’s immense goodness may grant it everlasting consolation in exchange for present tears: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

This passage can also be applied generally to the Church, which in the night of the present life endures the tribulation of persecutions and groans without worldly consolation, according to what the Truth himself says to the disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful” (John 16).

In the present life the Church does not seek consolation but searches for future joys. For as long as it is in the body, it knows that it is journeying away from its homeland and kingdom. Nevertheless, it does not doubt that through labors and struggles it will attain the crown, when sorrow will be turned into joy and, once the contest of this life is ended, it will receive the prize of eternal life, concerning which it is said in the psalm: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. 125).

For the cheeks are the holy preachers, of whom it is now said: “Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears were on her cheeks.” For in the Church’s adversity those who know how to crush the life of carnal people by preaching weep more deeply. Through them the holy Church crushes the wickedness of sinners and, as though swallowing them, converts them into its own members. Hence it is said also to the first preacher, as to the cheeks of the Church: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

Ghimel. “Judah has migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude. She dwelt among the nations and found no rest; all her persecutors seized her amid her anguish.”

The Jewish people migrated into dispersion among the nations because of the affliction of captivity. The people that had previously ruled over many nations under the leadership of a kingdom afterward labored in servitude among various peoples, because the vengeance deserved by their crimes overtook them.

Spiritual Judah migrated from its land because, by sinning, it provoked the Lord and aroused him to vengeance through its iniquities. Concerning this he spoke through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “You have made me serve because of your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities” (Isa. 43). Thus, assigned among the nations and polluted by their filth, it lost its freedom and fell into the hands of its enemies, who led it through various errors and allowed it neither to rest nor to draw breath even briefly.

Daleth. “The roads of Zion mourn because there is no one who comes to the solemn assembly. All her gates are destroyed; her priests groan, her virgins are squalid, and she herself is oppressed with bitterness.”

He says that the roads of Zion mourn—that is, that they are made mournful—because there are none who come to the solemn assembly to celebrate festive joys or perform the priests’ duties in the temple, since, after the temple was burned, the city walls were utterly demolished and the gates destroyed. Hence all her beauty grows squalid, and she herself, oppressed by bitterness, groans deeply over her children.

Mystically, the roads of Zion mourn when, after the fall of sin, the outward actions of a soul that once stood upon the citadel of the mind contemplating God appear shameful and mournful. Its affections no longer come, as formerly, to celebrate inward joys; rather, when its five bodily senses—signified here by the name of gates—have been destroyed through sloth, access lies open to various offenses. Ecclesiastical service also becomes contemptible, and the virtue of continence grows weak. Deprived of the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, the whole soul is therefore immersed in the bitterness of vices.

He. “Her enemies have become the head; her foes have grown rich, because the Lord has spoken against her on account of the multitude of her iniquities. Her little ones have been led captive before the face of the oppressor.”

The enemies of Jerusalem became her masters when her foes gained the upper hand, stripped the entire nation of divine things, subjected it to the bonds of captivity, and compelled it to go into a foreign land together with its women and children, while the Lord, against whom they had sinned, repaid them with a just judgment.

The enemies of deceived souls come to be at their head when evil spirits rejoice in their domination. Stripping the soul of its virtues, they drag its little thoughts here and there through harmful desires and do not permit it to possess any peace of mind.

(Greg.) Here we must consider what we stated above: the ancient enemy attacks our good deeds in three ways, so that what is done rightly before human beings may be corrupted in the sight of the inward Judge.

Sometimes he pollutes the intention in a good work, so that everything that follows in the action does not emerge pure and clean, because he disturbs it from its beginning. Sometimes he cannot corrupt the intention of the good work, but places an obstacle in the action itself, as though on the road, so that when someone ventures forth with a more secure purpose of mind, he is secretly killed by a vice inserted as though from ambush. Sometimes he corrupts neither the intention nor the course of the work, but entangles the good work at the end of the action. The farther he pretends to have withdrawn either from the house of the heart or from the road of the work, the more craftily he seeks the end of the good action to deceive; and the more he makes the unwary person believe that he is withdrawing, the more suddenly, and sometimes more harshly and incurably, he strikes him with a wound.

He pollutes the intention in a good work because, when he sees that human hearts are easy to deceive, he applies the breeze of passing favor to their desires, so that in doing what is right they incline toward seeking low things through a twisted intention. Hence, rightly, under the figure of Judea, the prophet says here concerning every soul caught in the snare of a wretched intention: “Her enemies have become the head.”

It is as though he were saying openly: When a good work is undertaken with a bad intention, the opposing spirits rule it from the very beginning of its thought. They possess it all the more completely because they hold dominion over it from its beginning.

When they cannot corrupt the intention, they conceal snares placed along the road, so that, in what is being done well, the heart may exalt itself and be diverted sideways into vice, and so that what someone began with one purpose may proceed in the action in a very different manner from that with which it began.

Often human praise meets a good work and changes the mind of the person acting. Although praise had not been sought, it nevertheless pleases when offered. When the mind of the person doing good is relaxed by this pleasure, it is scattered away from all the strength of its innermost intention.

Often anger attaches itself sideways to our justice once begun. When it disturbs the mind excessively in the zeal for rectitude, it wounds all the health of inward peace. Often sadness follows the gravity of the heart as though attached from the side, and strikes every work that the good mind begins with a veil of sorrow. Sometimes it is driven away all the more slowly because it serves the burdened mind as though it had arrived late.

Often immoderate joy attaches itself to a good work. When it demands that the mind rejoice more than is fitting, it drives all the weight of seriousness away from the good action. Because the Psalmist had seen that snares lay along the road for those who begin well, he rightly said, filled with the prophetic Spirit: “On the road along which I walked they hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141).

Vau. “All her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion; her princes have become like rams that find no pasture, and they have gone away without strength before the face of the pursuer.”

When Jerusalem was besieged by an external enemy, it lost inwardly all the beauty of its joy, especially as it suffered from famine and pestilence and was sustained by no one’s aid. Its princes and rulers, their strength dissolved and their hearts terrified, were thinking not of defending the citizens but of an idle flight.

Mystically, the daughter of Zion abandoned her beauty when, through negligence in her thoughts, the soul loses the adornment of virtues. Her princes—that is, rational reflections, with which she ought to have resisted her pursuing enemies—did not come to her aid. Her strength having failed, she was driven before the pursuing enemy into the pit of deception.

This sentence also condemns negligent rulers of the Church of God, through whose carelessness all the beauty of the Christian people perishes. They do not strive in meditation on divine law, in the worship of piety, or in the practice of sacred virtues; rather, at the suggestion of the compelling enemy, they are led away through various crimes into the luxury of pleasures. The evil of this danger especially concerns those who, placed in a position of rule, have chosen to follow secular desires rather than the footsteps of God’s commandments. Therefore they do not deserve to receive the glory of the heavenly kingdom with the holy teachers; instead, they are compelled to endure the punishment of Gehenna with the devil and his angels. Concerning this it follows:

### Zain

“And Jerusalem remembered the days of her affliction and of all her desirable things, which she had possessed from ancient days, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy and there was no helper. Her enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths.”

For not only did that earthly Jerusalem grieve that she had lost her joy and abundance of delights while situated among her enemies, but this mystical Jerusalem too is tormented with the greatest sorrow, when, already established in punishments, she too late regrets that she had then been negligent, when by good works and upright conduct she could have helped herself. [Col. 1189B] For she not only does not rejoice with the holy angels in eternal life, but, tortured with demons in hell, she fruitlessly laments her past sins, according to that passage which Scripture testifies that the wicked will utter in hell:

“Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us. We grew weary on the way of iniquity and destruction, and we walked difficult paths; but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did pride profit us, or what benefit did the abundance of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow of death, but in our wickedness we were consumed” (Wis. V).

Then the evil spirits themselves mock the idleness that the negligent uselessly pursued throughout the span of the present life. [Col. 1189C] Hence also it is now said through the prophet: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths.”

By command of the Law, one ceases from external work on the sabbath. The enemies see and mock the sabbaths when evil spirits draw the very periods of leisure toward unlawful thoughts. Every soul, in proportion as it is believed to be withdrawn from external actions in order to serve God, serves their tyranny all the more by thinking unlawful thoughts.

Holy men, however, because they are lulled to rest from the works of the world not in body but in virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could have remained awake. For in overcoming the activities of this age, they fight daily against themselves in a vigorous struggle, lest the mind grow sluggish through negligence; lest, once idleness has been subdued, it grow cold toward impure desires; lest it serve good desires beyond measure; and lest, under the appearance of discernment, by sparing themselves they grow weak in perfection. [Col. 1189D] The soul acts in this way, completely withdrawing itself from the restless desire of this world, abandoning the tumult of earthly activities, and, intent upon virtues through its devotion to quiet, keeping watch while it sleeps. For it is not led to contemplate inward things unless it diligently withdraws from those matters that entangle it outwardly.

Hence Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI). Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

### Heth

“Jerusalem sinned grievously; therefore she has become unstable. All who glorified her have despised her, because they saw her disgrace; and she herself groaned and turned backward.”

At the beginning of this statement he expressed the cause of the punishment: because of the magnitude of her crimes, Jerusalem deserved the destruction of exile. Those very people who had exalted her with praise while she was sinning later mocked her when she had been overwhelmed by captivity; they did not sympathize with her, nor offer any consolation to her groaning.

Hence the Lord says through Isaiah to the Jewish people: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you and confusing—or disturbing—the way of your steps” (Isa. III). The scribes and Pharisees—whom the same prophet had previously called exactors, not teachers, and earlier still mockers—because of the gifts that “blind the eyes even of the wise” (Deut. XVI), [Col. 1190A] not only failed to rebuke sinners among the people, but exalted them with praises for the sake of wealth and profit. Conversely, they called such people blessed, pillars of the house of God, and by other expressions of the sort that flatterers are accustomed to use. [Col. 1190B]

Yet such supporters offered no consolation to those afflicted on the day of tribulation. Rather, they exposed the shame of their crimes and revealed the disgrace of their hearts. Therefore the ecclesiastical teacher is one who provokes tears, not laughter; who rebukes sinners; who says that no one is blessed and no one is happy; and who does not distort the judgment of his Judge, as Holy Scripture says: “Do not call anyone blessed before death” (Ecclus. XI).

We also read elsewhere: “He who blesses his friend in the morning with a loud voice is no different from one who curses him” (Prov. XXVII). [Col. 1190C] Therefore, despising human judgments, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their slanders; but let us enter the straight way and the paths trodden by the holy prophets.

Let us hear this prophet saying elsewhere: “Stand upon the ways, and see, and ask about the everlasting paths of the Lord, which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. VI). [Col. 1190D]

### Theth

“Her uncleanness is upon her feet, and she did not remember her end. She has been cast down violently, having no comforter.”

He bears uncleanness upon his feet who pollutes the course of his conduct with evil works. He does not remember his end, nor the time of God’s just judgment. Therefore he has been cast down violently and handed over to the hands of his enemies, having no comforter, because at the appropriate time he did not wish to honor his Creator with the worship of piety.

The enemy alone will rule over her, because the true God, her friend, has abandoned her. Therefore, crushed by the greatest grief, she cries miserably to God: “See, Lord, my affliction, because the enemy has raised himself up.”

With no one resisting him, the wicked enemy rejoices in victory and, proud of his power against the Lord, raises himself up, attributing this to his own strength and not to God’s just judgment. For, according to the Psalmist: “He has no God before his eyes. His ways are polluted at all times; your judgments are removed from his sight” (Ps. IX).

### Iod

“The enemy stretched out his hand toward all her desirable things, for he saw nations entering her sanctuary, concerning which you had commanded that they should not enter your Church.” [Col. 1191A]

Because of the sins of the people, a hostile army devastated the temple of the Lord and cast down all its adornment, although it should neither have entered nor touched anything within it. For the Lord rejected his tabernacle, in which he had dwelt among human beings; he delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty into the hand of the enemy; he shut up his people by the sword and despised his inheritance.

If we too do not carefully guard the barriers of our hearts, and the ancient enemy finds an open entrance through any one of our senses, he enters the shrine of our soul through evil suggestions and unlawful desires, where the Holy Trinity has been accustomed to dwell through true faith. He strips it of the beauty of wisdom and the adornment of virtues, and we become wretched and entirely deserving of shame. [Col. 1191B]

### Caph

“All her people groan, seeking bread. They gave their most precious things for food, to revive the soul. See, Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.”

How many evils the Jewish people suffered through famine, pestilence, and slaughter is explained by the divine books, and Josephus’s history does not remain silent about it.

Spiritually, human delight is received through bread. Hence, while the prophet was lamenting the corrupt ways of the synagogue, he said: “All her people groan, seeking bread.” The perverse multitude of human beings is afflicted because it is not satisfied according to its desire with the delight of the present life. It gives all its precious things for food because it inclines the virtues of the mind toward the appetite for transitory pleasure, and it strives to revive the soul because it attempts to satisfy its perverse desires. [Col. 1191C]

Hence the voice of that chosen multitude appropriately adds immediately: “See, Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.” God’s people become vile when, as the number of the wicked among them increases, they pursue not what is lofty and heavenly but what is rejected and earthly. [Col. 1191D]

### Lamed

“O all you who pass along the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow. For he has harvested me, as the Lord spoke, on the day of his anger and fury.”

It is characteristic of those who grieve to consider their own suffering greater than that of others, because they do not know the sufferings of others. The more intensely they feel their own pain, the less willing they are to admit that another’s pain can equal it.

He says that the Lord harvested them on the day of his fury because, with the rule of justice prescribing it, he had already determined that they should reap the fruit of their labor.

But it must be considered why he invites only those who pass along the way to look upon his sorrow. Those who do not pass through the present life as through a road, but move toward it as toward their homeland, do not know how to contemplate the grief of the elect. He therefore seeks those who will consider his sorrow—those who have not fixed their soul in this world.

Hence Solomon says: “Open your mouth for the mute and for the causes of all the children who pass by” (Prov. XXXI). [Col. 1191D] The mute are those who do not resist the words of preachers by speaking against them. They are also called passers-by because they disdain to fix the intention of their mind in love of the present life.

### Mem

[Col. 1192A]

“He sent fire from on high into my bones and instructed me. He spread a net for my feet and turned me backward. He made me desolate, exhausted with sorrow all day long.”

When he says that God sent fire from heaven into his bones, he indicates a heavenly punishment by which he chastised them through inward torments, so that they might recognize to whom they ought in every way to be subject. He spread a net for their feet because he did not permit them to follow their pleasure to the end of life. He turned them backward so that they would experience sorrow instead of luxury and, deprived of the consolation of friends, would mourn throughout their lives among their enemies the evil they had done.

Mystically, when a soul burdened by sins is rebuked by the Lord for its iniquities, if, returning inwardly, it is pierced by salutary sorrow, it turns all its former luxury into tears by abstaining from sins. [Col. 1192B] It mourns while constraining itself all the more forcefully, in proportion as it remembers that it wandered for a longer time and more loosely through various desires.

### Nun

“The yoke of my iniquities has awakened in his hand; they have been bound together and placed upon my neck. My strength has been weakened; the Lord has handed me over to a hand from which I shall not be able to rise.”

He says that the yoke of his iniquities awakened in the hand of the Lord because the time of punishment, long deferred, finally came upon him. To rest securely and with impunity in the body of wickedness is like sleeping; to sustain the penalties of vengeance by suffering for the crime committed is like waking. Hence he asserts that his iniquities have been bound together and placed upon his neck, and that the vigor of his virtue has failed: he feels that the mass of sins which he accumulated through various transgressions over a long period weighs him down and makes him weak. [Col. 1192C]

Thus it is written: “Everyone is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V), because the strict Judge in no way permits a crime that is not corrected through repentance to remain unpunished. Concerning this it is also written in Job: “He leaves no sin unpunished.”

As for what follows—“The Lord has handed me over to a hand from which I shall not be able to rise”—this either indicates the powerful captivity of the Chaldeans or the excessively oppressive captivity of the Romans over the Jews.

Spiritually, it indicates that the final punishment is an infinite calamity for all the wicked and sinners, and that it never ceases from its torment. For in the outer darkness the worm of the wicked does not die, and the fire is not extinguished; [Col. 1192D] once someone enters there, he is no longer permitted to leave.

Truth himself shows this in the Gospel, saying: “Be reconciled quickly with your adversary, while you are on the way with him, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Truly I say to you, you will not come out from there until you repay the last quadrans” (Matt. V).

Just as the statement “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies beneath his feet” (I Cor. XV) is understood to mean that he will reign forever, since his enemies will forever be beneath his feet, so here too “You will not come out from there until you repay the last quadrans” can be understood to mean that he will never come out, because he is always repaying the last quadrans while paying the eternal penalties of earthly sins. [Col. 1193A]

### Samech

“The Lord has taken away all my mighty men from my midst; he summoned a time against me to crush my chosen ones.”

The Lord took away the mighty men of the Jewish people during their time of captivity, when, because of their wickedness and the multitude of their crimes, he did not allow them to retain among themselves the prophets and priests by whose help and teaching they had been chiefly sustained. The prophet Daniel bears witness to this in his prayer, saying:

“Lord, at this time there is neither prince nor prophet nor leader, neither burnt offering nor sacrifice nor incense nor place of firstfruits before you, so that we may find mercy” (Dan. III).

So too, after the enemy has led a soul deceived by the devil’s fraud inwardly captive from the state of right faith and upright, good conduct into the confusion of error, he removes from the sight of its heart, through forgetfulness, the teaching and examples of holy preachers. [Col. 1193B] He does this so that, stripped of virtues, he may possess it more easily in a foreign land, lest through recollection of sound doctrine and improvement of life it return to its former state.

### Ain

“The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep.”

We read in the prophet Isaiah that the Lord spoke concerning the winepress:

“I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me. I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath. Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my clothing. For the day of vengeance was in my heart; the year of my recompense has come” (Isa. LXIII).

We must therefore speak of the winepress. According to the usage of Holy Scripture, it sometimes signifies vengeance and the punishments of sinners, and sometimes the gathering of new fruits. It signifies punishments and torments when Jeremiah, lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem in the present Lamentation, says: “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep.”

In a good sense, Psalms VIII and LXXXIII are inscribed “For the winepresses.” In this winepress, punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good are trodden by the Savior. He alone trod it and had no helper. For no angel, archangel, throne, dominion, or any heavenly power assumed a human body, suffered for us, and trampled and crushed the hostile powers. [Col. 1193D] Only he did so who says in the Psalm: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. XI). So great was this reality that even the most confident apostle, Peter, firmest in faith, terrified by fear, fled and indeed denied the Lord three times (Matt. XXVI).

The Lord therefore trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah when he prepared the oppression of captivity for the unfruitful and long-sterile vine of the Jews, to whom it is said through Isaiah: “I waited for it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isa. V).

Mystically, the Lord treads the winepress for a soul unfruitful in virtues and empty of good works, producing no fruit of faith, when he makes it pay the penalties of a punishment proportionate to its barrenness and idleness. [Col. 1194A] Hence it follows:

“And my eye pours out water, because the comforter who restores my soul has been taken far from me. My children have become lost, because the enemy has prevailed.”

The great weeping of the sorrowing soul is described because, after the empty joy of this world, all consolation of the present life is taken away from it, the fruit of evil works is scattered, and the enemy alone rules amid its various torments.

### Phe

“Zion stretched out her hands, and there is no one to comfort her. The Lord commanded against Jacob; his enemies surround him. Jerusalem has become among them like a woman polluted by menstruation.”

Surrounded by the captivity of the Chaldeans, Zion sought someone to comfort her and found no one, because, as her sins demanded, she did not deserve to have the Lord as her true comforter. [Col. 1194B] He handed her over to her enemies for punishment because she refused to remain subject to him in obedience.

So too the soul of a believing person, which was once God’s mirror and the overthrower of vices, when for its evil merits it is handed over to spiritual wickedness, seeks a comforter outwardly in vain, having lost inward spiritual consolation.

“She has become,” he says, “among them like a woman polluted by menstruation.” Jerusalem is called polluted with menstrual filth because she refused to avoid bloody works and carnal desires in her wicked conduct.

Menstrual filth occurs when, each month, women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of impure blood. At that time, if a man has intercourse with a woman, the offspring conceived are said to contract a defect of seed, so that lepers and elephantiasis sufferers are born from such conception, and corrupted matter degenerates into foul bodily deformity or abnormality of the limbs in either sex. [Col. 1194C]

Therefore the Law of the Lord commands men (Lev. XV), not only concerning other women but also concerning their own wives, to whom they seem to be joined lawfully—since Scripture says, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth”—to know with discernment when intercourse is appropriate and when they should abstain from their wives. The Apostle and Ecclesiastes likewise proclaim: “A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces” (I Cor. VII; Eccles. III).

Let the wife therefore beware lest, overcome by the desire for intercourse, she entice her husband; [Col. 1194D] and let the husband beware lest he use force against his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at all times. Hence Paul says: “Let each one of you know how to possess his vessel in holiness and chastity” (I Thess. IV).

A saying in the brief maxims of Sextus the Pythagorean is aptly expressed: “He is an adulterer who is too ardent a lover of his own wife.” A certain person, transferring this book into Latin, sought to dignify it with the name of the martyr Sextus, without considering that throughout the entire volume—which he had foolishly divided into two parts—the name of Christ and of the apostles is wholly absent.

It is not surprising that he transformed a Gentile philosopher into a martyr and bishop of the city of Rome, since he also labeled the first book of Eusebius of Caesarea, written on behalf of Origen, with the name of the martyr Pamphilus, so that through such a laudatory sponsor he might more easily reconcile the utterly impious books *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) to Roman ears. [Col. 1195A]

### Sade
