“The Lord is just, because I provoked his mouth to anger. Hear, I beg you, all peoples, and see my sorrow. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.”

The mournful complaint is brought to recognition of the just Judge’s sentence. After this lamenting woman had recounted her calamity, she rightly acknowledged that she was suffering it, because a just judge can issue no sentence other than a just one.

“The Lord is just,” she says, “because I provoked his mouth to anger”—that is, by my evil merits I compelled the just Judge, naturally merciful, to issue a harsh sentence against me. Human limbs, like human emotions, are attributed tropologically to God, not literally, because boundless light and immeasurable majesty cannot be enclosed by bodily features. [Col. 1195B]

“Hear,” she says, “all peoples, and see my sorrow, because my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.” She invites very many people to see her sorrow because she considers her calamity exceedingly great, so that through the compassion of others she may in some way lighten her anxiety by bringing in comforters and supporters of her distress.

Such is the custom of human feeling: a person seeks others to share his sorrow or joy, so that through their consolation he may more easily bear the burden of sadness or gladness that has come upon him (Luke XV). Hence in the Gospel the man who searched for the lost sheep, and the woman who found the lost drachma, call together their friends and neighbors so that they may stand as witnesses and share in their joy. [Col. 1195C]

By lamenting that the young men and virgins had gone into captivity, she shows that she grieves most deeply because she saw the hope of her condition suddenly collapse. When she saw her offspring suddenly perish, she lost hope of future generations.

### Coph

“I called my friends, and they deceived me. My priests and my elders perished in the city, because they sought food for themselves in order to revive their souls.”

It must be asked how those who set a trap for their lovers can be called friends. For, as Scripture testifies, a true and faithful friend is a strong protection, a medicine of life and immortality. It is therefore clear that by antiphrasis someone is unjustly called a friend who is shown to be a deceiver. [Col. 1195D]

There are people who are called friends but prove rather to be enemies, because they go forth toward hostility, hatred, and strife, and expose insults. They become table companions and partners at the meal, but they do not remain on the day of necessity.

Such are those who even today live carnally, flatter those who follow their example, and are lovers of pleasures rather than of God. By consenting to this, they drag others with them into the abyss of sin, so that they make them participants in the eternal torment of their crime.

How great the power of true friendship is can be understood especially from this: from the infinite fellowship of the human race, which nature itself has brought together, friendship has been so contracted and narrowed that every affection is joined either between two people or among a few. [Col. 1196A]

For, as someone has said, friendship is nothing other than agreement concerning all divine and human matters, with goodwill and affection. Hence it is rightly written: “There is no comparison with a faithful friend, and no weighing of gold or silver is worthy against the goodness of his faith” (Exod. VI).

When he says that the priests and elders perished in the city, he shows that they died from hunger and thirst because of the scarcity of provisions, as frequently happened during the siege of Jerusalem by its enemies, according to the historical accounts.

Mystically, the soul that relies upon pleasures and desires of the flesh loses the dignity of priesthood and the maturity of counsel through lack of wisdom and poverty of virtues: “For the world passes away, and its desire” (I John II). Egypt will help in vain, and a broken reed-staff lacerates those who lean upon it and pierces their hand; [Col. 1196B] it can never grant complete prosperity to its lovers.

### Res

“See, Lord, for I am afflicted; my belly is troubled. My heart within me has been overturned, because I am full of bitterness. Outside, the sword kills, and inside there is a death like it.”

What does it mean that the prophet, speaking in the person of the people, invites the Lord to see his tribulation, unless it is that, recognizing his anxiety as excessive and immeasurable, he desires the help and mercy of the Lord alone to come to his aid?

Since he testifies that his belly is troubled and his heart overturned within him, he declares that he has not been touched by bitterness in part but filled with it, and that he is exhausted by a similar calamity both within and without. [Col. 1196C]

The apostle Paul wrote something similar to the Corinthians: “For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation that occurred in Asia: we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even became weary of living” (II Cor. VII). And again: “When we came to Macedonia,” he says, “our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every tribulation: conflicts outside, fears within” (ibid.).

It should be known that in sacred speech the word “belly” or “womb” usually signifies the mind. Hence Solomon says: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a human being, searching out all the hidden things of the belly” (Prov. XX). [Col. 1196D]

The light of grace that comes from above grants the human being breath for life. This light is said to search out all hidden things because it penetrates the secrets of the mind, bringing before the soul’s eyes, to be lamented, those things that had been hidden from it.

Hence Jeremiah himself says earlier: “My belly, my belly, I mourn” (Jer. IV). To show what he meant by his belly, he added: “The senses of my heart are troubled” (ibid.).

The womb therefore rightly signifies the mind, because just as offspring is conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind; and just as food is contained in the belly, so thoughts are contained in the mind.

A faithful soul wearied by various temptations rightly laments that it has been battered both within and without by a similar death, because it knows that it is torn outwardly by persecutions and inwardly by anxieties. Often we are worn down outwardly by scourges and inwardly wearied by carnal suggestion. [Col. 1197A]

Hence Jeremiah now laments in the present Lamentation, saying: “Outside, the sword kills, and inside there is a death like it.” The sword kills outside when vengeance strikes us outwardly and destroys us; but inside there is a similar death because, although it endures scourges, the conscience is not clean within from the filth of temptations.

Hence David says: “Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord afflict them” (Ps. I). For because a person is swept along in his heart by the breeze of temptation, he is raised like dust before the face of the wind. While divine strictness strikes amid these things, what else afflicts them but the angel of the Lord?

But these things occur differently in the reprobate and in the elect. The hearts of the former are tempted so that they consent; the latter indeed receive temptations, but resist them. [Col. 1197B] The heart of the former is captured with delight. If what is wickedly suggested displeases it for a time, it later becomes pleasing through deliberation. The latter, however, receive the arrows of temptations in such a way that they are always wearied by resisting. If at any time a tempted mind is carried as far as affection, it nevertheless quickly blushes at the stealthy pleasure and reproves it with strong judgment, whatever carnal thing it detects arising within itself.

### Sin

“They heard that I groan, and there is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my evil, Lord; they rejoiced because you did it. You have brought the day of consolation, and they will become like me.”

For an anxious soul afflicted by labors, the increase of its pain seems to be that the one in whom it had placed hope of consolation delays bringing the help of comfort. It also causes it the greatest sorrow that its enemies mock it, as though, frustrated in its hope, it had suffered this reproach from its Lord.

Such is the Psalmist’s statement: “Those who guarded my soul,” he says, “took counsel together, saying: God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him” (Ps. LXX).

In the Gospel the Jews also mocked the Lord hanging upon the cross, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him” (Matt. XXVII).

But such speech is manifest blasphemy. It does not injure the one in danger; it kills the blasphemer. God’s judgment, which is always just and disposes all things justly, must not be reproved by anyone; rather, it must be venerated and feared. For whatever the Lord wills, he does in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths. The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. He will not abandon all who hope in him; rather, he will hear their prayers and save them. [Col. 1197D]

It must be noted, however, that there are different kinds of striking. One kind is the striking by which a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve; another is that by which a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected; another is that by which someone is sometimes struck not so that he may correct past sins but so that he may not commit future ones; another is that by which neither past guilt is corrected nor future guilt prevented, but when unexpected salvation follows the striking, the power of the one who saves may be known and loved more ardently. When an innocent person is worn down by the scourge, the highest merit is heaped upon him through patience. [Col. 1198A]

This becomes clearer through examples. Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as is said to doomed Judea: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. XXX). And again: “Why do you cry to me over your destruction? Your pain is incurable.”

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “See, you have been made well; now do not sin” (John V). The words of the Savior indicate that the preceding sins had demanded the force of suffering.

Sometimes someone is struck not to cleanse a past fault but to prevent a future one. Paul clearly says this about himself: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me,” and so forth (I Cor. XII). [Col. 1198B] He does not say, “It exalts me,” but “lest it should exalt me,” plainly indicating that through that striking he was restrained so that the fault might not occur, rather than cleansed from a fault that had occurred.

Sometimes someone is struck neither for a past nor for a future iniquity, but so that the power of divine virtue alone may be displayed through the removal of the affliction. Thus, when the Lord was asked in the Gospel concerning the man born blind, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he should be born blind?” the Lord answered: “Neither did this man sin nor his parents, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John IX).

What is accomplished in this manifestation except that, through the scourge, the power of merits may be increased and great strength may be generated from patience? [Col. 1198C]

But since the Lord justly repays each person according to his works, we must consider what follows: “You have brought,” he says, “the day of consolation, and they will become like me.”

The consolation that the Lord grants to those unjustly oppressed, and the punishment that is deservedly inflicted upon their oppressors, proceed from God’s just judgment, so that each person may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

The punishment of the reprobate consists in being tormented by the happiness of others. Divine mercy therefore brings, after the chastisement of the scourge inflicted upon his servants, the paternal consolation of compassionate kindness, so that after long labor they may have the power to breathe again. Conversely, after the empty joy of the world, he will return to their torturers the enduring sorrow of just condemnation, so that they may receive in themselves what they unjustly did to their neighbors. [Col. 1198D]

Thus the patience of the saints is crowned and the injustice of the wicked is punished. The apostle Paul also shows this in his Epistle, saying:

“It is just with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Thess. I).

Concerning this it is further said:

### Thau

“Let all their evil come before you, and harvest them as you have harvested me because of all my iniquities. For my groans are many, and my heart is mourning.” [Col. 1199A]

This was the prayer of the multitude of the faithful: that the wound of their persecutors should be remembered in the sight of God, so that by a punishment proportionate to their deeds the just judgment of God might humble them through correction—those who in their pride had not feared to weary God’s confessors through manifold persecution.

To harvest is to reap the fruit of one’s works. The Lord harvests his enemies, who harvested his saints, when, in the future judgment, he makes them receive eternal vengeance in place of the temporal crushing by which they were permitted to oppress the saints for the purpose of testing them.

But it must be made clear that when holy men pray against their enemies in the manner of supplication, they do not do so from a desire for malice. Rather, by the spirit of prophecy they proclaim what they know beforehand will happen to them. [Col. 1199B] Or they pray against spiritual wickedness, which they know to be incorrigible, so that it may receive a just sentence from the Lord.

Hence the prophet prays in the Psalm against those who harm him, saying: “Judge, Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me” (Ps. XLIII).

The weakness assumed for our sake cries out that the guilty should be condemned—that is, the devil together with his ministers—for it knew that this would come to pass. For the wicked being judged means being condemned, since they cannot be acquitted in the trial, having always been shown to be entangled in evil deeds.

But, as has been said, this applies to the devil and his followers, through whom the iniquity of the Jewish will came about. For since the Lord himself commands, “Pray for your enemies,” this sentence cannot apply to human beings. [Col. 1199C]

He therefore asks that those be condemned whom, by the power of his foreknowledge, he knows are beyond the remedies of repentance. Later, when he comes to human beings, he desires that they be converted, not perish, as in the passage: “Let those who seek my soul be confounded and revere [you]; let those who think evil against me be turned backward and blush” (Ps. XXXIX).

Here, when he comes to corrigible human beings, not a curse is poured out but correction is requested. To be confounded is to blush at one’s deeds and to be changed to a better judgment. Those who are joined to punishment are also said to be confounded. But to show more clearly that he meant conversion, he added “let them revere [you]”—that is, once amended, let them worship the one whom they had thought ought to be persecuted.

## Chapter II

[Col. 1199D]

### Aleph

“Why has the Lord in his fury covered the daughter of Zion with darkness? He has cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel, and on the day of his fury he has not remembered his footstool.”

We have come to the second alphabetic section. Just as in the first, the prophet lamented in astonishment the unforeseen ruin of the city of Jerusalem and the unexpected downfall of the Jewish people, so now he asks in amazement: How has the most beautiful dwelling of Zion, and the illustrious race of the Israelites—which, supported by angelic ministry, was led across the Red Sea from the land of Egypt under the Lord’s own guidance, and which in the desert was educated for a very long time through Moses and Aaron by many miracles and divine consolations—now been cast down and trampled, as though from heaven to earth, from the greatest happiness into the utmost misery on the day of the Lord’s fury and the vengeance inflicted upon it? Because of the condition of divine worship, which at that time was especially prominent among that people, it was rightly called the Lord’s footstool.

In the mystical sense, however, the sinful soul, which once possessed the light of knowledge and the mirror of divine contemplation, when the feet of the Lord—that is, the traces of his commandments—rested in the secret place of its heart, has now, because of the blindness of its heart and the wickedness of its sinful conduct, fallen from the summit of the virtues into the foulness of earthly desires. By God’s just judgment it is despised and abandoned, and is trampled by its enemies. Therefore the prophet rightly mourns its ruin, because it has fallen from the highest honor into the greatest misery, so that it now lies exposed to everyone’s contempt and derision.

### Beth

“The Lord has cast down and has not spared all the beauties of Jacob; in his fury he has destroyed the fortifications of the daughter of Judah, and has thrown them to the ground; he has polluted the kingdom and its rulers.”

Because of the sins of the Jews and their transgressions—for by transgressing they did not keep God’s testimonies, serving foreign gods and worshiping their idols and images in imitation of the nations around them—the angry Lord handed his own people over to the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.

The Lord cast down all the beauties of Jacob: the magnificence that Jacob possessed in the adornment of the most renowned Temple and in the celebrated worship by which they believed themselves nobler than the other nations. In his fury he destroyed the fortifications of the cities of Judah, throwing to the ground the structure of their walls and towers. He also polluted the honor of the kingdom and its rule, so that their nobles were led away captive by their enemies and reduced to slavery, and were made eunuchs and disfigured, as the Book of Isaiah testifies. There the prophet himself spoke to King Hezekiah, saying:

“Behold, days are coming, and everything that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the Lord. And from your sons who will go out from you, whom you will beget, they will take some, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon” (Isa. 39).

In the mystical sense, the Lord destroys the beauties of Jacob when he despises the beauty of the soul, made decrepit by the devil’s craft, and demolishes the fortification of teaching founded upon secular wisdom, in which the soul placed its greatest confidence. He pollutes the honor and rule of the kingdom that the soul possessed through the reception of baptism and the anointing with sacred chrism, so that it no longer deserves to hear, together with the other faithful, the words of the apostle Peter:

“You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2).

This occurs when the soul serves various vices and obeys the evil persuasions of the ancient enemy. Concerning him it is also said:

### Ghimel

“He broke in the anger of his fury every horn of Israel; he turned back his right hand from before the enemy, and he kindled against Jacob a flame of fire devouring all around.”

The Lord not only destroyed the whole kingdom of the Jews, removing from them the protection of his right hand and handing their land over to their enemies for devastation; he also hands over the mystical Jerusalem, when it has withdrawn from the Lord and served foreign gods and various crimes, deprived of the protection of heavenly aid, to the flame of lust and the fury of its enemies, so that they may set it ablaze.

The right hand of God the Father is his only-begotten Son, through whom he grants consolation and protection to his faithful. But when, having offended him, we do not deserve to be freed from our enemies, we seem to have been handed over to them, since we have no defender. Therefore the prophet, lamenting in the Psalms that the Jewish people had been abandoned by the Lord, says:

“Why do you turn away your hand, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever?” (Ps. 73).

As though the Lord had been offended and angered, he says this because he did not wish to regard the sinful people, so that they might appear still to remain in their wickedness. For those whom he looks upon in his marvelous dispensation after being reconciled, he corrects; those upon whom he looks favorably, he reforms.

When he says, “Your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever,” he signifies that, just as Moses’ right hand, brought forth from his bosom at the Lord’s command, appeared leprous and, when drawn back into his bosom, was healed, so the Jewish people, going out from the Lord Christ, became unclean, but, when converted to him, returned to their former health.

### Daleth

“The Lord has bent his bow like an enemy; he has strengthened his right hand like an adversary; he has killed everything beautiful to behold in the tent of the daughter of Zion, and has poured out his indignation like fire.”

The Lord bent his bow like an enemy and strengthened his right hand like an adversary when he made the Chaldeans, or the Romans, who were fighting against Jerusalem, victorious, giving them power to burn the Temple and destroy the city walls. He himself, being angry, did not spare those for whom he had once been reconciled to their fathers and had distributed the land of various nations for their possession, as the Psalmist testifies, saying to the Lord:

“Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted the peoples and drove them out. For they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their own arm did not save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, because you were pleased with them.”

The Hebrews should not suppose that they had been triumphant through their own strength. He declares that they were not victorious by their own sword and that they had not seized the land of the nations by their own power. We call the arm “strength,” because battle is waged by it; but this arm could not free them from their enemies, although divine power had specifically saved them.

Thus, while the conduct of the Hebrews is explained, useful instruction is provided for the human race. The right hand signifies prosperity, the arm strength, and illumination counsel—gifts that the Lord bestows upon those who fight when he deigns to grant victory.

But lest they should say, “Our fathers pleased him by their own merit, and therefore they received such great benefits from the Lord,” he added that this was not given because of their merits. Rather, because it pleased God in this way—since everything he grants is freely given—he was also pleased with them, for from the whole world they alone were chosen as the nation from which the Lord the Savior would come. He is our arm, victory, and strength.

If we sin against him, and, after being patiently awaited by him for a long time, refuse to return to him through repentance, he bends the bow of his judgment against us. By the right hand of his power he scatters everything that we seemed to possess in the adornment of knowledge or virtues, and he exercises against us the vengeance of his indignation, because we refused to understand the mercy and beneficence of his boundless clemency.

### He

“The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel, he has cast down all its walls, he has destroyed its fortifications, and he has filled the daughter of Judah with a humbled man and a humbled woman.”

The Lord became like an enemy of the synagogue of the Jews when he caused it to be devastated by the enemy’s sword. He cast down its walls, destroyed its fortifications, and filled that people with humiliation and disgrace—that is, he made both sexes despicable through manifold shame.

According to the allegorical interpretation, just as walls in cities serve as adornment while fortifications serve for defense, so some gifts strengthen us and others adorn us. Prophecy, teaching, kinds of languages, and the power of healings are, as it were, walls of the mind. Even if someone does not possess these, he can remain securely established through faith and justice, although he may appear to lack the height of the adornment of the virtues.

Faith, hope, and charity, however, are not our walls but our fortifications. If we neglect to possess them, we lie exposed to the plots of our enemies. Therefore, because he took prophecy, teaching, and the signs of miracles away from Judaea, he cast down its walls. But because he permitted hope, faith, and charity to be taken away on account of its hardness, he undertook to destroy its fortifications.

The proper order has been preserved, so that the walls are said to have been destroyed first and the fortifications afterward. For when a sinful soul is abandoned, the gifts of the virtues that were given for the manifestation of the Spirit are first taken from it; afterward the foundations of hope, faith, and charity are destroyed. All these things the Lord, having taken them away from the faithless, granted to the Gentiles, and with what he took from unbelievers he adorned the minds of believers.

Hence it is also written: “To divide the spoils of the beauty of the house.” When he took the spoils of the virtues away from the Jews, he gave them as an adornment of gifts to the house of the hearts of the Gentiles, which he deigned to inhabit through faith. This was accomplished when the Jewish people received the words of God according only to the letter, which kills, while the converted Gentiles penetrated them through the Spirit, who gives life.

### Vau

“And he has demolished, like a garden, his tent; he has destroyed his tabernacle. The Lord has consigned festival and Sabbath to oblivion in Zion, and in the indignation of his fury he has treated king and priest with contempt.”

Because of the sins of the Israelites, he demolished his tent and destroyed his tabernacle like a garden. He consigned festivals and Sabbaths to oblivion, and, despising the whole nation together with its kings and priests, he handed it over to the reproach of captivity.

Although the names “tent” and “tabernacle” may seem to signify the same thing—for the term “tabernacles” derives from the fact that stretched curtains were hung by ropes over tabernacles standing within and supporting the tents—we may understand by “tent” the tabernacle that Moses constructed in the desert, and by “tabernacle” the Temple that Solomon built in the Promised Land. Because of the crimes of their inhabitants, the Lord handed both over to the hands of their enemies, as we read in the Psalter:

“He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle in which he dwelt among human beings; and he handed over their strength to captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy” (Ps. 77).

Again, through the present prophet, namely Jeremiah, the Lord said earlier:

“I will do to this house in which my name has been invoked, and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave you and your fathers, as I did to Shiloh. I will cast you from my presence, just as I cast away all your brothers, the whole seed of Ephraim” (Jer. 26).

Therefore we must take care lest, because of our iniquities, the Holy Spirit, who inhabits us, abandon the dwelling of our heart, reject our priesthood, and despise the order of our governance; lest we become like a devastated garden in which no fruit of the virtues is produced.

We must fear, then, lest, deprived of such sweetness and delight, we arrive at eternal bitterness and foulness. For the apostle Paul plainly says to the Corinthians:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 1).

And again:

“Do you not know,” he says, “that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 2).

### Zain

“The Lord has rejected his altar; he has cursed his sanctuary. He has handed over the walls of its towers to the hands of the enemy. They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn feast day.”

The Lord is said to have rejected his altar and cursed his sanctuary because he rejected the sacrifices offered there according to the law—which he calls salutary sacrifices—and rejected the altar on which those sacrifices were offered. Together with the city and its defenses, he handed them over to be plundered by the hands of the enemies.

Those same enemies raised a blasphemous cry in the house of the Lord, where once, on various solemn occasions, the priests and Levites sang praises with different instruments, while the Temple and its worship remained inviolate. The prophet Isaiah formerly lamented this, saying:

“Behold, look: we are all your people, and the city of your holy one has become deserted; Zion has become deserted. Jerusalem, the desolate house of our sanctuary, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruins” (Isa. 64).

Mystically, the Lord rejected his altar when, because our sins demanded it, he despised as ungrateful the altar of our heart and turned his face away from us—from the place from which we ought to have been saved—as it is written:

“Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79).

He neither heeds our prayers nor receives our offerings. He curses his sanctuary when he regards as polluted the Christian name in which we gloried and which we received in holy baptism through the anointing with sacred chrism, because our crimes and wicked deeds have deserved this.

He hands over to the hands of all our enemies all our weapons and fortifications in which we trusted, because in our entire way of life we have been reduced to nothing. We no longer deserve to have useful superiors or defenders, because in the house of the Lord, where the praise, honor, and glory of confession ought to resound, there resound instead shouting and blasphemy, and earthly commerce is practiced. For this reason the angry Lord made a whip of cords and drove everyone from the Temple; he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned the seats of those selling doves.

### Heth

“The Lord planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out his measuring line, and did not turn his hand away from destruction. The rampart mourned, and the wall was destroyed together with it.”

The city whose wall the Lord planned to destroy, stretching out his measuring line—that is, determining to repay it with a fitting and deserved recompense for its wickedness—is the synagogue of the Jews. It always acted proudly and contentiously against the Lord, persecuting his prophets and messengers sent to it; finally it killed the heir himself, that is, his only Son.

Therefore the Lord himself, the just judge who loves justice, did not turn his hand away from its destruction. Measuring its land as with a measuring line, he divided it among its enemies. He destroyed the wall and the rampart when he caused the angelic guardianship and protection that they had formerly possessed through the Lord’s mercy and the merit of their fathers to withdraw from them.

By contrast, there is another city, of which we read in Isaiah that, after the destruction of Moab, a famous song was composed. There it is written:

“On that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: ‘The Savior is the city of our strength; a wall and a rampart will be set in it.’ Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, the one keeping faith” (Isa. 26).

[MAURUS.] What city is this, unless it is the one situated on a mountain and unable to be hidden? Of it it is also written elsewhere:

“The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 43).

And again:

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86).

The founder of this city is the one of whom the Father says: “He will build my city.” Indeed, “the Savior is the city of our strength,” that is, Jesus. “A wall and a rampart will be placed in it”: a wall of good works and a rampart of right faith, so that it may be enclosed by a double protection. For it is not enough to have the wall of faith unless faith itself is confirmed by good works.

This wall and this rampart, or surrounding wall, are built from living stones, which, according to the Prophet, roll upon the earth, and so forth.

When he says, “Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, the one keeping faith,” the Lord commands the angels who preside over the gates of the Lord’s city to open the gates and let in the righteous nation that keeps faith—not the Jewish people, which has been rejected, but the righteous nation that received the name of faithful from faith. It is that people of whom the holy one speaks:

“Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. 117).

No one, however, will be able to enter these gates unless he has been freed from the gates of death and has said with the Psalmist:

“You who raise me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9).

When we have been snatched from the gates of death, then we shall be able to sing all the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion. Just as the gates of death are those guilty of sin, concerning whom it is said to Peter, “The gates of hell shall not prevail against you” (Matt. 16), so the gates signify all the works of the virtues. Whoever enters will find one gate, of which it is said:

“This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (John 14).

And just as one proceeds through many pearls toward one pearl, so through many ways and gates we arrive at him who says that he is the way and the gate through which we enter to the Father.

### Theth

“Her gates have been driven into the ground; he has destroyed and shattered her bars, her king and her princes among the nations. There is no law, and her prophets have not found a vision from the Lord.”

The prophetic word describes this: when earthly Jerusalem, or rather the synagogue of the Jews, was destroyed, its teachers and defenders—designated by the names of gates and bars—were shattered and dispersed; its kings and princes were destroyed; and its prophets were no longer present in it. It no longer possessed either an inviolate law or a prophetic vision from the Lord, because they had disdained to receive the true lawgiver and Lord of the prophets when he came to them in person.

He himself is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. He is also the true Prophet, announcing to believers the Father’s will and his own. Moses formerly said of him to the Israelites:

“The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him. And everyone who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from among his people” (Deut. 18).

### Iod

“They sat on the ground; the elders of the daughter of Zion were silent. They sprinkled their heads with ashes; they girded themselves with sackcloth. The virgins of Jerusalem cast their heads down to the ground.”

They sat on the ground because they pursued earthly rather than heavenly desires. Their elders were silent because they did not possess spiritual knowledge of God’s law, and therefore, once truth had been abandoned, they were no longer able to provide useful counsel to their hearers.

The daughters of Zion sprinkled their heads with ashes and girded themselves with sackcloth; they were clothed in a garment of mourning because they had not preserved the adornment of the virtues and spiritual wisdom by which they ought to have reached the bridal chamber of the heavenly king.

Therefore the virgins of Jerusalem cast their heads down to the ground when they depressed minds weighed down by earthly sadness into the depths and no longer dared in any way to aspire to heavenly joy.

All these things warn us not to be sluggish and lukewarm in learning divine wisdom and practicing works of virtue, lest our Creator, because of our negligence, despise and abandon us. Then, with the gates and bars destroyed, we would be deprived of kings and princes to lead us in the way of righteousness; the law of God and the utterances of the prophets would no longer illuminate our hearts; and we would sit upon the ground of our flesh, polluted as though with ashes and wrapped around with the bristles of vices.

We would lose all the glory that we might have possessed in the heavenly kingdom. We would lie upon the ground until our flesh returned to the dust from which it was taken and our end became everlasting destruction.

### Caph

“My eyes have failed from tears; my inward parts are troubled. My liver has been poured out upon the ground over the destruction of the daughter of my people, when the child and the nursing infant fainted in the streets of the town.”

Seeing the immense destruction of his people, the Temple burned, and the city devastated, and seeing that the enemies spared neither sex nor age in their killing, the prophet, shaken by overwhelming grief, laments with the greatest weeping. His eyes fail from tears, and every joy of desire is turned into anguish of heart.

For what could have been more grievous than that an ancient nation, the seed of patriarchs and friends of God, instructed by divine laws and repeatedly strengthened by the prophecies of the prophets, should have fallen into such great apostasy that, having forgotten its God, it was handed over, because of the enormity of its crimes, to enemies who blasphemed the name of God?

Even now, in the same way, we must mourn the ruin of souls that were once faithful. Redeemed at the price of Christ’s blood, washed from the filth of sins by the water of baptism, and consecrated by mystical anointing, they have again fallen into the mire and filth of vices. Those who seemed to imitate the innocence and simplicity of children are killed by spiritual enemies in the streets of the world and amid the desires of the age.

The Lord himself is read to have lamented this greatest ruin of the faithless city in the Gospel, where it is written:

“When Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘If you too had known, and indeed on this your day, the things that belong to your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with a rampart, hem you in on every side, and cast you and your children who are within you to the ground; and they will not leave in you stone upon stone, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation’” (Luke 19).

[Greg.] Once he did this when he announced that the city would perish; our Redeemer never ceases to do the same thing daily through his elect when he observes that some have passed from a good life into depraved conduct.

He mourns those who do not know why they are being mourned, who, in the words of Solomon, “rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). For if they had recognized the condemnation that threatens them, they would weep over themselves with tears.

Malign spirits press upon the soul from every side when they bring before it not only sins of action but also sins of speech and, beyond these, sins of thought. Thus the soul, which previously expanded itself widely in crime, is finally constricted by all of it in retribution.

Then the soul is cast down to the ground through awareness of its guilt, when the flesh that it believed to be life is forced to return to dust. Then its children fall into death, when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are scattered in the final punishment of life, as it is written: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.”

But then someone seeks the help of consolation in vain, when at the end the final judgment presses upon him. Rightly it follows:

### Lamed

“They said to their mothers, ‘Where is the grain and the wine?’ as they fainted like the wounded in the streets of the city, as they breathed out their souls in the bosoms of their mothers.”

At that time negligent hearers vainly seek from their teachers the grain of the word and the wine of spiritual grace, when, amid earthly affairs and the pleasures of the age, they have come to the end of the present life, and under the very nourishment of their teachers have wasted the time granted to them in sinful conduct.

For then it is no longer a time of remedy but of vengeance, when the strict judge will come to examine the conduct and life of each person through the discernment of a just judgment.

For this reason, in the Gospel, when the bridegroom comes, the foolish virgins ask the wise virgins to give them some of their oil, because their lamps are going out (Matt. 25). Yet they do not deserve to receive it, because whoever now wastes the time granted for his correction and improvement will then in no way obtain help from another’s work.

Then the door of the kingdom is closed to those who mourn, although now it is opened daily to those who repent. There will indeed then be repentance, but it will no longer be fruitful, because the one who lost the time suitable for forgiveness will not then find forgiveness.

Therefore Paul says:

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

The prophet also says:

“Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55).

For this reason the Lord does not hear those same foolish virgins when they call, because once the door of the kingdom has been shut, the one who could have been near is no longer near.

There, the person who asks cannot now earn from the Lord what he seeks, because here he did not wish to hear what the Lord commanded. Whoever has lost the proper time for repentance comes in vain with prayers before the door of the kingdom.

Therefore through Solomon the Lord says:

“I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked. You despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs. I also will laugh at your destruction, and I will mock when what you feared has come, when sudden calamity falls upon you, when tribulation and distress come upon you, and calamity and destruction rush upon you like a storm. Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (Prov. 1).

Therefore we must always fear the final day, whose coming we can never foresee. Behold, even now we receive the day in which we are speaking as a reprieve for conversion, yet we refuse to weep over the evils we have committed. We not only fail to mourn what we have done; we also increase what must be mourned.

Or, if some illness overtakes us, or signs of illness announce approaching death, we seek an extension of life in order to mourn our sins, and we ask for it with great ardor of desire—although, when such extensions are granted, we now regard them as worthless.

Therefore, seeing the incomparable ruin of the synagogue, or rather of the Christian soul, the prophet turns his speech toward Jerusalem itself, saying:

### Mem

“To whom shall I compare you, or to whom shall I liken you, daughter of Jerusalem? To whom shall I equate you, and how shall I console you, virgin daughter of Zion? For great as the sea is your destruction; who will heal you?”

The synagogue of the Jews, in the times of the law and the prophets, under kings and priests, surpassed many peoples and nations in dignity. The divine law was its royal guidance and form of worship. Through evangelical revelation and prophetic vision, the Lord himself revealed his mysteries to it and showed through his oracle what was to be avoided and what was to be done.

But after it abandoned God and, deceived by vain error, turned to idolatry, it was crushed by a violent collision and, like a sea in a storm, was shaken and submerged by the waves of persecutions.

Likewise, the Christian soul, whose fall from the state of right faith and the height of the virtues has been immense, has a misery that cannot be compared with that of anyone else. From fellowship with God and the society of holy angels it has fallen into the dominion of evil spirits. Having captured it through various vices and crimes, they drive it here and there through the surging pleasures and misfortunes of the age, push it into the pit of destruction, and strive to hurl it into the abyss of Gehenna, where it will be punished forever.

Therefore, showing from where such evils have come, the prophet continues:

### Nun

“Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not reveal your iniquity, so as to provoke you to repentance. They saw false burdens and banishments for you.”

Just as once the false prophets led the Jewish people astray with false prophecies and lying promises, so now heretics and schismatics strive, through fabricated opinions and deceitful arguments, to overturn the hearts of the simple from the truth of right faith and the state of good works.

The apostle Peter bears witness to this in his Epistle:

“There were indeed false prophets among the people, just as there will also be false teachers among you. They will introduce destructive sects, denying the Lord who bought them, and bring swift destruction upon themselves. Many will follow their wantonness, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will traffic in you with fabricated words. Their judgment has not been idle for a long time, and their destruction does not sleep” (2 Pet. 2).

For this reason it is also said through Isaiah:

“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5).

Whoever promises security from punishment to a sinner who attends to wicked deeds will be subject to the prophetic curse. Likewise, the person who, out of envy, disparages a good deed and opposes one who does good will have everlasting woe unless he corrects himself.

Therefore we must beware of following falsehood instead of truth, and darkness instead of light.

“For there are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end leads into the depths of hell” (Prov. 14). “There is also one who perishes in his righteousness, to whom it is said: ‘Do not be excessively righteous’” (Ecclus. 7).

For these reasons Israel promises that it will walk by the royal way, turning neither to the left nor to the right. And, to say what I think, who can easily escape this curse, when we frequently flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty?

Aquila therefore translated the passage more pointedly:

“Woe to those who say to the wicked, ‘You are good,’ and to the good, ‘You are wicked.’”

This corresponds to what Solomon says in Proverbs:

“Whoever declares the righteous wicked and the wicked righteous—both are an abomination before God” (Prov. 17).

### Samech

“All who passed along the way clapped their hands over you; they hissed and shook their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem, saying: ‘Is this the city of perfect beauty, the joy of the whole earth?’”

[Hieron.] This expresses the joy of the enemies, who rejoiced at the downfall of the Israelites. Clapping their hands, hissing with their mouths, and shaking their heads, they mockingly taunted them for having fallen from the highest happiness into the hands of their enemies.

The shaking of the head belongs to the custom of those who are exceedingly angry and burning with envy. For whenever we are inflamed by fury, we threaten with violent movements of the head.

Hence the passage in which the Jews, passing by the Lord Christ hanging on the cross, blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying:

“Ah! You who destroy the Temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matt. 27).

The following corresponds to the same meaning:

### Phe

“They opened their mouths against you; all your enemies hissed and gnashed their teeth. They said, ‘We shall devour. Behold, this is the day we awaited; we have found it, we have seen it.’”

[MAURUS.] The enemies had always desired that day to come, because then they would be permitted to devour the whole Jewish people at once with the sword of slaughter and devastation. But since this could not have happened unless the Lord, by the just judgment of their many impieties, had permitted it to happen, the prophet immediately continues:

### Aleph

“‘The Lord has done what he planned; he has fulfilled his word, which he commanded from ancient days. He has destroyed and shown no pity, and he has made the enemy rejoice over you; he has exalted the horn of your enemies.’”

(Hieronymus.) “Thus the synagogue of the Jews, repeatedly provoking the Lord, would long ago have deserved a just battle, had not the goodness of its Creator, enduring it for a long time, borne with it piously and patiently. But since it was unwilling to turn back and cease from the wickedness it had begun, at last it received, according to its merits, a punishment proportionate to them. Thus formerly, when Moses, his servant, was praying for the people who had turned to idolatry, the Lord answered him, saying: ‘I will forgive according to your word; nevertheless, on the day of vengeance I shall visit even this sin of theirs.’”

Hence he now says: “The Lord has done what he planned; he has fulfilled his word, which he commanded from ancient days; he has destroyed and shown no pity,” because, provoked to anger, he finally brought upon them the blows that he had often foretold by threats through the prophets and the Law.

Therefore, if earthly enemies then did these things against earthly Jerusalem, what will spiritual wickedness and the ministers of the ancient enemy do against spiritual Jerusalem—that is, the Christian soul—when, delivered to them by the Lord on account of its iniquities, they surround it everywhere with punishments and everywhere with pains? At that time nothing benefits it that in an earlier age it had possessed something of earthly happiness. Hence the Lord, under the figure of the city destined to perish, as we have already shown above, mourned over it, saying: “For if you too had known, and indeed on this your day, the things that are for your peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart and hem you in on every side.”

(Gregory.) The perverse soul has its own day: it rejoices in a transitory time, and the things present are for its peace. For while it rejoices in temporal possessions, while it is lifted up by honors, while it is dissolved in the pleasure of the flesh, while it is terrified by no fear of future punishment, it has peace in its own day—but in another’s day it will have the grave scandal of condemnation. There it must be afflicted where the righteous rejoice, and everything that now serves for peace will then be turned into the bitterness of strife, because it begins to quarrel with itself: Why was it not afraid of the condemnation it suffers? Why did it close the eyes of its mind to the evils that would follow?

Hence it is also said: “But now they are hidden from your eyes.” For the perverse soul, devoted to present things and dissolved in earthly pleasures, hides the evils that follow from itself, because it refuses to see the future things that disturb its present joy. And while it abandons itself to the delight of the present life, what else does it do but go toward the fire with its eyes closed? Hence it is rightly written: “In the day of good things, do not be mindful of evils” (Ecclesiasticus XI). And hence Paul says: “Those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not” (I Corinthians VII), because even if there is joy in the present time, it must be conducted in such a way that the bitterness of the coming judgment never departs from memory. Thus, while the fearful mind is pierced by dread of the final vengeance, present joy will be moderated in proportion to the anger that follows afterward.

For this reason it is written: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but whoever is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Proverbs XVIII). The anger of the coming judgment will then be borne all the more severely insofar as it is now scarcely feared even amid sins.

It continues: “For days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart.” Who are ever greater enemies of the human soul than the evil spirits? When it is departing from the body, they besiege the soul that they had cherished, while it was placed in love of the flesh, with deceptive pleasures. They surround it with a rampart when, bringing back before its mind the iniquities it committed, they hem it in and drag it toward the fullness of its condemnation. Thus, caught at the very extremity of life, it sees by what enemies it is enclosed, yet cannot find a way of escape, because it is no longer permitted to perform good works—works that, when it was permitted, it had despised.

We must reflect deeply on how terrifying the hour of our dissolution will be: what fear of sorrow, how great then the memory of all evils, what forgetfulness of past happiness, what dread and consideration of the Judge. What, then, should there be for us in present things that brings delight, when, although all things pass away together, what threatens us cannot pass away; when what is loved is completely brought to an end, and that begins where pain never ends?

Then the evil spirits seek the soul’s works when it comes forth; then they repeat the evils they persuaded it to commit, so that they may drag their companion to torments. The following may also be applied to this:

### Sade

“‘Their heart cried out to the Lord against the walls of the daughter of Zion.’”

(Hieronymus.) This cry signifies the mind’s intense purpose, not the raising of the voice. Perverse people—or spiritual wickedness—cry out before the Lord against the walls of the daughter of Zion when they attribute to their own power the authority by which they dominate a people or a sinful soul, rather than to the judgment of divine permission. Their blasphemy, by which they cry out against the Lord, will not escape a punishment proportionate to it. For when the judgments of the heavenly Arbiter have fulfilled their hidden purposes against his adversaries, they too will receive the just rewards of their guilt. They spare no persons, since they desire to harm all whom they can, to the extent permitted them, and seek to have them as companions in their own destruction.

(Gregory.) Hence it is not necessary to speak of this only with reference to the perverse soul, because they seek to hem it in when they come to each of the elect as they depart, and, if they prevail, seek something of their own in them. Yet there was one person who, before his passion, said with a free voice: “I shall no longer speak much with you; for the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV).

Because he saw this man as mortal, the prince of the world believed that he could find something belonging to himself in him; but he departed from the world’s corruption without any sin, just as he came into the world without sin.

Not even Peter presumed to say this of himself, although he deserved to hear: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI). Paul did not presume to say it either, although before paying the debt of death he reached the secrets of the third heaven (II Corinthians XII). Nor did John dare to say it, although, because of his exceptional love, he reclined at the breast of his Redeemer at supper (John XXI).

For when the Prophet says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm L), he could not be in the world without guilt who came into the world with guilt. Hence the same Prophet says: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII). Solomon says: “There is no person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiasticus VII). John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I). James says: “We all offend in many things” (James III).

For it is evident that all who were conceived through the pleasure of the flesh undoubtedly had something belonging to the prince of this world, whether in their action, speech, or thought. Yet he could neither seize them afterward nor hold them beforehand for this reason: the one who rescued them from their debts rescued them, the one who, without owing the debt of death, paid it for us, so that our debts would not hold us under the power of our enemy, because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humanity, freely repaid for us what he did not owe. For by paying the undeserved death of the flesh on our behalf, he freed us from the death we owed.

He says: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.”

Therefore, in accordance with what the Prophet exhorts us, saying: “Let your tears flow like a torrent by day and by night; do not give yourself rest, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent”—

(Maurus.) We ought at all times to pour out tears through compunction of heart, since we know that our Creator has been offended by our iniquities. Let us not be dissolved in sluggish inertia, nor let the pupil of our eye cease from tears through negligence and vain security. Let us anticipate the face of the Lord in confession, and sing praise to him in the psalms. Each night let us wash our bed with tears and water our couch; let us devote ourselves to works of mercy, give alms generously to the poor, and continually implore the Lord’s mercy both for ourselves and for our neighbors and those entrusted to us.

Hence it also follows:

### Coph

“‘Arise, praise in the night at the beginning of the watches; pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Lift your hands to him for the lives of your little ones, who have fainted from hunger at the head of every street.’”

(Hieronymus.) He rises in the night who shakes off from himself the torpor of negligence amid the tribulation of the present life. He praises at the beginning of the watches who conducts himself vigorously and cautiously in every aspect of his life and strives to turn whatever adversity he suffers entirely into an occasion for confessing God’s praise.

He pours out his heart like water before the face of the Lord who brings forth tears of compunction from the innermost affection of his heart. “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm L).

He lifts his hands to the Lord for the lives of his little ones, who have fainted from hunger at the head of all the chained: he undertakes works of mercy for the humble and the little members of Christ, who labor everywhere at the ends of the world from hunger and thirst, and does so out of sincere love. For no gift is more acceptable to God than compunction of heart brought forth from the root of true love.

Hence there is the passage in the Gospel in which, when the Lord had entered the house of a Pharisee and reclined for a meal, he valued the sinful woman’s tears more highly than the Pharisee’s delicacies. It is written:

“He entered the house of the Pharisee and reclined, and behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that he had reclined in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment. Standing behind him at his feet, she began to bathe his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with her hair and anointed them with ointment. But when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: ‘If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what and what kind of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner’” (Luke VII).

[Gregory.] But let us now hear by what judgment this proud and arrogant man is convicted. A parable is set before him concerning two debtors, one of whom owes less and the other more. After the debt of both has been forgiven, he is asked which of them will love the lender more. At once he replied: “The one to whom more is forgiven.”

In this matter it should be noted that, while the Pharisee is convicted by his own judgment, like a madman he carries the rope by which he is to be bound. The sinful woman’s good deeds and the supposed just man’s evil deeds are enumerated, when it is said:

“I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she has bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You did not give me a kiss, but she has not ceased kissing my feet since I entered. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment” (ibid.).

After this enumeration the judgment is added: “Therefore I say to you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (ibid.).

Whom does the Pharisee, relying on false righteousness, signify if not the Jewish people? And whom does the sinful woman, coming to the Lord’s feet and weeping, signify if not the converted Gentile people?

She came with an alabaster jar, poured out the ointment, stood behind the Lord at his feet, bathed his feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, and did not cease kissing the same feet that she had poured over and wiped. We are represented by that woman if, after our sins, we return to the Lord with our whole heart and imitate the grief of her repentance.

If, therefore, we perform righteous works by which we sprinkle the Church with the reputation of a good fragrance, what do we pour out upon the Lord’s body if not ointment? But the woman stood beside Jesus’ feet. We stood against the Lord’s feet when, placed in sins, we were held back from his ways. But if after our sins we turn to true repentance, we now stand behind his feet, because we follow the footsteps of the one whom we had opposed.

The woman bathes the Lord’s feet with tears. We too truly do this if, through the feeling of confession, we bow before any of the Lord’s least members; if we suffer with his holy ones in tribulation; if we regard their sorrow as our own.

The woman wiped with her hair the feet she had bathed. Hair grows excessively on the body, and what abundant earthly substance does not resemble hair? When it exceeds the use of necessity, even when cut off it is not missed. We therefore wipe the Lord’s feet with our hair when, out of charity, we sympathize with his holy ones and also show mercy from what is superfluous to us, so that the mind grieves through compassion in such a way that the generous hand also displays the feeling of grief.

He bathes the Redeemer’s feet with tears but does not wipe them with his hair who in some way sympathizes with the sorrow of his neighbors but does not show mercy from what is superfluous to him. He weeps but does not wipe who offers words of sorrow but, by failing to provide what is lacking, does not lessen the force of the sorrow.

The woman kisses the feet that she wipes. We too do this fully if we diligently love those whom we sustain through generosity, so that our neighbor’s need is not burdensome to us; so that the very want that is being supported does not become a burden; and so that, while the hand supplies what is necessary, the spirit does not grow sluggish in love.

(Maurus.) Therefore, after the Prophet had urged the wretched city to repentance and to the tears of prayer, he turns words of supplication toward the Lord himself, asking whether he might somehow appease him and turn him away from vengeance, saying:

### Res

“‘See, Lord, and consider whom you have harvested in this way. Shall women then eat their own fruit, infants of a palm’s measure, if priest and prophet are killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?’”

Among the other evils that befell the wretched Jewish people, this too occurred: their women ate their little children and the fruit of their womb because of the scarcity caused by famine. Hence there is the passage concerning the siege of Samaria, when a woman cried out to King Joram over the killing of her son, whom she had eaten with her neighbor, demanding that the other woman’s son likewise be given to both of them for food (IV Kings VI).

So too, in the final captivity under the Romans, during the rule of Titus and Vespasian, a certain woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, noble by birth and wealth, who belonged to the common people living beyond the Jordan, fled with a multitude of others and was received into Jerusalem, where she was besieged with the rest. When plunderers had stripped her of all her possessions and provisions, at last, compelled by the necessity of hunger, she killed her own nursing son, cooked and ate part of him, and reserved the other part to eat later. The plunderers were aroused by the smell of the roasted flesh; when they learned what had happened, they withdrew in great horror.

That priests and prophets, boys and old men, young men and virgins fell by the sword in the sanctuary of the Lord is clearly shown both by sacred history and by the books of Josephus the historian concerning the destruction of the city of Jerusalem.

Mystically, women will eat the fruit of their womb when sinful souls, with God as just judge repaying them, receive the fitting reward of their deeds. The prophet and priest is killed in the sanctuary of the Lord when the ministers of the altar and preachers of God’s word, because of their negligence and sloth, incur the deserved punishment of vengeance in the very office from which they ought to have been crowned.

### Sin

“‘They lay on the ground outside, boy and old man; my virgins and my young men fell by the sword. You killed them on the day of your anger; you struck them and showed no pity.’”

Boy and old man lie outside on the ground when those who pretended to possess childish innocence, or those who appeared to guide the people by their counsel, devote themselves to earthly desires and, because of their criminal life, are expelled from the city of the Lord and made equal to the earth to which they had clung in mind—dust being returned to dust.

Likewise, those who appeared to possess virginal chastity and to exercise the strength of youth in good works will be killed by the sword of future condemnation because of the hypocrisy they displayed before human eyes. Heavenly vengeance killed on the day of the Lord’s anger those who merely imitated sacred virtues, not those who truly practiced them.

Hence in the Gospel (Matthew XXV) the foolish virgins are read to have remained outside, begging beyond the door of the wedding feast, at the bridegroom’s arrival. And it is written in the Psalms that the young men were consumed by fire and that their virgins did not lament (Psalm LXXVII).

### Thau

“‘You summoned, as though to a solemn day, those who terrified me from every side, and on the day of the Lord’s anger there was no one who escaped and was left behind. Those whom I raised and nourished, my enemy consumed.’”

The enemies were summoned, as though to a solemn day, for the overthrow of the faithless city, because what they desired came about with the Lord’s permission. They were permitted to behold the destruction of the Jews that they desired.

Alternatively, enemies come as though summoned to a festival when, on the day of judgment, evil spirits gather exultantly to punish sinners. They rejoice over the ruin of souls because they know that the human race was created to fill the heavenly city from which they had fallen. Therefore, seeing that they have been deprived of eternal happiness, they hasten with all their strength, through envy, to cast human beings down so that they may not possess paradise.

Yet holy Church endures this with great sorrow when she sees her children—whom she has brought forth through baptism and instructed in the divine sacraments—falling daily through various crimes under the power of their enemies. This will be demonstrated clearly enough at the beginning of the following book, since we judge that the present book ends here.

## BOOK NINETEEN

[Col. 1215]

[Col. 1215B] (Hieronymus.) We have passed rapidly through the first part of Jeremiah’s Lamentation, which consists of two alphabets written, as it were, in Sapphic meter [Col. 1215C], since a heroic metrical clausula concludes three connected verses that nevertheless begin with the same letter, as has already been shown above in the exposition. Now let us come to the explanation of the second part, where there is a third alphabet written in trimeter, and where three verses begin with three letters, though the letters are the same.

First, we wish it to be understood that this part initially declares, in mourning, the calamity of the Jewish people—or rather of the human race; then it openly expresses the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and passion, in which the persecution of the Jews and the punishment and death of the innocent Christ are described.

## CHAPTER III

### Aleph

“‘I am a man who sees my poverty, under the rod of his indignation.’”

(Maurus.) The faithful people therefore lament their poverty under the correction of the Lord’s indignation, because they see many falling from the state of right faith and the pursuit of good works into the darkness of error and the abyss of vices: “For many are called, but few are chosen.”

### Aleph

“‘He led me and brought me into darkness, and not into light.’”

That is, he permitted me to fall into tribulation and did not preserve me in prosperity.

### Aleph

“‘He turns against me alone, and turns his hand all day long.’”

For the speaker understands that, by the sentence of the just Judge, what happens to him corresponds to his merits, and he recalls that he has deserved it by his own actions. Yet what he says must be considered: “He turns against me alone, and turns his hand.” For in Scripture “to turn” is often used for “to appease,” as in: “Turn, Lord, for a little while, and plead for your servants” (Psalm LXXXIX).

The Lord turns his hand when he justly sends due vengeance upon the guilty; and he turns back his hand when he mercifully suspends the sentence of vengeance. For it is written of him: “The Lord kills and makes alive; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts.” And in the song of Deuteronomy he himself says: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can rescue from my hands” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

### Beth

“‘The Lord has made my skin and my flesh old; he has crushed my bones.’”

By skin and flesh he expresses external and softer things; by bones, internal strength. Thus the Lord made the skin and flesh of the Jews old when, through want, he made them deformed in external matters. “He crushed their bones” when he diminished the hardness of their minds.

(Gregory.) Hence blessed Job also says: “My skin has become black upon me, and my bones have dried up from the heat” (Job XXX). This aptly corresponds to the words of holy Church, which deeply feels the pain of the final persecution in its weaker members; and while some perish through it, its stronger members are tormented by grief.

Its external cause is earthly administration; its internal cause is heavenly care. By the name “skin,” therefore, its weaker members are signified, those who now serve its external usefulness. By “bones,” however, its strong members are represented, in whom the entire structure of that body is strengthened.

Because many in the Church, either enticed by rewards or afflicted by persecutions, fall from the state of faith in their weakness, and afterward persecute the Church itself once they have fallen, what else does it suffer than the blackness of its skin? It appears afterward foul in those in whom it had previously appeared beautiful. For when those who formerly used to administer external things well later rage against God’s elect, the skin of the Church, as it were, loses the color of its former righteousness and becomes black with iniquity.

### Beth

“‘He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.’”

(Hieronymus.) What is “to build around” except to hem in with pressures on every side? And what is “to surround with gall and labor” except to confine one who has been filled with bitterness and toil? Hence it adds:

### Beth

“‘He placed me in dark places, like those who have been dead forever.’”

(Maurus.) He places him in dark places like those who have been dead forever when, deprived of every consolation, he does not allow the afflicted to hope for any comfort from the present life. Concerning this it adds further:

### Ghimel

“‘He built all around against me so that I could not escape; he made my fetter heavy.’”

(Hieronymus.) When he sees a siege built up against him with a rampart and earthworks, he declares his fetter to have been made heavy, because he finds no way of escaping his calamity. Holy Job expressed the same thing in similar words: “He fenced in my path so that I cannot pass, and he placed darkness on my road” (Job XIX).

[Gregory.] This also appropriately refers to the weaker members of holy Church, when, because they remember having acted wrongly, they are held back even from good works, and, timid through their own weakness, do not dare to undertake strong good deeds against these faults. Those who remember themselves to be weak in their actions fear beginning great good works.

And since they often do not even know what good they should choose, they shudder at the darkness placed, as it were, on their road. For the mind often becomes so uncertain about its own work that it has no idea at all what is virtue and what is guilt. He finds darkness on his road who does not know what he ought to choose among the things he desires to do.

Since sin is often committed through weakness and sometimes through ignorance, it is said of those weakened: “He fenced in my path, and I cannot pass.” But of those who are blind even to the good work they should choose, it adds: “And he placed darkness on my road.”

It is a punishment resulting from guilt to see the good one ought to do and yet be unable to accomplish it. And again: it is a more severe punishment resulting from guilt not even to see what one ought to do. Hence, against both conditions, the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm XXVI). Against the darkness of ignorance, the Lord is light; against weakness, he is salvation, since he both shows what should be sought in action and grants the strength by which what he has shown can be accomplished.

### Ghimel

“‘Even when I cry out and plead, he has shut out my prayer.’”

(Gregory.) Almighty God, knowing what can profit us, pretends not to hear the voice of those who grieve, in order to increase their benefit: so that life may be purified through punishment, and so that, since tranquility cannot be found here, the peace of rest may be sought elsewhere.

Some of the faithful do not understand this dispensation of grace; elsewhere, through blessed Job, it is said in their person: “Behold, I shall cry out, suffering violence, and no one will hear; I shall shout, and there is no one to judge” (Job XIX).

“There is no one to judge” is said when the one who is Judge himself delays judging, since, apart from him, there is no one to judge our case against the adversary. Yet it is not without judgment that judgment is delayed, because while blessed Job was saying these things, both the merits of the holy men and the punishment of their adversary were increasing. Thus the Judge’s delaying judgment was itself a judgment, so that each might receive in the future a reward proportionate to his merits.

### Ghimel

“‘He blocked my ways with squared stones; he overturned my paths.’”

(Maurus.) To show that she was hemmed in by powerful tribulations, she says that she was enclosed with squared stones and that the path of her steps had been overturned. For rocks possessing a solid, square form lie fixed wherever they are placed and cannot slide elsewhere.

Mystically, the people of the elect are enclosed by squared stones under the power of the wicked when their flesh is temporarily handed over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. He overturns their path because he does not allow them to escape his torments; nor is he content merely to afflict their flesh with tortures, but through deceit and snares he seeks to overthrow their soul utterly. Hence it adds:

### Daleth

“‘He became for me a bear lying in wait, a lion in hiding.’”

By these two most savage beasts he expresses the exceedingly deceitful and cruel persecution of the ancient enemy. Through his ministers he wishes to overturn one person by flatteries, another by threats, another by tortures, from the path of right faith, and to crush them, as though desolate, away from hope of heavenly assistance. Hence it follows:

### Daleth

“‘He overturned and broke my paths; he made me desolate.’”

The Prophet testifies in the Psalms concerning the snares of this lion, saying: “He sits in ambush with the rich in secret, to kill the innocent” (Psalm IX). “His eyes look toward the poor; he lies in wait secretly like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor; he seizes the poor when he draws him away. In his snare he humbled him; he bowed down and will fall when he has dominion over the poor.”

(Cassiodorus.) He compared the Antichrist’s activity to the practice of robbers, who lie in wait along hidden paths in order to kill the innocent. He says that the Antichrist’s kingdom will be of such a kind that it is clearly permitted for the crown of martyrs and the ruin of unbelievers.

For in sacred Scripture the rich are often understood in an evil sense, just as the poor are understood in a good sense. To kill the innocent is to make a religious person sacrilegious and to condemn his soul to everlasting death.

When he says that the Antichrist’s eyes look toward the poor, he does not look in order to observe them, but directs his attention toward destroying them. He calls the Antichrist a lion already placed in his den, because he will savagely and deceitfully tear apart the Christian people.
