At first the Church’s persecution was violent, when Christians were compelled by pagans, through confiscations, tortures, and killings, to sacrifice to idols. The second was deceitful, the one now carried on through heretics and false Christians. The final persecution remains, which is foretold as coming through the Antichrist; nothing will be more dangerous than it, since it will be exceedingly violent through the power of a single kingdom and deceptive through miracles, so that, as the Lord says in the Gospel, it will deceive, if possible, even the elect.

Accordingly, “lion” refers to force, while “in his den” refers to deceit; thus both of his iniquities are indicated by the individual expressions.

“To seize the poor” signifies the soul’s sudden danger, toward which that most wicked one strives to drag the innocent. “When he draws him away” means when he attempts to lead him from the truth of worship to veneration of his own name.

“In his snare he humbled him.” The snare signifies the deceit by which the hearts of the simple are caught and, as if by a knot, are lamentably bound in perversity. “He will humble” is rightly said, because those who are led into insane doctrines undoubtedly fall from true religion.

Here the statement now concerns the tyrant himself, who will rage against God’s servants by a power granted to him. “He will bow down,” that is, when he relaxes his spirit after acquiring an excessive number of the lost and, as though gorged on an abundance of evils, reaches a kind of repose after the punishments and afflictions of the saints.

Then the most wicked one will fall through his presumption, when sudden destruction overtakes him and his followers. He does not know the end of the age, because the Lord has reserved it within his own power.

### Daleth

“‘He bent his bow and set me up like a target for the arrow.’”

(Gregory.) That is, he revealed the sentence of his judgment against me and corrected me with a sure blow of chastisement.

In sacred speech, the name “bow” sometimes signifies the ambushes of the wicked, sometimes the day of judgment, and sometimes sacred Scripture itself. Ambushes are represented by the bow, as the Psalmist says: “They bent the bow for a bitter matter” (Psalm LXIII).

The day of judgment is also designated by the bow, as the same Psalmist says again: “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us to drink the wine of compunction. You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Psalm LIX).

With a bow, the farther the string is drawn, the more forcefully the arrow comes forth. In the same way, the more the day of the final judgment is delayed before it comes, the more severe the sentence that proceeds from it when it arrives.

For this reason we are now struck by various calamities, so that, corrected by them, we may then be found more prepared. Hence it was said beforehand: “You have shown your people hard things”—namely, the scourges of the age that precede the more grievous day of judgment that will follow. “You have given us to drink the wine of compunction,” so that earthly joys might be turned into tears. “You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

It is as though he were saying: This is the time of mercy; that will be the time of judgment. Through the scourges of the present time, therefore, you signify how you will strike [or: persecute] then, when you judge without sparing—since you now strike so sternly while sparing.

Sometimes sacred Scripture is also signified by the bow. The Church itself is a bow; it is the Lord’s bow. From it, just as arrows that wound come to human hearts, so terrifying judgments proceed. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “He bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he prepared the instruments of death; he made his arrows fiery” (Psalm VII).

The Lord bent his bow when through holy Scripture he displayed threats to all sinners. In this bow he prepared the instruments of death, because according to the sentence of his word he condemns as reprobate those who now neglect correction. In it he also made his arrows fiery, because he sends burning judgments of his words against those whom he corrects through fear.

“And he set me,” it says, “like a target for the arrow.” It is clear that a target is set precisely so that it may be struck by the discharge of arrows. The faithful people, therefore, have been set as a target for their enemy, who attacks them with his blows and afflicts them with his persecutions. Whoever continually endures evils in this life receives the blows of the one striking, as though placed at a target.

Hence the distinguished preacher, while enduring the evils of persecution and groaning under the persecution of adversaries, consoled the tender minds of his disciples concerning his afflictions, saying: “You yourselves know that we have been appointed for this” (I Thessalonians III). It is as though he were saying openly to them: “Why are you astonished at our wounds in this time? If we seek eternal joys, we have come here for this purpose: to be struck.”

### He

“‘He has sent the daughters of his quiver into my kidneys.’” (Jerome.) He calls arrows the daughters of the quiver. Thus he sent the daughters of his quiver into the kidneys when, according to the measure of his dispensation, he chastised carnal desires in human beings with fitting correction. Concerning this quiver it is written in Job: “For he has opened his quiver and afflicted me” (Job 30:11). What is signified by God’s quiver except his hidden counsel? The Lord casts an arrow from the quiver when, from the hidden counsel of his judgment, he issues an open sentence. We know that someone is scourged, but do we know from what cause the scourge comes? Yet when correction of life follows the scourges, the power of the counsel itself is also revealed. The closed quiver, therefore, is the hidden counsel; but we are afflicted when the quiver is opened, because through what follows the scourging we see by what counsel we are scourged. When the Lord sees sins and yet does not move his hand to vengeance, he holds the quiver, as it were, closed; but by striking, he shows how greatly displeasing to him was that which he had long tolerated while seeing it.

(Jerome.) Elsewhere, concerning the arrow and the quiver, we read in Isaiah, where it is written: “He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me,” and so forth (Isa. 49:2). When he says “chosen arrow,” he shows that God has very many arrows, and some that are not chosen. These arrows are the prophets and the apostles, who run throughout the whole world; concerning them it is also sung elsewhere: “Your arrows are sharp, most powerful; peoples shall fall beneath you.” And again: “The arrows of the mighty are sharp, with coals of desolation” (Ps. 44:6).

But Christ, from among the many arrows and the many sons, is one chosen arrow and the only-begotten Son, whom he hid in his quiver—that is, in a human body—so that the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily in him. Thus the faith of believers was rightly established, concerning which it is also said above: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know it” (Ps. 118:11). This arrow is also spoken of by the bride, receiving the wound, in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love.”

### He

“‘I have become a derision to all my people, their song all the day.’” (Maurus.) The prophet suffered the derision of his people when they did not believe his words, indeed opposed them, saying to him: “You are speaking a lie; the Lord our God did not send you” (Jer. 43:2).

Alternatively, these words describe the time of the holy Church when it is publicly mocked by the reprobate, when, as the wicked multiply, faith and truth will be treated as a disgrace: each person will be the more despised the more righteous he is able to be, and the more abominable the more praiseworthy. Thus, in the time of affliction, the holy Church of the elect becomes a proverb to the wicked, because when they see the good dying through torments, they take from them an example of cursing. For they see transitory death but do not see permanent life; and the less they attain inwardly, through understanding, to enduring goods, the more they flee present evils by mockery.

But the holy Church knows how to grow through sufferings and to maintain an honorable life amid reproaches. It knows neither to be cast down by adversity nor to glory in prosperity; against prosperity it knows how to lay its mind low in humiliation, and against adversity it knows how to raise its spirit toward the hope of the heavenly summit. It knows that its good things come from the mercy of the Redeemer, and that its evils are to be attributed to the justice of the Judge: it possesses good because he bestows it, and suffers evil because he permits it.

### He

“‘He has filled me with bitterness and intoxicated me with wormwood.’” (Maurus.) The prophet says that he was filled with bitterness because he was troubled not so much by his own calamity as by grief over the ruin of his people. Hence he compares himself to a drink made from a very bitter herb, because he sees himself grievously afflicted by the devastation of his enemies.

In a mystical sense, however, Jeremiah, taking upon himself the figure of all human conduct, complains in his lament, saying: “He has intoxicated me with wormwood.” A drunk person does not know what he is suffering; but one who is intoxicated with wormwood both finds what he has taken to be bitter and yet does not understand the same bitterness with which he is filled. The human race, therefore, rightly subjected by God’s judgment to its own pleasures [or, according to the supplied reading, “calamities”], and through those same pleasures handed over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood: what it endures for the love of this life is bitter, yet, through the blindness of desire, it fails to recognize that bitterness, as though through the insensibility of drunkenness.

For while thirsting for the glory of the world, it encounters many tribulations on its account; what it drinks is bitter. But because it has taken it in with excessive eagerness, it is no longer able, through that very drunkenness, to discern the evil of the bitterness. Perverse people love even the tribulations they endure for the glory of this world; they willingly serve it through every kind of toil and most devotedly submit their necks to the yoke of heavy labors. Concerning this he adds:

### Vau

“‘He has broken my teeth by number; he has fed me with wormwood.’”

“That is, he has taken away from me the use of eating and fed me with useless nourishment.” (Gregory.) In Holy Scripture, teeth are sometimes understood as preachers and sometimes as inward senses. Concerning the holy preachers of the bride it is said: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing” (Song 4:2). Hence, when one of them was shown the Gentiles in a vision, he was told: “Kill and eat”—that is, crush their oldness and convert them into the body of the Church, that is, into your members.

Since teeth are also customarily understood as inward senses, the prophet now says: “He has broken my teeth by number.” Food is broken by teeth so that it may be swallowed. Therefore we rightly understand the inward senses by teeth, since they chew and break up individually whatever they contemplate, as it were, and send it into the stomach of memory. The prophet says that they have been broken by number because, according to the measure of each person’s sin, blindness of understanding is generated in the senses; and according to what each person has done outwardly, he becomes dull in understanding what he might have perceived concerning inward and invisible things.

Hence it is rightly written also: “Every person who eats a sour grape—his teeth shall be set on edge” (Jer. 31:30). What is a sour grape except sin? A sour grape is fruit before its time. Whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life hastens to eat fruit before its time. Therefore, whoever eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge, because whoever feeds on the pleasure of the present world has his inward senses bound, so that he can no longer chew—that is, understand—spiritual things. For by whatever has given them pleasure outwardly, they become dull inwardly.

And while the soul feeds on sin, it cannot eat the bread of righteousness, because teeth bound by the habit of sin can in no way eat what is just and inwardly savory. Since, as we have said, in this passage teeth signify inward senses, we must carefully consider what the righteous are accustomed to do. Often, if they detect any carnal thing whatsoever in themselves, they reconsider it with their inward senses and vigorously pursue it within themselves; they crush themselves through affliction, judge even the least evil in themselves with great torments, and condemn it through repentance. They do this so that, insofar as possible, they themselves may be found blameless before the sight of the eternal Judge, and so that those who see them judging themselves in this way may burn with a desire to correct themselves from more serious faults.

(Maurus.) “He fed me,” he says, “with ashes”—that is, with something fragile and of little use; he sustained me with the support of food. This passage is also like what the penitent is read to have said in the Psalms: “All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me, because I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10–11). He explains why he was cursed to his face by friends or acquaintances, as it is clear that Job also endured this, whose life appeared filthy to his neighbors and friends because of its most grievous squalor.

Yet this verse must be examined more carefully, lest against ordinary human usage we suppose that the ashes of wood are the food of penitents. We know ashes to be the remains of burned coals; and we rightly compare them with sins, so that even the slightest remnants of faults may be consumed by the pains of affliction. For although only a small amount of sin remains, it does not deserve rewards but rather needs the forgiveness of sins. Hence the prophet cries in the fiftieth Psalm: “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.”

Therefore the most holy penitent rightly hastened to consume even the ashes of sins, lest anything remain that might prevent him from deserving the kingdom of heaven. “And I mingled,” he says, “my drink with weeping.” Although this may sometimes seem to occur literally, I think this too must be sought spiritually. The drink of souls is that satisfaction of which the seventy-fourth Psalm says: “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine with mixture, and he has poured from this into that.” This, then, is the drink which we rightly temper with tears; this is the cup which our tears make sweeter. For that heavenly drink enters the innermost parts of the soul when it is watered with devout weeping.

This was the cup that seemed unworthy to mockers; this was the food judged dreadful by the luxurious. But the good Christian ought all the more to love that by which he may be able to reach the banquets of the heavenly King.

### Vau

“‘And my soul has been rejected; I have forgotten good things.’”

### Vau

“‘And I said: My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.’”

If these words are considered historically, they express the great distress of the Jewish people, who, because of the impending tribulation of captivity, declare that they have been rejected from every earthly happiness and have forgotten past blessings. They say that they now have neither any end to their present tribulation nor any hope of consolation.

According to the mystical interpretations, however, the assembly of the elect confesses that it has been rejected from the prosperity of the age and has forgotten present goods; it shows that, in exchange for its present labor, it seeks from the Lord not a transitory reward but the future glory of the heavenly kingdom. “The world has passed away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.”

Hence blessed Job says: “My soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death; I have despaired; I shall no longer live” (Job 7:15–16). (Gregory.) What is signified by the soul except the intention of the mind, and by the bones except the strength of the flesh? Whatever is hung is undoubtedly raised up from below. The soul therefore chooses hanging so that the bones may die, because when the intention of the mind raises itself to lofty things, it kills in itself all the strength of outward life.

Holy men know with complete certainty that they cannot have rest in this life, and therefore choose hanging, because, abandoning earthly desires, they raise their minds to what is above. In being hung, they inflict death upon their bones, because, girded by love of the heavenly homeland for the pursuit of virtues, they pursue with the bond of humility what had previously made them strong in the world.

It is pleasing to observe how Paul hangs his soul, when he says: “I live, yet now it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). And again: “Having a desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Recalling the deeds of earthly strength, he counted, as it were, certain bones within himself, saying: “A Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee, according to zeal persecuting the Church of God” (Phil. 3:5–6).

But after hanging his soul, because he had killed these bones within himself, he immediately declares: “But the things that were gain to me, these I considered loss for Christ.” He indicates that these bones have been extinguished more forcefully within himself when he adds: “For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things and consider them as dung.” And he shows how lifelessly he hangs after the bones have died when he adds: “That I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Jesus Christ.”

But since, by citing his testimonies, we have shown Paul, hung on high and dead to the world, let us now show blessed Job fleeing the desire of outward life with the same spirit. He continues: “I have despaired,” he says, “I shall no longer live.”

There are some righteous people who seek heavenly things in such a way that they are nevertheless not at all broken in the hope of eternal things. They possess divinely granted estates for the support of necessity and retain honors temporarily bestowed upon them; they do not desire what belongs to others, and they use their own possessions lawfully. Yet they are detached from the very things they possess, because they are not held by desire for those things.

There are also some righteous people who, girded to attain the summit of perfection, seek higher things inwardly and abandon everything outwardly. They strip themselves of possessions, divest themselves of the glory of honor, and afflict themselves with continual sorrow through their desire for inward things; they do not wish to have consolation from outward things. While they draw near in mind to inward joys, they utterly kill within themselves the life of bodily pleasure.

### Zain

“‘Remember, Lord, my poverty and my transgression, my wormwood and my gall.’”

With an altered mode of expression, the prophet turns the words of prayer to the Lord himself on account of the people’s calamity, so that he who justly inflicted scourges upon sinners might extend the help of mercy to the afflicted. Because of transgression, therefore, they came into poverty and deserved to suffer the bitterness of devastation and captivity, expressed by the names “wormwood” and “gall.” But because the nature of divinity is merciful and kind, and more inclined to forgiveness than to vengeance—because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live—if anyone, after falling into sins, turns to true repentance, he will quickly obtain forgiveness of sins from the merciful Judge. The prophet also shows this in what follows, when he says:

### Zain

“‘Remembering, I will remember, and my soul shall languish within me.’”

### Zain

“‘Remembering these things in my heart, therefore I will hope [in God].’”

Whoever carefully examines himself and does not disdain to mortify his flesh and kill his desires on account of his sins ought to hope not only for forgiveness of sins but also for the heavenly reward from the true Savior and most merciful Judge, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth: “The Lord is merciful and gracious, patient and abundantly merciful” (Exod. 34:6).

Therefore the prophet, considering this unsearchable depth of God’s goodness and not being ignorant of the guilt and stubbornness of his people, immediately adds:

### Heth

“‘The mercies of the Lord are that we have not been consumed, because his compassions have not failed.’”

For the wicked and perverse nation of the Jews provoked and irritated the Lord to anger so many times that, if he had wished to judge it according to judgment and had not chosen patiently to endure it through mercy, it would long ago have perished under punishment and would have had no hope of restoration.

Isaiah also shows this when he says: “Woe to the sinful nation, the people laden with iniquity, wicked offspring, criminal children! They have forsaken the Lord; they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned backward. Upon what shall I strike you again, as you continue in transgression? Every head is sick and every heart sorrowful. From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it: wound, bruise, and swollen sore; it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” (Isa. 1:4–6). And shortly afterward: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

Hence Paul also says (Rom. 9:22–24): “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, and so forth.”

The apostle Paul discusses this passage more fully in writing to the same Romans (Rom. 11:1–2): “I say, then: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And shortly afterward: “So therefore, at this present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.”

From this it is shown that the foregoing threats spoken by the prophet Isaiah against Jerusalem and Judah are not to be referred to the time of the Babylonian captivity but to the final captivity under the Romans, when the remnants of the Jewish people were saved in the apostles, and three thousand and five thousand believed in a single day, and the Gospel was sown throughout the whole world.

The following sentence also supports this interpretation. For it continues:

### Heth

“‘They are new at dawn; your faithfulness is great.’”

The prophet is therefore speaking to the primitive Church in Jerusalem, praising its appearance. After the dawn of Christ’s resurrection, it put off the old person and manifested the beauty of the new person by its rising. Its faithfulness is also great, because, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, it called many to fellowship in the faith and to the Christian religion through the word of preaching and signs of virtue.

Hence it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 6:7): “The word of the Lord increased, and the number of the disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly; a great multitude of priests also obeyed the faith.” And again (Acts 4:32–35): “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them, brought the price of what they sold, and laid it at the feet of the apostles; it was distributed to each according as anyone had need.”

Therefore he subsequently says:

### Heth

“‘The Lord is my portion, my soul has said; therefore I will wait for him.’”

(Jerome.) The Lord’s portion is the ecclesiastical people redeemed by the blood of Christ, concerning whom Moses says in the song of Deuteronomy: “But the Lord’s portion is his people, Jacob the lot of his inheritance, Israel” (Deut. 32:9). Or rather, the Lord himself is his portion—the one whose love makes him despise all earthly things and choose to possess him alone above everything else, in whose future vision he also hopes to arrive.

In the person of this people the prophet says in the Psalms: “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (Ps. 72:26). (Cassiodorus.) “Failure” is so called because the effect is absent from it; and rightly carnal thought had failed, since it recognized that it had gone astray, but it confesses this to the one for whom revealing guilt is a remedy and confessing sins is security.

Notice that in one verse “heart” is used both for good and for evil: “My heart has failed”—that is, evil thought. “But God is the God of my heart”—that is, the author of good understanding, because no one possesses it without his grace.

God is the portion of that person who joins himself to his majesty through faith and commends himself to him by a worthy manner of life. The addition “forever” means that he promises always to cling to him. This is truly characteristic of the perfect: never to wish to depart from him without whom one continually falls into error.

### Theth

“‘The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.’” (Maurus.) The Lord is therefore good to those who hope in him, because the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy. Whoever seeks him will find him and reach blessed life. Hence the Psalmist says: “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Ps. 68:33).

Isaiah also says of him: “The saints who hope in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take wings like eagles, they shall fly and not grow weary” (Isa. 40:31). But because it is good for the one who hopes in the Lord and strives to reach his future life [or, according to the supplied reading, “vision”] to endure all adversity patiently and to pass through the present life without troubling others, he imitates the one of whom it is written: “Behold my servant; I will receive him; my chosen one, my soul has been pleased with him. I have given my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations. He shall not cry out, nor accept a person, nor shall his voice be heard outside. He shall not break a bruised reed, and he shall not extinguish smoking flax” (Isa. 42:1–3).

Therefore he says:

### Theth

“‘It is good to await silently the salvation of the Lord.’”

For the life of all good people is tranquil and peaceful, but among the proud there are always quarrels. Therefore Paul says to the Thessalonians: “We ask you, brothers, that you abound more and more, and that you make it your endeavor to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, to work with your hands as we commanded you, and to walk honorably toward those who are outside, and to desire nothing from anyone” (1 Thess. 4:10–12).

Because no one can do this perfectly unless he separates himself from the desires of the world and the affairs of the age, he continues:

### Theth

“‘It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.’”

### Iod

“‘He shall sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself.’”

The perfection of Christ’s soldiers is to have a mind withdrawn from all earthly affairs and from tumult, according to the Apostle’s saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2:4); and, insofar as human weakness permits, he hastens to unite that mind with Christ.

The good hermits and monks, who are bound by the monastic vow to the discipline of mystical life, strive to imitate this form of conduct. Yet this perfection is rare and granted by God to very few. For the person who is truly perfect, and not perfect only in part, is one who bears with equal greatness of soul both the squalor of solitude in the desert and the weaknesses of the brothers in the monastery.

Therefore it is difficult to find someone fully perfected in either profession: the anchorite cannot entirely attain contempt for and deprivation of material things, nor can the cenobite attain theoretical purity in its entirety. Yet the person who has experienced it knows how greatly the serenity of a tranquil life surpasses the turbulence of worldly conduct.

In the Gospel, the Lord distinguishes this in his judgment between two women, saying to Martha: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

Blessed David, defining this one thing as the sole necessity for human beings, desires to cling continually to God, saying: “But it is good for me to adhere to God, to place my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72:28). And elsewhere: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple” (Ps. 26:4).

There is therefore one and only one theoretical life—that is, contemplation of God—to which all the merits of righteousness and every pursuit of virtue are rightly subordinated. The active life fails with the body, but the contemplative life begins here so that it may be perfected in the heavenly homeland, because the fire of love that begins to burn here burns more intensely in love when it sees the one whom it loves.

The contemplative life is therefore not taken away; when the light of the present age is withdrawn, it is perfected. But above all, the protection of humility and patience is necessary for the servants of Christ, because whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever perseveres in the virtue of patience to the end shall be saved. Hence it follows:

### Iod

“‘He shall place his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there is hope.’”

The person who places his mouth in the dust is one who, thinking humbly, recognizes himself as fragile and confesses that he was made from dust and will return again to dust, saying with the patriarch Abraham: “I speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). He will also have hope of the future resurrection, because when he chastises himself through repentance and mortifies his flesh, he ought, through the Lord’s mercy, to possess the spirit of remission and future glory.

(Gregory.) Hence blessed Job, hearing the wise judgments of the Lord, reproves himself by recognizing that he is not wise, saying: “Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge” (Job 42:3). But since there is no knowledge of reproof if the laments of repentance do not also follow, he rightly adds after his reproof: “I repent in dust and ashes.”

To repent in dust and ashes is, after contemplating the highest essence, to recognize oneself as nothing but dust and ashes. Hence the Lord also says to the reprobate city in the Gospel: “If the miracles that have been performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11:21).

In sackcloth, harshness and contrition for sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead. Therefore both are customarily applied to repentance, so that in the piercing of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the dust of ashes discern what we have become through judgment. Let the piercing vices therefore be considered in the sackcloth, and in the ashes let the just punishment of vices that follows by the sentence of death be considered.

Because after sin the insults of the flesh arose, let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth what he did through pride, and in the ashes how far he has come by sinning. Sackcloth can also signify the piercing pain produced through recollection and repentance. For when blessed Job says, “I reproach myself,” he is pierced, as it were, by sackcloth, while his mind is rubbed by the sharp goads of reproof.

He repents in ashes because he carefully considers what he became through the just judgment of God after the first sin, saying: “I repent in dust and ashes.” As if he were plainly saying: “I take no pride in any gift of my Creator, because, having been taken from dust, I recognize that through the sentence of death inflicted upon me I must return to dust.” And because patience must accompany humility, the present prophet says:

### Iod

“‘He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches.’” (Maurus.) Thus he fulfills the Gospel command that says: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

David shows that those who return evil for evil, tooth for tooth, and eye for eye are also at fault, saying: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:5). Therefore the apostolic command is to be observed more faithfully: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Matt. 5:44; Rom. 12:20–21).

And because, beyond the calamity of this world, the Lord’s mercy will lift his elect from present tribulation, it follows:

### Caph

“‘For the Lord will not reject forever.’”

### Caph

“‘For if he has cast down, he will also have mercy, according to the multitude of his mercies.’”

The Lord does not reject forever those who wish to correct themselves and restrain themselves from sins. For if he has cast them down for a time and justly permitted them to be chastised by enemies, he again grants a benefit to those who have turned back, according to the multitude of his mercies.

A similar statement is found in David’s Psalms (Ps. 102:9–11): “The Lord will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant for eternity. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities; for according to the height of heaven above the earth, the Lord has confirmed his mercy over those who fear him.”

(Cassiodorus.) He will not be angry forever with those who, through devout satisfaction, recognize themselves, who love to return to him, and who despise the seductions of the age together with their author. Conversely, he will be angry forever with those to whom he will say: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

Great is the unhappiness of perishing under a merciful Lord. Do not delay in making satisfaction to the one before whom you recognize that you have gone astray, especially since you will not find your supplication empty if you recognize that you have offered it with an undivided heart.

This may also be understood of the Jewish people, whose conversion is known to occur at the end of the age. Concerning them the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and so all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

But when he says, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins,” the sentence is general, because there is no one who does not possess his grace freely, since the law has enclosed everything under sin, as the Apostle testifies: “God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32).

Nevertheless, he gives the spirit alike to the good and the wicked, grants salvation, removes necessities, and is universally good. To those who implore him he is so compassionate that he considers himself especially worthy to absolve a person when each one, having made satisfaction, strives to condemn himself.

The statement that the Lord’s mercy is so much greater than the merits of his faithful as the summit of heaven can be raised above the earth signifies this: just as heaven covers the earth and in its seasons grants fitting benefits to human beings—now pouring down rains, now providing fair weather, now tempering the air itself with health-giving winds—so the Lord’s mercy is known to bestow diverse benefits upon our frailty.

He sustains in order to correct, scourges in order to instruct, tests in order to grant benefits; and through the various works of his benefits his one will is to help sinners. But so that the force of the entire sentence may be understood, it must be stated briefly: if it is possible for heaven not to cover the earth, then it can be possible for the Lord not to protect those who serve him with complete purity.

### Caph

“‘For he has not humbled from his heart, nor cast away the sons of men.’” (Maurus.) The Lord did not so despise the human race from his heart and cast it away from the administration of his consolation that he would no longer wish to care for it because of its transgressions or sustain it through the help of his kindness. Rather, because of his goodness, he endures them with great patience, so that from vessels of wrath he may make vessels of mercy, because “the Lord is merciful and gracious, patient and abundantly merciful.”

Another Scripture says of him: “You have mercy on all, Lord, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance. For you love all things that exist, and hate nothing that you have made; nor did you establish anything while hating it” (Ps. 144; Wis. 11:23–26). How could anything remain unless you had willed it? Or how could anything that had not been called by you be preserved?

But you spare all things because they are yours, Lord, lover of souls. Your spirit is good and gentle in all things; therefore you correct those who go astray little by little and admonish them concerning the things by which they sin, so that, abandoning wickedness, they may believe in you, Lord.

Therefore it must in no way be thought that the most merciful Creator is the cause of the destruction of wicked people who refused to turn to God through repentance. Rather, each person will perish in his own sin: “For each person is bound by the cords of his sins, and the soul that sins shall itself die” (Prov. 5:22; Ezek. 18:4).

(Jerome.) That sins are called bonds we read frequently; among these is the Psalmist’s statement: “The cords of sinners have encircled me” (Ps. 118:61). And Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag sins as with a long rope.”

The Lord, reproving the delinquent people who had joined sin to sin, made a whip from cords, showing them how they had made the house of God a den of robbers and had turned the house of prayer into a house of commerce (John 2:15–16). The man who entered the banquet of the Lord’s supper without a wedding garment is likewise cast out, with his feet and hands bound, into the outer darkness.

And the Lord came to say to those who were in bonds, “Come out,” and to those who were dwelling in darkness, “Be revealed.” For he “releases those who are bound and gives light to the blind.” Jeremiah now calls them “bound to the earth,” saying:

Lamed. “To crush beneath his feet all the prisoners of the earth.” Nor are those to be lamented who began to sin and immediately ceased. “For there is no one on earth who does good and never sins” (Eccles. VII), but only one who has prolonged his sins with a long cord.

Hence, too, we read in Numbers (Num. XIX) that the red heifer, whose ashes are the people’s expiation, may be slain and offered upon the Lord’s altar only if it has performed no earthly work, has not borne a yoke, and has not been bound by the bonds of Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke. And in the prophet Isaiah, the daughters of Zion are girded with a cord instead of the belt of truth (Isa. III). Ahithophel and Judas also, one of whom betrayed David and the other the Lord (2 Kings XVII; Matt. XXVII), dragging their sins with a very long cord, perished by hanging, supposing that the evil of conscience would be ended by present death and that nothing existed after death.

(MAURUS.) The Lord’s judgment will in no way err, nor does anything happen on earth without cause. He condemns no one unjustly, rejects no one, and abandons no one without due reason, because he arranges, orders, and governs all things by number, measure, and weight. Nor should it in any way be believed, according to the opinion of the heretics, that anything in human affairs happens through the ignorance of its author. The following statement seems to have this meaning.

Lamed. “To turn aside the judgment of a man before the face of the Most High.”

Lamed. “To pervert a man in his judgment—the Lord did not know.” [Col. 1231C]

Something similar is also found in the Book of Job in the words of Eliphaz, where it is written: “Do you not think that God is higher than heaven and exalted above the summit of the stars (Job XXII)? And you say: ‘What does God know? Does he judge as though through a fog? Clouds are his hiding place, and he does not consider our affairs; he walks around the hinges of heaven?’”

(Greg.) There are many so dull that they know how to fear only what they see bodily. Hence they do not fear God, whom they cannot see. But because the heretics consider themselves wise, they utter words of mockery against Catholics and suppose that Catholics do not fear the one whom they cannot see bodily. As though through sluggishness of perception, they imagine that their author, because he is higher than heaven and exalted above the summits of the stars, cannot see from such a distance; and because regions of air lie between us and the heavenly dwelling, they suppose that, hidden in a cloud, he judges through a fog and, occupied with what is above, pays less attention to what is below; and that, while he surrounds and encompasses the hinges of heaven, he does not see what is within.

But who, even in his folly, would imagine such things of God? Though he is always omnipotent, he attends to all things in such a way that he is present to each, and he is present to each in such a way that he is never absent from all at once. For even if he abandons certain sinners, he is nevertheless present to those very people through judgment, though he is seen to be absent from them in assistance. [Col. 1231D]

Thus he encompasses outward things while filling inward things; he fills inward things while encompassing outward things; he governs the highest without abandoning the lowest; he is present to the lowest without withdrawing from the highest; he is hidden in his appearance and yet recognized in his activity; he is recognized in his work and yet cannot be grasped by the understanding of the one who recognizes him; he is present though he cannot be seen; and though he cannot be seen, his very judgments bear witness to his presence. He makes himself intelligible to us, yet veils from us the very ray of our understanding of him; and again, he restrains us with the darkness of ignorance, yet flashes into our minds with the rays of his brightness, so that the mind, lifted up, may see something, and, struck by the brilliance, may tremble; and because it cannot see him as he is, it may come to know him to some extent through seeing. [Col. 1232A]

But the heretics do not think that the holy Church knows these things, because in their foolish judgment they suppose that they alone are wise. Therefore this prophet immediately rebukes those who hold such opinions, saying:

Mem. “Who is this who said that something should happen when the Lord did not command it?”

Mem. “From the mouth of the Most High there do not proceed either good things or evil things.”

Mem. “Why has a living man murmured—a man because of his sins?”

(MAURUS.) There were heretics who said that God does not make evil things, contrary to what is written: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil [calamity]” (Isa. XLV). Conversely, there were others who said that God created evil things, contrary to what is written: “God made all things good” (Eccles. III). There were still others who said that from the beginning there had been two natures and two substances, namely, a good one and an evil one, although every nature is either the Creator or a creature. It is therefore false that any nature is evil, since the supreme and good Creator created a good creature, because “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. I).

Figuratively, therefore, God is said to make evil things—that is, to inflict adversity upon those who suffer—in accordance with what is written in Isaiah: “I am the Lord, and there is no other: forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil; I am the Lord, making all these things. I am,” he says, “the Lord, and there is no other outside me.” [Col. 1232B]

Apart from my word, reason, power, and wisdom, which is in me, there is no other God. “I have made these things,” so that the whole world, from east to west, may recognize that there is no other God besides me: “I am the Lord, and there is no other.” [Col. 1232C]

For the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, who says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X). In the Book of Ezra it is recorded that Cyrus wrote to all the nations that there is no God except the one God of Israel; or this may be understood to mean that the release of the captives and God’s mercy toward his people made God better known to all nations.

Therefore, the one who gave you strength and is himself the only God makes within himself things that are contrary to one another: light and darkness, that is, day and night; peace and evil, that is, leisure and war. By these he signifies that he was angry with his people when they endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of servitude, and again that he had mercy when they were sent back to their homeland and received peace and joy. Just as darkness is contrary to light, so war is contrary to peace. [Col. 1232D]

Hence, too, the heresy that considers God the creator of evil should be confounded, since here “evil” is not placed as the contrary of good but for affliction and war, in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matt. VI).

[Hieron.] Evils that have no existence by their own nature are not created by the Lord. Rather, the Lord designates the evils of his creature when he turns things that were well created into a scourge for us because of our evil actions. Thus those things are evils to sinners through the pain by which they strike them, while they are good through the nature by which they exist: poison, for example, is death to a human being but life to a serpent. [Col. 1233A]

For through love of present things we withdrew from love of our Creator; and when the perverse mind subjected itself to the pleasure of the creature, it separated itself from the fellowship of the Creator. It therefore had to be struck by the author through these very things, because in its error it had placed the author second, so that from the very source of its prideful refusal to fear guilt it might find corrective punishment; and so that it might turn back more quickly to what it had lost, the more clearly it saw that what it had sought had become the punishment of its pain.

(MAURUS.) “Who is this,” he says, “who said that something should happen when the Lord did not command it?” Nothing happens in the world except at God’s command or permission. Through mercy he heals those whom he wills, and in just judgment permits to perish those whom he does not choose to heal. [Col. 1233B]

Therefore a human being murmurs in vain against his Maker, who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. It is consequently better for us to follow the prophet’s admonition, by which he exhorts us, saying:

Nun. “Let us examine our ways, seek them out, and return to the Lord.”

Nun. “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven.”

It should be understood that whenever anyone disagrees in conduct with the Lord’s commandments, he is reproved and confounded in his heart whenever he hears them, because he is reminded of what he has done. For in whatever he recognizes that he has gone astray, his own conscience secretly accuses him.

Hence the prophet David prays, saying: “Then I shall not be confounded when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). A person is gravely confounded when he looks upon God’s commandments, whether by reading or hearing them, after having despised them in his life. [Col. 1233C]

Thus, too, the voice of John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask from him we shall receive” (1 John III); as though he were saying: If we do what he commands, we shall obtain what we ask.

For before the Lord these two things necessarily correspond with one another: prayer must be supported by action, and action by prayer. Hence Jeremiah now also says: “Let us examine our ways, seek them out, and return to the Lord; let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven.”

To examine our ways is to investigate the interior of our thoughts. A person lifts up his heart with his hands when he strengthens his prayer by his works. For whoever prays but refuses to act lifts up his heart but does not lift up his hands; whoever acts but does not pray lifts up his hands but does not lift up his heart. [Col. 1233D]

Accordingly, in keeping with John’s statement, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it, and the practice of good works accords with prayer.

Nun. “We have acted wickedly and provoked you to anger; therefore you are inexorable.”

Because of the people’s sins and their many transgressions, by which they provoked the Lord to anger from the beginning, they deserved to be destroyed together with the city. They were no longer worthy of pardon, since they despised the Son of God when he came to them and treated him with such contempt, as another prophet shows when he says: “Because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people are a reproach to all those around us.”

We, too, must therefore fear lest, if we despise God’s commandments and disobey the Gospel of Christ, we should experience the harsh retribution of Gehenna, since we do not wish to be corrected from sins toward righteousness. For the Apostle says (Hebr. X): “When we sin willingly after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains for us; rather, there is a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal [or accumulation] of fire that will consume the adversaries.” And again: “Anyone who rejects the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you suppose, will be deserved by the one who has trampled upon the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant—by which he was sanctified—unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” [Col. 1234A]

It continues:

Samech. “You have covered us in fury, struck us, killed us, and shown no mercy.”

Whenever God’s fury or anger is mentioned in Scripture, it expresses not a disturbance of mind but just vengeance in the punishment of the one who suffers. God is by nature pious, always good and peaceful; he is always the same, and his years do not fail. Of him it is written elsewhere: “But you, Lord of all, judge with tranquility and order all things” (Wis. XII). Therefore, when he strikes or kills anyone and does not spare him, he experiences no disturbance within himself; rather, remaining tranquil and peaceful, he compels the guilty to pay the punishments they deserve. [Col. 1234B]

Concerning this it is further added:

Samech. “You have placed a cloud before yourself, so that prayer may not pass through.”

God is said to place a cloud before himself when he declines to hear the thankless prayers of those who petition him. A cloud therefore seems to be placed before prayer when the mind is enveloped in a certain darkness and blindness, and does not deserve to be illuminated by the ray of divine contemplation. [Col. 1234C]

(Greg.) When God is not sought in prayer, the soul soon grows weary in prayer. For when a person asks for things that, according to God’s hidden judgment, he perhaps refuses to grant, the one who does not wish to give what is loved becomes burdensome to the petitioner as well.

The Lord, Creator of the universe, wishes to be loved more than the things he created, and wishes eternal things to be sought rather than earthly ones, since the Truth himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

For he did not say “they will be given,” but “they will be added.” He clearly judges that one thing is given as primary and another is added in addition. Since eternity should be our intention and temporality our use, the former is given and the latter is certainly added out of abundance. [Col. 1234D]

Yet often, while people ask in prayer for good temporal things and do not seek eternal rewards, they ask for what is added and do not desire that to which it should be added. They do not consider it a gain from their petition if they are temporally poor here but live eternally rich in blessedness there. Intent only upon visible things, they refuse to purchase invisible ones through the labor of petition; but if they sought heavenly things, they would already be performing their labor with profit. [Col. 1235A]

Hence James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask badly, so that you may spend it on your desires” (James I). He had said beforehand that they did not ask, and then he says that they ask badly, because one who asks badly seems, in the sight of the inward witness, to ask for nothing.

He asks badly who, while despising the Lord’s commands, desires heavenly benefits from the Lord. He also asks badly who, having lost love for heavenly things, seeks only to receive lower goods—not for the support of human weakness but for the overflow of unrestrained pleasure. This is what he means by “so that you may spend it on your desires.”

Samech. “You have made me an eradication and an outcast in the sight of the peoples.” [Col. 1235B]

(MAURUS.) The Jewish people assert that they were uprooted and cast away because in the Chaldean captivity they were often crushed for their crimes: first under Jehoiakim, then under Jeconiah, and third under Zedekiah, when the city was devastated, the temple burned, and the walls destroyed. Finally, the survivors who had been left by Nabuzardan, commander of the army, under Gedaliah to inhabit the land, contrary to the Lord’s command—which he had delivered to them through the prophet—went to Egypt and perished there among the nations.

In the Roman captivity, the entire city and land were so devastated and the people so scattered that they had no further hope of restoration; their desolation would continue to the end. [Col. 1235C]

Mystically, however, a sinful soul established among the peoples suffers uprooting and rejection from the Lord when it is so stripped of its virtues by evil spirits and so weakened in the root of faith that it is exposed not to honor but to everyone’s mockery. Its enemies themselves dominate it and taunt the deceived soul, because it is forced to endure, according to its merits, the punishments that Holy Scripture foretold to it and the snare of perdition.

Hence it follows:

Phe. “All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.”

Phe. “Terror and a snare have become for us prophecy and destruction.”

For the enemies then open their mouths against sinners when, as debtors, they hasten to devour them through various mutilations and torments. They show them no mercy and spare them nothing, but strive to cast them into the terror of punishments and the snare of perdition, in accordance with what the prophetic word foretold to sinners. [Col. 1235D]

Hence the prophet then lamented the destruction of his people in many ways, and now the holy Church unceasingly mourns the ruin of sinful souls, as is shown in the following statement.

Phe. “My eye has poured out streams of water because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

The prophet therefore declares that he has drawn streams of water from his eyes because of the destruction of the daughter of his people: he wept both over the perversity of her heart and over her ruin in sins and her destruction in devastation. So also now the company of the elect pours forth many sighs over a soul lost in sins, because it sees that she has gone astray in various crimes and strives with all its strength to see how it may be able to call her back from the wickedness she has embraced. [Col. 1236A]

Here it should be noted that the compunction of the elect is not always one and the same, but that their souls are pierced in different ways according to the variety of circumstances. For not every outpouring of tears arises from one feeling or one virtue.

One kind of weeping flows forth when the thorn of sins pricks our heart. Of this it is said: “I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; I shall water my couch with my tears.”

Another kind arises from contemplation of eternal goods and desire for that future love. From it still more abundant springs of tears burst forth because of the intolerable joy and immense gladness, while our soul thirsts for God, the living fountain, saying with the Prophet: “When shall I come and appear before the presence of God?” (Ps. CXIX.) “My tears have been my bread day and night,” as I cried out daily with wailing and lamentation: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged, and that my soul has been a sojourner for so long.” [Col. 1236B]

Tears of another kind flow without any consciousness of such crimes, yet arise from fear of Gehenna and remembrance of that terrible judgment. Struck by its terror, the Prophet prays to God: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII).

There is also another kind of tears, produced not by one’s own conscience but by the hardness and sins of another. Samuel is described as having wept for that city, Jerusalem; the Lord is also described in the Gospel as having wept for it; and Jeremiah in earlier times wept, saying: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?” (Jer. IX.) [Col. 1236C]

Or certainly, such are the tears of which the hundred-and-first Psalm sings: “For I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI). It is certain that these did not arise from the same feeling as those in the sixth Psalm, which emerge from the person of the penitent, but from anxiety about this life and the troubles and distresses by which the righteous, placed in this world, are oppressed. This is shown clearly not only by the text of that Psalm but also by its title, which is described from the person of that poor man of whom the Gospel says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V): “The prayer of the poor man when he is troubled and pours out his prayer before God.” [Col. 1236D]

The tears just mentioned therefore differ greatly from those extracted from dry eyes by a hardened heart. Although we believe that they are not entirely fruitless—for their emission is attempted with a good purpose—this outpouring of tears should not be forced from those who have not yet been able either to attain perfect knowledge or to be completely cleansed of the stain of their former or present vices. Still less should it be forced from those who have already passed into the disposition of the virtues.

Nor should the weeping of the outward person be pursued with excessive effort. Even if such tears are produced, they can never attain fully to the abundance of spontaneous tears. Rather, by distracting the suppliant’s mind through their own efforts, they humble it, plunge it into merely human concerns, and bring it down from that heavenly height in which the astonished mind of the one praying ought to remain steadfastly fixed. Once the intensity of its prayer has slackened, the mind begins to suffer over sterile and forced drops of tears. [Col. 1237A]

Ain. “My eye was afflicted and did not keep silent, because there was no rest.”

Ain. “Until the Lord looked down and saw from heaven.”

The prophet teaches us to possess urgency and perseverance in prayer. Whoever wishes to attain what he desires must not turn his mind away from the pursuit of prayer but must persevere more firmly in the intention he has begun.

Hence it is written in the Book of Kings concerning Hannah “that after she had prayed, her face was no longer turned in different directions” (1 Kings I). Hence also in the Gospel (Luke XVIII), that blind man who had heard Jesus passing through Jericho asked him to have mercy on him. When those going before Jesus ordered him to be silent, he cried out all the more, saying: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” [Col. 1237B]

(Greg.) Thus he deserved to receive from the Savior the light he had requested. But whom do those who precede the approaching Jesus signify except the crowds of carnal desires and the tumult of vices? Before Jesus comes to our heart, they scatter our thoughts with their temptations and disturb the voices of our heart in prayer.

Often, when we wish to turn back to God after committing vices, and when we try to pray against those very vices we have committed, the images of the sins we have done come before the heart. They strike back at the vision of our mind, confuse the soul, and suppress the voice of supplication.

Those who went before Jesus therefore rebuked the blind man and ordered him to be silent, because before Jesus comes to our heart, the evils we have done, striking our thoughts with their images, disturb us in our very prayer. Behold, the one whom the crowd rebukes for being silent cries out more and more, because the heavier the tumult of carnal thoughts presses upon us, the more ardently we must persist in prayer. [Col. 1237C]

The crowd contradicts us so that we may not cry out, because we often suffer the images of our sins even in prayer. Yet it is necessary that the voice of our heart, the more harshly it is repelled, should persist with greater force, so that it may overcome the tumult of unlawful thought and burst forth, through the excess of its importunity, to the merciful ears of the Lord.

Behold, the one who had been passing by stands still, because while we still suffer the crowds of images in prayer, we sense Jesus as somehow passing by. But when we persist vigorously in prayer, Jesus stands still to restore the light, because God is fixed in the heart and the lost light is restored. [Col. 1237D]

Jesus therefore hears the blind man crying out as he passes by and illuminates him when he stands still: through his humanity he had compassion on the voices of our blindness, while through the power of his divinity he infused us with the light of grace.

And notice what he says to the blind man who approaches: “What do you want me to do for you?” Did the one who could restore light not know what the blind man wanted? Rather, he wishes the man to ask for what he already knows both that we will ask and that he will grant.

For he urges us insistently to prayer, saying: “Your heavenly Father knows what you need” before you ask. He asks, therefore, so that the request may be made; he asks so that the heart may be stirred to prayer.

Hence the blind man immediately adds: “Lord, that I may see.” Behold, the blind man asks the Lord not for gold but for light. He considers it insignificant to seek anything outside the light, because even if a blind man can possess something, without light he cannot see what he possesses. [Col. 1238A]

Let us therefore imitate the one whom we have heard to have been saved both bodily and spiritually. Let us ask the Lord not for false riches, earthly gifts, or fleeting honors, but for light. Nor let us seek the light that is confined to a place, ended by time, altered by the interruptions of night, and seen by us in common with animals. Let us seek the light that we may see together with the angels, which neither beginning initiates nor ending confines. Faith is the way to that light.

(MAURUS.) Hence the reply made immediately to the blind man after he was illuminated is fitting: “See; your faith has saved you.” Whoever asks in full faith for what is beneficial will in no way be deprived of its fruit.

For the Lord looks down from heaven, receives the prayers of his faithful petitioner, and will save him because he has hoped in him. The Truth himself says: “Amen, I say to you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it will be done for you” (Mark XI). [Col. 1238B]

And because harmful desire often enters the mind through the sight of the eyes, it follows:

Ain. “My eye has plundered my soul among all the daughters of my city.”

He now gives the reason why he had said that his eye was afflicted because there was no rest: when, through carelessness, sight has opened an entrance to temptation, the troubled mind will scarcely find tranquility unless the gaze of divine mercy comes to its aid.

Hence blessed Job says (Job XIII): “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin.”

(Greg.) So that he might preserve the thoughts of his heart chastely, he made a covenant with his eyes, lest he first look carelessly upon what he would later love inwardly. For what the flesh drags downward is exceedingly powerful; once the appearance of a form has been fastened to the heart through the eyes, it is scarcely loosened except by the hand of a great struggle. [Col. 1238C]

Therefore, so that we may not turn slippery things over in our thoughts, we must take precautions, because it is not fitting to look upon what it is not permitted to desire. To preserve a pure mind in thought, the eyes must be restrained from the wantonness of their pleasure, as though they were robbers leading us into guilt.

For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree unless she had first looked upon it carelessly. It is written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Gen. III).

From this we should consider how carefully we must restrain our sight from unlawful things, we who live a mortal life, since even the mother of the living came through her eyes to death. [Col. 1238D]

Hence also now, in the voice of Judea, which by seeing outward things desired them and lost inward goods, the Prophet says: “My eye has plundered my soul.” By desiring visible things, it lost invisible virtues. Having therefore lost its inward fruit through outward sight, it suffered the plunder of the heart through the bodily eye.

Accordingly, to preserve purity of heart, we must also maintain discipline over the outward senses. However strong the mind may be in virtue, however firm in seriousness, the carnal senses nevertheless make a childish racket outwardly; and unless they are restrained by the weight of inward seriousness and by a kind of youthful vigor, they drag the enfeebled mind toward every fleeting and trivial thing. [Col. 1239A]

Up to this point the prophet, in the voice of one lamenting, has bewailed the ruin of his people, or of the sinful soul. Now he is about to introduce another person, who likewise laments his oppression, but differs in saying that it was inflicted gratuitously and without cause. This cannot in any way, by way of interpretation, be transferred to the sinner who suffers deserved punishments.

We must therefore understand, under the person of the prophet himself, the person of some just man—or rather, of our true Josiah, namely, the Lord and Savior himself. He is rightly called “the salvation of the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord,” because it is written of him: “He will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I). And the Prophet says of him: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Ps. CXVII).

His enemies therefore persecuted him without cause, since, finding no reason for death in him, they asked Pilate that he be killed. Hence it follows: [Col. 1239B]

Sade. “My enemies hunted me like a bird; they seized me without cause.”

(MAURUS.) The Lord himself is signified by the name “bird.” Although he was born on earth from a virgin mother, he nevertheless always sought heavenly things through his teaching and example, and continually lifted his members toward what is above by faith and hope as though by two wings, saying in the Gospel: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII). And again: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI). And again: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI).

Concerning this bird it is written in Job (Job XVIII): “The bird did not know the path, nor did it behold the eyes of the vulture.” [Col. 1239C]

(Greg.) Who is signified in this passage by the name “bird” except the one who, by ascending into the heavens, lifted aloft the fleshly body he had assumed? He is aptly also expressed by the name “vulture.”

When a vulture flies and sees a carcass lying below, it descends to eat the carcass; and often it is caught in death while coming down from the heights toward the dead animal. Thus our Mediator and Redeemer is rightly signified by the name “vulture.” Remaining in the height of his divinity, he saw from a kind of sublime flight the carcass of our mortality below, and lowered himself from the heavens to what was beneath.

He deigned to become human for our sake; and while he sought the dead animal, he found among us death, though he himself was immortal. But the eye of this vulture was the very intention of our resurrection, because, having died for three days, he freed us from eternal death. [Col. 1239D]

That faithless people—the Jews—saw him as mortal but paid no attention to the fact that by his death he would destroy our death. They did indeed see the vulture, but they did not behold the eyes of the vulture. By refusing to consider the ways of his humility, through which he lifted us to the heights, they did not know the path of the bird. They did not take care to weigh the fact that his humility would raise us to heavenly things and that the purpose of his death would restore us to life.

They therefore did not know the path of the bird and did not behold the eyes of the vulture: although they saw the one whom they held in death, they refused to see how much glory for our life would follow from his death. Hence they also burned with cruelty in their persecution, refused to receive the words of life, and drove away the preachers of the kingdom of heaven by prohibiting, raging, and striking them. [Col. 1240A]

Sade. “My life has slipped into a pit, and they placed a stone over me.”

(MAURUS.) After saying above that he had been captured in the hunt like a bird, he now adds that his life had slipped into a pit and that a stone had been placed over it.

What is it for life to slip into a pit except for bodily life to come all the way to decline? Christ’s life therefore slipped into a pit when his flesh reached the point of death. They placed a stone over him when, after he had been buried, they asked Pilate to order the tomb to be guarded, lest his disciples should come and steal him.

When Pilate replied, “You have a guard; go and guard it as you know how,” they went away and secured the tomb, sealing the stone together with the guards (Matt. XXVII). [Col. 1240B]

The name “pit” may also be understood as designating either hell or the profound calamity of this world. A pit is so called because its bottom is hidden when it is enclosed on all sides as a single hollow. Its level surface flatters the eyes with a deceptive tranquility, but conceals how deep it is.

Hence it is also written in the Psalm: “They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Ps. LXXXVII).

[Cassiod.] The pit, as we have said, stands for hell, for a burial hollow, and for the deepest calamity of this world. This is what he wished to be understood here: his persecutors placed him in the despised condition of death, so that, although they unjustly established that he was dead, they would not believe that he would be avenged. They left him in darkness—that is, under the blindness of oblivion—passed over and forgotten, with no one to seek him and no one to save him. [Col. 1240C]

The phrase “in the shadow of death” indicates the place of sinners, because the shadowy and dark spirits of the dead among the guilty endure this condition: joy does not shine upon them, and they are submerged in the perpetual darkness of their sadness. [Col. 1240D]

### Ṣade

“Waters flooded over my head; I said, ‘I am lost.’”

(Gregory.) In Holy Scripture, water sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit, sometimes sacred knowledge, sometimes erroneous knowledge, sometimes tribulation, sometimes peoples flowing away, and sometimes the minds of those who follow the faith. Through water, indeed, the infusion of the Holy Spirit is signified, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). The Evangelist, following this, added: “Now he said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

Again, sacred knowledge is signified through water, as it is said: “He gave them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 15). Erroneous knowledge, too, is sometimes called water, as when the woman in Solomon who bears the type of heresy beguiles with crafty persuasions, saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Proverbs 9).

The name “waters” is therefore sometimes understood as tribulations, as the Psalmist says: “Save me, God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Psalm 68). Peoples are designated by water, as John says: “The waters are peoples” (Revelation 17). Through water are signified not only the flowing current of peoples running onward, but also the minds of the good who follow the teachings of the faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isaiah 32). And the Psalmist says: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Psalm 28).

The waters, therefore, flooded over the Redeemer’s head when the seditious peoples of the Jews, stirring up persecution, disparaged the Redeemer’s divinity. The head of Christ is God, as the Apostle testifies. Out of envy, the Jews said to Pilate: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19).

[Cassiodorus.] Every sound mind confesses that Christ’s divinity is incapable of suffering. Yet he assumed our weakness, which could have been subject to destruction. Hence it is written here: “I said, ‘I am lost,’” that is, “I have reached the point of death.”

Accordingly, by that very dispensation he cries out in the Psalms, saying: “Save me, God, for the waters have entered even to my soul,” so that, since he ought not to flee from death, which he willingly endured, his humanity might more swiftly be saved through the aid of the resurrection. For he suffered because he willed to suffer. Martyrs suffer, but unwillingly. Thus the Lord himself said to the apostle Peter: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21).

The reason is now given why he asked to be saved: namely, because the waters had entered even to his soul. The waters must be understood as the uprisings of the populace and the agitation of the peoples, as divine Scripture often testifies. Thus it says: “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive like water.” And it continues: “The torrent passed over our soul; perhaps the water beyond endurance would have passed over our soul” (Psalm 123).

Therefore that Jewish people entered even to the soul of the Lord and Savior when, with criminal intent, it dared to crucify him. And because, having died on the cross, he descended to plunder hell, it continues:

### Qoph

“I called upon your name from the deepest pit.”

(Maurus.) For what should we understand by “the deepest pit” except the lower hell? Of it the Psalm says: “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell” (Psalm 85). Concerning this pit another prophet speaks to the Redeemer himself, saying: “But you, by the blood of your covenant, have brought out your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zechariah 9).

Our Redeemer therefore invoked the Lord’s name from the deepest pit when, in the power of his divinity, he descended to the dead; after breaking the prison-bars of Tartarus, he rescued his own whom he found there and ascended victoriously to the heights.

(Cassiodorus.) It is not unreasonable, perhaps, to think that hell is beneath the earth, since in the Old Testament we read concerning Dathan and Abiram: “The earth opened itself and swallowed them, and they went down alive into hell” (Numbers 16). But by what route souls are transferred there remains uncertain to us, since it is not stated in divine authority.

That hell has a lower region is attested by the Gospel passage which says that, when the impious rich man was being tormented by avenging flame, he lifted up his eyes and saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16). From this it appears that both were in hell, since they were able to see one another, and that the rich man lifted his eyes from a lower place to higher regions.

Although both seemed to be in hell, however, the teacher Augustine judges that, according to the distinction of their merits, the higher place should be assigned to the saints and the lower to sinners. Blessed Job also says: “All that I have will descend into the deepest hell” (Job 17), since it is evident that the righteous were held among the dead not in places of punishment but in the higher bosom of repose.

(Gregory.) A great question arises for us concerning what blessed Job means when he asserts: “All that I have will descend into the deepest hell.” For although he was going to descend into hell before the coming of the Mediator of God and humanity, it is nevertheless clear that he was not going to descend into the deepest hell.

Or do they call those higher regions of hell “the deepest,” because, in relation to the height of heaven, this expanse of air may rightly be called hell?
