Thus, since the apostate angels have been plunged from the heavenly seats into this dark air, the apostle Peter says: “God did not spare the sinning angels, but, having dragged them down with the ropes of hell, committed them to Tartarus, reserving them to be tormented at the judgment” (2 Peter 2).

If, then, in relation to the height of heaven this dark air is hell, in relation to the height of that same air the earth, which lies below, can also be understood as hell and as deep. In relation, however, to the height of that same earth, those regions of the lower world which are higher than the other receptacles of hell may here appropriately be designated by the expression “the deepest hell.” What air is to heaven and earth is to air, that higher bosom of hell is to the earth.

But it is very surprising that he adds: “All that I have will descend.” Since only the soul was going to descend to the regions below, what does the holy man mean by asserting that all that he has will descend there? Only that he saw himself to be wholly present where he understood the weight of recompense to be. For he abandons in the earth what in himself was insensible, until he returns to the incorruption of the resurrection; he does not perceive himself to exist.

He therefore asserts that all that he has will descend into the deepest hell, although he sees that only his soul will descend, because he is wholly there where he can feel what he is to receive. Or certainly, all that he has descends into hell because the recompense for all his labors was still confined to hell: he awaited its reception, and, as it were, everything he had done descended there, since there he found the repose of his recompense in respect of everything.

Hence the very repose for which he waits is added when it immediately continues: “Do you think that there will at least be rest for me there?” These words make clear what he desires, yet they also show that he is still uncertain about receiving rest—lest, after his holy deeds had been followed by so many scourges, enduring torments should follow his temporal scourges by the hidden judgment of the heavenly Judge.

In this matter we must consider with great fear which of us can now be secure about eternal rest, if even he still trembles concerning it whose virtues and praises both he himself and the Judge who strikes him proclaim.

“For if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the impious and sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4.)

Blessed Job knew that he would reach rest after his scourges. Yet, in order to shake our hearts with fear, he appears to doubt the recompense of eternal rest when he says, “Do you think”—so that we may understand how greatly we ought always to dread the coming judgment, since even he who was praised by the testimony of the Judge was not yet secure in his own words concerning the judgment’s recompense.

### Qoph

“You heard my voice; do not turn your ear away from my sobbing and cries.”

The divinity of the Lord heard the voice of his incarnation, because the salvation of the human race, which he requested according to his humanity, he granted according to his divinity. Therefore he says to the Father in the Gospel: “Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me; but I said this for the sake of the people standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me” (John 17).

“Do not turn your ear,” he says, “away from my sobbing and cries.” If we refer these words to the Lord himself, it was impossible for the Father to turn his ear away from his sobbing and cries, since he fulfilled everything he requested with the swiftest efficacy.

He wept, therefore, at Lazarus’s tomb and cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Lazarus, come out!” And immediately the man who had been dead came forth (John 11). Elsewhere, when he healed a deaf and mute man, he “looked up to heaven, groaned, and said, ‘Ephphatha’; and immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly” (Mark 7).

If it seems absurd to anyone to apply these words to the person of the Lord because it is written in Isaiah: “He will not cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Isaiah 53), and again: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth,” let him nevertheless know that elsewhere it is written concerning his person: “I have labored in crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Psalm 68).

[Cassiodorus.] Both statements, therefore, are true, and both were fulfilled. He was silent when he was handed over, so that his plan might reach its saving conclusion for the world; and he cried out openly: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17). Or this: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke 22); and again: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid.).

At that time too he labored in crying out, when he said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees! Woe to the world because of scandals!” and similar things. He labored in crying out when he was not heard by the faithless. Labor signifies a cry that goes unheard, because we do not say that those who have fulfilled their desire are laboring.

Thus it follows: “My throat has become hoarse.” When hoarseness takes possession of our throats, our words reach other ears in a confused manner. He rightly says, therefore, that his throat had become hoarse, because the sacrilegious people did not listen at all to his words.

(Maurus.) If, however, we understand these words as referring to his members, there is no doubt that they were heard. The martyrs themselves, although they were not heard according to their immediate desire on the day of their passion, were nevertheless completely heard unto eternal salvation, because from there they reached the eternal crown.

Hence it continues:

### Qoph

“You drew near on the day when I called upon you; you said, ‘Do not fear.’”

The divinity of the Savior drew near to his humanity when, through a sudden resurrection, it caused that humanity, according to its desire, to triumph over death.

Alternatively, the Lord drew near to his servants when they were afflicted and delivered them from their necessities, because he rescued their souls from the fear of the enemy. Thus they themselves prayed in Psalm 63: “Hear, God, my prayer when I am afflicted; rescue my soul from the fear of the enemy.”

(Augustine.) They were therefore heard and killed, and yet they were rescued from their enemies. Others, fearing, consented and lived, and yet they themselves were swallowed by their enemies. Hence comes the voice of thanksgiving: “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

Many were swallowed alive, many were swallowed dead. Those who thought the Christian faith empty were swallowed dead. But those who knew the preaching to be true—that Christ is the Son of God—and who believed this and held it inwardly, yet yielded to suffering and sacrificed to idols, were swallowed alive.

This, then, is what the martyrs’ voice prays: “Rescue my soul from the fear of the enemy,” not so that the enemy may not kill me, but so that I may not fear the one who kills. In the Psalm the servant prays to fulfill what the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna.”

Therefore, with certainty concerning future recompense, the voice follows, saying:

### Resh

“You have judged, Lord, the cause of my soul, ‘defender [redeemer] of my life.’”

(Maurus.) The Lord judged the cause of Christ’s soul when he brought the death of the innocent to the salvation of the human race and, by the triumph of his resurrection, confounded the authors of his death.

Alternatively, the Lord judged the cause of his faithful when he redeemed their souls and did not abandon all who hoped in him. He transferred his confessors to heavenly glory and plunged their persecutors into everlasting punishment. Their iniquity deserved this, because the recklessness of their minds did not allow them to fear and honor their Creator.

For they first rose up in the madness of their fury against the shepherd himself, saying: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance.” They seized him, threw him outside the vineyard, and killed him; and they beat one of his servants, killed another, and stoned another (Matthew 21). Thus the sheep of the flock were scattered. Therefore he now says:

### Resh

“You saw, Lord, their iniquity against me; judge my judgment.”

### Resh

“You saw, Lord, all their fury and all their thoughts against me.”

Their thought was evil and their words were filled with madness: they planned to kill the author of life and strove to reproach the words of truth. Concerning this it follows:

### Sin

“You heard their reproaches, Lord, all their thoughts against me.”

### Sin

“The lips of those who rose up against me, and their meditations against me, all day long.”

The chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel in order to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. Again: “The chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, so that they might hand him over to death, and they did not find any. Although many false witnesses came forward, at last two false witnesses came and said: ‘He said, “I can destroy this temple and rebuild it in three days”’” (Matthew 26).

When he had been crucified, those passing by therefore blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross.” Likewise the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wishes. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (Matthew 27).

Such was their meditation, such their fury and stubbornness, that they appointed witnesses to falsehood against the truth and repaid good with evil without cause. The Psalmist had long before foretold this, saying: “For without cause they hid from me the destruction of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul” (Psalm 34).

Truly “without cause,” since he had done them no evil. We call something gratuitous when it is given without compensation for anything.

(Cassiodorus.) “They hid it from me,” as they supposed, because they did not believe in the power of his divinity. For what can be hidden from him to whom nothing is hidden? He identified his betrayer at the supper, foretold his passion before it occurred, and nothing could be concealed from him, because he suffered everything according to the dispensation of his will.

Again he says: “Unjust witnesses rose up; they questioned me about things I did not know, and they repaid me evil for good, barrenness for my soul.”

The witnesses, therefore, who suddenly rise up with the violence of beasts and are not brought forward in a measured manner are without any doubt utterly false. He marks them with one powerful word when he says: “Unjust,” truly unjust, since they were about to speak against equity and justice.

He adds, “things I did not know,” that is, things I absolutely did not know myself to have said. Thus we speak of those who, by the Lord’s favor, guard themselves through upright conduct: “He does not know how to lie; he does not know how to steal; he does not know how to oppress.”

The Lord did not know how to blaspheme, which the chief priests charged against him when he said: “You will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Father.” The Jewish high priest followed, saying: “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses?” (Luke 22).

The following words reveal what kind of testimony this was: he did not say that they had convicted and questioned him as though they trusted in their own integrity, but that they were anxious to rely upon another’s voice.

“They repaid me evil for good,” namely, because while he had bestowed life upon believers, they preferred to return death. This kind of repayment is proved to be the extreme of all evils.

Barrenness of soul was also present when the good teacher could find in them no fruit of faith, nor did their hearts produce the shoots of belief; they had been hardened by stony stupor. And so that the Jews might not lightly regard themselves as condemned to this barrenness, he also cursed that fig tree, as the Gospel testifies (Mark 11), in which he found no fruit at all.

### Sin

“See their sitting and their rising; I am their psalm.”

(Maurus.) In their sitting he expresses the posture of judging; in their rising, their determination to carry out what they were plotting. But because the priests and leaders of the Jews sat in the chair of pestilence, lying in wait to kill the innocent (Psalm 1), they rose for this purpose: to complete by wicked action what they had wickedly planned.

There was misery in their ways, and they did not know the way of peace. Whatever he himself declared before them in truthful words, they strove wholly to turn into accusation and reproach. Thus, when he said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming in the clouds of heaven,” the chief priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed.” Then they spat in his face and struck him with blows; others slapped his face, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26.)

The Prophet had foreseen this in the Spirit and displayed it long ago, saying: “Those who sat at the gate were hostile to me, and those who drank wine sang against me” (Psalm 68). He says that his passion was a song for the Jewish people, who, as though their thought concerning the Lord’s death had been fulfilled, babbled drunkenly about it.

But because they were incorrigible and chose to persevere in evil rather than withdraw from it, defending themselves with proud intent as though they were executors of justice, it is said through Jeremiah. Hence it follows:

### Taw

“Repay them, Lord, according to the works of their hands.”

Immediately he expressed the same repayment more clearly, saying:

### Taw

“You will give them the shield of heart: your labor.”

(Gregory.) The labor of God appearing among human beings was his humanity capable of suffering. When the Jews, in their proud wisdom, looked upon it, they despised it; they scorned believing him immortal whom they saw mortal by nature and capable of suffering.

When they perceived his humility, hardened by the arrogance of pride, they took great care that the holy words of those preaching should not penetrate their minds. Thus, when the Lord repaid them for their evil works, he gave them the shield of heart that was his labor: by a just judgment, he displayed them as proudly hardened against him.

Hence he himself labored for us in weakness. They rejected the words of those preaching because they disdained the Lord’s weakness in suffering. They therefore held the Lord’s labor against the Lord himself as a shield of their hearts; it appeared all the more contemptible to those wise in their own conceit because he was humble for their sake.

This shield, as we have already said above, was first held by that sinner who, when the Lord asked why he had touched the forbidden tree, did not take the blame upon himself but replied that he had received it from the woman whom the Lord had given him, so that he might indirectly throw his guilt back upon the Creator who had given him a woman to persuade him to such things.

The woman likewise held this shield when she too did not take the blame upon herself but attributed it to the serpent’s persuasion, saying: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” Thus she also indirectly traced her guilt back to the Creator, who had permitted the serpent there, within her, to persuade her to such things.

The serpent, however, is no longer questioned, because his repentance was not being sought. But those whose repentance was sought brought forward the shield of a most wicked defense against the words of a most just correction.

Hence it continues to be drawn into the practice of sinners, so that when guilt is reproved it is defended, and from the very point where guilt ought to have been ended, it is increased.

### Taw

“You will pursue them in your fury and destroy them beneath the heavens, Lord.”

(Maurus.) These three statements that we have just enumerated, marked under their respective letters, correspond to the preceding ones, in which he had expressed the Jews’ iniquity and deceitful plotting. He shows what they deserved: in the fury of divine judgment, as God ordained, their enemies pursued them and crushed them severely in the present life, so that even now they are scattered throughout the whole world and suffer the evil of exile, sitting without a king, without royal priesthood, without a temple, and without the worship of piety.

Those who turn to Christ, however, will spiritually inherit that promise which was made to their fathers.

Finally, since the three alphabets have been completed, through which the prophet explained the first part of the Lamentation, we must now consider what he indicates in the fourth.

## Book Twenty

### Chapter 4

(Jerome.) The final book of Jeremiah is to be begun with the fourth alphabet, which, like the first and second, proceeds in Sapphic meter. In it the prophet likewise laments historically, in a mournful voice, the fall of the Jewish people and the devastation of the city, as in the other books; spiritually, however, he mourns miserably the fall of the faithful soul and its ruin in sins. He adds the prayer which, with tearful voice, he poured out to the merciful ears of the Lord on account of the destruction of his people, so that the gracious Lord, extending the hand of consolation to the wretched, might raise them again to their former condition and restore them to perfect health.

### Aleph

“How the gold has grown dim! How the finest color has changed! How the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street!”

(Maurus.) Although these words seem historically to speak of the destruction of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple, where all the former adornment was scattered and reduced to nothing, nevertheless, in a deeper sense they signify the overthrow of the mystical temple, which is daily darkened and destroyed in the life and conduct of the reprobate.

(Gregory.) What is signified by gold, which surpasses the other metals, except the excellence of holiness? What by the finest color, except the reverence of religion, beloved by all? What by the stones of the sanctuary, except persons of the sacred orders? What by the name of streets, except the breadth of the present life?

Since *platos* (πλάτος) means “breadth” in Greek, streets were plainly named from their breadth. Truth itself says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matthew 7).

Gold is therefore darkened when the life of holiness is polluted by earthly actions. The finest color is changed when the former esteem of certain people who were believed to live religiously is diminished. For when someone, after adopting the habit of holiness, involves himself in earthly actions, his reverence, as though its color had changed, grows pale and despised before human eyes.

The stones of the sanctuary are scattered in the streets when those who ought to devote themselves to the inner mysteries, as though within the sanctuary’s hidden places, for the adornment of the Church, seek the broad roads outside because of secular affairs.

For this purpose the stones of the sanctuary were made: to appear within the Holy of Holies on the vestment of the high priest. But when ministers of religion do not demand from their subjects the honor of their Redeemer on the basis of their life’s merit, the stones of the sanctuary are not on the priest’s vestment.

Those stones of the sanctuary lie scattered through the streets when persons of the sacred orders, devoted to the breadth of their pleasures, cling to earthly business. It should be noted that he does not say that they are scattered in the streets, but at the head of the streets, because even when they engage in earthly affairs they desire to appear exalted: thus they occupy the broad roads of pleasurable delight while still remaining at the head of the streets through the honor of holiness.

Nor is there any difficulty if we take the stones of the sanctuary as those very people from whom the sanctuary was constructed. They lie scattered at the head of the streets when men of the sacred orders devote themselves to earthly actions out of desire, although the glory of holiness had previously seemed to stand through their office.

Secular business may sometimes be tolerated out of compassion, but it should never be sought out of love, lest, when it burdens the mind of one who pursues it, it sink that mind, overcome by its weight, from heavenly things to the depths below.

### Beth

“The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed in the finest gold—how they have been counted as earthen vessels, the work of the potter’s hands!”

This sentence pertains to the same meaning as the preceding one: the sons of the Church, who were illustrious through the Christian religion and adorned with the radiance of wisdom and the beauty of virtues, are now softened by carnal desires and wasted away by earthly ambitions. They are compared to earthen vessels, which the rod of the Lord’s correction will crush and break at the future judgment, reducing them to nothing, so that no shard of pottery will be found from which a little fire might be carried away from the burning.

### Gimel

“Even the she-monsters exposed the breast; they nursed their young.”

In the *lamia*, the duplicity of the Jews and the pretense of hypocrites are expressed. The lamia has a human face but the body of a beast. Thus the Jewish people outwardly pretended to worship God, but in spirit were always hostile to him. Isaiah rightly displays this when he says: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29).

Similarly, all hypocrites display on their first face what appears to arise from the reason of holiness, but what follows is a bestial body, because the things they undertake under the appearance of good are exceedingly wicked.

Heretics can also be understood in the lamia: they possess a human face but, through impiety, carry bestial hearts. They expose the breast when they freely preach their error. They nurse their young when, by insinuating perversities, they nourish and confirm the childish souls of their evil followers in impiety.

“The daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness.”

As in the lamia, so also in the ostrich, historical meaning signifies the fiction and savagery of the Jews; in the mystical sense it signifies the pretense and inhumanity of hypocrites, who know how to fabricate works of virtue rather than perform them truthfully.

Concerning this ostrich, among other passages, it is written in the Book of Job: “She hardens herself toward her young, as though they were not hers” (Job 39). “She labored in vain, compelled by no fear.”

The cruel synagogue of the Jews was therefore hardened against the apostles and preachers of the New Testament, who had been born from that very people, as though they were not its sons. Hating them and counting them strangers, it persecuted them cruelly everywhere in the wilderness of the nations because of the Gospel of Christ.

Truth itself appears to have foretold this to them when he said: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized. They will make you expelled from the synagogues. But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God. And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father nor me” (John 16).

She labored in vain, compelled by no fear, because when she persecuted Christ as the destroyer of the nation and the overthrower of the kingdom, she preserved neither the stability of the kingdom nor the salvation of the nation, but rather destroyed them.

For, as the Gospel testifies, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus and said: “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we leave him alone, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John 11).

Caiaphas answered them: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and not that the whole nation should perish.”

They considered these things and went astray. Their wickedness blinded them; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. If they had sought salvation, they ought to have desired the Savior.

“They searched out iniquity; they failed in searching out their search. A man approached the deep heart, and God was exalted. The arrows of children became their wounds, and they made their tongues of no account against them. What the wicked feared came upon them: the boar from the forest destroyed them, and the solitary wild beast devoured them; and desolation will persist to their end” (Psalm 63).

Alternatively, the cruel ones are heretics, concerning whom John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”

(Gregory.) Like an ostrich, they harden themselves toward their children when they raise them not with paternal affection but with a stranger’s disposition.

True teachers therefore possess toward their disciples the inward compassion of fear through the power of charity. Hypocrites, however, fear those entrusted to them all the less because they do not even recognize in themselves what they ought to fear. Since they live with hardened hearts, they acknowledge even the children whom they beget without any tenderness of the love they owe.

For one whom the grace of charity does not shape so that he may teach his neighbor—even if he has begotten that neighbor for God—regards him as a stranger. Such are all hypocrites: while their minds always seek outward things, they do not grow tender toward their neighbor through any compassionate charity.

How tenderly Paul felt inwardly when he yearned for his children with such ardent love, saying: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord; and God is my witness, how greatly I long for you all in the inward parts of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1).

He also says to the Romans: “God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always make mention of you in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you; for I long to see you” (Romans 1).

To the Ephesians he says: “I ask that you not grow faint because of my tribulations for you, which are your glory” (Ephesians 3).

Behold, while placed in tribulation, he exhorts others and strengthens them by what he himself endures. He had not forgotten his children after the manner of ostriches. Rather, he feared greatly lest his disciples, seeing in their preacher the disgrace of so many persecutions, should despise the faith in him because countless insults of suffering prevailed against him.

For this reason he was less concerned about his own torments and more concerned that his children might be tempted by them. He regarded bodily wounds in himself as of little account while fearing wounds of the heart in his children. He received the wounds of suffering by enduring; he healed the wounds of their hearts by consoling his children.

Let us consider, therefore, how great his charity was, that amid his own pains he feared for others. Let us consider what kind of charity it is to seek the salvation of one’s children amid one’s own losses, and to preserve the state of mind of one’s neighbors even through one’s own humiliation.

But hypocrites do not know these inward feelings of charity. The more their minds are loosened outwardly through desire for the world, the more they are hardened inwardly in their affections and grow cold within, as an insensible body. For they soften outwardly through damnable love and cannot examine themselves, because they make no effort to think about themselves.

They cannot think about themselves because they are not wholly present to themselves. Nor do they suffice to be wholly present to themselves, because they are carried away by as many desires as they have; by so many forms they are scattered away from themselves. Scattered among lowly things, they lie there; gathered together, they could rise to the heights.

The mind of the righteous, however, because the discipline of vigilance breaks its appetite for the flow of all visible things, is gathered inwardly into wholeness within itself. It clearly sees what it ought to be toward God and neighbor, because it leaves nothing of itself outside. The more it is seen to be withdrawn from outward things, the more it is kindled inwardly; and the more it burns, the more brightly it shines for detecting vices.

### Daleth

“By thirst the tongue of the nursing child clung to the roof of its mouth; the little children asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them.”

(Gregory.) Understand this historically: the nursing children and infants of the Jews, deprived of the assistance of their mothers and nurses, suffered from hunger and thirst. Allegorically, however, it signifies that those who are still weak in understanding and less able to receive stronger food lack the nourishment of spiritual understanding because of the inertia and laziness of teachers. To such people the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, you are not even now able” (1 Cor. III).

“The little children,” he says, “asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them”—that is, the weak among the people asked that the stronger meanings of Holy Scripture be broken up and explained to them, but no one capable of undertaking the explanation could be found.

The prophet understood Scripture as drink when he said: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV). If the drink had not been open and accessible to the world, Truth itself would not have cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII). The prophet understood that both food and drink were lacking to Judaea when he said: “Her nobles perished from hunger, and her multitude withered from thirst” (Isa. V). For it belongs to only a few to know strong and hidden things, whereas many perceive the plain matters of history. Therefore he asserts that the nobles of Judaea perished not from thirst but from hunger, because those who seemed to preside, while giving themselves wholly to external understanding, had nothing inward [or: of the lesser things] to chew and digest by careful examination.

### Thet

“Those who feasted luxuriously perished in the streets; those who were brought up in saffron-colored garments embraced dung.”

(Maurus.) Who are those who feasted luxuriously, if not the Jews themselves, who were always devoted to earthly desires and the pleasures of the world, and who frequently murmured for food and drink, saying to Moses: “Surely you have brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey, and you have given us possession of fields and vineyards” (Num. XVI). Again they said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt; cucumbers and melons, leeks and onions and garlic come to mind. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna” (Num. XI).

“They themselves perished in the streets,” because they were destroyed on the broad and spacious way that leads to death. “And those who were brought up in saffron-colored garments embraced dung,” because, desiring the empty splendor of this world and following the historical tradition of the Law, they despised spiritual understanding and became filthy in that very external foulness. That the old observance of the Law’s ceremonies is compared with dung, Paul demonstrates by saying: “Whatever gains I had, I considered as dung for the sake of Christ” (Phil. III).

Tropologically, anyone who follows earthly greed and the delights of pleasure and completes the course of this life without correction will arrive not at the joys of eternal life but at the foulness of punishments.

### Vau

“The iniquity of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in an instant, and hands did not seize upon her.”

The iniquity of the Jewish people therefore became greater than the sin of Sodom, because the Sodomites transgressed only the natural law, whereas the Jews transgressed both the natural and the written law. They saw God’s miracles, were fed with heavenly food, and nevertheless remained continually ungrateful for his benefits.

Hence their teachers “did not seize hands upon them”: they found in them none of the fruits of their labor that would have been worthy of it. For they provoked their own lawgiver Moses with many insults and persecuted the prophets of God sent to them. Finally, they despised the heir himself—that is, the only-begotten Son of the Father—when he came to them to save and correct them from error; pursuing him with various accusations, they ultimately killed him through envy.

The Gospel shows how the iniquity of the Jews was greater than the sin of Sodom, where we read:

“Then Jesus began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not repented: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless I say to you: It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell; for if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained to this day. Nevertheless I say to you: It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you’” (Matt. XI; Luke X).

### Vau

“Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire.”

### Thet

“Their appearance has become blacker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets. Their skin clung to their bones; it dried up and became like wood.”

By these two statements it is shown how all the former beauty of the earlier people—which they possessed in the adornment of the Temple and in divine worship—withered because of their sins and, when enemies destroyed them, was reduced to nothing.

(Gregory.) Mystically, however, the prophet laments the fall of certain faithful souls. What is signified by the name of the Nazirites, if not the life of those who abstain and practice continence, which is said to be brighter than snow and milk? Snow freezes from water that comes from above; milk is pressed from flesh that is nourished by things below. What, then, is demonstrated by snow if not the whiteness of heavenly life? And by milk if not the administration of temporal dispensation?

Since men who practice continence in the Church often perform works so extraordinary that many who have maintained a heavenly life, and many who have administered earthly affairs well, seem to be surpassed by them, they are described as “whiter than snow and brighter than milk.” And because, through the fervor of the spirit, they sometimes seem to surpass the life of ancient and strong fathers, it is rightly added: “Redder than ancient ivory.” When the name of redness is impressed, the flame of holy desire is signified. We know that ivory is the bone of great animals. They are therefore “redder than ancient ivory,” because they often display before human eyes a more fervent devotion than certain fathers who preceded them.

To show all this together, it is added: “More beautiful than sapphire.” Sapphire is of a heavenly color. Because through their heavenly way of life they seem to surpass many who preceded them and who strive toward things above, they are said to have been more beautiful than sapphire.

Yet often, when an abundance of virtues prospers beyond what is fitting, the mind is brought to a certain confidence in itself; deceived by its own presumption, it is suddenly darkened when sin steals upon it. Hence it is rightly added: “Their appearance has become blacker than coals.” They become black after having been white, because, having lost God’s righteousness, they presume upon themselves and slip even into sins they do not understand. And because after the fire of love they come to the coldness of torpor, they are compared with extinguished coals. Sometimes, while abandoning the fear of God through confidence in themselves, they become even colder than cold minds.

Of them it is rightly added: “They are not recognized in the streets.” In accordance with Greek usage, *platea* means “street” because of its breadth. What is narrower to the human mind than breaking one’s own desires? Concerning this breaking, Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII). What is broader than resisting none of one’s own desires, and spreading oneself without restraint in whatever direction the impulse of the will leads?

Those who, through confidence in their holiness and after setting aside the judgment of better persons, follow themselves proceed as though through broad streets. Yet they are not recognized in the streets, because they had previously displayed something different in their lives, when by breaking their own desires they kept themselves on the narrow path.

And rightly it is added: “Their skin clung to their bones.” What is expressed by bone if not the hardness of strength, and by skin if not the softness of weakness? Their skin is therefore said to cling to their bones, because weakness of vice is regarded by those who think perversely as the hardness of virtue. What they do is weak; but, deceived by confidence born of pride, they join these things to strong suspicions, and the greater their opinion of themselves, the more disdainfully they refuse correction of their own wickedness.

Hence it is rightly added: “It dried up and became like wood.” Their guilt becomes so much more insensible the more it is considered praiseworthy by them. He rightly calls it dry, because it grows green through no reflection upon itself.

### Theth

“It was better for those killed by the sword than for those slain by hunger, because these wasted away, consumed by the barrenness of the earth.”

(Maurus.) As far as the brevity of death is concerned, the punishment of those suddenly killed by the sword was shorter than that of those long tormented by hunger and thirst. In the spiritual sense, however, it was better for the apostles and preachers of the Gospel to be punished for a time by a brief bodily suffering in Christ’s name and afterward crowned in eternal joy than for their persecutors to waste away through a prolonged famine of the word of God and, because of the barrenness and unfruitfulness of good works, finally to be burned in everlasting fire.

### Jod

“The hands of compassionate women cooked their own children; they became their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

Historically, this recapitulates what he had already said above: during the Chaldean captivity, and likewise during the Roman one, the Jewish people reached such distress, through lack of food, that some of their women slaughtered their own children and ate their cooked flesh.

According to the spiritual understanding, it is no small offense when evil teachers strip their hearers of their earthly goods and possessions because of their own greed, and do not give them the nourishment of the word by which they might be fed for eternal life. The Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel:

“Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves! Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, heal what was sick, bind up what was broken, bring back what was cast away, or seek what had perished; instead, you ruled over them with harshness and power. My sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field; they were scattered,” and so forth.

But that such conduct merits the Lord’s anger follows:

### Coph

“The Lord completed his fury, poured out the anger of his indignation, kindled a fire in Zion, and devoured its foundations.”

The Lord completed his fury and poured out the anger of his indignation upon the sinful nation when he not only exterminated the people but also, through their enemies, destroyed their dwellings down to their foundations and consumed the Temple and the city in fire.

He also completes his fury against evil teachers when, for their negligence and laziness, he will hand them over to everlasting fire. He punishes them not only for their evil works, but his vengeance reaches even to the foundations of their perverse thoughts.

### Lamed

“The kings of the earth did not believe, nor any of the inhabitants of the world, that an enemy and adversary would enter through the gates of Jerusalem.”

(Jerome.) While the Jewish kingdom remained secure and the worship of God there was most celebrated, it was difficult for the nations surrounding it to believe that an external enemy would dominate so distinguished a city and so famous a Temple—especially when they saw and heard that, from the beginning, that people had been made illustrious by signs and sustained and protected by divine aid.

Mystically, when we see the soul of any faithful person adorned with spiritual knowledge and the beauty of every virtue, we can scarcely believe that it could collapse in so sudden a fall: that one who had once, in a sense, ruled over spiritual enemies and expelled them from bodies they possessed by the word of prayer should now become the prey of those same enemies and be wholly subjected to their most wicked will.

But what gives rise to this great ruin, the prophet’s following statement shows.

(Maurus.) The captivity and devastation of Jerusalem occurred especially because of the sins of the Jewish scribes and Pharisees, as well as of the priests, who shed the blood of the Redeemer and of his prophets and apostles.

### Mem

“Because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst.”

Likewise now in the Church, because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, the gates of spiritual Jerusalem stand open for entry. When, through the cowardice of preachers and the negligence of God’s priests—who do not care to announce the Lord’s way to the people or restrain them from sins—the wicked enemy finds an entrance into the soul through the outward senses, he gains an opportunity to deceive it by various frauds.

Hence it is written: “Evil priests are the cause of the people’s ruin” (Lam. II). They are rightly said to shed the blood of the righteous, because when they withhold the word of consolation from the simple—who might perhaps be righteous through their innocence if they knew the straight paths of the Lord—they are held guilty of the blood that has been shed.

The divine word clearly demonstrates this to the prophet Ezekiel, saying:

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear words from my mouth and announce them to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, and do not speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you shall have saved your life.

“Even if the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, I will place a stumbling block before him; he shall die because you did not announce it to him. He shall die in his sin, and the righteousness he practiced shall not be remembered; but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce to the righteous that he should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it to him, and you shall have saved your life” (Ezek. III).

### Nun

“The blind wandered in the streets; they were polluted with blood. And when they could not, they held their tears [read: skirts].”

(Jerome.) Through the inertia of teachers, therefore, the crowds of the people, blinded by the darkness of ignorance, wandered in the streets, because, while surrendering themselves to the allurements of pleasure, they did not keep to the straight path of the divine commandments.

And it is rightly said: “They were polluted with blood,” because they were contaminated by association with bloodstained deeds. “When they could not”—that is, when they could not walk along the straight route—“they held their tears [read: skirts]” [the text has *lacrymas*, “tears”; the contextual correction is *lacinias*, “skirts”]. That is, they sought the guidance of others, so that, drawn along by examples of their conduct as though by certain skirts, they might imitate the steps of those who went before.

But since those who lead, and who ought frequently to guide their followers by the word of instruction and by good examples, often despise those who follow them through the arrogance of pride and drive them into despair, it follows:

### Samech

“‘Depart, polluted ones!’ they cried to them. ‘Depart, go away, do not touch us.’ For they quarreled and were agitated; they said among the nations, ‘He will no longer continue to dwell among them.’”

### Phe

“The face of the Lord divided them; he will no longer continue to regard them [or: rescue them]. They did not respect the persons of the priests, nor did they show mercy to the elders.”

(Maurus.) Such is the voice of proud teachers, who take from the flock the animal that is fat and cast away the one that is weak; they do not strengthen what is feeble or heal what is sick.

“‘Depart,’ they say, ‘polluted ones; depart, go away, do not touch us.’ Do not share anything with us. Your wounds are incurable and your sores cannot be healed. You are not worthy of Christian communion, so that the Holy Spirit should continue to dwell among you. The face of the Lord divides and rejects you, nor will he continue to receive you, because you did not respect the persons of your priests, nor did you meekly accept the admonition of your elders.””

Such speech does not enlighten the blind, heal the sick, or care for the weak; rather, it kills them and casts the one in danger into despair.

Good teachers, weighing the weaknesses of others from their own weakness, strive more through the soothing remedy of humility and gentleness to rescue sinners from the snare of error than to drive those wavering into the pit of destruction through severity. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles shows how he governed his subjects, saying: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all, so that I might save all.” Again he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (1 Cor. IX; 2 Cor. XI.)

[Gregory.] A ruler ought to be, through humility, a companion to those who act well, yet stand upright against the vices of offenders through zeal for justice. Thus he should in no way set himself above the good, but whenever the fault of the wicked demands it, he should immediately recognize the authority of his office. In this way, while suppressing his honor, he should consider himself equal to subjects who live well, yet should not fear to exercise the rights of righteousness against the perverse.

For it is clear that all human beings are born equal by nature; but as the order of merits varies, guilt places some below others. This very difference, which arose through vice, is administered by divine judgment, so that, because no human being can stand equally on his own, one is governed by another.

Therefore all who preside ought to consider not the power of their rank in themselves but the equality of their condition. They should not rejoice that they rule human beings, but that they benefit them. For our ancient fathers are remembered not as kings of human beings but as shepherds of animals. And when the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” he immediately added: “And let your fear and dread be upon all the animals of the earth.”

The fear and dread of these men is indeed commanded to be upon the animals of the earth, but is plainly forbidden to be upon human beings. A human being is naturally set above brute animals, not above other human beings. Therefore he is told to be feared by animals and not by human beings, because it is contrary to nature to be proud and wish to be feared by one’s equal.

Nevertheless, rulers must be feared by their subjects when they discover that their subjects have no fear of God, so that at least through fear of human beings they may fear to sin—those who do not fear divine judgments.

The preceding statements, in which the polluted are ordered to depart and are told amid quarrels that the Lord will no longer receive them or dwell among them, can also be understood as spoken by the enemies of the Jewish people. They taunted the captives when, by force, they expelled them from their land and brought them into a foreign land, saying that they had been deserted and abandoned by God, deprived of divine aid, that no hope of return remained for them, and that they would be condemned forever.

The following statement of the prophet makes clear why they were deserted by the Lord.

### Ain

“While we still endured, our eyes failed as we looked for our empty help, as we watched attentively for a nation that could not save us.”

(Maurus.) This recounts that, when they were rebuked by the Lord for their crimes, they did not turn to him through repentance or flee to his mercy, so that by his aid they might be rescued from their enemies. Instead, they sought help externally from other nations—namely, from the Egyptians or Assyrians—which could in no way deliver them.

Hence he says: “Our eyes failed as we looked for our empty help, as we watched attentively for a nation that could not save us.” In vain they sought comfort from those who could not defend even themselves.

This also led to what happened to the remnant of the Jews left by Nabuzardan, commander of the army, after the devastation of Jerusalem, to cultivate the land (2 Kings XXV). After Ishmael killed Gedaliah, whom the aforementioned Nabuzardan had appointed over the land, those remnants, terrified by fear, went against the word of God that had been delivered to them through Jeremiah and crossed into Egypt, as though they could be protected by the Egyptians against the weapons of the Chaldeans.

But their hope was vain. In the fifth year of the captivity of Jerusalem, as Josephus reports—the twenty-third year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar—the same Nebuchadnezzar encamped in Lower Syria, captured it, and subdued the Ammonites and Moabites. After subjecting these nations, he proceeded to Egypt and overthrew it. He killed the king who was then there, appointed another in his place, and once again led the Jewish captives to Babylon. Thus the race of the Hebrews met this end.

### Sade

“Our footsteps slipped on the paths of our streets; our end drew near. Our days were completed, because our end had come.”

Mystically, whoever, having abandoned the one true God, seeks help from spiritual Egypt—that is, from this world—and proceeds along the slippery footsteps of this age, deceived by empty hope, becomes the prey of spiritual enemies.

Hence it is written: “For Egypt will give help in vain” (Isa. XXX). Again: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. XVII).

### Coph

“Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursued us over the mountains and lay in wait for us in the wilderness.”

(Gregory.) By the swift flight of birds he signifies the powerful and rapid persecution of enemies, who pursued with extreme cruelty those who remained within their homeland and those who had fled after abandoning it.

In Holy Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes designates evil spirits, the robbers of souls; sometimes the powers of the present age; sometimes the most subtle understanding of the saints; and sometimes the incarnate Lord, who swiftly traverses the depths and soon returns to the heights.

The name “eagles” expresses ambushing spirits, as Jeremiah attests when he says: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven.” Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven when wicked people act against us with such force that, through their devices of malice, they seem even to outstrip the aerial powers.

The word “eagle” also figures earthly power. Thus the prophet Ezekiel says: “A great eagle, with great wings, long-limbed, full of feathers and variety, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of its branches.”

By this eagle none other than Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is signified. He is described as having great wings because of the vastness of his army; long limbs because of the long duration of time; being full of feathers because of his many riches; and being full of variety because of the countless forms of earthly glory.

He came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar and tore off the top of its branches because, attacking the height of Judaea, he removed the nobility of its kingdom like the marrow of a cedar; and when, by taking captive, he removed the tender offspring of its kings from the summit of their kingdom, he tore off, as it were, the top of its branches.

In another sense, the word “eagle” expresses either the subtle understanding of the saints or the flight of the Lord’s Ascension. Thus the same prophet, describing the four evangelists whom he had seen under the appearance of animals, testifies that the face of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared to him among them. Without doubt, by the eagle he signifies the fourth animal, John, who by flying abandoned the earth, because through subtle understanding he penetrated the inner mysteries by seeing the Word.

### Res

“The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured because of our sins; of him we said, ‘We shall live in your shadow among the nations.’”

(Maurus.) Different authors have explained this statement in different ways. Some have interpreted it as referring to the kings of the Jews, who were called *christs*—that is, anointed ones—under whose protection the Jewish people appeared to live. On this interpretation, they perished because of the people’s sins, like Josiah, who is said to have been righteous, and others of the same kind.

Others understand it as spoken about Jesus Christ, the true Lord of all and the life of faithful souls, under whose protection the Church exists among all nations. He himself is “the breath of our mouth,” “in whom we live and move and exist” (Acts XVII), and from whose savor we acquire whatever we rightly understand. He was handed over because of our sins and rose again because of our justification.

For the prophet Isaiah wrote most fully:

“Surely he himself bore our weaknesses and carried our pains; we considered him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded because of our iniquities, crushed because of our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. All of us, like sheep, have gone astray; each one has turned to his own way, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all.”

Again:

“Because of the crime of my people I struck him. He will give the wicked for his burial and the rich man for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he will see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord will prosper in his hand. Because his soul labored, he will see and be satisfied in his knowledge. The righteous one himself, my servant, will justify many, and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore I will allot him many, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because he handed over his soul to death and was reckoned among criminals. He himself bore the sin of many and prayed for transgressors” (Isa. LIII).

[Jerome.] Others interpret this according to what is read in Ezekiel, where the Lord says to the prophet:

“Son of man, have not the house of Israel, the provoking house, said to you, ‘What are you doing?’ Say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord God: This burden concerns the prince who is in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are in their midst. Say: “I am your portent; as I have done, so shall it be done to them. They shall go into exile and captivity. The prince who is in their midst shall be carried upon his shoulders. He shall go out in darkness; they shall break through the wall to bring him out. His face shall be covered so that he may not see the land with his eyes. I will spread my net over him, and he shall be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, into the land of the Chaldeans, but he shall not see it; there he shall die. And all those around him—his guards and his troops—I will scatter in every direction, and I will draw the sword after them. And they shall know that I am the Lord when I scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the lands. I will leave a few men among them, delivered from the sword, hunger, and pestilence, so that they may recount all their crimes among the nations to which they shall go, and they shall know that I am the Lord”’” (Ezek. XII).

According to the tropological interpretation, those who attempt to explain this concerning the Savior interpret the leader who is in the midst of Jerusalem as the one who went before as a portent and sign: both he and his companions are captives of this world, and, rising victorious from the underworld, he was carried upon the shoulders of angels.

He went out in darkness, unknown to unbelievers; after destroying the dividing wall, he made the two one. His face was covered so that he would not look upon the land of the Jews. Nor is it surprising that the Lord concealed his face, since to this day a veil lies before Moses’ face for the unbelieving people.

The Lord also spread his net over him, in accordance with what the bride says of him in the Song of Songs: “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, appearing through the lattices” (Song II).

Of him Jeremiah says: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord, was captured because of our sins,” and: “Although he had committed no sin, he was made sin for us.”

“And he shall be brought,” he says, “to Babylon”—the confusion of this world—and into the land of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as demons, so that he might recall to salvation those who had been enslaved to demons and lead the former captivity captive.

“He shall not see,” he says, “that land of the Chaldeans, and there he shall die,” so that by his death he might give life to us all. He scattered all his helpers, his apostolic companions and apostolic men, throughout the whole world, and drew his sword after them so that they might be crowned with various martyrdoms. Then they themselves, or those who had believed through them, would understand that he is the Lord, and that he had scattered them among the nations and dispersed them through the lands so that they might bear abundant fruit.

He left a few men among them, such as the apostle John and the others who were freed from sword, hunger, and pestilence and who escaped the onslaught of persecutions, so that they might recount the crimes of the Jews and the iniquities of all the nations to which they had gone. After doing penance, those nations would know that he was the Lord.

We have said these things, leaving the judgment to the reader’s discretion. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that it is dangerous to compare the captivity and death of an impious king with the mystery of God.

### Sin

“Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom, who dwell in the land of Uz; the cup will also come to you. You will become drunk and strip yourself naked.”

(Maurus.) Edom was the same as Esau, the brother of Jacob, from whom the Idumeans, enemies of Israel, arose. Uz was the son of Aram [Chorae], the founder of Trachonitis and Damascus, who held authority between Palestine and Coele-Syria. For this reason, in the Book of Job, where Hebrew has “the land of Uz,” the translators of the Septuagint rendered it “the region of Ausitis,” or “Usitis.”

When he tells the daughter of Edom to rejoice and be glad because the Lord’s cup has reached her, it should be read ironically, as in the Letter of the Apostle James: “Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, and the rich man in his humiliation” (James I). The verb “let him glory” is understood from the preceding verse, although the matter concerns not his glory but his humiliation and condemnation.

The Lord’s cup—that is, vengeance—came to the Idumeans when Nebuchadnezzar, after devastating Judaea, devastated the other nations in the same manner. It was fitting that the enemies of God’s people, who had rejoiced in its destruction, should themselves receive from their enemies a vengeance deserved for it.

Mystically, however, in the daughter of Edom—Edom being interpreted as “bloodied” or “earthly”—the synagogue of the Jews is signified, or more generally the crowd of all those who persecute the Church. They persecute the company of the faithful established throughout the world with the bitterest attacks, but a sure vengeance in the fire of Gehenna will remain for them.

David the prophet also remembers this daughter of Edom in the Psalms (Ps. CXXXVI), saying: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say, ‘Strip it, strip it down to its foundations.’”

(Cassiodorus.) The people of the Hebrews, now converted to the Lord, therefore beseech him not to permit many of those who tear the Church of God apart with savage denunciation to depart unpunished.

As we have said, some have thought that Edom should be interpreted as “bloodied,” others as “earthly”; there is no doubt, however, that both meanings can refer to carnal vices.

These, then, are the sons of Edom who persecuted the Christian people most severely and were not converted by any act of satisfaction. When he prays that, in the separation of the good, they should be brought to remembrance so that they might receive their due punishment, this is said—as has often been mentioned—in accordance with the prophetic outcome, not from a desire to curse. Our piety is not sought for those whom the Lord’s judgment condemns.

Hence it continues: “They say, ‘Strip it, strip it down to its foundations.’” These are the words of the sons of Edom persecuting the Christian people, drawn from the likeness of a cistern: if its water is diligently drawn out, one undoubtedly reaches its foundation.

But what benefit did it bring them to deprive such people of the light of this age, when those who were killed seemed rather to possess eternal life in the very foundation? For Christ the Lord is the foundation of the faithful, and he cannot be seized from the righteous, even though they may be proved to have everything belonging to this age taken from them.

Thus, while the persecutors sought to drain the Catholic religion, they bestowed upon the martyrs crowns that were most blessed and abundant. This appears to be signified by the following statement.

### Thau

“Your iniquity is complete, daughter of Zion; he will not continue to lead you into exile. He will visit your iniquity, daughter of Edom; he will uncover your sins.”

(Maurus.) When the persecution by which enemies are permitted to persecute God’s elect in this age—namely, for their testing, not for their condemnation—has been completed, they will no longer continue to lead them into exile, “for God has wiped away every tear from the eyes of his saints, and there will no longer be mourning, crying, or pain; the former things have passed away. But let the righteous rejoice in the presence of God and delight in gladness” (Rev. XXI). The impious and sinners, however, are sent with the devil into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

Therefore, after the lamentation—which, as we said, is marked beforehand in fourfold fashion at the appropriate places according to the sequence of the Hebrew letters themselves—there follows the prophet’s prayer. Historically, it laments the devastation of the city of Jerusalem and the downfall of the Jewish people; spiritually, it mournfully recalls the ruin of faithful souls and the desolation they have suffered from spiritual wickedness. Finally, it humbly beseeches the help and mercy of the Lord himself to come to the aid of the afflicted. [Col. 1262C]

## THE PRAYER OF JEREMIAH

“Remember, O Lord, what has happened to us; look and behold our reproach.” (MAURUS.) The prophets frequently used human ways of speaking when beseeching the Lord. “Remember,” or “be mindful,” is said to him who could never at any time forget anything. For the Divinity is not reminded so that something may return to his memory, since before him every past and future thing is always present. It is not fitting to attribute the injury of forgetfulness to that majesty. Rather, he is asked to remember or be mindful so that he may quickly bring help to those in need and make manifest what previously was hidden.

You will frequently find such tropes in the divine Scriptures, as in Genesis: “I will remember [Col. 1262D] my covenant” (Gen. IX). Or in Exodus: “The Lord remembered the covenant that he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exod. VI). Or what Moses said to the Lord: “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your faithful servants” (Exod. XXXII). David also says in the Psalms: “Remember your word to your servant” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. CXXXI).

“Remember,” he says, “O Lord, what has happened to us”: the wrong of devastation. “Look and behold our reproach,” which we have suffered at the hands of those who led us like captive slaves into a foreign land and abused us for their own service.

[Col. 1263A] “Our inheritance has been turned over to foreigners, our houses to strangers.” Different peoples, gathered from every side, possess the renowned land that you promised our fathers to give us as a possession.

“We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows.” For we have been deprived of a protector, like orphans, and have no persons who were accustomed to provide us with the consolations of nourishment; rather, like widows, we have been deprived of every provision and consolation.

“We drank our water for money; we bought our wood at a price.” He says that two elements by which human life is especially sustained, and whose use is common to all, had become difficult for them because of the deprivation of captivity: they could have neither water [Col. 1263B] for drinking nor wood for the fire without paying a price to redeem them.

“With our necks we were driven; no rest was given to the weary.” He says that they were driven with their necks bound, after the manner of beasts of burden, because their enemy allowed them no control over themselves. They were dragged wherever the impulse of the one directing them wished, and no opportunity was granted the weary for refreshment. Then he immediately adds where they sought relief, saying:

“We gave our hand to Egypt and to the Assyrians, that we might be filled with ‘bread.’” The Israelites had always turned their hearts toward Egypt and had frequently sought aid from the Assyrians. Therefore they were deservedly scourged by those to whom, after abandoning God because of their desire for earthly things, they chose to be subject.

[Col. 1263C] According to the allegory, however, this complaint applies to those who, having been stripped of their virtues because of their sins, were handed over to the power of spiritual enemies. It applies especially to the Jews, who, after Christ’s coming, relying on the ancient tradition, lost the law of Moses itself and the paternal blessing, which they seemed to possess by hereditary right; and these were given to the nations that believed in Christ, because in the seed of Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed.

[Col. 1263D] Hence, when they resisted and contradicted the preaching of Paul and Barnabas, the reply was made: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth’” (Acts XIII).

These people, therefore, became like orphans without a father, because they refused to have the true God as their father and chose another father, concerning whom it was said to them: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII).

Their mothers, namely the synagogues, became like widows, because on account of the fornication of idolatry they were not worthy to have their former husband, that is, God.

They redeem the water of knowledge by their desire to learn, as though by money supplied for the purchase. But because they do not find Christ in it, they perish from eternal thirst, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

Likewise, they buy wood at a price when they devote themselves to the exercise of virtues. But because they disdain to possess in it the ardor of charity, they expend all their labor in vain. [Col. 1264A]

“Their scribes and Pharisees drove them, as though bound by the neck, through various sects and useless traditions, and gave no rest to the weary.” And because they choose to serve spiritual Egypt and the Assyrians for the sake of the appetite rather than God, they will perish in eternal poverty. Their fathers acted in this way, devoted to earthly affairs and pleasures, and their children still do not cease to act likewise. Therefore it follows:

“Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities.” They bore their iniquities because they were imitators of their wickedness, according to what is written: “Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Jer. XXXI).

[Col. 1264B] And in Exodus: “I am,” he says, “the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. XX).

Nor is this passage contrary to the testimony of Ezekiel, where it says: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son,” because it immediately continues: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII).

He therefore resolves the question that a listener might have raised in opposition. “You are accustomed,” he says, “to ask: Why will the righteous son not bear the iniquity of his father?” And he himself replies: Clearly, because the son has acted well and has not committed his father’s offenses. It is just that, just as the sinner dies in his own wickedness, so the righteous should live in his own virtues; [Col. 1264C] that the soul which has sinned should die, and that the soul which has kept God’s commandments should live.

“Slaves have ruled over us; there was no one to redeem us from their hand.” He calls the Gentiles slaves, because they served idols and sacrificed to demons. Israel was handed over to their dominion because of its sins, although Israel had once been appointed in the place of sons. Hence it is written: “Out of Egypt I called my firstborn son, Israel” (Isa. XI). There was no one to redeem them from their hands, because they had not deserved to have God as their defender and liberator.

“With our lives we obtained our bread, in the desert, at the risk of the sword.” That is: while situated in the desert of the nations, we sought food for ourselves at the peril of our souls. It is deservedly subjected to slaves that willingly loses its freedom.

For if the Jews believed in Christ, they would truly be free and, nourished by the bread of life, would genuinely avoid the peril of their souls. But now, because they rejected—or rather crucified—the true liberator, they have been expelled from their land and wander as exiles and fugitives throughout the world. Roaming without fixed dwelling places, they acquire food at the risk of their lives.

The fratricide Cain prefigured this well. He received the sentence (Gen. IV) that he should wander as an exile, fearful and trembling, through various places, and should nowhere remain safe and secure.

“Our skin has been burned like an oven, because of the storms of famine.” By the burned skin he indicates the shameful deformity that they suffered, placed among enemies amid hunger, thirst, and nakedness.

[Col. 1265A] An oven is a vessel for baking bread, a rounded form fashioned from a bronze container, which burns within beneath consuming flames. In this likeness the sinful Jews are rightly placed, since at the future judgment they are to be tormented both by sorrow of spirit and by penal suffering, because they lived with obstinate minds against the Lord’s commands.

Hence it is written in the Psalms: “You shall place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence” (Ps. XX). The time of the Lord’s presence is the day of judgment, when the Son of Man will be seen by human beings; yet only the righteous will also behold him in contemplation of his divinity. For whoever is not worthy to be satisfied with heavenly bread is truly consumed by hunger.

“Women were humbled in Zion, virgins in the cities of Judah; princes were hanged by the hand; the faces of elders were not respected; they abused young men shamefully; and boys fell upon the wood.” [Col. 1265B]

He enumerates various forms of calamity that the wicked nation suffered during the devastation by the Chaldeans or the Romans. Their women were violated, their virgins oppressed in the cities, their princes bound by the hands, their old men deprived of honor, and young men and boys subjected to shameful abuse.

This happened to them because they refused to honor their Creator. Instead, they bestowed divine honor upon false gods and images fashioned by human art. Those who, because of their lust, had lived shamelessly in the worship of false gods were handed over to the power of their enemies and afflicted with every disgrace and humiliation.

[Col. 1265C] According to the allegory, whoever understands the savagery of spiritual enemies truly recognizes the immense confusion that they produce in souls deceived by their fraud. There every immodesty, impurity, violence, and dishonor reigns; there appear as many forms of confusion as there are kinds of vice.

“Elders have failed at the gates; young men from the choir of singers.” Counsel cannot mature where there is no order of judgment, nor can a choir of singers properly remain where pain and groaning are present. “Music in mourning,” as someone says, “is an untimely tale” (Ecclus. XXII). Hence it continues:

“The joy of our heart has failed; our choir has been turned into mourning. The crown has fallen from our head. Woe to us, because we have sinned.” [Col. 1265D]

It is rightly said that the choir has been turned into mourning where it is clear that the joy of the heart has failed and the honor of true religion has utterly perished. For where there is no gladness of mind, the melody of song sounds in vain.

Hence the Prophet speaks in the Psalms from the person of the captives (Ps. CXXXVI): “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, O Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.”

(CASSIODORUS.) The bitterness of their grief is intensified when they hung their pleasure, by which the people might have consoled themselves, upon the trees as though it were unnecessary. For what could sweet instruments do there, where the seasons of life were occupied with bitter lamentations?

[Col. 1266A] Hence blessed Job says: “My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

(JEROME.) The organ sounds through pipes and the harp through strings. The harp may signify right action, while the organ may signify holy preaching. The pipes of the organ can appropriately be understood as the mouths of preachers, and the strings of the harp as the intention of those who live rightly.

When this intention is stretched toward the life to come through affliction of the flesh, it sounds, like a thinned string on a harp, to the wonder of those who behold it. A string is dried and tightened so that it may produce a fitting sound on the harp; likewise holy men, disciplining their bodies, subject them to service and are stretched from lower things toward higher ones.

Whether holy preachers in the Church, or simple and abstinent people according to the strength they receive, render to their neighbors [Col. 1266B] a song of good exhortation. The wise diligently devote themselves to the fruit of preaching; and, to draw others toward life, they labor amid the sound of great disturbance.

Those who appear slower of understanding derive from the very merit of their life whatever authority of exhortation they perceive themselves able to possess toward others, and they do not cease to draw those whom they can toward the heavenly homeland.

But when the holy Church, pressed by the final persecutions, sees that her words are despised by the reprobate, she turns the grace of her love into lamentation alone, because she mourns for those whom she cannot draw by exhortation. Let her therefore say:

“My harp has been turned into mourning, and my organ into the voice of those who weep.”

[Col. 1266C] As though she openly confessed, saying: In the time of my peace, through some I preached small things in the manner of a harp, and through others great and resonant things in the manner of an organ. But now the harp and the organ have been turned into mourning, because, seeing myself despised, I lament those who do not hear the song of preaching.

(MAURUS.) And because the prophet complained that mourning had been imposed upon him and glory laid aside, he adds the cause of his affliction and grief: “Woe to us,” he says, “because we have sinned.”

The deserved vengeance for the sin committed and not corrected by worthy repentance and amendment of life followed, because what a person does not correct through repentance will await the sentence of divine retribution. Paul bears witness to this when he says:
