“Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. II).

“Because of this our heart has become sorrowful in pain; therefore our eyes have grown dark.” [Col. 1266D]

It is rightly said that the heart has become sorrowful because of sin. For where iniquity presses upon and inhabits the heart, there is no dwelling place for the Holy Spirit; rather, the whole mind is darkened by the gloom of sin, since the grace of the supreme Paraclete disdains to pour its brightness into it.

“For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and wisdom will not enter a malicious soul.”

Then, by adding another cause, he discloses the source of the grief:

“Because of Mount Zion, which has perished, foxes have walked upon it.” [Col. 1267A]

According to the historical sense, it was a fitting cause of sorrow that in the place where the sanctuary had been established and the worship of God had been most celebrated, there were now hiding places for beasts.

According to the allegory, however, it is no less—but rather more—grievous that in a Christian soul, where divine contemplation once existed, the folly of error should reign. By foxes we must understand none other than heretics, because of their deceit and cunning. Wherever they enter with their doctrine, they disturb the whole soul and blind it with the darkness of error.

“But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your throne from generation to generation. Why, then, will you forget us forever and abandon us for the length of our days?” [Col. 1267B]

Having enumerated the multitude of tribulations that the prophet recounted above, he proclaims the Lord’s eternal power and the majesty of his throne in supplicatory words, so that he may move him by humble petition to have mercy and to hasten timely aid, lest those who have been placed for a long time under the dominion of their enemies should utterly fail through despair.

When he says, “Why will you forget us forever?” he speaks in human fashion, as though the one who does not quickly help them seems to disregard them as completely forgotten, although elsewhere it is written of him: “He will not always be angry, nor will he threaten forever” (Ps. CII). And again: “The Lord will not reject his people, nor will he abandon his inheritance” (Ps. XCIV). [Col. 1267C]

The Lord did not reject the Jewish people in such a way that he no longer wished to have mercy upon them. Rather, “a partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.”

Even now, as he did formerly, he converts some each day to the faith of Christ and to ecclesiastical unity, so that the election may be preserved. For from that very people whom the Lord is known to have chosen for himself in the patriarchs came the prophets; from it also came the apostles and many faithful people who believed in the Lord with sincere minds, as the teacher of the Gentiles testifies, saying:

“What do we say, brothers? Has God rejected his people, whom he foreknew? Certainly not; for I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin, and so forth” (Rom. XI).

But he makes clear in what way its true salvation may come by adding:

“Convert us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be converted; renew our days as at the beginning.” [Col. 1267D]

Whomever the Lord converts will truly be saved; but whoever is disregarded by him no one will be able to correct.

When he says, “Renew our days as at the beginning,” he appears to ask that, just as at the beginning he made their first patriarchs—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—devoted to him with complete faith and love, so he may deign to make them faithful and devoted to him by the same gift.

Many think this was promised to them through the prophet Malachi concerning the coming of Elijah, where it says:

“Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest perhaps I come and strike the earth with a curse” (Mal. IV).

Therefore, before the day of judgment comes and strikes the earth with a curse—or “wholly” or “suddenly,” as the Septuagint translated it, for this is what the Greek word ἅρδην signifies—the Lord will send [Col. 1268A] Elijah, whose name is interpreted “My God,” and who is from the town of Thesbe, a name that signifies conversion and repentance.

The Lord will send the whole choir of the prophets, which will turn the heart of the fathers to the children—that is, of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the patriarchs—so that their descendants may believe in the Lord the Savior, in whom those patriarchs also believed. For Abraham “saw the day of the Lord and rejoiced” (John VIII).

[Col. 1268B] Or the heart of the father may be understood as the heart of God toward everyone who has received the spirit of adoption, and the heart of the children toward their fathers, so that Jews and Christians, who now disagree among themselves, may agree in equal devotion to Christ.

Hence it is said to the apostles, who proclaimed the seedbed of the Gospel throughout the whole world: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV).

For if Elijah has not first turned the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to their fathers, when the great and terrible day of the Lord comes—great for the saints, terrible for sinners—the true and just Judge will strike with a curse not heaven, nor those who dwell in heaven, but the earth and those who perform earthly works.

The Jews and Judaizing heretics think that Elijah will come before their ἠλειμμένος (“anointed one”) and restore all things. Hence the question is also put to Christ in the Gospel: “Why do the Pharisees say that Elijah is to come?” He answered them: “Elijah, whom you believe is to come, has already come,” understanding John in Elijah.

“But casting us away, you have rejected us; you have been exceedingly angry with us.” [Col. 1268C]

He did not speak these words as though despairing of the salvation of his people, but to reveal his great grief over the long-lasting destruction and rejection of his nation.

For by the prophetic Spirit he saw that the Jews themselves would not believe at Christ’s coming, but would oppose his Gospel and hand him over to death as the heir, as he had already declared in many places of this book.

Nevertheless, he in no way doubted its final conversion. Rather, he believed with complete certainty that in the seed of Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed, and the Jews themselves are certainly included in that universal company.

[Col. 1268D] But because his book ends with prophetic Lamentations, I too wish to bring our little work to an end with complaints and tears. My own misery and the crimes of those like me terrify me; punishments fill me with horror at future penalties; the world’s decline already weighs heavily upon me; and fear of the coming judgment draws rivers of tears down my cheeks, so that the prayer of our humility may move the clemency of the heavenly Judge to grant pardon.

I fear the day of judgment; I fear the day of darkness, the day of the trumpet, the bitter day, the harsh and sorrowful day. I consider the evil that I endure, but I fear more what remains. I mourn what I already suffer in this life, but I dread suffering worse things after this sentence. Although I already endure torments in punishment, nevertheless fear of Gehenna grievously tortures me because of my guilt. Present punishment now tears me apart, but future punishment troubles me more. The things I endure are severe; the things I fear forever are more severe.

[Col. 1269A] Our inner city, then, once surrounded by angelic protection, abounded within the bounds of faith in a wealth of virtues. Formerly it ruled over the desires of the flesh; now, through those very desires, it lies abandoned, and by sinning it pays tribute to enemies of many kinds of wickedness.

Therefore tears flow down its cheeks, and bitter weeping is poured out day and night. No one among all its loved ones consoles it, because those who once seemed to be its friends amid various delights now, despising it in its fallen state, prove themselves to be its true enemies.

[Col. 1269B] Our attention has been led captive into the foreign land of vices, where it finds no rest and is deprived of every consolation, because all its persecutors, who falsely seemed to be its lovers, prove in the end to be its genuine haters in every respect.

Therefore it now stands mournful amid its ruins, and no joy of celebration gladdens the outward senses through which entrance was opened within to the enemies. The seditious robber sat there and took captive with cruel chains. Hence they were stained by various vices, because they did not show obedience to the command of their teachers.

From this her continence appears squalid, and she is oppressed by the very bitterness of sins. Her enemies are at the head, and her foes exercise an unjust dominion over her. For because of the multitude of her iniquities, her little thoughts are led captive before the face of the one who afflicts her.

[Col. 1269C] Therefore the daughter of Zion has been stripped bare—she who once contemplated God with a pure mind in all his beauty. Nor does the spirit now exercise its own principate; rather, before the pursuing enemy, it falls daily before the ancient foe.

Our Jerusalem, once the vision of peace, remembers the day of its inner affliction and the downfall of its great misery, its former joy; and from this great anxieties weigh upon it, when enemies mock its repose and no one brings timely consolation.

It sinned grievously, and therefore, having become unstable, it fell. All who formerly glorified it with flattery later, when they saw its shame, despised and rejected it. Its filthy steps are dirty and soiled, and they find consolation in no purification.

[Col. 1269D] See, O Lord, our affliction, because you see that our enemy is stronger than we are. The enemy plunders what is desirable and by cunning tears away all the ornaments of virtue.

Adversaries enter your sanctuaries, although you commanded that your holy things be made inaccessible to strangers. Our multitude groans because of hunger for the word and no longer has anything with which to refresh the hunger of the soul.

See, O Lord, and consider how worthless the inner things of our souls have become. All who pass along the path of our sorrow, consider the power to which no other can be found similar, where the vengeance of divine fury burns.

It has burned and consumed our bones with fire and turned our feet backward. No place of escape is open, because the strength of our soul has utterly failed in every respect. When the Lord delivered us over, that hand pressed upon us, and no way out of escape was open.

[Col. 1270A] Our nobles, who nourished us, have been taken away, and our teachers have been crushed because of our sins. Misery alone presses upon us, and no consolations now comfort us.

The Lord, avenging our sins, has trodden the winepress; therefore our ceiling overflows with tears. All day long we stretch out our hands to our helper, but no one comes to our aid by offering consolation.

We are among enemies, like one polluted by menstruation, and no one cleanses us with the water of the heavenly river. You are just, O Lord, in all your judgments, because by our harmful sins we provoked you to anger.

Attend to our pain, all peoples, and with generous hearts share in our misery. Those whom we thought were our most faithful friends we have found to be our most savage enemies. They had promised us perpetual peace, but by laying ambushes they had prepared eternal captivity for us.

Therefore we are filled with bitterness within, and outside we have been handed over to the sword for slaughter by our enemies. [Col. 1270B] There is no consoler for our groans, because no one hears our outcry.

All our enemies heard of our evil, and because the Lord had abandoned us, they rejoiced with gladness. Let their iniquity, O Lord, enter before you, and repay them for the evil they committed against us, in death.

The Lord cast his Israel from heaven to earth and did not remember his footstool; because of its excessive transgression he hurled Jacob down.

In his fury he destroyed its fortified, sophistical defenses, and by throwing its kingdom and its princes to the ground he polluted them. [Col. 1270C]

Before the enemy he turned away his right hand and consumed his people like a devouring flame. He bent his bow like an enemy and killed everything beautiful to behold.

Like a garden he destroyed his tabernacle and consigned every festival of Zion to oblivion. The Lord rejected his sanctification and destroyed the wall of Zion.

By the strongest vengeance he destroyed its priests and princes, nor were divine visions revealed to its prophets. The elders of the daughter of Zion fell silent, and its virgins, girded with sackcloth, groaned.

At this our eyes also failed from tears, when they saw little children and sucklings fainting from hunger in the streets.

[Col. 1270D] O our watchtower, and once most beautiful fortress of Zion, your prophets saw false things for you and did not reveal your crimes by reproving you. For your offenses they promised you rewards and did not preach to you the torments of Gehenna that you feared.

Therefore, when your enemies ruled over you, they rejoiced over you, mocking and applauding with great delight. Pour out tears daily like a stream, and do not cease to utter mournful complaints.

Raise your hands to God with prayers for the souls of your little ones. Weep with groans; provide solemn funeral rites for your slain; and bury with tears the remains of your beloved ones.

See and consider how great are the evils of grief that we suffer. Many from our assembly fell by the sword of the enemies: children and elders; young men and virgins perished through scandal. For the vengeance justly pronounced by you took every consolation away from us.

[Col. 1271A] We acknowledge the deserved poverty of our need, since we endure a great lack of necessities. We have been filled with gall and labor and placed in darkness, counted as though dead.

We cry out to our judge day and night, but he does not hear. Rather, he closes our ways and overturns our paths. He stretches out bow and shield against us and sets us as a target for the arrow.

We have become a mockery to all our people, because, filling us with bitterness, he made us drunk with wormwood. He broke our teeth to the number, because, filling our souls, he fed us as though with ashes.

Because of poverty and transgression our life wastes away, but the hope that we have in the Lord does not fail at all. For it is not because of our merit, but because of the Lord’s great mercy, that we have not been utterly and [Col. 1271B] completely consumed, because the Lord is good to those who hope in him and exceedingly kind to the soul that seeks him.

It is good to await the salvation of the Lord in silence, because great is the mercy of the most compassionate Judge. It is good, therefore, for one who bears the yoke from his youth to sit alone and devote himself to divine contemplation, despising the pomp of the world, putting his mouth in the dust, and showing himself patient and exceedingly gentle toward the persecutions of enemies.

Although the Lord scourges him temporally, he will not reject or cast him away forever. The time of just recompense will come, when the just Judge will render to each according to his merits.

Who is there who says that anything happens to the Lord without his knowledge, when there is nothing in the world that does not happen at the Lord’s command or by his permission?

[Col. 1271C] Let us therefore examine our ways and return to the Lord. Let us lift our hearts with our hands to heaven, to God. We have acted wickedly and provoked him to anger; therefore we feel that he is angry and inexorable toward us.

He has set a cloud of darkness against us, so that prayer may not pass through, and has shown that the accusation against us was just. Therefore our eye has poured forth streams of water and many rivers of tears, and no rest is now granted us until firm hope and faith receive salvation.

We invoke your name, O Lord, from the deepest pit; I beg you, do not turn your ear away from our sobbing. Judge, O Lord, the cause of our soul, merciful Creator and Redeemer of our life.

You have seen the rage of our enemies against us; hear their reproaches and their thoughts against us. Repay them, O Lord, according to the works of their hands, and give them torments proportionate to the hardness of their heart.

[Col. 1272A] How the finest color of gold has become darkened! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered in the streets! How the renowned sons of Zion have been regarded as potters’ earthen vessels!

Even the lamiae (monstrous creatures), baring their breasts, suckled their young, while heretics, with bestial savagery and pernicious error, deceived their hearers. Like an ostrich toward its young, the mother synagogue became hostile toward her nurselings.

The tongue of the suckling clung to his palate in thirst, and the little children vainly asked for bread to break for themselves.

Our Nazarenes, whiter than snow, redder than ivory, more beautiful than sapphire, have been blackened beyond extinguished coals; and our limbs have become drier than dry wood. [Col. 1272B]

The Lord has fulfilled his fury in us and kindled the fire of his indignation. In mystical Zion, because of the sins of its prophets and the iniquities of its priests, the blind wandered in its streets; the face of the Lord divided them and scattered them like dust before the wind.

Our footsteps slipped on the road; our end in desolation has drawn near. Our Redeemer suffered for our sins, but we, in contrast, chose to live in our iniquities. Therefore vengeance was rendered for our evil works, and our crimes were exposed to the most savage enemies.

Remember, O Lord, what has happened to us, and behold the immense reproach that has come upon us. Our inheritance has been turned over to foreigners, and our labor is directed toward strangers.

[Col. 1272C] We have become orphans without a father; our mothers are like widows. The joy of our heart has failed, and the crown of our head has fallen. Woe to us, because we have sinned; therefore we have been handed over sorrowfully to our enemies.

But you, O Lord, remain forever, and you rule always and everywhere upon your throne through every generation. Why will you forget us forever and abandon us for the length of the days of the age?

Convert us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be converted; renew our days as at the beginning, and we shall be saved. We are yours, O Lord; we belong to you, and in your mercy you provide for us. We shall live forever before you.

Let your mercy, O Lord, always be upon us, so that we may proclaim your praise.

[Col. 1273]

## THE THIRTY BOOKS (TWENTY-NINE) OF THE EXPOSITIONS OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL

## PREFACE TO BISHOP SAMUEL

[Col. 1273A] To the holy and deservedly venerable Lord Samuel, bishop: Rabanus, the least of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ.

From the time I first saw you and recognized the excellence of your intellect and perceived the moderation of your character, I have always striven to love you with the devotion of my heart and have chosen you as my dearest friend. Therefore, sometimes in conversation and sometimes in writing, I have discussed with you the study of the divine Scriptures, whose reading was always sweet to me. Now, because I have heard that you wish to possess some part of my labor, which I have undertaken, insofar as I could, in the exposition of the sacred Scriptures, and especially in the Epistles of the blessed apostle Paul, I have sent to Your Holiness a certain collection from the little works of the holy Fathers on those same Epistles [Col. 1273B]. I recently composed it at the request of the monk Lupus, then a deacon, in order to satisfy your desire and to provide for the usefulness of others who wish to share in our labor.

Nor should the length of the work, which has been completed in thirty books, cause you weariness, because I did not wish to explain the opinions of the aforementioned Fathers in a condensed manner except by setting down their statements intact, just as they were published by them, lest, if I were to abstract anything indiscriminately, I should confuse the meaning of their understanding. Receive, then, the loan entrusted to you, and order diligent scribes to copy it more quickly onto parchment, so that, if anything useful can be derived from it for you, you may have it readily available [Col. 1274A], and that you may return to us more quickly what belongs to us—lest, while others are eating the desired food, our hunger should remain longer without the nourishment of apostolic dishes.

Everything of ours is ready for you, so that whatever you wish to take from it, or whenever you desire to have it, it may in every respect obey your will without hesitation, insofar as our ability permits. Only let your prudence be present, so that you request from us what you judge our ability capable of supplying, and what no impossibility prevents us from providing.

For the rest, I do not wish you to be unaware that in the present year I have been suffering from a serious illness, from which I have not yet been completely freed. Therefore I beg your affection to assist me with holy prayers before the almighty physician, who wounds and heals, puts to death and gives life [Col. 1274B], so that he may not afflict me with the punishments due according to my merits, but, according to his great mercy, may forgive all my offenses and grant that by the gift of his grace I may rejoice in his benefits; and that, under his dispensation, I may pass through the present life in such a manner that I may share in eternal life, which is in the presence of his glory. For it is best for me, throughout all the days of my life, here and hereafter, now and always, to live under his governance and to serve his will in all things.

I pray that you may always be well and advance daily in holy virtues. Holy father, remember us.

## Second Preface: To Lupus, Monk and Deacon

[Col. 1273]

[Col. 1273C] To the venerable brother and fellow soldier, Lupus, minister of Christ, Rabanus, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord.

After I was deprived of your desirable bodily presence [Col. 1274C], believe me, I was never empty of your affection in my heart. Rather, diligently recalling your zeal in meditating upon the divine law and the moderation of character by which, living among us, you were greatly loved by many [Col. 1275A], and mindful both of your request and of my promise, I composed a collection on the Epistles of the apostle Paul, insofar as I was able.

In it, as far as was permitted me and as far as ability allowed, with the assistance also of the companions of our reading, I gathered into one what the holy Fathers had set forth in their various works, each according to what the occasion of the discussion required. Since their writings, in keeping with their abundant eloquence, contained extensive exposition, I, desiring brevity, extracted from them what I judged necessary, so that, if anyone wished to read this work of ours, he would find the opinions of different teachers placed continuously before him; while anyone who disliked it could draw for himself from the purest sources of the Catholic commentators whatever he wished in their proper places.

No one is compelled against his will to make use of our labor, for I have labored only for the diligent, not for the disdainful. It seems better to me that someone should read with a calm mind, without envy of my name or contempt for the work, and without bitterness, those things which he believes useful to himself, than that, by reproving and mocking another’s work, he should incur the guilt of detraction and thereby acquire for his soul the death of sin through offending God [Col. 1275B].

But I admonish the one who has chosen to use our reading that, wherever he sees the names of the authors whose statements I have excerpted from their books, marked externally on the page by individual letters, or by two, or even by three, he should not be reluctant to pronounce them aloud while reading before others [Col. 1276A]. Otherwise, if he does not know who published this or that statement, he may confuse the hearer and make him suppose that the writing belongs to someone other than the one to whom it truly belongs.

For their opinions agree in some matters but differ in others. Therefore I consider it necessary that the attentive hearer should first hear the names of the individual authors written above the statements recited by the reader, so that he may know what each one thought in his reading of the apostolic text. Thus, gathering many things into his mind, he can judge individually what it is useful for him to take from each.

All these teachers were Catholic, except Origen; nevertheless, I have taken only those of his opinions which I believed had been expressed in a Catholic sense, while I have omitted the others. Nor have I set forth much from my own judgment in this work, as I did in my other little works, believing that a sober reader would find sufficient in what he discovers published in the opinions of the Fathers [Col. 1276B].

For the rest, I beg your loving charity, that you yourself may intercede with the Lord for my sins and urge those joined to you by fraternal love to do the same, so that through your intercessions I may deserve to receive forgiveness for my offenses from the divine mercy, and in the future life everlasting rest with God’s elect. May the eternal majesty of Christ deign to preserve your blessedness, holy brother, forever, endowed with sacred virtues.

## Prologue

[Col. 1275]

[Col. 1275C] First it is asked why, after the Gospels—which are the fulfillment of the Law and in which the fullest examples and precepts for living have been arranged— the Apostle wished to send these Epistles to each of the individual churches. The reason seems to have been that he might fortify the beginnings of the nascent Church when new circumstances arose, cut away present and emerging vices, and exclude future questions by the example of the prophets. For after the Law of Moses had been published, in which all God’s commands were read, they nevertheless continually restrained the sins of the people by their renewed teaching and transmitted them in books to our memory also as an example.

Next it is asked why he wrote no more than ten Epistles to the churches. There are ten, including the one called “to the Hebrews” [Col. 1275D]; for the remaining four were addressed specifically to disciples. He arranged his Epistles according to the number of the first commandments of the Decalogue, namely, to show that the New Testament does not differ from the Old and that he was not acting against the Law of Moses. As Moses instituted as many precepts for those liberated from Pharaoh, so the Apostle teaches in this number of Epistles those acquired from slavery to the devil and idolatry. The most learned men have also handed down that the two stone tablets prefigured the two Testaments.

Some people also ask why the example of the Romans is placed first, although reason shows that this Epistle was not written first [Col. 1276C]. For Paul testifies that he wrote it when he was setting out for Jerusalem, whereas he had already exhorted the Corinthians and others by letter to collect the ministry which he was going to carry with him. Hence some wish to understand that all the Epistles were arranged so that the first was placed first even though it was sent later, in order that through the individual Epistles one might advance to perfection by certain steps.

Most of the Romans were so uneducated that they did not understand that they had been saved by God’s grace and not by their own merits; and for this reason the two peoples were in conflict with one another. Therefore Paul asserts that they needed to be strengthened, first recalling the vices of their paganism.

To the Corinthians, however, he already says that the grace of knowledge has been granted, and he does not so much rebuke all of them as criticize them for not rebuking those who were sinning [Col. 1276D], as he says: “Fornication is heard of among you” (I Cor. V); and again: “When you are assembled with my spirit, to hand such a man over to Satan” (ibid.).

In the second Epistle they are praised and admonished to advance more and more. The Galatians are accused of no crime except this one: that they believed the most crafty apostles. The Ephesians, indeed, are worthy of no reproach but much praise, because they preserved the apostolic faith. The Philippians are praised still more, because they did not even wish to listen to false apostles.

The Colossians were such that, although they had not seen the apostle bodily, they were considered worthy of this praise [Col. 1277A]: “For although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Col. II).

He pursues the Thessalonians with every praise in two Epistles, because they not only preserved an unshaken faith in the truth but were also found steadfast in the persecution inflicted by their fellow citizens.

But what should be said about the Hebrews, whose imitators the Thessalonians—who are praised so greatly—are said to have become? As Paul himself says: “And you, my brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judea; for you suffered the same things from your fellow citizens as they did from the Jews” (I Thess. II). Among the Hebrews themselves he recalls the same things, saying: “For you also had compassion on those who were imprisoned, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your goods, knowing that you have a better and lasting substance” (Hebr. X).

## Book One: Exposition on the Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 1277]

### Argument

[Col. 1277B]

**(Ambrose.)** In order to have fuller knowledge of matters, their beginnings must first be sought. The reason for a matter can then be explained more easily if its origin is learned. When we have shown the manner and reason for which the Epistle was given, what we say can appear true.

**(Jerome.)** The Romans who had come to believe, both Jews and Gentiles, wished in their proud contention to place one another above the other. The Jews said:

“We are the people of God, whom he loved and cherished from the beginning. We are circumcised and descended from Abraham’s stock, from a holy race; and formerly God was known only in Judea (Psal. LXXVI). We were liberated from Egypt by God’s signs and powers and crossed the sea on dry foot, while the heaviest waves overwhelmed our enemies. For us the Lord rained manna in the desert and supplied heavenly food as though for his sons. By day and by night he went before us in a pillar of cloud and fire, to show us the way through an impassable region (Exod. XII, XIII, XIV and following passages).

“To say nothing of his other immeasurable benefits toward us, we alone were worthy to receive God’s law, to hear the voice of God speaking, and to know his will. In that law Christ was promised to us; to us also he himself testified that he had come, saying: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel’ (Matth. XV), whereas he called you dogs rather than human beings.

“Is it therefore right that today, having abandoned the idols which you served from the beginning, you should be made our equals, rather than being counted, by the authority and custom of the law, among proselytes? And you would not even deserve this, except because God’s abundant mercy has always wished to admit you for imitation of us.”

The Gentiles, on the other hand, replied:

“The greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the greater the crime of which you show yourselves guilty, for you were always ungrateful for all these things. With the very feet by which you crossed the dry sea, you played before the idols you had made; and with the very mouth with which, shortly before, you had sung to the Lord over the death of your adversary, you asked that images be made for you. With those eyes with which you used to behold the Lord in cloud and fire, you looked upon idols.

“Manna, too, became a source of disgust to you, and in the desert you constantly murmured against the Lord, desiring to return to Egypt, from which he had led you out with a mighty hand [Col. 1278B]. What more need be said? Your fathers so provoked the Lord by repeated rebellion that they all died in the wilderness, and no more than two men from among their elders entered the promised land.

“But why repeat ancient matters, when, even if you had not done those things, no one would judge you worthy of forgiveness for this one reason: that you not only refused to receive the Lord Christ, whom the voices of the prophets had always promised to you, but also killed him by a most shameful death? We, as soon as we came to know him, believed, although he had not previously been preached to us. Hence it is proved that, if we served idols, this must be attributed not to obstinacy of mind but to ignorance. For if we follow him immediately after coming to know him, we would certainly have followed him earlier if we had known him before.

“You boast of the nobility of your race as though imitation of character, rather than carnal birth, made you sons of the saints. Indeed, Esau and Ishmael, although they are descended from Abraham’s stock, are not counted among his sons.”

While they were quarrelling in this manner, the Apostle intervened between them and settled the questions of both sides in such a way as to show that neither had earned salvation by its own righteousness. He demonstrates that both peoples had sinned knowingly and gravely: the Jews, because by transgressing the law they dishonored God; the Gentiles, because, although they ought to have recognized the Creator from creation and venerated him as God, they exchanged his glory for images made by human hands.

He demonstrates with the soundest reasoning that both likewise obtained forgiveness and are equal, especially since it had been foretold in the same law that both Jews and Gentiles would be called to faith in Christ. Therefore, humbling them in turn, he exhorts them to peace and concord.

**(Ambrose.)** It is established that in the time of the apostles the Jews lived in Rome because they were under Roman rule. Those among them who had believed instructed the Romans that, while confessing Christ, they should preserve the law. The Romans, having heard the report of Christ’s miracles, were easily led to believe, being prudent—for they were not undeservedly called prudent, since, once wrongly instructed, they were immediately corrected and remained in the truth.

These Jewish believers in Christ, as can be understood, did not acknowledge that the Lord came from God, thinking him opposed to the one God. Therefore Paul denies that they had obtained the spiritual grace of God, and consequently says that they lacked confirmation.

These are the people who had also subverted the Galatians, so that they would withdraw from the apostles’ tradition. The Apostle was angry with the Galatians because, though they had been well taught, they had easily been led astray. But he ought not to be angry with the Romans; rather, he should praise their faith, because, seeing neither remarkable miracles nor any of the apostles, they had accepted the faith of Christ—though in a Jewish manner, in words rather than in understanding.

The mystery of Christ’s cross had not been explained to them. Therefore, when certain people arrived who believed correctly, questions arose about eating and not eating flesh, and whether the hope that is in Christ was sufficient or whether the law also had to be observed.

Thus he writes to the Romans in four ways, reproving from the beginning the human race by natural reasoning. For they are the head of all the Gentiles, so that the others, and all Gentiles, may learn through them.

The first method is that by which he shows who he is, what he was, and whose he is; by this he also strikes down the heresies.

The second method is that by which he reproves them for not submitting, by the reasoning of nature, to the one God, and for having committed shameful and disgraceful acts among themselves. For this they were so despised that believers rejoiced.

The third method is that they had despised the law given to them; hence he places the Jews before the Greeks.

The fourth method is that he teaches that the Jews had departed from the law and God’s promise in the matter of Christ, and had become like the Gentiles, so that both needed the mercy of God—not hoping for salvation through the law but through faith in Christ Jesus. For this reason he labors with all diligence to remove them from the law, because “the Law and the prophets were until John” (Luc. XVI), and to establish them in faith in Christ alone. Thus he seems to defend the Gospel against the law, not destroying the law but preferring Christianity.

He asserts that Christ was promised in such a way that, when he had been preached, the law would cease—not the whole law, because the law was abridged, so that it might grant salvation in a shortened form. For many things had been handed down to the ancients because of the hardness of their hearts, things that were burdensome; God’s mercy abridged them through Christ by granting forgiveness of past sins.

Therefore the person who wishes to remain under the law is ungrateful toward God’s mercy. For Moses had said: “You shall make those who fear thus, sons of Israel,” so that wherever they turned they would have the law and would by no means be without concern.

Thus, in order to teach that the hope of life and salvation must be placed in Christ without the law, and to show that the Lord himself is the Lord of all, he begins as follows: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ,” and so forth.

## Chapter One: The Apostle Shows That He Has Charity toward the Romans and Rebukes Their Vices, Since They Follow Their Own Desires

### Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ

The first question about Paul’s name seems to arise from this: why is he called Saul in the Acts of the Apostles but now called Paul? In the divine Scriptures we find that the names of certain ancient persons were changed: Abram was called Abraham, Sarai was called Sarah, and Jacob was called Israel. In the Gospels also, Simon was called Peter, and the sons of Zebedee were named “Sons of Thunder.”

But we read that these changes were made by God’s command. Nowhere, however, do we find that anything of this sort was done concerning Paul. On this matter some have thought that the Apostle took for himself the name of the proconsul Paul, whom he had subjected to the faith of Christ in Cyprus, so that, just as kings are accustomed to be named after those whom they have conquered—for example, Parthian after the Parthians and Gothic after the Goths—so the Apostle, after subjugating Paul, was called Paul.

We do not think this should be entirely dismissed. Nevertheless, since no such custom is found in the divine Scriptures, let us seek an explanation more particularly from examples that concern us. We find in the Scriptures that some people used two names, and others even three: Solomon, who was also called Jedidiah; Eliakim, who was also called Jehoiakim; Uzziah, who was also called Zechariah; and many others in the books of Kings and Judges whom you will find called by two names [Col. 1280B].

Nor do the Gospels reject this same custom. Matthew calls himself Matthew in his Gospel, whereas Luke calls him Levi in his Gospel. The same Matthew, in the catalogue of the apostles, says after many others: “Matthew the publican, and James of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, and Simon the Cananaean.” Mark, however, reports: “Matthew the publican, and Thomas, and James of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus.” This is the same person whom Matthew calls Lebbaeus and Mark calls Thaddaeus. Luke lists them as follows: “Matthew, Thomas, James, Judas of James.”

Thus the person whom Matthew called Lebbaeus and Mark called Thaddaeus, Luke wrote as Judas of James. It is certain that the Evangelists did not err in the names of the apostles; rather, because it was customary for Hebrews to use two or three names, each of them gave different names for one and the same man.

According to this custom, therefore, it seems to us that Paul also used two names. As long as he was ministering specifically to his own people, he was called Saul, a name that seemed more native to his country’s language; but he was called Paul when he wrote laws and precepts for Greeks and Gentiles.

This may also be understood in another way.

**(Ambrose.)** Among our ancient people names were formed according to their meaning: Isaac from laughter, and Jacob from heel. In the same way this man was called Saul because of his restlessness. But after he believed, he says that he became Paul from Saul—that is, changed; and because Saul, according to the meaning stated above, is interpreted as “restlessness” or “temptation,” when he came to the faith of Christ he says that he became Paul, that is, as though he had become peaceful, humble, or small from being a tempter.

“Servant,” he says, “of Christ Jesus.” By professing himself a servant of Jesus Christ, he shows that he has been stripped of the law. Therefore he used both names, Jesus Christ, so as to signify the person of both God and man, because he is Lord in both natures. As the apostle Peter also testifies, saying: “He is Lord of all.” Because, therefore, he is both Lord and God, as David says, “The Lord himself is God” (Psal. XCIX)—a truth that the heresies deny.

Marcion, because of his hatred of the Law, seems to deny Christ and his body while confessing Jesus. The Jews and Photinus, however, because of their zeal for the Law, deny that Jesus is God. For whenever he says either Jesus or Christ, he sometimes signifies God and sometimes man. Thus in this passage, among other things, he says: “And one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (I Cor. VIII), which certainly pertains to the Son of God insofar as he is God. Elsewhere he says: “Jesus,” he says, “advanced in age and wisdom” (Luc. II), which certainly applies to the man.

**(Gregory.)** It is asked what it means that Christ the teacher, in another passage, did not call the apostles servants but friends (Joan. XV), while the disciple of that same teacher—indeed, the Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking—called himself a servant. Since both expressions were spoken by Christ, we must carefully consider how they should be understood, especially since our Lord and Savior himself said to the same apostles, according to Luke: “Say: We are unprofitable servants, because we have done what we ought to do” (Luc. XVII); and again: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so” (Luc. XII); and again: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Luc. XIX).

Without prejudging a better interpretation, we should know that there are two kinds of good servitude: one of fear and one of love. One belongs to those who fear, like maidservants and servants; the other to sons who love and please. A maidservant fears being beaten; a married woman fears offending her husband’s feelings. But perfect love casts out the fear of servitude that has punishment. Perfect fear of servitude, however, not only has no punishment but reaches joy itself, as the Psalmist testifies by exhorting us: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Psal. LXXXV); and again: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psal. XVIII).

The holy angels also possess this fear, and the holy apostles certainly possessed it through the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom love descended into our hearts. For this reason the Lord called them not servants but friends, although they were called servants both by themselves and by the Lord—not, to be sure, because of fear, but because of their love of pleasing God.

### Called to be an apostle

**(Origen.)** This name, “called,” because it applies to all who believe in Christ, may seem general. But each person, according to what God foresees and chooses in him, is called either an apostle, a prophet, a teacher, free from a wife, or a servant in marriage. According to the diversity of grace, what is written is fulfilled: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matth. XX).

Nevertheless, it must be understood that someone may be a person called to be an apostle, a person called to be a prophet, or a person called to be a teacher, and, if he neglects the grace of his calling, may fall away from it. So it was with Judas: he was called to be an apostle, but, neglecting the grace of his calling, he became a betrayer. He was indeed called an apostle, but he was not chosen as an apostle.

The prophet who is reported in the Third Book of Kings to have prophesied about Jeroboam (III Reg. XIII) was called a prophet; but whether he was also chosen is a matter for examination, since, although forbidden to eat bread, he ate in Israel and was killed by a lion.

There are also many called teachers throughout all the churches of God, and many called ministers; but I do not know which of them are chosen teachers and chosen ministers. I think the same is true of certain people who are called to suffer for Christ but are not chosen—that is, called martyrs but not chosen martyrs—such as those who, after the trials of tortures and prisons, did not persevere to the end in confessing.

There is also a virgin who is called a virgin but is not a chosen virgin, namely one who has not been holy in body and spirit (I Cor. VII). There is a pastor who is called a pastor but is not a chosen pastor (Ezech. XLIII): he presides over the flock, uses its milk, and covers himself with its wool, but does not seek out the weak, does not bind up the lame, and harasses the strong with labor.

So too there is one who is called self-controlled but is not chosen as self-controlled: he fasts sadly and disfigures his face in order to please human beings (Matth. VI). Similarly, in each degree of grace you will find many called but few chosen (Matth. XX).

### Set apart for the Gospel of God

**(Gregory.)** “Set apart,” he says, “for the Gospel of God.” And according to John: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one” (Joan. XVII). If holy Paul believed that he had become one with those who had been preserved, what does it mean that he confesses himself to have been set apart?

For “set apart” is said as though separated from the flock, especially since the Lord said: “There will be one flock and one shepherd” (Joan. X), and the Holy Spirit spoke by command in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” [Col. 1282C] (Act. XIII).

It must first of all be understood that these testimonies not only do not disagree with one another but also agree with one another in unity. Paul and Barnabas were not separated from the flock but set apart—that is, they had been chosen for the work of the apostolate. Since they were of one heart and one soul with the flock (Act. IV), no separation could exist in any respect; nevertheless, they had been set apart from the flock because they had been chosen for the apostolate. Hands, too, are extended for working, yet they are not separated from the unity of the body.

**(Ambrose.)** He calls himself set apart for the Gospel of God. The Gospel is God’s good announcement, by which sinners are summoned to forgiveness. Since the Apostle held the position of a teacher in Judaism, being a Pharisee, he therefore says that he was set apart from the preaching of Judaism for the Gospel of God, so that, setting aside the law, he might preach Christ, who, where the law was powerless, was able to justify those who believed in him. Yet he is not against the law but in favor of the law, for the law itself says that this would happen, as the prophet Isaiah says:

“He will come from Zion, who will deliver and turn away captivity from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

### Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures

To prove that the hope of faith in Christ is valid and complete, he says that Christ’s Gospel had already been promised by God, so that he might show him to be a trustworthy guarantor of life. Before he came, testimony had been given to him, as the apostle Peter testifies: “For no other name,” he says, “has been given under heaven by which it is necessary for us to be saved” (Act. IV) [Col. 1283A].

“Through his prophets”—to signify more clearly that Christ’s coming would bring salvation. He has already indicated the persons through whom he made the promise known, so that from them it might be evident how true and magnificent the promise is. No one announces an insignificant matter through great heralds.

“In the holy Scriptures.” He added this to strengthen the force of his true declaration, to give believers greater confidence, and to commend the law. For the Scriptures are holy: they condemn vices, and contain the mystery of the one God and of the incarnation of the Son of God for the salvation of humanity, attested by signs and wonders.

### Concerning his Son

It was fitting that, since God was promising his own Son to the world, he should promise him through illustrious men, so that from them it might be known how powerful he was who was being proclaimed. He inserted his future coming into the holy Scriptures, so that what had been preached by the holy Scriptures could not appear false.

**(Origen.)** But whether “the Gospel promised by God through the prophetic Scriptures” should be understood simply, or whether it refers to a distinction from another Gospel—the eternal Gospel mentioned in John’s Apocalypse, which is to be revealed when the shadow has passed away, truth has come, death has been swallowed up, and eternity has been restored—this should be considered. And you, reader, should consider to which eternal Gospel those eternal years may also seem to belong, of which the Prophet says: “And I remembered the eternal years” (Psal. LXXVI). The book of life may also be joined to this, in which the names of the saints are said to be written (Apoc. III).

There are also those books which were opened in Daniel when the judgment had taken its seat (Dan. VII), and those which, according to the prophet Ezekiel, are said to be written within and without (Ezech. II). All these are said to have been written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.

Although it may seem dangerous to entrust discourse about these matters to little written booklets, the sayings of the wise and their enigmas must nevertheless not be passed over idly. They should be contemplated with a very subtle sharpness of mind, insofar as the matter permits, as though through a certain mirror. Otherwise, perhaps, the one who appeared as the Word made flesh, placed in the flesh—as the Apostle says, “he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels” (I Tim. III)—did not appear to the angels without the Gospel in that in which he appeared.

Nor did he appear without the Gospel to us human beings, to whom he says he was sent “to evangelize the poor, to release captives in remission, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. LXI).

If, therefore, when he appeared to us human beings he did not appear without the Gospel, it consequently seems to show that he also appeared to the angelic order not without the Gospel—perhaps that Gospel which we have explained above to be the eternal Gospel mentioned by John.

### Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh

**(Ambrose.)** He says that the one who was the Son of God according to the Holy Spirit—that is, according to God, because God is Spirit and is undoubtedly holy—was made, according to the flesh, the Son of God from the seed of David, in accordance with the saying: “The Word became flesh,” so that Christ Jesus might now be one Son of God and man.

For the one who had been the eternal Son of God was unknown to creation. When he wished to be manifested for human salvation, he had to become visible and corporeal, since he also wished to make himself known through power and to wash human beings from their sins in the flesh, death having been conquered. Therefore he became from the seed of David, so that, just as he had been born from God as King before the ages, so also according to the flesh he might receive royal origin from a king. He was made by the work of the Holy Spirit from a virgin—that is, he was born—so that, with reverence reserved for him, he might be recognized as more than human because his birth differed from human customary birth, as had been foretold by the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb,” and so forth (Isa. VII). Thus, when the event appeared new and worthy of praise, a certain providence of God concerning the visitation of the human race might be recognized as having been foretold.

[Col. 1284B] **(Augustine.)** In vain, Manichaean, do you strive to oppose the prophets. Behold, the Apostle says: “Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.” What the prophets foretold, the apostles saw and preached. He who was became what? He was the Word and became flesh; he was the Son of God and became the son of man; he was God and became man. He assumed humanity; he did not lose divinity.

You ask how Paul here says of Christ that he “was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh,” and, conversely, how he says elsewhere (II Cor. V): “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” Here we must consider how both statements can stand.

This can be resolved as follows: the Son of God was born as a man from the seed of David. The same Apostle says this in one place, and the holy Scriptures most openly proclaim it. But what he says—“Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him”—the context of that passage in Scripture sufficiently shows what the Apostle is discussing.

In his customary manner, he embraces our life in the future life, which has already been included in the mediator Christ Jesus, our head, who has risen. He considers it in certain hope as though it were already present and possessed. That life will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s life is now no longer according to the flesh. For in this passage he calls “flesh” the carnal condition of corruption, which then will no longer exist, because the transformed flesh will not decay.

Therefore we knew Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of the flesh—before he rose. But now we no longer know him in this way, because, as the same Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more,” and so forth (Rom. VI). Thus the two statements appear in no way to contradict one another: before Christ rose, the Apostle knew that he had mortal flesh; but after he rose, he believed that no corruption of death could touch him.

### Who was appointed Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification through the resurrection of the dead—Jesus Christ our Lord

**(Ambrose.)** By saying “Son of God,” he signified God the Father; by adding “the spirit of sanctification,” he disclosed the mystery of the Trinity. Therefore he who, when incarnate, concealed what he was, was then appointed—according to the spirit of sanctification—to be manifested as the Son of God in power when he rose from the dead, as it is written in Psalm 84: “Truth has sprung up from the earth.” For every ambiguity and uncertainty was trampled down and crushed by his resurrection. Indeed, while he was still hanging on the cross, the centurion, seeing the mighty deeds, confessed him to be the Son of God (Matt. 27). The disciples, however, doubted at his death, as Cleopas said at Emmaus: “We thought that he was the one who was beginning to redeem Israel” (Luke 24). The Lord himself says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8); and again: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12), that is, “then I will be recognized as Lord of all.”

He did not say, however, “from the resurrection of Jesus Christ,” but “from the resurrection of the dead,” because Christ’s resurrection grants a universal resurrection. For this appears to be the greater power and victory in Christ: that he should work by that power as one who was dead, by which he had also worked when alive. By this deed it became evident that he had assumed death in order to redeem us.

**(Augustine.)** When he says, “according to the spirit of sanctification through the resurrection of the dead,” he means that they received the gift of the Spirit. After mentioning his resurrection, he recalls the resurrection of the dead, because in him we are all crucified and rise again.

**(Origen.)** It should be noted, according to some authorities, that although *praedestinatus* (“predestined”) is usually found in Latin copies, nevertheless, according to the truth of the interpretation, *destinatus* (“appointed”) is written, not *praedestinatus*. For the one who is already in existence is appointed, whereas the one who does not yet exist is predestined, as in the Apostle’s words concerning those whom God foreknew: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. 8). Those who do not yet exist can be foreknown and predestined; but the one who exists and always exists is not predestined, but appointed.

We have said this because of those who speak impiously against the only-begotten Son of God. Ignoring the difference between *destinatus* and *praedestinatus*, they suppose that he must be counted among those who, although they had not previously existed, were predestined to exist. Yet he was never predestined to become a son; he always existed, just as the Father does. Therefore the one who always exists is appointed, as we have said, not predestined. The one who is predestined did not yet exist when he was predestined, but began to exist in time.

The Apostle therefore uses a necessary distinction when he says that the one who is from the seed of David according to the flesh was “made,” but that the one whom he names “Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification” was “appointed.” For when he had said “Son of God,” he did not add “in power” without reason. By this he indicates that, according to the spirit of sanctification, the Son is of the divine substance. Christ is called “the power of God” and “the wisdom of God,” which is also called “a breath of the power of God,” “a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty,” “the brightness of eternal light,” and “the image of God’s goodness” (Heb. 1).

But a question arises. If what is born from the seed of David is according to the flesh, while what is appointed in power according to the spirit of sanctification is the Son of God and is in the substance of God, how should we understand the soul of Jesus? Here it is not at all named together with the flesh and the substance of the spirit of sanctification or divine power. Yet elsewhere the Savior himself says of it: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and, “Now my soul is troubled” (Matt. 26; John 12). He lays it down from himself—or rather, it descended even to the underworld—and concerning it it is said: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld.”

For it is certain that this soul was not generated from the seed of David. He says that what was made from the seed of David is according to the flesh. Since, therefore, the soul appears to be included neither in what is according to the flesh nor in that in which the Son of God is appointed in power according to the spirit of sanctification, I think that here too the Apostle follows his customary usage. He knows that the soul always stands between spirit and flesh, so that it either joins itself to the flesh and becomes one with the flesh, or joins itself to the spirit and becomes one with the spirit. If it is with the flesh, people become fleshly; but if it is with the spirit, they become spiritual.

For this reason he does not name it separately, but names either flesh or spirit, since he knows that the soul must necessarily adhere to one of these two. Thus he says to certain people: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8); and: “He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body” (1 Cor. 6)—here calling the prostitute flesh or body. “But he who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit with him” (ibid.).

So also here, knowing that the soul of Jesus, joined and clinging to the Lord, had become one spirit with him—the spirit of sanctification—he did not name it separately, lest he divide Jesus. For “what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark 10). The spirit of sanctification is so called because it grants holiness to all, just as it is written elsewhere concerning him: “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1).

### Through whom we have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all the nations for his name

**(Ambrose.)** After the resurrection the Son of God is manifested in power. He gave grace, justifying sinners, and designated apostles, among whom he says that he is a companion, so that apostleship together with grace might be a gift of God.

**(Origen.)** Grace should be referred to endurance in labors, and apostleship to the authority of preaching. Christ himself is also called an Apostle, that is, one sent by the Father, since he says that he was sent to evangelize the poor. Therefore he gives his disciples everything that belongs to him. It is said that “grace was poured upon his lips” (Ps. 44); and he gives his apostles grace, with which they labor and say: “I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Cor. 15).

Since it was said of him, “Therefore, since we have a great high priest and Apostle of our confession, Christ,” he grants his disciples the dignity of apostleship, so that they too may become apostles of God. For the nations, who were alienated from God’s covenant and from the society of Israel, could not believe the Gospel except through the grace given to the apostles. Through this grace, when the apostles preached, the nations are said to obey in faith; and the sound of their grace concerning Christ is remembered as having gone out into all the earth (Ps. 14), so that it reached those who are in Rome. To them the Apostle says: “Among whom are you also, called by Jesus Christ our Lord.”

**(Ambrose.)** This means that, while we perform an embassy among all the nations on behalf of the name of Jesus Christ, you too are among those who have been called. The gift of God has been sent to all, so that when they hear themselves numbered among the other called ones, they may know that they ought not to live under the Law, since the other nations received the law of Christ without the law of Moses.

### To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints

Although he writes to the Romans, he signifies that he is writing to those who are in the love of God. Who are these, if not those who think rightly about the Son of God? These are holy, and they are called. Those who live under the Law understand Christ wrongly and do injury to God the Father when they doubt whether perfect hope of salvation is in Christ. Therefore they are not holy, nor are they called.

### Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ

He says that grace and peace belong to those who believe rightly. Grace is theirs because they have been released from sins; peace is theirs because, from being impious, they have been reconciled to their Creator. As the Lord says: “Into whatever house you enter, and they receive you, say: ‘Peace to this house’” (Matt. 10). And to teach that apart from Christ there is no peace or hope, he added that grace and peace come not only from God the Father but also from Christ Jesus.

He calls God “our Father” because of our origin, since all things are from him. He calls Christ “Lord” because, having been redeemed by his blood, we have been made sons of God.

**(Origen.)** I think that the blessing of peace and grace which the Apostle Paul gives to God’s beloved, to whom he writes, is no less than the blessing of Noah upon Shem and Japheth (Gen. 9), which was fulfilled through the Spirit in those who had been blessed. It is likewise no less than the blessing with which Abraham was blessed by Melchizedek, and Jacob by his father Isaac (Gen. 14), and the twelve patriarchs when they were blessed by their father Israel (Gen. 49), or the blessing of Moses with which he blessed the twelve tribes of Israel (Gen. 33).

I therefore do not consider this blessing of the Apostle, with which he blessed the churches of Christ, inferior to all those blessings. For he himself says of himself: “For I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7). In the Spirit, therefore, the Apostle writes, and in the Spirit he blesses. Through that same Spirit those who are blessed by the Apostle will receive blessings—provided that they are found worthy for his blessing to come upon them. Otherwise what is written will happen: “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, your peace will return to you.”

### First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world

**(Ambrose.)** Having completed his preface, he first of all declares his joy. As the Apostle of the nations, he rejoices that, although the Romans rule the world, they have subjected themselves to Christian faith, which appears humble and foolish to the wise of this age.

There were many things in the Romans from which he could rejoice. They had a noteworthy education and were eager and diligent in good works, being more concerned to do good than to speak—something not far removed from divine religion. Nevertheless, he says that he rejoices first in this: that their faith was spreading everywhere. Although it had not been handed down according to the rule of the truth delivered by its author, he congratulates them because, after the name of Christ had been introduced, they had begun to venerate what came from the one God, knowing that they could make progress.

By this he also displays his love for them, since he rejoices with them over their good beginning and urges them toward progress. He therefore says that he gives thanks only to his God, because their faith was not yet complete. For every fatherhood is from him, and every arrangement of our salvation is from God indeed, but through Christ, not through the Law or through some prophet.

**(Origen.)** We should note how, when writing to certain apostles, he says that he gives thanks for them all, as he now does to the Romans. When writing to others, he does give thanks, but does not add “for all.” If you observe carefully, you will find that wherever he says that he gives thanks for all, he does not heap serious faults or reproaches upon them; but wherever he points out or rebukes certain people, he does not add a thanksgiving in which he gives thanks for all, as he does with the Corinthians or the Colossians. To the Galatians he does not include any thanksgiving at all, because he is amazed that they are transferring themselves so quickly from the one who called them to another Gospel.

His first utterance therefore begins with thanksgiving. To give thanks means to offer a sacrifice of praise, and for this reason he adds “through Jesus Christ,” as through the great high priest. One who wishes to offer a sacrifice to God must know that he ought to offer it through the hands of the high priest.

Nor should what he says, “to my God,” be understood carelessly. This expression can belong only to the saints, of whom it is said, “the God of Abraham,” or “of Isaac,” or “of Jacob.” A person whose god is his belly, or greed, or worldly glory and the pomp of the world, or the power of perishable things, cannot call the Lord his God. Whatever each person worships above all else—that is his god.

But let us see for what the Apostle gives thanks to his God: “because,” he says, “your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

If we take “throughout the whole world” simply, it seems to indicate that in many places of the world—that is, of this earth—the faith and religion of those who are in Rome are being proclaimed. But if, as in certain other passages, the world here means that which consists of heaven and earth and all that is in them, it can also be understood in this way: the powers of whom it is said that they rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke 15) rejoice even more over the conversion and faith of the Romans, when the angels who ascend and descend to the Son of Man announce it to them.

For they too marvel at the conversion of the nations and at the fact that the sound of the apostles of Christ Jesus has gone out into all the earth. Finally, as they watch the struggles of the apostles, they rejoice in this world, just as the Apostle says: “We have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels and to human beings.”

It may also be understood in this way: the faith which the Romans possess is that same faith, and no other, which is proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world. It is preached not only on earth but also in heaven, because Jesus reconciled through his blood not only the things that are on earth but also those that are in heaven (Col. 1), and in his name not only earthly beings but also heavenly and infernal beings bend the knee (Phil. 2). This is for faith to be proclaimed throughout the whole world, through which the whole world is made subject to God.

### For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I remember you always in my prayers

**(Origen.)** God is a witness for his saints, who are themselves also witnesses of God, according to what the prophet says: “You are my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord” (Isa. 43, 44). The Savior likewise says to his disciples: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1), according to what is written: “Whoever confesses me, I will also confess him before my Father.”

**(Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.)** Nevertheless, since the person who calls upon God as a witness is swearing an oath, this passage must be considered carefully, lest the Apostle appear to have acted contrary to the Lord’s command. He often swore in this way, saying: “Now the things that I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1); and again: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I do not lie” (2 Cor. 11; Phil. 1).

The same applies to this statement: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, how without ceasing I remember you always in my prayers.” Unless perhaps someone says that an oath exists only when something is said by which one swears—so that the Apostle did not swear because he did not say “by God,” but said, “God is witness.”

It is ridiculous to think this. Nevertheless, for the sake of contentious people or those who are particularly slow to understand, lest anyone think that there is some difference, let him know that the Apostle also swears in this way when he says: “I die daily, by your glory” (1 Cor. 15).

Therefore, whoever understands that oaths should be used not for good things but for necessary ones should restrain himself as much as possible, so that he does not use one except under compulsion, when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath.

To this belongs the saying: “Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no.’” This is good and desirable. “Whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matt. 5). If you are compelled to swear, you should know that this arises from the weakness of those to whom something is being urged. That weakness is itself an evil, from which we daily pray to be delivered when we say: “Deliver us from evil.”

He did not say, “Whatever is more than these is evil.” You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath, which, although it is not good, is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another person of something that you are usefully urging. Rather, it is from the evil of the one whose weakness compels you to swear.

**(Ambrose.)** In order to commend his love, he calls God as witness—the God whom he serves and to whom he also makes prayer for them—not serving in the Law but in the Gospel of his Son. That is, he serves not in what Moses the servant handed down, but in what the beloved Son taught. For as great as the difference between a servant and a lord, so great is the difference between the Gospel and the Law—not because the Law is evil, but because the Gospel is better.

He therefore serves God in the Gospel of his Son, to show that it is God’s will that people believe in Christ. “Whom I serve”—how? “In my spirit,” he says—not in man-made circumcision, nor in new moons, Sabbaths, or distinctions of foods, but in the spirit, that is, in the mind. Since God is spirit, he must be served by the spirit, or rather by the soul; for one serves him in faith when one serves him with the soul.

The Lord also said this to the Samaritan woman, who thought that he wished to be worshiped on the mountain: “The hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit; those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4).

It is not a place that commends worship, but a devout mind: that is, to worship God the Spirit in truth and in the Spirit, and Christ, one from whom all things exist and one through whom all things exist. The Father seeks such worshipers.

He therefore insists that he remembers them in his prayers, so that he may sow love in them. For he creates in them a desire for himself. Who would not love one whom he hears remembering him? If they had gladly received teaching under the name of Christ from people who had not been sent, with adulterated words, how much more would they desire to hear from one whom they knew to be an Apostle and whose words were accompanied by power?

### Asking whether somehow, at last, I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you

**(Origen.)** He says that he prays without ceasing for those to whom he writes. Remembering his command, he fulfills in deed what he prescribed in speech. But when he says that he begs that somehow, at last, he may have a prosperous journey, so that by the will of God he may come to the Romans, we should consider that the Apostle of God, setting out for the work of the holy Gospel, waits until by his entreaties he obtains not merely a prosperous journey for himself, but a journey made prosperous according to the will of God.

For this reason, all the more should we, who possess neither such consciousness of labor nor such consciousness of merit, ask God for a prosperous journey whenever we plan to do something. I think, however, that the Apostle also wished this to be understood: the prosperity of a journey is not always accomplished according to the will of God.

Indeed, Balaam also had a prosperous journey in going to Balak to curse the people of Israel (Num. 22), but that prosperity was not according to the divine will. Many people also enjoy prosperous success in worldly matters and rejoice in their prosperity, but such prosperity is not according to the will of God except when the work of our journey is of the kind that the Apostle indicates here.

### For I desire to see you, so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift for your strengthening

**(Augustine.)** When he says, “so that I may impart to you a spiritual grace,” he means the love of God and neighbor, so that through the love of Christ they would not envy the nations called into the Gospel.

**(Ambrose.)** This strengthening requires three persons: God, who grants; the Apostle, who ministers; and the people, who receive. He now reveals the purpose of his desire—what his intention was concerning them.

When he says, “so that I may minister a spiritual grace to you,” he indicates that they had acquired a carnal understanding. Under the name of Christ they had not acquired what Christ had taught, but what had been handed down by the Jews. He himself desired to come quickly in order to draw them away from this tradition and give them a spiritual gift, to gain them for God by making them participants in spiritual grace, so that they might be perfect in their confession and faith.

For this reason he desires to be present, so that he may hand on evangelical teaching to them in the sense in which he writes, lest, under the authority of his letters, error should not be removed but strengthened. When present, he could persuade them by his power of what he could not persuade them to accept by words, so that the additions might benefit them more.

**(Origen.)** First of all we must learn that it is apostolic to desire one’s brothers, but for no other reason than to contribute some spiritual gift to them, if we can; or, if we cannot, to receive something from them. Apart from this, the desire to visit the brothers is not credible.

When he says, “so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you,” he seems to indicate that there is something which is a gift but is not spiritual. The gift of faith is undoubtedly spiritual, as are the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, and virginity. But when he speaks of marriage and virginity, he says: “Each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7).

He says that marriage too is a gift, since, as it is written, the woman is fitted by God to the man; but this is not a spiritual gift. Many other things may also be called gifts of God, such as riches, bodily strength, physical beauty, and earthly kingship. These too are given by God, as Daniel says (Dan. 2), because God makes kings and changes them; but they are not spiritual gifts.

Blessed, therefore, are those to whom the Apostle wishes to impart spiritual grace for the strengthening of their faith, so that they may no longer be children or be carried about by every wind of doctrine.
