### That is, that we may be mutually comforted among you by one another’s faith, both yours and mine

**(Ambrose.)** He says that he will be comforted with them if they apprehend spiritual things. Although he rejoices in their faith, he is nevertheless grieved because they were not receiving the right faith. The Apostle had this disposition: he grieved over the faults of others as though they were his own.

Accordingly, he says, “Let us be comforted by one single and identical faith,” so that all consolation might be one if they became of one faith in Christ. Thus the administration of spiritual grace, when the Apostle evangelized, would produce this result.

### For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I often intended to come to you, but have been prevented until now

He reveals his intention and desire. He does not doubt that they know this through the brothers who came to Rome from Jerusalem or the neighboring cities for some matter, whether religious or otherwise—such as Aquila and Priscilla—who made his desire known to the Romans.

Since he often wished to come but was prevented, it happened that he wrote the Epistle, lest, if they remained too long in an evil way of life, they should not easily be corrected. He calls them brothers not only because they had been reborn, but because among them there were at least a few who thought rightly.

Hence he says, “called as saints.” But what does “called as saints” mean? If they are already holy, how are they called in order to be made holy? This pertains to God’s foreknowledge: those whom God knows will become holy are already holy in his sight, and remain called.

He says that he was prevented until the time when the Epistle was given—by God, certainly, who, knowing that they were still unprepared, directed the Apostle to other cities that were already capable of receiving the truth. Although those cities lived under the name of the Savior, they were hindered by carnal vices from being worthy to learn spiritual things.

Thus, when Paul and Silas once wished to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16). Why, except because he knew that the proper disposition was still lacking? But among the Corinthians the Apostle was admonished when the Lord said: “Speak and do not be silent, because I have many people in this city” (Acts 18).

He therefore does not say that he was prevented without reason. He distinguished the causes of his delays and encouraged these people to prepare themselves, so that, hearing that spiritual grace was to be ministered to them, they might make themselves worthy to receive it by abstaining from carnal vices.

### So that I may have some fruit among you, as also among the other nations

He declared that he desired to come to them for the common benefit, so that they might obtain the spiritual grace of salvation and make firm the confession of their faith. Thus he might have fruit before God from his ministry, by which he urges them toward right faith through the example of the other nations. A person is more readily moved to accept what is delivered to him when he sees many others agreeing with it.

### I am a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish

**(Origen.)** We must now ask how the Apostle is a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish. What had he received from them by which he became their debtor?

I think that he became a debtor to the various nations because he received, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the ability to speak in the languages of all the nations, as he himself says: “I speak in tongues more than all of you” (1 Cor. 14). Since a person receives knowledge of languages not for himself but for those to whom he must preach, he becomes a debtor to all those whose languages he has received from God the ability to know.

He becomes a debtor to the wise because he received wisdom in the mystery hidden from the ages, which he would speak to the perfect and the wise. Similarly, he is a debtor to the foolish because he received the grace of patience and long-suffering toward them. For it is the mark of the greatest patience to endure the movements of the foolish.

**(Ambrose.)** By “Greeks” he means the Gentiles, including those who are called Romans, whether by nation or by adoption. By “barbarians” he means those who are not Romans, whose origin is foreign and who are not Gentiles.

By “wise” he means those who, educated in worldly disciplines, are called wise in this age: whether they are observers of the stars, or students of measurement, mathematics, grammar, rhetoric, or music. He shows all these people that such things are of no benefit and that they are not truly wise unless they believe in Christ.

He calls “foolish” those who follow simplicity and are unskilled in these matters. He testifies that he was sent to preach to all of them.

He says nothing about the Jews, because he is the teacher of the nations. In this way he professes himself to be their debtor, because he received teaching for the purpose of handing it on, and by handing it on he gains them.

**(Gregory.)** The excellent teacher is a debtor to the wise and the foolish. When he admonished certain Hebrews who were wise and others who were slower to understand, he overcame the wisdom of the former by an argument concerning the completion of the Old Testament, saying: “What is becoming obsolete and growing old is near to disappearing” (Heb. 8).

But when he saw that others had to be drawn by examples alone, he added: “Saints experienced mockeries and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were cut apart, they were tested, they died by the slaughter of the sword” (Heb. 11). Again he says: “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; contemplating the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (ibid.). In this way victorious reasoning would break the former, while gentle imitation would persuade the latter to climb toward greater things.

### Therefore, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you who are in Rome

**(Ambrose.)** Although he says that he was sent to preach to all the nations, he nevertheless declares himself ready to deliver the Gospel of God’s grace to the Romans, among whom the capital and seat of the Roman kingdom is located.

The welfare—or even the repose—of the members depends upon the head’s not being disturbed. For this reason he desires peace for the Romans, so that Satan may not boast greatly and so that the work of his ministry may bear more abundant fruit.

He testifies that he is ready, as he says elsewhere: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward” (1 Cor. 9). A person is ready to speak to the wise. Concerning the foolish, however, one should understand what he says: “But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship; and woe to me if I do not evangelize” (ibid.).

### For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes

**(Origen.)** Many insults against the Gospel arose at the beginning of its preaching. But Paul had learned patience from the prophets, who said: “Do not be overcome by their reproaches, nor yield to their contempt” (Isa. 51). He knew that he preached the Gospel not with persuasive words of human wisdom but in the power of the Spirit.

**(Ambrose.)** He is addressing those from whom they had received an incorrect faith. The power of the apostles commended their teaching, so that, since what was preached appeared incredible, the signs and wonders performed by the apostles might serve as testimony. One should not doubt what they said, since such great power was present in them.

There is no doubt that words yield to power. Therefore, since no power had appeared among those people, their preaching was without the power of God. He consequently says that he is not ashamed of the Gospel of God, while they are ashamed, because what had been handed on to them had become an object of reproach, was confirmed by no testimony, and disagreed with apostolic teaching.

The power of God, therefore, is what invites people to faith and grants salvation to every believer, forgiving sins and justifying, so that the believer cannot be held by the second death, having been marked with the mystery of the cross. For the preaching of Christ’s cross is an indication of death conquered, as the Apostle John says: “For the Son of God came for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3). Thus every believer is not held by death, because he bears the sign that death has been conquered.

**(Origen.)** Defining what the Gospel is, he declares:

“For the power,” he says, “of God is for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek.”

By saying that it is the power of God for salvation, he seems to indicate as though there were a power of God that was not for salvation but for destruction. For he knows that it is also written in the prophet: “And the caterpillar is my great power” (Joel 2), and that the Psalms say: “In your power, destroy them” (Ps. 58). For this reason he says here, “the power of God for salvation.”

We must consider whether, perhaps, through these different powers of God, God’s right and left hands are being designated, so that the power for salvation is called his right hand, while the power by which he destroys is called his left.

### To the Jew first and to the Greek

**(Ambrose.)** That is, to the one who is descended from Abraham and to the one who is from the nations. For by “Greek” he signifies a Gentile, while by “Jew” he means one descended from Abraham.

The Jews began to be called Jews from the time of Judas Maccabaeus, who, in the cause of the disaster, resisted the sacrileges of the nations, gathered the people through confidence in God, and defended his race. He was one of the sons of Aaron.

Although he places the Jew first on account of the patriarchs, he nevertheless says that the Jew too equally needs the gift of the Gospel of Christ. If, therefore, the Jew also is justified only through faith in Christ Jesus, what need is there to be under the Law?

**(Origen.)** Nor should we pass over the fact that the Greeks formerly classified the whole human race under two designations, calling each person either Greek or barbarian. Their distinction was such that everyone who was not Greek was regarded as a barbarian.

Paul, however, uses a much truer distinction when he says “Jews first,” and afterward “Greeks,” and finally “barbarians.” Since the Greeks, because they themselves lived according to laws, called all others barbarians as though they lived without laws, the Jews are rightly placed by the Apostle even before the Greeks. They began to live according to laws before the Greeks did, and their laws were promulgated by God, not by human beings.

For the righteousness of God is revealed in it, from faith to faith. (Ambrose) He says this because in the one who believes—whether he is a Jew or a Greek—the righteousness of God is revealed. He calls it righteousness because God freely justifies the ungodly through faith without the works of the Law (Gal. II), as he says elsewhere: “that I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the Law, but that which is from faith.” This righteousness, which is from God through faith, he says is revealed in the Gospel, when he gives a person the faith by which he may be justified. For the truth and righteousness of God are shown in him when he believes and confesses. It is God’s righteousness because he gave what he promised. Therefore, the believer, having obtained what God promised through his prophets, proves God to be just and is a witness to his righteousness.

“From faith to faith”—what else does “from faith to faith” mean except that the faith of God is in the fact that he promised what he had said concerning himself, and that there is also the faith of the person who believes the one making the promise? Thus, from the faith of God who promises to the faith of the person who believes, the righteousness of God is revealed. For in the believer God appears righteous, whereas to the one who does not believe he appears unrighteous; the person who does not believe that God has given what he promised denies that God is truthful. He is speaking here against the Jews, who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.

As it is written: “But the righteous person lives by faith.” Therefore he turns to the example of the prophet Habakkuk (Hab. II), to show that it was formerly declared that the righteous person lives by faith, not by the Law—that is, that a person is not justified before God through the Law, but through faith. For life from faith is not this present life, but the life to come, because the righteous person lives by faith, but lives before God.

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness. Just as the righteousness of God is revealed in the one who believes, as I mentioned above, so ungodliness and unrighteousness are revealed in the one who does not believe. For from the very structure of heaven God appears angry with them. He created the beautiful stars of heaven for this reason: so that from them it might be recognized how great and marvelous their creator is, and so that he alone might be worshiped. Hence it is written in the nineteenth Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.”

Therefore, through the natural law, he makes the human race liable, for they could grasp this through the law of nature. The structure of the world bears witness that God alone is the creator and is to be loved, a truth that Moses committed to writing.

(Augustine) When he says that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness, Solomon also says concerning the wise men of the world (Wis. XIII): “If they were able to know enough to estimate the world, how did they not more readily find its Lord and creator?” But those whom Solomon rebukes because they did not recognize the Creator through the creature, the Apostle also rebukes—not because they did not recognize him, but because “they did not give thanks”; and, while claiming to be wise, they became fools and fell into the worship of images.

For the Apostle himself clearly shows that the wise men of the nations did discover the Creator when he spoke to the Athenians. After saying, “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII), he added: “As even some of your own people have said.” He first rebukes the ungodliness of the nations with this purpose: to prove from it that converts can also attain grace. For it is unjust that they should suffer the punishment of ungodliness and not receive the reward of faith.

(Origen) We have spoken more fully elsewhere about the wrath of God, but a few things will be said here as well. The wrath of God is now said to be revealed not against some part, but against all ungodliness and unrighteousness; and not merely against all people, but against those alone who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness. They do suppress it, but they suppress it in unrighteousness. To them he also says that what is knowable about God is manifest, showing that there is something of God that is knowable and something that is unknowable.

He therefore says that the wrath of God is revealed to those who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. What is revealed from obscure and hidden places is brought into knowledge. Since, then, the wrath of God from heaven is said to be revealed even to those who do not ignore the truth but hold it—although they hold it wrongly—it seems that he is presenting reason and knowledge as the means by which the wrath of God is made manifest to those who know the truth, even though they suppress it in unrighteousness. As the following context makes clear, this is understood to refer to the wise men of this world, the learned, or the philosophers.

For what is knowable about God is manifest in them. (Ambrose) The knowledge of God has been made manifest through the structure of the world. Since God is invisible by nature, he made a work that would manifest its maker through its own visibility, so that the unknown might be known through the certain; and so that, through what is impossible for others, he might be believed to be the God of all, since he made this work.

(Origen) What is unknowable about God should be understood as the account of his substance or nature, whose character, I think, is hidden not only from us human beings but also from every creature. Or, if the rational nature will ever make such progress that it can attain this knowledge as well, God knows. Something of this kind seems to me to be hoped for from what the Savior says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Luke X). He would not have added “anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” unless he knew that there are some to whom he wishes to reveal him.

God made it manifest to them—that is, he made a work through which he could be recognized by faith. For his invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made, are seen from the creation of the world.

(Ambrose) He repeats the same meaning in order to teach more explicitly that, although the power and majesty of God cannot be seen by the eyes of creatures in themselves, they are seen through the work of the world when understood.

His eternal power and divinity also. (Augustine) We should certainly supply the words “are seen when understood.” Why should a person attend to the works and not seek the craftsman? You look at the earth producing fruit; you look at the sea filled with its creatures; you look at the air filled with birds; you look at the sky shining with stars—and you do not seek the craftsman of so great a work? But you say to me: “I see these things; I do not see him.” He gave bodily eyes for seeing these things, and the mind for seeing himself.

You do not see the human soul either. Just as you therefore understand the soul, which you do not see, from a person’s conduct and the management of the body, so understand the Creator from the ordering of the whole world and from the governance of the souls themselves.

So that they may be without excuse. (Ambrose) To make it entirely impossible for ungodliness to excuse itself, he added that the powers of God and his eternal divinity are known by human beings. The power of God, which is eternal, and his divinity, which is likewise eternal, are recognized by inferences drawn from creation. His power is that by which he rules all things; his divinity is that by which he fills the universe. By this, therefore, they become without excuse.

Alternatively, the eternal power of God is Christ, who established the things that did not exist, and in whom they remain. Even if his person was not formerly recognized, his works were nevertheless manifest. His divinity is shown by the fact that the elements of things endure within the work established by him. “So that they may be without excuse”: for in many ways the guilty person is proved unable to excuse himself.

For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts. (Augustine) When he says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks,” this is the beginning of sin, concerning which it is said: “The beginning of sin is pride” (Sir. X). If they had given thanks to God, who had granted them this wisdom, they would not have attributed anything to themselves in their thoughts. Therefore the Lord handed them over to the desires of their hearts, so that they might do what they ought not to do.

(Origen) Although God made himself manifest and they knew God, they did not worship him as was fitting or give thanks. Instead, through the vanity of their thoughts, while seeking forms and images for God, they lost the image of God in themselves. Those who seemed to boast of themselves in the light of wisdom were plunged into the deep darkness of folly. For what is so foul, so obscure, and so dark as to turn the glory of God toward the bodily and corruptible likeness of human form? This is what those who worship images are accustomed to do: they equate the majesty of God with birds, quadrupeds, and serpents.

Claiming to be wise, they became fools. (Ambrose) They consider themselves wise because they think that they have investigated the principles of nature, examining the courses of the stars and the qualities of the elements, while despising their Lord; therefore they are fools. For if these things deserve praise, how much more does their Creator!

Yet, ashamed of having neglected God, they often resort to a wretched excuse, saying that one can approach God through these beings just as one reaches a king through attendants. Come now: is anyone so insane, or so forgetful of his own safety, as to attribute the honor due to a king to an attendant? If anyone is found even to discuss such a matter, he is rightly condemned as guilty of treason. Yet these people do not consider themselves guilty when they offer the honor of God’s name to a creature and, abandoning the Lord, worship fellow servants, as though there were something greater that ought to be reserved for God.

People approach a king through tribunes or attendants because a human being is king and does not know to whom he should entrust the administration of the state. But to win the favor of God, from whom nothing is hidden—for he knows the merits of all—there is no need of an intermediary, but only of a devoted mind. Wherever such a person speaks to him, he will answer: “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man.”

Their heart was so blinded that they changed the majesty of the invisible God, whom they had recognized from these works, not into human beings, but—which is worse and an inexcusable crime—into the likeness of human beings. Thus God is called by them the form of corruptible man, that is, an image of man; and those whom they would not dare to honor by this name while alive, they receive as images of the dead into the glory of God.

What sickness, what folly, for these people to call this wisdom to their own condemnation—people among whom the dead have more power than the living, and the dead are preferred to the living! Turning away from the living God, they favor the dead. They are among those of whom it is written: “A mortal person fashions a dead image with wicked hands” (Wis. XV). Solomon’s Wisdom says this concerning such people.

And of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents. By adding these, he intensified the punishment for their dullness, so that such people might be beyond mere folly and vanity. They diminished the majesty and glory of God so far as to give honor to the likeness of those things that are least and smallest.

The Babylonians were the first to call their god an image of Bel, a dead man who was once said to have ruled over them. They also worshiped a serpent-dragon, which Daniel, the man of God, killed (Dan. XIV), and they possessed an image of it. The Egyptians worshiped a quadruped that they called Apis, in the likeness of a cow. Jeroboam imitated this evil when he set up cows in Samaria for the Jews to sacrifice to. They also worshiped birds, because the pagans have sacred crows. Yet the Egyptians worshiped images of all the things I have mentioned, as well as others that it is not necessary to mention now.

These practices were adopted by those who considered themselves wise in the world. Since they recognized the invisible God but did not honor him by doing these things, they were unable to exercise wisdom even concerning visible things. For it is difficult for a person who is prudent in greater matters to be wise in lesser ones.

Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves. (Augustine) When he says that they were “handed over,” this is understood to mean that he allowed them to follow the desires of their hearts. He says that they received from God a reciprocal reward: they were handed over to the lust of their hearts.

(Ambrose) How, he asks, did they deify images and likenesses of created things, to the dishonor of God the Creator? They were handed over to ridicule; and they were handed over not so that they might do what they did not wish to do, but so that they might accomplish what they desired. Here too God’s goodness is evident. It would have been fitting to subject them to doing what they did not wish and to torment them, since even something good is bitter and evil when it is done against one’s will. But these people, turning away from God, were handed over to the devil.

To hand over means to permit, not to incite or implant, so that the things they had conceived in their desires might be completed in action with the devil’s assistance. For they could not have such thoughts of good. They were therefore handed over to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves.

Since he recalls past events, he also signifies the evils of the present time, because they are handed over even now so that they may dishonor their bodies. People of that origin still exist to the present day, people who are said to dishonor one another’s bodies. Although the thought of the soul is what incurs guilt, the bodies are said to be dishonored. Why? Because bodily defilement is evidence of sin in the soul. When the body is polluted, no one doubts that the sin belongs to the soul.

(Cassian) We must nevertheless believe with unshaken faith that absolutely nothing is done in this world without God. We must confess that everything occurs either by his will or by his permission. Thus, things that are good are believed to be accomplished by God’s will and assistance, whereas things that are contrary to goodness occur by his permission, when, because of our wickedness and hardness of heart, divine protection abandons us and allows the devil or shameful bodily passions to rule over us.

The words of the Apostle teach this most clearly when he says: “Therefore God handed them over to passions of dishonor”; and again: “Because they did not believe that they should retain the knowledge of God, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do things that are not fitting.”

They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen. (Ambrose) By exchanging the truth of God for a lie—that is, by giving the name of God, who is true, to those who are not gods—they take away from stones, wood, and other metals what they are and give them what they are not. This is to change the true into the false. They are no longer called stone or wood, but God. This is to serve the creature rather than the Creator.

They do not deny God, but they serve the creature. This does not excuse them; rather, it accuses them all the more, because they recognize God but do not honor him, although he is blessed forever. Amen. This is true: God is called blessed forever because he remains God. But the gods of the nations receive honor for a time because of their ungodliness. Therefore this is not true of them; in God, however, truth remains.

The Apostle assigns this blessing to Christ elsewhere also, saying among other things: “And from them is the Christ according to the flesh, who is blessed above all forever. Amen” (Rom. IX). Either both passages refer to Christ, or he said of the Son what he also said of the Father.

(Origen) We frequently find in Scripture—and we have often explained this—that a human being is said to consist of spirit, soul, and body. But when it is said that “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V), the soul is unquestionably placed between them. It may either yield to the desires of the spirit or incline toward the desires of the flesh.

If it joins itself to the flesh, it becomes one body with it in its lust and desires. But if it associates itself with the spirit, it will be one spirit with it. For this reason the Lord says in Scripture concerning those whose souls had joined themselves wholly to the flesh: “My Spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI). But concerning those whose souls had been joined to the spirit, the Apostle says: “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. VIII).

Moreover, as we find in many passages of Scripture, there are also angels who support and assist either side or either way. The devil, his angels, and all the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places favor the desires of the flesh against the spirit, together with “the principalities and powers, the rulers of the darkness of this world,” against whom human beings struggle.

On the other hand, the angels of human beings favor the spirit as it struggles against the flesh and seeks to call back to itself the human soul, which stands in the middle. These are the ones concerning whom the Lord says: “Their angels continually see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Concerning them the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. I).

The Lord himself also favors the spirit, since he lays down his own soul for his sheep (John X). Yet discipline is maintained in the support given by both sides. The matter is not forced, nor is the soul compelled to incline toward either side. Otherwise neither guilt nor virtue could be attributed to it; neither the choice of good would deserve reward nor the rejection of evil punishment. Freedom of choice is therefore preserved for it in all things, so that it may incline toward whatever it wishes, as it is written: “See, I have set before you life and death, fire and water” (Sir. XV).

Life, therefore, is Christ, and death is the last enemy, who is the devil. The soul therefore has the choice either to choose life, Christ, or to incline toward death, the devil.

If the soul, recognizing God, does not embrace Christ as its life, and does not glorify him as God or give thanks, but becomes futile in its thoughts and exchanges the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents; and if in all these things it turns toward the flesh and those who favor the desires of the flesh, then it will unquestionably be abandoned and deserted by those who, through their support, were encouraging it to join itself to the spirit.

They will allow it—or hand it over—to the desires of its heart, by which it is joined and attached to the flesh. They will not force it, when it resists and recoils, back to the things it flees and rejects. If this image still seems obscure, we will make it clearer and more intelligible through a certain comparison.

Let us suppose there is a dwelling in which the soul lives together with the body and the spirit, as with two counselors. At the doors of this dwelling stands piety, together with all the virtues. On the other side stand ungodliness and every form of luxury and lust, waiting for the soul’s decision. The two groups observing the doors desire to know which choir the soul will invite into itself and which it will repel.

If the soul obeys the spirit, makes use of the better counselor, and summons to itself the choir of piety and chastity, will not the other, despised and rejected, depart? But if it follows the counsels of the flesh and brings into itself the company of ungodliness and lust, will not the whole crown of holiness and piety, to whose counsel the soul has preferred the counsel of evils, withdraw in justified indignation, leaving it to the desires of its heart, so that it may dishonor and disgrace its own body?

It has exchanged the truth of God for a lie; by bringing ungodliness and misery into itself, it worships and serves the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

(Augustine) Understand this carefully: either they worship an image or they worship a creature. Whoever worships an image turns the truth of God into a lie. The sea, for example, is true, while Neptune is a lie—the product of human manufacture. God made the sea, but human beings made an image of Neptune, thereby turning the truth of God into a lie. God likewise made the sun, but human beings, by making an image of the sun, turned the truth of God into a lie.

But lest they say, “I do not worship an image; I worship the sun,” he therefore said: “They worshiped the creature rather than the Creator.” But woe to you if you love created things and abandon the Creator. They are beautiful to you, but how much more beautiful is he who formed them?

Let your Charity pay attention, lest Satan steal upon you by saying what he usually says: “Let us enjoy the creature of God. Why did he make it, unless so that we might enjoy it?” And they become drunk, perish, and forget their Creator. They do not exercise restraint but use created things greedily; the Creator is despised. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.”

God does not forbid you to love these things, but he forbids you to love them as the source of blessedness. Rather, approve and praise them so that you may love the Creator. God has therefore given you all these things: love him who made them. For he intends to give you something greater—namely, himself, who made these things.

Therefore God handed them over to passions of dishonor. For their women exchanged natural use for that use which is contrary to nature. (Ambrose) He testifies that these things came upon the human race from an angry God because of idolatry: a woman desired a woman for shameful intercourse. Some interpret this differently because they do not perceive the force of the statement.

For what does it mean to exchange natural use for that use which is contrary to nature, except to abandon the permitted use and use it otherwise—to cause one and the same part of the body of each sex to offer itself to the other in a way different from what has been permitted? For if it is the bodily part that they suppose, how did they exchange the use of nature, since nature did not grant them such a use?

Earlier he had already said that they were handed over to impurity, but he had not yet shown the character of the act of impurity. He now explains it: “Likewise, the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned with desire for one another, males for males, committing shameful acts.”

He has now made clear how what he earlier said about the women should be understood. When he added, “Likewise the males,” saying that they “burned with desire for one another,” he showed the women’s sin plainly. And what is surprising about this, when even today women of this kind are found, so that just as the former practice was discovered by men, this one was discovered by women? In the end, women accuse one another, and men likewise.

It is evident that those who had already exchanged the truth of God for a lie also exchanged natural use for that use by which they were disgraced and made liable to the second death. Satan cannot give another law, for he has nothing of his own; he turns what has been permitted and lawful into another order, so that when things are done differently from what was permitted, they become sin.

And receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error. He calls this the compensation for their contempt of God—that is, shame and defilement. For this is the first cause of sin. What is worse, what is more destructive, than this sin? As idolatry is an extremely ungodly and grievous offense, so its recompense is a horrifying and exceedingly foul passion.

And just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do things that are not fitting. (Augustine) When he says again that God handed them over to a debased mind, and so forth, being filled with every unrighteousness, this is understood to concern the doing of harm—that is, the crimes he now mentions.

Earlier he was speaking of corruptions, which are called shameful acts, and from these one proceeds to crimes. For whoever follows the destructive sweetness of shameful acts and tries to remove the face of the person who obstructs him proceeds to crime. The passage in Solomon’s Wisdom (Wis. II) is distinguished in the same way. There, after listing the earlier shameful acts, he says: “Let us oppress the poor righteous person, because he is of no use to us,” and so forth.

(Ambrose) Because of their error concerning images, they were handed over to doing shameful things with one another, as was said. And because they considered these things to be unpunished, judging God to be unconcerned and therefore to be disregarded, it was added that, becoming increasingly dull, they would grow more ready to admit every evil. Thus they might believe that God would not avenge actions that they knew human beings could not fail to dislike.

He now lists all the evils that were added to them, so that perhaps they might turn back to natural understanding and recognize that these things had come upon them because God was angry.

(Gregory) Because they refused to glorify the Lord whom they had known, they were abandoned to a debased mind, so that they would not even know how to weigh the evils they were committing.

“Filled with all unrighteousness.” (Ambrose) He has spoken summarily here and then listed the members of unrighteousness: wickedness and fornication. This fornication includes adultery. If he had said “adultery,” he would have seemed to excuse fornication. Therefore he named the lesser offense, so that the greater might not be believed to go unpunished, together with the other things that are evident.

Greed, wickedness; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents.

How insolently they were seized, so that they did not even acknowledge their parents, whom they have as the authors of their birth; and although their parents rejoiced that they had been born, these people despised those through whom they had begun to exist! This means that they were without understanding and without the love of God. For there was among them the love of the flesh.

They knew the righteousness of God through the law of nature. They knew that these things displeased God, but they did not wish to take this to heart. For they knew that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them. For consent is participation.

Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death. All these evils form a body of sins to which they have been enslaved and made subject to the same power, so that they might do things deserving punishment.

This cause of evils began with the offense of the Sodomites against God, as was said above, and extended its branches into nearly every part of the world. It proclaimed idolatry as the cause of God’s wrath, because idolatry is the first part of error and ungodliness. He condemns it first, so that once it has been destroyed, the vices of conduct may easily be corrected. For when the seed of wickedness has been removed, the fruit of evil will wither. A tree whose roots have been cut does not bear fruit.

For this reason Moses also recorded what happened at Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. XIX), and did not conceal their destruction, so that he might instill fear of avoiding this deed. Therefore this vice and the defilement of a dishonored life are not admitted by one who keeps God in mind.

(Origen) We must therefore consider that we find the Apostle saying for the third time, “God handed them over.” He gives the causes of the first handing over: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks,” continuing through “serpents.” “Therefore,” he says, “God handed them over,” continuing through “their bodies.”

He seems to introduce the cause of the second handing over when he says that “they exchanged the truth of God for a lie,” continuing through “the Creator.” For this reason he says, “God handed them over to passions of dishonor.” This second handing over, however, appears subject to more serious shameful acts, for he says: “Their women exchanged natural use,” continuing through “that which is contrary to nature,” and likewise the males.

He also seems to give the cause of the third handing over when he says: “And just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do things that are not fitting,” filled with every unrighteousness, wickedness, and the other crimes that he subsequently lists.

Yet these distinctions among the causes do not seem to me to fit adequately the crimes assigned to each one. For how is the person who serves the creature rather than the Creator handed over to more shameful acts than the one who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, birds, quadrupeds, and serpents? Or how are those who did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge handed over to both of the former groups as though to an examination of evils?

Nevertheless, because the Apostle seems in these three categories to have enumerated all forms of ungodliness—those who worship images, those who serve the creature rather than the Creator, and those who did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge—I think that the first category indicates pagans indiscriminately, the second their wise men and philosophers, and the third heretics, whether those who deny their God the Creator or those who speak various blasphemies against the Most High.

Therefore, if each of the people we have mentioned, who err in the worship of the divinity, is designated by such headings of evils, let us who seem to be in the Church and to hold the right faith examine ourselves and weigh ourselves with every vigilance, lest perhaps we be separated from them only by the name of true worship while being joined to them in our deeds and actions.

For it is certain that whoever is filled with unrighteousness, wickedness, evil, and greed has not approved of retaining God in his knowledge and belongs to the number of those whom God handed over to a debased mind.

Again, those whose women or men, abandoning natural use, burn with desire for that use which is contrary to nature certainly belong to the number of those who serve the creature rather than the Creator and whom God handed over to passions of dishonor.

Likewise, if some dishonor their bodies through impurity, they belong to those who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God—except that a person who is already faithful and contaminates the temple of God is guilty of a more serious sacrilege than one who, while still profane, contaminates a temple of idols.

Nor should this apostolic statement be passed over: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of man.” It should be understood as rebuking not only those who worship images but also the Anthropomorphites, who, although placed in the Church, say that the bodily image of a human being is the image of God.

They do not understand what is written in Genesis: that the human being was made in the image of God. The Apostle interprets what should be understood by this human being when he says: “Putting off the old human being with his deeds and putting on the new, who was created according to God” (Col. III).

Do you hear that he says the new human being was created according to God? Elsewhere he calls this same new human being the inner human being. But he calls the corruptible one, whose image he rejects here, the outer human being, when he says: “Even if our outer human being is being destroyed, yet the inner human being is being renewed” (II Cor. IV).

Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them. (Augustine) When he says, “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them,” he signifies that whatever they did, they did not do without punishment. For when they consent to evil deeds, they also approve what they themselves have not done.

Therefore, concerning completed sins, he says: “Therefore you are without excuse, O human being, everyone who judges” (Rom. II). When he says “everyone,” he already includes not only the gentile but also the Jew, who wished to judge the gentiles according to the Law.

There are some who do not consider themselves guilty if they do not perform the evil deeds, although they consent to those who do them. To consent is to remain silent when one is able to rebuke; or, when hearing such stories, to flatter the person who tells them. Knowing that the impure and wicked person does not fail to realize that his deeds are known, and that he is not avoided but even honored, he perhaps boasts of being such a person and cannot be ashamed of these things when he sees others favoring and obeying him although they are not themselves like this.

Thus they provide fuel for the sins of others. It is therefore fitting that they be held guilty of the same crime.

There are others who not only do evil but also consent to those who do it, so that they both commit evil and consent to such people. Their wickedness is therefore double. Those who do evil but oppose those who do it are not so wicked; for, knowing the deeds to be abominable, they do not defend them. But those are exceedingly wicked who both do evil and consent to those who do it; they oppose [the object is unclear in the transmitted wording], desiring evils to increase without fear of God. For this reason they do not punish these acts, so that they may persuade others that such things need not be avoided.

## CHAPTER II

Paul rebukes the vices of the Jews, saying that they are guilty like the gentiles and, in certain respects, even worse.

Therefore you are without excuse, every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself, since you do the very things that you judge. Because he had shown that those who do evil and those who approve of its perpetrators are worthy of death [Col. 1304D], he teaches that the person who does evil but does not approve of those who do it is likewise without excuse, lest he should think that he could excuse himself. For it is not right that he should be granted impunity, since through hypocrisy he presents himself as not being such a person, although he is found to be worse: he deceives others so that, while deserving punishment, he may appear worthy of honor. If, then, he calls those without excuse who were able to perceive his invisible attributes through the things that have been made, yet did not obey the truth but remained unjust and ungodly, how much more without excuse are those who, instructed from his Law, trust that they themselves are guides of the blind, and who teach others without teaching themselves—those who preach that one must not steal, yet steal, and so forth, as the Apostle says concerning them. To them, indeed, he says: “Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself, since you do the very things that you judge.”

Human pride, presuming upon the powers of free choice, thinks itself excused when what it does seems to arise from ignorance rather than from the will. In accordance with this excuse, divine Scripture calls all who knowingly sin without excuse; yet it establishes the justice of God’s judgment and does not spare even those who have not heard. For “all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law,” and although they seem able to excuse themselves, he does not admit this excuse who knows that he made the human being upright and gave him a commandment of obedience, and that sin passed into his descendants only through the misuse of free choice. For those who have not sinned are not condemned, since that sin passes from one into all: before each person committed individual sins, all sinned together in that one. Consequently every sinner is without excuse, whether through the guilt of origin or through the addition of personal will—whether he knows or is ignorant, whether he judges or not. For ignorance itself is unquestionably sin in those who were unwilling to understand; but in those who were unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin. Thus in neither case is there a just excuse, but there is a just condemnation.

We know, however, that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things.

That is, we do not fail to know that God will judge such matters truthfully, when we ourselves judge them. For if they displease us, how much more do they displease God, who is more just and is zealous for his work? When he says, therefore, that God will judge them according to truth, he inspires fear, so that the one whom these people call unconcerned may be understood to judge the wicked according to truth—that is, to render the most truthful judgment according to each person’s measure and to spare no one.

(Origen.) But what seems to be shown in this passage is that judgment according to truth belongs to God alone. Some acts are committed in an evil deed but without an evil intention, as when someone commits homicide unintentionally; others are performed in a good deed but without a good intention, as when someone shows mercy not because of God’s commandments but in order to be praised by human beings. Other acts, however, are such that the intention agrees with the deed, whether the deed is good or evil. Since it belongs to God alone to know human hearts and discern the secrets of the mind, he alone is therefore able to judge according to truth.

But it may be asked whether God appears to preserve judgment according to truth concerning those whose iniquities have been remitted by the grace of baptism, whose sins have been covered through repentance, or to whom sin is not reckoned because of the glory of martyrdom. The truth of judgment demands that the wicked receive evil and the good receive good. Although God’s gifts and generosity by no means permit the scrutiny of one who investigates them, let us nevertheless show in this matter also how great is the truth of his judgment.

It is a common conviction that the good ought not to be punished and that the evil ought not to obtain good things. If, for example, someone has at some time done evil, it is certain that he was wicked when he did it. But if, repenting of his former deeds, he corrects his mind toward good things, does good, speaks well, thinks well, and wills what is good, does he not seem good to you, and does he not rightly receive good things? Likewise, if someone turns from good to evil, he will not be judged good because of what he was and is no longer, but evil because of what he is. Deeds, whether good or evil, pass away; but according to their quality they imprint and shape the mind of the one who performs them, leaving it either good or evil and assigning it either to punishment or to rewards.

Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape God’s judgment?

(Ambr.) That is: because you have been given the authority to judge evils and sexual sins, and because you do the same things while no one presently judges you, do you suppose that you will escape God’s judgment? Certainly not. For even if you have escaped God’s judgment in this world—since all authority and judgment come from God—you will not escape it in the future. God himself will judge, and before him flattery and partiality cease.

Or, if it seems just to anyone that such a person should be free from punishment, let him say so. But if it is just that he should not escape, let him believe that God will judge, so that what he judges to be just may prove true and be fulfilled, and let him acknowledge that God, the Creator of the world, providently and carefully seeks an account of the merits of his work. For if he made it and neglects it, he is called a bad craftsman, since by neglecting what he made he shows that he did not make good things. But since it cannot be denied that he made good things—for it is unworthy and incredible that the good should have made evil—he must necessarily be said to care for them. It would be an insult and an accusation against him if he were represented as neglecting the good things he made, especially since life itself is sustained by his will and providence through the service of the elements, as the Lord himself says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5).

(Origen.) If everything spoken by the Law is spoken to those who are under the Law, and what the Gospel or the Apostle says is spoken not to the rulers of the world or to kings but to the leaders and rulers of the churches—namely, to those who judge those within, bishops, presbyters, and deacons—then he says to these people that they should not suppose that they will escape God’s judgment if they themselves commit the acts for which they judge and condemn others. Therefore each person ought first to judge his own conscience and only then examine the deeds of the person whom he judges.

If this were done, all ambition for attaining ecclesiastical office would be completely cut off, if those who wish to rule the peoples were to think that they themselves would be judged rather than that they would judge. Let no one, therefore, suppose that he can escape God’s judgment, as the Prophet says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 138). Since these words are directed especially to those who preside and are judges of peoples, he says elsewhere also that judgment will begin from the house of God (1 Peter 4). And again the Lord says elsewhere: “Among those who draw near to me I will be sanctified” [Col. 1307A] (Leviticus 10), as happened with Nadab and Abihu when they offered strange fire—that is, fire that was not sacred—upon the divine altars. Judgment therefore begins first with the children, for God scourges everyone whom he receives among his children (Hebrews 11).

Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God’s goodness leads you to repentance?

(Ambr.) He says this so that no one should now think himself safe because God’s goodness allows him to sin for a long time, or should despise his patience as though he did not care about human affairs. Let him understand that God delays judgment because judgment has not been promised for this life but for the life to come, so that there he may regret not having believed that God is judge. For when placed in punishment, he will repent without benefit from repentance, because he did not believe in God’s judgment, which he then sees to be true. The one whom the long-suffering of patience did not correct must necessarily be corrected more severely—or rather, tormented by everlasting punishments. He speaks with the greatest severity, knowing that a wicked mind cannot easily be recalled from its vices except by fear.

(Origen.) The person who considers how many evils human beings commit daily on earth, and how almost all have turned aside and become useless (Psalm 13), walking along the broad and spacious way of destruction while neglecting the narrow path of life, can recognize the riches of God’s goodness. Yet, when they consider that God daily makes his sun rise for all these people and supplies them with rain, how many blaspheme against the Lord every day and stretch out their tongues toward heaven? What shall I say now about frauds, wealth, crime, sacrileges, and abominations? Yet in this passage those who judge others but themselves commit the very acts they punish in others seem to be preferred in wickedness.

If someone therefore despises this goodness of God, and his support—as some copies read—and his patience, he does not know that through these things he is being summoned to repentance. Support seems to differ from patience in this way: those who sin more from weakness than from intention are said to be supported, whereas those who, with obstinate minds, seem to insult God through their sins are said to be borne patiently. But just as God has made all things according to measure, weight, and number (Wisdom 11), so there is also a definite measure of his patience. We must believe that this measure was completed either with those who perished in the flood (Genesis 7) or with those who were destroyed by heavenly fire in Sodom (Genesis 19). Hence it is also said concerning the Amorites: “For the sins of the Amorites have not yet been filled up to this point” (Genesis 15).

God therefore bears patiently and awaits the repentance of each person. But do not let this make you careless or slow to conversion, because there is again a definite measure of his patience and support.

But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will render to each according to his works.

In Scripture, the heart is called hard when the human mind, bound by the cold of iniquity like wax, does not receive the seal of the divine image. Elsewhere this same condition is called a fat heart, as when he says: “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Matthew 13; Acts 28). The opposite of hard is soft, which in Scripture is called a heart of flesh; and the opposite of fat is subtle or thin, which the Apostle calls spiritual when he speaks of the person who examines all things.

Thus, when someone knows what is good but does not do it, he must be thought to possess, through hardness of heart, contempt for all good things. The fatness of his heart consists in the fact that it does not receive the sense of subtle and spiritual understanding. In this way an impenitent heart stores up wrath for itself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment: the good work is not done because of hardness, while good understanding is excluded because of the fatness of the heart.

Consider, beloved brothers, that God’s mercy has closed off our hardness. There is now nothing that a human being can find as an excuse. God is despised; he waits; he sees himself being despised and calls the sinner back; he receives the insult of contempt, and yet at some time he promises rewards to those who return. But let no one neglect this long-suffering of his, because he exercises a stricter justice in judgment in proportion as he has previously shown longer patience before judgment.

Here Paul says: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.”

The reprobate therefore store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath from the kindness of almighty God. While time is granted for repentance and opportunity is given for sin, the remedy of grace itself is turned into an increase of guilt. Thus almighty God, seeing that the remedies bestowed are being drawn into an increase of guilt, turns the very goodness he has conferred into the severity of judgment, so that he strikes more severely from the very point at which he now waits more patiently. Since the human being does not wish to abandon evil in order to live, he increases the means by which he will die.

The person who, through God’s long patience, not only refuses to correct himself but adds to his contempt and heaps up sins must necessarily be punished with a more severe penalty, or rather tormented by everlasting flames. When he says, “You store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath,” he uses “wrath” everywhere in the sense of vengeance; therefore he adds, “of God’s just judgment.”

It should be noted that God’s wrath is also mentioned in the New Testament. When people who oppose the old Law read of it in the Old Testament, they think that it should be condemned, although God is not subject to disturbances as we are, as Solomon says: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wisdom 12). “Wrath,” as has been said, is used in the sense of vengeance.

“You store up wrath for yourself.”

(Origen.) A treasury is so called because riches and wealth of various kinds are gathered into it. In Scripture we find three meanings of this term. The Gospel speaks of one treasury on earth, in which the Lord forbids people to store up treasure, and another treasury in heaven, in which he commands the faithful to deposit their riches. Here the Apostle now speaks of treasuries of wrath.

All people, through the things they do in this world, gather treasures in one of these three places. Someone may be unbelieving and unjust, and through hardness of heart and an impenitent heart may deposit his deeds in the treasuries of wrath. Or he may be earthly, thinking and speaking of earthly things; when his field produces abundant crops, he tears down his barns, builds larger ones, and stores up treasure on earth. The former is called hard, the latter foolish, for it is said to him: “Fool, this night your soul will be demanded from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12).

Or, if someone is wise and rich toward God, walking on earth but having his citizenship in heaven, and if everything he does is worthy of the kingdom of heaven, such a person stores the treasures of his riches in heaven.

(Ambr.) The day of wrath belongs to sinners, on which they will be punished; therefore it is a day of wrath for them, because they experience punishment on the day of the revelation of God’s just judgment. For what is now denied to be future will be revealed—that is, it will be recognized. It is called revelation because what is believed not to exist is shown to exist when it is disclosed. It is shown to those who deny it, since it is manifest to believers, so that even unwillingly they may confess God’s just judgment when he renders to each according to his works.

Will they not confess that these things are justly done when they see evils inflicted upon one another being avenged?

(Origen.) Clearly, in the pronouncements of the prophets, the day of wrath signifies the day of vengeance and judgment. Accordingly, the Apostle adds “and revelation” to “the day of wrath,” saying: “On the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment.” For everything is also designated as destined to be revealed in the Gospel, where it is said: “Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor covered that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10).

Some may rightly ask why this day, about which we have earlier stirred the prophetic books, has been appointed for the end of the world, so that all who have died from the beginning of the age until its end may be reserved for judgment on this final day. It is certain that the deeper reasons for this matter are concealed in more secret mysteries: “It is good to conceal the mystery of a king” (Tobit 12). Nevertheless, for the sake of explanation we shall say, insofar as it is possible to commit such matters to writing.

Many people, when they depart this life, leave behind seeds of either good or evil. From these, those who remain receive occasions either of salvation or of destruction. For example, this is true of all who established perverse sects alien to God among the philosophers, or who devised magical sacrileges, or who fabricated teachings and decrees concerning the stars. It is also true of those who among us became authors of heretics and perverse doctrines by publishing books, and of those who produced schisms, scandals, and dissensions in the churches.

On the other hand, the work and progress arising from the apostolic writings, the conversion of the whole Church to God, and the correction of the entire world are also spread through those who have departed. The causes of all these things will not be brought to a close until the end of the world itself. Therefore God’s judgment would not be just until the effects—whether progress or impediment—arising from each of these things had been brought to completion.

The Apostle also seems to signify this when he says: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but the sins of others follow after” (1 Timothy 5).

Moreover, if even those who are outside the body—the saints who are with Christ—do something and labor on our behalf, after the likeness of angels who provide ministries for our salvation; and if, again, sinners who are themselves outside the body also do something according to the purpose of their minds, after the likeness of the evil angels with whom Christ says they will be sent into everlasting fire, let this too be counted among the hidden things of God. These mysteries concerning the day of wrath and revelation are too great to be entrusted to a small page.

Let us inquire concerning the just judgment of God, in which he renders to each according to his works. First, the heretics who say that souls possess good or evil natures are excluded, and let them hear that God does not render to each according to his nature but according to his works. Second, the faithful are built up, lest they think that belief alone is sufficient for them; rather, they must know that God’s just judgment renders to each according to his works.

The Gentiles, however, will by no means seem capable of being excluded on this account, if perhaps they too do something good and act with greater uprightness. Yet another passage written in Ezekiel seems to oppose this interpretation. For he says: “When the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity according to all the iniquities that the wicked has committed, none of all his righteous deeds that he has done will be remembered in the transgression by which he transgressed; but in his sins that he has committed, in them he will die” (Ezekiel 18).

They will say: If nothing of the righteous person’s righteousness is remembered when he has fallen, how will God render to each according to his works?

But let us see whether the divine saying may perhaps contain its own explanation. If we observe how it is written, it says: “When the righteous has turned away from his righteousness.” But it was not sufficient to say merely, “When he has turned away from his righteousness”; it adds, “and has committed all iniquity, according to all the iniquities that the wicked has committed.” This seems secretly to introduce the following interpretation: if the righteous person has not committed all the iniquities that the wicked has committed, perhaps not all his righteousness is removed from memory; but if he has committed all the iniquities that the wicked has committed, then all his righteousness is removed from memory in his fall.

Although the Holy Spirit has concealed this in Scripture because of those who despise the riches of God’s goodness and patience, he has not completely taken it away. For the treasure hidden in the field (Matthew 13) is not found by everyone, lest it be easily plundered and perish; yet it is found by the prudent, who are able to go, sell everything they possess, and buy that field.

(Gregory.) The justice of the eternal Judge saves at the final examination the person whom his mercy here liberates from unclean works. But if anyone is believed to be saved here through the purity of his hands, so that he becomes innocent by his own powers, he is undoubtedly mistaken. For if heavenly grace does not precede the guilty person, he will never find one whom it can reward as innocent.

Hence Moses says in truthful words: “No one is innocent before you by himself” (Exodus 34). Heavenly mercy therefore first accomplishes something in us without us; then, when our free will follows, it accomplishes with us the good that we now desire. Yet through the abundant grace it rewards this in us at the final judgment as though it had proceeded from us alone.

Because divine goodness precedes us in order to make us innocent, Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15). And because our free will follows that same grace, he adds: “His grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.” Then, while recognizing that he was nothing in himself, he says: “Yet not I”; but because he found himself to be something together with grace, he adds: “But the grace of God with me.” For he would not have said “with me” if, together with prevenient grace, he did not also possess the free will that followed it.

Thus, to show that without grace he was nothing, he says, “Not I”; but to demonstrate that he worked together with grace through free will, he adds, “But the grace of God with me.” The innocent person will therefore be preserved in the purity of his hands, because the one who is here preceded by the gift that makes him innocent will be rewarded according to merit when he is brought to judgment.

For those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption, eternal life.

(Ambr.) Since he proclaims that God’s judgment is just, he explains what the future will be for the good. He speaks of those who, knowing that God’s patience is prolonged partly for correction and partly for the greater punishment of those who do not correct themselves, repent of their former deeds and live well, relying on the confidence of faith, lest by remaining here too long they suffer the loss of the promised life.

He will therefore give them glory and honor. And lest this should seem insufficiently great in comparison with the present life—for even here some appear glorious and honored—he adds “incorruption,” so that from this another glory and another honor may be understood, when incorruption accompanies them as well. In the present life, honor and glory are frequently lost, because both the giver, the gift, and the recipient are corruptible. But on the day of God’s judgment, incorruptible honor and glory will be given, so that their entire life may be eternal. Their substance itself will be glorified through a certain transformation of their merits.

Those, then, seek eternal life who are not merely of good profession but also of good life.

(Origen.) When he says “perseverance in good work,” he shows that labor and struggles await those who wish to do good work. There is a contest, as the same Apostle says, not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers and the rulers of this world (Ephesians 6). All these oppose good work, and therefore perseverance is necessary, because it is written: “By your perseverance you will gain your souls.”

Let us see what he means by “good work.” In the Gospel, concerning the woman who poured the alabaster of ointment over the Lord’s head, he declares: “She has done a good work in me” (John 12). He indicates that the person who pours ointment over himself with the word of God—that is, who joins works to the word—performs a good work. The word becomes fragrant, filled with the sweetness of every ointment, when it is adorned with work and deeds.

Let us now inquire what it means to seek glory and incorruption. According to the Apostle, there is a kind of glory that is not glorified, such as the glory that was on Moses’ face, which is said to have been destroyed. This may be understood as the letter of the Law, possessing the glory of commandments but unable to be glorified. There is also another glory that remains and is glorified in Christ. For when he ascended the mountain with Peter, James, and John, he is written to have been transformed into glory; and then, it says, Moses and Elijah appeared, speaking with him (Matthew 17).

This shows that the glory of the Law and the prophets appeared when Christ had been transformed into glory, so that the prophecy and Law, illuminated by his glory and with the veil of the letter removed, might be understood spiritually. This is to be considered the glory of God of which the Apostle writes to the Hebrews concerning the Son (Hebrews 1), saying that he is “the radiance of glory and the exact imprint of his substance.” Through this he declares that the Father is called the source of glory, from whom the Son, the radiance of glory, is generated. Through participation in him, all creatures are said to possess glory, as it is written concerning those who rise from the dead: “There is one glory of the sun [alternative reading: another brightness of the sun, etc.], another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15).

But since we have discussed glory as best we could, let us see what honor signifies, since those who hasten toward eternal life seek not only glory but also honor. For it is written: “Humanity, when it was in honor, did not understand; it was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48). Therefore he seeks the honor that he possessed before he was compared with foolish beasts: the honor he had in paradise before he sinned, the honor by which he was worthy to hear God’s voice, and the honor by which he enjoyed the fruits of paradise and the tree of life.

We shall quickly understand what incorruption signifies if we examine its opposite. Incorruption has corruption as its opposite. Corruption is said to occur in two ways, bodily and spiritually. Bodily corruption occurs when what is written comes to pass: “If anyone corrupts God’s temple, God will corrupt him” (1 Corinthians 3). Spiritual corruption occurs when what the Apostle likewise says comes to pass: “I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity of the faith that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 2).

If someone remains bodily and spiritually incorrupt in the matters mentioned above, he is said to seek incorruption, so that through this incorruption of conduct he may deserve to attain the incorruption that comes through resurrection.

Let us see what is given to those who seek these things. “Eternal life,” he says—life of which the Savior teaches when he says: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). Through this he shows that the substance of eternal life remains in the knowledge of God and Christ Jesus. How the knowledge of God may be possessed, we are taught in the Psalms: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45).

But for those who, through contention, distrust the truth and obey iniquity, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress.

(Ambr.) That is, repeated distress. They distrust the future judgment of God through Christ and therefore also despise his patience, striving to nullify what is true and firm. They believe in iniquity, for it is iniquity to deny what God has foretold will happen.

He therefore sets down three things corresponding to unbelief, saying: “wrath and indignation and distress.” Wrath does not belong to the one who judges but to the one who is judged, when he is found guilty. God is said to become angry so that he may be believed to avenge. For God’s nature is free from these passions. And so that he might be believed not only to become angry but also to avenge, he adds “indignation.” By adding indignation to wrath, he signifies that God will avenge the insult done to him. Distress is the condition in which one constrained by the sentence is afflicted in punishment.

Upon every soul of a human being who does evil.

In this expression he signifies not only deeds but also a profession of faithlessness. For he is speaking of the unbeliever, and therefore he says “upon the soul,” so that you may understand a spiritual rather than a bodily punishment, since the soul will be constrained by invisible punishments.

(Origen.) It should be noted that, when the Apostle enumerates the punishments deserved by sinners, he does not say “wrath and indignation” in such a way that these are to be referred to the one who renders them, as he had said above. Rather, he says: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress.”

Therefore the spiritual person who understands what the Spirit speaks through Paul says that the Apostle did not write these words through ignorance but through divine knowledge. He wrote them in order to show that the things which are to be rendered to those who seek glory and incorruption through perseverance in good work are rendered by God—namely, eternal life. But the things that will overtake those who through contention distrust the truth while obeying iniquity are not given by God—for his gifts are lasting and worthy of him—but arise as the consequence of their deeds. For those who do evil, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, according to what they have stored up for themselves.

Indeed, just as in the former passage he expressed “eternal life” in the accusative case, so here he would have expressed “wrath,” “indignation,” “tribulation,” and “distress” in the accusative case if he had wished to refer them to the person of God as the one who renders them. The same meaning is indicated in other passages of Scripture, as in the First Book of Kings, where the Lord says: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify; those who despise me will be despised” (1 Samuel 2). Here the Lord clearly shows that those who are to be glorified will be glorified by him, but concerning those who are to be despised he does not refer the matter to himself; he simply says that they will be despised.

For if God, just as he bestows good things by himself, also repaid evil by himself, it would follow that, just as he said, “Those who glorify me, I will glorify,” so he would say, “Those who despise me, I will despise.”

A similar point also seems to be shown elsewhere through the prophet, where those who go into the fire are said to find it kindled not by God but by themselves. Isaiah says: “Go, kindle your own fires and the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah 1).

To make this explanation still clearer, let us add the following. If a sick person, contrary to the physician’s command, takes the juices of harmful foods and, through the disturbance of his bodily constitution, falls into fevers and various illnesses of this kind, it is certain that he received the plague of sickness not through the physician but through his lack of self-control. But if he keeps the physician’s instructions and remains in good health, he will rightly be said to possess the blessing of health through the physician.

In the same way, God himself will consequently be seen to render to each person according to his works when those works are good; but evils are understood to come not from God but from the worst juices of intemperance and the raw perversity of one’s deeds.

But we must not leave unexplored the statement that those who, through contention, distrust the truth but obey iniquity. In each of these expressions the Apostle designates illnesses of the soul, whose cure no one will find unless he first recognizes the causes of the diseases.
