For this reason the illnesses of the soul are enumerated in divine Scripture and remedies are described, so that those who have submitted themselves to apostolic disciplines may, once their illnesses have been recognized through what is written, be healed and say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases” (Psalm 102).

One of the soul’s illnesses, and indeed one of the worst, must therefore be understood as contention, through which every perverse deed is performed. Through it heresies arise; through it schisms and all scandals are generated in the churches, while those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight defend as law whatever they please. Hence it happens that they distrust the truth but obey iniquity.

In Holy Scripture, “to distrust” is ordinarily found in the sense of “not to believe” or “not to obey,” as also in this passage. Perhaps the Latin translator would have rendered it more appropriately had he said: “Those who do not obey the truth but obey iniquity.”

Everyone, therefore, who enters upon a path alien to the truth and does not follow the one who said, “I am the truth,” distrusts the truth and is disobedient to it. The same is true of those who err not only in their actions but also in their thoughts and faith, which happens especially through contention.

Those who resist wisdom, justice, and sanctification also distrust Christ, who is not only truth but also wisdom and sanctification. Not to obey Christ, who is righteousness, is to obey iniquity, and to obey those deeds that unquestionably bring about the things written: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress.”

We have often said concerning wrath that at times even the torment inflicted upon the soul by the consciousness of sin is called wrath. Indignation signifies a kind of swelling of that wrath, and also the disturbance that follows it. For example, if we call some serious wound “wrath,” its swelling and distension may be called the indignation of the wound.

Tribulation, however, which is followed by distress, must not be considered like the tribulation of which the Apostle says that tribulation produces perseverance. That kind of tribulation does not have distress following it, as the Apostle himself says: “We suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed” (2 Corinthians 4). Indeed, the tribulation of the saints not only has no distress; it also possesses spaciousness. Thus the righteous says: “In tribulation you have enlarged me” (Psalm 4).

In this spaciousness of the hearts of the saints, God not only dwells but walks. In the hearts of sinners, however, where there is distress because they have given the devil a place to enter, he does enter, but not to dwell or walk about. There is distress there, but he enters in order to hide, like a serpent in a cave. Thus the unhappy soul that this most evil serpent has occupied is drawn along, stiff with the serpent’s cold, constricted, and driven into every kind of distress.

Jews first, and Greeks. (Ambrose.) He always places the Jew first because of the privilege of the Fathers, so that he may either be crowned first or condemned; for the one who believes is more honored on account of Abraham, while the one who distrusts must be treated more severely, because he rejected the gift promised by the Fathers.

But glory and honor and peace are for everyone who does what is good, for the Jew first and for the Greek. Just as he assigned three punishments to unbelievers, so also he assigns three splendid rewards to believers: that they may have honor doubly, as sons of God; glory, on account of transformation; and peace, because those who live well will be at rest in the future, disturbed by no agitation. Indeed, everyone who abstains from contrary things has peace with the Judge.

For there is no partiality with God. He shows that the Jew or the Greek is not despised by God, provided that he believes in Christ, but that the righteousness of faith is accepted in both. Likewise, he shows again that unbelievers are equally guilty, because circumcision without faith will be more harmful, while uncircumcision through faith will be beneficial; and by this he teaches that God is not a respecter of persons. For he does not follow the privilege of ancestry, accepting someone who distrusts on account of the merits of his fathers, or rejecting from himself someone who believes because of the unworthiness of his parents; rather, he either rewards or condemns each person according to his own merit.

Nevertheless, the Apostle seems to me to have established three orders in this passage. First, he speaks of those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption, and says that God will render eternal life to them. It is certain that perseverance in good work exists in those who endure the struggles and contests of piety; we have clearly explained above that this is said of Christians, among whom martyrs are made. This is also proved by what the Lord says to the apostles: “You have tribulation in this world, but the world will rejoice, while you will mourn” [the text reads *legebitis*; probably “you will mourn”] (John 16). A little later he adds: “In your perseverance you will possess your souls.” It therefore belongs to Christians to suffer oppression and mourn in this age, for theirs is eternal life.

And do you wish to know that no one has eternal life except the one who believes in Christ? Hear the Savior himself clearly identifying it in the Gospels: “This is eternal life: that they should know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). Therefore, everyone who has not acknowledged the Father alone and his Son Jesus Christ is alien to eternal life; for this very knowledge, and faith, is designated as eternal life.

There is therefore here a very large class of Christians, to whom eternal life will undoubtedly be rendered: those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption—the life that says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 11). Christ, who is eternal life, is the fullness of every good thing.

Second are placed those who act out of rivalry and who indeed distrust the truth but obey wickedness. For them, wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, are impending—that is, for everyone who works evil, for the Jew first and for the Greek. To these same people, however, the recompense of good is also assigned.

Third, with an equal distinction, a promise is made when he says: “But glory and honor and peace to everyone who does what is good, to the Jew first and to the Greek.” (Origen.) As far as I am able to understand it, he says this of Jews and Gentiles, both of whom are not yet believers. It can happen that someone from among those who are in the law, if he does not believe in Christ because of the common persuasion [or “general opinion”], nevertheless does only what is good: maintains righteousness, loves mercy, preserves chastity and self-restraint, and observes moderation and gentleness, performing every good work. Even if he does not possess eternal life, because, believing in the one true God, he did not also believe in his Son Jesus Christ whom he sent, nevertheless the glory, honor, and peace of his works may not perish.

Likewise, a Greek—that is, a Gentile—even though he does not have the law, is a law for himself, showing the work of the law in his heart and remaining steadfast by natural reason (Romans 14). Thus we see some among the Gentiles either maintaining righteousness, preserving chastity, or observing prudence, temperance, and moderation. Although he appears to be alien to eternal life because he does not believe in Christ, and cannot enter the kingdom of heaven because he has not been born again of water and the Spirit, it nevertheless appears that, on account of the things the Apostle says, he cannot altogether lose the glory, honor, and peace of good works.

For if, according to what we discussed above, the Apostle seems to condemn the Gentiles because, although they knew God by natural understanding, they did not glorify him as God, how could we not think that he can and should also praise those who, knowing God in these matters, glorify him? I therefore do not think it doubtful that one who would have deserved condemnation for an evil work, if he had performed a good work, would be considered worthy of the reward of that good work.

For you see the Apostle saying that we must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5). Thus, finally, he adds in this passage also: “For there is no partiality with God.”

But if this still seems doubtful to you, hear what Peter also declares in the Acts of the Apostles when he had entered the house of the Gentile Cornelius: “I have truly understood,” he says, “that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every place and among every nation, whoever does his will is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

Yet someone may object to us what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who believes in me will not be judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John 3). But let us see how we who believe in Christ are not judged, so that we may understand in what way the one who did not believe has already been judged.

Are we really to suppose that someone who has believed in Christ and afterward committed murder or adultery, or given false testimony, or done something of this kind—things that we sometimes see even believers commit—will not be judged for these acts because he has believed in Christ? It is certain that all these things will come to judgment. Therefore the Lord’s saying must be understood in this way: “Whoever believes in me will not be judged,” because, in accordance with what he has believed, he will not be judged as an unbeliever and faithless person. But he will undoubtedly be judged for his actions.

So also the one who does not believe has already been judged according to the fact that he did not believe. Just as judgment remains for the believer if he commits some sin outwardly, though his faith remains, so also, for the unbeliever, if he has done some good work, the reward will not perish apart from his unbelief—unless perhaps someone wishes to raise some grave and intolerable objection and say that the one who sins ought not to be counted among believers, because if someone believes, he does not sin; and if he sins, this very fact proves that he does not believe.

But how harsh this judgment is, I think no one can doubt. For how many people will be found on earth who have so freed their lives that they do not offend in the least? The apostle John also clearly rejects this sort of opinion in his Epistle, saying: “If anyone says that he has no sin, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. If we confess our sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus the righteous, who pleads for our sins” (1 John 1–2).

These matters, then, have been examined by us in this passage as far as we were able, while also considering what the Apostle says: “Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also.” Thus the explanation becomes clearer: this is how the Apostle places the Jews first and then the Greeks. Let it nevertheless remain to the reader’s judgment to approve what has been said; we have brought forward more material in our discussion so that we might not seem to leave any part of the Apostle’s meaning unexamined.

For all who sinned without the law will also perish without the law. How can anyone sin without the law, when we are all alike subject to the natural law? But he is speaking of the law of Moses, to which the Jews are subject, since they do not believe; and the Gentiles also, though they rejected it long ago, because they were unwilling to join themselves to it.

Unbelieving Gentiles therefore become guilty in two ways: they neither assented to the law given through Moses nor received the grace of Christ. Therefore it is just that they perish.

Thus, just as the one who sins without the law will perish, so also the one who keeps the law without the law will be justified. The one who naturally preserves righteousness is a keeper of the law; for “the law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Timothy 1), but for the unrighteous. Whoever does not sin is a friend of the law. He lacks only faith, through which he may become perfect; for it will do him no good before the Lord to abstain from opposing things unless he receives faith in God, so that he may be righteous in both respects: the former righteousness belongs to time, the latter to eternity.

(Origen.) Yet the one who sins without the law seems to be struck by a harsher sentence, since he is declared destined to perish, although someone who did not use the assistance of the law might appear worthy of compassion. Let us see whether here again, as we have taught elsewhere, something of the divine goodness may be concealed—something that he always hides from those who fear him.

Perhaps the Lord himself shows in the Gospel that he has a more solicitous care for those who are perishing when he says: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke 19). Again he says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10). And David says: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, Lord” (Psalm 118).

In the Gospel also, the woman finds the lost drachma after cleaning the house, and the father rejoices over the younger son who repents, because “he was dead and came to life again; he was lost and was found” (Luke 15). That younger son, as I think, had also been under the natural law; this seems to be indicated by the fact that he spent the portion of his father’s substance that belonged to him by living extravagantly.

Likewise, in the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 34), the shepherds are charged with not binding up the weak and not seeking what had perished. Shortly afterward the Lord himself says: “And what has perished,” he says, “I will seek.”

Nevertheless, we must observe that in all these passages God is never said to have caused anyone to perish. Rather, each person suffers this condition from himself. Thus he says here, “They will perish without the law”; and the Son of Man came to seek what had perished, not what he had destroyed; and he came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, not those whom he had destroyed.

When the Lord himself says, “All whom you have given me I have kept, and none of them has perished” (John 17), he did not say, “I destroyed none of them.”

Certainly, wherever God is said to destroy, you will find that the meaning is rather “to reject,” as when he says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent.”

When he says that as many as sinned in the law will be judged through the law, consider whether this may refer to the punishments written in the law, by which judgments were administered: when people were commanded to be stoned, handed over to the fire, sent to a city of refuge, or subjected to other such penalties. Perhaps the future judgment will likewise be carried out against those who have transgressed the law, since those who are under the law are said to serve as a type and shadow of heavenly things.

(Origen.) Since it is clear that Scripture speaks of different laws, if someone has fled from all of them to such an extent that even the natural law—which is lacking in almost no one—appears to have been erased and abolished in him through hardness or dullness of heart, it may be understood that the statement “he will perish without the law” was spoken of such a person.

But the one who lives under the law is said to be judged through the law, since the Apostle also testifies that everyone who circumcises himself is obligated to perform the whole law (Galatians 5).

(Augustine.) Who would dare to say that Jews who sin in the law will not perish, since they have not believed in Christ, when it has been said of them that “they will be judged through the law” in order that they may perish? For if the condition of those who do not know the law of God is worse than that of those who know it, then what the Lord says in the Gospel will be true: “The servant who does not know his master’s will, and does things deserving blows, will receive few blows” (Luke 12).

And all who sinned under the law will be judged through the law. (Ambrose.) The Jews have the law, in which salvation was promised to them. Since they do not believe or receive the promise, they will be judged under the law in which they lived. The law itself will accuse them, and they will pay the penalties; for the case of the Jews is almost more serious in their own eyes than that of the Gentiles.

Just as believers are preferred, so also, when they distrust, they are found to be worse. For the one who loses what he possessed is more displeasing than the one who could not obtain what he had not hoped for. The latter did not enter the royal palace; the former was sent outside.

# BOOK TWO

[Column 1319]

## CHAPTER 2 FOLLOWS

[Column 1319A]

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified. (Ambrose.) He says this because those who hear the law are not righteous, but those who believe in Christ, whom the law promised, are righteous; and this is what it means to do the law.

No one does the law who does not believe the law, since he does not receive the one to whom the law bore witness. But the one who seems not to be in the law because he is uncircumcised in the flesh, yet believes in Christ, is said to have done the law. The one who says that he is in the law—that is, the Jew—becomes a hearer of the law, not a doer, because he does not believe in Christ, who was written of in the law, as Philip said to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, whom Moses wrote about in the law, and the prophets” (John 1).

(Gregory.) The two disciples in the Gospel (Luke 24) who, after the Lord’s resurrection, were traveling with him on the road invite him to stay with them, prepare a table, and offer him food. They recognize the God whom they had not recognized in the exposition of sacred Scripture in the breaking of the bread.

Therefore, they were not enlightened by hearing God’s commandments, but were enlightened by doing them, because it is written: “The hearers of the law will not be justified before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” Whoever therefore wishes to understand what he has heard should hasten to fulfill in action what he has already been able to understand. Behold, the Lord was not recognized while he was speaking, but he deigned to be recognized while he was being fed.

For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law. “Gentiles” here means Christians, as he says elsewhere: “For I speak to you Gentiles”—those who are uncircumcised and observe neither new moons nor the Sabbath nor the law of foods—and who, guided by nature, believe in God and Christ, that is, in the Father and the Son. For this is what it means to keep the law: to acknowledge the Lord of the law.

The first part of wisdom is this: “Fear God the Father, from whom all things are,” and “the Lord Jesus, his Son, through whom all things are.” Nature itself recognizes its Creator by its own judgment, not through the law but through the reason of nature; for the work perceives its Maker within itself.

These people, who do not have the law, are a law to themselves, showing the work of the law written in their hearts. The meaning is the same: while they believe under the guidance of nature, they show the work of the law, not through the letter but through conscience.

The work of the law is faith. When they present this to God through their words, they show by natural judgment that they themselves are a law, because they spontaneously do what the law commands: they believe in Christ.

(Origen.) When he says “in their hearts,” it should not be thought that the law is said to be written in the bodily member called the heart. For how could flesh either emit such great perceptions of wisdom or contain them in such a great repository of memory?

Rather, we must understand that the rational power of the soul is accustomed to be called “the heart,” as a testimony of a sound conscience. Thus the Apostle says that they contain the law written in their hearts.

It therefore seems necessary to examine what this is that the Apostle calls “conscience.” Is it some other substance than the heart or the soul? For this conscience is also said elsewhere to reproach and not itself be reproached, and to judge a person without itself being judged, as John says: “If our conscience does not reproach us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John 3).

Paul himself also says elsewhere: “Our boasting is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1). Since, then, I see such freedom in it—that in good actions it always rejoices and exults, while in evil actions it does not accuse the conscience itself but reproves and accuses the soul to which it is attached—

Their conscience also bearing witness to them. (Gregory.) When he says that their conscience bears witness, he speaks in accordance with that passage of the apostle John in which he says: “Beloved, if our heart does not reproach us, God is greater than our conscience,” and so forth.

(Ambrose.) They believe with their inner conscience as witness, because they are conscious that what they believe is fitting for them. For it is appropriate for a creature to believe in and venerate its Creator; nor is it absurd that a servant should acknowledge his Lord.

Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Since he said that distrustful Jews would be judged through the law, the law will accuse them because it promised them Christ, whom they refused to receive when he came. But the Gentiles, who certainly do not have the law, will be judged through conscience if they refuse to believe.

First, believing Gentiles will be accusers of unbelieving Gentiles, just as the Lord says to unbelieving Jews concerning his disciples: “They will be your judges” (Matthew 12). The faith of the apostles, who were themselves Jews but believed while the others distrusted, will judge the unbelief of the Jews.

Then the Gentiles will be accused by their own thoughts if, being pricked in conscience, they refused to believe in the faith and power of the Creator, and if through some dullness they failed to consider that they should believe the Lord’s words and deeds. Their conscience will defend them on the day of judgment, because they did not think that they ought to believe; and they will be judged not as malicious but as ignorant. Nevertheless, they will not be without punishment, because they were not permitted to remain ignorant of this.

By “Gentiles” he signifies two groups: both believers and unbelievers. Above he speaks of believing Gentiles, and afterward he adds a discussion of those Gentiles who do not believe, so that just as believers are praised through their conscience, unbelievers may also be accused through their conscience.

I think this can also be understood if one believes that he spoke throughout about believing Gentiles. For he says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Corinthians 5); and: “Whoever has not believed has already been judged” (John 3); and: “The ungodly will not rise in the judgment” (Psalm 1).

Those who sin without the law will also perish without the law. Consequently, they will not be able to stand before the tribunal of Christ and give an account, because, after rising, they will be led to Gehenna.

Those whom he says are accused or defended by their thoughts on the day of God’s judgment are Christians who disagree with the Catholic faith, holding diverse views about Christ or about the meaning of the law within the Church’s tradition—whether Cataphrygians, Novatians, Donatists, or other heretics. Their thoughts will accuse one another on the day of judgment.

If someone understood that the Catholic faith was true but, not wishing to seem corrected, refused to follow it because he was ashamed to depart from what he had long held, he will be accused by his own thought on the day of judgment.

For two thoughts in a person will accuse one another: a good thought and an evil one. The good thought accuses the evil because it contradicted the truth; the evil thought in turn accuses the good because it did not follow what it recognized. By this the person is made guilty: he thought and recognized that the Catholic Church was good and true, yet remained in heresy or schism.

But his thoughts will defend one another if he always thought that what he followed was useful. For he will always say: “In my thoughts I considered what I followed to be useful; this was my faith.” Such a person will have a lighter case, although he must be corrected, because his conscience will not accuse him on the day of judgment.

In this way the hidden things of human beings will be judged on the day of God’s judgment through Jesus Christ our Lord.

(Origen.) Who could doubt that God’s judgment is just, when accusers, defenders, and witnesses are brought forward? Indeed, we human beings should take an example from this just judgment and never think that judgment can be just without an accuser, a defender, and witnesses.

Next, we must see how, on that day when God judges the hidden things of human beings, thoughts will either accuse or defend the soul—not the thoughts that will then exist, but those that now exist within us.

For whenever we think either good or evil thoughts, marks and seals of both good and evil thoughts are left in our heart, as in all other matters. These are now placed secretly within the breast, but on that day they are said to be revealed by none other than the one who alone can know the hidden things of human beings. Our own conscience will also testify that the causes of these signs and marks are not hidden from God.

(Gregory.) Therefore, because every faithful person knows that thoughts will be examined minutely in judgment, he examines himself intensely within before judgment, scrutinizing himself, so that the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully when he sees that the one whom he intends to examine has already been punished for his guilt.

But if you are called a Jew. (Ambrose.) The designation “Jew” derives from the privilege of the ancestors, by which they are called Israelites. Nevertheless, if we wish to comprehend everything that pertains to the matter, we must recognize that this name is understood in three ways.

First, they are sons of Abraham, who through the merit of his faith was made the father of all nations. Second, it is on account of Jacob, who was called Israel for the sake of increasing faith; for the dignity begun in the father is ennobled in the sons.

Third, they are called Jews not so much on account of Judah as on account of Christ, because he arose from Judah according to the flesh. They are called Jews because in Judah was signified what was to come in Christ.

For it was said: “Judah will be your leader”; and: “Judah, your brothers will praise you” (Genesis 49). This praise is not shown to have been given to Judah, but to Christ, whom all those who are pleased to call themselves his brothers praise daily. For he said to the women: “Go and tell my brothers that I am going before you into Galilee” (Matthew 28).

Who would not praise him by whose benefit he lives? Under this meaning, therefore, the Apostle wished to encompass everything: although Judah is later in numerical order, he is superior in merit. But the Jews, not understanding this, defend for themselves the name of the carnal Judah.

And you rest in the law, and boast in God, and know his will, and approve what is more useful, being instructed through the law. He does not wish it to appear very remarkable if a Jew believes, since he has been instructed through the law. But it is exceedingly dangerous if he does not believe, for he has the law as his guide.

Yet it is the merit of the fathers that causes the believer to be preferred; for although someone may flourish by himself, he is nevertheless ashamed in the presence of his own people.

And you trust that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing the form of knowledge and truth in the law. These things are true, because the teaching of the law is to instruct the ignorant, subject the profane to God, and summon the impious away from the worship of idols toward the hope of better things through the promise made in the law.

The teacher of the law therefore rightly boasts in these things, because he has handed down the form of truth. But if he has not received the one whom the law promised, he boasts of the law in vain and does it an injury, while he despises Christ promised in the law. He will no longer be an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, or a light of those who are in darkness, but a guide of them all toward destruction.

Therefore, you who teach someone else do not teach yourself. That is, you who accuse the Gentiles of being without the law and without God do not accuse yourself. For, distrusting Christ promised in the law, you are found guilty of the very things you accuse in them.

You who preach that one must not steal, steal. For you do what you preach must not be done: while you steal away the faith of Christ through a bad interpretation, you deny Christ our Lord, who was promised in the law.

You who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery. You adulterate the law when you remove the truth of Christ and put falsehood in its place. Hence he says elsewhere: “Adulterators of the word” (2 Corinthians 2).

[Column 1323A]

You who abhor idols commit sacrilege. You are sacrilegious when you deny Christ, whom the law and prophetic utterance signify as God.

For Isaiah says: “For you are God, and there is no God besides you; indeed, you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior” (Isaiah 45).

Were the Jews saying of God the Father, “You are God, and we did not know it,” when the whole law proclaims the authority of God the Father, from whom all things are? But because the Son of God always appeared while it remained hidden who he was, when he is recognized after the resurrection it is said to him in confession: “You are God, and we did not know it.”

For he was thought in the law to be only an angel and the leader of the Lord’s army. But when it is understood that he is the Son of God, it is said with thanksgiving: “You are God, and we did not know it.” By this, therefore, it signifies that he was the one who had indeed appeared to the patriarchs as God and was afterward incarnate, but had not been understood by everyone.

You who boast in the law dishonor God through transgression of the law. You are a transgressor of the law when you pass over the meaning of the law, which concerns the incarnation and divinity of Christ, and do not honor God by refusing to receive his testimony concerning his Son. For he himself said: “This is my beloved Son.”

For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written. The prophet Isaiah says this because the name of God was blasphemed among the Gentiles when they failed to recognize that the Jews had been handed over to them because of their crimes, but instead gave glory to their idols, as though they had conquered the God of the Jews through the Jews.

Likewise, in the time of the apostles the name of God was blasphemed in Christ, because the Jews, by denying Christ as God, blasphemed both Christ and the Father, as the Lord says: “Whoever receives me receives not merely me, but the one who sent me” (Luke 9). Therefore he was blasphemed among the Gentiles, because, when Gentiles were believing, the Jews tried to persuade them that Christ should not be believed to be God; thus the blasphemy of the Gentiles originated with the Jews, or with the followers of Photinus.

(Origen.) The Apostle indeed says these things to the one who is a Jew in name but not in conduct. Nevertheless, they can also apply to every person in whom there is only the name of religion and piety, while conduct, knowledge, and faith are lacking.

Therefore we ought to examine these matters more carefully in ourselves than in those who have not come to the faith of Christ, lest one of us, who through faith in Christ and the circumcision given in baptism has become a true Jew and rests in the law of Christ, should also boast that, having driven away the error of idols, he has acknowledged God and come to know his will.

Such a person knows how to approve what is good, pleasing, and perfect, and has advanced so far as to become a guide and teacher of the Church, illuminating those who are blind in knowledge and instructing little ones in Christ. Yet such a person may wish to teach others with great strictness and demand from those whom he instructs the highest discipline of chastity, while he himself is oppressed by intemperance and desire, and sometimes even burns with the flames of hidden lust.

To such a person, therefore, this apostolic saying is appropriately applied: “You who teach someone else do not teach yourself; you who preach that one must not steal, steal; you who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery.”

If, as sometimes happens, he were also to convert gifts offered to God and alms given for the use of the poor to his own profit, the words would rightly be said to him: “You who abhor idols commit sacrilege.”

If he should also fall into open disgrace, and public notoriety had already attached to him because of his greed, unjust judgments, and drunkenness, God would be dishonored by his actions. When it became known to the people that such a person was a teacher of the Church, the name of God would be blasphemed among the Gentiles; for disciples are certainly known to resemble their teacher.

These same things can also be applied, thirdly, to heretics. They too are called Christians, and some of them have also held to the law. Instructed by it, they claim to be guides of others and teachers of infants, and they approve what they say is more useful, though it has been hidden by ecclesiastical teachers.

But because they steal the words of God, snatch away their meaning through perverse interpretation, and introduce an adulterous understanding of the faith to the bride of Christ, the Church, into the royal chambers, the words are rightly said to them: “You who preach that one must not steal, steal; you who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery.” And those who abhor idols commit sacrilege, stealing precious vessels from the temple of God—that is, the pearls of the true faith in the Scriptures.

Through them also the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles, while they stain the chaste and honorable teachings of the Church with the corrupt and shameful errors of heretical perversity. From these people arose accusations of infanticide, incest, and other similar crimes, to bring the holy religion into disrepute.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that the Apostle says these things ironically to the Jews; for someone who truly rests in the law, boasts in God, and approves what is more useful should not be thought to do the things that have been listed.

Circumcision is indeed beneficial if you observe the law. (Ambrose.) One might argue the opposite: If circumcision is beneficial, why is it omitted? But it is beneficial if you observe the law. Circumcision must therefore be retained, and, in order that it may be beneficial, the law must be kept.

What, then, forbade what he showed to be beneficial if the law were kept? It therefore seems that what was forbidden was forbidden improperly: it is not displeasing in itself, but is said to be rendered fruitless through another’s negligence.

But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. This is what he says: if the law is not kept, a Jew becomes a Gentile.

But he used circumcision to signify Abraham’s lineage, because circumcision came from Abraham; for he could not build up what he had destroyed. He says this to teach that belonging to Abraham’s lineage is beneficial only if the law is kept—that is, if one believes in Christ, who was promised to Abraham. Those who are justified by faith have their own merit and are exalted by the honor of their fathers; for all salvation in the law concerns Christ.

Therefore, the one who believes in Christ keeps the law. But if he does not believe, he is a transgressor of the law, because he does not receive Christ, whom the law foretold would come for justification—justification that the law itself could not give.

It will do him no good to be called a son of Abraham, because according to merit the son of Abraham is the one who follows the faith through which Abraham became worthy of God.

Hence he says: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision”—that is, you have become like a Gentile because you do not believe in the one who, in the sign of circumcision, was promised to Abraham as his son.

Therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? The righteousness of the law is Christian faith, as he says elsewhere: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10).

It is therefore clear that if a Gentile believes in Christ, he becomes a son of Abraham, who is the father of faith.

And that which by nature is uncircumcised, while fulfilling the law, will judge you, who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law. The Gentile who believes in Christ, guided by nature, condemns the Jew, to whom the law had promised Christ but who refused to believe in him when he came. How much more, then, is the Gentile worthy of glory, who through nature alone recognized the Creator, as the apostle Peter says: “But you killed the Author of life” (Acts 3); so much more must the Jew be punished, who recognized Christ as Creator neither through nature nor through the law.

(Orig.) What circumcision is—the circumcision that the Apostle says is beneficial—and what law benefits us if it is observed, ought to be carefully investigated, so that, once we understand these things, we may also be circumcised. For if circumcision is beneficial according to the Apostle’s statement, “Circumcision is beneficial if you observe the law,” the Apostle himself teaches in what follows that it is not the circumcision in the flesh, which is outwardly visible, but the circumcision of the heart, made by the Spirit and not by the letter, whose praise comes not from human beings but from God. Elsewhere he says: “See the circumcision: for we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit and do not put confidence in the flesh.” This, in my opinion, is the circumcision that the Apostle says is beneficial if you observe the law—not the law of the letter, whose circumcision in the flesh you do not receive, but the law of the Spirit, according to which you are circumcised in the heart. “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), since the law of God is not written in ink but by the finger of God, which is his Spirit, and not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart.

Yet it may be objected to us that the Apostle says circumcision is beneficial. This can of course be understood as nothing other than the purification of the soul and the rejection of vices. How, then, does he add that this kind of circumcision is beneficial only if one observes the law, when this very circumcision appears to be produced only by observance of the law? But consider whether perhaps cutting away vices and ceasing from evil signify circumcision, while doing what is good and accomplishing what is perfect signify observing the law. For perfection does not consist in ceasing from evil, but in doing good, as we are taught more clearly in the Psalm, where it says: “Turn away from evil”; and it did not stop there, but added: “And do good” (Ps. 36). Likewise, the Apostle, being instructed in these matters, says that circumcision and the rejection of evil are beneficial only if one observes the law of good. For no one can be perfect merely by having done no evil, but only by having done some good.

Hence even the circumcision performed in the flesh was not signified without the image of this meaning, which we are now explaining. Indeed, it was given to infants on the eighth day, although they had not yet performed any work. But if someone should bring forward what is written at the beginning of the Book of Job in praise of him, where it says: “And Job was a truthful man, blameless, just, a worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil thing” (Job 1), why, after praise of his good works has preceded, is abstinence from evil mentioned at the end? I think the judgment is the one that often occurs: many people do what is good, but nevertheless mix in some evil deed; few, however, are like Job, who are so truthful and blameless, so just and worshipers of God, that, while doing all these things, they abstain from every evil thing.

“If, then,” he says, “you are a transgressor of the law,” as we explained above, by not doing what is good, “your circumcision has become uncircumcision,” since even what you appeared to have achieved by abstaining from evil is counted as unbelief against you because you do not perform the works of faith and righteousness. For it is impossible for anyone’s physical circumcision to become uncircumcision again, since once the flesh of the foreskin has been cut away, it cannot return.

It is therefore more appropriately and clearly understood that abstinence from evil conduct, which is signified by circumcision, is counted as impurity if it does not have the works of faith. In the Church, then, if one who has been circumcised through the grace of baptism afterward becomes a transgressor of the law of Christ, the circumcision of baptism will be counted for him as the foreskin of unbelief, since faith without works is called dead, and the portion of the wicked steward is placed with the unbelievers.

But if the uncircumcision observes the righteous requirements of the law, will not that which is uncircumcised by nature, while fulfilling the law, judge you who, with the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law?

Above he said that the Apostle discusses two Jews and two circumcisions, speaking now of the carnal and now of the spiritual. It therefore appears that in the present passage he calls “uncircumcision” the Gentiles who came in the uncircumcision of the flesh to faith in Christ, whom he sets alongside and compares with the Jews who, through the letter and circumcision of the flesh, are transgressors of the law. He says that these Jews will be judged by those in whom there is not circumcision of the flesh but observance of the law.

From this comparison we can also admonish our own people in the Church, for example, if we say that catechumens or even Gentiles are still in uncircumcision, while the faithful are circumcised through the grace of baptism. If, then, a catechumen who has not yet been circumcised through the grace of the washing observes the law of Christ, keeps its righteous requirements and commandments, will he not, by comparison, judge one who is called a believer but does not keep the commandments and despises the law and commandments of Christ? Finally, the Lord himself also said: “The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon” (Matt. 12).

For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh; rather, the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter; his praise comes not from human beings but from God.

(Aug.) When he says “in the Spirit, not in the letter,” this means that the law is to be understood according to the Spirit, not according to what the letter possesses. This occurs among those who have received circumcision more carnally than spiritually. When he says, “whose praise comes not from human beings but from God,” this applies to the one who is a Jew in secret.

(Ambr.) It is not obscure: he denies that circumcision of the flesh has praise with God—for Abraham was not justified because he was circumcised, but because he believed; afterward he was circumcised—but he declares that circumcision of the heart is praiseworthy with God. To circumcise the heart is, by cutting away error, to recognize the Creator. And because circumcision of the heart was to come, Moses first said: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart” (Deut. 10); and Jeremiah likewise: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Jer. 4).

He says this to the Jews who follow idols. For a veil lies around the heart, and when one turns to the Lord, he will circumcise it, because faith removes the cloud of error and grants perfect knowledge of God in the mystery of the holy Trinity, which had been unknown from the ages. The praise of this circumcision, therefore, comes from God and is hidden from human beings; for God regards the merit of the heart, not of the flesh.

The praise of the Jews, however, comes from human beings: they glory in the circumcision of the flesh because it comes from the patriarchs. Hence, among other things, he says: “And glory in their shameful parts, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. 3)—that is, those who think circumcision of the flesh a glory. For the one who glories in the flesh sets his mind on earthly things; but the one who glories in the Spirit has praise from God, for belief is in the Spirit, not in the flesh.

## CHAPTER III

He shows in what respect the Jews were superior to the Gentiles, proving that both Gentiles and Jews need the grace of Christ.

[Col. 1327C]

What, then, is the Jew’s advantage, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.

(Ambr.) Although there are many things that pertain to the honor and merit of Abraham’s offspring, he nevertheless mentions this one thing explicitly: their greatest praise is that they were judged worthy to receive the law, through which they would learn to distinguish right from wrong. Once this first point has been established, the character of the other matters can be understood.

Since he shows that testimony to descent benefits nothing carnal Jews—that is, unbelievers—he does not appear to have treated all Jews, including believers, harshly. Rather, he teaches that it is greatly beneficial to believing Jews, because they are children of Abraham. To them the oracles of God were entrusted: they receive the law, which had grown obsolete through human sins, as though people were sinning with impunity before God, restored on account of the merits of the patriarchs; and they are called the people of God.

Egypt, moreover, is struck with various plagues because of its injuries against them; they are fed with heavenly bread; they are a terror to all nations, as Rahab the prostitute testifies; and Christ the Savior was promised to them for sanctification. Therefore he says that it is greatly beneficial to Jews in every way, because they are children of Abraham. They are placed before the Gentiles—but only if they believe.

(Orig.) We must also consider the fact that he says the oracles of God were entrusted to them; he did not say that the letters were entrusted to them, but the oracles of God. From this a way is opened for us to understand that for those who read but do not understand, and read but do not believe, only the letter was entrusted—the letter of which the Apostle says, “The letter kills” (2 Cor. 3). But the oracles of God were entrusted to those who, understanding and believing what Moses wrote, also believe in Christ, just as the Lord says: “If you had believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5).

But suppose that the Jew has something greater in the letters and possesses some advantage in the oracles of God. Have those who come from the Gentiles to Christ been left with nothing at all, or do they too have some respect in which they possess something greater? Hear the Lord speaking to the believing Gentile centurion: “Truly I say to you, I have not found such faith even in Israel” (Luke 8). See, then, when it comes to faith, how much greater are the Gentiles, of whom the Lord says elsewhere: “They will come from the east and the west and from the four winds of the earth and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God; but the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. 6).

When, therefore, the subject is laws and letters, the Jews have much advantage in every way; but when the subject is faith, the Gentiles, comparatively speaking, have much advantage in every way.

It should also be investigated whether the same thing should be said of the Samaritans: were the oracles of God first entrusted to them, since the law of Moses appears to be observed among them as well? For my part, I would not say that even the letter, which is said to kill, was entrusted to them. The prophet says of them: “Woe to those who despise Mount Zion and trust in Mount Samaria” (Amos 6). For they make themselves strangers to the writings of God by rejecting the prophets.

Nor would I say that the oracles of God were entrusted to heretics who speak iniquity on high, who divide the unity of the Godhead by their impiety, and who separate the law from the Gospels, merely because the divine books appear to be read again among them. Since they perceive nothing spiritual in these books, nothing worthy of God, I would say that they possess only the letter, which kills.

But if perhaps the Jews were unwilling to accept the statement of our Apostle, which says that the letter of the law kills, and think that the law is dishonored if it appears to be despised according to the letter, let us return to Moses himself and see how highly he valued the letter of the law. When he had received tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God, he showed such honor to the letter of the law that he threw the tablets from his hands and shattered those written by the finger of God, yet he was not marked with the guilt of impiety on account of this.

You see, then, that it was not only Paul who despised the letter of the law; long before him Moses both despised and rejected it and shattered the letters of the law. In this he undoubtedly signified even then that the honor and power of the law were not in its letters but in its Spirit.

The Lord likewise, speaking to the Jews in the Gospel, says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.” I think that by “the kingdom of God” he meant the meaning of the law. It was taken away from the Jews, among whom only the letters of the law remained, and was given to the Gentiles, who could produce the fruit of the Spirit through faith.

[Col. 1329A]

What if some of them did not believe? Surely their unbelief will not annul the faithfulness of God? Certainly not.

(Ambr.) No, he says. Because some Jews did not wish to believe what God promised to the children of Abraham, this will not prejudice the other Jews, preventing them from being judged worthy to receive what God promised to believers, especially since the promise was made so that it might benefit those who believe.

Therefore God, not angered on account of their faithlessness—that is, the faithlessness of the Jews—will give the other believers the eternal life that he promised would come through faith in Christ. Those who did not believe made themselves unworthy, without prejudice to the others. By these words he commends believing Jews, because it does them no harm that many of their people refused to believe.

By “the faith of God” we may understand either the faith that God has toward those to whom he entrusts his oracles, or the faith by which those who receive the divine oracles from him believe God. We are therefore warned that the unbelief of those who either do not approach faith or fall away from it does not annul the faith of God that is in us—even if they perhaps mock us when we perform works of faith, whether when we fast, show mercy, devote ourselves zealously to the law of God, or even endure tortures for the martyrdom of Christ.

For God is truthful, and every human being is a liar, as it is written: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

To confirm what he said above—that God is faithful in his promise and every human being is a liar—he adds a prophetic example from the fiftieth Psalm. In it he marked both that God is justified by his words and that the human being is a liar because of unbelief. Both statements are read in the Book of Psalms: God is just and truthful, and every human being is a liar.

He calls the human being a liar when he does not believe what God has promised. For by denying that God will give what he promised, he is a liar; and he declares God a liar for many reasons when he does not believe his promises. Thus he calls every person a liar who distrusts God’s promises.

This applies above all to the Jews, whose case the Apostle is treating here. Although they saw Christ, they denied that he was the one whom God had promised, and for this reason they are pronounced liars. But God is truthful, because he sent Christ just as he promised.

And he prevails when he is judged, because he will give what he is denied to be about to give. For when he is not believed, he is judged a liar. But when he gives what he is judged not to be going to give, he prevails, showing himself truthful and the one who does not believe his words to be a liar.

He will see the Son of God in majesty, whom he denies; he will also see the resurrection of the flesh and will know that faithlessness has been defeated by God’s promise and truth [Perhaps: “by the promised faith and the truth of God”]. Christ also prevailed when he was judged: he was unjustly killed and made the devil guilty, although he had already overcome him by not sinning, so that, defeated a second time, the devil would lose those whom he was holding in the underworld. This means that every human being is a liar, but God alone is truthful.

Therefore, if God is truthful and alone truthful, while every human being is a liar, how will a human being become truthful unless he approaches the one who is not a liar? Finally, it is said to human beings: “You were once darkness” (Eph. 5). Behold, every human being is a liar.

But it is said to God: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35). Since God alone is truthful, because “God is light and there is no darkness in him at all” (John 1), human beings are darkness and God is light; the human being is a liar and God is truthful. When will the human being become truthful? “Approach him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33).

This, then, is what Scripture wished to show: every human being—absolutely every human being, insofar as he belongs to himself—is a liar. For he is not a liar except from what is his own, and he has nothing of his own except that he is a liar. This is not because he cannot be truthful, but because he will not be truthful from himself. Therefore, in order to be truthful, he says: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115). Take away “I believed,” and every human being is a liar.

When he withdraws from the truth of God, he remains in his own falsehood, because “the one who speaks falsehood speaks from what is his own” (John 8). Say, then: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. 115). “In my terror I said”—and I spoke truthfully—“Every human being is a liar.” But he will repay me not with punishment for my falsehood, but with good for evil; and by justifying the ungodly, he made the liar truthful.

“I said in my ecstasy: Every human being is a liar.” He calls terror “ecstasy,” the terror that human weakness suffers when persecutors threaten and sufferings loom. For we understand that the voice of the martyrs appears in this Psalm. The word “ecstasy” is also used in another way, when the mind is taken outside itself not by fear but by some inspiration of revelation.

Terrified, he perceived his weakness and saw that he must not rely on himself. Insofar as he belongs to himself, the human being is a liar; but by the grace of God he has been made truthful, lest, yielding to the pressures of his enemies, he fail to speak what he had believed and instead deny it, as happened to Peter because he had relied on himself.

Therefore it was most truthfully said: “Every human being is a liar.” They will not be liars to the extent that they will not be human beings, since they will be gods and sons of the Most High.

“So that you may be justified,” he says, “in your words and prevail when you are judged.” What does it mean that the future judge is to be judged? It means that the just one is to be judged by sinners and prevail in that judgment, because there was nothing in him that could be judged.

To this one, who had no sin, the prophet David says in the present tense: “Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil before you,” and so forth (Ps. 50). For you surpass all human beings and all judges; and the one who thinks himself just is unjust before you. Therefore you prevail when you are judged: you surpass them because you are more than human beings, and through you human beings were made.

But if our injustice commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?—I speak according to human reasoning. Certainly not.

(Amb.) The Apostle says this according to the sense of the prophet. When David had sinned in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, knowing that the promise could not be given to sinners, he pleaded that the justification of God’s words should prevail over the judgment by which sinners are judged, and that it should restore the repentant person by sanctifying him, so that God might give him what he had promised to the righteous.

For this reason he added: “But if our injustice commends the justice of God,” and so forth. That is, if, because we are sinners, God is justified, will he be unjust if he takes vengeance? For if our injustice benefited him, he would undoubtedly be unjust if he condemned sinners, since our injustice would make God just if, while we are sinners, he gave us what he promised to the saints. For although we are sinners, we are nevertheless restored through repentance, so that, no longer sinners but cleansed, we may deserve to receive the promise.

This, therefore, is not the meaning of the words of the prophet David when he says: “Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” That meaning is asserted by the perverse interpretation of wicked people, namely, that the sins and evil actions of human beings benefit God’s justification, that God appears good through our evils, and that our injustice demonstrates him to be just.

Since God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath, he is no longer justified by our sins. For if he were justified by our sins, he would be unjust if he took vengeance. But because he is not unjust when he takes vengeance, it is clear that our injustice does not commend God’s justice. If it commended it, he would not take vengeance, since he is just.

For this reason he added: “I speak according to human reasoning.” That is, far be it from us to call God unjust, since this belongs to the human being, who is plainly capable both of erring and being deceived, and of deceiving others. God, however, remains unchangeable and cannot fail to love what he has made.

Otherwise, how will God judge this world?

In this passage he calls “the world” the human beings who are in the world, just as we read elsewhere: “The whole world lies in the evil one” (1 John 5). This shows that the human beings who dwell in this world have been placed in wickedness. Yet it is true that it would not have been just for God to judge the world as a sinner if its sins benefited him, so that, when sinners pursued forgiveness at his will, God would appear good; and if they did not sin, he would not appear just. For if he did not sin, having no one to forgive, he would not be good.

(Orig.) Throughout the entire text of this Epistle he wishes to say what salvation was, before Christ’s coming, for those living according to the law, and how, through the Savior’s coming and Israel’s unbelief, salvation is again granted to the Gentiles. He also wishes to say that the Gentiles do not come to salvation in their entirety, but only those who believe, and that Israel is not rejected in its entirety, but the believing remnant is saved.

For this reason, as I have said, the order of the discourse appears confused, since he pursues the differences between believers and unbelievers in both groups. Necessarily, therefore, he also turns his speech toward God, so that through all these differences of acceptance and rejection he may show that the judgments of the true and just God are righteous.

He also shows that falsehood abounds greatly among human beings, and therefore says: “Let God be truthful, and every human being a liar,” as it is written: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50).

At this point, seeing that the contrary objection could plausibly be brought against him—that if God is truthful, every human being must be a liar, and if the justice of God is commended by human injustice, God would appear unjust when he inflicts wrath upon human beings, since he sees his justice approved through their injustice—he responds.

For if our—that is, human— injustice commends God’s justice, human beings will not appear worthy of punishment, since through them God’s justice is made more probable and more conspicuous.

“But far be it,” he says, “that we should accept this, that God who judges and inflicts wrath should appear unjust.” For how will the one who judges the world be considered unjust, when the very name “judge” shows that he does nothing without judgment? Where there is judgment, there is plainly justice, since both the judge and the judgment derive their names from justice.

“If, then,” they pretend that we assert, “the truth of God abounded through our falsehood, I am judged needlessly as a sinner.” But what they blasphemously accuse us of will instead appear in this: “If the truth of God is more clearly shown through human falsehood, and his justice is confirmed through human injustice, then let us do evil so that good may come from evil, and let us lie so that the truth of God may shine forth from our falsehood.”

But some people invent these accusations against us and blaspheme us, as though these things could be said or follow as a consequence of our own assertion. The reasoning of our teaching absolutely rejects this, since we understand God to be a just and truthful judge.

Perhaps for this reason the Apostle did not say that we unjust human beings commend the justice of God, but said: “If our injustice commends the justice of God,” showing that it is not God who is opposed to human beings but justice that is opposed to injustice. Wrath is brought upon human beings because they have given injustice a place within themselves.

God, who is justice, will not therefore appear unjust when he is angry against injustice, to which it is not fitting for him to be favorable. Rather, this wrath also reaches the human beings who have offered themselves as servants of the injustice at which God is angry.

For neither injustice nor justice can exist in nothing. Just as justice is the effect of a just and upright work, and is found first in God and then in those who imitate him, so injustice is the effect of an unjust and crooked work, and is first detected in the devil and then in those who wish to imitate him.

Therefore it is rightly said that wrath is inflicted upon them, although, through the contrast, God’s justice may seem to have been made clear by their injustice. For just as they received within themselves the inclination toward unjust and crooked work, they could have received, much more, the inclination toward what is upright and just. Thus wrath is rightly said to be brought by God upon all human beings.

For if the truth of God abounded through my falsehood to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?

(Ambr.) It is clear that if human falsehood benefits God’s glory, so that he alone appears truthful, sinners ought not to be called sinners, because they would appear to sin not by their own will but under his impulse. Far be this from us.

And not—as we are slandered, and as some claim that we say—“Let us do evil so that good may come.”

Now he reveals the reason why he discusses these matters so carefully and reverently. Wicked people were making this objection, as though this were the meaning of those who preach the remission of sins: that they should do evil and good should come, that is, that they should sin so that God might appear good by forgiving them, in accordance with what was said above.

He calls this blasphemy and rejects it as contrary to the meaning of divine teaching. Faith did not teach that one ought to sin, especially since it proclaims that God will judge. Rather, it counsels those who have fallen, so that, having recovered salvation and living under God’s law, they may sin no longer.

Therefore he added: “Their condemnation is just.” That is, the condemnation of those who, out of jealous envy, interpret what was said above about us in this way is just.

The Jews were making these accusations in order to attack apostolic teaching, saying that, when the apostles preached the remission of sins, they provided an incentive to sin, so that people, secure in the promise, would sin readily. Yet it is certain that after receiving faith it is dangerous to sin, and this is proclaimed to believers.

(Aug.) Grace produces this result so that those who had done evil may now do good, not so that they may continue in evil and think that good will be repaid to them. Therefore they ought not to say, “Let us do evil so that good may come,” but rather: “We did evil, and good came; now let us do good so that in the future age we may receive good for good, we who in this age receive good for evil.”

What then? Are we superior to them? Not at all. For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin.

(Ambr.) That is: why should we continue speaking at greater length? Having supplied the reasons, we have shown that Jews and Greeks—that is, Gentiles—are all guilty, and therefore that they observe the law in vain.

(Greg.) When the apostle Paul writes to the Romans that Jews and Greeks are all under sin, how does he later define not all but many as being made sinners through the disobedience of one human being, saying: “Just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5)?

We must explain how sinners can be many and not all, when the same Apostle says: “All have sinned.” We ought to distinguish between having sinned and being a sinner.

A sinner is one who, by committing many offenses, has already acquired the habit and, so to speak, the practice of sinning. Conversely, a righteous person is not one who has performed an act of righteousness once or twice, but one who, always acting justly, possesses righteousness through practice and habit.

For if someone is generally unjust in nearly all matters but once or twice performs some just work, he would be said to have acted justly in the particular work in which he practiced justice; nevertheless, he would not on that account be called just. Likewise, a just person is said to have sinned if at some point he commits something unlawful; yet he is not thereby called a sinner if he does not maintain the practice and habit of sinning.

It is like the physician who is not called a physician merely because he knows how to apply a spider’s web to a lightly torn scalp or to soothe the swelling of a wound with warm water, although these too may appear to belong to medicine. Rather, the physician is the one who possesses the practice, devotion, and discipline of healing.

From all this I think it has been sufficiently shown that having sinned is one thing and being a sinner another. For all may have sinned, even if they are holy, since no one is free from defilement—not even if his life has lasted only one day. Who is there who has not sinned either in deed, or in word, or—even if he is most cautious—in thought? Therefore he said that all will rightly be called people who have sinned, but not all will be made sinners; rather, many will.

(Ambr.) First he shows that the Greeks are guilty according to the law of nature, and that they have received neither the law of nature nor the law of Moses; hence their case is especially bad and extremely serious.

Then he also shows that the Jews are guilty, although they appear to live under God’s law and have rightly defended for themselves the dignity of their fathers, especially because they despised the promise made to the patriarchs, nullifying the grace of God.

To confirm this point he added a prophetic example from the thirteenth Psalm, saying:

As it is written (Ps. 13): “There is no one who is righteous.”

He began with their injustice in order to enumerate their evil works, and then added worse things, so that he might show that no hope appears in them unless they implore the mercy of Christ, who forgives sins.

Then he added: “There is no one who understands.” This is true, because if he devoted himself to understanding, he would not be unjust.

“There is no one who seeks God.” This too is not hidden, because if he understood what would benefit him, he would seek God—not like King Asaph of Judah, who, after many benefits from God, became so depraved that, while suffering from weakness in his feet and with a prophet present, he did not seek God (3 Kings 15).

All have turned aside together; they have become useless.

(Orig.) When he says this, it seems to me that no one is said to have turned aside except one who at some time stood on the straight path. Hence it appears that the first work of rational nature, which was made by God, was upright and placed, by the gift of the Creator himself, on the straight path.

But because it turned from this path toward the left-hand road of sin, it is rightly now said to have turned aside. An example is the first human being, Adam, who, from the straight path of paradise, turned through the serpent’s deceitful counsel toward the crooked and winding paths of mortal life.

(Ambr.) No one doubts that all who do not seek God incline away and seek help from vanity. Vanity is an idol; therefore they become useless.

The prophet Jeremiah also signifies all these people when he says, among other things: “Then they all rose up against the prophet of the Lord, wishing to kill him”; and he continues: “But all the people did not permit them” (Jer. 26).

Thus he says “all,” but the wicked; and “all,” but the good. For when he says “all have turned aside,” he does not mean the entire people without exception, but that portion of the people to which the prophet mentioned also refers, in which all the wicked have hidden themselves. For there are always two peoples within one people.

This is the people whom the Lord rebukes under the name of Jerusalem, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets” (Matt. 23); and elsewhere: “An evil and adulterous generation” (Matt. 12), and “brood of vipers.”

The prophet Isaiah also complains about such people, saying: “Woe to the sinful nation, to the wicked seed” [“to the worthless seed”] (Isa. 1). Through their evil will, while they produce evil fruits, they are a wicked seed. Yet because, if they wish, they can turn back, the Apostle’s statement in another Epistle proves this: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2).

There is no one who does good, not even one.

(Amb.) Because they neglected God and became useless, they cannot do good. For, already corrupted, they proceed from bad to worse.

Their throat is an open tomb.

Having already been enslaved to evil, they wished, if it could be done, to devour the good, so that their throat would be directed against the good just as a tomb lies open to receive corpses.

(Orig.) Paul appears in this passage to show a greater crime in those about whom he is speaking, when he calls them not a covered or closed tomb but an open one.

Closed tombs are said to be those whose shame restrains them somewhat from committing offenses openly and bringing their crimes into public view. But those are called an open tomb who display their filth and impurity openly. In them the persistence and habitual practice of crimes—the ultimate stage of evil—has even removed the shame of their offenses, so that they no longer open their mouths to bring forth the word of God, the living word, but open their throat and bring forth a dead word, the word of the devil, not from the heart but from the tomb.

They dealt deceitfully with their tongues.

(Ambr.) Since they were accustomed to such evil deeds, the things they said were marked by deceit.

(Orig.) Deceit occurs when someone says one thing with his tongue and turns another thing over in his heart. I do not know whether this crime leaves even the righteous and elect entirely free from guilt. But I think that one person has more of it and another less, yet no one is perfectly free from it except the one of whom it is written: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2).

The poison of asps is under their lips.

(Ambr.) He says this because the words of such people are snares. They speak in order to deceive; just as poison is poured through the lips of a serpent, so deceit and traps are poured through their lips.

(Orig.) This may also be understood of those who ensnare people through fabricated accusations. It may also refer to those who, through heretical teaching infected with the poison of the devil, deceive the souls of the simple.

Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. (Ambrose.) It is clear that the wicked always bring curses and bitter words against the good, bursting forth into their reproach and slander. (Origen.) “Cursing.” Yet bitterness is joined to it, because it is drawn out from the gall of anger: for through anger and fury the tongue is driven to curse.

Their feet are swift to shed blood. (Ambrose.) He said this concerning the killing of the prophets, whom they slaughtered without hesitation—slow to do good, swift to commit parricide. Destruction and misery are in their ways. Because they were quick to do evil, he declares their path, or their conduct, to be troubled and wretched. And they have not known the way of peace. The way of peace is smooth [Col. 1336A] and undisturbed; for every good life is tranquil, and modest actions are peaceful, and by these one goes to God. Therefore, refusing to know these things, they chose the way of troubles, by which one goes to Gehenna. (Origen.) Those who separate a soul from God by any kind of stumbling block are called “men of blood.” For just as the person who separates the body from the soul by which it is given life is called a homicide, so—and much more truly—he must be called a homicide who separates a soul from the true life, which is God. But in this passage understand “feet” as those of whom the Prophet says: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. LXXIII), that is, the counsel by which we travel the path of life. “Destruction,” he says, “and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace.” Hence he says in the Psalms: “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L), but he means that contrition by which sinners are said to break the Lord’s yoke and cast it from their necks. Likewise, “misery,” or as it is read elsewhere, “wretchedness,” is to be understood as that by which a person has become miserable and unhappy: although he was in honor, he did not understand, but was compared to senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. XLVIII). “And they have not known the way of peace.” Our peace is Christ; therefore the way of peace is the way of Christ. But even if we understand that sinners, while they are constantly oppressed by the wars of their vices, do not know the way of peace, we rightly understand it. For the Prophet says to the Lord: “Great peace have those who love your name, and there is no stumbling block for them” (Ps. CXVIII). That people also which was led out of Egypt walked the way of peace, so that it might come into the promised land and dwell in Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” just as the Prophet also says: “His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV). More fully, however, the one recognizes the way of peace who presses onward toward the dwelling of the heavenly Jerusalem, so that he may ascend to the holy city of the living God.

There is no fear of God before their eyes. Since such people are without understanding, they do not possess the fear of God. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I), Solomon says. And he did not say that these people do not have the fear of God, but: “There is not,” he says, “the fear of God before their eyes.” For because they see their utterly wicked deeds and do not recoil from them, they are said not to have the fear of God before their eyes. (Augustine.) Again, in another way: “There is none,” he says, “who does good; there is not even one.” “Even one” may be understood as including that one, so that no human being is meant, or as excluding that one, so that the Lord Christ is understood. Thus we say, “This field extends as far as the sea”; we certainly do not include the sea itself in the field. This is the better understanding: no one is understood to have done good as far as Christ, because no human being can do good unless he himself has shown the way; and this is true, because until a person knows the one God, he cannot do good.

Their throat is an open tomb. Either the voracity of a gaping appetite is signified, or, allegorically, the fact that they kill and, as it were, devour those whom they persuade to adopt the perversity of their ways. The contrary is similar to what was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts X), so that he might convert the nations to his faith [Col. 1337A] and good morals.

They dealt deceitfully with their tongues. Flattery accompanies the greedy, and all wicked people.

The poison of asps is under their lips. He calls it deceitful poison. “Of asps,” because they do not wish to hear the commandments of the Law, just as asps do not wish to hear the words of the enchanter.
