This is stated more clearly in another psalm: “Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness”—that is, the poison of asps. “Their feet are swift to shed blood,” through the habit of doing evil. “Destruction and misery are in their ways,” for all the ways of wicked people are full of labors and misery. Therefore the Lord cries out: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI) [Col. 1337B]. “And they have not known the way of peace”—that way, certainly, which the Lord, as I said, recalls in the easy yoke and the light burden. “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” They do not say, “There is no God,” but nevertheless they do not fear God.

(Origen.) We have already said that in this Epistle Paul, like a kind of arbiter between those who have believed from the circumcision and those who are from the nations, always moderates and balances his speech. At times he seems to rebuke one group, at times the other, in certain matters; and through the individual sections he lifts their souls upward by a sure hope of promise. Since, therefore, he seemed earlier to have said that if the uncircumcised person keeps the righteousness of the Law, he will judge the transgressor of the Law who is circumcised, he again added words to raise up those whom he had humbled: “What, then, is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision?” “Much in every way: first, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.” After this, having pursued certain matters in sequence, he added, and now says: “What, then, do we maintain as an advantage?” For we have charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin. But if all are under sin, there will be no cause for one to be elated over another, since each comes to salvation not through his own righteousness but through God’s mercy.

He therefore proved that the Greeks—that is, the gentiles—were under sin when he said: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed animals and serpents. Therefore God gave them over to a debased mind,” and the rest. He proved the Jews to be under sin when he said: “But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the Law,” and the rest, to which he added: “You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach not to steal, do you steal?” and so forth. After these things, therefore, he says that we have charged Jews and Greeks alike with all being under sin.

After this, as is his custom, he wishes to confirm what he has said from the Holy Scriptures, and at the same time offers an example to the teachers of the Church, so that what they speak to the people they may present not as presumptuous opinions of their own, but fortified with divine testimonies. For if so great and eminent an Apostle does not believe that the authority of his own statements is sufficient unless he shows that what he says is written in the Law and the Prophets, how much more must we carefully observe this, so that when we teach we may present not our own opinions but the judgments of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1338A].

Now we know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are in the Law. (Ambrose.) It is clear that the Law rebukes those who first did not believe their leader Moses, nor obey their fathers the prophets, whom they also persecuted and killed, nor their kinsmen according to the flesh, the apostles, whose blood they shed—always impious and rebellious against God—so that they might be condemned through the Law. For just as all evils have one common cause in evil, so all good things have one common cause in good; in these people, therefore, the evil of all who are alike is rebuked. These words concern the confusion of the Jews, who brought testimony from the Law on behalf of themselves and their fathers.

[Col. 1338B] So that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God. He says this because, with the Jews bound by sins, the whole world becomes subject to God. For no one doubts that the pagans are overwhelmed by transgressions and impieties, and therefore the whole world has been cast down before God, so that it may be able to attain forgiveness, because the whole world consisted of Jews and gentiles, from whom the faithful have been separated. Therefore, when he proves that the Jews, who received the Law from God and to whom the promise was made, are liable to sins, there is no doubt that all the Greeks are guilty of death. For this reason he says: “Let every mouth be stopped, and let the whole world become subject to God,” since all, having been proved guilty, need the mercy of God, both Jews and Greeks.

(Origen.) But let us inquire what he has called “the whole world” here. Will “the whole world” perhaps be understood as this earthly place, so that trees, stones, grasses, seeds, and streets that are in it are likewise included in the name? For each of these appears to be a part of this world. I do not think anyone could be found so foolish as to assert this. It remains, therefore, that by “the whole world” he means every rational creature; and just as everything irrational is excluded from this meaning, so no rational creature seems to me to be excluded from this condition. Therefore the whole world becomes liable to God because he has implanted the natural law in all creatures. Of these he also says elsewhere (Phil. II) that “at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth.”

(Augustine.) Scripture concluded all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ: Yes, Lord, do this; merciful Lord, command what cannot be fulfilled—rather, command what can be fulfilled only through your grace. So that, when human beings were unable to fulfill it by their own powers, “every mouth may be stopped,” and no one may regard himself as great; let all be made little, and let the whole world become guilty before you, because “no flesh shall be justified by the Law in your sight.”

For no flesh shall be justified before God by works of the Law. But what he says—that no flesh shall be justified before him in the Law, for through the Law comes knowledge of sin, and other similar statements, which some think are to be brought forward as an insult to the Law—must be read with great care, so that the Law may not appear to be rejected by the Apostle, nor free choice taken away from humanity. Let us therefore distinguish four stages of human beings: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace.

Before the Law, we follow the desire of the flesh. Under the Law, we are dragged along by it. Under grace, we neither follow it nor are dragged along by it. In peace, there is no desire of the flesh. Before the Law, therefore, we do not struggle, because we not only desire and commit sins but also approve of sins. Under the Law, we struggle but are defeated: for we admit that things are evil, since we do not wish to do them; but because grace is not yet present, we are overcome. In this stage it is shown to us how we lie prostrate; and while we are unwilling to rise, we fall and are afflicted more severely. Hence it is said: “The Law entered in so that the offense might increase” (Rom. V). Hence also the statement that “through the Law comes knowledge of sin,” which is not set down as the removal of sin; for sin is removed through grace alone.

The Law, therefore, is good, because it forbids what ought to be forbidden and commands what ought to be commanded. But when someone thinks that he can fulfill it by his own strength, not through the grace of his liberator, that presumption does him no good; indeed, it harms him so greatly that he is seized by a more intense desire to sin and is found to be a transgressor even in his sins. For where there is no Law, there is no transgression. When, therefore, someone lying prostrate recognizes that he is unable to rise by himself, let him implore the help of his liberator.

Grace then comes, forgiving past sins, aiding the one who strives, granting love of righteousness, and removing fear. When this happens, although certain desires of the flesh fight against our spirit while we are in this life, so that they may lead it into sin, nevertheless the spirit does not consent to these desires, because it is established in the grace and love of God, and it ceases to sin. For we do not sin in the wrongful desire itself, but in our consent. To this the same Apostle’s statement applies: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. VI).

For he shows here that there are desires which, when we do not obey them, do not allow sin to reign in us. But because the desires of the flesh arise from the mortality of the flesh—which we draw from the first sin of the first human being, from whom we are born carnally—they will not end until, after the resurrection of the body has transformed us, we receive what is promised to us, where there will be perfect peace, which we have placed in the fourth stage. He therefore says “perfect peace,” because nothing resists us, since we do not resist God. This is what the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII).

Free choice, therefore, existed perfectly in the first human being. In us, however, before grace, free choice does not exist in such a way that we do not sin, but only in such a way that we do not wish to sin. Grace, however, makes it possible not only for us to wish to do what is right but also to be able to do it—not by our own powers, but through the help of our liberator. He also grants us perfect peace in the resurrection, and this perfect peace follows upon a good will. For “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

(Ambrose.) He asserts that people are by no means justified before God, not because they did not keep the Law of righteousness in its commandments, but because they were unwilling to believe the sacrament of God’s mystery, which is in Christ. For God determined that human beings should be justified through this, not through the Law, because the Law justifies for a time, not before God. Therefore those who keep the Law in the present age are called righteous, but not before God, because they do not possess the faith by which human beings are justified before God. For faith is greater than the Law, because the Law pertains to us, while faith pertains to God. Therefore the Law possesses a temporal righteousness, but faith an eternal one.

By saying “all flesh,” he signified every human being, just as the prophet Isaiah also says: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. LI; Luke III)—that is, every human being shall see Christ God, in whom the salvation of all is contained. They are called “flesh” for this reason: because they are liable to sins. For just as righteousness makes people spiritual, so transgressions make them carnal, so that a person receives his name from his conduct.

Since it is one thing to be justified before God and another to be justified before human beings—that is, in comparison with other human beings—another person who has lived more correctly may appear righteous. In comparison with God, however, not only will no human being be justified, but, as Job said: “The stars also are not pure before him” (Job XXV). These stars are certainly considered pure and holy before us—that is, in comparison with human beings—but in comparison with God they cannot be pure.

For through the Law comes knowledge of sin. (Ambrose.) But through faith comes its abolition; therefore faith must be followed. What is this Law through which he says that sin is known, and how is it known? We see that the ancients were not ignorant of sin, since Joseph was sent to prison, although through false accusation, and the cupbearer and baker of Pharaoh were involved in the cause of sin. How, then, were sins hidden?

There are indeed three aspects of the Law. The first part concerns the sacrament of God’s divinity; the second corresponds to the natural law, which forbids sin; the third concerns the works of the Law—that is, the Sabbath, the new moon, circumcision, and so forth. This natural law, partly restored through Moses and partly confirmed through his authority, made sin known by restraining vices—not because sin was hidden, as I said, but because it showed that the sins people commit would not remain unpunished before God, lest someone who escaped punishment for a time should be thought to have mocked the Law. This is what the Law shows.

But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, bearing witness from the Law and the Prophets. It is clear that the righteousness of God appeared apart from the Law, but apart from the Law of the Sabbath, circumcision, the new moon, and vengeance—not, however, apart from the sacrament of God’s divinity, since the righteousness of God proceeds from God’s sacrament.

For when God’s righteousness forgave those whom the Law held guilty, he did this apart from the Law: those against whom the Law was going to exact punishment, he granted forgiveness of sin. And lest this should perhaps be thought to have been done against the Law, he added that the righteousness of God bears witness from the Law and the Prophets—that is, because the Law itself, in another respect, had long ago declared that this would happen, since the one who would save human beings was to come, a thing that had not been granted to the Law: to forgive sins.

It is called the righteousness of God, although it appears to be mercy, because it has its origin in a promise; and when God’s promise is fulfilled, it is called the righteousness of God. It is righteousness because what was promised has been given; and when righteousness receives those who flee for refuge to it, it is called righteousness because not to receive them would be iniquity.

(Augustine.) Grace found all transgressors through the Savior—some greater, some lesser. For the greater a person’s knowledge of the Law, the less excuse there is for sin, and the more manifest the transgression. It therefore remained that not their own righteousness but God’s—that is, righteousness given by God—should come to the aid of human beings.

Hence the Apostle says: “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin”—not, therefore, its removal, but its knowledge. “But now,” he says, “the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified by the Law and the Prophets.” Accordingly, this person also added: “Therefore I loved your testimonies,” as though he were saying: Since the Law—whether given in paradise, implanted naturally, or promulgated in written form—made all transgressors sinners of the earth, therefore I loved your testimonies, which are in your Law, concerning your grace, so that righteousness might not be mine but yours. For the Law is useful for this purpose: to send a person to grace.

Not only does it bear witness to the righteousness of God that is to be manifested, but by making people transgressors, so that even the letter kills, it compels them through fear to flee to the Spirit who gives life, through whom the totality of sins may be erased and love of right action inspired. “Through the Law,” he says, “comes knowledge of sin.”

(Origen.) By the Law of the Lord we recognize both what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided, as well as what is and what is not sin. Therefore, as heretics accuse the God of the Law, the Law is not an evil root or an evil tree through which knowledge of sin comes. For he did not say, “From the Law comes knowledge of sin,” but “Through the Law,” so that you may know that sin did not originate from the Law but was recognized through it.

For example, if we were to say, “Through the art of medicine knowledge of illness is given,” would medicine therefore seem to you to be the cause of illness, because through it the character of the illness is recognized? But just as medicine is plainly good because it provides understanding of disease, by which illness can be avoided, so the Law is also good, through which sin is detected and recognized.

“But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law.” What he says, therefore, is this: just as knowledge of sin comes through the Law, so the manifestation of the righteousness of God does not come through the Law. Rather, the righteousness of God is manifested apart from the Law. For the natural law could accuse the nature of sin and display knowledge of it; but the righteousness of God surpasses and rises above everything that the human mind can investigate through natural senses alone.

For the natural law is not sufficient to understand and contemplate every kind of human righteousness, much less the righteousness of God itself and the judgments that proceed from it—judgments of which it is said that they are “a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV), and that the righteousness and judgments of God are so profound that the Apostle says: “How unsearchable are the judgments of God!” (Rom. XI).

Wisdom also speaks to human beings as though the righteousness of God could not be known merely through the movements of nature, but must be sought through the study of teaching; therefore it says: “Learn righteousness, you who judge the earth” (Wis. I). For this reason, the natural law will provide no help at all toward knowing the righteousness of God, even if it seems to have some perception of human righteousness.

That law can perceive what is just among human beings—for example, that what a person does not want to suffer himself, he should not do to his neighbor. But can it naturally perceive that righteousness which says: “Be careful not to practice your righteousness before human beings,” and “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing”? (Matt. VI.) The natural law cannot dictate such righteous principles and others like them. Therefore the Apostle says: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law,” namely, the natural law, “bearing witness from the Law of Moses and the Prophets,” in which the Holy Spirit had written much about the righteousness of God through figures and riddles.

And do not be surprised that the one word “Law,” repeated twice in the same passage, has different meanings. We find this to be the custom of Scripture in other places as well, as in the passage: “Do you not say, ‘There are still four months, and then comes the harvest’? Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are white for harvest” (John IV). In this passage, is not “harvest,” mentioned twice, related first to the bodily harvest and then to the spiritual harvest?

So here, when the Apostle says that righteousness is manifested “apart from the Law,” the natural law is meant; but when he says “testified by the Law and the Prophets,” he designates the Law of Moses. This righteousness of God, which is Christ, is manifested apart from the natural law, but not apart from the Law of Moses or the Prophets. For the Law bears witness to it, just as Christ himself says: “Search the Scriptures, and they are the ones that bear witness about me” (John V).

The natural Law can indeed provide occasions and give understanding, as we have said, either concerning what equity requires to be done among all people, or even concerning the recognition that God exists. But who can naturally perceive concerning Christ that he is the Son of God? Therefore the righteousness of God, which is Christ, has been manifested apart from this Law, but testified by the Law of Moses and the Prophets.

Before we hurry on to what follows, this observation must not be omitted: in the case of sin I used the word “recognition,” but in the case of righteousness, “manifestation.” Everything that is manifested is light; and if what is manifested is light, sin, which is not light, is not manifested but recognized. I understand also the following in this way: “Nothing is hidden that will not be manifested, nor covered that will not be revealed.”

But let us return to the subject. The Law and the Prophets are witnesses to the righteousness of God, which righteousness is manifested through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe, with no distinction between those who believe from among the Jews and those from among the gentiles.

The righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ. (Ambrose.) For what else does “through faith in Jesus Christ” mean except that the manifestation of the righteousness of God is Christ himself? For through faith in the preaching of Jesus Christ, the gift long ago promised by God is recognized and received.

To all and upon all who believe. This means that the righteousness of God is seen to be upon all believing Jews and Greeks. For there is no distinction: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God.” Since he had said that the righteousness of God belongs to all Jews and Greeks who believe, to prove this he added: “For all have sinned.”

This must be understood generally, so that both Jews and Greeks are included. Hence he says, “There is no distinction.” Here he includes even the saints, to show that the Law was of no benefit without faith. For the Law was given in such a way that faith would be in the Law, hoping for the salvation that was to come.

Therefore the death of Christ benefits everyone, because in this world he taught what must be believed and observed, and he rescued everyone from the underworld. “For all have sinned”; but the one who came without sin alone came to those whom he found to be sinners.

The Apostle says this: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God,” so that he himself may deliver you, not you yourself, because you cannot deliver yourself. You need a liberator—so why do you boast? Why do you presume upon the Law and upon righteousness? Consider, then, and attend to the one who says: “I delight in the Law of God according to the inner person,” and so forth, until he says: “Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII).

Why grace? Because it is given freely. Why is it given freely? Because your merits did not precede it, but God’s benefits preceded you. Glory, therefore, belongs to him who delivers us.

Having been justified freely by his grace. They were justified freely because, doing nothing and rendering no repayment, they were justified by faith alone, through God’s gift.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. He testifies that the grace of God is in Christ, because by God’s will we have been redeemed by Christ, so that, having been set free, we might be justified. As he says to the Galatians: “Christ redeemed us, offering himself for us.” For he allowed himself to the raging devil, though the latter did not understand what he was doing. Thinking that he could retain Christ, he took possession of him, as it were; but because he could not endure Christ’s power, he lost, together with him, all those whom he held.

Whom God appointed as an expiation through faith. He says this because in Christ God appointed—that is, determined—that he would be propitious toward the human race if it believed.

In his blood. For this reason “in his blood,” because we were freed by his death, so that he might reveal him as dead and condemn death through his suffering.

For the demonstration of his righteousness—that is, so that he might make public his promise by which he would free us from sins, just as he had promised beforehand. When he fulfilled this promise, he showed himself to be righteous.

Because of the foregoing sins, in the patience of God. God knew the purpose of his kindness, by which he had determined to help sinners—both those who are above and those who were held in the underworld. He waited a very long time for both groups, setting aside the sentence by which it seemed just that all should be condemned. He wished to show us what he had long ago determined: to free the human race through Christ, just as he promised through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (Jer. XXXI).

And lest it should perhaps appear that he had promised this gift only to the Jews, he says through Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer among all nations” (Isa. LVI). For although the promise was made in connection with Judaism, God, foreknowing that the wicked Jews would reject his gift, promised to admit the gentiles to receive his grace. Provoked to jealousy by them, the wicked Jews would be driven to anger and suffer.

In this present time—that is, in our time, in which God has given what he had long ago promised to give, at the time when he gave it.

So that he himself might be just and justify the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. He rightly says this, because, in order to be just, God gave what he had promised. But he promised to justify those who believe in Christ. He says in Habakkuk: “But the righteous person shall live by my faith” (Hab. II), so that, possessing faith in God and in Christ, he may be righteous.

Therefore, through the propitiation of Christ’s blood, there is forgiveness of preceding sins [Col. 1344B] in God’s forbearance, for the demonstration of his righteousness. God’s forbearance is shown when the sinner is not immediately punished as soon as he sins, but, as the Apostle says in the same place, through God’s patience is led to repentance. In this passage God is said to demonstrate his righteousness.

He rightly adds, “in this present time.” In the time of the present age, God’s righteousness is expressed through forbearance; in the future age, through recompense. For it seemed just to the Lord that, since he had appointed the future age for judgment, he should assign the present age to forbearance and patience. If he punished the sinner in the present age, it would not seem just to summon again to judgment the one whom he had already punished. But if he exercises forbearance and patience in the present age, he will rightly be a just Judge in the future.

He therefore justifies the one who is of the faith, just as it is written concerning Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Since Abraham believed, he was justified by faith. Without doubt it follows that now also the one who believes God through faith in Jesus Christ is justified together with faithful Abraham.

Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. Through what law? The law of works? No, but through the law of faith. Having given the reason, he speaks to those who live under the Law, because they boast without cause, flattering themselves under the Law because they are Abraham’s offspring, while seeing that a person is not justified before God except through faith.

For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the Law. He says that a gentile is certainly regarded as a person who is justified by believing while doing none of the works of the Law—that is, without circumcision, new-moon observances, or veneration of the Sabbath.

(Augustine.) There were indeed people under the Law who boasted in the works of the Law, which perhaps they performed not from love but from fear. They wanted to appear righteous and to be preferred to the gentiles, who had not performed the work of the Law. But the Apostle, preaching faith to the gentiles, saw that those who were approaching the Lord were justified by faith, so that, because they had believed, they might do good works—not so that, because they had done good works, they might earn the right to believe. He therefore cried out confidently and said: A person can be justified by faith, apart from the works of the Law. Thus those who did what they did from fear were not truly righteous, since faith works through love in the heart, even if it does not emerge outwardly in a deed.

Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also. (Ambrose.) Without doubt, there is one God of all. For the Jews alone cannot claim that God belongs to them and not to the Gentiles, since they themselves acknowledge that all derive their origin from one Adam and that no outsider who wishes to approach the Law is forbidden. Indeed, some Egyptians came out with them into the wilderness; they were commanded to receive them, provided only that they were circumcised and ate unleavened bread or Passover together with them. Likewise, Cornelius—a Gentile who was not practicing Judaism—is shown to have received the gift of God (Acts 10), and his justification is confirmed by divine testimony, as it is written in the Psalms: “Remove from me the way of iniquity” (Psalm 118). And because the law of works entered in so that transgression might abound, he continues and says: “And have mercy on me according to your law.” According to what law, if not the law of faith? Hear the Apostle: “Where then is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith.” This is the law of faith, by which we believe and pray that it may be granted to us through grace to do what we cannot fulfill by ourselves, lest, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish our own, we fail to submit to God’s righteousness. In the law of works, therefore, there is the justice of God who commands; in the law of faith, there is the mercy of God who comes to our aid.

(Origen.) We who strive to maintain that the Apostle’s writing is complete and that everything stands in its proper order must consequently ask who was justified by faith alone, without works. As far as an example is concerned, I think the thief who was crucified with Christ is sufficient. He cried out: “Lord Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23). Nothing else concerning any good work of his is recorded in the Gospels; yet, for this faith alone, the Lord said to him: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid.).

Let us now apply the words of the Apostle Paul concerning this thief’s case, and say to the Jew: “Where then is your boasting?” Certainly, it has been excluded; it has been excluded not by the law of works, but by the law of faith. For this thief was justified by faith without the works of the Law, because the Lord did not ask what he had previously done, nor wait to see what work he would complete after believing; rather, by his confession alone, he took him as his companion into paradise, which he was about to enter. The only just boasting, therefore, is in faith in the cross of Christ, which excludes all that boasting that proceeds from the works of the Law.

These things have been said because the Apostle, as though asking a question, said: “Where then is your boasting?” He himself answered: “It has been excluded.” Then, as though asking again, he says: “By what law? Of works?” And he answers himself: “No, but by the law of faith.” “For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the Law.” We have already spoken above about these matters.

But because in the present passage also he again mentions two laws, speaking of the law of works and the law of faith, consider carefully, you who read, whether the discussion should be understood as referring to the Law of Moses and the natural law, or to the law of the letter and the law of the Spirit. For “the letter kills” and brings about death, whereas “the law of the Spirit of life” frees from the law of sin and death. Accordingly, in what follows he appropriately says: “Is he the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Indeed, of Gentiles also. Since God is one, he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.”

(Ambrose.) By “circumcision” he signifies the Jews, because they were justified by faith in the promise, believing that this was the Christ whom God had promised in the Law. By “uncircumcision” he signifies the Gentiles, justified before God through faith in Christ. For he justified Gentiles and Jews alike in no other way than by believing. Since there is one God of all, he justified all by one principle. What, then, does circumcision of the flesh profit, or what harm does uncircumcision do, when faith alone confers dignity and merit?

(Origen.) It does not seem to me that the Apostle’s change of prepositions here is without significance. We find him using these prepositions elsewhere not arbitrarily but carefully, and preserving the necessary distinction between them. Thus, speaking of God, he says: “From him and through him and in him are all things.” When he says “from him,” something primary seems to be indicated by the preposition. When he says “through him,” the notion of a subsequent cause is designated—that is, a cause which follows the primary one. For example, when he says “from him and through him and in him are all things,” “from him” signifies the first creation of all things and the fact that existing things began from God; “through him” signifies that things which had first been made are governed and administered through him, from whom they receive the beginning of their continued existence; “in him” signifies that those who have already been corrected and amended remain in his perfection.

Thus they teach that these distinctions possess a fully coherent meaning: that our existence is from God; that our being administered and governed is accomplished through him; and that our standing in the fullness of perfection is in him.

A similar distinction may perhaps be observed in the present passage, so that circumcision—which is justified as though in the first place and order—is said to be justified “from faith,” and not “through faith”; whereas uncircumcision, which is brought to justification in the second place, is said to be justified not “from faith” but “through faith.” Thus the one and same God justifies circumcision from faith and uncircumcision through faith.

If someone should inquire more inquisitively through whom those who are justified from faith are justified, and, again, from what those who are justified through faith are justified, although such curiosity may perhaps seem excessive, we can nevertheless answer appropriately: those who are justified from faith, having taken their beginning from faith, are perfected through the fulfillment of good works; those who are justified through faith, having begun with good works, receive the fullness of perfection through faith. Thus the two adhere to one another, and each is perfected from the other. For this reason, I think, the Apostle immediately placed what follows:

“Do we then abolish the Law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the Law.”

(Augustine.) When he says, “Do we abolish the Law through faith? By no means, but we justify the Law”—that is, establish it—how could the Law have been established except through righteousness? The righteousness that comes from faith did this, because through faith those very things that could not be fulfilled were fulfilled.

(Origen.) Since in the preceding discussion he seemed to refer everything to faith, he himself points out what another person might propose and says: If a person is justified through faith and not from the works of the Law; if God justifies circumcision from faith and uncircumcision through faith; then, Paul, do you destroy the Law of Moses through faith? He answers himself: “By no means; rather, we establish the Law,” that is, we confirm it.

It is worthwhile to see how he declares that he confirms the Law, when above he said that a person is not justified from the works of the Law. Our Savior says in the Gospel that Moses wrote about him. Therefore, whoever does not believe in Christ, about whom Moses wrote in the Law, destroys the Law. Whoever believes in Christ, about whom Moses wrote, confirms the Law through faith, because he believes in Christ.

By faith we mean a complete, full, and perfect faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which professes nothing diverse, nothing contradictory, and nothing foreign within the Trinity. For Marcion, who says that the God of the Law is one god and the Father of Christ another, does not establish or confirm the Law through his faith, but destroys it. Ebion does the same, as do all who insert some corruption into the Catholic faith.

I will also add appropriately that everyone who believes in Christ and acts well, keeping himself from every stain of sin, confirms the Law of God by living rightly. But whoever is driven headlong by the vices of sin and is stained by continual crimes without any restraint of repentance, even if he appears to believe in Christ, does not establish the Law through his faith but destroys it.

Nor should we pass over an objection that someone might raise: the Apostle seems to write things contrary to one another. In the present passage he says that the Law is not destroyed but confirmed; yet in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he writes: “If the ministry of death, carved in letters on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which is being destroyed, how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be in glory?” (2 Corinthians 3). A little later he says: “For if what is being destroyed came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (ibid.).

It may therefore be said that the glory of Moses’ face, which is being destroyed, and the statement, “If what is being destroyed came through glory,” contradict the present pronouncement: “We do not destroy the Law through faith, but establish and confirm it.” But see whether we can resolve the apparent difficulty in this way. “We destroy the Law” is not the same as “the Law is destroyed.” In the present passage Paul declares that he himself does not destroy the Law. If the Law is destroyed by a glory that surpasses it, it is not destroyed by Paul or by any other saint.

Thus the Lord himself said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5). None of the saints, not even the Lord himself, destroys the Law. Rather, its temporal and passing glory is destroyed and overcome by the eternal and abiding glory.

(Ambrose.) The Law is certainly not emptied of its meaning through faith but fulfilled. Its standing is confirmed when faith testifies that what it said would come has arrived. This is said because of the Jews, who think that the faith of Christ is hostile to the Law because they do not understand the meaning of the Law.

He does not abolish the Law when he teaches that it ought to cease, because he asserts that it was rightly given in its own time but that it should no longer be practiced. For the Law itself says that, at the time when the promise was fulfilled, the Law ought to cease. The angel Gabriel showed this to the prophet Daniel, who desired to know these things, saying among other matters that, when Christ came, the chrism—that is, the royal anointing, by which authority is understood—would cease. “And judgment,” he says, “shall no longer be,” which is the Law, “and my sacrifice shall be taken away” (Daniel 9, 11). He says “my” so that it might be understood that the former offering would cease.

The Savior, explaining this meaning, said: “The Law and the prophets were until John.” And because, when the Law of Moses ceased, God was going to give better commandments, the prophet Jeremiah proclaimed: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a New Covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers” (Jeremiah 31)—namely, with those who received Christ when he came according to the promise.

Therefore the Savior said: “I have not come to abolish the Law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.” And because the house of God was to exist not only in Jerusalem but also in other places, the prophet Zechariah said: “I will set Jerusalem among all the nations” (Zechariah 12), meaning the Church.

## CHAPTER IV

The Apostle declares by the example of Abraham that faith is required for salvation and that the old Law is insufficient.

### What, then, shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh?

(Ambrose.) After showing that no one can be justified before God through the works of the Law, he added that Abraham also could not have acquired anything according to the flesh. By “flesh” he means circumcision, because Abraham sought nothing through circumcision; he was justified before he was circumcised.

### For if Abraham was justified by works of the Law, he has glory, but not before God.

(Augustine.) When he says, “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God,” he means that Abraham, without the Law, while not seeking glory from the works of the Law, would seem to fulfill the Law by his own strength. But since this Law had not yet been given, that glory belongs to God, not to Abraham. It would not be unjust for him to obtain life from works; nevertheless, he was justified by the grace of God through faith. This is the point being proposed.

(Ambrose.) Abraham was justified by faith, which no one doubts; therefore he has glory before God. But because those who observe the Law—whether the Law of Moses or the natural law—are justified for the present, so that they may not be liable in the present judgment, he says: If Abraham was justified by works of the Law, he does not have glory before God. For it is written: “Whoever does the Law will live by it”—that is, he will not die as one liable to punishment. Yet he will not thereby have merit before God; rather, this is on account of faith.

### For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

He made clear that Abraham did not have glory before God because he was circumcised or because he abstained from iniquity, but because he believed God. For this reason he was also justified, and he will receive the reward of his praise in the future.

### But to the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt.

(Augustine.) When he says, “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt,” he speaks in the manner by which human beings pay wages to human beings. God, however, gave through grace, because he gave to sinners so that they might live righteously through faith—that is, so that they might act well. Therefore, whatever good we do after receiving grace must be attributed not to us but to him who justified us by grace. For if he wished to repay what was owed, he would also repay the punishment owed to sinners.

(Ambrose.) The matter is clear concerning the person who is subject to the law of works—that is, to the Law of Moses—or to the natural law: merit is not reckoned as a reward, so that he may have glory before God. He is obligated to perform the Law because the Law imposes a necessity upon him, so that, whether he wishes to or not, he must perform the Law lest he be condemned. As he says elsewhere: “Those who despise it acquire condemnation for themselves” (Romans 13), because they are liable in the present.

But believing or not believing belongs to the will. No one can be compelled to accept what is not evident; rather, a person is invited, because faith is not extorted but persuaded. Therefore the one who gives assent ought to be rewarded, as Abraham was, who believed what he had not seen.

(Origen.) Throughout this entire passage the Apostle seems to show that there are two kinds of justification: one, which he calls justification from works, and another, from faith. He says that the justification from works has glory in itself but not before God; the justification from faith, however, has glory before God, who examines human hearts and knows who believes secretly and who does not believe.

For this reason, the one who has glory before God alone has it rightly, since God sees the affection of his faith in secret. But the one who hopes for justification from works may have his works approved even by human beings. Whatever is manifested in a work is public and can be seen with the eyes. If faith is secret but works are public, it is appropriate to apply what is written: “The hidden things belong to the Lord your God, but the things that are manifest belong to you and your children” (Deuteronomy 29).

It is also appropriate to apply the statement: “The righteous person lives by my faith” (Habakkuk 2). Thus we may appropriately say that those who are circumcised according to the inner person and are Jews secretly, in spirit and not in letter, have their praise and glory not before human beings but before God.

Those who are justified by works, because their works are public and manifest, may have glory either before the saints and righteous, whom God grants authority to judge visible human works, or even before the angels and the other powers of the heavenly hosts, who can glorify the one whose works they have approved.

But because only God knows the secrets of the heart, he himself sees whether the affection of faith dwells in each person. Therefore the one who is justified by faith has glory before God alone, who possesses knowledge of hidden things and alone examines faith.

(Augustine.) Many people therefore boast of their works. You find many pagans unwilling to become Christians for this reason: they seem to be satisfied with their good life. “Living well is enough,” they say. “What will Christ command me? I commit no murder, no theft, no robbery; I do not covet another’s property; I am not defiled by adultery. Let nothing be found in my life that can be criticized, and let whoever criticizes me make himself a Christian.” Such a person has glory, but not before God—not, however, like our father Abraham.

Where, then, does Scripture say that Abraham was justified? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Abraham, therefore, was justified by faith.

“Then I may do whatever I wish, because even if I have no good works, provided that I merely believe in God, it is reckoned to me as righteousness.” I answer from the case of Abraham himself. We also find in the Epistle of another Apostle that he wished to correct those who had misunderstood this Apostle and who were unwilling to act well, relying on faith alone. He commended the works of Abraham, while Paul commended his faith. He says that Abraham’s work is known to all: he offered his son to God to be sacrificed.

If Abraham had done this apart from right faith, the work, whatever it might have been, would have profited him nothing. Likewise, if Abraham had held his faith in such a way as to question whether God had commanded him to offer his son as a sacrifice, he might have said to himself: “I will not do it, and yet I will believe, because God will rescue me even if I despise his commands.” Faith without works would have been dead, remaining barren and dry like a root without fruit.

### But to the one who does not work

(Ambrose.) That is, to the one who is liable because of sins, who does not do what the Law commands.

### But to the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness.

(Augustine.) When he says “who justifies the ungodly,” he means that he makes the ungodly godly, so that thereafter the person may remain in godliness and righteousness. He was justified for this purpose: to become righteous, not to suppose that he is permitted to sin.

(Ambrose.) He says this because, apart from the works of the Law, faith is reckoned as righteousness to the ungodly believer—that is, to the Gentile who believes in Christ—as it was to Abraham. How, then, do the Jews think to justify themselves through the works of the Law by Abraham’s justification, when they see that Abraham was justified not by the works of the Law but by faith alone?

The Law is therefore not necessary when the ungodly person is justified before God by faith alone. This accords with God’s purpose of grace. He says that God decreed that, when the Law ceased, people should seek the grace of God for salvation through faith alone.

David also says the same thing. He confirms this by the example of the prophet, speaking of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works. He calls blessed those concerning whom God decreed that they should be justified before him by faith alone, without labor or any observance.

He proclaims the blessedness of the time in which Christ was born, as the Lord himself says: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear, but they did not hear it” (Luke 10).

### Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered; blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.

They are plainly blessed: their iniquities are forgiven without any labor, and their sins are covered, no work of repentance being required of them, except only that they believe. This person is also blessed, to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.

“To forgive,” “to cover,” and “not to reckon” express one principle and one meaning; everything is obtained and given in the same way. Some, however, think that these statements have a threefold meaning, because the prophet used different words and descended from the plural number to the singular.

When he wishes to enumerate the words for sins in the abundance of God’s grace, since the names of sins are diverse, he speaks at greater length. Yet the expressions have one meaning: when God covers, he forgives; when he forgives, he does not reckon the sin. He speaks more expansively in praise of God’s grace in order to magnify it.

He made three degrees because of the variety of sins. The first degree is iniquity or impiety, when the Creator is not acknowledged. The second consists in the deeds of serious sins. The third consists in lesser sins. Yet he says that all these are blotted out in baptism. By these three degrees he signified the whole body of sin.

But how can the statement “Blessed are those whose sins have been covered” refer to repentance, when it is established that penitents acquire remission of sins through labor and groaning? Or how does the statement “Blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin” fit martyrdom, when we know that the glory of martyrdom is acquired through suffering and oppression?

The prophet, foreseeing the blessed time at the coming of the Savior, calls blessed those whose sins are forgiven, covered, and not reckoned through the washing of baptism, without labor or any work. Yet the Apostle, because the fullness of time has come and because there is more grace in the Apostles than there was in the prophets, declares greater things that we obtain through the gift of baptism. He professes that we not only receive remission of sins but are also justified and made children of God, so that this blessedness may possess complete security and glory.

### Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.

(Origen.) Iniquity differs from sin in this respect: iniquity is spoken of concerning those things that are contrary to the righteousness of faith about which the preceding passage says, as we have often stated, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

And not without reason: observance of the Law avoids punishment only, whereas the merit of faith awaits the hope of the promise. A command is imposed upon servants, but faith is sought from friends.

### For if those who are of the Law are heirs

(Ambrose.) That is, if those who are of the Law or under the Law are heirs through the Law, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished. It is clear that if the inheritance comes through the Law, the promise made to Abraham through faith has come to nothing.

But the promise was not made through the Law; the inheritance comes through the righteousness of faith. The Apostle shows the evil involved in hoping for an inheritance through the Law.

### For the Law brings about wrath.

When he says, “The Law brings about wrath,” he signifies vengeance. This belongs to the second degree, when a person is under the Law, so that he may show completely that a person cannot be justified before God through the Law, nor could the promise have been made through the Law.

“The Law,” he says, “brings about wrath,” for it was given to make transgressors liable: faith, however, is a gift of God’s mercy, so that those made liable through the Law may obtain forgiveness. Therefore faith produces joy. It does not speak against the Law but places faith above it, because those who could not be saved through the Law are saved through God’s grace by faith.

The Law itself is not wrath; rather, it produces wrath for the sinner—that is, punishment—because it does not forgive but avenges.

(Augustine.) Punishment is generated by wrath. Wrath arises from sin. For this reason, he wishes the person to leave the Law and flee to faith, which is known to release transgressions.

The promise would be destroyed if anyone were righteous through the Law. For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise abolished. The Law brings about wrath precisely so that God’s grace may be sought in order to escape wrath.

Why do you not understand, I ask, that they are not heirs through the Law because the Law brings about wrath? “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.” They are heirs through the promise because God himself does what he promised.

Whoever thinks that he fulfills the commandments of the Law through the free choice of his own will, without the Spirit of grace, wishes to establish his own righteousness rather than receive the righteousness of God.

(Origen.) Yet, as we have often said above, the Apostle introduces different laws in this Epistle. At one point he speaks of the Law of Moses; at another he names the law of faith, as when he says: “Where then is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith.”

He also introduces other laws, about which he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin” (Romans 7). Thus he passes from one law to another, so that, unless one’s understanding is alert and attentive, it is difficult to detect and follow him.

We must therefore consider whether the law that is in our members and takes us captive in the law of sin is perhaps the law that the Apostle says brings about wrath. It certainly produces wrath for the person whom it takes captive in the law of sin. Where this law is absent, it is certain that there is no transgression. Those who are under this law consequently will not be heirs.

Even if someone wishes to understand this as referring to the Law of Moses and to say that it brings about wrath, he could perhaps affirm this only because it commands that a person who sins against it be immediately stoned or burned with fire, or because some other punishment for sinners is decreed in the Law. Thus the punishment inflicted on the sinner by the Law may appear to be what the Apostle now calls wrath.

The same applies to transgression: he may not be speaking here of every transgression in general, but of the transgression of one who has sinned while placed under the Law, so that the offense of one who sins after being forbidden by the Law appears more serious than that of one who has received no warning from any law.

### For where there is no law, neither is there transgression.

(Ambrose.) He says this because, once those liable have been removed from the power of the Law and pardon has been granted, there is no transgression. Those who had been sinners through transgressing the Law have been justified.

The law of works therefore ceases—that is, the observance of Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, distinctions among foods, and the observance concerning a dead animal or the blood of a weasel [the final phrase is textually uncertain].

(Origen.) It can happen that there is a law without there being transgression; it cannot happen, however, that there is transgression where there is no law.

Even if we posit the Law of Moses, it does not immediately follow that everyone who lived under the Law of Moses became transgressors. Otherwise we would appear to involve the prophets and all righteous people in the same condemnation, unless someone should say that all the righteous and prophets lived not so much under the Law as under faith, whereas sinners and unrighteous people were bound by the chains of the Law.

The Apostle likewise says that “the Law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Timothy 1), but for the unrighteous and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and profane, those who kill their fathers and mothers, murderers, fornicators, those who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine.

If the Law has been laid down for such people, you will perhaps judge those better who did not lie with males in the manner of women: one of them was restrained by a commandment of the Law, and, if he had not feared it, might perhaps have committed the act; another, by the judgment of his own mind, did not even allow such a defiling thought to be heard.

Would you not prefer by far the person who, deterred by no threat of the Law, preserved himself free from contamination by such a disgrace? The same examination should be applied to the other sins.

Therefore, whether the Law of Moses is understood, or whether it is the law that is in our members and brings about wrath, those who are of that law cannot be heirs. Rather, heirs are those who are of the law of faith—the faith by which Abraham was justified.

Someone may perhaps ask how a person who is under the Law of Moses does not appear to be under the law of faith, since it is written in Exodus: “The people believed God and Moses his servant” (Exodus 14). Again, the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5).

It may seem that, just as he said of himself, “Whoever believes in me believes in him who sent me” (John 12), so Moses was told that, if they believed Moses, they would certainly believe Christ.

We answer that the statement in the wilderness, “The people believed God and Moses his servant,” is a narrative. It shows that, through Moses’ ministry, God provided signs and wonders, and the people believed this message.

But when he says, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also,” he accuses their unbelief. By refusing to believe him, they show that they do not believe the writings of Moses, in which the coming of Christ is contained in prophetic language.

When he says, “Whoever believes in me believes in him who sent me,” he speaks of the hope of believers, who are raised up to the Lord and Father. Just as the one who has seen the Son knows that he has seen the Father, so the one who believes the Son knows that he has believed the Father.

### Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the offspring.

(Ambrose.) The promise cannot be firm for all the offspring—that is, for every person from every nation—unless it is from faith. The origin of the promise is from faith, not from the Law, because those who are under the Law are liable; but the promise cannot be given to those who are liable.

Therefore they must first be purified through faith, so that they may become worthy to be called children of God and so that the promise may be firm. If those who are liable—that is, under the Law—call themselves children of God, their claim is not firm, because the children of God are free from sin.

If, then, those who are under the Law must be rescued from under the Law in order to deserve to receive the promise, how much more is this true of those who are not under the Law! It is therefore not beneficial to place oneself under the Law in order to find a remedy for one’s wound by a shorter route.

(Origen.) He distinguished reward from grace by saying that reward belongs to what is owed, whereas grace is owed to no one but is a benefit of goodwill.

In the present passage, therefore, wishing to show that God gives the inheritance of the promises not from debt but through grace, he says that the inheritance is granted by God to believers not as a debt owed for their reward but as a gift of faith.

For example, our very existence cannot be understood as though we exist as the reward for our work. Clearly, it is God’s gift that we exist, and it is the grace of the Creator who willed us to be. Likewise, if we receive the inheritance of God’s promises, it is due to divine grace, not to any debt or reward for works.

### Not only to the one who is of the Law, but also to the one who is of the faith of Abraham.

(Ambrose.) This means what he said above: “For all the offspring”—both the Jews, who certainly came from the Law, and the Gentiles, who follow the faith of Abraham, the faith that the Gentile possessed so that he might be righteous.

Abraham believed without the Law. Therefore Abraham is more closely joined to the Gentiles, so that the promise may be firm for those who believe in the one in whom he himself believed.

(Augustine.) When he says, “Before the God in whom you believed,” he signifies that faith belongs to the inner person and is in God’s sight, not in human display, as is the circumcision of the flesh.

### Who is the father of us all, as it is written: “I have appointed you father of many nations.”

(Ambrose.) By the example of the Law he confirmed that Abraham is the father of all, but of those who believe; and that the promise is thus firm if one withdraws from the Law for the sake of faith, because the promise of the kingdom of heaven is reckoned to the righteous, not to sinners. Those who are under the Law are under sin, because all have sinned; nor can anyone both be under the Law and obtain grace, as he also says to the Galatians: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified by the Law; you have fallen from grace” (Galatians 5).

Before God, whom he believed. (Origen) But it seems to me that when he says, “to all the seed,” “not only to the one who is of the law, but also to the one who is of the faith,” he here means by “law,” as we have often said, the natural law. He is asserting that the promise is not firm for those who come only from the natural law, but for those who add to the natural law by faith the faith that Abraham our father possessed. Thus he does not seem to be indicating two peoples—one from faith and the other from the law—but one and the same people, pleasing God not merely through the natural law, which all human beings use, but through the faith of which Abraham is the author. In this way he shows that if someone possesses intact everything that the natural law teaches, and his conscience reproaches him for no sin, yet does not also possess the grace of faith, he cannot be justified. For it is faith that is reckoned as righteousness; and understood in this way, the distinction yields a clearer interpretation.

Whatever offenses are committed are committed against the law. Hence the Greek expression calls iniquity ἀνομίαν (*anomia*), that is, something committed [against the law]. Sin, however, may also be understood as occurring when one transgresses against what nature teaches and conscience condemns. Everything is attributed to his grace, not to our merits.

(Augustine) Therefore sins are covered, concealed, and abolished—not sins in which no offenses have been found, but sins that have been covered. Why, then, did he say “covered sins”? So that they would not be seen. For what would it mean for God to see sins, except to punish sins? Thus you may know that for God to see sins is the same as to punish sins. What does he say to him in Psalm 50: “Turn your face away from my sins”? Let him therefore not see your sins, so that he may see you. How may he see you? As he saw Nathanael: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” The shade of the fig tree did not obstruct the eyes of God’s mercy.

(Gregory) Yet again, since it is written, “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4), how can those things be covered which cannot in any way be hidden from his eyes, to whom all things are naked? But because we put beneath us what we cover, and draw over it the material with which we cover it, we are said to cover sins when, as it were, we place them underneath by renouncing them and draw something else over them by afterward choosing the work of good action so as to put it first. Whoever, then, abandons his former evil and afterward does good covers his past wickedness by what he adds, placing over it the merits of good works.

Does this blessedness, then, remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? (Ambrose) That is, was this blessedness granted only to Abraham’s sons, or also to those who are uncircumcised? For if, at that time, the nations were not forbidden to approach the law and the promise made to Abraham, how could those coming to grace have been forbidden in the time of Christ, when God had fully stirred them by grace?

For we say—that is, if we speak according to the meaning of the law—that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. He begins from the origin in order to exclude every evasion and quibble. Whoever is excluded at the beginning has no point from which to begin raising the question.

How, then, was it reckoned? When he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith that he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe, so that righteousness might also be reckoned to them.

When Abraham was uncircumcised, he believed God. What did he believe? That he would have offspring—that is, a son in whom all the nations would be justified through faith while uncircumcised, just as Abraham himself was justified. For he received circumcision as the sign of the righteousness of faith: believing that he would have a son, he received a sign of what he had believed, so that it might be seen that he had been justified because he believed.

Circumcision, therefore, possesses no special dignity; it is only a sign. Abraham’s sons received this sign so that they might be recognized as the sons of the one who, believing God, had received this sign, and so that they might imitate their father’s faith and believe in Jesus, who had been promised to Abraham and whose figure was Isaac, born as a type. For it is not in Isaac that all the nations are blessed, but in Christ. “For there is no other name given under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4), says the apostle Peter.

And so he might be the father of circumcision, not only of those who are from circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised. He says this because, by believing, Abraham first became the father of circumcision—but of circumcision of the heart—not only of those who derive from his lineage, but also of those among the nations who believe in the same way. According to the flesh he is the father of the Jews; according to faith, however, he is the father of all believers.

(Maurus) He now proposes a question, from whose answer they may be taught, and from the very order of the times, that the blessedness of Abraham’s justification was given not in circumcision but while he was still uncircumcised.

(Origen) If Abraham, while he was still uncircumcised, was justified by faith, then everyone who believes God can also be justified by faith, even if he is uncircumcised, and this blessedness may also belong to him, of which it is said: “Blessed is the one to whom the Lord does not reckon sin.” He therefore shows that the Lord does not fail to reckon sin to just anyone, but that he does not reckon sins against the one who believes through his faith. For just as faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness, so also, whenever faith is reckoned as righteousness to every believer, sin is certainly not reckoned against him.

For he does not speak of the righteous, saying that faith is reckoned to them as righteousness. If this were the case, what grace would there seem to be in reckoning righteousness to a righteous person? Rather, he said that faith was reckoned as righteousness to the one who, before possessing this faith, did not have righteousness. This is the blessed person to whom God credits righteousness without works and to whom he does not reckon sin—the person whose iniquities have also been forgiven and whose former sins, if there were any, have been covered.

(Origen) But let us return once more to what he says: “And he received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had while uncircumcised.” Here we contemplate Paul’s profound wisdom. Perhaps to some he seems to repeat the same expression twice—that is, “sign” and “seal.” But it seems to me that the two expressions differ greatly from one another.

A sign is spoken of when, through something visible, something else is indicated. For example, the Lord says in the Gospel: “This generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man must be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. 12). This, then, is a sign: Jonah was seen, and Christ was understood. Similarly, in the Gospel it is said of the Lord himself: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2). The sign in which Christ had come was opposed, because one thing was seen in him and another understood. Flesh was visible, and God was believed.

Thus Abraham also receives a sign; and Scripture says in what follows that it is a sign: “Circumcision,” he says, “which would be a seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had before he was circumcised.” He therefore rightly called circumcision a sign in Abraham, because it too appeared to be one thing while it was understood as another. He shows that even then that bodily circumcision was a sign of spiritual circumcision, which is received not in the flesh but in the heart.

As for what he said by “seal,” I think it should be understood as follows. A seal is said to be placed upon something for safekeeping for a period of time, and no one may break it except the one who imposed it. Through this seal, therefore, as the apostle explains, the righteousness of faith that Abraham deserved to receive while uncircumcised is indicated, as well as his being the father of many nations. We believe that this seal will be broken when the fullness of the nations has entered and all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11). Then what the apostle says will come to pass: Abraham will be the father not only of the nations but also of the circumcision through faith.

Let us discuss the distinction between sign and seal still more clearly. A sign, as we have said, is present when something else is indicated through what is seen; a seal, however, encloses something for a time and is not open to view. It may therefore be understood that the mysteries foreshadowed in the law and in the patriarchs were of such a kind that they were both to be indicated by signs and preserved under seals.

Because these mysteries were to be indicated by signs, Abraham is said to have begun to be a sign among those from the nations who believed. But because those from the circumcision would not believe them, they were to be observed and concealed. He is said to have received a seal, and that seal will be revealed in its proper time, when, in the last days, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel will be saved.

For this reason Abraham is justified in faith before he is circumcised, and afterward he is circumcised, so that it might be shown that he would first become the father of many nations and afterward of those from the circumcision who would believe. For those who are born from Abraham according to the flesh are not to be called Abraham’s sons unless they possess Abraham’s faith and works.

Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel to the Jews who boasted that they were Abraham’s sons: “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would certainly do the works of Abraham” (John 8).

Would you like to be fully instructed from the Old Testament as well that someone may be called a son not of the one from whose physical seed he descended, but of the one whose conduct and works he imitates? Hear what Daniel says to one of those elders whom he accused of adultery: “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, appearance deceived you, and desire overturned your heart” (Dan. 13). You see that the man who physically descended from the stock of Judah is denied to be Judah’s son and is called a son of Canaan—namely, of the one whose conduct and works he followed.

Thus these men also, although they are said to derive their physical lineage from Abraham’s seed, are not called Abraham’s sons if they do not possess his faith. The prophet likewise says to them: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16). What united them was not kinship of descent but similarity of conduct.

“So that he might be the father of all who believe, while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them; and the father of circumcision”—not, however, of those who are from circumcision alone, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, the faith that he had while uncircumcised. Here he plainly declares, with regard to both peoples, as we said above, that what must be sought is not nobility of fleshly origin but nobility of faith.

For the promise to Abraham or to his seed—that he should be heir of the world—was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.

(Ambrose) It is clear that neither had the law yet been given nor had circumcision yet been instituted when the promise was made to the believing Abraham and to his seed, which is Christ, who would wash away the sins of human beings. Hence John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

He therefore became heir of the world not through the merit of having kept the law but through faith. An heir of the world is an heir of the earth, which he obtained in his children. Christ, however, is the heir of the nations, as David sings: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 1). For we die and live with him.

“For the promise to Abraham or to his seed—that he should be heir of the world—was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.”

(Origen) At this point the apostle seems to me to be arguing about the law of Moses and asserting that the promise made to Abraham—that he or his seed should receive the inheritance of the world, that is, of the whole earth—did not rest upon the law of Moses. This promise was made to Abraham before Moses gave the commandment concerning observance of the law.

Thus the promise to Abraham and to his seed, that he should be heir of the world, is not from the law but through the righteousness of faith. When this is understood more clearly, what might seem contradictory is found to be harmonious and mutually consistent.

(Ambrose) To teach that there is one God of all, he addresses the nations and says that Abraham himself believed in God and was justified before the God in whom the nations also believe, so that they may be justified. Thus there is no distinction between Jew and Greek in faith, because, with circumcision and uncircumcision removed, they become one in Christ. Abraham too, while uncircumcised, became one in Christ, because he believed and was justified while uncircumcised.

Who gives life to the dead and calls those things that do not exist as though they did. (Ambrose) By this statement he invites the nations to the faith of Abraham. While Abraham was uncircumcised, believing in God whose faith is now proclaimed in Christ, he was justified together with his wife.

Although they were advanced in age and their vigor had faded, they were renewed, so that he did not doubt that he would have a son by Sarah, whom he knew to be barren and in whom the natural flow of menstruation had already ceased. Through these things they are taught not to be concerned either with uncircumcision or with circumcision, but to be ready [*prompti*; the manuscript reading may be *rupti*] with regard to faith, secure because they believe in the one who gives life to the dead and because there is no other who possesses this power. Whenever he wills something that does not exist to exist, it immediately comes into being by his will.

Therefore, while Abraham was not yet a father, he was called the father of many nations, and he believed confidently in God’s power. To make it believed that the God in whom Abraham believed is also the Father of Christ, a sign like that given to Abraham and Sarah was given in Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1), when the promise was fulfilled in the world as Christ approached. Just as their aged bodies, dead with respect to generation, produced holy John, so Isaac had been born.

(Origen) By “the dead” we understand here those who are dead through the sin of the soul, since Scripture says: “The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18). Just as in bodily death the senses perish, so that a person can no longer receive through the body hearing, smell, taste, or touch, so those who have lost their spiritual senses in the soul—so that they do not see God, hear the word of the Lord God, receive the sweet fragrance of Christ, taste the good word of God, or handle with their hands anything concerning the word of life—are rightly called dead.

Christ’s coming found us in such a condition, but he gave us life by his grace, as the same apostle says elsewhere: “And when we were dead in our trespasses and sins, he raised us up together with him” (Eph. 2).

But let us also examine how the statement that follows—“and calls those things that do not exist as though they did”—should be understood. We have often explained elsewhere that God alone is the one who says: “I am who I am,” and that God’s substance alone always is. If someone joins himself to God, he becomes one spirit with him, and through the one who always is, he too is said to be. But one who is far from him, though he shares in him, is not even said to exist, as was the case with us Gentiles before we came to knowledge of the divine truth. Hence God is said to call those things that do not exist as though they did.
