Among those who exist—that is, who share in the one who is—are counted Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints. Since the nations, by believing, come into the faith of Abraham, the apostle consequently declares that God has called those things that do not exist as though they did.

This may also be understood in another way: in this passage the apostle seems to have poured himself out more fully in praise of God and to have recalled with wonder the beginning of his first creation, when he brought the universe into being from nothing and, by the power of his might, summoned into existence things that did not exist, as though they existed and had substance. In creating, nothing was difficult for him: when nothing existed, everything was suddenly called forth and was present as though it had always existed.

If someone objects to us with that statement of the apostle which he writes to the Corinthians—“God chose the contemptible things of the world, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast before God” (1 Cor. 1)—and says that, according to this interpretation, the things that are should be said to be destroyed when the things that are not have been chosen, we shall answer that in that passage he called some people “those who are,” while in this passage in the Epistle to the Romans he calls others by that name.

For he made clear in the letter to the Corinthians that he was speaking of those whom he had enumerated above. He said earlier: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.”

Thus, when he says that God chose the foolish things of the world—that is, the nations—in order to confound wisdom, he undoubtedly means the Jews; and by “the weak things of the world,” he means those chosen to confound the strong.

In the same order, in this passage he says of “the things that are not,” that they might bring to nothing “the things that are.” He shows that the nations were “not,” while the Jews were “those who are”—that is, those who were in the law but did not fulfill the law, so that they might be brought to nothing and those who were not in the law might be clothed with it and joined to the faith of Abraham through the merit of their belief.

Against hope he believed in hope. (Ambrose) It is clear that, when Abraham had no hope of begetting a child, he believed God, having faith that he would beget a child against hope, while knowing that God could do all things.

So that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said: “So shall your seed be.” This is in Genesis: showing him the stars of heaven, God said, “So shall your seed be.” Believing this, Abraham was justified.

For he believed what seems impossible to the world, since it does not accord with the nature of things that the aged should beget children and that their seed should multiply in such abundance that it could not be counted. Therefore faith is precious when it believes that what it knows or sees will happen contrary to that knowledge or sight. Abraham consoled himself with this hope, because God is the one who permits it; of God one may think more than human weakness can comprehend.

And he did not grow weak in faith, nor did he consider his own body, already dead, when he was nearly one hundred years old, or the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver in unbelief concerning God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to fulfill. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

(Augustine) When he says of Abraham, “giving glory to God,” this is set against those who sought their glory from works of the law before human beings.

(Ambrose) He proclaims Abraham worthy of praise because, knowing that he himself was unable, he strengthened his weakness by faith, believing that through God he could do what he knew could not happen according to the decrees of the world.

For one who believed God contrary to his own knowledge possesses great merit before God. He did not doubt that God, being God, could do what he knew could not happen according to the order of the world. He was firmly convinced that God transcends the order of the world. For no one should be said to be contained within what he created. Therefore the person who attributes more to his Creator than he himself understands deserves to be rewarded by God.

This would have no value if everyone held the same opinion; but the unbelief of many commends the faith of believers before God. He therefore urges the nations to this firmness of faith, so that they may receive God’s promise and grace without any hesitation, secure in Abraham’s example. The praise of the believer increases when he believes what is incredible and appears foolish to the world. For the more impossible what is believed appears, the more honorable the believer will be.

Yet it would truly be foolish to believe this if it were said to happen without God. Abraham’s faith is therefore so much more praiseworthy than that of others because it was not prompted by any prodigies of signs [*attractata*; perhaps *attracta*, “drawn or attracted”].

Because the world is governed and ruled by a definite law and power according to a fixed order, human beings, devoted through their love of the flesh to rational inquiry, neglected God, the maker of this order. To remove this error and show that he is God of all, God willed that it should be proclaimed that he both could do and had done what is impossible for the world. Thus those who believed this, while those who in their pride of worldly reason had neglected God were condemned, might be distinguished and saved, devoted to God’s dominion.

(Origen) Rightly, and in his customary manner, whenever the apostle treats of faith he joins hope to it, knowing that hope is inseparably connected with faith. Thus he teaches in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11).

Again, later in this same Epistle to the Romans, he says: “We were saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8).

When he says, “We were saved in hope,” this is the same as what he says elsewhere: “We were saved through faith”; and, “Your faith has saved you”; and, “Let it happen to you according to your faith.” These statements are made to those who, believing in Jesus, hoped that they could be healed by him.

Just as Abraham believed against hope in hope, so all who through faith are Abraham’s sons believe against hope in hope concerning each of the things they believe—whether the resurrection of the dead or the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. For in relation to human nature these things appear contrary to hope; in relation to God’s power, however, they are believed in hope. Abraham is their example, since whatever God has promised he is able also to accomplish, provided that faith, hope, and love remain in those who believe.

I think that faith is the beginning and foundation of salvation; hope is the progress and growth of the building; and love is the advancement and summit of the entire work. Hence love is said to be greater than all.

Abraham, therefore, believed against hope in hope, so that he might become the father of many nations, which would be like the stars of heaven not only in number but also in love [or “splendor,” *claritate*]. Faithfully believing the one who made the promise, he “did not grow weak in faith.”

When he says, “he did not grow weak in faith,” he seems to me to show that there is a certain weakness in faith. If there is weakness, there is undoubtedly also health, just as he shows elsewhere when he says: “Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith” (Titus 1). Blessed, therefore, is the one who does not grow weak in faith.

If someone does grow weak, the apostle describes his treatment when he says: “Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions. One believes that he may eat everything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables” (Rom. 14). By this he clearly indicates that “vegetables” of the word are to be offered to the one who is weak in faith, lest the full teaching of faith be forced upon those who hesitate in it and are, in a certain sense, sick.

Faith is called sound when it is perfect and lacks nothing. It is the faith that believes it may eat everything—that is, the faith capable of receiving all things. Whoever possesses it is called spiritual, judges all things, and cannot be scandalized by any word.

It is therefore plainly evident that there are degrees of progress in faith: some possess a small portion of faith, others a great one, and others the whole of faith. Hence the apostle said: “If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains” (1 Cor. 13). In the Gospels also the disciples say to the Lord, as though they did not yet possess complete faith: “Increase our faith.”

Consider carefully whether, according to what we say about increases in faith, we can understand increases in love in the same way, so that we might say of love, as that man said, “If I have all faith,” “If I have all love.” One possesses all love if he possesses all those things that properly belong to love, as the apostle says: “Love is patient, love is kind; it is not inflated, it is not jealous, it is not ambitious, it does not act improperly, it is not provoked; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13), and other things like these.

If someone possesses these qualities, it seems right to me to say that he possesses all love. Love undoubtedly consists of each of the parts that the apostle enumerated above. I think that the same may be said of mercy, piety, and the other virtues. Perhaps, just as it is said of faith that faith was reckoned as righteousness, so it may also be said of love that love, or piety, or mercy was reckoned to someone as righteousness.

But let us now examine what follows: “And he did not grow weak in faith, nor did he consider his own body, already dead, when he was nearly one hundred years old, or the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver in unbelief concerning the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith.”

As far as the simple meaning is concerned, he has given an evident explanation: when Abraham heard that offspring had been promised to him by God, he did not look to the dead powers of his hundred-year-old body, from which no succession could in any way have been expected. Rather, he looked to the power of the one who had made the promise and believed that nothing was difficult in what the Almighty promised. “He gave glory,” he says, understanding that the gift belonged to God alone, since the laws of human fertility had ceased to operate. Rightly, therefore, he gave glory to God, since he had been abandoned by the resources of nature.

As I said, this seems sufficient as far as the simple meaning is concerned. But if someone objects to us: How can Abraham, situated at the age of one hundred, be called dead in body, when, after he had received Isaac and Sarah had died—Sarah who had conceived him at the age of ninety and lived for one hundred twenty-seven years—and after Isaac had reached the age of forty and taken Rebecca, Scripture records all this: “Abraham again took a wife, whose name was Keturah; and she bore him Zimran [Jembran], Jokshan [Zexan], Medan, Midian, Ishbak [Jesoc], and Shuah [Soe]”?

How, then, can he be regarded as dead in body when, having grown much older than he was at that time, he was able to take a wife and beget six children?

To exclude these objections appropriately, we transfer the interpretation of “dead in body” to another sense. We say that Abraham was not dead through the weakness of human age, but according to that virtue which the saints first fulfill in themselves and then urge others to possess, saying: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Col. 3).

For I think it absurd if we do not believe that Abraham, the great patriarch whom the apostle even calls his father, possessed the good that Paul had in himself—for Paul would not have commanded others to possess what he had not himself done. Abraham therefore also possessed this mortification of the members. He was not stirred by lust, nor burned by desire, as were those of whom the apostle says: “It is better to marry than to burn.”

The same was true of Sarah, because the functions of womanhood had ceased in her. There was no wantonness of womanhood in her, nor dissolution of self-control, nor were they unwillingly driven toward the use of lust.

But when they heard of such great hope for their posterity and of the glory of their offspring, which would be made equal to heaven and the stars, they did not look to their own advantages—to the grace of continence or the mortification of their members. Rather, they regarded all these things, which they had considered gains, as losses, in order that they might gain Christ.

I would therefore have you consider what Paul intended when he promised us that, just as faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness when he believed, so it would also be reckoned to us who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

In this matter, as far as my limited understanding allows, I perceive that it is far more magnificent in the praises of God to raise Jesus our Lord from the dead than to make heaven and earth, create angels, and establish the heavenly powers.

For it was one thing to make what did not exist; this, however, was to restore what had perished. The former was to establish things not yet loved; the latter was to restore things already loved. The former was accomplished by command, the latter by suffering.

Yet the form and image of this great and magnificent mystery had preceded it in the faith of Abraham our father. He had believed in God when he was commanded to offer his only son, because God could also raise him from the dead. He had also believed that this event did not concern Isaac alone, but that the full truth of the mystery would be preserved for his seed, which is Christ.

Therefore he offered his only son with joy, because in him he contemplated not the destruction of his posterity but the restoration of the world and the renewal of the whole creation, which was restored through the Lord’s resurrection.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1363]

### CHAPTER 4 FOLLOWS

[Col. 1363C]

It is not written on his account alone, that it was reckoned to him as righteousness, but also on ours, who believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up on account of our sins and rose on account of our justification.

**(Amb.)** In Abraham, he says, an example was given to Jews and Gentiles, so that by his example we might believe in God, in Christ, and in the Holy Spirit, and righteousness might be reckoned to us. Although what is now believed differs, faith nevertheless possesses one gift. Thus we attain what we believe: for by believing that Christ is the Son of God, we are adopted by God as sons. He could give believers nothing greater than to be called sons of God, while the faithless are disowned. We are called sons of God, whereas they are not now worthy even to be called servants.

For in his infinite magnificence [Col. 1363D] God bestowed upon those who love him what is worthy of his majesty—not because human beings deserve it, since in a gift the greatness of the giver is considered more than that of the recipient. He receives the greater praise when, through Christ, he generously gives great gifts to little ones. Christ allowed himself to be killed for our sake so that, having received forgiveness, he might rescue us from the second death—that is, from the punishment of hell—and rose again so that, in the joy of the triumph by which death was conquered, he might grant us the grace of justification, making us worthy to be called sons of God.

Before the Passion, those who were baptized received only the remission of sins; out of envy of this [the antecedent is uncertain], Satan killed the Savior. After the resurrection, however, both those who had previously been baptized and those who were baptized later were all justified through the form of faith given in the Trinity, and after receiving the Holy Spirit, who is the sign of believers that they are sons of God.

And to increase the fullness of our justification, when he rose again he gave authority to his commandments, [Col. 1364C] so that this confidence in them might make us emulators of them and, through it by which we are justified, we might increase our merits; through it, having attained glory, we might appear radiant in the kingdom of God, because those who have been justified cannot be held by death. For by the Passion of the Savior death was conquered—death which previously held dominion because of sin—and it does not dare retain those whom he has justified.

[Col. 1364D] “He was delivered up on account of our sins, and rose on account of our justification.”

**(Aug.)** Just as we are sown through his death, so we are made to germinate through his resurrection. For his death signifies the destruction of our former life, and his resurrection signifies the newness of our life. On this subject the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6).

He did not say: “He was delivered up on account of our justification, and rose on account of our sins.” In his delivery, sin is proclaimed; in his resurrection, righteousness is proclaimed. Therefore, let sin die, and let righteousness rise.

“God commends his love in us.” First, it had to be made clear to human beings how greatly God loved us and what sort of people he loved: how greatly, so that we would not despair; what sort of people, so that we would not become proud. The Apostle explains this passage as follows: “God commends his love in us,” he says, “because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.”

For if we have risen with him who is righteousness, and walk in newness of life, and live according to righteousness, Christ rose for our justification. But if we have not yet put off the old man with his deeds, and live in unrighteousness, I dare say that Christ has not yet risen for our justification [Col. 1365A], nor has he been delivered up on account of our sins. For if I believe this, how can I love that for which he endured death? If I believe that he rose for my justification, how can I take pleasure in unrighteousness?

Christ therefore justifies only those who have embraced newness of life after the example of his resurrection and cast off, as the cause of death, the old garments of injustice and iniquity.

But I should like to inquire whether the Apostle says this only because it is written not for Abraham alone but also for us, when he says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Do you think that this statement, among all that are said about Abraham, was written not only on his account but also on ours? Or will other things also be seen to have been written not only on his account but also on ours? Or, indeed, are [Col. 1365B] everything said about him spoken not only on his account but also for us—and not only what is said about Abraham?

But see whether perhaps these same things must also be understood similarly of Isaac: that what was written about him concerns not him alone but also us; and likewise concerning Jacob and the other patriarchs. For it might seem reasonable to say that what was written about Abraham also pertains to us, but not to understand what was written about Isaac, Jacob, Judah, or Joseph in the same way. Yet if no reason appears why this should be understood in this manner of one patriarch and not also of the others, it follows that everything written was written not only on account of those who lived then but also on account of us.

I am especially persuaded [Col. 1365C] to think this by that Gospel passage in which our Lord and Savior replied to those who had said to him, “Abraham is our father”: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would certainly do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from my Father. Abraham did not do this” (John 8). By this he plainly showed that those who do the works of Abraham are the children of Abraham, and that what was written about Abraham was written for their sake.

## CHAPTER V  
### He demonstrates the power of faith in the justification of believers, since death reigned from Adam until Christ.

Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

**(Amb.)** Faith [Col. 1365D], not the law, makes us have peace with God. For faith reconciles us to God after removing sins, which had made us enemies of God. And because the Lord Jesus is the minister of this grace, through him we have been reconciled to God. Faith is greater than the law: the law is for our salvation, but faith is of God; the law pertains to present discipline, whereas faith pertains to everlasting salvation.

But one who does not think rightly about Christ will not be able to attain the rewards of faith, because he does not hold the truth of faith.

**(Orig.)** Most clearly, through this statement he invites the person who has understood what it means to be justified by faith and not by works to the peace of God, which surpasses every mind and in which the highest perfection consists. But so that we may perceive the Apostle’s meaning more carefully, let us inquire what [Col. 1366A] is meant by the name “peace,” and by that peace which comes through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Peace is said to exist where no one disagrees, no one is at variance, where nothing hostile or barbarous is being done. We, then, who were once enemies of God, following the enemy and tyrant, the devil, now—if we cast away his weapons and take up the standard of Christ and the banners of his cross—certainly have peace with God, but through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us to God through the sacrifice of his blood, as it is written concerning him: “When we were enemies of God, we were reconciled through the blood of the cross of his Son” (Romans 5).

And elsewhere Paul added these words: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5).

If, then, someone has peace with God and has been reconciled through the blood of Christ, let him no longer [Col. 1366B] engage in those things that are hostile to God. Do you wish to hear what those things are that are hostile to God? Paul himself teaches you, saying: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God” (Romans 8).

If, therefore, you think in a fleshly manner, or expose your life to the desires of the flesh and are weakened by an abundance of pleasures, or if you understand the law in a fleshly rather than spiritual manner, and defend it more by arguments acquired through human skill than through spiritual grace and a more subtle understanding, then through the wisdom of the flesh you become an enemy of God.

Nor does Paul alone write this in his letters. Hear also James, the brother of the Lord, declaring something similar when he says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (James 4). John also bears similar witness: “Little children, do not love the world or the things that are in the world, [Col. 1366C] because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from God” (1 John 2).

Therefore, whoever possesses these things cannot have peace with God; instead, he again arouses those hostilities for the sake of saving people from which Christ came.

**(Aug.)** “Having been justified,” he says, “in his blood.” We have plainly been justified in that we have been freed from all sins. We have been freed from all sins because the Son of God, who had no sin, was killed for us. Therefore we shall be saved through him from wrath—from the wrath, certainly, of God, which is nothing other than just vengeance.

For the wrath of God is not, as in a human being, a disturbance of the mind. Rather, his wrath is that of whom Holy Scripture says elsewhere: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wisdom 12). If, then, divine [Col. 1366D] vengeance has received this name, how is the reconciliation of God rightly understood unless that wrath comes to an end?

Nor were we enemies of God except in the way that sins are enemies of righteousness. When these sins are forgiven, such enmity comes to an end, and those whom he himself justifies are reconciled to the righteous God. Yet he loved even those who were enemies, since he did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all while we were still enemies.

The Apostle therefore rightly continued: “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son”—through which the forgiveness of sins was accomplished—“much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved in his life” (Romans 8): saved in his life, we who were reconciled through his death. For who would doubt that he will give his [Col. 1367A] life for friends, for whom he gave his death while they were enemies?

Through him we have access to this grace in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.

**(Amb.)** It is clear that through Christ we have access to the grace of God. For he is the mediator between God and human beings; by raising us up through his teaching, he made us hope for the gift of God’s grace, standing in his faith. We are said to stand because previously we lay prostrate; but by believing we have been raised up, glorying in the hope of the splendor that God promised us.

**(Orig.)** How we have access to grace through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior himself says: “I am the door, and no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 10). Through him, therefore, who is the door, we have access to grace.

But let us see what kind of door it is, so that we may know what sort of people those must be who enter [Col. 1367B] through him and gain access to grace. This door is truth, and liars cannot enter through the door of truth. Again, this door is righteousness, and the unrighteous do not enter through the door of righteousness. This door says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). Through the door of humility and gentleness, therefore, neither the angry nor the proud enters.

If someone wishes, in accordance with the Apostle’s word, to have access through our Lord Jesus Christ to the grace of the Lord—in which Paul says that he stands, and that those like him stand—he must be purified from all the things we have mentioned above. Otherwise, this door will not allow those who bear things alien to it to enter through it; it immediately closes and does not permit those unlike itself to pass through [Col. 1367C] it.

The Apostle Paul rightly says that he stands in grace, since elsewhere he also says: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15). Therefore, if there is someone else who labors more abundantly, who glories in his weaknesses, who is often exposed to dangers—dangers at sea, dangers in rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from false brothers (2 Corinthians 11)—and who nevertheless always stands firm in faith amid all these things, he too is said to stand in grace.

But let us also examine what follows: “And we glory in the hope of the glory of God.” What sort of statement is this? I am troubled by the fact that he did not say that he glories in the glory of God, but in the hope of the glory of God. Something seems to be lacking in the expression, so that we should understand: “in the hope of seeing the glory of God.”

Through this he teaches us, as [Col. 1367D] he himself says elsewhere (2 Corinthians 4), that “the things that are hoped for are eternal, but the things that are seen are temporal.” Moses is said to have seen the glory of God; the people are also said to have seen the glory of the God of Israel at the dedication of the Lord’s house.

But concerning this kind of glory, which could be seen, Paul—who was knowledgeable in the mysteries of God—dared to declare that the glory visible even on Moses’ face would be destroyed.

The glory that is hoped for, of which he says “in the hope of the glory of God,” will never be destroyed. It is that glory of which the same Apostle speaks concerning Christ: “Who is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance” (Hebrews 1).

Those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, [Col. 1368A], for they shall see God” (Matthew 5), possess the hope of seeing this glory. Then pain, sorrow, and groaning will have fled; the things that are now seen in a mirror and in an enigma will be destroyed, and those things will remain which are seen face to face (1 Corinthians 13).

If someone should perhaps object to our interpretation with the contrary statement that the Apostle himself says, “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3), and should ask how one who says that he already beholds the glory of the Lord with unveiled face and is transformed from glory to glory can still possess hope of glory, see whether we can resolve the objection in this way.

The Apostle seems to me to indicate differences among glories. One glory was revealed through the ministry of Moses, [Col. 1368B] concerning which we have already spoken above. Another was ministered at the Savior’s bodily coming, concerning which John also says in the Gospel: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1).

We cannot say that this is the glory that is to be hoped for, since the apostles say that they saw it; and that statement is true which says: “What does a person hope for if he sees it?” (Romans 8).

The true glory that is to be hoped for, concerning which the Apostle says in the present passage that he glories in the hope of the glory of God, may be understood as that of which the Savior says in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father and of the holy angels” (Mark 8).

When he said “of the Father and of the holy angels,” he did not mean that the glory of God the Father and that of the angels are one [Col. 1368C] and the same. Rather, it seems to me that he shows that the glories conveyed either through Moses to those who lived earlier, or to us through the bodily coming of Christ, were not the angels’ glories but human glories. They were ministered to human beings and were measured according to what human beings could receive.

But the glory in which the Son of Man will come for the judgment of the world will be so great that only angels can receive it. If some of the saints should also prove capable of that glory, they will surely be those of whom it is said that they will be “like the angels of God” (Matthew 22).

In this way, then, it seems rightly to have been said concerning the future glory that is to be hoped for, that the Son of Man will come in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels—that is, because it will not be earthly human beings [Col. 1368D] but holy angels who will be worthy to receive it. For God distributes the greatness of glories according to the capacity of minds.

Thus, this glory which the apostles say in the Gospel that they saw—“glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth”—[the sentence remains incomplete in the supplied text].

“We glory not only in this, but also in our tribulations.”

**(Aug.)** When he says, “not only this, but we also glory in tribulations,” and so forth, he leads us step by step all the way to the love of God, which he says we possess through the gift of the Spirit. He shows that everything we are able to attribute to God must indeed be attributed to him, since he has deigned to give the Holy Spirit through grace, because “through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Therefore he teaches that we must also glory in these things.

Tribulation added to hope [Col. 1369A] increases the reward. For tribulation is the evidence of a steadfast hope, bearing witness toward the crown. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed will you be when they persecute you and speak every evil against you for the sake of God’s righteousness. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5).

To despise present things and those that give pleasure, and not to yield under pressure because of hope in future things, is of great merit before God. Therefore one must glory in tribulation, because a person believes that he will receive so much more according as he sees himself stronger in tribulation.

“Knowing that tribulation produces endurance.”

**(Ambr.)** This means that tribulation produces endurance if tribulation itself does not undergo the movement of weakness or doubt. Endurance, however, produces testing. It is clear [Col. 1369B] that endurance, if it is such as we have described, will appear to be firm proof.

Testing produces hope. Hope is rightly spoken of in one who appears to have been tested. For he will be known to be worthy to receive a reward in the kingdom of God.

“Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Hope does not disappoint even when we are judged foolish and dull by the faithless because we believe things that lack worldly rationality. For we possess within us the pledge of God’s love: the Holy Spirit given to us. The Holy Spirit given to the apostles and to us proves that God’s promise is faithful. He enabled uneducated people to speak in different languages, with interpretations for the confirmation of hope, so that he might also commend the love of God in us.

Because it is impossible for those who are loved to be deceived, he made us secure concerning the promise: both because it is God who promised, and because he promised to those whom he wished to hold [Col. 1369C] dear.

**(Orig.)** The very first statement of this chapter immediately contains a certain ambiguity, for in what follows it does not say to what “not only” should refer. Therefore, let us see whether we can resolve the ambiguity of the expression in this way.

Above, he fully taught that many things had been granted to us through our Lord Jesus Christ: that we have been justified by faith through our Lord Jesus Christ; that through him we have access to this grace; and that through him we also glory in the hope of the glory of God. I think “not only this” [Col. 1369D] must refer to all these things that have been said—that is: “Not only this which I have said above, but also the fact that we glory in our tribulations, we possess through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

While others are saddened in tribulation, we, strengthened by the power of his glory, glory in tribulations. For through his instruction we have learned a new discipline: that through tribulations we may acquire the good of endurance. Once we possess the good of endurance, we are judged worthy; and having been tested through endurance amid many tribulations, we possess hope of future recompense from God. This hope is certain and true, and it does not disappoint those who hope.

The love of God follows faith and hope. It is the greatest of all things, and it not only fills our mind but also abounds and is poured out in our hearts, because it is not acquired by human skill on our part but [Col. 1370A] infused through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

This, according to the sequence of the statement itself or of the text, may serve as an explanation for opening up the Apostle’s language. Now let us investigate what the inner meaning contains.

First, let us examine the glorying, where he says, “We glory in our tribulations.” The language of glorying is sometimes used laudably in Scripture and sometimes blamefully. For when Jeremiah says:

“Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man glory in his strength, nor the rich man glory in his riches; but let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows me, because I am the Lord who establish mercy, judgment, and righteousness upon the earth” (Jeremiah 9),

he uses glorying both laudably and blamefully in one and the same chapter. [Col. 1370B]

For if someone, he says, glories either in his wisdom, strength, or riches, he glories blamefully. But if someone glories in knowing the Lord, and in understanding his judgments, mercy, and righteousness, he glories laudably.

Since this statement concerns both kinds, we must inquire in what things glorying is right and in what things it is less right. We shall be able to recognize this only if we distinguish the natures of things appropriately.

What we mean is this: everything that exists or happens is either good, evil, or indifferent. Although this matter deserves a more extensive discussion, we shall state as much as is sufficient for the present passage.

Those things are properly called good which pertain to the virtues of the soul; and only those things are defined as evil which pertain to wickedness [Col. 1370C] and are done against the law of God. The remaining things are indifferent—that is, they are to be called neither good nor evil—such as riches, bodily appearance, strength, height, and the things that serve the uses of the body.

If, therefore, someone does not recognize this distinction and glories in things that are not truly good and do not pertain to virtue of soul, he glories blamefully.

Paul, however, who was most experienced in these matters, after saying, “We glory in our tribulations,” lest anyone think that he was glorying in indifferent and intermediate things, immediately gives the reason and shows that his glorying in tribulations pertains to the virtues of the soul.

For he says that the tribulation in which he glories produces endurance; endurance produces testing; testing produces hope; and hope [Col. 1370D] does not disappoint because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. In this way he teaches that, through virtues succeeding one another, glorying in tribulations rises up to the summit of the Holy Spirit.

When the Apostle says in the present chapter that tribulation produces endurance, if endurance is clearly one of the virtues of the soul, then tribulation, which gives birth to the virtues of the soul, must without doubt be called neither evil nor indifferent but good.

Indeed, as we said above, endurance must be called a virtue of the soul to such an extent that he says that through endurance we are tested, and through testing hope is given. Since hope is placed in God, who is the Father of all virtues, it does not disappoint the one who hopes.

At the same time, along with hope, it holds an abundance [Col. 1371A] of love, which is joined to the spirit in the first place because love is greater than all things.

But if someone approaches us and says that tribulation is intermediate and indifferent, since we find even wicked and impious people suffering, and that their tribulation should not immediately be regarded as a virtue of the soul merely because they suffer for their evil deeds, see whether we can answer in this way: tribulation properly belongs to the saints, whereas the tribulation of the impious and unrighteous is called punishment.

Thus the Psalm says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Psalm 34); but concerning the others it says: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Psalm 32).

Perhaps for this reason tribulation and distress belong to the saints: they are the ones who walk along the narrow and constricted way, and for that reason they are said to suffer tribulation.

But when he says [Col. 1371B] that “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts,” we must consider more carefully in whose hearts the love of God is poured out.

I think it is poured out in the hearts of those who no longer have the spirit of slavery again in fear, but also in those in whom perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4), and to whom the Spirit of adoption is given, crying in their hearts, “Abba, Father.”

The love of God is therefore not poured out in the heart of just anyone, but only in that of a perfect person, such as Paul, through the Holy Spirit.

But this too must be considered: does he here mean the love by which we love God, or the love by which we are loved by God, which has been poured out through the Holy Spirit in our hearts?

If the statement is understood of the love by which we love God, [Col. 1371C], it requires defense. But if, because he said that God’s love has been poured out in our hearts, it is rather understood as the love by which we are loved by God, then it is certain that he presents love as the supreme and greatest gift of the Holy Spirit. He wishes us to understand that, having first received this gift from God, through it we are able to love God because we are loved by God.

**(Cass.)** Finally, the virtue of love is exalted to such a degree that the blessed Apostle John declares that it is not only a thing belonging to God but also God himself, saying: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

We see so clearly that love is divine [Col. 1371D] that we perceive the Apostle’s statement to be manifestly at work in us: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

This is as though he were saying that God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, and who, even when we do not know what we ought to pray for, intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.

But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because according to God he pleads for the saints.

Why, then, while we were still sinners, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time? For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps, indeed, someone might dare to die for a good person. (Origen) Since he wished more fully to demonstrate the power of charity, which he had said was poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, he explained for what reasons we ought to understand this. He teaches us that Christ died not for the godly but for the ungodly. For we were ungodly before we were converted to God; and Christ certainly underwent death for us before we believed. He would unquestionably not have done this unless he had possessed an excessive and most abundant charity toward us—whether it was our Lord Jesus Christ himself, dying for the ungodly, or God the Father, handing over his only-begotten Son for the redemption of the ungodly. (Ambrose) If Christ surrendered himself to death for unbelievers and enemies of God—and he died only for a time, since he rose again on the third day—how much more, when we believe in him, will he fortify us with his aid? For he died for us in order to acquire life and glory for us. Therefore, if he died for enemies, it must be understood how much he will provide for friends.

Among human beings, then—that is, according to time—he appeared to die; [Col. 1372B] for among the dead he was judging irreverent and wicked spirits for the salvation of souls. There are times in this world, where the sun rises and sets, the moon waxes and wanes, and day and night do not remain in their appointed condition. For whatever is subject to time and age is always mutable. Christ therefore died with respect to this time when he departed from the body. But where there is neither time nor age, there he was found not only alive but victorious.

For this reason he wished to commend the Savior’s affection toward us when he said: “Scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person.” But Christ died for the ungodly. For if someone scarcely dies for a righteous person, how can it happen that anyone should die for the ungodly? And if someone might perhaps dare to die for a good person—or perhaps might not dare, since he indicates that either course is difficult—how can it seem possible that anyone would dare to die for the ungodliness of many? If someone perhaps dares to die for a righteous or good person, he is drawn by a certain compassion or by affection for that person’s good works. But in the case of the ungodly, there is not only nothing to persuade someone to die; there is not even anything to move him to tears. Christ, however, died for the ungodliness of a people who were not yet his, so that he might make credible everything the world regards with disbelief.

He therefore established two grades, “righteous” and “good.” Although the righteous person must also be called good, he set out the categories themselves: by “righteous” signifying one who is righteous through practice, but by “good” one who is good by nature and is called innocent through simplicity. Thus, although—so far as this passage is concerned—the righteous person is of better standing than the good person, nevertheless he says, “Perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person,” indicating that, because the cause of innocence is more pitiable, someone might perhaps be compelled to do this. Indeed, parents wish to die for good children—not to mention wives for good husbands.

For if we wish to distinguish between the good and the righteous, sometimes we find the righteous to be better, and sometimes the good to be preferred. If, according to God’s law, the righteous person is better than the good person, this applies to one who has not yet labored with himself in order to increase himself through good works. Through practice, the righteous person will improve the goodness of his nature. But if the person is righteous according to the world, the good person is preferred to him because of his innocence; for worldly righteousness of this kind is not without ungodliness.

Thus every nature is good, whereas righteousness is the fitting fruit of nature according to God’s law. Therefore righteousness is goodness, and so righteous people are always called good. Yet good people are not always righteous, because they are called good not on account of their works but on account of their innocence. For perfect righteousness is goodness when it fulfills through action the good things proper to its nature.

(Jerome) On the occasion of this testimony, which they do not understand, two heresies blaspheme with different errors but equal ungodliness. Marcion, who makes the just God the creator of the law and the prophets, but the good God the author of the Gospel and the apostles—and whose Son he wishes Christ to be—introduces two gods, one just and the other good. He asserts that scarcely anyone, or only a few, met death for the just God, whereas for the good God, that is, Christ’s Father, countless martyrs arose.

Arius, moreover, refers “just” to Christ, of whom it is said: “Give the king your judgments, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 71); and Christ himself says in the Gospel: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He also says: “I judge as I hear.” But he refers “good” to God the Father, concerning whom the Son himself confesses: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God, the Father” (Mark 10).

Although he had been able to find paths leading astray this far in his blasphemy, he stumbles and falls in what follows. For how can anyone dare to die for the Father, while scarcely dying for the Son, when so much martyr blood has been shed for Christ’s name?

Someone who expounds this passage simply could therefore say that under the Old Law, in which there is justice, scarcely a few were found who shed their blood, whereas in the New Testament, in which there is goodness and mercy, countless martyrs appeared. But by saying, “Perhaps someone might even dare to die,” and tempering the statement with this hesitant qualification, he shows that some might be found who dare to die for the Gospel. This passage must not be understood in that way, however; its meaning must be considered from what precedes and follows.

For when the apostle Paul says that he rejoices in tribulations—because tribulation produces endurance, endurance approval, approval hope, and hope does not disappoint, since it possesses a sure promise from the fact that “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us,” in accordance with what God said through the prophet, “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Isaiah 44)—he marvels at Christ’s goodness: that he was willing to die for the weak, the ungodly, and sinners, [Col. 1373D] and to die at the opportune time, concerning which he himself says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (2 Corinthians 6); and again: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (ibid.). This was when all had sinned, all had become useless, and there was no one who did good, not even one (Psalm 52).

Unbelievable, therefore, is the goodness, and unheard-of the mercy, of dying for the ungodly. Scarcely does anyone shed his blood for a righteous and good person, since fear of death terrifies everyone. Yet sometimes it may be found that someone dares to die for a righteous and good person.

But God’s love toward us is demonstrated above all by this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. “His life was taken from the earth,” and “for the iniquities of the people he was led to death”; he “bore our sins,” “his soul was handed over to death,” and “he was reckoned among the wicked,” so that he might make us, the ungodly, weak, and sinful, godly, strong, and righteous.

Some interpret the passage in this way: If he died for us, the ungodly and sinners, how much more ought we, without any hesitation, to die for Christ, the righteous and good one. We should not think that “righteous” and “good” are different or that they specifically signify some person; they simply mean a righteous thing. Sometimes someone may be found who sheds his blood.

(Origen) The love of this life is so great that even when a just cause for death has arisen, scarcely anyone receives death patiently. A just cause of death seems to arise when death is imposed by the law of nature; and although it is just, by the condition of mortality, for the mind nevertheless scarcely embraces submission to the laws of nature. God, however, commends his love toward us.

(Ambrose) He commends his love in this way: while he is still benevolent toward enemies, he sends one who will save them, although they certainly do not deserve it.

For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath. He says this because, if God allowed his Son to be killed for sinners, what will he do for those who have been justified? He will preserve them from wrath—that is, he will keep them safe from the devil’s deception—so that they may be secure on the day of judgment, when vengeance begins to devastate the faithless.

Since God’s goodness wishes no one to perish, he gave a most worthy death so that, for those who understand God’s grace toward them, he might increase dignity and glory, while for the ungrateful he might multiply punishment. The ungrateful are those who, when God calls, dissent, rejecting God’s grace so that they may remain in their chosen error and wickedness.

(Origen) I certainly do not think that Paul’s variation in these words is pointless: that at one time he calls those for whom Christ died “weak,” at another “ungodly,” and at another “sinners.” Although he admits that he is unskilled in speech, I do not think that in this matter he varied through lack of skill, but rather through profound knowledge.

For through these three terms every kind of sin is gathered. Someone sins in darkness, either by ignorance of God, and is called ungodly; or, wishing to keep the commandment, is overcome by the weakness of the flesh and deceived by the attractions of the present life, and is called weak; or, knowingly and willingly, despises the commandment, hates God’s discipline, and casts his words behind him, and is called a sinner.

Thus Paul, who—as we have said—professes to be unskilled in speech, has embraced in these three distinctions all those for whom Christ is proclaimed to have died.

If sometimes even those who are under the law and appear to worship God are called ungodly in the divine Scriptures, this is because, abandoning the God of their fathers, they worship the gods of the nations.

As for Paul’s counting himself among sinners, although elsewhere he says: “We are Jews by nature and not sinners from the Gentiles” (Galatians 2), this is a virtue of his humility. For he imitates the one who, although he had committed no sin, “was made sin for us,” and although he was God, lived among human beings.

God therefore commends his love toward us.

(Origen) Here “commends” may be understood as “confirms,” or as “makes lovable” through the benefits he has bestowed. The fact that Christ died for us while we were still sinners gives us hope that, having been cleansed and justified from sin, he will much more save us through himself from the wrath that threatens sinners. He who loved strangers and enemies so greatly that he gave his only Son to death for us will much more grant eternal salvation to those who have become his own and have been reconciled to him.

“Much more,” he says, “now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath.” Earlier he had said: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God.” Now he says: “Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath.”

From this he shows that neither is our faith without Christ’s blood, nor does Christ’s blood justify us without our faith. Yet, from the two together, Christ’s blood justifies us much more than our faith does. For this reason it seems to me that, whereas earlier he simply said, “Having been justified by faith,” here he added, “Much more, therefore, now justified by his blood,” in order to teach that, even if our faith saves us from the coming wrath, and even if works of righteousness do so, nevertheless, above all these things, Christ’s blood saves us much more from the wrath to come.

For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. (Ambrose) It is clear that if God handed his Son over to death in order to reconcile us to himself, how much more will he save those who have been reconciled through his life? For he cannot fail to love friends, since he benefits enemies.

If the Savior’s death benefited us while we were still ungodly, how much more will his life benefit those who have been justified, when he rises from the dead? For just as his death rescued us from the devil, so his life will free us from God’s judgment on the day of judgment.

(Augustine) Christ therefore died for the ungodly, and Christ is God. How, then, did the righteous one, found in the life of God, reign, when the ungodly was sought in the death of God so that he might not perish? We shall be saved in the life of God because we had perished in our own life.

But when we hear of both the life of God and the death of God, let us distinguish what belongs to each. He brought life to us, but he received death from us—not, however, on account of his own merit, but on our account.

“For we too,” he says, “were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2). In this wrath, while human beings were subject to original sin, and all the more grievously and disastrously because they added greater or more numerous sins besides, a mediator—that is, a reconciler—was necessary. He would appease this wrath by the offering of a unique sacrifice, of which all the sacrifices of the law and the prophets were shadows.

When God is said to be angry, this does not signify a disturbance such as exists in the mind of an angry human being. Rather, by a term transferred from human emotions, his vengeance—which is always just—is called wrath.

That through the Mediator we are reconciled to God and receive the Holy Spirit, so that from enemies we may become sons—for “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Romans 8)—this is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

“For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life,” and so forth.

(Origen) It is clearly shown that we are a substance which, according to the definition of Marcion or Valentinus, is naturally hostile to God. Otherwise, if what is hostile were hostile by nature and not by will, it could not have reconciliation.

When someone changes from an enemy into a friend, it is certain that, while he performs those works that God does not love, he is an enemy of God. Each person becomes an enemy as grave and hateful as the number of works deserving enmity that he has multiplied.

There are therefore certain measures and degrees distinguished by the quality or quantity of sins among those who are enemies of God. Hence the one who sinned above all others is mentioned by Paul as the last enemy to be destroyed.

Conversely, and in due order, those who have been reconciled through the death of God’s Son are certainly regarded as friends. There is someone who is a friend in the manner in which Moses was called God’s friend. There are also others to whom the Savior says: “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15).

I believe, moreover, that there are still more intimate friends in heaven with God: either those who always behold God’s face, or those who always stand in the presence of the Most High. Thus, just as we said above that there is a final enemy, so there are there, according to the merits of their virtues, certain supreme friends.

Since this is so, I do not know whether one who still persists in those works that God hates, and on account of which there is enmity between God and human beings, can rightly be said to have been reconciled to God through Christ’s blood. For how has one who is an enemy been reconciled? Paul therefore rightly says both of himself and of those like him: “While we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the blood of his Son.”

Great shame is involved wherever such a reconciliation has taken place—where the enmity between God and human beings has been removed not by the sinner’s word but by the blood of the intercessor—and we nevertheless turn back again to enmity and do those things hated by the one to whom the outpouring of sacred blood alone had reconciled us.

Not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. (Ambrose) He teaches us to give thanks to God not only for the salvation and security we have received, but also to glory in God through Jesus Christ, who deigned to call us, though ungodly and enemies, his friends. Thus we rejoice that we have obtained all benefits through Christ.

Since through him we have come to know God, glorying in him, we should render him an honor equal to that rendered to God the Father, with Christ himself as a suitable witness, for he declares: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5).

After speaking of the providence of God the Father and of the gift he gave through Christ, in order to make the person of the Son pleasing to us—because through Christ we were redeemed by the one God the Father—he added:

“Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

Since above he demonstrated the grace of God given through Christ according to the order of truth, he now declares the order of the one God the Father through his one Christ, the Son. Just as one Adam—that is, Eve, for she too is Adam—sinned in all, so the one Christ, the Son of God, conquered sin in all.

And since he has shown the purpose of God’s grace toward the human race, in order to reveal the beginnings of sin he began with Adam, who first sinned. Thus he teaches that the providence of the one God restored through one person what had fallen through one person and been drawn into death.

This one, through whom we have been saved, deserves from us the reverence that we owe to God the Father, as Christ himself wills. For in another passage he says (Romans 14): “Whoever serves Christ in these things is pleasing to God,” although it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6).

If, then, the law says that one must serve God alone, and commands that Christ be served, Christ is included in the unity of God. He is not a different or another God, since, while the law urges that God alone be served, one who serves Christ is said to please God.

(Origen) Let us turn to the matter according to our strength, and first consider how through one man sin entered this world, and through sin, death.

Perhaps someone might ask: If the woman sinned before Adam—of whom it is said that she was deceived and became involved in transgression—and if the serpent sinned before her, for it sinned when it said to the woman, “Why did God say that you must not eat from every tree of paradise?”; and again, if it sinned when God had said, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die,” while the serpent said to the woman, “You shall certainly not die; but God knows that on whatever day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil”—

If, then, the woman sinned before Adam, and the serpent before the woman, and if elsewhere the apostle says that “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Timothy 2), how will sin appear to have entered through one man, and not rather through one woman?

For sin began with the woman, and before the woman with the serpent, or with the devil, of whom it is said in the Gospel that “he was a murderer from the beginning” (John 8).

But observe that in this matter the apostle maintained the order of nature. Since he was speaking of the sin through which death had passed to all human beings, he did not ascribe to the woman but to the man the succession of human posterity, which succumbed to this death arising from sin.

For posterity is not named from the woman but from the man, just as the apostle himself says elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11): “For man is not from woman, but woman from man”; and again: “Just as woman is from man, so also man is not from woman, but through woman.” For this reason mortal posterity and bodily succession are attributed to the man rather than to the woman, as to their author.

Consider carefully how he says that sin entered this world through one man. It is certain that here he calls “world” this earthly place in which human beings dwell. Ask whether sin entered in no other place, and whether it is not found in those places where “spiritual wickedness” is said to be “in the heavenly places.”

But also consider within yourself where sin entered this world from, or where it was before it entered here. Or, if it existed at all, whether it existed before the one to whom it is said: “Until iniquities were found in you, and for this reason I cast you down to the earth” (Ezekiel 18).

It is not safe for us to discuss these matters at greater length, since we see the apostle barely touching upon each of them in his words: “Through one man sin entered this world.”

As we have said, “world” must be understood either as the place in which human beings dwell or as earthly and bodily life, in which death has its place. The saints say that they were crucified to this world—that is, to earthly life—and are dead to it.

“And through sin,” he says, “death.” This is undoubtedly the death of which the prophet also says: “The soul that sins shall itself die.”

But let us see how death passed to all human beings: “in whom,” he says, “all sinned.” The apostle pronounced the statement absolutely, that the death of sin passed to all human beings in the one in whom all sinned, just as elsewhere: “For all have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Romans 3).

Therefore, even if you call Abel righteous, he cannot be excused. Yet it is unnecessary, at great risk, to enumerate each of the saints individually in these matters, since the apostle’s statement is sufficient: it says that death passed to all human beings, as does the statement of the one who said: “No one is clean from defilement, even if his life is but one day.”

But when this death of sin, which had passed to all, came to Jesus and tried to pierce him with its sting—for “the sting of death is sin”—it was repelled [Col. 1378C] and broken. For he was life, and death necessarily had to be driven out by life. Then it is said to death: “Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15).

Because he had conquered everything, it is said to death: “Where is your victory?”

Moreover, Paul did not say that sin entered into all human beings, but that it entered into the world; he did not say that death entered the world, but that it passed to all human beings; and he did not say that death entered, but that it passed through. I do not think that Paul used these differences without reason.

I believe that by “world” he here signifies those who are earthly and remain in an earthly way of life, whereas by “human beings” he means those who have already begun to recognize themselves and to know that they were made in the image of God.

He therefore says that sin entered those who are called worldly—that is, earthly—and he assigns no exit from them. But concerning those whom he now wishes to be understood as human beings, he says that sin passed through them: that is, it was indeed present, but was driven away through the conversion of repentance, and passed through without remaining in them any longer.

Thus it is evident that not even a single syllable in Paul’s writings should be considered devoid of mysteries.

(Ambrose) Death is the dissolution of the body, when the soul is separated from the body. There is also another death, called the second death, in Gehenna. We do not suffer this because of Adam’s sin, but acquire it through our own sins on account of that sin. The good are free from it, although they were in the underworld, as it were in an upper, free [custody], since they could not ascend to heaven.

They were held by the sentence pronounced against Adam; this written bond in the decrees was erased by Christ’s death. The provisions of the decree were that the body of one human being should be dissolved upon the earth, while the soul, held by the bonds of the underworld, should suffer destruction.

For sin was in this world until the law; but sin was not counted when there was no law. (Augustine) When he says, “For sin was in the world until the law,” this must be understood as extending until grace came. He says this against those who suppose that sins could have been removed through the law.

The apostle says that sins were made manifest through the law, but not removed, when he says: “Sin was not counted when there was no law.” He did not say, “It did not exist,” but “It was not counted.” Nor, when the law was given, was sin removed; rather, it began to be reckoned—that is, to become apparent.

Therefore, we should not think that “until the law” means that sin no longer existed under the law. Rather, “until the law” includes the entire period of the law, extending to the end of the law, which is Christ.

(Ambrose) He says that all sinned in Adam, as I mentioned above, and that until the law was given sin was not counted. People thought that they could sin with impunity before God, though not before human beings. For the natural law had not become entirely dull, since they knew that what they did not wish to suffer themselves they ought not to do to others.

Indeed, sin was so far from being unknown among human beings that when Laban, Jacob’s father-in-law, searched for his idols, he judged whoever was found to have stolen them worthy of death (Genesis 31). Joseph, although falsely accused, was nevertheless imprisoned as though he were guilty; the baker and cupbearer of Pharaoh likewise suffered punishment for an offense; and Moses, after killing the Egyptian, was terrified by the law.

How, then, was sin not counted when there was no law? Or how was it punished unless the law was known? The natural law has always existed and was never entirely unknown. People thought, however, that it possessed authority only for a time and did not make them guilty before God. They were ignorant that God would judge the human race, and thus sin was not counted—as though sin were not known to God—thereby representing God as unconcerned.

But when the law was given through Moses, it was revealed that God cares for human affairs and that those who do evil will not escape unpunished merely because, for whatever reason, they avoid punishment in the present.

For those who, with justice or nature as their teacher, judged that sins committed among themselves should not go unpunished—how much more should they not have failed to understand that God, whom they knew to be the creator of the world, would require an account of these things?

Certainly, since Sodom and Gomorrah were condemned to perish by fire, Moses made manifest in writing what forgetfulness had concealed, in order to establish that God would be the judge.

But when people abandoned God and began to receive images in his honor, their minds were corrupted, and they trampled underfoot the first part of the natural law.

For the natural law has three parts. The first is that the Creator, once recognized, should be honored, and that his glory and majesty should not be attributed to any creature. The second is the moral part: that one should live well, with moderation as one’s guide. For it is fitting that a human being who knows the Creator should restrain his life by law, lest that recognition prove fruitless.

The third is the teachable part: that knowledge of God the Creator and the example of good conduct should be handed down to others, so that they may learn how merit is established before the Creator.

This is true and Christian prudence.

But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come.

(Aug.) Concerning the statement, “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression …” ([Note: See the exposition of certain propositions from St. Augustine’s Epistle to the Romans in our *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, cols. 2067–2068. EDITOR.] This is shorter here.)

“This is the type of the one to come”: Adam, whom he had begun to discuss above, but whose order he had postponed while introducing certain distinctions; he now returns to that order and concludes it, saying: “Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all people,” and so forth. [Col. 1380B]

(Ambr.) Since sin was not reckoned before the law was given through Moses, as I have said, death reigned by the very impunity of usurpation, knowing that those people were devoted to it. Death therefore reigned through the security of its domination, both over those who escaped punishment for a time and over those who even here suffered penalties for their evil deeds. For it saw that all belonged to it, because “whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). Thinking that they could sin with impunity, they sinned all the more, especially in those matters which the world fostered as though they were permitted.

By this Satan rejoiced, confident that, because of Adam’s cause, the human being abandoned by God was in his possession. Death therefore reigned over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come, as we shall demonstrate below. It is therefore clear that death did not reign over everyone, because not everyone sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, not everyone sinned after despising God.

But who are those who sinned after despising God, except those who, neglecting the Creator, served the creature, establishing gods for themselves to worship, to God’s dishonor? The devil therefore rejoiced over these people, because he saw that they had become his imitators. For Terah, Abraham’s father, and Nahor, and Laban claimed particular gods for themselves (Gen. XI; Gen. XXXV).

Adam’s sin, too, is not far removed from idolatry: he transgressed, thinking that he would become God while remaining human. He judged that what the devil had suggested would benefit him more than what God had commanded, placing the devil in God’s position; hence he was subjected to the devil.

Likewise, these people sin in a similar, though not identical, manner when, having transgressed against God, they serve the creature; for similarity ordinarily contains something dissimilar. Nor can it be said that those who received the command not to eat from the tree were like Adam, whereas those who sinned did not transgress against God but against the natural law.

Whoever understood—whether through inherited tradition or through natural discernment—and reverenced God, assigning to no one the honor due to His name and majesty, if he sinned (for it is impossible not to sin), sinned under God, not against God, whom he recognized as judge. Therefore death did not reign over such a person. But, as I have said, it reigned over those who served the devil under the appearance of idols.

Because the authority of the law had not yet been promulgated, they could not foresee God as judge. Most of the world was ignorant that God would be judge; only very few were those over whom death did not reign. But those over whom it did reign, after this death—which is called the first—were taken up by the second death for future punishment and destruction. Those over whom it did not reign, because they did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, were reserved in hope for the Savior’s coming and liberation.

Thus Scripture speaks of Abraham: although he was in the underworld, he was nevertheless separated by a great distance, so that there was an immense chasm between the righteous and sinners (Luke XVI). If there was an immense chasm between the righteous and sinners, how much more was there one between the ungodly, so that there might be refreshment for the righteous, heat for sinners, and burning for the ungodly, and so that, even before the judgment, what was fitting for each person might not remain hidden?

Accordingly, death reigned over them because it saw that the works of its subtlety had advanced them toward punishment, as enemies. For it did not escape him that the human being had been made in the world for this purpose: to proclaim the rule of the one God, which Satan had transgressed.

And if the Greek is not guarded in this way, it is nevertheless written as follows: death is said to have reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. The whole passage seems to be included here, so that, since death—that is, dissolution—was brought about through the devil’s envy, he says that death reigned even over those who did not sin; for they die, and this is what Satan desires.

If this were true, however, it would not have been appropriate to say, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” if it reigns over everyone from beginning to end. Or perhaps it advanced by stages, so that it reigned from Adam to Moses, from Moses to Christ, and from Christ to the end. But to what advantage would this wording serve, since the passage is not shown to have been expressed even in that manner?

For he said: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” because the law had not been revealed, so that, once the law had been given, people might live under its authority, knowing what they should avoid, lest death reign over them. Therefore, if someone before the law, guided by nature, observed what the law afterward commanded, can it be said that death reigned over him?

Consider what is written about him: “Sin,” he says, “was not reckoned when there was no law.” And he added: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses”—precisely during the time when there was no law. It is therefore fitting that, because death reigned before the law was given, it should be said to have reigned over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as we mentioned above.

Just as, after the law was given, death reigned over those who served fornication or idols while despising the Lawgiver, so before the law death did not reign over those who anticipated the meaning of the law and honored its author. It is said to have reigned for this reason: because knowledge of the one God had vanished from the earth.

Finally, this is how the law began: “I am,” it says, “the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me, and you shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness” (Exod. XX). [Col. 1382A]

The law was therefore given so that death might not reign, and so that, once former sins had been abolished, the human race might obey the one God. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it” (Rom. VI). By this statement he shows that death still reigns if the law is despised.

For what is the kingdom of death except that its will is done, while it commands to the destruction of the one who obeys it? The will of that dominion is the root of idolatry.

And yet this is imposed upon us from the Greek manuscripts, as though the Greeks themselves did not disagree among themselves. This is caused by a zeal for contempt [or: contention]. Since no one can use his own authority to secure victory, he corrupts the words of the law so that he may assert his own meaning as though it were the words of the law, making it appear that authority, rather than reason, is decisive.

This is established by certain Latin manuscripts translated from old Greek copies, which the simplicity of earlier times preserved and confirms as uncorrupted. But after minds departed from concord and heretics began to torment them with troubling questions, many things were altered according to human interpretation, so that the written text would contain what seemed right to human beings. Consequently, the Greeks themselves possess different manuscripts.
