I regard this as true when reason, history, and authority are all observed. For what is today criticized in the Latin manuscripts is found placed in the same way by the ancients—Tertullian, Victorinus, and Cyprian.

The kingdom of death first began to be destroyed in Judea, because “God is known in Judah” (Ps. LXXV). Now, throughout all nations, it is daily being destroyed, as, to a great extent, children of the devil become children of God.

Therefore death did not reign over everyone, but over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as I mentioned above. Adam is a type of the one to come because already then, in the mystery, God had decreed through one Christ to repair what had become sin through one Adam, as I said in the Apocalypse of the apostle John: “The Lamb,” he says, “who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. XVII).

(Aug.) The Apostle discusses at greater length two human beings: the one and first Adam, through whose sin and death we, his descendants, have been bound as though by hereditary evils; and the other, the second Adam, who is not merely human but also God. Since he paid on our behalf what he did not owe, we have been freed from both inherited debts and our own.

Accordingly, it is just that the devil should release, because of this one man, all whom he held because of that one man—those generated through his corrupted carnal desire—namely, all those regenerated through this man’s spotless grace.

If the Apostle had intended this to be understood as imitation, he would have said that sin entered the world through the devil rather than through one human being. For it is written concerning the devil: “Those who are from his side imitate him.” But he said “through one human being,” from whom the generation of humanity began, in order to teach through generation that original sin exists.

For this reason he says: “Just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Just as they derive from that one human being, so infants cannot be free from the same sin unless they are released from its guilt through Christ’s baptism.

Whether it is sin, or death, or both, that is said to have passed through all human beings seems ambiguous; but which of these it is, the matter itself demonstrates plainly. For if sin had not passed through, no human being would be born with the law of sin that is in the members. If death had not passed through, all human beings would not die, insofar as this concerns the condition of mortals.

When the Apostle says, “in whom all sinned,” in whom can this be understood except in Adam, in whom he says that they die? For it was not just that punishment should pass through without guilt.

“For until the law, sin was in the world”—not because he meant that afterward sin existed in no one, but because what could be removed only by the Spirit of grace could not be removed through the written law. Thus no one, trusting in his own powers—not, I say, in the power of his will, but rather in his vanity—might suppose that the law could suffice through free choice and mock Christ’s grace.

Therefore the Apostle says: “For until the law, sin was in the world.” But “sin was not reckoned when there was no law.” He did not say, “it did not exist,” but “it was not reckoned,” because there was no law by which it could be exposed through accusation—whether the law of reason in children or the written law among the people.

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses,” because even the law given through Moses could not remove the kingdom of death, which only Christ’s grace removed. But over whom did it reign? Consider: “Even over those,” he says, “who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”

Death therefore also reigned over those who did not sin; but he shows why it reigned when he says, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” This is the better understanding of these words: after saying, “death reigned,” and “even over those who did not sin,” as though we might ask why it reigned over those who did not sin, he added, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”—that is, because the likeness of Adam’s transgression was present in their members.

The passage can also be understood in this way: death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because they were held by original vice within themselves after they had been born, while they did not yet possess the use of reason that Adam possessed when he sinned and had not received the commandment that Adam transgressed. Through this original fault the kingdom of death dragged them toward condemnation. [Col. 1383D]

The kingdom of death is absent only from those who, reborn through Christ’s grace, belong to his kingdom. For temporal death, although it too was propagated from original sin, kills the body in them but does not drag the soul to punishment.

He wished the kingdom of death to be understood in such a way that the soul, renewed by grace, would no longer die in Gehenna—that is, would not be alienated from or separated from the life of God. Temporal death, however, is left for the time being even in those redeemed by Christ’s death, for the exercise of faith and the struggle of the present contest, in which the martyrs also fought.

But temporal death itself will be taken up in the renewal of the body, which the resurrection promises. There death will be completely swallowed up in victory. For now Christ’s grace deprives it of its kingdom, so that it cannot drag the souls of Christ’s people to the punishments of Tartarus.

As for what he added concerning Adam, “who is a type of the one to come,” this too is not understood in only one way. Either he is a type of Christ by contrast, so that just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ; and just as through Adam’s disobedience many were constituted sinners, so through Christ’s obedience many will be constituted righteous.

Or he called him a type of the one to come because Adam himself inflicted upon his descendants the form of death. Yet the better interpretation is that Adam is believed to be a type by contrast, a point the Apostle strongly emphasizes.

Finally, lest the same correspondences in this type be regarded as entirely equal and opposite, he adds and says: “But the gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through the trespass of one, much more have the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ, abounded for many.”

Thus it is understood that he does not mean that the same many are involved in both cases, since the unrighteous who will be condemned are more numerous; rather, grace has abounded more greatly because, while the form of death from Adam operates temporally in those redeemed through Christ, the form of life through Christ will operate eternally.

“Although,” he says, “Adam is a type of the one to come, Christ nevertheless provides more abundantly for those regenerated than Adam harmed those generated from him.”

(Orig.) Therefore the death of sin reigned from Adam to Moses—that is, until the coming of Christ. For Moses is called “the law,” and the law, as it is written, remained in force until John’s baptism, from which time Jesus began to proclaim the kingdom of God.

But if, as is found in some copies, death is said to have reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, if this death, which would hold souls in the underworld, is said to have reigned—we understand that even the saints fell under this death, not under the law of sinning, but certainly under the law of dying.

Christ therefore descended into the underworld not only so that he himself would not be held by death, but also so that he might draw out those who were held there—not so much because of the guilt of transgression, as we have said, but because of the condition of dying.

As it is written: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose with him, and they entered the holy city” (Matt. XXVII). In this the words of the prophets are also fulfilled, when he says of Christ: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII).

In this way, through his resurrection, he already destroyed the kingdoms of death. Hence it is also written that he freed the captives. But hear when the Apostle says that the enemy himself—the tyrant whose kingdoms he dissolved—is to be destroyed: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. XV).

The kingdom of death has already been destroyed, and the captivity that was held under it has been led away. But since the enemy and tyrant himself is still to be destroyed at the last and at the end of the age, we now see him not so much reigning as committing robbery, driven from his kingdom and wandering through desolate and remote places, seeking for himself the hand of unbelievers.

For this reason the Apostle cried out: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI).

But let us be content to have briefly touched upon those things which the Apostle wished to leave concealed, and let us inquire into what follows. After this he added: “who is a type of the one to come.”

This seems ambiguous to me: is Adam called a type of the one to come from the time when the Apostle wrote these words, with “the one to come” meaning the age to come? Or is he called a type from Adam himself—that is, from the future Adam—so that it is understood as referring to Christ? That time was not future for the Apostle when he wrote these words, but past.

Yet elsewhere, when speaking about Adam and Eve, the same Apostle said: “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V). This seems to have given us greater assistance in understanding that Adam is called a type of the one to come because Christ came to unite the Church to himself.

I do not know, however, how one can fit Adam’s transgression, his sin, and the fact that through him death passed into all human beings into the form of Christ—unless perhaps these correspond to opposites, as the same Apostle explains above when he says: “Just as through one human being there is death, so also through one there is the resurrection of the dead”; and again: “Just as through the disobedience of one human being many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous.”

But if we understand the Apostle to have said, from his own time, when he wrote these things, that Adam was a type of the one to come, then it is more readily understood that just as in this age death reigned through one Adam and the entire human race became mortal, so in the future age life will reign through Christ and the entire human race will be endowed with immortality.

But the gift is not like the trespass.

(Ambr.) Because he called the one Adam a type of the one Christ, lest the cause of Adam be thought to signify something of the same kind as Christ’s cause, he therefore said: “But the gift is not like the trespass.” Adam is a type of Christ only in this respect: what one person sinned, one person repaired.

For if many died through the trespass of one, much more have the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ, abounded for the many.

That is: if many died through the trespass of one, imitating his transgression, much more have the grace and gift of God abounded for the many who flee to it. More people obtain grace than died through Adam’s trespass.

It is therefore clear that he did not refer to the death common to all, since absolutely everyone dies, yet not everyone obtains grace. Nor is it death over everyone that is meant, but death over those who died through Adam’s trespass, whom he says sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

These are the people whom he says died through the trespass of one, whereas the grace of God abounded for the many, because the grace of God abounded both in those said to have died through Adam’s trespass, who sinned in like manner, and in those who did not sin in this likeness of Adam’s transgression.

Although, by God’s judgment, they were in the underworld because of the ancestral sin, the grace of God abounded in the Savior’s descent, granting forgiveness to all and raising them triumphantly into heaven.

And the gift is not like what came through one sin; for the judgment arose from one trespass and led to condemnation, but the gift arose from many trespasses and led to justification.

[Col. 1386A]

The distinction is evident. Those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression were condemned through Adam’s one sin; but the grace of God through Christ justified human beings not from one trespass but from many, granting them the remission of sins.

He says this to magnify the mercy of God and Christ: although many are held by Adam’s trespass under the second death in the lower underworld, the gift of God’s grace—although it would have been just to punish them—not only forgives them but justifies them.

(Aug.) Let the heretics say how condemnation can arise from one trespass, unless it is because even one original sin, which passed into all human beings, is sufficient for condemnation.

Grace, however, leads from many trespasses to justification because it not only removes that one sin transmitted originally, but also the other sins added in each person through the movement of his own will.

For if death reigned through one person because of one trespass, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

“If death reigned through one person because of one trespass”—the trespass from which infants are cleansed through baptism—much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

They will reign in life all the more because the kingdom will be eternal life, whereas death passes through them temporally and will not pass through eternally.

Receiving the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness, they will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

(Ambr.) It must be observed that the meaning is one and does not differ at all. He says that death reigned, not that it reigns, because those who understood the judgment of God through the law were removed from its dominion.

It reigned because, without the revelation of the law, the fear of God was not on earth. The superior interpretation therefore is that, since death reigned from Adam to Moses over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, much more shall grace reign through the abundance of God’s gift unto life through the one Jesus Christ.

If death reigned, why should grace not reign all the more, since it justifies far more people than those over whom death reigned? How much more, then, must grace be believed to reign, since it bestows life through Christ!

Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.

That is: just as through one person’s trespass all deserved condemnation by sinning in like manner, so also through the righteousness of one all will be justified who believe.

But if some think that this condemnation is universal, they will likewise accept justification as universal. This is not true, because not all believe.

(Aug.) Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one justification justification unto life came upon all human beings. Let them persist in the vanity of their minds and say that one human being did not transmit a lineage but merely offered an example of sin.

How, then, did condemnation come upon all human beings through one trespass, and not rather through their many personal trespasses? It is because, even though that one trespass was but one, it is sufficient to bring about condemnation without any other trespasses being added, just as it brings about the condemnation of dying infants who are born from Adam if they are not reborn in Christ.

But concerning what seems to you to be contradictory—namely, that all go into condemnation through Adam and all into justification through Christ—you are altogether mistaken. No human being is drawn into condemnation except through Adam, and from that condemnation human beings are freed through the washing of regeneration. Nor is any human being freed from this condemnation except through Christ.

Therefore “all” are said on both sides, because no one comes to the condemnation of generation except through the one, and no one comes to the life of regeneration except through the other.

Accordingly, the universality of one side does not exclude the place of the other, because from those same people who universally die in Adam, Christ gives life to whomever he wills. He too is said to free all because he alone frees those whom he frees; just as he is said to enlighten every human being because no one enlightens anyone unless he himself does so.

For just as through the disobedience of one human being many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous.

(Ambr.) Those whom above he called “all,” here he signifies as “more numerous” and “many.” More people followed Adam’s trespass by transgressing, though not everyone; and many will be constituted righteous through faith in Christ, though not everyone.

Therefore death did not reign over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

(Aug.) See how he commends “one and one”—that is, Adam and Christ—the former unto condemnation and the latter unto justification—even though Christ came in the flesh so long after Adam. Thus we know that even the righteous of ancient times, whoever they may have been, were freed only through the same faith by which we are freed: the faith in Christ’s incarnation, which was foretold to them just as it is proclaimed to us.

For this reason he here calls Christ a human being, although he is also God, so that no one might think that the righteous of ancient times could be freed through Christ merely as God—that is, through the Word who was in the beginning—and not also through faith in his incarnation, by which Christ is called human as well.

But the law entered alongside, so that the trespass might abound.

When he says, “the law entered alongside, so that the trespass might abound,” the very wording sufficiently indicates that the Jews did not know through what dispensation the law had been given.

For it was not given because it could give life, since grace gives life through faith. Rather, the law was given to show how great and how tightly binding were the bonds of sins by which those who presumed upon their own strength to fulfill righteousness were held captive.

Thus sin abounded: concupiscence became more ardent through prohibition, and the crime of transgression was added to those who sinned against the law. This is understood by anyone who considers the second stage within those four stages.

(Ambr.) One might argue in opposition: then the law should not have been given, lest sins increase. For if there was less sin before the law, the law was unnecessary.

The law was plainly necessary, so that it might show that sins believed to be committed with impunity were nevertheless reckoned before God, and so that people might henceforth know what they ought to avoid.

Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “The law was given for assistance.” Since the seeds of righteousness are, in a certain way, implanted in nature itself, the law was added so that, through its authority and instruction, the natural disposition might progress toward producing the fruit of righteousness.

For just as birth perishes unless it has nourishment by which it may be nourished and grow, so the natural disposition toward righteousness, unless it has something to which it may look and which it may reverence, does not easily progress but grows weak; and when sins come upon it, it yields.

The habit of sinning weighs it down, preventing it from growing into fruit, and through this it is extinguished. The law was therefore given providentially, as the prophet testifies. But the people, following their old custom, multiplied their sins.

Through the very practice of sinning they began to sin more than they had sinned before. Thus it came about that, when the law was given, sins were not diminished but increased. For the Apostle shows what resulted from the giving of the law, not what the law itself accomplished.

But how did sins increase through any defect in the law, when the law threatened punishment so that people would not sin? Yet it is said to have entered alongside so that sin might abound.

This is true because it entered as though it would be beneficial, and with humility. But afterward it began to dominate those whom it had commanded not to sin, and they sinned.

The law began to reveal the abundance of sins when the things it had forbidden were committed more frequently than before. Thus the law was given so that the trespass might abound.

For, commending faith through which sins are certainly erased, the Apostle said that the law caused sins to abound, as I said above: it was not given so that sins might be abolished, but so that they might abound, since it showed sinners both before the law and afterward held everyone guilty.

But where the trespass abounded, grace abounded all the more.

It is clear that when sin abounded, grace abounded all the more: the gift of God came through the promise and covered the sins of all, so that the devil’s envy might lament that it had achieved nothing.

When the law had been given for the benefit of humanity, the devil contrived, by persuading people to do what was forbidden, to turn it upside down, so that what had been given for their benefit might work toward the contrary. The commandments were despised, and instead of benefit arising from the law, God’s judgment proceeded toward punishment.

Then the just and merciful God, wishing to empty the devil’s glory—the glory he had sought from his triumph over the human being—decreed that his Son would come and forgive all sins, so that joy arising from the gift of grace might become greater than the grief caused by sin.

The joy of God’s gift also benefits those over whom Satan could not triumph. For this reason grace abounded over the sin that Satan had instigated.

[Col. 1388D]

So that, just as sin reigned in death, grace might also reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Sin reigned because it saw its work advancing those who sinned toward death, in which it gloried. In the same way grace also reigns through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that just as sin began and reigned through Adam, grace might likewise reign through Christ.

Grace reigns through righteousness if, having received the remission of sins, we pursue righteousness. Then, when grace sees that it has borne fruit in the good whom it has redeemed, it reigns unto eternal life, knowing that we will become eternal.

Grace therefore abounded because sin reigned for a time, whereas grace reigns forever. The kingdom is God’s when grace reigns, just as it was the devil’s kingdom when sin reigned.

Yet he refers everything to Christ, so that all God’s grace may be learned from Christ.

(Aug.) But what he says—“the law entered alongside, so that the trespass might abound”—no longer pertains to the trespass transmitted from Adam, concerning which he earlier said, “death reigned through one.”

Whether we understand the law as the natural law, which appears in those stages of life when people can already use reason, or as the written law given through Moses, it could not itself give life or free anyone from the law of sin and death transmitted from Adam. Rather, it added increases of transgression: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

After the law given in paradise had been transgressed, the human being is born from Adam with the law of sin and death, concerning which it is said: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind,” and so forth (Rom. VII). Yet unless this law is later strengthened by an evil habit, it is more easily overcome, though not without the grace of God.

After the other law—the law operating in the rational soul’s use of reason—has been transgressed, all sinners of the earth become transgressors once they reach the age at which they use reason.

But after even that law which was given through Moses has been transgressed, the trespass abounds much more. The law therefore entered alongside so that the trespass might abound, whether people neglect what it says and commands, or, presuming upon their own strength, fail to ask for the assistance of grace and add pride to weakness.

But when, through divine calling, they understand to whom they ought to cry out, and invoke the one in whom they rightly believe, saying, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. L); and, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL)—when a person has stretched himself toward him and has lamented in this way, what follows will take place:

“Where the trespass abounded, grace abounded all the more.” Many sins are forgiven him because he loved greatly (Luke VII), and the love of God is poured into his heart. Thus the fullness of the law comes about—not through the powers of free choice that are in us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

Accordingly, just as sin reigned in death, so grace also reigns through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Now, when he had said, “so that, just as sin reigned in death,” he did not say “through one human being,” or “through the first human being,” or “through Adam,” because he had already said, “the law entered alongside so that the trespass might abound.”

This abundance does not pertain to the propagation of the first human being, but to the transgression of human conduct, which was added to that one trespass—by which alone infants are held bound—when people reached more mature ages and the abundance of iniquity increased.

But because grace through the Savior is also powerful to remove all this, including what does not pertain to the origin of that one trespass, after saying, “so that grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” he added, “through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Therefore let no arguments hinder infants from the salvation that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. We ought to speak on their behalf all the more because they cannot speak on their own behalf.

## CHAPTER VI

The Apostle declares that one must not remain in sins and that one must act virtuously.

[Col. 1390A]

What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? By no means. (Augustine.) Regarding his statement, “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? By no means. We who died to sin—how shall we live in it?” he shows here that it was because of past sins that they were forgiven, and that grace abounded in this respect, namely, that past sins might be remitted. Therefore, whoever still seeks an increase of sin in order to experience an increase of grace does not understand that he is acting so that grace may accomplish nothing in him. For it is the work of grace that we die to sin.

(Ambrose.) Does this mean that one must always sin, so that God’s gift may abound, covering our sins, and that, continually hoping for the remission of sins because God is merciful, we should place the grace of Christ first? Certainly not. For God had mercy on us through Christ so that, by no longer sinning, we might cause both our merit and God’s grace to reign in us. He removes the reign of God’s grace and hands himself over to sin who returns again to the old man, that is, to the manner of his former life. For we received mercy for two reasons: so that the devil’s kingdom might be excluded, and so that God’s authority might be proclaimed to those who were ignorant, while through this very thing dignity was acquired for us.

“We who died to sin—how shall we still live in it?” He says this because, while living in sin, we were dead before God; for whoever sins lives to sin, just as whoever does not sin lives to God. When God’s grace came upon us through Christ, and through faith regenerated us by the spiritual washing, we began to live to God and to be dead to sin, which is the devil. To die to sin, however, means to be liberated from sin and to become God’s servant. Therefore, now that we have died to sin, let us not return to our former evils, lest we live again to sin and, dying to God and having lost our dignity, incur the punishment from which we escaped.

(Augustine.) After he had spoken of the punishment that came through one man and of the grace that came through one man, he then commended the great mystery of holy baptism in the cross of Christ, in such a way that we understand Christ’s baptism to be nothing other than a likeness of Christ’s death. And the death of Christ crucified is nothing other than a likeness of the remission of sins: just as true death took place in him, so true remission of sins might take place in us; and just as true resurrection took place in him, so true justification might take place in us.

He therefore says: “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound?” For above he had said, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more”; and so he proposed this question to himself: whether, in order to obtain an abundance of grace, one ought to remain in sin. But he answered, “By no means,” and added: “If we died to sin, how shall we live in it?” Nothing could have been said more briefly or more effectively. For what more useful thing does God’s grace bestow upon us in this present evil age than that we should die to sin? And therefore the person who wishes to live in sin because of that grace through which we die to sin will be found ungrateful toward grace itself.

[Col. 1391A]

Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? (Ambrose.) He says this so that we may know that, once baptized, we ought no longer to sin, because when we are baptized we die with Christ. This is what it means to be baptized into his death: there all our sins die, so that, renewed and having laid aside death, we may appear to rise again, reborn to life. Thus, just as Christ died to sin and rose again, so we too may have the hope of resurrection through baptism.

Baptism, therefore, is the death of sin, so that another birth may follow—a birth that, while the bodily structure remains, renews the human being in mind, with the oldness of all evil actions buried. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the power of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

In saying this, he also signifies the first point: that Christ raised his body from the dead. For he himself is the power of God the Father, as he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He was speaking of the temple of his body (John 2). He rose into a new life that can no longer die. It is called “new” because it was given by Christ, namely, Christian discipline.

We, however, who were baptized were buried with Christ so that henceforth we might follow this life in which Christ rose. Baptism is therefore the pledge and image of resurrection, so that, remaining now in Christ’s commandments, we may not turn back again to our former ways. For whoever dies no longer sins; death is the end of sin.

For this reason baptism is celebrated with water: just as water washes away the uncleanness of the body, so we should believe that through baptism we are spiritually cleansed and renewed from every sin, so that what is incorporeal may be washed away invisibly. If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection.

He says that we can rise again happily if we have been planted in the likeness of his death—that is, if in baptism we lay aside all vices, are transferred into a new life, and henceforth do not sin. Through this we shall also be like his resurrection; for the likeness of death will produce a corresponding resurrection. The apostle John recalls this in his letter, saying: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3), that is, we shall rise immortal and glorious.

Nor will this likeness mean that there is no difference at all, because we shall be like him in the glory of the body, not in the nature of divinity. “Do you not know,” he says, “that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?”

(Augustine.) If, then, we are shown to have died to sin because we were baptized into his death, surely even infants who are baptized into Christ die to sin, because they are baptized into his death. For the statement was made without exception: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.” And it was said in order to prove that we have died to sin. But to what sin do infants die by being reborn, except that which they contracted by being born?

Accordingly, what follows also applies to them, where he says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life,” and so forth, until he says: “For the one who has died has died to sin once for all; but the one who lives lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

He had begun to prove from this that we ought not to remain in sin so that grace might abound, as he had said: “If we died to sin, how shall we live in it?” And, to show that we had died to sin, he had added: “Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” Thus he closed the whole passage in the manner in which he had begun it. For Christ indicated death in such a way that he even said that he himself had died to sin—but to what sin, except to the flesh? In him there was no sin, but there was the likeness of sin, and for that reason the flesh was called by the name “sin.”

Having therefore been baptized into the death of Christ, into which not only adults but also infants are baptized, he says: “So you also”—that is, just as Christ—“must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

Whatever was accomplished in Christ’s cross, burial, resurrection on the third day, ascension into heaven, and sitting at the right hand of the Father was accomplished in such a way that Christian life, as it is lived here, was conformed to these realities not only through mystical statements but also through enacted events.

Because of his cross it was said: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5). Because of his burial: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death.” Because of his resurrection: “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.” Because of his ascension into heaven and his seat at the Father’s right hand: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

[Col. 1392C]

Knowing this: that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer be slaves to sin.

Regarding his statement, “Knowing this: that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished,” it refers to what was said through Moses: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” The crucifixion of the old man was signified in the cross of the Lord, just as the restoration of the new man was signified in the resurrection.

It is clear that we act according to the old man, who is accursed, because of sin. No one doubts that this was said of the Lord: that he bore our sins, became sin for us, and condemned sin concerning sin. He himself explained what it means to abolish the body of sin: namely, that we should no longer serve sin. The statement, “If we died with Christ,” means, “If we were crucified with Christ.” For he says elsewhere (Galatians 5): “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

Moses therefore did not curse the Lord; rather, he prophesied what his crucifixion would reveal.

(Ambrose.) He interweaves and repeats many things in order to teach the baptized that they ought no longer to sin, especially that they must not return to idolatry, for this is the gravest crime and the source of all error: they must not lose the grace received from God through Christ.

He calls the old man past actions, because just as the new man is named from faith and a pure life, so the old man is named from unbelief and evil actions. He says that these actions have been crucified—that is, put to death—so that the body of sin might be destroyed, meaning all crimes. He calls all sins together a body, which he says is destroyed through a good life and catholic faith.

(Augustine.) The crucifixion of the inner man is understood as the pains of repentance and a certain health-giving suffering of self-restraint, by which the death of ungodliness is put to death. In this death God does not abandon us. Therefore, through such a cross, the body of sin is abolished, so that we no longer present our members as weapons of iniquity and sin.

This applies also to the inner man. Since he is renewed day by day, he was certainly old before he was renewed. For what takes place within is what the same apostle says (Colossians 3): “Put off the old man,” which he explains consecutively in this way: “Therefore, having put away falsehood, speak the truth.”

But where is falsehood put away except within, so that one may dwell on God’s holy mountain (Psalm 14), the one who speaks truth in his heart?

(Origen.) Yet it must be examined more carefully how he used the expression “body of sin.” There seem to be two possible interpretations: either he called our body the body of sin, or he said that sin itself has a particular body of its own, which must be destroyed by those who ought no longer to serve sin.

Since either meaning can be admitted in this passage, we shall explain what seems to us to be the case with respect to both. For if we suppose that sin has a body of its own, it will appear that, just as it was said of those who have been restored into the new man, “You are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Corinthians 12), so it can be said of those who have not yet crucified the old man that they are the body and members of sin, whose head is the devil, just as Christ is the head of the Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5).

The members of which this body of sin consists may be understood as those which the apostle listed above as “members on earth”: fornication, uncleanness, lust, avarice, contention, anger, deceit, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envy, revelries (1 Corinthians 6), and the like. This body of sin can rightly be said to consist of all these members, and this body can be called the old man.

If someone destroys it through the cross of Christ and is changed into the new man, who was created according to God, he will no longer be said to serve sin. Without doubt, however, he serves sin as long as he is subject to any of those members which we have explained above to be members of sin.

But if the apostle is understood to have called our own body the body of sin, it will certainly be taken according to that interpretation by which David also says of himself: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). The apostle himself likewise says elsewhere: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7). And again, he calls our body “the body of our humiliation.”

In another place he says of the Savior that he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to condemn sin in the flesh.” Here he shows that our flesh is indeed flesh of sin, whereas Christ’s flesh is like the flesh of sin. For he was not conceived from the seed of a man; rather, the Holy Spirit came upon Mary, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that what was born from her would be called the Son of the Most High.

Thus Paul, through the ineffable wisdom of God that was given to him, gazing upon some hidden and mysterious secret, calls our body the body of sin, the body of death, and the body of humiliation.

If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.

(Ambrose.) It is clear that those who have crucified the flesh—that is, the world together with its vices and desires—die to the world and die with Christ. They are also conformed to eternal and saving life, so that they may deserve to become like Christ in glory.

The flesh, that is, the body, is crucified when its desires are trampled down. These desires arise, while sin remains in the flesh, from the transgression begun by the first man. For the devil is crucified in the flesh; he is the one who deceives through the flesh.

“Flesh” may sometimes mean the world, that is, the elements; sometimes the human body; or even the soul insofar as it follows bodily vices.

Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and that death shall no longer rule over him: for the death by which he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life by which he lives, he lives to God.

(Gregory.) We had withdrawn from God in mind, returned to dust in the flesh, and were bound by the punishment of a double death. But he came to us, intending to die for us in the flesh alone, to join his single death to our double death, and to free us from both deaths. Concerning this Paul says: “The one who has died to sin has died once for all,” and so forth.

(Ambrose.) He shows the security of eternity in the Savior’s resurrection. We attain to it if we strive after a better life. For whoever lives to God by doing good truly lives, because he possesses eternal life.

“Knowing,” he says, “that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him.”

(Origen.) Did you dare to say this about Christ, O Paul—“Death shall no longer rule over him”—as though it had ever ruled him? His voice is proclaimed throughout the whole body of the Church, brighter than light, saying: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10).

Do you therefore say that death ruled him, who laid down his life not only willingly but also with authority; who alone among the dead was free; and whom death alone could not hold?

These and similar considerations, I think, will trouble those who are tenderly devoted to Jesus and cannot bear to hear anything lowly or unworthy about him. Someone may therefore give a more concise account of the matter by saying that here he calls death the common and intermediate death by which he died, as the same apostle says, “according to the Scriptures.” Nothing absurd will then appear in the fact that the one who had assumed the form of a servant endured the dominion of death, which certainly rules over all who are in the flesh and are reckoned to be under a servant’s condition.

Another person, however, who perceives a deeper meaning in Paul’s words through the power of the Spirit, will say that the death of which it is said that it shall no longer rule over Christ is to be understood as that final enemy who was prefigured by the great sea creature that had swallowed Jonah (Jonah 2). Concerning it, it is written in Job: “Let those curse it who curse the day” (Job 3)—the one who is destined to destroy the great sea creature.

Christ entered into this death as Jonah entered the belly of the sea creature, namely, into the place which the Savior himself called “the heart of the earth.” He said that the Son of Man would remain there for three days and three nights, following the example of Jonah, in order to release those who were held there by death.

To make this still clearer, we shall use another comparison. Let us suppose that a noble and just king wages war against an unjust tyrant who intends to fight in such a way that he will not appear to have conquered by a violent and bloody conflict, because the soldiers serving under the tyrant belonged to him and he wished not to destroy them but to free them.

Accordingly, by a better plan, he assumes the appearance of those who were with the tyrant and becomes in every respect like them until, placed under the tyrant’s domination, he persuades those who obeyed him to withdraw and return to the legitimate kingdom. At the proper time he binds the tyrant himself, strips him of his powers and authority, and carries away the captives whom he held.

In this manner Christ also, by his own will, emptied himself and took the form of a servant. He endured the tyrant’s domination and became obedient unto death (Philippians 2). Through that death he destroyed the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, in order to free those who were held by death.

After binding the strong one and triumphing over him on his cross, he also went into his house, the house of death, into hell, and from there seized his vessels—that is, he carried away the souls whom he held. From there, “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Psalm 67), namely, those who rose with him and entered the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem.

Accordingly, the apostle rightly says in the present passage that “death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans 6:9). For he will no longer give himself over to the tyrant’s domination, nor will he again empty himself, take the form of a servant, and become obedient unto death, lest once more, in the form of a servant—although placed there willingly and not by necessity—he endure the domination of the tyrant and of death.

We have said these things as best we could concerning the questions raised in this passage, so that it might become clearer how Christ died to sin once for all and no longer dies, and how the life by which he lives is life to God.

To live to God must be understood in this way: after completing what he had emptied himself of when he was in the form of God, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death, he remains again in the form of God and equal to the Father. Therefore, he appropriately says in what follows:

[Col. 1396A]

So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

This means that, by imitating Christ, we should die to sin, become alienated from it, live to God by joining ourselves to him, and become one spirit with him.

He did not say without reason, “Consider yourselves dead to sin.” In Greek this is expressed more aptly as, “Think of yourselves as dead to sin.” The matter under discussion exists more in thought and reasoning, because this kind of death must be held in thought rather than accomplished outwardly.

For whoever thinks and considers himself within as dead does not sin. For example, if desire for a woman draws me, or greed for silver, gold, or property presses upon me, and I place in my heart the conviction that I have died with Christ and think about death, desire is immediately extinguished and sin is driven away.

Or if, inflamed by hatred or anger, I rush toward the death of my enemy, and I consider myself dead with Christ and place thoughts of death in my mind, fury is undoubtedly extinguished, anger ceases, hatred grows calm, and sin is given no opportunity. In this way a person is found to die to sin and to live to God.

Nor does the addition, “alive to God in Christ Jesus,” seem superfluous to me. I think it is similar to saying, “alive to God in wisdom, in peace, in righteousness, in sanctification”—all of which Christ is. To live to God in these things, therefore, is to live to God in Christ Jesus.

And if no one lives to God without righteousness, peace, sanctification, and the other virtues, it is certain that no one lives to God except in Christ Jesus.

(Ambrose.) He speaks in such a way as to teach that it is impossible to die to sin and live to God except with all hope placed in Christ. He calls him “our Lord,” so that it may be understood that the law contributes nothing to attaining salvation in the age to come, when one can live to God only through Christ.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1395]

## CHAPTER VI FOLLOWS

[Col. 1395D]

Therefore, sin must not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires.

(Gregory.) He does not say, “Let it not exist,” but “Let it not reign,” because it cannot fail to exist, but it cannot reign in the hearts of the good. Therefore, whenever any fault assails an unjust heart, it finds it not resisting, but subjects it to its own domination.

(Ambrose.) The body is mortal because of the cause of Adam’s transgression, but through faith in Christ it is believed to become immortal. In order to reach this promise, he says that we must not obey sin, lest it reign in our mortal body. It reigns when it commands.

But if it does not reign, this body will not appear to be mortal, because it is held in the hope of eternity. He did not call the body mortal because of its dissolution, but because of the punishment of Gehenna: the person who is to be sent into Gehenna is called mortal, because those who obey sin do not escape the second death of hell, from which the Savior liberated those who believe in him.

By calling the body mortal, therefore, he signified the whole human being, because those who obey sin are called mortal. For he says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18), that is, the whole person. No one will be judged without the body.

(Origen.) Observe, nevertheless, that by showing that it lies within our power for sin not to reign in our mortal body, the apostle gives this command: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires.” If it were not within our power for sin not to reign in us, he would certainly not have given this command.

How, then, is it possible for sin not to reign in our flesh? If we do what the same apostle says: “Put to death your members that are on earth” (Colossians 3), and if we “always carry the death of Christ in our body.” For it is certain that where the death of Christ is carried, sin cannot reign.

Such is the power of Christ’s cross that, if it is placed before the eyes and faithfully retained in the mind, so that the mind’s eye gazes intently upon Christ’s very death, no desire, lust, anger, or envy can prevail. At its presence the entire army of sin and of the flesh that we enumerated above is immediately driven away. Sin itself does not persist, since its substance exists nowhere except in actions and deeds.

But I ask why he added, “in your mortal body,” when it would have been sufficient to say, “Therefore, let sin not reign in your body.” Why is “mortal” added, as though anyone could doubt that the body is mortal?

It seems to me, however, that he added this not without reason. Through it he indicated how sin can fail to reign in the body, in accordance with what he had said elsewhere: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

If, then, we know that our body can be mortified and be dead to sin, it can happen that sin does not reign in it. For according to this understanding the one who has died is said to be justified from sin. A dead person neither desires, nor grows angry, nor rages, nor seizes what belongs to another.

If, therefore, we restrain the body’s desire from all these things, the body is said to be dead to sin. This is what the apostle appears to be urging in the present passage by adding these words: “in your mortal body.”

Nor should you present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity.

(Ambrose.) He shows that the devil fights us with our own weapons. Opportunity is given to him through our sins, so that, when God abandons us, he may receive power to mock and destroy us. Therefore, we must restrain our members from every work of iniquity, so that our enemy, found unarmed, may be subjected.

He did not say, “Present your bodies,” but “your members,” because it is through the members, as servants, that one goes astray, not through the whole body. For above he did not say, “Let it not exist,” but “Let it not reign.” As long as sin necessarily exists in your members, at least remove its kingdom; do not do what it commands.

Anger rises: do not give your tongue to anger for cursing; do not give your hand or foot for striking. This irrational anger would not rise unless sin were in the members, but take away its kingdom. Let it have no weapons with which to fight against you. It also learns not to rise when it ceases to find weapons.

“Do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin”; otherwise you will be entirely taken captive, and there will be no possibility of saying, “With my mind I serve the law of God,” when you are servants of sin. You were free with respect to righteousness.

But present yourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead.

(Ambrose.) By “death” he signifies ignorance and unbelief together with an evil life, because life consists in knowing God through Christ. Since no one comes into life without a parent, and since all things originated from God for life through Christ, the person who does not acknowledge God through Christ as the parent of all is not said to possess life. Such a person is regarded as though he did not exist: he denies his own existence by thinking that he exists without God as his parent.

Therefore, ignorance and a shameful life are death. These vices acquire death for him—not the death common to all, but the death of Gehenna, as I mentioned above. Knowledge of God the Father and holy conduct, on the other hand, are life—not this life subject to decay, but that of the age to come, which is called eternal.

For this reason he says: “Present yourselves to God,” to whom, by coming to know him, you have advanced toward salvation, so that, renouncing a dishonorable life, you may be alive from the dead.

And present your members to God as weapons of righteousness.

He wishes us to govern our conduct with such great modesty that our actions, advancing in the righteousness of God rather than in the righteousness of the world—for the righteousness of the world is without the faith of Christ, and without that faith there is not life but death—may provide weapons for him to defend us. When we provide weapons for him through good works, we make ourselves worthy to be assisted by that righteousness, because the righteousness of God despises the unworthy.

For wherever the righteousness of God is, there the Holy Spirit dwells, to assist our weakness. Just as we provide weapons for sin when we act wickedly, so we provide weapons for righteousness when we conduct ourselves rightly, guarding our members from every disgrace.

(Origen.) Observe, in each detail, Paul’s wisdom and the necessary distinctions he employs. Where he says that weapons must not be presented to sin or iniquity, he speaks not of ourselves but of our members. But where he urges us to present ourselves to God, he does not say “our members,” because he wishes us to present ourselves to God—that is, our soul or our purpose.

When we have presented ourselves as godly to God and have joined ourselves to him, only then do we make our members also weapons of righteousness for God. And if we mortify the desire of sin in our mortal body, labor in the work of righteousness, and make all our members serve righteousness, we become as those who are alive from the dead: dead to sin and alive to righteousness. Consequently, our members also become weapons of righteousness for God.

He rightly preserves the metaphor introduced above: because he had said that sin reigns, he calls the members weapons of sin; and again, our members become weapons of righteousness for God the king.

Sin, however, shall no longer rule over you, for you are not under the law but under grace.

(Augustine.) His statement, “Sin shall not rule over you, for you are not under the law but under grace,” certainly belongs to that third stage in which a person already serves the law of God with the mind, although with the flesh he serves the law of sin.

He does not obey sin’s desire, although desires urge him toward it and provoke him to consent, until the body itself is given life and death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15). Since we do not consent to evil desires, we are in grace, and sin does not reign in our mortal body. Indeed, from the passage where he says, “We who died to sin—how shall we live in it?” he describes the person who has been placed under grace.

But the person over whom sin rules, although he resists sin, is still under the law, not under grace.

(Ambrose.) If we walk according to the commandments he gives, he says that sin cannot rule over us; for sin rules over those who sin. Those who do not walk as he commands are under the law. But if we do not sin, we are not under the law but under grace.

If we sin, however, we are brought under the law, and sin begins to rule over us, because whoever commits sin is a slave of sin. He must be under the law as long as he does not receive remission; for the authority of the law makes the sinner guilty of sin.

Accordingly, the person who has received remission and guards himself so that he will not sin thereafter is neither ruled by sin nor under the law. The authority of the law ceases in the case of one who has been freed from sin. For those whom the law holds guilty have been handed over to it by sin. Therefore, the one who has been stripped of sins cannot be under the law.

(Origen.) Here too observe the apostle’s remarkable caution in his wording. When he speaks about us, he says: “Sin shall not rule over you.” When he speaks about the Savior, he does not say, “Sin shall not rule over him”—for this was not an appropriate statement concerning him—but says: “Death shall no longer rule over him.” There was a place for death in him; there was no place for sin.

Conversely, it was not suitable to say of us, “Death shall not rule over you,” because we cannot avoid this. Instead he says, “Sin shall not rule over you,” which he certainly knew we could avoid, according to what we have said above, if we mortify the desires of the flesh, in which sin could exercise dominion.

For this reason he adds, “For you are not under the law but under grace,” and clearly shows by these words that we are not under that law which, placed in our members, he says conflicts with the law of the mind. For whoever mortifies his members is certainly not under the law of the members but under the grace of God.

Concerning this law he says elsewhere: “The power of sin is the law.” But if someone wishes to understand these words as referring to the law of Moses, he will certainly say that we are not under the law of the letter, which kills, but under the law of the Spirit, which gives life, and which he has here called grace.

(Theon.) Therefore, if we wish the deceptive imagination of dreams, the seducer of impure discharge, to be unknown either forever or at least—as I may say according to the humbler or common condition—for certain months, then, after that faith by which we ought continually to hope specifically for the gift of purity from God’s grace, we must restrain excess in food and drink.

For an overabundance of these necessarily produces such bodily humors in greater measure. Since, when congealed, they cannot fail to be discharged and expelled by the law of nature itself, they emerge under the pretext of any kind of irritation or nocturnal illusion.

When the satiety of food has been reduced, it follows that those impure discharges are also generated more slowly. Thus, just as their flow becomes less, so the illusion disturbs sleepers either more rarely or more subtly, because not only does discharge arise from imagination, but imagination also descends from an excess of discharge.

Therefore, if we wish to be freed from the allurements of these illusions, we must strive with all our strength. First, after conquering the passion of fornication, in accordance with the blessed apostle, sin must not reign in our mortal body so that we obey its desires.

Second, once the body’s alluring movement itself has been completely calmed and put to sleep, we must in no way present our members as weapons of iniquity to sin.

Third, after our inner man too has been utterly and thoroughly mortified to that titillation of lust, we must present ourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead. Thus, through this perfection [progress], reaching the perpetual rest of our body, we must also present our members as weapons—not now to lust, but to God’s righteousness.

When we have been established in this purity of chastity, sin will no longer rule over us. For we are not under the law, which, while commending the lawful rights of marriage, also nourishes and preserves within our marrow the burning passion through whose agency the work of unlawful fornication is accomplished. Rather, we are under grace, which, while introducing the incorruptibility of virginity, also destroys this innocent and simple movement of the body, as well as the pleasure of lawful intercourse itself.

What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means. (Ambrose.) Since the law is from God, and therefore lest anyone should object, he himself raised the question: “If the law is from God,” he says, “why should we not be under the law?” He clears this up and teaches that, in accordance with the will of God, who is the author of the law, we have been liberated by Christ from under the law. For although the law was rightly given—for it was given both to show before God those who had sinned before the law and to inspire fear, so that thereafter sin might not be committed—yet because the human race, through the weakness of its frailty, could not restrain itself from sins, it became liable to the death of hell. God, moved by the compassion of his mercy, by which he always comes to the aid of the human race, provided through Christ a means by which a remedy might now be given to those in despair: once they had received the forgiveness of sins, they would be rescued from the law that held them liable, relieved and restored, and, with God’s help through faith, would resist the vices by which they had previously been overcome. Therefore, we did not sin as though despising God’s law; rather, through Christ we followed his providence. “What then?” he says. “Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? By no means.” (Origen.) This seems similar to the statement that we explained above: “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means.” And therefore one and the same explanation is sufficient for both passages. The only apparent difference is that above the question is, “What then? Shall we remain in sin?”—as though it were being said to those who had not yet departed from sin that they must not remain in the condition in which they still seemed to be. Here, however, the question seems to be put as though to those who have already departed from sin. There the purpose was that grace, which did not yet exist, might abound; here, as though grace were already present, he says that we are not under the law but under grace.

Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness? (Ambrose.) Now, lest we profess one thing but do another, and, while we are called servants of God, be found by our deeds to be servants of the devil, he warns and declares beforehand that we are servants of the one whose will we fulfill by our works. It is no small evil to confess God as Lord while serving the devil by our actions. For God long ago points this out and condemns it, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15; Isaiah 29). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6). And it is said in the law: “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6).

(Origen.) This, then, is what the Apostle teaches in this passage: each person has it in his own hand and within his power of choice whether to be a servant of sin or of righteousness. For whichever side he inclines his obedience toward, and whichever side he wishes to obey, that side claims him as its servant. In this, as I have said, he plainly shows that freedom of choice exists within us, without any hesitation. It is within us to offer our obedience either to righteousness or to sin [or to righteousness or to sin]. But no one can serve two masters at the same time, sin and righteousness. Either he will hate the one—namely, sin—and love the other, that is, righteousness; or he will tolerate the one, sin alone, and condemn the other, that is, righteousness.

The same idea is expressed in what the Apostle said: “You are slaves of the one to whom you have rendered obedience, whether of sin or of righteousness”; and also: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). This latter statement is relevant, although he did not add, “Everyone who practices righteousness is a slave of righteousness.” Another person might perhaps think that this was omitted so that it should be understood as following by implication. Yet it seems to me that it was deliberately not added. For it would not have been fitting to say, “Everyone who practices righteousness is a slave of righteousness.” God himself practices righteousness, but for that reason he cannot be called a servant of righteousness; rather, he is Lord of righteousness. Therefore, it is not the case that everyone who practices righteousness is a servant of righteousness in the same way that everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin. The devil himself, without doubt, is a servant of sin, since he departed from the service of righteousness and rebelled in the sight of the almighty Lord; for this reason he has also been called an apostate.

It is therefore established from these words of Paul—“To whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one to whom you have rendered obedience, whether of sin or of righteousness”—that of our own will we present ourselves either to serve sin or, through our obedience, to serve righteousness, with no one compelling us. For this reason we must always remember these things, lest we bring forward empty complaints in excuse for sin, saying that the devil caused us to sin, or that the necessity of nature, or a fatal condition, or the course of the stars did so. But hear Paul’s clear judgment: “To whom you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one to whom you have rendered obedience, whether of sin or of righteousness.”

But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over. By believing in Christ, we have become servants of righteousness. (Ambrose.) We are called servants of the one whom we obey. And because it is right to obey Christ—for he himself is righteousness, and what he commands is righteous—he therefore says that we have become servants of righteousness from the heart, not from the law; from the will, not from fear, so that our profession may proceed from the judgment of the soul. By nature we have been led to faith, not by the law. In this pattern of teaching we have been formed by the command of God, who fashioned nature. For by nature we possess the ability to recognize from whom, through whom, and in whom we were created.

The pattern of teaching, therefore, is that into which the Creator has handed us over naturally. This is what he said above: “They are a law to themselves.” When they see that what they believe belongs to their nature, the Gentiles trust from the heart what the law and the prophets proclaimed to the Jews concerning Christ. For this reason he gives thanks to the Lord: although we were slaves of sin, we obeyed from the heart, believing in Christ, so that we might serve God—not through the law of Moses, but through the law of nature.

(Origen.) When he says, “Thanks be to God, because you were slaves of sin,” he shows that all human beings initially serve sin. For it is written: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.” It is first necessary that what is written be fulfilled in every person: “When the commandment came, sin revived.” But what follows he says of the few, namely, of those who are already being reformed: “Thanks be to God, because you were slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over.”

We were all therefore slaves of sin. But when the pattern of teaching was handed over to us, and we chose to obey it—not casually, nor with words alone, but from the heart, from the soul, with complete devotion—we are freed from slavery to sin and become servants of righteousness. As for what he says, “the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,” I think it should be examined how each person is handed over. For we find that God hands over those who do not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, according to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves (Romans 1); and that he hands over others who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God to dishonorable passions. I have discussed these matters in their proper places, as far as I was able.

God therefore also hands over those who present themselves as servants of righteousness through obedience, so that they may be trained and instructed according to the pattern of the teaching of righteousness. This also concerns me: he did not say, “You obeyed from the heart the teaching to which you were handed over,” but instead said, “the pattern of teaching.” I do not think that the Apostle regarded the teaching and the pattern of the teaching as the same thing. Rather, it seems to me that he knew the pattern of the teaching to be less than the teaching itself. At present, while we are in the body and this earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks about many things (Wisdom 9), we possess the pattern of the teaching, not the teaching itself. The same Apostle says elsewhere: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13). The teaching itself is that of which it is said: “Then we shall see face to face” (ibid.). Hence, in the present life, I think we can possess the pattern and shadow of the virtues; the virtues themselves will be ours when those things that are perfect have come. And therefore, as it seems to me, the righteous person now lives more in the shadow of the virtues than in the virtues themselves.

But having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness. This is an exposition of what we said above. For if you no longer serve sin, it is certain that, having been freed from it, you have become servants of righteousness. But the question arises: who is it that frees from sin? Without doubt, it is the recognition of truth. Thus Jesus said to the Jews who believed him: “If you believe my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8). It is truth, therefore, and the recognition of truth, that frees from sin. It is certain, moreover, that everyone who has been freed from sin serves righteousness.

When we say that he serves righteousness, since righteousness is one member of the choir of virtues, it is as though we were saying that if someone has been freed from sin, he will serve truth, wisdom, chastity, and piety. I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. (Ambrose.) By mentioning the weakness of the flesh, he indicates that he demands less from human beings in the worship of God than is deserved. Accordingly, he adds: “Just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification.”

In order to remove from us the fear of approaching the faith—because it might seem to us, as it were, unbearable and harsh—he commanded us to serve God according to the same measure by which we previously served the devil. Yet we ought certainly to serve God more eagerly than the devil, since the one produces salvation and the other condemnation. Nevertheless, the spiritual physician does not demand more from us, lest, while we flee from commandments that seem burdensome because we consider our weakness, we should remain in death. He stoops to the weakness of their bodies, as though he were saying to them more plainly: “If you can do no more, at least let your fruits in good works be such as you formerly were in the practice of vices.” Let not holy freedom find you weaker in good works than earthly desire formerly found you strong in the flesh.

(Origen.) What, then, is so human—that is, what is so easy, so free of burden, and so impossible for the weakness of the flesh to excuse? He says: “Just as you presented your members as servants to iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification.” It is indeed disgraceful to serve the virtues as one serves vices. Righteousness ought to be honored much more, and with much greater zeal. But, he says, “I am dealing with you humanely and in a common manner: I ask the same things and require comparable things.”

Formerly your feet ran to the temples of demons; now let them run together to the Church of God. Formerly they ran to shed blood; now let them run to deliver blood. Formerly your hands were extended to seize what belonged to others; now let them be extended to give away what belongs to you. Formerly your eyes looked around at a woman or at something belonging to another in order to covet it; now let them look around at the poor, the weak, and the needy in order to show mercy. Your ears took pleasure in vain talk or in disparaging good people; now let them turn to hear the word of God, to the exposition of the law, and to receiving the discipline of wisdom. Let the tongue accustomed to insults, curses, and shameful speech now turn to bless the Lord at all times; let it speak sound and honorable words, so as to give grace to those who hear, and let it speak truth with its neighbor.

But why pursue each item, when it is clear even to you that the service of each member, which it formerly offered to vices, must be adapted to the virtues, and that the action which it offered to impurity must now be turned toward chastity and sanctification? It seems that here he has named righteousness for all the virtues taken together, just as conversely he has placed iniquity for all the vices taken together. He also added “to righteousness for sanctification,” evidently commending chastity both as a part of the whole and specifically in itself. Observe also that throughout these statements he indicates the freedom of choice and shows that each person has it in his power to render to righteousness and sanctification the service that he formerly rendered to iniquity for iniquity, once his purpose has been turned toward what is better. This could not happen if either nature, as some think, resisted it, or the course of the stars obstructed it.

For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. (Ambrose.) It is clear that one who is free from God is a slave of sin. For when he sins, he departs from God and comes under sin.

(Augustine.) He says “free with respect to righteousness,” not “freed,” but of sin he does not say “free,” lest they attribute this to themselves. Rather, with the greatest care he preferred to say “freed,” referring this to the Lord’s statement: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 7). They are not free from righteousness, therefore, except through free choice; but they do not become free from sin except by the grace of the Savior. For this reason the admirable teacher carefully distinguished even the words themselves.

(Origen.) “When you were slaves,” he says, “of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness.” When someone serves sin, therefore, he is free with respect to righteousness—that is, alienated from righteousness. Here he calls “free” what is alienated, and rightly so. For no one can serve righteousness and sin at the same time, just as the Savior said: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6). But we have discussed these matters more fully above.

This should certainly be noted: there is a blameworthy freedom and a praiseworthy slavery. To be free from righteousness is a crime; to be its servant is praiseworthy. When he says that one becomes a servant of righteousness, understand at the same time that one becomes a servant of wisdom, piety, chastity, and all the virtues together. Conversely, whoever sins is at once a servant of evil desire, anger, rage, unchastity, robbery, and all vices and crimes together. Therefore, we must always examine ourselves in each thing we do and consider in every action whose servants we are: whether we belong to sin for iniquity, or to righteousness for sanctification.

What fruit, then, did you have at that time in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. Sacred Scripture teaches that there is fruit both of good things and of evil things, as the Savior himself says in the Gospels: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for a good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a bad tree produce good fruit” (Matthew 7). In this passage, a person’s purpose and will seem to be called either a good tree or a bad tree, while his works are its fruit.

If someone therefore turns his mind and purpose toward righteousness, he undoubtedly becomes ashamed and himself reproves his earlier deeds, which he performed while under sin, because their end is death. But I ask: what death? It is certain that it is not this common death. For no one turns to righteousness after death, nor does anyone become ashamed of past evil deeds. What, then, is meant? Does he seem to call the death of sin “death,” since “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18)? Or can it rather be understood that he is speaking of that death by which we die to sins with Christ and bring an end to vices and crimes, so that the Apostle seems to have said: “Their end is death”?

(Ambrose.) He called it the end—the departure from life and from actions, after which either death or life follows. But in this passage death is twofold, for one passes from death to death.

But now, having been freed from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life.
