That is, if, having received the forgiveness of sins, we become eager for good works, we shall acquire holiness; and our end—that is, our outcome—will be everlasting life. For from this death, which he called the end, we shall pass to the life that has no end.

(Augustine.) We cannot possess this fruit in sanctification—which fruit is certainly love, together with its works—at all by ourselves; rather, we possess it through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. For the divine Teacher was speaking of this very fruit when he said to the branches that remain in him: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

“You have,” he says, “your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life.”

(Origen.) He compares fruits with fruits. He declares that the fruits of sin, for which the saints are now ashamed—that is, after they have been freed from sin and become servants of God—end in death. But he says that the fruits of righteousness, which are found in sanctification, have eternal life as their end.

First, this must not be omitted: he did not wish to name the fruits for which we are now ashamed, nor to say what they are. But of the fruit of those who have been freed from sin and become servants of God, he says that it is found in sanctification. For we ought to remember good things more frequently than evil ones.

This too, I think, must be observed. Since we have said that the Apostle made a comparison between evil fruits and good fruits, when he spoke of the evil fruits he did not say, “You had your fruit in those things of which you are now ashamed,” but said, “What fruit, then, did you have?” When, however, he speaks of the good fruits, the word “your” has been added. For he writes: “You have your fruit for sanctification.” By this he seems to indicate to me that the evil fruit, the fruit of which one ought to be ashamed and repent, is not our fruit. For God did not plant in us the bad tree that would produce bad fruits, as he himself says through the prophet: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly fertile; how have you turned into the bitterness of an alien vine?” (Isaiah 5.)

Therefore, even if we produce bad fruits, they are not ours but belong to another—that is, to sin. But if we produce good fruits in sanctification, they are our fruits. Human nature received from its Creator the capacity to produce these fruits. For those alien fruits were not sown in us by God.

When he says “eternal life,” we must consider what the Savior himself said: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). The Apostle himself also says elsewhere that “we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4). Therefore, just as being always with the Lord has no end, so eternal life must be believed to have no end.

For the wages of sin is death. But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. (Ambrose.) He calls death the profit of sin, because death comes through sin. Accordingly, those who thereafter abstain from sins receive eternal life as their wages, because those who do not sin are strangers to the second death. For just as those who follow sin acquire death, so those who follow the grace of God—that is, the faith of Christ, which grants forgiveness of sins—will have eternal life, rejoicing that they are released for a time and knowing that they will attain this life, which is free from every weariness and has no succession.

(Augustine.) Therefore the Apostle calls eternal life itself, which is certainly the reward of good works, the grace of God. “The wages,” he says, “of sin is death. But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Wages are paid as what is owed for military service; they are not given as a gift. Therefore he said, “The wages of sin is death,” to show that death is brought upon sin not undeservedly but as something owed. But if grace is not freely given, it is not grace. We must understand, therefore, that even a person’s good merits are gifts from God, and that when eternal life is paid in return for them, what is being paid is nothing other than grace for grace.

(Ambrose.) This gift, given to us by God through Christ, our Lord, he himself confirms, so that we should give thanks to God the Father through no one other than his Son.

(Origen.) He rightly preserves the metaphor—that is, the figure—of military service introduced at the beginning. Since those serving under sin as king, or rather obeying its tyranny, receive wages, he says that the wages owed to them are paid out as death. But it was not fitting for God to give his soldiers wages as something owed; rather, he gives a gift and grace, which is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

I do not think that the addition “in Christ Jesus our Lord” is without significance. Perhaps he wished it to be known that eternal life by itself is one thing, and eternal life in Christ Jesus another. Those who rise to confusion and everlasting disgrace will indeed have eternal life, but not in Christ Jesus; rather, they will have it in confusion and everlasting disgrace. The righteous, however, who rise to eternal life in Christ Jesus, will have eternal life.

Sin therefore grants its soldiers, in whom it reigns, a fitting wage: death. By death we do not mean this bodily death, but that of which it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18).

## CHAPTER VII

The Apostle sets forth the cessation of the old law, which is the law of death, and treats of the law of the Spirit.

Or do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the law? (Ambrose.) To strengthen their minds in divine teaching, he uses the example of human law, persuading them of heavenly things through earthly things. Thus God is recognized from the creation of the world. Since everything belongs to one source, although things are different, they are nevertheless similar to one another in some respect.

The Romans know the law, since they are not barbarians but have grasped natural justice, partly from the Greeks, just as the Greeks did from the Hebrews. Although the law was not unknown before Moses, it lacked order and authority. For the laws of the Romans were brought from Athens.

Thus he says to those who know the law: “The law rules over a person for as long as he lives.” It is not hidden that the whole life of a human being is under the law of nature, which was given to the world. This is the general law. Now he sets forth another, particular law—although it too is general, but because it is not received by human beings it becomes particular—through which he wishes to prove his assertion. For he wishes to hand down the truth step by step. He therefore says:

“For the woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband. Accordingly, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man.”

(Augustine.) When he says, “The woman who is under a husband is joined to the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband,” and so forth, it must be observed that this analogy differs from the reality for which it is introduced in the following respect: here he says that the husband dies and that the woman marries whom she wishes, having certainly been freed from the law of her husband. There, however, he presents the soul as the woman and the passions of sins as the husband—passions that work in the members in order to bear fruit for death, that is, so that offspring worthy of such a union may be born.

The law that was given not to take away sin or to liberate from sin, but to display sin before grace, caused those placed under the law to be carried away by a more vehement desire to sin and to sin even more through transgression. Thus, although there are three elements there—the soul as woman, the passions of sins as husband, and the law as the husband’s law—he does not say that the soul is freed when sins die, as when the husband dies. Rather, he says that the soul itself dies to sin and is freed from the law, so that it may belong to another husband, namely Christ, when it has died to sin, even though sin itself still seems to be alive.

This occurs when, although desires and certain incitements to sin still remain in us, we nevertheless do not obey or consent to them, serving the law of God with the mind, because we have died to sin. Sin itself will also die when the reformation of the body has taken place in the resurrection, about which he later says: “He will give life even to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you.”

(Ambrose.) This law comes from the Gospel, not from Moses, nor from earthly righteousness. Thus, learning some things under the guidance of nature and some things from the law of Moses, they were made perfect through the Gospel of Christ.

By the following example, therefore, he argues more plainly that Christianity has been stripped of the law of deeds, not of every law. It is no longer advantageous to be under the law, lest, by returning under the law, one nullify the grace of God; for the grace of God has freed the human being from the law so that he may serve God in the spirit—that is, with the mind.

Just as a woman, when her husband dies, is freed from the law of her husband but not from the law of nature, so those who have been freed by God’s grace from the law under which they were held liable are freed from it as from something dead, so that, having been joined to Christianity, they are not adulterers. For if the law remains alive among them, they are adulterers, and it will profit them nothing to be called Christians, since they will be liable to punishment.

For he will be an adulterer not of the law but of the Gospel if, after the law has died and he has been joined to the Gospel, he returns to the law. The law is said to be dead when the person whom it held liable is forgiven and its authority ceases.

“But if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is joined to another man.” Those who have been removed from the law, having received the forgiveness of sins and having been joined to the Gospel, are not adulterers of the law, because the law has died among them. But if, while observing the law, they think that they are approaching the Gospel, they will be liable and adulterous, because they have joined themselves to the faith while the law was alive, and will be adulterers with respect to both.

(Origen.) Paul is therefore speaking to those who know the law—that is, to those who know the oldness of the letter and the newness of the Spirit that exist in the law. Whoever understands this well undoubtedly knows that the law rules over a person as long as he lives, just as a husband rules over a woman; and just as the woman is freed from the law of marriage by the husband’s death and receives the freedom to join herself to another husband, so the soul, whose husband is the law, when it recognizes the oldness of the letter in the law—for “what becomes old is near disappearance”—receives the power to marry another husband, who is the spirit of the law. “The Lord is the Spirit.”

When he says, “The law rules over a person for as long as he lives,” this does not refer to the person but to the law. He indicates this in what follows, where he says, “While her husband lives, she is bound to the law.” The very order of the example that has been adopted makes the same point more fully: he placed the law in the position of the husband and says of it, “But if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband.”

If this is understood as being said about the apostles or about those who believed from the circumcision, no difficulty will arise. For it is clear that they had the law as their husband, under whose power they lived. But when the fullness of time came, the law began to grow weak in the flesh, and death followed upon its weakness; and those who had lived under the power of this husband as a woman, when the letter had died, marry the Spirit by believing in Christ.

Those who from the Gentiles believed in the Lord, however, do not seem to have lived under the power of this husband—that is, under the power of the law—nor to have had the word of the law as their husband. Isaiah’s proclamation bears witness to this: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54).

He says that the desolate woman has many children, more than she who has a husband, because far more people from the Gentiles than from the circumcision believed. He shows that she who has a husband is the synagogue, which possesses the law; while the desolate woman, wandering and living without any power of the law, is the multitude of the Gentiles, which was barren, producing no offspring from any legitimate word.

Thus the person who lives under the law is placed by the Apostle in the position of the woman who is under a husband. He places the word of the law in the position of the husband, though he calls this husband mortal, since he is the word of the law according to the letter. But how he is dead must be carefully considered.

It may indeed also seem to me that he is dead when spiritual understanding excludes and, as it were, kills the bodily sense, showing that the letter which kills must be rejected and the Spirit that gives life must be followed. But this man’s death can be demonstrated even more clearly in this way.

For as long as the law bore the shadow of future goods, and earthly Jerusalem bore the type and image of heavenly worship, and the altar and priesthood remained, the word of the law—that is, the letter—seemed to live. For Christ had not yet entered the holy places not made with hands, nor approached the inner veil, which the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, interprets as Christ’s flesh (Hebrews 10).

But when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), earthly Jerusalem, together with the temple, the altar, and everything that was performed there, was overthrown by his presence. Then her husband died—that is, the law according to the letter.

Or is the word of the law not rightly said to have died when no sacrifices, no priesthood, and no ministries of the Levitical order are offered to it? It cannot punish a murderer or stone an adulteress; for Roman authority claims these matters for itself. Do you still doubt that the law is dead according to the letter?

Three times a year every male does not appear before the Lord; no sheep is slaughtered in the city that the Lord God is believed to have chosen at the feast of Passover; the sheaf of firstfruits is not offered; no offering is celebrated; no leprosy is cleansed, and no impurity is purified. Can it be doubted in all these matters that the letter of the law has died?

When it has therefore become clear through all these things that the former husband has died, there is no transgression in being joined to Christ as to another husband, just as it is no crime for a woman, after her former husband has died, to enter a second marriage. For this reason he says: “Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man,” to show that the human soul too, if it has already come to Christ and has been joined to Christ as to a second husband, must not in any way allow the oldness of the letter—like a former husband—to live within it. Otherwise, if it keeps him alive within itself, it will become an adulteress, since it has been joined to a second husband while the former still lives.

This is what he also said above under another figure: one must first die and then be buried together with Christ.

Therefore, my brothers, you too have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God.

**(Augustine.)** [Col. 1410B] Why have we died to the law through the body of Christ, if the law is good? Because we have died to the law that ruled us, having been freed from that disposition which the law punishes and condemns. For the law is more commonly so called when it rules, terrifies, and exacts punishment; the same commandment is “law” to those who fear it, but grace to those who love it. Hence the Gospel says: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). The very law that was given through Moses so that it might be feared became grace and truth through Jesus Christ so that it might be fulfilled.

Thus, then, “you have died to the law” was said as though it meant: “You have died to the punishment of the law through the body of Christ,” through which the sins that were held fast by the lawful punishment have been forgiven.

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1410B–1410D] Since the Savior permitted his body to be crucified by the devil, knowing that it would be for us and against him, he therefore says that we have been saved through the body of Christ. To die to the law is to live for God, because the law rules over sinners. Whoever, then, has his sins forgiven dies to the law—that is, he is freed from the law.

Therefore, through the body of Christ we obtain this benefit. For by handing over his body, the Savior conquered death and condemned sin. The devil sinned in him when he killed one who was innocent and entirely ignorant of sin. For when he defended his claim over humanity on account of sin, he was found guilty in the very one whom he accused.

Hence it came about that all who believe in Christ are rescued from the law, sin having been removed. Since sin—the devil—was conquered through the body of Christ, it has no authority over those who belong to him by whom it was conquered. For when he, though he did not sin, was killed as though he were guilty, he conquered sin by means of sin: that is, by the devil’s own sin, which he committed against him, he condemned the devil. He also erased the bond that had been decreed because of Adam’s sin when he rose from the dead, giving believers in him this pattern, so that they could not be held by the second death.

And so we have died to the law through the body of Christ. For whoever has not died to the law is guilty, and whoever is guilty cannot escape the second death.

**(Origen.)** [Cols. 1410D–1411A] You see how, although a diversity of figures may appear, everything nevertheless comes back to one meaning. For when he says that the law has died for us, this seems to mean the same as that we have died to the law through the body of Christ, in which body he carried our iniquities and bore our sins (Isaiah 53), and in which he stripped off rulers and authorities, triumphing over them in himself.

We must therefore hasten to this second marriage, which is far happier than the first. And see whether perhaps the law had already foreshadowed something of this kind when it commanded that, after a woman’s first husband had died—a husband from whom she had received no offspring, since he had been such as could not produce fruit—she should marry his brother. For the brother seems to be the law of the letter according to the spirit, so that the woman might bear fruit more fully from him. But this will be sought out more fully in its proper places.

For now, as we have said, we must first die to the law of the letter, so that in this way we may be joined to Christ, who rose from the dead.

When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins that come through the law were at work in our members, so that we might bear fruit for death.

**(Augustine.)** [Cols. 1411A–B] What, then, does “when we were in the flesh” mean, except “when we presumed upon the flesh,” that is, when we placed our confidence in ourselves? For “flesh” is said of a human being, just as it is said of humanity: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” What does “all flesh shall see” mean except “every human being shall see”? Therefore, when we were in the flesh—that is, when we were occupied with the desires of the flesh and placed all our hope, as it were, in ourselves—the passions of sins that come through the law, and are increased through the law, were at work in us. For by prohibiting, the law made a transgressor of the law, since the one who became a transgressor did not have God as his helper.

They were therefore at work in our members so that they might bear fruit—but for whom, except death? Therefore, do not be in the flesh; be in the spirit. What does “be in the spirit” mean? Place your hope in God.

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1411B–D] To be in the flesh can be understood in many ways. Every unbeliever is in the flesh, that is, carnal; a Christian who lives under the law is in the flesh; whoever hopes for something from human beings is in the flesh; if a Christian lives luxuriously, he is in the flesh; and whoever understands Christ wrongly is in the flesh.

Here, however, we shall understand “being in the flesh” in this way: before faith we were in the flesh; for we lived under sin, that is, following carnal perceptions, and we were subject to vices and sins. The understanding of the flesh is not to believe spiritual things: that a virgin gave birth without the involvement of a man; that a human being is born again from water and the Holy Spirit; and that the soul, once released from its union with the flesh, will rise again in the flesh. Whoever doubts these things is in the flesh.

Hence he says: “The vices of sins that are revealed through the law were at work in our members, so that they might bear fruit for death.” It is clear that whoever does not believe lives under sin and is dragged captive into committing vices, so that he may bear fruit for the second death. For death makes a gain when sin is committed.

Yet he says that the vices are at work in our members, not in the body, lest he provide an occasion for those who interpret the matter wrongly: the tongue is reproved for abusive speech, the hand is censured for theft, and the ears are rebuked in the one who pretends not to hear; and so with the other members. Although these things proceed from the heart, they are nevertheless carried out through the service of the members in action.

This discussion concerns Jews and those who are called Christians but wish to live under the law, so that, learning that they are carnal, they may withdraw from the law. Yet when he says that the vices of sins dominate those who live in the flesh, he shows that they are revealed through the law, not produced by the law. For the law is the indicator of sin, not its begetter: it makes sinners guilty.

But now we have been released from the law of death in which we were held.

[Col. 1412A] We have been released from the law when we received the forgiveness of sins. For it has no power over us; it rules over unbelievers and sinners. It is called the law of death because it punishes the guilty and puts sinners to death. It is therefore not evil, but just. Although what the law inflicts is evil for those who suffer it, the law itself is not evil, because it justly brings wrath.

Thus it is not evil toward sinners, but just; toward the good, it is spiritual. For who would doubt that it is spiritual to forbid sin? But because the law could not save a human being by forgiving sins, the law of faith was given, which would free believers from the dominion of the law, so that those whom the law held guilty of death could restore themselves to life. For the law of death belongs to those for whom it produces wrath on account of sin.

**(Origen.)** [Cols. 1412A–1413B] It is possible, however, that this should be understood not only of the law of Moses, which is according to the letter, but of every human being. For it is certain that, whatever institutions and whatever customs govern a person, he must be understood to live as though under the law that he follows. Either he himself must die to that law, or it must die to him, lest the soul, coming to Christ while placed under another husband, seem not so much to enter into his marriage as to become an adulteress, since it still lives according to the laws of its former husband.

The Apostle nevertheless brings the same meaning forward again under another figure of explanation. In the preceding passage he had discussed the law of the letter, which would seem to concern only those who had believed from circumcision. Now, by a hidden turn, he examines the law of the flesh and of the vices, so that this discussion would plainly appear to concern other human beings as well, and not only those who are from circumcision.

He therefore says, “when we were in the flesh.” Certainly, insofar as the matter itself is concerned, he was saying these things while he was in the flesh. But “when we were in the flesh,” that is, when we lived according to the flesh, “the vices of sins that were through the law were at work in our members.”

What law is this through which the vices of sins are at work? Is it the law of Moses, even if it were observed according to the letter? Does it generate the vices of sins? But it is evident that he is speaking of the law in the members that resists the law of our mind, concerning which we discussed earlier: how the law entered in so that sin might abound.

That, then, is the law which makes the vices of sins abound in those who live according to the flesh, so that they may bear fruit for death. For this law is in our members for the purpose of resisting the law of the mind, leading us captive to sin, and offering these fruits to death.

But now we have been released from the law of the dead in which we were held. From this law, then, we have now been released. When now? Clearly, when we died with Christ, were buried with him through baptism, and were crucified with him. Therefore he says, “we have been released from the law of the dead.” Unless someone has died with Christ, he is not released from this law.

I know that in other copies it is written, “from the law of death in which we were held.” But “of the dead” is read both more truly and more correctly.

As for what he added in conclusion—“so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” which plainly seems to have been said concerning the law of the letter—this could appropriately be understood in the following way.

While we were placed in the flesh and living according to the flesh, because of the vices of sins, the law that was in our members nourished them so that they might bear fruit for death. We could not serve in the newness of the spirit while that law of the members lived in us—or rather, while we lived according to that law.

But when Christ died for us, and we died with him to sin, and through him were freed from the law of sin in which we were held, we can now serve the law of God: to serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

Christ did not therefore draw us away from the law of sin so that we might serve the oldness of the letter—that is, so that we might receive circumcision and observe the Sabbaths and the other things contained in the oldness of the law—but so that we might serve the law of God in the newness of the spirit. That is, from everything written in it, we should receive, by the gift of the Spirit, its spiritual meaning.

As the same Apostle says elsewhere, a veil was placed over the face of Moses; but when someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. “For the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3).

I know that some, misunderstanding “the newness of the spirit,” have been led to say that the Spirit is new, as though he had not existed before or had not been known by the ancients. They do not realize that in this they blaspheme most gravely. For the same Spirit is in the law and in the Gospel; he is always with the Father and the Son; and he always is, was, and will be, just as the Father and the Son are.

He himself, therefore, is not new. Rather, he renews believers when he leads them from their former evils to the new life and the new observance of the Christian religion, and makes them spiritual instead of carnal.

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1413B–C] The old law is not the name of a crime, but of a time or age. It has grown old because it has ceased. The law of the spirit is itself the law of faith, because faith is in the mind. It is not learned through works, but believed in the heart. The mind itself understands that what it believes belongs to its nature; it is not seen with the eyes or touched with the hands. The gifts that are hoped for are not visible or earthly, but spiritual.

The old law, therefore, was formed on tablets of stone, but the law of the spirit is written spiritually on tablets of the heart, so that it may be eternal. The letter of the old law is worn away by age.

**(Augustine.)** [Cols. 1413C–D] Since the law is letter for those who do not fulfill it through the spirit of love, which belongs to the New Testament, those who have died to sin are freed from the letter by which they are held. For what else is the law to those who know how to read it but cannot fulfill it, except mere letter? It is not unknown to those for whom it was written. But because it is known only insofar as it is read as written, and not insofar as it is completed through love, it is nothing else to such people but letter.

That letter is not the helper of those who read, but the witness of sinners. They are therefore freed from its condemnation when they are renewed through the spirit, so that they are no longer bound by the letter for punishment, but joined to understanding through righteousness. Hence also the saying: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3).

And because he had said, “we have been released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” and thus might seem, through these words, to have criticized the law, he immediately added:

What, then, shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means.

**(Ambrose.)** [Col. 1414A] Since he calls it the law of death and rejoices that we have been rescued from it, and denies that we serve God in it, lest anyone should think that he was asserting it to be unjust, he removes this suspicion when he says, “By no means.”

But I did not know sin except through the law. The law, therefore, is not sin, but the indicator of sin. It reveals sins that were hidden and shows that they would not go unpunished before God. Once this became known, the human being became guilty.

**(Augustine.)** [Cols. 1414A–B] The law is therefore understood to have been given for this purpose: not so that sin might be introduced, nor so that it might be eradicated, but only so that it might be revealed. By revealing sin, it made the human soul, which had been secure as though innocent, guilty, so that, since sin cannot be conquered without the grace of God, the anxiety of guilt might turn the soul toward receiving grace.

Accordingly, he does not say, “I did not commit sin except through the law,” but “I did not know sin except through the law.” From this it is evident that desire was not implanted by the law, but revealed by it. It followed that, since desire could not yet be resisted without grace, it would also increase, because desire has greater force when the guilt of transgression is added to it than when it acts against no law.

For I would not have known desire unless the law said, “You shall not desire.”

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1414B–C] He did not distinguish desire from sin, but combined them, indicating this: when there was not even a suspicion that this thing was forbidden by God, he says, “I learned that it was sin.”

He conducts the general case under his own person. The law, therefore, forbids desire, which, because it is pleasurable, was not thought to be sin. It seemed a simple matter to desire something belonging to one’s neighbor; the law disclosed that this was sin. For worldly people think that nothing is so unpunished and harmless as pleasure.

But sin, having taken an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every desire.

**(Augustine.)** [Cols. 1414C–D] When he says, “sin, having taken an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every desire,” this must not be understood to mean that there had been every kind of desire before it was increased by prohibition. Desire is increased by prohibition when the grace that liberates is absent.

Before it is prohibited, therefore, it is not yet “every” desire. But when it has been prohibited and, as we have said, grace has withdrawn, desire grows so greatly that it becomes “every” desire in its own kind—that is, complete—so that it even acts against the law and accumulates the guilt of transgression.

When he says, “Apart from the law sin was dead,” he does not mean that sin did not exist; he says that it was dead because it was hidden. This he makes clear in what follows, when he says, “But sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.”

The law is good, but without grace it merely displays sins; it does not remove them. Sin existed even before, but not every sin existed, since the guilt of transgression was still lacking. Hence he says elsewhere: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

**(Jerome.)** [Cols. 1414D–1418B] How is medicine the cause of death if it reveals deadly poisons, even though evil people abuse them to bring about death, either killing themselves or plotting against their enemies? In the same way, the law was given to expose the poisons of sins, so that it might restrain the human being who was abusing his freedom badly—previously carried along without foresight and slipping over precipices—by the bridle of the law, and teach him to walk with measured steps, so that “we may serve in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.” That is, we should live under a command, whereas previously we lived like brute animals: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Corinthians 15:32).

But if, when the law entered—the law that teaches what we ought to do and forbids what we ought not to do—we are carried by our vice and lack of restraint against the legal commands, the law seems to be the cause of sin, since, by forbidding desire, it is recognized as inflaming it in a certain way.

There is a secular saying among the Greeks: “Whatever is permitted is desired less.” Conversely, therefore, whatever is not permitted receives nourishment for desire. Hence Tullius denies that Solon wrote among the Athenians concerning the punishments of parricides, lest he seem to be not so much prohibiting as reminding them.

Thus the law seems to be an occasion of offenses among those who despise it and trample upon its commands, since, by forbidding what it does not want to be done, it binds them with the chains of commandments. Previously, when they sinned without the law, they were not held by accusations.

We have said these things with the law given through Moses in mind. But because what follows speaks of “the law of God,” “the law of the flesh and of the members,” which fights against “the law of our mind” and leads us captive “in the law of sin,” and because I recognize that four laws are written as fighting among themselves in one passage, I do not think it irrelevant to ask how many kinds of law are mentioned in the holy Scriptures.

There is the law that was given through Moses, according to what is written to the Galatians: “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: Cursed is everyone who does not persevere in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them” (Galatians 3).

Again, in the same Epistle: “The law was established because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, having been ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (ibid.).

And again: “Thus the law was our pedagogue toward Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But after faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God through faith, which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid.).

Even history, which contains no commandments but reports what happened, is called “law” by the Apostle. “Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, have you not read the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman. But the one who was born from the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one from the free woman was born through promise” (Galatians 4).

The Psalms, too, are called law, so that the saying might be fulfilled that is written in their law: “They hated me without cause” (John 3; Psalm 68).

The Apostle also calls Isaiah’s prophecy law: “In the law it is written: ‘In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me,’ says the Lord.” I have found this written in Isaiah according to the Hebrew and Aquila.

The mystical understanding of the Scriptures is also called law: “We know that the law is spiritual.”

In addition to all these, the same Apostle teaches that the natural law is written in our hearts: “When Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, while their conscience bears witness to them” (Romans 2).

This law written in the heart embraces all nations, and there is no human being who does not know it. Hence the whole world is under sin, and all human beings are transgressors of the law. Therefore the judgment of God is just, since he writes it in the heart of the human race: “What you would not want done to you, do not do to another.”

Who does not know that murder, adultery, theft, and every desire are evil, from the fact that he does not want them done to himself? If he did not know that they were evil, he would never be pained when they were inflicted upon him.

Through this natural law Cain also recognized his sin when he said, “My guilt is greater than can be forgiven.” Adam and Eve recognized their sin as well, and therefore hid themselves beneath the tree of life.

Pharaoh, too, before the law was given through Moses, was stirred by the law of nature, confessed his crimes, and said: “The Lord is righteous, but I and my people are impious” (Exodus 9).

Childhood does not know this law, and infancy is unaware of it. A child who sins without a commandment is not held by the law of sin. He curses his father and mother, beats his parents, and, because he has not yet received the law of wisdom, sin is dead in him.

But when the commandment comes—that is, the time when he understands and desires good and avoids evil—then sin begins to revive, and he begins to die and become guilty of sin.

Thus it happens that the time of understanding, through which we recognize God’s commandments so that we may reach life, produces death in us if we act negligently, and if the opportunity for wisdom deceives, trips us up, and leads us to death.

This does not mean that understanding is sin—for the law of understanding is holy, just, and good—but that through the understanding of sins and virtues, sin is born in me. Before I understood that it was sin, I did not know it as sin. Thus what was given to me for good was changed into evil by my own fault.

And, to speak hyperbolically and use a new expression to explain my meaning: sin, which before I possessed understanding was without sin, begins, through the transgression of the commandment, to become for me a more sinful sin.

Let us first ask what this desire is of which the law says, “You shall not desire.”

Some think that the commandment is the one written in the Decalogue: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s property.” But we think that by “desire” all the disturbances of the soul are signified—those by which we grieve and mourn, fear, and desire.

The Apostle, the chosen vessel whose body was a temple of the Holy Spirit, said: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (1 Corinthians 13.) And elsewhere: “Christ redeemed us” (Galatians 3); and again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2).

He is not speaking about himself, but about one who, after sins, wishes to do penance. Under his own person he describes the fragility of the human condition, which endures the battles of two human beings—the inner and the outer—fighting against each other.

The inner human being consents to the written and natural law, because it is good, holy, just, and spiritual. The outer human being says, “I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I am doing, and I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7).

But if the outer human being does what he does not want and performs what he hates, he shows that the commandment is good, and that it is not he himself who performs what is evil, but sin dwelling in his flesh—that is, the vices of the body and the desires of pleasure, which have been implanted in human bodies for the sake of posterity and offspring, and which, if they go beyond their limits, are turned into sin.

If each person would consider matters carefully and accuse himself, examining the incitements of the vices—how often, both in speech and in thought and in the heat of the body, he speaks, thinks, and suffers what he does not want—I do not wish to say “does,” lest I seem to accuse holy men. Of them it is written: “That man was true and blameless, righteous, a worshiper of God, withdrawing from every evil work” (Job 1). And concerning Zechariah and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1).

The Apostles were also commanded: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” The Apostle would never have commanded this unless he knew that a human being could be perfect.

Unless perhaps we should say that “withdrawing from every evil” signifies correction, and a transition from the errors of childhood and the vices of a wanton age to correction and virtues; and that the righteousness praised in Zechariah and Elizabeth is outward, while the desire that is now said to dwell in our members operates inwardly.

But the Apostle does not command children; he commands those already of mature age to take up perfection, and we too confess that perfection exists in a perfected age.

In saying these things, we do not flatter the vices, but follow the authority of the Scriptures, which says that no human being is without sin: “God has enclosed all under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11). The exception is the one who did not commit sin, “nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2).

Hence Solomon says that the tracks of the serpent are not found upon the rock. And the Lord himself says of himself: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14)—that is, nothing of his work or his trace.

For this reason we are commanded not to reproach a person who returns from his sins, nor to despise an Egyptian, because we too were once in Egypt, built cities for Pharaoh from clay and bricks, and were led captive into Babylon by the law of sin that dwelled in our members.

And when there seemed to be utter despair—or rather, when it had been openly confessed that every human being is entangled in the snares of the devil—the Apostle, or rather the human being under whose person the Apostle speaks, turned back to himself and gave thanks to the Savior, because he had been redeemed by his blood, had put off his filth in baptism, and had put on the new garment of Christ. Having died to the old human being, he was born as a new human being who could say: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7.) “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord,” who freed me from the death of the body.

If anyone does not think that the Apostle is speaking about others under his own person, let him explain how Daniel, whom we know to have been righteous, speaks as though about himself when he intercedes for others: “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have acted impiously, and we have turned away and departed from your commandments and judgments. We did not obey your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings and princes, to our fathers, and to all the people of the land. To you, Lord, belongs righteousness, but to us confusion of face” (Daniel 9).

Likewise, in the thirty-first Psalm we read: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin. For this every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time.”

This is not appropriate to David, a righteous man—or, to speak plainly, to the prophet whose words are being related—but to a sinner. When the righteous man had poured out such words under the person of a penitent, he deserved to hear God say: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall walk; I will fix my eyes upon you.”

Likewise, in the thirty-seventh Psalm, whose title is “For a memorial,” teaching us that we must always remember our sins and do penance, we read: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins. For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they have been made heavy upon me. My wounds have rotted and festered because of my foolishness. I have been afflicted and humbled exceedingly.”

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1418B–1419A] Thus, by “every desire,” he signifies all sins. Above he mentions desire according to the law; now, adding the other vices, he says that every desire was produced in the human being through the impulse of the devil, whom he signifies by “sin,” so that the law given for the human being’s benefit might become its opposite.

When the devil saw the help provided for the human being through the law—one whom he rejoiced to have with himself in his condition because of that person’s transgression [or: “whom he rejoiced to have with himself in his condition because of Adam’s sin and because of the person’s own sin”]—he understood that it had been made against him. For when he saw the human being placed under the law, he was certain that the human being had been taken away from his dominion. The human being had learned how he might escape the punishment of hell.

At this the devil’s anger against the human being blazed up. He sought to pervert the law for him, so that, by committing what was forbidden, he would offend God again and fall once more under the devil’s power.

He began not to command but subtly to deceive, because, through the law that had been given, the devil had lost his dominion, knowing that thereafter the human being belonged to God’s judgment.

Apart from the law, sin was dead.

This must be understood in two ways: the devil is signified in sin, and the sin itself—which is called sin—is also signified. The devil is said to have been dead because, before the law, he ceased from the deception of the human being [variant: “for the deception of the human being”] and was, as it were, at rest. He was secure concerning his possession of the human being.

He said that sin was dead because it was thought not to be reckoned before God. Thus, in the human being it was dead, as though sin were committed with impunity.

For sin was not hidden, as I said above; rather, this was unknown: that God would judge. When this was made manifest through the giving of the law, sin was said to have revived.

Why did it revive, unless because it had lived before and was afterward considered dead through human negligence, although it was alive? Sin was thought not to be reckoned, even though it was reckoned; thus what was alive was regarded as dead.

I, however, was living apart from the law.

**(Augustine.)** [Col. 1419A] When he says, “I was once living apart from the law,” this must be understood as meaning, “I seemed to be living,” because before the commandment sin was hidden.

**(Ambrose.)** [Cols. 1419A–B] What does “apart from the law” mean, since the law has always existed, as I mentioned above? It means that the human being lived without fear of God, secure in the belief that God would not judge human actions.

But when the commandment came, sin revived. He therefore said that sin had revived to indicate that it had lived previously, but afterward was considered dead through human negligence, although it was alive. This is like the false reputation that sometimes arises concerning strangers.

This therefore signifies that at the beginning it had not been hidden that sin was reckoned before God—that is, that it was alive. But when the habit of sinning had erased this awareness, sin was considered dead, so that people thought the crime disappeared with the person.

When the law was given, or restored, sin revived among those among whom it had been considered dead. For they began to know that sin was reckoned.

But I died. The human being died because he saw himself guilty before God, whereas previously he had thought that he would not be held liable for the things he committed.

**(Augustine.)** [Cols. 1419B–C] “I died,” he says—that is, I learned that I was dead—or because the guilt of transgression threatened the certain punishment of death.

When he says that sin revived, he sufficiently indicated in this way that sin had once lived, that is, had been known, as I think, in the transgression of the first human being, because he too had received a commandment. For something cannot revive unless it once lived, but had died—that is, had been concealed—when mortal human beings, born without the commandment of the law, did not live according to it, following the desires of the flesh without any knowledge, because without any restraint.

Therefore he says, “I was once living apart from the law,” thereby making clear that he is not speaking from his own personal identity, but generally from the person of humanity.

And the commandment that had been given for life was found by me to be for death. (Amb.) This is true, because the law was given for life; but when it makes guilty a person who sins not only in the past but also in the future, the law given for life became, in the case of the sinner, [Col. 1419D] one that leads to death—though, as I said, for those who obey, it advances them toward life. (Aug.) For if the commandment is obeyed, it is certainly life; but it was found to be for death when it is violated, so that not only is sin committed, as it was even before the commandment, but it is committed more abundantly and more disastrously, now by one who knowingly transgresses. For sin, taking the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.

When he says that sin, having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me, this is said because the fruit of a forbidden desire is sweeter. Hence all sins committed secretly are also sweeter, although this sweetness is deadly. Therefore, in Solomon, a woman seated under the image of deceitful teaching [Col. 1420A] and inviting the foolish to come to her is written as saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. IX). This is the opportunity for sin found through the commandment; when it is desired, it certainly deceives, for it turns into greater bitterness. “Sin,” he says, “having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.” Sin, failing to use the law rightly, became sweeter because desire was increased by prohibition; and therefore it deceived, for it is a deceptive sweetness, since greater and more numerous bitter punishments follow. Since, then, those who have not yet attained spiritual grace admit more readily what is forbidden, sin deceives by a false sweetness; and because it also kills, the guilt of transgression kills.

(Amb.) In this passage understand “sin” as the devil [Col. 1420B], who is the author of sin. He found an opportunity through the law to satisfy his cruelty by the death of the human being: since the law threatened sinners, and a human being, at his instigation, continually admitted what was forbidden, he offended God and incurred the vengeance of the law, so that he was condemned by the very law that had been given for his benefit. Because the law had been given against his will, envy was inflamed against the human being, so that he might stain him more deeply with vicious pleasures and prevent him from escaping his grasp.

And so: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” (Aug.) For it commands what ought to be commanded and forbids what ought to be forbidden. The fault lies in one who uses it badly, not in the commandment itself, which is good; for the law is good if someone uses it lawfully. But one uses the law badly who does not submit to God with devout humility, so that the law may be fulfilled through grace.

[Col. 1420C] (Amb.) So that no unfavorable suspicion might remain against the law, he commends it in such a way that he declares it not only just but also holy and good. For the Gospel saying testifies that “commandment” means “law”; it says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. IX).

(Cass.) Finally, just as our goodness, when compared with the goodness above, is turned into wickedness, so also our righteousness, when compared with divine righteousness, is reckoned like a menstruous cloth, as the prophet Isaiah says: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV). And, to add something still clearer, even the life-giving precepts of the law itself—which are said to have been ordained through angels by the hand of the Mediator, and concerning which the same Apostle says, “Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good” (Gal. III)—when compared with the perfection [Col. 1420D] of the Gospel, are declared by the oracle to be not good at all. For he says: “And I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments by which they shall not live” (Ezek. XX). The Apostle likewise affirms, in the light of the New Testament, that the glory of the law has been dulled, declaring that, in comparison with the splendor of the Gospel, it was not even glorified, when he says: “For even that which was glorified was not glorious [shone in this respect], because of the surpassing glory” (II Cor. III).

What, then, was good became death to me? By no means. (Ambr.) Truly, by no means. For how can what is proved to be good be understood as death? Can it be praised more abundantly? A little earlier, by that word he said, “By no means,” he had defended it against accusation; he had not yet praised it [Col. 1421A]. Now, however: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” What, then, was good became death to me? By no means; for what is good is not death.

But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what was good. (Aug.) When he says, “What, then, was good became death to me? By no means; but sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what was good,” he clearly shows what he had said above: “Without the law sin was dead.” He said this because sin lies hidden. For now he says that it was not what was good—that is, the law—that became death to him, but that sin worked death through the good of the law, so that sin, which had been hidden without the law, might appear.

A person recognizes that he is dead [Col. 1421B] when he confesses that what was rightly commanded cannot be fulfilled by him, and when he sins more seriously by the crime of transgression than he would have done if he had not been forbidden. This is what he says below: “So that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment” (Rom. VII). Before the commandment it was lesser, because where there is no law, there is no transgression. The law is not death, but sin is death. He says, “Sin, so that it might appear to be sin”; he does not say, “so that it might become sin,” because it existed even when it did not appear. What does “so that sin might appear” mean? “I did not know desire except when the law said, ‘You shall not desire.’” He does not say, “I did not have desire,” but, “I did not know desire.” So here too he does not say, “so that sin might exist,” but, “so that sin might appear, it worked death in me through what was good.”

(Ambr.) In another way, he says that the devil received an opportunity through what was good to work evil against the human being, leading him astray into death [Col. 1421C]. The law was given and manifested in writing so that the things done wickedly before the law might be shown, through the enticement of desire, to be sins and might thereafter be avoided. Then Satan was inflamed, precisely through what was good: he saw that provision was being made for the human being and persuaded him to do what was unlawful, so that, instead of life through the law, death might come to him. This must indeed be attributed to human negligence, which so weakened the strength of its nature through the desire to sin that it could not restrain the suggestions of the adversary.

Yet the enemy, who is signified by sin, received through the law an opportunity to work death in the human being, so that he might appear to be an enemy. For while he persuades the human being to do what is unlawful, he is shown to be an enemy. Although even before the law he had procured death for the human being [Col. 1421D], apart from Adam’s first transgression, after the law he devised greater punishments for him in hell, where there is the second death. For it is a lesser crime to sin before the law has been revealed than after the law.

So that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment. (Aug.) “So that the sinner or sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment.” Why “exceedingly”? Because there is now transgression; for where there is no law, there is no transgression.

(Ambr.) What does “exceedingly” mean? Is it as though a measure had been assigned to those who offend, even though it is not permissible to sin? But these are the words of God: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete.” By this he shows that there is a certain measure of sins, and that when sinners have filled it, they are judged wholly unworthy of life [Col. 1422A]. So also with Pharaoh: because he had filled up this measure, God’s powers and signs were displayed against him, by which the others, struck with fear, might devote themselves to the benefits of life, so that life might be learned from one who had died.

But the Apostle considers another measure. To show that sin is greater under the law than it had been before the law, he signifies that, after the law, a greater measure of sins had grown through the envy and cunning of Satan, so that God’s providence might seem to have become contrary to the human being, even though he ought not to have sinned at all because of fear of the law. Therefore, in order to overcome the devil’s envy and establish his providence toward humanity, God changed the order of things, sending Christ the Savior, who would both conquer the devil and confirm God’s decrees concerning humanity.

(Orig.) In these passages it is often necessary for us to remind the reader of the diversity of laws [Col. 1422B]. For Paul intends, under the single name “law,” to transfer his meaning silently from one law to another, with the purpose, as I think, that the things spoken by the prophetic Scriptures under divine inspiration should not be placed openly before crude people who as yet bring little either of faith or of study, to be trampled underfoot, so to speak, and handed over for them to profane; rather, in accordance with what we said above by way of a certain comparison, the mystery of their king should reach the few more secretly.

He therefore says: “What, then, shall we say? Is the law sin?” You thought, he says, that I was speaking of the law of Moses when I said that it was [because it was] sin? “By no means, by no means.” Let this answer suffice for both questions: I am speaking neither of the law of Moses, nor do I say of that law itself that it is sin. But I did not know sin except through the law; for I did not know desire [Col. 1422C] unless the law said, “You shall not desire.”

Understand, he says, which law I am speaking about: if it did not exist, no one would recognize sin. Is it the law of Moses through which Adam recognized his sin and hid himself from the sight of God? (Gen. III.) Is it the law of Moses through which Cain recognized his sin and said, “My sin is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. IV)? Or the law through which Pharaoh recognized his sin and said, “The Lord is righteous, but I and my people are impious” (Exod. IX)?

If these men, and countless others before the law of Moses, recognized their sin, then without doubt it is not the law of Moses of which the Apostle says, “I did not know sin except through the law,” and of which he says, “I did not know desire unless the law said, ‘You shall not desire.’” Rather, it is that law of which we have often [Col. 1422D] spoken, the law written in human hearts—not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God—which teaches each person what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided.

It is therefore this law through which a human being recognizes his sin. Here he plainly calls it the natural law, which remains unknown to us until, as we advance in age, we learn to distinguish between good and evil and hear it from our own conscience. For it speaks to us within our conscience and says, “You shall not desire.”

But since this law is not always, nor from the beginning when a human being is born, found in a person, but for a time, while his age does not yet permit it, he lives without this law—as Paul himself admits when he says, “I was once alive without the [Col. 1423A] law”—during the time when we lived without the law we did not know desire. He did not say, “I did not have it,” but said, “I did not know it,” as though desire existed but it was not known what desire was.

When reason comes, however, and the natural law finds a place in us as we advance in age, it begins to teach us what things are good and to restrain us from evil. Thus, when it says, “You shall not desire,” we learn from it itself that the desire we previously did not know is evil.

But sin, having taken the opportunity, worked in me every desire through the commandment. The law of which he says, “I did not know desire unless the law said, ‘You shall not desire,’” is itself also called a commandment. He therefore says that, through the opportunity provided by this commandment by which we are forbidden to desire, sin burned more fiercely in us and [Col. 1423B] worked every desire in us.

For in that in which the flesh desires against the spirit—that is, against the law that says, “You shall not desire”—it also opposes the law and wages a kind of battle, so that it may not merely satisfy desire but also conquer its adversary. This, then, is the opportunity that he says comes from the commandment. For, in some inexplicable way, the things that are forbidden are desired more ardently. And so, although the commandment is holy, just, and good—for what forbids evil is necessarily good—when it forbids desire, it provokes and inflames it more strongly; through what was good, therefore, it worked death in me.

The Apostle nevertheless indicates here that the origin of sin arose from desire: when desire is forbidden by the law, whether by the law of Moses, which says, “You shall not desire,” or by the natural law, as we explained above, what is forbidden is sought with greater contentiousness [Col. 1423C].

It should certainly be understood that desire is presented here as blameworthy. Yet in many cases it is also praiseworthy, as we showed above:

“Without the law sin was dead. I was once alive without the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived. I died, and the commandment that had been given for life was found by me to be for death.”

Almost all these matters have already been treated fully above. Therefore, so that we do not go over the same things too often, we shall briefly recall what has been said.

We have shown that sin is dead in us without the law—that is, before the rational faculty within us became strong through age [Col. 1423D]—when we also gave the example of a child striking or cursing his father or mother. According to the law that forbids striking or cursing one’s father or mother, sin appears to be committed in such a case; but that sin is said to be dead because the law is not yet present in the child to teach him that what he is doing is not permitted.

It is certain that without this law both Paul and all human beings once lived—that is, during childhood. For at that time all were alike incapable of this natural law. Otherwise Paul’s statement would not appear to be true. For how could Paul be proved to have lived without the law of Moses, when he himself confesses that he was “a Hebrew of Hebrews” and circumcised on the eighth day according to the precepts of the law (Phil. [Col. 1424A] III)?

But in the manner we have described, he too once lived without the natural law, in childhood. At that time, he said, sin was not in a human being, but was dead; afterward it revived, when the natural law came and began to forbid desire. That law, as it were, raised sin from the dead. For the nature of sin is this: that what the law forbids should be done.

When sin revived, therefore, he says, “I died.” Who died? Clearly, the soul that had done what the law forbade. “The soul that sins,” as the prophet says, “it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). The commandment, then, which had been given for life, was found to be for death to the soul: it had been given to teach it the works of life, but it resulted in death when the soul did not so much flee what was forbidden as desire it more ardently.

Nevertheless, I am troubled by how he can say [Col. 1424B] that sin was dead and revived. It seems that nothing can be called dead unless it once lived and afterward lost its life. But when he says that it “revived,” he teaches that it did not receive a new life recently, but was restored to its former life. The very expression “revived” means to live again.

We, however, say that this death of sin was given as a benefit by God during the time when we lived without the law. Even when, at the coming of the commandment—which is holy, just, and good—sin revives in us and kills us, nevertheless “sin, having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.”

This does not accuse the commandment by saying that the opportunity through which sin killed me came from the commandment. Rather, the following is the meaning of the statement. The law is said to teach what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided [Col. 1424C]. It is necessary that what it says must be avoided should teach us what sort of thing it is, so that it may more easily be avoided through this knowledge; for no one can avoid what he does not know.

If someone, having been taught by the law what the thing is that he ought to avoid, does not so much avoid it as do it, he will appear to have received from the law the opportunity—the knowledge—that the thing ought not to be done. Yet the law did not teach him for this reason, so that he might do what he ought not to do and die, but so that he might not do it and live.

Thus sin, having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Or, since he says, “Sin through the commandment deceived me and through it killed me,” he may here have called “sin” the very author of sin, concerning whom it is written, “The serpent deceived me” (Gen. III); or he may have personified sin as someone who seemed to deceive the human being [Col. 1424D] through the opportunity provided by the commandment, making desire sweet, so that the soul, delighting in the sweetness of desire, might transgress the commandment that said, “You shall not desire,” and die.

But so that no one might attribute to the commandment of the law the fact that the soul was deceived and killed through the opportunity provided by the precept, the Apostle adds and says: “Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” For the commandment is good, and the law is holy; it commands good things and enjoins the observance of good things.

“What, then,” he says, “was good became death to me? By no means.” He necessarily refutes the objection that arises and says that it was not the good of the law and the commandment that brought death upon him, but that sin, so that [Col. 1425A] its wickedness might appear, brought death upon him through what was good.

The commandment is good if it is kept; but if it is not kept, it necessarily becomes evil for the one who has lost the good. Thus sin itself becomes exceedingly sinful through the opportunity provided by the commandment.

We said above that he has, as it were, personified sin, and that he speaks of sin itself as having become exceedingly sinful through the opportunity provided by the commandment. He speaks from the standpoint of that personification. For sin is less serious if one admits what is not forbidden; but if one commits what is forbidden and prohibited, one is, so to speak, exceedingly sinful, because one has not only committed what one ought not to have committed but has also transgressed a commandment.

When we said *peccatum* (“sin”), *peccator* (“sinner”), we preferred to accept a defect of expression rather than fail to convey the Apostle’s meaning completely [Col. 1425B]. For in Latin the noun *peccatum* (“sin”) constrained us, since it is declined in the neuter gender; in Greek, however, it is feminine, and therefore we called it *peccator* (“sinner”) in the masculine form, whereas there it can be called *peccatrix* (“female sinner”) in the feminine form.

We know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. (Aug.) When he says, “I have been sold under sin,” it must be understood that each person, by sinning, sells his soul to the devil, receiving as though a price the sweetness of temporal pleasure. Hence our Lord is also called the Redeemer, because we had been sold in the manner just described.

(Orig.) If that interpretation concerning the diversity of laws which we have maintained seemed to anyone to have been adopted too boldly, let him now observe in this chapter how not only a diversity of laws but also a diversity of persons [Col. 1425C] is introduced.

For Paul, who elsewhere said, “We do not live according to the flesh, but we wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X), says in the present passage that he is carnal, and here says that he has been sold under sin. Elsewhere he had said, “You were bought with a price” (I Cor. VII), and again, “Christ redeemed us” (Gal. III). Elsewhere again he said, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II), and again he says, “Because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. VIII). Now he says, “Good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.”

If good did not dwell in his flesh, how does he say that our body is the temple of God and the temple of the Holy Spirit? And how do the other statements in which he confesses that he is led captive by the law of sin that is in his members and that it struggles against the law [Col. 1425D] of his mind accord with apostolic dignity, and especially with Paul, in whom Christ both lives and speaks?

Let us therefore gather from these things how it is customary for divine Scripture to change secretly the persons, things, and causes about which it seems to speak, or rather to use the same names for different things in different places.

In the present passage the Apostle says: “We know that the law is spiritual.” Even in saying this—“We know that the law is spiritual”—he speaks with apostolic authority. For one who is carnal and sold under sin does not know that the law is spiritual; rather, the one who has the Spirit of God within him knows that it is spiritual.

This statement is appropriately understood of the law of Moses. It is the very law that, for one who understands spiritually [Col. 1426A], is a spiritual law and a life-giving Spirit; but for one who understands carnally, it is remembered as the law of the letter and the letter that kills.

When he says, “I am carnal, sold under sin,” he now assumes in himself the person of the weak, as a teacher of the Church. For this reason he also said elsewhere: “I became weak to the weak, that I might win the weak” (I Cor. IX). Thus, for those who are weaker—that is, the carnal and those sold under sin—Paul becomes carnal and sold under sin, and he speaks the things that it is customary for them to say, whether under a pretext of excuse or of inexcusable guilt.

Speaking of himself as though from their person, he says: “I am carnal, sold under sin”—that is, living according to the flesh and reduced, by the price of lust and desire [Col. 1426B], under the power of sin.

(Aug.) “We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal.” By this he sufficiently shows that the law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual people, and that they become spiritual only through grace. For the more similar a person becomes to the spiritual law—that is, the more he himself rises into a spiritual disposition—the more he fulfills it. The more he delights in it, the less he is oppressed under its name and the more he is enlivened by its light; for “the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII), and “the law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls” (ibid.), when grace grants forgiveness of sins and pours in the spirit of charity, so that righteousness is not merely moderate but also delightful.

It is written in Malachi: “Remember the law of Moses [Col. 1426C] my servant, which I commanded him in Horeb for all Israel, the precepts and judgments” (Mal. IV). “Remember,” he says, “the law of Moses my servant, which I gave him on Mount Horeb, which is Sinai, for all Israel, the precepts and judgments.” Yet the Apostle says, “We know that the law is spiritual.”

And blessed David says: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII). Spiritually, too, all were eating the heavenly manna, and the whole people of Israel were drinking from the same spiritual rock that followed them; “the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

Those who believe in Christ ought spiritually to observe the precepts of the law that he gave at Horeb—which is interpreted as “dryness,” through which the moisture of all vices is boiled away, and in the rays of the sun of righteousness the rheum of lust is dried up.

(Ambr.) He therefore calls the law of Moses [Col. 1426D] spiritual, the law that was given on tablets. Because it forbids sin, it is spiritual; for it prohibits the worship of invisible [visible] and carnal things. These statements serve to commend the law, so that it should not be thought worthy of blame because it exercised severity against sinners.

But he calls the human being carnal while he sins. “Sold under sin”: to be sold under sin means to derive one’s origin from Adam, who first sinned, and to become subject to sin through one’s own offense, as the prophet Isaiah says: “You have been sold because of your sins” (Isa. L). Adam first sold himself, and therefore all his offspring have been subjected to sin.

Consequently, a human being is weak in observing the precepts of the law unless he is strengthened by divine assistance. This is why he says [Col. 1427A]: “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin”—that is, the law is firm and just and free from blame, but the human being is fragile and subjected to his ancestral offense, so that he cannot exercise his own power in obedience to the law.

Therefore one must flee to God’s mercy, so as to escape the severity of the law and, released from sins, resist the enemy thereafter with God’s favor.

For what does it mean to be subjected to sin except to have a body corrupted by the fault of the soul? If sin enters [casts itself] into it and drives the human being like a captive into offenses, so that he does its will, the Lord says, among other things: “The devil comes and takes away what has been sown in their heart, so that they may not be saved” (Luke VIII).

Hence the same Apostle says in another Epistle: “Our struggle is not against flesh [Col. 1427B] and blood, but against rulers and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI), whom it is clear are Satan’s attendants.

Before the transgression of the human being, before he handed himself over to death, these powers did not have access to the human interior or the ability to insert contrary thoughts. Through his cunning, therefore, he arranged to surround the human being by speaking through the serpent. After he had surrounded and subjected him, he gained power over him, so as to strike the inner human being by joining himself to his mind. Thus a person cannot recognize what in his thought is his own and what belongs to the devil unless he looks to the law.

For what I do, I do not understand; for I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. (Orig.) When he says, “I do not know what I do,” he does not mean so much that [Col. 1427C] a carnal person is unaware of the act itself that he performs, but that he is said to be unaware of the cause of the act he performs.

When he says, “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate,” he shows that, although the one who speaks these words is carnal and sold under sin, he nevertheless attempts to resist vices to some extent, through the prompting of the natural law. But he is conquered by vices and overcome against his will, as often happens. For example, someone proposes to endure patiently one who provokes him, but finally he is conquered by anger and suffers this against his will: he becomes angry although he does not wish to be angry.

The same thing also commonly happens through the vice of fear, so that someone is frightened against his will by dread and terror. It often happens through the elation produced by sudden or unexpected honor, so that a person becomes more arrogant and more swollen with pride than he wishes.

(Aug.) “What I do,” he says, [Col. 1427D] “I do not understand.” For here the word is “I do not understand,” as though he did not know that he was sinning. This would contradict what he said: “But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what was good,” and the earlier statement: “I did not know sin except through the law.”

How, then, does sin appear, or how did he recognize what he does not understand? But it is said in the same way in which he will say to the wicked: “I never knew you” (Matt. VII). For nothing is hidden from God, when the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, “to destroy their remembrance from the earth” (Ps. XXXIII).
