Or, certainly, the expression in this passage, “What I do, I do not understand,” is used so that it may be understood as “I do not approve.” For just as darkness is not seen but is perceived by comparison with light, so “to perceive darkness” means “not to see” [Col. 1428A]. Thus sin, because it is not illuminated by the light of righteousness, is discerned by not understanding, just as darkness is said to be perceived by not seeing.

To this belongs what is said in the Psalm: “Who understands his transgressions?” (Ps. XVIII.)

But if I do what I hate, I consent to the law, because it is good. (Amb.) He proves that the law rightly forbids, since he confesses that he does unwillingly what the law forbids. He says that what the law commands belongs to his nature, because he declares that what he does outwardly is hateful to him.

(Aug.) If you do what the law hates, how do you consent to the law? Certainly, if I do what I do not want, I consent to the law because it is good. How so? The law commands, “You shall not desire.” My weakness does not fulfill the law, but my will consents to the law.

(Orig.) Nevertheless, insofar as he does not will evil, he consents to the law of God, because it is good [Col. 1428B], since it forbids evil. And the natural law is brought into a kind of harmony with the law of God, so that they will the same things and reject the same things.

If, then, we consent to the law of God according to our will, the evil that we do is no longer performed by us, but by the sin that is in us—that is, by the law and will of the flesh, which leads us captive under the law of sin that is in our members.

(Aug.) The law is sufficiently defended against every accusation. But care must be taken lest anyone think that these words take away from us the free choice of the will; that is not the case. The human being is now being described as placed under the law before grace.

The sinner is conquered when he tries to live righteously by his own strength without the help of God’s liberating grace. Yet within free choice he has the power to believe in the Liberator and receive grace, so that, once he has been liberated and assisted by the one who grants grace [Col. 1428C], he may no longer sin. Thus he ceases to be under the law and becomes with the law, or in the law, fulfilling it through the love of God, which he could not fulfill through fear.

Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. (Orig.) Here too Paul speaks as carnal when he says, “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” But Paul as spiritual says elsewhere: “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me” (I Cor. XV).

Just as this man attributes his labors not to himself but to the grace of God that worked in him, so the carnal man attributes his evil works not to himself but to the sin that dwells and works in him.

(Ambr.) Therefore he says, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” [Col. 1428D] For he saw that the law forbade what he was doing, and he agreed that it ought not to be done. By this he declares that the impulse by which these things are done belongs to something else, namely, sin.

He always names it “sin,” although it is known to be the devil with his angels, because these things would not have come about if the first human being had not sinned. Thus it is sin that does all these things.

[Col. 1429A] I know, then, that nothing good dwells in me—that is, in my flesh. (Orig.) For Christ does not yet dwell in him, nor is his body yet the temple of God. Nevertheless, the person here presented is not altogether alien to what is good. In intention and will he has begun to seek what is good, but he is not yet able to attain the good in deeds and actions. For there is a certain weakness in those who are beginning their way of life: although someone may immediately wish to do everything that is good, the result does not immediately follow the will.

Thus he deliberates within himself and resolves, for example, not to become angry, and fixes this determination in his will. But because the vice of anger has gained mastery over him through long practice and enduring habit, it resists his will and purpose as well; and the force of fury, following its accustomed path, bursts forth. The vice of lust acts similarly. Through the same disease of habit, lying also steals upon him, fear deters him, and in each of these matters the person who is now beginning his conversion appropriately says: “The will is present with me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish the good.”

[Col. 1429B] For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate. (Amb.) It should be noted that he does not say, as some think, that the flesh is evil, but that what dwells in the flesh is not good, namely, sin. How does sin dwell in the flesh, when it is not a substance but a transgression [or deprivation] of the good? Because the body of the first man was corrupted through sin so that it could be dissolved. The corruption of sin itself remains in the body by the condition resulting from the offense, retaining the force of the divine sentence pronounced upon Adam; this is the sign of the devil, at whose instigation he sinned. Therefore, because the cause of what was done remains, sin is said to dwell in the flesh. The devil approaches the flesh as though it were subject to his own law, and sin remains as it were within sin, because the flesh is now “of sin,” so that he may deceive the human being by evil suggestions [Col. 1429C], preventing him from doing what the law commands.

“The will is present with me.” He asserts that the things commanded by the law are good, and says that they naturally please him and that he wishes to do them. “But I do not find the ability to accomplish the good.” What the law commands therefore pleases him, and he has the will to do it; but the power and strength to fulfill it are lacking. For he is so oppressed by the power of sin that he cannot go where he wishes, nor is he able to resist, because another is lord over his power. The human being is already weighed down by the habit of sinning and more easily yields to sin than to the law, although he knows that the law teaches what is good. Even if he wishes to do good, habit presses upon him, with the enemy as his helper.

(Greg.) Hence it is written in Job (Job 38): “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who gave birth to the frost from heaven?” Thus Paul says, referring to the earth that has been soaked, how greatly it is oppressed by the ice of discipline [Col. 1429D]: “The will is present with me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish the good.” For the one who asserts that he possesses the will already shows, through the infusion of grace, the seeds hidden within him. But by saying that he does not find the ability to accomplish the good, he plainly indicates how greatly he is oppressed by the ice of the heavenly dispensation.

(Cassian.) Therefore let us investigate more carefully what the principal good was that the Apostle could not accomplish, although he wished to. We know many good things, and we cannot deny that the blessed Apostle and all men of similar merit both possessed them by nature and acquired them by grace. There is good chastity, praiseworthy continence, admirable prudence, generous kindness, watchful sobriety, moderate self-restraint, devout mercy, and holy justice [Col. 1430A]. There is no doubt that all these qualities were so full and perfect in the Apostle Paul and his companions that religion was taught by them more through the instruction of their virtues than through words.

And what of the fact that they were always consumed by unceasing care for all the churches and by vigilant solicitude? How great a good of mercy this is! How great a perfection it is to burn on behalf of those who cause scandal and to become weak with those who are weak! Since, then, the Apostle abounded in such gifts, what was that good whose perfection he lacked? We shall not be able to recognize it unless we advance into the disposition in which he himself spoke.

All the virtues we have mentioned, although they are like the most brilliant and precious gems, nevertheless, when compared with that illustrious and supreme pearl which the Gospel merchant sought and desired to purchase by selling all that he possessed [Col. 1430B], become so diminished and despised in worth that, once they have been sold without hesitation, the possession of that one good enriches the seller of countless goods.

What, then, is the one thing so incomparably superior to those many and such great goods that, once all else has been rejected and cast aside, it alone ought to be possessed? Surely it is that “better part.” When Mary preferred its magnificence and permanence to the task of receiving and showing hospitality, the Lord praised it in these words: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but few things are necessary—or even one. Mary has chosen the good [or better] part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10).

There is therefore one and only one *theoria*, that is, contemplation [Col. 1430C] of God, to which all the merits of justification and every pursuit of virtue are rightly subordinated. All those things that we said shone forth in the Apostle Paul are not merely good and useful, but also great and distinguished. Yet just as, for example, the metal tin, which was thought to possess some usefulness and value, becomes worthless when compared with silver, and silver in turn loses its worth when compared with gold, while gold itself is despised when compared with gems, and the multitude of gems, however distinguished, is surpassed by the brightness of a single pearl, so all those merits of holiness, although they are not only good and useful for the present but also obtain the gift of eternity, will nevertheless be judged worthless and, so to speak, saleable when compared with the merits of divine contemplation [Col. 1430D].

For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want. (Amb.) He repeats this often in order to make it clear. This is therefore what was said above: as a captive, through the causes mentioned earlier, he is compelled to do what sin wishes. If the will possesses judgment concerning the good, but the habit of carnal vices—which is called the law of the flesh or the law of the members—resists and snatches him away from the good will that he has, then, although he does evil, which he does unwillingly, he nevertheless consents to the law of God because it is good. For he hates evil and desires to do what the law commands as good.

If, then, against his will he does evil, overcome by the habit of vice and the practice of sinning, then it is no longer “I”—that is, the inner person—who does what I wish, namely, the good; rather, it is “sin dwelling in me.” For he has called the habit of sinning “sin”: “If I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” [Col. 1431A].

(Amb.) This is what he had already mentioned above: oppressed and subjected by sin, he fulfills not his own will but that of sin. Surely, because he says that a person sins unwillingly, he should therefore appear free from guilt because he does what he does not want, pressed by the force of its power? Certainly not. These things began through his own fault and negligence. Because he surrendered himself to sin by consent, sin rightly exercises dominion over him. It first persuades him, so that once he has been overcome it may rule him.

The Apostle explains these matters in order to give thanks to God and to show from how many evils God has freed the human being: what destruction he draws from Adam and what benefits he has obtained through Christ. In this way he demonstrates that the law could not help the person whom Christ rescued [Col. 1431B].

(Cassian.) Holy men perceive that they cannot accomplish the good they desire, but that they continually encounter the evil they do not want and hate—that is, movements of thought and concern for bodily matters. According to the inner person, they delight in the law of God; this inner person transcends all visible things and strives always to be united with God alone. Yet they see another law in their members, that is, one implanted in the nature of the human condition, which opposes the law of their mind and violently drags their understanding captive under the law of sin, compelling it, after abandoning that principal good, to submit to earthly thought.

Although this may appear necessary and useful to the body when it is undertaken in the administration of some religious necessity, nevertheless, in comparison with that good which delights the gaze of all the saints, it is judged by them to be evil and to be avoided, since through it they are withdrawn, in whatever manner or even for however brief a time, from the joy of perfect blessedness.

Truly, it is the law of sin that the transgression of its author introduced into the human race, through the guilt of the one upon whom the sentence of the most righteous judge was pronounced: “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat your bread by the sweat of your face” (Gen. 3). This, I say, is the law implanted in the members of all mortals. It opposes the law of our mind and keeps it from divine contemplation. The earth cursed in our works, after the knowledge of good and evil, began to produce the thorns and thistles of our thoughts; their prickles choke the native seeds of the virtues, preventing us from eating without the sweat of our face that bread of ours which descended from heaven and strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103) [Col. 1431D].

The whole human race is therefore universally subjected to this law without exception. No one, however holy, receives the bread mentioned above without the sweat of his face and the anxious concentration of his heart. But many rich people, as we see, eat this common bread without any sweat of their faces.

If I do what I do not want, he says, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. (Aug.) See how those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not commit sin and yet are not without sin, because it is no longer they themselves who commit it, but sin dwelling in them.

[Col. 1432A] Someone may ask: How did he do the evil he did not want, and how did he himself not do it, but sin dwelling in him? For he said both: “I do not do what I want,” and, “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” We must therefore understand that when the sin dwelling in us acts in us, we do not ourselves act, provided that our will in no way consents to it and even restrains the members of our body from obeying its desires. For what does sin do when we do not want it, except arouse permitted desires? If the consent of the will is not added to them, some emotion is indeed stirred, but no action is released for it.

The movement of illicit desire, however, which we do not obey and by which we therefore do not act, is nevertheless also said to be something we do because it is not the vigor of another nature but the weakness of our own. [Col. 1432B] From this weakness we shall be completely healed when we have become immortal in soul and body.

The guilt of this weakness and infirmity, from which illicit desires are aroused and which the Apostle calls sin, was entirely canceled through the sacrament of baptism, together with all the things we did, said, or thought while obeying it. Thereafter this weakness, although it remained within us, would not harm us if we never rendered obedience to its illicit desires, whether by action, speech, or silent consent, until it too should be healed.

I find, then, a law for me who wish to do good: evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person. (Orig.) [Col. 1432C] Here too, as we have often pointed out above, the expressions do not seem to be explained in their proper order, but are obstructed either by an abundance of conjunctions or by their particular usages. We should therefore read them in an arrangement of this kind, so that the meaning may become clearer:

“Since evil is present with me when I wish to do good, I find the law of God and delight in it according to the inner person.”

By this he shows that the inner person—that is, the will and purpose by which one begins to turn toward the Lord—consents to the law of God and delights in it. But, as we said above, once someone has willed to turn toward good, the practice of good action does not immediately follow. The will is quick and turns immediately, whether impediment is present or not; action, however, is slow, because it requires practice, skill, and labor in doing.

[Col. 1432D] To make this clearer, let us use an illustrative comparison. Suppose that someone wishes to become wise. He does not immediately become wise as soon as he wishes to do so, although the will precedes, and no one can become wise without the will. Nevertheless, once the will is present, labor, study, diligence, vigils, instruction, and training must be applied; only after long practice and continual meditation does he eventually become wise.

This person therefore had the will to be wise immediately from the beginning, but the work of wisdom was not immediately present. Even while he is being educated in order to become wise, how many foolish things he does, and how many things contrary to wisdom! Yet he is able to understand how foolishly he has acted, for he already possesses a devotion to wisdom. He is not yet so wise, however, that he can avoid admitting something foolishly [Col. 1433A].

The same order must be observed with regard to chastity: someone does not immediately fulfill chastity in action merely because he has decided to profess it, so that he is no longer troubled by any goads of desire. The same must be understood of gentleness, patience, and each of the virtues. In all these matters it is appropriate to say: “I delight in the law of God,” that is, in the virtues, “according to the inner person.”

(Amb.) He says that the mind delights in the things handed down by the law. This is the inner person, because sin does not dwell in the mind but in the flesh, which derives from the origin of sinful flesh, and through transmission all flesh becomes sinful. If the soul too were derived by transmission, and sin dwelt in the soul itself, then the soul of Adam sinned more than the body. But the sin of the soul corrupted the body.

[Col. 1433B] Sin therefore dwells in the flesh, as though at the doors of the soul, so that it will not permit the soul to go where it wishes. But if it dwelt in the soul, the human being would never recognize himself. Now, however, he recognizes himself and delights in the law of God.

But I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. (Orig.) What he had said above—“the will to do good is present with me”—he here calls the will for the good the law of the mind. This law of the mind agrees with the law of God and consents to it.

[Col. 1433C] But again he calls the movements of the body and the desires of the flesh the law of the members, which leads the soul captive and subjects it to the laws of sin. For it is certain that the desires of the flesh draw the soul toward sin and subject it to sin’s laws. Just as the law of the mind, which agrees with the law of God, brings the soul to the law of God if it is able to possess it, so the law that is in the members, through the desires of the flesh, subjects the soul to the laws of sin if it seduces it.

(Amb.) He names four laws. The first is the spiritual law, which is also natural, reformed through Moses and established with authority; this is the law of God. Next is the law of the mind, which consents to the law of God. Third is the law of sin, which he says dwells in the members as a result of the transgression of the first man. Fourth is the law that appears in the members when it suggests evil and then withdraws.

These laws, however, appear to be four repetitions, although they are two, namely, good and evil. The law of the mind is itself the spiritual law, or the law of Moses, which is called the law of God. The law of sin is the same as the law that he says appears in the members and contradicts the law of our mind [Col. 1433D].

(Aug.) He calls the law of sin that by which anyone entangled in the habit of the flesh is bound. He says that this law opposes the law of his mind and takes him captive under the law of sin. From this it is understood that the person being described is not yet under grace.

(Greg.) For if carnal habit merely opposed him without taking him captive, there would be no dominion. Its dominion consists in this: we obey and serve depraved and carnal desires. But if such desires arise and we do not obey them, we are not taken captive and are under grace. It is one thing to endure battles bravely, and another to be weakened and defeated by battles. In the former, virtue is exercised so that one may not be exalted inwardly; in the latter, virtue is utterly extinguished so that it cannot endure.

[Col. 1434A] Whoever, then, knows how to bear the trial of combat bravely, even when shaken by temptation, presides in the high citadel of tranquility. He sees within himself the conflicts of vices subject to him, and, broken by no pleasure, he gives them no consent.

“I see,” he says, “another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.” Where the law of sin struggles against the law of the mind, it is still dawn. The light has already appeared, but it has not yet completely driven away the darkness that is passing. It is still dawn because, while the law of the flesh strikes against the law of the mind and the law of the mind against the law of the flesh, light and shadow clash with one another in turn.

(Orig.) But after Paul had taught that these struggles are found within the human being when he assumed the more fragile person, and had shown that the soul is dragged into the power of sin, even against its will, through the desires of the flesh and the very practice of sinning, he uses an exclamation, still speaking in the person whom he has described, and says:

[Col. 1434B] Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? He sees himself as wretched, with so many laws opposing one another within him and so many battles being stirred up. The flesh fights against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; the law of the members opposes the law of the mind; the soul is led captive under the law of sin and is made subject to its yoke, even while the inner person delights in the law of God.

[Col. 1434C] (Amb.) He calls the human being wretched because he is born under sin. Is the human being not truly wretched when he has inherited this condition of transgression and has sin as an enemy within him, through which Satan gains access to him?

(Orig.) How, then, should a human being not call himself wretched amid so many and such great evils, and while dwelling in a body of death? It is rightly called a body of death because sin dwells in it, and sin is the cause of death.

This exclamation therefore comes from the person whom the Apostle describes as having received the beginnings of conversion: the will for good is present in him, but the good has not yet come into effect. He does not find the ability to accomplish the good because the practice and exercise of the virtues have not yet grown strong within him.

[Col. 1434D] The answer to his question—“Who will deliver me from this body of death?”—is given no longer in the person of that man but with apostolic authority: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” From this it is clear that the Apostle described all these things and set forth the evils that were being done within us in order finally to show and teach from how many evils and from how many deaths Christ has rescued us.

(Amb.) By the grace of God the human being has been delivered from this body of death. By “death” he means the death that he previously showed to have been devised in hell for the destruction of humanity through sin, which is called the second death. The body of death is all sins. For many sins constitute one body, and the individual sins are like members discovered by one author; from these the human being, rescued by the grace of God through baptism, has escaped the death mentioned above.

He would not say that a person placed in a fleshly body had been rescued from that very body. Rather, he called “body” that which, as he indicated above, is destroyed through baptism and observance of the law [Col. 1435A]. When he says “from the body of death,” he shows that there is another body which is not of death.

(Aug.) Next he begins to describe the human being established under grace. This is the third degree among the four that we distinguished. To this degree belongs what he immediately adds: “So then I myself, with the mind, serve the law of God, but with the flesh, the law of sin.” For although carnal desires exist, the person established under grace no longer serves them by consenting to commit sin; with his mind he serves the law of God, but with his flesh the law of sin.

By the law of sin he means the mortal condition resulting from Adam’s transgression, through which we became mortal. From this stain of the flesh carnal desire arises, and with reference to it he says elsewhere (Eph. 2): “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.”

[Col. 1435B] (Amb.) “I myself,” he says—that is, “I who have been delivered from the body of death”—serve the law of God with my mind or spirit, but with my flesh the law of sin, that is, of the devil, who through the flesh subject to him introduces evil suggestions into the soul.

Because the human being is twofold, consisting of flesh and spirit, he says that he serves the law of God with his mind because the spirit is devoted to God and, having recovered its own power, can resist the sin that acts through the flesh. For the flesh has been corrupted and subjected to death. It had been made in such a way that, through its fellowship and union with the soul, it would not die; but it received desires, whose burden it transfers, as it were, to the spirit, so that the spirit too is weighed down.

But because the grace of God rejects that death, he says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin,” as has been stated. For the spirit is now free and, restored to a good habit with the help of the Holy Spirit, can despise evil suggestions. Authority has been restored to it, so that it dares to resist the enemy.

[Col. 1435C] One who is no longer liable cannot in any way be pursued against his will. But the flesh, because it has no judgment and is incapable of discernment—for it is a brute nature—cannot close the entrance to the enemy, preventing him from entering and suggesting things contrary to the spirit. Therefore he says: “With the flesh I serve the law of sin.”

Since one human being consists of flesh and soul, in that part by which he understands he serves God, but in the other part, by which he is foolish, he serves the law of sin. If the human being had remained in the condition in which he was made, the enemy would not have had the power to approach his flesh and whisper things contrary to the soul.

But because the whole human being was not fully restored by the grace of God to his original state, the sentence pronounced upon Adam stood in the way. For it would have been unjust to dissolve a sentence justly issued. Therefore, while the sentence remained, God’s providence devised a remedy so that the salvation which the human being had lost through his own fault might be restored to him.

[Col. 1435D] Thus the person reborn here was to believe that his adversary, defeated by the power of Christ, would not dare, once the sentence of the first death had been pierced, to claim the human being for himself; with the race of Adam united, he now remains wholly immortal, lest he be restored to the condition of his first origin.

## CHAPTER VIII

He shows that one must adhere firmly to the law of Christ, since his law is the law of life and the law of the Spirit.

[Col. 1436A] Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. (Orig.) Above he taught what the difference was among those who, placed as it were in a contest, live according to the law of God in their mind but are driven by the desires of the flesh under the law of sin. Now he speaks of those who are no longer partly in the flesh and partly in the spirit, but are wholly in Christ, and he declares that nothing deserving condemnation exists in them, because the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed them from the law of sin and death.

The law of the Spirit of life is one and the same as the law of God, just as the law of sin is one and the same as the law of death. There will therefore be no condemnation for those who are completely freed from the law of sin, which is the law of death, and serve the law of God, which is the law of the Spirit [Col. 1436B].

To serve the law of God and to be under the law of the Spirit is to serve Christ. To serve Christ is to serve wisdom, to serve justice, to serve truth, and to serve all the virtues together.

It should not therefore be thought that someone is suddenly and immediately transferred from service to the law of sin and made to be in Christ Jesus as soon as he wishes, so that no condemnation on account of sin is now found in him. Justice requires its due in each person: it tests whether he has been so corrected and reformed that no unjust action can be found in him from which condemnation might follow.

Likewise, truth examines its due in each person, asking whether someone transferred from the law of sin is now found in no respect to contaminate the service of truth with falsehood. Chastity likewise examines its due, asking whether he is stained by no impure desires [Col. 1436C]. Piety and wisdom likewise examine their due in each person. When they find that these qualities remain in him rightly and completely, then he will be considered to be in Christ and to have no condemnation.

There is no doubt that these things are acquired through long practice and meditation and through vigilant labor. They do not happen to the idle or the sluggish, but gradually as one makes progress: first a few sins, then fewer, and finally, if one is able to attain it, none.

(Aug.) He clearly shows that there is no condemnation if carnal desires exist, provided that one does not obey them in order to sin. This occurs in those who are under the law, not yet under grace. For those under the law not only have a concupiscence that opposes them, but are also led captive when they obey it. This does not happen to those who serve the law of God with their mind.

[Col. 1436D] (Cassian.) “There is now no condemnation,” he says, “for those who are in Christ Jesus, for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death.” From this it is understood that the daily grace of Christ absolves all his saints from the law of sin and death, into which they are continually compelled to fall, even unwillingly, when they ask the Lord for the remission of their debts.

It therefore appears that the blessed Apostle uttered this sentence not in the person of sinners but in the person of those who are truly holy and perfect: “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I hate”; and, “I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” [Col. 1437A].

For the law, he says, of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death. (Amb.) He demands security for the human being through the grace of God, so that he need not be anxious about the suggestions of the devil, provided that he rejects them. They will do the human being no harm at the second death, because the law of faith—that is, of the Spirit—has freed the human being from the second death by condemning sin.

It no longer harms the human being that sin remains in the flesh, provided that he resists it, mindful of God’s help. Indeed, the person who suppresses the counsels of sin remaining in the flesh ought to be crowned. For it is a great skill to avoid the snares of a domestic enemy.

The law of the Spirit of life is therefore itself the law of faith. The law of Moses is also spiritual because it forbids sinning; [Col. 1437B] yet it is not the law of life, because it cannot remit sins to those deserving death so as to give life to the dying.

This law, because it both does not desire sin and turns a person away from death, is called the law of the Spirit of life. It does not consist in the letter but in the Spirit, because it is believed with the heart, and what is believed is spirit. This law, then, in Christ Jesus—that is, through faith in Christ—frees the believer from the law of sin and death.

The law of sin is the law that he says dwells in the members and strives to persuade one toward what is contrary. The law of death is the law of Moses, because it puts sinners to death. In another Epistle, among other things, he says concerning the authority of the law: “If the ministry of death, formed in stones, was in glory,” and so forth (2 Cor. 3).

It is therefore not surprising if the spiritual law is also called the law of death, since the Gospel is likewise so called. For elsewhere he says, among other things: “To some, an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” [Col. 1437C] (2 Cor. 2). For those whom the appearance or report of virtues or of deeds attracted to faith, the Gospel was an odor of life. But for those whose understanding was inflamed by the power of the deeds to contradict them, the preaching of faith was an odor of death.

Faith is therefore one, yet it produces different effects in people. So too the sun, although it is one, melts wax and hardens clay. Thus, according to the mind with which someone has perceived faith, so will it advance him.

Someone might say: If faith produces the same effects as the law, why is faith itself not also called in part the law of death? For it kills those who do not believe. But this is not so. Faith was given to justify those who flee to it, so that it might forgive those whom the law holds guilty and so that those who act under faith might be free from sin. Those who act under the law, however, are liable.

Those who do not obey faith will not be killed by faith but by the law [the text reads “under the law,” but the intended reading is evidently “by the law”], because those who do not approach faith remain held guilty by the law. Therefore all who perceive the words of faith with an evil disposition remain in death.

Let us now see what difference there is when the spiritual law and the law of the Spirit are mentioned. The spiritual law is so called because it gives commandments through which one does not sin; whoever does not sin is called spiritual, an imitator of the heavenly powers above. The law of the Spirit is so called because God, whose faith it is, is Spirit. There, then, are words; here, the reality. There are the things belonging to God; here, God himself [Col. 1437D].

[Col. 1438A] (Orig.) We must also not omit the fact that here the one who frees from the law of sin and death is called the Spirit of life, while in the Gospel according to John it is written that the Lord said: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will free you” (John 8). It seems to me that although these may appear different in their operation or in name, in reality they are one and the same. For Christ is life, and he is the one who frees; here too the Spirit of life frees.

How could there not be one freedom in both? What the Spirit does, Christ also does, and what belongs to Christ, the Spirit does. Just as those whom the Holy Spirit sanctifies, Christ sanctifies, so those whom the Spirit of life frees, life also frees.

[Col. 1438B] The only condition is that, once freed by the law of the Spirit of life, we remain in Christ and are no longer found serving the law of sin. For just as the person freed by the law of the Spirit of life remains in Christ, who is life, so the person who serves the law of sin remains in death, which comes from the condemnation of sin.

Because what the law could not do, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did: by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and on account of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh.

(Ambrose.) He says this in order to make the baptized secure, since they have been freed from sin. “What was impossible,” he says, “for the law.” Impossible for whom? For us, certainly: it was impossible for us to fulfill the commandment of the law, because we were subject to sin.

(Origen.) But since above he has named so many laws—for he spoke of the law of God, the law of the mind, and the law of the Spirit of life—and, conversely, also mentioned the law that is in the members, the law of death, and the law of sin, we must now ask which of these laws he means here. For when he says, “[Col. 1438C] what was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh,” choosing the intended meaning is no small matter.

Nevertheless, I think that here too, as we have often said in other places, the Apostle divides the law of Moses into two parts, naming in it sometimes the flesh and sometimes the spirit. He calls that observance which is performed according to the letter the understanding of the flesh, just as he says of such a Jew: “Vainly puffed up by the understanding of his flesh.” But he calls that which is received spiritually the spirit, just as elsewhere he says (II Cor. III): “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” Thus in this passage also, when he says, “what was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh,” the understanding according to the letter may be intended. For if it is understood according to the flesh—that is, according to the letter—it was itself both impossible and weak.

[Col. 1438D] For what is so impossible as the observance of the Sabbath according to the letter of the law, as we have already said in many places? One is commanded not to leave the house, not to move from one’s place, and not to lift any burden. Since these things appear impossible to Jews who observe the law according to the flesh, they devise various foolish and ridiculous interpretations by which they seem to patch up the impossibility of the law.

What, moreover, shall I say about the system of sacrifices, which has now become altogether impossible? For there is neither a temple, nor an altar, nor any place at all for offering sacrifice; and in each of these respects the law is not merely impossible and weak, but plainly dead. Before this death it was weak, when it attempted with the blood of calves and goats, [Col. 1439A] yet could not, to take away sins; and it was weak in the laws concerning leprosy, which it was never able either to explain or to fulfill. In all these matters, therefore, and in countless others, the law was both impossible and weak, insofar as the understanding of the flesh is concerned.

(Augustine.) There is another interpretation of the statement that the law was weakened through the flesh. He most clearly teaches by this that the very commandments of the law were not fulfilled because those to whom the law had been given, before grace, were devoted to carnal goods and desired to obtain happiness from them. They feared nothing except when adversity threatened their carnal goods; and therefore, whenever those temporal goods were disturbed, they easily withdrew from the commandments of the law.

Thus the law was weakened because what it commanded was not fulfilled—not through any fault of its own, but through the flesh, that is, through those people who [Col. 1439B], desiring carnal goods, did not love the justice of the law but preferred temporal advantages to it.

For this reason God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.

(Gregory.) He came, as it is written, “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII), so that he might condemn sin on account of sin. By setting the innocence of his flesh before the enemy, he wiped away the contagion of our flesh. The enemy held us captive through our flesh; through his own flesh he cleansed us and set us free, because what we had made an instrument of guilt was turned for us, through the Mediator, into a weapon of righteousness.

(Origen.) By saying “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he shows that we possess sinful flesh, whereas the Son of God possessed the likeness of sinful flesh, not sinful flesh itself. For all of us human beings, who have been conceived from the seed of a man in union with a woman, [Col. 1439C] necessarily use the words spoken by David: “For in iniquities my mother conceived me” (Ps. L).

But because Christ came to an immaculate body not from any pollution of a man, but solely when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, he possessed the nature of our body but did not possess at all the pollution of sin that is transmitted to those conceived through the movement of desire.

(Ambrose.) For this reason the virginal womb was chosen for the Lord’s birth: so that the Lord’s flesh might differ from our flesh in holiness. It is similar in origin, but not in the quality of sin’s substance. Therefore he called it “similar” because he derived it from the same substance of flesh, but did not have the same kind of birth, since [Col. 1439D] the Lord’s body was not subject to sin.

The Lord’s flesh was purified by the Holy Spirit, so that he might be born in a body such as Adam’s was before sin, except for the sentence pronounced upon Adam.

Therefore, when God sent Christ, he condemned sin on account of sin—that is, he condemned sin by means of sin itself. For when Christ was crucified by sin, which is Satan, sin sinned in the flesh of the Savior’s body. By this deed God condemned sin in the flesh, precisely where it had sinned, just as he says in another Epistle (II Cor. II): “Triumphing over them in him,” that is, in Christ.

For it is customary to ask of anyone who has been condemned: “For what offense was he condemned?” The answer is, for example, “for murder.” So also sin was condemned in the flesh—that is, in the sin that it committed in the flesh.

By this sin [Col. 1440A] Satan was made guilty; he lost dominion over the souls he had held captive, so that he would no longer dare to hold in the second death those marked with the sign of the cross by which he was defeated.

(Augustine.) There is another interpretation. Death is owed to sinful flesh; but the Lord’s death was an act of condescension, not the payment of a debt. Nevertheless, the Apostle also calls this “sin”: the assumption of mortal flesh, although not sinful flesh. He does so because the immortal one, when he dies, acts as though he were sin.

(Origen.) That Christ was made a sacrifice for sin and offered for the cleansing of sins is attested by all the Scriptures, and especially by Paul when writing to the Hebrews, where he says: “For he did this once, offering himself as a sacrifice” (Heb. VII); and again: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII).

[Col. 1440B] Through this sacrifice of his flesh, which is called a sacrifice for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “He appeared in the last days for the destruction of sin.” Again the prophet says: “He himself bore our sins and carried our iniquities” (Isa. LIII).

Therefore, “for sin”—that is, through the sacrifice of his flesh, which he offered for sin—he condemned sin in his own flesh.

## So that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit.

Through this sacrifice of the flesh, which was offered for sin and condemned sin—that is, drove sin away and removed it—the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in us, who keep the law according to the spirit and not according to the flesh. In the latter respect, [Col. 1440C] according to what we explained above, the law was impossible and weak.

(Augustine.) The Lord’s death accomplished this: that death should no longer be feared, and that temporal goods should no longer be desired, nor temporal evils feared. In these things consisted that carnal prudence through which the commandments of the law could not be fulfilled.

When this prudence was extinguished and removed in the Lord’s human being, the righteousness of the law is fulfilled, since one does not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Thus it was most truly said: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V).

The fullness of the law, therefore, is love (Rom. XIII), and love belongs to those who walk according to the spirit. For this pertains to the grace of the Holy Spirit: when there was not love of righteousness but fear, the law was not fulfilled.

(Ambrose.) [Col. 1440D] For this reason he says that sin was condemned, so that the righteous requirement of the law given through Moses might be fulfilled in us. For we have been removed from the condition of the law and made its friends; those who have been justified are friends of the law.

But how is its righteousness fulfilled in us unless forgiveness of all sins is granted, so that, once sins have been removed, the justified person may appear to serve the law of God with the mind? This is to walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit: the devotion of the mind, which is the spirit, must not consent to the desire of sin, because through the flesh it sows the soul’s desires, in which sin resides.

“If sin has been condemned by the Savior, how can it be present?” It was condemned by the Savior, and condemned in three ways.

First, he condemned sin by not sinning, [Col. 1441A] dissenting from sin. Then sin is said to have been condemned on the cross, because it sinned. From this its authority was taken away: as though it were itself the sinner, it had held human beings in hell on account of Adam’s offense, and thereafter it would not dare to hold those in whom the sign of the cross is present.

Third, he condemned sin by making offenses void through the granting of forgiveness. For when the sinner ought to have been condemned because of the sin committed, by forgiving him he condemned the sin in him.

Therefore, if we too do not sin after the example of the Savior, we condemn sin.

## For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the spirit.

(Origen.) Here he speaks more openly, as though placing the law of Moses between us and the Jews: [Col. 1441B] “Those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh.” That is, the Jews, whom he calls Israel according to the flesh, set their minds on the things of the flesh insofar as they understand the law according to the flesh. But “those who are according to the spirit”—speaking of those whom he calls Jews in spirit, not in letter—“perceive the things of the spirit.”

(Ambrose.) Another interpretation: Whoever obeys the suggestion made through the flesh sets his mind on the things of the flesh. For what he follows appears pleasant to him, while he seeks, contrary to what is right, the practice and judgment of the flesh’s error. In the flesh, worldly error is signified, in whatever form.

But those who are according to the spirit perceive the things of the spirit. It is clear that whoever restrains himself from the desires of the flesh lives according to the law of the mind; for he considers it useful to understand what agrees with the law.

[Col. 1441C] For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.

(Origen.) Is not the statement “the mind of the flesh is death” one and the same as “the letter kills”? The mind of the flesh, therefore, is death. Death for whom? Without doubt, for the soul. For whoever understands the law according to the flesh—that is, according to the letter—does not come to Christ, who is life. Therefore the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the spirit is life and peace. Whoever understands the law spiritually possesses life and peace, which is Christ.

(Ambrose.) Another interpretation: The mind of the flesh is sin, which produces death. It is called “mind” even though the matter is foolish, because to worldly people the errors conceived from visible things, whether in thought or in action, appear to be prudence against the law of God—especially because [Col. 1441D] all their industry and cleverness is directed toward sinning.

They seem wise to themselves if they devote themselves more carefully to this, although nothing is more foolish than sinning.

There is also another mind of the flesh, one inflated by worldly reasoning, which denies that anything can happen that lacks a worldly explanation. Hence it ridicules the Virgin’s birth and the resurrection of the flesh.

But the mind of the spirit is life and peace. This truly is wisdom, which acquires life and peace. For whoever follows spiritual things, despising the allurements of the present life, will have eternal life with peace—that is, without disturbance. For where there is disturbance, there is punishment also.

## For the mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.

(Origen.) [Col. 1442A] How could the mind of the flesh—that is, carnal understanding—not be hostile to God, when it opposes Christ, does not receive the one whom God sent, and says: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God”? (John XIX.)

How, then, could such a mind and such an understanding of the law not be called hostile to God and to his law? It is not subject, nor can it be subjected, to the law that is according to the spirit. For just as life and death are opposed to each other, so the letter of the law, which kills and is also the mind of the flesh, is opposed to the spirit, which gives life and is truly the law of God.

(Augustine.) By saying that the mind of the flesh is hostile to God, he shows what he means by “hostile,” so that no one might suppose that some nature arising from an opposing principle—one not created by God—exercises hostility against God.

[Col. 1442B] Someone is therefore called God’s enemy when he does not obey his law, and this occurs through the mind of the flesh: when he desires temporal goods and fears temporal evils. The definition of prudence is usually explained in the desire for goods and the avoidance of evils.

Accordingly, the Apostle rightly calls it the mind of the flesh when these things are desired as great goods, even though they do not endure in a human being, and when the loss of things that must eventually be lost is feared.

Such a mind cannot obey the law of God. The law is obeyed only when this mind has been extinguished and replaced by the mind of the spirit, through which our hope is placed neither in temporal goods nor our fear in temporal evils.

For the same nature of the soul possesses the mind of the flesh when it pursues inferior things, [Col. 1442C] and the mind of the spirit when it chooses and loves superior things—just as the same nature of water freezes in the cold and is dissolved by heat.

But when heat is applied and the water is dissolved and warmed, no one can still call it snow. Thus he says: “It is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.”

What does “nor indeed can it be” mean? It does not mean that the human being cannot, nor that the soul cannot, nor finally that the flesh itself cannot—for the flesh is God’s creature. Rather, the mind of the flesh cannot; vice cannot, but nature can.

It is as if one were to say: “Lameness is not subject to straight walking, nor indeed can it be.” The foot can walk straight, but lameness cannot. Remove lameness and you will see straight walking.

Therefore, when he says that the mind of the flesh is hostile to God, do not understand this as though that hostility could injure God. It is hostile by resisting, not by causing harm; it harms the one in whom the mind of the flesh exists.

(Ambrose.) [Col. 1442D] It should be noted that he did not say that the flesh is hostile, but that the mind of the flesh is hostile—that is, not the substance, but either evil actions or a thought or assertion arising from error.

The mind of the flesh is, first of all, the disputation about the stars invented by human beings; then it is delight in visible things. These are hostile to God because they equate the Lord of the elements and the Maker of the world with the things he made, asserting that nothing can happen beyond what the order of the world contains.

For this reason they deny that God caused a Virgin to give birth or that [Col. 1443A] the bodies of the dead will rise, saying that it is foolish for God to have done anything beyond what human beings can understand. “O wise men of the world,” who think that God ought not to act otherwise than his created creature acts, so that he himself may be thought similar to creatures!

Thus they have been blinded so that they do not see what insult they inflict upon God. For they condemn and call incredible and foolish the work that he graciously chose to perform for the proclamation of his own praise. Consequently, this disposition cannot be subject to the law of God, since it is exercised in opposing God’s deeds.

## Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.

(Origen.) “Those who are in the flesh,” he says—that is, those who follow the law according to the letter—“cannot please God.” This too was formerly [Col. 1443B] proclaimed by God through Isaiah, when he says: “Your fasts and festivals and your great day I cannot endure; your new moons and Sabbaths my soul hates” (Isa. I).

“But you,” he says, “in whom the Spirit of God dwells—if indeed he dwells—are not in the flesh but in the spirit.” That is, you do not follow a carnal understanding of the law but a spiritual one, through which you have come to the life-giving Spirit—if indeed your actions and manner of life are such that you deserve to have the Spirit of God within you.

Thus, as we have said, he divides the law of Moses into two parts, spirit and flesh. The things that are of the spirit he called the spiritual law and handed down to us; the things that are of the flesh he left to carnal Jews.

(Ambrose.) Another interpretation: The wise men of the world are in the flesh because, [Col. 1443C] looking toward the world, they resist spiritual wisdom, since the whole world is flesh. Everything visible is assigned to the flesh; the elements are related to the flesh, indeed are its elements. Therefore whoever obeys worldly things is in the flesh.

(Augustine.) Likewise, those are in the flesh who trust in the flesh, follow their desires, dwell in them, and take delight in their pleasures, establishing a blessed and happy life in those delights. They are in the flesh and cannot please God.

For he did not say, “Those who are flesh cannot please God,” as though it meant that human beings, insofar as they are in this life, cannot please God.

“But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit.”

(Ambrose.) Those who are situated in the flesh are said not to be in the flesh if, agreeing with the Apostle John, they do not love worldly things. [Col. 1443D] For a person’s judgment fashions its own nature, as it were, so that a person is called what he thinks.

(Gregory.) Those to whom he was sending the Epistles were not outside the flesh. But because they had conquered the passions of carnal desires, they were already free through the power of the spirit and were not in the flesh. To be no longer in the flesh is, as it were, to have nothing of the love of carnal things.

When the Apostle Paul says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV), he wants “flesh” to be understood according to guilt, not flesh according to nature. He immediately shows that he means flesh according to guilt by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

In the glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, flesh according to nature will exist, but flesh according to the desires of passion will not exist, because, once the sting of death has been defeated [Col. 1444A], it will reign in eternal incorruption.

“You are not in the flesh,” he says, “but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

(Augustine.) You are not in the flesh because you do not perform the works of the flesh by consenting to the desire of the flesh. But you are in the spirit because, according to the inner person, you delight in the law of God. Yet this is so only “if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

For if you presume upon your own spirit, you are still in the flesh. Therefore let the will dwell there so that you may call for help. “If indeed,” he says, “the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

(Ambrose.) He says this ambiguously because those who had been brought into the law did not yet possess perfect faith, although he saw in them the hope of perfection. Hence at times he speaks to them as though they were perfect, and at times as though they were about to become perfect; that is, at times he praises them and at times admonishes them.

If they live according to the law of nature, in accordance with what has been mentioned above [Col. 1444B], they are said to be in the spirit, because the Spirit of God cannot dwell in one who follows carnal things.

## If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.

(Origen.) It does not seem necessary for me now to explain how the Apostle Paul employs syllogisms gathered with consistency and dialectical skill, whether here or in his other Epistles. Otherwise we might appear to be asserting his skill in knowledge rather than in speech, in which he does not wish to be called learned.

Therefore we shall hasten instead to examine the meaning of the present passage. Above, when he said, “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you,” we explained in two ways what it means to be in the spirit: either to understand the law not according to the letter but according to its spiritual [Col. 1444C] meaning, or also, with the body mortified, to live according to the laws of the spirit and not of the flesh.

Now, when he says, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him,” and then adds, “But if Christ is in you,” we must ask whether it is something different for the Spirit of God to be in someone, for the Spirit of Christ to be in someone, for Christ himself to be in someone, or for the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead to be in someone.

But insofar as I consider either the sequence of the present passage or what the Savior says in the Gospel about the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father: “He will take from what is mine” (John XV)—and insofar as he joins an explanation of this saying below, saying, “Father, all that is mine is yours, and yours is mine; therefore I said, ‘He will take from what is mine’”—when I observe such unity between the Father and the Son, it seems to me that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are called one and the same Spirit.

[Col. 1444D] Nevertheless, we can understand his statement in this way also: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” For it truly seems to be stated abruptly, as though anyone who has not become so great and such a person as to be worthy of having the Spirit of Christ is immediately denied to belong to Christ, even though the Psalms say: “All the beasts of the forests are mine, the animals on the mountains, and the oxen” (Ps. XLIX).

If the wild beasts and cattle belong to him, how could human beings not belong to him? But it can, as I have said, be understood in the same way as the Gospel saying: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X).

Thus anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ—that is, anyone who is not [Col. 1445A] moved by the same spirit toward righteousness, truth, the proclamation of the word of God, the preaching of the kingdom of heaven, the rejection of the letter of the law and the opening up of its spirit, and resistance against sin; anyone who is not prepared to go even unto death for all these things—is not his disciple.

Whoever is not such a person and does not bear such a spirit within himself is indeed Christ’s creature, just as are the beasts of the forests, the animals on the mountains, and the oxen; but he is not Christ’s disciple.

Thus: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”

(Ambrose.) The Holy Spirit abandons a person for two reasons: when the person possesses either the understanding of the flesh or the deeds of the flesh. Through these considerations, therefore, he urges people toward a good manner of life. For although human beings are raised up by God’s goodness, they are not honored by being called children of God [Col. 1445B] unless they live in such a way that they do not appear unworthy of the name granted to them.

(Augustine.) Let no one, therefore, extend himself, boast, or claim strength for himself, when nature is needy and corrupted. “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” Let him not deceive himself.

Behold, with his mercy helping us, we have the Spirit of Christ. From our delight in righteousness, our undivided faith, and our catholic peace, we know that the Spirit of God is in us. But what shall we say about that mortal flesh? What about the law in our members that resists the law of the mind? What about that cry, “Wretched man that I am”? Hear what follows:

## But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the spirit is alive because of righteousness.

(Origen.) [Col. 1445C] In this passage “the Spirit of Christ” and “Christ” seem to me to mean one and the same thing. Wherever Christ is, he himself says that we always carry the death of Christ in our body. Death is imposed upon the body because of sin—that is, so that it may not sin.

If the body is dead to sin, the spirit necessarily lives in order to practice righteousness. For whoever is dead in the body and does not serve sin must live in the spirit and serve righteousness.

Thus the same Apostle says in another passage that he handed someone over to the destruction of the flesh so that his spirit might be saved (I Cor. V).

(Augustine.) Another interpretation: By “dead body” he means mortal body. For from its mortality the need for earthly things troubles the soul and arouses certain desires; one who already serves the law of God with the mind does not obey these desires so as to sin.

The body is called dead not only because it will die through the departure of the soul, which is still to come, but also [Col. 1445D] because of the weakness of flesh and blood. Thus the Apostle says: “The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.” This life has arisen from faith, because power lives from faith.

## But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies on account of his Spirit dwelling in you.

(Origen.) Since above he had spoken of those who mortify their bodies in imitation of Christ’s death so that they may not sin, he now necessarily mentions the one who raised Christ from the dead. In this way, and by the same reasoning by which they died and were buried with Christ, [Col. 1446A] they may know that through the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead they will be given life and raised from the dead in the likeness of Christ.

He shows how this happens when he says, “on account of his Spirit dwelling in you.” For if the Spirit of Christ dwells in you, it seems necessary that his dwelling place and temple be restored to the Spirit.

(Augustine.) You who are afraid, and who are anxious even about the flesh itself: “Not a hair of your head will perish.” Adam, by sinning, condemned your bodies to death. But if his Spirit is in you, God will also give life to your mortal bodies.

Thus you will be delivered from “this body of death,” not by having no body or by having another body, but by no longer dying. He will give life to your mortal bodies on account of his Spirit dwelling in you—not because of your merits, but because of his gifts—when “this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality” (I Cor. XV).

There perfect peace exists, because the soul will suffer no disturbance from the body, which will then have been given life and changed into a heavenly condition.

## Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.

(Origen.) Consequently he now adds that we are debtors, undoubtedly of those things that we have received from the Spirit of Christ.

“But we are not debtors to the flesh.” For God did not make us in his image so that we would be enslaved to the service of the flesh. Rather, he made us so that the soul, serving its Creator, might itself make use of the service and ministry of the flesh.

(Ambrose.) It is right and clear that we ought not to obey the device of Adam, who acted carnally. [Col. 1446C] By sinning first, he left death to us as an inheritance, assigning us to the flesh. We ought instead to serve the law of Christ, who by spiritual means redeemed us from the death mentioned above.

We are debtors to him, for he justified us, stained as we were by carnal vices, cleansing us through the washing of the Spirit, and made us children of God.

Previously, situated in the flesh, we lived subject to sins according to Adam’s example. Now, freed from sin, we ought to render obedience to the Redeemer. This obedience does not benefit him, who needs nothing, but acquires eternal life for us. For he loves us in such a way that he attributes to himself what benefits us.

(Origen.) But perhaps someone will say: “How are we not debtors to the flesh, when the necessity of nature compels us to provide it with food and clothing?”

To show that it is not providing something for the flesh that is condemned, but enslaving life itself to the flesh [Col. 1446D] is condemned, he therefore adds: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.”

What it means to live according to the flesh has often already been stated: it means indulging the desires of the flesh. In this respect, therefore, he denies that we are debtors, just as he says elsewhere: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII). He does not deny that provision must be made for the flesh in necessary matters, but denies provision made in its desires.

So here also: “If,” he says, “you live according to the flesh, you will die.”

(Augustine.) Above he had already said, “The mind of the flesh is death,” not because the flesh is evil, but because living according to the flesh is evil.

(Ambrose.) Nothing is truer than this: if we live according to Adam, we will die. For Adam, by transgressing, sold himself to sin and was assigned to the flesh.

[Col. 1447A] Every sin is flesh. Because vices and offenses arise outwardly from the senses—that is, from hearing, sight, touch, smell, or taste—they are assigned to the flesh. Every thought that looks outward incurs offense. The sin of the first human being also arose outwardly.

To live according to the flesh, therefore, is death, for every act of the flesh is outside the law.

## But if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.

He wants the body to be governed by the law of the soul. Therefore he shows that if, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the actions and plans of the flesh—contrived at the instigation of the powers of this world—are restrained so that they do not receive the power to act, life is granted.

They are said to be put to death if they cease. For if they cease, they are no longer present; sin does not exist if it is not committed.

(Origen.) [Col. 1447B] This too has already been said above: how the body ought to be dead because of sin, while the spirit is life because of justification.

Therefore whoever, acting according to the spirit, puts to death the deeds of the flesh will live because of the Spirit of life dwelling in him. Each person puts to death the deeds of the flesh in this way:

The fruit of the spirit is love; hatred is a deed of the flesh. Hatred is therefore put to death and extinguished through love.

Joy likewise is a fruit of the spirit, while the sorrow of this age, which produces death, is a deed of the flesh. This sorrow is therefore extinguished if the joy of the spirit is in us.

Peace is a fruit of the spirit; dissension and discord are deeds of the flesh. It is certain, however, that discord can be put to death through peace.

Likewise, patience of the spirit extinguishes impatience of the flesh; goodness destroys wickedness; gentleness [Col. 1447C] destroys ferocity; self-control destroys intemperance; and chastity kills immodesty.

In this order, whoever through the spirit has put to death the deeds of the flesh will live.

We must carefully observe that just as he speaks not of ordinary death but of the death of sin when he says, “If you live according to the flesh, you will die,” so also he speaks not of ordinary life but of eternal life, to which everyone will attain who, according to what we explained above, has perfected himself in the spirit and put the deeds of the flesh to death.

We must also know that this putting to death of the deeds of the flesh takes place through patience, not suddenly but gradually.

At first they must grow weak in those who are beginning. Then, when they have begun to make more ardent progress and to be filled with a more abundant spirit, the deeds of the flesh will begin not merely to grow weak but to waste away.

When they have reached perfection [Col. 1447D], so that absolutely no sign of sin arises in them—in deed, word, or thought—then they are to be considered to have fully put the deeds of the flesh to death and handed them over entirely to death.

(Augustine.) Since the Apostle had said, “If by the spirit you put to death the actions of the flesh, you will live”—that is, those desires of the flesh to which not consenting is greatly praiseworthy, while not possessing them is perfection—it is now necessary to beware lest someone again presume upon his own spirit for putting the actions of the flesh to death.

Therefore, lest the human spirit exalt itself and boast that it is capable and strong enough for this work, he added and said:

Whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. Not those who live according to their flesh, not those who live according to their own spirit, not those who are driven by the pleasure of the flesh, not those who are driven by their own spirit: but all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. Someone will say to me, “Then are we led, rather than acting?” I answer: “On the contrary, you both act and are led, and you are led well if you do what is good. For the Spirit of God who leads you is an assistant to you as you act; the very name ‘assistant’ prescribes this for you, because you yourself also do something.” For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

(Ambrose.) Not by the letter but by the Spirit; not by the law commanding, threatening, and promising, but by the Spirit exhorting, illuminating, and assisting—these, he says, are led by the Spirit of God. In their actions the counsels of the rulers and powers of this world are not seen; for in those in whom they are seen, they are not sons of God but of the devil, because whoever is born of God does not sin, as the apostle John says (1 John 5). For this is what distinguishes the sons of God from the devil’s sons. Hence the Lord said to the Jews, because they were acting wickedly and contemplating murder: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8).

(Origen.) It must be observed that, just as we have shown that different laws are mentioned in this Letter under the one designation “law,” and different deaths are named under the one designation “death,” so now we see different spirits indicated under the one name “Spirit.” Thus, in the present chapter he says: “For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.” Here he clearly means the Spirit of God himself. Again, in what follows: “For you have not received,” he says, “the spirit of slavery again in fear.” By this he shows that the spirit of slavery is different from the Spirit of God whom I mentioned above. Therefore he adds: “But you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Here he shows that the Spirit of adoption is the same one whom above he called the Spirit of God. Of this he also says again: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit”—that is, the Spirit of God himself, in whom we cry to God the Father, bears witness with our spirit.

Our spirit, unquestionably, is different both from the spirit of slavery, which is given in fear, and from the Spirit who bears witness to it through the invocation of the Father. All human beings, therefore, seem to be driven by some spirit, just as Paul himself wrote: “You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to mute idols, however you were led” (1 Corinthians 12). By this he shows that even the Gentiles are led toward idols by some spirit.

There is therefore the Spirit of God, who is also the Spirit of Christ and likewise the Holy Spirit. The Spirit of adoption also seems to be called the same, as the present apostolic statement makes clear. David too, who says, “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me, and establish me with your princely spirit” (Psalm 50), seems to speak of the same Spirit. I think he was called the “princely spirit” for this reason: to show that there are indeed many spirits, but that among them this Holy Spirit, who is also called princely, holds primacy and dominion.

For just as there are many sons of God, as Scripture says, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81), yet there is one Son by nature, the Only-Begotten from the Father, through whom all are called sons; so also there are indeed many spirits, but there is one who truly proceeds from God himself and grants to all the others the grace of his name and sanctification.

That there are many spirits is also declared by Paul himself when writing to the Hebrews: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1). David likewise says: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 102). Daniel also testifies, saying: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Daniel 3). In the present passage Paul says: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit” (Romans 8); and elsewhere: “May your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5). There is no doubt that all these statements concern rational spirits.

Moreover, there are evil spirits and evil angels, as David also says: “He sent upon them the fury of his anger, a sending through evil angels” (Psalm 77). And in the Books of Kings it is written concerning Saul: “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord suffocated him” (1 Kings 16). Likewise, in the Book of Judges it is reported: “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and between the men of Shechem” (Judges 9).

This evil spirit, then, which is said either to have gone out to suffocate Saul or to have been sent to divide Abimelech and the Shechemites, is to be understood as having been sent like an executioner to exact punishments from sinners. Although such spirits are called evil because of their purpose and will, nevertheless, among those who deserve punishment they perform a service for the divine will.

So too is the spirit mentioned by the prophet Micaiah: the lying spirit who, when God had said, “Who will entice Ahab for me?” answered, “I will entice him.” And the Lord said, “By what means?” He replied, “I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets, and I will say that he should go up to Gilead, and there he will fall.” And the Lord said, “Go; you shall entice him, and indeed you will prevail” (1 Kings 22). Thus even those called evil spirits perform for God the service of punishment.

There are also other spirits, of whom David says: “With a violent spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47). Spirits of storm and spirits of burning are also mentioned. Yet I would call these material rather than rational spirits.

Having first established this distinction among the designations of “spirit,” let us now pursue the remaining matters. When he says:

“For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’”

(Augustine.) The periods of the two Testaments are most clearly distinguished: the former belongs to fear, whereas the new belongs to love. But the question arises: What is the spirit of slavery? For the Spirit of adoption as sons is certainly the Holy Spirit.

The spirit of slavery in fear is the one who has the power of death, because, in that fear, those who were under the law and not under grace were held throughout their whole life as liable to slavery. Nor is it surprising that they received this spirit through divine providence, since they pursued temporal goods—not because the law and commandment belong to that spirit. For the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. But that spirit of slavery is certainly not good. Those receive it who are unable to fulfill the commands of the law that was given, while they serve carnal desires and have not yet been taken up by the grace of the Liberator into the adoption of sons.

The spirit of slavery itself has no one in its power except one who has been handed over to it according to the order of divine providence, with God’s justice assigning to each person what is his due. The Apostle had received such authority when he said of certain persons: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1). Again, concerning another he says: “I have already judged that such a one should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Corinthians 5).

Those, therefore, who are not yet under grace but are established under the law, overcome by sins so as to obey carnal desires, and increase the guilt of their offenses through transgression, have received the spirit of slavery—that is, the spirit of him who possesses the power of death.
