For if we understand the spirit of slavery as the human spirit itself, then the Spirit of adoption also begins to be understood as that same spirit, as though changed for the better. But because we have received the Spirit of adoption, namely the Holy Spirit, whom he clearly identifies when he says, “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit,” it remains that we understand the spirit of slavery as the one whom sinners serve. Just as the Holy Spirit conquers the fear of death, so the spirit of slavery, which possesses the power of death, holds the guilty in the terror of that same death, so that each person may turn to the help of the Liberator—even against the devil’s will, since the devil always desires to keep that person in his power.

“For you have not received,” he says, “the spirit of slavery again in fear.” What does “again” mean? As when you were terrified by a most burdensome tutor. What does “again” mean? As when you received the spirit of slavery on Mount Sinai.

Someone may say, “The spirit of slavery is one thing, and the spirit of freedom another.” If they were different, the Apostle would not have said “again.” Therefore it is the same spirit, but on tablets of stone it produces fear, whereas on tablets of the heart it produces love.

You have heard how the people standing far away were terrified on the mountain by voices, fire, and smoke; but you have also heard how, when the Holy Spirit came, he descended upon each of the disciples in tongues of fire. Therefore now it is not in fear but in love, so that we may be not slaves but sons.

Whoever still does good only because he fears punishment, and does not love God, is not yet among the sons—though would that he at least feared punishment. Fear is a slave; love is free. Do what is good even from fear of punishment, if you are not yet able to do so from love of righteousness. The mistress will come, and the slave will depart, because perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4).

(Gregory.) Therefore let the mind of the elect set aside the weight of fear, exercise itself in the strength of love, desire the dignity of its renewal, and pant after the likeness of its Creator. Since it is not yet able to behold him, it must necessarily await his eternity—that is, hungering for its inner nourishment.

(Origen.) It is also written in the prophet Malachi: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master; and if I am a Father, where is my honor? And if I am a Lord, where is my fear? says the Lord Almighty.” For it is certain that a person becomes a son of God through the Spirit of adoption, but a servant of God through the spirit of slavery.

The beginning of serving God, since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110; Ecclesiasticus 1), is accomplished through the spirit of fear, when someone is still called a little child. To little children fear is a tutor. Hence the Apostle says of such a little child: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, though he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father. So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world” (Galatians 4).

You see how Paul, according to the wisdom granted to him by God, calls the spirits of slavery given in fear “guardians and stewards” of children. Each of us, so long as he is a child, is guarded by them in fear according to the inner person, until he reaches that age at which he deserves to receive the Spirit of adoption as sons and becomes already a son and lord of all. For he says: “All things are yours,” and God “has given us all things with Christ.”

This, then, is what Paul teaches: after we have died with Christ, and his Spirit has come to dwell in us, we have not again received the spirit of slavery in fear. That is, we have not once more become little children and beginners; rather, as those who have already been perfected, we have received the Spirit of adoption once for all, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” For no one but a son calls him “Father.”

(Augustine.) This cry belongs to the heart, not to the throat or lips; it sounds within and sounds in the ears of God. With her mouth closed and her lips unmoving, this Susanna cried out in this voice (Daniel 12). Let the heart cry, “Our Father who are in heaven.” Why not simply “Father”? What does “Abba, Father” mean? If you ask what “Abba” means, you are answered: “Father.” For *Abba* means “father” in Hebrew. Why, then, did the Apostle wish to place both words? Because he saw the cornerstone that the builders rejected, which became the head of the corner (Psalm 117; Matthew 21). It was not without reason that it was called a cornerstone, except because it receives into one embrace both walls coming from different directions: from one side circumcision, from the other uncircumcision; from one side “Abba,” from the other “Father.” The walls’ concord is the glory of the corner.

(Ambrose.) Having therefore been freed from fear by God’s grace, we have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, so that, considering what we were and what we have obtained by God’s gift, we may order our lives with great care, lest the name of God the Father suffer insult in us and, like the ungrateful, we run back to all the things from which we escaped.

We have received such grace that we dare to say to God, “Abba”—that is, “Father.” For this reason he admonishes us lest the confidence we have received be turned into presumption. If we display a life unlike the voice with which we say, “Abba, Father,” we insult God by calling him Father. For in his goodness he has granted us this, which is beyond our nature, so that what we are unworthy to possess by substance we may deserve through our works.

“The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are sons of God.”

(Origen.) The Spirit of adoption, then, through whom a person is adopted as a son, bears witness and confirms our spirit that we are sons of God, after we have passed from the spirit of slavery into the Spirit of adoption, when no fear remains—that is, when we do nothing because of fear of punishment but accomplish everything because of love for the Father. “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are sons of God.”

(Augustine.) It is not our spirit that bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God, but the Spirit of God. The pledge bears witness concerning the thing promised to us.

(Ambrose.) When we act well, and the Holy Spirit therefore remains in us, the Spirit of God bears witness to the voice and mind with which we cry in prayer, “Abba”—that is, “Father”—by remaining in us, since we do not say “Abba, Father” presumptuously. Let us present a life worthy of this voice. This is the testimony of sons: that the paternal mark may be seen in them through the Spirit. “And if sons, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ.”

(Origen.) Here the Apostle constructs a syllogism and says: If we have received the Spirit of adoption, then we are sons. And if we are sons, then without doubt we are also heirs. A slave awaits wages, whereas a son hopes for an inheritance.

Again he adds another increase to the conclusion: “Heirs indeed of God, and joint heirs with Christ.”

(Ambrose.) Since God the Father can in no way be called dead, while Christ his Son is said to have died because of the incarnation, how can this one who died be called the heir of one who always lives, when heirs belong only to the dead? But this concerns his humanity, not his divinity. For with God what is called “inheritance” among us is the Father’s gift poured out upon obedient sons, so that the living may be heir of the living by personal merit, not by the necessity of the deceased.

Hence the Lord in the Gospel, signifying by a rationale that is not merely human but also divine that he had divided his living substance among the living, did so in a parable; for the parable is not composed irrationally. Thus, to make us ready to obey God the Father, he exhorts us with this hope, saying that we shall be heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ. Since the hope of the reward is great, we should be all the more devoted to God’s matters, setting aside concern for worldly things.

What it means to be a joint heir of the Son of God is taught by the apostle John. Among other things, he says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

(Origen.) A person also becomes an heir of God in this way, when he deserves to receive the things that belong to God: the glory of incorruption and immortality, and the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden away. He becomes a joint heir of Christ when Christ “will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body,” and also when he deserves to obtain what the Savior himself said: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17).

There is also this dignity of Christ’s joint heirs: the Father has given all judgment to the Son. But the Son also says to his joint heirs: “You also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). In this way Christ brings his joint heirs not only into a share in the inheritance but also into participation in authority.

“If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him.”

The one who says, “I have been co-crucified to the cross with Christ” (Galatians 2), suffers with Christ; and also the one who says, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (ibid.); and again the one who says, “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2); or even the one who can say, “I fill up in my body what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Colossians 1).

(Ambrose.) To suffer with Christ is to endure persecutions for the hope of things to come and to crucify the flesh with its vices and desires—that is, to reject the pleasures and pomp of this age. When all these things have died for a person, he crucifies the world, believing in the life of the age to come, in which he hopes to become a joint heir of Christ.

(Origen.) Just as God highly exalted Christ, because he had humbled himself and become obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Philippians 2)—and gave him the name that is above every name, so God also exalts with Christ into glory those who suffer with Christ and imitate the example of his sufferings. This is the way Christ opened for his joint heirs: they are exalted not through strength or wisdom but through humility, and through patient endurance of tribulations they obtain the glory of the eternal inheritance.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1453]

## CHAPTER VIII FOLLOWS

[Col. 1453B]

“I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

(Ambrose.) This exhortation relates to what came before. Through it he shows that the small things which the faithless can inflict here are insignificant in comparison with the ordained gift in the age to come. Therefore [he commands us] to be prepared for every kind of destruction, because great rewards have been promised in return for these things, so that the mind may console itself in tribulation and grow through hope.

For we know that some—indeed many—people, for the sake of present gains that will benefit them only briefly, undertake harsh and difficult labors, yet sometimes cannot reach the goals toward which they strive, since life itself is fragile and uncertain. Sailors entrust themselves to such storms and tempests for the sake of what advantages, when they know that in these dangers death is more before their eyes than life? Soldiers, too, because of hope for a present reward, do not hesitate to rise against swords, although victory is uncertain.

How much more, then, must one suffer for Christ, whose benefits have also been deferred for us, and who promises magnificent rewards for small things and everlasting rewards with glory for temporal things.

(Origen.) Nothing worthy of or comparable to the future glory can be found. For what can you compare mortal things with immortal things, visible things with invisible, temporal things with eternal, or perishable things with everlasting? Yet if in the present life certain seeds of future glory can in some way be gathered, these seeds, I say, are gathered from tribulations and sufferings, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “For this momentary and light affliction of ours produces for us an immeasurable weight of eternal glory,” when we do not look at the things that are seen but at those that are not seen (2 Corinthians 4).

Through this he shows that whoever looks toward the things that are unseen and eternal regards every tribulation that befalls him, however savage and however long it may seem, as momentary and light. Even if he is subjected to tortures, goads, and claws, while his body is being afflicted by punishments, if he looks toward the future glory that is to be revealed and considers how, after such tortures, this body of his lowliness will be transformed so that it becomes conformed to the body of the glory of God’s Son, he regards the present tribulation as momentary and light. But he considers the weight of future glory heavy—that is, great—and eternal. The more he sees the punishments of tribulations multiplied for him, the more he understands that the weight and greatness of glory are being heaped up for him.

When he says, “To the future glory that will be revealed in us,” I think we have already sufficiently demonstrated the difference among glories: what glory has already been revealed, what glory is to be revealed, and how now “we see through a mirror, in an enigma,” but then, when the Son of Man comes in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels, “we shall see face to face” (2 Corinthians 13), just as John also said, “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

That glory which is to be revealed may also be understood as arising when instruction concerning each of the world’s constituent principles, or concerning the things above the world, begins to be understood, and the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge are disclosed. For “the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.”

(Ambrose.) Since he has called the sufferings of the present time unworthy in comparison with the future glory, he adds that creation awaits this, so that the number of the sons of God destined for life may be completed; then creation itself may finally be freed from the slavery of corruption and cease in its defect.

(Origen.) He also says that creation, being rational, possesses a certain expectation and holds a hope for that time when the glory of the sons of God will be revealed—that is, when the things prepared for those who will deserve to be sons of God are revealed; or certainly when, after the veil by which they are covered has been removed, those who are sons of God themselves have been manifested.

“For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope; because creation itself will also be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.”

(Origen.) What creation is it, then, that awaits the revelation of the sons of God? This one, he says, which is now subjected to vanity. It was subjected not willingly or by its own choice, but by the will of him who orders all things. It was subjected, therefore, for his sake; but it was subjected not under a condition that it should remain forever subject to vanity, but with a certain hope.

He recalls what this hope is when he says: “Because creation itself,” he says, “will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.”

Let us therefore examine more attentively what this vanity is to which creation is said to be subjected, and what this corruption is from whose slavery it hopes to be freed. It seems to me that these statements concern the material and corruptible substance of the body. For corruption dominates nothing except the body. The inner person, who was created according to God and made in the image of God, is incorruptible and invisible and, according to his proper nature, may be called incorporeal.

The outer person, however, is called both corporeal and corruptible. For this reason Paul also said: “Although our outer person is being destroyed, our inner person is being renewed” (2 Corinthians 4). The renewal of the inner person, insofar as he is rational, consists in the mind’s knowledge of God and capacity for the Holy Spirit.

But, in order that we may commit something brief and concise concerning such profound matters even to these pages, and gather an image of the substance of the inner person—that is, of the soul and mind—let us consider how creation was subjected to vanity not willingly but because of him who subjected it in hope. Let us place Paul himself in the middle, if it seems fitting. His soul or mind, which is his inner person, surpasses and rises above everything corporeal, visible, and subject to sense and sight, and becomes capable even of the divine nature itself.

Yet this great and remarkable substance of his soul, which possesses the principles and understanding of heavenly and divine realities—for the reasons behind this, God knows—is subjected to the slavery of the corruptible body and bound to its vanity.

Consider the body’s necessities: the desire for food, the shame of digestion, the embarrassment of reproducing offspring, how a child is conceived, born, and nourished. Observe how much vanity and corruption there is in these matters, to which the noble and rational creation—that is, the soul—is subjected, though unwillingly; subjected, nevertheless, in hope, awaiting the time when it will be freed, when the time of the freedom of the sons of God arrives.

This is what the Apostle himself was already saying more plainly elsewhere: “While we are in this dwelling, we groan” (2 Corinthians 5). Wisdom also said through Solomon: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9). Paul likewise says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord”; and he desires rather “to be away from the body and to be with the Lord.”

He indicates and explains this still more clearly in the passage where he says: “I am hard-pressed between the two: I have the desire to return and be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain is more necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1). Here he plainly shows that, insofar as it concerned what he was conscious of in his soul, he did not willingly serve this corruption and vanity, but did so because of him who willed these things in this manner, and because of us, so that we might be saved.

He therefore remains in the flesh for our sake. But when the sons of God have been revealed and gathered into one through the Church, which he established in order to present a pure virgin to one man, Christ, then he too will be freed from the slavery of corruption, as he himself says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have finished the race; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4).

This is what it means to be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.

(Augustine.) When he says, “The expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God; for creation was subjected to vanity not willingly,” and so on, up to the point where he says, “And we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body,” it must be understood in such a way that we do not suppose that the sense of groaning and sorrow exists in trees, vegetables, stones, and other creatures of this kind—for this is the error of the Manichaeans.

Nor should we think that the holy angels have been subjected to vanity, or suppose that they will be freed from the slavery of destruction when they are certainly not destined for destruction. Rather, without doing violence to the text, we should understand the whole of creation in the human being.

For no creation can exist except as spiritual, as excels in the angels; animal, as is sufficiently apparent even in the life of beasts; or bodily, which can be seen or touched. All of these are also present in the human being, because the human being consists of soul and body.

Therefore creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God—everything in the human being that now labors and is subject to corruption—namely, that manifestation of which the same Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3).

John says: “Beloved, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

Creation therefore awaits this revelation of the sons of God—the creation that is now subjected in the human being to vanity, so long as it is devoted to temporal matters that pass away like a shadow. Hence it is said in the Psalms: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Psalm 143).

Solomon also speaks of this vanity when he says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance does a person have from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1, 3). David likewise says: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4).

He says that creation was subjected to vanity not willingly, because this subjection is punitive. For humanity was not condemned willingly, just as it sinned willingly. Yet this condemnation was inflicted upon our nature not without the hope of restoration.

Therefore he says, “because of him who subjected it in hope,” because creation itself will be freed from the slavery of destruction into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God—that is, so that it too may reach the freedom of the glory of the sons of God through faith. When faith was not present in it, it was called merely “creation.”

And you should refer to this what follows:

For we know that the creation groans together and suffers until now. [Col. 1457A] For there were still those who would come to believe, who even in spirit were subject to arduous errors. But lest anyone think that this had been said only of their labor, he adds also what concerns those who had already believed. Although in spirit—that is, in mind—they served the law of God, nevertheless, because in the flesh one serves the law of sin, as long as in this life we suffer the troubles and anxieties of our mortality, he therefore added, saying:

“Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we await adoption, the redemption of our body.”

For this adoption, which has already taken place in those who have believed, has taken place in spirit, not in body; for the body has not yet been transformed into that heavenly change, just as the spirit has already been changed by the reconciliation of faith, turned from [Col. 1457B] errors toward God. Therefore, even among those who have believed, that manifestation which will come about in the resurrection of the body is still awaited. It belongs to that fourth stage, where peace will be perfect in every respect and there will be eternal rest, with no corruption resisting us or troubling us in any part.

What he had promised—“I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us”—is therefore understood without absurdity. For earlier he had said: “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh,” which cannot happen without suffering, for which patience is necessary; and to this also belongs what he had said shortly before: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified.”

When he says, therefore, “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God,” I think he means this: [Col. 1457C] even this very thing within us that suffers when we put to death the deeds of the flesh—that is, when we hunger or thirst, or practice abstinence; when through chastity we restrain the pleasure of intercourse; when through patience we endure the wounds of injuries and the barbs of insults; when, having neglected and cast aside our pleasures, we labor for the fruitfulness of Mother Church—whatever in us suffers amid this and similar affliction is creation.

For the body and soul suffer, and both are certainly created things; and they await the revelation of the sons of God—that is, they await the time when what has been called in them will appear, the glory to which they have been called. Since the only-begotten Son of God cannot be called a creature, inasmuch as through him all things whatsoever God made were made, we too are distinctly called “creation” [Col. 1457D] before that evident manifestation of glory, and distinctly we are called “sons of God,” although we merit this by adoption; for the only-begotten is Son by nature.

Therefore, “the expectation of creation”—that is, our expectation—“awaits the revelation of the sons of God”: it awaits the time when what has been promised will appear, when it will actually be manifest what we now are in hope. For we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

This is the revelation of the sons of God, which the expectation of creation now awaits—not that creation awaits the revelation of another nature that is not creation, but that creation as it now is awaits the time when it will become what it is going to be. It is as though one were to say that, while the painter is at work and the colors have been placed before him and prepared for his work, the expectation of the colors awaits the manifestation of the image. They will not then be other colors, nor will they cease to be colors; they will simply possess another dignity.

“For creation,” he says, “was subjected to vanity” (Ecclesiastes I). This is the same as: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance does a man have in all his labor by which he labors under the sun?” To him it was said: “In labor you shall eat bread” (Genesis III).

Creation, therefore, was subjected to vanity, not willingly. It was rightly added: “not willingly.” For man sinned willingly, but he was not condemned willingly. Sin, then, was the voluntary act of doing contrary to the commandment of truth; the punishment of sin was subjection to deception.

Creation, therefore, was not willingly subjected to vanity, but because of him who subjected it [Col. 1458B] in hope—that is, because of his justice and mercy, who neither left sin unpunished nor wished the sinner to be incurable. For creation itself—that is, man himself—after losing through sin the seal of the image, remained merely creation. That is, he was not yet called the perfected form of the sons, but was called only creation. He will be freed from the slavery of destruction.

When he says, therefore, “it itself will be freed,” he makes us understand “it itself” in the same way as “us”: even concerning those who are not yet called sons of God, there is no despair. They have not yet believed and are therefore called merely creation; but they too will believe, and they will be freed from the slavery of destruction just as we shall be, who are already sons of God, although it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

It will therefore be freed [Col. 1458C] from the slavery of destruction into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God: that is, they too will pass from slavery into freedom and from death into glory in the perfect life that the sons of God will possess.

(Orig.) But, if you wish, ascend from these examples also to what was said above, and observe how the services of the sun itself, the moon, and the stars of heaven, and of the whole world, have been subjected to vanity and serve corruption. For they nourish the crops for human use, produce the fruits of trees and the grass of the fields, and roll on those same circles of the years, returning upon themselves. They restore what passes away, and allow what has been restored to pass away again.

(Amb.) Creation, having been placed under the power of the Lord and Creator, was certainly not willingly subjected to vanity; for its subjection is not beneficial to itself but to us. What, then, is meant by its being subjected to vanity, except that what it generates is perishable? It works to produce corruptible fruits; corruption, therefore, is vanity. For everything that is born in the world is weak, perishable, and corruptible, and therefore vain. They are vain because they cannot maintain their own condition. For all things, disfigured by continual flux, return confusedly into themselves, into nature.

Solomon says the same about these things: all is vanity. Nor does David disagree with this when he says: “Nevertheless every living man is vanity” (Psalm CXV). Is it not vanity to eat and drink and attend to the things of the world? Yet this very vanity is beneficial; for it profits those born into the world, so that through these things, being exercised in their bodies, they may learn the mystery of the Creator.

For in comparison with eternal things they are vain; but in themselves they are good, since they are necessary. “But because of him who subjected it in hope.” What hope? He immediately adds, saying: “For creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.”

Since creation cannot oppose its Creator, it has been subjected for his sake, not without hope. For, placed in labor, it has this consolation: it will have rest when all whom God knows will believe. For their sake also he subjected it.

(Greg.) Creation is subjected to vanity unwillingly, for man, who willingly abandoned the condition of his inborn steadfastness, now, pressed beneath the weight of mortality, unwillingly serves the corruption of his mutability. But this creation is then snatched from the slavery of corruption when, rising incorruptible, it is raised up into the glory of the sons of God. [Col. 1459B]

Here, therefore, the elect are bound by affliction, because they are still weighed down by the punishment of their corruption. But when we are stripped of corruptible flesh, we are released, as it were, from the bonds of affliction by which we are now constrained.

“Creation itself,” he says, “will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.” Punishment for corruption now burdens the elect, but then the glory of incorruption will exalt them; and insofar as the weight of present necessity is concerned, nothing of freedom is now displayed in the sons of God, but insofar as the glory of the freedom that follows is concerned, nothing of slavery will then appear in God’s servants.

Thus creation, stripped of the slavery of corruption and receiving the dignity of freedom, is transformed into the glory of the sons of God, because, united to God through the Spirit, it is shown to have passed beyond and risen above the very condition of being creation. [Col. 1459C]

For we know that every creature groans and suffers labor pains until now.

(Orig.) When he says that every creature groans and suffers labor pains, we shall understand “suffers labor pains” according to the sense in which the Apostle says that he begot through the Gospel those whom he brought to the light through the faith of Christ (1 Corinthians IV); or as he said of others: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV). Creation, therefore, suffers labor pains for those whom it regenerates for salvation.

(Aug.) Every creature is counted in man—not because all angels, the supereminent powers and authorities, or heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them are contained in him, but because every creature is partly spiritual, partly animal, and partly bodily.

Every creature is in man because he understands by the spirit, perceives by the soul, and moves locally by the body. Every creature, therefore, groans and suffers together in man. He rightly said “until now,” because even if some are already in Abraham’s bosom, and that thief, who was to be with the Lord in Paradise on the very day he believed, has ceased to suffer, nevertheless every creature still groans and suffers together until now, because in those who have not yet been freed, all creation is present through spirit, soul, and body. [Col. 1459D]

(Orig.) Above he had said: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory”; and after saying that he considered this to be so, here he says that he knows that every creature groans and suffers together, so that plainly there may be no uncertainty in this matter.

For although creation has been subjected unwillingly, nevertheless, since it yields to the will of him who subjected it, it also displays a certain affection and love toward those for whose sake it appears to have been subjected; it suffers on account of their sufferings and groans on account of their groans.

(Amb.) “Every creature,” he says, “groans and suffers through daily labor until now.” “Until now” signifies for as long as it is being read. For the elements themselves perform their functions with anxiety, because the sun and moon do not complete the spaces appointed to them without labor, and the spirit of animals is constrained with a great groan to perform its services. For we see those things, groaning, compelled unwillingly to labor.

All these things, therefore, await rest, so that they may be freed from servile work. But if this were the kind of slavery that advanced the cause of pleasing God, creation would rejoice rather than suffer; but because it has been subjected to the slavery of corruption for our sake, it suffers. For it sees its works perish every day; every day its work rises and sets. It rightly suffers, since its activity pertains not to eternity but to corruption.

So far as can be understood, they are sufficiently concerned for our salvation, knowing that their own liberation will be hastened if we come more quickly to recognize the Creator. Knowing this, therefore, let us show ourselves worthy through every care and diligence, so that we may also be an example to others—moved not only by compassion for ourselves, but also on its account, since it groans while suffering injuries day and night. For we are accustomed to keep more watchfully awake in the causes of others.

“Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we await the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body.” [Col. 1460C]

(Orig.) What he appears to say is this: Not only does every creature groan and suffer together, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, also groan inwardly. For we too await the adoption of the sons of God and the redemption of our body.

Although by the very fact that we believe in Christ we know that salvation has already been granted to us, this salvation is still in hope, not in visible sight [*visibilium*; perhaps *visibili*]. For if it were already seen, it would not be hoped for. One hopes in order to see. But if someone sees what he had hoped for, it is superfluous to continue hoping for what he sees.

We, however, do not place our hope in things that are seen, lest our hope be empty, but in things that are not seen. And because we hope for things that are not seen, and because they are so great and glorious that they are desired through many labors, tribulations, and dangers, we await them with patience, as though they might scarcely ever come.

We have said this by giving the apostolic words a certain direct and clearer order. Now, if you wish, let us see what he indicates by this new expression when he says: “But we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit.”

We read in the Apostle Paul that the gifts or graces of the Holy Spirit are called “spirits” in the plural, as when he says: “Since you are zealous for spirits, seek to abound in them for the building up of the Church” (1 Corinthians XIV). Paul therefore calls the various gifts of the Spirit “many spirits.”

Of these many gifts, whatever was highest and greatest was certainly obtained by the apostles, so that they might be suitable—as Paul himself says—as ministers of the New Testament, and so that they might fill the Gospel from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum.

This gift of the Holy Spirit, therefore, which had been bestowed upon them more sublimely and excellently than upon others, he rightly called the “first fruits of the Holy Spirit.” Hence he says: “But we ourselves.” In this he appears to designate particularly the apostolic dignity.

“We ourselves,” he says—that is, the apostles—“who have the first fruits of the Spirit,” who were chosen for this purpose, to receive the first fruits of the Spirit, “also groan inwardly.” There is no creature, he says, so free from pain and groaning that even we ourselves, who receive the highest and choicest gifts from the Holy Spirit, do not suffer and groan while awaiting the adoption of sons—that is, the perfection of those whom we were sent to teach and instruct—until we see them progress so far that they may merit adoption as sons.

So long, then, as we who are being instructed by them are negligent and delay, prolonging the time of our correction, and seek not invisible things but take pleasure in visible things, we stir up pains in the apostles and arouse, so to speak, the mourning and groaning of the whole creation. For the whole creation groans and suffers together, sighing over the damage caused by our hardness and hypocrisy.

But if you understand the statement, “We ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit,” as having been said of all who appear to have received the grace of baptism, then we must hope for what the same Apostle said: “If the first fruits are holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Romans XI). Even so, the first fruits of that lump in which the multitude of believers appears to be indicated were necessarily located in the apostles. For it is written that God placed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers.

Those who were placed in the first rank, therefore, will appropriately be believed to possess the first fruits of the Holy Spirit’s spiritual grace.

(Aug.) “Not only,” he says, “does every creature groan and suffer together, but we ourselves”—that is, not only do body, soul, and spirit together suffer in man because of bodily difficulties, but we ourselves, apart from the bodies, groan inwardly within ourselves.

He rightly said “having the first fruits of the Spirit”—that is, those whose spirits have already been offered to God like a sacrifice and seized by the divine fire of love. They are the first fruits of man, because truth first possesses our spirit, so that through it the rest may be possessed.

He therefore already has first fruits offered to God who says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans VII); and who says: “God, whom I serve in my spirit” (Romans I); and of whom it is said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew XXVI).

But since he still says: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans VIII), and since it is still said to such people: “He will give life even to your mortal bodies because of the Spirit dwelling in you,” the whole offering has not yet been consumed. It will be, however, when death is swallowed up in victory, when it is said to death: “Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Corinthians XV). [Col. 1462A]

Now, therefore, he says, not only does every creature—that is, together with the body—groan, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit—that is, we souls who have also offered our first-fruit minds to God—groan inwardly within ourselves, awaiting adoption apart from the body and the redemption of our body.

That is, the body itself, receiving the benefit of the adoption of sons, to which we have been called, will make it manifest that, after all troubles have passed, we are wholly free and, in every respect, sons of God.

(Orig.) But in another way, when he says “the redemption of our body,” I think he is referring to the body of the whole Church, just as he says elsewhere: “You are the body of Christ and members individually” (1 Corinthians VI). The Apostle therefore hopes for the redemption of the whole body of the Church and does not think that what is perfect can be given to each individual member unless the entire body has been gathered together into one.

This is why, when individuals pray for all, we pray that the kingdom of God may come. For then there will be the liberation of our body—that is, of all Christians. He signified everyone by the body, because “we are members of one another” (Romans XII).

(Amb.) From what has been said above, therefore, he demonstrates the force of the suffering that creation undergoes for our sake. We, whose benefit comes from its service and who have the Spirit of God as our helper, groan in order to be freed from this condition and to obtain the promised rewards.

How much more, then, does creation groan, since it neither has the Holy Spirit as its helper nor labors for its own sake? Add to this that it sees the things which it produces through its labor, so that they may serve as food for God’s servants, sacrificed unlawfully to idols.

Hence it suffers more and longs to be freed more quickly, knowing that this contributes to the insult inflicted upon the Creator.

“For in hope we were saved.”

(Amb.) He says this because, by hoping for what God promised us in Christ, we have acquired the merit by which we may be freed. We have therefore been freed in hope, because we expect nothing other than what we believe.

But hope that is seen is not hope. It is clear that what is seen is not hope, but what is not seen; and consequently believers are to receive rewards because they hope for what they do not see. For when someone sees something, why does he hope for it?

But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience. There is no doubt that what is not seen is hoped for; for future things are awaited. This expectation is patience, which merits much from God: day by day awaiting and desiring the coming of God’s kingdom, without doubting that he will grant it. [Col. 1462D]

(Orig.) We have already explained above how salvation is in hope, and that hope is placed not in things that are seen but in things that are not seen. We shall add only this brief point: from these words, and from those in which he says, “not looking at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen,” he teaches us that in the future blessings we ought to hope for none of the things that are now seen or can be seen—even if you see this visible heaven, even if you see the earth.

Hear what is said about these things: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew XXIV), for they are visible; and what you see, why do you hope for?

Therefore, absolutely nothing is to be hoped for in the future from the things that are seen. “Eye has not seen what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah LXIV; 1 Corinthians II). But the eye does see heaven and earth. Therefore, we must not believe that what is seen has been prepared by God for those who love him.

There is indeed heaven—or rather, heavens—far more eminent and higher than this firmament that can be seen with the eyes. The earth also is to be hoped for, but not this earth that is called dry land and lies before the eyes; rather, it will be that earth of the meek which the eye has not seen.

For the Apostle’s statement is clear: it teaches that in the future we are to hope not for visible and bodily things but for spiritual and eternal things, because “the things that are seen are temporary and come to an end with time, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians IV). These are what the Apostle teaches us to hope for.

For this reason also the restoration of our body is effected from corruptible to incorruptible, from mortal to immortal, from weakness to power, and from an animal body the body becomes spiritual, so that when it has become spiritual it may already be able to enjoy invisible blessings. Since we do not see these blessings in the present age, we hope for them through hope and await them with patience.

“Likewise, the Spirit also helps our weakness.”

After saying above that every creature groaned and suffered together with those who had been placed in the contest of this life—that is, that it labored with them and contributed strength—and after Paul had also mentioned that he and those like him uttered groans for those who were laboring, so that those engaged in the struggle might be encouraged when they saw all the saints and the whole creation laboring with them in affection and joining their groans, he now adds something higher and more exalted.

“Do not think it a small thing,” he says, “that the whole creation groans and suffers together with us; do not think it a small thing that we ourselves groan on account of your labors. Even in the divine nature itself there is, with respect to our struggles—for I include myself with you—a certain compassionate affection; and the Spirit himself helps our weakness.” [Col. 1463C]

(Ambr.) He helps the weakness of our prayer, because above he remembered that we groan and pray for liberation. Placed in suffering, we either want things said to be far in the future to happen immediately, or want the things through which we attain merit to be removed quickly; and we seem to pray with a weak prayer when its desired effect [*effectus*; text: *affectus*] is denied.

For the prayer is weak when it asks contrary to reason. Thus he shows that this weakness is assisted by the Holy Spirit given to us. He helps because he will not allow to happen those things that are requested either before they ought to be requested or that are contrary to our good.

(Aug.) When he says, “Likewise, the Spirit helps our weakness”—for we do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should—it is manifest that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit. This becomes clear in what follows, where he says: “Because he intercedes for the saints according to God.”

We do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should, for two reasons: both because what we hope for and toward which we are striving has not yet appeared, and because in this very life many things that are prosperous may seem to us adverse, and things that are adverse may seem prosperous.

For when tribulation befalls a servant of God, it sometimes appears useless to those who understand less, since it is intended for testing or correction. But if it is referred to what was said—“Give us help from tribulation; human salvation is vain” (Psalm LIX)—it is understood that God often helps us through tribulation, and that salvation is sought in vain when it is sometimes adverse, entangling the soul in the delight and love of this life.

Hence the statement: “I encountered tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXIV). When he says “I encountered,” he signifies something beneficial; for we do not rightly rejoice that we have found something unless it was what we were seeking.

Therefore, we do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should. God knows both what benefits us in this life and what he will give us after this life.

“But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groans.” He says that the Spirit groans because he makes us groan, stirring up through love the desire for the future life, just as he says: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deuteronomy XIII)—that is, to make you know; for nothing is hidden from God.

For we do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should.

(Orig.) Sometimes, compelled by weakness, we desire things that are contrary to salvation. For just as someone suffering from bodily illness asks a physician not for what contributes to health but for what the desire of his present weakness suggests, so we, languishing in the weakness of this life, sometimes ask God for what is not beneficial to us.

Accordingly, Paul himself, who speaks these things to you, when an angel of Satan had been given to him by the Lord to buffet him, lest he be exalted because of the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians XII), asked the Lord three times that it might depart from him, not knowing what he was praying for. And because he did not know how he ought to pray, the Lord did not grant his request but said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

Thus, we do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should.

(Amb.) There is also sometimes a proud and foolish request, as there was with the two apostles James and John, who asked for inappropriate and excessive things and were told: “You do not know what you are asking” (Matthew XX).

“But the Spirit himself asks on our behalf with unutterable groans.”

(Amb.) The Spirit of the Lord is said to ask on our behalf not in human speech but according to the manner of his nature. Since what is from God speaks of God, it must speak in the manner in which the one from whom it is speaks. No one speaks in one language with his fellow citizen and in another.

(Greg.) Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you” (John XIV).

In Greek usage, *paraclete*—παράκλητος—means in Latin “advocate” or “consoler.” He is called an advocate because he intervenes before the justice of the Father on behalf of sinners who have fallen through error. He is said to plead for sinners, being of one substance with the Father and the Son, because he makes those whom he fills into people who plead.

Hence Paul also says: “The Spirit himself asks on our behalf with unutterable groans.”

But the one who asks is inferior to the one who is asked. How, then, is the Spirit said to ask, since he is not inferior?

The Spirit himself asks because he inflames those whom he has filled so that they may ask. The same Spirit is called the Consoler because, while he prepares hope of pardon for those who mourn over the commission of sin, he lifts the mind from the affliction of sadness. [Col. 1464D]

(Orig.) But let us see what it means when he says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us.” John indicates that Jesus does this when he says: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone among us does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, who also intercedes for us” (1 John II).

Here too the Spirit intercedes for us.

(Aug.) What does “intercedes” mean except “makes us intercede”? To intercede with groans is evidence of need; but it is not lawful to believe that the Holy Spirit is in need of anything. He is therefore said to intercede because he makes us intercede and inspires in us the disposition to intercede and groan, as in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X).

Nor does this happen as though we did nothing. The help of the Holy Spirit is therefore expressed in such a way that he is said himself to do what he causes us to do.

For the Apostle himself sufficiently shows that the spirit of which it is said, “he intercedes with unutterable groans,” is not our spirit but the Holy Spirit, by whom our weakness is assisted. For he began in this way: “The Spirit helps our weakness”; then he added: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, as we should, but the Spirit himself asks for us.” [Col. 1465C]

(Cass.) Those worthy of it are sometimes carried away by a most fervent heart into that fiery prayer which cannot be grasped or expressed by human speech. Sometimes the mind that advances toward that true affection of purity, and has already begun to take root in it, is accustomed to conceive all these things together and at once, and, passing through everything like an incomprehensible and exceedingly consuming flame, to pour forth to God prayers of ineffable purity and strength.

The Spirit himself, interceding with unutterable groans, sends these prayers to God without our knowing it. At such a moment he conceives and pours out in supplication such things that, I will not say, can be traversed and expressed by the mouth, but that the mind itself cannot even recall at another time.

Hence, at whatever level a person may stand, he is sometimes found to utter pure and intent prayers. For from that first and humble order, which is concerned with remembrance of the future judgment, a person still held under the punishment and fear of examination is at times so pierced with compunction that he is filled with no less spiritual alacrity from the richness of observance than the one who, surveying and traversing God’s munificence through the purity of his heart, is dissolved in unspeakable joy and gladness.

For, according to the Lord’s saying, the one who knows that more has been forgiven him begins to love more.

(Orig.) The Spirit does this by helping our weakness. The Lord himself teaches what our weakness is when he says: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew XXVI). Our weakness therefore descends from the weakness of the flesh.

For it is the flesh that desires against the spirit; and while it presses its desires upon us, it hinders the purity of the spirit and obscures the sincerity of prayer.

But when the Spirit of God sees our spirit laboring in opposition to the flesh and cleaving to him, he extends his hand and helps its weakness. It is like a teacher taking up an inexperienced student who knows no letters at all: in order to teach and instruct him, the teacher must stoop to the student’s rudiments and first pronounce the name of the letter, so that the student may learn by responding. In a certain way, the teacher himself becomes like the beginning student, speaking and practicing what the beginner ought to say and practice.

So also, when the Holy Spirit sees our spirit disturbed by the assaults of the flesh and not knowing what it ought to pray for, he, as a teacher, first offers the prayer, which our spirit, if it wishes to be a disciple of the Holy Spirit, must continue.

He offers the groans by which our spirit is taught to groan, so that it may reconcile God to itself. But if the Spirit teaches and our spirit—that is, our mind—does not follow, the teacher’s instruction becomes fruitless for it through its own fault.

Knowing that this mystery takes place within a human being, Paul said: “For if I pray in tongues, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit” (1 Corinthians XIV), calling the grace of the Holy Spirit given by God to human beings “his spirit.”

And, exhorting us not to possess this benefit of the Holy Spirit fruitlessly, he adds: “What then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing a psalm with the spirit, and I will sing a psalm with the mind.”

“But he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he asks for the saints according to God.”

(Amb.) It is manifest that God, to whom nothing is silent or hidden, knows the prayer of every spirit—how much more that of the Holy Spirit, who is certainly of the same substance and speaks not through the impulse of air, nor like the angels or other creatures, but in the manner appropriate to his divinity.

He speaks to God when he appears silent to us, because he sees when he is not seen, and asks for those things that he knows are pleasing to God and beneficial to us. The same Spirit intervenes for us when he knows that through ignorance, not through boastfulness, we are asking for what is contrary to our good.

(Orig.) He shows that in prayer God weighs not so much our words as our heart and mind. For he is the one who searches hearts and kidneys.

When he says a second time that the Spirit intercedes, he means that he teaches that no small dispensation is also carried out through the Holy Spirit in all things. Although the only-begotten Son of God became incarnate and suffered for the salvation of the human race, destroyed death by his own death, and restored life through his resurrection, nevertheless, without the incarnation, magnificent works are also accomplished through the Holy Spirit.

The distinction is that Christ died for the ungodly; Paul himself shows this when he says: “For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans V). But the Holy Spirit now intercedes not for the ungodly but for the saints, and he intercedes not according to the flesh but according to God.

Christ, however, is not said to have died according to God but according to the flesh. Therefore the Spirit is said to offer intercessions for the saints not in words but in groans—and not in ordinary groans but in unutterable ones.

For how can it be explained what the Spirit of God speaks to God, when sometimes our own spirit cannot express in speech even what it feels and understands?

We know, however, that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose as saints.

(Origen) If, he says, the Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings, and the whole creation groans together and suffers pain until now—creation which will then finally be freed from the slavery of corruption, when the freedom of the glory of the children of God has come—how can it not rightly be declared that we know that all things work together for good for those who love God? Indeed, all things work together for good and labor together with those who love God to such an extent that the Spirit himself also assists and does not disdain to be the guide of the journey toward the good, although he is divine by nature.

(Augustine) Without the Lord either working in us so that we may will, or cooperating with us when we will, we can accomplish nothing in the good works of piety. Of the Lord’s working in us so that we may will it is said: “For God is the one who works in you both to will” (Phil. II). Of his cooperation with us once we already will and act by willing, he says: “For we know that all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. VIII). What does “all things” mean, unless it includes even those dreadful and savage sufferings? For a burden that is heavy to weakness becomes light to love. To people of this kind the Lord declared that his burden was light—such as Peter’s burden when he suffered for Christ, not such as it was when he denied Christ.

Through the disturbance caused by heretics, moreover, our diligence is roused from the sleep of our negligence, so that we may search the Scriptures more vigilantly and find a response with which the eyes of Christ may not be harmed. Thus, through the manifold grace of the Savior, God turns even what the enemy contrives for destruction into assistance. For those who love God, all things work together for good.

(Ambrose) Even if they have prayed ineptly, it will not harm them, because God knows the purpose of their hearts and does not impute to them the negligence by which they ask for adverse things; rather, he grants those things that ought to be given to those who love God. Hence the Lord also says: “Your Father knows,” he says, “what you need before you ask him” (Matt. VI). Those, then, are called according to his purpose whom God foreknows as destined to become fit for him when they believe, so that they were known before they believed.

For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

(Augustine) Predestination is something that cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. By predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to accomplish. Hence it is said: “He made the things that are to be.” But he can also foreknow things that he himself does not do, such as all sins. For even if there are certain things that are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sinners—whence it is said, “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting”—the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment. Therefore God’s predestination, which concerns the good, is the preparation of grace; while grace is the effect of that very predestination.

(Ambrose) Those whom he foreknew as destined to be devoted to him, he chose to receive the promised rewards. Thus those who seem to believe but do not remain in the faith they began are denied to have been chosen by God, because those whom God has chosen remain with him. Someone may be chosen for a time, as Saul and Judas were, not by foreknowledge but according to present righteousness.

(Origen) Concerning what he says, “to be conformed to the image of his Son,” I wish to inquire to which form they are said to be conformed. For we read that the Son of God is at one time in the form of God and at another time in the form of a servant. To which of these two forms does the Apostle say that those who love God, and for whom all things work together for good, will be conformed? This does not seem to me to be a distinction without significance.

I therefore think, in accordance with what this same Paul indicates elsewhere when he says, “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV), that he speaks of Christ being formed in those who strive toward perfection according to the fact that he is the Word, so that the purity of the Word of God may be perfectly formed in them; according to the fact that he is the truth, so that truth may remain in them without any admixture of deceit; and according to the fact that he is wisdom, so that the wisdom of God may be in them—the wisdom which Paul speaks among the perfect, preserved pure and without any deviation into error.

So also, according to everything that Christ is—whether righteousness, sanctification, or whatever other virtues there may be—if these are formed in them to perfection, they will be seen to have been conformed to that image, the form in which he is in the form of God (Rom. VIII).

But if someone is still living in the beginnings—for “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God” (Eccles. I; Ps. CX)—so that, while still established in fear, he receives the first elements of the worship of God according to the form of the servant, which he assumed for the purpose of teaching the fear of God to the inexperienced and ignorant, then those who receive the first beginnings in the fear of God are to be understood as being conformed to that form.

(Augustine) It can also be understood in this way: just as he became like us through mortality, so we may become like him through immortality. This indeed also pertains to the resurrection of the bodies.

(Origen) Concerning the fact that he said “he foreknew” and “predestined,” I think that, just as he did not speak of everyone who is predestined, so neither did he speak of everyone whom he foreknew and predestined. We must not think, according to the common opinion of the masses, that God foreknows good and evil alike; rather, we must understand it according to the usage of Holy Scripture.

Let anyone who is diligent in the Scriptures observe whether he ever finds Scripture saying that God foreknew the wicked, just as in the present passage it plainly says concerning the good that those whom he foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. For if those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and no wicked person can be conformed to the image of the Son of God, it is clear that he speaks only of the good: “He foreknew those whom he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” The others, however, are said not merely not to be foreknown by God, but even to be unknown to him.

“For the Lord knows those who are his.” To those who are not worthy to be known by God, the Savior says: “Depart from me, for I have never known you, workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII). Thus also in the present passage, those whom God foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; the others, however, are not said to be foreknown—not because anything can be hidden from that nature which is everywhere and absent nowhere, but because everything that is evil is unworthy of his knowledge or foreknowledge.

That he might be the firstborn among many brothers.

(Augustine) When he says, “that he might be the firstborn among many brothers,” he sufficiently teaches that our God and the firstborn are to be understood in different ways. When he is called the only-begotten, he has no brothers and is naturally the Son of God, the Word in the beginning through whom all things were made.

But according to the assumption of humanity and the dispensation of the incarnation, through which he also graciously called us—who are not sons by nature—to the adoption of sons, he is called firstborn with the addition of brothers. For where someone is called first, he is certainly not alone, but has brothers who will follow him into that which he has entered first.

Hence elsewhere he also calls him “the firstborn from the dead,” so that he himself might hold first place in all things. For there was no resurrection of the dead in such a way that they would no longer die before him; after him, however, there was the resurrection of many saints, whom he is not ashamed to call brothers because of their sharing in humanity.

As the firstborn from the dead, therefore, according to the same Apostle, he rose in glory from that death by which his flesh was sown in dishonor. According to this image of the Son, to which we are conformed through immortality, we also enact in the body what the same Apostle says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV). Thus, because we were mortal according to Adam, let us hold firmly, with true faith and certain hope, that we will be immortal according to Christ.

For now we can bear that same image—not yet in vision, but in faith; not yet in reality, but in hope.

(Ambrose) He is rightly called firstborn who, before every creature, was not made but born; after whose example God graciously adopted human beings as his sons. Christ is also the firstborn in regeneration; he is also the firstborn from the dead, whose nature is unknown; and he is also the firstborn who ascended into heaven after victory.

The firstborn, therefore, is called our brother in all things because he graciously consented to be born as a human being. He is nevertheless Lord, because he is our God, as the prophet Jeremiah said: “This is our God.”

And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

(Augustine) What he says, “those whom he called, he also justified,” can give rise to the question whether all who have been called are justified. Yet elsewhere we read: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). Nevertheless, since the chosen themselves were certainly also called, it is clear that no one is justified unless called, although not all who are called are so called according to his purpose, as he said above.

The purpose, however, is to be understood as God’s purpose, not theirs. He himself explains what “according to his purpose” means when he says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” For not all who have been called were called according to his purpose. This purpose pertains to God’s foreknowledge and predestination; and he predestined no one except one whom he foreknew as destined to believe and follow his calling—those whom he also calls chosen.

For many do not come, although many have been called; but no one comes who has not been called.

(Origen) Above he said, “Those whom he foreknew, he predestined”; and now he adds, “Those whom he predestined, he also called, and those whom he called, he also justified.” If we understand “foreknew” and “predestined” according to the common opinion, it will plainly appear that the one who was justified was justified because he was called; the one who was called was justified because he was predestined; and the one who was predestined was predestined because he was foreknown. Conversely, you will understand that if someone has not been justified, it is because he was not called; and if he was not called, it is because he was not predestined; and if he was not predestined, it is because he was not foreknown.

Observe into what absurd a conclusion those fall who understand God’s foreknowledge merely as his knowing in advance what will happen later. For, according to what we explained above, God is found not to have foreknown those whom he did not predestine [Ms.: “foreknew himself”]. And again, if the statement “those whom he called, he also justified” is referred to the common understanding, we open a huge window for those who deny that it lies within human power to be saved.

They say: “If God foreknew those whom he predestined; and if he predestined those whom he called; and if he justified those whom he called, then those who will not be justified are entirely without blame, because they were neither called, nor predestined, nor foreknown.”

Moreover, the fact that not everyone who is called is also justified openly contradicts this. The apostle Judas was called, but he was not justified. And if someone insists that he was justified simply by being called, certainly he was not glorified. Likewise, those of whom the Apostle says that they “suffered shipwreck concerning the faith” (I Tim. I) had indeed been called, but they were not justified.

According to the parables of the Gospel (Luke XIV), those to whom the servants had been sent and who excused themselves had been called, but were not justified. And the man who entered the king’s banquet (Matt. XX) without a wedding garment was called, but was not justified.

Since each of these cases is as stated, how will the Apostle’s statement appear to be true—the statement he made concerning foreknowing, predestining, calling, and even justifying?

But I think that, in accordance with what we explained above concerning how God knows or foreknows, we must return to the usage of Scripture. Scripture habitually uses the word “knowing” in this passage in a kind of ordinary sense, as when it says: “Adam knew his wife” (Gen. IV), meaning that he was joined to his wife. Again, concerning Rebekah it says: “She was a virgin; no man had known her” (Gen. XXIV).

It also says concerning the sons of Levi, when they were punishing transgressors, that “each one did not know his father or his mother” (Lev. XIX). This certainly shows that he did not join his affection and love to father or mother.

You will find many other passages in Scripture in which “knowing” is spoken of in this sense. Therefore, it is also clear that in the present passage the Apostle used the language of knowing according to the custom of Holy Scripture, in order to show that those people were foreknown by God in the sense that, knowing what they were like, God had placed his love and affection upon them, in accordance with what is written: “The Lord knows those who are his.”

As far as ordinary knowledge is concerned, God certainly does not fail to know not only those who are his but also those who have gone astray from him. But he is said to have known his own in the sense that he held them in love and joined them to himself.

Thus, those whom God foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified.

The solution to the earlier question still remains for us: how can those whom he called also be the ones he justified, when, according to what we said above, many are called but few are chosen?

It seems to me that there is a certain distinction in calling, according to what we explained in the preceding chapter: all are indeed called, but not all are called according to his purpose. Those who are called according to the good purpose and good will that they possess toward the worship of God are the ones who are said to be called according to his purpose. These are the ones who are justified when called.

Their good purpose lacked only the calling. Those, however, who do not possess a firm and good purpose either toward the worship of God or toward good works are also called, so that no excuse may be left to them and so that, when they are judged, they may not be able to make this very claim: “If we too had been called, we could certainly have been justified, and not only justified but also glorified.”

For this reason they too are called, but, as though the seed had been sown upon rocky ground, they spring up quickly; when the sun of tribulations rises, however, because they do not have the deep root of a good purpose, they immediately wither and perish. These are the ones of whom the Apostle says: “They have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith” (I Tim. I).

Those whom he called—that is, those whom he called according to a good purpose—he also justified. Even if “according to his purpose” is referred to God, meaning that they are said to have been called according to the purpose of God, who, knowing that a religious mind and a desire for salvation were present in them, called them, this too will not appear contrary to what we have explained.

In this way, therefore, neither the cause of our salvation nor that of our destruction rests upon God’s foreknowledge; justification does not depend solely upon calling; nor has glorification been taken entirely out of our power.

Even if we understand foreknowledge in the ordinary sense, something does not happen because God knows that it will happen; rather, because it will happen, it is known by God before it occurs. For even if, for example, we imagined that God did not foreknow something, what is to be would undoubtedly still be as it is.

For example, Judas became a betrayer, and the prophets foretold that this would happen. Judas did not betray because the prophets foretold it; rather, because he was going to be a betrayer, the prophets foretold the things that he would do out of the wickedness of his purpose.

Judas had it within his power to be like Peter and John, if he had wished. But he chose the desire for money over the glory of apostolic fellowship. The prophets, foreseeing that this would be his will, handed down in the monuments of their books what he was going to do.

But so that you may know that the cause of each person’s salvation is not placed in God’s foreknowledge but in his purpose and actions, consider Paul fearing that, after preaching to others, he himself might become disqualified, and therefore disciplining his body and bringing it into subjection.

Against those who raise such questions for us we can also say this: if he foreknew those whom he predestined, but did not predestine everyone, then he did not foreknow everyone; and, according to their reasoning, there will be certain things that God does not know.

But if “foreknowing” is understood according to what we said above—that is, as receiving someone into one’s affection and joining that person to oneself—it will be true that just as he did not predestine everyone, so neither did he foreknow everyone.

For in this sense Jesus too is said not to have known sin. Surely we will not say that Jesus did not know what sin was—that he did not know that murder, adultery, theft, and things of this kind were sins? Or is this what it means for him to be said not to know sin: that he did not mingle with sin or cleave to it?

So elsewhere it is written: “Whoever keeps the commandment will not acknowledge an evil word”—that is, he will not receive an evil word, believe it, willingly listen to it, or allow it to enter his mind.

Those, therefore, whom God foreknows in this sense, he also predestines; those whom he predestines, he calls, with the distinction in calling that we described; those whom he calls, he justifies; and those whom he justifies, he glorifies.

We can also understand glorification as occurring in the present age, according to what the Apostle says: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

There is, therefore, a glory that each of the justified receives in the present life, and there is also the glory hoped for in the future, when this body of our lowliness, which is sown in dishonor, will rise in glory; and when, just as one is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars, and star differs from star in glory, so also will be the resurrection of the dead.

What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also freely give us all things with him?

(Origen) How God is for us is evident from what he explained above: that the Spirit of God dwells in us; that the Spirit of Christ, or Christ, is in us; that the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in us; that we are led by the Spirit of God; that we have received the Spirit of adoption; that we are children of God and heirs, and fellow heirs with Christ; that we receive the firstfruits of the Spirit; that the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings; that the whole creation groans together and suffers with us; that all things work together for good for those who love God; and that we have been called according to his purpose, foreknown, predestined, justified, and glorified.

Making, as it were, an anakephalaion [recapitulation] of all these things, and repeating them all together, he says: “What then shall we say to these things?” That is, what shall we say to all the things we have mentioned above? If God is for us in such a way that he has granted all these things to us, who can be against us?

This does not mean that no one at all can be our adversary. Otherwise, how would Peter’s statement stand: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, walks about seeking someone to devour”?

Rather, he shows that when God acts for us, our adversary becomes contemptible and powerless.

David likewise says: “The Lord is my illumination and my savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” He does not therefore say that there is no one whom he fears or who opposes him. Rather, he says: “Although those who walk as my enemies should approach against me to eat my flesh, nevertheless, because the Lord defends my life, they were weakened and fell.”

He further gives a supreme indication of God’s immense love toward us. God loved us to such an extent, he says, that he did not spare even his own Son, but handed him over to suffering for us all.
