And in order to compel us to even greater amazement, he added words that disclose a great mystery, saying that he did not spare his own Son. For earlier he had said that we too, who receive the Spirit of adoption, are sons of God. Therefore, lest anyone think that by the common designation “sons” he had handed over one of those who appeared to have been adopted as sons, he added “his own Son,” so as to show that he meant the one who alone is generated from God himself by an ineffable birth.

For us all, therefore, the Father handed him over—not with the handing over of which it is written, “Brother will hand over brother to death, and parents their children,” but he is said to have handed him over in this sense: that, although he was in the form of God, he suffered himself to empty himself, to assume the form of a servant, and to reach the death of the cross.

Thus he placed in himself an example of obedience for all and opened the way of resurrection to the dead.

For us all, therefore, he handed him over—not only for the saints, not only for the great, but also for the least, and for absolutely all who are in the Church the Father handed over his own Son. Therefore, even if someone harms one of the least and weakest, striking his weak conscience, he is said to sin against Christ, because he scandalizes the soul for which Christ died.

Since the Father handed over his Son for all of us, no one at all—even the very least who is in the Church—is to be despised. Hence the Lord himself said: “If anyone causes one of these little ones, even the least of them, to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be fastened around his neck and that he be thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these to stumble.”

Therefore, God, who made us precious by pouring out for us the precious blood of his own Son, how will he not freely give us all things with him? For there is nothing among created things, whether visible or invisible, that can be compared with the Son. A creature can in no way be placed on a level with its Creator.

And if the Creator himself has been given to us, how will all creation not be given to us with him? Yet this statement can be understood in two ways: that he gave all things to us with him.

It may be understood in this sense: if we have Christ in us according to the fact that he is the Word, wisdom, truth, righteousness, peace, and all the other things written concerning him, then together with this fullness of virtues all things will be given to us, so that we will no longer occupy merely one small place among all creatures—the small portion of earth that we now seem to inhabit—but will possess with Christ all things whatsoever that God has created, visible and invisible, hidden and manifest, temporal and eternal.

It may also be understood in another way: when he says, “He will give us all things with him,” he means that, just as he is the heir and we are his fellow heirs, we will be granted to enjoy the whole of creation together with him.

Who will bring an accusation against God’s chosen?

(Ambrose) It is clear that no one dares or is able to reopen judgment and foreknowledge concerning us before God. For who can disapprove what God approves, when no one is God’s equal? “God is the one who justifies.”

This is found in the prophet Isaiah, and here he presents it as his own, because there is no one else who can accuse what God approves. Or perhaps he might accuse us himself, but he cannot accuse those whom he justifies.

Who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, and who also intercedes for us.

He denies that we can accuse God, because God justifies us. But we cannot condemn Christ, because he loves us with such affection that he died for us and, having risen, continually pleads our cause before the Father. His petition cannot be disregarded, because he is at the right hand of God—that is, in the honor that belongs to God—so that, secure in God the Father and in Christ his Son, who will judge, we may rejoice in faith.

This is what he says to the apostle Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII).

(Origen) It seems to me that by “Who will bring an accusation against God’s chosen?” he means the devil. For there is no one so chosen and so great whom the devil would not dare to accuse, except the one who committed no sin and who said: “Now the prince of this world has come, and he has found nothing in me” (John XII).

But although the devil displays the wickedness of his purpose, when God justifies and removes the iniquity of his chosen like a cloud, and their sins like a mist, whitening them from their former offenses like snow and making them white like wool (Isa. I), what does the accuser accomplish?

And when Christ has died for them—or rather, has risen from the dead—and is at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for them, who will be able to condemn them?

Above, he said, “The Holy Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings”; here, Christ Jesus, who died and rose again, himself intercedes for us. God, who handed over his own Son for us, himself justifies the chosen. Who, then, will dare to condemn them?

But observe more carefully how the Apostle nowhere departs from the caution inherent in his language. He did not say, “Who will bring an accusation against those who are called,” but “against the chosen.” Unless you have been chosen, unless you have shown yourself acceptable to God in all things, you will have an accuser.

If your case is bad, if your own crime binds you, what will an advocate profit you, even if it is Jesus who intercedes? For Jesus is the truth; therefore the truth cannot lie on your behalf.

He will help you in this: that you may not be entangled in the accuser’s calumnies, and that your former sins, which have been erased through baptism, may not be charged against you. But if, after these things, you sin again and do not wash these sins away with any tears of repentance, you will give your accuser material with which to indict you.

And although Jesus intercedes for us, Jesus cannot call darkness light, or bitter sweet.

Therefore, if you wish to prevail when you are judged, do what is written concerning the righteous: “Arrange your words in the judgment” (Ps. CXI); “Prepare your works for their outcome”; “Remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Eccli. VII), lest what is written concerning a certain person happen to you: “When he is judged, let him come out condemned” (Ps. CVII).

Consider how you should understand the statement that Jesus intercedes for us. He is the one of whom it is also written elsewhere: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). And just as he himself is both sacrifice and priest, and is both in the form of a servant and in the form of God, so he is both advocate and judge.

(Ambrose) In this way, then, the Savior intercedes for us. Knowing the shamelessness and arrogance of our adversary, when he rouses himself against us, if we do not yield to him, the Savior intercedes for us so that the adversary may not violently presume anything against us, and so that his insolence may be restrained.

For this reason the Son is said to intercede, although he himself accomplishes everything and is equal to God the Father. And because God is said to be one, lest the Father and the Son be thought to be a single person or a mere unity, Scripture speaks in this way to distinguish the persons: it presents the Son as not unequal, while giving precedence to the Father because he is Father and because all things are from him.

(Gregory) For the only-begotten Son to intercede for humanity means that he displays himself as human to the coeternal Father; and to plead for human nature means that he has assumed that same nature into the height of his divinity.

The Lord therefore intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the chosen, he set it free.

An advocate is therefore sought so that the desire may be heard, because unless the intercession of the mediator intervened for us, the voices of our prayers would undoubtedly be silent far from the ear of God.

Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.” But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us.

(Augustine) What he says—“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, distress, persecution,” and so forth—depends upon what he said above: “Provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified”; and, “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

The whole purpose of this passage is directed toward that exhortation: those to whom he speaks should not be broken by persecutions if they live according to the prudence of the flesh, by which temporal goods are desired and temporal evils feared.

(Origen) For all these things that we have enumerated above—that we are no longer in the flesh but in the Spirit; that the Spirit of God dwells in us; that Christ is in us, through whom the body is dead because of sin but the spirit is life because of justification; that we are no longer debtors to the flesh, so as to live according to the flesh, because by the Spirit we have put to death the deeds of the flesh; that through the Spirit of adoption we have become children of God, and, if children, also heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ; that the whole creation groans and suffers with us, awaiting the revelation of the children of God; that all things work together for good for those who love God; and that he foreknew and predestined us to be conformed to the image of his Son, having called us according to his purpose—

when, he says, we are established and rooted in the love of God for all these benefits that we have received, who will be able to separate us from it?

If tribulation comes, we will say to God: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. IV).

If there is distress from the world, arising from the necessity of the body, we will seek the breadth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, in which the world cannot constrict us. For I will return to the broadest fields of the divine Scriptures; I will seek the spiritual understanding of the Word of God, and no distress will confine me there. For I will ride through the very spacious expanses of mystical and spiritual understanding.

If I suffer persecution and confess my Christ before human beings, I am certain that he too will confess me before his Father who is in heaven (Matt. X).

If famine is present, it cannot disturb me. For I have the bread of life that descended from heaven and will refresh hungry souls; and this bread can never fail, for it is perfect and eternal.

Nakedness does not shame me. For I have put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and I hope to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven. For this mortal must put on immortality, and this corruptible must put on incorruption (I Cor. XV).

I will not fear danger. For “the Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. XXVI).

An earthly sword cannot frighten me. For I have with me a stronger sword, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI). With me is also the living and effective word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. IV).

Therefore, if the sword of the world comes against my neck, it increases my love for God. For I will say to him, as it is written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.”

It is not enough for me to die for Christ or to be tortured for a single hour, but to do so all day long—that is, throughout the whole period of my life. For if I spend my entire life in persecutions and dangers, I will say that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.”

The time of this life is brief, and the time we spend in persecutions is short; but what we await in glory is eternal and everlasting.

Therefore, in all these things, he says, we conquer—not by our own strength, but through him who loved us. For while we depend upon his love, we do not experience the sensation of pain. His love, with which he loved us and by which he draws our affection toward himself, does not allow us to feel the torture and pain of the body.

Therefore, in all these things we conquer.

I am convinced, then, that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither powers, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

**(Origen.)** The Apostle seems to have indicated two classes of beings who are accustomed to raise temptations against human beings. In those matters we discussed earlier, the class of human temptations is understood to have been described. Concerning these he also said to the Corinthians, since they were unable to bear greater trials: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human; but God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (I Cor. X). Now, however, in the words we have before us, he does not indicate human temptations, but temptations greater than human.

Therefore, I think that in the earlier passage, after enumerating each thing individually, he finally says: “But in all these things we prevail.” In these temptations of the second class, however, he does not say so confidently, “We conquer,” but states very cautiously that none of them will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus. Concerning human temptations, as though they were small and light, he confidently declares that we overcome them; but concerning those higher and more-than-human temptations, even if we are unable to overcome and overthrow them—for that is Christ’s work alone, since he stripped principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself (Col. II)—there is nevertheless victory even in this: if, after they have turned all the engines of their attacks against us, they are still unable to separate us from the love of God.

But let us now attempt to examine each point and, as far as our strength allows, explain what should be understood by each of the Apostle’s words. Although the Apostle appears to have touched upon matters higher than the power of our exposition can adequately explain, or than the brevity of our discussion permits, let us nevertheless inquire whether all the things he enumerated—or only some of them—are intent on trying to separate human souls from the love of God, and therefore devise against us all that we suffer.

**(Augustine.)** He says, then, “For I am convinced.” He did not say, “For I suppose.” He held the matter with complete faith: neither any death, nor any temporal life that is promised, nor any of the things that follow can turn the believer away from the love of God.

No one, therefore, can separate us—not even one who threatens death, because whoever believes in Christ, although he dies, will live; nor one who promises life, because Christ gives eternal life. The promise of temporal life is contemptible when compared with eternal life.

Nor can an angel separate us, because, he says, “Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what you have received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I).

Nor can a principality separate us—that is, an opposing principality—because Christ himself stripped these principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself.

Nor can things present or things future separate us, that is, temporal things: whether those that delight, those that oppress, those that offer hope, or those that produce fear.

Nor can power separate us. Here too, opposing power must be understood, according to the saying: “No one can plunder the goods of the strong man unless he first binds the strong man.”

Nor height nor depth (Matt. XII). Very often empty curiosity about things that cannot be discovered—or that are discovered without purpose—whether in heaven or in the abyss, separates a person from God, unless love prevails. Love summons us to certain spiritual realities, not through the vanity of outward things, but through inward illumination.

Nor can any other creature separate us. This can be understood in two ways. It may mean visible creation, since we too—that is, the soul—are creatures, though invisible; in that case he would be saying that no other creature separates us, meaning the love of bodies. Or it may mean that no other creature separates us from the love of God because there is no other creature between us and God that can oppose us and exclude us from his embrace. Above rational human minds there is no creature, but God.

**(Ambrose.)** These are all the things that the devil employs to draw us away, and he mentions them in order to fortify us, so that if any of them should arise, we may confidently rely on the hope and assistance of Christ and, armed with faith, resist them.

For what if death is inflicted? Is it not the greatest gain to find an opportunity by which one may enter more quickly into the promised kingdom? Nor, if the present life promised to us should be diminished in dignity, ought this to separate us from hope in Christ’s benefit, since we know that he will help us not only in the future but also in the present.

Nor, if an angel should appear to us in order to lead us astray, having been enlisted in the deceptions of his father, the devil, ought he to prevail against us, since we know that nothing should be preferred to Christ, the angel of the great counsel.

Nor, if a power should be performed by someone—as is said to have happened with Simon Magus, who supposedly flew upward through the air in order to scandalize Christ’s people—ought this to diminish the faith of those who know that the Savior, received by the service of a cloud, ascended above all the heavens.

Nor, if some being should display itself to us in the height of which the Apostle John says, “Do you not know the height of Satan?” (Rev. II), ought this to remove us from devotion to the Lord Jesus, whom we know to have descended from heaven in order to join earthly things to spiritual realities.

Nor, if through the phantasm by which it plans to seduce us it should display to us a depth terrifying to behold, by which we might perhaps be frightened and fall under its power, is it right for us on that account to break faith with Christ, whom we know to have descended for our sake into the depths of the earth and, by the pressure of death, to have liberated the human race.

Nor, if it should promise us future things, as it promised Eve, will we give it our assent, separating ourselves from Christ, whom we believe and know to be God in power and nature.

Nor, if by the art and elevation of its cunning it should temporarily fabricate another creature—as Jannes and Jambres fabricated things openly before Pharaoh (Exod. VII)—is it fitting that through this it should call us away from God the true Creator, who, as we know, through Christ his Son created a creature destined to exist forever.

Some think that by “another creature” he meant idols. But this is not true, because he ought to have signified the creature that Satan seemed to fabricate under the appearance of an astonishing deception. For which of the faithful would be deceived by things from which he has withdrawn after their error was exposed? Satan devises and fabricates such things so that he may be able to deceive the elect.

There are therefore no things that can separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus. For God displayed his love for us in Christ when he handed him over for our sake.

## CHAPTER IX

**The Apostle grieves over the obstinacy of the Jews, whom he shows not to have been deprived of the promise, and recalls that they were called before the Gentiles.**

“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself was wishing to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers.”

**(Origen.)** “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie,” and so forth, up to “forever.”

Paul saw that, if according to what he had explained above no power—whether heavenly or earthly, present or future—opposing him could separate him from the love of Christ, what he was now proposing to say would appear contradictory and unbelievable: that he wished to become accursed and alienated from Christ, whom he loved so inseparably. Therefore, lest he appear to incur the charge of falsehood, he first offers an assurance, so that no one may doubt his words. He says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit.”

But let us examine why he says, “I speak the truth in Christ,” as though indicating that there is some truth that is not in Christ. Let us see whether we can distinguish the truth that is in Christ from truth that is not in Christ in the following way. Elsewhere the same Paul says: “The truth of Christ is in me, because I do not lie” (II Cor. XI).

The truth of Christ, then, must be understood to be present wherever the other virtues that are described as belonging to Christ are present: where there is justice, where there is peace, where there is the word of God, there also is the truth of Christ.

Yet there is also truth in injustice. For example, the demonic spirit of Python mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, which had entered a certain slave girl and cried out after the Apostles, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of God” (Acts XVI): there was truth in these words, for what was said was true. But that truth was not in Christ. Therefore Paul turned to it and said: “Be silent and come out of her.”

What Caiaphas said was also true: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI). Nevertheless, this truth was not in Christ. Therefore the Apostle distinguishes Christ’s truth from the truth that is outside Christ by saying that he speaks the truth in Christ.

The same understanding seems to apply to his statement, “My conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit.” Conscience also bears witness among the Gentiles, as the same Apostle said earlier: “Their conscience also bears witness, and their thoughts accuse or even defend them.” In those whose thoughts contain something for which they may be accused, conscience comes forward as a witness; but it cannot be said that, on account of evil actions, conscience bears witness in the Holy Spirit.

In the Apostle, however, where his thought no longer has anything for which to accuse him, his conscience rightly bears witness in the Holy Spirit.

Consider, nevertheless, the greatness of the apostolic heart. He cannot be separated from the love of God; what he speaks, he speaks in Christ; what he holds in his conscience is contained by the Holy Spirit.

What heavens, what thrones, what vast minds of the heavenly powers, seated in such spacious places, could contain the whole Trinity?

“For I have great sorrow,” he says, “and continual pain in my heart.”

Suppose that you have sorrow; suppose that you feel pain over the destruction of your brothers, who are your relatives according to the flesh. Surely not to the point of wishing to become accursed and separated from Christ? What benefit is their salvation to you if you are separated from salvation? What will save others if you yourself perish?

“No,” he says, “that is not the case. I learned from my Teacher and Lord that whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will find it” (Luke IX).

**(Jerome.)** We can perceive the same affection in Moses and Paul toward the flock entrusted to them. “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; but the hired servant, when he sees the wolf coming, flees, because the sheep are not his own” (John X).

This is precisely what it means to say, “I was wishing to be accursed and separated from Christ,” and “to be erased from the book that you have written.” For those who are erased from the book of the living and are not written with the righteous become accursed and separated from the Lord.

At the same time, observe how great Paul’s love is in Christ: he desires to die for him and perish alone, provided that the whole human race should believe in him. But he means being struck down not forever, but for the present; for whoever loses his soul for Christ makes it safe.

**(Origen.)** What wonder, then, if the Apostle wishes to become accursed for his brothers, since he knows that the one who was in the form of God emptied himself of that form, assumed the form of a servant, and became a curse for us?

And what wonder if, when the Lord became a curse for his servants, the servant should become accursed for his brothers?

I think that Moses also, when the people had sinned, said to the Lord: “And now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, erase me from the book of life that you have written” (Exod. XXXII).

What then? Do you want Paul to appear inferior to Moses? Moses asks to be erased from the book of life for the sake of his brothers; should Paul not wish to become accursed for the sake of his brothers?

But perhaps someone may say that, by offering himself in this way, Moses deserved to obtain the people’s salvation, whereas Paul wishes for this but was not heard.

What if I show you that Paul was heard more than Moses? All those who had gone out of Egypt through Moses fell in the wilderness. Their descendants, however, who received the promised land, are even now wandering as exiles and outcasts from it.

But hear what Paul says about Israel: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery: a partial blindness has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

You see, therefore, that Paul was heard; and because he offered himself to become accursed, he obtained salvation for his brothers. For this reason it seems to me that he prefaced all those statements about his inability to be separated from the love of God, so that, when he offered himself as accursed for his brothers, you would not judge his fall possible. Rather, just as the one who is inseparable from the Father by nature and immortal came into death and descended into the underworld, so Paul, imitating his Teacher, though he cannot be separated from the love of Christ, becomes accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of his brothers—through devotion, certainly, not through transgression.

**(Ambrose.)** Since earlier he seems to have been speaking against the Jews, who think that they are justified by the law, he now displays his vow and affection toward them. With his conscience bearing witness, he says that he speaks in Christ Jesus and in the Holy Spirit, so that his testimony may not be rejected as though he were their enemy.

Therefore he gives Christ and the Holy Spirit, who conceal nothing, as witnesses—witnesses whose testimony cannot be rejected. They bear witness to the Apostle in this way: they commend him through the power of the signs that they perform through him.

Because Christ’s protection is so great, and because he displayed exceptional love toward the human race, promising glorious and immortal rewards through his gracious favor, Paul grieves over his own people according to the flesh, because by their unbelief they deprived themselves of this perpetual and saving benefit.

Therefore he says, “I was wishing,” not “I wish,” because he knows that it cannot happen that so honorable a member, without any preceding fault, should be cut off from the Christian body. Nevertheless, he displays his affection and love toward his own people.

**(Origen.)** That the Israelites are Paul’s relatives according to the flesh requires no explanation.

Their adoption as sons. The sons of Israel were adopted by God at the time “when the Most High divided the nations and dispersed the sons of Adam according to the number of the angels. And the portion of the Lord became Jacob, Israel the cord of his inheritance.” This, then, is the adoption as sons.

**(Ambrose.)** He rightly proves that he grieves when he proclaims the praise of their race: although they were once adopted sons, they made void the affection and favor of God the Father. He adds further matters in order to make others grieve for them as well, saying:

“The glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.”

He enumerates so many declarations of the nobility and dignity of the Jewish race and of the promises that he causes everyone to grieve over them, because, by not receiving the Savior, they lost the privilege of their fathers and the merit of the promise. They became worse than the Gentiles, whom they had previously abominated because they were without God. For it is a greater evil to have lost dignity than never to have possessed it.

**(Origen.)** What he says about “the glory and the covenant” has often already been said concerning the glory of the law that was given, just as the Apostle himself says: “If what is being brought to an end came through glory”—that is, the Old Testament—“much more will what remains be in glory” (II Cor. III), namely, the preaching of the Gospel.

But when he says “the covenant” and “the giving of the law,” he may perhaps seem to be saying one thing twice. For he calls the law that was given a covenant as well.

I, however, think that the distinction is this: there was one giving of the law, which took place once through Moses; but covenants were established frequently. For whenever they sinned and were rejected, they seemed to be disinherited; and again, whenever God was reconciled and recalled them, bringing them into the inheritance of his possession, he should be understood each time to have renewed the covenants and written them as heirs.

“And the worship and the promises”: by “worship” he means priestly services; by “promises,” those made to the fathers and expected to be given to those who through faith are called sons of Abraham.

It is certain, however, that not only the fathers but also Christ, according to the flesh, came from that very race, that is, from the Israelite race. As the Prophet also says: “Woe to them, because my flesh is from them.”

But why “woe to them”? Because Jesus was born “for the falling and rising of many” (Luke II), and because he was rejected by those whose flesh he shared but received by the Gentiles, who had not known him. As he also says through David (Ps. XVII): “A people whom I did not know served me.”

**(Augustine.)** When he says, “theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh,” and adds, “who is God over all, blessed forever,” he commends with the fullest faith the confession that, according to the assumption of flesh, we acknowledge our God as the Son of man, and that, according to eternity, he is the Word in the beginning, God blessed above all forever.

Because the Jews held only one part of this confession, they are refuted by the Lord. For when he asked them whose son they said Christ was (Matt. XXII), they answered, “David’s”—and this was according to the flesh. But concerning his divinity, that he is God, they answered nothing.

Therefore the Lord said to them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord?” He wanted them to understand that they had confessed only that Christ was the son of David, while they had kept silent about the fact that Christ was David’s Lord. The former concerns the assumption of flesh; the latter concerns the eternity of divinity.

**(Ambrose.)** When no mention is made of the name of the Father and the subject is Christ, it cannot be denied that he is called God. Scripture frequently speaks of God the Father in this way for the sake of confessing one God, and it calls the Father God and the Son God.

If anyone does not think that the words “who is God” were spoken about Christ, let him identify the person to whom they were spoken. No mention of God the Father has been made in this passage. But what wonder if, in this place, he openly called Christ God over all, since elsewhere in the Epistle he confirmed the same meaning in these words: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II)?

These are all the things over which Christ is God. For there are no others except these, so that Christ would not be God over all; nor can every creature bend the knee except to God.

Finally, the Apostle John, in his ignorance, wished to worship an angel, but heard from him: “Do not do this, for I am your fellow servant. Worship God” (Rev. XIX, XXII). The Lord would certainly not allow himself to be worshiped unless he were God. Otherwise he would be accused of usurpation and sin—which is impossible—since he himself, rebuking the devil, showed that the Lord God must be worshiped and that he alone must be served.

Nothing, therefore, is taken away from God the Father when Christ is worshiped as God, because although it is said that God alone must be served, Christ too is served. For he says elsewhere: “Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God” (Rom. XIV).

What remains, then, except that the Father is believed to be God, the Son God, and nevertheless both one God? Whether someone worships the Father or the Son, he says that he worships one God; whether he serves the Father or the Son, service is offered to one God.

There is therefore no distinction. Whoever worships the Son also prays to the Father, and whoever serves the Father serves the Son. To teach that this confession of divinity was not flattery, he placed “Amen” at the conclusion—that is, “truly”—so that he might show in truth that Christ, God over all, is blessed forever.

“But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are all sons; but ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called.’”

**(Origen.)** Since he had said above that he wished even to become accursed for the sake of his brothers, “who are his relatives according to the flesh, who are Israelites,” because theirs were the adoption as sons, the giving of the law, and the promise, he now says concerning them that the word of God has not failed—that is, the promise made to them has not vanished.

**(Ambrose.)** This is what happened, he says: God declared that those would not be called Abraham’s seed who were his sons according to the flesh, but those who received faith—the faith through which Isaac was born, reformed in the time of Christ, no longer particular but universal.

What Abraham believed concerning Isaac, these believe concerning God and Christ, because the Son of God was born for the redemption and salvation of the human race.

**(Origen.)** The true Israel is not merely one who derives his origin from Abraham according to the flesh, for “not all who are children of the flesh are children of God”; rather, the one who descends from Abraham according to the promise of faith also receives God’s promises.

There are many from the race of Israel, but not all are called Israel. Israel received its name from seeing God, as Jacob himself says: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Gen. XXXII). Therefore, because he saw God, he was called Israel. But whoever does not see him who said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John XIV), cannot be called Israel.

**(Ambrose.)** He therefore wishes it to be understood that people are not worthy merely because they are sons of Abraham. Those are worthy who are sons of the promise—that is, those whom God foreknew would receive his promise, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles.

These are worthy to be called Israelites, that is, “those who see God,” because they believe.

All these, certainly, are sons of Abraham through Isaac, because the entire Jewish race descends from Abraham through Isaac. Consequently, the other sons should not be called Abraham’s sons.

Abraham received Isaac because he believed, on account of his faith in God. In this was prefigured the mystery of future faith, so that those would be Isaac’s brothers who possessed the same faith in which Isaac was born. Isaac was born as a type of the Savior from the promise, so that whoever believed that Christ Jesus had been promised to Abraham would be Abraham’s son and Isaac’s brother.

It was therefore said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” This was not accomplished in Isaac himself, but in the one who was promised to Abraham in Isaac—namely, Christ—in whom all believing nations are blessed.

The rest of the Jews, therefore, are children of the flesh, since they are deprived of the promise. They cannot be reckoned as Abraham’s true offspring, because they do not follow the faith through which Abraham became worthy.

That is: “Not the children of the flesh are the children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as the seed.” It is clear that children of the flesh cannot be called children of God. The former were born from the desire of the flesh; the latter were born spiritually from faith, according to what was promised to Abraham, so that those who believe would be reckoned as the seed.

The word of the promise is this: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”

**(Origen.)** The Apostle has undertaken to establish that, although the people of Israel were rejected because of unbelief, God’s promises made to them had not fallen away or been frustrated. He teaches that, although Abraham had many sons, the promise was made in Isaac alone.

“For,” he says, “not the children of the flesh are the children of God.” He attempts to show how Isaac is not a child of the flesh but is the Son of God, and he returns to what is written about him in Genesis: “The word of promise is this: At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”

Isaac was therefore not born according to the order of carnal birth, especially since Abraham’s body was already considered dead and Sarah’s womb was barren, as was said above. Rather, he was born through the power of the one who said, “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”

He is rightly called not a son of the flesh but the Son of God, because he was born through the coming and word of God.

**(Ambrose.)** “The word of promise is this”: this was prefigured in Christ, so that Christ, who would fulfill the word of promise, might be promised as Abraham’s son, and so that all the nations of the earth might be blessed in Christ.

For when the promise was made to Abraham and he heard, “In your seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed,” Christ was certainly promised to him through the line of Isaac, in whom we see this fulfilled.

“Not only that, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father.”

**(Augustine.)** Not only was Isaac promised, when it was said, “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Gen. XVIII, XXV)—he who had certainly merited no works by which God should promise that he would be born and that the seed would be called in Isaac, that is, that those should belong to the portion of the saints which is in Christ who understood themselves to be children of the promise, not boasting in their merits but attributing it to the grace of their calling, so that they would be coheirs of Christ.

For when it was promised that they would exist, those who did not yet exist had certainly merited nothing. But Rebecca also, “having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father,” most carefully says “by one act of intercourse.” Twins were conceived at the same time, so that no one might attribute the distinction to the merits of the parents. Someone might perhaps say: “This son was born such because the father was disposed in that way at the time when he sowed in the mother’s womb,” or, “Because the mother was disposed in that way when she conceived him.” But both were conceived at the same time.

When they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works, but from the one who calls—it was said to Rebecca: “The older shall serve the younger,” as it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

**(Origen.)** This reasoning, then, he says, must be accepted not only concerning Isaac but also concerning Jacob. For Rebecca too, he says, did not give birth according to the order of carnal birth.

When she had conceived twins from one act of intercourse with Isaac, before the birth had occurred and before any good or evil actions of the children had taken place among human beings, divine election was directed toward Jacob. It was said: “The older shall serve the younger,” and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

He explains why these things were said: “So that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works, but from the one who calls.” That is, not those who are children of the flesh, but those who are children of God, are to be counted as the seed.

Just as from among many children of the flesh Isaac was chosen by God to be adopted as the Son of God, so here, from among two, the younger Jacob was chosen to be adopted as the Son of God. Thus it becomes true that God’s promises are established not in the children of the flesh but in the children of God.

All these matters serve to prove what the Apostle says: If either Isaac or Jacob had been chosen by God because of merits acquired while they were in the flesh, and if they had deserved to be justified through works of the flesh, their merit could certainly have extended by grace to their descendants according to flesh and blood.

But since their election was not made from works but from God’s purpose and from the decision of the one who calls, the grace of the promises is fulfilled not in the children of the flesh but in the children of God—that is, in those who, like them, are chosen according to God’s purpose and adopted as sons.

In these also is fulfilled what we explained above: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

**(Ambrose.)** God’s foreknowledge is required in these matters, because nothing can happen other than what God knows will happen. Knowing what each of them would become, he said: “This one will be worthy, since he will be the younger; the older will be unworthy.” He chose one through foreknowledge and rejected the other.

In the one whom he chose, God’s purpose remains, because nothing can happen other than what he knows and has purposed concerning him: that he should be worthy of salvation. And in the one whom he rejects, the purpose he formed concerning him likewise remains: that he should be unworthy.

He does this as one who foreknows, not as one who shows partiality. For he condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers.

This pertains to the case of the Jews, who defend their privilege by claiming that they are Abraham’s sons. The Apostle consoles himself because, although he had said that he bore continual pain in his heart on account of the unbelief of those whose adoption was as sons, whose was the giving of the law, and from whom Christ the Savior came—as he himself says, “salvation is from the Jews” (John IV)—after examining the law he discovered that not all who are from Israel would believe, nor should all who are called Abraham’s sons be called Abraham’s sons, as I mentioned above.

He therefore lessens his grief when he discovers that it was foretold long ago that not all would believe, so that only those should grieve who labor in unbelief through envy. They can believe God, as he makes clear from what follows. Nevertheless, those unbelievers who had been foretold should not be mourned excessively, because they were not predestined to life. For God’s foreknowledge had long ago determined that they would not be saved.

Who would grieve for someone who is considered to have died long ago?

But when the Gentiles entered—those who had previously been without God—and received the salvation that the Jews had lost, grief is revived. Yet again, because they themselves are the cause of their destruction, the grief is quieted.

God therefore, foreknowing that they would have an evil will, did not count them among the good. Nevertheless, the Savior says to the seventy disciples whom he had chosen in a second group, but who later withdrew from him: “Your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

He said this on account of justice, because it is just that each person should receive according to his merit. Since they were good, they were chosen for the ministry, and their names were written in heaven on account of justice, as I have said.

According to foreknowledge, however, they were numbered among the wicked. For God judges according to justice, not according to foreknowledge.

Thus he says to Moses: “If anyone has sinned against me, I will erase him from my book” (Exod. XXXII), so that according to the justice of the Judge he appears to be erased when he sins, whereas according to foreknowledge he had never been in the book of life.

The Apostle John also says concerning such people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II).

There is no partiality in God’s foreknowledge. For foreknowledge is that by which he has determined what each person’s will is going to be, in which he will remain, and through which he will be condemned or crowned.

Finally, those whom he knows will remain in goodness were often previously evil, and those whom he knows will remain evil were sometimes previously good. Thus complaint ceases, because God is not one who shows partiality.

Saul and Judas Iscariot had previously been good. Scripture says of Saul: “He was a good man, and there was none better among the sons of Israel” (I Reg. IX). Concerning Judas Iscariot, the Apostle Peter says: “He received a share in this ministry, in the performance of signs and wonders” (Acts I).

How could he have received a saving ministry unless he had been good? In the casting of lots there was God’s judgment: he was worthy at the time when he was chosen, just as were the seventy whom I mentioned above.

This is why Judas, after committing every evil crime, ended his life by hanging himself, moved by repentance. For all goodness cannot be utterly erased from anyone, since nature cannot be changed, though the will can. This is not the case in every matter, however, because something remains in nature that bears witness to the Creator.

What, then, shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. (Hier.) This signifies what the apostle Paul discusses in writing to the Romans: “What, then, shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not,” up to the passage where he says: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us offspring, we should have become like Sodom and have been made like Gomorrah.” The whole Epistle to the Romans requires interpretation and is enveloped in such great obscurities that, in understanding it, we need the help of the Holy Spirit, who dictated these very things through the Apostle. [Col. 1487B]

But especially this passage, in which certain people, wishing to preserve God’s justice by reference to preceding causes, say that Jacob was chosen in Rebecca’s womb and Esau rejected, just as Jeremiah and John the Baptist are chosen in the womb, and the apostle Paul himself is predestined in the Gospel before he is born. For our part, we approve nothing except what is ecclesiastical, and we are not afraid to say publicly in the Church—lest, following Pythagoras and Plato and their disciples, who introduce pagan doctrine under the Christian name, we should say that souls have fallen from heaven and, according to the diversity of their merits, suffer the punishments of ancient sins in these or those bodies—that it is much better simply to confess our ignorance and, among the other things we do not know, to avoid the obscurity of this passage as well. [Col. 1487C]

As long as we wish to prove God’s justice, we defend the heresy of Basilides and Mani and pursue the Iberian follies and Egyptian monstrosities. Let us say, then, as best we can, following the footsteps of the apostolic intention, and not departing from his judgments by even a point or, as they say, a crosswise fingernail. Above he had wept and, oppressed by the pain of his conscience, had called the Holy Spirit to witness that his brothers and kinsmen according to the flesh—that is, the Israelites—had not received the Son of God, although theirs were adoption, glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, worship, and the promise; from them also Christ himself, according to the flesh, was born of the Virgin Mary. He is so continually tormented by this grief of heart that he himself wishes to be accursed from Christ—that is, to perish alone—so that the entire Israelite race might not perish. [Col. 1487D] And because he had said this, he immediately foresees the question that would naturally arise:

“What, then, are you saying? Have all who are from Israel perished? And how have you yourself, the other apostles, and the innumerable multitude of the Jewish people received Christ, the Son of God?”

He resolves it as follows: Israel is called by two names in the holy Scriptures and is divided into two sons: one according to the flesh, and the other according to promise and the Spirit. Abraham had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac. Ishmael, who was born according to the flesh, did not receive his father’s inheritance; Isaac, who was generated through the promise from Sarah, is called the offspring of God. For it is written: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI), that is, “It is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.” [Col. 1488A]

And we show that this occurred not only in Isaac and Ishmael but also in Rebecca’s two sons, Esau and Jacob, one of whom was rejected and the other chosen. He says all this in order to signify, through the earlier brothers Ishmael and Esau, that the Jewish people were rejected; through the later ones, namely Isaac and Jacob, that the chosen people were the Gentiles—or those among the Jews who were going to believe in Christ.

And because, wishing to establish this, he had proposed the testimony concerning the twin sons Esau and Jacob, of whom it is written, “The elder shall serve the younger,” and in Malachi we read, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I), he proposes and discusses, in his usual manner, the question that arises incidentally, and once it has been resolved he returns to the subject with which he had begun. [Col. 1488B]

“If Esau and Jacob had not yet been born and had done nothing either good or evil by which they might please God or offend him, and if their election and rejection display not the merits of each individual but the will of the one who chooses and rejects, what then shall we say? Is God unjust?” This follows the example spoken to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exod. XXXIII).

“If we accept this,” he says, “so that God does whatever he wishes without regard to merit or works, either choosing someone or condemning him, then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy—especially since the same Scripture, that is, the same God, says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you, and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.’ [Col. 1488C] If this were so, he has mercy on Israel according to his will and hardens Pharaoh. Therefore it is useless to complain and argue that we have either failed to do good or have done evil, since it lies within his power and will, apart from good and evil works, either to choose someone or to reject him—especially since human frailty cannot resist his will.” [Col. 1488D]

This powerful question, woven together by the reasoning of the Scriptures and almost impossible to solve, the Apostle resolves in a brief statement, saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” The sense is this: by answering God and bringing accusations against him, you investigate so much in the Scriptures that you speak against God and inquire into the justice of his will. You show that you possess free choice and can do what you wish, and can remain silent, speak, or hold your tongue.

For if you think that you were created by God in the likeness of a clay vessel and cannot resist his will, consider this: a clay vessel does not say to the potter, “Why did you make me this way?” For the potter has power, from the same lump of clay, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. God, however, created all people under an equal lot and gave them freedom of choice, so that each might do what he wishes, whether good or evil. Indeed, he gave everyone such power that an impious voice may argue against its Creator and scrutinize the reasons for his will.

But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with great patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory, [Col. 1489A] whom he also called—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles—as he says in Hosea: “I will call ‘my people’ the one who was not my people, and ‘beloved’ the one who was not beloved; and in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. II), and the rest that follows—if, he says, God’s patience hardened Pharaoh and for a long time deferred punishment for Israel, so that he might condemn more justly those whom he had endured for so long, it is not God’s patience and infinite clemency that should be accused, but the hardness of those who abused God’s goodness for their own destruction.

Otherwise, the heat of the sun is one and the same, yet, according to the underlying substances, it melts some things, hardens others, loosens some, and contracts others. Wax melts and clay hardens, yet the nature of the heat is not different. So also God’s goodness and clemency [Col. 1489B] harden the vessels of wrath that are prepared for destruction—that is, the people of Israel.

But the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory and also called—that is, us, who are not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles—he does not save irrationally or without the truth of judgment, but on the basis of preceding causes: some did not receive the Son of God, while others willingly desired to receive him. These vessels of mercy are not only the people of the Gentiles but also those among the Jews who wished to believe, and one people was formed from believers.

Thus it is shown that it is not nations who are chosen but the wills of human beings. In this way what was said through Hosea was fulfilled: “I called ‘my people’ the one who was not my people”—that is, the people of the Gentiles—and those to whom it was formerly said, [Col. 1489C] “You are not my people,” are now called sons of the living God. And lest he seem to say this only about the Gentiles, he also calls those from the multitude of Israel who believed vessels of mercy and election.

For Isaiah cries out on behalf of Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X); that is, even if the multitude does not believe, a few will nevertheless believe. For God weighed the word, consummated and abbreviated, in his justice and humility, so that through Christ’s incarnation he might save those who wished to believe in him. Isaiah says the same thing elsewhere: “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us offspring, we should have become like Sodom and have been made like Gomorrah.”

After proposing testimonies in which a twofold calling is foretold—that of the Gentiles and that of the Jewish people—[Col. 1489D] he proceeds to the connected argument. Therefore he says that the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness because they did not become arrogant but believed in Christ. But a large part of Israel fell because it stumbled over the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense, and did not know God’s righteousness; seeking to establish its own righteousness, it refused to submit to the righteousness of God, who is Christ.

I have read in certain commentaries that the Apostle answered in such a way that he entangled the question more than he solved it. For in response to what he had proposed—“What, then, shall we say? Is there injustice with God?”—and to “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy; and he has mercy on whom he wishes and hardens whom he wishes; and who can resist his will?” [Col. 1490A] they say that the Apostle answered:

“O man, who are earth and ashes, do you dare to bring a question against God? O fragile and earthen vessel, do you rebel against your potter? Can the work say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? Therefore be silent in eternal silence, recognize your frailty, and do not bring a question against God, who did what he wished, so that he might be gentle toward some and severe toward others.”

(Orig.) “What, then,” he says, “shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.” The Apostle speaks from the person of one contradicting him: “Is there injustice with God?” And immediately at the outset he answers, “Certainly not,” so that, in all the other objections that must be raised from the person of the one contradicting him, the Apostle may always be understood to answer, “Certainly not.” [Col. 1490B]

(Ambr.) Because he loves one and hates another, does he say, “Is he unjust?” Certainly not, but just. For he knows what he is doing, and his judgment must not be reconsidered. This is found in the prophet Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I). Here he is speaking about judgment, whereas earlier he spoke about foreknowledge, saying that “the elder shall serve the younger.”

Likewise, by foreknowledge he condemned Pharaoh, knowing that he would not be corrected. But he chose the apostle Paul, who was persecuting him, knowing in advance that he would become good. He therefore anticipated him before the appointed time, because he was necessary, and condemned Pharaoh before the future judgment, so that he might be believed to be the one who would judge.

For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” Therefore, he says, “I will have mercy on him on whom I have had mercy”—that is, I will have mercy on him concerning whom I had foreknowledge that I would give mercy, knowing that he would convert and remain with me. “And I will show compassion to him to whom I show compassion”—that is, I will give mercy to the one whom I foresaw would return to me with a right heart after his error. This means giving to the one to whom it ought to be given and not giving to the one to whom it ought not to be given: calling the one whom he knows will obey, but not calling the one whom he knows will not obey. [Col. 1490C] To call is not to force someone to receive the faith.

(Aug.) This shows that there is no injustice with God, which some might say when they hear: “Before they were born, Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” “I will have mercy,” he says, “on whom I have mercy.” First God had mercy on us when we were sinners, in order to call us. “I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy,” he says, so that I may call him; I will have mercy on him still further when he has believed. [Col. 1490D]

But how again? Is it not so that he may give the Holy Spirit to the one who believes and asks? Once he has given him the Spirit, he will show mercy to the one on whom he has had mercy—that is, he will make him merciful, so that he may be able to do good through love. Therefore no one should dare to attribute to himself the fact that he acts mercifully, because God has given him love through the Holy Spirit, without which no one can be merciful.

God therefore did not choose those who were doing good, but rather those who were believing, so that he himself might make them do good. It is ours to believe and to will; it is his to give believers and those who will the ability [Col. 1491A] to do good through the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s love is poured into our hearts so that he may make us merciful.

Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.

(Ambr.) Rightly so, because what is requested ought to depend not on the will of the petitioner but on the judgment of the giver; for whether something should be given must be weighed by the giver’s judgment. When Saul sinned and asked forgiveness, he did not receive it; David, on the other hand, sinned, asked pardon, and obtained forgiveness. From this one must follow the judgment of God, who gives and does not give, because he does not judge unjustly—he who wishes all to be saved while justice remains intact.

For the Examiner of hearts knows whether the petitioner asks with the disposition that makes him worthy to receive. And although it is dangerous to discern God’s judgment, [Col. 1491B] nevertheless, for the sake of those who doubt, and so that their minds may obtain healing and not think God’s judgment unjust—saying, “He calls one and neglects another,” and thus supposing that those who are condemned can excuse themselves—let us prove this by facts rather than words. Where there are examples of events that actually occurred, no one dares to complain or offer any excuse.

There were two men, David and Saul. Let us examine their histories and see how each of them was found after God’s judgment, so that, if Saul is proved to have acted well after he did not receive mercy, we may regard God’s judgment as unjust—which God forbid—or, if David, having received mercy, is found to have despised God, whether he remained in the condition in which he obtained mercy.

To state the matter briefly, each of them endured a crisis in his kingdom. [Col. 1491C] And how great was David’s crisis, when his own son wanted to deprive him of his kingdom! In that crisis he traveled weeping and barefoot, fleeing as king and leader of God’s people. He was so humbled that he did not even answer when his own servant cursed him to his face, wishing through patience to make God favorable toward him, trusting that through God the kingdom would be restored to him.

Saul, however, was not found in such a crisis—for civil war is a greater evil than foreign war. Moreover, he took it badly that he had not been heard once and again, although he was unworthy, and he did not persist in prayer so as to acquire merit by which he might become worthy. Instead, impatient and indignant at God’s judgment, he sought help from the idols that he had previously condemned as worthless.

Behold, it is clear even to those unwilling to accept it that God’s judgment of foreknowledge is just. [Col. 1491D]

(Aug.) When he says, “Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy,” he does not abolish free choice; rather, he says that our willing is not sufficient unless God helps us by making us merciful for good works through the gift of the Holy Spirit. He refers this to what he said earlier: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

For we cannot even will unless we are called; and when, after the calling, we have willed, our will and our running are not sufficient unless God both supplies strength to those who run and brings them to the place to which he calls them.

(Orig.) As David also says in the psalm: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). [Col. 1492A] By this he shows that the person who builds the house does not do nothing, nor remain idle, while the Lord builds it; rather, the person expends as much concern and labor as lies within human capacity, but it belongs to God, once every obstacle has been removed, to bring the work to its result.

Since this teaches that a human being contributes labor and concern, while God grants success and completion to the work, it is pious and religious for a person to attribute the substance of the work that lies within him more to God than to himself.

Likewise, when Paul planted and Apollos watered, God is said to give the growth, and it is added: “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

Thus, in the present passage also, [Col. 1492B] we can say: “Therefore neither he who runs is anything, nor he who wills, but God who gives the result.” For the one who wills and the one who runs appear to be equivalent to the one who plants and the one who waters. But the Apostle says that the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing—not because they do nothing, but because, in comparison with God, who gives growth and brings the work to completion, they are considered nothing.

(Cass.) It is clearly proved that God’s grace and mercy are always at work within us, bringing about the things that are good. When he abandons us, the effort of the one who labors has no power, and however much the mind may strive, it cannot recover its former condition without his assistance once again. This saying is continually fulfilled in us: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” [Col. 1492C]

That grace, on the contrary, sometimes does not refuse to visit the negligent and lax with this inspiration, which is called holy, and with an abundance of spiritual thoughts. It inspires the unworthy, awakens those who sleep, illuminates those possessed by the blindness of ignorance, and mercifully rebukes and chastises us, pouring itself into our hearts so that, stirred by its own remorse, we may be urged to rise even in this way from the sleep of inertia.

Finally, often during these sudden visitations we are also filled with fragrances surpassing every sweetness of human composition, so that the mind, dissolved by this delight, is carried into a kind of spiritual ecstasy and forgets that it dwells in the flesh.

(Aug.) God did not therefore have mercy because Jacob willed and ran; rather, Jacob willed and ran because God had mercy. [Col. 1492D] “The will is prepared by the Lord, and the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Ps. XXXVI).

Furthermore, because this general statement—“It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy”—was spoken on account of Jacob, an example is also given from Pharaoh, in connection with what was said, “But Esau I hated,” and the text continues:

For Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you, and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

(Orig.) It is certain that God not only knows each person’s purpose and will but also foreknows them. Knowing and foreknowing, as a good and just steward, he uses each person’s impulses and purpose to accomplish those works that each person’s soul and [Col. 1493A] will have chosen.

For example, suppose we say that a wise and just head of a household, possessing a large number of servants, will observe as carefully as possible which of them is suited in mind to cultivate the fields and assign him to agricultural work; which is suited to trade; which to tending livestock; which to service; and which has the aptitude to attend and guard his chamber. Being wise, he will assign each one to appropriate duties.

But because it is not hidden from him—whether he is a head of household or a king—that subjects will sometimes rebel, violate the rules of discipline, and consequently require correction and blows, he must also choose from among all of them those dispositions suited to this purpose, if any have been driven to greater violence, who, although they are carried along by their own impulses, [Col. 1493B] may nevertheless provide the correction necessary for wrongdoers.

Let us suppose, then, that this head of household or king saw that the time had come when those who had committed many offenses against custom and discipline ought to be corrected, and chose someone especially harsh, much more severe even than those who were to be disciplined—someone who, because of his crimes, was no longer worthy of correction but of death.

Wishing his destruction to benefit the correction of the others, he sends him to those whom he wishes to correct through his death and says to him: “For this very purpose I raised you up, to show my power in you, and so that my name may be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.”

Observe that he did not say, “For this very purpose I made you”; otherwise the blame might seem to be referred to the creator. Instead he says, “For this very purpose I raised you up”—that is, so that through the wickedness of your mind, [Col. 1493C] which you acquired for yourself by living unrestrained and without fear of God, a useful and fruitful correction might be inflicted upon others, and upon yourself a most renowned destruction might be brought about as an example for posterity.

(Ambr.) Pharaoh was preserved for this purpose: so that many signs and plagues might be displayed against him, as against one already dead. He is said to have been raised up because, although he was dead before God, he received a short period in which he appeared to live. Thus there would be someone whose punishment and varied forms of torment, extending even to death, might cause all who were without God to look on, be terrified by fear, and confess with the greatest admiration that this God alone existed, from whom these acts of vengeance came.

By a similar method, ancient physicians, in the case of people deserving death or already condemned to death, investigated how the things hidden within the human body, once exposed, [Col. 1493D] might benefit the living, so that through them they might learn the causes of illness, and the punishment of the dying might contribute to the salvation of the living.

(Aug.) The fact, then, that Pharaoh did not obey God’s commands at that time already proceeded from punishment. No one can say that the hardening of his heart occurred undeservedly to Pharaoh; rather, it was the judgment of God, who repaid his unbelief with its due punishment.

Therefore what is not charged against him is that he did not obey at that time, since, with his heart hardened, he could not obey; rather, he is charged because he had made himself worthy to have his heart hardened by his earlier unbelief.

For just as, among those whom God chooses, works do not begin merit but faith, so that they may do good through God’s gift, so among those whom he condemns, unbelief and impiety begin the merit of punishment, [Col. 1494A] so that through that punishment they may do evil. As the same Apostle says above: “And because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting.”

Therefore the Apostle concludes as follows:

Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes.

(Orig.) When he says, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes,” he appears to take this from what is written in Exodus. For there he says: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not release the people.”

Pharaoh’s heart was hardened in this way: God did not wish to inflict sudden and complete vengeance upon him. Although he was utterly wicked, God, through his patience, had not even excluded for him the possibility of conversion. Therefore he used first gentler blows and then others gradually increasing in severity [Col. 1494B] against him.

But by what God was doing through patience, Pharaoh was hardened toward contempt, storing up greater wrath for himself, so that what the Apostle writes in Romans II might properly be said to him: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath.”

It is not, then, that God hardens the one whom he wishes; rather, the one who refuses to obey patience is hardened.

(Aug.) For the one on whom he has mercy he makes do good, and the one whom he hardens he leaves to do evil. But that mercy is granted on the basis of preceding merit of faith, and that hardening on the basis of preceding impiety, so that we may do good through God’s gift and evil through punishment.

Free choice of the will is not taken away—whether for believing in God, so that mercy may come to us, or for impiety, so that punishment may come to us. [Col. 1494C] Having brought this conclusion forward, he introduces a question as though from one contradicting him, for he says:

You say to me, then: “Why is anything still in question? For who resists his will?” He answers this inquiry in such a way that we may understand that, for spiritual men who are no longer living according to the earthly human being, the first merits of faith and impiety can become evident: how God, by his foreknowledge, chooses those who will believe and condemns unbelievers—not choosing the former on the basis of their works, nor condemning the latter on the basis of their works, but granting to the faith of the former that they may do good, and hardening the impiety of the latter by abandoning them, so that they may do evil. Since this understanding, as I have said, is open to spiritual people but far removed from carnal prudence, he rebukes the questioner in such a way that he understands that he must first lay aside the human being of clay, so that he may deserve to investigate these matters through the Spirit.

Therefore, he says, “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” So long as you are a thing formed, he says, and belong to the mass of clay, not yet brought to spiritual things so that you are spiritual, judging all things and judged by no one, you ought to restrain yourself from such an inquiry and not answer back to God. Whoever desires to know his counsel must first be received into his friendship; but this cannot happen except to spiritual people, who already bear the image of the heavenly human being: “For now,” he says, “I will no longer call you servants, but friends; for everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

So long as you are the potter’s vessel, that same vessel must first be broken within you by the iron rod of which it is said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod; as a potter’s vessel you shall break them” (Psalm 2). Thus, when the outer human being has been corrupted and the inner human being renewed, you may be rooted and grounded in love and comprehend “the breadth and length and height and depth,” and also “know the surpassing greatness of the knowledge of the love of Christ” (Ephesians 3).

Now, therefore, when from the same lump God has made some vessels for honor and others for dishonor, it is not for you to investigate the matter, if you are still living according to the same lump—that is, if you think in an earthly and carnal manner.

**(Origen.)** It is therefore superfluous for you, as an adversary, to say to the Apostle: “Why is anything still in question? For who resists his will?” Certainly no one opposes the will of God; but we must know that his will is just and upright. Whether we are good or evil depends upon our own will. But whether the evil person is destined for what punishments, and the good person for what glory, depends upon the will of God.

“O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” We also read in the Gospels that those who insolently and unbelievingly asked the Lord by what authority he did the things he was doing, and who had given him this authority, were not even considered worthy of an answer (Luke 20).

Likewise, in the present passage we see the Apostle moved against insolent questions and, by what he answered, confounding the obstinacy of the questioner. For he says: “O man, who are you to answer back against God?” A human being is to God what clay is to the potter. And just as a wicked servant, if he should see his master undertaking some work that appears to be full of reason and usefulness, might refuse to work and begin to examine what his master commands, asking him, “Why do you order this work to be done? What use is it? Why is it necessary?”—what answer could be more fitting for an insolent servant than to say to him, “Who are you to answer back against your master?”

I think, however, that the master would be pleased if a faithful and prudent servant asked questions because he wished to understand and marvel at his master’s wisdom. I do not think such a servant would be told, “Who are you?” Thus, when the prophet Daniel desired to know the Lord’s will—and for this reason was called “a man of desires” (Daniel 9–10)—he was not told, “Who are you?” Rather, an angel was sent to teach him about all God’s dispensations and judgments.

Therefore, if we desire to understand something of God’s secret and hidden matters, and if we are men of desire rather than of contention, let us faithfully and humbly seek the judgments of God inserted more secretly in the divine writings. For this reason the Lord also said: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5), knowing that these things are not opened to those who, occupied with other affairs, hear or read them superficially as they pass by, but to those who search the divine Scriptures more deeply with an upright and simple heart, continual labor, and unceasing vigils. I know very well that I am not one of these. Nevertheless, if there is anyone who seeks in this way, he will find. Let us, for our part, turn as best we can to the matters before us.

**(GG.)** “O man,” he says, “who are you to answer back to God?” The one who is called a human being is shown to be unable to answer God, because, having been taken from the earth, he is not worthy to investigate heavenly judgments.
