Hence it is written in Job: “Who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job 11).

The works of the Creator must always be revered without scrutiny, because they can in no way be unjust. To seek a reason for his hidden counsel is nothing other than to rebel proudly against his counsel. When the reason for his actions is not discovered, it remains for us to be silent with humility beneath his deeds, because the understanding of the flesh is entirely insufficient to penetrate the secrets of his majesty. Therefore, whoever does not see the reason in God’s works should consider his own weakness; in recognizing that weakness, he sees why he does not see the reason.

Accordingly, Paul adds immediately afterward: “Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” In recognizing himself to be a thing formed by the divine work, he reproves himself for rebounding against the hand of the worker, since the one who benevolently made what did not exist into what exists does not abandon it unjustly.

After being struck, therefore, let the mind return to itself and not seek what it cannot grasp. Otherwise, if it investigates the cause of divine anger, it may provoke that anger still further by its investigation, and pride may kindle what humility could have appeased inextinguishably.

“Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

**(Ambrose.)** It is clear that some vessels are made for honor, since they are needed for honorable uses, while others are made for dishonor, as utensils for kitchens. Nevertheless, they are of one substance; they differ according to the craftsman’s purpose in making them for honor. So also God, although we are all of one and the same substance and are all sinners, shows mercy to one and despises another—not without justice. In the potter there is only will; in God, however, there is will together with justice. For he knows to whom he ought to show mercy.

**(Origen.)** We also read something similar in the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 18), where God commands him to enter the potter’s house and watch him at work. The potter was gathering up again a vessel that had collapsed in his hands and reshaping it according to his will. “And the word of God,” he says, “came to him, saying: ‘Can I not deal with the house of Israel as this potter does?’” (ibid.)

Wisdom also says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests just men” (Ecclesiasticus 27). God therefore has authority over us, as the potter has authority over clay, to make from the same mass vessels for honor and vessels for dishonor.

Let this suffice for you who answer God insolently. But whoever desires to contemplate the works of God’s Wisdom in his dispensations should hear Paul, who is conscious of the divine mysteries, discussing these same matters elsewhere (2 Timothy 2): “In a great house,” he says, “there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor. If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.”

Do you hear how Paul, where he had no insolent adversary, disclosed the varieties of vessels? There, where the hearer was unworthy and was instead an adversary, he mentions only earthen vessels. Here, however, he says that there are vessels of gold, silver, wood, and earthenware, and that some are made for honor and others for dishonor. Likewise, where he mentioned the reason why some are made for honor and others for dishonor, he was silent there but disclosed it here.

For if anyone cleanses himself, he says, without doubt from the filth of sins, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. It follows, then, that whoever has not cleansed himself and washed away the stains of sins through repentance is a vessel for dishonor. If he increases his wickedness, refuses to convert through hardness of mind, and utterly despises repentance, he will now be not only a vessel of dishonor but also a vessel of wrath.

Thus the explanation that he closes to those who demanded it unworthily there, he opens here to those who seek it worthily. Through it, what he proposed shortly before concerning Jacob and Esau is also explained more clearly.

For Jacob’s soul had cleansed itself, so that Jacob might be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. God saw his purity and, having authority from the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, made Jacob—who, as we have said, had cleansed himself—a vessel for honor. But Esau, whose soul he saw was neither so pure nor so simple, he made from the same mass a vessel for dishonor.

To know that Jacob was made a vessel for honor because of the purity and simplicity of his soul, hear what testimony the divine Scripture gives concerning his simplicity: “Jacob,” it says, “was a simple man, dwelling at home” (Genesis 25). Therefore the Apostle says of them that, before they were born, it was said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

For if God, wishing to show wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—even us, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

**(Origen.)** We have often called attention to the Apostle’s awkward expressions and their deficiencies; the present passage likewise contains one. For what he says at the beginning of the chapter, “For if God, wishing…,” is not connected to anything. For example, elsewhere he himself says, “But if the firstfruits are holy, so also is the lump”; here he supplies nothing of that kind, but leaves the conjunction as something indefinite. Even if it is not taken up, the meaning becomes clearer without it. We may therefore read it as follows:

“God, wishing to show wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy.”

This seems to mean that, while God endures and patiently bears with unbelievers and faithless people, he makes both his patience and his power known to humanity: his patience, because he endures for a long time, in case they might repent and convert; his power, because at some point he punishes and does not leave crimes altogether unavenged.

And again, “in vessels of mercy”—that is, in those who have cleansed themselves from every stain of sin, from which “no one is clean, even if his life is but one day”—he makes known the riches of his glory. He prepared these vessels for glory not by some irrational or accidental grace, but because they themselves had cleansed themselves from the stains mentioned above.

**(Ambrose.)** The patience and long-suffering of God are such that, just as they prepare the wicked for destruction, so they prepare the good for a crown. The good are those in whom there is the hope of faith. He endures all, knowing the end of each one; thus it is patience that prepares for the glory of God those who are corrected from evil or who persevere in goodness.

The riches of glory are the manifold dignity prepared for believers. But those who change from good to evil and persist in what they have begun, he prepares for destruction.

This is what it means to make his power known “with much patience”: when people think that he will not avenge, because he delays for a long time, his power will become evident when he begins to avenge. Since he could avenge immediately but endured for a long time, the faithless cannot complain when they are condemned. To prepare is to know beforehand what will happen to each person.

**(Augustine.)** Here he sufficiently indicates that the hardening of heart which occurred in Pharaoh arose from the desert of a prior hidden impiety. God nevertheless patiently endured it until the time when vengeance could appropriately proceed against him, for the correction of those whom God had taught and intended to free from error, bringing them through piety to his worship and assisting their prayers and groans.

**(Origen.)** What he adds, “whom he also called us,” stands for “as he did us,” as though he had said: “Just as he did us, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.” The preceding discussion seems to have concerned Pharaoh, who was a vessel of wrath, and the children of Israel, who were vessels of mercy. Therefore, when he adds, “whom he also called us, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles,” he seems to be adopting an analogy, so that the statement may be understood in this way: “Just as we too are vessels of mercy, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.”

**(Augustine.)** The purpose of the whole of this discussion leads to the following conclusion: since he has taught that it is the mercy of God that enables us to do good, the Jews should not boast as though it arose from their works. When they had received the Gospel, they did not want it given to the Gentiles, thinking that it was being repaid to them as though it were owed for their merits. They must now abandon this pride, understanding that it is not from works but from God’s mercy and calling that believers are enabled to do good. This mercy must not be begrudged to the Gentiles, as though the Jews possessed a prior merit—which they do not.

**(Origen.)** This has been said insofar as it concerns the order of the Apostle’s discourse and the explanation of his words. Let us now briefly review some points and inquire into the inner meaning. How, then, does God make his wrath known? “Through vessels of wrath,” he says, “fitted for destruction.”

I am astonished within myself as I contemplate the counsel of the Holy Spirit in the divine books. He says that God’s wrath—which is foreign to his nature—is made known to humanity, as the present passage of the Apostle indicates; but he records that God’s goodness and sweetness, which belong properly to his nature, are hidden and concealed, as David says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Psalm 30).

What, then, shall we say is the reason that God reveals his wrath to humanity but conceals his sweetness? Without doubt he knows that the human race is fragile and inclined to fall through negligence. For such people it is more beneficial to remain under fear of wrath than to be relaxed by hope in God’s kindness and sweetness.

Thus the Wisdom of God also says: “He who spares the rod hates his son; for if you strike him with the rod, he will not die, but you will save his soul from death” (Proverbs 13).

God therefore makes his power known when he chastises and rebukes the impious, so that, in accordance with the saying of Scripture, “when the pestilent man is scourged, the innocent becomes wiser” (Proverbs 19).

He also makes known “the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.” God’s riches become known when his mercy is shown toward those who are despised and humble among human beings, who place their hope not in their riches or power but in the Lord. Thus, at that time, the Hebrew people, despairing in human eyes and rejected by God, obtained mercy. So also now the people of the Gentiles, who were despised by those who glory in circumcision, have obtained mercy.

But we must attend more earnestly to this point: they too obtained mercy, were called the people of God, and were beloved by God. Yet because they did not know how to preserve the grace they had received, it is said to them—of those among whom Israel’s dwelling was adulterated—“I dismissed her and gave her a bill of divorce into her own hands” (Jeremiah 3). And again elsewhere: “You have become a satiety to me; I will no longer forgive your sins” (Jeremiah 7).

Through the same Jeremiah the Lord says: “My inheritance has become like a hyena’s den.”

Let us therefore beware lest we too, who were not formerly the people of God but whom he called his people through the riches of his glory, and who were not beloved but became beloved and sons of the living God—if we do not walk as sons of light and sons of God, and if we do not act as God’s people so that, “seeing” our “good works,” people may “glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5)—fall under the Apostle’s warning, where he says (Romans 11): “If God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.”

“As he says in Hosea: ‘I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy’; and it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ that they shall be called sons of the living God.”

**(Ambrose.)** It is evident that this was foretold concerning the Gentiles. Formerly they were not the people of God; afterward, receiving mercy to the disgrace of the Jews, they were called the people of God. Those who previously were not beloved, after the Jews were rejected, were adopted as sons and became beloved, so that in the place where they were not called the people of God, there they might be called sons of the living God.

Formerly, sons of the living God were called such nowhere except in Judea—that is, in Jerusalem, where the house of God was—as he says in Psalm 75: “God is known in Judah.” But afterward, through the prophet Zechariah, he says: “I will set Jerusalem among all the nations,” because everywhere there would be sons of God and the house of God, which is the Church.

For this reason the Lord says to the Jews (Matthew 21): “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

**(Origen.)** There is another interpretation. The testimony that the Apostle takes from Hosea, insofar as the prophet’s own passage is concerned, does not appear to refer to the Gentiles but to the people of Israel themselves. As we said above, Paul takes an analogous example to show that, just as it was once said to them, when they had been rejected and despaired of, “You are not my people, and I am not your God,” and the prophet added, “And it shall be: in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God,” so also, he says, “we, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles”—who formerly were not his people—he has now called his people; and “the one who was not beloved, beloved”; and “in the place where it was said to us, ‘You are not my people,’ there we shall be called sons of the living God.”

But perhaps those who are from the circumcision will ask us and say: “Where was it said to you that you were not the people of God, so that you might be called sons of the living God there?” They will claim that God spoke these words in Judea—for he was known there alone—and that none of this concerns us, because “the law speaks to those who are under the law.”

On the contrary, I will show a much more worthy place where it was both fitting and possible for God to speak. God is not, properly speaking, said to speak in mountains, rocks, or other earthly places; rather, God speaks in the human mind, in rational understanding, and in the ruling faculty of the heart. There, when people who are unworthy and alienated from God are condemned by the rebuke of conscience, there, I say, it is pronounced and said to each one: “You are not my people.” But if anyone cleanses and purifies himself from these things, and “the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding,” begins to guard his heart, then—in the secret of his heart, when he has become peaceful—he will be called a son of God, with his conscience bearing witness.

But Isaiah cries out for Israel: “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

After Paul, through the wisdom of God that he speaks among the perfect, had explained the secret and hidden matters of the divine dispensation, and had shown by what method and order God either displays wrath in vessels of wrath or the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy; after he had taught that each person becomes a vessel of wrath by storing up wrath for himself through hardness and an impenitent heart on the day of wrath, while vessels of mercy are those who cleanse themselves from these things and prepare themselves for every good work—he now confirms these matters with greater authority by teaching that they were also prescribed in the Prophets.

“Isaiah,” he says, “cries out for Israel: ‘If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.’”

For the prophet, foreseeing the future, saw that many of Israel, and especially those compared with the sand of the sea, would through their hardness and impenitent heart become “vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,” not believing in their own life but crucifying the Lord of majesty. Therefore, he says, if they are “like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.” Those who are not saved are like the sand of the sea; but the remnant that will be saved is like the stars of heaven. For the statement contains both parts of the promise made to Abraham: “Your seed will be like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven” (Genesis 22).

**(Augustine.)** In another sense, when he says, “Isaiah cries out for Israel,” and so forth, he shows how the Lord is the cornerstone joining both walls in himself.

The testimony of the prophet Hosea was spoken concerning the Gentiles: “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved.” The testimony of Isaiah was spoken concerning Israel: “A remnant will be saved,” so that those who believed in Christ might themselves be reckoned as the seed of Abraham. Thus he makes both peoples harmonious according to the Lord’s testimony, where he says in the Gospel concerning the Gentiles: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

**(Gregory.)** The holy Church, enriched in its beginnings by the multitude of the Gentiles, scarcely receives at the end of the world the Jews whom it finds, gathering them at the end and placing them like the remnants of the harvest. Concerning these remnants Isaiah says: “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand, a remnant will be saved.”

**(Ambrose.)** Isaiah therefore cries out for those who believe in Christ. These are truly Israelites, as the Lord says to Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1): “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

When the Jews departed from the merit and promise of the fathers by refusing to receive it, those remained who persisted by believing in the faith of the promise made to the fathers. They depart from the Law who do not believe in the one whom the Law alone promised as sufficient for salvation. Therefore those who do not receive Christ must necessarily be regarded as apostates, since by rejecting Christ they are guilty of violating the Law.

Thus, from the very great multitude, he says that only believers are saved—those whom God foreknew.

For he is finishing and abridging the word in righteousness, because “the Lord will make an abridged word upon the earth.”

**(Origen.)** The “abridged word” is found where many are called but few are chosen. We may also call the whole teaching an abridged word, since what the Law and the Prophets formerly contained in the broad range of their commandments, the Lord, when he came, declared in these words: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22). In these two sayings he clearly abridged the Prophets and the Law.

“An abridged word” may also be understood as the faith of the creed handed down to believers, in which the whole summary of the mystery is contained in a few connected statements.

**(Ambrose.)** It is fitting that creation should obtain salvation through the sole name of the Lord the Creator—that is, through faith. For when all new moons, the Sabbath, circumcision, the law of foods, and animal offerings had been removed, faith alone was established for salvation. It is abridged from the Law, because what is in the faith is contained in the Law as its principal meaning, as the Savior says: “For he wrote about me” (John 5).

The Law, then, has been abridged. The remnant of the Jews is saved, but the others cannot be saved because they despise God’s decree by which he determined to save the human race.

And as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

**(Origen.)** What seed does Isaiah say was left by the Lord? Without doubt, the seed that the same Apostle explains elsewhere, when he says that it was spoken to Abraham: “To you I will give this land, and to your seed.” He did not say “to seeds,” as though referring to many, but “to your seed,” as referring to one, which is Christ (Galatians 3).

This, then, is what Isaiah says: “Unless the Lord had left us a seed”—that is, unless he had given us Christ, so that he might be born from us—we would have been like Sodom, insofar as the magnitude of our impiety is concerned, except that something even graver occurred among the Israelites.

For the Sodomites are reported to have been inhospitable, incestuous, and immoral; but the people of Israel became sacrilegious against the one who, although he is the Lord of majesty, wished to be called and to be their brother.

Unless, therefore, the Lord had left this seed through which the remnant would be saved and the vessels of mercy preserved, that people would have perished like Sodom. Yet Isaiah did not call what was left behind “seed” without purpose. Seed is what is sown in the earth and produces abundant fruit. Through this he also teaches that Christ would be sown—that is, buried in the earth—and would rise from it, bringing forth the abundant fruit of the whole multitude of the Church, as the Lord himself says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it bears no fruit; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

What shall we say, then? The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that comes from faith.

This may appear contrary either to what we said above, namely, that each person should cleanse and purify himself in order to become a useful vessel and a vessel of mercy, or to what we discussed earlier, namely, that the Gentiles also use the natural law, in which righteousness is certainly present. How, then, does he say here that “the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness”?

See whether we can answer in this way. To pursue something is one thing; to have it implanted within oneself is another. A person is said to pursue something when he desires to attain it through instruction and extensive reading. Hence such teachings, learned through human tradition, are called “schools” or “sects” from pursuing them.

The Gentiles, therefore, because they did not possess the Law written on tablets or in books, are not said to have pursued righteousness; nevertheless, they possessed within themselves what the natural law taught them. For this reason they were close to the righteousness that comes from faith—that is, to Christ.

**(Ambrose.)** True and enduring righteousness is in God, if he is acknowledged. For what is as just as to know God the Father, from whom all things exist, and Christ his Son, through whom all things exist?

The first righteousness, therefore, is to acknowledge the Creator; then it is to observe what he has commanded. Thus the Gentiles, who formerly did not seek righteousness—that is, the Law, which bore witness to the Creator—when Christ came found an overflowing righteousness, greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees. Those who previously did not pursue what was lesser afterward attained what was greater.

But the Jews, placed under the Law, ought to have advanced further; instead, they deteriorated.

Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness.

**(Ambrose.)** The perfection of the Law is faith. When the Gentiles apprehended it, they seemed to fulfill the whole Law. But the Jews, refusing to believe in the Savior out of envy, claimed the righteousness commanded in the Law—that is, the Sabbath, circumcision, and so forth—and did not attain the Law. This means that they did not perfect the Law; and those who do not perfect the Law are guilty according to the Law. For the one who fulfills the Law is the person who proceeds from the Law of Moses to faith in Christ.

Why? Because it was not from faith but, as it were, from works.

**(Origen.)** It is certain that Israel pursued the law of righteousness according to the letter, but did not attain the Law. Which Law? Without doubt, the Law of the Spirit. For the Apostle would not have said that Israel failed to attain the Law that it pursued, held, and possessed.

He therefore gives the reason why Israel could not attain the Law: “Because it was not from faith,” he says, “but as if from works.”

**(Ambrose.)** For, despising faith—which, as I have said, is the perfection of the Law—they said that they were justified by the works of the Law, that is, by the Sabbath, new moons, circumcision, and so forth, forgetting the Scripture’s statement that “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1).

The righteousness of the Law is so called because these things were given to the Jews by God’s just judgment on account of the hardness of their hearts. Thus, if someone happened to step on a dead weasel or touch some dead thing, or if a mouse fell into a vessel, it was called unclean. They observed these matters with great care, so that from any cause they might incur uncleanness.

If the blood of a weasel stained the floor, it had to be cleansed with no small care, and the person had to abstain from better foods. The Sabbath and circumcision, however, had their own righteousness in their proper time, because they were given as figures.

The Lord showed this through the prophet Ezekiel, saying among other things: “Therefore I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezekiel 20), because they were irreverent and faithless.

But at Christ’s coming, because he was going to give the gift of salvation, he proclaimed through Jeremiah: “I will give them a new covenant, not like the one I gave their fathers” (Jeremiah 31). He calls this covenant the Law that they did not attain, as I mentioned above.

For when believing Jews wished to impose this burden of observance upon believing Gentiles, the Apostle Peter said: “Why are you placing a yoke upon the neck of the brothers that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15).

From the time of Christ, the indulgence promised in the Law was granted. For the prophet Isaiah says: “He will come from Zion, who will remove and turn away impiety from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isaiah 59). This is the New Covenant promised by God in Christ.

They stumbled over the stone of stumbling and the rock of scandal, and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.

**(Origen.)** Because they pursued the Law not according to the works of God’s righteousness but according to the works of their own righteousness, they “stumbled over the stone of stumbling.” Concerning this it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

It must be known, however, that in the prophet Isaiah this testimony is written as follows (Isaiah 28): “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, a cornerstone, honorable in its foundations; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

The Apostle, however, seems to have inserted “the stone of stumbling and the rock of scandal” from another passage of the same prophet Isaiah, where it is written: “You shall not encounter him as a stone of stumbling, nor as a stone of falling” (Isaiah 8). Drawing from both passages whatever seemed suitable for his arguments, he adapted it to his purpose.

**(Ambrose.)** It has been established by the testimony of many that Christ is signified by the rock or stone. For the prophet Daniel (Daniel 2) calls him the stone that, cut from the mountain without hands, struck and crushed all kingdoms and filled the whole earth. This was evidently spoken of Christ.

In the Law also, the rock from which waters flowed was called Christ (Psalm 67; Exodus 17). “The rock,” he says, “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). And the Apostle Peter says among other things to the Jews: “This is the stone that was rejected by you builders.”

The stumbling block placed in Zion is therefore Christ. Zion means height, or the city of Jerusalem itself, which was not improperly called lofty because of its knowledge of God. In that city the Savior, placed by God the Father as a preacher, became an offense to the Jews when he proclaimed himself the Son of God, born of a woman through the Holy Spirit.

They were scandalized by his body and said: “Are not his mother and brothers with us?” How, then, does he say here, “Because I have come down from heaven”? They were unwilling to compare his words with his deeds, so as to recognize that what he said about having come down from heaven was not absurd—namely, that the body was working while God, hidden within it, was nevertheless revealing himself through his works.

This rock, therefore, is a scandal and an offense to the Jews. The rock is undoubtedly understood as the Savior’s body. It was cut without hands because it was made from a virgin by the Holy Spirit, without a man.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1505]

## CHAPTER 10

The Apostle prays for the Jews, showing that the righteousness which makes one worthy of eternal life comes solely from the Law and from faith in Christ.

[Col. 1505A]

Brothers, the desire of my heart and my supplication to God for them is for their salvation; for I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

(Aug.) Here he now begins to speak about the hope of the Jews, so that the Gentiles too may not dare to grow arrogant against the Jews. For just as the arrogance of the Jews had to be refuted, since they gloried as though in works, so the Gentiles also had to be addressed, lest, as though preferred to the Jews, they should become proud.

(Orig.) Since, then, in the matters recently expounded he used many testimonies of the prophets against Israel, so that he brought forward from Isaiah: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah”; and again: “If the number of the children of Israel were like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved”; and to these he added that Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law—therefore now, wishing once more to console that people and thereby invite them to faith, he says: “Brothers, the desire of my heart and my supplication before the Lord is for them, for their salvation.” He shows the reason why his desire and supplication for them are presented before God: “For,” he says, “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” Although, he says, they are entangled in the evils of so many and such great sins, nevertheless, because they possess an ineffable ardor and zeal for God, this reason moved me to beseech God on their behalf, so that at last they might somehow attain salvation. [Col. 1505B]

(Ambr.) Since, therefore, he wishes to remove them from the law, believing that it is a veil for the Jews, lest he should seem to do this out of hatred for Judaism, he displays his affection for them and grants much to the law; but he teaches that the time for observing the law has now passed, and thereby testifies that he wishes to provide for them, if only they will listen to him and recognize that he is not their enemy, since he also bears witness to the nobility of their ancestry and paternal tradition. “For,” he says, “they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

(Orig.) He proves how they do not have zeal for God according to knowledge: “For,” he says, “being ignorant of the righteousness of God, they submit to their own righteousness.” It is therefore of little benefit to have zeal for God and not to possess knowledge of zeal. Indeed, the Jews, thinking that they were acting out of zeal for God, became sacrilegious against the Son of God, because they were zealous not according to knowledge, as Phinehas son of Eleazar was, who, zealous according to knowledge, killed both the Midianite woman and the Israelite who was fornicating with her (Num. XXV); and as Elijah was, who said: “With zeal I have been zealous for the omnipotent God of Israel, because the children of Israel have forsaken you. They have killed your prophets and demolished your altars” (III Kings XIX); and as Mattathias was, of whom it is written in the First Book of Maccabees: “Because he was zealous for the law of God, his kidneys trembled, and his anger rose according to judgment.” The zeal and ardor of all these were according to knowledge. The zeal of the Jews, however, was not according to knowledge, because, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, they attempted to fulfill their own—that is, what appeared to human beings to be righteousness—when they ought rather to have obeyed the righteousness of God, which is Christ. [Col. 1505D]

But see now whether this saying may not seem to be addressed not only to them, because they have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. The Apostle could similarly speak about others, saying that they have fear of God but not according to knowledge; and about others, that they have love of God but not according to knowledge. For if someone has affection toward God but does not know that love must be patient, kind, not envious, not acting wrongly, not puffed up, not ambitious, not seeking its own interests (I Cor. XIII)—if he does not possess these and similar qualities in his love, but loves God only in affection, it may properly be said also of him that he has the love of God, but not according to knowledge.

Similarly, it may be said of another that he has faith in God, but not according to knowledge, if he does not know that “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II), and that the faith of God does not consist only in words, which are sometimes learned as composed or written by someone else, but in an affection of the mind such as that possessed by the woman who said within herself: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Matt. IX). If someone does not possess faith in such a way that he shows by his good actions in whom he believes, it may also be said of him that he has faith in God, but not according to knowledge.

It may also be said of another that he has purity before God, but not according to knowledge; and of another that he cares for the poor, but not according to knowledge, if he wishes to be praised by human beings; and another may be called temperate, but not according to knowledge, if he fasts in order to please people. Thus, with regard to each of the things we do, if we do not perform them according to knowledge and understanding, it may be said of us that we have zeal for a good work, but not according to knowledge. Therefore we must devote ourselves especially to works informed by knowledge, lest matters turn out disastrously for us: lest, while situated in faith, we be frustrated of faith, and, while possessing zeal for good things, we fall away from the good. [Col. 1506B]

Do you wish to know that someone can, if he lacks knowledge, become empty in faith? Listen to Paul himself speaking to certain people: “Unless you believed without cause” (I Cor. XV). Thus those who do not apply themselves to knowledge have believed without cause, so that in the thing in which they believed they may also receive an understanding of the truth.

Finally, the Apostles, recognizing this to be the distinction between faith simply handed down and faith that is according to knowledge, said to the Savior: “Increase our faith”—that is, grant that, possessing the faith that is not according to knowledge, we may also possess the faith that is according to knowledge. Thus Paul bears witness concerning the Jews that they have zeal for God, although not according to knowledge. Nevertheless, because they possessed in some fashion zeal for God, they gave the Apostle a reason to offer supplication to God for them. For it is better to have zeal for God, even if not according to knowledge, than not to have it at all. For whoever has, as it is written, “to him will be given” (Matt. XIII; Luke XIX), even at the end, when all Israel will be saved. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.

For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God.

(Ambr.) By “ignorance” he says that they did not believe in Christ. Although they had zeal for God, they did not know his will and purpose, and so they acted against the God whom they claimed to defend. He speaks of those who did not receive Christ out of malice or envy, but through error. To these the Apostle Peter also says (Acts III): “I know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance, as did your rulers.” For, being ignorant that this was the Christ whom God had promised, they said that another was to be awaited, placing before him their own righteousnesses, which they possessed from the law—although he is the righteousness of God through faith. For he himself is righteousness, because in him God fulfilled what he had promised. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

(Ambr.) He says this because the one who believes in Christ possesses the perfection of the law. Since no one was justified by the law, because no one fulfilled the law except the one who hoped in the promised Christ, faith was established, yielding to the perfection of the law, so that, everything else being set aside, faith might satisfy on behalf of the whole law and the prophets. [Col. 1507C]

For Moses wrote that the person who practices the righteousness that is from the law will live by it.

As for the righteousness that is from faith, he speaks in this way:

The righteousness of the law did not make them guilty for the time being, if it was observed; that is, they lived by doing the law, for they were debtors.

(Orig.) Earlier also the Apostle had mentioned two righteousnesses, when he said that Israel, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, sought to establish its own righteousness. Here again he speaks of two righteousnesses: one that is from the law and another that is from faith. But it seems to me that the righteousness which above he said Israel was ignorant of—the righteousness of God—is this righteousness that is from faith. The other, of which he says, “seeking to establish their own righteousness,” is the one which here also he indicates in the words of Moses: “The person who practices the righteousness that is from the law will live by it.”

But observe the difference between the righteousnesses, and likewise between the lives. That righteousness—that is, Christ—“who was made righteousness for us by God” and peace: see how he says, “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). This righteousness, therefore, not only grants life but eternal life. Of the righteousness of the law, however, he did not say that “the person who practices it will live eternally,” but only, “will live by it.”

And if Christ is the end of the law, as the Apostle said, neither will the person who does not receive Christ, the end of the law, be able to fulfill the righteousness that is from the law without Christ. This righteousness, therefore, which is from faith and which is Christ, as though living and subsisting, says:

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down—or, “Who will descend into the abyss?”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does Scripture say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.”

(Ambr.) He says that this righteousness is of faith, provided that there is no doubt concerning the hope that is in God and in Christ. Let no one, distrusting, say, “Who could ascend into heaven?” For he suffered for this reason: that, by the power of the Father, having stripped the underworld, conquered death, and risen, he might ascend into heaven with the souls he had rescued. For everyone who, having seen the Savior among the dead, hoped for salvation from him was liberated, as the Apostle Peter bears witness. He says that the gospel was preached even to the dead (I Pet. III). Whoever, therefore, does not doubt these things in his heart is justified by faith.

Justification from the law, however, is produced by fear. A person fears the law because he sees it inflict punishment on those who sin. Therefore the righteousness of the law is not great, nor does it confer merit before God, but only for the present. Faith, however, because it is foolishness to unbelievers, has a reward before God, from whom what is not seen is hoped for.

(Orig.) Nor should you be surprised that, although Christ himself is righteousness, he seems to speak these things about himself as though about someone else. In many places you will find the Savior speaking about himself as though about another, as in the Gospel he says (Matt. XXV): “He will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left, and he will say to those who are on his right,” and so forth. And again he says to those who are on his left the things that are written.

What he says, therefore—“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who ascended into heaven?’ or, ‘Who descended into the abyss?’”—apart from the words inserted in the middle, “that is, to bring Christ down,” or “to bring him back from the dead”—is followed by: “But Scripture says, ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.’”

This appears to be taken from Deuteronomy, where it is written in this manner: “This commandment, which I command you today, is not exalted above you, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you might say, ‘Who will ascend into heaven for us and bring it to us, so that we may hear it and do it?’ Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you might say, ‘Who will cross the sea for us and bring it to us, so that we may hear it and do it?’ The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart and in your hands, so that you may do it” (Deut. XXX).

Since, therefore, these words are taken from Deuteronomy, and the Apostle writes that the righteousness which is from faith says these very things, and that this righteousness is Christ, there is no doubt that the Apostle declares the words spoken in Deuteronomy to have been spoken by Christ. It is he, therefore, who said: “This commandment, which I give you today, is not exalted above you, nor is it far from you,” and the rest that follows.

What, then, does the Apostle teach through this? He teaches that we must not say in our heart or suppose that Christ is confined to some particular place and is not everywhere, diffused through all things. For, while he was on earth, he said that he was also in heaven. Thus he spoke to his Apostles (John III): “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” He did not say, “who was in heaven,” but “who is in heaven.” [Col. 1509A]

And again, lest we suppose that he is only in heaven and that his presence is absent from the abyss, the righteousness that is from faith says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” And, as though this were equivalent to saying, “to bring Christ down from heaven,” the Apostle added: “that is, to bring Christ down.” And again, if someone descends in mind and thought into the abyss, supposing that Christ is confined there alone, as though this were equivalent to bringing Christ back from the dead, he adds: “that is, to bring Christ back from the dead.”

But, he says, you ought to think of Christ as the Word, the Truth, the Wisdom, and the Righteousness of God. None of these is sought in a particular place; they are present everywhere. Nor are they summoned from the lower regions, but are grasped by the mind and understanding. Therefore, as the Word and Wisdom, he is near, in your mouth and in your heart.

(Ambr.) What we are told to believe is not far from our mind or mouth. Although it is not seen by the eyes, what we believe is nevertheless not contrary to the nature of souls or to the manner of speech. For in that very nature are implanted, as it were, seeds which, cultivated through hearing and the will, bring forth the testimony of the Creator.

(Orig.) We must also know that it is one thing for a possibility to exist in someone, and another for there to be efficacy or actual operation. The Greeks call these things δύναμις (*dynamis*, “capacity” or “potential”) and ἐνέργεια (*energeia*, “activity” or “actual operation”).

For example, a newly born child is potentially a rational human being, since he can become rational if he grows up. In potential he may also be called a craftsman, a helmsman, or a grammarian, for it is possible that he may become one of these. In actual efficacy or operation, however—that is, in reality and by the effect produced—he is none of these while he is a child. But when he begins either to be capable of reason or to produce something by the art of a craftsman or any other skill, then he is called rational, or a craftsman, or whatever else he demonstrates by the effect of his work.

In this same way Christ, who is the Word of God, must be believed to exist potentially alongside us—that is, alongside every human being—as reason exists potentially in children. But he is said to be with me in actual efficacy when I have confessed the Lord Jesus with my mouth and believed in my heart that God raised him from the dead.

Do you wish to know that he is present everywhere and is even in the midst of those who do not know him and do not confess him? Listen to how John the Baptist bears witness concerning him: “There stands in your midst,” he says, “one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John I). He is therefore also in the midst of those who do not know him, but he is in their midst potentially, not in actual efficacy. For they can receive him, but they do not yet receive him.

He is in the midst in actual efficacy or operation, however, among those to whom he said: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII). For these confessed the Lord Jesus with their mouth and believed in their heart that God raised him from the dead. Otherwise it seems absurd to say that he is in the midst both of those who gather in his name and of those who do not know him, unless this distinction is maintained: among the ignorant and those who do not yet believe, he is said to be in the midst potentially; among believers, in actual efficacy—that is, by the effect of the reality and the work itself. [Col. 1510A]

This is the word of faith that we preach.

(Ambr.) He speaks of no work of the law, but says that only faith is to be given in the cause of Christ.

(Aug.) This entire passage refers to what he said above: “For the Lord, completing and abbreviating, has made his word upon the earth.” Once the innumerable and manifold sacraments by which the Jewish people were burdened had been removed, it came about through the mercy of God that we should reach salvation through the brevity of a confession of faith.

For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

(Ambr.) What he spoke above he has here made explicit: this is the rule of faith—to believe that the Lord is Jesus, and not to be ashamed to profess that God, raising him from the dead, brought him bodily into heaven, from which he had come to be incarnate.

(Orig.) It will seem to some, from this passage, that even if someone lacks the distinction of good works, even if he has not devoted himself to the virtues, nevertheless, simply because he has believed, he will not perish but will be saved and will possess salvation, even if he cannot possess the glory of blessedness.

But see whether this should rather be understood in this way: the person who truly and not falsely confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart also confesses that he is subject to the lordship of wisdom, righteousness, truth, and all that Christ is. He no longer has Mammon as his lord—that is, neither greed nor injustice nor impurity nor falsehood rules over him. For once he has confessed Jesus Christ as Lord, he professes servitude to none of these.

And since he believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead, it is certain that he believes that he was raised for his justification. Otherwise, what benefit would it be for me to know and believe that God raised Jesus from the dead, if I do not have him raised within myself? Therefore, if I do not walk in newness of life and do not flee my old habit of sinning, Christ has not yet risen for me from the dead.

(GG.) The Apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: “But now remain faith, hope, and love.” The thief, suddenly filled with grace, received and preserved all three on the cross.

He had faith: he believed that the God whom he saw dying together with him would reign. He had hope: he requested entrance into his kingdom, saying, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII). He also vigorously maintained love in his death, for he rebuked his fellow criminal, who was dying for a similar crime, for his wickedness, and proclaimed to him the life that he himself had recognized, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong” (ibid.).

Behold what kind of man came to the cross through guilt, and what kind of man departed from the cross into grace. He confessed the God whom he saw dying with him in human weakness, at the time when the Apostles were denying him, although they had seen him perform miracles by divine power.

But those who assert that a human being is saved by his own powers suppose that this same confession of the man arose from the man’s own strength. If that were so, the Psalmist would not say in praise of God (Ps. XC): “Confession and magnificence are his work.” Therefore we have received from him the ability to confess rightly, from whom we also receive the ability to perform great works. To this meaning, too, the words that follow are appropriate:

For Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

(Orig.) This is written in Isaiah: “Everyone who believes in him does not blush with shame.” But everyone who sins is put to shame, just as Adam sinned, became ashamed, and hid himself. Whoever has incurred the shame of sin does not appear to believe.

(Amb.) When the examination of all things begins on the day of judgment, and all false inventions and doctrines are brought to shame, then those who believe in Christ will rejoice, seeing that it is made manifest to all that what they believed is true and that what was thought foolish is wise. They will see that, among the rest, they alone are glorious and wise who had been considered contemptible and foolish. For there is the true test, where there is reward and condemnation.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

(Amb.) He says generally that all will either be put to shame because of unbelief or raised up because of faith, since without Christ there is no salvation with God—rather, there is punishment or death. For neither the Jews can be commended by the privilege of the patriarchs or by the giving of the law, since they did not receive the merit and promise of the patriarchs; nor do the Gentiles possess any testimony by which they may be commended according to the flesh, unless they believe in Christ.

For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him. It is evident that this applies to everyone, whether Jews or Greeks, because without calling upon the Lord Christ no one lives with God.

(Orig.) That he is the same Lord of all is to be understood as follows: if righteousness, truth, wisdom, and sanctification—which altogether is Christ the Lord—rule over us. These are the riches, since in him are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II). Yet he did not say that he bestows these riches upon all human beings, but upon all who call upon his name.

(Amb.) Since, therefore, he is Lord of all, as the Apostle Peter agrees when he says, “He is Lord of all,” he is nevertheless rich only among those who call upon him, because they will receive the reward. He is not rich toward the faithless, because they do not share in his good things. For they will not receive what they did not believe he would give.

Yet he did not say that God is rich toward those who believe, but toward those who call upon him, so that, after believing, the mind may not cease to ask for what it has always been taught by God to seek. For in the Gospel of Luke he says, because of the adversary, who is subtle and crafty, that one must always pray.

To those who believe, forgiveness of sins alone is given; then it follows that, devoted to prayer, a person may be delivered from evil and may attain what God has promised to those who watch with their whole heart.

For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

(Ambr.) This is said in Micah. The same God who appeared to Moses says: “My name is Lord.” He is the Son of God, who is therefore called both Angel and God, so that he would not be thought to be himself the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom all things are. This is why he is called God: because the Father and the Son are one. He is called Angel because he was sent by the Father as the messenger of the promised salvation.

He is said to have been sent so that he would not be believed to be the Father himself, but begotten by him. Therefore everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. Moses also spoke in this sense (Deut. XVIII): “Whoever,” he says, “does not listen to that Prophet will be exterminated from the people.” If he is the Lord of all, he is invoked by servants.

(Orig.) Nevertheless, the saying which the Apostle presents—“Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved”—is written in the prophet Joel in this manner: “And I will give wonders in heaven above and on earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke; the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II).

It seems to me, however, that something great is designated in the divine Scriptures under the name of this invocation. For it is not written of just any sort of men, but of great and eminent ones, that “Enos first hoped to call upon the name of the Lord”; and in the Psalms: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name. They called upon the Lord, and he heard them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud” (Ps. XCVIII). [Col. 1512C]

How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?

(Orig.) By saying, “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” he clearly teaches that what he earlier presented as spoken by the prophet—“Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved”—must be referred to the Lord Christ.

For after saying, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved,” he adds: “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” The Jews did not believe in Christ.

At the beginning of the epistle which he writes to the Corinthians, likewise, when he says, “with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours” (I Cor. I), he declares that the one whose name is invoked is the Lord Jesus Christ.

If, therefore, Enos, Moses, Aaron, and Samuel “called upon the Lord, and he heard them,” without doubt they called upon Christ Jesus the Lord. And if calling upon the name of the Lord and praying to the Lord are one and the same, then, just as God is invoked, Christ must be invoked; and just as God is prayed to, Christ must also be prayed to.

Just as we offer our prayers first of all to God the Father, so we offer them to the Lord Jesus Christ; just as we offer petitions to the Father, so we offer petitions to the Son; and just as we offer thanksgiving to God, so we give thanks to the Savior. One honor must be given to both, that is, to the Father and the Son, as the divine word teaches when it says (John V): “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

(Aug.) Nevertheless, what he says—“How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard?”—can also be understood as spoken about the Gentiles.

For the teacher of the Gentiles wished to refute those who thought that the Gospel was to be preached only to the Jewish nation, and not to the uncircumcised Gentiles. Wishing to show that it pertained not only to the Jews but to all nations, he first presented the testimony of the prophet: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Then, after saying, “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard?” he immediately added: “How will they hear without someone preaching? Or how will they preach unless they are sent?” Thus he refuted those who denied that preachers of Christ should be sent to the uncircumcised Gentiles.

(Orig.) We have just cited the passage from the Epistles to the Corinthians, where the Apostle first says: “To the church of God that is in Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints” (I Cor. I). After this, as though speaking of people belonging to another rank and another order, he adds concerning certain others: “with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, theirs and ours.”

It may perhaps seem that there is some difference here: those he calls the church of God, sanctified and called saints; the others merely “those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

But see whether this apparent distinction may not indicate something like what the present chapter also seems to contain, where he teaches that the name of the Lord cannot be invoked unless one first believes in Christ.

When someone has believed in Christ, even if he has not yet been sanctified or joined to the body of the Church, it is nevertheless necessary that he already invoke the one in whom he has believed. For Christ came to reconcile the world to God and to offer those who believe in him to the Father.

Those whom he offers to the Father, the Holy Spirit receives, in order to sanctify them; and, as members of the heavenly Church of the firstborn, to give them life and restore them to the solidity and perfection of the whole body. Then at last it deserves to be called the Church of God, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V).

Before they approach this degree of perfection, therefore, they invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ as mediator of God and human beings. But after the Spirit of God has been in their hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII), that same Spirit teaches them also to invoke the name of the Father.

Therefore he says: “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” And by this he confines them within an exceedingly tight argument: Salvation exists only for the one who invokes. No one invokes who does not believe. Therefore, because you do not believe, you do not invoke; and because you do not invoke, you are not saved.

But how will they believe him whom they have not heard?

(Orig.) “Whom they have not heard” can be understood in this way: they either refused to hear him himself while he was present in the flesh, or they refused to hear his Apostles preaching about him. For the Lord himself also says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X).

It can also be understood that even now and always Christ, as the Word and Reason, speaks to each person in the heart, teaching piety, persuading toward righteousness, chastity, purity, and all the virtues together, just as he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X).

Thus, finally, he was speaking in Paul’s heart, so that Paul could say: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII).

The text continues:

How, then, will they hear without someone preaching?

(Orig.) In this he shows more clearly that Christ is heard through the speech of preachers, in whom, according to what we said above, Christ is shown to speak and teach.

How, then, will they preach unless they are sent?

(Ambr.) He says this because they will not be true Apostles unless they are sent by Christ, nor will they be able to preach without an authority. For no signs of virtue bear witness to them.

(Orig.) Yet a certain difficulty seems to arise for me in this statement. If we understand it in this way—that they do not preach because they are not sent, and that without someone preaching they will not hear, and if they do not hear they will not believe, and if they do not believe they will not invoke, and if they do not invoke they will not be saved—then it follows that the cause of their not being saved returns to the fault of the one who did not send preachers.

But let us turn instead to that path of interpretation which is more correct, and understand the words “How, then, will they preach unless they are sent?” as though the Apostle were saying:

“We heralds and preachers of Christ could not preach, nor would any power of announcing remain in us, unless the one who sent us himself were present with us. But if you do not wish to hear us when we preach, the fault is now yours; and if, after hearing, you do not believe, and if, not believing, you do not invoke, then, because you do not invoke, you cannot be saved.”

Therefore, because they were sent to preach, it is written concerning those whom he himself sent:

“​​How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things.”

**(Ambrose.)** The prophet Nahum says this. By mentioning “feet,” he signifies the coming of the apostles, who traveled throughout the world and proclaimed that the kingdom of God was approaching. Their arrival enlightened people, showing the way by which one proceeds in peace to God—a peace that John the Baptist had first come to prepare. This is the peace toward which those who believe in Christ hasten.

Finally, holy Simeon, because there is discord in the world, rejoiced at the Savior’s birth: “Now, Lord,” he said, “dismiss your servant in peace” (Luke 2); for the kingdom of God is peace. Once all discord has been cut away, everyone will bend the knee to the one God. Finally, the heavenly Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” and she is our mother.

**(Origen.)** That by “feet” here he means not bodily but spiritual feet, I think no one, however much a friend of the letter, can deny. For he would not reduce the apostolic meaning to absurdity by supposing that he calls the feet of the evangelists, which can be seen with bodily eyes, beautiful and attractive. Rather, those feet are beautiful and attractive that walk along the way of life. According to him who said, “I am the way” (John 14), understand as beautiful and attractive the feet of those who proclaim the gospel, who are worthy to walk along such a way.

These are the feet with which Paul said that he had run his course, and that he ran in such a way as to obtain the prize (1 Cor. 9; 2 Tim. 4)—that is, the vigor of the soul by which one strives and hastens toward heaven. You may also fittingly affirm that these feet are beautiful: the feet that Jesus washes for his disciples and dries with the towel with which he is girded (John 13). Although this was then fulfilled in bodily form, nevertheless, when Peter understood only what he saw being done and, as though out of concern for the honor due him, objected that the Lord should wash the feet of his servant, listen to the words in which a mystery of such depth is revealed: “If I do not wash you,” he says, “you will have no share with me.”

The feet, then, of those who proclaim good things are beautiful. For this reason the Lord Jesus does not wish to cover them with sandals and conceal their fair appearance, but commands them not even to have a sandal on the road (Luke 10).

Let us now consider what the good things are that they proclaim—that is, what they announce. Although the very expression “to proclaim the gospel” is interpreted as “to announce good things,” let us nevertheless inquire what those good things are that he has added to the word “good.” There is one true good: God, whose image of goodness is the Son, and his Spirit, who is called good. Since this one good exists in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he called it “good things.” For this is what the evangelists announce according to the command of our Lord and Savior: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28; Mark 16). These, then, are the good things proclaimed by the evangelists.

But since the one who announces is himself also called a good messenger, and since he announces good things, the meaning is that they not only announce good things, but announce good things well. For there are some who do indeed announce and preach about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but not sincerely or completely. Such are all heretics: they announce the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but they do not announce them well or faithfully. Either they wrongly separate the Son from the Father, saying that the Father has one nature and the Son another; or they wrongly confuse them, supposing either that God is composed of the three or that he possesses only a name consisting of three designations.

But whoever announces good things well will assign to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit the properties proper to each, while confessing that there is no difference in substance or nature. Those who proclaim the gospel in this way therefore not only announce good things; they announce good things well and worthily.

“But not all obey the gospel.”

**(Ambrose.)** This is true. Although the world is illumined by the splendor of the Lord’s teaching, there are nevertheless some who resist, calling light darkness. Their minds have been so blunted by error that they do not receive even the brightness of the true light. The gospel accuses them, saying: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1).

**(Origen.)** Not all from the Gentiles believed the gospel, nor did all from Israel; yet many more—far more—from the Gentiles believed than from Israel.

“Lord, who has believed our report?”

**(Ambrose.)** That is: Who has believed what we have heard and proclaim? By a prophetic example he established that the Jews are contradictors of evangelical truth. For the Law rebukes the Jews, because what was true among the ancients remains true now as well.

**(Origen.)** Since the Apostle states that Isaiah said, “Lord, who has believed our report?” we should observe that the word “who” is used to indicate rarity. In Scripture this expression is sometimes used of something rare and sometimes of something entirely nonexistent. For example: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Ps. 106), and: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. 23), and: “Who is the person who desires life?” (1 Pet. 3). In all these passages, “who” signifies someone rare.

But where it says, “Who has ascended into heaven?”—that is, to bring Christ down—or, “Who has descended into the abyss?”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead—“who” is understood as “no one.” For no one has ascended into heaven in order to bring Christ down from there.

Here, then, in the words, “Lord, who has believed our report?” which Isaiah speaks, “who” signifies rarity. We should nevertheless know that in Hebrew copies the word “Lord” is not present in the passage “Lord, who has believed our report?”; it is found in the translation of the Seventy elders, and the Apostle, confirming what is found among them, inserted “Lord.”

Yet Isaiah seems to prophesy these things in the person of the apostles, to whom the ministry of preaching had been entrusted. When they saw that believers were particularly few among the people of Israel, they said to the Lord: “Lord, who has believed our report?” If these words are instead referred to the persons of the prophets themselves, as though they were complaining to the Lord that no one, or scarcely anyone, from that people had believed what they had prophesied about Christ, this interpretation would not seem inappropriate.

Or should we not perhaps suppose that Moses says to the Lord: “Lord, no one has believed my report”? For if they had believed my writings, they would certainly also have believed Christ, since I wrote about him.

“Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”

**(Origen.)** Here “the word of Christ” signifies preaching about Christ. For it was not only those who heard the word from Christ the Lord himself as he spoke who believed in him; there are many more who heard others preaching him, just as the Lord himself had foretold when he said to Thomas: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20).

Every word, therefore, that the apostles—and anyone else who, having received grace from him, preached about Christ—spoke, he declares to be the word of Christ. Moreover, in the Church, if anyone speaks the wisdom that comes from God and God’s truth, if anyone teaches the way of God, which is Christ, and explains his righteousness, there is no doubt that what he speaks is the word of Christ.

“But I ask: Have they not heard?”

**(Ambrose.)** That is: They heard, but they did not wish to believe. Although faith comes from hearing, there are nevertheless those who do not believe even when they hear. They hear but do not understand, because their hearts have been blinded by ill will.

“And indeed their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” To such an extent he testifies that God’s preaching was heard by the Jews that he even declares the world to have been filled with the divine proclamation. For the very structure of the world proclaims its Creator.

What the Psalmist said about creation, the Apostle says here about the evangelists: it was heard everywhere, and the preaching of Christ’s name reached every place. Where the presence of the human preacher was absent, the sound and report nevertheless arrived, just as the report of the miracles performed in Egypt had reached all nations, as Rahab the prostitute testifies (Josh. 2). If it reached every place, the Jews could not have failed to hear the apostolic preaching, so that none of them might be excused from the charge of unbelief.

**(Origen.)** This may be understood in the following way: by “earth” he means all the uneducated and unteachable people, to whom not the words containing the reasoning of faith and the exposition of wisdom, but only the sound of faith through simple preaching, reached. By “the end of the world,” however, he means the more educated and prudent. For “end” indicates the perfection of things.

To such people, therefore, he declares that not merely the sound of the voice but the words and reasoning reached them. Hearing the discourse of faith, they can also examine and search the divine Scriptures, so as to recognize the truth of the words that were announced to them through the apostles.

Knowing this distinction between sound and words, the Apostle says in another passage: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Cor. 2). He thereby shows that “word” is the expression by which the wisdom of God is explained more clearly through the power of the Spirit, whereas “preaching” is what the Prophet means when he says, “Their sound has gone out into all the earth”—a simple announcement of faith, sufficient for the simpler among people.

“But I ask: Did Israel not know?”

**(Ambrose.)** That is: Did it not know? Since by the testimonies mentioned above he accuses the people of Israel of unbelief, and seemed to complain with grief about all the Israelites, he does not deny that Israel knew and attained what had been promised to it in the Law. Rather, he speaks of the one who is Israel more in spirit than in flesh, the one whom God had foreknown as destined to believe.

All heard, but not all believed. Therefore:

“First, Moses says, in the song of Deuteronomy: ‘I will make you jealous of a non-nation; I will provoke you to anger against an unintelligent nation.’”

**(Augustine.)** When he says, according to Moses’ testimony, “I will make you jealous of a non-nation, against an unintelligent nation,” this means that although all the people who worshipped idols constituted an unintelligent nation, the Gentile condition was laid aside through faith. Hence there is also the statement: “If the uncircumcision keeps the requirements of the Law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?” The sense is therefore: “I will make you jealous of that people which, by laying aside its Gentile condition through faith in Christ, has become a non-nation, although it had previously been an unintelligent nation through its worship of idols.”

**(Ambrose.)** These are the words of one who is indignant, because the Jews were always found to be unbelieving. He assigns one origin and one cause to all their evils. While rebuking those who are present, he touches upon those who are to come, to whom this also applies. For the condemnation of all such people is one if they persist in unbelief.

Jealousy therefore arose in them from envy, when they saw a people that previously, because it was without God, had been brutish in understanding, calling their own the God who had belonged to the Jews, and obtaining the gift that had been promised to them. Because of this they suffered jealousy and were stretched taut with anger, so that they might pay the wages of their wickedness and unbelief. Nothing consumes a person so thoroughly as jealousy. God therefore appointed it as an avenger of unbelief, because unbelief is a grave sin.

For whenever they are driven into anger, they are tortured when they hear that the Law and the Prophets belong to us who believe in Christ.

**(Origen.)** It might perhaps appear that Moses addressed the nation chosen by God on account of its faith and devotion in an insulting manner when he said “a non-nation,” as though he considered it so worthless that he did not even deem it worthy to call it a nation; or, if he did call it one, named it unintelligent.

But Moses is not insulting, being God’s friend, especially toward his chosen people. Nor will the language appear abusive if the reasoning behind it is understood. Each nation—for example, the Egyptians, Syrians, or Moabites—is called this or that nation because it is distinguished by its own boundaries, language, dress, customs, and institutions. Syrians are never called Egyptians, nor Moabites Idumeans, nor Arabs Scythians.

Christians, however, are not one nation; rather, from all nations there is one people. Therefore Moses, as a supreme honor, did not call them a nation, because they were not one nation but, if one may put it so, the nation of all nations.

Yet we may seem to be excluded by what follows, where he says: “I will provoke you to anger against an unintelligent nation,” since he has called it both a nation and unintelligent. But even here Moses, the servant of God, does not insult the people of God. He foresaw in the Spirit that if anyone wishes to be wise in this world, he must become foolish in order to be wise before God: “The world did not know God through wisdom; it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1). Through the preaching of Christ’s cross—which is foolishness to the Gentiles—a people would be gathered that would become foolish in this world in order to be wise before God.

The Jews therefore become angry because, while they excuse themselves and reject the invitation, the Gentiles have been invited to the king’s banquet. They do not consider what Isaiah long ago dared to say concerning this mystery: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me.”

**(Ambrose.)** Since above he used Moses’ words concerning the exclusion of the Jews, he has now added this example from the prophet Isaiah, so that through Isaiah’s fuller exposition he might teach more clearly that God, having cast out the Jews, freely offered grace to the Gentiles, to the Jews’ disgrace and destruction. Isaiah testifies to these things in the person of Christ.

**(Origen.)** Let us consider what the Apostle means when he says, “Isaiah dares and says,” and what sort of daring of the Prophet is being taught here. If we attend to the words of blessed Stephen—“Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute, who announced the coming of the Righteous One?” (Acts 7)—then we understand Isaiah’s daring. Although persecution and death had been set before him, he nevertheless dared to preach the coming of the Righteous One, and even dared to die for the good.

At the same time, this also shows that the prophets did not, as some suppose, fail to understand what they were saying and prophesy as though their minds were alienated. For when the Apostle says of Isaiah that “he dares and says,” he indicates that, despising death and the persecutions inflicted upon him, although he knew that danger threatened him, he nevertheless dared to preach the word of God.

Paul likewise said: “I know that bonds and imprisonments await me in Jerusalem, but I do not consider my life precious to myself” (Acts 20). Thus Isaiah also knew that he would be cut apart and killed by the ungodly, yet he dared, and in the person of Christ said: “I was found by those who were not seeking me.”

It is certain that these were the Gentiles, who neither knew how to seek Christ nor had learned to ask about him. Yet they found the one whom they had not sought, because he himself sought them first.
