For he is the good shepherd who sought the sheep that had been lost; and he is Wisdom, who sought the lost drachma and, seeking, found it (John 10; Luke 15).

The Jews, however, continue to seek Christ and to question the Scriptures about him, yet do not find him, because his cross is a stumbling block to the Jews.

“But to Israel he says: ‘All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe and who contradict me.’”

**(Ambrose.)** Here “Israel” is carnal Israel, that is, the sons of Abraham, but not according to faith. The true and spiritual Israel is the one who, by believing, sees God. “All day long” means “always,” for they have always been rebuked. They are therefore reproved as unbelieving, so that they may know that they themselves are the cause of their destruction.

This may also be understood of the Savior, who, with his hands extended on the cross, accused the sin of those who killed him. For that event cries out concerning the criminal deed of the Jews mentioned above. Isaiah dared to say of those who had been enemies of God that they would become friends, and that those who were called Israelites, because they were disobedient, would be rejected as enemies.

**CHAPTER 11.** The Apostle restrains the Gentiles’ contemptuousness toward the Jews, sets forth the Jews’ present blindness, and concludes the chapter with the depth of divine wisdom.

“But I ask: Has God rejected his people? Certainly not.”

**(Augustine.)** When he says, “Has God rejected his people? Certainly not,” this refers to what he said above: “The word of God cannot fail.” For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, nor, because they are Abraham’s descendants, are they all children; rather, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” Thus, from the Jewish people themselves, those are reckoned as descendants who believed in the Lord.

He also says above concerning this matter: “A remnant will be saved.”

**(Origen.)** From what was said above, the Jewish people might perhaps appear to have been rejected by God and to have no hope at all, since God had provoked them to jealousy against a non-nation and to anger against an unintelligent nation; since he had become manifest to those who were not seeking him, and had been found by those who were not asking about him.

Therefore the Apostle, wishing to correct these impressions and show that a way of salvation remains for the people of Israel if they believe—and that they were not rejected because they were Israelites but because they were unbelieving—says: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” To prove this by a present example, he adds: “For I also am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin,” and yet I teach and proclaim faith in Jesus, that he is the Christ.

If being an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, did not hinder me from believing in Christ and being justified by his faith, it is certain that God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.

**(Ambrose.)** By his own example he teaches that one part of Israel has been saved—those whom God foreknew as destined to be saved, or who may yet be saved—and that another part of Israel, because of its continual unbelief, has been assigned to destruction.

“God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” This is what the Savior says: “Father, those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished except the son of perdition” (John 17). Thus, of those whom God foreknew would believe, none has been rejected from the promise, because what happened was what God foreknew would happen.

**(Origen.)** But lest it should seem too little that the Apostle was teaching by his own example that the people of God had not been rejected, he seeks stronger examples and says:

“Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets; they have demolished your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.’ But what does the divine response say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.’”

**(Ambrose.)** These matters are clear. For he shows not only that Elijah remained, as one devoted to God and unwilling to worship idols (1 Kings 19), but also that many remained who continued in faith in God, just as not a few of the Jews believed.

The history also agrees with this, because many people hid in caves on account of Ahab, king of Samaria, and his wife Jezebel. They believed the false prophets, persecuted God’s prophets, and encouraged the people to idolatry.

Thus also in the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.

**(Origen.)** We must therefore show, as far as we can, how, just as it happened under Elijah—when the Prophet supposed that the whole people had been rejected, yet seven thousand men were found who remained in God’s covenant—it also happened at the coming of Christ and in the times when Paul preached.

Consider whether perhaps we can place John the Baptist, who preceded the Savior’s coming, in the position of Elijah. The gospel itself bears such witness to him, saying that he came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1), and the Lord himself said of him: “If you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. Let anyone who has ears to hear listen” (Matt. 11).

This man, then, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, had despaired so completely of that people that he did not call them the offspring of Abraham but “offspring of vipers,” and added: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3).

To him, therefore, as he complained about the people, our Lord and Savior responds: “I know whom I have chosen.” And again: “My sheep hear my voice, and I go before them, and my sheep follow me.” And again: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also” (John 10).

Let us also consider what that number—seven thousand men—indicates. The number seven pertains to rest: “For on the seventh day God rested.” Hear, then, how Christ also invites those who believe in him to rest, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

Everyone who comes to Christ, lays down the burdens of sin, and finds the rest of salvation belongs to this number seven. The Apostle therefore rightly says that at the present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. By “remnant” he means those from the circumcision who believed: both the apostles, among whom he includes himself, and the others who followed the faith of Christ with them.

But when he says that the remnant was saved according to the election of grace, this addition of “election” does not seem superfluous to me. He could have said merely, “The remnant was saved by grace.” Instead, he shows by this that grace exists both without election and with election.

All who are saved through faith are undoubtedly saved by grace. But those who are saved through the election of grace seem to me to be shown as more perfect in soul. For just as everyone who descends from the race of Israel is called Israel, while the true Israel is the one who sees God with a pure mind and sincere heart, so we may understand this passage as follows: all who come to the faith of Christ come by grace; but the one who adorns the gift of grace with works of virtue and purity of heart will be said to be saved by Christ not only through grace but through the election of grace.

Finally, if someone carefully observes the Apostle Paul’s words, he sees how he makes use of such distinctions. In one place he names Israel according to the flesh; elsewhere he makes no mention at all of the flesh, as in the present passage. When he said that God had not rejected his people and wished to explain the nobility of the Israelite soul, he said: “For I also am an Israelite.”

In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, however, when he is compelled to answer certain people who were boasting according to the flesh about their Israelite descent, observe what he said beforehand (2 Cor. 11): “What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness, in this matter of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.” And after a little he says: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.”

Thus, when he spoke of Israel according to the inner person—for such is the people whom God foreknew and did not reject—he did not say “Israel according to the flesh.” But to those who boasted in fleshly descent he first stated that he was speaking neither according to God nor in wisdom about such boasting, but, as he himself says, in foolishness.

Such, then, are the remnant “that has been saved according to the election of grace.”

“And if by grace, then it is no longer from works.”

**(Ambrose.)** It is clear that the grace of God is a gift, not a payment owed for works, but something granted freely through mercy. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

This is true: if it is a reward, it is not grace; but because it is not a reward, it is undoubtedly grace. For to grant pardon to sinners is nothing other than grace; and grace is offered even to those who do not seek it, so that they may believe.

Grace is therefore twofold, since it belongs to God, who abounds in mercy, both to seek those whom he may freely heal and to bestow his gift upon them.

**(Origen.)** We should know that the works which Paul rejects and frequently condemns are not the works of righteousness commanded in the Law. Rather, they are the things in which those who keep the Law according to the flesh boast: circumcision of the flesh, the rites of sacrifices, and the observance of Sabbaths and new moons.

These and similar practices, then, are the works by which he says no one could have been saved, and of which he says in the present passage, “not from works.” Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. For if someone is justified by these things, he is not justified freely.

But the person justified by grace is by no means required to perform these works. He must, however, take care that the grace he has received does not become void in him, just as Paul says: “His grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more abundantly than all of them” (1 Cor. 15). And again, as though mindful of grace, he adds: “Not I, but the grace of God that is with me.”

The person who adds works worthy of grace does not therefore make grace void, nor is he ungrateful to the grace of God. For whoever sins after receiving grace becomes ungrateful to the one who granted grace. But if you do not make grace void, grace will be multiplied for you, and, as though receiving the reward of a good work, you will obtain an abundance of graces. Thus Peter himself writes in his Epistle: “May grace and peace be multiplied for you in the knowledge of God” (2 Pet. 1); and again elsewhere: “As good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 4).

What, then, is the conclusion? What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it. The rest, however, were hardened, as it is written: “The Lord gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear, to this very day.” And David says: “Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling-block, and a recompense for them. Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually.”

In these words the Apostle divides Israel into two parts. One he calls “the elect,” who obtained what it was seeking [Col. 1522D]; the other he calls “the rest,” who not only did not obtain what they were seeking, but were also blinded by a spirit of compunction. He says that God gave them “eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear, to this very day,” that is, until the consummation of the age.

But a question arises for us: how can it fittingly be said of the good God that he himself gave eyes to the remnant of Israel with which they would not see, and ears with which they would not hear? Consider whether this may rather be a retribution and the reward of unbelief, in accordance with what we explained above, where it is said that, because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind. Here too he speaks of the eyes and ears of the heart, not of the body, by which they were blinded and do not hear—namely, those who, while seeing Christ bodily and hearing his teaching, nevertheless did not wish either to believe the works they saw or to obey the word they heard.

Indeed, we have spoken sufficiently about this very question in the earlier parts of this Epistle. Yet, although it is written there exactly as the Apostle says—“As it is written: God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear, to this very day”—I have so far been unable to find where it occurs. If anyone has searched the divine Scriptures more carefully than we have and has found it, let him make it known.

I nevertheless think that the Apostle spoke in this manner: “The rest were blinded”; and, as it is written concerning them, “God gave them a spirit of compunction.” Thus he seems to be saying in his own words that God gave them a spirit of compunction, in accordance with what was said through Isaiah concerning the blindness of the eyes and the hearing of the ears.

For Isaiah says:

> Go and say to this people:  
> “You shall hear by hearing and shall not understand;  
> and seeing you shall see and shall not see.  
> For the heart of this people has become dull,  
> and with their ears they have heard heavily;  
> and they have closed their eyes,  
> lest perhaps they should see with their eyes,  
> and hear with their ears,  
> and understand with their heart,  
> and turn and I heal them” (Isa. VI).

The Apostle therefore seems now to have expressed Isaiah’s meaning in his own words; but because he was stating the Prophet’s meaning, he added, “As it is written.”

He does something similar with the words that he declares to have been spoken through David. For he says:

> And David says:  
> “Let their table become a snare,  
> and a trap, and a stumbling-block,  
> and a recompense for them.  
> Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see,  
> and bend their back continually” [Col. 1523C].

For when he says, “Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling-block,” the words “and a trap” are not found written in the Psalm, neither in our copies of the Seventy translators nor in the Hebrew copies. And again, the Psalm has: “Let their table before them become a snare”; but the Apostle did not include “before them.”

We have mentioned these matters concerning the order of the words and the character of the testimonies employed in order to show point by point that the apostolic authority does not invariably confirm the Hebrew copies, nor always adhere to the wording of the interpreters; rather, it explains the meaning of the Scriptures in words suited to it.

Let us now see how the meaning of the proposed passage ought to be explained. He proves the blindness of the heart—namely, that the rest of Israel, those who did not believe, were blinded—by two prophetic testimonies, one apparently taken from Isaiah and the other from David; and in both the same meaning is expressed in a certain way. In the one passage, eyes are given to them with which they may not see, and ears with which they may not hear; in the other, it is desired that their table before them become a snare, a trap, a recompense, and a stumbling-block, and that their eyes be darkened so that they may not see.

It does not seem irrelevant to show how these things can fittingly be understood as being said, especially in the person of Christ in the Psalm. Consider, then, whether we can explain the question in this way.

Just as everyone uses bodily eyes to see either good or evil, and has the power either to raise his eyes toward heaven and, through what he sees, acknowledge and praise its Creator, or to turn them toward the spectacles of the circus or the theater, or toward the delights of any sordid sights, by which the mind may be inflamed either to lust, greed, or other vices—so understand also the eyes of the soul. Some use them to recognize the word of God and the teaching of truth and to make daily progress in his wisdom; others use these eyes in the opposite way, exercising themselves daily and seeking how they may undermine the doctrines of truth and attack the faith of Christ as far as they are able.

Suppose, then, that someone were to pray for those who are acute and clever in false knowledge and say: “May God give them eyes so that they may not see the subtleties of their perverse understanding, and ears so that they may not hear the teachers of falsehood; and may their eyes be darkened so that they may not see.” Would you not think that the person who wishes for them these things should be embraced, since through them their sins are diminished? For it is much better not to know than to know wrongly.

Do you not think, I ask, that Marcion, who composed blasphemous writings against God the Creator, or Basilides, or Valentinus, or the other authors of perverse doctrines, would have been blessed if they had not possessed the eyes of the heart with which they wrongly understood these matters? Concerning such people Isaiah says: “Woe to those who write; for in writing they write wickedness” (Isa. X).

Similarly, David prays in the Psalms for those who teach and speak wrongly, saying: “Let the lips of the wicked be made mute, which speak iniquity against the righteous in pride and contempt” (Ps. XXX).

Thus it is said also concerning Israel: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see,” and, “Let God give them eyes so that they may not see.” Let this suffice concerning the blindness of the eyes, which seems to have been given by God, as a kind of remedy, to unbelieving Israel that was seeing wrongly.

Now let us examine the table which is said to become for them a snare, a trap, a stumbling-block, and a recompense.

But first a few words must be said to those who reject allegories in the divine Scriptures and are accustomed to laugh at those who do not follow the historical meaning in every respect. Let them tell us: if the Prophet here means the table of the Jews at which they customarily lunch or dine, how is that very table to become a snare for them, so that it may catch them? Or if the table itself is to become a recompense for them, how are they to receive punishment from it for the things they have done wrong? Or let them explain how it is to be a stumbling-block for them.

If they cannot explain each of these points and see their laughter turned into confusion, then let them come with us and inquire from the divine Scriptures how this table can be understood as Israel’s table.

For our part, according to the capacity of our understanding, it seems to us that all the Scriptures which existed among Israel before the Lord’s coming—for “the oracles of the Lord were entrusted to them first”—and everything called the Old Testament constitute Israel’s table. At this table, if anyone wished to eat the word of God, he was nourished by the words of the Law and the Prophets set before him.

I think this is the table of which Solomon says:

> If you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man, understand intelligently what is set before you, and put your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things for yourself (Ecclus. XXXI).

And when the Savior says, “When you have eaten and drunk at my table,” what else do we understand his table to be except the place where he teaches those who are worthy and able to receive the word of wisdom and the knowledge of realities?

Solomon also bears witness to this in Proverbs, speaking of Wisdom:

> Wisdom built herself a house and set up seven pillars. She slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine in the bowl, and prepared her table (Prov. IX).

Every Scripture, therefore, is the table of Wisdom.

Let us see, then, how David prays that this table may become for unbelieving Israelites, in their presence, a snare, a stumbling-block, a trap, and a recompense.

The divine Scripture becomes a snare for them when they read the prophecies concerning Christ:

> “He shall build my city,  
> and he shall turn back the captivity of my people” (Amos IX),

and they say that these things were not fulfilled under Jesus. “He did not build the city of God,” they say, “nor did he bring back the captivity of the people.”

They say this because, sitting at the table of the powerful man, they do not do what Solomon urged: that they should understand intelligently the things set before them. Christ was prophesied to accomplish these things not visibly but intelligibly, that is, spiritually. For he truly built the city of God out of living stones, from which he raised up children for Abraham, and from them built the Church of God; and he turned back the captivity of the people—those whom the Devil held captive in sins.

For those who do not understand in this way, this table of divine Scripture became a snare and a trap.

This table may also be understood as the trap by which the Lord caught them when he said to them:

> What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?

They answered him, “David’s.” And the Lord said:

> How then does David call him Lord, saying, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand”? (Matt. XXII.)

And they were unable to answer him a word.

This table becomes a recompense for them, to state the matter briefly, according to the Lord’s word:

> Do you think that I shall accuse you before the Father? There is one who accuses you: Moses (John V);

and according to what the Apostle says:

> Whoever sinned under the Law shall be judged by the Law (Rom. II).

This table also becomes a stumbling-block for them in the following way. From the Scriptures the Jews had learned that “the Christ remains forever” (John XII). But when they saw Jesus in the flesh—and not only in the flesh, but also in death, and death on a cross (I Cor. XV)—they were scandalized by him, not knowing that although he suffered through the weakness of the flesh, he lives through the power of God.

Because they did not understand these things intelligently, they were scandalized by what had been set before them at the table of the powerful man. The very table of the divine Scriptures became for them a stumbling-block, and their eyes were darkened, as we said above, and their back was bent continually.

For those who have sinned against the Creator of heaven and against the Lord of majesty ought no longer to look toward heaven.

Each of us, too, must beware lest this table of the divine words, at which we seem to have sat down in order to receive, according to our ability, the food of God’s word, become for us a snare, a recompense, or a stumbling-block, if we do not receive from it, as we ought and with understanding, the pure, clean, and spiritual foods of wisdom.

We must also take care not to sit at the table of Wisdom in unclean and filthy garments—that is, with body or heart polluted—but, already contemplating the image of the future banquet in heaven, let us prepare each day, through conversion and repentance, garments ever cleaner and more fit for the wedding. Wearing these, may we deserve to enter the palace of Wisdom and the bridal chambers of the King’s Son.

I ask, then: Did they stumble in such a way as to fall? Certainly not; but through their trespass salvation came to the Gentiles, in order to provoke them to emulation.

**(Ambrose.)** He says this because they did not become so unbelieving that they would never again believe; that is, they were not so blinded on account of their wickedness that they could not be healed, just as we read that the Devil fell, when the prophet Isaiah says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer!” (Isa. XIV), signifying a fall and apostasy.

**(Augustine.)** He therefore does not say that they stumbled in such a way as to fall, but that on account of their stumbling they were dulled for a time. He does not say this because they did not fall, but because their fall was not fruitless, since it contributes to the salvation of the Gentiles. They did not sin in such a way as to fall—that is, merely to fall, as though only their own punishment were involved—but so that the very fact that they fell might benefit the Gentiles for salvation.

**(Origen.)** He shows how salvation is given to the Gentiles through their trespass: “in order to provoke them,” he says, “to emulation.” That is, when they see the conversion of the Gentiles, and the covenant of God—which they had first received—handed over to them, and the Law and the Prophets held among them in greater and more worthy observance, they may themselves be moved to zeal, at least in the last times. And just as their fall has now given salvation to the Gentiles, so the faith and conduct of the Gentiles may bring to Israel an emulation of conversion and salvation.

It must nevertheless be observed that Paul distinguishes between stumbling and sinning on the one hand, and falling on the other. For stumbling or sin he provides a remedy; but the statement that they had fallen, as though this involved some form of despair, he does not admit. For he says: “Did they stumble in such a way as to fall? Certainly not. But through their trespass salvation came to the Gentiles.”

It is remarkable how, despite all the many and important things that the entire text of the Epistle explains concerning them, the Apostle nevertheless denies that they have fallen. It seems to me that Paul knew well the distinctions among kinds of falling, and understood one kind of falling according to what is written: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV); and again: “Do not exult over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again” (Mic. VII); and according to what Jeremiah says: “Will one who falls not continue to rise? Or will one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. VIII).

Job also says concerning himself: “At the appointed time he is prepared to fall beneath others, and his house to be plundered by strangers.” And in the Fourth Book of Kings it is written: “Hezekiah fell through the pride of his heart” (IV Kings XX).

All these falls, of which we have recalled that Scripture speaks in the passages mentioned above, certainly have resurrection as their outcome, and their turning away has conversion as its outcome.

But in the present passage, as though the Apostle knew that if they had fallen they would be altogether unable to rise again, he denies that they have fallen and strongly excuses them in saying: “Did they stumble in such a way as to fall? Certainly not.”

Perhaps, then, with another fall in mind, the Apostle excuses Israel and denies that it has fallen—perhaps the fall of which our Lord and Savior said: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X), and also that of which Isaiah says: “How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. XIV).

With respect to such a fall, therefore, he denies that Israel has fallen. Israel’s conversion will occur at the end of the age, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI). But for the one who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be no conversion even at the end of the age.

Let us therefore understand that the kind of fall mentioned above—the kind in which the one who falls will continue to rise—is similar to the stumbling which the Apostle names in this passage and calls a trespass. This seems to me to be the meaning.

If a righteous person is overcome in some matter—for example, by the weakness of the flesh or by some other sin—and falls, but nevertheless does not abandon the observance of the whole Law, retaining righteousness, cultivating mercy, preserving faith, piety, and gentleness, and not neglecting to meditate on the Law of God, we can say concerning him: “Did he stumble in such a way as to fall? Certainly not.”

So also the Israelites, although they denied their Redeemer and stoned and persecuted those who were sent by him to preach salvation, nevertheless still retain something. They have meditation on the Law, although they do not believe or understand; they have zeal for God, although not according to knowledge.

For this reason the Apostle says that they did not stumble in such a way as to fall—that is, so as to withdraw entirely from every observance or meditation on the Law of God. He called this kind of fall a trespass.

“For through their trespass,” he says, “salvation came to the Gentiles.”

Therefore David too, knowing that there are trespasses of this kind, in which the one who falls rises again, and others in which the one who falls does not rise, not even at the consummation of the age, said:

> Trespasses—or falls—who understands them? (Ps. XVIII.)

The text continues:

> But if their trespass is the wealth of the world, and their diminution the wealth of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness!

**(Ambrose.)** It is clear that if their trespass benefited the world, since through their loss it has more good people—for the Gentiles are far more numerous than the Jews—and if their diminution, which is the loss of the promise, became the wealth of the Gentiles because they gained eternal life, how much more will their fullness do so!

It is evident that the world will be richer in good people if those who were blinded are also converted; for the world will be saved in large part. Here “the world” signifies human beings, as it was said concerning the Savior: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII).

**(Origen.)** In these words the wisdom of God is to be noted: with him not even trespasses and falls turn out uselessly. Although each person sins through the freedom of his own purpose, the dispensation of divine wisdom makes others rich by the very thing through which the sinner becomes poor as a result of his negligence.

For when God divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations, and so forth, as the inheritance of Israel. But when the angels to whom the portion of the nations had been assigned seduced, as it were, each person from the Lord’s portion and corrupted them, they caused them to stumble, so that the Lord said through the Prophet: “My desirable portion has become for me an abomination.”

It was therefore necessary that, once that portion had been rejected and repudiated, there should be another portion of the Lord upon earth, one that would receive the glory, the covenants, the legislation, and the services of the worship of God—all of which were the riches of the Lord’s portion—and that it should be called the Lord’s portion in place of the portion that had stumbled.

For this reason their trespass becomes the wealth of the world. Now it is no longer one Hebrew nation alone, but the whole world, that has become the Lord’s portion.

Thus the Savior says:

> I came not to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through me (John XII).

And lest the term “world” seem ambiguous—for “world” often refers to heaven and earth, often to the earth alone, and sometimes also to all human beings—therefore the Apostle repeats himself and indicates more clearly what he means by “world.” He says: “And their diminution is the wealth of the Gentiles.” What was diminished and taken away from those who stumbled has been transferred to the wealth of the Gentiles, who through faith have become the Lord’s portion and his inheritance.

He fittingly set “fullness” over against “diminution,” and it is not without profound meaning that Paul calls the people of Israel “fullness.” I understand something like the following, according to my ability.

At present, while all the nations are coming to salvation, the riches of God are being gathered from the multitude of believers. But as long as Israel persists in unbelief, the fullness of the Lord’s portion cannot yet be said to be complete. The people of Israel are lacking for its completeness.

When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and Israel has come to salvation through faith in the final time, that people—which was indeed first, but will come last—will in a certain way complete the fullness of God’s inheritance and portion.

It is therefore called “fullness” because, at the end, it will complete what was lacking in the Lord’s portion. Thus the dispensation of the almighty and good God makes the trespasses of some fruitful for others, just as in the present case Israel’s trespass makes the wealth of the world, and its diminution the wealth of the Gentiles.

> For I speak to you Gentiles: Insofar as I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to emulation and save some of them.

**(Ambrose.)** He shows with what affection he loves the Jews. For he honors his ministry, by which he is the Apostle of the Gentiles, if, because of his affection for his own race, he deliberately also wins the Jews to the faith. His ministry will be more greatly honored if he wins to life even those to whom he was not sent. For it will be a matter of the greatest praise for the fathers if he finds as brothers those who had perished.

**(Origen.)** Therefore, as long as Paul is the Apostle of the Gentiles, he says that he makes his ministry illustrious. And what is more fitting than that each person should adorn the ministry which, through God’s providence, he has received?

He adorns and makes his ministry illustrious who ministers well. Conversely, he dishonors his ministry and makes it blameworthy who ministers negligently and unworthily.

For example, in the ministry of the Church, the Apostle says: “He who has served well as a deacon acquires for himself a good standing and great confidence in the faith of Jesus Christ.” But if he has not served well—that is, if he has not shown himself to be as the Apostle describes him (I Tim. III): serious, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not seeking shameful gain, but possessing the ministry of faith with a pure conscience—then he acquires for himself not a good standing but a severe punishment, as one who has insulted the divine ministry.

Similarly, whoever assumes the rank of presbyter in the Church should strive sufficiently to make the ministry of the presbyterate illustrious. To him belong both the things that the Apostle writes to Titus concerning presbyters (Tit. I) and those that Isaiah writes when he says:

> The Lord himself will come to judgment with the presbyters [elders] of the people, and with its rulers he will be judged (Isa. III).

He adds:

> Why do you burn up my vineyard, and is the plunder of the poor in your houses? Why do you wrong my people and shame the faces of the poor? (ibid.)

In accordance with these things, a bishop also makes his ministry illustrious in the episcopate if he is as the Apostle describes him: blameless, watchful, prudent, well-ordered, hospitable, a teacher, not addicted to wine, not violent but moderate, not quarrelsome, not greedy, governing his own household well, having children obedient with all dignity, not puffed up with pride, lest he fall into the judgment of the Devil.

Whoever is such makes the ministry of his episcopate illustrious, so that he too may hear:

> Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things (Matt. XXV; Luke XIX).

Similarly, a widow, if she persists in prayers and supplications night and day, makes the ministry of her widowhood illustrious. But if she is as the Apostle describes her (I Tim. V)—idle and talkative, and not merely talkative but meddlesome, speaking things that ought not to be spoken—or if she lives in luxury and, while living, is dead, she has dishonored and not made illustrious the ministry of her widowhood.

In the same way, a virgin consecrated to God makes the ministry of her virginity illustrious if she is holy in body and spirit, thinks not about the things of human beings but about the things of God, and considers how she may please God.

But if she acts otherwise, she not only fails to make the ministry of her virginity illustrious and does not make her lamp shine; on the contrary, her light is extinguished, and she becomes one of the foolish virgins (Matt. XXV).

Let each person placed in the Church consider these matters within himself, so that, wherever he stands—whether among the clergy or among the people—he may make the ministry of his faith illustrious and perform such deeds that, when people see his good works, they may glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

Paul did this as well when he taught the Gentiles, of whom he was the Apostle: he cared for the weak, nourished the little ones with milk, supplied the strong with more substantial food of the word, and, with maternal affection, gave birth again to those who were wandering and wavering in the faith and had been reduced, as it were, to an aborted state, until Christ was formed in them [Col. 1530A] (I Cor. III; Gal. IV).

Through all these things he made the ministry of his apostleship illustrious, and brought his flesh—that is, his relatives according to the flesh—to emulation of the faith and zeal for good conduct, so that, if not all, at least some of them might be saved.

Thus, while he exercised vigilant care and constant concern for the teaching of the Gentiles and made their conduct and life highly commendable, he invited and provoked the Israelites who were his relatives according to the flesh to imitate those who were progressing in the faith of God. It is the glory of his ministry when, through their instruction, progress also comes to the Israelites.

> For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what is their acceptance except life from the dead?

The Apostle seems to show in these words that, after Israel had been rejected and preaching had necessarily been transferred to the Gentiles, the world was reconciled to God, according to what is written:

> God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them (II Cor. V);

and again, as Paul says:

> He placed in us the word of reconciliation,

through which word he said:

> We entreat you, on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.

Thus, he says, the rejection of this Israelite nation brought reconciliation to the world. And if such was the grace shown toward this nation that, once it had been removed, it was sufficient to reconcile the whole world to God, how much more, do you think, will the world receive when this nation too has deserved to be reconciled to God?

He briefly shows what the world will gain from Israel’s reconciliation when he says: “Life from the dead.” For Israel’s acceptance will occur when the dead also receive life, when the world passes from corruption to incorruption, and when mortals are given immortality.

It would indeed be absurd if, when their stumbling had granted reconciliation to the world, their acceptance did not bestow something greater and more excellent upon the world.

> For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what is their acceptance except life from the dead? And if the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches. But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree.

**(Ambrose.)** It is evident that what is of one substance is one; and therefore the first portion cannot be holy while the whole lump is unclean. He consequently shows that those whose fathers have already attained faith cannot be called unworthy of faith. For if one part of the Jews believed, why should it not be said that another part too can believe?

“And if the root is holy, so are the branches.” By changing the words, he repeats the same point, in order to reinforce the meaning through two examples.

“But if some of the branches were broken off”—that is, if some of them did not believe, having been cut off from the promise—“and you, although you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree.”

This signifies that, while many Jews did not believe, the Gentiles were grafted through faith into the hope of the promise, so that the Jews would be grieved.

**(Origen.)** Thus each person, by the power of his free choice, becomes either a good olive tree or a wild olive tree, whether of the Israelite race or of another culpable nation. Of one kind it is said:

> Sinners were estranged from the womb;  
> they went astray from the belly;  
> they spoke falsehood (Ps. LVII),

so that they are strangers to the covenants and foreigners to the promises of God.

Others, however, are cast upon God from the womb and say:

> Upon you I was cast from the womb;  
> from my mother’s belly you are my God (Ps. XXI).

But since, as we have said, freedom of choice always remains with this nature, it is possible for someone who belongs to the Israelite nation and is a branch of the good olive tree to fall into unbelief and be broken off.

Conversely, another who had chosen to belong to a culpable and sinful nation, and who was therefore called a branch of the wild olive tree, may turn to the faith—for he possesses within himself the freedom of choice by which he can turn toward the good—and may be grafted into the good olive tree through faith, becoming a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree.

Some call this root Abraham; others, Seth; others set down one or another of the deserving fathers. I, however, know no other holy root and holy first portion except our Lord Jesus Christ.

For he is the first fruits of all things, or the first portion, as we have in the Apostle in the present passage, according to what is said elsewhere of him:

> He is the firstborn of every creature (Col. I).

Everyone who is saved is grafted into this root, and from this holy first portion the entire mass of the human race is sanctified.

Indeed, just as a holy root, when its branches remain in it, supplies them with the richness of holiness—giving life to those who adhere to it through his Holy Spirit, cultivating them through the word, making them flourish through wisdom, and causing them to bear abundant fruits in the fullness of every virtue—so that they themselves may say concerning it:

> But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God (Ps. LI),

so too, if the branches that were broken off were broken off because of unbelief, and those that stand stand through faith, who else is it in whom they stand except Jesus Christ? And from whom else were they broken off through unbelief except from the one whom they did not believe?

Therefore, whenever foreigners came to the faith or to the way of life of Israel, they were enrolled in Christ, who was the true Israel. Especially from the time of his coming, many wild olive branches were grafted into this root—or into its branches, namely, the Apostles and Prophets of God—so that those grafted into them might become sharers in the root and richness of Christ.

> Do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, remember that you do not support the root; the root supports you.

Here the Apostle teaches that we cannot exalt ourselves against the root or against the broken-off Israelite branches, nor insult them, because we do not support the root; the root supports us. We do not possess anything that we have not received. “But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV.)

**(Ambrose.)** God is displeased if anyone rejoices in another’s evils, as Solomon says. They were not rejected for the sake of the Gentiles so that the Gentiles might rejoice, but because they did not believe, they provided an opportunity for preaching to the Gentiles.

“But if you boast, you do not support the root; the root supports you.” That is, if you exalt yourself over those into whose root you have been grafted, you insult the race that received you so that you might become good from what was evil. Nor will you stand if you destroy the very thing by which you stand.

He therefore says: “The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” Good; they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand through faith. “Do not be high-minded, but fear.” For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.

**(Origen.)** As though restraining some who were insulting the fallen with excessive boldness and saying, “The branches were broken off—good! They were broken off because of unbelief, so that I, who believed, might be grafted in,” the Apostle says:

They were indeed broken off because of unbelief, and you were grafted in through faith and stand in the faith. But remember that “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, XVIII). Therefore “do not be high-minded”; do not speak lofty and exalted things.

Although you stand in the root, and stand well, nevertheless fear, seeing that those whom you insult once stood where you now stand, while you were not there and were transferred from elsewhere to the root of this olive tree. It is possible for you too to sin. Indeed, by this very act of becoming proud and exalting yourself, you are already sinning.

**(Ambrose.)** Their rejection made room for the Gentiles. But they were not rejected by God so that the Gentiles might enter; rather, they made themselves reprobate by despising God’s gift. Thus they gave the Gentiles an opportunity for salvation.

Paul wishes to restrain this arrogance, so that people may rejoice in salvation rather than insult another’s misery; for the one who rejoices in another’s evils is easily deceived.

You rightly say that you were grafted in after the branches were broken off; but they were broken off because of unbelief—that is, not on your account, but through their own fault. Because they were unbelieving, you were called to salvation in order to provoke them to emulation.

Therefore you ought to give thanks for God’s gift through Christ, not insult them; but you should also pray that, if their evil has contributed to your salvation, they too may return to their origin. Then you will please God, who has shown mercy to you. For he called you for this reason: that through your emulation he might restore them also to grace.

“But you stand through faith.” Because the Jews fell through unbelief, he says that these stand through faith: previously they lay low because of unbelief, but through believing they began to stand.

“Do not be high-minded, but fear”—that is, do not be proud, but beware lest you too stumble.

“For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.” This is true. If he blinded those who, by the prerogative of the fathers, were worthy of such honor, to whom God had also made the promise that they would be adopted as sons, because of their unbelief, what will he do to those who, having been exalted by no distinction—for they possessed no dignity—were nevertheless honored, if they should doubt or exalt themselves?

**(Origen.)** After this, the one who is proud and insults the fallen is instructed by the Apostle in deeper lessons of humility, and is addressed as follows:

See, therefore, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off, and they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in—for God is able to graft them in again.

You who say these things—“See the goodness and severity of God”—when you see his severity toward the branches that were broken off, must fear lest, while you grow proud and insult those who have fallen, you yourself incur the severity of God, which presses hard upon sinners, by sinning. For his goodness remains in those who remain in goodness. Otherwise, by the same rule, you too, if you do not remain in goodness, will be cut off, and they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For it is not impossible for God to graft them in again if they withdraw from the unbelief because of which they were broken off; indeed, it seems easier to restore branches of their own tree to their root than to graft in branches from another tree.

*(Ambrose.)* He testifies that God is good to the Gentiles: although they followed idols and were certainly deserving of death, God in his patience waited for them; and, even though they were not yet seeking him, he called them of his own accord and forgave their sins. But he is severe toward the Jews: he blinded them because they rejected God’s gift. Yet by “these” he now signifies those Jews who, because of their own ill will, have been blinded forever. Hence he also says that they have fallen. Those whom he mentioned above as having stumbled, however, he does not say to have fallen, because he shows that they were blinded only for a time. Thus God was severe toward the apostates, so that they should be blinded forever.

But they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again. He shows that God’s justice does not remain in severity toward those whom he blinded for a time, because he did not cut them off in such a way that he could not graft them in again if they should convert—he who said through the prophet, “Those who return to me I will replant” (Jer. XXIV). Thus, knowing this, Gentile Christians should not insult the Jews, being certain that God’s mercy is reserved for them as for those who have fallen.

For if you were cut from a naturally wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree! Let us understand the olive tree as faith, by which Abraham was justified; and let us understand the wild olive tree—because it is wild and fruitless by nature—as signifying faithlessness. Therefore, if those who had always been enemies of God were converted to the faith of Abraham and grafted in, although they are not descended from him, how much more must the Jews, if they believe after their unbelief, be restored to their ancestral nature and grafted again into their own promise?

*(Origen.)* We must understand the nature of the olive tree or wild olive tree according to what we explained above: free choice has made each person by nature either a wild olive tree or a good olive tree. It should certainly be observed that those who fell from their own olive tree are said to have been broken off; but those who are grafted in from the wild olive tree, if they sin again, are not called “to be broken,” which would in any case be the lighter punishment, but “to be cut off.” This clearly indicates a more severe manifestation of God’s severity: after someone who was a wild olive tree, gathered from the forest of sinners and brought to the root of faith and holiness, again produces the bitter juices of wickedness.

Nor should we overlook the fact that the Apostle did not arrange the comparison of the olive tree and the wild olive tree in the order in which it is practiced among agriculturalists. They customarily graft the olive tree into the wild olive tree, rather than the wild olive tree into the olive tree. Paul, however, by apostolic authority, reversing the order, adapted realities more to their causes than causes to realities.

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: a partial blindness has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved.

Here again he addresses those who had believed from the Gentiles, as though they were elated and proud against the branches that had been broken off, and thought that they had obtained this not through God’s goodness and the ineffable dispensation of his wisdom, but through their own merits—that, once those branches had been broken off, they themselves, though wild olive trees, had been grafted into the good olive tree. He says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation.” To insult those who have fallen and boast against the branches that were broken off does not arise from God’s wisdom, but from a remarkable human wisdom that is ignorant of God’s mystery. For whoever is wise according to God will not insult those who have been cast down amid God’s benefits, but will give thanks with fear for the mercy that bestows them.

*(Ambrose.)* The dullness of blindness was therefore given to the Jews for a time—those who, while zealous for the law, did not see that the gift promised by God had come, the gift proclaimed by Christ. They were blinded by zeal, thinking that the law of works ought never to cease. Hence they were zealous for the Sabbath. Because of this offense they were partially dulled, so that on account of their unbelief they would suffer torment, seeing the Gentiles joyfully profess that they had obtained the promise made to Abraham. Yet, when the multitude of the Gentiles had been admitted, the darkness would be wiped away from the eyes of their minds, so that they might be able to believe; and the spirit of compunction that restrains their hearts—the spirit that grants them blindness—would give back to them the free choice of their will. For their unbelief did not arise from ill will, but they were to be corrected from error and afterward saved.

*(Origen.)* The mystery that was unknown to those who insulted others is therefore this: when the children of Adam were dispersed and the various nations were assigned according to the number of the angels, Israel became a particular portion, just as happened elsewhere where it was fitting—as we mentioned a little earlier concerning these very people—to whom the promises of blessings, the covenants, and the giving of the law were made.

Since that portion of the Lord remained in its own condition, it was not possible for us, who were Gentiles, to enter into God’s inheritance and succeed to the rights of his scepter. Therefore God permits blindness to occur in part—that is, not in all but in some of Israel—blindness undoubtedly inflicted by those angels who, through jealous rivalry, had received the rule over the other nations.

God therefore permitted it; although he could have prevented it, he did not wish to do so, in order that, on behalf of those who had been deceived by blindness—that is, who had fallen through dullness of heart—God might make the portions of those who had deceived them his own portion, so that they might in a certain sense be caught in the very thing by which they had begun to ensnare others.

For by turning God’s people toward themselves through the enticements of sin, they made room for the Gentiles to enter into God’s inheritance. God shared with them a certain and most equitable judgment: while they held God’s people captive in blindness, the number of the Gentiles would be restored, as it were, in exchange for those whom they had from the beginning withdrawn from God’s portion and his separated inheritance.

But when the fullness of the Gentiles had been completed, and Israel had begun, through rivalry over their salvation, to shake off the blindness of its heart, and, lifting its eyes, to behold Christ, the true light, then Israel, stirred up according to the preceding prophecies, would seek the salvation it had lost in its blindness, saying within itself that prophetic word: “I will return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now” (Hos. II).

That these things were promised to them through the prophets is found in many prophetic books. Nevertheless, we shall set down one testimony from Jeremiah sufficient for the present purpose, which reads as follows: “Though heaven should be exalted on high and the earth humbled below, I will not reject the race of Israel for all that they have done” (Jer. XXXI).

If, then, blindness came upon Israel because of all that they had done, in order that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, unquestionably, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the blindness will cease. But if you wish, says the Apostle, to know how Israel will also be saved after its blindness, hear how it is written:

He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns ungodliness away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.

*(Origen.)* It should certainly be known that in the prophet Isaiah (Isa. LIX), from whom Paul takes this testimony, instead of what the Apostle says, “He will come from Zion,” it is written, “He will come for Zion.” And what he says here, “when I take away their sins,” is not written there at all—not even among the Hebrews. Nevertheless, it has been assumed on the authority of the Apostle.

For the present, the Lord, coming from Zion, delivers and turns ungodliness away from Jacob. He turns ungodliness away from him according to what is written: “For the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from her midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning” (Isa. IV). And this was for them a covenant from God: that in this way ungodliness would be turned away from them and sins removed.

*(Ambrose.)* He says, therefore: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns ungodliness away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.” The meaning of this example always remains as long as there are those who believe. For this Lord Jesus, who was promised as coming from heaven for the liberation of the human race, himself forgives the sins of those who turn to him every day. He does not immediately condemn those who do not believe, but waits, knowing that they can advance toward knowledge of God.

*(Origen.)* But who this “all Israel” is that will be saved, or what this “fullness of the Gentiles” will be, God alone knows, together with his Only-begotten, and perhaps those who are his friends, to whom he says: “I no longer call you servants, but friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John XV).

Nevertheless, this may also occur to our understanding: just as Israel, so long as it remains Israel according to the flesh and has not also become Israel according to the spirit—so that it is a true Israelite, seeing God with the mind—cannot belong to salvation, so not all the Gentiles altogether can be saved, but only those who are found within the fullness, whatever that fullness may be which the Apostle names.

Thus the mystery of God is administered through an ineffable dispensation of his wisdom, so that even when the soul itself has brought upon itself the lot of evils, the one who knows how to arrange all things makes its rejection and the punishment of others into salvation.

I also think that in this passage we should examine more carefully the fact that he does not say that this blindness came upon all Israel, but only in part. For the remnant according to the election of grace has been saved. Concerning this remnant Isaiah also prophesied, saying: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed” (Isa. I).

These remnants, therefore, are joined in blessedness with the fullness of the Gentiles. But the rest of Israel who have been blinded are joined with those Gentiles who were unable to reach the fullness. Thus, whatever is found written in the words of the prophets concerning promises that contain blessedness, if it is said of Israel, pertains to these remnants who were chosen; if it is said of the Gentiles, it pertains to the fullness.

But if anything sorrowful is said—if it is said of Israel, it undoubtedly refers to the remaining Israelites who have been blinded; if of the Gentiles, it certainly concerns those who are outside the fullness.

Nevertheless, the end presses upon all things. Those who are blessed, whether they come from Israel or even from the Gentiles, are purified by the evangelical teaching of the present time, so that they may be like those to whom the Lord said: “Behold, you are already clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John XV).

But whoever rejects the purification of God’s word and evangelical teaching reserves himself for grievous and punitive purifications, so that the fire of Gehenna may cleanse him through torments—him whom neither apostolic teaching nor the evangelical word has purified—according to what is written: “And I will purify you with fire until you are pure” (Isa. I).

Nevertheless, we must always remember that the Apostle wished the present passage to be held as a mystery, so that the faithful and perfect should conceal such an interpretation within themselves in silence, as a mystery of God, and not proclaim it indiscriminately among the slain and those of lesser capacity. For, as Scripture says, “It is good to conceal the king’s mystery” (Tob. XII).

[Col. 1536C] According to the Gospel, they are indeed enemies for your sake.

*(Origen.)* Continuing to discuss Israel and the Gentiles, and charging the wild-olive branches that insulted the branches broken from the olive tree, the Apostle adds this also: Israel, according to the Gospel, has become an enemy of God because it did not believe in Christ.

*(Ambrose.)* Because of their unbelief they are enemies of the Gospel, so that their error and offense might open a way for the Gentiles to enter the faith before the appointed time, as I mentioned above. For it was first necessary that the word be preached everywhere to all the Jews; only afterward was it fitting that the Gentiles should also believe the word of God. But because they did not believe, the kingdom was taken from them and given to the Gentiles.

Therefore he warns that they should not be insulted, since their offense benefited the Gentiles. One should insult the person whose sin harmed others; for one must not rejoice in their faithlessness, but grieve if they delay in converting, so that just as the Gentiles rejoiced because they were saved through the Jews’ sin, they may rejoice in their conversion. For through the Jews’ occasion the Gentiles received God’s grace more quickly.

*(Origen.)* Yet, as we have often reminded you, the distinction in the present passage must also be observed: the Israel that is called God’s enemy is the one that cries out concerning Christ, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John XIX). For how could those who said or say such things—whether then or even now—not be called enemies of God?

And when he says “for your sake,” he means those whose salvation they envy, forbidding the apostles to speak to the Gentiles and persecuting those who proclaim Christ.

*(Augustine.)* For what else is meant by “according to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake” than that their hostility, by which they killed Christ, unquestionably benefits the Gospel, as we see?

But according to the election, beloved, they are for the sake of the fathers; for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.

*(Origen.)* As far as the honor bestowed upon the fathers is concerned, Israel was chosen and is held dear by God. Once election had been given to the seed of the fathers and love had been granted, God undoubtedly preserves his gifts and calling toward the seed of those to whom he granted them in some measure because of their merits. God does not experience regret, even if those to whom the benefits promised to the fathers are bestowed appear less worthy.

*(Ambrose.)* Although the Jews sinned grievously by rejecting God’s gift and are deserving of death, nevertheless, because they are the children of good ancestors, through whose prerogative and merit they received many benefits from God, they will be received with joy when they return to the faith; and God’s love toward them is aroused by the memory of their fathers.

*(Origen.)* As regards the remnant that is said to be saved, in which the election of believers from Israel has followed, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. Following their faith, they believe in him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead. In this respect, therefore, God’s gifts and calling toward such a seed are irrevocable.

*(Ambrose.)* For God’s grace in baptism does not require groaning, lamentation, or any work, but only a confession from the heart. They had sinned grievously by not receiving God’s promise, and grave sins attain forgiveness only through groaning and tears. Yet they were not to think that, because they did not see them grieving, they could no longer receive mercy. He shows that such grief is not required at the beginning of faith: God freely forgives sins in baptism as a gift.

*(Origen.)* After this he also reveals the hidden and deeper causes of their unbelief, and says: “For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now disbelieved in your mercy, so that they themselves may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.”

As he says: You Gentiles once did not believe God; nevertheless God did not wholly abandon you for that reason, but at the end you obtained mercy. Yet the occasion for mercy being bestowed upon you was the unbelief of the people of Israel. Likewise, those of the people of Israel who now did not believe and were abandoned because of their unbelief, so that God’s mercy might turn toward you, will not be left forever in their unbelief. After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, they too will obtain mercy.

In this the Apostle wishes to show God’s goodness, by which he makes the salvation of some arise through the unbelief of others. “God,” he says, “has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all”—not because he himself implanted in them the purpose of unbelief, but because, through their purpose of unbelief, he opened an avenue of belief to others who themselves had previously been unbelievers.

*(Ambrose.)* Moreover, the Gentiles had lived from ancient times in ungodliness and ignorance, being without God. For this reason the law was manifested in written form, by which the headlong might be restrained. And because the cunning of the adversary began to multiply sins, so that through prohibition a person might become more guilty, God, always providing for humanity through the clemency of his goodness, determined that what was sin without the law should also be capable of being removed under the law.

He therefore decreed that faith alone should be established, through which the sins of all might be abolished. Since there was no hope for all human beings through the law, they would be saved by God’s mercy. This is what it means that he enclosed all in unbelief: the ordained gift from God was to come when all were struggling with unbelief, so that the grace of the gift might be all the more welcome.

Therefore no one should boast; for it is miserable to be proud when one does not know.

*(Origen.)* While Paul was situated in these passages and contemplating more deeply such causes—how God does not immediately cut off and destroy an evil purpose, but allows it and preserves it, foreseeing that he will accomplish something good in others through another’s evil purpose—I think that from those about whom he was speaking he turned the eyes of his heart toward the very origin of wickedness.

God did not judge it useful from the beginning to cut off the wickedness that had arisen and was sprouting in those in whom it originated, whoever they may be, as it grew through freedom of choice. Rather, he permitted them to use their own purpose, knowing and foreseeing that the progress and benefit of many would arise from the occasion of their wickedness.

So great is the place given to virtue by the good God that, although the work of wickedness is destructive to the one from whom it proceeds, it is nevertheless dispensed so as to provide a benefit to the one against whom it stirs up conflicts, once it has been overcome.

Therefore, considering that God’s riches of goodness are so great, that such a work of divine wisdom is carried out toward rational natures, and that God is so rich in mercy and rich toward all who call upon him, and that his goodness, patience, and long-suffering are so immense, the holy Apostle suddenly looks upon these things with the inner eyes of his heart, perceives their immensity, and, struck at once with wonder and awe, cries out and says:

O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways.

*(Ambrose.)* He testifies, with every praise and thanksgiving, that God is exalted and immeasurable in the riches of his wisdom and knowledge. His counsel and judgment are incomprehensible.

For, knowing from the beginning the conduct and works of human beings—that the human race could be saved neither by the severity of justice alone nor brought to the goal of merit by mercy alone—he determined what should be preached at each time, while nevertheless permitting each person to follow his own judgment, since justice is recognized with nature itself as its guide.

And because the authority of natural justice had grown dull through the habit of sinning, the law was given so that the human race might be restrained by fear of the law once revealed. But because they did not restrain themselves and were held guilty by the law, mercy was proclaimed, so that it might save those who fled to it, while temporarily blinding those who rejected it. At the same time it invited the Gentiles to the promise, while those who had previously refused to follow the justice of God given through Moses, envying the Gentiles’ salvation, might through that very zeal return to the origin of the Savior’s root promised in the law.

This is “the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God,” who through manifold providence acquired both Jews and Gentiles for life.

*(Origen.)* How could the human mind have imagined that, while the freedom of each person’s will was preserved, the work of another’s wickedness would be turned into salvation for someone else, and that wickedness would confer a crown upon the one who conquered it, although it brings destruction to the one who uses it?

Having considered these matters according to a general argument, as it seems, the Apostle cries out and says that such is the depth of God’s riches, such the depth of his wisdom, and likewise such the depth of his knowledge—for the language of depth applies to all these—that no one is sufficient to scrutinize his judgments, by which he orders each soul and every rational nature, nor can anyone search out the ways of the Lord by which his providence proceeds.

By “anyone,” we mean not only human beings but the whole creation. For his judgments would not be called inscrutable and his ways unsearchable unless no creature were able either to investigate or to scrutinize them. The Son alone knows the Father, and the Holy Spirit alone “searches even the depths of God.”

Therefore he says that this depth of God, which he calls both inscrutable and unsearchable, is inscrutable and unsearchable to every creature. He could not say these things concerning the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: “Father, all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John XVII). And Paul himself declares concerning the Holy Spirit: “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (I Cor. II); so also no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of the Lord.

*(Cassian.)* Whoever believes that he can measure, by human speech or reasoning, the depth of that immeasurable abyss will try to diminish the wonder of this knowledge, which so great and distinguished a teacher of the Gentiles regarded with awe. For whoever confidently believes that he can fully conceive in his mind or explain in words the dispensations of God by which he works salvation in human beings has undoubtedly attacked the truth of the Apostle’s judgment. With profane boldness he has declared that God’s judgments are searchable and his ways searchable, although the Lord himself bears witness to them in these words: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are my ways your ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isa. LV).

For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid?

This is written in Isaiah. It is clear that God alone knows all counsels, and that he alone needs nothing, because all things are from him. Therefore his counsel is neither comprehended nor measured by anyone, because what is inferior cannot know the mind of what is superior.

Indeed, to believing Jews it seemed impossible that God’s counsel and will could be directed toward the redemption of the Gentiles. Likewise, it seemed difficult and incredible to the Gentiles that the Jews who had not believed could be converted, or that believers could be received so as to be saved. Among other things, this is the counsel of God that was hidden and could not be comprehended.

*(Origen.)* You see, therefore, that in the present chapter, when Paul says, “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”, he is speaking of creatures but excluding the nature of the Trinity, since it has nothing in common with creation except the work of beneficence.

And when he says, “Who has been his counselor?”, he does not mean that God himself was insufficient in counsel and needed another’s advice, but declares that there is no participant in his counsel among creatures.

Counsel, however, is necessarily present in the wisdom of the wise one, who is Christ, and in holiness, who is the Holy Spirit.

In the same way, the words “Who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid?” must also be understood. No one first contributed anything to his Maker, since each person received even his very existence from the Creator.

*(Gregory.)* Yet just as, when you give bread or clothing to a needy person, the Lord testifies that he has received it, so when sound counsel is given to someone who does not know, he himself receives it—he whose member is the person being instructed.

For all believers are members of our Redeemer. And just as he is nourished in us through the mercy of generosity, so he is assisted in us through the counsel of instruction.

For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

*(Ambrose.)* With this statement he disclosed the meaning that had been hidden from the world. Because God is the Creator of all things, all things are therefore from him. And because they are from him, they began to exist through his Son, who is of the same substance; the Son’s work is therefore the Father’s work.

Since he himself works through the Son, all things are through him. And since what exists is from God and through God, after being reborn in the Holy Spirit all things are in him, because the Holy Spirit too is from God the Father. Hence he knows the things that are in God.

Therefore the Father is also in the Holy Spirit, because what is from God the Father cannot be other than what God the Father is. Thus glory belongs to him, because all things are from him, through him, and in him.

Therefore those things that began to exist from him, through him, and in him cannot know his mind and counsel. But he knows all things, because all things are in him. He disclosed the mystery of God, which, as he said above, ought not to remain unknown to them.

*(Origen.)* You see how, at the end, he shows that in everything he said above he signified the mystery of the Trinity. For just as in the present passage, when he says, “For from him and through him and in him are all things,” this corresponds to what the same Apostle mentions elsewhere when he says, “One God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (I Cor. VIII), and likewise says that all things are revealed in the Spirit of God, thereby indicating that the providence of the Trinity is present in all things,

so also, when he says “the depth of riches,” he signifies the Father, from whom all things are; and by “the depth of wisdom” he reveals Christ, who is his wisdom; and by “the depth of knowledge” he declares the Holy Spirit, who knows even the depths of God.

Nevertheless, when he says “from him,” he indicates the fact that we exist; “through him,” the fact that we are ordered in life through his providence; and “in him,” that the perfection and end of all things will be in him, when God will be all in all (I Cor. XV).

Then glory will belong to him forever and ever. Amen.

“Forever” is said because the perfection of all things is not enclosed within a single age, but extends through many ages and is scarcely ever hoped to be completed. He also adds “Amen,” so that we may understand that through the one of whom it is written in Revelation, “Thus says the one who is Amen” (Rev. III), we must come to this blessedness.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1541]

## CHAPTER XII. The Apostle instructs the Romans both in matters pertaining to God and in matters pertaining to one’s neighbor.

[Col. 1541A]

Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service.

*(Ambrose.)* He exhorts them through the mercy of God, by which the human race is saved. After discussing the law and the faith of the people, and the nature of the Jews and the Gentiles, he exhorts them to lead a good life, for through this the hope of faith is obtained.

This exhortation therefore reminds them that they have received mercy and that they should be vigilant in the service of the one through whom they were freely justified from ungodliness.

*(Origen.)* Throughout the whole preceding text of the Epistle, the Apostle had taught how the central focus of religion had been transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles, from circumcision to faith, from the letter to the spirit, from shadow to truth, and from carnal observance to spiritual observance. He had shown through prophetic utterances that these things would happen.

Now he undertakes to establish the conduct and practices of this spiritual observance, to which he taught that the rite of worship of God had been transferred, and he says: “Therefore I appeal to you, brothers, through the mercy of God.”

Since, he says, we have shown that we must withdraw from carnal sacrifices, in accordance with what the prophet also says, “You did not desire sacrifice or offering” (Ps. XXXIX), and “you took no pleasure in them,” now I teach you what sacrifices delight God.

And I teach this not as one issuing commands—for the command of the law accomplishes nothing—but as one who has undertaken the duty of reconciling you to God. I appeal to you, brothers, and I appeal not through power but through the mercy of God.
