For, as I showed above, since all have been enclosed under sin, human salvation now rests not upon merits but upon God’s mercy.

What, then, is it that I ask of you? That you present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, so that your service may be reasonable.

Here he calls worship “service.” Since this worship formerly consisted in the bodies of mute animals, he now says that it should be offered in the body of a rational human being. Let your bodies, rather than the bodies of animals, become a sacrifice to God and be placed upon the sacred altars.

Those who mortify their members with respect to the incitements of lust and anger, and keep the actions of their bodies pleasing to God, offer a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God in a reasonable manner. They fulfill, according to spiritual understanding, the law of sacrifices that was given in Leviticus.

For example, there they offered first a calf, or second a ram, or third a goat, or fourth turtledoves, or even young pigeons, so that in these the soul of each person might be purified according to the character of his deeds. Now each person purifies these things in his own body and, discerning them in a spiritual sense, offers a living sacrifice to God in reasonable service.

When we discussed certain individual matters in the book of Leviticus, we tried, as far as we were able, to explain how each person, through reasonable service in the worship of God, should sacrifice a calf if he conquers the pride of his body; slaughter a ram if he overcomes anger; offer a goat as a burnt offering if he conquers lust; and sacrifice pigeons and turtledoves if he cuts off the wandering and slippery flights of his thoughts. But, as I said, anyone who thinks it worthwhile to know these things will find them discussed more fully there.

Now Paul appeals to those who believe in Christ to present their bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.

He calls it a living sacrifice because the one who carries life—that is, Christ—in himself says: “We carry the death of Jesus in our body, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our body” (II Cor. IV).

He calls it holy because the Holy Spirit dwells in it, according to what he said elsewhere: “Or do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Cor. III).

He calls it pleasing to God because it has been separated from sins and vices.

All these things constitute reasonable worship of God. A reason can be given for such worship, and it can be shown that it is fitting to offer such sacrifices to God. But no sound and honorable reason will accept that rams, goats, and calves be offered to the immortal and incorporeal God.

It will therefore appear especially that the living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice is an undefiled body.

Yet, because we see that some holy men, and even some apostles, had marriages, we cannot understand this as referring exclusively to virginity, although virginity may hold the first place among such sacrifices. Just as under the law there was one sacrifice of the priest, another of the ruler, another of the synagogue, and another of an individual soul,

and although in the Church the sacrifice of martyrs appears first after the apostles, that of virgins second, and that of the continent third, I nevertheless think that those who are married and, by mutual consent, abstain for a time for the sake of prayer—or who fulfill the vows of the Nazirite—should not be denied the ability to present their bodies as a “living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God,” provided that they act holily and justly in other respects.

Nor, on the other hand, should the bodies of virgins or continent persons be considered to have offered a holy and pleasing sacrifice merely because of bodily virginity, if they are stained either by the mark of pride, by the filth of greed, or by the uncleanness of a slanderous tongue or of falsehood.

For when a sacrifice was offered under the law, the priest examined it carefully—not only whether it was from clean animals, but also whether it had a defect in its eye, ears, or feet, lest a lame, one-eyed, or deaf animal be brought to the divine altar.

Thus the living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice, which is to be offered reasonably, is examined and tested in every one of its members.

And do not be conformed to this age. (Orig.) In this he shows that there is one form of this age and another of the age to come. Those who love the present age and the things that are in this world are adapted according to the form of the present age; but those who do not regard the things that are seen, but the things that are unseen and eternal, are transformed and renewed according to the form of the age to come. Hence it comes about that this world does not recognize them, but hates and persecutes them. Yet the angels of God, who belong to that future age, recognize this form.

This seems to me similar to the saying: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV). See, then, whether perhaps, when anger enters your heart, it makes you conform to this age. Likewise, evil desire, avarice, and the other vices in which the present age delights may impose upon you the form of the present age. But if, on the contrary, gentleness, patience, mildness, continence, faith, truth, and the other virtues dwell in your mind, they will make you conform to the age to come and will render your soul’s appearance so beautiful that the Word of God, who betrothed it to himself “in mercy and faith,” will say to it: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Cant. IV).

Consider more carefully what he says: “But be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” He thus shows that there is a culpable form: every soul formerly possessed the form of wickedness. But the apostolic word exhorts us, once that form has been cast aside, to be transformed into the appearance of each virtue, so that at last, with the face of our heart unveiled, we may contemplate the glory of the Lord, transformed from such an image.

How we are to be transformed into this form he teaches by saying, “by the renewal of your mind.” Our mind is renewed through the practices of wisdom, meditation on the word of God, and spiritual understanding of his law. The more someone advances each day through reading the Scriptures, and the more deeply his understanding penetrates, the more continually he becomes new—new each day.

It can nevertheless happen that not every aspect of the mind is able to be renewed and enlarged through the recognition of knowledge. The mind can be renewed toward justice; it can be renewed toward continence, mercy, faith, and patience. But see what the Apostle adds in what follows to this renewal of the mind: “so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

Certainly, unless the mind has been renewed toward every kind of knowledge and wholly illumined by the wisdom of God, it cannot prove what the will of God is. For in many matters what is thought to be the will of God is not. Those whose minds have not been renewed err and are deceived in this respect. It is truly the mind of one who is not merely renewed, but greatly renewed and, so to speak, re-formed according to the image of God, that can prove in each individual thing we do, say, or think whether it is the will of God, and can refrain entirely from doing, saying, or thinking anything that it recognizes as contrary to God’s will.

The will of God is whatever is good and perfect; nor can God will anything other than what is good. And whatever is good and perfect undoubtedly pleases God. It can indeed appear, as we said above, that every will of God is good, well-pleasing, and perfect. But something else may also be understood in these words: God’s will is always good, but we do not always deserve that his good will be administered to us in a well-pleasing and perfect manner.

For example, that Saul should be anointed king was indeed the will of God, but it was not well-pleasing or perfect. In anger against the people who had rejected God as king over them, he ordered that a human king be established over them. The prophet also says on God’s behalf: “I gave them over to the desires of their heart, so that they might go in their own cravings” (Ps. LXXX). Thus at times God’s will is done in the things we crave and desire. But the person whose mind has been renewed ought to discern whether this will of God is good, well-pleasing, and perfect, and not one that indulges our desires more than it consults our interests.

I say, through the grace given to me, to everyone who is among you: not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety, and to each according as God has divided the measure of faith.

First, it should be understood that where we have “to everyone who is among you,” the Greek has “to everyone who is in you.” This wording indicates that the statement is made to those who previously did not exist but have now begun to exist. For God, as the same Apostle says, “calls the things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV). Those who do not share in him who truly is do not exist—he who said to Moses: “Say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exod. III).

Therefore, when Paul says, “I say to everyone who is among you,” or, as we have said is found in the Greek, “to everyone who is in you,” it is as though he were saying: “I say to everyone who is in God: not to think more highly than one ought to think.”

He also seems to be applying this saying to the proud branches of the wild olive tree that insult the branches broken off from the good olive tree, saying to them that they ought not to think more highly than they should. This resembles the statement he made: “Do not think proudly” (Rom. XI); for this is to think more highly than one ought.

(Amb.) He clearly shows that we ought to think only what does not go beyond the boundaries of justice, so that it may be useful not only to ourselves but harmful to no one. For this is prudence: to benefit some rather than harm them, and to be content with the portion that God has measured out, according to each person’s faith. One should not claim for oneself what one sees has not been granted to oneself. This is what it means not to think more highly than one ought, since the whole cannot be granted to one person.

Nor, if someone is of good character, should he therefore claim for himself prudence in teaching; nor, because he possesses knowledge of the law, should he claim the services of the Levites for himself.

[Col. 1545A] (Greg.) Whoever strives to speak wisely should greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be confused by his eloquence. To give counsel to a fool is charity; to give it to a wise person is ostentation. But to give it to wisdom itself is perversity. Since those whom we have said to bear the appearance of heretics served ostentation rather than usefulness by their speech, it is rightly said in the Book of Job against Bildad: “You have displayed very great wisdom” (Job XXVI).

Everyone whose prudence is upright is not “very great” in this sense, because, in accordance with Paul’s saying, he does not desire to think more highly than he ought. But the one whose prudence is “very great” is not upright, because when it is stretched beyond measure it turns aside into some form of fault. Those display their prudence as “very great” who desire to appear more prudent than others. Hence it often happens that, because they do not know how to think with moderation, they speak foolishly.

(Ambr.) He therefore exhorts and teaches through the grace given to him. This grace is understood as knowledge of the Lord’s discipline, through which he teaches that one must devote oneself to humility and justice.

(Orig.) It should nevertheless be understood that other educated men also use this definition, placing the nature or cause of sin in the fact that something is added to or subtracted from the virtues. For example, justice is a virtue; and if someone does less than justice permits, he is undoubtedly unjust. But if someone, under the guise of justice, becomes excessive in seeking vengeance and pursues retaliation too harshly, he has slipped from justice into cruelty. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not become exceedingly just” (Eccl. VII).

Likewise, freedom is a virtue if it remains within its proper moderation; if it has less, it is called timidity; if more, recklessness. In the same way, prudence is a virtue if it remains within its proper measure; if it has less, it is imprudence; if it has more than it ought, it is called wickedness.

For this reason, I think, the serpent in Paradise is said to have been more prudent than the other beasts: that is, it exceeded the measure of prudence and slipped into the realm of wickedness. For this reason also the children of this age are said to be more prudent than the children of light (Luke XVI): they think more highly than they ought to think. Thus in each of the virtues someone can think more highly than he ought to think.

Someone can also think more highly than he ought about chastity, as do those “who attend to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods that God created” (I Tim. IV). These think more highly than they ought about chastity; whereas the lustful and incestuous person thinks less highly than he ought.

I say that the heretics think more highly than they ought about Christ when they deny that he is the Son of the creator God, assigning him instead to some other, I know not what, better God. Those also think more highly than they ought about Christ who deny that he came in the flesh and was born of a virgin, assigning to him a celestial body.

In all these matters, therefore, Paul wants us not to think more highly than we ought to think, but, he says, to think with sobriety. In Greek this is called *sōphrosynē* (σωφροσύνη); in our books—that is, in the divine Scriptures—our predecessors have translated it as “sobriety,” while other learned men render it “moderation.” This moderation is counted among the four general virtues. Accordingly, the Apostle’s words in this passage would shine more clearly if we too had written them according to the force of the Greek expression: “but to think with moderation”—that is, to maintain moderation in everything we do, say, or feel.

For in the matters we listed above, moderation alone knows how to preserve the proper measure, so that neither more nor less is done than ought to be.

As for his saying, “to each according as God has divided the measure of faith,” this means that each person should know and understand what measure of God’s grace is in him, the measure he has deserved to obtain through faith.

Sometimes someone receives from God the ability to be wise in the work of charity, or in the duty of visiting, or in mercy toward the poor, or in care for the weak, or in defending widows and orphans, or in the attentiveness required by hospitality. God has thus divided these individual gifts to each person according to the measure of faith.

But if the person who received grace to be wise in one of these matters does not understand the measure of grace given to him, and wishes to be wise concerning God’s wisdom, the word of teaching, and the reasoning of deeper knowledge—matters in which he has not received grace—and if he wishes not so much to learn as to teach what he does not know, then, although he has little understanding, he wants to think more highly than he ought. For he does not think with moderation, so as to preserve for each person the measure of faith that God has divided.

To make these matters still clearer, the Apostle introduces an example and says: “For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.”

By this he composes the entire body of the Church. Just as the individual members of the body each have their own functions and each serves through its own duties, yet it is impossible for them not to yield to one another by mutual agreement, so, he says, in the Church, which is the body of Christ, we each have different functions.

For example, one applies all his zeal to the wisdom of God and the teaching of the word, persists day and night in meditation on the divine law, and is the eye of this great body. Another, as we said above, cares for the ministry of the brothers and the needy, and is the hand of this holy body. Another is a diligent hearer of the word of God, and is the body’s ear. Another is diligent in seeing those who are bedridden, visiting those in distress, and rescuing those placed in need; he is undoubtedly called the foot of the ecclesiastical body.

In this way you will find each person especially inclined toward one particular duty and devoting himself to it in a more particular way, while regarding the other duties as secondary. We do not mean that one duty alone ought to be sufficient. Rather, following the pattern of the proposed example: just as the eye has the special function of seeing, yet is one member among all the members and performs all things together with them, while each of the individual members performs all things together with the eye, so the person who has merited one particular gift through the grace of faith administers that gift principally, but in all his actions is regarded as a companion and participant with the others.

(Ambr.) By the example of the body he teaches that none of us can do everything, since we are members of one another and one cannot be without need of the other. Therefore we ought to care for one another, and one should not obstruct another, because we need one another’s services. This will be loving Christ: if the members exhort one another to fulfill the measure by which the body is made perfect in Christ.

(Orig.) How this body is in Christ—that is, in truth, wisdom, justice, and sanctification, all of which Christ is—we have often already said.

But having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us.

(Amb.) Now he enumerates the particular duties assigned to the members according to the merit of faith, so that when one member sees what duty has been assigned to it, it may not make an outcry against another to whom it sees that something else has been entrusted, but may contribute to the perfection of the body of the Church.

(Cass.) No member can claim the ministries of other members for itself. The eyes do not use the function of the hands, nor the nostrils that of the ears. Therefore not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all teachers; not all possess gifts of healing; not all speak in tongues; not all interpret.

Those who have not yet been firmly established in the profession they have undertaken often hear certain people praised for various pursuits and virtues. They are then so inflamed by that praise that they immediately desire to imitate their discipline; in this matter human frailty necessarily expends its efforts in vain.

For it is impossible for one and the same person to shine at once with all the virtues I have described above. If someone wishes to pursue them all simultaneously, he must fall into this situation: while following everything, he achieves nothing completely, and suffers greater loss than progress through this change and variety. There are many roads by which one approaches God, and each person should complete the path he once undertook with unwavering determination, so that he may be perfect in whatever form of perfection he has chosen.

Whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith.

(Amb.) He begins with prophecy, which is the first proof that our faith is rational; indeed, after receiving the Spirit, believers prophesied. This gift is therefore given according to the capacity of the recipient—that is, as much as the circumstance for which it is given requires.

(Orig.) Having said that each of the believers is a member of the one body of Christ, he now enumerates, as it were, the diversity of the work of the different members. For example, just as sight belongs to the eye, so he assigns prophecy as a function to the mind, which is the inner eye; to another he assigns ministry as to a hand; to another he grants teaching as to a tongue; and likewise with the remaining gifts.

He therefore declares that the differences of gifts are given “according to the measure of faith” of each person: for example, someone receives grace to become this or that member in the body of Christ.

Writing to the Corinthians he says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is beneficial” (I Cor. XII); and shortly afterward he adds: “But one and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid.).

Therefore it seems to me that, writing both to the Romans and to the Corinthians, he teaches three ways in which grace is to be understood, showing that something is effected in us by our own agency, though the greater part rests in God’s generosity. He sets forth the “measure of faith,” through which someone receives grace; he says that it is given “for what is beneficial”; and he says that the Spirit distributes “as he wills.”

Thus, that faith may be found in us in such measure as to be able to merit a higher grace appears to be a matter of our work and diligence. But that it be given for what is beneficial and useful to the recipient is a matter of God’s judgment; indeed, whether he wishes to give it at all rests with him. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere (I Cor. XII): “But now God has placed each member in the body as he willed.”

God willed this either “according to the proportion” or “measure of faith” that is in us, or he “willed it for what is beneficial.” Unless perhaps someone wishes to understand the statement “God has placed each member in the body as he willed” in such a way that “as he willed” refers more particularly to the member—that is, “as he willed,” “as he chose,” “as he applied himself”—so that the power of free choice may not appear to be taken away from human beings.

Nevertheless, from his statement that grace is given “for what is beneficial,” it can happen that, even if someone possesses such a measure of faith as to deserve a higher grace, the Holy Spirit, foreseeing the future, may judge that it would not be beneficial for the recipient. He therefore necessarily distributes to each person as he wills and as is beneficial.

Thus we see some people receive the grace of teaching or exhorting the people, and through this very gift become exalted and turn to pride, falling into the judgment of the devil. Others indeed receive grace but corrupt it through negligence of mind and slothfulness of life. Hence there was also the man who wrapped the denarius he had received in a handkerchief and refused to do anything with it (Luke XIX).

For this reason the Apostle writes to his beloved son: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you” (I Tim. IV), as though he knew that grace could be lost through negligence.

As for his saying “according to the proportion,” or measure, “of faith,” I think that what faith is required of us, and what faith is given by God through grace, has already been fully explained above, in accordance with the same Apostle’s statement: “to another faith in the same Spirit,” and also with the Apostles’ saying to the Lord: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII).

The faith that hopes, believes, and trusts without any doubt is in us. But the proportion of that faith, its knowledge, and the perfect understanding of what we believe are given by God.

Someone may perhaps say: if all these things are given through grace, then a person is not at fault if he does not prophesy, minister, teach, exhort, give, preside, show mercy, or love, because he has not received the grace of any of these things.

To this we shall reply: just as there is the faith that we have taught is in us, and again there is the faith that is given through grace, as we said above is written, “to another faith in the same Spirit,” so also, in each of the things we have enumerated as being given by God through grace, there is something in us according to whose measure or proportion each person merits grace.

The statement written about wisdom should not be understood as applying only to wisdom: “Even if someone is perfect among the children of men, if your wisdom is lacking in him, he will be counted as nothing” (Wis. IX). In the same way we can say: even if someone is perfect in faith among the children of men, if the faith that comes from your grace is lacking in him, he will be reckoned as nothing.

Likewise, even if someone is perfect in teaching, if the grace of teaching that comes from God is lacking in him, he will be reckoned as nothing. And so in all the things enumerated there is a certain perfection among the children of men, which they attain through their own labor and diligence, whether in wisdom, teaching, or other duties. Yet if they do not have grace given by God, these things will amount to nothing, because if they lack the grace of the Spirit, they cannot be members of the body of Christ.

But the question arises whether there can be in us, or from us, some form of prophecy that does not have everything from God, but receives something also from human study. This will seem wholly impossible to others, but it is clearly demonstrated by Paul when he says: “Earnestly desire the greater gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (I Cor. XIV). Just as someone pursues ministry, teaching, exhortation, and the other gifts by applying diligence and labor to them, so the Apostle shows that the same must be done with prophecy.

Accordingly, the prophecy Paul teaches must be understood as not being the prophecy through which it is said, “Thus says the Lord” (Luke XVI). That prophecy continued only until John, as it is written in the Gospel: “The law and the prophets were until John.” Rather, it is the prophecy of which the same Apostle says: “The one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation” (I Cor. XIV).

Thus, according to Paul, prophecy is spoken when someone addresses people for their edification, when he speaks for exhortation, and when he speaks for consolation. It is therefore possible for us to apply diligence to this kind of prophecy. And when we devote ourselves to these things, it lies within our power that, according to the proportion or measure of faith, the prophecy that comes from God may also be added to us.

Let this suffice concerning the grace of prophecy. After this comes: Whether ministry, in ministering.

(Amb.) In order to provide service to the brotherhood, the minister is strengthened in proportion to his faith—how much he believes he ought to serve—so that, by laboring beyond his faith in service, he is not wearied in vain. For each person receives in accordance with what he strives for from the heart.

Whether the one who teaches, in teaching.

He likewise says that the teacher is assisted in teaching: to the extent that his faith is directed toward teaching, to that extent he is inspired to transmit heavenly discipline.

Whether the one who exhorts, in exhortation.

(Orig.) We can bring all these matters back to the rule given above: not to think more highly than one ought to think. Thus, for example, the one who ministers ought not, in ministering, to think more highly than he ought; the one who teaches ought not, in teaching, to think more highly than he ought; and the one who exhorts ought not, in exhorting, to think more highly than he ought.

Many, after receiving ministry or teaching, thought more highly than they ought. Then, lifted up into arrogance or dissolved in self-indulgence, they fell headlong.

Exhortation is a form of teaching and speech by which afflicted souls are wisely relieved through words of the divine Scriptures, suitably adapted and gathered together. It often happens that the soul, because of the excess of its tribulations, falls into despair and cannot easily be restored or refreshed by just any words, however polished and pleasing they may be. But if a word possessing the power of God’s grace is applied, it then penetrates the heart, offers consolation, and restores hope once despair has been removed, in accordance with what the Lord said through the prophet: “Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem.”

The one who gives, in simplicity.

(Amb.) He says that assistance is always supplied to the one who gives with a good disposition, the Spirit providing that the one who gives simply may not lack.

Solomon says: “The one who gives to the poor will not lack.”

(Orig.) The one who gives and provides for the needy ought, he says, to do this in simplicity of heart—that is, lest, while appearing to benefit the needy, he seeks praise from human beings in his heart. It is not simplicity if one thing appears to be done by the hands while something else is sought in the heart.

The one who presides, with diligence.

(Amb.) He says that the person who undertakes the care of presiding over the brothers receives vigilance and authority according to his faith, so that he may prosper in the matter for which he is diligent, having his fruit in those over whom he presides.

(Orig.) The one who presides over the brothers, or who presides over the Church, ought to be diligent—not with the diligence of human affairs or worldly matters, for this kind of concern ought to be foreign to those who preside over the Church—but he should receive the kind of concern the Apostle describes: “The daily pressure upon me, my concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (II Cor. XI).

The one who presides over churches ought to have this kind of concern, and ought absolutely not to have that other, worldly kind.

The one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

(Amb.) He says that this person, according to his disposition, performs mercy with a joyful spirit, and that he who does so gladly rather than as though unwilling is established and strengthened by God, so that he suffers no weakness in this matter. He knows what Solomon said: “While you have opportunity, do good” (Prov. III).

But this must be understood in many ways, for mercy is manifold though expressed under one name. If above he said, “The one who gives, in simplicity,” why was it necessary to repeat himself, unless he signified many good works under the one name of mercy? To forgive those who sin is mercy; to bring help to someone placed in difficulty or oppressed is mercy.

Therefore, if someone performs these works eagerly and without weariness, he will receive the reward of this work both in the present and in the future. Every act of mercy ought therefore to be performed both simply and joyfully: simplicity excludes hypocrisy, while joy bears witness to confidence in the hope of future reward.

(Orig.) It is one thing to give to a needy person and another to share with the needy person out of an attitude of mercy. Therefore he does not want sadness to be present in such a work. If someone spends his money while being faithless and despairing of receiving it back, he is necessarily saddened as though he had lost it. But the person who does these things with faith and hope acts with cheerfulness and joy, certain that these small gifts, which he spends in obedience to God’s command, will procure for him great riches of heavenly treasures and, in addition, eternal life.

Love without pretense.

I think that every love that is not according to God is pretended and not genuine. For God, the creator of the soul, inserted into it, together with the other virtues, the affection of love so that it might love God and the things God wills. When he has given this work to the soul, then whenever someone loves anything other than God and the things pleasing to God, the love in him must be called fictitious and pretended.

Likewise, if someone loves his neighbor but, when he sees him going astray, does not admonish or correct him, this love must be called pretended. Love ought therefore to contain nothing flattering and nothing artificial, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere (I Tim. I): “Love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

(Ambr.) The Spirit comes to the mind that reflects on this: one should love a brother because one knows that this pleases God the author, and should not do so through flattery motivated by the present life. Since this is sought with a devoted mind, the Spirit assists the person so that he may fulfill it through service. For they hear the Lord say: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII).

Hating evil, clinging to the good.

He does not say that it is enough to avoid evil unless one also clings to the good. The former arises from fear; the latter from love.

(Orig.) It may perhaps seem strange that hatred is included among the other good virtues and is set forth by the Apostle as necessary. It is therefore certain that the soul contains an affection of hatred. It is praiseworthy to hate vices and to hate sins.

Unless someone hates vices, he cannot love or preserve virtues. For example, if someone decides to guard chastity, he cannot safely preserve it unless he takes up a certain hatred and [execration] against impurity. That continence is difficult—indeed, extremely difficult—in which the thing from which one abstains is still desired, and the soul’s desire is restrained only by fear of future judgment.

These things are dangerous—indeed, extremely dangerous—unless, in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel, we hate evil and wage against it, as it were, unappeased battles of hatred, while clinging to the good. This too should be observed: just as he says elsewhere, “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI), so here also he says, “Let us cling to the good,” undoubtedly so that we may become one with the good.

Loving one another with brotherly affection.

This commandment, that we should love one another as God also loved us, although it is the first after the first—for the first is to love God, and among human beings this is again the first, that we love one another—is somehow despised among people as though it were the last and least necessary. The hatred that we said was implanted in us for the purpose of hating evil, we exercise in the wrong order against the good: loving the vices of the flesh and sins, we hate our brothers.

We do not otherwise come to hate what we ought not to hate except because we love what we ought not to love. We are therefore commanded to love our brothers, not to judge them.

If you think that someone is ungodly and therefore do not judge him worthy of love, hear that “Christ died for the ungodly.” Or if, because your brother is a sinner, you do not think him worthy of love, hear that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners (I Tim. I). But if he is righteous, he is all the more worthy of love, for “the Lord loves the righteous” (Ps. CXLV).

Preferring one another in honor. This is what the Lord also taught when he reproved the scribes and Pharisees for claiming the first places at banquets, and taught that, when you are invited to dinner, you should recline in the lowest place (Luke 14).

Not sluggish in diligence. (Ambrose) This is what the prophet Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the one who performs the works of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 48); for the person who is sluggish in divine conduct is without hope. Therefore he added: “Fervent in spirit.” This means that, in the practice of divine work or of the law, one must not be lukewarm, as it says in the Apocalypse of John: “Because you are lukewarm,” he says, “I will vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3). Daily meditation removes dullness and drowsiness and makes one vigilant. The works of the Lord are those which he commands to be done for the benefit of the Church, that is, of the brethren.

(Origen) For he wants us, who live under the law of the Spirit, to have nothing slack, nothing lukewarm within us, but to accomplish everything with the fervor of the Spirit and the warmth of faith.

Serving the Lord. A person serves the Lord who can say, “For us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8), and who is no longer dominated either by lust, greed, or empty glory. It should be noted that another edition reads, “serving the time.” (Ambrose) What it means to serve the time he explains elsewhere when he says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Eph. 5). Since he had said, “fervent in spirit,” lest they understand this in such a way that they might indiscriminately and inopportunely thrust religious words upon an unfriendly age, thereby perhaps causing scandal, he immediately added, “serving the time,” so that they might speak of the faith of religion modestly and honorably, at suitable times, in suitable places, to suitable persons, and at the appropriate moment. For even in this time of peace there are some who so dread the words of God that, when they hear them, they blaspheme the way of Christ with great anger.

He himself also served the time when he did what he did not wish to do. Unwillingly, he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16), and, after having his head shaved, he went up to the Temple to be purified according to the law (Acts 21), in order to calm the madness of the Jews.

Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, persevering in prayer. After saying, “serving the time,” he added, “rejoicing in hope,” so that if, because of the wickedness of the age, one was not permitted to speak publicly about the faith but had to remain in fear, one might nevertheless rejoice in hope, because this sorrow produces joy.

(Origen) The person rejoices in hope who does not look at the things that are seen but awaits the things that are not seen, and who knows that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). That same person will also be patient in tribulation, because “tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Rom. 5), provided that we fulfill the sentence that follows, namely, “persevering in prayer.” For where human weakness is insufficient, God’s help must be sought in prayers.

Sharing in the needs of the saints. I remember that the Latin manuscripts more commonly read: “sharing in the memories of the saints.” Yet we are disturbed neither by custom nor do we prejudice the truth, especially since both readings are suitable for edification. For by “sharing in the needs of the saints” he properly means not merely providing alms to those in need, but, in a certain manner, holding our resources in common with them, and remembering the saints, whether in solemn collections or so that we may profit from their remembrance. This seems apt and appropriate.

(Ambrose) Whoever wishes his prayers to be heard ought to be an imitator of the lives of the saints. For when he imitates them, he shares in them. Thus to remember and to share means to imitate their deeds; and, if they are in need of material support, we ought to share with them, as he says elsewhere: “from the collections made for the saints” (1 Cor. 16), and in Galatians: “that we should remember the poor” (Gal. 2).

Pursuing hospitality. (Origen) By saying that hospitality should be pursued, he does not show merely that we should receive a guest who comes to us, but that we should seek out guests, be solicitous, pursue them, and search for them everywhere—lest perhaps they be sitting in the streets or lying outside without shelter. Remember Lot, and you will find that it was not the guests who sought him but he who sought out guests (Gen. 19); and this was to pursue hospitality.

Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. As the Apostle develops the moral teaching more fully, he orders the conduct, mind, intention, mouth itself, and tongue of the disciples. He does not want those who believe in Christ to utter a curse from their mouths, but to speak well, bless, and pray for blessings, so that by this they may be recognized both as servants of a good master and as disciples of a good teacher.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that this language of blessing is used in different ways in Scripture. God is found blessing human beings, or the other things he created; and human beings, or the other creatures, are commanded to bless God. Yet God’s blessing always bestows some gift upon those whom he blesses, whereas human beings are said to bless God in the sense that they praise him and give thanks. Here, however, the Apostle says, “Bless, and do not curse,” as though, when we are provoked by enemies or incited by injuries, he were warning us not to return curses for them, but to do what he writes concerning himself: “We are cursed, and we bless” (1 Cor. 4).

Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. (Ambrose) This is what he says elsewhere: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12). For when someone offers consolation to a brother in need, he lifts his spirit and establishes merit for himself before God, because he loves a member of Christ’s body. And if he grieves together with an unbeliever, he urges that person all the more toward progress in the discipline of the Lord.

(Gregory) I see nothing so burdensome to the clerical order as bending the mind’s severity through compassion, changing one’s disposition according to the persons who come before one, and yet this is extremely necessary. For when, through his preaching, a sinner is brought to the grace of good works, does the one who preaches appear ungrateful? Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel, in the final section: “When the priests minister within, they shall wear linen garments.” Concerning these it is added: “When they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall remove the garments in which they ministered and place them in the treasury of the sanctuary” (Ezek. 44).

Woolen garments are, of course, the coarser garments; but when a priest approaches the holy ministry, when he enters within through compunction, he must be clothed, as it were, in a linen garment of more refined understanding. But when he goes out to the people, he ought to put away the garments in which he had ministered within and appear before the people clothed in other garments. For if he remains fixed in the severity of his compunction, if he continues in the grief that he experienced at the time of prayer, he does not admit the words of external matters. And what is the flock to do concerning its necessities if the shepherd refuses to hear and consider what the present time requires?

Therefore, when he goes out before the people, the priest should put on coarser garments, so that by his clothing he may adapt his manner even to enduring earthly things for the benefit of his children. Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, how great a labor it is for the watchman both to strive toward lofty things and suddenly to summon himself down to lowly matters; to make his mind less refined in the height of inward knowledge; and, because of the external concerns of his neighbors, so to speak, suddenly to become coarse in his thinking.

(Origen) A suitable and proper distinction must also be maintained here. For the joys of Christians are not to be joined to every kind of joy, nor are our tears to be united with every kind of weeping. If I see someone rejoicing over the acquisition of money, the extent of his possessions, or the prominence of worldly honor, I ought not to congratulate such a person, since I know that joys of this kind are followed by mourning and tears. Indeed, one should so little rejoice in such things that the Lord did not even permit his disciples to rejoice because they saw the demons subject to them. Rather, he said: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you, but rejoice because your names are written in the book of life” (Luke 10).

Accordingly, if we see someone performing such a work as deserves to be written in heaven—whether a work of justice, charity, peace, or mercy—and performing it in such a way that it merits being recorded in the book of life, we ought to rejoice with such people. Likewise, if we see someone converted from error, leaving behind the darkness of ignorance and coming to the light of truth, obtaining the forgiveness of sins and the grace of the Holy Spirit, we ought to rejoice with such people.

Similarly, “weep with those who weep.” We are not commanded to weep with those who mourn their dead or with those who mourn worldly losses, knowing that “the sorrow of this world produces death.” Our tears, therefore, are not to be joined with such people; rather, we ought to weep with those of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). If someone weeps for his sins, if someone turns to repentance after his offenses and washes away his error with tears, if someone, while dwelling in this habitation, sighs and longs to return to Christ, and washes his holy desire with an outpouring of tears, let us join our tears to theirs and add our groans to theirs. For “godly sorrow produces enduring salvation through repentance” (2 Cor. 7).

Having the same mind toward one another. This statement has become obscure not by its own nature but through interpretation. For this is what he says: that we should think of a brother as we think of ourselves, and wish for our neighbor what we wish for ourselves, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matt. 7).

Not setting your minds on high things. (Ambrose) To set one’s mind on high things is pride; even the devil apostatized when he conceived lofty thoughts. Let there not be exaltation in the mind, so that someone, perhaps presuming upon the soundness of his own conduct, does not sympathize with his brother but reproaches him as a sinner. This is pride: when it puts itself first, it gives offense. The Lord also censures this when he says: “First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matt. 7). Exaltation itself is sin; and even if a person were not a sinner—which is impossible—he becomes a sinner by becoming proud. Finally, Scripture says: “God resists the proud” (1 Pet. 5).

(Origen) He teaches that pride must be avoided in every way; for this is what he means by “to think high things.” And rightly pride must be fled, since Scripture says that “pride is the beginning of departure from God” (Ecclus. 10).

But associating with the humble. (Ambrose) This means that, having laid aside pride, one should make another’s cause one’s own and one’s own cause as though it belonged to another, so that one may have grace before the Lord, because “whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”

(Origen) He has expressed the instruction in humility well in a single phrase. To associate with the humble, to love the humble, and to bend oneself toward them means becoming accustomed to imitating the one who, although he was in the form of God, “took the form of a servant and humbled himself unto death” (Phil. 2). Hypocrite, if you say that you possess humility while believing that you have no sin, outwardly you feign humility, but inwardly you embrace vanity. Thus neither in mouth nor in heart do you possess the truth. What does it profit you to appear humble to people, if God sees that what you think is lofty?

Do not be wise in your own estimation. (Ambrose) This is written in the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 5), and here he sets it down almost as his own, so that justice may be held in common, rather than for someone to be just toward himself but unjust toward everyone else.

(Origen) Whoever appears wise to himself is foolish with arrogance, and cannot know the true wisdom of God, because he cherishes his own folly as though it were wisdom. Finally, in the preceding passage Paul himself teaches that this was the cause of the Jews’ unbelief, saying concerning them: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10).

[Gregory] Thus whoever is wise in his own estimation cannot be wise before God. Accordingly, the obstinate must be admonished in one way and the unstable in another. The former must be told that they think more highly of themselves than they are, and therefore do not yield to the counsels of others. The latter must be shown that, despising themselves excessively, they neglect themselves, and therefore, through the fickleness of their thoughts, are turned from their own judgment from moment to moment.

The former must be told that, unless they considered themselves better than others, they would never put everyone else’s counsels below their own deliberation. The latter must be told that, if they paid some attention to what they are, the breeze of instability would never toss them about through so many variations. To the former Paul says: “Do not be wise in your own estimation”; but the latter hear: “Let us not be carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. 4).

Returning evil for evil to no one. (Ambrose) This is what the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. 5). For the commandment in the law was: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” This, as it appears, is justice; but, so that the righteousness of Christians may abound, they are taught not to return evil for evil, so that they may be perfect and so that a reward may be given them for this at God’s judgment.

(Origen) If inflicting evil is sin, and returning evil is not, as some think, justice but a similar sin—or, as I judge, even a more serious one—for the one who first inflicted evil did not perceive that what he was doing was evil; whereas the one who returns evil, by the very fact that he is moved to take revenge, confesses that he perceived the evil of what he returned. Therefore, we must always look to the one who said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord (Heb. 10).

Providing good things not only before God but also before all people. (Ambrose) To provide means to hold future good things before one’s eyes, so that one may do those things which, once they have been done, cannot be brought into reproach but rather may be a matter of praise, whether before God or before human beings. No one should think that, because things permitted by God are not displeasing to him, it therefore does not matter if they cause scandal to a brother. He gives this warning because one must do what is displeasing neither to God nor scandalous to a brother. If something is permitted but scandalizes a brother, it does not please God, because God commands that one strive for salvation. Thus good things are provided before God and human beings when permitted things are done in such a way that they do not cause scandal.

(Origen) Whoever keeps the balance of his life, conduct, and actions in such a way that he cannot be reproved by anyone provides good things before all people. He does not say that we should please all people, but that we should provide good things before all people. This means that we should do good before all people, whether the good things please them or do not please them.

If possible, so far as it depends on you, living at peace with all people. (Gregory) Having urged the disciples to have peace with everyone, he first qualified it by saying, “If possible,” and then added, “so far as it depends on you.” For it was difficult that, if they corrected evil deeds, they could have peace with everyone. But when temporal peace is disturbed in the hearts of the wicked because of our correction, it is necessary that peace remain inviolate in our own hearts. He therefore rightly says, “so far as it depends on you,” as though he were saying: Since peace rests upon the agreement of two parties, but is driven out by those who are corrected, it must nevertheless be preserved whole in the mind of those who correct them.

Hence, again, he admonishes the disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey your word, mark him by letter and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed”; and he immediately added: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3). It is as though he said: Break external peace with him, but guard inward peace toward him from the depths of your heart, so that discord may strike the sinner’s mind with salutary fear, while peace does not depart from your hearts, nor is it denied by them.

(Origen) Since the Apostle knew that peace between those who are at peace does not consist in one party alone but in both, and lest the disposition of the other—if it should come in a state of hostility—seem to hinder us from the good of peace, he gave a most moderate command: our mind should always be prepared for peace, and the fault of discord should rest not with us but with the other person.

But perhaps someone may say: How can it happen that we have peace with all people? And what shall we do with the Scripture that says: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49)? For this reason the Apostle rightly added, “so far as it depends on you,” that is, insofar as this accords with your intention and your faith. To have peace and fellowship with the wicked does not accord with the intention of our faith. Yet another distinction may also be made here. It is one thing to love people and another to love crimes. Whoever loves people loves God’s creature; whoever loves crimes follows the devil’s inventions. Therefore those who are perfect, precisely by hating crimes, love people; and while hating in them what they do sinfully, they do not cease to love what God created.

(Ambrose) It can happen that, out of fear [Note: [Col. 1557D] In the printed edition, “of God” is added.], someone presents himself as peaceful toward one who hates peace. For when he does not wish to return evil for evil, he is peaceful; that is, he conquers evil by goodness, so that the one whom the commands of the law do not conquer may at least be conquered by acts of service.

Therefore, he says, “if possible, so far as it depends on you,” so that by acting well we may be seen to have peace. If the other person is not a lover of peace, you nevertheless should wish to be peaceful, so far as it concerns you. But if someone is irreverent and blasphemous, and you cannot have peace with him, this certainly cannot be charged against you, since the apostle John did not even permit those who deny that Christ came in the flesh to be greeted.

Let us therefore be prepared, if it can happen, to have peace with everyone. When others resist, it will become impossible—not because of us—provided that no complaint can be lodged against us. For whoever harms no one plainly appears to be peaceful.

Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. He warns that, if the bonds of peace are to be preserved, anger must be set aside, especially since sin is usually committed through anger: when someone is moved by rage, he demands more than the matter of the offense requires, or brings harm upon himself if he wishes to exact punishment for graver sins by a fitting [unfitting] vengeance. For he weakens the person whom he could have had corrected and sound.

Hence Solomon also says: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. 7); for, he says, there is one who perishes through his own righteousness. Wishing to respond to each individual sin, a person may find death in vengeance, both for himself and for the one whom he afflicts with blows; for people often sin in punishment.

He prohibits not only appropriate vengeance against those subject to us, but also vengeance against equals and superiors. That is, if perhaps a brother sins against us, we should not seek revenge, but should forgive, reserving the matter for God’s judgment, lest, while we are held by anger, the enemy find a place in which to suggest and persuade us to do what is against us.

For it is written—and, to make the point more forcefully, he confirms it by the example of the law: “It is written, I say: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Deut. 32; Heb. 10)—so that, if we fail to do what he teaches, he may show that God has been despised by us.

(Origen) There is also this way of giving place to wrath: when sinners, for the injuries they inflict, according to Paul’s own statement, “store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath,” when God will repay each person according to his works. If, therefore, we avenge ourselves, it is not a great thing that we return what we have received as an injury—for example, a slap for a slap, a stone for a stone, or an insult for an insult. But if we reserve these things for God’s vengeance, then in the one who injured us we give place to the wrath which he himself stores up for himself by his evil deeds, so that at God’s judgment it may exact penalties from him far more severe than those we could inflict.

(Cassiodorus) This sentence may also be understood in another way: “Not avenging yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath.” That is, do not proceed toward vengeance when anger compels you, but give place to wrath—do not let your hearts be so confined by the straits of impatience and faintheartedness that, when the violent storm of agitation bursts upon them, they cannot endure it. Rather, enlarge your hearts, receiving the hostile waves of anger within them, stretched out within the boundaries of charity, which “bears all things and endures all things” (1 Cor. 13). Thus, enlarged by the breadth of long-suffering and patience, the mind should contain within itself salutary retreats of counsel, in which the most foul smoke of anger, once received and dispersed, quickly vanishes.

Or certainly it should be understood in this way: We give place to wrath whenever we submit to another’s admonition with a humble and tranquil mind, so that, in a certain sense, confessing ourselves worthy of any injury, we comply as slaves to impatience. But those who so distort the meaning of apostolic perfection as to think that those give place to wrath who withdraw from the angry person seem to me not to cut off the fuel of dissension but to nourish it. For unless the anger of one’s neighbor is overcome immediately by humble satisfaction, the person who flees from it provokes it rather than averting it.

If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. (Augustine) What he says—“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head”—may seem to many to conflict with the statement in which the Lord commands us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. It may also seem to conflict with what the same Apostle said above: “Bless, and do not curse,” and again: “Returning evil for evil to no one.”

For how can someone love the person to whom he gives food and drink for the purpose of heaping burning coals upon his head, if the burning coals here signify some severe punishment? Therefore, it must be understood that this was said so that we might provoke the person who injured us to repentance for his deed by doing good to him. These burning coals are effective for burning—that is, for the anguish of the spirit, which is, as it were, the head of the soul; in it all wickedness is burned away when a person is changed for the better after repentance. They are the coals of which it is said in the Psalms: “What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, for your deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation” (Ps. 119).

(Ambrose) He shows that vengeance should not merely be left to God, but that benefits should also be bestowed upon enemies, so that we may truly show that we do not have enemies because of our own merits, since we strive to conquer them by acts of service so that they may cease from their hostility. If they persist in hostility because of the impiety of their mind, our acts of service will contribute to their punishment; or, pierced by the constancy of our service, they may revive like dead coals.

Therefore, in order to make us so perfect that we may acquire not only ourselves but also others for life, the Lord, through Solomon, not only forbids us to return evil to enemies but also urges us, by human kindness, to summon them to friendship.

Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good. This is the Apostle’s interpretation as he exhorts us not to return evil to our enemies, as was said. It will greatly benefit us if we yield to evil; for the person who seems for a time to be conquered by evil conquers it. The Savior also conquered evil in this way, by not resisting. Evil acts against itself, and, while it is being conquered, thinks that it is conquering. For the enemy’s purpose is to draw us away from our resolve, seeking an opportunity by which we may sin. Therefore, if, when provoked by him, we do not return evil to him, we conquer him with good.

For this reason we do not resist, so that we may preserve goodness while neglecting strict justice, since justice compels one to return what has been received.

(Origen) The person is conquered by evil who, provoked by evil, returns evil; but the person conquers evil with good who, having received evil, returns good. For it is certain that the nature of evil is to be increased and grow through what resembles it, just as fire grows if fire is added to it, and as the darkness of night is joined by the cloudiness of the air. But if good is applied, evil is driven out. For opposites are destroyed by opposites: fire is extinguished by water, and darkness is dispelled by light.

But perhaps someone may say that Paul, through inexperience in expression, has departed from his subject. For he proposed to speak about the gifts of grace that are given through the Holy Spirit, and indeed what he says—whether prophecy, ministry, teaching, or exhortation—can pertain to spiritual gifts. Perhaps what follows can also be joined to these: “the one who gives, in simplicity; the one who presides, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” But the things he enumerates after these—“let love be without dissimulation, hating evil, clinging to good, loving one another with brotherly love, preferring one another in honor,” and other things of this kind—he may seem to call commands rather than gifts.

Let us consider more carefully, lest perhaps, since he has begun to treat the moral subject throughout all these matters and to make the Christian not only stable and immovable in the faith of truth but also adorned in conduct, he therefore joins moral commands to the gifts of grace, in order to show that these too are given to Christians through God’s grace. For there are some gentiles who are well ordered in conduct and honorably disciplined, yet do not refer the very qualities they possess to God, nor confess that grace was given them by him, but attribute them either to their own diligence or boast about their teachers and instructors.

The Apostle shows us, however, that everything good is from God and is given through the Holy Spirit, just as the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1), so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1). Let us now see what else the Apostle adds in what follows.

## CHAPTER XIII

The Apostle teaches those of lower rank to obey those above them through assistance and love.

Be subject to all higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God. (Augustine) When he says, “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God,” he very properly warns that no one, because he has been called by his Lord into freedom and has become a Christian, should be lifted up into pride and fail to consider that, on the journey of this present life, his proper order must be maintained. Nor should he think that he need not be subject to the higher authorities to whom, for a time, the administration of temporal affairs has been entrusted.

Since we consist of soul and body, and so long as we are in this temporal life make use even of temporal things to support the conduct of this life, we ought, in that part of us which pertains to this life, to be subject to the authorities—that is, to human beings who administer human affairs with some degree of honor. But in that part by which we believe in God and are called into his kingdom, we ought not to be subject to any human being who wishes to overthrow in us the very thing that God has graciously granted for eternal life.

Therefore, if anyone thinks that, because he is a Christian, he need not pay a tax or tribute, or need not show the honor due to those authorities who administer such matters, he is in great error. Likewise, if anyone thinks that he must be subject in such a way that he believes the person who excels in some authority over temporal administration has power even over his faith, he falls into still greater error.

The measure prescribed by the Lord himself must be observed: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22; Luke 20). For although we are called to that kingdom where no such authority will exist, nevertheless, while we are traveling through this life, until we reach that age in which all principality and authority will be abolished, we must endure our condition according to the order of human affairs, doing nothing hypocritically and obeying in this very matter not so much human beings as God, who commands these things.

(Ambrose) Just as he commanded that the law of heavenly justice be followed, lest he seem to disregard the present life, so he commends this law as well, since, unless it is observed, the other cannot be kept. For this law is, as it were, a tutor who instructs children so that they may be able to follow the path of the higher justice. Mercy cannot be imputed to anyone unless he possesses justice. Therefore, in order to confirm the right and fear of the natural law, he testifies that God is its author and that those who administer it possess God’s ordinance. For this reason he added:

But those things that are are ordained by God. So that no one may think that human institutions are to be despised—for they see that divine law has been assigned to human authorities. Therefore, the person who abstains from what that authority forbids out of fear of God is subject to the power. (Orig.) If it is read as it appears in certain copies, “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,” it seems to me that he very commendably named the soul which he commands to be subject to the powers. For he would never have said, “Let every spirit be subject to the power,” but “every soul.” We have often already spoken of this distinction: sometimes a human being is named from the soul, sometimes from the flesh, sometimes from the spirit. When he is to be named from the better part, as one who ought to be understood as spiritual, he is called “spirit”; when from the lower part, “soul”; but when he is named from the worse part, he is called “flesh.” We have often brought forward testimonies to this effect from Scripture.

Now, since the Apostle is laying down precepts for believers, he wishes us, insofar as it lies within us, to preserve the quiet and peace of the present life. If, indeed, we are such as are joined to the Lord and are one spirit with him, we are said to be subject to the Lord. But if we are not yet such, and there is still in us the common soul that has something of this world and is in some way bound to worldly business, the Apostle gives this soul his commands and says that it must be subject to the powers of the world. For the Lord also said that those who have the emperor’s inscription upon them should render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Peter and John had nothing that they could render to Caesar, for Peter says: “Silver and gold I have none” (Acts III). Whoever has none of this has nothing to render to Caesar, nor anything by which he may be subject to the higher powers. But whoever has money, possessions, or any business in the world [Col. 1561D], let him hear: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.”

“For there is no power,” he says, “except from God.” Someone may perhaps say, “What, then? Is that power also from God which persecutes God’s servants, attacks the faith, and overturns religion?” We shall answer briefly: No one is unaware that sight, hearing, and sensation have also been given to us by God. Since these things are from God, however, it lies within our power to use sight for good or for evil, and likewise hearing, the movement of our hands, and the faculty of thought. In this consists God’s just judgment: we misuse for impious and wicked purposes those things that he gave for good uses. So too every power has been given by God “for the punishment of evildoers but for the praise of those who do good,” as the same Apostle says below. God’s judgment against those who have received power and govern it according to their own impieties rather than according to the divine laws will therefore be just. Hence he says: “Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God.”

(Orig.) Here he is not speaking of those powers that inflict persecutions upon the faith. In that case it must be said, “We must obey God rather than human beings.” Rather, he is speaking of the ordinary authorities, who “are not a terror to good conduct but to evil.” Whoever resists these authorities acquires condemnation for himself according to the character of his deeds.

(Amb.) This also applies against those who are powerful and therefore strong, or who do not believe that anything they do can be discovered by anyone, and who on that account think they can mock the law. He shows them that the law belongs to God [Col. 1562B], and that those who temporarily escape by some means will not escape God’s judgment. Those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves. It is clear that each person will either be justified or condemned by his deeds; for those who sin while hearing the law are without excuse.

“For rulers are not a terror to good works but to evil.” By “rulers” he means kings, who are established to correct conduct and prevent wrongdoing, bearing the image of God so that others may be subject to one. “Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” Praise arises from authority when someone is found innocent.

(Greg.) Good deeds are not to be done merely so that no power of this world may be feared, nor so that the glory of passing praise may be obtained through them. But when the preacher of outstanding merit considered that the weak mind could not rise to such strength as simultaneously to avoid wickedness and praise, he offered it something by his exhortation and removed something from it. By granting milder things, he took away harsher ones, so that a mind which could not rise at once to abandon everything might, while it familiarly retained one of its vices, be led without difficulty away from another vice.

“For he is God’s minister to you for good.” (Aug.) What he says—“Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it”—may trouble some people when they consider that Christians often suffered persecution from these very authorities. Did they not, then, do what was good, since they were not only not praised by those authorities but were afflicted with punishments and put to death? We must consider the Apostle’s words. He does not say, “Do what is good, and the power will praise you,” but, “Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” Whether it approves your good deed or persecutes you, you will have praise from it: either when you have won it over to the service of God, or when through its persecution you have earned a crown. This is also understood in what follows, when he says: “For he is God’s minister to you for good,” even if he is for himself a minister of evil.

(Ambr.) It is clear that rulers were appointed so that evil might not be done. But if you do evil, be afraid, for he does not carry the sword without reason. That is, he threatens so that, if he is despised, he may avenge. For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Since God has established a future judgment and wishes no one to perish, he appointed rulers in this world so that, by introducing fear, they might be like tutors to human beings, teaching them what they should observe lest they fall under the punishment of the future judgment.

(Orig.) Nevertheless, Paul’s words here raise a question: he calls the power of the world and the judgment of the world God’s minister—not once, but repeats it a second and a third time. I would therefore like to ask how the judge of the world can be God’s minister. We find it written in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles, meeting together, established decrees which we who have believed in Christ from the Gentiles ought to observe. They include the following:

“The apostles and presbyters to the brothers throughout Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia who have believed from among the Gentiles, greetings. Since we have heard that some have gone out from us and troubled you, to whom we gave no command” (Acts XV).

A little later it adds:

“It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you beyond these necessary things: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell” (ibid.).

In these precepts, then, where it says that no further burden should be imposed upon those from the Gentiles who believe except that they abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication, neither murder nor adultery nor theft nor intercourse between males nor the other crimes punished by divine and human laws is prohibited. If it says that Christians are to observe only those things mentioned above, it will seem to grant them permission concerning the rest.

But observe the ordinance of the Holy Spirit. Since the other crimes of the world are punished by the laws of the world, it seemed superfluous that those things which are sufficiently punished by human law should now be prohibited by divine law. The decree therefore concerns only those matters about which human law had said nothing and which seemed to belong particularly to religion. From this it is evident that the judge of the world fulfills a very large part of God’s law. For all the crimes that God wishes to be punished, he has willed to be punished not through the bishops and rulers of the churches but through the judge of the world. Knowing this, Paul rightly calls him God’s minister and an avenger against the one who does what is evil.

What he says concerning the power—“Do what is good, and you will have praise from it”—seems to me to require a deeper inquiry. It is not customary for the powers of the world to praise those who have not been criminals. They punish sinners; it is not their practice to praise those who do not sin.

But let us see whether perhaps Paul, even when he appears to teach moral matters, always inserts something concerning the mysteries. For he knows that “all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law”; and that the law will undoubtedly accuse each person in the judgment according to how he has lived. We have shown that the Holy Spirit has in many respects assigned a place to human law. It is therefore certain that on the day of judgment the person who has committed nothing against the established laws will also have praise before God from these laws, when the Lord says to him: “Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matt. XXV).

It must nevertheless be understood that “the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, for the impious, murderers, the defiled, perjurers, and others of this kind.” These are the ones who fear the law. But whoever does what is good—that is, whoever does what is good not from fear of the law but from love of goodness—no longer lives under the law of the letter but under the law of the Spirit.

Therefore you must be subject, because of necessity, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes: they are God’s ministers, serving for this very purpose.

(Aug.) What he says, “Therefore you must be subject, because of necessity,” serves to make us understand that, for the sake of this life, we must necessarily be subject and not resist if they wish to take something from us over which they have been given power—that is, temporal possessions. Since these things pass away, this subjection must also be established not in relation to goods that endure, as though they were permanent, but in relation to what is necessary for this present time.

Yet because he said, “You must be subject because of necessity,” lest anyone become subject to such powers without a wholehearted spirit and pure love, he added: “not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.” That is, not merely to escape wrath—which can also be done hypocritically—but so that in your conscience you may be certain that you act out of love for the one to whom you are subject, at the command of your Lord, “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II). When the Apostle said this, he was also speaking of these powers. This is what he elsewhere urges upon slaves: not to serve merely by outward appearance, as those who please human beings (Eph. VI), so that in being subject to their masters they may neither hate them nor seek to win their favor through deceit.

(Orig.) Through these words Paul orders the Church of God to conduct itself so that, doing nothing hostile toward the rulers and powers of the world, it may exercise the work of justice and piety through a quiet and tranquil life. For suppose, for example, that those who believe in Christ were not subject to the powers of the world, paid no taxes or tribute, showed fear to no one and honor to no one. Would they not thereby rightly cause the rulers and princes to turn their weapons against them, making their persecutors excusable but themselves blameworthy? It would then appear that they were being attacked not for the sake of the faith but because of insolence; and their cause of death would indeed be worthy, but the merit of their death unworthy.

(Ambr.) Therefore he rightly says that they ought to be subject, not only because of wrath—that is, present vengeance, for wrath produces retribution—but also because of future judgment.
