For if they escape here, punishment awaits them there, where they will be punished with their own conscience accusing them. “For this reason you pay taxes: they are God’s ministers, serving for this very purpose.” He says that taxes, including what are called fiscal payments, are to be paid so that they may demonstrate subjection, by which people know that they are not free but act under a power that is from God. For they are subject to their prince, who acts in God’s place, just as they are subject to God, as the prophet Daniel says: “The kingdom is God’s, and he gives it to whomever he wishes” (Dan. IV). Hence the Lord also says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Luke XX). They must therefore be subject to him as to God, and the proof of this subjection is that they pay him taxes.

[Col. 1565A] Therefore render to all what is owed. He wishes all people to render what is owed, because the powerful also owe something to their inferiors: they must respond to their merits. To whom tax is due, tax; to whom tribute is due, tribute. First he commands payment of what is owed to royal authority, because in these matters the cause or necessity is greater.

To whom fear is due, fear. Fear must be shown to the authority, because fear restrains sin; then it must be shown either to a parent or to an earthly master, so that he may give thanks in his son or in a Christian servant.

To whom honor is due, honor. This honor may also be shown toward those who appear exalted in the world, so that when they see the humility of Christ’s servants they may praise rather than blame the discipline of the gospel.

“Owe no one anything except to love one another.” He wishes us, if possible, to have peace with everyone, but love with the brothers—and even this with honor preserved. He calls them debtors because it is fitting and proper to bow before a person worthy of honor, whether present or future. One bows before the person from whom one has received honor; therefore he is called a debtor. If you do not do this toward your prince, you are proud. For a person is to be honored either because of merit or because of age.

(Orig.) Yet this very statement—“Render what is owed to everyone: to whom tax is due, tax; to whom tribute is due, tribute”—seems to me to be divided by what is added below, “to whom fear is due, fear; to whom honor is due, honor.” Taxes and tribute belong to those ministers whom we mentioned above, for they exact from us taxes on our land and tribute on our commerce.

And why should I speak of us? Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, while dwelling in the flesh, was charged a tax. He says that he paid it not because he was a debtor but so as not to cause scandal (Matt. XVII). If he who had nothing of Caesar in himself—he in whom, when the ruler of this world came, he found nothing of his own (John XIV)—paid the tax, though he was free (for he also came into death, so that he might be “free among the dead”), how much more must we pay these taxes of the flesh and of our commerce, if indeed we are trading in the pearls of the kingdom of heaven and, through various temptations, paying tribute to the spirits that exact it from us!

But fear and honor ought rather to be referred to the one who says through the prophet: “Do you not call me Lord and Father? And if I am Lord, where is my fear? And if I am Father, where is my honor?” (Mal. I).

The latter things he adds—“so that we owe no one anything”—clearly refer to the ministers, to whom a person becomes indebted when he has sinned. We have often and extensively shown that sin is a debt. Paul therefore wishes every debt of sin to be paid and no debt of sin to remain with us at all; yet he wishes the debt of love to remain and never cease from us. It is advantageous for us both to pay this daily and always to owe it. Finally, he sets out in what follows how great a virtue love is.

“For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” (Aug.) When he says, “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law,” he shows that the completion of the law consists in love, that is, in charity. Hence the Lord says that the whole law and all the prophets depend upon those two commandments, namely, love of God and love of neighbor (Matt. XXII). The one who came to fulfill the law therefore gave love through the Holy Spirit, so that what fear had previously been unable to fulfill, charity might afterward fulfill. Hence also the same Apostle says: “The fullness of the law is charity,” and: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I).

(Amb.) Whoever loves his neighbor fulfills the law given through Moses; for the commandment of the new law is also to love one’s enemies.

“For, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not kill,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not bear false witness,’ ‘You shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” [Col. 1566B]

(Orig.) Finally, briefly gathering the reason for so great a good, he says: “Love of neighbor does no evil; therefore love is the fullness of the law.” Above he had said that whoever loves his neighbor fulfills the law. Since it seemed difficult to understand how someone could fulfill the entire law in a single statement, he gives the fullest explanation by saying that love of neighbor does no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the law.

Apply love to each of the law’s commandments and you will see that all of them are easily fulfilled. Can one who loves his neighbor kill him? Certainly no one kills the person whom he loves. Love is therefore that by which the commandment “You shall not kill” is fulfilled. Again, can one who loves his neighbor commit adultery with his wife? Certainly not. If, then, you love your neighbor, you will not commit adultery. Likewise, one who loves his neighbor does not steal what belongs to him, and one who loves his neighbor does not bear false witness against him. The same is true of the other commandments: if love toward one’s neighbor exists, they are kept without any further labor.

(Amb.) He mentions what is supreme in the law in order to join the gospel to it, showing that the author’s meaning is one and the same. But because something had to be added in the time of Christ, he commanded that we love not only our neighbors but also our enemies. Hence it follows: “The fullness of the law is love.”

For justice consists in loving one’s neighbor, but abundant and perfect justice consists also in loving one’s enemies. What else is it to love an enemy than to wish that he cease from hatred and to ask nothing harsh against him? It is to love him by wishing for him those things through which he may have God’s favor. This is heavenly justice; it makes us like God the Father, because he gives annual gifts even to those who do not worship him. The Lord too, while hanging upon the cross, prayed for his enemies, so that he might demonstrate the fullness of the justice he had taught.

(Orig.) Nevertheless, I think that in this passage also the Apostle wished us to learn something more briefly. For if you inquire carefully who our neighbor is, you will learn from the Gospel (Luke X) that our neighbor is the one who came, placed us—wounded, lying there, and stripped by demons—upon the beast of his body, carried us to the inn of the Church, and entrusted two denarii of the New and Old Testament to the innkeeper for the expenses of our care—whether the innkeeper is Paul himself or anyone who presides over the Church. If, then, we love this neighbor, we fulfill the whole law and all its commandments in love for him.

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X). It is utterly impossible that one who loves Christ with all his heart and all his inward being should do anything that does not please Christ. Whoever loves him not only does not kill—the thing forbidden by the law—but does not even become angry with his brother. Delighted by the one whom he loves, he not only does not commit adultery but does not look upon a woman in order to desire her; rather he says: “My soul longs and languishes for the living God” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Whoever loves Christ—how could he think about the future, when he leaves behind everything he has in order to follow Christ? Whoever loves Christ—how could he bear false witness, when he knows that the one whom he loves was betrayed by false testimony? Necessarily, whoever loves Christ also loves his neighbor. For this is the sole sign by which someone is shown to be Christ’s disciple: that he has charity toward his neighbors. It is certain that whoever does not love his neighbor does not know Christ.

(Greg.) Hence Paul says: “The fullness of the law is love.” Again he says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). For what can the law of Christ more appropriately be understood to be than charity? We truly perfect it when out of love we bear our brothers’ burdens.

This same law is called manifold, because charity, with diligent care, expands into every work of virtue. It begins from two commandments but extends to innumerable things. The beginning of this law is love of God and love of neighbor. Love of God is distinguished in three ways, because the Creator is commanded to be loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all one’s strength.

Here we must note that when the divine word commands that God be loved, it not only tells us from what part of ourselves he is to be loved but also indicates the extent of that love, when it adds “with all.” Thus whoever desires to please God perfectly must reserve nothing of himself for himself.

Love of neighbor is derived into two commandments. Through a certain righteous man it is said: “What you hate being done to you by another, see that you do not do to another.” And Truth himself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. VII). Through these two commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained by one and kindness is conferred by the other: whoever does not do the evil he does not wish to suffer ceases from the work of harming, while by providing the good he wishes done to himself, he exercises himself in kindness for the benefit of his neighbor.

When these two things are considered with attentive intention, the heart is directed toward innumerable ministries of virtue: the restless mind must not burn with desire to inflict what it ought not, nor grow sluggish through idleness in offering what it ought. When it is careful not to do to another what it certainly does not wish to endure from another, it examines itself attentively, lest pride elevate it and, casting down the mind to contempt of its neighbor, exalt it; lest ambition tear apart its thoughts; and when it expands those thoughts toward desiring what belongs to another, lest lust narrow the heart, polluting it and corrupting it through unlawful desires; lest anger irritate it and inflame it to the point of uttering insults; lest envy bite it and, jealous of another’s prosperity, consume it with its own fire; lest excessive talkativeness drag the tongue along and extend it to the wantonness of detraction; lest hatred stir up malice and provoke it to the arrow of cursing.

Again, when it considers doing to another what it expects another to do to itself, it carefully weighs how to respond to evil with good and to good with better; how to show the gentleness of patience toward the insolent; how to offer the grace of kindness to those weakened by the disease of malice; how to reconcile the discordant in peace and lead those who are at peace toward desire for true peace; how to give what is necessary to those in need; how to show the way of uprightness to those who are wandering; how to soothe the afflicted by word and compassion; how to restrain by rebuke those inflamed by the desires of this world; how to mitigate the threats of the powerful by reasoned argument; how, insofar as it can, to relieve the distress of the oppressed by practical help; how to oppose those resisting outside with patience; how to offer, with patience, discipline to those who are proud within; how, toward the faults of subjects, gentleness may temper zeal so that it does not weaken the pursuit of justice; how zeal may burn for punishment without, in burning, crossing the limit of compassion; how to summon the ungrateful to love by benefits; how to preserve the grateful in love through acts of service; how to remain silent about the evils of one’s neighbors when one cannot correct them; and how, when they can be corrected by speaking, to fear that silence may be taken for consent.

Thus it tolerates what it keeps silent about, yet does not conceal within the soul the poison of grief. It offers the gift of kindness to the ill-disposed, yet does not, through favor, depart from the right of uprightness. It gives to its neighbors everything it can, yet does not grow swollen with pride in giving. In the good things it offers, it fears the precipice of self-exaltation, yet does not become sluggish in practicing goodness. It gives away what it possesses while considering how great is the generosity of the one who rewards; and when it distributes earthly goods, it does not consider its own poverty more than is necessary, nor allow sadness to obscure the light of joy in the offering of its gift.

The law of God is therefore rightly called manifold. Although charity is one and the same, when it fully takes possession of the mind it kindles it in many different ways toward innumerable works. We briefly express its diversity if, by touching upon them, we enumerate its good works in individual elect persons.

Through Abel it both offered chosen gifts to God and endured the sword of his brother without resistance (Gen. IV). It taught Enoch to live spiritually among human beings and also withdrew him bodily from human beings into the higher life. It showed Noah, despising everything else, to be pleasing to God alone; it exercised him in the construction of the ark through the diligence of long labor and preserved him alive for the world through his pious work (Gen. VII, VIII).

Through Shem and Japheth it humbly blushed with shame for their father and, throwing a cloak over their backs, concealed what they had not seen (Gen. IX). It made Abraham, who obediently raised his right hand for the death of his son, the father of innumerable nations (Gen. XXII). Because it always kept Isaac’s mind pure, it enlarged him, though his eyes were dim with age, to see things far in the future (Gen. XXVII).

It compelled Jacob both to mourn from the depths of his being for the loss of his good son and to endure with equanimity the presence of his wicked sons (Gen. XXXVII, XXXVIII). It taught Joseph, sold by his brothers, to endure servitude without a broken spirit and afterward to rule over those same brothers without an exalted mind (Gen. XXXVIII, XXXIX).

It brought Moses, when the people sinned, low in prayer even to the point of asking for his own death (Exod. XXXII); it raised him up, through zeal, even to the destruction of the people; and it moved him to expose himself to death for the people who were perishing and to rage immediately against the sinner in the place of the Lord who was angry (Lev. X).

It raised Phinehas’s arm in vengeance against sinners, so that he seized a sword and pierced the couple who were joined together, and, being angry, appeased the Lord’s anger (Num. XXV). It taught Jesus [Joshua] the explorer (Josh. IX) first to defend the truth in words against lying fellow citizens and afterward to bring it forward by the sword against enemies.

It made Samuel humble in authority and preserved him blameless in his deposition. Although he loved the people who persecuted him, he himself bore witness that he had not loved the height from which he had been cast down (I Sam. VII, XII). It moved David, before an unjust king, both through humility to flee and through piety to grant pardon. He fled from his persecutor in fear as from the Lord, yet when he found the power to strike him, he did not regard him as an enemy (I Sam. XIX, XXIII, XXVI).

It raised Nathan up against a sinful king in the authority of free rebuke, yet when the king’s fault was absent, it cast him humbly into petition (II Sam. XII). Through Isaiah it did not blush to display the nakedness of the flesh in preaching, and, withdrawing the carnal veil, it penetrated the heavenly mysteries.

It taught Elijah, who lived spiritually through the zeal of his fervor, to be taken bodily also into life (II Kings II). Because it taught Elisha to love his master with simplicity, it filled him twice over with the spirit of his master (ibid.). Through Jeremiah it resisted the people so that they would not go down to Egypt; yet, loving those who disobeyed the prohibition against going down, he himself went down with them (Jer. XLII, XLIV).

It first lifted Ezekiel away from earthly desires and afterward balanced him in the air by a lock of his head (Ezek. VIII). In Daniel, because it restrained his appetite from the royal foods, it also closed the mouths of hungry lions for him (Dan. XIV). In the three boys, because it subdued the fires of vice while they were at peace, it also tempered the flames in the furnace during the time of tribulation (Dan. III).

In Peter it bravely resisted the threats of rulers who sought to frighten him, yet in the matter of abolishing circumcision it humbly listened to the words of his inferiors. In Paul it humbly endured the hands of persecutors, yet in the matter of circumcision it boldly rebuked the opinion of one who was far superior to him (Acts IV and following).

This law of God is therefore manifold. It suits each individual circumstance without changing, and it joins itself to changing situations without itself being changed.

And this, knowing the time: that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. (Aug.) This refers to what has been said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” The time of the gospel is signified, as well as that favorable opportunity for saving those who believe in God.

(Orig.) There is also a kind of sleep belonging to the soul. For if, as we have often said, it has its own eyes, its own ears, its hands and feet—each of these being understood not so much as bodily members present in it but as virtues by which it is moved and impelled toward particular actions—then it certainly experiences sleep in relation to its eyes. If it does not do what belongs to God at the appropriate time but grows sluggish through laziness, it will rightly be called asleep.

(Ambr.) He therefore says that the time has come in which we ought to advance toward merit—that is, to rise from sleep and do what is good as in the day, openly. For unlawful things are done at night, that is, in secret. Now that we have been placed in manifestation, which means in the knowledge of God, and recognize what we ought to follow, we must take care to live purely and come to the promised reward, having shaken off sleep—that is, ignorance or negligence.

“For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed.” It is clear that after the washing, those who live well and devote themselves to love are not far from the merit of the promised resurrection. For the Christian’s good life is a sign of future salvation.

The night has passed; the day has drawn near. (Orig.) Paul, the herald of Christ, therefore goes throughout the world, which lies in the sleep of indolence, announcing that the light is already present and that it is time to rise from sleep. He declares that the night—that is, the time when ignorance held mastery over human beings—has passed, and that, as the Sun of righteousness approaches, the darkness is receding, the day of knowledge is already at hand. Therefore he cries out that we must awaken, lest anyone through sluggishness endure the night.

(Amb.) He signified the old human being by the night, the one who has been renewed through baptism. He says that this night has passed, while the day has drawn near, whose light has made the truth appear to us, so that we might know what we ought to do. Previously, in ignorance of Christ, we were in darkness; but when we learned, light arose within us, for we passed from falsehood to truth.

(Greg.) “The night has passed; the day has drawn near.” Here we must observe that when Paul said “the night has passed,” he did not add “the day has come,” but “the day has drawn near.” For when, after the departure of night, he indicates not that the day has already come but that it has drawn near, he clearly shows that after the darkness he is still before the sun, in the dawn. The holy Church of the elect will then fully be day, when no shadow of sin is mingled with it. It will fully be day when it shines with the perfect fervor of inward light. It will fully be day when, tolerating no memory of its evils to tempt it, it hides from itself even the remaining traces of darkness.

Thus this dawn is rightly shown as still in transition, when it is said through Job: “And you have shown the dawn its place” (Job XXXVIII). For whoever is shown its place is certainly called one thing from another. What is the place of the dawn except the perfect brightness of inward vision? When the dawn has arrived there, it will have nothing left of the darkness of the night that has passed.

Now, however, while still enduring the troubles of temptations, because the Church hastens toward something else through the intention of its heart, the dawn moves toward its place. If it did not see that place with the mind, it would remain in the night of this life. But as it strives each day, extending itself toward perfection and increasing daily into the light, it already sees its place and seeks for the sun to shine fully upon it. The dawn considers its place when the holy soul burns to contemplate the appearance of its Creator.

Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. (Ambrose) The works of darkness are the practices of a carnal life, driven by worldly enticements; this life deserves darkness, as the Lord says: “Take him away and, binding his hands and feet, cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII). To put on the armor of light means to perform good deeds, [Col. 1571B] because just as evil actions are assigned to darkness, since those who act wickedly do so secretly, so those who act well act openly, because they are not afraid but rejoice. Good actions, therefore, are the armor of light, attacking the darkness that consists in the vices of the flesh.

Let us walk honorably as in the day. It is true: since one does not sin publicly, let us act as one acts publicly, for nothing is as public as truth. (Origen) We should know, however, that the coming of this light and day is to be understood in two ways: both generally, for all, and particularly, for each individual. Light and day will come generally for everyone when the age to come arrives. In comparison with it, the span of the present world is called darkness. That time approaches as the days pass away daily, and the periods that are increased by what has passed are without doubt diminished by what is still to come; [Col. 1571C] therefore our salvation is nearer than when we believed, and it comes nearer every day. Thus, when the Lord distinguished the signs of the consummation of the age, he said: “When you see all these things, lift up your heads, because your redemption is near” (Luke XXI).

The coming of this day also takes place for each individual. For if Christ is in our heart, he makes the day for us; if the order of knowledge drives away our ignorance, and, turning away from unworthy actions, we pursue all that is pious and honorable, we have been placed in the light and walk honorably as in the day.

He next enumerates the works of darkness that must be cast off and says: Not in revelries and drunkenness. (Ambrose) Revelries are luxurious banquets, which are celebrated either through the contributions of all or are customarily offered in turn by companions, so that no one there is ashamed to say or do anything dishonorable. For people usually restrain themselves out of shame at another’s table, but at this sort of gathering they come together precisely so that disgraceful things may be done with an abundant supply of wine and various pleasures of lust may be aroused. Therefore he commands that such banquets be avoided.

Not in bedrooms and debauchery. (Ambrose) After the luxurious banquet and drunkenness he added what follows, namely, shameful intercourse; for this is the fruit of such wantonness.

Not in quarrelling and jealousy. He rightly warns that people be restrained from these, because every quarrel and jealousy produces hostility, which he calls darkness, since they cannot attain the reward of light.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. [Col. 1572A] He forbids provision for the flesh—that is, pleasure—so that nothing prohibited by the law may be desired, or at least, if desired, may be overcome. These are the works of the flesh: once stripped of them, they are to put on the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, having been renewed through Christ, they may keep themselves from these evils. (Origen) We have often said that Christ is wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and truth, together with all the virtues. Whoever takes these upon himself is said to have put on Christ. For if Christ is all these things, necessarily the one who possesses them also possesses Christ; and whoever possesses these things does not make provision for the flesh in its desires.

The Apostle uses his customary moderation when he does not deny that provision must be made for the flesh in every respect. It is certain that provision must be made for it in necessities, but in pleasures, luxury, and every kind of desire it must be completely excluded. [Col. 1572B] (Augustine) He therefore shows that care for the flesh is not to be blamed when provision is made for what contributes to the body’s necessary health. But if provision is made for excessive pleasures and luxury, so that a person delights in what the flesh desires, he is rightly reproved, because he is making provision for the flesh in its desires.

“For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh,” that is, the one who delights in carnal pleasures. (Gregory) He says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” But in these words of a leader and soldier we clearly recognize that the mind is then pierced by a mortal wound when the proper measure is not maintained. For those still living in mortal flesh cannot completely cut off care for the flesh; [Col. 1572C] rather, they are commanded to learn to use it with a moderate spirit.

Since the Truth forbids us to be anxious about tomorrow, he does not deny that we should have some care for present needs; he forbids that care to be extended toward the time that follows. And indeed, when Paul does not permit provision for the flesh to be made in desire, he clearly allows it in necessity. Care for the flesh must therefore be restrained by the discretion of great moderation, so that it serves and does not rule; so that, like a mistress, it does not conquer the mind, but, subdued by the mind’s dominion, serves like a handmaid; so that it is present when commanded and, when rejected at the heart’s command, springs away; so that it scarcely appears behind holy thought and never stands against the face of one thinking rightly.

## CHAPTER XIV. He exhorts the stronger not to despise or scandalize the weaker, but to build them up peacefully. [Col. 1572D]

Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over opinions. (Ambrose) Since there were Jews who had brought the Romans to the name of Christ, with the law intermixed, as I mentioned at the beginning of the Epistle, some thought that they ought not to eat meat that had been prohibited, while others, who followed Christ without the law, thought that eating it was permitted contrary to the law. On this account there were disputes among them. The Apostle, concerned for harmony and salvation, removes these disputes by divine argument, showing that eating does not benefit a person before God, nor does abstaining harm him.

He calls weak the person who fears to eat because the Jews had been forbidden to do so. He therefore wishes such a person to be left to his own judgment, lest, having been offended and separated from charity—which is, as it were, the mother of souls—he withdraw with a troubled mind, when Christians ought to be peaceful and quiet. [Col. 1573A] (Origen) It may indeed appear that this was said also to those who had believed from the Gentiles, who exalted themselves over those who had believed from the circumcision, because they considered nothing common or unclean, while the latter still observed, according to the traditions of the law, distinctions among foods. Thus he seems to restrain and admonish them not to insult those whom long custom in observing foods still stirred toward some discrimination and hesitation.

He therefore commands that the person who is weak in this faith be received rather than rejected, and not judged as though he were an unbeliever. For it is one thing to be an unbeliever and another to be weak in faith. An unbeliever is one who does not possess faith; a person weak in faith is one who doubts in some part of the faith. [Col. 1573B] (Augustine) This, then, is what he says: We should receive the one who is weak in faith and, through our strength, bear his weakness; nor should we judge his thoughts, that is, presume to pronounce sentence, as though we dared to pass judgment on another’s heart, which we do not see.

Therefore he continues and says: For one believes that he may eat everything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables. (Ambrose) Here, relying confidently on Scripture, he does not doubt that everything given for human use may be eaten. For he reads in Genesis that everything God created was very good. Therefore nothing should be rejected, since neither Enoch, who first pleased God, nor Noah, who alone was found righteous in the flood, nor Abraham, that friend of God, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor the righteous and friends of God among whom Lot also was, nor the other righteous are said to have abstained from these things. [Col. 1573C]

(Augustine) At that time many who were already strong in faith, knowing according to the Lord’s saying (Matt. XV) that what enters the mouth does not defile, but rather what comes out, took foods indiscriminately with a clear conscience. Others, however, who were weaker, abstained from meat and wine lest, even unknowingly, they fall into foods sacrificed to idols. For at that time all sacrificial meat was sold in the marketplace, and the Gentiles poured libations from the first of their wine to their images and performed certain sacrifices at the presses themselves.

The Apostle therefore commands those who used such foods and drink with a clear conscience not to despise the weakness of those who abstained from such food and drink; and he commands the weak not to judge those who ate meat and drank wine as though they were defiled. [Col. 1573D] This is the force of what he says next:

The one who eats must not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats. For the strong were insolently despising the weaker, and the weak were rashly judging the strong. (Ambrose) But let the one who is weak eat vegetables. Therefore, if someone thinks it useful to eat vegetables, he should not be persuaded to eat meat, lest he eat it with scruple and appear to sin because he has not kept his own purpose.

If someone eats, let him not despise the one who does not eat; and if someone does not eat, let him not judge the one who eats. For eating or not eating is a matter of will, and therefore no dispute should arise from it. Everything was made for this purpose: that it should be subject to the will, since it has been subjected to human dominion. [Col. 1574A]

Unless impatience often drove the minds of abstainers from the bosom of tranquility, Peter would certainly not have immediately added this exhortation when he said: “Supply virtue in your faith, and knowledge in virtue, and self-restraint in knowledge” (II Pet. I); and then, watchfully, he added: “and patience in self-restraint.” For he foresaw that patience was lacking in those who abstained, and he admonished them so that it might be present in them.

Again, unless the thoughts of abstainers were sometimes pierced by the fault of pride, Paul would certainly not have said: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.” And elsewhere, while binding the precepts of those who gloried in the virtue of abstinence, he added: “Things which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and not in sparing the body, and are not held in any honor for the satisfying of the flesh” [Col. 1574B].

God has received him. (Ambrose) He has been received by God when he was called to grace. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. It is clear that a servant ought not to judge the will of a fellow servant to whom the law has not been given in this matter. For God is the judge of the conscience with which a person eats or does not eat, since he is God’s servant.

(Augustine) He says, therefore, that in matters which can be done either with a good intention or with a bad one, we should leave judgment to God and not dare to pronounce sentence on another’s heart, which we do not see. But in matters that are so defined that it is clear they cannot be done with a good and chaste intention, it is not wrong for us to judge.

Thus, concerning food, since we do not know with what intention it is taken, he does not want us to be judges, but God. But concerning that wicked sexual crime in which a man had his father’s wife, he commanded that judgment be passed. For that man could not say that he had committed such an enormous crime with a good intention.

Therefore, whatever deeds are so manifest that one cannot say, “I did it with a good intention,” are to be judged by us. Whatever is done in such a way that the intention with which it is done is uncertain is not to be judged, but reserved for God’s judgment, as it is written: “The things that are hidden belong to God, but the things that are manifest belong to you and your children.”

(Cass.) Each person ought to judge only himself and guard himself carefully and watchfully in all things, not examining the conduct and life of others, in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “But why do you judge your brother? He stands or falls before his own master.” And: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. V).

But he will stand, for God is able to make him stand. (Ambrose) “He will stand,” he says, before his own Lord, because he will be neither guilty if he eats nor blameworthy if he does not eat, provided that he does this from devotion and does not avoid it as though it were something opposed to him.

(Origen) Yet Paul appears to have spoken these words with a deeper meaning. For the law had commanded nothing to those coming from the circumcision about eating vegetables, so that what he says—“the one who is weak should eat vegetables”—would seem to apply to them. Hence it is clear that he is treating here of the food of the word, and calls weak in faith the one who is not so perfect in understanding that he can take in every kind of food of God’s word.

Thus the Apostle himself says elsewhere: “Solid food belongs to the mature, those who by reason of practice have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil” (Heb. V). And again he says to others: “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able” (I Cor. III).

Would we be so foolish as to think that the Apostle, who was sent to preach the word of God, carried milk with him to give the Corinthians to drink? It is clear that he is speaking of the quality of the word. Therefore he says: If someone is weaker in understanding and is not so perfect in faith that he can grasp the word concerning the more secret mysteries, he must not be stirred up to disputes over opinions by matters that he cannot understand.

“For one,” he says, “believes that he may eat everything.” Paul is not by this urging his disciples to eat everything, nor is he a teacher of the belly and the throat. He is speaking without doubt of those whose faith is perfect and who are hindered by the many distinctions within the word of God. In another place the same Apostle calls such people spiritual when he says: “The spiritual person examines all things” (I Cor. II). He is the one of whom he says here: “Another believes that he may eat everything.”

Finally, before the apostles received the Holy Spirit, the Lord said to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot hear them now; when the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all things” (John XVI).

These, then, are the “all things” that the one who is capable of the more secret word through the perfection of faith bestowed by the grace of the Holy Spirit believes he may eat. Yet the weaker person also has something to receive from the word of God. There is a certain form of the word that this Apostle called vegetables, which does not so much make the hearer’s understanding robust and strong as sustain it and keep it from perishing.

In many places Holy Scripture speaks of the inner faculties of the soul as though they were bodily limbs. As we have often taught, the inner person is said to see, hear, and walk; so now the inner person is said either to be able to receive every kind of food, if perfect, or, if weak, to eat vegetables.

But in order to reconcile the harmony of the perfect and imperfect in the Church—as though they were dishonorable and honorable members of a body—and to ensure that there be no dissension among them, he says: “Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.” [Col. 1575D]

This is what is also said elsewhere: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you,’ nor the head to the feet, ‘I have no need of your service’; but rather, those members of the body that seem to be less honorable are more necessary.”

Therefore he commands those whose faith is so great that they can eat everything and grasp every form of the word not to become proud and despise those who are weaker. Conversely, he commands those who are incapable of the more perfect teaching not to judge those whose understanding is more receptive and whose intellect is more elevated. For the unlearned often perversely judge the learned, and the lazy judge the diligent.

Sometimes, however, those who have begun to acquire some initial knowledge also become inflated and exalt themselves against those who seem less capable. Therefore, by the interpretation grounded in the Apostle’s authority, Paul restrains the insolence of both sides when he says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master.”

When he says “stands or falls,” he speaks according to the understanding of the person whom he is rebuking. For the less learned person, if he sees someone perceiving something more deeply—something he himself cannot grasp—judges that person to have fallen from the state of faith. Conversely, those who are inflated by knowledge and do not act with charity, as Paul urges, form a similar opinion of the unlearned. For this reason he removed from a brother the power to judge his brother.

He rightly says “another’s servant,” because the Lord says: “But you are all brothers” (Matt. XXIII)—all, that is, the entire creation—and there is one Lord alone, Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all, rich toward all (Rom. X). At the same time he reveals God’s ineffable goodness when he says of the one who appears to have fallen—even if he has truly fallen—that God is able to make him stand; for “the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Ps. CXLIV).

For one judges one day above another; another judges every day. Let each be fully persuaded in his own understanding. (Augustine) Once the better interpretation has been set aside, this does not seem to me to have been said about two human beings, but about a human being and God. The one who judges alternate days is a human being: he can judge one thing today and another tomorrow. That is, someone whom today he has convicted and condemned as evil, tomorrow he may find to be good after that person has corrected himself; or, conversely, someone whom he praised as righteous today he may find corrupted tomorrow.

But the one who judges every day is God, because he knows not only what each person is [lacuna]. Therefore, “let each be fully persuaded in his own understanding,” he says—that is, let each dare to judge only as much as has been granted to human understanding, and not more than has been granted to any individual human being.

“He who observes the day,” he says, “observes it for the Lord.” That is, because he judges this very matter rightly with regard to the present day, he observes it for the Lord. To judge rightly concerning a day is to know that one must not despair of a person’s future correction because one has judged that person’s present fault.

Another, he says, understands certain things while passing over some; another recognizes all things possible to be seen as they are, in accordance with understanding. (Origen) Yet, according to the sequence of the Apostle’s words, this may be understood as concerning abstinence from foods or freedom regarding them. For the calling that is in Christ declares no food common or unclean, but the principle of abstinence persuades one to abstain even from what is lawful.

For, as he himself says elsewhere (I Cor. VI, X), “because all things are lawful,” it does not follow that “all things are beneficial” or that “all things build up.” The principle of abstinence itself, however, varies according to the vow and purpose of the one who makes the vow.

One person judges this matter and decides in his own mind to spend every day—that is, the whole period of his life—in abstinence. Another sets aside some period, as though by a vowed profession, during which he undertakes either perpetual or temporary continence. He grants each person’s understanding freedom. [Col. 1577A] Yet he promises that both are acceptable before the Lord.

“He who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and he who eats eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God.”

Therefore both give thanks to God: one for the fruit of continence, the other for the freedom to eat. But since, as we have shown earlier, the Apostle’s meaning is found to be deeper than the literal matter of bodily foods contains in its spiritual exposition, according to what we discussed above concerning those of whom one judges every day and another alternate days, we can understand the following:

In the divine Scriptures, each chapter that contains a doctrine of piety and faith is called a day. Truly, the day is that which illumines the mind, drives away the darkness of ignorance, and has within itself Christ, who is the sun of righteousness.

If there is someone who applies himself and devotes himself to the divine writings so as to examine and judge every day and every meaning of Holy Scripture, so that not one iota or one tittle of the law escapes him, he will seem to judge every day. But the person who is not so great in intellect will grasp alternate days—that is, a few meanings from among many. Even if these are not sufficient for the fullness of knowledge, they are certainly sufficient for the sum of faith.

Therefore, in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel, let both give thanks to God: the one who observes every day and eats everything—that is, who recognizes and understands everything—and the one who, although he does not eat everything and does not grasp the understanding of all things, is nevertheless saved by a brief confession of faith. Therefore even the one who does not eat everything and does not acquire knowledge of everything is said to give thanks to God.

No one among us lives for himself, and no one dies for himself. (Ambrose) Someone would live for himself if he did not act under the law. But the person governed by the law’s rein does not live for himself, but for God, who gave the law so that he might live according to God’s will. And the one who dies likewise dies for God, by whose judgment he will either be crowned or condemned.

The saints neither live nor die for themselves. They do not live for themselves because in everything they do they strive for spiritual gain, and by praying, preaching, and persevering in holy works they desire to increase the citizens of the heavenly homeland. They do not die for themselves because, in the sight of human beings, they glorify God through their death and hasten to reach him even by dying.

Let us therefore consider how much reproach the death of the saints received from unbelievers, but how great the praise of the Lord grew in the hearts of the faithful. If they had sought their own praise, they would surely have feared to endure so much reproach in death.

No one among us lives for himself and no one dies for himself who have sought their own glory neither in living nor in dying. Let us see whether the first shepherd of the Church himself, who did not live for himself, died for himself. Let John, his companion, be consulted; from the words of the Lord he speaks about the death of that same shepherd: “But he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God” (John XXI). Therefore he did not die for himself, since he glorified God in his death.

Let us learn, then, my brothers, to examine our intention carefully in everything we do and not to seek our own interests, if we wish to minister to almighty God. For whether we live, we live for the Lord; and whether we die, we die for the Lord. The meaning is the same: whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

(Ambrose) It is true that all of us belong to the Lord, as servants by our condition and by the dominion of the Redeemer, and that each person is treated according to his merit.

(Origen) What it means to live in Christ and what it means to die in Christ has often been said by us in the exposition of this Epistle, especially where we attempted to explain the Apostle’s statement: “But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him” (Rom. VI).

If we remember what was said there, the apostolic statement proposed here will also become clearer and more lucid: how no one among us lives for himself and no one dies for himself. For no one gives it to himself; rather, he receives from Christ the example of death. Christ alone died to sin, so that each person, by imitating him, might also become alienated from sin and dead to it.

Nor do we possess the example of life from ourselves; we receive it from Christ’s resurrection, as the same Apostle says: “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so you too should walk in newness of life.”

The newness of life by which we live in Christ through faith in his resurrection is assigned to the Lord, because it does not begin from us but from him. Therefore: “Whether we live, we live for the Lord; whether we die, we die for the Lord. Whether, then, we live or die, we belong to the Lord.”

By “death” he means that by which, as we have said, having been buried with Christ and baptized into his death, we have died to sin. By “life” he means that by which, having been made strangers to this world and, as he himself says, living from the dead, we live not for ourselves—that is, not for the flesh—but for God, in accordance with what he joins to this in what follows. [Col. 1578C]

For Christ died and rose again for this purpose: that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead. (Ambrose) Through Christ the Lord the creation that had been alienated from its author through sin and made captive was restored. God the Father, lest his work perish, sent his Son from heaven to earth and taught it, by what deed, to escape the hands of pirates.

For this reason he permitted himself to be killed by his enemies. Descending into hell, since he had been killed though innocent, he made sin guilty, so that he might release those whom it held in hell. Since he showed the living the way of salvation and offered himself for them, while he freed the dead from hell, he is Lord of both the living and the dead. For from the lost he reshaped them for himself once more as servants. [Col. 1578D]

(Origen) Someone might perhaps be troubled by the Apostle’s statement that Christ died and lived for this purpose, that he might be Lord of the dead and the living—as though it meant that, unless he had died, he would not have had dominion over the dead, and unless he had lived again after death, he would not have retained dominion over the living.

I think the answer should be given as follows. Christ’s dominion over every creature is established in two ways. The first is the dominion by which, as the creator of all and the holder of power over the universe, he has everything subject to him by the force of majesty and the necessity of power. Through this dominion he rules not only good and holy minds and spirits, but also the wicked and rebellious, and those whom divine Scripture calls evil angels.

For this reason he is called all-sustaining or almighty, as John indicates in the Apocalypse when he says: “Thus says the one who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Apoc. I). This, then, is one way in which Christ rules all things.

There is another way in which, as the good Son of a good Father, he does not wish rational spirits to be bent violently into obedience to his law. Rather, he waits for them to come willingly, so that they may seek the good by their will and not by compulsion; and by teaching rather than commanding, by inviting rather than extorting, he persuades them.

For this reason, finally, he deigned to approach death, so that he might leave to those who desire to die to sin and vices an example of obedience and a pattern of dying. For this reason the Apostle writes in the present passage that he died and lived so that he might rule the living and the dead: the living, certainly, who, following the example of his resurrection, lead a new and heavenly life on earth; and the dead, without doubt, who carry the mortification of Christ in their bodies and put to death their members that are upon the earth (Col. III). [Col. 1579B]

But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother, when, whether the mortification of the flesh’s vices is in you, it did not arise from you but was bestowed through Christ’s death; or whether you possess the newness of life and, while walking on earth, have your manner of life in heaven, you obtained this through Christ’s resurrection?

He rightly marked the characteristic fault of both with a common expression, saying to the one, “Why do you despise?” and to the other, “Why do you judge your brother?” For those who seem to have advanced somewhat in knowledge customarily despise and regard as worthless those less capable of higher understanding. Conversely, the unlearned and untaught judge—that is, accuse and condemn—those who investigate matters higher and deeper than they themselves can grasp or attain.

Therefore, wishing to cut away the fault arising on both sides, the Apostle commands the former not to despise and look down on the weaker, and the latter not to judge those who are superior, since they do not possess the skill to judge. Although he reproves both—the one who despises an inferior brother and the one who judges a superior one—nevertheless, to show that the latter sins more seriously in judging than the former does in despising his brother, he sets aside the fault of despising and emphasizes and condemns the presumption of the judging brother. Therefore he adds in what follows:

All of us will stand before the tribunal of God. For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God.” Therefore each of us will give an account of himself to God. Let us no longer judge one another, but rather judge this: that you do not place a stumbling-block or an occasion of scandal before your brother.

(Orig.) Taking up the causes of those who judge their brothers incorrectly, he introduces the upright and just form of divine judgment and says: “For we must all stand before the tribunal of God”—so that the one who judges his brother may recognize how great a crime of arrogance he incurs, assuming for himself the tribunal of God and anticipating the judgment of the Only-Begotten.

But let us consider what the Apostle means by mentioning the tribunal of God, and how it should be understood. For he refers to a tribunal not only here, but also in writing to the Corinthians, where he says: “Therefore we make it our aim, whether present or absent, to please him; for we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive in the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V).

We also find something similar concerning the form of judgment described by the prophet Daniel: “I saw,” he says, “and behold, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat, and his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A stream of fire flowed before him. Thousands upon thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII).

Likewise, in the book of the Twelve Prophets, it is said mystically that the Lord will judge his people in the valley of Jehoshaphat; and for this reason Paul calls that same valley the valley of judgment. But it would now be lengthy to discuss each of the things we have introduced by way of comparison. Nevertheless, when we compare what we said the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians with the present passage and with the other things we recalled as written among the prophets, we see that all these passages most certainly declare that God’s judgment is future. Its form, so that it might become more familiar to human beings, has been taken from what occurs among human beings. Thus we may understand that, just as an earthly judge ascends a higher place, called a tribunal, so that from it he may be higher and more eminent than those who are to be judged, and so that neither the punishments of the accused nor the pleas of the innocent may escape his notice, so also Christ, the Judge of all, is in nature and majesty exalted above all. He looks into the hearts and consciences of each person, reveals hidden and concealed things, grants praise for good deeds, and imposes upon the wicked the punishment they deserve.

If, then, God’s future judgment remains, and if it is such a judgment that each person will receive not only according to his deeds, but will also give an account for every idle or vicious word, in accordance with the Lord’s sentence, evil thoughts too will be refuted, with conscience bringing accusation; and each of us will give an account of himself to God.

“Let us therefore,” he says, “no longer judge one another,” and so forth. For, as I think, our heart will be laid bare before every rational creature, and hidden things will be brought to light, or even revealed—for there is a distinction between these. Those things that are “revealed” seem to belong to the wicked, concerning whom it is said: “For it will be revealed in fire” (I Cor. III). Those things that are “made manifest” seem to belong to the good; hence it is said: “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Ephes. V). And, like books written out or tablets engraved with letters containing the record of our deeds and thoughts, they will be read aloud before every rational creature, as we have said.

This, I think, is indicated through Daniel, where he says: “And the books were opened.” These books are wrapped up and covered within our heart, containing the things we do, furrowed with certain marks of conscience, yet known to no one except God alone. These books of our soul, or pages of our heart, will therefore be opened in the presence of the fiery throne, the wheels of burning fire, and the stream of fire flowing before the Ancient of Days. The angels will see and read these things, as will those thousands upon thousands of angels and those ten thousand times ten thousand ministers. Thus, for our crimes—when we are now ashamed to endure even one witness—we shall then endure innumerable hosts of heavenly powers as witnesses.

When Paul says, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of God,” and associates himself with those who will stand before God’s tribunal, who could deceive and mislead himself so far as not to think that he will come to Christ’s judgment and to the tribunal of his assessment? Who could fail to think that he will be revealed in the things he has done either rightly or wrongly?

In the present passage he says “the tribunal of God,” whereas to the Corinthians he says “the tribunal of Christ.” I do not think there is any difference preventing the tribunal of Christ and the tribunal of God from being one and the same tribunal, in accordance with what the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “All that the Father has is mine” (John XVI). And again: “Father, what is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (ibid.).

If, however, someone thinks that, since none of Paul’s words—or even syllables—is idle in his writings, an explanation should be sought for this variation, he might perhaps say something like the following. The name “Christ,” insofar as it belongs to the proper meaning of the designation itself—namely, the Word made flesh and reconciling the world to God—is an indication of this, as Paul himself says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V).

But the time-span of this reconciliation has been prolonged and extended by the delay of our conversion and by negligence in amendment. It will continue until he has abolished every principality and power, placed his enemies beneath his feet, and destroyed the last enemy, death. Until then he must reign, carrying out the ministry of the dispensation he undertook in the flesh, revealing the good, while the guilty each receive according to their works: “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (I Cor. XV). That is, when he has offered all who have been converted and amended to God, and has completed the mystery of the world’s reconciliation in its fullness, then, he says, he is said to stand before the tribunal of God, so that what follows may be fulfilled: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God.”

Every creature will bend the knee to God in the name of Jesus, through whom it has been reconciled to him, according to what the same Apostle says: “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II).

The Apostle took the expression “to bend the knee” and “for every tongue to confess to God” from the words of the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XLV). This, however, must not be understood carnally, so that we imagine that heavenly things—which, he says, bend the knee—do so with bodily limbs. For example, we must not suppose that the sun, moon, stars, angels, or whatever else is called heavenly bows on bodily knees to adore, or that it confesses God with a bodily tongue and an organ like that with which we human beings speak. Of these beings it is said that they are spirit and fire, according to what the prophet says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CIII). What knees, then, are to be believed to exist in spirits, or what tongue is to be sought in the form of fire?

“To bend the knee” means that all things are subject and obey the worship of God.

Something else from what we have taken from the Epistles to the Corinthians also troubles me. He says: “So that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.” Does he mean that in every human being there must be something good and something evil, and that no good person can be found who has not possessed some evil as well? Or, again, does he mean that among the wicked there is no one who has not possessed something good, on account of the Scripture that says: “The spirit is incorruptible in human beings”? Is this why he says that each person will receive good for his good deeds and evil for his evil deeds? Or does he call those “good” to whom nothing evil can be ascribed, and those “wicked” to whom no good at all is owed?

But if we adopt this last interpretation, we shall seem to contradict evident reason. For, as I have said, no one will be found so good that some evil is not implanted in him, as can very easily be gathered from the examples of many saints. Conversely, no one among the worst—even if Judas himself is taken as an example, who was wicked beyond all wickedness—will be found who does not seem to have possessed something good.

To pass over what he did while he was placed among the apostles as though he were one of them—although even there his good deeds were already mixed with evil, for he was greedy for money—this itself, that, moved by repentance, he returned the thirty pieces of silver to the priests and said, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” was something good.

From all this it seems to me that one and the same person cannot receive good and evil simultaneously. No one can at the same time be sent into paradise or the kingdom of heaven and into Gehenna. Rather, in those who are overwhelmed by evil, no account is taken of the good; and in those in whom good predominates, no account is taken of the evil, when repentance and conversion have erased the traces of their sins.

To return to the conclusion and end of the chapter under discussion: since, he says, the truth of God’s and his Christ’s judgment is so great, and the investigation of the future examination so thorough, “let us therefore,” he says, “no longer judge one another; but judge this instead, that you do not place an offense or a scandal before your brother.”

“Judge this,” that is, decide that, through observance of foods, you will not generate offenses or scandals for your brothers. We have already said above concerning offense and scandal that a scandal is something encountered as an obstacle on the road along which one travels, against which the feet of those climbing or walking stumble. This, then, is what happens to those who have recently entered upon the way of faith: they are offended by the disputes, negligence, contempt, or arrogance of those who came before them, and, recoiling from their examples, they are turned away from the faith.

I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through itself; but for the one who considers something common, for him it is common.

(Orig.) We have said elsewhere that in the holy Scriptures, by a kind of ordinary designation, whatever is not holy or clean is called “common” (*commune*). This designation is found more frequently in the New Testament; in the Old Testament I do not recall that it is used anywhere in this way. Thus the Savior says in the Gospel: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, fornications, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies; these are the things that defile a person. But eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Mark VII).

Although in some Latin copies they have placed *coinquinat* (“defiles”) instead of *communicat* (“makes common”), and although the force is the same, the proper wording is *communicat*. In the Acts of the Apostles, the Lord also says to Peter: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts X).

I think that this usage of the term arose in the following way. Since, for example, vessels set apart for the service of the temple were certainly called the Lord’s vessels, whereas the remaining vessels, in distinction from them, were called common, so also, for distinguishing foods, those that Scripture set apart as clean and lawful to eat were called clean, while all the rest were called common.

But the Jews, not understanding the force of the word, retained the usage without understanding its meaning when they called a person common. For foods created by God could not make a person common and unclean, whether they were taken ignorantly or simply. Rather, the mind of a human being, which is set apart for God alone, is rightly called clean.

But the mind that is alienated from God is possessed not by one unclean spirit but by many; therefore such a person is called common, as belonging to many, being the servant either of vices or of demons, according to the one who, when asked, “What is your name?” replied, “Legion,” because “we are many” (Luke VIII).

The same is true according to what the Savior says: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest and not finding it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it vacant, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there” (Luke XI). Such a person is plainly called common, having become the servant of all the evil spirits that dwell in him.

Knowing that this is the reasoning behind the term, Paul rightly says: “I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through itself.” Nothing in God’s creatures is unclean by nature. For it is evident that everything created by the good God is good and clean.

“But for the one,” he says, “who considers something common, for him it is common.” That is, a person who, with the intention of his heart, thinks something unclean and does not abandon his observance of distinctions. This is also what he says later: “Whoever makes a distinction, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith; for whatever is not from faith is sin.”

Yet he did not abolish the distinction made by the Law by simply saying that none of the things the Law declared unclean was common or unclean. He first stated the reason why nothing is called common through itself: “I know,” he says, “and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus.” In the Lord Jesus, then, nothing is common through itself—that is, by its nature. “But for the one,” he says, “who considers and thinks something common, for him it is common.”

Do not be surprised that the mind’s thought can make food unclean which by nature is neither common nor polluted, since conversely a truly polluted food—for truly polluted is food sacrificed to idols—may be acquitted of every suspicion of contamination by simplicity of mind and the absence of any scruple in thought. Again, even if food is clean, yet if someone suspects that it may have been sacrificed to idols, it is said to be polluted through the scruple of conscience.

For if your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to love.

(Orig.) Having established by apostolic doctrine that, through the Lord Jesus, nothing is to be considered common or unclean by nature, and having granted the faithful the fullest freedom concerning the use of foods, he again restricts the license of freedom for the sake of building up fraternal love, and says: “Even if nothing is common, and the use of all foods is freely permitted, nevertheless, if because of food—which you think may lawfully be eaten—you scandalize your brother, who does not yet possess this understanding in conscience, you are no longer walking according to love, nor are you displaying within yourself the affection of fraternal love.”

What harm would it do you, if, so as not to grieve your brother, you abstained even from things permitted? For you incur no guilt by abstaining from what is permitted; but for him, in matters in which he distinguishes and believes something not to be permitted, the use of it is condemnable.

(Ambr.) In another Epistle he says: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both the one and the other” (I Cor. VI). Since no one is pleasing or displeasing to God because of food, he therefore urges us to pursue love, through which God has deigned to free us. For he says: “But God, because of his exceedingly great love, had mercy on us.” Whoever remembers this benefit cultivates love and places nothing before it.

(Orig.) “Whoever makes a distinction, if he eats, is condemned.” If you do this, you certainly destroy your brother, for whom Christ died, and you acquire for him causes of destruction. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died.

(Ambr.) The value of a brother’s salvation is recognized from Christ’s death. Therefore the person who knows its cost ought to strengthen him, not scandalize him, so as to create a scruple for him out of something trivial and make him begin to hesitate over whether meat ought to be eaten, when perhaps he had been eating it simply and securely in his conscience.

But when disputes arise, he will begin, through disturbance, to sin against God’s creature, and the injury to the Creator will contribute to the destruction of the one who doubts. “Therefore,” he says, “let not our good be blasphemed.” This means that the Lord’s teaching, since it is good and salutary, must not be blasphemed on account of something trivial. It is blasphemed when doubt is cast upon God’s creature.

“Our good” may also be understood in this way: a person who possesses good works may obscure that good if he is censured in some other minor matter; then his good begins to be blasphemed through his evil.

(Orig.) Or it may mean that it is good to understand the Law spiritually and to avoid, as unclean and polluted foods, the impious and foolish doctrines of heretics or of those devoted to false philosophy. This is what is sanctioned by the spiritual Law.

Yet if, for example, someone from the Jews, or from those called Encratites, wishes to believe in Christ but still thinks that great importance attaches to observing continence, or to abstaining from foods prohibited by the Law, or from foods they regard as opposed to chastity—foods which some even think should be avoided on the authority of Scripture—if you press such a person to eat the common foods of all people, and tell him that he cannot otherwise be saved or attain the faith and grace of Christ unless he eats the foods from which he abstains, then the good of the spiritual teaching is truly blasphemed. The person you press will think that this is the faith held among us: that we believe no one can be saved unless he eats pork or other such common and indifferent foods.

For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

(Ambr.) It is clear that no one pleases or displeases God because of food. He says that those enter the kingdom of God who pursue righteousness, while possessing the Christian peace that the Lord gave when he said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV). From this peace arises joy in the Holy Spirit.

Argument, however, does not produce joy but anger. For this reason the Holy Spirit does not look upon it, since he rejoices only in those who are peaceful.

(Cass.) Therefore, if the kingdom of God is within us, and the kingdom of God itself is righteousness, peace, and joy, then whoever dwells in these things is unquestionably in the kingdom of God. Conversely, those who live in injustice, discord, and sadness, with death at work in them, are situated in the kingdom of the devil, in hell, and in death. By these judgments the kingdom of either God or the devil is distinguished.

Indeed, if we consider with the mind’s lofty gaze the state in which the heavenly and higher powers dwell—those who truly are in the kingdom of God—what else should we believe it to be than perpetual and unceasing rejoicing? For what is so proper to true blessedness and so fitting for it as continual tranquility and everlasting joy?

(Orig.) He therefore says: Why is it necessary to disturb fraternal peace and love so greatly over foods and the qualities of foods, when the kingdom of God, for which we labor and run, consists neither in foods nor in drink? These things are alien to the kingdom of God and to that future way of life.

For there, just as they “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God” (Mark XII), so they neither eat food nor drink, but are like the angels of God. Thus the Apostle has settled the matter with the clearest doctrine and evident judgment: in the kingdom of God, bodily foods and drink have no place, but righteousness and peace in the Holy Spirit do. Therefore he urges us to exercise ourselves in these things, and already here to meditate upon possessing those goods and that substance which can pass with us into the kingdoms of heaven.

Peace, righteousness, and whatever else is of this kind, acquired through the Holy Spirit, will themselves be our food and substance in the kingdom of God. Thus he teaches through these things that we must care not for bodily foods, which will have no place in the future, but for the virtues that remain with us in the present life and in the future kingdom of God.

Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by human beings.

(Ambr.) Because Christ redeemed us, he says, “Whoever serves Christ in this way,” as his redeemer, “is pleasing to God.” Why? Because God himself sent Christ to redeem the human race, just as the Lord himself says: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V). Therefore whoever pleases God is approved by human beings. How so? He has received the gift by which he may appear worthy of God.

(Orig.) This is what he says elsewhere concerning himself: “Just as I,” he says, “please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many” (I Cor. X). For this reason, although he was an apostle of Christ, he became as a Jew to the Jews, plainly so that, by pleasing the Jews, he might save them; and to those who were without the Law he became as one without the Law, so that, by pleasing them, he might save them.

He says that he pleases human beings not by indulging their vices, but by patiently bearing their weaknesses. Nor should we pass over carelessly what he says: “For whoever serves Christ in this”—that is, in the Holy Spirit—“is pleasing to God and approved by human beings.”

He says that he serves Christ in the Holy Spirit in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII). Paul himself therefore serves Christ in the Holy Spirit: having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, he serves the word of God, serves wisdom, serves righteousness, and serves all the virtues together, which Christ is said to be.

For this reason he is said to please God in these things, because he fulfills God’s will according to the word God himself proclaimed: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. IV). Whoever therefore listens to God and serves Christ, in whom God is well pleased, pleases God and is approved by human beings.

Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace and guard among one another the things that make for edification.

(Orig.) Above he said, “pursuing hospitality”; here likewise he says, “let us pursue the things that make for peace, and the things that make for edification among one another.” Just as we showed there how hospitality should be pursued, so here let us understand how peace should be pursued, since David likewise says: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII).

Although the Latin copies have *sequere eam* (“follow it”), *sectare* (“pursue it”) is also written there. This seems to me to show the following: since peace has been disturbed and driven away by many who act restlessly and insolently, and has as though fled from human beings, it must nevertheless be pursued and recalled in every possible way by those who have learned Christ and themselves serve him.

A person pursues peace when, even at personal labor, loss, disgrace, and, if necessary, even at the risk of life and reputation, he preserves those things by which peace can endure. These things preserve not only peace but also mutual edification.

The person who sees you seeking not what benefits you alone but what benefits others is himself built up; thus the building of faith grows, and the temple of God rises through the construction of love, from living stones.

Therefore he adds: “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food.” The person who places scandals before his brothers because of intemperance in food dissolves the work of God and destroys the building of love.

(Ambr.) A human being is the work of God, and again is the work of God when he is re-formed through generation [regeneration]. Food too is the work of God, but the human being was not made for food; food was made for the human being. There is therefore a great difference. Hence he says: Do not dissolve the work of God, which is glorious, for the sake of something that is most insignificant.

For the person who, through argument, again provokes to sin a brother freed from sin makes God’s benefit ineffective, undoing within him the works of Christ, which Christ performed to free the human being from sin.

Everything is clean, but it is evil for a person to eat through an offense.

(Ambr.) It is true and evident that everything is clean, since Genesis says that everything God made was very good. Although, by nature, all things are good and clean, they nevertheless become unclean for those who doubt. It will therefore be an offense to the person who eats while doubting, not with a clean conscience, because he does what he considers harmful to himself. For this reason no one should be contradicted who follows this [what in this] matter.

(Orig.) We must note that what he says, “Everything is clean, but it is evil for a person to eat through an offense,” resembles what he said above: “Nothing is common through itself, except for the one who considers something common; for him it is common.”

Therefore, according to their nature and according to the order of creation—for everything that exists was made by God—all things created by God are clean, and nothing is unclean or common. Yet he gives two causes by which things that are clean may become unclean, or things that are good may become evil.

In the present passage he says: “But it is evil for a person who eats through an offense.” What is good by its own nature becomes evil through an offense—that is, when your brother is offended because you use those foods through which he suffers scandal.

There is another cause by which something that is not unclean by nature becomes common or unclean: if someone considers it common and holds it to be so in his own mind. It becomes common or unclean only for the one who considers it so.
