Through these statements the Apostle clearly teaches that uncleanness and pollution consist not in things or substances, but in actions and thoughts that are less than upright, although the Law of Moses designated certain things as clean and others as unclean. Through these distinctions it wished to establish a separation, so that the people counted under the Law might appear to be distinguished from the other nations by such observances.

As long as that people was regarded as holy and separated from the other nations, a distinction between clean and unclean also seemed necessary—one that would separate and distinguish God’s special people from the nations whom ignorance of God and the worship of idols made unclean.

But when the door of faith was opened to the Gentiles and all were invited to God, all four-footed animals, reptiles, and birds were shown to Peter, spread out on a sheet that had been lowered from heaven, and he was told: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X).

When he, remembering the legal observance, answered the Lord and said: “By no means, Lord, for never has anything common or unclean entered my mouth,” the heavenly judgment was pronounced: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”

When, therefore, all nations are cleansed from contamination through knowledge of the faith, every food is purified by the word of the Lord and by prayer. For this reason the Apostle says that everything is clean, provided that what he adds in the following passage is avoided: that, through the offense of a brother, the clean things we eat should again become unclean.

It is good not to eat meat, and not to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened.

(Ambr.) Although he was speaking only about meat, he added drink as well, so that he might encourage those who abstain from these things by reminding them that both eating meat and drinking wine are permitted.

They were not to be saddened by those who use these things; he gave them the consolation of breathing freely, so that they might rest in their own choice and the dispute that produces discord might cease.

When it is recognized that eating meat and drinking wine are good, and conversely that not eating meat and not drinking wine are also good, no one quarrels. The creature has been given for the use of those who wish to use it; nevertheless, necessity has not been imposed either upon the one who wishes or upon the one who does not wish to use it.

(Orig.) What he says, “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine,” unless he had added, “nor to do anything by which your brother is offended,” might appear contrary to what came before. For he taught that eating meat and not eating it, drinking wine and not drinking it, are neither evil nor good, but matters that are intermediate and indifferent.

A bad person and one alienated from the faith can refrain from eating meat and drinking wine; indeed, it is certain that some do this for the sake of idols. Sometimes such an observance is also reported among practitioners of evil arts. It is certainly customary among not a few heretics to observe this, yet we do not immediately say: “It is good for them that they do not eat meat or drink wine.”

But in precisely the manner in which he states it below—“by which your brother is offended”—not eating meat and not drinking wine are no longer intermediate or indifferent, but truly good. For it is good not to place an offense or scandal before one’s brother.

He did not therefore wish the person who judges that meat should be eaten to compel the one who is offended by it to eat. Rather, for the sake of the one who does not think it should be eaten, he commands even those who judge that it should be eaten to abstain.

Everything must therefore be done so that the work of God is not destroyed. Meat should be eaten if a brother is built up by this, and it should not be eaten if through it the work of God does not grow. Wine should be drunk if through it a brother advances in faith, and it should not be drunk if through it your brother suffers loss of faith or you incur damage to charity.

Keep the faith that you have to yourself before God.

Here he calls “faith” that by which someone believes that all things may be eaten, as he said above: “One person believes that he may eat everything”—namely, the person who believes that nothing among God’s creatures is common or unclean.

“But it is enough for you,” he says, “to have this faith before God.” Nevertheless, another person who does not yet possess such faith as to believe that everything may be eaten must not for that reason be compelled to eat everything.

When he says, “You have it to yourself,” he cuts off ostentation, so that what we believe may be found more in virtue than in display. He adds, “Have it before God,” to teach that we must strive not for our faith to be publicized among human beings but for it to be approved before God.

It is a great thing to have faith that is approved before God; for before God even the faith of the apostles is judged small. Hence it is said to Peter: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV). For this reason the person who has faith approved before God is truly great.

Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves.

(Aug.) This should be referred chiefly to what he said above: “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.” For this is also what he now says, before this sentence: “Keep the faith that you have to yourself before God.”

Or it may refer to the fact that this faith is good—the faith by which we believe that all things are clean for the clean—and that we prove ourselves in this faith. Let us therefore use our good rightly, lest, when we have misused that good as an occasion of offense to weak brothers, we sin against our brothers and are judged in that very good in which we prove ourselves, when the faith itself pleases us and we scandalize the weak.

(Ambr.) He declares that each person is to be condemned by his own judgment if he does what he says he ought not to do. He calls blessed the person who does no more than what he proves useful to himself.

(Orig.) A person is called blessed not only if he does what is fitting, but also if he does not do what is unfitting. Thus the person who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly is called blessed (Ps. I); likewise the person who walks in the law of the Lord is blessed—“uselessly” [Note: [Col. 1589C] This is how it stood in the manuscript, but it should certainly be read otherwise.]—and the person who does not stand in the way of sinners is no less blessed, just as the one who meditates daily on the law of the Lord is blessed.

So also in the present passage the Apostle says: “Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves.”

But let us see what kind of conduct this blessedness concerns. There are many who approve doing something good—for example, those who, hearing about the rewards of chastity, approve and resolve to live chastely. But as time passes, whether through creeping negligence or overpowering lust, what they had approved as something to be observed becomes stained and corrupted.

That person is unhappy who, overcome in the very thing he had resolved to observe, judges and condemns himself. But the person who remains so fixed and stable in what he approves and resolves that he does not judge or reproach himself in anything is blessed.

But whoever makes a distinction, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith.

(Orig.) He says that this must also be understood concerning the observance of foods, according to the rule he established above. If someone, through the conscience of the spiritual Law, approves that everything may be eaten and that everything is clean, he should not afterward judge himself or begin to doubt whether he ought to partake or not.

For the person who makes such a distinction—that is, who doubts whether what he is taking is truly clean or unclean—is condemned by the very doubt of his mind, with conscience bringing accusation.

(Ambr.) It is true that the person who judges that he ought not to eat, yet eats, is condemned. For he condemns himself when he does what he declares to be harmful to himself.

(Orig.) He also explains the cause of this condemnation, saying: “Because it is not taken from faith,” but rather from doubt.

Whatever is not from faith is sin.

(Ambr.) He rightly calls sin what is done otherwise than it has been approved.

(Orig.) Through this saying he binds the careless and sluggish souls of believers with a tighter bond, so that they do nothing without faith, say nothing without faith, and think nothing without faith. For whether you have done something without faith, spoken without faith, or even thought without faith, you sin.

This is the same thing he says elsewhere: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (I Cor. X).

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 1589]

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 1589C] He goes on to exhort the stronger to support the weak and advance them in faith, and he excuses himself for not having visited the Romans bodily.

“We who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.”

(Cass.) For the weak never supports the weak, nor can one who is likewise sick endure or heal a sick person; rather, he will provide a remedy for the weak who is not himself subject to weakness. To him it is rightly said: “Physician, heal yourself.” He rightly says “we ought,” because teachers must strengthen the weak and instruct the unlearned with gentleness, lest, when provoked, they become contentious, or, while wishing to appear humble, advance toward something worse.

(Orig.) In these words Paul seems to declare himself strong. But do not understand this as though he were forgetful of that commandment which says: “Let your neighbor praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. XXVII). He therefore declares himself strong not for his own praise, but in view of the circumstances. For if he had avoided being counted among the strong under the pretext of humility, who among those responsible for bearing the weaknesses of others would have dared to undertake this duty, as though he himself were strong and were striving to bear the frailties of the weak?

For this reason he makes the duty common to all, so that each of us may bear the weakness of his neighbor in whatever respect he can—even if not in everything, nevertheless in the respect in which he appears stronger than his neighbor—just as he says elsewhere (Gal. VI): “Bear one another’s burdens.”

But there he seems to have called bodily necessities “burdens”: if someone is richer in possessions, let him bear the burden of the poorer and relieve his want by his abundance. In the passage where he says that the stronger should bear the weaknesses of the weak, nothing else can be understood than that those who are more robust should patiently endure the things in which others sin through weakness, and should not immediately despise, reject, or detest them if they are overcome in some fault arising from weakness. Nor should they drive them away from the assembly of the brethren and the fellowship of the Church under the pretext of a purer life.

For whoever does this is not an imitator of the one of whom Isaiah says: “He himself bears our weaknesses, and suffers for us; yet we thought that he was in pain, and under a blow, and in affliction” (Isa. LIII). If Christ bears our weaknesses, and God patiently endures our sins, how can we in no way tolerate the sins and negligences of those who seem somewhat inferior?

This is surely to turn Christ himself away from such affection, so that he may not wish to bear our weaknesses. No one is so perfect that he is not found weak in some respect before God, and is not borne by Christ. Therefore he teaches sympathy more particularly in this matter—that is, that we should have compassion on and suffer with one another—just as he also writes elsewhere (Col. III): “Forgiving one another your offenses, just as God in Christ forgave you.”

He does not command this in order to nourish those who sin or to dissolve the weak through excessive indulgence. Rather, he knows that, if the weak person is borne, either he will be ashamed to be borne any longer and will correct his sinful fault, or, if he cannot reform himself, the one who bears him will at least gain this fruit: the weak person will not progress toward worse things or become worse than himself, like those of whom the Apostle says (II Tim. III): “Wicked people and deceivers will advance toward worse things, deceiving and going astray.”

Along with bearing the weaknesses of the weak, we ought to add this also: [Col. 1591C] that we should not please ourselves, but our neighbor, as he said:

“Let each of you please his neighbor in what is good, for edification.”

(Orig.) The fault of self-love—that is, of pleasing oneself—the prophet also condemns in others when he says: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and learned in their own sight” (Isa. V). Similarly, we can say here: Woe to those who please themselves and appear good in their own sight.

For one ought first to please in the sight of God, and afterward in the sight of one’s neighbors. Just as the first commandment is to love the Lord God and the second one’s neighbor, so also one must first please God and afterward one’s neighbors.

But perhaps someone may say that Paul contradicts himself in commanding us to please our neighbors, since elsewhere he says (Gal. I): “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” This indeed seems contrary to the statement, “Let each of us please his neighbor,” and to what he says elsewhere (I Cor. X): “Just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking what is useful for myself, but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved.”

To this one must reply that it is one thing to be eager to please people in order to seek praise from them, and another thing to be eager to please people in such a way that one’s life is irreproachable among them and that all who see or hear such a person may profit from him.

One must not please people where what pleases them is contrary to faith, morality, or religion. This is why he says: “If I were pleasing people”—that is, unbelieving and faithless Jews—“I would not be a servant of Christ.”

For if Paul had wished to please the Jews, when he was sent to Damascus with letters (Acts IX), he would certainly have dragged men and women bound to Jerusalem and would not have believed the vision granted to him on the road or the heavenly voice. But when it is said, “Let each of you please his neighbor,” a necessary qualification is added, which clearly shows in what respect one should please one’s neighbor: “in what is good, for edification.”

When, therefore, we act well and teach well, we please our neighbor and edify him. He does not urge us to seek glory from human beings, but to give our neighbors edification through our conduct and speech, just as the Savior says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

By this he certainly does not exhort the disciples to seek glory from human beings, but so that, by living rightly and honorably, they may provide edification to those who see them, and so that God may be glorified, since he has opened to human beings the way of amendment and salvation.

“For Christ also did not please himself, but, as it is written: ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.’”

(Orig.) In this he seems to show that Christ also did not please himself, nor consider it robbery to be equal with God (Phil. II), but emptied himself. Yet, wishing to please human beings—that is, to save human beings—he endured the reproaches of those who reproached him, as it is written: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Ps. LXVIII).

This will become clearer if we recall what is written in the Gospel: in order to benefit people and save them, he ate and drank with sinners and tax collectors. For this reason the Jews reproached him, saying: “Why does your teacher eat with sinners and tax collectors?” (Matt. IX).

Again, when he did not prevent a sinful woman from touching his feet, washing them with her tears, wiping them with her hair, and anointing them with myrrh, the Jews reproached and upbraided him, saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke VII).

But if you ask why the example he brought from the Psalm is expressed as though the reproaches made against God had fallen upon Christ, we can explain it in this way: just as he said, “Whoever receives me receives the one who sent me” (Matt. X), so also this may be understood: whoever reproaches me reproaches the one who sent me.

The example he took from the sixty-eighth Psalm is written as follows: “I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to the sons of my mother. For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.”

(Ambr.) He says that the Savior did not please himself, but God the Father, because he says: “For I did not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John V, VI).

And because, while he was saying these things, he was killed by the Jews who contradicted him as though he were a sinner, the psalmist speaks in his person to God the Father, saying: “The slanders of those who reproached you fell upon me.” That is: While I was doing your will, they said that I was sinning against you. By not receiving me, whom you sent, they reproached you. For the Jews, while sinning against God by not receiving Christ whom he sent, even killed him as though he were sinning against God.

Thus the sins of those who sinned against God fell upon Christ: the innocent man was killed by sinners as a blasphemer, as it is written in the Gospel.

“For whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.”

(Orig.) This is like what he says elsewhere (I Cor. X): “These things were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

If it is asked how they were written for us, consider that this was written for us: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing.” For God is not concerned about oxen, but speaks about us (I Cor. IX).

It was also written for us that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Gal. IV), so that we might understand that these things are allegorical and that these are the two Testaments (ibid.).

It was written for us also that the people ate manna in the desert and drank water from the rock (Exod. XIV, XVI, XVII), so that we might understand that they ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink, drinking from the rock that followed them—and that rock was Christ (I Cor. X).

These and other matters of the same kind were mysteries hidden for eternal ages but now manifested through the prophetic writings and through the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

But so that it may become still clearer how what was written was written for us, concerning the earlier people the prophet says: “You shall hear with the ear and not hear; and seeing you shall see and not understand” (Ezek. XII; Jer. V).

But concerning us he says: “Those to whom he was not announced shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isa. LII).

Consider from this for whom what was written appears to have been written. For what is written is undoubtedly written for those who will understand, not for those who are said neither to see nor to understand.

Those who understand what is written will certainly find what follows: “so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope in God.” For it is not the person who neither believes nor understands who receives consolation from the Scriptures, but the one who both believes and understands.

“Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ.”

If patience is a virtue, and every virtue is from God, then patience also is from God. When, therefore, he is called the God of patience, this seems to show that God is said to be with those who possess the virtue of patience within themselves. Similarly, when he is called the God of justice, God is shown to be in those who preserve justice.

The same is understood of the God of truth and the God of wisdom. And when he is called the God of consolation, God is shown to be with those who receive spiritual consolation from the divine Scriptures through spiritual understanding.

“Therefore,” he says, “may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ.”

Here Paul, following the manner of the patriarchs and prophets whose blessings are recorded in Scripture, bestows blessings upon the Romans, praying that God may grant them to have the same mind toward one another.

Great is this blessing: that all should think and feel as one, and that each should desire for his neighbor what he desires for himself.

Would you like to know how powerful the grace of unanimity is? The Savior declares in the Gospel: “If two or three agree together concerning anything whatever that they ask from God, it will be done for them” (Matt. XVIII).

And again, speaking of himself, he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name”—that is, thinking the same thing and having the same mind in the name of Jesus Christ—“there I am in their midst” (ibid.).

Would you like another example of how Christ becomes present among those who are of one mind? See in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts I) how, after the Lord’s ascension, the eleven apostles, together with the others, raised their voice and prayed with one accord. The place where they stood was shaken, and they were deemed worthy of the presence of the Holy Spirit.

I also think that Paul does not join the names of others to his own in certain Epistles without purpose when he says, “Paul and Sosthenes the brother” (I Cor. I), and elsewhere, “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy” (I Thess. I). Rather, this shows that when two or three are united as one, the Holy Spirit draws one understanding from them and produces one utterance, so that those who wished to teach the Churches to say and think one thing should first demonstrate that they themselves said and thought one thing.

“So that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

(Ambr.) As though sent for salvation, the Apostle follows the people with a good prayer, wishing that God would grant them one understanding of wisdom according to Jesus Christ, so that they might think according to Christ’s teaching.

Then they will be able to preserve love, following the example of the Lord who says: “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends and brothers” (John XV). Thus, with one mouth and one confession, they may praise God the Father in Christ, if they exhort one another according to the mind of Christ, so that they may praise without ceasing God, who made all things through Christ and, after their fall into error, graciously raised them up and restored them again through the same one, granting a twofold benefit: mercy and knowledge.

(Orig.) “One mouth” is spoken of when one and the same understanding and speech proceeds from the mouths of different people.

The Apostle wisely added “according to Jesus Christ” when he said, “to have the same mind toward one another.” For it could happen that some might agree unanimously in wickedness and think as one toward evil. But whoever thinks according to Jesus Christ undoubtedly thinks whatever is good.

Therefore:

“Welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, for the honor of God.”

What he says, “Welcome one another,” refers to what he had proposed at the beginning, where those who held opposing opinions concerning clean and unclean foods were divided from one another. He says: “Welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you,” who recoiled from no one’s uncleanness and charged no one with his sins.

Therefore, do not judge the uncleanness of animals, just as he did not count the uncleanness of believers against them.

And whereas earlier he had said: “Let the one who eats not judge the one who does not eat, for God has welcomed him,” here he says that Christ has welcomed you, to show that being welcomed by God and being welcomed by Christ are one and the same thing.

He adds that being welcomed by Christ is also for the honor of God. For those whom Christ welcomes, he teaches to act in such a way that, when people see their good works, they may glorify the Father who is in heaven.

(Ambr.) We have been welcomed by Christ in this way: he took upon himself our weaknesses and bore our diseases, so that by this example we might strengthen one another’s weaknesses through patience, and so that the name and honor of God, having been bestowed upon us, might not be emptied of meaning. For by the grace of Christ we are called sons of God.

“For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the sake of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.”

(Orig.) There are two ways in which Christ may be understood to have been a minister of the circumcision for the establishment of the fathers’ promises.

The first is that he himself received circumcision in the flesh, so that it might be most clearly known that, coming from the seed of Abraham—to whom God had promised that all nations would be blessed in his seed (Gen. XXII; XXVI)—he fulfilled in himself what had been promised to the fathers.

This also accords with the order of the whole Epistle, in which he now restrains and suppresses those who believed from the circumcision and now those who believed from the nations, who were growing proud against one another. He teaches that those who remain occupied with observances of the Law must not be entirely judged, since Christ himself became a minister of circumcision in his flesh. He also teaches the Gentiles to understand that the Lord Christ was sent to the Jews, and that they should not become proud.

(Aug.) Because the Jews rejected what had been sent to them, the result was that the Gospel was preached to the Gentiles. This is also plainly recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles say to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word be preached to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

This accords also with the Lord’s own testimony when he says: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. XV), and again: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (ibid.).

If the Gentiles consider this carefully, they will understand, by that faith through which they now believe that all things are clean to the clean, that they ought not to insult those who may perhaps be weak among the circumcised and who, because of association with idols, dare not touch any meat at all.

(Orig.) Or he may be said to have been a minister of that circumcision concerning which the same Apostle says (Rom. II): “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; rather, he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God.”

And, according to what the same Apostle says elsewhere (Col. II): “In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh, but with the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism.”

Through this kind of circumcision, therefore, it is certain that the promises made to the fathers were fulfilled.

(Ambr.) Circumcision of the flesh was given to Abraham as a figure of circumcision of the heart. Circumcision of the heart consists in recognizing God the Creator, the Father, and his Son Christ, through whom he created all things, after the cloud of error has been removed, so that the truth of God might be fulfilled.

For he had promised that he would grant mercy, and he had promised it to the fathers of the Jews. For he had said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII).

And to David he said: “I will set the fruit of your womb upon your throne, if your sons keep my covenant, my testimonies, and the rest” (Ps. CXXXI).

And: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. XXIV).

“But for the Gentiles to glorify God because of his mercy.”

(Ambr.) Since they had received no promise, they were admitted to salvation as unworthy people solely through mercy, so that by confession they might glorify God, whom unbelievers dishonor.

“As it is written: ‘Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles, O Lord, and I will sing to your name.’”

(Ambr.) He proves this by prophetic example. For it is written in the seventeenth Psalm that the Gentiles were to be admitted to God’s grace in order to receive salvation.

These are the words of Christ, by which he foretold that his preaching would bear the fruit of confessing God’s mystery among the Gentiles. Therefore the Son gives thanks for this to the Father, because of the obedience of the Gentiles.

Hence in the Gospel he says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants, for so it was well pleasing before you” (Matt. XI).

This confession, therefore, is of the one God in the Trinity. From it arises joy, so that after confessing the truth he may joyfully sing of God’s mercy and gift.

And again he says: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people.” This is in the song of Deuteronomy.

And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and magnify him, all you peoples.” This is in the one-hundred-sixteenth Psalm.

He shows that God decreed long ago, through the intervention of his mercy, to make Jews and Gentiles harmonious, so that the Gentiles, having obtained grace, might become companions of the Jews, who themselves had once been called his people by God’s gift.

But now the Jews are noble, while these others, formerly ignoble, have been ennobled through mercy, so that all may rejoice together in the recognition of the truth. While the Gentiles praise him, let all peoples magnify God—the twelve tribes magnifying one God, who increased the number of his people by adding the Gentiles.

Finally, when the Jews argued against the apostle Peter concerning Cornelius, after he gave them his explanation they assented, magnifying the Lord and saying: “Perhaps God has also granted repentance to the Gentiles for the attainment of life” (Acts XI).

And again Isaiah says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises up to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope” (Isa. XI).

To give the Gentiles greater confidence and an unquestionable hope, he confirms by many testimonies that God’s decree was that all nations should be blessed in Christ. Thus the insolence of the unbelieving Jews would not grieve them or make the souls of believing Gentiles doubtful, as though they promised themselves hope in vain because Jewish faith is borne by the God received by Abraham [the Latin is uncertain]. In this way they would grow in joy and security.

Why, however, did Christ arise from the root of Jesse and not from the root of Boaz, the righteous man, or from the root of Obed?

Perhaps because he is called the son of David on account of the kingdom: just as, being born from God, he was born king, so also according to the flesh he would have his origin from David the king.

Therefore Jesse is the root of the tree of David, which bore fruit through the branch that is Mary the Virgin, who gave birth to Christ.

(Orig.) But it seemed better to discuss this statement concerning the root of Jesse in the exposition of Isaiah himself.

Nevertheless, in the present passage one may say that Jesse is interpreted in our language as “he is for me.” At Christ’s coming, therefore, everyone who believes in him rightly says, “He is for me.”

For the one of whom Moses said, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III), is himself “for me”—that is, I believe in the one who is, not in one who was made from nothing, as the impious wish, but in the one who is and always is.

This is his name, and he is the one who arose from the root of Jesse, and in him the Gentiles will hope.

Because of this mercy, which they have received from him, the one who always was is born from the root of Jesse to grant salvation to the Gentiles. For this mercy bestowed upon them, I say, the Gentiles glorify and magnify God.

“Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

(Orig.) Earlier he had said that it is written in Isaiah, “In him the Gentiles shall hope.” Gladly he added, “Now may the God of hope,” and the rest.

For if it had been written, “In him the Gentiles shall believe,” he would undoubtedly have added, “Now may the God of faith.” But because the Gentiles hope, he invokes the God of hope upon those who hope in him, praying that the gift of blessing may be increased for them by him.

The blessing is of this kind: “that they may be filled with all joy and all peace.”

Similarly, the Prophet says in one passage: “In his days righteousness and an abundance of peace shall arise, until the moon is taken away” (Ps. LXXI).

But since these things are said about Christ, we can rightly understand in him the abundance of peace, because through the blood of his cross he made peace not only the things on earth but also the things in heaven (Col. I).

How this prayer of the Apostle—that they may be filled with all joy and all peace—can be fulfilled in every respect seems difficult for me to explain, especially since the Apostle himself says that, among the things he attained through the grace of the Spirit, he knows and prophesies only in part (I Cor. XIII).

I think, however, that believers can possess the fullness of peace when they are reconciled to God the Father through faith, according to Paul’s word (II Cor. V): “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.”

They also possess it when they are restored to peace with the Son of God through the blood of his cross, and when they are joined to the Holy Spirit after cleansing themselves from every defilement and becoming holy vessels.

Thus someone may finally be considered filled with all peace if he believes in the fullness of the Trinity.

For this reason the Apostle adds and says: “May he fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

For if the believer is fortified by the power of the Holy Spirit, it is certain that he always possesses the fullness of joy and the fullness of peace.

“I myself am confident about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.”

(Orig.) By the same reasoning with which we said above that believers are filled with all joy and all peace, here also he confirms that those to whom he is speaking are full of goodness and all knowledge.

(Ambr.) These words are exhortative. By praising them he urges them toward better understanding and conduct. For whoever sees himself praised works diligently so that what is said may be true.

Therefore he did not say merely that they should teach one another, but also that they should admonish one another. What is known sometimes slips away from the mind; admonition is accustomed to bring it back.

(Orig.) Here he shows that each person ought, in what he has learned, also to admonish another, and that they should hold such conversations with fellow disciples that they admonish and edify one another.

Mutual exchange can contribute greatly to learning if it is conducted with love, and if, concerning deeper or more obscure matters, one seeks the judgment of the learned and perfect, according to what Moses also says: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will speak to you.”

“But I have written to you somewhat more boldly, brothers, partly as reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, to be a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.”

As one who is conscious that throughout the whole Epistle he has sometimes addressed those who are from the circumcision and at other times those who have believed from the Gentiles, and that he has touched upon some of the more secret and profound mysteries, revealing many things that had been hidden in his effort to give an account of them—although in each case he observed the dispensation of the word with careful moderation, indicating some things and weaving together again a great many others—he therefore says: “But I have written to you somewhat more boldly, partly as reminding you through the grace that has been given to me.”

Do you hear the Apostle saying, “I have written partly”? Therefore let no one be angry with us if we are unable to explain fully the meaning of the divine mysteries, when he hears that the one who handed these very things down to us handed them down only in part.

Nor should anyone walk about puffed up under the title of knowledge, as though he had understood everything, when Paul himself—the one from whom the word of knowledge has been transmitted to us—says that he writes and knows only in part.

I nevertheless think that, although Paul himself confesses that he knows only in part, he knew many more things—indeed, far more—than he wrote. It was as though he knew many things but did not dare to disclose many of them; therefore he says that he had dared to commit at least some things to writing.

When he says, “reminding you through the grace that has been given to me,” he indicates that he had already spoken to them about such matters and had often discussed the mysteries.

But because what is said only in speech is easily intercepted by forgetfulness, he says: Through these few things that I have written by the grace given to me, I recall to you those matters that I have often discussed with you at greater length.

We have already spoken above about the grace that Paul mentions as having been given to him. He says that this grace was given to him for this purpose: “to be,” he says, “a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles, sanctifying the Gospel of God.”

What we have as “sanctifying the Gospel of God,” the Greeks express more grandly as ἱερουργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, which, although not fully expressed by us, could be rendered “sacrificing the Gospel of God.” By this it is shown that announcing the Gospel is a priestly [sacrificial] work.

For this reason he adds: “so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit,” namely, so that the Gentiles may be offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice when, believing in Christ through the Gospel, they are sanctified.

As he says above: “Therefore I beseech you, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.”

Just as priests, when they offered sacrifices, necessarily had to ensure that the victim had no blemish, disgrace, or defect, so that it might be acceptable and pleasing to God, so also the person who sacrifices the Gospel and proclaims the word of God must take every possible care that no blemish arise in his preaching, no defect in his teaching, and no fault in his instruction.

Rather, so to speak, if possible, he must first sacrifice himself; he must first slaughter his own vices and put his own sins to death, so that through his offering he may make the salvation of his disciples acceptable to God not only through his teaching but also through the example of his life.

“Sanctified,” he says, “in the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit is the source of sanctification. Therefore the offering of the Gentiles, which is offered through Paul as the sanctifier, is said to be made acceptable to God not through observance of the Law but through the Holy Spirit.

I therefore have glory in Christ Jesus before God. For I would not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit.

True glory before God is only that which is in Christ. To glory in God without Christ is like someone saying that he can have glory before God without righteousness, without wisdom, and without truth; for Christ is all these things, and therefore true glory before God is found in Christ alone. This is like what he himself says elsewhere [Col. 1599D]: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” We have already discussed at greater length how blameworthy is every glory that lies outside Christ—for example, in riches, worldly honors, or the wisdom of this world, and in the other arts that are outside Christ. It should certainly be understood that here the Latins have used *gloria* for *gloriatio* (“glory” for “glorying”).

(Ambr.) He says that he has glory before God through Christ Jesus. For by believing in and serving Christ Jesus with a pure conscience, he acquired merit before God the Father, to such an extent that he says nothing is lacking which Christ did not accomplish through him for the exhortation of the Gentiles, giving signs and wonders through his hands, so that the power of his preaching might commend it.

(Orig.) [Col. 1600A] “The things I speak,” he says, “are not words belonging to another’s work, nor do I become the praiser of deeds belonging to others; rather, I write to you the things which I know Christ accomplished through me, which he fulfilled in me for the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed”—by the word of preaching, and by the work of signs and wonders.

We have already explained elsewhere at greater length what difference there is between signs and wonders, and here we shall set it forth more briefly. Signs are called those things in which, although there is something marvelous, something future is also indicated. Wonders, however, are those in which only something marvelous is displayed. He therefore said “signs and wonders” as though the expression contained both. Divine Scripture sometimes observes these distinctions, but at other times uses the terms loosely, putting “wonders” for “signs” and “signs” for “wonders.”

These matters should be observed and carefully maintained by the leaders of the churches [Col. 1600B], so that they may neither appear to speak of anything Christ has not accomplished through them, nor disfigure the labors and zeal of others. Someone speaks of things Christ has not accomplished through him in this way: if he speaks about continence and teaches it although he himself is not continent; or if he speaks about sobriety, justice, distributing wealth, and despising possessions for the sake of the kingdom of God, while Christ has accomplished none of these things in the very person who teaches them. For this reason the Apostle presents his own example and says that he speaks and preaches to others the things which Christ first fulfilled through him.

Thus, from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum, I have filled the Gospel of Christ. And I have made it my ambition to preach the Gospel not where Christ has already been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation.

[Col. 1600C] Paul, therefore, by the power of signs and wonders—which he performed in the power of the Holy Spirit—filled the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. God had given Moses and Aaron the power of signs and wonders, as it is written: “He placed in them the words of signs and wonders in the land of Canaan” (Psalm 104), so that, after chastising Egypt, they might free the children of Israel. Yet they were scarcely and only rarely able to convert anyone from the Egyptian people. Paul, having received the power of signs and wonders, converted not one nation, nor two or three peoples, but all the nations and peoples from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum, through the preaching of the word and through the power of works and mighty deeds, to the mysteries of Christ.

[Col. 1600D] He preached this Gospel in such a way that he did not insert his own discourse into the labors of others or add anything to another’s preaching, lest, where another had laid the foundations of faith, he himself should impose the structure of his own preaching and appear to steal the glory of another’s work.

(Ambr.) It is not without reason that he says he strives to preach there where Christ has not been named. For he knew that the false apostles were presenting Christ differently from what was proper. They went about for this purpose: under the name of Christ, they might enslave the people to other doctrines. Correcting this afterward was a work of the greatest difficulty. Therefore he wished to anticipate them, delivering to his hearers words of purified preaching, so that an unbroken and well-ordered surface might preserve the strength of the sound foundation. And since he had been appointed teacher of the Gentiles, he had to take careful care to teach there where Christ had not been proclaimed, so that he might both establish his authority and receive the full fruit of his labors from what he had planted.

[Col. 1601A] This is why he occupied all the places belonging to the Church. For afterward heresies, malignantly employing subtlety under the name of Christ, tried to corrupt the meaning of the law and the faith. He warned of this by the testimony of the law, saying: “But as it is written: ‘Those to whom he was not announced shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.’”

(Orig.) [Col. 1601B] The Apostle therefore carefully observed that, in accordance with prophetic speech, he should announce Christ to those to whom no one had announced him, so that they might understand concerning him what they had previously learned from no one. And this, I think, was the reason that frequently prevented him from proceeding to Rome, although he had been planning to go there. As he says: “For this reason also I was very much hindered from coming to you”; not, as he says elsewhere, hindered by Satan (1 Thessalonians 2), but detained by the task of founding churches, and founding them in places where no foundation of faith had preceded.

The example is taken from Isaiah and is given in the very words in which it is read in the prophet.

But now, having no further opportunity in these regions, and having had for many years a desire to come to you, when I begin my journey to Spain I hope to see you in passing and to be sent on my way there by you, after I have first enjoyed your company for a while.

[Col. 1601C] He seems to say this while situated in Achaia, near Corinth, as we have already demonstrated, to the best of our ability, in the earlier parts of the Epistle. Achaia is indeed near to and contiguous with Macedonia. Having lived in these regions and traversed each place, preaching the Gospel only within those boundaries where Christ had not previously been preached, and having filled everything with the knowledge of God, he says that he no longer has a place in these regions—that is, no place remains there for him where the preaching of Christ is lacking. He indicates that the time has now come when he should fulfill his desire to see those who are in Rome, a desire which he had carried within him for many years but which had been postponed and set aside until he had filled with the knowledge of the Gospel every place where Christ had not been preached.

(Ambr.) [Col. 1601D] He recalls what he said at the beginning of the Epistle: “I often intended to come to you, and I have been hindered until now.” Now he makes clear the reason why he was hindered: although he wished to come, he was doing something else that was pressing upon him, namely, excluding the corrupt arguments of the false apostles. Finally, after preaching throughout all the surrounding regions, he says that he is now free to come to Rome, which he had long desired.

He therefore corrects the Romans through the Epistle for the present, because they had been brought under the law. But those who had not yet heard the preaching would more profitably be taught by his presence, so that, being founded on the right faith, they might be less likely to accept something else. Nevertheless, he promised that he would come at the time when he was going to Spain, because Christ had not been preached there and he wished to occupy their minds. Since the journey was difficult for the false apostles, there would be no inconvenience if he went there later.

(Orig.) [Col. 1602A] When he says, “When I depart for Spain, I hope to see you in passing,” this should not be understood as though Paul felt so little love for the Romans that he judged them worthy to be seen only while passing through and then proceeding elsewhere. Consider what he adds afterward: “When I have first enjoyed your company for a while.” In this he seems to place in their power the time when the journey he had planned should be extended. In this way he somehow invites and nourishes their love for him: if they themselves are insatiable in their affection for the Apostle, they should know that he too intends not to depart from them or go to others before enjoying their love. Yet he anticipates that this love will be so great that it cannot be fully satisfied by his presence; hence he says, “for a while.”

[Col. 1602B] For he warns that in all circumstances the necessity of evangelizing must take precedence. Appropriately, therefore, he promises his presence and a somewhat longer stay to those whom he had not yet seen according to the flesh and to whom he had not yet come bodily. We receive goods more eagerly when we quickly fear that they will be taken away; but we neglect more securely what we think we shall retain for a longer time. He so nourishes the Romans’ affection for him and places his stay at their disposal that he says he is to be sent on his way by them to Spain, and to be sent only after he has first satisfied their love. If they show themselves especially eager, they will themselves give the Apostle reasons to remain longer.

[Col. 1602C] Now, however, I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have decided to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. For they have decided to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to minister to them in material things.

We can speak about this more fully from the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, in which he writes as follows: “We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia: in the midst of much testing through tribulation, their abundance of joy and their profound poverty overflowed into the riches of their generosity. For I bear witness that, according to their ability and beyond their ability, of their own accord, with many entreaties, they begged us for the grace and fellowship that is given to the saints,” and so forth (2 Corinthians 8).

[Col. 1602D] And just as in this passage he bears witness to the Macedonians, so again he exhorts the Corinthians, saying: “As you abound in everything—in faith, in word, in knowledge, and in your love for us—so you should abound in this grace also,” and so forth. In other passages as well, praising the Corinthians because they had been ready with regard to the fellowship of the poor in Jerusalem, he says: “I give an opinion in this matter, for this is expedient for you, who began not only to do but also to desire it from the previous year; now, therefore, complete it in deed.” Elsewhere, continuing his discussion of this same fellowship with the saints, he adds: “Concerning the ministry that is being performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you to the Macedonians, because Achaia has been prepared since the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up many” (2 Corinthians 8–9).

[Col. 1603A] That after this ministry of Macedonia and Achaia, which was performed for the saints in Jerusalem, the Apostle also proposed to see Rome is indicated in the Acts of the Apostles in this way: “When these things had been completed, Paul resolved in the Holy Spirit that, after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, he should go to Jerusalem, saying, ‘After I have been there, I must also see Rome’” (Acts 19).

[Col. 1603B] From all these words it is gathered that not only the First Epistle to the Corinthians but also the Second was written before this Epistle to the Romans that we now have in hand. At the same time, one observes that the later Paul is found in each Epistle, the more perfect he is, so that the saying he uttered may prove true: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling toward perfection” (Philippians 3).

When he says, “Macedonia and Achaia have decided to make some contribution for the poor among the saints,” he subtly and modestly exhorts the Romans while praising the Corinthians. Devoted minds are more easily invited to do good by examples than by words. But when he adds, “They have decided to do so, and they are their debtors,” what else does he wish the Romans to understand except that, if the Achaeans and Macedonians are debtors to the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem, the Romans likewise—who hold the faith of Christ—should recognize that they too have become debtors to these same people?

[Col. 1603C] For the Macedonians and Achaeans alone have not shared in the spiritual blessings of the saints who are in Jerusalem, so that they alone should owe them service in material things; the Romans have shared in them as well, and therefore are debtors under the same condition. But he speaks only of the former, so that the latter may know that they too are subject to the same judgment.

(Ambr.) He calls them debtors to the believing Jews, so that, just as they have shared in their spiritual blessings, they too may share in their bodily needs. In this way the believing Jews may rejoice and praise the providence of God in their salvation through the ministry of the Gentiles. These people, devoting themselves wholly to divine service and caring nothing for worldly things, offered believers an example of good conduct.

[Col. 1603D] Indeed, the Apostle wishes us to be so humane and merciful that he calls us debtors with regard to giving alms and practicing good works with a cheerful heart. For the one who hopes for mercy from God ought to be merciful, so that he may prove that he rightly hopes for it: if a human being shows mercy, how much more does God! This is the repayment, or reward: that those who receive mercy should show mercy. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matthew 5).

When, therefore, I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I shall depart through you to Spain. And I know that, when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ.

(Orig.) [Col. 1604A] See with what great caution he promises that he will seal the fruit of those who offer it. With what seal, do you suppose, does the Apostle seal the fruit of the holy work? I think with the seal in which the image of God is expressed—that is, so that in completing the work there may be no admixture of another’s manner of life, and that praise from human beings may not be sought; rather, the one who gives should give in simplicity of heart and not out of sorrow, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9). Whoever observes these and similar principles in the work of God seals his work with the seal of the divine image.

“When I have completed this,” he says, “then I shall depart through you to Spain.” He promises the Romans a great gift and says: “I know that, when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ.” He makes this promise only through the Holy Spirit and the grace of prophecy. For it is beyond human capacity to know future things—to know not only that he will come to them in the blessing of Christ, but that he will come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing. In this he indicates both the grace of the one who comes and the merits of those who receive him.

(Ambr.) [Col. 1604B] Being certain of God’s purpose and grace, he promised that he would come in the abundance of the blessing of the one whom he proclaims as Christ. This blessing is the power of signs, by which they were strengthened.

I appeal to you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, so that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea and so that the offering of my service may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem; that I may come to you with joy by the will of God and may find refreshment with you.

(Orig.) [Col. 1604C] Although earlier he said, “I know that, when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ,” nevertheless he also knew that prayer was necessary even in those things which he clearly knew were going to happen. For example, if prayer had not been offered, what had been prophesied would undoubtedly not have been fulfilled.

(Ambr.) Finally, he prays that he may be helped through their prayers, so that he may escape the hands of the unbelieving Jews—not because he himself deserves less, but because he follows the proper order, according to which the Church should pray for its own leader. For many who are insignificant, when gathered together in unity, become great, and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain what they ask.

[Col. 1604D] Who, then, reading this—that Paul asks those who are in Rome to pray for him—would despise or regard as unworthy the request for the Church’s prayers, even if those from whom prayer is requested seem to be inferior in merit? For here Paul, endowed with apostolic merits, not only asks the Romans to pray for him but also urges the Corinthians to do so.

(Orig.) Observe also with what powerful and sacred pledges he binds them: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” he says, “and through the love of the Spirit, I beg you to help me in your prayers to God.” What our translators rendered, “Help me in your prayers,” is more magnificently expressed among the Greeks by συναγωνίσασθαι (*synagōnisasthai*), “to contend together with me,” indicating: “Help me in the contest of prayer to God.” He shows that he himself has a contest and struggle of prayer, with those undoubtedly opposing him of whom he says: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 4).

[Col. 1605A] It is certain that all these powers, just as they oppose faith and resist godliness, and just as they are hostile to righteousness, truth, and every good thing, likewise undoubtedly resist and oppose prayer. Therefore Paul shows that there is no small struggle even in prayer, since in this struggle he believes that the help of those who are in Rome must also be implored.

For demons and hostile powers oppose prayer, first by preventing the one who labors in the contest of prayer from being found worthy to lift up pure hands without anger. Even if someone succeeds in obtaining this condition, namely, to be without anger, it is scarcely possible for him to be free from dispute—that is, from superfluous and vain thoughts [Col. 1605B]. For you will scarcely find anyone at prayer who is not visited by some empty or alien thought that turns aside and breaks the attention by which the mind is directed toward God, carrying it away through things that are unfitting.

Therefore prayer is a great contest: while enemies oppose and drag the mind of the one praying in different directions, the mind must always strive toward God with fixed and steady intention, so that the one praying may rightly say: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” (2 Timothy 4).

The Apostle therefore now prays to be helped in the contest of prayers, so that he may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, lest, being detained too long by their obstacles, he either present his ministry to the saints as less acceptable or delay for too long his desire to visit the Romans.

[Col. 1605C] “For if,” he says, “things proceed in such a way that my ministry is acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, and that, after being delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, I am not prevented from coming to you, I shall surely come to you rejoicing in the successful outcome, according to the will of God, and I shall find rest with you.” Paul is not seeking bodily rest, but that rest which brings consolation from God, just as he himself said earlier in this Epistle: “To be comforted among you through the faith that we share with one another, yours and mine.”

May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

He bestows a great blessing upon the Romans, praying that the God of peace may be with them—that is, that “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard their hearts in Christ Jesus, who is our peace.”

(Ambr.) He wishes them to be such people that the Lord Jesus Christ may be with them—he who, having cut away every discord arising from human error, gave and revealed what is true, so that they might remain peaceful in that very truth.

[Col. 1605D]

## CHAPTER XVI

He gives certain examples of good people and urges perseverance.

I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the church at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she herself also has assisted many, and me personally.

(Orig.) [Col. 1606A] This passage teaches, with apostolic authority, that women too are appointed to the ministry of the Church. Paul speaks of Phoebe, who held this office in the church at Cenchreae, with great praise and commendation. He enumerates her distinguished deeds, saying that she assisted everyone so greatly—that is, she was present in their necessities—that she also assisted me personally in my necessities and apostolic labors with complete devotion of mind.

Her work may be compared with the hospitality of Lot, who, because he always received strangers, once deserved to receive angels as guests (Genesis 19). Likewise Abraham, because he was always ready to welcome strangers, deserved that the Lord should turn aside with the angels to his tent (Genesis 18). So this religious Phoebe, because she assisted and served everyone, deserved also to assist and serve the Apostle.

Thus this passage teaches two things at once: that women, as we have said, are to be ministers in the Church, and that such women should be appointed to the ministry as have assisted many and, through good services, have deserved to attain even apostolic praise. [Col. 1606B] It also urges that those who devote themselves to good works in the churches should receive in return from the brothers both assistance and honor, so that, whenever necessary, whether in spiritual or even material services, they may be treated honorably.

(Ambr.) To persuade them to receive her without delay and assist her in her necessity, should she encounter it, he also testifies that she had assisted him, so that, the more exalted her person was in comparison with others, the more clearly he might show that the service owed to her should be rendered through love.

Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life. Not only I give thanks to them, but also all the churches of the Gentiles, and likewise the church in their house.

(Orig.) [Col. 1606C] It seems to me that these are the people of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “After this Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. Finding there a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy, together with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, he approached them. Since they practiced the same trade, he stayed with them and worked with them; for they were tentmakers” (Acts 18)—that is, shoemakers.

(Ambr.) Having become fellow workers with the Apostle, they believed so rightly that they themselves also exhorted others to the true faith. Indeed, although Apollos was well trained in the Scriptures, he was instructed by them more carefully in the way of the Lord. Therefore he calls them his fellow workers, but “in Christ Jesus,” for they were his co-workers in the Gospel of God.

[Col. 1606D] Aquila was the husband of Priscilla. It is clear that they did not come to Rome without purpose, for they were especially devoted to God. For the strengthening of the Romans, all those whom he greets here are understood to have belonged to this group. Hence he says that not only he but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks to them, thereby also touching upon the Romans, so that they may obey those whom they hear laboring for the progress of the Gentiles and for the encouragement of faith in Christ.

(Orig.) It is no wonder that Paul writes “Prisca” in the Epistle, whereas in the Acts of the Apostles she is written “Priscilla,” since the other details agree. It may be that those who at that time came to Corinth after the Jews had been expelled from the city by the emperor’s edict (*praeceptum*; variant *praecepto*) later returned to Rome [Col. 1607A] when the violence of the decree had ceased, and that Paul now greets them. Yet it is apparent that, when Paul was in danger because of the plots of the Jews, they exposed themselves on his behalf so that he might depart safely.

The Acts of the Apostles reports that a certain Jason did the same (Acts 17). The Apostle does not conceal their praise but transmits it for the admiration of all the churches. Therefore he says: “Not only I give thanks to them, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.”

It is consequently evident that they were dutiful and hospitable toward all the faithful brothers—not only those who had believed from the Jews but also those who had believed from the Gentiles. Great grace is found in the practice of hospitality, not only before God but also among human beings.

[Col. 1607B] Since this service depended not only upon the will and intention of the masters of the house but also upon the willing and faithful ministry of their servants, he called all those who faithfully fulfilled this ministry with them “the church in their house.”

Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ Jesus.

This Epaenetus seems to me to have been the first of all in Asia to believe. Hence he called him the beginning of the Church—or, as it is in Greek, the firstfruits of Asia—unless this expression signifies something deeper, so that we understand the angels of God, who preside over the churches, to offer to God as firstfruits each of those who believe.

Among them, however, those are judged to be firstfruits not who are first in time, but who excel in virtues and merits. Knowing through the Spirit Paul’s election concerning Epaenetus [Col. 1607C], and that the election of the angels had found him among the whole number of the faithful in Asia, he called him the firstfruits of Asia.

In another Epistle as well he speaks of certain people as the firstfruits of Achaia, undoubtedly recognizing the same sacramental principle in them.

Greet Mary, who has labored much for you.

(Ambr.) He reminds them by name of Mary, whom we understand to have labored especially for their encouragement, so that they may give thanks to her.

(Orig.) He also teaches that women ought to labor for the churches of God. For they labor when they teach young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to raise their children, to be modest and chaste, to manage their households well, to be kind, submissive to their husbands, to receive strangers hospitably, to wash the feet of the saints, and to practice all the other duties that are recorded concerning women’s responsibilities, in every form of chastity.

[Col. 1607D] Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and fellow prisoners, who are distinguished among the apostles and were in Christ before me.

(Ambr.) He calls them his kinsmen both according to the flesh and according to the spirit, just as the angel said to Mary: “And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman,” and so forth. He declares with his testimony that they also served the earlier apostles and suffered captivity with him for the sake of the faith, and therefore they are to be honored more fully.

(Orig.) It is possible to understand this also: perhaps they were among the seventy-two who are themselves called apostles. For this reason he calls them distinguished among the apostles, namely, among those apostles who were before him.

But I am also moved by the fact that he says, “my fellow prisoners.” What captivity of Paul was there in which he testifies that Andronicus and Junia were fellow prisoners with him? [Col. 1608A] Unless, perhaps, in a deeper mystery we should look to that captivity which Christ came to release, concerning which it is written (Isaiah 61) that he came “to grant release to captives and sight to the blind.” In that captivity these people seemed to be held in the same manner as Paul.

For example, if we say that when the people of Israel were captives among the Assyrians or Babylonians, all certainly appeared to be captives, but the reason for the captivity of the others differed from that of Daniel, Ananiah, Azariah, and Mishael (Daniel 4): the others were captives because of their sins, whereas these, for the consolation of the captives, were themselves also captives. Therefore, if Daniel had called some one person from the common people “my fellow prisoner,” it would not have seemed as fitting as if he had said this of Ananiah, Azariah, and Mishael; for in the latter there was one and the same reason for captivity, entirely different from that of the rest of the people.

[Col. 1608B] So Paul too, contemplating some such matter concerning himself, Andronicus, and Junia according to the meaning of the hidden mystery, calls them his fellow prisoners in this world and distinguished among the apostles.

Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

(Ambr.) He greets him as a friend, but as a friend in the Lord—not, however, as one who had shared his labor or captivity.

(Orig.) Although he seems to attribute no particular distinction to him in his praise beyond the others, nevertheless, by the very fact that he was beloved by Paul, he is made worthy of praise and worthy of this greeting.

Greet Urbanus, my fellow worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved.

He joins these two in his greeting, but places Urbanus before him in praise. For he calls the former a fellow worker in Christ, whereas Stachys is merely his personal beloved, as he also called Ampliatus. A fellow worker of the Apostle in Christ is understood to be nothing other than a participant in apostolic work.

[Col. 1608C] Greet Apelles, approved in Christ.

I think that this Apelles passed patiently through many tribulations and endured them bravely. For this reason the Apostle pronounced him approved, in accordance with what he himself said elsewhere (Romans 5): “Tribulation produces patience; patience, proven character; and proven character, hope.”

It should certainly be considered whether this is perhaps the same man who is called Apollos in the Acts of the Apostles—a native of Alexandria, learned in the Scriptures.

Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.

[Col. 1608D] Since nothing is added or omitted casually in the Apostle’s writings, he does not without reason call these people, who are from the household or family of Aristobulus, either beloved, approved, or fellow workers in Christ. Perhaps because they possessed none of these merits, he honored them only with the title of his greeting.

(Ambr.) This Aristobulus is understood to have been one who gathered brothers together in Christ. He approves his action in such a way that he designates those whom he gathered as worthy of his greeting.

Greet Herodion, my kinsman.

(Orig.) He too, like Andronicus and Junia, is called Paul’s kinsman. But he is not called a fellow prisoner as they are, nor is he called distinguished among the apostles—among those who were in Christ before Paul. Hence it should be understood that even among those whom Paul calls his kinsmen there is great difference, according to the principle which, as I think, we attempted to explain above.

Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.

(Ambr.) [Col. 1609A] This Narcissus is said to have been a presbyter at that time, as is read in other copies. Since he was not present, you see why he greets as holy those who were from his household, greeting them “in the Lord.” This Narcissus therefore performed the office of a presbyter among those living away from home, strengthening believers by his exhortations. Because the Apostle did not know the merits of those who were with him, he said: “Greet those who belong to the household of Narcissus in the Lord”—that is, greet in my name those among them whom you know to be worthy of my greeting, those who have placed their hope in the Lord.

Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.

(Orig.) [Col. 1609B] He gives good testimony concerning these women, whose labor he testifies to be not the labor of this world or of ordinary life, but labor in the Lord. For many labor, but it is not established that everyone’s labor is in the Lord.

Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored greatly in the Lord. (Ambrosiaster) She seems to have been placed before those mentioned above because she labored greatly in the Lord. This labor consists in exhortation, in service to the saints, in affliction, and in poverty for Christ’s sake, since they were abandoning their homes after being driven out and were objects of reproach to unbelievers.

Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother—and mine. He placed this Rufus before his mother because of the distinction of his administration of God’s grace, in which a woman has no place. For he was chosen, that is, advanced by the Lord to conduct his affairs. (Origen) Yet he had a mother so holy that the Apostle called her his own mother as well. I do not think that in these greetings the differences of praise and salutation assigned to each person are made without purpose. Whoever knows that Christ speaks through Paul is certain that, according to merit, one person is called approved by him, another beloved, another one who labors in the Lord, another one who labors greatly in the Lord, and another chosen.

This Rufus, of whom we have no further discussion, is greeted as chosen in the Lord because, I believe, Paul knew that he belonged not to the number of the many who are called, but of the few who are chosen. He also regarded Rufus’s mother as possessing such great merit that Paul called her his own mother, sharing with her—as Jesus did with John—the affection of a son toward his mother.

Greet Asyncretus [Asyncritus], Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. (Ambrosiaster) He greets these together because he knew them to be united in Christ, that is, joined in Christian friendship. He also greets together the brothers who were with them, whose names he has omitted. (Origen) Still, suppose that this Hermas is the author of the little book called *The Shepherd*. That writing seems to me very useful and, as I think, divinely inspired. But since he ascribed no praise to him, I believe the reason is that, as that writing itself indicates, he seems to have turned to repentance after many sins. Therefore he wrote no reproach against him, for he had learned from Scripture (Ecclesiasticus 8) not to reproach a person who turns away from sin. Nor did he attribute any praise to him, because Hermas was still placed under the angel of repentance, by whom, at the proper time, he was to be offered again to Christ. It is understood that these people lived together, since their greetings are joined.

Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olym—Olympiaden, and all the saints who are with them. (Ambrosiaster) All these are understood to have been of one mind; for this reason he greets them together. Their merit is recognized from those who were with them: he calls them saints, so that it may appear that he greets them deservedly. (Origen) It may be that Philologus and Julia were husband and wife, and that the others were their household members, to whom the simple greeting is directed.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. (Ambrosiaster) He commands all to whom he writes and whom he names to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, in the peace of Christ, not in carnal desire but in the Holy Spirit, so that the kisses may be religious, not carnal. (Origen) From this statement and several others like it, the custom was handed down to the churches that, after prayers, the brothers should receive one another with a kiss.

The Apostle calls this a holy kiss for two reasons: first, so that the kisses given in the churches may be chaste; second, so that they may not be feigned, as Judas’s was—he gave a kiss with his lips while plotting betrayal in his heart. A faithful kiss, then, should first be chaste, and finally should possess peace and sincerity in unfeigned love.

All the churches of Christ greet you. Is Paul not writing this while situated in one church? How, then, is it true that he sends the greetings of all the churches together to the church at Rome? We must understand either that one Spirit was in Paul and in all the churches of Christ, or that he says they greet the Romans because they are joined by faith and the Spirit. (Ambrosiaster) This also implies that there is a church that does not belong to Christ; hence David calls the conspiracy of the wicked “the church of the malicious.” He therefore says that the churches of all those places greet them, so that they may grow in faith. He refers this to the preceding meaning, to show that Christ is the one in whom salvation exists, that the faithful people belong to him, and that every creature lives by his will; for he is the author of life.

I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who create dissensions and stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly, and by their smooth words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.
