[Col. 1610D] He is understood to speak of those about whom he also wrote to Timothy, saying: “As I urged you to remain in Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might charge certain persons not to teach differently, nor to attend to myths and endless genealogies, which produce questions rather than God’s edification, which is in faith.” And to Titus: “For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those from the circumcision, who must be refuted. They overturn whole households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain.” One of their own prophets said of them: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.” To this refers what he says here: “For they do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly.” Of such people it is said elsewhere: “Their god is their belly.”

(Ambrosiaster) He is speaking of the persons of the false apostles, whom throughout the Epistle he warned them to avoid, as he does now, though without openly exposing their tradition he restrained it. They compelled believers to Judaize, so that they might make God’s benefit toward them fruitless, as I mentioned above. For they fitted together discourses composed of genealogical expressions to commend their tradition, through which they deceived the hearts of the simple.

(Origen) Paul must be understood to be writing these things through the Holy Spirit both to those who preside over the churches and to all believers, so that they may examine more carefully and discern who are the people who generate dissensions and stumbling-blocks in the churches, and who are strangers to that blessedness which God promised: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). For this, he says, you learned from the Lord through the Gospel: to be peacemakers. But to stir up dissensions or scandals is contrary to the teaching that you learned. Therefore let the person who stirs up disputes, sows quarrels, provokes lawsuits, and practices contentiousness be alien to you and not be received among you. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord, who is our peace, but their own belly.

The Spirit also reveals the reason why quarrels and lawsuits are stirred up in the churches: “for the sake of the belly,” he says—that is, for gain and greed. Hence certain people go around the houses speaking flattering words, with every kind of adulation and deceit—not to build souls toward virtue through the word of God, but to persuade them, by flattering and pleasant speeches, to remain or even advance in vices. They praise and call good those things that deserve correction, “making light darkness and darkness light, bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isaiah 5), and by these means they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Therefore one must carefully attend to the disposition [or: outlook] with which the teacher teaches: whether he seeks favor and honor from his hearers, or expects a reward from the Lord for the instruction and progress of those who are learning.

For your obedience has become known everywhere. I therefore rejoice over you, and I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil. (Origen) Paul subtly points out the undiscerning and overly ready obedience of the Romans, asserting that it is not merely praised everywhere but widely known. Yet, lest he make them disobedient again by criticizing them too openly on this account, he adds, “I therefore rejoice over you.”

But someone may say: How does he criticize their obedience as commonplace when he says that he rejoices over them? First, it is one thing to criticize a vice and another to criticize the people. It may be that he rejoiced in them because he had found many other good qualities in them, while he points out the vice that displeased him, so that they would not think that he too approved of it along with the rest.

The Apostle may also have said that he rejoiced in them for this reason: an obedient person can be led toward either evil or good, whereas a disobedient person can be led toward neither. If an obedient person is led toward useless things, the fault lies in ignorance, for he does not know that the things to which he offers his obedience are useless. But once he has learned which things are useless, possessing the good of readiness to obey, he immediately ascends by that virtue along the path of righteousness.

Paul therefore rejoices over those who obey, confident that, once he has taught them not to use the indiscriminate obedience that they heedlessly offer to everyone, but only that obedience by which one ought to obey God rather than human beings, they will abandon the rest and use this alone. Indeed, it is no small matter of discernment, but the mark of a tested and well-trained judgment, to know whose word or deed should be obeyed and whose resisted.

Finally, the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Beware of those who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7). Therefore an alert understanding and attentive mind are required—one able to recognize either the simplicity of a sheep lying openly before it or the hidden rapacity of a wolf. Hence observe how near to danger those become who neglect to exercise themselves in the divine writings, since from these alone the discernment required for such examination can be learned.

Immediately, then, he presents briefly the character of the distinction he has proposed and says: Since your obedience is ready and undiscerning, receive what you ought to keep and what you ought to avoid. “I want you,” he says, “to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.” This resembles what he writes to the Corinthians: “Be infants in malice, but mature in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14). It also accords with what the Lord says: “The sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation” (Luke 16).

The sons of this age are more prudent in evil because they always discover something deeper and subtler in it, by which they may do more harm and inflict more grievous injury. But they are foolish in what is good, for they scarcely find how they may advance in goodness. Paul, on the contrary, wants us to be wise in what is good—that is, always to discover and seek something more, and to think more deeply about what good we should do. Thus, even if someone’s wickedness prevents us from performing a good deed, if we are wise we should consider how, if we cannot perform the deed, we may at least speak a good word; and if even that is not permitted, we should at least show a good intention and disposition.

Thus we ought to be wise in what is good, but innocent in what is evil. If we are struck by wickedness or injured, we should not be crafty, seeking through the arguments of a deceptive art how we might repay evil for evil and wickedness for wickedness. In such a passage we must remember the saying: “If anyone wishes to be wise according to God, let him become foolish in this world” (1 Corinthians 3). Let us therefore be foolish by accepting injury and not returning it, so that we may be wise before God, who said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12; Hebrews 10; Deuteronomy 32).

Jeremiah also says of the wicked: “They are wise in doing evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4). The Lord’s saying also refers to this: that we ought to be innocent as doves and wise as serpents (Matthew 10).

If an unbeliever should cleverly confront us and say, “How can the same person be both wise and foolish?” we shall answer: Consider the arts practiced among human beings. A grammarian is found to be utterly ignorant in the craft of building; or again, how can the most learned pilot be found ignorant in the art of medicine? In the same way, it is possible to be wise in matters pertaining to God and foolish in matters pertaining to the world.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. (Ambrosiaster) That is, shortly. He speaks of his coming, because his coming will overpower the devil, on account of the fact that these people were to receive spiritual grace. Satan envies this, because he wants human beings to remain in error, so that they may belong to one confession despite their disagreements [?].

(Origen) The question arises whom he says will be Satan, whom God will soon crush under the feet of those to whom he writes. If this refers to one person, namely the one of whom it is said in the Gospel, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10), and who is shown to be Satan opposing the human race, then, if what Paul says is true, it would appear that Satan is soon to be crushed under the feet of those to whom he was writing at that time, so that Satan would no longer exist to stir up contests, struggles, and persecutions against believers. But faith in the realities of the matter does not permit this.

It seems to me, rather, that in this passage he calls every spirit that opposes believers “Satan”; for Satan is translated in our language as “adversary.” Whatever, then, resists and opposes the soul as it strives toward God, and whatever is contrary to peace, is truly called Satan.

Therefore he first says, “the God of peace”—that is, the God who delights in peace—will crush the one who is contrary to peace and produces dissensions. Thus, too, we read in the Books of Kings (3 Kings 11) that God raised up Satan [an adversary] against Solomon to ridicule him. That is, against Solomon, who was peaceful, he raised up Satan, who is contrary to peace.

But just as he promises those whom the Apostle teaches that, if they strive and show themselves to be what his teaching describes for the purification of life, the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet, so likewise the God of peace raises up Satan—an adversary—against the person who has not preserved his peace in a pure heart and a clean conscience. Thus the one who neglects the good of peace must endure the bitterness of attacks, and, placed amid opposition, finally remember the sweetness of the peace he violated.

Let us be built up by both passages of divine Scripture: God is said to raise up Satan against the negligent, but to crush and subject him to the diligent, stirring the former toward struggles while granting the latter the palm of victory over their prostrate adversary and bestowing the rewards of virtue.

We may also say, in each individual struggle, if we contend lawfully, that God will soon crush Satan under our feet. For example, if someone undertakes the struggle of chastity and perseveres to the end with an unstained conscience, it may be said of him that he has crushed Satan under his feet—that is, the spirit that opposed chastity. Likewise, if someone undertakes the struggle of faith and, standing before kings and governors, confesses the Lord Jesus Christ with confidence and remains steadfast in that confession to the end, God has crushed Satan under his feet, since he has conquered the spirit of unbelief.

The person who persistently cultivates harmony also crushes the demon of dissension under his feet; the person who preserves gentleness tramples Satan of anger under the footsteps of patience. This is precisely what the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 10): “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.”

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. (Ambrosiaster) He now wishes the grace that he promised them at his coming to be with them. For they deserve to receive it if it is already with them in hope. (Origen) It should indeed be understood that everything human beings possess from God is grace; they possess nothing by right of debt. For “who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans 11). Grace, therefore, is everything possessed by one who did not exist and now exists, receiving it from him who always was, is, and will be forever.

Timothy, my helper, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives, greet you. It seems to me that he intended something more concerning these men, whom he set apart from the entire list of those sending greetings. Thus he calls Timothy his fellow-worker and calls all of them his relatives. Concerning Timothy, the Acts of the Apostles gives a full account: he was a Hebrew citizen, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Gentile father. Paul himself says that he asked Timothy to remain in Ephesus so that he might charge certain persons not to teach differently or attend to myths and endless genealogies.

Some also maintain that Lucius himself was Luke, who wrote the Gospel, on the grounds that names are sometimes given according to their native inflection and sometimes according to Greek or Roman usage. Jason is the man of whom it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 17) that, when crowds were stirring up a riot at Thessalonica on Paul’s and Silas’s behalf, he surrendered himself so that he might secure the apostles’ freedom to depart. I suspect that Sosipater, who is joined with these men, is the same person described in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 20) as Sosipater, son of Pyrrhus, of Beroea.

(Ambrosiaster) Timothy was his companion in labor, almost a fellow bishop, and he governed the Church with great care, being placed in danger because of the Jews. For this reason he was circumcised at the outset on account of the Jews’ offense: since his mother was Jewish, he could not be a teacher while uncircumcised. He calls the others his relatives partly on account of their lineage and partly on account of their faith.

I, Tertius, who wrote the Epistle, greet you in the Lord. Tertius is his name, not his number. He was the scribe of the Epistle, to whom Paul granted permission to greet the Roman people in his own name, just as he writes to them to greet the others whom he names. At that time there were still only a few leaders of the churches in various places.

Gaius, my host, and the whole Church greet you. This Gaius is, I think, the man to whom the Apostle John writes, rejoicing in the love he displayed toward the brotherhood by providing them with the expenses they needed. Above he says, “All the churches of Christ greet you”; now he repeats, “The whole Church greets you.” I do not think that this repetition is pointless. For so great and accommodating a man placed nothing superfluous in his writing. When he says, “All the churches of Christ greet you,” he means all the saints, as he says elsewhere, “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Galatians 5). Now he adds that these others also greet them, those who follow, to signify the blessed people of the Church, because in every Church there are two peoples.

He may also have meant the churches of two provinces, saying first “all the churches” of one place and then of another—or perhaps those of the Jews and those of the Gentiles.

Erastus, the city treasurer, and Quartus [Marcus], the brother, greet you. A treasurer—that is, a steward or administrator—is like a curator who governed the city according to the dictates of justice, especially by regulating prices. He names all these people individually in his greeting to the Romans so that they might know what sort of people, and how important, were rejoicing together with them in their good undertaking.

(Origen) I think that this is the Erastus whom he says remained at Corinth, and who seems to be identified as the city’s steward. But I do not think that Paul would have made much mention of him in his Epistle on account of this office, unless he had perceived something greater in him and called him the treasurer—that is, the steward—of that city whose craftsman and founder is God. For this reason he did not give the name of the city, but merely called him its treasurer. Whether, then, this should be understood in some such way or rather taken simply, you who read must consider; nothing more should be sought in Paul’s writings.

Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, according to the command of the eternal God, made known among all the nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

(Ambrosiaster) He gives glory to God the Father, from whom all things exist, [Note: [Col. 1615D] The passage is obscure.] so that, because he is powerful, he may deign to complete what has been begun among the Romans by strengthening their minds in faith for the advancement of the Gospel, and by revealing the mystery hidden within mysteries—made manifest through Christ or in Christ. For the sacrament that had always been hidden in God was disclosed in the times of Christ, because God is not alone: with him from eternity are the Word and the Paraclete. In this truth he decreed that every creature should be saved through knowledge.

The truth of this sacrament had been indicated beforehand through the prophets by certain figures known only to the wise God, whose wisdom he also wished the Gentiles to share—the mystery that had been hidden from the human race. He alone, therefore, is wise, because all wisdom comes from him, as Solomon says: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him” (Ecclesiasticus 1). This Wisdom is Christ, because he is from him and was always with him. Through him belongs glory to God forever and ever.

Therefore nothing is complete without Christ, because all things are through him. When he is acknowledged, praise is given through him to God the Father, who is understood through Christ as through his Wisdom, in whom he saved believers. Glory, therefore, belongs to the Father through the Son—that is, glory belongs to both in the Spirit, because both share one glory.

(Origen) Let us return again and consider what has been said: “To him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the sacrament kept in silence through eternal times.” It does not seem to me that this strengthening of both kinds applies to everyone. The Gospel of Paul and the preaching of Christ certainly apply to all who believe. But the revelation of the sacrament kept in silence through eternal times applies not to the many but to the few and chosen, who are capable of God’s wisdom and knowledge; of them it is said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20).

Concerning his statement that the sacrament was kept in silence, we must ask whether he means that it was kept in silence so that absolutely no one knew it—not even those who proclaimed it, the prophets—or whether some deeper meaning of silence is intended. It seems very absurd to me to say that the prophets wrote about the divine sacraments without understanding the very things they were saying, since Scripture says: “The wise person understands what proceeds from his mouth, and carries understanding upon his lips” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

If the prophets did not understand what they themselves uttered, they were not wise. But since it is foolish to confess that they were prophets and deny that they were wise, it remains that they were wise, understood what they uttered from their own mouths, and possessed understanding upon their lips.

What, then, is the meaning of silence? Let us see whether it is the meaning that Paul himself taught as having been handed down to him for the dispensation of the sacraments, when he says that he was caught up into the third heaven and into Paradise, and heard unspeakable words that it is not lawful for a human being to utter. By this he certainly shows not that he himself was ignorant of what he had heard, but that he was not permitted to disclose to human beings what had been revealed to him.

Thus, in this passage too, the sacrament may be said to have been kept in silence through eternal times because the prophets knew it—for it is manifested through the prophetic Scriptures—but did not make it manifest or disclose it to human beings, that is, to the common people. Rather, they veiled it in silence according to the command of the eternal God until the time came for “the Word to become flesh and dwell among us” (John 1), and to be manifested to all the nations for the obedience of faith.

As for his saying “to the only wise God,” do not understand “wise God” as though wisdom had made him wise, in the way that a human being is called wise. Among human beings, each person is called wise by participation in wisdom. God, however, is called wise not as one who has been made wise from wisdom, but as the author and begetter of wisdom. For, as we have said, God is not wise from wisdom; rather, wisdom proceeds from the wise God.

He is rightly called “the only wise God,” for God alone is wise in such a way that he himself has begotten wisdom, rather than having been made wise from wisdom. And glory is rightly referred to him through Jesus Christ, because Christ Jesus, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, revealed that God alone is wise in such a way that he himself begot wisdom. “Forever and ever” is the customary way of divine Scripture to signify immensity through these temporal expressions.

He placed “Amen” at the end as a confirmation of everything written above; by it he signified, in the vernacular language of the Hebrews, that what has been written is true and trustworthy.
